scenes.title: Lesson Orientation: The Data Intelligence Platform

elements.content: The Data Intelligence Platform
Exam objective: describe the Data Intelligence Platform and its components.
Lesson 1 of 4: next come compute, SQL, Unity Catalog, and Git folders.
Lakehouse: object storage + warehouse-grade tables, history. [source p.242]
SQL is declarative: you declare results, the optimizer plans. [source p.339]
Control plane manages accounts and UI; the data plane holds your data.
Webhook ingestion is brittle; buffer events upstream. [source p.286]

Worked example: 500M rows × 2 KB/row = 1 TB.

Full overwrite = 1 TB/day × 30 days = 30 TB/month.

MERGE 2% = 10M × 2 KB = 20 GB/day = 0.6 TB/month.

actions.text: Welcome, everyone, and thank you for joining. Over this session we're going to work through the platform foundations unit for the Databricks Certified Data Engineer Associate exam. Our anchor for the whole course is this idea right here: the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform. Everything else we do today — compute, SQL, Unity Catalog, Git folders, Delta Lake — hangs off that one platform concept, so it's worth getting it crisp before we go any further.

Let me read you the exam objective in the exact wording the certification uses, because you should learn it the way it will be tested: describe the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform and the components a data engineer uses daily. Two halves to that verb — describe the platform as a whole, and name the daily-use components. Exam stems in this domain love to ask which component does which job, so our goal is not just recognition but precise attribution.

Here's the roadmap for the lesson. This is the first of four lessons in the platform foundations unit. Lesson one is where we are now: the platform itself. Then we move on to workspaces, notebooks and compute; after that, Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog; and finally, Git folders and the developer workflow. So think of today as the map, and the next three lessons as the territory.

On the architecture side, we'll unpack the lakehouse: object storage sitting underneath, paired with warehouse-grade tables and transactions on top. We'll separate the control plane — the managed layer that handles accounts, the web UI and orchestration — from the data plane, which is where your actual data and compute live inside your own cloud account. And we'll be explicit that SQL is declarative: you declare the result you want, and the optimizer decides how to produce it. That distinction shows up in exam questions more often than you'd expect.

One quick calibration before we start, just to set the level of rigor. Take a table of five hundred million rows at two kilobytes per row — that's one terabyte on disk. If a poor layout forces a full scan where a well-pruned query would touch a fraction of it, you have just paid for the whole terabyte. Every architectural choice in this unit exists to avoid exactly that kind of waste, so keep that number in the back of your mind.

Finally, how does this map to the certification blueprint? Today's material covers platform architecture, and it lays the groundwork for ingestion, transformation, and productionizing workloads in the domains that follow. If you keep that mapping in mind, each topic stops feeling like trivia and starts feeling like an answer to a specific exam question. Let's get moving.

scenes.title: What Is the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform?

elements.content: What Is the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform?

Managed, multi-cloud lakehouse built by the creators of Apache Spark; runs on AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud [source p.154].

Unifies data engineering, analytics, and ML on one copy of the data [source p.37].
Core service families — exam checklist

• Workspace and Notebooks — author and run code

• Compute — clusters and SQL warehouses

• Workflows / Jobs — scheduled orchestration

• Delta Live Tables — declarative pipelines

• Databricks SQL — BI on Delta tables

• Unity Catalog — unified governance
Note: native functions beat UDFs [source p.359].

Exam: "Which component should be used for X?"

Distractors swap similar service names, not functions.

Worked example: 2 TB/day JSON — streaming ingest 1 min vs nightly batch 45 min.

Map each service to its blueprint domain.

actions.text: Now that we've mapped the blueprint domains, let's put the first object under the microscope: Databricks itself. Before we can talk about lakehouses or Delta tables, we need to be able to answer one deceptively simple question — what is the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform?

Here is the sentence I want you to be able to say back to me verbatim. Databricks is a managed, multi-cloud lakehouse built by the creators of Apache Spark. Three words are doing the heavy lifting. Managed means Databricks runs the infrastructure and operational overhead for you — you are not babysitting a cluster of servers. Multi-cloud means the same platform is available on AWS, on Microsoft Azure, and on Google Cloud; the exam will happily swap the cloud provider on you just to check you know it's not single-cloud. And lakehouse is the architectural promise we'll unpack over the next several pages. If you can recite that one sentence, the platform-positioning questions are already yours.
That's the positioning. Now the practical half — and this is the part the exam actually tests. Here is the checklist of core service families that a data engineer touches day to day.

Start with the workspace and notebooks — that's where you author and run code. Then compute: clusters and SQL warehouses, the engines that actually execute what you write. Then Workflows, also called Jobs, which orchestrate your notebooks and queries into a schedule with dependencies and retries. Notice the shape of that list — you write code, you attach it to compute, and you orchestrate it. Those three questions come up constantly.

The second row continues the checklist. Delta Live Tables — and by the way, you'll also hear the newer product name Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines — gives you declarative pipelines: you state the transformation you want, and the platform figures out the dependency order, the retries, and the incremental processing. Databricks SQL is the warehouse-facing surface, where analysts and BI tools live. And Unity Catalog is the governance layer that spans all of it: one permission model across catalogs, schemas, tables, and files. Folder-level access from the old world is gone — governance in Databricks is a first-class service, and it's heavily examined.

One flagged note before we move on: native Spark functions beat Python UDFs. Don't worry about the mechanics yet — just file it away next to the compute family, because when we get to the UDF lesson we'll come back and prove why the exam keeps asking about it.

Now look at this bar chart — it's the relative exam blueprint weight by domain: platform, ingestion, transformation, and productionizing. Two things to read off it. First, no single domain is so dominant that you can skip the others; this is a broad exam, not a deep one. Second, platform knowledge — which is exactly what we're covering right now — is the substrate under all of the other domains. Every ingestion question assumes you know what a cluster is; every productionizing question assumes you know what Unity Catalog governs. This bar chart is why we spend the opening pages on orientation rather than syntax.

And here's the phrasing to expect, in the exam's own words: 'Which Databricks component should be used to accomplish X?' Notice what that question does — it never asks you to define a component. It gives you a scenario and asks you to name the tool. So the distractor options will always be other Databricks services, each plausible. Success depends on one thing: knowing the purpose of each service well enough to eliminate the near-misses. That's the skill we're building service by service, starting with the lakehouse on the next page.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Platform Positioning

questions.question: Which statement best describes Databricks' platform positioning in the cloud data ecosystem?

options.label: A single-cloud, self-managed Apache Spark distribution that requires customers to operate the control plane.
A managed, multi-cloud platform founded by the creators of Apache Spark that unifies data engineering, analytics, and machine learning on a single copy of data.
An open-source analytics engine that must be deployed on customer-managed Kubernetes clusters.
A proprietary SQL data warehouse that only supports structured data and cannot process streaming or machine learning workloads.

questions.analysis: Databricks is explicitly described as a SaaS offering available across multiple public clouds, which addresses multicloud needs and reduces data egress costs [source p.154]. It is also an example of a PaaS-like managed service that abstracts away operational details of distributed systems [source p.150]. The other options reflect common misconceptions: that Databricks is self-managed, single-cloud, or limited to SQL analytics. In reality, it is a managed, multi-cloud platform built on Apache Spark that unifies data engineering, analytics, and machine learning.

questions.question: Which of the following tasks are correctly matched to a Databricks service family? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Orchestrating a multi-step data pipeline with dependencies and scheduled runs → Workflows/Jobs
Building a declarative pipeline that maintains data quality and incrementally processes new data → Delta Live Tables
Running interactive SQL queries for business intelligence dashboards → Databricks SQL
Scheduling and monitoring production data pipelines → Databricks SQL

questions.analysis: Workflows/Jobs is the service family for orchestration, so A is correct. Delta Live Tables provides declarative pipeline building with data quality expectations, so B is correct. Databricks SQL is optimized for interactive SQL analytics and BI dashboards, so C is correct. Option D is incorrect because scheduling and monitoring production pipelines is the role of Workflows/Jobs, not Databricks SQL; this mirrors the exam trap of confusing an analytics service with an orchestration service. A proficient data engineer knows when to use SQL for analytics versus orchestration tools to combine multiple steps [source p.47].

actions.text: Before we move on to the lakehouse, let's lock in what we just covered with two quick checks. Take them one at a time — read each option fully, and for the multi-select, make sure every pairing you keep actually holds up before you submit.
Work through them on your own for now. Once you've submitted, I'll come back and we'll go through each one together, including why the ones that look tempting aren't the right pick.

scenes.title: The Lakehouse: Unifying Lake and Warehouse

elements.content: The Lakehouse: Unifying Lake and Warehouse
Data lakes hold open files but no ACID [source p.129]
Warehouses give ACID and fast SQL, but cost more
Lakehouse: open storage + metadata layer [source p.242]
Delta Lake: ACID, upserts, time travel [source p.243]
One copy serves BI, engineering, and ML [source p.243]
Example: 1 TB ÷ 128 MB = 8,000 files [source p.233]

actions.text: Now that we've closed out the positioning checkpoint, let's get into the architectural heart of the platform: the Lakehouse — the design that unifies the data lake and the data warehouse. This is where most of the exam's reasoning questions live, so I want you to understand not just what it is, but the problem it was invented to solve.

Start with the data lake. A data lake is simply low-cost object storage holding open-format files — Parquet, JSON, CSV — and 'open format' means no proprietary engine owns them; any tool can read them. The catch is that object storage has no transactional guarantees. There is no atomicity across files, no schema enforcement, no reliable isolation between two writers. Cheap and flexible, but not trustworthy on its own for a business report.

On the other side sits the data warehouse. Warehouses give you strong ACID transactions — atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability — plus fast SQL performance and real governance. But they historically store data in proprietary formats and they cost considerably more per terabyte. So we had a trade-off: economics on one side, reliability and governance on the other. The exam loves to test whether you can name which side gives which.

The Lakehouse refuses that trade-off. The definition you should memorise: keep the data itself in open formats in object storage — that's the lake economics — and add a transactional metadata layer on top of those files. That metadata layer is what supplies the reliability and governance the plain lake was missing. Open storage plus a metadata layer. That single sentence is the whole idea.

In Databricks, Delta Lake is that metadata layer. It sits over Parquet files and delivers ACID transactions, schema enforcement, upserts — meaning you can update or merge rows rather than rewriting whole partitions — and time travel, the ability to query an earlier version of the table. Notice what's happening here: the ACID guarantees come from the log-based metadata layer, not from the storage system underneath it.

And this is the practical payoff: one copy of the data — structured, semi-structured, and unstructured — serves BI analysts, data engineers, and machine learning workloads simultaneously. No copying data into a separate warehouse for SQL and a separate lake for ML. One governed copy, many consumers.

One quick number that matters later. In an object store, you manage files, not rows. If you ingest one terabyte and each file is about 128 megabytes, you land roughly eight thousand files. Remember that arithmetic — it explains why file layout and compaction become such a big deal in production, and we'll come back to it.

Finally, look at this comparison table. Read it across the columns — data types supported, ACID support, cost, and openness — and notice that the Lakehouse row is the only one that gets ACID and openness at lake-level cost. If you can reproduce this table from memory, you can answer almost any Lakehouse scenario question. Take a moment to scan it before we move on.

scenes.title: Data Lake vs. Data Warehouse vs. Lakehouse

elements.content: Dimension  |  Data Lake  |  Data Warehouse  |  Data Lakehouse

Storage format and openness
Data Lake: A data lake keeps raw files in open formats such as Parquet, JSON, and CSV inside object storage, so any engine that can read the format can read the bytes with no proprietary connector, which is why object storage is especially useful for semistructured and unstructured files [source p.378].
Data Warehouse: A data warehouse stores data in a proprietary, engine-internal table format, so external tools must import or export through connectors, and reserializing data out of that proprietary format incurs overhead in processing, time, and cost [source p.243].
Data Lakehouse: A data lakehouse keeps data in open table formats (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi) in object storage while still presenting warehouse-style tables, so various tools connect to the metadata layer and read data directly from object storage [source p.243].

Transactional guarantees (ACID)
Data Lake: A classic data lake offers no ACID guarantees at all: you simply pour in data and never update or delete it, so a partially written file or a concurrent overwrite is visible to readers and cannot be rolled back [source p.129].
Data Warehouse: A data warehouse delivers atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability as a core engine property, so every statement either commits fully or leaves the prior state intact, and readers never see a half-applied load [source p.129].
Data Lakehouse: A data lakehouse delivers the same atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability through a transactional metadata layer (the Delta transaction log) placed over object storage, which the source describes as a big departure from the original data lake [source p.129].

Workloads supported
Data Lake: A data lake is the natural home for machine learning feature engineering and for semistructured or unstructured data, because object storage can store any type of blob file and scales to a steady supply of files [source p.378].
Data Warehouse: A data warehouse targets SQL business intelligence: dimensional reporting, dashboarding, and high-concurrency analytical queries where a mature optimizer and governed semantics matter more than file openness.
Data Lakehouse: A data lakehouse runs both on one copy of the data, supporting SQL BI alongside ML and semistructured processing, because much of the data in a lakehouse may have no table structure imposed and warehouse features are applied only where they are needed [source p.243].

Schema and metadata management
Data Lake: A data lake is effectively schema-on-read only and its metadata lives at the file and directory level, so there is no built-in table history, no statistics layer, and no centralized place to enforce or evolve a schema.
Data Warehouse: A data warehouse provides robust table and schema support managed by the engine, with the catalog holding the authoritative definition of every table and view.
Data Lakehouse: A data lakehouse adds automated metadata management, robust table and schema support, and update/delete capabilities, and the complexities of managing the underlying files and storage are fully hidden from the user [source p.243].

Update, delete, and time travel
Data Lake: A data lake cannot update or delete rows natively, so correcting a bad load means rewriting or removing files outside any transaction and coordinating with every reader yourself.
Data Warehouse: A data warehouse supports UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE natively and can roll back an uncommitted transaction, but history is generally limited to what the engine chooses to retain.
Data Lakehouse: A data lakehouse supports table history and rollback by retaining old versions of files and metadata, and it provides explicit features for managing incremental updates and deletes [source p.242].

Cost and scaling model
Data Lake: A data lake is the cheapest tier because object storage holds petabytes at commodity blob prices, and there is no always-on query engine whose idle capacity you must pay for.
Data Warehouse: A data warehouse historically bundles storage and compute inside one proprietary system, so you pay proprietary storage rates plus compute credits, and you cannot scale one dimension without the other.
Data Lakehouse: A data lakehouse separates compute from storage so each scales independently, and the source notes that the architecture of cloud data warehouses has itself evolved to separate compute from storage and support petabyte-scale queries [source p.129].

Query performance and engine fit
Data Lake: A data lake requires an external engine such as Spark or Presto and typically performs full scans, with no table-level statistics for skipping files, so latency is unpredictable and depends entirely on how the data was laid out.
Data Warehouse: A data warehouse uses a purpose-built SQL engine with indexes, statistics, and materialized views, and some OLAP systems can even convert federated queries into materialized views to accelerate repeated access [source p.351].
Data Lakehouse: A data lakehouse uses the metadata layer to record file statistics and enable file skipping, delivering warehouse-class SQL performance without copying the data into a proprietary store [source p.242].

Interoperability and lock-in
Data Lake: A data lake offers maximum openness because any engine can read the files, but it offers no coordination guarantees when two writers touch the same prefix at the same time.
Data Warehouse: A data warehouse can reach outside itself through federated query and external tables — Snowflake external tables defined on S3 read from S3 at query time and can be joined to internal tables [source p.351] — but its own storage remains proprietary and reserializing out of it costs processing, time, and money [source p.243].
Data Lakehouse: A data lakehouse makes interoperability its key advantage over proprietary tools: data is easy to exchange between tools when it is stored in an open file format, and tools read directly from object storage through the metadata layer [source p.243].

Worked example: 12-month storage bill for 500 TB (illustrative unit prices)
Data Lake: Data lake: 500 TB x 1,024 GB/TB = 512,000 GB; at $0.023 per GB-month the annual bill is 512,000 x $0.023 x 12 = $141,312, and no additional engine cost is required just to keep the bytes.
Data Warehouse: Data warehouse: the same 512,000 GB in proprietary storage at $0.05 per GB-month costs 512,000 x $0.05 x 12 = $307,200 per year, which is about 2.17x the lake bill before any query compute is purchased, and every external read adds reserialization overhead [source p.243].
Data Lakehouse: Data lakehouse: you pay the object-storage rate ($141,312 per year in this example) plus the metadata and transaction layer, so the premium over a pure lake is small while you gain ACID transactions and governance [source p.242].

Primary failure mode
Data Lake: A data lake degrades into an unmanaged swamp when nothing enforces schema, deduplication, or quality, because the file system itself will happily accept contradictory and duplicate data.
Data Warehouse: A data warehouse becomes a cost and flexibility bottleneck: licensing and proprietary formats make ML and semistructured workloads expensive or impossible, so teams copy data out and lose a single source of truth.
Data Lakehouse: A data lakehouse depends on disciplined decisions about which datasets deserve table semantics, since much of the data in a lakehouse may remain raw or even unstructured while warehouse features are imposed only where needed [source p.243].

Takeaway — Choose a data lake when the workload is exploratory or ML-oriented, the data is semistructured or unstructured, and the dominant requirement is cheap, open blob storage with no transactional obligation [source p.378].

Takeaway — Choose a data warehouse when the workload is governed SQL BI at high concurrency and you are willing to accept proprietary storage and format lock-in in exchange for a mature optimizer and full ACID semantics out of the box [source p.129].

Takeaway — Choose a data lakehouse when you need both SQL BI and ML on one copy of data and want the ACID and history guarantees of a warehouse without giving up open formats, because the distinguishing features are the open format plus unified governance and metadata, not merely extra storage bolted onto a warehouse [source p.242].

Takeaway — Exam trap: the lakehouse is not 'a warehouse with extra storage'. The correct justification for choosing it cites the open table format, the transactional metadata layer, and the fact that tools connect to the metadata layer and read directly from object storage, whereas a warehouse requires reserialization at overhead in processing, time, and cost [source p.243].

Takeaway — Cost intuition: the lakehouse keeps the object-storage price line and adds only the metadata layer, so for the 500 TB example the storage bill stays at roughly $141,312 per year versus $307,200 per year in proprietary storage, while the ACID and governance capabilities that would otherwise force you into a warehouse are retained [source p.242].

actions.text: Now that we've reconstructed the lakehouse picture, let's put all three architectures on the same table and compare them across the dimensions exam questions actually test. The goal here isn't memorizing a list — it's being able to justify a choice under stated constraints.
This overview table is your anchor. We'll walk the rows top to bottom, then look at a worked cost example, the classic failure mode, and the four takeaways that capture the exam traps.

First, storage format and openness. A data lake stores raw files — Parquet, CSV, JSON — in open object storage. A warehouse keeps data in proprietary, closed table formats on managed storage. The lakehouse lands in between: open Delta tables sitting directly in object storage, which is what makes it readable by any compatible engine.

Second, transactional guarantees. A classic lake offers none — a partial write can leave you with corrupt or half-visible data. A warehouse gives full ACID. The lakehouse also gives full ACID, but achieved through the Delta transaction log written alongside the data files. Same guarantee, different mechanism — and that distinction shows up on the exam.

Third, workloads. A lake is the natural home for machine learning and semi-structured data — you can throw almost any shape of file at it. A warehouse is optimized for SQL BI: structured tables, repeatable analytical queries. The lakehouse's pitch is both on one platform, so you don't copy data between a lake for ML and a warehouse for BI.

Notice the schema and metadata row — on a lake, schema is typically enforced on read, so bad data is discovered late. A warehouse enforces schema on write. The lakehouse enforces on write by default too, and can evolve the schema deliberately when you need it to.

Next, update, delete, and time travel. A raw lake struggles with all three — overwriting files is awkward and there's no built-in history. A warehouse supports updates and deletes, and some versions offer time travel. The lakehouse supports updates, deletes, and time travel natively, because every commit is versioned in the log.

Cost and scaling is where the architectures really diverge. In a lakehouse, storage and compute scale independently — you store cheap object storage and spin compute up or down separately. A warehouse typically couples the two, so you pay for a sized cluster even when it's idle.

Two more quick rows. Query performance and engine fit: warehouses ship with a highly tuned SQL engine out of the box, while a lakehouse's performance depends on the engine you point at it and how well the table is laid out. And interoperability and lock-in: open formats mean low lock-in on a lake and lakehouse, versus higher lock-in on a proprietary warehouse.

Let's make the cost intuition concrete with this worked example — a twelve-month storage bill for 500 terabytes. Track how the open object storage side keeps the storage line low, and how decoupling compute is what actually drives the savings over a year.

And here's the primary failure mode to remember. A data lake degrades over time — small files pile up, schemas drift, and quality silently rots, which is why lake maintenance practices exist. A warehouse can become a cost and flexibility bottleneck. The lakehouse's own failure mode is governance and layout neglect: skip the maintenance, and it slides back toward being just a lake.
So the takeaways. Choose a lakehouse when you need both ML and BI on one governed copy of the data with open formats underneath.
Choose a data warehouse when the workload is purely structured SQL BI and you want a fully managed, tuned engine and are willing to accept the lock-in.

And here's the trap the exam loves: the lakehouse is not 'a warehouse with extra storage.' Its defining features are the open format and the unified governance layer — those are what let one platform serve both worlds. If you describe it as a warehouse plus a file store, you've missed the point.

Finally, the cost intuition: the lakehouse keeps the cheap, open storage of a lake while adding the reliability and governance of a warehouse — you get warehouse-grade guarantees without paying warehouse-grade storage prices. That single sentence is worth remembering, and it's exactly the trade-off the exam tests when it hands you a set of constraints and asks you to justify a choice.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Lakehouse Architecture

questions.question: A data engineer stores Parquet files in cloud object storage and wants ACID (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) transactions, table history and rollback, and reliable update/delete support without changing where the bytes physically live. Which statement best describes what Delta Lake adds to those object-storage files?

options.label: It rewrites the Parquet files into a proprietary columnar format that only Databricks engines can read, which is why a lakehouse is said to require a closed storage engine.

It adds a transactional metadata and file-management layer on top of the existing open files, delivering ACID transactions, schema and table support, and update/delete and time-travel capabilities while the data stays in object storage.
It adds an in-memory caching tier that pins the whole table on cluster-local SSDs so that object storage is used only as a cold backup and never read during queries.
It removes the need for a schema by converting every column to a semi-structured JSON string, so that schema enforcement and evolution are no longer part of the architecture.

questions.analysis: Delta Lake is an open source storage management system that a lakehouse system deploys as a metadata and file-management layer alongside data management and transformation tools; the lakehouse stores data in object storage just like a lake but adds robust table and schema support and features for managing incremental updates and deletes, and it typically supports table history and rollback by retaining old versions of files and metadata [source p.242]. Crucially, the transactional guarantees come from the metadata layer, not from relocating the data: the lakehouse supports ACID transactions while still housing data in object storage and supporting a variety of query and transformation engines, which is a big departure from the original data lake where you simply pour in data and never update or delete it [source p.129]. Option A states the classic exam misconception that a lakehouse requires loading data into a proprietary store; in fact the key advantage over proprietary tools is interoperability, because it is much easier to exchange data between tools when it is stored in an open file format, and reserializing data from a proprietary database format incurs overhead in processing, time, and cost [source p.243]. Option C is wrong because Delta Lake is a storage and metadata layer, not an SSD-pinning cache, and object storage remains the system of record that is read directly. Option D is wrong because Delta Lake enforces schema and supports schema evolution; it does not degrade structured columns into untyped JSON strings.

questions.question: A platform team is choosing between a classic data lake, a proprietary cloud data warehouse, and a Delta Lake lakehouse for a workload that must mix large batch transformations, semi-structured raw files, and governed SQL BI queries on one copy of the data. Which of the following statements are accurate characterizations of a lakehouse architecture? (select all that apply)

options.label: Because data remains in open file formats, different tools can connect to the metadata layer and read the data directly from object storage, avoiding the overhead of reserializing it into a proprietary database format.
To obtain ACID transactions, a lakehouse must load all data into a proprietary storage engine, after which the underlying files are no longer directly readable by other engines.
Warehouse features can be imposed only where they are needed: much of the data in a lakehouse may have no table structure at all, with other data left in a raw or unstructured format.

Object storage in this design performs well for large batch reads and writes and for a low rate of update operations that each modify a large volume of data, but is a poor fit for transactional workloads with many small updates every second.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: the key advantage of the data lakehouse over proprietary tools is interoperability, since it is much easier to exchange data between tools when it is stored in an open file format, and in a lakehouse architecture various tools can connect to the metadata layer and read data directly from object storage [source p.243]. Option C is correct and is a commonly missed nuance: it is important to emphasize that much of the data in a data lakehouse may not have a table structure imposed, and warehouse features are applied only where needed while other data stays raw or even unstructured [source p.243] — so a lakehouse is not an all-or-nothing conversion of every file into a governed table. Option D is correct: from the standpoint of data engineering, object stores provide excellent performance for large batch reads and batch writes, and while the folklore that object stores cannot handle updates is only partially true, they are an inferior fit for transactional workloads with many small updates every second, since those are better served by transactional databases or block storage; object stores suit a low rate of update operations where each operation updates a large volume of data [source p.233]. Option B is the distractor that mirrors a widespread misconception: it inverts the architecture. The lakehouse incorporates the controls, data management, and data structures found in a data warehouse while still housing data in object storage and supporting a variety of query and transformation engines, and it achieves ACID transactions through the transactional metadata layer rather than by moving data into a proprietary store [source p.129][source p.242].

actions.text: Time to check what stuck from that comparison. Two questions here: the first is single-choice, the second asks you to select every statement that applies — so read each option on its own merits before you settle on your set.

Work through them on your own without flipping back, and don't rush the multiple-select one; partial credit isn't a thing, so every box you tick has to hold up. Once you submit, I'll walk you through each option — including the distractors — and we'll line the reasoning up with the exam wording.

scenes.title: Inside the Lakehouse: Storage, Metadata, Compute, Governance

elements.content: Inside the Lakehouse
Storage · Metadata · Compute · Governance

Storage — Amazon S3, ADLS, GCS

Raw Parquet files, cheap [source p.242]

Metadata — Delta transaction log

ACID, time travel [source p.243]

Compute — Spark, Photon, SQL

No copies; reads storage [source p.126]

Governance — Unity Catalog

Access, lineage, audit [source p.129]
Compute and storage scale and price separately

Worked example: 1 TB ÷ 128 MB/file = 8,192 files

Each write = 1 commit; VACUUM cleans files [source p.304]

actions.text: With the lakehouse-versus-lake-versus-warehouse comparison behind us, let's open the box and see what's actually inside the Databricks lakehouse. Four layers do all the work here — storage, metadata, compute, and governance — and this page is the map we'll keep referring back to.

Read that subtitle as your mental index. Storage, metadata, compute, governance. Almost every architecture question on the Data Engineer Associate exam can be traced back to exactly one of these four words, so let's take them bottom to top.

Start at the bottom with storage. This is plain cloud object storage — Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, or Google Cloud Storage — holding raw Parquet files. It's cheap, it's effectively unlimited, and importantly, it's dumb: object storage knows nothing about tables, transactions, or schemas. It just holds bytes at a path.

So where does the intelligence live? In the metadata layer — specifically the Delta transaction log, that underscore delta underscore log directory. It records every commit as an ordered entry, and that single design decision is what buys us ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel on top of object storage that offers none of those things natively.

Above that sits compute — Spark clusters, the Photon-accelerated engine, and Databricks SQL warehouses. The key phrase on the slide is 'no copies.' These engines read the same files storage wrote; they don't move or duplicate the data to process it. That's a favourite distractor pattern, so hold onto it.

Finally, on top, governance — Unity Catalog. It's the unified catalog spanning tables, files, and models, and it supplies the access control, the lineage, and the audit trail. If an exam stem asks where lineage or auditing comes from, the answer is this layer, not the storage layer.

And here's the architectural payoff, the principle all four layers serve: compute and storage scale and price separately. Storage lives in your cloud account at cloud rates; compute spins up when you need it and you pay for the cluster or warehouse while it runs. You can grow one without touching the other — that decoupling is the whole reason the lakehouse works economically.

One quick number to make that concrete: divide one terabyte by 128 megabytes per file and you land on 8,192 files. That is the small-file reality of a raw ingestion landing zone, and it's exactly the problem that OPTIMIZE and file sizing will solve later in the course. Architecturally, that's the lakehouse in one breath: cheap storage, a log that makes it transactional, elastic compute that reads it, and a governance layer that watches over all of it.

content.html:
Explore the Lakehouse Architecture

Click a layer to see its job in the platform. Trace a query to find out where the bytes really go.

Control plane Data plane Your storage

Step-by-step reveal

Step 1 / 6

Workload toggle

Pick a workload: the same four layers are used, but the engine and the access pattern change.

Trace a query end to end

7 hops: request → planning → authorization → compute → Delta log → Parquet files → result.

Myth-busting

Does my data move into Databricks' control plane?

No. Only metadata, query plans and result sets pass through the control plane. Table bytes are read by compute in the data plane, directly from your storage account.

Where do the files actually live?

In your cloud object storage — ADLS Gen2, S3 or GCS — as Parquet files plus the _delta_log transaction log, under a path registered as an external location in Unity Catalog.

Is the lakehouse just a data warehouse?

No. It keeps the cheap, open storage of a data lake and adds warehouse features on top of the same files: ACID transactions, governance, indexes and statistics, and a vectorized SQL engine (Photon).

Must I copy data into Databricks to use it?

No. You can query Parquet directly with an external table, or run CREATE TABLE AS SELECT once to promote it to a managed Delta table. There is no separate ingestion silo.

Vocabulary (exam wording)

Medallion architecture
Bronze (raw) → silver (cleaned, conformed) → gold (business-level) refinement of the same Delta tables.
Slowly changing dimension (SCD)
How a dimension attribute changes over time: Type 1 overwrites in place, Type 2 keeps history with MERGE INTO.
Materialized view
A precomputed result stored as a Delta table and refreshed automatically — the lakehouse answer to warehouse summary tables.

nodes.title: Workspace & client
nodes.role: Where the request is born. A dashboard, a notebook or a Lakeflow job definition submits SQL or a job run. The workspace stores code, dashboards and job definitions — not your table data.
nodes.service: Databricks workspace (the user-facing surface of the control plane)
nodes.myth: The notebook does not hold the data. It holds code and cached results; the tables live in object storage.
nodes.tip: Exam phrasing: the workspace submits work; processing happens elsewhere.
nodes.blurb: Client — a dashboard, notebook or Lakeflow job submits SQL or a run request to the Databricks workspace.

nodes.label: Control Plane
nodes.title: Control plane
nodes.role: Runs in Databricks' own account. It parses and plans queries, schedules jobs, stores workspace metadata, notebook and job definitions, and hosts the Unity Catalog metastore. It routes results back — but it does not process table data.
nodes.service: Databricks-managed control plane (serverless, no VNet resources of yours inside)
nodes.myth: Data is not copied into the control plane when you query. Only metadata, plans and result sets pass through it.
nodes.tip: Control plane vs. data plane is a classic exam split: management + metadata on one side, actual processing on the other.
nodes.blurb: Control plane — plans the query, schedules the work, keeps metadata; it never touches the table bytes.

nodes.label: Unity Catalog
nodes.title: Unity Catalog
nodes.role: The governance layer: one metastore per region holding a three-level namespace (catalog.schema.table), plus grants, row filters, column masks, lineage, and audit logs. Every access is authorized here before compute opens a file.
nodes.service: Unity Catalog metastore (attached to one or more workspaces)
nodes.myth: Unity Catalog does not store your data — it stores metadata, permissions and lineage. The files stay in object storage.
nodes.tip: The metastore is the unified governance layer across workspaces, distinct from a workspace-local Hive metastore.
nodes.blurb: Unity Catalog — authorizes the read, returns table metadata and the storage location of the files.

nodes.label: Compute (Data Plane)
nodes.title: Compute — the data plane
nodes.role: The engines that actually read and process data, running in your cloud account / network boundary. SQL warehouses with Photon for BI, all-purpose and job clusters for Spark ETL, plus Lakeflow pipelines. Compute is ephemeral: it starts, does the work, and stops.
nodes.service: Databricks SQL warehouse with Photon · Lakeflow job clusters · serverless compute
nodes.myth: A SQL warehouse is not a database holding your tables — it is stateless compute that reads files on demand and caches results.
nodes.tip: Photon is the vectorized engine behind Databricks SQL and Spark; serverless compute runs in Databricks' account but inside your data-plane network boundary.
nodes.blurb: Compute — the work is scheduled onto the data plane: SQL warehouse with Photon, or a Spark job cluster.

nodes.label: Delta Transaction Log
nodes.title: Delta transaction log
nodes.role: The _delta_log/ directory sitting next to your data files: ordered JSON commits plus periodic checkpoints that record which Parquet files form the current table version, along with schema, partitioning, and file statistics. This is what gives ACID transactions, time travel and schema enforcement.
nodes.service: Delta Lake (open table format) — also powers Liquid Clustering, OPTIMIZE and Predictive Optimization
nodes.myth: Delta Lake is not a proprietary format: it is Parquet files plus an open-source transaction log that any engine can read.
nodes.tip: The Delta log is the single source of truth for a table's current state — readers list the log, not the whole directory.
nodes.blurb: Delta log — compute reads the log to get the current snapshot: exactly which Parquet files make up the table right now.

nodes.label: Cloud Object Storage
nodes.title: Cloud object storage
nodes.role: Cheap, durable, open storage in your own cloud account: Parquet data files, the Delta log, and raw landing zones. Bronze, silver and gold all live here as Delta tables — the medallion architecture (refining raw data in stages) is just a folder convention on top of one storage layer.
nodes.service: ADLS Gen2 · Amazon S3 · Google Cloud Storage (via external locations and storage credentials in Unity Catalog)
nodes.myth: The data does not live inside Databricks. The files live in your bucket; Databricks is the engine and the catalog on top.
nodes.tip: The testable claim is 'open format': any engine that understands Parquet + Delta can read the same data without Databricks.
nodes.blurb: Cloud storage — compute reads only the required Parquet files directly from your bucket. The bytes never enter the control plane.

actions.text: We just covered the four ingredients of the lakehouse — cheap object storage, a transactional log, elastic compute, and a governance layer. Now let's watch them work together as one architecture. On this diagram, each layer is something you can open and inspect.

actions.text: Next, the control plane. It parses and plans the query, schedules the job, stores workspace metadata, and routes results back. actions.text: So where do the files actually live? In your object storage, always. scenes.title: Checkpoint: Lakehouse Layers and Delta Lake

questions.question: A data engineer opens a Delta table's directory in cloud object storage and finds ordinary Parquet data files sitting next to a _delta_log directory. She must explain to a colleague where the table's ACID (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) guarantees, schema enforcement, and time travel actually come from. Which lakehouse layer is responsible for these capabilities?

options.label: The storage layer, because object storage such as Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, or Google Cloud Storage writes each Parquet file atomically and therefore enforces consistency on its own
The metadata layer, because the Delta transaction log records an ordered series of commits over the data files and supplies the transactional, schema, and history semantics
The compute layer, because Spark clusters and Databricks SQL warehouses hold the table state in memory while the query is running and write the final result back to storage
The governance layer, because Unity Catalog grants, lineage, and audit records make the writes on a Delta table isolated and durable

questions.analysis: Option B is correct. In the lakehouse architecture the storage layer is deliberately kept dumb and cheap: cloud object storage retains raw Parquet files, but object storage by itself offers no transactional guarantees, no schema, and no history. The transactional behavior lives in the metadata layer: the Delta transaction log (_delta_log) records commits as an ordered sequence of actions, which is what makes automated metadata management, table history, and update/delete capabilities possible while the complexities of the underlying files and storage stay hidden from the user [source p.243]. Option A is the classic storage-versus-metadata confusion: a PUT of a single object is atomic, but a multi-file table update is not, so object storage alone cannot give table-level ACID. Option C confuses execution with bookkeeping: compute reads files and applies a plan, but if compute crashed mid-job without a log there would be no record of whether the write should be visible. Option D confuses access control with transaction control: Unity Catalog decides who may read or write a table, not whether a half-written commit becomes visible to concurrent readers.

questions.question: Which of the following capabilities are supplied by the Delta Lake metadata layer rather than by the underlying object storage? Select all that apply.

options.label: ACID transactions over multiple files, so a reader never observes a partially written result
Time travel and rollback, achieved by retaining old versions of the data files and the metadata that points at them
Schema enforcement plus merge, update, and delete operations (upserts) applied to data kept in an open file format
Cheap, effectively unlimited, durable byte storage for the Parquet files themselves
Conversion of open Parquet files into a proprietary warehouse format before any other tool can query them

questions.analysis: Options A, B, and C are correct. A lakehouse adds warehouse-style features on top of raw files: robust table and schema support, features for managing incremental updates and deletes, and table history and rollback implemented by retaining old versions of files and metadata [source p.242]. Concretely, consider a nightly job that rewrites a 40 GB partition and produces 400 new Parquet files. Without a transaction log a reader starting at minute 3 could see 190 of those files and return a wrong aggregate; with Delta the commit is recorded once in the log, so the 40 GB partition flips from old to new in a single atomic step, and time travel to version 41 still reconstructs the previous state. Option D is wrong because cheap, unlimited byte storage is exactly what object storage provides, not what the metadata layer adds; the metadata layer is small by comparison. Option E states the opposite of the lakehouse value proposition: interoperability is the key advantage over proprietary tools, because storing data in an open file format avoids the overhead of reserializing data out of a proprietary database format, and many tools can connect to the metadata layer and read directly from object storage [source p.243]. Note also the precondition for options A through C: schema enforcement only applies to data written through a Delta-aware writer, so files dropped into the table directory by an external process must be registered before the table will honor them.

questions.question: A team runs a Spark ETL job that reads Parquet files directly from cloud object storage, and a BI team runs SQL queries against the same files through a Databricks SQL warehouse. The company is deciding whether to move the data into a proprietary MPP warehouse first. Which statement about the separation of compute and storage best justifies keeping the data where it is?

options.label: Because the data must first be copied into a proprietary MPP (massively parallel processing) system, the BI team will always see stale results unless the copy job runs continuously
Because storage and compute scale independently, each engine reads the same open files directly from object storage, so adding a second consumer does not require a second physical copy of the data
Because the data physically lives on the cluster's local disks, storage cost grows in proportion to the number of worker nodes the job requests
Because reading open file formats requires reserialization into a proprietary format, the ETL job and the BI queries must be scheduled so they never run at the same time

questions.analysis: Option B is correct. The last five years of data lake evolution produced a major migration toward separation of compute and storage: a move away from Hadoop toward cloud object storage for long-term retention of data [source p.242]. In that arrangement the object store holds one durable copy and any number of engines (Spark clusters, Photon-accelerated engines, SQL warehouses) attach to it, so a BI warehouse added later consumes the identical files rather than a duplicate copy. Options C and D describe the pre-lakehouse world: when data lived on the cluster's own disks, storage was coupled to compute, and reserializing out of a proprietary format incurred overhead in processing, time, and cost [source p.243]. Option A inverts the architecture by assuming a mandatory load into an MPP store. The edge case worth stating: decoupling does not mean storage is free of semantics. Cloud object storage is not the same as block storage attached to a VM, and cloud filesystem services such as Amazon EFS sit in yet another category, so a team must still confirm the consistency model and access pattern of the storage service it chooses [source p.202]. Note also that this abstraction trend extends upward: managed compute and managed Kubernetes services remove cluster-management work from the engineer, but they do not change the fact that the durable copy of the data remains in object storage [source p.171].

Take your time, read every option carefully, and pick the one you can justify. I'll be right here after you submit to go through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Control Plane and Data Plane: What Runs Where

elements.content: Control Plane and Data Plane: What Runs Where
Control plane: Databricks-managed backend runs the web app, editors, scheduler, cluster manager, and metadata.
Data plane: the customer's account holds cluster VMs and the object storage holding the data. [source p.229]
Compute: classic runs in the customer's subscription; serverless runs in Databricks' account. [source p.427]
Two-way traffic: control plane sends orchestration commands; results, logs, and metadata return. [source p.154]
Worked example: 1 TB (1,048,576 MB) scanned in customer storage; only ~50 MB returns = 0.005%.
Exam trap: customer data stays in customer cloud storage — it is never copied into the control plane.

actions.text: Now we come to one of the highest-yield topics in the whole blueprint: the control plane and the data plane. Every security, networking, and networking-cost question on the exam is really asking you one thing — which side of this boundary does this thing run on? So let's get the boundary razor sharp.

The control plane is the Databricks-managed backend. It lives in the Databricks cloud account, not yours. Think of everything you touch through the web UI: the notebook editor, the SQL query editor, the job scheduler, the cluster manager, and the workspace metadata. All of that is control plane. It is the brain that decides what should run — it is not where your data sits.

The data plane is the compute and the data in your cloud account. Two pieces matter: the cluster virtual machines that actually execute your Spark code, and the cloud object storage — S3, ADLS, or GCS — that holds the real files. This is the muscle, and it is deliberately inside the customer's perimeter.

Here is the nuance the exam loves. Classic compute launches in the customer's cloud subscription, which is why you get to attach your own instance profiles and network controls. Serverless compute is different: it runs in a Databricks-managed account, but in the same region as your workspace. Classic versus serverless is a recurring distractor pattern, so keep those two sentences separate in your head.

And this is not a one-way street. Communication flows in both directions. The control plane pushes orchestration and configuration commands down to the data plane — 'start this cluster, run this notebook, apply this cluster policy.' The data plane sends results, logs, and metadata back up. Two-way traffic, but only commands and metadata cross the line.

Let's make it concrete. A query scans one terabyte — that is one million forty-eight thousand five hundred and seventy-six megabytes — sitting in the customer's storage account. The control plane orchestrates the job, the data plane reads those bytes from customer storage, and only the result set and the logs travel back. The terabyte never moves into the Databricks account. That single sentence answers a surprising number of exam questions.

Which brings us to the trap. The tempting wrong answer is that Databricks copies your data into the control plane to process it. It does not. Customer data stays in customer cloud storage — encrypted with customer-managed keys if you configure them — and the control plane only ever sees metadata and commands. If an option says customer data is stored in the Databricks account, it is wrong, every time. Lock that down before we move on to the side-by-side comparison.

scenes.title: Control Plane vs. Data Plane

elements.content: Dimension  |  Control plane  |  Data plane

Physical location and ownership
Control plane: The control plane is the Databricks-managed backend that runs in Databricks' own cloud account, holding the web application, notebook and query editors, job scheduler, cluster manager, and workspace metadata, so the customer never has to provision or patch those servers.
Data plane: The data plane runs inside the customer's own cloud account and region, and consists of the cluster virtual machines, serverless compute, and the object storage buckets holding the data; because object storage is a regional resource, data written to an Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, or Google Cloud Storage bucket stays in the region the customer selected and moves between zones only invisibly and without direct networking charges [source p.427].

Contents: which components live in each plane
Control plane: The control plane contains the workspace UI and notebook editor, the job scheduler and workflow orchestrator, the cluster manager that hands out compute, and the metadata services (workspace objects, permissions, and Unity Catalog table and column metadata) - that is, everything that describes and coordinates work rather than performs it.
Data plane: The data plane contains the execution engines and the bytes: cluster VMs running the Spark executors and Photon-accelerated engine, serverless compute capacity, and the cloud object storage that holds the open-format Parquet data files plus the Delta transaction log (_delta_log) that makes those files transactional.

Data sensitivity: what actually gets stored
Control plane: The control plane stores configuration and metadata only - cluster specifications, job and notebook definitions, query text, access-control lists, and table, column, and lineage metadata - and it does not hold the row-level contents of the customer's tables.
Data plane: The data plane holds the sensitive payload itself: the Parquet and Delta files in the customer's object storage, which are governed by the customer's cloud permissions (IAM roles, bucket policies, KMS keys); because an object store is a key-value store for immutable objects, an UPDATE or DELETE is executed by writing new objects and committing the change in the Delta log rather than by editing a file in place [source p.232].

Security responsibility boundary
Control plane: Databricks is responsible for securing and operating the control-plane services, but the customer still owns the identity and authorization decisions inside the workspace, namely workspace users, groups, cluster policies, and Unity Catalog grants on securables.
Data plane: The customer is responsible for the cloud-side controls around data at rest and in transit: VPC and network configuration, storage firewall rules, encryption keys, and the cloud credentials (instance profiles, storage credentials, or service principals) that Databricks assumes to read the data.

Network topology and latency exposure
Control plane: Control-plane traffic travels between the customer's browser or workspace and the Databricks-managed account, crossing physical distance and multiple network hops through routers, and every additional hop adds latency and degrades perceived responsiveness [source p.427].
Data plane: Data-plane traffic is designed to stay local: classic HDFS and MapReduce deliberately pushed map jobs to the machines that held the data blocks so the scan was strictly local, which preserved bandwidth for the reduce-side shuffle and delivered better overall performance - the same colocation logic motivates reading object storage from compute inside the same region [source p.246].

Failure impact and blast radius
Control plane: A control-plane outage breaks the interface and the coordination layer: the workspace UI is unreachable, new jobs cannot be scheduled, and clusters cannot be created or resized, while already-running computations generally continue until they finish.
Data plane: A data-plane outage breaks execution - running jobs fail and clusters become unreachable - but results are usually recoverable because the data itself is stored separately in object storage and the job can simply be retried; the dangerous case is correlated failure, since entire cloud regions have failed in the past despite geo-redundant design [source p.427].

Cost model and who pays what
Control plane: Control-plane capability is bundled into the Databricks platform charge (measured in DBUs), so customers do not pay their cloud provider for the servers running the web app, scheduler, or cluster manager, and control-plane overhead is therefore mostly a latency concern rather than a line item.
Data plane: The data plane is billed directly by the cloud provider: VM instance hours for clusters and SQL warehouses, storage and request charges for object storage, and network charges that vary by distance, since VM-to-VM traffic between zones incurs nominal egress charges while movement between regions is slower and may incur higher egress fees [source p.427]; separating compute from storage is what makes this metering possible, because data can be housed in effectively limitless object storage and compute spun up or deleted on demand [source p.126].

Worked example: how much of job time is control-plane time
Control plane: Control-plane side of the worked example: suppose the scheduler takes about 2 s to place the job and the cluster manager about 1 s to launch the final executors, so the control plane contributes roughly 3 s of the job's wall-clock time - and if the workspace region is far from the user's browser, each additional network hop adds latency on top of that 3 s [source p.427].
Data plane: Data-plane side of the worked example: a 10-node cluster where each node sustains 1.5 GB/s of aggregate scan throughput delivers 10 x 1.5 GB/s = 15 GB/s, so scanning a 3 TB (3,072 GB) Delta table takes 3,072 / 15 = 205 s of pure scan time; total wall clock is 205 + 3 = 208 s, meaning the control plane accounts for only 3 / 208 = 1.4 % of the job, and if that job shuffles 200 GB between zones at a nominal $0.01 per GB egress rate the data-plane network bill for that step alone is 200 x $0.01 = $2.00, several times higher if the shuffle crosses regions instead of zones [source p.427].

Takeaway — Use the control plane to answer 'where does X live?' for anything describing or coordinating work - workspace objects, job definitions, schedules, cluster policies, and Unity Catalog metadata - and use the data plane to answer it for the bytes: VMs, serverless compute, and the object storage holding the Delta tables.

Takeaway — When a question asks 'who is responsible for securing Y?', route UI, workspace permissions, and managed-service patching to Databricks and route data-at-rest encryption, cloud IAM, bucket policies, and network isolation to the customer, because sensitive data never leaves the customer's storage and is governed by cloud permissions.

Takeaway — Prefer reasoning from the data plane when predicting job duration and cost, since the worked example shows data-plane scan time dominating control-plane overhead (205 s versus 3 s); control-plane sizing only matters when you are diagnosing UI slowness, scheduling delays, or cluster-launch failures.

Takeaway — Expect resilience from the split: a control-plane outage blocks scheduling and the UI but leaves running work alone, and a data-plane failure kills execution while leaving the data intact in object storage - so retries are cheap, but a region-wide event is a correlated failure that both planes share.

actions.text: Building on the split we just described, let's compare the control plane and the data plane dimension by dimension. This table is your reference sheet for exam scenarios — each row is a question the exam likes to ask.

Start with physical location and ownership. The control plane lives in a Databricks-managed account, while the data plane runs in your own cloud account or region. That single fact drives almost every other row on this slide, so anchor it first.

Next, contents — which components live in each plane. The control plane holds the workspace UI, the job schedulers, the cluster manager, and metadata. The data plane holds the virtual machines, the serverless compute, and the object storage where the actual data resides.

Now data sensitivity. The control plane stores configuration and metadata — not your sensitive records. Your data stays in your own storage and is governed by your cloud permissions. Notice the security responsibility boundary here too: the control plane is Databricks' responsibility, while the data plane's access control is yours.

Finally, failure impact and blast radius. A control plane outage affects the interface and scheduling; a data plane issue affects job execution. Because data is stored separately, results are typically resilient — that separation is precisely why the split exists. The same logic applies to network topology and the cost model: each plane has its own exposure and its own payer.
So how do you use this in the exam? Takeaway number one: when a question asks where something lives, reason from the control plane.
Takeaway number two: when a question asks who is responsible for securing something, the answer almost always points at the data plane, because that is where your data and your cloud account sit.

And takeaway number three: expect resilience from the split. If the control plane is briefly unavailable, your stored data is untouched — so eliminate any answer choice that claims the data is lost. Keep these three heuristics in mind, and the next checkpoint will feel straightforward.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Control Plane and Data Plane

questions.question: A European bank runs Databricks on Azure. Its engineers use a workspace with classic all-purpose clusters to transform 12 TB of Delta tables that live in an ADLS Gen2 account inside the bank's own Azure subscription in the West Europe region. The compliance team asks which components store or process data outside the bank's subscription. Which statement classifies the components correctly?

options.label: The notebook editor, job scheduler, and cluster manager run in the Databricks-managed control plane account, while the cluster VMs and the ADLS Gen2 Delta tables reside in the bank's own subscription.
The notebook editor and job scheduler run in the bank's subscription, while the cluster VMs, the Delta transaction log, and the table files run in the Databricks-managed control plane account.
Every component, including the cluster VMs and the Delta table files, runs in the Databricks-managed control plane account; only the browser rendering the dashboard runs in the bank's subscription.
The control plane stores the Delta data files because it owns the transaction log; the data plane stores only the compute VMs that read those files.

questions.analysis: Correct answer: A. The control plane is the Databricks-managed backend — web application, notebook and query editors, job scheduler, cluster manager, and workspace metadata — and it is hosted in a Databricks cloud account, not the customer's. The data plane is everything that actually touches the customer's data: the virtual machines of a classic cluster and the cloud object storage that holds the Delta tables. Delta Lake keeps data in open Parquet files in object storage and adds only a transactional metadata layer on top, so the table files never need to leave the customer's container. A useful order-of-magnitude check: the bank's 12 TB (12,000 GB) of table data stays in its own ADLS Gen2 account, while the corresponding control-plane objects — notebook code, job definitions, cluster configurations, query text — are on the order of kilobytes to a few megabytes each, because they describe work rather than contain the bulk data. This distinction is exactly the business-versus-technical metadata split: technical metadata such as job and cluster configuration is produced and consumed by systems, whereas definitions that answer who, what, where, and how are business metadata kept in a data dictionary or catalog [source p.79]. Option B swaps the two planes and, worse, relocates the Delta transaction log into the control plane. Option C collapses the model into a fully managed single plane, which is the serverless case at most and never moves the customer's Delta files out of the subscription. Option D confuses the transaction log (_delta_log), which sits beside the Parquet files in the customer's storage container, with the control plane. Two edge cases matter for the exam: (1) when the workspace uses serverless compute, the VMs run in a Databricks-managed serverless data plane, yet the table data is still read from the customer's own storage, so residency of the raw data is unchanged; (2) control-plane objects can still hold sensitive text such as SQL statements and source code, so a residency argument must cover metadata and not only table files.

questions.question: A platform team is reviewing plane responsibilities and failure modes before approving a multi-region Databricks deployment. Which statements are correct? (select all that apply)

options.label: A cluster that is already running on classic compute keeps executing the Spark workload it has been given even if the control plane is temporarily degraded, because execution happens on VMs in the customer's account.
The Delta transaction log for a Unity Catalog table is stored in the Databricks-managed control plane account, so a control-plane outage makes table reads impossible.

A serverless SQL warehouse or serverless job runs on compute in a Databricks-managed serverless data plane, while the query results and the underlying table data remain in the customer's cloud storage.
Because the workspace UI and job scheduler are customer-managed components deployed into the customer's cloud account, the customer can patch and upgrade them independently of Databricks.

questions.analysis: Correct answers: A and C. Statement A reflects the classic data-plane design: the cluster VMs sit in the customer's cloud account, so a workload that has already been dispatched continues to run; what an outage actually removes is the ability to start new clusters, submit new runs through the scheduler, and use the web UI and REST API. That split is not a theoretical nicety — user-facing, true real-time data applications deliver an action at the click of a button while performing extremely heavy work under the hood, and that work cannot afford to depend on the control plane for every read [source p.411]. Statement C describes the serverless data plane: Databricks runs the compute in a Databricks-managed account, and the customer's tables are still read from the customer's own storage over managed network connectivity, so the data-residency boundary of the raw data is preserved even though the VM boundary moves. Statement B is false because the Delta transaction log lives in the customer's storage container alongside the Parquet files; that is precisely why already-provisioned compute can keep reading and writing committed table versions during a control-plane interruption. Statement D is false because the workspace UI, scheduler, and cluster manager are Databricks-managed control-plane components hosted in the Databricks account, so the customer cannot patch them; the customer controls configuration and access, not the software lifecycle. A key preconditions-and-edge-cases point for the exam: read-only access to committed data survives a control-plane outage, but interactive actions (starting a cluster, editing a notebook, submitting a run) do not, and a workload whose ingestion depends on a scheduled trigger will stall even though the compute itself is healthy. Estimate the exposure: if a region's control plane is unavailable for 30 minutes on a pipeline that runs 24 jobs per hour, 12 scheduled runs fail to launch and must be backfilled, while the 12 TB of Delta data stays readable throughout.

questions.question: Explain why separating the control plane from the data plane helps an organization meet its security and compliance obligations. In your answer, address (a) data residency and where the bulk data physically lives, (b) the blast radius of a data leak or a security vulnerability, and (c) how moving to a serverless data plane changes — but does not remove — these obligations. Use Databricks terminology for the components you name.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100 points total): (1) Data residency — 35%: correctly states that the control plane (web application, notebook and query editors, job scheduler, cluster manager, workspace metadata) runs in a Databricks-managed account, while the customer's Delta table files and their _delta_log transaction log stay in the customer's own cloud object storage (S3, ADLS Gen2, or GCS); explains that a classic cluster's VMs also run in the customer's account, so regulated bulk data does not cross the boundary; notes the edge case that control-plane objects such as query text and notebook code are still customer content and may themselves be in scope for review. (2) Blast radius — 35%: explains that keeping data in the customer's subscription with tenant- or data-level security limits the impact of a single access-control failure, that a cross-tenant leak is a far more severe event than an internal access error, and that minimizing blast radius requires security applied at the storage layer and anywhere data could leak; links the plane split to least-privilege credential scoping. (3) Serverless nuance — 30%: states that serverless compute runs in a Databricks-managed serverless data plane, so the compute boundary moves into the Databricks account while the data remains in the customer's storage; correctly concludes that residency, access control, and audit responsibilities persist and must be re-verified rather than assumed away. Deduct for vague answers that only say 'it is more secure' or that confuse which plane owns the data.
questions.analysis: A strong answer covers three linked arguments. First, residency: the control plane is the Databricks-managed backend that hosts the workspace UI, notebook and query editors, job scheduler, cluster manager, and workspace metadata; the data plane holds the compute and the data in the customer's cloud account, so Delta tables remain in the customer's object storage with their transaction log beside them. For a bank or a health provider, this means the regulated bulk data — a 12 TB table, for example — is governed by the customer's own region pinning, encryption keys, and network controls, while only comparatively small control-plane objects describe the work. Second, blast radius: tenant- and data-level security inside storage keeps one customer's data out of another's view, and the consequence of getting it wrong differs enormously — an internal access error typically triggers a procedural review, whereas a leak between customers is a massive breach of trust with media attention and customer loss, which is why the guidance is to minimize blast radius and apply tenant- or data-level security anywhere leakage is possible [source p.72]. Third, the serverless case: with serverless compute the VMs move into a Databricks-managed serverless data plane, but the table data is still read from the customer's storage, so residency obligations, least-privilege credential scoping, and audit logging all remain in force — the boundary has moved, so the customer must re-verify it rather than assume the responsibility was transferred. A complete answer also notes the failure-mode benefit: already-running classic workloads survive a control-plane interruption, while interactive actions such as launching a cluster or submitting a new run do not.

actions.text: Now let's see how firmly that boundary has set. This checkpoint has a couple of multiple-choice items and one short written response — take each one on your own, and resist the urge to scroll back and forth hunting for the phrasing. For the written item, answer in complete sentences and name components with Databricks' own terminology, the way you would on the exam.

Give every question a genuine attempt before you submit, even the ones where you feel shaky — a wrong answer you commit to is worth more to you right now than a blank one. Once you're done, I'll walk through the reasoning behind each item with you.

Service Map — Exam Domains

Workspace hosts notebooks, queries, dashboards, Git Repos

Compute: all-purpose, job clusters, SQL warehouses

Workflows/Jobs schedule and orchestrate DAG pipelines

Delta Live Tables declare quality-enforced pipelines

Unity Catalog governs catalogs, permissions, and lineage

Databricks SQL serves BI-style queries on lakehouse data

Wrong engine choices implode under OLAP load [source p.359]
Exam Focus: Verb → Service

Schedule a DAG → Jobs; query → Databricks SQL

Trap: analytics swapped for orchestration

Exact names: Delta Live Tables, Unity Catalog

Match the prompt verb to one component

Next Lesson

Workspaces, Notebooks, and Compute

Worked example: 4 runs × 25 min = 100 job-cluster min vs 1,440 all-purpose min → 1 − 100/1,440 = 93% idle

SLA 10:00 — Jobs monitors the DAG and alerts when the overnight run misses its deadline [source p.91]

Takeaways: data stays in open Delta tables; the Delta log adds ACID and time travel [source p.242]

Control plane schedules and governs; the data plane executes compute and stores data [source p.126]

actions.text: Now that we've separated the control plane from the data plane, let's put names on the services themselves. This slide is your service map, and it's organized the same way the exam is organized by domain. If you can redraw this map from memory, you can answer a large share of the scenario questions by simply asking: which service does this verb?

Start with the Workspace. This is the developer's entry point — notebooks, queries, dashboards, folders, and Git-backed Repos all live here. Sitting underneath it is Compute: all-purpose clusters for interactive development, job clusters for scheduled runs, and SQL warehouses for SQL analytics. Here's the detail exam writers love: all of this executes in the data plane, inside your cloud account, while the control plane only orchestrates.

Next, governance and analytics. Unity Catalog governs catalogs, permissions, and lineage across every workspace attached to the metastore. Databricks SQL gives you BI-style querying directly on lakehouse data. And on the pipeline side, Workflows — that's Jobs — handles scheduling and orchestration, while Delta Live Tables, now framed as Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines, builds declarative, quality-enforced pipelines where you describe the target and the engine figures out the execution.

This box is the highest-yield thing on the page: verb maps to service. If the stem says schedule a DAG, or run this on a cron, the answer is Jobs. If it says query lakehouse data in a BI tool, or a warehouse that scales for concurrent analysts, the answer is Databricks SQL. The classic distractor is offering a job cluster when the workload is interactive exploration — remember, jobs are scheduled, all-purpose clusters are interactive. And watch the arithmetic trap too: a worked example here multiplies four scheduled runs by twenty-five minutes each to get one hundred job-cluster minutes of cost. The exam expects you to do that multiplication, not guess at it.

Before we leave this unit, hold onto the three takeaways: the lakehouse unifies storage and workloads on open formats, the control plane orchestrates while the data plane executes, and every exam scenario traces back to this architecture. That sets up our next lesson — Workspaces, Notebooks, and Compute — where we stop naming the services and start configuring the environment you'll use for the rest of the course.

elements.content: Lesson Orientation: Workspaces, Notebooks, and Compute
Objective 1 — Given a workspace, create a notebook, attach compute, and run cells in more than one language.
Objective 2 — Given a workload, select an appropriate cluster configuration rather than defaults [source p.379].
Builds on the lakehouse: data access now runs through the workspace, notebooks, and clusters [source p.382].
Worked example: 500 GB daily ETL, 144 cores, 4.4 GB/core-h.
