elements.content: Split clusters by use case, such as ETL [source p.379].
Compute selection is a graded task domain [source p.43].

actions.text: We've spent this first stretch naming the platform and drawing its architecture. Now we get our hands on it. This lesson is called Lesson Orientation: Workspaces, Notebooks, and Compute — and the title tells you exactly where we're going: from knowing what the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform is, to knowing how you actually work inside it.

Objective one, and notice the phrasing, because the certification phrases it the same way: given a workspace, the data engineer must create a notebook, attach it to compute, and run cells in more than one language. That is a task statement, not a definition. Create, attach, run — three verbs, three things you'll be asked to demonstrate before this course is over.

Objective two flips it. This time the requirement is given a workload description, select an appropriate cluster configuration. Notice the word "appropriate" — there is rarely one correct size on the exam. There is a defensible choice, and the distractor that looks cheaper but violates the constraint, or looks bigger but wastes the budget.

This builds directly on what we just covered. The lakehouse architecture we spent the last several pages unpacking — storage, metadata, compute, governance — is now accessed through the workspace, notebooks, and clusters. So think of it this way: last section was the blueprint, this section is the door you walk through to reach it.

And here's a worked example of exactly what objective two looks like in practice: five hundred gigabytes of daily ETL, one hundred and forty-four total cores, which gives us roughly four point four gigabytes per core per day. That little division is the arithmetic the exam expects you to do quietly in your head — total workload divided by available cores tells you whether the cluster is starved, comfortable, or over-provisioned.

One pattern worth banking now: split clusters by use case, such as ETL. A nightly batch job does not belong on the same cluster as an interactive analyst session, because one is throughput-oriented and the other is latency-oriented, and mixing them satisfies neither.

Which is why this page matters more than it looks: compute selection is a graded task domain. It is not background reading. Workspace navigation and cluster configuration are foundational Data Engineer Associate domains that every later lesson — SQL warehouses, Unity Catalog, Git folders, Lakeflow pipelines — simply assumes you already have. Over the next pages we'll cover workspace navigation, notebook and language basics, attaching clusters, configuration choices, and two applied decision scenes. Let's start with the workspace itself.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Workspace Navigation and Notebook Basics

questions.question: A new engineer opens the Databricks workspace for the first time and must satisfy four needs from one navigation surface: (a) find the shared folders and notebooks, (b) look up Unity Catalog tables, views, and volumes, (c) see clusters and SQL warehouses, and (d) inspect scheduled job runs. Which option correctly names the sidebar sections that map one-to-one onto these four needs?

options.label: The left sidebar sections Workspace, Catalog, Compute, and Jobs map one-to-one onto needs (a), (b), (c), and (d) respectively
The left sidebar sections Workspace, Catalog, SQL Warehouses, and Notebooks map one-to-one onto needs (a), (b), (c), and (d) respectively
The Catalog Explorer exposes workspace folders, Unity Catalog tables, cluster definitions, and job runs together in a single expandable tree
The account console exposes the workspace, the metastore objects, all compute, and complete job history for every workspace in the account

questions.analysis: The left sidebar is the single navigation surface for a Databricks workspace. Workspace gives you the collaborative file namespace of folders and notebooks; Catalog opens the Catalog Explorer for metastore objects such as tables, views, volumes, and functions; Compute lists clusters and SQL warehouses together with their state; and Jobs shows scheduled workflows and their run history. Option B is wrong because 'SQL Warehouses' and 'Notebooks' are not peer sidebar sections of the kind described: notebooks live inside the Workspace section, and SQL warehouses are a category of compute surfaced from the Compute section. Option C repeats the most common trap in this checkpoint: the Catalog Explorer is the data-governance browser for Unity Catalog objects only, so it will not show workspace folders, cluster definitions, or job runs. Option D confuses the workspace UI with the account console, which handles account-level concerns such as users, billing, and metastore assignment rather than day-to-day development objects. This separation of concerns mirrors the underlying architecture, in which HDFS colocates compute and storage on the same nodes while object stores keep them apart, so the tooling that manages each concern is deliberately distinct [source p.237].

questions.question: Browsing a workspace folder, you see three entries side by side: sales_ingest, bronze, and README. One opens a cell-based editor with a compute selector at the top, one expands to reveal child entries when selected, and one opens as static content. Which statement correctly distinguishes a notebook from a folder and from a non-notebook file?

options.label: All three entries are notebooks, because any item listed inside a workspace folder is by definition a notebook object

sales_ingest is a notebook (notebook icon, opens a cell-based editor with a compute selector), bronze is a folder (folder icon, expands a child listing instead of opening an editor), and README is a non-notebook file such as .md or .csv that opens as static content with no runnable cells
bronze is a notebook because it appears as a top-level entry in the tree, and sales_ingest is a folder because it contains code cells
README is a notebook and sales_ingest is a folder, because the workspace browser treats any entry carrying a file extension as a folder boundary

questions.analysis: The workspace browser is a file-and-folder namespace, so the dependable way to classify an object is by its icon and by what happens when you select it, not by its name or its depth in the tree. A notebook shows a notebook icon and opens a cell-based editor with a compute selector at the top; a folder shows a folder icon and expands to reveal the entries it contains instead of opening an editor; a non-notebook file such as a .md, .csv, .json, or .parquet file opens as static content with no runnable cells and no attached compute. Option A is false because a folder may contain any supported file type, not only notebooks. Option C reverses the roles: position in the tree says nothing about object type, and notebooks never 'contain' other notebooks. Option D invents an extension rule that Databricks does not apply — notebooks are frequently created without an extension, and many non-notebook files carry one. The right mental model is that the workspace browser keeps a directory and metadata catalog for your files, much as the HDFS NameNode maintains directories, file metadata, and a catalog of block locations [source p.237]. That namespace confers no transactional guarantee: ACID compliance is a property of the transactional layer, not of a file listing, and a system without it can return unexpected results such as dirty reads [source p.304]. Note also the deliberate boundary against the checkpoint's primary trap: a notebook is a development artifact, not a metastore object, so it will never appear beside Unity Catalog tables in the Catalog Explorer.

questions.question: Which statements about where cluster state (Running, Pending, Terminated) is displayed and what those states imply are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The Compute page lists each all-purpose cluster and SQL warehouse with a State column, so Running, Pending, and Terminated can be read without opening a notebook
A notebook's compute selector shows the state of the cluster attached to that notebook, which explains why cells cannot execute when the attached cluster is Terminated or still Pending
A Terminated cluster keeps its driver and worker virtual machines alive, so the next cell execution starts instantly against warm local caches
Cluster state is reported in the Catalog Explorer beside each table, because running SQL against a table requires an active cluster

questions.analysis: Cluster state is surfaced on the Compute page, where every all-purpose cluster and SQL warehouse appears in a list with a State column; the same state is echoed in the notebook's compute selector, so a cell that refuses to run is normally explained by a Terminated cluster (VMs released) or a Pending one (VMs still provisioning). Option C states the opposite of what happens: terminating a cluster releases its driver and worker virtual machines, and any data cached in local SSD or memory on those machines is lost with them. That is exactly the trade-off described for hybrid architectures, in which local storage is spun up during queries and pipeline stages while object storage provides long-term retention [source p.247]; caching buys speed only while those nodes exist. The classic reason to keep compute near data — pushing map work to the blocks that hold the data so that bandwidth is preserved for shuffling [source p.246] — pays off only while the nodes are alive, which is why restarting a cluster re-reads Delta files from object storage rather than resuming from a warm cache. Option D repeats this checkpoint's trap: the Catalog Explorer is the browser for Unity Catalog data objects and their permissions, and it never reports compute state, so seeing a table listed there tells you nothing about whether any cluster is running.

actions.text: Quick checkpoint before we go further — three questions on the workspace tour and notebook fundamentals we just covered: the sidebar areas, what actually distinguishes a notebook from a folder and a plain file, and where cluster state shows up. Take each one on your own, and remember the multiple-select items need every correct statement, not just the first one that looks right.
Work through them at your own pace — no hints from me until you submit. Once you're done, I'll come back and we'll walk through the reasoning behind each one together.

scenes.title: Navigating the Databricks Workspace

elements.content: Navigating the Databricks Workspace
Six sidebar services carry a data engineer's daily work: Workspace, Catalog, Compute, Jobs & Pipelines, SQL Warehouses, and Marketplace.
Workspace browser: your personal home folder versus shared folders; you create notebooks, folders, and files.
Worked example: worker-hours = workers × hours — 8 workers × 2 h = 16 worker-hours; a 2-worker job cluster for 15 min = 0.5. [source p.171]
Exam framing: match each 'Where would…' prompt to one sidebar service.
Jobs & Pipelines schedules DAG runs, alerting on failure. [source p.91]
Notebook: cells, results, cluster selector, Run all. [source p.382]

actions.text: We just cleared the workspace and notebook basics checkpoint, so now let's put a durable mental map on top of it. This page is about navigation: given any task the exam describes, how quickly can you point at the right service in the left sidebar?

Six sidebar services carry a data engineer's daily work: Workspace, Catalog, Compute, Jobs and Pipelines, SQL Warehouses, and Marketplace. Notice the organising principle — they are grouped by what you are trying to do, not by where the data physically lives. That is precisely why the certification likes stems of the form 'Where would the data engineer go to…': you are being asked to map a task onto a service, and nothing more.

Here is the schematic mockup. On the left you see the sidebar with those labeled services; on the right, the notebook editor with its four labeled regions — the cell list, the results pane, the cluster selector, and the Run and Run all controls. Learn those four regions by name. If a stem tells you the engineer ran a cell but saw no output, your first two suspects should be whether a cluster was attached and where the results pane is reporting.

Now the Workspace browser. Your personal home folder is private to you, while shared folders are how a team collaborates. Inside either one you will only ever create three object types: notebooks, folders, and files. That trio is a favourite distractor set — if an option offers you a 'worksheet' or a 'project', it is wrong. And note the boundary: when the task is scheduling rather than authoring, you leave the Workspace entirely and go to Jobs and Pipelines, which schedules the DAG runs and alerts on failures. The Compute tab is where all-purpose clusters, job clusters, and cluster policies are listed and managed — that is the tab you name when the question is about capacity, not about code.

Let's anchor this with the worked example: worker-hours equals workers times hours — eight workers for six hours is forty-eight worker-hours. The value of the arithmetic is not the number; it is the discipline of writing down which quantity is the rate and which is the duration before you compute. That same discipline is what the exam is testing when it hands you a scenario with two constraints and four plausible tabs.

So here is the exam framing, and this is the rule I want you to carry forward: match every 'Where would…' prompt to one specific sidebar service. Authoring goes to Workspace, discovery and metadata to Catalog, capacity to Compute, scheduling to Jobs and Pipelines, SQL execution to SQL Warehouses, and third-party solutions to Marketplace. When you meet a stem about clusters, code editing, or scheduled runs, you should be able to name the tab before you finish reading the options. Next, we open a notebook and look at what actually happens inside those cells when the language changes.

scenes.title: Multi-Language Cells and Magic Commands

content.html:
Multi-Language Cells & Magic Commands

Switch languages with %python, %sql, %md, %sh, %pip, %scala, %r — and watch the shared Spark session carry state across cells.
Loading Python runtime…
Notebook cells separate cells with # COMMAND ----------
Cell output id="output"
Run the notebook to see per-cell output. SQL prints a table, Python prints text or a DataFrame preview, %md renders markdown.
Tests —

Each test inspects what actually happened when your notebook ran — the magic commands you used, the views you registered, and where they were queried from.

Hints 0 / 0
Solution notebook

A complete notebook that satisfies every test. Compare it with your own cell structure — the important idea is that only session objects (tables, temporary views, files) cross the language boundary, never Python variables.

widgetConfig.description: Multi-Language Cells and Magic Commands — practise switching cell languages inside one notebook and observe how state is shared between language contexts.
widgetConfig.starterCode:
# A Databricks notebook is a list of cells.
# Separate cells with a line like:   # COMMAND ----------
# The FIRST NON-EMPTY LINE of a cell may be a magic command, which overrides
# the notebook's default language for that cell only.

# COMMAND ----------
%md
TODO 1 - markdown cell

Write one sentence about what a magic command is, then give this cell its own
heading line (start that line with # or ##).

# COMMAND ----------
%python
# TODO 2 - create a DataFrame and register it as SHARED state.
# rows = [(1, "Ada", 91.5), (2, "Grace", 78.0), (3, "Alan", 88.2)]
# df = spark.createDataFrame(rows, ["id", "name", "score"])
# df.createOrReplaceTempView("people")
print("TODO 2: register a temporary view named people")

# COMMAND ----------
%sql
-- TODO 3 - SQL can create a temporary view too.
-- CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY VIEW top_people AS
-- SELECT id, name, score FROM people WHERE score > 80;

# COMMAND ----------
%sql
-- TODO 4 - query, from SQL, the view you registered from Python.
-- SELECT * FROM people;

# COMMAND ----------
%pip
# TODO 5 - install a library into THIS notebook's Python environment.

testCases.input: A cell whose first line is %python
testCases.expected: The explicit %python cell runs without error
testCases.description: Use an explicit %python magic cell

testCases.input: A %sql cell containing CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY VIEW
testCases.expected: A temporary view is created in the notebook catalog
testCases.description: Create a temporary view from %sql

testCases.input: A %python cell that registers a DataFrame view, then a %sql cell that queries it
testCases.expected: The SQL cell resolves a view whose origin is Python
testCases.description: Share state across languages

testCases.expected: The markdown cell renders an h1/h2/h3 element
testCases.description: Render markdown with %md
Install a library with %pip

hints: Cells are separated by `# COMMAND ----------`. The first non-empty line of a cell is the magic command: `%python`, `%sql`, `%md`, `%sh`, `%pip`, `%scala`, `%r`. A cell with no magic command uses the notebook's default language (here: Python).

Register shared state from Python: `df = spark.createDataFrame([(1, "Ada")], ["id", "name"])` then `df.createOrReplaceTempView("people")`. The temporary view lives in the Spark session, and every cell of the notebook talks to that same session.

A `%sql` cell can now run `SELECT * FROM people;`. But a plain Python variable (for example `threshold = 80`) is NOT visible there — that is the classic trap. Only catalogs, tables and temporary views cross the language boundary.

`%md` renders markdown in the notebook (use `#` or `##` for headings). `%pip install faker` installs a library into the current notebook's Python environment only — not cluster-wide. `%sh` runs a shell command on the driver node.

Rendering differs per language: `%sql` returns a table, `%python` prints output or a DataFrame preview (the last expression in a cell is displayed), `%scala` returns a typed result such as `n: Long = 3`. The data underneath is the same because the session is shared.
widgetConfig.solution:
%md
## Multi-language cells: the session is shared, the languages are not
A temporary view registered from **Python** is queryable from `%sql`, because
both cells talk to the same Spark session.

# COMMAND ----------
%python
rows = [(1, "Ada", 91.5), (2, "Grace", 78.0), (3, "Alan", 88.2)]
df = spark.createDataFrame(rows, ["id", "name", "score"])
df.createOrReplaceTempView("people")
print("registered a temporary view with", df.count(), "rows")
df

# COMMAND ----------
%sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY VIEW top_people AS
SELECT id, name, score FROM people WHERE score > 80;

# COMMAND ----------
%sql
SELECT name, score FROM top_people ORDER BY score DESC;

# COMMAND ----------
%scala
println("Scala cell - same Spark session")
val n = spark.sql("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM people")

# COMMAND ----------
%pip
install faker

# COMMAND ----------
%sh
echo "driver node is up"

actions.text: So we open a notebook and look at what actually happens inside those cells when the language changes. Down here you have a notebook laid out cell by cell, and the rule the exam expects you to quote is this: the notebook has a default language chosen at creation, but any individual cell can override it with a magic command on its first non-empty line.

actions.content: Each cell begins with a magic command on its first non-empty line — that is the cell's language override.

actions.text: Notice the starter code separates cells with the COMMAND separator line, and the magics in play are the ones you must recognise on sight: percent-python, percent-sql, percent-scala, percent-r for language switching, percent-md for markdown, percent-sh for shell, and percent-pip for installing a library into this notebook's Python environment only.

actions.content: Run the notebook and watch each cell execute under the language its magic command declares.
Results render per language: SQL returns a table, Python prints output or a DataFrame preview, Scala returns a typed result.

actions.text: Now here is the classic trap, and I want you to feel it rather than just hear it. When a Python cell registers a DataFrame as a temporary view, a percent-sql cell can query that view immediately, because both cells talk to the same Spark session. But a plain Python variable, say a threshold of eighty, is not visible inside that SQL cell — only catalogs, tables, and temporary views cross the language boundary.

actions.content: Expand the test panel to confirm the five behaviours: an explicit Python cell, a temporary view from SQL, shared state across languages, a rendered markdown heading, and a successful pip install.
Compare your cells against the reference solution, which chains a Python view, a SQL view, a Scala read of the same session, and a shell command.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Notebooks, Cells, and Languages

questions.question: A data engineer is working in a Databricks notebook attached to an all-purpose cluster. The team needs a third-party Python library (for example, a specialized text-cleaning package) installed inside the notebook's Python environment so that later Python cells can import it. The lesson also stresses that bash tooling matters in pipelines, since data engineers routinely use command-line tools such as awk or sed to process files [source p.46]. Which magic command should the engineer use for this specific task?

options.label: Use %sh install so the package is installed by the cluster's shell interpreter, because bash is the command-line interface for Linux operating systems and the standard way to install tooling [source p.46].
Use %pip install so the package is added to the Python environment of the current notebook, leaving the other cells free to keep their own declared languages.
Use %md install so the dependency is declared as documentation in a Markdown cell and resolved by the cluster before the next run.
Use %run install so the installer executes as a separate notebook and its imports become globally available to the workspace.

questions.analysis: B is correct. %pip installs a package into the Python environment of the notebook it is run from, so subsequent Python cells in the same notebook can import it. A is wrong for the stated goal: %sh runs shell (bash) commands on the driver, and while bash knowledge genuinely improves a data engineer's productivity for scripting and OS operations [source p.46], a shell install does not target the notebook's Python interpreter. C is wrong because %md renders Markdown documentation; it never executes or resolves dependencies. D is wrong because %run executes another notebook inline within the current session; it does not accept a pip package name and does not create workspace-wide imports. A key supporting fact is that a notebook cell's language is declared per cell, so a magic command changes what one cell does, not the notebook's default language for all later cells.

questions.question: Consider a notebook attached to one all-purpose cluster. Cell 1 is a Python cell that reads a Delta table into a DataFrame named events_df and then calls events_df.createOrReplaceTempView("events_view"). Cell 2 starts with %sql and runs SELECT count(*) FROM events_view;. What is the correct prediction, and why?

options.label: The query succeeds, because all cells in a notebook attached to the same compute share one Spark session, so temporary views and tables created in one cell are visible to the others.
The query fails, because every cell runs in its own isolated session and the Python cell's session is destroyed as soon as that cell finishes executing.
The query succeeds only if the Python cell first writes the DataFrame to a managed table in Unity Catalog, because SQL cells can read only governed catalog objects.
The query fails, because Spark SQL cannot query temporary views and can query only permanent tables registered in the metastore.

questions.analysis: A is correct: the cells of one notebook attached to one cluster run against the same Spark session and execution context, so state that lives in that session — temporary views, cached tables, the Spark session itself — is shared across cells regardless of which language each cell uses. This is why data engineers are encouraged to compose SQL with other operations inside a framework such as Spark rather than treating them as separate worlds [source p.47], and why Spark SQL has been a first-class part of Apache Spark since early on [source p.339]. B is the classic trap: the claim that each cell runs in an isolated session is false for cells of the same notebook on the same compute. C is wrong because temporary views are session-scoped, not catalog objects, and Unity Catalog is not required for a temp-view read. D is wrong because Spark SQL queries temporary views routinely. Important edge cases to remember: a bare Python variable such as x = 5 is not visible by name in a SQL cell — only session-level objects such as temp views are, so a pandas DataFrame must be registered before SQL can query it; attaching a different cluster, restarting the cluster, or running cells out of order can also leave the SQL cell referencing an object that does not yet exist.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about notebook cells, magic commands, and execution languages are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The execution languages a cell can be set to are Python, SQL, Scala, and R; %md, %sh, and %pip are helper commands rather than languages.
%md renders the contents of the cell as formatted Markdown documentation instead of executing it as code.
Each cell of a notebook opens its own isolated session, so nothing created in one cell can be seen by any other cell in the notebook.
%sh runs shell commands on the driver, which is useful for OS-level work such as processing files with awk or sed, and is distinct from distributing a job across the cluster [source p.46].
%pip permanently switches the notebook's default language to Python, including for later cells that explicitly start with %sql.

questions.analysis: A, B, and D are correct. A is correct because the four notebook execution languages are Python, SQL, Scala, and R; anything starting with a percent sign that is not one of those four is a helper directive such as %md (documentation), %sh (shell), %pip (package installation), or %run (run another notebook). B is correct: %md is a rendering directive, not an execution language, so that cell never contributes rows to a query. D is correct: %sh executes bash commands on the driver, and bash is the Linux command-line interface whose awk/sed-style tools remain in daily use for file processing and for calling commands from orchestration frameworks [source p.46]. C is the intended trap and is false: cells of the same notebook on the same compute share a Spark session, so temp views and tables cross cell and language boundaries. E is false: %pip changes the Python environment only, and each cell still declares its own language, including %sql cells. Two further medium-level nuances worth recalling for the exam: JVM languages such as Scala are generally more performant than Python and expose lower-level APIs, which is exactly why PySpark is an API wrapper that pushes work into native Scala running in the JVM [source p.341], and SQL is a declarative language in which the compiler and optimizer decide the steps, so a SQL cell states the result it wants rather than the procedure [source p.339].

actions.text: Alright — time for a quick checkpoint on notebooks, cells, and languages. Three questions here, and they ask you to pick a magic command, predict what one cell can see from another, and separate the helper commands from the execution languages themselves. Take each one on your own and commit to an answer before you move on; that's exactly how the exam will ask it.
I'll be right here once you submit, and we'll walk through anything that gave you trouble — including the distractor patterns worth recognising.

scenes.title: Attaching Compute and Executing Cells

elements.content: Attach Compute, Run Cells
Attachment = the runtime binding of a notebook to a Running cluster.
• A detached notebook executes nothing; the binding is not permanent.
• Many notebooks can share one cluster runtime [source p.168].
• Detach = compute change only; data stays in storage [source p.221].
Worked example: 2 TB ÷ 128 MB = 16,384 tasks; 32 slots → 512 waves [source p.348].
Driver holds the Spark session; executors return results.
States: queued, running, finished, error; Run all: top-down.

actions.text: Good — checkpoint's behind us, so let's move into the next piece: attaching compute and executing cells. This page answers a very concrete question: what actually has to be true before a single line of your notebook runs?

Start with the definition, because the exam tests the wording. An attachment is the runtime binding of a notebook to a running cluster. It is not a copy of your code, and it is not a data movement step — it is a live link that says: this notebook executes on that cluster.

Which leads directly to the first rule. A detached notebook executes nothing. You can open it, you can type code into it, you can see the cells sit there perfectly formed — and absolutely nothing happens when you run them. No binding, no execution.

Now look at the diagram. The notebook on the left is bound to a cluster, and inside that cluster the work splits across two roles. The driver node coordinates the run and holds the Spark session. The executor nodes do the distributed work — and their results flow back to the driver, which is why your output appears in the notebook's results pane.
So keep that split sharp: driver holds the Spark session and results come back through it; the executors return results to the driver rather than writing into your notebook directly.

Here's the trap that catches people. Many notebooks can share one cluster runtime — and equally, one notebook can be re-attached to a different cluster. The attachment is a binding, not a permanent property of the notebook.
Which means detaching is a compute change only. Your data stays in storage. You are not deleting anything, you are not moving anything — you have simply unbound the notebook from that runtime.

Once you attach and run, each cell moves through recognisable states: queued, then running, then finished or error. And mind the two run controls — Run all executes cells top to bottom, while Run below executes from the cursor downward.

Finally, the worked example makes the driver-and-executor split concrete. Two terabytes divided into 128-megabyte partitions gives you 16,384 tasks; at 32 seconds per task, that arithmetic tells you how the cluster's parallelism turns into wall-clock time. That's the model to hold onto. Next we'll put it into practice by creating a notebook, attaching a cluster, and running multi-language cells.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Create a Notebook, Attach a Cluster, and Run Multi-Language Cells

elements.content: Problem 1

You are in a fresh Databricks workspace: no notebooks exist yet, no compute is running, and your home folder is /Users/de.associate@example.com. Build ONE notebook named sales_multilang_demo in your home folder, attached to ONE all-purpose cluster, that does three things: (1) a Python cell prints a greeting; (2) a second Python cell builds a Spark DataFrame from the inline rows below and registers it so that SQL can query it; (3) a %sql cell and a %scala cell each answer the same business question against that registered data. The rows are (region, product, units, unit_price): EMEA/Widget/120/9.50; EMEA/Gadget/40/22.00; AMER/Widget/300/9.50; AMER/Gadget/15/22.00; APAC/Widget/75/9.50. Business question: what is total revenue (units x unit_price) per region, highest revenue first, and how many line items back each region? Give the exact SQL result set and the exact cell code.
Hint: A Python variable is not a table. Register the DataFrame in the Spark session catalog before you leave the Python cell, then every language context can see it.

Worked solution
STEP 0 - Orient in the sidebar. The Workspace entry holds notebooks and folders; Compute holds clusters. Your personal home folder (/Users/... ) is private to you; shared folders are team-visible. Wait until Compute shows a cluster in state Running before you try to execute anything.

STEP 1 - Create the notebook. Sidebar > Workspace > open /Users/de.associate@example.com > Create > Notebook. Name it sales_multilang_demo (name states the purpose, so the reviewer knows what it demonstrates). Leave the default language as Python; you will override per-cell with magic commands. Leave the cluster selector detached for now.

STEP 2 - Create the all-purpose cluster. Sidebar > Compute > Create compute. Name: de-assoc-dev. Cluster mode: Multi node (a driver plus workers). Databricks runtime: the current LTS release offered by the workspace (an LTS runtime receives security updates and support for a longer window than a non-LTS one, which is why it is the safe default for a course-long dev cluster). Worker type: a general-purpose VM (for example Standard_DS3_v2 on Azure or an m5.xlarge-class instance on AWS), 2 workers, driver of the same family. Auto-stop ('Terminate after ... minutes of inactivity'): 30 minutes. Click Create compute and watch the state go Pending -> Running. Running means the driver VM is up and the Spark driver process is accepting work; Pending means it is still provisioning.

STEP 3 - Attach the notebook. Return to sales_multilang_demo, open the cluster drop-down in the notebook toolbar, and select de-assoc-dev. The notebook now has a live SparkSession. No code is required to create it - Databricks pre-binds a session object named spark in Python, Scala and R notebooks, and it is the SAME session object across languages.

STEP 4 - Cell 1 (Python, the greeting):

print('Hello, Databricks')

Output: Hello, Databricks

STEP 5 - Cell 2 (Python: build the DataFrame and publish it as a relation):

from pyspark.sql import Row

rows = [

Row(region='EMEA', product='Widget', units=120, unit_price=9.50),

Row(region='EMEA', product='Gadget', units=40, unit_price=22.00),

Row(region='AMER', product='Widget', units=300, unit_price=9.50),

Row(region='AMER', product='Gadget', units=15, unit_price=22.00),

Row(region='APAC', product='Widget', units=75, unit_price=9.50),

]

df = spark.createDataFrame(rows)

df.createOrReplaceTempView('regional_sales')

print('registered; rows =', df.count())

Output: registered; rows = 5

Note what createOrReplaceTempView actually does: it registers the DataFrame's logical plan under the name regional_sales in the SparkSession catalog. It does not copy the data and it does not persist anything to storage. df.count() is the action that forces the plan to execute.

STEP 6 - Cell 3 (SQL against the view). The magic command must be the very first line of the cell:

%sql

SELECT region,

SUM(units * unit_price) AS revenue,

COUNT(*) AS line_items

FROM regional_sales

GROUP BY region

ORDER BY revenue DESC

Result set:

AMER | 3180.00 | 2

EMEA | 2020.00 | 2

APAC | 712.50 | 1

Arithmetic check: AMER = 300*9.50 + 15*22.00 = 2850.00 + 330.00 = 3180.00. EMEA = 120*9.50 + 40*22.00 = 1140.00 + 880.00 = 2020.00. APAC = 75*9.50 = 712.50. Grand total = 3180.00 + 2020.00 + 712.50 = 5912.50, which is also the sum of 3420 + 1250 + 950... more directly: total units*price over all 5 rows = 1140 + 880 + 2850 + 330 + 712.50 = 5912.50, so the grouped result is complete.

STEP 7 - Cell 4 (Scala against the SAME view, no re-registration):

%scala

val topRegion = spark.sql("SELECT region, SUM(units*unit_price) AS revenue FROM regional_sales GROUP BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 1")

topRegion.show()

Output: AMER | 3180.00. Note that in the Scala context the session object is again named spark, and regional_sales resolves because it lives in the shared session catalog, not in the Python interpreter.

Deliverable: a 4-cell notebook, one attached all-purpose cluster, one Python greeting, one Python DataFrame + temp view, one %sql aggregate, one %scala aggregate, both aggregates returning the identical AMER/EMEA/APAC ranking.

Analysis — Why the method works: the notebook is bound to exactly one SparkSession on the attached cluster, and a temp view is registered in that session's catalog rather than in any one interpreter. Python, SQL, Scala and R cells are compiled to the same session, so regional_sales is visible to all of them; the Python object df is not, because df lives in the Python REPL's namespace. This is exactly the pattern in [source p.346], where a Spark job reads several sources into DataFrames, 'converting the data into a relational format', combines them into a single table, filters with a SQL statement, and writes the result out; the language used to describe the relation is an implementation detail, the relation itself is shared. SQL is a good fit for step 6 because it is declarative: you stipulate the final set (region, revenue, line_items) and the compiler and optimizer decide the physical steps [source p.339], which is why the same three-line query plans efficiently across many rows.

Where students go wrong: (1) writing a %sql cell that references a Python variable, e.g. SELECT * FROM df - there is no catalog entry named df, only the view you registered. (2) Forgetting that createOrReplaceTempView is lazy in the sense that it stores a plan; if the Python cell later mutates or overwrites df, the view may point at a re-evaluated plan. (3) Putting a comment or blank line above %sql, which turns the magic command into ordinary text and fails to parse. (4) Choosing a non-LTS runtime because it looks newer, which shortens the support window on a long-running course cluster [source p.168] describes the general hazard: workloads that share one long-lived environment accumulate dependency and version conflicts, which is precisely why ephemeral, purpose-built compute is preferred for repeatable jobs.

Edge cases and generalization: a temp view is scoped to the session and disappears when the cluster restarts or auto-stops; a global temp view (global_temp.name) is scoped to the Spark application and survives across sessions in the same running cluster but not across a restart; a persisted table (for example Delta Lake in Unity Catalog, catalog.schema.table) survives everything and adds ACID guarantees, including protection from dirty reads, at the cost of storage and commit bookkeeping [source p.304]. In production you register a temp view for exploratory joins and persist to Delta for anything another notebook or schedule must read.
Problem 2

You must recommend ONE compute configuration for a team of 6 data engineers doing interactive development against a 200 GB Delta table. Use these given rates: the driver consumes 0.5 DBU/hour, each worker consumes 1.0 DBU/hour, and all-purpose compute costs USD 0.40 per DBU. Each engineer runs one 3.0-hour interactive session per day, 20 days per month (120 sessions/month). Compare three candidates: (A) fixed multi-node, 1 driver + 2 workers, auto-stop 30 minutes; (B) autoscaling 1 driver + 2-8 workers, measured average 4.5 workers during the 3.0-hour session, auto-stop 30 minutes; (C) single-node cluster (driver only), auto-stop 30 minutes. (i) Compute the monthly cost of each. (ii) Recommend one and justify. (iii) Compute the monthly saving on your recommendation if auto-stop drops from 30 to 10 minutes. (iv) State what changes if the same logic is scheduled nightly instead of run interactively.
Hint: Bill the idle tail too: with auto-stop at 30 minutes, a 3.0-hour session is billed as 3.5 hours of DBU time.

Worked solution
STEP 1 - Establish the per-hour DBU rate for each option.

(A) Fixed 1 driver + 2 workers: DBU/h = 0.5 + (2 x 1.0) = 2.5 DBU/h. Cost/h = 2.5 x 0.40 = USD 1.00/h.

(B) Autoscaling, average 4.5 workers: DBU/h = 0.5 + (4.5 x 1.0) = 5.0 DBU/h. Cost/h = 5.0 x 0.40 = USD 2.00/h.

(C) Single node, driver only: DBU/h = 0.5. Cost/h = 0.5 x 0.40 = USD 0.20/h.

STEP 2 - Establish billed hours per session. Auto-stop terminates the cluster 30 minutes after the last activity, so each 3.0-hour session is billed for 3.0 + 0.5 = 3.5 hours.

STEP 3 - Monthly billed hours = 3.5 h x 120 sessions = 420.0 h.

STEP 4 - Monthly cost.

(A) 420.0 h x USD 1.00 = USD 420.00.

(B) 420.0 h x USD 2.00 = USD 840.00.

(C) 420.0 h x USD 0.20 = USD 84.00.

STEP 5 - Recommendation. Choose (A): a fixed 1 driver + 2 workers all-purpose cluster with a current LTS runtime and 30-minute auto-stop. Rationale: (C) is four times cheaper but is disqualified on capability - a 200 GB table plus concurrent joins and shuffles exceeds what one node's memory and cores can serve, and Spark work that does not fit in memory spills, which is visible in [source p.346] where one source is 'large enough that it must spill'. (B) costs exactly twice (A) for the same billed hours because 4.5 average workers is 2.25x the worker DBUs of (A); autoscaling is only worth its premium when the cluster is idle at 2 workers most of the day and spikes occasionally, which the measured 4.5-worker average says is not the case. Fixed 2 workers also gives 6 engineers predictable, reproducible parallelism, which matters for a shared dev cluster.

STEP 6 - Part (iii), tightening auto-stop to 10 minutes. Billed hours per session = 3.0 + (10/60) = 3.1667 h. Monthly = 3.1667 x 120 = 380.0 h. Cost = 380.0 x USD 1.00 = USD 380.00. Saving = 420.00 - 380.00 = USD 40.00/month, i.e. the 40 wrapped idle hours (0.3333 h x 120) priced at USD 1.00/h. Equivalently the idle tail falls from 40 h/month to 20 h/month.

STEP 7 - Part (iv), nightly scheduled job. The interactive all-purpose cluster is the wrong tool. A scheduled Workflows job should run on a job cluster created for that run and terminated at the end, which is the ephemeral-infrastructure pattern: 'each job gets its own temporary server or cluster installed with dependencies' [source p.168]. Benefits: only the job's dependencies need to be present, the cluster cannot be left running by a human, and a crashed run cannot corrupt the shared dev environment.

Analysis — Method choice: this is a cost model, so the only defensible way to compare options is to fix the unit (DBU), fix the billed time (session length plus auto-stop tail), then multiply. Students routinely compare only the headline per-hour rate and forget the tail; with a 30-minute auto-stop and a 3.0-hour session, 14.3% of billed time is idle (0.5/3.5 = 0.143), and across 120 sessions that is 40 idle hours per month - a real, avoidable line item.

Where students go wrong: (1) Treating auto-stop as free, or assuming the cluster stops exactly when the last cell finishes. Auto-stop is measured from the last activity, so the tail is always billed. (2) Assuming autoscaling always saves money; it saves only when the average worker count is materially below the fixed size, and here the measured average of 4.5 workers makes autoscaling strictly more expensive than fixed 2. (3) Applying the driver DBU rate to workers or vice versa; the two are priced differently and the driver is always billed while the cluster is up. (4) Choosing the single node purely on price, ignoring that the workload is 200 GB and multi-user - a configuration must satisfy the workload profile before price is compared.

Edge cases: autoscaling interacts with cluster state - a cluster scaled down to its minimum still bills its minimum; if the workload is bursty, average worker count over a day is a better cost input than the peak. Also, the cost model changes if the workload is not interactive: job clusters are created per run and terminated, so their idle tail is zero by construction [source p.168]. Finally, note that a SQL-only reporting workload of this shape would more naturally run on a SQL warehouse than on an all-purpose cluster; all-purpose compute is priced for interactive development, not for BI concurrency.
Problem 3

A colleague's notebook (default language Python) works in the morning and fails in the afternoon. Cell 1 (Python) builds the DataFrame and runs df.createOrReplaceTempView('regional_sales'). The cluster's auto-stop is set to 45 minutes. The engineer leaves for a one-hour lunch. Back at the keyboard, cell 2 is:

%sql

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM regional_sales;

and it fails with TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND. Cell 3 is:

%sql

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM df;

and it fails the same way. (a) Explain precisely why each cell failed, and what happened to the cluster during lunch. (b) Give two fixes that make SQL work for the rest of the current session, and one fix that survives the auto-stop. (c) The engineer's genuinely productive work in that session was 20 minutes; auto-stop was 45 minutes. Compute the percentage of billed cluster time that was idle, then recompute it for a 10-minute auto-stop. (d) Explain why the Python variable df was invisible to %sql even before lunch, while the cluster was running.
Hint: Nothing about the SQL changed. The session that held the catalog entry was terminated while the engineer was away.

Worked solution
(a) Timeline. At 12:00 the engineer's last cell executed; the cluster was Running. At 12:45, 45 minutes with no activity, auto-stop terminated the cluster and it moved to the Terminated state in the Compute list. Terminating the cluster tears down the Spark driver, and with it the SparkSession and its catalog. When the engineer pressed Run at 13:00, Databricks started a NEW cluster (Pending -> Running) and created a NEW SparkSession. That new session has an empty catalog: regional_sales, which was only ever a catalog entry pointing at a logical plan, no longer exists. Cell 2 fails with TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND for that reason. Cell 3 fails for a second, independent reason: there has never been a catalog object named df. df was a Python variable in the previous interpreter, and the interpreter died with the driver. The notebook's old cell outputs still appear on screen, which makes the failure look mysterious - but stored output is just text, not evidence that the objects still exist.

(b) Fixes that make SQL work for the rest of the current session: (1) re-run cell 1 - rebuilding df and calling createOrReplaceTempView('regional_sales') re-registers the view in the new session; (2) register the relation inside the SQL cell itself by rewriting the Python cell to end with spark.sql("CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW regional_sales AS SELECT ...") - or simply re-run cell 1 before any dependent cell, which is the practical habit. Fix that survives auto-stop: persist the data as a table rather than a temp view, e.g. df.write.mode('overwrite').saveAsTable('main.de_assoc.regional_sales') using the Unity Catalog three-level namespace, then query FROM main.de_assoc.regional_sales. That table is durable; the temp view is not.

(c) Billed time with a 45-minute auto-stop = 20 minutes of work + 45 minutes of idle tail = 65 minutes. Idle fraction = 45/65 = 0.6923, i.e. 69.2% of billed time was idle. With a 10-minute auto-stop: billed = 20 + 10 = 30 minutes; idle fraction = 10/30 = 0.3333, i.e. 33.3%. Idle minutes fall from 45 to 10, a reduction of 35 minutes per session (a 77.8% cut in wasted time) even though the productive work is unchanged. Re-running cell 1 after lunch costs seconds; the 45-minute tail is the expensive part.

(d) df was never a catalog object. It is a name bound in the Python interpreter's namespace to a DataFrame object (a Python wrapper around a logical plan). The %sql cell is not compiled by Python at all; the optimizer resolves identifiers against the SparkSession catalog, which contains databases, tables and views - not interpreter variables. A temp view is a catalog entry (session-scoped), which is why every language context can see regional_sales.

Analysis — Method: reason about SCOPE. Databricks notebooks offer three nested scopes and students conflate them. (1) Interpreter scope: Python variables and Scala vals - they exist only in the process that created them and are invisible to other languages. (2) Session scope: temp views registered in the SparkSession catalog - visible to every language bound to that session, destroyed when the session ends, i.e. when the cluster terminates or restarts. (3) Metastore scope: managed and external tables, including Delta Lake tables in Unity Catalog - visible to every session and every user with privileges, surviving restarts. Diagnosing TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND is a two-question decision tree: 'was the name ever a table or view?' and 'is the cluster still the same running cluster?' If the answer to the second is no, the fix is to re-run the defining cell; if the answer to the first is no, the fix is to register the object.

Common mistakes: (1) Running a cell while the cluster is Pending - the notebook is attached but the driver is not ready, so the cell may be queued or fail; the Compute page must read Running first. (2) Expecting %sql to see a raw Python variable - it cannot, and this is the single most common multi-language error. (3) Forgetting that auto-stop is destructive, not a pause: the cluster and the session are gone, along with cached data and any temp view; only persisted tables survive. In an exam item, 'the notebook returned results yesterday but fails today' is almost always a terminated cluster plus a non-persisted view.

Why persistence matters beyond convenience: a Delta table written to storage gives ACID semantics, so a reader does not see uncommitted writes (a dirty read) and the writer's atomicity is guaranteed [source p.304]; SQL over that table is declarative, with the optimizer choosing the physical plan [source p.339]. A temp view gives you none of that: it is a session-local pointer to a plan. Practical rule for this course: use temp views for intermediate steps inside one session, and write to Delta whenever a result must outlive the cluster, be shared with a teammate, or be read by a scheduled job.

actions.text: Let's put everything from this lesson together with a fully worked, end-to-end problem. This is exactly the kind of task the exam will ask you to reason through: create a notebook, attach compute, and run multi-language cells in a single session.

Here's the scenario. You're in a fresh Databricks workspace — no notebooks yet. Your job is to create a notebook in your home folder that prints a greeting in Python, computes an aggregate in SQL over a table registered from Python, and then reads that same table from a Scala cell — all while attached to one all-purpose cluster.

Walk through the solution. Step one: create the notebook, keep the default language as Python, and name it so its purpose is obvious. Step two: create an all-purpose cluster with a current LTS runtime, two workers, and an auto-stop timeout, then wait until its state reads Running. Step three: attach the notebook, run the Python cell to build a DataFrame and register it with createOrReplaceTempView, then run a %sql cell and a %scala cell against that very view.
Notice the hint here, because it's the heart of the whole task: a Python variable is not a table. To make data visible across language contexts, you have to register it as a temp view first.

Why does this work? Because one Spark session is bound to the notebook, so temp views are visible to every language context. That's the key insight — a Python variable stays in its own cell, but a registered view is shared. And watch the common pitfalls: running a cell while the cluster is still Pending, expecting %sql to see a raw Python variable, and forgetting that auto-stop terminates the cluster and clears notebook state.
Now a second one, this time about cost. You must recommend one compute configuration for a given workload.

The solution starts by establishing the per-hour DBU cost, and the hint reminds you to bill the idle tail too — with auto-stop at thirty minutes, that idle time still counts against your budget. Method-wise, this is a cost model, so reason step by step about hours, rate, and cluster size rather than guessing.

The third problem changes shape. A colleague's notebook, whose default language is Python, suddenly fails. The hint tells you nothing about the SQL actually changed — the session did. The method here is to reason about scope: Databricks binds a Spark session and its temp views to the notebook and cluster, so when the session context shifts, previously registered views can disappear. That is exactly the kind of scope reasoning the exam rewards. Keep these three patterns in mind, and the next checkpoint will feel straightforward.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Cluster Configuration Concepts

questions.question: A data engineer supports two workloads in the same workspace. Workload A is a 2 GB Delta table that one analyst explores interactively in a notebook, and the entire working set fits comfortably in a single machine's memory. Workload B is a nightly aggregation over roughly 3 TB of Delta and Parquet data that performs many joins and wide shuffles. Which pairing of cluster configurations is most appropriate?

options.label: Run Workload A on a single-node cluster (driver only, no worker nodes), and run Workload B on a multi-node cluster whose worker count autoscales between a configured minimum and maximum.
Run both workloads on a single-node cluster, because keeping everything on one machine eliminates the shuffle traffic that dominates Workload B.
Run both workloads on a multi-node autoscaling cluster, because a single-node cluster cannot start a Spark session and therefore cannot execute notebook cells.

Run Workload A on a multi-node cluster with exactly one worker, and run Workload B on a multi-node cluster whose minimum and maximum worker counts are set to the same value so autoscaling cannot add workers during the shuffle.

questions.analysis: A single-node cluster runs a driver with zero worker nodes, so it cannot distribute work across machines, but it does start a complete Spark session and can execute notebook cells (including SQL and DataFrame code). That makes it a strong fit when the dataset fits in the driver's memory and only one user is working at a time, which describes Workload A. Workload B cannot fit on one machine: distributing partitions across workers is the only way to obtain the parallelism that a 3 TB join and shuffle requires, so a multi-node cluster with an autoscaling worker range is required. Option B inverts the physics of shuffling: a single-node cluster does not make shuffles faster, it merely has no workers to shuffle between, so it avoids distribution rather than accelerating it. Option C is factually wrong because a single-node cluster is a genuine Spark cluster whose driver hosts the SparkSession. Option D is the classic over-correction: pinning Workload A to a one-worker multi-node cluster spends worker capacity that the driver alone could supply, and setting the minimum equal to the maximum removes autoscaling's ability to add capacity exactly when the shuffle phase needs it, so Workload B becomes slower and possibly fails on memory. Two further controls must be chosen together with the topology. Node type fixes the vCPU-to-memory ratio of each machine, so a memory-optimized instance family suits a wide aggregation that would otherwise spill to disk while a compute-optimized family suits CPU-bound parsing; changing node type changes memory per node, and worker count multiplies it. Runtime version fixes which engine capabilities exist, so a validated long-term-support (LTS) Databricks Runtime should be selected for both clusters rather than mixing versions. The economic logic underpinning the multi-node choice is the elasticity of separated compute and storage: because dynamic RAM is extremely expensive to own outright, the cloud lets a team rent a large quantity of memory for the duration of a job and release it when the job completes [source p.248]. Sizing also follows the standard ingestion questions of how frequently the data is accessed and in what volume it typically arrives [source p.66]. Finally, notice the isolation analogy that makes single-node compute attractive for a solo analyst: single-tenant architecture gives each group of tenants its own dedicated set of resources such as networking, compute, and storage, with nothing shared [source p.252].
questions.correctAnswer: A

questions.question: A team runs an all-purpose cluster configured with autoscaling between 2 and 16 workers and an auto-stop timeout of 20 minutes. Which statements about the cost and lifecycle behavior of this cluster are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: When autoscaling removes a worker, the meter for that worker's cloud instance and its DBUs stops for the remainder of the cluster's life, so a scaled-down cluster costs less per minute than the same cluster at full size.
Autoscaling lowers the cost of the driver node, because the driver is billed in proportion to the number of workers attached to it.

Auto-stop terminates the cluster after the configured idle period, which stops billing for the driver as well as the workers, while notebooks, workspace files, and data stored in cloud object storage continue to exist.
A cluster running a long continuous streaming job never becomes idle, so auto-stop never fires and the engineer must instead size the cluster and schedule its shutdown deliberately.
Auto-stop is triggered by low CPU utilization, so a cluster can terminate itself in the middle of a long-running command in order to save money.

questions.analysis: Statement A is correct because autoscaling changes the number of live worker nodes, and billing follows the live nodes: removing a worker ends both its cloud-instance charge and its DBU charge for the remaining life of the cluster, so the cost per minute falls as the cluster scales in. Statement B is false. Every cluster has exactly one driver, billed at the driver DBU rate regardless of how many workers are attached; autoscaling never changes the driver's price, and the driver is never multiplied by worker count. Statement C is correct and is the most commonly tested auto-stop fact: auto-stop terminates the cluster after the configured number of idle minutes, which stops all compute billing, driver included, but termination is not deletion. Notebooks, folders, Repos, cluster configuration, and Delta tables in the customer's cloud object storage persist independently of compute, and a later start simply re-attaches the cluster. Statement D is correct because idleness is defined by command and task activity, not by the clock: a streaming job keeps issuing work continuously, so the cluster never reaches the idle threshold and auto-stop cannot reduce its cost, which is why long-running streams should be placed on job clusters that terminate when the run ends or managed deliberately on a sized all-purpose cluster. Statement E is false because auto-stop is based on cluster inactivity rather than CPU utilization, and Databricks does not terminate a cluster in the middle of a running command. A concrete worked example shows the magnitude of both effects. Suppose the driver bills at 1.5 DBU per hour and each worker at 0.5 DBU per hour, and the job spends 30 minutes at 8 workers followed by 30 minutes at 2 workers. The first half hour costs 0.5 x (1.5 + 8 x 0.5) = 2.75 DBU and the second half hour costs 0.5 x (1.5 + 2 x 0.5) = 1.25 DBU, for a total of 4.0 DBU; running the whole hour at 8 workers would have cost 5.5 DBU, so autoscaling saved about 27 percent. Now suppose the engineer leaves the same cluster idle for 3 hours: the driver alone burns 1.5 x 3 = 4.5 DBU, more than the entire productive hour. That asymmetry is precisely the elasticity argument that makes separated compute and storage economical, since memory can be rented and then released when the job completes [source p.248]. It is also the reason total opportunity cost of ownership deserves a line in any configuration decision: choosing to leave one oversized, always-on cluster excludes the cheaper alternatives you could have run instead, and once that stack becomes part of production it carries its own support, training, and maintenance burden [source p.145].
correctAnswer: A
C
D

questions.question: A team complains that a SQL-heavy Delta Lake workload is too slow and proposes quote, turning on Photon, unquote. Which statement most accurately describes what Photon is and what enabling it on the compute actually does?

options.label: Photon is a vectorized query engine written in C++ that runs on the driver and executors alongside Spark and accelerates query execution; enabling it does not change how Delta data is stored on disk and is not a Unity Catalog governance feature.
Photon is the columnar file format that Delta Lake writes, so enabling it rewrites the tables into a faster on-disk layout that any engine can then read.
Photon is the Unity Catalog capability that captures column-level lineage and access grants, so enabling it improves governance rather than query speed.
Photon is a runtime version selector, so enabling it upgrades the cluster to the newest Databricks Runtime and is the only way to obtain a long-term-support (LTS) release.

questions.analysis: Photon is a native, vectorized query engine that replaces the execution operators of Spark SQL with a C++ implementation and runs on the driver and the executors of the cluster, accelerating SQL and DataFrame workloads on Delta and Parquet data. It therefore belongs to the compute layer. Option B is the trap this item is designed to catch: the columnar file format and the transaction log that enable ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and upserts are Delta Lake features that exist in storage, and Photon neither writes a table nor changes the layout that other readers see. Option C confuses Photon with Unity Catalog, which is the governance layer responsible for the metastore, grants, and lineage; enabling Photon grants no new permission and records no new metadata. Option D confuses Photon with the Databricks Runtime version selector: LTS runtimes are chosen independently of Photon, and Photon itself is available only on Photon-capable runtimes and instance families, so the driver and workers must be compatible node types. Two practical preconditions and edge cases matter for the exam. First, Photon helps most when the workload spends its time in CPU-bound operators such as scans, filters, joins, and aggregations; if the job is bound by remote object-storage reads or by a shuffle that saturates the network, the speed-up will be much smaller than the vendor benchmark suggests, so measure before standardizing. Second, Photon-capable compute carries a higher DBU rate, so the decision is a break-even calculation, not a free upgrade: if a job takes 3 hours at 2 DBU per hour without Photon (6 DBU total) and 1 hour at 3 DBU per hour with Photon (3 DBU total), the engine wins because the time saved outweighs the rate premium; if the engine only cuts the runtime from 3 hours to 2.5 hours, the higher rate can erase the gain. That trade-off is exactly the total opportunity cost of ownership calculation, in which choosing one stack excludes the alternatives and commits you to its support, training, setup, and maintenance [source p.145]. The elasticity of cloud compute is the lever that makes such an upgrade affordable in the first place: memory and CPU are rented for the duration of the job and released when it completes [source p.248], so a faster engine pays only if it genuinely shortens the rented interval.
questions.correctAnswer: A

actions.text: Before we move on, let's check that the cluster configuration controls from this stretch have settled in. This is a checkpoint on its own, so treat each question as a self-test rather than something to reason through out loud — read every option carefully, since a few of them are worded to sound plausible without being accurate.

Take your time and answer each one on your own. Once you submit, I'll walk through the whole set with you — including the distractors — so you can see exactly which terms you had sharp and which ones still need another pass. Go ahead and start when you're ready.

scenes.title: All-Purpose Clusters vs Job Clusters

elements.content: Dimension  |  All-Purpose Clusters  |  Job Clusters

Who creates it, and when it comes into existence
All-Purpose Clusters: A data engineer or workspace admin creates it explicitly from the Compute page, the Clusters REST API, or the Databricks CLI, so the cluster exists as a named, long-lived workspace object with its own cluster ID before any work is assigned to it.
Job Clusters: The Databricks job scheduler creates it automatically at the instant a task in a run starts, using the cluster specification embedded in the job definition, so no human creates it and it has no independent existence outside that single run.

Who can use it: sharing model and access control
All-Purpose Clusters: Multiple users in the workspace can be granted Can Attach To or Can Restart permission and share the same compute concurrently, which is exactly why it is called all-purpose; users are separated only by their notebook sessions, so one user's heavy cell can slow another user's cells. Access is granted through the workspace permission model, in the same way a filesystem stores per-entity permission metadata alongside each directory entry [source p.226].
Job Clusters: It is isolated to a single job run: only the tasks of that one run execute on it, and no other user, notebook, or job can attach to it, so noisy-neighbour interference between teams is structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged.

Lifecycle and termination (preconditions and edge cases)
All-Purpose Clusters: It stays Running until a human stops it, until the configurable auto-stop timer expires after a period of inactivity (120 minutes by default), or until the underlying cloud instance is terminated after an error; the edge case students miss is that auto-stop only counts idle time, so a cluster running a long interactive session never auto-stops. Idle time is a deliberate cost decision a human must make, much as retention length in object-storage-backed systems is a storage-cost decision rather than a correctness one [source p.306].
Job Clusters: It terminates automatically when the run completes, whether that run succeeded, failed, or was cancelled, so an idle job cluster burning DBUs is a configuration bug rather than normal behaviour; the edge case is that a failed run still terminates the cluster, which is why failure diagnosis must rely on logs, the Spark UI, and task output rather than on a surviving cluster.

Interactive capability: notebook attachment and shared state
All-Purpose Clusters: Notebooks and SQL editor sessions attach to it directly, and because the Spark session and cached data persist across cells and across detach/reattach cycles, developers iterate quickly, inspect intermediate DataFrames, and debug interactively.
Job Clusters: It cannot be attached to interactively: it exists only for the duration of the run, so there is no REPL to poke at, no cache to reuse between runs, and no way to re-enter the environment after the run ends. Each run is therefore a fresh start, the compute analogue of a truncate-and-reload pattern that builds a brand-new version instead of mutating a long-lived object [source p.342].

DBU cost and what drives the bill
All-Purpose Clusters: Databricks bills it at the higher All-Purpose Compute DBU rate, and because the cluster keeps Running between tasks, cost is driven by wall-clock uptime rather than by work performed; the cloud VM charges for the instances accrue in parallel for every idle minute.
Job Clusters: Databricks bills it at the lower Jobs Compute DBU rate, and because the cluster exists only while the run executes, cost is driven by actual run duration; the markdown is commonly around two to three times cheaper per DBU on list pricing, which is why production pipelines are expected to move off all-purpose compute.

Autoscaling support and sizing behaviour
All-Purpose Clusters: Autoscaling is supported, but it is coarse in practice because the minimum worker count stays provisioned whenever the cluster is Running; a cluster left on between meetings pays for workers doing nothing, and scaling decisions are made against an unknown, open-ended workload.
Job Clusters: Autoscaling is supported and far more effective because the scheduler knows the workload is finite: the cluster can scale up mid-run to absorb a shuffle-heavy stage and the entire allocation disappears at the end of the run, so workers provisioned map closely to work actually performed.

Primary use case and the interactive-versus-scheduled test
All-Purpose Clusters: Interactive development and exploration: developing and debugging notebooks, ad hoc analysis, exploratory SQL, collaborative debugging sessions, dashboard refreshes, and any workload where a human is waiting for a result and will iterate on it.
Job Clusters: Scheduled, automated production pipelines: recurring ingestion, transformation, and orchestration tasks launched by Workflows/Jobs on a trigger or schedule, where no human interacts with the compute and each invocation is expected to be repeatable and isolated.

Exam trap: can it run a job?
All-Purpose Clusters: Yes. A job or notebook task can be configured to run on an existing all-purpose cluster when you select an existing cluster instead of a job cluster, so the word 'job' in a question does not by itself imply a job cluster; the deciding signal is whether the work is interactive or scheduled, and whether the cluster should outlive the run.
Job Clusters: It is the default and recommended compute target for scheduled Workflows/Jobs, but it cannot be reused after the run ends, cannot be attached to a notebook, and cannot be shared with another job; it is created for one run and destroyed at the end of that run.

Cold start, warm start, and per-run overhead
All-Purpose Clusters: Warm start: libraries installed with %pip, cached tables, and the running Spark session persist between work sessions, so a developer pays cluster start-up once and reuses it for hours of iteration.
Job Clusters: Cold start on every run: cluster provisioning, library installation, and Spark session warm-up typically add several minutes before the first task executes, so a pipeline with a tight completion window must budget that overhead on every single invocation. Splitting one pipeline into 24 small runs a day makes start-up dominate and is the same anti-pattern as many small batch operations in batch-oriented systems [source p.273].

Worked cost example (illustrative list prices)
All-Purpose Clusters: Take a 6-DBU/hour cluster (1 driver plus 4 workers) billed at $0.55 per DBU on All-Purpose Compute: that is $3.30 per cluster-hour. Keeping it Running 8 hours a day for 22 working days costs 176 hours x $3.30 = $580.80 of DBUs for the month, and every idle minute between tasks is billed at the same rate.
Job Clusters: The identical 6-DBU/hour cluster on Jobs Compute at $0.15 per DBU costs $0.90 per cluster-hour; if the pipeline run takes 1 hour including a 5-minute cluster start, 22 runs cost 22 x $0.90 = $19.80 of DBUs for the month. The same work therefore costs roughly 29 times more in DBUs on an always-on all-purpose cluster, before any cloud VM charges are counted.

Takeaway — Use an all-purpose cluster when a human is in the loop: developing notebooks, exploring data, debugging, or iterating on transformations where warm caches and an attachable Spark session pay for themselves.

Takeaway — Use a job cluster for every scheduled, automated, or production pipeline run, because it is isolated to one run, billed at the lower Jobs Compute rate, and terminates automatically so no idle compute leaks cost.

Takeaway — Remember that an all-purpose cluster can also execute a job, so the exam keyword 'job' is not sufficient evidence; ask whether the workload is interactive or scheduled and whether the compute should outlive the run.

Takeaway — Treat auto-stop on an all-purpose cluster as a safety net, not a costing strategy, and size job clusters with autoscaling plus a realistic start-up allowance so that per-run overhead does not dominate short runs.

actions.text: Now let's turn to one of the highest-yield comparisons on the exam: all-purpose clusters versus job clusters. The exam constantly tests whether you can pick the right cluster category for a given workload, so we'll walk this table dimension by dimension.

This is a side-by-side comparison across the dimensions the exam cares about: who creates the cluster, who can use it, its lifecycle and termination, its relative DBU cost, autoscaling behaviour, and its primary use case. Let's start at the top.

First, who creates it. An all-purpose cluster is created manually through the UI or programmatically through the API, and it stays alive until someone stops it. A job cluster, by contrast, is created by the job scheduler for a single run and disappears when that run finishes — a human never types its configuration into the compute page.

Second, the sharing model. An all-purpose cluster is shared: multiple users can attach their notebooks to it simultaneously, subject to permissions. A job cluster is isolated to the single run that created it — nobody else attaches to it, and that isolation is a feature, not a limitation.

Third, lifecycle and termination. All-purpose clusters are stopped manually or by an auto-stop timer — that timer is a safety net, not a guarantee. Job clusters terminate automatically the moment the run completes, which is why they rarely leave idle compute burning DBUs.

Fourth, the DBU cost. All-purpose clusters carry a higher DBU rate because they support interactive, multi-user work. Job clusters are cheaper per DBU because they run a defined, isolated workload. That price difference is precisely why production pipelines should not run on all-purpose compute.

Fifth, the primary use case. All-purpose clusters exist for interactive development: notebooks, ad hoc exploration, and iterating on code. Job clusters exist for scheduled, automated production work: a pipeline that must run at 2 a.m. without a human watching. That interactive-versus-scheduled distinction is the heart of this whole page.

And here is the trap the slide calls out explicitly. An all-purpose cluster can also run a job. So if an exam question contains the word 'job', do not reflexively answer 'job cluster'. Ask yourself whether the work is interactive or scheduled — that determines the answer, not the word 'job' by itself.

Let's lock in the decision rule. Use an all-purpose cluster when a human is developing, exploring, or interactively working in notebooks. Use a job cluster for every scheduled, automated production pipeline — it's cheaper, it's isolated, and it cleans itself up when the run ends.

widgetConfig.description: Manipulate Databricks cluster configuration — worker node type, worker count, autoscaling min/max, runtime version, Photon acceleration and auto-stop timeout — and observe the resulting trade-offs between parallelism, wall-clock runtime and total cost.

actions.text: We just covered the vocabulary of cluster configuration on the checkpoint — now let's put real numbers on it. This simulator lets you size a cluster and watch three things move at once: parallel task capacity, wall-clock runtime, and total cost.

actions.content: Start here: worker count sets how many tasks can execute in parallel.

actions.text: Drag the worker slider up and down a few times before you change anything else. Watch how the task queue shrinks as the cluster grows, then notice that throughput eventually flattens out while the cost number keeps climbing. That flattening point is the signal that you have stopped buying speed and started buying idle capacity.

actions.content: Over-provisioned fixed cluster: 16 large workers, no autoscaling, one hour of idle billing.

actions.text: Look at the stats panel now. The queue is empty and the runtime is short — but check the total cost and the utilization figure. This is the over-provisioned fixed cluster, and it is exactly the pattern the exam describes as fast but wasteful. A large cluster is only 'best' if the workload can actually keep every worker busy.

actions.content: Right-sized alternative: autoscaling 1–4, Photon on, auto-stop set to five minutes.

actions.text: Same workload, very different profile: autoscaling lets the cluster shrink when demand drops, Photon accelerates throughput per hour, and the short auto-stop bounds how much idle time gets billed before the cluster terminates. So which configuration is correct? Neither — and that is the whole lesson. 'Best' always means best for a stated workload, not simply the largest. Give it a try with your own values, and remember this beats on the exam whenever a question hands you a constraint like a nightly SLA or a cost ceiling.
