scenes.title: Checkpoint: Choosing a Cluster Configuration for a Workload

questions.question: An analytics team runs a nightly batch transformation job. The job reads raw JSON files from cloud storage, joins and aggregates them, and writes the result as a Parquet-formatted Delta Lake table. A typical run takes about 40 minutes and must finish before the 06:00 reporting deadline. The job is only ever started by the scheduler at 01:00 — no analyst opens a notebook to develop or debug against it, and nobody queries the cluster interactively. Which cluster should you recommend?

options.label: A job cluster (job compute) that the scheduled run creates, uses for the transformation, and terminates automatically when the run finishes
An all-purpose cluster left running 24 hours a day so the 01:00 run never waits for a cold start
A large SQL warehouse whose auto-stop is disabled, because SQL warehouses execute SQL and the job contains SQL statements
A multi-node all-purpose cluster with autoscaling from 8 to 32 workers, kept running so the team can also debug interactively at any hour

questions.analysis: The workload is scheduled, unattended, and bounded in duration, so job compute (a job cluster) is the correct category: it is created for the run and terminated when the run completes, meaning the team is billed only for the roughly 40 minutes of work. Option B is the classic cost trap — an all-purpose cluster is billed for its uptime, so a 24/7 cluster for a 40-minute nightly job pays for over 23 hours of idle capacity per day. Option C confuses product surfaces: a SQL warehouse exists for SQL analytics and BI workloads, not for arbitrary multi-step Spark transformations that join, aggregate, and write a Delta Lake table. Option D is exactly the trap this checkpoint warns about: it picks the largest configuration and an always-on all-purpose cluster while ignoring the schedule and the cost constraint, and the 'debugging' justification is speculative because the stem states the job is never developed against interactively. Note also a batch-design principle that supports keeping the job as a single scheduled run rather than many small ones: batch-oriented systems perform poorly when users perform many small operations instead of a smaller number of large ones, forcing many small, suboptimal files and a high number of object-creation operations [source p.273]. A nightly, consolidated transformation is the pattern that avoids this.

questions.question: A single data analyst must explore a 2 GB CSV extract inside a Databricks notebook: profile the columns, compute a handful of aggregations, and render a small pandas-based chart on the collected result. There is no concurrency requirement, no second user, and the data fits comfortably in the memory and local disk of one machine. Which cluster configuration is most appropriate?

options.label: A single-node cluster (driver only) sized with enough memory and local disk to hold the 2 GB extract and its intermediate copies
A multi-node cluster with 8 workers, because Spark cannot execute transformations unless executor nodes are present
A multi-node cluster with 2 workers and autoscaling up to 16, so the configuration is ready when the extract eventually becomes a production table
A dedicated multi-tenant SQL warehouse with a large cluster size, so the analyst's resources are isolated from other users

questions.analysis: With a 2 GB dataset, one user, and a single-machine visualization step, a single-node (driver-only) cluster is the right size: Spark runs in local mode on the driver, no shuffle traffic crosses the network, and there are no idle executors to pay for. Option B reflects a real misconception — that a driver-only cluster cannot run Spark — but the driver hosts the Spark session and can execute jobs locally; workers add startup time, shuffle over the network, and DBU cost without improving a workload that already fits on one machine [source p.346]. Option C over-provisions for a hypothetical future ('ready when it becomes production'), which is the largest-configuration trap: the requirement is for today's 2 GB extract, and a cluster's size can be changed later in seconds. Option D misidentifies the product: a SQL warehouse serves SQL analytics, not notebook-based Python/pandas exploration, and 'multi-tenant' describes a shared-resource architecture in which resources such as networking, compute, and storage are shared among groups of users rather than dedicated to one [source p.252]. The governing principle is to size against your anticipated real-world data and query volume and evaluate performance and resource cost from a detailed evaluation of your own needs, not from a peak that has not arrived [source p.174].

questions.question: A team runs a scheduled Databricks job that ingests data from several partner APIs and transforms it into a Delta Lake table. Daily volume is genuinely unpredictable: it ranges from about 5 GB to 400 GB, some partners send nothing on a given day, and occasional backfills arrive with no warning. The team wants to avoid paying for capacity it is not using while still meeting the SLA on heavy days. Which TWO configurations should you recommend? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Enable autoscaling with a low minimum and a high maximum worker count, so the cluster acquires executors on heavy days and releases them when the load drops
Set a fixed worker count equal to the historical peak volume and keep the cluster running continuously, so the SLA is never at risk
Set a fixed worker count sized for the average daily volume, because autoscaling resizes only the driver node, not the workers
Pair autoscaling with an auto-stop (idle termination) timeout and use job compute for the scheduled run, so no cluster is billed between runs

questions.analysis: The defining property of this workload is variance, not size, so the fix is elasticity plus idle protection. Option A is correct: autoscaling adjusts the number of worker (executor) nodes between a configured minimum and maximum as demand changes, which is precisely the control that matches volume that swings from 5 GB to 400 GB. Option D is correct and complements A: autoscaling shrinks a cluster toward its minimum, but the minimum is still a running cluster, so an auto-stop timeout terminates the cluster entirely after a period of inactivity, and job compute means the cluster exists only for the scheduled run. Options B and C are the two distractors this checkpoint is designed to catch. Option B ignores the cost constraint: a fixed cluster sized for the historical peak is idle most days, and because volume is unpredictable the peak will eventually be exceeded anyway, so the 'no risk' claim is false. Option C states a false mechanism — autoscaling scales executors, not the driver — and sizing for the average guarantees SLA misses every time volume spikes. The broader trade-off is the one you must reason about explicitly: whether a given ingestion strategy costs more in time, money, maintenance, downtime, and opportunity cost than the simpler alternative [source p.67], and whether you have simulated the anticipated real-world data and query size rather than benchmarking against a comfortable sample [source p.174]. For a transformation that aggregates large daily volumes, prefer a design that performs a smaller number of large operations over many small ones, since many small writes create suboptimal files and force a high number of object-creation operations [source p.273].

actions.text: Time to check what stuck. Three scenario questions ahead — read each stem carefully, because the constraint in the wording is doing the real work, and pick the configuration you would actually recommend. Work through them on your own first.
Give every option a fair look before you commit — one of them will sound reassuringly oversized. Submit when you're done, and we'll walk through the reasoning together right after.

scenes.title: Decision Under Constraints: Right-Sizing a Nightly ETL Cluster

elements.content: Decision — A four-engineer data platform team runs a Databricks lakehouse whose nightly transformation reads roughly 500 GB of Parquet from bronze Delta Lake tables, deduplicates and applies slowly changing dimension logic (keeping a history of how a dimension row changed over time rather than overwriting it), joins the result to a curated silver dimension, and MERGEs about 120 GB into a gold table that the BI tool reads at 07:00. The decision is hard because four constraints bind at the same time and pull in opposite directions: the run must publish before 06:00, the monthly compute budget is fixed in DBUs and cannot be raised mid-quarter, the pipeline must survive spot-instance reclamation without producing partial or duplicated gold data, and the same four engineers need interactive notebook compute during the working day for exploration and incident debugging. A scheduling detail tightens the window further: the upstream CDC landing event fires at 02:30 in the p95 case, and the downstream BI contract consumes 30 minutes, so the transformation itself effectively has about three hours rather than the whole night. Availability is not free, because an always-on cluster bills every hour of the month whether or not data has arrived, so the team is really choosing between paying for idle headroom, paying for elasticity, and paying with runtime risk. The data being processed is warm data (touched nightly but not continuously), while an always-on all-purpose cluster keeps premium interactive compute in memory around the clock, which is closer to the hot-data cost profile than to the warm-data profile the workload actually has [source p.250]. Any acceptable option must also run a current LTS Databricks Runtime with Delta Lake and Unity Catalog, because the gold table's governance and time-travel guarantees are already established in this unit, and the job cluster should sit inside a single availability zone, where network traffic between nodes is free and latency is lowest for high-throughput shuffles [source p.426].

Constraints — The 500 GB nightly transformation must publish to gold before 06:00; with the p95 02:30 upstream CDC arrival and a 30-minute downstream BI contract, the effective transformation window is about three hours, not a full night.  •  Monthly compute spend is fixed in DBUs and cannot be increased mid-quarter, so idle capacity is as much a constraint violation as a missed deadline.  •  The pipeline must remain correct under spot-instance reclamation: a reclaimed worker must not leave partial or duplicated rows in the gold table.  •  Interactive notebook compute must stay available to four data engineers during the working day.  •  Every option must run a current LTS Databricks Runtime with Delta Lake and Unity Catalog governance for the gold table, and must keep the job cluster inside one availability zone to avoid cross-zone egress charges and added latency [source p.426].

Large fixed multi-node all-purpose cluster
+ Cells and jobs execute with no cluster start-up latency, so a late-arriving upstream file never waits for capacity to be provisioned.; + The same cluster doubles as the daytime interactive environment, which removes a second development cluster from the budget.; + Because no worker is ever reclaimed, the job needs no spot-retry logic and no special idempotent-write design.
− All-purpose compute carries the highest DBU rate, and the cluster bills every hour of the month: 8 nodes x 16 vCPU = 128 vCPU held for 720 hours is 92,160 vCPU-hours even on nights the pipeline finishes in 20 minutes.; − Capacity does not track volume, so the bill is a function of nodes deployed rather than data scanned, and a shrinking nightly file count produces no saving.; − It holds premium interactive compute idle all day for warm data that is only touched once at night, which is the wrong cost tier for this access frequency [source p.250].
Best for: A workload whose arrival time is unpredictable, whose SLA is measured in minutes, and where an engineer is often debugging interactively in the same environment while the job runs.

Autoscaling job cluster on a current LTS runtime with spot workers and Photon
+ Job-compute DBU rates are roughly one-third of all-purpose rates and the cluster exists only for the run, so idle hours drop to zero.; + Autoscaling matches capacity to the scan: map-side work is nearly perfect parallel work, and scan rate across the cluster scales close to linearly with the number of nodes [source p.348].; + Each run gets an isolated cluster, so the gold MERGE is never perturbed by an engineer running an ad-hoc notebook against the same JVM.; + Photon compresses the CPU-bound Parquet decode and aggregation stages, which is exactly where the three-hour window is won or lost.
− Spot reclamation can kill a worker mid-shuffle, so the job requires a retry policy and an idempotent Delta MERGE; without them a re-run can duplicate gold rows.; − Cluster start-up and spot acquisition add roughly 3 to 6 minutes to every run, which is real budget inside a three-hour window.; − Autoscaling reacts after a stage is already running, so the first stage runs at the minimum node count while the tail of the last stage pays for nodes that are idle.
Best for: Scheduled, volume-varying production pipelines with a hard runtime window and a fixed budget whose writes can be written idempotently.

Single-node cluster
+ One node is the cheapest possible configuration and pays no shuffle network cost, because all data stays in local memory and on local SSD.; + The operational story is trivial: no autoscaling policy, no spot retries, no executor failures, and no driver-to-executor sizing to reason about.; + For transformations over small reference data it is genuinely the correct answer and it still satisfies the LTS runtime and Unity Catalog requirement.
− Parallelism is capped by the cores in that one node and by a single JVM heap, so roughly 3.2 TB of stage I/O at an effective 200 MB/s is about 16,000 seconds, or 4.4 hours, before ramp-up and retries.; − The shuffle for the aggregate spills to a single local disk, and the scan stage cannot overlap the reduce stage the way a distributed map, shuffle, and reduce plan does when keys are redistributed by hash [source p.348].; − It is a single point of failure: one node loss or one out-of-memory during a large aggregation destroys the whole run with no executor to absorb the work.; − Writing output from a single node in many small operations creates many small files, which is the batch-size anti-pattern that forces high per-object creation overhead [source p.273].
Best for: Development, unit testing, and production jobs over datasets that fit comfortably in one node's memory and complete in minutes.

Recommendation: Autoscaling job cluster on a current LTS runtime with spot workers and Photon — The binding constraints are the roughly three-hour window and the fixed DBU budget, not raw speed, and only Option B satisfies both at once. Worked cost comparison: Option A holds 128 vCPU for 720 hours, which is 92,160 vCPU-hours per month; at an illustrative 0.40 DBU per vCPU-hour that is about 36,864 DBU. Option B averaging 12 workers of 16 vCPU for 2.5 hours across 30 nights is 12 x 16 x 75 = 14,400 vCPU-hours; at 0.15 DBU per vCPU-hour that is about 2,160 DBU, roughly 17 times cheaper, and even a pessimistic case of 20 workers x 16 vCPU x 3 hours x 30 nights = 28,800 vCPU-hours is about 4,320 DBU, still roughly 8.5 times under Option A. Worked runtime comparison: because scan throughput scales nearly linearly with node count [source p.348], 12 workers clear the project's approximately 3.2 TB of stage I/O in the order of 20 minutes plus shuffle barriers, whereas a single 16-core node at an effective 200 MB/s needs 3,200 GB divided by 0.2 GB/s, about 16,000 seconds or 4.4 hours, and misses the window; Option C is therefore eliminated by the deadline rather than by price. Option A meets the deadline but fails the budget constraint by paying a hot-data cost profile for a warm-data workload that is idle most of the day [source p.250]. Option B wins only if two preconditions hold, and both are engineering tasks the team controls: the gold write must be an idempotent Delta MERGE keyed on the business key plus a run identifier so a spot reclamation can be retried without duplicating rows, and the job cluster must be pinned to one availability zone, where intra-zone traffic is free and latency is lowest for the shuffle [source p.426]. Keep an all-purpose cluster running for the daytime interactive notebook work, which is the second half of the decision: scheduled work belongs on job compute, humans belong on all-purpose compute, and the cluster choice is justified with the schedule, size, latency target, and budget, never with the fact that it is the biggest.

actions.text: Now let's put that cluster-choice reasoning to work. Instead of just naming the options, we're going to walk through a real decision under constraints — the kind of scenario the exam loves to build around.

Here's the setup: a four-engineer data platform team runs a nightly pipeline from a 500 GB raw landing zone into a curated Delta table. Read the decision statement carefully — the team, the volume, and the goal are all fixed inputs. Everything else you choose has to answer to these facts, not to your personal preference for a particular cluster type.

These are the constraints, and they are the whole game. The 500 GB nightly transformation must finish before 06:00. The monthly compute budget is fixed. The pipeline must survive spot instance interruption. And the team still needs interactive notebooks during the day. Notice how each constraint rules something out — a schedule limits runtime, a budget limits how much idle hardware you can afford, and spot interruption demands a retry policy.

Option A is the big fixed multi-node all-purpose cluster. It satisfies the runtime window — it's fast, and it's always available. But it bills at the highest DBU rate, and when the pipeline finishes early, those nodes sit idle, burning the fixed budget you can't grow. Convenient, yes. Cheap, no.

Option B is an autoscaling job cluster on a current LTS runtime with spot workers and Photon enabled. This gives you the lowest cost per DBU, scales with the actual data volume, and is isolated per run — the cluster spins up for the job and terminates when it ends. The one catch is spot reclamation, so you need a retry policy to re-run interrupted tasks. Keep that in mind; it's the trade-off this option buys.

Option C is a single-node cluster. It's the cheapest and simplest configuration, and for small data it's genuinely great. But one node cannot parallelize a 500 GB transformation inside the before-06:00 window. Cheapest per hour, and still the wrong answer — cost alone never decides a cluster choice.

So the recommendation lands on Option B. The reasoning is the important part: the workload is scheduled, so job-cluster pricing applies; the volume varies, so autoscaling fits; and that combination meets the runtime window while respecting the budget. Meanwhile, keep the all-purpose cluster for daytime interactive work, where engineers are actually exploring in notebooks. And here is your exam takeaway — justify a cluster choice with the stated constraint, whether that's schedule, size, latency target, or budget. Never justify it with 'it is the biggest.'

actions.topic: Could Option A ever be the right call here — and what constraint would have to change for that to be true?
actions.prompt: Argue both sides. What would the runtime window, budget, or interruption requirement have to look like for a large fixed all-purpose cluster to beat the autoscaling job cluster?

scenes.title: Key Takeaways and Exam Checklist

elements.content: Key Takeaways and Exam Checklist
No attached compute means no execution: a detached notebook runs nothing.
One Spark session: a Python temp view is readable from SQL [source p.47].
Spark builds a DAG from your code; the driver plans the run [source p.346].
Choose category first: all-purpose for interactive work, job clusters for runs.
Then size the cluster: node type, workers, autoscaling, Photon, auto-stop.
Shuffle sends each key to one node; scans scale with nodes [source p.348].
Worked example: 2 idle workers × 30 min = 60 wasted node-minutes; auto-stop caps it.
Exam: map each question to a sidebar service. Next: Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog.

actions.text: Let's pull this whole lesson together into a quick recall checklist. Nothing new here — just the points you should be able to state from memory, because these are exactly the ideas the exam builds its questions around.

First, the core daily workflow. In the workspace you find or create a notebook, attach it to compute, and then run cells. The critical rule: with no attached compute there is no execution. A detached notebook is just text sitting still — nothing runs until it is bound to a cluster.

Second, one Spark session per notebook. That single session is why a temporary view written in a Python cell is immediately readable from a SQL cell — the session is shared. Magic commands like percent-python or percent-sql only switch the language for that one cell; they do not start a new session or wipe your temporary views.

Third, the cluster decision has an order. Choose the category first — all-purpose for interactive, exploratory work, job clusters for scheduled, automated runs. Only then do you size it: node type, number of workers, autoscaling, Photon, and auto-stop. Category answers the 'what for', sizing answers the 'how much'.

Keep that worked example in mind: two idle workers sitting for thirty minutes is sixty minutes of pure waste. Auto-stop and right-sizing are not cosmetic details — they are the difference between a healthy bill and an avoidable one. And remember that shuffle sends each key to one node, so scans scale with data size while shuffles scale with data movement.

Finally, the exam strategy. When a question asks 'where would the engineer go', map it to a sidebar service; when it asks you to choose a cluster, justify the choice with the workload's constraint. That is the pattern this whole lesson has been training. Next we move into Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog navigation, where these exact workspace and compute skills get applied to querying governed data.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Entering the Databricks SQL Workspace

questions.question: You are using Databricks SQL for the first time and need to locate the three SQL surfaces in the workspace. Which set of sidebar entries gives you direct access to the SQL warehouse list, the query editor, and the data catalog that Databricks SQL depends on?

options.label: Workspace, Compute, and Jobs & Pipelines — these three entries open the SQL editor and the warehouse list.
SQL Warehouses, SQL Editor, and Catalog Explorer — these are the dedicated SQL surfaces for compute, authoring, and metadata.
Compute, Marketplace, and Dashboards — the SQL Editor is a tab inside the Compute page.
Workspace, Catalog, and Repos — SQL queries are stored as notebooks, so the Workspace entry is the SQL editor.

questions.analysis: The Databricks SQL experience is exposed through its own sidebar entries: SQL Warehouses (the compute you attach to), SQL Editor (where you author and run queries), and Catalog Explorer (the metadata surface for catalogs, schemas, tables, and views). That is why option B is correct. Option A describes the notebook-oriented surfaces covered earlier in this unit — Workspace, Compute, and Jobs & Pipelines — which remain valid for notebook work but do not open the SQL warehouse list or the standalone SQL Editor. Option C is a common misconception: the Compute page manages all-purpose and job clusters, not SQL warehouses, and Marketplace and Dashboards are unrelated surfaces. Option D repeats the trap of treating the SQL Editor as just another notebook editor; although you can run SQL in notebook cells, the SQL Editor is a separate product surface, and Repos is a Git integration feature, not an editor. Note also that the catalog view surfaces the tables a warehouse queries, consistent with the wider analytics pattern in which a serving layer reads from governed, curated data rather than from source systems directly [source p.322].

questions.question: A teammate says: "I'll open the SQL Editor in my browser, pick my all-purpose cluster, and let the query run inside the browser tab." Which statement correctly describes what actually happens when the query executes?

options.label: The SQL Editor compiles the SQL to JavaScript and evaluates it in the browser, so no server-side compute is involved.

The SQL Editor sends the statement to a SQL warehouse (or, for a notebook cell, to the cluster attached to that notebook); execution happens on server-side compute and only the result set is rendered in the browser.
The SQL Editor always executes on the all-purpose cluster selected in the Compute page, and a SQL warehouse is used only when reading notebook temporary views.
A SQL warehouse is a storage layer, so the SQL Editor reads table files directly from cloud object storage without starting any compute.

questions.analysis: Option B is correct. The browser is only a thin client: the SQL Editor is an authoring and results surface, and the statement is actually planned and executed by a SQL warehouse (a server-side compute resource) or, inside a notebook, by the cluster attached to that notebook. Option A is wrong because SQL is not evaluated client-side; option C swaps the roles of warehouse and cluster, which is precisely the exam trap that confuses a SQL warehouse with a cluster. Option D mixes up compute and storage: modern cloud analytics deliberately separates the two so that data lives in cheap, effectively unlimited object storage while compute is spun up on demand and released when the workload ends [source p.126]. That separation does not mean the editor reads files itself — a query engine still has to scan and aggregate the data on compute nodes, and the classic reason analytics engines distribute that work across many machines is to scan massive volumes in parallel and keep the scan as close to the data as possible [source p.246]. Some engines go further and push the read into external storage without ingesting the data first, defining an external table on an object-store location and processing the files at query time, or issuing a federated query that combines object storage with tables from MySQL and PostgreSQL [source p.351]. In every one of those cases, an execution engine — not the browser — performs the work.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about SQL warehouses and all-purpose clusters in Databricks are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A SQL warehouse is a compute resource tuned for SQL analytics; it executes queries against tables and views but does not store those tables itself.
An all-purpose cluster must be running before you can open the SQL Editor at all.
A SQL warehouse can be started, resized, and stopped independently of the all-purpose cluster a data engineer uses for exploratory notebook work.
Stopping a SQL warehouse deletes the tables in Unity Catalog that the warehouse was querying, because the warehouse holds the data.

questions.analysis: Options A and C are correct. A SQL warehouse is compute, not storage: it provides the engines that parse, plan, and execute SQL, and its size determines throughput and concurrency. Because Databricks separates compute from storage, the warehouse and the notebook cluster have independent lifecycles — you can stop a warehouse to save cost while a cluster keeps running, and vice versa [source p.126]. Option B is the classic trap: the SQL Editor is a UI surface, and warehouse-backed queries never require an all-purpose cluster, which is why the two appear under different sidebar entries. Option D inverts the compute/storage relationship; dropping or stopping compute cannot delete catalog metadata, because the tables in Unity Catalog are governed objects registered over stored data, not objects that live inside the warehouse process. This separation is exactly what lets engines scale out cheaply: massively parallel systems were designed to scan enormous data volumes in parallel and return high-performance aggregations, and cloud architectures advanced this by putting data in object storage and scaling compute on demand [source p.125] [source p.126]. It is also why data can remain in an Inmon-style highly normalized warehouse acting as the single source of truth while downstream data marts and serving layers are rebuilt on fresh compute without duplicating the storage [source p.322]. A useful mental check for the exam: if the statement is about where bytes live, it is about storage (Unity Catalog, object storage, Delta Lake); if it is about CPU, memory, and query throughput, it is about compute (SQL warehouse or cluster).

actions.text: Before we go further into the Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog material, let's pause and check how much of that groundwork has settled. There are three questions ahead — take them one at a time, on your own.

Don't worry about getting everything right on the first pass; just answer honestly and commit to a choice for each one. Once you've submitted, I'll come back and we'll walk through the reasoning behind each question together.

scenes.title: The SQL Editor and the Query Lifecycle

elements.content: The SQL Editor and the Query Lifecycle
The editor is only a client: it submits SQL but computes nothing.
Every statement executes on a SQL warehouse, not in the editor.
Unity Catalog resolves table names and checks grants before any file is read, so a query sees one committed snapshot [source p.305].
Worked example: rerunning one 30-minute query 20 times a day burns 10 warehouse-hours; saving the result once costs 0.5 hours — a 95% cut [source p.335].
A 40-second cold query repeats in about 1 second from cache [source p.307].
Every hop can fail: a stopped warehouse, a missing GRANT, or a deleted Delta file.
1 · SQL editor
2 · SQL warehouse
3 · Unity Catalog
4 · Delta tables

actions.text: Now that we've stepped into the Databricks SQL workspace, let's trace exactly what happens between typing a query and seeing a result set. This is the SQL Editor and the Query Lifecycle — and understanding this path is what separates people who just click Run from people who can diagnose a failure.

First, a mental model that trips up a lot of candidates: the editor is only a client. It's a browser-based surface for writing, running, saving, and scheduling queries against Unity Catalog objects — but it does no heavy lifting itself. When you press Run, the editor simply submits your SQL and waits for results.

So where does the work actually happen? Every statement executes on a SQL warehouse, which is the compute. The editor never runs the query — the warehouse does. If the warehouse is stopped, nothing runs, no matter how perfect your SQL is.

Next, Unity Catalog resolves the table names and checks your grants before any data is touched. This is the governance gate. If you reference a table you don't have permission to read, the query fails here — long before it ever reaches storage.

So let's walk the four hops together: one, the SQL editor submits the statement. Two, the SQL warehouse provides the compute. Three, Unity Catalog resolves names and enforces permissions. And four, the query finally lands on the Delta tables in cloud storage, where the actual data lives.

Here's a worked example that makes the warehouse's role concrete. Imagine rerunning one 30-minute query twenty times. On a cold warehouse, every execution pays the full startup price. But once that warehouse is warm and the data is cached, the same query can come back in roughly a second.

Read that number again — a 40-second cold query repeats in about 1 second from cache. Same SQL, same result, dramatically different runtime. That gap is why SQL warehouses have warm-up behavior, and why 'just rerun it' is rarely the whole story on an exam question.

Finally, and this is the key takeaway: every hop in that chain can fail. A stopped warehouse, a missing grant in Unity Catalog, a deleted Delta table, or a malformed statement. When a query errors, your job is to ask which hop broke — compute, governance, or storage — and that single question usually narrows it down fast.

scenes.title: SQL Warehouses: Types, Sizing, and Scaling

elements.content: SQL Warehouses: Types & Scaling
Types. Serverless starts in seconds; Pro and Classic share a compute pool. [source p.351]
Sizes. Sizes run 2X-Small to 4X-Large; many small files still stall scans. [source p.273]
Scaling. Autoscaling spans a configured minimum and maximum cluster count.
Worked example. 2X-Large, min 1 / max 4 clusters → 4× peak concurrency.
Exam trap. Auto-stop suspends compute but never deletes Delta data. [source p.305]
Photon. Vectorized execution speeds up supported SQL with no rewrite.

actions.text: Now that you can locate and run queries in the SQL Editor, let's talk about the engine that actually executes them. This page covers SQL Warehouses — their types, their sizes, and how they scale.

First, warehouse types. Serverless warehouses start in seconds and let Databricks manage the underlying compute for you. Pro and Classic warehouses take longer to start, and the trade-off shows up in resource isolation and pricing model. For most workloads, Serverless is the default recommendation because you pay only for what you use.

This table lines the three types up across four dimensions — startup time, isolation, cost model, and best-fit workload. Keep it in mind as a decision aid, because the exam frequently asks which warehouse type fits a given scenario.

Next, sizes. T-shirt sizes run from 2X-Small all the way up to 4X-Large, and the size sets the number and size of clusters behind the warehouse. Here's the trap worth memorizing: you size up to handle concurrency — more simultaneous users — not to make a single bad query finish faster.

Scaling is configured with a minimum and maximum number of clusters. Autoscaling spins clusters up as demand rises and back down when it falls. In the worked example, a 2X-Large warehouse with a minimum of one and a maximum of four clusters can serve up to four clusters' worth of concurrent queries before it starts queuing.

Then there's Photon — Databricks' vectorized execution engine. It accelerates supported SQL workloads with no query rewrites required. You simply enable it and supported operators run faster on the same query.

Finally, the classic exam trap: auto-stop shuts the warehouse down after a set number of idle minutes. It suspends compute — it never deletes data or loses anything stored in your Delta tables. Storage is governed separately, so an idle warehouse is not a data-loss event.

To recap: choose a type based on startup and isolation needs, size for concurrency rather than single-query speed, configure autoscaling with a sensible minimum and maximum, and treat auto-stop as your cost brake — remembering that it only suspends compute, never your Delta data.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: SQL Warehouses and Query Execution

questions.question: A platform team is creating a new Databricks SQL warehouse for an executive dashboard. The requirement is that an analyst who opens the dashboard gets results within a few seconds even if nobody has queried the warehouse for twelve hours, and the team does not want to provision, patch, or pay for idle compute instances in its own cloud account. Which warehouse type and rationale is correct?

options.label: Serverless SQL warehouse: Databricks runs the compute in its own account and starts it on demand in seconds, so there is no cluster for the team to size or keep warm and no idle instance hours charged to the team's cloud account.
Classic SQL warehouse: the team selects instance types and keeps one cluster running at all times, because Classic has the fastest cold start of the three warehouse types.
Pro SQL warehouse: it starts in seconds because its compute runs inside the Databricks account, and it is the only type that supports multi-cluster autoscaling.
Classic SQL warehouse with Photon enabled: Photon removes the startup delay entirely because the vectorized engine keeps query results cached across restarts.

questions.analysis: Serverless SQL warehouses are built on the separation of compute from storage that cloud data warehouses popularized: the data stays in object storage while compute is spun up on demand and released when it is no longer needed [source p.126]. That architecture is exactly what makes a seconds-level cold start possible without the team owning any instances. Classic warehouses run in the customer's own cloud account, so their cold start is measured in minutes (node provisioning plus cluster start) rather than seconds, which contradicts option B. Multi-cluster autoscaling is available across warehouse types, and Pro compute runs in the customer's account, so option C is wrong on both counts. Photon is a vectorized execution engine that accelerates the scans, joins, and aggregations of queries that are already running; it addresses throughput, not cluster warm-up, so option D misattributes the cause of the delay.

questions.question: A Databricks SQL warehouse is configured with a minimum of 1 cluster and a maximum of 4 clusters. At 09:00, six analyst dashboards all refresh at the same moment. Which statements about what happens next are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Because the demand exceeds the capacity of the clusters that are already running, the warehouse adds clusters toward the maximum of four, and any queries that still do not fit are queued until a cluster frees up.
Setting the maximum to four reserves four clusters that run continuously, so the very first dashboard refresh never has to wait for a cluster to start.

When the dashboards close and demand falls, clusters above the minimum are removed after a scale-down delay rather than instantly, and with a minimum of one, one cluster stays available until auto-stop eventually shuts the warehouse down.
Raising the maximum from four to eight gives each individual cluster more memory, so a single heavy query scans less data and returns faster.

questions.analysis: A minimum/maximum pair is a floor and a ceiling on the number of identical clusters, not a reservation and not a per-cluster memory control. When concurrent queries exceed what the running clusters can serve, the warehouse scales out by adding more clusters of the same T-shirt size, up to the maximum, and further queries queue; this scale-out pattern is the same idea as moving a workload from a single machine to a distributed execution engine when it outgrows one node [source p.384]. Option B is a common misconception: the maximum is a limit on how many clusters may run, not a promise that they are already running, so the first refresh can still wait for a cluster to start. Option C describes real behaviour: scale-down is deliberately delayed rather than instantaneous, and the minimum keeps at least one cluster warm, which is the same on-demand elasticity that cloud warehouses introduced when they replaced fixed, pre-provisioned MPP systems [source p.126]. Option D confuses two independent dials: changing the maximum changes how many clusters exist, while changing the T-shirt size is what changes the vCPUs, memory, and cache available to each cluster.

questions.question: An analyst team runs an interactive BI dashboard workload with roughly 45 concurrent users between 09:00 and 17:00 and almost no queries overnight. The team has to justify its warehouse sizing and its auto-stop setting to a budget owner. Which rationale is the most defensible?

options.label: Size the warehouse to the observed peak concurrency with a Medium or Large T-shirt size, enable multi-cluster autoscaling with a minimum of 1 and a maximum that covers the peak, and set a short auto-stop timeout: auto-stop shuts the compute down and stops DBU billing, but the Delta tables in Unity Catalog are untouched.
Size to the peak concurrency and disable auto-stop, because auto-stop deletes the underlying Delta tables once the idle timeout elapses, which would force a full data reload every morning.
Choose the smallest T-shirt size and let the query queue absorb the load, because autoscaling will automatically upgrade the warehouse to a larger T-shirt size when concurrency rises.

Pick the T-shirt size from the monthly compute budget rather than from query concurrency, because T-shirt size controls only how long the warehouse stays running and not how many concurrent queries a single cluster can serve.

questions.analysis: T-shirt size sets the vCPUs, memory, and local caching of each cluster, so it determines how many concurrent queries one cluster can serve well; the minimum and maximum cluster counts then decide how far the warehouse scales out under peak concurrency. Sizing to the peak and letting autoscaling add and remove clusters is the elasticity that cloud warehouses introduced when they moved from fixed, multi-year MPP contracts to on-demand clusters that could be spun up for a workload and deleted afterwards [source p.126]. Auto-stop acts on compute only: it stops the clusters, which ends DBU billing, and it clears in-memory caches and session-scoped temporary objects, but the tables stored in Delta Lake on cloud object storage are unaffected because storage is a separate layer [source p.126]. Option B states the classic misconception that stopping compute destroys data; the data simply stays cold until the next query. Option C inverts how scaling works, since autoscaling changes the number of clusters, never the size of a cluster. Option D ignores what a T-shirt size actually controls. Spending on an always-warm warehouse overnight is also hard to justify against access patterns: data that is retrieved many times per day is hot and deserves fast compute, while data queried rarely behaves like cold data and does not need paid-for compute sitting idle beside it [source p.50].

actions.text: Time to check how those SQL warehouse ideas landed. Work through the four questions on your own — read each scenario carefully and pick the option you can actually justify, not just the one that sounds familiar.
Once you submit, I'll come back and we'll go through the reasoning together, including any traps you hit. Go ahead and give it your best shot.

scenes.title: Interactive: Tracing and Breaking the Query Path

content.html:
Tracing & Breaking the Query Path

Follow one SQL statement from the editor to Delta storage — then break it at each hop and predict the exact error Databricks returns.

Step 1 / 8

Query path control

Warehouse type · startup step

Inject a fault

Node detail

detail.role: Step 1 — the client holds the session and sends the statement
points: Submits your SQL to a SQL warehouse or all-purpose cluster over the Databricks SQL / REST protocol, and holds the session.
Renders result rows and error messages, but never opens a Delta file itself.
The only thing it knows about compute is the warehouse you selected.
detail.exam: Choose the wrong warehouse and the query dies right here: Unity Catalog is never consulted, no table is resolved, and no table-level audit entry is written.

detail.role: Step 2 — the warehouse plans and executes the query
points: Parses and plans the statement with the Catalyst optimizer, then executes it; Photon is the vectorized engine that accelerates the scan.
Schedules tasks, caches results, spills to disk, and streams rows back to the client.
Unity Catalog and storage errors are raised while this warehouse serves the query — so they are reported here even when the cause sits elsewhere.
detail.exam: Know the cold-start order of the startup step: Serverless starts in seconds, Pro in a few minutes, Classic is the slowest legacy type. A cold warehouse adds that delay before the first byte is returned.

detail.role: Step 3 — governance layer: name resolution, authorization, credential vending
points: Resolves the three-level namespace catalog.schema.table and confirms the object exists.
Authorizes the statement: USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT must all be granted to the principal.
Enforces fine-grained controls — row filters and column masks — and vends short-lived credentials for external locations.
Records lineage and audit logs for every access.
detail.exam: Unity Catalog is evaluated during query analysis, before a single file is opened. A denied query scans zero bytes — that is how you prove to an auditor that no data was read.

detail.role: Step 4 — storage layer: the Delta table on cloud object storage
points: A Delta table is a folder of Parquet data files plus the _delta_log: JSON commits and periodic checkpoints.
Compute reads the log to pin the snapshot, prunes files using min/max statistics (data skipping), then reads the surviving Parquet files.
The medallion architecture (bronze → silver → gold — raw, cleaned, business-ready layers) is just Delta tables living here.
detail.exam: Never mutate Delta files with cloud storage tools. Out-of-band deletes make the transaction log disagree with the folder and surface later as storage-level errors.

detail.role: Fault 1 — injected at the client → compute handshake
detail.inject: Point the notebook or BI tool at a warehouse that does not exist, that you have no CAN_USE on, or one you just created that is still starting.
detail.code:
PERMISSION_DENIED: User does not have CAN_USE on SqlWarehouse <warehouse-id>

— or —

INVALID_PARAMETER_VALUE: SqlWarehouse '<warehouse-id>' does not exist / is stopped
detail.surfaces: In the editor / client, at connect time. No query plan is built, Unity Catalog is never consulted, and no table-level audit entry appears.
detail.fix: Pick the correct warehouse in the editor's compute selector, GRANT CAN_USE (or ALL PRIVILEGES) on the warehouse, and warm a cold warehouse — or switch to Serverless for a sub-minute start.
detail.exam: Wrong-warehouse failures never reach the governance layer. The diagnostic clue is the missing Unity Catalog audit row for the query.

detail.role: Fault 2 — injected at the governance layer
detail.inject: REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE main.sales.orders FROM `analysts`;  — or leave out USE SCHEMA on the parent schema.
detail.code: PERMISSION_DENIED: User does not have SELECT on Table 'main.sales.orders'. SQLSTATE: 42501
detail.surfaces: Unity Catalog, during query analysis. The warehouse relays the message to the editor. Zero bytes scanned, no Parquet file opened.
detail.fix: GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG main; GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA main.sales; GRANT SELECT ON TABLE main.sales.orders; — all three levels are required.
detail.exam: SELECT alone is not enough: without USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA the statement still fails, even though the table grant exists.

detail.role: Fault 3 — injected at the governance layer (name resolution)
detail.inject: Reference an object that was renamed or dropped, or forget the session's current catalog / schema: SELECT * FROM main.default.orderz;
detail.code: TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND: The table or view `main.default.orderz` cannot be found. SQLSTATE: 42P01
detail.surfaces: Unity Catalog name resolution, reported in the editor by the warehouse. Nothing is read from storage.
detail.fix: Verify the three-level name: SHOW TABLES IN main.default, or query information_schema.tables. Check the current catalog and schema of the session.
detail.exam: A missing privilege and a missing table both fail at the governance layer — but the SQLSTATE differs: 42501 (permission) versus 42P01 (undefined object).

detail.role: Fault 4 — injected at the storage layer
detail.inject: Delete one Parquet file straight from the cloud bucket (bypassing Delta), or remove the storage credential's access to the external location.
detail.code:
FILE_NOT_FOUND: File s3://.../orders/part-00000-....snappy.parquet does not exist

— or —

DELTA_...: Failed to read the Delta transaction log / 403 Forbidden from cloud storage
detail.surfaces: The storage layer, while the warehouse opens the transaction log and reads Parquet. The message still appears in the editor, but the cause and the fix live in the storage account.
detail.fix: Restore the files (or use Delta time travel / RESTORE TABLE), run FSCK REPAIR TABLE for orphaned entries, and never write to a Delta path with non-Delta tooling.
detail.exam: Storage faults are the only ones that appear after a successful authorization: the query was allowed, but the bytes were not there.

actions.text: That checkpoint closed out SQL warehouses and how they execute a query. Now let's follow the full path a statement travels — and then break it on purpose at each node, so you can predict where the error surfaces and why. Work through the diagram with me, then drive it yourself.

actions.content: Step 1 — Client / SQL Editor: holds the session, sends the SQL, renders rows and errors.

actions.text: Start at the top: the client is your notebook, SQL editor, or BI tool. It knows exactly one thing about compute — which warehouse you selected — and it never opens a Delta file itself. The statement is then handed to the SQL warehouse, which parses and plans it with the Catalyst optimizer and executes it, with Photon vectorizing the scan.

actions.content: Step 3 — Unity Catalog: resolves the three-level name, authorizes, vends credentials, logs audit and lineage.

actions.text: Before any file is touched, governance runs. Unity Catalog resolves catalog dot schema dot table, checks USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT, applies row filters and column masks, and vends short-lived credentials. That ordering is the exam point: a denied query scans zero bytes, which is how you prove to an auditor that no data was read.

actions.content: Compare warehouse types: serverless starts in seconds, Pro in a few minutes, Classic is the slowest legacy type.

actions.text: Now toggle the warehouse type here. Serverless starts in seconds, Pro takes a few minutes, and Classic is the slowest legacy option — and remember that a cold start adds that delay before even the first byte comes back.

actions.content: Fault 1 — wrong or stopped warehouse: fails at connect time, no Unity Catalog audit row.
Fault 2 — REVOKE SELECT: SQLSTATE 42501, denied during analysis, zero bytes scanned.
Fault 4 — deleted Parquet file: FILE_NOT_FOUND, only storage fault that appears after authorization succeeds.

actions.text: Here is the pattern to carry into the exam. A wrong warehouse dies at the client, so there is no governance entry at all. A missing privilege and a missing table both fail at the governance layer, but the SQLSTATE separates them: 42501 is a permission problem, 42P01 is an undefined object. Storage faults are the only ones that show up after a successful authorization — the query was allowed, but the bytes were not there, so you repair with RESTORE or FSCK REPAIR TABLE. Step through each fault node now and predict the error before you read it, then ask yourself: which layer owns the fix?

scenes.title: Unity Catalog: The Three-Level Namespace

elements.content: Unity Catalog Namespace
1 metastore → 3 catalogs → 9 schemas → 27 tables.
• Every object name has three parts: catalog.schema.table.
• Fully qualified example: main.sales.orders [source p.331].
• Metastore owns identity and permissions [source p.322].
• Governs tables, views, volumes, functions [source p.351].
• Delta is the default format.
• Defaults: main catalog, default schema.
• USE CATALOG main; USE SCHEMA sales.

actions.title: 场景讲解
actions.text: Object names use three levels: catalog.schema.table, for example main.sales.orders。Above the catalog sits the metastore, which is attached to workspaces and owns the identity and permission model。Object types governed by Unity Catalog include tables, views, volumes, functions, models, and connections。Default names are the main catalog and the default schema; names can be fully qualified or set with USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA。Managed versus external tables, and Delta as the default table format。[Chart] Hierarchy diagram from metastore to catalog to schema to table with a highlighted fully qualified path。

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Unity Catalog Namespaces and Naming

questions.question: A notebook is attached to a cluster whose Unity Catalog session has the current catalog set to prod and the current schema set to sales. A colleague runs the statement SELECT * FROM orders in that same session. Which object does the statement actually read, and why?

options.label: It reads prod.sales.orders, because the session's current catalog and current schema are prepended to a one-part (unqualified) table name.
It fails, because Unity Catalog always requires the fully qualified three-part name catalog.schema.table for every read.
It reads main.default.orders, because one-part names always resolve against the workspace's built-in default catalog and default schema.
It reads hive_metastore.sales.orders, because unqualified names silently fall back to the legacy Hive metastore inside the workspace.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: Name resolution in Unity Catalog is positional and hierarchical: catalog.schema.object. When only one part is supplied, the session's current catalog and current schema are used as the missing prefixes, so orders becomes prod.sales.orders. The resolution happens during query compilation, before the optimizer produces its explain plan, which is why an incorrect default surfaces as a resolution error rather than a performance problem; understanding how the optimizer resolved the objects a query touches is part of reading an explain plan correctly [source p.303]. Option B is the over-correction trap: three-part names are always safe, but they are not always mandatory. Option C is wrong because main.default is only the metastore's fallback when no current schema has been selected (for example in a fresh SQL editor session or a job run with no USE SCHEMA), not a target that overrides an explicitly set current schema. Option D is wrong because hive_metastore is a distinct, explicitly named catalog in a Unity Catalog-enabled metastore; it is never an implicit fallback for a one-part name. Remember that the name resolves to a logical object whose data physically lives in cloud object storage, not to a file path, which is why the same table can be referenced identically from any workspace attached to the metastore [source p.233].

questions.question: Which of the following statements about one-part, two-part, and three-part object names in Unity Catalog are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: A one-part name such as orders resolves only when both the current catalog and the current schema of the session point at the object's real location.
A two-part name such as sales.orders is sufficient as long as the session's current catalog is set to the catalog that contains the sales schema.
A three-part name such as prod.sales.orders identifies the object independently of any session default, which makes it the safest form inside scheduled jobs and shared notebooks.
A two-part name such as sales.orders is always interpreted as catalog = main, schema = sales, so it resolves against the workspace default catalog rather than the session's current catalog.

correctAnswer: A
B
C
questions.analysis: The naming rule is that a statement must supply enough parts to be unambiguous given the session state. A one-part name requires both a current catalog and a current schema, because two prefixes have to come from somewhere; this is the same reason a query with an ambiguous column reference fails to compile. A two-part name schema.object requires only the current catalog, because the schema is stated explicitly and only the catalog prefix is missing. A three-part name catalog.schema.object supplies everything and therefore does not depend on session state at all, which is why it is the recommended form in production code where the session defaults of a job or another user are not under your control. Option D is the classic misconception: a two-part name is not anchored to main; main is merely the default catalog value when no current catalog has been chosen, and once a session sets a current catalog, the two-part name follows that catalog. When a query joins tables from several catalogs, as in the stream-enrichment pattern where events are enriched with reference data from another system, fully qualified names make the data lineage of each input obvious to the reader [source p.312]. The same discipline mirrors the readability argument for composing complex logic in named, readable units rather than relying on implicit context [source p.303].

questions.question: A data engineer works in Workspace A, where her interactive session default catalog is set to marketing, and she routinely runs INSERT INTO campaigns SELECT ... with campaigns resolving to marketing.ads.campaigns. She schedules the identical statement as a job that runs in Workspace B, and the run fails with TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: The job's session in Workspace B has a different current catalog, or no current schema at all, so the one-part name campaigns resolved against Workspace B's defaults instead of marketing.ads; the fix is to write the fully qualified name marketing.ads.campaigns.
Unity Catalog tables cannot be written to by job clusters, only by all-purpose clusters, so the INSERT is rejected regardless of how the table is named.
Job clusters are never attached to a Unity Catalog metastore, so marketing.ads.campaigns does not exist from the job's point of view and the table must be re-created in Workspace B.
Each workspace owns a private catalog namespace, so a table created in Workspace A can never be read or written from Workspace B under any name.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: This is the namespace-default trap: a one-part name carries no location, so it is resolved by whatever the executing session's current catalog and schema happen to be. The interactive session in Workspace A had marketing as its current catalog; the scheduled job in Workspace B does not inherit another user's interactive session state, so campaigns either resolves against a different catalog or fails outright. The durable fix is to make the statement self-describing with the three-part name marketing.ads.campaigns. Option B inverts the compute model taught earlier in this unit: job clusters are the recommended, cheaper compute for scheduled work and can read and write Unity Catalog tables subject to permissions. Option C confuses a catalog with a workspace; catalogs live in the metastore, and many workspaces can be attached to the same metastore, which is precisely why the storage layer is designed to be reachable from distributed compute across a network rather than pinned to one machine or one site [source p.221]. Option D overstates isolation: unless a catalog explicitly restricts access, a workspace attached to the same metastore sees the same catalog objects. Note also that once the name is fixed, a correctly targeted write still reads from the latest committed snapshot of the table, so other readers see a consistent picture of the data at a point in time [source p.305].

actions.text: Before we start querying across namespaces hands-on, let's put what we just covered to the test. This checkpoint has a few questions on how a statement's target object gets resolved and on one-part, two-part, and three-part names — so read each one carefully and think about how the session's defaults come into play.
Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer before you move on. Once you submit, I'll walk you through what each question was really probing and where the common traps hide.

scenes.title: Catalog Explorer: Browsing Metadata, Permissions, and Lineage

elements.content: Catalog Explorer Tour
• Navigate metastore → catalog → schema → table; search filters the tree.
• Details lists columns, types, and comments [source p.351].
• Overview gives location and owner; other tabs hold samples and grants.
• Grants cascade down to tables and show as inherited [source p.300].
• Lineage shows upstream sources and downstream writers [source p.278].
• Exam trap: without SELECT the name shows but sample data stays empty.
Worked example: GRANT SELECT ON CATALOG prod covers 3 schemas and 47 tables; REVOKE keeps 4 grants [source p.300].

actions.text: Now that we've nailed down the three-level namespace, let's see where you actually interact with it. Catalog Explorer is the graphical browser in the Databricks workspace that lets you tour Unity Catalog objects, inspect their metadata, read their grants, and trace their lineage — all without writing a single line of SQL.

Navigation follows the hierarchy you already know. You drill down from metastore, to catalog, to schema, to table, using the search box and filters to jump straight to what you need. At the table level, the simplest information you'll read is the column list — the column names, their data types, and any comments the author left behind. Comments matter more than learners expect; they often tell you the business meaning of a field that the name alone can't convey.

Once you open a table, you land on a set of detail tabs. The Overview tab gives you the physical location of the data — the cloud storage path — along with the owner of the object. The other tabs hold the richer signals: Sample Data lets you preview rows, Details shows the full schema, and Permissions and Lineage give you the governance picture. Think of Overview and Details as the 'what is this object' tabs, and Permissions and Lineage as the 'who can touch it and where does it come from' tabs.

The Permissions tab is where governance becomes visible. It shows granted privileges and inherited privileges side by side, so you can see exactly how grants cascade down the hierarchy — from catalog, to schema, to table. That cascade is the mechanic the exam keeps probing: a privilege granted at the catalog level flows down to every schema and table beneath it, and the UI labels it as inherited rather than granted directly on the object.

Next, the Lineage tab. This shows upstream sources and downstream writers — the tables that feed this object, and the tables, notebooks, or jobs that read and write it. When something looks wrong in a report, lineage is how you walk backwards to the source without guessing.

Now, the exam trap on this page — and it's a favourite. Catalog browsing is itself governed by privileges. A user without SELECT privilege can still see the table name in the tree, because knowing that an object exists is a weaker form of access. But they will not see sample data, and they won't be able to read column contents. Seeing the name does not mean seeing the data. Hold onto that distinction: existence is metadata, content requires SELECT, and the exam will absolutely test whether you can tell them apart.

So to wrap this page: Catalog Explorer is your read-only window into Unity Catalog. Navigate the tree, read names, types, and comments, open the detail tabs for location, owner, schema, permissions, and lineage, and remember that every one of those views is itself filtered by the privileges you hold.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Catalog Explorer and Governance Signals

questions.question: An analyst belongs to the group `sales_readers`. An administrator has issued exactly these Unity Catalog statements and nothing else: GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG main TO sales_readers; GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA main.sales TO sales_readers; GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA main.sales TO sales_readers. No GRANT statement has ever been issued on the table `main.sales.orders` itself. The analyst opens Catalog Explorer and browses to `main.sales.orders`. What does the analyst observe?

options.label: The table is absent from the object list entirely, because a table becomes visible in Catalog Explorer only when the principal holds a direct privilege recorded on the table object.
The table is listed and readable, but Catalog Explorer removes the Permissions tab and hides all inherited privileges from any principal that is not the table owner.

The table is listed, the Schema/Columns view and Sample Data preview are available, and the Permissions tab attributes the effective SELECT privilege to the schema `main.sales` as an inherited privilege rather than a direct grant on the table.

The table is listed and readable, and the Permissions tab shows `sales_readers` as a direct grantee of the table, because Unity Catalog copies each parent grant down onto every child object at the moment the parent grant is issued.

questions.analysis: Unity Catalog privileges are inherited down the three-level namespace: a grant on `main`, on `main.sales`, or on the table is additive, so the analyst can read the table without any grant being recorded on the table object itself. Option C is correct on both counts: visibility and read access succeed, and Catalog Explorer distinguishes an inherited privilege (shown with its parent scope, here the schema `main.sales`) from a direct grant (a row attached to the table). Option A encodes the most common misconception, that privileges do not flow downward and that visibility requires a table-level grant; in fact visibility needs only USE CATALOG plus USE SCHEMA, and reading needs SELECT, which the schema grant supplies. Option B invents tab-hiding behaviour; Catalog Explorer deliberately surfaces inherited privileges so that a reviewer can trace where access really comes from. Option D confuses inheritance with copying: no rows are materialized on the child, which is precisely why revoking the schema-level SELECT instantly removes the analyst's effective access even though the table still displays no direct grant of its own. This distinction matters because the whole point of a governed catalog is traceability of the access path, supporting the principle that a person receives only the privileges needed for the task and nothing more [source p.398]. It also rests on the schema-metastore idea that a governed table carries integrated structural information, the schema-on-write pattern in which any write must conform to a known schema held in a metastore [source p.245].

questions.question: A security review compares two ways of granting read access to `main.sales.orders`: GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA main.sales (which covers the table) versus GRANT SELECT ON TABLE main.sales.orders. Which statements correctly describe how these two grants differ? Select all that apply.

options.label: The schema-level grant is inherited by every table beneath the schema, so a user can read `main.sales.orders` even though that table records no grant of its own.
The table-level grant applies only to that one table and is not inherited by sibling tables such as `main.sales.returns` in the same schema.
If the schema-level SELECT is later revoked, the user loses effective read access to `main.sales.orders` immediately, even though the table itself never carried a direct grant.
When the schema-level grant is issued, Unity Catalog writes a copy of it onto each child table, so the table Permissions tab will list the user as a direct grantee of the table as well.
Because a broader grant is more authoritative, a schema-level grant overrides and cancels any conflicting or narrower table-level grant on the same object when the two are evaluated together.

questions.analysis: Unity Catalog evaluates privileges by walking the namespace from catalog to schema to table and unioning what it finds; it has no deny rules, so broader and narrower grants accumulate rather than compete. A is correct because inheritance flows downward, which is exactly why a table can be readable with an empty grant list of its own. B is correct because downward inheritance never travels sideways: a table grant says nothing about siblings, and schema-level grants are inherited only by the schema that received them, not by every schema in the catalog. C is correct and is the operational consequence of inheritance rather than copying: the effective privilege is computed at query time from the ancestor grant, so revoking the ancestor removes access in one step. D is the copying misconception; if grants were copied, revoking the parent would leave the child readable, which contradicts C and would defeat least privilege. E is the precedence misconception; Unity Catalog privileges are additive and there is no negative privilege, so a table-level grant can only add access, never be cancelled by a higher-level grant. Designing grants around schema and catalog scope is the practical application of least privilege, giving a principal only the privileges and data needed for the task at hand, and withdrawing them when the task ends, rather than handing out administrative access to everything [source p.398].

questions.question: You are asked to audit `main.sales.orders_gold`. Its Lineage tab shows three upstream nodes: the table `main.sales.orders_silver`, the notebook `/Repos/sales/build_gold`, and the scheduled job `nightly_sales_refresh`; the downstream side shows one dashboard. (a) Explain step by step how you would determine which asset actually wrote the table and how you would confirm it. (b) Then state which Catalog Explorer tab you would open to answer each of these four questions: who can read this table, what columns and data types does it have, what wrote it and what reads it, and how has it changed over time. Be explicit about which signals on the lineage graph you rely on.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric, 100 points total. (1) Lineage interpretation and correct attribution, 40 points: the answer identifies the notebook and the job as upstream producer nodes and distinguishes them by node type/icon and by the direction of the edges (arrows pointing into the audited table mean upstream); it states that both the notebook and the job can appear on the same path when the notebook is orchestrated by the job, so the correct attribution is the job run that executed the notebook, not the other upstream table, which is an input rather than the writer; it mentions using filters such as time range or workspace, and clicking through to the notebook or job run detail to confirm. Award partial credit for stopping at reading the node type without explaining confirmation. (2) Tab matching, 35 points, roughly 9 points per correct mapping: Permissions tab for who can read; Schema/Columns tab for columns and types; Lineage tab for what wrote it and what reads it; History (version/operation history) tab for how it has changed over time. Deduct for swapping Permissions and Lineage, which is the most frequent error. (3) Governance realism, 15 points: the answer notes that lineage is captured automatically from query plans when writes execute through Unity Catalog, that lineage visibility itself can depend on the viewer's privileges, and that a confirmed writer should be cross-checked against version history rather than assumed from graph position alone. (4) Clarity and terminology, 10 points: uses the terms upstream, downstream, lineage, three-level namespace, and inherited privilege correctly and writes in complete sentences.
questions.analysis: A strong answer treats the lineage graph as a directed graph of data assets and operations. Edges that point into `main.sales.orders_gold` are upstream producers; edges that leave it are downstream consumers. Reading the graph therefore yields `main.sales.orders_silver` as an input table and `/Repos/sales/build_gold` as a code asset; the `nightly_sales_refresh` job node is the orchestrator that ran that notebook, so the writer of record is the job run, and the notebook alone is not the complete answer because a notebook exists whether or not it ever produced this table. Confirmation comes from opening the notebook or job run detail, checking the time range filter so the edge corresponds to the version you are auditing, and cross-checking the History tab, which lists the write operations and versions of the Delta table. Note that expected consistency of what you see depends on how the writes were committed: a table produced by a sequence of operations should be read with an understanding of whether those operations were committed as a consistent set or as independent atomic writes, because concurrent readers can otherwise see intermediate states [source p.304]. The tab mapping follows directly from what each surface is built to display: Permissions answers who can read, and it distinguishes inherited privileges from direct grants; Schema/Columns answers what the data looks like, the integrated structural description that tells consumers how to read the table [source p.245]; Lineage answers what wrote it and what reads it; History answers how it changed across versions. Downstream nodes are worth reviewing because a gold table is typically an enriched dataset consumed by further assets, and enrichment joins a stream or table to other data to produce a new enhanced dataset, so a change to `orders_gold` propagates to every consumer shown downstream [source p.312]. Finally, the auditor should record privileges as well as structure: least privilege means each principal holds only what its task requires, so any principal that inherited read access through a schema or catalog grant should be documented as such rather than reported as a direct grantee [source p.398].

actions.text: Let's put those Catalog Explorer signals to the test. Take each question on your own — read carefully, and lean on what we just covered about how metadata, permissions, and lineage actually behave.
Work through them at your own pace, and once you submit, I'll walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Worked Problems: Locating, Qualifying, and Querying Objects

elements.content: Problem 1

A colleague tells you: "the orders table lives in the sales schema of the main catalog of our Unity Catalog metastore — just give me the five most recent orders." The table is main.sales.orders with columns order_id BIGINT, customer_id STRING, order_date DATE, order_total DECIMAL(10,2). It currently holds these six rows: (1007, 'C-44', DATE'2024-03-14', 250.00), (1006, 'C-19', DATE'2024-03-12', 89.99), (1005, 'C-02', DATE'2024-03-09', 1004.50), (1004, 'C-77', DATE'2024-03-09', 42.00), (1003, 'C-31', DATE'2024-02-27', 512.75), (1002, 'C-44', DATE'2024-02-25', 66.10). Write the query that returns exactly the five most recent orders, explain every clause, and give the exact result rows.
Hint: Translate the English first: 'five most recent' = sort descending on the business date, then cut the list after the sort.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Resolve the name before writing any logic. The colleague gave you a catalog (main), a schema (sales) and a table (orders), so the fully qualified three-part name is main.sales.orders. Writing all three parts is not cosmetic: it removes any dependence on whatever the session's current catalog and current schema happen to be, which is the single most common reason a query that works in one notebook fails in another.

Step 2 — Recognize the operation. This is the read pattern of CRUD: a query is a request to read a pattern of records [source p.299]. The 'pattern' here is a projection (four columns), a sort (descending order_date), and a row cap (five rows).

Step 3 — Decide what 'most recent' sorts on. It sorts on the business date order_date, not on any ingestion timestamp, because the requirement is about when the customer ordered.

Step 4 — Handle the tie. Rows 1005 and 1004 both have order_date = 2024-03-09, so `ORDER BY order_date DESC` alone leaves their relative order undefined and the LIMIT cut is nondeterministic. Add order_id DESC as a deterministic tiebreaker.

Step 5 — Order of clauses. SQL evaluates ORDER BY logically before LIMIT, so sorting then capping gives the top five of the sorted list, not five arbitrary rows that happen to get sorted afterwards.

The query:

SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_total

FROM main.sales.orders

ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC

LIMIT 5;

Trace of the sort (6 rows in, 5 rows out):

2024-03-14 (1007) → 2024-03-12 (1006) → 2024-03-09 (1005, tiebreak 1004) → 2024-02-27 (1003) → 2024-02-25 (1002)

Result rows:

1007 | C-44 | 2024-03-14 | 250.00

1006 | C-19 | 2024-03-12 | 89.99

1005 | C-02 | 2024-03-09 | 1004.50

1004 | C-77 | 2024-03-09 | 42.00

1003 | C-31 | 2024-02-27 | 512.75

Sanity check with an independent aggregate: SELECT MAX(order_date) FROM main.sales.orders returns 2024-03-14, which equals the order_date of the first row returned — the two computations agree, so the ordering is right.

If the requirement were 'every order on the five most recent dates', LIMIT would be the wrong tool because it truncates on row count, not on date. The correct form uses a window function:

WITH ranked AS (

SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS d

FROM main.sales.orders

)

SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, order_total

FROM ranked WHERE d <= 5;

Analysis — The method works because SQL's logical evaluation order fixes the semantics: FROM (resolve main.sales.orders) → WHERE → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. The optimizer may physically push the sort and the limit down, but it must preserve that meaning, which is why `LIMIT 5` written before `ORDER BY` in the text is still applied after the sort. Two failure modes dominate student answers. First, `LIMIT 5` with no `ORDER BY` returns an arbitrary five rows; in a Delta table the order often looks like insertion order, so 1002–1006 may come back and the student concludes the query 'works' until the table is rewritten. Second, sorting on the wrong column — a `created_at`/ingestion timestamp instead of the business date — silently produces the five most recently loaded orders, which is a different business question. Also note that ties make `LIMIT` nondeterministic at the boundary: if six orders shared 2024-03-09, the fifth row returned would be an arbitrary choice, which is why production code that must be reproducible adds a unique tiebreaker. Nullable dates deserve an explicit decision too: Spark's default null placement in a DESC sort is not identical to every other engine's, so if order_date can be NULL, state `NULLS LAST` explicitly rather than relying on the default. Finally, this read pattern is only the front half of a real pipeline; a three-part qualified read like this is exactly what a streaming enrichment join uses when it looks up reference rows while processing events [source p.312]. For anything more complex than three clauses, prefer a CTE over nested subqueries because the readable flow lets a reviewer see the sort and the filter, and check the explain plan when latency matters [source p.303].
Problem 2

You inherit an unfamiliar workspace whose metastore you have never seen. Write the exact statement sequence that discovers (a) every catalog, (b) every schema in the target catalog, and (c) every table in the target schema, then shows how to stop typing fully qualified names. Then do the arithmetic: the discovery returns 3 catalogs, 4 schemas in main (information_schema, sales, marketing, hr) and 47 objects in main.sales; the other three schemas hold 12 objects each on average. How many distinct three-part names exist under the catalog main, and how many of them did the exploration touch in the first three statements?
