Hint: Discovery is metadata-only: you never touch data, you only walk catalog → schema → table.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Catalogs. Every workspace attached to a metastore sits above all catalogs, and catalogs are the top level of the three-part namespace (main.sales.orders)[source p.245].

SHOW CATALOGS;

This is metadata-only: it reads the metastore's catalog registry and returns one row per catalog name. A typical result is `main`, `analytics`, `legacy_raw`.

Step 2 — Schemas inside a chosen catalog. Pick the catalog you were told to work in and ask for its schemas:

SHOW SCHEMAS IN main;

-- equivalent long form: SHOW SCHEMAS IN CATALOG main;

The result is `information_schema`, `sales`, `marketing`, `hr`. Note that `information_schema` is itself a real schema that exists in every catalog; you can query it programmatically with `SELECT table_catalog, table_schema, table_name FROM main.information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'sales';` when you want to filter or join the listing instead of reading it by eye.

Step 3 — Tables inside a chosen schema:

SHOW TABLES IN main.sales;

This returns one row per table and view, with columns including `tableName` and `isTemporary`. Temporary views exist only inside the current session, so they are not part of the persisted namespace.

Step 4 — Pin the names to the session so unqualified names resolve. Discovery and execution are different privileges and different states: the three SHOW statements never change what `SELECT ... FROM orders` means. To do that:

USE CATALOG main;

USE SCHEMA sales;

SELECT current_catalog(), current_schema(); -- returns main, sales

SELECT order_id, order_date FROM orders LIMIT 3; -- one-part name now resolves

Step 5 — The arithmetic. Distinct three-part names under `main` = objects in sales + objects in the other schemas = 47 + (3 × 12) = 47 + 36 = 83. The first three statements returned 3 catalogs + 4 schemas + 47 tables = 54 rows of metadata; they displayed 47 of the 83 names in `main` and named none of the objects in the other two catalogs. Reproducing the full inventory means one SHOW SCHEMAS and one SHOW TABLES per catalog — a nested walk, not one flat statement: for 3 catalogs × 4 schemas you would issue 1 + 3 + 12 = 16 statements to see every table name in the metastore.

Analysis — The method works because Unity Catalog is a strict three-level hierarchy with the metastore above the catalog, and each SHOW statement only reveals the level immediately below the one you name. This is why a single 'show me everything' statement does not exist: the metastore deliberately makes you traverse, so that the traversal itself is subject to privilege checks. A subtle consequence is that a short listing is not proof of absence. SHOW results are filtered by what your identity is permitted to see, so if `SHOW TABLES IN main.sales` returns 40 rows where a teammate sees 47, the difference is usually privilege, not a deleted table. Common mistakes: using the legacy synonym SHOW DATABASES and forgetting that in Unity Catalog a 'database' and a 'schema' are the same level of the hierarchy; assuming SHOW TABLES lists only tables when views appear too; and treating `information_schema` as a system catalog when it is a per-catalog schema you must qualify as main.information_schema. Schema itself is the Rosetta stone here — it is the information that tells a reader how to interpret the files and columns below it, which is why discovery starts with names and ends with DESCRIBE TABLE, not the other way around [source p.245]. Finally, the count matters operationally: 83 names is small enough to grant by hand once, but the point of the exercise is that you should not grant by hand at all, which is the subject of the cascade problem below.
Problem 3

User `analyst_maria` must be able to open Catalog Explorer, navigate to main.sales, see the table main.sales.orders in the list, and inspect its columns and comment — but if she runs SELECT * FROM main.sales.orders she must receive a permission error. Write the exact GRANT statements that implement this, state precisely what each privilege does and does not grant, and explain what she would see if you granted only the two USE privileges.
Hint: Separate three questions that students habitually merge: can she walk to the object, can she see the object, can she read the object's rows.

Worked solution
The three questions map onto three different privileges, all evaluated on top of the catalog → schema → table hierarchy.

1) Can she walk the namespace? Navigation is granted by USE:

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG main TO `analyst_maria`;

GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA main.sales TO `analyst_maria`;

USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA are prerequisites for referring to objects in that catalog/schema with two-part or one-part names, but they confer no rights on any table. They are the corridor, not the room key.

2) Can she see the object's metadata (name, columns, comment, table type) without reading rows? That is exactly what BROWSE is for:

GRANT BROWSE ON TABLE main.sales.orders TO `analyst_maria`;

-- scalable variant that covers every current and future table in the schema:

-- GRANT BROWSE ON SCHEMA main.sales TO `analyst_maria`;

3) Can she read rows? That requires SELECT, which you deliberately do not grant:

-- intentionally omitted:

-- GRANT SELECT ON TABLE main.sales.orders TO `analyst_maria`;

-- and, if she previously had it:

-- REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE main.sales.orders FROM `analyst_maria`;

Expected outcomes after the three grants above:

- Catalog Explorer shows main → sales → orders; she can open the table page, see the column list, types and comment.

- SELECT * FROM main.sales.orders fails with a permissions error of the form: User does not have SELECT on Table main.sales.orders (error class INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS). The error is a governance rejection, not a 'table not found' — she has already proven she can see the table, so the only thing missing is the data privilege.

- SHOW TABLES IN main.sales and DESCRIBE TABLE main.sales.orders succeed, because both are metadata operations covered by BROWSE plus USE SCHEMA.

If you granted only the two USE privileges and nothing else, the deterministic, exam-safe answer is: navigation succeeds, but metadata visibility on the table is not guaranteed. Depending on metastore settings and runtime version, objects she holds no privilege on are either hidden from the listing or rendered with a lock icon. Because that behaviour is version-dependent, do not rely on it — grant BROWSE explicitly when the requirement is 'see but do not read'.

Analysis — The trap this problem tests is the belief that permissions are monotonic down the hierarchy — that USE CATALOG somehow implies 'some access' to the tables inside. They are three independent checks, and a query only succeeds when all applicable ones pass: the session resolving the name (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA), the object being visible (BROWSE or any stronger privilege), and the row read being authorized (SELECT). The cleanest way to remember the relationship is that SELECT is a superset in one direction: a user who can read a table can obviously see it, so granting SELECT also makes the table visible; BROWSE exists precisely for the case where you want visibility without data access, and there is no privilege that grants data access without visibility. A second edge case is ownership: a table's creator/owner has implicit rights and cannot be locked out by REVOKE, so 'granted nothing but seems to see everything' is usually ownership, not a privilege leak. Third, privileges attach to the securable object, so DROP TABLE followed by a re-CREATE produces a brand-new object with no grants and silently breaks every consumer that relied on the old grants; renaming the table, by contrast, keeps the object identity and the grants. Finally, note what BROWSE does not do: it does not let her run the query, and it does not let her see data through a view that selects from the table — a view runs with the *definer's* privileges only under specific configurations, so 'hide the table behind a view with BROWSE-only' is a design that must be tested, not assumed. When the business wants 'see the catalogue entry, never the rows', the audit trail to show is exactly this: USE at both upper levels, BROWSE at the object or schema level, and a documented, deliberate absence of SELECT.
Problem 4

A platform team governs 12 schemas that average 25 tables each (about 300 tables) for 6 consumer identities: 3 analyst groups, 2 BI service principals and 1 ML training job. The old runbook grants SELECT table by table. (a) Compute how many GRANT statements the per-table approach needs versus granting at the schema level. (b) The environment adds 40 new tables per year; estimate the annual maintenance load per-table, and the expected number of ungoverned tables per year if each manual grant has a 2% chance of being forgotten. (c) State the general rule about which direction privileges cascade, and name the anti-pattern.
Hint: A privilege granted on a container applies to every child object that exists now and every one created later — count the containers, not the leaves.

Worked solution
(a) Statement counts. Per-table: 300 tables × 6 consumers = 1,800 GRANT statements (3,600 if the runbook also writes the matching REVOKE for periodic review). Schema-level: each consumer needs one catalog grant and one grant per schema it may read. Assume every consumer reads the 12 schemas: 6 × 12 = 72 schema grants, plus 6 × 1 = 6 catalog USE grants = 78 statements. The ratio is 1,800 / 78 ≈ 23 : 1 in favour of the schema level.

(b) Annual maintenance. New tables per year = 40. Per-table discipline needs 40 × 6 = 240 additional statements per year, and each statement is a place a human can make a mistake: at a 2% error rate the expected number of bad grants is $240 \times 0.02 = 4.8$ per year, i.e. roughly one ungoverned object every 2.5 months (12 / 4.8 ≈ 2.5). At a generous 2 minutes per grant-and-verify cycle, 240 statements cost $240 \times 2 = 480$ minutes ≈ 8 hours of pure grant maintenance per year, and that cost grows linearly with every new consumer and every new table. Under schema-level grants the marginal maintenance for the same 40 tables is zero, because a privilege granted on a schema applies to every object in it, including objects created after the grant.

(c) The cascade rule. Unity Catalog privileges cascade *downward* on the hierarchy catalog → schema → table (and its siblings such as views and volumes). A grant on a catalog applies to all schemas in it; a grant on a schema applies to all tables in it; a grant on a table applies to nothing else. Privileges never cascade upward (SELECT on one table does not let you list the schema) and never sideways (a grant on main.sales does not leak into main.marketing). The anti-pattern is *per-table grants as the primary governance mechanism*: it is unmaintainable at scale, it drifts the moment a schema grows, and the drift is invisible until an audit or a broken dashboard surfaces it.

The scalable pattern keeps the same least-privilege intent without the statement explosion: split schemas by audience (for example a `shared` schema every analyst can read versus a `restricted` schema that most identities cannot enter), grant SELECT once at the schema level to the appropriate group, and handle the genuinely sensitive columns or rows with column masks and row filters rather than by withholding the table-level grant. Concretely, if 5 of the 25 tables in a schema are sensitive, isolating them into a second schema costs 6 extra schema grants (36 statements to switch from 1,800 to ~90) and buys back roughly 230 statements per new table cohort.

Analysis — The cascade exists because Unity Catalog stores privileges as tuples on securable objects and evaluates a query by checking the object and then walking up its ancestors; inheritance is the natural implementation of that walk, and it means a single grant has a well-defined meaning for an unbounded set of future objects. Per-table grants invert that economy: they turn a governance decision into a maintenance backlog whose size is the product of consumers and tables, which is exactly why it is called an anti-pattern rather than merely 'less convenient'. Two edge cases make the anti-pattern worse than pure arithmetic suggests. First, DROP-and-recreate destroys the object identity and therefore the grants, so a pipeline that rebuilds a table every night and a runbook that granted per table will silently produce a table nobody can read; renaming a table keeps grants, recreating it does not. Second, grants on a schema do not survive as 'grants on tables' — if you later DROP the schema, the child-level grants vanish with it, which is fine for schema-level design but destroys evidence of per-table work you may be relying on. The correct mental model from the query side is that the user writes one query, and the platform answers three questions behind it: can the session resolve the name (USE), is the object visible (BROWSE or stronger), is this specific read authorized (SELECT). Answering all three with two or three container-level grants is the whole point: it keeps the answer correct as the environment grows, instead of correct only as of the last time somebody remembered to run a script.
Problem 5

A notebook session in workspace A runs the query SELECT * FROM sales.orders and fails with TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND, even though the table plainly exists as main.sales.orders in the metastore that workspace A is attached to. Investigation shows that workspace A's default catalog is `analytics` and its default schema is `default`, and that the catalog `analytics` contains no schema named `sales`. Explain exactly how the engine resolved the name, give three fixes with their scope, and state how the error message would have differed if the real problem were a missing privilege.
Hint: Count the parts of the name: without a catalog part, the engine must borrow one from the session.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Parse the name. `sales.orders` has exactly two parts, so it is interpreted as schema.table, not catalog.schema. A two-part name is only complete when the session can supply the missing catalog.

Step 2 — Read the session state. The current catalog is `analytics` and the current schema is `default`. Print it rather than assume it:

SELECT current_catalog(), current_schema();

-- analytics, default

Step 3 — Complete the resolution. The engine prefixes the session's current catalog, so `sales.orders` becomes:

analytics.sales.orders

Check whether that exists: SHOW SCHEMAS IN analytics returns the schemas of `analytics`, and there is no `sales` among them. The lookup therefore fails before any privilege check can even be reached, producing the error class for a missing object, TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND. Nothing is wrong with the table; the *name* pointed somewhere else.

Fix 1 — Fully qualify the name (most portable, no session mutation):

SELECT * FROM main.sales.orders;

The three-part name carries its own catalog, so it resolves identically in every workspace attached to the same metastore.

Fix 2 — Change the session defaults, then use a short name:

USE CATALOG main;

USE SCHEMA sales;

SELECT * FROM orders; -- one-part name now means main.sales.orders

This is session- or notebook-scoped: re-running the notebook re-establishes the default, which is why the USE statements must sit at the top of the notebook rather than in someone's muscle memory.

Fix 3 — Set the defaults explicitly at the start of the session:

SET CATALOG main;

-- optionally SET SCHEMA sales;

In the Databricks SQL editor the equivalent control is the catalog/schema picker above the editor; setting it there changes what the editor's session resolves to, but it does not change what a notebook session resolves to.

Step 4 — Distinguish the two failure classes, because the fix is completely different.

- Wrong namespace → TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND (or a schema/catalog-not-found error at the parent level). The object exists; your name did not reach it.

- Right namespace, insufficient rights → a permissions error such as User does not have SELECT on Table main.sales.orders or a permission denied error class. The object exists and was found; you were not allowed to read it.

Diagnostic rule: if a teammate runs the identical three-part statement and succeeds, the problem is namespace resolution or privileges, not the data. If they succeed with the two-part name from their session and you fail with the identical text, it is almost certainly a session-default difference.

Analysis — The pitfall is a category error: students treat a table name as an absolute address when a one- or two-part name is really a *relative* path anchored to session state. The engine resolves names by filling missing left-hand parts from the session (current catalog, then current schema), so the same text can name different objects in different workspaces, different notebooks, and even the same notebook after one USE CATALOG. This is why the exam-style question 'does this reference resolve?' is answered by counting parts and reading the session defaults, never by intuition about where the table 'should' be. Three consequences deserve emphasis. First, portability is monotonic in the number of parts: one-part names are the least portable (they move with both defaults), two-part names are portable only when the default catalog matches, and three-part names are portable across every workspace attached to the same metastore because Unity Catalog names are metastore-scoped, not workspace-scoped. Second, migration to a shared metastore is exactly when this bites: a job that ran for years with `sales.orders` in a workspace whose default catalog happened to be `main` breaks the moment it is scheduled from a workspace whose default is something else — nothing about the table changed, only the anchor. Third, the habit that prevents all of this is cheap: begin every notebook with USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA or with fully qualified names, and never sign off on a query whose correctness depends on a default you have not printed with SELECT current_catalog(), current_schema(). Because a query implicitly assumes its inputs — including that the names it mentions are the objects you meant — stating the namespace explicitly is part of making the query correct, not just readable [source p.303].

actions.text: Now let's put the Unity Catalog navigation we just covered into practice. This page walks through five fully worked problems, each one translating a plain-English request into correct namespace and query syntax. Let's take them in order.

Problem 1 starts with a colleague's offhand description: the orders table lives in the sales schema of the main catalog, and we need the five most recent orders. The critical move is to resolve that human sentence into a fully qualified three-part name before writing a single line of SQL.

Stepping through the solution: the name resolves to main.sales.orders — catalog, then schema, then table. From there the query is mechanical: select everything from that table, order by order_date descending, and apply a limit of five. Because we qualified the name completely, there is no ambiguity about which orders table we mean.

Problem 3 tests a distinction that trips up a lot of candidates. Here a user must be able to open the table in Catalog Explorer, yet be prevented from reading its rows. The worked answer separates three questions: USE on the catalog and USE on the schema let the user navigate and see metadata, while SELECT on the table itself is what actually governs access to the data. Grant the navigation privileges, withhold the SELECT.

And Problem 5 lands the most common pitfall of all: assuming a two-part name resolves the same way in every workspace. Without a catalog prefix, a name falls back to the session's default catalog and schema — and those defaults can differ entirely from one workspace to the next. This is the exact trap the exam likes to set.

Notice the recurring pattern across all five problems: parse the name, qualify it fully, and only then reason about privileges. Keep that sequence in mind and these stop being tricky and start being mechanical. Feel free to pause and rework any of them on your own before we move on.

scenes.title: SQL Warehouse vs. All-Purpose Compute

elements.content: Dimension  |  SQL Warehouse  |  All-Purpose Compute

Primary interface and entry point
SQL Warehouse: A SQL warehouse is driven from the Databricks SQL editor in the browser, where you write, run, save, and schedule queries, and it is the same compute that backs dashboards and alerts, so the editor is only a client while the warehouse does the execution.
All-Purpose Compute: An all-purpose compute cluster is driven from a notebook: you find or create a notebook in the workspace, attach it to the cluster, and run cells, and with no attachment there is no execution at all.

Supported languages
SQL Warehouse: A SQL warehouse is SQL-only, which is precisely why its optimizer, Photon vectorized engine, and result caching can be tuned for relational scan-aggregate-join workloads rather than for arbitrary code.
All-Purpose Compute: All-purpose compute is multi-language, running Python, Scala, R, and SQL cells inside one Spark session, where magic commands such as %python, %scala, or %sql switch the language per cell and temporary views created in one language are visible to the next.

Workload shape and optimization target
SQL Warehouse: A SQL warehouse is optimized for BI and dashboard workloads, meaning high-concurrency, short-to-medium, repetitive aggregation queries over Delta tables where columnar scanning and result reuse pay off.
All-Purpose Compute: All-purpose compute is optimized for Spark ETL, exploratory data analysis, and machine learning, spanning long-running transformations, feature engineering, and model training, which fits the software-engineering observation that you may write transformations in Python powered by a distributed system such as Spark instead of in SQL. [source p.359]

Concurrency behavior
SQL Warehouse: A SQL warehouse scales for concurrency by adding clusters between its configured minimum and maximum, so the correct remedy for many simultaneous dashboard users is to raise the max cluster count or photograph size rather than assume a single query got faster.
All-Purpose Compute: An all-purpose cluster serves the interactive sessions attached to it, and concurrent notebooks compete for the same fixed worker pool plus fixed driver, so adding users does not automatically add execution capacity the way a warehouse's cluster autoscaling does.

Startup behavior
SQL Warehouse: A SQL warehouse startup depends on its type: serverless starts in seconds because Databricks manages the compute in its own account, Pro offers faster startup with resource isolation, and Classic starts slowest because clusters are provisioned in the customer's cloud account.
All-Purpose Compute: All-purpose compute startup is a cluster launch, so a cold cluster takes minutes as cloud VMs boot, the Spark runtime installs, and the cluster registers with the workspace; the same cluster type also has to be chosen before sizing (node type, workers, autoscaling, Photon, auto-stop).

Cost model and lifecycle
SQL Warehouse: A SQL warehouse is billed on warehouse usage with auto-stop shutting it down after a configured number of idle minutes, and the serverless tier bills on a consumption unit price that folds in the managed infrastructure, while data in Delta tables in cloud storage is unaffected by auto-stop and remains stored and queryable.
All-Purpose Compute: All-purpose compute is billed per DBU for the cluster's uptime from launch until termination, so an idle notebook cluster still burns DBUs, which is why auto-stop and aggressive auto-termination matter; this mirrors the shift that Google BigQuery and Snowflake popularized by separating compute from storage so data lives in object storage with virtually limitless capacity. [source p.126]

Fit with dashboards, alerts, and scheduling
SQL Warehouse: A SQL warehouse is the only surface that backs dashboards, alerts, and the query scheduler, so if a stakeholder needs a refresh-on-schedule dashboard or a threshold alert, the query must live on a SQL warehouse.
All-Purpose Compute: All-purpose compute can run scheduled jobs, but those jobs are notebooks, not dashboard queries; a notebook cannot substitute for the query that powers a built-in dashboard or alert tile, even though a notebook cell may contain SQL.

Governance integration
SQL Warehouse: A SQL warehouse queries Unity Catalog objects by their three-level names, for example main.sales.orders, and it inherits the metastore's identity and permission model, so a SELECT run in the SQL editor is authorized exactly as the same SELECT in a notebook would be.
All-Purpose Compute: All-purpose compute also reads the same Unity Catalog metastore, but its Spark session adds its own layer of catalog and schema resolution, so learners must be able to distinguish one-part, two-part, and three-part names and use USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA to make unqualified references resolve. [source p.382]

Worked example: sizing the same workload on each surface
SQL Warehouse: A dashboard with 30 concurrent viewers issuing 5 queries per minute each is 150 queries per minute; if a 2X-Small warehouse sustains roughly 12 concurrent queries per cluster before queueing, you set minimum = 2 and maximum = 12 clusters, because size up for concurrency and not to make a single bad query fast.
All-Purpose Compute: The same 150-queries-per-minute pattern expressed as a continuous Spark job over a 200 GB Delta table is one notebook that runs for 40 minutes; at the cluster's DBU-per-hour rate the job's cost is fixed by that single run's wall-clock time, so the tuning lever is partition and shuffle efficiency rather than cluster count.

Takeaway — Choose a SQL warehouse whenever the deliverable is SQL consumed by a person or a system: the SQL editor, scheduled queries, dashboards, and alerts are all delivered by a SQL warehouse, and its cluster autoscaling is the mechanism that absorbs BI concurrency.

Takeaway — Choose all-purpose compute when the work is notebook-driven and polyglot: exploration, feature engineering, Spark ETL, and machine learning that needs Python, Scala, or R alongside SQL in one Spark session.

Takeaway — Avoid the two classic exam traps: do not treat a SQL warehouse as a general-purpose cluster for arbitrary code, and do not expect an all-purpose cluster to back a dashboard, because the dashboard path terminates at a SQL warehouse and nowhere else.

Takeaway — Both surfaces obey the same Unity Catalog governance, so a query that fails on one for a missing catalog.schema.table reference or a missing privilege will fail on the other for the same reason; changing compute does not change permissions.

actions.text: Having mapped out where objects live in Unity Catalog, we now have to answer the practical question: which compute surface do I actually run my SQL on? This table lays out both options side by side across the dimensions that matter — interface, languages, workload shape, concurrency, startup, cost model, and fit with dashboards and alerts.

Start with the primary interface. A SQL warehouse is reached through the SQL editor, dashboards, alerts, and scheduled queries — it is the entry point for anything that speaks SQL natively. All-purpose compute, by contrast, is reached through a notebook: you attach it, you write cells, you run them.

That difference in entry point shows up again in supported languages. A SQL warehouse runs SQL, full stop. An all-purpose cluster gives you Python, Scala, R, and SQL in the same notebook — which is exactly why it is the home for Spark ETL, data exploration, and machine learning workloads.

Workload shape follows from that. SQL warehouses are optimized for BI-style, set-oriented queries — aggregations, joins over curated tables, high concurrency from many analysts at once. All-purpose clusters are optimized for iterative, code-driven transforms where the shape of the work is a program, not a query.

Notice concurrency and startup behavior. SQL warehouses are built to fan out across many concurrent users and support serverless, pro, and classic types, so they can start almost instantly. All-purpose clusters are generally long-lived, single-team resources that take minutes to spin up and are not designed to serve a hundred simultaneous dashboard users.

This row is the one exam writers love. Dashboards, alerts, and query scheduling are delivered by a SQL warehouse. If a question describes a dashboard that must refresh on a schedule and fire an alert when a threshold breaks, the backing compute is a SQL warehouse — never an all-purpose cluster.

One thing both surfaces share: they obey the same Unity Catalog governance model. The same three-level namespace, the same grants, the same lineage — so your security decisions do not change based on which compute you pick.

The worked example sizes the same workload on each surface, and the conclusion is consistent: the SQL warehouse wins on concurrency and startup, the all-purpose cluster wins on flexibility and multi-language processing. Same data, same catalog, different tool.

So let's lock in the takeaway and the two classic exam traps. Trap one: treating a SQL warehouse as a general-purpose cluster for arbitrary code — it is not, it is SQL-only. Trap two: expecting an all-purpose cluster to back a dashboard or an alert — it will not. Remember the distinction clearly: a notebook can contain SQL, but the SQL editor, alerts, and dashboards are delivered by a SQL warehouse. Hold onto that phrasing; it is worth easy points on the exam.

scenes.title: Lesson Checkpoint: Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog Navigation

questions.question: A data engineer opens the SQL editor on a serverless SQL warehouse, runs USE CATALOG main; and USE SCHEMA default;, then executes SELECT count(*) FROM orders; The statement fails with TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND, yet a teammate runs the identical statement text successfully. The production object is main.sales.orders. Which explanation and minimal fix are correct?

options.label: The single-part name orders is resolved as current_catalog.current_schema.orders, that is main.default.orders, so the failure is namespace resolution rather than a compute fault; running USE SCHEMA sales; or writing the two-part name sales.orders would resolve it to main.sales.orders.
The SQL warehouse cached the catalog tree when it started, so any table whose metadata changed after warehouse startup stays invisible until the warehouse is stopped and restarted.
Unity Catalog always requires a three-part name of the form metastore.main.sales.orders, because the metastore is the outermost level of the object namespace.

The SQL editor is bound to the wrong compute, so USE SCHEMA was sent to an all-purpose cluster instead of to the warehouse; switching the editor connection from serverless to classic warehouse resolves the name.

questions.analysis: Unity Catalog uses a three-level namespace, catalog.schema.table, and a query's reference is resolved against the session's current catalog and current schema before the optimizer plans anything. The rules are conditional, not optional: a one-part name (orders) resolves as current_catalog.current_schema.orders and never searches other schemas; a two-part name (sales.orders) resolves as current_catalog.sales.orders; only a three-part name (main.sales.orders) is immune to session context. Because the session had set USE CATALOG main and USE SCHEMA default, the one-part reference deliberately pointed at main.default.orders, which does not exist. Option A therefore states both the mechanism and a correct minimal fix, since USE SCHEMA sales changes current_schema for subsequent statements while sales.orders explicitly overrides it for that statement. Option B is a common misconception that confuses compute lifecycle with governance: stopping a warehouse terminates compute, it does not re-synchronize a name-resolution binding, and a Unity Catalog table is immediately resolvable once the path and privileges are correct. Option C is wrong on a definitional point - the metastore is not a fourth name level; it is the top-level container attached to workspaces that holds catalogs and owns the identity and permission model, so main.sales.orders is already fully qualified. Option D confuses compute with governance; USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are session settings resolved by the governance layer, and the warehouse type affects startup latency and isolation, not whether a name binds to an object. As a debugging habit, when a reference misbehaves it helps to read the query plan and confirm which database objects the optimizer actually resolved and how it planned the query, since the explain plan reports the objects used (tables, indexes, cache) together with resource consumption and performance figures [source p.303]. Edge case to remember: if the session has no current catalog or schema at all, even two-part names fail, which is why notebooks and scheduled jobs should either set the context explicitly or write three-part names.

questions.question: A team runs a 2X-Small pro SQL warehouse that autoscales between a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 2 clusters. Between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. about 60 analysts share one dashboard, and by 1 p.m. queries queue for several minutes. Overnight, a single ELT query runs for about three hours. Select the TWO statements that are correct for this scenario.

options.label: Raising the maximum cluster count and/or moving up the T-shirt size is justified, because warehouse size and autoscaling govern how many concurrent queries are executed in parallel, which is what the 1 p.m. queue reflects.
Moving from 2X-Small to 4X-Large will shorten the three-hour overnight ELT query in roughly the same proportion as the increase in warehouse size, so the same resize solves both problems.
Setting auto-stop to 5 minutes will delete the underlying Delta files of the dashboard tables after five idle minutes, so the nightly load will have to reload the source data.

A serverless warehouse is the better fit if the team's binding constraint is startup latency for interactive ad-hoc queries, because serverless, pro, and classic differ in startup latency, resource isolation, and pricing model.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct because of how the sizing knobs actually bind. T-shirt size sets the size and number of clusters in a warehouse, minimum and maximum clusters bound autoscaling, and concurrency is the resource being purchased: size up for concurrent work, not to make one slow query fast. A concrete worked example makes the symptom predictable. If a dashboard refresh issues queries that each consume about 20 seconds of compute and the warehouse can execute 3 of them in parallel, one refresh wave for 60 analysts demands 60 x 20 = 1200 query-seconds and completes in (60 / 3) x 20 = 400 seconds, which is nearly seven minutes of perceived queueing - exactly the reported 1 p.m. behavior. Using the conventional doubling between T-shirt sizes, moving from 2X-Small to Large multiplies raw compute capacity by roughly 16x (2X-Small to X-Small, Small, Medium, Large is four doublings), which is why raising the maximum cluster count and/or the size addresses concurrency. Option B is the classic misconception and is false: a larger warehouse adds parallel capacity, but a single statement is bounded by its own plan, its partition count, and the parallelism the query can actually exploit, so the three-hour ELT job will not scale proportionally with warehouse size. Reading the explain plan is the disciplined way to see where the cost really sits, because the plan reports the objects used and resource consumption and performance figures rather than raw size alone [source p.303]. Note also that query speed is a modeling question as well as a compute question: a star schema keeps fact tables surrounded by a small number of dimensions, which yields fewer joins and faster query performance, so reshaping a wide, heavily joined model can beat resizing [source p.327]. Option C is false on a definitional point: auto-stop shuts down the warehouse compute after a configured number of idle minutes, and it does not touch stored data, because Delta tables live in cloud storage while the warehouse is only compute. Option D is correct: serverless, pro, and classic warehouses differ in startup latency, resource isolation, and pricing model, so when the pain is warehouse startup for ad-hoc interactive users rather than steady-state concurrency, serverless is the defensible choice.

questions.question: An analyst holds USE CATALOG on main plus USE SCHEMA and SELECT granted on the schema main.sales. In Catalog Explorer she opens main.sales.orders, and the Permissions tab shows no explicitly granted privilege on the table itself. Select the TWO statements that are correct.

options.label: She can read orders, because the schema-level SELECT is inherited by every table in the schema, and the Permissions tab separates directly granted privileges from inherited ones.
She cannot read orders, because Unity Catalog requires an explicit table-level grant for every read, so an empty Permissions tab on the table means no access.
If the schema-level SELECT were revoked and SELECT granted directly on orders alone, orders would remain readable for her while the sibling tables in main.sales became unreadable.
The Lineage tab records write operations only, so it can identify the notebook that wrote orders but can never show which downstream dashboards read it.

questions.analysis: Unity Catalog grants cascade downward from catalog to schema to table, and Catalog Explorer exists precisely to make that cascade legible: the Permissions tab distinguishes privileges granted directly on the object from privileges inherited from an ancestor. Preconditions matter here. Inheritance is only useful if the path resolves: a user needs USE CATALOG on the catalog and USE SCHEMA on the schema before the schema's SELECT becomes effective, so the edge case to remember is a table-level grant with no parent USE privileges, which still fails to produce a readable table. The converse edge case is also true and is the reason option C is correct: revoking the schema-level grant removes the inherited path for the whole schema, but a direct grant on one table is a separate grant row and survives, leaving orders readable while its siblings become unreadable. Option B states the misconception that every read needs a table-level grant, which would make schema-level grants meaningless and would contradict the cascade the Permissions tab is designed to display. Option D is false because lineage graphs are directional and cover both upstream and downstream: they let you identify which notebook or job wrote a table and which downstream consumers read it. Interpreting metadata correctly is an exam-relevant governance skill because in many architectures the business logic is applied when the data is queried rather than baked into the stored objects, and modern platforms blur the storage boundary further by letting warehouse engines read external data locations and even convert federated queries into materialized views [source p.351]. Modeling choices reinforce the point: in a Data Vault, business logic is created and interpreted at query time, and a Data Vault can serve as the landing zone for analytical data that is then re-modeled separately [source p.331]. That means privilege enforcement happens per query against resolved objects, which is why inherited versus direct grants must be read from Catalog Explorer rather than inferred from the stored table.

questions.question: Explain why catalog, schema, and table are three distinct privilege levels in Unity Catalog rather than a single table access checkbox. In your answer address (a) what each level protects and who typically administers it, (b) how a grant at one level interacts with grants above and below it, including the edge case of a user who holds a table grant but no USE CATALOG or USE SCHEMA privilege, and (c) why three levels reduce administrative cost as object counts grow, using a concrete numeric example.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Level semantics and administrators, about 35 percent - must state that the catalog is the top-level container beneath the metastore used to separate domains, environments, or business units and is administered centrally by platform or account administrators; that the schema (database) is a logical grouping of related tables, views, volumes, functions, and models typically owned by a domain team; and that the table is the finest grain, the level at which row and column level controls and masking policies apply. Definitions must include a precondition, for example that a catalog must exist and be attached through the metastore before schemas and tables can be granted. (2) Inheritance, the resolution path, and the edge case, about 35 percent - must explain that privileges cascade downward from catalog to schema to table, that a user therefore needs USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA before an inherited table privilege becomes usable, that an explicit table grant without those parent USE privileges still fails, that revoking a parent grant removes the inherited path for all children while direct child grants survive, and that a schema-level grant applies to objects created in that schema later. (3) Numeric argument for administrative cost, about 20 percent - must build a concrete example such as one catalog with 12 schemas and 40 tables each, giving 12 x 40 = 480 table-level grants versus 12 schema-level grants, and state the scaling rule that administration cost then grows with schemas rather than tables. (4) Expression and vocabulary, about 10 percent - uses Unity Catalog terms accurately (metastore, catalog, schema, table, grant, inheritance, USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA) in exam-style phrasing. Deduct for answers that treat the metastore as a fourth name level or that claim table-level grants are always required.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. Each level answers a different governance question, which is why collapsing them into one checkbox is a category error. The catalog is the outermost object level beneath the metastore and is used to separate domains or environments (for example main for production and a separate catalog for sandbox work); the metastore itself is not a name level but the container attached to workspaces that owns identity and the permission model. The schema is a logical database inside a catalog that groups related objects such as tables, views, volumes, functions, and models, and it is the level at which a domain team is usually made owner. The table is the finest grain and the point where row filters, column masks, and column-level grants attach. Inheritance runs downward along the resolution path: a grant on the catalog flows to its schemas and their tables, and a grant on a schema flows to its tables. Two preconditions and edge cases must appear for full credit. First, inheritance is not the same as resolution: a user with only a table grant but no USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA cannot resolve the name, so the grant is inert until the parent USE privileges exist. Second, revoking a parent grant removes the inherited path for every descendant but does not erase grants written directly on those descendants, so a single explicitly granted table can stay readable after the schema-level grant is gone. The cost argument is arithmetic: with 1 catalog, 12 schemas, and 40 tables per schema, table-by-table administration requires 12 x 40 = 480 grant statements, whereas schema-level administration requires 12, and each new table in a granted schema is covered automatically without a new grant. Administrative cost therefore scales with the number of schemas rather than the number of tables, which is the whole design rationale. Good answers also note that this layering is what makes cross-domain data products workable: models such as the Data Vault deliberately defer business logic to query time, and a Data Vault is often the landing zone for analytical data that is then modeled separately, commonly as a star schema [source p.331]. Because logic and joins are applied per query rather than baked into stored structures, access must be enforced against resolved objects at each level rather than once at rest. Realistic schema design also keeps those resolved object sets small and understandable: the star schema deliberately places a fact table at the center surrounded by the necessary dimensions, producing fewer joins and faster query performance while staying flexible enough to answer the critical questions [source p.327]. Finally, source schemas are messy in the wild - APIs vary, application internals leak into the data, and engineers must study a source schema before ingesting from it, which is exactly why a two-tier grouping (catalog and schema) above the table is needed to keep that complexity administrable [source p.268].

actions.text: That wraps up our tour through the SQL workspace and the governance layer around it. Now it's your turn to put it together — this checkpoint pulls from the SQL editor and query lifecycle, warehouse types and sizing, the Unity Catalog naming model, and what Catalog Explorer actually tells you.

Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer, even where you're not fully certain — that is exactly where the learning happens. Read the scenario details carefully, since the wording usually decides between two plausible-sounding choices. Once you submit, I'll be right here to walk through your results with you and sort out anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Lesson Orientation: Git Folders and the Developer Workflow

elements.content: Orientation: Git Folders
Data engineering underpins analytics [source p.29].
Git folders connect a remote repo to your workspace.
Branches isolate work before merging to main.
Each commit records who changed which notebook.
Version control is lifecycle work [source p.59].
The exam tests repo connection and branch operations.
You already know navigation, notebooks, and compute.

Worked example: two engineers share one ETL notebook.

A commits 3 files at 09:10; B's push at 09:15 fails.

B pulls, merges 1 conflict, then pushes: 0 files lost.

Engineers work in teams, not alone [source p.57].

actions.text: Now we shift into a brand-new lesson: Git Folders and the Developer Workflow. Everything we've built so far — the workspace, notebooks, compute, SQL and Unity Catalog — lives inside our own little corner of Databricks. This lesson is about how that work gets shared, versioned, and shipped as a team.

Before we dive in, a quick prerequisite check. You already know how to navigate the workspace, create notebooks, and attach compute — those came up earlier in this unit. Today we reuse all of that, but we put it under version control.

Here's the bigger picture. Data engineering underpins analytics — nothing downstream works if the pipelines aren't reliable. And reliability, in a team setting, starts with version control. That is lifecycle work, not an afterthought.

So what is a Git folder? A Git folder connects a remote repository — think GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps — directly to your Databricks workspace. You pull code down, work on it locally in the workspace, and push your changes back. Same repository, same folder, shared by the whole team.

Two of the concepts doing the heavy lifting are branches and commits. Branches isolate your work before it's merged into main, so you can experiment without stepping on a teammate's changes. And each commit records exactly who changed which notebook, and when — a durable history you can always trace back through.

Now, why should you care specifically? Because the Data Engineer Associate exam tests this directly. You'll be asked about connecting a repository and performing branch operations inside the workspace — so pay close attention to the exact steps and terminology here.

And you won't just hear theory. We'll walk through a worked example where two engineers share a single ETL notebook, and you'll see how branching and committing keep them from overwriting each other's work.

Here's our roadmap for the lesson: Git folder concepts first, then connecting a remote repository, then branches, then the pull-commit-push loop, and finally how this all comes together for team collaboration. Let's start by defining exactly what a Databricks Git folder is.

scenes.title: What Is a Databricks Git Folder?

elements.content: What Is a Databricks Git Folder?
Definition: a workspace object that syncs a remote Git repository with a workspace folder [source p.226].
Remotes: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps.
Prerequisites: a workspace admin enables Git integration; each user links a PAT or OAuth credential [source p.357].
Rename: 'Repos' → 'Git folders' (same object). Files: notebooks, .md, .yaml, .json [source p.418].

Example: /Workspace/Repos/acme/etl ↔ github.com/acme/etl.

Exam trap: a Git folder is not a workspace folder.

actions.text: Let's start by defining exactly what a Databricks Git folder is, since everything else in this lesson builds on that definition.

A Git folder is a workspace object that syncs a remote Git repository with a folder inside the Databricks workspace. That sync runs in both directions — you pull changes from the remote down into the workspace, and you commit and push the changes you make in the workspace back up to the remote. So a Git folder is really a working copy that lives inside Databricks.

On the remote side, Databricks supports the major hosted providers — GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps. From the exam's perspective, just remember: the remote is an external Git host, and the Git folder is the local mirror of it inside your workspace.

There are two enablement prerequisites you need to know. First, a workspace admin must enable Git integration for the workspace. Second, each individual user must link their own credential — either a Git personal access token, or an OAuth credential. The key trap here is that this is per-user, not workspace-wide. Enabling the feature for the workspace does not grant you access to a repository on its own.

Now for a terminology point that trips people up. This feature used to be called Repos — short for repositories — and it was renamed to Git folders. It is the same object, just a new name. Exam items may use either term, so treat Repos and Git folders as synonyms.

Here's a concrete example of the mapping. The workspace path on the left points at a folder inside slash Workspace slash Repos slash acme slash etl, and that folder is bound to the remote repository github.com slash acme slash etl on the right. Change a notebook in one and sync, and the other reflects it.

Notice one important distinction as you look at this: a Git folder is not the same object as a plain workspace folder. A regular workspace folder holds files, but those files are not version-controlled. Only a Git folder participates in Git — branching, committing, and history. Keep that contrast in mind, because we'll compare all three — Git folder, workspace folder, and a local Git client — later in this lesson.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Git Folder Fundamentals

questions.question: A team keeps a notebook and a helper Python module in a workspace folder at /Workspace/Users/ana@example.com/etl. The same week, they create a Git folder called etl-repo that is linked to a remote repository. Which statement correctly distinguishes a Git folder from a workspace folder and from a notebook?

options.label: A Git folder is a workspace folder whose contents are tracked against a remote Git repository, so each notebook inside it is an individual version-controlled file; a plain workspace folder is a container that exists only inside the workspace; a notebook is a single document such as .ipynb, .py, .sql, .r, or .scala that can live in either kind of folder.
A Git folder is a single notebook that has been converted into a repository, so the original workspace folder is deleted once the conversion finishes.
A Git folder, a workspace folder, and a notebook are three names for the same object; the only real difference is the icon Databricks shows in the sidebar.
A workspace folder is always backed by a remote Git provider, whereas a Git folder is a local snapshot that is stored only inside Databricks and never pushed anywhere.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: A Git folder is a container in the workspace that is linked to a remote Git repository, so Databricks compares the state of the files inside it against that remote and exposes commit, pull, and branch operations. A plain workspace folder is only a container that lives inside the workspace: it has no remote history and no commit log. A notebook is not a container at all but a single tracked file (.ipynb, .py, .sql, .r, or .scala) that can sit inside either kind of folder. Option B is wrong because linking a repository never turns a notebook into a repository and never removes the surrounding folder; the folder simply becomes repository-backed. Option C is wrong because the three objects have different lifetimes and different version-control semantics, not merely different icons. Option D reverses the relationship: it is the Git folder, not the workspace folder, that is backed by a remote provider. The practical consequence mirrors the brittleness the book describes for tightly coupled monolithic systems, where one break anywhere forces a full restart and leaves no audit trail of what changed [source p.166]. Putting notebooks under version control is also the same integration discipline the book describes when it argues that modern integration happens through general-purpose APIs rather than bespoke, ad hoc connections [source p.84].

questions.question: A workspace admin has already turned on Git integration for the workspace. A new user can see the Git folders entry point, but the clone of a private repository fails. According to the Databricks repository enablement model, which additional prerequisite is missing?

options.label: The user must add a Git credential for that provider in their own user settings (for example a personal access token or an OAuth connection), because Git integration is enabled once at the workspace level but authentication is per user.
The user must be granted USE CATALOG on the main catalog, because Git folders are Unity Catalog objects and inherit catalog privileges.
The user must attach a serverless SQL warehouse to the notebook, because the clone operation needs SQL compute to run on.
The user must be a workspace admin, because only admins are permitted to authenticate against an external Git provider.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: Connecting a Databricks Git folder requires two independent enablement steps. First, an admin enables the Git integration setting for the whole workspace, which makes the feature visible. Second, each individual user supplies a Git credential for the provider — a personal access token or an OAuth/SSO-based connection — because the workspace setting grants capability, not identity. Option B is a genuine confusion with the Unity Catalog three-level namespace: Git folders live in the workspace's /Repos or Git folders area and are not governed as catalog objects, so USE CATALOG has no effect on cloning. Option C confuses the storage of files with the compute that runs them; a clone is a workspace and provider operation and needs no SQL warehouse. Option D is wrong because any user with the workspace setting enabled and a valid credential can connect; admin rights are needed only to flip the workspace switch. The credential is a secret travelling over the network to an external service, so it should be sent over an encrypted connection and scoped as narrowly as possible, consistent with the least-privilege network practice of allowing only the addresses and users that genuinely need access [source p.403]. Also note the edge case: if Git integration is disabled at the workspace level, a perfectly valid personal token will still not make the Git folders feature appear.

questions.question: Which of the following remote Git providers can be connected directly to a Databricks Git folder? Select all that apply.

options.label: GitHub
GitLab
Bitbucket
Azure DevOps
AWS CodeCommit
Amazon S3

correctAnswer: A
B
C
D
questions.analysis: Databricks supports Git folders against four provider families: GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps. Options A through D are therefore all correct, and each still requires its own per-user Git credential on top of the workspace-level Git integration setting. Option E is the most common misconception: AWS CodeCommit is a Git service, but it is not one of the providers Databricks connects to for Git folders, so choosing it because it is 'a Git host in AWS' is a category error. Option F is a different kind of mistake altogether: Amazon S3 is object storage, not a version-control host — it stores files and blobs but has no branches, commits, or merge semantics. That distinction matters because a pipeline may well pull data from an API, land it in object storage, and then have Spark read it, with the Git folder holding only the code that does the work [source p.84]. A useful diagnostic habit: ask whether the endpoint can answer 'what commit is this file at?' If it cannot, it is storage rather than a Git provider, and Git-folder operations such as clone, pull, and branch switching will not apply to it.

actions.text: Time for a quick checkpoint on what we just covered about Git folders. Go ahead and work through each question on your own — no peeking back at the earlier pages if you can help it.

Take your time, answer all three, and submit when you're ready. Once you do, I'll come back and we'll go through anything that gave you trouble, including how Git folder, workspace folder, and notebook actually differ and what each provider connection requires.

scenes.title: Connecting a Remote Git Repository

elements.content: Connecting a Remote Git Repository
① Credential — under user settings add a PAT or OAuth token; grant minimal scopes [source p.402].
② Create → Git folder — paste the repo URL, then pick the branch [source p.226].
③ Sparse checkout — check out only selected monorepo directories [source p.273].
Exam trap — creation failures are usually credential or permission problems, not the repo [source p.402].
Permissions — CAN READ / CAN RUN / CAN EDIT / CAN MANAGE on the Git folder are separate from workspace object permissions [source p.402].
Worked example — github.com/acme/etl, branch release/2024.11, sparse src/jobs/: 38 of 1,240 files (3%).

actions.text: Now that we know what a Git folder is, let's actually connect one to a remote repository. This is a short, very mechanical procedure, and the exam expects you to know the order of the steps.

Step one happens outside the workspace entirely. Under your user settings, you add a Git credential for your provider — either a personal access token, a PAT, or an OAuth connection. Until that credential exists, Databricks has no way to authenticate to GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket on your behalf, so nothing downstream will work.

Step two happens back in the workspace. You use Create, then Git folder, paste the repository URL, and select the branch you want to check out. That branch is what lands in the folder — you are not cloning every branch, just the one you asked for.

Step three is optional but very useful in real projects. Sparse checkout restricts the checkout to selected directories, so you only pull the monorepo subfolder you actually work in. On a large repository, that keeps the folder small and the sync fast.

Here's a concrete example. Suppose the repository is github.com/acme/etl and you want the release branch. You paste that URL, select release, and if the repo is a monorepo you point sparse checkout at just the pipeline directory you own. Three decisions: credential, URL plus branch, and optionally a path.

Now the exam trap. When creating a Git folder fails, the overwhelming majority of the time the cause is the credential or a permission on the repository — not a problem with the repository itself. If your token expired, or the credential was never added for that provider, or your account lacks access to that repo, creation fails. So the diagnostic order is: credential first, permissions second, repository contents last.

Finally, a distinction people miss. Git folder permissions — CAN READ, CAN RUN, CAN EDIT, CAN MANAGE — control what a user can do inside the Git folder. Those are completely separate from workspace object permissions on the notebooks and files inside it. A user can have CAN EDIT on the Git folder and still be denied access to a specific notebook, because the two permission models are independent.

To recap this page: credential first, then Create, Git folder with URL and branch, then optional sparse checkout for monorepos. Remember that failures usually point at credentials or permissions, and remember that Git folder permissions are not the same thing as workspace object permissions.

scenes.title: Interactive: The Sync Cycle Between Remote Repository and Git Folder

content.html:
🔁

The Sync Cycle: Remote Repository ↔ Databricks Git Folder

Click any stage to see the Databricks UI action and its Git equivalent.

Step 1 / 8
Remote Inbound (clone / pull) Outbound (push) Remote event Conflict

nodes.label: Remote Repository
nodes.details: The shared branch hosted on GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, or Bitbucket. This is 'origin' — the single source of truth every workspace syncs against. Databricks reaches it through a Git credential (personal access token or OAuth) attached to the Git folder.
nodes.ui: Workspace → Create → Git folder (in older UIs: Repos → Add repository). Paste the repository URL, choose a Git credential, select the branch, then Create.

nodes.label: Clone branch
nodes.details: Clone copies the selected branch into the workspace and creates the Git folder. From this moment everything you do happens against your local checkout — not against the remote. A teammate will not see your edits until you push.
nodes.ui: In the Create Git folder dialog: repository URL + Git credential → select the branch → Create. Databricks then shows the folder together with the branch name and the latest commit.

nodes.label: Databricks Git folder
nodes.details: This is your working tree — the local checkout that Databricks tracks and mirrors to the branch. Notebooks and files here can be edited directly in the workspace editor. The Git dialog lives on this folder and always shows the current branch, the latest commit, and any changed files.
nodes.ui: Right-click the folder → Git… to Commit, Push, Pull, or Create branch. The folder header shows the branch and an 'out of date' indicator when the remote has moved ahead.

nodes.label: Uncommitted local edits
nodes.details: Edits live only in your workspace until you commit them. Databricks marks the Git folder with a change indicator and lists the modified notebooks in the Git dialog. Nothing has reached the remote yet — a teammate cannot see these changes.
nodes.ui: Edit notebooks in the workspace. The Git dialog lists the modified files and requires a commit message before it will publish anything.

nodes.label: Commit & Push
nodes.details: A commit is a snapshot recorded in your local branch; push publishes that snapshot to the remote branch so teammates can pull it. Databricks performs both steps from a single dialog and can additionally open a pull request (PR) for review.
nodes.ui: Git folder → Git… → select the branch → type a commit message → Commit & Push (or Commit & Push with PR). An empty commit message is rejected.
nodes.git:
git add -A
git commit -m "message"
git push origin <branch>

nodes.label: Pull
nodes.details: Pull = fetch + merge: it downloads the new commits from the remote branch and merges them into your local checkout. Databricks deliberately blocks the pull when you have uncommitted changes, so your work is never overwritten silently.
nodes.ui: Git folder → Git… → Pull (or click the 'out of date' indicator and pull). If the workspace is dirty, Databricks first asks you to commit your changes.
nodes.git:
git fetch origin
git pull origin <branch>   # or git pull --rebase

nodes.label: Teammate pushes
nodes.details: Another engineer commits and pushes to the same branch. The remote now holds commits your checkout does not have, and your Git folder stays on the older commit until you pull. This is the classic 'remote moved ahead' divergence.
nodes.ui: Databricks surfaces the divergence: the Git folder shows an 'out of date' badge and the Git dialog offers Pull so you can catch up.
nodes.git:
git fetch origin
git log HEAD..origin/<branch> --oneline

nodes.label: Conflict checkpoint
nodes.details: Scenario: you have uncommitted edits AND a teammate pushes. Pull is blocked. Choose one path: (a) commit your work, then pull, resolve any conflicts in the editor, commit the merge, and push; or (b) stash, pull, then re-apply. Databricks never silently discards local work.
nodes.ui: Pull fails with 'You have uncommitted changes'. The Git dialog forces a decision — commit your changes, or discard them — before the pull can run.
nodes.git:
git stash
git pull origin <branch>
git stash pop   # resolve conflicts, then commit

actions.text: Now that we've covered credentials and permissions, let's walk the sync cycle that keeps a Databricks Git folder aligned with its remote repository. Use the Next button to step through each stage.

actions.content: Remote repository: the shared origin.
Clone creates the Git folder from the selected branch.

actions.text: From here, your edits stay local. Databricks marks changed files, but nothing reaches the remote until you commit and push. Commit records a snapshot; push publishes it so teammates can pull.

actions.content: Commit & Push publishes your snapshot to the remote branch.
Pull fetches and merges remote changes into your local checkout.

actions.text: But if a teammate pushes while you have uncommitted edits, Databricks blocks the pull to protect your work — that's the conflict checkpoint. Click any stage to see the Databricks UI action and the equivalent Git command.

actions.content: Uncommitted changes block a pull: commit or stash first.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Connecting Repositories and Syncing Changes

questions.question: In a Databricks Git folder, which sequence correctly describes the routine collaboration loop when a teammate has already committed new work to the remote repository since your last sync?

options.label: Edit in the workspace folder, then pull, then commit to the remote, then push your branch
Pull to bring remote commits into your workspace folder, edit your notebook or file, commit to record the change in local history, then push to publish your commits to the remote
Commit your edits, push them, pull the teammates' commits, then edit again to reconcile the two histories
Push your local snapshot first, edit in place on the remote, then pull the merged result back into the workspace folder

questions.analysis: The correct order is pull, edit, commit, push. A pull is a read from the remote into your working checkout: the remote is the source and your Git folder is the target, which is exactly the pull model described in the lifecycle chapter, where 'a pull strategy (Figure 7-8) entails a target reading data directly from a source' [source p.270]. The equivalent ingestion framing is that in timestamp-based CDC 'an ingestion system queries the source database and pulls the rows that have changed since the previous update' [source p.68] - a git pull fetches precisely the commits that changed since your last sync. Only after that read do you edit, because editing against a stale base is what creates divergence. The commit then records a consistent snapshot in your local repository history, which is the same notion as a database commit, a change such as creating, updating, or deleting a record or object that keeps a consistent state [source p.304]. Push is the opposite direction: a push strategy 'involves a source system sending data to a target' [source p.270], so push is the step that makes your commits visible to teammates. Option A is wrong because commit is a local operation and cannot 'commit to the remote'. Option C inverts the loop and produces a rejected push as often as not. Option D is wrong because a push cannot succeed while the remote tip has moved ahead of your base, and because you cannot edit 'in place on the remote' through a Git folder - the workspace folder is your working checkout.

questions.question: You edit a notebook in your Git folder, run a commit, and the push fails with 'Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally.' Your local branch tip is a91c4d2, which was created from parent commit 3de8f70, but the remote branch now points at f37e2b1. What is the correct diagnosis and the correct first corrective step?

options.label: Your personal access token expired, so the credential must be re-entered before the push can reach the remote

Your local commit was built on a base that the remote tip has since moved past, so the push is a non-fast-forward rejection; pull the remote commits, resolve any overlap with your edits, then push again
Unity Catalog privileges on the owning catalog were revoked, so you need USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA before the push can complete
The Git folder lost its branch state because it is attached to an all-purpose cluster instead of a SQL warehouse, so restart the cluster and re-push

questions.analysis: The rejection message is a non-fast-forward error, and the evidence is in the parent relationship: your commit a91c4d2 descends from 3de8f70, but the branch on the remote has advanced to f37e2b1, which is not an ancestor of your commit. Git refuses to overwrite f37e2b1 with a history that does not contain it. This is the classic divergence produced by skipping the pull step of the pull-edit-commit-push loop. The fix is to reconcile first: pull the remote commits into your workspace folder so the remote commit joins your local history, resolve any textual overlap between your edits and the teammate's edits, then push the merged result. The reconciliation-before-write discipline mirrors the streaming consumer pattern, where subscribers 'read messages from a topic and confirm when they have been processed' [source p.276] - you confirm you have integrated the remote state before you publish your own. Thinking of a commit as a consistent snapshot also clarifies why the base matters: a commit keeps a consistent state of the repository across a sequence of changes, and a commit built on an outdated parent is simply not the state the remote is expected to accept [source p.304]. Option A is wrong because an authorization or credential failure surfaces as an authentication error, not as a message about remote work you do not have locally. Option C confuses Unity Catalog governance with Git transport; catalog privileges govern table access, not repository writes. Option D is wrong because compute type has no bearing on Git refs - branch state lives in the repository, not in the cluster.

questions.question: Select all statements that correctly distinguish what a pull does to the working checkout from what a commit does to the remote repository. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A pull changes files in your workspace working checkout by bringing in the commits that exist on the remote branch since your last sync.
A commit records a snapshot in the local repository history inside the Git folder, but it sends nothing to GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps until a push succeeds.
A commit publishes your changes to the remote immediately, so the remote branch is already updated even if the subsequent push fails.
A push is what makes your commits visible to teammates on the remote, and until that push succeeds the remote branch still points at its previous tip.
A pull overwrites the remote branch with your local edits, so pulling after a rejected push resolves the conflict by discarding the teammate's work.

questions.analysis: A pull is a read in the inbound direction: the remote is the source and your workspace folder is the target, matching the pull model in which 'a target reads data directly from a source' [source p.270]. Concretely, a pull brings in only the new commits - the equivalent of the CDC case where the reader 'pulls the rows that have changed since the previous update' [source p.68] - which is why option A is correct and why nothing outside your working checkout changes. Option B is correct because a commit is a local durability and consistency operation. Commits exist to keep a consistent state of the repository while it is active and in the event of a failure, and they handle isolation when concurrent editors touch the same objects [source p.304]; none of that requires the remote to be contacted, so a commit is invisible to teammates until it is pushed. Option D is correct and is the mirror image of B: pushing is the outbound direction, where a source writes data out to a target, so the remote branch tip only advances when the push is accepted [source p.270]. Option C is the single most common student misconception - it conflates commit with push. If C were true, a rejected push would be harmless, yet a rejected push is exactly the signal that the remote was never updated. Option E inverts the direction of transfer and of conflict resolution: a pull reads from the remote into your checkout, it never writes to the remote, and the standard resolution preserves both histories through a merge or rebase rather than discarding the teammate's commit. The practical rule to carry into the exam is directional: pull and push move commits across the workspace-remote boundary in opposite directions, while commit and branch are local Git state that only becomes shared data after a push.

actions.text: You've just walked through the sync cycle stage by stage, so let's see how much of it sticks. There are three questions ahead — one of them asks you to select all that apply, so read the options carefully before you lock anything in.
Work through each one on your own; I'll hold off on commenting until you've submitted. Once you're done, I'll come back and we'll go through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Branches Inside a Databricks Git Folder

elements.content: Branches Inside a Databricks Git Folder
• Branch control creates a branch at the current commit and switches to it inside the workspace.
• A switch needs a clean tree: commit, discard, or resolve conflicting edits first [source p.304].
• Merge locally, or open a pull request when branch policies require review [source p.290].
• Each branch is an independent tree of files, so parallel edits never overwrite one another [source p.290].
• Revert records a new commit that undoes an earlier one and preserves shared history.
• Discard throws away uncommitted local edits and adds nothing to shared history.

Worked example — main → release-2.1 with 2 modified notebooks: attempt 1 fails on 2 uncommitted files.

Commit both edits → 0 conflicts → attempt 2 switches successfully; reverting the merge later keeps both revisions [source p.304].

Jobs run against a Git reference (branch, tag, commit).

Databricks runs the sync as a managed service [source p.171].

actions.text: Nice work on that checkpoint. Now that we understand how a Git folder connects to a remote repository and how changes sync back and forth, the next piece is branching — because almost no real team commits straight to main. Let's walk through how branches actually behave inside a Databricks Git folder.

The title says it plainly: branches live inside the Databricks Git folder. That means you can create, switch, and reconcile branches without ever leaving the workspace — you don't need a local Git client to do the day-to-day work.

First, creation. The branch control in the Git folder creates a branch at the current commit, then switches you onto it. From that point on, every notebook edit you make is committed to that branch, not to main.

Here's the rule that trips people up. Databricks requires a clean working tree before it will switch branches. If you have uncommitted edits, you must commit them, discard them, or resolve any conflicting changes first — the switch simply won't happen otherwise.

Worth remembering why: each branch is an independent tree of files. The notebooks you see on one branch can be completely different from another, so Git needs a tidy state to swap the working directory safely.

Once the work is finished, you reconcile it. You can merge the branch locally inside the Git folder, or push it and open a pull request when your team's branch policies require review. Both paths end in the same place — the changes land on the target branch.

Now two operations that look similar but are not. Revert records a new commit that undoes an earlier commit — the shared history is preserved, so everyone who has pulled still has a consistent timeline. Discard, by contrast, throws away uncommitted local edits and never touches shared history at all. Exam items love to test which one keeps history intact: that's revert.

And the reason branching matters beyond source control — jobs run against a Git reference, whether that's a branch, a tag, or a specific commit. That's the mechanism by which versioned code reaches production, and it's why the branch you commit to has real consequences for what runs.

The worked example ties it together: going from main to a release-2.1 branch with two modified notebooks. Create the branch, make and commit the edits, then merge or open a pull request — and if something goes wrong downstream, revert rather than discard. Next up, you'll get hands-on with exactly this in the branch and merge sandbox.

actions.text: We just covered how branches live inside a Databricks Git folder — now let's watch that divergence happen live. In this sandbox, main and a feature branch are two separate lines of commits, and you control how far each one moves.

actions.content: Each dot is a commit, each line is a branch, and the dotted link marks where the two branches last shared history.
Load the clean feature branch: Alice and Bob edit different lines of notebook.ipynb.
The merge base — the common ancestor — is the last commit both branches share before they diverged.

actions.text: Notice that Alice's branch is ahead of main while Bob's is on a separate line of work. Edits landing on different lines merge cleanly — but as soon as both engineers touch the same line of the same notebook, Git has no way to decide which version wins.

actions.content: Now both branches edit line 5 of notebook.ipynb.
Read the conflict flag here — this is exactly where Databricks reports a merge conflict inside the Git folder.
Switch Bob to committing directly on main and compare how much larger the conflict surface becomes.

actions.text: Take a minute to drive this yourself: pull Bob back to a different line and watch the conflict clear, then push the merge base depth to three or four commits and see how the common ancestor moves.
