scenes.title: Checkpoint: Branches and the Developer Workflow

questions.question: You are working in a Databricks Git folder checked out on the branch feature/order-cleanup. You have edited transformations/orders_silver.sql in your working tree but have not staged or committed anything. You now use the Git folder's branch selector to switch to main. Assume that transformations/orders_silver.sql has different content on main than on feature/order-cleanup. What does Databricks do?

options.label: Databricks silently discards the uncommitted edits, because a branch switch always resets the working tree to the target branch's HEAD.
Databricks automatically commits the edits to feature/order-cleanup before switching, so the work is preserved and main now contains a new commit.

Databricks refuses the switch for that file and reports a checkout conflict, leaving you on feature/order-cleanup with the edits intact, because applying them to main would overwrite content that differs.
Databricks stashes the edits into a hidden stash, and you must run a Restore stash operation before the edits reappear in either branch.

questions.correctAnswer: C
questions.analysis: Branch switching inside a Git folder follows Git checkout semantics rather than Databricks-specific magic. The precondition for a clean switch is that, for every file you have modified, the target branch either does not modify that file or holds byte-identical content. When that precondition holds, your edits simply carry over and appear as uncommitted changes on the newly checked-out branch: Databricks does not commit them for you (so option B is wrong) and does not throw them away (so option A is wrong). When the precondition fails, as stated in the question, checkout would have to overwrite your work, so the operation aborts and Databricks surfaces the conflict for that file exactly as option C describes; you remain on the original branch until you commit, discard, or reconcile the file. Edge cases worth memorising: Databricks has no automatic stash and no Restore stash command (option D describes a feature that does not exist), and the risk is asymmetric — a clean working tree can always be switched, while a dirty tree can be blocked by a single overlapping file. The deeper reason to care is that an uncommitted edit is not a durable state; as with database commits, a change becomes a recoverable, consistent boundary only at the moment it is committed [source p.304]. Finally, note the difference between switch-time conflicts and pull-time conflicts: switching can only fail on overwrite risk, whereas merge conflicts are reported during pull or merge.

questions.question: A teammate's commit to the shared main branch of your Git folder introduced a broken transformation in the Silver layer of your medallion architecture (Bronze holds raw ingested data, Silver holds cleaned and conformed data, Gold holds aggregated business-level tables). The commit has already been pushed and three other engineers have pulled it. You need the branch to return to its previous behaviour without changing the history those engineers already hold. Which operation do you use?

options.label: Use Discard changes on the modified file in the Git folder, which removes the bad commit from the branch.
Open the Git history for the branch, choose Revert on the offending commit, and push the new commit that Databricks creates.
Reset the branch to the previous commit with a hard reset and force-push so the bad commit disappears from history.
Detach the checkout at the previous commit and then re-clone the repository into a new Git folder.

questions.correctAnswer: B
questions.analysis: Revert and discard operate on different layers, and confusing them is the most common error in this workflow. Discard changes acts only on the working tree: it throws away edits that were never committed and cannot touch anything already recorded in history, so option A is wrong by construction. Revert creates a new commit whose diff is the inverse of the offending commit, so history retains both the bad commit and its reversal; because it only moves the branch forward, it is safe on a branch that teammates have already pulled, which makes option B correct. Reset plus force-push rewrites published history: every engineer who pulled the bad commit now holds a diverged branch, their next push is rejected or silently resurrects the discarded work, and any local commits they made on top are at risk — that is the classic misconception in option C, and it is acceptable only on a private branch that has never been pulled by anyone. Option D neither restores what other engineers see nor preserves your own local work. The general principle is to select the operation that matches the state of the shared system rather than the operation with the shortest description, which is the same judgement the source material demands when it tells you to understand the appropriate update pattern for the database or data store you are working with [source p.273]; shared branches are precisely the case where loosely coupled teams must still agree on common standards, ownership, and accountability [source p.116].

questions.question: Databricks reports a merge conflict in a Git folder under which of the following conditions? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Your working tree holds uncommitted edits to specific lines, and a pull brings in remote commits that changed those same lines.
One branch modifies a file while the branch being merged into it deleted or renamed that same file.
Two branches each commit changes to the same region of the same file, and you merge one branch into the other.
Two engineers edit different files in the same repository and one of them pulls after committing.
You switch branches with a clean working tree, and the files you previously touched are identical on both branches.

questions.correctAnswer: A,B,C
questions.analysis: Merge conflicts are deterministic rather than random: Git reports one only when it cannot combine the two sides without a human decision, and there are three recurring conditions. First, both sides changed the same region of the same file, which covers option A (a dirty working tree versus incoming remote changes to those exact lines) and option C (two branches committing edits to the same region and then being merged). Second, a modify/delete collision: one side edits a file while the other deletes or renames it, as in option B, because Git cannot decide whether the file should exist at all. Third, by contrast, non-overlapping work never conflicts — edits to different files, or to disjoint regions of the same file, are merged automatically, so options D and E are wrong; option E is doubly wrong because a clean working tree can never produce a conflict, only the possibility of stale or overwritten content. Two edge cases are worth stating precisely. Conflicts are reported at pull or merge time, not at switch time, so 'I changed branches and nothing happened' is not evidence that a later merge will be clean. And resolution is only complete once the conflict markers the Databricks editor inserts are edited away and the result is staged, committed, and pushed; until then the merge stays unresolved. Practically, conflict probability scales with how many small, overlapping commits accumulate on diverging branches before integration — the same clutter effect the source material warns about when many small commits are made instead of a smaller number of larger, coherent ones [source p.304]. Because collaborative data engineering is fundamentally a team discipline in which the role sits at the center of the modern data platform [source p.3], these conflict rules are part of the assessed collaboration vocabulary rather than an optional detail.

This checkpoint covers switching branches, merging, reverting, and discarding, plus when Databricks actually reports a conflict. Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer before moving on; the reasoning matters more than the guess.
Take your time, especially on the multiple-select one — read every option carefully. Once you submit, I'll walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Git Folder vs. Workspace Folder vs. Local Git Client

elements.content: Dimension  |  Git folder  |  Workspace folder  |  Local Git client

Version control and history model
Git folder: A Git folder is an actual checkout of a remote repository (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps) inside the workspace, so every notebook and file in it carries the commit graph, blame, and diffs of the branch that was checked out.
Workspace folder: A workspace folder is only a container in the workspace's own metadata store, so each save overwrites the previous content in place and no commit graph, diff, or blame exists anywhere.
Local Git client: A local Git client keeps the authoritative history in the developer's clone and in the remote, so the workspace only ever sees whichever revision the developer explicitly synced in.

History semantics under concurrent or repeated edits
Git folder: A Git folder behaves like the insert-only update pattern described in the course material: new commits are appended rather than overwriting earlier ones, so the current state of a file is found by resolving its newest revision [source p.342].
Workspace folder: A workspace folder behaves like the truncate-and-reload update pattern: the prior content is cleared and the transformation is rerun to produce a new version, so an in-place save replaces the previous version and leaves nothing recoverable [source p.342].
Local Git client: A local Git client also follows insert-only history, but the append happens outside the platform, so the workspace copy diverges silently from the repository the moment someone edits directly in Databricks.

Native Databricks execution and revision pinning
Git folder: Notebooks in a Git folder execute natively in the workspace, and a job can be pinned to a specific branch, tag, or commit, so a production run against commit 9f3c2a1 is reproducible on demand.
Workspace folder: Notebooks in a workspace folder also execute natively, but a job points at a mutable path with no branch awareness, so any edit changes production behavior on the next run with no rollout gate.
Local Git client: Code authored in a local Git client never executes on the platform as-is; it must be imported, uploaded, or built into a wheel or Asset Bundle and synced before a job can reference it.

Permissions and access control model
Git folder: Access to a Git folder is layered across three independent control planes: workspace folder permissions (CAN VIEW, CAN RUN, CAN EDIT, MANAGE) govern who can open and modify the checkout, the remote provider governs who can push to the branch, and Unity Catalog governs which data the code may read.
Workspace folder: A workspace folder is governed only by the workspace ACL, so a user holding edit rights can silently overwrite a shared notebook and no repository-level review or branch protection exists to intercept the change.
Local Git client: A local Git client is governed by the remote's repository permissions plus each developer's personal access token or OAuth credential, while the workspace sees only artifacts that were synced in and the local filesystem itself is ungoverned by Databricks.

Synchronization mechanics and conflict handling
Git folder: The sync cycle is explicit in a Git folder: Pull fetches and merges remote changes into the checkout, edits are staged, and Commit & Push publishes them, and Databricks requires a clean working tree before a branch switch, so pending changes must be committed, discarded, or resolved first.
Workspace folder: A workspace folder has no sync cycle at all, because the workspace copy is the only copy, so two engineers editing the same notebook produce last-writer-wins overwrites with no merge step and no warning.
Local Git client: A local Git client resolves pull, rebase, and merge conflicts with full local diff and merge tooling, and the workspace receives only the merged result that the developer or pipeline subsequently pushes or syncs.

CI/CD suitability and promotion gates
Git folder: Commits pushed from a Git folder can trigger the provider's CI, and Databricks Asset Bundles read job and pipeline definitions straight from the repository, which is what makes the analytics-as-code practice of treating transformations as reviewable, testable software artifacts enforceable through pull requests and automated tests [source p.359].
Workspace folder: A workspace folder emits no commit event to trigger a pipeline, so promotion means copying files through the workspace API or exporting notebooks by hand, and drift between development and production is unavoidable and unauditable.
Local Git client: A local Git client supports CI/CD fully because the same repository is built and tested locally and in the pipeline, but any notebook created only inside the workspace is invisible to that pipeline until someone commits it back to the repository.

Backup and recoverability (the documentation exam trap)
Git folder: A deleted or corrupted notebook in a Git folder is restored by checking out the prior commit, and even deleting the entire workspace folder does not lose history because the remote still holds every commit.
Workspace folder: A workspace folder has no version history and no dependable restore point, so an overwritten notebook, a failed refactor, or a deleted folder loses the content permanently; the exam trap is assuming workspace folders are versioned or recoverable, which they are not.
Local Git client: Recovery in a local Git client depends entirely on what was committed: work pushed to the remote is fully recoverable, while code typed directly into a Databricks notebook and never synced back to the local clone is just as exposed as it would be in a workspace folder.

Fit with touchless production and development-to-production separation
Git folder: A Git folder directly supports touchless production, because engineers develop and test against simulated or cleansed data in development and staging environments and automated code deployments then promote the committed code to production without anyone hand-editing a production workspace [source p.291].
Workspace folder: Authoring directly in a production workspace folder is the opposite of touchless production, and when a bug cannot be reproduced without live data the compensating control is a broken-glass process that requires at least two approvals before production data is touched [source p.291].
Local Git client: A local Git client is the strongest fit for touchless production because code is never authored in production at all; the workspace receives only pipeline-built artifacts and production data is reached through automated deployment rather than interactive editing [source p.291].

Toolchain and code portability
Git folder: The repository is the unit of portability for a Git folder: the same branch checked out on Windows, Linux, or macOS yields identical files, and SQL, Python, and JVM-based transformation code are versioned together, an advantage analogous to shipping a single JDBC driver that any JVM language can use instead of maintaining native binaries per architecture and OS [source p.277].
Workspace folder: Portability for a workspace folder is manual, because content lives in workspace metadata, so moving it to another workspace or a CI runner requires exporting notebooks one by one or calling the workspace API, and no single artifact can be consumed by a second system.
Local Git client: For a local Git client the clone plus the remote is portable to any machine with Git installed, but Databricks-specific glue such as job definitions, cluster policy references, and Unity Catalog grants is not portable unless it is captured in versioned configuration such as Databricks Asset Bundles.

Worked example: onboarding and recovery cost for an eight-engineer team
Git folder: Worked example: onboarding a new hire on Git folders costs about 30 minutes (add a PAT or OAuth credential, choose Create, select Git folder, paste the repository URL, pick the branch) plus roughly 5 minutes to clone a 2,000-file monorepo over a 100 Mbit/s link, and restoring a notebook deleted at 17:00 takes one checkout of the previous commit, about 5 minutes of work.
Workspace folder: Worked example: the same hire on workspace folders costs 4 to 6 hours of manually re-sharing folders and undocumented walkthroughs, and the 17:00 deletion is unrecoverable, so re-deriving a 300-line transformation notebook from memory and job logs typically costs 1 to 2 engineer-days per incident.
Local Git client: Worked example: the same hire on a local Git client costs 2 to 3 hours to install the toolchain, clone the repository, and configure the Databricks CLI or Asset Bundle, but the workspace is then updated only by a pipeline or an explicit sync command, adding a build-and-ship latency that a 15-minute hotfix must absorb.

Takeaway — Choose a Git folder whenever code is shared, must be versioned, or must run against a specific branch, tag, or commit, since pinning a job to an immutable revision is the only way to make a production run reproducible.
Takeaway — Use a plain workspace folder only for scratch exploration and genuinely non-versioned work, and never treat it as a backup: workspace folders are not versioned and are not recoverable.

Takeaway — Choose a local Git client when developers edit outside Databricks and sync code in only when it needs to run on the platform, accepting that anything created directly in the workspace stays outside the repository until someone commits it.

Takeaway — Whichever option you pick, keep job definitions, cluster policy references, and Unity Catalog grants in versioned configuration, so reproducing a production run requires a clone and a credential rather than a walkthrough of the workspace.

actions.text: We just worked through branches and merges inside a Git folder. Now let's zoom out and answer a question the exam asks in several different ways: where should a data engineer actually keep code in a Databricks-centric workflow? There are three options, and each one is the right answer in a specific situation.

This table lines up the three options — a Databricks Git folder, a plain workspace folder, and a local Git client used outside Databricks — against the dimensions that actually drive the decision: version control, execution, permissions, CI/CD, backup, and portability. Read it as a decision matrix, not as a list of features.

Start with the version control and history model. A Git folder is backed by a remote repository, so every change is committed, branches exist, and you can roll back to any earlier state. A plain workspace folder has no history at all — whatever is in it is simply whatever the last person saved. A local Git client keeps full history too, but that history lives in your local repo and the remote, not inside Databricks.

Next, native Databricks execution and revision pinning. A Git folder runs natively on the platform and can be pinned to a branch, a tag, or a specific commit — exactly what you need when a job must run against a frozen revision. A workspace folder also executes natively, but there is nothing to pin. A local Git client only helps once you sync the code in; the source of truth stays on the developer's machine.

Careful, this is the row the exam loves. Backup and recoverability. A Git folder is recoverable, because the remote repository is a real backup. A local Git client is recoverable too, provided the work is pushed to a remote. A workspace folder is neither versioned nor recoverable — if someone deletes it, it is gone. The trap is assuming that because a workspace folder lives inside Databricks, it must be versioned or restorable. It is not.

So, three takeaways. Choose a Git folder whenever code is shared, versioned, and something — a notebook or a job — must run against a branch, a tag, or a commit. Use a plain workspace folder only for scratch exploration and non-versioned work; it gives you no history and no backup. And choose a local Git client when developers edit outside Databricks and only sync code in when it needs to run on the platform.

And whichever option you pick, keep job definitions and production logic in a versioned place. The workspace folder is a convenience, never a system of record. On the next page we'll put this into practice by recovering a diverged feature branch.

scenes.title: Exercise: Recover a Diverged Feature Branch

elements.content: Problem 1

Your Databricks Git folder is connected to `https://github.com/acme/retail-lakehouse.git`. You are on branch `feature/total-sales-by-region`, based at merge base $B$. In `notebooks/sales_report.py`, cell 3 at $B$ is:

```sql

SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total_sales FROM sales GROUP BY region;

```

Your feature branch has commit $A1$ changing cell 3 to:

```sql

SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total_sales FROM sales WHERE region = 'EMEA' GROUP BY region;

```

A teammate has merged `main` at commit $M2$, which changes the same cell 3 to:

```sql

SELECT region, SUM(amount_net) AS total_sales FROM sales GROUP BY region;

```

and adds a new cell 4 computing `SUM(tax)`. You also have an uncommitted edit in cell 2 that changes `date >= '2024-01-01'` to `date >= '2024-04-01'`. When you pull or merge `origin/main` into your feature branch, Databricks reports a conflict on `notebooks/sales_report.py`. Give the exact recovery sequence that preserves both teammates' edits, including the resolved cell 3, the commands or UI actions, commit message, push, and pull request. Use concrete branch names and hashes.
Hint: commit your local work first, then merge `origin/main`, resolve each conflicting cell in the diff view, commit, push, and open a PR.

Worked solution
Step 1: make the working tree clean. Databricks requires a clean working tree before branch changes or merges, so commit the cell 2 edit on `feature/total-sales-by-region`:

```bash

git add notebooks/sales_report.py

git commit -m 'Add April 2024 filter to sales report'

```

This creates commit $A2$. Now `git status` is clean.

Step 2: fetch and merge the remote main branch into the feature branch. In a Databricks Git folder, use the pull/merge action for `origin/main`; from a terminal or local clone the command is:

```bash

git fetch origin

git merge origin/main

```

The merge stops with a conflict on `notebooks/sales_report.py`.

Step 3: inspect the conflicting notebook in the Databricks diff view. The conflicted cell 3 contains text markers:

```text

<<<<<<< HEAD

SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total_sales

FROM sales

WHERE region = 'EMEA'

GROUP BY region

=======

SELECT region, SUM(amount_net) AS total_sales

FROM sales

GROUP BY region

>>>>>>> origin/main

```

Resolve cell 3 by combining both intents: keep the teammate's corrected net-amount column and keep your EMEA filter. The resolved cell is:

```sql

SELECT region, SUM(amount_net) AS total_sales

FROM sales

WHERE region = 'EMEA'

GROUP BY region;

```

Do not delete cell 4; it was added only on `main`, so it should remain. Cell 2 was changed only on your branch, so it should also remain with the April filter.

Step 4: stage and commit the resolution:

```bash

git add notebooks/sales_report.py

git commit -m 'Merge origin/main into feature/total-sales-by-region; resolve total_sales conflict by combining amount_net with EMEA filter'

```

Step 5: push the feature branch:

```bash

git push origin feature/total-sales-by-region

```

Step 6: open a pull request from `feature/total-sales-by-region` into `main`. In the Git provider, confirm the PR no longer reports conflicts, request review, and merge. The final branch history contains $A1$, $A2$, $M2$, and the merge commit.

Analysis — Git uses the merge base $B$ to perform a three-way merge. It compares $B$ to your branch and $B$ to `origin/main`. Cell 3 conflicts because both sides changed the same SQL lines. Cell 4 does not conflict because only $M2$ changed it. Cell 2 does not conflict because only you changed it. This is exactly the isolation problem that transactions solve in databases: a commit is a change such as creating, updating, or deleting a record, and transactions keep a consistent state while multiple concurrent events read and write the same objects [source p.304]. Without that consistency boundary, users can get conflicting information [source p.304]. Git commits play the same role for branches. A pull is a pull-model operation: data, here commits, is retrieved from the source remote rather than pushed from it [source p.68]. The common pitfall is to discard changes instead of resolving them; that silently destroys a teammate's edits. An edge case is that if both branches make the identical change on the same line, Git may auto-merge without a conflict. Another edge case is `.ipynb` notebooks: Databricks may present cell-level conflict resolution, and you must choose or combine cells rather than edit raw JSON. Dependency conflicts are a constant problem when many services share one codebase [source p.168]; branch isolation reduces blast radius, but shared notebooks still require deliberate merge resolution.
Problem 2

During the same conflict, a teammate opens the Databricks Git folder, sees the conflicted `notebooks/sales_report.py`, and clicks `Discard changes` to make the conflict disappear. They then pull `origin/main`, commit, and push. Explain exactly what is lost, why the loss can be silent, how to recover the teammate's `amount_net` change and your `region = 'EMEA'` change, and what operation should have been used. Include one concrete recovery command sequence.
Hint: Discard resets the working tree; it is not a merge resolution.

Worked solution
What is lost: `Discard changes` resets the file to the last committed state on the current branch, which is HEAD of `feature/total-sales-by-region`. It removes the conflict markers and also removes any uncommitted edits in that file. If your `WHERE region = 'EMEA'` change was still uncommitted, it is gone from Git. If the teammate's `SUM(amount_net)` change exists only in `origin/main` and has not been merged, discarding the conflict means the feature branch never incorporates that change. If the teammate then commits and pushes, the later PR can drop the `amount_net` fix when it merges into `main`, because the feature branch never recorded it.

Why it is silent: Git does not track uncommitted working-tree changes. There is no commit, no branch, and no reflog entry for a discarded edit. The loss appears only when someone later notices that the notebook reverted to old SQL. Databricks notebook cell history may help, because cell-level version history can retain earlier cell contents even when Git does not.

Recovery if the discard was not committed: open the notebook's version history or cell history in Databricks and recover the lost cell text. Then redo the merge:

```bash

git fetch origin

git merge origin/main

```

Resolve cell 3 to combine both changes:

```sql

SELECT region, SUM(amount_net) AS total_sales

FROM sales

WHERE region = 'EMEA'

GROUP BY region;

```

Recovery if the bad discard was committed and pushed: find the pre-discard state in the reflog, then create a corrective branch or revert. For example:

```bash

git reflog

# identify <good> before the discard commit

git branch recovery/pre-discard <good>

git diff recovery/pre-discard -- notebooks/sales_report.py

```

If the bad commit is already on the shared remote, do not force push. Instead create a corrective commit that restores the lost `amount_net` logic and re-applies the merge resolution, then open a new PR.

The correct operation is: edit the conflicted cell, remove the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers, choose or combine the cell contents, then `git add` and `git commit`. In the Databricks diff view, use the per-cell accept/keep/merge controls rather than `Discard changes`.

Analysis — `Discard` is dangerous because it is a working-tree operation, not a merge resolution. A database analogy is a dirty read: a row is read while an uncommitted transaction has altered it, so the reader sees a state that may never be committed [source p.304]. Discarding the conflict is like ignoring the concurrent change and then committing a state that never included it. The loss is silent because Git does not version uncommitted work. The edge case is that if the teammate had already committed the conflict resolution, recovery is easier: Git keeps that commit in the reflog until garbage collection. If the notebook has Databricks cell history, recovery may be possible even for uncommitted cell edits. The general rule is to commit or stash before any destructive operation. Databricks enforces a clean working tree before branch changes precisely to prevent this class of silent data loss. At team scale, dependency conflicts are a constant problem when many services share one codebase [source p.168]; a discarded merge resolution is a human-driven version of the same conflict, and it can propagate into the main branch as a missing dependency or missing column.
Problem 3

On shared branch `feature/total-sales-by-region`, commit `9f3c2a1` was accidentally pushed. It adds `notebooks/debug_scratch.py` with a hard-coded test credential and also changes cell 5 of `sales_report.py` to print a debug DataFrame. Two teammates have already pulled `9f3c2a1`. You must undo it. Compare `git revert 9f3c2a1` with `git reset --hard 9f3c2a1~1` followed by `git push --force-with-lease origin feature/total-sales-by-region`. Give the exact commands for each, state which one is safe here, and explain the consequence for the teammates and for the merge base when the feature branch is later merged to `main`.
Hint: Shared history should be corrected by appending, not rewriting, unless everyone agrees.

Worked solution
Safe option: `git revert 9f3c2a1`. Exact commands:

```bash

git switch feature/total-sales-by-region

git revert 9f3c2a1

# if conflicts occur, resolve them, then:

git revert --continue

git push origin feature/total-sales-by-region

```

This creates a new commit $R$ that inverses the changes from `9f3c2a1`. History becomes `... -> 9f3c2a1 -> R`. Teammates who already pulled simply run `git pull` and receive $R$. Their local branches remain compatible because the branch only moved forward. When `feature/total-sales-by-region` is merged to `main`, the net diff excludes the debug file and the debug cell because the revert cancels them.

Risky option: `git reset --hard 9f3c2a1~1` followed by a force push:

```bash

git reset --hard 9f3c2a1~1

git push --force-with-lease origin feature/total-sales-by-region

```

This rewrites the shared branch so `9f3c2a1` is removed from the branch tip. Teammates who already pulled `9f3c2a1` now have a divergent history. Their next pull will fail as non-fast-forward, or if they force pull they may reintroduce the bad commit. Their local merge base with `main` still descends from the old history, so their later PRs can contain duplicate commits or unexpected conflicts. The safe choice is revert for any commit that has already been pushed and pulled by others.

Edge case: if `notebooks/debug_scratch.py` contains a real credential, revert removes it from the tip but not from Git history. You must rotate the credential immediately and coordinate a history purge with tools such as `git filter-repo` or BFG, then have every teammate re-clone or reset. If branch protection disables force push, the revert must go through a pull request.

Analysis — A commit is a durable change in a versioned history, analogous to a database commit that creates, updates, or deletes objects [source p.304]. Revert preserves history and appends a corrective transaction, which is the safest model for shared branches. Reset --hard rewrites history, changing the identity of every descendant commit. For anyone who already pulled, this creates a divergent state where the remote and local no longer share the same commit graph. The pull-versus-push distinction matters: a normal pull retrieves remote work, while a force push overwrites the remote reference without retrieving others' work [source p.68]. Dependency conflicts are a constant problem when many services share one codebase [source p.168]; rewriting shared history multiplies those conflicts because every teammate's local dependencies on commit hashes become invalid. Use revert for shared branches. Reserve reset and force push for private branches, or for cases where every collaborator explicitly agrees to reset and re-clone.
Problem 4

A Databricks Git folder is on branch `feature/a` with an uncommitted edit to `notebooks/job.py`. You try to switch to `main`. Which statement is correct? A) Databricks automatically stashes the edit and switches. B) Databricks switches and carries the uncommitted edit to `main`. C) Databricks blocks the branch switch until the working tree is clean; you must commit, discard, or resolve changes first. D) Databricks deletes the edit and switches. Choose one and justify your choice.
Hint: Think about what a branch switch would do to work that has no commit.

Worked solution
Correct choice: C. Databricks requires a clean working tree before a branch switch. It does not auto-stash the edit and it does not carry an uncommitted edit across branches, because that would make the edit appear on a branch where it was never committed. It also should not silently delete the edit. The platform presents commit, discard, or resolve options. If you commit, the edit becomes a commit on `feature/a`. If you discard, the edit is removed from the working tree. If you resolve, you address any conflict first. After handling the file, `git status` should be clean and then the switch to `main` succeeds. Edge case: untracked files may or may not block the switch depending on workspace policy, but modified tracked files do require resolution.

Analysis — The rule exists because an uncommitted change has no commit identity. If Databricks carried it across branches, the same working-tree state would be interpreted against a different HEAD, creating ambiguity about which branch owns the change. This is the same isolation problem that database transactions solve: without a commit or transaction boundary, concurrent operations can read and write inconsistent state [source p.304]. A common mistake is choosing `Discard` just to get unstuck, which silently destroys work. Another mistake is assuming Databricks behaves like a local Git client with `git stash`; Databricks Git folders expose commit, pull, and branch controls, but the safe habit is to commit or deliberately discard before switching. Generalization: treat branch switch as a transaction boundary. The pull-push model also applies: pulling retrieves remote commits [source p.68], and you should not mix uncommitted local edits with a remote update unless you intend to resolve the merge.

actions.text: Now let's put the Git folder workflow into practice. This page works through four progressively harder problems on recovering a diverged feature branch — the exact kind of scenario the exam likes to package as a real ticket.

Problem 1 sets up the classic case: your Git folder is on a feature branch, your teammate has already merged into main, and the next pull throws a conflict on a shared notebook. The key move here is to look at the hint — make your working tree clean first, then merge origin/main. Committing local work before you merge is what keeps you from losing it, and it is also what Databricks requires before you switch branches.

The worked solution is worth memorizing as a sequence: pull, open the conflicting notebook in the diff view, resolve each conflicting cell, then commit and push, and finally open a pull request. Notice that resolution happens cell by cell inside Databricks — you are not editing raw conflict markers in a terminal.

The analysis explains why: Git uses the merge base, the common ancestor commit, to decide which cells actually conflict. Cells changed on only one side merge cleanly; only the cells both you and your teammate touched need a human decision. That is why a clean working tree matters before any branch change — uncommitted edits have no commit to be compared against.

Problem 2 is the trap that catches people in production. A teammate opens the Databricks Git UI mid-conflict and clicks Discard changes. Discard is not a merge operation — it resets the working tree and silently throws away those cell edits with no commit to recover them. Read that hint carefully: it resets, it does not resolve.

Problem 3 pushes you onto a shared branch where an accidental commit has already been pushed. Here the safe answer is git revert — an append-only fix that records a new commit undoing the bad one, leaving shared history intact for everyone who already pulled. Rewriting history with a reset or force-push would force every teammate to reconcile a branch that suddenly moved underneath them.

Problem 4 ties it back to the platform rule: with uncommitted changes, Databricks will refuse to switch branches, and the correct exam answer is the one that commits first. As we covered on page 46, a branch switch swaps the entire working tree, so any uncommitted edits would simply vanish — the restriction exists to protect your work, not to slow you down.

So the thread running through all four: keep the working tree clean before structural Git operations, resolve conflicts cell by cell against the merge base, and never rewrite shared history when revert will do the job. That combination is what recovers a diverged branch without breaking your teammates.

actions.topic: When, if ever, is rewriting shared history the right call instead of using revert?
actions.prompt: Think about a branch only you have pulled, versus a branch your whole team has already fetched. Does the answer change?

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Version Control in Collaborative Data Engineering

questions.question: A data engineering team keeps a shared transformation library plus its notebooks in a Databricks Git folder. Which statement best explains how the Git folder lets the team share reviewed, versioned code inside the workspace?

options.label: Each teammate's Git folder is backed by the remote repository, so a reviewer can approve a feature branch in the Git provider and every teammate then pulls the same reviewed commit into their own workspace checkout, where notebooks execute directly against that revision.
The Git folder copies the repository into each user's home directory at login, so edits made by one teammate appear automatically in another teammate's folder without any pull.
The Git folder stores notebooks as Unity Catalog objects, so version history is inherited from catalog object history and no remote repository is involved.
The Git folder is one shared directory that all teammates edit simultaneously, and Databricks serializes concurrent edits the way a transactional database serializes commits.

questions.analysis: A Git folder is a workspace checkout of a remote Git repository, not a copy of files inside the workspace. Each user clones the repository into their own Git folder, runs notebooks and jobs straight from that checkout, and synchronizes with the remote through pull, commit, and push. Sharing therefore happens through the remote repository: a change becomes shared, reviewed code only after it is committed, pushed to a branch, reviewed, and merged, and other engineers see it after a pull. Option B is wrong because Git folders are not auto-synchronized between users; without a pull, another user's `main` stays at its old commit. Option C is wrong because a Git folder holds files tracked by Git in a remote provider (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps); Unity Catalog governs data objects, not notebook source history — the two systems solve different problems. Option D is wrong because a Git folder is a per-user checkout with its own working tree, and Git does not serialize concurrent edits; conflicts are detected at merge time, not prevented by locking. This sharing responsibility is exactly why version control belongs to the data engineer's remit: data engineers exist to maintain data and code so it stays available and usable by others, and to operate the organization's infrastructure for downstream analysts and scientists [source p.29].

questions.question: Describe the full path a change takes from a feature branch in a Databricks Git folder to a reviewed merge into main. Name each operation in order, state exactly where human review happens and what artifact the reviewer inspects, and explain what blocks the merge if the reviewer requests changes. Also state the condition Databricks imposes on the working tree before you can switch branches to do this work.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Branch creation and clean-tree precondition — 25%. Candidate must state that the feature branch is created from the Git folder's branch control and that Databricks requires a clean working tree before a branch switch or creation, so uncommitted edits must first be committed, discarded, or resolved. (2) Commit and push — 25%. Candidate must state that changes are staged and committed locally with a commit message, then pushed to publish the branch to the remote provider, and that a push is rejected if the remote branch has advanced since the last pull (pull first, then re-push). (3) Review location and artifact — 30%. Candidate must place review in the Git provider (pull request / merge request), not in the Databricks workspace UI, and identify the artifact the reviewer inspects as the diff of the feature branch against main plus commit history; optionally branch protection rules and required CI checks. (4) Merge and post-merge sync — 20%. Candidate must state that the merge is executed in the provider (or locally in the Git folder when no policy requires review), that a conflict on a shared notebook must be resolved before the merge completes, and that teammates pick up the merged result with a pull so their checkouts advance to the reviewed commit. Deduct for vague answers that say review happens in Databricks, or that omit the pull-before-push rule.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: (1) Start from a clean working tree — Databricks refuses a branch switch while uncommitted changes exist, so commit, discard, or resolve them first. (2) Create the feature branch from the Git folder's branch control, which checks out the new branch inside the workspace; no local Git client is required. (3) Edit notebooks and files in the checkout, stage the changes, write a commit message, and commit; the commit records a snapshot in the branch history of the local checkout only. (4) Push the branch to the remote provider, which publishes the commits and makes them visible to reviewers; if the remote branch has commits the checkout does not have, the push is rejected and you must pull, resolve, then push again. (5) Open a pull request (merge request) in the Git provider — this is where review happens, against the diff of the feature branch versus main, together with the commit history and any required status checks. (6) The reviewer approves or requests changes; if changes are requested, the merge is blocked and the author returns to step 3, committing and pushing more commits onto the same branch, which updates the pull request. (7) Merge in the provider once policies are satisfied, or merge locally in the Git folder when no review policy applies. (8) Everyone else pulls to advance their checkouts to the reviewed, merged commit. Note that the merge step is where trouble concentrates in practice — data teams coming from row-based warehouses and column-based cloud systems routinely misjudge merge semantics, and the same is true of Git merges over shared notebook files, where overlapping edits on the same cell region surface as conflicts at merge time [source p.343]. If a merge policy requires review, the Databricks-side merge is not the review; the pull request is.

questions.question: A data engineer wants to create a Git folder from the team's private repository, for example https://github.com/acme/etl-lib. They open Create, then Git folder, paste the URL, select the main branch, and the operation fails with an authentication or permission error, even though the engineer can open the repository in a browser while signed in. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The engineer has no valid Git credential linked for that provider in user settings, or the existing personal access token is expired, revoked, or scoped too narrowly to read the repository, so Databricks cannot authenticate on the engineer's behalf.
Databricks can only create Git folders from public repositories; private repositories must be handled with a local Git client on the engineer's laptop.
The branch selector accepts only a tag or a commit SHA, so choosing a branch name such as main is what causes the checkout to fail.
A sparse checkout pattern must be configured before any Git folder can be created, because Databricks rejects a full repository checkout for private repositories.

questions.analysis: Creating a Git folder has two enablement prerequisites: a workspace admin must enable Git integration for the workspace, and each user must link their own Git credential — a personal access token or OAuth — for the provider. Browser access proves nothing, because that session belongs to the engineer's browser, not to the Databricks workspace; Databricks authenticates with the credential stored under the user's settings, so an absent, expired, revoked, or under-scoped token is the classic cause of an authentication failure on a private repository. Option B is wrong: Databricks supports private repositories on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps, and a local Git client is an alternative workflow, not a requirement. Option C is wrong: the branch control accepts branches, tags, and commits, and selecting main is the normal case. Option D is wrong: sparse checkout is an optional optimization that limits the checkout to selected directories, useful for large monorepos, and is never a precondition for creation. The deeper lesson generalizes: as the field moves quickly, an engineer's durable skill is diagnosing which layer of the stack is actually failing rather than assuming the newest-looking component is at fault [source p.405].

questions.question: Which of the following statements about commit, push, pull, merge, and revert in a Databricks Git folder are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Commit writes a snapshot of the staged changes into the local checkout's branch history; by itself it does not change anything in the remote repository until a push occurs.

Push publishes the checkout's local commits to the remote branch, and Databricks rejects the push when the remote branch holds commits that the local checkout does not have, so a pull is required first.
Pull fetches remote commits and merges them into the local checkout, and uncommitted local edits that overlap the incoming changes can block the update or surface as a conflict.
Merge always creates a distinct merge commit, including when the two branches never diverged and no conflict occurs.
Revert removes the offending commit from the branch history entirely, so after the next push that commit no longer exists on the remote branch.

questions.analysis: A, B, and C are correct. Commit is a local operation: it records a snapshot on the checked-out branch inside the Git folder, and only push transfers that history to the remote, which is why a teammate sees nothing until the author pushes and the teammate pulls. Push is publication, and it fails when the remote has advanced — the standard fix is pull, resolve, then push again, which is the same ordering rule taught for the sync cycle and is a frequent exam scenario. Pull is fetch plus merge into the checkout, so it can be interrupted by uncommitted overlapping edits; Databricks will not silently discard or overwrite a dirty working tree. Option D is wrong because a fast-forward merge, where the target branch has not diverged, simply moves the branch pointer forward and creates no merge commit. Option E is wrong because revert is additive: it creates a new commit that undoes the effect of an earlier one while preserving history, which matters for shared branches; obliterating a commit from history is the behavior of a reset plus force push and is unsafe on shared branches. Note also that the word commit is overloaded in this domain — a database commit is a change within a database, such as creating, updating, or deleting a record or table, and consistency expectations for concurrent readers depend on how the database handles commits and transactions, so do not blur that meaning with a Git commit in exam items [source p.304].

actions.text: Time to check how well that sync cycle and branch workflow stuck. This checkpoint covers the version control objective — sharing reviewed, versioned code in a workspace, the path from feature branch to reviewed merge, creating a Git folder from a private repository, and telling commit, push, pull, merge, and revert apart. Take each question on your own, and write out the short answer in full order — the sequence and the review point are what's being assessed.

Work through them without looking back first — that's how you'll find the gaps. Once you submit, I'll walk through anything that tripped you up, especially the operations that behave differently than people expect.

scenes.title: Lesson Wrap-Up: Version Control in the Databricks Workflow

elements.content: Version Control: Lesson Wrap-Up
A Git folder syncs a remote repository into the workspace; the admin enables integration and you link a PAT or OAuth.
The loop. Connect a credential, create a Git folder, then branch, commit, and push inside the workspace.
Why it matters. Version control makes notebooks shared, reviewable, and production-safe for a data team. [source p.359]
Worked example. 4 engineers, a 12-directory monorepo; Ana edits cells 5–8, Ben edits 30–33, so those cells conflict.
Exam checklist. The Repos-to-Git-folders rename, both prerequisites, and the clean-tree rule before a branch switch.
Next up. Ingesting, transforming, and building pipelines — durable lifecycle ideas. [source p.66] [source p.405]

actions.text: That brings us to the wrap-up for version control in the Databricks workflow. We've covered a lot of ground with Git folders, so let's pull the threads together and make sure everything is locked in for the exam.

Start with the loop, because it's the single most testable idea on this page. You connect a credential, create a Git folder that points at a remote repository, and then you branch, commit, and push exactly like you would with any Git workflow — except it all happens right inside the workspace. Same mental model, different surface.

Then ask yourself why any of this matters. Version control is what makes notebooks shared, reviewable, and production-safe for a data engineering team. Without it, you're emailing files around and hoping nobody overwrites your work — with it, every change is traceable and every branch is reversible.

Here's the exam-ready checklist. Know the rename from Repos to Git folders — that terminology shift shows up in questions. Know the prerequisites, meaning what has to be in place before you can even create the folder. And know the clean-tree rule: you must commit or discard outstanding changes before you switch branches. A dirty working tree blocks a branch switch, and that scenario is a classic trap.

Looking ahead, we're moving into the next stretch of the certification path: working with data on the platform — ingestion, transformation, and pipelines. Everything we just built with Git folders becomes the delivery mechanism for that work, so keep the workflow fresh in your mind as we shift into data movement.

scenes.title: Delta Lake Architecture at a Glance

elements.content: Delta Lake Architecture at a Glance
Delta Lake adds a transaction protocol over Parquet data files in cloud object storage [source 4].
Components: Parquet files, the _delta_log transaction log, and the metadata actions that bind them [source 3].
The log is ordered and immutable, so ACID guarantees hold via optimistic concurrency control [source 3].
Storage and compute are decoupled: Spark and Databricks SQL read the same table state [source 1].
Version history plus timestamp mapping lets you query the table by version number or timestamp [source 2].
Worked example: v0 = 1,000,000 rows; commits 1-3 add 200,000 rows each, so replaying to v3 gives 1,000,000 + 600,000 = 1,600,000 rows [source 5].
Exam focus: Delta Lake is the storage layer; Databricks is the platform that implements and manages it [source 1].

actions.text: Now that we've covered how code moves around in Databricks, let's turn to what that code actually reads and writes. This page frames Delta Lake as the storage layer of the lakehouse, so keep this picture in mind for the rest of this unit.

Delta Lake Architecture at a Glance. The one-sentence definition you want to memorize: Delta Lake is an open table format plus a transaction protocol layered on top of Parquet data files in cloud object storage.

That matters because raw Parquet on object storage is just a pile of files with no guarantees. Delta Lake adds a transaction protocol over Parquet, which is what turns that untrusted pile into a reliable, transactional table.

Architecturally there are three components. First, the Parquet data files themselves — the actual rows. Second, the _delta_log transaction log directory. Third, the metadata and protocol actions that bind the two together. Data plus log plus metadata — that's the whole architecture.

If you look at the stack diagram, read it bottom to top. Cloud object storage at the bottom holds the bytes. The Delta protocol and transaction log sit in the middle. The compute engines sit on top — Spark, Databricks SQL, and others all reading that same table state from the same files.

That layering is why we say storage and compute are decoupled. You can swap engines or scale compute independently without rewriting your data, because the table state lives in the log and the files, not in any single engine.

And here's the property that makes all of it possible: the log is ordered and immutable. Each commit appends a new entry; nothing gets rewritten in place. That ordering is exactly what gives you ACID guarantees on top of storage that offers none natively.

Because the log keeps full version history, plus a timestamp-to-version mapping, you can query any prior state of the table — that's what time travel is built on, and we'll unpack it in detail later in this unit.

Let's ground it with the worked example on the slide. Start at version zero with one million rows. Commits one through three each append a change. If you query version two, you see the table exactly as it existed after that second commit — not before, not after.

Finally, the exam focus, and this is the distinction candidates get wrong most often: Delta Lake is the storage layer. Databricks is the platform that implements and manages it. Don't conflate the two in an answer. Next up, we'll test exactly what Delta Lake adds on top of plain Parquet.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: What Delta Lake Actually Adds

questions.question: Delta Lake stores table data in cloud object storage. Which statement most accurately describes what the Delta protocol adds on top of the Parquet data files themselves?

options.label: It adds an ordered, immutable transaction log (_delta_log) plus the metadata and protocol actions that bind the log to the Parquet files, enabling ACID transactions, time travel, and schema evolution.
It replaces the Parquet files with a proprietary closed binary format that only Databricks engines are licensed to read.
It renames the Parquet directory to _delta_log so that object storage can enforce row-level locking on each file.
It adds a caching layer in memory only, so the underlying files remain plain Parquet and no persistent metadata is written to storage.

questions.analysis: Delta Lake is an open table format plus a transaction protocol layered on top of Parquet data files in cloud object storage [source 6]. The Parquet files stay Parquet; what is added is the _delta_log, an ordered, immutable log of all table operations, together with the metadata and protocol actions that bind the log to those files. That log is 'the foundational mechanism that transforms object storage into a reliable lakehouse platform' and is what delivers ACID guarantees through optimistic concurrency control and time travel via version history and timestamp mapping [source 3]. Option B is the most common trap: it assumes Delta 'replaces' Parquet with a proprietary closed format, but the data files are still ordinary Parquet and Delta implementations are open, not vendor-locked. Option C confuses the transaction log directory with the data directory — the log is a sibling of the data files, not a rename, and object storage does not provide row-level locking; concurrency is handled optimistically by the protocol. Option D is wrong because the log and its actions are persistent files in the same object storage, not an in-memory-only cache; without persisted metadata, none of the reliability properties would survive a cluster restart.

questions.question: A colleague says: 'Delta Lake is just Databricks, and it only works because of the Spark engine.' Which statement best corrects this?

options.label: Delta Lake is an open table format and protocol that any compatible engine can read; Databricks is a platform that implements it and Apache Spark is one engine that can read and write it.
Delta Lake is a feature of Apache Spark itself, so it is available in Spark but cannot be used by Databricks SQL or any non-Spark engine.
Delta Lake is a Databricks-managed storage service, so tables must physically live in Databricks-managed storage to be queryable.
Delta Lake is a Spark library only, which is why it requires pip install pyspark delta-spark before any engine can read a Delta table.

questions.analysis: Storage and compute are decoupled in Delta Lake: the table state lives in object storage as Parquet files plus the _delta_log, and Spark, Databricks SQL, and other engines can read that same table state from the same files [source 6]. That separation is exactly why Delta Lake cannot be equated with either the platform (Databricks) or the engine (Apache Spark). The open-source entry path described in the material — install Apache Spark and the delta-spark package, then configure the Spark session with Delta-specific settings that enable SQL extensions and designate Delta as the default catalog — is about configuring a Spark session, not about defining what Delta Lake is [source 1]. Option B inverts the relationship: Delta is a format/protocol, not a Spark feature, and Databricks SQL reads Delta tables natively without the Spark engine driving the query. Option C mistakes the protocol for a managed storage service; Delta tables are plain directories in the customer's own object storage bucket, which is precisely what makes the format portable. Option D confuses a convenience installation step (pip install pyspark delta-spark enabling SQL extensions and the default catalog) with a hard runtime dependency, and ignores that once the data and log exist on storage, any compatible reader can consume them. The behaviors the colleague is implicitly describing — ACID transactions, time travel, automatic schema evolution, and optimized metadata management — are properties of the protocol, not of a single vendor's platform [source 1].

Once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning behind each one with you, including the traps the distractors are built around. Go ahead and give it your best shot.

scenes.title: Delivering ACID on Top of Object Storage

elements.content: Delivering ACID on Top of Object Storage
Object stores give no multi-file transactions and no schema [source 1].
Example: replaying commits 1–7 in order rebuilds version 7 [source 5].
Atomicity: each commit writes one JSON file all-or-nothing [source 3].
Consistency: snapshots come from the log, which enforces schema [source 4].
Isolation: optimistic concurrency control serializes commits [source 3].
Durability: data and log files both live in replicated storage [source 1].

actions.text: Now let's get to the heart of what makes Delta Lake special. This page answers a question that trips up a lot of candidates: how do you get full ACID guarantees when your underlying storage is just cloud object storage — something that was never designed for transactions?

The title says it all: delivering ACID on top of object storage. Keep this framing in mind, because the exam loves to test whether you understand that Delta doesn't change the storage layer — it wraps guarantees around it.

Start with the constraint. Object stores like S3 or ADLS give you cheap, durable, virtually unlimited capacity — but they give you no multi-file transactions, no schema enforcement, and historically weak consistency on listings. So writing ten Parquet files either all lands or partially lands, and a reader can catch that half-written state. That is exactly the problem Delta must solve.

First letter, Atomicity. Every commit is a single JSON file, written all-or-nothing under a monotonically increasing version number. Because the commit itself is one atomic object write, the table never appears half-updated — the log either has the new commit file or it doesn't.

Next, Consistency. Snapshots are derived from the log, which enforces a defined schema. A reader asking for a version always sees a complete, self-consistent picture of the table — never a partial write. And closely related, Isolation uses optimistic concurrency control to serialize writers, so concurrent commits don't corrupt each other.

And Durability falls out naturally: both the Parquet data files and the log entries live in replicated object storage. Object stores are already built for eleven-nines durability, so Delta simply inherits it — no extra mechanism required.

Here's the mental model to lock in. Replaying commits one through seven, in order, rebuilds version seven of the table. The log is the source of truth, the data files are just the payload, and that's what lets a plain object store behave like a transactional database.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: ACID Guarantees in Delta Lake

questions.question: A team runs a large INSERT into a Delta Lake table. A Spark job writes hundreds of new Parquet data files, then the writer crashes after only some of those files have been uploaded to cloud object storage, before it records the commit. A reader queries the table one second later. Why does the reader never observe a partially written table state?

options.label: Because the cloud object store guarantees atomic multi-file uploads, so the object store itself rolls back the half-uploaded Parquet files on the reader's behalf.

Because Atomicity in Delta Lake is delivered by writing a single commit entry (a JSON transaction-log file) all-or-nothing under a monotonically increasing version number; until that commit is recorded in the _delta_log, the newly added Parquet files are not part of the table state. [source 3]
Because Delta Lake physically rewrites the whole table on every INSERT, so there is only ever one file version and partial writes are impossible on object storage.
Because Spark buffers the entire INSERT in memory and only flushes it to disk after the query finishes, which prevents readers from seeing intermediate files.

questions.analysis: Atomicity belongs to the Delta transaction protocol, not to the object store. Each commit is recorded as one JSON file in _delta_log under a monotonically increasing version number, written all-or-nothing; the ordered, immutable log of table operations is what lets Delta deliver ACID guarantees through optimistic concurrency control [source 3]. Option A is the classic trap of crediting object storage with transactional guarantees it does not have — object stores provide cheap, durable storage but no multi-file transactions. Option C is false because Delta does not rewrite the whole table per INSERT. Option D is false because a large INSERT spills Parquet files to storage as it runs; the protection comes from the log, not from buffering.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly attribute an ACID property to the Delta Lake mechanism that actually provides it, rather than to object storage? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Atomicity: the commit is a single transaction-log entry written all-or-nothing under a monotonically increasing version number, so a failed write is simply never committed.
Isolation and consistency: readers resolve a consistent snapshot through the transaction log, so they never see a half-written table. [source 3]
Durability: the object store may forget recent writes, which is why Delta must periodically re-upload Parquet files to survive node failures.
Time travel and data versioning: the transaction log's version history lets you recreate a table's state at any earlier point by processing only the commits made before that point. [source 5]

questions.analysis: Options A, B, and D correctly map properties to Delta mechanisms. Atomicity comes from all-or-nothing commit entries in the log; the log's ordered, immutable record of operations delivers ACID guarantees through optimistic concurrency control and lets readers see a consistent snapshot [source 3]; and because the log preserves version history, you can recreate the table state at any point in time by replaying only the commits made prior to that point [source 5]. Option C is the exact trap this quiz targets: it credits object storage with being unreliable while demanding Delta compensate for it. Object storage is durable, but it lacks table-level transactions and schema enforcement — that is why Delta Lake layers a transaction log on top [source 4]. Durability here is a division of labor, not a Delta-only repair job.
