scenes.title: The Log as the Source of Truth: Concurrency and Isolation

elements.content: The Log as the Source of Truth: Concurrency and Isolation
Readers take a snapshot from the log; writers commit optimistically — no locks on data files
Read Path — Snapshot from the Log

Readers never list the data directory to discover files. They read the log (commit JSONs plus the newest checkpoint via _last_checkpoint) to build a consistent snapshot, then open only the Parquet files that snapshot references [source 3].

Because snapshot state is rebuilt by replaying the commits prior to a point in time, an identical read path yields time travel for free [source 5].

If reader R reads up to version 8 while writer W commits version 9, R still answers from the version-8 snapshot: the half-committed version 9 is invisible, so a partially written table can never be observed [source 3].
Write Path — Optimistic Concurrency

1. Read the current version N

2. Precompute and write new Parquet data files

3. Attempt a commit at N+1 [source 3]

4. If another writer won the race, retry from step 1

No lock is ever taken on the data files — the log is the coordination point.
Worked Example: The Race
W0 (both) → commit f0 @ v42
W1 → commit f1 @ v43 ✓
W2 → commit f2 @ v43 … conflict → retry at v44 ✓
Serializable isolation

Concurrent writers may request version 43 simultaneously, but only one commit file for version 43 can exist. The loser replays, recomputes and commits 44 — so the outcome equals some serial order [source 3].

The monotonic version number powers time travel, audit history and reproducible debugging [source 2].
Exam trap: concurrency is coordinated through the log — not through locks on the data files. Multiple readers and multiple writers are fully supported [source 3].

actions.text: Now let's build on the log layout we just covered and ask a deeper question: why is the transaction log called the source of truth? The answer is that the log, not the data files, is what coordinates both readers and writers. Everything about concurrency and isolation in Delta Lake flows from that one design decision.

Let's start with the read path. A reader takes a snapshot from the log — meaning it reads the log to determine exactly which set of files constitutes the table at some version — and then it opens only those Parquet files that the snapshot references.

The critical detail here is what readers never do: they never list the data directory to discover files. That's what makes reads fast, consistent, and immune to the partial writes happening concurrently. There's no directory scanning, no guessing — just a snapshot from the log.

The write path uses optimistic concurrency control. Optimistic here means the writer assumes it will succeed — it does its work first and only checks for conflict at the moment of commit. That's a very different posture from pessimistic locking, where you'd grab a lock before doing anything.

Here's the three-step write protocol. Step one: read the current version, call it N. Step two: precompute and write out any new data files — this is the expensive part, and it happens without any coordination. Step three: attempt the commit at version N+1. If nobody else committed version N+1 in the meantime, you win.
Let's walk through a worked example of the race, because this is where the exam likes to test you. Two writers start at the same time on the same table.

Both writers, W0 and W1 in our numbering — call them W0 and W2 if you like — read the current version, which is 42. They each compute their new files independently. Then one of them commits file f0 at version 42, advancing the table to version 43.
The first writer to attempt the commit at version 43 succeeds — its commit of file f1 lands cleanly, and the table is now at version 44. Victory for W1.

But W2 is still trying to commit at version 43, and version 43 is already taken. That's a conflict. Delta detects it and retries W2's transaction at the next available version, 44. Now W2 commits successfully and the table advances to 45. Notice that nobody was blocked, nobody was locked out, and both writers eventually landed their data.

This retry mechanism is how Delta delivers serializable isolation. Serializable isolation means concurrent transactions produce the same result as if those transactions had been run in some serial ordering — one after another, one at a time. The log's version number is the arbiter that establishes that ordering.

Multiple writers can request version 43 at the same time. The log decides which one gets it, and the other retries. The version number itself — monotonically increasing — is also what makes time travel, audit history, and reproducible debugging possible. If you can name a version, you can reconstruct exactly the table state at that point.

Here's the exam trap. A lot of candidates assume concurrency is coordinated through locks on the data files. It is not. Concurrency is coordinated through the log. Data files are immutable and never locked. That's why Delta supports multiple concurrent readers and multiple concurrent writers — optimistic concurrency with retry, driven by the log. If you remember nothing else from this page, remember that sentence.

scenes.title: Comparison: Delta Table vs. Raw Parquet Lake vs. Warehouse Table

elements.content: Dimension  |  Raw Parquet Data Lake  |  Delta Lake Table  |  Cloud Data Warehouse Table

ACID transactions (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability)
Raw Parquet Data Lake: A raw Parquet data lake provides no transaction boundary across files: each write is just a set of independent object PUTs, so a reader that lists the bucket during a multi-part write can observe a partially written dataset with no way to roll it back, and there is no mechanism to guarantee serializable isolation between concurrent writers.
Delta Lake Table: A Delta Lake table provides full ACID guarantees by writing one atomic JSON commit per transaction into the _delta_log, using optimistic concurrency control so that concurrent writers read the current version and attempt a commit at version N+1, retrying if they lose the race, which yields serializable isolation [source 3].
Cloud Data Warehouse Table: A cloud data warehouse table provides ACID guarantees natively inside the warehouse's own storage and metadata layer, but the transaction scope ends at that engine's boundary, so external tools cannot independently read or write the same committed table state without going through the warehouse's API.

Schema enforcement and schema evolution
Raw Parquet Data Lake: A raw Parquet data lake stores whatever the writer emits, so a downstream reader can find missing columns, renamed fields, or type mismatches, and it has no table-level schema enforcement to reject a malformed batch at write time [source 4].
Delta Lake Table: A Delta Lake table enforces the table schema on write and rejects non-conforming records by default, while also supporting explicit automatic schema evolution to add new columns when the data structure changes [source 1].
Cloud Data Warehouse Table: A cloud data warehouse table enforces a rigid declarative schema: writes that violate column types or nullability are rejected, and schema changes are typically DDL operations that must be planned and migrated rather than inferred at ingest.

UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE support
Raw Parquet Data Lake: A raw Parquet data lake cannot update or delete individual rows: the only realistic mutation path is rewriting entire files and partitions, and there is no atomic MERGE primitive, so slowly changing dimensions (SCD — tracking how a dimension value changes over time for a business entity) must be implemented manually.
Delta Lake Table: A Delta Lake table supports row-level UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE statements by rewriting only the affected Parquet data files and recording add and remove actions in the log, which makes implementing slowly changing dimensions (SCD) a first-class table operation.
Cloud Data Warehouse Table: A cloud data warehouse table supports row-level UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE through the warehouse SQL engine, but the rewrite work happens inside the warehouse's proprietary storage and compute, so cost and concurrency are bound to that vendor.

Time travel and historical versioning
Raw Parquet Data Lake: A raw Parquet data lake has no built-in version history: you can only recover a previous state if you happened to keep physically separate copies or a snapshot directory, and there is no query syntax to read an older version of a logical table.
Delta Lake Table: A Delta Lake table exposes built-in time travel by version number and by timestamp because the transaction log orders every commit, so you can recreate the state of the table at any point in time by processing only the commits made before that point [source 5]; deleting historical data files limits which versions remain queryable [source 2].
Cloud Data Warehouse Table: A cloud data warehouse table typically offers some form of time travel or cloning, but the retention window and the precise semantics are vendor-defined, and historical state is not exposed as an open file set you can read with an arbitrary engine.

Concurrency model
Raw Parquet Data Lake: A raw Parquet data lake has no writer coordination: two concurrent jobs can overwrite each other's files or produce duplicate rows with no detection, so correctness under concurrency is the application's problem and usually requires external locking or partitioning conventions.
Delta Lake Table: A Delta Lake table handles concurrency through optimistic concurrency control: writers read the log, attempt a commit at version N+1, and retry if another writer won the race, so concurrent transactions produce the same result as some serial ordering [source 3].
Cloud Data Warehouse Table: A cloud data warehouse table handles concurrency with its own internal locking and scheduling, which is robust for concurrent SQL sessions inside the warehouse, but the isolation boundary does not extend to engines outside the warehouse.

Open format and engine interoperability
Raw Parquet Data Lake: A raw Parquet data lake is fully open: the files are standard Apache Parquet, so Spark, Databricks SQL, Trino, DuckDB, and other engines can read them directly without a proprietary catalog [source 4].
Delta Lake Table: A Delta Lake table keeps data in an open, engine-agnostic format: the data files remain Parquet, and the _delta_log is a publicly specified protocol of JSON actions and Parquet checkpoints, so Spark, Databricks SQL, and other conforming engines read the same table state from the same files [source 3].
Cloud Data Warehouse Table: A cloud data warehouse table typically stores data in a proprietary internal format and exposes it only through vendor SQL endpoints or exports, so readers must go through the warehouse rather than reading files directly.

Cost model
Raw Parquet Data Lake: A raw Parquet data lake has the lowest storage cost because you pay only for cheap, durable cloud object storage, but you pay the hidden engineering cost of building your own transactions, schema checks, and update logic.
Delta Lake Table: A Delta Lake table inherits the low storage cost of cloud object storage because Delta is a format and protocol layered on top of Parquet files, and you pay compute only when you actually read or write, so storage stays cheap while reliability is added in software [source 1].
Cloud Data Warehouse Table: A cloud data warehouse table charges for both storage and warehouse compute units, and the per-query cost can be much higher than reading Parquet directly from object storage, especially for large scans that a lakehouse would serve from cheap object storage.

Metadata management and query performance
Raw Parquet Data Lake: A raw Parquet data lake relies on directory listings and partition folder conventions for metadata, which becomes slow and fragile as the table grows, and there is no automatic statistics layer for file skipping.
Delta Lake Table: A Delta Lake table maintains optimized metadata management through the transaction log, including checkpoints so readers do not replay the entire log and file-level statistics that enable faster query performance [source 1].
Cloud Data Warehouse Table: A cloud data warehouse table maintains its own optimized metadata and statistics inside the warehouse, often delivering very fast queries but only for data already loaded into that warehouse's storage.

Typical use case
Raw Parquet Data Lake: A raw Parquet data lake is a reasonable choice for immutable append-only archives, cold raw-landing zones in a medallion architecture (the bronze/silver/gold layering of progressively refined data), and one-off analytics where no row-level mutations or concurrent writers are needed.
Delta Lake Table: A Delta Lake table is the right default for bronze, silver, and gold layers of a medallion architecture, streaming ingestion with Auto Loader, SCD workloads, and any table that must be updated, audited, or read by multiple engines while still living cheaply on object storage.
Cloud Data Warehouse Table: A cloud data warehouse table is appropriate when the workload is dominated by SQL BI users inside one warehouse, when strict vendor-managed governance and SLAs matter more than open file access, and when the data volume and cost profile fit the warehouse's pricing.

Takeaway — Choose a raw Parquet data lake only for immutable, append-only raw storage where no ACID, schema enforcement, or row-level updates are required, because it lacks transactions, schema enforcement, and built-in time travel [source 4].

Takeaway — Choose a Delta Lake table when you need ACID transactions, row-level UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE, time travel, and concurrency safety on top of cheap object storage while keeping data in an open, engine-agnostic Parquet format [source 3].

Takeaway — Choose a cloud data warehouse table when your workload is entirely SQL inside one vendor's platform and you accept a proprietary storage format and warehouse compute pricing in exchange for managed performance and governance.

Takeaway — For the exam, justify the selection by explicitly mapping the workload's concurrency level, update/delete frequency, and cost sensitivity to the dimensions above, and state that Delta Lake is the lakehouse position that combines the openness and low cost of object storage with the reliability of a warehouse.

actions.text: We've just seen how the transaction log gives Delta Lake its atomicity and concurrency guarantees. Now let's put that into perspective by comparing three storage options side by side — a plain Parquet data lake, a Delta Lake table, and a cloud data warehouse table.

This table organizes the comparison across the decision dimensions that actually matter when you're designing a Databricks data architecture. Read it column by column, not row by row — that's how the exam frames it.

Start with ACID transactions — atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability. A raw Parquet data lake on object storage gives you none of these. Both the Delta table and the warehouse deliver full ACID guarantees. This is the first fork in the road.

The next differentiator is UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE support. Again, plain Parquet cannot do this — you'd rewrite entire files. Delta and the warehouse both handle row-level mutations natively. And notice the pattern emerging: the Delta table matches the warehouse on every capability, but adds something more.

That something is the open format and engine interoperability dimension. Parquet and Delta both store data in open, engine-agnostic formats — any engine can read them. A cloud data warehouse typically locks you into a proprietary format and that vendor's compute.

Look at the cost model row as well. A raw Parquet lake is the cheapest to store but the most expensive in engineering effort, because you build reliability yourself. Delta Lake sits in the sweet spot: object storage economics with warehouse-grade reliability.
Time travel is another capability only Delta and the warehouse offer — the ability to query historical versions of your data. For a Parquet lake, that's simply not there.

Here's the takeaway. Choose a raw Parquet data lake only when your workload is purely append-only, has no update or delete requirements, and you're optimizing strictly for the lowest storage cost with no concurrency needs. That's a narrow case.

Choose a Delta Lake table when you need ACID, updates, time travel, and open-format portability at object-storage cost. That's the lakehouse position — combining the openness and low cost of the lake with the reliability of the warehouse. This is the default choice for Databricks data engineering.

Choose a cloud data warehouse table when your workloads are primarily SQL analytics, concurrency is high but read-heavy, and you're willing to accept the proprietary format and higher cost in exchange for a fully managed serving layer.

And here's the exam tip you can't miss: on a scenario question, don't pick an answer because it sounds modern. Justify your selection against three things — the workload's concurrency requirements, its update and delete behavior, and its cost constraints. Walk through those three filters and the answer becomes obvious. Let's apply that reasoning next.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Concurrency, Isolation and Architecture Choices

questions.question: Two writers, W1 and W2, both read version 7 of a Delta table and then each attempts to add a distinct Parquet data file as a new commit. Assume neither transaction conflicts logically (both are simple appends with no overlapping remove actions). Under Delta Lake's optimistic concurrency control, what is the outcome when both writers attempt to commit?

options.label: Exactly one writer succeeds by writing commit file 00000000000000000008.json, and the other writer's commit is rejected outright and its data is permanently discarded.

Both writers succeed; 00000000000000000008.json serialises as one commit, and the loser re-attempts its commit as version 8 by replaying its read against the current log and checking for conflicts before writing the next commit file.
Both writers succeed immediately because object storage provides multi-file transactions that serialise concurrent writes at the storage layer.
Both writers are blocked and queued by the Delta log until a writer holding a table-level write lock releases it, after which the queued writers commit in arrival order.

questions.correctAnswer: Both writers succeed; 00000000000000000008.json serialises as one commit, and the loser re-attempts its commit as version 8 by replaying its read against the current log and checking for conflicts before writing the next commit file.
questions.analysis: Delta Lake uses optimistic concurrency control: each writer reads the current version, attempts to write commit file N+1, and if another writer won the race for that version number, the loser retries by re-reading the log and re-checking for conflicts before writing the next commit file [source 3]. Because object storage has no multi-file transactions and no native locking, options A, C and D describe mechanisms (hard rejection, storage-level transactions, table-level write locks) that Delta does not rely on; the optimistic protocol is what turns object storage into a reliable lakehouse [source 3]. The key exam trap is crediting object storage or a global lock with serialisation that Delta actually provides through the log's ordered, immutable commits [source 3].
answer: Both writers succeed; 00000000000000000008.json serialises as one commit, and the loser re-attempts its commit as version 8 by replaying its read against the current log and checking for conflicts before writing the next commit file.

questions.question: A reader opens a Delta table at a fixed version number V while a writer simultaneously commits version V+1. Which statements correctly describe what snapshot isolation guarantees in this scenario? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The reader sees only the Parquet files referenced by the log state at version V; files added in V+1 are invisible to that reader.
The reader never observes a half-written table because the commit at V+1 is an atomic, all-or-nothing JSON commit that either exists fully or does not exist at all.
The reader's snapshot is defined by the version number, and the same version number always reconstructs the same set of active files regardless of when the reader queries the table.
The reader must acquire a shared read lock on the Delta table's Parquet files to prevent the writer from mutating them mid-read.

questions.correctAnswer: The reader sees only the Parquet files referenced by the log state at version V; files added in V+1 are invisible to that reader.,The reader never observes a half-written table because the commit at V+1 is an atomic, all-or-nothing JSON commit that either exists fully or does not exist at all.,The reader's snapshot is defined by the version number, and the same version number always reconstructs the same set of active files regardless of when the reader queries the table.
questions.analysis: Delta delivers isolation through the log rather than through read locks: readers read the log to obtain a snapshot and open only the files that snapshot references, so a version V reader ignores V+1 additions [source 3]. Atomicity is provided by the commit being a single all-or-nothing JSON file written under a monotonically increasing version number, meaning a partially applied table state can never be observed. The version number is the identity of the snapshot; replaying commits 0..V always yields the same active file set, which is the mechanism behind time travel [source 5]. Option D mirrors a common misconception that Delta uses shared read locks; the architecture is snapshot-based and lock-free with respect to readers [source 3].
answer: The reader sees only the Parquet files referenced by the log state at version V; files added in V+1 are invisible to that reader.,The reader never observes a half-written table because the commit at V+1 is an atomic, all-or-nothing JSON commit that either exists fully or does not exist at all.,The reader's snapshot is defined by the version number, and the same version number always reconstructs the same set of active files regardless of when the reader queries the table.

questions.question: A team needs a single storage option for a workload with these characteristics: (1) concurrent streaming appends from multiple writers, (2) SQL readers on Databricks that must not see partially written files, (3) the ability to query the table as it existed yesterday to reproduce a report, and (4) the data must remain readable as plain Parquet files in object storage by an external engine. Which option best fits the stated requirements?

options.label: A plain Parquet data lake directory in cloud object storage, because Parquet files are the most portable representation and readers will simply ignore incomplete files.
A cloud data warehouse table, because it provides ACID and time travel and removes the need to worry about file layout in object storage.

A Delta Lake table on object storage, because the transaction log adds ACID through optimistic concurrency and enables time travel via version history while the underlying data files remain Parquet [source 3].
A single large Parquet file written with overwrite mode, because replacing the whole file on each write gives atomicity without needing a transaction log.

questions.correctAnswer: A Delta Lake table on object storage, because the transaction log adds ACID through optimistic concurrency and enables time travel via version history while the underlying data files remain Parquet [source 3].
questions.analysis: The requirements combine ACID with concurrent writers, snapshot isolation for readers, time travel, and Parquet portability. Delta Lake satisfies all four: the transaction log tracks every change, promotes consistency and enables features like time travel [source 4], and it delivers ACID guarantees through optimistic concurrency control and time travel via version history and timestamp mapping [source 3]. Option A fails requirement 2 because a raw Parquet lake lacks table-level features such as transactions and schema enforcement [source 4], and readers scanning the directory have no atomic snapshot. Option B abandons the requirement that external engines read plain Parquet files directly on object storage, since a warehouse table is not a Parquet directory. Option D trades away concurrency (a single overwriting writer) and time travel (no version history), and rewrite-a-whole-file is not an ACID commit protocol in the Delta sense [source 3].
answer: A Delta Lake table on object storage, because the transaction log adds ACID through optimistic concurrency and enables time travel via version history while the underlying data files remain Parquet [source 3].

actions.text: Time for a harder checkpoint. This one pulls together the transaction-log mechanics and the architectural reasoning we just covered, so read each question carefully — some of the distractors are written to sound plausible.

Work through all three on your own and pick the option that matches what the log actually does. Hold your reasoning — once you submit, I'll go through each one with you and we'll pick apart the traps together.

scenes.title: Reading the Log: A Version Timeline

elements.content:
Active Parquet file count by commit version (with DELETE at v8 and compaction at v10) (line)
Commit version (zero-padded _delta_log JSON version) → Active Parquet files referenced by the log snapshot
Step chart. Each step is one atomic commit file in _delta_log (e.g. 00000000000000000008.json). The y-value is the number of active add-actions minus remove-actions as of that version; row counts per file are given in the unit note of each claim.
Active Parquet files: 0→2   1→3   2→3   3→4   4→4   5→6   6→6   7→7   8→4   9→5   10→2   11→3   12→3

Claim 1 — Refuted
The rows removed by the DELETE committed at version 8 were physically erased from cloud object storage at the moment version 8 was committed.
Why: The chart shows the active-file count dropping from 7 at version 7 to 4 at version 8, which only means the log snapshot at version 8 no longer references three files. Because commits are atomic actions recorded as newline-delimited JSON in _delta_log [source 5], a remove action is a logical tombstone in the log, not an object-store DELETE call. The underlying Parquet objects remain physically present; Delta Lake treats them as no longer active for readers of versions 8 and later. The claim conflates logical log state with physical storage state.

Claim 2 — Supported
Because the log is an ordered, immutable sequence of commits, the table state as of version 7 remains readable after versions 8 through 12 have been committed.
Why: The series shows version 7 at 7 active files while versions 8-12 move to 4, 5, 2, 3, 3. Nothing in the plotted data overwrites earlier versions; the change is additive commits. Delta Lake recreates any earlier state by starting from the original table and processing only the commits made prior to the target point, which is what enables time travel [source 5]. Time travel by version number is a built-in Delta Lake feature that the transaction log makes possible [source 2]. So version 7 will show 7 active files whenever it is queried.

Claim 3 — Refuted
The number of active Parquet files increases monotonically with every commit from version 0 through version 12.
Why: The series rises from 2 files at version 0 to 7 files at version 7, but then falls to 4 at version 8 (DELETE) and falls again to 2 at version 10 (compaction). Monotonic increase is violated at versions 8 and 10. A compaction commit rewrites many small files into fewer larger ones, and the log records both add actions for the new files and remove actions for the old ones. The chart's y-value is a snapshot of the active set, not a cumulative count.

Claim 4 — Supported
Between version 9 and version 10 the active file count fell by exactly 3 files, and this drop is consistent with a compaction rewriting the active set rather than with data being lost.
Why: Version 9 plots 5 active files and version 10 plots 2, so the arithmetic drop is 5 - 2 = 3. Row counts are conserved: 5 files of 200 rows each = 1,000 rows, and 2 files of 500 rows each = 1,000 rows. A compaction commit replaces the many small files with fewer consolidated files while preserving the logical row set, which is exactly the pattern a remove/add pair of actions in one atomic commit produces. Losing data would not preserve the row arithmetic.

Claim 5 — Insufficient
At version 12 the table is exactly 3 Parquet files and no other Parquet objects that were ever part of this table exist in storage.
Why: The chart only reports the count of active files per version, which is 3 at version 12. It gives no information about how many files were previously added and later removed, and it gives no information about whether VACUUM has run. Files removed at versions 8 and 10 are tombstoned in the log and may still exist physically until VACUUM. The data supports the active count of 3 but is silent on total objects in storage, so the universal part of the claim cannot be decided.

Claim 6 — Supported
If two writers both read version 11 (3 active files) and each tries to commit at version 12, at most one commit will succeed at version 12 and the loser will retry at version 13.
Why: This is the optimistic concurrency control pattern: a writer reads the current version, attempts a commit at version N+1, and retries if another writer won the race [source 3]. The chart's version axis is itself the evidence that commit numbers are strictly ordered and unique; the series has exactly one point per version from 0 to 12, so two commits cannot both occupy version 12. The retry then lands at version 13, consistent with the monotone version axis. Note the chart does not show the contents of either competing commit, only the version numbering that enforces exclusivity.

Claim 7 — Refuted
Using the log, a reader at version 12 must scan the object-store directory listing of the table directory to discover which Parquet files to open.
Why: Readers never scan the directory for files; they read the log to obtain a snapshot and then open only the Parquet files that snapshot references. The chart is precisely that snapshot: the y-values are the count of active files per version, which is derived from the log, not from a directory listing. The transaction log tracks every change and promotes consistency, which is why time travel and consistent snapshots are possible [source 4]. A directory scan would return tombstoned files and would also break isolation.

Claim 8 — Refuted
The total logical row count of the table at version 6 is greater than at version 7, assuming each active file contains 200 rows.
Why: Version 6 plots 6 active files and version 7 plots 7 active files. With 200 rows per active file, version 6 = 6 x 200 = 1,200 rows and version 7 = 7 x 200 = 1,400 rows. The added commit at version 7 increases the logical row count by 200, so the table is larger at version 7, not smaller. Students who read the chart as a cumulative insert count rather than a snapshot can invert this comparison; the step chart is a snapshot, not a running total.

actions.text: Now let's put that log reasoning into practice. What you see here is a version timeline — a step chart where the X-axis is the commit version from 0 to 12, and the Y-axis is the number of active Parquet files. Two events are annotated directly on the chart: a DELETE at version 8, and a compaction at version 10.

This is the chart itself. Trace the staircase carefully. Notice how the file count steps up with each commit, then watch what happens at those two annotation points — they break the pattern, and that's exactly where the exam wants you to look.

Here's the raw data behind the chart. At version 0 there are zero active Parquet files — an empty table. By version 1 we have three, and so on up the ladder. Read this legend alongside the step chart; every step in the chart corresponds to one of these counts.

Claim 1 states that the rows removed by the DELETE at version 8 were physically erased from object storage. That claim is refuted. Delta is immutable at the file level — the DELETE writes new Parquet files and a new log entry marking the old ones as removed. The original bytes are still sitting in object storage until a VACUUM reclaims them. This is the heart of the logical-versus-physical distinction.

Claim 3 says the active file count increases monotonically with every commit. That's refuted too — look at the drop after version 10. Compaction merges many small files into fewer larger ones, so the active count falls even though no data was lost. Monotonic growth is a trap assumption; the file count reflects layout, not data volume.

Claims 2 and 6, on the other hand, are supported. Because the log is an ordered, append-only sequence of commits, the state as of version 7 remains readable after versions 8 through 12 land — nothing overwrites it in place. That immutability is precisely what enables time travel and what keeps concurrent readers isolated.

actions.topic: What does a verdict of 'insufficient evidence' actually tell us about reading a Delta log?
actions.prompt: Claim 5 was judged insufficient because the table is empty at version 12 — the log gives us no rows to reason about. Think about when the log alone cannot answer a question, versus when the answer is simply refuted. What kinds of claims require more than the version timeline — for example, column-level data, retention settings, or the physical cloud paths?

scenes.title: Tradeoffs: Choosing a Table Format for a Workload

elements.content: Decision — A data platform team of four engineers supports an analytics pipeline for a mid-sized SaaS company and must choose a storage format for a nightly batch job that appends new event records only, with multiple writers occasionally overlapping and a hard requirement for predictable cost plus strong debugging ability. The decision is difficult because the cheapest raw-file option appears to satisfy the append-only pattern at first glance, but the team has been burned before by silent schema drift and unreproducible row counts, and the governance-rich warehouse option is attractive for auditing yet threatens both budget predictability and engine openness. The team has already studied how the Delta Lake transaction log provides atomic commits under monotonically increasing version numbers and how readers obtain consistent snapshots from the log rather than by listing the directory, so the conversation now turns to applying those transaction-log concepts to a concrete workload choice.

Constraints — The job appends new event records only; no updates or deletes are performed by the batch process.  •  Multiple writers occasionally overlap in time, so concurrent-write safety is required.  •  Cost must be predictable and preferably low, with no unbounded per-query or per-storage growth surprises.  •  Strong debugging ability is required, meaning the team must be able to inspect history, reproduce past row counts, and identify what changed.  •  The storage format must support schema enforcement to prevent silent schema drift.  •  The solution must remain compatible with SQL engines and non-SQL engines where possible, rather than locking the team into a single proprietary query surface.

Plain Parquet files in object storage
+ Lowest raw storage and write cost because there is no transaction-log overhead, no commit coordination, and no periodic checkpoint maintenance. [source 4]; + Maximum engine openness because any engine that reads Parquet can query the files directly, and no proprietary protocol is involved.
− No ACID transactions, so concurrent writers can interleave file writes and produce a table directory that no single reader can interpret as a consistent snapshot. [source 3]; − No schema enforcement and no version history, so a bad write cannot be rolled back and debugging requires reconstructing intent from raw file listings rather than replaying an ordered log. [source 4] [source 5]
Best for: Append-only archival or staging zones where writers never overlap, schema is externally controlled, and nobody needs historical reproduction.

Delta Lake table
+ ACID commits backed by optimistic concurrency control make overlapping writers safe: each writer reads the current version, attempts a commit at the next version, and retries if another writer won the race. [source 3]; + The ordered _delta_log gives version history and time travel, so debugging can start from the exact commit that changed the active file set rather than from directory guesses. [source 5]; + Schema enforcement plus a small per-commit log overhead preserves predictable cost because the log is compact and readers use checkpoints instead of replaying the entire log. [source 4]
− Each commit adds a small log write and periodic checkpoint maintenance, so there is a nonzero operational overhead compared with writing raw Parquet. [source 5]; − The team must adopt Delta-aware tooling or configure engines for Delta compatibility, which is a migration and training cost rather than a pure drop-in replacement.
Best for: Append-only pipelines that nonetheless need concurrent-write safety, schema enforcement, and reproducible history for debugging.

Managed warehouse table
+ Strongest built-in governance, SQL tooling, and out-of-the-box access controls, which reduce the engineering effort required to enforce policies and audit queries.; + Managed compute and storage tuning can simplify operations because the warehouse vendor handles concurrency, compaction, and many maintenance tasks.
− Higher and less predictable cost, since warehouse pricing typically bundles compute and storage in ways that can grow with query volume rather than with committed data volume.; − Less openness for non-SQL engines, so Spark, Python, or custom machine-learning jobs may be forced through a narrower interface or a separate copy of the data.
Best for: Teams whose analysts live in SQL, whose governance requirements are strict, and whose budget tolerates managed-service pricing.

Recommendation: Delta Lake table — The stated constraints decide this: multiple writers occasionally overlap, so the absence of ACID transactions in plain Parquet is disqualifying because concurrent writers can corrupt the reader's view [source 3]. Strong debugging ability requires version history and time travel, which only the ordered transaction log provides [source 5]. Schema enforcement prevents silent drift in an append-only feed, and the small per-commit log overhead is predictable and bounded rather than query-dependent, satisfying the cost constraint. By contrast, the managed warehouse satisfies governance but fails the openness and predictable-cost constraints, while plain Parquet fails the concurrency and debugging constraints outright. Therefore Delta Lake is the only option that satisfies every hard limit simultaneously, and its overhead is a justified price for reproducible, safe, debuggable appends. [source 4]

actions.text: Now that we understand how the transaction log drives versions, concurrency, and isolation, let's put that knowledge to work. This page presents a real design decision: a data platform team must choose a table format for a specific workload, and you need to justify the choice using the log concepts we just covered.

Here's the scenario. The team is four engineers. They need a table format that fits their workload and their operational constraints — not the theoretically best format, but the right one for their situation.

Look carefully at the constraints, because these are what drive the decision. The job is a nightly batch that appends new event records only — no updates, no deletes. But multiple writers occasionally overlap, so concurrent writes do happen. And the team wants predictable cost and strong debugging ability. Hold those four facts: append-only, overlapping writers, predictable cost, debuggability.

Option A is plain Parquet files in object storage. It has the lowest raw cost and no log overhead. But there's no ACID, no schema enforcement, and no version history — and concurrent writers here are genuinely unsafe. On our constraint list, it fails on overlapping writers and on debuggability, since there's no history to inspect.

Option B is a Delta Lake table. This is where everything we just learned pays off. ACID commits backed by optimistic concurrency mean overlapping writers are safe. Schema enforcement protects the append path. Version history gives the team exactly the debugging ability they asked for. The tradeoff is a small per-commit log overhead and periodic maintenance.

Option C is a managed warehouse table. It gives the strongest built-in governance and the best SQL tooling, but at higher cost and with less openness for non-SQL engines. That's more capability than this workload needs, and it doesn't match the 'predictable cost' constraint as tightly.

So the recommendation is Option B, the Delta Lake table. Even though the pattern is append-only, we still need concurrent-write safety, schema enforcement, and version history for debugging. Because the log overhead is small, it's easily justified against those requirements. Before we move on — pause and ask yourself: what would have to change in these constraints for Option A to become the right answer? That reasoning is exactly what the exam tests.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Delta Table Baseline

questions.question:
A data engineer runs the following statement in a Databricks workspace without specifying any format clause:

CREATE TABLE main.sales.orders (
  order_id BIGINT,
  customer_id BIGINT,
  order_ts TIMESTAMP,
  amount DECIMAL(10,2)
);

Which table format does Databricks apply by default when the table is created this way?

options.label: Delta Lake, because Delta is the default format for tables created through the Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog managed-table path
Raw Parquet, because Databricks writes the underlying data files as Parquet and therefore treats the table as a plain directory of Parquet files
Apache Hive ACID ORC, because all SQL-created tables in the lakehouse inherit the legacy Hive transactional format
No format is chosen until the first INSERT runs; the format is inferred from the engine that performs the first write

questions.analysis: Delta is the default table format on Databricks: a bare CREATE TABLE (no USING clause) produces a Delta table whose data files are Parquet and whose metadata lives in the _delta_log directory. Option B is the classic misconception this unit flags — it is true that Delta stores data as Parquet, but the table is not 'just Parquet'; the transaction log is what makes it a Delta table [source 3]. Option C confuses Delta with legacy Hive ACID tables that predate the lakehouse. Option D is wrong because the format is resolved at CREATE TABLE time, not deferred to the first write. Note the precondition: the default applies when the session/catalog is configured for Delta (Delta Lake-specific settings that enable SQL extensions and designate Delta as the default catalog) [source 1].

questions.question: You need a quick, single-statement report that returns a Delta table's physical storage location, the number of data files that currently make up the table, and the total on-disk size of those files. Which statement should you run?

options.label: SELECT * FROM main.sales.orders LIMIT 1;
LIST '/mnt/lake/sales/orders';
DESCRIBE DETAIL main.sales.orders;
DESCRIBE EXTENDED main.sales.orders;

questions.analysis: DESCRIBE DETAIL returns table-level metadata including the format, the physical location, the number of files (numFiles) and the total size in bytes (sizeInBytes) — exactly the three values requested. Option A returns rows, not storage metadata. Option B lists raw objects in a path: it may work for an external table's directory, but it reports every object including the _delta_log JSON and checkpoint files, so it does not give you the count and size of the active data files of the table as Delta defines it. Option D returns schema and table properties but not the file count/size summary. Because readers obtain a snapshot from the log and not by scanning the directory, the authoritative 'which files are active' answer comes from table metadata, not from a filesystem listing [source 3].

questions.question: A colleague claims: 'A Delta table is basically just a folder of Parquet files — there is no log, so you can point any Parquet reader at it and you get the same table.' Which of the following statements correctly identify what the claim gets wrong? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The table directory also contains a _delta_log folder holding newline-delimited JSON commit files (00000000000000000000.json, 00000000000000000001.json, ...) plus periodic checkpoint files, and that log — not the Parquet listing — defines which files are part of the table.

Because each commit is written all-or-nothing under a monotonically increasing version number, a reader can reconstruct the state of the table at any point in time by processing only the commits made before that point, which a bare folder of Parquet files cannot support.
The claim is essentially correct: Delta Lake replaces Parquet with a proprietary closed format, so a Parquet reader would fail on a Delta table's data files.

Parquet files can remain physically present after a DELETE or UPDATE, because a remove action only marks them inactive in the log; a naive reader that lists the directory would therefore return deleted rows that a Delta reader would never see.

questions.analysis: A is the core correction: the transaction log is the source of truth and it stores atomic actions (add, remove, metadata, protocol, commitInfo) as newline-delimited JSON, with checkpoints so readers do not replay the entire history. B captures the time-travel consequence: you can recreate the state of a table at any point in time by starting with an original table and processing only commits made prior to that point [source 5]. D captures the practical failure mode of directory-scanning: removes are logical, so stale Parquet files linger and a raw listing over-reports. C is the distractor this unit explicitly debunks — data files are still Parquet in an open format; what Delta adds is the ordered, immutable log that delivers ACID guarantees through optimistic concurrency control and time travel [source 3], not a closed container format.

actions.text: Let's see how the Delta Lake foundations we just covered have settled in. This one is a quick knowledge check, so read each item carefully and answer on your own.
Take your time with each question — try every one before you submit, and I'll walk through the reasoning with you once you're done.

scenes.title: Creating a Managed Delta Table

elements.content: Creating a Managed Delta Table
Goal: write CREATE TABLE DDL that produces a managed Delta table — the default path in Databricks.
Managed by Default: Format and Physical Location

• CREATE TABLE students (id INT, name STRING); creates a managed Delta table.

• Delta is the default format — no USING clause is required to get transactional behaviour.

• Data lands in the metastore's managed warehouse directory (e.g. /user/hive/warehouse/students).

• DROP TABLE removes both metadata and data files; internal queries take the optimized fast path [source 1].
Worked Example — where the files go

CREATE TABLE sales (id INT, amt INT);

INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,10),(2,20);

Result: 2 rows stored as Parquet in .../warehouse/sales, plus a commit 00000000000000000000.json in _delta_log [source 4].
One-Statement Variants: Create or Fully Replace

• CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE and CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT create and fully replace a table in one atomic commit — readers never see a partially rebuilt table, because each commit writes a single new log version [source 5].

• CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is a no-op when the table already exists; no new version is committed.

• PARTITIONED BY and TBLPROPERTIES (e.g. 'delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite' = 'true') are declared at creation time and are visible in the table metadata action of the log.

data.text: Creates a new managed Delta table; errors if the table already exists
No-op (succeeds silently) when the table already exists
Creates or atomically replaces the table and its data in one commit
Creates the table from a query result, replacing it atomically if it exists

actions.text: Now that we've established the Delta table baseline, let's put it into practice. On this page we're going to create a managed Delta table — and the key thing to remember is that the default CREATE TABLE path in Databricks already gives you Delta. You don't have to specify a format at all.

Here's our objective: write CREATE TABLE DDL that produces a managed Delta table. 'Managed' means Databricks owns both the metadata and the physical data files, so you never have to point at a storage location yourself.

This is the part exam questions love. Delta is the default format, so a simple statement like CREATE TABLE students with id INT and name STRING creates a managed Delta table. Its files live in the metastore's managed warehouse directory — you didn't specify a LOCATION, and you didn't need to.

Let's walk a worked example so you can see where the files actually go. We create a table called sales and insert a couple of rows — and then we ask: on disk, where did those Parquet files land? Under the managed warehouse directory, in a folder named after the table.

Notice the pattern here. The CREATE TABLE defines the schema; the INSERT writes the first data files; and Delta automatically creates the _delta_log alongside them. That log, which we studied earlier, is what makes this a Delta table rather than just a folder of Parquet.
There are also one-statement variants that create or fully replace a table. These are worth memorizing because they behave very differently from one another.

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE and CREATE TABLE AS SELECT both create and fully replace a table in one atomic commit — the old data is gone. By contrast, CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is a no-op when the table already exists: it succeeds silently and leaves your data untouched.

This table summarizes the four variants side by side with their effect, and it also reminds us that PARTITIONED BY and TBLPROPERTIES — for example delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite — are declared at creation time and show up in the table metadata. Read this table carefully; it's the highest-yield part of this page for the exam.

scenes.title: External (Unmanaged) Delta Tables

elements.content: External (Unmanaged) Delta Tables
Objective: create an external Delta table with an explicit LOCATION, then predict exactly what DROP TABLE destroys and what it leaves behind.

Definition. An external table pairs a schema in the metastore with data at a path you name. The catalog stores only the schema and the pointer — never the bytes. Precondition: the table is unmanaged, so deleting it cannot delete storage it does not own [source 4].

Path options. The LOCATION may be a DBFS path or cloud storage (S3, ADLS, GCS) you control. Edge case: a path that already contains Parquet files plus a _delta_log directory is a live Delta table whether or not the metastore knows it [source 4].

elements.html: \text{CREATE TABLE t USING DELTA LOCATION '/mnt/data/t'
\text{SELECT * FROM delta.\texttt{`}/mnt/data/t\texttt{`}

elements.content: Register an existing Delta directory with an explicit LOCATION, or read it unregistered with the delta.`path` syntax — no catalog entry required.
DROP TABLE behavior — the recurring exam trap

Managed table: DROP TABLE removes the metadata and the underlying data files. The metastore owns both, so both are destroyed.

External table: DROP TABLE removes only the metadata. The data, the _delta_log, and the pointer's target all survive [source 5].
Worked example. Table sales_ext has LOCATION s3://bucket/sales (1.2 GB, 40 Parquet files). DROP TABLE leaves 1.2 GB intact in S3; only the metastore entry vanishes.

Trap: deleting files by hand. If you delete an external table's files in cloud storage while the catalog entry survives, the registered table now points at nothing — queries fail, yet DROP TABLE still runs cleanly because metadata and storage are decoupled [source 5].
Practice — predict the outcome. You have events_ext with LOCATION /mnt/events, 3 GB of Parquet files, and no managed copy. You run DROP TABLE events_ext. What remains?
A. The 3 GB of Parquet files are deleted from /mnt/events.
B. The files remain, but the catalog entry is gone — data is orphaned.
C. Nothing changes; the table is still queryable by name in the metastore.

Answer: B. External tables decouple metadata from storage — only the catalog entry is removed. Misconception A confuses this with managed-table behavior; C ignores that DROP TABLE always removes the metastore entry [source 5].

1. External tables keep data at a path you own; the metastore stores only the schema and the pointer.

2. DROP TABLE removes metadata only for external tables, but metadata and data for managed tables.

3. An existing Delta directory can be read with delta.`path` and registered later with LOCATION.

4. Deleting an external table's files by hand leaves a registered table pointing at nothing.
Sources: transactional guarantees and time travel [source 5]; table-level features and schema enforcement [source 4]; time travel via the transaction log [source 2].

actions.text: Now we move from managed tables to external tables — also called unmanaged tables. These are the ones where the data lives at a path you own, and the metastore stores only the schema and the pointer to that path.
Our objective on this page is twofold: first, create an external Delta table with an explicit LOCATION, and second, be able to predict exactly what DROP TABLE does to an external table.

Here's the definition. An external table pairs a schema registered in the catalog with data that physically lives outside of the managed warehouse. The metadata and the data are decoupled — that single idea drives everything else on this page.
For the location, you can use a DBFS path or a cloud storage path such as an S3 or ADLS bucket. Whatever path you choose, that's where the actual Parquet files sit — not in the managed storage root.
The syntax is straightforward: CREATE TABLE using DELTA, with a LOCATION clause pointing at the directory. Let's look at the DDL on the slide so you can see how the path is wired in.
A really useful pattern: you can register an existing Delta directory with an explicit location. That means you can query raw files first and register them later — no data movement required.
Notice the SELECT statement — you can read a Delta directory without registering it at all, just by using the delta backtick path syntax. The metastore is optional for reading.
Now, the recurring exam trap: DROP TABLE behavior. This distinction between managed and external tables is where certification questions love to trip people up.

For a managed table, DROP TABLE removes both the metadata and the data. For an external table, it removes only the metadata — the files at your LOCATION survive untouched. Say that distinction out loud to yourself; it's worth a point on the exam.

Here's a worked example. Table sales_ext has a LOCATION on S3. If we drop this table, the catalog entry disappears but the 3 gigabytes of Parquet in S3 remain — fully readable if we re-register the table later.

And here's the inverse trap: deleting files by hand. If you delete an external table's files directly in cloud storage, the catalog entry still exists and still points at that path — you've created a registered table that queries nothing. The catalog and the storage are decoupled, and that decoupling is a feature and a hazard at the same time.
Let's practice. You have events_ext, an external Delta table with 3 GB of Parquet at /mnt/events. You run DROP TABLE events_ext. What happens?
Option A claims the files are deleted. That would only be true for a managed table.
Option B says the files remain but the catalog entry is gone. That matches exactly what we just covered about external tables.
Option C claims nothing changes and the table is still queryable. But without a catalog entry, the table name no longer resolves — so that can't be right.
The answer is B. External tables decouple metadata from data — the DROP strips the catalog entry, the Parquet files stay put, and the table is fully re-registrable from the same location later.

Let's recap the key takeaways. External tables keep data at a path you own. The metastore stores only the schema and the pointer. And DROP TABLE removes metadata only for external tables — the data is yours to keep.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Managed vs External Behavior

questions.question: A Databricks workspace contains two tables: `events_managed` (a MANAGED table) and `events_external` (an EXTERNAL table whose LOCATION points to a folder in the same Unity Catalog managed storage volume). An analyst runs `DROP TABLE events_managed;` and then `DROP TABLE events_external;`. Which statement correctly describes the state of storage immediately after both statements succeed?

options.label: Both the metadata and the underlying data files are deleted for both tables, because DROP TABLE always purges everything Databricks created.

For `events_managed`, Databricks deletes both the table metadata in the metastore and the data files it owns; for `events_external`, Databricks deletes only the table metadata, and the files at the specified LOCATION remain in storage.

For `events_managed`, Databricks deletes only the metadata and keeps the data files; for `events_external`, Databricks deletes the metadata and the data files because the LOCATION resides inside managed storage.
Both tables retain their metadata, because Delta Lake is an immutable log and no version can ever be physically removed from object storage after it has been committed.

questions.analysis: This question targets Objective 1: predicting the storage state after DROP TABLE for each table type. Managed (internal) tables are owned end-to-end by the metastore: dropping them removes both the catalog entry and the data files, because the table's lifecycle is bound to the catalog. External tables deliberately decouple lifecycle from data: the metadata entry disappears so the name can be reused, but the files at the LOCATION are kept so another engine or workspace can still read them. Option A over-generalizes by treating DROP like a purge for both types. Option C inverts the two behaviors, which is the single most common student error. Option D confuses the immutability of the Delta transaction log — which is why time travel works within a retained version history [source 5] — with physical file deletion; dropping an external table's metadata does not mean the log and files cannot be deleted or that they are protected forever, and dropping a managed table does delete its files.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about identifying and reasoning about MANAGED versus EXTERNAL tables in Databricks are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: `SHOW TABLES` alone is sufficient to report whether a given table is MANAGED or EXTERNAL, because it lists the table type column alongside the name.

`DESCRIBE EXTENDED <table_name>` (or `DESCRIBE DETAIL <table_name>` in Databricks SQL / PySpark) reports the table type and, where applicable, the storage LOCATION, so it can be used to determine whether a table is MANAGED or EXTERNAL.

A common exam distractor claims that an EXTERNAL table cannot support UPDATE or DELETE; in reality an external Delta table supports `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, and `MERGE` exactly like a managed Delta table, because the operations are driven by the Delta transaction log, not by the table's lifecycle type [source 3].
Because an EXTERNAL table's data is outside Databricks' lifecycle, an external table also loses ACID guarantees and time travel; those are reserved for MANAGED tables in Unity Catalog.

questions.analysis: Objective 2 (identify the statement that reports table type) and Objective 3 (recognise the trap distractor) are both tested here. `DESCRIBE EXTENDED` (or its Databricks SQL / PySpark `DESCRIBE DETAIL` counterpart) surfaces the table type and location, so it is the reliable way to distinguish MANAGED from EXTERNAL — B is correct. The classic trap is that external tables somehow lose DML; they do not: `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, and `MERGE` work on any Delta table because correctness comes from the transaction log and optimistic concurrency control, not from where the files happen to sit [source 3], so C is correct. A is wrong: `SHOW TABLES` lists table names (and, depending on catalog, can show a type column but does not universally and reliably indicate MANAGED vs EXTERNAL for the purposes of this exam objective — the authoritative way is DESCRIBE). D is wrong because ACID guarantees and time travel come from Delta Lake's ordered, immutable log and version history [source 3][source 5]; a managed vs external distinction changes the *lifecycle* of the files, not the transactional semantics of the table.

questions.question: A data platform team must publish a curated analytics dataset that (a) will be read by a separate Databricks workspace and by an external engine, (b) must be updated nightly with corrections using `MERGE`, and (c) must allow engineers to query the previous seven days of data for regulatory audit (time travel). Which table type and storage choice best satisfies all three requirements?

options.label: A plain Parquet folder in cloud object storage, because open format alone satisfies (a) and (b) and Parquet contains all historical versions for (c).
A MANAGED Delta table in the source workspace, because it is the only type that supports `MERGE` and time travel.

An EXTERNAL Delta table whose LOCATION is an open cloud storage path registered in Unity Catalog, because Delta Lake provides ACID transactions, `MERGE`, and time travel [source 3] while the external LOCATION keeps the files accessible to other workspaces and engines.
A cloud data warehouse table, because it is the only option that simultaneously provides ACID transactions, update support, and an open, engine-agnostic format.

questions.analysis: Objective 4 requires mapping business requirements to the correct table type. Requirement (a) demands openness and cross-workspace readability: the files must be in an open format outside a single metastore's life cycle, so EXTERNAL is appropriate. Requirement (b) demands `MERGE`, which Parquet cannot provide because there is no transaction log to record the merge atomically [source 4]. Requirement (c) demands time travel, which Delta Lake delivers via its ordered, immutable log and version history [source 3][source 5]. Option C combines the open storage of an external LOCATION with Delta's transactional engine features, satisfying all three. Option A is wrong because plain Parquet is not ACID, has no `MERGE`, and has no version history [source 4]. Option B is wrong because a MANAGED Delta table would still provide `MERGE` and time travel, but it binds the files to the source workspace's metastore lifecycle, which conflicts with the cross-workspace/engine requirement. Option D is wrong because data warehouses use proprietary, closed formats; Delta's key differentiator is combining an open format with warehouse-grade reliability [source 3].
