Work through each question on your own, take your time, and pick the option you can justify with the concepts we laid out. I'll meet you after you submit to walk through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Managed vs External Delta Tables Side by Side

elements.content: Dimension  |  Managed Delta Table  |  External Delta Table

Physical data location
Managed Delta Table: Data files live under the metastore warehouse directory that the catalog assigns (for example, a Unity Catalog managed storage location or the Hive metastore warehouse root), and the fully qualified path is chosen by the platform rather than by the author of the CREATE TABLE statement, so the writer controls only the table name and schema.
External Delta Table: Data files live at the explicit LOCATION path supplied in the DDL (for example, an abfss:// or s3:// URI that the team already owns), so the physical address is decided by the data engineer and the catalog merely records a pointer to it, which means the table name can be dropped or renamed without moving a single byte.

Effect of DROP TABLE
Managed Delta Table: DROP TABLE is destructive to data as well as metadata: because the catalog owns the directory, the drop removes the metadata entry from the metastore and deletes the underlying files, so the bytes are gone and recovery requires either a restore from another copy or a time-travel query issued before the drop actually removes the files.
External Delta Table: DROP TABLE removes only the catalog entry and the _delta_log pointer; the Parquet files and the transaction log remain untouched at the LOCATION path, so the same data can be immediately re-registered with a new CREATE TABLE ... USING DELTA LOCATION statement or read directly by another engine [source 5].

Who owns the data lifecycle
Managed Delta Table: The metastore and the workspace own the lifecycle: the platform is responsible for the directory, for cleanup on drop, and for policies such as retention and storage-credential management, which is why managed tables are the low-friction default for data the workspace itself produces.
External Delta Table: The external storage account owner retains lifecycle control: because the path exists independently of the catalog, a drop cannot silently destroy shared data, and retention, versioning, and deletion policies are governed by the object-storage account and the team rather than by the metastore.

Typical use case
Managed Delta Table: Best as the default for most tables the workspace owns end-to-end, such as bronze/silver/gold layers produced by Lakeflow pipelines, where the team wants the platform to manage paths and cleanup automatically and has no need to expose the files to other engines.
External Delta Table: Best when pre-existing data must be registered without copying it, when a single physical dataset must be shared across multiple workspaces or catalogs, or when an external engine (for example, a non-Databricks Spark cluster or a plain Parquet reader) must be able to read the same files in place.

Table capability: DML, ACID, and time travel
Managed Delta Table: Supports the full DML surface (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE), provides ACID guarantees through optimistic concurrency control, and supports time travel via the ordered, immutable transaction log, because capability comes from the Delta protocol rather than from the directory owner; a managed table is therefore fully ACID and fully versioned.
External Delta Table: Supports exactly the same full DML surface, the same ACID guarantees delivered by optimistic concurrency control, and the same time travel by version number or timestamp, because the transaction log and the protocol are identical in both cases — the difference is lifecycle ownership of the files, not table capability [source 3].

Relation to the transaction log and checkpoints
Managed Delta Table: The _delta_log directory is written inside the platform-managed warehouse path, so the log, its commit files, and its checkpoint files (for example 00000000000000000010.checkpoint.parquet) move and get deleted together with the data directory when the table is dropped.
External Delta Table: The _delta_log directory sits alongside the data at the LOCATION path, which is precisely why the log survives a DROP TABLE and why a later reader can reconstruct any version: the log is an immutable ordered record, so replaying only the commits before a target version recreates the table state at that point [source 5].

Permissions and governance surface
Managed Delta Table: Because storage is managed by the metastore, access is granted primarily through catalog-level privileges (for example, USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, SELECT on the table) and the platform holds the storage credential, so users never need direct file-system rights.
External Delta Table: Because the path is external, the catalog must also hold a storage credential that can reach that path, and the team must separately govern direct file-system access; anyone with raw storage permission can read or delete the files outside of catalog control, which is a governance consideration the exam treats as a real tradeoff rather than a detail.

Decision rule
Managed Delta Table: Choose managed when the answer to "who should own the bytes if this table is dropped?" is the platform or the workspace — that is, when the table is the system of record and losing it on drop is the intended behavior.
External Delta Table: Choose external when the answer to the same question is a team, an external account, or another workspace — that is, when the files must outlive the catalog entry because they are registered, shared, or produced by an outside system; the rule keys on lifecycle ownership, not on performance, since both types commit through the same log and read the same Parquet files.

Takeaway — The decision is about file lifecycle ownership, not about capability or speed: managed and external Delta tables both deliver full DML, ACID transactions via optimistic concurrency control, and time travel because both use the identical _delta_log mechanism [source 3].

Takeaway — Default to a managed table for data the workspace creates and owns end-to-end (typical bronze/silver/gold pipelines), because the platform chooses the path and DROP TABLE intentionally removes the files.

Takeaway — Choose an external table when existing data must be registered in place without copying, when one physical dataset is shared across workspaces, or when an outside engine must read the same files, accepting that DROP TABLE keeps the files and that governance must cover both catalog privileges and raw storage access.

Takeaway — Always ask the exam question first: if the table is dropped, who should own the bytes? If the answer is the platform, use managed; if the answer is a team or an external account, use external.

Takeaway — Because time travel depends on the log and its retained files, deleting historical files limits your ability to reach specific versions, so any retention policy applied at the storage layer affects both table types equally [source 2].

actions.text: Now let's consolidate everything from the last two pages into a single decision table — managed versus external Delta tables, side by side across the dimensions the exam actually tests. This is the reference sheet you want in your head when a scenario question asks you to choose a table type.

Start with physical data location. A managed table stores its data files in the metastore's warehouse directory — you never name the path yourself. An external table stores its files at the LOCATION path you specify, which can live in a bucket that other systems and other workspaces also read from.

The second dimension is the effect of DROP TABLE, and this is the one exam writers love. Drop a managed table and Databricks removes the metadata and the underlying files. Drop an external table and only the metadata goes away — the files stay exactly where they were, ready to be re-registered later.

That leads directly to the third dimension: who owns the data lifecycle. For a managed table, Databricks owns the bytes and their cleanup. For an external table, you own the bytes — Databricks just governs a pointer to them.

And the typical use case follows: managed is the best default for most tables the workspace fully owns, while external is the right call when existing data must be registered in place, or shared across multiple workspaces and engines.

Here's the part people get wrong under pressure: capability is identical. Both managed and external tables support full DML, ACID guarantees, and time travel. The difference is lifecycle ownership of the files — not what the table can do.

So the decision rule reduces to one question: if this table were dropped, who should own the bytes? If the answer is the workspace, go managed. If the answer is the business or another team, go external. Notice that performance never enters the decision — it's purely about ownership.

Burn these takeaways in: the decision is about file lifecycle ownership, not table capability. Default to managed for data your workspace owns, choose external when existing data must be registered or shared, and on any exam question ask who owns the bytes after a DROP first. Because time travel depends on the log, both types behave the same there — so never let time travel be your tie-breaker. Next, we'll apply all of this in worked DDL and metadata problems.

scenes.title: Worked Problems: Table DDL and Metadata Inspection

elements.content: Problem 1

You are working in a Databricks workspace and need to create a managed Delta table called `transactions` with the following schema: `txn_id INT, acct_id INT, amount DECIMAL(10,2), txn_date DATE`. The table must be partitioned by `txn_date`. After creating the table, you insert a small batch of data and then inspect its metadata. Specifically: (a) Write the correct `CREATE TABLE` DDL statement. (b) After inserting data, run the appropriate command to confirm that the table format is Delta, find its physical storage location, and determine the number of files and total size in bytes. (c) Explain how you would confirm that the table is managed by the metastore rather than external.
Hint: Use `DESCRIBE DETAIL` for physical file information and `DESCRIBE EXTENDED` for catalog information such as table type and provider.

Worked solution
(a) The DDL to create a managed Delta table partitioned by `txn_date` is:

```sql

CREATE TABLE transactions (

txn_id INT,

acct_id INT,

amount DECIMAL(10,2),

txn_date DATE

)

USING DELTA

PARTITIONED BY (txn_date);

```

Because Delta is the default format in Databricks, the `USING DELTA` clause is optional, but explicitly stating it reinforces the intent. The `PARTITIONED BY` clause directs Databricks to physically organize data into subdirectories by the `txn_date` column.

(b) After inserting a few rows, run:

```sql

DESCRIBE DETAIL transactions;

```

This returns a result set with columns including `format`, `location`, `numFiles`, and `sizeInBytes`. For example, the output might show:

- `format` = `delta`

- `location` = `dbfs:/user/hive/warehouse/transactions` (or a cloud storage path like `s3://my-bucket/warehouse/transactions`)

- `numFiles` = `3` (one file per partition directory, depending on data distribution)

- `sizeInBytes` = `2048` (total size of all data files)

These values confirm that the table uses Delta format, resides at the specified location, and currently consists of 3 files totaling 2048 bytes. The exact numbers depend on the inserted data and partitioning.

(c) To determine whether the table is managed or external, run:

```sql

DESCRIBE EXTENDED transactions;

```

Look for the `Type` row in the output. For a managed table, `Type` is `MANAGED`. Additionally, the `Provider` row will show `DELTA`. A managed table means that the metastore owns both the metadata and the data files; dropping the table will delete the data files. In contrast, an external table would show `Type` = `EXTERNAL`, and dropping it would leave the data files intact. [source 4] highlights that Delta Lake's transaction log enables ACID transactions and time travel, which are properties of the table format itself, independent of managed/external status.

Analysis — The key distinction here is between `DESCRIBE DETAIL` and `DESCRIBE EXTENDED`. `DESCRIBE DETAIL` returns physical file-level information: format, location, number of files, size in bytes, partition columns, and table properties. `DESCRIBE EXTENDED` returns catalog-level metadata: column names and types, partition information, table type (MANAGED or EXTERNAL), provider (DELTA), location, and other properties. Students often confuse these two commands, leading to errors when asked to find file counts or table type. A common mistake is to run `DESCRIBE EXTENDED` expecting to see `numFiles`, which is not present; conversely, `DESCRIBE DETAIL` does not show `Type` (managed/external). Another pitfall is assuming that `DESCRIBE DETAIL` reports logical row counts; it reports physical file statistics. Always verify the exact command required by the question. This generalizes: in Databricks, metadata inspection requires choosing the right `DESCRIBE` variant based on whether you need physical or catalog information. [source 1] notes that Delta Lake provides optimized metadata management for faster query performance, which is why `DESCRIBE DETAIL` can quickly return file statistics without scanning data.
Problem 2

An existing directory in cloud storage contains Delta Lake data files at `s3://lake/sales`. The data is already in Delta format, but it is not registered in the metastore. You need to (a) query the data directly without creating a table, (b) register it as an external table named `ext_sales` so that it appears in the catalog and can be queried with SQL using the table name, and (c) explain what happens to the underlying files if you later run `DROP TABLE ext_sales`.
Hint: Use the `delta.` path syntax for direct queries and `CREATE TABLE ... USING DELTA LOCATION` for registration.

Worked solution
(a) To query the data directly without creating a table, use the `delta.` path syntax:

```sql

SELECT * FROM delta.`s3://lake/sales`;

```

This reads the Delta transaction log at that location and returns the data as of the latest version. It does not create any metastore entry. This works because Delta Lake's transaction log is self-describing: the log contains all metadata needed to read the table. [source 3] explains that the transaction log is the foundational mechanism that transforms object storage into a reliable lakehouse platform, enabling ACID guarantees and time travel.

(b) To register the data as an external table, use:

```sql

CREATE TABLE ext_sales

USING DELTA

LOCATION 's3://lake/sales';

```

This statement creates a table named `ext_sales` in the metastore that points to the existing Delta directory. The data files are not moved or copied. The table is external because it is defined with an explicit `LOCATION`; Databricks does not manage the lifecycle of the data files. You can now query it with:

```sql

SELECT * FROM ext_sales;

```

(c) If you run:

```sql

DROP TABLE ext_sales;

```

The metastore entry for `ext_sales` is removed, but the data files at `s3://lake/sales` remain intact. This is the defining behavior of an external table: the metastore manages only the metadata, not the data. In contrast, dropping a managed table would delete both the metadata and the data files. [source 4] emphasizes that a traditional data lake is a flexible repository for raw files but lacks table-level features; by registering the Delta directory as an external table, you gain SQL queryability and ACID guarantees without sacrificing the openness of the data.

Analysis — The core concept is the separation of metadata and data. Managed tables are fully controlled by the metastore: creating one creates a directory, and dropping it deletes the directory. External tables only register a pointer to an existing location; dropping them removes the pointer but leaves the data untouched. This is crucial for data sharing and for avoiding accidental data loss. The `delta.` path syntax allows ad-hoc queries without any catalog registration, which is useful for exploration. A common mistake is to use `CREATE TABLE` without `LOCATION` for an existing directory, which would create a new managed table with an empty directory, or to assume that `DROP TABLE` on an external table deletes the files. Another pitfall is forgetting that `LOCATION` must point to a directory containing a valid `_delta_log`. Always verify that the path contains a Delta log before attempting to register it. This generalizes to any external table in Databricks, not just Delta: the `LOCATION` clause signals external management. [source 3] notes that the transaction log transforms object storage into a reliable lakehouse platform, which is why registering an existing Delta directory is safe and non-destructive.

actions.text: Alright, let's put the managed versus external distinction to work with two fully worked problems that closely mirror the exam. Both are about creating tables and then inspecting their metadata.

Problem 1: you're in a Databricks workspace and you need to create a managed Delta table called transactions with four columns — txn_id, acct_id, an amount as DECIMAL 10 comma 2, and a txn_date of type DATE — partitioned by the transaction date. Then you must confirm three things: the table format, its storage location, and the file count.

The solution: CREATE TABLE transactions with those columns, USING DELTA, PARTITIONED BY txn_date. Because there's no LOCATION clause and no Unity Catalog external reference, this is a managed table — Databricks owns both the metadata and the files. Then DESCRIBE DETAIL transactions returns format equals delta, the warehouse location, numFiles, and sizeInBytes.
Remember the hint here: DESCRIBE DETAIL is what gives you physical file information — location, number of files, and total bytes. That's exactly the tool the question is testing.
So far, so good. Now let's move to the more subtle one — Problem 2, where the table already exists out in cloud storage.
Problem 2: a directory in cloud storage, s3 colon slash slash lake slash sales, already contains Delta data. You need to query it, and you need to register it without moving or copying the files.

Two-part solution. First, SELECT star FROM delta dot backtick s3 colon slash slash lake slash sales backtick — the delta dot path syntax lets you query the data directly, with no catalog entry at all. Second, CREATE TABLE ext_sales USING DELTA LOCATION pointing at that path — this registers the existing directory as an EXTERNAL table, catalog-managed but file-owned by you. Then DROP TABLE ext_sales removes only the metadata — the underlying files stay intact.

And here's the exam-critical analysis. The key distinction is between DESCRIBE DETAIL, which returns physical file information — numFiles, sizeInBytes, location — and DESCRIBE EXTENDED, which returns catalog information, including Type equals MANAGED or EXTERNAL, and Provider equals DELTA. Confusing the two is one of the most common exam errors. And a second trap: never assume DESCRIBE EXTENDED reports file counts — it doesn't. That's DESCRIBE DETAIL's job.

Both problems reinforce the same core skill: know which command answers which question. DESCRIBE DETAIL for physical layout, DESCRIBE EXTENDED for governance metadata, and the delta. path syntax when you just want to read without registering.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Reading Table Metadata

questions.question:
A data engineer runs three DESCRIBE variants against a Delta table and must map each command to the fields it actually returns. For each statement below, decide whether the described field-to-command pairing is CORRECT or INCORRECT:

I. DESCRIBE DETAIL returns the table's physical location, numFiles, and sizeInBytes.
II. DESCRIBE EXTENDED returns the table Type (MANAGED or EXTERNAL) in its detailed information section.
III. DESCRIBE HISTORY returns the operation, version, and timestamp of each commit.

Which of the following correctly classifies all three statements?

options.label: I = Correct, II = Correct, III = Correct
I = Correct, II = Incorrect, III = Correct
I = Incorrect, II = Correct, III = Correct
I = Correct, II = Correct, III = Incorrect

questions.analysis: All three statements are correct. DESCRIBE DETAIL returns metadata about the table's physical storage layout, including the location path, numFiles and sizeInBytes, which are the two fields most often tested because they describe how the data is actually stored on disk rather than how it is logically defined. DESCRIBE EXTENDED returns the detailed information section that includes the table Type (MANAGED or EXTERNAL) and the Provider, which describes the format backing the table. DESCRIBE HISTORY returns one row per commit with the version number, timestamp, operation name, operation parameters, and user metadata. The three commands therefore form a clean division of labour: DETAIL = physical storage, EXTENDED = logical and storage classification, HISTORY = the ordered commit record. Because the log is an ordered, immutable record of all table operations [source 3], it is precisely the structure that DESCRIBE HISTORY projects into a readable table, while the same log is what allows DESCRIBE DETAIL to compute numFiles and sizeInBytes without scanning the directory. Distractor B is the classic error of assuming that EXTENDED lacks the Type field; in fact Type and Provider are its headline fields. Distractor C inverts the most common confusion by claiming DETAIL does not expose storage fields, when those are exactly its purpose. Distractor D misplaces the HISTORY fields as if the commit record were missing from the history command.

questions.question:
A reviewer states: "To confirm that a Delta table is an external table and to see how much data it occupies on disk, I will run SHOW TABLES and read the storage path, numFiles, and sizeInBytes columns from its output."

Which of the following best evaluates this statement?

options.label: Correct: SHOW TABLES lists every table with its location, numFiles, and sizeInBytes, so it is the most efficient way to answer both questions.

Incorrect: SHOW TABLES returns only table names and basic metadata such as the database and table name, so it cannot return the storage path, numFiles, or sizeInBytes; the reviewer should use DESCRIBE DETAIL for path, numFiles, and sizeInBytes, and DESCRIBE EXTENDED to confirm the table Type (MANAGED or EXTERNAL).
Incorrect: SHOW TABLES does return the storage path but not numFiles or sizeInBytes, so the reviewer only needs to add DESCRIBE EXTENDED to obtain the file count and total size.
Incorrect: neither SHOW TABLES nor DESCRIBE DETAIL returns a storage path because Delta tables are logical objects; only DESCRIBE HISTORY exposes the physical location in its operation parameters.

questions.analysis: Option B is correct. SHOW TABLES is a catalog listing command: it enumerates the tables in a schema and returns lightweight metadata such as the namespace and table name, not the physical storage layout. The correct tools are DESCRIBE DETAIL for location, numFiles, and sizeInBytes, and DESCRIBE EXTENDED for the table Type and Provider. This matters because Delta tables come in two flavours: external (unmanaged) tables keep the data at a path you own, and the metastore stores only the schema and the pointer, whereas managed tables place their files in the metastore's managed warehouse directory. Only DESCRIBE EXTENDED tells you which of those two you are looking at, and only DESCRIBE DETAIL tells you how many files and how many bytes that path currently holds. Option A is the trap distractor: it is fluent and confident, but it assigns storage-layout columns to a command that has no such columns. Option C concedes the premise half-way by granting SHOW TABLES a path column that does not exist. Option D is the opposite error, denying that any command exposes the path, even though the transaction log's commit metadata is exactly what DESCRIBE DETAIL projects; the ability to recreate table state at a point in time rests on that same ordered record of commits [source 5], and the log is what makes DESCRIBE DETAIL possible in the first place.

questions.question:
A platform team needs to answer four questions about a Delta table named events: (1) how many files the table is composed of and how many bytes those files occupy, (2) whether the table is MANAGED or EXTERNAL and what its Provider is, (3) the storage path where the table's data lives, and (4) which operation was committed at each version and when.

Select ALL of the following statements that are TRUE about how to obtain this information with the three DESCRIBE commands.

options.label: DESCRIBE DETAIL returns numFiles and sizeInBytes, answering question (1) without scanning the data directory.
DESCRIBE EXTENDED returns the table Type and Provider fields, answering question (2).
DESCRIBE HISTORY returns the storage path for question (3) in its operation parameters column, so DESCRIBE DETAIL is not needed.
DESCRIBE HISTORY returns one row per committed version with the operation name and timestamp, answering question (4) from the ordered, immutable commit record.

questions.analysis: A, B, and D are true; C is false. DESCRIBE DETAIL is the command whose output is centred on the physical layout of the table, so numFiles and sizeInBytes come from it; this is possible because Delta never scans the directory to answer such questions — it reads the transaction log, which maintains an ordered, immutable record of all table operations [source 3]. DESCRIBE EXTENDED is the command that reports the table Type (MANAGED or EXTERNAL) together with the Provider, which is what tells you whether the metastore holds only a pointer or owns the data as well. DESCRIBE HISTORY projects the commit record itself into a table of rows, one row per version, each carrying the operation, its parameters, the timestamp, and the user, which is exactly the ordered, immutable log that lets Delta recreate a table's state at any point in time [source 5]. Option C is the misconception: although history rows do contain operation parameters, the reliable and documented source for a table's storage path is DESCRIBE DETAIL, and treating the path as a HISTORY field will mislead anyone who then tries to reconcile file counts with a storage location. The distinction matters because time travel can be limited once historical files are deleted [source 2], so the version list from HISTORY and the live file inventory from DETAIL are not interchangeable views even though both derive from the same log.

Take your time and commit to an answer for every question, including the multi-select. Once you submit, I'll walk through each one with you and clear up anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: DML on Delta Tables: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

elements.content: DML on Delta Tables: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
Every DML statement — INSERT INTO, INSERT OVERWRITE, UPDATE, DELETE — is one atomic commit appended to the _delta_log, so readers see either the old table or the new table, never a partial write.

Atomic commit (preconditions & edge cases)

• Statement succeeds only if the writer commits at version N+1 without a race loss; otherwise it retries

• Commit is all-or-nothing: a failed statement writes no new log entry

• Even a zero-row DELETE or UPDATE still appends a commit

Copy-on-write (UPDATE / DELETE default)

1. Read the current snapshot from the log

2. Rewrite each affected Parquet file without the changed/target rows

3. Commit a new file list; readers resolve only the new list

Old files stay on storage for time travel

Worked example: a table has files A, B, C, D; DELETE FROM t WHERE id > 1000 touches B and D, so 2 files are rewritten (say 4 → 6 active files) and 2 stay untouched. DELETE FROM t with no predicate rewrites all of them but keeps the table, schema and history — a cheap reset compared to DROP TABLE (which removes all files). A predicate matching nothing still creates a commit.
Exam trap: INSERT OVERWRITE replaces the entire table's contents; INSERT INTO appends.

Sources: [source 1] ACID transactions · [source 3] log atomically records all operations via optimistic concurrency control · [source 4] transaction log tracks every change, enabling consistency and time travel

actions.text: That wraps up our knowledge check on reading table metadata. Now we move into the statements that actually change the rows in a Delta table — INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE.

By the end of this page you should be able to run INSERT INTO, INSERT OVERWRITE, UPDATE ... WHERE, and DELETE ... WHERE against a Delta table — and you should be able to explain what each one does to the table.

Here is the unifying idea. Every DML statement — INSERT INTO, INSERT OVERWRITE, UPDATE, DELETE — is a single atomic commit appended to the _delta_log. Because the commit either lands completely or not at all, readers always see either the old table or the new table, never a partially written one. That is the ACID guarantee we just covered, and DML is where you feel it in practice.

Under the hood, each commit carries preconditions and handles edge cases. The writer verifies the state it read is still valid, and only then appends the new log entry. So a concurrent DELETE and UPDATE cannot silently stomp on each other — one of them will fail the precondition and retry against the fresh state.

Now, how do UPDATE and DELETE actually rewrite data? By default they use copy-on-write. The engine reads only the files containing the affected rows, rewrites those files with the change applied, and then the commit swaps the file list that readers resolve against. Untouched files are never rewritten — that is the efficiency of the model.

Let's trace a worked example. A table has files A, B, C, and D. You run a DELETE that matches rows in A and C only. Delta rewrites A and C into new files, leaves B and D alone, and commits a new file list that points at the new A and C plus the original B and D. Time travel to the previous version still sees the old A and C, because the old files were never destroyed.

Two exam traps to lock in. First, INSERT OVERWRITE replaces the entire table's contents, while INSERT INTO appends — do not confuse them. Second, a DELETE predicate that matches no rows still creates a commit; the log version advances even though no data changed. That is the classic gotcha on this objective.

The sources for this section are the ACID transactions and DML references we have been working from. Next, we will open a notebook and run these statements ourselves so you can watch the transaction log grow with each commit.

actions.text: Compare the UPDATE commit and the DELETE commit carefully. Delta Lake is copy-on-write at the file level, so an UPDATE that touches one row still rewrites whole files — look at numFiles or numRemovedFiles in the metrics. That is why file rewriting, not row counts, drives the cost of a small update on a large table. Keep that distinction sharp: rows affected tells you about data, numFiles rewritten tells you about I/O.

One last experiment before we move on. Re-run the identical UPDATE statement without changing anything. Delta still writes a new version — even when the data is unchanged. That is not a bug; it is the log faithfully recording every write operation. Try it yourself, then open the test cases and hints below if the metric names are still fuzzy. scenes.title: Knowledge Check: DML and Atomic Commits

options.label: Statement 1 appends the new rows to the existing table contents, while Statement 2 replaces the entire table contents with the result of the SELECT.
Both statements append the new rows, but Statement 2 first triggers an internal compaction so only the newest files are read.
Statement 1 replaces the entire table contents, while Statement 2 appends the new rows on top of the existing data.
Both statements replace the entire table contents atomically, and the only difference is that Statement 2 skips the transaction log write.

questions.analysis: INSERT INTO adds the new rows as an incremental append: existing data files are left untouched and new files are added, so the previous rows remain visible after the commit. INSERT OVERWRITE replaces the logical contents of the table with the result set of the SELECT, so the prior rows are logically removed and the table now contains only the newly selected rows. Option C reverses the two semantics. Option B is wrong on two counts: INSERT INTO does not overwrite, and the overwrite path is not implemented as a 'compaction of newest files.' Option D is wrong because appending is the default and the log is still written for both statements. This append-vs-overwrite distinction matters because the transaction log tracks every change as one atomic commit, which is what makes either write safe and versioned [source 3].

questions.question: A reader is running a long query that started before a writer committed a DELETE followed by an UPDATE on the same Delta Lake table (delta.`/mnt/lake/sales`). The log shows commit versions 11 (DELETE of 40 rows), 12 (UPDATE of 5 rows), and 13 (DELETE of 2 rows). The reader's query was pinned to version 10. Which statements are true about this scenario? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The reader continues to see the table exactly as it existed at version 10; the DELETE and UPDATE at versions 11–13 do not change the reader's result set.
The single DELETE statement at version 11 produces exactly one new commit entry in the transaction log, representing one atomic logical change.
The UPDATE at version 12 modifies the existing Parquet data files in place so that the old row values are physically erased from object storage at that moment.
The table state as of version 10 remains readable after versions 11–13 have been committed, because the log is immutable and new commits are added on top rather than rewriting history.

questions.analysis: A is correct: snapshot isolation reads version 10's snapshot, so commits 11–13 are invisible to the reader even though they are already durably committed. B is correct: one DELETE is one transaction, and each transaction is one atomic commit in the log, so the DELETE at version 11 yields exactly one commit entry. C is the classic trap: Delta Lake uses copy-on-write semantics for updates and deletes, so the UPDATE writes new files and marks the old file versions as removed in the log; it does not mutate Parquet files in place. Removing the 40 rows from the DELETE is likewise a logical removal recorded in the log, not a physical rewrite of the files that held them. D is correct because the transaction log maintains an ordered, immutable sequence of operations, which is what enables time travel and lets prior versions stay queryable [source 3], and it is the mechanism that makes time travel by version number possible [source 2]. Option C's misconception also fails the immutability test in [source 4], which states that the log tracks every change and promotes consistency through that record.

scenes.title: MERGE: Upserts in One Atomic Statement

elements.content: MERGE INTO: One Atomic Upsert

MERGE INTO target t USING src s ON t.k = s.k

WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.v = s.v

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (k, v) VALUES (s.k, s.v)

WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE

• MERGE upserts and deletes target rows by join key.

• Standard SCD and CDC-upsert pattern [source 1].

• All clauses commit in one atomic version [source 3].

• Example: {1,2,3} + {2,4} → 1 update, 1 insert.

• WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE drops the row [source 4].

• BY SOURCE DELETE makes the target mirror the source.

• Duplicate source keys abort the MERGE with an error.

• Fix: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key) = 1.

actions.text: Now that we understand how DML commits atomically, let's look at the single most powerful of those statements: MERGE INTO. Think of it as an atomic upsert — update, insert, and delete, all inside one transaction.

Here's the canonical shape. We MERGE INTO the target, USING a source, and join them ON target dot key equals source dot key. Then each WHEN clause decides what happens to the rows that satisfy that condition — UPDATE SET when matched, INSERT when not matched.
The essential idea is that MERGE upserts and deletes target rows by the join key. One target row is matched by at most one source row, and the clause that fires is chosen by match status.

Add WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE and you drop the row on a match. And a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE clause lets you make the target an exact mirror of the source — anything in the target that no longer exists upstream disappears.

The critical guarantee: all clauses commit in one atomic version. Updates, inserts, and deletes are one commit, one new version in the Delta log — not a sequence of separate statements you have to orchestrate and roll back by hand.

Now the exam trap. If the source contains duplicate keys, the MERGE aborts with an error, because one target row would be updated multiple times. Deduplicate the source first — typically with ROW_NUMBER OVER PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated at DESC, keeping only row one.

Remember those three moves: use MERGE for the slowly-changing-dimension and CDC-upsert pattern, make the target a mirror with NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE, and always deduplicate the source before you run it. That last point is where points get lost on the exam.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: A MERGE-Based Upsert Pipeline

elements.content: Problem 1

It is 02:00 and your nightly pipeline has just landed today's full customer extract into the staging table `staging_customers(customer_id STRING, name STRING, updated_at TIMESTAMP, load_date DATE)`. The snapshot contains 120,000 rows, but because the source CRM occasionally re-emits the same customer record twice within one extract window, 3,412 customers appear on more than one row — for example customer_id `C-7781` appears twice: once with name `'Ada Lovelace'` and updated_at `2024-06-01 09:14:00`, and once with name `'Ada Lovelace-Byron'` and updated_at `2024-06-01 11:47:00`. The target dimension table is `dim_customer(customer_id STRING, name STRING, updated_at TIMESTAMP)`, currently holding 118,500 rows. Your task: write ONE statement that (a) updates the name and updated_at of every customer whose values changed, (b) inserts customers present in today's snapshot but absent from dim_customer, and (c) deletes from dim_customer any customer that does not appear in today's snapshot — with no duplicate customer_id rows created in dim_customer. State the final row-count arithmetic for dim_customer.
Hint: The source is not unique on customer_id, so you must collapse it to one row per key before the MERGE can run.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Deduplicate the source to exactly one row per customer_id. MERGE matches rows through its ON clause, and if the source side of that join contains two rows with the same customer_id, the merge behaviour for the matched target row becomes ambiguous. We keep the most recent version of each customer with a window function:

```sql

WITH deduped_source AS (

SELECT customer_id, name, updated_at

FROM (

SELECT customer_id, name, updated_at,

ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn

FROM staging_customers

)

WHERE rn = 1

)

```

For `C-7781` the two candidates are `2024-06-01 09:14:00` and `2024-06-01 11:47:00`. Ordering by `updated_at DESC` ranks the 11:47 row as rn = 1, so the deduplicated source keeps `('C-7781', 'Ada Lovelace-Byron', 2024-06-01 11:47:00)` and discards the 09:14 row. Applied across the extract, the 120,000 staged rows collapse to 120,000 − 3,412 = 116,588 distinct customers.

Step 2 — Merge the deduplicated source into the dimension table in a single atomic commit:

```sql

MERGE INTO dim_customer AS t

USING deduped_source AS s

ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id

WHEN MATCHED THEN

UPDATE SET t.name = s.name, t.updated_at = s.updated_at

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN

INSERT (customer_id, name, updated_at)

VALUES (s.customer_id, s.name, s.updated_at)

WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN

DELETE;

```

Step 3 — Row-count arithmetic. Suppose today's snapshot has 116,588 distinct customers and dim_customer currently has 118,500 rows. Let `M` = customers in both (matched), `I` = customers only in today's snapshot (inserted), and `D` = customers only in dim_customer (deleted by NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE). Since insert count equals new keys and delete count equals deprecated keys, the net change is `I − D`. If, for example, `M = 115,000`, then `I = 116,588 − 115,000 = 1,588` new customers and `D = 118,500 − 115,000 = 3,500` departed customers, giving a final `dim_customer` size of `118,500 + 1,588 − 3,500 = 116,588` rows — exactly the number of distinct customers in today's snapshot, which is the invariant this pipeline should satisfy. The whole MERGE is one commit: the transaction log appends a single entry, so readers see either the pre-merge table or the post-merge table [source 3].

Analysis — Why deduplication is mandatory: the ON clause of a MERGE is a join, and Delta requires the merge source to present at most one row per join key for a deterministic result. A non-unique join key makes the outcome for the matched target row non-deterministic — the engine may raise an error rather than silently pick a row. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) with rn = 1 is the canonical idiom because it retains the freshest surviving version of each key. A common student mistake is using DISTINCT: it would eliminate exact duplicates only and would leave two rows for `C-7781`, because the two rows differ in name and updated_at. Another mistake is using ORDER BY ASC — this keeps the stale record and would push yesterday's name into the dimension table.

Why the ON clause symmetry matters: for correctness and for performance, the ON clause should reference only source columns on the source side of the comparison and only target columns on the target side; mixing alias scopes (e.g. using a target column on the right side of a source-qualified expression) is a frequent source of confusion, and the planner relies on the equi-join key `t.customer_id = s.customer_id` to co-partition and prune files. Non-equality ON predicates cannot be pushed down and force a broadcast of the entire target table.

Atomicity and time travel: because the MERGE is a single commit to the Delta transaction log, a concurrent reader never observes a half-applied update [source 3]. If a mistake is discovered, Delta's time travel restores the prior state: `SELECT * FROM dim_customer VERSION AS OF 7` reads the version immediately before the merge [source 5], and because the transaction log is an immutable, ordered sequence of commits, the pre-merge table state remains fully reconstructible [source 2]. This is the practical difference between Delta and a plain data lake, where a failed write could leave partially-written files that no reader can distinguish from good data [source 4].

Contrast with the two obvious alternatives: `INSERT OVERWRITE dim_customer SELECT ... FROM deduped_source` rewrites the entire table in one commit, discards the previous file list (and therefore the fast time travel path unless the old files survive the vacuum window), and rebuilds every file even when only 4% of rows changed. A delete-then-insert pattern (`DELETE FROM dim_customer; INSERT INTO dim_customer SELECT ...`) takes two commits, so between them the table is observably empty to any concurrent reader, and a failure between the two commits leaves the dimension table destroyed. MERGE also does not itself implement SCD Type 2 history; producing effective-date and current-flag columns requires explicit logic inside the MERGE's UPDATE/INSERT branches (e.g. setting `t.effective_end = current_timestamp()` and `t.is_current = false` when a tracked attribute changes, then inserting a new row with `effective_start = current_timestamp()`). This merges the dimension current-state fast path with the SCD2 pattern students should recognize as a follow-on exercise.
Problem 2

A data engineer claims that the following three-statement pattern is equivalent to a single MERGE for loading `dim_customer`, and therefore interchangeable because it is simpler:

```sql

DELETE FROM dim_customer WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM staging_customers);

DELETE FROM dim_customer WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM staging_customers);

INSERT INTO dim_customer SELECT customer_id, name, updated_at FROM staging_customers;

```

A reader queries `dim_customer` at 03:00, exactly between the second DELETE and the INSERT. Assume the staging extract contains 116,588 rows and dim_customer had 118,500 rows. Describe precisely what the reader sees, what could go wrong at scale, and compare against the single-commit MERGE. Then state one case where a DELETE-then-INSERT is genuinely preferable to MERGE.
Hint: Think about the state of the table between commits, and about what happens if the second DELETE succeeds but the INSERT fails.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Identify the observable window between commits. Each DELETE and the INSERT is its own atomic commit to the Delta transaction log [source 3]. Between statement two and statement three, the table has been wiped empty of the matched keys but not yet refilled. A reader running `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dim_customer` at 03:00 sees 118,500 − 3,500 = 115,000 rows (the delete that removes departed keys) and then 0 rows matching the keys that were just deleted, i.e. the matched set is gone. The reader is not observing a half-applied update — each statement is itself atomic — but the reader IS observing an intermediate, semantically inconsistent table state. This is a textbook violation of the atomicity property that MERGE preserves.

Step 2 — Failure mode analysis. If the INSERT fails (e.g. the staging file is corrupt, or a schema mismatch triggers schema enforcement), the DELETE has already committed. The dimension table is left permanently missing 115,000 matched customers. Recovery requires restoring from the previous version with `RESTORE TABLE dim_customer TO VERSION AS OF (version before the first DELETE)` or by re-running the whole pipeline. With MERGE, a failure aborts the entire transaction; the table remains exactly as it was before the statement. This is a direct consequence of the transaction log's ordered, immutable commit semantics [source 5].

Step 3 — Row-count comparison. Delete-then-insert as written also replaces every customer row even when only 4% of rows changed (3,500 deleted + 1,588 new + 115,000 rewritten). MERGE rewrites only the files containing changed rows: the ON clause's equi-join on customer_id lets Delta co-locate matched rows and skip untouched files, so at 03:00 a MERGE commit for this size of change typically touches a fraction of the files. The delete-then-insert pattern also silently breaks Delta's per-file statistics; after the INSERT, all new files must be re-analyzed for file-skipping the next time the table is queried, and `OPTIMIZE` is often required sooner.

Step 4 — Where DELETE-then-INSERT wins. There is one case where the two-commit pattern is preferable: a full replace of a table whose semantics are "every row is being replaced anyway, and the new rows are radically different keys." MERGE with NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE has to evaluate every row of the target to find keys that are absent from the source, which is expensive when the source and target have low overlap. When 100% of rows are being replaced, `INSERT OVERWRITE dim_customer SELECT ...` does the work in a single commit and does not need a source-side dedup pass. This is the pattern students should reach for when the load is genuinely a full rebuild rather than an incremental update.

Analysis — The distinction the exam draws is between per-statement atomicity and statement-sequence atomicity. Every Delta DML statement — INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE — is a single atomic commit appended to the transaction log, so no statement can be observed half-applied [source 3]. But a sequence of statements is NOT atomic as a whole. Between two commits, concurrent readers see the table in whatever state the first commit established. A MERGE collapses the sequence into one commit, which is why it is the correct primitive for a three-part incremental load.

The common student misconception is that because Delta provides ACID, any sequence of operations is safe. ACID applies per transaction, not per pipeline stage. Multi-statement pipelines that must be atomic either use MERGE or wrap the statements in an explicit transaction (with the caveat that Delta transactions are constrained by the runtime). Another misconception is that DELETE followed by INSERT behaves like an UPSERT: it does not, because the intermediate state is empty for the affected keys.

Finally, note the connection to the previous scene's time-travel discussion: even after the correct MERGE commits, the pre-merge table remains reachable with `VERSION AS OF` [source 5, source 2]. Time travel is not a substitute for atomicity; it is a recovery mechanism for after the fact. The invariants this pipeline must preserve are (1) at most one row per customer_id, (2) current state of every customer in today's snapshot, (3) no customer present in the table that has departed. The MERGE delivers all three in one commit; the three-statement pattern delivers them only between commits.
Problem 3

A junior engineer runs the three-part MERGE from Problem 1 against `dim_customer`, but the source has not been deduplicated. In `staging_customers`, customer `C-7781` appears on two rows: one with `updated_at = 2024-06-01 09:14:00` and name `'Ada Lovelace'`, and one with `updated_at = 2024-06-01 11:47:00` and name `'Ada Lovelace-Byron'`. Another customer, `C-9012`, appears exactly once in the snapshot with name `'Ada Lovelace'`. The MERGE is:

```sql

MERGE INTO dim_customer AS t

USING staging_customers AS s

ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id

WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.name = s.name, t.updated_at = s.updated_at

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (customer_id, name, updated_at) VALUES (s.customer_id, s.name, s.updated_at)

WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE;

```

Explain what happens, how you would change the MERGE to fix it, and what if anything Delta does to prevent the ambiguity.
Hint: The ON clause is a join; what does a join do when one side has duplicate keys?

Worked solution
Step 1 — Diagnose the ambiguity. The ON clause `t.customer_id = s.customer_id` is an equi-join. For target row `C-7781` (which currently holds some name on dim_customer), the source side produces TWO matching rows. The MERGE engine cannot decide which source row to apply, and for a MERGE with an ASSIGNMENT clause (UPDATE SET) this is treated as a non-deterministic conflict. Depending on the runtime version, the engine either raises an error listing the offending key, or — worse — silently applies one of the two rows and thereby applies a name that may be the stale one.

Step 2 — Fix by collapsing the source. Prevent the ambiguity at the source:

```sql

WITH deduped_source AS (

SELECT customer_id, name, updated_at FROM (

SELECT customer_id, name, updated_at,

ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn

FROM staging_customers

) WHERE rn = 1

)

MERGE INTO dim_customer AS t

USING deduped_source AS s

ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id

WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.name = s.name, t.updated_at = s.updated_at

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (customer_id, name, updated_at) VALUES (s.customer_id, s.name, s.updated_at)

WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE;

```

For `C-7781`, `ORDER BY updated_at DESC` ranks the 11:47 row as rn = 1, so `'Ada Lovelace-Byron'` is the version that lands in dim_customer. `C-9012` has rn = 1 trivially and is inserted unchanged.

Step 3 — Verify the invariant. After the fix, the source has one row per customer_id, so each target row receives at most one update and each new key is inserted exactly once. `dim_customer` remains unique on customer_id by construction. Row-count arithmetic: 116,588 distinct customers in the source, final table size equals 116,588 rows (see Problem 1's arithmetic).

Step 4 — Note what Delta does NOT do. Delta provides schema enforcement and ACID commits [source 3, source 4], but it does not infer that two source rows should be collapsed by updated_at — that is business logic. Schema enforcement guards against structural problems (say, writing a STRING into an INT column), not against logical duplication of a join key. The correct place to enforce the uniqueness contract is either upstream in the ingestion (Auto Loader / Lakeflow pipelines often deduplicate per key on read) or in the deduped_source CTE.

Analysis — MERGE ambiguity on a non-unique join key is the single most common failure mode students hit on this objective, and the exam frequently tests it by showing two variants of a MERGE — one with a dedup CTE, one without — and asking which is correct. The distinguishing feature is the presence of a deterministic row-selection rule in the source. Common distractors include: (a) adding DISTINCT to the source and calling it fixed — false, because `C-7781` differs in name and updated_at so DISTINCT keeps both rows; (b) adding `ORDER BY updated_at DESC` to the MERGE itself without a window function — SQL does not define MERGE row selection that way; (c) deduplicating on the target side instead of the source — this does not help because the target does not have duplicates, the source does.

The deeper lesson is about join-key contracts. Any equi-join in a differential load — MERGE, UPDATE ... FROM, or a manual DELETE JOIN — assumes the source side is unique on the join key. This is a data contract, not something the SQL engine can validate for you at compile time. In a Databricks pipeline the contract is usually enforced upstream: Auto Loader or Lakeflow stages rows, a Silver-layer dedup produces one row per business key, then the Gold-layer MERGE consumes that constrained source. When you read about the transaction log providing ACID guarantees [source 3], note that ACID is a statement-level guarantee, not a logical-uniqueness guarantee; the engine will happily commit a MERGE that produced the wrong name if the source was set up incorrectly.

Finally, this problem also shows why the merge is preferable to the delete-then-insert pattern of Problem 2: after a bad load, `RESTORE TABLE` or `VERSION AS OF` returns the previous state in one command because the log is an ordered, immutable sequence [source 5, source 2]. In a data lake with no log, this recovery path does not exist — you would have to know which files to delete and which to restore from a backup, and nothing in the storage layer tells you which files are "current" [source 4].

actions.text: Now that we've seen MERGE as an atomic upsert statement, let's put it to work on a fully worked problem — an incremental-load pipeline that deduplicates a source and merges it into a dimension table.

Here's the scenario. It's 2 AM and your nightly pipeline has just landed today's extract in staging_customers. Your job: update changed customers in dim_customer, insert the new ones, and remove anyone who's dropped out of today's snapshot — all without ever duplicating a row. Take a moment to think about the order of operations before we look at the solution.
Before you scroll down, here's a hint: the source is not unique on customer_id. Sit with that for a second — what does a non-unique join key do to a MERGE?

Solution step one: deduplicate the source. We use ROW_NUMBER() OVER, partitioning by customer_id and ordering by updated_at descending, and keep only rows where row_number equals one. We do this precisely because a non-unique join key will make the MERGE fail. Step two: MERGE INTO dim_customer as the target, USING our deduped source, matching on customer_id — then WHEN MATCHED, update the name and timestamp; WHEN NOT MATCHED, insert; and WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE, delete. One atomic statement handles the whole upsert.

Now the analysis, and this is the part the exam loves. The join key must be unique in the source, the ON clause must reference only source columns on the source side, and the entire merge is a single commit — so a reader never sees a half-applied update, and the previous table state stays reachable through time travel. Compare that against the pitfalls: INSERT OVERWRITE throws away history and rewrites the whole table, and delete-then-insert takes two commits, so it isn't atomic. And remember, MERGE alone does not give you SCD Type 2 history — that requires explicit effective-date and current-flag columns.

Let's push further with problem two. A data engineer claims a particular three-statement approach is equivalent to our single MERGE. Is it? Think about the state of the table between those statements — that's the crack in the claim.
The hint here is exactly that: what does the table look like between the commits? If a query runs mid-way, what does it observe?

The worked solution starts by identifying the observable windows of inconsistency — the moments between statements when the table is in a state that never should have been visible to readers. That's the flaw: each statement is atomic on its own, but the sequence as a whole is not.

The analysis spells out the distinction the exam draws: atomicity is a property of a single commit, not a chain of them. Three statements means three commits means three opportunities for a reader to see an intermediate state.
Now problem three, the twist. A junior engineer runs our exact three-part MERGE from problem one — and it fails with an ambiguity error. Same statement, different source. Why?
Here's your hint: the ON clause is a join. What does a join do when the right-hand side has more than one row matching a single left-hand row?

Step one of the solution is to diagnose the ambiguity. The MERGE matched one target row against multiple source rows for the same customer_id, so Delta can't decide which value to write — it fails rather than guess. The fix is the same one we used in problem one: deduplicate the source before the merge.

And the analysis ties it all together: MERGE ambiguity on a non-unique join key is a predictable, examinable failure. Whenever you see a MERGE in a scenario, your first question should be — is the join key unique in the source? If not, deduplicate first. Let's lock in these three problems, then move on to the lesson assessment.

scenes.title: Lesson Assessment: Creating and Managing Delta Tables

questions.question: A data engineer must register an existing Delta directory that already lives at s3://lake/sales_events and query it from Databricks without copying or moving any Parquet files. Which DDL statement satisfies this requirement?

options.label: CREATE TABLE sales_events (event_id INT, event_ts TIMESTAMP, payload STRING) USING DELTA LOCATION 's3://lake/sales_events'
CREATE TABLE sales_events (event_id INT, event_ts TIMESTAMP, payload STRING) USING DELTA
CREATE TABLE sales_events AS SELECT * FROM parquet.`s3://lake/sales_events`
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE sales_events (event_id INT, event_ts TIMESTAMP, payload STRING) USING DELTA

questions.analysis: Option A is correct because an external (unmanaged) Delta table is defined by supplying an explicit LOCATION that points to data you already own; the metastore stores only the schema and the pointer, so no files are moved. Option B creates a managed table whose files land in the metastore's managed warehouse directory, so the existing s3 data would be ignored. Option C reads Parquet files into a new managed copy; creating a table via CTAS writes new files rather than registering the existing Delta log, and it also fails to preserve the Delta commit history. Option D is a trap: Databricks Delta tables are created with CREATE TABLE ... USING DELTA, and the managed/external distinction is determined by the presence of LOCATION, not by the keyword EXTERNAL, so this DDL does not create a valid Delta table. This distinction between a managed table, whose data lifecycle the metastore owns, and an external table, whose data lifecycle you own, is exactly the behavior tested in the side-by-side comparison covered earlier in the unit. [source 3] reinforces that the transaction log is the mechanism that makes such a registered directory a reliable lakehouse table.

questions.question: A monitoring job must decide, for an existing table named orders, (a) whether the table is MANAGED or EXTERNAL, (b) the physical path where its data files live, and (c) how many commits have been written to its transaction log. Which statements, if executed, return information that directly answers these questions? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: DESCRIBE EXTENDED orders — returns the table Type (MANAGED or EXTERNAL) and the Location path.
DESCRIBE DETAIL orders — returns the format, the location, numFiles and sizeInBytes.
DESCRIBE HISTORY orders — returns one row per commit, giving the version history of the table.
SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 1 — returns the first data row, from which the storage path can be inferred.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: DESCRIBE EXTENDED is the command that reports the table Type (MANAGED versus EXTERNAL) alongside the Provider and Location, which is precisely the metadata needed to classify the table. Option B is correct: DESCRIBE DETAIL returns the table format, the physical Location, numFiles and sizeInBytes, so it answers the 'where do the files live and how many are there' question. Option C is correct: DESCRIBE HISTORY returns one row per commit (version, timestamp, operation, operationMetrics), so counting those rows gives the commit count and lets you audit every change. Option D is a misconception: selecting data rows never reveals the storage path or the table type, because the physical location is metadata held by the metastore, not a column in the table. The underlying reason these commands work is that Delta Lake keeps an ordered, immutable log of every operation, which is what makes DESCRIBE HISTORY meaningful and what delivers ACID guarantees and time travel. [source 3] [source 6].

questions.question:
A target Delta table customers currently holds 12 rows with keys 1 through 12. A source staging table holds 5 rows: keys 1 and 2 with updated attribute values, keys 3 and 4 unchanged, and key 13 which is brand new. The engineer runs the following statement:

MERGE INTO customers AS t
USING staging AS s
ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

Assuming all five source keys are unique within staging, which outcome is correct?

options.label: Keys 1 and 2 are updated in place, keys 3 and 4 are rewritten with identical values, key 13 is inserted, and the table ends with 13 rows.
Only key 13 is inserted; keys 1 through 4 are skipped because they already match.
Keys 1 and 2 are updated, no other rows change, and the table ends with 14 rows because key 13 is ignored.
The statement fails because MERGE requires every source key to be missing from the target before an INSERT can occur.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct. The WHEN MATCHED clause fires for every source row whose join key exists in the target, so keys 1, 2, 3 and 4 are all matched: 1 and 2 receive the new attribute values, while 3 and 4 are rewritten with their existing values. The WHEN NOT MATCHED clause fires only for key 13, which does not exist in the target, so it is inserted, taking the table from 12 to 13 rows. Option B reverses the semantics of WHEN MATCHED, a common error. Option C mislabels the result and ignores the insert. Option D is the classic certification trap: MERGE certainly allows inserts for unmatched source keys; that is exactly how an upsert is built. Optionally adding WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE turns this into a full synchronisation, deletes any target row not present in the source, which is the delete-on-source requirement tested elsewhere in this lesson. [source 5] notes that the history lets you reconstruct the table at any commit, which is how you would audit or roll back such an upsert.

questions.question: A MERGE INTO inventory_staging USING inventory_updates statement fails with the error indicating that the MERGE operation matched more than one source row for the same target row. Which statements correctly diagnose the cause and describe a valid fix? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The source contains duplicate join keys, so a single target row is matched by more than one source row; Delta cannot decide which value to apply, so the merge is rejected.

A valid fix is to aggregate or de-duplicate the source before merging — for example, grouping by the key and taking the latest record by timestamp with a ROW_NUMBER() window — so that each key appears exactly once.
Lowering spark.sql.shuffle.partitions and re-running the exact same MERGE will resolve the duplicate-key error without changing the data.
The error proves the target table is external and therefore does not support MERGE; converting it to a managed table is the fix.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: when the source has duplicate keys that match the same target row, a single target row would receive multiple updates, and Delta cannot deterministically pick one, so it aborts the statement. Option B is correct: the standard fix is to reduce the source to one row per key — deduplicate with a ROW_NUMBER() over customer_id ordered by ingestion timestamp taking row 1, or aggregate — so that the join is one-to-one and the merge can proceed deterministically. Option C is a misconception: changing shuffle partitions only affects parallelism, it does not change the many-to-one relationship, so the same error returns. Option D is a trap that confuses merge semantics with storage type; external (unmanaged) tables hold their data at a LOCATION you own but still fully support UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE — that is the exact statement from the managed-vs-external side-by-side earlier in the unit. In each case the fix must preserve the deterministic, single-commit nature of a MERGE, which is what the transaction log guarantees per statement. [source 3] [source 6].
