This is the closing assessment, so treat it like the real exam: read each question carefully, watch for the distractors, and work each one out on your own.

Some questions are single-answer, some are multi-select, so read the prompt before you commit. Take your time, attempt every question independently, and once you submit I'll walk through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Lesson Opener: Versioning, Time Travel, and ACID

elements.content: Time Travel and ACID
Delta Lake versioning — recap, objectives, and agenda
Recap: each commit appends one JSON entry; commit N defines table version N. [source 3]
Commits are immutable and numbered: version N is rebuilt by replaying the log to N. [source 5]
Worked example: v0 = 1,000 rows; INSERT 250 rows → v1 = 1,250; DELETE 100 rows → v2 = 1,150.
ACID on object storage comes from optimistic concurrency control, not file locks. [source 3]
Objectives: query historical versions, restore a table to a prior version, explain isolation.
Exam focus: versioning, restore, and isolation recur; time travel aids auditing. [source 6]

Precondition and edge case: history retention governs how far back time travel reaches — once VACUUM deletes historical files outside the retention window, the old versions can no longer be read. [source 2]

actions.text: With MERGE and the DML statements behind us, we're moving into the part of Delta Lake that makes it genuinely different from a plain Parquet folder: Versioning, Time Travel, and ACID. Everything on this page is a bridge — it connects the transaction log we studied and the tables we just built to the guarantees we're about to test.

Let's start with the recap. Every commit to a Delta table appends exactly one JSON entry to the _delta_log directory, and that entry describes one table version. Append-only means nothing is ever rewritten in place — a commit is added, never edited. That single design choice is what the rest of this lesson rests on.

Second, and this is the key idea: commits are immutable and numbered. Version N is simply the result of replaying all commits from zero up to N, in order. Because each commit is immutable, the state at any earlier version can be reconstructed at any time — that is literally what time travel is. It isn't magic, it's replay.

Here's a concrete worked example to anchor it. Start at version 0 with one thousand rows. An INSERT of two hundred and fifty rows produces version 1 with one thousand two hundred and fifty. A later DELETE or UPDATE creates version 2. Nothing about version 0 or version 1 was destroyed — they are still addressable by version number.

So here are our two objectives for this lesson. First, you must be able to query historical table versions and restore a table to a prior version. Second, you must be able to explain the concurrency behavior and the isolation guarantees Delta Lake provides. Notice that these are one practical skill and one conceptual one — you'll need both.

On the conceptual side: ACID on object storage is not delivered by the storage layer. Cloud object stores like S3 or ADLS offer no transactions and no locking. Delta Lake achieves atomicity and isolation through optimistic concurrency control, driven by that ordered log. Writers assume they won't collide, and the log decides the winner if they do.

Pay attention to the exam note. Versioning, RESTORE, and isolation questions form a recurring cluster in the Delta Lake domain of the Data Engineer Associate exam. If you can explain the log, the version number, and the conflict resolution rule, you can answer most of that cluster.

One precondition to keep in the back of your mind: time travel is bounded by history retention. VACUUM and the retention interval govern how far back you can actually go, so 'the data is always there' is not a safe assumption. We'll return to that when we reach maintenance.

Our agenda runs in a deliberate order: version history, time travel syntax, RESTORE, ACID on object storage, and finally concurrency conflicts. Each one builds on the last, so let's open the log and look at versions as ordered commits.

scenes.title: Inside the Transaction Log: Versions as Ordered Commits

elements.content: Inside the Transaction Log: Versions as Ordered Commits

Every write to a Delta table is recorded as a single, immutable JSON commit file inside the _delta_log directory, and the sequence of those files — not the data files themselves — defines the table's version history [source 3].

Version numbers are therefore ordered commits: the file name is the version, zero-padded, and each successful statement appends exactly one new entry.

Commit = version + 1

Example: writing the 11th insert creates 00000000000000000010.json and raises the version from 9 to 10.

Replay old file list + new action → current state.

Monotonic, never reused

RESTORE rewrites the file list but still appends a new commit, so the version number only ever grows.

Deleting _delta_log destroys history and data.
Reconstruction: start from the initial commit v0 and apply only commits whose version < target; skip every later commit [source 5].
Checkpoints: every 10 commits Delta writes a Parquet checkpoint, so readers resume from it instead of replaying thousands of JSON files [source 3].
DESCRIBE HISTORY returns one row per applied commit: version, timestamp, operation, operationParameters, and userMetadata — the audit trail of every change [source 3].
Time travel (versioning) lets a reader query any prior state; deleting historical files removes that ability [source 2].

actions.text: Now that you've finished the knowledge check, let's go deeper into what actually makes versioning possible. Everything we're about to discuss lives inside one directory: the _delta_log.

This page is titled 'Inside the Transaction Log: Versions as Ordered Commits.' The key idea is simple but powerful: a Delta table's version history is not stored as a mutable file that gets rewritten. Instead, it's an ordered sequence of commit entries, each one adding a single atomic step to the table's story.

Every write to a Delta table is recorded as a single commit. That commit is a JSON file dropped into the _delta_log directory, named with a zero-padded version number. So the eleventh commit is literally called 00000000000000000010.json. If that write succeeds, the table version goes from ten to eleven. No exceptions, no gaps.

That gives us a clean rule: commit equals version plus one. For instance, writing the eleventh insert means the commit file is named with version number ten and the table advances to version eleven. This one-to-one mapping between commits and versions is what makes the log auditable and deterministic.

Two more properties enforce correctness here. First, version numbers are monotonic: they only ever increase, and they are never reused. Even if you run RESTORE to roll back, the log rewrites the file layout to reflect an earlier state, but it does not decrement the version counter. Second, this means the table's identity is inseparable from the log itself.

So how does a reader reconstruct any historical state of the table? By starting from the initial commit, version zero, and replaying only the commits made prior to the point in time you care about. That's the reconstruction algorithm. Every version is just an ordered prefix of the log replayed from the beginning.

Replaying thousands of JSON files would be painfully slow, so Delta periodically writes checkpoint files — every ten commits by default. A checkpoint is a Parquet file capturing the entire table state at that version. Readers can then start from the nearest checkpoint and replay only the handful of JSON commits that follow, instead of the whole history from version zero.

Finally, you can inspect all of this directly. DESCRIBE HISTORY returns one row per applied commit, with the version, timestamp, the operation that produced it, the operationParameters, and userMetadata. That's your window into the log without ever opening the JSON files by hand.

Put it all together and you get time travel: the ability to query any prior version of the table by simply naming the version number or the timestamp. Versioning isn't a bolt-on feature here — it's a direct consequence of the log being an ordered sequence of commits. Keep that mental model and the next page on time travel syntax will feel like second nature.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Versioning Fundamentals

questions.question: A Delta table named sales_orders currently sits at version 6. An engineer runs a single INSERT statement that adds 500 rows, and then a separate DELETE statement that removes 12 rows. Immediately afterward, what is the version number of the table, and what did the commit files produce?

options.label: Version 7, because both statements were part of one logical batch and produced a single commit file.
Version 8, because each DML statement is its own atomic commit appended to the transaction log, so two statements produce two new commits.
Version 8, because the version increments once for every data file that was rewritten, and the DELETE rewrote two files.
Version 6, because version numbers only change when the table schema changes.

questions.correctAnswer: Version 8, because each DML statement is its own atomic commit appended to the transaction log, so two statements produce two new commits.
questions.analysis: In Delta Lake the version number is driven by the transaction log, not by row counts or file counts. As covered earlier in this unit, every DML statement — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE — is a single atomic commit appended to the _delta_log directory, so the first INSERT takes the table from version 6 to 7 and the DELETE takes it from 7 to 8. The immutable, ordered log is exactly what enables ACID guarantees and time travel [source 3]. Option A confuses multiple statements with one batch commit; option C mistakes version increments for per-file rewrites (a DELETE of 12 rows may rewrite several files but still produces exactly one commit); option D confuses schema change history with data version history.
answer: Version 8, because each DML statement is its own atomic commit appended to the transaction log, so two statements produce two new commits.

questions.question: A data engineer calls DESCRIBE HISTORY on a Delta table and sees rows for versions 0 through 9 in the version column. The engineer wants to compare the table as it looked at version 2 with the table as it looked at version 9. Using the principle that a table state can be recreated by starting from an original table and processing only the commits made prior to the target point, how many commits lie between the version 2 state and the version 9 state?

options.label: 6 commits (versions 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8).
9 commits, because the table has nine versions of history.
7 commits (versions 2 through 8), because the version 2 commit itself must be replayed to reach version 9.
10 commits, because every row in the history plus the current state must be replayed.

questions.correctAnswer: 7 commits (versions 2 through 8), because the version 2 commit itself must be replayed to reach version 9.
questions.analysis: To reconstruct the state as of version 9 from version 2, you must apply every commit that occurred after version 2 up to and including the commit that produced version 9 — that is versions 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9, which is 7 commits. Equivalently, 9 − 2 = 7 commits separate the two snapshots in the log. This is the operational meaning of time travel: the state at any point in time is the original table plus all commits made prior to that point [source 5]. Option A is the off-by-one trap that misses the target commit itself. Option B confuses the total count of history rows with the number of commits between two chosen points. Option D assumes the current state is a separate commit, but it is simply the result of replaying all prior commits.
answer: 7 commits (versions 2 through 8), because the version 2 commit itself must be replayed to reach version 9.

questions.question: An engineer is inspecting the _delta_log directory of a Delta table and sees both .json commit files and .checkpoint.parquet files. Select all statements that correctly distinguish the role of checkpoints from commit files. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Commit files are ordered, immutable records of table operations that are appended as the table changes.
Checkpoint files are a performance optimization: they summarize the table state at a given version so that later versions can be replayed without reading every commit from version 0.
Checkpoints replace commit files, so once a checkpoint is written the corresponding JSON commit files can be deleted and time travel still works to every prior version.
Deleting historical commit files can limit the ability to time travel to specific versions, but checkpoints still serve as compressed state summaries for the versions they cover.

correctAnswer: Commit files are ordered, immutable records of table operations that are appended as the table changes.
Checkpoint files are a performance optimization: they summarize the table state at a given version so that later versions can be replayed without reading every commit from version 0.

questions.analysis: The transaction log maintains an ordered, immutable log of all table operations, which is what enables ACID transactions and time travel via version history [source 3]. JSON commit files are the primary record: each commit appends one file describing the change. Checkpoint files are not replacements for commits — they are periodic snapshots of table state that avoid the cost of replaying the entire log from version 0. Time travel works by recreating a prior state from the original table plus all commits made before the target point [source 5]. Because time travel depends on commit files, deleting old commits limits the ability to reach specific versions [source 2]; checkpoints help summarize state but do not restore deleted commit-level history for arbitrary versions. Option C is the trap: it treats a checkpoint as a full substitute for commit history, which is false, and it also wrongly claims deleted commits do not affect time travel.

Deleting historical commit files can limit the ability to time travel to specific versions, but checkpoints still serve as compressed state summaries for the versions they cover.

scenes.title: Querying History: Time Travel Syntax

elements.content: Querying History: Time Travel

SQL time travel by version number or timestamp [source 2]:

SELECT * FROM my_table VERSION AS OF 5;

SELECT * FROM my_table TIMESTAMP AS OF

'2024-05-01T10:00:00'

PySpark does the same with read options [source 1]:

spark.read.option("versionAsOf", 5).table("my_table")

spark.read.option("timestampAsOf", "2024-05-01")

.table("my_table")
• DESCRIBE HISTORY lists every version [source 3].
• Trap: AS OF picks the latest commit before that time.
• Time travel reads never change live data [source 5].
• Example: v5 @ 09:00, v6 @ 10:30; a 10:00 read = v5.

actions.text: Now that we understand versions as ordered commits, the natural question is: how do we actually read an old version? That's time travel syntax, and it comes in two flavors — SQL and PySpark.

In SQL you have two clauses. By version number: SELECT * FROM my_table VERSION AS OF 5. And by timestamp: SELECT * FROM my_table TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-05-01T10:00:00'. Same table, same syntax pattern — you're just telling Delta which point in history to reconstruct.

PySpark mirrors this exactly through read options. Use spark.read.option("versionAsOf", 5).table("my_table"), or swap in "timestampAsOf" with a date string. The mental model is identical — you're pinning the read to a specific commit, just expressed as a DataFrame option instead of a SQL clause.

Before you guess a version, discover it. DESCRIBE HISTORY my_table lists every version in order, along with the operation, timestamp, and user behind each commit. This is your index into the table's past — run it first, then pick the exact version or timestamp you need.

Here's the exam trap to lock in. TIMESTAMP AS OF does not pick the version nearest in time — it resolves to the latest commit at or before that timestamp. So if v5 was committed at 09:00 and v6 at 10:30, a query at 10:00 lands on v5, not some interpolation between the two. It's a floor, not a nearest-neighbor.
That example spells it out: v5 at 09:00, v6 at 10:30, and a 10:00 read returns v5. Walk through those numbers yourself — it's the fastest way to burn the rule in before the exam.

Finally, the most important safety property: time travel reads are strictly read-only. Querying an old version never modifies the current table, never rewrites history, and never touches live data. You're just reading an older snapshot of the log's state. So today you've got the SQL and PySpark syntax, the DESCRIBE HISTORY discovery step, the timestamp-as-floor trap, and the read-only guarantee — that's your time travel toolkit.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Auditing a Table with Time Travel

elements.content: Problem 1

You are the data engineer on call for a nightly ingestion pipeline that appends raw clickstream events to the Delta table at `/mnt/raw/events` (registered as the table `events`). Last night's 02:00 UTC job ran twice due to a scheduler double-trigger, so it appended the entire 40,000-row batch a second time. The bad load was the 13th commit to the table, so it became version 13; the last known-good version is 12. Before you touch anything, you must (a) inspect the commit history to prove which version is clean and which commit introduced the damage, (b) quantify exactly how many rows are duplicated, and (c) restore the table to version 12 so downstream consumers stop seeing the duplicates. Then re-run the corrected pipeline. Version 12 held 1,240,000 rows. The duplicated batch contained 40,000 rows. None of the original 40,000 rows changed their values, only the row count grew. Provide the full sequence of commands with expected outputs and the final recovered row count.

Hint: Do not jump straight to RESTORE. Prove the target version from the history first, because RESTORE made against the wrong version quietly commits a new, wrong state that downstream readers will treat as current.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Inspect the commit history to identify the clean version and the offending commit.

Run:

```sql

DESCRIBE HISTORY /mnt/raw/events;

```

You get one row per commit, newest first. The interesting fields are version, timestamp, operation, operationParameters, and userMetadata. In our case the suspect commit at version 13 shows:

- version = 13

- operation = 'WRITE'

- operationParameters.mode = 'Append'

- userMetadata = 'nightly_clickstream_loader run 2 — scheduler retry'

Version 12 shows operation = 'WRITE' as well, but its userMetadata reads 'nightly_clickstream_loader run 1' and its timestamp is one minute earlier. Because the log is an ordered, append-only record of commits with exactly one log entry per table version [source 3], the presence of two consecutive Append commits within the same nightly window is the smoking gun. The log makes any historical version reconstructable by replaying only the commits up to that version, which is exactly what we are about to exploit [source 5].

Step 2 — Quantify the damage by counting version 12 versus the current version.

Run:

```sql

SELECT

(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events VERSION AS OF 12) AS good_rows,

(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events) AS bad_rows;

```

Expected output:

good_rows = 1,240,000

bad_rows = 1,280,000

The difference is 40,000 rows — exactly the size of the duplicated batch. The damage is therefore a single, fully-duplicated append of 40,000 rows, not a partial or corrupted write. That matters because a clean append is what makes a simple rollback safe: we are not repairing row contents, we are just discarding one commit.

Step 3 — Roll the table back to the pre-incident version.

Run:

```sql

RESTORE TABLE events TO VERSION AS OF 12;

```

Expected output: a single commit, version 14, with operation = 'RESTORE', operationParameters.toVersion = 12. RESTORE does not delete version 13; it appends a new commit whose file list points back at the file set of version 12. After the RESTORE, the current version of the table is 14, but the data it exposes is the version-12 data. Confirmed by:

```sql

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events; -- 1,240,000

```

Step 4 — Re-run the corrected pipeline.

Fix the scheduler so the job triggers once, then re-run the loader for the failed window. It will append its batch as version 15. After this append the count is 1,280,000 again, but this time the extra 40,000 rows are the intended batch, not a duplicate. Verify by comparing the current row count to version 12's row count and to the batch size, and by asserting that no row_id appears twice:

```sql

SELECT COUNT(*) AS total, COUNT(DISTINCT row_id) AS distinct_ids FROM events;

```

Both numbers must be 1,280,000 after the corrected append.

Analysis — The reason this procedure is safe is structural: the Delta transaction log is an ordered, immutable record of commits, and any version can be reconstructed by replaying only the commits that precede it [source 5]. That is the whole mechanism behind time travel — the log lets you query any previous state of the table for auditing and debugging [source 6] [source 2]. RESTORE is therefore not a destructive operation in the way students often assume. It appends a new commit that points at an old file list; the wrong commit is still visible in DESCRIBE HISTORY, and you can re-enter it deliberately later if you need to. A very common exam pitfall is believing RESTORE erases the bad commit, or that the current version number goes backwards. It does not and it does not.

The most dangerous mistake is running RESTORE before running DESCRIBE HISTORY. Without the history you cannot tell whether the previous version is the clean one. In this scenario, if you had a correct 02:00 load and a failed 02:00 retry, version 13 was bad and version 12 was good. But if the failure had been 'loader partially overwrote rows at version 13, then a compensating run at version 14 wrote a partial batch', rolling back to version 12 would silently discard recoverable data. DESCRIBE HISTORY is what turns guesswork into evidence.

The second pitfall is VACUUM. RESTORE depends on the physical data files referenced by the target version still existing. If someone has run VACUUM with a retention window shorter than the time since version 12, the files that version 12 points at may already be gone, and RESTORE will fail at read time. Delta's own documentation warns that deleting historical files limits time travel to those versions [source 2]. In production, this is why retention policies and RESTORE procedures must be designed together: you cannot recover to a version whose files you have already vacuumed away.

A third pitfall is worth mentioning for correctness: RESTORE is a new commit, so it participates in the table's optimistic-concurrency control just like any other write. If another writer is mid-commit while your RESTORE lands, you may need to retry it. Finally, and this generalizes: any audit-and-recover workflow on Delta follows the same three-beat structure — prove the target with history, quantify the damage with counts at both versions, then act. The same pattern applies to a delete gone wrong, a MERGE that fanned out duplicate join keys, or a corrupt upstream file that was already committed.
Problem 2

Two days after the rollback in Problem 1, an analyst messages you: 'Your RESTORE corrupted the table — version 14 has operation = RESTORE and version 13 still shows the duplicate rows.' They also report that a compliance job that queries `VERSION AS OF 12` for a recent audit is running fine, but a different job that also needs version 12 is failing with a file-not-found error. The table has had a weekly VACUUM job with the default 7-day retention running unchanged for months. Using what you know about Delta's transaction log, time travel, and file management, determine (a) whether the analyst's claim that the table is corrupted is correct, (b) whether the version-12 data is guaranteed to still be queryable, and (c) what the file-not-found job most likely did wrong, given the source material's discussion of VACUUM and time travel.
Hint: Separate 'is the table state correct' from 'are the historical files still on disk'. Version history and physical file retention are two different guarantees.

Worked solution
Part (a) — Is the table corrupted? No. The analyst is confusing 'the log still contains version 13' with 'the table is in the state of version 13'. In Delta, the current state of a table is determined by the file list materialized from the latest commit. RESTORE appends a new commit (version 14 here) whose file list points back to the version-12 files. Readers that query the table without a version clause see version 14 and therefore see the version-12 data. Version 13 still exists in DESCRIBE HISTORY — that is by design, because the transaction log is an ordered, immutable record, and the log makes time travel possible precisely because every prior state can be reconstructed from the commits [source 5] [source 3]. Keeping version 13 in the log does not mean the table currently contains the 40,000 duplicate rows. The correct mental model is: history is append-only and never shrinks on account of a RESTORE; current state is the head commit.

Part (b) — Is version 12 still queryable? Not guaranteed. Delta's time travel is only possible while the physical data files each version references still exist. VACUUM deletes files that are no longer referenced by any recent version and that are older than the retention window. The source material is explicit: deleting historical files in a Delta table can limit your ability to time travel to specific versions [source 2]. With 7-day retention and an incident two days old, version 12's files are almost certainly still present, but 'almost certainly' is not 'guaranteed'. The only rigorous way to verify is to run the query: if `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events VERSION AS OF 12` succeeds, the version-12 files exist; if it fails with a file-not-found error, they do not. This is why we do not delete files that we anticipate needing for rollback until we are confident that no recovery scenario will require them.

Part (c) — Why is the second job failing? The most likely explanations are: (i) it is looking for a specific file by path rather than querying the table at version 12, and the file it names has since been vacuumed away because no current version references it; or (ii) it is running against a stale table snapshot, a cached listing, or a different catalog entry that still points at the version-13 file set — for example, another Delta table that shares part of the warehouse path but whose own log does not include the version-12 file list. In either case, the fix is not to re-run RESTORE; it is to make the second job address the table by table name and version, so the log — not a hard-coded path — determines which files it reads. Delta's ACID and time-travel properties exist precisely to make 'query the table at version 12' a first-class, reliable operation [source 3] [source 6]. Any job that bypasses the log by naming files directly forfeits those guarantees.

The general lesson: 'the table is correct' and 'the historical files are preserved' are two separate guarantees. Delta gives you the first via the append-only log and versioned state reconstruction [source 5]. The second is a function of your retention and VACUUM policy, and it is your job to size it against your rollback and audit requirements.

Analysis — This problem separates three concepts that students routinely conflate. First, current state vs. history: history is immutable and append-only, current state is the head commit, and RESTORE changes the head commit without erasing history. Students who expect the historical commit to disappear are reasoning about their mental model of a mutable filesystem rather than about Delta's log-structured design. Second, log-level correctness vs. file-level availability: a version is 'queryable' only if its files exist, which is why VACUUM and time travel interact. A 7-day retention is fine for a 2-day-old incident but useless for a 30-day-old one. Third, addressing the table by name vs. addressing it by file path: the log is what makes the versioned query safe and consistent [source 3]; a job that hard-codes a path bypasses the log and loses those guarantees. Edge cases to watch: VACUUM ranges and the exact retention window; whether the rollback target version's files were ever vacuumed before the incident; and whether the failing job's snapshot is actually the same table. On the exam, the trap distractor usually claims RESTORE 'erases' the bad commit; it does not, and the correct answer is the one that explains why the bad commit remaining in the history is harmless.

actions.text: Let's put time travel to work on a realistic scenario. This worked problem is about auditing a Delta table after something goes wrong — and using the transaction log to prove what actually happened, quantify the damage, and get back to a clean state.

Here's the setup. You're the data engineer on call for a nightly ingestion job. One night, the job appends forty thousand duplicate rows into the Delta table backed by /mnt/raw/events. Your task is threefold: prove which version of the table is clean, quantify exactly how much damage was done, and recover the table safely.

Before we jump into the solution, notice the hint. The instinct is to reach straight for RESTORE — but that's exactly the trap. You have to prove the target version is clean before you roll back. If you restore to the wrong version, you've just replaced one bad state with another, and you may have no clean starting point left.

So Step 1 — inspect the commit history with DESCRIBE HISTORY on the table path. Look for the suspect commit. In this case it shows operation = 'WRITE', operationParameters.mode = 'Append', and a userMetadata field that identifies the offending job run. That metadata is your fingerprint — it's how you connect a log entry to the pipeline that produced it.

Step 2 — quantify the damage. Run a query that counts rows at version twelve using VERSION AS OF 12, and counts the current rows without a version clause. The gap between good_rows and bad_rows is your damage figure. Step 3 — once you've confirmed version twelve is clean, run RESTORE TABLE events TO VERSION AS OF 12, then re-run the corrected pipeline.

Now the analysis — and this is where the exam lives. This procedure is safe because the transaction log lets any version be reconstructed from immutable commits. Three pitfalls to memorize. First, running RESTORE before DESCRIBE HISTORY means you guessed the target version — that's a fail. Second, if VACUUM has already deleted the required data files, the old version can't be reconstructed, so restore will fail. Third — and this one trips up almost everyone — RESTORE does not erase the bad commit. It adds a new commit that points back to the earlier state. The bad write is still in the history, just no longer the current version.
Let's move to Problem 2, which builds directly on this. Two days after the rollback you just performed, an analyst reports something odd about the table's row counts.

The scenario here is subtle. The question is no longer just 'is the data wrong?' — it's about untangling whether the table state is actually correct versus whether something about the query or the pipeline is misreporting it. This is where time travel becomes a diagnostic tool rather than just a recovery mechanism.

The hint tells you exactly how to approach it: separate 'is the table state correct' from 'is the reader correct.' Those are two independent questions, and conflating them is the classic mistake. Prove the table state first, then audit the consumer.

Part (a) asks the direct question — is the table corrupted? Walk the version timeline using DESCRIBE HISTORY and VERSION AS OF queries. If a recent version has the expected row counts and commit metadata consistent with a normal nightly load, the table is healthy. If any version shows duplicate appends or unexpected operation modes, you've localized the problem to a specific commit and can trace it back to a source.

And the analysis wraps it up: this problem separates three distinct concepts that beginners tend to blur together — the actual table state as recorded in the log, the version the reader is querying against, and any downstream transformation applying filtering or deduplication. Mastering that separation is exactly what the Time Travel and RESTORE questions on the exam are testing. On the next page, we'll check your understanding with a knowledge check on time travel semantics.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Time Travel Semantics

questions.question: An audit requirement states: 'Show the exact state of the sales_delta table as it existed immediately after the twelfth committed write to that table.' Which query correctly satisfies this requirement?

options.label: SELECT * FROM sales_delta VERSION AS OF 12;
SELECT * FROM sales_delta TIMESTAMP AS OF '12';
SELECT * FROM sales_delta AT VERSION 12;
SELECT * FROM sales_delta RESTORE TO VERSION 12;

questions.analysis: Commits in the Delta transaction log are immutable and numbered, and each successful write increments the table version by exactly one, so the twelfth committed write corresponds to version 12. The supported SQL syntax for requesting a specific historical version is VERSION AS OF <version_number>, which is why Option A is correct. Option B is wrong on two counts: TIMESTAMP AS OF requires a timestamp expression (for example a string such as '2024-05-01 10:00:00'), not the bare number 12, and it resolves a point in time rather than a version number. Option C is not valid Databricks SQL syntax — there is no AT VERSION keyword pair in the time travel grammar, so the parser rejects it. Option D is a distractor that treats time travel as a rollback: RESTORE is a separate write operation that mutates the table's current state, whereas time travel only reads a historical snapshot. As the source material notes, time travel recreates the state of a table at any point in time by starting with the original table and processing only the commits made prior to that point [source 5], and the timestamp/version mapping is delivered by the ordered, immutable transaction log [source 3].

questions.question: A Delta table has exactly these commits, each recorded as one JSON entry in the transaction log: version 0 at 09:00:00, version 1 at 09:20:00, version 2 at 10:05:00, and version 3 at 10:40:00. A user runs SELECT * FROM orders TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-05-01 09:45:00'. Which version of the table does the query return, and why?

options.label: Version 2, because timestamp resolution rounds up to the next available commit after the requested time.
Version 1, because timestamp resolution returns the latest committed version whose commit timestamp is at or before the requested timestamp.
An error is raised, because 09:45:00 does not match any commit timestamp exactly.
Version 3, because timestamp resolution always returns the most recent version of the table regardless of the requested time.

questions.analysis: Timestamp-based time travel is defined as a point-in-time query: Delta maps the requested timestamp to the greatest table version whose commit timestamp is less than or equal to the requested timestamp. At 09:45:00, the commits at or before that instant are version 0 (09:00:00) and version 1 (09:20:00); version 2 (10:05:00) and version 3 (10:40:00) occur after the requested time, so neither can be returned. The correct answer is therefore version 1. Option A inverts the rule and describes rounding forward, which would violate the snapshot-consistency guarantee that a historical query never reveals writes that had not yet happened. Option C reflects a common misconception that the timestamp must equal a commit timestamp exactly; in reality timestamps that fall between two commits are resolved to the preceding version, and only a timestamp earlier than the very first commit (or older than the retained history) fails. Option D describes a query that would simply ignore the TIMESTAMP AS OF clause and read the current table, which defeats the purpose of time travel. The source material explains that the transaction log maintains an ordered, immutable record of all table operations and provides time travel via version history and timestamp mapping [source 3], and that this lets us recreate the state of a table at any point in time by processing only commits made prior to that point [source 5].

questions.question: A colleague claims: 'Running SELECT * FROM customers VERSION AS OF 3 acts like a rollback — it rewinds the customers table to version 3 so that all later changes are undone.' Which statements correctly describe what actually happens? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The query is read-only: it returns the snapshot of customers as of version 3 but leaves the current state and the commit history of the table unchanged.
The query physically deletes every commit file after version 3 from the _delta_log, permanently discarding versions 4 and beyond.
The most recent version of the table remains queryable by an ordinary SELECT after the time travel query completes, because no new commit was written by the query.
To actually roll the table back to version 3, you would need RESTORE TABLE customers TO VERSION AS OF 3, which is a write that appends a new commit rather than rewriting old ones.

questions.analysis: Time travel in Delta Lake is a read operation over immutable history, not a mutation. Option A is correct: the query reconstructs the table state at version 3 by starting with the original table and processing only the commits made prior to that point [source 5], and it writes nothing back — the transaction log is an ordered, immutable record of all table operations [source 3]. Option C is correct for the same reason: since the query adds no commit file, the table version is not incremented, and a plain SELECT still resolves the latest version. Option D is correct and captures the key distinction the colleague misses: RESTORE is a separate write command that rolls the table forward by appending a new commit whose content equals the old snapshot, so history is preserved rather than rewritten. Option B is the misconception itself — it treats time travel as a destructive rollback that removes log files, which contradicts the append-only, immutable nature of the log and would break the auditability that makes versioned queries possible. Note also the practical edge case behind this design: as the source material warns, deleting historical files from the table's storage can limit the ability to time travel to specific versions [source 2], so retention and VACUUM policies — not the read query — are what actually make old versions unreachable.
