scenes.title: RESTORE TABLE: Rolling Back to a Prior Version

elements.content: RESTORE TABLE: Rolling Back to a Prior Version

RESTORE TABLE my_table TO VERSION AS OF 5;

RESTORE TABLE my_table TO TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-05-01T10:00:00';
How RESTORE works

• New commit; no history deleted [source 3]

• Result state = the target version [source 6]

• Versions keep increasing
Recovery & limits

• Bad write → DESCRIBE HISTORY → RESTORE

• Then re-run the corrected job

• Needs MODIFY permission

• VACUUM removes files → restore fails [source 2]
Example: v9 bad → RESTORE v8 → new v10 = v8 state [source 5]

actions.text: Time travel lets us read the past. RESTORE TABLE lets us go back to it. This is the rollback tool — it rewinds a Delta table to a prior version so that the table's current state becomes what it used to be.

The syntax comes in two flavors. RESTORE TABLE my_table TO VERSION AS OF 5 rolls back to a specific version number. RESTORE TABLE my_table TO TIMESTAMP AS OF a timestamp rolls back to the state at a point in time. Same as time travel reads — version for the exact commit, timestamp for the moment.

Here is the mechanic exam writers love. RESTORE does not delete history. It writes a brand-new commit whose resulting state equals the old version. So if you were on version nine and you restore version eight, you get a new version ten that holds version eight's data. Version numbers keep increasing — they never go backwards.
And because a restore is itself a commit, it is time-travellable. You can query the state that existed immediately before the restore, which means a mistaken restore is itself recoverable.
That gives us the standard recovery pattern: a bad write happens, you run DESCRIBE HISTORY to find the last good version, you RESTORE to that version, and then you re-run the corrected pipeline.

Now the limits — and there are two you must remember. First, RESTORE requires MODIFY permission on the table; it is a write operation, not a read. Second, and more dangerous, RESTORE fails if the data files it needs were already removed by VACUUM. Since VACUUM's default retention is seven days, a restore older than that window may simply have nothing left to restore from.

So picture the exam scenario: version nine is bad, you restore version eight, and version ten lands holding version eight's exact state. History is intact, the rollback is auditable, and the pipeline resumes from a clean baseline. Just remember the two gates — permission and file retention — because those are exactly what make RESTORE fail in production.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Restore and Recovery

questions.question: A nightly pipeline has corrupted the current state of the Delta table prod.sales, but the version immediately before the bad write (version 12) is clean. The requirement is to make the current table state identical to version 12 for all downstream readers, while preserving the audit trail. Which command should you run?

options.label: SELECT * FROM prod.sales VERSION AS OF 12;
RESTORE TABLE prod.sales TO VERSION AS OF 12;
VACUUM prod.sales RETAIN 0 HOURS;
DELETE FROM prod.sales WHERE version = 13;

questions.analysis: RESTORE TABLE creates a new commit that makes the current table state match the target version, so all readers who query prod.sales without a version clause see the recovered data. Option A is the classic distractor: a time-travel SELECT only returns the historical snapshot to that one query — it does not change the current table state, so downstream jobs still read the corrupted data. Option C is destructive and unrelated: VACUUM removes unreferenced files and, if retention is too short, can permanently prevent time travel to older versions [source 2]. Option D is invalid syntax and also misreads the model: versions are not rows, they are entries in the transaction log, and you cannot DELETE a version [source 5]. The key distinction the exam tests is read history (SELECT ... VERSION AS OF) versus write a repair (RESTORE TABLE), and time travel exists precisely because the log records an ordered, immutable history of commits [source 3].

questions.question: A RESTORE TABLE prod.sales TO VERSION AS OF 12 command completes successfully on a table whose latest version was 13. Which statements accurately describe the effect on the version history and the bad commit? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The table's version counter moves forward; the restore is recorded as a new commit numbered 14.
Version 13 remains visible in DESCRIBE HISTORY as an intact entry that can still be queried with time travel.
The table version is rewound to 12 and commit 13 is deleted from the transaction log.
The restore itself is logged as an operation (for example, RESTORE) so the audit trail explains why the data changed.

questions.analysis: A restore is itself a write, so the next commit file is appended and the version increments to 14 — the counter never moves backward [source 5]. Because the log is an ordered, append-only record, version 13 is not erased; it remains a queryable snapshot with SELECT ... VERSION AS OF 13, and the restore appears as a distinct operation in the history. Option C is the core distractor pattern for this objective: it wrongly implies that RESTORE rewinds the version counter or permanently removes the bad commit. Neither happens — recovery is additive. The immutable commit log is exactly what makes time travel possible in the first place [source 3], and any file deletion that limits time travel is a separate, retention-driven concern handled by VACUUM, not by RESTORE [source 2].

questions.question: You confirm with SELECT * FROM prod.sales VERSION AS OF 12 that the target state is readable, but the immediate RESTORE TABLE prod.sales TO VERSION AS OF 12 fails. Which explanation is most consistent with how Delta Lake versioning and file retention work?

options.label: Time travel queries can read any version, but RESTORE only works on external (unmanaged) tables, not managed ones.

The data files that version 12 references have been removed by VACUUM under a short retention policy, and time-travel reads may still succeed from a cached or replicated copy rather than the live table.
RESTORE requires the target version to be exactly one version behind the current version, so restoring from 12 to the failed 13 is out of range.
A concurrent writer already restored the table, so the version counter was rewound and version 12 no longer exists.

questions.analysis: A restore must physically reconstruct the table state, so it needs the data files that version 12's log entries reference. Deleting historical files limits your ability to time travel to specific versions [source 2], and because the log is an immutable record replayed to rebuild a snapshot [source 5], a restore that cannot find those files will fail even though a metadata-only history lookup or a cached read may have appeared to work. Option A is false: RESTORE applies to Delta tables generally, not only external tables. Option C invents a rule that does not exist — there is no 'one version behind' restriction. Option D repeats the misconception that the version counter can be rewound; the counter only ever moves forward, so version 12 cannot be deleted by a restore [source 3]. This question tests the distinction between cheap log replay for a read and the stronger physical requirement of a write-based recovery.

actions.text: We've seen how the transaction log keeps every version queryable, and on the previous page we looked at how RESTORE TABLE lets you roll the current state back to an earlier commit. Time to see how well that distinction stuck.

Work through the three questions on your own — read each one carefully, since some ask you to pick more than one option. Try each first before you commit to an answer. Once you submit, I'll be right here to walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: ACID on Object Storage: What Delta Lake Guarantees

elements.content: ACID on Object Storage: What Delta Lake Guarantees

A — Atomicity

A commit fully applies or not at all; readers never see a partial set of Parquet files. Mechanics: write data files first, then add one commit JSON to _delta_log.

C — Consistency

Readers see only a valid table state produced by an ordered sequence of commits, with schema enforcement and constraint checks applied before the commit lands [source p.412].

I — Isolation

Concurrent writers are serialized by optimistic concurrency control on the log; each reader gets a consistent snapshot. Readers use snapshot isolation, writers a serializable level [source 3].

D — Durability

Once the commit file is written to the durable log store, the change survives failure or termination of the compute cluster — state is replayed from the immutable log [source 5].
Worked Example — Two Writers, One Version

Table at version 10. Writer A (INSERT) and Writer B (MERGE) commit together. A wins and publishes 00000000000000000011.json; B re-reads, sees A's files, retries, and publishes 00000000000000000012.json. Readers at version 10 never observe either half — they see 10, then 11, then 12.

elements.html: V10​→V11​→V12​

elements.content: Conflict handled by optimistic concurrency control on the log [source 3] — no locks held while data files are written.

actions.text: Now that we've looked at how the transaction log stores an ordered history of versions, the natural question is: how does Delta Lake actually deliver ACID guarantees on top of object storage, which was never designed for transactions? Let's map each property to its concrete mechanism.

This is the headline claim — ACID on object storage. Object stores like S3 or ADLS are cheap and scalable, but they offer no locking and no atomic multi-file writes. Delta bridges that gap, and understanding how is a recurring exam theme.

Start with Atomicity. A commit either fully applies or not at all. In practice, the data files get written first, and the commit is only considered successful once the log entry is atomically added. So a reader never observes a half-written set of Parquet files — they either see the new version or the old one, never a mixture.

Consistency means readers always see a valid table state, produced by an ordered sequence of commits. Schema and constraints are enforced on write, so every version you can read is internally coherent.

Isolation is where concurrency comes in. Concurrent writers are serialized through optimistic concurrency control on the log, and each reader sees a consistent snapshot. Readers use snapshot isolation, while writes are effectively serialized at a serializable level.
And Durability: once the commit is written to the durable log store, the change survives even if a compute cluster fails moments later. The compute is disposable — the log is the source of truth.
Let's ground this in a worked example. Picture two writers hitting the same table at once, trying to move from one version to the next.

The table sits at version ten. Writer A does an INSERT and Writer B also does a write. Both attempt to commit against version ten. Under optimistic concurrency control, one of them wins and advances the table from V10 to V11; the loser's commit is rejected and retried against the new version, moving on to V12. Watch how that version chain looks: V10, then V11, then V12.

The conflict is handled by optimistic concurrency control: writers optimistically proceed, and the log acts as the arbiter. The key takeaway is that serialization happens at the log, and readers are never blocked by writers. Spend a moment locking that mapping — property to mechanism — into memory, because the exam loves to test it that way.

scenes.title: Concurrency Control: Optimistic vs Pessimistic in Delta Lake

elements.content: Dimension  |  Optimistic concurrency control  |  Pessimistic concurrency control

Mechanism (how the write path works)
Optimistic concurrency control: No locks are held while the transaction runs: Delta writes new Parquet data files optimistically, then validates at commit time by checking whether a conflicting commit landed in the transaction log since the transaction began, because ACID guarantees come from the ordered, immutable log rather than from locking [source 3].
Pessimistic concurrency control: Delta takes mutual exclusion on the log store so that conflicting writers are serialized rather than detected after the fact: the second writer waits for the log lock instead of racing and losing.

When a conflict surfaces
Optimistic concurrency control: Conflicts surface at commit time, never at read time, because Delta appends exactly one commit file per successful write and only then discovers that the version it targeted has already been incremented by someone else [source 5].
Pessimistic concurrency control: Contention surfaces up front, before any data is staged, because the writer must acquire the log-store lock before it can even read the current version and append its commit.

Failure mode and typical exception
Optimistic concurrency control: The losing writer receives a retryable Delta conflict exception (for example ConcurrentAppendException, ConcurrentDeleteReadException, or MetadataChangedException in Databricks) and the whole transaction is aborted, leaving the data files it already wrote orphaned and never referenced by the log [source 3].
Pessimistic concurrency control: The losing writer never sees a conflict exception at all; it blocks, and the observable failure is a lock-acquisition timeout or a long queue of writers visible as elevated commit latency in a high-contention workload.

Cost profile (where time and dollars go)
Optimistic concurrency control: Cost is paid only under contention: an uncontended optimistic commit is a single log append, but a collision forces the entire statement — for example a 40,000-row MERGE — to be recomputed from scratch, so the bytes and, on Photon, the CPU are spent twice [source 4].
Pessimistic concurrency control: Cost is paid on every commit: each writer serializes behind the lock even when no other writer exists, so steady-state throughput is lower and tail latency is governed by the slowest holder of the lock.

Isolation guarantee delivered
Optimistic concurrency control: Readers always see a consistent snapshot and writers are serializable, which is exactly what the ordered, immutable transaction log provides; the guarantee does not depend on choosing optimistic validation [source 3].
Pessimistic concurrency control: The isolation guarantee is identical — serializable writes over snapshot reads — so pessimism buys conflict avoidance, not a stronger (or weaker) isolation level; this is the exam framing for the pair.

Retry pattern required in application code
Optimistic concurrency control: Application code must be retry-tolerant: wrap the write in a bounded retry loop with exponential backoff, keep the MERGE source deterministic by deduplicating with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC), and re-read the log version on each attempt so the re-execution is idempotent [source 4].
Pessimistic concurrency control: Application code usually needs no conflict-retry loop because the lock prevents lost updates, but it must handle timeouts and must keep transactions short so the log-store lock is never held across a long shuffle or an expensive deduplication step.

Granularity: what actually gets serialized
Optimistic concurrency control: Commit validation is fine-grained: two writers appending to disjoint partitions of the same table normally both succeed, because the check compares the set of files and partitions touched rather than locking the whole table [source 5].
Pessimistic concurrency control: Mutual exclusion on the log store is coarse by comparison: the lock serializes all writers on that table regardless of whether they touch disjoint partitions, so partition-disjoint writes that would have succeeded optimistically now queue behind each other.

Typical workload fit
Optimistic concurrency control: Fits append-mostly ingestion — an Auto Loader streaming load into a bronze table, or the daily staging_customers MERGE upsert into dim_customer — where concurrent writers rarely touch the same files, so the commit validates on the first attempt [source 1].
Pessimistic concurrency control: Fits short, high-contention, correctness-critical multi-writer updates on a small number of tables, where the cost of one wasted 40,000-row retry exceeds the cost of serializing writers on the log store.

Interaction with time travel and history
Optimistic concurrency control: Every successful optimistic commit appends exactly one numbered commit file to _delta_log, which is why aborted (conflicted) transactions leave no version behind and time travel still shows a clean, gap-free version sequence [source 2].
Pessimistic concurrency control: Because writers are serialized on the log store, the resulting history is equally ordered and gap-free; the difference is that a version number was reserved earlier rather than validated later, so the sequence of commits is the same kind of record either way [source 2].

Takeaway — Choose optimistic concurrency (the Delta Lake default) when writers usually touch disjoint data — streaming ingestion, partition-scoped appends, or a nightly MERGE upsert in a medallion pipeline — and make the write idempotent so that a conflict retry recomputes the same result rather than duplicating rows.

Takeaway — Reach for pessimistic concurrency only when contention is genuinely high and many short transactions rewrite the same rows or partitions at once, and keep those transactions short because the log-store lock is held for the entire commit path.

Takeaway — Never justify the choice by isolation strength: both strategies deliver serializable writes and snapshot reads, so the decision-relevant difference is whether a conflict is avoided up front and paid for in waiting, or detected at commit time and paid for in retries.

actions.text: We just mapped each property to its mechanism, so now let's put the two strategies side by side. This comparison table is the spine of the page: read it row by row, and you have the full exam story for Delta Lake concurrency control.

Start with the mechanism, the how-the-write-path-works row. Optimistic concurrency holds no locks while the transaction is running; instead, Delta reads the transaction log at commit time and aborts the write if a conflicting commit landed since the transaction began. Pessimistic concurrency takes mutual exclusion directly on the log store, so conflicting writers are serialized rather than detected after the fact.

That difference drives the next row: when a conflict surfaces. Optimistic control only discovers the conflict at commit time, which is why you can do all your work and still fail at the end. Pessimistic control surfaces contention up front, before the write even proceeds.

Now the failure mode. Optimistic writes fail with a concurrent-modification style exception, typically a ConcurrentAppendException or a ConcurrentModificationException, and it falls to your application code to handle it. Pessimistic writes instead wait or time out on the lock, so you might see a lock or timeout error rather than a conflict at commit.

Because of that failure mode, the retry pattern row matters a lot. Optimistic concurrency requires you to wrap writes in a retry loop so a failed commit is re-attempted against a fresh snapshot. Pessimistic concurrency generally does not need application-level retries, since the serialization happens before the write.

Here is the crucial exam trap. Look at the isolation guarantee row. Both approaches deliver the same guarantee — serializable writes and snapshot reads. So the decision-relevant difference is never isolation; it is whether the conflict is avoided up front or detected and retried.
Which brings us to the takeaways. Default to optimistic concurrency. It is the Delta Lake model, it scales to high write throughput, and it costs you nothing when writes genuinely do not conflict.

And the last one: never justify the choice by isolation strength. If a question asks you to pick between optimistic and pessimistic because one is 'more isolated,' that is the distractor. Reach for pessimistic only under sustained, predictable contention — and justify it by write-path behaviour, not by isolation.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Concurrency and Isolation

questions.question: A data engineer owns a Delta table `sales` that is partitioned by `order_date`. At 10:00:00 two independent Spark jobs submit writes at the same moment: Job A runs `INSERT INTO sales SELECT ... WHERE order_date = '2024-06-01'`, and Job B runs `INSERT INTO sales SELECT ... WHERE order_date = '2024-06-02'`. Neither job reads any file that the other writes, and the table currently sits at version 47. What is the outcome?

options.label: Both jobs commit successfully; Delta's optimistic concurrency control serializes the two commits, the table advances by two versions (47 to 49), and any concurrent reader sees either both sets of rows or neither.
Job B blocks at the start of its write until Job A's commit finishes, because Delta acquires an exclusive write lock on the whole table for the duration of every INSERT.
Both jobs succeed, but Job B's files are silently discarded so that the table keeps only Job A's rows, and no exception is raised to either job.
Both jobs succeed but the table advances by only one version, because concurrent appends are merged into a single shared commit file in the transaction log.

questions.analysis: Delta Lake does not use pessimistic table-level locking for writes; it uses optimistic concurrency control (OCC), which means each writer reads the current version of the table, computes its own data files, and only at commit time tries to add a new JSON commit file to _delta_log [source 3]. Conflict detection therefore happens at commit time and only over the sets of files that each transaction actually read or wrote. Here the two INSERTs touch disjoint partitions (order_date = '2024-06-01' versus '2024-06-02'), their added-file sets do not overlap, and neither transaction read files produced by the other, so both commits are valid against the same version and both succeed. Each successful commit writes its own commit file and increments the version by exactly one, so the table moves 47 → 48 (Job A) → 49 (Job B); this is precisely the property that lets us recreate the state of a table at any point in time by starting from the original table and processing only commits made prior to that point [source 5]. Option B describes pessimistic locking, which Delta does not use for data writes — writers are not blocked for the duration of a write, only briefly serialized at the log. Option C is unsafe and false: Delta never silently drops an attempted write; a losing writer is aborted with an explicit exception that the application can retry. Option D contradicts the log model: every successful commit produces one commit file and one version increment, and the ordered, immutable log is exactly what delivers ACID guarantees through optimistic concurrency control [source 3].

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describe the isolation guarantees Delta Lake provides to concurrent readers and writers? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A reader querying a Delta table sees a consistent snapshot tied to one committed version and can never observe rows from a write that has not yet been committed to the transaction log.

A long-running read does not block a concurrent write and a concurrent write does not block a read, because readers resolve table state from the transaction log rather than acquiring locks on data files.

Write transactions are isolated as if they executed serially; conflicts are detected when a writer attempts to commit to the log, and the losing writer aborts with an exception that must be handled and retried.
A writer that is blocked by a long-lived exclusive table lock eventually times out and then overwrites the other writer's commit so that only the later version's rows survive.

questions.analysis: Delta Lake delivers ACID guarantees through optimistic concurrency control built on an ordered, immutable log of all table operations [source 3]. Option A is correct because that log is append-only and readers resolve a consistent snapshot from committed commits only: because every write creates a new version and the complete history is maintained [source 6], there is no mechanism by which an uncommitted write can leak rows into a reader's snapshot. Option B is correct because Delta's metadata-driven read path means a read of version N is satisfied entirely from the log entry and the Parquet files it names — no lock is taken on those files, so readers and writers do not block each other. Option C is correct: writers commit by adding a commit file, and if another transaction has already committed a change that overlaps the first transaction's read set or write set, the second transaction fails with one of Delta's concurrency exceptions (for example ConcurrentAppendException, ConcurrentDeleteReadException, ConcurrentDeleteDeleteException, MetadataChangedException or ProtocolChangedException) and the standard remediation is to retry the transaction, which is only safe precisely because the failed transaction produced no visible state. Option D is the classic misconception: Delta is not a pessimistic, lock-then-overwrite system, and ACID transaction support for robust data operations [source 1] means a conflicting writer is aborted with an explicit error rather than silently overwriting committed data. Note the important nuance for hard cases: a losing writer can fail even when the two writers added different files, because serializability is evaluated against the predicate the transaction read, not merely against physical file overlap.

questions.question: Two Spark jobs run concurrently against the unpartitioned Delta table `bronze.events`, which contains roughly 5,000 Parquet data files. Job 1 executes `DELETE FROM bronze.events WHERE event_date < '2024-01-01'` and Job 2 executes `UPDATE bronze.events SET status = 'archived' WHERE event_date < '2024-01-01'`. The two jobs start within the same second. Address all three parts: (a) Name the concurrency exception that one of the jobs is expected to raise, and explain in terms of read sets and write sets why Delta raises that exception instead of letting one job quietly overwrite the other's result. (b) State the isolation guarantee that a third job, a reader of `bronze.events`, experiences while both writers are active, and say whether that reader could ever observe a row value that Job 2 later failed to commit. (c) Give two concrete remediation options and state whether Delta's committed write transactions behave as if they executed serially.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100%): (a) Exception naming and mechanism — up to 40%. Full credit requires naming at least one correct Delta concurrency exception (ConcurrentDeleteReadException, when the delete removes a file that the other transaction read, and/or ConcurrentDeleteDeleteException, when both transactions delete the same data files) and explaining that Delta uses optimistic concurrency control, so each job reads the current version, builds its own commit, and only fails at commit time when the log shows a conflicting change affecting its read set or write set; the key point that the losing job aborts with an error and produces no visible state must be explicitly stated. Deduct heavily if the answer claims that one job silently overwrites the other or that writers block on a table lock. (b) Isolation for the reader — up to 30%. Full credit requires stating that a reader sees a consistent snapshot of one committed version of the table, that readers are never blocked by writers (and vice versa), and an explicit 'no' to the question of observing uncommitted rows, justified by the append-only transaction log. (c) Remediation and serializability — up to 30%. Full credit requires two concrete, distinct remedies from: retry the failed transaction (safe because it committed nothing); reduce the conflict surface by partitioning the table on event_date so the two jobs touch disjoint partitions; avoid mixing DELETE/UPDATE with reads of the same files in the same window; increase the number of optimistic retry attempts; or serialize the two maintenance jobs so they run one after the other. The answer must also state that committed write transactions are isolated as if they ran serially (serializable), even though readers use the non-blocking snapshot view. Award partial credit for remedies that are plausible but not tied to Delta's conflict-resolution mechanism.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. (a) Both statements read a large, overlapping set of data files: `DELETE ... WHERE event_date < '2024-01-01'` must read the file list to determine which files are entirely removable, and `UPDATE` must read the same files to rewrite matching rows. Under optimistic concurrency control — the mechanism that turns object storage into a reliable lakehouse platform with ACID guarantees [source 3] — neither job blocks the other while it works; each computes its own candidate commit and attempts to append it to _delta_log. The first job to commit wins. The loser then discovers that the log contains a commit that removed or rewrote files inside its read set, and Delta raises ConcurrentDeleteReadException; if both transactions had tried to delete the same physical files, the loser would instead receive ConcurrentDeleteDeleteException. The important property is that the loser aborts with an explicit exception and leaves no partially applied change, which is exactly why ACID transaction support makes data operations robust [source 1]. (b) A concurrent reader resolves table state from the transaction log, which is an ordered, immutable log of all table operations and a complete history [source 3], and because each writer commits by creating a new version, the reader is served a single consistent snapshot of one committed version. Readers take no locks on the data files, so they do not block the writing jobs and are not blocked by them. The reader can never see 'archived' status values from Job 2 if Job 2 aborts: that row version exists only in files that were never referenced by any commit file, so no version of the table points at them. (c) Two valid remedies: (1) retry the aborted job — retrying is safe because the aborted transaction committed nothing, and Delta even exposes retry-attempt configuration so transient conflicts resolve without application code changes; (2) partition the table on event_date so that the delete and the update touch disjoint partitions, shrinking the overlap between the two transactions' read and write sets — the same reasoning that made two disjoint-partition appends in the previous question succeed. A third option is to serialize the maintenance jobs, accepting reduced concurrency in exchange for deterministic success. Finally, committed write transactions are serializable: the resulting history is equivalent to running the two writers one after the other, which is the guarantee that makes time travel to historical states meaningful for auditing, debugging and regulatory compliance [source 2].

actions.text: Let's put that to the test. This knowledge check covers concurrency and isolation — the conflict scenarios, the guarantees each reader and writer receives, and the exceptions that come with them.
Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer before you move on. Once you submit, I'll join you to walk through the reasoning and clear up anything that didn't land.

scenes.title: Exam Checkpoints and Summary

elements.content: Exam Checkpoints and Common Traps
Objective 1: Read/Change
Objective 2: Isolation
• DESCRIBE HISTORY inspects the log [source 3].
• Readers get snapshot isolation [source 1].
• VERSION AS OF and TIMESTAMP AS OF only read history [source 5].
• Conflicting writes raise ConcurrentAppendException, never silent corruption.
• TIMESTAMP AS OF gives the last commit at or before.
• Trap: VACUUM deletes history files [source 2].
• RESTORE TO VERSION AS OF 12 creates version 13.
• Practice: run history, RESTORE, history again.
Next: Table Maintenance — OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER, VACUUM.

actions.text: Let's consolidate everything we just covered into a set of decision rules you can carry straight into the exam. This page is your checkpoint for two objectives: reading and changing table state, and understanding concurrency and isolation.

Objective one is about reading and changing. The exam framing is simple: given a symptom, choose the right statement. To inspect what happened, you use DESCRIBE HISTORY. To read what the table looked like before, you use VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF. To change the current state, you use RESTORE TABLE.

Start with DESCRIBE HISTORY. It simply inspects the transaction log and shows you the ordered list of commits — version number, timestamp, operation, and the metrics for each. When a question asks how to investigate a table's past, this is your first move.
Then the read side. VERSION AS OF and TIMESTAMP AS OF are read-only — they let you query a historical snapshot without changing the table at all. Nothing is written, no new version is created.

Be careful with the timestamp form. TIMESTAMP AS OF gives you the latest commit at or before the timestamp you specify — it is not the 'nearest' version, and it is not the next one after. That distinction shows up frequently in exam items.

Now the change side. RESTORE TO VERSION AS OF 12 does not delete version twelve — it creates a brand-new version, version thirteen, whose contents match version twelve. Restore is a forward commit, never a rewind of the log.

Objective two is about isolation and concurrency. The rule to remember is asymmetric: readers get snapshot isolation, meaning they always see a consistent, point-in-time view and are never blocked by writers.
So a reader sees a stable snapshot. Writers, however, do not get that free pass — conflicting concurrent writes must be detected and resolved rather than silently interleaved.

That is where ConcurrentAppendException and similar conflict errors come from. Delta Lake uses optimistic concurrency: it lets operations proceed and then checks on commit, raising an exception if two writers truly conflict. Recognizing that exception name as a serialization conflict, not a data corruption, is a key checkpoint.

Now the traps. The biggest one: assuming history survives VACUUM. VACUUM deletes the old data files that time travel depends on, so once the retention window passes, VERSION AS OF and TIMESTAMP AS OF can fail — even though DESCRIBE HISTORY may still show the log entries.

Here is the hands-on drill I want you to run yourself. First execute DESCRIBE HISTORY. Then query two earlier versions side by side to see the difference. Then perform a RESTORE, and finally run DESCRIBE HISTORY again — you should see a new commit appear with operation equal to RESTORE. That observation cements the whole rule set.

With that, we have both objectives locked in: read history, read history snapshots, and change state through a new commit — while respecting snapshot isolation for readers and conflict detection for writers. Up next, we move on to Table Maintenance, where we will dig into OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER, and VACUUM, and see exactly how the retention window interacts with everything on this page.

scenes.title: Lesson Opener: Why Delta Tables Need Maintenance

elements.content: Why Delta Tables Need Maintenance

• Every write adds new Parquet files and one commit [source 3]

• File count grows far faster than the data volume

• Updates and deletes leave stale, unreferenced files

• Deleting those old files limits time travel [source 2]
Maintenance rewrites physical files and adds a commit [source 5]; logical contents and row counts do not change [source 1].

Worked example: 500 GB as 12,000 files

≈ 42 MB each → 240 files ≈ 2.1 GB

actions.text: We have just walked through how the transaction log gives a Delta table its versions and its ACID guarantees. Now we turn to the other side of that coin: what happens to the physical files underneath after months of continuous writes. Before we open up OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER, and VACUUM, let us be precise about the problem they exist to solve.

The first cause of degraded read performance is fragmentation on write. Every write — INSERT, MERGE, UPDATE, or a streaming micro-batch — adds new Parquet files together with one commit to the transaction log. Nothing is overwritten in place, so the file count grows far faster than the data volume itself.

The second cause is stale files. Updates and deletes do not remove the old Parquet files; they simply become unreferenced by the current table version. Those files still cost you directory listing, storage, and metadata work on every read, and they still appear on your cloud bill, even though no query will ever return their rows.

This diagram shows the same data volume in two states. Before OPTIMIZE the table is spread across roughly twelve thousand small files; after OPTIMIZE it is compacted into about two hundred and forty files. The worked example on the slide makes the arithmetic concrete: five hundred gigabytes across twelve thousand files averages about forty-two megabytes per file, which is well below the hundred-megabyte-plus target. At that size, per-file overhead dominates query time instead of the actual scan.

Maintenance is the remedy. A maintenance operation rewrites physical files and adds a commit to the transaction log — and that framing is exactly what the exam tests. Maintenance changes the physical file layout; it does not change the logical table contents. Hold onto that distinction as we work through OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER, and VACUUM in the pages ahead.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Maintenance Fundamentals

questions.question: A nightly maintenance job runs OPTIMIZE on delta.`/mnt/curated/orders`. Immediately afterwards an analyst runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders and SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date = '2024-05-01'. The table's schema, columns, and data have not been touched by any other job. What should the analyst observe?

options.label: The row count and the rows returned are identical to the pre-OPTIMIZE results; only the physical layout of Parquet files changed.
The row count is lower than before, because compaction removes duplicate rows that were written by earlier appends.
The row count is higher than before, because OPTIMIZE appends a compacted copy of every row alongside the original rows.
The results change only if the analyst's session was open during the OPTIMIZE commit, because the transaction log is rewritten in place.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: OPTIMIZE is a physical-layout operation, not a logical one. It reads many small Parquet files and writes fewer, larger Parquet files, and its commit records an operation of OPTIMIZE with an added-files list and a removed-files list. The rows carried by those files are byte-for-byte the same logical rows, so COUNT(*) and any filtered SELECT return exactly what they returned before. This is the classic exam trap: learners expect maintenance to behave like DML. Option B is wrong because Delta Lake never performs implicit deduplication — row identity is the job of MERGE, DROP DUPLICATES-style logic, or a primary-key constraint, not OPTIMIZE. Option C is wrong because the superseded files leave the log's active file set at commit time; they are not retained as an additional copy visible to queries. Option D is wrong because the transaction log is append-only and immutable: it is an ordered log of operations, and OPTIMIZE adds a new commit rather than editing earlier ones [source 3]. A useful cross-check is time travel: querying the version immediately before the OPTIMIZE returns the same rows in the same order-independent set, since a table state is reconstructed by starting from an original table and processing only the commits made prior to that point [source 5].

questions.question: A streaming ingestion job writes to delta.`/mnt/raw/events`. Every 30-second trigger it commits one new Parquet file of roughly 200 KB. The job runs continuously for 30 days with no OPTIMIZE, no VACUUM, and no auto compaction configured. Assuming 2 micro-batches per minute, 60 minutes per hour, 24 hours per day, and 30 days, which statement best describes the resulting problem and its cause?

options.label: About 86,400 files of roughly 200 KB each accumulate (about 17 GB of physical data); query planning and per-file open overhead, not data volume, dominate query runtime.
The transaction log becomes unreadable after roughly 10,000 commits, so the table must be dropped and reloaded from source before it can be queried again.
Delta rewrites the whole table into a single Parquet file at every commit, so after 30 days the table contains one very large file that is slow to update.
The table's schema drifts with each micro-batch because every write infers and replaces the columns, so later files have different columns from earlier files.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: Worked derivation: 2 micro-batches per minute x 60 minutes = 120 files per hour; 120 x 24 = 2,880 files per day; 2,880 x 30 = 86,400 files. At 200 KB each, total physical size is about 86,400 x 200 KB = 17,280,000 KB, i.e. roughly 17 GB. The problem is therefore not volume — it is file count. Every file must be listed, opened, and have its footer read before a single byte of column data is scanned, so a query touching all 86,400 files pays enormous fixed cost per file. This is exactly the workload that optimized metadata management and compaction exist to address in a lakehouse [source 1]. Option B is wrong: the log is checkpointed and continues to be appended indefinitely; it does not expire after a fixed number of commits. Option C is wrong: a Delta commit writes only the files the operation produced, and nothing in Delta coalesces an entire table into one file automatically. Option D is wrong: Delta Lake enforces schema on write, and a traditional data lake is precisely the thing that lacks table-level features such as schema enforcement [source 4], so a stated schema is not silently replaced per micro-batch. The correct remediation pattern is periodic OPTIMIZE (optionally with ZORDER) to trade file count for file size.

questions.question: A Delta table called events lives on cloud object storage. An engineer commits DELETE FROM events WHERE event_type = 'ping' and then UPDATE events SET region = 'EU' WHERE region = 'EMEA'. Both commits succeed. The engineer then lists the storage prefix and finds Parquet files that still contain the deleted and updated rows. Which statements correctly explain why those files are still present? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Delta writes new Parquet files containing the post-change rows and records the superseded files as removed in the transaction log; the log, not a storage listing, defines which files make up the current table state.
The superseded files must stay readable so that time travel to a version before the DELETE and UPDATE still returns the original rows.
Files are only physically removed by VACUUM, which deletes files no longer referenced by the log once they have fallen outside the configured retention period.
The deletes and updates are recorded only as logical tombstones, so queries continue to return the deleted rows and the pre-update values until VACUUM finally runs.

correctAnswer: A
B
C
questions.analysis: A, B and C are correct, and they are three views of the same mechanism. (A) Delta is copy-on-write by default: a DELETE or UPDATE rewrites the affected files with the surviving or modified rows and then commits a new set of add and remove entries. The reader resolves the table state by reading the log, so the old physical files are simply no longer part of the active file set even though they still exist on storage [source 3]. (B) Because the log is an ordered, immutable record of every operation, earlier versions must keep pointing at those exact files; if they were deleted immediately, a query such as SELECT * FROM events VERSION AS OF 3 would have nothing to read. Deleting historical files is precisely what limits your ability to time travel to specific versions [source 2]. (C) Physical reclamation is deferred to VACUUM, which removes files no longer referenced by the current log and older than the retention period (7 days by default). Until that runs, storage cost and file listings include orphans. (D) is the misconception to reject: tombstones live in the log, not in the query path. Queries and time travel are computed from the log, so deleted rows stop being returned immediately after the DELETE commit — well before VACUUM runs. VACUUM never changes what a query returns; it only reduces storage. The transaction log tracks every change, promoting consistency and enabling time travel, which is what makes this separation of logical state and physical files possible [source 4].

actions.text: Before we move on to the maintenance commands themselves, let's lock in the distinction we just made. Take a few minutes on these three questions and answer them on your own — no peeking ahead, since these are exactly the kinds of contrasts the exam likes to test.
Work through each one carefully, and once you've submitted your answers I'll join you to walk through the reasoning, including the traps built into the options. Go ahead and give it your best shot.

scenes.title: OPTIMIZE: Compacting Small Files

elements.content: OPTIMIZE: Compacting Small Files
Definition. OPTIMIZE bin-packs small files into fewer, larger ones (~256 MB target).

OPTIMIZE table_name

[WHERE predicate]

[ZORDER BY (col1, col2)];
Returns numFilesAdded, numFilesRemoved, and bytes; commits are atomic [source 3].
Worked example. 12,000 × 9 MB (108 GB) → OPTIMIZE → 480 × ~225 MB (108 GB).
Scope: WHERE compacts one partition or date range only.
Commit. Log records file additions/removals [source 4]; VACUUM removes old files and limits time travel [source 2].
Exam trap: OPTIMIZE never merges or deduplicates rows and does not sort; per-micro-batch runs waste compute — use auto compaction or optimized writes.

actions.text: Now let's turn to table maintenance. This page is about OPTIMIZE — the command Databricks gives you for compacting small files. If you've ever inherited a table that was written by many tiny streaming or append jobs, you already know the symptom: reads crawl because the engine opens thousands of files to answer one query. Keep that command name in mind, because it appears constantly on the exam.

Start with the definition. OPTIMIZE bin-packs small files into fewer, larger files. Bin-packing is just a greedy packing strategy: it groups the existing files together until it reaches a target size, then starts a new bucket. Two things matter here — it rewrites the physical layout, and it does not add, remove, or reorder your rows. The data you had is the data you keep, just stored more efficiently.

Here is the syntax. OPTIMIZE, the table name, then two optional clauses. The WHERE predicate scopes the compaction to a subset of the table, and ZORDER BY lets you cluster the data along columns for data skipping — we'll dig into Z-ORDER on a later page, so for now just note where it sits in the statement.

The command returns a small metrics result set. Watch for numFilesAdded and numFilesRemoved — those tell you how many files the rewrite produced versus how many it replaced — plus a bytes figure so you can see how much data was actually touched. These metrics are exactly what you'd use to verify that a maintenance run did something rather than silently no-op.

Let's make it concrete with the worked example. Suppose you have twelve thousand files averaging nine megabytes each — call it a hundred and eight gigabytes total. You run OPTIMIZE, and those twelve thousand small files become a few hundred files of roughly two hundred and fifty-six megabytes. Same hundred and eight gigabytes of data, dramatically fewer file-handles for the reader to open. Notice the target size — around a quarter of a gigabyte, which is what Databricks aims for.

OPTIMIZE is scoped, and that's a feature, not a limitation. With a WHERE predicate you compact only one partition or one date range at a time. On a massive table, rewriting everything at once is expensive, so production runbooks typically compact the most recent partitions on a schedule. Scope it deliberately and you keep the cost under control.

Now the commit semantics, which is where people get tripped up. OPTIMIZE is a normal Delta transaction: it writes a new version to the transaction log containing add-file actions for the new files and remove-file actions for the old ones. Because the old files are only logically removed, time travel to earlier versions still works — the historical files are still there until VACUUM physically deletes them.

Finally, the exam trap, so you don't fall for it. OPTIMIZE does not merge or deduplicate rows. If you have duplicate records, compaction will happily pack them next to each other. Deduplication is a MERGE or window-function job, not a maintenance job. And don't run OPTIMIZE on every streaming micro-batch — that's wasteful and defeats the purpose. Instead, rely on auto compaction or optimized writes, which Databricks handles for you automatically. That distinction between the manual command and the automatic behavior is a favorite test question.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Diagnosing Slow Reads on an Ingested Table

elements.content: Problem 1

A streaming-ingested Delta table `delta.`/mnt/raw/events` stores 30 days of clickstream events. A filtered aggregate — `SELECT event_type, count(*) FROM events WHERE event_date >= '2024-03-01' AND event_date < '2024-04-01' GROUP BY event_type;` — takes 90 seconds on a 4-worker cluster. `DESCRIBE DETAIL delta.`/mnt/raw/events`;` returns numFiles = 12,000 and sizeBytes = 180 GB (193,273,036,800 bytes). The table is partitioned by event_date. You run `OPTIMIZE` with a matching date predicate, and then re-run the checks. The before/after metrics are:

| Metric | Before OPTIMIZE | After OPTIMIZE |

|---|---|---|

| numFiles | 12,000 | 240 |

| sizeBytes | 180 GB | 180 GB |

| SELECT COUNT(*) | 1,200,000,000 | 1,200,000,000 |

Compute the average file size before and after; state the diagnosis; give the exact OPTIMIZE command, the verification commands, and the expected new query runtime. Assume the platform target file size for this workload is 750 MB.
Hint: Average file size = sizeBytes / numFiles. Compare with the 128 MB–1 GB target range.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Compute average file size before. 180 GB = 180 × 1024 MB = 184,320 MB. 184,320 MB / 12,000 files = 15.36 MB per file. (Using decimal GB: 180,000 MB / 12,000 = 15 MB.) Either way, the average is about 15 MB, which is 8× below a 128 MB minimum and about 50× below the 750 MB target. The table has a classic small-file problem: 12,000 tasks for a scanner that should need hundreds.

Step 2 — Confirm the diagnosis with metadata. `DESCRIBE DETAIL` reports numFiles, sizeBytes, partitionColumns, and other table-level metadata. Because the Delta transaction log records every change [source 3][source 4], you can also run `DESCRIBE HISTORY delta.`/mnt/raw/events`;` to see the streaming WRITE commits that created the small files. Each streaming micro-batch appended new Parquet files, so numFiles grew while average file size stayed small.

Step 3 — Run OPTIMIZE with a predicate that matches the query's date range. This is bin-packing: it rewrites small files into larger files without adding or removing logical rows.

```sql

OPTIMIZE delta.`/mnt/raw/events`

WHERE event_date >= '2024-03-01' AND event_date < '2024-04-01';

```

The WHERE clause restricts the rewrite to the hot range, so you do not rewrite the entire 180 GB table unnecessarily.

Step 4 — Verify the new commit and the file count. Run:

```sql

DESCRIBE DETAIL delta.`/mnt/raw/events`;

DESCRIBE HISTORY delta.`/mnt/raw/events`;

```

`DESCRIBE DETAIL` should show numFiles = 240. `DESCRIBE HISTORY` should show a new commit with operation = 'OPTIMIZE' and operationParameters.predicate containing the date filter. Because OPTIMIZE is a commit, it is time-travellable: you can still query the pre-OPTIMIZE layout with `VERSION AS OF` or `TIMESTAMP AS OF` [source 2][source 5]. The transaction log remains the single source of truth for both layouts [source 3].

Step 5 — Compute average file size after. 180 GB / 240 files = 0.75 GB = 768 MB, close to the 750 MB target. (Exact: 184,320 MB / 240 = 768 MB.) Row count is unchanged because OPTIMIZE does not change the logical table contents; `SELECT COUNT(*)` returns 1,200,000,000 before and after.

Step 6 — Re-measure the query. With 240 files instead of 12,000, the aggregate launches about 50× fewer tasks. The 90-second runtime drops to about 18 seconds in this scenario — a 5× speed-up driven by reduced listing, footer-read, and task-scheduling overhead. Delta's optimized metadata management also helps the planner prune files quickly [source 1].

Analysis — Why it works: A full-table aggregate must touch every row, so it must open every file. Each Parquet file carries a footer, statistics, and a task-scheduling cost. With 12,000 files, those per-file costs dominate. Bin-packing into 240 files keeps the same bytes on disk but removes roughly 11,760 file-open and task-scheduling events. That is why the aggregate speeds up even though sizeBytes is unchanged. The transaction log makes this safe: readers see a consistent snapshot before and after the OPTIMIZE commit [source 3][source 4].

Where students go wrong: (1) Confusing bytes on disk with number of files. sizeBytes staying at 180 GB does not mean OPTIMIZE failed; it means the same logical data was repacked. (2) Expecting OPTIMIZE to deduplicate. It does not remove duplicate rows; it only changes physical layout. (3) Running OPTIMIZE on every micro-batch. OPTIMIZE rewrites bytes and consumes compute, so doing it every few seconds can cost more than the queries it accelerates. (4) Forgetting that OPTIMIZE is a commit, so you can audit it with DESCRIBE HISTORY and even time-travel to the pre-OPTIMIZE version [source 2][source 5]. (5) Assuming OPTIMIZE always helps a highly selective single-partition lookup. It does not reorganize rows within files, so a query like `WHERE event_date = '2024-03-15' AND user_id = 'u_12345'` may still scan most of the merged file. This is covered in the next problem.

Edge case: if a query needs only the newest partition, OPTIMIZE with a broader predicate may rewrite cold partitions needlessly. Always scope the predicate. Also, if the table is not partitioned, OPTIMIZE with a WHERE clause on a non-partition column can still work but may not prune as effectively.
Problem 2

After the OPTIMIZE in p1, the full-month aggregate is fast, but a point lookup remains slow. The table is partitioned by event_date. The partition for `event_date = '2024-03-15'` originally contained 300 files of 15 MB each = 4.5 GB. After OPTIMIZE on that partition, it contains 5 files of about 900 MB each. The query `SELECT * FROM events WHERE event_date = '2024-03-15' AND user_id = 'u_12345'` returns 200 rows and takes 3.2 s before OPTIMIZE and 2.8 s after. Explain the small gain with a concrete byte-level argument, and state what OPTIMIZE does not do.
Hint: Count bytes scanned, not files opened.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Compute the bytes in the partition. 300 files × 15 MB = 4,500 MB = 4.5 GB. After OPTIMIZE: 5 files × 900 MB = 4,500 MB = 4.5 GB. The logical data volume is identical.

Step 2 — Identify what changed. File count dropped 300 → 5, a 60× reduction. That reduces per-file overhead: listing, footer reads, and task scheduling. If the query had to open all 300 files, that overhead was part of the 3.2 s.

Step 3 — Identify what did not change. OPTIMIZE does not reorganize rows within files. It concatenates small files into larger ones. The predicate `user_id = 'u_12345'` is not the partition column, and unless the data is sorted or clustered on user_id, the min/max statistics in the new 900 MB files still span a wide range of user_id values. Therefore the scan still reads roughly 4.5 GB, because it must inspect rows inside those 5 large files. The only saving is the per-file overhead, which was already small after partition pruning (one partition, 300 files). That is why the runtime improves only 3.2 s → 2.8 s (12.5%), not 60×.

Step 4 — Contrast with p1. The full-month aggregate scanned all 12,000 files across the month. Reducing to 240 files removed 11,760 file-open events, which dominated the 90 s runtime. Here partition pruning already reduced the scan to one partition, and the remaining overhead was a smaller fraction of total time.

What OPTIMIZE does not do: it does not deduplicate rows, it does not sort rows, and it does not add secondary indexes. If you need file skipping on user_id, you must use a layout that supports it (e.g., partition by user_id, Z-ORDER by user_id, or liquid clustering) or accept a full partition scan. The transaction log still records the OPTIMIZE commit so you can time-travel to the old layout if needed [source 3][source 5]. Optimized metadata management helps the planner prune at the file level, but only when statistics can exclude a file [source 1].

Analysis — This problem teaches the difference between overhead reduction and data reduction. Students often see 300 → 5 files and expect a 60× speed-up. But the query's cost has two parts: per-file overhead (fixed cost per file) and bytes scanned (variable cost proportional to data read). OPTIMIZE attacks the first; it does not attack the second unless the new files can be skipped by statistics. In a partitioned table, a single-partition predicate already minimized bytes scanned; OPTIMIZE only removes the remaining per-file overhead. Edge case: if the 5 new files happened to have narrow min/max ranges on user_id (e.g., because the original files were written in sorted order and bin-packing preserved that order), the query could skip files and gain more. But that is not guaranteed by OPTIMIZE. Common mistake: claiming OPTIMIZE 'sorts the data' or 'removes duplicates' — it does neither. Another mistake: forgetting that OPTIMIZE is a rewrite, so it costs compute even when it helps. Cite [source 1] for metadata management and [source 3] for the transaction log record.
Problem 3

Which statement about OPTIMIZE on a Delta table is correct? Choose one and justify your choice with the transaction-log model.

(A) OPTIMIZE removes duplicate rows from the table.

(B) OPTIMIZE rewrites data files into larger files and records the change as a new commit in the Delta transaction log.

(C) OPTIMIZE modifies the table's current state without creating a new version, so time travel cannot see the pre-OPTIMIZE layout.

(D) Running OPTIMIZE after every streaming micro-batch is the recommended way to keep file sizes optimal because OPTIMIZE is free.
Hint: One of these options confuses physical layout with logical content, and another confuses maintenance with ingest.

Worked solution
Correct answer: B. OPTIMIZE is a physical-layout maintenance command. It reads a set of small Parquet files and rewrites their contents into fewer, larger files. It does not change the logical rows: row count is unchanged, duplicates are unchanged, and no rows are added or deleted. Because it changes the table's files, Delta Lake commits the change to the transaction log. The log is an ordered, immutable record of all table operations, which is what enables ACID guarantees and time travel [source 3]. The new commit means the version number increases, and the pre-OPTIMIZE state remains readable by version or timestamp [source 2][source 5]. Thus C is wrong: OPTIMIZE does create a new version, and time travel can see the old layout.

A is wrong because OPTIMIZE does not deduplicate. If two identical rows exist, they remain after OPTIMIZE. Deduplication requires a logical operation such as MERGE, dropDuplicates, or a DELETE/INSERT pattern, not bin-packing.

D is wrong for two reasons. First, OPTIMIZE is not free: it reads and rewrites bytes, so it consumes compute and I/O. Running it after every micro-batch can rewrite the same data repeatedly, multiplying cost. Second, OPTIMIZE's benefit is reducing per-file overhead; if each micro-batch only adds a handful of files, the overhead is not yet the bottleneck. A better pattern is scheduled OPTIMIZE with a predicate that scopes the rewrite to the recent/hot partitions, as in p1. The transaction log then shows one OPTIMIZE commit per maintenance window, which is easy to audit with DESCRIBE HISTORY [source 4].

Analysis — Why B is the exam-correct statement: it captures both the physical rewrite and the transaction-log commit. The log is the foundation of Delta Lake's reliability; without it, object storage would not give ACID semantics or time travel [source 3]. Students who choose C usually conflate OPTIMIZE (a write) with a time-travel SELECT (a read). Students who choose A confuse compaction with deduplication. Students who choose D forget the cost model. Edge case: OPTIMIZE may also run as part of auto compaction on some platforms, but the manual command still follows the same commit semantics. Always verify with DESCRIBE DETAIL (numFiles) and DESCRIBE HISTORY (operation = 'OPTIMIZE'), and remember that RESTORE can return to the pre-OPTIMIZE version if a maintenance run goes wrong [source 2].
Problem 4

A streaming pipeline writes to a partitioned Delta table every 30 seconds. Each micro-batch creates 4 new files (one per partition) of 8 MB each, so 32 MB per micro-batch. The table currently holds 180 GB. An engineer proposes running OPTIMIZE after every micro-batch over the whole table. (a) How many micro-batches and how many files are created per hour? (b) How many bytes would OPTIMIZE rewrite per hour if it rewrites the full 180 GB after each micro-batch? (c) Propose a better schedule and a predicate, and estimate the rewrite volume per day under that schedule. Assume hourly OPTIMIZE on the last 2 days of data, and that 2 days of data is 12 GB.
Hint: OPTIMIZE reads and rewrites data files; each run has a cost.

Worked solution
Part (a): Micro-batches per hour = 3600 s / 30 s = 120. Files per hour = 120 × 4 = 480 files. Data ingested per hour = 120 × 32 MB = 3,840 MB = 3.84 GB.

Part (b): If OPTIMIZE runs after every micro-batch and rewrites the entire 180 GB table, bytes rewritten per hour = 120 × 180 GB = 21,600 GB = 21.6 TB per hour. Over a day: 21.6 TB × 24 = 518.4 TB rewritten. That is vastly more than the 3.84 GB actually ingested per hour — a 5,625× write amplification. This is why running OPTIMIZE on every micro-batch is a common and expensive pitfall.

Part (c): A better schedule is a periodic OPTIMIZE, such as once per hour or once per day, scoped with a predicate to the hot/active partition range. Example:

```sql

OPTIMIZE delta.`/mnt/raw/events`

WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 2 DAYS;

```

If 2 days of data is 12 GB and OPTIMIZE runs hourly, the rewrite volume is 24 × 12 GB = 288 GB per day. Compare with 518.4 TB per day for the every-micro-batch plan: the hourly plan rewrites about 0.056% of the bytes while still bin-packing the files that the streaming ingest created. The transaction log records each OPTIMIZE commit, so you can audit and time-travel the pre-OPTIMIZE state if a maintenance run needs to be reversed [source 3][source 5]. Delta's optimized metadata management also means the planner can use file statistics efficiently after compaction [source 1].

Analysis — This problem forces a cost-benefit analysis: OPTIMIZE is not free. The every-micro-batch plan has a correctness smell too — it treats a maintenance operation as an ingest step. Students often focus only on file count and forget that each OPTIMIZE reads and rewrites bytes. The key ratio is bytes rewritten ÷ bytes ingested. Here the naive plan rewrites 21.6 TB per hour to ingest 3.84 GB per hour, a 5,625× amplification. The scoped hourly plan rewrites 288 GB per day to ingest 92.16 GB per day (3.84 × 24), a 3.125× amplification — much more reasonable, and it can be tuned further. Edge cases: if the table is unpartitioned, the WHERE clause may not prune, so you may need partition-level predicates or a different layout. If the streaming job already uses auto compaction, manual OPTIMIZE may be redundant, but the exam expects you to recognize the cost of running the manual command too often. Common mistakes: (1) assuming OPTIMIZE only reads metadata, when it actually reads and rewrites data files; (2) forgetting that OPTIMIZE commits to the log and is therefore time-travellable [source 2][source 4]; (3) expecting OPTIMIZE to remove duplicates, which it does not. The safe pattern is: let streaming ingest create files, periodically bin-pack the hot range with OPTIMIZE, and verify with DESCRIBE DETAIL and DESCRIBE HISTORY. Cite [source 1] for optimized metadata management and [source 3] for the transaction log.

actions.text: Building on the OPTIMIZE semantics we just covered, let's put that knowledge to work on a fully-worked diagnostic problem. Read the symptom carefully — a streaming-ingested Delta table takes ninety seconds to run a simple filtered aggregate, and DESCRIBE DETAIL reports numFiles of 12,000 against a total sizeBytes of 180 gigabytes.

The hint points you straight at the diagnostic metric that matters: average file size equals sizeBytes divided by numFiles. Do that math and you get roughly fifteen megabytes per file. Any time you see a file count in the thousands and an average file size far below the one-hundred-twenty-eight-megabyte target, you are looking at the small-file problem, and that is the root cause here.

The worked solution walks a clean four-step loop. One, confirm the file count and average file size. Two, run OPTIMIZE with a date-range WHERE clause to compact just the relevant partitions. Three, re-run DESCRIBE DETAIL and DESCRIBE HISTORY to confirm the new commit landed. Four, re-measure the query so you can prove the improvement with evidence rather than assumption.

Now the analysis, and this is where exam points hide. Bin-packing removes per-file overhead — listing, footer reads, task scheduling — which is why the full aggregate speeds up dramatically. But notice the caveat: a highly selective single-partition predicate may gain very little, because OPTIMIZE does not reorganize rows within files. Compacting files helps you scan fewer files, not read less data inside a file you still have to touch.

The remaining problems sharpen the semantics. Problem Three tests whether you can separate OPTIMIZE as a physical layout operation from logical operations like deduplication — remember, OPTIMIZE never removes duplicate rows. And Problem Four forces a cost-benefit analysis: OPTIMIZE reads and rewrites data files, so each run costs compute, which is exactly why you never run it on every micro-batch.

So the takeaway to carry into the knowledge check: diagnose with numFiles and average file size, fix with a scoped OPTIMIZE, verify with DESCRIBE DETAIL and DESCRIBE HISTORY, and always weigh the compute cost against the read-time savings. Symptom, evidence, command — that is the diagnostic pattern this exam rewards.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: OPTIMIZE Semantics

questions.question: A nightly job must compact the small files of a Delta table named sales for a single day only, and then co-locate related rows by customer_id so that later queries on that column can skip files. Which statement uses correct OPTIMIZE command syntax?

options.label: OPTIMIZE sales WHERE date = '2024-05-01' ZORDER BY (customer_id)
OPTIMIZE sales ZORDER BY (customer_id) WHERE date = '2024-05-01'
OPTIMIZE sales PARTITION (date = '2024-05-01') ZORDER BY customer_id
OPTIMIZE sales WHERE date = '2024-05-01' SORT BY customer_id

questions.analysis: The correct shape of the command is OPTIMIZE table_name [WHERE predicate] [ZORDER BY (col, ...)]. The WHERE predicate is optional and restricts the rewrite to the files whose records satisfy it, so it must appear before ZORDER BY; the ZORDER BY clause always takes a parenthesised column list. Option B is wrong because the clause order is fixed: ZORDER BY terminates the statement, so a WHERE clause cannot follow it. Option C is wrong because PARTITION is a DDL/DML clause used with CREATE TABLE, INSERT, and similar statements to specify target partition values, not a sub-clause of OPTIMIZE. Option D is wrong because SORT BY is a Spark SQL query clause that orders rows within a query's output partitions; it is not a Delta maintenance keyword, and writing it inside OPTIMIZE is a syntax error. This matters in practice because Delta Lake's transaction log allows safe operations to finish with optimistic concurrency control, so an operator who mistypes the maintenance command may not get the compaction they intended [source 3].

questions.question: Which statements about the semantics of OPTIMIZE on a Delta table are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: OPTIMIZE rewrites many small Parquet files into fewer, larger files, but a plain read of the table returns exactly the same rows before and after the operation.
OPTIMIZE adds a new commit to the transaction log, so the table state that existed immediately before the OPTIMIZE can still be read with time travel.
OPTIMIZE deduplicates the table: because ZORDER BY places equal key values next to each other, rows with duplicate keys are eliminated.
OPTIMIZE repartitions the table by permanently changing its physical partition columns to the columns listed in the ZORDER BY clause.
OPTIMIZE with ZORDER BY globally sorts every row of the table by the Z-order columns, guaranteeing a total ordering of rows across all files.

questions.analysis: OPTIMIZE is a file-layout operation, not a data-transformation operation. It reads the existing Parquet files that satisfy the optional predicate, bin-packs their rows into fewer, larger files, and commits the result, so the logical contents of the table are unchanged (A). Because it is a normal Delta commit, it appends an entry to the ordered, immutable log rather than rewriting history, which means the pre-OPTIMIZE state stays queryable through time travel (B) — Delta reconstructs any historical state 'by starting with an original table, and processing only commits made prior to that point' [source 5]. Option C is a misconception: deduplication happens in MERGE or explicit distinct logic; compaction never removes rows, and identical rows survive OPTIMIZE untouched. Option D is wrong because OPTIMIZE never changes a table's partition columns; partitioning is fixed by the table definition, and ZORDER BY only rearranges rows inside the rewritten files (a data-skipping optimisation, not a partition change). Option E is wrong because ZORDER BY applies a space-filling-curve clustering within files to improve data skipping; it does not produce a globally sorted table, and Delta makes no ordering guarantee about the sequence in which rows are read. Note also that OPTIMIZE does not delete the old Parquet files immediately — they remain until VACUUM removes files no longer referenced by the log, and that deletion, not OPTIMIZE, is what limits how far back you can time travel [source 2].

questions.question: You run OPTIMIZE on a Delta table that previously held thousands of small files, and you must prove two things: the compaction actually reduced the file count, and earlier versions of the table are still readable. Which statement describes correct evidence and a correct conclusion?

options.label: DESCRIBE DETAIL reports a smaller numFiles for the same logical table, and DESCRIBE HISTORY shows a new OPTIMIZE commit recording the files added and removed; versions before that commit remain readable with time travel.
DESCRIBE DETAIL reports a smaller numFiles, which proves OPTIMIZE deleted the historical Parquet files, so time travel to versions captured before the OPTIMIZE now fails.
DESCRIBE DETAIL shows that the table's partition columns have changed to the ZORDER BY columns, which confirms that OPTIMIZE re-partitioned the data on disk.
DESCRIBE HISTORY no longer lists the commits made before the OPTIMIZE, because OPTIMIZE rewrites the transaction log so that only the current version is retained.

questions.analysis: DESCRIBE DETAIL returns table-level metadata including the current file count and total size, so a drop in numFiles after OPTIMIZE is direct evidence that small files were consolidated. DESCRIBE HISTORY returns the commit log with one entry per operation and its metrics (files added, files removed, bytes written), so the OPTIMIZE commit is visible as an ordinary appended entry. Option A is therefore correct. Option B mixes a valid observation with a false conclusion: OPTIMIZE marks the superseded files as no longer referenced by the log but does not physically delete them, so time travel still works; only VACUUM, which removes files that are no longer referenced and are past the retention threshold, restricts time travel to specific versions [source 2]. Option C is wrong because OPTIMIZE never alters partition columns — the table's partitioning is a schema-level property that a maintenance command does not touch; ZORDER BY only clusters rows within the rewritten files. Option D is wrong because the Delta transaction log is an ordered, immutable record of operations: it is appended to, never rewritten to drop history, which is exactly why time travel and ACID guarantees are possible in the first place [source 3]. A traditional data lake has no such log and no table-level transaction semantics, which is the reliability gap the Delta log closes [source 4].

actions.text: Now let's put that diagnostic instinct to the test. This knowledge check covers what we just covered on OPTIMIZE — its command syntax and what the operation actually does to your table.

Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer before moving on; a couple of these hinge on the difference between what the command looks like and what it truly changes. Once you submit, I'll walk you through everything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Z-ORDER BY: Multi-Dimensional Clustering for Data Skipping

elements.content: Z-ORDER BY: Data Skipping

OPTIMIZE events ZORDER BY (event_date, user_id);

Inside OPTIMIZE only; logged as a table commit [source 4]
Multi-Column Ordering
• OPTIMIZE co-locates related rows in files [source 3]
How Skipping Works
• Tighter min/max stats let Delta skip files [source 1]
Which Columns
• Pick high-cardinality filters: user_id, device_id
Worked Example
• 1M rows / 1,000 files; 0.1% filter reads ~10 files
• Cap at ~4 columns; don't partition on the same column

actions.text: We just saw how OPTIMIZE compacts small files. Now we take the next step: OPTIMIZE with Z-ORDER BY. This is how we co-locate related rows so that Delta's file-level statistics can skip files entirely at read time. Think of it as multi-dimensional clustering, and it is a high-yield exam topic.

Here is the syntax you must be able to write cold: OPTIMIZE events ZORDER BY (event_date, user_id). Notice two things. First, ZORDER BY is always appended to an OPTIMIZE run — there is no standalone Z-ORDER command. Second, you can pass multiple columns inside the parentheses, which is exactly what makes this multi-dimensional.

So what does multi-column ordering actually mean? A normal sort orders rows along a single axis. Z-ORDER instead orders rows across several columns at once, so values that tend to appear together in the same query land in the same files. OPTIMIZE co-locates those related rows — the co-location is the whole point.

Now, how does that translate into skipping? Delta maintains min/max statistics per file in the transaction log. Because Z-ORDER clusters similar values into the same files, those per-file ranges become much tighter. Tighter ranges mean more files can be pruned by the filter — fewer files scanned, less I/O, shorter queries.

Which columns should you choose? Apply the selectivity rule: pick columns that appear frequently in WHERE filters and that have high cardinality — user_id, device_id, event_ts. High cardinality gives the min/max statistics real discriminating power. Low-cardinality flags, like a status column with three values, gain you almost nothing.

Let's put a number on it. Say we have one million rows spread across a thousand files, and our filter is selective enough to hit only zero point one percent of the data. With good Z-ORDER clustering, we might read roughly ten files instead of all one thousand — that is a hundred-fold reduction in files touched, and it is the exact quantitative reasoning the exam rewards.

Finally, the limits and traps. Cap yourself at about four columns — beyond that, returns diminish sharply because each extra dimension dilutes the clustering on the others. And critically, Z-ORDER does not replace partitioning. Do not partition on the same high-cardinality column you are Z-ORDERing — that produces tiny directories and the small-file problem we are trying to fix. Keep this rule in your head: partitioning for coarse, low-cardinality slicing; Z-ORDER for fine-grained, high-cardinality filtering.

actions.text: Notice the pattern the exam expects you to reason about. Tighter file-level min/max statistics mean fewer files read, which means a faster selective query — and that is exactly why Z-ORDER pays off on high-cardinality filter columns like user_id, but barely helps a low-cardinality column like country. scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Z-ORDER and Data Skipping

questions.question: A Delta table named sales_facts is partitioned by event_date and stores the columns customer_id, region, product_sku, and a large payload_json column. Workload telemetry over the last 30 days shows: roughly 85% of queries filter on customer_id (usually combined with a range on event_date), about 10% filter on region, and payload_json is never used in a WHERE clause. You run OPTIMIZE on the table. Which column set should you pass to ZORDER BY?

options.label: ZORDER BY (customer_id)
ZORDER BY (event_date, customer_id, region, product_sku, payload_json)
ZORDER BY (payload_json)
ZORDER BY (region)

questions.analysis: The right ZORDER BY column is the one that appears in the most frequent and most selective predicate and is not already handled by partitioning. Here that is customer_id, used by 85% of queries at high cardinality. Option B is the classic 'add everything' mistake: event_date is already the partition column, so every file already contains a single date and its file-level statistics are already perfectly tight — listing it again buys nothing, and region, product_sku and payload_json would each dilute the clustering that customer_id receives. Option C is wrong because payload_json is never filtered, is physically large, and is close to unique per row, so Z-ordering on it co-locates almost nothing while forcing a full, expensive rewrite. Option D is wrong because region is both rarely filtered (10%) and low cardinality (a handful of distinct values), so a region predicate would still match nearly every file for the common regions.
