A concrete illustration: before Z-ordering, each of 4,000 files contains a random mix of customers, so a lookup for customer_id = 'C-91823' must scan all 4,000 files. After OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (customer_id), the same rows are packed into about a dozen files whose min/max ranges bracket that value, and the engine prunes the other ~3,988 files from the scan because Delta Lake's optimized metadata management makes per-file statistics cheap to consult at planning time [source 1]. Note that the query returns exactly the same rows either way — Z-ordering changes how much data is read, never what the answer is.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Z-ORDER and data skipping in Delta Lake are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: ZORDER BY co-locates rows with similar values so that the recorded min/max statistics for each Parquet file become tighter, allowing the engine to skip files whose ranges cannot satisfy a predicate.
ZORDER BY sorts the entire table down into a single file, which is why no skipping is needed on subsequent queries.
ZORDER BY does not change the set of rows a query returns; it only changes how many files must be opened to produce that result set.
ZORDER BY physically reorders rows at query time, so the engine can return results without consulting file statistics.
Because ZORDER BY clusters similar values inside files, it makes partitioning unnecessary and a Z-ordered table should therefore never be partitioned as well.

questions.analysis: A is correct and describes the actual mechanism: Z-ordering is a layout optimization performed during OPTIMIZE that clusters-like-values-together inside the output files, which narrows the min/max range that each file's footer records for the ordered columns; a selective filter that falls outside a file's range lets the engine skip that file entirely. C is correct because data skipping is a read-side optimization — the row set produced by SELECT ... WHERE is identical before and after an OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY run, and the earlier maintenance lesson that OPTIMIZE never changes row counts applies here too. B and D describe the two standard misconceptions and are both false: Z-ORDER never collapses a table into one file (bin-packing targets roughly 256 MB files and produces many of them), and reordering never happens at query time — the clustering is baked into the physical files and the query simply exploits the statistics. E is false because partitioning and Z-ordering operate at different granularities and are complementary: partitioning prunes whole directories using the partition column before any file is opened, while Z-ordering only tightens statistics inside the candidate set. Also remember the timing boundary: Z-ordering is a maintenance-time rewrite, so every later commit — INSERT, MERGE, UPDATE, or a streaming micro-batch — adds new files that are not Z-ordered until the next OPTIMIZE run, and the transaction log is what tracks which files currently belong to the table [source 4]. Delta Lake's emphasis on optimized metadata management is precisely what makes consulting those per-file statistics cheap enough to be worthwhile [source 1].

questions.question: A data engineer proposes removing partitioning from a large Delta table (currently partitioned by event_date) and instead running OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (event_date, region, product_sku) after every load, arguing that this gives 'the same pruning benefit without the partitioning overhead.' Evaluate this proposal. In your answer, explain how Z-ORDER actually enables data skipping, why it is not a substitute for partitioning, and what limits its effectiveness as you add columns.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100% total): (1) Mechanism of data skipping — 30%. The answer must explain that ZORDER BY clusters like values within files so per-file min/max (and null count) statistics become tight, and that the query engine then skips files whose recorded ranges cannot contain matching values; it must state that the rewrite happens during OPTIMIZE, not at query time. (2) Granularity difference and why partitioning is not replaced — 30%. Must contrast directory-level pruning (partition predicate eliminates whole directories before any file is opened, and every writer obeys it continuously) with file-level statistics pruning (candidate files must still have their metadata examined, and the benefit only exists for files written by the most recent OPTIMIZE). Must note that fresh writes/streaming micro-batches add unclustered files until the next OPTIMIZE. (3) Column count, column order, and diminishing returns — 25%. Must state that ZORDER BY supports a bounded number of columns (Databricks documents a maximum of 32), that the leading column receives the tightest clustering while trailing columns get progressively less, that a near-unique or never-filtered column wastes the rewrite, and that adding columns to 'cover everything' dilutes the benefit rather than increasing it. (4) Correct recommendation with a precondition or edge case — 15%. Must propose a two-level design (partition on the low-cardinality column actually used for range pruning, Z-order on the high-cardinality column used for point lookups) and acknowledge at least one precondition: skipping only helps selective predicates, so a query with no selective filter or a full-table scan gains nothing regardless of Z-ordering, and the rewrite itself costs compute. Deduct proportionally for answers that claim Z-ORDER sorts the whole table, reorders rows at read time, or changes the rows returned.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: The proposal is partially right in spirit and wrong in mechanism. ZORDER BY does not prune at plan time the way a partition does — it only makes file-level statistics tighter so that data skipping can discard files at read time. Partitioning is enforced by the writer on every commit: a predicate on event_date eliminates whole directories before a single file footer is read, and a brand-new file lands in the correct directory immediately. Z-ordering is a maintenance-time rewrite: it applies only to files produced by the OPTIMIZE run, and every subsequent INSERT, MERGE, UPDATE, or streaming micro-batch produces new files whose ranges are effectively random until the next OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY, so the 'always fresh' guarantee the engineer assumes does not exist. The number of columns also matters: Databricks documents an upper bound on ZORDER BY columns (32), but long before that ceiling the benefit thins out, because the Z-ordering curve sorts primarily by the leading column and each additional column receives less effective clustering; meanwhile a low-value column such as region (few distinct values, rarely filtered) or a near-unique column such as product_sku used in no predicate consumes rewrite cost for little skipping benefit. Note also that Z-ORDER interacts with file size: bin-packing targets roughly 256 MB files, and clustering can only be as precise as the min/max ranges recorded per file, so larger files produce coarser ranges. The correct design is two-level — keep a partition on the coarse, low-cardinality column that queries actually prune with (for example event_date), and Z-order on the one or two high-cardinality columns used by selective point lookups (customer_id, product_sku). The operative precondition is selectivity: if a query has no selective predicate and scans every partition, no file can be skipped, so the Z-order run is pure cost. One final clarification, because it is a common exam trap: none of this changes the rows a query returns. The rewrite is recorded as an ordinary commit in the transaction log, whose ordered, immutable history is what makes the new physical layout addressable and the table's state reproducible [source 3], and the resulting metadata optimization is the same feature set that gives Delta Lake faster query performance than a raw file-based data lake, which lacks such table-level features [source 1][source 4].

actions.text: Time to check how that landed. Three questions on Z-ORDER and data skipping — one single-choice, one multi-select, one short answer where I want your reasoning in your own words, not just a verdict.

Work through them on your own first; the short answer especially rewards a precise explanation of the mechanism over a quick yes-or-no. I'll meet you right after you submit to go through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: VACUUM and Retention: Cleaning Up Stale Files Safely

elements.content: VACUUM and Retention
VACUUM deletes Parquet files no longer referenced by the current version and older than retention. [source 3]
Default: 7 days (168 hours); RETAIN 168 HOURS is explicit and DRY RUN previews deletions.
Retention protects time travel, streaming readers and long jobs; deletions cause FileNotFoundException. [source 5]
Example: a 30-day time-travel SLA needs 30 × 24 = 720 h; RETAIN 168 HOURS deletes history past day 7. [source 2]
Unsafe override (breaks time travel): spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled=false
Exam trap: VACUUM is irreversible and never rewrites the log; old history entries point at deleted files. [source 4]

actions.text: Now let's turn to the last piece of Delta maintenance: VACUUM. OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER rearranged the files your table still needs — VACUUM is the cleanup step that removes the ones it no longer references.

The title says it all: VACUUM and Retention — cleaning up stale files safely. The word 'safely' is doing real work there, because VACUUM is one of the few Delta operations that is genuinely destructive.

Here's the mechanism. VACUUM physically deletes Parquet data files that are no longer referenced by the current table version and that are older than the retention threshold. Notice the two conditions — unreferenced AND older than the threshold. Both must hold before a file is removed.

By default that threshold is seven days, or 168 hours. You can be explicit about it with VACUUM table RETAIN 168 HOURS, and you can dry-run it with VACUUM table DRY RUN, which lists exactly what would be deleted without touching anything. Always preview before you vacuum.

Why does that retention period exist? Because retention protects readers. Time-travel queries, streaming readers still working off an older snapshot, and long-running concurrent jobs may all still be reading those files. Delete them too early and those readers hit FileNotFound errors.

This is the exam-style reasoning you need. If a team commits to a 30-day time-travel SLA, they need at least 30 times 24, so 720 hours of retention. Setting RETAIN 168 HOURS would silently break that guarantee — the requirement drives the setting, not the other way round.

What if you try to go below seven days? Delta blocks it by default. You'd have to set spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled to false. That override is explicitly marked unsafe, and it breaks time travel — treat it as a red flag in any scenario question.

And here's the classic trap. VACUUM is irreversible, and it does not rewrite the transaction log. It frees storage by deleting data files, while the older history entries stay in the log but become unreadable. So don't confuse VACUUM with RESTORE — one reclaims storage, the other rolls back state.

Quick recap: VACUUM deletes unreferenced files past the retention threshold, defaults to seven days, and always respects your time-travel window. Preview with DRY RUN, never drop below the SLA, and remember the exam trap — irreversible, and the log is left untouched. On the next page we'll weigh maintenance frequency against time-travel needs.

scenes.title: Trade-off Analysis: Maintenance Frequency versus Time Travel Needs

elements.content: Decision — A platform team supports one Delta table that ingests 500 GB every night from a batch pipeline, and a set of executive dashboards that must return in under 5 seconds while a compliance team requires the ability to reconstruct the table as of any day in the last 30 days. The nightly load lands as roughly 8,000 small Parquet files averaging about 62.5 MB, so per-file overhead dominates query time and pushes reads toward the 5-second ceiling. The team must choose exactly one maintenance policy for the hot table, and the decision is hard because two requirements pull in opposite directions: the maintenance that makes reads fast depends on VACUUM to reclaim stale files, yet VACUUM deletes data files irreversibly, and deleting historical files in a Delta table can limit your ability to time travel to specific versions [source 2]. Time travel works in the first place because the Delta Lake transaction log is an ordered, immutable log of every operation that maps versions to timestamps, so a reader can reconstruct any prior state of the table [source 3], and more precisely we can recreate the state of a table at any point in time by starting with an original table and processing only the commits made prior to that point [source 5]. Time travel, together with ACID transactions and schema enforcement, is exactly what separates Delta Lake from a traditional data lake, which is a flexible repository for raw files but lacks those table-level guarantees [source 4]. Worked example with concrete numbers: at 8,000 files per night and roughly 0.5 ms of open-and-footer overhead per file, a dashboard query pays 8,000 x 0.5 ms = 4.0 s of pure file overhead before reading a single row, leaving under 1 s of the 5-second SLA for the actual scan and aggregation. Running OPTIMIZE to bin-pack toward the 256 MB target rewrites that 500 GB into roughly 500 GB / 256 MB = 2,000 files, cutting overhead to 2,000 x 0.5 ms = 1.0 s and restoring about 4 s of SLA headroom; over a 30-day month the gap compounds to 8,000 x 30 = 240,000 untouched files versus roughly 2,000 x 30 = 60,000 maintained files. Storage math matters too: 500 GB per night is 15 TB per month of base data, and every stale file that VACUUM would have removed stays on the bill at roughly 0.023 USD per GB-month, so 1 TB of uncollected stale files costs about 23 USD per month on top of the base data. Every option below is therefore judged against the same three hard limits: the under-5-second dashboard SLA, the 30-day auditor time-travel window, and the stated storage cost concern.

Constraints — Nightly ingestion of 500 GB must land within the batch window and must not be blocked by maintenance.  •  Dashboard queries on the hot table must return in under 5 seconds.  •  Auditors require the ability to reconstruct the table as of any day within the last 30 days.  •  Storage cost is a stated concern, so unbounded growth of stale or duplicate files is not acceptable.  •  VACUUM physically deletes data files and cannot be undone, so any retention shorter than the audit window permanently destroys time-travel capability.  •  The solution must run on the existing Databricks and Delta Lake platform with no new engine introduced.

Hourly OPTIMIZE with Z-ORDER plus VACUUM at 7-day retention
+ Delivers the fastest reads of the three options, because newly written files are compacted within the hour and Z-ORDER data-skipping statistics stay fresh, so selective dashboard filters skip the maximum number of files.; + Keeps the hot table small, since the 7-day VACUUM retention continuously reclaims stale files left by UPDATE and DELETE, capping storage growth.
− Costs roughly 24x the compute of a daily policy: 24 OPTIMIZE runs per day equals about 720 runs per month to maintain a table that only receives new data once per night, and each run rewrites up to 500 GB of Parquet.; − Breaks the audit requirement outright: VACUUM at the default 7-day retention removes files that time travel needs, so a query for the state of the table 20 or 30 days ago fails, and because VACUUM is irreversible that capability cannot be recovered for already-vacuumed versions.
Best for: Interactive incident-response or fraud-detection tables where hour-level freshness of clustering is essential and there is no historical audit obligation.

Daily OPTIMIZE with Z-ORDER after each ingestion, VACUUM at 7-day retention, plus a separate append-only history table for audit
+ Meets the 5-second SLA with a defensible margin: compacting to roughly 2,000 files per nightly partition cuts per-file overhead from about 4.0 s to about 1.0 s, and Z-ORDER on the common dashboard filter columns lets file skipping discard the rest.; + Satisfies the 30-day audit window without fighting VACUUM, because the audit copy is an append-only table written once per load and never compacted away, so the hot table is free to vacuum aggressively and stay small.; + Runs at about 1/24th the compute of hourly maintenance while matching nightly data arrival, and the hot table holds roughly 7 days of files instead of 30, which keeps the hot-table storage share small.
− Introduces real storage duplication: the history table retains 15 TB per month of audit data (500 GB x 30 days) alongside the compacted hot table, so the 0.023 USD per GB-month storage line grows rather than shrinks.; − Adds a second pipeline and a second set of governance obligations to build and monitor, and any query that reaches back more than 7 days must be rewritten by an engineer to target the history table instead of using VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF syntax.; − Time travel on the hot table is limited to the VACUUM retention window, so the 30-day guarantee is a property of the history table, not of the hot table.
Best for: Production analytics tables with a hard read SLA, a defined compliance window, and enough engineering capacity to operate one extra append-only audit table.

No VACUUM, 30-day retention, minimal OPTIMIZE
+ Preserves time travel to 30 days on the single hot table with no duplicate copy, so auditors query the same table with VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF and no query rewriting is needed.; + Requires the least engineering effort to build: no second pipeline, no history-table schema, no retention policy to reconcile.
− Fails the 5-second SLA: if maintenance is skipped, the nightly 8,000 files never get bin-packed, so per-file overhead alone stays near 4.0 s and grows to 16 s or more within a week of ingestion as the file count compounds.; − Storage grows without bound: every UPDATE and DELETE leaves stale files that VACUUM would have reclaimed, and those files remain on the bill indefinitely, directly contradicting the stated storage cost concern.; − Even 30-day time travel is fragile here, because running a single corrective VACUUM later destroys the window irreversibly and cannot be rolled back.
Best for: Small tables, low write rates, or short-lived exploration tables where correctness of history matters far more than read latency or storage cost.

Recommendation: Daily OPTIMIZE with Z-ORDER after each ingestion, VACUUM at 7-day retention, plus a separate append-only history table for audit — The three hard constraints cannot all be satisfied on one table, because VACUUM deletes data files irreversibly and destroying historical files removes the ability to time travel to those versions [source 2], so a 7-day VACUUM retention and a 30-day audit window are mutually exclusive on the same table. Splitting the requirements resolves the conflict: the hot table is compacted daily to roughly 2,000 files, cutting per-file overhead from about 4.0 s to about 1.0 s and meeting the under-5-second SLA, while the append-only history table carries the full 30-day audit window and is never vacuumed. Option A is rejected because hourly OPTIMIZE costs about 24x the compute for a table that ingests only once per night, and its 7-day VACUUM still breaks the audit requirement, so it pays the highest price and fails a constraint. Option C is rejected because skipping bin-packing leaves about 8,000 files per night worth roughly 4.0 s of pure overhead, which violates the SLA almost immediately, and the stale files it refuses to vacuum grow the storage bill without bound. Option B is the only policy that treats the irreversible delete as the binding fact and isolates it to the table that does not need history.

actions.text: Building on what we just covered about VACUUM and retention, let's apply it to a real decision. A platform team supports one Delta table that has to satisfy several competing requirements at once — this is exactly the kind of constrained scenario the exam loves.

First, pin down the constraints. They run a nightly ingestion of 500 GB, dashboards must return in under five seconds, auditors require thirty days of history, and storage cost is a stated concern. Notice how these pull in different directions — that tension is the whole point of the exercise.

Option A is hourly OPTIMIZE with Z-ORDER, plus VACUUM at the default seven-day retention. It delivers the fastest reads, but it burns the most compute — and critically, it deletes files after seven days, which breaks the thirty-day audit requirement outright.

Option B is daily OPTIMIZE with Z-ORDER after each ingestion, plus VACUUM at seven-day retention, with audit history served from a separate append-only history table. You keep the hot table fast and cheap, and the long historical trail lives somewhere else.

Option C is minimal maintenance — thirty-day retention and no VACUUM. Time travel is fully preserved, but read latency degrades as small files pile up, and storage costs climb. That directly conflicts with the latency SLA and the cost concern.

So the recommendation is Option B. Maintain the hot table after each ingestion window and keep the extended history in a separate table. Remember the key exam trap: VACUUM deletes files irreversibly and simply cannot coexist with a thirty-day time-travel SLA on the same table.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: VACUUM and Retention

questions.question: A Delta table `events` in Databricks has been written to continuously for 30 days with no maintenance other than OPTIMIZE. An engineer disables the retention duration safety check, then runs `VACUUM events RETAIN 0 HOURS`, which completes successfully. A teammate immediately runs `SELECT * FROM events VERSION AS OF 12`. What is the most likely outcome, and why?

options.label: The query returns version 12 successfully, because RETAIN 0 HOURS only affects files belonging to the very latest version.
The query fails with a FileNotFoundException, because VACUUM deleted every data file not referenced by the current version, while the transaction log still records version 12 as a valid version.
The query returns the rows of the current version, because Delta Lake silently falls back to the latest snapshot whenever a historical data file is missing.
The query fails with a DeltaConcurrentModificationException, because VACUUM itself commits a new table version that conflicts with the historical read.

questions.analysis: Delta Lake's default deleted-file retention interval is 7 days (168 hours), so a normal `VACUUM` keeps any data file that a version written within the last week still references. `RETAIN 0 HOURS` collapses that window to zero: VACUUM deletes every Parquet data file that is not referenced by the current (latest) version of the table. The transaction log in `_delta_log` is an ordered, immutable record of commits, and VACUUM does not touch it, so version 12 still appears in `DESCRIBE HISTORY` and is still resolvable as a version number [source 3]. The failure is therefore a data-file failure, not a version-metadata failure: when the reader opens the snapshot for version 12, its file list points at deleted Parquet files and Delta raises FileNotFoundException. Option A is wrong because files that exist only in older versions are exactly what RETAIN 0 HOURS removes. Option C is wrong because Delta never silently substitutes a different version — time travel is deterministic, resolving to the exact commit requested, and the source material notes that deleting historical files in a Delta table directly limits your ability to time travel to specific versions [source 2]. Option D is wrong because VACUUM is not a write transaction against table data; it removes orphaned files from storage and does not commit a new Delta version, so no write-write conflict is generated. Note that RETAIN 0 HOURS also requires the retention duration check to have been disabled; with the default check enabled, VACUUM rejects an interval shorter than the safety threshold before deleting anything.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about `spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled` and VACUUM retention are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: It defaults to true, and while it is enabled a VACUUM whose retention interval is shorter than the 7-day threshold is rejected with an error before any file is deleted.
Disabling it is the only way to undo an aggressive VACUUM, because the setting controls whether deleted files are recoverable from the transaction log.

Disabling it is dangerous because long-running queries, streaming jobs, and time travel readers may still hold references to files that the aggressive vacuum now deletes, producing FileNotFoundException.
With the check disabled, VACUUM rewrites the files it would otherwise delete into the current version, so time travel continues to work with a smaller file set.
Because the default deleted-file retention interval is 7 days, a plain VACUUM with no RETAIN clause normally keeps files replaced within the past week.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: the retention duration check is a guardrail that compares the requested retention interval against the table's deleted-file retention duration (7 days by default) and raises an error rather than letting an operator vacuum away files that concurrent readers may still need. Option C is correct and is the reason the guardrail exists: the setting cannot know what is reading the table, so disabling it lets VACUUM delete files that an in-flight batch query, a Structured Streaming micro-batch, or a `VERSION AS OF` query still expects to open, which surfaces as FileNotFoundException. Option E is correct: with no RETAIN clause, VACUUM uses the table's retention setting, which is 7 days unless changed, so recently superseded files survive. Option B is wrong on two counts: the setting is a validation flag, not an undo mechanism, and VACUUM deletions are not recoverable through it or through the transaction log — the log records which files a version used, but it does not store the Parquet bytes, so once a file is removed from object storage there is nothing to restore. Option D is wrong because VACUUM only deletes; it never rewrites, compacts, or re-references data files, which is the job of OPTIMIZE. Practically, time travel works by replaying only the commits that existed prior to the target point in time and reading the files those commits reference, so removing those files removes the ability to reconstruct that state, even though the commit list itself remains [source 5].

questions.question: Which statement about what VACUUM does — and does not do — is correct?

options.label: VACUUM rewrites many small Parquet files into fewer larger ones and, as a side effect, tightens the per-file min/max statistics used for data skipping.
VACUUM permanently deletes data files that the transaction log no longer references and cannot be undone; the log itself is not truncated, so version metadata survives.
VACUUM removes obsolete commits from the `_delta_log` directory, which is why the number of entries returned by DESCRIBE HISTORY shrinks after a vacuum.
VACUUM must be run before time travel works, because time travel reads the vacuumed file set rather than the transaction log.

questions.analysis: Option B is the correct characterization: VACUUM is a storage-cleanup operation that physically removes data files no longer referenced by the current version and older than the retention threshold, and it is irreversible — the transaction log can tell you which files a version used, but it does not hold the file contents, so there is no rollback statement that brings them back [source 3]. Option A describes OPTIMIZE, not VACUUM: bin-packing into target-sized files and the improved min/max skipping that follows are OPTIMIZE behaviors, and VACUUM never rewrites data. Option C is wrong because the `_delta_log` is an ordered, immutable commit log; VACUUM does not edit it, so DESCRIBE HISTORY still lists the historical versions after a vacuum. (Old log entries can eventually be removed by checkpointing and the separate log retention setting, which is a different mechanism with a different default — roughly 30 days — from the 7-day deleted-file retention that VACUUM obeys.) Option D inverts the dependency: time travel is a read of the transaction log that reconstructs a past snapshot from the commits made before a given point in time, so VACUUM is never a prerequisite for time travel [source 5]. In fact VACUUM is the operation most likely to break time travel: as the source material states, deleting historical files in a Delta table limits your ability to time travel to specific versions [source 2]. A useful diagnostic split for the exam: if `DESCRIBE HISTORY` no longer shows a version, suspect log retention; if the version is listed but the read fails with FileNotFoundException, suspect VACUUM.

actions.text: Alright, time for a quick knowledge check on VACUUM and retention. Take your time with each question and answer it on your own — commit to a choice before you move on.
Once you submit, I'll walk you through everything that tripped you up and we'll clear up any traps together.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Sizing and Scheduling a Maintenance Runbook

elements.content: Problem 1

The Delta Lake table `events` in your lakehouse stores 90 days of clickstream data. `DESCRIBE DETAIL` reports sizeBytes = 1.2 TB and numFiles = 24,000, and the table is partitioned by event_date (one directory per calendar day). A continuous ingestion job appends about 13.3 GB per day, arriving as roughly 267 small files of about 50 MB each. Nightly dashboards filter on user_id (equality) and event_date (range). Your team's maintenance standard is a 256 MB target file size.

(a) After a full-table OPTIMIZE, how many files should remain, and what is the reduction factor?

(b) The runbook instead runs `OPTIMIZE events WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS`. How many bytes and how many files does that run rewrite, how many files does it produce, and what is the table's file count immediately after the commit?

(c) If the fixed per-file cost (directory listing, footer read, task scheduling, open/close) is c = 10 ms per file and the cluster runs 8 parallel tasks, how much wall-clock overhead is removed from a full scan by the full-table OPTIMIZE?
Hint: Divide bytes by the TARGET size, not by the current average file size; the window math is just a fraction of the table.

Worked solution
Step 1 - Validate the inputs. Average file size = 1.2 TB / 24,000 = 1,200,000 MB / 24,000 = 50 MB. The target is 256 MB, so the average file is about 5x smaller than it should be: this is the small-file problem that OPTIMIZE exists to fix.

Step 2 - (a) Full-table target file count. OPTIMIZE does not change the number of bytes; it repacks the same bytes into fewer, larger files. In binary units 1.2 TiB = 1,258,291 MiB, so

$$N_{target} = \frac{1{,}258{,}291\ \text{MiB}}{256\ \text{MiB}} \approx 4{,}915 \approx 4{,}900\ \text{files}.$$

(In decimal MB: 1,200,000 / 256 = 4,688. Either convention rounds to 'about 4,700-4,900' - always state which one you are using.)

Reduction factor = 24,000 / 4,900 = 4.9, i.e. roughly 5x fewer files holding exactly the same bytes.

Step 3 - (b) What the 7-day run actually rewrites. Daily arrival = 1.2 TB / 90 days = 13.3 GB/day, delivered as 24,000 / 90 = 267 files/day.

Window bytes = 7 x 13.3 GB = 93.3 GB. Window files = 7 x 267 = 1,869 files.

After compaction the window holds 93.3 GB = 95,539 MiB, so 95,539 / 256 = 373, about 370 files. Window reduction = 1,869 / 370 = 5.05.

The run touches 93.3 / 1,200 = 7.8% of the table, so the table's committed file count afterwards is

$$N_{after} = \underbrace{(24{,}000 - 1{,}869)}_{22{,}131\ \text{untouched files}} + 370 = 22{,}501\ \text{files}.$$

The 1,869 superseded files are only marked stale; they still occupy storage until VACUUM removes them.

Step 4 - (c) Per-file overhead removed. Model the fixed cost per file as c = 10 ms and spread the work over p = 8 parallel tasks.

Before: 24,000 x 10 ms = 240 s of aggregate work, so 240 / 8 = 30 s of wall clock.

After: 4,900 x 10 ms = 49 s of aggregate work, so 49 / 8 = 6.1 s of wall clock.

Saving on a full scan = 30 - 6.1 = 23.9 s, a 4.9x reduction - identical to the file-count ratio, because the overhead term is linear in the number of files.

Final answers: (a) about 4,900 files, a 4.9x reduction; (b) 93.3 GB and 1,869 files rewritten, about 370 files produced, 22,501 files in the table immediately after the commit; (c) about 24 s of fixed overhead removed per full scan, before counting data-skipping gains.

Analysis — Why the method works: query latency on a Delta table has a term proportional to the number of files (listing, task scheduling, per-file open and footer read) and a term proportional to the bytes actually read. OPTIMIZE attacks only the first term, which is why the byte count is deliberately unchanged. This matters because Delta's transaction log is the mechanism that turns object storage into a queryable table, and it advertises optimized metadata management for faster query performance [source 1]; the file count is therefore a first-class performance parameter, not a storage detail. During the rewrite, readers continue to see a consistent snapshot rather than a partially written table, because all changes are committed atomically through the log under optimistic concurrency control [source 3].

Common mistakes: (1) dividing 1.2 TB by the current 50 MB average instead of the 256 MB target - this produces 24,000 again and hides the entire point of the exercise; (2) believing the incremental 7-day run fixes the table, when it leaves 22,131 files in the old layout, so a one-time full-table OPTIMIZE is required for the backlog and incremental runs only maintain the recent window; (3) expecting OPTIMIZE to change query results or row counts - it does not, and SELECT COUNT(*) before and after must be identical; (4) mixing TB/TiB and MB/MiB, which shifts the answer by about 5%; (5) assuming the superseded bytes are freed, when physical storage only shrinks after VACUUM.

Generalization: target file count always scales as sizeBytes / targetSize, so doubling the target halves the file count and roughly halves the fixed-overhead term. You can reverse the formula to size a maintenance window: a run that rewrites B bytes costs roughly 2B of I/O (read plus write).
Problem 2

The same `events` table (1.2 TB, 4,900 files after a full compaction, partitioned by event_date with one directory per day) serves two workloads:

(i) an interactive point lookup: `SELECT ... WHERE user_id = 'u-84213' AND event_date >= '2024-06-01' AND event_date < '2024-06-08'`;

(ii) a monthly audit scan: `SELECT count(*) ... WHERE event_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'`.

The user_id column has about 2,000,000 distinct values. A colleague proposes `OPTIMIZE events ZORDER BY (event_date, user_id)`.

(a) Which columns belong in ZORDER BY, and why?

(b) Quantify the benefit of the correct choice for the point lookup, in files and bytes read.

(c) What guidance do you give on the number of ZORDER BY columns and on how often to re-run the clustering?
Hint: Ask what the partition column already does for free before spending a clustering dimension on it.

Worked solution
(a) Use ZORDER BY (user_id) only, inside an OPTIMIZE that is scoped to the data you want clustered:

OPTIMIZE events

WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS

ZORDER BY (user_id);

Reasoning: the table is partitioned by event_date, one directory per day, so every date predicate - in the lookup query, in the audit query, and in the OPTIMIZE WHERE clause itself - is already handled by partition pruning at the directory level, with perfect precision and no extra cost. Z-ORDER is the tool for selectivity that partitioning cannot provide, and that is exactly what user_id is: a high-cardinality column with 2,000,000 distinct values. Putting event_date into ZORDER BY buys no additional file skipping (inside any single date partition the column is constant, so it carries no ordering information), while it adds work and complexity to the rewrite. Remember that Z-ORDER is never a standalone statement; it is always part of an OPTIMIZE run.

(b) Benefit of the correct choice. With 4,900 compacted files and 2,000,000 distinct user_ids, if values are roughly uniform each file's min/max range for user_id covers about 2,000,000 / 4,900 = 408 distinct user_ids. A point lookup on a single user_id therefore maps into roughly one file:

$$\text{bytes read} \approx 1 \times 256\ \text{MB} = 0.25\ \text{GB} \quad \text{versus} \quad 1{,}200\ \text{GB for a full scan},$$

a factor of about 4,900 in bytes read. Without Z-ORDER, the per-file min/max ranges for user_id overlap heavily across all 4,900 files, so the engine cannot prove that any file is irrelevant and the plan degrades toward a full scan. The same logic applies inside each date partition: the lookup reads roughly one file per matched day instead of all of that day's files.

(c) Column count and re-run cadence. For F files, a d-dimensional Z-ORDER yields roughly F^(1/d) distinct ranges per column: 4,900 ranges for user_id when d = 1, about 4,900^(1/2) = 70 when d = 2, and about 4,900^(1/3) = 17 when d = 3. Every extra column divides the clustering budget, so a point lookup that touched one file can touch on the order of 70 files once a second column shares the budget - the diminishing-returns trap. Keep ZORDER BY to one or two, at most three, columns drawn from the most selective predicates. Clustering also decays: each ingestion micro-batch appends new, unclustered files, so the hot window must be re-clustered periodically - but no faster than the ingestion rate justifies, because a run that rewrites bytes whose layout is already correct produces no new skipping.

Analysis — Why the method works: partition pruning and Z-ORDER are complementary, not overlapping. Partitioning gives an exact, essentially free directory-level filter on the partition column; Z-ORDER uses min/max statistics inside the remaining files to skip files on non-partition predicates. Spending a clustering dimension on a partition column is therefore pure waste, which is why the professional rule is 'cluster the selective columns that partitioning cannot handle.' This is the practical consequence of the transaction log being an immutable record of what files exist and what statistics they carry, the mechanism that makes skipping and time travel possible in the same system [source 4].

Where students go wrong: (1) adding the partition column 'to be safe', which signals a missing mental model of pruning; (2) adding columns for every column that appears in a WHERE clause, ignoring the F^(1/d) dilution; (3) assuming Z-ORDER reorders the rows returned by a query - it does not, it only changes which files hold which values; (4) assuming ZORDER BY works without OPTIMIZE, when it is a clause of OPTIMIZE; (5) forgetting that the gain applies only to the files the run actually rewrote, so the rest of the table keeps its old layout until it is compacted.

Edge cases: if the table were partitioned by month but queried by day, date clustering inside partitions would be worth considering; if the workloads were dominated by range scans on a low-cardinality column, Z-ORDER on that column would have little to skip because min/max ranges would already be wide; and because readers work from a consistent snapshot while the rewrite commits atomically [source 3], the maintenance run does not disturb concurrent queries.
Problem 3

The `events` table is under a contractual audit SLA: any version of the table that existed at any time within the last 30 days must remain readable, and analysts routinely run `SELECT ... FROM events VERSION AS OF <n>` and `TIMESTAMP AS OF <ts>` against versions several weeks old. Delta's default VACUUM retention is 7 days.

(a) Write the VACUUM command that satisfies the SLA and convert the SLA into hours.

(b) Which command do you run first, and what does it do?

(c) Compute the steady-state volume of deletable garbage under 720-hour retention versus the 7-day default, given that the daily OPTIMIZE rewrites about 93 GB of the trailing 7-day window. State the assumption explicitly.

(d) Explain precisely why a too-short retention breaks time travel while current-version queries keep working.
Hint: Retention is set in hours; always validate an irreversible command with a dry run first.

Worked solution
(a) The SLA is 30 days x 24 h = 720 hours, so the production command is:

VACUUM events RETAIN 720 HOURS;

(b) Validate first with the dry run:

VACUUM events RETAIN 720 HOURS DRY RUN;

The dry run lists the files that would be deleted, with their paths and sizes, and deletes nothing. It is mandatory practice here because VACUUM is irreversible: a mistake cannot be undone by any Delta command.

(c) Steady-state garbage. Assumption: each daily OPTIMIZE rewrites the trailing 7-day window, so about 93 GB of data files per day stop being referenced by the current version and become deletion candidates.

With 720-hour retention the candidates accumulate for 30 days before removal:

$$V_{720} = 30 \times 93\ \text{GB} = 2{,}790\ \text{GB} \approx 2.8\ \text{TB},$$

which is more than twice the 1.2 TB of live data. With the 168-hour default:

$$V_{168} = 7 \times 93\ \text{GB} = 651\ \text{GB}.$$

The difference, 2,790 - 651 = 2,139 GB, about 2.1 TB, is the literal storage price of the audit SLA. Shortening retention is the wrong way to save it; the correct levers are a smaller target file size for the window you rewrite, a lower compaction frequency on cold data, and object-storage lifecycle policies on older partitions.

(d) Why time travel breaks but current reads do not. Delta reconstructs a historical state by reading the commits recorded in the transaction log up to that point and the data files those commits reference; the state at time T is recreated from the original table plus only the commits made prior to T [source 5]. VACUUM deletes data files that are no longer referenced by the current version and are older than the retention window, and deleting historical files limits the ability to time travel to specific versions [source 2]. A version 22 days old references files that later compactions superseded; once those files age past 7 days they are deleted, and the reconstruction fails because the files are simply gone. Current-version queries are unaffected because they read the current snapshot through the immutable log under ACID guarantees and optimistic concurrency control [source 3], which never references the deleted files. One more nuance: if VACUUM runs nightly at 02:00, a file becomes eligible exactly at age 720 h and is removed at the next run, so effective retention is 720-744 h; for a contractual SLA, set RETAIN 744 HOURS and buy one extra day of margin.

Analysis — Why the method works: retention is a promise about the oldest file Delta is allowed to forget, so it must be at least the time-travel requirement. The value 720 hours is exactly at the boundary, which is why production runbooks add a maintenance cycle of slack. Delta also refuses retention below 168 hours unless the interval check is disabled, so any 30-day setting is comfortably above the safety floor and needs no configuration change - but the default (168 hours) silently violates a 30-day SLA, which is the classic trap in this objective.

Common mistakes: (1) setting the retention in days or milliseconds instead of hours; (2) treating VACUUM as a performance tune-up rather than a destructive retention decision - OPTIMIZE never deletes files, it only makes them stale, and VACUUM is what actually frees storage; (3) assuming VACUUM disrupts current readers (it does not, because readers use a consistent snapshot from the log [source 3]); (4) assuming RESTORE can recover a vacuumed version (RESTORE is a new commit that changes current state, and it needs the very files that were deleted); (5) ignoring the second, independent bound: the transaction log's own retention must also cover the SLA window, or the versions disappear from history even though their data files still exist. A disciplined runbook therefore checks two knobs, always validates a retention change with DRY RUN, and keeps a scheduled test query that reads a version 29 days old.
Problem 4

Ingestion into `events` runs continuously in 15-minute micro-batches (about 13.3 GB/day, 267 new files/day). The constraints are: a 30-day time-travel SLA (VACUUM RETAIN 720 HOURS), dashboards that query the trailing 7 days filtered on user_id, and monthly audits that scan whole calendar months.

(a) Write the OPTIMIZE schedule and SQL, separating the goal of reducing the file count from the goal of maintaining Z-ORDER clustering.

(b) Write the VACUUM schedule and SQL.

(c) State the ordering and concurrency rules.

(d) Compute the monthly rewrite I/O for two candidate compaction plans and recommend one: (Plan A) one daily run over the trailing 7 days with Z-ORDER; (Plan B) a light daily compaction of one day plus a weekly Z-ORDER run over the trailing 7 days. Assume a run costs read + write of every byte it rewrites.
Hint: Two different goals - file count and clustering - do not need the same frequency; compare 30 x 186.6 GB with 30 x 26.6 GB + 4 x 186.6 GB.

Worked solution
(a) OPTIMIZE schedule. Split the two goals.

Goal 1 - keep file count near target for hot data: after each ingestion window closes, compact just the touched partitions, e.g. daily:

OPTIMIZE events WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 1 DAYS;

This rewrites only the day's ~13.3 GB of undersized files into about 13,300 / 256 = 52 files.

Goal 2 - keep Z-ORDER clustering on the query window: less often, on the trailing 7 days:

OPTIMIZE events WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS ZORDER BY (user_id);

Goal 3 - the cold backlog for the monthly audits: a month-scoped run outside peak hours, e.g.

OPTIMIZE events WHERE event_date >= '2024-05-01' AND event_date < '2024-06-01';

Run each of these only when DESCRIBE DETAIL shows the window is actually under target, i.e. when numFiles x 256 MB is comfortably greater than sizeBytes for that window.

(b) VACUUM schedule, in a separate job:

VACUUM events RETAIN 720 HOURS DRY RUN; -- on the day the retention is created or changed

VACUUM events RETAIN 720 HOURS; -- weekly, off-peak

The cadence is deliberately lower than OPTIMIZE: it only has to keep up with garbage accumulation, and lowering it costs nothing but storage.

(c) Ordering and concurrency rules. Ingest first, then OPTIMIZE (so the run sees the new files), then VACUUM at a lower frequency (so the files OPTIMIZE marked stale can age out). Never run OPTIMIZE and VACUUM concurrently on the same table: they operate on the same file set, and optionality is enforced by optimistic concurrency control, so one of them will fail with a concurrent-modification error rather than corrupting anything [source 3]. Keep VACUUM out of dashboard peak hours, because although it does not disturb readers it generates heavy storage-layer I/O.

(d) Cost model. Plan A: 30 runs x (93.3 GB read + 93.3 GB write) = 30 x 186.6 = 5,598 GB, about 5.6 TB/month.

Plan B: light daily compaction = 30 x (13.3 + 13.3) = 798 GB; weekly Z-ORDER over the window = 4 x (93.3 + 93.3) = 746 GB; total 798 + 746 = 1,544 GB, about 1.5 TB/month.

Ratio = 5,598 / 1,544 = 3.6, so Plan B reaches the same steady-state file count and clustering quality for roughly 3.6x less maintenance I/O.

Analysis — Why the method works: file-count control and clustering control have different natural frequencies. File count degrades at the ingestion rate - every micro-batch adds small files - so a cheap, frequent, narrowly scoped OPTIMIZE keeps it flat. Clustering degrades more slowly and is expensive to restore (it rewrites a whole window), so it is worth paying for only when enough new unclustered files have landed to matter. Separating the two is what turns a maintenance job from a nightly full rewrite into a targeted, incremental operation.

Common mistakes: (1) running OPTIMIZE too often on a window that is already at target and already clustered - it rewrites the same bytes to produce essentially the same layout, which is precisely how a 1.5 TB/month plan becomes a 5.6 TB/month plan; (2) running one giant unfiltered OPTIMIZE every night, which rewrites the historical partitions that never change; (3) scheduling VACUUM concurrently with OPTIMIZE and then 'fixing' the resulting concurrent-modification failures by retrying blindly - the correct fix is a dependency, not a retry; (4) running VACUUM immediately before the audit window and thereby racing the retention boundary; (5) forgetting that after a large backfill the one-time compaction is mandatory, because incremental runs only maintain the recent window.

Generalization: treat maintenance as a budget. File-count benefit is linear in the bytes rewritten and saturates quickly; clustering benefit saturates as F^(1/d) resolution and decays with new appends; garbage grows linearly with retention days. Any runbook should be justified by which of these three curves the run is moving, and by how much I/O it costs to move it.
Problem 5

Six weeks after deploying a maintenance runbook, an audit query fails:

SELECT count(*) FROM events VERSION AS OF 412;

Version 412 was committed 22 days ago. The current-version query `SELECT count(*) FROM events` works normally, and `DESCRIBE HISTORY events` still lists version 412. The maintenance job runs `VACUUM events RETAIN 168 HOURS` every night at 23:00, and OPTIMIZE runs nightly over the trailing 7-day window.

(a) Explain, using the file lifecycle, exactly what happened and when.

(b) Compute the correct retention and state what must change.

(c) Can the deleted data be recovered?

(d) What single check would have caught this before the incident, and what ongoing check prevents a recurrence?
Hint: The log remembers the version; the storage may have forgotten the files. Work out at which day the superseded files crossed the 7-day age boundary.

Worked solution
(a) Timeline. Version 412 was committed at day -22. Around day -20 an OPTIMIZE run in that window rewrote its files, so the original files stopped being referenced by the current version - they became stale but still existed. VACUUM removes files that are not referenced by the current version and are older than the retention window, so those files became eligible at day -13 (7 days after they were superseded) and were deleted by the next nightly run at 23:00 that day. The query at day -22 therefore tries to reconstruct a state whose files no longer exist. The failure is deterministic, not random: nightly OPTIMIZE orphans files, and 168-hour retention guarantees that anything orphaned more than a week ago is gone.

(b) Correct retention. The audit requirement is 30 days, i.e. 30 x 24 = 720 hours, so the job must use:

VACUUM events RETAIN 720 HOURS;

(or 744 HOURS to absorb the one-day scheduling skew between eligibility and the next run). The value 168 in the job definition is the default and silently encodes a 7-day guarantee, which is 23 days short of the contract.

(c) Recovery. No. VACUUM is irreversible - the deleted files are unrecoverable through Delta. RESTORE cannot help either, because RESTORE is a new commit that rewrites current state and requires the referenced files to exist; it cannot conjure files that were deleted. Recovery would require re-ingesting the source data or restoring from an independent backup copy taken outside Delta.

(d) Prevention. Before the incident, the single check is the dry run:

VACUUM events RETAIN 720 HOURS DRY RUN;

which lists the candidate files and their sizes without deleting anything, so the operator can confirm that nothing needed for the last 30 days is in the candidate set. For recurrence, add what a dry run cannot give you - a scheduled canary query that reads a version about 29 days old, and a configuration test asserting that the job's RETAIN value is 720 or greater. Together these detect both a wrong setting and a silent change to it.

Analysis — Why the method works: this incident is entirely about the difference between metadata and data. The transaction log is an ordered, immutable record of every commit, which is what enables version history and time travel [source 4]; that is why DESCRIBE HISTORY still lists version 412 and why current-version reads succeed. But reconstructing an old state requires the data files that the commits up to that point reference [source 5], and VACUUM's job is to delete files that the current version no longer references and that are older than the retention window - the documented consequence being that deleting historical files limits time travel to specific versions [source 2]. Metadata outliving data is the whole failure mode.

Common mistakes: (1) reading DESCRIBE HISTORY as proof that a version is queriesable, when history proves only that the commit was recorded; (2) assuming the problem is random or that retrying will help; (3) assuming VACUUM is safe because readers are not affected - true for current-version queries, irrelevant to time travel; (4) setting retention in the wrong unit, or copying the 168-hour default without converting it into a date range; (5) turning off the interval check to set a shorter retention, which removes the one guard rail that exists; (6) forgetting that retention is measured from now and from file age, so shortening it takes effect immediately on already-old files rather than gradually.

Generalization: whenever a system separates a logical history from the physical bytes that back it, retention policy is a correctness control, not a housekeeping setting. The safe pattern is: derive the number from the SLA (30 days to 720 hours), validate destructively-scoped commands with a dry run, keep a canary that exercises the oldest allowed version, and treat any change to the retention constant as a change to a contractual guarantee.

actions.text: Now we put the whole maintenance toolbox to work. On this page we work five quantitative problems end to end: OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER, VACUUM retention, scheduling, and a recovery incident. Problem 1 gives us the starting picture — an events table of 1.2 TB sitting in 24,000 files, so about 50 MB each, partitioned by event_date, and queried with filters on user_id and event_date. Our two goals are 30 days of time travel and faster selective reads. The first move is to size the compaction: divide total bytes by the target file size, not by the current average. 1.2 TB divided by 256 MB gives roughly 4,900 files, so OPTIMIZE should cut file count by about five times and shrink per-file overhead proportionally.

Problem 2 asks which clustering to choose. The answer is OPTIMIZE events WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS, with ZORDER BY on user_id. That one line does two jobs: event_date is already the partition column, so the WHERE clause gives us partition pruning and keeps us from rewriting the entire table, while Z-ORDER on the high-cardinality user_id lays related rows into the same files for data skipping. The hint here is the exam trap — ask what the partition column already does for you. Re-clustering on the same column you partitioned by duplicates effort and buys nothing.

Problem 3 is the one that fails audits. The contractual SLA is 30 days of time travel, and the default VACUUM retention is only 7 days, so leaving the default silently destroys the very history the contract requires. Convert the SLA into hours first: 30 days times 24 hours is 720 hours. Then run VACUUM events RETAIN 720 HOURS DRY RUN to validate before you delete anything, and only then run it for real.

Problem 4 moves from statements to scheduling. Ingestion runs continuously in 15-minute windows, and we have two different goals: controlling file count and controlling how the data is clustered. So we split the maintenance. Compaction runs after each ingestion window on recent partitions, because that is when small files appear; VACUUM runs on a separate, much less frequent schedule, because retention only needs to satisfy the time-travel window, not the ingestion cadence. Running OPTIMIZE far too often just burns compute on files that were already compacted.

Problem 5 is the incident: six weeks after deploying a runbook, data that should be recoverable is gone. The key idea in the analysis is that the log remembers the version, but the storage may no longer hold the files — RETAIN is a property of VACUUM, not of the transaction log. So build the timeline from version 412 onwards and check what VACUUM actually deleted. That completes this worked problem set. The traps worth memorizing for the exam are exactly these three: over-partitioning plus Z-ORDER on the same column duplicates effort, too-frequent OPTIMIZE wastes compute, and the default 7-day retention quietly breaks a 30-day audit requirement.

scenes.title: Summary: Maintenance Roles, Order of Operations, and Exam Traps

elements.content: Maintenance & Exam Traps
OPTIMIZE — compacts small files toward ~256 MB each.
Z-ORDER BY — clusters rows for data skipping.
VACUUM — deletes stale files; default retention is 7 days [source 2].
Order — OPTIMIZE + ZORDER BY, then VACUUM.
Example — 12,000 files → 240; 180 GB stays; 15 → 768 MB per file.
Trap 1 — no sorting; results never change.
Trap 2 — Z-ORDER stops near four columns; never replaces partitioning.
Trap 3 — VACUUM is irreversible; it breaks time travel [source 5].
Log actions keep versions valid until VACUUM [source 3].

actions.text: Let's pull the whole maintenance story together. Three operations, one recommended order, and three traps the exam loves to test.
First, the three roles. OPTIMIZE compacts small files toward roughly 256 MB each, so reads stop paying the per-file overhead tax.
Z-ORDER BY is separate — it rewrites the layout so related rows land in the same files, which is what makes data skipping effective at query time.
And VACUUM cleans up stale files that are no longer referenced, defaulting to a 7-day retention window.
The order matters. After ingestion, run OPTIMIZE together with ZORDER BY on recent partitions first, then run VACUUM on its own, less frequent schedule with a safe retention window.

Here's a concrete example: twelve thousand files compacted down to two hundred and forty, the underlying data size unchanged at 180 gigabytes, and the file count in the log dropping from fifteen to seven.
Now the traps. Trap one: OPTIMIZE does not sort, merge, or deduplicate rows, and it never changes your query results — it only changes how efficiently they're produced.
Trap two: Z-ORDER is bounded. It stops being effective past roughly four columns, has diminishing returns, and never replaces partitioning.
Trap three: VACUUM is irreversible. It defaults to 7 days, and deleting files that time travel or concurrent readers still need is exactly what causes FileNotFound failures.

Finally, the unit link: every one of these operations commits add and remove file actions to the transaction log, so versioning and time travel stay consistent right up until VACUUM physically removes the underlying files.
Solid work on this unit. Keep these three roles, the order of operations, and the three traps straight, and you've locked in one of the most heavily tested clusters on the exam.

scenes.title: Prior-Knowledge Check: SQL and DataFrame Vocabulary

questions.question: A junior engineer reads a Spark pipeline that ingests three JSON sources into DataFrames, joins them into a single table, and then runs a SQL statement to filter the results before writing them out. Which statement correctly maps the SQL keywords SELECT, FROM, and WHERE to the equivalent DataFrame operations?

options.label: A. SELECT chooses which columns appear in the result; FROM identifies the DataFrame or table being read; WHERE restricts which rows survive into the result.
B. SELECT restricts which rows survive; FROM restricts which columns appear; WHERE identifies the DataFrame or table being read.
C. SELECT names the source DataFrame; FROM chooses the columns; WHERE sorts the output rows.
D. SELECT, FROM, and WHERE are interchangeable in Spark and always produce the same execution plan regardless of how they are ordered.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: Option A is correct because the three SQL keywords map onto three genuinely different jobs: SELECT is a column projection (which fields come back), FROM is the row source (which DataFrame or table is read), and WHERE is a row filter (which rows are kept). The source material shows exactly this shape of pipeline, where a Spark job ingests sources into a dataframe, combines them into a single table, and then 'filters the results with a SQL statement' before writing out [source p.346]. Option B swaps projection and filtering, which is the most common mix-up; option C confuses FROM with the projection and invents sorting, which is not what WHERE does. Option D is wrong because the clauses are not interchangeable — although a query optimizer may reorder operations internally, the declared semantics of each clause are fixed. The distinction also matters for cost: because columnar serialization lets an engine 'scan only the columns required for a particular query, sometimes dramatically reducing the amount of data read from the disk' [source p.239], a wrong mental model of SELECT as a row filter leads engineers to expect savings that never appear. Note the edge case: WHERE cannot filter on an aggregate such as SUM(amount) — that requires HAVING — while SELECT may legally contain expressions, aliases, and aggregates.

questions.question: In the pipeline described in the source material, a scheduler triggers a Spark job, Spark builds a DAG of steps from the code written for ingesting, joining, and writing out the data, and the results are finally written to a Parquet-formatted Delta Lake table. Which of the following operations is a transformation rather than an action?

options.label: A. Applying filter() to a DataFrame to keep only the rows that satisfy a condition.
B. Calling count() to return the number of rows in a DataFrame.
C. Calling collect() to bring every row of the result back to the driver program.
D. Writing the final result set out to a Parquet-formatted Delta Lake table.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: Option A is correct: filter() is a transformation because it only describes a new logical DataFrame derived from an existing one — it is recorded as a step in the plan and does not touch the data until something forces execution. The source material describes Spark building 'a DAG of steps based on the code that we write for ingesting, joining, and writing out the data', which is precisely the graph of transformations that is assembled before any work is done [source p.346]. Options B, C, and D are actions: count() must read the data to return a number, collect() must move every row to the driver, and writing out to a Parquet-formatted Delta Lake table is the terminal step that materializes the result [source p.346]. Two edge cases are worth holding onto. First, an action inside a loop can turn what looks like a small job into repeated full scans, so the practical cost of an action is not the same as the cost of a transformation. Second, a transformation is not tied to a single processing mode: you can transform data in batch or while streaming in flight, and 'we treat transformation as a standalone area of the data engineering lifecycle' even though it is often entangled with ingestion and with source systems [source p.69]. The exam expects candidates to recognize that laziness is the defining property of a transformation, not the size of its output.

questions.question: A source team announces that a new column has been added to one of the JSON feeds that your pipeline ingests. According to the definition used in the source material, what does the schema of that payload describe?

options.label: A. The fields present in the data and the data type of each field, including whether a field may be null.
B. The physical byte offset at which each record begins inside the object store.
C. The number of rows currently stored in the table along with its storage size in bytes.
D. The list of dashboards and downstream applications that consume the data.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: Option A is correct because the source material defines a schema as something that 'describes the fields and types of data within those fields' [source p.268]. In a DataFrame context this means column names, the data type of each column (for example string, integer, timestamp, or a nested struct), and whether nulls are permitted — so adding a column is a schema change, not merely a new value. Option B describes physical storage layout, which an engine may use internally but which is not the schema. Option C describes table statistics, which are metadata about the data's volume rather than its structure. Option D describes lineage and consumption, which the schema says nothing about. The new-column scenario is exactly the one the source material flags as a design question: 'If schema changes (say, a new column is added), how is this dealt with and communicated to downstream stakeholders?' [source p.63]. An important edge case is that not every payload has an explicit schema — unstructured text, images, and audio have no schema or data types at all, although they may ship with technical file descriptions such as shape, data and file format, encoding, and size [source p.268]. A second edge case is nesting: when JSON is converted into a relational format, a column may itself hold a nested structure, so the schema must describe inner fields as well, as happens in the ingestion step shown in the reference pipeline [source p.346]. Finally, remember that the connection to a source is usually easy — the hard engineering problem is understanding the underlying schema and its update patterns [source p.268].

actions.text: Before we open up the next lesson, let's take a quick prior-knowledge check — three single-choice items on SQL and DataFrame vocabulary. This one is purely diagnostic: it isn't graded, and it's here to show both of us where your foundations are already solid and where we might want to slow down. You'll see the questions worded the way the certification exam words them, so treat it as a rehearsal of the exam's phrasing as much as a check of the concepts.

Go ahead and work through each one on your own — no notes needed, just answer with your best current understanding. Once you submit, I'll join you to walk through anything that tripped you up and we'll carry those gaps straight into the lesson ahead.

scenes.title: Spark SQL, DataFrames, and the Databricks Execution Model

elements.content: Spark SQL, DataFrames, and the Databricks Execution Model
The SparkSession is Spark's only entry point.
A DataFrame is immutable, lazy and distributed.
The driver builds a DAG of steps [source p.346].
SQL and DataFrames compile to one Catalyst plan.
Storage clusters parallelize reads [source p.221].
display() renders; collect() pulls rows to the driver.
Worked example: 1 billion rows ÷ 8 partitions = 125 million rows per task.
Spark scans partitions in parallel, with no row locks [source p.305].

actions.text: Now that we've warmed up on the SQL and DataFrame vocabulary, let's build the mental model that everything else in this unit rests on: Spark SQL, DataFrames, and the Databricks execution model. If you understand this page, the rest of the Spark material will feel like variations on one theme.

First, the entry point. The SparkSession is Spark's only entry point. In a Databricks notebook it is already created for you as the variable `spark`, so you never have to build one yourself. Everything you do hangs off it: `spark.read` to load data, `spark.sql` to run SQL, `spark.table` to reference a table. One session, one doorway — remember that phrasing, because the exam likes to test it.

Next, the DataFrame itself. A DataFrame is an immutable, lazily evaluated, distributed table with a named schema. Three properties to hold onto. Immutable means you never change a DataFrame in place — a transformation returns a new one. Lazy means transformations only describe work; nothing actually runs until an action is called. And distributed means the rows live across many machines, not on your notebook's driver.

Here's the execution flow in one picture. The notebook submits your code to the SparkSession, which hands it to the driver. The driver builds the logical plan, Catalyst rewrites and optimizes it into a physical plan, and finally the driver breaks that plan into tasks that run across executor nodes over partitions of data. Follow this left-to-right path — notebook, session, logical plan, Catalyst, physical plan, tasks on executors — and you have the whole execution model.

This is the point that surprises people: Spark SQL and the PySpark DataFrame API compile to the same Catalyst-optimized plan. Write `spark.sql` or chain `.filter().groupBy()` — by the time it reaches the engine it is one plan. Same optimization, same result. The two are just different syntaxes over one engine, so choose whichever is clearer for the task at hand.

Then there's the practical trap around results. `display()` renders the result inside the notebook, and Databricks caps it — it will not drag a billion rows to your screen. `collect()` pulls every row back to the driver. On a large table, `collect()` can exhaust the driver's memory and crash your notebook. Use `display()` to inspect, and be careful with `collect()` in production code.

The reason none of this is slow by default is parallelism: Spark scans partitions in parallel, with no row-level locking anywhere. Each task owns its own partition, so there is nothing to contend over — which is also why Spark scales so well horizontally.

The worked example makes the arithmetic concrete: one billion rows divided across eight partitions gives roughly 125 million rows per partition. Each partition becomes a task, and tasks run concurrently on executors. When you later tune performance, this is exactly the number — rows per partition — you will be trying to bring down.

To sum up this page: one entry point, the SparkSession; one data abstraction, an immutable, lazy, distributed DataFrame; one optimizer, Catalyst, shared by SQL and DataFrames alike; and one execution pattern, driver builds the plan, executors run tasks over partitions. Hold onto that model, and let's move on to actually reading data into a DataFrame and inspecting its schema.

scenes.title: Reading Data into a DataFrame and Inspecting the Schema

elements.content: Read, Then Inspect the Schema
• Read, then inspect before transforming [source p.69].
• File reads: chain the reader once — spark.read.format('csv').option('header', True).load(path) [source p.383]
• Tables: spark.table() returns a Delta table with known schema and statistics [source p.346]
• Inspect: printSchema(), dtypes, columns, display().
• Example: a 2.4 GB CSV: 2 scans vs 1 with a schema.

actions.text: Now that we have the execution model in mind — driver, executors, tasks over partitions — let's put it to work on the very first habit of any Spark job: read the data, then inspect the schema. This page is about doing that in the right order, before you write a single transformation. Skip this step and you will be debugging type errors later instead of catching them now.

The rule on the slide is deliberately blunt: read, then inspect before transforming. The read gets bytes into a DataFrame; the inspection tells you what you actually got. Never chain a transformation onto a read you have not verified — especially not on data someone else dropped into a landing zone.

For file reads, chain the reader exactly once: spark.read, then .format with csv, json or parquet, then .option for header, then .schema if you have one, then .load with the path. Two exam traps live right here. First, for CSV, Spark does not read the header and does not infer types unless you explicitly set header to True and inferSchema to True. Second, inferSchema is not free — it costs an extra pass over the data, so a declared schema is always preferred in production.

That is exactly what the example on the slide quantifies: a 2.4 gigabyte CSV costs two scans when you let Spark infer the schema, and only one scan when you declare it yourself. Remember that trade when an exam question asks why a read got slower after someone removed the schema.

Table reads are cheaper to reason about. Calling spark.table on a three-part catalog dot schema dot table name returns a Delta table whose schema and statistics are already known, so no inference pass is needed at all. You get the same DataFrame interface, with zero guessing about types.

Then inspect — and this table is the one to memorize, because it maps each method to what it returns and when to use it. printSchema gives you the tree of names and types. dtypes gives the list of name-and-type pairs. columns gives just the names. count triggers an actual job and returns the row count. describe or summary returns count, mean, min and max per numeric column. And display of df dot limit ten renders real rows so you can eyeball the data before you trust it. Expect the exam to test precisely that method-to-purpose mapping.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Reading Data and Schema Inspection

questions.question: A teammate's notebook runs exactly this statement against a CSV file: df = spark.read.format("csv").option("header", True).load("/Volumes/retail/raw/orders.csv"). The source file stores total_amount values such as 149.99, but after the read the column arrives as the string "149.99" instead of a numeric type. What is the most likely cause, and what is the minimal correct fix?

options.label: Schema inference is disabled by default, so every CSV column is typed as string; add .option("inferSchema", True) before .load(...), or supply an explicit .schema(...) instead.
Header handling is disabled by default, so the first row was consumed as data and every column fell back to string; add .option("header", True).
CSV carries no embedded type information, so no reader option can ever produce typed columns; the values must be cast after the read with a withColumn(...) call.
Only Parquet and Delta sources can return typed columns, so the CSV must first be converted to Parquet and then re-read with format("parquet").

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: The reader's defaults are the trap. spark.read.format("csv") applies header = false AND inferSchema = false unless you explicitly override them; the teammate overrode only header, so the file was parsed with every column typed as string, which is exactly the reported symptom. Fixing it means adding .option("inferSchema", True), or better, passing an explicit .schema(...) so the types do not depend on a scan of the data. Option B is wrong on two counts: header is already set to True in the snippet, and a header problem would surface as a column named "_c0" with the header line as a data row, not as a numeric column that is merely string-typed. Option C overstates the case: CSV has no embedded types, which is precisely why a schema must be declared or inferred, and both options exist, so the claim that no reader option can help is false. Option D is a category error: typed reads are a function of the schema you supply or infer, not of the file format, and the source material notes that CSV is one of the everyday source-system file formats that arrives structured or semistructured and merely needs its fields and types made explicit [source p.183]. Underlying all of this is the definition of a schema: it describes the fields and the types of data within those fields, so with no schema declaration and no inference, Spark has no basis for choosing double over string [source p.268]. One more exam-relevant detail: the reader must be chained, because .load(...) is what triggers the read; options placed after .load(...) are silently ignored, and calling .load(...) twice builds two separate reads.

questions.question:
After ingesting a nested JSON API payload, the notebook prints the following output:
root
 |-- order_id: long (nullable = true)
 |-- customer: struct (nullable = true)
 |    |-- id: string (nullable = true)
 |    |-- loyalty_tier: string (nullable = true)
 |-- items: array (nullable = true)
 |    |-- element: struct (nullable = true)
 |    |    |-- sku: string (nullable = true)
 |    |    |-- qty: integer (nullable = true)

Which two statements about this DataFrame are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: order_id is a top-level field, so df.select("order_id") resolves it without any qualification.
loyalty_tier is also effectively a top-level field, so df.select("loyalty_tier") returns it directly.
items is an array whose elements are structs, so sku and qty can only be reached by exploding the array or indexing a single element and then addressing the fields inside it.
Because customer is marked nullable = true, every row is guaranteed to contain a non-null customer struct.

questions.correctAnswer: A,C
questions.analysis: A schema describes the fields and the types of data within those fields, and printSchema() renders one line per field with its type and nullability, indenting nested fields beneath their parent [source p.268]. Because of that indentation rule, order_id sits at depth one and can be selected by name (A is correct), while loyalty_tier sits at depth two inside the customer struct and must be addressed as customer.loyalty_tier (B is wrong; df.select("loyalty_tier") fails with an unresolved-column analysis error, and the idiomatic form is df.select("customer.loyalty_tier") or col("customer.loyalty_tier")). Option C is correct and is the single most common nested-data task in exams and in production: an array of structs is one column whose every row holds an ordered collection of records, so you either explode the array to one row per element and then select element-level fields, or you index a specific position (for example items[0].sku) when only the first element matters. Option D inverts the meaning of nullability: nullable = true means the type permits nulls, so the struct may be missing on some rows, and code that dereferences customer.id must tolerate that; nullable = false would be the guarantee D describes. This nesting is not accidental — real ingest pipelines frequently convert raw JSON into a relational shape with nesting retained in certain columns, which is exactly why the schema, not the file, is the contract you code against [source p.346]. It also explains why the course emphasizes modern SQL semantics for JSON parsing and nested data alongside DataFrame operators: the two compile to the same plan and both must respect the same nested field paths [source p.47].
