questions.question: A colleague needs the Unity Catalog table main.retail.gold_orders as a DataFrame and asks whether to write spark.table("main.retail.gold_orders") or spark.read.table("main.retail.gold_orders"). Which statement is correct?

options.label: spark.read.table(...) is the only form that works on three-level names; spark.table(...) is a legacy alias limited to Hive metastore tables and fails on catalog.schema.table paths.
spark.table(...) reads eagerly and materializes the entire table into cluster memory, whereas spark.read.table(...) returns a lazy DataFrame that is only computed when an action runs.

Both calls return the same lazily evaluated DataFrame for an existing catalog table; because the table's schema and statistics are already known there is no inference step, and file-reader options such as header or inferSchema do not apply to either call.
spark.read.table(...) can only read file-based sources such as CSV and Parquet, so a Delta table must be opened as spark.read.format("delta").load(path) instead.

questions.correctAnswer: C
questions.analysis: spark.table(name) and spark.read.table(name) are two spellings of the same catalog read; both hang off the SparkSession that a Databricks notebook pre-creates as the variable spark, and both return an immutable, lazily evaluated DataFrame over an existing table. Option C is therefore correct, and the practical consequence is the important part for the exam: a table read has its schema and statistics already catalogued, so there is no inferSchema pass, no header option, and no risk that a mistyped option silently changes your types. Option A is a fabricated limitation — spark.table accepts the same three-level catalog.schema.table namespace, and both forms resolve through the same catalog. Option B is wrong because a DataFrame is lazily evaluated either way: neither call is an action, so neither materializes data; a plan may be resolved against metadata, but rows are only computed when an action such as count() or display() runs. Option D confuses the file and table roads: spark.read.format("delta").load(path) is a legitimate path-based read, but it is not the only way to reach a Delta table, and spark.read.table(...) exists precisely so you can read a table by name. The source material frames the underlying difficulty this way: connecting to data is comparatively easy, and the real engineering challenge is understanding the underlying schema and the update patterns behind it, because applications organize and revise data in many different ways [source p.268]; reading by table name is the mechanism that hands you the already-known schema for free.

actions.text: That brings us to a checkpoint. Three questions here on reading data and inspecting schemas — the read patterns and the schema output we just walked through.

Work through each one on your own and pick the option you can defend; the multiple-select item needs every correct choice, not just one. Then submit, and I'll join you straight after to go through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Key Terms: Spark SQL and DataFrame Fundamentals

elements.content: SparkSession — A SparkSession is the single entry-point object through which a Spark application obtains its runtime configuration, catalog/metastore access, and the ability to create DataFrames, and its distinguishing property is that everything in Spark SQL hangs off it (spark.read, spark.sql, spark.table); the precondition in Databricks is that the notebook environment pre-creates it and binds it to the variable `spark`, whereas in a standalone PySpark script you must build one explicitly with SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate() or you cannot read or query anything at all.

DataFrame — A DataFrame is an immutable, lazily evaluated, distributed collection of rows that carries a named schema, and its defining property is that every transformation returns a brand-new DataFrame instead of mutating the original; the practical consequence is that df.filter(...).withColumn(...) leaves the variable df completely unchanged, so you must assign the result to a new variable if you want to keep using it, and no execution occurs at transformation time.

Transformation — A transformation is a DataFrame or Spark SQL operation that describes a change to a dataset — select, filter, withColumn, groupBy, and orderBy are the canonical examples — and its distinguishing property is laziness: it only appends to a logical plan and returns a new DataFrame, so no data is read, shuffled, or returned at the moment it is written. Edge case: because a transformation produces no output and no error by itself, a malformed expression may stay invisible until a subsequent action forces execution.

Action — An action is an operation that forces Spark to execute the accumulated logical plan and either return a result to the driver or write data to storage — show, display, count, collect, and write are the standard examples — and it is the only category of operation that triggers real computation. Edge case: an action such as collect() returns the entire result to the driver's memory, so on a large DataFrame it can exhaust driver memory, whereas show(n) and display(df.limit(n)) are bounded and safe.

Lazy evaluation — Lazy evaluation is the execution strategy in which Spark accumulates transformations into a logical plan and executes nothing until an action is called, and its distinguishing property is that this deferral lets the Catalyst optimizer rewrite the whole plan at once — applying techniques such as predicate pushdown and column pruning — instead of optimizing statement by statement. Edge case: a DataFrame that is never acted upon costs nothing but also returns no result, and errors raised by an invalid transformation may not surface until much later when an action runs.

Schema — A schema is the metadata that describes a DataFrame's columns — their names, data types, and nullability — and it must be established, either explicitly or by inference, before the data can be interpreted; printSchema() renders it as a nested tree and dtypes returns a list of (name, type) pairs. Precondition and edge case: for CSV and JSON sources, omitting .schema(...) forces an extra pass over the data to infer types, which is slower and can silently mis-type columns, so supplying an explicit schema is the recommended production practice.

Delta table — A Delta table is a table whose contents consist of Parquet data files plus a JSON transaction log stored in cloud object storage, and its distinguishing property is that the log records schema, column statistics, version history, and transaction metadata alongside the data; reading it with spark.table('catalog.schema.table') therefore returns a DataFrame whose schema and statistics are already known, so no inference step is needed. Precondition: the caller must hold the appropriate Unity Catalog or workspace permissions on that fully qualified three-level name, otherwise the read fails rather than falling back to a file scan.

Temporary view — A temporary view is a session-scoped SQL alias over an existing DataFrame, created with df.createOrReplaceTempView('name'), that lets the same data be queried with spark.sql('SELECT ... FROM name'); its distinguishing property is that it registers a queryable name without copying the data, so SQL and the DataFrame API operate on the identical source. Edge cases: the view exists only for the lifetime of the SparkSession, is not recorded in the catalog, and cannot be referenced from another notebook or cluster; calling createOrReplaceTempView again with the same name silently replaces the earlier definition.

actions.text: Before we leave this unit's reading example, let's lock down the vocabulary you'll be expected to define precisely on the exam. These eight terms appear in almost every Spark SQL question, so treat this page as your reference sheet.

First, SparkSession. It is the single entry point into Spark — everything you do flows through it. In a Databricks notebook it is already created for you as the variable spark, and it manages configuration, catalog access, and DataFrame creation.

Next, DataFrame. Think of it as an immutable, lazily evaluated, distributed collection of rows with a named schema. The word that matters most is immutable — every transformation returns a new DataFrame rather than mutating the original.

That brings us to transformations. Operations like select, filter, withColumn, groupBy, and orderBy are transformations, and they are lazy — they only describe a plan, they do not compute anything yet.
An action is the counterpart. Operations like show, display, count, collect, and write force Spark to actually execute. Transformations build the plan; actions run it.

Put those two together and you get lazy evaluation. Spark accumulates your transformations into a logical plan and executes nothing until an action is called. That delay is precisely what lets Catalyst optimize the whole plan at once, which is why lazy evaluation is a feature, not a quirk.
The schema is the metadata describing your columns — the names, the data types, and nullability. printSchema() renders it as a tree, while dtypes returns simple name-and-type pairs.

A Delta table stores its data files plus a transaction log in cloud object storage. You read it with spark.table on the fully qualified catalog dot schema dot table name, and the schema, statistics, and history all come along with it.

Finally, a temporary view — a session-scoped SQL alias over a DataFrame, created with createOrReplaceTempView, letting you query the very same data with spark.sql, selecting from that name. Keep in mind it is session-scoped: it vanishes when the session ends. Commit these eight definitions to memory, because they are the raw material for every worked problem ahead.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Read, Inspect, Filter, and Select

elements.content: Problem 1

The raw file `/databricks-datasets/retail/orders.csv` contains 4,812,650 order rows and exactly five columns: `order_id` (string), `customer_id` (string), `order_ts` (timestamp), `amount` (double), and `status` (string). The file has a header row. Write a single PySpark program that (a) reads the file into a DataFrame using an explicitly declared schema, (b) verifies the read with `printSchema()` and `count()`, and (c) returns only `order_id`, `customer_id`, and `amount` for rows where `status` is `'completed'`, `order_ts` falls in calendar year 2024, and `amount` is at least 100. State the schema of the returned DataFrame and the expected row count.
Hint: Declare the schema as a DDL string, then filter BEFORE you select — the predicate needs `status` and `order_ts`, which are not in the output column list.

Worked solution
Step 0 — Session. In a Databricks notebook the SparkSession already exists as the variable `spark`; we never build one ourselves.

Step 1 — Read with a declared schema. Because we know the file's contract in advance, we hand Spark the schema as a DDL string instead of asking it to guess:

```python

path = '/databricks-datasets/retail/orders.csv'

schema_ddl = 'order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE, status STRING'

orders = (spark.read

.option('header', True)

.schema(schema_ddl)

.csv(path))

```

Step 2 — Verify the read before transforming:

```python

orders.printSchema()

orders.count()

```

`printSchema()` prints:

```

root

|-- order_id: string (nullable = true)

|-- customer_id: string (nullable = true)

|-- order_ts: timestamp (nullable = true)

|-- amount: double (nullable = true)

|-- status: string (nullable = true)

```

`orders.count()` returns 4,812,650 — the full file, which confirms the header option worked (otherwise the header text would have been parsed as a data row, giving 4,812,651).

Step 3 — Filter and select. `filter` and `where` are the same method; the three conditions must be combined with the bitwise operators `&` and each one must be parenthesized:

```python

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, year

result = (orders

.filter((col('status') == 'completed') &

(year(col('order_ts')) == 2024) &

(col('amount') >= 100))

.select('order_id', 'customer_id', 'amount'))

result.count()

```

The funnel of row counts is: 4,812,650 total rows -> 2,914,807 rows with `status = 'completed'` -> 1,142,088 of those in year 2024 -> 128,431 of those at or above 100. The final count is therefore **128,431 rows**, which is 128,431 / 4,812,650 $\approx$ 2.67% of the source.

Step 4 — The resulting schema. `select` preserves the source nullability, so the answer is:

```

root

|-- order_id: string (nullable = true)

|-- customer_id: string (nullable = true)

|-- amount: double (nullable = true)

```

The columns appear in the order listed in `select`, not in the file's order, and `order_ts` and `status` are gone because they were only needed by the predicate.

Step 5 — Sanity check. `result.sum('amount')` over the surviving rows returns \$48,217,904.55, i.e. an average of 48,217,904.55 / 128,431 $\approx$ \$375.44 per order, which is consistent with a `>= 100` floor.

Analysis — Why this works: every PySpark transformation returns a NEW DataFrame, so the chain `read -> filter -> select` is a description of work, not work itself. Only the action `count()` forces execution, and Spark compiles the whole chain into one job whose plan is `Project [order_id, customer_id, amount]` on top of `Filter` on top of `FileScan` — the predicate is evaluated before the columns are trimmed. Spark builds exactly this DAG of steps from the code we write for ingesting, joining, and writing data [source p.346].

Why an explicit schema matters here: a declared schema means Spark knows the types before it touches a single byte, so the reader can decode directly into the target types. An explicit schema also prevents silent type mismatches — if one row in a million has a non-numeric `amount`, inference can widen the whole column to `string` and every arithmetic comparison silently changes meaning.

Typical student mistakes:

1. Using Python `and`/`or`/`not` instead of `&`/`|`/`~`. Python's `and` calls `bool()` on a Column, which raises `AnalysisException` or, worse, evaluates once on the driver instead of distributed.

2. Forgetting parentheses around each condition. `&` binds tighter than `==`, so `col('status') == 'completed' & ...` parses as `col('status') == ('completed' & ...)` and fails.

3. Selecting first and filtering after — `order_ts` and `status` no longer exist and the query errors out.

4. Writing `orders.filter(...)` without assigning the result. DataFrames are immutable; the original object is unchanged and the notebook prints the unfiltered data. Capture the return value: `result = orders.filter(...)`.

5. Assuming `select` tightens nullability. Spark keeps `nullable = true` because the declared schema says the column is nullable; only a filter with a proven non-null predicate would let the optimizer consider otherwise, and it does not rewrite the public schema.

Edge cases and generalization: this read -> validate -> filter -> project shape is the standard Bronze-to-Silver move in a medallion architecture (a layered refinement pattern: raw Bronze tables, cleaned Silver tables, business-level Gold tables). Once the pattern is internalized, every additional requirement (deduplication, joins to a customer dimension, aggregation) is appended as another lazy transformation before the next action.
Problem 2

A teammate rewrites the read as `spark.read.option('header', True).option('inferSchema', True).csv(path)` instead of declaring the schema. The CSV is 92 GB in object storage, the cluster reads at an aggregate 9.6 GB/s, and 37 rows contain the literal string `N/A` in the `amount` column. (a) How much extra wall-clock time does inference add per run, and how much cluster time does it consume across 200 daily runs? (b) What type will Spark infer for `amount`, and what does the predicate `amount >= 100` then actually compute? (c) Demonstrate with two concrete values that the filter result differs from the numeric answer, and quantify the error if 1,204,300 rows genuinely satisfy the numeric condition while 1,268,455 rows satisfy the string condition.
Hint: Ask yourself what data type a column must have if even one of its values is a non-numeric string, and what comparison operator Spark then applies.

Worked solution
(a) Cost of inference. With `inferSchema = True`, Spark performs an additional pass over the data to read values and infer types before the real read; for CSV the default sampling ratio is 1.0, so the pass covers every row, not a sample. The extra time is therefore one full scan:

$$t_{\text{extra}} = \frac{92\ \text{GB}}{9.6\ \text{GB/s}} = 9.58\ \text{s} \approx 9.6\ \text{s per run}$$

Across 200 daily runs: $200 \times 9.58\ \text{s} = 1{,}916\ \text{s} \approx 31.9$ minutes, i.e. roughly 0.53 cluster-hours per day of pure metadata guessing. Declaring the schema eliminates that pass entirely.

(b) Inferred type. Type inference works bottom-up over all values: as soon as one value in the column cannot be parsed as a number, the column's type is widened to `string`. With 37 rows holding `N/A`, Spark infers `amount: string`. The predicate `col('amount') >= 100` is then a STRING comparison, because `100` is coerced to the string `'100'`. String comparison is lexicographic (character by character, by ASCII code), not numeric.

(c) Concrete counterexamples:

- `'99.5' >= '100'` -> compare the first characters: `'9'` has ASCII 57 and `'1'` has ASCII 49, so `'9' > '1'` and the whole comparison is **TRUE**. Numerically, 99.5 >= 100 is FALSE. A \$99.50 order is wrongly admitted.

- `'1000.00' >= '100'` -> the first three characters tie (`'1','0','0'`), the left string is longer, so it is **TRUE**. Here the string answer happens to agree with the numeric one, which is exactly why the bug survives casual inspection.

Error magnitude for the full day: $1{,}268{,}455 - 1{,}204{,}300 = 64{,}155$ spurious rows, a relative inflation of

$$\frac{64{,}155}{1{,}204{,}300} = 5.33\%$$

Every downstream aggregate built on this filter is inflated by about 5.3%.

Analysis — Why the method works: a declared schema is a contract. Handing Spark the contract up front lets the CSV reader decode bytes directly into `DOUBLE` and `TIMESTAMP` without a discovery pass, and it fails loudly (or nulls the value, depending on mode) when the file violates the contract instead of silently redefining the column's meaning. Inference buys convenience on ad-hoc exploration and costs a full scan plus the risk of a type that depends on the data of the day.

This matters even more in columnar storage: a columnar format reads only the columns a query selects, and packing similar values together yields high compression, so a scan that touches 3 of 5 columns is genuinely cheaper than a row-by-row read [source p.239]. An extra inference pass defeats part of that advantage because it must touch every column of every row. Nulls are also essentially free in columnar storage, which is why wide, sparse schemas are tolerable there and catastrophic in a row store [source p.332].

Typical student mistakes:

1. Believing `inferSchema` samples a few rows. It reads all rows by default; the cost scales with file size, so a 92 GB file pays 92 GB of extra I/O.

2. Believing the inferred type is stable. Adding one bad row tomorrow changes `amount` from `double` to `string` and silently changes every comparison in the pipeline — a classic schema-evolution trap.

3. Assuming a filter on a string column raises an error. Spark coerces `100` to `'100'` and the query succeeds with wrong semantics; only arithmetic (e.g. `amount * 1.1`) would fail loudly.

Edge cases and generalization: when the source genuinely is untyped, prefer an explicit schema with a deliberate recovery strategy — set `mode` to `PERMISSIVE` and add a malformed-record column (`_corrupt_record`) so bad rows are quarantined rather than silently contaminating the column type. Reading from a table (`spark.table('catalog.schema.table')`) sidesteps the issue entirely because the Delta table already carries its schema and statistics. Finally, ingesting data from a new source always requires studying the source schema itself, and that study happens in the transformation stage of the engineering lifecycle, not after ingestion [source p.268].
Problem 3

Take the verified DataFrame `orders` (columns `order_id`, `customer_id`, `order_ts`, `amount`, `status`) and answer the requirement — completed 2024 orders with `amount >= 100` — a second time in pure Spark SQL. Register the DataFrame as a temporary view named `orders`, write the SQL statement, then use `explain()` on both the DataFrame result and the SQL result to prove they compile to the same plan, and explain what a genuine difference between the two plans would tell you.
Hint: `createOrReplaceTempView` makes a DataFrame queryable by name for the life of the session; both APIs feed the same Catalyst optimizer.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Expose the DataFrame to the SQL namespace:

```python

orders.createOrReplaceTempView('orders')

```

The view is session-scoped and stores the logical plan, not the data.

Step 2 — The SQL statement:

```sql

SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount

FROM orders

WHERE status = 'completed'

AND YEAR(order_ts) = 2024

AND amount >= 100;

```

Run it with `sql_result = spark.sql(open_sql_text)` (or paste the text directly). `sql_result.count()` returns the same 128,431 rows as the DataFrame path, and `sql_result.columns` returns `['order_id', 'customer_id', 'amount']` in the same order, because `SELECT` fixes the projection order just as `.select(...)` does.

Step 3 — Compare the plans:

```python

df_result.explain(True)

sql_result.explain(True)

```

Both print the same shape, for example:

```

== Physical Plan ==

*(1) Project [order_id#12, customer_id#13, amount#15]

+- *(1) Filter ((((isnotnull(status#16) AND isnotnull(order_ts#14)) AND isnotnull(amount#15))

AND (status#16 = completed)) AND ((year(order_ts#14) = 2024) AND (amount#15 >= 100.0)))

+- *(1) FileScan csv [order_id#12, customer_id#13, order_ts#14, amount#15, status#16]

Batched: false, Format: CSV, Location: /databricks-datasets/retail/orders.csv

```

Three observations prove equivalence:

1. The operators are identical and in the same order: `Project` over `Filter` over `FileScan`.

2. Both plans contain the same number of `isnotnull` tests. Neither SQL nor the DataFrame API ever asked for them — Catalyst inserted them because a comparison with NULL yields NULL, never TRUE, so the optimizer adds null checks to keep the operator three-valued-logic safe.

3. The `AQS`/scan node reads the same five columns and the same file location in both plans.

If the plans differed — say one had an extra `Exchange` (a shuffle) or one fell back to a `Generate`/UDF node — that would tell you one of the two expressions is not expressible in Catalyst's built-in function set and is being evaluated row-by-row instead of by the code-generated engine.

Step 4 — A sharper predicate. `YEAR(order_ts) = 2024` wraps a function around a column, which blocks predicate pushdown for that condition. The equivalent range form is pushdown-friendly:

```sql

WHERE order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:00:00'

AND order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2025-01-01 00:00:00'

```

On a Delta table this allows file-level statistics (min/max per file) to skip entire files; on the CSV source here it mainly keeps the door open for future pruning. The row count is unchanged: 128,431.

Analysis — Why both paths agree: Spark SQL and the DataFrame API are two front ends to the same engine. SQL text is parsed into an unresolved logical plan and bound to the catalog; the DataFrame API builds a logical plan through method calls. Both then pass through the same analyzer, the same rule-based and cost-based optimizer, and the same physical planner. That is why `explain()` is a legitimate proof of equivalence rather than a coincidence.

The role of `createOrReplaceTempView` is often misunderstood: it does not copy data, does not persist anything, and disappears when the session ends. It simply gives the logical plan a name the SQL parser can resolve. Persisting across sessions requires a real table (`saveAsTable`) or a managed object such as a materialized view.

Typical student mistakes:

1. Using Python operators inside SQL-like strings, e.g. `spark.sql("SELECT ... WHERE status = 'completed' AND amount >= 100")` is fine, but writing `col('status') == 'completed' and col('amount') >= 100` in PySpark is not — the `and` short-circuits on the driver. SQL's `AND` and PySpark's `&` are the distributed forms; Python's `and`/`or` never are.

2. Assuming `=` in SQL and `==` in PySpark behave differently. Both compile to `EqualTo`, and neither matches NULL.

3. Comparing plans by row counts only. A slow-but-correct plan and a fast one return identical rows; only `explain()` reveals the missing predicate pushdown or an unnecessary shuffle.

4. Assuming the optimizer will fix a function-wrapped predicate for you. `year(order_ts) = 2024` is computable but not pushdown-able to file statistics, so it is a residual filter applied after the scan.

Edge cases and generalization: the equivalence breaks only when one side uses something the other cannot express — a Python UDF, an RDD operation, or a dialect feature such as `QUALIFY`. When that happens, `explain()` shows the diverging subtree, and the practical fix is to rewrite the expression using built-in functions so both paths converge on the same generated code. As a rule, register the DataFrame and use SQL when the logic is easier to express declaratively, but keep the DataFrame version around for testing, because plan comparison is the cheapest correctness check available.
Problem 4

A seven-row sample of the `orders` data is shown below. For each row, decide whether it survives the predicate `status = 'completed' AND YEAR(order_ts) = 2024 AND amount >= 100`, and state exactly why or why not:

| order_id | order_ts | amount | status |

|---|---|---|---|

| O-1001 | 2024-03-15 10:22:00 | 250.00 | completed |

| O-1002 | 2024-07-04 09:00:00 | 99.99 | completed |

| O-1003 | 2024-11-30 23:59:00 | 500.00 | pending |

| O-1004 | 2023-12-31 23:59:00 | 150.00 | completed |

| O-1005 | 2024-05-05 12:00:00 | NULL | completed |

| O-1006 | 2024-06-06 12:00:00 | 320.00 | NULL |

| O-1007 | NULL | 200.00 | completed |

Then, if the full table has 4,812,650 rows with 9,431 NULL `amount`, 512 NULL `status`, and 87 NULL `order_ts` values, explain how many rows are lost purely to NULL logic, and rewrite the query so that NULL `status` rows are deliberately retained as `completed` candidates rather than silently dropped.
Hint: In a WHERE clause only the value TRUE admits a row. Anything that evaluates to NULL or FALSE is discarded — and NULL is not the same as FALSE.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Evaluate the predicate row by row. The predicate is a conjunction, and SQL/PySpark use three-valued logic: `TRUE`, `FALSE`, and `NULL` (unknown). A row passes only when the whole conjunction is `TRUE`.

| order_id | status = 'completed' | YEAR(order_ts) = 2024 | amount >= 100 | Conjunction | Verdict |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| O-1001 | TRUE | TRUE | TRUE | TRUE | **kept** |

| O-1002 | TRUE | TRUE | FALSE (99.99 < 100) | FALSE | dropped — order too small |

| O-1003 | FALSE (`pending`) | TRUE | TRUE | FALSE | dropped — wrong status |

| O-1004 | TRUE | FALSE (2023) | TRUE | FALSE | dropped — wrong year |

| O-1005 | TRUE | TRUE | NULL | NULL | **dropped — NULL amount** |

| O-1006 | NULL | TRUE | TRUE | NULL | **dropped — NULL status** |

| O-1007 | TRUE | NULL | TRUE | NULL | **dropped — NULL timestamp** |

Result: 1 of 7 rows is returned, namely O-1001. Note that O-1002, O-1003, and O-1004 are dropped for honest business reasons, while O-1005, O-1006, and O-1007 are dropped for a reason nobody stated in the requirement.

Step 2 — The three-valued truth table for `AND`, which is why this happens:

| `A` | `B` | `A AND B` |

|---|---|---|

| TRUE | TRUE | TRUE |

| TRUE | FALSE | FALSE |

| TRUE | NULL | NULL |

| FALSE | FALSE | FALSE |

| FALSE | NULL | FALSE |

| NULL | NULL | NULL |

Row O-1005 illustrates `TRUE AND TRUE AND NULL = NULL`; row O-1006 illustrates `NULL AND TRUE AND TRUE = NULL`. In both cases the conjunction is NULL, and a `WHERE` clause keeps only TRUE.

Step 3 — Scale the loss. Of the full 4,812,650 rows, at least 9,431 + 512 + 87 = 10,030 rows contain a NULL in a column the predicate touches, and every one of them is excluded regardless of the other two conditions. Concretely, if all 512 NULL-`status` rows were in 2024 and above 100, the current query still returns 128,431 instead of 128,943 — a silent under-report of 0.4%.

Step 4 — Rewrite to make the choice explicit. If the business rule is "a missing status means the order was never cancelled, so treat it as completed", say so in code:

```python

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, year

result = (orders

.filter(((col('status') == 'completed') | col('status').isNull()) &

(year(col('order_ts')) == 2024) &

(col('amount') >= 100))

.select('order_id', 'customer_id', 'amount'))

```

SQL equivalent:

```sql

SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount

FROM orders

WHERE (status = 'completed' OR status IS NULL)

AND YEAR(order_ts) = 2024

AND amount >= 100;

```

Note the parentheses: `OR` binds looser than `AND`, so `(A OR B) AND C` must be written with brackets or the query becomes `A OR (B AND C)`.

Step 5 — Do NOT "fix" NULL amounts by filling. `orders.na.fill({'amount': 0.0})` makes the row non-null but 0.0 < 100, so it is still dropped, and you have now corrupted the column for every other aggregate. If a NULL amount should count as zero revenue for reporting, do that in an explicit `coalesce(col('amount'), lit(0.0))` projection with a comment, not in the filter.

Analysis — Why the method works: filtering with a conjunction is a probabilistic-safe operation only under closed-world assumptions, and NULL breaks them. Nullability is exactly the property the DataFrame schema advertises with `nullable = true`, so a schema that says every column is nullable is telling you that three-valued logic will apply. Spark's optimizer even materializes this fact: it rewrites `status = 'completed'` into `(isnotnull(status) AND status = 'completed')`, which is why `explain()` shows null checks nobody typed. Nulls are essentially free to store in columnar formats, so wide, sparse tables with many NULLs are routine rather than exotic [source p.332], and a directory of such tables is often compared with the relational row-store equivalent, where the same sparsity is expensive because every row must allocate space for every field.

Typical student mistakes:

1. Reading NULL as "false" or as "empty string". `status ='' ` and `status IS NULL` are different predicates with different results; `NULL = NULL` is NULL, never TRUE.

2. Using `col('status') != 'cancelled'` intending "not cancelled". This silently drops NULL statuses too, because `NULL != 'cancelled'` is NULL. If you want "not cancelled or unknown", write `(col('status') != 'cancelled') | col('status').isNull()`.

3. Filling NULLs with a sentinel so the predicate "works". A sentinel for `amount` (0.0) or `status` (`'unknown'`) changes the domain of the column and pollutes every downstream join and aggregate.

4. Counting with `count(col('amount'))` and expecting the row count. `count(col)` skips NULLs, while `count('*')` counts rows; on this data the two differ by 9,431 in the source table.

5. Assuming `amount >= 100` alone protects against NULL amounts because "100 is a number". Comparison with NULL is NULL, not FALSE.

Edge cases and generalization: the same three-valued logic governs joins — an `=` join condition never matches two NULL keys, so NULL foreign keys vanish from inner joins, while Delta Lake's `MERGE` requires distinguishing `NULL = NULL` from `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` semantics. When a requirement says "include missing values", that sentence is a data-quality convention that belongs in the transformation, written explicitly with `isNull()`, `coalesce`, or `na.fill` and justified in a comment. Discovering it after the fact means re-running the pipeline and reconciling against historical reports. Finally, note that examining a source schema's quirks is part of ingestion planning itself [source p.268], and that obtaining correct row and column access to the underlying files is a prerequisite the data engineer usually arranges before any of this code runs [source p.383].

actions.text: Now let's put those fundamentals to work. This page is a fully worked end-to-end problem that chains together everything we just covered: reading a raw CSV with an explicit schema, inspecting it, then filtering and selecting columns in both the DataFrame API and Spark SQL. We'll walk through four problems in sequence, and each one builds on the DataFrame produced by the last.

Problem 1 sets the stage. The raw file at /databricks-datasets/retail/orders.csv has five columns — order_id, customer_id, order_ts, amount, and status — and we need to return only order_id, customer_id, and amount for completed orders placed in 2024 with an amount of at least 100. We also have to state the resulting schema, so the output types matter just as much as the rows.

The hint nudges you the exam way: declare the schema as a DDL string, then filter with a single chained expression. Look at the worked solution — we read with option('header', True) and pass the schema as a string literal: order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE, status STRING. Then we verify with printSchema() and count(). Verifying is not optional — it is the habit that catches a wrong delimiter or a misaligned column before it poisons everything downstream.

The analysis explains why this works: every PySpark transformation is lazy. Nothing is read until an action like count() forces execution. And because the schema is explicit, Spark skips the extra pass over the file that inference would require and cannot silently mistype a column.

Problem 2 puts that claim to the test. A teammate rewrites the read using option('inferSchema', True) instead of a declared schema. Your job is to explain what changes. Notice the trade: inference is convenient, but it costs an extra scan and it guesses types from sampled data.

The worked solution separates two costs. First, the performance cost of inference: Spark reads the data once purely to determine types, then reads it again to build the DataFrame — two passes where a declared schema needs one. Second, and more dangerous, the correctness cost: inferred types depend on the sample. A column of all-digit strings can come back as a numeric type, and a column with leading zeros can lose them. A declared schema makes the contract explicit and reproducible.

Problem 3 moves us into SQL. Take the verified orders DataFrame, register it with createOrReplaceTempView, and write the equivalent query. As the worked solution shows, once the DataFrame is a temp view, Spark SQL and the DataFrame API are two syntaxes over the same engine — and calling explain() on both confirms they compile to the same logical plan.

Problem 4 is where exam traps live. We are given a seven-row sample of the orders data and asked which rows survive the filter. Remember the hint: in a WHERE clause, only the value TRUE admits a row. If amount or status is NULL, the whole predicate evaluates to NULL, not TRUE — so those rows quietly disappear. That is not a bug, it is three-valued logic, and you must handle it deliberately with isNull() or na.fill() rather than assume it away.

So the through-line of this page is short and worth memorizing: declare your schema, verify it with printSchema and count, build the filter with col and the & operator — never Python's 'and' — parenthesize every condition, and capture the returned DataFrame, because DataFrames are immutable and nothing changes unless you reassign. Next, we'll checkpoint these skills before moving on to derived columns and conditional logic.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Selecting, Filtering, and Deriving Columns

questions.question: The DataFrame `orders` was read with the declared schema: order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE, status STRING, region STRING. You must return a new DataFrame containing exactly two columns: order_id, and net_total — defined as amount multiplied by 0.8 and stored as DECIMAL(10,2). Which single statement does exactly this and nothing more?

options.label: orders.selectExpr('order_id', 'CAST(amount * 0.8 AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS net_total')
orders.select('order_id', 'amount * 0.8 AS net_total')
orders.withColumn('net_total', col('amount') * 0.8).cast('DECIMAL(10,2)')
orders.drop('status', 'region').withColumnRenamed('amount', 'net_total')

questions.analysis: Option A is correct because selectExpr parses each argument as a SQL expression, so both the arithmetic (amount * 0.8) and the alias (AS net_total) are interpreted as SQL; only order_id and net_total are projected, and the explicit CAST fixes the result type to DECIMAL(10,2) rather than leaving it as DOUBLE. Option B is the classic exam trap: in the DataFrame API, select('order_id', 'amount * 0.8 AS net_total') treats the second string as a literal column NAME, not an expression, so the analyzer raises UNRESOLVED_COLUMN — the string form of select only resolves existing names and never parses SQL syntax. Option C is wrong on two counts: DataFrame.cast('DECIMAL(10,2)') casts EVERY column it can convert (order_id, a STRING, would be coerced toward a decimal type, or leave an unusable schema), and it also retains customer_id, order_ts, status and region instead of projecting two columns. Option D keeps four columns (order_id, customer_id, order_ts, net_total) and only renames amount — the value stays DOUBLE with no explicit cast, so the declared type requirement is unmet. A useful mental model: the explicit schema you declared at read time is a contract, and a derived column is only 'converted' when YOU say so with cast or a typed SQL expression; otherwise Spark picks a wider type such as DOUBLE to avoid silent precision loss. Finally, recall that this whole statement is a transformation: it returns a NEW immutable DataFrame and nothing is computed until an action such as display(), count() or write() is called. Projecting only the two columns you need is not cosmetic either — with columnar serialization the engine can read only the required columns instead of full rows, which 'can dramatically reduce the amount of data that must be scanned to execute a query' [source p.419], and columnar serialization 'allows a database to scan only the columns required for a particular query' [source p.239].

questions.question: For the DataFrame `orders` (columns order_id, amount, status, region, coupon_code), which of the following filter statements are semantically correct in PySpark 3.x for the intent stated next to them? Select all that apply.

options.label: orders.filter((col('status') == 'completed') & (col('amount') >= 100)) — Intent: keep rows that are both completed and worth at least 100.
orders.filter((col('status') == 'completed') and (col('amount') >= 100)) — Intent: keep rows that are both completed and worth at least 100.
orders.filter(col('region') == None) — Intent: keep rows where the region value is missing.
orders.filter(col('region').isNull()) — Intent: keep rows where the region value is missing.
orders.filter(col('coupon_code') != 'SAVE10') — Intent: keep every row that did not use coupon SAVE10, including rows that have no coupon code at all.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: & is the bitwise/boolean AND that Column objects overload into a Catalyst predicate, and each comparison is wrapped in parentheses because & binds tighter than == in Python — omitting the parentheses is the single most common real-world mistake here. Option B is the other classic trap: Python's `and` evaluates truthiness of the left operand, and a Column has no boolean value, so PySpark raises an error about converting a column into a bool instead of building a predicate; the same holds for `or` versus `|` and `not` versus `~`. Option C is wrong because Python None is turned into a literal null in the expression, and a comparison against null yields null (unknown) for every row, never true — the predicate compiles and runs but silently returns zero rows, which is why it looks harmless in a notebook. Option D is correct: isNull() is the null-aware predicate that returns a non-null boolean for every row, and its siblings are isNotNull() and the null-safe equality operator eqNullSafe, which treats null as a comparable value rather than as unknown. Option E is wrong on exactly the null-safe point: in SQL's three-valued logic, null != 'SAVE10' evaluates to null, the row is not true, and the filter DROPS the very rows (uncoded orders) the analyst wanted to keep; the correct form would be (col('coupon_code') != 'SAVE10') | col('coupon_code').isNull(). Two exam-level habits follow from this. First, label every filter with the intent it is supposed to satisfy and test it mentally against a null row, because null handling is where the intended and actual result sets diverge. Second, remember that a filter is a lazy transformation that goes into the plan — Spark composes the read, the joins and the filter into a DAG of steps based on the code you write [source p.346] — so a wrong operator does not raise at definition time, it silently changes the data that later stages and the final write must process.

questions.question: Using the PySpark DataFrame API on a DataFrame named `orders` whose columns are order_id (STRING), order_ts (TIMESTAMP), amount (DOUBLE), status (STRING), region (STRING), write a SINGLE-LINE filter predicate (assigned to a variable and then applied with orders.filter(...)) that keeps rows satisfying all three conditions at once: (1) status is 'completed'; (2) amount is at least 100; (3) region is either exactly 'EU' or is NULL. Your one-line predicate must be correct under Spark's null semantics and must not raise an error at definition time. Then state, in one or two sentences, what the result set would be if you replaced your region handling with col('region') == 'EU' alone.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric, 20 points total: (1) Boolean operator correctness — 25%: uses the & operator (not the Python keyword and), and parenthesises each individual comparison so that & applies to two fully-formed boolean Columns. A submission that uses `and` or omits the parentheses scores zero on this criterion. (2) NULL-safe region handling — 35%: keeps EU rows AND null rows, e.g. (col('region') == 'EU') | col('region').isNull(), or the null-safe form col('region').eqNullSafe('EU'). Using `== None`, `.isna()` on a Region, or a bare `col('region') == 'EU'` alone does not satisfy the condition. (3) All three conditions present and correctly conjoined — 20%: status == 'completed', amount >= 100, and the region disjunction combined with & in a single expression; penalise partial credit for missing a condition or using | where & is required. (4) Single-line / API correctness — 10%: uses col(...) or equivalent and produces one filter expression that can be passed to orders.filter(...) without error; a multi-statement helper function or a SQL string inside .filter('...') with unparenthesised AND/OR also loses this portion. (5) Explanation of the null behaviour — 10%: correctly states that col('region') == 'EU' evaluates to null (unknown) for rows with a missing region, so those rows are dropped and the result set shrinks to EU-only rows. Deduct for answers that claim nulls are treated as false but still retained, or that claim the comparison errors out.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: flt = (col('status') == 'completed') & (col('amount') >= 100) & ((col('region') == 'EU') | col('region').isNull()), then orders.filter(flt). An equivalent region clause is col('region').eqNullSafe('EU'), which returns a definite boolean for null input instead of an unknown value. Three points make this the only correct shape. First, operator precedence: in Python, & binds more tightly than ==, so (col('status') == 'completed') & (col('amount') >= 100) without parentheses is parsed in a way that does not build the predicate you intended, and the Python keyword `and` is worse still — it forces a truth-value test on a Column and raises instead of constructing a boolean Column. Second, null semantics: comparisons in Spark follow three-valued logic, so `region == 'EU'` is null — not false — when region is null, and filter keeps only rows where the predicate is true; that is why the OR with isNull() (or eqNullSafe) is required rather than optional. Third, the intent of drawing a boundary: replacing the disjunction with == 'EU' silently removes every unknown-region row, which changes revenue totals and row counts downstream without raising a single exception — exactly the kind of quiet defect that survives code review. Remember too that this predicate is a transformation that merely extends the plan: Spark builds a DAG of ingestion, joining and filtering steps from the code you write [source p.346], and the read-side benefit of touching fewer columns or fewer rows comes from the engine pruning columns and partitions rather than from the filter statement itself, since with columnar storage the engine 'allows us to read data from only a subset of fields rather than having to read full rows at once' [source p.419], an advantage that 'can dramatically reduce the amount of data that must be scanned to execute a query' [source p.239]. In practice, always test a null-sensitive predicate against a row where the column IS null, because that single row is the difference between a correct answer and a distractor on the exam — and between a correct and a wrong data product in production.

scenes.title: Selecting, Filtering, and Deriving Columns

elements.content: Select, Filter, and Derive Columns
DataFrame API: df.select('order_id','amount') keeps two columns and df.drop('status') removes one.
SQL mirror: SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' returns the same rows [source p.346].
df.filter() and df.where() are the same; join conditions with & and add parentheses.
Columnar storage prunes columns [source p.419] and compresses repeats [source p.239].
Worked example: 250.50 * 1.08 = 270.54 via withColumn, then cast to decimal(10,2).
Every transformation returns a NEW DataFrame; reassign or chain.

actions.text: Let's consolidate everything we just practiced into a single reference slide: selecting, filtering, and deriving columns. This is the core transformation vocabulary you'll be tested on, so treat this page as a checklist you can come back to.

On the left we have the DataFrame API. To pick columns, use df.select with column names, or col expressions when you need to rename — col('amount').alias('amount_with_tax'). To drop columns, use df.drop. And selectExpr lets you write SQL-style expressions inline, like 'amount * 1.08 AS amount_with_tax'.

On the right is the SQL mirror. The same operation is SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders WHERE amount > 100. The important takeaway for the exam is that the DataFrame API and Spark SQL describe the same underlying operations — you should be able to translate between them fluently in either direction.

For row filtering, remember that df.filter and df.where are literally identical — neither is deprecated, so don't let an exam question trick you into thinking one behaves differently. When you combine predicates, use the ampersand, pipe, and tilde operators, and wrap each condition in parentheses to control precedence.

Here's the worked example that ties it together. We derive a taxed amount with withColumn, multiplying amount by lit 1.08 — so 250.50 becomes 270.54. And notice the explicit cast on the same line: col('amount').cast('decimal(10,2)') forces a predictable numeric type instead of leaving you at the mercy of implicit conversion.

And the rule that trips up more candidates than any other: every one of these transformations returns a NEW DataFrame. DataFrames are immutable — nothing is modified in place. So either reassign, df = df.withColumn(...), or chain the calls together into a single expression.

Look at this transformation-chain diagram. Source DataFrame flows into filter, then select, then withColumn, producing a new DataFrame. Notice the original DataFrame sitting beneath the chain, completely unchanged — that's immutability made visual. Keep this picture in mind, because it's the mental model the rest of the lesson builds on.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Derived Columns, Casting, and Conditionals

questions.question: A DataFrame `sales` has the schema (order_id STRING, region STRING, amount DOUBLE). A teammate writes: sales.select('*', round(col('amount'), 2).alias('amount')). The cell runs without error, and the printed schema shows two columns that are both named 'amount'. Which statement best explains what happened and gives the correct single-column rewrite?

options.label: Spark permits duplicated output names in a select projection, so the original DOUBLE 'amount' and the rounded 'amount' both survive; any later unqualified reference to 'amount' fails as an ambiguous reference, and the intended rewrite is sales.withColumn('amount', round(col('amount'), 2)), which replaces the existing column in place.

Spark keeps only the last output column that carries a given name, so the result already holds a single rounded 'amount'; withColumn would have produced the same values but would have appended an extra column named 'amount_rounded'.

The projection should have failed during analysis with a duplicate-alias error, so the only legal way to round the column in place is to drop 'amount' first and then append the rounded value with withColumn under the same name.

The Catalyst analyzer collapses the two identically named output columns into one as part of optimization, so the duplicate name never reaches the executor and the two expressions become a single physical vector.

questions.analysis: A select projection is a list of output expressions, and nothing in the DataFrame API forbids two of those expressions from being given the same alias: select('*', round(col('amount'), 2).alias('amount')) therefore returns a DataFrame whose schema literally contains two fields called 'amount' (the untouched DOUBLE from the star expansion and the rounded expression). The duplicate is not removed by the analyzer or the optimizer, so it survives into the physical plan; what breaks is the NEXT operation that refers to the name without qualification, which fails during analysis with an ambiguous-reference error (for example when you select 'amount', join on it, or write it to a Delta table whose schema cannot hold two identical field names). Option B is wrong because Spark does not perform last-wins de-duplication of names, and withColumn never invents an 'amount_rounded' name. Option C is wrong because nothing at analysis time rejects the duplicate alias, and dropping then re-adding a column is unnecessary. Option D is wrong because Catalyst analyzes and optimizes the plan but does not merge two distinct output expressions into one field. The idiomatic rewrite is withColumn('amount', ...), whose semantics are: if the name already exists, the expression replaces that column and keeps its original position in the schema; if the name is new, the column is appended at the end. Both the broken select and the correct withColumn are transformations that return brand-new DataFrames, and because they are lazy the failure only surfaces when the plan for the next action is analyzed. This matters for derived metric work, where replacing a metric in place keeps the pipeline readable: complex business measures such as profit before marketing costs versus profit after marketing costs are computed as derived columns, and you want exactly one authoritative column per metric rather than two same-named competitors [source p.346].

questions.question: A Delta table is read into a DataFrame `payments` whose column `raw_amount` is STRING and holds values such as '12.50', 'abc', and '300'. The session runs with Databricks' default configuration, meaning ANSI mode (spark.sql.ansi.enabled) is disabled. Which of the following statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Casting the malformed value 'abc' to INT returns NULL for that row while the query still succeeds, so a later average or count that ignores NULLs silently drops the bad row instead of alerting anyone.

Enabling ANSI mode turns the same cast of 'abc' into a hard query failure rather than a NULL, which is the central trade-off to reason about when casting a STRING column whose contents you do not control.
Casting the DOUBLE value 12.9 to INT yields 13, because Spark rounds a floating-point value to the nearest integer whenever it narrows the type.
Casting the integer literal 300 to TINYINT returns NULL under non-ANSI behavior because 300 overflows the TINYINT range of -128 to 127, whereas the same cast raises an error when ANSI mode is on.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct and is the single most common production trap: with ANSI mode disabled, a cast that cannot parse the input produces NULL for that row rather than failing the job. The query succeeds, the schema still says INT, and the corruption is invisible unless you explicitly count nulls before and after (compare count('raw_amount') with count(cast_amount)). This is a data-quality problem rather than a syntax problem, and it is worse in modern pipelines because analytics are increasingly replaced by automation, so a silently nulled value flows straight into an automated action instead of being spotted by a human reading a report [source p.411]. Option B is correct: ANSI mode changes the contract from 'null on failure' to 'fail fast', raising a runtime error for a value such as 'abc' that violates the target type's format. Option D is correct in the same way: integral casts are range-checked, so 300 does not fit in TINYINT (-128 to 127); under non-ANSI behavior the result is NULL, and under ANSI behavior the cast errors out. Option C is wrong: since Spark 3.0, casting a floating-point or decimal value to an integral type truncates toward zero rather than rounding, so cast(12.9 AS INT) is 12 and cast(-12.9 AS INT) is -12. Notice the two independent failure modes being tested here: a parse failure ('abc') and an overflow failure (300 as TINYINT). Both are silent under non-ANSI behavior, which is why the certification expects you to predict the result of a cast rather than assume it 'just works'.

questions.question: You have a DataFrame `customers` with columns customer_id STRING, tier STRING, and lifetime_value DOUBLE (nullable). A requirement asks for a derived column `segment` defined as: 'platinum' when lifetime_value >= 10000, 'gold' when lifetime_value >= 5000, 'silver' when lifetime_value >= 1000, and 'bronze' in every other case. (a) Write the PySpark expression that adds `segment`, and explain the order in which the branches are evaluated. (b) A colleague writes the branches in ascending order (silver first, then gold, then platinum, then otherwise('bronze')) and reports that 'gold' and 'platinum' are never produced. Using the concrete value lifetime_value = 12000, explain exactly why those branches are unreachable. (c) State what the column contains for a row whose lifetime_value IS NULL and explain why, and describe what changes if the otherwise() call is omitted entirely.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100%): (1) Correct code, 30% — a single withColumn (or an equivalent select/selectExpr) that assigns the result to a NEW DataFrame, uses when/otherwise with the four thresholds in DESCENDING order, and uses >= rather than >. (2) Evaluation-order explanation, 25% — states that the when-chain is evaluated top-down and returns the value of the FIRST branch whose condition evaluates to true, so once an earlier (broader) condition matches, every later branch is permanently unreachable. (3) Concrete trace for lifetime_value = 12000, 20% — shows that 12000 >= 1000 is already true, so the 'silver' branch fires and the 'gold' and 'platinum' branches are dead code; must give the number 12000 explicitly. (4) NULL semantics, 15% — explains that when lifetime_value is NULL every comparison evaluates to NULL (unknown, not true), so control falls through to otherwise('bronze'); and that omitting otherwise() leaves those rows as NULL rather than raising an error. (5) Clarity and terminology, 10% — correct use of when/otherwise, branch, first-match-wins, fallback, and a clear statement that the resulting column type is STRING.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. (a) Code: from pyspark.sql.functions import col, when; then segmented = customers.withColumn('segment', when(col('lifetime_value') >= 10000, 'platinum').when(col('lifetime_value') >= 5000, 'gold').when(col('lifetime_value') >= 1000, 'silver').otherwise('bronze')). The chain is a nested CASE expression: Spark walks the branches in the order written, evaluates each condition, and returns the value of the first condition that evaluates to true; only if no condition is true does it return the otherwise() value. The order in the source code is the order of evaluation, which is why the thresholds must run from most restrictive to least restrictive. (b) With the branches reversed, the trace for lifetime_value = 12000 is: 12000 >= 1000 is true, so the expression returns 'silver' immediately. The conditions 12000 >= 5000 and 12000 >= 10000 are never evaluated, because the chain already produced a value — the 'gold' and 'platinum' branches are dead code. Every value of 1000 or more becomes 'silver', so the only surviving outputs are 'silver' and 'bronze'; the bug is silent, no error is raised, and the segment counts simply look wrong. (c) If lifetime_value IS NULL, each comparison is NULL, and NULL is not true, so it does not satisfy any branch and control falls to otherwise('bronze'). In other words a missing value is silently labelled as the lowest-value customer, which may or may not be the business intent; to make it explicit you would prepend when(col('lifetime_value').isNull(), 'unknown') — and the null check must come FIRST, because of first-match-wins ordering. If otherwise() is omitted, the expression has no ELSE, so any row that matched nothing (including the NULL rows) receives NULL, the column type is still STRING, and downstream filters on segment = 'bronze' quietly lose those rows. Practical notes: the identical logic written in SQL as CASE WHEN lifetime_value >= 10000 THEN 'platinum' ... ELSE 'bronze' END compiles to the same Catalyst plan, and because the expression is deterministic and free of non-deterministic functions, repeated identical queries can be served from a cached result set instead of being recomputed — the query results cache is a canonical example of hot data [source p.250]. Finally, keep all branch values the same type: mixing, say, a numeric branch with string branches forces Spark to find a common type and can produce unexpected stringifying of the output.
