scenes.title: Worked Problem: Derive a Revenue Report with when/otherwise and Casts

elements.content: Problem 1

An e-commerce pipeline lands raw orders in a DataFrame `orders` with schema `order_id STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE, status STRING`. Six concrete rows are:

| order_id | order_ts | amount | status |

|---|---|---|---|

| A-1001 | 2024-03-05 10:00:00 | 1250.00 | completed |

| A-1002 | 2024-03-06 11:30:00 | 99.99 | completed |

| A-1003 | 2024-04-01 09:15:00 | 150.00 | completed |

| A-1004 | 2024-04-02 16:45:00 | 1000.00 | completed |

| A-1005 | 2024-04-03 12:00:00 | 45.50 | completed |

| A-1006 | 2024-02-29 08:00:00 | 250.00 | completed |

Produce a revenue report with exactly these output columns and types: `order_id STRING`, `order_date DATE` (from `order_ts`), `amount DECIMAL(10,2)`, `amount_with_tax DECIMAL(10,2)` where $amount\_with\_tax = amount \times 1.08$, and `revenue_band STRING` in {high, medium, low} using the thresholds $amount \geq 1000 \Rightarrow$ high and $amount \geq 100 \Rightarrow$ medium, otherwise low. Sort by `amount` descending. Write the DataFrame API version, the equivalent Spark SQL version over a temporary view, and show that both compile to one and the same physical plan.
Hint: Remember that predicates in the same SELECT list see the source column, not the freshly aliased output column.

Worked solution
Step 1 — read with a declared schema so nothing is inferred:

```

orders = (spark.read.option('header', True)

.schema('order_id STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE, status STRING')

.csv('/databricks-datasets/retail/orders.csv'))

```

Step 2 — DataFrame API: derive all five columns in ONE projection, then sort.

```

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, to_date, when

report_df = (orders

.select(

col('order_id'),

to_date('order_ts').alias('order_date'),

col('amount').cast('decimal(10,2)').alias('amount'),

(col('amount') * 1.08).cast('decimal(10,2)').alias('amount_with_tax'),

when(col('amount') >= 1000, 'high')

.when(col('amount') >= 100, 'medium')

.otherwise('low').alias('revenue_band'))

.orderBy(col('amount').desc()))

```

Step 3 — per-row arithmetic. The tax is computed on the raw DOUBLE and only then cast; the cast to `DECIMAL(10,2)` rounds HALF_UP:

* A-1001: $1250.00 \times 1.08 = 1350.0000 \rightarrow 1350.00$; band = high ($1250 \geq 1000$)

* A-1004: $1000.00 \times 1.08 = 1080.0000 \rightarrow 1080.00$; band = high ($1000 \geq 1000$)

* A-1006: $250.00 \times 1.08 = 270.0000 \rightarrow 270.00$; band = medium

* A-1003: $150.00 \times 1.08 = 162.0000 \rightarrow 162.00$; band = medium

* A-1002: $99.99 \times 1.08 = 107.9892 \rightarrow 107.99$; band = low ($99.99 < 100$)

* A-1005: $45.50 \times 1.08 = 49.1400 \rightarrow 49.14$; band = low

Step 4 — sorted result (descending `amount`):

| order_id | order_date | amount | amount_with_tax | revenue_band |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| A-1001 | 2024-03-05 | 1250.00 | 1350.00 | high |

| A-1004 | 2024-04-02 | 1000.00 | 1080.00 | high |

| A-1006 | 2024-02-29 | 250.00 | 270.00 | medium |

| A-1003 | 2024-04-01 | 150.00 | 162.00 | medium |

| A-1002 | 2024-03-06 | 99.99 | 107.99 | low |

| A-1005 | 2024-04-03 | 45.50 | 49.14 | low |

Resulting schema: `order_id string, order_date date, amount decimal(10,2), amount_with_tax decimal(10,2), revenue_band string`.

Step 5 — Spark SQL over the identical data:

```

orders.createOrReplaceTempView('orders_v')

report_sql = spark.sql('''

SELECT order_id,

to_date(order_ts) AS order_date,

CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS amount,

CAST(amount * 1.08 AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS amount_with_tax,

CASE WHEN amount >= 1000 THEN 'high'

WHEN amount >= 100 THEN 'medium'

ELSE 'low' END AS revenue_band

FROM orders_v

ORDER BY amount DESC''')

```

Step 6 — equivalence: `report_df.schema == report_sql.schema` returns True, and both `report_df.explain()` and `report_sql.explain()` print the same shape, e.g.

```

== Physical Plan ==

*(2) Sort [amount#10 DESC NULLS LAST], true, 0

+- Exchange rangepartitioning(amount#10 DESC NULLS LAST, 200), ENSURE_REQUIREMENTS

+- *(1) Project [order_id#1, to_date(order_ts#2) AS order_date#3, ...]

+- *(1) FileScan csv [...] PushedFilters: [], ReadSchema: struct<...>

```

The Sort, the Exchange, the Project and the FileScan are the same nodes, because the SQL parser and the DataFrame API both build one unresolved logical plan that Catalyst rewrites into one physical plan.

Analysis — Both front-ends are the same engine: SQL text is parsed into a logical plan and the DataFrame API builds that same plan programmatically, so `CASE WHEN` and `when().otherwise()` become the same expression node and the optimizer emits one physical plan — the equivalence is structural, not coincidental. A single `select` is the correct shaping primitive because it is a projection that declares the whole output schema in one place, allowing the optimizer to push the projection into the scan and let a columnar reader touch only five columns instead of every column of `orders`; columnar serialization exists precisely so a query 'can scan only the columns required for a particular query, sometimes dramatically reducing the amount of data read from the disk' [source p.239]. Casting money to `DECIMAL(10,2)` avoids accumulating binary floating-point error, and the cast rounds HALF_UP, so $99.99 \times 1.08 = 107.9892$ becomes 107.99. The branch order (>= 1000 before >= 100, `otherwise` last) is mandatory because a searched CASE is evaluated top-down and the first TRUE branch wins; putting a broad predicate first makes later branches unreachable. A subtle edge case: inside one SELECT list, sibling aliases are not visible, so `amount` in every `when` predicate — and in the SQL `CASE` — refers to the raw DOUBLE source column, not to the rounded DECIMAL being produced. A stored value of 99.999 therefore displays as amount 100.00 but is banded 'low'; making the band consistent with the displayed amount requires a second projection or a CTE that first rounds, then bands. Finally, `orderBy` is still a transformation: it appends a Sort node to the plan and returns a new lazy DataFrame, and not a single row moves until an action such as `display()`, `count()`, or `write()` runs.
Problem 2

A junior engineer writes this report, using the same six orders (amounts 1250.00, 99.99, 150.00, 1000.00, 45.50, 250.00):

```

bad = (orders

.withColumn('revenue_band',

when(col('amount') >= 100, 'medium')

.when(col('amount') >= 1000, 'high')

.otherwise('low')))

```

A production CSV also occasionally contains the string `'N/A'` in the `amount` column. Answer three questions: (a) which rows receive the wrong band and why; (b) what value does `col('amount').cast('decimal(10,2)')` produce for `'N/A'`, and what band does that row then receive; (c) write a corrected expression that is safe against both faults.
Hint: Reordering alone repairs the 'high' band; it does not repair the NULL that a failed cast produces.

Worked solution
(a) The first branch `amount >= 100` is broader than the second, so it swallows every row that could have reached 'high':

* 1250.00: $1250 \geq 100$ is TRUE $\rightarrow$ 'medium' (wrong; should be 'high')

* 1000.00: $1000 \geq 100$ is TRUE $\rightarrow$ 'medium' (wrong; should be 'high')

* 250.00: $\rightarrow$ 'medium' (correct)

* 150.00: $\rightarrow$ 'medium' (correct)

* 99.99: both predicates FALSE $\rightarrow$ 'low' (correct)

* 45.50: both predicates FALSE $\rightarrow$ 'low' (correct)

The second `when` is dead code: the value 'high' is never produced. The rule is that a searched CASE is evaluated top-down and the first TRUE branch wins, so branches must run from the narrowest/most restrictive condition to the broadest, with `otherwise` as the final fallback.

(b) Casting the string `'N/A'` to DECIMAL(10,2) cannot produce a number. In Spark's non-ANSI mode the cast returns NULL instead of raising (`try_cast` makes that behavior explicit); with ANSI mode enabled the same cast raises an error. Either way the downstream `when` is affected: `NULL >= 100` evaluates to NULL, which is not TRUE, so the first branch is skipped; `NULL >= 1000` is also NULL, so the second branch is skipped; execution lands in `otherwise`, and the record is silently labelled 'low' while its `amount` is NULL. The report now contains a row that looks like a genuine low-revenue order but is actually corrupt input.

(c) Corrected, defensive expression — validate the type first, order branches most-restrictive-first, and make the NULL case explicit instead of letting it fall through:

```

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, when

safe = (orders

.filter(col('amount').rlike(r'^-?\\d+(\\.\\d+)?$')) # drop non-numeric strings

.select(

col('order_id'),

col('amount').cast('decimal(10,2)').alias('amount'),

when(col('amount') >= 1000, 'high')

.when(col('amount') >= 100, 'medium')

.when(col('amount').isNull(), 'invalid')

.otherwise('low').alias('revenue_band')))

```

With this code the 1250.00 and 1000.00 rows are 'high', 250.00 and 150.00 are 'medium', 99.99 and 45.50 are 'low', and a malformed row is either filtered out at the source or surfaced as 'invalid' rather than being disguised as 'low'.

Analysis — The ordering fault is not a syntax error — it is a semantic error that the compiler cannot catch, which is exactly why CASE ordering is a favourite exam and code-review trap: the plan is valid, the job succeeds, and only the business numbers are wrong. NULL handling is the second trap. SQL uses three-valued logic, so a predicate over NULL is UNKNOWN, not FALSE, and a CASE treats UNKNOWN the same way it treats FALSE by falling through to the next branch and eventually to ELSE; `when(cond, x).otherwise(y)` therefore silently maps unknown inputs onto the ELSE label. Silent cast failure is the third trap, and it is grounded in ingestion reality: comma-separated text does not natively encode schema and 'data engineers are often forced to work with CSV data and then build robust exception handling and error detection to ensure data quality on ingestion' [source p.284]. The robust pattern is to validate before casting, or at minimum to add an explicit `isNull` branch and a quarantine table so a corrupt value is visible instead of being resolved to a plausible-looking band. Note also that the correct fix is not merely to reorder the branches — reordering fixes 'high' but a NULL amount would still fall to 'low', so both fixes are required together.
Problem 3

You inherit a notebook that builds the revenue report from a 200-column wide Delta table `silver.orders` (which contains `order_id`, `order_ts`, `amount`, `status` and 196 other columns). The inherited code is:

```

df = spark.table('silver.orders')

df = df.withColumn('order_date', to_date('order_ts'))

df = df.withColumn('amount', col('amount').cast('decimal(10,2)'))

df = df.withColumn('amount_with_tax', (col('amount') * 1.08).cast('decimal(10,2)'))

df = df.withColumn('revenue_band', when(col('amount') >= 1000,'high')

.when(col('amount') >= 100,'medium')

.otherwise('low'))

df = df.drop('status')

df = df.orderBy(col('amount').desc())

display(df)

```

(a) Rewrite it as a single projection that emits exactly the report columns. (b) Explain what each chained `withColumn` contributes to the logical plan and why the rewrite is better for a columnar engine. (c) State at which line the sort actually executes, and why the original `silver.orders` table is never modified.
Hint: Nothing runs until `display`; everything before it only appends nodes to a lazy plan.

Worked solution
(a) One projection, one sort:

```

from pyspark.sql.functions import col, to_date, when

report = (spark.table('silver.orders')

.select(

col('order_id'),

to_date('order_ts').alias('order_date'),

col('amount').cast('decimal(10,2)').alias('amount'),

(col('amount') * 1.08).cast('decimal(10,2)').alias('amount_with_tax'),

when(col('amount') >= 1000, 'high')

.when(col('amount') >= 100, 'medium')

.otherwise('low').alias('revenue_band'))

.orderBy(col('amount').desc()))

display(report)

```

(b) Each `withColumn` call returns a NEW DataFrame whose logical plan wraps the previous plan in another `Project` node. The first three calls each add one 200+1-column projection, the fourth call adds the band, and `drop('status')` adds yet another projection that removes one column from the 201-column stream. In the inherited code the 196 unused columns are still carried through five stacked projections before they are finally discarded. Spark's optimizer often collapses adjacent projections, but stacked projections inflate the logical plan, make `explain()` hard to read, and can defeat projection pushdown — the very optimization that makes a columnar store efficient, since a columnar reader 'can scan only the columns required for a particular query' [source p.239]. The single `select` declares the five output columns up front, so the scan reads five columns and the exchange and sort shuffle five columns instead of 200. Chained `withColumn` calls are also the wide-table pattern that manufactures 'hundreds or more' columns without a deliberate model, and whose updates are 'very painful' [source p.332].

(c) Nothing executes until `display(df)` on the last line. Every statement before it — `spark.table`, all five `withColumn`s, `drop`, `orderBy` — merely builds a plan. The sort is a `Sort` node appended by `orderBy`, and the rows physically move only when the terminal action `display` is evaluated. Because DataFrames are immutable, `df = df.withColumn(...)` rebinds the Python variable to a new DataFrame; the Delta table `silver.orders` and any previously bound DataFrame are untouched, so no data is written back.

Analysis — `withColumn` is convenient for adding or replacing one column by name, but it is a projection, not a mutation, and its cost is structural: N chained calls produce N stacked `Project` nodes, each of which must reintroduce every column of the input. On a narrow table the difference is cosmetic; on a 200-column wide table it is measurable, because the intermediate rows and the shuffle for the sort carry 200+ columns until the final projection prunes them. This matters more on a columnar engine, where efficiency comes from reading only the needed columns and where record-level updates are inherently expensive — changing one field forces the engine to decompress a column file, modify it, recompress it and write it back, which is why 'columns are broken into many files, typically using partitioning and clustering strategies' [source p.419]. The same economics explain why `withColumn` chains that mimic row-at-a-time edits are an anti-pattern in batch pipelines: a batch-oriented system performs poorly when asked to do 'many small in-place update operations' [source p.273]. Finally, laziness is the point students most often misread. `orderBy` returns a new DataFrame with a Sort node; the sort happens during the action, and the original table is untouched because transformation never writes. Debugging follows from this: call `df.explain()` to inspect the plan before the action, and only then call `display()` or `write()`.
Problem 4

You have two DataFrames that are supposed to be identical: `df_api` from the DataFrame API solution and `df_sql` from `spark.sql(...)` over the temporary view, both with schema `order_id STRING, order_date DATE, amount DECIMAL(10,2), amount_with_tax DECIMAL(10,2), revenue_band STRING`, both sorted by `amount` descending. Describe and execute three verification steps: (1) compare schemas, (2) prove the row sets are equal regardless of order, (3) compare physical plans. Then state precisely what it would mean if step 2 failed while step 3 passed, and what a sort-column bug would look like in this test set.
Hint: Treat the pipeline as three independent contracts: types, contents, and plan shape — each catches a different class of bug.

Worked solution
Step 1 — schema equality. Compare the full schemas, including types and nullability, not just names:

```

df_api.schema == df_sql.schema # True

df_api.dtypes == df_sql.dtypes # [('order_id','string'), ('order_date','date'),

# ('amount','decimal(10,2)'), ...]

```

A type mismatch such as `decimal(10,2)` versus `decimal(12,4)` fails here even when every displayed number looks the same.

Step 2 — row-set equality, order-insensitive. Use the multiset difference in both directions:

```

diff_api_only = df_api.exceptAll(df_sql).count() # 0

diff_sql_only = df_sql.exceptAll(df_api).count() # 0

assert diff_api_only == 0 and diff_sql_only == 0

```

`exceptAll` preserves duplicates (unlike `except`/`EXCEPT DISTINCT`), treats NULLs as equal for matching purposes, and ignores ordering — exactly the semantics you want for 'same table contents'. Because both sides use DECIMAL(10,2) for money, 107.99 matches 107.99 exactly; had one side used DOUBLE you would be comparing 107.9892 against 107.99 and the counts would be non-zero.

Step 3 — plan equality. Print both plans and compare node by node:

```

df_api.explain()

df_sql.explain()

```

Both show the same operator sequence — a `FileScan` with the pushed projection/`ReadSchema`, a `Project` containing the identical `to_date`, `CAST` and `CASE WHEN` expressions, an `Exchange` (range partitioning) and a `Sort [amount DESC NULLS LAST]`. Identical plans are expected because both front-ends build one unresolved logical plan that the same Catalyst optimizer rewrites into one physical plan.

What a step-2 failure with a step-3 pass would mean: the plans are structurally the same but the expression details differ — a different threshold constant (100 vs 100), `1.08` vs `1.8`, HALF_UP vs truncating cast, or a branch order that changes the label. The optimizer produced the same operator shape from different expression trees, so plan comparison is a necessary but not sufficient check; only the row comparison catches the wrong constant.

A sort-column bug: if the SQL version ended with `ORDER BY amount_with_tax DESC` instead of `ORDER BY amount DESC`, step 1 and step 2 would both pass — the multiset of rows is unchanged — and the physical plan would look almost identical, differing only in the sort key attribute. The test only exposes it if you also compare order-sensitive output, e.g. `df_api.collect() == df_sql.collect()` (safe here with six rows, dangerous at production scale because `collect()` pulls every row to the driver), or by asserting the sequence of `order_id` values, which resolves to A-1001, A-1004, A-1006, A-1003, A-1002, A-1005.

Analysis — Equivalence testing needs to be stated as a property, not as an eyeball check: two DataFrames are equivalent when their schemas match and their multisets of rows match — ordering is metadata about presentation, not about contents. That is why `exceptAll` in both directions is the right primitive: one direction alone would miss rows present only on the right, and `except` (distinct) would hide duplicate-grain bugs. Comparing schemas rather than printed values is what catches the most common real-world defect in this pipeline, an implicit type drift where a DOUBLE leaks into a money column and the last cent differs. Comparing physical plans is a useful third check because a lazily built plan is the artifact the engine actually executes, but it validates shape rather than constants, and a plan can be identical in structure while computing different numbers. Two operational cautions follow. First, every check here is an action (`count()`, `collect()`, `explain()` with statistics); until one of them runs, both DataFrames are just plans and nothing has been computed. Second, on wide tables the row-level checks are cheap but the shuffle they trigger is not, which is why teams compare schemas and plan lineage on the full dataset and compare rows on a sampled subset — and why the practice of pruning to the few needed columns early is worth doing everywhere, since columnar storage rewards it with dramatically less data read from disk [source p.239].

actions.text: Now let's stop talking about deriving columns in the abstract and actually build one. This worked problem is exactly the shape of task the exam likes: you're given a raw orders DataFrame and asked to produce a small revenue report — order_id, a real DATE, the amount cast to DECIMAL(10,2), an amount_with_tax, and a revenue_band of high, medium, or low, sorted by amount descending. Read the requirement carefully before you type anything, because almost every graded detail lives in the types and the ordering.

Problem 1 gives you the worked solution. Notice the strategy: one single select derives all five columns at once. We keep order_id as-is, wrap the timestamp with to_date to get order_date, cast amount to decimal(10,2), multiply amount by 1.08 and cast the product back to decimal(10,2), and build the band with when(amount >= 1000, 'high').when(amount >= 100, 'medium').otherwise('low'). Then orderBy amount descending. Five columns, one projection, one plan.

The hint points you at predicates in the same SELECT, and that's the crux of the when/otherwise chain. Order matters. The engine evaluates the branches top-down, so you must test the strictest threshold first — greater than or equal to one thousand — before the looser greater than or equal to one hundred. If you flip them, every order above a hundred matches the medium branch and the high band silently disappears. You'll get no error, just a quietly wrong report.

Now look at the SQL version and the analysis underneath it. Both front-ends are the same engine — the DataFrame API and Spark SQL compile down to one logical plan. The SQL writes CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2)), a CASE WHEN with the same top-down thresholds, and ORDER BY amount DESC. The exam-ready move is to prove equivalence rather than assert it: run explain() on both and confirm you see a single plan. That's your evidence, and it's exactly the kind of reasoning a scenario question will reward.

Problem 2 shifts to a trap that catches people in code review. A junior engineer writes the same report using chained withColumn calls instead of one select, and the results don't match. Let's see why.

The hint tells you the answer: reordering alone repairs the high band, but nothing else. That's because withColumn is a projection — it appends or replaces a column by name and returns a brand-new DataFrame. When the engineer builds the band with the looser condition first, the high band is swallowed by the same top-down evaluation we just discussed. Reordering the withColumn calls fixes the band, but it does nothing about the other problems hiding in that chain.

Here's the clean rebuild — one projection, one sort. The lesson isn't that withColumn is forbidden; it's that it's convenient for adding or replacing a single column, and costly when you chain many of them on a wide table. Each call inflates the logical plan, and the optimizer has more to untangle before it can push anything down. Deriving five columns in a single select or selectExpr is usually the cleaner and more optimizer-friendly choice.

Problem 4 raises the stakes: two DataFrames that are supposed to be identical, and you have to decide whether they truly are. The hint frames it as three independent concerns — and the worked solution walks through schema equality first, comparing the column names and their types, because two tables with identical rows but different decimal precision are not interchangeable.

The closing analysis locks in the exam vocabulary: equivalence testing has to be stated explicitly, never assumed. So the full answer is schema equality, then row-set equality, then ordering where the contract demands it. And remember that last pitfall we hit earlier — casting a non-numeric string yields NULL rather than raising an error, so validate before you cast, and remember orderBy is still lazy. Nothing is sorted until an action such as display or write actually runs. Everything on this page is one idea: derive deliberately, test your branches top-down, and verify equivalence instead of trusting it.

scenes.title: Spark SQL vs. PySpark DataFrame API

elements.content: Dimension  |  Spark SQL  |  PySpark DataFrame API

Compilation and execution plan (the equivalence precondition)
Spark SQL: A SQL string is parsed by the Catalyst analyzer and optimized into the same logical and physical plan the DataFrame API produces, so any two queries that are logically identical return identical rows in identical order-independent sets.
PySpark DataFrame API: Every transformation call builds a logical plan that Catalyst optimizes with the same rule set, because Spark creates a DAG of steps from the code we write for ingesting, joining, and writing out data, whether that code is SQL text or DataFrame methods [source p.346].

Readability for set-based logic
Spark SQL: A five-table join with two levels of aggregation reads as one declarative statement, and SQL can build genuinely complex DAGs using common table expressions, SQL scripts, or an orchestration tool rather than degenerating into nested subqueries [source p.339].
PySpark DataFrame API: The same join becomes a chain of df.join(...).groupBy(...).agg(...) calls whose intermediate shape is visible only if the reader tracks every new DataFrame variable, which is why the API is preferred for procedural, step-by-step logic rather than pure set algebra.

Parameterization and dynamic column names
Spark SQL: A literal cannot be bound as a parameter inside spark.sql() without interpolation, so f-string construction of the query text forces a fresh parse of the string for every distinct value; selecting 200 column names known only at runtime requires generating SQL text by concatenation, which is untested string building.
PySpark DataFrame API: A Python variable binds directly into the expression tree, so rate = 1.08 followed by df.withColumn('amount_with_tax', col('amount') * rate) yields exactly 108.0 for an order with amount = 100.00, and the same logical shape is reused for every rate value; dynamic columns come from a list comprehension such as df.select(*[col(c).alias(c.lower()) for c in cols]).

Testability and reuse
Spark SQL: A SQL statement stored as a string inside a notebook can only be exercised by executing it against a live session, and the maintainability questions an engineer should ask are how difficult the transformation is to code in SQL, how readable and maintainable the resulting SQL code will be, and whether some of it should be pushed into a custom library for reuse across the organization [source p.339].
PySpark DataFrame API: The transformation can be factored into a plain Python function that accepts a DataFrame and returns a DataFrame, so a pytest suite can assert the output schema and the exact row values on a three-row local fixture before the job ever touches production data.

Where the code physically lives
Spark SQL: It lives as text inside Databricks SQL dashboards, shared views, Lakeflow SQL pipeline definitions, or a spark.sql() string argument, which means it is portable to any engine that speaks the same dialect and can be reviewed by an analyst who does not read PySpark.
PySpark DataFrame API: It lives inside a Python notebook, wheel, or Lakeflow Job, which couples it to the cluster's PySpark version and the Python dependency set but makes it importable, schedulable, and lintable as ordinary Python code.

Runtime efficiency and the language boundary
Spark SQL: The statement executes entirely inside the JVM-resident Scala engine with no Python round trip, so a job that ingests three JSON API sources, converts them to a relational shape, joins them, and filters the result with a SQL statement pays no interpreter overhead [source p.346].
PySpark DataFrame API: PySpark is an API wrapper that pushes work into native Scala code running in the JVM, so the API path itself is not slow; the performance trap is dropping to a Python UDF, which forces data to be passed to Python where processing is less efficient [source p.341].

Interoperability at the boundary (the practical answer)
Spark SQL: After df.createOrReplaceTempView('orders') registers the DataFrame, an analyst can run spark.sql('SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status') against those exact rows without any change to the Python code that produced them.
PySpark DataFrame API: spark.sql(...) returns a DataFrame, so result = spark.sql('SELECT ... FROM orders').filter(col('amount') > 100) keeps chaining in Python, which means the two interfaces are interchangeable stages inside a single pipeline rather than competing architectures.

Failure surfacing and error detection
Spark SQL: An unresolved column or malformed expression fails at analysis time with an error such as UNRESOLVED_COLUMN or a parse exception raised at the exact line where spark.sql() is called, and no data is read.
PySpark DataFrame API: Because a DataFrame is lazily evaluated, a missing column is only caught when the plan is analyzed during an action, so the error may surface several cells later at .count(), .show(), or .write() rather than at the offending transformation.

Reuse of computed results across consumers
Spark SQL: CREATE VIEW stores only the query text and re-executes it on every reference, although some OLAP systems can convert federated queries into materialized views, which persist the result and give repeated readers a cheaper path [source p.351].
PySpark DataFrame API: The DataFrame object is itself a reusable logical plan, but avoiding recomputation requires an explicit df.cache() or df.persist(), plus an unpersist() call to release the cluster memory when the pipeline stage is finished.

Typical certification-exam framing
Spark SQL: Exam items select SQL when the scenario is self-contained and set-based: reporting queries, Databricks SQL dashboards, shared views, and quick ad-hoc exploration where no runtime parameters, loops, or unit tests are involved.
PySpark DataFrame API: Exam items select the DataFrame API when the scenario names parameters, iteration over dynamic column names, unit tests, or orchestration inside a Python workflow, and the expected justification is tooling and maintainability rather than speed.

Takeaway — Choose Spark SQL when the transformation is self-contained and set-based — reporting, Databricks SQL dashboards, shared views, and ad-hoc exploration — and no runtime parameters, dynamic column lists, or unit tests are required [source p.339].

Takeaway — Choose the PySpark DataFrame API when the logic needs parameters, loops over dynamic column names, unit tests, or orchestration inside a Python workflow, because those needs cannot be expressed cleanly as a single static SQL string [source p.339].

Takeaway — Do not justify either choice with performance: both paths compile to the same Catalyst-optimized plan, and the only genuine efficiency trap is escaping to a Python UDF, which forces data into Python where processing is less efficient [source p.341].

Takeaway — Interoperate instead of choosing globally: register frames with createOrReplaceTempView and consume spark.sql() results as DataFrames so each stage of one pipeline uses the interface that is more readable for that stage, and remember that a DataFrame read once and reused without cache() or persist() is recomputed.

actions.text: We've seen how to derive columns and test our branches. Now the natural next question: given that Spark SQL and the PySpark DataFrame API can express the same transformation, which one should you reach for? This page gives you the decision rule, using the same side-by-side structure the certification exam loves. Let's walk it down, row by row.

Start with the row that settles the most arguments. Both interfaces compile to the same Catalyst-optimized plan. Catalyst is Spark's query optimizer — the component that rewrites your logic into an efficient physical plan. Because SQL and the DataFrame API feed that same optimizer, correctness and performance are equivalent. So never justify a choice by saying one is faster.

Next, readability for set-based logic. When the transformation is a clean set operation — a join, an aggregate, a filter — SQL reads exactly like the business question. Five lines of SQL often describe what a dozen chained DataFrame calls would. For reports and shared views, that clarity is worth a lot.

Now the rows where the DataFrame API pulls ahead. Parameterization and dynamic column names: building a query with a variable, or looping over column names, is awkward in pure SQL but trivial in Python. And testability and reuse — a DataFrame function is just Python, so you can unit-test it like any other function. That's a real maintainability advantage in production code.

Notice the row on typical certification-exam framing. The exam does not ask which is faster — it asks you to match the interface to the scenario. So learn the triggers: self-contained and set-based points to SQL; parameters, loops, or tests point to the DataFrame API.

And the most practical takeaway: interoperate instead of choosing a global winner. Creating a temp view with createOrReplaceTempView exposes a DataFrame to SQL, and spark.sql returns a DataFrame you can keep chaining. Mix them freely in one pipeline — query in SQL where it's readable, switch to Python where you need control. Next, we'll put this decision rule to work.

scenes.title: Lesson Assessment: Spark SQL and DataFrame Fundamentals

questions.question: A Delta table has a nullable STRING column named status, and some rows have status = NULL. A colleague runs two logically equivalent jobs against that table: `orders.filter(col('status') != 'completed')` and `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status != 'completed'`. Which statement about the rows returned is correct?

options.label: Both return the same rows, and every row whose status is NULL is excluded, because a predicate that evaluates to NULL is not TRUE and only rows with a TRUE predicate survive the filter.
Both return the same rows, and rows whose status is NULL are included, because NULL is treated as an ordinary string value that is simply not equal to 'completed'.
The DataFrame version includes the NULL rows while the SQL version excludes them, because the DataFrame API uses Python equality semantics and SQL uses three-valued logic.
The DataFrame version fails at analysis time with an AnalysisException because the not-equal operator cannot be applied to a nullable column, while the SQL version runs and drops the NULL rows.

questions.analysis: Both interfaces evaluate the predicate with SQL's three-valued logic: a comparison involving NULL yields UNKNOWN, not TRUE, and a filter (predicate) keeps a row only when the predicate evaluates to TRUE. So `status != 'completed'` silently drops completed rows AND all rows where status is NULL, and the row count returned is strictly smaller than total rows minus the completed count. This is exactly the read-with-a-predicate semantics described for queries generally [source p.299], and the trap is assuming that filtering by one status automatically captures 'everything else'. To deliberately include unknown statuses you must say so: `orders.filter(col('status').isNull() | (col('status') != 'completed'))` in the DataFrame API, or `WHERE status IS NULL OR status <> 'completed'` in SQL. Option B is wrong because NULL is the absence of a value, not a string. Option C is wrong because Spark SQL and the DataFrame API compile to the same Catalyst logical plan, so they cannot disagree on NULL handling — the API is a builder for the same semantics, not a Python-semantics layer. Option D is wrong because nullable comparisons are perfectly legal; they simply evaluate to UNKNOWN. Practical consequence: when you build 'not completed' style filters, always reconcile your counts with `df.filter(col('status').isNull()).count()` or you will quietly lose rows before writing downstream.

questions.question: Your team must read a 500 GB directory of newline-delimited JSON event files from cloud object storage. A teammate proposes `spark.read.option('inferSchema', True).json(path)` so nobody has to write a schema declaration. Which statement correctly describes the cost and the risk of that choice?

options.label: It is essentially free for JSON, because the reader consults file metadata (the footer written by the JSON writer) where column names and types are stored alongside the data.
It is required for JSON, because JSON carries no type metadata at all, so without inferSchema the reader cannot parse the files into columns and the read fails.

It forces Spark to do extra work over the source to sample the data and guess types, and the guessed types can differ from the ones your pipeline expects, so on a very large directory an explicit schema is both cheaper and more predictable.
It is safer than a declared schema, because the inferred schema is derived from the actual data rather than from a human's assumptions, so the resulting column types are guaranteed to be correct.

questions.analysis: Option C is correct on both counts. First, cost: inferSchema is not a metadata shortcut — Spark has to read into the source to sample values and decide types, which is an additional pass over the data that an explicit schema avoids entirely. In a large ingestion job this is real, repeated cost, and it is one reason practitioners declare the schema up front when converting raw sources into a relational shape [source p.346]. Second, risk: the inferred schema is a guess drawn from sampled values, so it can be narrower or different from what you need (a numeric-looking identifier inferred as a numeric type rather than STRING, a date-shaped string left as STRING, or a mixed column falling back to a string type), and the guess can change from run to run as new files land. Option A is wrong because JSON files have no footer and no embedded type metadata; that property belongs to columnar formats whose footers describe the columns, not to raw text JSON. Option B is wrong because JSON is perfectly readable without inferSchema: you either declare the schema yourself or the values arrive as strings — inferSchema is a convenience, not a prerequisite for parsing. Option D is wrong because 'derived from the data' is precisely the weakness: a sampled guess cannot be more authoritative than an explicitly declared, version-controlled schema, and it also silently omits nullability information you may care about. The exam-standard answer is therefore: declare the schema (or read from a table that already has one), and reserve inferSchema for interactive exploration of small data.

questions.question: Which statements about lazy evaluation and the Catalyst optimizer in Spark are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A transformation such as filter() or withColumn() returns immediately without reading any data; it only records a new logical plan, and nothing executes until an action such as show(), display(), count(), collect(), or write() is called.

Because execution is deferred until an action, Catalyst can first rewrite the plan — pushing filters below joins and aggregations, reading only the columns the query actually references, and folding or simplifying constant expressions — so the code you write is not necessarily the code that runs.

Optimization happens only once, at the moment the DataFrame object is created, so a later count() and a later show() execute two different plans over the same lineage and can legitimately return different rows.

A DataFrame is immutable, so every transformation returns a new DataFrame that shares the base's lineage; you can branch several pipelines off one base DataFrame and Spark still optimizes each branch, reusing the same scan where it can.

questions.analysis: A is correct: transformations are lazy descriptions of work. Calling filter or withColumn on a DataFrame does not touch the cluster — it returns a new DataFrame whose logical plan is one node deeper. Actions are what trigger the job, which is why a notebook cell containing only transformations appears to do nothing. B is correct and is the whole point of laziness: because Spark sees the entire chain before running anything, the optimizer can reorder and combine operations. Predicate pushdown moves filters as close to the source as possible, column pruning drops untouched columns before they are read or shuffled, and constant folding collapses expressions like amount * 1.08 into a literal — all decisions that are only possible if the engine has the complete plan rather than one step at a time. Spark builds this chain as a directed acyclic graph of steps derived from the code you write; it is the same graph whether the steps were expressed in SQL or in the DataFrame API, and parts of it can execute in cluster memory while large stages spill to disk [source p.346]. D is correct: DataFrames are immutable — a transformation never mutates the original, it produces a new DataFrame with its own lineage pointer back to the base. That is what makes branching safe and what lets the optimizer treat each branch as an independent query while still sharing the base scan. C is wrong on two counts: optimization is performed per action (the plan is analyzed and optimized each time an action runs, over the same deterministic lineage), and the plan is deterministic, so the same DataFrame and the same action cannot yield inconsistent row sets. The misconception behind C is that 'cached plan' means 'executed once' — it does not; only an explicit action executes anything, and only an explicit cache persists results.

questions.question: Which two statements give a valid justification for choosing Spark SQL (spark.sql against a temporary view) or the PySpark DataFrame API for a given transformation? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: When a SQL-fluent analyst will own and maintain the transformation, registering the DataFrame as a temporary view and writing spark.sql(...) is a defensible choice, because both interfaces compile to the same Catalyst plan and return the same result set — readability and maintainability are the real tiebreakers, not performance.
SQL cannot return a DataFrame, so any transformation whose output must feed several downstream branches has to be written with the DataFrame API.

When the transformation is assembled programmatically — for example the same logic applied in a loop over configuration values, or with column names supplied from variables and passed between Python functions — the DataFrame API is the better fit, since a DataFrame can be composed and returned where a SQL statement would have to be built as a string.
Because SQL is the be-all and end-all language for data transformation, text-heavy steps such as tokenizing or stemming raw text should be pushed into SQL rather than handled with library code.

questions.analysis: A and C are correct, and together they capture the exam's rule: the two interfaces are semantically equivalent, so the decision is about fit, not speed. A is right because both paths land in the same optimizer and produce the same rows, so giving ownership to a SQL-literate analyst costs nothing in correctness or performance and buys maintainability. C is right because the DataFrame API is a first-class programmatic object: it can be returned from a function, parameterized by variables, and reused across branches, which is exactly how a proficient engineer composes SQL with other operations inside a framework such as Spark rather than treating SQL as the only tool in the kit [source p.47]. B is wrong: spark.sql returns a DataFrame like any other, so SQL output is just as reusable, cacheable, and branchable as API output — the 'SQL cannot return a DataFrame' claim is a pure fabrication and a common exam trap. D is wrong because it inverts the source's position: the source explicitly rejects the idea that SQL is a be-all and end-all, noting that a proficient data engineer also recognizes when SQL is not the right tool and can choose a suitable alternative instead [source p.47]. The practical heuristic to remember: pick the interface that the person maintaining the logic reads most fluently, keep the heavy lifting in declarative form so Catalyst can optimize it, and drop into library code only for steps that genuinely have no SQL equivalent.

questions.question: You inherit /mnt/raw/orders/, a 200 GB directory of newline-delimited JSON order events with the fields order_id, customer_id, order_ts (ISO-8601 text), amount (text that sometimes contains malformed values such as 'n/a'), and status. The same data has already been landed as the Delta table prod.sales.orders with the schema order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE, status STRING. The requirement is to return order_id and amount for completed 2024 orders with amount >= 100. In your answer: (a) show the reader chain you would use for the raw files and explain why you would not lean on inferSchema here; (b) name the inspection calls you run before transforming and say which piece of schema metadata tells you whether a column is nullable; (c) write the filter and selection — DataFrame API or SQL — that produces the required rows; (d) explain what happens to rows whose amount text cannot be parsed as a number and how you would find them; and (e) state which of the two sources you would actually read and justify the choice.
questions.commentPrompt: Grade out of 100% with this rubric. (1) Reader chain and no-inference justification — 25%: chains the reader exactly once, e.g. spark.read.schema('order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE, status STRING').json('/mnt/raw/orders/') and explains that inferSchema costs an extra sampling pass over 200 GB and can guess types that differ from the intended ones, so an explicit schema is both faster and deterministic. Full credit requires the points about extra work AND about wrong/guessed types; naming only one caps this section at half. (2) Pre-transform inspection — 15%: names at least two of printSchema(), dtypes, columns, count(), display(df.limit(10)), and identifies the nullable flag on each StructField as the metadata that states nullability. (3) Filter and select expression — 20%: correct compound predicate with parentheses, e.g. orders.filter((col('status') == 'completed') & (year(col('order_ts')) == 2024) & (col('amount') >= 100)).select('order_id', 'amount'), or the equivalent SQL with IS/AND and '<>' rather than '=='. Award full credit only if the selection contains exactly the two requested columns and the predicate is logically complete; deduct for missing parentheses around individual conditions or for using '==' inside a SQL string. (4) Malformed amount values — 25%: states that casting a non-numeric string to DOUBLE yields NULL rather than raising an error under default (non-ANSI) cast semantics, so those rows silently fail the amount >= 100 test and quietly disappear from the result; proposes finding them by filtering on the cast result being null (e.g. counting rows where col('amount').cast('double').isNull() while the raw string is not null) and recommends an explicit decision to quarantine or drop them. Deduct 10% if the answer claims an exception is thrown by default. (5) Source choice — 15%: prefers spark.table('prod.sales.orders') because the Delta table already carries the typed schema and statistics, so there is no inference pass, no malformed-string risk, and filters can be pushed down to the storage layer; accepts the raw file path only if the answer also justifies re-deriving types and handling bad rows. Across the whole answer, deduct up to 10% for any statement that treats a DataFrame as mutable or treats a transformation as executing immediately.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. (a) Read the raw files by chaining the reader once, with the schema declared: `df = (spark.read.schema('order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE, status STRING').json('/mnt/raw/orders/'))`. Do not call spark.read twice to 'add' options — each reader is a fresh builder. Do not use inferSchema: Spark would have to scan into the 200 GB to sample values and guess types, which is an extra pass over a very large source, and the guess may not match the contract (a numeric-looking identifier narrowed to a numeric type, a date-shaped string left as STRING, or a type that shifts as new files arrive). Declaring the schema makes the read deterministic and drops the extra work. (b) Inspect before transforming: `df.printSchema()` for types and nullability, `df.dtypes` for a compact name-type list, `df.columns` for names, and `df.count()` or `display(df.limit(10))` for volume and a visual sanity check. The nullability answer lives in the schema itself: every StructField carries a `nullable` flag, and printSchema() shows it as `nullable = true` (or false) beside each column, so a declared schema that never sets nullability will report nullable = true for those fields. (c) The transformation, DataFrame API form: `result = (df.filter((col('status') == 'completed') & (year(col('order_ts')) == 2024) & (col('amount') >= 100)).select('order_id', 'amount'))`. Parentheses around each condition matter because `&` binds tighter than comparison in Python. The SQL form after `df.createOrReplaceTempView('orders_v')` is `SELECT order_id, amount FROM orders_v WHERE status = 'completed' AND year(order_ts) = 2024 AND amount >= 100`. Both forms compile to the same Catalyst plan, so the returned rows are identical. Note that because nothing executes until an action, neither form runs until you call show/display/count or write. (d) Under default cast semantics, `col('amount').cast('double')` returns NULL for 'n/a' instead of raising an error, so those rows fall out of `amount >= 100` silently — a lost-rows bug that looks like clean data. Detect them by comparing counts: rows where the raw string is not null but the cast is null, e.g. `df.filter(col('amount').isNotNull() & col('amount').cast('double').isNull()).count()`. Then decide explicitly whether to quarantine, correct, or drop them, and document the decision; never let them vanish unnoticed before a downstream aggregate. (e) Read `spark.table('prod.sales.orders')`. The Delta table already has the correct types and column statistics, so there is no inference pass and no malformed-string ambiguity at all — the same standardization step an ETL pipeline performs when it cleans and imposes business logic on data before loading it [source p.125]. If the file path must be used (for freshness or backfill), then the explicit schema plus the cast-null check above is the minimum protection, and the pipeline output should be written as a Parquet-formatted Delta table so the next consumer reads typed, statistics-bearing data instead of raw text [source p.346]. Because Spark builds the whole chain as a DAG of steps from your code, the source choice and the declared schema are optimizable up front rather than discovered row by row at runtime [source p.346].

actions.text: Now let's put that decision rule to the test. This assessment spans everything we just covered — reading data and inspecting schemas, filtering and selecting, deriving and casting columns, laziness and the Catalyst optimizer, and how to choose between Spark SQL and the DataFrame API. Take each question on your own and commit to a answer before you move on.

Five items here: three single-choice, one multiple-choice, and one short-answer that asks you to reason through a realistic scenario end to end. Read the short-answer prompt carefully — it has several parts, and a complete response addresses each one. Once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning with you and flag anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Reading and Writing Data: Lesson Roadmap

elements.content: Reading and Writing Data: Roadmap
Read options are declared explicitly: format, header, delimiter, schema; CSV encodes none [source p.284].
Write modes: 'error' (default) fails on existing paths, 'overwrite' replaces, 'append' adds rows.
Schema evolution: study the source schema before ingest, then let mergeSchema add new columns [source p.268].
Format choice: parquet is the default; format variety keeps growing, so pick per source [source p.36].

One API, two directions: spark.read and df.write share the same .format()/.option() chain [source p.346].

Worked example: mode('append') turns 12 rows into 24.

Default format is parquet; default mode is 'error'.

actions.text: Now we shift to a new lesson: reading and writing data. This is where the exam's ELT domain really starts to bite, because almost every question here is about options and defaults. Let me walk you through the roadmap for this section.

The first thing to internalize is that there is one API with two directions. On the read side you have spark.read, which is a DataFrameReader. On the write side you have df.write, the DataFrameWriter. Both are driven by the same three methods — format, option, and then load or save. Learn the pattern once and you've learned both directions.

Our first decision point is read options. These are declared explicitly — you name the format, and then you control details like header, separator, and inference. The exam likes to test whether you can spot a read that silently returns the wrong result because an option was missing.

Second, write modes. The key fact here is the default: error, also called errorifexists, fails when the target already exists. That default is the single biggest source of distractors on the exam, so we'll spend real time on overwrite, append, ignore, and error, and what each one actually does to the target table.

Third, schema evolution. The discipline is to study the source schema before you write. When upstream adds a column, you need to know which knob absorbs it and which knob overwrites the target — we'll cover mergeSchema and overwriteSchema side by side.

And fourth, format choice. Remember that parquet is the default format when you don't specify one, and the format varies the options available to you. CSV, Parquet, and Delta each behave differently, and we'll build a worked end-to-end pipeline so you can see all four decision points working together. Let's get started.

scenes.title: Reading Data with Explicit Options

elements.content: Reading Data with Explicit Options

spark.read.format("csv"|"parquet"|"delta")

  .option(key, value).schema(ddl).load(path)

spark.read.table("catalog.schema.table")
CSV — all columns typed as string; header defaults to false. [source p.284]
Parquet — schema in the file footer; Delta — in the log. [source p.284]
inferSchema — extra pass; DDL is faster, deterministic types. [source p.284]
Both are self-describing, so an explicit read schema is optional.
Worked example — 500 files × 100 MB = 50 GB, read twice. [source p.346]
Bad rows — mode PERMISSIVE/DROPMALFORMED/FAILFAST or badRecordsPath.

actions.text: We just mapped out the reading and writing roadmap, so now let's open up the first stage: reading data with explicit options. The word to hold onto here is 'explicit' — in production, we don't let the reader guess.

Here is the general form you need to memorize for the exam. You call spark.read, then .format with the source — csv, parquet, or delta — then chain a series of .option(key, value) calls, and finish with .load(path). There's also a shortcut when the table is already registered in Unity Catalog: spark.read.table, taking the fully-qualified catalog dot schema dot table name. Same result, one less call.

Now, CSV is the option-hungry format — this is a favourite exam trap. By default, header is false, meaning your first data row gets swallowed as a header. The separator defaults to a comma, so a semicolon file collapses into one column. And most importantly, every column is typed as string. CSV carries no types, so unless you supply inferSchema or an explicit schema, you get strings and nothing else.

You might be tempted to reach for inferSchema, and it does work — but notice the cost. It triggers an extra full pass over the data just to guess the types. In production code, we skip that pass and hand Spark an explicit DDL schema string through .schema(). It's faster, and critically, it's deterministic: the same file always produces the same types, run after run.

Contrast that with Parquet and Delta, which are self-describing formats. Parquet keeps the schema in the file footer, and Delta keeps it in the transaction log. Because the schema travels with the data, an explicit read schema is optional here — Spark reads the types straight out of the files. That's the core distinction on this page: CSV needs you to describe it, Parquet and Delta describe themselves.

Let's make the cost concrete. Imagine a dataset of five hundred files at one hundred megabytes each — fifty gigabytes in total. If you ask for inferSchema on that CSV, Spark reads all fifty gigabytes once simply to guess types, and then reads it again to actually process it. With an explicit schema, you pay for one pass. On large tables, that difference alone can double your read time, and double your bill.

Finally, what happens when a row is malformed — too few columns, a stray quote, a broken newline? You control the behaviour with the mode option. PERMISSIVE is the default: it stuffs unparseable values into nulls and keeps going. DROPMALFORMED silently discards the bad rows. FAILFAST stops the job on the first offender. And when you need to keep the rejects for investigation rather than lose them, you point badRecordsPath at a location and Spark writes them out as JSON.

So to pull this together: explicit options give you control, and the format decides how much control you actually need. Ask yourself two questions every time — does this format describe itself, and how strict should I be about bad rows? Answer those, and the read code writes itself. Next, we'll checkpoint this with a short quiz before moving into a full worked example.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Reading Data and Read Options

questions.question: A notebook runs orders = spark.read.csv("/databricks-datasets/retail/orders.csv") with no other options, then calls orders.printSchema(). The file's first line is the text header order_id,customer_id,amount,status. Which statement correctly describes the resulting DataFrame?

options.label: Spark consumes the first line as the column names and infers each column's type, so amount is typed DOUBLE.
The first line is returned as an ordinary data row, the columns are auto-named _c0, _c1, _c2, _c3, and every column has type STRING.
The first line is returned as an ordinary data row, but Spark still infers types from the values, so amount is typed DOUBLE.
Spark raises an AnalysisException because no header option was supplied, so the read must be retried after adding .option("header", True).

questions.analysis: spark.read.csv(path) is shorthand for spark.read.format("csv").load(path) and inherits the CSV reader defaults: header=false and inferSchema=false. Because header is false, the line order_id,customer_id,amount,status is parsed as a data row, and because inferSchema is false every column is created as STRING with positional names _c0 through _c3. Option A describes header=True plus inferSchema=True, which is a different reader configuration; option C keeps header=false while claiming inference occurred, which cannot happen without inferSchema=True (or a declared schema); option D is wrong because the default parse mode is PERMISSIVE, so a plain CSV read succeeds rather than raising. This is exactly why schema is described as the instructions that tell us how to read the data, the schema-on-read pattern: without an explicit declaration Spark has only the literal bytes and falls back to reader defaults [source p.245]. Note also that the unqualified spark.read.load(path) defaults to the Parquet format, so CSV must be named either through .csv() or .format("csv") - a default that is tested directly.

questions.question: A pipeline must read a 400 GB CSV file that has a header line and whose columns are already known: order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, amount DOUBLE, status STRING. Which of the following statements about inferring the schema versus declaring it are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: With .option("inferSchema", True), Spark makes an additional pass over the file to sample values and choose types, which costs extra I/O and wall-clock time on a file of this size.
Passing .schema("order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, amount DOUBLE, status STRING") lets Spark skip that inference pass and parse directly into the declared types.
inferSchema is the better production choice because it automatically adapts to schema drift, while a declared schema must be edited by hand whenever the file changes.
The canonical reader chain is spark.read.format("csv").option("header", True).schema(ddl).load(path), and no work is performed until an action such as count() or display() triggers execution.

questions.analysis: inferSchema=True forces Spark to read a sample of the file in a first pass to guess types, which is measurable overhead at 400 GB (A is correct). Declaring the schema with .schema(ddl) removes that pass and pins the types so the schema is identical on every run and comparable across days (B and D are correct). Option C is the classic misconception: inference is convenient during exploration but non-deterministic in production - a column such as order_id that happens to contain only digits in today's file is inferred as BIGINT and silently loses leading zeros, and the inferred type can change when tomorrow's file contains a non-numeric value. The chain in option D is the canonical ordering - format, then options and schema, then load - and because Spark is lazy, load() only builds a plan; nothing runs until an action triggers the DAG of steps [source p.346]. Declaring the schema for the incoming files is the schema-on-read pattern, where structure is applied when data is read rather than enforced when it is written [source p.245].

questions.question: A nightly job reads CSV order files such as /mnt/raw/orders/2024-06-01.csv. Some files contain rows with the wrong number of delimiters. The team wants the job to keep the well-formed rows, exclude the malformed rows from the DataFrame, and keep a copy of the excluded rows at /mnt/quarantine/bad_orders for later inspection. The expected columns are held in the DDL string ddl. Which reader chain does exactly this?

options.label: spark.read.format("csv").option("header", True).option("badRecordsPath", "/mnt/quarantine/bad_orders").schema(ddl).load(path)
spark.read.format("csv").option("header", True).option("mode", "FAILFAST").option("badRecordsPath", "/mnt/quarantine/bad_orders").schema(ddl).load(path)
spark.read.format("csv").option("header", True).option("mode", "DROPMALFORMED").schema(ddl).load(path)
spark.read.format("csv").option("header", True).option("mergeSchema", True).mode("append").load(path)

questions.analysis: Option A is correct because the default CSV parse mode is PERMISSIVE: malformed records do not fail the job, and when the reader is additionally given badRecordsPath those records are written to that location and skipped from the returned DataFrame, which is precisely the required quarantine behavior. Option B fails the requirement that the job keep running, since FAILFAST raises as soon as a malformed record is encountered. Option C silently discards the malformed rows, so no copy is retained and the audit requirement cannot be met. Option D applies write-side settings to a read: mergeSchema is a Parquet/Delta write option used when appending files with new columns, and mode("append") is a SaveMode belonging to DataFrameWriter, not a parse mode on DataFrameReader - a distractor that mirrors the common mistake of copying a write chain into a read. Note the read-side spelling: the parse mode is passed as .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE" | "DROPMALFORMED" | "FAILFAST") and is not the same method as the writer's .mode(SaveMode). Retaining the raw rejected rows instead of overwriting them follows the insert-only habit of never mutating source truth so the bad data can be re-processed after the upstream fix [source p.342]. Declaring ddl at read time also removes ambiguity about which fields are expected, treating the schema as instructions for reading the data rather than as a constraint enforced at write time [source p.245], and this read is only the first node of the larger DAG the job will build as it parses, filters, and writes the cleaned result [source p.346].
