scenes.title: Schema Evolution: mergeSchema and overwriteSchema

elements.content: Schema Evolution on Write: mergeSchema vs. overwriteSchema
Default: Delta enforces the target schema on write — a mismatched append fails [source p.346].
mergeSchema — additive on append

df.write.option("mergeSchema", "true")

.mode("append").format("delta").save(path)

Additive only — never drops or retypes columns.

A new field is a metadata change [source p.332].
overwriteSchema — replace on overwrite

df.write.option("overwriteSchema", "true")

.mode("overwrite").format("delta").save(path)

Ignored on append — only fires with mode overwrite.

Breaks readers and cached plans [source p.343].

Worked example: append-only fact table [source p.324].

Target = 3 columns, 500 rows; source adds `region`.

Plain append of 3 rows → schema mismatch error.

mergeSchema=true → 4 columns, 503 rows, nulls.

Quiz: a full refresh must REPLACE the target schema.

A) mergeSchema + append

B) overwriteSchema + append

C) overwriteSchema + overwrite

actions.text: Now we come to the write option that trips up more candidates than almost any other: schema evolution on write. This page contrasts mergeSchema and overwriteSchema, and by the end you should know exactly which option unlocks which behaviour.

Start with the default. Delta enforces the target schema on write. If your incoming DataFrame carries a column the table does not have, the append fails outright rather than silently reshaping the table. That is a deliberate safety guarantee, not an inconvenience — it stops a stray upstream column from quietly changing your contract with downstream consumers.
When you do want new columns absorbed, you opt in with mergeSchema. Think of it as additive on append: the new columns get folded into the target schema and existing rows simply carry nulls for them.

Here is the syntax you should be able to write from memory. Set the option mergeSchema to true on the writer, keep the format as delta, and in this case use mode append, then save to the path. Because it is additive, it is the right tool for a steadily growing source that keeps adding attributes.

But be precise about what additive means. mergeSchema can never drop a column, and it can never retype a column. If the incoming type conflicts with what is already there, mergeSchema will not save you — that failure has to be resolved upstream or with an explicit cast.

The second knob is overwriteSchema, and it plays a completely different game. This one replaces the target schema entirely. It is the option you reach for on a full refresh, when the new data is meant to redefine the table rather than extend it.
Note the pairing in the code: overwriteSchema set to true, but this time with mode overwrite. That combination is what makes it fire.

And here is the classic exam trap. overwriteSchema is ignored on append — it only takes effect with mode overwrite. So if a question shows you option overwriteSchema with mode append, the answer is that nothing happens to the schema; the option is silently skipped. Lock that pairing into memory.

Let's ground it with the worked example on the slide: an append-only fact table. New attributes arrive from source over time, so you use mergeSchema with append and the table grows its columns additively. Now suppose the upstream system renames or retypes a field and you need a clean cut. That is a schema change, not an append — so you run a full refresh with overwriteSchema and mode overwrite, and the target schema is rebuilt from the incoming data.

Before you turn the page, answer the quiz prompt in your head: a full refresh must replace the target schema. Which option, and with which mode? If you said overwriteSchema with mode overwrite, you have got it. One last caution while you are here: a full schema overwrite invalidates existing readers and cached plans, so any downstream consumer of that table needs to be checked before you ship it.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Schema Evolution and Write Options

questions.question: A Delta table stored at /mnt/silver/orders currently declares three columns: order_id, customer_id and amount. Tonight's batch produces a DataFrame with those same three columns plus two new ones, fulfilment_centre and promised_date, and the job must add only the new rows to the table without disturbing the 400 million rows already stored there. Which write call is correct?

options.label: df.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").save("/mnt/silver/orders")
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("overwriteSchema", "true").save("/mnt/silver/orders")
df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("mergeSchema", "true").save("/mnt/silver/orders")
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").option("overwriteSchema", "true").save("/mnt/silver/orders")

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: The two options are not synonyms; they answer two different questions. mergeSchema answers 'may the target table grow to accommodate columns the incoming data brings?', while overwriteSchema answers 'may the target table's declared schema be replaced outright by the incoming one?'. Only mergeSchema is compatible with adding rows, so only option A satisfies both requirements: mode("append") preserves the existing 400 million rows, and option("mergeSchema", "true") performs schema evolution (the ability of a table to absorb structural change, here the arrival of two new columns, without rewriting existing data). Option B pairs the option that replaces a schema with the mode that refuses to replace anything — the two controls come from different worlds and do not compose. Option C does merge the new columns into the schema, but mode("overwrite") discards the existing table contents, which the requirement explicitly forbids. Option D stacks both schema options on an append write, which is contradictory: one option asks Delta to extend the schema and the other asks it to substitute the schema, and the combination is rejected rather than resolved. This pairing of option and mode is a direct instance of the traditional schema-on-write contract, in which a table has an integrated schema and any write to that table must conform to it [source p.245]; Delta merely relaxes that contract in a controlled way through mergeSchema. Note the operational cost of the relaxed contract: once columns can be added automatically, downstream transformations that select an explicit column list can break silently, which is exactly the risk described for automated schema updates in columnar systems [source p.344].

questions.question: A colleague writes df.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("overwriteSchema", "true").save(path), believing the call will append the new rows and also adopt the incoming schema. What actually happens at write time?

options.label: The rows are appended and the table's schema is replaced by the incoming DataFrame schema.
The write is rejected with an error: overwriteSchema is only honoured when the mode is overwrite, so nothing is appended and the table schema is untouched.
The rows are appended and overwriteSchema is silently ignored, so the write succeeds even when the incoming schema differs from the table's.
Specifying overwriteSchema implicitly promotes the write to overwrite mode, so the whole table is rewritten with the new schema.

questions.correctAnswer: B
questions.analysis: overwriteSchema is a schema-replacement instruction, and schema replacement is only meaningful when the write itself is a replacement. Delta therefore validates the option against the mode and refuses the combination: an append write carrying overwriteSchema fails rather than quietly doing half the job. The exact error string differs between runtime versions, but the outcome is stable and is what the exam tests — the call does not append rows, and the schema of the target table is not modified. Option A describes overwriteSchema semantics attached to the wrong mode. Option C describes the dangerous fantasy that an incompatible option is silently dropped; Delta is deliberately strict here, because silently ignoring the option would produce the very surprise of a table that does not match the code that wrote it. Option D is the mirror-image misconception: the option does not steer the mode, the mode constrains which options are legal. The design intent behind this strictness is the schema-on-write contract, in which a table's integrated schema governs every write to it [source p.245]. Contrast this with the legitimate pairing: when you genuinely want the new shape of the data to become the table's shape, you use mode("overwrite") with overwriteSchema, accepting that the old definition and the old rows are both replaced. A related organisational lesson applies: schema change is cheap mechanically, but uncoordinated schema change is what breaks downstream consumers, which is why versioning or a review path for schema changes is recommended when evolution is frequent [source p.274].

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Delta Lake write-time schema behaviour are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: With mode("append") and no schema option, an incoming DataFrame whose columns do not match the table is rejected at write time: the default behaviour is schema enforcement, not schema evolution.
option("mergeSchema", "true") can add brand-new columns to the target table, but it cannot remove an existing column and it cannot change the data type of an existing column.
Because it is a write-time schema tool, mergeSchema lets you drop a column that is no longer produced upstream, as long as mode("overwrite") is also used.

To make the target table's schema become exactly the incoming DataFrame's schema, including removed columns and re-typed columns, you use mode("overwrite") together with option("overwriteSchema", "true").
mergeSchema and overwriteSchema are interchangeable aliases: both merge the incoming schema into the existing table schema and differ only in spelling.

questions.correctAnswer: A, B, D
questions.analysis: Statement A is correct and is the default that candidates most often forget. Delta enforces schema on write: the table owns an integrated schema, and a write that does not conform is refused, which is the classic data-warehouse pattern in which any write to a table must conform to that table's schema [source p.245]. Consequently an append whose DataFrame has extra or differently typed columns fails with a schema-mismatch error instead of silently inventing columns; you must opt in to evolution explicitly. Statement B is correct because mergeSchema is an additive, union-style operation: it can widen the table by appending new columns, optionally filled with nulls for the pre-existing rows, but it has no vocabulary for subtraction or retyping. Removing a column or changing a column's type is a destructive change to the table's contract, and an additive option invalidates none of the historical data that depends on the old contract. Statement C is therefore false: dropping a column is exactly what mergeSchema cannot do — overwriteSchema is the option that can, and only under overwrite mode. Statement D is correct and is the paired behaviour the exam expects you to associate: overwriteSchema under mode("overwrite") makes the incoming schema authoritative, so columns absent from the new DataFrame disappear from the table definition and a column whose type changed is re-declared with the new type. The trade-off is that the previous schema and the rows written under it are replaced, so this is a deliberate schema migration rather than a routine nightly load. Statement E is false; it is the central distractor of this checkpoint. The two options sound interchangeable because both mention schema, but one governs addition and the other governs substitution, and they are legal under different write modes. This distinction matters operationally because the sources of change are outside the data team's control: an IoT device receiving a firmware update adds fields to its events, and a third-party API can alter its payload shape, which is precisely why schema evolution is described as common in event pipelines and as something with unintended downstream impact [source p.274]. For a university-level treatment, note the governance layer on top of the mechanics: columnar storage makes adding, deleting and renaming columns easier than row storage does, yet the organisational questions — which updates are automated, who reviews them, which downstream processes break — remain the hard part [source p.344]. A correct mental model is that Delta gives you three distinct contracts on write (enforce, extend additively, replace wholesale), and choosing the wrong one is a semantic error even when the job returns success.

actions.text: Time to check how well those two options have settled in. Work through each question on your own — read the write calls carefully and pick the one you'd actually ship.
I'll be right here once you submit, and we'll walk through anything that tripped you up together.

scenes.title: CSV vs Parquet vs Delta: Which Format, When

elements.content: Dimension  |  CSV  |  Parquet  |  Delta

Schema handling: where the schema lives and how it is applied
CSV: CSV carries no embedded schema, so every column arrives typed as string unless you pass an explicit DDL schema string to .schema() or accept the extra full pass over the data that inferSchema costs, and the header option supplies only names, never types.
Parquet: Parquet is self-describing: the physical schema — column names, types, nullability and nested structure — travels inside the data files themselves, so a reader recovers correct types with no inference pass and with no separate metadata file to keep in sync.
Delta: Delta stores its schema in the transaction log and enforces it on every write, rejecting a batch that does not conform unless schema evolution is explicitly enabled with mergeSchema or autoMerge, so a misconfigured upstream producer cannot silently corrupt the table.

Physical storage layout and compression mechanism
CSV: CSV serializes complete rows as sequential text, so a query that needs 4 of 40 columns still reads and parses 100% of the bytes and pays text-parsing CPU on every scan.
Parquet: Parquet pivots the data by column, storing each column in its own set of file pages inside row groups, which lets the engine read only the subset of fields a query touches and packs similar values next to each other for high compression ratios with minimal compression overhead [source p.419], [source p.239].
Delta: Delta adds no new data encoding: it stores Parquet files exactly as Parquet does and layers the _delta_log commit protocol on top, so it inherits columnar pruning and compression while the log records which data files belong to which table version.

Required read/write options and option surface
CSV: CSV is the option-hungry format: header defaults to false and sep defaults to comma, so production code must chain .option('header', True), .option('sep', '|') and .schema(...) before .load(path) to get deterministic names and types.
Parquet: Parquet needs essentially no options — spark.read.format('parquet').load(path) is sufficient — and options appear only for pruning (partition filters, basePath) rather than for basic correctness.
Delta: Delta reads require only spark.read.format('delta').load(path) or the spark.read.table('catalog.schema.table') shortcut, but writes may require options such as mergeSchema, overwriteSchema or replaceWhere to control how the table evolves.

Atomicity, ACID support, and concurrent-write safety
CSV: CSV offers no atomicity whatsoever: a failed or interrupted write leaves a truncated file in the prefix, two concurrent writers to the same path can interleave, and readers can observe a torn or half-written file.
Parquet: Parquet gives atomicity only at the level of a single file replacement — a reader sees either the old file or the new one — but a multi-file overwrite is not transactional and there is no isolation from a concurrent writer touching the same directory.
Delta: Delta's log-based commit protocol makes multi-file writes atomic and serializable: readers see a consistent snapshot, conflicting concurrent writers are detected and retried, and no reader ever observes a partially committed write.

Time travel, auditability and rollback
CSV: CSV keeps no version history at all, so recovering yesterday's data means restoring a separate copy from object-store versioning or a backup that you had to configure in advance.
Parquet: Parquet keeps no version history either; overwriting the directory destroys the previous state unless your object store happens to retain its own object versions, which is a storage-level property, not a table property.
Delta: Delta keeps every commit in the _delta_log, so you can read a prior state with .option('versionAsOf', N) or .option('timestampAsOf', ...) and roll the table back with RESTORE TABLE, which makes it the only one of the three that supports reproducible point-in-time queries.

Incremental ingestion and streaming support
CSV: CSV files are read in batch, or ingested by file-arrival tooling such as Auto Loader that treats each new file as a new object; there is no mechanism to read only the rows appended since your last query.
Parquet: Parquet is likewise an immutable-file format: incremental processing means tracking externally which files are new, and a streaming read over Parquet is still a directory scan with file-level bookkeeping.
Delta: Delta is natively both a streaming source and a sink: spark.readStream.format('delta').load(...) reads only newly committed files, and a Delta sink provides exactly-once streaming writes backed by checkpointed idempotent commits.

Typical role in the medallion lakehouse (the bronze/silver/gold layering of a lakehouse)
CSV: CSV belongs at the edge — bronze landing of files arriving from outside the platform and interchange with systems that can produce nothing else — so it is a raw ingredient rather than a serving format.
Parquet: Parquet is the columnar exchange format that databases export natively in order to bypass JDBC/ODBC and land data directly in the lake [source p.278], and it is a reasonable choice for immutable, read-mostly files when no transactional guarantee is needed [source p.346].
Delta: Delta is the default table format for refined layers: the bronze-to-silver conversion, every silver and gold table that is updated, appended incrementally or queried concurrently, and the write target of streaming pipelines that combine multiple sources and filter them with SQL before landing [source p.346].

Worked example: selective query cost over a 400 GB, 40-column table
CSV: If the 400 GB arrives as pipe-delimited CSV, a query selecting 4 columns with WHERE amount > 1000 still reads all 400 GB, parses every text field and applies the filter afterwards, so the scan equals 100% of the data and the parse cost is paid on every run.
Parquet: Stored as Parquet, the same 400 GB is organized as 40 column chunks per row group, so reading 4 of 40 columns touches roughly 10% of the bytes — about 40 GB before compression — and per-row-group min/max statistics let the reader skip row groups whose range excludes amount > 1000.
Delta: Delta reads the identical ~40 GB of Parquet data but first reads the tiny _delta_log, then prunes whole files by partition value and file-level statistics, so it is at worst equal to Parquet on scan cost and strictly cheaper whenever entire files can be skipped.

Cost of the dominant write patterns (overwrite, update, append)
CSV: A CSV overwrite deletes and rewrites the whole prefix, so correcting one day in a 40-million-row landing job rewrites 400 GB, and an append is only as safe as the writer's ability to complete the file.
Parquet: A Parquet overwrite rewrites every file in the target directory, and because files are immutable a single late-arriving record can force a full rewrite of the affected partition rather than an in-place update.
Delta: A Delta overwrite removes the old files from the current snapshot atomically and registers the new ones, while MERGE and UPDATE rewrite only the files containing matching keys, so updating 1% of the table touches roughly 1% of the data plus one log commit.

Takeaway — Choose CSV only at the boundary: raw external files, human-readable interchange and small one-off inspections, where the lack of schema and atomicity is tolerable because nothing has been refined yet.

Takeaway — Choose Parquet for immutable, read-mostly analytic files and for columnar export/import between engines, because schema travels with the data and column pruning shrinks scans, but accept that there is no ACID, no time travel and no concurrent-write safety.

Takeaway — Choose Delta the moment data is refined, updated, appended incrementally or queried by more than one writer, because ACID commits, schema enforcement, time travel and streaming sources and sinks are all required at that point.

Takeaway — Apply the decision rule end to end: land raw external files as CSV or JSON into bronze, then convert to Delta for anything refined, mutable, incrementally appended or concurrently queried, which is also the framing the exam tests.

actions.text: Now that we've worked through write modes and schema evolution, let's pull it all together and answer the question you'll face on nearly every pipeline: which format should I actually use? This side-by-side decision table compares CSV, Parquet, and Delta across the dimensions that really drive the choice.

Start with the orientation of the table. Each row is a format — CSV, Parquet, Delta — and each column is one dimension we care about: schema handling, storage layout, required read and write options, atomicity, incremental and streaming support, and the typical role it plays in the medallion lakehouse. Read it row by row, not column by column.

First, schema handling — where the schema actually lives. CSV is plain human-readable text with no embedded schema, so you must supply header, separator, and inferSchema yourself, and every reader guesses. Parquet is self-describing: the schema travels with the data, which is why column pruning and predicate pushdown work so well. Delta inherits Parquet's self-describing files but adds a transaction log that enforces and evolves the schema for you.

Next, the physical storage layout and compression. CSV is row-oriented and uncompressed by default, so a query that needs two columns still reads the whole file. Parquet is columnar and compressed, so you only read the columns you ask for. Delta is Parquet data files plus that _delta_log transaction log on top — same efficient columnar reads, but now with a source of truth for table state.

Then the one that trips people up on the exam: atomicity and ACID support. CSV has none — a failed write leaves you with a half-written file and no way to roll back. Parquet alone doesn't give you transactions either; it's immutable files with no concurrent-write safety. Only Delta, through the log, gives you ACID writes, isolation, and safe concurrent access.

That same log is what unlocks incremental ingestion and streaming. Delta tables are natural streaming sources and sinks, which is exactly what Auto Loader and Structured Streaming rely on. CSV and plain Parquet can't track what's already been processed, so you end up re-reading or over-counting on every run.

Let's make that concrete with the worked example. Picture a 400-gigabyte table and a selective query that filters one column and projects two more. Over CSV, you scan the entire 400 gigabytes. Over Parquet, column pruning and predicate pushdown cut that to a fraction. The storage format alone determines whether that query is cheap or expensive.

So here's the decision rule you should carry into the exam: land raw external files as CSV or JSON into bronze, then convert to Delta the moment the data becomes refined — updated, appended incrementally, or queried concurrently. CSV only at the boundary, Parquet for immutable read-mostly data, Delta for everything that's live. Let's move on and apply this write mode to a real daily refresh.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Choosing and Applying a Write Mode for a Daily Refresh

elements.content: Problem 1

A Delta Lake table lives at /mnt/silver/events in the silver layer of a medallion architecture (a bronze/silver/gold layering in which each layer holds progressively cleaned and conformed data). The table is partitioned by event_date, a DATE column: one directory per calendar day. Every night a scheduled job must replace the data for exactly one calendar day — tonight, 2024-06-01 — with a late-arriving batch of events, while every other day stays untouched. The orchestrator retries failed tasks, so the job must be re-runnable: running it once or three times must leave exactly the same table. Current state: the table holds 5,000,000 rows spread over 30 day partitions, and the 2024-06-01 partition currently holds 120,000 rows. Tonight's batch is a DataFrame df_late with 130,000 rows, every one of which has event_date = 2024-06-01. (a) Write the write statement for Option A, replaceWhere. (b) Write the write statement for Option B, dynamic partition overwrite, including the configuration line it requires. (c) State the precondition each option places on the target table and on df_late. (d) Compute the expected row count of the 2024-06-01 partition and of the whole table after one successful run, and after a second identical run.
Hint: Both options keep mode("overwrite"); they differ in how the writer decides which files 'overwrite' actually removes.

Worked solution
**Option A — replaceWhere.** We keep the overwrite mode and narrow it with a predicate:

df_late.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("replaceWhere", "event_date = '2024-06-01'").save("/mnt/silver/events")

Because the predicate mentions only the partition column event_date, Delta can resolve the matching files from table metadata instead of scanning data. One atomic commit then removes the data files of the 2024-06-01 partition (120,000 rows) and adds the new files containing all 130,000 rows of df_late. No other partition directory is touched.

**Option B — dynamic partition overwrite.** We flip the session-level behaviour of the overwrite mode from static to dynamic:

spark.conf.set("spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic")

df_late.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/mnt/silver/events")

The writer inspects the partition values present in df_late, finds only 2024-06-01, and replaces exactly those partitions. Everything else is left alone.

**Preconditions.** (i) The table must be partitioned by event_date. Partitioning means splitting one logical table into subtables by a field value, which is why date-based partitioning is so common for time-ranged analytics [source p.240]. (ii) With Option B, the DataFrame must contain every row you want to keep for every partition it touches — a partition that appears in df_late is deleted in full and rebuilt from df_late. (iii) With Option A, df_late should contain only rows satisfying the predicate; the predicate column must be the partition column for the fast, metadata-only replacement path. (iv) In both cases df_late must be a complete snapshot of the day, not just the newly arrived rows; this is the same requirement as the truncate-and-reload pattern, where a target is cleared of data and transformations are re-run into it, generating a new table version [source p.342].

**Arithmetic.** Non-target days: 5,000,000 − 120,000 = 4,880,000 rows. Target day after the write: 130,000 rows (the old 120,000 are gone). Whole table: 4,880,000 + 130,000 = 5,010,000 rows. On a second, identical run the predicate/dynamic scope still resolves to 2024-06-01 only: that partition is deleted (130,000 rows) and rewritten (130,000 rows), so the table still holds 4,880,000 + 130,000 = 5,010,000 rows. The operation is idempotent — the observable state after n runs is the state after one run.

Analysis — The teaching point is that 'overwrite' is not one behaviour but two nested scopes. mode("overwrite") alone is a table-scoped instruction: it removes the entire target and replaces it. Both solutions keep the mode but add a finer scope — a predicate (replaceWhere) or the set of partition values present in the DataFrame (dynamic overwrite). Mathematically we can write the result as a set operation: new_table = (old_table − P) ∪ D, where P is the set of rows removed and D is the DataFrame. For replaceWhere, P = {r ∈ old : r.event_date = 2024-06-01}; for dynamic overwrite, P = {r ∈ old : r.event_date ∈ {values present in D}}. Idempotency then follows because P and D are the same on every run. The classic mistakes: (1) assuming mode("overwrite") is 'safe' because it is atomic — it is atomic, but it atomically deletes 4,880,000 rows you wanted; (2) assuming dynamic partition overwrite is a default — spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode defaults to static, so the conf line is mandatory and is a favourite exam trap; (3) forgetting that dynamic overwrite deletes the whole partition, so a partial day-batch silently truncates that day. Choose replaceWhere when the replacement set is expressible as a predicate and you want the guard rail that non-matching rows in the DataFrame are caught; choose dynamic overwrite when the DataFrames you write are already scoped by their own partition values, e.g. a parametrised job that is handed one day at a time. This is exactly the kind of decision a Spark job in an Airflow-triggered pipeline must make before it writes its result [source p.346], and it matters wherever event data arrives late [source p.313].
Problem 2

Use the same table: /mnt/silver/events, partitioned by event_date, 5,000,000 rows total, of which 120,000 belong to 2024-06-01. The nightly batch df_late has 130,000 rows, all for 2024-06-01. Two engineers propose alternatives to the partition-scoped overwrite. Engineer 1 writes: df_late.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("/mnt/silver/events"). Engineer 2 writes: df_late.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/mnt/silver/events") and changes nothing else. (a) Give the whole-table row count and the 2024-06-01 row count after 1, 2, and 3 runs of Engineer 1's job. Derive the general formula. (b) Give the state of the table after Engineer 2's first run. (c) Explain, in terms of the re-runnability requirement, why neither job is acceptable, and state the minimal repair for each.
Hint: Append never removes anything (so repeats accumulate); plain overwrite with the default static setting removes everything (so one run is already fatal).

Worked solution
**(a) Engineer 1 — append.** Append adds new files without touching, deleting, or rewriting existing data, and it is the natural mode for incremental loads and streaming micro-batches.

Run 1: whole table = 5,000,000 + 130,000 = 5,130,000; 2024-06-01 = 120,000 + 130,000 = 250,000.

Run 2: whole table = 5,000,000 + 2 × 130,000 = 5,260,000; 2024-06-01 = 120,000 + 260,000 = 380,000.

Run 3: whole table = 5,000,000 + 3 × 130,000 = 5,390,000; 2024-06-01 = 120,000 + 390,000 = 510,000.

General formula after n runs: whole table = 5,000,000 + 130,000n; partition 2024-06-01 = 120,000 + 130,000n. Because the late batch is not a pure insert — the events already exist in the target — every retry multiplies the day by a factor and silently inflates downstream aggregates (sums, counts, distinct-user metrics) by 130,000 rows per retry.

**(b) Engineer 2 — plain overwrite, static mode (the default).** mode("overwrite") replaces the data in the target; with Delta this is an atomic replacement of data files, not a drop-and-recreate of the table. But the scope is the entire table: the writer first clears all data files, then writes df_late. Result: whole table = 130,000 rows, all with event_date = 2024-06-01. The 4,880,000 rows of the other 29 days are gone in a single commit, and — because the operation is atomic and successful — no error is raised.

**(c) Why both fail, and the minimal repair.** Re-runnability (idempotency) requires f(f(T)) = f(T). Append gives f(T) = T ∪ D, and since D ∩ T ≠ ∅, each application adds 130,000 rows: f(f(T)) ≠ f(T). Plain static overwrite gives f(T) = D for every T, which is idempotent in the narrow sense but is not a *refresh*: it destroys 29 days of data, so it fails the 'all other days stay untouched' requirement instead. Minimal repairs: for Engineer 1, add .option("replaceWhere", "event_date = '2024-06-01'") and keep mode("overwrite") — do not simply switch append to overwrite without the scope, which recreates Engineer 2's bug. For Engineer 2, either add the replaceWhere option or set spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode to dynamic before the write, as both make the effective write set exactly the 2024-06-01 partition.

Analysis — This problem isolates the two failure directions that any refresh job can take: under-deletion (append, duplicate rows) and over-deletion (unscoped overwrite, lost partitions). A useful mental checklist for a nightly refresh is: (1) does the operation remove the previous version of exactly the target day? (2) does it leave everything else byte-for-byte intact? (3) is the result of two runs the same as one? Append answers no to (1); plain overwrite answers no to (2); only a partition-scoped overwrite answers yes to all three. Common student errors: believing Delta's overwrite is partition-aware by default (it is not — the default is static, so the whole table is cleared); believing that 'the table is not dropped' means 'the data is safe' (the data files are replaced atomically, which is still total loss of unread rows); and reasoning that duplicates 'do not matter because the downstream query uses distinct'. Aggregates such as count(*) and sum(amount) are not idempotent under duplication, so a retried append corrupts every nightly metric derived from that partition. This matters more than usual in pipeline design because retries are normal, not exceptional: orchestrators such as Airflow routinely re-trigger failed tasks, and the Spark job they call is expected to be safely re-runnable [source p.346]. Note also that append is not 'wrong' in general — it is precisely right for an insert-only pattern where new versions of records are genuinely new rows and a view resolves the current state by newest key [source p.342]. The mistake is using an insert-only mode for a replace-one-day operation.
Problem 3

The table is /mnt/silver/events, partitioned by event_date, 5,000,000 rows total. Partition 2024-06-01 holds 120,000 rows and partition 2024-06-02 holds 150,000 rows. A filter bug means tonight's DataFrame df_late does not contain only the target day: it has 130,000 rows for 2024-06-01 and 500 spilled rows for 2024-06-02, for 130,500 rows in total. The write is: df_late.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("replaceWhere", "event_date = '2024-06-01'").save("/mnt/silver/events"). (a) Describe the outcome on an engine that validates the DataFrame against the predicate, and on one that does not; in the latter case compute the total row count and the 2024-06-02 row count. (b) Now suppose the predicate is instead too broad — 'event_date >= '2024-06-01'' — while df_late still contains only 2024-06-01 rows. Compute the row count per partition and for the table. (c) Write the guard you would put in the job before the write.
Hint: replaceWhere deletes everything matching the predicate and inserts everything in the DataFrame; the two sets must be the same set.

Worked solution
**(a) Mismatch between DataFrame and predicate.** The contract of replaceWhere is that the predicate describes exactly the rows you are supplying. Delta resolves the predicate against the partition column, removes all data files matching event_date = '2024-06-01' (120,000 rows), and then writes every row of df_late. On Delta versions that validate the write, the job fails with an error to the effect that the data written out does not match the replaceWhere condition — a safe failure, and the table is unchanged. On an engine without that validation, the 130,000 matching rows are written into the (now empty) 2024-06-01 partition, and the 500 non-matching rows are written into the 2024-06-02 partition — whose original files were never removed, because the predicate did not select them. Result: 2024-06-02 = 150,000 + 500 = 150,500 rows (500 duplicates), whole table = 5,000,000 − 120,000 + 130,500 = 5,010,500 rows, and 500 of those rows are wrong by construction. Note the failure is asymmetric: the mistake produces *duplication* in the untouched partition, never an error, so downstream counts stay plausible until someone audits the day.

**(b) Over-broad predicate.** With the predicate 'event_date >= '2024-06-01'', Delta removes *all* files whose event_date satisfies it, i.e. 2024-06-01 through 2024-06-30 — 30 days. Those partitions held 5,000,000 rows in total only if the table starts at 2024-06-01; if the table spans a wider range, the predicate removes every day from 2024-06-01 onward. It then writes only the 130,000 rows of df_late, which all belong to 2024-06-01. So 2024-06-01 = 130,000, every later day = 0 rows, and the table = (rows before 2024-06-01) + 130,000. Rows that existed inside the predicate but were not in the DataFrame are simply gone: this is precisely the case where 'rows outside the DataFrame can be lost', because the delete side of replaceWhere is driven by the predicate, not by the data.

**(c) Guard before the write.** Validate that the DataFrame and the predicate describe the same set, and fail fast if not:

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

TARGET = "2024-06-01"

bad = df_late.filter(F.col("event_date") != F.lit(TARGET)).count()

assert bad == 0, f"df_late contains {bad} rows outside {TARGET}"

assert df_late.count() > 0, "refusing to overwrite a partition with an empty batch"

Then write with the same literal used in the assertion:

df_late.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("replaceWhere", f"event_date = '{TARGET}'").save("/mnt/silver/events")

Deriving both the predicate and the assertion from one variable removes the class of bug where the filter and the predicate drift apart.

Analysis — replaceWhere is best understood as a two-sided contract: the predicate selects what to *delete*, the DataFrame determines what to *insert*, and correctness requires delete-set = insert-set. Students usually reason about only one side. If they think about the DataFrame, they miss the over-broad-predicate failure (b), where a single character error in a date comparison silently annihilates 29 partitions. If they think about the predicate, they miss failure (a), where innocuous extra rows are inserted into partitions that were never cleared, producing duplicates that look like legitimate events. The safe engineering pattern is to treat the predicate as code with a unit test: assert on the data first, then write. Two related edge cases worth knowing: (i) the predicate must be deterministic — a non-deterministic expression such as current_date() cannot be used for file-level replacement; (ii) for replaceWhere to prune at file level rather than scan, the predicate should reference partition columns. That second point is exactly why date- and time-based partitioning is so common: partitioning splits the table into subtables so that a query (or a write) can touch only the relevant subset [source p.240]. Practical advice: prefer the conjunction 'event_date = ''2024-06-01'' AND region = ''EU''' style of predicate when the table is partitioned on more than one column, and log the two counts (rows deleted, rows written) from the operation's metrics so an audit can confirm the swap was balanced. Finally, note that replaceWhere is not the only correct tool for a same-key refresh: the upsert/merge pattern looks up source records against a target by a primary key and updates matches while inserting non-matches, which tolerates a partial feed and can also express deletions [source p.343]. replaceWhere is the cheaper, sharper tool when the day is delivered as a complete snapshot; MERGE is the tool when it is delivered as a delta.
Problem 4

Same table /mnt/silver/events, partitioned by event_date, 5,000,000 rows total: 2024-06-01 = 120,000 rows, 2024-06-02 = 150,000 rows, 2024-06-03 = 160,000 rows, remaining 27 days = 4,570,000 rows. A backfill DataFrame df_backfill was built by a broken filter and spans three days: 130,000 rows on 2024-06-01, 90,000 on 2024-06-02, 75,000 on 2024-06-03. Three sub-questions. (a) The job runs with spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode = dynamic and df_backfill.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/mnt/silver/events"). Give the row count of each of the three partitions and of the table, and identify the data lost. (b) The same broken df_backfill is written with replaceWhere "event_date = '2024-06-01'" on an engine with no predicate validation. What are the counts now? (c) A correct backfill DataFrame for 2024-06-01 contains only 90,000 of the 130,000 rows it should, because the source export was truncated. What does the dynamic-overwrite job do to the partition, and would a MERGE behave differently?
Hint: Dynamic overwrite replaces partitions wholesale — whatever the DataFrame does not contain disappears with the old files.

Worked solution
**(a) Dynamic partition overwrite with an over-wide DataFrame.** Dynamic mode computes the set of partition values present in the DataFrame: {2024-06-01, 2024-06-02, 2024-06-03}. Each of those partitions is deleted in full and rebuilt from df_backfill. Results: 2024-06-01 = 130,000; 2024-06-02 = 90,000 (was 150,000, so 60,000 rows lost); 2024-06-03 = 75,000 (was 160,000, so 85,000 rows lost); the other 27 days = 4,570,000 unchanged. Whole table = 4,570,000 + 130,000 + 90,000 + 75,000 = 4,865,000 rows, down from 5,000,000: 145,000 rows were destroyed by a filter bug, with no error and no warning. Dynamic overwrite is a deletion scope, not an insertion scope.

**(b) replaceWhere with the same over-wide DataFrame.** Now the delete side is the predicate: only files with event_date = '2024-06-01' are removed, and all 295,000 DataFrame rows are written. So 2024-06-01 = 130,000; 2024-06-02 = 150,000 + 90,000 = 240,000 (90,000 duplicates); 2024-06-03 = 160,000 + 75,000 = 235,000 (75,000 duplicates); other days = 4,570,000. Whole table = 5,000,000 − 120,000 + 295,000 = 5,175,000 rows. On a Delta version that validates the predicate, this write fails instead. Note that the same broken DataFrame therefore produces *opposite* damage under the two options: silent data loss under dynamic overwrite, silent duplication under replaceWhere.

**(c) Truncated but correctly-scoped DataFrame.** Dynamic overwrite deletes the whole 2024-06-01 partition (120,000 rows) and writes the 90,000 rows it was given: partition = 90,000, and 30,000 rows vanish. The job reports success, because from the writer's point of view nothing is wrong. A MERGE on a business key (say event_id) would instead read the 90,000 incoming rows, update or insert only matching keys, and leave the 30,000 rows that the truncated export never mentioned exactly where they were — the partition stays at 120,000 rows (or grows, if any incoming event_id is new). MERGE is therefore the right tool when the incoming feed is a partial delta rather than a complete daily snapshot; dynamic overwrite is the right tool when the feed is authoritative for the whole day.

Analysis — This problem turns the two options into a comparison of failure modes, which is the real decision criterion. Dynamic overwrite is *scoped by data*: whatever partitions appear in the DataFrame are replaced wholesale. replaceWhere is *scoped by a predicate*: the delete set is fixed by the predicate, and extra DataFrame rows leak in. Neither is unconditionally safer; each is safe only when the DataFrame is exactly what you think it is. The engineering conclusion is that the choice must be paired with a data contract — for dynamic overwrite, the contract is 'this DataFrame is the complete truth for every partition it contains'; for replaceWhere, the contract is 'this DataFrame contains nothing outside the predicate'. Both contracts can be enforced by assertions on distinct partition values and row counts before the write, and both should be, because the failure modes are silent. A second lesson concerns partial feeds. Real pipelines frequently receive a delta rather than a snapshot, especially with late-arriving events whose arrival can be delayed arbitrarily long — a session close, or an event produced offline and delivered only when the device reconnects [source p.313]. When the feed is a delta, wholesale partition replacement is the wrong shape of operation and MERGE, which matches source rows to target rows by key and updates or inserts accordingly [source p.343], is the correct one. Finally, be aware that dynamic overwrite only has partitions to replace if the table is partitioned at all; on a non-partitioned table the setting has nothing to scope and the write degenerates into a full overwrite.
Problem 5

A production table is /mnt/silver/events: 5,000,000 rows, 30 partitions by event_date, about 166,667 rows per day. The nightly late-arriving batch is 130,000 rows for a single day, and the target day already holds 120,000 rows. The platform team must pick a strategy that satisfies three requirements simultaneously: (R1) the job is re-runnable — one run and three runs must give the same table; (R2) partitions other than the target day are not modified; (R3) the job does not rewrite the whole table. Which of the following satisfy R1, R2 and R3? Give the row count or state change per run for each. (A) df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(path), default settings. (B) df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save(path). (C) df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("replaceWhere", "event_date = '2024-06-01'").save(path). (D) spark.conf.set("spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic") then df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(path). (E) A MERGE statement keyed on event_id that updates matching rows and inserts new ones.
Hint: Score each option against the three requirements independently before comparing them.

Worked solution
Score each option on R1 (idempotent), R2 (other partitions untouched) and R3 (no full-table rewrite).

**(A) Plain overwrite, default settings.** The default partitionOverwriteMode is static, so mode("overwrite") clears the table and writes the DataFrame. Run 1 leaves 130,000 rows; run 2 leaves 130,000 rows. R1: satisfied trivially. R2: violated — 4,880,000 rows outside the target day are destroyed (table goes from 5,000,000 to 130,000 rows). R3: satisfied in the narrow sense that only 130,000 rows are written, but the surviving table is not the table anyone wanted. Verdict: rejects R2.

**(B) Append.** Run 1: table = 5,130,000, target day = 250,000. Run 2: table = 5,260,000, target day = 380,000. Run 3: 5,390,000 / 510,000. General: 5,000,000 + 130,000n and 120,000 + 130,000n. R1: violated (f is not idempotent; the day grows by 130,000 every retry). R2: satisfied (nothing else is touched). R3: satisfied (130,000 rows written). Verdict: rejects R1.

**(C) replaceWhere.** Rows removed = 120,000 (the target day); rows written = 130,000. Table after run 1 = 5,000,000 − 120,000 + 130,000 = 5,010,000; target day = 130,000. Run 2 removes 130,000 and writes 130,000: table stays at 5,010,000. R1: satisfied. R2: satisfied — the predicate selects only the target partition's files. R3: satisfied — about 250,000 rows of work (120,000 deleted + 130,000 written) out of 5,000,000, i.e. 5% of the table. Verdict: satisfies all three.

**(D) Dynamic partition overwrite.** The DataFrame contains one partition value, so exactly the target partition is replaced: identical arithmetic to (C) — 5,010,000 rows and 130,000 on the target day after every run. R1, R2, R3 all satisfied, *provided* the DataFrame never contains more partition values than intended and provided the conf line is actually set; if the conf is forgotten, (D) collapses into (A). Verdict: satisfies all three under that contract.

**(E) MERGE keyed on event_id.** Correctness: the merge reads the 130,000 incoming rows, updates the target rows whose event_id matches, and inserts the rest. Row count depends on how many incoming event_ids are already present — say 95,000 match and 35,000 are new — giving 5,000,000 − 0 + 35,000 = 5,035,000 rows, with the target day at 120,000 + 35,000 = 155,000. Re-running with the same 130,000 rows changes nothing (the second run matches 130,000 keys and inserts 0), so R1 and R2 hold and R3 holds (only files containing matching keys are rewritten). Verdict: satisfies all three, but it is a different semantics — it *merges into* the day rather than *replacing* it, so it is the right answer only when the day is delivered as a delta of changed events rather than as a complete snapshot of the day.

**Conclusion.** (C) and (D) satisfy all three requirements with the same cost profile and the same target semantics; (E) also satisfies them but answers a different question. (B) fails re-runnability and (A) fails partition preservation.

Analysis — The value of this problem is the framing: a write-mode choice is a multi-objective decision, and exam questions frequently hide one unmet requirement behind two satisfied ones — (B) is perfectly safe for R2 and R3 and still fatally wrong. Two structural facts explain the whole table. First, with Delta, overwrite is an atomic replacement of data files, not a drop-and-recreate of the table, so an unscoped overwrite is a *silent* catastrophe: no error, a successful commit, and 4,880,000 rows gone. Second, partition scoping can come from either the code (replaceWhere) or the session configuration (partitionOverwriteMode = dynamic), and the default is the dangerous one. Cost reasoning follows the same structure: work is proportional to the rows deleted plus the rows written, so (C)/(D) touch about 250,000 of 5,000,000 rows while (A) touches 130,000 rows and destroys the rest — the cheap option is cheap because it does almost nothing. On a non-partitioned table, note that (D) degenerates to (A) and (C) loses its pruning advantage, so a large unpartitioned table that must be refreshed in place requires MERGE or a full truncate-and-reload [source p.342], and MERGE is also the only one of the five that can express hard deletions [source p.343]. Prefer partitioning a table on the freshness dimension that both queries and refreshes use — typically time — precisely so that both read and write can address a day at a time instead of the whole table [source p.240].
Problem 6

A second table, /mnt/silver/events_flat, holds the same 5,000,000 events but is NOT partitioned: it is a single directory with no partition columns, and event_date is an ordinary DATE column inside the files. The nightly job must again replace the 120,000 rows of 2024-06-01 with a 130,000-row batch df_late. Two engineers try the two solutions from the previous problems. Engineer X sets spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode to dynamic and writes with mode("overwrite"). Engineer Y writes with mode("overwrite").option("replaceWhere", "event_date = '2024-06-01'"). (a) What happens to the table in each case? Give row counts. (b) Explain why each of the two mechanisms behaves differently on a non-partitioned table than on a partitioned one. (c) Recommend a correct and reasonably cheap approach for this table, using the 5,000,000-row scale to justify the cost argument.
Hint: Both mechanisms are scopes over partitions. With no partitions, one scope disappears and the other loses its fast path.

Worked solution
**(a) What happens.** Engineer X: dynamic partition overwrite has nothing to scope to. With no partition directories, the writer cannot restrict the overwrite to a subset of the data, and the write degenerates to a plain table overwrite: the whole table is replaced by df_late. Result: 130,000 rows, all 2024-06-01; the other 4,880,000 rows are gone. Engineer Y: replaceWhere still functions as a predicate over rows, but with no partition column the engine cannot resolve the matching files from metadata. It must examine data to find the rows satisfying event_date = '2024-06-01', then rewrite the table so that those rows are replaced and the other 4,880,000 are preserved by being copied forward. The observable end state is correct — 4,880,000 + 130,000 = 5,010,000 rows, 2024-06-01 = 130,000 — but the write is no longer a metadata-only, file-pruning operation; it reads and rewrites data far beyond the 120,000 rows it is logically replacing.

**(b) Why the behaviour differs.** Partitioning means physically splitting one logical table into subtables by a field value [source p.240]. That physical split is what both mechanisms exploit. Dynamic overwrite works by inspecting the partition values in the incoming DataFrame and replacing the corresponding *directories*; if the table is one directory, the only possible scope is 'everything', so the mode silently reverts to static overwrite semantics. replaceWhere works by mapping the predicate onto partition values so it can remove exactly the files whose metadata says they belong to the target day. When the predicate column is not a partition column, that mapping does not exist, and the engine falls back to a data-level operation — correct but much more expensive. The predicate column being a partition column is therefore not a stylistic preference for replaceWhere; it is the precondition for the cheap, file-level replacement path.

**(c) Recommendation.** For a single-directory table with no partition column, add partitioning on event_date (a one-time rewrite: 5,000,000 rows written once, after which every nightly refresh touches 250,000 rows instead of 5,000,000), or use a MERGE keyed on a business key such as event_id. The scale argument is decisive: at 5,000,000 rows per night, a data-level rewrite means reading and rewriting roughly 5,000,000 rows every day — 1.825 billion rows per year — to change 130,000 rows, a write amplification of about 38×. Partitioning or keying on the refresh dimension reduces the nightly work to roughly 250,000 rows, a 20× reduction, and it simultaneously speeds up the time-range analytics that motivated the table in the first place. If the incoming batch is a delta rather than a complete snapshot, MERGE on event_id is the appropriate choice: it reads the 130,000 incoming rows, matches them against the target by key, updates what matches (say 95,000 rows) and inserts what does not (35,000 rows), leaving the table at 5,035,000 rows and touching only the files that contain matching keys.

Analysis — This problem exposes the hidden precondition behind both correct answers in the previous problems: both are *partition-scoped* mechanisms, and neither scoping mechanism survives on an unpartitioned table. The general rule to remember is that replaceWhere requires the predicate to reference partition columns to be cheap, whereas dynamic overwrite requires the table to be partitioned at all to be correct. Exam distractors exploit the first half of this rule and hide the second: students remember 'replaceWhere works on any table' (it does, but expensively) and 'dynamic mode only replaces the partitions in the DataFrame' (true only if partitions exist; otherwise it is a full overwrite). The cost framing — write amplification of roughly 38×, reduced to about 20× less work after partitioning — is the reason partitioning is a design decision made before the table gets big, not an optimisation applied afterwards. Two caveats are worth stating. First, partitioning is not free: too many partitions (thousands of tiny directories) hurts listing and planning, which is why clustering within partitions, finer-grained sorting by one or a few fields, is often combined with coarse date partitioning [source p.240]. Second, if the source data itself is a stream of changed records rather than a daily snapshot, the right primitive from the start is the merge pattern — matching source records to target records by key and updating matches while inserting non-matches [source p.343] — because it is the only one of these mechanisms that tolerates a partial feed without deleting the rows the feed did not mention. Whatever mechanism is chosen, it must be safe to re-run, since the orchestrator that triggers the Spark job will retry failed tasks [source p.346].

actions.text: Now let's put those write modes to work on a real decision problem. This page walks through six worked scenarios, all built around the same partitioned Delta table at /mnt/silver/events. Let's start with the first one and extract the repeatable pattern.

Problem one sets the scene. We have a Delta table living at /mnt/silver/events, partitioned by event_date. Every night, one day of late-arriving events needs to be replaced, while every other day must stay completely untouched. And critically, the job has to be re-runnable — running it twice must not corrupt the table.

Here are the two correct solutions, and notice both keep mode overwrite — the difference is in the scope. Option A uses replaceWhere with the predicate event_date equals the target day. That atomically replaces only the partitions matching that predicate. Option B flips the table-level setting spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode to dynamic, then writes with mode overwrite so that only the partitions present in the incoming DataFrame get replaced.

The analysis is the exam-worthy point here. Plain mode overwrite with dynamic overwrite turned off would delete the entire table — that's catastrophic. And mode append would duplicate the day's rows on every single re-run. Neither satisfies the re-runnability requirement. So the options narrow to replaceWhere or dynamic partition overwrite, and the exam will test whether you know which knob controls which behavior.

Problem two drills into the same table but isolates the failure modes. If you append, repeats accumulate and uniqueness breaks; if you overwrite without a scoped predicate, you wipe the table. Notice the pattern across all six problems: idempotent + scoped write. That is the design principle this page is teaching, and it's exactly what the certification wants you to reason about on scenario questions.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Integrated Reading and Writing Scenarios

questions.question: A nightly pipeline lands /mnt/raw/orders.csv into the existing Delta table /mnt/bronze/orders, which already holds the rows loaded on previous nights. The arriving file is pipe-delimited, has a header row, and production code supplies an explicit DDL schema string. Only the rows in the new file may be added; every row already in the target must remain untouched. Which code block does this correctly?

options.label:
df = spark.read.format("csv").option("header", "true").option("sep", "|").schema(ddl).load("/mnt/raw/orders.csv")
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("/mnt/bronze/orders")

df = spark.read.format("csv").option("header", "true").option("sep", "|").option("mergeSchema", "true").schema(ddl).load("/mnt/raw/orders.csv")
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("/mnt/bronze/orders")

df = spark.read.format("csv").option("header", "true").option("sep", "|").schema(ddl).load("/mnt/raw/orders.csv")
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("header", "true").save("/mnt/bronze/orders")

df = spark.read.format("csv").option("header", "true").schema(ddl).load("/mnt/raw/orders.csv")
df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/mnt/bronze/orders")

questions.analysis: Option A is correct on both sides of the API boundary. On the read side, CSV is the option-hungry format: sep defaults to a comma, so a pipe-delimited file read without option("sep", "|") collapses each line into one string column, and once the explicit DDL schema is applied every numeric or timestamp field beyond the first resolves to null. Supplying .schema(ddl) also avoids inferSchema, which would cost an extra full pass over the data just to guess types. On the write side, mode("append") adds new files to /mnt/bronze/orders without removing or rewriting anything already there, which is exactly the 'add only new rows' requirement; Delta commits that write atomically, so readers see either all of the new files or none of them [source p.305]. This mirrors the pipeline described in the source material, where a Spark job ingests sources, combines them into a single table, filters the result, and writes it out as a Delta Lake table in object storage [source p.346]. Option B is wrong because mergeSchema is a Delta write-side reconciliation option; a raw CSV file carries no schema metadata, so the option has nothing to reconcile and changes nothing. Option C is wrong because header is a reader-only option: DataFrameWriter ignores it, and Delta stores parquet data files plus a transaction log, not delimited text, so no header row can be manufactured. Option D is wrong twice: dropping sep means the pipe is never treated as a delimiter, and mode("overwrite") deletes every previously loaded row, turning an intended incremental append into a destructive full refresh.

questions.question: A nightly job performs a full refresh of the Delta table /mnt/silver/customers. Last night the upstream source added two new columns (loyalty_tier and is_gift) and retired one legacy column. The refreshed target must contain today's data only and must expose exactly the new column set, including the two additions and without the retired column. Which write call satisfies this?

options.label: df.write.option("mergeSchema", "true").mode("append").format("delta").save("/mnt/silver/customers")
df.write.option("overwriteSchema", "true").mode("overwrite").format("delta").save("/mnt/silver/customers")
df.write.option("overwriteSchema", "true").mode("append").format("delta").save("/mnt/silver/customers")
df.write.option("mergeSchema", "true").mode("overwrite").format("delta").save("/mnt/silver/customers")

questions.analysis: Option B is the only call that satisfies both halves of the requirement: mode("overwrite") clears the target so only today's rows survive, and option("overwriteSchema", "true") authorises Delta to replace the stored table schema with the incoming one, adding loyalty_tier and is_gift and dropping the retired column. This is the truncate-and-reload pattern, in which a table is cleared of data and transformations are rerun into it, effectively generating a new table version [source p.342]. Schema replacement is cheap in a columnar store precisely because adding or removing a field is initially just a change to metadata rather than a rewrite of every row [source p.332]. Option A uses the right option in the wrong mode: mergeSchema with append widens the table by the two new columns but keeps every historical row, so it is not a full refresh, and mergeSchema by definition only adds columns — it can never drop or retype the retired column. Option C pairs overwriteSchema with append, a combination Delta rejects: append is defined as never removing or rewriting existing data files, so it cannot be granted permission to replace the target's schema. Option D is the mirror-image error, placing the append-side option in overwrite mode; mergeSchema widens an existing schema, but a refresh that must also remove a column needs overwriteSchema, and combining a schema-widening option with a full replace leaves the retired column and the stale schema in place.

questions.question: A developer ships this job: df.write.format("delta").save("/mnt/silver/customers"). It ran successfully last night against an empty location. Tonight the scheduler runs the identical, unchanged code. What happens, and what is the correct fix?

options.label: The run fails with a path-already-exists AnalysisException before anything is written, because the default save mode is error/errorifexists; the fix is to choose the intended behaviour explicitly with .mode("append") for an incremental load or .mode("overwrite") for a full refresh.
The run succeeds and replaces the target contents, because save() defaults to overwrite for Delta tables.
The run succeeds and appends the new rows, because save() defaults to append for Delta tables.
The run fails with an incompatible-schema error, and the fix is to add .option("mergeSchema", "true").

questions.analysis: Option A is correct. DataFrameWriter's default mode is error (also spelled errorifexists), so the second run detects the existing Delta table at /mnt/silver/customers and fails before writing anything — a deliberate safety default that prevents a careless re-run from destroying production data. The diagnosis follows directly from the four save modes: error fails on an existing target, overwrite replaces the data atomically (removing the existing data files and committing a new table version, the truncate-and-reload pattern [source p.342]), append adds files without touching what exists, and ignore silently does nothing. The fix therefore depends on intent, not on the error text: append for incremental loads and streaming micro-batches, overwrite for a genuine full refresh. Options B and C are false because no API default silently chooses destructive or additive behaviour; a job that overwrites without being told to would be an unacceptable surprise. Option D misdiagnoses the failure: the schema here is not the problem, the existing target path is. mergeSchema addresses the separate case of appending a DataFrame that carries a new column, and it would not clear the path-already-exists condition that error mode raises.

questions.question: A team is writing a standards document for Delta Lake read and write options. Which statements are technically accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: PERMISSIVE and FAILFAST are read-side CSV parse modes that govern what happens to malformed records; neither is a legal value for df.write.mode(...).
option("header", "true") configures the reader only; passing it to DataFrameWriter neither writes a header row into the Delta files nor changes the target schema.
mergeSchema can add new columns during an append, but it cannot drop a column or change an existing column's data type.
option("overwriteSchema", "true") can be paired with mode("append") to evolve the target schema without deleting any existing rows.
Because Delta enforces schema on write, appending a DataFrame that contains an extra column silently widens the target schema unless the writer is told otherwise.

questions.analysis: A is accurate: read-side parse modes (PERMISSIVE, DROPMALFORMED, FAILFAST) describe how the CSV reader handles corrupt records, while write-side modes (error/errorifexists, overwrite, append, ignore) describe what the writer does when the target already exists; the two vocabularies are not interchangeable, and passing PERMISSIVE to df.write.mode(...) is a category error. B is accurate: header, sep, inferSchema and schema are properties of DataFrameReader, and DataFrameWriter ignores them — Delta targets store parquet data files plus a transaction log, so there is no delimited text in which to place a header row. C is accurate: mergeSchema is an additive reconciliation rule for appends; it lets a write introduce new fields, but Delta will not let it remove a field or retype one, because silently changing a column's type would invalidate data already stored. Adding a field is cheap in a columnar store — initially just a change to metadata, and wide tables typically arise exactly this way, through gradual schema evolution [source p.332]. D is false: overwriteSchema is the schema-replacement switch for a full refresh, and Delta rejects pairing it with append, since append is defined as never removing or rewriting existing data files. E is false: Delta enforces schema on write by default, so an append carrying an unrecognised column fails loudly instead of quietly widening the table — the fail-closed behaviour that keeps insert-only loaders and downstream consumers safe [source p.342].

actions.text: Time to put the last few pages together. This checkpoint mixes reading options, write modes, and schema evolution into single scenarios, so read each question carefully and pay attention to which direction each option is pointing.

Take each one on your own and commit to an answer before moving on — that is how these pay off. Once you submit, I'll join you to walk through the reasoning behind every item, including the tricky distractors.

scenes.title: Summary and Exam Traps

elements.content: Summary and Exam Traps
Read: format → option → load; CSV needs header/sep/schema [source p.284]; Parquet/Delta self-describe.
Write: df.write.format().mode().option().save(); default mode is error, not append [source p.346].
Modes: overwrite replaces · append adds · ignore no-ops silently · error fails fast.
Schema: Delta enforces schema on write [source p.245]; mergeSchema extends, overwriteSchema replaces.
Traps: append ≠ default · overwriteSchema + append · read options ≠ write modes · CSV for updates.

actions.text: Let's pull this lesson together. Here on the summary page, we're going to turn everything about reading and writing data into a short decision checklist — and then name the specific defaults and mispairings that quietly cost people points on the exam.

First, the read side. The pattern is always the same three steps: format, then option or options, then load. What changes is how much you have to tell the reader. CSV is the demanding one — it carries no type information, so you must state the header, the separator, and often an explicit schema. Parquet and Delta are self-describing: they read their schema from the data itself, so you rarely need to declare it.

The write side mirrors it: df.write, then format, then mode, then option, then save. One detail to commit to memory — the default mode is error, also written as errorifexists. That means if you do nothing, an existing target will not be touched; the write fails fast. Treat that default as something you must consciously override, never something you inherit by accident.

Now the four write modes in one line each. Overwrite replaces the target. Append adds new rows to it. Ignore no-ops silently — no error, no change, the write simply doesn't happen. And error fails fast. If you can say those four out loud without hesitating, you've covered a large share of what gets tested here.

Schema evolution is the next piece. Use mergeSchema when you're appending additively and a new column shows up — it lets the existing table absorb the addition. Use overwriteSchema when you're doing a full refresh and the shape genuinely changes. And remember the pairing rule: overwriteSchema only works with mode overwrite. Those two belong together, always.

Finally, the traps. Four of them account for most lost points. One: assuming append is the default — it is not, error is. Two: pairing overwriteSchema with append, which is invalid. Three: confusing read-side options with write modes — they are different systems entirely. And four: reaching for CSV where the requirement is updates or concurrency, when Delta is what actually delivers that.

So use this page as your pre-exam checklist: read pattern, write pattern, the four modes, the two schema-evolution knobs, and those four traps. If all five come to mind instantly, you're ready for the questions on this topic. Let's move on to aggregations, joins, and window functions.

scenes.title: Lesson Roadmap: Aggregations, Joins, and Window Functions

elements.content: Lesson Roadmap: Aggregations, Joins, and Window Functions
Unit 3 · Querying Data with Spark SQL and PySpark · Prerequisite: read a DataFrame and inspect its schema

1 · Grouped Aggregates

GROUP BY, SUM, HAVING

2 · Multi-Table Joins
