3 · Window Functions

RANK, running totals
Exam Objective Mapping
The Certified Data Engineer Associate exam assesses foundational data engineering tasks on the Data + AI Platform, including querying and transforming data.
SQL is powerful but not enough alone; engineers compose SQL with Spark operations [source p.47] and favor modular, interoperable tools [source p.36].
Skill Checkpoints & Teaching Pattern

Each pattern coded twice: SQL and DataFrame API.

Aggregates, joins, windows: GROUP BY, INNER/LEFT, RANK.

Prefer native SQL over slow Python UDFs [source p.359].

Worked example: amounts 10, 20, 5 in time order.

GROUP BY → 35; SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ts) → 10, 30, 35.

Read → join → filter → Delta write [source p.346].

actions.text: Let's step back and frame where we are. This page is our roadmap for the next stretch of the course: Aggregations, Joins, and Window Functions — the three query patterns that show up again and again on the Data Engineer Associate exam.

We're in Unit 3, Querying Data with Spark SQL and PySpark. Everything we do here builds directly on the reading and schema inspection we just covered — you already know how to load a DataFrame, so now we're going to make it answer analytical questions.

First checkpoint: grouped aggregates. That's GROUP BY for grouping, aggregate functions like SUM and COUNT, and HAVING for filtering the groups themselves rather than the rows. This is how you collapse a detailed table into a business summary.
Second: multi-table joins. We'll work through INNER and LEFT semantics carefully, and we'll cover broadcast joins — the fast path when one side of the join is small enough to ship to every executor.

Third: window functions. These let you compute across a partition without collapsing rows — perfect for ranking with RANK, calculating running totals, and our personal favorite for the exam: deduplicating a change feed with ROW_NUMBER.

Now, why these three? Start with the exam objective mapping. The Certified Data Engineer Associate exam explicitly assesses foundational data engineering tasks on the Databricks Data plus AI Platform — and querying and transforming data sits right at the center of that.

So treat this lesson as direct exam preparation. If you can read an aggregation, a join, and a window function and predict the output, you're covering a large share of the transformation questions you'll see on test day.
One more thing about how we'll learn it. Look at the teaching pattern for the whole lesson — this is where it gets practical.

Every pattern we cover gets coded twice: once in Spark SQL, and once in the PySpark DataFrame API. Why? Because SQL is powerful but not enough alone — engineers working on Databricks move between both, and the exam expects you to read either. And each demo uses a tiny, traceable dataset — small enough that you can work out the answer by hand before you run a single line of code. That's how the mechanics stick.

Here's a taste of that. Imagine amounts 10, 20, and 5 in time order. A grouped sum gives you one number — 35 — the rows are gone. A windowed running total gives you 10, 30, 35, keeping every row. Same data, different question, different shape of answer. Holding that distinction in your head is the single most useful thing you can take from this page.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Aggregation Vocabulary and Prior Knowledge

questions.question: You run two statements in a Databricks notebook against a Delta table named sales. Statement 1 is: SELECT count(*) FROM sales. Statement 2 is: SELECT region, count(*) FROM sales GROUP BY region. Which description of the result shapes is correct?

options.label: Both statements return a single row; the GROUP BY version simply adds a region column to that one row.

Statement 1 collapses the whole table into exactly one row with one column (and returns the row even when the table is empty, with a value of 0); statement 2 returns one row per distinct value of region, which means zero rows when the table is empty and an extra null-keyed row whenever region is NULL.
Statement 1 returns one row per source row; statement 2 collapses every source row into a single row.
Both statements return one row per distinct region; statement 1 just leaves the region column out of the projection.

questions.analysis: B is correct. An aggregate with no GROUP BY clause (an ungrouped aggregate) has no grouping keys, so the entire input is treated as one group and the output is always exactly one row with one column per aggregate expression. This is a precondition that surprises people: even when the table contains zero rows, SELECT count(*) still returns one row containing 0, because the empty input is still one (empty) group. A grouped aggregate behaves differently: the number of output rows equals the number of distinct grouping-key combinations actually present in the data, so an empty input yields zero rows, not one row of zeros. The edge case that costs people marks is NULL: GROUP BY treats NULL as a legitimate group value, so a nullable region column produces an additional row whose region is NULL, and that group is easy to miss when you are eyeballing totals. Option A is wrong because the ungrouped query has no per-row identity left to attach a column to; the collapse has already happened. Option C reverses the two result shapes. Option D is wrong because statement 1 knows nothing about regions at all, and statement 2 does not materialise rows for regions that are absent from the table. This matters in practice because teammates consume analytics results as a consistent snapshot of many rows at a point in time, and an unexpected row count (or a missing row) breaks downstream joins [source p.305].

questions.question: A nightly job must report, per order_date, the number of order rows in a Delta table and the number of distinct customers who ordered. The customer_id column is nullable. Which of the following statements about count(*) and count(col) / countDistinct(col) are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: count(*) counts every row in the group, including rows where some or all columns are NULL.
count(customer_id) counts only rows where customer_id is not NULL, so a count that is lower than the row count is usually caused by that column silently dropping NULLs rather than by missing data.

countDistinct(customer_id) / F.countDistinct("customer_id") counts distinct non-NULL values, so a group in which every customer_id is NULL contributes 0 to that measure while still contributing its rows to count(*).
count(customer_id) is always the correct way to count rows because it reads only one column instead of the whole row.

questions.analysis: A, B and C are correct. count(*) is a row count: it is defined over the row itself, so it is unaffected by NULLs anywhere in the row. count(col) is a value count with a built-in filter: it increments only when the argument is not NULL, and the filter is applied silently, with no warning and no error. That silent NULL-dropping is the classic exam distractor and the most common cause of a total that is 'slightly too low' in a production report. countDistinct(col) (PySpark: F.countDistinct("col")) follows the same NULL rule and counts distinct non-NULL values only, so a group whose customer_id is entirely NULL yields 0 for the distinct measure but a positive count(*). The precondition to remember is that all three are exact only over the rows the query actually reads: if a filter or a partition prune removes rows first, all counts shrink uniformly. Option D is wrong on correctness and on performance: count(*) is the only count that answers 'how many rows', and it should be used for row counts. The performance nuance is the opposite of the distractor — columnar storage lets a scan read only the columns a query needs, so count(customer_id) may read less data than a wide projection, but the saving is measured in I/O, not in correctness, and choosing it for a row count is simply wrong [source p.239]. In large batch pipelines these aggregates are often executed against a replica rather than the primary system precisely so that the wide scan does not overload transactional traffic [source p.162].

questions.question: A colleague needs a per-day table containing, for each order_date in a Delta table orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount): (a) the total number of order rows, and (b) the number of distinct customers who ordered. customer_id is nullable. (1) Write the Spark SQL statement. (2) Write the logically equivalent PySpark DataFrame API expression, naming the import you need for the aggregation functions. (3) State which of the two counts silently drops NULLs, describe the exact symptom a reviewer would see in the results, and explain how you would obtain a count of rows whose customer_id is NULL if the business actually needs it.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100% total). (1) Correct Spark SQL — 30%: full credit only if the answer includes SELECT order_date, count(*) AS order_count, count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS distinct_customers FROM orders GROUP BY order_date, with GROUP BY on the non-aggregated column and an explicit alias for each aggregate. Deduct for grouping on an alias, for omitting GROUP BY, or for using count(customer_id) where a row count is required. (2) Correct DataFrame API — 30%: must show from pyspark.sql import functions as F (or an equivalent import of functions), then orders.groupBy("order_date").agg(F.count("*").alias("order_count"), F.countDistinct("customer_id").alias("distinct_customers")) — accept F.count(F.lit(1)) in place of F.count("*"). Deduct for .count() alone when a second measure is also required, for using .select() where .agg() is needed, or for a missing alias. (3) NULL behaviour and remedy — 40%: must state that count(DISTINCT customer_id) / F.countDistinct filters out NULLs while count(*) does not; must describe the symptom, i.e. distinct_customers can be 0 for a day whose order_count is greater than 0, and the two measures therefore do not reconcile; must give a concrete remedy, e.g. F.count(F.when(F.col("customer_id").isNull(), 1)).alias("null_customer_rows"), or F.sum(F.when(F.col("customer_id").isNull(), 1).otherwise(0)), or the SQL equivalent sum(CASE WHEN customer_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). Award partial credit for identifying the NULL behaviour without a working remedy. Deduct for claiming countDistinct counts NULL as a distinct value, and for claiming count(*) ignores NULL rows.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. (1) Spark SQL: SELECT order_date, count(*) AS order_count, count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS distinct_customers FROM orders GROUP BY order_date; — one output row per distinct order_date actually present, and zero rows if the table is empty. (2) PySpark: from pyspark.sql import functions as F; orders.groupBy("order_date").agg(F.count("*").alias("order_count"), F.countDistinct("customer_id").alias("distinct_customers")) — F.count(F.lit(1)) is an equally correct row-count idiom. The two forms are logically equivalent: the same aggregation, grouping keys and NULL rules are expressed once and then built into the same job plan, whether you hand Spark a SQL string or a DataFrame expression chain [source p.346]. (3) count(*) counts rows and is NULL-safe; count(DISTINCT customer_id) counts distinct non-NULL values only. The symptom is a day row with order_count = 5000 and distinct_customers = 1200 where the gap is not explained by repeat customers — the missing customers are the rows with NULL customer_id, which appear in neither the distinct measure nor any error message. To measure them explicitly, count conditionally: F.count(F.when(F.col("customer_id").isNull(), 1)).alias("null_customer_rows"), or sum(CASE WHEN customer_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) in SQL. A second edge case worth stating: if the source were reached through a federated query combining object storage with an OLTP database, the remote engine would apply its own NULL and distinct semantics to the same column, so the same aggregation can disagree across engines unless the NULL rule is pinned down [source p.351].

actions.text: Now let's see where you stand before we dig into aggregations, joins, and window functions. These three questions are a quick diagnostic, so treat them as a chance to check what already sticks and what doesn't.
Have a go at each one on your own — no peeking ahead. Once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning with you and we'll clear up anything that felt shaky.

scenes.title: Aggregating Data: groupBy, agg, and Spark SQL GROUP BY

elements.content:
Aggregating Data: groupBy, agg,

and Spark SQL GROUP BY

df.groupBy("region").agg(sum("amount").alias("revenue"))

SQL: SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM sales GROUP BY region [source p.348]
Worked example: (A,100), (A,200), (B,50), (C,NULL) → A=300, B=50, C=NULL; no key: SUM=350, COUNT=3.

data.text: Aggregates read only the referenced columns [source p.239].

elements.content: Data spreads across many servers [source p.215].
HAVING filters groups; WHERE filters rows; ORDER BY the alias.
Exam trap: no key → one row, not an error.

actions.text: Let's move from vocabulary into mechanics. Aggregation is the workhorse of the ELT domain — it's how we turn raw rows into something a business can read. Today we'll cover grouping keys, aggregate functions, and post-aggregation filtering, in both Spark SQL and the PySpark DataFrame API.

Start with the two equivalent forms of the same query. In the DataFrame API, we write df.groupBy("region").agg(sum("amount").alias("revenue")). In Spark SQL, we write SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM sales GROUP BY region. These produce the same physical plan — the exam sometimes shows you one form and asks you to recognize the other. Notice the alias call: it names the aggregated column, which you'll need if you want to order or filter on that result later.

One thing worth internalizing early: that grouping key is not free. Data spreads across many servers, so grouping requires a shuffle — a wide transformation that moves rows across the network so every value of a key lands on the same partition. Every cost conversation about aggregation starts here.

Here's the aggregate function reference you'll want to know cold. count(*) counts rows, including rows with nulls. count(col) skips nulls — so count(*) and count(col) can return different numbers on the same data, and that difference is usually the point of the question. avg, min, and max also skip nulls. countDistinct gives you exact distinct counts but costs a shuffle. And stddev and percentile_approx are there when you need distribution rather than a single number. The middle column — what each function ignores — is the column the exam tests.

Let's trace a worked example. Values: A with 100, A with 200, B with 50, and C with a null. Group by the key and sum the amount: A gives 300, B gives 50, and C gives null — not zero. That's the trap in miniature. Sum skips the null and, because C's only row had nothing to add, the result stays null. If you need zero, wrap it in coalesce.

Now the ordering of filtering, which trips people up constantly. WHERE filters rows before aggregation. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. So "regions with more than ten thousand in revenue" is a HAVING clause on the aggregated alias, while "only rows from 2024" is a WHERE clause. And ORDER BY goes at the very end, sorting the grouped result — again, by the alias, not the raw column. Get those three in the right slots and most of these questions resolve themselves.

Finally, the exam trap on the board: an aggregate with no grouping key does not error. SELECT sum(amount) FROM sales with no GROUP BY returns exactly one row — the total across the whole table. Candidates see a missing GROUP BY, panic, and pick "this query fails." That's almost never the intended answer. One row is the answer. Next, we'll take this pattern and build a full monthly revenue report by region.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Monthly Revenue by Region

elements.content: Problem 1

The Delta table `sales` is registered in Unity Catalog with the schema `region STRING, order_date DATE, amount DECIMAL(10,2), customer_id BIGINT` (customer_id is nullable). It currently holds exactly these ten rows:

| region | order_date | amount | customer_id |

|---|---|---|---|

| East | 2024-01-05 | 120.00 | 1 |

| East | 2024-01-19 | 80.50 | 2 |

| East | 2024-02-10 | 200.00 | 1 |

| East | 2024-03-02 | 99.50 | 3 |

| West | 2024-01-08 | 300.00 | 4 |

| West | 2024-01-30 | 150.00 | 4 |

| West | 2024-03-15 | 250.00 | 5 |

| West | 2024-03-28 | 400.00 | NULL |

| North | 2024-02-01 | 50.00 | 6 |

| North | 2024-04-02 | 999.00 | 7 |

Write one query that returns, for every region and month in Q1 2024 (2024-01-01 through 2024-03-31 inclusive), the region, the month, the total revenue (`SUM(amount)`), the number of orders (`COUNT(*)`), and the number of distinct customers (`COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)`), sorted by revenue from highest to lowest. Give the solution in both the PySpark DataFrame API and Spark SQL, and state the exact result set.
Hint: Filter rows first, derive the month column second, aggregate third — SQL's WHERE runs on rows, HAVING runs on groups, and the DataFrame API has no HAVING at all.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Read the source. Because `sales` is a Delta table registered in Unity Catalog, `spark.table('sales')` (equivalently `spark.read.table('sales')`) returns a DataFrame carrying the stored schema; there is no `inferSchema` step and no format guessing to do.

Step 2 — Filter to Q1. `col('order_date').between('2024-01-01','2024-03-31')` is inclusive at both ends, so 2024-03-31 is kept and 2024-04-01 is not. The string literals are implicitly cast to DATE for the comparison. This drops the North row of 2024-04-02 (999.00) and leaves 9 of the 10 rows. That 999.00 must never appear in the output.

Step 3 — Derive the month key. `withColumn('month', date_trunc('month', col('order_date')))` maps every date to the first day of its month. Note the return type: `date_trunc` yields a TIMESTAMP (2024-01-01 00:00:00), whereas `trunc(date_col, 'month')` yields a DATE. Either works for grouping; the difference matters only when you later compare the value to a DATE literal.

Step 4 — Group and aggregate.

```

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

q1 = (

spark.table('sales')

.filter(F.col('order_date').between('2024-01-01', '2024-03-31'))

.withColumn('month', F.date_trunc('month', F.col('order_date')))

.groupBy('region', 'month')

.agg(

F.sum('amount').alias('revenue'),

F.count('*').alias('orders'),

F.countDistinct('customer_id').alias('customers'),

)

.orderBy(F.desc('revenue'))

)

q1.display()

```

Step 5 — The same logic in Spark SQL:

```

SELECT region,

date_trunc('month', order_date) AS month,

SUM(amount) AS revenue,

COUNT(*) AS orders,

COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers

FROM sales

WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-03-31'

GROUP BY region, month

ORDER BY revenue DESC;

```

`GROUP BY region, month` (referring to the SELECT alias) works in Spark SQL because group-by-alias resolution is enabled by default in Databricks Runtime; `GROUP BY region, date_trunc('month', order_date)` is the portable spelling that also works in engines without alias resolution.

Step 6 — Verify by hand. There are six surviving region-month groups:

- East/Jan 2024: 120.00 + 80.50 = 200.50; 2 orders; customers {1, 2} = 2.

- East/Feb 2024: 200.00; 1 order; customers {1} = 1.

- East/Mar 2024: 99.50; 1 order; customers {3} = 1.

- West/Jan 2024: 300.00 + 150.00 = 450.00; 2 orders; customers {4} = 1 (customer 4 appears twice).

- West/Mar 2024: 250.00 + 400.00 = 650.00; 2 orders; customers {5} = 1 (the NULL customer_id is not counted).

- North/Feb 2024: 50.00; 1 order; customers {6} = 1.

Check: 650.00 + 450.00 + 200.50 + 200.00 + 99.50 + 50.00 = 1650.00, which equals 120.00 + 80.50 + 200.00 + 99.50 + 300.00 + 150.00 + 250.00 + 400.00 + 50.00 — so no Q1 row was lost and the April row was correctly excluded.

Step 7 — Final answer, ordered by revenue descending:

| region | month | revenue | orders | customers |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| West | 2024-03-01 | 650.00 | 2 | 1 |

| West | 2024-01-01 | 450.00 | 2 | 1 |

| East | 2024-01-01 | 200.50 | 2 | 2 |

| East | 2024-02-01 | 200.00 | 1 | 1 |

| East | 2024-03-01 | 99.50 | 1 | 1 |

| North | 2024-02-01 | 50.00 | 1 | 1 |

Analysis — The query is deliberately written in the order filter → derive → group → aggregate → sort, and that order is the whole lesson. `groupBy('region','month')` groups on keys that are not the table's partition columns, so the engine cannot satisfy the grouping locally: it must repartition rows by the hash of (region, month), which is a shuffle — data is written to local disk, pulled across the network, and read back. Because the shuffle happens after the filter in this plan, only the Q1 rows are ever shuffled. Prefiltering before the aggregation is exactly the technique of applying filters early to reduce the amount of data processed in each stage [source p.337]; on a real table, moving the predicate from after the aggregation to before it is usually the single highest-leverage change available.

Two type details are worth committing to memory. First, `countDistinct` is exact but keeps an in-memory set per group; on a high-cardinality key with millions of groups it can dominate memory, and `approx_count_distinct(customer_id, 0.05)` (a HyperLogLog sketch with 5% relative error) is the standard escape hatch. Second, `SUM(amount)` where every amount is NULL returns NULL rather than 0, because SQL uses three-valued logic; wrap it in `coalesce(SUM(amount), 0)` if the report must show a zero.

The common mistakes are all structural. Putting the region filter after the aggregation (`df.filter(col('revenue') > 500)`) raises an AnalysisException, because `revenue` does not exist as a column until the aggregation has run — in SQL you would need HAVING for that. Forgetting `month` in `groupBy` collapses the three East months into one row. Using `count('customer_id')` instead of `countDistinct('customer_id')` reports 2 for West/Jan instead of 1, silently over-counting repeat buyers, and using `count('customer_id')` where `count('*')` is meant under-counts orders whenever the customer is unknown. Finally, `ORDER BY revenue DESC` alone is not a total order: two regions with identical revenue can come back in either order across runs, so add a tiebreaker (`ORDER BY revenue DESC, region`) whenever the output is compared in a test or written to a downstream table.
Problem 2

A second Delta table `refunds(region STRING, amount DECIMAL(10,2), customer_id BIGINT)` holds exactly four rows, all for region East: (amount 100.00, customer_id 1), (amount 200.00, customer_id 2), (amount NULL, customer_id 3), (amount 300.00, customer_id NULL).

(a) Compute `AVG(amount)`, `SUM(amount) / COUNT(*)`, and `SUM(amount) / COUNT(amount)` and state which one is the true arithmetic mean.

(b) Compute `COUNT(*)`, `COUNT(amount)`, `COUNT(customer_id)` and `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)`.

(c) Suppose a later requirement is to keep only region-months whose revenue exceeds 500.00. Write the correct Spark SQL and the equivalent PySpark, and explain why filtering before the aggregation is not simply an alternative spelling but a different (and usually better) plan.
Hint: Aggregate functions skip NULL inputs; COUNT(*) does not skip anything.

Worked solution
(a) The mean.

- `AVG(amount)` = (100.00 + 200.00 + 300.00) / 3 = 600.00 / 3 = 200.00. The NULL amount is dropped from BOTH the numerator and the denominator.

- `SUM(amount) / COUNT(*)` = 600.00 / 4 = 150.00. SUM ignores the NULL, but COUNT(*) counts all four rows, so the two terms disagree about the population.

- `SUM(amount) / COUNT(amount)` = 600.00 / 3 = 200.00 — identical to AVG.

The true mean is 200.00, and the identity to remember is:

$$AVG(x) = \frac{SUM(x)}{COUNT(x)}$$

not `SUM(x) / COUNT(*)`. The 150.00 figure is the classic wrong answer produced by mixing a NULL-ignoring numerator with a NULL-counting denominator.

On data types: `AVG` over an integral column returns a DOUBLE in Spark SQL, not an integer. `AVG` of the INT values (1, 2) is 1.5, never 1. The pitfall of an integer average silently truncating belongs to engines and languages that perform integer division; in Spark SQL the `/` operator itself also produces a floating-point result, so `SUM(amount) / COUNT(*)` does not truncate either. Assume floating point and round explicitly at the presentation layer (`ROUND(..., 2)`) if the report needs two decimals.

(b) The counts.

- `COUNT(*)` = 4 — every row.

- `COUNT(amount)` = 3 — the NULL amount is skipped.

- `COUNT(customer_id)` = 3 — the NULL customer is skipped.

- `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` = 2 — the distinct set is {1, 2}; NULL is neither counted nor treated as a value that can equal another NULL.

So a business question phrased as "how many refund events?" must be `COUNT(*)` = 4, while "how many known customers?" is `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` = 2. Choosing the wrong column is not a cosmetic difference: it changes the metric.

(c) Filtering on the aggregate.

Spark SQL — the aggregate is filtered with HAVING:

```

SELECT region,

date_trunc('month', refund_date) AS month,

SUM(amount) AS revenue

FROM refunds

WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-03-31'

GROUP BY region, date_trunc('month', refund_date)

HAVING SUM(amount) > 500.00

ORDER BY revenue DESC;

```

PySpark — the DataFrame API has no HAVING keyword; the equivalent is `.filter()` placed after `.agg()`:

```

(spark.table('refunds')

.groupBy('region', 'month')

.agg(F.sum('amount').alias('revenue'))

.filter(F.col('revenue') > 500.00))

```

The two placements are not interchangeable. A `WHERE` predicate is evaluated per row before grouping and can shrink what gets shuffled; a `HAVING` predicate is evaluated per group after the aggregation and therefore cannot remove a single row from the shuffle. If the requirement really is `SUM(amount) > 500.00`, only `HAVING` can express it — the value does not exist row by row. But if the requirement can be rewritten as a row predicate (for example, keep only `amount > 50.00` contributions), pushing it into `WHERE` reduces the shuffled bytes before the exchange even starts [source p.337].

Analysis — This problem isolates three-valued logic, which is where most aggregation bugs originate. SQL NULL means "unknown", not "zero", so every aggregate except `COUNT(*)` ignores NULL inputs: `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX`, `COUNT(col)`, and `COUNT(DISTINCT col)` all work on the non-NULL subset, and each may be computing over a different population of rows. The practical rule is to decide per metric whether NULL is a missing value to be skipped or a category of event to be counted, and then choose the column argument accordingly.

The HAVING-versus-WHERE distinction is the other exam-relevant edge case. Logically the engine evaluates FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY, which is why a SELECT alias like `revenue` is visible in ORDER BY and HAVING but not in WHERE. A student who writes `WHERE revenue > 500` gets an unresolved-column error on the alias; a student who writes `HAVING amount > 50` gets either an error or a reference to an arbitrary row inside each group, which is worse because it can silently succeed under some engines. Note also that HAVING cannot save you a shuffle: it operates after the exchange.

The generalisation is that a filter's position in the plan is a performance decision, not just a syntax decision. Column pruning and predicate pushdown work because each column is stored as its own set of files, so a query can read a subset of fields instead of reconstructing full records [source p.419]. Push a predicate down to the scan and the same reduction applies to the shuffle. The edge case to watch is a predicate that depends on an aggregate, a window function, or a join result — it cannot be pushed below the operator that produces it, so it stays in HAVING or in a post-aggregation `.filter()`.
Problem 3

The `sales` table from Problem 1 has, at production scale, 40 columns, 2.4 billion rows, and 1.2 TB on disk. It is a Delta table partitioned by `order_date`. The Q1 region-month revenue query references only four columns (`region`, `order_date`, `amount`, `customer_id`), and Q1 rows account for 12% of all rows.

(a) Estimate the bytes read from storage and the bytes shuffled under three plans: (i) no column pruning and no prefilter, (ii) column pruning only, (iii) column pruning plus the Q1 prefilter. Express the improvement as ratios.

(b) Explain precisely why this group-by forces a shuffle, and what partitioning and clustering would each contribute.

(c) Name the two shuffles that appear in the physical plan of the final query and give one mitigation for each.
Hint: Bytes per column = total bytes / number of columns; multiply by the selectivity of the filter.

Worked solution
(a) Volume estimate.

Assume columns are roughly equal in size (an approximation we will revisit):

- Average bytes per column = 1.2 TB / 40 = 30 GB.

- Four referenced columns = 4 x 30 GB = 120 GB.

- Q1 selectivity = 12% = 0.12, so the post-filter volume = 120 GB x 0.12 = 14.4 GB.

Plan (i), no pruning, no prefilter: the engine touches all 40 columns and all rows, and everything eligible for the aggregation must reach the shuffle, so the shuffle traffic is approximately the full table: 1200 GB.

Plan (ii), pruning only: because columnar storage stores each column in its own set of files, the scan can read only the four needed fields rather than reconstructing full rows [source p.419]. Scan and shuffle traffic drop to 120 GB. Improvement factor: 1200 / 120 = 10x.

Plan (iii), pruning plus prefilter: the 120 GB is reduced by the Q1 row filter to 14.4 GB before the shuffle. Improvement over (ii): 120 / 14.4 = 8.33x. Improvement over (i): 1200 / 14.4 = 83.3x, i.e. the query processes roughly 1.2% of the naive volume.

In practice the scan of plan (iii) is even smaller than 14.4 GB, because `order_date` is a partition column: partition pruning means the reader never opens the partitions for the other nine months, so the bytes read approach the Q1 fraction directly at the file level rather than filtering after reading. Partitioning exists precisely because analytics workloads scan time ranges, and splitting the table on the date field makes those scans cheap [source p.240].

(b) Why the shuffle is unavoidable here.

Grouping requires that all rows sharing a group key land in the same task. The rows are laid out by partition (`order_date`) and, within a partition, by whatever order they arrived; two West rows from January and one West row from March live in different files, and probably on different machines. The engine therefore hashes each row on (region, month) and repartitions the data so that all rows for a given region-month are co-located; that repartition is the shuffle, and it costs a local write, a network transfer, and a local read for every row. Because the group keys are unrelated to the partition column, no amount of partitioning by date eliminates the exchange — it only shrinks the input to it.

Partitioning by `order_date` helps by pruning files at scan time. Clustering — sorting data within partitions by one or a few fields — helps differently: it colocates similar values, which improves filtering, sorting, and joining on those values [source p.240]. If the table were clustered (or Z-ordered / liquid-clustered) on `region`, the rows for each region would sit in contiguous file ranges, so the aggregation could skip data more aggressively and read fewer, denser files. Columnar storage also puts similar values next to each other, which is why columnar layouts are normally combined with compression [source p.419] — the 30 GB-per-column figure is itself an average, and in a real table the four narrow columns in this query are typically far cheaper than the wide text columns they sit beside.

(c) The two shuffles.

The physical plan of `... GROUP BY region, month ... ORDER BY revenue DESC` contains:

1. An Exchange with hash partitioning on (region, month), followed by the final HashAggregate. Mitigation: push the WHERE predicate below the aggregation, prune to four columns, and rely on partition pruning; these are exactly the reductions quantified above. Adaptive Query Execution in Databricks Runtime then coalesces small post-shuffle partitions, so you rarely need to hand-tune `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` for the automatic case.

2. An Exchange with range partitioning on revenue DESC, followed by a Sort for the global ORDER BY. Mitigation: only ask for the global order if the consumer needs it — a downstream writer that re-sorts anyway pays twice — and keep the sort on the small aggregated result (six rows here), never on the 2.4-billion-row base table.

Analysis — This problem turns an intuition ("filter early, select few columns") into arithmetic. The two levers are independent and multiplicative: pruning cuts columns, and prefiltering cuts rows, so their combined effect here is about 83x. That factorization is the reason query tuning notes usually list "select only what you need" and "filter before you aggregate or join" as separate items rather than as one tip. The unit is shuffled bytes, not rows, because the shuffle is a disk-write plus network-read per row — it is the dominant cost in almost every distributed aggregation, and it is also the easiest quantity to reason about with a spreadsheet.

The methodological caveat is that the "total bytes divided by number of columns" estimate assumes uniform column sizes. Real tables have skewed columns — long free-text or nested columns can be 10x the average — so the estimate is a first-order sanity check, not a measurement. The correct engineering practice is to confirm with the query profile's scan and shuffle byte metrics rather than to trust the arithmetic.

Common mistakes at this stage: calling `.count()` or `.show()` on an intermediate DataFrame to "check" a transformation, which triggers an extra full job over the data; writing the filtered Q1 rows to an intermediate Delta table and re-reading them, which adds a full write and read to save a filter that costs nothing in the same job; wrapping `date_trunc` in a Python UDF, which blocks predicate pushdown and adds serialization overhead; and `persist()`-ing the 1.2 TB base table to "speed up" a single-use query, which just moves the cost into the cache. The generalisation is that on Delta Lake the cheap wins are all metadata wins — partition pruning, file skipping on statistics, column pruning — and they are available before you change a single line of the business logic.
Problem 4

Using the Q1 result produced in Problem 1 — West/2024-01 with 450.00, East/2024-01 with 200.50, East/2024-02 with 200.00, North/2024-02 with 50.00, West/2024-03 with 650.00, East/2024-03 with 99.50 — write a query that returns exactly one row per month of Q1 giving the highest-revenue region for that month. Then extend the solution so that (i) if two regions tie for the top revenue in a month, both are returned, and (ii) every month of Q1 appears in the output even if no region had orders in that month. Finally, state the difference between `ROW_NUMBER`, `RANK` and `DENSE_RANK` for the tie case, and say which one a "return all tied winners" requirement demands.
Hint: Aggregate first, rank second — a window function over raw rows ranks individual orders, not regions.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Compute the monthly figures first. A window function cannot rank regions before the revenue exists, so the aggregation from Problem 1 becomes a subquery (a common table expression in SQL, a DataFrame in PySpark):

```

WITH monthly AS (

SELECT region,

date_trunc('month', order_date) AS month,

SUM(amount) AS revenue

FROM sales

WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-03-31'

GROUP BY region, date_trunc('month', order_date)

),

ranked AS (

SELECT region,

month,

revenue,

RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rk

FROM monthly

)

SELECT month, region, revenue

FROM ranked

WHERE rk = 1

ORDER BY month;

```

The PySpark equivalent uses `Window`:

```

from pyspark.sql import Window

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

w = Window.partitionBy('month').orderBy(F.col('revenue').desc())

(q1.withColumn('rk', F.rank().over(w))

.filter(F.col('rk') == 1)

.select('month', 'region', 'revenue')

.orderBy('month'))

```

Step 2 — Compute the answer by hand. Partitioning by month gives three independent windows, each sorted by revenue descending:

- January 2024: {West 450.00, East 200.50} → West, 450.00.

- February 2024: {East 200.00, North 50.00} → East, 200.00.

- March 2024: {West 650.00, East 99.50} → West, 650.00.

| month | region | revenue |

|---|---|---|

| 2024-01-01 | West | 450.00 |

| 2024-02-01 | East | 200.00 |

| 2024-03-01 | West | 650.00 |

Note that January contains East/2024-01 at 200.50; a careless answer that ranks on amount rather than on aggregated revenue would return the single largest order of the month and produce a completely different (and meaningless) result.

Step 3 — Ties. `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY revenue DESC)` assigns 1 to every region tied at the top, so `WHERE rk = 1` returns them all. The three ranking functions differ only in what they do after a tie. For revenues 450.00, 450.00, 300.00: `ROW_NUMBER` gives 1, 2, 3 — the tie is broken arbitrarily, and the winner can change between runs because the pre-window row order is not guaranteed; `RANK` gives 1, 1, 3 — it leaves a gap; `DENSE_RANK` gives 1, 1, 2 — no gap. Both `RANK` and `DENSE_RANK` satisfy "return all tied winners"; `ROW_NUMBER` never does, because it is defined to emit distinct integers. The requirement therefore demands `RANK` (or `DENSE_RANK`, which is equivalent for the `= 1` predicate but differs if you later ask for the top three places).

Step 4 — Gap months. A month with no orders produces no group at all, so no window row exists and the month simply vanishes from the output. If North had no February orders, February would still appear because East has one; but a month in which no region sold anything would disappear entirely. Two standard fixes:

- Build the grid explicitly and left-join the facts onto it. In Spark SQL: create a month dimension with `SELECT explode(sequence(to_date('2024-01-01'), to_date('2024-03-01'), interval 1 month)) AS month`, cross join it with `SELECT DISTINCT region FROM sales`, then `LEFT JOIN monthly` on both keys and `coalesce(revenue, 0)`.

- Or maintain a small persistent date/calendar table in Unity Catalog and join against it — the usual production answer, because the calendar is reusable across every report.

Step 5 — Schema detail. `date_trunc('month', order_date)` returns a TIMESTAMP at midnight. If the consumer expects a DATE column, add `CAST(date_trunc('month', order_date) AS DATE)`, or use `trunc(order_date, 'month')`, which returns a DATE directly.

Analysis — The key structural point is that this is a two-stage problem: aggregate, then rank. A window function is computed after the FROM/WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING phases and before the final ORDER BY, so it can only see the rows that the aggregation produced. Students who apply the window to the base table rank individual orders; students who try to mix `GROUP BY` and a window over the same ungrouped columns get an error or, worse, a silently arbitrary row. The safe pattern is always CTE-with-aggregation → window → filter.

The tie-handling discussion generalises beyond this query. `ROW_NUMBER` is the right operator when you genuinely want one row and can supply a deterministic tiebreaker as a secondary sort key (`ORDER BY revenue DESC, region`); without that tiebreaker it is non-deterministic, which is exactly the kind of bug that passes in development and fails in a nightly job. `RANK` is the right operator for "all winners". `DENSE_RANK` differs from `RANK` only beyond the tie block, so a "top 3" report written with `RANK` can return two rows while one written with `DENSE_RANK` returns three — a genuine definitional choice that must be made with the business, not by the engineer.

The gap-month edge case is a data-modelling point rather than a Spark point: an aggregation can only return groups that exist, so any report that must show a value for every period needs a driving dimension table (a calendar, a region list) and a LEFT JOIN. A fact table stores events at the lowest grain available — an order is one row, with the customer and date attributes resolved through dimension tables [source p.324] — and because facts only exist when something happened, the dense grid has to come from dimensions. The remaining mistake to avoid is the loop anti-pattern: running one query per month with `LIMIT 1`. That scans the fact table N times and produces N jobs; a single windowed query does it in one pass.

actions.text: Let's put that aggregation pattern straight to work. This page walks through four worked problems on the same sales table, and each one is a trap the exam loves to set. Problem one is the full monthly revenue report: from sales — region, order_date, amount, customer_id — return each region's monthly revenue, order count, and distinct customer count for Q1, ordered by revenue descending. Notice it asks for three metrics at once, and one of them counts distinct customers.

The hint flags the two highest-leverage moves. Filter the rows before you group, so fewer rows ever get shuffled. And derive the month column directly from order_date, then group on that — never try to aggregate on the raw timestamp.

Here's the worked solution. In PySpark we filter order_date into the Q1 window, add a month column with date_trunc, then groupBy region and month and aggregate sum of amount, count star, and countDistinct of customer_id, finishing with orderBy descending revenue. The Spark SQL version is the direct translation: WHERE the date range, GROUP BY region and the truncated month, ORDER BY revenue descending. Practise writing either form from memory.

Now the analysis, and this is the part worth memorising. We're grouping on region and month, which are not the partition columns, so Spark is forced to shuffle. Filtering before grouping shrinks the shuffled bytes, and that is the single highest-leverage optimisation here. Keep the common pitfalls in mind as well: using WHERE on an aggregate instead of HAVING, expecting avg() of an integer column to return a decimal, and reaching for count of customer_id when the nulls must also be counted.

Problem two moves to a refunds table and isolates three-valued logic — how aggregate functions skip NULL inputs, and why COUNT of a column behaves differently from COUNT star. Problems three and four build on the same theme: estimating table volume from column statistics, and then ranking the monthly figures with a window function once you've aggregated. Work through all four on your own — if you can write problem one cold, the rest are variations on the same pattern.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Aggregations Under Exam Conditions

questions.question: A Delta table named silver.sales holds one row per order line with the columns region, product, order_id, and amount. You need a result set that contains exactly one row per distinct combination of region and product, showing the total amount for that combination. Which query returns that result?

options.label: SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM silver.sales GROUP BY region, product;
SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region, product) AS revenue FROM silver.sales;
SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM silver.sales GROUP BY region;
SELECT DISTINCT region, product, amount FROM silver.sales;

questions.analysis: Option A is correct because a GROUP BY clause defines the grouping keys, and the aggregation contract is one output row per distinct key combination: every order line in the same (region, product) pair is collapsed into a single row with its amounts summed. This is exactly the pattern the distributed aggregation pipeline is built around: partial aggregates are computed locally, then the grouping key is hashed so that each key lands on exactly one node, where the partial results are combined into the final row [source p.348]. Option B is the classic window-function misconception. A window expression does not reduce the row count at all; it annotates every input row with a value computed over its window, so a table with 10,000 order lines still returns 10,000 rows, many of which repeat the same (region, product) pair and the same total. Option C is not just wrong, it fails: the select list contains product, which is neither present in the GROUP BY clause nor wrapped in an aggregate, so Spark raises an analysis error along the lines of 'expression product is neither present in the group by, nor is it an aggregate function'. Option D is not an aggregation at all. DISTINCT applied to (region, product, amount) de-duplicates whole triples, so a single region/product combination with five different amounts still produces up to five rows, and the amounts are raw rather than totaled. A precondition worth memorizing for exam items: GROUP BY never synthesizes rows that do not exist in the data, so if a region has no sales at all it will be absent from the output; producing a zero row for it requires an outer join against a region dimension or a calendar-style cross join. Also note that MPP engines were explicitly optimized for this workload — high-performance aggregation over massive parallel scans is their core design goal [source p.125] — which is why grouped aggregates are the canonical 'one row per group' construct rather than DISTINCT or a window. Points are awarded for selecting A; choosing B indicates confusion between grouping and windowing, and choosing C or D indicates a missing grasp of the GROUP BY contract.

questions.question: You are reviewing an aggregated query that measures daily revenue per region. Select the TWO statements that correctly describe WHERE versus HAVING and the effect of filtering on the amount of data that must be shuffled across the cluster.

options.label: A row-level predicate written in WHERE, such as WHERE event_date = '2024-06-01' AND amount IS NOT NULL, is applied before the grouping and before the exchange, so it reduces the number of rows that are written to and read from the shuffle.
A predicate inside HAVING, such as HAVING amount > 100, filters individual rows before the grouping and therefore reduces shuffled data exactly as much as the equivalent WHERE clause does.
The engine cannot push a WHERE predicate below the aggregation, so a WHERE filter on a row-level column is always evaluated after the shuffle, which is why WHERE and HAVING have identical cost.

HAVING may reference aggregate expressions such as HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000 and is applied to the already-grouped result, so it can remove entire groups but cannot reduce the volume of data that was shuffled.

questions.analysis: Options A and D are correct, and they describe the two halves of the same optimization story. Option A states the pre-aggregation filter: predicates on ordinary row-level columns belong in WHERE because the logical plan applies them before the grouping operator, so filtered rows never reach the exchange. Query optimizers treat the early application of filters as a top priority precisely because it can dramatically reduce the amount of data processed by everything downstream [source p.337]. When the filtered column is also the partition key — for example event_date on a table partitioned by event_date — the predicate additionally enables partition pruning, so entire directories are never listed or read. Option D states the HAVING contract correctly: HAVING is evaluated after grouping, its predicates may reference aggregates such as SUM(amount) or COUNT(*), and its only leverage is to drop finished groups. Dropping a group after the shuffle saves downstream work, but the rows of that group were still hashed, serialized, and moved over the network, so the shuffled byte volume is unchanged. This matters because the shuffle is the expensive step: it redistributes data by key so that each key ends up on exactly one node [source p.348], and every byte crossing the network competes for the same cluster bandwidth that the local, embarrassingly parallel map-side scans depend on [source p.246]. Option B is a misconception about evaluation order. HAVING is not applied to individual rows before grouping; 'HAVING amount > 100' is either an error (amount is not aggregated and not a grouping key, so the engine complains) or, in dialects that tolerate it, a post-grouping filter that behaves nothing like the row-level WHERE. Option C inverts the truth twice: WHERE filters are routinely pushed below the aggregation, and the whole point of that pushdown is that WHERE and HAVING do not have identical cost. A useful memory hook for the exam: WHERE decides which rows reach the aggregate, HAVING decides which groups survive it.

questions.question: A nightly revenue report reads a Delta table and returns the following result. For EMEA it reports 600.00 as the average order value, but the reporting team insists the true average order value for EMEA is 200.00. The table contains these order lines: (region=EMEA, order_id=1, customer_id='C1', amount=100), (region=EMEA, order_id=2, customer_id=NULL, amount=200), (region=EMEA, order_id=3, customer_id=NULL, amount=300), (region=APAC, order_id=4, customer_id='C2', amount=50), (region=APAC, order_id=5, customer_id='C3', amount=50). The query is: SELECT region, COUNT(customer_id) AS paying_orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue, ROUND(SUM(amount) / COUNT(customer_id), 2) AS avg_order_value FROM sales GROUP BY region; Diagnose why the EMEA figure is wrong, show the arithmetic that produces both the reported number and the correct number, explain which other aggregate functions in this query are or are not affected by NULLs, and give at least two concrete rewrites that would produce the correct metric.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric, total 100 percent. (1) Correct root cause, 40 percent: the answer must state that COUNT(customer_id) counts only rows where customer_id IS NOT NULL, so the two EMEA guest-checkout rows (order_id 2 and 3, amount 200 and 300) are excluded from the denominator while their amounts remain in SUM(amount). Award full credit only if the answer names COUNT(col) null-elimination as the cause and identifies which column is nullable; award partial credit if the answer says 'NULL problem' without naming COUNT(customer_id) as the specific culprit. (2) Correct arithmetic, 25 percent: reported EMEA figure is 600 / 1 = 600.00 because SUM(amount) = 100 + 200 + 300 = 600 and COUNT(customer_id) = 1; the correct figure is 600 / 3 = 200.00 because there are three order lines. Full credit requires both the numbers and the implied conclusion that the metric was overstated by 3x (200 percent). (3) Collateral damage analysis, 20 percent: the answer should note that SUM(amount) is unaffected here only because no amount is NULL (SUM ignores NULLs but the amounts are present), that COUNT(*) would return 3 for EMEA, and that COUNT(DISTINCT col) also skips NULLs. Award credit for stating that any metric built as a ratio of a NULL-sensitive count to an amount, price, or quantity column is at risk, and that COUNT(*) is the correct row-count aggregate while COUNT(col) answers a narrower question. (4) Concrete rewrites, 15 percent: acceptable answers include replacing COUNT(customer_id) with COUNT(*) or COUNT(1) or COUNT(order_id) when order_id is a non-nullable key; alternatively keeping COUNT(customer_id) but renaming the column to orders_with_known_customer and computing avg order value as SUM(amount) / COUNT(*); or using COUNT_IF(customer_id IS NOT NULL) if that narrower metric is genuinely intended. Full credit requires at least two distinct rewrites. Deduct for any answer that simply adds a WHERE clause to remove NULL customer rows without noting that this also changes the revenue total, since that alters the measure rather than fixing it.
questions.analysis: The report is wrong because COUNT(customer_id) is a NULL-eliminating aggregate: it counts rows in the group where the argument is not NULL, so it counts 1 in EMEA rather than the 3 order lines that exist. SUM(amount) has no such problem in this example because none of the amount values are NULL; SUM ignores NULL amounts but still adds the 100, 200, and 300, giving 600. The metric is then formed as 600 / 1 = 600.00 instead of 600 / 3 = 200.00, a threefold overstatement that survives every visual check of the query, because the SQL is syntactically perfect and the engine raises no warning. The trap generalizes to any derived metric built from a null-sensitive count: revenue per paying customer, average order value, conversion rate, and fill rate are all vulnerable when the denominator uses a nullable column. Note also that the grouping itself is unaffected here: the aggregation pipeline hashes the grouping key region so that every EMEA row is combined on one node while the partial sums from each scan are merged [source p.348], and that distributed aggregation is precisely the workload MPP and lakehouse engines were designed to run at scale [source p.125]. The correctness defect is entirely in the choice of aggregate, not in the execution. Two safe fixes are: SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue, ROUND(SUM(amount) / COUNT(*), 2) AS avg_order_value FROM sales GROUP BY region; or, if the business genuinely wants the count of identified customers, keep COUNT(customer_id) but rename it orders_with_known_customer and compute the average against COUNT(*) — the definition must match the label, otherwise the number is technically computable but semantically false. A common wrong fix to flag in review is adding WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL, which silently deletes 500 of the 600 EMEA revenue and changes the measure being reported rather than repairing it. One further edge case: if the source table were a CSV read with inferSchema, the NULL customer_id values could instead arrive as the empty string, in which case COUNT(customer_id) would return 3 and the bug would disappear while a string-equality filter elsewhere would quietly break — which is why explicit schemas and explicit NULL semantics are worth defending in the mediation (bronze/silver/gold) layers of the lakehouse.

Take your time, answer every part including the written one, and I'll walk through anything that tripped you up once you submit.

scenes.title: Joining Datasets: Types, Semantics, and Row Counts

elements.content: Join Semantics and Row Counts

PySpark: df.join(other, on='customer_id', how='left')

SQL: SELECT * FROM orders LEFT JOIN customers ON customer_id
INNER keeps matches only. LEFT/RIGHT OUTER keep all rows from one side and NULL-fill the other. FULL OUTER keeps rows from both sides.
LEFT SEMI returns left columns only for matches. LEFT ANTI returns left rows with no match. CROSS pairs every left row with every right row.
Broadcast: spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold decides; else shuffle [source p.337].
Watch for: ambiguous columns, key type mismatches, NULL keys that never match.
Worked example: key 'this' appears 5× in A, 10× in B → 5 × 10 = 50 output rows [source p.323]. Row explosion can exhaust resources; prune unneeded columns [source p.304].

actions.text: Now that we've seen how aggregations collapse rows, let's look at the operation that multiplies them: the join. This page covers join semantics and, just as importantly, the row counts each join type produces.

Start with the core join types. INNER keeps only matched rows. LEFT OUTER keeps all rows from the left table and fills nulls where the right side has no match; RIGHT OUTER mirrors that. FULL OUTER keeps everything from both sides, with nulls on whichever side is missing. Being able to predict the output row count from the join type is exactly what the exam tests.

Two types deserve special attention. LEFT SEMI returns only the left-hand columns for rows that have a match — it behaves like a filtered left table, not a widening one. LEFT ANTI does the opposite: it returns left rows that have no match at all. Neither one adds columns from the right side, which is a very common trap.

For syntax, you'll use both APIs. In PySpark it's df.join(other, on='customer_id', how='left'), and the same operation in SQL is a LEFT JOIN with an ON clause. Same semantics, two spellings — you should be fluent in both.

Now the performance lever. A broadcast join replicates the small table to every executor, which eliminates the shuffle entirely. Databricks applies this automatically when one side falls below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, so knowing that setting tells you why an otherwise expensive join suddenly gets fast.

Watch for the classic failure modes: ambiguous column names after the join, join-key type mismatches that silently return nothing, duplicate column names, and null join keys that never match anything. Each of these is a frequent exam distractor.

Finally, the worked example. When a key appears five times in table A and ten times in table B, an inner join produces fifty rows — five times ten. That multiplication is the heart of join row counts, and it's why an unexpected row explosion almost always traces back to a non-unique key on one side.

So the mental checklist is: know what each join type keeps, be able to write it in SQL or PySpark, and always ask whether your keys are unique before you trust the row count. Let's put that to the test on the comparison page coming up.

scenes.title: Comparison: Which Join Type Returns Which Rows?

elements.content: Dimension  |  Left Join (Left Outer Join)  |  Left Semi Join  |  Left Anti Join

Rows returned relative to the left input (contrasted with inner join)
Left Join (Left Outer Join): A left outer join returns every row of the left table: an inner join would keep only the matched pairs, whereas the left join additionally emits each unmatched left row exactly once with NULLs in every right-side column.
Left Semi Join: A left semi join returns each left row exactly once if and only if at least one right row satisfies the join predicate, so on the same data it returns the same rows as an inner join but without the right-side columns and without duplication.
Left Anti Join: A left anti join returns each left row exactly once if and only if no right row satisfies the join predicate, making it the exact complement of the semi join and the empty-result counterpart of the inner join on the same left input.

Row multiplicity and row-explosion risk (worked example)
Left Join (Left Outer Join): If the join key value 'this' appears 5 times in the left table and 10 times in the right table, a left join emits 5 × 10 = 50 rows for that one key value, because it materialises every matched pair [source p.323].
Left Semi Join: Under the same 5 × 10 repetition pattern a left semi join emits exactly 5 rows — one per left row — so duplication of the key on the right side cannot multiply the output, which is why semi joins are the safe choice for existence checks [source p.323].
Left Anti Join: Under the same 5 × 10 repetition pattern a left anti join emits 0 rows for that key value, since every left row has at least one match, and it therefore has no multiplicative failure mode at all [source p.323].

Null handling on the join key
Left Join (Left Outer Join): Spark evaluates equality join predicates with three-valued logic, so NULL never equals NULL; a left row whose key is NULL is not matched and is preserved as an unmatched row with NULL right-side columns, which superficially looks like a genuine match.
Left Semi Join: A left row whose join key is NULL is dropped by a left semi join, because the predicate never evaluates to TRUE and no existence can be established, which surprises learners who assume a filter-like operator will 'keep' such rows.
Left Anti Join: The same NULL-key left row is retained by a left anti join, because 'no right row satisfies NULL = right_key' is trivially true, which is exactly why left anti join is the idiomatic way to find records with missing keys.

Columns present in the output schema
Left Join (Left Outer Join): The output schema is the concatenation of all left columns plus all right columns (with identically named join keys de-duplicated), so downstream code may legally select right-side attributes such as product_name or customer_segment.
Left Semi Join: The output contains only the left table's columns, because a semi join is a filtering operation rather than a column-adding operator; a subsequent select of any right-side column fails at analysis time, and this is the classic exam distractor.
Left Anti Join: The output likewise contains only left-side columns, so an anti join that answers 'rows in A that have no B' gives you no access to B's attributes and usually forces either a second join or a NOT EXISTS subquery.

Effect on downstream counts and aggregation
Left Join (Left Outer Join): count(*) is inflated by the join multiplicity — one row per matching pair — so counting distinct left entities requires count(DISTINCT left_id) or a pre-join aggregation to recover the true cardinality.
Left Semi Join: count(*) already equals the number of matching left entities, so count(DISTINCT left_id) is redundant and semi joins are the safest inner step before a grouped aggregate.
Left Anti Join: count(*) directly measures the number of non-matching left entities, which makes left anti join the direct way to compute a metric such as 'how many customers never ordered'.

Storage and I/O cost characteristics
Left Join (Left Outer Join): A left join must materialise the right-side payload columns for every matched pair, so bytes moved and shuffle volume scale with the match multiplicity rather than merely with the two input row counts.
Left Semi Join: A semi join only needs the right-side join key to decide existence, and because columnar serialization lets an engine scan only the columns a query requires, this can dramatically reduce the data read from disk and over the network [source p.239].
Left Anti Join: An anti join has the same narrow-column advantage as the semi join for the probe side, though it must still confirm the absence of any matching key, which is why it is often paired with a broadcast of the small right-side key set.

Typical use case and question-wording mapping
Left Join (Left Outer Join): Use a left join when the requirement says 'including customers with no orders' or when you are enriching a stream with reference data, as in the enrichment pattern where incoming events are joined to product and demographic lookups and the enriched events flow on downstream [source p.312].
Left Semi Join: Use a left semi join when the requirement says 'customers who ordered' — it answers an existence question and, in relational designs, mirrors the index-assisted foreign-key lookup that decides whether a matching parent record exists [source p.239].
Left Anti Join: Use a left anti join when the requirement says 'customers who never ordered', and it is also the standard incremental-load pattern for selecting only source IDs that are not yet present in the target table.

Syntax, optimizer behaviour, and failure modes
Left Join (Left Outer Join): Spark SQL spells it LEFT OUTER JOIN and the DataFrame API uses how='left', but optimizers may reorder joins and predicates, so a row explosion produced at an early stage can still fail the query even when a later predicate would have removed those rows [source p.323].
Left Semi Join: Spark SQL spells it LEFT SEMI JOIN and the DataFrame API uses how='left_semi'; it is planned as an existence operator that can be satisfied by a broadcast semi-join when the right side is small, so it never needs the right-side payload.
Left Anti Join: Spark SQL spells it LEFT ANTI JOIN and the DataFrame API uses how='left_anti'; the optimizer frequently rewrites NOT EXISTS (and NOT IN when NULL semantics permit) into a left anti join, which is precisely why the 'filter, not column-adder' mental model is the one to hold.

Takeaway — Choose a left outer join when the deliverable must present right-side attributes or must preserve unmatched left rows in the output schema — 'including customers with no orders' — and accept that non-unique right-side keys will multiply rows.

Takeaway — Choose a left semi join when the deliverable is a filtered subset of the left table whose existence in the right table is the only criterion; it is duplicate-safe, column-narrow, and maps to 'customers who ordered'.

Takeaway — Choose a left anti join when the deliverable is the complement of that existence test — 'customers who never ordered', missing keys, or rows not yet loaded into a target — remembering that NULL keys always land in the anti result and never in the semi result.

Takeaway — Before writing any of them, check the cardinality of both sides of the join key: a 5 × 10 key repetition turns 15 input rows into 50 output rows, and no amount of later filtering is guaranteed to save the query once that explosion has occurred [source p.323].

actions.text: Here's the comparison table you'll want burned into memory. We're lining up four join types side by side — inner, left, left semi, and left anti — across the dimensions the exam actually tests: rows returned, null handling, output columns, and typical use case.

Start with row counts. An inner join keeps only matching pairs. A left join keeps every row from the left input — matched rows get their right-side columns filled in, unmatched rows get nulls. Left semi keeps each left row that has at least one match, exactly once. Left anti keeps the left rows that have no match at all. Notice those last two keep one copy of the left row, never a multiplied set.

Null handling on the join key is the trap. In Spark, a null key never matches anything — not even another null. So a left join on a nullable key will not produce a match for those rows; it produces them as unmatched, with nulls on the right. Inner join drops them entirely. Semi and anti treat them as non-matching, which means anti will actually return them.

Now the output schema. Inner, left, and left outer joins add the right-side columns into the result. Semi and anti do not — they are filters, not column-adders. This is the frequent distractor: the question asks for a result that includes right-side columns, and an answer option offers a left semi join. That option is always wrong, because semi joins can only ever return left-side columns.

Then there's row multiplicity. If your join key isn't unique on the right side, a left join multiplies left rows — that's row explosion. Semi and anti are immune to it, because they never duplicate a left row. So when you see counts suddenly triple after a join, the first thing to inspect is key cardinality.

The use case column is really a translation table for question wording. "Customers who ordered" means semi. "Customers who never ordered" or "products with no sales" means anti. "Including customers with no orders" means left. Read the wording carefully — the phrasing is deliberately chosen to point at exactly one join type.

First takeaway: choose a left outer join when the deliverable must include unmatched left rows and needs the right-side columns present. If the expected output carries right-side fields, you're in left join territory, not semi.

Second: choose a left semi join when the deliverable is pure filter semantics — keep the left rows that have a match, and the right side contributes nothing to the output. It's also the efficient way to express an EXISTS-style condition.

Third: choose a left anti join when you want the rows that never found a partner. It's your anti-join pattern, it never duplicates left rows, and unlike an inner join followed by a null filter, it's the clean and correct expression.

And the meta-takeaway before you write any of them: check the cardinality of your join keys first. Verify whether the right key is unique, consider whether nulls can appear on either side, and confirm the expected row count. Do that, and the join type almost selects itself. On the next page we'll lock this in with a checkpoint.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Joins and Join Strategies

questions.question:
You have two DataFrames in a Databricks notebook. orders contains 5 rows and has a column customer_id; customers contains 3 rows and its customer_id column is a unique primary key. Exactly 4 of the 5 order rows have a customer_id value that also exists in customers; the remaining order row references customer_id 999, which is absent from customers. Which statement correctly predicts the row count of each join?

  inner = orders.join(customers, "customer_id", "inner")
  left  = orders.join(customers, "customer_id", "left")

How many rows does each result contain?

options.label: inner returns 4 rows and left returns 5 rows, because a left join preserves every row of the left table while an inner join discards unmatched left rows.
inner returns 5 rows and left returns 5 rows, because both joins keep the full left table and only differ in whether right-side columns are null.
inner returns 4 rows and left returns 4 rows, because the unmatched order row is dropped by both joins since no match exists on the right side.
inner returns 5 rows and left returns 6 rows, because the left join adds one synthetic null row for every unmatched key.

questions.analysis: An inner join keeps only the rows that satisfy the join predicate, so the one order whose customer_id is 999 has no partner in customers and is discarded, leaving 4 rows. A left (outer) join preserves every row of the left input regardless of whether a match exists, so all 5 orders survive; the unmatched row is padded with nulls for the customers columns. Joins are the most common means of combining datasets, which is exactly why the two semantics must be distinguished before you run the job [source p.301]. Option B is the classic misconception that a left join is just an inner join with extra null columns added, which misstates the row count as well. Option C inverts the rule and drops the unmatched row from the left join. Option D invents an extra row: a left join emits one output row per surviving left row, not one extra row per unmatched key. One important edge case: with a unique right-side key, left returns exactly 5 rows, but if customers.customer_id were not unique, a single order could match several customer rows and the left result would grow beyond 5 through one-to-many repetition [source p.323]. Always check key uniqueness before trusting the predicted row count.

questions.question: A Databricks job joins a 2 TB fact table (fact_sales) to a small dimension table (dim_store) on store_id. Under which conditions will the query optimizer select a broadcast join rather than a shuffle hash join? Select all that apply.

options.label: One side of the join is small enough to be collected and broadcast to every executor, typically because its collected statistics fall below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (default 10 MB).
The small side has been pre-filtered down to a handful of rows, or the query carries an explicit hint such as /*+ BROADCAST(dim_store) */ that forces the plan.
Both inputs exceed the broadcast threshold and neither side can fit on a single node.
The join is written as a left outer join, because outer joins are always executed as broadcasts.

questions.analysis: A broadcast (map-side) join is chosen when one input is small enough to be copied to every executor, so no shuffle of the large table is needed; the engine makes this decision from statistics and the configured threshold, and you can also force it with a broadcast hint. In practice the broadcast side is often a down-filtered larger table that the engine collects and broadcasts, and prefiltering data to create broadcast joins where possible is one of the highest-leverage optimizations available, because query optimizers prioritize early filter application and join reordering to shrink what each join must process [source p.337]. Option C describes the opposite case: when neither table fits on a single node, the engine falls back to a shuffle hash join, which repartitions both sides by a hash of the join key [source p.337]. Option D is a fabricated rule: the join type (inner versus left outer) does not determine the physical join strategy, and a broadcast join is legal for outer joins as long as the broadcast side is the one whose non-matching rows may be null-padded. Choosing the right strategy matters because joins are how we create value by combining datasets, so the access path is as important as the join type [source p.301].

questions.question:
You join events (left) to promo_lookup (right) on a promo_code column. In events, the value 'SPRING' appears 5 times; in promo_lookup, the value 'SPRING' appears 10 times. All other promo_code values appear at most once on each side.

(a) Exactly how many output rows does the 'SPRING' value contribute to the join result, and what is this phenomenon called? Show the arithmetic.
(b) Explain the operational risk this creates on a large production table and name one mitigation the optimizer or the engineer can apply.
(c) An analyst asks: 'Which customers placed at least one order in Q1 2024?' The orders table has one row per order line. Would you write an inner join or a left semi join, and why?
(d) The same analyst now asks for the total amount of every Q1 order together with the customer name. Which join do you use, and what must you still guard against?
questions.commentPrompt: Grade out of 100%, then scale to the question's point value. (1) Part (a) - 25%: must state 5 x 10 = 50 rows and name row explosion (many-to-many / non-unique join key). Award partial credit if the multiplication is right but the term is missing. (2) Part (b) - 25%: must explain that row explosion can consume massive resources or make the query fail, and must give at least one credible mitigation: pre-filtering to shrink inputs, broadcast the small side, deduplicate the key before joining, or reorder joins so filters apply early. (3) Part (c) - 25%: must select left semi join and justify it - it returns each left row at most once (no duplication even when multiple orders match), returns only left-side columns, and answers an existence question; an inner join would return one row per matching order, so you would need DISTINCT. (4) Part (d) - 25%: must select an inner (or left) join because right-side columns such as customer name are required, and must still guard against non-unique keys inflating the result - verify uniqueness or aggregate first. Deduct up to 15% for a vague answer that names a join without mechanics.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. (a) This is row explosion. Because the join key is repeated, the engine pairs every 'SPRING' row from the left with every 'SPRING' row from the right: 5 x 10 = 50 output rows, even though the left table contributed only 5 rows. The source describes exactly this case - a join key repeated five times in table A and ten times in table B produces 5 x 10 = 50 rows via a cross-join of the matching rows [source p.323]. (b) Row explosion often generates enough rows to consume a massive quantity of database resources or even cause a query to fail, and if it happens in an early stage of the plan the query can fail even though a later predicate should have filtered the result correctly [source p.323]. Mitigations: prefilter both sides so the small input can be broadcast, deduplicate the join key (for example with dropDuplicates or a GROUP BY before joining), or rely on early filter pushdown and join reordering [source p.337]. (c) Use a left semi join. The question is an existence question ('at least one order'), and a semi join returns each left row at most once and only the left-side columns, so a customer with seven Q1 orders appears once rather than seven times. An inner join would also work semantically only if you wrap it in DISTINCT or a GROUP BY, and it would additionally multiply rows whenever the right key is non-unique. (d) Use an inner join (or a left join if customers with no orders must be preserved), because the customer name lives on the right side and semi joins cannot project right-side columns. You must still guard against the non-unique key: either confirm customer_id is unique in the dimension table or aggregate the order lines first, otherwise a duplicated customer row silently inflates the totals.
