scenes.title: Window Functions: Partition, Order, Frame

elements.content: Window Functions: Partition, Order, Frame
Anatomy: fn() OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY t ROWS BETWEEN a AND b)
A window keeps every row; GROUP BY returns one row per group.
row_number() unique; rank() leaves gaps; dense_rank() none.
Dedup: row_number() = 1 keeps the latest row [source p.343]
Partitioning prunes scans [source p.240]; PKs unenforced [source p.342].
Worked example: amounts 100, 50, 25 → running total 100, 150, 175.

actions.text: Good — with joins behind us, let's move on to the last query pattern in this lesson: window functions. This is where a lot of people get tripped up on the exam, because the syntax looks unusual even though the underlying idea is simple.

Start with the anatomy. A window function is just a normal function followed by the OVER clause. Inside OVER you have three optional parts: PARTITION BY, which splits rows into independent groups; ORDER BY, which sequences rows within each partition; and the frame clause — that ROWS BETWEEN ... AND ... — which defines exactly which neighbouring rows feed each output row. Miss any one of these and the result changes, so read the clause like a sentence, left to right.

Here's the mental model that matters most: a window keeps every row. GROUP BY collapses your table down to one row per group — you lose the detail. A window function computes per-partition, per-sorted-row values while leaving the original rows intact. That single difference is why window functions can do ranking, running totals, and deduplication, all things plain aggregation can't express.

Look at the diagram. Rows are first split into partitions, then ordered inside each partition, and that highlighted sliding frame shows which rows feed each output row. As the frame moves, its contents change — that's precisely what makes a cumulative total grow row by row instead of returning a single number.

Now the ranking family, and this is heavily tested. row_number gives every row a unique number — ties get broken arbitrarily but numbers never repeat. rank assigns the same value to tied rows but leaves gaps afterward. dense_rank also ties rows together, but with no gaps. Remember it as: row_number never ties, rank gaps, dense_rank no gaps. If the exam asks which one is safe for picking one row per group, that's row_number.

And the frame clause is what turns a window into a running total. With ORDER BY order_date and a frame of UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW, amounts of 100, 50, and 25 produce a cumulative 100, 150, 175 as you move down the rows — each row sees itself plus everything before it in the partition.

Finally, the deduplication pattern — you'll reuse this constantly in Delta pipelines. Partition by the primary key, order by updated_at descending, and keep row_number equal to one. That preserves exactly the latest version of each record and discards the rest. Memorise that skeleton, because page after this one we'll hand you a messy change feed and ask you to apply it — and the interactive playground is waiting right after this to let you try it yourself.

hints: Window functions execute AFTER WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING but BEFORE ORDER BY and LIMIT. PARTITION BY splits the rows into independent groups; the ORDER BY inside OVER() defines the order that rank(), row_number() and running totals see.

Put the SAME OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC) on ROW_NUMBER(), RANK() and DENSE_RANK() in one SELECT. ROW_NUMBER() gives 1,2,3,4,5,6 — never a repeat. RANK() gives 1,1,3,4,5,6 — it skips after a tie. DENSE_RANK() gives 1,1,2,3,4,5 — it never skips.

Deduplication is a two-step pattern: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn inside a subquery, then WHERE rn = 1 in the outer query. You cannot write WHERE rn = 1 in the same SELECT that defines rn, because the window is computed after WHERE is applied.

A windowed SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region) returns exactly the same totals as GROUP BY region, but it keeps every input row. That is the trade-off: GROUP BY collapses rows, a window function annotates them.

An ORDER BY inside OVER() implies the default frame RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Leaving the ORDER BY out gives you the entire partition. ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts physical rows, while RANGE treats tied rows as peers and includes them all at once.
widgetConfig.solution:
-- ============================================================
--  Reference solutions for every check in this playground
-- ============================================================

-- 1) Ranking with ties -------------------------------------
SELECT region, rep, amount,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC, rep) AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC)       AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC)       AS drnk
FROM sales
ORDER BY region, rn;

-- 2) Deduplication: keep the most recent row per customer --
SELECT customer_id, city, updated_at
FROM (
  SELECT customer_id, city, updated_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM customer_updates
)
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;

-- 3) Windowed SUM vs GROUP BY -----------------------------
SELECT region, rep,
       COUNT(*)    OVER (PARTITION BY region) AS rows_in_region,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region) AS region_total
FROM sales
ORDER BY region, rep;

SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS region_total
FROM sales
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY region;   -- same numbers, only 2 rows

-- 4) Running total + explicit frame ------------------------
SELECT rep, month, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY rep ORDER BY month
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY rep) AS rep_total
FROM sales
WHERE region = 'East'
ORDER BY rep, month;

-- 5) LAG(): month-over-month delta -------------------------
SELECT rep, month, amount,
       LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY rep ORDER BY month) AS prev_amount,
       amount - LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY rep ORDER BY month) AS delta
FROM sales
WHERE region = 'West'
ORDER BY rep, month;

actions.text: We just covered how PARTITION BY splits rows into independent groups and how the ORDER BY inside OVER() defines the order that rank functions and running totals actually see. Now you get to drive that yourself — this playground is a live SQL sandbox seeded with a sales table that contains deliberate ties and a customer_updates table.

actions.content: The editor already holds a working query — this is where you will edit the OVER (...) clauses.

actions.text: Notice the starter query puts ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK side by side using the exact same OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC). That is the whole point of the exercise: identical window specification, three different numbering behaviours.

actions.content: Run the query, then change only the OVER clauses and run it again.
Compare the rn, rnk and drnk columns row by row — focus on East/Ben at 200 and West's four rows at 250.

actions.text: Here is what you should be seeing on those ties: ROW_NUMBER never repeats, RANK skips after a tie, and DENSE_RANK never skips. West's four rows at 250 are the clearest case — RANK jumps from 3 to 6, DENSE_RANK stays flat at 3, and ROW_NUMBER just keeps counting.

Now push further on your own. Write the deduplication pattern — ROW_NUMBER inside a subquery, then filter rn = 1 in the outer query — and confirm exactly one row survives per customer_id. Then compare a windowed SUM with the GROUP BY version: identical totals, but the window keeps all twelve rows while the grouping collapses them to two. Finally, add the frame clause ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW and watch the running total rebuild as the ORDER BY walks forward. The checkpoint right after this will test exactly that reasoning.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Window Functions and Deduplication

questions.question: A Delta table scores(user_id, attempt_id, score) holds five rows for user_id = 'U1': (a1, 90), (a2, 90), (a3, 80), (a4, 80), (a5, 70). You run: SELECT attempt_id, score, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY score DESC) AS rn FROM scores WHERE user_id = 'U1'. Which statement about the values of rn is correct?

options.label: rn takes the values 1, 1, 3, 3, 5 - each pair of tied rows shares one number and the next number skips the positions already consumed by the tie.
rn takes the values 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 - each pair of tied rows shares one number and the next number does not skip.

rn takes the five distinct values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 exactly once each, but which tied row (a1 or a2, a3 or a4) receives which number is arbitrary and may change between runs; adding a tiebreaker such as attempt_id makes the result reproducible.
The query fails with an AnalysisException because ORDER BY score DESC is not a total order and row_number() requires a deterministic ordering.

questions.analysis: row_number() guarantees uniqueness, not determinism. Its only postcondition is that inside each partition the assigned integers form a strictly increasing sequence 1..n that respects the ORDER BY expression, so rows with equal sort keys (peers) must still receive different numbers. Because nothing in the specification says which peer comes first, the assignment depends on the physical order in which rows reach the window operator, and that depends on shuffle partitioning, file ordering inside each partition, and task retries. The values 1, 1, 3, 3, 5 in option A describe rank(), which gives every peer the same number and then jumps past the positions the tie has consumed. The values 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 in option B describe dense_rank(), which also gives every peer the same number but never skips. Option D is wrong: Spark does not require a total order for row_number() or any other ranking function; an incomplete sort simply produces an arbitrary but still valid tiebreak. Note that the tie does not disturb the parts of the result that are genuinely determined: a5 (score 70) always receives rn = 5 and each 90-score row always receives rn 1 or 2, because row_number is monotone with respect to the ORDER BY key. Preconditions and edge cases matter here: if the ORDER BY key is unique within the partition, row_number, rank and dense_rank all produce identical output, which is why the defect is invisible on clean test data. The practical consequence is that a deduplication query filtering rn == 1 without a tiebreaker is non-idempotent: re-running the same job on the same data can keep a different physical row, silently changing downstream email, plan or payload values. The remedy is a total order, for example Window.partitionBy('user_id').orderBy(col('score').desc(), col('attempt_id').asc()), which collapses the tie into a defined sequence. This level of care about repeatability is warranted because query engines are explicit that a query is evaluated against a snapshot of the data rather than against a fixed physical layout [source p.305]; when the ordering inside the window is under-specified, even an unchanged snapshot can hand back a different row.

questions.question: A DataFrame df has columns customer_id, event_ts (a timestamp) and amount. The requirement is a per-customer running total of amount in ascending event_ts order: for each row, the sum of amount over that same customer_id for all rows whose event_ts is less than or equal to this row's event_ts. Which of the following window specifications, used as df.withColumn('running_total', sum('amount').over(spec)), satisfy the requirement as written? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Window.partitionBy('customer_id').orderBy('event_ts').rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
Window.partitionBy('customer_id').orderBy('event_ts')  (no frame clause given)
Window.partitionBy('customer_id')  (no orderBy, no frame clause)
Window.orderBy('event_ts').rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)  (no partitionBy)
Window.partitionBy('customer_id').orderBy('event_ts').rowsBetween(Window.currentRow, Window.unboundedFollowing)

questions.analysis: Only A and B express 'from the beginning of this customer's history up to and including this row'. Option A spells the frame out explicitly: rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow) is a ROWS frame, measured in physical rows, and it grows by exactly one row per step. Option B is also correct, and this is the trap the item is testing: when an ORDER BY is present and no frame clause is supplied, Spark's default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which is also cumulative. The difference between the two is the unit of measurement, and it is observable. A ROWS frame counts rows; a RANGE frame includes every peer sharing the same ORDER BY value. Therefore, if two rows for the same customer carry an identical event_ts, option B includes both of them in each other's total (their running totals are equal), while option A includes only the rows that physically precede. Both are defensible readings of the requirement, which is why the requirement itself should state what to do about ties. Option C drops the orderBy: with partitionBy alone the window is the whole customer partition, so the frame is the entire history and the same total is repeated on every row - that is a partitioned total, not a running total. Option D drops partitionBy, producing one global running total across all customers, which is not per-customer at all; Spark additionally emits a warning that no partition is defined for the window operation and that moving all data to a single partition can cause serious performance degradation, because the whole table must be funnelled through one task. Option E reverses the direction of travel: rowsBetween(Window.currentRow, Window.unboundedFollowing) is a suffix sum that decreases as event_ts grows. The governing precondition is that a window is evaluated independently per partition, never across partitions, which is the same per-key semantics the source describes for session windows: session windows are per key, each user gets their own set of windows, and the system accumulates data per user [source p.309]. Edge cases to keep in mind: rows with a NULL event_ts still participate in the frame (in Spark, nulls sort first in ascending order), and a customer with a single row produces a running total equal to that single amount under every correct specification, which is exactly why single-row test data never catches a missing frame clause.

questions.question: The Delta table customers_raw(customer_id, updated_at, email, plan) holds multiple historical versions per customer, and some versions share an identical updated_at value: customer C1 has two rows both stamped 2024-05-01, while customer C2 has one row stamped 2024-05-01 and one stamped 2024-06-01. Write the PySpark code that returns exactly one row per customer_id holding the most recent version, using a window function. State which ranking function you use and justify the choice, explain precisely what changes if you substitute rank() or dense_rank() while keeping the filter rn == 1, and describe what your query does and does not guarantee on a repeated run.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (total 100%): (1) Correct query structure, 40% - the answer must use withColumn to attach row_number().over(Window.partitionBy('customer_id').orderBy(col('updated_at').desc())) (a further tiebreaker such as email or an ingestion timestamp is acceptable and should be acknowledged), then filter rn == 1, then drop the helper column; code that ranks without partitioning, or that filters before ranking, or that forgets to drop the helper column, loses part of this component. (2) Justification of row_number versus rank and dense_rank, 30% - the answer must state that row_number guarantees a unique rn == 1 per partition, whereas rank and dense_rank assign 1 to every peer in a tie, so the rn == 1 filter would keep two rows for C1. (3) Concrete numeric illustration, 20% - the answer must show the actual assigned values for C1 and C2 (for C1: row_number 1 and 2 in arbitrary order, rank 1 and 1, dense_rank 1 and 1; for C2: 1 and 2 for all three), and should note the rank-versus-dense_rank difference with a three-way tie followed by a lower row (1,1,1,4 versus 1,1,1,2). (4) Determinism and repeatability, 10% - the answer must say that without a tiebreaker the surviving row is not guaranteed to be the same on a re-run, and must name a remedy (a total ordering key, or an idempotent Delta MERGE downstream).
questions.analysis: Reference solution: w = Window.partitionBy('customer_id').orderBy(col('updated_at').desc()); deduped = customers_raw.withColumn('rn', row_number().over(w)).filter(col('rn') == 1).drop('rn'). row_number() is the correct ranking function because its contract is exactly the one the requirement needs: within each partition it returns a strictly increasing sequence of distinct integers starting at 1, so exactly one row per customer_id receives rn = 1. rank() and dense_rank() have a different contract - they are deterministic functions of the ORDER BY values alone and give every peer (every row sharing the same sort key) the same number. Worked derivation with the data from the question: for C1, whose two rows both carry updated_at = 2024-05-01, ordering by updated_at DESC makes them peers, so row_number assigns 1 and 2 in an order the query does not define, rank assigns 1 and 1, and dense_rank assigns 1 and 1. Filtering rn == 1 therefore keeps one row under row_number and two rows under rank or dense_rank - the deduplication silently fails, and the customer is duplicated. For C2, whose timestamps differ, row_number, rank and dense_rank all produce 1 and 2, so the rn == 1 filter keeps exactly one row whichever function is used. This is what makes the mistake dangerous: it is conditional on a tie at the top of a partition, so it passes on clean test data and appears only for certain keys in production. Extending C1 to three rows tied at 2024-05-01 plus one older row shows the rank/dense_rank divergence directly: rank gives 1, 1, 1, 4 while dense_rank gives 1, 1, 1, 2, and both still keep three rows after the rn == 1 filter. Two further points decide whether the answer is actually correct rather than merely runnable. First, 'the most recent version' is ambiguous when updated_at ties, so a defensible solution must either add a business tiebreaker (for example orderBy(col('updated_at').desc(), col('ingestion_ts').desc())) or state explicitly that the surviving row is arbitrary; with the tiebreaker the query is deterministic and idempotent, because re-running it on the same snapshot returns the same rows. That distinction matters because, as the source notes, an engine reads from the latest committed snapshot rather than from a frozen physical layout [source p.305] - so reproducibility has to come from the query's own ordering, not from the storage layer. Second, the mechanics of writing the result: the window forces a wide shuffle so that all rows for a customer land in the same task, and replacing the whole table should be done as one large, atomic operation (an overwrite or a Delta MERGE on customer_id) rather than a loop of tiny row-level updates, because repeating many small write operations forces the creation of many small suboptimal files and a high number of object-creation operations, and in-place updates force a scan of each existing column file [source p.273]. If the source table is wide, project only customer_id, updated_at, email and plan before the window, since columnar storage lets the engine read only the columns a query requires [source p.239]. Finally, note the guarantee boundary: the query deduplicates the DataFrame it is run on, but it does not prevent duplicates from re-entering customers_raw on the next load, so production pipelines pair it with a Delta MERGE or an Auto Loader-style ingestion rule that enforces the key constraint at write time.

actions.text: Time to put that window-function reasoning to the test. These questions are deliberately tougher than the earlier checkpoints, so read each one carefully before you commit to an answer.
Work through all three on your own — no hints from me until you submit. Once you do, I'll walk through the reasoning behind each one and clear up anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Deduplicating a Change Feed

elements.content: Problem 1

The table `customers_cdc` is an append-only change-data-capture (CDC) feed — a CDC feed is an ordered log in which every insert, update and delete emitted by a source system arrives as a new row, so one customer can appear many times. Its schema is `(customer_id INT, name STRING, email STRING, updated_at TIMESTAMP, op STRING)`, where `op` is one of `'insert'`, `'update'`, `'delete'`. The current 8 rows are:

| customer_id | name | email | updated_at | op |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 101 | Alice | alice@old.example | 2024-01-01 09:00:00 | insert |

| 101 | Alicia | alicia@new.example | 2024-02-15 10:30:00 | update |

| 101 | Alicia | alicia@new.example | 2024-02-15 10:30:00 | update |

| 102 | Bob | bob@old.example | 2024-01-05 08:00:00 | insert |

| 102 | Bob | bob@new.example | 2024-03-01 12:00:00 | update |

| 102 | Bob | NULL | 2024-03-20 09:00:00 | delete |

| 103 | Carol | carol@example | 2024-02-01 07:00:00 | insert |

| 104 | Dan | dan@example | NULL | insert |

Return the current state of each customer: exactly one row per `customer_id` carrying the payload (`name`, `email`, `updated_at`) of the most recent event, and no row at all for a customer whose most recent event is a delete. Write the query in Spark SQL and in the PySpark DataFrame API, and state the exact result set.
Hint: Rank inside each `customer_id`, then filter on the rank — never filter the feed first.

Worked solution
Step 1 — fix the output grain. "One row per customer_id" means the answer has at most COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) = 4 rows (101, 102, 103, 104); the delete rule will remove some of them.

Step 2 — rank events inside each key. The window `PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, op ASC` numbers each customer's events newest-first, so rn = 1 is that customer's latest event.

Step 3 — keep rn = 1 and drop deletes. Both predicates are applied to the ranked result, not to the raw feed (problem 3 shows what happens otherwise).

Spark SQL:

WITH ranked AS (

SELECT *,

row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id

ORDER BY updated_at DESC, op ASC) AS rn

FROM customers_cdc

)

SELECT customer_id, name, email, updated_at

FROM ranked

WHERE rn = 1 AND op <> 'delete';

PySpark:

w = Window.partitionBy('customer_id').orderBy(col('updated_at').desc(), col('op').asc())

(df.withColumn('rn', row_number().over(w))

.filter((col('rn') == 1) & (col('op') != 'delete'))

.drop('rn'))

Step 4 — trace the ranking.

| customer_id | updated_at | op | rn | kept? |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 101 | 2024-02-15 10:30:00 | update | 1 | yes |

| 101 | 2024-02-15 10:30:00 | update | 2 | no |

| 101 | 2024-01-01 09:00:00 | insert | 3 | no |

| 102 | 2024-03-20 09:00:00 | delete | 1 | no — filtered by op |

| 102 | 2024-03-01 12:00:00 | update | 2 | no |

| 102 | 2024-01-05 08:00:00 | insert | 3 | no |

| 103 | 2024-02-01 07:00:00 | insert | 1 | yes |

| 104 | NULL | insert | 1 | yes |

Step 5 — final result: 3 rows.

| customer_id | name | email | updated_at |

|---|---|---|---|

| 101 | Alicia | alicia@new.example | 2024-02-15 10:30:00 |

| 103 | Carol | carol@example | 2024-02-01 07:00:00 |

| 104 | Dan | dan@example | NULL |

Customer 102 disappears because its newest event (2024-03-20) is a delete. Customer 101's two newest rows are fully tied, so `row_number()` may assign rn = 1 to either physical row — but both carry the identical payload, so the returned values are the same.

Analysis — This problem is the textbook statement of the change-feed dedup task: given an append-only feed you must "deduplicate, find the latest version of each record by key, and not show any record whose latest version shows deleted" [source p.343]. The reason the feed is append-only rather than updated in place is a property of the storage layer: in columnar storage "to change one field in one record, we must decompress the column file, modify it, recompress it, and write it back to storage" [source p.419], so the cheap pattern is to append the new version and pay the deduplication cost at read time. The method works because a window function evaluates the ranking over the whole partition before the outer `WHERE` runs; the `WHERE rn = 1` is a post-ranking filter, which is exactly what makes "the latest per key" expressible in one pass. Two mistakes dominate in practice. First, students filter `op <> 'delete'` inside the CTE — that makes deleted customers reappear (problem 3). Second, students reach for `row_number()` but then write `rank()`, which returns 1 for every tied row, silently producing two rows for one key and causing fan-out when the result is joined downstream. Generalisation: the identical shape produces a Type 1 slowly changing dimension — a slowly changing dimension (SCD) is a dimension table that models how entity attributes change over time, Type 1 overwriting the old value while Type 2 keeps every version as a new row — and it is how Master Data Management teams build a golden record, that is, a single trusted, deduplicated version of an entity [source p.82].
Problem 2

Use the same `customers_cdc` feed from problem 1 (8 rows, customers 101–104) and the query:

WITH ranked AS (

SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, op ASC) AS rn

FROM customers_cdc

)

SELECT customer_id, name, email, updated_at FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 AND op <> 'delete';

(a) A colleague rewrites it with `rank()` instead of `row_number()`. Compute the exact output of the rewritten query on this data and say what contract it breaks. (b) Then consider a new customer 105 whose feed contains two events at exactly the same instant:

| customer_id | name | email | updated_at | op |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 105 | Eve | eve@example | 2024-05-01 00:00:00 | update |

| 105 | Eve | NULL | 2024-05-01 00:00:00 | delete |

Explain which event `op ASC` selects as rn = 1, what the opposite direction would return, and state a general rule for choosing a deterministic tiebreaker.
Hint: `rank()` gives equal ranks to equal sort keys; `row_number()` never does. 'delete' < 'insert' < 'update' lexicographically.

Worked solution
(a) With `rank()`, the two fully tied rows for customer 101 both receive rank 1 (the next row receives 3). The trace becomes:

| customer_id | updated_at | op | rank | kept at rank = 1? |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 101 | 2024-02-15 10:30:00 | update | 1 | yes |

| 101 | 2024-02-15 10:30:00 | update | 1 | yes |

| 101 | 2024-01-01 09:00:00 | insert | 3 | no |

| 102 | 2024-03-20 09:00:00 | delete | 1 | no (op filter) |

| 103 | 2024-02-01 07:00:00 | insert | 1 | yes |

| 104 | NULL | insert | 1 | yes |

The result is 4 rows instead of 3, with customer 101 duplicated. The broken contract is "exactly one row per key": downstream, joining this 4-row result to an orders table on `customer_id` doubles every order belonging to 101.

(b) For customer 105 both events share the timestamp 2024-05-01 00:00:00, so the tie is decided by the second sort key, `op ASC`. Alphabetically 'delete' < 'insert' < 'update', so the delete row sorts first, receives rn = 1, and is removed by the outer filter: customer 105 is correctly absent. Reversing the tiebreaker to `op DESC` puts the update first, so 105 reappears as a live customer holding a state the source already deleted — a silent resurrection.

General rule for a deterministic tiebreaker:

1. Order by the business timestamp `DESC`.

2. Add a semantic second key that encodes precedence for genuinely simultaneous events (`op ASC` makes deletes terminal).

3. If two rows can still tie on both keys, add a monotonically increasing technical column (ingest timestamp `_ingest_ts`, a file offset, or a source sequence number) so that a re-run of the same query on the same data always chooses the same physical row. If no such column exists, the choice is arbitrary — accept it only when the tied rows are payload-identical, as they are for customer 101.

Analysis — The method choice here is `row_number()` over `rank()` (and over `dense_rank()`). `row_number()` is a total order within the partition: it can never return the same number twice, so `rn = 1` is guaranteed to select exactly one row per partition key and the "one row per key" contract is enforced by construction. `rank()` and `dense_rank()` are only partial orders — they answer "how good is this row?", not "which single row is it?" — so they are the right tool for leaderboards and the wrong tool for deduplication. The tiebreaker direction is a semantic decision, not cosmetic: because 'delete' precedes 'insert' and 'update' lexicographically, `op ASC` makes a delete win any exact-timestamp tie, which is the safe default for CDC, since a delete is terminal and resurrecting a removed entity is usually worse than dropping a legitimate update. The common student mistake is to assume tied rows are "the same row" and therefore harmless; they are harmless only when the payload is identical, which you must verify, not assume. The second common mistake is to rely on the physical order of the files or partitions, which Databricks does not guarantee to be stable across reruns, compactions, or a `OPTIMIZE`/rewrite of the underlying Delta table — results then differ between two runs of the same query. Edge cases worth stating: when a partition has exactly one row the tiebreaker never fires; when the tiebreaker column is NULL, NULL sorts last under `ASC` in Spark (see problem 5), which can flip the winner.
Problem 3

A teammate "optimises" the query by pushing the delete filter into the CTE, arguing that deleted rows should never be ranked at all:

WITH filtered AS (SELECT * FROM customers_cdc WHERE op <> 'delete'),

ranked AS (SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM filtered)

SELECT customer_id, name, email, updated_at FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

Using the 8-row `customers_cdc` table from problem 1, compute the output of this query, compare it with the correct result from problem 1, and name the phenomenon. Then state the general condition under which the two orderings agree.
Hint: Which row becomes the "latest" for customer 102 once its delete row has been thrown away?

Worked solution
Step 1 — apply the inner filter. Removing the two delete rows (only customer 102 has one) leaves 7 rows:

101 insert 2024-01-01 09:00:00; 101 update 2024-02-15 10:30:00; 101 update 2024-02-15 10:30:00; 102 insert 2024-01-05 08:00:00; 102 update 2024-03-01 12:00:00; 103 insert 2024-02-01 07:00:00; 104 insert NULL.

Step 2 — rank what remains. For customer 102 the newest surviving row is now the 2024-03-01 update, so it gets rn = 1 and survives:

| customer_id | name | email | updated_at | rn |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 101 | Alicia | alicia@new.example | 2024-02-15 10:30:00 | 1 |

| 102 | Bob | bob@new.example | 2024-03-01 12:00:00 | 1 |

| 103 | Carol | carol@example | 2024-02-01 07:00:00 | 1 |

| 104 | Dan | dan@example | NULL | 1 |

Step 3 — compare with problem 1. The correct answer had 3 rows and no 102; this query returns 4 rows, including a live customer 102 that the source deleted. The customer was resurrected: discarding the delete before ranking rewrites history so that the last non-delete event becomes "latest".

Step 4 — when do the orders agree? Only when no customer's newest event is a delete, or, more precisely, when for every key the maximum-timestamp event is not a delete. Because that condition is data-dependent, the two formulations are not interchangeable: the pre-filter version is wrong precisely on the rows the delete rule exists to remove. The correct order is always rank first, filter on `rn = 1` AND `op <> 'delete'` second.

Analysis — This is the single most common production bug in change-feed deduplication, and it is a semantics bug, not a performance bug: the delete row is not "noise to be discarded", it is the most recent fact about the entity, and it has to participate in the ranking in order to win it. The same trap appears in the upsert/merge family of update patterns, where "the merge pattern adds to the [upsert] the ability to delete" and both "consistently cause the most trouble for data engineering teams, especially for people transitioning from row-based data warehouses to column-based cloud systems" [source p.343]. A useful mental model: deduplication is a two-phase operation — phase 1 establishes *which* event is current (the window), phase 2 interprets that event (the `op` predicate and the payload projection). Predicates that change *which event is current* must never be pushed into phase 1. Predicates that only remove rows which can never be current, such as a filter on a partition column (`WHERE event_date = '2024-03-01'`) that is provably implied by the window's ordering, are safe to push down. Edge cases: if the feed contains deletes followed by a genuine re-insert for the same key, the latest event is the re-insert and the customer must reappear — the ranking handles this automatically, whereas a naive `WHERE op <> 'delete'` on the whole table (without any window) would keep every non-delete version and still produce duplicates. On the performance side, the ranked-then-filtered form is not slower in practice: it reads the same columns (columnar storage scans only the columns a query requires, which is the main reason column-oriented layout is fast for analytics [source p.239]), performs one shuffle on `customer_id`, and adds no join.
Problem 4

A reviewer proposes replacing the window function with the classic aggregate-and-join idiom:

SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, c.email, c.updated_at

FROM customers_cdc c

JOIN (SELECT customer_id, MAX(updated_at) AS max_ts

FROM customers_cdc GROUP BY customer_id) m

ON c.customer_id = m.customer_id AND c.updated_at = m.max_ts

WHERE c.op <> 'delete';

Run it by hand on the 8-row `customers_cdc` table from problem 1. Give the exact output, identify every defect you find (including rows that are missing), and explain why the window version is preferable. Then write the minimal repair that makes the self-join semantically correct, and say what it still costs relative to the window version.
Hint: What does `NULL = NULL` evaluate to in SQL, and what does that do to customer 104?

Worked solution
Step 1 — compute the aggregate.

| customer_id | max_ts |

|---|---|

| 101 | 2024-02-15 10:30:00 |

| 102 | 2024-03-20 09:00:00 |

| 103 | 2024-02-01 07:00:00 |

| 104 | NULL |

Step 2 — join on equality of the timestamp and apply the delete filter.

| customer_id | matched rows | after `op <> 'delete'` |

|---|---|---|

| 101 | 2 rows (both 2024-02-15 10:30:00) | 2 rows — duplicate key |

| 102 | 1 row (the 2024-03-20 delete) | 0 rows — correct by luck |

| 103 | 1 row | 1 row |

| 104 | 0 rows: `NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN, not TRUE | 0 rows — Dan is lost |

Final output: 3 rows — `101 Alicia` twice, `103 Carol` once. Two defects:

1. Duplicate key. The tied timestamps for 101 match two rows, so the equality join fans out and violates "one row per customer_id".

2. Silent data loss. `c.updated_at = m.max_ts` is never true when both sides are NULL, because three-valued logic returns UNKNOWN. Customer 104 disappears entirely, and unlike 102 there is no delete to justify it.

Step 3 — minimal repair. Use a null-safe equality and add a second ranking step to collapse ties:

SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, c.email, c.updated_at

FROM customers_cdc c

JOIN (SELECT customer_id, MAX(updated_at) AS max_ts FROM customers_cdc GROUP BY customer_id) m

ON c.customer_id = m.customer_id AND c.updated_at <=> m.max_ts -- null-safe

QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY c.customer_id ORDER BY c.op ASC) = 1

AND ... -- and the delete predicate, applied after the ranking

(the `<=>` operator is Spark's null-safe equality; in PySpark the equivalent is `df.updated_at.eqNullSafe(m.max_ts)`).

Step 4 — cost. The repaired form performs a shuffle for the GROUP BY, a second shuffle (or broadcast) for the join, and still needs a window pass to break ties — three distributed operations where the original query needed one.

Analysis — The reason the aggregate-and-join idiom is popular is historical: in a hand-indexed row store, looking up `MAX(updated_at)` and then fetching the matching record is cheap, because "indexes provide a map of the table for particular fields and allow extremely fast lookup of individual records" [source p.239]. In a distributed, columnar engine that reasoning inverts: there is no row-level index to fetch from, so the self-join buys nothing and costs an extra shuffle and an extra aggregation. The window version exploits a total order that the engine can compute in a single pass per partition and cannot produce a duplicate row for a tie. Two subtleties students miss. First, moving the `op <> 'delete'` predicate *inside* the subquery reintroduces the resurrection bug of problem 3 — here it would make MAX(updated_at) = 2024-03-01 for customer 102 and bring Bob back. Second, the NULL timestamp case is easy to miss because the query returns a plausible-looking three rows; the defect is the row that *isn't* there. Spark's `<=>` (and PySpark's `eqNullSafe`) is the correct tool whenever a join key may be null, though for this particular problem the cleaner answer is a data-quality rule: an event with no timestamp is malformed and should be quarantined rather than silently ranked. Generalisation: the same reasoning applies to `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE max_ts IS NULL` "anti-join" rewrites, and it is why deduplication is normally expressed with window functions rather than self-joins in Spark SQL.
Problem 5

Customer 104 now has two events, and the timestamp of one of them is missing (a malformed event, common when a source sends partial records):

| customer_id | name | email | updated_at | op |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 104 | Dan | dan@example | NULL | insert |

| 104 | Danny | danny@example | 2024-04-01 06:00:00 | update |

Using `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC)`, state which row is rn = 1 under Spark's default NULL ordering, and which row wins if you write `ORDER BY updated_at DESC NULLS FIRST`. Say which answer is correct here, why the implicit default is a portability hazard, and give two data-engineering remedies.
Hint: Spark's defaults are ASC → NULLS FIRST and DESC → NULLS LAST; write the clause explicitly if you depend on it.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Spark's default. Under `ORDER BY updated_at DESC` Spark places NULLs last (its defaults are NULLS FIRST for ascending order and NULLS LAST for descending order). Ranking customer 104 therefore gives:

| name | updated_at | op | rn (default) |

|---|---|---|---|

| Danny | 2024-04-01 06:00:00 | update | 1 |

| Dan | NULL | insert | 2 |

rn = 1 is `Danny` with `updated_at = 2024-04-01 06:00:00`, `op = 'update'`, which is not a delete, so the customer is kept and the returned state is Danny. That is the correct answer: the April update really is the newest known state.

Step 2 — the explicit opposite. `ORDER BY updated_at DESC NULLS FIRST` puts the row with the unknown timestamp at the top:

| name | updated_at | op | rn (NULLS FIRST) |

|---|---|---|---|

| Dan | NULL | insert | 1 |

| Danny | 2024-04-01 06:00:00 | update | 2 |

Now rn = 1 is `Dan` with `updated_at = NULL`, and the pipeline silently reverts a customer to a stale state — a correctness bug introduced purely by sort-direction syntax.

Step 3 — why it is a portability hazard. The SQL standard leaves null ordering implementation-defined; Spark's defaults happen to be ASC → NULLS FIRST, DESC → NULLS LAST, and the choice of ASC versus DESC therefore flips which default applies. Code that omits `NULLS FIRST`/`NULLS LAST` behaves differently on another engine, and any future change to the ordering clause can flip the winner without a single data change.

Step 4 — remedies. (1) Never rank on a nullable ordering key: filter or quarantine rows with `updated_at IS NULL` before the window and alert on them, or coalesce to a sentinel such as `COALESCE(updated_at, TIMESTAMP '1970-01-01 00:00:00')` so the row is unambiguously oldest. (2) Always spell the null placement out: `ORDER BY updated_at DESC NULLS LAST, op ASC` so the intent is in the query text and survives a review or a port.

Analysis — Null handling is where declarative queries and intuition part company. A student's instinct is that "missing timestamp" means "no information", but the engine must still order the row, and it must do so according to some rule — so the missing value silently becomes a decision about which version of the customer is current. The three-valued logic of SQL makes this doubly dangerous: the definition of the winner is spelled with comparison operators, and `NULL` never compares true. This is a concrete instance of the general warning that upsert-style state reconstruction is fragile on columnar cloud systems, where the team — not the database — is responsible for the key semantics: "it's the responsibility of the data engineering team to manage this primary key by running appropriate queries. Most columnar systems will not enforce uniqueness" [source p.343]. Because uniqueness is not enforced, a query that picks the wrong survivor does not error; it just returns a plausible, wrong answer. Common mistakes: (1) assuming the newest row is "the one the file wrote last" rather than the one the sort key selects; (2) assuming DESC means "nulls last" everywhere; (3) forgetting that the same NULL ordering rule applies to the `op` tiebreaker when `op` itself is null. Edge cases to state explicitly: a partition containing only NULL-timestamp rows will still yield an rn = 1 survivor, so a NULL ordering key does not by itself remove a customer; and `MAX()` over an all-NULL group returns NULL, which is what broke the self-join in problem 4.
Problem 6

Three variants of the ranking window are proposed for the `customers_cdc` data of problem 1 (customers 101–104, 8 rows, with customer 101 having two names and two event types, and customer 104 having a NULL timestamp):

(A) `PARTITION BY customer_id, name ORDER BY updated_at DESC`

(B) `PARTITION BY customer_id, op ORDER BY updated_at DESC`

(C) no `PARTITION BY` clause at all, with `ORDER BY updated_at DESC`

For each variant, keeping the outer predicate `rn = 1 AND op <> 'delete'`, compute how many rows the query returns, list the surviving `customer_id`s, and explain the rule that predicts the failure. Then state what happens to rows whose partition key (`customer_id`) is NULL, and why adding more columns to `PARTITION BY` never makes the query cheaper.
Hint: The partition granularity must equal the grain of uniqueness you want in the output.

Worked solution
Rule: the number of surviving rows per customer equals the number of distinct partitions that customer's rows fall into, because `row_number()` restarts at 1 in every partition. To return exactly one row per key, `PARTITION BY` must list exactly the key columns you want to be unique.

Variant A — `PARTITION BY customer_id, name`. Customer 101 splits into two partitions ('Alice' and 'Alicia'), so each gets its own rn = 1:

| partition | rn = 1 row | op | kept? |

|---|---|---|---|

| (101, 'Alice') | 2024-01-01 insert | insert | yes |

| (101, 'Alicia') | 2024-02-15 update | update | yes |

Customers 103 and 104 each form one partition and survive; 102 is dropped because its rn = 1 is a delete. Total: **4 rows** — Alicia *and* the stale Alice, i.e. a duplicate key in the output.

Variant B — `PARTITION BY customer_id, op`. Customer 101 has both 'insert' and 'update' events, so it splits into two partitions and again yields two survivors (the 2024-01-01 insert and one of the 2024-02-15 updates); customer 102 splits into three partitions whose rn = 1 rows are the insert, the update, and the delete — the delete is filtered, but the update partition's rn = 1 is the 2024-03-01 update, which is kept, resurrecting Bob. Total: **5 rows** (101 twice, 102 once, 103, 104).

Variant C — no `PARTITION BY`. All 8 rows form one global partition, so exactly one row in the entire dataset has rn = 1: the newest non-null timestamp, customer 102's 2024-03-20 delete. The `op <> 'delete'` predicate then removes it, leaving **0 rows**. The query compiles, runs, and returns an empty table.

NULL partition keys: `PARTITION BY customer_id` groups every row with a NULL `customer_id` into a single partition, and `row_number()` still numbers them 1, 2, 3, … so `rn = 1` keeps exactly one of them and silently discards the rest. Worse, those rows are unrelated entities that merely share a missing key, so the survivor is arbitrary. The remedy is to quarantine NULL-keyed rows (`WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL`) and report the count, never to let them into the dedup window.

Why more partition columns is not cheaper: the window operator must shuffle the data so that all rows of a partition land on one executor regardless of how the partition is defined, and the total number of rows moved is the same. Adding `name` or `op` shrinks each partition but multiplies the number of partitions, so shuffle volume and task overhead stay flat or grow, while correctness breaks. The partition key is a semantic contract, not a tuning knob.

Analysis — The window function's contract is: *one output row per (partition key, rank) pair*. Students learn the syntax `PARTITION BY <something>` and treat the column list as an implementation detail, when it is in fact the specification of the output grain. The diagnostic drill is mechanical: count the distinct partitions per entity; if that number exceeds one, you will get duplicates, and if the partition key is the whole table, you will get a single survivor. Note that variant B is not merely wasteful but actively wrong in a way that resembles problem 3: partitioning by `op` means each operation type ranks independently and the delete can never suppress the update it was meant to cancel, so the delete rule is defeated even though the predicate is written correctly. Variant C illustrates that a window without a partition is a *global* ranking — the correct tool for "top N overall" questions, which is why exam items often contrast `row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ...)` with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)`. The rule generalises to every dedup frame: partition by the entity key, order by the event time with a deterministic tiebreaker, keep rank 1. On cost, one shuffle on `customer_id` is unavoidable and buys the correctness; extra shuffle keys buy nothing, and the physical layout work that does reduce scan cost — partitioning and clustering strategies that organise the table according to query and update patterns — belongs to the storage layer, not to the window clause [source p.419]. Finally, the NULL-key case is a data-quality signal, not a query-design problem: a feed whose entity key can be null cannot be deduplicated reliably, because the very notion of "the same entity" is undefined.

actions.text: Now let's put all of that into practice. This page walks through six worked problems built around one change feed table, `customers_cdc`, and each one isolates a different failure mode of window-function deduplication. Follow along with the solution, then compare it to what you wrote.

Problem 1 states the core requirement: `customers_cdc` is append-only — every change to a customer appends a new row — and we need exactly one surviving row per `customer_id`: the latest record by `updated_at`, with any record whose `op` is `delete` removed entirely. Notice that this is really two operations glued together: deduplication and deletion filtering, and the order in which you apply them matters.

Here is the worked solution in Spark SQL. The ranked CTE attaches a `row_number()` partitioned by `customer_id` and ordered by `updated_at DESC, op ASC`. The outer query then keeps `rn = 1` and filters `op <> 'delete'`. The PySpark version is the exact same logic — `Window.partitionBy('customer_id').orderBy(col('updated_at').desc())`, add the row number as a column, filter on it, then drop the helper column. The `op ASC` in the ORDER BY is not decoration; it is your deterministic tiebreaker, so that when two rows share the same timestamp, the same physical row wins on every single rerun.

The analysis explains why this is the textbook pattern. `row_number()` is preferred over `rank()` because `rank()` assigns equal ranks to ties — if two rows for the same customer share a timestamp, `rank()` returns rank 1 for both, and your filter on `rn = 1` now emits two rows per key. That silently breaks the deduplication contract. And if you omit a tiebreaker entirely, Spark is free to pick an arbitrary row, so the same query can produce different results across runs. Determinism in a pipeline is not a nicety; it is what makes your downstream tests meaningful.

Problem 2 pushes directly on that point using the same feed. With `rank()`, two fully tied rows both receive 1, so the result set for that customer explodes from one row to two. With `row_number()` and a tiebreaker, exactly one row survives. The lesson to carry into the exam: any time a question asks for the single latest record, `row_number()` is the answer, and `rank()` is the trap.

Problem 3 is the most common production bug on this pattern. A teammate 'optimises' the query by pushing the `op <> 'delete'` filter into the inner query, before the ranking. That looks harmless and even more efficient — but it changes which row is ranked, so the surviving 'latest' record for a customer can become an older, non-deleted row. The rule is simple: filter on the result of the window function, never on the input to it. Rank first over the complete history, then discard.

Problem 5 covers null handling, which is where declarative query languages most often surprise people. Spark's defaults are `ASC → NULLS FIRST` and `DESC → NULLS LAST`. So a null `updated_at` sorts first when ascending and last when descending — which, in a descending latest-record query, means null timestamps quietly sink to the bottom and lose. If nulls should win or should be excluded outright, you must say so explicitly with `NULLS LAST` or a filter. Never leave it to the default and hope.

Problem 6 gives you the one-line rule that ties all six problems together: the number of surviving rows equals the number of distinct values in the partition key. If you partition by the wrong column — say by `name` instead of `customer_id` — you get duplicates back, because two customers who happen to share a name collapse into one partition. Partition granularity must equal the granularity of the key you are deduplicating.

So, to summarise the page: `row_number()` with a deterministic tiebreaker for the single latest row; filter after the window, never before; be explicit about null ordering; and match the partition key to the deduplication key exactly. Those four habits resolve every problem on this page and most of the exam questions built on this pattern. Let's move on to the lesson summary, where we'll collect these traps into a checklist you can rehearse.

scenes.title: Lesson Summary: Query Patterns and Exam Traps

elements.content: Query Patterns and Exam Traps

Three Patterns to Recall

• Grouped aggregate: GROUP BY keys, then SUM/COUNT

• Typed join: inner, left, semi; match join key types

• Window: rank, running total, dedupe [source p.350]

Exam Traps to Memorise

• count(col) skips NULLs; count(*) counts all rows

• Semi join filters; it adds no right-side columns

• Set ROWS frames; rank() ties, row_number() never ties
• 10 rows, 3 amounts NULL → COUNT(col) = 7, count(*) = 10

Performance Levers

• Prefilter, then broadcast the small table [source p.337]

• Filter first; project only needed columns [source p.304]

• Self-check: write each pattern in SQL and PySpark

• Next: UDFs, higher-order functions, efficient patterns

actions.text: Let's consolidate everything from this lesson into one page you can rehearse before the exam. We're covering three clusters of knowledge: the query patterns themselves, the traps that cost marks, and the performance levers that show you understand how Spark actually executes.

First, the three patterns you should be able to write from memory. The grouped aggregate: groupBy or GROUP BY, followed by agg with sum, count, or avg — remember that aggregation is a wide transformation, so a shuffle happens. Second, the correctly-typed join: match the join keys and their data types, and know whether you want an inner, left semi, or left anti join. Third, the windowed pattern: partitionBy, orderBy, and a frame, used for rank, running totals, and deduplication.

Now the exam traps — this is where marks quietly disappear. count of a column silently skips nulls, while count star or count one counts every row. Semi versus inner join confusion is the next big one: a left semi join returns each left row at most once, with only the left columns, whereas an inner join can multiply rows when the right side has duplicates. Then window defaults versus an explicit frame, and finally rank versus row_number when there are ties — rank leaves gaps, row_number never does.

Here's the classic illustration. Ten rows, three of the amount values are null. Count of amount returns seven, but count star returns ten. Same table, two different answers — and the exam loves to test whether you notice which function was used.

Next, the performance levers. Filter before you group so less data reaches the shuffle. Broadcast the small table in a join to avoid a full shuffle altogether. Project only the columns you need rather than dragging wide rows through the pipeline. And never use SELECT star on wide tables in a production query — it forces the scan and shuffle to carry columns nobody asked for.

Finally, your self-check before moving on. Can you write each of those three patterns from memory, in both Spark SQL and the PySpark DataFrame API? If any of them still requires looking something up, that's your revision list for tonight. Next, we move into UDFs, higher-order functions, and efficient query patterns.

scenes.title: Prior-Knowledge Check: Native Functions and Query Vocabulary

questions.question: A DataFrame has a column tags of type array<string>. You must uppercase every element of every array while keeping exactly one output row per input row. Which of the following performs this transformation as a built-in higher-order function, without row-by-row Python serialization overhead?

options.label: df.withColumn('tags', transform(col('tags'), lambda t: upper(t)))
df.withColumn('tags', make_upper_udf(col('tags'))), where make_upper_udf = udf(lambda t: [x.upper() for x in t], ArrayType(StringType()))
df.withColumn('tags', explode(col('tags')))
df.select('tags').collect(), then rebuild the column in Python with a list comprehension

questions.analysis: transform is the built-in higher-order function in this scenario: a higher-order function is any function that accepts another function (here written as the lambda expression 'lambda t: upper(t)') together with an array or map column, and applies that function element by element while preserving the shape of the array. Because transform is a Catalyst built-in, it executes inside the JVM directly on Spark's internal binary row representation, the optimiser can fuse it into whole-stage code generation, and no data crosses the process boundary. Option B is a Python UDF, which is evaluated row by row: for every row the engine serialises the array out of the JVM into a Python object, runs the interpreter, and serialises the Python list back into an internal row. That round trip is what the vocabulary calls serialization overhead, and [source p.340] documents how punishing it becomes, reporting JavaScript UDFs that increased query time from a few minutes to several hours, while noting that SQL UDFs often perform reasonably well. A worked example makes the magnitude concrete: on 8,000,000 array rows spread over 4 executor cores, the native transform path at roughly 200,000 rows per second per core finishes in about 8,000,000 / (200,000 x 4) = 10 seconds, whereas a Python UDF costing even 40 microseconds per row adds 8,000,000 x 40 microseconds = 320,000,000 microseconds = 320 seconds, stretching a 10-second stage past five minutes. Option C is wrong because explode is indeed a built-in, but it flattens one array row into n rows, so it multiplies row counts instead of transforming elements and it breaks the one-row-per-record guarantee. Option D is wrong because collect() pulls the whole data set onto the driver, contradicting the distributed, in-cluster-memory processing model described in [source p.346], where ingestion, joining and filtering all happen across the cluster and only the final result is written out.

questions.question: Given df, a DataFrame containing a string column named region, which of the following return exactly the same result set AND the same output column name as df.select(upper(col('region')).alias('region_upper'))? Select all that apply.

options.label: df.select(upper('region').alias('region_upper'))
df.selectExpr("UPPER(region) AS region_upper")
df.groupBy('region').agg(upper('region').alias('region_upper'))
df.selectExpr("UPPER(region)")

questions.analysis: Options A and B are correct and are the exam's canonical example of two equivalent forms of the same query. In the PySpark DataFrame API a bare string passed to a Column-accepting function is implicitly wrapped in col(), so upper('region') and upper(col('region')) are semantically identical; the explicit col() call is a style choice, not a different function. selectExpr is a thin wrapper that parses a SQL string into the very same Catalyst expressions, so 'selectExpr("UPPER(region) AS region_upper")' produces an identical logical plan, which is then compiled to the same physical plan. Option C is wrong for two reasons: agg expects aggregate functions and UPPER is a scalar (row-level) function, so Spark raises an AnalysisException because upper(region) is not a registered aggregate; conceptually it is also wrong because agg collapses the DataFrame to a single row, which is exactly the GROUP BY versus ungrouped aggregate distinction covered earlier in this unit. Option D is the near miss that catches careless readers: it returns the correct values but names the output column 'UPPER(region)' instead of 'region_upper', so any downstream code referring to region_upper breaks even though the data looks right. This equivalence matters in practice because the pipeline described in [source p.346] ingests three JSON sources into DataFrames, combines them, and then filters the results with a SQL statement against the same engine, showing that SQL text and DataFrame operators are two front ends for one execution engine. [source p.340] reinforces why both forms must be fluent for the certification: SQL engines can store user-defined functions as objects inside a database, but they lack a natural notion of reusable libraries, so engineers routinely move between SQL and DataFrame code for the same transformation.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why a built-in column function outperforms a Python UDF that computes exactly the same value?

options.label: A Python UDF must convert each row out of Spark's internal binary representation into a Python object and convert the result back, so the cost is paid row by row and the optimiser cannot fold the function into whole-stage code generation.
A Python UDF is slower only because Python is an interpreted language, but it still operates directly on Spark's packed binary buffers, so no data conversion takes place.
A Python UDF is slower because Spark must collect the entire DataFrame to the driver before the function can run on each row.
A Python UDF is slower because it forces an extra shuffle that repartitions the data by the UDF's input column before evaluation.

questions.analysis: Option A states the mechanism correctly: Spark stores data in a packed internal binary format, and a Python UDF interrupts that representation, serialising each row out to a Python object, executing interpreted code, and serialising the result back into an internal row, so the overhead is charged per row rather than per column and the function becomes opaque to the Catalyst optimiser. Two pieces of evidence from the source material support this. First, [source p.340] quantifies how far this can go, reporting JavaScript UDFs that pushed query time from a few minutes to several hours while noting that SQL UDFs often perform reasonably well, which tells us the penalty is about the row-by-row interpreter boundary rather than about SQL versus DataFrame syntax. Second, [source p.239] explains the advantage that is being thrown away: columnar serialization lets an engine scan only the columns a query needs and packs similar values next to each other, giving high compression ratios with minimal compression overhead, so scans move faster from disk and over the network. A worked example on 50,000,000 rows makes the difference tangible: at 30 microseconds of conversion and interpreter cost per row the UDF alone adds 50,000,000 x 30 microseconds = 1,500,000,000 microseconds = 1,500 seconds = 25 minutes, whereas a vectorised built-in over the same column typically completes in roughly one to two minutes, because it is executed in batches inside the JVM. Option B is wrong because it denies the serialization step that actually causes the slowdown, and even a JIT-compiled Python runtime would still pay it. Option C is wrong because UDFs run in the executors alongside the partitions, not on the driver; collect() is a separate, explicitly driver-bound operation and the three-source pipeline in [source p.346] shows data being ingested and combined in cluster memory with only the final result written out. Option D is wrong because a UDF does not inherently create a shuffle; shuffles are caused by operations such as groupBy, join and repartition, and the edge case worth remembering is that vectorised pandas/Arrow UDFs reduce this overhead by amortising serialization over batches, though they still cannot be fused into whole-stage code generation the way a native built-in can.

actions.text: Before we move into UDFs and higher-order functions, let's do a quick prior-knowledge check — three short questions on the native-function and query vocabulary we'll be leaning on for the rest of this lesson.

Work through each one on your own, no notes needed — treat it as a diagnostic rather than a graded test. Submit when you're finished and I'll walk through the reasoning behind each one with you after that.

scenes.title: Lesson Roadmap: UDFs, Higher-Order Functions, and Query Patterns

elements.content: Lesson Roadmap: Three Parts
Builds directly on aggregation, joins, and windows.
Part 1 — Native over Python UDFs: Catalyst and Tungsten optimize JVM code, never Python [source p.341].
Part 2 — Higher-order functions: transform, filter, exists and aggregate work on whole arrays and maps.
Part 3 — Query patterns: dedup, top-N per group, pivot, anti-joins; prefilter to broadcast [source p.337].
Worked example: 25M rows (12M+8M+5M) joined; 2 Python UDFs ship 50M rows to Python, native ships 0 [source p.346].
Exam signal: slow row-by-row answers often expect a native rewrite [source p.341].

actions.text: With that prior-knowledge check behind us, let's set the map for this lesson. We're going to move through three parts, and each one builds on the aggregation, join, and window function material we just covered on page 143.

Nothing here is a brand-new world. Deduplication, ranking, and grouped calculations are all things you already did with GROUP BY, joins, and window functions. What changes in this lesson is how you express them — and how efficiently Spark can execute them.

Part 1 is about why native Spark functions beat row-by-row Python UDFs. We'll look at the Catalyst optimizer, which plans your query, and Tungsten, which handles the low-level memory and code generation. Those two are the reason a built-in function can run many times faster than equivalent Python code applied row by row.

Part 2 covers higher-order functions — transform, filter, exists, and aggregate — which let you work directly with arrays and maps inside a column, instead of exploding the array into extra rows first.
Part 3 is a set of reusable query patterns: deduplication, top-N per group, pivot, and anti-joins. These are the shapes that show up again and again, both in real pipelines and in the exam.

To make this concrete, we'll work through an example with twenty-five million rows, split roughly twelve million, eight million, and five million, joined together — with a couple of Python UDFs in the pipeline. You'll see exactly where the time goes and how the rewrite changes it.

And here is the exam signal, so listen closely. When a question describes a solution that works but is slow, and the logic is applied row by row, that is almost always a prompt to rewrite it with native functions. Working-but-slow is the tell. Keep that in mind as we go.
Let's start with Part 1 and the execution model underneath Spark.

scenes.title: Why Native Spark Functions Beat Python UDFs

elements.content: Native vs Python UDFs
Codegen: Catalyst parses native functions and fuses them into JVM codegen.
Boundary: Every UDF row pays a JVM-to-Python copy. [source p.341]
Black box: The explain plan shows the UDF as an opaque node. [source p.303]
pandas UDFs: Arrow batches cut per-row cost, but rewrites stay blocked.
Decision rule: prefer built-ins; keep a UDF as a last resort. [source p.359]
Worked example: 10M rows × 1 µs ≈ 10 s overhead.

actions.text: Now we get to the heart of this lesson: why native Spark functions beat Python UDFs. This is one of the most testable topics in the certification, and the good news is that once you understand the execution model, the preference stops being a rule you memorize and becomes a conclusion you can justify.

Start with the native path. When you use a built-in function like upper, datediff, or a higher-order function like transform, Catalyst can see exactly what it does. Because the operation is a known node in the logical plan, the optimizer can rewrite it, push filters through it, and then fuse it into whole-stage code generation. That means the entire pipeline, scan through projection, compiles down into a single tight block of JVM bytecode, with no per-row interpretation overhead.

A Python UDF is the opposite. Catalyst cannot inspect it. Look at the explain plan and you will literally see it surface as an opaque operator, often labeled as a BatchEvalPython or ArrowEvalPython node. Because the optimizer has no idea what is inside, it cannot push predicates through it, cannot reorder it, and cannot fuse it into the codegen stage. The rest of the plan has to be split around it, and that split alone can cost you the entire benefit of whole-stage code generation.

Then there is the boundary problem, and this is where the arithmetic gets painful. A regular Python UDF executes row by row. Every single record has to be serialized in the JVM, handed across the JVM-to-Python process boundary, deserialized in the Python worker, processed, and then the result is sent all the way back. That per-record copy, combined with process transfer, is the real killer. It is not that Python is slow, it is that crossing that boundary a million times is slow.

Here is a quick worked example to make it concrete. Suppose the boundary crossing and serialization cost you about one microsecond per row. On ten million rows, that is roughly ten seconds of pure overhead, before your actual Python logic even runs. And if your UDF does anything nontrivial, the per-row cost is often far higher than a microsecond.

This is exactly why pandas UDFs exist, sometimes called vectorized UDFs. Instead of shipping one row at a time, they ship Arrow batches, often thousands of rows per call. The per-row serialization cost collapses dramatically, and that single change can be an order of magnitude faster. But note the catch: a pandas UDF is still opaque to the optimizer. You cut the boundary cost, but you still block predicate pushdown, reordering, and codegen. So vectorization fixes the transport, not the visibility.

This table pulls the three options side by side, and I want you to study each column. Where does the code execute? How much per-row overhead does it pay? And crucially, what can the optimizer see? Read it as a trade-off triangle: native functions win on every axis, pandas UDFs buy back some throughput at the cost of optimizer visibility, and plain Python UDFs lose on both. Commit those three rows to memory, they map directly to exam questions.

So here is the decision rule, and it is the one I want you to carry into the exam and into your own pipelines. Always prefer a built-in or a higher-order function first. Reach for a UDF only when no native expression can capture the logic at all. And when you truly must, keep it as small and rare as possible, or push it into a vectorized pandas UDF to blunt the boundary cost. The default assumption should always be that native can express it until you have proven otherwise.

To recap this page: native functions are visible to Catalyst and fuse into codegen; Python UDFs are opaque, block optimizer rewrites, and pay a per-row boundary tax; pandas UDFs shrink that tax with Arrow batches but remain a black box. With that execution model in hand, you are ready for the checkpoint that follows.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: UDF Mechanics and Performance Vocabulary

questions.question: A PySpark job applies a Python UDF to a string column. Catalyst still rewrites the surrounding DataFrame plan, but it never rewrites anything inside the UDF. Which statement best explains why?

options.label: Catalyst can only plan against the expressions it understands; the body of a Python UDF is an opaque function that runs in a separate Python worker process, so it cannot push predicates into the UDF, fold constants inside it, or rewrite its internal logic.
Catalyst can optimise the inside of a Python UDF, but only when the function is registered with spark.udf.register() instead of the @udf decorator.
Catalyst disables optimisation for the whole query as soon as any UDF appears, so joins, filters and aggregations elsewhere in the same plan also run unoptimised.
Catalyst does optimise Python UDF internals, but only when the UDF is invoked through the DataFrame API instead of through SQL.

questions.analysis: A query optimizer works by breaking a query into appropriate steps in an efficient order, assessing joins, indexes, data scan sizes and other factors so that the query executes in the least expensive manner [source p.301]. Catalyst does that work on expression trees it can inspect: filters, projections, join types, aggregates. A Python UDF enters the plan as a single opaque call, so Catalyst sees the call but not the logic inside it, and therefore cannot perform the intra-expression rewrites (constant folding, predicate pushdown into the function, null-propagation reasoning) it applies to native expressions. Note the precise scope of the claim: the plan AROUND the UDF is still optimised - a filter above the UDF can be pushed below it, unused columns can be pruned, a broadcast join can still be chosen - only the UDF's interior is off-limits. That is exactly the distractor in option C, which overstates the damage by claiming the entire plan is abandoned. Option B is wrong because the registration mechanism (decorator versus spark.udf.register) changes only how the function is resolved by name, not how opaque it is to the planner. Option D is wrong because the calling API (DataFrame versus SQL) is syntactic sugar over the same logical plan; the real difference is the language boundary, and the JVM is generally more performant than Python and may expose lower-level features that the Python API does not [source p.46]. This is also why a Scala or Java UDF is cheaper than a Python one: it is compiled into the same JVM process as the executor, so the planner can treat it as an ordinary expression and there is no cross-language boundary to cross.

questions.question: A 10-million-row DataFrame is processed through three sequential Python UDFs, each of which rewrites a string column. Which statements correctly describe the cost structure of this job? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Each row must be serialised (flattened and packed into a standard format that the reader can decode) before it leaves the JVM executor, deserialised inside the Python worker, then serialised again on the way back - so the boundary is crossed twice per row per UDF.
The JVM executor and the Python worker share the same heap, so rows are passed by reference and no serialisation is required at all.
The overhead is charged per row, not per distinct value: the plan pays roughly 10,000,000 x 3 x 2 = 60,000,000 boundary crossings even if the column contains only a dozen distinct strings.
The cost is bounded by the size of the source table on disk, because the UDF reads the serialised data directly from storage instead of from the executor's memory.

questions.analysis: Serialisation is the process of flattening and packing data into a standard format that a reader will be able to decode; a serialisation algorithm encodes types, imposes rules on the data structure, and exists precisely to allow exchange between programming languages and CPUs [source p.222]. A Python UDF forces exactly that exchange, because the function does not run in the JVM executor: it runs in a separate Python worker process, so each row (or each batch of rows) must be written to a transferable format on the JVM side, read and reconstructed in the worker, and the return value written back in the same way. That is option A, and it is the single most important mechanical fact about UDF cost. Option B is a classic misconception: there is no shared heap between the JVM and a Python worker process, and that is why serialisation is needed in the first place. Option C is correct and is the part students most often get wrong - the cost is per row, not per distinct value, so deduplication or low cardinality does not rescue you. Worked example: 10 million rows x 3 UDFs x 2 crossings = 60,000,000 boundary crossings. If each crossing costs even 1 microsecond of pure serialisation overhead (packing the value, framing it, shipping it, unpacking it), that is ~60 seconds of overhead spent doing no useful work, and it is paid again on every run of the job - before counting the interpretation cost of Python bytecode, which is far slower per operation than JVM-compiled code [source p.46]. Option D is wrong because the data is read and decoded by the JVM executor first; the UDF never touches storage, and the scan cost is an additive, not a bounding, term. This is also why small local tests mislead: benchmark data that fits comfortably in memory on a laptop will look fast while hiding the per-row boundary cost entirely, so real-world evaluation must simulate anticipated production data and query sizes [source p.174].

questions.question: Which situation genuinely makes a user-defined function the correct choice rather than a built-in function or a window expression?

options.label: The transformation must call logic that has no equivalent in the built-in function library - for example a proprietary hashing routine or third-party NLP library - so it can only run as arbitrary code outside the optimizer's set of known expressions.
The transformation cleans a string column by trimming whitespace, changing case, and replacing a substring matched by a regular expression.
The transformation needs a per-customer running total ordered by order date and a ranking that leaves no gaps after ties.
The transformation converts a Unix epoch integer column into a timestamp column for a downstream Delta table.

questions.analysis: The precondition for a UDF is narrow and should be stated as such: a UDF is justified only when the required logic cannot be expressed with the built-in function set and cannot be reduced to a SQL expression - typically because it delegates to external code, such as a proprietary hash, a signature-verification routine, or a third-party NLP or ML library whose internals are not open to reimplementation. The edge case matters too: even when a UDF is unavoidable, the cost is not fixed. A Scala or Java function stays inside the JVM and avoids the cross-language boundary, whereas a Python UDF pays per-row serialisation on every invocation; a vectorised (Arrow-backed pandas) UDF amortises part of that cost by shipping batches rather than single rows. Options B, C and D are all expressible natively and therefore fail the unavoidability test. Trimming, case-folding and regex replacement are handled by built-in string functions; a running total and a gap-free rank are exactly the window patterns - SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) and dense_rank() - that were covered earlier in this unit, which is precisely why the exam offers them as UDF distractors. Epoch-to-timestamp conversion is a built-in cast/conversion. Behind all of this sits the optimiser: it exists to execute a query in the least expensive manner by choosing efficient steps [source p.301], and it can only do that for code it can inspect, so pushing work into an opaque function removes optimisation opportunities that built-ins keep. Where a UDF is truly required, the JVM-native route remains preferable on performance grounds, since the JVM is generally more performant than Python and can reach lower-level features [source p.46].
