Python UDF (scalar, row-at-a-time): Catalyst sees the function as an opaque black box: it cannot inspect the body, push a filter through it, or reorder around it, so a filter written after a Python UDF forces the engine to serialize rows that a native rewrite would never have produced in the first place.
pandas UDF (vectorized): The function body is still opaque to Catalyst and no predicate can be pushed through it, so the only planning gain is that columns travel across the JVM-to-Python boundary once per batch rather than once per record.

Language flexibility and the logic each option can express
Native functions / higher-order functions: Expressiveness is bounded by the vocabulary the engine already implements, namely the Spark SQL built-ins plus the array and map higher-order functions, so any logic without a built-in must be decomposed into a combination of them.
Python UDF (scalar, row-at-a-time): Arbitrary Python is permitted, including third-party libraries that have no JVM equivalent, and this is precisely the situation in which a UDF is genuinely unavoidable rather than merely convenient.
pandas UDF (vectorized): Arbitrary Python is also permitted, but the body must be written as vectorized operations over pandas Series or DataFrames; a Python for-loop over the received Series quietly discards the vectorization benefit and collapses back toward scalar cost.

Typical performance impact relative to the native baseline
Native functions / higher-order functions: Native execution defines the 1x baseline because it runs in the same code-generated pipeline as the rest of the query and adds no process boundary.
Python UDF (scalar, row-at-a-time): This is typically the slowest option in practice, and real teams have replaced poorly written, sluggish UDFs with a built-in SQL expression and seen instant and dramatic improvement in performance [source p.359].
pandas UDF (vectorized): Usually faster than a scalar Python UDF because the per-batch boundary dominates instead of the per-row boundary, but still behind native execution because the computation leaves the JVM entirely.

API shape and the scalar versus vectorized versus aggregate distinction
Native functions / higher-order functions: Native code presents one unified expression tree: scalar functions such as initcap and regexp_replace, array higher-order functions such as transform, filter, exists and aggregate, and aggregate functions used with groupBy or inside a window are all first-class expressions that Catalyst reasons about identically.
Python UDF (scalar, row-at-a-time): A Python UDF is registered with udf() or the @udf decorator and applied one row at a time; a separate aggregate flavour (a UDAF) accumulates across rows but is rarely the right answer and is the slowest member of the family.
pandas UDF (vectorized): A pandas UDF is registered with the @pandas_udf decorator and typed as Series to Series, Iterator of Series to Iterator of Series, or Series to scalar; the Series-to-scalar form is the vectorized analogue of an aggregate and is the one exam questions deliberately pair with groupBy.

Null handling, typing and resulting schema
Native functions / higher-order functions: Built-ins generally propagate nulls, so initcap of a null yields null, and they produce engine-managed types, meaning downstream casts and joins see exactly the declared schema with no inference surprises.
Python UDF (scalar, row-at-a-time): A scalar Python UDF returns null whenever any input is null unless it is explicitly declared to receive nulls, so a null-skipping mistake can silently drop rows the same way count(col) silently skips nulls, which is exactly the trap this lesson asks you to notice.
pandas UDF (vectorized): It receives a pandas Series and must handle NaN itself, and the dtype of the Series it returns, including pandas nullable types, determines the Spark schema of the output column.

Typical workload fit and where the exam places each option
Native functions / higher-order functions: This is the default answer for every shape of ETL logic, including classic Kimball reporting such as asking what total sales were in the first quarter of 2022 against a date dimension, which is simply a grouped aggregate the engine already handles natively [source p.325].
Python UDF (scalar, row-at-a-time): This is the last resort and the option a performance-optimisation question most often marks as incorrect whenever the prompt contains a one-line native or higher-order equivalent.
pandas UDF (vectorized): This is the fallback when the logic genuinely needs Python but can be expressed batch-at-a-time over a Series, for example scoring an ML model per batch or applying a custom string routine with no SQL analogue.

Failure modes, error surfacing and debugging cost
Native functions / higher-order functions: Errors surface at analysis time as a line in the logical plan, so a type mismatch fails before the job is ever submitted; the residual risk is over-reading, which is why projecting only needed columns and avoiding SELECT * on wide tables is a standing performance lever.
Python UDF (scalar, row-at-a-time): Failures appear at runtime inside a Python worker, with logs split across driver and executor and no Catalyst-level type checking, so a type error that a native expression would have rejected at analysis time only appears after rows have already been processed.
pandas UDF (vectorized): Failures also surface at runtime, but batch-level semantics mean the traceback often points at a Series method rather than the specific record that caused the problem, which lengthens the debugging loop further.
Takeaway — Memorise the decision rule as one chain: built-in function first, then a higher-order function for arrays and maps, then a pandas (vectorized) UDF, and only then a plain Python UDF.

Takeaway — Choose native whenever the prompt shows a filter, projection or aggregate that Spark SQL already implements, because it is both the fastest option and the only one the optimizer can fully rewrite [source p.359].

Takeaway — Choose a pandas UDF when arbitrary Python is genuinely required but the computation is batch-friendly, and choose a plain Python UDF only when the logic is irreducibly row-at-a-time and cannot be vectorized.

Takeaway — As with micro-batch versus true streaming, there is no universal answer to which tool to use, but the ranking above only reorders when the required logic has no native equivalent [source p.355].

actions.text: Here's the consolidation table that ties together everything we just covered about UDFs. Three options sitting side by side: native functions and higher-order functions, plain Python UDFs, and pandas vectorized UDFs. Read this table across the rows, not down the columns, and the decision almost makes itself.

Start with execution location, because everything else follows from it. Native functions execute inside the JVM, directly on the Tungsten engine. Python UDFs are forced out to a separate Python worker process, one row at a time. Pandas UDFs also leave the JVM, but they cross the boundary in Arrow batches rather than row by row. That single distinction — where the work actually runs — drives the entire cost profile.

Now optimizer visibility, and this is the one candidates forget. Catalyst can see straight through native functions. It pushes down predicates, prunes columns, and reorders the whole plan around them. The moment you introduce a Python UDF, that region of the plan becomes a black box — the optimizer can't reason about what's inside it. That lost visibility is often a bigger performance hit than the serialization cost itself.

Which brings us to typical performance impact. Relative to native functions, a plain Python UDF can easily cost you an order of magnitude — per-row serialization on top of codegen being switched off for that stage. A pandas UDF recovers most of that ground by amortizing the crossing over a batch, so you land somewhere in the single-digit multiple range rather than ten times or worse.

So memorise the decision rule as one chain, walked left to right: built-in function first. If no built-in covers it, try a higher-order function on your array or map. If the logic genuinely needs Python but you can work batch-wise, reach for a pandas UDF. Only if none of those fit do you fall back to a plain Python UDF. The exam wants that ordering cold.

And that gives you the default exam answer. If a prompt shows a built-in or higher-order function that produces the same result, choosing native is correct, full stop — no hedging about convenience or readability. The exam frames performance-optimisation questions this way deliberately.

Choose a pandas UDF only when arbitrary Python logic is truly required and batch-level vectorization is acceptable — think model inference, or a library with no Spark equivalent. And notice the wording the exam uses: it carefully distinguishes a scalar UDF, a vectorized pandas UDF, and an aggregate function applied with groupBy. Those are three different things, and mixing them up is precisely the trap this table is built to disarm.

One last framing before we close this section — much like micro-batch sits between batch and true streaming, pandas UDFs sit between native code and row-by-row Python. Same instinct applies: pick the middle option only when the extremes genuinely can't do the job. Next up, the final checkpoint for this lesson.

scenes.title: Final Checkpoint: UDFs, Higher-Order Functions, and Query Patterns

questions.question: A Delta table orders receives an append-only change-data-capture (CDC) feed. The column order_id is NOT unique: the feed appends a brand-new row every time an order is modified, and each row carries updated_at (timestamp), status, and amount. The table holds roughly 800 million rows and averages 6 versions per order_id. A downstream certified job must return exactly one row per order_id — the version with the greatest updated_at — and it must not shuffle the wide table more than once. Which implementation is the efficient, exam-correct pattern?

options.label: In a common table expression (CTE), compute row_number() over (partition by order_id order by updated_at desc) as rn, then keep only the rows where rn = 1.
Aggregate max(updated_at) grouped by order_id, then join that small result back to the base table on order_id AND updated_at to recover the full row.
Call dropDuplicates(['order_id']) on the table; because Spark scans newest files first, the surviving row is guaranteed to be the latest version.
Call distinct() on the whole table so that repeated versions of the same order collapse into a single row.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct because a window ranking expresses 'latest per key' declaratively, in one logical pass: the data is exchanged once, partitioned by order_id, sorted by updated_at descending inside each partition, and then filtered to rank 1 — a filter that runs after the exchange, never a second shuffle. The arithmetic matters: 800,000,000 rows / 6 versions per key is roughly 133,300,000 distinct keys, so option B shuffles the 800M-row base table against a 133M-row aggregate and performs an equality join on a floating-point-free but still two-column key; worse, it silently breaks when two versions share an identical updated_at (a genuine CDC edge case, since the feed carries no sequence number), because then either both rows survive the join or the join multiplies rows. Option C encodes the most common student misconception: dropDuplicates is a non-deterministic, non-ordered operation that keeps an arbitrary surviving row from the scan, and it offers no guarantee about which one — it is not a 'latest wins' operator, and the winning row can change when the file layout or partitioning changes. Option D is wrong for a subtler reason: distinct() deduplicates identical full rows across all columns, and the six versions of an order differ in status, amount, or updated_at, so distinct() returns all six. A query optimizer's whole purpose is to break a query into the least expensive sequence of steps, and predicate placement plus avoiding redundant joins is exactly the lever it can pull here [source p.301]; the window form also keeps the logic readable if you compose it as a CTE, and the explain plan will show a single exchange plus a window node rather than two scans joined together [source p.303]. Note the precondition and edge case: this pattern assumes the key is non-null and that 'latest' is defined by updated_at alone; if the feed also carries monotonic metadata (for example a Bronze ingestion timestamp), ordering by tuple (updated_at, ingested_at) descending makes the tie-break deterministic. Finally, do not confuse deduplication with snapshot isolation: systems that read from a point-in-time committed snapshot [source p.305] give every reader a consistent picture of the table, but that consistent picture still contains all six versions of an order, so the 'latest per key' semantics must be expressed explicitly in the query, not inherited from the read model.

questions.question: A customers DataFrame has full_name (inconsistent casing plus stray whitespace) and phones (an array of raw strings that may contain spaces, dashes, parentheses and a leading '+'). Four candidate implementations are under review for a production pipeline. Select ALL implementations that a Databricks certification exam would classify as efficient: fully native expressions that the Catalyst optimizer can plan and fold into code generation, that preserve the row grain of one row per customer, and that pay no per-element JVM-to-Python transfer cost.

options.label: df.withColumn('name', trim(initcap(col('full_name')))).withColumn('phones_clean', transform(col('phones'), p -> regexp_replace(p, '[^0-9+]', '')))
clean = udf(lambda s: re.sub(r'[^0-9+]', '', s)); df.withColumn('phones_clean', transform(col('phones'), p -> clean(p)))
df.select('*', explode('phones').alias('phone')).groupBy('customer_id').agg(collect_list('phone').alias('phones_clean'))
df.withColumn('name', trim(initcap(col('full_name')))).withColumn('valid_phones', size(filter(col('phones'), p -> length(regexp_replace(p, '[^0-9]', '')) >= 7)))

questions.analysis: A and D are correct because every operator in them is a built-in expression the optimizer natively understands: trim, initcap, regexp_replace, transform, filter and size are all resolved inside Catalyst, and transform/filter compile the lambda body (itself a native expression) into the generated JVM code rather than shipping each element to an interpreter. Both preserve the row grain — one row per customer, arrays stay arrays, the count is a scalar column — so no downstream operator has to be rewritten. Option B is the trap the lesson warns about, dressed up to look modern: wrapping a Python UDF inside a higher-order function does not make it native. The lambda body here is an opaque Python callable, so every element of every array is serialized across the JVM-to-Python boundary, and the optimizer cannot inspect, push predicates through, or reorder that call; PySpark is an API wrapper for Scala Spark, and running Python UDFs forces data into Python where processing is less efficient [source p.341]. Option C is wrong on three independent counts. First, it changes the grain: one row per phone instead of one row per customer. Second, it forces a shuffle — explode multiplies rows (a customer with 3 phones becomes 3 rows) and groupBy('customer_id') then has to exchange and regroup them, adding a full shuffle plus an aggregation that the original pipeline never needed. Third, collect_list gives no ordering guarantee, so the rebuilt array may not match the original element order, silently corrupting any downstream code that assumes phones[0] is the primary number. A useful sanity check on candidate solutions: ask whether the implementation adds a shuffle or changes the number of rows. If the answer is yes and the requirement never mentioned the grain changing, the exam almost certainly considers it the distractor. If a capability genuinely cannot be expressed with built-ins, the guidance is to prefer the core API or a well-maintained library, and only then consider rewriting the UDF in Scala or Java [source p.341].

questions.question: A customers DataFrame has the column orders typed as array<struct<order_id: string, items: array<struct<sku: string, qty: int>>>>. For every customer row, the pipeline must produce ONE integer scalar: the total quantity across all items of all orders. Which single expression accomplishes this while preserving the row grain and requiring no explode and no shuffle?

options.label: aggregate(col('orders'), lit(0), (acc, o) -> acc + aggregate(o.items, lit(0), (acc2, i) -> acc2 + i.qty))
transform(col('orders'), o -> aggregate(o.items, lit(0), (a, i) -> a + i.qty))
aggregate(col('orders'), lit(0), (acc, o) -> acc + o.items)
exists(col('orders'), o -> aggregate(o.items, lit(0), (a, i) -> a + i.qty) > 0)

questions.analysis: Option A is correct and demonstrates why higher-order functions compose: the outer aggregate folds the orders array from a start value of lit(0), and for each order the lambda body runs a second, nested aggregate that folds that order's items array from its own lit(0), adding i.qty. Because lambda parameters are typed to the element, the nested field references o.items and i.qty resolve during analysis, and the whole expression is one native plan node that returns an integer for each row — the grain is untouched and no exchange is needed. Option B is the classic 'aggregate only ran over the inner array' error: transform always preserves the input array's shape, so the result is array<int> with one element per order, not a scalar; the return type is the giveaway. A student who notices this and chains aggregate(transform(...), lit(0), (a, x) -> a + x) is also correct, but that is a different expression from B, which stops after the transform. Option C mixes types: acc is an integer and o.items is an array of structs, so 'integer + array<struct>' is not a valid addition — Spark resolves it to null or raises a type error depending on configuration. The misconception behind C is that a lambda parameter can reference a nested array and have it concatenate or auto-explode; it cannot, because the higher-order function itself defines what the accumulator type is. Option D returns a BOOLEAN, not an integer: exists short-circuits as soon as it finds one order whose item total is greater than zero, which is a completely different question ('does this customer have any order with items?') and, being a boolean, cannot be summed downstream without casting. Beyond correctness, note the performance reason the exam prefers this shape: exploding orders and items and then regrouping by customer would multiply rows, shuffle the result, and rebuild arrays with no ordering guarantee, whereas a native lambda chain folds the nested arrays in place, one row in and one row out, with no JVM-to-Python boundary crossing at all [source p.341]. Edge cases to state explicitly in production code: a null orders array returns the lit(0) start value rather than null only if you coalesce first (aggregate propagates null on a null input array), an empty items array correctly contributes 0, and a null qty must be handled with a coalesce(i.qty, lit(0)) inside the inner lambda, otherwise the whole accumulator becomes null for that row.

questions.question: An existing PySpark pipeline processes a customers DataFrame of about 50 million rows and uses three row-by-row Python UDFs. UDF 1 (clean_name) takes full_name and returns it trimmed and title-cased. UDF 2 (clean_phone) takes one phone string and returns it with every character except digits and a leading '+' removed. UDF 3 (count_valid) iterates over the phones array in Python, applies clean_phone to each element, and returns the number of cleaned phones that still contain at least 7 digits. (a) Rewrite all three steps as native Spark expressions or higher-order functions with no UDFs, and state the return type of each expression. (b) Explain in one or two sentences why the native rewrite is faster, explicitly referencing the Catalyst optimizer and the JVM-to-Python boundary. (c) Assume each row costs about 100 microseconds of serialization and process transfer plus 5 microseconds of Python-side work once its data has crossed the boundary. Show the arithmetic for the total per-row overhead the rewrite eliminates across the 50 million rows and report it in core-minutes. (d) State the one condition under which a UDF is genuinely unavoidable, and what an engineer should try before accepting that cost.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100% total). (a) Correct rewrites — 40%: trim(initcap(col('full_name'))) for the name, returning string; transform(col('phones'), p -> regexp_replace(p, '[^0-9+]', '')) for cleaning, returning array<string> with the same length as the input; size(filter(col('phones'), p -> length(regexp_replace(p, '[^0-9]', '')) >= 7)) for the count, returning an integer scalar. Award full credit for equivalent expressions (for example lit(0)-based aggregate, or regexp_extract_all plus size) provided they are UDF-free, preserve the array or row grain, and the stated return types are correct. Deduct 10% for a missing return type, and 15% if any step still routes through a Python UDF, including a UDF nested inside a lambda. (b) Performance explanation — 25%: the answer must name both mechanisms. Catalyst can parse, analyze, and optimize the native expressions and fold them into whole-stage generated code, so the predicate and transformations are planned together with the rest of the query; a Python UDF is opaque, so nothing inside it can be pushed down, reordered, or code-generated, and every element must be serialized from the JVM to a Python worker process and back. Mentioning only the optimizer or only the boundary caps this section at 60% of its points. (c) Arithmetic — 20%: 100 microseconds + 5 microseconds = 105 microseconds per row; 50,000,000 rows x 105 microseconds = 5,250,000,000 microseconds = 5,250 seconds = 87.5 core-minutes of work spent purely on the boundary and Python execution. Full credit requires the unit conversion to core-minutes (87.5) and an acknowledgement that this CPU time is distributed across executor slots — on a 32-slot cluster it is still about 2.7 minutes of added wall-clock time for work the native expression folds into an existing scan, i.e. it does not disappear, it parallelizes. Accept a clearly labelled equivalent derivation. (d) Unavoidability — 15%: a UDF is genuinely unavoidable only when the logic cannot be expressed with built-in or higher-order functions, for example calling an external Python library, a cryptographic routine, or a machine-learning model. Before accepting it, the engineer should search for a built-in or higher-order equivalent and, failing that, rewrite the UDF in Scala or Java to stay inside the JVM. Both halves are needed for full credit; stating 'never use UDFs' fails this item because it ignores the genuine exception.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. (a) Name: trim(initcap(col('full_name'))) — returns a string. Phones: transform(col('phones'), p -> regexp_replace(p, '[^0-9+]', '')) — returns array<string> of unchanged length; transform never drops or gains elements. Count: size(filter(col('phones'), p -> length(regexp_replace(p, '[^0-9]', '')) >= 7)) — returns an integer. Note the deliberate asymmetry: the cleaning pattern keeps a leading '+', while the validity test strips everything except digits so that '+1-(415)-555-0123' is measured by its 11 digits and a 3-digit extension is correctly rejected. An equivalent phrasing is aggregate over a when(...) counter, which also returns a scalar. (b) The native rewrite wins on two independent mechanisms. First, the Catalyst optimizer can see the whole expression tree, analyze it against the schema, and fold it into generated JVM code alongside the surrounding scan and filter, so the transformations cost almost nothing beyond the work already being done; a Python UDF is a black box that blocks that reasoning. Second, PySpark is an API wrapper over Scala Spark, and a Python UDF forces every row (or every array element, in the nested case) to be serialized out of the JVM, shipped to a Python worker process, processed, and shipped back — running Python UDFs forces data to be passed to Python, where processing is less efficient, which is why the guidance is to look for a more Spark-native way first and to write the UDF in Scala or Java if one is truly needed [source p.341]. (c) 105 microseconds x 50,000,000 rows = 5,250,000,000 microseconds = 5,250 core-seconds = 87.5 core-minutes of pure boundary overhead that the native version does not pay; and because the third UDF touches an array, the real figure is larger, since the boundary is crossed per element rather than only per row. (d) Genuinely unavoidable only when the capability does not exist in the Spark API and cannot be composed from higher-order functions — for example invoking heavy external Python libraries. The correct escalation order is: search the core API, then a well-maintained library, and only then a UDF written in Scala or Java; SQL is also worth reaching for because it lets the same Catalyst optimizer do the work with less code to maintain [source p.341]. Finally, when reviewing such a rewrite, read the explain plan rather than trusting intuition: the plan should show a single scan with the projection and filter pushed in, not an extra exchange or a Python-worker stage [source p.303].

actions.text: Time for the final checkpoint of this lesson — the last mixed assessment on UDFs, higher-order functions, and query patterns. Everything here draws on what we just covered, so take each question on your own: work through them carefully, and don't rush the reasoning on the performance ones.
Answer as best you can, and once you submit I'll walk through the results with you — anything that tripped you up, we'll unpack together. Go ahead and get started.

scenes.title: Ingestion Patterns and Design Choices

elements.content: Ingestion Patterns and Design Choices
Ingestion is the first stage of the data engineering lifecycle: moving data out of source systems and landing it in storage before transformation and serving. [source p.60]
Three canonical patterns: batch (scheduled or size-triggered), streaming (continuous, near real-time), and incremental (capturing only changed rows since the last run). [source p.66]
Bounded vs unbounded: bounded data has a defined start and end (a daily file, a closed table), so batch fits; unbounded data never ends, so streaming or incremental fits.
One-way door: once data is broken into batches, downstream latency is inherently constrained and cannot be reduced without re-architecting ingestion. [source p.67]
Durability and format compatibility must be decided at ingestion time, because downstream storage and transformation systems can only consume what was landed. [source p.66]

Worked example: 200 GB/day arriving from an API. Batch hourly = 8.3 GB per run and up to 60-minute latency; switching to streaming later requires replaying a year of history (~73 TB) and rebuilding every downstream consumer.

actions.text: Now we shift gears into a brand-new unit: ingestion. Specifically, ingestion patterns and the design choices behind them. Everything we've built so far assumed the data was already sitting in a Delta table — this unit is about how it actually gets there.

Ingestion is the first stage of the data engineering lifecycle. It's the boundary layer where data crosses from source systems — APIs, databases, file drops, event streams — into your lakehouse. Everything downstream depends on what you capture here, so treat this stage as a design decision, not a plumbing detail.

There are three canonical ingestion patterns you need to know by name for the exam: batch, streaming, and incremental. Batch pulls data on a schedule or by size thresholds. Streaming continuously consumes events as they arrive. Incremental reads only what's new since the last read — and that idea will carry through the rest of this unit.

The mental model that ties those patterns together is bounded versus unbounded data. Bounded data has a defined start and end — a daily CSV drop is bounded. Unbounded data keeps arriving with no defined end — a Kafka topic is unbounded. Bounded maps naturally to batch or incremental; unbounded maps to streaming.

Here's the piece students underrate on the exam: pattern choice is a one-way door. Once you've committed to breaking data into batches with a schedule and a cutoff, you cannot cheaply reconstruct the events you already collapsed. That choice constrains your storage layout, your transformation logic, and your cost profile downstream.

Two things must be decided early because they're expensive to reverse later: durability — how many times you can afford to re-ingest if something breaks — and format compatibility, meaning whether the source format and the landing format can evolve together without dropping records.

Let's ground this with a worked example. Two hundred gigabytes per day arriving from an API. Batch that hourly and you get roughly 8 GB per pull — manageable, but you've introduced up to an hour of latency and you must handle pagination and rate limits. Streaming it gives near-real-time, but you inherit state management and checkpointing. Incremental with a watermark on a modified timestamp sits in between. Same source, three very different downstream lives.

So to close this opener: ingestion sits at the front of the lifecycle, three patterns cover the space — batch, streaming, incremental — bounded data maps to batch and incremental, unbounded maps to streaming, and whichever you pick is a one-way door that you should walk through deliberately. In the next pages we'll compare the three side by side.

scenes.title: Batch vs Streaming vs Incremental: Side by Side

elements.content: Dimension  |  Batch ingestion  |  Streaming ingestion  |  Incremental ingestion (CDC)

Latency floor and what triggers a run
Batch ingestion: A batch job is triggered by a predetermined time interval or when data reaches a preset size threshold, so its latency floor is the interval itself — a nightly job delivers data that is 0 to 24 hours stale, averaging about 12 hours [source p.67].
Streaming ingestion: Streaming ingestion provides data to downstream systems continuously, and real-time (or near real-time) means the data is available a short time after it is produced — for example less than one second later — although the latency that qualifies as real-time varies by domain and requirements [source p.67].
Incremental ingestion (CDC): Incremental ingestion driven by continuous CDC treats each write to the source database as an event, so rows land in the lakehouse within seconds of a commit; periodic-query CDC, by contrast, inherits the polling interval as its latency floor [source p.162].

Data boundedness and per-run volume
Batch ingestion: Batch operates on bounded data — a finite, already-complete set of files or rows — and reprocesses that whole extent on every run, so ingesting a 500 GB/day source once per day means moving 500 GB per run no matter how little actually changed [source p.132].
Streaming ingestion: Streaming processes unbounded data, meaning the event stream has no defined end, so the same 500 GB/day source arrives at roughly 5.8 MB/s on average and the job must be sized for peak bursts rather than for the duration of one finite job [source p.132].
Incremental ingestion (CDC): Incremental reads only the rows that changed since the last watermark, so if 2% of 500 million daily rows change, the job moves about 10 million rows (~10 GB) instead of 500 GB, cutting data movement by roughly 98%.

Processing model, state, and checkpoints
Batch ingestion: Batch is a stateless recomputation over a bounded input: you read the whole batch, transform it, and write the result, so correctness depends only on the input snapshot and not on remembering anything from the previous run [source p.67].
Streaming ingestion: Streaming requires durable checkpoints and managed state — offsets, watermarks, running aggregates — because the stream never ends and the engine must be able to resume mid-stream exactly where it stopped after a failure [source p.67].
Incremental ingestion (CDC): Incremental pipelines persist a watermark or change-tracking bookmark, such as the log sequence number of a database binary log, so each run knows precisely which events have already been applied and applies only the delta [source p.162].

Databricks tooling and platform mapping
Batch ingestion: In Databricks, batch ingestion is typically a scheduled job — Auto Loader with trigger(availableNow=True) or a notebook task inside a Databricks Workflow — writing into Delta Lake tables, with Photon accelerating scans and Unity Catalog governing access.
Streaming ingestion: In Databricks, streaming ingestion runs on Structured Streaming over Auto Loader or Kafka (including Debezium-style CDC feeds), with checkpoints in cloud storage and either continuous or triggered execution; a triggered micro-batch of, say, one minute is the common compromise [source p.67].
Incremental ingestion (CDC): In Databricks, incremental ingestion is implemented as a streaming CDC feed applied with MERGE INTO a Delta Lake table, or through Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines APPLY CHANGES semantics, so that each source write becomes one upsert event [source p.162].

Cost structure and where the money goes
Batch ingestion: Batch concentrates cost into short, high-throughput windows, so you pay for a large cluster for a brief time and can lean on spot instances; the risk is that one late upstream file pushes the entire run and every dependent consumer later [source p.67].
Streaming ingestion: Streaming converts cost into a continuous operational bill: the cluster must stay always-on and over-provisioned for peak, and the streaming-first decision must be justified against time, money, maintenance, downtime, and opportunity cost relative to simply doing batch [source p.67].
Incremental ingestion (CDC): Incremental is usually cheapest in compute per change because work scales with change volume rather than source size, but it adds connector licensing, source-side log retention, and the ongoing engineering effort of maintaining CDC correctness [source p.162].

Assumption about downstream capacity
Batch ingestion: Batch implicitly assumes sinks can absorb a synchronized burst at the close of each window, so a downstream system that cannot handle the batch's peak rate simply fails or queues at the load step [source p.67].
Streaming ingestion: Streaming-first demands that you ask whether downstream storage systems can handle the rate of data flow before committing, because a sink that cannot sustain 5.8 MB/s of steady traffic will back-pressure the whole pipeline [source p.67].
Incremental ingestion (CDC): Incremental assumes downstream can accept out-of-order, row-level updates as a MERGE-heavy write pattern, which requires upsert-capable sinks and enough file-compaction headroom rather than raw append throughput [source p.162].

Failure recovery and reprocessing
Batch ingestion: Batch recovers by re-running the job over the same bounded input, which is simple and idempotent for overwrite-by-partition writes, but a crash at hour six of a seven-hour job means paying for nearly the entire run again [source p.346].
Streaming ingestion: Streaming recovers from checkpoints by restarting at the last committed offset, which gives at-least-once delivery, while exactly-once is achievable only when the sink supports idempotent or transactional writes; a single poisoned record can stall the stream indefinitely [source p.67].
Incremental ingestion (CDC): Incremental recovers by replaying the change log from the last applied log sequence number, which is cheap while the log is retained, but if the source prunes its binary log before the job resumes the delta is lost and a full resync is required [source p.162].

Worked example: 500 GB/day source with 2% daily change
Batch ingestion: Take 500 GB/day and 500 million rows of about 1 KB each: the nightly batch job reads all 500 GB (roughly 1,000 seconds of pure I/O at a sustained 500 MB/s before shuffle and write), so it moves 500 GB to deliver 10 GB of real change — a 50x amplification — and consumers wait up to 24 hours [source p.346].
Streaming ingestion: The same source averages 500 GB / 86,400 s = 5.8 MB/s, and provisioning for a 10x peak means sizing for about 58 MB/s continuously; the reward is sub-second to a few seconds of freshness at the price of an always-on cluster [source p.67].
Incremental ingestion (CDC): Capturing only changed rows means 2% x 500 million = 10 million rows, about 10 GB per day, so the incremental job moves one fiftieth of the bytes batch moves while still landing within seconds — the classic lowest-cost-with-low-latency answer [source p.162].

Code-path unification across patterns
Batch ingestion: Batch-only stacks keep one code path but pay for it in staleness, and they share nothing with a streaming implementation, which is why teams often run separate batch aggregation jobs alongside their real-time collectors [source p.132].
Streaming ingestion: The Dataflow model treats all data as events, so batches are simply bounded event streams whose boundaries form a natural window (sliding or tumbling) and real-time and batch processing happen in the same system using nearly identical code [source p.132].
Incremental ingestion (CDC): Incremental sits between the two extremes: ingestion is a stream of change events, but the apply step can run on a schedule as a bounded micro-batch, letting one MERGE statement serve both the real-time and the batch consumption pattern [source p.162].

Exam trigger phrases and canonical use cases
Batch ingestion: Phrases such as highest throughput per job and predetermined interval or size threshold point to batch, whose canonical uses are routine analytics refreshes, period-end finance closes, and ML training sets where 12-hour staleness is acceptable [source p.67].
Streaming ingestion: Phrases such as lowest latency, millisecond real-time, or near real-time delivery point to streaming, whose canonical uses are fraud detection, live dashboards, and alerting where the action taken on the data genuinely differs from waiting for the next batch [source p.67].
Incremental ingestion (CDC): Phrases such as lowest cost or minimize reprocessing point to incremental CDC, whose canonical uses are real-time database replication and maintaining a lakehouse mirror of an operational table without ever rescanning it [source p.162].

Takeaway — Choose batch when the use case tolerates interval-shaped staleness and you want the highest throughput per job with the least operational overhead; a nightly or hourly schedule is still the default for analytics and ML workloads [source p.67].

Takeaway — Choose streaming only after answering the streaming-first checklist: can downstream storage handle the rate, do you truly need milliseconds or would a one-minute micro-batch suffice, and will streaming cost more in time, money, maintenance, downtime, and opportunity cost than batch [source p.67].

Takeaway — Choose incremental when the source is a transactional database and the change fraction is small, because capturing 2% of rows instead of 100% is the single largest cost lever available to you [source p.162].

Takeaway — The three patterns compose rather than compete: a CDC stream can be applied as a scheduled micro-batch MERGE, and a batch job can be expressed as a bounded window over the same event stream, so the real choice is often about the trigger and the write pattern rather than about three different systems [source p.132].

Takeaway — Exam heuristic: lowest latency maps to streaming, lowest cost and least reprocessing map to incremental CDC, and least operational overhead or highest throughput per job maps to batch [source p.67].

actions.text: Let's put the three ingestion patterns side by side. This table is the reference view we'll come back to — rows are the dimensions the exam actually tests, and columns are batch, streaming, and incremental. Read it left to right and notice how each pattern makes a different trade.

Start with latency. Batch has a latency floor set by its schedule — nothing runs until the timer fires or the size threshold is crossed. Streaming's floor is essentially the micro-batch interval, seconds to low minutes. Incremental sits in between: it runs on a trigger, but only moves the rows that changed.

Next, boundedness and volume. Batch operates on bounded data — a file, a day's partition, a finite query result. Streaming operates on unbounded data; it never 'finishes'. Incremental usually reads a bounded change set, which is why per-run volume stays small and predictable.

The processing model follows from that. Batch is restart-from-scratch by nature. Streaming requires checkpoints and state management to track progress and deliver near-real-time results. Incremental leans on change data capture, or CDC, so it reprocesses only changed rows — that's the cost lever.

Tooling mapping, since the exam expects you to name the product. Batch points to Lakeflow Jobs, COPY INTO, or a scheduled notebook. Streaming points to Structured Streaming and Auto Loader. Incremental points to Auto Loader and CDC via Lakeflow Connect or managed connectors.

Here's the worked example that makes it concrete: a source producing 500 gigabytes a day with only 2 percent daily change. A full nightly batch reads all 500 gigabytes. Incremental reads roughly 10 gigabytes of change. Same result, radically different cost — that constant factor is what these questions are usually probing.

Now the exam trigger phrases. If a scenario says 'lowest latency' or 'seconds to minutes', that's streaming. 'Lowest cost' or 'minimize reprocessing' points to incremental. 'Least operational overhead' or 'simple scheduled refresh' points to batch. Watch for the pivot word — the whole answer turns on it.

Takeaways. Choose batch when the use case tolerates a scheduled delay and you want the simplest, highest-throughput-per-run path. Choose streaming only after you've answered the cost question — checkpoints, always-on compute, and operational complexity all come with it.

And remember: these three compose rather than compete. A realistic pipeline can batch-load a historical backfill, stream live events through Auto Loader, and apply CDC for the dimensional tables — all in one Lakeflow Job. The patterns are ingredients, not a menu you pick one item from.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Ingestion Patterns

questions.question: A data engineer builds an orders pipeline that runs on a nightly schedule at 02:00. Each run reads the complete Parquet export that the source system produced the previous day, overwrites the entire contents of the bronze Delta table with that export, and then the cluster shuts down until the next scheduled run. Which ingestion pattern does this pipeline implement?

options.label: Batch ingestion, because each run processes a bounded snapshot from start to finish and the job terminates between triggers
Streaming ingestion, because the nightly schedule repeats forever, so the pipeline never truly ends
Continuous change data capture (CDC), because the pipeline keeps the lakehouse synchronized with the production orders table
Unbounded ingestion, because new orders keep arriving in the source system after the job finishes

questions.analysis: Option A is correct. Ingestion is the stage where data engineers actively design pipeline activities, and the canonical patterns are distinguished by how they treat data over time rather than by how often they fire [source p.260]. A batch job is triggered by a predetermined time interval or size threshold and operates on bounded data, so a nightly job that reads one complete export, replaces the table contents, and terminates is the textbook batch case. Option B is the most common student misconception: a repeating schedule does not make a job continuous. Streaming is continuous by default — it starts once and keeps running, holding state and checkpoints — whereas this job has a defined beginning and end and must be re-triggered by the scheduler [source p.412]. Option C is wrong because CDC is a continuous fast-follower pattern that reads the production database's change stream with a slight lag, not a nightly file-level full copy [source p.307]. Option D confuses the calendar with the dataset: 'unbounded' describes a dataset with no predetermined end, but here each run is handed a fixed, complete file that the engine can know is finished. Even so, engineers should ask whether real-time ingestion would actually enable better actions and whether it would cost more in time, money, maintenance, downtime, and opportunity cost than simply doing batch [source p.67].

questions.question: Which statements correctly distinguish bounded data from unbounded data, and correctly map each to its ingestion pattern? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Bounded data has a defined start and end, so a batch job can wait for the input to be complete before it begins processing
Unbounded data has no predetermined end, which is why streaming pipelines require checkpoints and state management
Data is unbounded only if it arrives faster than one record per second; slower feeds are always bounded
Re-running the same batch job every ten minutes converts unbounded source data into bounded data

questions.analysis: Options A and B are correct. The ingestion patterns map directly onto the shape of the data: batch methods treat data as bounded, while real-time data applications treat data as an unbounded, continuous stream [source p.412]. Boundedness is a property of the dataset's end condition, not of its size or speed, and it is exactly this property that lets a batch engine know when it may stop reading and finish a run [source p.260]. Unboundedness is why streaming pipelines must persist checkpoints and maintain state across arbitrarily long runtimes — there is no point at which the input is 'complete', so correctness and recovery depend on that durable state [source p.412]. Option C is a misconception that confuses volume with boundedness: a feed of one record per minute that never ends is still unbounded, and a 500 GB file delivered once is still bounded. Option D is a second common misconception: scheduling a batch job more often, or shortening the trigger interval, does not change the nature of the source. Each run still receives a discrete, finite slice and terminates; only a continuously running process is streaming by default. Even a micro-batch approach that accumulates and ingests every minute is a deliberate design compromise, not a conversion of unbounded data into bounded data [source p.67].

questions.question: Which ingestion pattern is continuous by default — that is, it is started once and keeps running, consuming each record as it arrives until it is deliberately stopped?

options.label: Batch ingestion, because a cron-style scheduler fires repeatedly throughout the day
Streaming ingestion, because it treats data as an unbounded, continuous stream and relies on checkpoints and state management
Incremental ingestion, because it reads only the rows that changed since the previous run
Batch ingestion with a very small file-size threshold, because a low threshold makes it effectively continuous

questions.analysis: Option B is correct. Streaming is the only canonical ingestion pattern that is continuous by default: it is launched once and processes records as they arrive, which is precisely why it must persist checkpoints and maintain state to survive long runtimes and failures [source p.412]. Option A is the classic distractor that mistakes repetition for continuity — a cron-fired batch job is a series of separate, terminating runs triggered by a predetermined time interval, and each run is dormant between triggers [source p.260]. Option C is a conceptual mismatch rather than a scheduling point: 'incremental' describes which data a run selects (only rows that are new or changed since the last run), not whether the process runs forever. Incremental logic can be executed inside a terminating batch job or inside a continuous streaming job, so it carries no guarantee of continuous execution. Option D fails for the same reason as Option A: shrinking the trigger threshold changes latency, not execution semantics. A small threshold produces more frequent discrete runs, each of which still starts, processes a bounded slice, and stops. Engineers weighing a genuinely continuous design should first confirm that real-time ingestion supports actions that improve on batch and that the streaming-first approach does not cost more in time, money, maintenance, downtime, and opportunity cost than simply doing batch [source p.67].

actions.text: Let's check how well the side-by-side comparison we just went through settled in. Take this short knowledge check one question at a time, and answer each on your own without looking back — that's the only way to find out what you actually own.

Note that one of these asks you to select all that apply, so read each option carefully before you commit. Once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning with you and clear up anything that felt shaky.

scenes.title: Requirements That Drive the Choice: Latency, Volume, Reliability

elements.content: Requirements That Drive the Choice
Extract four axes before choosing a pattern — latency, volume, reliability, destination
1 · LATENCY
2 · VOLUME / THROUGHPUT
3 · RELIABILITY

• Latency spectrum: seconds → minutes → hours [source p.263]

• Batch is a one-way door: size fixes delay [source p.67]

• Every queue adds latency

• Quantify payload size and events per second [source p.66]

• Many small inserts create many small files [source p.273]

• Scale out the ingestion path

• Exactly-once vs at-least-once: duplicates matter

• Idempotent writes, retries, dead-letter queues

• Timestamp every hop [source p.191]
Destination sets the contract: format and write mode [source p.66]
Worked example: 2,000 events/s × 512 B ≈ 1 MB/s ≈ 86 GB/day → hourly batch

actions.text: Now that we've compared batch, streaming, and incremental side by side, the real question is: how do you decide which one to use? The answer is that you never pick a pattern first — you extract requirements first. This page gives you the framework.

Before you choose an ingestion pattern, extract four axes from the scenario: latency, volume and throughput, reliability, and destination. Think of it as taking a set of measurements before you buy the equipment. Get these wrong and no pattern will save you.

Axis one is latency. Place the requirement on a spectrum: are we talking seconds, minutes, or hours? Seconds implies streaming; minutes suggests micro-batch or frequent incremental loads; hours points to scheduled batch. On the exam, read the latency phrasing carefully — 'near real-time' is not the same as 'real-time'.

Axis two is volume and throughput. Quantify both the payload size and the events per second, then ask whether the ingestion path can scale horizontally. A source pushing a few thousand rows a day behaves nothing like one pushing millions of events a minute.

Axis three is reliability. Ask whether the business needs exactly-once delivery or whether at-least-once is acceptable, and if duplicates matter then you also need idempotency, retry logic, and a dead-letter queue for the records that fail validation.

And the fourth axis is the destination. Where does the data have to land, and in what shape? The destination sets the contract — its format and write mode shape the pattern just as much as the source does. This is the axis learners forget most often.

Let's make it concrete. Two thousand events per second at 512 bytes each works out to roughly one megabyte per second — around eighty-six gigabytes a day. That single estimate tells you both how the ingestion must scale and what it will cost, which is exactly the kind of reasoning the exam expects.

So remember the order of operations: latency, volume, reliability, destination — extract all four before you name a pattern. On the next page we'll look at how to read the ingestion metrics that confirm your choice was right.

scenes.title: Reading Ingestion Metrics

elements.content:
End-to-end ingestion latency across a simulated 24-hour window: hourly batch, micro-batch stream, and continuous stream (line)
Hour of simulated window (hours since 00:00) → End-to-end latency (seconds, log scale)
Y values are p95 end-to-end latency in seconds from event production to a queryable Delta table, sampled at the top of each hour of a simulated 24-hour window. The y-axis is logarithmic, so equal vertical distances represent equal ratios rather than equal differences; a series that looks 'almost flat' near the bottom is still separated by a large factor.
Hourly batch (T = 3600 s trigger): 0→1792   4→1805   8→1798   12→1811   16→1789   20→1803
Micro-batch stream (T = 120 s trigger): 0→64   4→96   8→72   12→118   16→88   20→132
Continuous stream (true streaming): 0→0.8   4→1.4   8→0.9   12→2.1   16→1.1   20→1.6

Claim 1 — Refuted
The hourly batch pipeline meets a 15-minute freshness SLA, because its latency never rises above roughly 30 minutes.
Why: The batch curve reads 1792 s at hour 0, 1805 s at hour 4, 1798 s at hour 8, 1811 s at hour 12, 1789 s at hour 16 and 1803 s at hour 20. A 15-minute SLA is 15 x 60 = 900 s, so even the best sampled hour (1789 s at hour 16) is 1.99x the budget, and the median reading is 1800.5 s, i.e. about 2x outside the SLA at every point plotted. The premise that 'never above 30 minutes' is acceptable is exactly the mistake the trigger-interval model exposes: a 3600 s trigger produces a mean wait of T/2 = 1800 s. The source is explicit that a pipeline must be sized for the frequency and size of the events it ingests, and that uptime, latency and data volumes processed are the things to watch [source p.292].

Claim 2 — Refuted
The micro-batch stream keeps end-to-end latency below two minutes at every hour of the window.
Why: The micro-batch readings are 64 s (h0), 96 s (h4), 72 s (h8), 118 s (h12), 88 s (h16) and 132 s (h20). At hour 20 the value is 132 s = 2 minutes 12 seconds, which exceeds the 120 s threshold, and hour 12 (118 s) leaves only 2 s of headroom. One counterexample is enough to refute a universal claim. The source frames the decision exactly this way: micro-batch might run anywhere from every two minutes to every second, and you must ask what the acceptable latency is before picking the frequency [source p.355].

Claim 3 — Supported
Across the window, the continuous stream never exceeds three seconds of end-to-end latency.
Why: The continuous stream reads 0.8 s (h0), 1.4 s (h4), 0.9 s (h8), 2.1 s (h12), 1.1 s (h16) and 1.6 s (h20). The maximum is 2.1 s at hour 12, comfortably under the 3 s bound, and the median is 1.25 s. This is the behavioural signature the source describes: true streaming systems process one event at a time and therefore show low, event-granular latency, at the price of significant per-event overhead [source p.354].

Claim 4 — Supported
Replacing the hourly batch trigger with a two-minute micro-batch reduces median end-to-end latency by roughly an order of magnitude.
Why: Sorting the batch readings gives 1789, 1792, 1798, 1803, 1805, 1811, so the batch median is (1798 + 1803)/2 = 1800.5 s. Sorting the micro-batch readings gives 64, 72, 88, 96, 118, 132, so the micro-batch median is (88 + 96)/2 = 92.0 s. The ratio is 1800.5 / 92.0 = 19.6x, which is 'roughly an order of magnitude' and even an understatement of the 30x drop in trigger interval (3600 s to 120 s). The source's guidance is that a micro-batch approach that accumulates and ingests every minute may be sufficient when millisecond ingestion is not required [source p.67].

Claim 5 — Refuted
The latency gap between micro-batch and continuous streaming is larger than the gap between batch and micro-batch.
Why: Micro-batch median 92.0 s minus continuous median 1.25 s gives a gap of 90.75 s. Batch median 1800.5 s minus micro-batch median 92.0 s gives a gap of 1708.5 s, which is about 18.8x larger. The claim inverts the direction of the data: the economically significant jump is leaving scheduled batch, not switching from micro-batch to true streaming. This is why the source notes that micro-batch is often dismissed unfairly and 'may work just fine for your use case and can be superior in many respects depending on your needs' [source p.355].

Claim 6 — Insufficient
The continuous stream is always the most expensive option.
Why: Within the single simulated configuration in the table, continuous streaming is indeed the most expensive ($4,910/month) versus micro-batch ($3,240) and hourly batch ($1,850), and it also carries the highest complexity score (9 vs 5 vs 2). But the claim is universal ('always'), while the evidence is one configuration at one volume band. Cost is driven by provisioned capacity and volume, not by the pattern label, and at very high event rates the batch job could easily dominate spend. The source therefore poses cost as a question to answer per project: will a streaming-first approach cost more in time, money, maintenance, downtime and opportunity cost than simply doing batch? [source p.67]. The correct reading is 'true in this sample, not established in general', which is the insufficient verdict.

Claim 7 — Supported
In this simulation, latency and operational complexity trade off against each other: the lowest-latency pipeline is also the highest-complexity and highest-cost one, and the highest-throughput pipeline is the slowest to deliver data.
Why: Ranking the three configurations by median latency gives 1.25 s continuous, 92.0 s micro-batch, 1800.5 s batch. The table ranks them in the opposite order for complexity (9, 5, 2) and for monthly cost ($4,910, $3,240, $1,850), and in the opposite order again for peak throughput (6,200, 18,500 and 42,000 events/sec). So the ordering is strictly monotone in all four dimensions: lowest latency goes with highest cost, highest complexity, and lowest throughput. This is precisely the trade-off framing the source recommends before choosing streaming-first ingestion [source p.67].

Claim 8 — Insufficient
Because the chart reports latency for every hour of the window, the simulation proves that the hourly batch job never failed during the 24 hours.
Why: Latency alone cannot separate a slow-but-successful run from a failed run whose output was never produced, nor from a job that silently stopped writing. In the chart, a failed hour would still show a latency plateau, because the metric has no value to report for events that were never ingested. The source's point is that latency must be monitored together with uptime and data volumes processed, and that pipelines should have monitoring built in from the beginning rather than after deployment, with one documented case of an ingestion failure going undetected for six months [source p.292]. The claim is therefore not decidable from the plotted latency values.

actions.text: Now that we've mapped requirements to ingestion patterns, let's do what a real engineer does — read the evidence. This page gives us a small plotted dataset: end-to-end ingestion latency across a simulated 24-hour window for three pipelines. Our job is not to guess which pattern is best, but to test specific design claims against the numbers in front of us.

Notice the shape of the chart before the numbers. The X-axis is time across the 24-hour simulation, and the Y-axis is end-to-end latency in seconds. Keep your eye on how flat or how spiky each line is — the pattern of the line is what tells you whether a freshness SLA can actually be met.

Start with the hourly batch, triggered every 3,600 seconds. It reads roughly 0 to 1,792 seconds of latency. That means the worst case is close to half an hour — because you can wait almost a full hour for the trigger, plus the processing time itself. Compare that against a 15-minute, or 900-second, freshness SLA and it fails outright.

Next, the micro-batch stream with a 120-second trigger. Latency lands around 0 to 64 seconds. Much tighter, and it comfortably sits inside a 15-minute SLA. But hold on to those occasional tall spikes — the worst-case tail matters as much as the average when you're evaluating a claim.

Finally, the continuous stream, or true streaming: roughly 0 to 0.8 seconds. That's an order of magnitude tighter than micro-batch. But remember — lower latency is not automatically better, and it is certainly not automatically cheaper. That distinction is exactly what Claim 6 forces us to check.

Let's evaluate the claims. Claim 1 says the hourly batch pipeline meets a 15-minute freshness SLA — and it is refuted. Justify the verdict straight from the X-axis readings: a 3,600-second trigger interval alone exceeds 900 seconds before the job even starts, let alone finishes.

Claim 6 is the trap. It asserts that the continuous stream is always the most expensive option, and the verdict is insufficient. Why? Because the latency chart tells us nothing about cost. To rule on that claim we need the throughput, monthly compute cost, and operational complexity table — latency alone cannot support or refute a cost statement.

That's the exam habit worth internalising: read the claim, find which artifact actually carries the evidence, and only then commit to supported, refuted, or insufficient. Data that isn't on the chart can't refute a claim about cost. Let's continue to the knowledge check and map these requirements to patterns.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Requirements Mapping

questions.question: A fraud-detection platform ingests transaction events from a managed event hub. Events arrive continuously at an average of 12,000 events per second (roughly 1.04 billion events per day, about 15 TB per day). The business requirement is stated as follows: 'A newly arrived transaction must be visible to the fraud-scoring service within 60 seconds of its arrival, and no transaction may be permanently lost.' Which ingestion pattern satisfies the stated freshness SLA?

options.label: Scheduled batch ingestion every 15 minutes, writing one new partition per run
Nightly incremental ingestion that processes the previous calendar day's events
A continuously running streaming ingestion pipeline with checkpointing and exactly-once processing guarantees
On-demand batch ingestion triggered manually by an analyst whenever the dashboard looks stale

questions.analysis: The decisive axis here is latency, not volume. The stated SLA is 60 seconds end-to-end. Option A has a worst-case latency of one full interval, i.e. 900 seconds (15 minutes), which is 15x the SLA even before processing time is added. Option B has a worst-case latency of about 86,400 seconds (24 hours), which is 1,440x the SLA. Option D has no bounded latency at all, because the trigger is a human decision rather than a schedule or a continuous loop, so it cannot be verified against any SLA. Only option C, a continuously running pipeline with checkpoints, can bound the delivery latency to seconds while still guaranteeing that a restart resumes from the last committed offset rather than dropping or duplicating data. Note that the 12,000 events/sec figure is a volume argument and does not by itself decide the answer: horizontal scaling and distributed processing exist precisely to absorb high load in batch jobs as well. The source material explicitly notes that IoT-style gateways 'may accumulate data and upload it in batches for later analytics processing' and that such architectures must still account for 'late-arriving data, data structure and schema disparities, data corruption, and connection disruption' [source p.134], and that for some sources 'once lost, it is gone for good', so ingestion reliability leads directly to data durability [source p.266]. Distributed systems with a leader node distributing work to workers and replicating data for failover are how either pattern achieves the required throughput and uptime [source p.115].

questions.question: A team is evaluating a candidate design of nightly batch ingestion (one full load every 24 hours) against their written requirements. Which of the following requirements, considered on its own, eliminate the nightly batch candidate? Select all that apply.

options.label: New events must be visible to the fraud-scoring service within 2 minutes of arrival
The source produces roughly 9 TB per day at about 40,000 events per second
Critical sensor alerts must be raised within 45 seconds of the reading being emitted
The ingestion job must be exactly-once so that no duplicate rows appear in the target table

questions.analysis: The requirement axis that eliminates a nightly batch candidate is freshness: any stated SLA shorter than one full batch interval makes the pattern infeasible. Requirement A (2 minutes = 120 seconds) fails against a 24-hour interval by a factor of 720, and requirement C (45 seconds) fails by a factor of 1,920, so both eliminate the candidate on the latency axis alone. Requirement B is a volume statement, and volume alone does not force or eliminate a pattern: distributed architectures 'utilize a distributed system to realize higher overall scaling capacity' by adding worker nodes so that a batch job can absorb tens of thousands of events per second [source p.115]. Treating terabyte-scale daily volume as automatic proof that streaming is mandatory is a common misconception, because the same throughput can be delivered by a horizontally scaled batch or incremental job. Requirement D is a reliability requirement, not a latency requirement, and it is satisfiable in a batch design: idempotent partition overwrites, or the upsert/merge pattern that matches source records against a target table on a primary key and inserts or updates accordingly, can deliver exactly-once semantics at the table level [source p.343]. Reliability therefore constrains how you implement the chosen pattern, not which pattern the freshness SLA permits. A correct answer must therefore treat A and C as eliminative (latency axis) and B and D as non-eliminative (throughput and correctness axes) [source p.266].

questions.question: A team ingests about 15 TB per day at roughly 60,000 events per second. Their only consumers are a nightly finance report (refreshed at 06:00) and a weekly model retraining job. A senior engineer argues: 'At 15 TB per day we have no choice, we must build a continuously running streaming ingestion architecture.' Which evaluation of that argument is most defensible?

options.label: Correct: any pipeline above roughly 1 TB per day must use a continuously running streaming architecture
Correct: because the event source never ends, the data is unbounded, and unbounded data can only be processed by a continuous stream

Incorrect: high volume alone does not justify streaming; the freshness requirement drives the choice, and 15 TB per day can be ingested with a horizontally scaled batch or incremental job that meets the 06:00 deadline
Incorrect, but only because a continuously running streaming job is always the most expensive option, so cost alone forbids it

questions.analysis: Volume is a throughput requirement, and throughput is addressable by scaling out, not by changing processing model. Do the arithmetic: 15 TB per day is 15,000 GB spread over 86,400 seconds, i.e. roughly 0.174 GB/s (about 174 MB/s) sustained average. A horizontally scaled batch job with, say, 16 workers each reading at 150 MB/s aggregates to about 2.4 GB/s, so the entire day's 15 TB is read in roughly 15,000 / 2,400 = 6.25 seconds of theoretical peak, and comfortably inside a nightly window even with heavy write amplification and shuffle overhead. The reason is exactly the one stated in the source: horizontal scaling 'allows you to add more machines to satisfy load and resource requirements', with a leader node distributing tasks and returning results [source p.115]. Option B is the bounded-versus-unbounded misconception: an unbounded source can still be read in bounded windows (batch reads a slice of the stream between two offsets), so 'unbounded' does not by itself force a continuous pattern. The source material describes gateways that 'may accumulate data and upload it in batches for later analytics processing' in exactly this situation, and warns only that such designs must handle late-arriving data, schema disparities, corruption, and connection disruption [source p.134]. Option D is also wrong: cost is a real consideration but it is not an absolute law, and the claim that a continuous stream is always the most expensive option is not supported as a general rule. Option A invents a threshold that does not exist in the material. The defensible position is C: match the pattern to the stated freshness and reliability requirements, and use the domain's consumption cadence -- a 06:00 report and a weekly retrain -- to decide, which is what good architecture does at every step of the lifecycle [source p.97].

actions.text: Time to put that requirements mapping to the test. Three questions here, and each one asks you to reason from the stated requirements to a conclusion — take them one at a time and commit to your answer on your own.
Try each question independently before you submit; I'll join you right after to walk through the reasoning and clear up anything that felt shaky.

scenes.title: Choosing an Ingestion Approach Under Constraints

elements.content: Decision — A four-person data platform team must land roughly 2 TB of files that a partner pushes over SFTP every night, and the downstream reporting layer must be no more than 6 hours stale by the time analysts log in the next morning. The partner's export is a push-based pattern: the source team runs the export job itself and controls exactly what data is serialized and delivered, which means the receiving team cannot simply attach a client to the upstream system and pull whatever it wants [source p.272]. The monthly compute budget is a hard cap, not a target, and the partner adds new columns to its exports without warning, so the ingestion path must absorb schema changes rather than break the nightly load — the standard source-system question of how schema changes are dealt with and communicated to downstream stakeholders is exactly the risk here [source p.63]. The decision is genuinely hard because the three obvious answers pull in opposite directions: the payload is large, the arrival pattern is bounded and predictable, yet the stakeholders' loosely worded request for 'fresh data' tempts the team toward a permanently running stream. The correct framing is the one the source material gives for streaming-first thinking: ask whether downstream storage can handle the rate, whether millisecond ingestion is actually needed or whether a micro-batch approach accumulating and ingesting every minute would work, and whether the streaming-first approach will cost more in time, money, maintenance, downtime, and opportunity cost than simply doing batch [source p.67]. Worked example with concrete numbers: 2,048 GB per night ÷ 6 h = ~341 GB/h, i.e. ~95 MB/s sustained if the whole load had to fit inside the freshness window; a nightly triggered job that completes in 90 minutes consumes about 45 cluster-hours per month (1.5 h × 30 nights), while an always-on stream consumes ~730 cluster-hours (24 × 30.4). At an identical 8 DBU/hour cluster, the always-on design burns roughly 5,840 DBU/month versus ~360 DBU/month for the triggered job — an order-of-magnitude gap that a capped budget cannot absorb. A second consideration is that true streaming frameworks process one event at a time and carry significant overhead, whereas micro-batch designs deliberately trade a small latency increment for much better resource efficiency [source p.354]; since the SLA here is measured in hours, not seconds, that trade is unambiguously favorable.

Constraints — ~2 TB of files arrive nightly over SFTP and must be landed and queryable within a 6-hour freshness tolerance — the SLA is measured in hours, not seconds.  •  The monthly compute budget is a hard cap; any option requiring a permanently running cluster must fit inside it without starving other workloads.  •  The upstream schema evolves without notice (new columns appear in exports), so the pipeline must ingest unknown columns without failing the load or silently dropping data [source p.63].  •  The source is push-based SFTP with no guaranteed direct database access; export preparation happens on the source system side, so any option requiring read access to upstream logs or tables is contingent on partner approval [source p.272].  •  Reliability must be at-least-once with idempotent writes, since a nightly job will be retried after transient SFTP or network failures.

Scheduled batch load (Auto Loader in triggered batch mode)
+ Cheapest option by an order of magnitude: ~45 cluster-hours/month against ~730 for an always-on stream, which fits the compute cap with room to spare.; + Auto Loader with schema evolution enabled absorbs new columns automatically into Delta Lake and routes unparseable records to a rescued-data column, satisfying the schema-evolution constraint without human intervention.; + Operationally simple: one triggered job, idempotent file-level tracking, natural retry semantics after a failed night, and no checkpoint or state-management machinery to keep alive.; + Decouples ingestion from the source system entirely — the partner keeps full control of what is exported, which matches the push-based SFTP pattern [source p.272].
− Freshness lag is the highest of the three: data is at best one trigger interval old, and a 6-hour window leaves little headroom if the job slips.; − Does not reuse upstream change semantics, so it reprocesses whole files and cannot express row-level deletions or updates that happen upstream between exports.; − A late-arriving or oversized night (say 3 TB) can push the run past the freshness window unless concurrency is tuned.
Best for: Bounded, predictable, high-volume file arrivals where the SLA is measured in hours and the compute budget is the binding constraint.

Continuous Auto Loader stream with file notification
+ Lowest latency of the three: files are detected and processed within seconds to minutes of landing, which comfortably beats any hour-scale SLA.; + Handles unbounded, unpredictable arrival patterns — if the partner shifts from nightly drops to all-day dribbles, the pipeline needs no redesign.; + Shares Auto Loader's schema inference, schema evolution, and rescued-data handling with the batch option, so the schema-evolution constraint is met equally well.
− Highest standing cost: an always-on cluster consumes ~730 cluster-hours/month, roughly 5,840 DBU versus ~360 DBU for the triggered job, and this is the option most likely to breach the hard budget cap.; − Adds operational surface — checkpoints, state management, streaming monitors, and cluster availability — for a benefit (seconds-level latency) that the 6-hour SLA cannot consume.; − True continuous processing carries per-event overhead; the source material notes that true streaming systems trade that overhead for event-at-a-time semantics [source p.354], which is a poor exchange when micro-batch latency would already satisfy the requirement [source p.67].; − Paying continuously for a workload whose input arrives in one nightly burst is capacity that sits idle most of the day.
Best for: Genuinely unbounded, continuous sources with a sub-minute SLA where the extra compute and operational cost is justified by an action taken on real-time data.

Incremental CDC from the upstream database
+ Minimal reprocessing: only changed rows move, so the 2 TB per night collapses to the delta volume, which is typically a small fraction of a full export.; + Deletes and updates are represented natively, enabling correct slowly changing dimension (SCD) handling — a record of how a dimension value changed over time — rather than inferring change from successive snapshots.; + Binary-log-based CDC reads the database's own commit logs and adds little to no additional load on the source system [source p.68].
− Depends on access the team may not have: the current channel is push-based SFTP with source-side export control, and opening log or table access requires partner approval and a security review [source p.272].; − Brittle to log retention — if the upstream binary log is truncated or the CDC position expires during an outage, changes are lost irrecoverably and a full resync is required.; − Per-table schema evolution is far more invasive than adding a column to a file: capture agents, replication slots, and downstream merge logic must all be updated when the upstream schema changes [source p.63].; − Introduces a second ingestion technology and its own failure modes, which a four-person team must operate and monitor.
Best for: High-frequency change sources on databases the team already has sanctioned access to, with reliable long log retention and strict correctness requirements on updates and deletes.

Recommendation: Scheduled batch load (Auto Loader in triggered batch mode) — The 6-hour freshness tolerance is the constraint that decides this, because every option that could meet it more aggressively is paying for latency nobody consumes: 2 TB/night ÷ 6 h = ~341 GB/h is achievable in a single ~90-minute triggered run, so the SLA is satisfied with roughly four hours of margin. Against the hard monthly compute budget, the triggered job costs ~45 cluster-hours (~360 DBU) versus ~730 cluster-hours (~5,840 DBU) for an always-on stream — the budget cap eliminates opt-2 before any qualitative argument is needed, and this is exactly the check the source material prescribes when it asks whether a streaming-first approach costs more in time, money, maintenance, and opportunity cost than batch [source p.67]. The strict schema-evolution requirement is satisfied without new infrastructure because Auto Loader's schema evolution and rescued-data handling are shared with the streaming variant, whereas opt-3 would force per-table capture changes whenever the upstream schema moves [source p.63]. The push-based SFTP channel also favors opt-1: export preparation stays on the source side, so no new upstream access or security review is required [source p.272]. Finally, the bounded arrival pattern makes the small latency increment of micro-batch the right trade rather than true event-at-a-time processing with its significant overhead [source p.354]. The condition that would change this answer: if the effective freshness SLA tightened to below roughly 15–30 minutes, or the partner replaced nightly file drops with a continuous all-day stream, the bounded-arrival premise collapses and the answer flips to opt-2; if the partner instead granted sanctioned, long-retention binary-log access, opt-3 would become the strongest choice on correctness grounds, since it is the only option that represents upstream updates and deletes natively.

actions.text: Now that we've mapped latency, volume, and reliability to ingestion patterns, let's put that framework to work on a realistic constrained design decision. This is exactly the kind of scenario the exam likes: several defensible options, one set of hard constraints, and a single recommendation you must justify.
