actions.text: We just saw that COPY INTO reports a no-op when you re-run it over files it has already processed, because a delta table metadata store keeps track of which source files have been ingested. Now let's make that behavior tangible over several simulated overnight runs. This widget puts a landing folder on one side and the COPY INTO tracker on the other.

actions.content: This button runs COPY INTO against whatever files are currently in the landing path.

actions.text: Keep an eye on three live counters as we go: files loaded, files skipped, and cumulative rows inserted. Those are the exact numbers you'll be asked to read on the exam.

actions.content: Start with a fresh landing path of three files, modified one hour ago, on a single run.

actions.text: Go ahead and hit Run. First load should ingest all three files — watch the loaded counter jump while skipped stays at zero, and note that each file contributes its configured rows to the running total.

actions.content: Advance the clock: two new files land just now, then run COPY INTO two more times.

actions.text: Here's the incrementality test. On these subsequent runs you should see the two new files loaded, and the original three skipped — not re-ingested. The counters aren't guessing which is which; the tracker is comparing file metadata like modification time against what's already committed, which is the mechanism that makes COPY INTO idempotent.

actions.content: Classic gotcha: existing files are overwritten, and the simulated clock moves more than seven days past their original load.

actions.text: Look closely at what the overwrite triggers. When a file is overwritten with a new modification timestamp, COPY INTO treats it as a brand-new file and re-ingests it — so your counters climb again. But once the clock pushes beyond the seven-day retention window, the tracker's remembered metadata for the older runs expires, and you lose the ability to skip those stale files entirely. That's the trap: your retention window defines how far back idempotency is guaranteed. Try sliding the file count and timestamp yourself and predict whether each run loads or skips before running it.

scenes.title: Choosing the Statement: COPY INTO vs INSERT INTO vs MERGE

elements.content: Dimension  |  COPY INTO  |  INSERT INTO  |  MERGE

Input shape accepted
COPY INTO: Reads file-based batches from cloud object storage or Unity Catalog volumes — CSV, JSON, PARQUET, AVRO, ORC, TEXT, and BINARYFILE — via a directory path, an explicit FILES list, or a glob PATTERN, and lands those files as new rows in an existing Delta table.
INSERT INTO: Reads rows supplied literally by VALUES or produced by a SELECT over tables, views, or a DataFrame write, so the input is a relation rather than a set of files and there is no file-level state to track.
MERGE: Reads a source relation (staging table, view, or subquery) and joins it to the target Delta table on a business key or another logical condition, so the input is always a pair: matched rows to update and unmatched rows to insert.

Target table precondition
COPY INTO: The target Delta table must already exist, because COPY INTO loads into a table but does not create it; the statement fails if the table or its parent schema is missing.
INSERT INTO: The target must already exist as well, since INSERT INTO appends to an object that exists and creation is a separate step such as CREATE TABLE or CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE.
MERGE: The target must exist and must be a Delta table that supports transactional merges, because the update/insert/delete decisions are committed atomically against the current snapshot.

Idempotent on re-run?
COPY INTO: Yes, at file granularity: Databricks records each processed file's path, size, and last-modified timestamp and skips a file only when all three match, so a second identical run inserts 0 rows.
INSERT INTO: No: the statement keeps no record of previous runs, so retrying an INSERT INTO that already committed appends the same rows again — a retry after a timeout is a duplicate-producing retry.
MERGE: Conditionally: MERGE reproduces the same final state on a re-run only if the ON clause keys on the true business key, because each source row is then matched and updated in place instead of being inserted again.

Row-level deduplication
COPY INTO: None — COPY INTO deduplicates files, not rows, so two differently named files that both contain order_id = 1001 both load and the table ends up with two rows for that key.
INSERT INTO: None — INSERT INTO performs no key lookup of any kind, and the engine does not enforce uniqueness, so deduplication must be engineered downstream.
MERGE: This is the row-level tool: the ON clause matches source records to target records by a primary key or another logical condition, updates matched target records, and inserts the ones with no match [source p.343].

Update and delete semantics
COPY INTO: Append-only: COPY INTO can only add rows, so rewriting existing data requires a separate pattern such as truncate and reload, which wipes the table and regenerates a new table version [source p.342].
INSERT INTO: Insert-only: new records accumulate without changing or deleting old ones, so current state must be reconstructed by finding the newest record per primary key, which can be extremely computationally expensive at query time [source p.342].
MERGE: Upsert plus delete: the merge pattern adds to upserting the ability to delete records, expressed as WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE, so one statement can insert, update, and remove in a single commit [source p.343].

Schema evolution behavior
COPY INTO: New columns discovered in the files can be absorbed by enabling schema-evolution COPY_OPTIONS, so the target gains the added columns while pre-existing columns keep their types and the file-tracking metadata is unaffected.
INSERT INTO: The INSERT column list must be compatible with the target, so adding a column first requires ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMNS, or the statement must supply only the subset of columns the target already has.
MERGE: MERGE can propagate new source columns to the target when schema evolution is enabled, but every column referenced in the ON condition must already exist in the target because the match key cannot be invented mid-merge.

Cost profile of a re-run (worked example)
COPY INTO: Take a daily drop of 24 files x 250,000 rows = 6,000,000 rows: the first run inserts all 6,000,000, and an identical re-run inserts 0 because 24 of 24 files match on path, size, and timestamp, so the retry cost collapses to 24 metadata comparisons.
INSERT INTO: Re-inserting that same 6,000,000-row batch yields 12,000,000 rows, a 100% duplicate rate; the check SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM orders returns 6,000,000, and every downstream consumer must now pay to deduplicate.
MERGE: Merging the same batch on order_id yields, say, 5,800,000 matched rows updated in place and 200,000 unmatched rows inserted, a net growth of 200,000 rows; running it twice produces the identical final state of 6,000,000 distinct source keys with 0 duplicates.

State the mechanism keeps
COPY INTO: A per-file ledger of path, size, and last-modified timestamp held in the Delta table's transaction log — this ledger is the entire reason its idempotency works and it requires no primary key on the data.
INSERT INTO: No state about prior writes at all; the writer is stateless with respect to duplicates, so idempotency has to be engineered elsewhere, for example with a streaming checkpoint.
MERGE: No run ledger either, but the deduplication rule is encoded declaratively in the ON clause and evaluated against the latest committed snapshot, consistent with the point-in-time full table commit model in which a query reads one committed version no matter how long it runs [source p.305].

Uniqueness enforcement and its failure mode
COPY INTO: No key enforcement: the failure mode is silently duplicated business keys when the same logical record arrives inside two differently named files.
INSERT INTO: No key enforcement either; columnar systems generally do not enforce primary keys, so the primary key is an engineering construct and an insert-only feed drifts into duplicates without an explicit dedup step [source p.343].
MERGE: No enforced uniqueness, but because MERGE joins source to target, a source holding two rows for the same business key triggers a nondeterministic multi-match inside one statement, so the source must be deduplicated by key before merging [source p.343].

Fit with derived-table pipelines
COPY INTO: Poor fit for computed results, since COPY INTO is defined over landing files; a Spark job that ingests three JSON API sources into a dataframe, combines them, and writes the result out does that as a table write, not as a file ingest [source p.346].
INSERT INTO: Natural fit for computed results: once the Spark job has ingested, joined, and filtered the three sources, INSERT INTO (or an equivalent write) lands the derived rows into the Parquet-formatted Delta Lake table [source p.346].
MERGE: Fit when the computed result must be reconciled against existing rows rather than merely appended: the same transformed dataframe becomes the merge source and the business key drives the update-versus-insert decision [source p.346].

Typical exam scenario that makes it correct
COPY INTO: "Files land in a storage path on a schedule and the orchestrated job may be retried, but duplicate rows are unacceptable" maps to COPY INTO, because retrying is safe by design.
INSERT INTO: "Populate an existing Delta table from a query or a fixed set of values in a one-shot step that will not be retried" maps to INSERT INTO, accepting that any retry duplicates data.
MERGE: "Apply a daily change feed that must upsert on a business key, and a re-run must not duplicate rows" maps to MERGE, the row-level deduplication tool.

Boundary: continuous, ever-arriving files
COPY INTO: Not the right mechanism here: COPY INTO is built for discrete, bounded drops, so continuous, high-volume, ever-arriving ingestion is handled by a different mechanism covered in the next lesson (Auto Loader / Lakeflow).
INSERT INTO: Also not the mechanism here: repeated INSERT INTO against an ever-arriving feed either duplicates rows or needs external state to decide what is new.
MERGE: Not the mechanism either: MERGE can be driven inside a streaming microbatch, but the guarantee then comes from the streaming checkpoint rather than from the SQL statement itself.

Takeaway — Choose COPY INTO when the input is files in cloud storage or a volume, the target Delta table already exists, and the pipeline must be safely retried — file-level tracking of path, size, and timestamp turns a re-run into a no-op instead of a duplicate load.

Takeaway — Choose INSERT INTO when you are appending a relation (VALUES or a SELECT result) in a step that will not be retried, or when duplicates are acceptable or removed downstream; never treat it as idempotent, because a retry after partial failure appends the same rows again.

Takeaway — Choose MERGE when a re-run must not duplicate rows and the decision must be made per business key: MERGE is the only one of the three that performs row-level upsert and delete, making it the tool for change-data-capture feeds, slowly changing dimensions (SCD — a table that retains historical versions of each record keyed by business key), and idempotent incremental loads [source p.343].

Takeaway — Exam traps to reject: "COPY INTO deduplicates rows sharing a primary key" and "INSERT INTO is retriable like COPY INTO" — file-level idempotency is not row-level idempotency, and only MERGE reads existing target rows to decide an outcome.

Takeaway — Sequencing tip: land raw files with COPY INTO, transform in Spark, then reconcile the derived result with MERGE — in a medallion architecture (bronze/silver/gold layering of progressively refined tables) the three commands are complements rather than competitors [source p.346].

actions.text: Now that you've had a crack at the knowledge check, let's pull it all together. This page is the decision table you'll want burned into memory: three ways to put data into a Delta table — COPY INTO, INSERT INTO, and MERGE — laid out side by side against the same set of dimensions. Read it top to bottom and the pattern jumps out.

Start with the input shape, because that's what quietly decides everything else. COPY INTO reads file-based batches — you point it at a path and it consumes files. INSERT INTO takes rows or the result of a query — you're already holding the data. MERGE takes a source relation and applies it against a business key. Input shape is the first filter.

The second filter is idempotency — what happens when you re-run. COPY INTO is idempotent at file granularity: it remembers which files it has already loaded, so re-running does not duplicate them. INSERT INTO has no such tracking, so a retry duplicates rows. MERGE is idempotent at the row level, because it matches on a key rather than blindly inserting.

So the takeaways crystallize. Choose COPY INTO when the input is a file drop and file-level, re-run-safe loading is exactly what you need — this is the landing pattern, the classic daily CSV or Parquet drop into a bronze table.

Choose INSERT INTO when you are appending rows you already trust, and a duplicate on retry is either acceptable or impossible. It's the simplest hammer — but remember, it has no memory, so any scheduled retry is a duplication risk.

Choose MERGE when a re-run must not duplicate rows and you have a business key to match on. MERGE gives you row-level deduplication and full upsert semantics — insert the new, update the changed — all in one atomic statement.

One boundary note before we close. This table is about landing and upserting discrete data. Continuous, high-volume, ever-arriving file ingestion — the case where files keep showing up and you need incremental discovery at scale — is a different mechanism entirely, and that's Auto Loader, which we'll cover next lesson.

And here's your exam trap list. Reject any option that says COPY INTO deduplicates rows — it deduplicates files, not rows. Reject any option that claims INSERT INTO is safe to retry. And reject any option that uses MERGE purely for a bulk file load with no key. Situation drives choice: file drop, append, or keyed upsert. If you can name the situation, you can name the statement.

scenes.title: Exam Trap Drill: COPY INTO

questions.question: A nightly batch job drops files named part-0001.csv, part-0002.csv, and so on into the Unity Catalog volume path /Volumes/landing/sales/. The Delta table dwh.sales already exists and already holds yesterday's rows. The upstream team never deletes and never rewrites files; they only add new ones. The pipeline must be safe to re-run against the same directory without adding a second copy of rows that were already ingested. Which single statement meets this requirement?

options.label: COPY INTO dwh.sales FROM '/Volumes/landing/sales/' FILEFORMAT = CSV PATTERN = 'part-*.csv'
INSERT INTO dwh.sales SELECT * FROM read_files('/Volumes/landing/sales/', format => 'csv')
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dwh.sales AS SELECT * FROM read_files('/Volumes/landing/sales/', format => 'csv')
COPY INTO dwh.sales FROM '/Volumes/landing/sales/' PATTERN = 'part-.*\.csv'

questions.analysis: Option A is the correct ingestion command for this scenario. It targets the existing table dwh.sales, supplies the required FILEFORMAT = CSV, and narrows the input with a glob PATTERN. Re-running it is safe because COPY INTO keeps a ledger of every file it has loaded, keyed on file path, file size, and last-modified timestamp; a re-run therefore processes only files that are new or changed, which is exactly the 'must be re-runnable' requirement in the stem. Put concrete numbers on it: if day 1 lands 40 files holding 1,000,000 rows, and day 2 adds 6 files holding about 150,000 rows, the re-run reports 6 files loaded and the table grows from 1,000,000 to 1,150,000 rows. Option B is the plain insert trap: INSERT INTO re-reads the whole directory on every execution, so the same 46 files are appended again and the table reaches 2,150,000 rows with a full duplicate of the earlier data. That is precisely the insert-only update pattern, whose downside is that any notion of current state has to be reconstructed at query time by finding the newest record per key, a step that gets expensive on a columnar store [source p.342]. Option C is the truncate-and-reload trap: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE clears the table and rebuilds it from everything in the landing path, so it produces the right row count but destroys table history, breaks concurrent readers, and pays the full cost of reprocessing the entire directory every night rather than only new files [source p.342]. Option D is the syntax trap in disguise: it omits FILEFORMAT, which is mandatory, and it writes a regular-expression-style pattern where PATTERN expects glob syntax, so the backslash is treated as a literal character and the pattern will not match part-0001.csv. One further design note: the correct statement loads the directory as a single set-based operation rather than issuing one statement per file, because batch-oriented systems degrade when they are driven by many tiny operations that create many small, suboptimal files and force a high number of object-creation calls [source p.273].

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the COPY INTO contract are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The target must already exist: COPY INTO loads into an existing Delta table and errors out instead of creating the table for you.
FILEFORMAT is mandatory, even when the file extension already makes the format unambiguous.
PATTERN applies glob wildcards (*, ?, [abc]) to file names, while the FILES clause names exact files instead.
PATTERN is a regular expression, so PATTERN = '.*\.csv$' is the idiomatic way to select every CSV file.
COPY INTO refuses to load a file whose rows would duplicate a primary key that the target table already contains.

questions.analysis: A is correct and is the single most common exam trap: COPY INTO is a loader, not a DDL statement, so the target Delta table must pre-exist; if it is missing you get an error, not an auto-created table. B is correct: the three required pieces are the target table, the FROM source path or external location, and FILEFORMAT. Omitting FILEFORMAT is a parse error even when the CSV extension seems self-evident, and the same is true if you forget to quote the path as a string. C is correct: PATTERN performs glob matching against file names, where '*' matches any run of characters, '?' matches a single character, and '[abc]' matches a character class; FILES is the alternative clause that lists exact file names when the selection cannot be expressed as a glob, and VALIDATE reports on the files a run would process without inserting anything. D is the regex trap and is false: '$', '.*', and backslash escaping are regular-expression ideas that glob does not implement, so a pattern written that way silently fails to match the files the engineer expected. E is false for two reasons. First, COPY INTO is a file-level loader: its only uniqueness notion concerns files, not rows. Second, uniqueness is generally not enforced by columnar systems at all; a primary key is a construct the data engineering team maintains through its own queries, and the upsert/merge pattern is the tool that uses a key or another logical condition to match source records against the target table and update matches while inserting non-matches [source p.343]. Remember also that successful ingestion still depends on the right credentials and privileges for the source file path and the target table, so a permissions problem produces a failure rather than a duplicate or a silent skip [source p.383].

questions.question: An engineer claims: 'Because we run COPY INTO every night into dwh.orders, that table can never contain two rows with the same order_id.' Which statement best explains why this claim is wrong?

options.label: COPY INTO skips a file only while its path, size, and last-modified timestamp still match the recorded values; if the upstream job re-exports a file so that its size or timestamp changes, those rows load a second time, and COPY INTO has no concept of order_id uniqueness at all.
COPY INTO skips nothing, so every nightly run reloads the entire directory and appends a full extra copy of the data.
COPY INTO does deduplicate on a primary key, but only when the target table is registered in Unity Catalog with a declared primary key.
COPY INTO becomes idempotent only after a MERGE statement has been run against the target table at least once.

questions.analysis: A is the correct explanation. The idempotency of COPY INTO is a file-level property, not a row-level one: Databricks records the file path, its size, and its last-modified timestamp for every file it loads, and a file is skipped only when all three values still match. Two escape hatches therefore remain open. First, a file rewritten in place defeats the ledger. Suppose an upstream export writes orders_2024_06_01.csv at 10 MB, COPY INTO loads its 80,000 rows, and the vendor then re-exports the same day with a corrected total so the file becomes 12 MB at a later timestamp; the re-run sees a different size and timestamp, treats the file as new, and inserts the same 80,000 orders a second time. Second, there is no key logic anywhere in the statement: COPY INTO does not look at order_id, does not enforce uniqueness, and does not know which rows a previous run inserted. The durable remediation is a row-level one, either an upsert/merge that matches staged rows against the target on the natural key [source p.343] or a deduplicating read that collapses to the newest row per key [source p.342]. Option B states the reverse trap: it denies the very guarantee that makes COPY INTO retriable, because unchanged files are in fact skipped and a second identical run over an unchanged directory is a no-op. Option C invents primary-key enforcement in the catalog; key declaration is not what protects this table, and matching records by key is the job of the merge pattern rather than of the loader [source p.343]. Option D inverts the tooling relationship: MERGE is the row-level upsert/merge pattern that may be used downstream, and running it is never a prerequisite for COPY INTO to skip already-processed files.

questions.question: A pipeline loads device telemetry with COPY INTO from /Volumes/landing/telemetry/ into the Delta table dwh.telemetry. Gateways buffer events while they are offline and upload whole files in batches once connectivity returns, and the job was paused for 10 days before being re-run. Which statements about that re-run are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Retained file metadata expires after roughly seven days, so files loaded before the pause may no longer be recognised as already processed and can be ingested again.
Any batch file that was overwritten in place during the pause (same name, new content) is treated as a new file because its size or last-modified timestamp changed.
Because COPY INTO is not a row-level deduplication tool, the durable fix is to MERGE the loaded rows on the natural key, or otherwise deduplicate at read time.
The re-run is guaranteed to be a no-op simply because the statement text is identical to the earlier run.
If the job fails halfway through because a storage credential or path permission was revoked, the safest recovery is to delete the target table and reload everything from scratch.

questions.analysis: A is correct: the processed-file ledger is retained for a limited window, on the order of seven days, after which the recorded path, size, and timestamp entries expire. A ten-day pause therefore sits outside the retention window, so files that a short re-run would have skipped can be treated as unprocessed and ingested again. The exam-ready formulation is that 're-running loads only new or changed files' is a statement about a re-run inside the retention window, not an unconditional promise. B is correct: the skip test compares path, size, and last-modified timestamp, so a file that was overwritten in place during the pause has at least one differing value and is re-ingested, duplicating the rows it contributed earlier. C is correct and is the defensive design conclusion: because COPY INTO operates at file granularity, the guarantee against duplicate business keys must be enforced downstream by an upsert/merge that matches on a key or logical condition and updates matches while inserting non-matches [source p.343], or by deduplicating at query time, which is the trade-off the insert-only pattern accepts [source p.342]. D is false: the no-op behaviour comes from the file-metadata ledger, not from the statement text being character-for-character identical, which is why a 10-day pause and an in-place overwrite both change the outcome. E is false and actively harmful: a credentials or permissions failure is fixed by repairing the access and re-running, because COPY INTO is retriable by design and only counts files it actually committed, whereas deleting and reloading is the truncate-and-reload pattern that wipes data and regenerates the table version [source p.342]. The scenario itself is realistic rather than contrived: gateway-based ingestion commonly accumulates measurements and uploads them in batches only when a cellular or WiFi network is reachable, and the resulting late-arriving data, schema disparities, corruption, and connection disruption are exactly the conditions engineers must design for [source p.134].

actions.text: Time to put that decision-making under pressure. This next set is scenario-shaped — the kind of wording the real exam leans on — so read each one carefully before you commit. Attempt every question on your own and don't second-guess yourself into changing a well-reasoned answer.
Work through it solo for now; once you submit, I'll come back and we'll go through each one together, including the ones that felt easy.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Tripled Row Counts After a Re-Run

elements.content: Problem 1

An orchestrated job runs a single `COPY INTO` statement against the Delta table `dwh.orders` (target table already exists), ingesting the daily CSV drop at `/Volumes/landing/orders/`. On day 1 at 00:00 UTC the job loaded one file, `part-00000.csv`, and reported `120000 rows loaded`. The job was then paused. It was resumed on day 9 at 02:00 UTC and again on day 10 at 02:00 UTC, and BOTH resumed runs also reported `120000 rows loaded`, even though upstream wrote no new files and never rewrote `part-00000.csv` in place. Today `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dwh.orders` returns `360000`, and `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM dwh.orders` returns `120000`.

(a) Compute the duplication factor and the number of redundant rows, and compute how many rows each individual resumed run contributed.

(b) Databricks retains COPY INTO processed-file metadata for 7 days from the moment a file is processed. With $t_{\text{proc}} = $ day 1 00:00 UTC, compute the exact expiry moment and the elapsed time at the day-9 run. Decide whether the file was still tracked.

(c) State the exact condition under which COPY INTO skips a file, and say which of the three identity attributes changed in this incident.
Hint: The row-count arithmetic identifies the shape of the failure; the retention-window arithmetic identifies its cause.

Worked solution
**(a) Duplication arithmetic.**

Let $u = 120000$ be the number of distinct business keys and $T = 360000$ the current row count.

$$d = \frac{T}{u} = \frac{360000}{120000} = 3.000$$

$$E = T - u = 360000 - 120000 = 240000 \text{ redundant rows}$$

The two resumed runs each reported exactly $120000$ rows, and $120000 / 120000 = 1$ full copy per run, so the table received exactly three full copies of the same file: day 1, day 9, day 10. What matters is that the *load counter* was truthful: the file really was ingested again each time. COPY INTO did not silently mishandle the file; it decided the file was new.

**(b) Retention-window arithmetic.**

Retention $R_{\text{ret}} = 7$ days $= 7 \times 24 = 168$ h.

$$t_{\text{exp}} = t_{\text{proc}} + 168\ \text{h} = \text{day 8, 00:00 UTC}$$

Elapsed time at the day-9 run:

$$\Delta = (9-1)\ \text{days} + 2\ \text{h} = 8 \times 24 + 2 = 194\ \text{h}$$

Overshoot past expiry:

$$194 - 168 = 26\ \text{h}$$

Since $\Delta = 194\ \text{h} > R_{\text{ret}} = 168\ \text{h}$, the processed-file record for `part-00000.csv` had already been evicted when the day-9 run started. The lookup found no matching record, so the file was classified as brand new and ingested in full. The day-10 run was 218 h after day 1 and was equally out of window.

**(c) The skip predicate.**

COPY INTO skips candidate file $f$ if and only if a retained processed-file record matches on all three attributes simultaneously:

$$\exists\, p \in P_{<168\text{h}} : p.\text{path} = f.\text{path} \;\wedge\; p.\text{size} = f.\text{size} \;\wedge\; p.\text{mtime} = f.\text{mtime}$$

In this incident, path was unchanged and size was unchanged (upstream did not rewrite the file), and the timestamp was unchanged too. The predicate failed for a different reason: the set $P_{<168\text{h}}$ no longer contained the record at all. So the answer to 'which attribute changed?' is 'none of the three — the record expired.'

**Verification.** `DESCRIBE HISTORY dwh.orders` should show three write commits on the load days, each with `numOutputRows = 120000`. And `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)` stuck at $120000$ proves no new business keys arrived: the extra $240000$ rows are three copies of the same $120000$ keys, not new data.

Analysis — **Why this method works.** The row-count ratio is the fastest triage instrument available. If the table holds an integer multiple of the known unique-key count ($d = 3$ exactly), then each run appended a complete copy, which points at the *file-identity* decision rather than at a partial or overlapping load. If the ratio had been non-integral (say $d = 2.4$), you would instead suspect a PATTERN that matches only part of the directory, or files that changed mid-run.

**Where students go wrong.** (1) Assuming COPY INTO deduplicates on a primary key. It does not; it compares file identity, and columnar systems typically do not even enforce a primary key, so the notion of 'the current version of a record' is the engineering team's responsibility [source p.343]. (2) Measuring the pause from the last successful *job* rather than from the moment the *file* was processed — the retention clock starts at processing time, so a long backfill can expire metadata for the earliest files while the latest ones are still tracked. (3) Treating a truthful '120000 rows loaded' message as evidence of new upstream data instead of checking `COUNT(DISTINCT key)` first.

**Generalization.** Any ingestion mechanism whose idempotency record has a time-to-live imposes a maximum safe cadence on the pipeline. State that maximum explicitly as a pipeline SLA: here, any pause of 168 h or more guarantees full re-ingestion of every file. The safe operating rule is to keep the worst-case gap strictly below the retention constant with a margin, which is exactly the constraint derived in the prevention problem.
Problem 2

You have two candidate explanations for the 3× row count in `dwh.orders`:

- **H1 (eviction):** the processed-file metadata expired because the gap between successful runs was $194$ h, longer than the $168$ h retention window, so the already-ingested file looked new.

- **H2 (mutation):** upstream rewrote `part-00000.csv` in place, giving the same path a new last-modified timestamp (and possibly a new size), so the identity triple no longer matched even though the metadata record still existed.

Available evidence: (i) the table holds $360000$ rows; (ii) `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)` was $120000$ before and after the incident; (iii) each of the two resumed runs reported exactly $120000$ rows loaded; (iv) the run gap was $194$ h and the retention window is $168$ h.

Build the decision table, name the single decisive observation, explain how `DESCRIBE HISTORY dwh.orders` corroborates the diagnosis, and explain why the row-count evidence alone cannot rule out H2.
Hint: Eviction is about the absence of a record; mutation is about a change in the record's values. Only the source object's identity triple separates them.

Worked solution
**Decision table.**

| Observation | H1: retention expiry | H2: in-place rewrite |

|---|---|---|

| Source `path` vs day 1 | identical | identical (that is the point of H2) |

| Source `size` vs day 1 | identical | may differ |

| Source `mtime` vs day 1 | identical | different (newer) |

| Run gap $g > 168$ h required? | Yes — necessary for H1 | No — irrelevant to H2 |

| Rows appended per resumed run | full file ($120000$) | full file ($120000$), content may differ |

| `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)` | unchanged ($120000$) | unchanged if the rewrite is row-for-row; may change if upstream added/removed keys |

**The decisive observation.** The *current* `mtime` and `size` of `part-00000.csv` read from cloud storage (for example with `dbutils.fs.ls('/Volumes/landing/orders/')`), compared against the values recorded on day 1.

- If both are unchanged AND the gap is $194\ \text{h} > 168\ \text{h}$, H1 is confirmed and H2 is excluded: nothing about the file changed, so only eviction can explain the reload.

- If `mtime` differs, H2 is active. Note that H1 and H2 are **not mutually exclusive** — a file can be both rewritten and have had its metadata evicted, in which case you still reload it and you additionally cannot tell *which* copy of the rows you already hold.

**Why the counts cannot separate them.** If upstream re-emits a fixed-format partition with the same number of rows (a very common pattern: a corrected daily export that keeps its schema and grain), then H2 appends $120000$ rows per run exactly as H1 does. The signature '$d = 3$ with $u = 120000$' is identical under both hypotheses. The only discriminator is the file identity triple, which is precisely the quantity COPY INTO itself compares. This is the reason to record `path`, `size` and `mtime` in your own load ledger at ingest time: the platform's copy of those values is bounded by the retention window, yours need not be.

**Corroboration with commit history.**

```sql

DESCRIBE HISTORY dwh.orders;

```

Expect three write operations at versions 0, 1 and 2 on day 1, day 9 and day 10, each with `numOutputRows = 120000` in `operationMetrics`. This does two things: it confirms there were exactly three appends (no partial loads, no unseen compaction), and it localizes each bad append in time so that a targeted rollback such as

```sql

DELETE FROM dwh.orders WHERE _ingest_ts >= '2025-03-09T02:00:00Z';

```

is available as a coarse repair before doing key-level deduplication.

**Following up on H2 if it is active.** Hash the file bytes and compare with a recorded digest; if the file changed, decide which version is authoritative. A useful secondary test is whether the three copies of a given key are byte-identical in the payload columns: identical payloads point to eviction or a harmless re-emit, while differing payloads mean upstream republished corrected data and the newest copy is the one to keep.

Analysis — **Method choice.** This is a hypothesis-discrimination exercise, and the discipline it teaches is to identify the *one observation* whose values differ across hypotheses before running any repair. Eviction leaves the file untouched but the record absent; mutation leaves the record present but its values changed. Since COPY INTO's skip decision is a conjunction over `(path, size, mtime)`, the two failure modes must be probed with exactly those three quantities.

**Common student mistakes.** (1) Going straight to a deduplication script. A repair that deletes $240000$ rows while the root cause is still live will be followed by another $240000$ duplicates on the next run — you have fixed the symptom twice and the disease zero times. (2) Reading the file from a cached path listing rather than from the storage layer. (3) Forgetting that the retention clock is per-file and starts at processing time, not at job start; in a backfill that ingests a year of files in one run, the oldest records expire while the newest are fresh, which produces *partially* duplicated history and a non-integral duplication factor. (4) Assuming the two causes are mutually exclusive.

**Generalization.** The same discrimination pattern applies to every idempotency key you will ever build: an event ID, a message offset, a Kafka partition-offset pair. In each case ask 'what could make the key look new?' and enumerate (a) the key store losing the entry, (b) the key's components changing, (c) two producers emitting different keys for the same logical record. Case (a) is a retention/TTL problem, case (b) is a producer-contract problem, case (c) is a key-design problem — and each has a completely different fix.
Problem 3

The diagnosis is confirmed: `dwh.orders` holds $360000$ rows comprising three copies of each of $120000$ `order_id` values, with copies distinguishable by the load column `_ingest_ts` (and, if you added it, `_source_file`).

Write the repair: (a) the pre-flight query that quantifies the excess rows, (b) the backup step, (c) a `MERGE` statement that keeps the most recent copy per `order_id` and deletes the surplus, (d) a tie-breaking variant for the case where two copies of a key carry the identical `_ingest_ts`, and (e) the post-repair verification query. Compute the expected number of rows deleted. Finally, explain why `SELECT DISTINCT *` would NOT repair this table.
Hint: Think of the MERGE source as the survivor set, then delete every target row that has no partner in it.

Worked solution
**(a) Pre-flight quantification.**

```sql

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_total,

COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS keys_distinct

FROM dwh.orders;

-- 360000 | 120000

SELECT SUM(c - 1) AS excess_rows

FROM (SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS c

FROM dwh.orders

GROUP BY order_id);

-- 240000

```

Each of the $120000$ keys has $c = 3$ copies, so the excess is $\sum (c_i - 1) = 120000 \times (3 - 1) = 240000$ rows. That is the exact number the repair must remove; if your MERGE deletes a different number, stop and investigate before committing anything downstream.

**(b) Backup.**

```sql

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dwh.orders_bak DEEP CLONE dwh.orders;

```

`DEEP CLONE` physically copies the data. `SHALLOW CLONE` is far cheaper but produces a new table whose pointers reference the same underlying files, so the copies are not independent artifacts in the way students usually assume [source p.249]; for a destructive repair, prefer a deep clone or an explicit `SELECT ... AS` snapshot.

**(c) The repair MERGE (survivor-set pattern).**

```sql

MERGE INTO dwh.orders AS t

USING (

SELECT order_id, MAX(_ingest_ts) AS keep_ts

FROM dwh.orders

GROUP BY order_id

) AS k

ON t.order_id = k.order_id

AND t._ingest_ts = k.keep_ts

WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE;

```

Read it as: the source is the survivor set — exactly one row per key, the newest. Target rows that find a partner survive; the two older copies of each key find no partner and are deleted. Accounting: $360000 - 120000 = 240000$ deleted, $120000$ remain.

**(d) Tie-breaking variant.** If two copies of the same key share an identical `_ingest_ts` (for example, if the column is stamped at file-write time rather than load time, or two appends land in the same clock tick), the `MAX(_ingest_ts)` source yields two survivors and the duplicate persists. Make the survivor deterministic with a window function:

```sql

MERGE INTO dwh.orders AS t

USING (

SELECT order_id, _ingest_ts, _source_file

FROM (

SELECT order_id, _ingest_ts, _source_file,

ROW_NUMBER() OVER (

PARTITION BY order_id

ORDER BY _ingest_ts DESC, _source_file DESC

) AS rn

FROM dwh.orders

) WHERE rn = 1

) AS k

ON t.order_id = k.order_id

AND t._ingest_ts = k._ingest_ts

AND t._source_file = k._source_file

WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE;

```

`ROW_NUMBER()` returns exactly one row per partition, so the ON clause is guaranteed to match a single target row per key even under exact ties.

**(e) Verification.**

```sql

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_total,

COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS keys_distinct,

(SELECT SUM(c - 1) FROM (SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) c

FROM dwh.orders GROUP BY order_id)) AS excess

FROM dwh.orders;

-- 120000 | 120000 | 0

```

A post-check that returns $120000 / 120000 / 0$ proves both halves of the repair: no surplus rows, and no keys were lost. Never accept a deduplication that reduces the row count *below* the distinct-key count.

**Why `SELECT DISTINCT *` fails.** Take a single key with its three copies:

$$(1001,\ 250.00,\ 2025\text{-}03\text{-}01\text{T}00{:}05\text{Z})$$

$$(1001,\ 250.00,\ 2025\text{-}03\text{-}09\text{T}02{:}01\text{Z})$$

$$(1001,\ 250.00,\ 2025\text{-}03\text{-}10\text{T}02{:}01\text{Z})$$

`DISTINCT *` compares whole rows. The `_ingest_ts` values differ, so all three rows are distinct and the deduplicated result still has three rows for key 1001 — the table stays at $360000$ rows and the repair accomplishes nothing. Deduplication must be keyed on the *natural key* (`order_id`), not on row equality. This is also why a whole-row `DROP DUPLICATES`-style rewrite is sufficient only for the special case where the extra copies are exact duplicates of every column, which is not the case once a load-timestamp column is present.

**Cost consideration.** On object storage, an update or delete is implemented by rewriting whole files, not by editing rows in place — file-based systems use copy-on-write [source p.343]. A MERGE that touches every key in the table therefore rewrites the entire table. If only the day-9 and day-10 appends are suspect, restrict the survivor set to those partitions or filter by `_ingest_ts >= '2025-03-09'` so that older files are never rewritten.

**Downstream follow-through.** Any aggregate table, dashboard extract or materialized view computed on the $360000$-row version is now wrong by a factor of three and must be recomputed; a materialized view that derives the current state of each record by key has to be refreshed after the repair [source p.342].

Analysis — **Why this method works.** The survivor-set MERGE is the general-purpose row-level deduplication primitive for Delta tables: build the set of rows you want to keep, match the target against it, and delete everything that fails to match. It is idempotent by construction — running it a second time rebuilds the same survivor set, every target row matches, and nothing is deleted. That property matters because a repair script run twice during a long maintenance window must not over-delete.

**Choosing which copy to keep.** Here the copies are payload-identical, so keeping the newest is arbitrary but harmless. In the variant where upstream republished corrected data, keeping the newest is *substantively* correct — this is the merge/upsert semantics of

actions.text: Now let's put everything we just covered about COPY INTO idempotency to work. This is a three-part worked problem, and each part builds on the last, so follow along closely.

Part one sets up the evidence. An orchestrated job runs a single COPY INTO statement against a landing folder. On day one it loads 120,000 rows. Then on day nine and day ten, the same job runs again and loads the same 120,000 rows each time, so the table now holds 360,000 rows. Before we reach for any fix, we need to read the row-count arithmetic and figure out what shape of failure this is.

Here the workout shows the arithmetic directly. Multiply 120,000 by three and you land exactly on 360,000. That clean multiple tells us the duplication is whole-file, not partial. There is no key-level corruption and no column scrambling — entire files were ingested more than once.

And this is why the method works. Row-count arithmetic is a diagnostic tool. When the total is an exact multiple of a single run's load, you are looking at re-ingestion of file identity, which points straight at the COPY INTO metadata rather than at your data content.
Part two shifts to diagnosis. You have two candidate explanations for that three-times row count, and you need to decide which one is real. This is genuine hypothesis testing, not guessing.

The decision table lays the two explanations side by side. Explanation one: the job was paused longer than the seven-day metadata retention window, so every file looked new on re-run. Explanation two: upstream rewrote the files in place with fresh timestamps. Both would produce duplicates — but the way to tell them apart is by looking at whether the source records are actually new.

The hint sharpens the distinction. Eviction is about the absence of a record — the tracking metadata is gone. A rewrite is about the presence of the same record under a new identity. One is a gap, the other is a disguise.

Part three is where the diagnosis gets confirmed. The orders table holds 360,000 rows, and now we have to repair it. The fix is a deduplication pass — either a MERGE or DROP DUPLICATES against a natural key.

The pre-flight quantification shows the survivor set logic. In a MERGE-based cleanup you have to decide, before you touch a single row, which version of each duplicate survives — and you must express that decision as an explicit rule, typically the latest load timestamp or the highest version, so the same cleanup run is reproducible every time.

And here is the takeaway that carries into the exam. Idempotency is a property of file identity, not of table content. COPY INTO tracks files, not rows, so it must never be relied on for row-level deduplication. For prevention, schedule your loads inside the retention window, scope PATTERN to immutable partition prefixes, and land files in write-once folders such as landing/orders/ingest_date equals YYYY-MM-DD. Keep that principle in mind as we look next at a week of real COPY INTO runs.
