elements.content:
Nightly COPY INTO run log: files loaded vs. files skipped (Mon–Sun) (line)
Day of week (Mon = 1 … Sun = 7) → Files (count)
Synthetic seven-day run log from one nightly COPY INTO job against an existing Delta table. Landing-path contents per day: Mon 12, Tue 17, Wed 17, Thu 17, Fri 26, Sat 26, Sun 26 files. Monday is the first run ever against this path (it loads the 12 pre-existing files); new drops arrive on Tuesday and Friday only. Rows inserted: Mon 480,000; Tue 210,000; Wed 0; Thu 0; Fri 1,350,000; Sat 0; Sun 0. Elapsed seconds: Mon 96; Tue 41; Wed 9; Thu 8; Fri 305; Sat 9; Sun 8. landing = skipped + loaded on every day.
Files loaded: 1→12   2→5   3→0   4→0   5→9   6→0   7→0
Files skipped: 1→0   2→12   3→17   4→17   5→17   6→26   7→26

Claim 1 — Refuted
Re-running the nightly COPY INTO job reloads every file that is still present in the landing path, so Monday's 12 files should reappear in Tuesday's loaded count.
Why: The chart shows Tuesday with loaded = 5 and skipped = 12: exactly Monday's 12 files stayed unprocessed because each still matched a previously loaded path, size and last-modified timestamp. Wednesday repeats the pattern with loaded = 0 and skipped = 17 of 17 landing files, so the re-run is a no-op rather than a full reload — the property that makes an orchestrated nightly trigger safe to retry [source p.91].

Claim 2 — Supported
Loaded files track new arrivals: on each day a fresh drop landed the loaded count equals the number of newly arrived files, and on every day without a new drop the loaded count is zero.
Why: Tuesday lands 17 files with 12 skipped, so loaded = 17 − 12 = 5 new files; Friday lands 26 files with 17 skipped, so loaded = 26 − 17 = 9 new files; Monday's first-ever run loads all 12 pre-existing files (loaded = 12, skipped = 0). The four no-drop days — Wed, Thu, Sat, Sun — all plot loaded = 0 while skipped holds at 17, 17, 26 and 26.

Claim 3 — Supported
A no-op night is not free: Wednesday, Thursday, Saturday and Sunday each inserted 0 rows yet still consumed 8–9 seconds of elapsed job time, so an orchestrated nightly trigger keeps running even when there is nothing new to load.
Why: The chart gives loaded = 0 for all four of those nights, and the run log's elapsed column reads 9 s (Wed), 8 s (Thu), 9 s (Sat) and 8 s (Sun) against rows inserted = 0 on each. An orchestration system that stays online to sense and monitor continuously still fires the trigger and pays that overhead; setting an expected completion time such as 06:00 is what converts a silent stall into an alert [source p.91].

Claim 4 — Supported
On every day of the week the file-level identity loaded = landing − skipped holds, which is the arithmetic signature of a file-level idempotency check rather than row-level deduplication.
Why: Mon: 12 − 0 = 12 loaded; Tue: 17 − 12 = 5; Wed: 17 − 17 = 0; Thu: 17 − 17 = 0; Fri: 26 − 17 = 9; Sat: 26 − 26 = 0; Sun: 26 − 26 = 0. The account balances on all seven days, and it balances on files, not rows — COPY INTO never inspects a primary key, so rows re-arriving inside a rewritten file still land in the table.

Claim 5 — Refuted
Wednesday inserted a smaller but non-zero number of rows, which would indicate that one or two files partially overlapped the previous night's drop.
Why: Wednesday's plotted loaded count is 0 with 17 of 17 landing files skipped, and the run log records rows inserted = 0 for that day. A partial overlap would necessarily show loaded ≥ 1, so no file overlapped: the night was a complete no-op, not a partial re-ingest.

Claim 6 — Refuted
Elapsed job time scales with the number of files loaded, so Monday's 12-file run should be the slowest run of the week.
Why: Monday loaded 12 files in 96 s, but Friday loaded only 9 files and took 305 s — 3.2 times longer with 25% fewer files. File count alone cannot explain the runtime: batch systems behave badly when a run is forced into many small-batch operations and small objects, while a small number of very large files shifts the profile the other way [source p.273].

Claim 7 — Insufficient
Elapsed time is proportional to rows inserted, so seconds per 1,000 rows inserted should be roughly constant across the three productive runs.
Why: Worked ratios from the log: Mon 96 ÷ 480 = 0.200 s, Tue 41 ÷ 210 = 0.195 s and Fri 305 ÷ 1,350 = 0.226 s per 1,000 rows. They look close, but the three runs vary simultaneously in files loaded (12, 5, 9), rows inserted (480,000 / 210,000 / 1,350,000) and file-size distribution — the longest run processed the fewest files yet contained the largest single file. The log records no bytes read and no compute size, throughput scales with the number of nodes [source p.348], and each job may run on its own ephemeral cluster with its own dependency set [source p.168], so one week of data cannot separate row count from file size and cluster size. The claim is not decidable from this log.

Claim 8 — Insufficient
The four nights with 0 rows inserted prove that the landing files were byte-for-byte identical to the files loaded earlier in the week.
Why: The log reports only counts — skipped 17, 17, 26, 26 and loaded 0 on Wed/Thu/Sat/Sun — while a skip requires merely that path, size and last-modified timestamp all match a previously processed file. A file rewritten in place with different contents but an identical size and timestamp is skipped too, and the log carries neither checksums nor byte sizes, so the data is consistent with byte-identity but does not establish it.

Claim 9 — Supported
Week-level insertion volume is dominated by Friday's drop: the three productive runs total 2,040,000 rows, of which Friday contributes 1,350,000, about 66%.
Why: Worked example from the run log: 480,000 (Mon) + 210,000 (Tue) + 1,350,000 (Fri) = 2,040,000 rows inserted across the week, and 1,350,000 ÷ 2,040,000 = 0.662, i.e. 66.2%. Friday therefore carries roughly two thirds of the week's volume while contributing only 9 of the 26 files, and Wednesday, Thursday, Saturday and Sunday contribute 0 rows each.

Claim 10 — Insufficient
Sunday skipped all 26 landing files because COPY INTO's retained file metadata still covered every one of them, including Monday's 12 files.
Why: Sunday's plotted skipped = 26 and loaded = 0 show that nothing was re-ingested, but the chart has no path or timestamp column, so it cannot show which metadata rows were still retained or whether the seven-day history had begun to expire. The observation is consistent both with full coverage and with a partly expired history in which the remaining matches were kept alive by size and timestamp; the log as given cannot settle it.

actions.text: Building on the idempotency idea we just covered, here's what a real week of nightly COPY INTO runs actually looks like. This log records one row per day: how many files were sitting in the landing path, how many were skipped, how many were loaded, how many rows came in, and how long the job ran.

Start with the files-loaded column. Look at how spiky it is — some nights load twelve files, others load five, and several nights load exactly zero. That pattern is the fingerprint of COPY INTO tracking which files it has already processed.

Now pair it with the files-skipped column. On those same nights where loaded is zero, skipped jumps to twelve or more. The file counts add up: every file in the landing path is either new and loaded, or already seen and skipped. Nothing is silently reprocessed.

So let's judge the claims. Claim one says re-running the nightly job reloads everything. That's refuted — if it were true, skipped would always be zero and loaded would match the full landing path. The high skip counts on the unchanged days prove otherwise.

Claim two says loaded files track new arrivals. That one is supported — on each landing day, the loaded count equals exactly the number of new files that dropped, and it's zero on every day when nothing new arrived.

Claim three says elapsed time is proportional to rows inserted. This is the interesting trap — it's insufficient data to conclude. The longest run actually processed the fewest files but the largest single file. File size and row count don't move together here, so the log simply doesn't give you enough to decide. That distinction between refuted and insufficient is exactly what the exam rewards.

When you face a claim like this in the exam, ask two questions: what would the numbers look like if the claim were true, and does the data actually contain that signal? If the evidence contradicts the claim, it's refuted. If the evidence is simply absent, it's insufficient. Keep that test in mind as we look at exam trap drills next.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Ingestion Foundations

questions.question: A team receives a 40 GB CSV drop once per hour into a Unity Catalog volume and loads it into an existing Delta table. A teammate argues: 'Always go streaming-first — streaming ingestion always means lower latency and lower cost, so there is no reason to keep running a batch job.' Which response best reflects the ingestion trade-offs you should actually weigh before accepting that argument?

options.label: Accept it: streaming is strictly cheaper because true streaming frameworks process one event at a time and therefore pay none of the overhead that micro-batch frameworks pay.

Reject the blanket claim: you should ask whether downstream storage can absorb the real-time rate, whether a micro-batch that accumulates and loads, say, every minute already satisfies the business need, and whether streaming-first would cost more in time, money, maintenance, downtime, and opportunity cost than batch.
Reject it because streaming can never write into a Delta table, so COPY INTO is the only ingestion pattern Databricks supports for file drops.

Accept it partially: the only deciding question is whether millisecond latency is required, and whenever it is, streaming is guaranteed to be both lower latency and lower cost than any batch alternative.

questions.correctAnswer: B
questions.analysis: Option B is correct because the decision is a trade-off analysis, not a slogan. The source material lists the questions to ask before choosing a streaming-first design: whether downstream storage can handle the rate of data flow, whether millisecond real-time ingestion is genuinely required or whether a micro-batch approach that accumulates and ingests data (for example every minute) would work, what specific benefit streaming delivers that batch would not, and whether streaming-first costs more in time, money, maintenance, downtime, and opportunity cost than doing batch [source p.67]. Option A is wrong on a factual point: micro-batching is designed for this use case and performs well at high batch frequency, whereas true streaming systems process one event at a time and that 'comes with significant overhead', so streaming is not automatically cheaper [source p.354]. Option C is wrong because incremental file ingestion — including COPY INTO into an existing Delta table — is a supported pattern; nothing about Delta prevents streaming writes. Option D is wrong because latency need is only one of several questions; even when low latency is required, cost, maintenance, and downstream capacity must still be evaluated separately [source p.67]. Note the underlying vocabulary: micro-batch means processing accumulated data on a short interval (roughly every second to every couple of minutes) rather than one event at a time, and streaming-first means making that latency pattern the default architecture rather than a justified requirement.

questions.question: You load a bounded set of roughly 200 new CSV files per day from a Unity Catalog volume into the existing Delta table dwh.orders using one scheduled COPY INTO statement executed on a SQL warehouse. Which of the following statements about this COPY INTO design are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: COPY INTO fits this scenario because the input is a bounded file set, the logic can be expressed in SQL, and the statement is retry-safe at the directory level: files that have not changed are skipped on a re-run.
For every loaded file, Databricks records the file path, the file size, and the last-modified timestamp, and a file is skipped only when all three values match a previously processed file.
COPY INTO deduplicates rows on a natural or primary key, so the same business record arriving in two differently named files cannot create duplicate rows in the target table.

If the scheduled job is paused longer than the metadata retention window (about 7 days), the recorded file metadata expires, the old files look new again, and a re-run can load the same data a second time.
Splitting the daily load into 200 separate single-file COPY INTO statements is preferable, because many small operations are faster on columnar storage than a few large ones.

correctAnswer: A
B
D
questions.analysis: A, B, and D are correct. A captures the fit criteria: COPY INTO is the SQL-first tool for a bounded, landing-file drop and it is idempotent at the file level, so retrying an orchestrated job does not reload unchanged files. B states the exact bookkeeping rule — path, size, and last-modified timestamp must all match before a file is skipped — which is why overwriting a file in place with new content forces a reload. D describes the retention edge case that produced the classic triple-count incident: pause the job beyond roughly 7 days and the retained file metadata expires, so every file looks new. C is the row-level confusion trap: COPY INTO does not compare primary keys or deduplicate rows; MERGE is the row-level tool, and duplicates can still arrive from rewritten files or after metadata retention expires. E is wrong for a database-physics reason stated in the source material: batch-oriented systems perform poorly when users execute many small-batch operations instead of a smaller number of large operations, because doing so forces the creation of many small, suboptimal files and a high number of create-object operations [source p.273]. The same reasoning applies here — 200 single-file statements is the anti-pattern, one statement over the directory is the pattern.

questions.question: A reviewer claims: 'COPY INTO already remembers which files it has seen, so it gives you the same per-file state that an incremental streaming ingestion framework maintains. Just point a streaming reader at it and you get exactly-once, low-latency ingestion for free.' Which evaluation of that claim is most defensible?

options.label: Correct: because COPY INTO records file path, size, and last-modified timestamp, it is functionally equivalent to an incremental ingestion state store, and any streaming reader can simply resume from that record.

Incorrect on both counts: COPY INTO's bookkeeping belongs to the target table's load history and has a finite retention window (about 7 days), it is not a streaming-resumable state store, and it provides no row-level uniqueness — so latency and exactly-once guarantees would still have to be designed explicitly.
Correct, and also cheaper: because COPY INTO is a batch operation, it always consumes fewer compute resources than any streaming alternative, regardless of data volume or arrival frequency.
Incorrect, but only because COPY INTO cannot be re-run safely at all: every re-run reloads all files from the beginning and therefore duplicates the entire table.

questions.correctAnswer: B
questions.analysis: Option B is correct because it separates two things that sound similar but are not the same: skipped-file bookkeeping and a resumable incremental ingestion state. COPY INTO's record is scoped to the target table's load history, is keyed on file path, size, and last-modified timestamp, and expires after the retention window (roughly 7 days), at which point old files look new again and can be reloaded. That is file-level idempotency for retries on a bounded directory, not a streaming state store that a reader can resume from with per-record progress, and it certainly makes no claim about row-level uniqueness — MERGE, not COPY INTO, is the row-level tool. Option A states the exact misconception this lesson warns about. Option C over-generalizes cost: even where streaming is growing in prevalence, the cost comparison has to be made on the specific workload [source p.67], and true streaming designs carry their own significant overhead when processing one event at a time [source p.354]. Option D is a different error — COPY INTO re-runs are safe for unchanged files, which is the whole point of the recorded metadata; what breaks is long pauses beyond the retention window, not re-running itself. The broader industry trend is real — as streaming ingestion becomes more prevalent, batch ingestion becomes less common [source p.412] — but a trend toward streaming does not turn COPY INTO's load history into a per-file state store, and the historical shift from batch computing to event streaming [source p.34] does not remove the need to pick the pattern that matches the workload.

actions.text: Time for a knowledge check on what we just built up — the ingestion foundations we've been working through, from pattern selection down through COPY INTO. Three questions here, mixing single-answer and multi-select, so read each option carefully before you commit.

Take your time and work through them on your own — no peeking ahead. Once you've submitted, I'll come back and we'll walk through the reasoning together, especially the traps worth flagging for the exam. Go ahead and start when you're ready.

scenes.title: Auto Loader: Incremental Cloud File Ingestion at Scale

elements.content: Auto Loader: Incremental Cloud File Ingestion at Scale
The cloudFiles structured streaming source — ingest only what is new, from thousands to billions of objects [source p.242]

Incremental discovery

Detects only files new since the last run — no full-prefix re-list

Schema inference

Infers and evolves schema; schema hints or rescued data column handle surprises

Checkpoint / state store

Tracks seen files so restarts resume exactly where the last run stopped

Definition (with preconditions): Auto Loader is the cloudFiles structured streaming source. Precondition — the source path must be a cloud object store prefix (S3, ADLS Gen2, GCS) or a Unity Catalog external location or volume. Edge case — two runs pointed at different source prefixes maintain independent file-discovery state, so an object written under a new prefix is never missed or double-counted. [source p.272]

Worked example (lakehouse medallion path [source p.242])

Object store prefix holds 2,000,000 files on day 1; only 5,000 are new on day 2. Auto Loader scans the 5,000 new objects, not the full 2,000,000 — COPY INTO would re-list the whole prefix. Cumulative files scanned in 1 month ≈ 5,000 × 30 = 150,000 vs. 2,000,000 × 30 = 60,000,000.

[source p.67]

Micro-batch chosen over millisecond streaming — Auto Loader's trade-off for scale.

actions.text: That file-level idempotency is exactly what breaks down when you scale. When you have millions or billions of objects landing continuously in a cloud bucket, re-listing the prefix every run becomes the bottleneck. That's where Auto Loader comes in.
Auto Loader: incremental cloud file ingestion at scale. This is the Databricks mechanism designed for exactly the scenario COPY INTO struggles with — high file counts and continuous arrivals.

Under the hood, Auto Loader is the cloudFiles structured streaming source. It ingests new files incrementally and, critically, it only reads the files that appeared since the last run — it does not re-scan the entire prefix.

Formally: Auto Loader is a structured streaming source that scales to thousands — even billions — of objects, detects new files incrementally, and integrates schema inference and evolution out of the box. Think of it as COPY INTO's big sibling for continuous workloads.
First pillar: incremental discovery. Auto Loader detects only the files that are new since the last run. This is the core differentiator — you never list the whole prefix again.

Second pillar: schema inference. Auto Loader infers the schema from your data and can evolve it as new columns appear. You can let it infer automatically, or supply an explicit schema for stricter control.

Third pillar: the checkpoint or state store. This tracks which files have already been seen, so restarts and re-runs pick up exactly where they left off — giving you that same idempotent behavior, but at scale.

Here's the worked example in a lakehouse context. Cloud storage lands files into the bronze layer through Auto Loader using cloudFiles, and the destination is a Delta table. Bucket in, incremental ingest, Delta out — the classic medallion path.

One note on timing: Auto Loader defaults to micro-batch rather than millisecond-level streaming. That's a deliberate tradeoff — micro-batching keeps costs and complexity down while still delivering near-real-time latency for most ingestion needs.

So to summarize this page: Auto Loader is a cloudFiles structured streaming source that incrementally discovers new files, infers and evolves schema, and uses a checkpoint state store for reliable, idempotent ingestion — the go-to choice when COPY INTO's full-prefix listing no longer fits.

scenes.title: Under the Hood: State, Schema, and Discovery Modes

elements.content: Under the Hood: State, Schema, and Discovery Modes

Auto Loader stays incremental because it keeps its own bookkeeping: a RocksDB state store of processed files, a persisted inferred schema, and a pluggable file-discovery mechanism. Under a schema-on-read landing zone, no integrated table schema exists, so the reader must supply the structure contract itself [source p.245].
State Store & Schema Store

1. File-level idempotency needs a durable ledger, so records that match neither the prior state nor the new file set cannot be re-emitted; this mirrors how commit-driven systems must periodically clean stale file references or they accumulate clutter [source p.304].

2. The inferred schema is persisted separately as the contract for reads and writes.

3. New columns trigger schema evolution, not a failure.

4. Misfit records route to _rescued_data.

5. Trap: schemaLocation and checkpointLocation must differ.
Discovery Modes

Directory listing (default): the prefix is re-listed on every trigger, which is cheap per listing but expensive when the prefix holds millions of objects.

File notification: a cloud-native event subscription feeds the queue, so the trigger reads events instead of scanning the whole prefix.

The discovery mode only changes how new files are found; the state store still decides which are already processed. Metadata plumbing (naming, permissions, pointers) is the filesystem's job [source p.226].
Worked Example: One Day of a Streaming Load

Trigger 1 lists 100 files, processes 100, state store = 100.

Trigger 2: 20 new files land plus 3 rewritten in place. The ledger plus the rewrite rule yields 100 + 20 + 3 = 123 processed entries, so only 23 files are read.

If the ledger is lost, every file looks new and the stream re-ingests 123 files — the same false-new pattern that balloons batch row counts after metadata expiry.

Fix legacies upstream by repairing with a key match: when a source record matches the target key the target row is replaced, and when no match exists the row is inserted — the upsert/merge path handles records the loader never saw [source p.343].

actions.text: Building on the Auto Loader foundation we just covered, let's now go under the hood. We'll look at the three mechanisms that make Auto Loader scale to millions of files: the state store, the schema store, and the two discovery modes.

First, the state store and schema store. Auto Loader keeps an internal RocksDB state store under the checkpointLocation, and that ledger records every file it has already processed. This is what makes ingestion incremental and effectively idempotent at the file level — on each trigger it consults the ledger rather than reprocessing everything.

Notice this point: file-level idempotency needs a durable ledger, which is why the checkpointLocation must live in reliable storage and must be consistent across restarts. Separately, the schemaLocation persists the inferred schema, so when a new file introduces a new column, Auto Loader evolves the schema automatically. Any records that don't match land in the _rescued_data column instead of failing the stream, governed by cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode. And here's the classic exam trap — schemaLocation and checkpointLocation are different directories and must never point at the same path.

Now the two discovery modes. Directory listing is the default, and it re-lists the entire prefix on every trigger — simple, but it gets expensive as the directory grows, because the cost scales with the number of files, not the number of new files. File notification subscribes to cloud-native file events from the storage service instead, so it only sees the arrivals. The tradeoff is that it requires extra cloud permissions and setup, but it avoids full-prefix listing altogether.

Let's make this concrete with the worked example. In one day of a streaming load, the first trigger lists one hundred files, processes all one hundred, and the state store records them as done. The next trigger re-lists the prefix but sees nothing new to ingest. If an upstream process rewrites a file with the same name but different content, the state store still considers it processed — which is why the note reminds us to fix such legacies upstream with a key-matching repair rather than expecting Auto Loader to re-read it.

So to recap: the state store under checkpointLocation gives you incremental, effectively idempotent ingestion; schemaLocation holds the evolving schema and routes mismatches to _rescued_data; and you choose between directory listing and file notification depending on scale and permissions. Keep those two directories separate — that's the trap most candidates fall into.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Auto Loader Foundations

questions.question: A data engineer configures an Auto Loader (cloudFiles) streaming read over a landing path and supplies both checkpointLocation and schemaLocation. Which statement correctly describes what each location stores and the consequence of pointing it somewhere new?

options.label: checkpointLocation stores the inferred schema and its evolution history, while schemaLocation stores the per-file processing bookkeeping; either one can be repointed at a fresh path on every run without affecting incrementality.

checkpointLocation stores the stream's progress state, meaning which files have already been discovered and ingested, while schemaLocation stores the inferred schema and its evolution history; both must be stable, dedicated paths per stream, because a new checkpoint forces reprocessing and a new schema location forces schema re-inference.

Both are optional performance hints. If they are omitted, Auto Loader reconstructs identical state on every run by comparing each file's path, size and last-modified timestamp, so no progress information is ever lost.
checkpointLocation is required only when the trigger is availableNow, and schemaLocation is required only when a PATTERN is used; a default streaming run needs neither.

questions.analysis: Auto Loader keeps two distinct pieces of durable state, and confusing them is the classic exam error. checkpointLocation is the Structured Streaming checkpoint: it records the stream's progress, including the set of source files that have already been discovered and ingested. It is what makes the read incremental, so a second run over an unchanged prefix commits zero new rows. schemaLocation is a separate directory in which Auto Loader caches the inferred schema plus a schema log; without a stable location, the schema must be re-inferred each time the stream starts, which is slower and can yield a different result for the same underlying data. Both paths must be stable and dedicated to exactly one stream: if two Auto Loader streams share a checkpoint directory their progress interferes, and if a pipeline is pointed at a brand-new checkpoint path, every file under the prefix looks new, so the whole history is reprocessed and duplicated. Repointing schemaLocation alone does not reload data, because progress lives in the checkpoint, but it discards the previously inferred schema and forces fresh inference. Option A simply swaps the two roles. Option C describes the file-identity bookkeeping used by COPY INTO, which this unit covered earlier, not Auto Loader's checkpoint state. Option D invents constraints that do not exist: every Auto Loader read needs a durable checkpoint, regardless of the trigger type or whether a glob pattern is used. The same discipline of never casually deleting state directories applies to databases that retain old files for failure checkpoint references, which accumulate until they are cleaned up [source p.304].

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Auto Loader's incremental file processing and its runtime requirements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: On each trigger Auto Loader discovers the files under the source path and compares them against the files recorded in its checkpoint state, so files that were already ingested are not read again and the full prefix is never silently reprocessed.
Auto Loader requires a cluster that stays up 24 hours a day to keep watching the directory, because a scheduled job that starts a cluster, runs one batch and stops cannot preserve streaming progress.

Auto Loader can be driven by a scheduled job that starts a cluster, ingests everything newly arrived using trigger(availableNow=True), and then stops; progress persists in the checkpoint location, so the next scheduled run continues where the previous one ended.
Deleting the checkpoint directory between runs is safe housekeeping, because Auto Loader rebuilds exactly the same state by comparing file paths, sizes and last-modified timestamps.

questions.analysis: Statement A is correct: Auto Loader is incremental by design. On every trigger it discovers files, either by listing the directory or through file notification mode backed by cloud notifications, and compares that discovery against the files already recorded in checkpoint state. Files already ingested are skipped rather than re-read, so a normal run never silently reprocesses the whole prefix. Statement C is correct and is the point most often missed in practice: Auto Loader does not need a cluster running around the clock. A scheduled job can start a cluster, run the stream with trigger(availableNow=True), which processes all newly discovered data and then stops the stream, and shut the cluster down. Because the checkpoint lives in durable cloud storage, the next scheduled run picks up exactly where the previous one stopped, giving incremental behaviour with a fraction of the cost. That choice should be made against the standard ingestion design questions: expected data volume, file format, and whether genuine in-flight processing is required [source p.261], plus how frequently data should be pulled from the source and whether it arrives as periodic snapshots or as update events [source p.63]. Statement B is false; it describes an always-on architecture that Auto Loader does not require and that wastes compute. Statement D is also false: path, size and last-modified timestamp is COPY INTO's file-identity model from earlier in this unit, whereas Auto Loader's progress lives in the checkpoint. Deleting that directory makes every file still present look new, which forces a full reprocess and produces duplicates rather than restoring equivalent state.

questions.question: A nightly Auto Loader job ingests JSON order files from a landing volume into a bronze Delta table. The inferred schema declares order_id as an integer. One file arrives in which a single record has order_id set to the string N/A and also carries an extra field promo_code that is not in the schema. The job runs with default rescued-data behaviour, meaning no explicit rescuedDataColumn option and no FAILFAST mode. What is the outcome?

options.label: The micro-batch fails with a schema mismatch error, the job stops, and the same file is retried on every trigger until upstream corrects the data.

The stream continues and commits the batch; the offending record loads with order_id nulled out and the original raw payload preserved in the automatically added _rescued_data column, which also captures the unexpected promo_code field instead of discarding it.
The stream continues but the offending record is silently dropped from the batch and only surfaces later as a dropped-records metric, so the original payload is unrecoverable.
Auto Loader halts the stream and waits for the schema to be extended with an ALTER TABLE statement before it will commit the batch.

questions.analysis: Under the default permissive behaviour, and with no explicit rescuedDataColumn option, Auto Loader automatically adds a column named _rescued_data. Any field that cannot be cast to the declared type, here the string N/A in an integer column, is set to null in the typed column, and any field that is not part of the schema, here promo_code, is not materialised as its own column. In both cases the original JSON fragment is preserved verbatim in _rescued_data rather than being dropped. That yields three properties worth memorising. The micro-batch still commits, so one malformed record never brings down a nightly ingestion job. Nothing is lost silently, because the raw payload is retained for auditing and later repair. And a new field appearing in a later file does not, by itself, break the pipeline or force an immediate schema change. Option A describes FAILFAST-style behaviour or a schema-enforcement assertion rather than the default. Option C describes DROPMALFORMED semantics, which discard the payload and leave only a metric behind. Option D is wrong because schema evolution is an opt-in mode that adds columns when they are detected; Auto Loader does not block a batch waiting for a manual ALTER TABLE. Two edge cases are worth remembering. First, rescue applies only to data that can be parsed at all, so a genuinely corrupt or truncated file still fails the read. Second, rescued records are not revisited automatically: once the file is checkpointed, fixing the schema or the source data later does not re-read it, so repairs must be driven from _rescued_data or by deliberately reprocessing that file. This is exactly why data-quality checks for late, missing or malformed data belong in the ingestion design before options are chosen [source p.63], and it reflects the long shift from purely batch pipelines toward continuously arriving event data [source p.34].

actions.text: Now let's check how well the Auto Loader foundations settled in. Three questions here — two single-answer, one multiple-select — so take each one at your own pace and answer from what we just covered on state, schema, and incremental processing.

Work through them independently and commit to an answer before moving on; the multiple-select in particular rewards reading every option carefully. Once you submit, I'll come back and we'll unpack the reasoning together — including a couple of traps worth remembering for the exam. Go ahead and start whenever you're ready.

scenes.title: Configuring Auto Loader: Essential Options

elements.content: Auto Loader: Minimal Read + Production Options

# Minimum viable Auto Loader read

spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles")

.option("cloudFiles.format", "json")

.load("abfss://path")

Worked example

Day 9 pause creates 1 checkpoint; on day 10 a 1-CSV drop loads 1,000 rows in < 5s.

Production-critical

cloudFiles.schemaLocation — schema store

checkpointLocation — streaming state

Detection mode

useNotifications=true → file notification mode

without it → directory listing, rescans the prefix [source p.346]

Trigger choice

processingTime → continuous

availableNow → scheduled batch [source p.354]

Exam trap: .option("cloudFiles.format", ...) describes the file format (json, csv, parquet, avro) and is NOT interchangeable with .format("cloudFiles"). [source p.183]

Definitions: cloudFiles is a Structured Streaming source needing a checkpoint for state; schemaLocation stores the schema bookkeeping. [source p.342]

Schema evolution: new files widen the schema; mismatched fields are diverted to _rescued_data.

actions.text: Now that we understand the two discovery modes, let's put Auto Loader together — starting with the absolute minimum you need to get a stream running, then layering on the options production actually demands.

Here is the minimum viable read. You call spark.readStream, then format("cloudFiles") — that string is the Auto Loader source itself, not the file format. Then you chain .option("cloudFiles.format", "json") to say the underlying files are JSON, and finally .load() with your cloud path. That's the entire skeleton. Everything else is optional, but the exam expects you to know which options are effectively mandatory once you leave the sandbox.

In production, two options become non-negotiable. First, cloudFiles.schemaLocation — this is where Auto Loader persists the inferred schema, so it can evolve it safely over time instead of re-inferring from scratch. Second, checkpointLocation, which stores the streaming state that tracks which files have already been processed. Lose either one and you either lose schema history or reprocess everything from the beginning.

Then there's detection mode. Setting cloudFiles.useNotifications to true switches the source away from directory listing and into file notification mode. Instead of listing the whole prefix, Auto Loader subscribes to file events through the cloud provider's queue service — far cheaper and far faster at scale. Directory listing is fine for small volumes or when you can't grant notification permissions; notifications are the default recommendation otherwise.

Finally, your trigger choice shapes how the stream actually behaves. processingTime keeps it running continuously, waking up on a fixed interval to process new files. availableNow processes everything currently pending, then stops the stream — this is how you turn Auto Loader into a scheduled incremental batch job. Same source, same semantics, but two very different cost and latency profiles.

Let's walk the worked example. A nine-day ingestion pause produced exactly one checkpoint, and on restart Auto Loader resumed from that checkpoint rather than reprocessing all nine days of files. That's the whole point of the checkpoint — it makes recovery incremental instead of a full replay.

And here's the exam trap to burn in. .option("cloudFiles.format", "json") describes the format of the files being read — json, csv, parquet, or avro. It is not interchangeable with .format("cloudFiles"), which names the data source. Swap them and your stream either fails or silently does the wrong thing. Read the question carefully: if it's asking about the files, it's an option; if it's asking about the source, it's format.

This diagram shows what happens as new files arrive with a wider schema. Auto Loader evolves the stored schema to absorb new columns, while fields that don't match the expected type get diverted into the _rescued_data column instead of breaking the pipeline. So you keep ingesting, keep the good data, and still have the mismatched records quarantined for inspection. In the next section we'll compare directory listing and file notification head to head and migrate a pipeline between them.

hints: Start with the options dict: {"cloudFiles.format": fmt}. Then add "cloudFiles.schemaLocation" ONLY when schema_location is not None, and always add "cloudFiles.useNotifications" as the STRING "true" or "false" - Auto Loader options are strings, never Python booleans.
Build the statement as a list of lines and join them with "\n". Keep the .option(...) lines in the same order as options.items() so the generated code is deterministic and easy to test.

Notification mode (useNotifications = true) needs a queue: S3 -> SQS, ADLS -> Event Grid + Queue, GCS -> Pub/Sub, plus IAM permission to consume that queue. Listing mode replaces all of it with plain LIST calls on the container - simpler IAM, but slower for very large directories.

The two locations are not really optional in practice. schemaLocation persists the inferred schema and its evolution log; checkpointLocation persists stream progress. Without schemaLocation a schema change cannot be recovered on restart; without checkpointLocation the query cannot be resumed at all.

Trigger choice changes the run pattern: availableNow=True processes one incremental batch per trigger and then stops - the right choice for scheduled jobs. processingTime="10 seconds" keeps the stream running continuously with micro-batches every 10 seconds.
widgetConfig.solution:
NOTIFICATION_INFRA = [
    "Notification mode: storage -> queue -> Auto Loader (S3+SQS / ADLS+Event Grid / GCS+Pub/Sub)",
    "IAM: permission to consume the notification queue (e.g. sqs:ReceiveMessage)",
]

LISTING_INFRA = [
    "Listing mode: Auto Loader lists the directory on every micro-batch",
    "IAM: list permission on the storage container only, no queue needed",
]


def build_autoloader(fmt, path, use_notifications=False, schema_location=None,
                     checkpoint_location=None, schema=None, trigger="availableNow"):
    options = {"cloudFiles.format": fmt}
    if schema_location is not None:
        options["cloudFiles.schemaLocation"] = schema_location
    options["cloudFiles.useNotifications"] = "true" if use_notifications else "false"

    lines = ["df = (spark.readStream", '    .format("cloudFiles")']
    for key, value in options.items():
        lines.append('    .option("{}", "{}")'.format(key, value))
    if schema is not None:
        lines.append('    .schema("{}")'.format(schema))
    lines.append('    .load("{}"))'.format(path))
    lines.append("")

    if trigger == "availableNow":
        trigger_clause = ".trigger(availableNow=True)"
    else:
        interval = trigger.split("=", 1)[1]
        trigger_clause = '.trigger(processingTime="{}")'.format(interval)

    lines.append("(df.writeStream")
    if checkpoint_location is not None:
        lines.append('    .option("checkpointLocation", "{}")'.format(checkpoint_location))
    lines.append("    " + trigger_clause)
    lines.append("    .start())")

    warnings = []
    if schema_location is None:
        warnings.append(
            "Missing cloudFiles.schemaLocation: the inferred schema is tracked only inside "
            "the checkpoint, so a schema change cannot be recovered on restart.")
    if checkpoint_location is None:
        warnings.append(
            "Missing checkpointLocation: the query keeps no progress metadata and cannot "
            "be resumed after a restart.")
    if not use_notifications:
        warnings.append(
            "Listing mode is active: Auto Loader lists the whole directory on every "
            "micro-batch, which is slow for very large directories.")

    infra = NOTIFICATION_INFRA if use_notifications else LISTING_INFRA

    return {
        "options": options,
        "statement": "\n".join(lines),
        "warnings": warnings,
        "infra": infra,
        "trigger": trigger_clause,
    }

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Auto Loader Configuration

questions.question: A data engineer must configure an Auto Loader stream that ingests CSV files landing in a cloud storage prefix every few minutes. Which configuration snippet correctly declares both the streaming source and the file format of the incoming files?

options.label: .format('cloudFiles').option('cloudFiles.format', 'csv')
.format('csv').option('cloudFiles.format', 'cloudFiles')
.format('cloudFiles').option('format', 'csv')
.format('cloudFiles') with no cloudFiles.format option, relying on automatic format detection

questions.analysis: Correct answer: A. In a Structured Streaming read, .format() names the source that Spark uses to discover and read data, and for Auto Loader that source name is exactly the string 'cloudFiles'. The file format of the discovered objects is a separate, source-specific concern carried by the option cloudFiles.format, whose legal values are the reader formats Auto Loader supports (csv, json, parquet, avro, orc, text, binaryFile). Option B inverts the two roles: Spark would look for a source registered under the name 'csv' and would then hand that source an option called 'cloudFiles.format', which no CSV source understands, so the read fails at planning time rather than producing rows. Option C keeps the correct source but invents an option name; there is no plain 'format' option inside the cloudFiles source, so the file format is never explicitly declared and the parse is left to chance. Option D relies on format autodetection, and the source material is explicit that autodetection is merely a convenience feature and is inappropriate for production ingestion [source p.284]. This matters because CSV is by no means a uniform format: engineers must stipulate the delimiter, quote characters and escaping to export and re-ingest string data correctly, and CSV does not natively encode schema information or nested structures, so encoding and schema details must be configured in the target system [source p.284]. The same reference describes CSV as a catchall for delimited text with flexibility in escaping, quote characters and delimiter, advises avoiding CSV inside pipelines where the exchange format is under the engineer's control, and requires a complete technical description of the serialization configuration whenever CSV is used for archival [source p.418]. Declaring cloudFiles.format explicitly is therefore not a formality: it is the difference between a deterministic parse and silent data-quality damage.

questions.question: A team is promoting an Auto Loader job from a laptop prototype to a production streaming workload that must restart cleanly after cluster failures and must never re-read files it already ingested. Which options must be present or explicitly configured for that production-grade read? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: cloudFiles.format, so Auto Loader knows how to decode every discovered object
checkpointLocation, so the stream's progress log and Auto Loader's file-tracking state store survive a restart
cloudFiles.useNotifications set to true, because Auto Loader otherwise cannot detect new files
schemaLocation pointed at exactly the same directory as checkpointLocation, so schema state and file state stay together

questions.analysis: Correct answers: A and B. cloudFiles.format is required because Auto Loader is a source that must be told how to decode each object it finds; a file format is not inferable from the source name 'cloudFiles' itself, and guessing the format per file would make the parse non-deterministic, which is precisely the failure mode the reference warns about when it says autodetection is inappropriate for production ingestion [source p.284]. checkpointLocation is required because Auto Loader's incrementality is physically implemented by an internal RocksDB state store that records which files have already been processed; that store, together with the stream's progress log, lives under checkpointLocation, and it is what lets a restarted stream resume at the right position instead of re-listing and re-reading the whole prefix. Option C is wrong: cloudFiles.useNotifications is an optional switch, not a prerequisite, and its default is false, meaning Auto Loader uses directory listing mode and re-lists the prefix on every trigger; enabling notifications changes the discovery mechanism to a subscription to cloud-native file events, which is a scalability and cost optimisation rather than a functional requirement. Option D is wrong and is one of the classic configuration traps: schemaLocation already defaults to a 'schema' subfolder inside the checkpoint directory, so the two options persist different artefacts, and collapsing them onto the same path mixes the inferred schema and its evolution log with stream progress and file-tracking state. Keeping many small state and metadata artefacts in one location also has a storage cost that has to be reclaimed periodically, a general property of systems that write new files for each commit and retain older ones for failure checkpoints, as the source material describes [source p.304]. Architecturally, this read is the extract-and-load half of an ELT pattern: raw files are landed with minimal transformation and cleaned later inside the lakehouse, which is why the source material notes that modern warehouse and lakehouse systems absorb raw data first and transform it in place [source p.338]. Getting the two mandatory options right is what makes that pattern restart-safe.

questions.question: An engineer writes an Auto Loader stream and sets both .option('cloudFiles.schemaLocation', '/mnt/checkpoints/orders') and .option('checkpointLocation', '/mnt/checkpoints/orders') to the same directory. Why is this a defect, and what is the correct practice?

options.label: The two options persist different state: checkpointLocation holds stream progress and Auto Loader's file-tracking store, while schemaLocation holds the inferred schema and its evolution log; they must be different directories, and by default schemaLocation is a schema subfolder inside the checkpoint directory
There is no defect: the two options are aliases for one directory, and Auto Loader simply uses whichever one appears first in the option list
The defect is only cosmetic: ingestion still works, but Databricks re-infers the schema on every micro-batch and therefore emits a warning
The defect is that checkpointLocation must reference a table rather than a path, so both options should instead be set to a Unity Catalog table name

questions.analysis: Correct answer: A. checkpointLocation and cloudFiles.schemaLocation are not aliases; they persist two logically different kinds of state. checkpointLocation is where Structured Streaming writes query progress and committed offsets, and it is also where Auto Loader stores the RocksDB state store that lists already-processed files and therefore makes the read incremental and effectively idempotent across restarts. cloudFiles.schemaLocation is the directory where Auto Loader persists the inferred schema and the log of schema changes it has observed, which is what allows a new file with an extra column to evolve the schema rather than break the stream or, worse, be silently dropped. Collapsing both onto one path means the schema artefacts and the progress and file-tracking artefacts are interleaved in the same namespace, so a schema change or a clean-up of one artefact can damage the other, and tooling that inspects either location can no longer tell the two apart. Option B is a misconception worth naming precisely: the options are never interchangeable, because streaming checkpoints and schema logs have different writers, different formats and different recovery semantics. Option C understates the risk by treating it as a warning-only cosmetic issue; the reference material on commit and state management makes clear that systems which write new files for each state change accumulate clutter and may need that storage reclaimed, so mixing state namespaces is an operational hazard rather than a cosmetic one [source p.304]. Option D confuses a path-valued option with a catalog object; checkpointLocation and cloudFiles.schemaLocation both accept storage paths, not Unity Catalog table names. The correct practice is to give the checkpoint its own directory and let schemaLocation default to the 'schema' subfolder beneath it, or, if you set schemaLocation explicitly, point it at a separate, dedicated path. Doing so is part of the same discipline that makes CSV ingest safe in the first place: because CSV does not natively encode schema information, the schema must be configured or persisted in the target system rather than guessed at read time [source p.284], and any CSV-based exchange should carry a complete description of its serialization configuration for future consumers [source p.418].

actions.text: Time for a quick knowledge check on Auto Loader configuration — option names, required paths, and how file-format options differ from source-format options. Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer, even when two choices look close.
I'll be right here once you submit, and we'll unpack the reasoning together — including a couple of traps worth remembering for the exam. Go ahead whenever you're ready.

scenes.title: Directory Listing vs File Notification

elements.content: Dimension  |  Directory Listing  |  File Notification

Initial setup effort
Directory Listing: Directory listing needs only cloudFiles.format plus a cloudFiles.schemaLocation on the read; it is the default discovery mode, so a developer can ship a working incremental stream in one notebook cell with no cloud-side changes.
File Notification: File notification needs the developer to provision a cloud event queue and wire its identifier into the reader — cloudFiles.useNotifications true, plus the queue ARN, Event Grid queue resource ID, or Pub/Sub subscription option — before the first stream can start, which usually means an infrastructure ticket and a second iteration.

Cloud infrastructure required
Directory Listing: Nothing beyond the storage container, the Databricks compute, and a checkpoint location; the listing calls are ordinary storage API requests handled by the same managed filesystem pattern in which the vendor owns networking, disk clusters, and failure handling [source p.202].
File Notification: A cloud-native notification pipeline in the same region: SQS or SNS on AWS, Event Grid paired with a Storage Queue on Azure, or Pub/Sub on Google Cloud, each subscribed to the container's object-created events. Those events keep metadata transfer inside one region, consistent with the hybrid pattern that holds egress costs near zero by analyzing data where it already lives [source p.154].

IAM permissions required
Directory Listing: Only read and list permission on the storage path — exactly the access COPY INTO already needs — which makes directory listing the only viable mode in locked-down environments where the data team may not create queues or attach roles to a service principal.
File Notification: Requires the queue itself plus permissions to consume from it (for example s3:GetObject for the backfill and sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, and sqs:GetQueueAttributes for the queue), and a role that the Databricks compute can assume. Denied queue permissions are a classic silent failure: the stream starts cleanly, reports no error, and simply never sees a file.

Per-trigger cost model
Directory Listing: Cost scales with re-listing on every trigger, because one LIST call returns at most 1,000 keys. Worked example: a prefix holding 1,000,000 objects needs 1,000 LIST requests per sweep; at the published USD 0.005 per 1,000 requests that is about USD 5.00 per trigger, and a one-minute trigger costs roughly 1,440 x USD 5.00 = USD 7,200 per day even when zero new files arrived. Cloud storage meters performance this way explicitly — Amazon EBS publishes separate IOPS and throughput tiers with higher-performance SSD-backed tiers costing more per gigabyte [source p.229] — and object listing is metered the same way, per request.
File Notification: Cost is proportional to arrivals, not to inventory: each new file produces one small queue message plus one notification event, so the charge is nearly flat with respect to prefix size and stays small even for very large prefixes. The expensive listing sweep is paid only by the low-frequency backfill, which is why notification mode becomes cheaper the larger and more static the prefix is.

Latency to detect a new file
Directory Listing: Detection latency is bounded below by the trigger interval, because a file exists to Auto Loader only when the next listing sweep runs: a ten-minute scheduled availableNow job averages about five minutes of discovery delay and can be as slow as ten. Windowed micro-batch processing runs every few seconds or every few minutes depending on the configured trigger, so the interval you choose is literally the freshness your downstream consumers experience [source p.355].
File Notification: Detection latency is the event-delivery time, typically sub-second to a few seconds, plus the small trigger interval the stream uses to drain the queue, which is what makes this mode compatible with low-latency targets and near-real-time medallion-architecture (bronze to silver to gold) pipelines.

Practical file-volume ceiling
Directory Listing: Comfortable for thousands of files and low-frequency scheduled runs; sweep time and LIST spend grow linearly with object count, so a prefix in the tens of millions of objects becomes both slow and expensive. Deciding between a frequent small scan and a continuous event-driven pipeline has no universal answer — it depends on the acceptable latency and the team's existing expertise [source p.355].
File Notification: Built for prefixes in the thousands to billions of objects, because the marginal cost of one more file is one more event rather than one more key inside a full re-listing, so throughput scales with arrivals rather than with total inventory.

Recovery when discovery is interrupted (the exam trap)
Directory Listing: Discovery is stateless, so nothing outside the RocksDB state under checkpointLocation can expire: after a pause, the next run simply re-lists and discovers everything that appeared, which is why directory listing is the natural fallback and audit mechanism.
File Notification: Queue and notification events expire after a retention window, and any file that landed while the queue, the event subscription, or the stream was down is never announced to Auto Loader at all. Notification mode therefore still needs a periodic directory-listing backfill — a scheduled availableNow read over the same prefix — to catch those orphans, because transiently stored events are lost when the resource is torn down, exactly as an instance store volume loses its contents when the VM shuts down [source p.230].

Best-fit operational scenario
Directory Listing: The right default for small landing zones, SQL-first teams, permission-restricted workspaces, and scheduled overnight runs where several minutes of extra detection latency is invisible to consumers.
File Notification: The right choice when a very large prefix must be watched continuously with low-latency targets and the platform team can own a queue plus role as permanent infrastructure.

Takeaway — Memorise the decision rule: a high file count combined with low-latency targets pushes you to file notification, while small volumes and restricted IAM permissions push you back to directory listing.

Takeaway — In cost terms, directory listing bills you for inventory (every object, on every trigger) and file notification bills you for arrivals (one message per new file), so a prefix that grows monotonically forever eventually forces the switch to notification.
Takeaway — Directory listing is the safer default because it needs no extra infrastructure and cannot orphan a file; it is the mode to reach for when you cannot create queues or attach roles.

Takeaway — Whatever mode you select, schedule a low-frequency directory-listing backfill: notifications are missed whenever the queue or its subscription is unavailable, and a purely notification-driven pipeline will silently skip those files until the backfill runs.

actions.text: Now that we've configured Auto Loader's essential options, there's one configuration choice that deserves its own page, because it drives cost, latency, and permissions all at once — the discovery mode. Let's compare directory listing and file notification side by side.

This table is laid out along the dimensions that actually drive the selection decision. Read it left to right: the dimension, then how directory listing behaves, then how file notification behaves. If you can recall these rows, you can answer almost any Auto Loader design question on the exam.

Start with initial setup effort. Directory listing needs essentially nothing beyond the cloudFiles source path itself — you point Auto Loader at a location and it goes. File notification, by contrast, requires you to provision and wire up a notification service and grant Auto Loader the rights to consume from it before your first file is ever detected.

That leads directly to cloud infrastructure. Directory listing requires no extra cloud resources at all. File notification requires a cloud event queue — on AWS that's SQS or SNS, on Azure it's Event Grid paired with a Storage Queue, and on Google Cloud it's Pub/Sub. Notice the pattern: each cloud has its own native messaging service, and Auto Loader can drive all three.

Because of that queue, file notification also needs IAM permissions — an identity that is allowed to create the queue or subscription and to read messages from it. Directory listing only needs read access to the storage location itself. This is the single most common reason a team is forced to stay on directory listing: their security posture will not hand out queue and subscription permissions.

Now the cost model, and this one is worth memorising precisely. Directory listing bills per trigger, and the cost scales with how many objects you re-list on every single run — so it grows with the size of the prefix, not with the number of new files. File notification inverts that: the queue does the discovery work, so you stop paying to repeatedly list a huge prefix.

Latency to detect a new file is the next dimension. File notification is near-real-time — the moment the object lands, the event fires and the stream picks it up. Directory listing is bound to your trigger interval, so its detection latency is only as good as how often you schedule the stream.

And then there is the practical file-volume ceiling. Directory listing is fine for thousands of files or low-frequency scheduled runs; once you are dealing with millions of objects under a prefix, re-listing on every trigger becomes both slow and expensive, and file notification becomes the only sane option.

Here is the row most candidates miss, and it's a classic exam trap. Neither mode is self-sufficient in production. Even in file notification mode you still need a periodic directory-listing backfill, because files can arrive while the queue or the notification service is unavailable. Those files never generate an event, so nothing tells Auto Loader they exist — only a scheduled listing sweep will find and ingest them.

Putting the dimensions together gives you the best-fit operational scenario for each mode. Directory listing fits small volumes, strict permission boundaries, and low-frequency scheduled batches. File notification fits high-volume landing zones, near-real-time targets, and teams that can manage the cloud queue.

So here's the decision rule to memorise: a high file count combined with a low-latency target pushes you to file notification. Small volumes, or a restricted permission environment, push you back to directory listing.

And when you're genuinely unsure, remember what the second takeaway tells you: directory listing is the safer default. It comes with fewer moving parts, no cloud-side infrastructure to maintain, and no extra permission grants — it just costs you more as the prefix grows.

In cost terms specifically, the comparison is tidy: directory listing bills for repeatedly reading the directory, whereas file notification pays a small fixed amount for the queue and then scales with the events rather than the prefix size.

Whatever mode you ultimately select, schedule a low-frequency listing job as a safety net. It costs almost nothing, and it guarantees that any file that slipped past the notification path still gets ingested. That single habit is the difference between a demo pipeline and a production one.

To sum up: setup effort, cloud infrastructure, and IAM permissions all favour directory listing. Cost at scale and detection latency favour file notification. Extend your Auto Loader options with a discovery mode only after checking which of those constraints your environment actually allows — and always keep the backfill sweep in the schedule.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Migrating to File Notification Mode

elements.content: Problem 1

A production pipeline ingests 4,000,000 new small JSON files per day into the prefix s3://raw-events/, landing them in a Bronze Delta table. The business SLA is that a file must be queryable in Bronze within 5 minutes of landing in S3. Today the stream runs Auto Loader in its default discovery mode (directory listing of the prefix) on a 5-minute trigger, and it spends most of its wall-clock time issuing LIST calls. Assume: the S3 ListObjectsV2 API returns at most 1,000 keys per request; one trigger must page through the whole prefix to discover new files; S3 LIST costs $0.005 per 1,000 requests; SQS costs $0.40 per million requests; a single sequential LIST round trip takes about 5 ms. Compute (a) LIST requests per trigger, (b) LIST requests per day, (c) the daily and annual LIST cost, (d) the equivalent notification-mode request cost for the same day, and (e) what happens to (b) and (c) if a 10-day retention policy lets the prefix grow to 40,000,000 objects.
Hint: The key quantity is not files per day — it is objects in the prefix multiplied by triggers per day.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Requests per full prefix scan. S3 returns at most 1,000 keys per page, so one complete scan of a prefix holding 4,000,000 objects costs

$$\lceil 4{,}000{,}000 / 1{,}000 \rceil = 4{,}000 \text{ LIST requests}.$$

In directory-listing mode this scan is repeated on every trigger, because the source has no way to know which objects changed since the last trigger other than by asking for the listing again. This is the O(total objects) behaviour described in the unit: the source re-lists the prefix on every trigger.

Step 2 — Requests per day. At a 5-minute trigger,

$$\frac{24 \times 60}{5} = 288 \text{ triggers/day}$$

so the daily LIST volume is

$$288 \times 4{,}000 = 1{,}152{,}000 \text{ LIST requests/day}.$$

Step 3 — Wall clock. 4,000 sequential round trips at 5 ms each is $4{,}000 \times 0.005 = 20$ seconds of pure API latency per trigger, before a single byte of JSON is parsed. That is 20 s out of a 300 s SLA budget, i.e. 6.7% of the budget consumed by discovery alone.

Step 4 — Cost. $1{,}152{,}000 / 1{,}000 = 1{,}152$ thousand-request units at $0.005 each gives $1{,}152 \times \$0.005 = \$5.76$ per day, or $\$5.76 \times 365 = \$2{,}102.40$ per year.

Step 5 — Notification mode on the same day. In file notification mode the queue delivers one message per new object, so the request count is 4,000,000 messages/day $= 4.0$ million requests:

$$4.0 \times \$0.40 = \$1.60 \text{ per day} = \$584 \text{ per year}.$$

Saving: $\$5.76 - \$1.60 = \$4.16$ per day, a 72.2% reduction in discovery API cost.

Step 6 — The growth scenario. With a 10-day retention policy the prefix holds $4{,}000{,}000 \times 10 = 40{,}000{,}000$ objects. Listing cost per trigger becomes $40{,}000$ requests, so per day $288 \times 40{,}000 = 11{,}520{,}000$ requests $= \$57.60$/day $= \$21{,}024$/year, and the sequential latency balloons to $40{,}000 \times 0.005 = 200$ seconds (3 min 20 s) of the 5-minute budget. The notification-mode bill stays at $\$1.60$/day, because it is proportional to the 4,000,000 objects that are actually new, not to the 40,000,000 that exist.

Analysis — The method here is an orders-of-magnitude argument, not a benchmark: you bound the discovery work with a formula and compare two cost functions. Directory listing is $O(T \times N_{total})$ per day where $T$ is the number of triggers and $N_{total}$ is the objects in the prefix; file notification is $O(N_{new})$. The two diverge as soon as retention lets the prefix grow, which is the normal case in production. Notice that notification mode is not free and is not even fewer API calls at current volume — 625,000 fewer LIST calls versus 4,000,000 SQS messages, so the raw request count actually goes up while the cost goes down by 72%. Students commonly mis-apply this by claiming 'notifications eliminate API cost'; the honest claim is that notifications eliminate the cost and latency that scale with the total size of the prefix. This mirrors the general shift the source describes from a query engine acting as an 'external observer' polled by a cron job to computations 'triggered directly from the data itself' [source p.309]. A second common mistake is to ignore the wall-clock term entirely: at 40 million objects, discovery latency alone consumes two thirds of the 5-minute SLA, and no amount of tuning the ingestion step recovers it. Edge cases worth stating: list throttling can make the tail far worse than the average, so a 20 s mean is a lower bound rather than a plan; S3 request pricing varies by region and by storage class; and if the prefix is partitioned, listing only the relevant partition reduces $N_{total}$ but never removes the dependence on total object count.
Problem 2

You must now flip the existing stream to file notification mode. Write the complete Auto Loader read and write configuration for two variants: (A) Databricks provisions the notification resources (SNS topic, SQS queue, IAM role) on an account where the job principal has permission to create them; (B) the account is locked down, so an already-provisioned SQS queue must be supplied. For variant B, list the queue URL option, the region option, and the two permission sets that must already exist. State explicitly what must not change during this edit.
Hint: The only discovery-related option that changes is cloudFiles.useNotifications (plus region/queueUrl in variant B).

Worked solution
Variant A — let Databricks provision the notification resources. The read side becomes:

spark.readStream .format("cloudFiles") .option("cloudFiles.format", "json") .option("cloudFiles.useNotifications", "true") .option("cloudFiles.region", "us-east-1") .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "s3://meta/raw-events/schema") .load("s3://raw-events/")

and the write side is unchanged:

.writeStream .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://meta/raw-events/checkpoint") .trigger(processingTime="4 minutes") .toTable("bronze.raw_events")

With cloudFiles.useNotifications = "true" and no queue supplied, Auto Loader creates the SNS topic, the SQS queue, and the IAM role that allows S3 to publish bucket events and allows the job to consume them. That requires the principal to hold the corresponding create/pass-role permissions on the account.

Variant B — supply an existing queue. Add exactly one option to the variant A read:

.option("cloudFiles.queueUrl", "https://sqs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/123456789012/autoloader-raw-events")

Two permission sets must already be in place, and neither is created by the job:

1. The SQS queue policy must allow the SNS topic for s3://raw-events/ to send messages to the queue, and the S3 bucket must have an event notification configured with that topic as the destination.

2. The identity running the stream must be able to consume the queue — sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage, sqs:GetQueueAttributes — plus s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on the bucket itself, because the queue carries only the object path; the data is still read with a GET.

The region option (cloudFiles.region) must name the region of the bucket, not the region of the cluster.

What must not change: cloudFiles.schemaLocation and checkpointLocation stay exactly as they are. The switch from directory listing to file notification changes how new files are discovered; it does not change the RocksDB state store that records which files have already been processed. Keeping both paths byte-for-byte identical is what prevents a full re-read of everything already ingested.

Analysis — The method choice here is a substitution, not a rewrite: Auto Loader exposes discovery as a single option so that migration is a one-line diff plus an optional queue URL. The reason that is safe is architectural — discovery mode is a plug-in in front of the same state store, so the seen-file set survives the switch. Preconditions and edge cases to state precisely: the bucket must be in a region the option names correctly, or the source subscribes to a topic that never fires; S3 event notifications must exist for the prefix (a bucket-level notification is not the same thing as a topic); in locked-down accounts the queue may already be shared by several streams, in which case each stream must still have its own checkpointLocation or the two streams will fight over the same state directory. The classic student error is to 'clean up' by pointing checkpointLocation at a new path during the migration 'so we start fresh' — that empties the state store and reprocesses the entire prefix (quantified in the next problem). A second error is to believe the queue holds the migration state: it does not. Deleting or recreating the SQS queue loses only undelivered events; the record of what has been ingested lives in the checkpoint, and that is why the backfill pass, not the queue, is the completeness mechanism. Note also that the option is a string ("true"), not a Python boolean, in the option() API — a small but frequent source of silent misconfiguration in exam-style questions.
Problem 3

A junior engineer proposes moving the checkpoint from s3://meta/raw-events/checkpoint to s3://meta/raw-events/checkpoint-v2, arguing that 'we are changing the source mode, so the state should start clean'. The Bronze table currently holds 3.4 billion rows from 90 days of ingestion. Files land at 4,000,000 per day, the prefix keeps 30 days of retention, and the average file carries 25 JSON records. Compute (a) how many files sit under the prefix at the moment of the change, (b) how many rows would be appended if the new checkpoint path were used, (c) the resulting table size and growth percentage, (d) how long the re-read would take at a measured throughput of 333 files/second, and (e) the correct action.
Hint: The state store is keyed by file path. An empty state store means every file under the prefix looks brand new.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Objects under the prefix. With 30 days of retention at 4,000,000 files/day:

$$N_{prefix} = 4{,}000{,}000 \times 30 = 120{,}000{,}000 \text{ files}.$$

Step 2 — Rows appended. The RocksDB state store under checkpointLocation is the only record that these files were already processed. A new path starts with an empty state store, so every one of the 120,000,000 files is treated as new:

$$120{,}000{,}000 \times 25 = 3{,}000{,}000{,}000 \text{ rows appended}.$$

Step 3 — Table impact. New size $= 3.4 + 3.0 = 6.4$ billion rows, an increase of

$$\frac{3.0}{3.4} \times 100 = 88.2\%.$$

Every business metric computed on Bronze — counts, sums, distinct users — is now roughly double-counted, and no error is raised anywhere: the job reports success.

Step 4 — Wall clock. At 333 files/second, re-reading the prefix takes

$$\frac{120{,}000{,}000}{333} \approx 360{,}360 \text{ s} \approx 100 \text{ hours}$$

of continuous compute — over four days of re-ingesting data that was already there.

Step 5 — Correct action. Preserve both paths verbatim:

.option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "s3://meta/raw-events/schema")\n .option("checkpointLocation", "s3://meta/raw-events/checkpoint")

The migration touches exactly one option, cloudFiles.useNotifications. If a path must genuinely move, the only two safe routes are (i) copy the checkpoint directory tree to the new location so the state store is not empty, or (ii) accept the re-read and follow it immediately with a deduplicating MERGE against a natural key such as (source file path, record id), which collapses the duplicated rows back to 3.4 billion.

Analysis — This problem isolates the difference between configuration state and data state. Auto Loader's per-file bookkeeping lives in the checkpoint, not in the queue and not in the table, and it is keyed by file path — the same design that makes COPY INTO idempotent at the directory level is here applied per file. Because the key is the path, losing the store is indistinguishable from a brand-new dataset, which is why the failure is silent and expensive. Two edge cases deserve explicit statement. First, schemaLocation is a separate store: moving only schemaLocation causes schema re-inference against a sample of files rather than a full re-read, so it produces a wrong-but-cheap failure — the schema may come back narrower or with a different inferred type, and the sink write then fails or silently drops columns. Second, checkpoint directories are ordinary object-store prefixes: an S3 lifecycle rule that expires s3://meta/... after N days will delete the state store and trigger exactly the disaster computed above on the next run. This generalizes: whenever a pipeline has durable correctness state, that state's retention policy is part of the pipeline's correctness contract. The exam distractor to expect is a plausible-sounding 'start clean after a migration' instruction, and the reasoned answer is always that discovery mode is orthogonal to ingestion state. Note also the retention interaction flagged in the source: databases backed by object storage retain old files until vacuumed, and Databricks in particular retains data indefinitely until manually vacuumed, so the extra 3 billion rows also consume real S3 spend until a VACUUM plus rewrite runs [source p.306].
Problem 4

With notification mode enabled you must pick a trigger interval that satisfies the 5-minute freshness SLA and schedule the one-off backfill for the migration window. Measured facts: 4,000,000 files/day arrive uniformly; sustained ingestion throughput is 333 files/second; queue delivery plus commit overhead adds roughly 15 seconds to end-to-end latency. (a) Derive the largest trigger interval T (in whole minutes) that meets a 5-minute SLA. (b) State whether a 5-minute trigger meets the SLA. (c) A colleague proposes maxFilesPerTrigger = 10,000 as a safety cap — compute the backlog after 24 hours. (d) The migration window is 40 minutes; size the backfill pass and specify how it is configured.
Hint: End-to-end latency is approximately T (waiting for the trigger) plus the batch processing time, not just the processing time.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Arrival rate.

$$r = \frac{4{,}000{,}000}{24 \times 60} = 2{,}777.8 \text{ files/minute} = 46.3 \text{ files/second}.$$

Step 2 — Batch size and processing time for an interval T. Files per batch $= 2{,}777.8\,T$. At 333 files/second the processing time is

$$t_{proc} = \frac{2{,}777.8\,T}{333} = 8.34\,T \text{ seconds} = 0.139\,T \text{ minutes}.$$

Step 3 — End-to-end latency versus the SLA.

$$L = T + 0.139T + 0.25 \text{ min (queue + commit)} = 1.139\,T + 0.25.$$

Require $L \le 5$:

$$1.139\,T \le 4.75 \implies T \le 4.17 \text{ minutes}.$$

The largest whole-minute interval that meets the SLA is T = 4 minutes, giving $L = 1.139 \times 4 + 0.25 = 4.81$ minutes and roughly 11 seconds of headroom per cycle.
