questions.analysis: The source is explicit that credentials should never be embedded in code and that secrets must be handled as configuration, never committed to version control, using a secrets manager where possible [source p.399]. It also warns that embedding credentials directly in code is a major security risk and that they frequently leak into version-control repositories and get passed around through messages and email [source p.383]. That rules out all three distractors. Option A fails because workspace readability is not a security control — the literal still lands in the notebook's version history, in any git-backed repo, and in exported run output. Option C is exactly the anti-pattern the source calls out: credentials in code and credentials circulated by email [source p.383]. Option D confuses transport encryption with secrecy — a URL is just a string like any other and is visible in notebook code, Spark logs, and Spark UI, so it is no safer than option A. Option B is correct because a secret scope keeps the value outside the code, injects it at runtime, supports rotation and auditing, and lets you apply the principle of least privilege — never grant more access than the job requires [source p.399].

actions.text: So let's see how that landed. This knowledge check covers the JDBC configuration and security decisions we just walked through, so take each question on your own and commit to an answer before you move on.
Once you submit, I'll be right here to go through anything that gave you trouble — especially the options that look right but aren't. Go ahead and give it your best shot.

scenes.title: Change Data Capture: Initial Snapshot Plus Increments

elements.content: Change Data Capture: Initial Snapshot + Increments
Keeping a Delta table synchronized with a source database without full reloads
What CDC Actually Captures

CDC reads the source transaction log or database triggers to emit change records for every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — not just the current row state.

Database binary logs record every change sequentially, so a CDC tool can replay them as events [source p.162].

Two delivery modes:

• Batch-oriented: periodic deltas via an updated_at filter [source p.278]

• Continuous: each write treated as an event for near real-time, e.g. log-based CDC feeding Kafka/Debezium [source p.162]
Initial snapshot, then change records (INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE)
The Standard Pattern: Snapshot First, Then MERGE INTO

data.text: Full read of all rows at T0; establishes the baseline in the Delta target
Pull rows changed since the last watermark (band-oriented CDC filter on updated_at) [source p.278]
Match on primary key + sequence; UPDATE when matched, INSERT when not, DELETE for tombstones [source p.343]

elements.content: Merge requires a primary key managed by the data engineering team — columnar engines generally do not enforce uniqueness [source p.343]
Exam Trap: Full Reload vs. True CDC

A nightly full reload is not CDC. A truncate-and-reload clears the table and reruns transformations, producing a new table version — that is a reload pattern, not change capture [source p.342].

True CDC requires change records — it must represent INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. An insert-only feed cannot express deletes: queries must deduplicate by key and exclude any key whose latest version is a deletion [source p.342–343].

Small-row-at-a-time operations are also an anti-pattern for columnar targets — many tiny files and per-file scans for every update [source p.273].
Cumulative Rows Processed — Full Reload vs. Snapshot + CDC
Assuming a 1,000,000-row table with 4–5% daily change volume — 30-day cumulative rows
Worked Example: 30 Days of a 1,000,000-Row Table

Full reload, nightly, 30 days: 30 × 1,000,000 = 30,000,000 rows processed. Rows scale linearly with elapsed time, not with change volume.

Snapshot + CDC, nightly: initial snapshot = 1,000,000 rows; daily increments assume a 1,000,000 × 4% = 40,000-row change volume growing ~1% per day. Day 30 increment ≈ 40,000 × 1.0129 ≈ 53,300 → 30-day increment total ≈ 1,260,000, so the 30-day grand total ≈ 2,260,000 rows.

That is roughly 13.3× less work than full reload (30,000,000 / 2,260,000 ≈ 13.3) — and the gap widens every additional day.
Step 1 — Snapshot: read the full source once at T0 into the Delta target.
Step 2 — MERGE INTO: apply each daily delta on primary key + sequence; handle deletes as tombstones [source p.343].
Rule to remember: CDC = initial snapshot + true change records (INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE) applied by MERGE INTO on primary key + sequence. A scheduled full reload is reloading, not CDC.

actions.text: Now let's build directly on the JDBC connection we just covered. JDBC gets you a copy of a database table — but what if you need that copy to stay in sync as the source keeps changing? That's where Change Data Capture comes in.

Change Data Capture — CDC — is the mechanism that keeps a Delta table synchronized with a source database without reloading the whole thing every night. Instead of copying all the rows, you capture only what changed.

So what does CDC actually capture? Three kinds of events: INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. And how does it find them? It reads the source transaction log or database triggers — it doesn't scan the tables. That's the key idea to hold onto for the exam.

That gives us the pattern in a single line: an initial snapshot first, then change records flowing in — inserts, updates, and deletes. The snapshot establishes the baseline; the change records keep it current.
This is the standard pattern you'll be tested on: snapshot first, then MERGE INTO. You read the full source once, and from that point forward you apply each delta.

And notice what makes that MERGE possible — a primary key managed by the data engineering layer. Without a stable key, you can't match incoming changes to existing rows, and the whole pattern collapses.

Now here's the exam trap, and it catches a lot of people. A nightly full reload is not CDC. A truncate-and-reload is not CDC either. Think about why: neither one produces true change records, and critically, neither one represents deletes correctly. CDC requires genuine change rows — including deletes.

Let's make that concrete with the chart. This line chart shows cumulative rows processed over 30 days, comparing a full reload against snapshot plus CDC. Assume a one-million-row table with four to five percent daily change — so roughly forty to fifty thousand rows changing each day.

Do the math with me. Full reload, nightly, thirty days: thirty times one million — thirty million rows processed. Snapshot plus CDC: one million for the initial snapshot, then thirty days at about forty-five thousand changes each — roughly 1.35 million more. So the total lands near 2.35 million.
Let me walk the two steps. Step one — the snapshot: read the full source once at time zero and land it as your Delta baseline. That's the only full read you ever pay for.

Step two — MERGE INTO: apply each daily delta on the primary key, using a sequence column to make sure the latest change wins. And that's the difference between thirty million rows and two and a third million. Same result, a fraction of the cost.

So here's the rule to remember, and I want you to carry it into the next page: CDC equals an initial snapshot plus true change records — inserts, updates, and deletes — applied forward, not a repeated full copy. Next up, we'll put this pattern to work in our interactive CDC pipeline explorer.

widgetConfig.description: Simulate CDC operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) flowing into a Delta table. Compare batch-oriented vs continuous mode and observe MERGE INTO behaviour.

actions.text: Now that we have seen how Auto Loader handles incremental cloud file ingestion, let's look at the other major ingestion pattern: change data capture, or CDC. CDC is the technique of capturing inserts, updates, and deletes from a source system and replaying them into a target Delta table, so the target stays in sync without full reloads.

This simulation puts you in the driver's seat. On the left you control the source operations; on the canvas you will watch changes flow from the source database into the target Delta table. Let's start by examining the controls.

actions.content: Use this slider to choose INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE on the source table.
This switches between batch-oriented and continuous CDC mode.
Let's begin with Continuous CDC so we can see how quickly increments are picked up.
The status badge shows the current mode and whether the pipeline is actively syncing.

actions.text: I want you to experiment with the operation slider. Notice that when you slide to UPDATE, the change is not appended as a new row in the target — MERGE INTO matches on the key and applies the update. Slide to DELETE and watch the corresponding row disappear from the Delta table. All of those operations are resolved by a single MERGE statement on the target.

Now switch the CDC mode slider from Continuous to Batch-oriented and compare how long it takes for the change to appear. In continuous mode, increments flow in near real time; in batch mode, they wait for the snapshot schedule. This latency-versus-cost trade-off is exactly what the CDC knowledge check on the next page will test, so play with both modes here before we move on.

actions.content: Hit Reset any time to replay the initial snapshot capture from a clean state.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Change Data Capture

questions.question: A source PostgreSQL system supports an order-management application. The analytics team currently runs a nightly query that reads the entire orders table and overwrites yesterday's copy in the lakehouse. They now want to capture inserts, updates, and deletes as they occur, without re-reading the full table each night. Which statement best distinguishes the recommended approach from what they do today?

options.label: Enable change data capture so each row change in the source is emitted as an event containing the operation type and change payload, rather than relying on periodic full-table snapshots.
Continue the nightly full refresh but increase the query frequency from daily to hourly so that deletes and updates are eventually overwritten by the next snapshot.
Append every row read from the source table to a Delta table without a merge key, so the newest version of each order naturally ends up at the end of the file.
Replace the full refresh with a JDBC read that uses partitionColumn and numPartitions to parallelize the extract, which is what makes the read capture deletes.

questions.analysis: Change data capture (CDC) is 'the process of ingesting changes from a source database system' [source p.278], so it delivers the stream of row-level changes rather than repeated full snapshots. Continuous CDC 'captures all table history' and 'treats each write to the database as an event' [source p.162], which is exactly what is needed to see updates and deletes as they happen. Option B merely re-snapshots more often; a periodic snapshot model is the extract (E) of traditional ETL, which queries 'a current source table snapshot on a fixed schedule' [source p.68] and never exposes a delete as a first-class event. Option C is an append-only anti-pattern: appending without a merge key never retracts or updates a previously written row, so it cannot represent deletes and leaves stale duplicates. Option D is a misconception from the JDBC lesson: partitionColumn/lowerBound/upperBound/numPartitions only control read parallelism and predicate pushdown; they change how a snapshot is read, not whether changes are captured.

questions.question: You are landing a CDC event stream from an operational database into a Delta Lake silver table. The stream contains insert, update, and delete operations for a customer table keyed on customer_id. Which statements about the correct MERGE semantics and the evidence you should keep are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: When the CDC row is a delete, MERGE should match on customer_id and execute a DELETE branch; simply appending the delete event leaves the customer visible to downstream consumers.
When the CDC row is an update, MERGE should match on customer_id and SET the changed columns to the new values so exactly one current row per key survives.
Appending every CDC event to an append-only table is sufficient because the last event for a given key will always be the correct current state at query time.
Keeping the raw CDC events in a bronze table preserves the full change history, so the silver table can be re-derived from bronze if the merge logic is later corrected.

questions.analysis: MERGE is the correct primitive for CDC because the incoming stream mixes operation types against a stable business key. A delete event must hit a WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE branch keyed on customer_id, otherwise the row is never retracted and the customer remains in the silver table (A is correct). An update event must hit WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET, writing the new column values onto the single row for that key so the table stays at one current row per customer_id (B is correct). Option C describes the append-only trap: it mirrors the earlier warning that appending deletes is not a delete. If you append and only 'latest wins' at read time, the table still contains the deleted and superseded rows, so any consumer that does not implement that deduplication reads wrong results, and file counts grow without retraction. Option D is correct and reflects the medallion architecture (bronze = raw ingested data, silver = cleaned/conformed data): retention of the raw change events in bronze is what makes the silver merge reproducible, and it aligns with the source's practice of capturing 'all table history' [source p.162]. Note that CDC is 'the process of ingesting changes from a source database system' [source p.278], so the ingestion layer is expected to hand you operation-coded events, not a pre-merged table.

questions.question: A team must ingest changes from a source database. Their freshness requirement is that changes must be visible in the lakehouse within about two minutes of occurring. The database cannot enable binary logging, and the platform team has confirmed they cannot create any cloud event queues, topics, or IAM roles on the account. Given these constraints, which choice is most defensible, and why?

options.label: Continuous (log-based) CDC, because a two-minute target can only be met by reading the database binary log and streaming each change as an event.
Continuous CDC via a managed event stream, because managed CDC automatically provisions the queue and IAM role even when the platform team cannot.
Frequent ordered snapshot pulls of the changed rows with a fully-merged target, because the two blocking constraints remove the log-based and event-stream options that continuous CDC depends on.
A single full-table snapshot once per day with append-only writes, because CDC cannot be configured and the snapshot is the only remaining way to see all the data.

questions.analysis: This item tests choosing between continuous versus batch-oriented CDC against a stated latency requirement plus real-world blockers, a mode-selection discipline introduced in this unit. Continuous CDC can be implemented in two common ways: log-based CDC that reads 'the database binary log' and forwards events to a target [source p.162], and a managed variant where 'many cloud-hosted databases can be configured to directly trigger a serverless function or write to an event stream' [source p.162]. The stem removes BOTH of those foundations: binary logging is disabled, and no queues/topics/IAM roles may be created. Under those constraints the only achievable mechanism is a very frequent interval pull (a short-interval micro-batch/streaming read) whose target is maintained with MERGE so updates and deletes are applied — that is the point of C. Option A fails because log-based CDC requires the binary log to be enabled; you cannot read a log that is not being written. Option B fails by asserting automatic provisioning: the earlier unit's warning about recommending notification mode where the team cannot create queues or roles applies directly, and here even the ingestion-side notification plumbing is forbidden. Option D fails on the stated two-minute freshness requirement: a once-daily snapshot can never deliver two-minute visibility, and append-only writes also fail to retract updates and deletes. Always start from the freshness requirement AND the permission model before naming a technique.

actions.text: Before we open the pipeline explorer, let's check how well the CDC picture has settled. Three questions here — work through each one on your own and pick the option you'd actually defend on the exam. I'll join you right after you submit to talk through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Snapshot Plus CDC from SQL Server to Delta

elements.content: Problem 1

Your on-premises SQL Server holds a table `sales.orders` with 48,000,000 rows. `order_id` is a monotonically increasing BIGINT primary key; the minimum value is 1 and the current maximum is 48,000,000. The nightly job must land the full table into a Bronze Delta table `bronze_orders`, and it must not hard-code credentials. (a) Write the PySpark JDBC read using 8-way parallelism, pulling the password from the Databricks secret scope `prod-secrets` under key `sqlserver-password`. (b) Compute how many rows each JDBC partition will read. (c) If a single task can pull 25,000 rows per second, estimate the wall-clock time, and explain whether adding a 32-core cluster would help.
Hint: lowerBound and upperBound do not filter anything — they only tell Spark how to slice the key range.

Worked solution
Step 1 — the read statement. The four parallelism options are mandatory together: `partitionColumn`, `lowerBound`, and `upperBound` are ignored unless `numPartitions` is also set, and `numPartitions` alone leaves you with a single partition.

```python

pw = dbutils.secrets.get(scope='prod-secrets', key='sqlserver-password')

orders = (spark.read

.format('jdbc')

.option('url', 'jdbc:sqlserver://sqlsrv01.corp.internal:1433;databaseName=sales')

.option('dbtable', 'sales.orders')

.option('user', 'etl_reader')

.option('password', pw)

.option('partitionColumn', 'order_id')

.option('lowerBound', 1)

.option('upperBound', 48000000)

.option('numPartitions', 8)

.load())

(orders.write.format('delta').mode('overwrite')

.saveAsTable('bronze_orders'))

```

The password is retrieved at runtime from the secret scope and never appears in the notebook text; `spark.read.format('jdbc')` is a batch read, so no checkpoint is needed for the snapshot itself.

Step 2 — partition arithmetic. Spark computes the stride as

$$\text{stride} = \frac{\text{upperBound} - \text{lowerBound}}{\text{numPartitions}} = \frac{48{,}000{,}000 - 1}{8} = 5{,}999{,}999.875$$

Spark issues eight `WHERE` predicates against `order_id` (on SQL Server this is a range scan on the clustered index): partitions 0 through 6 cover the half-open ranges $[1, 5{,}999{,}999 \ldots)$ up to $[41{,}999{,}999, 48{,}000{,}000)$, and partition 7 is the closed tail. Rounding the stride, the seven lower partitions each hold about 6,000,000 rows and the last holds the remaining 6,000,000 rows because the maximum key equals the upper bound. Total check: $8 \times 6{,}000{,}000 = 48{,}000{,}000$ rows.

Step 3 — time budget. One partition's work is

$$t_{\text{partition}} = \frac{6{,}000{,}000\ \text{rows}}{25{,}000\ \text{rows/s}} = 240\ \text{s} = 4\ \text{min}$$

The eight ranges are read concurrently, so the wall clock is roughly 4 minutes plus cluster startup and the Delta write. Crucially, each JDBC range becomes one Spark task: a 32-core cluster (8 workers x 4 cores) would still run at most 8 such tasks at once, leaving 24 cores idle. To use them you must raise `numPartitions` to 32 (stride $= 1{,}499{,}999.97 \approx 1{,}500{,}000$ rows, about 60 s per task), which trades wall clock for 32 simultaneous connections to the source database — a licence and load consideration on the SQL Server side.

Step 4 — pushing work to the source. If the nightly snapshot only needs a window, put the filter in `dbtable` as a subquery so SQL Server executes it: `.option('dbtable', '(SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, status, updated_at FROM sales.orders WHERE updated_at >= \'2024-01-01\') AS o')`. `partitionColumn` must still be exposed by the subquery, which it is here.

Analysis — The method choice here is deliberate: `partitionColumn`/`lowerBound`/`upperBound`/`numPartitions` is the cheapest way to parallelise a relational read, because it converts one serial cursor into N independent server-side range scans. The critical subtlety students miss is that the bounds are planning hints, not predicates: rows with `order_id < lowerBound` are still returned and are pushed into partition 0, and rows above `upperBound` are pushed into the last partition. That is why an out-of-date upper bound silently creates skew (see problem p5). A second common mistake is putting a non-indexed or highly skewed column (for example `status` with three values) into `partitionColumn`; the source then executes 8 full scans instead of 8 index-range scans. A third is writing the password inline 'just for testing' — the correct pattern is always a secret scope, and in Unity Catalog-managed workspaces, a service principal or secret-backed connection rather than a personal credential. Finally, remember that a multi-partition JDBC read is not a transactionally consistent snapshot of the source: each range is read at a different instant, which is precisely why the high-watermark logic in p2 must be conservative. Also note the general trade-off that pulling wide rows over JDBC is itself expensive because columns must be reserialized as rows on the wire, and many sources now support native Parquet/ORC/Avro export or REST APIs that bypass JDBC entirely [source p.278]. Many teams therefore keep JDBC as a reader process that writes objects into cloud storage and let orchestration handle the rest of the pipeline, rather than reading straight into the final table [source p.278].
Problem 2

The snapshot in p1 was launched at 2024-03-15 02:00:00 UTC and its final partition finished writing to `bronze_orders` at 02:42:00 UTC. The source publishes an hourly change batch at five minutes past each hour: the 03:05 batch contains every row whose `updated_at` falls in the clock hour 02:00:00.000-02:59:59.999, and so on. (a) Which timestamp should be stored as the high-watermark that the next incremental run starts from? (b) Does the 03:05 batch overlap with the snapshot, and is that a problem? (c) What goes wrong if instead you store `max(updated_at)` observed in the snapshot, which for this run happened to be 02:41:58? (d) The 03:05 batch contains 412,000 rows. Show that the pipeline is safe to re-run.
Hint: Snapshot reads are not atomic across partitions, so the watermark must be the run's start time, not the last thing you happened to read.

Worked solution
Step 1 — choose the watermark. Store the snapshot's **start** instant, `2024-03-15T02:00:00Z`, as `watermark_ts` in the control table (for example `bronze_ingest_control`), together with `source = 'sales.orders'` and `status = 'SUCCESS'`. Advance the watermark only after the snapshot write commits, never before.

Step 2 — reason about overlap. The 03:05 batch covers 02:00:00-02:59:59.999, which straddles the snapshot window. Rows mutated between 02:00 and 02:42 appear twice: once as whatever version the snapshot's parallel readers saw, and once as the authoritative version in the batch. Overlap is intentional and is not a correctness problem, provided the apply step is idempotent. The alternative — starting the increment exactly at 02:42:00 — *creates* a gap, because a row updated at 02:10 in a partition that Spark had already finished reading is in the snapshot as a stale value and would never be re-read.

Step 3 — why `max(updated_at)` is wrong. `max(updated_at)=02:41:58` is merely the newest value any of the eight independent range scans happened to observe; it is not a consistent cut of the source. A row in partition 7 might have been read at 02:05 with `updated_at = 01:50`, then updated at 02:30. The 03:05 batch carries it with `updated_at = 02:30`, but $02{:}30 < 02{:}41{:}58$, so a filter of `updated_at > watermark` would discard it and the Bronze table would keep the stale 01:50 value forever. Recording 02:00:00 admits exactly the rows at risk and no more.

Step 4 — proves re-runnability. With the watermark at 02:00:00, the 03:05 batch (412,000 rows) is applied; suppose the job fails at 03:20 and is re-run. The same 412,000 rows are read again and merged again. Because the merge is keyed on `order_id` and guarded by a monotonic `change_seq` (p3), applying a change row twice produces exactly the same target state as applying it once: the update is a function of the source row, not a delta on the target. Idempotency is what makes the overlap free. Concretely, the second run touches the same 412,000 keys, rewrites the same Delta files, and leaves row counts and column values unchanged, so the re-run is a no-op semantically even though it costs compute.

Step 5 — bookkeeping. After each successful apply, write `watermark_ts = 03:59:59.999` (the end of the interval the batch covered) — not the batch's arrival time 03:05 — so the next run's lower bound is unambiguous.

Analysis — This is the standard 'snapshot plus incremental' change data capture pattern, in which a full copy establishes a baseline and periodic deltas keep it current. The design principle to internalise is *at-least-once delivery plus idempotent apply*, rather than *exactly-once delivery*: you deliberately reprocess the boundary hour and rely on the merge to converge. Students typically fail this in three ways. First, they set the watermark to the job's end time and silently lose every change that landed on a row already read by an early partition — the classic off-by-one-hour data gap. Second, they treat the source's `updated_at` column as a reliable ordering key when it is only a timestamp: two transactions in the same millisecond, or a clock skew between application servers, make ties ambiguous, which is why a monotonic `change_seq` is preferred and a tiebreaker (`>=` plus dedup) is required otherwise. Third, they advance the watermark before the Delta write commits, so a failed write leaves the watermark past data that was never landed — the watermark must be committed in the same logical step as the load. Note also that upsert and merge are the patterns that cause the most trouble for teams moving from row-based warehouses to column-based systems, because columnar targets usually do not enforce primary keys, so uniqueness is an engineering responsibility rather than a database guarantee [source p.343]. If the merge becomes too expensive, the alternative is the insert-only pattern with a deduplicated view that selects the newest record per key [source p.342]; but finding the latest record at query time can be extremely expensive, so a pre-computed materialised view is the usual mitigation [source p.342].
Problem 3

Design and trace the incremental apply step. The hourly extract lands in `staging.orders_changes` with columns `order_id BIGINT`, `customer_id STRING`, `amount DECIMAL(12,2)`, `status STRING`, `op STRING` (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), `change_seq BIGINT` (monotonic per source transaction), `updated_at TIMESTAMP`. The current `bronze_orders` contains:

- 1001 | C-77 | 250.00 | SHIPPED | change_seq 101

- 1002 | C-12 | 90.50 | PENDING | change_seq 88

- 1003 | C-45 | 410.00 | PENDING | change_seq 95

The incoming batch holds five rows: (1002, seq 104, amount 120.00, UPDATE), (1003, seq 103, op DELETE), (1001, seq 105, amount 250.00, status DELIVERED, UPDATE), (1004, seq 106, C-90, 55.25, INSERT), (1001, seq 102, amount 200.00, UPDATE — this one arrived late). Write the dedup and the `MERGE` statement, then give the exact resulting table.
Hint: Order the MERGE clauses carefully — in Delta, when several clauses of the same type match, the first one wins.

Worked solution
Step 1 — collapse the batch to one row per key, keeping the newest version. This removes the ambiguity of two source rows matching one target row:

```python

from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

changes = (spark.table('staging.orders_changes')

.withColumn('rn', F.row_number().over(

Window.partitionBy('order_id').orderBy(F.col('change_seq').desc())))

.filter('rn = 1')

.drop('rn'))

changes.createOrReplaceTempView('changes')

```

Step 2 — the guarded merge. Clause order matters: the delete branch is tested first, then the sequence-guarded update, then the insert guarded against re-inserting a delete:

```sql

MERGE INTO bronze_orders AS tgt

USING changes AS src

ON tgt.order_id = src.order_id

WHEN MATCHED AND src.op = 'DELETE' THEN DELETE

WHEN MATCHED AND src.change_seq > tgt.change_seq THEN UPDATE SET *

WHEN NOT MATCHED AND src.op <> 'DELETE' THEN INSERT *

```

Step 3 — dedup result. Per key the surviving row is: 1001 -> seq 105 (DELIVERED), 1002 -> seq 104, 1003 -> seq 103 (DELETE), 1004 -> seq 106. The late row (1001, seq 102) is dropped, so five source rows become four.

Step 4 — clause-by-clause trace.

- 1001: matched; `op = 'UPDATE'` so the delete branch is not taken; $105 > 101$, so `UPDATE SET *` rewrites the row to 250.00 / DELIVERED / seq 105.

- 1002: matched; $104 > 88$, so amount becomes 120.00 and seq 104. The write actually changes a value, unlike a blind `UPDATE SET *` of an identical row.

- 1003: matched and `op = 'DELETE'`, so the first clause fires and the row is physically removed.

- 1004: no target match and `op = 'INSERT'`, so the row is inserted.

Step 5 — resulting `bronze_orders` (three rows, down from three but with different membership: one delete, one insert):

- 1001 | C-77 | 250.00 | DELIVERED | change_seq 105

- 1002 | C-12 | 120.00 | PENDING | change_seq 104

- 1004 | C-90 | 55.25 | (status from source) | change_seq 106

Step 6 — invariants to assert after the merge: `count(*)` equals previous count plus inserts minus deletes, no `order_id` appears twice, and no row with `op = 'DELETE'` survives in the target.

Analysis — The reason a guard such as `src.change_seq > tgt.change_seq` is mandatory is that the change feed is only *eventually* ordered: network retries, partitioned staging writes, and backfills routinely deliver sequence 102 after sequence 105. Without the guard the merge applies whatever row it happens to see last, so the outcome depends on file order and is non-deterministic across runs. Deduplicating before the merge buys the same safety at the batch level and also avoids Delta's multiple-source-match ambiguity, where two source rows matching one target row can raise an error or silently pick one. The delete problem is subtler: a `DELETE` change row for a key that is already absent from the target has no match, so an unconditional `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *` resurrects a deleted order as a live row, usually carrying `op = 'DELETE'` in a column nobody inspects. That is the single most common production defect in CDC merges. The fix is the ordering used above — a matched delete clause to remove existing rows, and a not-matched clause restricted to non-delete operations so a delete never inserts. A final design note: if the organisation's policy forbids hard deletes (audit or regulatory retention), replace the `THEN DELETE` clause with a soft delete, add an `is_deleted` flag, and expose a view that filters `is_deleted = false` — that is the insert-only pattern, though materialising the current state as a view rather than recomputing it per query is what keeps it cheap [source p.342]. The merge pattern is formally upsert plus delete capability: matched keys are replaced, unmatched keys are inserted, and a match can additionally trigger removal [source p.343]. Both are write operations on stored records, i.e. the C and U of CRUD, and a property of query languages worth keeping in mind when reasoning about what a statement is allowed to mutate [source p.299].
Problem 4

A colleague's version of the merge runs nightly and has been reported as 'mostly working'. It reads:

```sql

MERGE INTO bronze_orders AS tgt

USING staging.orders_changes AS src

ON tgt.order_id = src.order_id

WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *

```

After the 03:05 batch, two symptoms appear. (a) Order 1003, which the source deleted with `op = 'DELETE', change_seq 103`, is present in `bronze_orders` again with `status = PENDING` and a literal `op = 'DELETE'` column value. (b) Order 1001, whose amount was legitimately raised to 250.00 at `change_seq 105`, now shows 200.00, because the same batch also contains a late `change_seq 102` row for that key. Diagnose both defects, explain the mechanism, and state whether the fixed pipeline is safe to re-run three times.
Hint: Two symptoms, two independent missing guards: one for deletes that do not match, one for ordering.

Worked solution
Step 1 — defect (a): resurrection of a deleted key. The 03:05 batch contains a single `DELETE` row for 1003. But 1003 was already deleted by an earlier apply, so the source row finds no target row, falls through to the only unmatched clause, `WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *`, and inserts the whole change record — including the `op` column set to `'DELETE'`. The table now holds a row that means 'this order is deleted' while being itself an active row. The mechanism is that the statement has one unmatched clause and no conditional filtering, so delete events are indistinguishable from insert events. Fix: add `WHEN MATCHED AND src.op = 'DELETE' THEN DELETE` before the update clause, and restrict the insert with `WHEN NOT MATCHED AND src.op <> 'DELETE' THEN INSERT *`.

Step 2 — defect (b): last-writer-wins on unordered keys. The batch holds two rows for 1001 with `change_seq` 105 and 102. With `WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *` and no ordering predicate, whichever source row the merge encounters last for that target row wins. Delta does not guarantee that ordering when multiple source rows match a single target row, so 1001 flips between 250.00 and 200.00 depending on file layout and retry history. Fix, in order of robustness: (i) deduplicate the batch with `row_number()` over `order_id` ordered by `change_seq DESC` so exactly one row per key reaches the merge; then (ii) add the guard `WHEN MATCHED AND src.change_seq > tgt.change_seq THEN UPDATE SET *` so even a wrongly ordered batch cannot roll the target backwards.

Step 3 — corrected statement:

```sql

MERGE INTO bronze_orders AS tgt

USING changes AS src -- changes = deduped, one row per order_id

ON tgt.order_id = src.order_id

WHEN MATCHED AND src.op = 'DELETE' THEN DELETE

WHEN MATCHED AND src.change_seq > tgt.change_seq THEN UPDATE SET *

WHEN NOT MATCHED AND src.op <> 'DELETE' THEN INSERT *

```

Step 4 — is it idempotent under three re-runs? Yes. The dedup is deterministic (highest `change_seq` wins, ties broken by `updated_at` then by the row's arrival order if you must), and each clause is a pure function of the surviving source row. Run 2 reads the same four rows: 1001 has $105 > 105$? No — equal, so the guard is false and the row is untouched. 1002 has $104 > 104$? No. 1003 no longer exists in the target and its `op = 'DELETE'` is excluded from the insert clause, so nothing happens. 1004 already has seq 106, so no update. The table after run 2 and run 3 is byte-for-byte semantically identical to the table after run 1. The broken version, by contrast, is not idempotent in any useful sense: each run re-applies the 102 row and re-inserts the 1003 delete marker, and the final state depends on physical file order.

Step 5 — the cost of getting it wrong downstream. A resurrected delete propagates into Gold layer revenue as a phantom order, and an amount that flips between 200.00 and 250.00 breaks any reconciliation against the source ledger. Both are silent: no job fails, which is why the guards must be structural rather than caught by monitoring row counts.

Analysis — The pedagogical point is that a merge is only as correct as its predicates. `UPDATE SET *` means 'take every column from the matched source row', not 'take the columns that changed', so any defect in the source rows — a stale version, a delete marker, a partial backfill with NULLs — is written straight into Bronze. This is why the upsert/merge family is described as the pattern that consistently causes the most trouble, particularly for teams transitioning from row-based warehouses to column-based cloud systems [source p.343]. The edge cases worth enumerating explicitly: (1) a key that is deleted then re-inserted later gets a new `change_seq` and correctly reappears, so the delete branch must not be a permanent tombstone; (2) NULL `change_seq` values — if the source cannot supply a sequence, the fallback is `updated_at` plus a tiebreaker and a tolerant `>=` guard, accepting that ties are resolved arbitrarily; (3) schema drift where a new source column arrives as NULL for existing rows and `UPDATE SET *` blanks a populated target column — a reason to enumerate columns rather than use `SET *` in regulated pipelines; (4) soft-delete policies that require an `is_deleted` flag plus a filtered view instead of physical removal [source p.342]. Finally, the pattern generalises: for each operation type in the change feed, ask what the statement must do when the target row exists and when it does not, and write one clause per cell of that 2x2 table. Missing cells are exactly where bugs of this kind live.
Problem 5

Your JDBC snapshot was tuned in p1 with `partitionColumn = order_id`, `lowerBound = 1`, `upperBound = 48000000`, `numPartitions = 8`, when the table really did contain 48,000,000 rows with a maximum key of 48,000,000. Six months later the table holds 60,000,000 rows and `MAX(order_id) = 60,000,000`, but nobody changed the options. The nightly job now takes 12 minutes, and task timings show seven tasks finishing in about 4 minutes and one task taking about 12 minutes. (a) Compute the exact row count in each partition. (b) Explain the timing. (c) Give the fix and the new expected runtime, assuming 25,000 rows per second per task.
Hint: Values above upperBound are not filtered out — they are all routed to the final partition.

Worked solution
Step 1 — recompute the stride. The JVM is still using the stored options, so

$$\text{stride} = \frac{48{,}000{,}000 - 1}{8} \approx 6{,}000{,}000$$

Step 2 — count rows per partition. Partitions 0-6 each scan the half-open interval of width 6,000,000:

$$\text{rows}_{0..6} = 6{,}000{,}000 \times 7 = 42{,}000{,}000$$

Partition 7 is the closed tail `order_id >= 42,000,000`, and because Spark does not discard keys above `upperBound`, every one of the 18,000,000 rows with `order_id` from 42,000,001 to 60,000,000 lands there:

$$\text{rows}_{7} = 60{,}000{,}000 - 42{,}000{,}000 = 18{,}000{,}000$$

Check: $42{,}000{,}000 + 18{,}000{,}000 = 60{,}000{,}000$. The distribution is $6{:}6{:}6{:}6{:}6{:}6{:}6{:}18$ — the last partition is three times heavier than its peers.

Step 3 — explain the timings. Time is proportional to rows, because a range scan is I/O bound:

$$t_{0..6} = \frac{6{,}000{,}000}{25{,}000} = 240\ \text{s} = 4\ \text{min}, \qquad t_{7} = \frac{18{,}000{,}000}{25{,}000} = 720\ \text{s} = 12\ \text{min}$$

Seven tasks finish in 4 minutes and sit idle while partition 7 runs for 12 minutes, so the job's wall clock equals the slowest task. Effective parallelism during the last two-thirds of the run is 1, not 8: you are paying for a cluster and using one eighth of it.

Step 4 — the fix. Query the current maximum before building the read, then pass it as the bound:

```python

hi = (spark.read.format('jdbc')

.option('url', url).option('user', user).option('password', pw)

.option('query', 'SELECT MAX(order_id) AS hi FROM sales.orders')

.load()).first()['hi']

# hi = 60,000,000

```

Now stride $= (60{,}000{,}000 - 1)/8 = 7{,}499{,}999.875 \approx 7{,}500{,}000$, so each partition reads about 7,500,000 rows:

$$t_{\text{new}} = \frac{7{,}500{,}000}{25{,}000} = 300\ \text{s} = 5\ \text{min}$$

A balanced 5-minute job beats a skewed 12-minute one even though it reads slightly more per task. If 5 minutes is still too slow, raise `numPartitions` to 16 (stride 3,750,000, about 2.5 minutes) and accept 16 concurrent source connections. Cache the `MAX` query's result in the control table and refresh it monthly, or recompute it nightly — it is a single index lookup on the primary key and costs almost nothing.

Step 5 — guard rails. Persist `min(order_id)`, `max(order_id)`, `row_count`, and the bounds used, in the same control table that holds `watermark_ts`. Alert when `max(order_id)` drifts more than 10 percent above the recorded `upperBound`, which would have flagged this problem on day one.

Analysis — This problem is about the single most misunderstood aspect of parallel JDBC reads: `lowerBound` and `upperBound` are not filters, they are the endpoints used to compute the stride of the partition predicates. Spark emits `WHERE order_id >= ? AND order_id < ?` for the interior ranges and `WHERE order_id >= ?` for the final one, so the cost of an out-of-date bound is entirely concentrated in the last task. The same skew appears in the opposite direction if the key is sparse: a table with only even `order_id` values and a stride of 6,000,000 still gets eight even ranges, but a table whose key distribution is bimodal (for example an ID space where old IDs are dense and new IDs sparse) produces very uneven partitions regardless of equal numeric width — equal key ranges do not imply equal row counts. That is why production pipelines compute bounds from quantiles of the key rather than from `MIN`/`MAX` when the distribution is known to be skewed, and why the number of partitions must be reconciled with the source database's connection limit and licence. There is also a network argument for pushdown: the more selective the predicate executed on the source, the fewer rows are serialised and shipped, since relational rows are converted to rows on the wire and byte volume dominates transfer time [source p.278]. Finally, note where this work happens: the ingestion lands in cluster memory and Spark builds a DAG of read, transform, and write stages, so a single straggler task in the read stage delays every downstream stage [source p.346]. Keeping bounds current is therefore not a cosmetic tuning detail but a correctness-of-throughput requirement, and recording them alongside the watermark makes the tuning auditable when the job's runtime changes.

actions.text: Now that we've seen how CDC works conceptually, let's walk through a fully worked ingestion problem. This one takes an on-premises SQL Server and lands the sales.orders table into a Bronze Delta table — a nightly snapshot plus hourly change capture. It's a very realistic pattern for the exam.

Problem 1 sets the scene. Your source is a SQL Server table, sales.orders, and the target is bronze_orders in Delta. The design is a nightly full snapshot followed by hourly incremental applies from a change feed. Read the JDBC statement carefully — there's a deliberate trap in it.

The hint tells you exactly where to look: lowerBound and upperBound do not filter anything. They only control how the read is split into partitions. If you rely on them to select a range of rows, you'll silently ingest extra data or miss records entirely. Keep that in mind as we trace the solution.

Step 1 of the worked solution walks through the read statement: url, dbtable, partitionColumn=order_id, lowerBound, upperBound, and numPartitions=8. That gives us eight parallel reads for the snapshot. Then we land the result into bronze_orders and record the high-watermark timestamp so the next run knows where to resume.

The analysis is the exam-critical part. The method choice is deliberate: the bounds are a partitioning device, not a filter. And in the apply step, a sequence or timestamp is required so out-of-order changes don't overwrite newer values, plus a WHEN MATCHED AND op = 'DELETE' THEN DELETE branch to handle deletes properly. Get those two guards right, and you've got this pattern.

scenes.title: Kafka and Event-Streaming Platforms

elements.content: Kafka and Event-Streaming Platforms
Topics, partitions, and consumer offsets feeding continuous streaming data into the lakehouse
1. A Kafka Topic Is a Distributed, Append-Only Log

• Kafka stores records in an append-only log; records are never edited in place and are deleted only by retention policy or compaction [source p.190].

• A topic is split into partitions; the partition is chosen by hashing the record key — identical to the IoT rule of routing one device's messages to one server [source p.207].

Worked example — partition by remainder

Key = numeric ID; partition = ID mod 3.

ID 4 → 4 mod 3 = 1; ID 7 → 7 mod 3 = 1 → same partition, guaranteed order [source p.207].

Trap: hotspotting on the partition key

Keying by US state overloads CA, TX, FL, NY and starves other partitions [source p.207].

Choose a key that distributes evenly.

actions.text: Now that we've covered snapshot-plus-increment CDC, let's turn to the last major streaming source in this lesson: Kafka and event-streaming platforms. Kafka is the backbone of continuous streaming ingestion, and understanding how it feeds data into the lakehouse is a favorite exam topic.

Start with the core mental model: a Kafka topic is a distributed, append-only log. Producers write records into that topic, and the topic is split into partitions. The partition a record lands in is determined by its key. That means Kafka is not a queue that you 'drain' — it's a durable log that keeps records and lets consumers read them at their own pace.

Consumers track their position with offsets — think of an offset as a bookmark into the log. Here's the critical exam point: ordering is guaranteed only within a single partition, never across the whole topic. Once a topic has multiple partitions, there's no global ordering to rely on.

That's the pipeline shape: topics, partitions, and consumer offsets feeding continuous streaming data into the lakehouse. You simply connect the streaming source, read with a structured streaming query, and land records into a Delta table where the rest of the medallion architecture takes over.

Let's walk the worked example. Partitioning is done by a simple remainder: key equals the record's numeric id modulo the number of partitions. If a record maps to partition two, it always lands in partition two. The key and the partition count together fully determine placement.

Now the trap — hotspotting. If you key by user id and one user dominates your traffic, all their records pile into a single partition while others sit idle. That's a skew problem, and it's exactly the kind of scenario the exam wants you to recognize. Choose a high-cardinality, evenly-distributed key whenever possible.

And remember the other exam traps from the objectives: Kafka does not delete messages just because they were consumed — retention is time or size based, not consumption based. And a consumer cannot re-read in global order after a restart. Ordering lives inside a partition, nothing more. Get those right and this section is yours.

scenes.title: Knowledge Check: Kafka and Streaming Ingestion

questions.question: A data engineer writes a Spark Structured Streaming job that reads from Kafka and wants strict ordering guarantees for events within a single log partition. Which configuration approach best satisfies that ordering requirement?

options.label: Rely on the topic-level partitioning of Kafka, since ordering is inherently guaranteed per topic regardless of how Spark reads it
Read the Kafka topic using the subscribe option and process each partition in order without introducing an explicit repartition or shuffle that would reorder records
Set startingOffsets to "latest" so that only newly arriving records are consumed
Use the subscribePattern option instead of subscribe so that multiple topics can be read in parallel

questions.analysis: Ordering is guaranteed per Kafka partition, not per topic, and only if the stream does not reorder records downstream. Reading with subscribe keeps the per-partition order intact, so option B is correct. Option A confuses per-partition with per-topic guarantees — a topic with several partitions delivers no global ordering. Option C controls only where consumption starts, not ordering. Option D changes topic subscription but does not address partition-level ordering. This matches the ingestion-context reasoning discussed in the source [source p.66], where streaming sources may require in-flight consideration before reaching their destination.

questions.question: Which attributes are required to make a JDBC read parallel, so that the data is split into multiple partitions rather than producing a single partition? Select all that apply.

options.label: partitionColumn, naming the numeric column used to divide the data
lowerBound and upperBound, defining the range of values for the partition column
numPartitions, specifying how many parallel read partitions to create
numRecordsPerPartition, limiting the number of rows returned in each partition

questions.analysis: A parallel JDBC read needs partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound, and numPartitions together; without any of these the read falls back to a single partition. Option D is a distractor: Spark's JDBC reader does not use numRecordsPerPartition to control read parallelism. Option A, B, and C are the required options. This connects directly to the prior worked problem on snapshot plus CDC from SQL Server to Delta, where the snapshot read used partitionColumn=order_id with matching lowerBound, upperBound, and numPartitions=8 to parallelise ingestion.

questions.question: A streaming ingestion job uses checkpointing and writes into a Delta table. Which statement best describes the role of checkpoints in achieving exactly-once ingestion?

options.label: Checkpoints record which offsets have been consumed and the state of the stream, so a restarted query resumes from a consistent point without reprocessing or dropping data
Checkpoints compress the incoming records so that duplicates are eliminated before they land in the target table
Checkpoints are only needed for batch-oriented jobs and have no effect on streaming exactly-once guarantees
Checkpoints replace the need for a Delta transaction log by storing the final results of each micro-batch

questions.analysis: Checkpointing tracks consumed offsets and stream state, allowing the engine to resume consistently so all records are processed exactly once. Option B is a misconception: checkpoints do not deduplicate or compress records; deduplication is typically handled by the sink or by MERGE with a key. Option C is wrong because streaming jobs rely on checkpoints to guarantee exactly-once. Option D is wrong; checkpoints and the Delta transaction log serve different purposes. This reflects the broader reliability and durability concern in the source: ingestion systems must not lose or corrupt data, and downstream processes may run late if they break temporarily [source p.266].

scenes.title: Lakeflow Connect and Managed Connectors

elements.content: Lakeflow Connect & Managed Connectors
Managed connectors move SaaS and database data into the lakehouse with minimal code — but they are not zero-configuration.

• Connector handles authentication so you don't store credentials per pipeline.

• Schema drift is reconciled automatically on each ingest.

• Incremental extraction pulls only new/changed rows, not full reloads.

• Sources: databases (JDBC) and SaaS platforms such as Salesforce.

• Destination: Unity Catalog tables in the lakehouse.

• Runs on a schedule you define — you pick the SLA.

Worked example — Salesforce nightly load: 500 rows change per day; a full refresh transfers 4,000,000 rows (3.2 GB).

Connector incremental mode transfers 500 rows (~400 KB) per run — a ~8,000x reduction in data moved [source p.346].
Exam trap: destination schema, schedule, and grants are still your responsibility [source p.304].

actions.text: Now that we've covered JDBC, change data capture, and Kafka, let's move to the most hands-off ingestion path on the exam: Lakeflow Connect and managed connectors.

Here's the core idea. Managed connectors move SaaS and database data into your lakehouse with almost no code. Instead of writing and maintaining your own extract logic, you point the connector at a source, and Databricks handles the mechanics.

Three things the connector takes off your plate: it handles authentication so you don't store and rotate credentials yourself, it absorbs schema drift as the source changes, and it performs incremental extraction so you only pull what's new. That's what we mean by not hand-rolling every pipeline.

The sources fall into two families: databases over JDBC, and SaaS platforms such as Salesforce. Lakeflow Connect lands that data into Unity Catalog tables on a schedule, and for on-premises sources, ingestion gateways and private connectivity keep the traffic inside your own network.

Let's walk the worked example: a Salesforce nightly load of five hundred rows. You configure a destination table in Unity Catalog, set the schedule, and the connector extracts only the changed records each night. No custom API client, no bespoke pagination code.

And here's the exam trap. Managed connectors are not zero-configuration. They still require a destination schema, a schedule, and correct grants. Remember the decision rule as well: reach for a managed connector first, and drop down to JDBC or CDC only when it can't meet your source or latency requirement.

scenes.title: Choosing an Ingestion Path: JDBC vs CDC vs Kafka vs Managed Connector

elements.content: Dimension  |  JDBC batch  |  Snapshot + CDC  |  Kafka streaming  |  Managed connector

Refresh latency (freshness)
JDBC batch: Latency is bounded by the batch schedule, so a nightly job yields data roughly 24 hours stale and an hourly job yields at best one-hour staleness, with no sub-hour guarantee without redesign.
Snapshot + CDC: Continuous CDC captures each database write as an event and can push it to the target in seconds to minutes, whereas batch-oriented CDC applies periodic deltas that land on the schedule interval [source p.162].
Kafka streaming: Kafka is a distributed append-only log that keeps records available for consumers, and the end-to-end latency is set by how quickly the consumer commits offsets, so a well-tuned stream typically sustains near-continuous (sub-minute) freshness.
Managed connector: Freshness is governed by the connector's built-in extraction schedule, and managed connectors handle authentication, schema drift, and incremental extraction without custom code [source p.225], so the achievable latency depends on the schedule the connector offers.

Incremental support and change semantics
JDBC batch: Only full re-reads are native, so you must express incrementality yourself; a simple high-watermark predicate on an updated_at column approximates incremental load but cannot see deletes, and any missed run requires a backfill window.
Snapshot + CDC: The standard pattern is an initial snapshot followed by applying subsequent changes with MERGE INTO using a primary key plus a sequence column, which correctly resolves repeated updates and removes deleted rows.
Kafka streaming: Incremental by construction: each record is an event appended to a topic partition, and consumers replay from stored offsets, so updates and deletes must be encoded as event types (for example tombstone records) rather than inferred from a table state.
Managed connector: Connectors typically extract incremental changes automatically, removing the need to hand-code watermark logic, but the change-capture mechanics are abstracted, so you must read the connector documentation to confirm whether deletes and schema changes are propagated.

Source system impact
JDBC batch: Each run re-reads and transfers the selected rows across the network, so a nightly full-table JDBC read of a large table competes with production traffic for connection slots, CPU, and I/O.
Snapshot + CDC: Log-based CDC reads the database binary log rather than querying the tables, which adds little to no additional load to the source database [source p.68]; timestamp-based or trigger-based CDC still issues queries, so it affects the source more than log-based CDC.
Kafka streaming: Kafka streaming bypasses a backend database entirely because data is pushed directly to an endpoint and buffered by the event-streaming platform [source p.68], so the load falls on producers and the Kafka cluster rather than on an operational database.
Managed connector: Because the connector is managed, the vendor handles the extraction strategy, authentication, and incremental extraction, which is the lowest-effort option overall, though the underlying read pattern (log read vs. polling query) still determines the residual source load.

Operational effort and code volume
JDBC batch: Code volume is small (a single spark.read.format("jdbc") call with url, dbtable or query, user, and a password from a Databricks secret scope), but you own the schedule, watermark bookkeeping, retries, and backfills.
Snapshot + CDC: Effort sits in the middle: you build and maintain the initial snapshot load, the MERGE INTO upsert logic, and the CDC agent or log reader, which is more code than pure JDBC but less than a bespoke streaming pipeline.
Kafka streaming: Effort is highest when hand-rolled because you must manage brokers, topics, partitions, consumer groups, offsets, delivery semantics (at-most-once through exactly-once with idempotent sinks), and checkpoints for fault tolerance.
Managed connector: Effort is lowest overall: Lakeflow Connect handles authentication, schema drift, and incremental extraction so you do not hand-roll each pipeline [source p.225], and configuration replaces most code.

Consistency and exactly-once guarantees
JDBC batch: Consistency is whatever the source database provides at query time, and databases often support consistency configuration at the individual query level (for example, DynamoDB eventually consistent reads versus strongly consistent reads) [source p.225], so the batch you read is a point-in-time view.
Snapshot + CDC: MERGE INTO with primary key plus sequence makes the target converge to the source state under at-least-once delivery, because a later sequence number overwrites an earlier one, but duplicate events without a sequence can double-apply an update.
Kafka streaming: Kafka guarantees ordering only within a partition, never across the whole topic, so per-key processing must partition by the business key; end-to-end exactly-once requires transactions plus an idempotent sink and durable checkpoints.
Managed connector: Guarantees are defined by the connector, not by you; users must verify whether the connector offers at-least-once or exactly-once semantics and how it tracks offsets before relying on the sink being duplicate-free.

Typical use case and decision trigger
JDBC batch: Choose JDBC batch when the freshness requirement is a day or an hour, the table is small enough that a re-read is affordable, and the source can tolerate the added read load.
Snapshot + CDC: Choose snapshot + CDC when you need seconds-to-minutes freshness for a transactional table and cannot accept full re-reads, especially when deletes and updates must be reflected in the target.
Kafka streaming: Choose Kafka streaming when data originates outside a database, such as fleets of IoT sensors emitting readings, where each reading is an event and an event-streaming platform buffers the flow [source p.68].
Managed connector: Choose a managed connector when the lowest-effort path that meets the freshness and source constraints is acceptable, because the connector supplies authentication, schema drift handling, and incremental extraction out of the box.

Takeaway — Pick the lowest-effort path that satisfies the freshness and source constraints rather than defaulting to Kafka: if a nightly batch read meets the SLA, JDBC batch is the correct engineering choice.

Takeaway — Use snapshot + CDC when you need sub-hour freshness on a transactional table with reliable update and delete semantics, and prefer log-based CDC because it adds little to no additional load to the source database [source p.68].

Takeaway — Use Kafka streaming when the source is already an event stream and there is no backend database to read; accept that ordering holds only per partition and that exactly-once requires transactions, idempotent sinks, and checkpoints.

Takeaway — Check the source consistency model (for example, eventually consistent versus strongly consistent reads [source p.225]) before assuming a JDBC or CDC read captures the committed state you intend.

Takeaway — Managed connectors are the first choice when a supported source exists and its schedule meets the SLA, since they absorb authentication, schema drift, and incremental extraction complexity that you would otherwise implement and operate.

actions.text: Building on that rule, let's put all four paths side by side one last time so you can see exactly which dimension separates them. This table is your decision reference for the exam.

Here is the comparison grid: JDBC batch, snapshot plus CDC, Kafka streaming, and managed connectors, scored across five dimensions — latency, incremental support, source impact, operational effort, and code volume. Notice there is no single winner; each row trades something off.

Start with freshness, because that is usually the requirement that eliminates options first. JDBC batch typically gives you daily or hourly data, CDC brings it down to seconds or minutes, Kafka is effectively continuous, and a managed connector follows whatever schedule it exposes. If a business user needs data within the hour, plain JDBC is off the table immediately.

Then weigh source system impact. Each JDBC run re-reads and loads the source database, which can hurt production. CDC instead reads the transaction log, so it touches the source far more gently, and managed connectors offload that whole concern to the platform.

Operational effort and code volume move together. JDBC means hand-written extraction code, scheduling, and watermark bookkeeping you maintain yourself. CDC adds snapshot handling and merge logic. Managed connectors are the lowest effort overall because the connection, schema, and incremental state come out of the box.

And don't forget change semantics. Batch gives you no incremental support, CDC delivers inserts, updates, and deletes as explicit changes, Kafka delivers an ordered event stream, and managed connectors inherit whatever the source supports.

So the takeaway that ties it all together: pick the lowest-effort path that still satisfies your freshness and source constraints. Do not reach for Kafka when a nightly JDBC read is sufficient. That single sentence answers most exam questions on this topic.

questions.question: A team must ingest a SaaS CRM such as Salesforce into Unity Catalog with a near-real-time freshness requirement (data should land within minutes, not hours). The source exposes both a REST API and no transaction-log access, and the team has limited engineering headcount. Per the lesson's guidance on Lakeflow Connect and managed connectors, which ingestion path is the most appropriate choice?

options.label: A hand-rolled JDBC batch pipeline scheduled nightly with a full truncate-and-reload
A managed connector (Lakeflow Connect) ingesting from the SaaS source into Unity Catalog tables on a schedule
spark.read.format("jdbc") with a single partition and an inline password in the notebook
A Kafka topic that the team must build and operate themselves to mirror the CRM's internal objects

questions.correctAnswer: A managed connector (Lakeflow Connect) ingesting from the SaaS source into Unity Catalog tables on a schedule
questions.analysis: Managed connectors are precisely the right tool for this scenario: the lesson teaches that 'managed connectors handle authentication, schema drift, and incremental extraction so you do not hand-roll each pipeline' and that 'Lakeflow Connect ingests from databases and SaaS sources such as Salesforce into Unity Catalog tables on a schedule'. The source material reinforces the underlying motivation: before writing a connector, 'ask yourself: has this already been created? Furthermore, is there a service that will manage the nitty-gritty details of this connection for me? [source p.282]'. Option A is wrong because a nightly truncate-and-reload full refresh cannot meet a minutes-level freshness target and also wastes compute; it also contradicts the warning that deciding on streaming should weigh its benefits against batch [source p.67]. Option C is wrong on two counts: JDBC batch does not target SaaS REST APIs well, and placing a password inline violates the credential-handling rule taught in the JDBC lesson (credentials must come from a Databricks secret scope). Option D is wrong because building and operating a Kafka topic to mirror a SaaS CRM's objects is exactly the 'complicated plumbing' the managed-connector approach is meant to spare the team, and it does not provide the catalog-integrated, schedule-driven sync that Lakeflow Connect offers.
answer: A managed connector (Lakeflow Connect) ingesting from the SaaS source into Unity Catalog tables on a schedule

questions.question: You are comparing a managed connector against a hand-rolled JDBC pipeline for extracting an operational database into Delta Lake. Select ALL statements that correctly characterize the trade-offs the lesson emphasizes.

options.label: A managed connector removes the need to build and maintain custom connector code, because the vendor or cloud fully manages and monitors data syncs [source p.282]
A hand-rolled JDBC pipeline gives you full control over partitioning, so it is always cheaper and lower-maintenance than a managed connector over the long run

Managed connectors typically let you configure the source and target, choose an ingestion mode such as CDC, replication, or truncate-and-reload, and set credentials and update frequency [source p.282]
A hand-rolled JDBC pipeline automatically handles schema drift and incremental extraction without any additional engineering effort

correctAnswer: A managed connector removes the need to build and maintain custom connector code, because the vendor or cloud fully manages and monitors data syncs [source p.282]

Managed connectors typically let you configure the source and target, choose an ingestion mode such as CDC, replication, or truncate-and-reload, and set credentials and update frequency [source p.282]
questions.analysis: Options A and C are directly supported by the source material: managed connector platforms provide 'a standard set of connectors available out of the box to spare data engineers building complicated plumbing', and 'the vendor or cloud behind the scenes fully manages and monitors data syncs' [source p.282]. The same page enumerates the configuration surface: 'set a target and source, ingest in various ways (e.g., CDC, replication, truncate and reload), set permissions and credentials, configure an update frequency' [source p.282]. Option B is a common exam trap: hand-rolling gives control, but the source explicitly frames managed connectors as offloading the 'nitty-gritty details' and ongoing maintenance, so 'always cheaper and lower-maintenance' is false. Option D is also false: schema drift and incremental extraction are called out as things the managed connector handles for you, not something a plain JDBC batch read gives you for free. A hand-rolled pipeline still needs explicit logic to detect new columns or to devise an incremental high-watermark strategy, which is exactly the kind of effort the managed approach is designed to absorb.
answer: A managed connector removes the need to build and maintain custom connector code, because the vendor or cloud fully manages and monitors data syncs [source p.282]

Managed connectors typically let you configure the source and target, choose an ingestion mode such as CDC, replication, or truncate-and-reload, and set credentials and update frequency [source p.282]

questions.question: A source table receives both inserts and hard DELETEs throughout the day, and downstream consumers must reflect row removals within minutes. A nightly batch reload is rejected by the business. According to the CDC lesson, which approach is required and why?

options.label: A nightly truncate-and-reload is sufficient because it is 'incremental' as long as the schedule is daily
Continuous change data capture, because it captures INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE from the source transaction log and applies them near-real-time so deletes propagate promptly
Batch-oriented CDC run once per hour, because it naturally removes deleted rows without any MERGE logic
A single JDBC snapshot taken at the end of each day, because JDBC reads automatically detect and drop rows deleted on the source

questions.correctAnswer: Continuous change data capture, because it captures INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE from the source transaction log and applies them near-real-time so deletes propagate promptly
questions.analysis: The CDC lesson defines the mechanism: 'CDC captures INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE by reading the source transaction log or database triggers', and 'continuous CDC applies change rows to the target near-real-time', with the standard pattern being 'take an initial snapshot, then apply subsequent changes with MERGE INTO using primary key plus sequence'. Because the business requires deletes to propagate within minutes, continuous CDC is the correct choice. Option A is the classic exam trap: a full reload is NOT incremental even if it is scheduled daily, and the description mislabels a full refresh as incremental. Option B is wrong because batch-oriented CDC applies periodic deltas and still requires explicit MERGE semantics to remove deleted rows; it does not remove them 'naturally'. Option C is wrong because a JDBC snapshot is a point-in-time bounded read: it will not detect or drop source-side deletions that occurred mid-day, so deleted rows would linger in the target until the next manual reconciliation. The source material also warns that real-time applications treat data as 'an unbounded, continuous stream' distinct from bounded batch techniques [source p.412], which is precisely why a bounded nightly read cannot satisfy a minutes-level delete-propagation requirement.
answer: Continuous change data capture, because it captures INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE from the source transaction log and applies them near-real-time so deletes propagate promptly

scenes.title: Lesson Recap and Exam Takeaways

elements.content: Lesson Recap and Exam Takeaways
Four ingestion paths — JDBC batch, snapshot + CDC, Kafka streaming, managed connector. Decide by source type + freshness, then pick the lowest-effort path that meets latency.

Batch Sources

JDBC • CDC

Streaming Sources

Kafka • Managed

Decision Rules

Map • Choose
JDBC re-reads source; partitionColumn + numPartitions control parallelism [source p.308]
Kafka: offsets, per-partition ordering, at-least-once default; checkpoints for EOS [source p.191]
Match source type to ingestion path; freshness sets the latency budget [source p.134]
Exam Strategy

1. Source type → possible paths

2. Freshness → latency budget
Next: Transform and Model
Take ingested Bronze data → Silver transformations

actions.text: Let's pull together everything we just covered in this lesson on databases, Kafka, and managed connectors. This recap page is your bridge into the exam, so I want you to leave here with a clear decision framework, not just a list of facts.

We walked through four ingestion paths: JDBC batch, snapshot plus CDC, Kafka for event streams, and managed connectors. Each one maps to a different kind of source and a different freshness requirement.

For batch sources, reach for JDBC when it's a simple, low-frequency read of a database. Reach for CDC — change data capture — when you need to capture updates and deletes incrementally rather than re-reading the whole table.

For streaming sources, Kafka handles continuous event streams with offsets, per-partition ordering, and at-least-once delivery. Managed connectors give you SaaS and database sources with minimal code, which is often the lowest-effort path in the exam.

Here's the decision rule that carries into the exam: map the scenario to the source type plus the freshness requirement, then choose the lowest-effort path that still meets the latency. Don't over-engineer — if batch meets the SLA, batch is the answer.

Two details worth carrying forward. On the JDBC side, remember that it re-reads the source each run, and partitionColumn plus numPartitions controls how that read is parallelized. That's a common exam detail.

On the Kafka side, keep offsets, per-partition ordering, and at-least-once semantics straight. And regardless of path, always account for credential handling, schema drift, ordering guarantees, and exactly-once semantics.

So your exam strategy in two steps: first, identify the source type to narrow possible paths; second, check the freshness requirement to decide where late-arriving data and staleness live in the design.
That closes the ingestion unit. Next, we move into Transform and Model — taking the Bronze data you've just ingested and turning it into Silver transformations and beyond. See you there.

scenes.title: Medallion Architecture: The Three Layers

elements.content: Medallion Architecture: The Three Layers
Medallion architecture is a data design pattern that organizes lakehouse data into Bronze, Silver and Gold layers to progressively improve data quality and structure [source 2].

Bronze — raw

Landing hop. Data is ingested as-is via Auto Loader or Lakeflow, preserving the source schema, including duplicates and nulls.

Silver — validated

Cleansing hop. Records are deduplicated, type-cast, and conformed with slowly changing dimensions (SCD) before joining facts.

Gold — enriched

Consumption hop. Highly aggregated business tables (e.g., daily revenue) are stored as materialized views for BI and ML.
Worked example: one row entered Bronze 3 times (duplicate + null email); Silver keeps 1 clean row; Gold aggregates it into a daily revenue figure.

Each layer guarantees atomicity for efficient analytics, and the terms bronze (raw), silver (validated), and gold (enriched) describe the quality of data in each layer [source 6]. The pattern addresses the problem of data arriving in inconsistent, raw states before reaching analysts or models [source 1].

actions.text: We've now crossed into the Transform and Model unit, and the first thing to understand is the medallion architecture — sometimes called the multi-hop architecture. It's a data design pattern that organizes the data in your lakehouse into three layers: bronze, silver, and gold. As data moves through these layers, its quality and structure improve step by step.

Here's the core idea. Instead of asking analysts and models to cope with messy raw data, the medallion pattern front-loads the cleanup. Each layer is a purpose-built table with a clear job, and that decouples three concerns that used to be tangled together: ingestion, cleansing, and consumption. That separation is what makes pipelines easier to reason about and maintain.

The first hop is Bronze — your raw landing zone. Data is ingested exactly as it arrives, no cleanup, no transformation. But it isn't a dumb file dump: typically Bronze is append-only Delta tables that capture the source faithfully, including its duplicates, gaps, and odd formats. Raw here doesn't mean unmanaged — it means faithfully preserved.

Next comes Silver — the validated layer. This is the cleansing hop: records are de-duplicated, types are enforced, schemas are conformed, and bad rows are filtered or quarantined. Silver is where the data becomes trustworthy and consistent, but it's still organized around the entities themselves — customers, orders, events — not yet shaped for business reporting.

Then Gold — the enriched, consumption hop. Here you find highly aggregated, business-level tables: revenue by region, daily active customers, whatever the BI dashboards and machine-learning models actually query. Gold tables are the ones analysts trust because the business logic has been applied once, consistently, upstream. Now notice this worked example on the slide — one row entered Bronze three times due to duplicate ingestion.

That single duplicated row is a perfect illustration of the whole point: Bronze keeps all three copies because ingestion is raw, Silver removes the duplicates down to one trusted record, and Gold presents that clean record already shaped for consumption. Each hop improves the data step by step, so the problems of inconsistent raw data never reach your analysts.

And remember — each of these hops is an atomic, transactional table. That means if something fails mid-way, you don't get half-written garbage propagating forward. Every layer guarantees atomicity for efficient analytics. On the exam, expect questions that ask you to identify the quality level or the purpose of each layer — raw, validated, enriched — so make sure that mapping is second nature before we move on.
