actions.text: Let's put that layer-mapping instinct to the test. Take each question on your own — no peeking back — and answer honestly so we know exactly where you stand. I'll walk through anything that trips you up once you submit.

scenes.title: Bronze: Raw, Append-Only Ingestion

elements.content: Bronze: Raw, Append-Only Ingestion
The landing layer stores source data exactly as received — no cleansing, no deduplication, no type coercion, insert-only.

• Contents: JSON, CSV, Parquet, log lines, CDC feeds — one raw table per source object.

• Ingest tools: Auto Loader or COPY INTO write new files as new rows; nothing is overwritten in place.

• Added columns are minimal metadata only: _ingest_ts, _source_file, _batch_id.

• No column renaming, no PII masking, no join logic at this hop.

• Consumers: data engineers and pipelines, not analysts or BI tools.

Replay

Rebuild silver and gold from the untouched original when logic changes [source 1]

Audit

Prove what the source actually sent, and when [source 3]

Schema evolution

Absorb new source columns without breaking re-reads [source 3]

Worked example — reordering is provably safe: a raw order feed has 5 deliveries: order_id 1,2,2,3,1. Bronze stores all 5 rows unchanged plus metadata [source 6]. A Silver step keyed on order_id yields 3 distinct orders — 1,2,3 — and the 2-row gap proves the feed needed no bronze-side fix. Because the append preserves every arrival, a later rule change ("2 rows = a cancelled duplicate") is re-runnable against the same bronze file with zero re-ingestion.

actions.text: Now that we've mapped the medallion architecture as a whole, let's zoom into the first layer: bronze — raw, append-only ingestion. If silver is where data gets cleaned and conformed, bronze is where it simply lands, untouched.

Bronze stores source data exactly as received — byte-for-byte, with nothing corrected, nothing filtered, nothing reformatted. Notice the wording: no transformations. The whole point of this layer is source fidelity.

So what actually lands here? Typical bronze content is JSON, CSV, Parquet files, raw log lines, and change data capture — that's a CDC feed, meaning a stream of inserts, updates and deletes captured from a source system. On Databricks you'll ingest these with Auto Loader or COPY INTO, and exam questions love testing which tool fits which pattern.

Why preserve source fidelity at all? Four reasons. First, replay — if your transformation logic changes, you can rebuild silver and gold from the untouched original rather than re-requesting data from the source system. That alone is worth the storage cost.
Second, audit. Bronze is the evidence of what the source actually sent, and when it sent it — invaluable when a business stakeholder asks why a number looks wrong.

Third, schema evolution — bronze can absorb new source columns without breaking, because we haven't locked in a rigid contract. And fourth, reprocessing after logic changes, which follows directly from replay.

Let's look at the worked example — reordering is provably safe. Because bronze is append-only, rows are never mutated in place; a new ingest simply appends. That means the order in which batches arrive never changes the final result once silver applies its deterministic logic. This is exactly the property that makes full reprocessing trustworthy.

One more pattern to remember: bronze updates are insert-only, or insert plus minimal metadata — an ingestion timestamp, the source file name, and a batch ID. And who consumes bronze? Data engineers, not analysts and not BI tools. Analysts should be reading silver and gold. That distinction is a classic exam trap.

scenes.title: Silver: Validated, Conformed, Deduplicated

elements.content: Silver: Validated, Conformed, Deduplicated

Silver = the trusted entity layer: one clean row per customer, order, or product, assembled from many bronze feeds.

Cleansed, validated, and conformed — but not aggregated into business metrics.

Core silver transformations

Type casting, null and constraint handling, dedup, CDC MERGE, cross-source joins

Schema enforcement & evolution

Stable, predictable columns for every downstream consumer

Silver tables are validated, deduplicated, and conformed records that combine multiple bronze sources [source 4]. The layer guarantees atomicity so partial writes never leak into analytics [source 6].

Typical work: cast strings to typed columns, enforce NOT NULL and referential constraints, dedup, MERGE, then join across sources.
Worked example — dedup + MERGE on orders

Bronze lands 3 rows for order_id=42 from retries: ($19.99, 2024-01-05), ($19.99, 2024-01-05), ($24.99, 2024-01-06). Silver keeps the latest (version by ts) → 1 row, $24.99. Downstream consumers now see one order, not three.
Exam trap: silver is cleaned entity data — if a question asks for project-level business metrics, that belongs to gold [source 6].

actions.text: So bronze is raw and append-only. What comes next? Silver. If bronze is the landing zone, silver is where the data actually earns trust. Think of silver as validated, deduplicated, and conformed records — the layer where we turn messy source data into something we're willing to build on.

Here's the key framing: silver is your trusted entity layer. One clean row per entity — per customer, per order, per product. And crucially, silver is where multiple bronze sources get combined into a single conformed view of that entity.

What does the transformation work look like in practice? Type casting to enforce correct data types, null and constraint handling so bad rows don't silently pass through, deduplication to keep a single authoritative row, MERGE for change-data-capture upserts, and joins across sources to stitch the entity together.

Then there's schema enforcement and evolution. Downstream consumers — analysts, BI tools, other pipelines — need stable, predictable columns. So silver is where we decide: do we reject a mismatched record, or do we evolve the schema to absorb it? Either way, the contract stays clean for everyone downstream.

Let's walk the worked example on the slide — dedup plus MERGE on orders. Imagine bronze lands three rows for order_id equal to 42 because the source system retried. A retry, a duplicate delivery, whatever the cause. Bronze faithfully keeps all three — that's its job. Silver is where we collapse them into one correct row.

And watch out for this classic exam trap. Silver is cleaned entity data. It is not project-level business metrics. If a question asks where aggregated revenue by region lives, or a KPI for a dashboard — that is gold, not silver. Silver gives you one trustworthy row per entity; gold gives you the business numbers built on top of it. That distinction comes up again and again on the exam.

questions.question: A data engineering team is reviewing a set of candidate transformations to decide where each belongs in a Databricks lakehouse. Which of the following transformation tasks is the most appropriate responsibility of the silver layer?

Deduplicating records, casting columns to correct types, and applying MERGE upserts to produce validated, conformed tables
Computing monthly revenue rollups and customer lifetime value metrics for executive dashboards
Publishing gold-layer outputs as shared data products across domain teams in a data mesh

questions.analysis: The silver layer is defined as containing validated, deduplicated, and conformed records that combine multiple bronze sources, and its core transformations include type casting, null and constraint handling, deduplication, and MERGE for CDC upserts [source 4]. Option A describes bronze-layer ingestion, which preserves raw source fidelity and is append-only. Option C describes gold-layer business aggregation, which is enriched and business-ready [source 6]. Option D describes data mesh governance, which occurs after gold outputs exist [source 1]. Deduplication, type casting, and MERGE are all explicitly listed as silver responsibilities, making B the correct answer.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describe the silver layer in the medallion architecture? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Silver tables store unaltered source records so the pipeline can be replayed and audited after logic changes
Silver tables are described as conformed and validated because they enforce type casting, null handling, and constraints
Silver tables combine records from multiple bronze sources using joins and MERGE operations
Silver tables apply business aggregation such as revenue rollups before data reaches analysts

questions.analysis: Silver is described as validated, deduplicated, and conformed records that combine multiple bronze sources, and its core transformations include type casting, null and constraint handling, deduplication, MERGE for CDC upserts, and joins across sources [source 4]. Option A is incorrect because preserving unaltered source records for replay and audit is the purpose of the bronze layer, not silver [source 3]. Option D is incorrect because business aggregation is a gold-layer activity, not a silver-layer responsibility; the quality progression places enriched and business-ready data in gold [source 6]. Therefore B and C are correct.

questions.question: A reviewer claims that business aggregation tasks such as building quarterly sales summaries belong in the silver layer. Which statement best explains why this claim is incorrect?

options.label: Business aggregation belongs in the bronze layer because bronze stores the most complete set of raw records
Business aggregation belongs in the gold layer because gold tables are enriched and business-ready, while silver is limited to validated, conformed, and deduplicated data
Business aggregation is not part of the medallion architecture and should be performed only in an external BI tool
Business aggregation belongs in silver only when the source data arrives in an inconsistent raw state

questions.analysis: The medallion architecture progressively refines raw data into trusted, business-ready tables, with a clear quality progression: bronze is raw, silver is validated, and gold is enriched and business-ready [source 6]. Because business aggregation produces enriched, business-ready outputs, it belongs in the gold layer. Silver is scoped to validation, deduplication, conformance, and combining sources, not to business aggregation [source 4]. Option A is wrong because bronze preserves raw source fidelity for replay and audit, not aggregation [source 3]. Option C is wrong because aggregation is a recognized gold-layer activity, not something excluded from the medallion pattern. Option D is wrong because inconsistent raw data is handled before silver, and raw state does not relocate aggregation into silver. Option B is the correct explanation.

scenes.title: Gold: Business-Level Tables Analysts Trust

elements.content: Gold: Business-Level Tables Analysts Trust

Gold tables are project- and business-specific data products: aggregates, dimensional models (star schemas — fact tables plus conformed dimension tables), and curated metrics that encode business logic [source 5].

Because gold is the enriched layer of the medallion progression, rows are no longer raw events or validated records: they are pre-computed answers, so a BI tool can chart them without applying any transformation [source 6].

The grain (the level of detail one row represents) shifts in gold: it is summarized to exactly the level the business question needs — per day, per store, or per customer segment — never the transaction-level grain inherited from bronze [source 3].

Worked example: 40M raw order lines in bronze become a 12M-row silver order table after deduplication. Gold then aggregates to a daily grain: a region-by-day fact table of about 3,650 rows (10 regions × 365 days) joined to store and date dimensions.
Gold is consumed by BI dashboards, scheduled reporting, and data-science feature inputs, and it is refreshed on a schedule or in streaming mode — not queried ad hoc from raw sources [source 1].

actions.text: Now we reach the top of the medallion architecture: the gold layer. These are the business-level tables that analysts actually trust and query every day.

Gold tables are project- and business-specific. Instead of raw or conformed data, gold holds aggregates, dimensional models — that's star schemas with fact and dimension tables — and curated metrics that map directly to a business question.

The big shift here is grain — the level of detail one row represents. Gold tables are summarized to exactly the level the business question needs: per day, per store, or per customer segment. You deliberately give up fine-grained detail to make queries fast and answers unambiguous.

Here's a concrete example. Forty million raw order lines in bronze get aggregated down to a gold table with maybe a few thousand rows — one row per store per day. Same underlying data, radically different grain.

Gold is consumed by BI dashboards, scheduled reports, and data science feature inputs, refreshed either on a schedule or streaming. And because the business logic lives in gold — not scattered across every dashboard — every report shows the same numbers. That's the design goal: a trustworthy, self-service layer analysts can query without re-deriving logic.

scenes.title: Hands-On: Assemble the Layered Flow

content.html:
Hands-On: Assemble the Layered Flow

Medallion architecture — bronze → silver → gold on Databricks

Step 1 / 6

Layer Inspector

click a node
🗄️
Source

Source Systems

Layer map

  • Bronze Ingest raw JSON
  • Silver Deduplicate · Conform types
  • Gold Aggregate to daily KPIs
  • Consume Dashboard / BI

Exam tip: raw data lands in Bronze, cleaned and conformed rows live in Silver, and business-level aggregates ready for BI live in Gold.

nodes.label: Source Systems
nodes.details: Landing point for raw data: operational application databases (via change data capture — CDC, which streams every row-level insert, update, and delete), Kafka / Azure Event Hubs event streams, and REST API endpoints. Data arrives exactly as the producer wrote it. Exam tip: no cleaning, deduplication, or type casting happens at the source layer.

nodes.label: Ingest Raw JSON
nodes.details: Bronze layer — raw and append-only. Land JSON exactly as received using Auto Loader (cloudFiles) or a Lakeflow pipeline, adding ingestion metadata such as file path and ingest timestamp. Schema evolution is allowed; there is no deduplication, no type casting, and no business logic. Delta Lake keeps every version so the raw data can be replayed.

nodes.label: Deduplicate
nodes.details: Silver layer — validated and cleansed. Deduplicate on the business key with MERGE INTO or dropDuplicates, keeping the latest record. When history matters, model a slowly changing dimension (SCD — a technique that tracks how an entity's attributes change over time; Type 2 keeps prior rows with valid-from / valid-to dates).

nodes.label: Conform Types
nodes.details: Silver also conforms data types and enforces quality: cast raw strings to TIMESTAMP, DECIMAL, and BOOLEAN; apply expectations and constraints; and unify naming across sources into one canonical schema. Tables are governed by Unity Catalog, which provides lineage and fine-grained access control.

nodes.label: Aggregate to Daily KPIs
nodes.details: Gold layer — business-level aggregates. Roll silver rows into daily KPIs with GROUP BY and window functions, or publish a materialized view (a precomputed result table that Databricks refreshes automatically as the source data changes) so BI queries stay fast. Gold tables are the certified, consumer-ready layer.

nodes.label: Dashboard / BI
nodes.details: Consuming workloads read gold: Databricks SQL dashboards, Power BI / Tableau, and ML feature tables. End-to-end lineage runs source system → bronze (raw) → silver (cleansed and conformed) → gold (aggregated) → dashboard, and Unity Catalog records every hop.

actions.text: Now we pull the whole medallion architecture together by hand. Think of the medallion architecture as a layered pipeline where raw data enters bronze, gets cleaned and conformed in silver, and becomes trusted business aggregates in gold. Let's walk the layers one by one, starting from where data is born.

actions.content: The full end-to-end flow: source systems down through bronze, silver, and gold, to the consuming dashboard.

actions.text: Use the next button to step through each node in order, then check the side panel to read what that operation actually does and which layer owns it.

actions.content: Step 1: Land the raw JSON exactly as it arrived — no cleaning, no casting.
Bronze is raw and append-only. Schema evolution is allowed, but deduplication, type casting, and business logic are not.

actions.text: Here's the exam trap to internalize: if you place deduplication or type casting in bronze, you've broken the layer's contract. Those belong in silver. Step forward and confirm where the dirty-work operations live.

actions.content: The detail panel exposes the layer's rules, so you can verify each operation belongs where it's been placed.

scenes.title: Check: Mapping Data to Layers

questions.question: A data engineer is onboarding a new source into a Lakeflow pipeline. The requirements state: 'Land change data capture (CDC) events from the source system exactly as received, without altering values, dropping rows, or applying business rules. This table must support full replay and reprocessing if transformation logic changes later.' According to the medallion architecture, which target layer should this table be assigned to, and why?

options.label: Bronze, because bronze tables are raw, unaltered copies of data exactly as received from source systems and are typically append-only, preserving source fidelity for replay and audit [source 3].
Silver, because silver is the layer where change data capture feeds are upserted via MERGE and deduplicated into conformed records [source 4].
Gold, because gold tables are business-ready and therefore must contain the CDC events the business has approved.
Bronze, because bronze is where type casting, null handling, and deduplication are performed so that analysts can query it directly.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct. The requirement is pure ingestion-time fidelity: keep the record exactly as received, do not change values, and retain the ability to replay. Bronze is defined as the raw, unaltered copy of source data, typically append-only, which preserves source fidelity for replay, audit, schema evolution, and reprocessing after logic changes [source 3]. Option B describes a real silver activity (MERGE for CDC upserts, deduplication) but that is a modeling-time concern applied after the raw landing, not the correct home for data that must remain unaltered [source 4]. Option C inverts the medallion quality progression: gold is enriched and business-ready, so raw CDC events cannot belong there [source 6]. Option D is a deliberately blended distractor that attributes silver-layer work (type casting, null handling, deduplication) to bronze; that conflation is the most common student misconception when mapping transformations to layers.

questions.question: A junior engineer proposes a shortcut: 'Why keep a separate bronze layer at all? We can land raw events and immediately cleanse, deduplicate, and aggregate them in one step, then skip straight to the gold KPI table.' In one short, well-reasoned paragraph, explain (a) why raw events must land in bronze before any cleansing occurs, and (b) predict the concrete effect of placing business aggregation directly on raw bronze data instead of on validated silver data. Use the terms ingestion-time concern and modeling-time concern in your answer.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100% total): (1) Bronze-before-cleansing justification - 40%: the answer must state that bronze preserves source fidelity as an unaltered, typically append-only copy, and that this enables replay, audit, schema evolution handling, and reprocessing when transformation logic changes [source 3]. It should note that cleansing is destructive if done at ingestion, so raw data must survive untouched first. (2) Predicted effect of aggregating on bronze - 30%: the answer must predict concrete failures such as double-counted rows from duplicates, wrong totals from bad types or nulls, unstable KPI values when source systems replay or resend events, and an inability to reproduce or correct a dashboard metric because the raw evidence was mutated or discarded. (3) Distinction between ingestion-time and modeling-time concerns - 20%: ingestion-time concerns are capture, fidelity, and replayability; modeling-time concerns are validation, deduplication, conformance, and business aggregation, and these belong to different layers [source 1][source 4]. (4) Clarity and correct use of Databricks/medallion vocabulary - 10%.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: Raw events must land in bronze because bronze is the unaltered, append-only landing zone that preserves source fidelity, enabling replay, audit, schema evolution, and reprocessing after logic changes [source 3]. Cleansing is a modeling-time concern: it is lossy by design (dropping rows, coercing types, overwriting via MERGE), so performing it at ingestion-time destroys the evidence needed to fix a bug or answer an audit question. If business aggregation is placed directly on raw bronze data, the aggregate inherits every defect of the source: duplicate CDC events inflate sums, malformed or null values corrupt averages, and the metric changes whenever the source resends data, breaking stability and comparability. It also violates the progressive-refinement principle that inconsistent, raw inputs require refinement before reaching analysts or models [source 1]. The correct flow is bronze (ingest raw) → silver (validate, deduplicate, conform) → gold (aggregate to business KPIs), where each layer resolves only the concerns appropriate to it [source 4][source 6].
