Work through all three independently, and once you submit, we'll walk through the reasoning together and pick apart any distractors that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Star Schema: The Shape of a Trusted Gold Table

elements.content: Star Schema: The Shape of a Trusted Gold Table
A star schema is one central fact table joined outward to denormalized dimension tables. It is the classic gold-layer shape for a single analytical domain [source 1].
fact_sales (grain: one row per order line)
Foreign keys: DateKey, CustomerKey, ProductKey · Measure: LineAmount
dim_date: DateKey, Year, Quarter, Month, Day. One row per calendar day, shared by every fact table in the domain.
dim_customer: CustomerKey plus effective-date columns so historical attributes stay true to the transaction.
dim_product: ProductKey plus category and brand. Each join uses surrogate keys, not natural IDs.
Denormalization is a deliberate trade: you store redundant attributes to avoid joins, spending a small amount of storage for far simpler queries and faster columnar scans [source 3].
Conformed dimensions (a shared dim_date and dim_customer) let two different fact tables be compared on identical terms instead of re-defining "month" per dashboard [source 1].
Star-schema gold tables are stored as Delta tables, so Databricks SQL, BI tools, and notebooks read the same trusted shape [source 4].

Worked example: 10 million order-line rows share only 2,000 customers. Normalized, "customer tier" costs 10M lookups; denormalized once into dim_customer it is a 2,000-row lookup joined by CustomerKey.

actions.text: Now let's pull everything we just covered about facts, dimensions, and grain into a concrete shape: the star schema. This is what a trusted gold table actually looks like when you lay it out on the page.

A star schema is one central fact table joined out to a set of denormalized dimension tables. Picture it drawn on a whiteboard: the fact table sits in the middle, and the dimensions radiate outward like the points of a star. That visual shape is where the name comes from.

At the center is the fact table — here, fact_sales. Notice the grain statement: one row per order line. That's the same grain declaration we practiced earlier, and it's the most important sentence in the whole model. Every measure you add later must stay consistent with that grain.

The fact table connects to the dimensions through foreign keys: DateKey, CustomerKey, ProductKey, and so on. These are surrogate keys — meaningless integers generated by the warehouse — not the natural business keys from the source system. Surrogate keys keep joins fast and insulate the model from upstream changes.

Now look at the dimensions. dim_date carries DateKey, Year, Quarter, Month, and Day as a single flat table. In a normalized warehouse model you'd split those into separate tables and join them back — the star schema deliberately collapses them together.

dim_customer adds effective-date columns alongside CustomerKey — that's how we version a customer's history over time, which points forward to the SCD strategies coming up shortly. And dim_product carries ProductKey plus category and brand, flat and ready to filter on.

That flattening is denormalization, and it's a deliberate trade. You store redundant values — the category name repeated on every product row — and in exchange you get far simpler queries and much better performance on columnar, distributed engines. On a system like Databricks, the storage is cheap and the joins you avoid are expensive, so the trade almost always pays off.

One more design idea: conformed dimensions. When two different fact tables share the same dim_date and the same dim_customer, you can compare them on consistent terms. Same definition of a month, same definition of a customer — no reconciliation headaches.

And in the lakehouse, those gold tables are stored as Delta tables. That means Databricks SQL, your BI tools, and notebooks all read the very same table — one copy of the truth, governed and queryable from anywhere.

So to recap this page: central fact table with a declared grain, dimensions radiating outward via surrogate keys, denormalization as a performance trade, conformed dimensions for cross-table consistency, and Delta as the storage format underneath. On the next page we'll sort columns into the star so you can test that mental model yourself.

scenes.title: Check: Star Schema Design Decisions

questions.question:
A lakehouse team lists four Gold-layer table candidates. Which listing represents a star schema (rather than a snowflake schema or a fully normalized 3NF model)?

(A) d_product (product_id, name, subcategory_id), d_subcategory (subcategory_id, category_id), d_category (category_id, name), f_sales
(B) f_sales (sales_key, date_key, product_key, store_key, quantity, net_amount), d_date (date_key, day, month, year), d_product (product_key, sku, product_name, category_name), d_store (store_key, store_id, store_name, city, region)
(C) f_sales joined to d_product joined to d_subcategory joined to d_category, with no denormalized attributes carried on d_product
(D) A single 3NF schema in which product, category, subcategory, store, city, and region each occupy one separate table with only foreign keys to their parent table

Choose the best answer.

options.label: Option A
Option B
Option C
Option D

questions.analysis: Option B is a star schema: one central fact table (f_sales) with surrogate keys pointing to a small number of wide, denormalized dimension tables (d_date, d_product, d_store) whose descriptive attributes such as category_name, city, and region live directly on the dimension rather than in further-joined parent tables. Option A and Option D are snowflake / 3NF shapes because the product hierarchy is split across d_product, d_subcategory, and d_category with only foreign keys connecting them. Option C describes the join path a snowflake forces you to traverse, not a star. The distinction matters because a star schema collapses a hierarchy into a single dimension grain so that a BI query touches one dimension join per level, while a snowflake requires a chain of joins. The medallion source establishes the broader context: the Gold layer holds business-ready tables, and the two patterns are composable — 'For a single analytical domain—say, sales reporting or inventory tracking—a well-designed star schema with fact and dimension tables delivers faster query performance and simpler governance than a full medallion pipeline' [source 1].

questions.question:
A retailer runs two business processes: (1) point-of-sale order capture and (2) warehouse shipment reconciliation. Both processes need to report facts grouped by the same calendar period and the same physical store. Which statements correctly describe a conformed dimension in this model? Select all that apply.

A dimension is 'conformed' when it is shared consistently across multiple business processes with the same meaning, grain, and key. A dimension is 'conformed' when it is duplicated per process with a locally invented key so each pipeline can move independently. A dimension is 'conformed' when a single physical d_date and a single physical d_store are reused by both f_orders and f_shipments so cross-process comparisons reconcile on identical member keys. A dimension is 'conformed' when the two processes each maintain their own date table but share the same column names. A dimension is 'conformed' when the same calendar dimension is built once at the Gold layer and every downstream fact references it rather than re-deriving calendar attributes from raw timestamps.

options.label: Option A: Shared across processes with identical meaning, grain, and key
Option B: Duplicated per process with a locally invented key
Option C: Single physical date and store dimension reused by both facts
Option D: Each process keeps its own date table but shares column names
Option E: Built once at Gold and referenced by every downstream fact

questions.analysis: A conformed dimension is shared, not replicated. Option A states the definitional precondition (same meaning, grain, and key). Option C is the worked instance: because f_orders and f_shipments both join to the same physical d_date and d_store, a report that groups both facts by month or store reconciles on identical member keys. Option E is the medallion consequence — the calendar is modeled once at the Gold layer instead of being re-derived from raw timestamps in every pipeline. Option B is the classic student misconception that parallelism requires separate keys, but duplicate dimensions with different keys silently break cross-process comparisons. Option D is subtler: identical column names do not make a dimension conformed; shared identity and shared grain do. The source material frames the layering implication: the medallion architecture 'organizes data in a lakehouse across bronze, silver, and gold layers, progressively refining raw data into trusted, business-ready tables' [source 3], and the conformed dimension is part of that Gold-layer contract.

questions.question: A source CRM system reuses business keys: when a customer account is closed, its customer_id is later reassigned to a new customer. Meanwhile, some accounts transition between tiers without changing customer_id, and a small number of customer_id values are recycled from a legacy system that no longer exists. Explain the role of the surrogate key in the warehouse dimension when the source business key is reused, recycled, or changed, and describe what breaks if you build the dimension on the business key instead.
questions.commentPrompt:
Grading rubric (100% total):
(1) Definition and necessity of surrogate key — 30%. The response must define the surrogate key as a warehouse-generated, meaningless integer (or hash) that uniquely and stably identifies a dimension row, independent of any source-issued identifier, and note the precondition that it must be generated once and never reassigned to a different member.
(2) Handling of reused business keys — 30%. The response must explain that a recycled customer_id is a different real-world entity and therefore must map to a new surrogate key; the old surrogate key is retained for historical fact rows, so historical facts keep pointing at the right person while new facts point to the new surrogate key. A response that only says 'dedupe on customer_id' earns no credit here.
(3) Handling of changed attributes (SCD) — 20%. The response must mention slowly changing dimensions (a warehouse pattern in which historical attribute values are preserved by versioning dimension rows) and note that a change such as a tier transition either overwrites the row (Type 1) or creates a new version row with a new surrogate key (Type 2), and that the surrogate key is what allows two versions of the same business key to coexist.
(4) Failure mode of business-key-only design — 20%. The response must identify the concrete break: building the dimension on the business key overwrites history when the key is reused or its attributes change, causing historical facts to retroactively attribute revenue to the wrong entity. Deduct for vague answers that do not name the historical-accuracy failure.
Award partial credit proportionally; do not award full credit if either the reused-key or SCD discussion is missing.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: The surrogate key is a warehouse-generated identifier whose only job is to be a stable, unique handle for one dimension member. When a customer_id is recycled, the CRM is asserting that a new real-world person now owns that number; the warehouse must issue a new surrogate key and leave the prior surrogate key intact so that facts already recorded against the old member continue to resolve to the old member. When a non-key attribute such as tier changes, we treat it as a slowly changing dimension (SCD): a Type 1 update overwrites the row, while a Type 2 update writes a new version row with a new surrogate key and effective-dating columns, so the same business key legitimately maps to more than one surrogate key. If the dimension is keyed on customer_id, both events cause collapse: a recycled key makes historical facts join to the wrong person, and an attribute change silently rewrites what last quarter meant, which destroys the auditable history that the Gold layer is supposed to provide. The source establishes the quality contract this depends on: 'The terms bronze (raw), silver (validated), and gold (enriched) describe the quality of the data in each of these layers' [source 6], and a conformed, surrogate-keyed dimension is part of what makes the Gold layer trustworthy for cross-process reporting [source 1].

scenes.title: Type 1 vs Type 2 vs Type 3: Comparing SCD Strategies

elements.content: Dimension  |  Type 1 SCD  |  Type 2 SCD  |  Type 3 SCD

Definition and preconditions
Type 1 SCD: Type 1 is the overwrite strategy: when an attribute changes, the existing value in the dimension row is replaced in place, and the precondition is that the business key remains unique because no new rows are created. Edge case: if the dimension row is referenced by fact rows whose values were derived from the old attribute (for example, a fact computed from the old ZipCode), those facts silently lose their historical context after the update [source 6].
Type 2 SCD: Type 2 is the versioning strategy: each change produces a new dimension row carrying EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate (9999-01-01 for the open record), and an is_current flag, so the current row is identified either by is_current = true or by EFF_EndDate = 9999-01-01. The precondition is a surrogate key because the business key is no longer unique once multiple versions exist [source 3].
Type 3 SCD: Type 3 is the prior-value strategy: the original and current values of a changed attribute are stored side by side in additional columns such as Original_ZipCode and Current_ZipCode, keeping exactly one physical row per entity. The precondition is that the set of tracked attributes and the number of retained prior versions are fixed at design time, so it must be extended with new column pairs to hold more than one historical step [source 6].

History preserved
Type 1 SCD: Type 1 preserves no history at all, so after a correction the previous value exists only in the source system, in a backup, or in the Bronze layer's raw append-only records that earlier lessons described as the replay point [source 5].
Type 2 SCD: Type 2 preserves full history indefinitely as long as every change is inserted as a new row, and the set of closed versions forms an auditable timeline of that entity; this is the direct dimension-layer application of the trusted-history principle from the medallion recap.
Type 3 SCD: Type 3 preserves only the immediately previous value per tracked attribute, so a value that changes twice (A to B to C) loses the A state entirely unless additional column pairs are added at design time.

Rows added per change
Type 1 SCD: Type 1 adds zero rows: the change is an UPDATE of the existing row, so entity count and row count stay 1:1 and the table's size tracks the source entity count rather than the change count [source 6].
Type 2 SCD: Type 2 adds exactly one row per change: the previous version is closed by setting its EFF_EndDate and is_current, and a new open version is inserted, so an entity with c changes occupies 1 + c rows.
Type 3 SCD: Type 3 adds zero rows: only the column values on the single existing row are updated, because both the prior and current values live in their own dedicated columns.

Extra columns required
Type 1 SCD: Type 1 requires no additional columns beyond the natural attributes, so if the source always had a ZipCode it simply overwrites that column; a common design mistake is also omitting a load timestamp, which makes it impossible to reconstruct when the overwrite happened.
Type 2 SCD: Type 2 requires at least three metadata columns: EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate (with the 9999-01-01 sentinel for the open record), and is_current, plus a surrogate key if the business key cannot be trusted to remain unique across versions [source 3].
Type 3 SCD: Type 3 requires two columns per tracked attribute (for example, Original_ZipCode and Current_ZipCode), so tracking n attributes costs 2n extra columns and the schema grows linearly with the number of history-bearing attributes.

Key handling
Type 1 SCD: Type 1 keeps the existing key unchanged, so the business key remains a valid dimension key and every fact table foreign key continues to resolve to exactly the same row for the same entity [source 6].
Type 2 SCD: Type 2 requires a surrogate key because the business key is no longer unique once multiple versions exist: the exam trap is that inserting a second version without a surrogate key breaks both the primary key constraint and every fact-to-dimension join by multiplying fact rows across versions [source 3].
Type 3 SCD: Type 3 keeps the same key, which is why the strategy is sometimes described as a Type 1 with history and is favored when foreign keys cannot be remapped, at the cost of a constrained history window.

Reporting impact
Type 1 SCD: Type 1 changes the meaning of historical facts that were computed from the old attribute: a report that groups facts by the attribute will show the new value even for periods before the correction, so it is right for fixing errors but wrong when the attribute is a real reporting slice [source 6].
Type 2 SCD: Type 2 supports as-was and as-is reporting: joining facts to the dimension version whose effective interval contains the fact's event date reproduces the historical state, while filtering is_current = true collapses the dimension back to one current row per entity.
Type 3 SCD: Type 3 supports only as-was and as-is comparison for the current and immediately previous values, so it cannot answer questions that need three or more historical states without extending the schema.

Implementation effort and mechanics
Type 1 SCD: Type 1 is the lowest-effort option: a single MERGE with matched-update and no insert branch, run on the same watermark logic used in the Silver-layer upsert pattern from the earlier retail worked problem.
Type 2 SCD: Type 2 is the highest-effort option because the load must close the matching open record (set EFF_EndDate and is_current = false) and insert the new open record atomically, which is naturally expressed as a MERGE with matched-update plus not-matched-insert or a two-statement transaction, and the version dates must be derived from the change timestamp to avoid overlapping intervals [source 3].
Type 3 SCD: Type 3 is moderate effort but front-loaded: the first implementation is simple, yet every time the business asks to track another historical step the schema must be altered and the load logic rebuilt, so its lifetime cost grows with requirements.

Worked example: two ZipCode changes on one customer
Type 1 SCD: Start: customer 4471 has ZipCode 10001 and one dimension row. After an overwrite to 20002 the table still holds one row for 4471 showing ZipCode 20002, so the historical value 10001 is unrecoverable from the dimension table alone and total rows remain 1, illustrating the Type 1 row-count formula rows = number of entities [source 6].
Type 2 SCD: Start: customer 4471 has one row (version 1, EFF_StartDate 2023-01-01, EFF_EndDate 9999-01-01, is_current = true). A change to 20002 closes version 1 with EFF_EndDate = the change date and inserts version 2 as the open row, then a change to 30003 closes version 2 and inserts version 3: after two changes, total rows = 1 + 2 = 3, and querying the fact stream for events on 2023-06-15 joins to whichever version's interval contains that date [source 3].
Type 3 SCD: Start: customer 4471 has one row. After a change to 20002, the single row shows Original_ZipCode = 10001 and Current_ZipCode = 20002. After a change to 30003, the row shows Original_ZipCode = 20002 and Current_ZipCode = 30003, so the very first value 10001 is lost because the column pair holds only two states, i.e. versions tracked = 2 and total rows stay 1.

Typical use and when it is the right choice
Type 1 SCD: Type 1 is right for correcting data-entry errors (a misspelled city, a wrong sign), normalizing inconsistent source encodings, and attributes that are reassignments rather than business history, where reporting genuinely should reflect only the corrected value [source 6].
Type 2 SCD: Type 2 is right when compliance, audit, or as-was analysis requires the complete timeline, for example tracking a customer's segment or a product's price over years, and it is the standard choice for a conformed customer dimension in the Gold layer described in earlier lessons [source 3].
Type 3 SCD: Type 3 is right for narrow, bounded comparisons such as current-vs-previous region or current-vs-original credit band when foreign keys must stay stable and only the most recent change matters, and it is rarely used because it cannot answer open-ended history questions [source 6].
Takeaway — Choose Type 1 when the change is a correction, not a business event: it minimizes rows, effort, and schema churn, but accept that no history survives the overwrite [source 6].

Takeaway — Choose Type 2 by default for dimensions that drive historical reporting, audit, or compliance, and budget for the surrogate key plus EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate, and is_current on every row [source 3].
Takeaway — Choose Type 3 only when the history requirement is bounded to one prior value and key stability outweighs completeness, remembering that two changes exhaust the pair of columns.

actions.text: Now that we've sorted columns into a star schema, let's tackle the next big modeling decision: what happens when an attribute of a dimension actually changes over time? This is where slowly changing dimensions, or SCDs, come in — a technique for tracking how a dimension's attributes evolve.

This table lines up the three classic strategies — Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3 — across the dimensions that actually decide an implementation: history preserved, rows added per change, extra columns, key handling, reporting impact, and implementation effort. Let's walk through each row of comparison.

Start with history. Type 1 preserves no history at all — you simply overwrite the old value in place. Type 2 preserves full history by adding a brand-new row version every time the attribute changes. Type 3 keeps only a limited window of history, typically just the previous value alongside the current one.

This connects directly to row counts. Type 1 adds zero rows — the count stays flat. Type 2 grows the table with every change, one new row per version. Type 3 adds no rows either, because it stores the change in extra columns rather than new rows.

On extra columns: Type 1 requires none. Type 2 adds EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate — with 9999-01-01 marking the open current record — and an is_current flag. Type 3 adds paired columns like Original ZipCode and Current ZipCode, which caps you at a fixed number of changes.

Key handling is where the exam trap lives. Type 1 keeps the existing key, so nothing downstream breaks. Type 2 requires a surrogate key, because once multiple versions of the same business entity exist, the business key is no longer unique. Type 3 keeps the key unchanged but adds the history columns.

The reporting impact follows from that. Type 1 changes the meaning of historical reports, because past facts now point at the corrected value. Type 2 lets you report on the value as it was at the time — you preserve point-in-time accuracy. Type 3 lets you compare only the current value against the immediately previous one.

Finally, effort. Type 1 is the simplest — a plain update. Type 2 is the most involved: merge logic, key generation, and date-stamping. Type 3 sits in the middle but is rarely used, because the fixed-column limit makes it brittle in practice.

So the takeaway: choose Type 1 when the change is a correction of bad data and you genuinely don't need the old value. Choose Type 2 by default whenever the history itself matters for analysis or audit. And reserve Type 3 for narrow cases where only the previous value is ever needed.

actions.topic: Choosing an SCD strategy under real requirements
actions.prompt: Consider a retail customer dimension where the marketing team needs to compare this year's regional sales against the region each customer lived in at time of purchase — but a separate team only ever wants the customer's current email address. Which attributes in this dimension would you model as Type 1, which as Type 2, and why?

scenes.title: Worked Problem: A Type 2 SCD Row-Versioning Walkthrough

elements.content: Problem 1

Your gold-layer customer dimension `dim_customer` is a Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD Type 2: a dimension that preserves history by writing a new row for every version of an entity instead of overwriting the old one). Its primary key is a surrogate key (`customer_sk`), an artificial integer generated by the pipeline; its business key, often called the natural key, is `customer_id`, the identifier the source system itself uses. Before the change, the table contains exactly one row for the customer with `customer_id = 4471`:

| customer_sk | customer_id | zip | eff_start_date | eff_end_date | is_current |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 981 | 4471 | 10001 | 2021-06-01 | 9999-01-01 | true |

On 2024-03-15 this customer relocates from ZIP 10001 (New York, NY) to ZIP 94105 (San Francisco, CA). Show the required change: (a) the two DML statements, in the correct order; (b) the complete contents of the table afterwards; (c) the four invariants that must hold for customer 4471; (d) the two values that must never appear in the modified row 981.
Hint: Expire first, insert second, and touch nothing else on the old row.

Worked solution
Step 0 — declare the grain in words before writing any code: one row per customer per version, that is, one row per (customer_id, eff_start_date). Every rule below follows from that one sentence. If a change creates a new version, it creates a new row; if it does not create a new version, no row may be added.

Step 1 — expire the current version. The old row is terminated, not rewritten:

UPDATE dim_customer

SET eff_end_date = DATE '2024-03-15',

is_current = false

WHERE customer_sk = 981;

Notice what is deliberately absent from the SET clause: `zip`. The value 10001 must remain byte-for-byte on row 981, because row 981 is the only surviving record that customer 4471 lived in ZIP 10001 from 2021-06-01 to 2024-03-15. The columns `customer_id`, `zip` and `eff_start_date` are never touched on an existing Type 2 row.

Step 2 — insert the new version under a brand-new surrogate key:

INSERT INTO dim_customer

(customer_sk, customer_id, zip, eff_start_date, eff_end_date, is_current)

VALUES

(1492, 4471, '94105', DATE '2024-03-15', DATE '9999-01-01', true);

1492 is produced by the pipeline — a monotonically increasing sequence, an IDENTITY/GENERATED column, or a deterministic hash such as sha2(customer_id || eff_start_date, 256). It has no arithmetic relationship to 981; it is simply the next unused version identifier for this entity.

Steps 1 and 2 must execute as one atomic unit of work (a single table transaction, or one MERGE statement). If a concurrent reader queries the table between them, that reader sees either zero current rows for 4471 or the wrong current row.

Step 3 — the table afterwards, two rows:

| customer_sk | customer_id | zip | eff_start_date | eff_end_date | is_current |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 981 | 4471 | 10001 | 2021-06-01 | 2024-03-15 | false |

| 1492 | 4471 | 94105 | 2024-03-15 | 9999-01-01 | true |

Row count for this customer: 1 before, 2 after. Total table row count increases by exactly 1.

Step 4 — the invariants that must hold for customer 4471:

1. Version count: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dim_customer WHERE customer_id = 4471 returns 2.

2. Exactly one current version: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dim_customer WHERE customer_id = 4471 AND is_current = true returns 1.

3. Contiguous, non-overlapping validity intervals: under the half-open convention [eff_start_date, eff_end_date), row 981 covers 2021-06-01 through 2024-03-14 and row 1492 covers 2024-03-15 onward. No date is covered by both rows, and no date from 2021-06-01 to today is covered by neither. Equivalently, successor.eff_start_date = predecessor.eff_end_date.

4. Surrogate-key uniqueness: SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT customer_sk) FROM dim_customer returns 0 for the whole table.

Step 5 — the values that must never appear in the modified row 981: the new ZIP 94105 must never be written into row 981 (that is the in-place update error), and is_current = true must not survive on row 981. Symmetrically, the retired ZIP 10001 must never be written into the new row 1492. A Type 2 row is immutable once written: only its closing metadata (eff_end_date, is_current) may ever change.

Analysis — Why this works: the surrogate key is a version identifier, not a customer identifier. Facts loaded before 2024-03-15 were stamped with 981, so they keep pointing at the 10001 row forever, and facts loaded after 2024-03-15 carry 1492 and resolve to 94105. History is preserved in the dimension rather than re-derived from the fact table, which is the entire point of Type 2.

Where this sits in the architecture: the raw relocation event arrives from the source system as a change-data-capture record in bronze, the layer where data arrives in inconsistent, raw states that require progressive refinement before reaching analysts or models [source 1]. The versioned row set written above is the refined, validated form of that event. The medallion architecture organizes lakehouse data across bronze, silver and gold layers that progressively refine raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3], and the terms bronze (raw), silver (validated) and gold (enriched) describe the quality of the data in each of those layers [source 6]. A conformed, historically complete `dim_customer` is exactly the kind of table that must be shared, unchanged, by every fact table in the domain.

The three classic failures, and what each one costs:

Updating in place — running SET zip = '94105' on row 981 — is a Type 1 change, not a Type 2 change. Row 981 still carries the surrogate key referenced by every historical sale, so every sale made in Manhattan before 2024-03-15 now reports against a San Francisco ZIP. The error is silent: no query fails, the numbers are just wrong.

Reusing surrogate key 981 for the new version makes the join from fact to dimension one-to-many. Every fact row that references 981 now matches two dimension rows, so every historical revenue figure fans out and doubles. This is the single most damaging SCD mistake because it corrupts the fact table's numbers without touching the fact table.

Deleting the old row instead of expiring it orphans the historical facts. In an inner join those sales disappear entirely; in a left join they appear with NULL ZIPs. Both outcomes are revenue losses that nobody notices until a reconciliation fails.

Interval convention: choose either half-open [start, end) or closed [start, end] and enforce it everywhere. Under the half-open convention used here, expiry is written as the successor's start date (2024-03-15); under the closed convention it would be 2024-03-14. Mixing the two conventions produces exactly one day of double counting per change — small enough to survive testing, large enough to fail an audit.

Generalization: the expire-then-insert pattern is identical for any history-tracked attribute — product price, employee department, account tier, supplier terms. The decision rule is always the same question: must an analyst be able to ask what was true on a past date? If yes, Type 2 with a fresh surrogate key per version; if the old value was simply wrong, see the Type 1 discussion in the next problem.
Problem 2

`fact_sales` in the gold layer is at the grain one row per sales transaction, with columns (sale_sk, sale_date, customer_sk, net_amount). Two transactions belong to customer 4471, whose dimension history is the two-row table produced in the previous problem:

| customer_sk | customer_id | zip | eff_start_date | eff_end_date | is_current |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 981 | 4471 | 10001 | 2021-06-01 | 2024-03-15 | false |

| 1492 | 4471 | 94105 | 2024-03-15 | 9999-01-01 | true |

The fact rows are:

| sale_sk | sale_date | customer_sk | net_amount |

|---|---|---|---|

| 55210 | 2024-02-10 | 981 | 250.00 |

| 55211 | 2024-03-20 | 1492 | 175.50 |

(a) Write the SQL that reports revenue by ZIP and compute the exact result. (b) An intern rebuilt the same report but keyed the fact table on the natural key `customer_id` and joined on it with no date predicate; show the result set of that join and quantify the error in the grand total and in each ZIP. (c) Write the point-in-time predicate that repairs the natural-key join, and state the single interval-convention decision it depends on.
Hint: Count the join rows before you sum anything.

Worked solution
(a) Surrogate-key join with a defensive point-in-time predicate:

SELECT d.zip, SUM(f.net_amount) AS revenue

FROM fact_sales f

JOIN dim_customer d

ON f.customer_sk = d.customer_sk

WHERE f.sale_date >= d.eff_start_date

AND f.sale_date < d.eff_end_date

GROUP BY d.zip;

Each fact row matches exactly one dimension row, because customer_sk is unique in the dimension:

- sale 55210 carries customer_sk = 981, whose row holds ZIP 10001 and covers 2021-06-01 up to but excluding 2024-03-15. 2024-02-10 falls inside, so it counts against 10001.

- sale 55211 carries customer_sk = 1492, whose row holds ZIP 94105 and covers 2024-03-15 onward. 2024-03-20 falls inside, so it counts against 94105.

Result: ZIP 10001 = 250.00, ZIP 94105 = 175.50, grand total = 425.50. Two input fact rows, two output join rows — a one-to-one match.

(b) The natural-key version:

SELECT f.sale_sk, d.zip, f.net_amount

FROM fact_sales f

JOIN dim_customer d

ON f.customer_id = d.customer_id;

Both fact rows carry customer_id = 4471, and the dimension holds two rows with customer_id = 4471, so each fact row matches both dimension rows. The join returns 2 x 2 = 4 rows:

| sale_sk | zip | net_amount |

|---|---|---|

| 55210 | 10001 | 250.00 |

| 55210 | 94105 | 250.00 |

| 55211 | 10001 | 175.50 |

| 55211 | 94105 | 175.50 |

Grouped by ZIP: ZIP 10001 = 250.00 + 175.50 = 425.50; ZIP 94105 = 250.00 + 175.50 = 425.50; grand total = 851.00.

Error quantification against the true figures: the grand total is overstated by 851.00 - 425.50 = 425.50, which is 100 percent of the true total (one extra copy of every fact). ZIP 10001 is overstated by 425.50 - 250.00 = 175.50, a relative error of 175.50 / 250.00 = 70.2 percent. ZIP 94105 is overstated by 425.50 - 175.50 = 250.00, a relative error of 250.00 / 175.50 = 142.5 percent. Note that the per-ZIP numbers are wrong in both directions and both ZIPs report the identical, meaningless figure of 425.50 — a strong tell that a fan-out has occurred.

(c) The repair is the point-in-time predicate:

AND f.sale_date >= d.eff_start_date

AND f.sale_date < d.eff_end_date

This restores exactly one matching dimension row per fact row and returns the correct 425.50. It works only because the interval convention is half-open: a sale on the boundary date 2024-03-15 matches the new version (94105) and not the expired one. With closed intervals you would need `f.sale_date <= d.eff_end_date`, and you would have to guarantee that expiry is always written as one day before the successor's start date — otherwise boundary days are counted twice. The convention must be documented and enforced by tests, because it is invisible in the data itself.

Analysis — This problem is the proof of why the surrogate key exists. The surrogate key is a version identifier that the fact table copies at load time; the natural key is a customer identifier that is stable across versions. Joining facts to a versioned dimension on the natural key produces a many-to-many match, and many-to-many matches inflate aggregates silently — nothing errors, the number is simply doubled. A useful rule of thumb: if a join between a fact table declared at transaction grain and a dimension returns more rows than the fact table contains, the surrogate key or the point-in-time predicate is wrong.

Why the point-in-time predicate is still worth writing even with surrogate keys: late-arriving facts. If an order that actually occurred on 2024-03-10 arrives in the warehouse on 2024-04-02, a pipeline that stamps the surrogate key at load time (2024-04-02) would stamp 1492 and place a Manhattan sale in San Francisco. A corrected load that back-dates the event to 2024-03-10 should be resolved by the interval predicate, which requires the old row to still exist. This is the operational reason a Type 2 dimension must never have its expired rows deleted or collapsed.

The `is_current = true` trap: many BI tools simplify reporting by always filtering the dimension to `is_current = true`. That is correct for a report about customers as they are today, and catastrophically wrong for any historical revenue report, because it re-labels every historical fact with the current address. Every report must therefore make an explicit choice between the current view (filter on is_current) and the historical view (filter on the validity interval). Mixing them within one model is a governance failure, not a query-writing failure.

A further convention check: with the half-open interval used above, using `BETWEEN eff_start_date AND eff_end_date` would put any activity on 2024-03-15 into both versions, adding one day of double counting per attribute change — small enough to pass casual testing. Teams should pick half-open intervals, document the choice in the table description, and add an automated overlap test.

Schema context: for a single analytical domain — sales reporting, say — a well-designed star schema with fact and dimension tables delivers faster query performance and simpler governance than a full medallion pipeline [source 1]. That advantage depends entirely on the dimension behaving as one row per version with a unique surrogate key; star schemas with broken SCD logic under-perform hand-written SQL and mislead more confidently. The overall purpose of this pipeline is unchanged: creating reliable, scalable systems that transform raw inputs into trusted insights [source 5].
Problem 3

Two change requests arrive for `dim_customer` on the same day.

Request (i): the stored name for customer 4471 is `Jon A. Smith`, but the source system confirms it should always have been `John A. Smith` — a data-entry typo that has been carried since 2021, not a real-world event.

Request (ii): customer 9044, whose only row is (customer_sk = 3050, zip = 85001, eff_start_date = 2022-02-01, eff_end_date = 9999-01-01, is_current = true), moves to ZIP 85251 on 2024-04-01.

(a) Classify each change as Type 1 or Type 2, justify the classification with the decision rule, and show the resulting table state for each. (b) Compute the row counts after the changes. (c) Then suppose customer 4471 changes ZIP three more times, on 2024-07-01, 2024-11-20 and 2025-02-14, and receives two further typo corrections; compute the number of rows and the number of current rows for this customer, and say how many rows each typo correction touches. (d) Name the four wrong answers a grader would expect to see and explain what each one breaks.
Hint: Ask whether the previously stored value was wrong, or whether the world changed.

Worked solution
(a) Request (i) is a Type 1 change (overwrite, no history). The previously stored value was wrong; nothing about the customer changed in the real world. The repair is:

UPDATE dim_customer

SET full_name = 'John A. Smith'

WHERE customer_id = 4471;

This statement updates 2 rows — the expired 10001 version (customer_sk = 981) and the current 94105 version (customer_sk = 1492) — because in a Type 2 dimension the descriptive attribute is repeated on every version of the entity, and leaving the typo on the older version would make history internally inconsistent. No new surrogate key is generated, no new row is inserted, and the row count is unchanged. Note the deliberate choice to filter on the natural key rather than on customer_sk: a Type 1 correction applies to the entity, not to one version of it.

Request (ii) is a Type 2 change (new version, history preserved). The customer really moved; the previously stored value 85001 was correct until 2024-04-01. The repair is the expire-then-insert pair:

UPDATE dim_customer

SET eff_end_date = DATE '2024-04-01',

is_current = false

WHERE customer_sk = 3050;

INSERT INTO dim_customer

(customer_sk, customer_id, zip, eff_start_date, eff_end_date, is_current)

VALUES

(2101, 9044, '85251', DATE '2024-04-01', DATE '9999-01-01', true);

The decision rule that separates the two cases: if the previously stored value was wrong, overwrite it (Type 1); if the previously stored value used to be right, keep it and add a version (Type 2).

(b) Row counts. Customer 4471: 2 rows before the name correction, 2 rows after, of which 1 is current. Customer 9044: 1 row before, 2 rows after, of which 1 is current. Total table row count increases by 1 (the single new 9044 version).

(c) Customer 4471 after all changes. Start: 1 initial row. The first relocation on 2024-03-15 added 1 row; the three later relocations (2024-07-01, 2024-11-20, 2025-02-14) each add 1 row, so rows = 1 + 4 = 5. The two typo corrections add no rows: rows remain 5. Current rows remain exactly 1, because each relocation closes the previous version before opening the next. Each typo correction touches all 5 rows, since the name attribute is repeated on every version of the entity and consistency demands that all versions agree.

Check queries: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dim_customer WHERE customer_id = 4471 returns 5; the same query with AND is_current = true returns 1. Storage growth for a population of 50,000 customers under an assumed 12 percent annual movership rate is 50,000 x 0.12 = 6,000 extra rows per year — about 12 percent growth per year in the dimension, which is negligible next to the transaction-grain fact table. The cost of Type 2 is therefore almost entirely query complexity, not storage.

(d) The four wrong answers and what each breaks:

1. Updating the ZIP in place for request (ii) — that is Type 1 applied to a genuine Type 2 change. Every historical fact row pointing at customer_sk = 3050 is re-labelled with 85251, so revenue that genuinely occurred while the customer lived in 85001 is reported against 85251. History is destroyed irreversibly unless the table has time travel or full history enabled.

2. Reusing customer_sk = 3050 for the new version — the dimension now contains two rows with the same primary key. The join from fact to dimension becomes one-to-many and every historical fact for this customer doubles in any aggregate.

3. Inserting a new row for the typo in request (i) — the dimension gains versions that differ only by a misspelling, with identical ZIPs and overlapping or adjacent intervals. Version counts, customer counts built on the dimension, and the interval invariants all become ambiguous, and the analyst can no longer tell a real move from a data-entry fix.

4. Deleting the old row after expiring it — a superficially tidy answer that orphans every historical fact row referencing customer_sk = 3050. Inner joins drop those sales entirely; left joins return NULL ZIPs. The dimension looks clean and the revenue number is wrong.

A fifth, subtler error worth flagging: leaving `is_current = true` on the expired row while also inserting the new current row. Any consumer using the standard current-view filter then sees two current rows for one customer and reports the customer twice.

Analysis — The classification rule is the whole examinable content: wrong value, overwrite (Type 1); value used to be right, add a version (Type 2). Where an attribute is genuinely corrected rather than changed, most warehouse designs apply the correction across all versions of the natural key so that history stays internally consistent — a hybrid that is sometimes labelled Type 2 with a Type 1 correction, and which must be documented because it means some columns of a Type 2 row are, exceptionally, mutable.

Alternatives that exist and when they are used: Type 3 keeps a previous-value column alongside the current one and tracks exactly one prior state — cheap but useless beyond a single change and awkward in queries. Type 6 combines a current-value column, a historical value column and Type 2 rows to support both fast current-state filtering and full history. Neither replaces Type 2 when the requirement is full temporal reconstruction, which is the usual requirement in a lakehouse serving BI plus data science.

Cost model: Type 2 moves cost from storage to semantics. Rows grow linearly with the number of genuine changes, and one current row per entity must be maintained as an invariant. Type 1 moves cost from semantics to truth: it is cheaper to store and impossible to query historically. The choice should be driven by the stated reporting requirement, exactly as grain is declared before writing code.

Where the choice is registered in the architecture: medallion architecture is a data design pattern that organizes lakehouse data into Bronze, Silver and Gold layers to progressively improve data quality and structure [source 2]. The Type 1 or Type 2 decision is part of the silver-to-gold modeling contract, because downstream facts inherit whatever identity semantics the dimension exposes. Once a fact table has been loaded against natural-key semantics, switching to surrogate-key Type 2 semantics is a migration, not a configuration change: the fact table must be re-keyed by a point-in-time lookup, and any aggregate built on the old join must be rebuilt.

Common student errors to watch for: treating every correction as a new version (version inflation), treating every change as an overwrite (history loss), filtering Type 1 corrections on customer_sk instead of customer_id so the old version keeps the typo, and asserting that Type 2 is always the right answer. Type 2 is right only when the business question requires historical state; for an attribute nobody ever queries historically — a marketing opt-in flag used only for suppression lists — versioning adds interval logic and join fan-out risk for no analytical benefit.
Problem 4

A junior engineer rebuilt `dim_customer` overnight. The documented convention for this table is that `eff_end_date` is exclusive (its value equals the successor version's `eff_start_date`, and 9999-01-01 is the open-ended sentinel). The audit query SELECT * FROM dim_customer ORDER BY customer_id, eff_start_date returns exactly these six rows:

| customer_sk | customer_id | zip | eff_start_date | eff_end_date | is_current |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 981 | 4471 | 10001 | 2021-06-01 | 2024-03-15 | false |

| 981 | 4471 | 94105 | 2024-03-15 | 9999-01-01 | true |

| 1655 | 4471 | 94105 | 2024-03-15 | 9999-01-01 | true |

| 3050 | 9044 | 85001 | 2022-02-01 | 2023-12-31 | false |

| 3061 | 9044 | 85251 | 2024-01-01 | 9999-01-01 | true |

| 2077 | 9910 | 30301 | 2022-05-01 | 2024-05-01 | true |

(a) List every invariant violation, naming the responsible rows and the concrete downstream error each one causes. (b) Write the DML that repairs the table. (c) Show the repaired table. (d) Write the production validation queries that would have caught each defect before it shipped. (e) Explain the most likely pipeline bug that produced the duplicate row 1655.
Hint: There are four independent defects, and one of them is only visible because the interval convention is exclusive.

Worked solution
(a) Four invariant violations.

Defect 1 — surrogate key not unique. Rows 1 and 2 share customer_sk = 981 while holding different ZIPs. One primary key identifies two versions, so every fact row that was loaded against 981 matches two dimension rows when joined. Impact: all historical revenue for customer 4471 is counted twice, and the two copies land in different ZIPs, so both per-ZIP figures are wrong. This is the failure mode that corrupts a fact table without touching the fact table.

Defect 2 — more than one current row for one natural key. Customer 4471 has two rows with is_current = true (the 94105 versions with sk 981 and sk 1655), and they carry identical zip values and identical validity intervals. Impact: any consumer that uses the standard current-view filter, WHERE is_current = true, returns customer 4471 twice, so current-customer counts, per-customer averages and any gold aggregate built on that view are double counted. The two rows being exact duplicates confirms this is a repeated write, not a genuine version.

Defect 3 — a gap in coverage. Customer 9044 has row 3050 closing at eff_end_date = 2023-12-31 and row 3061 starting at 2024-01-01. Because eff_end_date is exclusive, row 3050 covers up to and including 2023-12-30; the date 2023-12-31 belongs to no version at all. Impact: a fact row dated exactly 2023-12-31 disappears from an inner join (silent revenue loss) or returns a NULL ZIP from a left join (silent misattribution). The invariant here is successor.eff_start_date = predecessor.eff_end_date; the repair is to push 3061's start back to 2023-12-31.

Defect 4 — a row that is simultaneously closed and current, and a natural key with no open version. Row 2077 for customer 9910 carries is_current = true while also carrying a finite eff_end_date of 2024-05-01, which contradicts itself. Reading the row as an expiry, the real defect is that the successor version was never inserted: after 2024-05-01 customer 9910 has neither a current row nor any covering interval, so every fact row for this customer dated 2024-05-01 or later falls outside all versions and vanishes from every point-in-time join.

(b) Repairs, one statement group per defect:

Defect 1 — give the newer version its own key (rather than renumbering the older one, which fact rows already reference):

UPDATE dim_customer

SET customer_sk = 1492

WHERE customer_sk = 981

AND zip = '94105';

Defect 2 — delete the redundant duplicate. Only run a delete after proving the row is a pure duplicate of a surviving current row in every attribute except the surrogate key:

DELETE FROM dim_customer

WHERE customer_sk = 1655;

Defect 3 — close the gap by moving the successor's start date back to the predecessor's end date:

UPDATE dim_customer

SET eff_start_date = DATE '2023-12-31'

WHERE customer_sk = 3061;

Defect 4 — correct the flag and open the missing version (the post-move ZIP from the source feed is 30305):

UPDATE dim_customer

SET is_current = false

WHERE customer_sk = 2077;

INSERT INTO dim_customer

(customer_sk, customer_id, zip, eff_start_date, eff_end_date, is_current)

VALUES

(2098, 9910, '30305', DATE '2024-05-01', DATE '9999-01-01', true);

(c) Repaired table, six rows, all invariants satisfied:

| customer_sk | customer_id | zip | eff_start_date | eff_end_date | is_current |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 981 | 4471 | 10001 | 2021-06-01 | 2024-03-15 | false |

| 1492 | 4471 | 94105 | 2024-03-15 | 9999-01-01 | true |

| 3050 | 9044 | 85001 | 2022-02-01 | 2023-12-31 | false |

| 3061 | 9044 | 85251 | 2023-12-31 | 9999-01-01 | true |

| 2077 | 9910 | 30301 | 2022-05-01 | 2024-05-01 | false |

| 2098 | 9910 | 30305 | 2024-05-01 | 9999-01-01 | true |

Per-customer check: 4471 has 2 rows and 1 current; 9044 has 2 rows and 1 current; 9910 has 2 rows and 1 current. Six rows, six distinct surrogate keys, three current rows for three customers.

(d) The four validation queries, run as post-load assertions; each should return zero rows.

Surrogate-key uniqueness:

SELECT customer_sk, COUNT(*)

FROM dim_customer

GROUP BY customer_sk

HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

One current row per natural key:

SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*)

FROM dim_customer

WHERE is_current = true

GROUP BY customer_id

HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Overlaps and gaps, expressed as one self-join over consecutive versions:

SELECT a.customer_id, a.customer_sk, a.eff_end_date, b.eff_start_date

FROM dim_customer a

JOIN dim_customer b

ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id

AND a.customer_sk <> b.customer_sk

AND a.eff_start_date < b.eff_start_date

WHERE a.eff_end_date <> b.eff_start_date;

Any row returned is either an overlap (a.eff_end_date greater than b.eff_start_date) or a gap (a.eff_end_date less than b.eff_start_date). Pair it with an explicit overlap test on half-open intervals, which is cleaner to reason about:

SELECT a.customer_id

FROM dim_customer a

JOIN dim_customer b

ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id

AND a.customer_sk <> b.customer_sk

AND a.eff_start_date < b.eff_end_date

AND b.eff_start_date < a.eff_end_date

GROUP BY a.customer_id;

Flag and interval consistency:

SELECT *

FROM dim_customer

WHERE (is_current = true AND eff_end_date <> DATE '9999-01-01')

OR (is_current = false AND eff_end_date = DATE '9999-01-01');

(e) The likely pipeline bug behind row 1655: a non-idempotent merge. If the MERGE matches the incoming change only on customer_id plus the condition is_current = true, then a retry of the same micro-batch finds no current row to update at the moment of evaluation — for example because the previous run's update and insert were not committed in one transaction, or because the match condition also included the new ZIP, which does not yet exist — so the insert branch fires a second time and produces a byte-identical current row. The fix is to key the merge deterministically: match on (customer_id, eff_start_date) or on the source change event identifier (the CDC log position or event id), so that replaying the same batch is a no-op. Equivalently, express the whole change as one MERGE statement with a stable match key and wrap it in a transaction, because atomic application of the expire and the insert is what makes the operation idempotent and re-runnable. Lakehouse table formats are described as guaranteeing atomicity for efficient analytics [source 6], which is exactly the property being relied on here.

Analysis — These four checks are not optional hygiene; they are the definition of the grain one row per customer per version. Each invariant maps to a specific way a report breaks: a duplicated surrogate key causes fan-out and doubled aggregates; a duplicated current row causes double-counted customer counts; a gap causes silently dropped or NULL-attributed facts; a stale or contradictory is_current flag causes an entire entity to vanish from time-based joins. Of the four, the two that cause the most damage are the ones that produce no error message at all — fan-out and gaps — because the pipeline reports success and the dashboard reports a plausible wrong number.

The engineering lesson is that a Type 2 dimension needs both a correct write path and an enforcing test suite. Write path: one atomic MERGE with a deterministic match key, applying expire-then-insert. Test path: the four queries above as post-load assertions, failing the job rather than logging a warning. In a Databricks lakehouse these are naturally expressed as data-quality expectations attached to the pipeline, so a violating batch is quarantined instead of published. The medallion architecture organizes data in a lakehouse across bronze, silver and gold layers, progressively refining raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3], and that refinement is only real if the invariants that define the table's grain are checked at every hop.

Generalization beyond customers: the same five invariants (unique surrogate key, one current row per natural key, contiguous non-overlapping half-open intervals, flag/interval consistency, no orphaned facts) apply to every Type 2 dimension in the warehouse — product, employee, account, supplier. They are also the reason a Type 2 dimension is a poor candidate for naive materialization into every reporting view: each view that filters on `is_current = true` gets the current view, and each that filters on the interval predicate gets the historical view, but mixing the two in one model silently double counts. Finally, the broader objective of the whole exercise remains the one that motivates the medallion pattern in the first place: creating reliable, scalable systems that transform raw inputs into trusted insights [source 5], with the SCD invariants as the check that keeps the word trusted honest.

actions.text: Now that we've compared the three SCD strategies, let's make Type 2 concrete. This slide walks through a fully worked row-versioning example — exactly the kind of question the exam will ask you to reason through.

Problem 1. Our gold-layer dimension is dim_customer, and it's modeled as a Type 2 slowly changing dimension — meaning we keep history by adding new rows rather than overwriting old ones. The scenario: customer_id 4471 moves from ZIP code 10001 to 94105 on 2024-03-15. Your job is to show the exact row change required.

Here's the setup. Before the change, we have exactly one active row: surrogate key customer_sk 981, customer_id 4471, zip 10001, with EFF_StartDate of 2021-06-01 and an EFF_EndDate of 9999-01-01, flagged is_current equals true. And the hint gives away the pattern — expire first, insert second, and touch nothing else.

Step 0 is to declare the grain in words: one row per customer per version of that customer's attributes. Step 1 — expire the current row. Set EFF_EndDate to 2024-03-15 and flip is_current to false. Critically, you never overwrite the old ZIP value in a Type 2 dimension — that 10001 stays exactly where it is.

Step 2 — insert the new version as a brand-new row: a fresh surrogate key, customer_sk 1492, the same customer_id 4471, the new zip 94105, EFF_StartDate of 2024-03-15, EFF_EndDate of 9999-01-01, and is_current true. So after the change there are two rows for this customer — the closed historical version and the open current version.

Why does this work? Because the surrogate key is what keeps historical facts pointing at ZIP 10001 after the change. Any fact row loaded before March 15 still references customer_sk 981, so it resolves to the old ZIP forever. The two classic pitfalls are updating in place — which is really Type 1 — and reusing the same surrogate key for the new version, which silently destroys the history.
Let's build on that with Problem 2, which flips the perspective — now looking at the fact table side.

fact_sales in the gold layer sits at the grain of one row per order line. The hidden trap here is the join. If you join to a Type 2 dimension using the natural key customer_id instead of the surrogate key, the same customer matches multiple historical rows and your fact rows multiply. The hint says it plainly — count the join rows before you sum anything.

The worked solution: always join on the surrogate key, with a defensive check that it produces exactly one match per fact row. This problem is really the proof of why the surrogate key exists — it's the guardrail that protects your measures from fan-out.
Problem 3 gives us two change requests arriving at dim_customer on the same day, and asks us to classify each one as Type 1, Type 2, or Type 3.

The diagnostic question to ask yourself is simple: does the previously stored value need to be preserved for analysis? If the answer is yes, that's Type 2 — new versioned row, old row closed. If it's no, that's Type 1 — a plain overwrite. And Type 3 only when you need the prior value stored in a dedicated column, not full history.

Request one is a Type 1 change — a correction of a misspelled attribute where we don't care about the old value, so we simply update it in place. Request two is a Type 2 change, because it affects a value that historical reporting depends on, so we expire and insert a new version. The classification rule is the whole exercise here: the strategy follows the analytical requirement, not the other way around.
Problem 4 is our debugging drill. A junior engineer rebuilt dim_customer overnight and something went wrong.

The hint tells us there are four independent defects, and one of them is a violation of a check that's easy to skip. Your task is to identify all four invariant violations — things like duplicate current rows for the same natural key, overlapping effective date ranges, null surrogate keys, and reused surrogate keys across versions.

The worked solution lists the four defects and pins each one to the invariant it breaks. This is deliberate practice — spotting broken versioning by inspection is a skill the exam tests directly, because these errors are invisible until they corrupt your measures.

And here's the closing insight: these four checks are not optional hygiene. They're the data-quality guardrails that make a Type 2 dimension trustworthy. Exactly one current row per natural key, no gaps or overlaps in effective dates, and a stable surrogate key — enforce these and your history will hold up under any audit.

scenes.title: Check: Choosing and Detecting SCD Types

questions.question: A sales operations team states the requirement: 'We must retain the sales territory a rep was assigned at the moment each sale closed, so a rep who later moves regions does not silently change the territory credited on historical sales.' Based on this stated requirement, which slowly changing dimension (SCD) type best represents the assignment of sales territory to a rep over time? Type 1 = overwrite in place (no history kept); Type 2 = add a new versioned row with validity dates, preserving prior versions; Type 3 = keep a limited number of prior values in extra columns.

options.label: Type 1 — overwrite the rep's territory value in place so the dimension has exactly one row per rep
Type 2 — insert a new versioned row for the rep with effective dates, so each sale joins to the territory that was active when it closed
Type 3 — keep only the current territory plus one prior territory in an 'old_territory' column
Type 0 — never change the territory value at all, freezing the rep's very first assignment permanently

questions.analysis: The requirement is explicitly about preserving history: the territory credited to a sale must reflect who owned that territory when the sale closed, even after the rep moves. This is the canonical Type 2 use case — the dimension gets a new versioned row with validity (effective/expiration) dates, and the fact table joins to the version active at the event time. Type 1 is a distractor that fails the requirement because overwriting in place destroys the historical territory attribution. Type 3 is a distractor that partially preserves history but only for a small, fixed number of prior values, which cannot support arbitrary historical repointing and is fragile. Type 0 (often summarized as 'retain original') is wrong because it freezes the very first assignment and cannot represent the move at all. Type 2 is the standard pattern whenever the requirement includes auditable history with point-in-time correctness [source 1]; the medallion framing matters because this Type 2 logic typically lives in the silver layer, where records are validated and conformed before serving [source 3][source 6].

questions.question: A junior engineer 'optimizes' a Type 2 rep-territory dimension by switching it to Type 1 (overwrite in place). Which downstream consequences would you expect to observe? Select all that apply. (Assume the original Type 2 dimension had one row per rep per assignment period, and the fact table joined on the version active at sale close.)

options.label: Previously published reports that broke sales down by historical territory will silently change numbers, because the overwrite rewrites the territory that past sales attribute to
The dimension table's row count drops to one row per rep, so there are no longer multiple active versions of the same business key

A query that historically returned several rows for one business key (the version history) now returns exactly one row, so any code depending on version columns like effective_date/expiration_date will behave differently or fail
The fact table's row count for historical sales will automatically double, because each sale now matches two dimension rows

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: Type 1 overwrite is destructive — it replaces the current value and therefore changes the historical attribution of any fact rows that joined on that dimension. This is the 'silent rewrite' trap: reports that were correct yesterday can produce different historical numbers today with no change to the fact table. Option B is correct: the defining property of Type 2 is multiple versioned rows per business key; collapsing to Type 1 removes those extra versions, so row count falls to one row per rep. Option C is correct: columns like effective_date, expiration_date, is_current, and version_number are artifacts of Type 2. If downstream SQL references them, the query semantics change or the columns may no longer exist. Option D is incorrect: Type 1 does not create additional matches; it reduces dimension rows, so it cannot cause the fact table to double through join multiplication in the way described. This question tests exactly the distractor pattern of mixing Type 1 and Type 2 consequences: row counts, duplicate business keys, and join behavior. The reason this is architecture-relevant is that the dimension is a silver/gold artifact — the medallion layers promise progressively refined and trusted data, and overwriting history in place breaks that trust contract [source 1][source 3].

questions.question: Using a concrete example with numbers, explain how converting a Type 2 dimension (SCD Type 2 = a new versioned row per change, with validity dates) to a Type 1 overwrite (SCD Type 1 = update the value in place with no history) can silently rewrite the history of previously published reports. Then describe the validation check that would detect an unexpected Type 2 version explosion — i.e., more active versions per business key than expected.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Mechanism of silent history rewrite — must explain that Type 1 modifies the single dimension row, so facts that joined to it before (via a surrogate key or business key) now attribute to the new value even though the fact rows did not change; correct answers should note that reports re-executed after the overwrite produce different historical numbers with no change to the source facts — 40%. (2) Concrete numeric example — e.g., rep R107 sold $12,500 in Q1 2023 under Territory East; actual rep moved to West in Q2 2023; Type 1 overwrite changes the dimension row from East to West, so rerunning the 'Q1 2023 sales by territory' report now shows $12,500 under West instead of East (or splits incorrectly, depending on join design) — 25%. (3) Version-explosion validation check — must name a detectable condition such as: group by business key and count rows with is_current = true (or count rows with overlapping validity intervals); if the count exceeds the expected threshold (e.g., 1 current row per business key, or more than N versions per key per period), raise a data-quality alert. Should mention this can be implemented as a Delta Lake job / expectation on the silver dimension table and that a non-zero overlap of validity intervals is also a red flag — 25%. (4) Clarity, use of Databricks terminology (silver layer, Delta Lake, medallion architecture), and correct use of terms like business key, surrogate key, effective_date, expiration_date, is_current — 10%.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: Type 1 updates the dimension row in place. Facts typically store either a surrogate key or join on the business key at query time. In the surrogate-key case, if the dimension ETL loads a new surrogate key on each Type 1 overwrite, the old fact rows dangle or must be remapped; if the ETL reuses the surrogate key, the facts that pointed to the old value now point to the new value. Either way, a report that aggregates sum(sales_amount) grouped by territory will produce different historical results after the overwrite. Concrete example: rep R107, Territory East, closes $12,500 in Q1 2023; rep is reassigned to Territory West in Q2 2023; Type 1 overwrites the dimension so R107 is now West. Re-running 'Q1 2023 sales by territory' now attributes the $12,500 to West. The fact rows are unchanged, but the published report changes — this is the silent rewrite. A Type 2 design would have kept two rows (R107 / East / 2023-01-01–2023-06-30 and R107 / West / 2023-07-01–9999-12-31) and the Q1 report would still show East. Validation check for version explosion: SELECT rep_id, COUNT(*) AS active_versions FROM dim_rep_territory WHERE is_current = true GROUP BY rep_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; on a well-formed Type 2 the expected count is exactly 1 current version per business key. Additionally check for overlapping effective/expiration intervals, which indicates the SCD Type 2 merge logic is inserting versions incorrectly. This can be wired as a Delta Lake expectation on the silver-layer dimension so violations surface before they reach gold [source 3][source 6]; the medallion architecture's purpose is to progressively refine raw data into trusted, business-ready tables, and a broken SCD merge breaks that refinement chain [source 1].

scenes.title: Implementing SCD Type 1 and Type 2 on Databricks

elements.content: Implementing SCD Type 1 and Type 2 on Databricks

Slowly changing dimensions become concrete: a dimension change is just a Delta write that must preserve (Type 1) or version (Type 2) history. Both patterns are refinements inside the gold layer — trusted, business-ready tables [source 3].
Where this lives: dim_customer is a gold-layer dimension. Type 1 overwrites it; Type 2 keeps every historical version [source 5].
Type 1 — MERGE INTO (overwrite)

• Wrong email or mis-typed city: fix the current value in place.

• One statement handles update + insert:

• ON dim_customer.customer_id = staging.customer_id

• WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET ...

• No history kept — cheap, irreversible.
Type 2 — two-step MERGE (version)

Step 1 — expire the current row:

• EFF_EndDate = source change date

• is_current = false

Step 2 — insert the new version:

• new surrogate key, same customer_id

• EFF_StartDate = change date, End = 9999-01-01

Worked example: customer_id 4471 moves ZIP 94107 → 10001 on 2024-06-15. Step 1: old row EFF_EndDate 9999-01-01 → 2024-06-15, is_current true → false. Step 2: new row EFF_StartDate 2024-06-15, EFF_EndDate 9999-01-01, is_current true. Querying where is_current still returns one row per customer.

actions.text: Now that we've compared Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3 strategies conceptually, let's make it concrete. In this page we map slowly changing dimensions — SCDs — onto the actual mechanisms Databricks gives you: Delta MERGE for Type 1, and either a two-step MERGE or APPLY CHANGES INTO for Type 2.

First, where does this live? Our dimension table, dim_customer, is a gold-layer dimension table in the lakehouse. Everything we do here is a Delta table operation, so it inherits the ACID guarantees and the transaction log we discussed on the earlier Delta Lake pages.

Let's start with Type 1. Type 1 is the overwrite strategy — we simply correct the current value in place. A single MERGE INTO statement does the job: we match on customer_id, and when matched, we update the attribute columns to the staged values. No history is preserved, and that's exactly the point.

When do you reach for Type 1? Classic cases like a wrong email address or a mis-typed city in the source system. Fixing the value is the whole requirement — you don't need a version history for a typo. Just be aware that the old value is gone forever, so reach for it deliberately.

Type 2 is where it gets interesting. Delta doesn't have a built-in SCD Type 2 command via plain SQL MERGE, so we use a two-step MERGE pattern: first we expire the current row, then we insert the new version. Let's look at step one in detail.

Step 1 — expire the current row. We match on the business key and a filter that the row is currently active, then we set EFF_EndDate to the change date and flip is_current to false. That closes the old version cleanly, so at this instant the customer has no current row — which is why step 2 must follow immediately.

Here's a worked example: customer_id 4471 moves from ZIP 94107 to 94110 on March 15th. Instead of overwriting the ZIP, we close the existing row with EFF_EndDate of 2024-03-15 and insert a brand-new row with a fresh surrogate key, EFF_StartDate of 2024-03-15, and is_current set to true. Point-in-time queries now return the correct ZIP for any date — that's the whole value Type 2 delivers.

One trap worth memorizing before we move on: always derive the effective date from the source change timestamp, never from the pipeline run time. If you use the run time, a backfill that reprocesses old events will stamp them with today's date, and your history is corrupted forever. Use the source's change timestamp, and backfills stay safe.
