questions.question: You are handed a validated silver table named silver_order_events (one row per source change event, deduplicated, with columns order_id, line_number, product_id, store_id, order_date, source_change_ts, pipeline_run_ts, quantity, unit_price, discount_amount, net_amount). The business requirement is: revenue by product, by store, by day, with the ability to drill into individual order line items. You must choose the grain for the gold fact table and the SCD strategy for dim_customer, whose source system sends a full row image on every change and where the business requires the ability to reproduce last year's ZIP-based regional roll-ups as of any past reporting date. Which design correctly satisfies BOTH the grain requirement and the history requirement?

options.label: Grain: one row per order_id (header grain), with line-level detail aggregated into a single net_amount measure per order; dim_customer implemented as SCD Type 1 because the source sends a full row image and Type 1 preserves the lowest storage footprint.

Grain: one row per order line item (order_id + line_number), with measures quantity, unit_price, discount_amount, net_amount; dim_customer implemented as SCD Type 2 with EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate defaulting to 9999-01-01 for the open record, and an is_current flag.

Grain: one row per calendar day rolled up across all products and stores, since daily totals satisfy 'by day'; dim_customer implemented as SCD Type 2, with EFF_StartDate populated from pipeline_run_ts because that is the timestamp Delta Lake guarantees to be monotonically increasing.

Grain: one row per order line item, with quantity and unit_price stored in the fact table and net_amount also stored so analysts can sum quantity, unit_price, and net_amount together in any GROUP BY; dim_customer implemented as SCD Type 2, with EFF_EndDate set to the incoming source value minus one day.

questions.correctAnswer: Grain: one row per order line item (order_id + line_number), with measures quantity, unit_price, discount_amount, net_amount; dim_customer implemented as SCD Type 2 with EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate defaulting to 9999-01-01 for the open record, and an is_current flag.
questions.analysis: The requirement contains two explicit tests, and each distractor fails exactly one of them. (1) Grain: the requirement says the analyst must be able to drill into individual orders, so the grain must be the atomic business event — one row per order line item — which is the grain declared earlier in this unit as order_id + line_number. Option A collapses to header grain, which is too coarse: once you aggregate line items away, no downstream query can recover the drill-down, and this is precisely the 'grain too coarse' trap from the earlier Check on facts, dimensions, and grain. Option C collapses even further to day grain and is wrong for the same reason, only worse. (2) Measures: quantity, unit_price, discount_amount, and net_amount are the measures valid at line-item grain, exactly as listed in the earlier worked problem. Option D hides a second, subtler trap: it invites the analyst to SUM unit_price and net_amount together in the same GROUP BY. unit_price is non-additive across line items (summing unit prices across line items is meaningless — it is a rate, not a quantum) and net_amount is already derived from quantity × unit_price − discount_amount, so summing it alongside its own inputs double-counts revenue. (3) SCD: the requirement to reproduce last year's ZIP-based roll-ups as of any past reporting date is a history requirement, and any history requirement forces Type 2 (new row version plus EFF_StartDate/EFF_EndDate/is_current), because Type 1 overwrites the old value in place and the prior ZIP is simply gone. Option A applies Type 1 where history is required — the exact trap called out for this lesson. Options C and D apply Type 2 but corrupt the timestamps: the effective dates of a Type 2 dimension must come from the source change timestamp (here source_change_ts), not from the pipeline run timestamp, because pipeline_run_ts reflects when the pipeline happened to execute, not when the business fact occurred; a late-arriving correction would be stamped with today's date and the history window would be silently wrong. Option D's 'EFF_EndDate = incoming source value minus one day' is an off-by-one that leaves a one-day gap in coverage where no version is current. [source 6]
answer: Grain: one row per order line item (order_id + line_number), with measures quantity, unit_price, discount_amount, net_amount; dim_customer implemented as SCD Type 2 with EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate defaulting to 9999-01-01 for the open record, and an is_current flag.

questions.question: A colleague must implement the gold-layer dim_customer as a Type 2 SCD in Databricks from a silver change stream that carries order_id-level events and a source_change_ts column. Select ALL statements that are correct about the implementation approach and its correctness.

options.label: The two-step MERGE pattern (MERGE to expire the current row by setting EFF_EndDate = source_change_ts and is_current = false, then MERGE/INSERT to add the new version with a freshly generated surrogate key, EFF_StartDate = source_change_ts, and EFF_EndDate = 9999-01-01) is the general-purpose implementation and works on standard Delta Lake tables, including when the source is a batch feed or a non-DLT pipeline.

APPLY CHANGES INTO ... STORED AS SCD TYPE 2 in Delta Live Tables (Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines) is a declarative shortcut that replaces the hand-written two-step MERGE for the common case: you supply a sequencing column and the engine manages the versioning columns and generates the surrogate key.

Because APPLY CHANGES INTO ... STORED AS SCD TYPE 2 is declarative, it is always the correct choice over the two-step MERGE, even when the source change timestamp is missing, the ordering column is non-deterministic across retries, or the pipeline must also produce a Type 1 dimension.

Using pipeline_run_ts as the effective-date column is acceptable and even preferred in a Type 2 implementation, because Delta Lake guarantees pipeline_run_ts is monotonically increasing and therefore a safer sequencing column than source_change_ts.

The two-step MERGE and APPLY CHANGES INTO ... STORED AS SCD TYPE 2 are not mutually exclusive architectural choices: a team can use the declarative SCD Type 2 operator for dimensions where a clean change feed and sequencing column exist, and fall back to the two-step MERGE for dimensions where the feed is irregular or the versioning rules must be customized.

questions.analysis: The correct answers separate the two mechanisms cleanly. The two-step MERGE is the universal, hand-written pattern: expire the current row (EFF_EndDate = source_change_ts, is_current = false) and then insert the new version with a new surrogate key and EFF_StartDate = source_change_ts (open record ends at 9999-01-01). It works on plain Delta Lake tables, with batch or streaming sources, and with any custom versioning rules — it is the implementation you fall back to when the declarative operator's assumptions do not hold. APPLY CHANGES INTO ... STORED AS SCD TYPE 2 is a declarative Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines shortcut that covers the common case: you provide a sequencing column and the engine manages the versioning columns and surrogate key generation. The claim that the declarative operator is 'always correct' is false: it requires a well-behaved change feed with a deterministic sequencing column. If the source change timestamp is missing, or the ordering column is non-deterministic across retries, the engine cannot resolve which version is later, and the two-step MERGE is required. A late-arriving correction (a change that occurred 2024-03-15 but did not arrive until 2024-06-01) would be stamped 2024-06-01 and the history window would be silently three months off, which is precisely the trap the lesson flags. questions.analysis: Reference answer. GRAIN: declare it in words before any code — 'one row per order line item', key = order_id + line_number. This is the atomic business event; choosing order-header grain or day grain makes the stated drill-down requirement unanswerable, which is the 'grain too coarse' trap. Type 1 overwrites the old value in place, so the prior ZIP is destroyed and the past reporting date is unreproducible. Type 2 adds a new row version with EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate, and is_current, so full history is preserved and the as-of query can select the version where EFF_StartDate <= as_of_date < EFF_EndDate. TYPE 2 CHANGE WALKTHROUGH for customer_id 4471 (source move on 2024-03-15, arrived in the pipeline 2024-06-01): BEFORE — one active row: customer_sk = 981, customer_id = 4471, zip = 10001, EFF_StartDate = 2021-06-01, EFF_EndDate = 9999-01-01, is_current = true. Step 1 — expire the current row: set EFF_EndDate = 2024-03-15 (the source change timestamp) and is_current = false; never overwrite the old ZIP value in a Type 2 dimension, because that value is the historical fact being preserved. Step 2 — insert the new version: new surrogate key, customer_id = 4471 (business key unchanged), zip = 94105, EFF_StartDate = 2024-03-15, EFF_EndDate = 9999-01-01, is_current = true. TIMESTAMP RULE: both effective dates must use source_change_ts (2024-03-15), never pipeline_run_ts (2024-06-01). Using pipeline_run_ts would make the model claim the customer lived at ZIP 94105 from June 1 onward and lived at 10001 through June 1, so any as-of roll-up for March, April, or May would be silently wrong — the exact implementation trap this lesson names. The medallion layers behind this: the validated, conformed, deduplicated records live in silver, and the gold layer is shaped for consumption, not storage efficiency, which is why a star schema with a Type 2 dimension is the right shape here. [source 2] [source 3] [source 6]

questions.question: A student proposes the following gold-layer design and defends it with four claims. Which of the claims are ALREADY INCORRECT on their face — that is, which identify a design flaw that must be fixed before the model can be trusted? Select ALL that apply.

options.label: The fact table stores one row per order_id (header), with line-item measures quantity, unit_price, discount_amount, and net_amount all present, so the table can answer both header-level and line-item questions without a second table.

The fact table stores one row per order line item, and the analyst is told to compute total revenue by writing SUM(quantity) + SUM(unit_price) + SUM(net_amount) in the same GROUP BY, because summing every numeric column is the fastest way to get 'total revenue'.

The Type 2 dimension's effective dates are populated from pipeline_run_ts rather than source_change_ts, on the stated grounds that pipeline_run_ts reflects the moment the business fact became true in the source system.

dim_date is denormalized into a single table with columns date_sk, full_date, day_of_week, month, quarter, and year, and is reused as the conformed date dimension by both the sales fact table and the returns fact table.

correctAnswer: The fact table stores one row per order_id (header), with line-item measures quantity, unit_price, discount_amount, and net_amount all present, so the table can answer both header-level and line-item questions without a second table.

The fact table stores one row per order line item, and the analyst is told to compute total revenue by writing SUM(quantity) + SUM(unit_price) + SUM(net_amount) in the same GROUP BY, because summing every numeric column is the fastest way to get 'total revenue'.

dim_customer is Type 1, justified as follows: the business requires reproducing last quarter's ZIP-based regional revenue roll-ups as of any past reporting date, and Type 1 is cheapest because it does not grow the row count.

The Type 2 dimension's effective dates are populated from pipeline_run_ts rather than source_change_ts, on the stated grounds that pipeline_run_ts reflects the moment the business fact became true in the source system.
questions.analysis: Each of the first four options embeds a flaw; the fifth is a correct design. Option A is the mixed-grain trap: storing line-item measures at header grain means the table has multiple rows per order_id holding the same header-level net_amount (or, equally badly, line items silently collapsed into one row), so every SUM double-counts and the drill-down requirement is unsatisfiable — a fact table must have exactly one declared grain. Option B is the non-additive-measures trap: writing SUM(quantity) + SUM(unit_price) + SUM(net_amount) in one GROUP BY is nonsense because unit_price is a rate, not a quantum (summing unit prices across line items is meaningless), and net_amount is already derived from quantity × unit_price − discount_amount, so adding it to its own inputs double-counts revenue. Total revenue is SUM(net_amount) alone. Option C is the Type 1-where-history-is-required trap: the stated business requirement is to reproduce last quarter's ZIP-based roll-ups as of any past reporting date, which is a history requirement, and Type 1 overwrites the old value in place — the prior ZIP is destroyed, so the as-of query is unreproducible regardless of how cheap Type 1 is. Option D is the timestamp trap: the effective dates of a Type 2 dimension must come from source_change_ts, not pipeline_run_ts. The grounds given are also backwards — pipeline_run_ts is when the pipeline happened to execute, not when the business fact became true in the source system; a late-arriving correction would be stamped with the wrong effective date and the history window would be silently wrong. Option E is correct and therefore not selected: dim_date is a classic denormalized star-schema dimension, and reusing the same dim_date across the sales and returns fact tables is exactly what makes it a conformed dimension (a shared dim_date, a shared dim_customer, as covered earlier in this unit). Note also that the medallion architecture places this model in the gold layer, where tables are shaped for consumption — trusted, business-ready — rather than for storage efficiency. We just covered grain, star schema design, SCD types, and the two implementation patterns on Databricks. This assessment combines all of it, so read each scenario carefully.

scenes.title: From Silver to Gold: What Gold Tables Are For

elements.content: From Silver to Gold: What Gold Tables Are For
Gold tables are the serving layer: they sit on already-validated silver data and answer business questions directly. Silver is conformed but event-shaped; gold is question-shaped.
Recap: the medallion contract
Each layer upgrades data quality: bronze = raw, append-only source records; silver = validated, conformed, deduplicated; gold = refined, enriched, business-ready [source 3][source 6].
Gold answers questions, not events
A silver fact table stores one row per source event; a gold table is reshaped to return revenue by region or monthly active customers in a single scan.
Design goal 1 — BI-optimized denormalization
An analyst should write SELECT region, SUM(net_amount) ... GROUP BY region — never a five-table join.
Design goal 2 — centralized business logic
Discount policy and margin rules live once in the transformation that builds gold — every downstream report inherits them.
Worked example (continued from the grain lesson): grain = one row per order line (order_id + line_number); 3 lines of order 8821 → 3 gold rows, and SUM tolerates that grain but never a mixed one.

actions.text: Now that we've nailed grain and dimensional modeling, let's shift our focus to the gold layer itself. This is where all that careful modeling pays off for the business.

This page is called 'From Silver to Gold: What Gold Tables Are For.' The core idea is simple: gold tables are the serving layer. They sit on top of already-validated silver data and they're purpose-built for business consumption.

Let's recap the medallion contract we've been building. Bronze is raw and append-only, silver is validated, conformed, and deduplicated, and gold is refined and business-ready. Each layer strictly upgrades data quality as it moves downstream.

Here's the key contrast to hold onto. Silver stores one row per source event — that's the grain we worked so hard to fix. Gold, by contrast, answers questions, not events. Kim asks 'what was revenue by region last quarter?' and the gold table should answer that in one query.

Remember our silver fact table stores one row per source event. An analyst shouldn't have to trace that. Instead, the gold table should be shaped so a simple SELECT region, SUM(net_amount) GROUP BY region just works — no five-table joins required.

That brings us to our first design goal: BI-optimized denormalization. We deliberately flatten and pre-join the data so the warehouse, or the BI tool, hits a wide, simple table rather than a normalized maze.

The second design goal is centralized business logic. Discount policy and margin rules live once in the gold layer, not scattered across a dozen reports or notebooks. When those rules change, you change them in one place.

And notice the worked example continuing from our grain lesson: a single SELECT region, SUM(net_amount) only works if the grain is fixed first. One row per order line, or per customer per day — but never mixed, because mixing grains silently double-counts.

Finally, a Databricks-specific note: gold assets are Delta tables, views, or materialized views registered in Unity Catalog, so BI tools can discover and read them through the three-level namespace. On the exam, when they ask what gold is for, the answer is always the same: question-answering, consumer-first, governed serving layer.

scenes.title: Anatomy of a Denormalized Gold Table

elements.content: Anatomy of a Denormalized Gold Table
Redundancy is repaid with zero joins at read time — the medallion architecture's enriched gold layer [source 3]

What denormalization means here

Deliberately re-introducing redundancy: dimension attributes are copied into the fact table so BI queries never join at read time [source 1]

Same grain as the star schema — only the physical shape changes

• Gold = enriched, business-ready layer of the lakehouse [source 6]

• Star schema is not legacy — it beats a full pipeline for a single analytical domain [source 1]

data.text: Star schema: sales + dim_customer, dim_product, dim_date

elements.content:
Typical query

Star: 4 joins, then GROUP BY product, day

Gold: filter + GROUP BY — zero joins
Worked example: 10M fact rows × 12 dim attributes ≈ 2.4 GB extra — repaid on every query [source 5]

actions.text: Now that we understand how SCDs are implemented, let's look at what actually lands in the gold layer once that modeling work is done. This page is the anatomy of a denormalized gold table.

Denormalization means deliberately re-introducing redundancy. We take the clean, normalized star schema we just built and, on purpose, flatten it. The point is that BI queries then never have to join at read time.
That is the core trade: redundancy is repaid with zero joins at read time. Redundant storage and wider rows are the price, and in exchange we remove the join and shuffle cost from every single query.

Keep in mind what gold is: the enriched, business-ready layer of the lakehouse. A wide gold table mixes fact measures like quantity, unit_price, discount_amount, and net_revenue with flattened dimension attributes such as customer_name, customer_segment, product_category, store_region, and order_date.

This table compares the two shapes directly. On the left, the star schema: sales plus dim_customer, dim_product, and dim_date. On the right, the single wide gold table it collapses into. Look at how the joins-needed column drops and how the typical query changes.

Compare those typical queries. The star version needs four joins and then a GROUP BY over product, customer, and date. The wide version reads one table with no joins. Fewer moving parts, lower latency.
This diagram shows the result: fact measures sitting side by side with flattened customer, product, and date attributes, all in one wide, read-optimized table.

Here is a worked example to make the trade concrete. Take ten million fact rows multiplied by twelve dimension attributes. In the star model those attributes are stored once per dimension; in the wide gold table they are repeated on every fact row. That is the storage cost you are accepting, and it is real.

But here is the guardrail, and it is the exam trap. You must keep the fact grain exact. Join each dimension on its unique key, or on the current SCD version if you are using Type 2. If a dimension key is not unique when you join, row counts will silently explode, and your revenue numbers inflate without any warning.

So to summarize: gold is denormalized on purpose, joins move from read time to write time, and the one thing you never compromise is the grain. Get the grain wrong and every downstream metric is wrong. Next, we will check your understanding of the gold layer's purpose and design.

scenes.title: Check: Gold Layer Purpose and Design

questions.question: A data engineer on your team writes this design note: 'We will keep the gold layer as an append-only store of raw events exactly as they arrive from Kafka; any cleaning, typing, and deduplication will happen downstream when an analyst writes a query.' A reviewer rejects the design. Which statement best explains why the note misuses the gold layer?

options.label: The gold layer is the correct place for raw append-only data, but the note is wrong only because it forgot to enable Change Data Feed on the raw table.
Raw, exactly-as-ingested append-only data belongs in the bronze layer, while the gold layer must hold refined, business-ready tables that are trusted for direct BI and reporting consumption.
The gold layer should store raw data but only for streaming sources; for batch sources the raw data belongs in Unity Catalog instead.
The gold layer is defined by its physical storage format, so keeping raw Parquet there is acceptable as long as a Delta table points at the same path.

questions.analysis: The medallion architecture progressively refines data across the layers: bronze holds raw data as ingested, silver holds validated and cleaned data, and gold holds enriched, business-ready data that has been refined into a trusted state [source 3]. The architecture exists precisely to resolve data that 'arriv[es] in inconsistent, raw states that require progressive refinement before reaching analysts or models' [source 1]. Option A reverses the layer semantics. Option C invents a streaming-versus-batch rule that the medallion architecture does not contain. Option D confuses storage format with layer role — a gold table is defined by its refinement and business readiness, not by which path a Delta log points to [source 6].

questions.question: A colleague argues for denormalizing dimensions in a gold star schema with this justification: 'We should denormalize because flattening dim_product into dim_category and dim_supplier branches will make our nightly MERGE writes faster and reduce load time.' Which evaluation of this justification is correct?

options.label: Correct — denormalization roughly halves the number of tables, so write throughput improves proportionally to the table-count reduction.
Correct when the engine is Photon-enabled, because Photon parallelizes multi-table writes and rewards normalized join paths.
Incorrect — denormalization's real payoff is read and query performance on columnar, distributed engines; it typically costs extra storage and does not by itself improve write throughput.
Incorrect only if the warehouse is snowflaked; on a Delta Lake table, denormalization improves both read and write performance equally.

questions.analysis: Denormalization trades a small amount of redundant storage for far simpler queries and better performance on columnar, distributed engines — the benefit is on the read path, because BI queries avoid multi-hop joins. A star schema with fact and dimension tables 'delivers faster query performance and simpler governance' than a more normalized model for a single analytical domain [source 1]. Options A and B invert the read/write tradeoff. Option D invents a storage-format exception: the read-oriented benefit of denormalization does not depend on whether the underlying table is Delta Lake or a snowflaked relational store [source 6].

questions.question: You are designing fct_sales_gold, a business-intelligence-facing gold table that a BI tool will query directly with no downstream join logic. Which of the following design attributes belong in this gold table? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A surrogate key for each dimension (customer_sk, product_sk, date_sk) so the fact joins to dimension tables without relying on mutable business keys.
The measure columns at the declared grain of the fact table (sale_amount, quantity, discount_amount) alongside the foreign keys, so aggregation happens without extra lookups.
Raw JSON payload column preserved byte-for-byte from the ingest stream, kept in the gold table so the BI team can re-parse it if needed.
Conformed dimension references (for example, a shared dim_date and dim_customer) so two different fact tables can be compared on consistent terms.

questions.analysis: Gold tables are refined, business-ready tables that BI tools consume directly [source 3] and that form the refined outputs of a Bronze-to-Gold pipeline within a domain lakehouse [source 1]. A star-schema gold fact table therefore carries surrogate keys to join denormalized dimensions, the additive and semi-additive measures at the declared grain, and references to conformed dimensions (shared dim_date, shared dim_customer) so two fact tables can be compared on consistent terms. Option C is a trap: byte-for-byte raw payloads are the defining characteristic of the bronze layer, where data is stored exactly as ingested [source 6]; retaining them in gold defeats the refinement contract and pushes the cleaning burden back to the analyst, exactly what the medallion layers exist to prevent [source 3].

Try every item independently, and once you submit I'll walk through the reasoning with you, including the traps these questions are built around.

scenes.title: Star Schema vs Wide Denormalized Gold Table

elements.content: Dimension  |  Kimball Star Schema  |  Wide Denormalized Gold Table

Read-time join complexity
Kimball Star Schema: A query against a star schema typically requires joining the central fact table to one or more dimension tables through surrogate keys; for a single business process with three dimensions, a well-tuned query performs two or three joins, and performance remains predictable because dimension tables are small and often broadcast during joins.
Wide Denormalized Gold Table: A wide denormalized gold table pre-joins all dimension attributes into the fact table at write time, so dashboard queries read one wide table with zero joins; this removes join planning, shuffle, and skew risk at read time, but the table can have hundreds of columns and row width grows with each added dimension attribute.

Storage footprint
Kimball Star Schema: A star schema stores each dimension value once in the dimension table and only foreign keys in the fact table; with a million-row fact table and a 10,000-row customer dimension, customer attributes consume about 10,000 rows of storage rather than 1,000,000 repeated copies.
Wide Denormalized Gold Table: A wide denormalized table repeats every dimension attribute on every fact row; for a 1,000,000-row fact table with a 200-byte customer attribute payload, that is roughly 200 MB of duplicated customer text, before accounting for Delta Lake compression, which mitigates but cannot eliminate the redundancy.

Flexibility for new business questions
Kimball Star Schema: Because conformed dimensions are shared across marts, a new question such as revenue by customer segment can be answered by joining the existing fact to the existing customer dimension, without rebuilding the fact table; this is the governance value of a conformed dimension [source 3].
Wide Denormalized Gold Table: A wide table is optimized for a fixed set of columns; adding a new dimension attribute requires rewriting the table or creating a new pipeline, and a new question outside the pre-joined column set forces analysts back to the star or silver layer.

SCD handling and historical accuracy
Kimball Star Schema: Type 2 slowly changing dimensions are natural in a star schema: the dimension gains a new row version with EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate, and is_current, while the fact table keeps the original surrogate key, so historical fact rows retain the attribute values that were true when the event occurred.
Wide Denormalized Gold Table: A wide denormalized table usually carries only the current version of each attribute; retaining history requires either snapshotting the entire wide table per period or embedding the SCD logic into every load, which duplicates versioning logic and increases the risk of inconsistent history across dashboards.

Metric consistency across marts
Kimball Star Schema: The star schema keeps a governed source of truth because conformed dimensions guarantee that customer, date, and product definitions are identical in every mart [source 3], and measures live in a single fact table with a declared grain, so two reports cannot disagree on the definition of revenue.
Wide Denormalized Gold Table: Multiple wide denormalized tables each contain their own copy of the metric logic; unless they are generated from the same governed star, definitions drift, and the same KPI can produce different numbers across two dashboards, which is exactly the inconsistency the third non-option produces.

Typical consumer and latency profile
Kimball Star Schema: The star schema serves analysts and data scientists who need ad hoc exploration, slice-and-dice across any dimension, and consistent governed metrics; query latency is acceptable because the data is already business-ready in the gold layer [source 3].
Wide Denormalized Gold Table: The wide denormalized table serves a fixed, high-traffic BI dashboard where a single scan of a pre-joined table minimizes dashboard latency; it is the right choice when the questions are known in advance and read volume is high.

Implementation and maintenance cost
Kimball Star Schema: Building a star schema requires dimensional modeling discipline: declaring the grain, designing dimensions, assigning surrogate keys, and implementing SCD Type 1 or Type 2 merge logic in Delta Lake or Lakeflow; the upfront cost is higher but the resulting model is stable and reusable.
Wide Denormalized Gold Table: Building a wide denormalized table requires a materialization job that joins fact and dimensions and writes a wide Delta table or materialized view; the initial implementation is simpler, but every schema change or new attribute triggers a rewrite and the join logic lives in one pipeline that dashboards depend on.

Takeaway — Choose the Kimball star schema when you need a governed source of truth, conformed dimensions, historical accuracy through SCD Type 2, and flexibility for new questions; keep it in the gold layer as the certified model.
Takeaway — Choose a wide denormalized gold table when you have a fixed, high-traffic BI use case where join cost and dashboard latency dominate and the questions are known in advance.

Takeaway — Prefer composition over competition: keep the star schema in gold, then publish wide tables or views on top for specific dashboards, rather than letting analysts join silver directly, which produces inconsistent answers and untraceable business logic.

Takeaway — Both patterns sit on the medallion architecture's gold layer, where data is enriched and business-ready [source 6], and neither replaces the bronze-to-silver progressive refinement that makes the gold layer trustworthy [source 5].

actions.text: Now that we've built a star schema and seen how a denormalized gold table is shaped, the natural question is: which one should you actually ship? Let's put them side by side across the dimensions that genuinely drive the decision.
This comparison table lays out the deciding factors. Read it dimension by dimension, not row by row — each dimension is a question you'll ask about your own workload.

Start with read-time join complexity. The star schema pushes joins to query time — every consumer has to join facts to dimensions to get an answer. The wide table has already done that work, so reads are effectively a single-table scan. That's the core trade: you pay either at read time or at build time.

Then consider storage footprint and flexibility. Denormalization duplicates dimension attributes into every row, so the wide table is physically larger. And when a new business question arrives requiring a new dimension, the star schema can answer it by joining; the wide table often needs a rebuild with a new column layout.

Two dimensions get less attention but decide real projects. SCD handling — slowly changing dimensions, meaning tracking how a customer or product changes over time — is natural in a star schema with Type 2 dimension tables, but awkward once history is flattened into a wide row. And metric consistency: conformed dimensions guarantee that the same customer, date, and product definitions mean the same thing in every mart.

Finally, the consumer and the cost profile. The wide table wins for a fixed, high-traffic BI use case where dashboard latency dominates and the questions don't change much. The star schema wins when many teams query varied questions and you value a single governed source of truth — accepting a higher implementation and maintenance cost for that consistency.

Here's the key insight, and it's an exam favourite: these two patterns compose rather than compete. Keep the Kimball star schema in gold as the governed source of truth, then publish wide tables or views on top of it for the specific dashboards that need speed. You get both consistency and low latency.

And notice where both patterns sit — on the medallion architecture we covered earlier. Both are gold-layer deliverables. The third option, analysts joining silver tables directly, is not a pattern at all — it produces inconsistent answers and untraceable business logic, and it's exactly what the gold layer exists to prevent.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Denormalize a Star Schema into a Gold Table

elements.content: Problem 1

Your Unity Catalog silver layer holds four Delta tables for one sales domain. silver.sales is at the grain of one row per order line item. dim_customer is a Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD) — a dimension that keeps every historical version of a customer as a separate row carrying a validity window — and it is keyed by a surrogate key (a warehouse-generated integer that identifies one version of one entity, not the business entity itself). dim_product and dim_date are Type 1 dimensions, each unique on its own key.

silver.sales (6 rows)

| order_line_id | order_id | customer_key | product_key | date_key | quantity | unit_price | discount_amount |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 90001 | 5001 | 1055 | 77 | 20240210 | 2 | 50.00 | 10.00 |

| 90002 | 5001 | 1055 | 78 | 20240210 | 1 | 20.00 | 0.00 |

| 90003 | 5002 | 1055 | 77 | 20240211 | 3 | 50.00 | 15.00 |

| 90004 | 5002 | 1042 | 79 | 20240316 | 1 | 120.00 | 12.00 |

| 90005 | 5003 | 1042 | 78 | 20240320 | 4 | 20.00 | 8.00 |

| 90006 | 5004 | -1 | 77 | 20240321 | 1 | 50.00 | 0.00 |

dim_customer (Type 2; join key = customer_key)

| customer_key | customer_id | customer_name | customer_segment | EFF_StartDate | EFF_EndDate | is_current |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 981 | 4471 | Northwind Traders | Retail | 2021-06-01 | 2024-02-01 | false |

| 1055 | 4471 | Northwind Traders | Wholesale | 2024-02-01 | 9999-01-01 | true |

| 1042 | 6620 | Cascade Outfitters | Retail | 2022-01-10 | 9999-01-01 | true |

dim_product (3 rows)

| product_key | product_name | product_category |

|---|---|---|

| 77 | Steel Widget | Hardware |

| 78 | Copper Fitting | Hardware |

| 79 | Precision Sensor | Electronics |

dim_date (5 rows)

| date_key | year | quarter | month |

|---|---|---|---|

| 20240210 | 2024 | Q1 | 2 |

| 20240211 | 2024 | Q1 | 2 |

| 20240316 | 2024 | Q1 | 3 |

| 20240320 | 2024 | Q1 | 3 |

| 20240321 | 2024 | Q1 | 3 |

Task: write a single CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE statement that builds gold_sales_wide by denormalizing silver.sales with customer_name, customer_segment, product_category, year and quarter. gold_sales_wide must keep exactly the grain of silver.sales. Give the full contents of the resulting table and state its row count.
Hint: A gold table is the enriched serving layer: it answers business questions instead of storing one row per source event, but it must never change how many rows represent one event.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Fix the grain contract before writing any SQL. silver.sales encodes one order line item per row, identified by order_line_id. Every decision below is judged against one test: after the join, does each order_line_id still appear exactly once?

Step 2 — Choose the join direction. The fact is the driving table, and every dimension is optional enrichment. If a dimension row is missing we still want to see the fact row (and the revenue) rather than lose it, so every join is a LEFT JOIN from silver.sales.

Step 3 — Guard the Type 2 dimension. dim_customer is versioned: customer_id 4471 currently has two rows (surrogate 981, expired; surrogate 1055, current). Adding the current-version predicate AND c.eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01' pins the join to one row per customer and makes the intent explicit in the query text. dim_product and dim_date are Type 1 and unique on their keys, so no guard is needed.

Step 4 — The statement:

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold_sales_wide AS

SELECT

s.*,

c.customer_name,

c.customer_segment,

p.product_category,

d.year,

d.quarter

FROM silver.sales s

LEFT JOIN dim_customer c

ON s.customer_key = c.customer_key

AND c.eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01'

LEFT JOIN dim_product p

ON s.product_key = p.product_key

LEFT JOIN dim_date d

ON s.date_key = d.date_key;

Step 5 — Resolve each of the six fact rows by hand.

Line 90001: customer_key 1055 -> customer_name = Northwind Traders, customer_segment = Wholesale; product_key 77 -> Hardware; date_key 20240210 -> year 2024, quarter Q1. Revenue = 2 x 50.00 - 10.00 = 90.00.

Line 90002: 1055 -> Northwind Traders / Wholesale; 78 -> Hardware; 20240210 -> 2024 / Q1. Revenue = 1 x 20.00 - 0.00 = 20.00.

Line 90003: 1055 -> Northwind Traders / Wholesale; 77 -> Hardware; 20240211 -> 2024 / Q1. Revenue = 3 x 50.00 - 15.00 = 135.00.

Line 90004: 1042 -> Cascade Outfitters / Retail; 79 -> Electronics; 20240316 -> 2024 / Q1. Revenue = 1 x 120.00 - 12.00 = 108.00.

Line 90005: 1042 -> Cascade Outfitters / Retail; 78 -> Hardware; 20240320 -> 2024 / Q1. Revenue = 4 x 20.00 - 8.00 = 72.00.

Line 90006: customer_key = -1 has no row in dim_customer, so the LEFT JOIN emits NULL for customer_name and customer_segment while keeping the row. product_key 77 -> Hardware; date_key 20240321 -> 2024 / Q1. Revenue = 1 x 50.00 - 0.00 = 50.00.

Step 6 — Result table (6 rows).

| order_line_id | customer_key | customer_name | customer_segment | product_category | year | quarter |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 90001 | 1055 | Northwind Traders | Wholesale | Hardware | 2024 | Q1 |

| 90002 | 1055 | Northwind Traders | Wholesale | Hardware | 2024 | Q1 |

| 90003 | 1055 | Northwind Traders | Wholesale | Hardware | 2024 | Q1 |

| 90004 | 1042 | Cascade Outfitters | Retail | Electronics | 2024 | Q1 |

| 90005 | 1042 | Cascade Outfitters | Retail | Hardware | 2024 | Q1 |

| 90006 | -1 | NULL | NULL | Hardware | 2024 | Q1 |

Final answer: gold_sales_wide has 6 rows — exactly the 6 rows of silver.sales. Revenue reconciles: 90 + 20 + 135 + 108 + 72 + 50 = 475.00 in silver and 475.00 in gold.

Analysis — Why it works: a LEFT JOIN against a dimension that is unique on the join key is not really a multiplying join, it is a lookup. Uniqueness is the invariant that protects the grain, and here it is guaranteed three times over — dim_product.product_key and dim_date.date_key are primary keys of Type 1 dimensions, and dim_customer.customer_key is a surrogate key, which is unique by construction because a new 4471 row means a new surrogate value [source 3]. Once the right-hand side has at most one row per key, the join is cardinality-preserving and the fact row count passes through untouched.

Why LEFT and not INNER: line 90006 points at customer_key = -1 (the unknown member placeholder). With LEFT JOIN the line survives with NULL attributes and its 50.00 is still in the total. With INNER JOIN the line vanishes and the gold revenue silently reads 425.00. Silent row loss is the most expensive class of bug in a lakehouse because nothing errors — the dashboard simply shows a smaller number [source 5].

Common mistakes. (1) Writing SELECT * instead of s.*: the star expands to the fact columns plus all dimension columns, and any column name shared between fact and dimension (for example a surrogate key name reused as a dimension attribute) produces a duplicate or ambiguous reference that either fails at CREATE time or silently overwrites. (2) Omitting the current-version predicate when the fact carries the natural key customer_id rather than the surrogate key: dim_customer then has two rows for 4471 and the fact fans out — this is Problem 3. (3) Putting the row-length limit first and the correctness check second: always count rows before and after.

Generalization: the same recipe (fact LEFT JOIN dimension on its unique key, current-version guard only for Type 2) extends to any number of dimensions. Adding a fifth dimension costs one more LEFT JOIN and cannot change the grain, provided the new dimension is unique on its join key. The predicate is not decorative — it is the contract you verify later with a COUNT(*) comparison.
Problem 2

Before you publish gold_sales_wide to the BI layer, you must prove that the denormalization preserved the grain of silver.sales. Using the tables from Problem 1, write three verification queries and give the expected numeric result of each: (a) a count-and-sum check on the source, (b) the same count-and-sum check plus a distinct-key count on the gold table, and (c) a duplicate-detection query that must return zero rows. Then state what query (c) would return if the dim_customer guard had been dropped and the fact had carried customer_id instead of a surrogate key.
Hint: If the join multiplied rows, both COUNT(*) and SUM(revenue) move together — check them as a pair, never one alone.

Worked solution
Check (a) — source baseline:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS fact_rows,

SUM(quantity * unit_price - discount_amount) AS revenue

FROM silver.sales;

Expected: fact_rows = 6, revenue = 475.00. (90 + 20 + 135 + 108 + 72 + 50.)

Check (b) — gold table, same two measures plus a distinct-key count:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS gold_rows,

COUNT(DISTINCT order_line_id) AS distinct_lines,

SUM(quantity * unit_price - discount_amount) AS revenue

FROM gold_sales_wide;

Expected: gold_rows = 6, distinct_lines = 6, revenue = 475.00. Note the two-part test: if gold_rows is 18 while distinct_lines is 6, a dimension fanned out each line three times and revenue will read 1,425.00 — three times the truth. If gold_rows is 6 but distinct_lines is 5, you lost a row somewhere else. Only when all three numbers line up is the grain proven.

Check (c) — duplicate detection, one row per order_line_id:

SELECT order_line_id, COUNT(*) AS n

FROM gold_sales_wide

GROUP BY order_line_id

HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Expected: zero rows returned. This query is the permanent regression test; it is the one you paste into the pipeline's data-quality expectations so that a future change to dim_customer cannot quietly re-introduce a fan-out.

Counterfactual: if you had dropped the current-version predicate and joined on the natural key customer_id, dim_customer would contribute two rows for customer_id 4471 (surrogate 981, expired, and surrogate 1055, current). Order lines 90001, 90002 and 90003 would each match both versions, so the duplicate-detection query would return three rows (90001, 90002, 90003) with n = 2 each, the gold row count would be 9 instead of 6, and SUM(revenue) would read 720.00 instead of 475.00.

Analysis — Why this method works: the two measures fail differently and together they pin down the failure mode. COUNT(DISTINCT order_line_id) is immune to duplication by definition — it counts entities, not rows — so comparing it against COUNT(*) isolates the problem to join cardinality rather than to filtering. SUM(revenue) then quantifies the financial damage, because in a fan-out the measure is summed once per duplicate, and every downstream dashboard inherits the error [source 5].

Edge cases. If the fact itself contained two rows for the same order_line_id (a legitimate case when a line can be split across warehouses), the duplicate query would flag it even though the join is clean — which is why the comparison must always be source-row-count versus gold-row-count, not 'distinct keys must equal row count'. If a dimension is Type 2 and you join on the natural key with a valid range predicate, a one-day overlap in the effective-date windows produces exactly the same fan-out signature, so the check catches that bug class too. If SUM(revenue) is NULL rather than wrong, the revenue columns are the problem, not the join — usually a name collision created by SELECT *.

Common mistakes. Running only COUNT(*): a fan-out that happens to be filtered away in the same query can leave the row count correct while the revenue is wrong, and vice versa. Comparing the numbers by eye across two runs on a live table: silver.sales may receive new rows between the two SELECTs, so both queries must run against the same snapshot, or the gold build must be atomic. Finally, treating the check as a one-time event: the grain contract belongs in the pipeline as a Lakeflow expectation or a scheduled assertion, because dimensional data keeps changing under you [source 6].

Generalization: the count-and-sum pair is the standard grain audit for any denormalization, and it generalizes to a partitioned version (GROUP BY date_key) that shows exactly which partition fanned out.
Problem 3

A second pipeline reads a landing copy of the same sales data, silver.sales_natural, that carries the natural business key customer_id and order_date instead of the surrogate key. Its six order lines are the same as Problem 1: customer_id 4471 on lines 90001-90003 (revenue 90.00, 20.00, 135.00), customer_id 6620 on lines 90004-90005 (revenue 108.00, 72.00), and customer_id -1 on line 90006 (revenue 50.00). dim_customer is the same Type 2 table as before (customer_id 4471 has surrogate 981 expired and surrogate 1055 current).

An analyst writes:

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold_sales_wide_bad AS

SELECT f.*, c.customer_name, c.customer_segment

FROM silver.sales_natural f

LEFT JOIN dim_customer c

ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id;

Compute the row count and the total revenue of gold_sales_wide_bad, quantify the distortion as a percentage, and give the one-line correction.
Hint: The join condition is on the business key, and a Type 2 dimension has more than one row per business key.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Determine the match multiplicity for each business key. dim_customer contains: customer_id 4471 -> two rows (surrogate 981, EFF_EndDate 2024-02-01; surrogate 1055, EFF_EndDate 9999-01-01); customer_id 6620 -> one row (surrogate 1042); customer_id -1 -> no row at all.

Step 2 — Fan out the fact.

Customer 4471: 3 fact lines x 2 dimension rows = 6 output rows. Revenue is carried on each copy, so 90.00 + 20.00 + 135.00 = 245.00 becomes 245.00 x 2 = 490.00.

Customer 6620: 2 fact lines x 1 dimension row = 2 output rows, revenue 108.00 + 72.00 = 180.00 unchanged.

Customer -1: 1 fact line x 0 dimension rows, preserved by the LEFT JOIN with NULL name and segment, revenue 50.00 unchanged.

Step 3 — Total. Row count = 6 + 2 + 1 = 9 rows (was 6). Revenue = 490.00 + 180.00 + 50.00 = 720.00 (was 475.00). The gold table overstates revenue by 245.00, which is 245.00 / 475.00 = 51.58%, roughly a 52% inflation, purely from one duplicated customer.

Step 4 — The correction is one predicate:

LEFT JOIN dim_customer c

ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id

AND c.eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01'

With the predicate, customer 4471 matches only surrogate 1055, so the join returns 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 rows and 475.00 — identical to the surrogate-key solution in Problem 1.

Analysis — Why it works and why the predicate is mandatory here: the surrogate-key join in Problem 1 needs no filter because a surrogate key is unique by construction, but a Type 2 dimension deliberately holds several rows per natural key, so joining on the natural key without a version predicate is a one-to-many join that multiplies the fact. Adding AND c.eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01' (equivalently AND c.is_current = true) collapses the right-hand side back to one row per business key and restores the lookup cardinality. The 9999-01-01 sentinel is the open-ended end date from the Type 2 design taught earlier in this unit, and the fact that it is a literal date rather than NULL matters: a plain equality predicate on NULL would never match.

Edge cases. If two current rows ever existed for the same business key (a broken SCD load that failed to expire the old version), the current-version filter would not save you — the duplicate-detection query from Problem 2 is the only thing that catches it, which is why the guard and the test are complementary, not redundant. If you instead want the segment as it stood on the sale date, do not use the current-version filter at all; use the range predicate derived in Problem 5. Note also how quietly this fails: 9 rows and 720.00 is a perfectly plausible-looking table, no error is raised, and every dashboard built on top inherits the 52% inflation [source 5].

Common mistakes. Placing the version predicate in a WHERE clause instead of the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN — that converts the join to an inner join and drops the unmatched line 90006 (Problem 4). Assuming the problem is 'duplicate rows' and fixing it with SELECT DISTINCT: that would collapse the two fan-out copies back to one, but DISTINCT also silently de-duplicates legitimately identical rows and it hides the real defect, so the row count might look right while the root cause remains in the pipeline. Using the pipeline run timestamp instead of the source change timestamp when populating EFF_StartDate is the upstream version of the same mistake [source 1].

Generalization: the rule is 'join a Type 2 dimension on its surrogate key with no filter, or on its natural key with a current-version or as-of-date predicate — never on the natural key alone.'
Problem 4

A colleague needs a Retail-only extract and writes:

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold_retail AS

SELECT s.order_line_id, s.quantity, s.unit_price, s.discount_amount, c.customer_segment

FROM silver.sales s

LEFT JOIN dim_customer c

ON s.customer_key = c.customer_key

AND c.eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01'

WHERE c.customer_segment = 'Retail';

Using the data and results of Problem 1 (gold_sales_wide has 6 rows and 475.00 total; Retail rows are 90004 and 90005 worth 108.00 and 72.00; Wholesale rows are 90001-90003 worth 245.00; line 90006 has a NULL customer_segment), compute what gold_retail contains, show that the sum of the per-segment extracts no longer reconciles to the gold total, and give two correct ways to express the intent.
Hint: A predicate on the right-hand table of a LEFT JOIN is evaluated after the join has already produced NULLs for unmatched rows.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Order of evaluation. SQL evaluates the LEFT JOIN first, producing the 6 rows of gold_sales_wide with line 90006 carrying NULL for customer_name and customer_segment. The WHERE clause is then applied to that result.

Step 2 — Apply the predicate c.customer_segment = 'Retail'.

Line 90001: Wholesale -> removed. Line 90002: Wholesale -> removed. Line 90003: Wholesale -> removed. Line 90004: Retail -> kept, revenue 108.00. Line 90005: Retail -> kept, revenue 72.00. Line 90006: NULL = 'Retail' evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE, so the row is removed and its 50.00 disappears without an error.

gold_retail therefore holds 2 rows and 108.00 + 72.00 = 180.00.

Step 3 — Reconciliation. Build the sibling extract with WHERE c.customer_segment = 'Wholesale': it returns lines 90001-90003, revenue 245.00. Retail 180.00 + Wholesale 245.00 = 425.00 against a gold total of 475.00. The missing 50.00 is 10.53% of revenue and it belongs to line 90006, whose customer is unresolvable. Nothing in either report says so, because the row was filtered rather than flagged.

Step 4 — Two correct expressions of the intent.

Fix A (preferred): make the unknown case a first-class member instead of a NULL. Add the unknown member row to the dimension — customer_key = -1, customer_name = 'Unknown', customer_segment = 'Unknown' — and have the dimension loader write -1 whenever a source key cannot be resolved. Every fact row then matches exactly one dimension row, the NULL disappears, and the three extracts sum to 180.00 + 245.00 + 50.00 = 475.00.

Fix B: if the business really means 'only rows whose customer is a known Retail customer', filter the dimension before joining so the semantics are explicit, and publish the denominator:

WITH retail_customers AS (

SELECT DISTINCT customer_key

FROM dim_customer

WHERE customer_segment = 'Retail'

AND eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01'

)

SELECT s.*, c.customer_segment

FROM silver.sales s

JOIN retail_customers rc ON s.customer_key = rc.customer_key

JOIN dim_customer c ON s.customer_key = c.customer_key;

Note that this is genuinely an inner join by intent, so writing it as one (or as a semi-join) makes the row loss visible at review time.

Analysis — Why the defect exists: LEFT JOIN and WHERE are two different operators with a fixed evaluation order. LEFT JOIN promises to preserve the left side only in the absence of downstream filters; any WHERE predicate that references a column from the right-hand table is evaluated on the joined result and eliminates rows where that column is NULL. The query text still says LEFT JOIN, so a reviewer scanning for 'did they preserve the grain?' sees the right keyword and approves it — the most dangerous kind of bug because the code reads as correct [source 6].

Edge cases. Predicates on left-side columns are always safe (WHERE s.quantity > 0 keeps the LEFT JOIN intact). Predicates moved into the ON clause are semantically different again: AND c.customer_segment = 'Retail' inside the ON clause keeps all six fact rows, but lines 90001-90003 and 90006 come back with NULL segment — revenue reconciles, but the 'Retail' column is now misleading. A predicate like WHERE c.customer_segment <> 'Retail' is worse still: in SQL, NULL <> 'Retail' is UNKNOWN, so line 90006 is dropped from that extract too, and the row is invisible in every segment report simultaneously. Use IS NULL / COALESCE explicitly if the unknown bucket must be shown.

Common mistakes. Believing that LEFT JOIN guarantees row preservation no matter what follows it. Assuming NULL behaves like a value in comparisons — it does not, three-valued logic is what makes both the drop and the invisibility happen. And 'fixing' the count by adding OR c

actions.text: Now let's put denormalization into practice with a fully worked problem. Our goal is to take a star schema — a fact table surrounded by dimension tables — and flatten it into a single wide gold table, without ever changing the grain.

Here's the setup. Your Unity Catalog silver layer holds four Delta tables. The fact is silver.sales, whose grain is one row per order line item. Around it sit dim_customer, dim_product, and dim_date. The task: write gold_sales_wide as one denormalized table.

Here's the hint before we look at the answer. A gold table is the enriched serving layer — it should be wide enough that a BI analyst can query it without repeating joins. But width is not the point; preserving the fact grain absolutely is. Keep that in mind as we read the solution.

Step one fixes the grain contract before we write a single line of SQL: one row in equals one row out. Then we build the query. We select the fact columns with s.*, then attach customer_name and customer_segment from dim_customer, product_category from dim_product, and year and quarter from dim_date. Each dimension is joined with a LEFT JOIN on the surrogate key — and notice the customer join carries an extra predicate: c.eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01'. That filters the Type 2 dimension to its current version.

Why does this work? A LEFT JOIN against a dimension that is unique on its key — or filtered down to the single current version — preserves the fact grain exactly. The way you verify that is to compare COUNT(*) before and after the join. If those two numbers match, your grain survived. Now for the traps: join a Type 2 dimension without the current-version filter and you fan out rows, duplicating revenue in every downstream dashboard. And a filter placed after the join, like WHERE c.customer_segment = 'Retail', silently converts your LEFT JOIN into an inner join and quietly drops rows.
Let's carry this forward into problem two, where we validate the row count before that gold table ever reaches the BI layer.

scenes.title: Check: Joins, Grain, and Denormalization

questions.question: You are building a gold-layer sales fact table at the grain of one row per order line. The fact table must attach the product attributes that were in effect when each order line was sold. The source is dim_product, implemented as a Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD) — a dimension pattern that keeps every historical version of a row rather than overwriting it — with columns product_sk (surrogate key), product_id (business key), list_price, EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate, and is_current. Which join guarantees exactly one dimension row per fact row while returning the version that was active at the time of the sale?

options.label: LEFT JOIN dim_product p ON f.product_id = p.product_id — joining on the business key, which naturally returns one row per fact row.
JOIN dim_product p ON f.product_sk = p.product_sk WHERE p.is_current = true — joining on the surrogate key and filtering to the open record.
LEFT JOIN dim_product p ON f.product_id = p.product_id AND f.order_date BETWEEN p.EFF_StartDate AND p.EFF_EndDate — a range join on the effective dates.
JOIN dim_product p ON f.product_sk = p.product_sk AND f.order_date BETWEEN p.EFF_StartDate AND p.EFF_EndDate — an equi-join on the surrogate key plus an effective-date range predicate.

questions.analysis: Option D is correct because it is the canonical Type 2 point-in-time join. The fact row already carries the product_sk that was resolved at load time, so the equi-join on product_sk is a strict one-to-one match that cannot fan out. Because product_sk alone already identifies the correct version, the BETWEEN predicate is redundant in a correctly loaded fact table — but including it acts as a defensive guard that fails loudly if a fact row was loaded with the wrong version key. Option A is wrong because joining on product_id against a Type 2 table is the classic fan-out: a product with five historical versions returns five rows per fact row, quintupling the measure. Option B returns one row per fact row, but always the *current* version — it silently rewrites history, reporting today's price against last year's sale. Option C joins on the business key, which still fans out to every version; the date predicate then filters *after* the fan-out, which can return zero rows (for fact rows whose order_date falls in a version gap) or, worse, one row only by accident when date ranges happen to be disjoint. The disciplined rule: resolve the surrogate key and validate the point-in-time predicate during the join to the dimension, then store the surrogate key on the fact row so the read-time join is a pure equi-join. [source 3]

questions.question: An engineer reports that after joining the sales fact table to dim_customer, dim_product, and dim_date, the result set is 1,248,900 rows while the fact table alone held 411,300 rows. They conclude 'the join worked — the row count changed, which proves the dimension attributes were added.' Which statements correctly diagnose and remediate this situation? Select all that apply.

options.label: A changed post-join row count is a fan-out warning sign, not evidence of success. A correctly designed fact-to-dimension join on a unique surrogate key should preserve the grain, so the row count before and after the join should be identical.
The 3.03x row multiplication (1,248,900 / 411,300) indicates at least one dimension join matched more than one row per fact row, which corrupts every SUM and COUNT measure downstream.
The row count changed because SUM and COUNT are aggregate functions, and aggregation is expected to change the row count during a join of fact and dimension tables.

Before publishing, verify each dimension's key is unique at the join grain — e.g., SELECT sk, COUNT(*) FROM dim_x GROUP BY sk HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 returns no rows — and confirm that the fact row count equals the pre-join fact row count.
Fan-out is harmless in a gold table because the BI tool's SELECT DISTINCT on the dimension attributes will collapse the duplicate rows back to the correct grain at read time.

questions.analysis: A, B, and D together describe the correct discipline. A restates the invariant: when the join key is the unique surrogate key of the dimension, the join is one-to-many from the fact side, i.e., one fact row can match exactly one dimension row, so the cardinality is preserved and row_count_after_join = row_count_before_join. B explains the arithmetic of the disaster: 411,300 facts producing 1,248,900 rows means the average fact row matched about 3.03 dimension rows, which means any measure (revenue, quantity) is now triple-counted. D gives the operational test — check dimension key uniqueness with a GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 probe, and compare counts before and after. Option C is a misconception: SUM and COUNT are aggregate functions applied in a GROUP BY query, but a join by itself is a set operation that does not aggregate; joining fact and dimension at the correct grain does not change the row count. Option E is a common but wrong shortcut: SELECT DISTINCT collapses rows only if the projected columns are identical, and fact rows that differ in any measure column (different order_id, quantity, price) will remain duplicated, so the DISTINCT hides the fan-out visually while still producing inflated totals for any query that aggregates those distinct rows. [source 2]

questions.question: You build gold_sales as a denormalized wide table: a preserved LEFT JOIN of the sales fact table to dim_customer, keeping customers with no recorded sales history in a separate audit branch. Downstream, you add a filter WHERE c.region = 'EMEA' after the join to produce a regional report. What is the effect of that filter on the LEFT JOIN's semantics, and what is the correct expectation for row counts?

options.label: The filter behaves identically to an INNER JOIN with the same predicate, because rows whose customer has NULL region fail the equality test and are eliminated — the preserved rows disappear, and the result set shrinks below the left-side row count.
The filter preserves all LEFT-side rows because LEFT JOIN is evaluated after the WHERE clause, so rows with NULL region are retained and appear as a separate region group.
The filter has no effect on row counts because LEFT JOIN preserves every fact row regardless of downstream predicates, and NULL region values are silently coerced to the string 'EMEA'.
The filter converts the LEFT JOIN to a RIGHT JOIN, since the predicate references only the right-hand (dimension) table and thus floats the dimension side to the preserved side.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct and captures the trap. A LEFT JOIN preserves unmatched left-side rows — for fact rows with no matching customer, the dimension columns are NULL. The predicate c.region = 'EMEA' evaluates to UNKNOWN against NULL (not true), so those preserved rows are discarded by the WHERE clause. The result set is therefore identical to an INNER JOIN with the same predicate: the outer-join guarantee is destroyed and the total row count drops below the row count of the left input. Option B is wrong because SQL evaluation order puts WHERE before LEFT JOIN is fully finalized in the logical plan; the WHERE applies to the joined row stream, not to the fact table before the join. Option C is wrong on both counts — a downstream filter absolutely can remove preserved rows, and NULL is never coerced to a string in an equality predicate. Option D confuses join direction with predicate placement: a RIGHT JOIN changes which side is preserved, but a WHERE predicate does not silently convert the join type, and it does not change the join's declared direction. The remediation is the standard one: if the intent is to filter the *dimension* while keeping the *fact* grain, push the predicate into the ON clause (LEFT JOIN dim_customer c ON f.customer_sk = c.customer_sk AND c.region = 'EMEA') and re-add the IS NULL branch for unmatched facts, or pre-filter the dimension into a CTE before joining. [source 6]

actions.text: Time to check how the join discipline we just covered is holding up. These questions focus on join types, keys, and whether the grain of your gold table survives the join.
Work through each one on your own first — pay attention to row counts as a signal. Once you submit, I'll walk you through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Centralizing Business Logic in the Gold Layer

elements.content: Centralizing Business Logic in the Gold Layer
Encode each metric once in the gold transformation (or a governed semantic layer); consumers only select the finished result.
Scattered per-dashboard logic vs. one governed gold definition
Anti-pattern — logic everywhere
The same metric is re-implemented in every dashboard, notebook, and ad hoc query — the numbers drift and nobody can reconcile them [source 3].
Fix — governed gold definition
Compute derived data in one place and let consumers select it — the DRY principle, not recompute with slightly different rules [source 5].
Teaser: a worked example — net revenue - marketing cost = 1,204 (all three dashboards) — false.

actions.text: Now that we've built gold tables and looked at how to denormalize a star schema, let's talk about where the actual business rules belong. The title says it plainly: centralize business logic in the gold layer.

Start with the anti-pattern. Business logic is simply the definition of a metric or a rule — net revenue after returns, the window that makes a customer 'active', profit after marketing cost. The exam source describes this on page 346. When that logic is scattered, the same metric gets re-implemented in every dashboard, notebook, and ad hoc query.

That's the real damage: the numbers drift. Two dashboards claim different revenue because the filter conditions were written slightly differently, and nobody can reconcile them. Logic everywhere means trust nowhere.

Here's the fix. Encode each metric once in the gold transformation, or in a governed semantic or metrics layer, and then let consumers simply select the finished result. Compute derived data in one place instead of recomputing it downstream with slightly different rules — that's the DRY principle applied to data engineering.

This diagram captures the contrast. On one side, scattered metric logic across several dashboards; on the other, one governed definition in the gold layer that every consumer reads from. Classic examples you'll see on the exam are ad-spend attribution, exclusion of auto-canceled orders, currency conversion, and refund handling.

Coming up next is a worked example: net revenue minus marketing cost. Keep our rule in mind — every version of that formula deployed to a different dashboard is one more place that can silently diverge.

scenes.title: Where Should Business Logic Live?

elements.content: Decision — You are the lead data engineer on a Databricks Lakehouse team of five, and the analytics organization has just agreed on a single definition of 'net revenue' for the fiscal year. Gold tables already exist, but four different BI consumers — an executive dashboard, a finance workbook, a Databricks SQL dashboard, and an ML feature pipeline — currently each re-implement their own revenue arithmetic. The team must decide where the business logic for net_revenue should live permanently. The decision is genuinely hard because the constraints pull in opposite directions: the CFO's team demands sub-second dashboard latency at 9am on quarter-end, the finance team revisits the definition of net revenue (returns, credits, and tax treatment) roughly once a quarter, three downstream tools cannot adopt a new semantic engine within this fiscal quarter, and a prior audit found six conflicting revenue numbers that cost two days of reconciliation. Each candidate location for the logic optimizes one of these pressures while taxing another, so there is no free option.

Constraints — Sub-second interactive latency on the executive net-revenue dashboard during quarter-end morning traffic  •  The governed definition of net_revenue must change at most quarterly without breaking downstream consumers  •  At least one consumer (the finance workbook) cannot adopt a new semantic layer engine inside this fiscal quarter  •  Audit requires end-to-end lineage from raw bronze events to the published net_revenue number in Unity Catalog  •  Storage and compute budget cannot support full daily rewrites of a multi-terabyte gold fact table plus a parallel semantic-layer scan on every query

Option A — materialized net_revenue columns in the gold table
+ Reading a single pre-computed column is the fastest possible path: the executive dashboard and the ML feature pipeline get sub-second performance with no join and no runtime arithmetic.; + There is exactly one physical definition of net_revenue in the lakehouse, which directly satisfies the audit requirement for a single governed number [source 1].; + Because the gold table is already the refined, business-ready layer of the medallion architecture, adding measures there fits the contract instead of fighting it [source 3].
− Any change to the net_revenue formula requires rewriting and backfilling the entire gold table, and at multi-terabyte scale that is expensive and slow.; − Historical correctness becomes a versioning problem: either old rows keep stale arithmetic or you must choose a single effective formula, which risks a Type 1-style silent rewrite of previously published reports.; − Team-specific or exploratory revenue variants cannot be expressed without altering the shared table, so you either bloat the schema or block the request.
Best for: Metrics that are stable, high-traffic, and used by many consumers with a single agreed definition — exactly the case where the formula changes less often than it is read.

Option B — gold views and materialized views
+ Logic stays expressed as SQL, so any change to the formula is a code change, not a data backfill; the underlying fact rows never move.; + Materialized views give the dashboard fast reads while keeping the definition queryable and reviewable in the gold layer [source 5].; + A Databricks SQL materialized view can be refreshed on a schedule, so the staleness window is explicit and bounded rather than accidental.
− Every refresh costs compute, and the constraint budget cannot absorb a full re-scan of a multi-terabyte fact plus a separate semantic-layer scan on each query.; − Consumers see staleness up to the refresh interval, which is unacceptable for a same-morning quarter-end close where the CFO expects last night's transactions.; − A plain (non-materialized) view pushes the arithmetic into every query, reintroducing per-query CPU cost on the busiest dashboard.
Best for: Volatile definitions where the formula changes often and consumers can tolerate an explicit, documented staleness bound.

Option C — a governed semantic / metrics layer
+ One definition serves every tool — the dashboard, the workbook, the SQL dashboard, and the feature pipeline — which is the strongest structural cure for metric drift [source 1].; + Definition changes are centralized and version-controlled, so a quarterly revision of net revenue is a single governed edit rather than six edits.; + Consumers keep their own tooling (with connectors) rather than each re-implementing SQL, and lineage stays anchored to one governed metric.
− Adopting and maintaining the layer is real ongoing cost and ownership work [source: p.346].; − The finance workbook cannot adopt the layer inside this fiscal quarter, so it would either read the old number or require a temporary bridge.; − A semantic-layer scan can add latency and compute on the very query path that must be sub-second during quarter-end.
Best for: Organizations with many consumers and frequent definition churn who have the staffing and time to operate a governed shared layer.

Option D — logic inside each dashboard
+ No platform change and no cross-team coordination; each dashboard team implements exactly the arithmetic it wants today.; + Each team moves at its own speed and can ship a dashboard this week without waiting on governance.
− It duplicates definitions, breaks lineage, and guarantees metric drift — the exact audit finding that cost two days of reconciliation.; − There is no single number to certify, so the audit requirement for end-to-end lineage cannot be met.; − It recreates the six-conflicting-revenue-numbers failure that motivated this decision.
Best for: Nothing in this scenario; per the scene guidance, per-dashboard logic is rejected.

Recommendation: Option A — materialized net_revenue columns in the gold table — The binding constraints are the sub-second quarter-end latency requirement, the audit's demand for one governed lineage-complete number [source 1], and the budget that forbids both a multi-terabyte backfill on every change and a parallel semantic-layer scan on every query. Net revenue is a stable, high-traffic metric whose formula changes at most quarterly, so the backfill cost of Option A is amortized over many months of reads while the latency win is paid on every dashboard load — the asymmetry favors materialization. Worked comparison: suppose the fact has 500 million rows, a net_revenue expression costs 40 ms per 1 million rows when evaluated at query time, and a materialized view refresh costs $X per run. Pre-computing the column makes the dashboard read effectively free at query time, whereas a non-materialized view adds roughly 500 × 40 ms = 20 s per full-fact query — impossible on the quarter-end morning path. Option B trades that latency for refresh cost and staleness, which the quarter-end close rejects; Option C is the correct destination for the volatile, team-specific definitions and provides the governed shared definition long-term, but its adoption cost [source: p.346] and the finance workbook's inability to integrate this quarter make it ineligible as the sole home for net revenue right now; Option D is rejected outright because it duplicates definitions, breaks lineage, and guarantees metric drift. Operationally, materialize the stable high-traffic metrics as gold columns, keep volatile or team-specific variants in a governed semantic layer, and never encode them per dashboard — this hybrid satisfies the constraints while preserving a migration path to Option C as the finance workbook's tooling catches up [source 3][source 5].

actions.text: So if duplicated logic is the disease, the real question is where the cure lives. You're the lead data engineer on a Databricks lakehouse, and you've been handed a decision: where should business logic actually live?

Before we compare options, let's ground this in the constraints. We need sub-second interactive latency on the gold tables, and we're bound by the golden rule we just covered — one definition, one place to change it. Any option that violates either of those is off the table.

Option A — materialized net_revenue columns written directly into the gold table. This gives the fastest possible reads and exactly one physical definition. The tradeoff: any change to the formula means rewriting and backfilling that table.

Option B — gold views and materialized views. Your logic stays queryable and refreshable rather than baked into physical columns. The cost is that materialized views in Databricks SQL add refresh cost and introduce staleness between refreshes.

Option C — a governed semantic or metrics layer. One governed definition serves many tools, which is exactly what a single source of truth demands. The price is adopting and maintaining that layer as its own system to operate.

Option D — logic inside each dashboard. We reject this outright: it duplicates definitions, breaks lineage, and guarantees metric drift. This is the exact anti-pattern we've been warning about all lesson.

So the recommendation: materialize stable, high-traffic metrics as gold columns, which is Option A for the metrics we know won't change often. Keep volatile or team-specific definitions in a governed semantic layer. And never — under any circumstance — encode business logic per dashboard. That layered answer is the exam-ready one: stabilize what's stable, govern what's volatile, and reject duplication entirely.

scenes.title: Check: Business Logic and Derived Data

questions.question: A BI team proposes: 'Each BI team should define profit in its own dashboard for flexibility.' Following the gold-layer governance principles taught in this unit, what is the primary problem with this approach?

options.label: It makes the dashboards load too slowly because each team computes profit separately.
It is the classic source of irreconcilable numbers: the same metric name means different things in different dashboards, so no one can reconcile totals.
It causes duplicate business keys in the dimension tables, violating SCD Type 2.
It violates the bronze layer contract, which requires raw append-only storage.

questions.analysis: The trap here is the phrase 'for flexibility.' When each consumer independently defines profit — e.g., one includes discounts, another excludes tax — the same metric label produces different numbers across dashboards, and reconciliation becomes impossible. The medallion architecture is meant to progressively refine raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3], and the gold layer exists precisely so that a governed, shared definition is materialized once. Option A is a misconception about performance (denormalization and materialization are about read performance, not dashboard fragmentation). Option C confuses SCD mechanics with metric definitions; duplicate keys relate to Type 2 versioning, not metric logic. Option D misapplies the bronze contract — bronze stores raw data, so it has nothing to do with how profit is defined in gold.
