questions.question: A metric such as 'monthly active customers' is frequently reused across many dashboards, its definition rarely changes, and it is expensive to compute from raw events. According to Databricks' gold-layer guidance, where should this metric be materialized?

options.label: In a view in the bronze layer so it can trace back to raw events.
In the silver layer as a deduplicated conformed table.
In the gold layer as a materialized, business-ready table.
In a table in Unity Catalog that each BI team can query live without materialization.

questions.analysis: The medallion architecture progressively refines raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 5], and the gold layer is where refined, consumer-oriented data lives. A metric that is frequently reused, stable in definition, and expensive to compute is exactly the candidate for materialization in gold so analysts can write a simple SELECT ... GROUP BY instead of rebuilding the metric each time. Option A is wrong because bronze is raw and append-only — it is not where business metrics live. Option B is tempting because silver is validated/conformed, but silver still holds cleaner entity-level data rather than ready-to-consume aggregate metrics. Option D is a distractor that confuses governance with the materialization decision: putting the table in Unity Catalog does not decide whether it should be materialized.

questions.question: Which of the following are real risks of deriving the same metric inconsistently across multiple consumers (select all that apply)?

options.label: The same metric name yields different values in different dashboards, so totals cannot be reconciled.
Business decisions are made on conflicting numbers, eroding trust in the data platform.
The bronze layer stops being append-only and begins overwriting history.
New consumers cannot reuse a governed definition and must re-derive the logic themselves, multiplying the divergence.

questions.analysis: Duplicated logic across consumers is the classic source of irreconcilable numbers. Option A captures the direct symptom: the same metric label produces different results, so cross-dashboard reconciliation fails. Option B captures the downstream consequence: decisions get made on conflicting numbers, which damages trust — the opposite of what the medallion architecture is meant to deliver, since it progressively refines raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3]. Option D captures the compounding effect: without a governed definition to reuse, each new consumer re-implements the logic, and each implementation drifts further. Option C is a misconception: inconsistent metric derivation is a logic/governance problem in the gold and consumption layers, not a change to the bronze layer's append-only contract. The three correct risks are therefore A, B, and D.

actions.text: Time to check how the business-logic and derived-data principles we just covered have settled in. Take each question on your own — no need to rush — and once you submit, I'll walk through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Encode Profit Logic Once

elements.content: Problem 1

Your team owns the WEB-channel P&L. The Databricks job has already refined raw order events into three silver tables, all for trade date 2024-03-15, channel 'WEB'.

silver.order_lines — grain: one row per order line item

order_id | line_id | order_date | channel | product_category | order_status | gross_amount | discount_amount | cogs_amount

5001 | L1 | 2024-03-15 | WEB | Outdoor | COMPLETE | 400.00 | 40.00 | 180.00

5001 | L2 | 2024-03-15 | WEB | Outdoor | COMPLETE | 200.00 | 0.00 | 90.00

5002 | L3 | 2024-03-15 | WEB | Kitchen | COMPLETE | 300.00 | 30.00 | 140.00

5003 | L4 | 2024-03-15 | WEB | Kitchen | COMPLETE | 100.00 | 0.00 | 45.00

5004 | L5 | 2024-03-15 | WEB | Outdoor | AUTO_CANCELED | 500.00 | 50.00 | 200.00

silver.refunds — grain: one row per refund event (the same order line can be refunded more than once)

refund_id | line_id | refund_date | refund_amount

R1 | L1 | 2024-03-16 | 60.00

R2 | L1 | 2024-03-16 | 40.00

R3 | L3 | 2024-03-16 | 20.00

silver.marketing_spend — grain: one row per spend_date x channel

spend_date | channel | spend_amount

2024-03-15 | WEB | 243.00

Business rules:

(a) net revenue per line = gross_amount - discount_amount - every refund posted against that line, with refunds attributed back to the original order_date so the metric stays reproducible;

(b) AUTO_CANCELED lines (payment authorization failure) never produce revenue or COGS and must not participate in the allocation base at all;

(c) marketing spend is allocated to product categories in proportion to each category's net revenue within the same date x channel;

(d) net profit = net revenue - COGS - allocated marketing.

Compute net revenue, COGS, allocated marketing and net profit per product category for 2024-03-15 WEB, plus the day total, and write the SQL that lands the result in a gold table at grain profit_date x product_category.
Hint: Pre-aggregate refunds to the line grain, remove AUTO_CANCELED lines first, and only then compute the allocation denominator.

Worked solution
Step 0 — Fix the grains before touching any arithmetic. The refund table is at refund-event grain, the marketing table is at date x channel grain, and the fact we must publish is at date x category grain. Every join in the pipeline has to move data to the grain of the join key, never past it.

Step 1 — Pre-aggregate refunds to the line grain, so each line carries one refund number:

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW refunds_by_line AS

SELECT line_id, SUM(refund_amount) AS refund_amount

FROM silver.refunds

GROUP BY line_id;

Result: L1 = 100.00 (60.00 + 40.00), L3 = 20.00. L2 and L4 have no refunds.

Step 2 — Build the line-grain net table and exclude AUTO_CANCELED lines BEFORE the allocation step, using a LEFT JOIN so lines without refunds survive:

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW line_net AS

SELECT l.line_id, l.order_date, l.channel, l.product_category,

l.gross_amount - l.discount_amount AS net_sales,

l.gross_amount - l.discount_amount - COALESCE(r.refund_amount, 0) AS net_revenue,

l.cogs_amount

FROM silver.order_lines l

LEFT JOIN refunds_by_line r ON l.line_id = r.line_id

WHERE l.order_status <> 'AUTO_CANCELED';

L1: 400.00 - 40.00 - 100.00 = 260.00; COGS 180.00

L2: 200.00 - 0.00 - 0.00 = 200.00; COGS 90.00

L3: 300.00 - 30.00 - 20.00 = 250.00; COGS 140.00

L4: 100.00 - 0.00 - 0.00 = 100.00; COGS 45.00

L5 is gone: no revenue, no COGS, and — critically — no place in the allocation base.

Step 3 — Allocation base per date x channel: 260.00 + 200.00 + 250.00 + 100.00 = 810.00, split Outdoor 460.00 and Kitchen 350.00.

Step 4 — Allocate spend pro rata using a window function. The marketing join is 1:1 on (spend_date, channel), so it does not change the row count and the window denominator is computed over exactly the eligible lines:

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW line_alloc AS

SELECT n.*,

s.spend_amount * n.net_revenue

/ SUM(n.net_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY n.order_date, n.channel) AS allocated_marketing

FROM line_net n

JOIN silver.marketing_spend s

ON s.spend_date = n.order_date AND s.channel = n.channel;

Allocation rate = 243.00 / 810.00 = 0.30 exactly.

L1 = 260.00 x 0.30 = 78.00; L2 = 200.00 x 0.30 = 60.00; L3 = 250.00 x 0.30 = 75.00; L4 = 100.00 x 0.30 = 30.00.

Category totals: Outdoor = 78.00 + 60.00 = 138.00; Kitchen = 75.00 + 30.00 = 105.00; check 138.00 + 105.00 = 243.00, equal to the spend row.

Step 5 — Aggregate once to the gold grain:

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold.category_daily_profit AS

SELECT order_date AS profit_date, product_category,

SUM(net_revenue) AS net_revenue,

SUM(cogs_amount) AS cogs,

SUM(allocated_marketing) AS marketing_allocated,

SUM(net_revenue) - SUM(cogs_amount) - SUM(allocated_marketing) AS net_profit

FROM line_alloc

GROUP BY order_date, product_category;

Outdoor: 460.00 - 270.00 - 138.00 = 52.00

Kitchen: 350.00 - 185.00 - 105.00 = 60.00

Day total: 810.00 - 455.00 - 243.00 = 112.00

Step 6 — Reconcile before publishing: category net revenue sums to the line-grain total (810.00), allocated marketing sums to the spend row (243.00), and net profit equals net revenue - COGS - allocated marketing for every row. Any consumer that reads this gold table now gets the exact same number, because the exclusion rule, the refund netting, and the allocation rule exist in exactly one place.

Analysis — The method works because each rule is applied at the only grain where it is true. Refunds are true at refund-event grain, so they must be collapsed to line grain before being joined to a line-grain table; COGS and gross amount are true at line grain; marketing spend is true at date x channel grain; and profit is only meaningful at date x category grain. Following the medallion contract, silver is validated and conformed data and gold is the enriched, business-ready layer [source 6] that progressively refines raw inputs into trusted tables [source 3], so the gold table is where the metric definition belongs — not in each dashboard.

Typical student mistakes: (1) using an INNER JOIN on refunds, which silently deletes every never-refunded line and understates revenue; (2) computing net_revenue as a single SUM(gross - discount - refund) at the wrong grain; (3) allocating spend after filtering in some runs and before in others, which makes the table non-reproducible; (4) using DOUBLE for money and then failing the reconciliation check by a cent — cast to DECIMAL(18,2). Edge cases to design for: a fully refunded line has net_revenue = 0 and therefore receives 0.00 of allocation, which is correct but must not be dropped by the join; if an entire date x channel has zero net revenue the window denominator is 0 and the division fails, so guard it with a CASE expression that assigns 0.00 or falls back to an explicit equal-split rule; and refunds posted in a later month must still be attributed to the original order_date, or the same day's profit changes every time the job runs. The rule generalizes: whenever a metric mixes grains, pre-aggregate to the finest grain that carries all the keys, allocate with a window function partitioned by the allocation dimensions, and aggregate exactly once at the end.
Problem 2

Before the job ships, a reviewer proposes this compressed one-shot query to produce the gold table:

SELECT l.product_category,

SUM(l.gross_amount - l.discount_amount - COALESCE(r.refund_amount, 0)) AS net_revenue

FROM silver.order_lines l

LEFT JOIN silver.refunds r ON l.order_id = r.order_id

WHERE l.order_status <> 'AUTO_CANCELED'

GROUP BY l.product_category;

(a) Using the 2024-03-15 WEB data from the previous problem, compute the net revenue per category this query actually returns. (b) Explain precisely why it differs from the correct figure — name the grain mismatch and give the fan-out factor. (c) Show the minimal change that makes the refund deduction count exactly once per line, and recompute Outdoor to prove it.
Hint: Count how many rows of silver.refunds share order_id 5001, and how many lines order 5001 has.

Worked solution
(a) The join key is order_id, but neither side is unique on order_id. Order 5001 has two lines (L1, L2) and two refund rows (R1, R2, both against L1). A left join on order_id therefore produces 2 x 2 = 4 rows for order 5001:

(L1, R1): 400.00 - 40.00 - 60.00 = 300.00

(L1, R2): 400.00 - 40.00 - 40.00 = 320.00

(L2, R1): 200.00 - 0.00 - 60.00 = 140.00

(L2, R2): 200.00 - 0.00 - 40.00 = 160.00

Outdoor SUM = 300.00 + 320.00 + 140.00 + 160.00 = 920.00.

Order 5002 has one line (L3) and one refund (R3), so it fans out 1 x 1: 300.00 - 30.00 - 20.00 = 250.00. Order 5003 has one line (L4) and no refund, so the LEFT JOIN yields a single row with NULL: 100.00 - 0.00 = 100.00. Kitchen SUM = 250.00 + 100.00 = 350.00 — correct by accident, because Kitchen orders happen to have a single line each.

The query returns Outdoor 920.00 and Kitchen 350.00, a day total of 1270.00 instead of 810.00.

(b) The grain mismatch is order-level key versus line-level and refund-event-level measures. Algebraically, the fanned set gives:

Outdoor = 2 x (360.00 + 200.00) - 2 x (60.00 + 40.00) = 1120.00 - 200.00 = 920.00.

Both the line net sales and the refund amounts are multiplied by the fan-out factor of 2 — the number of lines in the order, which happens to equal the number of refund rows here. The correct answer is 460.00, so Outdoor net revenue is overstated by 460.00, exactly 100%. Kitchen is unaffected only because its orders have no fan-out, which is precisely why this bug survives a casual spot check on one category.

(c) Move the refunds to the line grain first, then join on the line key:

WITH refunds_by_line AS (

SELECT line_id, SUM(refund_amount) AS refund_amount

FROM silver.refunds

GROUP BY line_id

)

SELECT l.product_category,

SUM(l.gross_amount - l.discount_amount - COALESCE(r.refund_amount, 0)) AS net_revenue

FROM silver.order_lines l

LEFT JOIN refunds_by_line r ON l.line_id = r.line_id

WHERE l.order_status <> 'AUTO_CANCELED'

GROUP BY l.product_category;

Outdoor now recomputes as (260.00 + 200.00) = 460.00: L1 carries its two refunds as one 100.00 deduction, L2 carries 0.00, and no row is duplicated.

Analysis — A join on a non-unique key is a many-to-many join, and its row count is the product of the two multiplicities. The safe habit is to state the grain of each input in a comment and assert uniqueness on the join key (for example, a COUNT(*) = COUNT(DISTINCT key) check) before the join runs. Students often reason that a LEFT JOIN is harmless because it only preserves rows — but the LEFT keyword controls which unmatched rows survive, not how many matched combinations are produced. The second trap is the misleading partial validation: one category reconciles perfectly while another is 100% wrong, so a test suite that only checks the day total or a single category passes. This matters most for gold-layer tables that feed BI dashboards and data products, because downstream consumers cannot see the raw events that would reveal the inflation [source 1]. The same fan-out risk applies to any measure joined at the wrong grain — payments, shipments, support tickets, web sessions — so always pre-aggregate the transaction table to the grain of the entity you are enriching.
Problem 3

Same 2024-03-15 WEB data. A second engineer keeps the refund pre-aggregation correct but allocates marketing spend before applying the AUTO_CANCELED exclusion: the spend row is joined to all five lines, the window denominator SUM(net_revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY order_date, channel) is computed over all five lines, and only at the very end, immediately before the GROUP BY, is WHERE order_status <> 'AUTO_CANCELED' applied.

(a) Compute the window denominator this pipeline uses. (b) Compute the marketing dollars that survive the final filter, per category and in total. (c) Compute the per-category net profit this pipeline reports and quantify the error against the correct answer. (d) State the single one-line reconciliation check that would have caught it.
Hint: The canceled line L5 has net revenue 500.00 - 50.00 = 450.00 and receives an allocation it will never pay for.

Worked solution
(a) Denominator over all five lines: L1 260.00 + L2 200.00 + L3 250.00 + L4 100.00 + L5 450.00 = 1260.00. The canceled line's 450.00 of net revenue inflates the base by 55.6% relative to the correct 810.00.

(b) Allocation rate = 243.00 / 1260.00 = 0.192857 per dollar of net revenue. Per line:

L1 = 243.00 x 260/1260 = 50.14

L2 = 243.00 x 200/1260 = 38.57

L3 = 243.00 x 250/1260 = 48.21

L4 = 243.00 x 100/1260 = 19.29

L5 = 243.00 x 450/1260 = 86.79

Sum = 243.00, so the allocation itself still balances — until the filter runs.

After WHERE order_status <> 'AUTO_CANCELED', L5 is removed and its 86.79 of allocated spend disappears with it:

Outdoor = 50.14 + 38.57 = 88.71

Kitchen = 48.21 + 19.29 = 67.50

Surviving total = 156.21, versus 243.00 in silver.marketing_spend. 86.79 of real cost has evaporated.

(c) Reported profit:

Outdoor: 460.00 - 270.00 - 88.71 = 101.29

Kitchen: 350.00 - 185.00 - 67.50 = 97.50

Day total: 198.79

Correct answer: Outdoor 52.00, Kitchen 60.00, day total 112.00. The pipeline overstates the day by 86.79 — exactly the marketing cost allocated to the canceled line — which is a 77% overstatement, and Outdoor alone is reported 94.8% too high (101.29 instead of 52.00). Note the direction of the bias: dropping cost inflates profit, so the error looks like good news and rarely gets escalated.

(d) Reconcile the allocated cost back to the source: SUM(marketing_allocated) per profit_date x channel must equal SUM(spend_amount) from silver.marketing_spend for the same date and channel. Here 156.21 <> 243.00 and the job fails immediately. The filtering has to happen inside the allocation base — either in a WHERE clause before the window is evaluated, or with an explicit FILTER (WHERE order_status <> 'AUTO_CANCELED') clause on the window function — so that the eligible lines absorb the full spend.

Analysis — The allocation is a partition-level invariant: the parts must sum to the whole. That invariant holds only if the row set used in the denominator is exactly the row set that is written out. Filtering after the window silently changes the denominator, and because the change is proportional, every ratio downstream shifts without any error being thrown — the row count is smaller, the numbers are plausible, and no exception fires. This is the classic 'quiet shift' failure mode, and it is dangerous precisely because the medallion architecture's promise is that gold holds trusted, business-ready output, while the pipeline that owns it can quietly redefine the denominator [source 3]. Domain teams own their own Bronze-to-Gold pipelines and publish gold outputs as data products [source 1], so consistency is a governance property of that single pipeline, not something a downstream analyst can repair.

Where students go wrong: assuming a WHERE clause 'obviously' applies early, when in SQL the filter placement is a logical-order decision that changes what the window sees; forgetting that the same trap applies to refunds (a refunded-to-zero line must still count as an eligible line, or the base shrinks), returns, and promo discounts; and testing only the grand total, which here still reconciles at 243.00 before the filter, hiding the defect. Edge cases: a date x channel with all lines canceled leaves a zero denominator — decide explicitly whether to write a zero-profit row or no row at all; a canceled order that was partially refunded may still need its refund recorded somewhere for finance, so exclude it from the P&L fact but not from the refund fact; and if the business later wants allocation by units or by gross margin instead of net revenue, the denominator changes and the reconciliation test must change with it. The general rule: a window function's denominator must be computed over the post-exclusion population, and every allocation must be paired with a parts-sum-to-whole assertion.
Problem 4

The gold table is defined and populated as:

CREATE TABLE gold.category_daily_profit (

profit_date DATE, product_category STRING,

net_revenue DECIMAL(18,2), cogs DECIMAL(18,2),

marketing_allocated DECIMAL(18,2), net_profit DECIMAL(18,2)

);

The nightly job writes it with INSERT INTO gold.category_daily_profit SELECT ... FROM line_alloc GROUP BY 1, 2. Assume the table already holds 2024-03-15 with Outdoor 52.00 and Kitchen 60.00. The 2024-03-15 batch fails partway through and the retry succeeds and inserts the same rows again.

(a) Show the state of the table for 2024-03-15 after the retry and quantify the effect on a 'profit over the last 30 days' dashboard that runs SUM(net_profit) with no deduplication. (b) Rewrite the write so that re-running any day, any number of times, leaves the table byte-identical — an idempotent write. (c) Give one alternative write pattern and state when it is preferable. (d) State the precondition the source must satisfy for the MERGE to be deterministic.
Hint: Idempotence means the second run produces exactly the same table state as the first run, not the same table plus the same rows.

Worked solution
(a) INSERT appends unconditionally. After the retry the table contains, for 2024-03-15:

Outdoor row twice: (460.00, 270.00, 138.00, 52.00) and (460.00, 270.00, 138.00, 52.00)

Kitchen row twice: (350.00, 185.00, 105.00, 60.00) and (350.00, 185.00, 105.00, 60.00)

SUM(net_profit) for that date = 224.00 instead of 112.00, SUM(net_revenue) = 1620.00 instead of 810.00, SUM(cogs) = 910.00 instead of 455.00, SUM(marketing_allocated) = 486.00 instead of 243.00. The 30-day dashboard overstates profit by exactly 112.00 — one whole day counted twice — and because the duplicate is a plausible-looking date, no consumer can tell which row is the phantom. Retrying a job must never change a published number.

(b) Encode the write as an upsert on the table's declared grain, date x category:

MERGE INTO gold.category_daily_profit AS t

USING (

SELECT order_date AS profit_date, product_category,

SUM(net_revenue) AS net_revenue,

SUM(cogs_amount) AS cogs,

SUM(allocated_marketing) AS marketing_allocated,

SUM(net_revenue) - SUM(cogs_amount) - SUM(allocated_marketing) AS net_profit

FROM line_alloc

GROUP BY order_date, product_category

) AS s

ON t.profit_date = s.profit_date AND t.product_category = s.product_category

WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET

t.net_revenue = s.net_revenue,

t.cogs = s.cogs,

t.marketing_allocated = s.marketing_allocated,

t.net_profit = s.net_profit

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT

(profit_date, product_category, net_revenue, cogs, marketing_allocated, net_profit)

VALUES

(s.profit_date, s.product_category, s.net_revenue, s.cogs, s.marketing_allocated, s.net_profit);

The second execution matches both existing rows on (profit_date, product_category) and overwrites them with the recomputed values, so the table returns to exactly 112.00 for the day. The match condition must be the full grain: matching on profit_date alone would update two categories with one source row and corrupt the table.

(c) When the job recomputes whole days or whole partitions, use an atomic partition replacement instead — for example INSERT INTO gold.category_daily_profit REPLACE WHERE profit_date = DATE'2024-03-15', or a full dynamic-partition overwrite of the day being rebuilt. This is preferable when the day is fully recomputed and late-arriving adjustments can delete a category entirely: REPLACE WHERE removes rows that no longer exist, while MERGE leaves stale rows in place because it has nothing to match them against. Use MERGE when the source is partial (only changed categories arrive) and REPLACE WHERE when the source is complete for the partition.

(d) The source s must be unique on (profit_date, product_category). If the staging query produces two rows for the same date and category, Delta cannot decide which one wins: it raises DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE (or, on older runtimes, applies a nondeterministic update and writes different results on different runs). Deduplicate or pre-aggregate the source before the MERGE, exactly as the GROUP BY above does.

Analysis — Idempotence is what makes a pipeline operable: retries, backfills, and late-arriving data all become safe, and the only write that satisfies it at row grain is a deterministic upsert keyed on the table's full grain. The reason this belongs in the gold layer is architectural — the medallion architecture guarantees atomicity of these writes and distinguishes raw from validated from enriched data [source 6], and it exists to turn raw inputs into trusted insights [source 5]; a gold table that doubles a day's profit after a retry has broken that contract. Bronze is append-only, so re-ingesting an event there is expected and deduplication handles it downstream in silver; gold is the opposite — it is a published, aggregated artifact, so its write must be keyed and idempotent.

Common mistakes: assuming MERGE is automatically idempotent regardless of key (it is not — a partial key creates duplicates under the same date); running MERGE without a partition predicate on the merge key, which forces a full-table scan instead of partition pruning; and using UPDATE-only logic that silently drops a brand-new category — always include the WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT branch. A subtler mistake is fixing the write path but not the read path: a dashboard that concatenates two daily files instead of reading the table will still double the day.

Edge cases: a category that disappears after a restatement needs the partition-replacement pattern, not a MERGE; concurrent writers on the same partition can conflict, so serialize the job per date; and if the source contains NULL in the match key, the ON clause never matches and you get a new row on every run — reject NULLs in the grain columns before writing. The generalization is the definition worth memorizing: a transformation is idempotent when applying it twice produces the same state as applying it once, and the practical test is to run the job twice in a row and assert that COUNT(*) and SUM(net_profit) per profit_date are unchanged.

actions.text: Now let's put that principle to work on a concrete case. This is the worked problem where we encode the profit logic once — and only once — so every team downstream reads the same number.

Problem 1: your team owns the WEB-channel profit and loss statement, and the Databricks gold table shows a refund deduction that is inflated far beyond what finance reports. Before you touch any code, ask yourself where the grain mismatch could be coming from.

The hint is the key: pre-aggregate refunds to the line grain first. Each refund relates to an order, and orders contain multiple lines — so if you join at transaction grain without pre-aggregating, kauf the same refund appears once per line item and the total deduction explodes.

The worked solution lays out Step 0: fix the grains before anything else. Then join marketing cost allocated by date and channel, aggregate once to date by category, and write to gold. Every consumer now reads the same profit figure.

And the analysis explains why the method works: each rule is a small, testable transformation. When you break profit into discrete steps — exclude canceled orders, net refunds, allocate cost — each step can be validated independently, which is exactly what the exam expects you to reason about.

scenes.title: Lab: Build and Query a Gold Table in Databricks

content.html:
Lab: Build and Query a Gold Table · Databricks

PySpark · Medallion
🐍 Python (PySpark) ⏳ Loading Pyodide…
Initializing…
📋 Output — 
> Ready to run code...
✅ Reference Solution (conceptual):
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

gold = (silver_orders
    .join(silver_customers, "customer_id", "left")
    .join(silver_products, "product_id", "left")
    .select("order_id", "customer_id", "product_id", "order_date", "amount", "customer_name", "product_name")
)

# Validate grain
assert gold.count() == silver_orders.count()

# BI aggregate
result = (gold.groupBy("customer_id", "customer_name")
          .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total_spend"))
          .orderBy(F.desc("total_spend")))
result.show()

actions.text: Now let's put that gold-layer theory into practice. In this lab you'll write the PySpark join that turns silver orders, customers, and products into a single wide gold table, then query it the way a BI consumer would.

actions.content: Write your transformation here — start with the join across silver_orders, silver_customers, and silver_products.

actions.text: As you build the join, keep the grain front of mind. The gold table's grain is one row per order, so every join key you add must be unique on the right-hand side — otherwise you'll silently fan out rows.

actions.content: These checks validate grain: they compare your gold row count against the silver order count and flag fan-out or rows lost to an accidental inner join.
Run your code to see the row count and grain validation.

actions.text: Once the transform passes, write the aggregate BI query the gold table was designed to make trivial — for example, revenue by region and month. Notice how much simpler it is than joining the silver tables directly every time.

actions.content: Execute and compare your gold query against the same aggregation over raw silver joins.

actions.text: If the feedback flags fan-out, rows lost, or columns violating the declared grain, use the hint panel to diagnose which join key isn't unique. Fixing the grain here is exactly the discipline the exam rewards — encode the logic once in gold, and every downstream metric stays trustworthy.

scenes.title: Check: Building Gold Tables End to End

questions.question: A team proposes making the gold layer self-contained by storing every dimension attribute from every source system inside each wide gold table, so that downstream analysts 'never need to join anything ever again.' From a design standpoint, what is the primary objection to this proposal?

options.label: It improves query speed but has no material downside, since storage in Delta Lake is effectively free.
The gold table becomes arbitrarily wide and its flattened attributes go stale the moment a dimension changes, because they are copied snapshots rather than governed references.
Storing dimension attributes in gold breaks the medallion contract, because gold is defined as raw append-only data exactly as ingested.
It forces every query to perform a five-table join at read time, which is exactly what denormalization was meant to prevent.

questions.analysis: Denormalization is a deliberate trade: redundancy is reintroduced to improve read/query performance, at the cost of storage and maintenance. Copying every dimension attribute into gold expands column count without bound and, more seriously, freezes each attribute as a snapshot. When an SCD Type 2 dimension later changes a customer_segment or a product_category, the copied value in the already-built gold table no longer matches the governed dimension, so the gold layer silently drifts from the source of truth. Option A is wrong because the storage and staleness costs are real and compounding. Option C inverts the medallion contract: raw append-only data is bronze, while gold is refined and business-ready [source 3]. Option D is backwards — denormalization exists precisely to remove read-time joins, not add them. The correct answer is the trap the lesson calls out: unbounded width and stale attributes are the cost of storing every dimension attribute in gold.

questions.question: Before publishing a newly built denormalized gold table to consumers, which validations should the engineer run? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Confirm the fact grain is unchanged after the dimension joins, e.g. COUNT(*) on silver.sales equals COUNT(*) on the joined gold result.
Verify each LEFT JOIN against an SCD Type 2 dimension matches only the current version (eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01') so it returns exactly one row per fact row.
Ensure the gold table stores raw events exactly as ingested, with no cleaning or refinement applied.
Check that the metric business logic is defined once, so a single metric (for example net revenue after returns) has one consistent definition across all consumers.

questions.analysis: Publishing a gold table safely means reconciling the count before and after the join so that no fan-out has occurred. A LEFT JOIN against a dimension that is unique on its key — or filtered to the current SCD Type 2 version — preserves the fact grain, and you verify this by comparing COUNT(*) before and after, exactly as the worked denormalization example does. Business logic should be encoded once in the gold transformation (or a governed semantic/metrics layer) so that the same metric does not drift across dashboards, notebooks, and ad hoc queries [source 5]. Option C is the classic trap distractor: gold is refined and business-ready, not raw; raw append-only data belongs to bronze [source 6]. The three correct validations are grain reconciliation, SCD Type 2 version filtering, and single-definition metric logic.

questions.question: A gold_sales_wide table was built six months ago. Its source dim_customer is an SCD Type 2 dimension, and a customer's segment was legitimately changed three months ago. The gold table still shows the customer under their original segment. What is the correct response?

options.label: Ignore it — the historical gold table is an immutable snapshot and should never be rebuilt after publication.
Edit the gold_sales_wide rows directly and update the stale segment values in place, without touching the pipeline.
Rerun the gold_sales_wide build so the LEFT JOIN picks up the current SCD Type 2 version (the row whose eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01'), restoring alignment with the governed dimension.
Convert the dimension from Type 2 to Type 1 so that future segment changes overwrite history and no rebuild is ever needed.

questions.analysis: The gold table copied a snapshot of a dimension attribute, so when the SCD Type 2 dimension gained a new current version, the flattened attribute became stale. The fix is to re-run the gold transformation so the join re-matches the current version (eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01') and the flattened column reflects the governed source of truth. Option A is wrong: a gold table is a derived artifact and must be rebuilt when its inputs change. Option B is the manual-patch anti-pattern — hand-editing breaks reproducibility and auditability, and the next run would overwrite the fix anyway. Option D destroys the historical tracking that the Type 2 modeling was implemented to preserve, so it trades a rebuild for permanently lost history. As the source notes, a well-designed dimension with proper versioning keeps the governed definitions consistent; the medallion layers are progressively refined sources of truth [source 3].

questions.question: Three BI tools — a tableau-style dashboard, a notebook-based ad hoc analysis, and a scheduled report — all read from the same gold layer. Describe, in plain terms, how you keep a single metric definition (for example, 'net revenue after returns') consistent across all three consumers, and name one concrete failure mode that occurs if you do not.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Identifies that the metric is defined ONCE — either inside the gold transformation or in a governed semantic/metrics layer — and exposed to all three tools from that single source, rather than being re-implemented per tool (40%). (2) Explains why this works: each tool reads the same pre-computed column or governed metric, so the SQL expression is not duplicated (25%). (3) Names a concrete failure mode — for example, 'the numbers drift: the dashboard and the report disagree on net revenue because one silently excludes returns and the other does not, and nobody can reconcile them' (20%). (4) Expression clarity and use of accurate terminology (15%).
questions.analysis: Reference answer: Encode the business logic for 'net revenue after returns' exactly once, inside the gold transformation (for example, net_revenue = gross_revenue - returns_amount computed in gold_sales_wide) or in a governed semantic/metrics layer that all three tools query. The dashboard, the notebook, and the scheduled report then each read the same governed column or metric rather than re-deriving the formula in their own SQL. This eliminates metric drift, where each tool independently re-implements the definition and the numbers slowly diverge. The stated anti-pattern is exactly this: the same metric re-implemented in every dashboard, notebook, and ad hoc query, so that the numbers drift and nobody can reconcile them. The medallion architecture supports this by making gold the refined, business-ready layer that all consumers share, progressively refining raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 5].

actions.text: Let's pull all of that together now. This one is a capstone check — it mixes gold layer design, join discipline, and where business logic belongs, so read each item carefully before you commit. Take your time and work through every question on your own.
Hold off on second-guessing yourself mid-question — answer what you think is right, and I'll walk through anything that tripped you up once you submit. Go ahead and give it your best shot.

scenes.title: Summary and Exam Focus

elements.content: Summary and Exam Focus
Gold-table design and centralized business logic — consolidated for the certification exam
1. Gold tables are built for the consumer

• Fix the grain first: one row per order line item, never fanned out.

• Denormalize deliberately — flatten dimensions before BI reads (facts alone reduce to bronze/silver).

• Push join work upstream: an analyst should write a simple SELECT ... GROUP BY, not a five-table join [source 4].
2. Denormalization trades storage for query latency

• Redundancy is re-introduced on purpose: fewer joins, faster dashboards, larger footprint.

• Always verify row counts — a dimension join that fans out is the fail signal [source 6].
3. Centralize business logic once
• Define each metric once in gold or a governed semantic layer — never per dashboard.

actions.text: We've reached the summary page for this section on gold-table design and centralized business logic. Let's consolidate everything into exam-ready takeaways, because these three ideas show up repeatedly on the Data Engineer Associate exam.
Here's the through-line: gold tables are built for the consumer, and business logic should be centralized. Everything else on this page flows from those two principles.

First, gold tables are built for the consumer. That means you fix the grain first — one row per order line item, for example — and you push join work upstream so analysts query a single table instead of assembling it themselves.

Second, denormalization trades storage for query latency. Redundancy is re-introduced on purpose — fewer joins mean faster reads. But here's the trap: always verify your row counts, because a dimension join can silently fan out and multiply rows. That single check saves more exam points than almost anything else.

Third, centralize business logic once. Define each metric a single time — in gold or in a governed semantic layer — and never redefine it per dashboard. Duplicated logic is the most common source of inconsistent numbers in production. Watch for the recurring exam traps too: mistaking gold for bronze or silver, calling denormalization a write optimization, and picking the option that computes the metric inside each BI tool. Next lesson we'll go deeper into business logic, derived data, and metrics layers.

scenes.title: Business Logic and Derived Data

elements.content: Business Logic and Derived Data
Medallion architecture · gold layer
Business logic = the rules that convert raw events into decision-ready values.
Precondition: the rule is agreed and versioned before it is encoded anywhere.
Derived data = any value computed from other data, never captured at the source.
Edge case: if the inputs change, every derived value must be recomputed and backfilled.
Worked example — profit is a rule, not an event:

elements.html: profit=revenue−cost−marketing spend

elements.content:
• Every gold column, dashboard metric, and ML feature is a derived artifact carrying business logic [source 3].

• If 12 teams each restate profit, the numbers drift and no one can reconcile them.

elements.html: 3×105×0.62=1.86×105

elements.content: Same three inputs, two customers, one agreed definition.

A: revenue $500,000 − cost $150,000 − spend $40,000 = $310,000

B: same inputs defined per team = $385,000

Gap = $75,000 of pure definitional drift [source 5].

actions.text: As we just saw, the gold layer is where your trusted tables live. But what actually makes them trustworthy? The answer is business logic and derived data — and these are the two most politically sensitive objects in the entire lakehouse, because when they disagree, two teams can walk into the same meeting with two different numbers.

Start with the definition. Business logic is the set of rules that convert raw events into decision-ready values. Raw events are just facts: a sale happened, a cost was incurred, a click was recorded. They carry no opinion. Business logic is the opinion — the rule that says profit equals revenue minus cost minus marketing spend. Notice that the rule is not stored anywhere in the source system; it is invented by the business.

And there is a precondition you must respect: a rule only counts as business logic once it is agreed upon and versioned before you encode it. If two engineers independently decide what profit means on a Friday afternoon, you do not have a rule — you have two rules, and you will discover that in the next quarterly review.

That leads to the second term. Derived data is any value computed from other data rather than captured at the source. Revenue is captured at the source. Profit is derived. Lifetime value is derived. Conversion rate is derived. Anything you calculate is derived data, and by definition it inherits the logic used to calculate it.

Here is the edge case that trips people up. If the inputs change, every derived value downstream changes too — not just the one you were looking at. A single late-arriving cost record silently rewrites profit, margin, bonus accruals, and any dashboard that reads them. This is why derived values are described as politically sensitive: they are the numbers people are held accountable for.
Let's make it concrete with the worked example on the slide.

Profit equals revenue minus cost minus marketing spend. Say revenue is five hundred thousand, cost is one hundred and fifty thousand, and marketing spend is forty thousand. Profit is three hundred and ten thousand. But key point: profit is a rule, not an event. Nobody 'captured' profit. We computed it — and the moment that formula lives in two places, the two copies can drift.

Now look at the layer map. Bronze holds raw events with no logic applied. Silver holds conformed facts — cleaning, deduplication, conformance — still no business opinion. Gold is where business logic lives. That placement is deliberate: it gives you exactly one place to look when a metric is contested.

And remember the scope of this. Every gold column, every dashboard metric, every ML feature is a derived artifact carrying business logic. If the logic is wrong, every consumer inherits the error — the table, the report, and the model. That is why this page frames the rest of the lesson: how rules become derived values inside transformations, and why a single source of truth is not just good hygiene, it is a governance requirement.

scenes.title: Check: Business Logic and Derived Data

questions.question: A data engineer is reviewing a silver table for an e-commerce pipeline. The table contains a column named order_timestamp, which is copied directly from the source system's transactional log, and a column named profit_after_marketing, which is computed as net_revenue minus cogs minus allocated_marketing_cost. How should these two columns be classified according to the medallion architecture principle of separating captured data from derived data?

options.label: order_timestamp is captured data because it is recorded at the source and copied into the lakehouse, while profit_after_marketing is derived data because it is computed from other columns.
order_timestamp is derived data because it can be recalculated from the ingestion batch ID, while profit_after_marketing is captured data because marketing cost is stored in the source.
Both columns are captured data because they both appear in the silver table, and silver is defined as validated raw data.
Both columns are derived data because they are stored in the lakehouse rather than queried directly from the source system.

questions.analysis: Captured data is the raw fact recorded at the source and brought into the lakehouse without transformation; order_timestamp is exactly this kind of data. Derived data is produced by applying a formula or rule to captured data; profit_after_marketing is computed from net_revenue, cogs, and allocated_marketing_cost, so it is derived. The medallion architecture progressively refines raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3], and the same progressive refinement is described as a pattern that improves data quality and structure across Bronze, Silver, and Gold [source 2]. Option B inverts the definitions. Option C confuses the layer with the classification: silver contains validated data, but validated captured data remains captured data. Option D misapplies storage location as the criterion; storage in the lakehouse does not make a value derived.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about where business logic belongs in the medallion layers are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Bronze should stay raw and append-only; business logic should not be applied there just because bronze is closest to the source.
A rule applied during validation in silver (for example, excluding auto-canceled orders from a revenue metric) is still business logic, not merely data quality.
Silver should carry all business logic because it is the validated layer and consumers never query bronze or gold directly.
Gold is the appropriate home for stabilized, reusable metric definitions such as net revenue after returns or profit after marketing cost.

questions.analysis: Bronze is the raw layer, and the medallion architecture is explicitly about progressively refining raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3]; baking business logic into bronze destroys the raw record and makes re-derivation impossible, so A is correct. A business rule is the definition of a metric or rule, not a technical quality check; excluding auto-canceled orders changes the meaning of the metric, so it is business logic even when implemented inside silver validation, making B correct. Gold is the refined, business-ready layer where stable, reused definitions belong, so D is correct. Option C is the trap distractor: silver validates and conforms data, but placing all business logic in silver would force consumers to repeat metric logic downstream and defeat the purpose of a governed gold layer. The medallion pattern is also composable with other patterns and does not require every rule to live in one layer [source 1].

questions.question: A stakeholder argues that because bronze is 'closest to the source,' business logic should be applied there so that every downstream layer inherits the rules automatically. Which response best reflects the medallion architecture guidance?

options.label: Reject the argument: bronze should remain raw and append-only so the original record is preserved for replay and re-derivation, and business logic belongs in the refined layers.
Accept the argument: because bronze is closest to the source, it is the most natural place to encode metric definitions and avoid duplication.
Accept the argument only for time-based rules, since timestamps must be fixed at ingestion and cannot be recalculated later.
Reject the argument, but replace it with the rule that business logic must be applied in silver validation so that gold stays purely presentational.

questions.analysis: The medallion architecture organizes data into bronze, silver, and gold layers that progressively refine raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3], and the terms bronze (raw), silver (validated), and gold (enriched) describe the quality of data in each layer [source 6]. Preserving bronze as raw and append-only is what makes replay and re-derivation possible when a metric definition changes. Option B is the classic trap distractor: 'closest to the source' is an intuitive but incorrect justification for putting business logic in bronze. Option C mistakes ingestion-time values for business rules; timestamps are captured data, not metric logic, and replay still depends on the raw record. Option D overcorrects by forbidding all logic in gold, but stabilized, reusable metric definitions are exactly what gold is for.

actions.text: Let's put that to the test. Try each question on your own — sorting captured data from derived data and placing business logic in the right layer is exactly the kind of distinction the exam loves to probe.
Take your time, commit to an answer for each one, and I'll walk through the results with you once you've submitted.

scenes.title: Where Duplicated Logic Creeps In

elements.content: Where Duplicated Logic Creeps In
The same business rule gets re-implemented in the notebook, the ETL script, the dashboard calculated field, and the ad-platform export — one rule, four definitions.

Duplicated business logic appears whenever the same rule is re-implemented in more than one place: the notebook, the ETL script, the dashboard calculated field, and the ad-platform export each carry their own copy of the definition. The medallion architecture keeps the raw, validated, and enriched layers distinct so that progressive refinement produces trusted, business-ready tables [source 3].

Running example — marketing cost attribution. The pipeline computes one 'profit' number by allocating marketing spend inside the gold transform, and the analyst's spreadsheet recomputes profit by dividing spend across rows with its own method. The two numbers disagree because the rule was copied, not reused; the layer design is only as reliable as the discipline that funnels every consumer through the enriched layer [source 6].

Attribute-derived values diverge fastest. Clicks weighted by price, naive attribution, and last-click each change the moment the weighting rule is varied — and that rule is variation-prone, so two teams can agree on the raw clicks and still report different attributed revenue. Each domain should own its Bronze-to-Gold pipeline so the enrichment is defined once, then shared as a data product [source 1].
Rule ownership — for every derived metric, record where it is currently computed, who owns it, and which consumers read it. If one metric has four computation sites, it is already fragmented.

actions.text: Now that we understand why business logic and derived data matter, let's get concrete about where duplicated logic actually creeps in. This is the page where the abstract becomes a checklist you can apply during the exam.

Here's the core idea: duplicated business logic appears whenever the same rule is re-implemented in more than one place. That means a notebook, an ETL script, a dashboard calculated field, and an ad-platform export can each carry their own copy of the same rule. Four surfaces, one rule — and now four places to change when that rule evolves.

A useful way to spot it: ask whether the logic has a single owner. If the answer is 'it's computed here, and also over there,' you already have duplication — even before anyone notices the numbers disagree.

Our running example is marketing cost attribution. The pipeline computes profit one way by attributing marketing cost across campaigns, and an analyst's spreadsheet computes it again with its own assumptions. Same data, two 'profit' numbers — and both can be defended by whoever built them.

Attribute-derived values diverge fastest. A metric like clicks weighted by price, a naive attribution, or a last-click model all depend on a weighting rule — and that weighting rule is exactly the thing that gets varied accidentally. Change one coefficient in one place and the two metrics quietly drift apart.

So the discipline is rule ownership. For every derived metric, record where it is currently computed, who owns it, and which consumers actually read it. That single table is often the fastest way to expose duplication you didn't know existed.

And one exam trap to flag now: a consistent silver table does not guarantee consistent metrics. The table can be perfectly clean while the metric definition varies across consumers. The variation lives in the definition, not the table — hold onto that, because we'll return to it on the next page.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Profit After Marketing Costs

elements.content: Problem 1

An ad platform reports that order O1 attracted 10 clicks at a total spend of $80. Order O1 contains two line items: item X, price $40, credited with 6 of the 10 clicks; and item Y, price $60, credited with 4 of the 10 clicks. For each item compute (i) the allocated marketing cost and (ii) the profit defined as price − allocated marketing cost, under two defensible rules: (a) click-weighted attribution (equal cost per click) and (b) price-weighted attribution (spend allocated in proportion to item price). Report the order total under each rule, and state the per-item change in profit for item X caused purely by the choice of rule.
Hint: Both rules must distribute the entire $80 pool: exhaustiveness (nothing left over) and additivity (parts sum to the whole) are the two tests a valid allocation has to pass.

Worked solution
Step 0 — collect and check the givens. Total order revenue $R = 40 + 60 = \$100$. Total spend to allocate $S = \$80$. Total clicks $C = 6 + 4 = 10$. The spend is one pool that must be split across exactly two items, so the weights must sum to 1 and the allocated costs must sum to $80.

(a) Click-weighted attribution (equal cost per click). Cost per click $c = S / C = 80 / 10 = \$8$.

Allocated cost $a_X = c \times 6 = 8 \times 6 = \$48$; $a_Y = c \times 4 = 8 \times 4 = \$32$.

Exhaustiveness check: $48 + 32 = \$80$ ✓ (nothing unallocated).

Profit: $\pi_X = 40 - 48 = -\$8$; $\pi_Y = 60 - 32 = \$28$.

Order total: $-8 + 28 = \$20$, which agrees with the independent check $R - S = 100 - 80 = \$20$.

(b) Price-weighted attribution. Weights $w_i = p_i / \sum_j p_j$, so $w_X = 40 / 100 = 0.40$ and $w_Y = 60 / 100 = 0.60$; note $w_X + w_Y = 1$.

Allocated cost $a_X = 0.40 \times 80 = \$32$; $a_Y = 0.60 \times 80 = \$48$.

Exhaustiveness check: $32 + 48 = \$80$ ✓.

Profit: $\pi_X = 40 - 32 = \$8$; $\pi_Y = 60 - 48 = \$12$.

Order total: $8 + 12 = \$20$ ✓ — identical to rule (a).

(c) The pure rule effect. $\Delta \pi_X = 8 - (-8) = +\$16$: item X flips from an $8 loss to an $8 profit, which is a change of sign, while $\pi_Y$ moves the opposite way by the same $16 (from $28 to $12). The order-level profit is unchanged at $20 under both rules.

Analysis — Why the total is invariant. Any attribution rule of the form $a_i = S \cdot w_i$ with non-negative weights satisfying $\sum_i w_i = 1$ is exhaustive and additive, so $\sum_i \pi_i = \sum_i (p_i - S w_i) = R - S$. The rule can move dollars between items, but it cannot create or destroy a dollar at the order level. That is precisely why two analysts can each be defensibly right about the order total ($20) and simultaneously disagree about a single item (X is −$8 under one rule and +$8 under the other). Per-item profit is a modelling convention, not a measurement; the correct professional habit is to name the rule as part of the metric definition, which is exactly the discipline the gold layer exists to impose — the medallion architecture arranges the lakehouse in bronze, silver and gold layers that progressively refine raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3], and bronze/silver/gold describe the quality level of the data in each layer [source 6].

Where students go wrong. (1) Believing one rule is 'true'. Both pass exhaustiveness and additivity; the choice is a causal argument about how clicks create value, not a fact that can be looked up. (2) Forgetting the second item when computing a weight, so the weights sum to less than 1 and spend is silently left unallocated. (3) Treating 'equal cost per click' as equal allocation per item — it is not: X receives 60% of the cost precisely because it received 60% of the clicks. (4) Reporting a per-item margin without the rule, which makes it unreproducible by anyone else.

Edge cases. If $C = 0$ the click-weighted rule is undefined (division by zero) and must fall back to price-weighted or to an unallocated-cost line. If $\sum_j p_j = 0$ (all prices zero, e.g. promotional freebies) the price weight is undefined. If prices can be negative (returns, credits) the weights can become negative and the allocation stops being monotone; clip or exclude such lines explicitly and document it. Finally, an item credited with zero clicks receives zero cost under rule (a) but a positive cost under rule (b) — a genuine free-rider artefact of click-weighted attribution that analysts should flag when someone asks 'why is this item so profitable?'.

Generalization. The same two formulas, $a_i = S \cdot c_i / \sum_j c_j$ and $a_i = S \cdot p_i / \sum_j p_j$, are the shared-cost allocation problem in general form: substituting order counts, headcount or floor space for clicks or price gives cost allocation in logistics, manufacturing overhead and store-level cost accounting.
Problem 2

A nightly job computes daily profit by joining the order-line fact `silver.sales` (one row per order line item) to `silver.ad_spend`, which stores one row per (date, channel). On 2024-03-01 the channel `paid_search` has spend = $80, and order O1 has two line items on that date and channel: X (price $40) and Y (price $60). The job runs:

SELECT s.item_id, s.price, a.spend

FROM silver.sales s

JOIN silver.ad_spend a

ON s.order_date = a.date AND s.channel = a.channel

WHERE s.order_date = DATE'2024-03-01';

(a) Compute SUM(price), SUM(spend) and SUM(price) − SUM(spend) over the joined result. (b) State the general size of the error in terms of the fan-out. (c) Give the correct price-weighted per-item allocation and rewrite the query so the join cannot corrupt the spend. (d) Give the one reconciliation query that proves the rewrite preserved the spend.
Hint: Ask what the grain of each input is before you join: a join is safe only when the right-hand side is unique on the join key.

Worked solution
(a) The join matches one `ad_spend` row to each of the two fact rows, so the result is:

(X, 40, 80)

(Y, 60, 80)

Row count = 2, which equals the fact grain — the row count did NOT change, yet the spend column was duplicated. Then SUM(price) = 40 + 60 = $100 (correct), SUM(spend) = 80 + 80 = $160 (wrong; the source day has only $80), and "profit" = 100 − 160 = −$60. The true profit is $20, so the reported figure understates reality by $80. Per item the broken numbers are $\pi_X = 40 - 80 = -\$40$ and $\pi_Y = 60 - 80 = -\$20$, which sum back to −$60$ and so look internally consistent — the classic signature of a fan-out bug.

(b) If a spend row at parent grain joins to $n$ fact rows, each of the $n$ output rows carries a full copy of the spend row, so $\text{SUM}(spend) = n \times S$ and the overstatement is $(n - 1) \times S$. Here $n = 2$, $S = \$80$, so the inflation is $1 \times 80 = \$80$. Note that the error grows with basket size: a 7-line order would inflate the day's spend by a factor of 7.

(c) Correct price-weighted allocation at the line-item grain, where $w_X = 40/100 = 0.40$ and $w_Y = 60/100 = 0.60$:

$a_X = 0.40 \times 80 = \$32 \Rightarrow \pi_X = 40 - 32 = \$8$;

$a_Y = 0.60 \times 80 = \$48 \Rightarrow \pi_Y = 60 - 48 = \$12$;

total allocated spend $= 32 + 48 = \$80$ ✓ and total profit $= 8 + 12 = \$20$ ✓.

Corrected query — allocate FIRST, using a window function partitioned at the order, so each spend dollar is divided rather than copied:

WITH allocated AS (

SELECT s.order_id, s.item_id, s.price,

a.spend * s.price

/ SUM(s.price) OVER (PARTITION BY s.order_id) AS alloc_cost

FROM silver.sales s

JOIN silver.ad_spend a

ON s.order_date = a.date AND s.channel = a.channel

WHERE s.order_date = DATE'2024-03-01'

)

SELECT item_id, price, alloc_cost, price - alloc_cost AS profit

FROM allocated;

(d) Reconciliation — the invariant to assert after every run:

SELECT

(SELECT SUM(alloc_cost) FROM allocated) AS allocated_total,

(SELECT SUM(spend) FROM silver.ad_spend

WHERE date = DATE'2024-03-01') AS source_total;

These two numbers must be equal ($80 = $80); a mismatch is the fan-out alarm. The complementary check is COUNT(*) before versus after the join, which must be unchanged from the fact grain.

Analysis — Why the rewrite works. The fan-out happens because `ad_spend` is at a coarser grain (date × channel) than the fact (order line item), so the join is many-to-one in the wrong direction: every fact row matches the same spend row and inherits its full value. Allocating inside the joined set with a window function distributes the spend exactly once per order before any aggregation, so the sum over the partition recovers the original $80. The same principle is why the medallion architecture insists on validated silver tables with known grains before enrichment: the layers progressively refine raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3], and the medallion pattern is simply a pipeline broken into bronze, silver and gold stages [source 4]. Gold is where the enriched, consumed version lives; if the enrichment step itself multiplies rows, gold inherits the lie and every downstream dashboard reports it.

Common student errors. (1) Assuming an unchanged row count proves the join is safe — it does not: this example has an unchanged row count and a $80 error. (2) The popular shortcut `a.spend / COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY a.date, a.channel)` — it happens to give the right total here but imposes an equal split, silently overriding the attribution rule you claimed to be using; it also breaks if a third item exists with a different price. (3) Pre-aggregating the fact to the order grain and then joining spend, which loses the per-item breakdown entirely. (4) Writing the fix as `SELECT DISTINCT`, which deduplicates rows but leaves the spend value attached to an arbitrary item.

Edge cases. If an order spans two channels, spend from both channels arrives on both line items and the allocation must partition by (order_id, channel), not by order_id alone. If a line item has price 0, the window denominator still works but that item receives zero allocated cost; decide deliberately whether that is intended. If `ad_spend` is missing a row for a (date, channel) that the fact references, use an explicit LEFT JOIN and surface the unmatched spend as a data-quality alert rather than dropping the fact rows.

Generalization. Any join where the right side is coarser than the left side and carries an additive measure (spend, quota, budget, freight cost) will fan out. The fix pattern is always the same three moves: identify the coarse grain, allocate or divide at the fine grain, then aggregate — and then reconcile the total against the source of truth.
Problem 3

The gold table `gold.item_profit` stores allocated marketing cost keyed by (date, order_id, item_id) and is refreshed each night with `INSERT INTO gold.item_profit SELECT ... FROM allocated;`. For 2024-03-01 the source spend is $80 and the correct price-weighted allocation is X = $32, Y = $48 on prices $40 and $60 respectively. The job runs twice in one night because of a transient-failure retry, and a third time the next evening as a backfill. (a) Compute total allocated cost and per-item profit after run 2 and after run 3. (b) Give a general formula for the reported profit after k runs. (c) Give an idempotent write pattern that makes a re-run a no-op, and name the constraint that would have caught the bug immediately.
Hint: Idempotent means f(f(x)) = f(x): applying the transformation twice must produce exactly the same state as applying it once.

Worked solution
(a) Each run appends two rows, $32 and $48, so each run adds $80 of allocated cost to a day whose true spend is $80.

After run 2: allocated X = $64, Y = $96, total = $160. Profit $\pi_X = 40 - 64 = -\$24$; $\pi_Y = 60 - 96 = -\$36$; total $= -\$60$.

After run 3: allocated X = $96, Y = $144, total = $240. Profit $\pi_X = 40 - 96 = -\$56$; $\pi_Y = 60 - 144 = -\$84$; total $= -\$140$.

The per-item attribution ratio is preserved (X always carries 40% of the inflated pool), so the error is invisible in any 'share of spend' chart and only visible in the absolute total.

(b) After k runs, allocated cost $= k \cdot a_i$ and reported profit $= R - k S = 100 - 80k$. At k = 1 the answer is +$20; at k = 2 it is −$60; the sign flips once $k > R/S = 1.25$, i.e. from the second run onward the order is reported as a loss. The error is linear in the number of executions, which is why a retry storm converts a profitable day into a catastrophic one without a single line of query logic changing.

(c) Idempotent write patterns, in order of preference:

1. Partition overwrite (rebuild the affected slice from scratch):

INSERT OVERWRITE gold.item_profit

PARTITION (order_date = DATE'2024-03-01')

SELECT order_date, order_id, item_id, price, alloc_cost, price - alloc_cost AS profit

FROM allocated;

2. Keyed upsert — re-running updates the same keys instead of appending new ones:

MERGE INTO gold.item_profit AS t

USING allocated AS s

ON t.order_date = s.order_date

AND t.order_id = s.order_id

AND t.item_id = s.item_id

WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET

t.price = s.price, t.alloc_cost = s.alloc_cost, t.profit = s.profit

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

3. Full rebuild: `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold.item_profit AS SELECT ... FROM allocated;`

The constraint that catches the bug at write time is a primary key (or Delta unique constraint) on (order_date, order_id, item_id): the second INSERT then fails loudly instead of silently doubling the cost. If you must keep an append-only audit trail, add an `allocation_run_id` column and make every consumer read only the latest run_id per key.

Analysis — Why non-idempotency is the quiet killer. A transformation that appends is correct only if the input never repeats — which retries, backfills, and late-arriving data all violate. The failure mode is especially dangerous because every individual item looks plausible: X's cost is still exactly twice Y's cost in proportion to price, the row count doubled in a way that looks like growth, and no error is raised. Trustworthy pipelines are defined by turning raw inputs into reliable, reproducible insights [source 5]; reproducibility is exactly the property that an append-on-retry job destroys, because two runs over identical input produce two different tables.

Common student errors. (1) Confusing 'at-least-once delivery' with 'exactly-once effect' — the orchestrator may deliver a task twice by design, so the write must be the thing that absorbs the duplicate. (2) Believing a MERGE is automatically idempotent: if the ON keys are wrong (for example, matching on date and channel but not on item_id), a MERGE produces duplicate keys just as an INSERT does. (3) Fixing the symptom with `SELECT DISTINCT` at read time, which hides the growth in storage and cost while leaving the table wrong for anyone who queries it directly. (4) Deduplicating by timestamp instead of by business key, which keeps the last write of a retry pair but breaks as soon as a legitimate late correction arrives with an older timestamp.

Edge cases and validation. Partitioned overwrite must name every partition the run touched, or unlisted partitions keep stale rows; if the run is a partial backfill, MERGE is safer than a broad overwrite. After any pattern, run the reconciliation from the previous exercise: `SUM(alloc_cost)` for the day must equal `SUM(spend)` in the source spend table. An idempotency test belongs in CI: execute the transform twice against a fixed fixture and assert the two resulting tables are byte-identical.

Generalization. The same reasoning applies to incrementally maintained aggregates and materialized views: any derived table that is refreshed rather than recomputed must be refreshed by key, never by append. 'Recomputing a metric non-idempotently so totals drift on each run' is one of the four classic attribution defects, alongside mixed rules, cross-grain recomputation, and join fan-out.
Problem 4

Two dashboards publish 'profit by item' for order O1 (prices $40 and $60, $80 of ad spend, total profit $20). Dashboard A uses click-weighted attribution and reports X = −$8, Y = $28. Dashboard B uses price-weighted attribution and reports X = $8, Y = $12. An analyst exports both, unions them into one table, and reports total profit = −8 + 8 + 28 + 12 = $40. (a) Show that each dashboard's own total is $20 and explain arithmetically where the extra $20 came from. (b) Give the reconciliation test that would have caught the error and the schema change that prevents it structurally. (c) State the governance fix. (d) A colleague argues both numbers should be kept 'for flexibility' and the reconciliation left to the analyst. Answer the argument.
Hint: Each attribution rule is a redistribution of the same $20, not a separate profit stream — two decompositions of one quantity, not two quantities.

Worked solution
(a) Dashboard A: $-8 + 28 = \$20$. Dashboard B: $8 + 12 = \$20$. Both equal the invariant $R - S = 100 - 80 = \$20$. The union sums four numbers, but they are two valuations of the same two items: −$8 and +$8 are two values of $\pi_X$; $28 and $12 are two values of $\pi_Y$. Summing them counts each item once per rule, so the reported total is $k \times 20 = 2 \times 20 = \$40$, where k = 2 is the number of attribution rules unioned. The extra $20 is not new profit; it is the same $20 counted twice.

(b) Reconciliation test — compare each rule's total against the invariant computed directly from the fact, never against another rule's output:

SELECT attribution_rule,

SUM(profit) AS reported_profit,

SUM(price) - SUM(spend_unallocated) AS invariant_profit

FROM gold.item_profit

GROUP BY attribution_rule;

Both rows must show reported = invariant = $20. Sorting, unioning or grouping across `attribution_rule` is the operation that must be forbidden. The structural fix is to make the rule a column (a genuine dimension of the metric), so that the union produces a visible `attribution_rule` column rather than four anonymous rows — an analyst who sums across a labelled dimension has at least done so knowingly.

(c) Governance fix: define 'profit after marketing cost' once, in the gold layer or a governed metrics/semantic layer, choose one allocation rule as the published default, and let both dashboards select the finished column instead of each re-deriving it. If the business genuinely needs both views, publish two explicitly named metrics — `profit_click_weighted` and `profit_price_weighted` — never one metric called 'profit'. For a single analytical domain, a well-designed star schema with fact and dimension tables can deliver faster query performance and simpler governance than a sprawling pipeline [source 1], which is a reminder that the governance fix is organizational as much as technical: one domain, one definition, one owner.

(d) The flexibility argument is the classic source of irreconcilable numbers. The costs of per-consumer definitions are asymmetric in a way that defeats the flexibility benefit: each team saves minutes of effort, while the organization pays in reconciliation meetings, disputed KPIs, and decisions made on doubled numbers. Flexibility is preserved better by parameterizing a single definition (a rule column, a governed metric parameter) than by duplicating the definition — the duplication is what destroys the ability to compare, and comparability is the only reason the metric exists.

Analysis — Why the totals agree and the items do not. Every admissible attribution rule is a redistribution: $\sum_i (p_i - S w_i) = R - S$ whenever $\sum_i w_i = 1$ and the weights are non-negative. Total profit is therefore invariant under the choice of rule, and per-item profit is exactly the quantity the rule governs. Analysts who only ever check totals conclude the two dashboards agree; analysts who check items conclude they contradict each other; both are correct. This is the mechanical root of duplicated metrics, and it generalizes far beyond advertising: the same structure appears in freight allocation across order lines, cloud cost allocation across teams, and overhead allocation across product lines.

Where students go wrong. (1) Recomputing a metric at a different grain than it was defined at — computing profit per order and then averaging, comparing or summing those order-level numbers against item-level numbers gives a third inconsistent answer, because the aggregation is no longer over the same unit of analysis. (2) Double counting spend when joins fan out (the defect from the previous exercise), which corrupts the total rather than just the split. (3) Recomputing non-idempotently, so the total drifts on each run and no two dashboards ever see the same input. (4) Treating a named rule as boilerplate and dropping it from the output schema, which makes the mixing bug invisible until someone totals the columns.

Edge cases. A rule that fails exhaustiveness (leaving spend unallocated) or additivity (allocating the same spend twice within a rule) breaks the invariance proof, so the reconciliation against $R - S$ will fire even without any mixing — that is the test doing its job. Allocation rules based on fractional shares produce rounding residues: with three items sharing $80 the shares may not sum to exactly $80 at cent precision, so define a deterministic remainder policy (largest-remainder allocation to the highest-value line) and reconcile to the cent. Finally, if the rule itself changes over time, the metric's history is not comparable across the rule change; record the rule and its version as slowly changing dimension attributes (slowly changing dimensions — the technique for tracking how a dimension attribute changes over time, so that historical facts keep the attribute value that was true when they occurred) so old and new periods can be compared knowingly.

Generalization. The three questions that resolve any attribution dispute are: what is the total (invariant), what is the split (rule-dependent), and which rule was used (must be stored). Everything else — the choice of clicks versus price versus a hybrid model — is a business argument that belongs in a written metric definition in the gold layer, not in five notebooks.

actions.text: Let's make that abstract point concrete with a fully worked problem. This is exactly the kind of scenario the exam loves, because two rules that both look correct will hand you two contradictory profit numbers for the same item.

Here is the setup. An ad platform reports that order O1 attracted ten clicks and eighty dollars of spend. That order contains item X, priced at forty dollars, which received six of those clicks, and item Y, priced at sixty dollars, which received the other four. Before writing any SQL, note the two grains in play — the spend is recorded at the order level, but the profit we want is at the item level.

The hint tells us the one invariant we must respect: both rules have to distribute the entire eighty dollars. No spend can be invented, and none can be dropped — the allocation must be exhaustive and additive. Keep that constraint in your head, because it is what makes the next two answers agree on the total even when they disagree on the parts.

Rule (a), naive attribution, is equal cost per click: eighty dollars across ten clicks is eight dollars a click. Item X takes six clicks, so forty-eight dollars of cost against forty dollars of price — a profit of negative eight. Item Y takes four clicks, so thirty-two dollars of cost against sixty dollars of price — a profit of positive twenty-eight. Add them up and the order total is twenty dollars.

Now rule (b), price-weighted attribution, which splits spend by price share instead of click share. Item X is forty out of one hundred, so it carries forty percent of the spend — thirty-two dollars — leaving a profit of eight. Item Y carries the remaining sixty percent — forty-eight dollars — leaving a profit of twelve. Look closely at item X: the same data, a different rule, and the sign flips from minus eight to plus eight. The total, though, is still twenty dollars, because the analysis confirms both allocations are exhaustive and additive.

That is the mechanical root of duplicated metrics. Two consumers can each pick a defensible rule, both totals reconcile, and the per-item numbers still contradict each other. The pitfall list is worth memorizing for the exam: mixing attribution methods across consumers, recomputing at a different grain — order versus item — letting joins fan out and double-count spend, and recomputing a metric non-idempotently so totals drift on every run. Notice that when we fan out on the join, the spend gets duplicated, and when we recompute at a different grain, we get a row count explosion — the same warning signs you saw earlier when we discussed join semantics. Next, let's put these rules side by side and judge what each one gets right and wrong.

scenes.title: Check: Consistency of Derived Metrics

questions.question: A data engineer owns two computations of the same headline metric, 'net revenue after returns,' on the same silver orders table. Computation A is a materialized column baked into the gold table during the last full rewrite. Computation B is a gold view that was re-pointed to the same silver table. Both read the same partitions, and the raw order rows are byte-identical. Nevertheless, A and B disagree by roughly 4 percent on days where refunds were issued. Based on what you learned about business logic and derived data, which statement best explains and resolves that disagreement?

options.label: Computation A is wrong because a materialized column is stale by construction; rebuild it every hour and the gap will close.
Computation B is wrong because a view always re-derives logic at read time and therefore double-counts; replace it with a copy of A's column.

Both computations are calculations, and the disagreement lives in the rule they encode, not in the underlying data; reconcile the refund-handling and cancellation definitions into one governed definition and point both consumers at it.
The tables cannot be reconciled; pick whichever table has the fresher update timestamp and treat that as the source of truth going forward.

questions.analysis: The stem deliberately removes the usual suspects: same table, same partitions, byte-identical raw rows. When the data is the same and the numbers differ, the difference is definitional — the rules that turn raw events into decision-ready values (profit = revenue minus cost minus marketing spend) are being applied in two places and have drifted. Returning refunds differently (order-line grain vs. transaction grain), or excluding auto-canceled orders in one path but not the other, produces exactly this symptom. Option C names the right diagnosis and the right fix: encode the logic once in the gold transformation or a governed semantic/metrics layer and let consumers select the finished result. Option A is a plausible-sounding but false claim that materialization alone causes disagreement; a materialized column and a view that encode the same rule agree. Option B inverts the actual risk; nothing about a view 'double-counts' by definition. Option D is the trap distractor the test points warn about — 'the fresher table is the correct one' confuses recency with correctness. A fresher table that encodes the wrong rule is still wrong.
