Note also that the medallion architecture progressively refines raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3], and the whole premise of that refinement is that the gold layer carries the trusted definition; two gold artifacts encoding two definitions defeats the purpose.

questions.question: An analyst reports that a dashboard field labeled 'revenue' is about 30 percent higher than the corresponding 'revenue' column in the certified gold table, even though both are fed from the same Delta source. Select ALL of the following that are legitimate hypotheses you should test before concluding that the gold column is wrong. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The dashboard field is computed at order-header grain and joined onto item-level rows, so each order's header amount repeats once per line — a grain mismatch that inflates totals.
The dashboard definition of 'revenue' includes shipping fees and pre-refund amounts, while the gold definition is net of refunds — a rule difference, not a data difference.
The dashboard's underlying table was refreshed more recently than the gold table, which proves the gold column is the incorrect one.
The dashboard's query joins a dimension that fans out rows (for example, an SCD Type 2 dimension joined without a point-in-time filter), multiplying the measure.

questions.analysis: Options A, B, and D are the three canonical explanations for a metric that disagrees across two consumers of the same source: grain mismatch, definition/rule mismatch, and join fan-out. A grain mismatch is the classic inflation pattern — you join an order-header spend number onto item-level rows and each order's amount appears once per line, so the SUM is inflated by the average number of line items per order. A definition mismatch is a rule problem: 'revenue' with or without shipping, gross vs. net of refunds, recognized vs. booked. Fan-out from a badly joined dimension is the same inflation mechanism as A but introduced by the join rather than the source grain. Option C is the distractor the test points flag — 'the fresher table is the correct one.' Freshness is not correctness. A table can be refreshed every minute and still encode the wrong definition, and a stale table can encode the right one. Always trace a discrepancy to the rule (Definition A vs. Definition B) or the grain (which rows are you summing over?) before you decide which number is right. The medallion architecture exists precisely to give you one progressively refined, trusted definition [source 6], so a disagreement between a gold field and a dashboard field is a signal that the dashboard is re-implementing logic that the gold layer already owns.

questions.question: A gold table `fact_sales` is at the order-line grain, and each row carries `order_id`, `line_id`, `unit_price`, `quantity`, and `line_amount`. A dashboard author wants total order value per region. They write a query that joins `fact_sales` to `orders` (header table, one row per order) on `order_id`, joins to `regions` on `region_id`, and selects SUM(o.order_total) grouped by region. The result is roughly 2.7x too high. Which single change most directly fixes the inflation while preserving the intended per-region total?

options.label: Pre-aggregate to the order grain before joining: SELECT SUM(order_total) FROM orders grouped by region via the region dimension, or equivalently select the distinct order totals per order before summing.
Switch the join type from LEFT to INNER to drop the rows that are causing the doubling.
Add DISTINCT to the SELECT list so the duplicate order totals collapse to one value per region.
Refresh the gold table so the order totals are current; inflated totals are a freshness symptom.

questions.analysis: The correct answer is A. The bug is a grain mismatch: `order_total` lives at the order grain, but the query sums it over order-line rows, so each order's header amount is counted once per line item. If the average order has about 2.7 lines, you get the observed 2.7x inflation. The fix is to make the summation grain match the measure's grain — either aggregate `orders` to the region grain directly (since `order_total` doesn't need the line rows at all), or pre-aggregate order totals to one row per order and then join. Option B is wrong: LEFT vs. INNER changes which rows survive, not how many times a header amount is repeated. Dropping rows would lower the number, but it would silently bias the metric rather than fix it. Option C is wrong and dangerous: SELECT DISTINCT applied after the join does not collapse partial sums inside SUM(), and even at the row level DISTINCT would discard legitimate distinct line values. Option D is the trap distractor again: freshness has nothing to do with grain. A perfectly fresh fact table joined at the wrong grain is still inflated. Remember the medallion principle — the layers progressively refine raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3] — and grain, not freshness, is what makes a table business-ready. Verify the fact grain before any join and confirm the row count is unchanged when the join is supposed to be one-to-one.

scenes.title: Risks of Duplicated and Inconsistent Metrics

elements.content: Risks of Duplicated and Inconsistent Metrics

When the same business logic is re-implemented across multiple consumers, the medallion guarantee of 'one trusted gold layer' [source 3] is broken. The consequences are business-facing, not just technical.
Trust Erosion
Two dashboards show different revenue → stakeholders revert to spreadsheets.
Silent Drift
A rule fixed in one copy but not others → definitions diverge with no error.
Reconciliation Cost
Engineers and analysts trace which number is correct instead of acting.
Hidden Coupling
A dashboard silently depends on another team's notebook logic — a small refactor breaks it.
Worked Example: Drift in Daily Profit

Dashboard A and B both compute daily profit. A pre-aggregates refunds at order-line grain; B joins refunds at transaction grain. One order-line has 3 transactions and 1 refund of $10 → A deducts $10, B deducts $30, inflating the refund by $20. Neither job fails; neither raises an alert. The gold layer was bypassed, violating the principle that logic be encoded once [source 5].
Exam Trap: Recomputing a metric in the BI tool 'for speed' creates a second definition — the classic source of irreconcilable numbers.

actions.text: Now that you've seen where duplicated logic creeps in, let's talk about what it actually costs you — because the damage goes well beyond a slightly messy notebook.
This page is about the risks of duplicated and inconsistent metrics. Every one of these is a real, observable consequence, and the exam expects you to recognize them by name.

First, trust erosion. When two dashboards show different revenue for the same period, stakeholders stop believing both numbers — and they quietly go back to their own spreadsheets. Once that happens, your platform has lost its authority, even if one of those numbers was actually correct.

Second, silent drift. Someone fixes a rule — say a refund exclusion — in one copy of the logic but not in the others. Nothing errors, nothing alerts, and the two definitions quietly diverge over weeks. Silent drift is the most dangerous of the four precisely because it raises no signal at all.

Third, reconciliation cost. Engineers and analysts burn hours tracing which number is the right one, instead of acting on it. That time is pure waste, and it scales with every additional copy of the logic you maintain.

And fourth, hidden coupling. A dashboard silently depends on logic buried in another team's notebook. That team refactors one cell, and your reporting breaks — with no warning and no obvious link back to the change.

Let's make this concrete. Dashboard A and Dashboard B both compute daily profit. A previous correction to how refunds are handled was applied to only one of them. Both run without error, but they now disagree — that's silent drift producing trust erosion, and the root cause is the duplication itself.

Finally, the exam trap. If a question frames 'recompute the metric inside the BI tool for speed' as a good practice, be careful — that is not a performance technique, it creates a second definition of the metric. The sound answer is to define it once and reuse it. Keep these four risk names in mind, because the next page shows the three places you can actually put a definition.

scenes.title: Three Places to Define a Metric

elements.content: Dimension  |  Transformation-layer (gold) definition  |  BI calculated field  |  Governed metrics/semantic layer

Who owns the definition
Transformation-layer (gold) definition: The data engineering team owns it, because the rule is implemented as a column or aggregate inside the gold transformation that produces the table consumed downstream.
BI calculated field: The report author or BI developer owns it, because the rule is re-implemented as a calculated field inside a single report or dashboard artifact.
Governed metrics/semantic layer: A central analytics-engineering or governance function owns it, because the rule is declared once as a first-class metric object that consumers reference rather than restate.

Consistency across all consumers
Transformation-layer (gold) definition: Consistency is strongest, because every consumer reads the same physically written column, so SQL, BI, and ML all see identical values by construction.
BI calculated field: Consistency is weakest by default, because each report reproduces the arithmetic independently and two authors can weight or filter differently without anyone noticing.
Governed metrics/semantic layer: Consistency is enforced by design, because the metric is defined once and served to SQL, BI, and notebooks from the same governed source.

Coupling to a single tool
Transformation-layer (gold) definition: Consumers are decoupled from any one BI tool, since the value lives in the lakehouse table and any engine that can read Delta Lake sees it.
BI calculated field: Consumers are tightly coupled to the BI tool, because the logic exists only inside that tool's expression language and is invisible to ML training code and notebooks.
Governed metrics/semantic layer: Consumers are coupled to the metrics layer's API and runtime, which becomes a shared dependency that every consumer must adopt.

Change cost
Transformation-layer (gold) definition: Highest change cost, because editing the rule means editing the pipeline and re-running it, which rewrites and backfills the affected gold partitions before the new value appears.
BI calculated field: Lowest change cost for the author, because the field can be edited in seconds in the report, but the cost is deferred and multiplied when other consumers must be updated separately.
Governed metrics/semantic layer: Moderate change cost, because one edit to the metric definition propagates to all consumers, but the edit is gated by the layer's review, versioning, and deployment process.

Auditability
Transformation-layer (gold) definition: Auditability is strong at the code level, since the rule is a reviewable, version-controlled transformation, but the lineage of a specific published number depends on knowing which pipeline run produced the partition.
BI calculated field: Auditability is poor, because a calculated field can be changed in place with no code review, no lineage record, and no notification to downstream consumers.
Governed metrics/semantic layer: Auditability is strongest conceptually, because the layer is meant to hold a single versioned definition with documented lineage from metric to source column.

Fit for ML consumers
Transformation-layer (gold) definition: Well suited, because feature engineering code and training notebooks can read the same gold column that BI reads, so training and serving inputs match.
BI calculated field: Poorly suited by default, because ML and notebook consumers cannot see the BI tool's calculated field at all, so they re-derive the value and create training-serving skew.
Governed metrics/semantic layer: Well suited when the layer exposes a programmatic interface, because notebooks can request the governed metric instead of hand-coding the formula.

Failure and staleness behavior
Transformation-layer (gold) definition: If the pipeline fails or is not re-run, the gold column silently retains yesterday's logic and value, and consumers cannot tell without checking the pipeline run metadata.
BI calculated field: The field always recomputes against whatever data the report query returns, so it is never stale relative to the query, but it is also never validated or reconciled by anyone else.
Governed metrics/semantic layer: If the layer is unavailable or its cache is stale, every consumer that depends on it fails together, which is the availability price of centralization.

Typical use
Transformation-layer (gold) definition: Best for stable, frequently reused metrics that many consumers need identically, where the transformation-layer rewrite and backfill cost is justified by downstream reuse.
BI calculated field: Best for exploratory, one-off, or presentation-only calculations that no other consumer will ever need to reproduce.
Governed metrics/semantic layer: Best for metrics that must be shared across SQL, BI, and notebook consumers while remaining governed and changeable in one place.
Takeaway — Define the metric once and let consumers read it: a gold transformation column wins when the metric is stable and reused enough to justify a pipeline run on every change.
Takeaway — A BI calculated field is acceptable only for one-off exploration, because it duplicates logic per report and is invisible to ML and notebook consumers [source 1].
Takeaway — Adopt a governed metrics/semantic layer when one definition must serve SQL, BI, and notebooks, accepting the cost of operating an extra platform component [source 3].
Takeaway — On the exam, choose the option that defines the metric once and lets consumers read it, never the option that re-implements it per consumer.

actions.text: We just listed the risks of duplicated logic, so now let's make it concrete. This table compares the three places you can define a derived metric, judged across the same set of dimensions: who owns the definition, consistency across all consumers, coupling to a single tool, change cost, auditability, fit for ML consumers, failure and staleness behavior, and typical use.

Start with the ownership dimension. In the transformation layer, one team — the data engineering pipeline owner — owns the definition. In a BI calculated field, the definition is owned by whoever builds the report, which is usually a business analyst. In a governed metrics layer, ownership is explicit and centralized. Ownership is the first thing exam questions probe, because it determines who is accountable when the number is wrong.

Consistency follows directly from ownership. When the metric is defined in the transformation layer, every downstream consumer — SQL, notebooks, dashboards, ML — reads the same computed column, so consistency is strongest. In a BI calculated field, only that one report sees the logic; the notebook team never does. That is the classic source of two different revenue numbers in the same meeting.

Now the change-cost dimension, and this is the key trade-off. Defining the metric in the transformation layer gives you the strongest consistency, but every single change means editing the pipeline and re-running it, so the change cycle is slow. A BI calculated field is fast to write and fast to change — which is exactly why duplicated logic creeps in. The governed metrics layer sits in between: you change it once in a central place, and it propagates to all consumers.

Look closely at fit for ML consumers. A metric defined in the transformation layer or in a governed metrics layer is readable by notebooks and ML feature pipelines, because it exists as a queryable object. A BI calculated field is invisible to ML — the model has to re-implement the logic in Python, and now you have two definitions drifting apart silently.

So the recommended pattern for production is the governed metrics or semantic layer. One governed definition is served to SQL, to BI, and to notebooks through a single interface. The cost you accept is an extra platform component to operate — someone has to configure it, publish the definitions, and monitor it. That operational overhead is real, but it is far cheaper than reconciling four different profit formulas every quarter.

Here is the exam framing, and it is refreshingly simple: choose the option that defines the metric once and lets consumers read it, and never choose the option that re-implements the metric per consumer. If an answer choice describes copying the same CASE WHEN expression into three different dashboards, eliminate it immediately. If it describes a single governed definition consumed by SQL, BI, and notebooks, that is your answer.

One nuance before we move on: a BI calculated field is acceptable only in a genuinely narrow case — a one-off, single-consumer, exploratory view that will never be reused and never needs to match another report. The moment a second consumer needs that number, the definition has to move out of the BI tool. Recognizing that moment is the skill the exam is testing.

scenes.title: Check: Single Source of Truth Principles

questions.question: A retail lakehouse team needs a 'profit after marketing' metric delivered to four executive dashboards and consumed as a training feature by two ML models. Leadership wants exactly one number that all six consumers agree on. Which design best satisfies the single-source-of-truth principle?

options.label: Define the profit formula once in a governed gold table or semantic layer, then have all four dashboards and both ML models read that single definition.
Let each BI team implement the formula in its own dashboard calculated field so teams stay autonomous and can tune the metric to their own audience.
Precompute the metric in an analyst's spreadsheet and email the resulting CSV to dashboard owners and the ML engineers whenever the logic changes.
Store the raw revenue and cost columns in bronze and require every consumer to recompute profit at query time using its own SQL.

questions.analysis: Defining the metric exactly once in a governed gold table or semantic layer is the single-source-of-truth pattern: all four dashboards and both ML models then resolve to the same derived value, so a rule change is made in one place. The medallion architecture refines raw data into trusted, business-ready tables, and the gold layer is where that consumption-ready logic belongs [source 3][source 6]. Option B duplicates the formula across four dashboard fields, the exact 'each team defines profit for flexibility' anti-pattern that produces irreconcilable numbers. Option C is worse: a spreadsheet is an ungoverned, unversioned copy. Option D pushes business logic down into bronze, but bronze is raw, validated-only input and must not carry derived business logic [source 6].

questions.question: A platform owner proposes copying the profit-after-marketing formula into every consumer 'for convenience and speed.' Select ALL of the risks that correctly justify rejecting this duplication.

options.label: Two implementations of the same attribution rule diverge silently, so the same order shows different profit in different consumers.
A single bug fix or rule change must be applied in N places, so one consumer is easily left on a stale version of the logic.
No single owner can certify the number, so audit and reconciliation cost rises even though the underlying data is identical.
Duplicating the formula makes the dashboards run faster, which by itself justifies the maintenance burden.

questions.analysis: Duplicated logic is the classic source of irreconcilable numbers: the same rule re-implemented in more than one place (notebook, ETL script, dashboard calculated field, ad-platform export) drifts apart, so option A is a real risk. Option B is the maintenance risk — a rule change made once upstream but missed in a copied field silently produces stale results. Option C is the governance risk: with no single source of truth, nobody can certify the metric, and reconciliation work grows. Option D is the distractor: a local copy may feel faster, but 'convenience and speed' never outweighs correctness and governance, and the maintenance burden is exactly what duplication creates.

questions.question: A team must publish a gold-layer 'daily category profit' metric. The upstream gold aggregate already exists and is cheap to query, but latency-sensitive dashboards need sub-second responses and the metric is refreshed only once per day. Which choice respects single-source-of-truth while meeting the requirement?

options.label: Re-implement the profit formula inside each dashboard so latency improves without changing the pipeline.
Keep the gold table as the single definition and add a materialized view over it, so the precomputed result is reused rather than the logic being re-authored.
Copy the gold aggregate into a separate per-team table and edit the copy whenever a dashboard needs a tweak.
Move the metric definition down into silver so each consumer inherits a slightly different version of the rule.

questions.analysis: A materialized view over the existing gold table keeps one authored definition while caching the precomputed result for low-latency access — the DRY (don't repeat yourself) principle applied to derived data. The medallion architecture progressively refines raw data into trusted, business-ready tables, and materialization is a performance concern layered on top of that single definition, not a second definition [source 3][source 5]. Option A re-authors the logic per dashboard, reintroducing duplication. Option C forks a per-team copy that will drift. Option D pushes business logic into silver, where the rule would be re-derived differently by each consumer — the opposite of a single source of truth.

Give every question your best attempt before you submit. Once you're done, I'll be right here to walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Consolidate the Profit Logic

content.html:
Consolidate the Profit Logic

Rewrite a duplicated profit calculation as one shared metric definition — then watch every consumer re-render from the same source.

Loading SQL engine (WebAssembly)… Engine: SQLite (sql.js) · ANSI-standard SQL Target grain: 1 row per month
metric_profit.sql
output
Run your metric definition to see the result set here. Use the chips above to inspect the source tables — pay attention to how many rows one month has in each table.
validation
hints
Hint 1 — grain before join orders is one row per order. marketing_spend is one row per campaign-date. Join them raw and both sides fan out — every order is repeated once per spend row, and every spend row once per order. Aggregate each table to the month first, then join.
Hint 2 — build the month key Use substr(order_date, 1, 7) to get '2024-01', and substr(spend_date, 1, 7) for the spend side. Revenue counts only status = 'complete' rows — refunded orders are not revenue.
Hint 3 — two CTEs, one join Write one CTE that groups orders to the month, one CTE that groups marketing_spend to the month, then JOIN them on the month key. Aliasing the CTEs keeps the final SELECT readable and keeps the metric definition in one place.
Hint 4 — exact output contract The final SELECT must return exactly four columns named month, revenue, marketing_spend, profit, with revenue - marketing_spend AS profit, and end with ORDER BY month.
-- One shared metric definition: monthly profit after marketing costs
WITH revenue AS (
  SELECT substr(order_date, 1, 7) AS month,
         SUM(revenue)             AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'complete'
  GROUP BY 1
),
spend AS (
  SELECT substr(spend_date, 1, 7) AS month,
         SUM(spend)               AS marketing_spend
  FROM marketing_spend
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT r.month,
       r.revenue,
       s.marketing_spend,
       r.revenue - s.marketing_spend AS profit
FROM revenue r
JOIN spend s ON s.month = r.month
ORDER BY r.month;
Worked example — the numbers your metric must reproduce

These totals are the single source of truth. Every consumer (dashboard tile, finance close, exec summary) must re-render identically from your one definition.

Jan revenue
500
Jan spend
250
Jan profit
250
Feb revenue
600
Feb spend
150
Feb profit
450
  • Revenue = SUM(orders.revenue) where status = 'complete'. Order 1004 ($300) is refunded and never counts. Total revenue across both months must be 1,100.
  • Marketing spend = SUM(marketing_spend.spend) at campaign × date grain. Total across both months must be 400. If you see 1,050 or 1,600, a fan-out join is multiplying spend.
  • Profit = revenue − marketing spend, computed after both sides are already at month grain.

The engine is an in-browser SQLite build, so substr() and CTEs work exactly as they do in Databricks SQL. Medallion architecture (bronze → silver → gold layers, where each layer is progressively cleaner) is the pattern behind this exercise: the shared metric definition is a gold-layer object.

The two divergent definitions you are replacing

Snippet A — "Order Explorer" dashboard tile. Joins at raw grain, so every order is repeated once per marketing row. Revenue inflates to 2,000 and spend to 750.

SELECT substr(o.order_date,1,7) AS month,
       SUM(o.revenue)             AS revenue,
       SUM(m.spend)               AS marketing_spend,
       SUM(o.revenue) - SUM(m.spend) AS profit
FROM orders o
JOIN marketing_spend m
  ON substr(o.order_date,1,7) = substr(m.spend_date,1,7)
WHERE o.status = 'complete'
GROUP BY 1;

Snippet B — "Finance close" notebook. Correct totals, but no profit column, a correlated subquery instead of a join, and a status filter written as <> 'refunded' — which silently breaks the moment a new status such as 'pending' appears.

SELECT substr(order_date,1,7) AS month,
       SUM(revenue)           AS revenue,
       (SELECT SUM(spend) FROM marketing_spend
         WHERE substr(spend_date,1,7) = substr(order_date,1,7)) AS marketing_spend
FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'refunded'
GROUP BY 1;

Two definitions, two answers, and every downstream consumer picks whichever one it was wired to. Consolidate into one.

Source schema
  • orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, revenue, status) — order grain. status ∈ {complete, refunded}.
  • order_items(order_id, item_id, amount) — item grain. Joining this to orders fan-outs revenue; that is a grain mismatch (two tables at different levels of detail joined without pre-aggregation).
  • marketing_spend(campaign_id, spend_date, channel, spend) — campaign × date grain. Multiple rows per month.

scenes.title: Where Should the Profit Rule Live?

elements.content: Decision — A four-person data team maintains a Databricks lakehouse whose gold layer feeds four dashboards, two machine learning models, and ad hoc analyst SQL. The team must decide where the definition of 'profit after marketing costs' should live: inside each BI dashboard's calculated fields, as a materialized column produced by the gold transformation, or in a governed metrics/semantic layer served over the gold tables. The decision is hard because the three placements trade off build speed against cross-consumer consistency, freshness, and the ongoing cost of governing an additional component, and the team is small enough that any new operational surface has to be justified by a consumer that genuinely needs it [source 3].

Constraints — Attribution rules are formally rechecked every quarter, so whatever holds the definition will be edited at least four times a year.  •  The team has four engineers total, so operating an additional always-on service must be weighed against the maintenance capacity it consumes.  •  The two ML models require point-in-time consistency, meaning the profit value used at training time must be reproducible against the data as it existed at that point, not recomputed under today's rule.  •  All four dashboards, both models, and ad hoc analyst SQL must be able to consume the same metric without exporting or copying the underlying data.  •  The medallion architecture already organizes the lakehouse into bronze, silver, and gold layers, and the team wants the definition to live at the layer where data is already enriched and business-ready [source 6].

Define profit as a calculated field in each dashboard
+ Fastest possible iteration: an analyst can add or tweak the field in minutes without touching the pipeline or waiting on a deployment.; + No new pipeline runs are required when the rule changes, so there is no recompute latency to plan around.; + Each dashboard can locally tailor the metric to its own audience without coordinating with anyone else.
− Five definitions of the same rule will inevitably drift: a correction made in one dashboard is invisible to the other four [source 3].; − The ML models cannot consume a BI calculated field at all, so the models must re-implement the profit rule somewhere else, guaranteeing silent divergence.; − Every quarterly attribution recheck becomes a five-place edit with no audit trail proving all copies now agree.; − It directly violates DRY (don't repeat yourself): the same business rule is re-implemented in more than one place, which is exactly how duplicated logic creeps in.
Best for: One-off exploratory analysis where the result will never be reused and the metric has exactly one consumer.

Materialize profit as a column in the gold transformation
+ One owner, one place to edit: the quarterly attribution recheck becomes a single, version-controlled pipeline change.; + The profit column is automatically visible to every SQL consumer, including ad hoc analyst queries, because it lives in the gold table itself.; + The definition sits in the enriched, business-ready gold layer that medallion architecture already designates for business logic [source 3].; + The rule change is auditable: the diff shows exactly what changed, and the recomputed column can be compared against the prior version before publication.; + Point-in-time consistency for the ML models is achievable if the gold table preserves historical rows rather than overwriting them.
− Every rule change requires a recompute of the gold table, so there is a measurable latency window during which dashboards show the old definition.; − The column is physically stored, so historical snapshots must be retained if the ML models need to train on the rule as it existed at that date.; − Non-SQL consumers such as notebooks must still read the gold table directly rather than query a metric by name, which requires a little more discipline from analysts.
Best for: A small team that needs one trustworthy definition with minimal new infrastructure and can tolerate a bounded recompute window on quarterly rule changes.

Define profit in a governed metrics/semantic layer over gold
+ One definition is served everywhere, including notebooks and BI tools, so every consumer queries the metric by name rather than by column [source 3].; + Governance metadata (definition, owner, consumers) travels with the metric, which makes the quarterly review a governance action rather than a code hunt.; + New consumers get the metric automatically instead of copying a formula from an existing dashboard.
− The team must operate and govern another always-on component, which is real maintenance load for four engineers.; − Every rule change may now require both a gold recompute and a semantic-layer update if the metric is defined above the column, adding coordination.; − If the semantic layer is not itself version-controlled, it can become a new unauthorized place where the definition silently forked.; − Adoption is not automatic: an analyst who writes raw SQL against gold can still bypass the metric and reintroduce a second definition.
Best for: A team where more than one non-SQL consumer genuinely needs the same metric and the organization can absorb the operating cost of governing a semantic layer.

Recommendation: Materialize profit as a column in the gold transformation — The binding constraints are the small team, the quarterly rule change, and the need for point-in-time consistency, and materializing the column in gold satisfies all three without adding a service to operate. Option one is ruled out because it violates DRY: the same rule would be re-implemented five times, which is precisely the duplicated-logic pattern that causes dashboards to disagree and stakeholders to revert to spreadsheets [source 3]. Option three is the correct long-term target but not the correct base, because the team currently has only one non-SQL consumer class (the models, which can read gold directly), so it would pay the operating cost of a governed metric layer before any consumer actually requires it. Materializing in gold also places the definition in the enriched, business-ready layer that medallion architecture is designed to produce, and the recompute latency on a quarterly cadence is acceptable. The semantic layer should be layered on later, once a second non-SQL consumer needs the metric served by name rather than by column.

actions.text: Let's put all of that single-source-of-truth theory to work on a concrete case. Here's the decision we have to make: where should the profit rule actually live?

Start with the situation. A four-person data team maintains a Databricks platform, and the metric 'profit after marketing costs' is consumed in three very different ways: four dashboards, two ML models, and whatever ad hoc SQL an analyst writes on a given afternoon.

Before we pick a placement, look at the constraints. Attribution rules are formally rechecked every quarter — so the definition of profit will change on a schedule, not never. The team is small, so every extra component is a maintenance tax. And the ML models need point-in-time consistency, which means whatever we choose must reproduce the exact value that was correct as of a given date.

Option A is the tempting one: define profit as a calculated field inside each dashboard. It's the fastest to build and it's invisible to reviewers — but it gives us no cross-consumer consistency, the ML models never see it at all because they don't read dashboard definitions, and we're stuck maintaining five separate copies. That last point is the killer: it violates DRY, don't repeat yourself.

Option B moves the logic into a gold transformation that materializes a profit column. Now there's one owner, one definition, and the column is consistent and auditable — every consumer, SQL or Python, reads the same materialized value. The cost is recompute latency: every time the quarterly rule changes, we rebuild that column across the whole history.

Option C goes further: put profit in a governed metrics or semantic layer over the gold data. One definition then serves everything, including notebooks and ML. But you now operate and govern another component — real overhead for four people. Hold that thought while we look at the recommendation.

Here's the recommendation: take B as the base — a materialized, tested, version-controlled gold column — and layer C on top only once more than one non-SQL consumer genuinely needs the same metric. Rule out A entirely, because duplication guarantees drift. Notice how the constraints, not the technology, drove the answer: quarterly changes favor one owned definition, and point-in-time needs favor a materialized column. Now let's test whether you can apply this reasoning yourself.

scenes.title: Check: Metrics, Layers, and Exam Traps

questions.question: A company maintains four dashboards and two production ML models that all need the same governed definition of 'profit after marketing spend'. Which placement of the definition guarantees that every one of these consumers reads the exact same rule, with no chance of divergence?

options.label: Define the metric once in a governed metrics/semantic layer that all consumers query
Write the metric as a calculated field in each dashboard, copy the query, and paste it into each ML notebook
Store the definition as a formula in a shared spreadsheet that each team references manually
Let each team own its own version of the metric in its own tool, since the numbers will agree in practice

questions.analysis: A governed metrics/semantic layer defines the metric exactly once and exposes that single definition to every consumer — dashboards, notebooks, and ML models — so the same rule is executed everywhere and any change propagates from one owner. Option B is the classic 'copy the query' distractor: duplicating the SQL into each report and notebook creates as many definitions as there are copies, and silent drift is guaranteed when one is later corrected. Option C relocates the definition to an ungoverned spreadsheet, so no pipeline, catalog, or ML feature can programmatically resolve which version is authoritative. Option D is the 'let each team own its own version' trap — independent ownership means no reconciliation mechanism exists when the versions disagree, which is exactly the trust-erosion failure mode the exam tests. The medallion architecture progressively refines raw data into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3], and the semantic layer is where those trusted tables get one shared business definition rather than one per consumer.

questions.question: Which of the following scenarios silently create a SECOND, competing definition of an existing metric that already lives in a gold table or governed semantic layer? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: An analyst copies the gold table's profit query into a personal dashboard and tweaks the cost-attribution join condition locally
A team stores the metric formula in a spreadsheet and recomputes profit per campaign there each week
The pipeline re-runs the same published gold transformation that produced the table the semantic layer already reads
Each business unit ships its own 'official' version of the metric in its own BI tool to avoid waiting on the central pipeline

questions.analysis: Options A, B, and D all fork the definition: A and D duplicate the metric into per-report or per-team BI artifacts with independently editable logic, and B moves it into an ungoverned spreadsheet where nothing can reconcile it with the pipeline value. Because attribute-derived values such as cost attribution diverge fastest — the weighting rule is easy to vary accidentally — a locally 'tweaked' join condition is precisely the kind of edit that silently creates a second definition. Option C is not a fork: re-running the same published transformation that materializes the table the semantic layer already reads keeps a single authorship of the rule, so the number cannot diverge. Note that layered architectures are explicitly designed so bronze raw, silver validated, and gold enriched data carry increasing quality and structure [source 6], which only holds if the business rule is authored in the enriched layer once, not re-authored in four downstream tools.

questions.question: An engineer argues: 'Our gold table is materialized with a scheduled pipeline, so the table itself IS our semantic layer.' Why is this reasoning exam-incorrect?

options.label: A metrics/semantic layer holds the authoritative metric definition and serves it to all consumers; the materialized gold table is only one physical realization of that definition for one delivery path
It is incorrect because materialized tables can never be read by BI tools, only by ML workloads
It is incorrect because a materialized view is always refreshed on read while a semantic layer is always refreshed by a scheduled job
It is incorrect because the semantic layer must live in Unity Catalog while the gold table must live in a separate metastore

questions.analysis: The distinction the exam tests is authoring versus realization. A metrics/semantic layer owns the definition of the metric and resolves it for every consumer — BI reports, notebooks, and ML feature pipelines — so the number means the same thing everywhere. A materialized gold table is a physical realization of that definition along one delivery path; if the definition lives only inside the table's SQL and nowhere governed, there is nothing to serve a second consumer consistently, and a BI calculated field will quietly re-implement it. Option B is false: gold tables are routinely exposed to BI tools. Option C garbles refresh semantics in both directions. Option D invents a metastore-location rule that is not part of the metrics-versus-materialization distinction. The medallion pattern refines raw data into trusted business-ready tables [source 3], but holding trusted rows is not the same as holding the single governed metric definition that all consumers resolve against.

questions.question: An order contains item X (price $40, 6 clicks) and item Y (price $60, 4 clicks); the ad platform reports $80 of total spend for the order. Compare naive attribution (equal cost per click) with price-weighted attribution. Which statement correctly characterizes the two results?

options.label: Per-item profit changes between the two methods (X is −$8 naive but +$8 weight-adjusted; Y is $28 naive but $12 weight-adjusted) while the order-level total stays $20 under both
Both the per-item breakdown and the order-level total change, because changing the attribution rule always changes the total
Neither the per-item breakdown nor the total changes, because the attribution rule only affects reporting labels, not dollars
The per-item breakdown is identical under both methods, but the naive total is $20 while the weighted total is $28

questions.analysis: Naive: cost per click is $80 / 10 = $8, so X pays 6 × $8 = $48 for a profit of $40 − $48 = −$8, and Y pays 4 × $8 = $32 for a profit of $60 − $32 = $28; the total is $20 (allocation conserves the order's dollars). Price-weighted: X's share is 40 / (40 + 60) = 40%, so X pays $32 and profits $8, while Y's 60% share is $48 and profits $12; the total is again $20. So the attribution rule redistributes per-item profit — even flipping X's sign — while conserving the order total, which is why a discrepancy between a gold column and a dashboard field is a definition problem, not a freshness problem, and why the distractor 'the fresher table is the correct one' must be rejected. Option B overgeneralizes by claiming the total must move. Option C undergeneralizes by claiming allocation is cosmetic. Option D misstates both the unchanged breakdown and the weighted total. This is exactly why the metric must be defined in one governed place: attribute-derived values like advertising attribution diverge fastest because the weighting rule is easy to vary accidentally.

actions.text: Time to put that reasoning to work. Take your time on each question and answer them on your own — don't second-guess yourself by peeking ahead or teaming up.
Once you submit, I'll be right here to walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Design Checklist: Single Source of Truth

elements.content: Design Checklist: Single Source of Truth
Define each derived metric exactly once, as far upstream as consumers allow.

A design pattern organizes lakehouse data across bronze (raw), silver (validated), and gold (enriched) layers, progressively refining raw inputs into trusted, business-ready tables [source 3][source 6]. This checklist turns that principle into an actionable audit for every metric you ship.
1

Define once, upstream. Derived data is any value computed from other data rather than captured at source, so each derived metric belongs in a single gold column or governed metric definition, not per dashboard.
2
Document the definition. Record formula, grain, attribution rule, null and negative handling, and refresh cadence where consumers can read it.
3
Serve, don't copy. Publish views, a metrics or semantic layer, or shared transformation functions instead of pasting per-consumer SQL.
4
Version and test the logic. Unit-test the rule on known inputs and reconcile aggregates against silver on every run.
Worked example: profit after marketing
Order: 10 clicks, $80 spend. Item X: $40, 6 clicks. Item Y: $60, 4 clicks.
Naive: cost = $8/click. X = 6x8 = $48, profit = -$8. Y = 4x8 = $32, profit = $28. Total = $20.
Price-weighted: X = 40/100 = 40%, cost $32, profit $8. Y = 60%, cost $48, profit $12. Total = $20.
The total agrees, but the per-item breakdown flips. That is why one definition must be served, not re-implemented.
Exam traps to reject
One table per metric. Multiplies copies of the same rule and guarantees silent drift.
SQL copied into each team's notebook. A rule corrected once stays wrong everywhere else.
Fix the number in the dashboard. Patching the output without fixing the rule hides the defect.

actions.text: Building on the consistency problems we just walked through, here is the payoff — a design checklist for the single source of truth. This consolidates everything about derived metrics into four rules you can actually apply when designing transformations. Let's take them one at a time.

Rule one: define once, upstream. The definition should live as far upstream as your consumers allow — typically as a documented gold column or a governed metric. One metric, one definition, one place. If you find yourself re-deriving the same value in two notebooks, that is the smell that this rule has been broken.

Rule two: document the definition. And notice what the slide demands you record — the formula, the grain, the attribution rule, how nulls and negatives are handled, and the refresh cadence. This is exactly the level of detail the exam expects, because a metric without a stated grain or an attribution rule is not really defined at all.

Rule three: serve, don't copy. Publish the definition through views, a metrics or semantic layer, or shared transformation functions — anything that lets consumers reference the logic instead of reimplementing it. The moment a team copies your SQL into their own notebook, you have two definitions and no source of truth.

Rule four: version and test the logic. Unit-test the rule on known inputs, and reconcile aggregates against silver on every run. If a nightly load silently changes the profit number, the reconciliation is what catches it — and versioning is what lets you get back to the last good definition.

Now the exam traps to reject, and these are worth memorizing as anti-patterns. One table per metric — that multiplies copies of the same rule until they drift apart. SQL copied into each team's notebook — a rule corrected in one place while the others quietly go stale. And fixing the number in the dashboard without fixing the rule — patching the output instead of the pipeline.

Before we close this lesson, run the profit-after-marketing example once more against these four rules. Define the cost allocation once, document the price-weighted attribution, serve it rather than copy it, and test it — and the per-item breakdown stops flipping depending on who ran the query.

So to recap: define once upstream, document formula and grain, serve instead of copy, and version and test. Four rules, one trustworthy definition per metric. That is the design discipline for the rest of your pipelines.

scenes.title: Unit Glossary: Transformation and Modeling Terms

elements.content: Business logic — The set of rules that converts stored, source-level data into decision-ready values, such as profit = revenue − cost − marketing spend; it is distinct from raw capture because it encodes an interpretation of the data rather than recording an event, and it must reside in exactly one authoritative place to remain trustworthy.

Derived data — Any value that is computed from other data rather than captured at the source, including every gold-layer metric, KPI, dashboard field, and ML feature; because derived values inherit the correctness of both their inputs and their formula, a change to either can silently alter the output without any error being raised.

DRY (don't repeat yourself) — The design principle that each piece of knowledge — including a metric formula such as profit after marketing costs — has exactly one authoritative representation; it applies to derived data whenever the same rule could be re-implemented in more than one consumer, and its violation is the root cause of silent metric drift.

Single source of truth (SSOT) — The design rule that a metric is defined once and every consumer reads that single definition instead of re-implementing it; it requires a governed definition artifact and fails when consumers are permitted to copy the formula for convenience, speed, or team autonomy, in which case the copies diverge.

Metrics layer / semantic layer — A governed catalog of metric definitions — each specifying formula, grain, and available dimensions — that serves the same computation to SQL, BI, notebooks, and ML consumers; because it is decoupled from any single tool, it gives the strongest cross-consumer consistency and ML reusability, at the cost that every definition change must be published through the layer rather than edited locally.

Attribution model — The rule that assigns shared costs, such as advertising spend, to individual items or channels; a naive attribution model splits cost equally (for example, equal cost per click), while a price-weighted model allocates cost in proportion to each item's price share, and because the weighting rule is easy to vary accidentally, attribution-derived values diverge faster than most other derived metrics.

Grain — The level of detail at which a fact or metric is recorded — for example, order, item, or day — and which determines what a single row represents; comparing or joining metrics that were computed at different grains produces silently wrong numbers, so grain must be stated explicitly in every metric definition before the values are combined.

Conformed dimension — A dimension, such as date or customer, that is shared by multiple fact tables and uses identical keys, values, and meaning across them; it is the precondition that allows metrics from different fact tables to be combined consistently across the warehouse, and without it cross-subject joins yield inconsistent or duplicated results.

actions.text: Before we move into data quality, let's lock down the vocabulary from this unit. These are the terms the exam expects you to use precisely, so we'll walk through them one at a time and anchor each to the medallion and dimensional-modeling material we just covered.

First, business logic. This is the set of rules that converts stored data into decision-ready values. The classic example: profit equals revenue minus cost minus marketing spend. Notice that none of those three inputs is a decision on its own — the rule is what turns them into something a business can act on.

Next, derived data: any value computed from other data rather than captured at the source. And this definition is broader than it sounds — every gold metric, every KPI, and every machine learning feature is derived data. If you didn't capture it from the source system, it's derived.

DRY — don't repeat yourself — is the principle that each piece of knowledge, including a metric formula, has exactly one authoritative representation. Read that carefully: the formula itself is knowledge, and it counts as something you should not duplicate.

That leads directly to the single source of truth, or SSOT. This is the design rule that a metric is defined once, and every consumer reads that definition instead of re-implementing it. SSOT is the goal; DRY is the principle that gets you there.

The metrics layer, also called the semantic layer, is the mechanism. It's a governed catalog of metric definitions — formula, grain, and dimensions — served consistently to SQL, BI tools, notebooks, and ML consumers. One definition, many consumers.

Now attribution model: the rule that assigns shared costs to items or channels. Naive attribution splits costs equally, while price-weighted attribution allocates proportionally to price. Same underlying data, two different answers — which is exactly why the rule must be defined once.

Grain is the level of detail at which a fact or metric is recorded — order, item, or day. This one carries an exam trap: comparing metrics at different grains produces silently wrong numbers. No error is raised; the answer is just incorrect.

And finally, conformed dimension: a dimension such as date or customer that is shared by multiple fact tables, so metrics can be combined consistently across the warehouse. Conformed dimensions are what let you compare a sales metric to an inventory metric and trust the result.
Keep these eight terms handy — we'll lean on business logic, derived data, grain, and SSOT repeatedly in the pages ahead. Take a moment to skim the glossary once more before we move on.

scenes.title: Diagnostic Check: What Is Data Quality?

questions.question: A retail analytics team loads nightly point-of-sale transactions into a Delta table. A data steward reports that roughly 12% of customer records have an empty value in the 'postal_code' column, even though the column must be populated for every sale. Business stakeholders ask: 'Which data quality dimension is being violated?' Identify the dimension that best fits this business statement.

options.label: Completeness, because required values are absent from records that should contain them
Accuracy, because the stored postal codes do not match the real mailing addresses
Uniqueness, because the same customer may appear more than once across rows
Validity, because postal codes do not conform to a permitted format or pattern

questions.correctAnswer: Completeness
questions.analysis: Completeness measures whether all required values are present. The report describes empty values in a mandatory column, which is the textbook description of missing data. The source material states that any patterns or significant amounts of missing data should be taken into consideration when conducting an analysis, and that you can report missing data when writing up results [source 5]. Distractor B describes accuracy (wrong values), which is different from absence; C describes uniqueness (duplicate rows); D describes validity (format or domain conformance). This item calibrates the learner's ability to map business language ('empty value in a required field') to the formal dimension of completeness.

questions.question: A data engineer receives a raw customer export and must prepare it for a Databricks Lakehouse gold-layer dashboard. She notices two separate anomalies: (1) several customer_id values appear on more than one row with identical attributes, producing duplicate records; and (2) some email values are stored as 'not-an-email@@example' with clearly invalid syntax. Select ALL statements that correctly classify these anomalies and the required cleaning action.

options.label: The duplicate rows are a uniqueness problem; the engineer should remove duplicates as part of data cleaning
The malformed email values are a validity problem; the engineer should standardize or fix them before analysis
The malformed email values are a completeness problem because the value 'not-an-email@@example' is effectively unusable
The duplicate rows are an accuracy problem because duplicated records make the row count wrong

correctAnswer: The duplicate rows are a uniqueness problem; the engineer should remove duplicates as part of data cleaning
The malformed email values are a validity problem; the engineer should standardize or fix them before analysis
questions.analysis: Data cleaning is the process of identifying and fixing errors, inconsistencies, and quality issues in raw data so it is accurate, consistent, and ready for analysis, and it typically includes removing duplicates and standardizing values [source 2]. Duplicate rows violate uniqueness, not accuracy, so option A is correct and option D is a common trap: duplication is a structural repetition issue, not a wrong value. Malformed emails violate validity because the value does not conform to the expected pattern or domain; option B is correct. Option C is a distractor that confuses 'unusable-looking' with 'absent' — completeness is specifically about missing values, not malformed ones. This item directly tests the exam trap that duplicate-row stems map to uniqueness, and the completeness-versus-accuracy distinction.
answer: The duplicate rows are a uniqueness problem; the engineer should remove duplicates as part of data cleaning
The malformed email values are a validity problem; the engineer should standardize or fix them before analysis

questions.question: An executive asks: 'We run dashboards on a gold layer that is built from silver and bronze tables. Why can we trust the dashboard only if upstream quality checks pass?' Which explanation is the most technically correct one-sentence justification for this dependency?

options.label: Because downstream metrics are computed from upstream records, so any defect present upstream is propagated and reproduced in the dashboard output
Because dashboards run on Photon, and Photon silently drops any row that fails a quality rule before aggregation
Because Unity Catalog automatically rewrites incorrect bronze values as part of every read operation
Because gold-layer materialized views are recalculated only when upstream tables contain zero rows

questions.correctAnswer: Because downstream metrics are computed from upstream records, so any defect present upstream is propagated and reproduced in the dashboard output
questions.analysis: The valid reasoning is propagation: every downstream layer derives from upstream data, so a defect at bronze or silver is inherited and shown in gold-layer metrics. The source material makes this concrete by noting that flawed data leads to skewed results, and that cleaning ensures the analysis reflects the true representation of the data, preventing misleading conclusions and fostering more accurate insights [source 6]. A second supporting source says quality control checks in the field should catch most errors in data collection, and that further steps are needed to prepare collected data for analysis [source 4]. Option B is false: Photon is a vectorized query engine, not a silent quality-rule filter. Option C is false: Unity Catalog is a governance and catalog layer; it does not rewrite incorrect values on read. Option D is false: materialized views refresh based on the underlying data and schedule, not on upstream tables being empty. This item calibrates causal reasoning about the medallion architecture (a layered bronze/silver/gold data refinement pattern).
answer: Because downstream metrics are computed from upstream records, so any defect present upstream is propagated and reproduced in the dashboard output

actions.text: Before we dive into data quality, let's run a short diagnostic check to see how well you already map business language to formal quality dimensions — this is a warm-up, so a few of these may be new to you, and that's exactly the point.
Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer. Once you submit, I'll join you to walk through the reasoning, including the traps where these dimensions get confused for one another.

scenes.title: Why Bad Data Breaks the Pipeline

elements.content: Why Bad Data Breaks the Pipeline
A defect introduced at ingestion is not a local problem — it is amplified at every downstream hop.
FAILURE CHAIN — ONE NULL COLUMN, FOUR DECISIONS WRONG
customers rows with NULL customer_id
join drops 2,000 of 10,000 rows
revenue totals understated 20%

Region C reads $8.0M instead of $10.0M

→ $500k of promotion budget withdrawn

Worked example — impact of a silent NULL:
10,000 rows → 2,000 dropped → 80% survive.
Observed total: $8.0M. Actual total: $10.0M.

elements.html: Understatement=10.010.0−8.0​=20%

elements.content: Why cleaning matters: flawed data yields skewed results, and cleaning keeps analysis a true representation of the data [source 6].
Scope of cleaning: identify and fix errors, inconsistencies, duplicates and missing values so data is accurate and analysis-ready [source 2].
Quality is an undercurrent spanning generation → ingestion → storage → transformation → serving; a "quality pass" at the end recovers nothing already propagated.

actions.text: Now let's tie those quality dimensions to something very concrete: why bad data actually breaks the pipeline. This is the motivating case for the whole unit on data quality, and it's exactly the kind of scenario the exam likes to frame as a story.

Here's the core principle. A defect introduced at ingestion is not a local problem. It doesn't stay in the bronze table — it propagates silently through every downstream transformation, dashboard, and ML model, because each layer happily consumes the output of the layer before it.

So let's walk the failure chain end to end — one null column, four decisions wrecked. Follow it step by step, because this sequence is the mental model I want you to carry into every quality discussion.
Step one: the customers table lands with rows that have a NULL customer_id. No validation at ingestion, so nothing blocks it.
Step two: the join against orders drops those rows. Two thousand of ten thousand rows simply disappear — and the job reports success, because the query itself didn't fail.
Step three: the revenue totals are understated by twenty percent. The dashboard renders, the numbers look plausible, and nobody has any reason to suspect them.

Step four: Region C reports eight million dollars instead of ten million. That's half a million dollars of profit misattributed to the wrong place — and an executive makes a decision on the wrong number. The defect never announced itself; it just quietly changed the answer.

Notice what the worked example is really teaching: silent failures are more dangerous than loud ones. A crash pages you at 3 a.m.; a NULL that quietly drops rows can survive for months in your reporting layer.

That's why cleaning matters. Flawed data yields skewed results, and data cleaning is what makes the analysis reflect a true representation of the data — not a version of it that has quietly lost a fifth of its rows.

So what does cleaning actually cover? Identifying and fixing errors, inconsistencies, and quality issues so the data is accurate, consistent, and analysis-ready. Note the scope — it's not just fixing typos, it's reconciling disagreement between sources.

And the key phrase to remember: quality is an undercurrent spanning generation, ingestion, storage, transformation, and serving. It runs beneath every stage of the data engineering lifecycle, and it cannot be bolted on at the end. If your only quality check sits at the dashboard, you've already lost every upstream battle.
That's the motivation. Next we'll define the core data quality dimensions you can actually test against, and then we'll look at where quality checks belong in the pipeline.

scenes.title: The Core Data Quality Dimensions

elements.content: The Core Data Quality Dimensions

Six dimensions test a table before it is trusted. Each is framed as the question it answers plus a concrete check — cleaning rows and columns into a well-defined row/column relationship is the precondition [source 1].
Quality checks apply at Bronze, Silver and Gold stages.
Dimension Comparison

data.text: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(customer_id); null rate per column
Reconcile to system of record / trusted table
Is the data fresh enough for its use case?
Does it conform to domain and format rules?
Value in allowed domain list; regex format match

elements.content:
Worked example

orders table: 100,000 rows, 12,000 null customer_id, 1,240 duplicate order_id, 2,400 rows past 24h freshness. Rules: null rate < 5%, 0 duplicates, latency < 24h.
[source 4] [source 1] [source 2] [source 6]

Rule-by-rule verdict

Completeness: 12% > 5% → FAIL

Uniqueness: 1,240 duplicates → FAIL

Timeliness: 2,400 rows late → FAIL

Accuracy/Validity/Consistency: reconcile and rule-check before Gold promotion.

Exam takeaway: name the dimension first, then the check that implements it. The six dimensions form the quality gate before any analysis — flawed data skews results, so cleaning ensures the analysis reflects the true data [source 6].

actions.text: Let's define the dimensions you'll measure any table against. Think of each dimension as a question you ask about the data before you decide to trust it. In the exam, and in real pipelines, quality checks rarely use all six — you pick the two or three that matter for the use case.

The six dimensions are completeness, accuracy, timeliness, uniqueness, validity, and consistency. Completeness asks: are the values we need actually present? You test it by comparing COUNT(*) against COUNT of a specific column, or by measuring the null rate per column.

This table is your reference for the exam. For each dimension, it gives you the question answered, an example failure, and a concrete check expression. Accuracy is about whether the values reflect reality, so you reconcile against a system of record. Timeliness asks whether the data is fresh enough for its use case, usually tested against a maximum ingestion timestamp. Uniqueness means each real-world entity appears once, verified by comparing COUNT(*) to COUNT(DISTINCT business_key).

Notice that these checks apply at every layer of the medallion architecture — that's the Bronze, Silver, Gold naming pattern we covered earlier. Bronze catches basic completeness and validity on raw ingest, Silver enforces uniqueness and consistency, and Gold adds timeliness and accuracy against business expectations.

Here's a worked example you might see on the exam. An orders table has one hundred thousand rows, but twelve thousand of them have a null customer_id. That's a twelve percent null rate against a five percent threshold. Walk through each rule: which dimension is violated, and does the verdict pass or fail? Completeness fails. Working the arithmetic out loud is exactly what the exam expects.

The single most important takeaway here: always name the dimension first, then the check that implements it. Don't just say 'the data is bad' — say 'completeness on customer_id fails because the null rate exceeds the threshold.' That structure is what gets you full marks. Next we'll look at how to translate business expectations into testable rules.

scenes.title: Dimension Identification Drill

questions.question: A nightly Lakeflow (Databricks' orchestration framework for scheduled data pipelines) job loads orders from a source system into a Bronze Delta table in your medallion architecture (a layered Bronze/Silver/Gold organization in which Bronze holds raw ingested data, Silver holds cleaned and conformed data, and Gold holds business-level aggregates). An engineer notices that hundreds of rows in the Bronze table have order_id populated but customer_id is NULL. Which data quality dimension does this defect most directly violate?

options.label: Completeness — a required value (customer_id) is absent where it should be present.
Accuracy — the NULL is numerically wrong because a customer truly exists.
Uniqueness — a missing customer_id creates duplicate order records.
Timeliness — the NULLs indicate the partition was loaded too late.

questions.analysis: Completeness asks whether required values are present, and the standard check is COUNT(*) versus COUNT(customer_id) or a NULL rate per column measured on the actual data. Because customer_id is declared a required attribute yet arrives as NULL, the defect is a presence problem, so Option A is correct. Option B tempts students because a real customer exists in the world, but accuracy concerns whether a populated value reflects reality — a NULL is not a wrong value, it is an absent one. Option C confuses completeness with uniqueness: NULLs do not generate duplicates; duplicates are a separate dimension tested by comparing COUNT(*) against COUNT(DISTINCT order_id). Option D mislabels the defect as a freshness problem even though lateness would be evidenced by a missing or stale partition key, not by NULLs inside a correctly loaded partition. Note the edge case: if customer_id were genuinely optional (for example, guest checkout), the NULLs would not violate completeness at all, and the presence rule must be stated as a precondition before declaring a failure. Data cleaning, as the source material defines it, is the process of identifying and fixing errors, inconsistencies, and quality issues so data is accurate, consistent, and ready for analysis [source 2].

questions.question: An auditor runs SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS distinct_ids FROM sales.silver.orders and receives rows = 2,000,000 and distinct_ids = 1,900,000. Which TWO statements about this result are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The result is a uniqueness defect: 100,000 rows share order_id values with other rows.
The result is a completeness defect because the table is missing 100,000 rows relative to ideal volume.
The result alone cannot establish an accuracy violation because accuracy requires an external source of truth.
The result is a validity defect because order_id values fall outside the allowed format.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct because uniqueness is exactly the dimension that asks whether each real-world entity appears once. With 2,000,000 total rows but only 1,900,000 distinct order_id values, at least 100,000 rows are redundant, a classic exam trap: the large row count seduces candidates into answering 'completeness,' but the table is not short of rows — it has too many for the same key. Option C is correct because accuracy asks whether values reflect reality, and verifying that requires reconciliation against a source system of record or a trusted reference table; an internal COUNT/DISTINCT check has no external anchor and therefore cannot prove or disprove accuracy, making accuracy the hardest dimension to test without a source of truth. Option B mirrors the most common student misconception, conflating the gap between rows and distinct_ids with missing records, but a completeness check is COUNT(*) versus COUNT(col) per column, not distinct counts. Option D confuses uniqueness with validity: validity concerns format and range rules for individual values, and nothing in this query reveals malformed order_ids. The general lesson matches the source material's guidance that quality assurance checks are performed to verify data accuracy, which presupposes a trusted reference rather than a purely internal aggregate [source 1].

questions.question: A Silver table's partition for processing_date = 2024-03-15 still contains data as of 2024-03-10, and the pipeline's maximum business_date in that partition equals 2024-03-10. Which dimension is most directly violated, and why is that the best-fitting answer?

options.label: Timeliness — the partition for the 15th is stale because its newest record is five days old.
Accuracy — the dates are wrong representations of reality.
Completeness — 2024-03-11 through 2024-03-14 records are absent, so the partition has missing rows.
Consistency — two partitions disagree about the meaning of processing_date.

questions.analysis: Timeliness asks whether data is fresh enough for its intended use, and a partition labeled for 2024-03-15 whose newest business_date is 2024-03-10 is demonstrably stale, so Option A is the best fit. The question deliberately forces ranking of overlapping candidate defects: the missing intermediate dates could also be framed as completeness, but completeness specifically asks whether required values are present within the records that exist (measured by NULL rate per column), whereas a lagging maximum business_date is the canonical freshness signal. This illustrates the exam principle that one defect can violate more than one dimension, and the candidate must choose the dimension the scenario's evidence most directly demonstrates. Option B is weaker because accuracy demands an external system of record to show the stored dates misrepresent reality, and here the dates are probably faithfully copied — they are merely late. Option D invokes consistency between partitions, but the scenario describes a single partition's content, not contradictory semantics across partitions. In line with the source material's cautions about patterns of missing data being taken into account during analysis [source 5], a stale partition can silently bias trend analysis if it is not detected before aggregation, which is why freshness checks must run as an automated gate in the pipeline and not as a manual afterthought.

actions.text: Time for a quick drill. We've just walked through the core data quality dimensions, and now I want to see how well you can match a realistic defect to the right one. Work through each question on your own — read the scenario carefully and pick the best-fitting answer. Some defects can touch more than one dimension, so think about which one the question is most directly pointing at.
Take your time, submit when you're ready, and I'll be right here to walk through anything that tripped you up once you're done.

scenes.title: Completeness vs. Accuracy vs. Timeliness vs. Uniqueness

elements.content: Dimension  |  Completeness  |  Accuracy  |  Uniqueness

Question answered
Completeness: Are the required values physically present in the column, regardless of whether those values are correct?
Accuracy: Do the stored values agree with the real-world state of affairs as recorded in a system of record or trusted reference dataset?
Uniqueness: Does each real-world business entity appear exactly once, so that counting rows does not overstate the entity population?

Preconditions that must hold before the dimension is even measurable
Completeness: The schema must declare which columns are required, because a column that is optional by contract can be 100% NULL and still be complete.
Accuracy: A trusted reference must exist (source system of record, reconciled extract, or golden table) and must be joinable to the target on a declared business key.
Uniqueness: A business key must be explicitly declared by the data owner; without that declaration, no uniqueness violation can be defined or detected.

Primary metric and typical Databricks check pattern
Completeness: NULL rate per required column, computed as 1 - COUNT(col)/COUNT(*) in Spark SQL, or equivalently (COUNT(*) - COUNT(col)) / COUNT(*) * 100 expressed as a percentage; this is exactly the COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) pattern introduced when we first defined the dimension.
Accuracy: Reconciliation delta, computed by joining the target to the source of record on the business key and counting rows where the compared measures disagree, for example SUM(CASE WHEN t.amount <> s.amount THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) after an inner join on order_id.
Uniqueness: Duplicate rate, computed as (COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT business_key)) / COUNT(*) * 100; in Databricks this is a single aggregate over the Delta table or a Lakeflow expectation such as EXPECT (COUNT(*) = COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)) applied on the target.

Typical failure mode observed in production
Completeness: Placeholder and sentinel values such as 'N/A', '0000-00-00', or -1 are physically present, so the column is technically complete while remaining analytically useless — this is the exact reason completeness proves presence, not correctness.
Accuracy: Silent divergence: the target contains a plausible value that disagrees with the source of record, often introduced by a join that duplicated a dimension row or a transformation that applied the wrong business rule.
Uniqueness: Row multiplication from an unqualified join, a retried Auto Loader or Lakeflow pipeline that appended the same batch twice, or a late-arriving update inserted instead of merged as a slowly changing dimension (SCD, a pattern that preserves history when an attribute changes).

Worked example with concrete numbers
Completeness: A customer table holds 1,000,000 rows and the email column is required; COUNT(email) returns 940,000, so the NULL rate is (1,000,000 - 940,000) / 1,000,000 * 100 = 6.0%, which fails a 1% completeness SLA and would be flagged by a Lakeflow expectation.
Accuracy: Reconciling 1,000,000 orders against the source system of record on order_id returns 1,000,000 matched rows of which 12,500 have a differing amount, giving an accuracy disagreement rate of 12,500 / 1,000,000 * 100 = 1.25%, which exceeds a 0.5% tolerance and blocks the gold-layer publish.
Uniqueness: The same 1,000,000 rows contain only 950,000 distinct order_id values, so the duplicate rate is (1,000,000 - 950,000) / 1,000,000 * 100 = 5.0%; this is precisely the '2 million rows but 1.9 million distinct order_ids' exam trap from the drill, and it tests uniqueness, not completeness.

What the dimension does NOT prove
Completeness: A 100% completeness score does not prove correctness: a row full of placeholder values is complete but inaccurate, which is why completeness must never be presented as an accuracy guarantee.
Accuracy: A 100% accuracy score on matched rows does not prove completeness or uniqueness, because rows missing from the target simply never enter the reconciliation join and therefore cannot be counted as disagreements.
Uniqueness: A 100% uniqueness score on the business key does not prove that each row is about a different real-world entity, because uniqueness enforced on a surrogate key or a partition column such as ingest_date is meaningless — the same entity can arrive once per partition and still pass.

Cost and operational overhead of enforcing it
Completeness: Completeness is the cheapest dimension to enforce because it needs only column-level aggregates over the target and no external data; it scales linearly with table size under Photon and can run on every micro-batch.
Accuracy: Accuracy is the most expensive dimension because it requires moving or joining a reference dataset, and the cost grows with the size of the reconciliation window; a full reconciliation is typically scheduled rather than run per micro-batch.
Uniqueness: Uniqueness sits in between: it needs a COUNT(DISTINCT business_key) aggregation, which is cheaper than an external join but more expensive than a NULL count and can dominate runtime on very wide high-cardinality keys.

When it is the right primary check
Completeness: Choose completeness first when the requirement is a contract about required fields, such as 'every order must carry a customer_id', and you are validating ingestion before any business logic runs.
Accuracy: Choose accuracy when a business decision depends on the value itself — pricing, regulatory reporting, financial reconciliation — and a source system of record or trusted reference table is available to compare against.
Uniqueness: Choose uniqueness when downstream counts or joins would be inflated by repeated entities, such as deduplicating before a MERGE into a gold-layer materialized view (a precomputed, automatically refreshed result table).

Takeaway — Treat the three dimensions as independent axes, not a hierarchy: completeness proves presence, accuracy proves agreement with reality, uniqueness proves one-row-per-entity, and passing one says nothing about the others [source 1].
