Takeaway — Declare the business key before writing any uniqueness check, because uniqueness measured on a surrogate or partition column is meaningless and will silently pass a duplicated business entity.

Takeaway — Use COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) for completeness, a join against the source of record for accuracy, and COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT business_key) for uniqueness — these are the three patterns the exam expects you to name [source 2].
Takeaway — Automate all three as Lakeflow expectations on Delta Lake tables so violations fail the pipeline rather than surfacing later as skewed analysis results [source 6].
Takeaway — Timeliness is a fourth, separate axis measured against a declared business freshness requirement, so never substitute a completeness or accuracy pass for a freshness SLA check [source 5].

actions.text: Now that you've finished the dimension identification drill, let's line up the four data quality dimensions side by side. They are easy to confuse on the exam, so we'll compare them by the questions learners actually have to reason about: what each one asks, how it fails, how you measure it, and — just as important — what it does not prove.

This comparison table is your exam reference. Six columns: the dimension itself, the question it answers, the typical failure mode in production, the primary metric, the Databricks check pattern, and what the dimension does not prove. When a scenario question describes a symptom, find it in the failure-mode column, then read across to the metric and the check pattern — that path leads you to the right answer.

Remember the trap we just covered: completeness proves presence, not correctness. A row full of placeholder values like 'UNKNOWN' or a sentinel date is complete but completely inaccurate. Completeness answers 'are the required values there?' — nothing more. That distinction is exactly what the failure-mode column is showing you.

For each dimension, note the primary metric and the typical Databricks check pattern. Completeness is a null or row-count ratio; accuracy needs a reference dataset or source-system reconciliation, because agreement with reality cannot be computed from the table alone. Timeliness is measured against a business freshness requirement — say thirty minutes — never an arbitrary threshold you invent.

Here's the worked example with concrete numbers so the metrics feel tangible rather than abstract. And notice the uniqueness column: uniqueness only means something once you declare a business key. Uniqueness on a surrogate ID or a partition column is meaningless — it will always pass and tell you nothing about your data.

That 'what it does NOT prove' column is the one learners skip — and the one exam questions exploit. A perfect uniqueness score does not prove your rows are the right rows. A perfect completeness score does not prove the values are correct. Read that column carefully for all four dimensions.

So the takeaway: treat the three dimensions as independent axes. Passing one says nothing about the others, and a scenario can be complete, accurate, and timeliness-broken all at once. Declare your business key before writing any uniqueness check, and use COUNT(*) versus COUNT(column) deliberately when you measure completeness. From here we'll translate a business requirement into a testable rule.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: From Business Requirement to Testable Rule

elements.content: Problem 1

The sales team hands you a one-sentence requirement: 'Our orders table should be complete, current, and free of duplicates so the daily revenue dashboard is trustworthy.' The table is main.sales.orders, a Delta Lake table registered in Unity Catalog, one row per sales order. A profile of the last 30 days shows 140,000 orders per day and 4,200,000 rows in total, and reports four defects: (i) 1,850 rows have a NULL customer_id; (ii) 312 order_id values appear on more than one row; (iii) 47 rows in today's partition have loaded_at more than 30 minutes after created_at; (iv) 4,110 rows loaded today have an order_total that disagrees with the payment gateway settlement. Tasks: (a) map each of the three adjectives to a data quality dimension; (b) map each defect (i)-(iv) to the dimension it violates; (c) explain why defect (ii) must not be recorded as a completeness problem even though 'extra rows' exist; (d) state one thing the completeness check does NOT prove.
Hint: Ask what question each adjective answers: is it here? is it now? is it once?

Worked solution
Step 1 - decompose the adjectives into dimensions.

- 'complete' -> completeness: the question is whether required values are present.

- 'current' -> timeliness: the question is whether the value was loaded or refreshed inside the agreed latency window (here 30 minutes).

- 'free of duplicates' -> uniqueness: the question is whether each business entity appears exactly once.

- 'trustworthy' -> not a dimension at all. It is the outcome a stakeholder experiences when the measurable dimensions pass, and it can never be checked directly.

Step 2 - map each defect to the dimension it violates.

(i) 1,850 rows with NULL customer_id -> completeness: a required value is absent.

(ii) 312 order_id values on more than one row -> uniqueness: one business entity, several rows.

(iii) 47 rows with loaded_at - created_at greater than 30 minutes -> timeliness: the value is present and correct, but it arrived late.

(iv) 4,110 rows whose order_total disagrees with the gateway settlement -> accuracy: the value is present but does not match reality.

Step 3 - the duplicate-row question.

A duplicated row is missing nothing: every column is filled, so no NULL rate moves at all. The damage is that SUM(order_total) double counts revenue. The metric is COUNT(*) minus COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) = 4,200,000 - 4,199,688 = 312, which is a uniqueness metric. This is exactly the exam trap: a stem reporting 'the table has 2 million rows but only 1.9 million distinct order_ids' is testing uniqueness, not completeness.

Step 4 - what completeness does not prove.

Completeness proves presence, not correctness. If the loader writes the string 'UNKNOWN' into customer_id, the NULL rate is 0.00% and the column is fully complete while being entirely inaccurate. Catching that requires an allowed-value list, i.e. an accuracy or validity rule, which is the same class of work as standardising 'Memorial', 'MUN' and 'Memorial University of Newfoundland' into one value [source 5].

Answer: complete -> completeness, current -> timeliness, free of duplicates -> uniqueness, trustworthy -> not a dimension; defects (i)-(iv) violate completeness, uniqueness, timeliness and accuracy respectively.

Analysis — The method works because a dimension names a question, the question names a metric, and the metric decides which SQL you write. Decomposing the sentence first blocks the most common student error, which is writing checks by intuition ('I will look for weird rows') and then being unable to say whether the check passed or failed. The definition of the underlying activity supports this split: data cleaning is the process of identifying and fixing errors, inconsistencies and quality issues in raw data so it is accurate, consistent and ready for analysis, and it typically includes removing duplicates and handling missing values [source 2] - note that the definition keeps the duplicate problem and the missing-value problem in separate boxes, which is precisely the distinction tested in part (c). A second pitfall is scope: 1,850 nulls in 4,200,000 rows (0.0440%) and 62 nulls in a 140,000-row daily partition (0.0443%) are the same defect measured at two scopes, and a rule that does not name its scope cannot be reproduced or argued about. Third, a single defect can violate more than one dimension - a duplicated order that also arrived three hours late breaks uniqueness and timeliness simultaneously - so the profile should record the best-fitting dimension as primary and the rest as secondary. Generalisation: in a medallion architecture (bronze = raw ingested data, silver = cleaned and conformed data, gold = business-level aggregates for consumption), completeness and uniqueness are enforced at the bronze-to-silver boundary where you still have the raw evidence, while accuracy requires an external reference and is therefore checked against a source system of record, a table that is authoritative for a given entity.
Problem 2

Using main.sales.orders (columns: order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, order_total DECIMAL(18,2), created_at TIMESTAMP, loaded_at TIMESTAMP, order_date DATE) and the gateway reference table main.sales.gateway_settlements (order_id STRING, settled_amount DECIMAL(18,2)), write one executable assertion per dimension as Databricks SQL. Every assertion must return a single scalar number, must be deterministic (identical inputs produce an identical number), and must be scoped to today's partition of 140,000 rows. Report the value each query returns, given: 62 NULL customer_ids today (1,850 over 30 days), 14 duplicated order_ids today (312 over 30 days), 47 late rows, and 4,110 accuracy mismatches at a 0.01 currency tolerance. Finally, explain why a query that returns the list of offending rows is a poor scheduled assertion.
Hint: Each rule should reduce to one number that you compare with one threshold; keep the row list as a debugging tool, not as the rule.

Worked solution
Write every assertion so that it returns one scalar count, then compare that count with a threshold.

Rule 1 - completeness:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS null_customer_id

FROM main.sales.orders

WHERE order_date = current_date() AND customer_id IS NULL;

Result today: 62. The same query without the order_date filter returns 1,850 over the 30-day table.

Rule 2 - uniqueness:

SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS duplicate_rows

FROM main.sales.orders

WHERE order_date = current_date();

Result today: 14. Over 30 days: 312. On a very large table the same scalar comes from a grouped subquery as SUM(cnt - 1) over groups kept by HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, which avoids a full distinct shuffle.

Rule 3 - timeliness:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS late_rows

FROM main.sales.orders

WHERE order_date = current_date() AND loaded_at > created_at + INTERVAL 30 MINUTES;

Result: 47.

Rule 4 - accuracy (reconciliation against the source of record):

SELECT COUNT(*) AS mismatched_rows

FROM main.sales.orders o

LEFT JOIN main.sales.gateway_settlements g ON o.order_id = g.order_id

WHERE o.order_date = current_date()

AND (g.order_id IS NULL OR abs(o.order_total - g.settled_amount) > 0.01);

Result: 4,110.

Comparison with thresholds (from the rule catalogue): 62 against 70 allowed (0.05% of 140,000) is a pass; 14 against a strict 0 is a failure; 47 against 140 allowed (0.10%) is a pass; 4,110 against 700 allowed (0.50%) is a failure.

Why a row list is a poor scheduled assertion: a list of offending rows has no single value to compare with a threshold, so a human must read it and judge it, and the verdict is then neither reproducible nor auditable. Keep the scalar count as the rule; keep the row list as an optional debug query that is executed only after the count has failed.

Databricks note: the same predicates can be promoted to Lakeflow pipeline expectations or Delta Lake constraints so the count is evaluated at write time rather than by a separate scheduled job.

Analysis — Determinism is the property that separates an engineering control from an opinion. The queries above are deterministic because they depend only on stored columns and a fixed partition key; the moment you write WHERE loaded_at > current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR inside the predicate, the rule returns a different number on every re-run of the same data and cannot be reproduced during an incident review. Avoid RANDOM(), avoid unseeded TABLESAMPLE, and avoid aggregating without pinning the window. The uniqueness pattern is also a place where students lose marks: COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) counts excess rows, not distinct duplicated keys, so a key appearing three times contributes 2. If the business asks how many orders are affected rather than how many extra rows exist, use COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) on the grouped HAVING result instead - both are correct, they answer different questions. The accuracy rule is the only one that needs an external dataset, which is why quality assurance checks that verify accuracy are treated as a separate activity from tidying the data set itself [source 1]. Finally, the absolute thresholds (70, 0, 140, 700) are just percentages multiplied by the row count of the evaluated scope, so a rule written as a percentage stays valid when daily volume grows, whereas a rule written as a magic number of rows silently changes meaning.
Problem 3

Today's partition of main.sales.orders holds 140,000 rows. The four assertions from the previous step returned: completeness 62 rows with NULL customer_id, uniqueness 14 duplicated order_ids, timeliness 47 rows later than 30 minutes, accuracy 4,110 rows mismatching the gateway at a 0.01 tolerance. The rule catalogue defines: completeness passes at or below 0.05% of daily rows, warns from 0.05% to 0.20%, and is critical above 0.20%; uniqueness passes only at exactly 0 duplicated order_ids and is critical otherwise; timeliness passes at or below 0.10%, warns from 0.10% to 0.50%, critical above 0.50%; accuracy passes at or below 0.50%, warns from 0.50% to 1.00%, critical above 1.00%. Compute the failure rate for each rule, convert each threshold into an absolute row count, assign the verdict, name the owner and the alert action, and state whether the daily revenue materialized view (a precomputed, stored query result) may be published. Then state what would happen to the on-call engineer if the completeness threshold were set to zero instead.
Hint: Convert every threshold to a row count first; it makes the comparison mechanical and removes unit confusion.

Worked solution
Step 1 - convert each threshold into an absolute row count for a 140,000-row partition.

- completeness: 0.05% of 140,000 = 0.0005 x 140,000 = 70 rows; warn ceiling 0.20% = 280 rows; critical above 280.

- uniqueness: 0 rows, always.

- timeliness: 0.10% = 140 rows; warn ceiling 0.50% = 700 rows; critical above 700.

- accuracy: 0.50% = 700 rows; warn ceiling 1.00% = 1,400 rows; critical above 1,400.

Step 2 - compute the observed rates.

- completeness: 62 / 140,000 = 0.0004428 = 0.0443%. Compare with 0.05% -> PASS, and it is close to the boundary.

- uniqueness: 14 / 140,000 = 0.0001 = 0.01%, but the rule is a strict zero -> FAIL, critical, because a duplicated order_id inflates SUM(order_total) and corrupts the revenue number itself.

- timeliness: 47 / 140,000 = 0.000336 = 0.0336%, below 0.10% -> PASS.

- accuracy: 4,110 / 140,000 = 0.029357 = 2.94%, far above 0.50% and above the 1.00% critical line -> FAIL, critical.

Step 3 - severity, owner, action.

- completeness, pass: owner ingestion platform on-call; no notification is sent. Silent success is a required behaviour, not laziness.

- uniqueness, critical: owner is the order-service team that produces the events; action is to page immediately and block publication of the gold revenue materialized view, because double-counted revenue is worse than no revenue.

- timeliness, pass: owner is the streaming ingestion owner (Auto Loader / Lakeflow pipeline); no notification, but the rate is trended because 0.0336% is one third of the way to the 0.10% ceiling.

- accuracy, critical: owner is the payments integration team; action is to page and hold the publish.

Step 4 - publish decision.

Two of four rules fail, both at critical severity, so the daily revenue materialized view must not be published from today's partition. The partition is quarantined (held out of the gold layer) until uniqueness and accuracy are resolved, or the dashboard is published with an explicit 'partial data' banner.

Step 5 - the zero-threshold counterfactual.

If completeness were set to 'fail on any NULL', the rule would fire 62 times per day, every day, on a defect that the business has already accepted at 0.05%. An on-call engineer who receives dozens of technically-correct pages that require no action learns to ignore the channel, which is alert fatigue: the alerting channel stops transmitting information even though every individual alert is true. A threshold is what turns a measurement into a decision.

Analysis — The threshold is not part of the measurement, it is an encoding of business tolerance, and it has to be derived from the cost of the defect: a duplicated order_id is not tolerable at 0.01% because revenue is a sum, whereas a 0.04% NULL customer_id is tolerable because the dashboard groups revenue by product, not by customer. That asymmetry is why uniqueness gets the strict zero and completeness gets a percentage band. The absolute-row-count conversion is a technique, not a formality: teams that store thresholds as percentages in code and compare them with raw counts ship off-by-100x bugs, and teams that store raw counts must edit the rule every time volume grows. Keeping both - a percentage in the rule catalogue and a computed row count in the alert payload - removes the ambiguity. Two edge cases routinely break this design. First, a rate computed on a partial partition (a day with only 40,000 rows loaded so far) will look artificially good or bad; the rule must only evaluate partitions whose load window has closed, or must scale the threshold to the rows present. Second, near-boundary passes such as 0.0443% against 0.05% are unstable: the correct engineering response is a warn band or a moving average, exactly as the timeliness rule above shows, so that a rule that is about to break announces itself before it breaks. Flawed data leads to skewed results, and cleaning ensures the analysis reflects the true representation of the data [source 6] - a threshold that lets 2.94% of revenue rows pass unremarked would defeat exactly that purpose.
Problem 4

You inherit five candidate rules written by colleagues and must audit them for testability. R1: 'The data looks reasonable this morning.' R2: 'The revenue dashboard number should not drop.' R3: 'There must be no duplicate order_ids.' R4: 'customer_id must be populated.' R5: 'The dashboard must be accurate.' For each rule: classify it as testable or not testable, and if not testable explain the exact defect (missing predicate, missing scope, missing reference value, missing threshold, or dependence on human judgement). Then rewrite each one into an executable rule with a predicate, a scope, a reference, a threshold, a severity and an owner. Finally, give one concrete input that flips each rewritten rule from pass to fail, and check the rewritten rules for determinism.
Hint: A rule is falsifiable when you can name the input that makes it fail; a rule is deterministic when re-running it on the same data always gives the same verdict.

Worked solution
R1 'The data looks reasonable this morning.' Not testable: no predicate (what is measured?), no scope (which table, which partition?), no reference value, no threshold, and the verdict depends on human judgement. Rewrite: 'The NULL rate of customer_id in main.sales.orders for order_date = current_date() must be at or below 0.05% of rows; scope: today's partition; reference: the 0.05% tolerance in the rule catalogue; threshold: 70 rows; severity: warn at 0.05%-0.20%, critical above 0.20%; owner: ingestion platform on-call; action: page the on-call rotation.' Flipping input: 71 NULL rows out of 140,000 = 0.0507%, which crosses 0.05% and fails the rule.

R2 'The revenue dashboard number should not drop.' Not testable: a drop can be legitimate (fewer orders, a promotion ending, a season), so there is no reference that makes a drop wrong. The rule confuses a business trend with a data defect. Rewrite it as a reconciliation rule against the system of record: 'The count of rows in main.gold.revenue_daily must equal the count of orders present in main.sales.gateway_settlements for the same business date; threshold: 0 rows of difference; severity: critical; owner: analytics engineering; action: block the materialized view refresh.' Flipping input: a gold row count of 139,900 against 140,000 gateway orders fails by 100 rows.

R3 'There must be no duplicate order_ids.' Partially testable but under-specified in two ways: no scope, and no definition of duplicate. A retried delivery from a producer can legitimately land the same event twice within the load window and be merged afterwards, so an unscoped rule fires on valid retries. Rewrite: 'COUNT(*) minus COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) = 0 for order_date = current_date(), evaluated 45 minutes after the load window closes; severity: critical; owner: order-service team; action: page and quarantine the partition.' Flipping input: order 88123 landing on two rows makes the scalar 1 and fails the rule.

R4 'customer_id must be populated.' Not testable as written because 'populated' is ambiguous: NULL, empty string, whitespace and the literal placeholder 'UNKNOWN' are four different states with four different meanings. This is the completeness versus accuracy boundary. Rewrite as two rules: a completeness rule, 'COUNT(*) WHERE customer_id IS NULL OR trim(customer_id) = 0 must be 0', and an accuracy or validity rule, 'COUNT(*) WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM main.reference.customers) must be 0', with severity critical and owner the master-data team. Flipping input: 100 rows containing the string 'UNKNOWN' pass the completeness rule and fail the referential rule, which is exactly why one rule cannot cover both.

R5 'The dashboard must be accurate.' Not testable directly: accuracy is defined as agreement with a reference, and here neither the reference nor the comparison is named. Rewrite by decomposition into the four measurable rules already built (completeness, uniqueness, timeliness, accuracy against the gateway), all gated on the same partition, with a publish rule: 'publish the revenue materialized view only if all four upstream rules are at pass severity.' Flipping input: today's accuracy count of 4,110 against a 700-row threshold blocks the publish.

Determinism check: all rewritten rules reduce to a scalar count over a named partition and compare it with a stored threshold, so re-running them on unchanged data returns the same verdict. Any version that used current_timestamp() inside the predicate, RANDOM(), or an unseeded sample would not be deterministic and would be rejected at review.

Analysis — The audit uses one test: can you name the input that makes the rule fail, and would two engineers running it on the same data agree on the outcome? If either answer is no, the rule is documentation, not a control. The five failure modes are distinct and examiners test them separately - missing predicate (R1), missing reference (R2), missing scope or definition (R3), ambiguous predicate (R4), missing decomposition (R5) - so a good answer names the mode rather than saying 'too vague'. The R4 case is the deepest one, because it is the point where completeness stops and accuracy begins: a row full of placeholder values is complete but inaccurate, and no NULL-rate check will ever detect it. Standardising those placeholder values is the same class of work as reconciling spelling variants and name variants across sources [source 5]. On determinism, the trap is subtle: a rule evaluated with current_timestamp() reads a different predicate value on every execution, so an incident review cannot reproduce the alert, and the team cannot tell whether the data changed or the rule did. Freeze the evaluation window as a partition column or a job parameter, and record the parameter value with the alert. One caveat about zero-threshold rules: uniqueness genuinely deserves a strict zero because a single duplicate corrupts a SUM, but applying the same strictness to every dimension produces alert fatigue, and an ignored channel is functionally identical to no monitoring at all.
Problem 5

The accuracy rule from the previous steps compares order_total with settled_amount using a tolerance of 0.01 and flags 4,110 of today's 140,000 rows as mismatched, which is a critical failure at the 0.50% threshold. Investigation shows that 3,970 of those rows are orders with a partial refund, where the gateway record is the original charge and the refunds table main.sales.refunds (order_id, refund_amount) holds the later reduction; the remaining 140 rows are genuine capture errors such as a failed capture or a currency-rounding fault. Tasks: (a) compute the failure rate and verdict of the current rule; (b) rewrite the rule to normalise refunds and compute the new rate and verdict; (c) compute alert precision (true faults divided by all alerts) before and after, and explain the consequence for the on-call engineer; (d) state the tolerance choice, threshold, severity, owner and the condition under which the rule may run.
Hint: Reconcile the business quantity that both sides of the comparison are supposed to represent, not the raw column that happens to be named similarly.

Worked solution
Step 1 - the rule as written.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS mismatched_rows

FROM main.sales.orders o

LEFT JOIN main.sales.gateway_settlements g ON o.order_id = g.order_id

WHERE o.order_date = current_date()

AND (g.order_id IS NULL OR abs(o.order_total - g.settled_amount) > 0.01);

Result: 4,110 rows out of 140,000 = 0.02936 = 2.94%, above the 0.50% pass line and above the 1.00% critical line, so the verdict is FAIL critical and the revenue publish is blocked.

Step 2 - normalise the refund before comparing.

The quantity the gateway settled is the net amount, so the comparable business quantity on the order side is order_total minus any refund already settled.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS mismatched_rows

FROM main.sales.orders o

LEFT JOIN main.sales.gateway_settlements g ON o.order_id = g.order_id

LEFT JOIN main.sales.refunds r ON o.order_id = r.order_id

WHERE o.order_date = current_date()

AND (g.order_id IS NULL

OR abs((o.order_total - coalesce(r.refund_amount, 0)) - g.settled_amount) > 0.01);

Result: 140 rows out of 140,000 = 0.001 = 0.10%, at or below the 0.50% pass line, so the verdict becomes PASS.

Step 3 - alert precision before and after.

Before: 140 genuine faults out of 4,110 alerts, precision = 140 / 4,110 = 0.0341 = 3.41%. The on-call engineer pages 4,110 times a day for a 140-row problem; 96.6% of the pages require no action, which is alert fatigue measured numerically.

After: 140 genuine faults out of 140 alerts, precision = 140 / 140 = 100%, and total alert volume falls by a factor of 4,110 / 140 = 29.4. The same 140 faults still fire, so nothing real was suppressed.

Step 4 - rule metadata.

Tolerance 0.01 in the order currency (one cent, matching the DECIMAL(18,2) rounding of both sides); threshold 0.50% of daily rows = 700 rows for pass, 0.50%-1.00% = 700-1,400 rows warn, above 1.00% = above 1,400 rows critical; severity critical on breach; owner payments integration team; action: page on-call and block the gold revenue materialized view refresh. Precondition: the rule may only run after the settlement and refund windows for the business date have closed, otherwise refunds that arrive later are indistinguishable from capture errors and the rule reports false failures.

Analysis — The method here is business-quantity alignment: the order table stores the gross charge and the gateway stores the net settlement, so comparing the two columns directly compares two different quantities, and every partial refund becomes a false failure. This is the most common real-world source of accuracy-rule false positives, and it generalises to any reconciliation where one side is a snapshot and the other is a running balance. The precision calculation is what makes the argument to stakeholders concrete: the rewritten rule does not weaken the control (all 140 true faults still fire) but it converts 3,970 daily false pages into zero, which is the difference between a channel that is read and a channel that is muted. Note the deliberate tension with the uniqueness rule: there the threshold is a strict zero, here it is a percentage band, because a single mis-captured payment is a rounding-level nuisance while a single duplicated order corrupts an aggregate. Quality assurance checks exist precisely to verify that data is accurate against such references [source 1], and quality control checks upstream may catch most collection errors, but preparation steps are still required afterwards [source 4] - reconciliation against the settlement system is one of those steps, not a duplicate of them. The edge cases to state explicitly are: a currency-conversion row where the gateway amount is in a different currency than the order amount, which needs a conversion join rather than a wider tolerance; a refund that is authorised but not yet settled, which is a timeliness problem masquerading as an accuracy problem; and the temptation to widen the tolerance until the rule passes, which would hide the 140 genuine errors and make the rule unfalsifiable. A useful generalisation is to express this as a slowly changing dimension (a table that keeps the history of how a record changed over time, here the order-to-refund lifecycle) so the comparison always uses the version of the order that was current at settlement time.

actions.text: Now let's put everything together in a fully worked problem. We'll take one vague sentence from the business and translate it into executable, testable quality rules.
Problem 1. The sales team hands you a one-sentence requirement, and your job is to turn it into something a pipeline can actually enforce.

They say: 'our orders table should be complete, current, and free of duplicates so the daily revenue dashboard is trustworthy.' Notice how many adjectives are packed in there — complete, current, free of duplicates. Each one is hiding a separate quality dimension we need to unpack.

Here's a useful hint: ask what question each adjective answers. Complete — is every required column populated? Current — how fresh is the data? Free of duplicates — is there exactly one row per business key? That reframing is what turns vague language into measurable dimensions.

In the worked solution, Step 1 decomposes those adjectives into four dimensions: completeness over customer_id and order_total, uniqueness on order_id, timeliness against the order-creation timestamp, and accuracy against the payment gateway. Step 2 writes each as an executable SQL assertion — for example, a COUNT of rows where customer_id IS NULL, expected to return zero. And Step 3 attaches a threshold, a severity, and an owner to each rule so the test can fail loudly instead of silently.

The analysis here is the key takeaway: the method works precisely because a dimension name tells you what to measure, the assertion tells you what value is acceptable, and the threshold tells you when to raise an alarm. Rules must be falsifiable and deterministic — a rule like 'the data looks reasonable' can never fail, and a rule with no threshold just produces alert fatigue.

scenes.title: Translating Expectations into Rules

questions.question: A data team is asked to translate the business expectation 'the daily revenue dashboard should be trustworthy' into a single rule at the order-header grain (one row per order). Which rule is both testable and dimension-appropriate for the expectation 'ordered quantity per order is internally consistent'?

options.label: Assert that the number of line items in order_lines matches the line_item_count recorded on the order header for each order_id; expected result: 0 mismatched orders.
Assert that COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) on the line-item table equals COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) on the order-header table; expected result: 0 difference.
Assert that the revenue dashboard 'looks reasonable' compared to last week's numbers; expected result: the reviewer agrees.
Assert that the order_lines table has fewer than 5% nulls in the product_id column; expected result: null rate below 0.05.

questions.analysis: Option A produces a deterministic numeric assertion (the count of mismatched orders must be 0) and it operates at the correct grain — it compares a per-order aggregate (line_item_count on the header) to the count of child rows, which is a classic cross-grain consistency check. Option B is the exam trap: comparing COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) across two tables only confirms that the same set of orders appears in both places, it does not verify an expected cardinality or any threshold, and it tests the wrong granularity for an internal-consistency expectation. Option C is a subjective human judgement, not an executable assertion, so it can never fail deterministically. Option D tests completeness (presence), not the internal consistency of quantities; a product_id null rate tells you nothing about whether line_item_count matches reality. As covered earlier in this unit, a rule must yield a deterministic boolean or numeric result to be testable, and the dimension must match the expectation being validated [source 1].

questions.question: Select ALL statements that correctly describe why a proposed rule is defective for a quality-assurance check. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A rule states 'order_total should be accurate' but no reference source (payment gateway or source-system extract) is identified; expected result: unspecified.
A rule checks COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) on a line-item grain table to detect duplicate orders; expected result: 0 difference.
A rule asserts COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL equals 0; expected result: 0.
A rule states 'data should be clean'; expected result: the data engineer confirms it looks fine.

questions.analysis: Option A is defective because accuracy checks require a reference source: without a system of record or trusted reference table, agreement with reality cannot be validated [source 1]. Option B is the exam trap described in the test points — checking COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) on a line-item grain table does not verify uniqueness of orders; the correct check must be at the order-header grain (COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) on the orders table). Option D is defective because it has no threshold, no measurable assertion, and no failure semantics; it relies on subjective judgement and therefore cannot produce a deterministic boolean or numeric outcome [source 1]. Option C is a valid rule: it is executable, has a clear threshold (0), and is dimension-appropriate for completeness (presence of customer_id). Note that as taught earlier, a row full of placeholder values can pass a completeness check while still being inaccurate — this distinction is why Option A's missing reference source is a genuine defect [source 5].

questions.question: A stakeholder states: 'The customer master table should be clean and reliable so marketing can trust segment counts.' Translate this expectation into at least two testable rules. For each rule, specify (a) the dimension, (b) the executable assertion with an expected result, and (c) the reference source if the rule is an accuracy check. Explain why any rule without a threshold or failure semantics would be rejected.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Rule 1 is dimension-appropriate with a deterministic assertion and explicit expected result — 30%. (2) Rule 2 is dimension-appropriate with a deterministic assertion and explicit expected result — 30%. (3) Accuracy rules cite a concrete reference source (e.g., CRM extract, source-system reconciliation) — 20%. (4) Explanation rejects rules lacking thresholds or failure semantics as untestable/subjective — 20%. Deduct for rules that mix dimensions incorrectly (e.g., claiming a uniqueness rule tests accuracy) or that check the wrong grain.
questions.analysis: A strong answer decomposes 'clean and reliable' into named dimensions and writes executable assertions. Example: (1) Completeness — SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customer_master WHERE customer_id IS NULL OR email IS NULL; expected result 0. (2) Uniqueness — SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM customer_master; expected result 0. (3) Accuracy — reconcile customer_name and address against the CRM extract of record; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customer_master c FULL OUTER JOIN crm_extract r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id WHERE c.customer_name <> r.customer_name OR c.address <> r.address; expected result 0. The accuracy rule explicitly names the reference source because, as established earlier, accuracy proves agreement with reality and requires a trusted reference [source 1]. A rule such as 'the table should be clean' with no threshold and no failure semantics relies on subjective judgement and cannot produce a deterministic boolean or numeric result, so it cannot be validated, scheduled, or alerted on; such rules must be rewritten before deployment [source 1]. Note also that completeness proves presence, not correctness — placeholder emails would pass Rule 1 but fail accuracy reconciliation, which is exactly why the reference-based rule is required [source 5].

actions.text: Time to put that into practice. This quick quiz checks whether you can translate a business expectation into a rule that is genuinely testable and dimension-appropriate. Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer — I'll join you right after you submit to walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Reading a Quality Metrics Report

elements.content:
Daily data quality metrics for the orders dataset (Mon to Sun) (line)
Day of week (Mon=1 ... Sun=7) → Percentage (%) / Lag (min)
customer_id_null_pct and duplicate_order_pct are percentages of total_rows; max_ingestion_lag_minutes is a count of minutes. Tolerances: null rate target <= 1.0%, duplicate target <= 0.1%, ingestion lag SLO <= 30 minutes. Table below shows total_rows per day.
customer_id_null_pct: 1→2.1   2→1.6   3→1.4   4→1.9   5→1.2   6→0.9   7→0.7
duplicate_order_pct: 1→0.05   2→0.06   3→0.04   4→0.12   5→0.08   6→0.07   7→0.03
max_ingestion_lag_minutes: 1→22   2→25   3→28   4→35   5→27   6→24   7→20

Claim 1 — Refuted
Completeness, as measured by the customer_id null rate, improved steadily every single day of the week.
Why: The null rate falls from 2.1% on Mon to 1.4% on Wed, but then regresses upward to 1.9% on Day 4 (Thu) before resuming its decline. Because Wednesday and Thursday both break monotonicity, the claim of steady daily improvement is false. Note the precondition: null rate is a completeness proxy only for the customer_id column, not for the whole row. [source 1] frames these checks as quality assurance checks necessary to verify data accuracy; here the check detects a presence defect, not a correctness defect.

Claim 2 — Refuted
Uniqueness is within tolerance for the entire week because the duplicate-order percentage stays within the 0.1% threshold on all days.
Why: The threshold is 0.1%. Thursday (Day 4) records 0.12% duplicates, which exceeds 0.1% by 0.02 percentage points. The other six days are within tolerance (Mon 0.05%, Tue 0.06%, Wed 0.04%, Fri 0.08%, Sat 0.07%, Sun 0.03%), but 'entire week' is contradicted by Day 4. In terms of raw rows, Thursday's total_rows was 500,000, so 0.12% equals 0.0012 * 500,000 = 600 duplicate-flagged rows. Recognizing this as a uniqueness violation rather than a completeness violation is exactly the exam trap introduced earlier in this unit. [source 2] lists removing duplicates as a core part of data cleaning.

Claim 3 — Refuted
Timeliness never breached its 30-minute service-level objective (SLO) during the measured week.
Why: Max ingestion lag equals 35 minutes on Thursday (Day 4), which exceeds the 30-minute SLO by 5 minutes. All other days are under 30 minutes (Mon 22, Tue 25, Wed 28, Fri 27, Sat 24, Sun 20). Because at least one day breaches the SLO, the universal claim 'never breached' is false. Note the metric is max lag, not average lag; a single late partition is sufficient to fail the SLO.

Claim 4 — Refuted
Every dimension passed at least one day, so the dataset is fully trustworthy for the week.
Why: Each dimension passes on some days, but the claim's conclusion does not follow. Completeness (null rate <= 1.0%) only passes on Sat (0.9%) and Sun (0.7%); the other five days are above 1.0%. Uniqueness (<= 0.1%) fails on Thu only. Timeliness (<= 30 min) fails on Thu only. Therefore not every day passes every dimension, and the week as a whole contains failures. The logical error is aggregation: per-day passes cannot be summed into a week-level 'fully trustworthy' verdict when any dimension fails on any day. [source 6] warns that flawed data leads to skewed results.

Claim 5 — Supported
Thursday is the only day on which two or more dimensions failed simultaneously.
Why: Define a dimension failure as: null rate > 1.0%, duplicate rate > 0.1%, or lag > 30 min. On Thursday: null rate 1.9% (fail), duplicate rate 0.12% (fail), lag 35 min (fail) — three failures. Mon: null 2.1% (fail); duplicates 0.05% (pass); lag 22 (pass) — one failure. Tue: null 1.6% (fail) only. Wed: null 1.4% (fail) only. Fri: null 1.2% (fail) only. Sat: null 0.9% (pass), dup 0.07% (pass), lag 24 (pass) — zero failures. Sun: null 0.7%, dup 0.03%, lag 20 — zero failures. So Thursday is indeed the unique day with two or more simultaneous failures.

Claim 6 — Insufficient
The 0.02 percentage-point excess on Thursday is negligible and can be ignored.
Why: The data alone cannot decide whether 0.02 pp is negligible, because no business risk tolerance or financial impact statement is given in the metrics report. In raw rows, 0.02% of Thursday's 500,000 rows equals 0.0002 * 500,000 = 100 rows, which is non-zero but small. Judging materiality requires an external threshold (for example, 'no more than 50 duplicates per day' or 'any duplicates trigger downstream double-counting in revenue'). This is the classic case where the rule exists but the failure semantics or severity threshold is missing — exactly the defective-rule pattern flagged earlier in this unit. [source 5] notes that missing data patterns should be taken into consideration when conducting an analysis, which by analogy also applies to missing tolerance thresholds.

Claim 7 — Supported
The data quality rule set should validate customer_id null rate, duplicate_order_pct, and max_ingestion_lag_minutes as separate assertions, each with its own threshold and failure semantics.
Why: The week's evidence shows each dimension moves independently: null rate is high early and improves late; duplicate rate spikes only on Thursday; lag breaches only on Thursday. A per-dimension assertion is the only way to localize failures. Worked derivation of a completeness assertion: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL; expected result = 0 rows. Given Mon's total_rows = 400,000 and null rate = 2.1%, the null count on Monday is 0.021 * 400,000 = 8,400 rows, which is non-zero and therefore fails the assertion. This aligns with [source 1]'s emphasis on quality assurance checks to verify data accuracy and with [source 4]'s point that field-level quality control should catch most errors before analysis, though not all.

Claim 8 — Refuted
Because the duplicate rate and the lag both pass on Sunday, the dataset is complete on Sunday.
Why: Sunday passes uniqueness (0.03% <= 0.1%) and timeliness (20 min <= 30 min), but completeness on Sunday has a null rate of 0.7%, which is below the 1.0% target — so in this dataset Sunday's completeness also passes. However, the claim's reasoning is invalid: passing uniqueness and timeliness does not by itself establish completeness, because completeness is measured by the customer_id null rate, a separate column. The correct reading is that Sunday passes all three dimensions, not that one dimension implies another. [source 2] treats duplicate removal and missing-value handling as distinct cleaning tasks, reinforcing that dimensions are independent.

Claim 9 — Supported
If the Wednesday null rate of 1.4% were compared against a stricter 1.0% threshold, the completeness assertion would fail on Wednesday.
Why: 1.4% > 1.0%, so with the stricter threshold Wednesday fails completeness. With the original target of 1.0% it also fails (1.4 > 1.0). The distinction matters only for analyzing the shape of improvement: under the 1.0% target, completeness passes only on Sat (0.9%) and Sun (0.7%), and under a 1.5% target it would additionally pass on Wed. The worked comparison is: 1.4% vs 1.0% gives 0.4 pp over target; 1.4% vs 1.5% gives 0.1 pp under target. Threshold choice is therefore a first-class part of the rule definition, not a detail. [source 1] and [source 4] both stress that checks are only meaningful when their acceptance criteria are explicit.

actions.text: Now let's put everything from the previous pages to work. This is the orders dataset quality metrics report — a week of daily numbers. Read it the way an engineer would: column by column, not claim by claim.

Start with the completeness column — customer_id_null_pct. Day one is 1 percent, then it climbs, peaks mid-week, and comes back down. Remember what we just covered: a claim about 'steadily improving' has to match this curve exactly, including any regression.

Next, uniqueness — duplicate_order_pct. Compare every value here against the stated 0.1 percent tolerance threshold. This is a per-dimension check: the duplicates can be well within tolerance even when the null rate is misbehaving.
And timeliness — max_ingestion_lag_minutes. The SLO is 30 minutes. Scan the whole column and ask whether any single day breached it. One breach is enough to refute a claim that says 'never breached'.

Here's Claim 1: 'Completeness improved steadily all week.' Check it against the null-rate trend, and notice that the trend is not monotonic — there is one mid-week regression. That single bump is enough to put the claim in the Refuted column.

Claim 2 says 'Uniqueness is within tolerance.' This one is straightforward — the duplicate rates sit comfortably under the 0.1 percent threshold, so the verdict is Supported. Always read the metric against its own stated threshold before judging.

Claim 3: 'Timeliness never breached its 30-minute SLO.' The max lag column pushes past 30 on at least one day, so this claim is Refuted. One number in one cell can overturn an entire statement — that's the exam trap here.

Claim 4: 'Every dimension passed at least one quality rule.' Look carefully at the rule-passes column — if any dimension never passed a rule across the whole week, the claim is Refuted. This forces you to read the table per-dimension, not just per-day.

Claim 5 is a different flavor: 'Thursday is the only day on which…' — a day-level assertion, not a dimension-level one. Supported here, but only after you've cross-referenced Thursday's row against every column in the table.

Claim 6 is the interesting one — 0.02 percentage points. That number is too small and too noisy to support a firm conclusion, so the verdict is Insufficient, not Refuted. Know the difference: 'the data says no' versus 'the data can't say'.

Claims 7 and beyond round out the exercise. Claim 7 — the rule set should be tightened — is Supported. Claims 8 and 9 chain two metrics together, so you must reason about them jointly rather than one at a time. The key takeaway: a metric can pass its own threshold while the dataset still violates a related dimension.

actions.topic: When a metric passes its own threshold but the dataset still violates a related dimension, which claim verdict should you record — Supported, Refuted, or Insufficient?
actions.prompt: Pick one claim from the report and argue it both ways. What evidence from the table would flip your verdict? Where is the line between 'data refutes' and 'data is insufficient'?

scenes.title: Hands-On: Implementing Quality Checks in Databricks SQL

content.html:
🧪 Quality Checks in Databricks SQL

Write and run dimension-specific quality queries (completeness, uniqueness, timeliness) against a sample orders table. Watch thresholds flip assertions from PASS to FAIL.
Initializing SQL engine…
▸ Output
Ready
✅ Test cases ▼

Hint 1: For completeness, compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(customer_id). The null rate is (COUNT(*) - COUNT(customer_id)) / COUNT(*).

You can also use this pattern for any column to detect missing values.

Hint 2: Uniqueness check: compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(DISTINCT order_id). If they differ, return the duplicate order_id values.

Hint 3: Timeliness: use MAX(order_timestamp) or MAX(_ingest_timestamp) and compare to a freshness threshold (e.g., CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() - INTERVAL 1 DAY).

📘 Reference solution (one possible approach): 
-- Completeness: null rate for customer_id
SELECT 'completeness' AS check_name,
       (COUNT(*) - COUNT(customer_id)) / COUNT(*) AS null_rate,
       CASE WHEN (COUNT(*) - COUNT(customer_id)) / COUNT(*) > 0.05 THEN 'FAIL' ELSE 'PASS' END AS status
FROM orders;

-- Uniqueness: duplicate order_id
SELECT 'uniqueness' AS check_name,
       order_id,
       COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- Timeliness: freshness
SELECT 'timeliness' AS check_name,
       MAX(order_timestamp) AS latest_order,
       CASE WHEN MAX(order_timestamp) > CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() - INTERVAL 1 DAY THEN 'PASS' ELSE 'FAIL' END AS status
FROM orders;

actions.text: We've talked about data quality dimensions in the abstract — completeness, uniqueness, timeliness. Now let's make them concrete. In this sandbox you'll write real Databricks SQL queries that assert those rules against a sample orders table, and you'll watch each check flip from PASS to FAIL as the data changes.

actions.content: This is your query editor. Write one quality check here at a time.

actions.text: Start with completeness. A simple rule: the null rate on customer_id. Compare COUNT star against COUNT of customer_id — the difference over the total gives you the fraction of missing keys. That ratio is your testable assertion.

state.code: SELECT (COUNT(*) - COUNT(customer_id)) * 1.0 / COUNT(*) AS null_rate FROM orders;

actions.content: Run a completeness check for null customer_id keys.
The result panel shows the computed metric — that value is what your threshold compares against.

actions.text: Now uniqueness. Count rows versus COUNT DISTINCT order_id. If those diverge, duplicates have crept in. Notice that both checks follow the same shape: compute a metric, compare to a threshold, decide pass or fail.

state.code: SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS duplicate_rows FROM orders;

actions.content: Run a uniqueness check and surface the duplicate count.

actions.text: Finally, timeliness. Take MAX of the order timestamp or the ingest timestamp and compare it against your freshness threshold. Toggle the threshold on the toolbar, or inject a few nulls and duplicate rows, and re-run — you'll see the same assertion flip. That flip is the whole point: a quality check is just a metric plus a threshold plus a decision.

scenes.title: Check Implementation Checkpoint

questions.question: A Databricks SQL quality rule for the silver orders table states: 'No order row may have a missing customer_id.' You want to express this as an executable assertion. Which expression correctly counts only the offending rows — the rows that actually violate the completeness rule?

options.label: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL;
SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(customer_id) FROM orders;
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;

questions.analysis: The rule is a row-level predicate: a row is a defect when customer_id IS NULL. Option A counts exactly those rows with a WHERE clause, returning 0 when the rule passes. Option B is tempting but denormalizes the intent and, more importantly, invites confusion because COUNT(customer_id) silently ignores NULLs — the very masking behavior the exam traps test. Option C measures distinct non-null customers, which is a uniqueness/cardinality metric, not a completeness count. Option D returns total table rows, which tells you nothing about missing values. Note that COUNT(*) in option D or A would include NULL rows — in option A that is the desired behavior because the WHERE clause already isolates the defective rows. For completeness checks, always combine an explicit NULL predicate with a count so the result has deterministic failure semantics: 0 rows = pass, >0 = fail.

questions.question: A nightly Lakeflow job produces a quality metrics report. The report shows customer_id_null_pct = 3.4% for the orders table, and the data contract states the completeness threshold for customer_id is <= 1.0%. Which statements about this result are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The completeness check fails because 3.4% exceeds the 1.0% threshold, so the batch should be quarantined or held back from the gold layer.
A query written as COUNT(*) - COUNT(customer_id) would silently return 0 for this defect if customer_id contains NULLs, because COUNT(customer_id) ignores NULLs.
Because the null rate is under 5%, the batch may safely proceed to the revenue dashboard without remediation.
The rule 'reject rows where customer_id IS NULL before writing to silver' would prevent the defect from reaching the table in the first place.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: the reported null rate 3.4% > 1.0% threshold, so the rule fails and the batch violates the contract, matching the earlier lesson that rule outputs must have deterministic failure semantics. Option B is correct and is a classic exam trap — COUNT(col) skips NULLs, so a naive `COUNT(*) - COUNT(customer_id)` expression is only correct when the intent is genuinely row-level completeness; when misused it masks the defect by returning 0. Option C is wrong because the stated threshold, not an arbitrary 5%, governs acceptance; accepting an out-of-tolerance batch is exactly the failure mode the checkpoint is designed to catch. Option D is correct: filters applied in the ingestion path prevent (rather than detect) the defect, which is the preventive-vs-detective distinction being tested. Given the source note that data cleaning should ensure 'accurate, consistent, and ready for analysis' results [source 2], quarantining the batch aligns with controlling the defect rather than merely reporting it.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a completeness rule that DETECTS a defect and a completeness rule that PREVENTS one, using a concrete SQL example for each on an orders table with a NOT NULL customer_id requirement. Include in your answer: (a) the exact SQL you would write for each, (b) what a result of 0 means for each, and (c) why writing COUNT(customer_id) inside a check can silently mask a completeness defect.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Correct distinction between detection (measure/assert defect) and prevention (block/filter defect) — 30%. (2) Concrete SQL for detection, e.g. 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL' with expected 0 — 20%. (3) Concrete SQL for prevention, e.g. a filtered write 'INSERT INTO silver.orders SELECT * FROM bronze.orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL' or a constraint/expectation that rejects or quarantines null rows — 20%. (4) Explanation that COUNT(customer_id) ignores NULLs, so a row lacking customer_id is excluded from the count and the violation is hidden — 20%. (5) Clarity and correct Databricks terminology (silver/bronze/gold, Lakeflow, expectations) — 10%.
questions.analysis: A strong answer separates the two roles. A DETECTIVE rule is a query that measures or asserts; for example: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL; expected result is 0 when the batch is complete. A PREVENTIVE rule stops the bad row from entering the table: for example, INSERT INTO silver.orders SELECT * FROM bronze.orders WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL, or a Lakeflow expectation that DROPS null-customer_id rows (or quarantines them) before the write. In both cases the number 0 is meaningful — for detection it means the assertion passed; for prevention it means no rows were filtered/dropped. The masking hazard is that COUNT(customer_id) excludes NULLs by definition, so a row where the required value is missing is not counted at all; an expression like COUNT(*) - COUNT(customer_id) or a bare COUNT(customer_id) comparison against a row count will therefore under-report or falsely report zero defects. This connects to the earlier lesson that cleaning must make data accurate and consistent [source 2], and to the caution that patterns of missing data must be surfaced rather than hidden [source 5]. Always pair a completeness metric with an explicit IS NULL predicate on the required column so the failure mode is unambiguous.

actions.text: Let's see how well the check implementation ideas landed. Take your time and work through each question on your own — try to commit to an answer before you look ahead.
Give it your best shot without backtracking to the slides. Once you submit, I'll walk you through anything that tripped you up, especially the traps around how these checks behave in practice.

scenes.title: Where Should Quality Checks Live?

elements.content: Decision — A retail analytics platform ingests order events into a bronze layer, refines them into a silver table joined with customer and product dimensions, and publishes a gold aggregate for an executive revenue dashboard. The question is where in the medallion architecture (bronze = raw ingested data, silver = cleansed and conformed data, gold = business-level aggregates) each quality check should physically execute. The decision is hard because each placement is a different bet on when a defect is caught, how much data must be repaired after the fact, and how much engineering capacity a small platform team must spend maintaining the checks. Enforcing everything at ingestion maximizes early detection but risks quarantining raw data and hiding upstream fixes; enforcing everything at serving directly protects executives but means defects have already persisted through two layers and remediation becomes an expensive backfill. Because the three options score differently on detection latency, remediation cost, and team effort, the team cannot simply pick the 'safest' layer.

Constraints — 30-minute freshness SLO (service-level objective, a measurable target) for the executive dashboard — no quality gate may push end-to-end latency past this window.  •  1% maximum null tolerance on customer_id, measured on the published gold contract; exceeding it must block publication rather than silently degrade the dashboard.  •  A small platform team that cannot maintain three fully independent rule suites, so every check must have a named owner and a single authoritative layer.  •  Defects must be detected deterministically and expressed as boolean or numeric assertions with explicit thresholds, not subjective reviews.  •  Raw data must remain replayable, so no ingestion-layer gate may permanently discard source records.

Enforce quality at ingestion (bronze)
+ Detection is earliest possible and remediation is cheapest because bad records never propagate downstream, which aligns with the principle that quality control checks should catch most errors before they reach analysis [source 4].; + Completeness, uniqueness, and schema checks are cheap and deterministic, matching the rule-design guidance that every rule should produce a numeric assertion with a declared threshold rather than a subjective judgement.; + Because raw records are quarantined rather than deleted, the ingested data stays replayable and an upstream producer can still fix the root cause.
− A hard ingestion gate sits directly in the critical path, so a slow or failing check directly threatens the 30-minute freshness SLO for the executive dashboard.; − Blocking raw data can mask upstream fixes: when the source system is corrected, the quarantined batch must be reprocessed and reconciled separately.; − Business-rule accuracy checks cannot run here because joins with customer and product dimensions do not yet exist at bronze grain.
Best for: Teams that can tolerate pauses in ingestion in exchange for never letting a defect enter the lakehouse.

Enforce quality during transformation (silver)
+ Checks execute exactly where business rules and joins already exist, so accuracy checks against a source-of-record reference can be expressed naturally as part of the same transformation.; + It keeps ingestion unblocked, which preserves the 30-minute freshness budget for the executive dashboard.; + Quality logic is centralized in one place, reducing the surface area that a small platform team must maintain.
− Defects have already persisted into bronze, so the 'cheap remediation' advantage of early detection is partially lost [source 2].; − Some defects are silent at the silver row grain — for example, a duplicate order line may survive a join and only become visible in the gold aggregate.; − Reconciliation against the source of record requires an extra trusted reference table, which the small team may not yet maintain.
Best for: Teams whose transformations already encode rich business semantics and whose ingestion path cannot afford added latency.

Enforce quality at serving (gold)
+ Checks run directly against the published contract, so the executive dashboard is protected by construction and can never consume a violation unknowingly.; + The published contract is the smallest and most business-readable surface, which makes assertions like the 1% customer_id null tolerance easy to express and audit.; + It provides a final safety net independent of any upstream change, which is valuable when upstream producers are external.
− Detection is latest possible, so by the time a violation fires the defect has already crossed bronze and silver and must be repaired by an expensive backfill.; − Blocking publication at gold is exactly the layer the 30-minute freshness SLO depends on, so a late check directly threatens the executive dashboard availability.; − It cannot distinguish an upstream source defect from a transformation bug, which makes root-cause analysis slower for the small platform team.
Best for: Publishing externally facing data products where a contract violation must never reach a consumer, regardless of cost.

Layered hybrid: critical checks at bronze, business rules at silver, contract assertion at gold
+ It matches the layered recommendation by placing critical, cheap, deterministic checks (completeness, uniqueness, schema) at ingestion, business-rule accuracy checks in silver, and a final serving-layer assertion on the published contract.; + Only the bronze checks sit in the ingestion path, and because they are cheap set comparisons they add negligible latency, protecting the 30-minute SLO.; + Each rule has exactly one authoritative owner and layer, which is the only realistic way for a small platform team to maintain coverage without triple-maintaining rules.
− It requires a rule-placement policy (which dimension belongs to which layer) and a documented interface for the published contract.; − The same logical rule appears at more than one layer by design, which risks drift if the layers are not versioned together.; − The silver accuracy check still depends on a trusted reference table that the team must build and maintain.
Best for: Teams operating a medallion architecture with a hard freshness SLO and limited headcount, where neither pure early nor pure late enforcement is affordable.

Recommendation: Layered hybrid: critical checks at bronze, business rules at silver, contract assertion at gold — The binding constraints are the 30-minute freshness SLO, the 1% null tolerance on customer_id at the published contract, and a small platform team that cannot afford to maintain three independent rule suites. A pure ingestion gate defeats the freshness SLO because it sits in the critical path, and a pure serving check makes remediation prohibitively expensive because the defect must be backfilled across two prior layers. The hybrid resolves both simultaneously: the cheap, deterministic bronze checks (completeness, uniqueness, schema) catch most defects early and add negligible latency, which honors the principle that quality control should catch most errors before analysis consumes them [source 4]; the silver layer owns accuracy because that is where business rules and joins already exist [source 2]; and a single final assertion on the published gold contract enforces the 1% customer_id null tolerance so the executive dashboard is protected by construction. Because each rule has exactly one authoritative layer, the small team maintains coverage rather than duplicating it, and the raw layer remains replayable so quarantined records can be reprocessed once the upstream source is fixed [source 1].

actions.text: In the last checkpoint you learned how to translate business expectations into testable rules. Now comes the architectural question every data engineer eventually faces: where should those quality checks actually live? This is a constrained design decision, and the Databricks exam loves to test whether you can reason about the tradeoffs rather than memorize a single answer.

Before we compare options, let's anchor on the constraints — because in a real design decision, the constraints do most of the arguing for you. We have three: a 30-minute freshness SLO for the executive dashboard, a 1% null tolerance on customer_id, and a small platform team. That word 'small' matters enormously. Any solution that requires heavy operational overhead is effectively off the table, no matter how elegant it looks on paper.

Option A is enforcement at ingestion — the bronze layer. The upside is obvious: you catch defects the earliest, and remediation is cheapest because the bad data never propagated downstream. This is the completeness, uniqueness, and schema territory — deterministic checks that cost almost nothing to run. But there's a real downside: you either block the ingestion or quarantine raw records, and doing that aggressively can mask upstream problems by silently absorbing them. Bronze should stay faithful to the source; over-filtering there hides the fact that a producer is broken.

Option B moves checks into the silver transformation layer. The advantage here is that business rules and joins already exist at that point, so accuracy checks have real context — you can validate a computed margin, not just a nullable column. The catch is that by the time data reaches silver, defects have already persisted into bronze, so you're catching issues one hop later, and your freshness budget is already partly spent.

Option C places checks at the serving layer, the gold tables. This protects consumers directly and lets you assert on the published contract — the columns and guarantees your dashboard actually depends on. But detection is late, and remediation means expensive backfills. If a bad batch has already reached the executive dashboard for even ten minutes, you've burned the SLO and your credibility along with it.

So here's the recommendation, and notice it's a layered hybrid rather than a single choice. Put critical, cheap, deterministic checks — completeness, uniqueness, schema — at bronze, where they're fastest and cheapest. Move business-rule accuracy checks into the silver transformation, where the logic genuinely exists. And keep a final assertion at the serving layer on the published contract. Each layer does what it's uniquely good at, and the small team only maintains checks once, in the place they belong.

A quick exam-orientation tip: when a question gives you a freshness SLO plus a small team plus a null tolerance, and asks where a specific check belongs, the deciding factor is almost always whether the check is deterministic and cheap, or whether it needs business context. Deterministic goes early; context-dependent goes later. That single rule resolves most of these scenarios. Let's now work through computing and thresholding those quality metrics on the next page.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Computing and Thresholding Quality Metrics

elements.content: Problem 1

A nightly batch loads the Delta table sales.orders, which is declared at order grain (exactly one row per order_id). Profiling after the load returns three raw counts: total rows = 5,000,000; rows with customer_id IS NULL = 175,000; distinct order_id values = 4,992,500; MAX(_ingest_timestamp) = 2024-06-14 09:59:00Z and MAX(order_timestamp) = 2024-06-14 09:12:00Z. The data contract states: customer_id null rate must be <= 1.0%, duplicate row rate must be <= 0.10%, and freshness lag must be <= 30 minutes. Compute the three metrics, give the pass/fail verdict for each dimension, and state the overall batch verdict.

Hint: Compute each rate as a ratio over total rows, then compare against the tolerance in the same unit — and convert the tolerance into a row budget so you can see how far over the line the batch is.

Worked solution
Step 0 — fix the grain and the denominator before computing anything. sales.orders is declared at order grain, so the denominator for every rate is the total row count, 5,000,000. Rates and thresholds must be stated on the same base, otherwise the pass/fail decision is not reproducible.

Step 1 — completeness (are required values present?). The metric is the null rate of a required column:

$$\text{null rate} = \frac{\text{rows with customer\_id IS NULL}}{\text{total rows}} = \frac{175{,}000}{5{,}000{,}000} = 0.035 = 3.5\%$$

The same number in Databricks SQL: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(customer_id) FROM sales.orders gives COUNT(*) = 5,000,000 and COUNT(customer_id) = 5,000,000 - 175,000 = 4,825,000 (COUNT(col) skips NULLs), so 1 - 4,825,000/5,000,000 = 0.035. Comparison: 3.5% > 1.0% tolerance, so the completeness check FAILS. Convert the tolerance into a row budget to size the breach: 0.010 x 5,000,000 = 50,000 allowed nulls; observed 175,000, which is 175,000 - 50,000 = 125,000 rows over budget, i.e. 3.5x the allowance.

Step 2 — uniqueness (is each business key represented once?).

$$\text{duplicate rows} = \text{total rows} - \text{distinct keys} = 5{,}000{,}000 - 4{,}992{,}500 = 7{,}500$$

$$\text{duplicate rate} = \frac{7{,}500}{5{,}000{,}000} = 0.0015 = 0.15\%$$

Comparison: 0.15% > 0.10% tolerance, so the uniqueness check FAILS. Row budget: 0.0010 x 5,000,000 = 5,000 permitted duplicate rows; observed 7,500, i.e. 2,500 rows over budget and 1.5x the allowance. In Databricks SQL the same check is SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM sales.orders, and the offending keys come from GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.

Step 3 — timeliness (freshness). The freshness lag is the gap between the newest event in the source and the newest row actually ingested:

$$\text{lag} = \text{MAX}(\_ingest\_timestamp) - \text{MAX}(order\_timestamp) = 09{:}59 - 09{:}12 = 47 \text{ minutes}$$

Comparison: 47 minutes > 30-minute SLO, so the timeliness check FAILS. Note the shape of this expression: it is MAX minus MAX, not the average of per-row latencies.

Step 4 — overall verdict. Completeness FAIL (3.5% vs 1.0%), uniqueness FAIL (0.15% vs 0.10%), timeliness FAIL (47 min vs 30 min). All three dimensions are breached in the same batch, and even under the most lenient reading of the contract at least two dimensions (completeness and uniqueness) are unambiguously out of tolerance, so the batch is NOT promotable to the gold layer. The publish job should stop and route the batch to quarantine: duplicates must be resolved (removing duplicates is an explicit part of data cleaning [source 2]) and the customer_id gap characterised and reported rather than silently averaged over [source 5].

Analysis — Method choice: quality metrics are ratios plus a threshold, and the ratio's denominator is dictated by the table's grain. Because sales.orders is one row per order_id, total rows is the only defensible denominator for both the null rate and the duplicate rate, and expressing the threshold as a row budget (0.010 x 5,000,000 = 50,000; 0.0010 x 5,000,000 = 5,000) makes the breach magnitude auditable instead of just a yes/no. Converting thresholds into row budgets is the step students most often skip, and it is the step that tells you whether a failure is a rounding wobble or a systemic defect. Edge cases to watch: (1) COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) ignores NULLs, so if any order_id were itself NULL those rows would be counted as "duplicates" by the subtraction although they are really a completeness defect — pair the uniqueness check with a NOT NULL check on the key. (2) The freshness lag is a MAX-minus-MAX statistic and is therefore set by a single straggler event; it answers "is anything late?" not "is the batch typically late?". (3) 3.5% missing customer_id may be tolerable for a marketing attribution use case but not for financial reporting, so the threshold is a business statement, not a technical constant. Common mistakes: reporting the null rate against non-null rows (3.627% instead of 3.5%), mixing absolute counts with percentage tolerances, and treating "the job succeeded" as "the data is good". Generalisation: the same three-step template — define grain and denominator, compute the ratio, compare to a pre-declared threshold with explicit failure semantics — applies unchanged to every dimension you will be asked to implement. Finally, the three breaches are not independent: duplicated order rows inflate any downstream SUM, which is exactly why flawed data produces skewed results and misleading conclusions if it is analysed before cleaning [source 6].
Problem 2

A teammate runs the uniqueness check from the previous exercise against sales.order_lines, a line-item table with 12,480,000 rows and 1,860,000 distinct order_id values, and reports a "duplicate rate of 85.1%" — a five-alarm failure against the same 0.10% tolerance. The declared grain of sales.order_lines is one row per (order_id, line_number). Profiling the composite key shows 12,479,000 distinct (order_id, line_number) pairs. Compute the naive metric, compute the metric at the correct grain, and state which verdict is correct and why.
Hint: Uniqueness is only ever defined relative to a declared key; ask what one row is supposed to represent before you count duplicates.

Worked solution
Step 1 — reproduce the naive metric. The teammate applied the order-grain rule to a line-item table:

$$\frac{12{,}480{,}000 - 1{,}860{,}000}{12{,}480{,}000} = \frac{10{,}620{,}000}{12{,}480{,}000} = 0.85096 = 85.10\%$$

That is arithmetically correct and analytically meaningless, because it measures lines per order, not duplication. Confirm with the ratio the teammate actually computed: 12,480,000 / 1,860,000 = 6.71 lines per order, which is a perfectly ordinary basket size.

Step 2 — deduplicate the key definition, not the data. The grain of sales.order_lines says one row per (order_id, line_number), so the uniqueness key is the pair, not order_id alone. Count distinct composite keys: 12,479,000.

Step 3 — recompute at the correct grain.

$$\text{duplicate rows} = 12{,}480{,}000 - 12{,}479{,}000 = 1{,}000$$

$$\text{duplicate rate} = \frac{1{,}000}{12{,}480{,}000} = 0.0000801 = 0.00801\% \approx 0.008\%$$

Comparison: 0.008% <= 0.10% tolerance, so the uniqueness check PASSES. Row budget: 0.0010 x 12,480,000 = 12,480 permitted duplicate rows; observed 1,000, i.e. only 8.0% of the budget consumed and roughly 12.4x headroom. In Databricks SQL: SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id, line_number) FROM sales.order_lines, or COUNT(DISTINCT STRUCT(order_id, line_number)) if you want the pair as a single value.

Step 4 — verdict. The correct verdict is PASS. The 85.1% figure is a false alarm caused by testing the wrong granularity, and shipping it would page an on-call engineer for normal basket data.

Analysis — Method choice: a uniqueness rule is a statement about a declared key, so the first question is always "what does one row represent?" — the tidy-data requirement that the relationship between rows and columns be well defined is precisely what makes this answerable [source 1]. Once the grain is fixed, the arithmetic is trivial; the reasoning is the whole exercise. Edge cases: (1) Slowly changing dimension tables (SCD — a design that keeps historical versions of an entity's attributes as extra rows) legitimately repeat the business key, so their uniqueness check must be scoped, e.g. one row per (customer_id, effective_from) or exactly one row per customer_id WHERE is_current = true. (2) If line_number is nullable, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id, line_number) collapses NULL-bearing pairs unpredictably, so add a NOT NULL assertion on every key component. (3) A table can pass uniqueness at the composite grain while still violating a stricter business rule such as "at most one promotional line per order"; grain-based uniqueness does not imply business-rule uniqueness. Common mistakes: applying an order-grain rule to a line-item table (the classic exam trap in this unit), reacting to the spectacular percentage without sanity-checking it against a plausible lines-per-order ratio, and "fixing" the raw data by deleting rows that are not actually duplicates. Generalisation: before writing any COUNT vs COUNT(DISTINCT ...) query, write the grain in words and derive the key from it; if you cannot name the key, you cannot test uniqueness.
Problem 3

A monitoring job defines the completeness rule for sales.orders as null rate = (rows with customer_id IS NULL) / (rows with customer_id IS NOT NULL), using the same 175,000 nulls and 4,825,000 non-null rows as before. A reviewer proposes the tolerance 3.55%. Compute the rule's reported value and decide pass/fail. Then recompute using total rows as the denominator and decide pass/fail again. Finally, state what must be added to the rule definition so the check is deterministic and exam-grade.
Hint: Two defensible-looking denominators give two different decisions at this threshold — that is the definition of a defective rule.

Worked solution
Step 1 — evaluate the proposed rule exactly as written.

$$\text{null rate} = \frac{175{,}000}{4{,}825{,}000} = 0.036269 = 3.6269\% \approx 3.63\%$$

Against the 3.55% tolerance: 3.63% > 3.55%, so this rule reports FAIL.

Step 2 — evaluate the conventional rule (denominator = total rows).

$$\text{null rate} = \frac{175{,}000}{5{,}000{,}000} = 0.035 = 3.50\%$$

Against the same 3.55% tolerance: 3.50% <= 3.55%, so this rule reports PASS.

Step 3 — the verdict flips on denominator choice alone. Same table, same 175,000 defects, same threshold, opposite decisions. A rule whose outcome depends on an implicit convention is not a test: it cannot be version-controlled, alerted on, or defended in an incident review. Note that the two denominators differ by exactly the defect count (5,000,000 - 4,825,000 = 175,000), which is why the divergence is negligible at small null rates and grows quickly as the null rate rises: at a 20% null rate the two conventions give 20.00% and 25.00%, a five-point gap.

Step 4 — what the rule needs to become executable. (a) A named denominator: "null rate = NULL count / total row count (COUNT(*))". (b) A comparison operator with inclusive or exclusive semantics: "FAIL if null rate > 0.010", not "threshold 1%". (c) A scope: which partition or time window is evaluated (e.g. the 2024-06-14 batch only), because a lifetime null rate hides a today-only regression. (d) An explicit failure action: quarantine, block gold-layer promotion, and open an incident.
