(e) A tolerant-of-NULLs note on the key column used for COUNT(DISTINCT ...), since COUNT(col) and COUNT(DISTINCT col) both ignore NULLs. With those five elements the rule is a deterministic assertion that returns a boolean and a numeric evidence value, which is what a data contract requires.

Analysis — Method choice: the denominator is part of the metric definition, not an implementation detail, because every threshold in a contract is quoted relative to a stated base. Total rows is the conventional base for missing-value checks because it is stable — it does not move when the column you are measuring changes — and because it matches how reviewers read a table ("3.5% of orders have no customer"). The non-null base has legitimate uses (it answers "of the customers we do know, what fraction is affected?") but it must be labelled explicitly and must never be mixed with total-row thresholds. Edge cases: the divergence is largest exactly when the defect rate is largest, i.e. when the alert matters most; and lowering the threshold to make a rule pass is threshold gaming, not remediation. Common mistakes: dividing by a filtered row count (e.g. only un-quarantined rows) so the metric improves as data is removed from scope; quoting "3.5%" without stating the base; treating a threshold as a target to be met by redefining the metric. Generalisation: write every quality metric as a complete sentence with a numerator, a numerator's scope, a denominator, a comparison operator, a threshold, an evaluation window, and a consequence. If any element is missing, the rule is defective no matter how correct its SQL looks — and note that a rule can also be defective for testing the wrong granularity, which is the same failure mode as problem 2 expressed at the column level.
Problem 4

A monitoring table records the end-to-end freshness lag (minutes between the newest source event and the newest ingested row) for ten consecutive micro-batches of sales.orders: 4, 6, 7, 9, 11, 14, 19, 26, 31, 47. Two SLO proposals are on the table: SLO A, mean lag <= 30 minutes; SLO B, p95 lag <= 30 minutes (nearest-rank percentile, rank = ceil(p x n)). Compute the mean, the median, the p90, the p95 and the maximum, then state the verdict under each SLO, and explain which SLO is the better contract for this table.
Hint: Sort first, then use rank = ceil(p x n) for percentiles — with n = 10, p95 lands on the largest observation.

Worked solution
Step 1 — order the data (already sorted): 4, 6, 7, 9, 11, 14, 19, 26, 31, 47. There are n = 10 micro-batches.

Step 2 — mean.

$$\bar{x} = \frac{4 + 6 + 7 + 9 + 11 + 14 + 19 + 26 + 31 + 47}{10} = \frac{174}{10} = 17.4 \text{ minutes}$$

Step 3 — median (n even, so average the two central values, positions 5 and 6).

$$\text{median} = \frac{11 + 14}{2} = 12.5 \text{ minutes}$$

Step 4 — percentiles by nearest rank, rank = ceil(p x n).

$$\text{p90: rank} = \lceil 0.90 \times 10 \rceil = 9 \Rightarrow x_{(9)} = 31 \text{ minutes}$$

$$\text{p95: rank} = \lceil 0.95 \times 10 \rceil = 10 \Rightarrow x_{(10)} = 47 \text{ minutes}$$

$$\text{max} = x_{(10)} = 47 \text{ minutes}$$

Step 5 — verdicts. Under SLO A (mean <= 30): 17.4 <= 30, so PASS. Under SLO B (p95 <= 30): 47 > 30, so FAIL. The statistic choice, not the data, decides the outcome — and note that 47 minutes is exactly the MAX-minus-MAX lag computed from the raw timestamps in problem 1, which is the same single straggler event surfacing in both metrics.

Step 6 — interpretation. Nine of ten micro-batches are at or below 31 minutes; the mean is dragged to 17.4 by the low tail, and the max is dragged to 47 by one late event. A mean-based SLO lets a table be "fresh on average" while a dashboard reading the newest partition is nearly an hour stale, which is the failure users actually notice. SLO B is the better contract for a table that feeds a near-real-time revenue dashboard, because it bounds the experience of the user querying the most recent data. A reasonable refinement is to state both: p95 <= 30 minutes for the contract, with an alert-only threshold on max lag.

Analysis — Method choice: a freshness SLO is a promise about what a user will observe, so the summary statistic must be chosen to match where the pain occurs. Latency distributions are right-skewed — most batches are fast, a few stragglers are slow — so the mean is pulled toward the bulk and hides the tail, whereas high percentiles describe the tail directly. Edge cases: with small n, nearest-rank percentiles are jumpy (p95 on ten batches can only take the tenth value; dropping the 47 makes p95 = 47... no — dropping the 47 changes n to 9 and gives rank = ceil(0.95 x 9) = 9, i.e. 31), so a p95 SLO should be evaluated over a rolling window with enough observations to be stable. Also distinguish event-time from processing-time lag: MAX(_ingest_timestamp) - MAX(order_timestamp) measures end-to-end delay including source lag, whereas comparing two ingestion timestamps measures only pipeline delay — the two numbers can differ wildly and mixing them invalidates the SLO. Common mistakes: reporting the mean by default because it is the first function taught; computing percentiles with rank = round(p x n) or p x n + 1 and getting a neighbouring value; leaving lag in minutes and comparing it with a threshold expressed in seconds. Generalisation: for any latency or volume metric, decide whether the contract is about the typical case (mean, median) or the worst case (p95, p99, max) before you compute anything, and state the window and the sample size alongside the number. Reporting the lag distribution rather than a single figure is also what lets you report the pattern of deficient data honestly rather than averaging it away [source 5].
Problem 5

The same nightly batch from problem 1 must be reconciled for accuracy. The warehouse reports SUM(order_total) = 41,980,300.00 USD for the day, while the payment gateway — the source of record — reports 41,915,120.00 USD for the same window. The accuracy tolerance is <= 0.05% variance, measured against the source of record. Compute the absolute variance, the variance rate, and the verdict. You then have capacity to fix exactly one defect today; using the average order value implied by the warehouse total and the 7,500 duplicated rows from problem 1, estimate how much of the accuracy gap the duplicates could explain, and state which defect you fix first and why.
Hint: Compute the variance against the gateway (the reference), then ask whether 7,500 duplicated rows at the average order value could account for the gap.

Worked solution
Step 1 — define the comparison and name the reference explicitly. Accuracy is agreement with reality, so the reference is the payment gateway (source of record), and the variance is measured as a rate over the gateway figure.

$$\text{absolute variance} = 41{,}980{,}300.00 - 41{,}915{,}120.00 = 65{,}180.00 \text{ USD}$$

$$\text{variance rate} = \frac{65{,}180.00}{41{,}915{,}120.00} = 0.0015551 = 0.1555\% \approx 0.16\%$$

(For the record, using the warehouse figure as the denominator gives 65,180.00 / 41,980,300.00 = 0.1553% — the denominator convention must be written into the contract for exactly the reason shown in problem 3.)

Step 2 — verdict. Tolerance budget in dollars: 0.0005 x 41,915,120.00 = 20,957.56 USD. Observed variance 65,180.00 USD exceeds it: 65,180.00 / 20,957.56 = 3.11x the allowance, and 0.1555% > 0.05%. The accuracy check FAILS.

Step 3 — estimate the duplicate contribution. Average order value in the warehouse:

$$\bar{v} = \frac{41{,}980{,}300.00}{5{,}000{,}000} = 8.39606 \text{ USD per row}$$

If the 7,500 duplicated rows each carry an order_total at that average, they inflate the sum by approximately 7,500 x 8.39606 = 62,970.45 USD, which is 62,970.45 / 65,180.00 = 96.6% of the observed variance. The residual is 65,180.00 - 62,970.45 = 2,209.55 USD, i.e. 0.00527% of the gateway total — within the 0.05% tolerance.

Step 4 — fix order. Deduplicate sales.order_lines/sales.orders on the declared key first, then re-run the reconciliation. If the hypothesis holds, one fix removes ~96.6% of the accuracy gap and converts two failures (uniqueness and accuracy) into one open problem (residual 2,209.55 USD). Only then quantify and route the 175,000 NULL customer_id rows, because completeness failures degrade segmentation and attribution but, unlike duplicates, cannot silently double-count revenue.

Step 5 — note what cannot be checked without a reference. The accuracy check is only runnable because a gateway extract exists; nothing inside the warehouse can validate order_total against reality. By contrast, completeness, uniqueness and timeliness are all computable from the table alone.

Analysis — Method choice: accuracy is the only one of the four dimensions that requires an external reference, so the first design decision is naming the source of record and the second is the join key and time window used for the comparison — an off-by-one-day window will manufacture a variance that looks like a data defect. Expressing the variance as both dollars and a rate lets you compare against a rate-based tolerance while still seeing the cash impact. Edge cases: (1) reconciling at order grain but comparing at day grain masks offsetting errors and can show a false PASS — reconcile at the finest grain the reference supports, then aggregate. (2) Variance rate conventions differ (over the reference vs over the warehouse); pick one and document it. (3) A tolerance of 0.05% on a large revenue number is a tight budget: 20,957.56 USD here, so a handful of mispriced high-value orders can breach it. Common mistakes: assuming a failed accuracy check is a pipeline bug when it is usually a duplicate or join-grain artefact upstream (as Step 3 shows); reporting "revenue is close enough" without quantifying the gap; and fixing the most visible defect (missing customer_id) rather than the one with the largest blast radius (duplicated financial rows). Generalisation: dimensions interact — one root cause (duplicate rows) can breach both uniqueness and accuracy simultaneously, so rank remediation by causal reach, not by which alert fired first. Verifying data accuracy through quality assurance checks before analysis, rather than after, is the whole point of this stage of data processing [source 4], and cleaning is what makes the resulting analysis reflect the true state of the business [source 6].

actions.text: Now let's put that into practice. On this page we have a worked problem where you compute completeness, uniqueness, and freshness from raw counts, and then decide pass or fail against stated thresholds.

Here's the setup. A nightly batch loads the Delta table sales.orders, giving us five million total orders, a hundred and seventy-five thousand rows with a NULL customer_id, and 4,992,500 distinct order_id values. The latest ingest timestamp is forty-seven minutes behind the latest order.
Before diving in, keep the hint in mind: compute each rate as a ratio over total rows. That framing matters — it keeps every dimension comparable and it's exactly the arithmetic the exam expects.

Step one, completeness. Null rate equals 175,000 divided by 5,000,000 — that's 3.5%. Against a 1.0% tolerance, that exceeds the threshold, so the check fails. Step two, uniqueness. The duplicate rate is 5,000,000 minus 4,992,500, divided by 5,000,000, which is 0.15%. That breaches the 0.10% tolerance, so uniqueness also fails. Step three, timeliness: a forty-seven-minute lag breaks the thirty-minute freshness SLO. Two of three dimensions breached in the same batch.

The analysis is where the exam traps live. Thresholds must match the grain of the table and the business use case. Notice that a 0.15% duplicate rate on a line-item table would be a false alarm, because line-item grain legitimately repeats order_id. So always ask: what does one row actually represent before you judge a metric?

actions.topic: If a duplicate rate breaches tolerance only because of legitimate line-item grain, what should change — the threshold, the grain, or the table?
actions.prompt: Think about which lever gives you a metric that is both defensible and meaningful to the business.

scenes.title: Lesson Assessment: Data Quality Dimensions and Expectations

questions.question:
A retail data platform ingests a nightly feed of point-of-sale transactions. A review of the raw Delta table surfaces four independent defect scenarios. For each scenario below, select EVERY option that correctly names a data quality dimension that the scenario directly violates or tests. (Select all that apply.)

Scenario A: The customer_id column is NULL for 43,000 of 2,000,000 rows because the POS terminal did not capture a loyalty card swipe.
Scenario B: The order_total of an order reads 199.99, but the payment gateway's settlement record for that same order reads 189.99.
Scenario C: The table contains 2,000,000 rows but only 1,950,000 distinct order_id values.
Scenario D: The settlement_date for a subset of rows is January 3 when the cashier's timestamped receipt shows January 5.

options.label: Scenario A primarily tests completeness.
Scenario B primarily tests accuracy and requires a reference source to prove.
Scenario C primarily tests uniqueness rather than completeness.
Scenario D primarily tests timeliness against a freshness threshold.
Scenario A primarily tests validity because NULL is an out-of-domain value.
Scenario C primarily tests completeness because 50,000 rows are effectively lost.

questions.analysis: Scenario A is a textbook completeness defect: a required value (customer_id) is absent, and the correct check is a null rate computed as COUNT(*) minus COUNT(customer_id). Scenario B is an accuracy defect: the stored value disagrees with reality, and proving it requires reconciliation against a source system of record such as the payment gateway, since completeness alone cannot prove correctness. Scenario C is the classic certification trap: a gap between COUNT(*) and COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) tests uniqueness (the table should have one row per order_id), not completeness, even though a naive reader might think rows were 'lost'. Scenario D is not a timeliness question at all — timeliness measures freshness (for example MAX(_ingest_timestamp) against a 30-minute threshold), whereas a wrong calendar date on a row is an accuracy defect because the value does not reflect what actually happened. Options E and F are the distractor traps taught earlier in this unit: NULL is a missing value (completeness), not an invalid domain value, and duplicate rows are a uniqueness problem, not a completeness problem. Data cleaning exists precisely to identify and fix errors, inconsistencies, and quality issues so the data is accurate and consistent [source 2], and flawed data leads to skewed results, which is why each dimension must be checked on its own terms [source 6].

questions.question: The order operations manager states this business expectation verbatim: 'Our silver orders table must be trustworthy, and I want to guarantee the daily revenue dashboard is never inflated by the same physical order being counted twice.' The silver table is at order-header grain (one row per order_id, with line items already aggregated upstream). Which single rule best encodes this expectation as a deterministic, executable assertion that a Databricks SQL quality check can evaluate automatically?

options.label: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM silver_orders WHERE order_id IS NULL; expected result: 0, fail the batch if any null order_id is found.
SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS duplicate_count FROM silver_orders; expected result: 0, quarantine the batch if duplicate_count > 0.
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM silver_orders; expected result: greater than zero, pass the batch if the table is non-empty.
SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT line_item_id) AS duplicate_count FROM silver_orders; expected result: 0, fail the batch if duplicate_count > 0.

questions.analysis: Option B is the only choice that both encodes the stated expectation (no order counted twice for revenue) and operates at the correct grain. Because the table is at order-header grain, COUNT(*) minus COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) directly measures the number of duplicate physical orders, and a clean executable rule sets an explicit threshold (expected 0) with explicit failure semantics (quarantine). Option A tests completeness of order_id, not uniqueness — a null order_id is a presence problem, and it will not detect a fully-populated row that appears twice. Option C is a smoke test only; a non-empty table can still be full of duplicates, so it gives no assurance about double-counting. Option D is the exact exam trap taught in this unit: it tests uniqueness on the wrong grain — line_item_id is finer than the order-header grain, so it can never reveal a duplicated order header. Selecting the rule that produces a deterministic boolean or numeric assertion rather than a subjective judgement, and rejecting rules that test the wrong granularity or carry no failure semantics, is the core skill of translating expectations into rules.

questions.question: A Databricks quality job runs a batch of 400,000 silver order rows. It reports total_rows = 400000, customer_id_not_null_count = 386400, and distinct_order_id_count = 399600. The governance policy sets a null-rate threshold of 1.5% on customer_id and a duplicate-rate threshold of 0.5% on order_id. Which statement correctly computes the metrics AND makes the right pass/quarantine decision?

options.label: Null rate = 3.4%, duplicate rate = 0.1%. The batch passes because only the duplicate rate is within tolerance.
Null rate = 3.4%, duplicate rate = 0.1%. The batch must be quarantined because the null rate exceeds the 1.5% threshold.
Null rate = 1.36%, duplicate rate = 0.1%. The batch passes because both metrics are within tolerance.
Null rate = 3.4%, duplicate rate = 0.4%. The batch passes because the duplicate rate is within tolerance.

questions.analysis: Null rate = (total_rows - customer_id_not_null_count) / total_rows = (400000 - 386400) / 400000 = 13600 / 400000 = 0.034 = 3.4%. Duplicate rate = (total_rows - distinct_order_id_count) / total_rows = (400000 - 399600) / 400000 = 400 / 400000 = 0.001 = 0.1%. Comparing to policy: the duplicate rate of 0.1% is below the 0.5% threshold, so uniqueness is acceptable; but the null rate of 3.4% exceeds the 1.5% completeness threshold, so the batch must be quarantined. Option B is therefore correct. Option C is the classic COUNT(col) null-masking trap: it divides the wrong way (13600 / 400000 was mis-set, or the learner inverted the formula and used 1.5% vs. the derived value incorrectly), yielding 1.36% — suspiciously just under the threshold, which is exactly the kind of near-miss a careless implementer would wave through. Option D errors on the duplicate-rate arithmetic, inflating 0.1% to 0.4% and still concluding 'pass' on the wrong basis. Option A computes both metrics correctly but then makes a defective decision: passing a batch while acknowledging a breached completeness threshold contradicts the requirement that a rule must carry failure semantics. Any patterns or significant amounts of missing data must be taken into consideration when conducting an analysis [source 5], and cleaning ensures the analysis reflects the true representation of the data so results are not skewed [source 6].

questions.question:
A data engineering team is building a medallion architecture (bronze = raw ingested data, silver = cleaned and conformed data, gold = business-level aggregates and marts) on Databricks with Delta Lake, and they must decide where each of the following three quality checks belongs, and justify the placement:

(1) A landing-zone schema and nullability check verifying that every record from Auto Loader contains the mandatory keys `order_id`, `store_id`, and `event_ts` before the record is allowed to proceed downstream.
(2) A reconciliation check comparing the silver `order_total` against the payment gateway settlement table to confirm recorded values agree with the system of record.
(3) A business-level freshness check confirming the gold `daily_revenue` table was refreshed within the last 60 minutes before the dashboard is served.

For EACH check, state which medallion layer it belongs to, name the data quality dimension it enforces, and justify why that layer is the correct placement using the principle of failing as close to the source as possible while still having the reference data required to evaluate the rule.
questions.commentPrompt: Score against four criteria. (a) Correct layer-to-check mapping (40%): (1) belongs in bronze — it is a raw-ingest/schema-and-nullability gate, e.g. a landing-zone completeness check on mandatory keys, and it should fail early so bad records never contaminate downstream layers; (2) belongs in silver — accuracy reconciliation against the payment gateway requires the conformed, keyed silver table and a trusted reference source, so it cannot be evaluated reliably at raw bronze grain; (3) belongs in gold — it is a business-freshness (timeliness) SLA on the served table, so it is defined at the consumption layer, not the raw layer. (b) Correct dimension naming (30%): (1) completeness; (2) accuracy; (3) timeliness. (c) Justification quality (20%): explains the trade-off between failing as close to the source as possible and the need for the reference data or SLA that only a specific layer provides; must name failure semantics (quarantine the batch / quarantine the record) for at least two of the three checks. (d) Clarity and vocabulary (10%): uses correct Databricks and data engineering terminology (bronze, silver, gold, Delta Lake, Auto Loader, system of record, quarantine) without inversion.
questions.analysis: A strong answer maps (1) to bronze, (2) to silver, and (3) to gold, naming the dimensions completeness, accuracy, and timeliness respectively. The reasoning rests on a single governing principle from this unit: quality checks must span generation, ingestion, storage, transformation, and serving, and cannot be bolted on at the end. The completeness gate for mandatory keys is evaluated best at bronze because a record missing `order_id` or `event_ts` will only compound into worse errors downstream, so the cheapest, most local place to catch it is the landing zone. The accuracy reconciliation must live in silver because it needs both conformed keys and a trusted reference source (the payment gateway settlement table) — and accuracy by definition proves agreement with reality only against a reference dataset, which raw bronze alone cannot provide. The timeliness SLA belongs in gold because freshness is a consumption-layer guarantee: it is the dashboard consumer who cares that `daily_revenue` was refreshed within 60 minutes, and the check is meaningless against a raw landing zone that is overwritten every few minutes. Confusing these layers — for example, running the payment-gateway reconciliation on raw bronze or the freshness SLA on bronze — is the systemic error this lesson guards against. Missing data, whether sparse or patterned, must be surfaced rather than silently absorbed [source 5], and cleaning exists to make data accurate and analysis-ready [source 2], which is precisely why each layer's check must match the layer's purpose.

actions.text: Keeping that grain question in mind, this next section is a set of exam-style items covering the data quality dimensions we just worked through — classification of defect scenarios, choosing the executable rule that encodes a business expectation, computing quality metrics against a threshold, and justifying where a given check belongs in the medallion architecture.

Treat these as the real thing: read each question carefully, watch the wording of the options, and work them through on your own without looking back. Take your time and commit to an answer for each one — once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning with you, including any of the traps that caught you.

scenes.title: Why Duplicates and Late Data Break Pipelines

elements.content: Why Duplicates and Late Data Break Pipelines

Recall Unit 6 Lesson 1: cleanliness spans the whole pipeline and cannot be bolted on at the end [source 2].

Uniqueness and timeliness are two of the core quality dimensions; this lesson makes them operational.

Duplicates — Uniqueness

Silently inflate counts, revenue, and conversion rates.

No error is raised; the number is simply too high. Cleaning removes duplicates as a standard step [source 2].

Lateness — Timeliness

Silently under-report the current period; the window closes before the row lands.

No error is raised; the number is simply too low.

Worked example: 100 real orders, 6 duplicated by a retry, 4 late rows arriving after the cutoff.

Naive COUNT(*) = 106 (+6% inflation); windowed revenue captures only 96 of 100 orders (−4% under-report).

Lesson roadmap

1. Where duplicates come from

2. Dedupe: primary key + window function

3. Idempotent MERGE upserts

4. Watermarks & late-arriving records

Shared root cause + exam objective

Pipelines assume each record arrives exactly once, in order, in real time — almost always false [source 1].

Objective: identify the source before choosing a fix.

actions.text: Now that we can measure data quality, let's turn to two failure modes that quietly wreck pipelines even when every check passes at the wrong moment: duplicates and late-arriving data.

Recall from our earlier lesson on data quality dimensions — uniqueness and timeliness were two of the core dimensions we defined. Today we make them operational: how do these two dimensions actually break, and how do we fix them in Databricks?

First, duplicates — the uniqueness dimension. A duplicate record silently inflates counts, revenue, and conversion metrics. Nothing errors out. Your dashboard just reports a number that is wrong, and you only find out when someone reconciles against the source system.

Second, lateness — the timeliness dimension. A late record silently under-reports the current period. The data for last Tuesday shows up on Thursday, but Tuesday's report was already published. Again, no error, just a number that quietly drifted.

Here is a worked example that makes both concrete. Say we have one hundred real orders, but six got duplicated by an at-least-once retry, and eight arrived late. Our count reads one hundred and six instead of one hundred, and our current-period revenue is short by whatever those eight late orders were worth. Two silent distortions from one pipeline.

Notice both problems share one root cause: our pipelines assume every record arrives exactly once, in order, and in real time. That assumption is almost always false. And the exam objective here is precise — identify the source of the duplication or the lateness before you choose a remediation technique. Diagnose first, then fix.

So here is our roadmap for this lesson: first, where duplicates come from; second, deduplication by primary key using a window function; third, idempotent MERGE upserts; and fourth, watermarks and late-arriving records. Let's start by tracing where duplicates actually come from.

scenes.title: Where Duplicates Come From

elements.content: Where Duplicates Come From

Duplicate rows are a uniqueness defect, not a completeness or accuracy defect: every row can be present and correct and the table still fails the one-row-per-order_id rule. Diagnose the source before you deduplicate.

Data cleaning is the process of identifying and fixing errors, inconsistencies, and quality issues so data is accurate, consistent, and ready for analysis [source 2].
1

At-least-once delivery. Message queues and event-streaming platforms (Amazon SQS, Kafka, Kinesis) redeliver a message whenever the consumer fails before acknowledging it, so exactly-once is not guaranteed at the transport layer.
2

Replayed ingestion. Re-running a batch job, reprocessing a checkpointed stream from an earlier offset, or backfilling a historical window appends the same events a second time into the same target table.
3
Non-idempotent writes. An append-only (INSERT) pipeline writes a fresh copy of every record on every run, so a pipeline re-run that should have been a no-op instead multiplies row counts.
4
CDC and source-system quirks. Database replication and change-data-capture can emit an update as a new row rather than an in-place change, and a multi-row update emits one row per modified record.
Worked example — counting the damage
1,000,000 source orders loaded by 3 non-idempotent runs → 3,000,000 rows; if each order legitimately had 2 updates captured as new rows, the target holds 6,000,000 rows for 1,000,000 orders.
Duplication factor = 6,000,000 rows ÷ 1,000,000 distinct order_id = 6×; row-count growth alone will not reveal this, so the uniqueness check must compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(DISTINCT order_id).
Exam trap — MERGE

A MERGE whose SOURCE contains multiple rows for the same key is not a deduplication fix: it can fail with a duplicate-match error or multiply target rows.

Deduplicate the source first, then merge.
Quality assurance checks verify accuracy after cleaning [source 1]; any patterns or significant amounts of duplicated or missing data should be reported with the results [source 5].

actions.text: Before we move into deduplication strategies, we need to answer a more fundamental question: where do duplicated rows actually come from? If you can pinpoint the root cause, you can choose the right fix instead of blindly deduplicating after the damage is done.
We'll walk through four concrete sources, and then look at a worked example and the classic exam trap behind this topic.

The first thing to internalize is this: a duplicate row is a uniqueness defect, not merely a cosmetic annoyance. It violates a data quality dimension we just covered, and it can silently corrupt downstream aggregations, joins, and business metrics.

Source number one: at-least-once delivery. Services like Amazon SQS, Kafka, and Kinesis guarantee that a message is delivered at least once — but not exactly once — at the transport layer. If a consumer fails to acknowledge before a timeout, the platform redelivers the same message, and your pipeline processes it twice.

Source number two: replayed ingestion. Re-running a batch job, restarting a checkpointed stream from an earlier offset, or backfilling a historical window will append the same events a second time. The data is correct, but it is inserted twice.

Source number three: non-idempotent writes. An append-only INSERT pipeline creates a brand new copy of every record on every run. Run the exact same job three times, and you get three copies — the row count multiplies with each execution.

Source number four: CDC and source-system quirks. Change data capture and database replication can emit an update as a brand new row rather than modifying the existing one, and a multi-row update emits one change record per affected row. Those change events then land as extra rows in your Delta table.

Let's put numbers on the damage. Suppose one million source orders are loaded by three non-idempotent runs. Each run appends the full set, so you do not end up with one million rows — you end up with six million.

That gives a duplication factor of six: six million rows divided by one million distinct orders. If a dashboard sums revenue over this table, every order is now counted six times, and the report overstates the business by five hundred percent.

Now the exam trap. A MERGE whose SOURCE contains multiple rows for the same key is not a deduplication fix. In a MERGE, when the source has several rows matching one target key, the statement can fail with a duplicate-match error, or it can silently multiply the rows in the target. If you suspect a MERGE is duplicating data, inspect the source first — a MERGE is a correction tool only when the source is already unique.

One last point to keep in mind: quality assurance checks verify accuracy after cleaning — they do not prevent duplicates. So the goal is not to inspect later; it is to design each source of ingestion so duplicates are either impossible or immediately detectable.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Sources of Duplication

questions.question: A streaming pipeline uses Apache Kafka as transport and writes events into a bronze Delta table. The downstream silver table has exactly 1,912,400 rows but only 1,900,000 distinct order_id values, and the brokers were rebooted once during the window. Which statement best classifies the duplication mechanism, given that message transport guarantees at-least-once delivery?

options.label: The duplication is a uniqueness defect caused by at-least-once delivery, because transport redelivers unacknowledged records after a broker reboot, and no MERGE with a deterministic key was applied on the write path to collapse redeliveries.
The duplication is a completeness defect, because missing rows forced the transport to replay records and inflate the row count beyond the distinct-key count.
The duplication was created by the write pattern: an un-deduplicated MERGE into the silver table re-inserted every matching source row on each micro-batch.
The duplication originates at the source system before ingestion, so the key count exceeds distinct keys, and the transport is not responsible.

questions.correctAnswer: The duplication is a uniqueness defect caused by at-least-once delivery, because transport redelivers unacknowledged records after a broker reboot, and no MERGE with a deterministic key was applied on the write path to collapse redeliveries.
questions.analysis: At-least-once delivery is a transport-level semantic, not a uniqueness guarantee; after a broker restart, records without committed offsets are redelivered. The observed pattern (row count > distinct key count) is a uniqueness violation [source 1], and the mechanism is duplicate delivery plus a non-idempotent write that never applied a deterministic MERGE key. Option B is wrong because completeness concerns presence, not count inflation. Option C describes the non-idempotent append/re-run pattern, which is a distinct mechanism and is only a contributing factor here, not the primary classifier named in the stem. Option D inverts the causal direction: the source-duplicate trap applies when the same business key genuinely exists twice upstream before any transport handoff. Note also that data cleaning explicitly includes removing duplicates [source 2], and a defect of this shape must be treated as a duplicate-handling task, not a missing-data task [source 5].
answer: The duplication is a uniqueness defect caused by at-least-once delivery, because transport redelivers unacknowledged records after a broker reboot, and no MERGE with a deterministic key was applied on the write path to collapse redeliveries.

questions.question: A student claims: 'We use Kafka with at-least-once delivery, therefore our Delta table is exactly-once.' Select every statement that correctly explains why this reasoning is invalid (select all that apply).

options.label: Exactly-once is an end-to-end property of the whole pipeline (transport + write + checkpoint/offset management), and message transport alone cannot provide it.

At-least-once delivery explicitly permits redelivery, so duplicates can reach the sink; the pipeline must make the write idempotent, for example by MERGE on a deterministic business key or by using a deduplication stage, to achieve an exactly-once effect.
Exactly-once is only achievable if the source system itself guarantees no duplicate business keys, because transport semantics are irrelevant once rows arrive.
A non-idempotent append of micro-batches on every retry will accumulate duplicate rows in Delta, so an exactly-once *effect* requires an idempotent write or an explicit deduplication step.

correctAnswer: Exactly-once is an end-to-end property of the whole pipeline (transport + write + checkpoint/offset management), and message transport alone cannot provide it.

At-least-once delivery explicitly permits redelivery, so duplicates can reach the sink; the pipeline must make the write idempotent, for example by MERGE on a deterministic business key or by using a deduplication stage, to achieve an exactly-once effect.
A non-idempotent append of micro-batches on every retry will accumulate duplicate rows in Delta, so an exactly-once *effect* requires an idempotent write or an explicit deduplication step.
questions.analysis: The first, second, and fourth statements are all correct: exactly-once is a pipeline-wide property spanning transport, write semantics, and offset/checkpoint management. At-least-once delivery explicitly permits redelivery, so idempotent writes or explicit dedup stages are required to produce an exactly-once effect. The third statement is the classic distractor that mirrors the exam trap: it inverts the reasoning and claims the transport is irrelevant. In a real pipeline, a perfectly clean source can still produce duplicate sink rows due to transport redelivery and non-idempotent writes (the non-idempotent append pattern). Making a duplicate-handling decision requires treating it as a data-cleaning task [source 2], and the underlying discipline of preparing collected data for analysis [source 4] applies identically whether the source is clean or not. The other trap here is that 'exactly-once' is often asserted as a transport feature; you must always ask what the write pattern does on retry.
answer: Exactly-once is an end-to-end property of the whole pipeline (transport + write + checkpoint/offset management), and message transport alone cannot provide it.

At-least-once delivery explicitly permits redelivery, so duplicates can reach the sink; the pipeline must make the write idempotent, for example by MERGE on a deterministic business key or by using a deduplication stage, to achieve an exactly-once effect.
A non-idempotent append of micro-batches on every retry will accumulate duplicate rows in Delta, so an exactly-once *effect* requires an idempotent write or an explicit deduplication step.

questions.question: A silver-layer Delta table is produced by running INSERT INTO silver.orders SELECT * FROM bronze.orders (an append) after each batch. Stakeholders report duplicate order_id values, and a teammate proposes fixing it by re-running the job with DELETE WHERE order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM silver.orders GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) before the INSERT. Evaluate this proposal. In your answer (a) classify the duplication mechanism, (b) state whether the proposed fix is a trap or a sound solution and why, and (c) describe a more robust remediation using MERGE semantics, being explicit about the source-side precondition.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Mechanism classification — 30%: must correctly identify this as a non-idempotent append plus job re-run pattern (append on every batch/retry accumulates duplicates), not as a source-side duplicate or transport-only issue. (2) Trap evaluation — 30%: must state the DELETE+re-INSERT is fragile (race conditions, partial failure between steps, grain mismatch) and does not make the write idempotent, so retries can reintroduce duplicates. (3) MERGE remediation — 30%: must describe MERGE INTO silver.orders USING (deduplicated batch) ON o.order_id = s.order_id with explicit WHEN MATCHED UPDATE and WHEN NOT MATCHED INSERT, keyed on the stable business key, and must state the source-side precondition that the incoming batch itself must be deduplicated (e.g., ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC) = 1) before MERGE; otherwise MERGE will still insert duplicates if the source stage contains duplicate keys. (4) Clarity and use of course vocabulary — 10%: uses terms such as idempotent, business key, grain, deterministic; and cites or paraphrases the cleaning discipline [source 2] and the preparatory processing steps [source 4].
questions.analysis: A strong answer begins by classifying the mechanism: the sink duplicates are produced by an append write that is re-run on each batch, i.e., a non-idempotent append plus job re-run pattern. This is distinct from at-least-once transport redelivery and from the source-duplicate trap. On the fix: DELETE+re-INSERT is a trap. It is not atomic with the INSERT (a failure between steps leaves the table inconsistent), it can delete legitimate rows if the grain of the silver table differs from the proposed key, and it does not make the overall write idempotent, so the next retry re-creates duplicates. A robust remediation is a MERGE INTO the silver table keyed on the stable business key (for example order_id): WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE and WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT. The crucial precondition is that the incoming batch must itself be deduplicated before MERGE; if the source stage contains duplicate keys, MERGE will match one row and insert the rest, so the source must be collapsed first with a deterministic window such as ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC) = 1. This is the trap the checkpoint is designed to expose: an un-deduplicated MERGE source looks like a solution but merely relocates the duplicate rows. This aligns with the general cleaning objective of identifying and fixing errors and removing duplicates [source 2], and with the broader discipline of preparing collected data for analysis [source 4], while still reporting residual missing-data patterns [source 5] when they coexist.

scenes.title: Deduplication Strategy: Key Plus Ordering

elements.content: Deduplication Strategy: Key Plus Ordering
The general recipe: pick the key, pick a deterministic tie-break, keep exactly one row per key.

Step 1 — Choose the key

Use the natural / business primary key. A line-item entity needs a composite key: order_id + line_item_id. Removing duplicates means identifying and fixing errors and inconsistencies in raw data [source 2].

Step 2 — Tie-break

Winner = MAX(updated_timestamp), MAX(version), or MAX(ingestion_time). Signals like these must be taken into consideration before analysis [source 5]. Must be deterministic.

Step 3 — Keep one row

Window function ROW_NUMBER() per key, or an insert-only pattern read with MAX(created_timestamp) at query time. Quality checks then verify the result [source 1].
Worked example (composite key)
Rows 2, 5, 9 share order_id=A1 & line_item_id=3. MAX(version) keeps only row 9 if versions differ; if versions tie, fall back to MAX(updated_timestamp) — otherwise output is non-deterministic.
Exam traps

• dropDuplicates() on all columns only removes fully identical rows — one differing field and the duplicate survives. • ORDER BY with no unique tie-breaker makes 'latest' non-deterministic when timestamps match.

actions.text: Now that we've seen where duplicates come from, let's build the strategy for getting rid of them. The general recipe for deduplication is a key plus an ordering — and once you internalize this three-step pattern, you'll be able to handle almost any deduplication question the exam throws at you.

Here's the overall recipe in one line: pick the key, pick a deterministic tie-break, then keep exactly one row per key. Notice the word deterministic — that's the heart of it. If your tie-break can produce two different winners on two different runs, your pipeline isn't idempotent, and that's a problem both in production and on the exam.

Step one: choose the key. Use the natural or business primary key for the entity. If the entity isn't the whole order but a line item within the order, you need a composite key — for example, order_id together with line_item_id. Getting the grain of the key right is what makes the whole deduplication correct.

Step two is the tie-break. When several rows share the same key, which one wins? The rule is the record with the maximum updated_timestamp, the maximum version, or the maximum ingestion time — whichever field reliably captures recency in your data. The crucial requirement is that this comparison must be deterministic, so the same input always yields the same winner.

Step three: keep exactly one row per key. The standard approach is a window function — ROW_NUMBER over the key, ordered by your tie-break — and then filter to row number one. The alternative is an insert-only pattern where you append every change and read the latest with MAX of the created timestamp at query time. Both give you one row per key; the choice depends on whether you want the dedup materialized or applied on read.
Let's ground this in a worked example using a composite key.

Rows two, five, and nine all share the same order_id of A1 and the same line_item_id — so they represent the same logical line item. Because we partition by that composite key and order by the latest timestamp, only the row with the newest timestamp survives; the other two are dropped as duplicates of the same entity.

Now the exam traps, and these are the ones that catch people. First, DataFrame.dropDuplicates on all columns only removes rows that are identical across every single column. The moment one field differs — say a status changed but everything else matches — the duplicate survives. So dropDuplicates without a key column subset rarely gives you the dedup you actually intend.

The second trap is subtler: an ORDER BY without a unique tie-breaker makes 'latest' non-deterministic whenever two records share the same timestamp. If you only order by timestamp and there's a tie, Spark is free to pick either row — and that can flip between runs. Always add a unique column to your ordering to break those ties. Keep both traps in mind, and you'll be ready for the ROW_NUMBER lab coming up next.

widgetConfig.title: ROW_NUMBER Deduplication Lab
widgetConfig.description: Students write and run window-function deduplication queries against a messy orders table and see exactly which row survives.
widgetConfig.starterCode:
-- orders(order_id, dedupe_key, customer, amount, status, updated_at, ingestion_time, seq)
-- 13 rows in the source, but only 5 distinct dedupe_key values.

-- TODO: keep exactly ONE row per dedupe_key — the newest by updated_at.
-- Rank rows inside each key with ROW_NUMBER(), then keep only rn = 1.

SELECT
    order_id,
    dedupe_key,
    status,
    updated_at
FROM (
    SELECT
        *,
        -- TODO: replace 0 with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dedupe_key ORDER BY updated_at DESC)
        0 AS rn
    FROM orders
) AS ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

testCases.description: Exactly one row per dedupe_key (down from 13 messy source rows).
The surviving row is the one with the latest updated_at.
Tie on updated_at is broken by ingestion_time DESC.
Tie on updated_at AND ingestion_time is broken by the monotonic seq column.
Identical-looking rows still resolve deterministically — the highest seq wins.

hints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) has two parts. PARTITION BY dedupe_key is the group that must end up unique; ORDER BY updated_at DESC decides which row inside that group wins.

Window functions are computed AFTER WHERE, so you cannot filter on ROW_NUMBER() in the same SELECT that creates it. Wrap it in a subquery or CTE and filter outside: WITH ranked AS (SELECT o.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dedupe_key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM orders o) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

Watch the ties. B-200 has two rows with an identical updated_at, and C-300 has two rows that also share ingestion_time. Add tie-breakers to the ORDER BY: ORDER BY updated_at DESC, ingestion_time DESC, seq DESC. The monotonic seq column guarantees one stable, reproducible winner every run.

Why not GROUP BY? SELECT dedupe_key, MAX(updated_at) FROM orders GROUP BY dedupe_key returns the right timestamps, but every other column is pulled from an arbitrary row of the group — status and amount would not belong to the max row. Either join back to orders on (dedupe_key, updated_at) or use the window-function pattern above. Databricks' dropDuplicates() has the same trap: it deduplicates on the columns you list, so if status differs between two rows of the same key, BOTH rows survive.
Final shape: rank in a CTE with PARTITION BY dedupe_key, ORDER BY updated_at DESC, ingestion_time DESC, seq DESC; then WHERE rn = 1 and ORDER BY dedupe_key.
widgetConfig.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        o.*,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY dedupe_key
            ORDER BY updated_at DESC, ingestion_time DESC, seq DESC
        ) AS rn
    FROM orders AS o
)
SELECT
    order_id,
    dedupe_key,
    customer,
    amount,
    status,
    updated_at,
    ingestion_time,
    seq
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY dedupe_key;

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Window-Function Deduplication

questions.question:
A silver-layer table `events_raw` holds clickstream events at raw event grain. A data engineer runs the following deduplication query to keep exactly one record per (user_id, session_id) pair:

SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY user_id, session_id
    ORDER BY event_timestamp
  ) AS rn
  FROM events_raw
) WHERE rn = 1

The table currently contains three rows for a single (user_id, session_id) pair, and two of those rows share the identical maximum value of `event_timestamp`. Which single best statement describes which row survives the filter `rn = 1`?

options.label: Exactly one row survives, but which one is non-deterministic because the ORDER BY tie is broken arbitrarily by the engine — a secondary deterministic tiebreaker is required.
All rows sharing the maximum `event_timestamp` survive, because ROW_NUMBER() assigns rn = 1 to every tied row.
The row that arrived last (largest `_ingest_timestamp`) always survives, because ROW_NUMBER() automatically falls back to ingestion order.
No row survives the filter, because the query fails with a cardinality error when ORDER BY values are tied.

questions.analysis: ROW_NUMBER() is defined to produce a strictly increasing sequence with no gaps and no ties, so exactly one row per partition receives rn = 1 and the filter keeps exactly one row per (user_id, session_id) — option B is therefore wrong. However, when the ORDER BY expression is tied, the ordering among tied rows is non-deterministic: the engine may pick any of them, so the surviving record can change between runs, which makes the whole pipeline non-reproducible (option C's claim of an automatic ingestion-order fallback is a common misconception; ingestion order is only used if you explicitly write it into the ORDER BY). The query does not error on ties (option D is incorrect). The correct engineering practice is to make the ordering total by adding a deterministic secondary key, for example ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC, _ingest_timestamp DESC, event_id DESC, so that the surviving row is stable across re-runs. This mirrors the unit's warning that you must identify the source of duplication and control which copy survives, since a non-deterministic winner silently changes downstream aggregates [source 2][source 4].

questions.question: A table `line_items` has the composite grain (order_id, line_item_id): a single order contains many line items, and line_item_id is only unique within an order. The table is loaded by an append-only (INSERT) pipeline that is re-run after a failure, and multiple Kafka consumers write to it with at-least-once delivery semantics. A proposed fix uses `df.dropDuplicates(['order_id'])`. Select ALL statements that correctly identify problems with this proposed fix. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: PARTITION BY must use the composite grain (order_id, line_item_id); partitioning by order_id alone collapses every line item of an order into one surviving row and destroys valid data.
Even with the correct partition key, dropDuplicates removes rows based only on the key columns and offers no ordered, deterministic choice of which duplicate survives when ties exist.
dropDuplicates(['order_id']) is sufficient because it removes duplicates by comparing across all columns of the DataFrame, not just the listed keys.

Because the source is at-least-once delivery plus a re-run append-only writer, duplicates can only be eliminated by a window function (for example ROW_NUMBER() with a total ORDER BY) that selects exactly one row per composite key.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: the table's grain is the composite key (order_id, line_item_id). PARTITION BY order_id alone would treat all line items of one order as one partition and keep only a single surviving line, silently deleting valid line items and corrupting order totals — an instance of the exam trap where the deduplication key tests the wrong granularity. Option B is correct: dropDuplicates/`SELECT DISTINCT`-style semantics are key-based, not order-aware, so they cannot guarantee that a specific (for example latest) record survives when duplicates disagree; they simply collapse rows. Option D is correct: the two named duplication mechanisms — at-least-once message delivery (Kafka consumers) and a non-idempotent append-only re-run — mean deterministic, order-aware deduplication is required, and a window function with ROW_NUMBER() and a total ORDER BY is the tool that does this. Option C is a misconception: dropDuplicates with an explicit column subset deduplicates using ONLY those columns; it does not compare all columns, so it cannot be sufficient here. Note the unit's principle that duplicates arise from identifiable mechanisms (at-least-once delivery, replayed ingestion, non-idempotent writes) and must be attributed to a mechanism before a remediation is chosen.

questions.question: Write a Databricks SQL (or Spark SQL) statement that deduplicates a `silver.orders` table down to one row per `order_id`, keeping the record with the largest `order_timestamp`, and guarantees a deterministic result whenever `order_timestamp` is tied. In your answer, (a) give the complete SQL, including PARTITION BY, ORDER BY, the ROW_NUMBER() expression, the outer filter, and the tiebreaker; (b) state one concrete edge case where your tiebreaker can still fail to be total, and how you would fix it; and (c) explain, in one or two sentences, why the ORIGINAL (pre-dedup) append-only pipeline is the root cause that made this deduplication necessary at all.
