Award full credit only if the statement has all four required elements: an inner subquery/CTE computing ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY order_timestamp DESC, <tiebreaker>), an alias such as rn, and an outer WHERE rn = 1. Deduct proportionally for any missing element (each missing element costs 10% of the item).
(2) Deterministic tiebreaker — 20%. The ORDER BY must include at least one additional column that is unique within each partition (for example `_ingest_timestamp DESC` or `event_id DESC`); a bare ORDER BY order_timestamp DESC is a 0 on this component because it leaves ties non-deterministic.
(3) Edge case — 20%. Full credit requires a concrete, plausible edge case AND a stated fix. Acceptable examples: the tiebreaker column itself is nullable or NULL for some rows (fix: add a COALESCE/NULLS LAST ordering or fall back to a monotonically increasing ID); the tiebreaker is itself duplicated by the same replayed ingestion (fix: add a monotonically increasing surrogate/offset such as Kafka offset + partition); the tiebreaker is a timestamp of insufficient precision (fix: use a higher-precision type or a deterministic concatenation of two keys). A purely hypothetical or vague answer earns at most half this component.
(4) Root-cause explanation — 20%. Must explicitly name at least one duplication mechanism from the lesson, i.e. at-least-once delivery (message queues / streaming platforms such as Kafka) or a non-idempotent append-only (INSERT) pipeline re-run. Naming 'the pipeline appended duplicates' without naming the mechanism earns half credit; naming the wrong mechanism (for example claiming exactly-once is guaranteed at transport) earns 0.
Do not award any credit for reasons that conflate deduplication with a completeness/null-handling check: the item is about uniqueness and determinism, not completeness.
questions.analysis:
A reference answer is:

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY order_id
           ORDER BY order_timestamp DESC, _ingest_timestamp DESC, event_id DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM silver.orders
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;

The critical design decisions are, first, that PARTITION BY order_id matches the actual grain of the orders table (order_id is the entity key), and second, that ORDER BY must be TOTAL, not merely ordered by the business timestamp. Because ROW_NUMBER() assigns rn = 1 to exactly one row per partition and cannot produce ties, any tie in the leading ORDER BY key is broken arbitrarily by the engine, so the surviving row would change across runs. Adding _ingest_timestamp DESC and a unique event_id DESC (or a Kafka offset) makes the ordering total and therefore the result reproducible. Edge case: if the tiebreaker column can itself be NULL (for example _ingest_timestamp missing on some bronze rows), the ordering is still not total unless you add NULLS LAST or COALESCE it; if the tiebreaker is duplicated by the same replays (for example a batch re-run preserves _ingest_timestamp), even _ingest_timestamp can tie, and the fix is a monotonic surrogate such as a Kafka offset combined with partition, or a monotonically increasing sequence. Root cause: the duplication was produced upstream — Kafka consumer groups deliver at-least-once so a failure causes redelivery, and an append-only INSERT pipeline re-run appends a second copy of every row — which is exactly why an order-aware, deterministic winner-selection is required. Correctly identifying the mechanism before choosing a remediation is the exam-oriented first step in this unit.

actions.text: Time to put that reasoning to the test. This checkpoint covers what we just walked through — reading PARTITION BY and ORDER BY logic, picking the right partition key, spotting non-deterministic ordering, and knowing when dropDuplicates won't cut it.
Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer before you submit. Once you're done, I'll be right here to go through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Deduplicate Then Upsert into Delta

elements.content: Problem 1

bronze.orders_events is an append-only Delta table fed by an at-least-once CDC (change data capture) feed. In production it holds 1,800,000 rows spread over 1,000,000 distinct order_id values — an average of 1.8 rows per order_id — because (a) every status change is appended as a new version of the order, and (b) a backfill re-delivered a historical window, creating exact copies that differ only in their ingestion timestamp. The downstream job must write a target table whose grain is exactly one row per order, so the first task is to reduce this source to one current row per order_id. Work the six-row extract below by hand, give the deduped result set, and then give the exact SQL.

Extract from bronze.orders_events, shown as order_id | status | amount | updated_at | ingestion_time:

1. O-1001 | placed | 50.00 | 2024-05-01 09:00:00 | 2024-05-01 09:00:05

2. O-1001 | shipped | 50.00 | 2024-05-02 14:30:00 | 2024-05-02 14:30:11

3. O-1002 | placed | 20.00 | 2024-05-01 11:00:00 | 2024-05-01 11:00:03

4. O-1002 | placed | 20.00 | 2024-05-01 11:00:00 | 2024-05-03 02:00:00

5. O-1003 | placed | 75.00 | 2024-05-02 08:00:00 | 2024-05-02 08:00:02

6. O-1004 | packed | 12.50 | 2024-05-02 19:15:00 | 2024-05-02 19:15:09

Rows 3 and 4 are the same business event delivered twice; row 4 is the backfill copy. The target grain is one row per order_id.
Hint: You need a ranking, not a DISTINCT: rank rows inside each order_id partition by the business version column, then keep rank 1.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Fix the grain before writing any SQL. Tidy, analysis-ready data has a well-defined relationship between rows and columns [source 1]; here that relationship is one row per order_id, so the unit of deduplication is the entity (the order), not the physical row. The natural/business key is order_id.

Step 2 — Choose the ordering columns. The current version of an order is the row with the largest updated_at. Because at-least-once transport and the backfill can produce ties, updated_at alone is not enough to define a unique winner, so we add ingestion_time DESC as a tie-break.

Step 3 — Compute ROW_NUMBER() manually. The window PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, ingestion_time DESC assigns:

- Partition O-1001: row 2 (2024-05-02 14:30:00) gets rn = 1; row 1 (2024-05-01 09:00:00) gets rn = 2.

- Partition O-1002: rows 3 and 4 both have updated_at = 2024-05-01 11:00:00, so the tie-break decides. ingestion_time 2024-05-03 02:00:00 > 2024-05-01 11:00:03, so row 4 gets rn = 1 and row 3 gets rn = 2.

- Partition O-1003: single row, rn = 1.

- Partition O-1004: single row, rn = 1.

Step 4 — Filter rn = 1. The deduped result set is 4 rows:

- O-1001 | shipped | 50.00 | 2024-05-02 14:30:00

- O-1002 | placed | 20.00 | 2024-05-01 11:00:00 (the backfill copy is retained; the payload is identical, but the choice had to be deterministic)

- O-1003 | placed | 75.00 | 2024-05-02 08:00:00

- O-1004 | packed | 12.50 | 2024-05-02 19:15:00

Rows removed = 6 - 4 = 2, a 2/6 = 33.3% row reduction on the extract. Scaled to production the same operation collapses 1,800,000 rows into 1,000,000, removing 800,000 rows; by the duplicate-rate definition used earlier in this unit that is $\frac{1{,}800{,}000 - 1{,}000{,}000}{1{,}800{,}000} = 0.4444 = 44.4\%$.

Step 5 — The SQL. Note the outer SELECT uses * EXCEPT (rn) so the view schema matches the target table exactly (the MERGE in the next problem uses UPDATE SET * and INSERT *, which fail if the source carries a stray rn column):

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW deduped AS

SELECT * EXCEPT (rn)

FROM (

SELECT *,

ROW_NUMBER() OVER (

PARTITION BY order_id

ORDER BY updated_at DESC, ingestion_time DESC

) AS rn

FROM bronze.orders_events

) WHERE rn = 1;

Step 6 — Sanity check on the view: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM deduped must return equal numbers (4 and 4 on the extract; 1,000,000 and 1,000,000 in production).

Analysis — Why ROW_NUMBER and not DISTINCT: DISTINCT deduplicates whole physical rows, not entities. Rows 3 and 4 differ in ingestion_time, so SELECT DISTINCT * would keep both and the view would still hold two rows for O-1002 — 6 rows in, 6 rows out. Removing duplicates is a core data-cleaning operation [source 2], but it only works when the deduplication key is chosen at the entity level.

Why not RANK() or DENSE_RANK(): on a tie, RANK() assigns 1 to every tied row, so WHERE rn = 1 returns two rows for O-1002 and the source is no longer unique per key. That breaks the next step of the pipeline: the MERGE would try to modify the same target row from two source rows.

The ordering must be a total order, not a partial one. If updated_at and ingestion_time can both tie (identical backfill files, second-precision timestamps, a batch-constant ingestion_time), ROW_NUMBER falls back to an implementation-defined order that is not guaranteed stable across cluster restarts or repartitioning. The tie-break column must therefore be a stable, source-assigned attribute — never a wall-clock current_timestamp() evaluated at write time, which is a property of the run rather than of the data. This is developed further in the last problem of this scene.

A very common exam distinction: the source having duplicates (at-least-once delivery, CDC replays, backfills) is a different failure from the write pattern creating duplicates (non-idempotent append-only INSERT). Step 1 addresses the first; the MERGE in the next problem addresses the second. Choosing a remediation technique before classifying the mechanism is the standard mistake.

The pattern generalizes to any versioned entity: pick the entity key, pick a deterministic total order over versions, rank, filter to 1. The same expression handles customers, accounts, inventory snapshots, or device telemetry; only the key and the version column change.
Problem 2

The deduped view from the previous problem is ready to be written to silver.orders, which currently holds 1,000,000 rows (one per order_id; the target key is unique by contract). Re-reading bronze.orders_events and re-deduplicating it yields a source of 1,000,000 rows, decomposed as follows: 15,000 order_id values are not present in silver.orders at all (brand-new orders), and 985,000 already exist. Of those 985,000 existing orders, 42,000 carry a strictly newer updated_at than the stored row; the remaining 943,000 incoming rows carry exactly the same updated_at as the stored row.

(a) Write the statement that performs the upsert (update-if-exists, insert-if-not). (b) Compute exactly how many target rows are written on run 1, on run 2 with a byte-identical source, and on run 3 when the source contains 3 brand-new orders and 5 orders whose status changed. (c) Compute the same figures for run 1 and run 2 if the predicate used >= instead of >, and state the ratio of wasted writes.
Hint: MERGE INTO target USING source ON key WHEN MATCHED AND <version is newer> THEN UPDATE WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT.

Worked solution
Step 1 — The statement.

MERGE INTO silver.orders AS t

USING deduped AS s

ON t.order_id = s.order_id

WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET *

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

The ON clause defines identity (which row is the same order). The WHEN MATCHED predicate defines whether the incoming version is allowed to overwrite the stored one. Because the update overwrites in place and keeps no previous version, this is a slowly changing dimension (SCD) Type 1 implementation — the older attribute values are discarded rather than historised.

Step 2 — Run 1 arithmetic. Every source row is evaluated against the ON clause exactly once:

- matched = 985,000, of which the version predicate is true for 42,000;

- not matched = 15,000 (all of which are inserted);

- rows written = 15,000 inserts + 42,000 updates = 57,000;

- target cardinality afterwards = 1,000,000 + 15,000 = 1,015,000 (updates replace in place, so they do not change the count).

The 943,000 matched rows whose version predicate is false match no WHEN clause and are left untouched.

Step 3 — Run 2 with the identical source. The source still has 1,000,000 rows, but silver.orders now contains every one of those keys, so:

- matched = 1,000,000, not matched = 0;

- the version predicate is true for 0 rows, because s.updated_at equals t.updated_at for all of them;

- rows written = 0; target cardinality stays at 1,015,000.

This is what idempotency means formally: running the job $n$ times produces the same end state as running it once, $f(f(x)) = f(x)$. The write is a function of the data, not of the run count.

Step 4 — Run 3 (three new orders, five genuine status changes): rows written = 3 + 5 = 8, and cardinality becomes 1,015,003. The job cost scales with change volume, not table size — that is the payoff of doing the reduction and the comparison inside the engine.

Step 5 — The >= variant, run 1. If the predicate were s.updated_at >= t.updated_at, all 985,000 matched rows satisfy it, so:

- rows written = 15,000 + 985,000 = 1,000,000;

- no-op rewrites = 985,000 - 42,000 = 943,000, i.e. $\frac{943{,}000}{1{,}000{,}000} = 94.3\%$ of the write is useless;

- write amplification versus '>' = $\frac{1{,}000{,}000}{57{,}000} \approx 17.5\times$.

Step 6 — The >= variant, run 2. The source is unchanged, but every one of the 1,000,000 matched rows still satisfies >=, so the job rewrites 1,000,000 rows again — and every subsequent run does the same. Critically, the row count after the run is still 1,015,000, so a count-based verification would report success while the table churns on every execution.

Analysis — The reason this works is that the MERGE predicate makes the write a function of the data rather than of run count. Two guarantees are needed, and they are supplied by different parts of the statement: the ON clause needs the source to be unique per key (guaranteed by the deduped view) AND the target to be unique per key (guaranteed by the table contract), and the WHEN MATCHED predicate needs a monotone version column.

Skipping the dedupe step is the classic failure. Delta requires that each target row be modified by at most one source row; if the source contains 985,000 duplicated keys instead of 1,000,000 unique ones, the merge either fails with a multiple-source-row-matching-target-row error or, in configurations that tolerate it, applies a nondeterministic update — which row wins depends on the execution plan, so the same job can produce different results on consecutive runs. The duplicate-match error is a symptom of a missing Step 1, not a MERGE bug.

Using >= instead of > is the second classic mistake. It is not merely slower: it makes the job non-idempotent in effect even though it is idempotent in result. Every re-run rewrites every matched row, which creates new Parquet files, advances the Delta table version on every run, and invalidates any downstream materialized view (a precomputed, stored query result that refreshes when its source changes) or streaming read of that table. Under >= the count-based check is blind to the problem, which is why the verification step in the next problem must read the write metrics, not only the row count.

One nuance about row counts versus file counts: Delta rewrites whole files, not individual rows (unless deletion vectors are enabled, in which case an update can be recorded as a deletion marker plus a new row rather than rewritten in place). So 42,000 updated rows can still touch many files if the changes are scattered across the table. That is why the operation metrics reported by DESCRIBE HISTORY include both numTargetRowsUpdated and numTargetFilesAdded / numTargetFilesRemoved.

Finally, note where this logic lives. This upsert runs in the silver layer, where the business key and the version rule already exist — the transformation-stage placement of quality work discussed earlier in this unit. Running the same dedupe at bronze would force a choice between blocking the raw feed and letting defects persist downstream.
Problem 3

The pipeline from the previous problem has run twice with the same source. silver.orders now contains 1,015,000 rows. (a) Write the two verification queries that prove the table satisfies its grain contract (exactly one row per order_id) and that a re-run did not change the table, and state the exact expected output of each. (b) Give the DESCRIBE HISTORY metrics you would read to distinguish a truly no-op run 2 from a run that rewrote every row. (c) Suppose the duplicate query returns exactly two offending rows, O-7712 with 3 rows and O-8890 with 2 rows. Name the three most likely causes and give the single query you would run first to discriminate between them.
Hint: A GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 returns zero rows when the grain holds; a no-op run is proven by the write metrics, not by the row count.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Query (a)(i), the grain check:

SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS row_count

FROM silver.orders

GROUP BY order_id

HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Expected output: zero rows. Rows are grouped per entity key and the HAVING clause keeps only keys that violate the one-row-per-key contract, so an empty result set is the proof of uniqueness. Note that this is the same COUNT(*) versus COUNT(DISTINCT ...) logic used for the uniqueness rule earlier in this unit, expressed per key so that it also names the offending keys for remediation.

Step 2 — Query (a)(ii), the aggregate form and the rate:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS k FROM silver.orders;

Expected output: n = 1,015,000 and k = 1,015,000, so the duplicate rate is $\frac{n - k}{n} = \frac{0}{1{,}015{,}000} = 0.00\%$, inside the 0.10% tolerance used by the quality report earlier in this unit.

Step 3 — Query (a)(iii), re-run invariance: capture SELECT COUNT(*) FROM silver.orders before the second run and after it. Both must return 1,015,000. More precisely, the count must be unchanged for a byte-identical source, and it must change by exactly (new keys) on a source with new orders — 1,015,003 after the run 3 described in the previous problem.

Step 4 — Part (b), the write metrics. Run DESCRIBE HISTORY silver.orders and read the operationMetrics of the two MERGE commits:

- Run 1: numSourceRows = 1,000,000, numTargetRowsInserted = 15,000, numTargetRowsUpdated = 42,000, numTargetRowsDeleted = 0.

- Run 2 with an identical source: numSourceRows = 1,000,000, numTargetRowsInserted = 0, numTargetRowsUpdated = 0, numTargetRowsDeleted = 0, and numTargetFilesAdded should be 0 (or only commit metadata).

This is the discriminating measurement: a job that had used >= would report numTargetRowsUpdated = 1,000,000 on run 2 while the row count stayed at 1,015,000. Row count alone cannot tell a no-op from a full rewrite; the metric can.

Step 5 — Part (c), diagnosis. The three most likely causes:

1. The write pattern created duplicates. The source was not reduced to one row per key (Step 1 skipped, or the rn filter lost), so two source rows modified the same target row, or a prior non-idempotent append-only INSERT already put duplicate keys in silver.orders.

2. NULL keys. The ON clause t.order_id = s.order_id can never be TRUE when order_id is NULL, because NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE. Every NULL-keyed source row is therefore classified as NOT MATCHED on every run and inserted again — a completeness defect upstream, in a column used as a join key, silently converted into an unbounded uniqueness defect downstream.

3. Concurrent writers. Two runs of the pipeline overlapping in time (a retried job, an Auto Loader stream plus a scheduled backfill) both read the same target snapshot and both insert the same new key.

Run this first, against the deduped source (not against silver):

SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows,

COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS distinct_keys,

SUM(CASE WHEN order_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS null_keys

FROM deduped;

Interpretation: if total_rows > distinct_keys, cause 1 is confirmed and Step 1 of the previous problem is broken. If null_keys > 0, cause 2 is confirmed — the rows accumulate by exactly null_keys per run, so after 10 runs there would be 10 x null_keys extra rows and the GROUP BY check would show a single NULL group with COUNT(*) = 10 x null_keys. If both are clean and silver still has duplicates, the defect predates this job (cause 1's append-only history) or is concurrency (cause 3), and you can confirm the history with DESCRIBE HISTORY silver.orders plus the ingestion timestamps on the offending rows.

Analysis — Verification is a test of a written contract, and the contract here has two clauses that need two different queries: uniqueness (structural) and invariance under re-run (dynamic). Removing duplicates and verifying accuracy is explicitly part of preparing collected data for analysis, not an optional final flourish [source 4].

The subtle lesson is that a count-based check is necessary but not sufficient. It detects duplicated keys; it cannot detect a run that rewrote every row, and it cannot detect a run that wrote a different value for the same key (that failure mode is the subject of the next problem). Reading numTargetRowsUpdated / numTargetRowsInserted from the Delta commit closes the first gap, and a value fingerprint closes the second.

NULL keys deserve emphasis because they are an exam trap in two layers. At the query level, COUNT(col) ignores NULLs — the trap already seen in the completeness check — so a null count taken on the wrong column hides the defect. At the join level, SQL three-valued logic means NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, so a MERGE never matches NULL-keyed rows and inserts them forever. The remediations are to enforce NOT NULL on the natural key before the write, or to use a null-safe equality in the ON clause (Databricks SQL supports the null-safe equality operator).

A useful debugging primitive: Delta time travel lets you compare the state before and after a commit, e.g. SELECT COUNT(*) FROM silver.orders VERSION AS OF <n-1>, so you do not have to reconstruct what the table looked like before the run.

Finally, note the placement decision. This verification runs in the transformation layer, where the business key already exists; placing an equivalent check only at serving (gold) would protect consumers but detect the defect after the expensive MERGE has already been committed, and remediation would need a backfill.
Problem 4

The upstream CDC connector stores updated_at as a TIMESTAMP truncated to second precision, and the ingestion job populates ingestion_time with a batch-level constant (every row written by one run of the backfill receives the identical value). A backfill file contains two rows for the same order, shown as order_id | status | amount | updated_at | ingestion_time:

1. O-2001 | placed | 100.00 | 2024-05-04 10:00:00 | 2024-05-04 12:00:00

2. O-2001 | cancelled | 100.00 | 2024-05-04 10:00:00 | 2024-05-04 12:00:00

The upstream truth is that the placed event occurred at 10:00:00.100 and the cancelled event at 10:00:00.900; truncation to seconds made them look simultaneous, and the backfill gave them the same ingestion_time. Run A of the pipeline wrote cancelled into silver.orders. After a cluster restart, which changed the shuffle partitioning, run B wrote placed. In both runs the duplicate query returned zero rows and SELECT COUNT(*) returned 1,015,000. Explain why the verification passed, quantify the downstream impact given that gold.orders_placed_by_day counts orders with status = placed and that 2024-05-04 has 12,000 orders, and give a fixed dedupe expression plus a verification that would have caught the flip.
Hint: ROW_NUMBER produces an arbitrary winner when the ORDER BY has a tie; a stable total order needs a tie-break that is a property of the data, not of the run.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Why the row choice was undefined. The ranking expression is ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, ingestion_time DESC), evaluated for O-2001:

- row 1: updated_at = 2024-05-04 10:00:00, ingestion_time = 2024-05-04 12:00:00;

- row 2: updated_at = 2024-05-04 10:00:00, ingestion_time = 2024-05-04 12:00:00.

Both ordering columns compare equal, so the two rows are tied and the window's ORDER BY defines a partial order, not a total one. Spark is free to return either row as rn = 1, and which one it returns depends on the shuffle layout, partition ordering, and sorting stability — all of which can change between runs. Run A and run B are both correct executions of the same query; they simply observed different tie orders.

Step 2 — Why the verification passed. The structural contract is one row per order_id, and both runs satisfied it: for every key exactly one row was produced, so GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 returned zero rows, and the cardinality check returned 1,015,000 both times. The check verifies the grain, not the value. Nothing in the two queries inspects which of the tied source rows survived, so a deterministic-but-wrong choice and a nondeterministic choice look identical.

Step 3 — Quantify the downstream impact. gold.orders_placed_by_day for 2024-05-04:

- run A: O-2001 has status cancelled, so it is excluded; count = 12,000 - 1 = 11,999;

- run B: O-2001 has status placed, so it is included; count = 12,000.

Absolute difference = 1 order; relative difference = $\frac{1}{12{,}000} = 0.0083\%$. That looks negligible, but the size of the error is not bounded by this example — it equals the number of conflicting keys in the batch. With 4,000 conflicting keys in a day, the reported figure swings by up to 4,000, i.e. 33% of 12,000, and any report built on the table inherits the swing. The real defect is that the pipeline is not a function of its input: identical input, different output.

Step 4 — The fix, in order of preference.

(a) Repair the ordering data so a total order exists. Store the full-precision timestamp (microseconds) instead of a second-truncated TIMESTAMP: 10:00:00.100 and 10:00:00.900 are then comparable and cancelled wins deterministically.

(b) If the truncation cannot be fixed, add a stable, source-assigned tie-break that is unique within the partition:

ROW_NUMBER() OVER (

PARTITION BY order_id

ORDER BY updated_at DESC,

ingestion_time DESC,

event_id DESC

) AS rn

event_id is written by the source and is therefore reproducible across runs. If no such column exists, use file provenance, which is also stable for a given file:

ROW_NUMBER() OVER (

PARTITION BY order_id

ORDER BY updated_at DESC,

_metadata.file_modification_time DESC,

_metadata.file_path DESC

) AS rn

(c) Never use a wall-clock current_timestamp() as an ordering column. It is a property of the run, not of the data, so a re-run of a backfill assigns new values and can reorder history. Prefer ingest-time metadata supplied by the platform (file modification time and path from the Auto Loader-style _metadata column), which is a deterministic function of the input.

(d) If two genuinely contradictory events exist at the same instant, do not silently pick one — encode a business rule such as a status precedence (cancelled > shipped > placed) in a CASE expression inside the ORDER BY, and raise a data-quality alert for the conflicting key.

Step 5 — The verification that would have caught it. Compare a value-level fingerprint across the two runs:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS n,

COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS k,

SUM(CRC32(CONCAT_WS('|', order_id, status, CAST(amount AS STRING)))) AS value_fingerprint

FROM silver.orders;

Run A and run B both give n = k = 1,015,000, but they produce different value_fingerprints. Recording that fingerprint per run, or using a row-level hash column in silver (which makes changed rows visible in a single pass), turns nondeterminism into a failed check rather than a silent drift.

Analysis — The distinction this problem teaches is between a structural contract and a semantic one. 'Exactly one row per key' is structural: it is checkable with COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT key), and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, and it is what most candidates verify. 'The same input produces the same output' is semantic and dynamic: it requires either a value fingerprint or a comparison of the write metrics plus a value hash across runs. A deduplication job can satisfy the first contract perfectly while violating the second, and the resulting table looks healthy by every count-based test.

Why the tie happens is a data-modelling lesson rather than a SQL lesson. A ranking is only well defined when the ORDER BY is a total order on each partition; ties hand the decision to the execution engine. Truncating a timestamp to seconds, or populating an ordering column with a batch-constant run timestamp, destroys the total order. The same class of defect appears with inconsistent categorical values: if the source emits 'cancelled' in one row and 'Canceled' in another, the two rows are not merely tied on time, they also fail to group together in downstream aggregation, so standardisation of values is part of cleaning, not a cosmetic step [source 5].

The consequences are exactly the ones data cleaning is meant to prevent: flawed input produces skewed results and misleading conclusions [source 6]. A non-idempotent, non-deterministic silver table propagates into every downstream metric, dashboard, and model, and because the count checks pass, the defect is discovered by a business stakeholder noticing a number that moves on its own rather than by the pipeline's own tests.

Finally, the fix generalises past this example. Any time a window function chooses 'the latest' row, ask two questions: is the ORDER BY a total order, and is every ordering column a reproducible property of the data? The first question is answered by adding a unique tie-break; the second by refusing to order on anything generated at run time. The same discipline applies to SCD Type 2 pipelines that must decide which incoming version closes the previous one.

actions.text: Now let's put everything we just covered about window-function deduplication to work in a full end-to-end problem. This is the capstone exercise for this section: deduplicate a change feed and then upsert it into Delta.

Here's the setup. bronze.orders_events is an append-only Delta table. On average it holds 1.8 rows per order_id, each with a different updated_at value, and a backfill job has added re-run duplicates on top of that. Your goal: build silver.orders with exactly one current row per order_id, and make the job safe to re-run any number of times.
Before scrolling to the solution, here's your hint. You need a ranking, not a DISTINCT. Rank rows within each order_id and keep only the winner.

Step one — fix the grain before writing anything. We CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW deduped, selecting from a subquery that adds ROW_NUMBER OVER PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, ingestion_time DESC as rn, then filter WHERE rn = 1. Notice the tie-break on ingestion_time — without it, 'latest' could flip between runs.

Why ROW_NUMBER and not DISTINCT? DISTINCT eliminates identical rows, but our duplicates are not identical — they differ in updated_at. ROW_NUMBER lets us deterministically pick one row per key, which is exactly the grain contract silver.orders needs.
Problem two builds on that view. The deduped view from the previous problem is read as the source for an upsert into silver.orders.
Hint for this one: MERGE INTO target USING source ON key, and then WHEN MATCHED and WHEN NOT MATCHED branches to describe what should happen in each case.

Step two — upsert idempotently. MERGE INTO silver.orders AS t USING deduped AS s ON t.order_id = s.order_id. WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET star. WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT star. That single statement handles both the update and the insert atomically.

And here's the analysis — why this works. Because the window function reduced the source to one deterministic row per key, the MERGE never sees duplicate matches on the join key. And the predicate s.updated_at > t.updated_at makes the write a function of the data rather than of how many times the job ran.
Problem three asks you to verify. The pipeline from the previous problem has run twice. Hint: a GROUP BY with HAVING COUNT(star) > 1 will return the offending order_ids if the grain is broken.

Step three — the verification query. SELECT order_id, COUNT(star) FROM silver.orders GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(star) > 1 must return zero rows, and the row count must be unchanged after a second run.
Verification is a test of a written contract, not just a smoke test. It proves both uniqueness — one row per order — and idempotence — same result after re-runs.
Now problem four — the subtle one. The upstream CDC connector stores updated_at as a timestamp with millisecond precision, and two events for the same order can share the same updated_at.
Hint: ROW_NUMBER produces an arbitrary winner when the ordering columns tie. So what do you need to add to make the result deterministic?

Step one — the row choice was undefined when both sides of the ORDER BY tied. The fix is a tie-break column that is guaranteed unique or at least monotonic, such as ingestion_time or an event sequence number from the connector.

The distinction this problem teaches: updated_at captures business time, but it doesn't guarantee total ordering. A deterministic dedupe needs both the business ordering and a stable tie-break. And when you write the MERGE, remember to strictly use greater-than, not greater-than-or-equal, otherwise a second run with equal timestamps will rewrite identical rows and churn the table's version history. Framed this way, you now have the exact vocabulary the certification assesses: deterministic dedupe, idempotent upsert, and version churn.

scenes.title: Comparison: Four Deduplication Patterns

elements.content: Dimension  |  dropDuplicates()  |  ROW_NUMBER window + filter  |  Delta MERGE upsert  |  Insert-only append + MAX(created_timestamp)

Correctness when non-key columns differ
dropDuplicates(): Only removes rows that are byte-for-byte identical across every column, so two records with the same order_id but different shipping addresses both survive and the key remains duplicated.
ROW_NUMBER window + filter: Keeps exactly one row per partition key because ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_timestamp DESC) = 1 deterministically ranks and discards the losers, so non-key column conflicts are resolved by the chosen tie-break.
Delta MERGE upsert: Updates the target row's non-key columns with the matched source values, so divergent addresses, statuses, or amounts are reconciled to the newest source version rather than merely discarded.
Insert-only append + MAX(created_timestamp): Never compares or overwrites anything; every version of every record is retained and the reader must resolve conflicts by selecting the row whose created_timestamp equals MAX(created_timestamp) per key at query time.

Safe to re-run (idempotency)
dropDuplicates(): Idempotent only against exact duplicates already present in the same DataFrame; re-running a job that appends then calls dropDuplicates() on the union still reproduces the duplicate if the source re-delivers a differently-versioned row.
ROW_NUMBER window + filter: Idempotent as a batch transformation because the window ranking is recomputed from the full input each run, so re-processing the same partition yields the same single surviving row.
Delta MERGE upsert: Idempotent by construction: the MERGE match condition (target.order_id = source.order_id) means a second run matches the row it just wrote and updates it in place instead of inserting a copy.
Insert-only append + MAX(created_timestamp): Not idempotent at write time; re-running the ingestion appends a second physical copy of the event, and correctness is restored only by the read-time MAX(created_timestamp) filter that hides the older duplicate.

Compute and storage cost
dropDuplicates(): Cheapest option: a single shuffle-free (or single-shuffle) exact-row comparison over the DataFrame, with no window sort and no join against a target table.
ROW_NUMBER window + filter: Moderate cost: requires a full shuffle and sort per partition key because ROW_NUMBER must order all candidate rows before filtering, and the sort cost grows with the number of versions per key.
Delta MERGE upsert: Highest cost of the three write-side patterns: each MERGE performs a join between source and target plus a rewrite of every matched and inserted file, and on a 5,000,000-row target an unconditional full-table MERGE can rewrite gigabytes for a handful of changed keys.
Insert-only append + MAX(created_timestamp): Lowest write-side cost per event (pure append, no join, no sort) but the highest read-side and storage cost, since the table grows without bound and every downstream query pays an aggregation over all historical versions.

Preserves history
dropDuplicates(): No: duplicate rows are deleted, so the fact that a record was ever redelivered is erased along with the row.
ROW_NUMBER window + filter: No: all but the winning row are dropped by the filter, so prior versions of the entity are permanently lost unless a separate history table was written first.
Delta MERGE upsert: Optionally yes: history can be preserved only if the MERGE is paired with an SCD Type 2 (slowly changing dimension — keeping one current row plus dated prior versions) target design or Change Data Feed; a plain MERGE keeps no audit trail.
Insert-only append + MAX(created_timestamp): Yes by design: the full stream of versions is retained, which makes late arrivals first-class rather than exceptions, at the price of table growth, lookup overhead, and the need to define a record sunset date that periodically prunes obsolete versions.

Typical use case
dropDuplicates(): Cleaning an already-assembled batch where suspicion is simple exact-row duplication, such as a CSV landed twice with identical contents.
ROW_NUMBER window + filter: The general-purpose batch workhorse: producing one current row per key in a silver table after a join or union has multiplied rows, exactly the pattern exercised in the ROW_NUMBER deduplication lab.
Delta MERGE upsert: Required when you must update a target incrementally and stay idempotent on re-run — for example, applying CDC (change data capture) events into a Delta Lake target so that a replayed Kafka offset does not double-count.
Insert-only append + MAX(created_timestamp): The append-only landing/bronze pattern for streaming ingestion where nothing may be discarded, late events are expected, and the current state is always derived by reading MAX(created_timestamp) per key.

Worked example: 5,000,000 orders with replays and late data
dropDuplicates(): If all 5,000,000 rows are exact duplicates of a prior 5,000,000-row load, dropDuplicates() returns 5,000,000 rows and the duplicate rate the uniqueness check measured earlier — (5,000,000 - 4,992,500) / 5,000,000 = 0.15% — drops to 0%, so the batch passes the 0.10% tolerance.
ROW_NUMBER window + filter: If the same order_id appears three times with updated_timestamp values 09:00, 11:00, and 13:00, ROW_NUMBER() = 1 keeps only the 13:00 row, so the batch emits 4,992,500 distinct keys and the duplicate rate falls to 0% while preserving the newest attribute values.
Delta MERGE upsert: If the source re-delivers yesterday's batch, MERGE matches all 5,000,000 keys, updates the existing rows, and inserts 0 new rows; a second identical run also inserts 0 rows, so counts stay flat and the 0.15% duplicate rate never reappears.
Insert-only append + MAX(created_timestamp): Under insert-only, the table now holds 10,000,000 physical rows for 5,000,000 logical entities; a query with MAX(created_timestamp) still returns 5,000,000 rows, but it scans and aggregates twice the data, and a late event timestamped 47 minutes behind the latest order is simply an extra version rather than an error.

Fit with the quality checks already implemented
dropDuplicates(): Feeds directly into the uniqueness query COUNT(*) versus COUNT(DISTINCT order_id): after dropDuplicates(), duplicate rate = (COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)) / COUNT(*) must be 0%, and any residual signals non-exact duplication the pattern cannot fix.
ROW_NUMBER window + filter: Produces the clean silver input that the completeness check expects, so a null rate of 175,000 / 5,000,000 = 3.5% is still measured on the surviving current rows and still fails the 1.0% tolerance independently of deduplication.
Delta MERGE upsert: Because it rewrites the target in place, MERGE must run before the uniqueness check, otherwise the check would compare an already-clean target against a replayed source and report a false defect.
Insert-only append + MAX(created_timestamp): Because duplicates remain physical, the uniqueness check will report the true physical duplicate rate (for example 50% after one full replay) and must be paired with a logical-count check that filters on MAX(created_timestamp) per key. [source 2]

Takeaway — Choose dropDuplicates() only when duplication is exact-row duplication and re-run idempotency is not required; it is the cheapest pattern and the one to name when the exam says 'identical rows' or 'exact duplicates'. [source 2]

Takeaway — Choose ROW_NUMBER window + filter when a batch job must emit exactly one current row per key and non-key columns may differ; it is the general-purpose workhorse and the deterministic tie-break (MAX(updated_timestamp), MAX(version), or MAX(ingestion_time)) is what makes it defensible. [source 1]

Takeaway — Choose Delta MERGE upsert whenever the requirement says 'must be idempotent on re-run' or the target must be updated incrementally, since the match condition on the business key makes a replayed batch an update rather than an insert. [source 2]

Takeaway — Choose insert-only append + MAX(created_timestamp) when the full history must be preserved and late arrivals must be first-class, accepting table growth, lookup overhead, and the obligation to set a record sunset date. [source 5]

Takeaway — Exam guidance: match the pattern to the stated requirement before computing anything — 'must be idempotent on re-run' points to MERGE, 'must keep one current row per key in a batch job' points to ROW_NUMBER, and only 'remove exact duplicate rows' justifies dropDuplicates(). [source 1]

Takeaway — Whichever pattern is chosen, verify it with the uniqueness check already taught — COUNT(*) versus COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) and a duplicate-rate threshold — because a deduplication pattern that is never measured is a claim, not a guarantee. [source 6]

actions.text: We've just built up the ROW_NUMBER deduplication technique, and now it's time to widen the lens. This decision table puts four deduplication patterns side by side, and it's exactly the kind of comparison the exam likes to draw on. The rows are our four candidates: dropDuplicates, ROW_NUMBER window plus filter, Delta MERGE upsert, and the insert-only append pattern where you query MAX of created_timestamp. The columns are the dimensions that actually decide the choice.

Start with cost, because it's often the first thing people reach for. dropDuplicates is the cheapest option — one pass, no shuffle on extra keys, no merge machinery. But that cheapness comes with a hard limit we'll see in a moment.

Here's the catch on correctness. dropDuplicates only matches on exact rows — if two records share the same key but differ in any non-key column, dropDuplicates keeps both. ROW_NUMBER is the general-purpose workhorse here, because you control the ordering and can keep exactly one row per key regardless of what the other columns look like.

Next, idempotency — safe to re-run. Both dropDuplicates and ROW_NUMBER are idempotent when they write to a fresh target, because a second run produces the same result. MERGE is the one that's designed from the ground up to be re-run safely against a live target, which is why the exam ties the phrase 'must be idempotent on re-run' directly to MERGE.

Then there's history. dropDuplicates and ROW_NUMBER both discard duplicates, so they don't preserve history. The insert-only append pattern is the opposite: it never deletes anything, so every replay and every late arrival lives in the table. That makes late-arriving data first-class, but you pay for it with table growth, lookup overhead, and the need for a record sunset date.

Finally, typical use case. dropDuplicates is for cleaning an already-ingested batch where you know duplicates are exact repeats. ROW_NUMBER is the batch workhorse when you must keep one current row per key. MERGE is required whenever you must update a target incrementally. And insert-only is for audit-style tables where nothing may be thrown away.

Let's ground this with the worked example on the slide: five million orders with replays and late corrections. dropDuplicates would collapse exact replays cheaply, but it would leave a corrected order sitting alongside its original. ROW_NUMBER would keep the newest version of each order. MERGE would let you upsert the correction straight into the target. And insert-only would preserve both, letting MAX(created_timestamp) pick the winner at query time.

Lock in the exam guidance: match the pattern to the requirement, not the other way around. If the requirement says 'must be idempotent on re-run', that points to MERGE. If it says 'must keep one current row per key in a batch job', that points to ROW_NUMBER.

And whichever pattern you choose, the closing takeaway stands: verify it. Confirm the row counts, confirm the key is unique in the target, and confirm a second run changes nothing. That verification step is what separates a working pipeline from one that merely passed once.

actions.topic: Your team must ingest a daily change feed into a Delta table, and the auditors require that every correction be preserved for twelve months.
actions.prompt: Given the four patterns we just compared, which one would you reach for, and which column of the decision table drove your choice most strongly?

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Choosing a Deduplication Pattern

questions.question: A nightly Delta Lake pipeline ingests order events from Kafka, writes them to a bronze table with an append-only INSERT pattern, and must remain safe to re-run after a mid-job failure. Late deliveries and replays WILL occur, so the transport layer provides at-least-once delivery only. Which deduplication pattern best satisfies the explicit requirement that the pipeline be idempotent under re-runs?

options.label: Add a DISTINCT clause to every SELECT so that duplicate rows are dropped before they reach the target table, leaving the target append-only.

Keep one row per business key by applying ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_timestamp DESC, ingestion_time DESC) and filtering to row_number = 1, then writing the surviving rows with a MERGE on order_id so a re-run converges to the same target state.
Partition the bronze table by ingestion_date and prune partitions older than seven days so that the volume of duplicate rows stays bounded over time.
Switch the pipeline from append-only inserts to blind INSERT OVERWRITE of the whole target table on every run so that each run starts from a clean slate.

questions.analysis: The stated requirement is idempotency under re-runs, and only the ROW_NUMBER plus MERGE pattern is idempotent: the tie-break is deterministic, so the same key always resolves to the same surviving row no matter how many times the job runs, and MERGE on the business key makes the second run a no-op rather than a second copy. Option A is the classic misconception that DISTINCT equals deduplication: DISTINCT compares entire rows, so two events for the same order_id that differ in timestamp or status are both 'distinct' and both survive, so a re-run still multiplies rows. Option C is the 'manage the symptom' trap — pruning reduces storage but does not stop each new run from appending another copy, so counts are still inflated and the pattern is not idempotent. Option D is destructive and non-idempotent in effect: a failed run that overwrites before completing can leave the table truncated or half-written, and blind overwrite destroys the history that a key-plus-ordering dedupe pattern preserves. This test point is the headline judgement the checkpoint assesses: select the pattern that satisfies an explicit idempotency requirement rather than one that merely reduces duplicate volume [source 2].

questions.question: A data engineer proposes a solution to the duplicate-row problem in a silver fact table that currently contains 8,400,000 rows. The proposal is: 'Run a single dedupe job that keeps the highest updated_at per order_id and writes the result with INSERT OVERWRITE, then move on.' Which statements correctly describe the limitations of that proposal? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: 'Remove duplicate rows' and 'maintain one current row per key' are different goals, and the proposal collapses them into one step, which means the table silently loses all prior versions of each order instead of retaining history for slowly changing dimensions (SCD) analysis.

INSERT OVERWRITE is idempotent in the sense that each run produces the same row set, but it is not safe under partial failure: if the job dies after the overwrite begins, the target can be truncated without the surviving rows ever being written.
Because the dedupe key is order_id and the ordering column is updated_at, the surviving row is deterministic, so duplicates cannot reappear on a subsequent ingestion of the same batch.

The proposal's win is bounded by the maximum updated_at per key, so 8,400,000 input rows collapse to at most the number of distinct order_id values, and any downstream metric computed on the pre-dedupe table would have been overstated by the ratio of rows to keys.

questions.analysis: Correct selections A, B and D map to the three cost and history implications this checkpoint tests. A is correct because dropping duplicate rows is a set operation on the current batch, while maintaining one current row per key is a stateful contract that also implies deciding what happens to prior versions — an SCD (slowly changing dimensions, i.e. tracking how an entity's attribute values change over time) design question that INSERT OVERWRITE simply deletes away [source 2]. B is correct because deterministic output per run does not make a destructive write safe if it aborts partway; the classic remedy is a MERGE or a write-to-staging-then-swap, not a direct overwrite. D is correct and is the concrete arithmetic: if 8,400,000 rows represent k distinct order_id values, the pre-dedupe table overstates any row-count-based revenue or conversion metric by 8,400,000 / k, so removing duplicates is not cosmetic [source 6]. C is the distractor that mirrors a real student misconception — it confuses local determinism with global idempotency. A deterministic tie-break guarantees WHICH row survives, but if the pipeline is append-only and re-ingests the same batch, the duplicate rows still arrive and a one-shot overwrite job that only runs once will not re-clean them. This checkpoint's emphasis on spotting idempotency failures in proposed solutions is exactly what C inverts.

questions.question: A colleague hands you this remediation plan for a silver orders table: 'Stream from Kafka into bronze with append-only writes, MERGE bronze into silver on order_id, then after the MERGE run a dedupe pass to remove duplicate rows from silver.' Using the key-plus-ordering pattern, explain the correct ordering of dedupe-then-merge steps, state the deterministic tie-break you would choose and why, and describe one concrete way the colleague's ordering produces a wrong result on a re-run.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Correct ordering stated explicitly — dedupe to one row per key in the staging/bronze layer BEFORE the MERGE (roughly 40%). (2) Deterministic tie-break justified — e.g. updated_timestamp DESC, then ingestion_time or a monotonic version column as a secondary key so ties resolve identically on every run (about 30%). (3) Concrete wrong-result demonstration of the colleague's ordering — e.g. duplicates from an at-least-once redelivery reach silver first, MERGE into a non-unique key can raise an ambiguous-match error, or the post-hoc dedupe deletes rows that later ingestion legitimately needed, so a re-run does not converge to the same table state and counts are inflated by the duplicate rate (about 30%). Award partial credit for naming ROW_NUMBER or MERGE correctly but reversing the order.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. The correct sequence is: (1) ingest to bronze with a raw append, (2) apply dedupe in the staging/bronze layer using ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_timestamp DESC, ingestion_time DESC) and keep row_number = 1, (3) then MERGE the single-surviving-row-per-key result into silver on order_id. The tie-break must be deterministic because the whole point of the pattern is that a re-run produces the same winner; updated_timestamp DESC breaks the primary tie, and ingestion_time (or a monotonic version column) breaks ties between rows that share a timestamp, so the result is stable across runs. The colleague's ordering is wrong on two counts. First, it MERGEs before dedupe, so the at-least-once redeliveries described in the unit's sources reach silver as duplicate keys; MERGE on a non-unique key can raise an ambiguous-match error or, worse, apply an arbitrary match. Second, running dedupe on silver AFTER the MERGE is a late remedy: duplicates have already been joined and aggregated downstream, and a destructive dedupe pass can discard rows that a later run would have needed. On a re-run, silver never converges to the same state — its row count inflates roughly by the duplicate rate — so the pipeline fails the idempotency requirement, and the fix is to move the dedupe upstream and make the MERGE consume a unique key. This ordering discipline is what this checkpoint calls 'explain the correct ordering of dedupe-then-merge steps' [source 1] [source 4].

actions.text: Now let's check whether the four deduplication patterns we just compared have settled in. This checkpoint is all about pattern-selection judgement, so read each scenario carefully and think about what the explicit requirement actually demands before you pick.

Work through each question on your own — there's a mix of single-answer, multi-select, and a short written explanation here, so don't rush the last one. I'll be right here once you submit to walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Late-Arriving Data: Event Time vs Process Time

elements.content: Late-Arriving Data: Event Time vs Process Time
A record has three distinct timestamps, and conflating them is the root cause of both missed and double-counted results.

Three clocks in one pipeline

• Event time — when the action happened at the source

• Ingestion time — when the record reached the platform

• Process time — when the pipeline actually handled the record

A record arriving late still carries its original event time; only process time moves.
Late data is normal, not an error. Offline mobile devices, network outages, batch backfills, clock skew, and timezone bugs all deliver events out of order [source 4].

Windowed aggregates computed on process time place the event in whichever window the pipeline was in — not the window the event belongs to. Re-running the window appends a second answer instead of replacing the first.

Worked example

Event at 11:58 arrives at 12:07. Process-time window [12:00–13:00] counts it in the wrong hour; the [11:00–12:00] window already closed.
Watermarks bound how long a streaming query waits for late events, trading result latency against state size and dropped records.
Exam trap: append-only writes + process-time windows both miss late events and duplicate recomputed windows.
Sources: MUN data processing chapter [source 1]; field quality-control checks [source 4]; data-cleaning definition and duplicate handling [source 2].

actions.text: Now that we've seen how duplicates creep in, let's tackle the other half of that same problem: late-arriving data. This is one of the most commonly tested conceptual distinctions on the associate exam, so let's get it precise.

The topic is late-arriving data, and the key idea is the tension between event time and process time. When those two disagree, records land in the wrong window — and that is where results get missed or double-counted.

Every record in a pipeline carries three distinct clocks. Event time is when the action actually happened at the source — the real-world timestamp on the transaction. Ingestion time is when that record reached the platform. And process time is when the pipeline actually handled it. Those three clocks can be minutes, hours, or even days apart.

Here's the crucial one: process time. It is simply the wall clock on the machine when the record gets handled. It has nothing to do with when the business event occurred. Timestamps drift between those two all the time — a phone that was offline for hours sends its events the moment it reconnects.

And here's the mindset shift: late data is normal, not an error. Offline mobile devices, network outages, batch backfills, clock skew, and timezone bugs all deliver events out of order. A healthy pipeline is designed to expect that, not to reject it.

Walk through the worked example on the slide. An event happens at 11:58, but it arrives at 12:07. If you window on process time, that event gets assigned to the 12:00 window — the wrong bucket entirely. And if the job later re-runs and appends a second answer, you've both missed the original count and double-counted the corrected one.

This is where watermarks come in. A watermark bounds how long a streaming query waits for late events before it commits a result. It's a deliberate trade-off: a longer watermark catches more late data but grows state and delays results, while a shorter watermark produces answers faster but drops stragglers.

Finally, memorize this exam trap: append-only writes combined with process-time windows both miss late events and duplicate results when a window is recomputed. When you see that pairing in a question, that's almost always the answer they're steering you toward. Next, we'll put watermarks to work in an interactive lab.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Late-Arriving Data

questions.question: A streaming pipeline uses event-time windows of 10 minutes and a watermark defined as 'max observed event_time minus 5 minutes'. A new event arrives whose event_time falls inside a window that the engine has already closed and emitted because the watermark had passed the window end. Databricks documentation calls this a late, out-of-order event. According to exam-oriented watermark semantics, which handling is correct?

options.label: The engine will reopen the closed window automatically and re-emit a corrected aggregate, because watermarks only delay, never finalize

The event is dropped from the aggregate result by default; teams that must not lose it rely on an explicit policy such as allowing lateness, writing to a separate 'late' sink, or reprocessing the affected window from the raw source
The event is inserted into the already-emitted result as an extra row without touching the existing aggregate, so the count stays correct with no extra logic
The event is converted to the current processing time and placed in the current open window, because event time is only used for display

questions.analysis: A watermark is a promise that the engine believes no data older than the watermark will still arrive. Once the watermark passes a window's end, the engine can finalize and emit that window and discard its state. By definition, an event arriving after that point is 'late' with respect to the watermark, and the default behavior of event-time engines is to drop events that fall before the watermark because the window state no longer exists. Reopening a closed window (option A) is not the default; it would require a stateful engine that retains all closed windows, which defeats the purpose of bounded state. Option C confuses an append-only fact table that includes a status flag or a retraction model with a streaming aggregate that has already emitted; simply appending a row breaks the aggregate unless the downstream consumer is designed to re-aggregate. Option D is exactly the mistake of substituting processing time for event time, which corrupts the answer to the question 'when did this happen in the real world?' The exam objective is to pick an explicit remediation (allowed lateness, side output, or reprocessing) before assuming the engine will fix it, which is consistent with the data quality dimension of timeliness discussed earlier in this unit [source 2].

questions.question: A team runs a Spark Structured Streaming job that writes to a silver Delta table using an append-only INSERT pattern. The job has a 5-minute event-time window and a watermark of 2 minutes. Several sources of duplication and lateness are combined below. Select ALL pipeline designs that will DOUBLE COUNT a given event's contribution when a window is recomputed or reprocessed. (Choose all that apply.)

options.label: A kafka consumer that redelivers a message after a broker failure, plus an append-only INSERT into the silver table that has no deduplication key logic
A batch job that is re-run with the same input window, appending the same events again into a table read by a downstream SUM() with no MERGE and no deduplication
A stream that is stopped after emitting window W, restarted from an earlier checkpoint offset, and allowed to re-emit window W as new rows without a Delta MERGE keyed on the window identity

A stream that writes each final window result with MERGE INTO silver_agg t USING new_batch s ON t.window_start = s.window_start AND t.window_end = s.window_end WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *

questions.analysis: Duplication is created whenever the same logical event is written more than once AND the downstream read is a pure append that counts rows rather than a set-valued operation keyed on the entity. Option A is the classic at-least-once delivery combined with a non-idempotent append: the transport does not guarantee exactly-once, so re-delivery is possible, and with no dedupe key the second copy is a real row [source 5]. Option B is the job re-run collision: re-running a batch that reads the same window and appends to a table read with SUM() adds a second copy of every row [source 2]. Option C is the checkpoint-replay collision: restarting from an earlier offset forces re-emission of window W, and without a window-scoped MERGE the second emission is appended as fresh rows [source 6]. Option D is the correct idempotent pattern: the MERGE uses a deterministic business key (window_start + window_end) so a recomputation updates the existing aggregate instead of adding a second one. The key discriminator the exam tests is whether the write pattern is keyed and set-valued (idempotent) or append-only (non-idempotent). This mirrors the earlier lesson's point that duplicates originate in at-least-once delivery, replayed ingestion, and non-idempotent writes, not in the analytical query itself.

questions.question: A team states a business requirement: 'For each 10-minute event-time window, we need a count of distinct user sessions that is correct within a bounded state footprint. Events may arrive out of order by up to 4 minutes, and after that we are willing to drop them. The streaming engine must retain only a bounded amount of state.' Explain how you would choose the watermark and allowed-lateness parameters to meet this requirement, why state remains bounded, and describe one concrete scenario in which the team would still see double counting unless an additional idempotency mechanism is added. Be explicit about the trade-off you are making.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Correctly defines the watermark as max(observed event_time) minus an allowed-lateness/lag bound and sets that bound to 4 minutes to match the stated out-of-order tolerance (35%). (2) Explains that with a bounded lateness of 4 minutes and a 10-minute window, the engine keeps at most the current window plus a fixed look-back (roughly one to two window lifetimes) in state, and discards a window once the watermark passes its end, so state does not grow with total event count or with time (30%). (3) Gives a concrete double-counting scenario and the fix: e.g., an at-least-once source redelivering a session event, or a job restart re-emitting a window, combined with an append-only write, and notes that the fix is an idempotent write keyed on (window_start, window_end, session_id) via MERGE, or an insert-only table queried with MAX/ROW_NUMBER deduplication; also notes that '4 minutes tolerated and 5 minutes arrives' means the late event is intentionally dropped and must be reported as missing data rather than silently counted twice (25%). (4) Expression clarity and use of exam vocabulary (watermark, event time, allowed lateness, bounded state, idempotent write, drop-vs-reprocess decision) (10%).
questions.analysis: Watermark = max(observed event_time) minus 4 minutes, i.e., lag equal to the advertised out-of-order tolerance. A window is eligible for emission when the watermark passes window_end, and the engine can then drop its state. Because the tolerance is fixed at 4 minutes and the window is 10 minutes, the engine needs to retain only a bounded look-back, so total state is proportional to the number of simultaneous keys in the look-back, not to the size of history or the number of events ever seen. This is the same bounded-state argument the certification expects: watermarking is the mechanism that converts an unbounded stream into a sequence of finalizable windows. The residual double-counting risk does not come from lateness but from the write pattern: if the stream redelivers (at-least-once transport) or a restart re-emits a closed window, and the silver writer is an append-only INSERT, the second copy of every session contributes twice, which is the non-idempotent-write problem noted in the deduplication comparison. The remedy is an idempotent write keyed on the window identity and the session key, or an insert-only table read with ROW_NUMBER/MAX at query time. Events arriving later than 4 minutes are intentionally dropped; per earlier lessons on timeliness and completeness, that degradation must be measured and reported rather than hidden, and the pipeline should expose a late-event counter so downstream consumers know the window may under-report [source 2][source 5][source 6].

actions.text: Time for a checkpoint on late-arriving data. There are three questions here — one single choice, one multiple select, and one short answer that asks you to reason through a design trade-off. Take your time, work through each one independently, and be as explicit as you can on the written response.

Once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning with you — especially the ones that tend to trip people up, like state growth and where double counting sneaks in. Go ahead and give it your best shot.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Late Data Without Double Counting

elements.content: Problem 1

bronze.orders_events is an append-only Delta table of order events with columns (order_id, region, event_time, amount, updated_at, ingestion_time). It holds an average of 1.8 rows per order_id because the Kafka topic delivers at-least-once and a Monday backfill appended the same orders a second time. You must maintain gold.daily_revenue with exactly one row per (calendar day, region) holding the total order amount whose event_time falls inside that day. Three hard constraints apply: (i) orders can arrive up to 48 hours after their event_time; (ii) the pipeline is stopped every night at 02:00 UTC for maintenance and re-run over the last 3 days of source data, so the same event-time window is aggregated and written more than once; (iii) neither SUM(revenue) nor COUNT(*) in gold.daily_revenue may change because of a restart. Worked data for region EU and day 2024-03-05, in USD: ORD-1001 = 400 (event 09:15), ORD-1002 = 500 (event 13:40), ORD-1007 = 300 (event 18:05), ORD-1042 = 150 (event 22:10, arrived 2024-03-07 01:12, lag 27 h 02 m), ORD-1055 = 200 (event 23:55, arrived 2024-03-07 23:40, lag 47 h 45 m). Runs 1, 2 and 3 execute on 2024-03-06, 2024-03-07 and 2024-03-08 at 02:00 UTC. Design the pipeline, compute the contents of gold.daily_revenue after each run, and compute what an append-only INSERT implementation would have produced instead.
Hint: Recompute the whole window each run, then replace the row that has the same (day, region) key - never add to it.

Worked solution
Step 0 - Fix the grain before writing any code. Tidy data means the relationship between rows and columns is well defined [source 1]: gold.daily_revenue has exactly one row per (day, region), where day is a DATE (the start of the event-time window), region is a STRING and revenue is DECIMAL(18,2). The composite primary key is (day, region). This is the aggregate grain, and it is deliberately the same thing that will become the MERGE key. Every later step is correct only because of this decision.

Step 1 - Deduplicate the source. 1.8 rows per order_id means that for the five distinct orders of run 3 we scan 9 raw rows and keep 5. Removing duplicates is an explicit part of data cleaning, alongside fixing errors and inconsistencies [source 2]:

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW deduped AS

SELECT * FROM (

SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id

ORDER BY updated_at DESC, ingestion_time DESC, amount DESC) AS rn

FROM bronze.orders_events) WHERE rn = 1;

The tie-break chain updated_at, ingestion_time, amount is deterministic, so two runs over the same input always keep the same physical row and the check in Step 5 cannot flake.

Step 2 - Event-time windows plus a watermark. Group by the 1-day window on event_time and by region, and attach a watermark of 2 days so the streaming state lives long enough for realistic lateness:

agg = (spark.readStream.table('bronze.orders_events')

.withWatermark('event_time', '2 days')

.groupBy(F.window('event_time', '1 day').alias('day'), 'region')

.agg(F.sum('amount').alias('revenue')))

Watermark arithmetic: watermark = max(event_time observed) - 2 days. The window W = [2024-03-05 00:00, 2024-03-06 00:00) is finalized once watermark >= 2024-03-06 00:00, i.e. once an event with event_time >= 2024-03-08 00:00 has been seen. In our data the first event of 2024-03-08 arrives at 00:04, so W is finalized at 2024-03-08 00:04 - only 24 minutes after ORD-1055 landed at 2024-03-07 23:40. Two days is therefore exactly at the SLA edge (48 h of lateness plus the engine's own event-time progress leaves no slack); a 3-day watermark is the safer production choice, which Problem 2 quantifies.

Step 3 - Make the write keyed and idempotent with foreachBatch, using the aggregate grain as the MERGE key:

def upsert(batch_df, batch_id):

batch_df.selectExpr('day.start AS day', 'region', 'revenue').createOrReplaceTempView('batch')

batch_df.sparkSession.sql('''

MERGE INTO gold.daily_revenue t

USING batch s

ON t.day = s.day AND t.region = s.region

WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.revenue = s.revenue

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (day, region, revenue) VALUES (s.day, s.region, s.revenue)

''')

query = (agg.writeStream.foreachBatch(upsert)

.outputMode('update')

.option('checkpointLocation', 'abfss://.../chk/daily_revenue')

.start())

Step 4 - The key idea: recompute, then overwrite by key. Because the streaming aggregation is stateful, each micro-batch (and each re-run over the last 3 days) carries the complete, or at least more complete, value for the (day, region) key. MERGE with WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET revenue = s.revenue replaces the stale value; it never adds to it. That is what makes the write idempotent: applying the same batch twice leaves the same row.

Step 5 - Compute the actual contents. Run 1 (2024-03-06 02:00) sees ORD-1001, ORD-1002, ORD-1007: revenue = 400 + 500 + 300 = 1,200 USD. The MERGE finds no matching target row, so it inserts one: gold[(2024-03-05, EU)] = 1,200, COUNT(*) = 1.

Run 2 (2024-03-07 02:00) sees those three plus ORD-1042: revenue = 400 + 500 + 300 + 150 = 1,350 USD. The MERGE matches (2024-03-05, EU) and updates the row from 1,200 to 1,350. COUNT(*) is still 1.

Run 3 (2024-03-08 02:00) sees all five orders: revenue = 400 + 500 + 300 + 150 + 200 = 1,550 USD. The MERGE updates 1,350 to 1,550. COUNT(*) is still 1.

Final state: one row, 1,550 USD.

Step 6 - Compare with append-only. A plain INSERT of every batch would give three rows for the same key with 1,200, 1,350 and 1,550. SUM(revenue) = 4,100 USD instead of 1,550 USD - an overstatement of 2,550 USD, i.e. 4,100 / 1,550 = 2.645 times the truth, or 164.5% too high. The row count drifts from 1 to 3, and the drift grows without bound with the number of restarts.

Step 7 - Verify. The duplicate test must return zero rows, and the total must be unchanged after a replay:

SELECT day, region, COUNT(*) FROM gold.daily_revenue

GROUP BY day, region HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; -- must return 0 rows

SELECT SUM(revenue) FROM gold.daily_revenue; -- 1,550 for this slice, unchanged after a re-run

Reconciliation to the source of truth closes the loop: recompute the same window from the deduplicated bronze view and compare SUM(revenue) with the gold value. Quality assurance checks are what confirm the numbers are actually accurate, not merely present [source 1], and the preparation step is not optional even when upstream controls exist [source 4].

Analysis — Why it works: the merge key is the aggregate grain (day + region), so a replay of a window is a replace of one row rather than an increment. Idempotence is a property of the write pattern, not of the transport: at-least-once delivery guarantees that the same event can be seen twice, so the sink must be able to absorb a repeat without changing the result. Choosing the key is the whole design - once ON t.day = s.day AND t.region = s.region is fixed, an arbitrary number of re-runs converges to the same table.

Where students go wrong: (1) Appending instead of upserting, which turns every restart into new revenue; this is the single most common failure and it is invisible in development, where jobs are usually run once. (2) Keying on a surrogate column - a fresh batch UUID, monotonically_increasing_id() or an auto-increment row id - so each run creates new rows for the same logical key; the MERGE still 'succeeds' and the totals still inflate. (3) Choosing a watermark shorter than the real arrival lag, so late events are silently dropped rather than double counted - the totals drift downwards and no error is raised. (4) Leaving the state unbounded because no watermark was set at all. (5) Assuming that a passing duplicate check proves correctness: HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 catches inflation but can never catch a dropped late order.

Edge cases: the MERGE target must be unique on the key - if gold.daily_revenue already contains duplicates, MERGE updates the matching rows but does not remove the surplus ones (repairing that state is Problem 4). A source batch with more than one row per merge key is rejected by Delta, so the aggregation (which guarantees one row per group) must happen before the write. On replay, ordering of UPDATE and INSERT across keys is irrelevant because the operation is keyed, not positional.

Generalisation: the pattern 'recompute the affected grain, then MERGE on that grain' is the general remedy for late data in gold-layer aggregates, and it is the same reasoning that makes MERGE the required pattern when a target must be updated incrementally rather than rewritten.
Problem 2

The same EU job runs with withWatermark('event_time', '2 days'). Measured arrival lag (ingestion_time - event_time) over the last 90 days for the EU feed is: p50 = 12 min, p95 = 26 h, p99 = 44 h, and max = 61 h 05 m, driven by one partner that batches its feed on Monday mornings. gold.daily_revenue for (2024-03-05, EU) currently holds 1,550 USD. Now ORD-2210 arrives with event_time = 2024-03-05 23:55, amount = 200 USD, ingestion_time = 2024-03-08 13:00. Between those two moments, an unrelated event with event_time = 2024-03-08 12:00 was processed at 2024-03-08 12:00. (a) Show the watermark arithmetic and state whether ORD-2210 is included. (b) Quantify the resulting error in gold.daily_revenue and the share of revenue it represents. (c) Recommend a watermark, compute the state cost of the change on a 1-day x 8-region key space, and state the latency trade-off. (d) Explain what happens if no watermark is declared at all. (e) Would the duplicate-detection query from Problem 1 have caught this bug?
Hint: The window closes on event-time progress, not on wall-clock time; compare the arrival lag with the watermark length before anything else.

Worked solution
(a) Watermark arithmetic. watermark = max(event_time observed) - 2 days. The window W = [2024-03-05 00:00, 2024-03-06 00:00) is finalized as soon as watermark >= 2024-03-06 00:00, which requires max(event_time) >= 2024-03-08 00:00. The 2024-03-08 12:00 event processed at 12:00 pushes max(event_time) to 2024-03-08 12:00, so watermark = 2024-03-06 12:00 >= 2024-03-06 00:00: the window is closed and its aggregate of 1,550 USD has already been emitted to gold. ORD-2210 then arrives at 13:00 with a lag of 2024-03-08 13:00 - 2024-03-05 23:55 = 61 h 05 m, which exceeds the 48 h watermark by 13 h 05 m, so it is dropped silently: no exception, no retry, no row in gold.

(b) Error. gold keeps 1,550 USD where the truth is 1,550 + 200 = 1,750 USD. Under-report = 200 / 1,750 = 11.43% of that day's EU revenue, and the error is permanent unless the day is recomputed. The systematic part is worse than the average: the partner that batches on Mondays is always the slowest feed, so the loss concentrates on exactly the days where late volume is highest.

(c) Watermark recommendation. Size the watermark from the maximum observed lag, not from the median: max lag = 61 h 05 m, so 3 days (72 h) leaves 10 h 55 m of slack and covers every arrival in the 90-day window; 2.5 days (60 h) would already have dropped the worst observed case. State cost: each open window must retain one entry per active key. With 1-day windows and 8 regions, a 2-day watermark holds 8 x 2 = 16 key entries, a 3-day watermark holds 8 x 3 = 24, i.e. 1.5x the state and 1.5x the checkpoint size. Latency cost: the earliest a final number can appear moves from T+2 days to T+3 days (2,880 minutes to 4,320 minutes). If the business cannot wait three days, split the problem: emit a revisable estimate with a short watermark for dashboards, and schedule a batch reconciliation that recomputes the last 7 days from bronze and MERGEs on (day, region) - safe, because the merge key is the aggregate grain, so the repair replaces the estimate instead of adding to it.

(d) No watermark at all. In update mode, the stateful aggregation has no event-time expiry rule, so every key ever seen stays in the state store forever: memory and checkpoint growth are unbounded in the number of distinct keys, and a long-running job eventually spills or fails.
