scenes.title: Tracking Quality Metrics Over Time

elements.content: Tracking Quality Metrics Over Time
Persist per-run counts to a Delta metrics table, derive pass_rate, and read it as a time series to catch regressions early.

Capture per-run counts

• rows_in, rows_valid, rows_quarantined recorded for every pipeline run

• pass_rate is derived, not stored raw: pass_rate = rows_valid / rows_in

• Each run writes one row keyed by run_id with a run timestamp

• Metrics measure detection, not handling — the quarantine table still holds the rejected records

Chart: pass_rate over 30 days

A source-side change lands mid-window, so the line dips below the alert threshold before recovering.

Without a persisted series, this regression would reach downstream consumers first.

Worked example: rows_in = 1,000,000; rows_valid = 862,000; rows_quarantined = 138,000.

pass_rate = 862,000 / 1,000,000 = 0.862 — a 13.5% drop versus the prior run's 0.997.
Unify metrics across tables — the same run_id/pass_rate schema on every source — to build a single dashboard and flag regressions before downstream consumers notice. [source 4] [source 1] [source 2]

actions.text: Now that we can route invalid records to quarantine, the next question is: how do we know whether our data quality is getting better or worse over time? The answer is to stop treating quality checks as one-off events and start treating them as a time series. So we persist per-run counts to a Delta metrics table, keyed by run_id and stamped with a run timestamp. Every pipeline run writes one row of metrics — no exceptions.

Here's what we capture per run: rows_in, the raw count coming in; rows_valid, the records that passed every expectation; rows_quarantined, the ones we isolated; and rows_quarantined. From just these two numbers we derive the pass rate. capture rows_valid and rows_in, and then derive pass_rate. Those four columns are the minimum viable metrics table — small, cheap to store, and enough to reconstruct your entire quality story.

Let's ground that with the worked example on the slide. Say rows_in equals 1,000,000, and rows_valid equals 996,000. The pass_rate is simply rows_valid divided by rows_in — 996,000 over 1,000,000 — which gives us 0.996, or 99.6 percent. Keep that number in mind; it's the single figure you'll trend over time and alert on. Note the formula carefully, because the exam loves to test whether you divide valid by input, not quarantined by input.

Now watch what happens when we plot that pass_rate as a line chart over thirty days. Notice the visible dip in the middle of the series. That dip lines up exactly with a source-side change — an upstream system altered its data, and our pass rate dropped almost immediately. This is the whole point of tracking metrics over time: the chart turns an abstract quality rule into a regression signal you can actually see.

One more piece, and it matters for scale: unify metrics across tables. The same run_id and pass_rate schema should be used everywhere, so that every table's metrics land in one consistent shape. That way you can build a single quality dashboard across your whole pipeline instead of stitching together ad-hoc reports. And the payoff is exactly what this page is about — metrics let you detect regressions before downstream consumers notice them. You catch the dip on the chart; they never see bad data in their reports. On the next page, we'll read these metrics in detail and practice spotting regressions from the numbers alone.

scenes.title: Reading the Metrics: Detecting Regressions

elements.content:
Ingest pipeline quality metrics vs. day (30-day window) (line)
Day (calendar day of the 30-day monitoring window) → Metric value (pass_rate in %, quarantined rows in records)
pass_rate is a percentage (rows_valid / rows_in). Quarantine volume is an absolute count of records per calendar day. Both series come from the same per-run metrics table keyed by run and date. A source schema change (upstream added loyalty_tier) was deployed on day 11; day 1-10 are the pre-change baseline. To make both series readable on one axis, quarantine volume is plotted as its raw count while pass_rate is plotted in percent; they share the numeric axis but not the unit.

pass_rate (%): 1→99.2   2→99   3→99.3   4→98.9   5→99.1   6→99.2   7→99   8→99.3   9→99.1   10→99.2   11→97.8   12→96.4   13→95.1   14→94.2   15→94.6   16→94   17→94.3   18→93.9   19→94.1   20→94.2   21→94.4   22→94   23→94.3   24→94.1   25→94.5   26→94.2   27→94   28→94.4   29→94.1   30→94.3

quarantined (records): 1→42   2→44   3→39   4→47   5→43   6→45   7→41   8→44   9→46   10→43   11→118   12→190   13→267   14→331   15→302   16→348   17→336   18→361   19→344   20→352   21→340   22→357   23→349   24→338   25→346   26→350   27→355   28→342   29→347   30→344

Claim 1 — Supported
pass_rate declined after the source schema change: the mean pass_rate over days 1-10 (pre-change) is approximately 99.1%, while the mean over days 11-30 (post-change) is approximately 94.2%, a drop of about 4.9 percentage points.
Why: Summing the pre-change values (99.2+99.0+99.3+98.9+99.1+99.2+99.0+99.3+99.1+99.2 = 991.3) and dividing by 10 gives a pre-change mean of 99.13%. Summing the post-change values (97.8+96.4+95.1+94.2+94.6+94.0+94.3+93.9+94.1+94.2+94.4+94.0+94.3+94.1+94.5+94.2+94.0+94.4+94.1+94.3 = 1883.9) and dividing by 20 gives 94.20%. The difference is 99.13 - 94.20 = 4.93 percentage points. Note the day-11 value of 97.8% already sits far outside the pre-change range [98.9, 99.3], so the break begins the day the change was deployed. Quarantine counts rise in lockstep (day-10 = 43, day-11 = 118, day-14 = 331), which is the corroborating second signal you should always look for before calling a regression [source 1]. This claim is a description of the plot, not a root-cause attribution.

Claim 2 — Refuted
The quarantine spike is explained by seasonality, because the spike recurs on a regular weekly cycle within the 30-day window.
Why: Divide the post-change window into weeks. Days 11-17 (118, 190, 267, 331, 302, 348, 336) and days 18-24 (361, 344, 352, 340, 357, 349, 338) have near-identical weekly means of roughly 270 and 349; the second week is not a repeat of the first, it is a further step up before plateauing. There is no oscillating peak-trough-peak pattern of the kind a weekly seasonality would produce; instead we see a monotone ramp (43 to 331 over days 10-14) followed by a flat regime around 340-357. A seasonal explanation also cannot account for the abrupt regime change coinciding exactly with the day-11 deployment. Verdict: the pattern is inconsistent with seasonality. Beware that 'seasonality' is a classic confound: a spurious correlation with day-of-week can make a release-day regression look cyclic [source 6].

Claim 3 — Insufficient
Reading the metric alone proves the root cause: the pass_rate drop and quarantine spike prove that the added loyalty_tier column caused the failures.
Why: The plot establishes correlation and a temporal sequence (change deployed day 11, metrics break day 11), but a time series of pass_rate and quarantine counts cannot discriminate among competing causes: a new NOT NULL rule, an unenforced schema mismatch, an upstream ordering change, or a change in the downstream consumer could each produce the same curve. To move from correlation to causation you need the quarantine table contents — the failed_rule and rejection_reason columns — which the metric chart does not contain. Because the evidence required to decide is not present in this dataset, the correct verdict is insufficient, not refuted: the metric is consistent with the claim but does not prove it [source 6].

Claim 4 — Refuted
The magnitude of the second break is larger than the first: the pass_rate drop from day 11 to day 14 (3.6 points) matches the drop from day 11 to day 12 (1.4 points) plus the drop from day 12 to day 13 (1.3 points), which is 2.7 points, so the claim that the two sub-drops sum to the total is arithmetically false.
Why: Read the values directly: day 11 = 97.8, day 12 = 96.4, day 13 = 95.1, day 14 = 94.2. The total drop day 11 to day 14 is 97.8 - 94.2 = 3.6 points. The first sub-drop is 97.8 - 96.4 = 1.4 points; the second is 96.4 - 95.1 = 1.3 points; their sum is 2.7 points. But 1.4 + 1.3 = 2.7 omits the day 13 to day 14 drop of 95.1 - 94.2 = 0.9 points, and 2.7 + 0.9 = 3.6, which is the correct total. The claim as stated declares 2.7 = 3.6, which is false; a decomposition over n intervals must include all n intervals. This is the same error as forgetting a term in a sum.

Claim 5 — Supported
In the post-change regime the quarantine count has stabilised: the standard deviation of quarantined rows over days 18-30 is small relative to its mean, whereas over days 11-14 it grows monotonically.
Why: Days 11-14 quarantine counts are 118, 190, 267, 331 — a monotone ramp, each day exceeding the last, with a 4-day range of 213 records. Days 18-30 are 361, 344, 352, 340, 357, 349, 338, 346, 350, 355, 342, 347, 344. Their mean is (361+344+352+340+357+349+338+346+350+355+342+347+344)/13. Sum = 361+344=705; +352=1057; +340=1397; +357=1754; +349=2103; +338=2441; +346=2787; +350=3137; +355=3492; +342=3834; +347=4181; +344=4525. 4525/13 = 348.1 records. The range is 361 - 338 = 23 records, and the values sit within roughly ±7% of the mean, so the regime is plateaued, not drifting. Diagnostically this matters: pass_rate is flat at approximately 94.2% post-change, so the pipeline has not healed, it has simply stopped getting worse and is now shedding about 5.8% of every batch [source 2].

Claim 6 — Supported
Because rows_valid is derived as rows_in minus rows_quarantined, a pass_rate of 94.2% on a day with 6,000 rows_in implies roughly 348 rows quarantined, which is consistent with the plotted quarantine series on those days.
Why: The definitional chain is pass_rate = rows_valid / rows_in x 100, and rows_valid = rows_in - rows_quarantined. Rearranged, rows_quarantined = rows_in x (1 - pass_rate/100) = 6000 x (1 - 0.942) = 6000 x 0.058 = 348. The plotted quarantine counts for the plateau days (e.g. day 16 = 348, day 21 = 340, day 26 = 350) sit in exactly this range, and the day-16 value of 348 matches the derivation to the record. When rows_in varies, the absolute count moves while pass_rate holds: on a 12,000-row day the same 94.2% implies 12000 x 0.058 = 696 quarantined rows. Any single-point metric is a ratio, so it is only interpretable alongside the volume it was computed from [source 5].

Claim 7 — Supported
Averaging the 30 daily pass_rate values and reporting 'about 96% overall' would understate the regression, because the unweighted mean is pulled upward by the 10 clean baseline days even though no post-change day exceeds 97.8%.
Why: The unweighted mean of all 30 days is (991.3 + 1883.9)/30 = 2875.2/30 = 95.84%, which rounds to about 96%. But 20 of 30 days sit between 93.9% and 97.8%, and 19 of the 20 post-change days are below 95.2%. Reporting the 30-day mean therefore describes a regime the pipeline has not been in since day 11. An unweighted mean over a series with a structural break averages two different regimes and describes neither; the correct practice is to segment at the break, as in claim-1, and report each regime separately [source 4].

Claim 8 — Refuted
The quarantine spike and the pass_rate decline on day 11 are explained by the spike being a delayed consequence of the pass_rate decline, since the quarantine count begins rising on day 11 while pass_rate does not reach its plateau until day 14.
Why: Both series break on the same day, 11: pass_rate falls from 99.2 on day 10 to 97.8 on day 11, and quarantine jumps from 43 to 118 on day 11. A delayed consequence would show pass_rate changing first and quarantine responding some days later, but here the day-11 change is simultaneous in both. Nor is the 'plateau' a separate event: pass_rate on day 11 is itself already 1.4 points above the eventual plateau, so the day-11 shift is the same regime change, continuing to day 14. The two series are two views of one event (the day-11 deployment), not cause and delayed effect, and neither proves causality on its own, which is why claim-3 is insufficient rather than supported [source 6].

actions.text: Here's the trend we saved from the last page: thirty days of ingest pipeline quality metrics, with pass_rate on one line and quarantine volume on the other. Now the real skill — reading this chart like an engineer, not just admiring it. We're going to evaluate a set of written claims against the plotted evidence, and for each one decide whether it's supported, refuted, or insufficient.

Start with pass_rate. Look at the daily numbers: it begins around 99.2 percent, drifts down slightly, holds steady for a stretch, then drops sharply in the second half of the window, landing as low as 96 percent before recovering. So there are two distinct breaks in this series — not one smooth decline.

The quarantine volume tells a different story. At the start it sits around forty-two to forty-four records a day — that's your baseline noise, normal rejected rows. Then on the day of the second break it jumps to nearly three hundred records, and it stays elevated in the post-change regime. That magnitude is far outside anything the first twenty days ever produced.

Claim one: pass_rate declined after a source schema change. Supported. The timing lines up — the sharp break in pass_rate coincides with a documented change, and the decline persists rather than bouncing back, which is exactly what a structural problem looks like.

Claim two: the quarantine spike is explained by seasonality. Refuted. Seasonality means a recurring, predictable pattern — but this spike is a single, abrupt, sustained jump right at the change point, with no matching rhythm in the earlier weeks. Correlation with a pattern is not the pattern itself.

Claim three: the metric alone proves the root cause. Insufficient. The chart shows us what happened and when, but it can't tell us why. To establish the root cause you'd need to inspect the failing records, the error messages, and the schema diff — the numbers narrow the search, they don't close it.

Claim four: the magnitude of the second break was small. Refuted. The quarantine count went from roughly forty to nearly three hundred — that's a sevenfold jump, and the pass_rate drop was equally steep. A break that size is not a small fluctuation.

Claim five: in the post-change regime the quarantine volume stays elevated. Supported. This is where you separate a one-off blip from a regime change. After the second break, the daily quarantine numbers never return to their old baseline — they stay high, which means the new behavior is the new normal until someone intervenes.

Claim seven: averaging the thirty daily pass_rate values gives a representative picture of the pipeline. Supported — but carefully. Mathematically the average is valid, yet it's representative of nothing useful here. It smooths over two distinct breaks and hides the regression entirely. This is the trap: a correct computation can still be the wrong way to read the metric.

Claim eight: the quarantine spike and the pass_rate decline are the same event viewed twice. Refuted. Watch the timing — the pass_rate decline and the quarantine surge are not perfectly simultaneous; the quarantine jump is concentrated at the second break, while pass_rate erodes more gradually. Two related effects can still be two distinct signals, and treating them as one would send you chasing the wrong lead. When you read any quality trend on the exam, check the timing, the magnitude, and whether the change persists — those three questions will resolve most supported-versus-refuted claims for you.

actions.topic: When do the numbers justify a conclusion, and when do they only justify a hypothesis?
actions.prompt: Pick any one metric from the chart — pass_rate or quarantine volume. What would you need to see beyond this single plot before you'd feel confident naming a root cause?

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Regression Detection

questions.question: You operate a nightly ingestion job whose quality metrics are persisted to a Delta metrics table keyed by run_id. Over 30 days the daily pass_rate (rows_valid / rows_in) is stable at approximately 0.985. On day 19 the upstream source silently adds a new nullable column to the feed; on day 20 pass_rate drops to 0.72 and rows_quarantined rises from ~150 to ~4,200, but rows_in stays essentially flat. Days 21–24 show pass_rate climbing slowly back toward 0.86 while quarantine volume declines steadily. Which interpretation of the regression window is most defensible?

options.label: The regression window begins on day 19 and the recovery trend across days 21–24 indicates the checkpoints were gradually adjusted or the inflow of malformed records diminished, so the day-20 drop is a genuine data regression rather than a metrics-capture fault.
The regression window begins on day 20, and because pass_rate eventually climbs back, the entire event is best classified as expected seasonality and requires no further action.
Because rows_in did not change, the drop in pass_rate proves the metrics-capture logic is broken and the run_id rows for days 20–24 should be deleted before any schema investigation.
The regression window cannot be identified from a pass_rate time series alone, so the correct action is to recompute pass_rate using rows_quarantined / rows_in and treat the result as the true trend.

questions.analysis: A quality-metric time series is built from per-run counts — rows_in, rows_valid, rows_quarantined — with pass_rate = rows_valid / rows_in persisted to a Delta metrics table keyed by run_id and a run timestamp, and it exists precisely so you can locate a change point in a trend. Here the change point coincides with the silent upstream column addition on day 19, and the gradual recovery across days 21–24 is consistent with the checkpoints adapting to the new shape rather than with a broken capture path, so option A is the defensible reading. Option B mislabels a step change as seasonality; seasonality would show a recurring pattern, not a single sustained shift anchored to a schema event. Option C is a real student misconception: a flat rows_in does not diagnose a capture bug, and the training rule is that a write failing with a schema mismatch is testing that you do not reach for a destructive fix first. Option D uses the wrong denominator — rows_quarantined / rows_in is the quarantine rate, not pass_rate [source 1].

questions.question: Your team must decide how to alert on the pass_rate signal for a nightly ingest, and separately must decide whether a sudden pass_rate collapse is a genuine data regression or a metrics-capture bug. Select all statements that correctly reflect sound practice. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A fixed threshold alert (for example, fire when pass_rate < 0.95) is simple and auditable, but it can stay silent on a slow multi-week drift and can misfire on a legitimately volatile low-volume feed.

A baseline-deviation alert (for example, fire when today's pass_rate deviates from a trailing baseline by more than k standard deviations) adapts to each feed's normal behaviour but needs enough history and can be noisy right after a deliberate, well-understood upstream change.

If rows_in also collapses at the same moment as pass_rate, that joint movement points toward a genuine data regression caused by an upstream schema change rather than a metrics-capture bug, because a broken capture path typically leaves the raw inflow intact.

Because hand-written quality checks cannot be wrong, any disagreement between the trend chart and the quarantine table should be resolved by trusting the chart and deleting the conflicting quarantine rows.

questions.analysis: A and B are the two legitimate alerting strategies with their genuine tradeoffs: a fixed threshold is transparent but blind to gradual drift and brittle to volatile feeds, while a baseline-deviation alert adapts per feed but requires sufficient history and can produce false positives immediately after an intentional upstream change. C is the key diagnostic heuristic: a metrics-capture bug corrupts how the run's counts are recorded, so the underlying inflow should still be present, whereas a real regression driven by an upstream schema change typically perturbs rows_in and the valid/quarantine split together. D is the misconception to reject — quality checks are code and can be wrong, and the quarantine table exists precisely to preserve the original record payload plus rejection_reason, failed_rule, ingest_timestamp, source_table, and batch_id so the disagreement can be investigated rather than deleted [source 4].

actions.text: Let's put that regression-detection thinking to the test. There are two questions here — one single-answer, one multi-select — and they ask you to interpret a metric trend and to reason about how you'd alert on it. Work through each one on your own and commit to an answer before you submit.

scenes.title: Quarantine Strategy: Fail Fast vs Quarantine vs Drop

elements.content: Decision — A team operates a Databricks Lakeflow ingestion job in a medallion architecture (the bronze/silver/gold layering convention) that feeds dozens of downstream tables. A subset of incoming records violates declared quality rules: some have NULL customer_id, some have order_amount outside the contractual range, and some carry malformed event timestamps. The engineering team must choose how the pipeline responds when a row fails these rules, and the choice is hard because the three candidate strategies optimize for mutually incompatible objectives — safety of the dataset, availability of fresh data, and operating cost — while the binding external constraints are the pipeline's uptime SLA, an audit requirement that every rejected record be recoverable, and an unknown tolerance for gaps in downstream aggregates. Earlier in this unit you learned to separate detection (a quality check) from handling (routing) as distinct design steps, and you learned that a quarantine table stores the original record payload intact alongside rejection metadata columns such as rejection_reason, failed_rule, ingest_timestamp, source_table, and batch_id.

Constraints — The pipeline must honour a stated uptime/freshness SLA, so an option that halts the job indefinitely on the first bad row is only acceptable where the SLA explicitly permits downtime.  •  Audit and regulatory requirements demand that every rejected record be preserved and explainable, which rules out any handling that destroys the evidence of a rejection.  •  Downstream consumers have a finite tolerance for gaps: aggregates computed over valid rows only are still correct as totals over the surviving population, but referentially dependent joins may break if a parent record is missing.  •  Whatever handling is chosen must be expressible inside the existing Databricks Lakeflow/Delta Lake job without introducing a separate processing service, because the team has no budget for new infrastructure this quarter.  •  Quality metrics (rows_in, rows_valid, rows_quarantined, pass_rate) must continue to be captured per pipeline run so regressions remain detectable.

Fail fast on the first invalid record
+ Highest safety: the pipeline never writes a run in which an invalid row is silently absent, so downstream tables can never be subtly wrong due to a swallowed error [source 2].; + Makes the failure immediately visible to the on-call engineer via the job's own failure state, satisfying the doctrine that flawed data leads to skewed results and that identification of errors must precede any repair [source 6].; + Requires no quarantine table, no metadata columns, and no routing logic, which minimizes schema and code surface.
− Lowest availability: a single NULL customer_id in a batch of millions stops the entire feed and can breach the uptime SLA for every downstream table, not just the one affected by the bad row.; − It conflates two very different failure classes: an isolated bad record (a routine data-quality event) and a critical referential-integrity violation (a genuine contract break), so operators lose the ability to triage by severity.; − It scales the cost of one bad row to the full batch: if 0.01% of rows are bad, the pipeline may never complete a run at all, which is the exact anti-pattern this unit warned about when it argued that failing an entire pipeline on one bad record is costly.
Best for: Critical referential-integrity violations where continuing would corrupt the meaning of the dataset — for example, a fact row whose foreign key has no matching dimension after a schema change, or any run where the audit requirement is in fact complete-data-set correctness rather than record-level explainability.

Quarantine invalid records and continue the run
+ Preserves availability: valid rows flow to silver and gold on schedule while invalid rows are isolated in a quarantine Delta table with their payload and rejection metadata intact, so fresh data keeps arriving within the SLA.; + Satisfies audit and regulatory requirements literally, because every rejected row is recoverable and carries rejection_reason, failed_rule, ingest_timestamp, source_table, and batch_id, and can be reprocessed after an upstream fix — the definition of quarantine rather than deletion.; + Keeps detection and handling as separate, testable design steps, so quality rules can be toggled and their effect measured as a change in the rows_valid/rows_quarantined split, which is exactly what the routing lab demonstrated.; + Extends naturally to regression detection: because runs still complete, per-run metrics (rows_in, rows_valid, rows_quarantined, and pass_rate = rows_valid / rows_in) can be persisted to a Delta metrics table keyed by run_id and read as a time series.
− Downstream aggregates computed over the surviving population are totals over valid rows only, so they are not identical to the totals the source system would report; any consumer that treats them as complete will be wrong by exactly the quarantined volume.; − Quarantine tables grow without bound unless an operator defines a retention and reprocessing policy, and every such table adds governance overhead in Unity Catalog (Databricks' unified catalog for data and AI assets).; − The pipeline now has a second success mode — 'completed with quarantined rows' — which is easy to misread as a fully healthy run if nobody is watching pass_rate against a baseline.
Best for: Monitored or regulated pipelines where isolatable record-level defects are expected, the SLA forbids downtime, and the auditor's question is 'can you show me every rejected record and why' rather than 'was the batch complete' — which, as the unit established, is the recommended default for exactly these conditions.

Drop invalid records and continue the run
+ Lowest operating overhead: no quarantine table, no metadata wiring, and no retention policy, so the job is the simplest of the three to build and the cheapest to run.; + Maximum availability: the pipeline never stops and never needs an operator decision at ingest time.; + Output tables contain only rows that passed the rules, so downstream code needs no special case for 'known bad' records.
− Destroys the evidence of the rejection, which is mutually exclusive with the audit constraint: the unit is explicit that dropping silently destroys evidence and that quarantine exists precisely to preserve it.; − Produces silent data loss: a declining pass_rate becomes invisible because there is no quarantined volume to observe, so a regression after an upstream schema change cannot be distinguished from a seasonality effect in the metrics — the central failure mode of the regression-detection exercise.; − If a bad row is a missing parent in a referential relationship, dropping it silently changes a query that should have raised an integrity error into one that silently returns incomplete results, which is the worst of both safety worlds.
Best for: Almost nothing. The only defensible use is a genuinely disposable telemetry stream with no audit obligation, no referential dependencies, and an explicit written acceptance of silent loss — a combination that is rare in regulated pipelines and never acceptable where the audit constraint applies.

Recommendation: Quarantine invalid records and continue the run — The three constraints do the deciding, and only quarantine satisfies all three simultaneously. The uptime SLA forbids fail-fast as the default because halting on one bad row breaches the SLA for every downstream table, and the audit requirement forbids drop because it destroys the recoverable evidence of each rejection. Quarantine is the only option that keeps valid data flowing on schedule while writing each bad row to a Delta table with its intact payload and rejection metadata (rejection_reason, failed_rule, ingest_timestamp, source_table, batch_id), and it is the only option that keeps the per-run metrics needed to detect a regression. This does not make fail-fast obsolete: it should be reserved for critical referential-integrity violations, where continuing would silently corrupt results, and it should be implemented as a rule-level escalation inside the quarantine job rather than as the pipeline's blanket behaviour. Concretely, on a run of 1,000,000 rows with 150 NULL customer_id and 50 out-of-range order_amount, quarantine yields rows_valid = 999,800, rows_quarantined = 200, and pass_rate = 999,800 / 1,000,000 = 0.9998, within a 99.9% SLA, whereas fail-fast would have produced rows_valid = 0 and a breached SLA, and drop would have produced a healthy-looking 1,000,000-row write with 200 rows and their rejection reasons permanently gone.

actions.text: Now that you can track quality metrics over time and spot regressions, the next question is a design decision: when a pipeline encounters an invalid record, what should it actually do? This page frames that as a decision under explicit constraints.

Here's the scenario. A team operates a Databricks Lakeflow pipeline that ingests records from an upstream source. Their job is to pick a strategy for handling records that fail validation — and that choice has real consequences for data integrity and for how fresh the downstream tables stay.

The constraints shape everything. The pipeline must honour a stated SLA, meaning downstream consumers expect fresh data on a schedule. There may be audit or regulatory requirements that dictate every record be accounted for. And there's a limit to how much downstream consumers will tolerate gaps. Any strategy we choose has to live inside those boundaries.

Option A: fail fast on the first invalid record. The pipeline stops the moment it sees bad data. This gives you the highest safety — nothing questionable ever reaches the target — but the lowest availability, because the run halts and downstream data goes stale until someone investigates.

Option B: quarantine invalid records and continue the run. Bad rows are routed aside into a quarantine table where they can be inspected, while valid data keeps flowing. This preserves availability and gives you a full audit trail of what was rejected — exactly what monitored or regulated pipelines need.

Option C: drop invalid records and continue the run. This has the lowest overhead — no extra table, no extra logic — but it carries the highest risk of silent data loss. The data simply vanishes, and if nobody's watching, you might not notice until a business report looks wrong.

So the recommendation: quarantine by default for any monitored or regulated pipeline, because it balances safety with availability and keeps a durable record of rejects. Reserve fail-fast for critical referential-integrity violations — cases where continuing would corrupt a foundational table. And treat dropping as a last resort only for low-stakes, high-volume streams where you've decided the data is expendable. Notice how the constraint always drives the choice — that's the exam framing you want to internalise.

scenes.title: Worked Exercise: Building a DQ Metrics Pipeline

elements.content: Problem 1

Pipeline: the silver ingest `ingest.orders_raw` reads `bronze.orders_raw`, applies quality predicates, and routes failures to a quarantine Delta table. The run `run_id = 'r-2024-06-14-0200'` (with `run_timestamp = '2024-06-14T02:00:00Z'`) finished with rows_in = 1,248,000, rows_valid = 1,215,310 and rows_quarantined = 32,690. (a) Verify the counting identity and compute pass_rate to six decimal places. (b) Write the PySpark that assembles the single metric row (run_id, run_timestamp, rows_in, rows_valid, rows_quarantined, pass_rate). (c) Write the Delta write so that a retry of the same run_id does not create a second row for the run. (d) The job is retried at 02:14:00, and a partial first attempt had already emitted rows_in = 400,000, rows_valid = 389,600, rows_quarantined = 10,400. Compute exactly what an append-only write does to the daily rollup, and compare it with what the keyed write does.
Hint: Write the identity rows_in = rows_valid + rows_quarantined on paper first; if it fails, fix the counters before touching the metrics table.

Worked solution
Step 1 - Counting identity. Every input row must land in exactly one bucket, so the contract is $\text{rows\_in} = \text{rows\_valid} + \text{rows\_quarantined}$. Check: $1{,}215{,}310 + 32{,}690 = 1{,}248{,}000$. The identity holds, so the three counters are mutually consistent and safe to persist. This is the numeric form of the quality assurance check that verifies accuracy before data is used downstream [source 1].

Step 2 - Derive pass_rate. $\text{pass\_rate} = \dfrac{\text{rows\_valid}}{\text{rows\_in}} = \dfrac{1{,}215{,}310}{1{,}248{,}000} = 0.973806$ (97.3806%). The complement is the quarantine rate $32{,}690 / 1{,}248{,}000 = 0.026194$, and $0.973806 + 0.026194 = 1.000000$. Store the raw counts, not only the ratio: the ratio can always be recomputed from counts at any granularity, but a stored ratio cannot be un-mixed back into counts.

Step 3 - Assemble the metric row.

```python

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

run_id, run_ts = 'r-2024-06-14-0200', '2024-06-14T02:00:00Z'

rows_valid = valid_df.count() # passed every quality predicate

rows_quarantined = quarantine_df.count() # routed out with rejection metadata

rows_in = rows_valid + rows_quarantined # valid ONLY because the split is exhaustive

metrics_stage = (spark.createDataFrame(

[(run_id, run_ts, rows_in, rows_valid, rows_quarantined)],

'run_id string, run_timestamp string, rows_in long, rows_valid long, rows_quarantined long')

.withColumn('pass_rate', F.round(F.col('rows_valid') / F.col('rows_in'), 6)))

assert metrics_stage.count() == 1, 'one metric row per run_id, or the MERGE key is not unique'

```

Step 4 - Idempotent write. The target is `ops.quality.metrics`, keyed by `run_id`. A MERGE makes the write a set-to-latest-value operation instead of an append:

```sql

MERGE INTO ops.quality.metrics AS t

USING metrics_stage AS s

ON t.run_id = s.run_id

WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET

t.run_timestamp = s.run_timestamp,

t.rows_in = s.rows_in,

t.rows_valid = s.rows_valid,

t.rows_quarantined = s.rows_quarantined,

t.pass_rate = s.pass_rate

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT

(run_id, run_timestamp, rows_in, rows_valid, rows_quarantined, pass_rate)

VALUES (s.run_id, s.run_timestamp, s.rows_in, s.rows_valid, s.rows_quarantined, s.pass_rate);

```

Step 5 - The retry, in numbers. Attempt 1 wrote a partial row: $389{,}600 + 10{,}400 = 400{,}000$ (identity holds) with $\text{pass\_rate} = 389{,}600/400{,}000 = 0.974000$. Attempt 2 wrote the full row from Step 2.

Append-only daily rollup:

- $\text{rows\_in} = 400{,}000 + 1{,}248{,}000 = 1{,}648{,}000$, i.e. $1{,}648{,}000 / 1{,}248{,}000 = 1.3205$, an inflation of +32.05%.

- $\text{rows\_quarantined} = 10{,}400 + 32{,}690 = 43{,}090$, i.e. $43{,}090 / 32{,}690 = 1.3181$, an inflation of +31.81%.

- $\text{rows\_valid} = 389{,}600 + 1{,}215{,}310 = 1{,}604{,}910$.

- pooled $\text{pass\_rate} = 1{,}604{,}910 / 1{,}648{,}000 = 0.973853$.

Keyed MERGE rollup: one row survives, so $\text{rows\_in} = 1{,}248{,}000$, $\text{rows\_quarantined} = 32{,}690$, $\text{pass\_rate} = 0.973806$.

Comparison: the appended pass_rate is wrong by only $0.973853 - 0.973806 = 0.000047$, i.e. 0.0047 percentage points - invisible on a dashboard - while the quarantine volume is overstated by 31.81%, which is exactly the magnitude of a real incident. The metric that would hide the bug is the ratio; the metrics that expose it are the raw counts.

Analysis — Why the method works: a metric row is a fact about a run, and a run has a stable identity (`run_id`). Writing facts under their natural key with MERGE turns retries into overwrites, which is the definition of an idempotent write. That matters because job retries are routine, not exceptional: a cluster preemption, a throttled source API, or a transient Unity Catalog permission error all cause the same `run_id` to be processed twice, and each of those retries is a chance to double-count.

Common mistakes. (1) Computing `rows_in` as `rows_valid + rows_quarantined` is only legal when the routing step is exhaustive and mutually exclusive; if a branch silently drops rows (for example a `filter` that removes duplicates before the quality split), the identity becomes a tautology and the dropped rows vanish from every count. In that case read `rows_in` from the source table and let the identity assertion fail loudly. (2) Using `INSERT OVERWRITE` on the whole day's partition to get idempotency: it works only if the rerun of one pipeline also recomputes every other pipeline writing to that partition, otherwise it deletes their rows. (3) Assuming MERGE is idempotent when the merge key is not unique - if a run writes one row per source table, key on `(run_id, source_table)` and deduplicate the staging frame with `row_number()` first, otherwise Delta raises `DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW` or writes a nondeterministic result. (4) Keying on `run_timestamp` instead of `run_id`: timestamps differ between attempt 1 and attempt 2, so the retry inserts a second row and you are back to double counting.

Generalisation and the exam framing: whenever a question says a job retried and the numbers look inflated, the answer is a keyed write (MERGE with a deterministic key), not a bigger cluster and not a `dropDuplicates()`. The related principle is that counting and ratio metrics move differently under a bug: ratios are self-normalising and hide multiplicative errors, counts are not and expose them. Because flawed or double-counted data leads to skewed results, the counts must be persisted alongside the derived rate so the trend charts still reflect the true representation of the pipeline [source 6]. Finally, note the reporting consequence: any run whose counters are not mutually consistent should be blocked from publication rather than written with a caveat, because the cleaning and verification step exists precisely to catch these inconsistencies before analysis [source 2].
Problem 2

The table `ops.quality.metrics_daily` holds one row per ingest day for the pipeline from Problem 1, with `rows_in` constant at 1,240,000 because the source delivers a fixed daily batch. Data:

| run_date | rows_in | rows_valid | rows_quarantined | pass_rate |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2024-06-01 | 1,240,000 | 1,216,688 | 23,312 | 0.9812 |

| 2024-06-02 | 1,240,000 | 1,214,952 | 25,048 | 0.9798 |

| 2024-06-03 | 1,240,000 | 1,218,300 | 21,700 | 0.9825 |

| 2024-06-04 | 1,240,000 | 1,215,324 | 24,676 | 0.9801 |

| 2024-06-05 | 1,240,000 | 1,213,836 | 26,164 | 0.9789 |

| 2024-06-06 | 1,240,000 | 1,181,844 | 58,156 | 0.9531 |

| 2024-06-07 | 1,240,000 | 1,167,088 | 72,912 | 0.9412 |

(a) Write SQL that computes a trailing baseline (mean and standard deviation of pass_rate) and the deviation of the current day from it. (b) Compute the baseline mean and population standard deviation from 2024-06-01 to 2024-06-05 and the z-score of 2024-06-06. (c) The on-call alert rule is a fixed threshold of pass_rate < 0.95. On which date does it fire, and how many extra quarantined rows are produced before it fires? (d) State the regression window.
Hint: The trailing window must exclude the current row; otherwise a regression contaminates its own baseline and the z-score stays small.

Worked solution
Step 1 - Trailing-window SQL. The window frame is `ROWS BETWEEN 5 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING` - the `1 PRECEDING` is the critical detail, it excludes the day being tested.

```sql

WITH b AS (

SELECT run_date, pass_rate,

AVG(pass_rate) OVER (ORDER BY run_date

ROWS BETWEEN 5 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS baseline_mean,

STDDEV_SAMP(pass_rate) OVER (ORDER BY run_date

ROWS BETWEEN 5 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS baseline_sd

FROM ops.quality.metrics_daily

)

SELECT run_date, pass_rate, baseline_mean, baseline_sd,

pass_rate - baseline_mean AS deviation,

(pass_rate - baseline_mean) / baseline_sd AS z_score,

rows_in, rows_quarantined

FROM b

ORDER BY run_date;

```

Step 2 - Baseline statistics for 2024-06-01 to 2024-06-05.

$$\bar{p} = \frac{0.9812 + 0.9798 + 0.9825 + 0.9801 + 0.9789}{5} = \frac{4.9025}{5} = 0.9805$$

Deviations from the mean: $+0.0007$, $-0.0007$, $+0.0020$, $-0.0004$, $-0.0016$; they sum to zero, which is the arithmetic check that the mean is correct. Squared deviations: $4.9\times10^{-7}$, $4.9\times10^{-7}$, $4.0\times10^{-6}$, $1.6\times10^{-7}$, $2.56\times10^{-6}$, summing to $7.70\times10^{-6}$.

Population variance $= 7.70\times10^{-6} / 5 = 1.54\times10^{-6}$, so $\sigma = 0.001241$. (If you use `STDDEV_SAMP`, as the SQL above does, the denominator is 4 and $s = 0.001388$; the choice matters for the size of z, never for the sign or the alert date.)

Step 3 - z-score of 2024-06-06: $z = \dfrac{0.9531 - 0.9805}{0.001241} = \dfrac{-0.0274}{0.001241} = -22.1$. The day is 22 population standard deviations below an extremely tight baseline. For 2024-06-07: $z = \dfrac{0.9412 - 0.9805}{0.001241} = -31.7$.

Step 4 - Fixed-threshold comparison. Threshold $0.95$:

- 2024-06-06: $0.9531 \ge 0.95$ - the rule stays silent even though pass_rate fell 2.58 percentage points in one day.

- 2024-06-07: $0.9412 < 0.95$ - the alert fires.

The baseline mean quarantine volume for 2024-06-01 to 2024-06-05 is $(23{,}312 + 25{,}048 + 21{,}700 + 24{,}676 + 26{,}164)/5 = 120{,}900/5 = 24{,}180$ rows/day. On 2024-06-06 the quarantine table received $58{,}156$ rows, an excess of $58{,}156 - 24{,}180 = 33{,}976$ rows - nearly one and a half days of normal quarantine volume - before the fixed threshold said a word. So the baseline-deviation rule fires on 2024-06-06 and saves 33,976 bad rows' worth of latency; the fixed threshold fires one day late.

Step 5 - Regression window. The break is one-sided and sustained: the last in-control day is 2024-06-05, the first out-of-control day is 2024-06-06, and the degradation continues through 2024-06-07 (0.9412). The regression window is therefore $[2024\text{-}06\text{-}06,\ \ge 2024\text{-}06\text{-}07)$, open on the right until a fix day returns pass_rate inside the baseline band. The magnitude grows ($-2.58$ pp then $-3.77$ pp), which is consistent with a source schema change that started dropping one field for a growing share of the batch, not with an instantaneous one-off glitch.

Analysis — Why the method works: a fixed threshold encodes an absolute business tolerance, whereas a trailing baseline encodes the pipeline's own recent behaviour. On a stable pipeline the baseline standard deviation is tiny ($\sigma = 0.0012$ here), so a 2.7-point move is astronomically unlikely under the baseline - this is exactly the situation in which baseline-deviation alerts beat fixed thresholds. The deviation approach answers 'is today different from yesterday's normal?', the threshold approach answers 'is today unacceptable in absolute terms?'. Mature monitoring runs both and routes them to different people.

Common mistakes. (1) Including the current row in the baseline (`BETWEEN 4 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`). With a 5-day window the regressed day contributes 20% of its own baseline, pulling the mean down and the z-score up toward zero; on 2024-06-06 it would raise the baseline mean to $\frac{0.9805 \times 5 + 0.9531}{6} = 0.97593$ and cut the apparent deviation by roughly 18%. (2) Using `STDDEV_SAMP` with a window of a single preceding row, which returns NULL and silently nulls the z-score column. (3) Reading the trend from a bar chart of `pass_rate` alone: because `rows_in` is pinned at 1,240,000 here, the pass_rate axis doubles as the quarantine axis, but the moment volumes move the two decouple and the chart lies. Always plot pass_rate and quarantine volume together. (4) Treating a one-day blip as a regression window, or a sustained drift as noise: the test is whether the deviation persists past the alert, which is why the window is stated with an open right end.

Generalisation: the same construction works for any per-run ratio - null rate, duplicate rate, schema-violation rate - and the trailing window length is a bias/variance trade-off: short windows adapt fast but raise false positives, long windows are stable but slow. Thirty days of trending data is the minimum useful span for distinguishing a genuine data regression from a metrics-capture bug, because the latter typically shows as a discontinuity in one metric while its companion metrics stay flat [source 5]. It is equally important that the metric stream itself is stable before you interpret it: the cleaning and preparation steps that make raw data analysable are the same steps whose failure produces a metrics artefact that looks like a regression [source 4].
Problem 3

The payments ingest `ingest.payments_raw` writes one metric row per day. Four consecutive runs produced:

| run_date | rows_in | rows_valid | rows_quarantined | pass_rate |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 2024-07-01 | 1,240,000 | 1,216,688 | 23,312 | 0.9812 |

| 2024-07-02 | 1,240,000 | 1,215,310 | 0 | 0.9801 |

| 2024-07-03 | 620,000 | 607,600 | 12,400 | 0.9800 |

| 2024-07-04 | 1,240,000 | 1,181,844 | 58,156 | 0.9531 |

For each row, decide whether it is (A) a healthy baseline, (B) a metrics-capture bug, (C) an upstream volume/delivery incident, or (D) a genuine data-quality regression. Justify each answer with arithmetic, and state the diagnostic invariant you used.
Hint: Test rows_in = rows_valid + rows_quarantined first; then ask which of the three counters actually moved relative to the baseline.

Worked solution
Step 1 - Apply the invariant to all four rows. The invariant is $\text{rows\_in} = \text{rows\_valid} + \text{rows\_quarantined}$.

- 2024-07-01: $1{,}216{,}688 + 23{,}312 = 1{,}240{,}000$ - holds. Also $1{,}216{,}688/1{,}240{,}000 = 0.9812$, matching the stored pass_rate. Consistent.

- 2024-07-02: $1{,}215{,}310 + 0 = 1{,}215{,}310 \ne 1{,}240{,}000$. Gap $= 1{,}240{,}000 - 1{,}215{,}310 = 24{,}690$ rows unaccounted for. pass_rate $= 1{,}215{,}310/1{,}240{,}000 = 0.980089 \approx 0.9801$, matching the stored value.

- 2024-07-03: $607{,}600 + 12{,}400 = 620{,}000$ - holds. $607{,}600/620{,}000 = 0.980000$ exactly.

- 2024-07-04: $1{,}181{,}844 + 58{,}156 = 1{,}240{,}000$ - holds. $1{,}181{,}844/1{,}240{,}000 = 0.953100$.

Step 2 - Interpret each row against the baseline of 2024-07-01, where the normal quarantine load is 23,312 rows/day (quarantine rate $0.0188$).

Row 2024-07-01 - diagnosis A, healthy baseline. All three counters are self-consistent and pass_rate 0.9812 is in the normal band. It defines the reference: rows_in 1,240,000, quarantine rate 1.88%.

Row 2024-07-02 - diagnosis B, metrics-capture bug. The data quality looks fine (pass_rate 0.9801, even a hair better than baseline), but the quarantine counter is zero while the identity demands 24,690 rows. Two readings are possible. Either the rows were genuinely not routed to quarantine - which would mean the routing step dropped them silently, the highest-risk failure mode in the whole design - or the counter was never read from the routing step and the metrics row defaulted to zero. The tell is that pass_rate is normal while its complement is zero: a real data problem moves both counters together; a capture bug moves one. The remedy is to recompute the row from the quarantine table rather than from the counter, and to gate the metric write on the identity assertion from Problem 1, so an inconsistent row never reaches `ops.quality.metrics`.

Row 2024-07-03 - diagnosis C, upstream volume/delivery incident. The identity holds and pass_rate is 0.9800, essentially identical to baseline - the quality of what arrived was fine. What moved is rows_in: $620{,}000$ versus $1{,}240{,}000$, exactly half, a drop of 50%. Quarantine volume fell proportionally ($12{,}400$ versus $23{,}312$, a ratio of 0.532) because there were simply fewer rows, not because fewer were bad. A pass_rate-only alert would have missed this day entirely; a volume alert on rows_in catches it immediately. The root cause is upstream (a missing daily partition, a truncated export, a partially loaded source table), so the incident should be routed to the data producer, not to the quality owner.

Row 2024-07-04 - diagnosis D, genuine quality regression. The identity holds, rows_in is back at exactly 1,240,000, and the movement is all on the failure side: rows_quarantined $= 58{,}156$, which is $58{,}156 / 23{,}312 = 2.495$ times baseline, and rows_valid fell from 1,216,688 to 1,181,844, a loss of 34,844 valid rows. pass_rate drops $0.9812 - 0.9531 = 0.0281$, i.e. 2.81 percentage points, or a factor of $\dfrac{1 - 0.9531}{1 - 0.9812} = \dfrac{0.0469}{0.0188} = 2.495$ on the quarantine rate - the two statements are the same fact. Because volume is normal, the failure rate genuinely rose.

Step 3 - Diagnostic rule in one line: the identity detects capture bugs, and comparing which counter moved against the baseline separates a quality regression (rows_quarantined up, rows_in flat) from a volume incident (rows_quarantined and rows_in both down proportionally, pass_rate flat).

Analysis — Why the method works: with only three counters there is one hard constraint ($\text{rows\_in} = \text{rows\_valid} + \text{rows\_quarantined}$) and two degrees of freedom. The constraint catches internal inconsistency - the signature of a bug in the measurement apparatus - while the degrees of freedom locate the change relative to a baseline: which counter moved tells you whether the data changed or the world did. This is the operational version of separating detection from handling that was established when the quarantine table was designed: a quality check detects, routing handles, and the metric layer independently verifies that both happened.

Common mistakes. (1) Believing the pass_rate column. Because pass_rate is a ratio it is self-normalising: on 2024-07-02 it looked healthy and on 2024-07-03 it looked healthy, yet one day had a broken counter and the other had half the data. Ratios must always be read together with their denominators. (2) Assuming a quarantine spike is seasonality without evidence. Here the spike on 2024-07-04 is accompanied by an unchanged rows_in and a loss of valid rows, which excludes seasonality as an explanation; seasonality would raise quarantine volume while keeping the failure mix proportional to volume. (3) Treating a drop in rows_in as a data-quality problem and paging the quality owner - the fix lives upstream. (4) Fixing the 2024-07-02 row by editing the number to 24,690 instead of re-deriving it from the quarantine table; the edited value is a guess, and the underlying capture bug remains for the next run. (5) Reusing one alert for both signals. Volume anomalies and quality regressions need different thresholds and different responders, which is why the metrics table stores rows_in as well as pass_rate.

Generalisation: the same triage applies whenever a monitoring number moves - ask first whether the number could be wrong (invariant test), then whether the denominator moved (volume test), then whether the numerator moved against a stable denominator (quality test). Note also why quarantined rows are counted rather than dropped: if 2024-07-04's 58,156 rows had been silently discarded instead of routed, rows_in would still be 1,240,000, the identity would still hold, and the only surviving evidence would be a pass_rate drop with no counterexample material to reprocess after the fix. Preserving the invalid records with their rejection metadata is what makes the follow-up investigation possible at all, and it is the same principle that makes cleaned data trustworthy in any analysis pipeline [source 2].
Problem 4

On 2024-06-14 the orders ingest ran once per source stream and wrote two metric rows into `ops.quality.metrics`:

| run_id | source_table | rows_in | rows_valid | pass_rate |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| r-2024-06-14-0200-orders | bronze.orders_raw | 1,000,000 | 980,000 | 0.980000 |

| r-2024-06-14-0215-partner | bronze.partner_orders_raw | 10,000 | 5,000 | 0.500000 |

(a) Compute the day's pass_rate two ways: as the unweighted `AVG(pass_rate)` over the two rows, and as the pooled ratio `SUM(rows_valid) / SUM(rows_in)`. (b) Write the SQL for both, and say which one belongs on a trend chart. (c) The partner stream's pass_rate degrades to 0.50 while its volume stays at 10,000 rows. Quantify how much the unweighted daily number moves versus the pooled number, and express the amplification factor.
Hint: An unweighted average of ratios is a weighted average in disguise, and the weights are equal row counts - which is almost never what you mean.

Worked solution
Step 1 - Unweighted average of the two per-run ratios.

$$\overline{p} = \frac{0.980000 + 0.500000}{2} = \frac{1.480000}{2} = 0.740000$$

Step 2 - Pooled (volume-weighted) ratio, which is what the identity actually supports.

$$p_{\text{pooled}} = \frac{\text{rows\_valid}}{\text{rows\_in}} = \frac{980{,}000 + 5{,}000}{1{,}000{,}000 + 10{,}000} = \frac{985{,}000}{1{,}010{,}000} = 0.975248$$

Step 3 - The gap: $0.975248 - 0.740000 = 0.235248$, i.e. 23.52 percentage points. The unweighted figure implies that roughly a quarter of all rows failed, while in fact 1.475% failed. Notice also that the unweighted mean happens to equal the weighted mean only when all weights are equal - here the weights are 1,000,000 and 10,000, a 100:1 ratio, so the equal-weighting is badly wrong.

Step 4 - SQL for both.

```sql

-- WRONG for a trend line when run volumes differ

SELECT run_date,

AVG(pass_rate) AS avg_pass_rate

FROM ops.quality.metrics

GROUP BY run_date;

-- RIGHT: pooled pass_rate, rebuilt from counts

SELECT run_date,

SUM(rows_in) AS rows_in,

SUM(rows_valid) AS rows_valid,

SUM(rows_quarantined) AS rows_quarantined,

SUM(rows_valid) / SUM(rows_in) AS pass_rate

FROM ops.quality.metrics

GROUP BY run_date

ORDER BY run_date;

```

Step 5 - Sensitivity. Fix the partner stream's volume at 10,000 rows and move its pass_rate from 0.980000 down to 0.500000 (valid rows $9{,}800 \to 5{,}000$).

- Unweighted: $\overline{p}$ moves from $\frac{0.980 + 0.980}{2} = 0.980000$ to $0.740000$, a change of $-0.240000$.

- Pooled: $p_{\text{pooled}}$ moves from $\frac{980{,}000 + 9{,}800}{1{,}010{,}000} = \frac{989{,}800}{1{,}010{,}000} = 0.980000$ to $0.975248$, a change of $-0.004752$.

- Amplification factor: $0.240000 / 0.004752 = 50.5$. The unweighted daily number overreacts by a factor of about 50 to a change in a stream that carries 1% of the volume.

The trend chart must use the pooled ratio (Step 4's second query). The unweighted mean is defensible only when comparing runs of comparable volume - for example two nightly runs of the same source - and even then it should be reported with the weights attached.

Step 6 - Weighted-average identity. Averaging per-run pass_rates weighted by rows_in is algebraically identical to the pooled ratio:

$$\frac{\sum_i \text{rows\_in}_i \cdot p_i}{\sum_i \text{rows\_in}_i} = \frac{\sum_i \text{rows\_in}_i \cdot (\text{rows\_valid}_i / \text{rows\_in}_i)}{\sum_i \text{rows\_in}_i} = \frac{\sum_i \text{rows\_valid}_i}{\sum_i \text{rows\_in}_i} = p_{\text{pooled}}$$

Check on the data: $\frac{1{,}000{,}000(0.98) + 10{,}000(0.50)}{1{,}010{,}000} = \frac{980{,}000 + 5{,}000}{1{,}010{,}000} = 0.975248$, matching Step 2 exactly, as it must.

Analysis — Why the method works: an average of ratios is only interpretable if you know the weights, and `AVG()` silently imposes equal weights. Because rows_in is the natural weight for a per-row pass rate, the pooled ratio is the correct daily aggregate: it answers 'what fraction of the rows we processed yesterday were valid?', which is the question the trend chart is asking. The unweighted mean answers 'how did the average stream behave?', which is a different and usually less useful question - and it is dominated by whichever stream happens to have the smallest volume.

Common mistakes. (1) Averaging the stored pass_rate column because it is the column that looks like the metric. The underlying counts are required; a table that stores only pass_rate makes the correct daily aggregate unrecoverable. (2) Using the pooled ratio to compare streams. Pooling hides the partner stream entirely - a stream at 50% pass rate contributing 1% of volume barely moves the daily number, so per-source monitoring must use the per-run rows, not the daily rollup. Both views are needed: per-run for diagnosis, pooled for trend. (3) Weighting by the number of metric rows instead of rows_in, which is just the unweighted mean again. (4) Treating the 0.24 swing produced by the unweighted mean as a real incident and paging an on-call engineer for a stream carrying 10,000 rows.

Generalisation and exam framing: this is the same class of error as mixing granularities anywhere in a medallion pipeline (bronze, silver, gold - raw, cleaned, and business-aggregated layers) - the aggregate must be computed from counts at a consistent grain, never by averaging a derived rate whose denominator changed. It also interacts with the retry problem from Problem 1: double-counting inflates rows_in, which shifts the pooled weight of a stream, so an idempotent keyed write is a precondition for a correct trend, not an unrelated nicety. Finally, the reason the whole exercise insists on counts rather than ratios is accuracy of conclusions: cleaning and monitoring exist to keep analysis reflecting the true state of the data, and a mis-weighted dashboard is exactly the kind of skewed result that produces misleading conclusions about whether the pipeline is healthy [source 6]. Track the counts over time, and report the data you set aside rather than quietly averaging it away [source 5].

actions.text: Now let's pull everything together with the exercise you've been building toward — a data quality metrics pipeline. This is exactly the kind of task the exam loves, because it forces you to combine counting, identity checks, and idempotent writes into one workflow.

Problem 1 gives you the silver ingest, `ingest.orders_raw`. The task is to emit per-run quality metrics — rows_in, rows_valid, rows_quarantined, and pass_rate — into a Delta metrics table. Before you write any aggregation, stop and notice the identity.

That's the hint on screen: every input row must land in exactly one bucket. rows_in equals rows_valid plus rows_quarantined. If those two don't reconcile to the total, you've dropped or double-counted rows somewhere — and your pass_rate is now a lie.

The worked solution walks it in steps. Step 1 is the counting identity — aggregate the run's DataFrames, compute the four counts, and union them with the run metadata: run_id and run_timestamp. Step 2 is the write. Here's the critical part: persist with MERGE keyed on run_id.

And the analysis explains why the method works: a metric row is a fact about a single run, so run_id is its natural key. If you used a plain append and the job retried, you'd write the same run's metrics twice — double-counting that re-run and corrupting every trend you plot afterward. MERGE on run_id makes the write idempotent: retrying simply overwrites the same row.

The remaining problems reinforce the same theme from different angles — trailing-window queries, quarantined-row invariants, and the pitfall of averaging ratios instead of computing them from the raw counts. Notice that every one of them traces back to a single principle: metrics must be exact, and writes must be safe to repeat. That's the mindset you want walking into this domain's exam questions.

scenes.title: Lesson Assessment: Monitoring and Quarantine

questions.question: You are designing a quarantine Delta table schema for a streaming ingestion pipeline that writes raw JSON events from Auto Loader into a bronze table. Every violating record must be preserved with enough context for investigators to trace it back to its origin and reprocess it after an upstream fix. Which set of columns BEST satisfies the anatomic requirements of a quarantine table?

options.label: payload, rejection_reason, failed_rule, ingest_timestamp, source_table, batch_id
payload_id, error_code, retry_count, created_at
record_hash, is_valid, processed_flag, updated_at
payload, cleaned_payload, quarantine_flag, load_date

questions.analysis: The lesson established that a quarantine table must store the original record payload intact alongside rejection metadata, and the required columns are rejection_reason, failed_rule, ingest_timestamp, source_table, and batch_id. Option A matches this exactly, preserving both forensic context and reprocessing capability. Option B loses the raw payload and the rule that failed, so records cannot be reprocessed after an upstream fix. Option C keeps only a hash and flags, which destroys the evidence needed for investigation. Option D adds a cleaned_payload but omits rejection_reason, failed_rule, source_table, and batch_id, so investigators cannot attribute a rejection to a rule or a source. This builds on the earlier separation of detection (a quality check) from handling (routing), as described in the lesson and reinforced by the principle that flawed data leads to skewed results when not isolated and cleaned [source 6].

questions.question: A data engineer is routing invalid records to quarantine in a Spark pipeline that reads a daily batch into a DataFrame with columns id, amount, and event_ts. Quality predicates are: amount IS NOT NULL, amount >= 0, amount <= 10000, and event_ts IS NOT NULL. Which of the following statements about the routing implementation are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: A single boolean condition (all rules pass) should define valid rows, with the complement routed to quarantine.
Rejection metadata such as rejection_reason, failed_rule, and ingest_timestamp should be attached using conditional when() expressions.
Rows failing multiple rules should be dropped so only the first failure is recorded.
The valid/quarantine split should be idempotent so reruns produce the same partition of rows given the same input.

questions.analysis: The lesson's worked exercise explicitly specified defining quality predicates and splitting with a single condition where valid equals all rules passing, otherwise quarantine (A). It also specified attaching rejection metadata via conditional when() expressions (B). Idempotency is essential because metric writes and quarantine writes are often retried; the same input must yield the same split on rerun (D). Option C is wrong: silently dropping rows that fail multiple rules destroys evidence, contradicts the principle that invalid records must be isolated rather than dropped, and prevents the correct failed_rule attribution. As the source notes, cleaning must identify and fix errors and inconsistencies so data is accurate and ready for analysis, which requires retaining rather than discarding invalid rows [source 2].

questions.question: You maintain a dq_metrics Delta table keyed by run_id with a run_timestamp. Over 30 days the daily pass_rate is stable near 0.98, then on day 22 it drops to 0.71 for three consecutive runs before recovering to 0.97 on day 25. rows_in is unchanged, but rows_quarantined increases by an order of magnitude. A source schema change was deployed on day 21. Which alerting approach is MOST appropriate, and what does the trend indicate?

options.label: Use a fixed threshold of 0.95; the drop below threshold indicates a likely data regression tied to the day 21 schema change.
Use baseline-deviation alerting against the 0.98 baseline; the three-run dip is a regression window beginning at day 22.
Ignore the dip because pass_rate recovered by day 25, indicating seasonality.
Treat the dip as a metrics-capture bug since rows_in is unchanged.

questions.analysis: The lesson distinguished fixed-threshold alerts from baseline-deviation alerts and taught interpreting pass_rate as a time series to identify a regression window. Baseline-deviation is more appropriate here because it detects the departure from the 0.98 baseline even before a hard threshold is crossed and localizes the regression window to days 22-24 (B). Option A would also fire, but a fixed threshold is less sensitive and does not by itself localize the window as cleanly. Option C is wrong because a recovery does not imply seasonality; seasonality would typically affect rows_in or show a periodic pattern, which is absent. Option D is wrong because rows_in stability with a quarantine spike points to upstream data problems, not a capture bug, and the day 21 schema change plus the sustained three-run dip support a genuine regression. This aligns with the lesson's guidance on detecting regressions from trends and matches the source principle that flawed data leads to skewed results, so quality assurance checks are necessary to verify data accuracy [source 6].

questions.question: Design and justify a quarantine table schema for a bronze-to-silver pipeline in Unity Catalog, then explain how you would capture and monitor quality metrics to detect a regression. Your answer must: (1) list the required quarantine columns and the purpose of each; (2) state the quality predicates used for routing and show at least one concrete routing condition; (3) define rows_in, rows_valid, rows_quarantined, and pass_rate and give the pass_rate formula with a worked numeric example; (4) describe how you would detect a regression from the metrics time series and distinguish it from a metrics-capture bug.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Quarantine schema - 30%: names rejection_reason, failed_rule, ingest_timestamp, source_table, batch_id, and specifies that the original payload is stored intact; explains forensic and reprocessing purpose of each. (2) Routing design - 20%: defines quality predicates, uses a single all-rules-pass condition for valid rows with the complement to quarantine, and shows a concrete when() or equivalent conditional attaching rejection metadata. (3) Metrics definitions - 30%: accurately defines rows_in, rows_valid, rows_quarantined, and states pass_rate = rows_valid / rows_in with a correct worked example (e.g., 10000 in, 9700 valid -> 0.97). (4) Regression detection - 20%: explains baseline-deviation vs fixed threshold, identifies a regression window from the time series, and distinguishes a genuine data regression from a metrics-capture bug (e.g., rows_in constant with quarantine spike and correlated source change indicates real regression).
questions.analysis: A strong answer mirrors the lesson's quarantine anatomy and worked exercises. Quarantine columns: rejection_reason (human-readable cause), failed_rule (which predicate failed), ingest_timestamp (when observed), source_table (origin), batch_id (which run/batch), plus the intact raw payload for reprocessing after an upstream fix. Routing: valid = amount IS NOT NULL AND amount >= 0 AND amount <= 10000 AND event_ts IS NOT NULL; rows where this is false go to quarantine; metadata is attached with when() expressions. Metrics: rows_in = total rows read this run, rows_valid = predicate-passing rows, rows_quarantined = complement, pass_rate = rows_valid / rows_in. Worked example: 10,000 rows in, 9,700 valid -> pass_rate = 9700/10000 = 0.97. Regression detection: persist per-run metrics keyed by run_id with run_timestamp and treat pass_rate as a time series; use baseline-deviation against a rolling baseline rather than only a fixed threshold to localize the regression window; distinguish a real regression (rows_in stable, quarantine spike correlated with a source schema change) from a capture bug (e.g., metrics not written, run_id collisions, or rows_valid + rows_quarantined != rows_in). The lesson's emphasis on isolating invalid records rather than dropping them and on identifying and fixing errors and inconsistencies aligns with the source's principle that cleaning ensures accurate analysis and prevents misleading conclusions [source 2], and with the general data preparation guidance that quality assurance checks verify accuracy [source 1].

scenes.title: Why Declarative Pipelines Exist

elements.content: Why Declarative Pipelines Exist
Declare datasets and queries — the framework derives the execution order
What "declarative" means here

A declarative pipeline is one where the developer writes only the dataset definitions and their queries; the engine builds a dependency graph from those definitions and decides execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures [source 5].

Precondition: each dataset is defined as a query over other datasets. Edge case: the engine still resolves the graph at runtime, so a cyclic definition is a compile-time error, not a silent loop.
Worked example: 7 datasets, 1 declared chain
Declare bronze_orders → silver_orders → gold_daily_sales. You write 3 queries; the engine infers 2 dependency edges and the run order for you.
Imperative wiring vs. engine-derived graph

Contrast

Imperative: you hand-wire task order, dependencies, retries, schedules (Airflow DAGs, notebook job chains).

Declarative: the framework owns dependency resolution, orchestration, incremental refresh and error handling [source 3].
Pipeline = graph of datasets, not a list of tasks

actions.text: Now that you've had a chance to work through the monitoring and quarantine assessment, let's shift gears. So far we've been writing transformation logic step by step — read this, filter that, write here. In this lesson we're going to look at a fundamentally different way of expressing a pipeline: declaring what you want rather than scripting how to do it.

This is the title question: why do declarative pipelines exist at all? The short answer is that orchestration — deciding what runs when, in what order, and what to do when a step fails — is a lot of repetitive, error-prone work that has almost nothing to do with the actual business problem you're solving.

So let's define the term precisely. A declarative pipeline is one where the developer declares datasets and their queries, and the framework derives the execution order. You describe the relationships between the data, and the engine works out the sequence. Hold on to that phrasing — it is exactly the kind of definition the exam likes to test.

Now contrast that with imperative orchestration, which is what most of you have probably done before. In an imperative setup, you hand-wire the task order, the dependencies, the retries, and the schedules yourself. Airflow DAGs are the classic example, and so are chained notebook jobs where task two only fires after task one succeeds. All of that glue code is yours to write and yours to maintain.

Here's a worked example that makes this concrete. We declare bronze_orders, then silver_orders, then gold_daily — a chain of seven datasets in total. Notice that we never say 'run bronze first, then silver.' We simply declare how each dataset is built, and the dependency graph falls out of the definitions automatically.

That leads to the mental model shift I want you to internalise: a pipeline is a graph of datasets, not a list of scheduled tasks. Once you see it that way, it becomes obvious why the framework can own dependency resolution, orchestration, incremental refresh, and error handling on your behalf. And one exam trap worth flagging early — declarative does not mean no code. You still write the transformation logic; you just don't write the orchestration.

scenes.title: Anatomy of a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline

elements.content: Anatomy of a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline
Three Dataset Types You Can Define

Streaming tables

Append-only. Record is processed once, then never reprocessed. Use for raw events ingested continuously.

Materialized views

Result of a full query is stored and refreshed incrementally. Use for aggregated business marts.

Temporary views

Pipeline-local only, not persisted. Use as reusable staging steps within the pipeline.
How the Pipeline Graph Is Inferred

• Each dataset = a name + query; no separate task object.

• Any query that references another dataset becomes its downstream dependency.

• DAG is built from these references automatically.
  Example: SELECT * FROM silver_events in gold_daily_sales creates silver → gold edge.

• Multiple unrelated queries = independent parallel branches.
Worked Example: Define bronze_events → reference in silver_events → reference in gold_daily_sales. Framework extracts order: bronze → silver → gold. Only gold’s last-read offset must be stored.
Sources: [source 5] Declarative dependencies and data quality; [source 3] SQL and Python batch/streaming; [source 2] pipeline graph tracking

actions.text: Now let's open up a Lakeflow declarative pipeline and look at its anatomy. What are the actual building blocks you write? It comes down to datasets — and every dataset is just two things: a name and a query.

A pipeline can define three dataset types, and the exam expects you to name all of them. First, streaming tables — append-only, where each record is processed once as it arrives. Second, materialized views — the result of the query is the product, refreshed on demand. And third, temporary pipeline-local views — intermediate steps that live only inside the pipeline and are never published to the catalog.

Here's the key distinction on streaming tables: the word 'append-only' is doing a lot of work. A record is processed once, and you never rewrite it. That is fundamentally different from a materialized view, which recomputes its result whenever the underlying data changes.

So how does the pipeline know what depends on what? This is the part that trips people up. There is no separate task object, no DAG you declare by hand. The graph is inferred: any dataset that references another dataset automatically becomes its downstream dependency.

Read that again — each dataset is a name plus a query, and there is no separate scheduled task. The framework builds the dependency graph for you by reading your references, then refreshes datasets in dependency order and processes only what needs to change. That's the whole value proposition.

Let's walk the worked example. You define bronze_events as a streaming table. Then a silver dataset simply references bronze_events in its FROM clause. Nothing else is declared — that single reference is what tells the framework the dependency exists and dictates the refresh order.

And remember, one pipeline can mix SQL and Python source files freely, and it can blend batch and streaming execution in the same graph. So to recap this page: three dataset types, name plus query, inferred graph, ordered refresh. Those four ideas are exactly what the certification will test.
