scenes.title: Declarative Pipelines vs. Imperative Orchestration

elements.content: Dimension  |  Lakeflow declarative pipeline  |  Imperative orchestration (Airflow / notebook jobs)

Definition unit (the primitive you author)
Lakeflow declarative pipeline: The authoring primitive is a dataset (a streaming table, materialized view, or temporary pipeline-local view) defined as a name plus a query, and there is no separate scheduled task object because publishing and ordering are properties the framework attaches to that dataset.
Imperative orchestration (Airflow / notebook jobs): The authoring primitive is a task plus its schedule: a PythonOperator, a notebook task, or a Spark submit task is registered on a DAG with a cron/schedule and an explicit execution operator, so the task object itself — not the data it produces — is the unit of definition.

Source of dependency ordering
Lakeflow declarative pipeline: Dependencies are inferred: because the pipeline is declarative, the engine builds a dependency graph from your definitions and determines the execution order, so any dataset whose query references another dataset automatically becomes its downstream dependency and the developer never writes a DAG edge [source 1][source 5].
Imperative orchestration (Airflow / notebook jobs): Dependencies are explicit: the engineer hand-codes upstream/downstream links (Airflow's set_upstream/set_downstream, TaskFlow wiring, or a notebook chain in a job's task list), so order is a property of the authored graph and a missing edge silently produces stale reads.

Refresh behaviour / incremental processing
Lakeflow declarative pipeline: Refresh is framework-managed: the engine decides where to process incrementally and reprocesses only the affected portion of the graph, and you select trigger modes (continuous, triggered on a schedule, or manual refresh) as pipeline-level configuration rather than as task logic [source 2][source 5].
Imperative orchestration (Airflow / notebook jobs): Refresh is developer-written: you own the MERGE INTO, INSERT OVERWRITE, or watermark filter inside each task, plus the backfill command (for example `airflow dags backfill -s 2024-01-01 -e 2024-01-31`), so correctness under late-arriving data depends on your hand-written idempotency.

Failure recovery and retry semantics
Lakeflow declarative pipeline: Recovery is graph-aware: the engine determines how to recover from failures and restarts from the failed dataset's boundary rather than from the head of the pipeline, and data quality expectations declared alongside the transformation are enforced by the framework, quarantining or dropping bad records according to your rules [source 5].
Imperative orchestration (Airflow / notebook jobs): Recovery is task-scoped: retries are configured per operator (retries=3, retry_delay=timedelta(minutes=5)), a failed task blocks its downstream dependents, and a rerun re-executes that task's write logic — which is safe only if you wrote it idempotently.

Testing and validation model
Lakeflow declarative pipeline: Testing centres on dataset semantics: you assert row-level expectations inside the pipeline (for example `CONSTRAINT valid_amount EXPECT (amount >= 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW`), and the framework enforces them at runtime, so validation is continuous and the pipeline event log reports which expectations fired [source 2].
Imperative orchestration (Airflow / notebook jobs): Testing centres on orchestration contracts: you unit-test task callables and DAG structure offline (great_expectations suites, pytest against the DAG), and the 'does the DAG load and produce the right order' question is separate from 'are the rows correct?'

Cost and control granularity
Lakeflow declarative pipeline: You get consistency and lose per-step control: the trade-off is that declarative authoring removes orchestration code but hands scheduling granularity to the framework, so you cannot tune each step's compute profile, retry policy, or SLA independently — an intentional constraint that keeps the graph coherent.
Imperative orchestration (Airflow / notebook jobs): You keep per-step control and pay for it: each task can specify its own cluster, queue, retry, timeout, and SLA in code, but the pipeline is only as reliable as the hand-wired graph and incremental logic you maintain.

Takeaway — Choose a Lakeflow declarative pipeline when the workload is a set of related datasets whose order is implicit in their queries, when incremental refresh and data-quality enforcement should be framework-owned, and when you value consistency over per-step tuning [source 3][source 6].

Takeaway — Choose imperative orchestration (Airflow / notebook jobs) when the workflow is heterogeneous or crosses system boundaries — sending files to a partner, calling an external API, branching on an operational condition — where explicit control of each step's compute, retries and SLA is the requirement.

Takeaway — Do not treat them as mutually exclusive in production: a common pattern is a declarative pipeline for the medallion layers (bronze/silver/gold) invoked as a single task inside an Airflow DAG that owns the cross-system dependencies.
Takeaway — Exam rule of thumb: if the question asks 'who determines execution order?', the declarative answer is always 'the framework, from dataset references'.

actions.text: Good work on that checkpoint. Now let's compare the two design styles side by side across the dimensions the certification actually tests. This table is your reference sheet: each row is a dimension where declarative pipelines and imperative orchestration diverge, so let's walk each one.

First, the definition unit — the primitive you actually author. In a Lakeflow declarative pipeline, you declare a dataset plus its query, and that's it. In imperative orchestration like Airflow or notebook jobs, you author a task plus its schedule. Same goal, but you're writing the 'when' and the 'in what order' by hand.

Second, where dependency ordering comes from. Declaratively, the framework infers it from dataset references — if one dataset reads another, the edge exists automatically. Imperatively, you explicitly code the upstream and downstream links yourself, so every dependency is a line of code you own and must maintain.

Third, refresh behaviour and incremental processing. The declarative framework manages incremental processing for you. On the imperative side, the developer writes the MERGE or overwrite logic that makes the refresh incremental. That's where most of the hand-written complexity lives.

Fourth, failure recovery and retry semantics. In a declarative pipeline the framework handles retries and recovery at the dataset level, tracking state so a failed refresh picks up correctly. With imperative orchestration, retry behaviour is something you configure task by task — timeouts, retry counts, intervals — so your recovery semantics are only as good as your configuration.

Fifth, the testing and validation model. Declaratively, expectations are first-class — you attach quality rules to datasets and the framework enforces and logs them. Imperatively, you build validation as separate tasks or assertion steps, which means the discipline has to be imposed by you rather than the runtime.

And sixth, cost and control granularity. This is the real trade-off: declarative removes orchestration code, but it hands scheduling granularity to the framework — you gain consistency and lose per-step control. If you need to tune one step's cluster or retry policy independently, imperative gives you that knob.
So takeaway one: choose a Lakeflow declarative pipeline when the work is naturally dataset-shaped and consistency across refreshes matters more than micromanaging each step.

Takeaway two: choose imperative orchestration with Airflow or notebook jobs when you need fine-grained control over per-task scheduling, dependencies, and failure handling that the framework won't give you.

Takeaway three, and this one matters: do not treat them as mutually exclusive. A Lakeflow Jobs workflow can orchestrate declarative pipeline tasks alongside notebook and SQL tasks — so the exam answer is often 'both, at different levels of the pipeline.'

And takeaway four — your exam rule of thumb: if the question asks who decides the order or the refresh granularity, that tells you which style is expected. If the ordering is data-driven and inferred, it's declarative. If it's hand-coded and scheduled, it's imperative. Hold that rule and the scenario questions on this topic get much easier.

scenes.title: SQL Syntax: Declaring Datasets

elements.content: SQL Syntax: Declaring Datasets
Every dataset is declared with a name plus a query — the framework infers the rest [source 5].
Streaming table (ingest)

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_orders AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(raw_orders);

Adds only new rows each run — no full reload.
Materialized view (recompute)

CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_daily_sales AS SELECT date, SUM(amount) ... ;

Result cached; framework refreshes on change.
Dependencies & options

• Read a dataset by name to create a dependency [source 1].

• Use LIVE. to force resolution to the pipeline-local dataset.

• Same statement: COMMENT, PARTITIONED BY, CLUSTER BY, TBLPROPERTIES, CONSTRAINT ... EXPECT [source 4].
Exam trap

No separate INSERT or MERGE job. Refresh is owned by the pipeline — your statement declares what, not when [source 5].

Imperative DAGs schedule tasks; declarative pipelines derive order [source 3].
Worked example: raw_orders → bronze_orders (streaming table) → gold_daily_sales (materialized view), dependency auto-inferred from name reference.

actions.text: Now let's move from the concepts of declarative pipelines into the syntax itself. In a Lakeflow declarative pipeline, every dataset — whether a streaming table or a materialized view — is declared with a name plus a query. That single statement is the whole definition; there is no separate loading step.
Start with the streaming table, which handles incremental ingest. You write CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE, give it a name like bronze_orders, and then an AS SELECT that reads from your source.

Notice the STREAM() wrapper around raw_orders. That is what tells the framework to process this incrementally — read each new batch as it arrives rather than reprocessing everything. Drop the STREAM() wrapper and you lose the incremental behavior.

Next is the materialized view, the recompute-style dataset. Here you write CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, name it gold_daily_sales, and again follow with AS SELECT. The difference is semantic, not syntactic: the framework recomputes the full result rather than ingesting incrementally.

Dependencies come for free. You create them simply by reading another dataset by name in your SELECT — the pipeline graphs those references automatically. When a name must resolve to the pipeline-local dataset rather than a physical table with the same name, prefix it with LIVE.

And here is the exam trap worth memorizing: there is no separate INSERT or MERGE job. Refresh is owned by the pipeline, not by your statement — your SQL just declares what the dataset should be, and the framework decides when and how to refresh it.

questions.question: You need to declare a bronze dataset that continuously ingests new order records arriving from an external event stream, with each new record processed exactly once as it arrives. Which SQL statement form should you write in a Lakeflow declarative pipeline?

A materialized view (option B) is a recomputed dataset: the framework recomputes the result rather than ingesting incrementally, so it is the wrong semantic for an append-only event feed. Option C (a manual INSERT) and option D (a plain CREATE TABLE) are imperative or non-refreshable forms that push the incremental logic back onto the developer instead of letting the declarative engine own incremental refresh, violating the core premise that the developer declares datasets and the framework derives execution order and incremental placement [source 5].

questions.question: A teammate proposes the following pipeline definition and asks you to review it for a dataset that must be recomputed whenever upstream silver_sales data changes: CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_sales AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(silver_sales). Explain whether the statement form and the source clause are appropriate, and describe what the framework would do with this definition if it were run as written.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Correctly identifies that MATERIALIZED VIEW is the recomputed dataset type and that a materialized view should not read a STREAM() source - a materialized view is recomputed rather than incrementally ingested, so STREAM(silver_sales) is a semantic mismatch - 40%. (2) Explains that the correct form for incremental ingest would be CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE ... AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(...), and the correct form for recomputation is a materialized view reading the upstream dataset by name (optionally with LIVE. to bind to the pipeline-local dataset) - 30%. (3) States that the framework infers a dependency edge on silver_sales and derives the refresh order, so no manual INSERT/MERGE or execution order is needed - 20%. (4) Clarity and use of Databricks terminology (streaming table, materialized view, dependency graph) - 10%.
questions.analysis: A strong answer distinguishes the two dataset types by processing semantics. A streaming table is the incrementally ingested type and pairs with STREAM(...) as its source, so CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE gold_sales AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(silver_sales) is the form for continuous ingest. A materialized view is the recomputed type: the framework recomputes the result rather than ingesting records incrementally, so pairing MATERIALIZED VIEW with a STREAM() source mixes incompatible semantics. The corrected definition for recomputation is CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_sales AS SELECT * FROM silver_sales (using LIVE. if the name must resolve to the pipeline-local dataset). In both cases, because the pipeline is declarative, the engine builds a dependency graph from these definitions and determines execution order and failure recovery automatically, so no manual INSERT, MERGE, or explicit ordering is required [source 5] [source 1].

scenes.title: Python Syntax: Declaring Datasets

elements.content: Python Syntax: Declaring Datasets
Decorators register a name and a query — the framework infers the dependency graph, execution order, and incremental refresh strategy from your definitions alone.

@dp.table(

    name="silver_orders",

    comment="cleaned orders"

)

def silver_orders():

    return spark.readStream.table("LIVE.bronze_orders")

@dp.view                 # pipeline-local, not persisted

dp.read("silver_orders")         # batch snapshot

dp.read_stream("bronze_orders")   # streaming dependency

import pyspark.pipelines as dp  # legacy: import dlt

Definition. @dp.table decorates a function that returns a DataFrame to declare a streaming table; the decorator does not compute the data, it registers the dataset name, comment, options, and dependencies with the pipeline graph [source 2].

Precondition. The function body may only call dp.read, dp.read_stream, or spark.readStream.table — calling an arbitrary spark.read inside a pyfunc breaks dependency inference and forces full recompute on every pipeline run.

Edge case. If a dataset's dependencies are 2+ and one is streaming while the other is batch, the framework picks the union — streaming semantics dominate, and the batch side becomes a one-time snapshot at pipeline start.

Worked example. Given 3 datasets — bronze_orders (@dp.table), silver_orders (@dp.table reading LIVE.bronze_orders), gold_sales (@dp.materialized_view) — the framework infers 3 dependency edges and 1 valid topological order (bronze → silver → gold). Adding a 4th dataset silver_customers that reads the same upstream creates 4 edges and 2 independent branches, so a full refresh of silver_customers does not force a recompute of silver_orders.

Choice. dp.read() materialises a static snapshot for the run; dp.read_stream() creates a streaming dependency with checkpoint offsets that carry over between pipeline updates. Choosing wrong turns a 12-minute incremental update into a full scan of the upstream table.

Migration. Legacy code uses import dlt; @dlt.table; current code uses import pyspark.pipelines as dp; @dp.table [source 3]. The concept — a decorated function that declares a dataset — is identical; only the module name changed.
Sources: declarative framework and dependency graph [source 2], dataset types and automatic dependency resolution [source 5], Python decorators over a declarative pipeline [source 3].

actions.text: Now that we've seen how declarative datasets are declared in SQL, let's look at the Python side. The same declarative idea applies — you're just expressing it with decorators instead of DDL.
The pattern is straightforward: you decorate a plain Python function, and the function body returns a DataFrame. That combination is what declares a dataset in the pipeline.

The definition is worth committing to memory. The @dp.table decorator turns a function into a registered dataset. The decorator supplies the name and the comment, and it inspects the function body to figure out what that dataset depends on.

Here's the concrete syntax. @dp.table takes name and comment arguments — for example, name equals silver_orders. Inside the function, you read an upstream pipeline dataset with spark.readStream.table, using the fully qualified name LIVE.bronze_orders. That readStream call is exactly what declares a streaming dependency between the two datasets.

Use @dp.view instead when you want a temporary, pipeline-local view — something that isn't materialized as a durable table but is still tracked in the dependency graph. And when reading, dp.read() gives you batch semantics while dp.readStream() gives you streaming semantics. Which one you pick determines the refresh behaviour of the whole dataset.

The key discipline: keep the function body to the transformation only. The decorator is responsible for registering the dataset name, its options, and its dependencies. Don't bury side effects, file writes, or logging inside that body — the framework owns the execution.

Let's walk the worked example. Given three datasets — bronze_orders upstream, silver_orders in the middle, gold_revenue downstream — you declare silver with @dp.table and read bronze via readStream, and you declare gold with another @dp.table reading silver. The framework joins them into a single dependency graph; you never write the orchestration.

And the exam trap: older material and legacy code use import dlt with @dlt.table, while newer code imports pyspark.pipelines as dp. The concept is identical — only the module name changed. If you see dlt in a question, read it exactly the same way you'd read dp.

To sum up this page: decorator declares the dataset, readStream declares the streaming dependency, @dp.view is for temporary views, and dp.read versus dp.readStream chooses batch or streaming. Coming up next, we'll put SQL and Python side by side in a bronze-to-gold worked problem.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Bronze to Gold in SQL and Python

elements.content: Problem 1

A retail team lands raw clickstream and purchase events as newline-delimited JSON files in a Unity Catalog volume at `/Volumes/retail/landing/raw_events/`. A single file, `events_2024-06-01.json`, has just arrived with the following 12 records (columns: `event_id`, `user_id`, `event_ts` = the UTC time the event happened, `amount`, `ingested_at` = the time the ingestion job copied the file):

| # | event_id | user_id | event_ts | amount | ingested_at |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 1 | E1 | U1 | 2024-06-01 08:01:00 | 10.00 | 2024-06-01 08:01:02 |

| 2 | E2 | U1 | 2024-06-01 09:15:00 | 25.50 | 2024-06-01 09:15:03 |

| 3 | E3 | U2 | 2024-06-01 10:00:00 | 5.00 | 2024-06-01 10:00:01 |

| 4 | E1 | U1 | 2024-06-01 08:01:00 | 10.00 | 2024-06-01 08:07:44 |

| 5 | E4 | U3 | 2024-06-01 12:30:00 | NULL | 2024-06-01 12:30:02 |

| 6 | E5 | U2 | 2024-06-01 23:59:00 | 40.00 | 2024-06-01 23:59:05 |

| 7 | E6 | U4 | 2024-06-02 00:30:00 | 7.25 | 2024-06-02 00:30:01 |

| 8 | E5 | U2 | 2024-06-01 23:59:00 | 45.00 | 2024-06-02 01:10:00 |

| 9 | E7 | U1 | 2024-06-02 07:00:00 | 100.00 | 2024-06-02 07:00:00 |

| 10 | E8 | U4 | 2024-06-02 08:00:00 | 0.00 | 2024-06-02 08:00:01 |

| 11 | E9 | U5 | 2024-06-02 09:45:00 | 12.10 | 2024-06-02 09:45:00 |

| 12 | E1 | U1 | 2024-06-01 08:01:00 | 10.00 | 2024-06-02 02:00:00 |

Business rules for the cleaned layer are: (i) drop any record whose `amount` is NULL; (ii) keep exactly one row per `event_id`, namely the copy with the greatest `ingested_at`, because a later copy is a correction; (iii) an `amount` of `0.00` is a valid value and must be kept.

Declare the complete three-dataset medallion pipeline in Databricks SQL (bronze = raw landing, silver = cleaned and conformed, gold = business-level aggregates, the standard layering vocabulary): a bronze streaming table that incrementally ingests arriving files, a silver streaming table that applies the three rules, and a gold materialized view (a dataset the framework recomputes for you) that reports one row per event date with `event_count` and `total_amount`. Include no ordering hints of any kind. Then state the exact silver rows and gold rows this file produces.
Hint: Choose the read mode (streaming vs batch) separately from the statement type, and remember that gold aggregates on event time `event_ts`, not on ingestion time `ingested_at`.

Worked solution
**Step 1 — Declare the three datasets (Databricks SQL).** The script contains only dataset definitions; there is no `-- run after` comment, no `%run`, no manual `INSERT`:

```

-- Bronze: incrementally ingest newly arriving files

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_events

AS

SELECT *

FROM STREAM read_files(

'/Volumes/retail/landing/raw_events',

format => 'json'

);

-- Silver: drop NULL amounts, keep the latest copy per event_id

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE silver_events

AS

SELECT event_id, user_id, event_ts, amount, ingested_at

FROM (

SELECT

*,

row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY ingested_at DESC) AS rn

FROM STREAM(LIVE.bronze_events)

WHERE amount IS NOT NULL

)

WHERE rn = 1;

-- Gold: one row per event date

CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_daily_event_value

AS

SELECT

date(event_ts) AS event_date,

count(*) AS event_count,

sum(amount) AS total_amount

FROM LIVE.silver_events

GROUP BY date(event_ts);

```

Three points about the syntax. `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE` declares a dataset that is processed incrementally; the `STREAM` keyword on the read makes the source a streaming source. `LIVE.bronze_events` is not a physical path: the `LIVE` prefix forces the name to resolve to the pipeline-local dataset, which is what records the dependency edge. Gold uses a plain `SELECT ... FROM LIVE.silver_events` (a batch read) inside a `MATERIALIZED VIEW`, because a grouped aggregate is recomputed rather than appended.

**Step 2 — Silver row-by-row derivation.**

Rule (i), drop NULL `amount`: row 5 (E4, NULL) is removed. That leaves 11 rows.

Rule (ii), keep the greatest `ingested_at` per `event_id`:

- `E1` appears in rows 1, 4 and 12. Greatest `ingested_at` = 2024-06-02 02:00:00 (row 12), so rows 1 and 4 are dropped. Remaining value: `amount = 10.00`, `event_ts = 2024-06-01 08:01`.

- `E5` appears in rows 6 and 8. Greatest `ingested_at` = 2024-06-02 01:10:00 (row 8), so row 6 is dropped. Remaining value: `amount = 45.00`, not `40.00`.

- `E2, E3, E6, E7, E8, E9` each appear once and are kept unchanged. `E8` keeps `0.00` because rule (iii) forbids filtering on zero.

Duplicates removed: 3 rows (rows 1, 4, 6). Final silver cardinality: $12 - 1 - 3 = 8$ rows.

| event_id | user_id | event_ts | amount |

|---|---|---|---|

| E1 | U1 | 2024-06-01 08:01:00 | 10.00 |

| E2 | U1 | 2024-06-01 09:15:00 | 25.50 |

| E3 | U2 | 2024-06-01 10:00:00 | 5.00 |

| E5 | U2 | 2024-06-01 23:59:00 | 45.00 |

| E6 | U4 | 2024-06-02 00:30:00 | 7.25 |

| E7 | U1 | 2024-06-02 07:00:00 | 100.00 |

| E8 | U4 | 2024-06-02 08:00:00 | 0.00 |

| E9 | U5 | 2024-06-02 09:45:00 | 12.10 |

**Step 3 — Gold arithmetic.** Group the eight silver rows by `date(event_ts)`:

2024-06-01: $10.00 + 25.50 + 5.00 + 45.00 = 85.50$, `event_count = 4`.

2024-06-02: $7.25 + 100.00 + 0.00 + 12.10 = 119.35$, `event_count = 4`.

| event_date | event_count | total_amount |

|---|---|---|

| 2024-06-01 | 4 | 85.50 |

| 2024-06-02 | 4 | 119.35 |

Cross-check: $85.50 + 119.35 = 204.85$, which equals $10.00 + 25.50 + 5.00 + 45.00 + 7.25 + 100.00 + 0.00 + 12.10$.

Analysis — The framework builds a dependency graph from the definitions and then determines the execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures [source 5]; that is why this script needs no ordering hints even though gold textually depends on silver, which depends on bronze. The key method choice is that read mode and dataset type are two independent decisions: `STREAM(...)` selects incremental processing, while `MATERIALIZED VIEW` versus `STREAMING TABLE` selects whether the framework appends or recomputes. Reading `LIVE.silver_events` by name — not by a storage path — is what creates the graph edge, and the same form appears in Python, since Lakeflow pipelines are a declarative framework for building batch and streaming pipelines in both SQL and Python [source 3].

Edge cases a marker scheme should test. First, late data: event `E5` has `event_ts` on 2024-06-01 but was ingested on 2024-06-02, and it lands in the 2024-06-01 gold row because gold keys on event time. If you keyed gold on `date(ingested_at)` you would instead get 2024-06-01 = 40.50 and 2024-06-02 = 164.35 — a different, and for most businesses wrong, answer. Second, idempotency of corrections: `E5` arrives twice with different amounts, and the ordering key `ingested_at DESC` makes the newest copy win, so the pipeline is deterministic regardless of how many times the file is re-read. Third, the `row_number` dedup keeps state for every `event_id` ever seen; without restricting the retained window (for example by watermarking on `event_ts`), that state grows without bound, and Databricks recommends `dropDuplicates` with a watermark or an `apply_changes`/AUTO CDC flow when late-arriving corrections are a first-class requirement.

Common student errors. (1) Writing `CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW silver_events ... FROM LIVE.bronze_events` — legal SQL, but it silently converts incremental ingestion into a full recomputation of the whole history on every refresh. (2) Filtering `amount != 0` and losing `E8`. (3) Deduplicating with `SELECT DISTINCT *`, which keeps both `E5` rows because 40.00 and 45.00 differ. (4) Replacing `LIVE.silver_events` with the physical path, which removes the edge from the graph and lets gold run before silver exists.
Problem 2

Declare exactly the same three-dataset pipeline as in Problem 1, but in Python using the Lakeflow Pipelines decorator API. Requirements: (a) state which module you import and what makes a plain function become a dataset; (b) bronze must use Auto Loader (the `cloudFiles` source) so it tracks newly arriving files, and must add an `ingested_at` audit column with `current_timestamp()`; (c) silver must read the upstream pipeline dataset `bronze_events` with streaming semantics, drop rows with NULL `amount`, and keep one row per `event_id`; (d) gold must read `LIVE.silver_events` with batch semantics and return one row per event date with `event_count` and `total_amount`. No function may read a storage path for `bronze_events` or `silver_events`.

Hint: `spark.readStream.table('LIVE.bronze_events')` declares a streaming dependency; `spark.read.table('LIVE.silver_events')` declares a batch dependency. The decorator, not the function body, declares the dataset.

Worked solution
**Step 1 — Import and dataset declaration.** In the modern package the import is `from pyspark import pipelines as dp` (older material and many existing repos use `import dlt`, where `dlt` is the same API under its legacy name). A function becomes a dataset when it is decorated and returns a DataFrame; the function name (or the explicit `name=` argument) becomes the dataset name, and the returned DataFrame becomes its query.

**Step 2 — The three datasets.**

```

from pyspark import pipelines as dp

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

@dp.table(

name='bronze_events',

comment='Raw events incrementally ingested from the landing volume'

)

def bronze_events():

return (

spark.readStream

.format('cloudFiles') # Auto Loader

.option('cloudFiles.format', 'json')

.option('cloudFiles.schemaLocation',

'/Volumes/retail/checkpoints/bronze_events/schema')

.load('/Volumes/retail/landing/raw_events')

.withColumn('ingested_at', F.current_timestamp())

)

@dp.table(

name='silver_events',

comment='Deduplicated, amount-complete events'

)

def silver_events():

return (

spark.readStream.table('LIVE.bronze_events')

.filter(F.col('amount').isNotNull())

.withWatermark('event_ts', '2 days')

.dropDuplicates(['event_id'])

)

@dp.materialized_view(

name='gold_daily_event_value',

comment='Daily event count and total amount by event date'

)

def gold_daily_event_value():

return (

spark.read.table('LIVE.silver_events')

.groupBy(F.to_date('event_ts').alias('event_date'))

.agg(

F.count('*').alias('event_count'),

F.sum('amount').alias('total_amount')

)

)

```

**Step 3 — Where the dependency comes from.** The dependency is created by the *name* passed to the read, not by the position of the function in the file. In `silver_events()`, `spark.readStream.table('LIVE.bronze_events')` resolves to the pipeline-local dataset `bronze_events`, so the framework records the edge bronze to silver. In `gold_daily_event_value()`, `spark.read.table('LIVE.silver_events')` records the edge silver to gold. Because nothing in the file is ordered, a reader can move the three functions into any order and the graph is identical.

**Step 4 — Verify on the Problem 1 data.** Bronze contains the 12 rows plus `ingested_at`. Silver drops the NULL-`amount` row (E4) and collapses the duplicated `event_id` values, giving the same 8 rows as the SQL version. Gold gives 2024-06-01: `event_count = 4`, `total_amount = 85.50`; 2024-06-02: `event_count = 4`, `total_amount = 119.35`. Total $= 204.85$ in both languages.

Analysis — The decorated-function form and the SQL form are two surface syntaxes for the same semantic object — a name plus a query — which is why Lakeflow can offer one declarative framework for batch and streaming pipelines in SQL and Python [source 3][source 6]. The framework then tracks the data dependencies through the pipeline graph [source 1] and infers order, so the developer never writes a scheduler.

Method choice. `dp.table` declares incremental processing; `dp.materialized_view` declares full recomputation. Mixing them is deliberate in the medallion pattern: bronze and silver are append-mostly streams, while gold is a small aggregate whose cheapest correct implementation is recompute-from-scratch. The batch-versus-streaming read inside each function must agree with the dataset type, otherwise the pipeline fails at analysis with a message of the form 'a streaming table must be defined on a streaming query'.

Edge case: deduplication semantics differ subtly from the SQL solution. `dropDuplicates(['event_id'])` keeps the *first* record seen for a key within the watermark window, whereas the SQL `row_number() OVER (ORDER BY ingested_at DESC)` kept the *latest* copy. On the Problem 1 file, `E5` arrives as 40.00 and then 45.00; `dropDuplicates` keeps 40.00 if the first arrival is processed before the correction lands, giving 2024-06-01 `total_amount = 80.50` instead of 85.50. If corrections must win, either use an explicit windowed `rank()` over `ingested_at` inside the function, or model the entity with a slowly changing dimension (SCD) flow such as `dp.create_auto_cdc_flow`, which applies sequenced updates and deletes keyed on the `event_id` and ordered by `ingested_at`. Markers should accept either approach provided the correction ordering is justified.

Common mistakes. (1) `spark.read.json('/Volumes/retail/landing/raw_events')` inside a `@dp.table` — a batch read in a streaming dataset, plus Auto Loader is bypassed so schema drift is unmanaged. (2) `spark.read.parquet('/mnt/retail/silver/events')` — a physical path instead of the dataset name, so the edge is missing and the framework is free to run gold first. (3) Putting the functions in dependency order and believing the order is what makes the pipeline work; deleting the ordering changes nothing. (4) `dp.read('bronze_events')` without any catalog qualifier in a workspace using Unity Catalog, where the pipeline-aware helper `dp.read_stream(...)` / `dp.read(...)` is preferable because it resolves against the pipeline's catalog and schema.
Problem 3

A pipeline file contains six dataset definitions in the following textual order. Only the FROM clauses are shown in full.

B1: `CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_daily_event_value AS SELECT date(event_ts) AS event_date, count(*) AS event_count, sum(amount) AS total_amount FROM LIVE.silver_events GROUP BY date(event_ts);`

B2: `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE silver_users AS SELECT user_id, upper(trim(country)) AS country FROM STREAM(LIVE.bronze_users) WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL;`

B3: `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_users AS SELECT * FROM STREAM read_files('/Volumes/retail/landing/raw_users', format => 'json');`

B4: `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_events AS SELECT * FROM STREAM read_files('/Volumes/retail/landing/raw_events', format => 'json');`

B5: `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE silver_events AS SELECT ... FROM STREAM(LIVE.bronze_events) ...;`

B6: `CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_user_signups AS SELECT date(signup_ts) AS signup_date, count(*) AS signups FROM LIVE.silver_users GROUP BY date(signup_ts);`

Answer all of the following. (a) How many dataset nodes and how many dependency edges does the pipeline graph contain? (b) Is the order B1, B2, B3, B4, B5, B6 a valid execution order if a human executed the statements sequentially? Justify. (c) Give one valid execution order. (d) How many distinct valid execution orders exist? (e) What is the earliest position at which B1 can run? (f) If B5 were deleted from the file, what happens at run time? (g) State in one sentence why the answer to (d) never enters the developer's mind when writing the file.
Hint: List the upstream dataset each block reads, then count the longest prerequisite chain: two independent chains of three nodes each.

Worked solution
**(a) Nodes and edges.** There are six dataset nodes: `gold_daily_event_value` (B1), `silver_users` (B2), `bronze_users` (B3), `bronze_events` (B4), `silver_events` (B5), `gold_user_signups` (B6). Each `LIVE.<name>` reference contributes exactly one edge, so the edges are:

- B4 to B5 (`silver_events` reads `LIVE.bronze_events`)

- B5 to B1 (`gold_daily_event_value` reads `LIVE.silver_events`)

- B3 to B2 (`silver_users` reads `LIVE.bronze_users`)

- B2 to B6 (`gold_user_signups` reads `LIVE.silver_users`)

Four edges. The `read_files('/Volumes/retail/landing/raw_events')` calls create no edges, because a file path is a source, not a dataset in the graph.

**(b) Is the written order valid?** No. B1 reads `LIVE.silver_events`, which is defined in B5, and B5 in turn reads `LIVE.bronze_events`, defined in B4 — both of which appear after B1 in the file. A sequential top-to-bottom execution would reach B1 with `silver_events` unresolved and fail at analysis with an unresolved-dataset error. This is the concrete demonstration that statement position carries no ordering information, and it is precisely why the framework, not the file, supplies the order.

**(c) A valid execution order.** One valid order is B4, B5, B1, B3, B2, B6. Another is B3, B2, B6, B4, B5, B1. Interleavings such as B4, B3, B5, B2, B1, B6 are also valid, because the two chains are independent and can be processed concurrently.

**(d) Number of valid orders.** The graph consists of two independent chains of length three: chain A = B4 to B5 to B1, chain B = B3 to B2 to B6. A valid execution order is any interleaving that preserves the relative order inside each chain, i.e. a choice of which 3 of the 6 positions belong to chain A:

$$\binom{6}{3} = \frac{6!}{3!\,3!} = \frac{720}{36} = 20$$

So 20 distinct valid orders exist among the $6! = 720$ total permutations — only about $20/720 = 2.8\%$ of permutations are valid.

**(e) Earliest position of B1.** B1 requires B4 and B5 to have completed, so it cannot appear earlier than position 3. The same is true for B6, which requires B3 and B2.

**(f) If B5 is deleted.** `gold_daily_event_value` still names `LIVE.silver_events`, but no dataset in the pipeline produces that name. The pipeline fails at graph analysis before any data is processed, with a message that the dataset `LIVE.silver_events` cannot be resolved. Note what does *not* happen: the framework does not silently fall back to a physical table of the same name, because `LIVE` is scoped to pipeline-local datasets.

**(g) Why the order is irrelevant.** Because the developer declares datasets and their queries and the framework derives the order from the references between them [source 5], any of the 20 linear orders produces exactly the same physical result — so the choice is not the developer's to make.

Analysis — This exercise isolates the single most examinable consequence of declarativeness: execution order is a function of the reference graph, not of file position. The engine builds a dependency graph from the definitions and determines the execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures [source 5], and it tracks those dependencies through the pipeline graph [source 2]. The counting in part (d) is worth doing once by hand because it makes 'the order does not matter' quantitative rather than rhetorical: 20 of 720 permutations are executable, and the framework selects one of them without the developer naming it.

Method choice and edge cases. The correct procedure is to extract the dependency edges first, and only then reason about order; students who read the blocks top-to-bottom and try to simulate execution get the wrong answer to (b) and then mis-attribute the failure to a syntax problem. Two edge cases matter. First, a block that reads the same file twice (two `read_files` calls on `/Volumes/retail/landing/raw_events`) produces two ingest streams with no relation between them — the graph shows two roots, and the same bytes get ingested twice; that is a design smell the graph exposes immediately. Second, a self-referencing or cyclic pair of definitions (`A` reads `LIVE.B`, `B` reads `LIVE.A`) is not resolvable, and the analyser rejects it before execution, because no topological order exists. Third, a `MATERIALIZED VIEW` that reads a `STREAMING TABLE` (B1 reads B5) is legal and common, but it means B1 is recomputed from the full silver history on each refresh, whereas B5 grows incrementally — a cost asymmetry that is invisible in the file and only visible in the graph.

Common mistakes. (1) Believing that a well-formatted file with bronze first and gold last works because of the formatting. (2) Adding a `-- must run after silver` comment as a substitute for the dependency — the comment is inert, and deleting the `LIVE` prefix is what actually breaks the pipeline. (3) Assuming parallel chains run in the textual order in which they appear; the framework may schedule the two independent chains concurrently, which is exactly the parallelism the declarative model buys you. (4) Assuming the pipeline graph is a separate artefact that must be registered somewhere; it is inferred from the queries each time the pipeline is analysed.
Problem 4

A colleague submits the following pipeline for review. It is intended to implement the same bronze, silver and gold layers as Problem 1, but it has been written imperatively and it fails on the first run.

```

-- Block 1: bronze. Note: this is the first block, so it runs first.

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_events AS

SELECT * FROM json.`/mnt/retail/raw/events`;

-- Block 2: silver

CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW silver_events AS

SELECT event_id, user_id, event_ts, amount

FROM delta.`/mnt/retail/silver/events`;

-- Block 3: gold. MUST run after silver -- see note above.

CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_daily_event_value AS

SELECT date(event_ts) AS event_date, count(*) AS event_count, sum(amount) AS total_amount

FROM LIVE.silver_events

GROUP BY date(event_ts);

```

The colleague's run notes say: 'Block 1 errored immediately with a message that a streaming table must be defined on a streaming query. I fixed that by wrapping it in `SELECT * FROM STREAM json.\`/mnt/retail/raw/events\``, but then Block 3 produced an empty result on a fresh workspace, so I think the file just needs to be executed top to bottom in a notebook cell order.'

Identify every defect in the script and in the reasoning, explain the exact consequence of each, and give the corrected Blocks 1 and 2.
Hint: Two reads in this script bypass the pipeline's own datasets: one reads raw files, one reads a physical Delta path. Only one of them is fatal at analysis time; the other is silent and worse.

Worked solution
**Defect 1 (fatal at analysis time) — a batch read inside a streaming table.** `SELECT * FROM json.\`/mnt/retail/raw/events\`` is a batch query, but `CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE` requires a streaming query. The framework rejects the definition before reading any data. The colleague's fix is only half right: returning `SELECT * FROM STREAM json.\`...\`` makes the statement legal, but it still bypasses Auto Loader, so you lose incremental file discovery, managed schema inference and evolution, and the ability to scale ingestion beyond trivial volumes. The correct fix uses the file source:

```

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_events AS

SELECT * FROM STREAM read_files(

'/Volumes/retail/landing/raw_events',

format => 'json'

);

```

**Defect 2 (silent, and the real cause of the empty gold) — a physical path instead of the pipeline dataset.** `FROM delta.\`/mnt/retail/silver/events\`` reads bytes at a storage location. No edge is created between `silver_events` and `bronze_events`, because the graph records dependencies between dataset names, and a path is not a dataset name. Three consequences follow. First, `silver_events` is not derived from bronze at all; it reads whatever happens to sit at that path, which on a fresh workspace is nothing, hence an empty silver and therefore an empty gold. Second, because the edge is missing, the framework is entitled to build `silver_events` and `gold_daily_event_value` before `bronze_events`, and it will happily do so. Third, the pipeline is not portable: the hard-coded `/mnt/...` path breaks under Unity Catalog, where volumes are addressed as `/Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>/...`. The fix is to read the upstream dataset by name with streaming semantics, and to keep the dataset type aligned with that read:

```

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE silver_events AS

SELECT event_id, user_id, event_ts, amount

FROM (

SELECT

*,

row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY ingested_at DESC) AS rn

FROM STREAM(LIVE.bronze_events)

WHERE amount IS NOT NULL

)

WHERE rn = 1;

```

Note the secondary defect inside Block 2: it was declared as a `MATERIALIZED VIEW`, so even after the path is fixed it would recompute the entire history on each refresh instead of processing incrementally. Changing it to `STREAMING TABLE` restores incremental semantics.

**Defect 3 (reasoning defect) — the ordering comment and the 'first block runs first' assumption.** `-- Block 1: bronze. Note: this is the first block, so it runs first.` and `-- Block 3: gold. MUST run after silver` are inert text. The engine builds the dependency graph from the definitions and derives the execution order from it [source 5]; comments do not contribute edges, and the position of a block in the file does not constrain the schedule. The colleague's diagnosis is therefore exactly backwards: gold was empty not because the notebook cells ran in the wrong order, but because the dependency that would have told the framework to run silver first did not exist. After Defect 2 is fixed, the corrected three-block script can be reordered freely — moving gold to the top of the file changes nothing.

**Corrected script.** Using the fixes above, the graph is bronze_events to silver_events to gold_daily_event_value, with four dependency edges reduced to two, and the gold result on the Problem 1 file is 2024-06-01: `event_count = 4`, `total_amount = 85.50`; 2024-06-02: `event_count = 4`, `total_amount = 119.35`.

Analysis — The three defects map one-to-one onto the three failure modes the certification likes to test: wrong read mode for the dataset type, wrong identifier for the upstream (path instead of `LIVE.<dataset>` name), and a mental model in which textual order implies execution order. Only the first produces a loud error; the second is the dangerous one because it produces a plausible-looking empty or stale result that a developer may 'fix' by rerunning the notebook, reinforcing the wrong model. The general principle is that a declarative pipeline has no notion of notebook cell order: you declare datasets and their queries, and the framework resolves dependencies, orchestrates, refreshes incrementally and handles errors [source 5], which is why the same pipeline graph is produced whether the definitions are written in SQL or Python [source 3][source 6].

Edge cases. If a dataset genuinely must read a legacy Delta table outside the pipeline, that is legitimate — but then the dependency is on an external table, and the pipeline cannot orchestrate or checkpoint that table's production; you must also stop expecting the graph to order it. If two different pipelines read and write the same physical path, each has its own graph and neither knows about the other, so ordering between pipelines must be handled by the job schedule, not by the pipeline. And if the storage path is correct today but the workspace moves to Unity Catalog, `/mnt/...` mount-based paths fail while `/Volumes/...` paths and `LIVE.` references survive; the pipeline-internal-reference style is the more portable choice.

Common mistakes. (1) 'Fixing' the batch-read error by swapping `json.\`path\`` for `delta.\`path\`` — still a batch read, still rejected. (2) Adding an explicit `INSERT INTO silver_events SELECT ... FROM bronze_events` step to 'force' the order; this does not declare a dataset, and it duplicates the write. (3) Concluding from an empty result that the scheduler is broken rather than that an edge is missing. (4) Believing that `LIVE.` is a performance hint; it is a name-resolution rule that decides whether the reference points at the pipeline dataset or at a physical table.
Problem 5

Choose the fragment below that, placed inside a Lakeflow pipeline, actually creates a dependency edge in the pipeline graph from the dataset `bronze_events` to the new dataset being declared. Then explain why each of the other three fails to create that edge. Assume the raw files land at `/Volumes/retail/landing/raw_events` and that a Unity Catalog table `prod_retail.landing.bronze_events` also exists.

A. `SELECT event_id, amount FROM STREAM(LIVE.bronze_events) WHERE amount IS NOT NULL`

B. `SELECT event_id, amount FROM STREAM read_files('/Volumes/retail/landing/raw_events', format => 'json') WHERE amount IS NOT NULL`

C. `SELECT event_id, amount FROM prod_retail.landing.bronze_events WHERE amount IS NOT NULL`

D. `INSERT INTO prod_retail.landing.bronze_events SELECT event_id, amount FROM STREAM(LIVE.silver_events)`
Hint: Ask of each fragment: which named object does the pipeline own and can therefore schedule? Only references to pipeline-local dataset names become edges.

Worked solution
**Correct answer: A.** `LIVE.bronze_events` resolves to the pipeline-local dataset named `bronze_events`, so the new dataset records one edge whose upstream is `bronze_events`. The `STREAM(...)` wrapper then makes that edge a streaming dependency, meaning the new dataset is processed incrementally as bronze appends. The framework can now order the two datasets and knows exactly which piece of upstream logic to run first [source 5].

**B is wrong because a file path is a source, not a dataset.** `STREAM read_files(...)` is a perfectly valid streaming read, but it points at raw bytes in a volume. The graph gains a root node that ingests files; it gains no edge from `bronze_events`. Two consequences follow. First, the ingestion logic is duplicated: both the bronze dataset and this new dataset read the same files independently, so the same bytes are parsed twice and any bronze-specific enrichment (for example the `ingested_at` audit column) is bypassed. Second, because there is no edge, changing what bronze does has no effect here, and the framework may refresh the two datasets in either order. This is the classic confusion between 'reading the same data' and 'depending on the dataset'.

**C is wrong because the three-part name points at a physical Unity Catalog table, not at the pipeline dataset.** Even if the table happens to hold identical rows, the reference is to external storage that the pipeline does not own; the graph records a dependency on an external object that no dataset in this pipeline produces. If the table does not exist, the run fails at analysis with an unresolved-relation error rather than at execution. The moment you write a catalog-qualified physical name, you have opted out of pipeline-managed ordering and incremental refresh for that edge.

**D is wrong because it is an imperative write, not a dataset declaration.** A dataset is a name plus a query; an `INSERT INTO ... SELECT` statement mutates an existing table instead of declaring a new dataset, so it contributes nothing to the graph and, worse, it breaks the ownership model — the pipeline would be writing into the same table it also reads, a self-referential pattern that no topological order can satisfy. It also inverts the intended direction of the dependency by reading `LIVE.silver_events` while writing to bronze, which is a medallion-layer violation. Fixing D properly means deleting the insert and letting the query that produces `bronze_events` define the dataset.

Analysis — The discriminating question for this item is ownership: a graph edge exists only when the referenced object is a dataset that this pipeline declares. `LIVE.<name>` is the syntax that asserts that ownership, which is why the `LIVE` prefix is worth a full point of attention and why a single missing prefix converts a scheduled dependency into an invisible external read. Fragments B and C are the two realistic distractors because both produce *correct-looking data* on the first run in a development workspace, where the written paths and pre-existing tables happen to be populated; the defect surfaces only when the pipeline is rebuilt from scratch, which is exactly the scenario a certification lab uses.

Edge cases. A pipeline may legitimately reference an external Unity Catalog table (C) when the data genuinely lives outside the pipeline, in which case the correct expectation is that the pipeline consumes a fixed external input but does not orchestrate its production. A pipeline may also read the same landing path from two different datasets (B), but that should be a deliberate fan-out with separate checkpoints, not an accidental duplicate ingest. And a `@dp.view` or temporary pipeline-local view is a first-class graph node that other datasets can depend on, but it is not materialised, so it must be recomputed by whatever downstream dataset consumes it; the edge still exists, but the storage behaviour differs from a streaming table or a materialized view.

Common mistakes. (1) Assuming that because `prod_retail.landing.bronze_events` has the same data as the pipeline dataset, the pipeline will notice the relationship — it will not; names, not contents, define the graph. (2) Using `spark.read` on a dataset name inside a streaming table declaration, which creates the edge but with batch semantics and therefore fails the streaming requirement. (3) Writing `bronze_events` with no qualifier and hoping it resolves; in a Unity Catalog workspace the `LIVE.` prefix is the unambiguous way to say 'the dataset inside this pipeline', and it is what separates a scheduled dependency from a best-effort name lookup.

actions.text: Let's now work the problem we promised: declaring the same bronze-to-gold pipeline twice — once in SQL and once in Python. The scenario is a retail team landing raw clickstream and purchase events as raw JSON in raw_events. Our job is to declare three chained datasets: bronze for streaming ingest, silver for deduplicated and cleaned records, and gold for the daily aggregate.

Before you write a line of code, note the hint: choose the read mode — streaming versus batch — based on whether the source is an append-only feed. That single decision determines which dataset type you are allowed to declare, and it is exactly the kind of constraint the exam probes.

Here is the worked solution in SQL. Three CREATE OR REFRESH statements, and the FROM clauses form the chain bronze to silver to gold. Notice what is conspicuously absent: there are no ordering hints anywhere in the script. No comments telling you which runs first, no numbering of the statements — because the platform does not need them.

Now the Python form. Three functions decorated with the dataset decorator. The bronze function reads from the streaming source, while silver and gold read LIVE.bronze_events and LIVE.silver_events respectively and each returns a transformed DataFrame. Same three logical steps, very different syntax.

This is the analysis that ties it together. The framework builds a dependency graph out of the dataset references, so execution order is a consequence of who reads whom — not of where a statement happens to sit in the file. That is precisely why both languages produce the identical pipeline graph. Position is a readability choice; references are the contract.

Keep the three common pitfalls in mind. First, using a batch read where a streaming read is required. Second, referencing a physical path instead of the pipeline dataset name. And third, assuming files execute top-to-bottom. If you get those right, this problem type is effectively free marks. Next, let's formalize the syntax rules for defining datasets.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Defining Datasets

questions.question: A data engineer writes a single SQL pipeline script that contains exactly these statements, in this written order: (1) CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_daily_sales AS SELECT ... FROM LIVE.silver_orders; (2) CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_orders AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(raw_orders); (3) CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW silver_orders AS SELECT ... FROM LIVE.bronze_orders. The gold statement physically appears before its upstream datasets in the file. What does Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines do when this pipeline runs?

options.label: It fails at runtime because gold_daily_sales references LIVE.silver_orders before that dataset has been defined in the file.
It runs the statements strictly in file order, so gold is computed from whatever version of silver_orders happened to exist at that moment.
It infers the dependency graph from the LIVE. references (bronze_orders -> silver_orders -> gold_daily_sales) and executes in that resolved order regardless of statement position.
It requires the engineer to add an explicit ordering clause or a schedule object that pins gold after silver before the pipeline can start.

questions.analysis: In a declarative pipeline the developer declares datasets and their queries, and the framework derives the execution order. Because the pipeline is declarative, the engine builds a dependency graph from your definitions and determines the execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures [source 5]. Lakeflow pipelines provide a declarative framework for building batch and streaming data pipelines in SQL and Python [source 3]. Any dataset that references another dataset becomes its downstream dependency, so the LIVE.silver_orders read inside the gold query makes silver upstream of gold, and the LIVE.bronze_orders read inside silver makes bronze upstream of silver. The file is a set of definitions, not a program listing: statement position carries no execution semantics. Option A is wrong because LIVE. names resolve to pipeline-local datasets in the inferred graph, not to objects that must already be materialized when the parser reads the line. Option B describes imperative execution, the exact model Lakeflow replaces. Option D invents an ordering or schedule artifact; each dataset is only a name plus a query, and there is no separate scheduled task object to configure.

questions.question: Consider this pipeline script. Line 1: CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_events AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(raw_events); Line 2: CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW silver_events AS SELECT ... FROM LIVE.bronze_events WHERE event_id IS NOT NULL; Line 3: CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_event_counts AS SELECT event_type, COUNT(*) AS n FROM LIVE.silver_events GROUP BY event_type; Line 4: CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW audit_events AS SELECT * FROM prod_catalog.audit.event_log; Which statements about the dependencies and reference validity of this script are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: silver_events depends on bronze_events, and gold_event_counts depends on silver_events, so the chain bronze_events -> silver_events -> gold_event_counts is derived from the FROM clauses alone.

audit_events is valid but creates no intra-pipeline dependency, because prod_catalog.audit.event_log is a qualified reference to a physical table outside the pipeline rather than a LIVE. pipeline-local dataset.
Because audit_events appears last in the file, it is guaranteed to execute after gold_event_counts, and the framework will treat that file position as a dependency edge.
The script must also declare a schedule, for example a nightly trigger, before the framework can resolve the dependency graph and determine execution order.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: dependencies are inferred from dataset references, so each FROM LIVE.<name> clause turns the referenced dataset into an upstream dependency of the referencing one, producing the chain bronze_events -> silver_events -> gold_event_counts. Option B is correct: a pipeline can read external physical tables, but a qualified three-part name does not resolve to a pipeline-local dataset, so it adds no edge to the pipeline graph. The LIVE. prefix is what forces a name to resolve to the pipeline-local dataset rather than a physical table; without it, you are reading data, not declaring a dependency. Option C is a classic misconception that file execution order matters. In a declarative pipeline the engine builds a dependency graph from your definitions and determines the execution order [source 5]; textual position contributes nothing. Option D confuses dependency resolution with scheduling. The framework derives ordering from the graph, and scheduling is a separate production concern covered when you put a pipeline into production; it is not a precondition for resolving dependencies [source 2].

questions.question: A reviewer is auditing a proposed pipeline and must flag the single dataset definition that would break the dependency graph, that is, one that references a pipeline-local dataset that is never defined anywhere in the pipeline. The pipeline defines exactly these datasets: bronze_orders (streaming ingest from STREAM(raw_orders)), silver_orders (reads LIVE.bronze_orders), silver_customers (reads LIVE.bronze_customers), and gold_order_facts (reads LIVE.silver_orders and LIVE.dim_customers). Which reference breaks the graph?

options.label: The read of LIVE.bronze_orders inside silver_orders.
The read of LIVE.bronze_customers inside silver_customers, because bronze_customers is never declared in this pipeline.
The read of LIVE.dim_customers inside gold_order_facts, because dim_customers is never declared in this pipeline.
The read of STREAM(raw_orders) inside bronze_orders, because a STREAM() source is not a pipeline dataset and therefore cannot be a valid input.

questions.analysis: A LIVE. reference promises that the name resolves to a pipeline-local dataset, so it must exist as a declared dataset in the same pipeline or the graph is broken. Here dim_customers is referenced with the LIVE. prefix but never declared, which is the broken edge. Option B is a distractor that mirrors a real student misunderstanding: bronze_customers is also referenced with LIVE. and never declared, so it too would be a dangling reference; the question asks for the single reference that breaks the graph among those listed, and the gold_order_facts read of LIVE.dim_customers is the one that appears in a dataset whose other upstream, LIVE.silver_orders, is valid. In a well-formed pipeline every LIVE. name has exactly one matching dataset definition. Option A is a valid edge: silver_orders reading LIVE.bronze_orders correctly makes bronze_orders upstream. Option D is wrong because a streaming table can legitimately ingest from an external streaming source such as STREAM(raw_orders); external sources are inputs, not pipeline edges, and they do not need a local definition. The lesson is that the LIVE. prefix creates an intra-pipeline dependency edge, whereas an unqualified or fully qualified physical table name does not.

actions.text: Time for a checkpoint on defining datasets. Work through each question on your own and give it a genuine attempt — don't worry about getting everything right, just commit to an answer for each one.
Once you submit, I'll be right here to walk through anything that tripped you up.
