widgetConfig.description: Build the Pipeline Graph — declare datasets with CREATE ... AS SELECT ... and watch Lakeflow-style dependency resolution build the DAG and the refresh order.
widgetConfig.starterCode:
-- Declare pipeline datasets.
-- Each CREATE ... AS SELECT ... becomes one node in the graph.
-- A plain name in FROM / JOIN becomes a dependency edge.
-- A dotted name (catalog.schema.table) is an external source, not a node.

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE raw_events
AS SELECT *
FROM STREAM(source_catalog.events.raw);

CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW clean_events
AS SELECT event_id, user_id, event_ts
FROM raw_events
WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL;

testCases.description: Declare at least two datasets in the pipeline.
clean_events depends on raw_events (a FROM/JOIN on another declared dataset creates an edge).
Every non-dotted reference resolves to a declared dataset.
The refresh order is a valid topological order of the graph.

hints: Every `CREATE ... AS SELECT ...` statement becomes exactly one NODE in the graph. The dataset name is the node identity — not the SELECT body.

Edges are inferred, not declared. A bare identifier after `FROM` or `JOIN` that matches another declared dataset becomes an EDGE from that dataset to this one. That is why `FROM raw_events` is enough to wire the graph.

Not every `FROM` is an edge. `FROM STREAM(source_catalog.events.raw)` reads an EXTERNAL source — the dotted 3-part name is a catalog table, not a node in your pipeline, so it creates no edge and no unresolved flag.

A *materialized view* (batch semantics) is refreshed by recomputing it from its inputs; a *streaming table* is refreshed incrementally and must read its input with `STREAM(...)`. Both appear as nodes in the same graph — the graph is about dependencies, not about refresh mode.

The refresh order is the topological sort: sources first, then each dataset once all of its upstream dependencies have been processed. A cycle — or a reference to a dataset that was never declared — makes that order unresolvable, which is why the node is flagged in red.

To see failure propagation, pick a dataset in the 'Simulate failure at' dropdown and press Refresh. Everything downstream of a failed dataset is BLOCKED, because a dependent can never be considered fresh while its input is stale.
widgetConfig.solution:
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE raw_events
AS SELECT *
FROM STREAM(source_catalog.events.raw);

CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW clean_events
AS SELECT event_id, user_id, event_ts
FROM raw_events
WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL;

CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW events_by_user
AS SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS event_count
FROM clean_events
GROUP BY user_id;

actions.text: The framework decides when and how to refresh, but the graph of what depends on what is still inferred from what you declare. So let's build that graph ourselves. This editor on your left is pre-seeded with two declarations: a streaming table, raw_events, and a materialized view, clean_events, that reads from raw_events. On the right is the live pipeline graph. Run it and watch the nodes and edges resolve.

actions.content: Each CREATE ... AS SELECT ... statement declares one dataset — that becomes one node.
Running the declarations builds the graph.

actions.text: Two nodes, one edge — from raw_events into clean_events. Notice that nothing declared that edge explicitly. The bare identifier after FROM, raw_events, matches another declared dataset, so the framework draws the dependency for you. Edges are inferred, not written.

actions.content: Arrow = a FROM or JOIN reference to another declared dataset.

actions.text: Look closer at raw_events, though. It reads FROM STREAM(source_catalog.events.raw) — a dotted three-part name. That is an external catalog table, not a dataset in this pipeline, so it creates no node and no edge. That distinction matters: dotted names are external sources, bare names are internal dependencies.

actions.content: Refresh processes datasets in dependency order.

actions.text: Now press Refresh and watch the order. raw_events turns green first, then clean_events — the topological sort, sources before dependents. Add a third dataset that reads from clean_events, and it will land at the end. Try it in the editor, and also try a reference to a dataset you never declared — you will see that node flagged with a red dashed border, because its order cannot be resolved.

scenes.title: Key Terms: Declarative Pipelines

elements.content: Declarative pipeline — A pipeline expressed as a set of dataset definitions rather than as explicitly ordered tasks, in which the execution engine infers execution order, retries, and refresh behaviour from the dependency graph formed by those definitions; it applies only when datasets are declared with the supported CREATE OR REFRESH or @dp.table APIs, because the framework cannot infer orchestration from arbitrary procedural code.

Dataset — The named output of a pipeline, produced by exactly one query and materialised as one of three forms — a streaming table, a materialized view, or a temporary (pipeline-local) view; a dataset is the unit of declaration and dependency in a declarative pipeline, so a name must be defined exactly once within a pipeline, and temporary views are not persisted outside the pipeline's lifetime.

Pipeline graph — The directed acyclic graph whose nodes are datasets and whose edges are inferred from the tables each dataset's query reads; an edge exists whenever one dataset references another by name (directly or through the LIVE schema), and because the graph must remain acyclic, a declaration that would make a dataset depend on itself, directly or transitively, is rejected at analysis time.

Streaming table — A dataset that the framework processes incrementally as new data arrives, declared with CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE in SQL or with @dp.table over a streaming read in Python; it is the correct dataset type when the source is append-only or when the query reads from a streaming source such as STREAM(raw_orders) or spark.readStream, and it is not appropriate for a query that must recompute the full result set on every refresh.

Materialized view — A dataset whose contents the framework recomputes as its inputs change, declarable in both SQL (CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW) and Python (@dp.table without streaming semantics); it is the appropriate type when the query performs aggregations, joins, or deduplication that must reflect updates to upstream data, and unlike a streaming table it can incorporate changes to already-processed rows.

LIVE schema — The pipeline-local namespace used to reference another dataset in the same pipeline instead of a physical table name, written as LIVE.dataset_name in SQL and as LIVE.dataset_name in spark.readStream.table() or spark.read.table() in Python; it resolves to the current pipeline's definition of that dataset, so it fails if no dataset with that name exists in the same pipeline, and it never resolves to an external table of the same name.

Expectation — A declarative data-quality rule attached to a dataset that can warn, drop, or fail rows at refresh time; it is evaluated when the dataset is refreshed, so it applies to the data flowing through that dataset rather than to stored data at rest, and the chosen action determines whether offending rows are retained, discarded, or cause the refresh to abort.

Pipeline mode and trigger — The settings that determine whether a pipeline runs continuously or on demand, covering the pipeline mode and the trigger configuration that schedule refreshes; these settings are declared at the pipeline level rather than inside individual dataset definitions, and they control when the framework evaluates the graph, not what the graph contains.

actions.text: Let's lock in the vocabulary for this unit, because these are the exact terms the certification exam reuses. First: a declarative pipeline. It's a pipeline expressed as a set of dataset definitions. You describe what each dataset should be, not how to run it — the engine infers execution order, retries, and refreshes from the resulting graph.

Second: a dataset. This is a named output of a pipeline, produced by exactly one query, and materialised either as a streaming table, a materialized view, or a temporary view. The key point is one dataset, one defining query.

Third: the pipeline graph. This is the directed acyclic graph of datasets connected by references. You never declare the edges yourself — they are inferred from the tables each query reads. That inference is what makes the pipeline declarative.

Fourth: a streaming table. This is a dataset the framework processes incrementally as new data arrives. You declare it with CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE in SQL, or with the @dp.table decorator over a streaming read in Python.

Contrast that with number five: a materialized view, where the framework recomputes the contents as its inputs change. It's declarable in both SQL and Python. Remember the distinction — streaming table for incremental processing, materialized view for full recompute.

Sixth: the LIVE schema. This is the pipeline-local namespace you use to reference another dataset in the same pipeline, instead of pointing at a physical table name. It keeps your pipeline definitions portable.
Seventh: an expectation. This is a declarative data-quality rule attached to a dataset. At refresh time it can warn, drop, or fail rows — we'll unpack those three actions in a later lesson.

And eighth: pipeline mode and trigger — the settings that decide whether a pipeline runs continuously or on demand. We'll cover those in detail later in this unit. For now, make sure all eight terms feel familiar, because from here on I'll use them without stopping to define them.

scenes.title: Lesson Checkpoint: Concepts and Syntax

questions.question: A Lakeflow declarative pipeline is authored as a set of dataset declarations rather than a set of scheduled tasks. A student claims that the engine can only resolve the graph correctly if the developer writes the datasets in true execution order (bronze first, then silver, then gold) inside one file. Which statement best explains why this claim is false?

options.label: The engine builds a dependency graph from the definitions themselves and determines the execution order, so any dataset that references another dataset becomes its downstream dependency regardless of file or statement position [source 5].
The engine alphabetizes dataset names and executes them in that order, so physical ordering in the file is irrelevant only when names are already alphabetical.
The engine requires the developer to list upstream datasets explicitly in a dependency metadata object, and file order only matters if that list is omitted.
The engine executes every dataset in parallel and reconciles the results afterward, so no ordering information is ever needed.

questions.correctAnswer: The engine builds a dependency graph from the definitions themselves and determines the execution order, so any dataset that references another dataset becomes its downstream dependency regardless of file or statement position [source 5].
questions.analysis: Lakeflow declarative pipelines infer the pipeline graph from dataset references: 'the engine builds a dependency graph from your definitions and determines the execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures' [source 5]. Because dependency is derived from a read of another dataset (for example a FROM clause or a LIVE.name reference), the position of statements within a file or across files cannot change the graph. Option B invents an alphabetical heuristic that does not exist. Option C re-imports imperative thinking: there is no required dependency metadata object. Option D is wrong because datasets process in dependency order, not arbitrarily in parallel, and 'upstream failures block downstream nodes' in the earlier lesson.
answer: The engine builds a dependency graph from the definitions themselves and determines the execution order, so any dataset that references another dataset becomes its downstream dependency regardless of file or statement position [source 5].

questions.question: A team is defining a pipeline that ingests raw JSON events as an incrementally ingested bronze dataset and then publishes a daily aggregate as a gold dataset. Which of the following declarations are valid Lakeflow declarative pipeline syntax for that requirement? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_events AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(raw_events);
CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_daily_events AS SELECT event_date, COUNT(*) AS events FROM LIVE.bronze_events GROUP BY event_date;
schedule: "0 0 * * *" CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_events AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(raw_events);
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_events AS SELECT * FROM raw_events; INSERT INTO bronze_events SELECT * FROM STREAM(raw_events);

correctAnswer: CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_events AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(raw_events);
CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_daily_events AS SELECT event_date, COUNT(*) AS events FROM LIVE.bronze_events GROUP BY event_date;
questions.analysis: A streaming table declared with CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE ... AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(...) is the canonical incrementally ingested dataset, and a CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW ... AS SELECT ... is the canonical recomputed dataset; reading LIVE.bronze_events is what creates the dependency edge from gold to bronze rather than copying physical data. Options C and D are distractors imported from imperative orchestration: a cron-style schedule object does not belong in a dataset declaration, and a manual INSERT step violates the rule that the FROM clause creates a dependency without an imperative write step.
answer: CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE bronze_events AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(raw_events);
CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_daily_events AS SELECT event_date, COUNT(*) AS events FROM LIVE.bronze_events GROUP BY event_date;

questions.question: A pipeline graph fails to resolve one dataset reference. The failing node is a Python dataset defined with @dp.table(name='silver_events') whose body contains the line: df = spark.read.table('bronze_events'). The bronze dataset in the same pipeline is named bronze_events. Which diagnosis is most consistent with Lakeflow declarative semantics?

options.label: The reference resolves to a physical table in the catalog instead of the pipeline-local dataset, so the graph has no upstream edge; using spark.readStream.table('LIVE.bronze_events') would resolve to the pipeline-local dataset and declare the dependency.
The reference is correct, but the pipeline cannot resolve it because @dp.table requires the function name to match the dataset name exactly.
The reference is correct, but the graph will still resolve only if the developer also adds an explicit dependency list to the @dp.table decorator.
The reference is correct, but the pipeline requires a schedule object before it can resolve cross-dataset references at analysis time.

questions.correctAnswer: The reference resolves to a physical table in the catalog instead of the pipeline-local dataset, so the graph has no upstream edge; using spark.readStream.table('LIVE.bronze_events') would resolve to the pipeline-local dataset and declare the dependency.
questions.analysis: The LIVE. prefix is what makes a name resolve to the pipeline-local dataset rather than a physical table. Without it, spark.read.table('bronze_events') is read as an ordinary catalog lookup and contributes no graph edge, which is why the graph fails to resolve the intended dependency. Option B is a misconception about decorator naming versus the name= argument. Option C re-imports manual dependency lists that declarative pipelines do not use. Option D imports a required schedule object, which the earlier lesson explicitly rejected as an imperative-orchestration distractor.
answer: The reference resolves to a physical table in the catalog instead of the pipeline-local dataset, so the graph has no upstream edge; using spark.readStream.table('LIVE.bronze_events') would resolve to the pipeline-local dataset and declare the dependency.

questions.question: In your own words, explain why a Lakeflow declarative pipeline can be defined with its dataset declarations written in any file order and still refresh correctly. In your explanation, contrast this with imperative orchestration, and name at least two responsibilities that the framework owns rather than the developer.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Graph inference - 35%: the answer states that the framework derives the dependency graph from the dataset definitions themselves, where a reference to another dataset creates the upstream/downstream edge, and that this derivation is what determines execution order. (2) Imperative contrast - 25%: the answer contrasts declarative datasets-plus-queries with imperative tasks-plus-schedules, noting that imperative orchestration requires engineers to hand-wire upstream/downstream links and schedules. (3) Framework responsibilities - 25%: the answer names at least two of dependency resolution, orchestration, incremental refresh, and failure recovery as framework-owned. (4) Clarity and correct use of Databricks terminology - 15%: the answer uses Delta Lake, Lakeflow, streaming table, materialized view, pipeline graph, or LIVE. correctly and reads clearly.
questions.analysis: A strong answer covers: Lakeflow pipelines provide a declarative framework for building batch and streaming data pipelines in SQL and Python [source 3]; the developer declares datasets and their queries, and the engine builds a dependency graph from those definitions to determine execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures [source 5]; the supported dataset types include streaming tables, incrementally updated materialized views, automated CDC, and declarative data quality expectations [source 4]; and the course covers how Spark/Lakeflow declarative pipelines track data dependencies through the pipeline graph and how to configure compute, trigger modes, and scheduling at deployment time [source 1][source 2]. Because a dataset is a name plus a query with no separate scheduled task object, file order carries no ordering information, so the same set of declarations always produces the same graph and the same refresh behaviour.

scenes.title: The Core Decision: Which Dataset Type Do You Declare?

elements.content: The Core Decision: Which Dataset Type Do You Declare?
Objective: distinguish streaming tables from materialized views, and select the correct dataset type for a stated requirement.
Three dataset types, one pipeline

A Lakeflow declarative pipeline produces three dataset types: streaming tables, materialized views, and temporary views [source 5].

Each dataset is a name plus a query; the declaration you write — not a schedule object — fixes the type.

Lakeflow runs batch and streaming pipelines from SQL and Python declarations [source 3].
Semantics differ by declaration

Streaming tables ingest only new data incrementally; materialized views persist a query result and recompute it at each pipeline update [source 5].

Exam trap: "every dataset is a materialized view" is false — CREATE STREAMING TABLE and CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW carry different semantics.

Lakeflow adds native streaming tables and incrementally updated materialized views [source 4].

Worked example: raw_events lands 12,000,000 records/day; silver drops 2% as duplicates.

As a materialized view, gold reprocesses all 12M rows per update. As a streaming table, it processes only the 12M − 240,000 = 11,760,000 new rows.

Lesson roadmap

Semantics → selection criteria → refresh behavior → incremental processing and cost

actions.text: Now that you can build a pipeline graph in both SQL and Python, we arrive at the question that trips up more candidates than almost any other on this exam: which dataset type do you actually declare? This is the core decision, and it drives semantics, refresh behavior, and your production bill.

Our objective for this page is narrow and testable: distinguish a streaming table from a materialized view, and select the right dataset type for a given requirement. If you can do that, you can answer the scenario questions in this unit.

Remember the framing from the previous page: a Lakeflow declarative pipeline can produce three dataset types — streaming tables, materialized views, and views. The type is not inferred by the engine. It is fixed by the declaration you write in the pipeline source.

So look at the semantics. A streaming table ingests only new data incrementally — it is append-oriented and built for continuous or scheduled ingestion. A materialized view persists the result of a query and refreshes that persisted result during a pipeline update. Same pipeline, same graph, but radically different behavior depending on that one keyword.

Here is the worked example that makes the cost dimension concrete. Suppose raw_events lands twelve million records, and the business wants a daily refreshed aggregate on top of it. If you declare a streaming table for the raw layer, you only ingest the new increment per run. If you declare a materialized view for a layer that should be incremental, every refresh reprocesses the full result — and you pay for that recompute.

Which brings us to the exam trap, and I want you to memorize the exact wording: the statement that 'every dataset in a declarative pipeline is a materialized view' is false. The declaration governs the semantics. CREATE STREAMING TABLE and CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW are not interchangeable, and the question stem will try to blur that line.

Our roadmap for the rest of this unit is a sequence: first the semantics of each dataset type, then the selection criteria, then refresh behavior, and finally how incremental processing connects to cost. Keep that order in mind — each page builds the vocabulary you will need for the side-by-side comparison coming next.

scenes.title: Side-by-Side: Streaming Table vs Materialized View

elements.content: Dimension  |  Streaming table  |  Materialized view

Processing model
Streaming table: A streaming table is produced by incremental, append-oriented processing: each pipeline update reads only the new data that has arrived since the last checkpoint and appends the transformed rows to the existing table, so the amount of work per update scales with the size of the new increment rather than the size of the history [source 4].
Materialized view: A materialized view is produced by executing a defining query whose result is persisted, and the framework recomputes that query when the pipeline updates; the engine can refresh it incrementally when the defining query is incrementally computable, otherwise the whole result is rebuilt [source 4].

Data semantics: what history looks like
Streaming table: A streaming table records an append-only event history: rows are never silently rewritten by the framework, so the table is the accumulated sequence of records ingested across updates, and handling updates to existing keys requires explicit change-data-capture (CDC) logic — the automated CDC support that Lakeflow provides — rather than a blind overwrite [source 4].
Materialized view: A materialized view holds the current answer to a query, so its contents after each refresh are the query result at that moment; a row that changes in an upstream table can cause the corresponding output row to change, or to disappear, because the persisted result represents state rather than an append log [source 4].

Typical source
Streaming table: A streaming table consumes streaming sources: cloud files read with Auto Loader, message buses such as Kafka or Event Hubs, or another streaming table whose increment it continues downstream, which is why it is the natural landing point for change-data-capture (CDC) feeds and event streams [source 4].
Materialized view: A materialized view is defined over existing tables — typically the datasets already in Unity Catalog, including the streaming tables upstream of it — because the query it materializes is an ordinary SELECT-style query evaluated against whatever those tables currently contain [source 5].

Refresh behaviour
Streaming table: A streaming table advances its checkpoint with each pipeline update and processes only the unconsumed increment; it is therefore naturally idempotent per update and does not need to re-read the full source, which is what makes continuous, low-latency ingestion viable [source 5].
Materialized view: A materialized view is refreshed on each pipeline update as well, but the refresh is only incremental when the defining query is incrementally computable; queries whose logic the engine cannot invert — certain window functions, non-deterministic expressions, or joins the engine cannot delta-maintain — force a full recomputation of the result [source 4].

Compute cost and scaling
Streaming table: Cost for a streaming table is proportional to the increment: if 2 million new orders arrive in an update against a 500-million-row history, the update processes roughly 2 million rows, so the marginal cost per update stays roughly flat as the table grows [source 4].
Materialized view: Cost for a materialized view depends on whether the refresh is incremental: an incrementally refreshed view behaves like the streaming case, but a full recomputation over the same history must scan and recompute from the source tables each update, so its cost grows with the size of the inputs rather than with the size of the change [source 4].

Refreshing on a full recompute — worked example
Streaming table: Streaming table, worked case: 10 million new events arrive per day into a 2-billion-row streaming table; each daily update touches approximately 10 million rows, i.e. 0.5 percent of the stored history, so the incremental pass is the dominant cost driver and the rest is storage [source 4].
Materialized view: Materialized view, worked case: a gold view defined as SELECT date, sum(amount) FROM silver GROUP BY date is incrementally computable, so only new silver rows feed the aggregate; if instead the query contained a non-invertible expression requiring a full refresh, the same 2 billion-row silver table would be recomputed end-to-end on every pipeline update, roughly 200 times the incremental row volume in the example above [source 4].

Definition syntax in the pipeline
Streaming table: Declared with CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE ... AS SELECT ... FROM STREAM(source), or in Python with a @dp.table function that reads an upstream dataset through spark.readStream.table('LIVE.upstream'); the STREAM() wrapper (or read_stream) is what marks the dependency as an increment [source 5].
Materialized view: Declared with CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW ... AS SELECT ..., or in Python with a @dp.table function that reads an upstream dataset through the batch reader; no STREAM() wrapper appears, because the defining query is evaluated as a query, not as an increment [source 5].

Where each sits in the medallion architecture (a layered bronze/silver/gold data organization pattern)
Streaming table: Streaming tables usually occupy bronze and parts of silver: they land raw events, apply CDC semantics, and feed the next dataset downward, which matches append-only ingestion from streaming sources [source 4].
Materialized view: Materialized views usually occupy silver and gold: they express joins, aggregations and serving-layer business logic over tables that already exist, which is exactly the query-shaped work for which a persisted query result is appropriate [source 5].

What does NOT distinguish them
Streaming table: Both are registered in Unity Catalog as regular tables, so a streaming table can be read with an ordinary SELECT by any downstream consumer; the fact that a consumer reads it with SELECT tells you nothing about how it was produced [source 5].
Materialized view: Both are registered in Unity Catalog as regular tables, so a materialized view can likewise be queried with an ordinary SELECT and joined by other datasets; the distinguishing property is the processing contract behind the name, not the read path [source 5].

Best-fit use case and decision rule
Streaming table: Choose a streaming table when the source delivers appends or change data and you need low-latency, incremental capture of that stream; the shape of the data is an event history, not a question whose answer must be recomputed [source 4].
Materialized view: Choose a materialized view when the work is a complex join, an aggregation, or serving-layer business logic over existing tables, and you want the framework to persist and keep that answer fresh rather than writing the maintenance logic yourself [source 5].

Takeaway — Decision rule: if the input arrives as appends or change data from a streaming source (Auto Loader over cloud files, a message bus, or another streaming table), declare a streaming table — that is the case where increment-only processing is both correct and cheap [source 4].

Takeaway — If the requirement is a complex join, aggregation, or serving-layer business logic over existing tables, declare a materialized view; the framework persists the query result and refreshes it on each pipeline update, incrementally where the query is incrementally computable [source 5].

Takeaway — Do not choose based on how the dataset is read: both types are Unity Catalog tables readable with plain SELECT, so the decision must be made from the processing contract — append-only incremental ingestion versus a persisted, refreshed query result [source 5].

Takeaway — Size the choice with the increment: when the daily change is a small fraction of the stored history (for example 10 million new rows against 2 billion stored), a streaming table's cost tracks the increment, while a non-incremental materialized view would recompute the full input on every update [source 4].

actions.text: Now that you can declare datasets, the real question is which type to declare. This page puts streaming tables and materialized views side by side across the dimensions that actually drive the decision — and that the exam loves to test.

Here's the comparison table. Notice it's organized by dimension: processing model, data semantics, typical source, refresh behavior, compute cost, and best-fit use case. We'll walk each dimension, but keep the table in view — this is the artifact you should be able to redraw from memory.

Start with the processing model. A streaming table is incremental and append-only: each run only processes the new data that arrived since the last run. A materialized view persists the result of a query and refreshes it on each pipeline update — and it can refresh incrementally when the defining query is incrementally computable.

Next, data semantics — what history looks like. A streaming table is a log of appended records; you see every increment as it landed. A materialized view shows you the current answer to a query, not the history of how that answer changed. That distinction is the root of almost every downstream difference.

That leads directly to the typical source. Streaming tables consume streaming sources: cloud files read with Auto Loader, message buses like Kafka, or another streaming table. Materialized views are defined over existing tables — they read from your lakehouse tables rather than from a raw event stream.

Refresh behavior follows from all of this. A streaming table advances the stream — it only ever processes new data, so it never re-reads what it has already consumed. A materialized view may be incrementally refreshed, but if the query isn't incrementally computable, the engine falls back to a full recompute of the entire result. That fallback is where surprises live.

Which brings us to compute cost and scaling. For a streaming table, cost is roughly proportional to the size of the increment — steady, predictable, and it scales with new data volume. For a materialized view, cost depends on whether the refresh is incremental or a full recompute; a full recompute means re-reading and re-processing everything, so cost scales with total data size, not just the new data.

Let's make that concrete with the worked example in front of you. Suppose you 100 GB of historical data and 1 GB of new data per day. On a streaming table, a daily run touches about 1 GB — the increment. On a materialized view whose query is not incrementally computable, that same daily refresh re-reads all 100 GB plus the new day. Same daily cadence, roughly a hundred times the scanned data. That gap is why the refresh behavior dimension matters so much in practice.

In syntax, the keyword you declare is what commits you to the semantics. You declare a streaming table to get incremental, append-only processing; you declare a materialized view to get a persisted query result. Pick the keyword deliberately — it isn't a stylistic choice.

Now here's the trap. Both are registered in Unity Catalog as ordinary tables, both can be read with a plain SELECT, and both appear in the same catalog and schema. So how you read them does NOT distinguish them. If an exam question asks you to tell them apart based on how you query them, that's a distractor — the difference is in how they are declared, how they process data, and how they refresh.

In the medallion architecture — bronze for raw ingested data, silver for cleaned and conformed data, gold for business-level tables you serve from — streaming tables typically do the bronze ingestion work, while materialized views are more natural for silver and gold layers where you're aggregating, joining, and shaping tables that already exist.

So here's the decision rule, and it's the one line worth memorizing. If the input arrives as a stream — append or change-data-capture semantics from a streaming source — declare a streaming table. If the requirement is a complex join, an aggregation, or serving-layer business logic over existing tables — declare a materialized view. Match the declaration to the shape of the input and the shape of the output.

One more guardrail: do not choose based on how the dataset looks or how you'll read it. Both look like tables and both read the same way. Choose based on where the data comes from and what transformation you're performing on it.

And size the choice with the increment. When the increment is small relative to the total — a steady stream of new events — streaming tables keep cost proportional to what's new. When you genuinely need the whole result recomputed, be honest about that cost. The final decisions here are also captured in the takeaways on this page, so use them as your summary before we check your understanding.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Telling the Two Dataset Types Apart

questions.question: A data engineer needs to continuously incrementally ingest new order records from a raw source as they arrive, appending only new data on each refresh rather than recomputing the full result. Which SQL declaration is the correct choice for this requirement?

options.label: CREATE STREAMING TABLE bronze_orders AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(raw_orders)
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW bronze_orders AS SELECT * FROM raw_orders
CREATE TEMPORARY VIEW bronze_orders AS SELECT * FROM raw_orders
CREATE TABLE bronze_orders AS SELECT * FROM raw_orders; then run an INSERT INTO statement each refresh

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: a streaming table is the dataset type designed for continuous incremental ingestion, reading from a streaming source such as STREAM() or Auto Loader. As the source material states, Lakeflow provides native support for streaming tables, incrementally updated materialized views, and automated CDC [source 4]. A materialized view (Option B) is intended for a result the framework recomputes, not for append-only incremental ingestion; a temporary view (Option C) does not persist data as a dataset; and Option D reintroduces the manual INSERT step that declarative pipelines are meant to eliminate. The framework infers how to process incrementally from your declaration rather than relying on a hand-written write step [source 5].

questions.question: Which of the following statements about dataset types in Lakeflow declarative pipelines are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A materialized view whose query is incrementally computable is not recomputed from scratch on every update; the engine can apply incremental updates.
A streaming table can natively apply updates and deletes to already-ingested rows without AUTO CDC or APPLY CHANGES.
The engine builds a dependency graph from your dataset definitions and determines execution order and where to process incrementally.
A materialized view can only ever be reprocessed by fully recomputing its entire result from scratch on each refresh.

questions.analysis: Options A and C are correct. Lakeflow supports incrementally updated materialized views as a first-class capability [source 4], so when the query is incrementally computable the framework applies incremental updates rather than a full recompute. And because the pipeline is declarative, the engine builds a dependency graph from your definitions and determines the execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures [source 5]. Option B is a distractor that mirrors a common misconception: applying updates and deletes to ingested rows is the job of automated CDC via AUTO CDC / APPLY CHANGES, not something a plain streaming table does natively [source 4]. Option D is the opposite error, overstating recomputation.

questions.question: A pipeline already has a bronze-layer streaming table named bronze_events. The team now needs a daily sales aggregate, refreshed by the framework when upstream data changes, that reads from bronze_events. Which declaration correctly expresses this dataset?

options.label: CREATE STREAMING TABLE gold_daily_sales AS SELECT date, SUM(amount) AS total FROM bronze_events GROUP BY date
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_daily_sales AS SELECT date, SUM(amount) AS total FROM LIVE.bronze_events GROUP BY date
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_daily_sales AS SELECT date, SUM(amount) AS total FROM /mnt/bronze_events GROUP BY date
CREATE TEMPORARY VIEW gold_daily_sales AS SELECT date, SUM(amount) AS total FROM bronze_events GROUP BY date

questions.analysis: Option B is correct. An aggregation over an upstream dataset is a result the framework refreshes, so a materialized view is the right declaration, and reading LIVE.bronze_events resolves the name to the pipeline-local dataset and creates a dependency edge rather than reading a physical copy. Option A misdeclares an aggregation as a streaming table, which is not the correct dataset type for a recomputed aggregate. Option C hard-codes a storage path, breaking the graph's name-based reference model. Option D uses a temporary view, which is pipeline-local and not a persisted gold dataset. Because references create the dependency graph and the engine infers execution order and incremental processing from the resulting graph [source 5], declaring the correct type and a valid LIVE. reference is what allows the pipeline graph to resolve correctly [source 1].
