scenes.title: Streaming Tables: Incremental, Append-Only Ingestion

elements.content: Streaming Tables: Incremental, Append-Only Ingestion
Processing semantics of a streaming table dataset in a Lakeflow declarative pipeline

1. Incremental processing: each pipeline update consumes only data not yet processed — every record is read exactly once across runs. [source 5] A stream is therefore unbounded and never fully recomputed.

2. Native append-only semantics: a streaming table only appends new rows. To apply updates and deletes, use AUTO CDC (APPLY CHANGES) in Python or APPLY CHANGES INTO in SQL — the append-only default alone cannot apply them. [source 4]
3. Checkpointing: streaming tables are backed by Delta Lake and use checkpoints to track source offsets already consumed, which enables incremental reads and restart-from-failure. [source 5]

4. Typical sources: cloud object storage via Auto Loader, event-streaming platforms, and upstream streaming tables. A batch table read with readStream-style semantics is not a streaming source. [source 3]
Worked Example — Checkpoint Offset Arithmetic

If an offset checkpoint records offset 4,321 the next incremental run reads from offset 4,322 only — earlier records are never reread [source 5].

Filtered query (status = 'paid'): 10,000 source rows in, 6,400 emitted.

The output is still a streaming table because the declaration stays CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE — a transformation does not change dataset type [source 3].
Exam trap: adding a filter or cast does not turn a streaming table into a materialized view; the declaration decides the dataset type.

actions.text: Now that we can tell the two dataset types apart, let's zoom into the first one: streaming tables. This is a streaming dataset declared in a declarative pipeline, and our job here is to understand exactly how it ingests data, not just how it looks in a cell.

Here is the processing semantics in a single sentence. A streaming table behaves like a streaming dataset: each pipeline update consumes only the records it has not seen before. That property — incremental processing — is the whole reason streaming tables exist. They are ingest-first datasets designed to keep landing new arrivals without ever re-reading your entire history.

Let's break that into four exam-relevant points. First, incremental processing. Each pipeline update continues from where the previous one stopped, so we never reprocess the same records. That means the cost scales with new data, not with the size of the table.

Second, native append-only semantics. A streaming table appends. That is all it does. It cannot natively update or delete rows in place. If your source sends updates and deletes — which almost every real source does — you must layer AUTO CDC on top, called APPLY CHANGES in Python or APPLY CHANGES INTO in SQL. If you skip that and try to mutate a streaming table row directly, you are off the rails, and the exam knows it.

Third, checkpointing. Streaming tables are backed by Delta Lake, and they maintain checkpoints that record the source offsets already consumed. This is what makes incremental reads possible in the first place — and it is what lets a pipeline restart from a failure without replaying data it already landed. No checkpoints, no exactly-once.

Fourth, typical sources. Cloud object storage through Auto Loader, event-streaming platforms like Kafka, and upstream streaming tables themselves. Notice what is missing: reading a batch table with readStream-style semantics is not a valid streaming source. The table has to actually be streamable; you cannot wish it into being one.
Let's make checkpointing concrete with this worked example on offset arithmetic.

If an offset checkpoint records offset 4,321, then the next pipeline update resumes from the very next record. It does not start at zero. It does not reprocess 4,321. Read this as a plain statement of the incremental guarantee: offset recorded, resume after it. That one line of arithmetic is the mechanism behind the word 'incremental'.

And finally, the exam trap I want you to carry out of this page. Adding a filter or a cast does not turn a streaming table into a materialized view. The declaration decides the dataset type, not the transformation. You can filter, cast, join, and aggregate inside a streaming table definition and it is still a streaming table. So before you answer any question about dataset type, look at how the dataset was declared, never at what the body of the query does.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Declaring the Right Dataset for an Ingestion-to-Serving Pipeline

elements.content: Problem 1

Acme Retail runs an orders pipeline on Databricks Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines. JSON order files land continuously in cloud storage under the path s3://acme-landing/orders/, at a rate of about 4,200 files per day, each averaging 430 KB (so roughly 1.806 GB per day of new raw data). The landing zone retains 540 days of history, which is about 2,268,000 files and roughly 975 GB of raw JSON. Two requirements must be met. Requirement (a): the BI team needs a dataset named daily_revenue with one row per calendar day containing the total order amount in USD, and it must be refreshed hourly. Requirement (b): the pipeline must not re-read the entire 975 GB history on every hourly update. Write the two SQL dataset declarations that satisfy both requirements, classify each hop as an ingestion hop or a serving hop, and check with numbers whether the design actually delivers requirement (b).
Hint: Ask which hop sees brand-new data arrive (incremental at the edge) and which hop transforms already-landed data (recomputable at the serving layer).

Worked solution
Step 0 - Decompose the requirement into two hops. The requirement describes two distinct movements of data. Hop 1 is ingestion: the landing zone in cloud storage to a first pipeline dataset called raw_orders. Hop 2 is serving: raw_orders to the aggregated dataset daily_revenue. Crucially these hops have different physics. At hop 1, new data appears from outside the pipeline, so the only question is which files have already been read. At hop 2, the data already sits in a pipeline-managed table and the query is a deterministic transformation of it. Step 1 - Declare the ingestion hop as a streaming table. Continuous file arrival is a streaming source. A streaming table ingests new data incrementally, and Lakeflow provides native support for streaming tables [source 4]. In SQL, the streaming read of a directory of files is written with the STREAM read_files(...) function (Auto Loader), so: ```sql CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE raw_orders AS SELECT * FROM STREAM read_files( 's3://acme-landing/orders/', format => 'json', schemaLocation => 's3://acme-checkpoints/orders/_schema' ); ``` Three things make this declaration the correct one. First, STREAMING TABLE tells the engine to keep file-discovery state, so a file already read is not read again. Second, STREAM read_files is Auto Loader in SQL: it lists (or receives notifications about) new files and processes only the unseen ones. Third, schemaLocation persists the inferred JSON schema so the schema is not re-inferred from scratch on every update. Step 2 - Declare the serving hop as a materialized view. The daily revenue requirement is a grouped aggregation over an existing dataset, so the declaration is: ```sql CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS SELECT date_trunc('day', order_ts) AS day, sum(amount) AS revenue_usd FROM raw_orders GROUP BY 1; ``` Note that the FROM clause reads raw_orders by name. That reference, not a physical copy, is what creates the dependency edge in the pipeline graph, and the engine builds that graph from the definitions and determines execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures [source 5]. Both statements may appear in any file order because the graph is inferred from the FROM clauses, not from the order in which the statements are written [source 1]. Step 3 - Verify incrementality with concrete numbers. Full history in the landing zone: $$2{,}268{,}000 \text{ files} \times 430\ \text{KB} = 975{,}240{,}000\ \text{KB} \approx 975\ \text{GB}$$ If the ingestion hop were instead declared as a materialized view, the query would be recomputed, meaning the whole directory would be listed and read: 2,268,000 files and 975 GB per update. Now compute what actually happens per hourly update under the streaming table. New files per hour: $$\frac{4{,}200}{24} = 175\ \text{files/hour}$$ New bytes per hour: $$175 \times 430\ \text{KB} = 75{,}250\ \text{KB} \approx 75.3\ \text{MB}$$ The ratio of the wrong design to the right design per update is: $$\frac{975{,}000\ \text{MB}}{75.25\ \text{MB}} \approx 12{,}958$$ Over a full day: the correct design reads 1.806 GB (each file exactly once), while a materialized-view ingestion hop would scan 24 x 975 GB = 23.4 TB per day. That is a factor of about 13,000, and it is the single number that settles the design. Step 4 - Check the serving hop is incrementally refreshable. The engine can refresh daily_revenue incrementally for two reasons. The aggregation is deterministic: for a fixed input, sum(amount) group by day always returns the same rows. The input is effectively append-only: new rows arrive in raw_orders and existing rows are not silently mutated. Under those conditions the engine only has to recompute the day-partitions touched by new data - in a typical hourly update that is one day, occasionally two when a late file lands - and it merges those updated aggregate values into the materialized view rather than re-reading 540 days of history. Lakeflow provides this as incrementally updated materialized views [source 4]. Final answer: ```sql CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE raw_orders AS SELECT * FROM STREAM read_files('s3://acme-landing/orders/', format => 'json', schemaLocation => 's3://acme-checkpoints/orders/_schema'); CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS SELECT date_trunc('day', order_ts) AS day, sum(amount) AS revenue_usd FROM raw_orders GROUP BY 1; ```

Analysis — Why the split works. The two hops answer different questions. The ingestion hop asks 'what is new outside the pipeline?', which is exactly what a streaming table tracks through checkpointed file-discovery state with Auto Loader, so the incremental work is proportional to new data (~75.3 MB per hourly update). The serving hop asks 'what does the business want to see?', and because the query is a deterministic grouped aggregate over an append-only input, the answer can be produced by merging recomputed day-partitions instead of a full rescan. Lakeflow pipelines are a declarative framework for both batch and streaming workloads in SQL and Python [source 3], and the framework decides where to process incrementally from the definitions themselves [source 5]. The recommended recipe is therefore 'incremental at the edge, recomputable at the serving layer'. Typical learner mistakes. (1) Declaring the ingestion hop as a materialized view, usually by dropping the STREAM keyword: 'CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW raw_orders AS SELECT * FROM read_files(...)'. This runs and returns correct rows, which is the trap - the dataset looks right while doing 12,958 times the I/O per update. (2) Writing a batch read inside a streaming table: 'CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE raw_orders AS SELECT * FROM read_files(...)' without STREAM, which is not a streaming source. (3) Reintroducing imperative control: adding an explicit INSERT/MERGE step, hard-coding a physical table path in the FROM clause, or adding an ORDER BY-style execution hint. None of these are needed, and each breaks either the incremental state or the graph edge. (4) Believing that the file order in the notebook matters. It does not; the graph is derived from references [source 1]. Edge cases to reason about. Late-arriving files are still new to the checkpoint, so they will be ingested, and the affected day in daily_revenue will be recomputed - correctness is preserved. If an upstream system sends corrections to historical orders, raw_orders remains append-only from the pipeline's perspective, but the MV must then recompute the corrected day; incrementality survives because the recompute is day-local. If order_ts were replaced by a nondeterministic expression such as current_timestamp(), incrementality would break because the same input row would produce a different output on each refresh. That is the general rule: incrementality requires determinism plus an append-only or change-tracked input. Generalization. Whenever a requirement contains the words 'files arrive continuously' or 'new events', the edge dataset is a streaming table; whenever it contains 'aggregate', 'join' or 'report', the downstream dataset is a candidate for a materialized view. The correct declaration is the one whose refresh semantics match how the data actually moves.
Problem 2

A colleague on the Acme Retail team submits this pipeline code for review. The pipeline is scheduled to run every hour, and the landing zone still holds 2,268,000 JSON files totalling about 975 GB: ```sql CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW raw_orders AS SELECT * FROM read_files('s3://acme-landing/orders/', format => 'json'); ``` The colleague argues it is fine because the daily_revenue numbers it produces are correct. (i) Identify the defect in the declaration. (ii) Rewrite it correctly. (iii) Quantify the wasted I/O per day, and state one reliability problem in addition to the cost problem.
Hint: Correct results and correct refresh semantics are two different acceptance criteria. Ask what state each dataset type keeps between updates.

Worked solution
(i) The defect. The statement is syntactically valid and produces correct rows, but the dataset type does not match the shape of the source. A materialized view persists the result of a query and refreshes it during a pipeline update; a streaming table ingests new data incrementally [source 4]. Because raw_orders is declared as a materialized view over a raw directory path, every hourly update recomputes the query, and the query is a full batch read of the landing directory. The engine has no persistent notion of 'files I have already read'. Two further symptoms follow from the same root cause: the read is not a streaming read (read_files without STREAM is batch), and the FROM clause points at a storage path rather than at a pipeline dataset name, so no incremental state can be attached to a source object. (ii) The correction. Replace the materialized view with a streaming table and make the file read streaming: ```sql CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE raw_orders AS SELECT * FROM STREAM read_files( 's3://acme-landing/orders/', format => 'json', schemaLocation => 's3://acme-checkpoints/orders/_schema' ); ``` The downstream daily_revenue statement does not change at all, because it reads raw_orders by name; only the producer of raw_orders changed. This is a good illustration of why dependency edges are created by names and not by paths. (iii) Quantifying the waste. Per update, the wrong declaration lists and reads: $$2{,}268{,}000\ \text{files}, \quad 975\ \text{GB}$$ The correct declaration reads only the files that arrived since the last update. At 4,200 files/day and a 1-hour schedule, that is: $$\frac{4{,}200}{24} = 175\ \text{files/hour} \quad \Rightarrow \quad 175 \times 430\ \text{KB} = 75.3\ \text{MB}$$ Daily totals, at 24 updates per day: $$\text{wrong: } 24 \times 975\ \text{GB} = 23{,}400\ \text{GB} = 23.4\ \text{TB/day}$$ $$\text{right: } 24 \times 75.3\ \text{MB} \approx 1{,}807\ \text{MB} \approx 1.81\ \text{GB/day}$$ $$\text{ratio } = \frac{975{,}000\ \text{MB}}{75.25\ \text{MB}} \approx 12{,}958\ \text{times the I/O per update}$$ At 2,268,000 file-open operations per update, the wrong version performs about 54.4 million file listings/opens per day. On cloud object storage, where each listing call has latency and a per-request price, that is the difference between a pipeline that finishes in minutes and one that spends the whole hour scanning. (iv) The reliability problem. A materialized view over a raw path has no resumable position. If the pipeline fails halfway through an update, the next run starts again from the beginning of the directory with no record of what it already consumed. A streaming table keeps checkpoint state, so a retry resumes from where it stopped; the engine recovers from failures using the state implied by the dataset definitions [source 5]. Under the wrong declaration the pipeline is also fragile with respect to the schema: without a schema location, every update re-infers the JSON schema across the whole history, and one malformed historical file will fail every future update rather than just the update that ingested it.

Analysis — The method choice here is the distinction between 'recompute the query' and 'advance the source'. Both dataset types produce correct rows, so correctness of output cannot be the acceptance test; the acceptance test is whether the declaration matches the motion of the data. A rule of thumb: if the source is outside the pipeline and grows over time (files, Kafka topics, event hubs), the producer must be a streaming table so the engine can hold a position. If the source is already a pipeline dataset and the transformation is a deterministic query over it, a materialized view is the natural declaration, and the framework will still refresh it incrementally when it can [source 4]. Where students typically go wrong. The most common error is reading the requirement 'I just need a table of all orders' and picking MATERIALIZED VIEW because it sounds more permanent than STREAMING TABLE. A second is copying a batch snippet (read_files without STREAM) into a pipeline and assuming the pipeline will make it incremental. A third is 'fixing' the cost problem by adding a manual incremental job: a MERGE or INSERT that appends only new files, plus an explicit schedule or dependency list. That reintroduces the imperative machinery declarative pipelines exist to remove, and it breaks the graph that the engine builds automatically [source 5]. A fourth is confusing the two failure modes: this bug does not produce wrong data, so it will not be caught by a row-count test - it will only be caught by watching the refresh duration or the bytes scanned. Edge cases. If the landing zone is a small, fixed set of files that is fully replaced on each run, the materialized-view form is defensible, because there is nothing incremental to track; that is the genuine exception. If the ingestion needs schema evolution, the streaming table is still the right answer, and the schema location is what makes evolution safe. Finally, note that the same correction applies when the source is a Delta table with change data feed rather than files: the point is not 'files' but 'a source the engine can advance a position on'. Generalization. When reviewing any dataset declaration, ask three questions: Is the source external and growing? Are the transformations deterministic? Is the input append-only or change-tracked? If yes to all three, the declaration at the edge is a streaming table, and the rest of the pipeline can be materialized views refreshed incrementally on top of it.
Problem 3

Acme's BI team now asks for a second serving dataset, top_customers, which lists every customer with their lifetime spend in USD and a rank column, ranking all customers from 1 (highest lifetime spend) downward. The candidate query is: ```sql SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) AS lifetime_spend_usd, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY sum(amount) DESC) AS rank FROM raw_orders GROUP BY customer_id; ``` Known sizes: raw_orders holds 380,000,000 rows over 540 days, averaging 0.24 KB per row in Delta, so about 91.2 GB. A separate materialized view customer_lifetime, defined as `SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) AS lifetime_spend_usd FROM raw_orders GROUP BY customer_id`, holds 1,400,000 rows at about 64 bytes each, so about 89.6 MB. During a refresh, a single new order of 12,000 USD from customer 8817 arrives, which moves that customer from rank 40 to rank 3. Answer: (i) can the rank column be maintained incrementally by merging a delta? (ii) exactly how many of the 1,400,000 rank values change? (iii) what is the cheapest correct declaration, and how much data does a full recompute touch compared with reading raw_orders directly?
Hint: A global window function is not a grouped aggregate: the value of one row depends on rows that did not change at all.

Worked solution
(i) Can the rank be merged incrementally? No. The reason is structural. A grouped aggregate such as sum(amount) GROUP BY day is a fold: it is associative, so new input rows can be folded into the existing partial results and only the touched groups need rewriting. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY sum(amount) DESC) is not a fold. The rank of each customer is defined by its position relative to all other customers, so a change anywhere can change rows everywhere below it. The engine cannot merge a 38-row delta into a rank column that is defined by global order, so it recomputes the window over its full input. Important nuance: the dataset type does not change. It is still declared as a materialized view, because it is a persisted query result that the framework refreshes [source 4][source 5]. Choosing MATERIALIZED VIEW is not evidence that the refresh is cheap; it says only that the result is stored and recomputable. What controls the cost is the size of the input the query reads, which is a design decision you control through layering. (ii) How many rows actually change. Before the update, order the customers by descending spend; call them c(1), c(2), ..., c(1,400,000). Customer 8817 is c(40), so the incoming 12,000 USD order moves them to position 3. Removing them from position 40 and inserting them at position 3 gives: - old c(3) through old c(39) each move down one position, so 37 customers change rank by +1; - old c(40), which is customer 8817, changes rank from 40 to 3, so 1 more customer changes. Everyone else is unaffected: exactly the same number of customers sit above old c(41) before and after, so old c(41) stays at rank 41. $$\text{rows changed} = 37 + 1 = 38 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{38}{1{,}400{,}000} = 0.0027\%$$ So 0.0027% of the output changes, yet a global window forces a recompute over 100% of the input. That asymmetry is the whole lesson of this problem. (iii) Cheapest correct declaration. Keep MATERIALIZED VIEW, but read the small aggregated dataset rather than the 380-million-row fact table: ```sql CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW customer_lifetime AS SELECT customer_id, sum(amount) AS lifetime_spend_usd FROM raw_orders GROUP BY customer_id; CREATE OR REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW top_customers AS SELECT customer_id, lifetime_spend_usd, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY lifetime_spend_usd DESC) AS rank FROM customer_lifetime; ``` customer_lifetime is a deterministic grouped aggregate over an effectively append-only input, so the engine refreshes it incrementally - only the customers with a new order need their sum rewritten (in a typical hourly update, a few hundred to a few thousand of 1.4 million rows). top_customers then pays a full window recompute, but over 89.6 MB instead of 91.2 GB. Compare the recompute cost: $$\text{direct over raw_orders: } 380{,}000{,}000 \times 0.24\ \text{KB} = 91{,}200{,}000\ \text{KB} = 91.2\ \text{GB}$$ $$\text{layered over customer_lifetime: } 1{,}400{,}000 \times 64\ \text{B} = 89{,}600{,}000\ \text{B} \approx 89.6\ \text{MB}$$ $$\frac{91{,}200\ \text{MB}}{89.6\ \text{MB}} \approx 1{,}018\ \text{times less data scanned}$$ In row terms it is 380,000,000 / 1,400,000 = 271 times fewer rows, and the byte ratio is larger (about 1,018x) because a raw order row carries many columns while customer_lifetime carries two. Final answer: declare customer_lifetime and top_customers both as materialized views, chain them so the expensive global window sits on the small aggregated input, and accept the full window recompute because it now costs about 89.6 MB rather than 91.2 GB.

Analysis — Why this works. The cost of a refresh is determined by two independent things: what the engine must recompute (fixed by the query shape) and how much it must read to recompute it (fixed by where the query sits in the graph). ROW_NUMBER over a global order fixes the first: no incremental merge is possible because ranks are relational, not per-row. Layering fixes the second: by inserting a cheap, incrementally refreshed aggregate between the fact table and the window, the unavoidable full recompute lands on a 1000x smaller input. This is the same reasoning that makes medallion architecture (a layered bronze/silver/gold arrangement in which each layer narrows and cleans the data before the next) pay off: put expensive global operations as high in the graph as possible, on the smallest correct input. Where students typically go wrong. The biggest error is the belief that 'materialized view' automatically means 'avoided all recomputation'. A materialized view is recomputed; the engine merely tries to refresh it incrementally when the query allows [source 4]. A second error is the mirror image: assuming that because the rank cannot be merged, the dataset must be declared as a streaming table. A streaming table requires an incremental source with a tracked position; a global window over a whole table is not a streaming source, and declaring it as one does not make the recompute disappear. A third error is computing the size of the change (38 rows, 0.0027%) and concluding the engine 'should' only touch those rows. Engines do not reason about semantic minimality; they reason about query structure. A fourth error is forgetting that customer_lifetime must itself be correct before the window runs - if it were declared with a nondeterministic expression, its own incremental refresh would be impossible, and the whole chain would degrade into full recomputes. Edge cases. Ties matter: with ROW_NUMBER, two customers with the same lifetime spend receive different ranks (order then depends on the engine's scan order), whereas RANK gives them the same rank and skips the following number. If the business wants deterministic behaviour on ties, add a tie-breaker such as ORDER BY lifetime_spend_usd DESC, customer_id ASC - without it, the output is not stable across refreshes, which also undermines any incremental refresh logic. Another edge case is a partitioned window: if the business question were reformulated as 'top customer per day' with `PARTITION BY day`, the window becomes local to each day, and a change to one day leaves the other days' rows unchanged - a structure the engine can exploit for a partial refresh. The global ranking in this problem offers no such locality. Finally, if customer_lifetime were defined over an input that receives updates to old rows (not just appends), the aggregate still refreshes correctly, but the engine must read the changed rows; append-only inputs remain the cheapest case. Generalization. Faced with any expensive serving requirement, first classify the query: is it a fold (grouped aggregate, associative merge) or a relational reordering (window, ranking, deduplication by global order)? Then classify its input: how many rows and bytes must be read? Optimize the second, because the first is usually not negotiable. This is also the exam-relevant vocabulary: streaming table for incrementally ingested data, materialized view for query results the framework recomputes, and views for pipeline-local temporary results [source 3][source 5].

actions.text: Now let's put that rule into practice with a fully worked problem. This one takes a realistic requirement all the way from classification through SQL declaration, and then we'll analyze why the split works and where learners typically go wrong.

Here's the scenario. Acme Retail runs an orders pipeline on Databricks. JSON order files land continuously in cloud storage, a daily revenue aggregate must be served to BI, and critically, the pipeline must not reprocess the entire history on every update. Hold onto that last constraint — it drives everything that follows.

Before you look at the solution, here's the hint that should shape your thinking: ask which hop sees brand-new data arrive incrementally. That single question tells you the dataset type for the ingestion edge, while the serving layer answers a different question entirely.

Let's walk the worked solution step by step. Step one — classify the ingestion hop. Continuous file arrival means we declare a streaming table: CREATE STREAMING TABLE raw_orders AS SELECT ... FROM STREAM read_files(...), which is Auto Loader under the hood. Step two — classify the serving hop. That's a grouped aggregation over an existing table, so it becomes a materialized view: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS SELECT date_trunc('day', order_ts) AS day, sum(amount) FROM raw_orders GROUP BY 1. Step three — verify incrementality. The aggregation is a deterministic grouped aggregate over an append-only input, so the engine can refresh it incrementally rather than recomputing the full history.

Now the analysis — why the split works. The two hops answer two different questions: the edge needs incremental ingestion, and the serving layer needs a recomputable result. Incremental at the edge, recomputable at the serving layer. And notice the pitfall: if you declared the ingestion hop as a materialized view instead, every update would force a rescan of the landing zone — exactly the full-history reprocessing the requirement forbids. That's the trap this problem is built to expose.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Semantics and Syntax of Streaming Tables

questions.question: A Lakeflow declarative pipeline contains a streaming table named bronze_events that ingests JSON files landed in cloud storage via Auto Loader, plus a downstream streaming table silver_events that reads from bronze_events. The pipeline has already processed files 001 through 100. A new file, 101, lands in the source path, and the engineer triggers a normal pipeline update (not a full refresh). Which data does the pipeline reprocess during that update?

options.label: Only the new data — file 101 flowing through bronze_events into silver_events — because a streaming table is incremental and append-only, so already-processed files 001–100 are not read again unless a full refresh is explicitly requested.
All source files 001–101 from scratch, because any pipeline update rebuilds each streaming table from its underlying source as a fresh batch computation.
Only silver_events, because downstream streaming tables are always recomputed in full on every update while upstream streaming tables stay frozen.
Nothing until the engineer manually runs an INSERT or MERGE statement, because a streaming table is passive storage that does not react to a pipeline update.

questions.commentPrompt: N/A (single choice)
questions.analysis: A streaming table applies incremental, append-only processing: it consumes only new data from its streaming source on each update. Files 001–100 were already committed, so file 101 is the only new input, and it flows through bronze_events into silver_events in dependency order inferred by the pipeline graph [source 5]. Option B describes a full refresh, which happens only when explicitly requested. Option C inverts the semantics — a downstream streaming table does not recompute its whole history every update. Option D is a distractor built on the misconception that manual INSERT/MERGE steps drive streaming tables; declarative pipelines infer execution from the graph instead [source 1][source 2].

questions.question: An engineer must maintain a silver streaming table that reflects the latest state of an orders feed, where the source produces inserts, updates, and deletes keyed by order_id. Which statements about implementing this correctly are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: AUTO CDC (also written APPLY CHANGES) is the correct tool: it processes the change feed and applies inserts, updates, and deletes into the target, which is the supported way to get non-append-only semantics on a streaming table.
Hand-writing a MERGE statement that targets the streaming table directly and running it as part of the pipeline update is the standard supported pattern for applying deletes and updates.

Checkpoints let the framework remember how far each streaming query has progressed, so after a failure it resumes from the last committed offset rather than reprocessing the entire source, which is central to fault recovery in incremental processing.

A streaming table is best understood as a cached query result: it stores whatever the query returned the last time it ran, and it is refreshed by re-running the query and replacing the cached output, much like a materialized view.

questions.commentPrompt: N/A (multiple choice)
questions.analysis: Option A is correct: automated CDC (AUTO CDC / APPLY CHANGES) is the native way to apply row-level deletes and updates to a streaming target; a hand-written MERGE is not the supported mechanism for streaming tables (Option B is the classic misconception). Option C is correct: checkpoints record processing progress so recovery resumes incrementally after failure instead of restarting from the beginning [source 5]. Option D is a category error — it describes a materialized view, not a streaming table. Lakeflow provides streaming tables and incrementally updated materialized views as distinct dataset types, and the streaming table's defining property is incremental append-only ingestion, not cached query results [source 4][source 5].

questions.question: Which statement best describes the role of checkpoints in a streaming table's incremental processing and fault recovery within a Lakeflow declarative pipeline?

options.label: Checkpoints record the progress of each streaming query — the offsets and state already committed — so that after a failure or a normal update the query resumes from where it left off instead of reprocessing all source data from the beginning.

Checkpoints are scheduled snapshots that the engineer must configure manually before the pipeline can start; without an explicit checkpoint schedule, the pipeline cannot process incrementally and falls back to full recomputation on every run.
Checkpoints cache the query's final results so that downstream datasets can read the output without touching the target table, which is why a streaming table behaves like a materialized view.
Checkpoints are optional performance hints only; a streaming table that loses its checkpoint state simply continues from the newest file in the source with no behavioral change.

questions.commentPrompt: N/A (single choice)
questions.analysis: Checkpoints are the mechanism that makes incremental processing durable: they track how far each streaming query has progressed so the framework can resume from the last committed point after a failure, rather than reprocessing the whole source. This is part of how the pipeline engine 'determines the execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures' [source 5]. Option B invents a manual checkpoint schedule requirement that does not exist — the framework manages checkpoints automatically [source 1][source 2]. Option C misuses the term to mean result caching, which conflates streaming tables with materialized views. Option D understates the stakes: losing checkpoint state forces a restart of the stream, which can mean reprocessing from the earliest available offset rather than simply the newest file.

actions.text: Now let's check how well the semantics and syntax of streaming tables have settled in. We've covered a lot about how these datasets behave incrementally, how they handle change data, and how recovery works — so take your time, read each question carefully, and work through them on your own.
Once you submit, I'll walk through anything that gave you trouble. Go ahead and give it your best shot.

scenes.title: Interactive Decision Tree: Streaming Table or Materialized View?

content.html:
Streaming Table or Materialized View?

Interactive decision tree · Databricks certification prep
1 / 7

nodes.label:
Source continuous
& append-only?
nodes.title: Decision 1 — Look at the source
nodes.details:
Ask: does the data arrive continuously and append-only — new files landing in storage, a message bus (Kafka, Event Hubs), or another streaming table?

  • Yes → the native declaration is a streaming table: Lakeflow ingests each record once, as it arrives.
  • No → the dataset is produced by querying tables that already exist. Go on to Decision 2.

Glossary: append-only means the source only ever adds new records — it never updates or deletes the ones already written.

nodes.label:
CREATE STREAMING
TABLE
nodes.title: CREATE STREAMING TABLE — continuous, append-only source
nodes.details:
CREATE STREAMING TABLE bronze_events
AS SELECT *
FROM STREAM read_files('/landing/events', format => 'json');
-- or: FROM STREAM kafka_source
-- or: FROM STREAM upstream_streaming_table

Why it fits: a streaming table is a Delta table that ingests each source record exactly once, incrementally. Auto Loader, message buses and upstream streaming tables are all streaming sources.

Why the other choice fails: a materialized view (a query result kept up to date by re-running the query) recomputes its whole definition at every refresh. Facing a continuous source it cannot consume the stream record-by-record, and you would have to schedule refreshes and pay for repeated recomputation.

Watch the keyword STREAM in the subquery — that is what marks the read as incremental.

nodes.label:
Result is a query
over existing tables?
nodes.title: Decision 2 — Look at the shape of the result
nodes.details:
Is the output a query over tables that already exist — joins, aggregations, business logic — that should be refreshed rather than appended to?

  • Yes → a materialized view declares exactly that.
  • No → you are not declaring a Lakeflow dataset at all.

The tell-tale words are "result of a query over existing tables" and "kept fresh by re-running".

nodes.label:
CREATE MATERIALIZED
VIEW
nodes.title: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW — query result over existing tables
nodes.details:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW gold_sales_by_region
AS SELECT region, sum(amount) AS revenue
   FROM sales
   GROUP BY region;

Why it fits: a materialized view stores the result of a query over existing tables and keeps it fresh by re-running that query on a schedule or trigger. Joins, aggregations and updates are all legal because nothing is ingested incrementally.

Why the other choice fails: a streaming table requires an append-only streaming source. A query over existing Delta tables produces updates and retractions, not clean appends — so "recompute this query over what exists" is a materialized view, never a streaming table.

nodes.label:
No dataset declaration
— notebook / job
nodes.title: Neither — no Lakeflow dataset declaration
nodes.details:
If the source is not continuous and the output is not a maintained query result, you are not declaring a managed dataset:

  • A one-off or batch computation → a notebook or a scheduled job that writes a Delta table.
  • Query-only logic that must always be current at read time → a plain VIEW (no storage, recomputed on every read).

Reach for CREATE STREAMING TABLE or CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW only when you need a managed, continuously fresh dataset.

nodes.label:
Trap: refresh a MV
over a stream
nodes.title: Exam trap — "Refresh a materialized view over continuously arriving files"
nodes.details:
Why it sounds right: a materialized view is also a managed dataset inside a pipeline, and the word "refresh" sounds like "keep it current".

Why it is wrong: a materialized view does not ingest — it re-runs its defining query. Pointed at Auto Loader, Kafka or an upstream streaming table it either cannot read incrementally, or it forces full recomputation over an ever-growing input.

Rule to memorise: continuous + append-only source → CREATE STREAMING TABLE. Refresh a query result over existing tables → CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW.

nodes.label:
Trap: streaming table
for a batch query
nodes.title: Exam trap — "Wrap a join or aggregation in CREATE STREAMING TABLE"
nodes.details:
Why it sounds right: streaming tables are the modern, incremental option, so learners reach for them whenever "freshness" is mentioned.

Why it is wrong: a streaming table expects an append-only streaming source. A join or aggregation over existing tables emits updates and deletes, so the declaration does not express "recompute this query over what already exists" — that is a materialized view.

Rule to memorise: "incremental ingest from a stream" → streaming table. "Result of a query over existing tables" → materialized view.

actions.text: We just compared streaming tables and materialized views side by side, so now let's put that distinction to work with a decision tree. Walk through it the same way you would on the exam: answer each question, follow the branch, and read the reasoning at every leaf.

actions.content: The tree starts at the top decision node and branches left or right depending on your answer.
Node 1 asks whether the source is continuous and append-only — new files, a message bus, or another streaming table.

actions.text: Answer that first question honestly. If the source keeps arriving and never updates existing records, you already know the declaration: a streaming table ingests each record exactly once, incrementally. Notice the keyword STREAM inside the subquery — that is what marks the read as incremental.

actions.content: Advance to the streaming table leaf so you can see the full declaration template.

actions.text: Now take the other branch. When the answer is no — the source is not continuous — the second question asks whether the result is a query over tables that already exist. Joins, aggregations, and business logic that should be refreshed rather than appended all point to a materialized view, kept fresh by re-running its defining query.

actions.content: Each leaf shows the correct declaration plus the reason the other choice fails, so the contrast is what you memorise.

actions.text: Try the trap branches too. Refreshing a materialized view over continuously arriving files sounds right because refresh implies freshness, but a materialized view does not ingest — it recomputes. And wrapping a join in CREATE STREAMING TABLE ignores that a streaming source must be append-only. Continuous plus append-only means streaming table; a query result over existing tables means materialized view. That rule is what the exam is testing, and we will build on it when we look at materialized view refresh behaviour next.

scenes.title: Materialized Views: When the Result Is the Product

elements.content: Materialized Views: When the Result Is the Product

Definition. A materialized view (MV) is a dataset whose declaration persists the result of a query as a queryable Delta table in Unity Catalog — the output rows are stored, not recomputed at read time.

Precondition: produced by exactly one query; refreshed as part of a pipeline update.
Full recompute (left) vs incremental refresh (right)
Refresh rule. The engine refreshes incrementally only when the defining query is incrementally computable; otherwise it recomputes the entire result on each update [source 4].

Worked example: refresh cost. A gold MV aggregates 1,000,000 fact rows.

• Incremental: new day = 5,000 rows → process ≈5,000 rows (0.5%).

• Full recompute: process all 1,000,000 rows (100%) — 200× more work.
Non-deterministic kill switch. current_timestamp(), rand() and similar functions make a query non-incrementally-computable, forcing a full recompute of the affected MV.
Non-deterministic kill switch. current_timestamp(), rand() and similar functions make a query non-incrementally-computable, forcing a full recompute of the affected MV.
Best fit. Serving-layer aggregations, multi-table joins and dimensional models that business consumers query repeatedly [source 5].
Exam trap: a plain VIEW recomputes at query time and caches nothing — not an MV.
Sources: [source 5] Lakeflow dataset types & dependency graph · [source 4] incrementally updated materialized views · [source 1] pipeline graph dependencies

actions.text: Welcome back. On the previous page you picked between streaming tables and materialized views in a decision tree. Now let's zoom in on the right-hand branch: the materialized view, or MV — a dataset where the result itself is the product.

Here is the definition you need to memorize: a materialized view stores the result of a query and refreshes that result as part of a pipeline update. The key word is persisted — it is a real, queryable table in Unity Catalog, not a recipe that runs on demand. Consumers read it like any other table, and the refresh work is done for them by the pipeline.

Now look at this image. On the left you see full recompute — every update throws away the old result and rebuilds it from scratch. On the right, incremental refresh — the engine only processes the changed rows and merges them into the existing result. Same logical answer, very different cost.

So when does the engine choose which? The refresh rule is: incremental refresh is used only when the defining query is incrementally computable. Aggregations that can be updated, filters, projections, and joins over append-only streams typically qualify. If the engine can't prove that the new result follows from the old result plus the delta, it silently falls back to a full recompute on each update — correct, but expensive.

Here's the worked example. A gold MV aggregates a large fact table. If the aggregate is incrementally computable, adding one new day of data touches one day of rows. If it's not, every pipeline update rescans the entire history. That difference is what shows up on your bill and on your refresh latency.

And here is the classic cause of that fallback: non-deterministic expressions. current_timestamp(), rand(), and similar functions produce a different value every time they run. The engine cannot reason about 'old result plus delta' when the function itself is unstable, so it forces a full recompute of the affected materialized view. This is a favorite exam trap — expect a scenario where someone sprinkles now() into a gold aggregate and wonders why refresh cost exploded.

Where do MVs fit best? Serving-layer aggregations, multi-table joins, and dimensional models that business consumers query repeatedly. In other words — anything where many readers hit the same precomputed answer, and you don't want each of them paying for the join.

One last trap before the checkpoint. A plain VIEW is not a materialized view. A view is just stored SQL — it recomputes at query time and caches nothing. So if the exam asks which object delivers materialized-view performance for a repeated heavy join, the answer is the MV, never the view. Let's move to the checkpoint and test this.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Refresh Behavior and Full Recompute Triggers

questions.question: A pipeline defines a materialized view with the following defining query: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_daily_orders AS SELECT order_id, order_ts, customer_id, amount FROM raw_orders WHERE amount > 0 AND order_ts >= current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS. On each pipeline update, what happens to this materialized view, and why?

options.label: It is recomputed in full on every update because current_timestamp() is non-deterministic; the engine cannot reuse previously computed rows, so the whole defining query is re-evaluated against all source data.
It is refreshed incrementally on every update because the filter predicate amount > 0 is a deterministic row-level expression that the engine can push down and only new raw_orders rows are read.
It is refreshed incrementally on every update because order_ts >= current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS is treated as a sliding window and the engine only reprocesses the last 7 days of raw_orders.
It is never recomputed after creation; materialized view results are frozen at first materialization unless you explicitly drop and recreate the dataset.

questions.analysis: The correct answer is A. A materialized view is incrementally refreshed only when its defining query is incrementally computable, meaning the engine can derive the new result from the old result plus newly arrived source data. current_timestamp() is a non-deterministic function: it returns a different value on every evaluation, so the set of rows that pass the filter changes between runs even if raw_orders itself does not change. There is no stable delta to merge, so the engine must drop the prior result and recompute the entire query in full. Option B is a common misconception: a deterministic predicate like amount > 0 is not sufficient on its own, because the query also contains a non-deterministic expression; a single non-deterministic function anywhere in the definition is enough to force full recompute. Option C is also a misconception: the engine does not infer a 'sliding window' from a time expression involving current_timestamp(), and this is not how Lakeflow decides incrementality. Option D is simply false — materialized views are persisted and refreshed on each pipeline update, not frozen. This distinction is foundational: Lakeflow declarative pipelines produce datasets with distinct processing semantics, and the engine determines where to process incrementally and how to recover from failures from the definitions you write [source 5].

questions.question: You are asked to decide which of the following materialized view definitions are guaranteed to be incrementally refreshable (that is, the engine can derive the new result from the previous result plus newly arrived source data, without recomputing the entire query). Select all that apply.

options.label: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_a AS SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total FROM sales GROUP BY region — a deterministic grouped aggregation over an append-only source.
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_b AS SELECT order_id, uuid() AS tracking_id FROM raw_orders — a projection that generates a random identifier per row.

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_c AS SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders_7d FROM raw_orders WHERE order_ts >= current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS GROUP BY customer_id — a sliding 7-day count driven by the current time.
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_d AS SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount FROM raw_orders WHERE amount > 0 — a deterministic filter over an append-only source.

questions.analysis: The correct answers are A and D. Both definitions are deterministic and depend only on the source rows and their values, so when new rows arrive in raw_orders the engine can fold the new rows into the existing result: a grouped SUM can add the new group contributions, and a filter can simply evaluate incoming rows against amount > 0. Option B is incorrect because uuid() is non-deterministic: each evaluation produces a different value, so the engine cannot reuse any previously materialized row and must recompute the whole query. Option C is incorrect for the same class of reason: current_timestamp() changes on every evaluation, so the set of qualifying rows changes even with no source change, which forces full recompute. The general rule to memorize is that a materialized view can be incrementally refreshed when the defining query is incrementally computable; a single non-deterministic function in the definition is the trigger that makes it not incrementally computable. This is exactly the behavior described for materialized views in Lakeflow, where the result of a query is persisted and refreshed on each pipeline update and can be incrementally refreshed when the defining query is incrementally computable [source 4][source 5].

questions.question: A pipeline contains a streaming table raw_events (created with CREATE STREAMING TABLE while reading continuously arriving files via Auto Loader) and a materialized view mv_events_hourly (a deterministic hourly aggregate over raw_events). The team currently runs a regular pipeline update. They propose switching to a full refresh of the pipeline in order to 'pick up the new files more quickly.' Explain precisely what a full refresh does to the streaming table and to the materialized view, how this differs from a normal pipeline update, and why the proposal is misguided. Then also reject the following distractor in your own words: 'A full refresh only re-ingests new source rows for a streaming table, leaving previously processed data untouched.'
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100% total): (1) Correctly defines a regular pipeline update — it processes only new data, i.e. each update consumes only data that has not been processed before, with the streaming table using checkpoints to track source offsets already consumed — 30%. (2) Correctly defines a full refresh — it clears the dataset's existing data and recomputes/reprocesses the dataset from the source definition (for the streaming table this means reprocessing the full history rather than only new rows; for the materialized view it means recomputing the entire defining query, even if that query is incrementally computable) — 30%. (3) Explicitly rejects the distractor: a streaming table's native semantics are append-only and it uses checkpoints to track source offsets, so a full refresh resets/ignores that incremental state and reprocesses source data rather than merely appending new rows; the claim that 'previously processed data is untouched' is false — 25%. (4) Clarity, correct use of Databricks terminology (streaming table, materialized view, Auto Loader, checkpoint, pipeline update, full refresh), and a coherent conclusion explaining why full refresh is more expensive and unnecessary for simply 'picking up new files' — 15%. Award no credit for answers that claim a full refresh only affects the materialized view, or that conflate full refresh with a normal incremental update.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. A regular pipeline update runs the pipeline graph and processes only new data: a streaming table is incremental and append-only, and each pipeline update consumes only data that has not been processed before. The engine uses checkpoints, stored alongside the Delta Lake table, to track the source offsets already consumed, which is what enables incremental reads and restart-from-failure. So newly landed files are picked up automatically by a normal update; there is no need for a full refresh to 'pick up new files.' A full refresh is a different operation: instead of advancing incrementally from the last checkpoint, it clears the dataset's existing contents and recomputes the dataset from its definition over the available source data. For the streaming table raw_events this means reprocessing the full history rather than only the new rows — the checkpoint state is effectively reset for that dataset. For mv_events_hourly, the materialized view is recomputed from its defining query; because the query is a deterministic hourly aggregate it is incrementally computable under a normal update, but a full refresh recomputes the entire query anyway. The distractor must be rejected: the statement that a full refresh 'only re-ingests new source rows for a streaming table, leaving previously processed data untouched' confuses a full refresh with an ordinary incremental update. Streaming tables are append-only by native semantics and rely on checkpoints to know which source offsets were already consumed; a full refresh discards that incremental position and reprocesses data from the source, so previously processed data is not left untouched. The proposal is misguided because it trades a cheap incremental update for an expensive full recomputation while delivering something a normal update already does. This aligns with the framework's role: because the pipeline is declarative, the engine builds a dependency graph from your definitions and determines the execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures [source 5], and Lakeflow provides native support for streaming tables and incrementally updated materialized views [source 4].

scenes.title: Controlling Refresh: Updates, Full Refresh, and Incremental Processing

elements.content: Controlling Refresh: Updates, Full Refresh & Incremental Processing
Objective: control refresh behavior and incremental processing per dataset type. [source 1][source 2]
A. What a Pipeline Update Processes
New data available
Definition changed
Full refresh requested
A pipeline update processes each such dataset plus every dataset that depends on it. [source 5]
Worked example: files land hourly; 3 of 10 datasets get new data → 3 process incrementally, 7 skip.

actions.text: Now that you've been selecting dataset types, the next question is a refresh question: when a pipeline run actually happens, what gets reprocessed? This page is all about controlling refresh behavior and incremental processing — and it's one of the more heavily tested topics.

The objective here is precise: you should be able to control refresh behavior and describe incremental processing for each dataset type. So we'll look at three things — what a pipeline update decides to process, when a full refresh is actually warranted, and how the refresh policy interacts with streaming tables versus materialized views.
Let's start with part A: what a pipeline update processes. Think of a pipeline update as a decision procedure — it walks the graph and asks, for each dataset, do I need to run you on this trigger?

There are three triggers that cause a dataset to be processed. First, new data is available at the source. Second, the dataset's definition changed — you edited the query or logic. Third, a full refresh was explicitly requested on it. Notice these are yes-or-no conditions, not a priority ranking.

Here's the part people forget on the exam: a pipeline update processes each dataset that meets one of those three conditions, plus every dataset that depends on it downstream. So marking one table for processing can cascade through the whole graph below it.

Quick worked example: files land hourly, and only three of your ten datasets have new data. The update processes those three — and anything that reads from them. The other seven are untouched, so you're not paying to recompute work that didn't change. That cost avoidance is exactly why incremental processing matters.

Remember the key distinction: a normal update is incremental and selective, while a full refresh clears the selected dataset and its dependents and reprocesses everything from source. Reserve full refreshes for backfills, logic corrections, and unrecoverable schema changes — and watch the trap that a full refresh on a streaming table can replay the entire available source history, which is not equivalent to an incremental update. Let's check your understanding on the next page.

scenes.title: Choosing a Refresh Strategy Under Cost and Latency Constraints

elements.content: Decision — You are the data platform lead for a retail analytics team. A 2-billion-row sales history table must power a BI dashboard that carries a 4-hour freshness SLA (service level agreement: the maximum permitted age of the data shown on the dashboard at any time). The team has a strict monthly compute budget that rules out reprocessing the entire two-billion-row history every 15 minutes, and the pipeline must also support scheduled replays of history during a nightly backfill window and survive schema changes. The hard part is that three design dimensions pull in different directions: data volume (2 billion rows), update frequency (continuous operational events), and the cost of every pipeline update must satisfy the freshness SLA without exceeding the budget, while still leaving a path to replay or backfill history. Prior lessons in this unit established that a declarative pipeline produces exactly three dataset types, and the type is fixed by the declaration you write: streaming tables are incremental and append-only, materialized views persist the result of a query and refresh on each pipeline update, and views store nothing [source 5][source 4][source 3].

Constraints — 4-hour freshness SLA on the dashboard — the served aggregate may never be older than 4 hours.  •  Monthly compute budget rules out full reprocessing of the 2-billion-row history every 15 minutes.  •  The pipeline must support replays and backfills of history on demand (a full refresh is allowed only for backfills and schema changes).  •  The team may declare only the three dataset types available in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines (streaming table, materialized view, view); no hand-rolled incremental orchestration outside the declarative build [source 5][source 3].  •  Applying updates and deletes to ingestion must use AUTO CDC (APPLY CHANGES), not a hand-written MERGE into a streaming table.

Option A: Streaming table ingestion + incrementally refreshed materialized view for the aggregate
+ The ingestion edge is append-only and consumes only data not processed before, so each pipeline update reads a small slice of new events rather than the full 2-billion-row history [source 5].; + The serving materialized view is incrementally refreshed when its defining aggregation is incrementally computable, so steady-state cost scales with new data, not with total table size [source 4].; + Explicitly leaves full refresh available for backfills and schema changes, which is the exact escape hatch the constraints require.
− More moving parts than a single full-refresh job: you must reason about checkpoint state and about which operations are incrementally computable.; − The materialized view is append-only through the streaming edge; applying updates and deletes requires AUTO CDC (APPLY CHANGES) to be inserted correctly, which adds schema and correctness work [source 5].; − Incremental refresh can silently degrade to a full recompute if the defining query stops being incrementally computable, so the pipeline needs monitoring and event logging [source 1][source 2].
Best for: A high-volume, continuously updated source that must meet a freshness SLA on a fixed compute budget while retaining a backfill path.

Option B: Full-refresh materialized view every 15 minutes
+ Simplest model to reason about: every refresh defines the truth from scratch, so correctness reasoning does not depend on checkpoint state.; + No ingestion-edge streaming semantics to reconcile — the pipeline is almost entirely a single materialized view declaration [source 3].
− Recomputes the full 2-billion-row history on every pipeline update, which directly violates the monthly compute budget constraint.; − The freshness benefit of 15-minute refresh is mostly wasted because the SLA only requires 4 hours — the extra frequency buys nothing the SLA asks for.; − Backfills and schema changes are handled, but the cost model is the worst of the three under this constraint set.
Best for: Small or medium tables where full recompute is cheap and simplicity outranks cost; in this scenario it is ruled out by the budget.

Option C: Plain view over the streaming table, queried directly by BI
+ Zero storage and zero pipeline-update cost: a view stores nothing, so no materialization is charged [source 5].; + Always reflects the latest available data at query time, which superficially matches the 4-hour freshness SLA.
− All compute is pushed to query time with no caching, so every BI interaction re-aggregates the two-billion-row history — the exact cost pattern the budget forbids, just moved from the pipeline to the BI layer.; − No persisted aggregate means no way to guarantee the dashboard's 4-hour freshness SLA against query latency or contention; the SLA depends on query-time behaviour you do not control.; − No materialization also weakens lineage, monitoring, and data-quality enforcement hooks that the declarative framework provides for persisted datasets [source 1][source 2].
Best for: Ad-hoc exploration on small to medium datasets where freshness is irrelevant and repeated scans are acceptable; unsuitable here.

Recommendation: Option A: Streaming table ingestion + incrementally refreshed materialized view for the aggregate — Option A is the only design that satisfies all stated constraints at once. The 4-hour freshness SLA and the budget cap are simultaneously met because each pipeline update consumes only data not processed before, so steady-state cost scales with new events rather than with the 2-billion-row history [source 5][source 4]. Option B is ruled out directly by the budget constraint: it reprocesses the full two-billion-row history every 15 minutes, which is the exact cost pattern the constraint forbids. Option C is ruled out because it moves the same total compute to query time with no caching, so it cannot guarantee a 4-hour SLA and offers no persisted aggregate to monitor. Option A additionally preserves the required backfill path: the incremental design can be full-refreshed on demand for history replays and schema changes, and updates and deletes on ingestion are handled by AUTO CDC (APPLY CHANGES) rather than a hand-written MERGE, which is what the declarative framework expects [source 5][source 3]. The residual risks — checkpoint correctness, incremental computability of the serving aggregation, and silent degradation to full recompute — are operational monitoring problems handled by pipeline event logging, not design blockers [source 1][source 2].

actions.text: Now let's apply everything we just covered about refresh behavior to a realistic constrained decision. You are the data platform lead for a retail company, and you've been handed a two-billion-row sales history, a dashboard that must be no more than four hours stale, and a monthly compute budget that simply won't tolerate reprocessing the entire history again and again. Your job is to pick a refresh strategy that satisfies all three at once.

Before we look at any design, let's nail down the constraints, because in an exam these are the facts that eliminate wrong answers. We have four hours of freshness tolerance on the dashboard — that's the latency ceiling. We have a hard monthly compute budget. And that budget rules out one very tempting but very expensive option: reprocessing the whole two-billion-row table every fifteen minutes. Notice how the freshness SLA and the cost ceiling pull in opposite directions.

Option A proposes streaming table ingestion at the edge — that's incremental, append-only capture of only the new records — feeding an incrementally refreshed materialized view, which is a precomputed result that the engine updates by processing only what changed, rather than rebuilding from scratch. This gives us the lowest steady-state cost and the best latency, because we never touch the old two billion rows again.

Option B is the simplest to reason about: a full-refresh materialized view every fifteen minutes. There's no incremental logic to debug, but the catch is brutal — every single update recomputes the entire two-billion-row history. That's the option our budget already disqualified.

Option C is a plain VIEW over the streaming table, queried directly by BI. A view stores nothing and caches nothing, so every dashboard load pushes all the work to query time. Cheap on storage, expensive and unpredictable on every read — and it doesn't fit a shared dashboard.

So our recommendation is Option A. Five decision dimensions drove it: data volume, update frequency, freshness SLA, cost per pipeline update, and the need to replay or backfill history. Option A wins on all of them, while we reserve full refresh for the rare cases that genuinely require it — backfills and schema changes. That distinction — incremental for the steady state, full refresh only for backfills and schema changes — is exactly the kind of nuance the exam likes to test.

scenes.title: Lesson Assessment: Selecting and Refreshing Datasets

questions.question: A Lakeflow declarative pipeline must continuously ingest JSON order files that arrive in cloud storage without reprocessing history, and a downstream daily revenue aggregate must be served to BI. Using the interactive decision tree and the worked ingestion-to-serving example, which pair of declarations correctly classifies the ingestion hop and the serving hop?

options.label: CREATE STREAMING TABLE raw_orders AS SELECT ... FROM STREAM read_files(...); CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS SELECT date_trunc('day', order_ts) AS day, sum(amount) FROM raw_orders GROUP BY 1
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW raw_orders AS SELECT ... FROM read_files(...); CREATE STREAMING TABLE daily_revenue AS SELECT date_trunc('day', order_ts) AS day, sum(amount) FROM raw_orders GROUP BY 1
CREATE VIEW raw_orders AS SELECT ... FROM read_files(...); CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS SELECT date_trunc('day', order_ts) AS day, sum(amount) FROM raw_orders GROUP BY 1
CREATE STREAMING TABLE raw_orders AS SELECT ... FROM raw_orders; CREATE STREAMING TABLE daily_revenue AS SELECT date_trunc('day', order_ts) AS day, sum(amount) FROM raw_orders GROUP BY 1

questions.analysis: The ingestion hop is continuous file arrival, which the decision tree classifies as a streaming table declared with CREATE STREAMING TABLE over STREAM read_files(...), i.e. Auto Loader; the serving hop is a grouped aggregation over an existing table, which is a materialized view declared with CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW [source 5]. A materialized view persists the result of a query and refreshes it during a pipeline update, and it can be incrementally refreshed when the defining query is incrementally computable, so the daily aggregate does not reprocess all history on every update [source 4]. Option B swaps the types and fails because a materialized view is not the continuous append-only ingestion primitive, and a streaming table is append-only rather than a grouped aggregation result. Option C misuses a plain view, which is not the persisted, refresh-managed serving dataset. Option D declares a streaming table that reads from itself, which cannot resolve to a real source and does not address the file-arrival requirement.

questions.question: Which statements about incremental update behavior versus full refresh behavior for streaming tables and materialized views are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A streaming table processes only data that has not been processed before on each pipeline update, unless a full refresh is explicitly requested.
A materialized view is not recomputed from scratch on every update when its defining query is incrementally computable.
A streaming table natively applies updates and deletes to existing rows without AUTO CDC or APPLY CHANGES.
A materialized view always recomputes its entire result from scratch on every pipeline update regardless of the query.
Checkpoints let a streaming table track source offsets already consumed, enabling incremental reads and restart-from-failure.

questions.analysis: Streaming tables are incremental and append-only: each pipeline update consumes only unprocessed data unless a full refresh is requested, and Delta Lake-backed checkpoints record consumed source offsets so incremental reads and failure recovery work [source 4]. Materialized views persist a query result and refresh on each pipeline update, but they are incrementally refreshed when the defining query is incrementally computable rather than always recomputed in full [source 5]. Option C is a documented exam trap: streaming tables do not apply updates and deletes natively; you must use AUTO CDC (APPLY CHANGES) in Python or APPLY CHANGES INTO in SQL. Option D is the mirror-image trap stating materialized views always recompute in full, which contradicts incremental refresh. Option E correctly states the checkpoint role in incremental processing and fault recovery.

questions.question: A materialized view is defined over existing Delta tables. Which query characteristics prevent the materialized view from being incrementally refreshed and force a full recomputation on pipeline update? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The query uses a non-deterministic expression such as current_timestamp() in a way that depends on the run time.
The query performs an aggregation with GROUP BY over append-only source tables, such as sum(amount) grouped by day.
The query filters source rows using a window function whose result depends on the full partition, such as row_number() over an unbounded window.
The query returns a simple projection and filter over an append-only source table, such as SELECT id, amount FROM raw_orders WHERE amount > 0.
The query joins two source tables in a way that cannot be computed incrementally from only the newly arrived rows.

questions.analysis: Incremental refresh is possible only when the defining query is incrementally computable. Non-deterministic expressions that depend on run time, window functions whose results depend on full-partition state, and joins that cannot be derived from only newly arrived rows all break incrementality and force a full recomputation [source 5][source 4]. By contrast, a grouped aggregation over append-only sources (option B) and a simple projection and filter over an append-only source (option D) are classic incrementally computable patterns, so they do not prevent incremental refresh. This distinguishes the correct understanding from the distractor that a materialized view always recomputes in full.

questions.question: A pipeline ingests a continuous stream of change events, applies updates and deletes to maintain current state, and serves a daily revenue aggregate to BI. In exam-objective terms, explain which dataset type you declare for each hop, why the alternative fails, and why the answer must not rely on the traps that views cache results, streaming tables natively handle deletes, or materialized views always recompute in full. Cite specific framework behavior in your justification.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Ingestion hop declared as CREATE STREAMING TABLE with Auto Loader/read_files over the continuous source, justified as incremental append-only ingestion — 30%. (2) CDC hop using AUTO CDC / APPLY CHANGES (SQL: APPLY CHANGES INTO) rather than hand-written MERGE into a streaming table, since streaming tables are natively append-only — 30%. (3) Serving hop declared as CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW for the grouped daily revenue query, noting it persists and refreshes each pipeline update and can be incrementally refreshed when incrementally computable — 25%. (4) Explicitly rejects the three exam traps: views do not cache results, streaming tables do not natively handle deletes, and materialized views do not always recompute in full — 15%.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: the ingestion hop is a streaming table because continuous file or event arrival maps to incremental, append-only processing via CREATE STREAMING TABLE over STREAM read_files(...) (Auto Loader), with checkpoints tracking consumed offsets [source 4]. Applying updates and deletes requires AUTO CDC (APPLY CHANGES) in Python or APPLY CHANGES INTO in SQL because streaming tables are append-only by native semantics. The serving hop is a materialized view declared with CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW; it persists the query result and refreshes on each pipeline update, and it is incrementally refreshed when the defining query is incrementally computable [source 5]. A declarative pipeline produces these dataset types and the declarative engine builds the dependency graph, determines execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures [source 5]. The three traps are rejected because views do not cache results, streaming tables do not apply updates and deletes natively without AUTO CDC / APPLY CHANGES, and materialized views are not always recomputed in full when their query is incrementally computable.
