scenes.title: Why Declarative Pipelines Need Expectations

elements.content: Why Declarative Pipelines Need Expectations

In a Lakeflow declarative pipeline you declare data quality expectations alongside the transformations, and the framework enforces them, quarantining or dropping bad records according to your rules [source 5].

The engine builds a dependency graph from your definitions, decides execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures [source 5].

Declared, not validated after load

An expectation is a named constraint attached to a dataset; it is evaluated on every pipeline update.

Definitions and rules travel in the same file, so the engine — not a human scheduler — chooses order and incremental steps [source 1].

Precondition: only declared on a dataset (streaming table or materialized view), never on a bare SELECT.

Edge case: evaluating each update means a transient early failure can be re-checked on the next update rather than baked into the output.

One declaration, three actions

warn — keep the record, log the violation.

drop — discard the bad record, continue the update.

fail — stop the update; the dataset does not advance.

Example: CONSTRAINT amount_not_null EXPECT (amount IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW.

Exam trap: expectations are not a replacement for pipeline modes or triggers — they only govern what happens to an invalid record.

Sample update: 10,000 records in the raw stream; validation drops 400 records (expectation on amount), 9,600 records reach the target — warn would have kept all 10,000 and logged 400 violations [source 5].
Sources: [source 5] expectations enforce quarantine/drop; [source 3] declarative framework for batch and streaming; [source 1] dependency graph and expectations module.

actions.text: We've covered streaming tables and materialized views, so now let's tackle the question that trips up a lot of candidates: why do declarative pipelines need expectations at all? Let's frame the problem first.

In a Lakeflow declarative pipeline, you declare datasets — not the procedural steps that build them. That means the platform decides how to read, transform, and write your data. So if you never look at the records yourself, where does data quality control fit in?

That's the gap expectations fill. Quality is declared, not validated after the load. An expectation is a named constraint attached to a dataset, and the engine evaluates it on every pipeline update. Contrast that with the imperative habit of loading first and then running a separate validation query — by then, bad records are already in your table.

One declaration maps to three possible actions: warn keeps the record and flags it, drop discards the record, and fail stops the update entirely. Remember this as one line of code, three distinct outcomes — and the outcome you choose is a business decision, not a technical one.

Now look at this bar chart. For one sample update we plot three bars: records in the raw stream, records that passed validation, and records dropped or failed. Read the gap between the first two bars — that gap is your invalidity rate, and it's exactly the number you'd monitor on a production pipeline.

Concretely: 10,000 records arrived in the raw stream, and validation passed a large majority. The remainder is where your expectation action decided their fate. If those had been warn, they'd still be loaded and merely counted. If drop, they'd be silently gone. If fail, the whole update would have halted.

Before we move on, lock in the exam trap shown here. Expectations enforce quarantine rules on records — they do not replace pipeline modes or triggers, and they don't govern when a pipeline runs. Modes and triggers decide when; expectations decide what happens to invalid rows. Mixing those up is a classic distractor. Next up, we'll look at the actual SQL and Python syntax for declaring expectations.

scenes.title: Expectation Syntax: SQL and Python

elements.content: Expectation Syntax: SQL and Python

Every expectation is declared alongside the transformation and enforced by the framework, which quarantines or drops bad records according to your rules [source 5]. Expectations are attached at the dataset level, so the same dataset can carry several of them.

SQL — CONSTRAINT … EXPECT … ON VIOLATION

CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW; omitting ON VIOLATION means warn only.

Python — decorators on the dataset

Use @dp.expect("valid_email", "email RLIKE '^[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@'") to warn, @dp.expect_or_drop for row-level removal, and @dp.expect_or_fail to abort.

Worked example: a 1,000-row batch contains 40 rows with a NULL order_id. With warn-only, all 1,000 rows are kept and the violation count is logged; with ON VIOLATION DROP ROW or @dp.expect_or_drop, the 40 offending rows are dropped and exactly 960 reach the target.

Expectations sit on streaming tables and materialized views alike, and they are evaluated on every pipeline update rather than once at definition time. Lakeflow ships native support for declarative data quality expectations alongside streaming tables, incrementally updated materialized views, and automated CDC [source 4].
Exam trap: expect_or_drop removes only the violating rows in this dataset — it never deletes rows from upstream tables — and expect_or_fail aborts the entire pipeline update, not just the bad rows.

actions.text: Now let's get concrete about the syntax. Databricks gives you two ways to declare an expectation, and both express the same idea: a name, a condition, and what to do when the condition is violated. First we'll walk the SQL path, then the Python path.

The unifying idea first: every expectation is declared alongside the transformation that produces the dataset, not in some separate validation script. That's what makes these declarative — the rule travels with the dataset definition, and it's re-evaluated on every update.

In SQL, you add a CONSTRAINT clause to your dataset definition. Here we write CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT, followed by the boolean expression order_id IS NOT NULL. Then ON VIOLATION DROP ROW tells the pipeline what to do with the bad records. And note this carefully, because the exam loves it: if you omit the ON VIOLATION clause entirely, the default is warn only — the rows still flow through, you just get logged metrics.

In Python, the same concept is expressed with decorators on the dataset function. Plain @dp.expect takes a name and a condition — that's the warn-only behaviour. @dp.expect_or_drop removes the violating rows before they land. And @dp.expect_or_fail aborts the entire update. So the decorator you choose is exactly the violation action you're selecting.

A couple of scoping facts while we're here. Expectations are attached at the dataset level, and a single dataset can carry many of them. They're evaluated per update — and that holds equally for streaming tables and materialized views, so you don't need a separate mental model for each.

Let's make it concrete with the worked example on the slide. A batch of one thousand rows contains forty that fail an expectation. With expect_or_drop, you keep nine hundred and sixty rows and forty are discarded. With plain expect, all one thousand land and you simply recorded forty violations — do the arithmetic before you answer.

Finally, the exam trap. expect_or_drop removes only the violating rows from the dataset being written — it does not reach upstream and delete rows from the source tables. And expect_or_fail doesn't drop anything at all: it aborts the entire update. Keep those two straight, and you'll handle most of the expectation questions you'll see.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Expectation Actions

questions.question: In a Lakeflow declarative pipeline, you want a data quality expectation that flags every record violating the rule while still writing ALL records (both good and bad) to the target table, so downstream engineers can inspect the failures. Which keyword or decorator on the expectation produces this warn-only behavior?

options.label: expect_or_fail(...) — the expectation that aborts the update on any violation
expect(...) — the default expectation that records the violation in metrics without removing the record
expect_or_drop(...) — the expectation that silently removes the violating rows
ON VIOLATION WARN — a mandatory clause that must follow every expectation keyword

questions.analysis: A bare expectation — expect(...) in Python, or CONSTRAINT <name> EXPECT (<expr>) with no ON VIOLATION clause in SQL — produces warn-only behavior: the pipeline still completes, every record (including violators) reaches the target, and the violation count is emitted in the expectation metrics. This is the mechanism by which declarative pipelines let you observe data quality problems without blocking ingestion, consistent with the framework enforcing expectations while 'quarantining or dropping bad records according to your rules' [source 5]. Option A is wrong because expect_or_fail escalates a violation into a pipeline failure rather than warning. Option C is wrong because expect_or_drop physically removes violating rows, which contradicts the requirement of keeping all records. Option D is wrong because ON VIOLATION is optional syntax used to upgrade an expectation's severity; WARN is its default, and it is a clause, not a keyword that produces warn-only behavior by itself. Because Lakeflow manages expectations declaratively so the engine enforces them according to your rules [source 4], the correct recall pairing is: warn = plain expect / no ON VIOLATION clause.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguish the warn action, the drop action, and the fail action for Lakeflow data quality expectations? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Warn (plain expect, or EXPECT with no ON VIOLATION clause) forces ALL violating records to remain in the target table while incrementing the expectation's violation metrics.
Drop (expect_or_drop / ON VIOLATION DROP ROW) removes the violating rows from the target but lets the pipeline update finish successfully.
Fail (expect_or_fail / ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE) aborts the entire pipeline update the moment a violating record is encountered, rather than failing only that record.
Writing an expectation keyword without any ON VIOLATION clause is a syntax error because ON VIOLATION is mandatory.

questions.analysis: Options A, B, and C are all correct. A: warn is the default only when no escalation clause is present — the violating rows survive and are merely counted, which is the mechanism the framework uses when it does not quarantine or drop records [source 5]. B: drop removes the offending rows from the target table but still completes the update, matching the framework's ability to quarantine or drop bad records according to your rules [source 5]. C: fail throws an error that terminates the whole update — the trap distractor. Students often assume expect_or_fail fails only the violating record, analogous to a row-level quarantine; in reality it fails the entire pipeline update, so every downstream dataset in that update is blocked. Option D is the syntax-error misconception: ON VIOLATION is NOT mandatory. Omitting it produces warn-only behavior, so its absence is valid syntax rather than an error. This is why the earlier checkpoint distinguished 'a syntax error (missing ON VIOLATION)' from a deliberate warn action. Because Lakeflow provides declarative data quality expectations as a first-class framework feature [source 4], you should reason about each keyword by its escalation semantics, not by assuming any clause is required.

actions.text: Time for a quick checkpoint on expectation actions. This one's about recalling which keyword or decorator produces which behavior, so read each option carefully and take a shot at every question on your own.
Give it your best attempt — I'll be right here after you submit to walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Warn vs Drop vs Fail: Choosing the Action

elements.content: Dimension  |  WARN  |  DROP  |  FAIL

SQL keyword and Python decorator syntax
WARN: In SQL you attach the expectation as a named constraint on the output dataset using the WARN form (for example, CONSTRAINT valid_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION WARN, or the legacy EXPECT ... WARN clause); in Python you decorate the pipeline dataset function with @dp.expect('valid_amount', 'amount > 0') so violations are counted but never removed.
DROP: In SQL the clause becomes CONSTRAINT valid_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION DROP (historically EXPECT ... DROP); in Python the equivalent is @dp.expect_or_drop('valid_amount', 'amount > 0'), which is a distinct decorator from the warn variant because the violation-handling behavior is baked into the decorator name.
FAIL: In SQL the clause becomes CONSTRAINT valid_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE (historically EXPECT ... FAIL); in Python the equivalent is @dp.expect_or_fail('valid_amount', 'amount > 0'), and the FAIL semantics apply to the pipeline update as a whole, not to a single row.

Effect on the violating record
WARN: The violating record is retained unchanged in the target dataset and written to the output exactly like every conforming row; only a counter and an event-log entry are incremented, so a WARN expectation never alters the data itself.
DROP: The violating record is removed from the target dataset before it is written (quarantined at the dataset boundary, not stored in a separate quarantine table by default), which silently reduces the row count of that dataset relative to its input.
FAIL: The violating record is not removed and no partial result is committed; instead the entire pipeline update is aborted, so no rows from the violating dataset are written at all in that update.

Effect on the update / transaction outcome
WARN: The pipeline update completes successfully and commits all data, because WARN never raises a data-quality error; success is reported even when violations occurred, which is why it is the right choice when you only want to observe quality before enforcing it [source 1][source 2].
DROP: The pipeline update also completes successfully and commits, just with fewer rows than were read; DROP therefore preserves pipeline continuity and does not block the schedule, since the engine treats removal as normal processing rather than a failure [source 5].
FAIL: The pipeline update fails and does not commit the affected dataset, blocking the schedule until the data or the rule is fixed; this is the hard gate that protects downstream consumers at the cost of pipeline availability [source 5].

Effect on downstream tables
WARN: Downstream tables receive every row, including bad ones, so an aggregation such as SUM(amount) can be inflated or skewed by values the expectation flagged; because nothing is blocked, bad data propagates all the way to serving layers.
DROP: Downstream tables receive only surviving rows, so aggregates are computed on a reduced population; because the same rule is applied consistently, downstream results are internally consistent, but they are silently biased toward the records that passed.
FAIL: Downstream tables receive no new data at all from the violating dataset, because the update aborts; they stay on the last good version of their input, which protects them from corruption but can leave them stale if failures are frequent.

Typical use case
WARN: Use WARN for monitoring before enforcement: when you are rolling out a new expectation, want a baseline violation rate, or are diagnosing a source you do not yet control, and you must not disturb the pipeline schedule [source 2].
DROP: Use DROP when you need pipeline continuity plus a bounded blast radius: the bad rows are genuinely unusable (for example, malformed JSON that cannot be parsed into a typed column), but the rest of the batch must keep flowing.
FAIL: Use FAIL when correctness is contractual: a revenue figure, a regulatory report, or an SLA-backed metric that must never be computed from incomplete input, so stopping the update is preferable to publishing a wrong number [source 5].

Main risk / failure mode
WARN: The main risk is complacency: because the update always succeeds, a growing violation rate can go unnoticed unless you alert on the violation metrics recorded in the pipeline event log, and unmonitored WARN is effectively no quality control at all [source 1].
DROP: The main risk is silent volume loss: because DROP removes rows without failing, downstream aggregates drift over time and a slow leak in row counts can distort monthly totals or medallion-architecture KPIs long before anyone notices [source 5].
FAIL: The main risk is availability: a single bad batch or an over-tight rule can halt a production pipeline, and over-zealous FAIL rules have caused more outages in practice than bad data itself, since the failure blocks every dependent dataset in the graph.

Metric and audit visibility
WARN: WARN records a per-expectation violation count (and, in the event log, the number of rows that failed the condition) while keeping the data, so you can chart the violation rate over time to decide when to escalate to DROP or FAIL [source 1].
DROP: DROP records the same violation count as WARN, so the metric exists, but the metric reflects only the number of rows removed from the target dataset and, if not alerted on, the emitted count is the only evidence that data was dropped.
FAIL: FAIL records the violation and then aborts the update, so the strongest signal is the pipeline failure itself plus the event-log entry identifying the expectation that triggered it; recovery requires fixing the input or relaxing the rule and re-running the update.

Quarantine semantics (the exam trap)
WARN: WARN does not quarantine: the record stays in the target dataset and remains available to downstream readers, so it is not isolated from the rest of the data.
DROP: DROP is the only action that behaves like a quarantine: the record is excluded from the target dataset before it can reach consumers, which is functionally the same as holding it back from the output [source 5].
FAIL: FAIL does not quarantine either: the record is neither isolated nor written, because the whole update is rolled back, so no per-record state change is observable in the target dataset — only an update-level failure.

Interaction with pipeline refresh and incremental processing
WARN: Because WARN never drops or blocks rows, a subsequent pipeline update continues incrementally: only unprocessed data is consumed and each new batch adds its own violation counts, so the violation metric accumulates across updates unless you reset the dataset [source 1][source 2].
DROP: Because DROP removes rows before they are written, the checkpoint still advances past the input offsets, so the dropped records are never retried on the next incremental update; to recover them you must fix the rule and perform a full refresh of the affected dataset [source 5].
FAIL: Because FAIL aborts the update, the checkpoint does not advance past the failing batch, so the same input is reprocessed on the next run; this is intentional for correctness but means a persistent violation can wedge a pipeline indefinitely until the input or the rule changes.

Worked example: 10,000-row batch with a 2% violation rate
WARN: If 10,000 order rows arrive and 2% violate amount > 0, WARN writes all 10,000 rows and records 200 violations; a downstream SUM(amount) over the batch includes the 200 bad rows, and the daily revenue figure is overstated by whatever those rows carry.
DROP: Under the same 10,000-row / 2% input, DROP writes 9,800 rows and records 200 removals; the downstream aggregate is now computed over 9,800 rows, so revenue is understated by the value of the dropped orders — a 2% population loss that compounds across 30 daily batches into a systematic monthly distortion.
FAIL: Under the same input, FAIL writes 0 rows and aborts the update; the downstream table remains at its previous version, so the day’s revenue is missing entirely rather than wrong, which is the correct trade-off when the report is contractual but the wrong one when the 2% of bad rows are trivial.

Choosing under cost and latency constraints
WARN: WARN adds essentially no compute beyond the predicate evaluation and keeps every row, so it is the cheapest action per update and is the right default while you are still measuring whether a rule is worth enforcing.
DROP: DROP adds only the cost of filtering the violating rows out of the write path, so it is nearly as cheap as WARN, but it changes the dataset’s row count and therefore the semantics of every downstream incrementally refreshed materialized view built on top of it [source 4].
FAIL: FAIL may appear free per batch, but a single failure blocks the pipeline update and every dependent dataset, so its true cost includes re-runs and on-call time; use it only where the cost of a wrong downstream number exceeds the cost of a stalled pipeline [source 5].

Takeaway — Choose WARN when you are still measuring data quality or rolling out a new rule and cannot afford to disturb the schedule; it preserves all rows, records violation metrics, and lets you decide later whether to escalate to DROP or FAIL [source 1][source 2].

Takeaway — Choose DROP when bad records are genuinely unusable but the rest of the batch must keep flowing; it is the only action with quarantine-like semantics, but it silently reduces row counts, so alert on the drop metric to catch slow aggregate drift [source 5].

Takeaway — Choose FAIL when correctness is contractual and a wrong downstream number is worse than a stalled pipeline; it protects consumers by preventing any partial commit, at the cost of pipeline availability and re-runs.

Takeaway — The exam trap is conflating 'the update fails' with 'the record is quarantined': only DROP isolates the record from the target dataset; FAIL rolls back the whole update and WARN leaves the record in place, so neither of them quarantines anything.

actions.text: Now that you've attempted the checkpoint on expectation actions, let's lock in the decision itself. Everything on this page compares the three actions across the dimensions you must weigh in production. Start with the syntax row: WARN maps to the SQL keyword WARN and the Python decorator expect, DROP maps to DROP and drop, and FAIL maps to FAIL and fail. In Databricks declarative pipelines, the keyword in SQL and the decorator name in Python are what the certification tests, so memorize the pairing.

Next, the effect on the violating record. WARN keeps every row, including the bad ones, and simply tallies them into a metric. DROP removes the violating record from the result. FAIL rejects the entire update — not just the bad row. This single row is where most exam candidates slip, so read it carefully.

Then think about what each action does downstream. WARN lets everything through, so downstream tables inherit the questionable rows. DROP keeps the pipeline running but silently reduces volume — and that shrinkage can distort downstream aggregates if nobody is monitoring it. FAIL halts the update entirely, which protects downstream consumers at the cost of pipeline availability.

So how do you choose? WARN is what you reach for when you're still measuring — you want visibility before you start enforcing. DROP fits when you'd rather keep the pipeline flowing and the bad rows are clearly not valuable. FAIL is the hard gate you use when correctness is a contract and no bad data may ever reach consumers.

And here is the classic exam trap on this page. People conflate 'the update fails' with 'the record is quarantined' — they are not the same thing. Only DROP behaves like a quarantine: the bad record is pulled out and set aside while the rest proceed. FAIL does not quarantine anything; it blocks the whole update. Keep that distinction sharp in your head.

To summarize the three takeaways: choose WARN when you're still measuring and want metrics without stopping flow, choose DROP when bad records are genuinely disposable, and choose FAIL when correctness is a contract you cannot break. The trap is mixing up what 'the update fails' actually means. On the next page we'll write expectations for a real orders pipeline and match each action to its requirement.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Writing Expectations for an Orders Pipeline

elements.content: Problem 1

A retail platform streams order events into the raw table `raw_orders`, which has columns `order_id STRING`, `customer_email STRING`, `amount DECIMAL(10,2)`, and `order_ts TIMESTAMP`. You must declare a silver streaming table `silver_orders` with three data-quality expectations: (a) a row with a NULL `order_id` must be rejected; (b) a row whose `customer_email` does not contain an `@` must be dropped; (c) a negative `amount` must stop the update. One batch arrives with exactly these six rows:

1. `(O-1001, ana@example.com, 120.50)`

2. `(NULL, bob@example.com, 80.00)`

3. `(O-1003, not-an-email, 45.00)`

4. `(O-1004, carla@example.com, -250.00)`

5. `(O-1005, bogus-address, -10.00)`

6. `(O-1006, dan@example.com, 0.00)`

Write the SQL declaration, state the exact order of the `CONSTRAINT` clauses, and justify that order row by row.
Hint: Ask which row violates two rules at once — that row is what makes the ordering decision, not the single-rule rows.

Worked solution
Step 1 — choose the declaration. The source is a continuous stream, so the target is a streaming table, which is the dataset type for append-only ingestion hops in the declarative pipeline model [source 5].

```sql

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE silver_orders (

CONSTRAINT non_negative_amount EXPECT (amount >= 0) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE,

CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW,

CONSTRAINT valid_email EXPECT (customer_email RLIKE '@') ON VIOLATION DROP ROW

)

AS SELECT order_id, customer_email, amount, order_ts

FROM STREAM(raw_orders);

```

Step 2 — map each requirement to an action keyword. Requirement (a) and (b) are row-level noise, so they use `DROP ROW`; requirement (c) is a contract break, so it uses `FAIL UPDATE`. The three expectations are declared *inside the dataset definition*, which is what makes them declarative rather than a separate validation job: the framework enforces them, quarantining or dropping bad records according to your rules [source 5].

Step 3 — order the clauses by severity, most severe first. The engine evaluates the `CONSTRAINT` list in order and applies the action of the first violated expectation, so the list is an ordered decision procedure, not a set.

Step 4 — trace the batch under this ordering.

- Row 4 `(O-1004, -250.00)`: violates `non_negative_amount` first. The expectation list is ordered, so `FAIL UPDATE` fires: the update aborts and the offending record is surfaced for diagnosis. The dataset is not updated with that batch.

- Row 5 `(O-1005, bogus-address, -10.00)`: violates *both* `non_negative_amount` and `valid_email`. Because the fail-level rule is first, row 5 is reported as a money-contract break. This is exactly why the ordering matters.

- Row 2 `(NULL, 80.00)`: the first expectation passes (`80.00 >= 0`), the second fails → `DROP ROW`. The row is excluded from the target and counted in the expectation metric.

- Row 3 `(O-1003, not-an-email, 45.00)`: first passes, second passes, third fails → `DROP ROW`.

- Row 6 `(O-1006, 0.00)`: `0.00 >= 0` is TRUE, so it is retained. Zero is a valid amount under `>= 0`.

- Row 1 `(O-1001, 120.50)`: passes all three and is written.

Step 5 — state the outcome. In this batch the update aborts, so rows 1 and 6 are *not* committed either: `FAIL UPDATE` is not a row-level filter, it stops the update. Re-run the trace for the realistic case where the upstream refund bug is fixed and rows 4 and 5 never arrive: row 2 and row 3 are dropped, rows 1 and 6 land in `silver_orders`, and the two drops appear as failed-record counts on their expectations.

Step 6 — justify the relative order of the two drop rules. Swapping `valid_order_id` and `valid_email` changes nothing observable, because both actions are `DROP ROW` and a row that violates both is dropped either way. Order them cheap predicate first (`IS NOT NULL` before a regex) for scan cost and readability. The only order that has behavioural consequences is the fail-level rule relative to the drop rules.

Analysis — The method works because a Lakeflow pipeline is declarative: the engine builds the dependency graph from your definitions and determines execution order, incremental processing, and failure recovery, so the quality rules ride along with the definition rather than living in a separate script [source 5]. The exam-relevant insight is that severity and action are two separate decisions: `EXPECT (<predicate>)` alone means warn (keep the row, record the metric), `ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` filters the row out, and `ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE` aborts. Choosing the keyword is the design decision; ordering the list is the correctness detail.

Where students go wrong:

1. Writing `order_id <> ''` instead of `order_id IS NOT NULL`. For a NULL `order_id`, `<> ''` evaluates to NULL, not TRUE. A NULL expectation result is treated as a violation, so the row is dropped — the right outcome by accident, with the wrong predicate. `IS NOT NULL` is total: it always returns TRUE or FALSE.

2. Assuming `RLIKE '@'` is a real email validator. It is a coarse smoke test: it accepts `a@`, `@@`, and `x@y`. That is usually the correct trade-off, because a strict regex rejects rare but legal addresses and *increases* the drop rate. If you tighten it, use a character-class form: `RLIKE '^[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+[.][A-Za-z]{2,}$'`.

3. Forgetting that a NULL email makes `RLIKE` return NULL, which counts as a violation, so NULL-email rows are dropped by the email rule. That is defensible, but you must know it is happening — check the expectation's failed-record count rather than assuming the rule is inert.

4. Believing `FAIL UPDATE` drops only the bad row. It does not; it stops the update, so valid rows in the same batch are withheld. This is precisely the trade-off quantified in problem 3, and it is why `FAIL UPDATE` is reserved for contract breaks.

The pattern generalises to any ingestion-to-silver hop: one ordered constraint list per dataset, severity-ordered, with the fail-level rule first so a coincidental secondary violation can never mask it.
Problem 2

Re-express the three expectations from problem 1 using the Python declarative-pipeline API instead of SQL. Produce the full decorated function for `silver_orders`, state the exact API name used for each of the three actions, then fill in a mapping table with columns *rule*, *Python API*, *SQL equivalent*, and *record fate*. Finally, explain where the dropped rows' counts are visible after the update and why a Python `expect_or_fail` and a SQL `ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE` must not be mixed carelessly inside the same pipeline.
Hint: Two of the three decorators differ by a single word; the third returns a different object entirely because it does not drop rows.

Worked solution
Step 1 — import the pipeline module. The current import path is `pyspark.pipelines`; older code and older exam references use the alias `import dlt`. Both name the same decorator set, so read the import before judging a snippet.

Step 2 — write the function with one expectation per rule:

```python

from pyspark import pipelines as dp

@dp.table

def silver_orders():

return spark.readStream.table("raw_orders")

@dp.expect_or_fail("non_negative_amount", "amount >= 0")

@dp.expect_or_drop("valid_order_id", "order_id IS NOT NULL")

@dp.expect_or_drop("valid_email", "customer_email LIKE '%@%'")

def silver_orders():

return spark.readStream.table("raw_orders")

```

(The first block shows the bare dataset; the second is the final form. In practice you write only the second, with `@dp.table` outermost.)

Step 3 — name the APIs precisely. `expect_or_drop(name, condition)` excludes violating rows and records the failure. `expect_or_fail(name, condition)` aborts the update on a violation. `expect(name, condition)` is the third action: it keeps every row and records the violation as a metric — the shadow mode used in problem 5. Grouped variants exist (`expect_all_or_drop`, `expect_all_or_fail`) that take a dictionary of `{"name": "condition"}` pairs; use them when a whole family of rules shares one action.

Step 4 — the mapping table:

| Rule | Python API | SQL equivalent | Record fate |

|---|---|---|---|

| `amount >= 0` | `@dp.expect_or_fail("non_negative_amount", "amount >= 0")` | `CONSTRAINT non_negative_amount EXPECT (amount >= 0) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE` | Update aborts; no rows committed |

| `order_id IS NOT NULL` | `@dp.expect_or_drop("valid_order_id", "order_id IS NOT NULL")` | `CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` | Row excluded from target, counted as failed |

| `customer_email LIKE '%@%'` | `@dp.expect_or_drop("valid_email", "customer_email LIKE '%@%'")` | `CONSTRAINT valid_email EXPECT (customer_email RLIKE '@') ON VIOLATION DROP ROW` | Row excluded from target, counted as failed |

Step 5 — say where the counts appear. Passed and failed record counts per named expectation are written to pipeline event logging, which is the mechanism the course introduces for monitoring pipeline performance and health [source 1]. Practically: after a run, group the data-quality metrics by expectation name and dataset to see that, say, `valid_email` failed 2,400 records while `valid_order_id` failed 610. A rule whose failure count is permanently zero is dead weight; a rule whose failure count jumps is your incident signal.

Step 6 — the mixing caution. A single dataset should have one governing rule set. If the same dataset is declared once in Python with `expect_or_fail` and once in SQL with `DROP ROW`, you now have two definitions of one table — the pipeline graph cannot resolve that into one node, and which action wins becomes an ordering accident rather than a design decision. Choose one language per dataset, and if you need the explicit "first violated expectation wins" ordering, express the run of rules as an ordered SQL `CONSTRAINT` list.

Analysis — The declarative framework supports both SQL and Python for building batch and streaming pipelines, and native declarative data-quality expectations are available in both [source 3][source 4]. That symmetry is the point of this exercise: the *decision* (drop, fail, or warn) is a data-contract decision that is independent of the language, so you should be able to translate between the two without re-deciding anything.

Why the API names are what they are: `expect_or_drop` and `expect_or_fail` are named for the *consequence*, not the *condition*, which forces you to state what happens to a bad row at the moment you write the rule. Students who reach for a generic `expect` everywhere get no enforcement at all — the pipeline logs the violation and happily writes the bad row.

Common mistakes:

1. Using `@dp.expect` when the requirement says "reject". `expect` is warn-only; nothing is removed. The requirement wording ("reject", "must not be loaded", "stop") is the signal for which decorator to choose.

2. Writing the condition in the wrong dialect. Python expectations accept Spark SQL expression *strings*; `LIKE '%@%'` is Spark SQL syntax, not a Python `in` check. Passing a Python lambda works in some helper APIs but not in the declarative expectation string, and a lambda cannot be pushed to the engine.

3. Losing the uniqueness of the decoration target. `@dp.table` must wrap the final returned DataFrame; expectation decorators sit between the table decorator and the function. If you place `@dp.table` innermost by accident, the dataset is registered without its rules and the pipeline runs green with no enforcement.

4. Believing `expect_or_fail` fails only the offending partition. It fails the update flow, so a scheduled pipeline can burn every trigger of the day on the same single bad record — quantified in problem 4.

The generalisation: one dataset, one language, one ordered severity policy, and the expectation names treated as first-class monitoring identifiers that you can alert on. Treat the names as part of your schema contract, because dashboards and alerts bind to them.
Problem 3

The `silver_orders` pipeline lands 12,000,000 orders per day with an average order value of $68.40. An upstream release starts emitting refund events as negative amounts instead of as a separate refund record: 0.4% of daily rows are affected, and their amounts average -$120.00. Separately, 0.02% of rows carry malformed emails because one legacy integration writes them.

Design A drops negative amounts (`ON VIOLATION DROP ROW`). Design B fails on negative amounts (`ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE`) and drops malformed emails. For each design, compute the revenue figure that the `daily_revenue` materialized view publishes for one day, compute the error versus the true net figure, and quantify the quarterly error. Then justify the choice in terms of the pipeline graph and the freshness SLA.
Hint: A negative amount is money leaving the business; removing it does not remove its effect on the total — it removes the subtraction.

Worked solution
Step 1 — baseline gross revenue. $$12{,}000{,}000 \text{ rows} \times 68.40 = \$820{,}800{,}000 \text{ per day}$$ (As written without LaTeX: 12,000,000 * 68.40 = $820,800,000.)

Step 2 — size the negative-amount population. 0.4% of 12,000,000 = 48,000 rows. Total value of those rows = 48,000 * (-$120.00) = -$5,760,000 per day.

Step 3 — compute the true net figure. $$820{,}800{,}000 - 5{,}760{,}000 = \$815{,}040{,}000 \text{ per day}.$$

Step 4 — evaluate Design A. Dropping the 48,000 negative rows leaves the aggregate at $820,800,000. Reported minus true = 820,800,000 - 815,040,000 = +$5,760,000 overstated, which is 5,760,000 / 815,040,000 = 0.71% of the true net. Over a 90-day quarter that is 5,760,000 * 90 = $518,400,000 of overstated revenue. The pipeline runs green every day while the number is wrong.

Step 5 — evaluate Design B. The negative-amount row violates `non_negative_amount` and the update aborts. Because the pipeline is declarative, the engine builds the dependency graph from your definitions and handles execution order and failure recovery automatically [source 5]; `daily_revenue` depends on `silver_orders`, so an aborted upstream update means the downstream materialized view cannot refresh. The dashboard keeps yesterday's value, the freshness SLA is breached, and an alert fires. The failure is loud, attributable, and fixable at the source within the SLA window.

Step 6 — evaluate the email drop in the same units. 0.02% of 12,000,000 = 2,400 rows dropped per day. At $68.40 average they represent 2,400 * 68.40 = $164,160 per day of revenue that is silently unattributed — only 0.02% of the total, so the arithmetic is not the concern. The concern is bias: if all 2,400 come from the legacy integration, then that channel's revenue is not 0.02% short, it is 100% missing, and any per-channel comparison is invalid.

Step 7 — verdict. Negative amounts → `FAIL UPDATE`. Malformed emails → `DROP ROW`, with the failed-record count monitored per source system so a correlated drop is detected early.

Step 8 — the decision rule, stated generally. Fail when the violation is an upstream contract break whose silent handling biases a reported number (money, quantities, identity keys). Drop when the violation is independent row-level noise whose loss costs one row's value and does not systematically bias an aggregate.

Analysis — This is the core of the scene: `FAIL UPDATE` is not the "strict" option and `DROP ROW` is not the "lenient" option; they are tools for two different failure modes, and picking the lenient one here does not make the pipeline robust, it makes it *quietly wrong*.

The reasoning has three parts. First, the decision is about the *aggregate*, not about the row. A dropped malformed email removes one customer's $68 row from an attribution report — measurable, small, and arguably acceptable. A dropped negative amount removes a subtraction from a sum, so the aggregate is biased upward by the full magnitude of every dropped row, and the bias grows with the volume of the upstream bug rather than staying constant. Because the bug arrived with a release, it is systematic, not random, and it will not average out.

Second, the failure mode of `FAIL UPDATE` is visible; the failure mode of `DROP ROW` is not. A stopped update breaches the SLA, pages someone, and is resolved. An overstated revenue number is consumed by a forecast or a bonus calculation before anyone notices — detection can take a quarter.

Third, the blast radius must be priced. `FAIL UPDATE` withholds the valid rows in the same batch, and in a streaming pipeline the dependency graph propagates that stall to every downstream dataset, including the daily revenue materialized view [source 5]. At 12,000,000 rows/day you are choosing between one day of stale dashboard and roughly half a billion dollars of quarterly overstatement; the stale dashboard is the cheaper failure.

Edge cases and traps:

1. Zero amounts. `amount >= 0` admits 0.00. If zero is also a contract break (a free order should carry a promotion id), the predicate is `amount > 0` — but check the drop counts first, because free orders are usually legitimate.

2. Negative amounts that are legitimate. If refunds are modelled in the same column by design, `amount >= 0` is simply the wrong predicate, and no choice of action saves you. Fix the model: refunds belong in their own stream, and the expectation should encode the contract you actually have.

3. Assuming drops are free. A drop is a silent write of a nonzero failure count; if nobody reads the expectation metric, the drop is indistinguishable from a bug [source 1].

4. Regressing the whole pipeline to `FAIL UPDATE` after this exercise. The malformed-email rule would then stop the pipeline on a single record from a legacy integration — the pitfall quantified next.
Problem 4

A team reacts to problem 3 by declaring all 20 of its expectations with the fail action. The pipeline processes 12,000,000 rows per day, and each expectation is violated by 0.005% of rows. (a) Compute the probability that any individual row violates at least one of the 20 expectations, using the small-`p` approximation and then the exact value. (b) Compute the expected number of violating rows per update. (c) Compute the probability that a daily update completes without failing, and interpret it. (d) State the remediation and the monitoring that justifies it.
Hint: You are exponentiating a per-row probability over 12 million rows — use the Poisson limit rather than a 12-million-term product.

Worked solution
Step 1 — per-row, per-expectation violation probability. p = 0.005% = 0.00005.

Step 2 — probability a row violates at least one of 20 expectations. Treat violations as independent across expectations (an idealisation; correlated violations only make the result worse).

Approximation: 20 * p = 20 * 0.00005 = 0.001.

Exact: $$1 - (1-p)^{20} = 1 - (0.99995)^{20}.$$ Expanding: (0.99995)^20 = 1 - 20(0.00005) + 190(0.00005)^2 - ... = 1 - 0.001 + 0.000000475 = 0.999000475, so the per-row violation probability is 0.000999525, i.e. 0.09995% — the approximation 0.001 is accurate to about 5 parts in 10,000.

Step 3 — expected violating rows per update. 12,000,000 * 0.000999525 = 11,994.3, so roughly 12,000 bad rows per day, or ~500 per hour if the pipeline is triggered hourly.

Step 4 — probability of a clean run. $$P(\text{no violation}) = (1 - 0.000999525)^{12{,}000{,}000}.$$ Take logarithms: ln P = 12,000,000 * ln(0.999000475) = 12,000,000 * (-0.000999975) = -11,999.7. Therefore P = e^{-11,999.7}, roughly 10^{-5,211} — zero for any practical purpose.

Step 5 — interpret. The update does not fail occasionally; it fails essentially every run, and because the row-level checks are evaluated as data streams through the operator, the abort typically lands in the first micro-batch containing a bad row. The team's "strict" configuration therefore produces a pipeline that commits nothing, ever, while each individual rule is violated by only 5 rows in 100,000. The strictness bought no correctness for the money column and destroyed throughput for the other nineteen rules.

Step 6 — remediation. Demote nineteen rules to `DROP ROW` (for row-level noise) or warn-level `EXPECT` (for rules whose violation rate you have not yet measured), and keep `FAIL UPDATE` for the one or two rules that represent genuine contract breaks. Recompute the expected outcome: with one fail-level rule at p = 0.00005, the expected violating rows per day is 12,000,000 * 0.00005 = 600 per day. If that rule is the negative-amount rule from problem 3, 600 rows/day at -$120 is about -$72,000/day of real money, which is worth stopping for — the quantity justifies the strictness.

Step 7 — the justifying monitoring. Shadow-run each candidate rule at warn level, read its failed-record count from pipeline event logging [source 2], and promote only rules whose measured violation rate and business meaning justify a stop. The count, not the intent, decides the action.

Analysis — This problem makes the cost of strictness quantitative, and the mathematics has a clean shape: the probability that a *run* stays clean decays exponentially in the number of rows, so it is governed by `rows * rules * p` — the expected number of violating rows. When that product is well above 1, the run fails; the only way to bring it below 1 is to shrink the number of fail-level rules, shrink the row count (not possible), or shrink p at the source. Strictness is therefore budgeted, not maximised.

The Poisson/first-order step is the standard large-n, tiny-p approximation: `(1-p)^n = e^{-np}` when np is order 1 or larger. Students who try to multiply `0.999^12,000,000` by hand usually mis-handle the exponent; taking logarithms first is the reliable route.

Common mistakes:

1. Reporting the per-row probability (0.001) as the run failure probability. Off by six orders of magnitude in the exponent — the whole point.

2. Treating the expectations as one combined rule. Twenty rules each with a 0.005% violation rate is twenty times the exposure, which is why the failing rule count matters as much as the row count.

3. Assuming violations are anti-correlated so that a row "can only break one rule". In real data, a single upstream schema change breaks many rules at once on the same rows, so the true per-row violation probability is often *higher* than the independent calculation, and the pipeline fails even more reliably.

4. Remediating by lowering the check to warn everywhere and never promoting anything back. Warn-level rules with no promotion path are documentation, not enforcement; the promotion decision is the job.

5. Forgetting that `FAIL UPDATE` failures are retried by the pipeline. A continuously triggered pipeline can rediscover the same bad record every trigger, converting a data defect into a compute-cost incident.

The design rule to carry into the exam and into production: at most a small, explicitly argued set of fail-level rules per dataset, chosen because the violation represents a broken upstream contract; everything else drops or warns, with the failed-record metrics driving subsequent promotion decisions [source 2].
Problem 5

You want to add two rules to `silver_orders` without risking a production stoppage: (i) `currency_code` must be one of USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, CAD; (ii) `order_ts` must not be in the future. You are considering the predicate `order_ts <= current_timestamp()`. Write both constraints in their shadow (non-blocking) form, state what each action does to a violating row, give concrete promotion criteria with numbers assuming 12,000,000 rows/day, and explain why the wall-clock predicate is a defect in the rule itself.
Hint: The absence of an `ON VIOLATION` clause is itself the decision — it means warn, and warn means the row survives.

Worked solution
Step 1 — write the shadow declarations. Omit the `ON VIOLATION` clause entirely. That omission is the warn action: the row is retained and the violation is recorded as a metric.

```sql

CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE silver_orders (

CONSTRAINT valid_currency EXPECT (currency_code IN ('USD','EUR','GBP','JPY','CAD')),

CONSTRAINT order_ts_not_future EXPECT (order_ts <= current_timestamp())

)

AS SELECT order_id, customer_email, amount, currency_code, order_ts

FROM STREAM(raw_orders);

```

Step 2 — state what each action does to a violating row, in the three-action vocabulary. Warn: the row is written to the target and the expectation's failed-record count increments. `DROP ROW`: the row is not written and the count increments. `FAIL UPDATE`: the update aborts; no rows from that batch are written. Warn is the only action that changes nothing about the data while changing everything about the information you have, which is why it is the correct first phase for an unmeasured rule [source 5].

Step 3 — set promotion criteria before running, so the decision is not made emotionally at the end of the window. Measure over 7 days. At 12,000,000 rows/day the window contains 84,000,000 rows.

- Failed records = 0 across the window: the rule is always true on current data. Either keep it at warn as cheap regression detection, or delete it. Do not promote it to `DROP ROW`; a rule that has never fired is an untested code path, and promoting it adds only the risk of a future silent drop.

- 0 < failed < 0.01% of rows (fewer than 1,200/day, and randomly distributed across sources): promote to `DROP ROW`. The violations are row-level noise.

- failed >= 0.01% of rows (1,200/day or more), or failures concentrated in one source system: escalate to `FAIL UPDATE` and notify the source owner. A systematic violation is a broken contract, and the same argument as problem 3 applies — a correlated failure that is silently dropped biases every downstream aggregate.

- Any rule still failing after escalation while the source is blocked: keep warn, document it in the dataset definition as known-debt, and alert on the trend rather than the absolute count.

Step 4 — explain the wall-clock defect. `current_timestamp()` is non-deterministic. Consider one row with `order_ts = 2024-06-01 10:00`: today the predicate is TRUE and the row passes; on a full refresh run six months later it is still TRUE, so this particular rule looks stable — but consider the boundary case. A row arriving with a clock-skewed timestamp of "now + 4 seconds" passes when evaluated at t+10s and fails when the same batch is replayed. The predicate is evaluated against a different clock on every run, so the *same historical data* can produce different expectation outcomes on different runs. That breaks reproducibility: a full refresh of the pipeline — the operation you use for backfills and logic corrections — can suddenly fail on rows that were perfectly fine when they originally landed, and the failure is not reproducible from the data alone.

Step 5 — replace it with a deterministic bound. Use a value derived from the data or the batch, for example compare `order_ts` against the maximum timestamp present in the batch, or against a partition date carried in the file metadata, or simply assert a fixed sanity window such as `order_ts >= '2020-01-01' AND order_ts <= '2030-01-01'`. Deterministic predicates give the same answer on every replay.

Step 6 — flag the NULL edge case in the currency rule. For a NULL `currency_code`, `currency_code IN (...)` returns NULL, and a NULL expectation result counts as a violation, so NULL-currency rows are flagged by the warn rule. If the intent is “a missing currency is a violation,” write it explicitly as `currency_code IS NOT NULL AND currency_code IN ('USD','EUR','GBP','JPY','CAD')` so the rule documents its own intent and always returns TRUE or FALSE rather than NULL.

Analysis — Shadow deployment (warn) is the only honest way to introduce an expectation, because enforcement strength is a claim about data you have not yet measured. Declaring a rule at `DROP ROW` on day one asserts that you know the violation rate and that the business can absorb it; declaring it at warn asserts nothing and costs almost nothing, and the failed-record metric supplies the evidence for the promotion decision. This is why the course frames expectations as declarative data quality integrated into the pipeline rather than as validation bolted on afterwards [source 4].

Why the deterministic-predicate point matters beyond this rule: the pipeline model treats dataset definitions as reproducible computations, and the same engine that decides incremental processing and recovery depends on the definition producing the same result given the same input [source 5]. A wall-clock predicate injects hidden state (the current time) into the definition, which makes the dataset's output a function of *when* it ran as well as *what* it read — the same class of problem the course attributes to non-deterministic expressions in incrementally refreshed materialized views. Determinism is a property of the whole definition, not only of the columns.

Edge cases and traps:

1. Forgetting that `WARN` is spelled by omission. Learners often write `ON VIOLATION WARN` by analogy; the shadow form is the bare `EXPECT (predicate)`, and inventing keywords produces a syntax error.

2. Promoting a rule because it "looks important" rather than because the metric supports it. Promotion is an evidence-based decision with a numeric threshold, as in step 3.

3. Treating a zero-failure rule as proof of data quality. Zero failures over 84,000,000 rows usually means the predicate is trivially true, not that the data is clean; check that at least one historical sample would have failed the rule before trusting it.

4. Adding a rule at fail level directly to "save time". That is the pitfall from problem 4 with a new name: the first batch containing a violation stops the pipeline, and you learn the violation rate from an outage instead of from a metric.

5. Forgetting that `order_ts` rules often need a *source-specific* window. A single global upper bound may be correct for one integration and wrong for a batch integration that deliberately backdates records; scope the rule to the dataset where it is true rather than weakening it globally.

The generalisable workflow: draft the rule at warn level, attach a metric review to the 7-day window, promote to `DROP ROW` or `FAIL UPDATE` against a pre-agreed threshold, and keep the fail-level set deliberately small so that a failure always means something.

actions.text: Let's put the three expectation actions to work. Here's a fully worked problem: a retail platform streams order events into a raw orders table, and we need to write expectations that reject null order IDs, drop malformed emails, and fail on negative amounts. Then we'll justify the ordering — this is exactly the kind of scenario the exam hands you.

Read the requirement carefully and notice that it names three different actions for three different rule violations. The table is a streaming ingestion target with columns order_id, customer_email, amount, and order_ts. Each expectation must map to the right violation action — and the requirement is deliberately written so that guessing 'fail for everything' is wrong.

Before you read the solution, try the hint: ask which row would violate two rules at once. If a row has both a null order_id and a negative amount, what should happen to it? That thought experiment is what forces you to reason about ordering, not just syntax.

Now the SQL solution. We declare a CONSTRAINT valid_order_id with a predicate of order_id IS NOT NULL, and we set ON VIOLATION DROP ROW. Same pattern for valid_email: the predicate checks that customer_email matches the email pattern with RLIKE, and again we drop the row. Finally, non_negative_amount checks that amount is greater than or equal to zero, but this one uses ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE — the whole update aborts. Drop, drop, fail — three rules, two different failure semantics.

Why does this ordering work? Because a Lakeflow declarative pipeline evaluates expectations in declaration order and stops at the first failure action that aborts. By putting the cheap row-level drops first and the fail last, we filter obvious noise before we hit the one rule that must halt the pipeline. If a row is malformed, it never reaches the fail check — that's how you avoid a single bad record killing your whole refresh. The Python equivalent mirrors this with @dp.expect_or_drop for the first two and @dp.expect_or_fail for the amount rule, giving you the same semantics in a different syntax.

Problem 2 flips the perspective. Instead of writing the declaration, you're given three plain-English expectations and asked to re-express them in the declarative framework. This tests whether you can translate a business requirement into a predicate and pick the right action — the real exam skill.

The hint here is a gift: two of the three decorators differ by a single word. expect_or_drop and expect_or_fail look almost identical, and mixing them up is the most common mistake. Read each decorator name character by character — the action is baked into the name.

Step 1, you import the pipeline module — conventionally aliased as dp. Step 2, you decorate the dataset definition with the appropriate expect variant for each rule. The convention is to order them from most permissive to most strict, so drops come before fails. And note the pattern: the decorator name is the action, and the two string arguments are the rule name and the SQL predicate. That's the entire mental model.

The analysis point: the declarative framework supports both SQL and Python expression of the same expectation. What matters is that the semantics are identical — same predicate, same action, same result. You are free to choose the language your team maintains best, but you must be able to read both.
Problem 3 adds scale. This time you have a silver_orders pipeline that lands twelve million order rows, and you need to reason about the consequences of your action choices at that volume.

Here's the key insight the hint points to: a negative amount isn't a bad row, it's money leaving the business. That's a semantic signal, not noise. Treating it as row-level garbage would silently corrupt your revenue reporting.

This is the heart of the scene: FAIL UPDATE. When you fail on negative amounts, the pipeline stops and forces a human to look upstream. That's intentional. Drops absorb the noise; fails surface a contract break you cannot safely swallow. The exam will test whether you can distinguish these two reasons for using fail instead of drop.

Problem 4 is the trap scenario. A team reacts to the previous problem by declaring all twenty of their expectations as expect_or_fail. The hint warns you not to exponentiate a per-row probability — a rule that fails on any single row, multiplied across millions of rows, has an almost certain chance of halting the pipeline.

The worked solution lays out per-row, per-expectation violation math. If each rule has even a tiny chance of a single bad row, the probability that at least one rule fires approaches one as row count grows. Strictness is not free — every fail you add is another reason the pipeline will stop, and at scale that cost compounds fast.

The takeaway: choose the failure action based on the meaning of the violation, not on how strongly you feel about data quality. Fails belong on contract breaks; drops belong on row-level noise. Making everything fail is a fragility anti-pattern.

Finally, problem 5 asks: how do you add two new rules to silver_orders without breaking the existing pipeline? This is the production rollout question — you can't just ship stricter rules and hope for the best.

The hint is that the absence of an ON VIOLATION clause is important. When you omit it, the expectation defaults to warn — it records the violation but lets the row through. That default is exactly what you want during a trial period.

Step 1 of the worked solution is to write a shadow declaration: the new rules, deployed with warn semantics, running alongside the production rules. You observe how often they fire before you decide whether to escalate them to drop or fail. This is the shadow deployment pattern for expectations.

The analysis closes the loop: shadow deployment with warn is the only safe way to introduce new expectations into a live pipeline. You get the data you need to set thresholds, and you get it without risking an outage. So the full playbook is: warn to observe, drop to filter noise, fail to protect contracts — and at scale, protect the fail rule for the violations that truly matter.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Matching Actions to Requirements

questions.question: A data engineer is building a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline that ingests order events from a message bus into a bronze streaming table. The stated quality requirement is: 'Records with a NULL customer_id must be rejected and stored for later investigation, but ingestion must continue and the pipeline update must not stop.' Which expectation action satisfies this requirement?

options.label: EXPECT (customer_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
EXPECT (customer_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
EXPECT (customer_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION WARN
EXPECT (customer_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION QUARANTINE ROW

questions.analysis: The requirement has three parts and must be read carefully. First, bad records must be 'rejected', which rules out WARN (Option C), because WARN keeps the record in the target dataset rather than rejecting it. Second, 'ingestion must continue and the pipeline update must not stop' rules out FAIL UPDATE (Option B), because failing the update halts the entire pipeline update the moment the constraint is violated. Third, the record must be 'stored for later investigation'. In Lakeflow, dropping a row on violation does not silently discard it: the dropped record is recorded and can be surfaced through the expectation's event metrics and pipeline event logging, which is how you 'store' the bad record for investigation while ingestion continues. That is exactly the behavior of ON VIOLATION DROP ROW, Option A. Option D is a trap distractor: many engineers assume there is a dedicated QUARANTINE action alongside WARN, DROP, and FAIL, but no such keyword exists as a fourth action — the three actions map to three outcomes: warn keeps the record, drop discards it, and fail stops the update. The key reasoning, per the pipeline semantics, is that bad records are either quarantined or dropped according to your rules [source 5], and only WARN, DROP, and FAIL are available as violation actions.

questions.question: A Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline has a streaming table named bronze_events and a downstream materialized view named mv_daily_counts that aggregates bronze_events. On a given pipeline update, the incoming batch contains 10,000 rows, of which 400 rows violate an expectation. Two scenarios are compared: (Scenario D) the expectation uses ON VIOLATION DROP ROW; (Scenario F) the expectation uses ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE. Select ALL statements that correctly describe the outcome. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: In Scenario D, all 10,000 rows enter the streaming table, and the expectation only records a warning.
In Scenario D, the 400 violating rows are discarded, so 9,600 rows are written to bronze_events and flow through to mv_daily_counts.
In Scenario F, the 400 violating rows are discarded but the update continues, so mv_daily_counts still receives 9,600 rows.
In Scenario F, the update fails before the batch is committed, so no new rows reach mv_daily_counts and the downstream materialized view is not updated for this run.
In Scenario D, only 9,600 rows reach mv_daily_counts, because drops remove rows from the dataset before downstream datasets are computed.

questions.analysis: The core distinction is whether a violation stops the update or merely removes rows and lets the run proceed. Under DROP ROW (Scenario D), the 10,000 incoming rows are evaluated, the 400 violating rows are discarded, and the remaining 9,600 rows are written to bronze_events. Because Lakeflow tracks dependencies through the pipeline graph and flows data downstream to dependent datasets [source 2], the materialized view mv_daily_counts sees only those 9,600 rows — so Option E is correct, and it also corrects Option A, which wrongly claims all 10,000 rows enter the table (that is WARN behavior, not DROP). Option B restates the 9,600-row outcome correctly. Under FAIL UPDATE (Scenario F), a violation aborts the update: the batch is not committed, and the downstream materialized view is not refreshed for that run — so Option D is correct. Option C is the classic misconception: it borrows DROP's row count (9,600) but pairs it with FAIL's label, which is contradictory, because FAIL does not discard-and-continue; it halts. The framework enforces declared expectations, quarantining or dropping bad records according to your rules [source 5], and the dependency graph determines what runs after a failure.

questions.question: A product requirement states: 'Bad telemetry records must never silently disappear; they must be counted and visible to the on-call team, but a single malformed record must not block the night's ingestion run.' You are choosing between three expectation actions on a streaming table. Which actions are consistent with the requirement as written, and which single action is the trap to avoid? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: WARN — keep the record, record a metric, and continue the update; acceptable when the requirement is to observe and continue.
DROP ROW — discard the record, record the drop, and continue the update; acceptable when the requirement is to reject a record and continue.
FAIL UPDATE — halt the update on the first violating record; this satisfies the 'must not block the run' clause.
FAIL UPDATE — the correct trap distractor, because it contradicts the 'must not block the night's ingestion run' clause even though it satisfies 'never silently disappear'.
QUARANTINE ROW — a fourth dedicated action that is identical to FAIL UPDATE but does not stop the update.

questions.analysis: The requirement has two clauses that must be satisfied simultaneously: bad records must never silently disappear (they must be counted and visible), and a malformed record must not block the run. WARN (Option A) satisfies both: it keeps the record, records a metric, and lets the update continue. DROP ROW (Option B) also satisfies both: it discards the record while recording the drop event, and the update continues. FAIL UPDATE (Option C) satisfies the first clause but violates the second, because it halts the update on the first violation — so it is the trap to avoid, and Option D correctly identifies it as the trap distractor. Option E is a fabrication: there is no fourth QUARANTINE ROW action. Only three actions map to three outcomes — warn, drop, and fail [source 5] — and bad records are quarantined or dropped according to your rules within those three actions. This is precisely the trap called out in the checkpoint description: choosing expect_or_fail when the requirement says 'quarantine bad records and continue'.

actions.text: Now let's put that to the test. These questions push you to match an action to a stated requirement and to reason about where rows end up downstream — so read each scenario carefully and commit to your best answer on your own.
Work through each one independently, then hit submit. Once you're done, I'll come back and we'll walk through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Where Expectation Results Land: The Pipeline Event Log

elements.content: Where Expectation Results Land: The Pipeline Event Log
Objective: Locate expectation results in the pipeline event log and read their structure — the authoritative source for programmatic alerting [source 1].
What each data-quality event carries

• dataset — the dataset the update wrote

• expectation name — the declared constraint

• passed_records — rows satisfying the predicate

• failed_records — rows violating the predicate
One event is emitted per expectation, per update — expectation name is the unit of record [source 2].
Worked example — one update, 10,000 rows

valid_id: passed_records = 9,980, failed_records = 20 (warn)

not_null_id: passed_records = 10,000, failed_records = 0

Written row count = 10,000 (warn keeps rows).
failed_records = 0 means none failed — not “not evaluated”.

Warn vs drop: warn keeps the row (failed_records rises, count unchanged); drop discards it (failed_records rises, dataset row count falls). The action — not a separate counter — distinguishes them [source 5].

actions.text: We just wrote expectations for the orders pipeline, so now let's answer the natural follow-up question: where do those expectation results actually go? Your objective here is to locate expectation results in the pipeline event log and read their structure correctly. This matters because on the exam, and in production alerting, you need to know exactly which field to query.

Every expectation you declare produces a structured event. In the Lakeflow declarative pipeline model, these data-quality events are emitted into the pipeline event log — the same event stream that carries flow progress and errors. Let's look at what each event actually carries.

Each event names the dataset the update wrote to, and then, per expectation, it records the expectation name, the dataset it applies to, passed_records, and failed_records. Two counters, always both present. The key idea on this slide comes next: one event is emitted per expectation, per update.

Notice that phrasing: one event per expectation, per update. So on a pipeline with three expectations, each micro-batch run produces three data-quality events — not one combined summary. If you're parsing the log programmatically, you filter to data-quality events, then key on the expectation name to aggregate counts over time.
Let's ground this in the worked example: one update processing 10,000 rows. Here's a real event payload you might see in the log for a valid_id expectation.
valid_id shows passed_records = 9,980 and failed_records = 20. That tells you 20 rows had a null or malformed id. The expectation was evaluated, and 20 violations occurred. Straightforward.

Now the exam trap. If you see failed_records = 0, do not conclude the expectation was skipped. Zero failures means the expectation was evaluated and nothing violated it — an empty violation set, not an absent check. The evaluator still ran. Read that distinction carefully; it is a favorite distractor on the exam.

And finally, the warn-versus-drop distinction. Warn keeps the row, so failed_records rises but the dataset's row count is unchanged. Drop removes the offending rows, so failed_records rises and the dataset's row count falls. The counters don't tag rows as warned or dropped — the expectation's action is what tells you which happened. That is the whole slide: event structure, a worked example, the failed_records = 0 trap, and the warn-versus-drop signal. Next, you'll build an expectation and watch these results land in the log yourself.
