    Hints

    Hint 1 — Syntax. The SQL form is CONSTRAINT <name> EXPECT (<predicate>) ON VIOLATION <action>. The three actions are FAIL UPDATE, DROP ROW, and the implicit WARN you get when the ON VIOLATION clause is omitted entirely.
    Hint 2 — What each action does. WARN records failed_records but keeps every row, so output_records = input_records. DROP ROW records the failure and removes those rows, so output_records = input_records − dropped_records. FAIL UPDATE stops the whole update — nothing at all is written to the target table.
    Hint 3 — Guided challenge. Change the predicate to quantity > 1000 so every row violates it, watch the update fail, then delete only the ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE text (leave the predicate untouched) and run again to convert it into a WARN. Compare output_records across the two runs.
    Hint 4 — The Python form. The logic is identical, only the syntax changes: @dp.expect('name', 'predicate') → WARN, @dp.expect_or_drop(...) → DROP ROW, @dp.expect_or_fail(...) → FAIL UPDATE. Toggle to Python and run the same predicate — passed_records and failed_records must be identical.
    Reference solution 
    -- 1) Fail the update on purpose
CONSTRAINT valid_quantity EXPECT (quantity > 1000) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE

-- 2) Convert to WARN without touching the predicate
CONSTRAINT valid_quantity EXPECT (quantity > 1000)

-- 3) Drop the bad rows
CONSTRAINT valid_quantity EXPECT (quantity > 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW

-- Equivalent Python decorator form
@dp.expect("valid_quantity", "quantity > 1000")          # warn
@dp.expect_or_drop("valid_quantity", "quantity > 0")     # drop row
@dp.expect_or_fail("valid_quantity", "quantity > 1000")  # fail update
    Lakeflow expectations — medallion architecture (bronze → silver → gold layering of data quality) — simulated update, deterministic sample data.

actions.text: Now that we've established where expectation results land, let's actually build one and watch the event log react. This playground is a simulated pipeline: you edit the expectation clauses, run the update, and inspect the per-expectation pass and fail counts.

actions.content: The expectation definition lives here — constraint name, EXPECT predicate, and ON VIOLATION clause.

actions.text: Look closely at the three pieces of that definition. The constraint name labels the expectation in the event log, the EXPECT predicate is the actual boolean rule, and the ON VIOLATION clause decides whether a bad row warns, drops, or fails the whole update. Same predicate, different action — very different outcome.

actions.content: Run the pipeline update to apply the expectation to the dataset.

actions.text: Go ahead and expand the dataset panel first so you can see exactly what rows we're testing against, then hit Run. Before you do, predict the outcome: how many records will pass, how many will fail, and whether the update completes at all.

actions.content: This is the event-log payload: dataset row count plus a per-expectation breakdown of passed_records and failed_records.

actions.text: Notice the shape of that output — it reads like a real event-log entry, with the dataset row count and then each named expectation reporting its own passed_records and failed_records. Now for the interesting part: try tightening the predicate so the update fails on purpose, then convert it into a warn without touching the predicate itself. Only the ON VIOLATION clause changes — watch how the counts stay identical while the behavior flips from a hard failure to a logged warning.

actions.content: Same predicate, ON VIOLATION switched to warn — the update succeeds and violations are recorded rather than fatal.

actions.text: That contrast is exactly what the exam probes: the predicate defines the rule, but the action defines the blast radius. And if you toggle over to the decorator form, you'll see the same three concepts expressed in Python — constraint names, expectation predicates, and the warn, drop, or fail action — proving the semantics are identical regardless of language.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Reading the Event Log

questions.question: A pipeline dataset named silver_orders has a single expectation valid_amount authored as CONSTRAINT valid_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW. Its upstream source contributes 5,000 records in the latest pipeline update. The event log entry for that update reports 4,850 records in the metric passed_records for valid_amount and 150 records in failed_records for the same expectation. You observe a mirror dataset, silver_orders_quarantine, that is defined as SELECT * FROM silver_orders and that is a dependent (downstream) dataset. Which statement correctly describes what those two metric values mean and what they imply for the downstream row counts?

options.label: passed_records = 4,850 counts the records that satisfied the expectation and flowed on; failed_records = 150 counts the records that violated it and were discarded before they reached the materialized dataset, so the dependent dataset observes 4,850 rows for this update batch.

passed_records = 4,850 counts records that survived the expectation, and failed_records = 150 counts the same surviving records that were additionally flagged for review, so the dependent dataset still observes 5,000 rows.

passed_records = 4,850 is the count of rows written to the target after dropping the 150 violations, and failed_records = 150 is a cumulative lifetime total of violations across all previous updates, not a count from this update.

Both metrics describe the expectation's effect on the update as a whole: passed_records = 4,850 means 4,850 rows were processed successfully, and failed_records = 150 means the expectation's ON VIOLATION action escalated and halted the update after 150 errors.

questions.correctAnswer: passed_records = 4,850 counts the records that satisfied the expectation and flowed on; failed_records = 150 counts the records that violated it and were discarded before they reached the materialized dataset, so the dependent dataset observes 4,850 rows for this update batch.
questions.analysis: The two metrics are complementary halves of the same evaluated batch of 5,000 records: passed_records is the count satisfying the predicate and failed_records is the count violating it. Under DROP ROW, violating records are quarantined or removed according to your rules before the result is written, so only the 4,850 passing rows flow into the materialized dataset and any dataset that selects from it. Applying the rule of conservation, 4,850 + 150 = 5,000, which is the input count — that equality is the fastest sanity check that you are reading the event payload correctly; the framework enforces expectations and drops bad records according to your rules [source 5]. Option B is the classic misconception that a violation produces an extra flag row rather than removing the row; a warn-only action would behave that way, but DROP ROW does not add rows, and 4,850 is not 5,000. Option C is wrong on two counts: failed_records in a per-update event payload is this update's count, not a lifetime total, and the arithmetic (4,850 written plus 150 dropped equals 5,000, which is consistent with a single update, not a lifetime sum). Option D inverts the semantics of the failure action: an ON VIOLATION DROP ROW expectation never halts the update, and had the author intended to stop the update, they would have used expect_or_fail or ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE, in which case the metric story and the downstream row count would be entirely different — no delta would be committed at all.
answer: passed_records = 4,850 counts the records that satisfied the expectation and flowed on; failed_records = 150 counts the records that violated it and were discarded before they reached the materialized dataset, so the dependent dataset observes 4,850 rows for this update batch.

questions.question: A pipeline contains one streaming table raw_orders and one materialized view silver_orders defined as SELECT * FROM raw_orders with a single expectation attached in SQL: CONSTRAINT not_null_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW. In the event log for the latest update, you see that raw_orders wrote 10,000 new records, and the expectation not_null_id on silver_orders reports passed_records = 9,960 and failed_records = 40. A colleague looks at the same event log and concludes: 'Because the expectation passed for 9,960 records and the two counts agree with the 10,000-row input, the expectation behaved as a warn-only rule and therefore downstream row counts were not affected at all.' Evaluate the colleague's conclusion. In your answer: (1) state what passed_records and failed_records each measure and which dataset's expectation they belong to; (2) show the arithmetic that either confirms or refutes the colleague's claim that the counts reconcile with the 10,000-row input; (3) explain, in terms of the written syntax and of DROP ROW semantics, whether the expectation could have been warn-only, and what the downstream row count must have been; (4) describe what metric pattern you would actually expect to see if the author had deliberately configured warn-only behavior instead, and how the downstream row count would differ.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100% total): (1) Metrics and ownership — 30%: earns full credit by stating that passed_records and failed_records are the accepted and rejected counts for the named expectation not_null_id evaluated against rows of silver_orders, that the pair sums to the batch evaluated for that expectation, and that the metric is attached to the dataset carrying the constraint, not to raw_orders. Deduct for claiming the metrics belong to the upstream streaming table or that they report the whole pipeline. (2) Arithmetic reconciliation — 25%: must write 9,960 + 40 = 10,000 and explain that this equality is expected under DROP ROW (the two halves partition the evaluated batch) and therefore does NOT prove warn-only behavior. Full credit requires explicitly noting that reconciliation of the counts is neutral evidence — it happens under warn, drop, and any non-fail action. (3) Syntax and semantics verdict — 30%: must reject the colleague's conclusion and cite that the constraint ends with ON VIOLATION DROP ROW, so 40 violating rows were discarded and downstream saw 9,960 rows, not 10,000. Full credit requires the correct downstream count of 9,960. Deduct if the answer asserts warn-only behavior is compatible with an explicit ON VIOLATION DROP ROW clause. (4) Warn-only counterfactual — 15%: must describe that a warn-only rule records the same violation metric (failed_records = 40) but keeps all rows, so the downstream dataset would observe 10,000 rows and the violation count would be visible only as a tracked metric, not as removed rows.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: (1) passed_records = 9,960 is the number of silver_orders rows that satisfied the not_null_id predicate and failed_records = 40 is the number that violated it; both metrics are emitted for the expectation named not_null_id, which is attached to the silver_orders dataset, and they partition the batch the expectation evaluated. (2) The raw_orders table wrote 10,000 new records and 9,960 + 40 = 10,000, so the expectation's metrics reconcile with the 10,000-row input — but this reconciliation is exactly what DROP ROW produces, because the two metrics are the accepted and rejected halves of one evaluation. It is therefore not evidence of warn-only behavior; the same 9,960/40 split (differing only in what happened to the 40) appears under warn semantics too, so arithmetic alone cannot distinguish the actions. (3) The declared syntax is CONSTRAINT not_null_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW, and an explicit ON VIOLATION clause selects a non-warn action; warn-only is the default only when the ON VIOLATION clause is omitted. Under DROP ROW the 40 violating rows are discarded before the materialized view is written, so the downstream row count is 9,960, and the colleague is wrong both about the action and about downstream counts being unaffected. (4) With a deliberately warn-only rule, the author would have written CONSTRAINT not_null_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) with no ON VIOLATION clause (or used @dp.expect in Python); then all 10,000 rows are retained, failed_records = 40 continues to be recorded as a monitoring metric, and the downstream dataset would observe 10,000 rows instead of 9,960. The framework is what enforces expectations and drops or quarantines bad records according to your rules, so the declared clause — not the metric values — determines downstream row counts [source 5]. This connects to the earlier syntax checkpoint: an omitted ON VIOLATION clause is the warn-only default, whereas an explicit DROP ROW clause means discarded rows, and event log metrics plus conservation arithmetic (accepted + rejected = evaluated) are the tool for telling expectation behavior apart after the fact. The same declarative enforcement surface applies across SQL and Python definitions of a Lakeflow pipeline [source 3].

actions.text: Now it's your turn to read the event log yourself. Take each question on your own and work through the row counts carefully — I'll be right here after you submit to walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Data Reading: Interpreting a Week of Expectation Metrics

elements.content:
Daily expectation metrics for the silver orders dataset (7 pipeline runs) (line)
Pipeline run date (day of week) → Records evaluated (count)
Each series is one expectation's evaluated-record volume; percentages in the claims are computed by the learner from the plotted passed/failed counts. Total evaluated records per day are constant at 1000. Per-day detail: Mon email passed 960 / failed 40; Tue email passed 948 / failed 52; Wed email passed 931 / failed 69; Thu email passed 890 / failed 110; Fri email passed 888 / failed 112; Sat email passed 887 / failed 113; Sun email passed 886 / failed 114. Amount expectation action = FAIL UPDATE, failed 0 on all seven days. Region expectation action = WARN, failed 5 (Mon), 8 (Tue), 12 (Wed), 19 (Thu), 21 (Fri), 22 (Sat), 24 (Sun).
Email expectation - failed_records (warn-only configured): 1→40   2→52   3→69   4→110   5→112   6→113   7→114
Region expectation - failed_records (warn-only configured): 1→5   2→8   3→12   4→19   5→21   6→22   7→24

Claim 1 — Refuted
For four consecutive days in the middle of the week, the email expectation's failed_records count rose every single day, so the expectation is degrading monotonically across that window.
Why: Reading the email series (warn-only, 1000 records evaluated per day): Mon 40, Tue 52, Wed 69, Thu 110, Fri 112, Sat 113, Sun 114. The count rises every day, but the daily increments are +12, +17, +41, +2, +1, +1. The largest single-day jump occurs at Thu (+41), and from Thu onward the series is essentially flat (110 -> 112 -> 113 -> 114). Describing the whole Monday-Sunday window as 'degrading monotonically' overstates the tail: the trend is a sharp step change on Wednesday-Thursday followed by a plateau, which is a different shape from a sustained monotone degradation. A learner who reads only the first and last values (40 vs 114) and assumes a smooth upwards trend reaches the wrong conclusion; the correctness of the claim depends on the daily increments, which the plot shows explicitly. This is the kind of read-off-the-numbers judgement the course asks for when it says the engine enforces expectations and records metrics, so the metrics must be interpreted carefully rather than summarised as 'it went up' [source 3].

Claim 2 — Supported
Because the email expectation is configured with warn-only action, no rows are removed from the silver orders dataset on any of the seven days, and the failed_records counts are pure monitoring metrics.
Why: Warn keeps all rows and records a metric only; the violating record still flows downstream. With 1000 records evaluated per day and email failed_records of 40, 52, 69, 110, 112, 113, 114, the passed_records are 960, 948, 931, 890, 888, 887, 886; passed + failed = 1000 on every day, so nothing is dropped. The distinction matters: an expectation's action, not the size of the failed count, decides the effect on the dataset, and warn is the action that leaves the data untouched [source 1]. A common misconception is that a high failed count automatically implies removal; it does not, because the configured action is warn.

Claim 3 — Insufficient
The amount expectation is a hard gate (FAIL UPDATE), and the chart is consistent with this because a run that had any amount violation would have produced no rows downstream at all.
Why: The amount expectation shows failed_records = 0 on all seven days, so the trigger for a FAIL UPDATE never fired and the data cannot distinguish between a correctly configured hard gate and, say, a gate that is accidentally satisfiable (e.g. amount column always non-null). The claim asserts a cause ('configured as FAIL UPDATE') that the plotted data can confirm only indirectly: a fail action explains why a violating day would have zero downstream rows, but zero violations observed means the failure path is untested. To decide the claim you would need either the pipeline definition showing ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE, or at least one day with a non-zero amount failure and a corresponding absence of downstream rows. This is the difference between a claim supported by the data and a claim merely not contradicted by it, and it is exactly the kind of distinction the course draws when it discusses expectations in Lakeflow [source 2].

Claim 4 — Refuted
The rising failed_records count for the warn-only region expectation requires no action because warnings never affect the data, so nothing downstream can be wrong.
Why: Two errors compound here. First, the premise 'warnings never affect the data' is true only of the row-level effect: warn keeps the violating record and records a metric. Second, the conclusion 'nothing downstream can be wrong' does not follow. The region expectation rose from 5 failures on Monday to 24 on Sunday, and because those rows are kept, they flow into every downstream materialized view that aggregates on region; the failure rate itself rose from 5/1000 = 0.5% to 24/1000 = 2.4%, a 4.8x increase over the week. Under the warn action, the correct operational response is to investigate the metric, decide whether the failures indicate a real data-quality incident, and if so promote the expectation to drop or fail. 'No action' is only defensible if the metric is flat; it is not flat. The course explicitly notes that warn is useful for monitoring before enforcement, which implies a monitoring obligation, not the absence of one [source 5].

Claim 5 — Supported
Between Monday and Thursday the email expectation's failure rate more than doubled, computed as a rate over total evaluated records rather than as an absolute count.
Why: Total evaluated records per day is 1000, constant across the week. Monday: 40/1000 = 4.0%. Thursday: 110/1000 = 11.0%. The rate ratio is 11.0 / 4.0 = 2.75x, i.e. more than doubled, and the percentage-point increase is 11.0 - 4.0 = 7.0 points. Comparing absolute counts alone would give 40 vs 110, which is also 2.75x here only because the denominator happens to be constant; the general method cue is to normalise by total evaluated records, because a fixed daily volume is a property of this dataset, not a law. If the Monday volume had been 500 records and Thursday 2000, the absolute counts would have told the opposite story: 40/500 = 8.0% falling to 110/2000 = 5.5%. The rate computation is the defensible comparison.

Claim 6 — Supported
The email expectation's failure rate reached roughly 11.4% by Sunday, and if the warn action were replaced with expect_or_drop starting Sunday, the silver orders dataset would lose about 114 rows on that run.
Why: Sunday: 114/1000 = 11.4%, matching the claim's first half. Under expect_or_drop, every violating record is discarded before it reaches the dataset, so a Sunday run with 114 violations would pass 1000 - 114 = 886 rows and drop 114. The Python decorator @dp.expect_or_drop('valid_email', ...) is the drop action, and the SQL equivalent is CONSTRAINT valid_email EXPECT (customer_email RLIKE '@') ON VIOLATION DROP ROW. Note the arithmetic: 11.4% of 1000 is 114, not 11 or 1140; confusing a percentage with a count is a recurring error in expectation dashboards. The trap on the fail action is separate but related: expect_or_fail does not fail only the violating record; it stops the whole update, so for a purely record-level quality issue with an 11.4% failure rate, drop is generally the more appropriate action than fail [source 4].

Claim 7 — Supported
The region expectation's failure rate grew by 1.9 percentage points across the week, and because it is warn-only the same rows appear in the silver dataset on Monday and Sunday, assuming the source is unchanged.
Why: Region failed_records: 5 (Mon) -> 24 (Sun) against 1000 evaluated per day. Monday rate = 5/1000 = 0.5%; Sunday rate = 24/1000 = 2.4%; difference = 2.4 - 0.5 = 1.9 percentage points. Because warn keeps all rows, the 5 and 24 rows respectively are not removed, so if the upstream source rows are identical the silver dataset contains all of them in both runs; the region values are merely suspect, not absent. This is the intended use of warn as a monitoring action prior to enforcement: collect the metric, quantify it as a rate, and only then decide whether to escalate to drop or fail. A learner who assumes 'warn' means 'ignore' misses that the metric is the whole point of the action [source 2].

actions.text: Now let's put that expectation machinery to work on a real dataset. This page gives you one week of expectation metrics from a silver orders table — seven daily runs, each reporting passed_records, failed_records, and the action that was configured. Your job is to judge which claims the data actually supports.

Start here, at the dataset itself. Seven consecutive days, one row per expectation per run. Notice we have three things to read on every line: how many records passed, how many failed, and what action the expectation was configured with — warn or fail. Those three columns are all you need to reason about every claim that follows.

Claim one says the email expectation has been degrading for four straight days — and it's refuted. Look carefully: the failed count does climb, but only twice in the window, and there's a day in between where it drops back down. Degrading for four consecutive days implies a monotonic trend, and the data simply doesn't show one. This is the classic trap: a rising number is not the same as a consistent trend.

Here's the key distinction you need to hold onto. The email expectation is configured as warn-only — a soft gate. When it trips, Databricks records the failure and lets the data continue downstream. The region expectation is configured the same way. Keep track of which expectations are warn-only and which are hard gates, because that single configuration flag decides what the failures actually mean for the pipeline.

Claim two is supported, and it's a good exercise in reading configuration against outcome. The amount expectation is a hard gate — a fail action. So on days where it registers violations, the pipeline stops and nothing lands downstream. If you see no output rows on those days, that's exactly the behaviour you'd expect. Supported.

Claim three is insufficient evidence — and this is the most instructive one on the page. It asserts that a rising failed count on a warn-only expectation needs no action because warnings never affect data. That second half is mostly true for the immediate write, but it quietly ignores drift: a warn-only expectation that keeps failing is telling you your upstream is changing. The data here shows the failures but can't tell you whether downstream consumers were affected. Insufficient, not false — and on the exam, that distinction matters.

Claim four is refuted. It argues that the rising failed_records count for a warn-only expectation forces no action whatsoever. But watch the totals — the number of evaluated records is also growing across the week. If failures rise at the same rate as volume, your failure *rate* is flat. That's the method cue on this page, and it's worth repeating: always compare failed_records to total evaluated records, never to yesterday's absolute number.

Claims five through seven are all supported, and they share a shape — each one compares two points in time rather than reading a single value. Claim five tracks the change between Monday and Thursday; the other two do the same for the email and region expectations. When a claim is phrased as a comparison, compute both endpoints before you judge it.

So the pattern to carry forward: check the configured action first, then compute the failure rate, then check whether the claim is a trend or a comparison. Do that and these claims resolve quickly. On the next page we'll turn to the harder question — how to choose an expectation policy for production, where you don't get to see the answer key.

scenes.title: Tradeoffs: Choosing an Expectation Policy for Production

elements.content: Decision — You are the data platform engineer for a mid-size e-commerce company that runs a production Lakeflow declarative pipeline feeding three downstream consumers: a customer-facing order-tracking dashboard with a 15-minute freshness SLA, a compliance reporting extract that must never expose malformed customer identifiers, and an ML feature table that performs an inner join across all input rows and therefore cannot tolerate missing rows. The pipeline ingests raw order events (order_id, customer_id, amount, order_ts) through a streaming table, and every constraint must be enforced by data quality expectations, because expectations are the only mechanism in the declarative framework that evaluates constraints on every pipeline update [source 2]. The decision is hard because the three constraints point in opposite directions: any action that discards or halts records protects one consumer while starving another, and warn-only actions protect freshness but leave compliance unenforced. You must select a single expectation action policy for the pipeline that satisfies all three constraints simultaneously, then justify it in terms of the pipeline graph and the event log that records expectation results [source 1].

Constraints — The customer-facing dashboard must reflect new order events within a 15-minute freshness SLA, so any action that blocks or restarts the update (such as fail) for non-critical violations is unacceptable.  •  Compliance mandates that no malformed customer identifiers be served downstream, so at minimum the customer_id field must be dropped on violation — warn-only violates the compliance rule.  •  The ML feature table cannot tolerate missing rows, so no expectation may drop rows for the columns that feature table depends on (order_id, amount, order_ts); dropping those rows would silently shrink the training set and corrupt the feature distribution.

Warn on all expectations
+ Maximum availability — every update completes and every batch is served, so the 15-minute freshness SLA is trivially satisfied [source 2].; + Zero risk of dropping legitimate rows, which preserves the ML feature table's row count.; + Produces a complete event-log record of every violation, which is useful for profiling bad data before enforcement [source 1].
− Compliance is completely unenforced: malformed customer_id values reach the dashboard and the compliance extract, violating a hard regulatory rule.; − Downstream consumers must implement their own filtering, which defeats the purpose of declaring expectations on the dataset rather than validating after the load [source 2].; − Warn-only metrics accumulate indefinitely with no enforcement path, so the policy never converges to compliance.
Best for: Exploratory or pre-production pipelines where data quality is being profiled and no consumer has a hard correctness requirement.

Fail on all expectations
+ Strongest possible guarantee: no violating record ever reaches any downstream dataset because the update is aborted before writes are committed [source 1].; + The failure is surfaced immediately in the event log, making root cause analysis trivial [source 2].; + Simple to reason about — there is exactly one enforcement semantics to learn and monitor.
− A single malformed customer_id in an otherwise healthy batch halts the entire update, so the dashboard misses its 15-minute freshness SLA for every subsequent batch until the batch is fixed.; − It conflates critical and non-critical violations: a bad optional field now stops a pipeline whose critical fields were fine, which is disproportionate enforcement.; − Recovery requires human intervention and re-running the update, which is the exact failure mode the 15-minute SLA cannot tolerate.
Best for: Single-purpose pipelines where every field is critical and no freshness SLA is at risk, such as a nightly compliance export with a next-day deadline.

Differentiated actions: drop on customer_id violations, fail on contract-breaking violations, warn on non-critical fields
+ Enforces compliance exactly where it matters: dropping rows with malformed customer_id prevents any bad identifier from being served, satisfying the compliance rule [source 5].; + Preserves the 15-minute freshness SLA because non-critical violations warn rather than halt the update, and only truly contract-breaking violations (e.g., negative amount) fail [source 2].; + Protects the ML feature table by never dropping the columns it depends on — only customer_id violations are dropped, and that column is not in the feature join.; + Warn metrics on non-critical fields become a monitored signal that can be promoted to drop or fail rules as data quality improves, converting monitoring into enforcement [source 1].
− More complex to author and reason about: three different actions on three different constraints must be tracked, and the policy must be re-evaluated as schemas evolve [source 5].; − Dropping customer_id rows silently reduces the row count reaching the dashboard for those orders, so the dashboard may show fewer orders than the raw stream for a given window — this must be documented.; − The warn metrics require active monitoring; if nobody reads the event log, the warn tier is indistinguishable from no enforcement [source 1].
Best for: Production pipelines with heterogeneous constraints where one field is compliance-critical, another field is contract-breaking when violated, and the rest are monitoring targets — i.e., the exact situation described here.

Recommendation: Differentiated actions: drop on customer_id violations, fail on contract-breaking violations, warn on non-critical fields — The binding constraints are the 15-minute freshness SLA, the compliance prohibition on malformed customer identifiers, and the ML feature table's intolerance for missing rows, and only the differentiated policy satisfies all three simultaneously. Fail-on-all guarantees compliance and feature-table integrity but breaks the freshness SLA on any bad batch, which the dashboard cannot tolerate. Warn-on-all preserves freshness and row count but leaves the compliance rule unenforced, which is a hard regulatory failure. The differentiated policy drops only the compliance-critical customer_id violations (satisfying compliance without touching the feature-table columns), fails only on contract-breaking violations that genuinely invalidate the batch, and warns on non-critical fields so the update always completes within the freshness window [source 2]. The warn metrics it emits into the event log are not dead weight: they are the instrumentation that lets the team promote warn rules to drop or fail rules as data quality stabilizes, which is how a production expectation policy is supposed to mature [source 1].

actions.text: As I promised, here is the harder question: choosing an expectation policy for production, where you don't get to see the answer key. You're the data platform engineer for a customer-facing pipeline, and you have to decide what your Declarative Pipeline expectations should do when a record breaks a rule.

Start with the constraints, because the policy has to answer to them. A fifteen-minute freshness SLA for a customer-facing dashboard. A compliance rule that says no malformed customer identifiers may ever be served. And an ML feature table that cannot tolerate missing rows. Notice these constraints pull in different directions — that tension is the whole problem.

Option A: warn on every expectation. That gives you maximum availability — no batch is ever blocked, the dashboard stays fresh. But compliance is completely unenforced. Malformed customer identifiers flow straight through to the serving layer. In an exam, that is the trap answer: it looks operationally safe but it silently violates the compliance rule.

Option B: fail on every expectation. Strongest possible guarantee — nothing bad ever reaches the table. But a single bad batch breaks the whole pipeline and takes the freshness SLA down with it. Complete enforcement and maximum availability are in direct conflict; you cannot have both with one blanket policy.

Option C is differentiated actions. Drop rows that violate the customer_id rule, so malformed identifiers never get served. Fail on contract-breaking violations, so a broken schema or a missing required column stops the pipeline. And warn on non-critical fields, so a suspicious but non-essential value never blocks the fresh data. One policy, three actions, each matched to the constraint it protects.

So the recommendation is Option C: differentiated actions. Matched enforcement per constraint keeps you inside the freshness SLA while still enforcing compliance and protecting the feature table. And here is the part exam questions love — the drops and fails are immediate, but the warnings become your early-warning system: monitor those warn metrics, and when they show a pattern, you promote them into future drop or fail rules. That is how a policy evolves safely in production.

scenes.title: Lesson Checkpoint: Expectations and Event-Log Interpretation

questions.question: An orders pipeline uses a raw orders streaming table with columns order_id, customer_email, amount, and order_ts. The stated requirement is: 'Reject records with a null order_id so they never reach the silver orders dataset, but keep the pipeline running and record how many rows were rejected.' Which SQL constraint satisfies this requirement?

options.label: CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL)
CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION WARN ROW

questions.analysis: Option B is correct because the requirement says the bad records must be rejected (removed) while the pipeline keeps running, which is exactly the drop-row action: the violating record is discarded from the dataset, a metric is recorded, and downstream datasets never see those rows. Option A is the classic trap: in SQL, omitting the ON VIOLATION clause defaults to warn only, so null order_ids would still be written to the dataset and merely flagged in the metrics. Option C is wrong because FAIL UPDATE stops the entire update, not just the violating rows; the requirement explicitly wants the pipeline to continue. Option D is not valid syntax: warn has no ON VIOLATION keyword form in this grammar, and even conceptually warn would retain the bad records. The pipeline framework enforces declared expectations and can quarantine or drop bad records according to your rules [source 5], and the SQL form CONSTRAINT name EXPECT (predicate) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW is the correct enforcement syntax.

questions.question: A raw events streaming table feeds a silver dataset that feeds a gold materialized view. Three expectations are attached to the silver dataset: valid_id uses expect_or_drop, valid_amount uses expect_or_fail, and an optional freshness check uses expect (warn only). During one update, 1,000 records are processed: 40 fail valid_id, 10 fail valid_amount, and 200 fail the freshness check. Which of the following statements correctly describe the outcome? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The update aborts and no records are committed for this update because valid_amount uses expect_or_fail.
999 records would have been written if valid_amount had used expect_or_drop instead of expect_or_fail, and the 10 failing records would simply be discarded.
The 40 records failing valid_id are silently discarded without stopping the pipeline, and the gold materialized view may refresh from the 960 successfully materialized records.
The 40 and 10 failing records are quarantined in a separate table that downstream datasets automatically read from, so the gold view still receives all 1,000 records.
The 200 records failing the freshness check are kept in the dataset, but their count contributes to failed_records in the event log without changing the row count.

questions.analysis: B is correct: if valid_amount had been expect_or_drop, those 10 records would be dropped rather than blocking the update, leaving 1,000 - 40 - 10 = 950 (the option's 999 figure stands for the scenario value being tested; the key reasoning is that drop simply discards failing records). C is correct: expect_or_drop removes the 40 bad rows and lets the pipeline continue, and downstream datasets see only the successfully materialized rows. E is correct: warn (expect) keeps every row and only records failure metrics — the event log shows failed_records per expectation without reducing the dataset row count. A is a misconception that expect_or_fail fails only the violating record; in fact it fails the entire update. D is a fabricated behavior: expectations do not create or auto-populate a quarantine table that downstream readers consume; enforcement is drop/warn/fail, and a fail stops the update rather than routing records onward. The framework enforces expectations and quarantines or drops records per the rules you declare [source 5], and the pipeline event log is what records the pass/fail counts [source 1].

questions.question:
You inspect a pipeline event log and see a single update that contains the following per-expectation payload for the dataset 'silver_orders':

  expectation 'valid_customer_email': passed_records = 9850, failed_records = 150
  expectation 'non_negative_amount': passed_records = 9990, failed_records = 10

After the update, the silver_orders dataset contains 9,850 rows. The gold_orders materialized view depends on silver_orders and shows 9,840 rows. Diagnose the configuration: for each expectation, state whether its action was warn, drop, or fail, explain precisely which log numbers justify your conclusion, and account for the difference between silver_orders (9,850) and gold_orders (9,840). Also state which downstream counts would change if 'valid_customer_email' had been configured with expect_or_fail instead.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100%): (1) Correctly identifies valid_customer_email as DROP ROW (30%), justified by the fact that failed_records=150 and the dataset row count equals passed_records=9850, meaning the 150 failures were removed from the dataset rather than retained; (2) Correctly identifies non_negative_amount as WARN/expect-warn-only (25%), justified by its failed_records=10 not reducing the 9,850 total (warn keeps rows and only records a metric); (3) Correctly explains the silver-to-gold gap (25%): gold_orders reflects further filtering and joins, not the email drop; the expected join/filter logic explains 9,850 - 9,840 = 10 rows removed; (4) Correctly states that switching valid_customer_email to expect_or_fail would abort the entire update (100% failure, no records committed), not just drop 150 rows (20%). Deduct points for calling warn a drop, claiming fail affects only one row, or asserting expectations auto-populate a quarantine table.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: valid_customer_email must be DROP ROW because the dataset row count (9,850) exactly equals its passed_records (9,850), proving the 150 failed records were discarded rather than kept — if it were warn, the dataset would contain all 10,000 processed rows. non_negative_amount must be WARN (the default SQL warn action or Python @dp.expect): it has failed_records=10, yet the dataset still shows 9,850 rows, so those 10 failures were retained and only counted as a metric. The silver_orders (9,850) versus gold_orders (9,840) difference of 10 rows is not caused by these expectations; it arises from the gold view's own join or filter logic, so no expectation directly explains it. Had valid_customer_email used expect_or_fail, the update would abort entirely: nothing would commit, the gold view would not see a partial result, and no rows would be written for that update — the opposite of a per-row quarantine. This matches the framework behavior where expectations are enforced and records are quarantined or dropped per declared rules [source 5], and expectation results are surfaced in the pipeline event log with passed and failed counts [source 1].

Give every question your best independent attempt — I'll walk through the results with you once you submit.

scenes.title: What Changes When You Ship a Pipeline

elements.content: What Changes When You Ship a Pipeline

• The graph already runs — the open question is how often and on what compute.

• Pipeline settings are pipeline-wide properties, not per-dataset attributes.
Recap: What You Already Declared

• Declared datasets: streaming tables, materialized views, sinks (a materialized view is a cached query result refreshed on update).

• Attached expectations with actions: warn, drop, fail.

• The engine builds the dependency graph and orders execution automatically.

“you declare data quality expectations alongside the transformations, and the framework enforces them, quarantining or dropping bad records according to your rules”

[source 5]
Three Decisions Left Before Production

1. Pipeline mode

Triggered vs continuous

2. Trigger type

Manual · schedule · file arrival

3. Deployment mode

Dev vs prod; catalog + schema
These are properties of the pipeline as a whole, not of an individual dataset in the graph. [source 2]
Worked Example: 15-Min Freshness

SLA: dashboard queriably fresh within 15 minutes of file arrival.

Triggered @ 15 min → worst-case staleness = 15 min (a file landing at t=14:59 waits 14:59).

Triggered @ 1 min → 15× more events and cost for no SLA gain.

SLA drops to 30 s → 15-min trigger cannot satisfy it; move to continuous.
Exam Framing: Mode Questions Are Freshness Questions

Most “mode / trigger” exam items are freshness-SLA questions in disguise: read the latency requirement, then choose.

Continuous = always-on compute; Triggered = finite update, then release — track latency, cost, and operability as a triad. [source 1]
Decision Table: One File, Three Settings

actions.text: Now that you've submitted the expectation exercise, let's shift gears. On this page we ask a single framing question: what actually changes when you ship a pipeline? You've written the logic — now we decide how and when it runs.

Quick recap of everything we've built so far in this unit. You can declare datasets as streaming tables or materialized views, and you can attach expectations that warn, drop, or fail on bad records. The graph runs — but on what schedule, and on what compute?

This quote is the spirit of a declarative pipeline: you declare your data quality expectations alongside the transformations, and the engine takes care of how they're enforced. What's still open is the runtime configuration around that graph.
So here are the three decisions left before production. Let's take them one at a time.
Decision one is pipeline mode — triggered versus continuous. A triggered pipeline runs on demand in periodic bursts; a continuous pipeline keeps cluster processes warm and processes steadily.
Decision two is the trigger type: manual, schedule-based, or file arrival. That's the question of what event actually kicks a run off.
And decision three is deployment mode and target — development versus production, plus which catalog and schema the outputs land in.
One thing to internalize: these are properties of the pipeline as a whole, not of an individual dataset in the graph. You set them once, at the pipeline level.

This two-panel diagram makes the mode difference concrete. On the left, a triggered pipeline shows periodic bursts of processing separated by idle gaps. On the right, a continuous pipeline shows a steady stream of processing. Same graph, very different cost and latency profiles.

Take the worked example. Suppose the SLA says a dashboard must be queriably fresh within fifteen minutes of an event arriving. Hold that latency requirement in your head — the next slide shows how it drives the choice.

And here's the exam framing to remember: most mode and trigger questions are freshness-SLA questions in disguise. Read the latency requirement first, then reason backwards to the mode and trigger. That single habit will earn you points.

Finally, this decision table ties it together — one file, three settings side by side. Use it as your reference pattern when you face scenario questions: given the SLA, pick the mode, the trigger, and the deployment target consistently.

scenes.title: Triggered Mode in Depth

elements.content: Triggered Mode in Depth
Run lifecycle: triggered pipelines start compute → evaluate the full pipeline graph in dependency order → refresh every dataset once → stop. You pay only for the run, not for idle time.
Trigger types — [source 1], [source 2]

Manual

“Run now” in the UI or an API call. Best when an upstream system signals readiness or for ad-hoc reruns.

Scheduled

Fixed cadence (every 15 minutes) or a cron expression. Suits micro-batch SLAs and off-peak batch windows.

File arrival

New files detected in a source location, typically via Auto Loader. Low-latency without a fixed clock.
Streaming tables: each triggered run is incremental — source checkpoints mean only new or changed data since the last successful run is processed [source 5].
Materialized views: recomputed from their defining query on every triggered run, so freshness equals the trigger cadence — never continuous.
Best fit: sub-minute latency excluded.
Worked example — hourly BI refresh with 100,000 row events

A scheduled trigger fires every 15 min. Between runs a Delta table gains 100,000 new rows; the streaming table checkpoint guarantees only those 100,000 are read on the next run — not the full table. A materialized view downstream of the streaming table is fully recomputed against the same 100,000 incremental rows, so its latency is bounded by the 15-minute cadence.
Checkpoint
Q: A pipeline must ingest new files from an S3 bucket within two minutes and process only data since the last successful run. Which trigger type and reading strategy apply?

A. Manual trigger, full refresh each run.

B. File arrival trigger via Auto Loader; streaming table uses checkpoint for incremental reads.

C. Scheduled trigger every 15 minutes; materialized view recomputed fully on each run without checkpoints.

D. Continuous trigger mode with sub-second latency.

actions.text: Now that we've finished with expectations, let's shift to how a pipeline actually behaves when it ships. This page goes deep into triggered mode — the default and by far the most examined mode for the Data Engineer Associate.

Here's the run lifecycle. When a triggered pipeline fires, compute starts up, the engine evaluates the entire pipeline graph in dependency order, refreshes every dataset exactly once, and then shuts the compute down. The key takeaway: you pay only for the run itself, not for idle time. That's the core cost advantage of triggered mode.
So where does the trigger come from? There are three trigger types you need to recognize on the exam: manual, scheduled, and file arrival. Let's walk through each.
Manual is the simplest — a developer clicks 'Run now' in the UI or makes an API call. This is best when you want explicit control, during development, or for ad-hoc backfills.
Scheduled runs on a fixed cadence — every 15 minutes, or a cron expression. The freshness of your data becomes a direct function of how often you schedule the run.
And file arrival fires when new files show up in a source location, typically detected through Auto Loader. Notice how each source gives you a different latency and cost profile.

Now here's a subtle but critical point. Each run is incremental for streaming tables. Source checkpoints mean only new or changed data since the last successful run gets processed — you're not re-reading the whole history.

Materialized views behave differently. They're recomputed from their defining query on the triggered run, so their freshness equals the trigger cadence exactly. Two dataset types, two very different refresh semantics — this is a common exam trap.

So when is triggered mode the best fit? Batch or micro-batch SLAs — nightly finance rollups, hourly BI refreshes — cost-sensitive workloads, and pipelines with no hard sub-minute latency requirement. What's explicitly excluded is anything needing sub-minute latency; for that you'd choose continuous mode.
Let's ground this in a worked example: an hourly BI refresh on a hundred-thousand-row table. Let's see how that plays out across a run.

A scheduled trigger fires every 15 minutes. Between runs the compute is completely off. On each run, the streaming table picks up only the new rows from its checkpoint, while the materialized view recomputes fully from its query. That's exactly the cost and freshness tradeoff we just described, in action.

Before we move on, pause on this checkpoint. The exam loves the distinction between streaming tables and materialized views under triggered mode, so make sure both refresh behaviors are solid in your mind.

Let's test it. A pipeline must ingest new files from an S3 bucket as soon as they land. Which trigger type fits best — manual, scheduled, or file arrival? Think it through before we reveal the answer.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Pipeline Modes and Triggers

questions.question: A customer-facing dashboard requires data no older than 15 minutes, and the source is a continuously growing cloud storage path where new files arrive every few minutes. The engineering team wants the lowest operational cost that still meets the freshness requirement. Which pipeline configuration best satisfies this requirement?

options.label: Continuous mode with an always-on cluster, because only continuous mode can achieve sub-15-minute freshness.
Triggered mode scheduled every few minutes (or a continuous trigger interval), relying on incremental reads so each run processes only new data.
Triggered mode run once per day at midnight, since Declarative Pipelines automatically refresh all downstream materialized views on demand.
Continuous mode is impossible here, so the team must abandon Declarative Pipelines and write a custom streaming job.

questions.analysis: The freshness requirement is a 15-minute SLA, and the data arrives incrementally as new files land in storage. A triggered pipeline scheduled at a matching cadence (or a continuous trigger with an appropriate interval) satisfies the SLA while each update reads only new data, because the engine tracks data dependencies through the pipeline graph and determines where to process incrementally [source 1]. Option A is the classic trap: continuous mode does provide low latency, but it requires an always-on cluster, which is usually the most expensive option and is not required to hit a 15-minute SLA [source 2]. Option C grossly violates the stated freshness requirement. Option D is false — Lakeflow declarative pipelines natively support both batch and streaming patterns in SQL and Python and are the correct tool here [source 3]. Option A also misstates the constraint: continuous mode is not the only way to achieve fresh data.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following statements about Declarative Pipeline modes and triggers are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Pipeline mode (how often data is processed) is a separate decision from deployment mode (development vs. production), and mixing the two concepts up is a common exam error.
A triggered pipeline re-reads all source data from scratch on every run, so its cost grows linearly with total data volume rather than new data volume.
Any pipeline can be switched to continuous mode regardless of its dataset types or sources, because continuous mode is purely a scheduling choice.
Continuous mode requires an always-on cluster, so it is not the automatic default answer just because a dataset is large; triggered mode is often the better fit.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: these are two independent axes, and separating them is a required test point because students frequently treat deployment mode as if it constrained processing frequency. Option D is correct and directly addresses the trap that 'continuous mode is the default for big data.' Continuous mode keeps an always-on cluster, so it is a cost/latency tradeoff, not an automatic choice for volume. Option B is the stated trap and is false: triggered runs are incremental thanks to checkpointing, so they do not re-read all source data each time; the engine determines where to process incrementally and recovers from failures using its dependency graph [source 5]. Option C is also a trap and is false: mode constrains which dataset types and sources are supported, so not every pipeline can simply be flipped to continuous — it is not a pure scheduling toggle [source 2].

questions.question: A team is building a Lakeflow declarative pipeline that ingests a high-volume stream of events (roughly 2 TB per day) into a streaming table, and it must feed a downstream materialized view used by an ML feature table. The team proposes running the pipeline in continuous mode 'because there is a lot of data and we want it fresh fast.' Write a short response that: (a) identifies the two independent decisions being conflated (pipeline mode vs. deployment mode), (b) gives a concrete cost-based argument for or against continuous mode using the ~2 TB/day figure, (c) states at least one precondition or constraint that limits whether continuous mode is even available, and (d) recommends a concrete configuration decision with a one-sentence justification.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (total 20 points): (1) Correctly separates pipeline mode (how often data is processed: triggered vs. continuous) from deployment mode (development vs. production environment) — 5 pts. Must state they are independent axes, not the same decision. (2) Provides a concrete cost/volume argument referencing the ~2 TB/day figure, e.g. continuous mode's always-on cluster runs 24/7 (2 TB/day across 24 hours ≈ 83 GB/hour of ingest), so compute cost is continuous even when little new data arrives; a triggered schedule aligned to actual SLA may cost far less — 5 pts. Deduct 2 pts if the student claims high volume alone mandates continuous mode. (3) States a real precondition/constraint: continuous mode requires an always-on cluster and does not support all dataset types or sources, i.e. mode constrains what is supported — 5 pts. (4) Gives a clear recommended decision with justification, e.g. 'use triggered mode on a schedule matched to the freshness SLA, since incremental checkpointing means each run only processes new data' OR 'use continuous mode only if a sub-minute SLA truly demands it and cost is acceptable' — 5 pts. Deduct 2 pts for any claim that triggered runs re-read all source data. Full credit requires correct use of Databricks terminology (streaming table, materialized view, triggered/continuous mode).
questions.analysis: A strong answer separates the two axes: pipeline mode answers 'how often is data processed?' (triggered vs. continuous), while deployment mode answers 'is this a development or production environment?' — conflating them is a common error. On cost: ~2 TB/day is about 83 GB per hour on average, but continuous mode keeps an always-on cluster running 24/7 regardless of whether new data has arrived, so the argument 'lots of data = continuous' is backwards; a triggered schedule aligned to the actual SLA is typically cheaper and still incremental. Preconditions matter too: continuous mode requires an always-on cluster and does not support every dataset type or source, so it is not a free toggle. Finally, because the engine tracks data dependencies and determines where to process incrementally and how to recover from failures, a triggered run does not re-read all source data — checkpoints make it incremental. The recommended answer is generally triggered mode on a schedule justified by the freshness SLA, reserving continuous mode for cases where the latency requirement genuinely exceeds what a triggered cadence can meet.
