Once you submit, I'll walk you through anything that gave you trouble. Give it your best shot.

scenes.title: Triggered vs Continuous: Choosing Under Real Constraints

elements.content: Dimension  |  Triggered (scheduled) pipelines  |  Continuous pipelines

Freshness and the stale-data window
Triggered (scheduled) pipelines: In a triggered pipeline the data's age is bounded below by the trigger cadence: if the schedule fires every 15 minutes, the freshest possible gold table is at most 15 minutes old plus the run duration, so freshness is a schedule-design parameter you control directly.
Continuous pipelines: In a continuous pipeline the streaming tables refresh as new data arrives and the observable latency is seconds to a few minutes, bounded not by a clock but by micro-batch sizing and source availability, so 'fresh' means 'as fresh as the ingestion path allows' rather than 'as fresh as the cron allows'. The declarative framework still builds the dependency graph, decides where to process incrementally, and recovers from failures on your behalf [source 5].

Compute cost model and idle behavior
Triggered (scheduled) pipelines: Triggered runs bill per run: the cluster starts at the trigger, processes the delta since the last successful update, and terminates, so an idle pipeline costs nothing and total cost scales with the number of runs and volume processed per run.
Continuous pipelines: Continuous runs bill for an always-on cluster, so the monthly cost is approximately cluster_hourly_rate x 24 x days regardless of whether data arrived, and the mode is only economically justified when a hard latency SLA makes the idle hours worth paying for (e.g., a cluster at 4 DBU/hour costs roughly 4 x 24 x 30 = 2,880 DBU per month in idle-only terms).

Setup and operational overhead
Triggered (scheduled) pipelines: Triggered pipelines need a schedule or job trigger plus a policy for overlapping and backfilled runs; configuration effort is mostly scheduling and dependency management, and you configure compute resources, data assets, and trigger modes as explicit advanced options [source 1] [source 2].
Continuous pipelines: Continuous pipelines need always-on compute sized for peak ingest, checkpoint and state management for the streaming sources, and monitoring of an uninterrupted process, which shifts effort from calendar scheduling to cluster-lifetime and state-store operations.

Failure behavior and retry semantics
Triggered (scheduled) pipelines: A failed triggered run is visible as a failed job run; the next scheduled trigger retries the delta, and because the update is incremental, already-committed data is not reprocessed, though a missed SLA window is lost until the next trigger.
Continuous pipelines: Continuous pipelines with automatic retries are a production capability: only the production deployment mode supports continuous pipelines with automatic retries, while development mode is for iteration and not for always-on serving, so a continuous design tested only in development mode will not have the retry guarantee at serve time.

Typical use case
Triggered (scheduled) pipelines: Triggered pipelines fit reporting and analytics where a 15-minute to daily cadence satisfies the consumer, such as nightly silver-to-gold rebuilds or hourly materialized view refreshes, and they are the default when no consumer has a sub-minute latency requirement.
Continuous pipelines: Continuous pipelines fit operational, customer-facing, or event-driven consumers with a hard sub-minute SLA, such as fraud scoring or live dashboards, and are usually paired with expectations so that quarantining or dropping bad records keeps the always-on stream healthy [source 4].

Data-quality enforcement interaction (link to expectations)
Triggered (scheduled) pipelines: In a triggered pipeline a failing expectation aborts one run and the next scheduled trigger retries the delta, so a fail policy costs at most one cadence window of freshness and any dropped rows are deduplicated only on the next successful update.
Continuous pipelines: In a continuous pipeline a fail expectation can stop the always-on process and the outage is immediate, so production stream designs typically favour expect_or_drop for malformed records and reserve expect_or_fail for invariants that must never be served, since the declarative engine enforces expectations and quarantines or drops bad records according to your rules [source 5].

Hybrid pattern and decision rule
Triggered (scheduled) pipelines: The common production pattern is a continuous pipeline for bronze and silver streaming tables feeding a scheduled triggered pipeline that rebuilds gold materialized views, so cost is spent only where latency is required [source 4].
Continuous pipelines: A fully continuous medallion is rarely justified: choose continuous end-to-end only when the consumer's SLA is measured in seconds to low minutes and you can pay for an always-on cluster, otherwise keep the triggered mode for gold and beyond.

Takeaway — Choose triggered when the consumer's SLA is minutes to hours, when idle time should cost nothing, and when a lost cadence window is tolerable; the freshness you get equals the trigger cadence you configure.

Takeaway — Choose continuous only when a hard seconds-to-minutes latency SLA exists and your budget can absorb an always-on cluster, and only deploy it in production mode because automatic retries for continuous pipelines are a production-mode capability, not a development-mode one.

Takeaway — Prefer the hybrid of continuous bronze/silver plus triggered gold materialized views when you need fresh raw and conformed data but can tolerate a scheduled rebuild for analytics-facing tables.

actions.text: Now that we've seen how triggered mode actually behaves, let's put the two modes side by side and decide when each one earns its keep. Start with the dimension that usually forces the decision: freshness. With a triggered pipeline, your data freshness is exactly your trigger cadence — if it runs hourly, you get data that is up to an hour old. It does not refresh the moment new data lands.

Continuous pipelines flip that. A streaming table refreshes as new data arrives, with seconds-to-minutes latency. But notice the trade-off on cost: triggered bills per run and goes quiet when idle, while continuous bills for an always-on cluster. That means continuous has to be justified by a hard latency SLA, not by preference.

Setup and operational overhead tell the same story. With triggered mode, the cluster spins up, does the work, and shuts down — so configuration stays simple and idle cost is basically zero. Continuous pipelines keep a cluster alive around the clock, so they demand more care in sizing and monitoring. That ongoing overhead is real, and it belongs in your decision.

Then there's failure behavior and retry semantics — a favorite exam topic. Only production deployment mode supports continuous pipelines with automatic retries. Development mode is for iteration, not for always-on serving. So if you need continuous with automatic retries, the answer must be production mode.

In practice, most real deployments don't pick one or the other — they pick both. The common hybrid pattern is a continuous pipeline for bronze and silver streaming tables, feeding a scheduled triggered pipeline that rebuilds gold materialized views. You get low-latency ingestion where it matters, and predictable, cost-controlled refresh where it doesn't.

So here's the decision rule to carry into the exam and into production: choose triggered when the consumer's SLA can tolerate the trigger cadence — minutes to hours is fine — and you want predictable, idle-friendly cost. Choose continuous only when a hard seconds-to-minutes SLA truly justifies an always-on cluster, and remember that requires production mode with automatic retries. When in doubt, prefer the hybrid: continuous bronze and silver, triggered gold. Keep this table in mind — it drives several of the exam scenarios we'll work through next.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Selecting Modes and Triggers for Three Pipelines

elements.content: Problem 1

You own three production pipelines in one Databricks workspace, and your team has two hard constraints: every SLA must be met, and compute spend must stay near zero between runs except where an SLA makes that impossible. Pipeline A — the nightly finance rollup: source rows are appended all day, the rollup is rebuilt once per day from the previous day's data, and the finance team's first consumer opens the table at 07:00; the agreed SLA is 'complete and correct by 06:45 daily, one build per day'. Pipeline B — fraud-risk signals: an alerting service polls the output table continuously and the risk team's SLA is 'no emitted signal older than 60 seconds at p99'. Pipeline C — partner ingestion: between 1 and 40 CSV files per day land in a landing volume at unpredictable times, and each file must be ingested and validated within 5 minutes of landing, with no work existing between arrivals. For each pipeline, state (i) the pipeline mode (triggered or continuous), (ii) the trigger type (manual, scheduled, or file arrival), and (iii) the deployment mode and target catalog/schema, and justify each choice with the SLA and the cost constraint. Finally, compare the total daily compute consumption of your design against a naive 'continuous everywhere' design, using a hypothetical cost rate of 1 compute-unit per compute-hour, and assuming A's update takes 45 minutes, B runs 24 hours, and C needs about 1 minute of compute per arrival.

Hint: Ask two separate questions per pipeline: what signal tells you new work exists (a clock, a human, or an external event), and how stale may the output be? The mode follows staleness; the trigger follows the signal.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Split the decision in two. In a Lakeflow declarative pipeline the engine builds a dependency graph from your dataset definitions and determines the execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures, so you never schedule table-by-table work yourself [source 5]. What remains yours to choose is compute behaviour (the pipeline mode) and what starts an update (the trigger) [source 1]. Mode answers 'how stale may the output be'; it is a latency decision with a direct cost consequence. Trigger answers 'what tells the pipeline new work exists'; it is a clock, a human, or an external event. Data volume is not part of either question — volume sizes the cluster, it does not pick the mode.

Step 2 — Pipeline A: staleness budget of one day, delivered as a deadline. There is no consumer between 07:00 and the next build, so continuous mode would run compute for ~24 hours per day to satisfy a requirement that is really 'be finished by 06:45'. Choose triggered mode, scheduled trigger, aligned so the update completes before the deadline: start at 02:00, leaving 4 h 45 min of slack for the worst case. Deploy with the production deployment mode and target the production catalog and schema (for example catalog finance_prod, schema gold) so the schedule, retries, and access controls apply to the artifact finance actually reads; development mode exists for iterating on definitions before promotion [source 2]. Compute is alive only for the ~45-minute update, then terminates, so between-run cost is effectively zero.

Step 3 — Pipeline B: staleness budget of 60 seconds at p99. A triggered pipeline cannot promise this. If the schedule period is T and an update takes R seconds, a row can land just after one update reads its snapshot, so worst-case staleness is approximately $T + R$. Even T = 1 minute with R = 45 seconds gives about 105 seconds > 60 seconds, and overlapping runs cannot repair the gap. The only way to hold 60 seconds at p99 is compute that is already running and processing incrementally, so choose continuous mode with always-on compute, deployed in production mode into the production catalog/schema. This is the single place where the cost constraint is deliberately traded for latency.

Step 4 — Pipeline C: the signal for new work is an external event (a file landing), not a clock. Choose triggered mode with a file-arrival trigger, implemented with Auto Loader detecting new files in the landing volume (a cloudFiles streaming source on a streaming table, with the pipeline's trigger set to file arrival). Auto Loader tracks which files have already been discovered, so each arrival starts one update that processes only the new files, and ingestion begins seconds after landing — comfortably inside the 5-minute SLA — while the pipeline terminates afterwards, keeping compute near zero between arrivals. Deploy in production mode, writing validated output to the production catalog/schema.

Step 5 — Cost check with concrete numbers. Using 1 compute-unit per compute-hour as a hypothetical rate, purely to compare the shapes of consumption:

- A: 45 min = 0.75 compute-hours/day.

- C: worst case 40 arrivals × 1 min = 40 min ≈ 0.67 compute-hours/day.

- B: 24 compute-hours/day (required by its SLA).

Selected design total ≈ 0.75 + 0.67 + 24 = 25.42 compute-hours/day.

Naive 'continuous everywhere' design: 3 × 24 = 72 compute-hours/day.

Saving = (72 − 25.42) / 72 ≈ 64.7%, achieved without breaking any SLA — B keeps its 60-second latency precisely because continuous mode is what its SLA demands.

Analysis — The method works because mode and trigger are answers to two independent questions rather than one 'is this streaming?' question. Freshness SLA determines the mode: a requirement expressed in days or hours is satisfiable by discrete updates, while a requirement expressed in seconds at a percentile is satisfiable only by always-on compute. The signal for new work determines the trigger: a deadline is a clock problem (scheduled), an unpredictable arrival is an event problem (file arrival), and an ad hoc backfill is a human problem (manual). Once you separate the two axes, the three pipelines resolve mechanically and the cost constraint falls out as a consequence rather than a compromise. Note that 'triggered' does not mean 'batch only' — a triggered pipeline can still declare streaming tables and use Auto Loader to process incrementally per update; the mode governs when compute exists, not whether the data is read as a stream [source 3].

Edge cases that break the naive answer. First, SLAs must be read at the right granularity: 'daily by 07:00' is a deadline, not a 24-hour latency, so an hourly or 15-minute schedule is also wrong (it over-provisions) and a 1-minute schedule is absurd. Second, the trigger must be aligned to upstream arrival, not just the deadline: if the source file for A lands at 03:00, a 02:00 start reads an incomplete partition and silently ships a wrong rollup — schedule after the upstream landing, before the deadline. Third, file-arrival triggers require idempotency per file; without Auto Loader's file tracking, a restart or a re-listed directory re-ingests everything. Fourth, the 5-minute SLA for C could also be met by a scheduled trigger with period T satisfying $T + R ≤ 300$ seconds; that is a valid but more expensive design, so the correct answer is the one that satisfies the SLA at the lowest cost, not merely the one that satisfies the SLA. Fifth, these decisions are re-derived when inputs change: if partner arrivals grow to hundreds per minute, the event rate itself becomes the new work signal and continuous mode may become correct for C.

Common mistakes and the certification distractor. The classic distractor is choosing continuous mode for a daily dashboard — paying 24/7 compute for data nobody reads until the morning [source 1]. It sounds modern and it does satisfy the SLA, so a student checking only the SLA will pick it; the cost constraint is what eliminates it. The mirror-image mistake is choosing a schedule for event-driven ingestion, which caps latency at the schedule period and quietly violates the SLA. A third mistake is conflating data velocity with required freshness: high-volume data that is only consumed daily is still a scheduled, triggered pipeline, and low-volume data consumed by a real-time service is still continuous. Finally, forgetting the deployment decision: development mode is for iteration, production deployment mode with an explicit catalog and schema is what the SLA-bound artifact should run under [source 2].
Problem 2

A team runs a nightly revenue dashboard. The source appends rows all day, the dashboard is consumed from 09:00 to 17:00, and the business requirement is only that the morning refresh reflects all data through midnight. The engineer set the pipeline to continuous mode because 'the source is streaming data', and the pipeline was left in development deployment mode. Telemetry shows the continuous pipeline consumes 24 compute-hours per day; a triggered pipeline doing the same transformation completes in 15 minutes. (a) Identify the two configuration errors and explain why each one is wrong. (b) Compute the daily and monthly compute-hour difference between the current configuration and the corrected one, assuming a 30-day month. (c) State the corrected configuration.
Hint: The source being a stream tells you how the data arrives, not how often the consumer needs it. The constraint that matters is the consumer's freshness requirement.

Worked solution
(a) Error 1 — continuous mode for a once-daily consumer. Continuous mode exists to hold a latency SLA measured in seconds; here the requirement is a single deadline (morning refresh, complete through midnight). Nobody reads the table between the refresh and 09:00, so between 09:00 and the next midnight the always-on compute produces rows that no consumer will ever see in that state. Continuous mode is not 'more correct' than triggered mode — it is a latency purchase, and this pipeline has nothing to buy. Error 2 — development deployment mode. Development mode is the iteration mode for building and testing pipeline definitions; production SLAs, the scheduled run cadence, and the governed target catalog/schema belong to the production deployment. Shipping a business-critical refresh under development mode means the artifact the dashboard reads is not the governed production artifact [source 2].

(b) Cost arithmetic. Continuous baseline: 24 compute-hours/day. Corrected triggered pipeline: 15 minutes = 0.25 compute-hours/day. Daily difference = 24 − 0.25 = 23.75 compute-hours/day saved. Monthly difference = 23.75 × 30 = 712.5 compute-hours saved per month. As a percentage, the corrected design uses 0.25 / 24 ≈ 1.04% of the original compute, a reduction of ≈ 98.96%.

(c) Corrected configuration: pipeline mode = triggered; trigger = scheduled, firing once per day early enough that the 15-minute update finishes well before 09:00 and after the midnight data is complete (for example 04:00); deployment mode = production, with an explicit production catalog and schema as the target; the transformation itself keeps its streaming table declarations — the mode change does not require rewriting the pipeline as a batch job, because a triggered pipeline still processes streaming sources incrementally per update [source 3].

Analysis — The point of this exercise is to make the student distinguish the velocity of the data from the freshness the consumer actually needs. The engine builds the dependency graph and decides execution order, incremental processing, and failure recovery regardless of which trigger you attach, so the trigger setting is purely a question of when compute exists [source 5]. Continuous mode is justified only when the cost of staleness exceeds the cost of always-on compute; on a nightly dashboard it never does.

Edge cases worth noting. A 'nightly' job is not automatically safe: if the source's last rows for the previous day land at 02:30, a 01:00 schedule produces a rollup missing the previous evening, and the dashboard is confidently wrong at 09:00 — a silent correctness failure that no amount of compute savings excuses. Likewise, switching from continuous to triggered can change the shape of downstream processing: a streaming table fed by an event-driven trigger processes bounded micro-batches per update rather than a continuous stream, which is fine for a dashboard but would matter if a downstream consumer expected second-level latency. Where a pipeline writes a materialized view (a precomputed, incrementally refreshed result table) the refresh inherits the pipeline's trigger, so the freshness of the view is bounded by the trigger period — this is exactly why the trigger choice must be derived from the consumer SLA rather than from engineering habit.

The common mistakes mirror certification distractors precisely. Distractor 1: 'the source is streaming, therefore continuous mode' — conflates arrival mechanism with required latency. Distractor 2: 'always choose triggered to save cost' — fails on the fraud-signal pipeline, where a 60-second p99 SLA makes continuous the only correct answer, so neither mode is universally right. Distractor 3: leaving the pipeline in development mode after promotion, which decouples the tested definition from the governed production artifact [source 2]. Distractor 4: changing the mode and forgetting the schedule alignment to upstream arrival, which converts a cost problem into a correctness problem.
Problem 3

Pipeline C ingests partner files that land unpredictably in a landing volume. Each file must be ingested and validated within 5 minutes (300 seconds) of landing; an update takes about R = 60 seconds of compute; the pipeline is triggered, so no compute exists between runs. (a) If you insisted on a scheduled trigger instead of a file-arrival trigger, derive the maximum schedule period T that still satisfies the SLA, and explain the margin problem at that value. (b) Choose a period with at least 60 seconds of worst-case margin and compute the number of daily runs and the daily compute-hours it implies. (c) Compute the daily compute-hours for the file-arrival design with 40 arrivals per day at 1 minute of compute each, and compute the percentage saving. (d) Compare the latency profiles of the two designs and state which you would ship and why.
Hint: Model worst-case staleness as the schedule period plus the update runtime: a row or file can arrive just after one run has read its inputs, so only the next run picks it up.

Worked solution
(a) Model worst-case staleness. With a schedule of period T and an update runtime R, a file that lands immediately after a run has started waits until the next run plus the runtime of that run, so worst-case staleness ≈ $T + R$. Requiring $T + R ≤ 300$ seconds with R = 60 gives $T ≤ 240$ seconds = 4 minutes. At T = 4 minutes the design sits exactly on the SLA boundary with zero margin: any variance in runtime — a larger file, a slower cluster start, a retried micro-batch — pushes worst-case staleness past 300 seconds and the SLA is breached. A boundary-tight schedule is therefore not a production design even though the arithmetic works.

(b) Period with margin. Applying a 60-second margin means $T + R + 60 ≤ 300$, so $T ≤ 180$ seconds = 3 minutes. Choose T = 3 minutes. Daily runs = 1440 / 3 = 480 runs per day. At roughly 1 minute of compute per run (the 60-second update), daily compute = 480 × 1 min = 480 min = 8 compute-hours/day. Worst-case staleness at this setting is about 3 min + 1 min = 240 seconds, i.e. 60 seconds inside the SLA.

(c) File-arrival design. With 40 arrivals per day and 1 minute of compute per triggered update, daily compute = 40 × 1 min = 40 min ≈ 0.67 compute-hours/day. Saving versus the 3-minute schedule = (8 − 0.67) / 8 = 7.33 / 8 ≈ 91.6%, and versus the tight 4-minute schedule (360 runs × 1 min = 6 compute-hours/day) the saving is (6 − 0.67) / 6 ≈ 88.8%.

(d) Latency comparison. File arrival: detection plus update start is seconds, so typical staleness is well under a minute and worst case is roughly R plus detection overhead — far inside 300 seconds even with a 60-second update. Scheduled: average staleness is approximately T/2 + R ≈ 90 + 60 = 150 seconds at T = 3 minutes, and worst case 240 seconds, so the SLA is met but with a design that spends 12 × more compute and still delivers worse freshness. Ship the file-arrival trigger with Auto Loader: it starts work exactly when work exists, it is roughly an order of magnitude cheaper, and its latency distribution dominates the schedule's. Note that the file-arrival trigger is a mode-and-trigger choice layered on top of the same declarative dataset definitions, so the transformations, expectations, and dependency graph are unchanged [source 5][source 3].

Analysis — This problem makes the cost-versus-latency trade-off explicit instead of leaving it qualitative. The key modelling move is writing worst-case staleness as $T + R$ rather than T alone; forgetting R is the single most common error, because a schedule that fires every 5 minutes does not deliver 5-minute freshness when each run takes 60 seconds. The second move is noticing that satisfying an SLA at the boundary (T = 4 minutes here) is not the same as satisfying it robustly, and that a certification answer keyed on 'meets the SLA' will still prefer margin where the cost is unchanged.

Edge cases. If the update runtime R itself grows past the SLA budget — say R = 320 seconds with a 300-second SLA — no schedule period can fix the problem, because even a zero-period schedule fails; the fix is making the update faster (fewer files per update, smaller cluster-to-data ratio, Photon-enabled compute, or filtered/partitioned reads) or moving to continuous mode so the SLA is met by an always-running process. A second edge case is arrival clustering: if 30 files land within one minute, a file-arrival trigger may coalesce them into a single update, so the per-arrival compute assumption in (c) understates or overstates cost depending on the trigger's batching behaviour — the correct approach is to measure the coalesced update count, not the raw file count. A third edge case is a duplicate-arrival storm from a partner retry; Auto Loader's file tracking prevents reprocessing and therefore prevents the cost model from being invalidated, but only if the landing path is the same path the stream is tracking.

Common mistakes. Distractor 1: treating the schedule period as the freshness guarantee, ignoring runtime. Distractor 2: choosing continuous mode for C to 'guarantee' freshness, which pays 24 compute-hours/day to beat a 5-minute SLA that file arrival already meets for under one compute-hour. Distractor 3: assuming that because files arrive unpredictably, the pipeline must be event-driven in mode as well as trigger — mode and trigger are independent, and triggered mode with a file-arrival trigger is the combination that satisfies both the SLA and the near-zero-between-runs cost constraint. Distractor 4: picking the 4-minute schedule because it is the largest period that satisfies the SLA, which is mathematically correct but leaves zero tolerance for runtime variance [source 1][source 2].

actions.text: Now let's put the mode-and-trigger decision into practice. This worked problem gives you three pipelines with very different freshness SLAs, and your job is to pick the right mode and trigger for each. This is exactly the pattern the exam tests, so follow along closely.

Here are the three pipelines. Pipeline A rebuilds a nightly finance rollup that's read at 07:00. Pipeline B emits fraud-risk signals that must be at most one minute stale. And Pipeline C must begin ingesting the moment a file lands in the landing zone. Notice how each one gives you a different freshness requirement.

Before solving, here's the method. Ask two separate questions per pipeline: what is the freshness SLA, and what signal tells you new work has arrived? The first question drives the mode; the second drives the trigger type. Keep those two questions in mind as we work through each case.

Now the worked solution. Pipeline A is triggered with a scheduled trigger aligned to the nightly window, running in production deployment mode. Pipeline B needs continuous mode with always-on compute in production. Pipeline C is triggered with a file-arrival trigger — that's Auto Loader detecting new files. In each case the trigger type matches what signals new work.

Here's why this method works. The mode comes from the freshness SLA, not from data volume. The trigger comes from what signals new work — a clock or an external event. And the pitfall to avoid is choosing continuous mode for a daily dashboard, which pays 24/7 compute for data nobody reads until the morning. That's a classic distractor on certification questions.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Deployment Targets and Modes

questions.question: A team defines one Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline whose settings specify the target catalog "analytics_prod" and the target schema "silver". Downstream, the same pipeline also declares a materialized view named gold_orders_mv. A developer opens the Unity Catalog explorer after a successful run and searches only inside analytics_prod.silver, but cannot find gold_orders_mv anywhere under that schema. Which statement best explains where each dataset is actually registered?

options.label: Every dataset in the pipeline is registered under the pipeline-level target catalog and schema, so gold_orders_mv must appear as analytics_prod.silver.gold_orders_mv and the search simply missed it.
Only streaming tables use the pipeline-level target; materialized views inherit the schema of the source table they read from, so gold_orders_mv lives wherever its upstream table lives.

All datasets in the pipeline are registered under the pipeline-level target catalog and schema unless a dataset explicitly overrides its own catalog and schema, so gold_orders_mv would be analytics_prod.silver.gold_orders_mv unless the definition sets different values.
Materialized views are never registered in Unity Catalog; they exist only inside the pipeline's own storage account and cannot be queried from SQL, which is why the explorer shows nothing.

questions.analysis: The deployment target (catalog + schema) is a property of the pipeline as a whole, not of an individual dataset, and every dataset the pipeline produces lands there by default; a dataset can only escape that default by explicitly declaring its own catalog and schema in its definition. Option A is wrong because it asserts the outcome dogmatically without acknowledging the override mechanism, and it treats the search as the problem rather than the inheritance rule. Option B inverts the semantics: materialized views do not inherit a schema from upstream tables; they inherit the pipeline's target. Option D reflects a common misconception that materialized views live outside Unity Catalog, but Lakeflow registers them as governed Unity Catalog objects. Recall that a pipeline's settings cover "data assets, trigger modes, and other advanced options" as whole-pipeline properties [source 1].

questions.question: A data engineering team is preparing a pipeline for a customer-facing dashboard and must choose a deployment mode. Select all statements that correctly describe the operational difference between development mode and production mode. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Development mode runs on isolated compute sized for fast iteration, so a developer can validate logic quickly without competing for the production cluster's capacity.
Production mode uses configured compute and applies automatic retries, so transient failures in a scheduled run do not immediately require human intervention.
Development mode and production mode are the same field as pipeline mode (triggered vs continuous); choosing continuous mode automatically puts the pipeline into production mode.
Production mode is the intended runtime for workflow/Jobs scheduling or Databricks Asset Bundles deployment, whereas development mode is optimized for a single engineer iterating interactively.

questions.analysis: Development mode prioritizes fast iteration on isolated compute, while production mode uses configured compute with automatic retries and is the mode used when the pipeline is deployed through Jobs or Databricks Asset Bundles. Option C is the central trap of this checkpoint: pipeline mode (triggered vs continuous) controls processing cadence, whereas deployment mode controls runtime behaviour and reliability; conflating the two is a real student error because both appear as pipeline-level fields in the settings UI. The course frames these as whole-pipeline settings alongside trigger modes and compute configuration [source 1], and the production story explicitly includes "scheduling options, and enabling pipeline event logging to monitor pipeline performance and health" [source 2].

questions.question: Give one concrete reason why a team should keep Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline dataset definitions (streaming tables, materialized views, expectations) in version control rather than authoring and editing them only in the workspace UI. In your answer, name the deployment mechanism you would pair with version control and explain how it preserves the production configuration. Additionally, state one operational setting that must be explicitly preserved by that mechanism and why it matters for reliability.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric (total 100%): (1) Identification of a valid versioning/CI benefit — 40%. Accept any of: review of changes before they reach production, ability to roll back to a known-good definition, diffable history of who changed an expectation and when, reproducibility of environments. A vague answer like "so we don't lose it" earns partial credit. (2) Explicit naming of Databricks Asset Bundles (or an equivalent Jobs-based deployment invoking the pipeline from a bundle/repo) as the deployment mechanism — 30%. Naming only "Git" with no deployment mechanism earns half of this portion. (3) Preservation of a specific production setting with justification — 30%. Strong answers cite production deployment mode (which carries automatic retries on configured compute) and/or the Unity Catalog target catalog/schema, and/or trigger configuration (schedule or file arrival). Answers should note that if these are only typed into the UI, a UI-only change is invisible to review and can silently regress production reliability — e.g., a pipeline quietly reverted to development mode loses automatic retries and runs on isolated compute.
questions.analysis: A strong answer links three ideas: (a) definitions and expectations are code-like artifacts whose history matters, (b) Databricks Asset Bundles (or an equivalent Jobs deployment) is the supported path to promote them through environments, and (c) production deployment mode plus its configured compute and retries, along with the pipeline's target catalog and schema, are whole-pipeline settings that must be captured in the bundle so promoting the code does not silently change runtime behaviour. Teams that edit only in the workspace UI lose the ability to review and roll back expectation changes, which matters because expectations govern whether malformed records reach a compliance-sensitive dataset. The course positions "putting a pipeline into production, including scheduling options, and enabling pipeline event logging" as a distinct concern from the dataset definitions themselves [source 2], and treats compute, data assets, and trigger modes as pipeline-level configuration [source 1].

actions.text: Let's put what we just covered to the test. Take your time and work through each one on your own — try to answer from your own understanding before you submit.
Once you've submitted, I'll walk through anything that gave you trouble and we'll sort out the sticking points together.

scenes.title: Deploying with Unity Catalog: Target Catalog and Schema

elements.content: Deploying with Unity Catalog: Target Catalog and Schema
One pipeline → exactly one target catalog and one target schema. Publishing registers every dataset in Unity Catalog.
Target binding & publication

• One target catalog + one target schema per pipeline

• Datasets publish as managed tables and views

• Full column-level lineage: source → consumption

• No manual DDL or CREATE TABLE required

• Example: catalog prod, schema sales_gold → prod.sales_gold.daily_orders [source 3]
Governance & ownership

• Access via Unity Catalog grants

• USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, SELECT, MODIFY

• Applied to owner or service principal

• Running a pipeline never bypasses grants

• One pipeline owns its schema — two writers can conflict [source 5]
Development mode uses an isolated on-demand cluster and does not auto-retry failures. Production mode uses the compute policy and retries failed runs. [source 1]

actions.text: Now that we understand modes and triggers, let's talk about where a pipeline actually lands its data. This is the deployment side of the picture: binding your pipeline to a Unity Catalog target.

The title here says it directly — Deploying with Unity Catalog. When you configure a pipeline, you specify a target catalog and a target schema, and that becomes the governed home for everything the pipeline produces.

The rule to memorize: one pipeline maps to exactly one target catalog and one target schema. Every dataset the pipeline declares is published into that single location and registered in Unity Catalog automatically. No manual DDL, no CREATE TABLE — the datasets simply appear as managed tables and views with full column-level lineage.

Let's look at target binding and publication more closely. Because one pipeline owns its target schema, two pipelines writing to the same schema can conflict. So the design principle is simple: separate consumers get separate pipelines, or at least separate schemas. This also means development mode uses an isolated on-demand cluster that does not automatically retry failures — that's for iteration — while production mode uses the configured compute policy and retries failed runs.

Finally, governance and ownership. Access is controlled entirely by Unity Catalog grants — USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, SELECT, and MODIFY — applied to the pipeline's owner or its service principal. Know this exam trap well: running a pipeline never bypasses Unity Catalog permissions. The pipeline runs with exactly the privileges its identity has, nothing more.

So in summary: one pipeline, one target catalog and schema; datasets auto-registered with lineage; dev mode is isolated and non-retrying while prod mode retries; keep one owner per schema; and every access path is still gated by Unity Catalog grants. Next, we'll decide when you need one pipeline versus two for dev and prod.

scenes.title: One Pipeline or Two? Deploying Dev and Prod

elements.content: Decision — A four-person data platform team has built a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline that reads raw order events, lands them in a bronze layer, cleans them into a silver table, and materializes a gold revenue aggregate consumed by a customer-facing dashboard. The pipeline works. Now the team must decide how to deploy it so that developers can keep iterating on the silver transformation rules without ever endangering the production tables that finance reconciles against. The difficulty is that the pipeline is a single declarative artifact: the same source repository defines every dataset, and Lakeflow derives the execution order for the whole pipeline graph at run time, so there is no natural built-in boundary between 'the code I am editing' and 'the data my customers are reading' [source 5]. The team must also respect the unit's earlier distinction between pipeline mode (triggered versus continuous) and deployment mode or target (which catalog and schema the datasets publish into); those are properties of the pipeline as a whole, not of any individual dataset, which means the choice made here propagates to every table the graph produces. The team has six weeks before the finance team's quarterly close, the production workspace already carries a Unity Catalog catalog with a governed revenue schema, and the operations budget covers roughly one full-time engineer's attention for pipeline maintenance, no more.

Constraints — Production datasets must be protected from developer mistakes: no manual or misconfigured run may write into the production catalog and schema.  •  Iteration must stay fast and cheap: developers need a place to re-run the graph many times a day, including full refreshes, without paying for production-scale compute or waiting on review.  •  Pipeline definitions must remain reproducible and reviewable: the same source repository is the single source of truth, and any promotion into production must be an auditable, repeatable action rather than an ad-hoc click.  •  The operational budget is one small team: at most a modest amount of extra configuration is tolerable, and anything requiring a dedicated operations role is out of scope.  •  Data-quality expectations must remain enforced identically in both environments so that a rule verified in development means the same thing in production [source 6].

Option A — One pipeline with a parameterised target schema switched by deployment mode
+ Minimal setup: a single pipeline definition with one configurable catalog/schema parameter, so there is nothing to keep in sync between two artifacts.; + Lowest cost and lowest cognitive load, because there is exactly one pipeline object to schedule, monitor, and reason about.; + Developers can flip the parameter and immediately see the production code path, which makes deployment-mode behaviour easy to inspect in a demo.
− A single misconfigured run — a forgotten parameter override, a stale job definition, or a developer running the pipeline interactively — writes directly into the production schema, which is precisely the failure the constraint forbids.; − There is no promotion step to audit: the difference between development and production is a runtime parameter, so the source-control history does not show what was promoted or when.; − Concurrent development and production runs contend for the same pipeline definition, so editing a transformation to test it changes the artifact production executes.
Best for: Throwaway exploration, demos, and internal pipelines whose target data nobody reconciles against — acceptable only where a mistaken production write is merely annoying, not a governance incident.

Option B — Separate development and production pipelines built from the same source repository, each with its own target catalog
+ Full isolation: the development pipeline publishes to a development catalog and the production pipeline publishes to the governed production catalog, so no run in development can reach production tables.; + A clean, auditable promotion path: the same source repository feeds both pipelines, so promotion is a reviewable source-control action plus a production pipeline update, and the deployment history is visible in version control.; + Development runs can use cheaper compute and full refreshes on a schedule of their own choosing, satisfying the fast-iteration constraint without touching the always-on cost profile of production.; + Expectation definitions are shared because they live in the same repository, so a rule validated in development is the same rule that gates production [source 6].
− Extra configuration to maintain: two pipeline objects, two target catalogs, two sets of permissions, and a convention that keeps their parameters aligned as the graph evolves.; − Promotion is a deliberate two-step action (merge, then update the production pipeline), which adds latency compared with simply re-running one pipeline against a different parameter.; − Drift risk: if a developer edits only the development pipeline's parameters or datasets, the two pipelines can silently diverge until the next promotion reconciles them.
Best for: Any pipeline whose outputs are consumed by other people or systems and whose definitions must be reviewable — the normal case for production data engineering work.

Option C — One pipeline writing straight to production, with developers using manual runs
+ Simplest possible arrangement: one pipeline, one target, no environment parameters and no second artifact to keep aligned.; + Developers never wonder which catalog they are pointed at, because there is only one answer.
− There is no safe place to iterate, so every experiment — including a deliberately broken EXPECT predicate used to see how a hard gate behaves — executes against the production schema [source 5].; − There is no promotion process at all, so nothing in the source-control or pipeline history records when a change became live, violating the reproducibility constraint outright.; − Manual runs by developers are indistinguishable from scheduled production runs in the event log, which destroys the audit trail the team needs to attribute a bad batch to a change.
Best for: Nothing in a governed environment; it is defensible only for a single-developer sandbox whose output is never consumed downstream.

Recommendation: Option B — Separate development and production pipelines built from the same source repository, each with its own target catalog — Two of the stated constraints are absolute rather than graded: production datasets must be unreachable from developer activity, and promotion must be reproducible and reviewable. Option A fails the first because its isolation is a runtime parameter on a shared pipeline object — one forgotten override and a development run writes into the governed production schema — and it fails the second because a parameter flip leaves no promotion event in source control. Option C fails both constraints by construction and additionally destroys the event-log attribution the team relies on to diagnose bad batches. Option B is the only candidate that satisfies all five constraints simultaneously: separate target catalogs give hard isolation, the shared source repository plus an explicit production pipeline update gives an auditable promotion path, development compute can be smaller and freely refreshed, and expectations remain textually identical across environments because they are declared once in the repository [source 5][source 6]. Its cost — a second pipeline object and a permission model per catalog — is bounded configuration that a four-person team can maintain inside its operations budget, whereas the cost of Option A is an unbounded risk of a production write. This matches the unit's broader principle that deployment mode is a property of the pipeline as a whole and that a development/production mode switch is not a substitute for a genuinely separate non-production target.

actions.text: Now that we've settled deployment targets and modes, here's a decision you'll actually face on the job: when you deploy a pipeline to both development and production, do you build one pipeline or two? Let's work through this together.

Here's the scenario. A four-person data platform team has built a Lakeflow pipeline and now needs to run it in both development and production. Everything else about the design flows from how we answer that one question.

Before we choose, let's pin down the constraints. Production datasets must be protected from developer mistakes. Iteration needs to stay fast and cheap. Pipeline definitions must remain reproducible and reviewable through version control. And a small team simply can't afford heavy operational overhead. Those four constraints are the lens we judge every option through.

Option A is a single pipeline with a parameterised target schema, switched by deployment mode. It's minimal setup and the lowest cost, but there's the rub — one misconfigured run can write straight into the production schema. You're relying on configuration discipline to protect your most important data.

Option B keeps separate development and production pipelines built from the same source repository, each with its own target catalog. You get full isolation and a clean promotion path, at the cost of a small amount of extra configuration to maintain.

Option C is one pipeline writing straight to production, with developers running it manually. It's simple, but notice what's missing: there's no safe place to iterate and no promotion process you can audit. For a certification question, that absence of an auditable promotion path is almost always a disqualifier.

So the recommendation is Option B. Isolation and a reproducible promotion path outweigh the extra configuration for a team shipping to production. Option A stays acceptable only for throwaway exploration, and remember — the development/production deployment mode is not a substitute for a separate non-production target. That distinction shows up in exams, so hold onto it: one pipeline or two comes down to isolation and auditability, and for production work, that's Option B.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Pipeline Modes, Triggers, and Deployment

questions.question: A team defines one Lakeflow declarative pipeline with `target = "prod"` and `catalog = "retail"`. They now need the same transformation logic to also write a physically separate copy of every dataset into `retail_sandbox.sandbox` for ad-hoc analysts, refreshed by the same pipeline run. According to how deployment target is configured on a pipeline, which statement is correct? (Choose one.)

options.label: They can simply add `sandbox` to a list of target schemas on the pipeline; one pipeline can deploy to several target schemas simultaneously.

This is not possible in a single pipeline: a pipeline has one target catalog and one target schema, so a second physical copy requires a second pipeline (or a downstream consumer) pointed at the other schema.
It works only if they set the deployment mode to development, because development mode allows multiple target schemas per pipeline.
It works only if they set the deployment mode to production, because production mode replicates each dataset into every schema that the Unity Catalog metastore contains.

questions.analysis: Deployment target (catalog + schema) is a property of the pipeline as a whole, not of an individual dataset in the graph, and a pipeline resolves to a single target catalog and schema. Option A is the classic trap: 'you can deploy one pipeline to several target schemas simultaneously' is false. Options C and D invert the meaning of development vs production deployment mode, which controls isolation and retry/optimization behaviour, not the number of physical write targets. Because the declarative engine derives one dependency graph and lands its datasets in one namespace, producing a second materialized copy in another schema means a separate pipeline (or a downstream job reading the first output). [source 5] and [source 2] both frame the pipeline as a declarative framework whose assets, trigger modes, and compute are configured at the pipeline level. [source 3] reinforces that the pipeline is the unit of declaration for batch and streaming assets. [source 4] is relevant because CDC and streaming-table semantics assume one governed destination per dataset.

questions.question: An engineer toggles a pipeline from production deployment mode to development deployment mode to iterate faster. Which of the following statements correctly describe the resulting behaviour? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Automatic retries are disabled, so a transient task failure surfaces immediately instead of being retried by the pipeline's retry policy.
The pipeline runs on isolated compute that is dedicated to that development session rather than sharing the production pipeline's cluster.
Unity Catalog permissions are bypassed during development runs, so the developer can read and write any table without grants.
Development mode changes the trigger type from scheduled to continuous so that developers always see the freshest data.

questions.analysis: Development mode is the fast-iteration configuration: it disables automatic retries so failures are visible immediately, and it runs on isolated compute so a developer's experiments cannot contend with or destabilise the production pipeline's resources. Option C is the second classic trap — 'pipeline runs bypass Unity Catalog permissions' is false. A pipeline runs with the identity and grants of its owner or service principal in every deployment mode, so development mode does not grant the developer access they do not already have; the opposite is true, and a missing grant will fail the run. Option D confuses dimensions: deployment mode (development vs production) is orthogonal to pipeline mode (triggered vs continuous) and to trigger type. [source 5] and [source 2] both describe configuring pipeline compute resources, data assets, and trigger modes as pipeline-level settings, which is exactly why an isolation/retry setting such as deployment mode must be reasoned about separately from the trigger.

questions.question: A fraud-risk pipeline must emit signals that are at most one minute stale at all times, and the operations team insists that a task-level failure must be retried automatically without human intervention. Which combination of pipeline mode, trigger, and deployment mode satisfies these requirements as a single coherent pipeline? (Choose one.)

options.label: Triggered mode + scheduled trigger every 1 minute + development deployment mode.
Triggered mode + file-arrival trigger + production deployment mode.
Continuous mode + always-on compute + production deployment mode, with the streaming tables refreshing as new data arrives.
Continuous mode + manual trigger + development deployment mode.

questions.analysis: A hard one-minute latency bound is the textbook justification for continuous mode: streaming tables refresh as new data arrives with seconds-to-minutes latency, and the pipeline holds an always-on cluster, which is precisely why continuous mode is billed for idle time and must be justified by a latency SLA. Option A looks superficially plausible because '1 minute' matches the cadence, but (i) development deployment mode disables automatic retries, directly violating the retry requirement, and (ii) a scheduled trigger equal to the freshness bound gives no headroom, so any run longer than a minute breaks the SLA. Option B is wrong on the trigger: file arrival restarts only when a file lands, so quiet periods produce stale output with no upper bound. Option D is internally inconsistent — continuous mode is not driven by a manual trigger, and development mode again removes automatic retries. [source 5] and [source 1] establish that dependencies, execution order, incremental processing, and failure recovery are derived by the declarative engine from the graph, which is why mode, trigger, and compute must be chosen together.

questions.question:
A colleague proposes the following design for a customer-facing pipeline: 'I will declare one Lakeflow pipeline, set it to development deployment mode so I can keep iterating, give it a scheduled trigger every 15 minutes to meet the freshness SLA, and point it at both `prod.gold` and `analytics.features` so that one run writes both copies. Then Unity Catalog does not matter, because pipeline runs bypass permissions anyway.'

Identify every incorrect or unsafe claim in this proposal, state the correct behaviour for each one, and explain how the corrections interact. Ground your answer in how the pipeline's settings are configured and how Unity Catalog governs pipeline execution.
questions.commentPrompt:
Grading rubric (100 points total):
(1) Target schema claim — 30 points. Must state that a pipeline has a single target catalog and single target schema, and that deploying one pipeline to several target schemas simultaneously is impossible; a second physical copy requires a second pipeline or a downstream consumer. Award full credit only if the correct fix is given, not just the identification of the error.
(2) Deployment mode claim — 25 points. Must state that development deployment mode disables automatic retries and runs on isolated compute, so it is inappropriate for a production SLA; production deployment mode should be used. Full credit requires an explicit link between 'no automatic retries' and the reliability risk for a customer-facing 15-minute refresh.
(3) Unity Catalog permissions claim — 25 points. Must state that pipeline runs do NOT bypass Unity Catalog permissions; the pipeline runs with the identity and grants of its owner or service principal. Full credit requires mentioning that missing grants cause run failures rather than being silently ignored.
(4) Freshness/auditability claim — 15 points. Should note that a 15-minute scheduled trigger satisfies freshness only if each run completes well within 15 minutes, and that event logging should be enabled to verify performance and health.
(5) Clarity, structure, and correct Databricks terminology (pipeline mode vs deployment mode vs trigger) — 5 points. Deduct for conflating deployment mode with pipeline mode or trigger type, or for describing the settings as per-dataset rather than pipeline-level.
questions.analysis: Model answer. (1) Target: deployment target is a property of the pipeline as a whole, so one pipeline resolves to exactly one target catalog and one target schema; the proposed dual-target run is invalid. Correct fix: keep `prod.gold` on the production pipeline and create a second pipeline (or a downstream consumer) for `analytics.features`. (2) Deployment mode: development mode disables automatic retries and uses isolated compute, so it must not be relied on for a customer-facing 15-minute SLA; switch to production deployment mode so failures are retried and the run uses governed production compute. (3) Permissions: the claim that runs bypass Unity Catalog is false. The pipeline executes with the identity and grants of its owner or service principal in all deployment modes, so every source and destination table it touches needs a valid grant; an ungranted table causes the run to fail rather than being ignored. (4) Freshness: a scheduled trigger every 15 minutes meets the SLA only if each triggered run (start compute, evaluate the graph in dependency order, refresh once, stop) completes inside the window; enable pipeline event logging so run durations and failures are observable. (5) These corrections interact: production deployment mode restores retries and governed production compute, the single-target rule forces a second pipeline for the feature copy, and Unity Catalog grants must be issued to the pipeline's owner or service principal for both pipelines before either can succeed. [source 5] and [source 2] both state that the engine builds the dependency graph and that compute resources, data assets, and trigger modes are configured as pipeline-level advanced options; [source 1] confirms that scheduling and pipeline event logging are the mechanisms used to put a pipeline into production and monitor its performance and health; [source 4] supports the Unity Catalog assumption because CDC and streaming assets are written under governed namespaces.
