scenes.title: Worked Problem: Deploying an Orders Pipeline Step by Step

elements.content: Problem 1

Your team is promoting the orders_pipeline from the previous lesson to production. The pipeline declares exactly three datasets: orders_bronze, a streaming table fed by Auto Loader from abfss://landing@acmeorders.dfs.core.windows.net/orders/; orders_silver, a materialized view carrying the data-quality expectations; and orders_gold, a materialized view that rolls the orders up by order date and region. The deployment requirement is that every dataset must be queryable as prod_catalog.sales.<dataset_name>, with no path-based access anywhere in the BI layer. (a) Write the two target settings the pipeline needs. (b) Give the fully qualified name of each dataset after deployment. (c) Explain what breaks if the target is left unset. (d) Explain what breaks if a second pipeline, returns_pipeline, is pointed at the same target schema.
Hint: The target is a property of the pipeline as a whole, not of an individual dataset in the graph — set it once and every declared dataset inherits it.

Worked solution
(a) Set the pipeline target catalog to prod_catalog and the pipeline target schema to sales. In the pipeline settings these appear as Target catalog and Target schema; both are deployment-scope properties rather than per-dataset options.

(b) Unity Catalog names objects with a three-level namespace, catalog.schema.object, so the pipeline's declared names become the third level. After deployment the three datasets are:

- prod_catalog.sales.orders_bronze

- prod_catalog.sales.orders_silver

- prod_catalog.sales.orders_gold

You never write CREATE TABLE statements for them. The pipeline is declarative: the engine builds a dependency graph from your definitions and determines execution order, where to process incrementally, and how to recover from failures, then publishes each output and auto-registers it in Unity Catalog [source 5]. Lakeflow pipelines provide that declarative framework for building batch and streaming data pipelines in SQL and Python [source 3], which is exactly why the target, not the DDL, is what fixes the physical location of the data.

(c) If the target is left unset, each dataset lands in the pipeline's default location — the developer's own default catalog and schema, or a pipeline-scoped internal schema — instead of prod_catalog.sales. The run still succeeds, so nothing obvious fails on the surface, but every BI query written against prod_catalog.sales.orders_gold returns nothing, and the lineage for the promoted pipeline is split across two namespaces: development lineage under one name and production lineage under another. Promotion from dev to prod therefore silently becomes a consumer-rewrite project rather than a configuration change.

(d) If returns_pipeline is pointed at the same target schema, prod_catalog.sales ends up with two independent writers. Ownership of the schema can only belong to one principal, so the second pipeline's service principal either cannot create its objects or, worse, is granted enough privilege to overwrite objects the first pipeline believes it owns. A refresh of orders_pipeline and a refresh of returns_pipeline can then race on the same names, and a table that one pipeline recreates can invalidate the expectations and downstream consumers configured for the other. The deployment rule is one target schema per writing pipeline: confirm the schema is owned by this one pipeline and that no other pipeline writes to it.

Analysis — This problem isolates the first of the three remaining deployment decisions: where the output lives. The reason the target is a pipeline-level setting is architectural rather than stylistic. Because a declarative pipeline infers its execution graph from dataset definitions [source 5], the only place left to specify physical placement is the pipeline itself; there is no per-table CREATE statement to edit. Students typically go wrong in three ways. First, they assume a successful run means the objects were published to the requested catalog, when in fact a pipeline happily publishes to whatever default it inherits. Second, they confuse the target schema with the pipeline's workspace folder, which stores source code and logs, not data. Third, they treat schema sharing as harmless because the two pipelines write different table names — but ownership, permissions, and refresh cadence are all schema-scoped, so sharing a schema couples two pipelines that should be independent. The generalization is the promotion pattern: keep one pipeline definition, change only the target between development and production, and never let a schema have more than one writing pipeline.
Problem 2

The orders_pipeline must satisfy three constraints at once: (i) a customer-facing dashboard whose contract says no value it displays may be more than 40 minutes old; (ii) a budget ceiling of 15 DBU per day for this pipeline; (iii) an operations rule that a failed scheduled run must be retried automatically rather than waiting for a human. The graph bronze -> silver -> gold runs in 6 minutes of wall-clock time on the compute selected by the configured cluster policy, which provisions one driver and two workers. The driver is billed at 0.5 DBU/hour and each worker at 0.75 DBU/hour. (a) Choose the pipeline mode, the trigger type and cadence, and the deployment mode. (b) Compute the worst-case data staleness for a clean run. (c) Compute the worst-case staleness when the first attempt aborts after 1 minute, there is a 2-minute delay before an automatic retry, and the retry runs the full 6 minutes; then compute it again if the retry policy allowed a second retry with the same delays. (d) Compute the daily DBU cost of your configuration, the daily cost of the always-on alternative, and the ratio between them. (e) State what changes if the dashboard contract were tightened to 25 minutes.
Hint: Freshness for a triggered pipeline is not the cadence alone: add the run duration, and add the retry path when a run fails.

Worked solution
(a) Pipeline mode = triggered. Trigger = scheduled, cadence every 30 minutes (cron 0 0/30 * * * ?). Deployment mode = production, so compute comes from the configured cluster policy and a failed scheduled run is retried automatically.

(b) Worst-case staleness for a clean run is the cadence plus the run duration:

$$t_{stale} = t_{cadence} + t_{run} = 30 + 6 = 36\ \text{minutes} \le 40\ \text{minutes}$$

Headroom = 4 minutes. The 30-minute cadence is chosen precisely because it is the largest round cadence that fits the contract.

(c) With one failed attempt: the first attempt aborts after 1 minute, 2 minutes pass before the retry starts, and the retry takes the full 6 minutes:

$$t_{stale} = 30 + 1 + 2 + 6 = 39\ \text{minutes} \le 40\ \text{minutes}$$

Headroom = 1 minute, so the contract still holds but only just. With a second allowed retry the bound becomes 30 + 1 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 = 47 minutes, which breaches the 40-minute contract. The retry policy must therefore be capped at one automatic retry; more retries would need a shorter cadence to stay under the SLA.

(d) Cluster billing rate = 0.5 + (2 x 0.75) = 2.0 DBU/hour. Per run:

$$0.20\ \text{DBU} = 2.0\ \frac{\text{DBU}}{\text{h}} \times \frac{6}{60}\ \text{h}$$

Runs per day = 24 x 2 = 48, so daily cost = 48 x 0.20 = 9.6 DBU/day, which is under the 15 DBU ceiling. The always-on alternative bills 2.0 x 24 = 48 DBU/day, a ratio of 48 / 9.6 = 5x the triggered configuration, and 3.2x over budget.

(e) Under a 25-minute contract a 30-minute cadence fails immediately: 30 + 6 = 36 > 25. The cadence must satisfy t_cadence <= 25 - 6 = 19 minutes, and the smallest practical choice is 15 minutes, costing 0.20 x 96 = 19.2 DBU/day, which breaks the 15 DBU ceiling. At that point continuous mode becomes the honest candidate, but it must be justified by the latency SLA itself: continuous mode needs an always-on cluster, so it is not the default answer for volume or freshness in general, only for a hard latency requirement that a cadence cannot meet.

Analysis — The method here is to treat the four deployment axes as independent: mode (how often the graph is evaluated), trigger (what starts an evaluation), deployment mode (which compute and failure semantics apply), and target (where output lands). Freshness is then derived rather than assumed — the key insight is that a triggered pipeline's freshness window equals the trigger cadence plus the run duration, and failure handling adds to that window. Two common mistakes follow from skipping that arithmetic. The first is choosing continuous mode by default because it sounds more production-grade; the calculation above shows it costs 5x more here for latency nobody asked for. The second is forgetting that automatic retry, while it protects the SLA from transient errors, also extends the worst-case staleness, so the retry count is itself a freshness parameter. The edge case worth remembering is the near-miss: configurations that pass the SLA with 1 minute of headroom are fragile, because any growth in graph runtime consumes the remaining margin. The generalization is to write the freshness inequality as t_cadence + t_run + (retry penalty) <= SLA and choose the largest cadence that satisfies it.
Problem 3

Before the first production run you must provision Unity Catalog privileges for the pipeline's service principal sp-orders-pipeline (application ID 4f9c1e22-7b6a-4d3e-9c10-2ab7f0e55d31) and for the BI consumer group bi_dashboard_users. The pipeline publishes into prod_catalog.sales. (a) Write the GRANT statements for the pipeline's service principal. (b) Write the GRANT statements for the consumer group. (c) Determine whether sp-orders-pipeline can create the three datasets in prod_catalog.sales using only the grants from (a), and explain the role of schema ownership. (d) State the checks that prove the schema is owned by this one pipeline and that no other pipeline writes to it. (e) Explain why granting MODIFY to bi_dashboard_users would be a mistake.
Hint: USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are traversal privileges; they let a principal reach objects but not create them.

Worked solution
(a) For the pipeline's service principal:

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG prod_catalog TO `sp-orders-pipeline`;

GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA prod_catalog.sales TO `sp-orders-pipeline`;

GRANT SELECT, MODIFY ON SCHEMA prod_catalog.sales TO `sp-orders-pipeline`;

(b) For the consumer group:

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG prod_catalog TO `bi_dashboard_users`;

GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA prod_catalog.sales TO `bi_dashboard_users`;

GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA prod_catalog.sales TO `bi_dashboard_users`;

Note the absence of MODIFY.

(c) Not reliably. USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are traversal privileges: they let a principal name and reach objects under the catalog and schema, but they confer no create or write rights on their own. SELECT and MODIFY act on objects that already exist. Creating an object requires CREATE TABLE on the schema, or ownership of the schema, which carries all privileges on the schema and the objects inside it. On a cold start — the first production run, when prod_catalog.sales.orders_bronze, orders_silver, and orders_gold do not exist yet — the pipeline would be able to read and modify existing tables but could not publish the new ones. The resolution used here is to make sp-orders-pipeline the owner of prod_catalog.sales, which is also what satisfies the one-writer-per-schema rule; the alternative is to keep ownership elsewhere and add GRANT CREATE TABLE ON SCHEMA prod_catalog.sales TO `sp-orders-pipeline`. Ownership is the stronger choice because it keeps the schema's lifecycle tied to the one pipeline that writes into it, but it must be granted deliberately: ownership also carries the ability to alter and drop the schema's objects.

(d) Two checks together. First, DESCRIBE SCHEMA EXTENDED prod_catalog.sales returns Owner = sp-orders-pipeline, and no other principal holds MODIFY or CREATE TABLE on the schema. Second, the audit log for the last 30 days shows no write events (CREATE TABLE, WRITE, ALTER, DROP) on prod_catalog.sales by any principal other than that service principal. The first check proves the intended configuration; the second proves the actual behaviour, which is what you need, because a stray grant to a group containing a second pipeline's service principal would pass the first check and fail the second.

(e) MODIFY lets a principal update and delete rows. If bi_dashboard_users holds MODIFY on prod_catalog.sales, a consumer can change or delete rows that the pipeline considers its own output. The next pipeline refresh recomputes those datasets, so the consumer's edit silently disappears — or, worse, the edit and the incremental refresh interleave and the resulting table is a mixture that neither party can reproduce. The pipeline's expectations were also evaluated against the pipeline's own writes, not against consumer edits, so the quality guarantee no longer describes the data being served. Consumers of a pipeline-owned dataset need SELECT; write access belongs to the writing pipeline's service principal alone.

Analysis — This problem separates three privilege categories that students routinely blur. Traversal privileges (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA) are prerequisites — without USE CATALOG, a schema-level grant is unusable, and the error message is misleading, which is the single most common permissions bug: a principal holds SELECT on the schema but still sees an authorization failure because the catalog grant is missing. Object and data privileges (SELECT, MODIFY) act on things that exist. Creation rights (CREATE TABLE) or ownership determine whether the pipeline can publish new datasets at all. The deeper principle is that a target schema should have exactly one writer, expressed through ownership, because ownership, refresh cadence, and expectations are all schema-scoped and therefore cannot be shared safely. The generalization to any deployment: compute the privilege set from the role (writer pipeline versus reader consumer), verify the negative case as well as the positive one — that no unintended principal holds write rights — and re-verify after every team or group change, since group membership silently expands privilege sets.
Problem 4

Deployment is complete. You trigger the pipeline manually with Run now and the run reports SUCCESS after 6 minutes 12 seconds. The landing zone holds 1,248,310 order records. orders_silver carries the expectation that customer_id must not be null, configured with the drop action, and 312 of the landing records have a null customer_id. orders_gold rolls the surviving rows up by order date and region, and all 90 distinct order dates with all 6 regions have at least one surviving order. A scan of the last 7 days of query history shows 7 queries still reading the raw landing path. Verify the deployment: (a) state the expected row count of each of the three datasets; (b) list the verification checks that must pass before the deployment is declared complete, including the lineage check; (c) state what must be done about the 7 queries still hitting the landing path and why; (d) explain why the SUCCESS status of the run is not evidence that the deployment worked.
Hint: A green run tells you the graph executed, not that it published to the right place or that anyone is reading the result.

Worked solution
(a) orders_bronze ingests every landing record, so 1,248,310 rows. orders_silver drops the records that violate the non-null customer_id expectation, so 1,248,310 - 312 = 1,247,998 rows. orders_gold has one row per (order date, region) group, so 90 x 6 = 540 rows, given that every combination has at least one surviving order.

(b) Four checks, all of them necessary:

1. Target check: DESCRIBE TABLE prod_catalog.sales.orders_bronze (and silver, gold) succeeds, and the Catalog Explorer entry for each dataset shows the expected catalog and schema — that is, the datasets really are in prod_catalog.sales and not in a development default.

2. Content check: the row counts match 1,248,310 / 1,247,998 / 540. A count of 0 in any dataset means the pipeline published an empty object, which a SUCCESS status does not rule out.

3. Data-quality check: the 312 dropped rows are accounted for, and the expectation outcome is consistent with the drop action — a count of 1,248,310 in orders_silver would mean the expectation was silently reconfigured to warn.

4. Lineage check: in Catalog Explorer, the lineage of prod_catalog.sales.orders_bronze traces back to the landing path abfss://landing@acmeorders.dfs.core.windows.net/orders/, orders_silver traces to orders_bronze, and orders_gold traces to orders_silver. Lineage back to the landing zone is what proves the production dataset is fed by the production source rather than by a leftover development copy.

(c) The 7 queries must be repointed at prod_catalog.sales.orders_gold (or orders_silver where row-level detail is needed) and re-tested. As long as they read the raw landing path they bypass the whole pipeline: they see records that have not passed the customer_id expectation, they are not covered by lineage, and they will not break when the source format changes because they were never registered as consumers. The deployment is only complete when every consumer queries prod_catalog.sales rather than the raw source.

(d) SUCCESS means the dependency graph was evaluated and every dataset in it was refreshed without an unhandled error. It says nothing about where the outputs went, whether the consumers were repointed, or whether the target schema is the one the business agreed on. In the worst case, all three datasets could be published into a development schema with the same content and the run would still be green; the lineage graph would simply point at a different namespace. Success is therefore a necessary condition for a completed deployment, not a sufficient one. The deployment is complete only when the target is confirmed, the row counts and expectation outcomes are confirmed, lineage reaches back to the landing zone, and the consumers have been repointed.

Analysis — This problem teaches the difference between execution verification and deployment verification. Execution verification asks whether the graph ran; deployment verification asks whether the result is in the right place, contains the right data, and is being consumed by the right readers. The row-count arithmetic also enforces a discipline: expectation outcomes must reconcile. If landing holds 1,248,310 records, silver holds 1,247,998, and 312 records violated a drop expectation, the numbers balance; any mismatch means either the expectation action changed or the pipeline is not reading the source you think it is. Two edge cases deserve attention. First, bronze equals the landing count only because the production target is fresh and the streaming checkpoints start empty; a second run of the same source data adds zero rows, because streaming tables process incrementally. Second, gold equals 90 x 6 only if every date-region combination has at least one surviving order — a group with zero rows simply produces no row, not a zero row, so a group-by rollup must be validated against the expected key space and not just against a total. The generalization: after any deployment, verify placement, content, quality, lineage, and consumption, and treat the run status as the weakest of the five signals.
Problem 5

A colleague hands you this configuration sheet for the orders_pipeline and asks you to ship it as-is.

- Pipeline mode: continuous

- Trigger: none configured; the pipeline is started manually with Run now during testing

- Deployment mode: development

- Target catalog: not set

- Target schema: dev_sandbox

- Grants: GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON CATALOG prod_catalog TO `all_users`

- Schema ownership: prod_catalog.sales shared with returns_pipeline

Requirements: datasets must land in prod_catalog.sales, refresh every 30 minutes, retry automatically on failure, hold least privilege, and have exactly one writing pipeline per schema. All compute numbers from the previous problem still apply: the graph takes 6 minutes, the driver and two workers bill 0.5 + 2 x 0.75 = 2.0 DBU/hour. For each of the six fields, state the fault, the corrected value, and the concrete consequence of shipping it as-is; then compute the daily cost penalty of the mode error alone.
Hint: Each field is a separate deployment axis. A single wrong axis can pass a manual test and still be a production failure.

Worked solution
Field 1, pipeline mode: continuous. Fault — an always-on cluster for a workload with a 40-minute freshness contract. Correction — triggered. Consequence as-is: the cluster bills 2.0 x 24 = 48 DBU/day instead of 48 x 0.20 = 9.6 DBU/day, a penalty of 38.4 DBU/day, 5x the triggered cost, with no improvement the business asked for. Continuous mode is only justified by a hard latency SLA that a cadence cannot meet.

Field 2, trigger: none, manual Run now only. Fault — manual triggering means a human is the scheduler, so the refresh happens when someone remembers. Correction — a scheduled trigger every 30 minutes, plus the production retry semantics. Consequence as-is: freshness degrades to whenever the last manual run happened, silently violating the 40-minute dashboard contract the first time someone is in a meeting. Note also that the trigger type is what makes a failed run retryable on a schedule; a pipeline with no trigger never gets the automatic retry at all.

Field 3, deployment mode: development. Fault — development mode is meant for iterative authoring, not for the serving path. Correction — production, which takes compute from the configured cluster policy and retries failed runs automatically. Consequence as-is: compute may be provisioned ad hoc rather than from the policy, the run is not treated as a production run, and there is no automatic retry, so the 1-minute headroom computed in the freshness analysis disappears entirely — a single transient storage error leaves the dashboard stale until a human intervenes.

Field 4, target catalog: not set. Fault — the datasets inherit a default catalog rather than prod_catalog. Correction — set the target catalog to prod_catalog. Consequence as-is: the objects are published somewhere other than the agreed namespace, the run still reports SUCCESS, and every consumer query against prod_catalog.sales returns nothing until the target is fixed and the pipeline re-run.

Field 5, target schema: dev_sandbox. Fault — production output would land in a development schema. Correction — target schema sales, giving the fully qualified names prod_catalog.sales.orders_bronze, orders_silver, and orders_gold. Consequence as-is: production and development artifacts share a namespace, lineage is split across two schemas, and any development experiment can overwrite the datasets that consumers depend on.

Field 6, grants: GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON CATALOG prod_catalog TO `all_users`. Fault — a catalog-wide grant to an everyone-group is the opposite of least privilege. Correction — USE CATALOG on prod_catalog and USE SCHEMA plus SELECT and MODIFY on prod_catalog.sales for the pipeline's service principal only; USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, and SELECT for the consumer group; no catalog-wide grants to all_users. Consequence as-is: every user in the workspace can read, modify, and potentially drop objects across every schema in the catalog, which also destroys the one-writer-per-schema property, because any user can write into prod_catalog.sales.

Field 7, schema ownership: prod_catalog.sales shared with returns_pipeline. Fault — two writing pipelines in one schema. Correction — prod_catalog.sales is owned solely by orders_pipeline's service principal, and returns_pipeline targets its own schema. Consequence as-is: ownership belongs to one principal only, so the second pipeline is either blocked from publishing or is over-privileged; in the latter case its refreshes can overwrite or drop objects that orders_pipeline and its consumers depend on, and neither pipeline's expectations describe the data that ends up in the schema.

Daily cost penalty of the mode error alone: continuous = 48 DBU/day, triggered = 9.6 DBU/day, difference = 38.4 DBU/day, a factor of 5.

Analysis — The point of this problem is that deployment settings compose multiplicatively in failure modes: each field is individually defensible-looking and jointly catastrophic, and no single passing test reveals the combination. Students typically diagnose only the loud failures (wrong target, missing grants) and miss the quiet ones: continuous mode looks more production-ready than triggered, development mode looks like a harmless leftover, and a manual test that succeeds looks like evidence that the trigger is configured. The discipline that catches all of them is to walk the axes explicitly — mode, trigger, deployment mode, target, permissions, ownership — and ask for each one what it must be and what happens if it is wrong. Two edge cases are worth remembering. First, a manual run during testing can produce exactly the same green status as a scheduled production run, so run status can never confirm the trigger configuration; the trigger must be inspected directly. Second, ownership is a single-valued property: sharing a schema is not a middle ground between two independent schemas and one owner, it is a configuration where one pipeline's lifecycle can invalidate the other's objects. The generalization for any certification scenario: enumerate the deployment axes, give each one an expected value with a stated rationale, and verify the negative cases — what must not be true — alongside the positive ones.

actions.text: Let's put everything we've covered about deployment into a full worked problem. This one walks through deploying the orders_pipeline end to end — five stages, each isolating one deployment concept.

Problem 1 starts with the target. Your team is promoting the orders_pipeline from development into production, and the datasets need to land in prod_catalog.sales. The hint points you straight at it: the target is a property of the pipeline itself, not something you configure on individual datasets.

The worked solution confirms this. Set the pipeline's target catalog to prod_catalog and the target schema to sales. Every declared dataset is then published there automatically and registered in Unity Catalog — you never qualify each table by hand. Notice the analysis note: this problem isolates the very first deployment axis, where the data lands.

Problem 2 moves to the timing axis. The pipeline must satisfy three constraints at once: refresh every 30 minutes, keep compute coming from the configured policy, and automatically retry when a run fails.

The solution: pipeline mode stays triggered, you add a scheduled trigger for every 30 minutes, and you set deployment mode to production so compute comes from the policy and failed runs retry. The key trap here is freshness. Freshness for a triggered pipeline is not the same as continuous mode — triggering every 30 minutes gives you that cadence without paying for always-on compute.

Problem 3 is permissions. Before the first production run you must provision access for the pipeline's service principal — and the hint reminds you that USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are traversal privileges, so they come first.

The solution grants USE CATALOG on prod_catalog, then USE SCHEMA plus SELECT and MODIFY on sales to that service principal. You also confirm the schema is owned by this one pipeline and that no other pipeline writes to it. The analysis separates three privilege layers: catalog traversal, schema traversal, and table-level read and write — get the order right and access checks pass cleanly.

Problem 4 is the verification stage. Deployment is complete and you trigger the pipeline manually. It runs green — so are you done? The hint says a green run tells you the graph executed, nothing more.

Here's the crucial insight: orders_bronze ingests every landing file, and a successful run proves nothing until you check the schema and repoint the consumers. You confirm each dataset appears in Catalog Explorer with lineage back to the landing zone, and you confirm downstream consumers now query prod_catalog.sales instead of the raw source. This problem teaches the difference between a pipeline that ran and a deployment that actually succeeded.

Problem 5 is the synthesis. A colleague hands you a configuration sheet — mode, trigger, deployment target, permissions, everything — and you have to read it field by field and decide whether it's correct.

The worked solution takes each field in turn: pipeline mode, trigger configuration, deployment mode, the target catalog and schema, and the granted privileges. The hint frames it perfectly — each field is a separate deployment axis. The analysis note is the punchline: deployment is not one setting, it's several independent decisions that must all be consistent. Read the sheet field by field and check each against the requirement.

So to recap this page: target tells you where data lands, mode and trigger tell you when and how compute runs, permissions tell you who can traverse and modify, and verification tells you whether it actually worked. Master those four axes and you can reason through any deployment scenario on the exam.

scenes.title: Lesson Capstone: End-to-End Pipeline Configuration

questions.question: A payments team runs a fraud-risk scoring pipeline with a hard SLA: no emitted risk signal may be more than 1 minute stale during trading hours. The pipeline reads from a Kafka-backed bronze streaming table and writes an incrementally updated silver scoring table that a downstream application polls. The team also has a nightly finance rollup that is only read at 07:00 and a landing-zone ingestion job that must start the instant a file appears. Which combination of pipeline mode, trigger type, and deployment mode is correct for the fraud-risk pipeline, and why does it differ from the other two?

options.label: Triggered mode with a 5-minute scheduled trigger in production mode, because scheduled triggers are the Databricks-recommended default for any low-latency consumer and continuous mode is reserved for batch rollups.

Continuous mode with always-on compute in production mode, because only continuous mode refreshes streaming tables as new data arrives with seconds-to-minutes latency, whereas the rollup should be triggered on a nightly schedule and the ingestion job should use a file-arrival trigger.
Triggered mode with a file-arrival trigger in development mode, because development mode avoids retries that would otherwise mask SLA violations during testing.
Continuous mode with a manual trigger in development mode, because a manual trigger lets an operator decide when each micro-batch starts, which is how sub-minute latency is achieved.

questions.analysis: The fraud pipeline has a hard latency SLA (at most 1 minute stale), so it requires continuous mode with always-on compute; continuous mode is the only mode in which streaming tables refresh as new data arrives with seconds-to-minutes latency, and the always-on cluster cost must be justified by exactly this kind of hard latency SLA. The nightly finance rollup inverts every dimension: freshness equals trigger cadence, so a triggered pipeline with a scheduled trigger aligned to the nightly window keeps compute cost near zero between runs, and it belongs in production mode. The landing-zone job needs a file-arrival trigger (Auto Loader detecting new files) rather than a time-based cadence. Option A is wrong because a 5-minute schedule cannot meet a 1-minute SLA and because continuous mode is not 'reserved for batch rollups'. Option C is wrong because development mode is for iteration (isolated compute, no automatic retries) and a file-arrival trigger does not match a Kafka source. Option D is wrong because manual triggers are operator-driven and cannot guarantee sub-minute freshness; it also confuses deployment mode with pipeline mode [source 2]. Pipeline mode, trigger type, and deployment mode are properties of the pipeline as a whole, not of an individual dataset [source 1].

questions.question: A staff engineer claims: 'If I set the pipeline to continuous mode, I can stop worrying about expectations, because continuous ingestion means the data is always fresh and therefore always clean.' Which of the following statements correctly refute this claim, and which correctly describe how expectations behave across modes? Select all that apply.

options.label: Expectations are declared alongside transformations and are enforced by the framework regardless of whether the pipeline runs in triggered or continuous mode; data quality checks apply in every mode.

A continuous pipeline that ingests a malformed timestamp field will still fail, drop, or quarantine the offending records according to the configured expectation action (warn, drop, or fail), and the action is observable in the event log.
Continuous mode replaces the expectation framework by re-reading source data until the records become valid, so expectations become redundant once continuous mode is enabled.
The correct way to relax enforcement in continuous mode is to remove expectations entirely and rely on downstream consumers to filter bad records.

questions.analysis: The claim conflates freshness with correctness. Freshness is a function of pipeline mode and trigger cadence; correctness is a function of expectations, which are declared alongside the transformations and enforced by the framework [source 5]. Option A is correct: expectations apply in every mode, because they are a property of the dataset definition, not of the schedule. Option B is correct: for warn, drop, and fail, the configured action still governs record disposition, and the failure is diagnosable from the event-log payload. Option C is a real student misconception: continuous mode does not re-read invalid data until it becomes valid; it simply processes new data as it arrives, so the expectation still must be declared and the action still must be chosen. Option D is also a misconception: removing expectations silently pushes the cost of bad data downstream to consumers, which is the opposite of declarative data quality. This is the deliberate trap described in the unit — 'continuous mode removes the need for expectations' is false [source 4].

questions.question: A team needs to ingest files as soon as they land in a cloud storage landing zone, but their CFO has imposed a compute-cost ceiling that forbids an always-on cluster. They propose a triggered pipeline with a file-arrival trigger using Auto Loader. A reviewer objects that 'a triggered pipeline cannot serve near-real-time consumers.' Which evaluation of the reviewer's objection is correct?

options.label: The objection is correct; only continuous mode can achieve sub-minute freshness, so the team must violate the cost ceiling or accept a multi-hour stale-data window.

The objection is incorrect; a triggered pipeline with a file-arrival trigger (or a very frequent scheduled trigger such as every 15 minutes) can deliver short freshness windows at much lower cost than an always-on cluster, because compute starts, evaluates the full pipeline graph in dependency order, refreshes every dataset once, and then stops.
The objection is incorrect only if the team also switches from production mode to development mode, because development mode gives the pipeline higher scheduling priority.
The objection is incorrect because file-arrival triggers bypass the pipeline graph and write directly to the target catalog without evaluating expectations.

questions.analysis: Triggered pipelines start compute, evaluate the full pipeline graph in dependency order, refresh every dataset once, and then stop — you pay only for the run, not for idle time. A file-arrival trigger fires the moment Auto Loader detects new files, and a frequent scheduled trigger (for example, every 15 minutes) achieves a bounded freshness window equal to the cadence. Both deliver short stale-data windows at far lower cost than an always-on cluster, which is why 'triggered cannot serve near-real-time consumers' is a false trap [source 1]. Option A overstates the requirement: freshness in a triggered pipeline equals the trigger cadence, so cadence choice directly trades cost for freshness. Option C confuses deployment mode with scheduling; development mode is for isolated iteration with no automatic retries and gives no scheduling advantage. Option D is factually wrong: file-arrival triggers are a trigger type on the pipeline as a whole; the pipeline graph is still evaluated and expectations are still enforced [source 2].

questions.question: A platform team is deploying three pipelines into the same Unity Catalog metastore. All three currently point at target catalog 'prod' and target schema 'silver'. During the first production run, pipeline A's materialized view and pipeline B's streaming table collide on the same registered object name, and a downstream dashboard begins reading stale data. A teammate proposes the fix: 'Just let every pipeline write into the same target schema; Unity Catalog will merge the objects by name and lineage.' Explain why a pipeline's target catalog and schema should be owned by exactly one pipeline, and describe what a correct deployment looks like instead. Your answer should address (a) the one-pipeline-one-target rule, (b) what gets published into that target (managed tables and views, column-level lineage), (c) the operational risk of shared targets, and (d) a concrete corrected layout for the three pipelines.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric — award full credit only if all four parts are addressed with precision: (a) State the rule that a pipeline has exactly one target catalog and one target schema, and that every dataset the pipeline declares is published into that location; 25%. (b) Explain that datasets appear as managed tables and views registered in Unity Catalog with full column-level lineage from source to consumption, and that no manual DDL or CREATE TABLE is required; 25%. (c) Explain the operational risk of shared targets: name collisions between a streaming table and a materialized view, ambiguous lineage, a failed pipeline overwriting or blocking another pipeline's object, and the impossibility of clean rollback or per-pipeline ownership; 25%. (d) Provide a concrete corrected layout — for example, prod.silver_a, prod.silver_b, prod.silver_c (or separate schemas per pipeline), with dataset names unique within each schema, and note that development mode uses an isolated target so iteration never touches production objects; 25%. Deduct marks for answers that propose sharing schemas with naming conventions alone, or that claim Unity Catalog merges objects automatically. Accept a well-argued alternative layout if it enforces single-pipeline ownership.
questions.analysis: A pipeline has exactly one target catalog and one target schema; every dataset the pipeline declares is published into that location and registered in Unity Catalog [source 2]. Datasets appear as managed tables and views with full column-level lineage from source to consumption, and no manual DDL or CREATE TABLE is required [source 1]. The one-pipeline-one-target rule is not stylistic: shared targets create name collisions (a streaming table and a materialized view cannot both claim 'silver.orders'), ambiguous lineage, cross-pipeline failure coupling, and no clean rollback path. The correct deployment is single ownership — e.g., prod.silver_a, prod.silver_b, prod.silver_c — with each pipeline registering its own managed tables and views; development mode uses an isolated target so iteration never touches production objects. The teammate's claim that Unity Catalog 'merges objects by name' is a misconception: Unity Catalog registers objects as they are published, it does not reconcile conflicting definitions [source 5].

actions.text: This is the capstone for the lesson, so these questions pull together everything we've built across dataset types, expectations, pipeline mode, triggers, and deployment targets — all in full end-to-end scenarios rather than one concept at a time.

Work through each one on your own before submitting, including the written response. Take the scenarios slowly and justify each choice to yourself as you go. Once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning behind each answer and the traps that were hiding in the wording.

scenes.title: Batch vs Streaming: Bounded and Unbounded Data

elements.content: Batch vs Streaming: Bounded and Unbounded Data

• Bounded data: a fixed, complete dataset with a known start and end; batch jobs process the entire finite set, so results are deterministic and repeatable.

• Unbounded data: a dataset that keeps arriving with no predefined end; processing follows the stream and typically materializes results into Delta tables [source 4].

• Precondition: batch needs the full partition available; unbounded streams are only queried incrementally, so a plain non-streaming read typically fails on them.
Why streaming? End-to-end latency comparison

Worked example — a 1.8 million ms batch job is 1,800,000 ÷ 3,000 = 600× slower than micro-batch and 1,800,000 ÷ 4 = 450,000× slower than true streaming [source 6].

Alerts inside a 4 ms window must use streaming; a nightly 30-minute report can stay batch.
Common streaming sources
Kafka · Kinesis · Pub/Sub — connected via standard connectors [source 5]

actions.text: Now that you've seen the full range of ingestion patterns, let's shift gears into streaming itself. This is a foundational concept for the exam, so I want you to lock in the vocabulary early.
The title says it all: batch versus streaming, and the two concepts that anchor everything else — bounded and unbounded data.

Bounded data is a fixed, complete dataset with a clear beginning and end — think a CSV drop from last night, or a full table scan. Batch processing is built for exactly this: the data is already sitting there, fully known before you start. Unbounded data, by contrast, is a continuously arriving stream with no predefined end — sensor readings, click events, Kafka topics. The dataset never 'finishes'; it just keeps flowing.

So why choose streaming at all? The answer is latency. This chart compares end-to-end latency across approaches. Look at the bar for batch — minutes to hours, because you're waiting for a scheduled job to fire. Micro-batch sits in the seconds range. And true streaming lands in milliseconds, up to the millisecond. That gap is exactly why streaming exists: when a business decision must be made on data that just arrived, batch can't cut it.

Here's a worked example to make the numbers concrete. Suppose a batch job takes 1.8 million milliseconds — that's roughly thirty minutes. Now notice: at thirty minutes of latency, a fraud detection model is useless. The transaction has already cleared. This is the kind of reasoning the exam expects when it asks you to justify a streaming choice.

When you need streaming, where does the data come from? The common sources are message queues and event-streaming platforms — Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, and Google Cloud Pub/Sub are the three you'll see most on the exam. In Databricks, these are connected through standard connectors, and they're what feed your streaming DataFrames.

One exam trap before we move on: unbounded does not mean schema-less. Streaming DataFrames are still structured — they require a schema, just like batch. If you see an answer choice that says 'streaming data has no schema,' that's a distractor. Let's carry that forward as we look at how batch and streaming DataFrames differ.

scenes.title: Batch DataFrame vs Streaming DataFrame

elements.content: Dimension  |  Batch DataFrame  |  Streaming DataFrame

Creation API
Batch DataFrame: A batch DataFrame is created with spark.read followed by a format-specific loader such as .format("parquet").load("path") or .table("catalog.schema.table"), and the call returns immediately because the data already exists and is bounded.
Streaming DataFrame: A streaming DataFrame is created with spark.readStream instead of spark.read, and the call is a lazy declaration of a continuous source, so no data is read and no rows are materialized until a writeStream action starts the query.

Underlying data model
Batch DataFrame: A batch DataFrame is a fixed, fully materialized logical table whose contents are determined at the moment the read is resolved, consistent with the bounded-data model covered earlier in this unit.
Streaming DataFrame: A streaming DataFrame is modeled as an unbounded table that logically grows as new data arrives, so the DataFrame is a declarative plan over a table with no known upper bound rather than a snapshot of rows. [source 3]

Schema handling
Batch DataFrame: A batch DataFrame over a well-formed source such as a Delta table or Parquet directory can infer its schema directly from the data and use Delta Lake transaction log metadata for a stable schema without user intervention.
Streaming DataFrame: A streaming DataFrame must declare the schema explicitly for most sources, so the engineer supplies StructType definitions or uses the schemaLocation option with Auto Loader, because the planner cannot sample an unbounded source to infer types. [source 3]

Execution model
Batch DataFrame: A batch DataFrame executes once as a single job: a catalyst-optimized physical plan runs to completion over a fixed number of partitions and then terminates, which makes shuffle cost predictable and bounded.
Streaming DataFrame: A streaming DataFrame executes as a continuous Structured Streaming query that processes one micro-batch (or one continuous processing interval) at a time, maintaining processing state for fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics. [source 5]

Supported operations
Batch DataFrame: A batch DataFrame supports the full DataFrame API, including arbitrary aggregates, sorts, joins, repartitioning, and window functions, because the bounded input lets the engine see all rows before producing output.
Streaming DataFrame: Only a limited set of operations is supported on a streaming DataFrame: stateless select, filter, and withColumn are always allowed, stateful aggregations and stream-stream joins require watermark and state, while non-deterministic operations such as full outer joins without watermarks and sorting are unsupported or error-prone.

Persistence API and typical sink
Batch DataFrame: A batch DataFrame persists with df.write, typically using saveAsTable or insertInto to land a bounded result into a Delta Lake table or an external warehouse, and overwrite semantics are available because the run is finite. [source 1]
Streaming DataFrame: A streaming DataFrame persists with df.writeStream, typically using .format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", ...).outputMode("append").trigger(processingTime="1 minute").start(), landing append-only data into a streaming table for low-latency ingestion. [source 5]

Correctness guarantees and durability
Batch DataFrame: A batch write is atomic per job but does not need a checkpoint: re-running overwrite simply recomputes the bounded result, and Delta Lake's transaction log protects concurrent readers from partial writes. [source 1]
Streaming DataFrame: A streaming write requires a checkpoint location to record offsets and processing state, and the Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the same table. [source 1]
Takeaway — Choose a batch DataFrame when the input is bounded and latency is not the driver: spark.read + df.write with the full API keeps the plan simple and the cost predictable.

Takeaway — Choose a streaming DataFrame when the input is unbounded and near-real-time or sub-minute latency is required: spark.readStream + df.writeStream plus a checkpoint location is the only combination that gives exactly-once end-to-end semantics. [source 1][source 5]

Takeaway — Exam trap to internalize: the transformation logic on the two DataFrames is deliberately identical, so the distinguishing signals in a question stem are read() vs readStream(), write() vs writeStream(), the presence of a checkpointLocation, and the trigger/laziness discussion, not the bodies of the transformations.

Takeaway — A streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines is simply a Delta table with streaming and incremental support designed for append-only ingestion, so the same DataFrame code can be promoted from pipeline to pipeline when chained for very large volume and low latency. [source 2][source 3]

actions.text: So this is where the earlier distinction becomes concrete. Here we have a side-by-side comparison of the Batch DataFrame and the Streaming DataFrame across five dimensions: creation API, underlying data model, schema handling, execution model, and the typical sink. This table is essentially the exam's cheat sheet, so let's walk each row carefully.

Row one, the creation API. A batch DataFrame is created with spark.read — you point it at a bounded source and it materializes. A streaming DataFrame is created with spark.readStream. That single word in the middle, 'stream', is the whole difference at creation time. There is no separate class you instantiate.

Row two, the underlying data model. A batch DataFrame is a fixed table — a bounded set of rows that you can count and exhaust. A streaming DataFrame is modeled as an unbounded table that logically grows as new data arrives. Think of it as a table that never finishes being written to.

Row three, schema handling. Both carry a schema, but the streaming case has to be more careful. If your source has no declared schema, the streaming engine cannot safely evict or retain state, so it will refuse to proceed until you give it one. That's a favorite exam trap — streaming does not mean 'schemaless'.

Row four, the execution model, and this is the heart of it. A batch DataFrame executes eagerly — you call an action, the work happens once. A streaming DataFrame is lazy in a deeper sense: you define the plan, and it is only realized when you start a query and the engine drives it continuously over micro-batches. Nothing runs until you start the stream.

Row five, supported operations. On a batch DataFrame virtually everything works. On a streaming DataFrame only a limited set of operations is supported — some require state, like windowed aggregations or stream-stream joins, and others are simply unsupported, such as certain forms of sorting and deduplication without a watermark.

And the persistence side mirrors creation exactly: df.write persists a batch DataFrame, df.writeStream persists a streaming one, and you choose output modes and a sink — typically a Delta table — rather than simply overwriting files.

One more dimension worth calling out even though it isn't always in the table: correctness guarantees and durability. In batch, retry the job and you get the same result. In streaming you rely on checkpoints and idempotent sinks to get exactly-once semantics — that's what makes a streaming pipeline as trustworthy as a batch one.

Now the headline takeaway and the exam trap. The transformation logic looks identical. filter, select, withColumn — the same code, character for character. The difference is readStream and writeStream, plus the laziness, not the transformations themselves. If an exam question shows you a body of transformation code and asks whether it's batch or streaming, look at the read and write calls, not at the middle.

So choose a streaming DataFrame when the input is genuinely unbounded and you need low-latency, incremental processing — and choose a batch DataFrame when the source is bounded and you simply want a repeatable, run-to-completion job. Most production pipelines use both, feeding streaming data into a Delta table and then running batch transformations on top of it.

And keep one forward-looking point in mind: a streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines is effectively a declaratively-managed streaming DataFrame. The same readStream semantics under the hood — you just declare it instead of writing the imperative query. That connection will matter when we reach the pipeline unit later in the course.

scenes.title: Check: Streaming Concepts

questions.question: A fraud-detection team must flag suspicious card transactions within milliseconds of authorization, and the transaction feed never terminates. Which processing approach is the correct design choice?

options.label: Batch processing, because the team can schedule a job every few minutes over the full historical table
Streaming processing, because the data is unbounded and must be acted on with near-real-time latency
Batch processing, because decision latency is irrelevant as long as the final report is accurate
Streaming processing, because streaming is always faster than batch regardless of the workload

questions.analysis: Bounded vs unbounded data is the first design decision. Here the transaction feed is continuously arriving with no predefined end, so it is unbounded data, and the requirement is near-real-time action (milliseconds). That combination points to streaming: streaming processes a continuously arriving dataset with no predefined end and is chosen when data must be acted on with near-real-time latency. Option A is a common misconception — a micro-batch or scheduled job over a full historical table is still batch semantics and cannot reliably hit millisecond decisions. Option C inverts the actual requirement (latency does matter). Option D is a false absolute; streaming is not automatically 'faster' for every workload, it is the right fit when the data is unbounded and latency-sensitive, and Databricks explicitly positions streaming tables for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming where workloads have very large data volume and low latency requirements [source 3][source 2].

questions.question: Which of the following statements about creating and using a streaming DataFrame in the Databricks/Spark Structured Streaming API are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A streaming DataFrame is created by reading a source with the streaming reader API rather than the standard batch reader, and it is modeled as an unbounded table that logically grows as new data arrives
Only a limited set of operations is supported on streaming DataFrames; some require state and others are entirely unsupported
Writing a streaming DataFrame to a Delta Lake table gives exactly-once processing guarantees, even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against that table
Because it is a DataFrame, every batch transformation is automatically supported on a streaming DataFrame without exception, so no operation is ever restricted

questions.analysis: A is correct: the defining creation API is the streaming reader, and the underlying data model is an unbounded table that grows as new data arrives. B is correct: the supported operation set is deliberately restricted — stateful operations such as streaming aggregations and joins need state management, and some operations (for example, certain sorts without a watermark) are simply unsupported. C is correct: Delta Lake as a streaming sink relies on the Delta transaction log, which guarantees exactly-once processing even with concurrent streams or batch queries against the same table [source 1][source 5]. D is the classic student misconception — reusing the batch DataFrame API does not mean batch semantics carry over unchanged; the streaming API is a restricted subset precisely because unbounded input breaks assumptions that batch transformations can make.

questions.question: A team ingests clickstream events from Kafka with very large data volume and a strict low-latency requirement, wanting the target to be a Delta table with append-only ingestion. Which Databricks-aligned choice best matches the platform's own terminology for this pattern?

options.label: A batch-view materialization that recomputes the whole clickstream table on every scheduled run
A streaming table, which is a Delta table with support for streaming and incremental processing, designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming
A managed external table populated only by nightly full refreshes
A non-Delta file sink that overwrites the target directory each micro-batch

questions.analysis: B is correct and uses Databricks' own vocabulary: a streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines is a Delta table with support for streaming and incremental processing, designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 3][source 4]; DLT streaming pipelines are built on Spark Structured Streaming and Python DLTs can ingest directly from an event bus like Kafka, which supports chaining pipelines for very large volume with low latency requirements [source 2]. Option A is wrong because recomputing the full table on each scheduled run is batch-style, not incremental streaming. Option C is wrong because a nightly full refresh cannot satisfy a strict low-latency requirement. Option D is wrong on two counts: it abandons Delta Lake, losing the transaction log that provides exactly-once guarantees, and a non-append overwrite conflicts with append-only ingestion semantics [source 1][source 3].

actions.text: Before we move into execution internals, let's make sure the foundations from the last couple of pages have settled. This check focuses on bounded versus unbounded data and the streaming DataFrame API — the vocabulary you just picked up.
Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer before moving on. Once you submit, I'll be right here to go through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Micro-Batch Execution and Triggers

elements.content: Micro-Batch Execution and Triggers

By default, Structured Streaming runs on the micro-batch engine: the engine repeatedly queries the source for newly arrived rows and processes each chunk as one small Spark job. It is not a per-record engine — each chunk is a scale-out batch job executed against the same logical streaming DataFrame you defined earlier [source 5].
Lifecycle of one micro-batch

1. Query the source for data not yet consumed.

2. Append those rows to the unbounded input table.

3. Optimize and plan the streaming DataFrame.

4. Execute the plan as an ordinary Spark job.

5. Commit results and offsets atomically to the sink.

The result is near-real-time latency (seconds, not milliseconds) while keeping the reliability, fault tolerance and exactly-once semantics of a batch job — Delta Lake's transaction log guarantees exactly-once even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the same table [source 1][source 5].
One streaming query = an unbounded input table drained by successive micro-batches on a timeline.
Triggers: the cadence knob
processingTime ("every 5 seconds") — fixed wall-clock cadence. availableNow — drain all available data, then stop. once — one batch, then stop. continuous (experimental) — no micro-batches.
Worked example

A topic producing 10,000 events/s with .trigger(processingTime='5 seconds') yields batches of ~50,000 rows (10,000 x 5); at 'every 1 second' each batch holds ~10,000 rows. Smaller intervals = more, smaller batches = lower latency but higher per-batch overhead.

Exam trap: continuous mode is a distinct, experimental low-latency engine that abandons micro-batches; it is not the same as the default micro-batch engine with a processingTime trigger. Default = micro-batch; continuous must be explicitly enabled.

Exam trap: continuous mode is a distinct, experimental low-latency engine that abandons micro-batches; it is not the same as the default micro-batch engine with a processingTime trigger. Default = micro-batch; continuous must be explicitly enabled.

actions.text: Now that we've seen how a streaming DataFrame differs from a batch DataFrame, let's look at the engine that actually runs them: micro-batch execution, and the triggers that control it.

By default, Structured Streaming does not run continuously. It uses the micro-batch engine. The query repeatedly asks the source for data it has not yet consumed, and processes each chunk as a small batch. So a stream is really a sequence of tiny batch jobs, one after another, forever.

Here is the lifecycle of one micro-batch. First, query the source for data not yet consumed. Second, write the new offsets so the engine knows where it left off. Third, execute the logical plan as an ordinary Spark job against the streaming DataFrame. Finally, commit the results to the sink. Then the loop immediately starts again.

The mental model to hold onto: one streaming query is an unbounded input table that grows forever. Each micro-batch reads only the newly appended rows and produces an incremental update to the result table. The plan itself is static; only the data keeps arriving.

The payoff is near-real-time latency — seconds, not hours — while keeping the reliability and exactly-once semantics of batch processing. That combination is the real selling point of micro-batch: stream-like freshness with batch-like correctness.
Triggers are the cadence knob. They do not change what the query computes; they decide how often the next micro-batch fires.

processingTime, for example trigger every five seconds, fires a fixed interval repeatedly. availableNow processes everything currently available and then stops — ideal for incremental batch-style loads. once processes one batch and stops. And continuous is a very different engine, experimental, offering millisecond latency but without the same guarantees. Don't confuse that last one with a processingTime trigger — this is a classic exam trap.

A worked example makes the trade-off concrete. A topic produces ten thousand events per second, and the query uses trigger processing time every five seconds. So each micro-batch covers roughly fifty thousand events. Shrink that interval and latency drops, but you run more, smaller jobs and pay more overhead. Widen it and cost falls, but latency rises.

Two exam takeaways to lock in. The default is the micro-batch engine with a processingTime trigger. And continuous mode is a distinct, experimental low-latency engine — not the same thing as a short micro-batch interval. Keep those separate and you'll avoid the most common trap on this topic.
