scenes.title: Check: Micro-Batch Model

questions.question: A data engineer is building a Structured Streaming pipeline on Databricks and does not explicitly configure a trigger. Which execution model will the pipeline use by default?

options.label: The micro-batch engine, which repeatedly queries the source and processes each new chunk of data as a small batch
The continuous processing engine, which processes each record with up-to-the-millisecond latency as it arrives
A single bounded batch job that reads all available data once and then terminates
A synchronous engine that blocks the source until the sink confirms each individual record

questions.analysis: By default, Structured Streaming uses the micro-batch engine: it repeatedly queries the source for new data and processes each chunk as a small batch, and each micro-batch is an ordinary Spark job executed against the logical streaming DataFrame. Option B describes the experimental continuous mode, which is not the default. Option C describes the once/availableNow-style behavior of a single bounded pass, not the default cadence. Option D invents a synchronous per-record engine that Structured Streaming's micro-batch model does not provide. The micro-batch default is also consistent with the Lakeflow view that a streaming table is a Delta table with support for streaming and incremental processing designed for append-only ingestion and low latency [source 4]: the Delta Lake transaction log then guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the table [source 1].

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Structured Streaming triggers and micro-batch behavior are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Setting a shorter processingTime interval typically reduces end-to-end latency but can increase per-batch overhead and reduce throughput
availableNow processes all currently available data in one or more micro-batches and then stops the query, making it suitable for incremental batch-style backfills
A longer processingTime interval groups more events into each micro-batch, which generally improves throughput but raises latency
The once trigger is the recommended setting for continuously updating dashboards that must reflect new events within milliseconds

questions.analysis: Trigger interval is a latency-versus-throughput trade-off. A shorter processingTime interval means the engine wakes up more often, so new data is processed sooner (lower latency), but each tiny micro-batch carries fixed scheduling and job-launch overhead, which lowers effective throughput; this matches the interactive exercise where adjusting the trigger interval changes how incoming events are grouped, batch size, and end-to-end latency. availableNow drains all currently available data across one or more micro-batches and then stops, so it fits incremental batch-style backfills rather than perpetual streaming. A longer interval amortizes overhead across larger batches, improving throughput at the cost of latency. Option D is wrong on two counts: once is a single-pass finite trigger, not a continuous one, and up-to-the-millisecond latency is the territory of the experimental continuous trigger (and even then, ordinary micro-batch cadence is not millisecond-level). Using Delta Lake as the sink preserves exactly-once processing across these choices, since the transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when concurrent streams or batch queries touch the table [source 1].

questions.question: You are configuring the trigger for a Structured Streaming ingestion job that writes to a Delta Lake table. Explain how the choice of processingTime interval creates a trade-off between end-to-end latency and throughput, and describe how you would adjust the interval for (a) a dashboard with a 1-second freshness requirement and (b) a nightly-cost-sensitive bulk ingest. In your answer, refer to the default execution engine and to exactly-once delivery.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Correctly identifies the default execution engine as micro-batch and explains each micro-batch as a Spark job over the growing logical streaming DataFrame - 30%. (2) Articulates the latency-versus-throughput trade-off: shorter processingTime intervals reduce latency but add fixed per-micro-batch overhead that lowers throughput, while longer intervals group more events per micro-batch to improve throughput at the cost of latency - 30%. (3) Matches scenario (a) to a very short interval (for example every 1 second) to satisfy freshness, and scenario (b) to a long interval or a finite trigger such as availableNow/once to minimize cost - 25%. (4) States that exactly-once delivery is preserved because the Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even with concurrent streams and batch queries, so changing the interval does not weaken correctness - 15%.
questions.analysis: A strong answer states that Structured Streaming defaults to the micro-batch engine, which repeatedly queries the source and runs each new chunk as a small Spark job against the unbounded, logically growing streaming DataFrame. The interval controls cadence: a short processingTime interval means more frequent, smaller micro-batches, lowering end-to-end latency but adding per-batch scheduling overhead that reduces throughput; a long interval yields larger, less frequent micro-batches with higher throughput but higher latency. For (a), a 1-second freshness goal argues for a short interval such as 'every 1 second' (and, if the workload and sink support it, the experimental continuous trigger, though it is not the default). For (b), a cost-sensitive bulk ingest argues for a long interval or a finite trigger such as availableNow or once. Interval choice does not break correctness: Delta Lake's transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently [source 1], and the Delta Lake sink preserves exactly-once processing guarantees for streaming sources and sinks [source 5].

actions.text: Let's check how the micro-batch model and trigger settings settled in. Work through each question on your own — I'll walk through anything that tripped you up once you submit.

scenes.title: Reading from Streaming Sources

elements.content: Reading from Streaming Sources

Every streaming pipeline begins with a streaming read: spark.readStream returns a streaming DataFrame over an unbounded source, whereas spark.read returns a bounded batch DataFrame. The source is never fully consumed — new data simply appends to the logical streaming table as it arrives, which is why an unbounded DataFrame has no "end".
The canonical readStream call and its four builder steps

A streaming read is constructed by chaining four builder methods before any data is touched: format(...) selects the connector, option(key, value) configures it (endpoint, topic, path, offsets), schema(...) declares the columns, and load() materializes the stream. In PySpark: df = spark.readStream.format("kafka").option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092").option("subscribe", "events").load().
Four connectors you must recognize for the exam

Kafka — the standard message-bus source; read with format("kafka") and a subscribe option; DLT Python pipelines ingest directly from Kafka via Structured Streaming [source 2]. Delta tables — a Delta table can itself be a streaming source with exactly-once guarantees [source 1]. Files / cloud storage — via Auto Loader for incremental file discovery. Rate source — a built-in test source that generates rows at a fixed rate for development and benchmarking.
Why streaming reads require an explicit schema

Schema inference on a stream is dangerous: the first micro-batch may see only a subset of columns, so the inferred schema is incomplete and later files with new fields are silently dropped or fail. Always provide an explicit schema(...). Delta tables can carry their own schema, but for evolving file sources Auto Loader or explicit DDL is required.
A streaming query is lazy until a sink and trigger are defined

Calling load() builds a plan but executes nothing. Execution begins only when you declare writeStream, a sink (.format("delta").start()), and a trigger; the stream then runs continuously or until availableNow/once completes. Rate limiting and stateful operators are configured here to keep batch sizes stable [source 5].
Exam trap: each new file is new data, not a re-read

Reading a directory as a stream does not re-process the same batch each trigger — it detects newly arrived files and treats each one as new rows appended to the streaming table. Re-reading a fixed set of files requires a batch query or Auto Loader's file-tracking state. Streaming tables in Lakeflow are append-only by design for this reason [source 3][source 4].

Worked example: 5,000 events/s arrive with a 10 s processingTime trigger → each micro-batch holds ~50,000 rows. Halve the interval to 5 s and each micro-batch holds ~25,000 rows, lowering latency but doubling the number of Spark jobs and checkpoints — the classic latency-throughput tradeoff [source 5].

actions.text: Now that we've traced how micro-batches execute and what triggers control them, let's open the next layer: where does the data actually come from? This page is about reading from streaming sources.

Every streaming pipeline begins with a streaming read. The canonical call is spark.readStream, and just like the batch reader you already know, it's a builder — you chain format, option, and load. Same fluent style, only the entry point changes from read to readStream.

There are four source connectors you must recognize for the exam. First, Kafka — the standard message-bus source, read with format("kafka") and configured through bootstrap servers and topic options. Second, Delta tables, which we'll cover in depth on the next page. Third, files and cloud storage, best handled by Auto Loader. And fourth, the rate source — a synthetic generator used purely for testing and demos.

Next, schema. Unlike batch file reads, a streaming read generally requires an explicit schema. Why? Because inference on a stream is dangerous: the first micro-batch may see only a partial file, or no file at all, so the inferred schema could be wrong or empty and then lock in. For evolving file sources, always declare the schema yourself — or let Auto Loader manage it for you.

Here's a subtle but heavily tested point: a streaming query is lazy. Calling load() builds a logical plan but executes nothing. Nothing runs until you define a sink, choose a trigger, and call start() on a running query. Remember the phrase — build the plan, define the target, then start.

And the classic exam trap: reading a directory as a stream does not re-process the files that are already there. Each newly arrived file is treated as new data, appended to the stream. It is not a re-read of the same batch. So if you expect a full re-scan every run, you'll be surprised — the stream only picks up what's new since the last checkpoint.

To sum up this page: readStream plus format, option, load builds the source; Kafka, Delta, files, and rate are the four connectors; declare your schema explicitly; and the query stays lazy until a sink and trigger start it. Keep the trap in mind — new files mean new data. Next, we'll put it into practice by reading and writing a streaming DataFrame end to end.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Read and Write a Streaming DataFrame

elements.content: Problem 1

Acme Retail drops JSON event files into cloud storage under s3://acme-retail/raw/events/ at an average rate of 12,000 events per second. Each file holds about 6,000 events (~2 MB), so a new file lands roughly twice per second. Every event record has five fields: event_id (string), event_ts (ISO-8601 string), store_id (integer), event_type (string, either 'page_view' or 'purchase'), and amount (double, null for non-purchase events). Roughly 8% of all events are purchases with amount > 0. Build a Structured Streaming pipeline on Databricks that (a) reads the arriving files as an unbounded stream, (b) keeps only purchase events with amount > 0, (c) appends the result to the Delta table main.retail.silver_purchases, (d) triggers every 30 seconds, and (e) survives a cluster restart with no duplicated and no lost rows. Write the code and justify every option you pass.
Hint: Define the schema first, then spark.readStream, then a stateless filter/select, then writeStream with both a Delta sink and a checkpointLocation.

Worked solution
Step 1 - fix the schema before touching the source.

events_schema = 'event_id STRING, event_ts TIMESTAMP, store_id INT, event_type STRING, amount DOUBLE'

A file-based streaming source must be given an explicit schema. If the engine inferred the schema it would have to read records to guess types, and the guess could change as new files arrive, while the contract of a streaming DataFrame is a schema that is fixed for the life of the query. A concrete failure mode: if the first files contained only page_view rows, amount would be inferred as a string column, and the later predicate amount > 0 would silently compare text to a number instead of filtering on a double.

Step 2 - create the streaming DataFrame.

events = (spark.readStream

.format('json')

.schema(events_schema)

.option('maxFilesPerTrigger', 200)

.load('s3://acme-retail/raw/events/'))

readStream (not read) is what makes the result an unbounded logical table rather than a fixed batch. maxFilesPerTrigger is a rate limit: it caps how many files a single micro-batch may consume, which keeps batch sizes stable when a backlog of files appears.

Step 3 - apply stateless transformations.

from pyspark.sql.functions import col

purchases = (events

.filter((col('event_type') == 'purchase') & (col('amount') > 0))

.select('event_id', 'event_ts', 'store_id', 'amount'))

filter and select here are exactly the operators used on a batch DataFrame - there is no separate streaming API. Because both are stateless, they require no watermark and no state store, and each input row produces at most one output row.

Step 4 - write the stream.

query = (purchases.writeStream

.format('delta')

.outputMode('append')

.option('checkpointLocation', 's3://acme-retail/_checkpoints/silver_purchases')

.trigger(processingTime='30 seconds')

.toTable('main.retail.silver_purchases'))

Step 5 - check that the trigger and the rate limit agree. Let the arrival rate be lambda = 12,000 events/s and the retained fraction be f = 0.08. The retained rate is rho = lambda x f = 12,000 x 0.08 = 960 rows/s. With trigger interval T = 30 s, the batch size is B = rho x T = 960 x 30 = 28,800 rows per micro-batch. Files per micro-batch = 2 files/s x 30 s = 60 files, which is below maxFilesPerTrigger = 200, so the file cap is not binding: the trigger interval, not the option, sets the batch size. The committed payload is about 28,800 rows x 80 bytes = 2.3 MB per micro-batch.

Step 6 - reason about latency. End-to-end latency is L = T + B/R, where R is cluster throughput. On 2 workers x 4 cores = 8 cores at 5,000 rows/s per core, R = 40,000 rows/s, so B/R = 28,800/40,000 = 0.72 s and L is about 30.7 s plus the Delta commit. Halving the trigger to 15 s halves the batch to 14,400 rows and the latency to roughly 15.4 s, but doubles the commit rate from 2 to 4 per minute, which doubles the small-file pressure on the target table.

Step 7 - restart safety. The checkpointLocation is not optional: it is the engine's durable memory of which source offsets have been consumed and which micro-batches have been committed, and it is what enables fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5]. On the sink side, the Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries are running concurrently against the same table [source 1]. The same read - transform - write pattern is what a Lakeflow pipelines streaming table packages for you: a Delta table with incremental processing designed for append-only ingestion and low latency [source 3], and it is built on Spark Structured Streaming, which is also why a pipeline can ingest directly from an event bus such as Kafka [source 2].

Analysis — The method works because a streaming read is only a declaration: readStream builds an unbounded logical table, and the physical work happens once a writeStream query is started and its trigger fires. Filters and projections stay stateless, so the engine can stream rows through without keeping state, which is why this pipeline has no watermark anywhere. The two options a student is most likely to omit are the explicit schema and the checkpointLocation, and both fail loudly in production rather than in a notebook test: without a checkpoint the query cannot resume and a Delta sink rejects the write, and with an inferred schema the column types can shift between micro-batches. A second classic mistake is choosing the output mode by habit: append is correct here because every output row is final as soon as it is produced, but the same append mode silently breaks the moment a streaming aggregation or deduplication is added without a watermark (see problem p3). A third trap is putting the checkpoint on cluster-local storage or reusing one checkpoint directory for two queries - both destroy the offset bookkeeping that makes restarts correct. Finally, note the trade-off knob: the trigger interval controls latency and commit frequency, not throughput, so shrinking it does not make a slow cluster faster; it only produces more, smaller Delta commits. This generalizes to any file-to-Delta ingestion: pin the schema, keep transformations stateless where possible, give the sink a checkpoint, and size the trigger against the arrival rate so a micro-batch is large enough to be efficient but small enough to meet the latency objective.
Problem 2

The pipeline from problem p1 is running in production. Its checkpoint directory is s3://acme-retail/_checkpoints/silver_purchases and it has committed 47 micro-batches. During micro-batch 48, the driver is killed by the cloud provider after workers have written 12,000 of the expected 28,800 rows to the target table but before the micro-batch completes. (a) List what lives in the checkpoint directory for this query. (b) Explain what the engine does on restart and why the table ends up with neither duplicates nor missing rows. (c) A colleague deletes the checkpoint directory and starts a query against the same source path and the same target table. Predict the effect and explain why it differs from (b). (d) State precisely what the number 47 tells you - and what it does not tell you.
Hint: Exactly-once is a contract between two durable logs: the checkpoint's offset/commit logs on the source side and Delta's transaction log on the sink side.

Worked solution
(a) What the checkpoint contains. The directory holds a metadata file that records the query id and the configuration fingerprint of the query, a sources/ subdirectory containing the offset log (one entry per micro-batch describing which files or offsets that batch will read), a commits/ subdirectory containing the commit log (one entry per micro-batch once its output has been durably written), and a state/ subdirectory that would hold operator state for stateful operations. Because this query only uses filter and select, state/ stays empty - there are no aggregation or deduplication keys to remember. Storing this processing state is exactly what enables fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5].

(b) Restart behaviour. The offset log is written before processing begins (a write-ahead record), while the commit log entry is written only after the output has been durably accepted by the sink. On restart the engine replays both logs and finds that micro-batch 48 has an offset entry but no commit entry, so batch 48 is re-executed and the same 28,800 rows are re-derived from the same source files. The 12,000 rows that had already been written are not visible to readers if the sink transaction never committed - those files are orphans that the retry supersedes - and if the sink transaction did commit, the Delta sink recognises the (stream id, batch version) pair as already applied and does not append it a second time. The Delta Lake transaction log is what makes each micro-batch commit atomic and idempotent, which is the stated guarantee of exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries write to the table concurrently [source 1]. The cost of the recovery is only the recomputation: 28,800 rows / 40,000 rows per second = 0.72 s of work.

(c) Deleting the checkpoint. The checkpoint is the only record of what has already been consumed. Deleting it resets the query's memory: no offsets are known, so every file still present in s3://acme-retail/raw/events/ (that is, everything inside the storage retention window) is listed and read from the beginning, and the idempotency records in the Delta transaction log no longer match the new query identity. The re-ingested data is appended as ordinary new rows, so the target table receives roughly the full retained history a second time. The difference from (b) is that (b) replayed a single unfinished micro-batch under an intact identity, whereas (c) removes the source-side replay point entirely and turns a resumable stream into a fresh one. Correct handling: never delete the checkpoint of a live production query; to restart from scratch, write to a new target table and swap it in, or deduplicate downstream on a key such as event_id.

(d) The number 47. It is the id of the highest micro-batch with a commit log entry, i.e. the number of micro-batches durably applied. It says nothing about row counts (each committed batch here carried 28,800 rows, so 47 batches is about 1.35 million rows), nothing about the number of input files consumed, and nothing about how much work the following micro-batch will be - batch 48 was already 3.4x larger than the average only because of the timing of the crash.

Analysis — Structured Streaming achieves exactly-once by pairing two independently durable logs. The checkpoint answers the source-side question 'which input have I already consumed and which batches have I finished?', and the Delta transaction log answers the sink-side question 'has this batch's write already been applied?'. Remove either half and the guarantee collapses: no checkpoint means the stream replays its source from the beginning, and a non-transactional sink (for example plain Parquet) means a retried batch appends duplicate files because nothing records that the batch already succeeded. The most common student errors are (i) assuming the Delta transaction log alone is sufficient, when the replay point for an unfinished batch lives in the checkpoint; (ii) placing the checkpoint on cluster-local or temporary storage so it disappears exactly when it is needed; (iii) pointing two different queries at one checkpoint directory, which corrupts the offset numbering; and (iv) editing the transformations or the schema while reusing a checkpoint, which makes the stored offsets inconsistent with the new query plan and produces errors or silently wrong output. A good mental model for the exam: batch id + query identity + offset log on the source side, batch id + table version on the sink side, and the two must agree before a row is considered delivered. This reasoning generalises to any sink that supports idempotent commits, which is why Delta Lake and Lakeflow streaming tables are the recommended streaming targets on Databricks [source 1][source 5].
Problem 3

Using the same events stream (12,000 events/s; fields event_id, event_ts, store_id, event_type, amount; 8% purchases), four candidate streaming queries are proposed. For each, decide whether it runs as written; if it does not, give the error condition and the minimal fix. Q1: events.filter(col('event_type') == 'purchase') written to Delta with outputMode('append'). Q2: events.groupBy('store_id').count() written to Delta with outputMode('append') and no watermark. Q3: events.orderBy(col('event_ts')) written to Delta with outputMode('append'). Q4: events.dropDuplicates(['event_id']) written to Delta with outputMode('append') and no watermark. Then state which output modes a Delta Lake streaming sink accepts and why the others are excluded.
Hint: Append mode may only emit a row once the engine is certain that row can never change; ask for each query what makes that certainty possible.

Worked solution
Q1 runs. filter is a stateless operator, so each input row maps to at most one output row and that row is final the instant it is produced. Append mode is the natural fit and no watermark or state is required.

Q2 fails at analysis time with the error 'Append output mode not supported when there are streaming aggregations on streaming DataFrames/DataSets without watermark'. In append mode the engine may emit a group only when it is certain the group can never be updated again. A count for store_id = 17 changes with every new event for store 17, so without a watermark the engine would have to wait forever. Two minimal fixes: (i) add a watermark and a window, e.g. events.withWatermark('event_ts', '10 minutes').groupBy(window('event_ts', '5 minutes'), 'store_id').count() with append mode, so each 5-minute window is finalised once the watermark passes its end; or (ii) keep the raw groupBy and switch to outputMode('update'), which writes only the groups that changed in each micro-batch and is accepted by the Delta sink. Both fixes are correct; they answer different questions (closed-window aggregates versus a continuously refreshed view).

Q3 fails with a sorting error: sorting is not supported on streaming DataFrames or DataSets except after a streaming aggregation in complete output mode (exact wording varies by Spark version). A global sort is only meaningful once all rows are known, and an unbounded logical table never has all its rows. The fix is to remove orderBy from the streaming query and sort in the downstream batch read: spark.read.table('main.retail.silver_purchases').orderBy('event_ts'). Pushing the sort into a batch consumer is always safe because a Delta table is a bounded source.

Q4 runs, but with a state cost that the student must name. dropDuplicates is stateful: the engine must remember every event_id it has seen in order to suppress a later repeat, and without a watermark that memory grows for the entire life of the query. It is not an error, it is a slow leak. Adding events.withWatermark('event_ts', '1 hour') before dropDuplicates lets the engine discard keys older than the watermark, bounding the state at the cost of emitting a duplicate if an event arrives more than an hour late. Note also that the deduplication is over the unbounded history of the stream, not over a single file.

Output modes accepted by the Delta sink. A Delta Lake table as a streaming sink accepts append and update. Complete mode is rejected because it would require the sink to rewrite the entire result set on every trigger, which contradicts the append-only, transaction-log-based storage model of a Delta table; complete mode belongs with memory or console sinks used interactively in a notebook. Append is therefore the correct mode for Q1, update for the aggregation in Q2, and update is what makes a dashboard-style 'latest value per store' query viable on Delta.

Analysis — All four cases reduce to one rule: append mode may emit a row only when the engine can prove the row is final. Stateless operators (filter, select, withColumn, a union of stateless streams) make that proof immediately. Stateful operators (aggregations, dropDuplicates, stream-stream joins) cannot make it until a watermark tells them that no earlier record can still arrive - which is precisely why watermarks and state stores exist, and why only a limited set of operations is supported on streaming DataFrames, with some requiring state and others being unsupported outright. Students typically go wrong in three ways: they assume any batch operator can be lifted into a stream (orderBy, count without watermark, show or collect on a streaming DataFrame); they believe that changing append to update is a cosmetic switch, when in fact it changes the semantics from 'emit each final row once' to 'emit the rows that changed in this micro-batch', so downstream consumers of a Delta table will see updated rows repeatedly; and they add a watermark as a magic incantation without reasoning about the late-data threshold, which either bloats state (threshold too large) or drops legitimate late events (threshold too small). The generalisable design habit is to classify each operator as stateless or stateful before writing the query, then choose the output mode that the class permits.
Problem 4

Before enabling live traffic, the team must backfill 4.2 TB of history: 900,000 JSON files averaging 4.7 MB each, already sitting in the same cloud path. The backfill cluster has 3 workers x 4 cores = 12 cores, and each core parses JSON at about 25 MB/s. Each Delta commit adds roughly 1 s of overhead per micro-batch. (a) With maxFilesPerTrigger set to 1000, how many micro-batches will the backfill run? (b) Estimate the wall-clock time with trigger(processingTime='30 seconds') versus trigger(availableNow=True). (c) Which trigger belongs to the backfill and which to the live tail, and what exactly changes between the two? (d) What is the small-file consequence of the backfill, and what does raising maxFilesPerTrigger to 5000 buy you?
Hint: processingTime waits until the next tick even if the work is done; availableNow runs back-to-back until the available input is exhausted, then stops.

Worked solution
(a) Number of micro-batches. 900,000 files / 1,000 files per micro-batch = 900 micro-batches.

(b) Wall clock for each trigger. Bytes per micro-batch = 1,000 x 4.7 MB = 4,700 MB. Cluster throughput R = 12 cores x 25 MB/s = 300 MB/s. Compute time per micro-batch T_c = 4,700 MB / 300 MB/s = 15.7 s, plus about 1 s of commit overhead, so the engine is busy for roughly 16.7 s per batch.

With trigger(processingTime='30 seconds') the engine starts a micro-batch every 30 s regardless of how fast the previous one finished, so the period is max(30, 16.7) = 30 s. Total time = 900 x 30 s = 27,000 s, i.e. about 7.5 hours - and the query never terminates on its own, because a processingTime trigger is meant for an unbounded stream.

With trigger(availableNow=True) the engine processes all data available at the moment the query starts, running micro-batch after micro-batch back-to-back, and then stops the query. The period is now the work itself: 900 x (15.7 + 1) = 900 x 16.7 s = 15,030 s, i.e. about 4.2 hours. The speed-up is 27,000 / 15,030 = 1.8x, purely from removing idle waiting; no extra compute was needed.

(c) Which trigger where. availableNow for the bounded backfill: the input is finite, the job must end, and there is no reason to idle. Then start a second query with trigger(processingTime='30 seconds') for the unbounded live tail, pointing at a checkpoint directory of its own. Note the semantic difference: availableNow consumes the data that is available at the start of the query; files that land while it is running are not part of that set and will be picked up by the live query. The legacy once trigger did something similar and is superseded by availableNow.

(d) Small files and the effect of a larger file cap. Each micro-batch writes output files sized by the shuffle and partition layout; with roughly 4.7 GB per micro-batch and 128 MB target files you get about 36 files per batch, so 900 batches produce on the order of 32,000 small files, which forces later readers to open and plan over a very large manifest. Raising maxFilesPerTrigger to 5000 gives 900,000 / 5,000 = 180 micro-batches, each reading 5,000 x 4.7 MB = 23.5 GB, taking 23.5 GB / 300 MB/s = 78.3 s of compute plus 1 s of commit, so 180 x 79.3 s = 14,274 s, i.e. about 4.0 hours. The elapsed time barely moves because the backfill is compute-bound, not trigger-bound; what improves is the commit count (180 instead of 900) and the number of output files, and what worsens is the retry granularity if a micro-batch fails. Rate limits such as maxFilesPerTrigger exist precisely to keep batch sizes consistent and prevent processing delays when a backlog appears [source 5]. Finish with a compaction pass (OPTIMIZE or automatic compaction) so the freshly written small files are coalesced.

Analysis — The choice of trigger is a statement about whether the input is bounded or unbounded. processingTime assumes an endless stream and imposes a cadence, so it wastes whatever slack exists between the trigger interval and the actual work - here 13.3 s of idle time in every 30 s cycle - and never stops. availableNow assumes a finite snapshot, drains it as fast as the cluster allows, and terminates, which makes it the correct tool for backfills and for scheduled incremental jobs. The generalisable formula is period = max(trigger interval, compute time + commit overhead), and total time = number of micro-batches x period; a student who writes that formula down will never again mis-estimate a backfill. Common mistakes: running a backfill with a 30-second trigger and being surprised that it takes 7.5 hours and never ends; setting maxFilesPerTrigger very low 'to be safe', which multiplies commits and output files without reducing total compute; and forgetting that the backfill and the live tail must use separate checkpoint directories, since sharing one corrupts offset bookkeeping. In medallion architecture terms (bronze = raw ingested data, silver = cleaned and conformed data, gold = business-level aggregates), this backfill populates the bronze-to-silver step and the live query keeps it current, after which a scheduled batch job builds the gold layer by reading the Delta table - the place where ordering, deduplication and joins that streaming cannot express are finally applied. Store the processing state that makes both phases fault-tolerant, and rate-limit input so batch sizes stay stable [source 5].

actions.text: Now that we understand how micro-batches are triggered, let's make it concrete with a fully worked problem. Here we'll build a minimal streaming read, transform, and write pipeline in PySpark — exactly the pattern the exam expects you to recognize.

Problem one sets the scene: Acme Retail drops JSON event files into a cloud storage location, and our job is to read them, filter down to a subset, and continuously append the results to a Delta table. Read the full statement carefully — every constraint in it matters.

Before you peek at the answer, note the hint: define the schema first, then create the streaming DataFrame with spark.readStream. That ordering is deliberate — it's the single most common place people lose points.

Here's the worked solution. Step one: declare the schema explicitly rather than relying on inference. Step two: apply stateless transformations — filter and select — that look exactly like plain batch DataFrame code. Step three: write with writeStream, set format to delta, use outputMode append, and critically, provide a checkpointLocation and a trigger. Every one of those pieces is load-bearing.

Why does this method work? Because a streaming DataFrame is really just a batch DataFrame plus an unbounded source and a checkpoint that remembers progress. The analysis flags the common pitfalls: a missing checkpoint means no fault tolerance, a wrong output mode can break the write, and some operations simply aren't supported in streaming. Keep this pipeline shape in mind — it's the backbone of the next several problems.

scenes.title: Check: Streaming Reads and Writes

questions.question: You need to build a streaming DataFrame that continuously reads new JSON event files as they land in a cloud storage location. Which API call creates the streaming DataFrame so that the source is treated as an unbounded, ever-growing input table?

options.label: spark.readStream.format("json").schema(eventSchema).load("/mnt/events/raw")
spark.read.format("json").schema(eventSchema).load("/mnt/events/raw")
spark.readStream.format("json").load("/mnt/events/raw").rdd
spark.sql("SELECT * FROM json.`/mnt/events/raw`").writeStream

questions.correctAnswer: spark.readStream.format("json").schema(eventSchema).load("/mnt/events/raw")
questions.analysis: A streaming read is created with spark.readStream, not spark.read: spark.readStream.format('json').schema(eventSchema).load(path) returns a streaming DataFrame modeled as an unbounded table that grows as new files appear [source 1]. Option B is the batch API (spark.read) and only performs a single re-read over the files present at that moment — a common misconception that produces a bounded DataFrame that will never refresh. Option C attempts to convert the streaming DataFrame to an RDD, which is unsupported because streaming queries are executed as a series of incremental micro-batches rather than a single RDD computation. Option D is malformed: writeStream is a sink operation and cannot be used inside a spark.sql statement to produce a source. A best practice on file sources is to define the schema explicitly, since schema inference is not streaming-friendly for evolving sources, and to consider Auto Loader for efficient incremental file discovery [source 5].

questions.question: You are writing a streaming DataFrame to a Delta Lake table so that the pipeline can recover after a restart without reprocessing or losing records. Which two options MUST be configured on the write to guarantee this behavior? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: checkpointLocation — specifies where Structured Streaming persists progress and state for fault tolerance
output mode (for example, append) — defines how results are emitted to the sink on each micro-batch
trigger(processingTime='30 seconds') — sets the micro-batch cadence
option('mergeSchema', 'true') — enables automatic schema evolution during the write

questions.correctAnswer:
checkpointLocation — specifies where Structured Streaming persists progress and state for fault tolerance
output mode (for example, append) — defines how results are emitted to the sink on each micro-batch
questions.analysis: For any streaming write, Structured Streaming must know where to store processing state so it can resume exactly-once after failure: checkpointLocation is required and stores progress and state, enabling fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5]. The output mode is likewise required because it tells the engine how to deliver results to the target on every micro-batch (append, update, or complete) [source 5]. A trigger option (C) controls cadence but is optional — the default micro-batch engine runs continuously. mergeSchema (D) is an optional Delta write capability for evolving schemas, not a requirement for resumable streaming. Delta Lake's transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the same table [source 1], but only if checkpointing is in place.

questions.question: A teammate has built a pipeline that reads events from a cloud storage folder using spark.read.format('json').load(path) and then writes them with .write.mode('append').save('/mnt/delta/events'). They claim this is a streaming pipeline because new files keep arriving in the folder. In 3–5 sentences, explain why this is a batch re-read rather than a streaming read, describe what the source will return if the folder is not re-read, and state what needs to change to make the pipeline continuous and fault-tolerant.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric (100 points total): (1) Correctly identifies that spark.read creates a bounded, batch DataFrame evaluated once over files present at load time — 40%. (2) Explains the unbounded-table behavior of the streaming source: with spark.readStream the DataFrame is modeled as an unbounded table that grows as new files arrive [source 1]; the batch DataFrame does not automatically pick up new files [source 5] — 30%. (3) States that a streaming write requires checkpointLocation and an output mode to persist state and enable exactly-once delivery, and that Delta Lake's transaction log provides exactly-once guarantees [source 1] [source 5] — 30%. Full credit requires the student to contrast 're-read' vs 'continuously grows' and to mention at least one of checkpointLocation or output mode.
questions.analysis: spark.read is the batch reader: it produces a bounded DataFrame evaluated once over whatever files exist at the moment load() is called, so the result is a single, fixed re-read. To make the source truly continuous, use spark.readStream, which models the source as an unbounded table that logically grows as new files arrive [source 1]. On a streaming source, processing state and progress are persisted at the checkpoint location, and the write needs an output mode so the engine knows how to emit results to the sink on each micro-batch [source 5]. Finally, writing into a Delta table via Structured Streaming gives exactly-once guarantees because the Delta Lake transaction log tracks commits, even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently [source 1].

elements.content: Writing to Streaming Sinks and Output Modes
df.writeStream requires a sink, an output mode, and a checkpoint — the three decisions that determine correctness and latency
Sink
Delta table, Kafka, files, or console / foreach for debugging
Output Mode
append, update, or complete — which rows reach the sink each micro-batch
Checkpoint
checkpointLocation stores offsets and state for restart recovery
Worked Example — Append to Delta with Exactly-Once Semantics

Reuse the JSON read from the earlier worked problem, then add .option("checkpointLocation", "/ckpt/orders").format("delta").start("/mnt/silver/orders"). If micro-batch 7 commits offsets up to 1,000,000 but the driver crashes before the log write, on restart Spark replays from the last committed offset only — no duplicate and no gap. [source 1]
Sources: [source 1] Delta Lake transaction log exactly-once; [source 5] sinks, rate limits, checkpoint state; [source 3] streaming tables as append-only Delta sinks

actions.text: Now that we understand how to read from streaming sources, let's turn to the other half of the equation: writing the results out. This page covers `df.writeStream`, the sinks you can write to, the output modes that control which rows reach the sink, and the checkpoint that makes exactly-once processing possible.
Writing to streaming sinks is a core skill for the Data Engineer Associate exam, so let's walk through each required piece carefully.

A `df.writeStream` call requires three things: a sink where the data lands, an output mode that decides which rows are emitted, and a checkpoint location. Miss any one of them and your query either fails to start or cannot recover.

The sink is simply the destination. Typical choices are a Delta table, Kafka, plain files, or the console and `foreach` sinks you use for debugging. For production work, Delta is almost always the answer.

Output mode controls which rows are written on each micro-batch. `append` emits only new rows, `update` emits only rows that changed, and `complete` rewrites the entire updated result — which you must use with aggregations when you want the full picture.
The checkpoint is the recovery anchor. `checkpointLocation` stores the source offsets and any state, so if the query restarts it picks up exactly where it left off — no missing rows, no duplicates.

Let's ground this in a worked example. We reuse the JSON read from our earlier problem and append it to a Delta table with `checkpointLocation` set — that combination is what gives us exactly-once processing, thanks to Delta's transaction log.

One exam trap to flag now: with aggregations, `append` mode only emits results once they're finalized after the watermark. If you need earlier or full results, reach for `update` or `complete` instead.

scenes.title: Lesson Check: Structured Streaming Fundamentals

questions.question: A team is building a pipeline that reads change events from Kafka, performs a stateful aggregation per account, and must never double-count an event even after a mid-batch executor failure. The pipeline writes results to a Delta Lake table. Which combination of design choices best satisfies the exactly-once requirement?

options.label: Use foreachBatch with a custom deduplication table and disable checkpointing to avoid stale state.
Use a Delta Lake sink so that the Delta transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing, and persist processing state via a checkpointLocation for fault tolerance.
Use the complete output mode with a console sink and rely on the driver to discard duplicate records.
Set the trigger to availableNow and store offsets only in memory so each run restarts from the earliest offset.

questions.analysis: Delta Lake as a streaming sink provides exactly-once processing because the Delta Lake transaction log makes the write idempotent together with checkpointed progress; the source material states that the Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently [source 1], and that storing processing state enables fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5]. Option A is wrong because disabling checkpointing removes the fault-tolerance mechanism; a custom dedup table cannot restore progress after failure. Option C is wrong because complete mode with a console sink is a debugging pattern, has no durable sink transaction, and cannot discard duplicates. Option D is wrong because in-memory offsets are lost on restart, re-reading from the earliest offset and re-emitting already-emitted rows.

questions.question: A developer is configuring a Structured Streaming query that reads JSON files from cloud storage and writes to a Delta table. Which statements about the read/write API contract are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: spark.readStream.format(...).schema(...).load(path) creates the streaming DataFrame, and an explicit schema should be provided rather than relying on inference for evolving file sources.
The write requires a checkpointLocation and an outputMode in addition to a sink such as a Delta table.
Because the source is a directory of files, the same spark.readStream call can be swapped for spark.read and will produce identical incremental results.
Stateless transformations such as filter and select can be applied to the streaming DataFrame in the same way they are applied to a batch DataFrame.

questions.analysis: A is correct: a streaming DataFrame is created with spark.readStream, and streaming reads generally require an explicit schema because inference is not streaming-friendly for evolving file sources. B is correct: a streaming write needs a sink plus a checkpointLocation and an outputMode to be durable and well-defined. D is correct: stateless operations like filter and select behave identically on streaming and batch DataFrames, as shown in the worked read/write problem. C is wrong because spark.read performs a one-time bounded batch read of whatever files exist at that moment, while spark.readStream keeps querying the source for new data as the unbounded table grows. Delta Lake tables can serve as both streaming sources and sinks with exactly-once guarantees [source 5].

questions.question: A dashboard must show a continuously updated running count of orders per region with the lowest practical latency, and late-arriving orders must update the already-published counts. The team wants the sink to contain the entire refreshed result set after every micro-batch. Which output mode and trigger choice is the best fit?

options.label: append mode with a Trigger.processingTime('1 hour') to reduce write amplification.
complete mode with a short processingTime trigger, so each micro-batch republishes the full updated aggregation result.
update mode with Trigger.once(), because once mode guarantees the lowest end-to-end latency.
append mode with the experimental continuous trigger, because append is the only mode compatible with aggregations.

questions.analysis: Complete mode republishes the entire updated result after each micro-batch and is the mode designed for aggregations where previously emitted rows may change; pairing it with a short processingTime trigger keeps latency low, and micro-batches are ordinary Spark jobs executed against the growing logical streaming table. A is wrong because a one-hour trigger produces unacceptably high latency for a dashboard and append mode will not re-emit updated counts. C is wrong because once/availableNow processes only what is currently available and then stops, so it cannot provide continuously updated low-latency results. D is wrong because append mode is not the only aggregation-compatible mode and continuous mode is experimental. Delta Lake sink semantics also matter here: the Delta Lake transaction log supports exactly-once processing [source 1], and streaming tables are designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 4].

questions.question: Explain how Structured Streaming's micro-batch execution model, the output modes (append, update, complete), and the Delta Lake sink together deliver exactly-once processing. In your answer, refer to the role of the checkpoint location, the trade-off controlled by the trigger interval, and one concrete failure scenario in which a design without checkpointing would produce incorrect results.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric (100 total): (1) Micro-batch model - 25%: correctly describes that Structured Streaming repeatedly queries the source for new data and processes each chunk as a small Spark job against the growing logical streaming DataFrame, and that the trigger (processingTime, availableNow, once, continuous) controls the cadence. (2) Output modes - 20%: correctly distinguishes append (only new rows), update (only changed rows), and complete (the entire updated result, used with aggregations), and links the chosen mode to whether prior rows are re-emitted. (3) Exactly-once mechanism - 30%: must state that the Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even with concurrent streams or batch jobs [source 1], and that storing processing state enables fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5]; must reference the checkpointLocation as the place where progress/offsets and state are persisted. (4) Trigger trade-off - 15%: explains that shorter trigger intervals reduce latency but increase the number of small micro-batches and overhead, while longer intervals raise latency but improve per-batch efficiency/throughput. (5) Failure scenario - 10%: gives a concrete example, e.g., an executor dies mid-batch and without a durable checkpoint the query restarts from the earliest offset and re-emits rows, duplicating counts in the sink. Deduct points for vague claims such as 'checkpointing makes it reliable' without naming the persisted progress/state or the Delta transaction log.
questions.analysis: A strong answer should cover: (a) Structured Streaming defaults to micro-batch execution, where the unbounded input table is queried repeatedly and each new chunk becomes an ordinary Spark job; triggers set how often this happens. (b) Output modes decide what the sink receives per batch: append = new rows only, update = changed rows only, complete = the full updated result (typically for aggregations). (c) Exactly-once is achieved by combining idempotent writes to Delta Lake, whose transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently [source 1], with durable progress and state stored at the checkpoint location enabling fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5]. (d) The trigger interval trades latency for throughput: very short intervals give low latency but many small batches, while longer intervals reduce overhead but increase latency. (e) Without a checkpoint, a failure forces the query to restart from the earliest available offset, re-emitting already-emitted rows and producing duplicates or inflated aggregations, since there is no durable record of what has been processed. Delta Lake can serve as both streaming source and sink with exactly-once guarantees, and streaming tables are designed for append-only, low-latency ingestion [source 4].

scenes.title: Delta Tables as Streaming Sources and Sinks

elements.content: Delta Tables as Streaming Sources and Sinks
Two exam objectives: read a Delta table as a stream, and write a stream into Delta

One Delta table holds one or more roles in a pipeline: streaming source (a readStream reader) and/or streaming sink (a writeStream target).

Precondition: the table must be Delta-format and transaction-logged, so batched and streaming writers never lose rows. [source 1]

Source: spark.readStream.table(

"events") — the same table can serve batch and streaming readers concurrently.

Sink: df.writeStream.format("delta")

.option("checkpointLocation", ...)

.toTable("silver_events")
Worked example — exactly-once under concurrent writes

elements.html: 10,000+2500×4=20,000 rows committed

elements.content: A batch job appends 10,000 rows; a streaming writer commits 4 micro-batches of 2,500. The Delta transaction log commits each write atomically with a monotonically increasing version, so no read or replay ever sees a row twice. [source 1]
Rows appended per micro-batch by two concurrent writers [source 5]
Takeaway: Delta Lake is both a valid streaming source and a valid streaming sink; the transaction log is what makes this safe. [source 1][source 5]

actions.text: Now that we've got the streaming fundamentals down, let's see how a Delta table fits into a Structured Streaming pipeline. A Delta table can play two distinct roles: it can be a streaming source, and it can be a streaming sink — sometimes the exact same table does both at once.

Keep these two exam objectives in mind throughout this page. First, identifying the two roles a Delta table can play in a pipeline. Second, explaining why the Delta transaction log lets us guarantee exactly-once processing — even when other writers are touching that same table.

Let's start with the source side. To read a Delta table as a stream, you call spark.readStream.table, passing the table name, for example "events". The key insight here is that the same table can simultaneously serve batch readers and streaming readers — there's no lock, no conflict, no interference between them.

On the sink side, writing a stream into Delta looks like this: df.writeStream.format("delta"), plus a checkpointLocation option, and then .toTable with a target like "silver_events". That checkpoint location is not optional — it is what lets the stream remember exactly where it left off if the query restarts.
Here's a worked example that ties it all together — exactly-once behavior under concurrent writes. Watch carefully, because this is precisely the kind of scenario the exam likes to test.

Imagine a batch job appends ten thousand rows to a table, and at the same time, a streaming writer is appending micro-batches. The transaction log serializes these commits: each writer adds its own commit entry, and readers see a consistent snapshot at whatever version they happen to read.

This bar chart shows rows appended per micro-batch by the concurrent batch writer versus the streaming writer on the same Delta table. The logs guarantee that no row is double-counted and every committed micro-batch appears exactly once, even though both writers are active at the same time.

So the takeaway is: Delta Lake is both a valid streaming source and a valid streaming sink. The transaction log is what makes exactly-once semantics possible when multiple writers — batch or streaming — hit the same table. In the next segment, we'll go hands-on and actually read a Delta table as a stream.

scenes.title: Check: Streaming Reads from Delta

questions.question: A data engineer wants to expose an existing Delta table named `main.sales.events` as an unbounded streaming DataFrame within a Structured Streaming query, without redefining any schema or pointing at a physical storage path. Which API call correctly returns a streaming DataFrame from this Delta table?

options.label: spark.readStream.table("main.sales.events")
spark.read.table("main.sales.events").stream()
spark.readStream.format("path").load("main.sales.events")
spark.readStream.load("main.sales.events")

questions.analysis: The correct call is spark.readStream.table("main.sales.events"). This is the catalog/table-based streaming read API: readStream selects the streaming (unbounded) execution path, and table(...) resolves the Delta table by its fully qualified name through the catalog. This mirrors the Delta-specific pattern taught in the unit — spark.readStream.table("events") — which lets the same Delta table act as both a streaming source and a batch source concurrently, since the Delta Lake transaction log tracks committed versions that streaming readers consume incrementally [source 1]. Option B is wrong because spark.read.table(...) returns a batch DataFrame, and there is no .stream() method on a DataFrame in PySpark. Option C is wrong because the format("path").load(...) file-source pattern expects a storage path and a format string (e.g. "delta"), not a catalog table identifier; even when reading files, the format option must be supplied. Option D is wrong because readStream.load(...) with a bare table name does not resolve catalog tables — load() is the path-based entry point for file formats, not the table-based entry point. Recognizing that readStream.table() is distinct from read.table() and from a path-based file source is precisely the exam trap this question tests.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describe the behavior and API surface of reading a Delta table as a stream? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A streaming query can read a Delta table while a separate batch writer appends new data to that same table, because the Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the table.
spark.read.table(...) and spark.readStream.table(...) are interchangeable: both return a streaming DataFrame as long as the target is a Delta table.
After creating a DataFrame with spark.readStream.table(...), df.isStreaming returns True, which distinguishes it from an equivalent batch DataFrame.
Reading a Delta table as a stream requires an explicit schema because streaming reads never support schema inference.
A Delta table can act as both a streaming source and a streaming sink, which is why a streaming table is described as a Delta table with support for streaming and incremental processing.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: the Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing, even when there are other streams or batch queries running concurrently against the table, so a streaming reader and a batch writer can safely operate on the same table at the same time [source 1]. Option C is correct: the definitive runtime check that a DataFrame is a streaming DataFrame is df.isStreaming — after spark.readStream.table(...) it returns True, whereas after spark.read.table(...) it returns False. Option E is correct: a Delta table serves both roles (streaming source and streaming sink), and this duality is exactly why a streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines is described as a Delta table with support for streaming and incremental processing, designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 3]. Option B is a classic misconception — read returns a batch DataFrame and readStream returns a streaming DataFrame; they are not interchangeable, and the streaming path must be selected explicitly. Option D is a misconception: explicit-schema requirements apply to file/cloud-storage sources where schema evolution is a concern; a Delta table read through the catalog already has a defined schema in the metastore, so schema inference is not the binding requirement here.

questions.question: You are designing a pipeline where a streaming query reads a Delta table named `main.ops.transactions` and writes results into another Delta table while a nightly batch job appends new rows to `main.ops.transactions`. Explain: (1) the exact API call you would use to obtain the streaming DataFrame; (2) how you would verify at runtime that the DataFrame is indeed streaming; and (3) whether this concurrent read-while-writing pattern is safe, citing the mechanism that makes it safe.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Correct API (40%): The answer must state a call of the form spark.readStream.table("main.ops.transactions") — readStream for the streaming execution path and table(...) for the catalog-resolved Delta table. Naming read.table() or a bare path without format is a deduction. (2) Runtime verification (25%): Must reference df.isStreaming and state that it returns True for a streaming DataFrame (and False for the batch equivalent). (3) Concurrency safety (35%): Must explain that the pattern is safe because the Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the table. Partial credit for mentioning the transaction log without the exactly-once/concurrency clause; no credit for simply asserting 'it works' without the mechanism.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: (1) The streaming DataFrame is created with spark.readStream.table("main.ops.transactions"). The readStream entry point selects the unbounded execution path and table(...) resolves the Delta table by its fully qualified catalog name — this is the same streaming-table read pattern demonstrated in the unit. (2) Verification: call df.isStreaming; a properly constructed streaming DataFrame returns True, which is how the hands-on lab confirms that the DataFrame will be executed by the micro-batch engine rather than as a single batch job. (3) Safety: yes, the pattern is safe. Delta Lake's transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries are running concurrently against the table [source 1]. The streaming reader consumes committed versions from the log incrementally, so a concurrent batch append shows up as new data in a subsequent micro-batch rather than corrupting or duplicating state. This is the operational form of the claim that Delta tables are used as streaming sources and sinks with exactly-once processing guarantees [source 5], and it is why a Delta-based streaming table can support append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming simultaneously [source 3].
