scenes.title: Controlling Output Modes: Append, Update, Complete

elements.content: Controlling Output Modes: Append, Update, Complete

Append — emits only rows added since the previous trigger; each micro-batch contributes a new, non-overlapping chunk.

Update — emits only rows whose values changed since the last trigger; unchanged rows are suppressed.

Complete — rewrites the entire result table on every trigger, regardless of what changed.

Worked Example (rows emitted per trigger)

Source adds 40 rows at t₀. A later trigger revises 12 and adds 8.

append → 40, then 8.

Rows written: 40 + 8 = 48

update → 40, then 12 changed rows only.

complete → 40, then the full 48-row result.

Worked Example (rows emitted per trigger)

Source adds 40 rows at t₀; a later trigger revises 12 and adds 8.

append → 40, then 8 (total written = 48).

update → 40, then only the 12 changed rows.

complete → 40, then the full 48-row result table.

Accepted by a Delta Sink

Delta streaming sinks require append: a Delta table is an append-only, incrementally processed store [source 3].

An attempt to write update or complete into Delta raises an analysis error — the mode is not supported for that sink [source 1].

Accepted by a Delta Sink

Delta streaming sinks require append: a Delta table is an append-only, incrementally processed store [source 3].

Attempting update or complete against Delta raises an analysis error — unsupported mode for that sink [source 1].

Default & exam cue: append is the default output mode and the only one that safely and incrementally appends to a Delta table. Exactly-once is guaranteed by the Delta transaction log even with concurrent batch or streaming readers [source 1].
Distractor alert: “update mode updates only changed rows in the Delta target” is false — Delta streaming sinks accept neither update nor complete [source 2].

actions.text: Now we come to a decision point that shows up constantly on the exam: controlling output modes. When you write a streaming DataFrame to a sink, you must tell Spark how to emit rows each micro-batch. There are exactly three options to know — append, update, and complete — and each behaves very differently.

Let's start with append mode. Append emits only the rows added since the previous trigger — nothing else. It never revisits rows that were already written, which is precisely why it can be applied incrementally to a Delta table without reprocessing history.

Here's your exam cue: append is the default output mode. If a question doesn't specify a mode, assume append — and remember that it's the only mode that safely and incrementally appends to a Delta table.

This worked example walks through how many rows each mode emits per trigger. Watch the row counts as new events arrive: append grows monotonically, while update re-emits only the rows that changed, so the same key can appear multiple times across batches.

Now the critical constraint for a Delta sink. Delta streaming sinks accept only append mode. Update and complete are not accepted as Delta sinks — complete mode rewrites the entire result table every trigger and is intended for aggregated results displayed interactively, not for a streaming Delta target.

And finally, the distractor alert. A tempting wrong answer states that 'update mode updates only changed rows in the Delta target table.' That sounds plausible, but it's false — Delta streaming sinks do not support update or complete output modes at all. Read the sink before you read the mode. That single check resolves most of these questions.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Choosing an Output Mode and Sink

elements.content: Problem 1

Scenario: a retail company streams click events from a Kafka topic called clicks (12 partitions, about 1.2 million events per hour, average event payload 800 bytes, Kafka retention 24 hours) into a Bronze Delta table named clicks_bronze. (Bronze = the raw ingestion layer of the medallion architecture, the layered raw-to-refined data design pattern in which bronze holds raw ingested data, silver cleaned data, and gold business-level aggregates.) The Databricks job runs every 15 minutes on a cluster that starts for the run and then terminates; there is no always-on cluster. There is no aggregation and no update of previously emitted rows - the Bronze table is append-only. Requirement: a downstream SQL dashboard that queries clicks_bronze must see every event exactly once (no duplicates, no lost events), and the delay for a new event must stay under 16 minutes on average. Task: write the complete read and write code and justify the choice of output mode, trigger, and sink. State explicitly where the exactly-once guarantee comes from and why checkpointLocation is not optional.

Hint: Separate the problem into three independent decisions: (1) which sink can give exactly-once delivery? (2) which output mode is legal for a non-aggregated, append-only stream? (3) which trigger lets a scheduled job consume everything that arrived and then stop the cluster?

Worked solution
Step 1 - Read the stream with spark.readStream.

```python

clicks_raw = (spark.readStream

.format('kafka')

.option('kafka.bootstrap.servers', 'broker1:9092,broker2:9092')

.option('subscribe', 'clicks')

.option('startingOffsets', 'earliest')

.option('maxOffsetsPerTrigger', 50000)

.load())

```

The Kafka source has a fixed schema (key, value, topic, partition, offset, timestamp, timestampType), so no schema inference is required here. File-based sources (JSON, CSV, Parquet, and Auto Loader) do require an explicit schema, because schema inference is not streaming-friendly for evolving file sources.

Step 2 - Parse the payload with stateless transformations (identical in form to batch transformations).

```python

from pyspark.sql.functions import from_json, col

schema = 'event_id STRING, user_id STRING, page STRING, event_time TIMESTAMP'

clicks = (clicks_raw

.select(from_json(col('value').cast('string'), schema).alias('e'))

.select('e.*'))

```

Step 3 - Write with writeStream, choosing sink, mode, trigger, and checkpoint.

```python

(clicks.writeStream

.format('delta')

.outputMode('append')

.option('checkpointLocation', '/checkpoints/clicks_bronze')

.trigger(availableNow=True)

.toTable('clicks_bronze'))

```

Step 4 - Justify the SINK: Delta Lake. Delta is the only sink in this problem that can deliver exactly-once end to end, because the Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing, even when other streams or batch queries are running concurrently against the table [source 1]. A plain Parquet directory sink gives atomic file writes but no transaction log, so a replayed batch would create duplicate files instead of a no-op.

Step 5 - Justify the OUTPUT MODE: append. The stream is non-aggregated and append-only, so every micro-batch consists of new rows only, which is exactly the definition of append mode. Two distractors fail:

- complete mode is rejected by Spark for non-aggregated streams ('Complete output mode not supported when there are no streaming aggregations on streaming DataFrames/DataSets'), and even where it is legal it rewrites the entire result table on every trigger, which is absurd for a table that grows forever.

- update mode emits only rows that changed since the previous trigger. In a non-aggregated, append-only stream nothing is ever 'updated', so update mode adds configuration risk with zero benefit; it exists for aggregation results whose previously emitted rows change.

Step 6 - Justify the TRIGGER: availableNow=True. This trigger processes all data currently available in one or more micro-batches and then stops the query, which matches a job that runs every 15 minutes on a non-always-on cluster. Using trigger(processingTime='15 minutes') instead would keep the cluster running 24/7 waiting between triggers - the same data freshness at a much higher cost.

Size the batches to confirm the cluster is adequate: 1.2 million events/hour divided by 4 runs per hour equals 300,000 events per run; 300,000 divided by 50,000 rows per micro-batch equals 6 micro-batches per run; per-micro-batch raw payload is 50,000 x 800 bytes = 40 MB, and per-run raw payload is 300,000 x 800 bytes = 240 MB. That footprint is small enough for a two-worker cluster with the default memory budget.

Step 7 - Justify the CHECKPOINT: checkpointLocation is mandatory for Delta and file sinks; the query simply will not start without it. The checkpoint directory is where Spark durably records the source offsets it has consumed, the IDs of committed batches, and any state for stateful operators. Exactly-once is a two-sided contract:

- source side: the checkpoint stores the Kafka offsets, so a restart resumes at the last committed offset instead of re-reading a retention window or skipping ahead to latest;

- sink side: the Delta transaction log makes a replayed batch idempotent. If the write committed but the checkpoint record of that batch did not, the retried batch is committed under the same transaction identity and Delta recognises it as already applied [source 1].

Delta tables are usable as both streaming sources and sinks with exactly-once guarantees, and storing processing state in the checkpoint is what enables fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5].

Step 8 - Check the latency budget. Worst case an event arrives one second after the 15-minute job starts, waits 15 minutes for the next run, plus roughly 30 seconds of processing: 15.5 minutes, which satisfies the 16-minute requirement. If the requirement had been under one minute, the correct answer would change to trigger(processingTime='10 seconds') with an always-on job, or to a Lakeflow pipeline streaming table, which is a Delta table with support for streaming and incremental processing, designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 3].

Final answer: sink = Delta (toTable('clicks_bronze')), outputMode = append, trigger = availableNow=True, checkpointLocation = /checkpoints/clicks_bronze, plus maxOffsetsPerTrigger = 50000 for batch-size control.

Analysis — The reason this combination works is that it separates three concerns that beginners fuse into one: durability of the sink (Delta transaction log), semantics of the emitted rows (output mode), and scheduling of the work (trigger). Exactly-once requires both halves of the contract - a source-side record of consumed offsets (checkpoint) and a sink-side idempotent commit (Delta log) [source 1]. Remove either half and you get at-least-once (duplicates) or at-most-once (loss).

The most common exam mistakes are: (a) choosing update mode 'because it writes less data', when update mode is designed for changed aggregation rows and does nothing useful for an append-only stream; (b) choosing complete mode with a small mental model of the data, forgetting that complete rewrites the full result on every trigger; (c) choosing processingTime='15 minutes' to match the job schedule, which keeps the cluster alive between triggers; (d) omitting checkpointLocation, which for Delta sinks raises an error at query start rather than failing silently.

Edge cases to know: append mode with aggregation requires a watermark (covered in the next problem); schema changes on the source need Delta schema evolution options such as mergeSchema; and adding a second writer to the same table is fine for exactly-once only because each query keeps its own checkpoint and Delta serialises concurrent commits against the transaction log [source 1]. This pattern generalises to any stateless bronze ingestion: Kafka or Auto Loader as source, append-only Delta as sink, availableNow for scheduled runs, and processingTime for always-on low-latency runs. On Lakeflow pipelines the same idea appears as a streaming table, which is a Delta table that supports streaming and incremental processing and is designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 3]; a Lakeflow pipeline is itself built on Spark Structured Streaming and can ingest directly from an event bus like Kafka [source 2].
Problem 2

Now the business adds an aggregation. From the same clicks stream, the analytics team wants a Delta table clicks_per_page_1m containing, for each 1-minute tumbling event-time window and each page, the number of clicks. The upstream producer sometimes retries, so about 3% of events are exact duplicates by event_id. Measurements show events can arrive up to 4 minutes 10 seconds later than their event_time. The stream carries 1.2 million events per hour and about 15,000 distinct page URLs per hour. Task: write the aggregation pipeline, choose the output mode, trigger, and watermark, add duplicate removal, and compute (a) the memory held by the deduplication state with and without a watermark, and (b) the delay before an append-mode window result is final. Then state what you would change if the dashboard required results to appear within 2 minutes.

Hint: A watermark is a lateness budget, not a timer. Round the observed 4 minutes 10 seconds of lateness up to a 5-minute watermark, then ask when the watermark can possibly pass the end of a 1-minute window.

Worked solution
Step 1 - Separate the deduplication from the aggregation, because they have different correctness rules.

```python

from pyspark.sql.functions import window, col

deduped = (clicks

.withWatermark('event_time', '5 minutes')

.dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(['event_id']))

agg = (deduped

.groupBy(window(col('event_time'), '1 minute'), col('page'))

.count())

query = (agg.writeStream

.format('delta')

.outputMode('append')

.option('checkpointLocation', '/checkpoints/clicks_per_page_1m')

.trigger(processingTime='60 seconds')

.toTable('clicks_per_page_1m'))

```

Step 2 - Justify the watermark value. The watermark is the maximum lateness you are willing to tolerate. Observed maximum lateness is 4 minutes 10 seconds, so the smallest safe round number is 5 minutes. Setting it to 1 minute would silently drop late events (they would be considered 'too late' and ignored); setting it to 60 minutes would keep window state alive far longer than necessary and delay every result.

Step 3 - Justify the deduplication operator. dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(['event_id']) removes duplicate event_ids and, crucially, lets the watermark garbage-collect the keys. Quantity check: 20,000 events per minute (1.2M per hour) x 5 minutes of watermark = at most 100,000 event_ids retained in state; at roughly 150 bytes per state entry that is about 15 MB - trivially small. Compare with plain dropDuplicates(['event_id']) and no watermark: state retains every key it has ever seen, so 28.8 million keys per day (1.2M x 24) x 150 bytes is about 4.3 GB per day, roughly 30 GB per week, and the query eventually fails with out-of-memory or a checkpoint too large to recover. Plain dropDuplicates with a watermark is also bounded, but it holds each row until the watermark passes it before emitting; dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark emits immediately and discards late duplicates that fall inside the watermark (available in Spark 3.5+ / DBR 13.3 LTS and above). Number of duplicates removed per day: 3% x 28.8M = 864,000 rows.

Step 4 - Justify the output mode and compute the latency. With window(col('event_time'), '1 minute') the window is a tumbling event-time window of width 1 minute. In append mode, Spark emits a window only when it is certain no more rows can belong to it, i.e. when the watermark passes the window end. The watermark equals (maximum event time seen so far) minus 5 minutes, so the window [10:00, 10:01) becomes final when the watermark reaches 10:01, that is when the maximum observed event time reaches 10:06. The delay from window start is therefore $$1 + 5 = 6 \text{ minutes}$$ and from window end it is 5 minutes. Adding the 60-second processing-time trigger, the worst case is about 7 minutes. Also note: append mode with a streaming aggregation and no watermark is illegal - Spark raises 'Append output mode not supported when there are streaming aggregations on streaming DataFrames/DataSets without watermark'.

Step 5 - Answer the 2-minute question. Append mode cannot meet it: final results are structurally at least watermark + window size late. Two legitimate changes: (a) shrink the budget - if lateness were truly under 30 seconds you could use a 1-minute watermark with 30-second windows for about 1.5 minutes - but the measured 4 min 10 s lateness makes that unsafe here; or (b) use outputMode('update'), which emits the rows that changed since the previous trigger, so the dashboard sees provisional counts within one trigger interval (60 seconds), while final values settle at the ~6-minute mark. Update mode requires a sink that can express row-level changes; Delta's sink writes the changed rows as a transaction, whereas Spark's generic file sink supports append and complete only.

Final answer: watermark 5 minutes on event_time; dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark on event_id; 1-minute tumbling windows grouped by page; append mode for final, stable counts (about 6 minutes after window start); processingTime trigger of 60 seconds; dedicated checkpoint /checkpoints/clicks_per_page_1m. Use update mode if provisional sub-2-minute visibility is mandatory, accepting that displayed values can still change.

Analysis — The method choice here follows from two independent correctness requirements. Duplicate removal requires keyed state, and any unbounded keyed state must be bounded by a watermark, otherwise the query degrades over days and dies - this is the single most common production failure of streaming deduplication. Aggregation output requires deciding whether you can wait for certainty; append mode buys correctness (each window emitted once, never revised) at the price of lateness equal to watermark + window size, while update mode buys freshness at the price of provisional values and a sink that supports updates.

Typical mistakes: (1) using withWatermark but forgetting it only takes effect for the stateful operators downstream of it - placing withWatermark after the aggregation does nothing; (2) assuming the trigger interval controls window finalisation (it does not - the watermark does); (3) setting the watermark below the observed lateness, which converts late data into silently dropped data with no error; (4) choosing complete mode for a group-by whose key space is unbounded (15,000 pages per hour means millions of distinct (window, page) keys over a day, and complete mode must produce every key on every trigger, so state cannot be safely discarded and output volume explodes); (5) running dropDuplicates on the whole row instead of on the business key event_id, which fails to remove retries that carry a new ingestion timestamp.

This generalises to a rule you can apply in any exam scenario: stateful streaming operator + unbounded key space = you must define a watermark, and the watermark value is a business decision about how much lateness you accept. The same reasoning applies to joins (watermark both sides plus an event-time range condition) and to sessionisation.
Problem 3

Incident review. A junior engineer wants to 'double throughput', so they deploy a second copy of the p1 pipeline that writes to the same clicks_bronze table using the same .option('checkpointLocation', '/checkpoints/clicks_bronze'). The second query does not behave as expected. The engineer then deletes the /checkpoints/clicks_bronze directory to 'start clean' and restarts with startingOffsets='earliest'. One day later the dashboard shows inflated click counts. Quantify the damage in rows for both possible settings of startingOffsets (earliest and latest) given 1.2 million events per hour, a 24-hour Kafka retention, and a 20-minute restart window; then give the correct fix and explain what is stored in a checkpoint directory.

Hint: A checkpoint path is the identity of a streaming query, not a scratch directory. Sharing it means two queries claim the same offsets; deleting it means the query forgets which offsets it already consumed.

Worked solution
Step 1 - Diagnose the two-writer attempt. A checkpoint directory identifies one query: it holds the consumed source offsets the query is advancing. Starting a second, concurrent query against the same checkpoint location is rejected - Spark refuses to start it because that checkpoint is already owned by a running query (the exact exception text varies by version) - or, if the first query has stopped, the second query resumes from the stored offsets rather than starting fresh, so you get exactly the same throughput as before, not double. Either way, the second query never delivers 'two readers on one Kafka topic'.

Step 2 - Quantify the effect of deleting the checkpoint with startingOffsets='earliest'. The query loses the record of consumed offsets, so it re-reads from the beginning of what Kafka still retains: 24 hours x 1.2 million events/hour = 28.8 million events replayed. At roughly 500 bytes per stored row that is about 14.4 GB of duplicated data, and every event is now counted twice by the dashboard, so measured click counts for the affected period are inflated by up to $$\frac{28.8\text{M}}{28.8\text{M}} = 100\%$$ for the replayed window. (Because the sink is Delta with a checkpoint that has been destroyed, the replayed batch carries a new transaction identity and is not deduplicated.)

Step 3 - Quantify the effect with startingOffsets='latest'. Now there is no replay but a gap: the query jumps to the end of each partition and discards everything produced between the last checkpointed offset and the restart. With 1.2 million events/hour = 20,000 events/minute and a 20-minute restart window: $$20{,}000 \times 20 = 400{,}000$$ events are silently lost, and no error is raised - the job simply looks healthy while the table is wrong.

Step 4 - Give the correct fix. (a) Never share a checkpoint path between two queries; if you genuinely need two writers to one table, give each its own path (for example /checkpoints/clicks_bronze_w1 and _w2) - concurrent writers to the same Delta table are safe because the transaction log serialises commits and still guarantees exactly-once [source 1]. (b) Do not solve throughput with a second writer at all. Scale inside the single query: increase Kafka partitions, tune maxOffsetsPerTrigger, add workers, or enable Photon. (c) If the pipeline must be restarted from scratch deliberately, use a new checkpoint path and expect reprocessing; declare the operation as a backfill, not a fix.

Step 5 - State what the checkpoint actually contains. Structured Streaming writes four kinds of artefacts under checkpointLocation: offsets/ (the source offsets committed for each batch), commits/ (a marker per completed batch, used to prove that a batch finished before offsets are advanced), metadata (the query identity and plan information), and state/ (the keyed operator state for stateful operations such as aggregations and deduplication). The checkpoint is the source-side half of the exactly-once contract; Delta's transaction log is the sink-side half, which is what makes a replayed batch idempotent [source 1]. Together they are what the platform documentation means by storing processing state to enable fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5].

Final answer: the second writer must have a unique checkpoint; deleting a checkpoint converts a correct exactly-once pipeline into either a 28.8-million-row duplication event (startingOffsets='earliest') or a 400,000-event silent loss (startingOffsets='latest'). Scale within one query instead.

Analysis — Why this is subtle: a checkpoint is invisible in normal operation, so students treat it as configuration noise. It is actually the query's durable memory - the answer to 'which inputs have I already consumed?' - and therefore the precondition for exactly-once. Without it, restart behaviour is decided entirely by startingOffsets: earliest duplicates, latest loses data. Neither is 'safe'.

Edge cases worth memorising: reusing the same checkpoint path after materially changing the query's stateful plan can fail with a checkpoint incompatibility error rather than silently misbehaving; moving a checkpoint path is equivalent to deleting it; and deleting a checkpoint while a query is running corrupts the recovery contract. A second writer on the same table with a distinct checkpoint is legitimate and safe because Delta's transaction log guarantees exactly-once even with other streams or batch queries running concurrently against the table [source 1].

Generalisation: whenever you see 'exactly-once' in a scenario, look for two artefacts - a source-side offset record (checkpoint) and a sink-side idempotent commit (Delta transaction log) [source 5]. If either is missing, the guarantee is at-least-once or at-most-once, no matter how correct the transformations look. This is also why rate limiting options such as maxOffsetsPerTrigger belong next to the read, not the write: they bound batch size without touching the offset bookkeeping that the checkpoint manages [source 5].
Problem 4

Code review, second trap. A developer must produce a Silver table named checkout_events containing only the clicks whose page equals '/checkout'. They write:

```python

df = spark.read.table('clicks_bronze')

(df.filter(col('page') == '/checkout')

.writeStream

.format('delta')

.outputMode('append')

.option('checkpointLocation', '/checkpoints/checkout_events')

.toTable('checkout_events'))

```

The job fails at once. (a) Identify the exact error and explain it. (b) Give the corrected code. (c) A colleague 'fixes' it by changing the destination back to clicks_bronze in the toTable call, so the stream reads and writes the same table. The job runs successfully. Explain what happens to the table over one day, assuming 15-minute runs and 300,000 new Bronze events per run, and give the correct architectural pattern instead.
Hint: Check the return type of the read call before you check anything else - and remember that isStreaming is a property you can assert on rather than hope about.

Worked solution
Step (a) - Diagnose. spark.read.table('clicks_bronze') returns a static (batch) DataFrame. Calling writeStream on it raises exactly this error:

AnalysisException: 'writeStream' can be called only on streaming Dataset/DataFrame

This is not a configuration problem: the query is not streaming at all, so there is nothing for a trigger, output mode, or checkpoint to control. The trap is that no error appears until the write, so the read line looks innocent. The corrected read is spark.readStream.table('clicks_bronze'), which returns a streaming DataFrame whose .isStreaming property is True; the equivalent batch call .read.table() on the same table is perfectly valid and is used by batch jobs, which is why the mistake is easy to copy from a batch notebook.

Step (b) - Corrected code.

```python

from pyspark.sql.functions import col

df = spark.readStream.table('clicks_bronze')

assert df.isStreaming

(df.filter(col('page') == '/checkout')

.writeStream

.format('delta')

.outputMode('append')

.option('checkpointLocation', '/checkpoints/checkout_events')

.trigger(availableNow=True)

.toTable('checkout_events'))

```

A Delta table can serve as both a streaming source and a streaming sink, and a path-based or table-based streaming read picks up new commits incrementally rather than re-scanning the whole table.

Step (c) - The feedback loop. If the stream filters clicks_bronze and writes the survivors back into clicks_bronze, every micro-batch appends rows that the very next micro-batch reads and appends again. Each 15-minute run adds 300,000 rows, all of which are re-read and re-written by the next run, so after 24 hours (96 runs) the table has accumulated $$96 \times 300{,}000 = 28{,}800{,}000$$ extra rows - roughly one duplicated day of checkout events on top of the real data. The job reports success the whole time; only the row counts and downstream revenue figures reveal the loop. Nothing about Delta, checkpoints, or exactly-once prevents this, because each individual batch is written correctly - the defect is architectural.

Step (d) - Correct pattern. Follow the medallion architecture (raw bronze, cleaned silver, business-level gold): read Bronze, write Silver (checkout_events), and never write a stream into the table it reads. If a genuine in-place enrichment is unavoidable, the write must target a different table or a different path, or the read must be filtered so that it cannot see the pipeline's own output (for example by reading only rows written before the query started, or by carrying an explicit lineage column that the read filters out). Read and write are separate stages with separate table identities.

Final answer: the failure is a batch read feeding a streaming write ('''writeStream' can be called only on streaming Dataset/DataFrame'); the fix is spark.readStream.table(...) plus a distinct destination table; writing a stream back into its own source creates an unbounded self-amplifying duplicate loop, 28.8 million extra rows per day at these volumes.

Analysis — Why the method works: streaming and batch reads return different DataFrame types, and only streaming DataFrames carry the incremental-progress machinery (offsets, watermarks, state) that writeStream requires. Asserting df.isStreaming immediately after the read turns a confusing write-time error into a clear read-time failure.

Common mistakes: copying a batch read into a streaming job because both compile; assuming readStream is a performance switch rather than a different execution model; and 'fixing' a failing pipeline by pointing the sink at whatever table is already available, which produces the self-read loop. A less obvious variant: reading a table and writing to a different table is safe, but reading a table that another job writes every 15 minutes is only safe because Delta readers snapshot a consistent version - a streaming reader continues from the last version it saw, while a batch reader takes the latest version, and mixing them up changes whether you reprocess or skip data.

Edge cases: writing to the same table with a *different* checkpoint and no filter is still a loop; a stream-to-stream join requires watermarks and event-time bounds on both sides; and when the source and sink are both Delta, retention and vacuum settings matter because VACUUM can remove the versions a slow streaming reader still needs. This generalises to one design rule for the exam: every streaming pipeline should be expressible as bronze -> silver -> gold, with each stage reading one table and writing a different table.

actions.text: Now let's put output modes to work. This is a worked, exam-style problem: you need to choose the output mode, the trigger, and the sink together, and justify every choice — not just pick one and hope.

Problem 1 sets the statement. A retail company streams click events from Kafka, and those events must land in a Delta table with exactly-once semantics so a downstream query sees each event exactly once. Notice the phrase 'exactly once' — that single requirement drives the entire design.

Here is the worked solution. Step 1 reads the stream with spark-dot-readStream, using the Kafka format and subscribing to the clicks topic. Step 2 writes it: format delta, an explicit checkpointLocation, output mode append, trigger availableNow set to true, and toTable clicks-underscore-bronze to land it in the catalog.

Now the analysis — why this combination works. Append is the only Delta-compatible output mode for this case, checkpointLocation is mandatory for exactly-once recovery, and the Delta transaction log makes replayed batches idempotent. That's the key insight: replays are safe because the log absorbs them.

Keep the hint in mind: separate the problem into three independent decisions — mode, trigger, and sink — then justify each separately. Let's move to Problem 2, where the business adds an aggregation and the picture changes.

Problem 2: the business now wants an aggregation over the same stream. The moment you aggregate, append alone can't express the result — you need to reason about output modes again, and about how late data is handled.

The hint here is important: a watermark is a lateness budget, not a timeout. It tells Spark how long to wait for late events before finalizing a window's state. Misreading that definition is one of the most common exam traps.

The worked solution separates deduplication from aggregation as two distinct stages, then applies a watermark before the aggregation and a dropDuplicates call. That separation matters: cleaning the stream first, then aggregating, gives predictable semantics.

The analysis explains why the method choice follows from two constraints at once: the need for correctness under retries, and the need to bound state. The watermark bounds state; dropDuplicates handles the duplicates that aggregation would otherwise double-count.
Problem 3 shifts from design to incident review. This is a different skill — diagnosing a running system rather than writing new code, and the exam tests both.

The scenario: a junior engineer wants to 'double up' — run a second query writing to the same sink, presumably to speed things up. Your job is to explain why that breaks exactly-once, and what the correct fix is.

The hint is a definition worth memorizing: a checkpoint path is the identity of a streaming query. Two queries pointing at the same checkpoint path are not two writers working together — they collide.

The worked solution starts by diagnosing the two-writer attempt. The correct approach is not to share the checkpoint — it's to give each query its own checkpointLocation, or better, to run a single query and scale it, since that's what the sink actually supports.

The analysis calls this subtle for a reason: a checkpoint is invisible until it's wrong. You only see the failure on restart, when the query either replays the source or throws a new-query error because it found an existing checkpoint that doesn't belong to it.
Problem 4 is a code review with a second trap — and this one is about the read side, not the write side.
Here a developer must produce a certain result and has written code that looks plausible. Your job is to spot what's wrong before you explain the fix — read the code the way an examiner would.

The hint points you straight at it: check the return type of the read call before blaming the write. A readStream call returns a streaming DataFrame, and a read call returns a batch DataFrame — mixing the two is the trap.

Step A of the worked solution is the diagnosis: spark-dot-read-dot-table produces a batch DataFrame, which cannot be used in a streaming pipeline. Step B is the correction: swap it for spark-dot-readStream configured for the appropriate source, so the query stays streaming end to end.

The analysis lands the point: streaming and batch share the same DataFrame API and the same operators, but not the same constructors. That's why this bug is so easy to introduce and so easy to miss on a first read. With all four problems worked, the pattern is clear — mode, trigger, sink, and checkpoint, decided together and justified separately. Apply that checklist to any streaming question on the exam.

scenes.title: Check: Output Modes and Delta Sink Constraints

questions.question: A pipeline ingests clickstream JSON files from cloud storage and must continuously land new events into an existing Delta table named silver_events. Existing rows must never be rewritten, each micro-batch must add only its newly arrived records, and the pipeline must tolerate restarts without duplicating data. Which combination of output mode and sink configuration satisfies these requirements?

options.label: outputMode("append") with a Delta sink configured via .format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", ...).toTable("silver_events")
outputMode("complete") with a Delta sink configured via .format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", ...).toTable("silver_events")
outputMode("update") with a Delta sink configured via .format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", ...).toTable("silver_events")
outputMode("append") with a console sink so that rows can later be copied into the Delta table by a batch job

questions.analysis: Append mode emits only rows that were newly produced since the previous trigger, which is exactly the semantics required for incremental landing into an existing table, and Delta Lake guarantees exactly-once processing because its transaction log records which micro-batches have been committed [source 1][source 5]. Option B is wrong because complete mode rewrites the entire updated result on every trigger; a Delta sink rejects complete mode for streaming writes because it is not an incremental operation. Option C is wrong because update mode is designed for emitting changed rows from stateful operations (for example, aggregation results) and is not the safe incremental append path for a raw event stream. Option D is wrong because a console sink is a debugging sink, not an incremental persistence mechanism, and manually copying rows would lose the checkpoint-based fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery guarantees described in [source 5].

questions.question: A developer configures a streaming write with df.writeStream.outputMode("complete") and targets a Delta table as the sink. Which statements correctly describe what happens or why? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The write fails because complete mode emits the entire updated result table every trigger, which is not an incremental change a Delta sink can append.
Complete mode is intended for use with stateful operations such as aggregations, where the full aggregated result must be re-emitted each trigger.
Delta Lake's transaction log still provides exactly-once processing, so complete mode would merely be slower but still valid against a Delta sink.
The safe default for appending new events to a Delta table is append mode, because it emits only new rows since the last trigger.

questions.analysis: Complete mode rewrites the entire updated result each trigger; it is defined for stateful aggregations rather than incremental row arrival, so a Delta sink does not accept it as an append-style write. Delta's exactly-once guarantee relies on the transaction log recording committed micro-batches [source 1], but that guarantee does not make complete mode a valid incremental write to Delta. Append mode is the default and the safe incremental path for landing new events [source 5]. Option C is the common misconception: students conflate the exactly-once guarantee with output-mode validity. Exactly-once processing concerns not duplicating committed batches, not whether the mode itself is compatible with the sink.

questions.question: Explain how update mode differs from append mode in what is emitted per micro-batch trigger. In your answer, (a) state the precise rows each mode emits, (b) give one scenario where update mode is the correct choice and one where append mode is the correct choice, and (c) explain why append mode is the only mode that safely and incrementally appends to a Delta table without rewriting existing rows.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Accurate definition of append (only newly produced rows since the previous trigger) and update (only rows changed since the previous trigger) — 40%. (2) Correct scenario pairing, e.g., update for stateful aggregations emitting changed aggregate rows, append for raw event landing to Delta — 30%. (3) Explanation tying append's incremental, non-rewriting behavior to Delta's transaction log and exactly-once guarantees — 30%. Deduct for confusing complete mode with update mode or claiming Delta accepts complete mode incrementally.
questions.analysis: Append mode emits only rows newly produced since the previous trigger and never rewrites previously emitted rows. Update mode emits only rows that changed since the previous trigger, which is useful when a stateful operator (such as an aggregation) updates existing keys and only the changed keys need to be re-emitted. Complete mode, by contrast, rewrites the entire updated result every trigger and is used with aggregations where the full result must be re-emitted. Append is the default and the only mode that safely and incrementally appends new events to a Delta table without rewriting existing rows, with Delta Lake's transaction log guaranteeing exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the table [source 1]. A streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines is likewise a Delta table designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 3], reinforcing that append semantics are the intended landing pattern for event ingestion.

scenes.title: Checkpoints, Triggers, and Exactly-Once into Delta

elements.content: Checkpoints, Triggers, and Exactly-Once into Delta

A Structured Streaming query is only as trustworthy as the state it keeps outside the data itself. The checkpoint directory, the trigger setting, and the Delta transaction log together decide whether a restart replays events or silently reprocesses them.
What a checkpoint location stores

1. Source offsets — the exact position already consumed in the source (for example, a Kafka partition/topic map or the file path consumed), recorded once per micro-batch.

2. Commit log — the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) that records which batch was sent to the sink, so an interrupted batch can be redelivered rather than lost or duplicated.

3. State store — present only for stateful operators: aggregations, dropDuplicates and stream-stream joins keep their intermediate state here.

It is user-specified storage, not a system-managed artifact, which is why checkpointLocation must be set on writeStream before the query starts.
Exactly-once into Delta

Two mechanisms must combine for exactly-once delivery. The checkpoint supplies the restart position; the sink must independently detect that a batch already landed.

Delta Lake contributes an idempotent commit keyed by batch ID. On retry, Delta finds that ID in its own transaction log and rejects the duplicate write, so an offset replay after a crash does not append the same rows twice.

Concurrent batch writers and other streams against the same Delta table are tolerated — the transaction log version numbering serializes them safely [source 1].
Worked example — crash mid-stream, then restart

A Kafka stream writes to a Delta sink. At T0 the checkpoint records offsets 0–500; the sink commits batch 001 and records offset 500. At T1 offsets 501–999 arrive as batch 002: the checkpoint is written but the process dies before Delta commits.

On restart, Spark relocates itself at offset 500 because that is the last committed batch. It reprocesses and re-sends batch 002. Delta's transaction log still holds batch 002's ID, so the commit is skipped. Result: no gaps, no duplicates.
Triggers change latency, not correctness — default micro-batch, processingTime, availableNow, and continuous all consume the same log
Each trigger reuses the same checkpoint offsets; only the pacing of micro-batches changes. Even continuous mode, which abandons micro-batching, still commits through the same idempotent mechanism.
Preconditions: checkpointLocation must be set and stable; the sink must be Delta or another idempotent sink; output mode must be append for a Delta table.
Edge case — stateful queries: aggregations and stream-stream joins additionally need the state store directory, and their recovery can take as long as the window length.

Pitfall — deleting or changing the checkpoint directory: the query starts as a brand-new query, loses its offsets, and replays the source from the earliest offset. With a Kafka source using earliest, that means re-ingesting the entire retained topic history, and because the batch IDs no longer match the Delta log, the duplicate rows land in the table for real [source 5].
Reset deliberately: if you truly want a clean replay, stop the query, copy the old checkpoint aside, point checkpointLocation at a new path, and expect a full re-read — never delete in place.

actions.text: Now let's connect everything we just covered about streaming reads and writes into a single correctness story: checkpoints, triggers, and exactly-once delivery into Delta. These three pieces fit together, and the exam loves to test whether you understand how they interact.

Here's the framing to hold onto. A Structured Streaming query is only as trustworthy as its checkpoint location. If that location is lost or corrupted, the query can no longer guarantee that it won't reprocess or skip data. Everything downstream depends on it.

So what does a checkpoint location actually store? Think of it as the query's memory. It records the exact progress of the stream, so that after a crash or restart, the engine knows precisely where to resume. Let's look at what goes in there.

First, the source offsets — the exact position already consumed from each source. For a Kafka stream, that's the topic, partition, and offset per partition. Second, there's a commit log that records what logical batches have been completed. And third, for stateful queries, the state store itself is checkpointed. That means aggregations and stream-stream joins can be recovered without losing the accumulated state.
Now, how do we get exactly-once into Delta? This is a key exam point, so pay attention. It's not the checkpoint alone that guarantees it — two mechanisms have to combine. Let's look at those.

Two mechanisms must combine for exactly-once delivery. One, the checkpointed offsets tell the engine where it left off. Two, the idempotent commits — recorded in the Delta transaction log — let the sink detect and skip a batch that was already written. The checkpoint gives you position; the Delta log gives you deduplication. Together, they close the loop.

Let's walk through a concrete example. A Kafka stream is writing into a Delta sink. At time T0, the cluster crashes mid-stream, right after a micro-batch was written but before the checkpoint was updated. On restart, the engine reads the checkpoint, replays the uncommitted data, and the Delta transaction log lets it verify the batch was already applied — so it skips the duplicate. No lost rows, no double counting.

This brings us to triggers. A trigger controls when each micro-batch runs. The default micro-batch trigger runs as fast as data arrives. A processingTime trigger runs on a fixed interval, say every thirty seconds. availableNow processes everything currently available and then stops. And continuous mode pushes latency down to milliseconds. The critical insight: triggers change latency, not correctness. Exactly-once still holds regardless of which trigger you pick.

Here's the pitfall that trips people up — and one the exam absolutely tests. If you delete or change the checkpoint directory, the query restarts as a brand-new query. It has no memory of what was processed, so it replays the source from the earliest offset. That can mean reprocessing every historical record — and potentially double-writing into your sink. If you truly want a clean replay, do it deliberately by resetting the checkpoint and starting from a controlled position.

One last contract to remember: the preconditions. The checkpointLocation must be set, and for Delta sinks the table must be a Delta table, because that's what gives you the idempotent commit log. Get those preconditions right and the correctness story holds. Get them wrong, and no amount of tuning will save you. Let's move on to comparing our sink options.

scenes.title: Sink Comparison: Delta Table vs Parquet Files vs Kafka

elements.content: Dimension  |  Delta table sink  |  Parquet directory sink  |  Kafka (message-bus) sink

Exactly-once delivery guarantee
Delta table sink: A Delta sink provides exactly-once processing because the Delta Lake transaction log atomically commits each micro-batch, so a replayed batch after a failure is detected via the checkpoint and never duplicated, even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the table [source 1].
Parquet directory sink: A Parquet directory sink offers only at-least-once delivery in practice: the file write itself is not transactional, so a task that writes part files and then fails before the checkpoint commit can leave orphaned files that a retry re-emits, producing duplicates on the next successful attempt.
Kafka (message-bus) sink: Kafka can achieve effectively-once end-to-end only when the producer is idempotent (enable.idempotence=true with a stable producer ID and increasing sequence numbers) or when the consumer uses transactions (isolation.level=read_committed); the broker alone makes no claim about your Spark write path.

Output modes accepted
Delta table sink: Delta accepts append mode for incremental inserts and update mode for changed rows, but complete mode is rejected because rewriting the entire result table each trigger would invalidate the append-only transaction log semantics; append is the default and only mode that safely and incrementally appends [source 1].
Parquet directory sink: A Parquet file sink effectively requires append mode only, because there is no table abstraction to update in place; using update or complete against a file sink either raises an analysis error or silently rewrites whole partitions, defeating incremental processing.
Kafka (message-bus) sink: Kafka accepts append mode for publishing each new row as a message and update mode for emitting upsert-style records keyed by a message key; complete mode is unsupported because a message bus has no concept of a full result set to re-emit each trigger.

Schema evolution behavior
Delta table sink: Delta enforces schema on write by default and supports controlled evolution with mergeSchema, so a new column in the source can be admitted explicitly and recorded as a schema change in the transaction log, keeping downstream readers consistent [source 1].
Parquet directory sink: Parquet files are self-describing per file, so a new column appears only in newly written files and old files simply lack the field; downstream readers must reconcile heterogeneous schemas themselves, and there is no central record of when the change happened.
Kafka (message-bus) sink: Kafka messages are opaque byte payloads with no broker-side schema enforcement unless you attach a schema registry (e.g., Avro/Protobuf with a compatibility policy), so evolution is governed entirely by producer and consumer discipline, not by the sink.

Small-file handling and maintenance
Delta table sink: Delta mitigates small files through its transaction log and the OPTIMIZE command, which compacts many small files into fewer large ones while the log keeps readers consistent; this is the operational consequence of a file-based sink that Delta specifically addresses [source 1].
Parquet directory sink: A Parquet directory accumulates one or more part files per micro-batch with no compaction mechanism, so a stream running with a 10-second trigger for one hour produces roughly 360 files per partition, and you must run an external compaction job yourself [source 1].
Kafka (message-bus) sink: Kafka does not accumulate files at all; it appends to segmented log partitions and reclaims space by retention policy (retention.ms or retention.bytes), so the small-file problem is replaced by a retention and partition-count management problem.

Downstream consumption and queryability
Delta table sink: A Delta sink is directly queryable with SQL and DataFrame APIs and supports concurrent batch readers with snapshot isolation, which is why it wins when downstream consumers need SQL queryability plus ACID guarantees alongside streaming and incremental processing [source 3][source 4].
Parquet directory sink: A Parquet directory is queryable with SQL engines that can scan a directory of files, but consumers must handle partially written batches and inconsistent snapshots unless they coordinate with the writer's commit protocol.
Kafka (message-bus) sink: Kafka is consumed by subscribing clients rather than queried by SQL; it is optimized for fan-out to many independent subscribers, and analytics typically requires landing the topic into a table store first [source 5].

Concurrency with batch writers and readers
Delta table sink: Delta allows a stream and concurrent batch queries to operate against the same table because the transaction log serializes commits and gives readers a consistent snapshot, which is the mechanism behind its exactly-once claim under concurrency [source 1].
Parquet directory sink: A Parquet directory has no commit log, so a batch reader that lists files mid-write can see a partial batch and return torn results, and concurrent writers can overwrite or duplicate partitions without detection.
Kafka (message-bus) sink: Kafka handles concurrent producers and consumers natively through partition assignment and offset management, but a consumer group rebalance during processing can cause duplicate delivery unless offsets are committed transactionally.

Fan-out to multiple subscribers
Delta table sink: A Delta sink does not fan out; multiple consumers each query the table, so scaling to many independent readers means scaling query compute rather than relying on the sink to push data to each subscriber.
Parquet directory sink: A Parquet directory likewise does not fan out; each consumer independently scans the directory, and adding subscribers adds scan cost rather than leveraging any push mechanism.
Kafka (message-bus) sink: Kafka is explicitly designed for fan-out: each consumer group tracks its own offsets independently, so N independent subscribers each receive the full stream without the producer knowing or caring about them [source 5].

Checkpointing and fault tolerance
Delta table sink: A Delta sink relies on checkpointLocation to store processing state and enable fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics, combined with the transaction log to make the commit atomic [source 5][source 1].
Parquet directory sink: A Parquet file sink also depends on checkpointLocation to record which batches were written, but because the file write is not atomic with respect to the checkpoint, a crash between the two can leave the system in an inconsistent state that neither side can fully repair.
Kafka (message-bus) sink: Kafka's fault tolerance comes from replication (replication.factor) and consumer offset commits; Spark's checkpoint still stores query state, but end-to-end correctness depends on committing offsets only after the sink write succeeds [source 5].

Typical role in a medallion architecture (a layered bronze/silver/gold refinement pattern)
Delta table sink: A Delta sink is the standard choice for bronze and silver layers, where you need append-only ingestion into a streaming table with low latency and incremental processing, and for gold layers that need ACID and SQL queryability [source 3][source 4].
Parquet directory sink: A Parquet directory is typically an intermediate or archival landing zone rather than a serving layer, because its lack of ACID and compaction makes it a poor fit for gold-layer analytics.
Kafka (message-bus) sink: Kafka typically serves as the ingestion backbone between producers and the medallion layers, feeding Spark or Lakeflow pipelines rather than acting as the analytical store itself [source 2].

Worked example: 1 million events/hour with 10-second triggers
Delta table sink: With 1,000,000 events/hour and a 10-second trigger, you get 360 triggers/hour; Delta commits each trigger atomically to the transaction log, so a downstream SELECT sees exactly the 1,000,000 events once, and OPTIMIZE later compacts the 360 small files per partition into a handful of large files [source 1].
Parquet directory sink: The same workload into a Parquet directory produces 360 part files per partition per hour = 8,640 files/day with no atomic commit, so a crash mid-batch can duplicate or lose events and you must schedule external compaction and deduplication.
Kafka (message-bus) sink: The same workload into Kafka publishes 1,000,000 messages/hour across N partitions; if the topic has 12 partitions, each partition receives about 83,333 messages/hour, and correctness depends on idempotent producers or transactional offsets rather than on any table commit.

Cost and operational overhead
Delta table sink: A Delta sink adds transaction-log storage and periodic OPTIMIZE/VACUUM jobs, but the log enables concurrency and exactly-once without custom locking, which usually dominates the marginal storage cost [source 1].
Parquet directory sink: A Parquet directory has the lowest storage overhead but shifts cost into custom deduplication, compaction, and consistency handling that you must build and operate yourself.
Kafka (message-bus) sink: Kafka adds broker infrastructure, replication, and retention-tier storage, and its cost scales with partition count and retention window rather than with query volume, so it is expensive for long-term analytical storage but efficient for high-fan-out delivery [source 5].

Exam signal: which scenario points to which sink
Delta table sink: If the requirement mentions SQL queryability, ACID guarantees, downstream analytics, or exactly-once into a table, the answer is a Delta table sink [source 1][source 3].
Parquet directory sink: If the requirement mentions a low-cost landing zone or raw file archival with no ACID need, a Parquet directory is acceptable, but be alert to distractors that ignore small-file and consistency costs [source 1].
Kafka (message-bus) sink: If the requirement mentions fan-out to many subscribers, decoupling producers from consumers, or an event bus feeding multiple pipelines, the answer is Kafka [source 5][source 2].

Takeaway — Choose a Delta table sink when downstream consumers need SQL queryability plus ACID guarantees, exactly-once delivery, and concurrent batch and streaming readers against the same data [source 1][source 3].

Takeaway — Choose a Kafka (message-bus) sink when you must fan out the same stream to many independent subscriber groups or decouple producers from consumers, and accept that analytics requires a second hop into a table store [source 5].

Takeaway — Choose a Parquet directory sink only for low-cost archival or intermediate landing where at-least-once is tolerable and you are prepared to operate your own compaction, deduplication, and consistency logic [source 1].

Takeaway — Regardless of sink, always set checkpointLocation to store processing state and enable fault tolerance and exactly-once semantics, and prefer append mode when writing to a Delta table [source 5][source 1].

actions.text: Now let's put the three big sink options side by side. This comparison table is exactly the kind of thing the exam probes, so let's walk through it dimension by dimension.

Here's the full comparison grid. Reading across the rows, we compare Delta tables, Parquet directories, and a message bus like Kafka against the dimensions that matter most: exactly-once support, the output modes each one accepts, schema evolution, small-file handling, and how downstream consumers actually read the data.

Start with the delivery guarantee. A Delta table sink gives you exactly-once delivery end to end, because the checkpoint records which offsets have been committed and the transaction log makes each micro-batch commit atomic and idempotent. That combination is what lets you state confidently that no record is lost or processed twice.

Then look at output modes. Delta accepts append and update modes, and complete mode is allowed when the aggregation is stateless enough to recompute the whole result. But there's a trap here: append mode only works when the operation is append-only, and any aggregation with a watermark or stateful shuffle will force update mode instead. Know which mode each scenario really needs.

Schema evolution behaves differently too. Delta lets you evolve the schema safely through mergeSchema or autoMerge, and because the new columns land as real table metadata, downstream queries pick them up automatically. A raw Parquet directory gives you none of that — the reader has to infer whatever shape it finds on disk.

Now the small-file problem. Every file-based sink, Delta or Parquet, accumulates tiny files as micro-batches land, and those fragments wreck read performance. Delta gives you a way out: run OPTIMIZE to compact them, driven through the transaction log. A Parquet directory has no such mechanism — you're left manually rewriting files or living with the degradation.

Finally, downstream consumption. Because a Delta sink is a real managed table, any consumer can point SQL at it, query it interactively, and rely on ACID guarantees while readers and writers run concurrently. That's the difference between a queryable table and just a pile of files.

Flip the situation around and a message bus wins. When you need fan-out to many independent subscribers, each replaying the stream at its own pace and with its own logic, Kafka is the natural choice. Delta's strength is a single queryable source of truth; Kafka's strength is broadcasting events to whoever wants them.

So the takeaway to memorize: choose a Delta table sink when downstream consumers need SQL queryability plus ACID guarantees. Choose a Kafka sink for fan-out to multiple subscribers. Choose a Parquet directory sink only for simple archival or cheap batch handoff where nobody needs transactional reads.

And regardless of which sink you pick, always configure a checkpoint location. It's the recovery anchor that makes restart-after-failure correct, and skipping it is one of the most common exam traps. Next we'll check your understanding of these tradeoffs.

scenes.title: Check: Checkpoints, Triggers, and Sink Choice

questions.question: A streaming job reads clickstream events from Kafka and writes them to a Delta table named clicks_bronze using output mode append, with a checkpoint location configured at /checkpoints/clicks. The job is stopped and restarted after a transient cluster failure. After the restart, a downstream analyst reports that some click events appear twice in clicks_bronze, even though the source Kafka topic did not replay any records. Which of the following is the MOST likely cause of the duplicated rows?

options.label: The checkpoint location was deleted or changed between runs, so the restarted query treated the Kafka source as brand new and re-processed offsets it had already committed.
Delta Lake cannot guarantee exactly-once processing when the sink is a Delta table, so duplicate rows are expected on every restart.
The output mode was set to append, but append mode always rewrites the entire result table on each trigger, producing duplicate rows.
Kafka itself delivered duplicate messages because the consumer group was not committed, so the duplicates originate in the source rather than from the checkpoint.

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: The Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing, even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the table [source 1]. That guarantee depends on the checkpoint location storing the source offsets, commit log, and (for stateful queries) the state store, so that on restart Structured Streaming knows exactly which offsets were already committed. If the checkpoint directory is deleted, moved, or pointed at a different path, the restarted query has no record of prior progress, re-reads the Kafka source from its configured starting offset, and re-writes those records as new rows — producing duplicates. Option B is wrong because Delta sinks explicitly provide exactly-once semantics via the transaction log [source 1]. Option C is wrong because append mode emits only new rows per trigger; it does not rewrite existing rows. Option D is wrong because the question explicitly states the source did not replay any records; duplicates originate from the lost checkpoint state, not from Kafka redelivery.

questions.question: A data engineer must choose a sink for a low-latency ingestion pipeline that reads from an event bus (Kafka) and lands raw events for downstream analytics. The downstream requirement is stated as follows: 'The sink must support exactly-once processing, allow concurrent batch reads and concurrent streaming writes without corrupting the table, support schema evolution and time travel for auditing, and be readable by a streaming downstream query.' Which of the following statements correctly justify choosing a Delta Lake table over a Parquet file sink? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Delta Lake tables can be used as streaming sources and sinks with exactly-once processing guarantees, whereas a raw Parquet directory does not provide a transaction log to commit offsets idempotently.
A streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines is a Delta table with support for streaming and incremental processing, making it the appropriate construct for append-only, low-latency ingestion.

Delta Lake provides a transaction log that guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the same table, which a plain Parquet sink cannot guarantee.
Parquet is preferred over Delta for streaming sinks because Parquet files are immutable and therefore eliminate all duplicate writes without needing a checkpoint.

correctAnswer: A
B
C
questions.analysis: Options A, B, and C are correct. Delta Lake tables are designed to serve simultaneously as streaming sources and sinks with exactly-once guarantees [source 5]. A streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines is defined as a Delta table with streaming and incremental processing support, explicitly designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 3] [source 4]. The Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently [source 1], which directly satisfies the concurrency requirement. Option D is a misconception: Parquet files are indeed immutable, but immutability alone does not give idempotent commits tied to checkpointed offsets — without a transaction log there is no way to atomically record which offsets were committed, so a restart can still re-write files and duplicate data.

questions.question: Explain the relationship between triggers and end-to-end latency in a Structured Streaming pipeline writing to a Delta Lake sink. In your answer, (a) define what a trigger controls, (b) compare at least two trigger strategies — for example, a fixed processing-time interval such as trigger(processingTime='10 seconds'), a continuous/low-latency trigger, and trigger(availableNow=True) — and explain how each affects latency and throughput, (c) describe how the checkpoint location interacts with triggers to preserve exactly-once semantics across restarts, and (d) give a concrete scenario (for example, a clickstream ingestion job with a stated SLA) where you would pick one trigger over the others, and justify the choice. Use Databricks and Delta Lake terminology precisely.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric (total 30 points): (1) Definition of a trigger — Trigger controls when each micro-batch is executed / how often the streaming query processes new data; it does not change what data is emitted, that is governed by output mode. 5 points. (2) Comparison of at least two trigger strategies — must correctly describe processingTime interval (e.g., '10 seconds'), availableNow (process all available data as one or more micro-batches then stop, useful for scheduled/backfill), and/or continuous/real-time trigger (ms-level low latency, restricted operations). Must explain the latency/throughput trade-off (shorter intervals → lower latency, more overhead; longer intervals → higher throughput per batch, higher latency). 8 points. (3) Checkpoint interaction — Checkpoint location stores source offsets, commit log, and state store; combined with the Delta transaction log's idempotent commits this yields exactly-once processing across restarts regardless of trigger cadence [source 1][source 5]. 7 points. (4) Concrete scenario — A specific job with a stated SLA where a specific trigger is chosen and justified (e.g., '5-second processingTime for a 10-second-latency clickstream SLA', or 'availableNow for an hourly scheduled Bronze ingest where cost beats latency'). 6 points. (5) Use of Databricks/Delta terminology (Delta Lake, checkpointLocation, micro-batch, output mode, exactly-once, Lakeflow streaming table) — 4 points. Deduct up to 3 points for vagueness, no numbers, or missing justification.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: A trigger controls when each micro-batch of a Structured Streaming query is executed — it schedules processing, but it does not determine which rows are emitted; that is the role of the output mode (append, update, complete). A fixed processing-time trigger such as trigger(processingTime='10 seconds') runs a micro-batch every 10 seconds, so end-to-end latency is bounded roughly by the trigger interval plus processing time; shorter intervals reduce latency but increase scheduling overhead and can lower per-batch throughput. trigger(availableNow=True) processes all currently available data as one or more micro-batches and then stops, which is ideal for scheduled or backfill jobs where the SLA is in minutes or hours rather than seconds, since it maximizes throughput per run and lets the cluster shut down. Continuous/lower-latency triggers minimize latency (milliseconds) but restrict the operations supported and are not required for typical Delta sink ingestion. Whatever the trigger, the checkpoint location stores source offsets, the commit log, and (for stateful queries) the state store, and combined with the idempotent commits recorded in the Delta transaction log it preserves exactly-once processing across restarts; this is why Delta Lake tables can serve as streaming sources and sinks with exactly-once guarantees even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently [source 1][source 5]. Concrete example: a clickstream ingestion job with a 30-second freshness SLA writing to clicks_bronze would use trigger(processingTime='10 seconds') with output mode append and a checkpoint at /checkpoints/clicks, because 10s < 30s SLA and the interval is short enough to keep micro-batches small; by contrast an hourly partition backfill into the same Delta table would use trigger(availableNow=True) to process everything in one run and save cost.
