elements.content: Streaming Tables, Declarative Pipelines, and Exam Traps

Streaming table: a Delta table with native support for streaming and incremental processing, designed for append-only ingestion and low latency [source 3][source 4].

Precondition: data arrives as an append-only change feed; edge case: updates and deletes must first be expressed as CDC events.
Plain Structured Streaming vs. Declarative Pipelines
Why Upserts and Deletes Need CDC

• You write the pipeline: readStream → transform → writeStream, one query per stage.

• Declarative pipelines (Delta Live Tables / Lakeflow) add dependency management and chaining.

• Chaining is built on Spark Structured Streaming and suits very large volumes with low latency [source 2].

• A Python pipeline can ingest from an event bus such as Kafka directly [source 2].

• An append stream only adds rows; it cannot express "this key now equals X."

• Upserts and deletes therefore arrive as change data capture (CDC) events with an operation column.

• A construct such as apply_changes replays those operations into the target table.

• Worked example: keys K1, K2 are appended, then an update row for K1 and a delete row for K2 arrive — the applied row count goes 2 → 3 → 2.
Traps: append-only Delta sinks · missing checkpointLocation · schema inference errors on streaming sources · unbounded small files without OPTIMIZE

actions.text: Now that we've covered how Delta tables act as streaming sources and sinks, let's extend that append-only story to managed streaming tables and CDC ingestion — and then consolidate the traps the exam loves to test.
Our title frames the three things we'll work through: streaming tables, declarative pipelines, and exam traps. Let's start with the definition that anchors everything else.

A streaming table is simply a Delta table with native support for streaming and incremental processing. It's designed for append-only ingestion and low latency. The key point for the exam: it's still a Delta table underneath, so all the log, ACID, and time travel behavior you already learned applies.

Here's the distinction that trips people up. With plain Structured Streaming, you write the pipeline yourself: readStream, transform, writeStream. With a declarative pipeline — think Delta Live Tables or Lakeflow — you just declare the datasets, and the engine chains multiple streaming stages together for you. Same append-only semantics, very different level of authoring control.
That first bullet is the imperative pattern in a nutshell: you own every stage of the chain.

Now the crucial limitation. An append stream only adds rows — it can never express an update or a delete. So if your source needs upserts or deletes, you can't fake it with a plain append; you need CDC ingestion constructs like apply_changes to interpret the change feed correctly.
That's the row that says it plainly: append-only means append-only. Hold onto that when we hit the traps.

Finally, the trap list to memorize. Append-only Delta sinks will reject updates and deletes. A streaming write requires a checkpointLocation — leave it out and the query fails. Streaming sources can throw schema inference errors, so define your schema explicitly. And without regular OPTIMIZE, low-latency ingestion produces unbounded small files that quietly destroy read performance. Lock these four in — they show up again and again on the exam.

scenes.title: Lesson Assessment: Streaming Reads and Writes with Delta

questions.question: A data engineer builds a clickstream pipeline. A Kafka source is read with spark.readStream.format("kafka").option("subscribe", "clicks").load(). The engineer then writes the stream with .writeStream.format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/clicks").outputMode("complete").toTable("clicks_bronze"). The job fails immediately at analysis time. Which root cause best explains the failure?

options.label: The Delta sink rejects complete output mode because complete mode rewrites an entire result table each trigger, which is incompatible with incrementally appending to a Delta table; append is the only mode that safely and incrementally appends to a Delta sink [source 1].
The Kafka source does not support structured streaming and must be replaced with a Parquet file source before any output mode can be used.
The checkpointLocation option is missing a trailing slash, so offsets cannot be committed idempotently into the Delta transaction log.
Complete mode is valid only when the query also sets .trigger(continuous="1 second"), because continuous triggers are required for full-table reconciliation.

answer: The Delta sink rejects complete output mode because complete mode rewrites an entire result table each trigger, which is incompatible with incrementally appending to a Delta table; append is the only mode that safely and incrementally appends to a Delta sink [source 1].
questions.analysis: The failure is an output-mode/sink incompatibility, not a source or syntax issue. Complete mode rewrites the whole result table on every trigger, whereas a Delta sink commits incremental append transactions into the Delta transaction log, so the pairing is invalid; append is the safe incremental mode for a Delta sink [source 1]. Option B is wrong because Kafka is a standard streaming source used via Structured Streaming connectors, including from Delta Live Tables written in Python [source 2]. Option C is wrong because checkpointLocation is a directory path, not a string whose trailing slash determines idempotency; exactly-once is provided by checkpointed offsets combined with idempotent Delta commits [source 1][source 5]. Option D is wrong because trigger choice changes latency, not which output modes a sink accepts, and continuous mode is not a prerequisite for complete mode.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about using a Delta table as a streaming source and sink are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: Writing a stream into a Delta table provides exactly-once processing guarantees, even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the same table [source 1].
A Delta table can serve as a streaming source while batch writers concurrently append to it, and the stream will pick up newly committed data on subsequent micro-batches [source 5].
Adding a checkpointLocation is optional when writing to a Delta sink, because the Delta transaction log alone provides fault tolerance without storing source offsets [source 5].

answer: Writing a stream into a Delta table provides exactly-once processing guarantees, even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the same table [source 1].
A Delta table can serve as a streaming source while batch writers concurrently append to it, and the stream will pick up newly committed data on subsequent micro-batches [source 5].
questions.analysis: The first statement is the core Delta streaming guarantee: the Delta Lake transaction log enforces exactly-once processing even with concurrent batches and streams [source 1]. The second statement reflects the design of Delta as a streaming source and sink with exactly-once guarantees; a streaming reader sees newly committed files as micro-batches advance [source 5]. The third statement is a classic exam distractor: checkpointing is not optional. Fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery require storing processing state and source offsets to a durable checkpoint location, which is then combined with idempotent commits recorded in the Delta transaction log [source 1][source 5]. Without a checkpoint, a restarted job cannot resume from correct offsets and will reprocess or skip data.

questions.question: A streaming pipeline reads change data capture (CDC) records — row-level inserts, updates, and deletes with an operation column — from a message bus and must apply them to a Delta target so that downstream SQL consumers see the latest state of each key exactly once, without duplicated rows. Explain how you would model the target (plain streaming write vs. streaming table with CDC upserts), justify the guarantee this relies on, and diagnose one failure mode that produces duplicates.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Correctly distinguishes a plain streaming append write from a CDC/upsert merge pattern, and states that a Delta streaming table (a Delta table with streaming and incremental processing support) is the right construct for keyed upserts — 35%. (2) Justifies exactly-once using two combined mechanisms: checkpointed source offsets plus idempotent transactions recorded in the Delta transaction log [source 1][source 5] — 30%. (3) Diagnoses a concrete duplication failure mode, e.g., restart without a valid checkpointLocation, checkpoint deleted or pointed to a different path, or using append mode for CDC deletes — 25%. (4) Uses correct Databricks terminology (streaming table, Delta transaction log, checkpoint, CDC/upsert) and writes clearly — 10%.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: A plain streaming write with append mode only appends new rows and cannot express updates or deletes, so CDC records that require keyed upserts should target a streaming table — a Delta table with support for streaming and incremental processing, designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 3][source 4]. The correctness of the upsert path relies on exactly-once processing: source offsets are persisted to the checkpoint location, and the corresponding idempotent commits are recorded in the Delta transaction log, so a restarted query resumes from the correct offset and does not re-apply already-committed batches [source 1][source 5]. A common duplication failure mode is a restart without a valid checkpoint location (missing option, deleted path, or a different path per run), which forces the query to re-read from the earliest or default offset and re-apply batches; using append mode on a CDC stream with updates and deletes produces stale or duplicated key states instead of a single latest version.

questions.question: A team must land streaming events into a Delta table with exactly-once semantics and minimal latency, while a downstream analyst runs SQL queries over the same table. Which combination of sink and trigger best satisfies both the correctness and latency requirements?

options.label: A Delta sink with checkpointLocation set and a processingTime trigger, because exactly-once comes from checkpointed offsets plus idempotent Delta commits, and processingTime controls latency without affecting correctness [source 1][source 5].
A Parquet directory sink with complete output mode and a continuous trigger, because Parquet supports exactly-once commits through its own transaction log.
A Kafka sink with append mode, because Kafka provides SQL queryability and ACID guarantees to downstream analysts.
A Delta sink with no checkpointLocation and a default trigger, because removing the checkpoint avoids I/O overhead and improves exactly-once performance.

answer: A Delta sink with checkpointLocation set and a processingTime trigger, because exactly-once comes from checkpointed offsets plus idempotent Delta commits, and processingTime controls latency without affecting correctness [source 1][source 5].
questions.analysis: A Delta sink is correct when downstream consumers need SQL queryability plus ACID guarantees; exactly-once is achieved by persisting source offsets and state to a checkpoint location and combining them with idempotent commits in the Delta transaction log [source 1][source 5]. Trigger choice (default micro-batch vs. processingTime vs. availableNow) changes latency, not correctness, so a processingTime trigger legitimately reduces latency while preserving guarantees. Option B is wrong because Parquet files do not provide a transaction log, so they cannot guarantee exactly-once commits, and complete mode rewrites results rather than incrementally appending. Option C is wrong because a message bus is chosen for fan-out to many subscribers, not for SQL queryability, and a Kafka sink does not give downstream analysts direct table-style SQL access with ACID guarantees. Option D is wrong because omitting the checkpoint destroys fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery, and the default trigger would not improve correctness either.

actions.text: We've covered how Delta tables behave as streaming sources and sinks, along with the output modes, triggers, and checkpoint settings that decide whether exactly-once actually holds. Time to put that under exam pressure.

Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer before moving on. Once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning with you — especially the traps around output modes and sink choice — and we'll clear up anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Event Time, Processing Time, and Why Windows

elements.content: Event Time, Processing Time, and Why Windows

Event time = when the event actually occurred, carried as a timestamp column inside the data itself. Processing time = when Spark processes the record. Ingestion time = when the record first entered the system.

Structured Streaming windowed aggregations operate on an event-time timestamp column, never on the wall clock.

The three time concepts are independent: a late record can have event time 09:00, ingestion time 09:45, and processing time 10:02 — all in the same row.

Why window? An unbounded stream never ends, so a single aggregation like sum(amount) would never return a finite answer. Windows slice the stream into finite, incrementally emitted groups so each trigger produces a bounded result.

This is the same principle that makes our Delta sink safe to read: an event-time window transforms an infinite input into a sequence of bounded outputs, and exactly-once delivery from checkpointed offsets keeps those outputs consistent even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently [source 1].

A streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines is a Delta table with support for streaming and incremental processing, designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 3].

Worked example (5-minute tumbling window, 09:00–09:05):

Row A: event time 09:03, arrives 09:04 → lands in window [09:00, 09:05).

Row B: event time 09:04, arrives 09:40 (late) → still lands in [09:00, 09:05) under event time, but would land in [09:35, 09:40) under processing time.

Row C: event time 09:06, arrives 09:07 → lands in [09:05, 09:10). Switching the time column silently moves B without changing the window size — the exam trap to watch for.
Three window families you must recall: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding (fixed size, overlapping by slide interval), session (dynamic, gap-defined).

Exam trap: switching from event time to processing time changes which records land in which window whenever data arrives late — the schema and results look valid, but the wrong rows are aggregated. Cite [source 5]: exactly-once semantics depend on checkpointed state, not on the time column choice.

actions.text: So far we've been reading and writing streaming data with Delta tables, and we've looked at output modes and sink choice. Now we need to confront a question that catches almost everyone: when we say 'time' in a stream, which time do we actually mean? Let's unpack that.

This is the core of event-time semantics — event time, processing time, and the reason windows exist at all. These three ideas are the foundation for everything else in this unit, so let's take them in order.

Event time is when the event actually occurred, and that timestamp is carried inside the data itself — a sensor reading, a click, an order. Processing time is a completely different thing: it's when Spark actually processes that record. And there's a third one you should be able to name for the exam, ingestion time — the moment the record arrived in the system. Keep these three straight and most window questions become straightforward.

Now, why do we need windows at all? A stream is unbounded — it never ends — so you can't aggregate it 'in one shot' the way you'd aggregate a fixed table. A window partitions that endless stream into finite, incrementally emitted groups, so you get a result for each group instead of waiting forever for a total that never comes.

There are three window families you must recall by name. Tumbling windows are fixed-size and non-overlapping. Sliding windows are also fixed-size, but they overlap — the same event can land in more than one window. Session windows are different: they're defined by gaps in activity, so their length depends entirely on the data. Tumbling for regular intervals, sliding for moving averages, session for user behavior.

Here's a worked example to make this concrete. Take a five-minute tumbling window over the 09:00 to 09:05 range. The windowed aggregation in Structured Streaming operates on an event-time timestamp column, not the wall clock — so an event that occurred at 09:03 but only arrives at 09:07 still belongs in the 09:00 window. That's the behavior the exam is testing.

And here's the classic trap. If you silently switch your window from event time to processing time, which records land in which window changes — especially when data arrives late. The same late event that would have joined the 09:00 window under event time now shows up in whatever window processing time happens to place it in. Nothing errors, nothing warns you — the numbers just quietly change. Remember: the exam objective says Structured Streaming windowed aggregations run on an event-time timestamp column, so always confirm which time you're grouping by before you trust the result.

That's the groundwork. Next we'll compare the three window types side by side and see how event-time assignment works in the DSL — then watermarks will show up, and this whole picture will click together.

scenes.title: Tumbling vs Sliding vs Session Windows

elements.content: Dimension  |  Tumbling windows  |  Sliding windows  |  Session windows

Window length: fixed vs dynamic
Tumbling windows: Tumbling windows have a fixed, pre-declared duration that never changes at runtime, so with a 10-minute duration the timeline is cut into the rigid segments [09:00,09:10), [09:10,09:20), [09:20,09:30); the window length is a compile-time constant and not a function of the data.
Sliding windows: Sliding windows also have a fixed, pre-declared duration, but that duration is paired with a separate slide interval that determines how far the window advances each time; with duration 10 min and slide 5 min the windows are [09:00,09:10), [09:05,09:15), [09:10,09:20), so the length is fixed while the stride is independently configurable.
Session windows: Session windows have no fixed length at all: the length is data-driven and equals the span between consecutive events once the inactivity gap is bridged, so an active session may last 40 seconds or 40 minutes depending entirely on when events stop arriving.

Extra parameter beyond the duration
Tumbling windows: Tumbling windows require no parameter beyond the duration itself, because the window start times are fully determined by aligning the event timestamp to the duration boundary.
Sliding windows: Sliding windows require exactly one extra parameter, the slide interval, and that parameter is what creates overlap; the duration and the slide are independent knobs, so a slide smaller than the duration produces overlap and a slide larger than the duration produces gaps.
Session windows: Session windows replace the duration with a timeout parameter, the inactivity gap, and the window closes only after no event has arrived for that gap; the gap is the sole boundary-setting parameter and there is no window length to declare.

Overlap between adjacent windows
Tumbling windows: Tumbling windows never overlap: the segment [09:00,09:10) ends exactly where [09:10,09:20) begins, so the union of all windows tiles the timeline with no double coverage and no gaps.
Sliding windows: Sliding windows overlap whenever the slide interval is strictly smaller than the duration; with duration 10 min and slide 5 min, each instant of the timeline is covered by exactly two windows, and reducing the slide to 1 min would cover each instant ten times.
Session windows: Session windows generally do not overlap because sessions are partitioned by the inactivity gap, but they can be non-adjacent or arbitrarily spaced, and a later session simply starts after the gap rather than tiling the timeline.

Can a single event appear in multiple windows
Tumbling windows: In a tumbling window every event belongs to exactly one window, because the duration boundaries partition the timeline; an event at 09:12:30 falls only into [09:10,09:20) and into no other window.
Sliding windows: In a sliding window an event belongs to every window whose interval contains its timestamp, so the 09:12:30 event falls into [09:05,09:15), [09:10,09:20), and [09:00,09:10) is excluded because it has already closed; with duration 10 min and slide 5 min, most events land in exactly two windows.
Session windows: In a session window an event is assigned by the gap logic, and because gap boundaries can be re-evaluated as late events arrive, a single event can end up merged into a session that spans many earlier events, so the same event can be counted once per session definition that the engine emits.

Aggregate semantics and duplicate counting
Tumbling windows: Tumbling windows produce one non-overlapping aggregate per period, so summing the per-window counts gives a correct total that equals the raw event count with no double counting.
Sliding windows: Sliding windows produce overlapping aggregates, so summing the counts across windows double counts events; the correct interpretation is that each window answers a separate rolling question such as events in the last 10 minutes as of each 5-minute mark.
Session windows: Session windows produce one aggregate per contiguous burst of user activity, and the same event may be counted in more than one session if the session boundaries are recomputed when late data arrives, so session counts are per-session and not additive across sessions.

Watermark and late-arrival behavior
Tumbling windows: Tumbling windows close at deterministic wall-clock boundaries, so a watermark of 2 minutes lets the engine finalize [09:00,09:10) at 09:12 and reject or drop events older than that boundary.
Sliding windows: Sliding windows close many overlapping boundaries, so with duration 10 min and slide 5 min a 2-minute watermark causes roughly two window boundaries to be finalized per 5-minute period, and each late event must be routed to every still-open window whose interval contains it.
Session windows: Session windows close only when the inactivity gap has elapsed in event time, so with a 30-minute gap and a 5-minute watermark the engine must hold state for at least 30 minutes plus the watermark lag before it can safely finalize a session; sessions are the most state-intensive of the three.

State footprint and runtime cost
Tumbling windows: Tumbling windows keep state for exactly one open window per key, so the state store holds at most one partial aggregate per key and memory scales linearly with the number of distinct keys.
Sliding windows: Sliding windows keep state for every window that is still open, so duration 10 min with slide 5 min holds two overlapping partial aggregates per key and slide 1 min would hold ten, multiplying the state store and merge cost by duration divided by slide.
Session windows: Session windows keep state for every open session per key until the gap plus watermark elapses, and because the gap is typically much longer than a tumbling duration, sessions can hold state for far longer and are the most likely to trigger state-store growth warnings.

Typical use cases
Tumbling windows: Tumbling windows are the default choice for fixed reporting periods such as events per 10-minute interval, hourly billing rollups, and KPI dashboards fed by an append-only streaming table into Delta [source 3].
Sliding windows: Sliding windows are used for rolling or moving metrics such as a 10-minute rolling average refreshed every 5 minutes, anomaly detection over a moving baseline, and any smoothed metric that should not jump at hard boundaries.
Session windows: Session windows are used for user-session analytics such as clickstream funnel analysis, where a 30-minute inactivity gap defines a visit, and for any workload whose natural unit is a burst of activity rather than a fixed clock period.

Worked example: 20 events in a 20-minute span
Tumbling windows: Assume 20 events, one per minute from 09:00 to 09:19, with a tumbling duration of 10 minutes; the engine emits [09:00,09:10) = 10 events and [09:10,09:20) = 10 events, and the sum 10 + 10 = 20 equals the raw count, confirming no overlap.
Sliding windows: With the same 20 events and a sliding duration of 10 minutes with a 5-minute slide, the engine emits windows at 09:00, 09:05, and 09:10; the 09:00 window contains events 09:00-09:09 = 10, the 09:05 window contains 09:05-09:14 = 10, and the 09:10 window contains 09:10-09:19 = 10, so the sum 10 + 10 + 10 = 30 counts each interior event multiple times.
Session windows: With the same 20 events and a session gap of 3 minutes, an event arriving every minute never lets the gap elapse, so the entire 09:00-09:19 span forms one session of 20 events; if the stream paused from 09:09 to 09:14 the gap would be exceeded at 09:12 and the data would split into two sessions of 10 events each.

Exam trap: duration equals slide
Tumbling windows: A tumbling window is the special case of a sliding window whose slide interval equals its duration, but you should declare the tumbling form explicitly when the requirement is non-overlapping periods, because a reader can misread a slide equal to the duration as an independent design choice.
Sliding windows: Setting duration = slide = 10 min makes the sliding window advance by a full duration each time, so the windows [09:00,09:10), [09:10,09:20), [09:20,09:30) are non-overlapping and each event lands in exactly one window, which is behaviorally identical to tumbling; the exam expects you to spot that these two configurations produce the same output.
Session windows: Do not confuse duration with gap: setting a session gap equal to a tumbling duration does not make a session behave like a tumbling window, because the session boundary is driven by inactivity while the tumbling boundary is driven by clock alignment.

Integration with Delta and exactly-once sinks
Tumbling windows: Tumbling-window aggregates can be written with append mode into a Delta table, and the Delta transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the table [source 1].
Sliding windows: Sliding-window aggregates are best written with update mode or to a merge target, because the same logical window may be revised as late data arrives; this matches the pattern of using Delta Lake tables as both streaming sources and sinks with exactly-once guarantees while state is stored for fault tolerance [source 5].
Session windows: Session-window aggregates rely on substantial state, so the state store must persist to the checkpoint location; the same fault-tolerance mechanism that enables exactly-once delivery for Structured Streaming also carries the open sessions across restarts [source 5].

Declarative pipeline fit
Tumbling windows: Tumbling windows are the natural fit for a streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines, because a streaming table is a Delta table designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 3][source 4].
Sliding windows: Sliding windows fit chained streaming pipelines such as workloads with very large data volume and low latency, where Delta Live Tables written in Python ingest from an event bus like Kafka using Spark Structured Streaming and re-window the data downstream [source 2].
Session windows: Session windows also run on the same Structured Streaming substrate, but because sessions merge and hold state they are best placed on a dedicated stateful pipeline rather than mixed into a stateless append-only ingestion streaming table [source 2][source 3].

Takeaway — Choose a tumbling window when the requirement names fixed reporting periods and the aggregates must sum to the raw event count; it is the only type with no overlap, one window per event, and minimal state.

Takeaway — Choose a sliding window when the requirement names a rolling or moving metric; remember that duration is the lookback, slide is the refresh stride, and setting slide equal to duration silently degenerates into tumbling.

Takeaway — Choose a session window when activity is grouped by user behavior rather than the clock and the gap of inactivity defines the unit; budget for the largest state store because sessions cannot finalize until the gap plus the watermark has elapsed.

Takeaway — Regardless of window type, write results into a Delta sink when downstream consumers need SQL queryability and ACID guarantees, since the Delta transaction log provides exactly-once processing even with concurrent readers and writers [source 1].

actions.text: Now that we've established event time versus processing time, let's put the three windowing options side by side. Start with the first dimension: window length. A tumbling window has a fixed, single duration. A sliding window also has a fixed duration, but it adds a second parameter — the slide interval. And a session window has no fixed length at all; its boundaries are determined dynamically by inactivity.

That brings us to the extra parameter beyond duration. For a tumbling window, there isn't one — you specify the duration and you're done. For a sliding window, you must also specify the slide interval, which sets how far apart consecutive windows begin. For a session window, the extra parameter is the session gap, the period of inactivity that closes one session and opens the next.

Next, overlap between adjacent windows. Tumbling windows never overlap — they tile the timeline end to end. Sliding windows do overlap whenever the slide is shorter than the duration. And session windows never overlap by construction, because a new session only begins after the gap.

This leads to a question the exam loves: can a single event appear in multiple windows? With tumbling windows, no — every event belongs to exactly one window. With sliding windows, yes, an event can fall into several overlapping windows. Session windows are trickier: a session can merge with a neighboring session when a late event arrives, so an event may end up contributing to more than one logical session.

Here's the worked example that pulls this together. Picture 20 events arriving over a 20-minute span. A tumbling window of 5 minutes gives you four disjoint windows with 5 events each — clean and non-overlapping. A sliding window with duration 10 and slide 5 produces seven overlapping windows, and because of the overlap, events are counted in more than one. A session window instead groups by activity bursts, so the number of windows depends entirely on where the gaps fall.

And here's the trap to memorize: a sliding window with duration equal to its slide becomes behaviorally identical to a tumbling window. If you see duration 10 minutes and slide 10 minutes, treat it as tumbling — there's no overlap. This single detail catches a lot of test-takers, so make sure it's locked in.

One more dimension worth flagging before we move on: state footprint. Tumbling windows carry the smallest state because each event lives in one place. Sliding windows multiply the state by the number of overlapping windows, and sessions accumulate state per active key until the gap closes. That cost difference matters when you're sizing a streaming job.

So to summarize the decision: choose tumbling when you need clean, non-overlapping periodic aggregates; choose sliding when the requirement is a rolling view over a recent period; and choose session when you're analyzing bursts of activity bounded by inactivity. On the next page we'll check your understanding with a quick drill, and then we'll bring watermarks into the picture.

scenes.title: Check: Window Types and Event-Time Assignment

questions.question: A fraud-detection team needs a running total of transactions per card, refreshed every minute, and the requirement reads: "for each card, report the sum of the last 15 minutes of activity, recomputed each minute so amounts falling out of the 15-minute horizon are removed." Which window type does this requirement imply?

options.label: Tumbling window of 15 minutes with a 1-minute trigger
Sliding window of 15 minutes with a 1-minute slide interval
Session window with a 15-minute inactivity gap
Global window with a 1-minute processing-time trigger

questions.analysis: The phrase "recomputed each minute so amounts falling out of the 15-minute horizon are removed" is the signature of a sliding (hopping) window: a fixed window length of 15 minutes combined with a smaller slide interval of 1 minute, producing overlapping windows that are re-emitted every slide. A tumbling window (A) would use a non-overlapping 15-minute window, so a card's events are counted once and a minute-by-minute roll-off never appears. A session window (C) is bounded by a gap of inactivity rather than a clock duration, so it cannot guarantee a 15-minute horizon. A global window (D) accumulates the entire stream forever and never evicts old events. Note that the underlying mechanics are standard Structured Streaming aggregation, the same engine layer that Delta Live Tables (DLT) builds on when you chain multiple streaming pipelines [source 2], and locking in exactly-once results for the target Delta table relies on the Delta Lake transaction log guaranteeing exactly-once processing even when batch queries run concurrently against the table [source 1].

questions.question: A sliding window of length 10 minutes with a slide interval of 2 minutes is applied to a clickstream. Which of the following statements about event-time window assignment are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A single click event can be assigned to more than one window, because consecutive 10-minute windows overlap by 8 minutes.
An event's window membership is decided by the event timestamp carried in the record, not by the wall-clock time at which the record is processed.
Because the slide interval (2 minutes) is smaller than the window length (10 minutes), each event lands in exactly one window.
If a 12-minute-late event arrives after its windows have already been emitted, the engine cannot retroactively change prior results, so that work is dropped or handled by the watermark rule.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: with a 10-minute length and a 2-minute slide, windows start every 2 minutes and each covers 10 minutes, so an event at time t belongs to the windows that start at t, t-2, t-4, ... t-8 — up to five overlapping assignments. Option B is correct and is the definitional point of event-time processing: assignment uses the timestamp embedded in the data (event time), which is also the basis for the watermark that bounds late data. Option C is the classic distractor that swaps event time for the slide relationship: overlapping only stops when slide = length (a tumbling window); a smaller slide produces more, not fewer, memberships. Option D is correct because once downstream results for a window have been emitted, a later-arriving record whose event time is beyond the watermark is dropped (or the pipeline must be designed with a larger allowed lateness). This event-time discipline is what lets a delta sink keep exactly-once semantics in a streaming table, which is defined as a Delta table with support for streaming and incremental processing designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency [source 3][source 4], and the transaction log provides the exactly-once guarantee even with concurrent batch writers [source 1].

questions.question: A pipeline reads a Kafka topic of page-view events into a Delta table with exactly-once semantics, and a downstream analyst wants a per-page count over the previous 30 minutes refreshed every 5 minutes. A junior engineer proposes: "Use a tumbling 30-minute window with a 5-minute processing-time trigger, and write the aggregate with complete output mode into the same Delta table as the raw events." Identify two distinct problems with this proposal, explain how each violates a constraint on window type or sink correctness, and describe the corrected design. Your answer should explicitly distinguish event time from processing time and explain the role of the slide interval and the Delta sink's accepted output modes.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Window type error — 35% — the student must state that a 30-minute tumbling window with a 5-minute trigger is not the same requirement as 'previous 30 minutes refreshed every 5 minutes', and that a sliding window of length 30 minutes with slide interval 5 minutes is the correct choice because consecutive windows must overlap by 25 minutes; mentioning that each qualifying event therefore falls into multiple overlapping windows (as many as length/slide = 6) earns full credit for this criterion. (2) Sink/mode error — 30% — the student must state that 'complete' output mode is incompatible with a Delta sink, because complete rewrites the entire result table each trigger and does not support incremental appends to a Delta table; the safe and exam-default mode is append, and if updates to existing rows are needed the correct primitive is an upsert/CDC construct such as apply_changes rather than a plain append stream. (3) Event-time vs processing-time reasoning — 20% — the student must clarify that window assignment is driven by the event timestamp embedded in the record, and that the trigger and processing-time settings only control when results are emitted (latency), not which window an event belongs to or whether it can appear in more than one window; mixing them up is the distractor to avoid. (4) Corrected end-to-end design — 15% — the student should propose: read from Kafka with readStream, apply a sliding window of 30 minutes with 5-minute slide, write the aggregate with outputMode('append') and a checkpointLocation to a dedicated Delta sink (separate from raw events), and rely on the Delta transaction log for exactly-once semantics.
questions.analysis: The proposal has two independent flaws. First, a tumbling window of 30 minutes with a 5-minute trigger does not satisfy 'previous 30 minutes refreshed every 5 minutes' — a tumbling window is non-overlapping and is emitted only at the end of its 30-minute duration, so an event is counted once in one window and roll-off is coarse. The requirement dictates a sliding window: window length = 30 minutes, slide interval = 5 minutes, which means each event is assigned to six overlapping windows (30 / 5 = 6). Second, 'complete' output mode is fundamentally incorrect for a Delta sink. Complete mode rewrites the entire result table on every trigger and is rejected by Delta as a sink, whereas append mode emits only new rows since the last trigger and is the only mode that safely and incrementally appends to a Delta table. Because windows overlap, results for old windows would effectively need rewrites if you were not using append with proper watermarks, which is exactly the scenario where an upsert/CDC construct like apply_changes is required rather than a plain append stream. Structurally, DLT pipelines can chain multiple streaming stages on top of Spark Structured Streaming precisely so the raw Kafka ingest [source 2] and the aggregated sliding-window result can live in separate streaming tables — defined as Delta tables with native support for streaming and incremental processing for append-only, low-latency workloads [source 3][source 4] — and the exactly-once guarantee comes from the Delta Lake transaction log, which holds even when batch queries run concurrently against the target [source 1].

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Assigning Events to Tumbling and Sliding Windows

elements.content: Problem 1

A stream of user events has event times (in minutes from the start of the session) $t = 0, 3, 7, 12$. Assign each event to (a) tumbling windows of 5 minutes and (b) sliding windows of 10 minutes duration with a 5-minute slide. For each case, list every window interval and the set of event times it contains. State how many output rows each event produces and the total number of output rows.
Hint: Use half-open intervals $[\text{start}, \text{end})$ and compute the primary window start as $\lfloor t / \text{slide} \rfloor \times \text{slide}$.

Worked solution
Part (a) — Tumbling windows of 5 minutes. Duration $D = 5$, slide $S = 5$. Windows are disjoint: $[0,5)$, $[5,10)$, $[10,15)$, $[15,20)$, … For each event, the window start is $\lfloor t / 5 \rfloor \times 5$.

- $t = 0$: $\lfloor 0/5 \rfloor \times 5 = 0$ → $[0,5)$. Check $0 \le 0 < 5$: yes.

- $t = 3$: $\lfloor 3/5 \rfloor \times 5 = 0$ → $[0,5)$. Check $0 \le 3 < 5$: yes.

- $t = 7$: $\lfloor 7/5 \rfloor \times 5 = 5$ → $[5,10)$. Check $5 \le 7 < 10$: yes.

- $t = 12$: $\lfloor 12/5 \rfloor \times 5 = 10$ → $[10,15)$. Check $10 \le 12 < 15$: yes.

Assignment: $[0,5) \to \{0, 3\}$; $[5,10) \to \{7\}$; $[10,15) \to \{12\}$. Every event appears in exactly one window. Total output rows = 4.

Part (b) — Sliding windows, duration $L = 10$ minutes, slide $S = 5$ minutes. Window starts are multiples of 5: $0, 5, 10, 15, \ldots$ An event at time $t$ belongs to every window starting at $w = k \cdot 5$ such that $w \le t < w + 10$.

- $t = 0$: candidate $w = 0$: $0 \le 0 < 10$ → yes. So only $[0,10)$.

- $t = 3$: $w = 0$: $0 \le 3 < 10$ → yes. So only $[0,10)$.

- $t = 7$: $w = 0$: $0 \le 7 < 10$ → yes; $w = 5$: $5 \le 7 < 15$ → yes. So $[0,10)$ and $[5,15)$.

- $t = 12$: $w = 5$: $5 \le 12 < 15$ → yes; $w = 10$: $10 \le 12 < 20$ → yes. So $[5,15)$ and $[10,20)$.

Assignment: $[0,10) \to \{0, 3, 7\}$; $[5,15) \to \{7, 12\}$; $[10,20) \to \{12\}$. Event multiplicities: $t=0$: 1, $t=3$: 1, $t=7$: 2, $t=12$: 2. Total output rows = $1+1+2+2 = 6$. The test-point summary lists only $[0,10)$ and $[5,15)$ to highlight overlap; the complete assignment includes $[10,20) \to \{12\}$, so event 12 also appears in two windows.

Analysis — Half-open intervals $[\text{start}, \text{end})$ are mandatory for tumbling windows: if closed intervals $[\text{start}, \text{end}]$ were used, an event exactly on a boundary (e.g., $t=5$) would belong to two tumbling windows, violating the definition of tumbling. The window start formula $\lfloor t / S \rfloor \times S$ works because it finds the largest multiple of the slide that is $\le t$. For sliding windows, this formula gives the primary (most recent) window start, and all earlier windows that still cover $t$ are found by subtracting $S$ repeatedly. The number of windows covering an event is at most $\lceil L/S \rceil$; when $L$ is a multiple of $S$, it is exactly $L/S$ for most events, but events near the start of the stream (e.g., $t=0$) may belong to fewer windows if negative starts are excluded. Common mistake: assuming sliding windows produce the same number of rows as tumbling; they produce roughly $L/S$ times more output rows, which increases sink write volume and checkpoint state. Delta Lake's transaction log still guarantees exactly-once processing for each emitted row, even when other streams write concurrently [source 1]. However, exactly-once does not mean the event appears once in the result; it means each window assignment is written exactly once. State stores keep open windows for late events, enabling fault-tolerant exactly-once delivery [source 5]. Therefore, the output row count is a design decision: sliding windows give richer overlap at the cost of more output rows.
Problem 2

An event has event time exactly $t = 10$ minutes. (a) Which tumbling window of 5 minutes contains it? (b) Which sliding windows of 10 minutes duration and 5-minute slide contain it? (c) If a stream contains 1,000 events uniformly distributed over a long period, estimate the total number of output rows for tumbling windows of 5 minutes and for sliding windows of 10 minutes duration with a 5-minute slide. Explain the ratio.
Hint: Boundary events test the half-open interval convention; output volume for sliding windows scales with duration divided by slide.

Worked solution
Part (a) — Tumbling 5 minutes. Windows are $[0,5)$, $[5,10)$, $[10,15)$, … Because the interval is half-open, $t=10$ is excluded from $[5,10)$ (since $10 < 10$ is false) and included in $[10,15)$ (since $10 \le 10 < 15$ is true). Answer: the window $[10,15)$.

Part (b) — Sliding 10 minutes duration, 5-minute slide. Window starts are multiples of 5: $0, 5, 10, 15, \ldots$ For $t=10$:

- $w=10$: $10 \le 10 < 20$ → yes.

- $w=5$: $5 \le 10 < 15$ → yes.

- $w=0$: $0 \le 10 < 10$ → no.

So $t=10$ belongs to two windows: $[5,15)$ and $[10,20)$.

Part (c) — Output volume. Tumbling windows are disjoint, so each event belongs to exactly one window. 1,000 events → 1,000 output rows. Sliding windows with $L=10$ and $S=5$: each event belongs to approximately $L/S = 10/5 = 2$ windows (exactly 2 for events not near the stream boundaries, since $L$ is a multiple of $S$). Therefore 1,000 events → approximately $1000 \times 2 = 2000$ output rows. The ratio is 2. More generally, the average number of windows per event is $L/S$; if $L$ is not a multiple of $S$, some events fall into $\lfloor L/S \rfloor$ windows and others into $\lceil L/S \rceil$ windows, but the average remains $L/S$.

Analysis — This problem isolates the boundary convention. A common student error is to use closed intervals $[a,b]$, which makes $t=10$ belong to both $[5,10]$ and $[10,15]$ for tumbling, violating the 'exactly one' property. The half-open convention is standard in Spark Structured Streaming and most stream processors. For output volume, the factor $L/S$ is the key insight: sliding windows multiply the number of rows written to the sink. This matters for Delta Lake because more output rows mean more commits and larger checkpoints. The checkpoint stores source offsets and state store, including open windows for late events [source 5]. If you underestimate the output volume, you may hit write throughput limits or create many small files. Note that the Delta transaction log still provides exactly-once for each row [source 1], but it cannot reduce the number of rows you intentionally emit. A streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines is designed for append-only ingestion; if you use sliding windows that emit multiple rows per event, the table remains append-only, but the downstream consumer must be aware that each event appears in multiple window rows [source 3]. Always estimate output volume as input volume times the overlap factor before choosing window parameters.
Problem 3

A developer writes a Structured Streaming query that reads from Kafka and groups events using $\text{window}(\text{current\_timestamp}(), '5 minutes')$ instead of the event-time column $\text{event\_time}$. A micro-batch arrives and is processed at wall-clock time 20 minutes after the stream started. The batch contains events with event times $t = 0, 3, 7, 12$ minutes. (a) What window assignment does the faulty query produce for these four events? (b) What is the correct event-time tumbling window assignment? (c) Explain how this mistake interacts with exactly-once semantics and a Delta sink.
Hint: Processing time uses the system clock at processing moment; event time uses the timestamp embedded in the data. Exactly-once does not fix wrong window keys.

Worked solution
Part (a) — Faulty query. The window key is $\text{current\_timestamp}()$ evaluated when the micro-batch is processed. If processing occurs at wall-clock time 20 minutes (relative to stream start), all four events in that batch receive the same processing timestamp, approximately 20 minutes. With 5-minute tumbling windows, the window start is $\lfloor 20/5 \rfloor \times 5 = 20$, so all four events are assigned to the single window $[20,25)$. Output: $[20,25) \to \{0, 3, 7, 12\}$. If processing time crosses a window boundary during the batch, events might split across two processing-time windows, but the key point is that the window key depends on when the query ran, not on the event times. Running the query again at a different wall-clock time gives different window assignments for the same data.

Part (b) — Correct query. Use $\text{window}(\text{event\_time}, '5 minutes')$. With half-open tumbling windows: $[0,5) \to \{0,3\}$; $[5,10) \to \{7\}$; $[10,15) \to \{12\}$. Total output rows = 3 (because $0$ and $3$ share a window).

Part (c) — Exactly-once and Delta sink. Delta Lake's transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing for each row emitted, even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the table [source 1]. However, that guarantee applies to the write of each computed row; it does not validate the window key. The faulty query will still write output exactly once per micro-batch, but the content is wrong because the window key is processing time. If the same event is reprocessed due to a failure and restart, the checkpoint ensures the same offsets are not reprocessed, so the wrong output is written once. But if you run the query again on the same data at a different wall-clock time, you get different window assignments. Exactly-once does not repair the semantic error. The checkpoint stores source offsets and state, including window state, to enable fault tolerance [source 5], but if the window key is processing time, the state tracks the wrong windows and late events are handled incorrectly. A streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines is designed for append-only ingestion and incremental processing [source 3]; processing-time windowing breaks the append-only contract because the same event can be placed into different windows across runs. If you chain multiple streaming pipelines, the error propagates downstream [source 2]. The fix is to replace current_timestamp() with the event-time column and define a watermark if late events must be handled.

Analysis — This is the most common pitfall in streaming windowing: using processing time when you mean event time. Event time is the timestamp embedded in the data, recording when the event actually occurred. Processing time is the wall-clock time when the system processes the event. They diverge due to network delays, backpressure, or reprocessing. The window start formula for event-time tumbling windows is $\lfloor t / D \rfloor \times D$; for processing time it is $\lfloor \text{current\_timestamp} / D \rfloor \times D$, which depends on the query execution. Exactly-once guarantees in Delta Lake [source 1] ensure that each computed row is written exactly once, but they do not validate the row's window key. Checkpoints store the state needed to resume and to guarantee exactly-once delivery, including open windows for late events [source 5]. If you accidentally use processing time, the state store will track the wrong windows and late events will be handled incorrectly. Streaming tables and declarative pipelines [source 3] assume append-only, event-time-correct ingestion; introducing processing-time windowing makes the table's contents non-deterministic across runs, which breaks downstream time-series joins and aggregations. A common mistake is to believe that exactly-once semantics will somehow detect or correct the wrong window key — it will not. Always verify that the window function references the event-time column, not the system clock, and test the query by replaying the same data at different wall-clock times to confirm deterministic output. The correct event-time assignment for the given events is $[0,5) \to \{0,3\}$, $[5,10) \to \{7\}$, $[10,15) \to \{12\}$, which matches the test-point summary.

actions.text: Now let's make all of that concrete. Window boundary arithmetic is exactly the kind of thing the exam loves to test, so we'll work a full problem where you assign events to tumbling and sliding windows by hand.

Problem 1: we have a stream of user events with event times of 0, 3, 7, and 12 minutes. Our job is to assign each event to, part (a), tumbling windows of five minutes, and part (b), sliding windows of ten minutes duration with a five-minute slide. Notice we're using event time, not the wall clock — hold onto that, because it becomes the trap in Problem 3.

The hint gives us the key convention: windows are half-open intervals, closed on the left and open on the right. So an interval from 0 to 5 includes 0 but excludes 5. An event landing exactly on a boundary belongs to the later window, never both adjacent tumbling windows.

Here's the worked solution. For tumbling: the window from 0 to 5 holds events 0 and 3; the window from 5 to 10 holds event 7; and the window from 10 to 15 holds event 12. Every event falls into exactly one window. Now for sliding: the window from 0 to 10 holds 0, 3, and 7; the window from 5 to 15 holds 7 and 12. Notice event 7 appears in two windows — that's the defining property of sliding windows.

And here's the analysis the university-depth question demands. For sliding windows, the window start is floor of event time divided by slide, times slide. So any event lands in every window it overlaps — and an event near a boundary is emitted once per window it belongs to. That's precisely why sliding windows produce more output rows than tumbling windows over the same stream. Same events, more rows. Keep that cause and effect straight.
Problem 2 now isolates the boundary convention. An event has an event time of exactly 10 minutes. Which windows does it belong to? This is where the half-open interval does all the work.
Remember: closed on the left, open on the right. So an event at t equals 10 is excluded from the window ending at 10, and included in the window starting at 10.

For tumbling five-minute windows, t equals 10 belongs to the window from 10 to 15 — not to the window from 5 to 10, because 10 is the open right edge there. It goes to exactly one tumbling window. For sliding, with a ten-minute duration and a five-minute slide, t equals 10 appears in the window from 5 to 15, and also in the window from 10 to 20. Two windows again — because sliding windows overlap.

So the takeaway from Problem 2: a boundary event lands at the start of a window, never at the end. That single convention eliminates double counting in tumbling windows while still allowing overlap in sliding ones.

Problem 3 shifts from arithmetic to a pitfall. Here a developer writes a Structured Streaming query that windows by current_timestamp instead of the event-time column. The results look plausible in a demo — and then become non-reproducible.

The hint spells it out: processing time uses the system clock at processing time on the cluster running the query. Event time comes from the data itself. Mixing them means your window assignment depends on when the query ran, not when the event happened.

The worked solution shows what goes wrong. In part (a), the faulty query puts events into windows based on wall-clock arrival, so a replayed or late-arriving event gets filed under the wrong window, and aggregate totals shift every time you re-run the pipeline. The fix is to window on the event-time column and use watermarks to bound how late data can arrive.

And this is the most common pitfall in stream processing — grouping by the wall clock instead of the event-time column. On the exam, whenever a question asks why a streaming aggregation is unstable or produces different results on each run, check first whether the window is anchored to event time. If it isn't, that's your answer.

actions.text: We just saw how trigger intervals control micro-batch cadence. Now let's look at the other half of the streaming problem: event time. This simulation shows how events get assigned to windows and when the watermark lets those windows close.

actions.content: Window duration sets the size of each window.
Slide interval controls how far each window advances.

actions.text: When window duration equals slide interval, every event lands in exactly one window — that is a tumbling window. When the slide is smaller than the duration, windows overlap and the same event belongs to several windows at once. A much larger duration with a large slide behaves like a session window, grouping bursts of activity together.

actions.content: Switch to a sliding 10s window with a 5s slide.
Each event flows into every window whose range covers its event timestamp.

actions.text: Now watch the watermark. The watermark trails the maximum event time by the delay you set. Any event that arrives after the watermark passes its window's end is late — depending on the delay, it is included, dropped, or held until the window closes.

actions.content: Apply the late-events scenario to see how long delay keeps stragglers alive.
Open-window state is evicted only after the watermark crosses the window end.

actions.text: Finally, toggle arrival order and compare event time versus processing time. The same events produce a different result because windows are anchored to event time, not to when the records happened to reach the stream. This is exactly the behavior that withWatermark(...).groupBy(window(...)) encodes in code — the delay bounds state, and the window spec decides assignment.

scenes.title: Check: Window Assignment and Late Data

questions.question: A Structured Streaming query aggregates events using a sliding window defined as window(event_time, '10 minutes', '5 minutes'). An event arrives with event_time = 12:07. Into which window(s) does this event fall, and why does the answer differ from a tumbling window of the same 10-minute duration?

options.label: Only the window [12:00, 12:10), because the event belongs to exactly one window just as it would with a tumbling window
The window [12:05, 12:15) only, because the slide interval shifts the start of every window forward by 5 minutes
Both [12:00, 12:10) and [12:05, 12:15), because a sliding window overlaps and an event can be assigned to multiple windows
Both [12:00, 12:10) and [12:10, 12:20), because sliding windows place each event in the window that starts and the window that ends at that timestamp

answer: Both [12:00, 12:10) and [12:05, 12:15), because a sliding window overlaps and an event can be assigned to multiple windows
questions.analysis: A sliding window takes a fixed duration PLUS a slide interval, and because the slide (5 minutes) is smaller than the duration (10 minutes), consecutive windows overlap, so a single event can belong to several windows. The sliding windows starting at 12:00 and 12:05 both cover 12:07, giving [12:00, 12:10) and [12:05, 12:15). A tumbling window of 10 minutes has no slide parameter and is non-overlapping, so 12:07 would land in exactly one window. Option A wrongly applies tumbling behavior; Option B ignores the earlier overlapping window; Option D invents a 'start-and-end' rule that does not exist — the second covering window begins at 12:05, not 12:10.

questions.question: A Structured Streaming query reads from an event stream with a watermark of 5 minutes and performs a 10-minute tumbling aggregation on event_time. Records are annotated below. Which records are dropped (excluded from further window updates) once the watermark has advanced past them? Select all that apply.

options.label: Record R1 with event_time = 10:02, arriving at processing time 10:14
Record R2 with event_time = 10:04, arriving at processing time 10:09
Record R3 with event_time = 10:03, arriving at processing time 10:20
Record R4 with event_time = 10:06, arriving at processing time 10:08

answer: Record R1 with event_time = 10:02, arriving at processing time 10:14
Record R3 with event_time = 10:03, arriving at processing time 10:20
questions.analysis: With a 5-minute watermark, Spark tracks max(event_time) - 5 minutes; any record whose event_time falls before that watermark is late and is discarded from the aggregation. Trace the observed max event_time as records arrive in processing order: R4 (10:06) at 10:08 sets the watermark to 10:01; R2 (10:04) at 10:09 is on time and advances the watermark to 9:59; R1 (10:02) at 10:14 arrives after the watermark has moved past 10:02, so it is dropped; R3 (10:03) at 10:20 also arrives after the watermark has passed it and is dropped. R2 and R4 both arrive before the watermark crosses their event_time, so they are processed. The discarded records never update window aggregates, even though they physically exist in the stream — this is how a watermark bounds state.

questions.question: A student claims: 'To increase throughput, I can point my append-only Structured Streaming write at a Delta table and switch to complete output mode, since a Delta sink accepts any output mode.' Which statement best corrects this misconception and explains the correct behavior?

options.label: Complete mode is fine for a Delta sink as long as the checkpoint location is set, because the Delta transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing [source 1]
A Delta sink does not support complete mode, because complete mode rewrites the entire result table each trigger, which is incompatible with appending incremental changes to a Delta table
Complete mode works with a Delta sink but only if the query is a streaming table defined in Lakeflow, since streaming tables are Delta tables with native streaming support [source 3]
Complete mode is accepted by a Delta sink as long as the trigger is set to availableNow rather than the default micro-batch trigger

answer: A Delta sink does not support complete mode, because complete mode rewrites the entire result table each trigger, which is incompatible with appending incremental changes to a Delta table
questions.analysis: Complete output mode re-emits the full result table on every trigger, which would require rewriting the entire Delta table rather than appending incremental changes; a Delta sink therefore rejects complete mode and demands append or update. The checkpoint location (Option A) or the trigger type (Option D) does not change which output modes a Delta sink accepts — a checkpoint enables the exactly-once guarantee with the Delta transaction log [source 1], but it does not make an unsupported mode legal. Option C inverts the point: streaming tables in Lakeflow are Delta tables designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 3], so they rely on append/upsert semantics, not complete-mode rewrites.
