scenes.title: Watermarks: Bounding State and Handling Late Data

elements.content: Watermarks: Bounding State & Handling Late Data

Definition — A watermark is a moving threshold computed as (max event time seen so far − allowed delay). Events older than the threshold are considered too late to be processed in that window.

Precondition: an event-time column exists and withWatermark is applied to it. Edge case: delay = 0 means a single straggler instantly closes the window.

Why Watermarks Bound State

The watermark tells Spark that no event with an older event time can still arrive, so completed windows can be evicted from the state store — without it, the state store grows forever [source 5].

This keeps checkpointed state bounded, which is what makes exactly-once recovery into Delta feasible [source 1].

Exam Rule & Common Trap

withWatermark must be applied to the event-time column before the aggregation or join, or it has no effect.

Trap: a watermark does not change window boundaries and does not delay arrival of individual records — it only governs when results finalize and state is cleaned up.
Worked Example — Tumbling 5-min windows, delay = 2 min

Events at t = 0, 3, 7, 12 → window [0,5) closes when max event time ≥ 5 + 2 = 7; window [5,10) commits at 7 + 2 = 9. A record with event time 6 arriving at processing time 10 falls behind the watermark (9) and is dropped in append mode.

Under update or complete mode, the late record is still folded into its window result, but the window can never reopen once state has been evicted.

actions.text: Now let's tackle one of the most tested streaming concepts on the exam: watermarks. This is where we finally answer the question of how Spark knows when it's safe to forget about old data.

Here's the definition. A watermark is a moving threshold, computed as the maximum event time seen so far minus a delay that you specify. Any event whose timestamp is earlier than that threshold is considered too late to be processed. Think of it as a moving line that trails behind the newest event you've observed, and the delay you choose determines how far behind it lags.

So why does this matter? The watermark tells Spark when it can safely evict a completed window from the state store. In a streaming aggregation, Spark holds window state in memory across micro-batches. Without a watermark, that state grows forever — it never knows a window is truly finished, so it keeps everything. The watermark is what bounds that state and lets Spark clean it up.

Now the exam rule you must memorize: withWatermark has to be applied to the event-time column before the aggregation or the join. If you call it after the groupBy or after the join, it has no effect at all. This is the single most common trap on the exam — order of operations determines whether the watermark does anything.

Let's walk through the worked example. We have tumbling five-minute windows and a delay of two minutes. Events arrive at t equals zero, three, seven, and twelve. The window zero to five closes when the watermark passes its end — and the watermark is the max event time minus two. So watch how each event advances the threshold and which windows get finalized.

Notice this key line: events at t equals zero, three, seven, and twelve, and window zero to five closes when the watermark passes its end. In append mode, once that window is finalized, any record arriving later for that window is simply dropped — it cannot update a result that's already been emitted. That's the behavior the exam wants you to predict.

One final warning, and it's a big one: a watermark does not change your window boundaries, and it does not delay individual records. It only governs when results are finalized and when state is cleaned up. Keep that distinction sharp, because the exam will absolutely try to blur it.

scenes.title: Design Tradeoff: Choosing the Watermark Delay

elements.content: Decision — A 4-engineer team operates a real-time aggregation pipeline that reads clickstream events from Kafka through Lakeflow streaming tables and writes one-minute revenue aggregates to a Delta table; the pipeline uses event-time tumbling windows, so the team must now pick the single watermark delay value that closes each window before it is emitted. The decision is hard because the three quantities the team cares about move in opposite directions: shrinking the delay makes results appear sooner and keeps the state store small, but it silently discards events that arrive later than the delay; growing the delay recovers those late events, but memory held in the state store grows with the delay and every dashboard tile gets staler. There is no free option, and because the pipeline is a chain of streaming stages feeding a Delta sink with exactly-once guarantees, the choice cannot be changed casually once state has been written [source 5]. The engineering question is therefore not 'what is the most accurate watermark' but 'what delay can this deployment justify under its SLA and its observed event skew, and how will the team know the choice has gone wrong?'

Constraints — The pipeline is a chain of streaming stages built on Spark Structured Streaming with a Delta sink that must preserve exactly-once processing, so state is checkpointed and any delay change is a stateful restart [source 5]  •  The cluster's state store is a fixed memory budget: state size scales roughly linearly with the watermark delay, so an unbounded or long delay risks out-of-memory failures on the stateful aggregation  •  The dashboard's freshness SLA is under 10 minutes end to end, and the pipeline only emits a window's result once the watermark passes the window end  •  Events carry an event-time column and arrive out of order; the pipeline cannot wait forever for stragglers because an unbounded stream has no natural end and only the watermark advances window finalization  •  The team must be able to explain to auditors why events were dropped, so dropped-late-event counts have to be observable rather than invisible

Short watermark delay of 1 minute
+ Lowest result latency: a 1-minute window is finalized roughly one minute after its end, comfortably inside the 10-minute SLA.; + Smallest state store, because only one minute of window state plus its buffered events must be held in memory at a time, which respects the cluster memory budget.; + Fastest failure recovery after a restart, since there is very little accumulated state to rehydrate.
− Every event that arrives later than one minute after its event time is dropped from the aggregation, so revenue totals are silently understated.; − The pipeline becomes fragile to the briefest Kafka consumer lag or connector pause, because lag inflates apparent lateness and converts on-time events into dropped events.; − Because very little of the stream can be corrected, the pipeline behaves like a processing-time system and loses the event-time correctness that motivated windowing in the first place.
Best for: Pipelines where latency is contractual and a small, measured undercount is acceptable, such as live operational counters.

Long watermark delay of 30 minutes
+ High completeness: windows wait long enough that almost all out-of-order events are incorporated before the aggregate is emitted.; + Robust against consumer lag and connector hiccups, because a 30-minute buffer absorbs delays that would destroy a 1-minute configuration.; + Produces auditable totals close to a batch recomputation of the same event-time data, which simplifies reconciliation.
− Breaks the under-10-minute freshness SLA outright: a 1-minute window cannot emit until roughly 31 minutes after it starts.; − State growth is proportional to the delay, so 30 times as many windows and buffered events are resident compared with a 1-minute delay, pushing the fixed memory budget toward OOM.; − Recovery and checkpoint replays are much slower, because the runtime must restore 30 minutes' worth of window state before it can emit again [source 5].
Best for: Correctness-critical batch-like reconciliation where an hourly or daily cadence is acceptable and memory is provisioned for it.

No watermark at all
+ No event is ever dropped, because windows are never closed by a watermark and nothing is classified as too late.; + Conceptually the simplest configuration: the team never has to choose a lateness threshold.
− State grows without bound, because the aggregation must retain every window's accumulating state indefinitely and the cluster memory budget is fixed.; − Append output mode cannot finalize a window, so the Delta sink cannot receive a complete result and downstream consumers see either nothing final or endlessly revised rows.; − Stateful exactly-once semantics degenerate in practice: checkpoints grow without limit and a restart may never complete, which is fatal for production [source 5].
Best for: Exploratory notebooks where the stream is bounded or short-lived and no production SLA applies; never in a production pipeline.

Delay set to the observed p99 event lateness, with dropped-event metrics
+ Aligns the delay with measured data rather than a guess: if the 99th percentile of (ingestion time minus event time) is, say, 4 minutes, a 4-minute delay retains 99% of events while keeping latency far inside the 10-minute SLA.; + State and latency costs are bounded and predictable, because the delay is a concrete, monitored number proportional to the measured skew.; + Emits a dropped-late-event counter, so the residual 1% loss is visible and auditable rather than invisible, and the team has a trigger for revisiting the setting.; + Works whether the aggregation is a plain Structured Streaming stage or a chained Lakeflow pipeline, since both run on the same watermark mechanism [source 2].
− Requires an additional measurement job to compute event lateness percentiles before the delay can be chosen, which is engineering time the team must spend up front.; − p99 is a snapshot: a product launch, a mobile client release, or a timezone bug can shift the lateness distribution and silently push loss above 1% until someone checks the metric.; − Leaves at most 1% of events dropped by construction, so it is not 'complete', merely 'complete enough', and that must be stated explicitly in the SLA.
Best for: Production pipelines with a measurable event-lateness distribution and a defined freshness SLA, which is exactly this case.

Recommendation: Delay set to the observed p99 event lateness, with dropped-event metrics — The 10-minute freshness SLA eliminates the 30-minute delay before accuracy is even considered, and the fixed state budget eliminates unbounded growth. Within those two hard limits, the only defensible number is one derived from the data: set the delay to the p99 measured lateness so that latency stays well under 10 minutes while state stays proportional to a known quantity, and emit a dropped-late-event metric so the residual loss is observable. Because the pipeline is a chain of streaming stages on a Delta sink with exactly-once state [source 5] and low-latency append-only ingestion [source 3][source 4], the delay is a checkpointed parameter that should be revisited whenever the SLA or the event-skew distribution changes.

actions.text: Now let's put that watermark knowledge to work on a real design decision. Your team has four engineers running a real-time aggregation pipeline, and you have to pick a watermark delay. That single number controls three things at once: how fresh your results are, how complete they are, and how much state your cluster has to hold in memory.

Remember the constraint that shapes everything here: the pipeline is a chain of streaming stages, so the watermark propagates downstream. Whatever delay you pick at the source ripples through every aggregation after it. You cannot tune each stage independently — you are choosing one number for the whole chain.

Option A: a short delay, say one minute. This gives you the lowest result latency and the smallest state footprint, which is great for memory and cost. The tradeoff is accuracy — anything arriving more than a minute late is silently dropped, and silent is the dangerous word here.

Option B: a long delay, around thirty minutes. Completeness goes up because you are willing to wait for stragglers, but your state store grows accordingly and your results are thirty minutes stale. For a dashboard that needs to react quickly, that latency may simply be unacceptable.

Option C: no watermark at all. Nothing is ever dropped and you never emit a final result — but state grows without bound and you lose append-mode finalization entirely. That is not viable for production, so cross it off.

So how do you actually choose? You measure. Take the observed p99 event lateness in your stream — the value that ninety-nine percent of your events beat — and set the delay there. That gives you a defensible answer backed by data, not a guess, and it is exactly the reasoning the exam rewards.

And that is the recommendation to carry forward: set the delay to the observed p99 lateness, emit a metric for dropped-late-events so you can see the silent losses, and revisit the decision whenever your SLA or your event skew changes. Freshness, completeness, and memory — you are always trading between the three.

scenes.title: Check: Watermarks and State Management

questions.question: A Structured Streaming aggregation reads events carrying an event-time column `event_ts`. The query is written as `(df.withWatermark("event_ts", "10 minutes").groupBy(window("event_ts", "5 minutes")).count())`. At a given instant, the maximum event time observed so far is 14:47. Which value is the current watermark, and what does it bound?

options.label: 14:37 — a moving threshold equal to (max event time seen so far − delay) that bounds how long the engine must retain window state
14:47 — a moving threshold equal to the max event time seen so far, used to delay records until the clock catches up
14:42 — the midpoint between the max event time and the delay, used to close windows exactly at their end boundary
14:57 — the max event time plus the delay, used to buffer records that arrive out of order

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: The watermark is defined as (max event time seen so far − delay), so with a maximum event time of 14:47 and a delay of 10 minutes the watermark is 14:37. Its purpose is to bound state: the engine commits to never see events older than that threshold, so window state whose end boundary lies at or below the watermark can be finalized and evicted. Option B drops the delay entirely and repeats the misconception that a watermark postpones records; Option C invents a midpoint formula that has no basis in the watermark definition; Option D adds the delay instead of subtracting it, which would push the watermark ahead of real time and incorrectly drop valid late data. Note that the delay here is the delay parameter of withWatermark, and the watermark only starts advancing after the first micro-batch in which an event time is observed.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about `withWatermark` placement, state eviction, and late-event handling are correct for a streaming aggregation? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: withWatermark must be called on the streaming DataFrame before the aggregation operator (groupBy/window), not after it, for the watermark to bound the aggregation's state
Window state can be evicted only after the watermark crosses the window's end boundary, so a window ending at 15:00 with a 10-minute delay is not finalized before the watermark reaches 15:00
A watermark deliberately delays the delivery of records to the sink until the watermark passes their event time, which is how out-of-order arrivals are reordered
Events whose event time is older than the current watermark are dropped rather than being added to window state, which is the trade-off that makes state eviction possible

correctAnswer: A
B
D
questions.analysis: Option A is correct: withWatermark must be applied to the input DataFrame before the aggregation so the aggregation carries the watermark and can use it to bound state; applying it after the aggregation (or at the wrong stage) means the aggregation has no watermark to evict with. Option B is correct: the watermark is a monotonic threshold and eviction happens when the threshold crosses the window's end boundary, so with a 10-minute delay and a window ending at 15:00 the earliest the watermark can be 15:00 is when max event time reaches 15:10 — until then the window stays open. Option C is the distractor: a watermark is not a reordering or buffering mechanism and does not delay delivery of records; it bounds state and defines a lateness cutoff. Option D is correct: once the watermark has advanced past an event's event time, adding that event would reopen (or fail to close) a window, so the engine drops it — this is exactly the trade-off that makes bounded state possible. Streaming Delta sinks preserve exactly-once semantics for the events that are not dropped [source 1][source 5].

questions.question: A tumbling window aggregation uses 5-minute windows and `withWatermark("event_ts", "2 minutes")`. At processing time T the engine has observed a maximum event time of 12:20. A record with event time 12:14 arrives in the next micro-batch. Which statement best describes its treatment, and why?

options.label: The record is dropped because 12:14 is older than the current watermark 12:18, so the [12:10, 12:15) window has effectively been finalized conceptually and the engine will not reopen it
The record is held in a buffer until the watermark advances past 12:14, at which point it is delivered to the sink in event-time order
The record is always accepted because window state is never evicted while the query is running; eviction only happens when the stream terminates
The record is dropped because its event time falls in a window [12:10, 12:15) that has not yet been emitted and is therefore invalid by definition

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: The watermark is (max event time − delay) = 12:20 − 0:02 = 12:18. The arriving event has event time 12:14, which is older than the watermark, so by the definition of the watermark behavior it is treated as too late and is dropped — the engine cannot add it to the [12:10, 12:15) window without contradicting the guarantee that the watermark bounds state. Option B repeats the misconception that a watermark buffers and reorders records; it does not. Option C is wrong because state eviction is a continuous, per-window process driven by the watermark crossing each window's end boundary, not an end-of-stream event. Option D is wrong because the drop is caused by the event being older than the watermark, not by the window being un-emitted — an un-emitted window that is still above the watermark would normally accept the event. This precisely illustrates the distractor the unit warns against: the watermark is not a delay of records; it is a bound on state.

actions.text: Time to check how well the watermarks and state management material settled in. Work through each question on your own and commit to your best answer — and for the multi-select, consider every option carefully before you decide.
Once you submit, I'll walk through each question with you and we'll untangle anything that gave you trouble. Go ahead and give it your best shot.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: A Stream-Stream Join with Watermarks

elements.content: Problem 1

**Scene: a stream-stream join with watermarks, part 1 — which pairs actually match?**

A Databricks Structured Streaming job ingests two Kafka topics into two Lakeflow streaming tables and joins them to attribute ad clicks to ad impressions. The **left** side is impressions, the **right** side is clicks. Both DataFrames call `.withWatermark('event_time', '10 minutes')`, and the join is expressed as:

```python

clicks.alias('c').join(

impressions.alias('i'),

expr('c.ad_id = i.ad_id AND c.event_time >= i.event_time '

'AND c.event_time <= i.event_time + INTERVAL 30 MINUTES'))

```

Events arrive one per micro-batch, in this order (all event times are on the same day and live in the event-time column carried by the data):

| batch | stream | ad_id | event_time |

|---|---|---|---|

| 1 | impression | A | 10:00 |

| 2 | impression | B | 10:05 |

| 3 | click | A | 10:04 |

| 4 | impression | A | 10:20 |

| 5 | click | B | 10:22 |

| 6 | click | A | 10:25 |

Answer: **(a)** What is the watermark on each side after every micro-batch? **(b)** Which (impression, click) pairs satisfy the join predicate, and in which micro-batch is each pair emitted? **(c)** How many rows does the job write to the sink, and which input rows produce more than one output row?

Hint: Two different numbers govern this join: the 10-minute watermark delay is a state-retention knob, and the 30-minute range condition in the ON clause is the actual matching rule. They are not the same thing.

Worked solution
**Step 1 — Write down the two rules before touching the data.**

Rule 1 (matching): a pair $(i, c)$ is a match iff `c.ad_id = i.ad_id` **and** $i.event\_time \le c.event\_time \le i.event\_time + 30$ minutes. The 30-minute range is what a click stream can be bounded by; the equi-join on `ad_id` alone is not enough to bound state.

Rule 2 (watermark): each input has its **own** watermark, $W = (\text{max event time seen on that input so far}) - 10\ \text{minutes}$. The two watermarks advance independently and never move backwards, because the max event time never decreases.

**Step 2 — Watermark trace, one row per micro-batch.**

| batch | event | max event time (impressions) | $W_{imp}$ | max event time (clicks) | $W_{clk}$ |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| 1 | i1 A 10:00 | 10:00 | 09:50 | — | not defined |

| 2 | i2 B 10:05 | 10:05 | 09:55 | — | not defined |

| 3 | c1 A 10:04 | 10:05 | 09:55 | 10:04 | 09:54 |

| 4 | i3 A 10:20 | 10:20 | **10:10** | 10:04 | 09:54 |

| 5 | c2 B 10:22 | 10:20 | 10:10 | 10:22 | **10:12** |

| 6 | c3 A 10:25 | 10:20 | 10:10 | 10:25 | **10:15** |

Note batch 4: a single impression at 10:20 moves $W_{imp}$ from 09:55 to 10:10, i.e. the impression side has now decided that any impression older than 10:10 is too late to be processed. The click side is unaffected — this is the whole point of having two watermarks rather than one.

**Step 3 — Enumerate candidate pairs and test the predicate.**

There are $3 \times 3 = 9$ candidate pairs. Impression times: i1 = 10:00, i2 = 10:05, i3 = 10:20. Click times: c1 = 10:04, c2 = 10:22, c3 = 10:25. The allowed upper bound for each impression is i1 → 10:30, i2 → 10:35, i3 → 10:50.

| pair | ad_id match? | $c \ge i$ ? | $c \le i + 30$ min ? | verdict | emitted in batch |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| (i1, c1) | A = A yes | 10:04 ≥ 10:00 yes | 10:04 ≤ 10:30 yes | **MATCH** | 3 |

| (i1, c2) | A ≠ B no | — | — | no | — |

| (i1, c3) | A = A yes | 10:25 ≥ 10:00 yes | 10:25 ≤ 10:30 yes | **MATCH** | 6 |

| (i2, c1) | B ≠ A no | — | — | no | — |

| (i2, c2) | B = B yes | 10:22 ≥ 10:05 yes | 10:22 ≤ 10:35 yes | **MATCH** | 5 |

| (i2, c3) | B ≠ A no | — | — | no | — |

| (i3, c1) | A = A yes | 10:04 ≥ 10:20 **no** | — | no (click is before the impression) | — |

| (i3, c2) | A ≠ B no | — | — | no | — |

| (i3, c3) | A = A yes | 10:25 ≥ 10:20 yes | 10:25 ≤ 10:50 yes | **MATCH** | 6 |

**Step 4 — Answer.**

- (a) The watermark trace is the table in Step 2. After batch 6: $W_{imp}$ = 10:10 and $W_{clk}$ = 10:15.

- (b) Four matches, emitted as they are detected: (i1, c1) in batch 3, (i2, c2) in batch 5, and both (i1, c3) and (i3, c3) in batch 6.

- (c) The job writes **4 output rows**. Row i1 (impression A at 10:00) fans out to two clicks (c1 and c3), and click c3 (A at 10:25) fans out to two impressions (i1 and i3). The join is not one-to-one; a single impression can be credited with several clicks inside the 30-minute range.

The matched pairs are then written append-only into a Delta table. Because the Delta transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even with other concurrent readers and writers [source 1], the output can be modelled as a streaming table — a Delta table with native streaming and incremental processing, designed for append-only ingestion and low latency [source 3] — and safely re-run after a restart without double-counting clicks.

Analysis — **Why this method works.** The ON clause is doing three separate jobs and students routinely collapse them into one. The equi-join on `ad_id` is what makes the join feasible at all: Spark can hash-partition and shuffle both sides by `ad_id`, so a click only ever has to look at impressions with the same key. The **time-range condition** is what makes the *state* finite: an impression at 10:00 can only ever match clicks up to 10:30, so there is a computable moment after which the impression is useless. The **watermark** is what makes that moment *knowable at runtime*: $W_{clk}$ is Spark's running estimate of the oldest click that can still show up, so once $W_{clk}$ passes 10:30 the impression at 10:00 can be thrown away. Remove the time-range condition and no amount of watermarking bounds the state, because a click at 11:00 next year could still share the same `ad_id`. Remove the watermark and the time-range condition still cannot be *enforced*, because Spark has no evidence about which clicks are still coming. This is why both appear in the query.

**Common mistakes.** (1) Reading the 10 minutes as the join window — 'a click joins if it arrives within 10 minutes of the impression'. It does not; the watermark delay is a lateness budget used for state retention. In this problem (i1, c3) matches even though the click's event time is 25 minutes after the impression and the delay is 10 minutes, and (i3, c3) matches although c3 arrived *after* the impression watermark moved past its own event time. (2) Assuming a match is lost because the matching row arrived in a later micro-batch. Spark buffers both sides in the state store [source 5]; the pair (i1, c3) spans 5 micro-batches and still matches. (3) Assuming the output is symmetric: it is not. One impression can produce many output rows (fan-out), so downstream aggregations must be written to tolerate duplicate impression ids, e.g. by aggregating with a window on the click's event time rather than counting impression rows. (4) Assuming that once a click is emitted its impression can be dropped — the impression must stay until no *future* click can match it, which is exactly the eviction rule quantified in the next problem.

**Generalisation.** The pattern 'equi-join key + event-time range + watermark on both sides + append-only Delta sink' is the standard bounded stream-stream join template, and it composes into chained pipelines — streaming DLT/Lakeflow pipelines are built on top of Structured Streaming and are the recommended shape when you need to chain several streaming stages with high volume and low latency, and Python pipelines can ingest directly from an event bus such as Kafka [source 2]. The identical arithmetic appears in windowed aggregations: a window is retained exactly until the watermark passes its end, and a join row is retained exactly until the watermark of the other side passes its event time plus the range bound.
Problem 2

**Scene: a stream-stream join with watermarks, part 2 — when is state evicted, and how big does it get?**

Take the same job and the same six events as before: i1 (A, 10:00), i2 (B, 10:05), c1 (A, 10:04), i3 (A, 10:20), c2 (B, 10:22), c3 (A, 10:25), each in its own micro-batch, with the same 10-minute watermark on `event_time` and the same ON-clause range `c.event_time BETWEEN i.event_time AND i.event_time + 30 MINUTES`. Two more batches then arrive:

| batch | stream | ad_id | event_time |

|---|---|---|---|

| 7 | impression | C | 10:40 |

| 8 | click | A | 11:00 |

Answer: **(a)** Derive the eviction rule Spark applies to each side of the state store, from the join predicate and the watermark definition alone. **(b)** After which micro-batch is each buffered row evicted? State explicitly which rows survive after batch 8 and why. **(c)** How many rows sit in the state store after batch 8, and what does that tell you about whether the state is bounded? **(d)** If both streams then go completely idle for an hour, what happens to the state?
Hint: A row is evicted by the watermark of the *opposite* stream, not its own. Ask: after this point, could any new row on the other side still be able to match it?

Worked solution
**Step 1 — Derive the eviction rule from the predicate (not from memory).**

*Impression side.* An impression at time $t_i$ matches clicks in the closed interval $[t_i,\; t_i + 30\ \text{min}]$. If $W_{clk} > t_i + 30\ \text{min}$, then every click still able to arrive has an event time strictly greater than $t_i + 30$ minutes (anything older would be below the click watermark and is therefore too late to be processed), so the impression at $t_i$ can never match again. **Impression rows are evicted once $W_{clk} > t_i + 30$ min.**

*Click side.* A click at time $t_c$ matches impressions in $[t_c - 30\ \text{min},\; t_c]$. The only impressions that could still arrive and match it are ones with event time $\le t_c$. If $W_{imp} > t_c$, no such impression can arrive any more. So the 30-minute offset does *not* appear on this side: **click rows are evicted once $W_{imp} > t_c$.**

Notice that each rule uses the watermark of the *other* input. That is not an accident: a row can only be discarded when the side that could still touch it has promised not to.

**Step 2 — Watermark trace including batches 7 and 8.**

| batch | event | $W_{imp}$ | $W_{clk}$ |

|---|---|---|---|

| 6 (end of part 1) | c3 A 10:25 | 10:10 | 10:15 |

| 7 | i4 C 10:40 | **10:30** | 10:15 |

| 8 | c4 A 11:00 | 10:30 | **10:50** |

**Step 3 — Apply the rules row by row.**

| buffered row | event time | evicted when | evicted at batch |

|---|---|---|---|

| c1 (click A) | 10:04 | $W_{imp} > 10$:04 | **4** (after i3 pushed $W_{imp}$ to 10:10) |

| c2 (click B) | 10:22 | $W_{imp} > 10$:22 | **7** (after $W_{imp}$ = 10:30) |

| c3 (click A) | 10:25 | $W_{imp} > 10$:25 | **7** (after $W_{imp}$ = 10:30) |

| i1 (impression A) | 10:00 | $W_{clk} > 10$:30 | **8** (after $W_{clk}$ = 10:50) |

| i2 (impression B) | 10:05 | $W_{clk} > 10$:35 | **8** (after $W_{clk}$ = 10:50) |

| i3 (impression A) | 10:20 | $W_{clk} > 10$:50 | **not yet** — $W_{clk}$ = 10:50 exactly, and the test is strictly greater |

| i4 (impression C) | 10:40 | $W_{clk} > 11$:10 | not yet |

| c4 (click A) | 11:00 | $W_{imp} > 11$:00 | not yet ($W_{imp}$ = 10:30) |

Key detail: c1 was evicted in batch 4, yet its match (i1, c1) had already been emitted in batch 3. **Eviction never retracts output; it only removes rows that can no longer produce *new* output.** Also note that c2 and c3 were both evicted the instant i4 arrived, even though i4 has `ad_id = C` and matches nothing — eviction is driven by the watermark, not by the data on the matching key.

**Step 4 — What is left after batch 8.**

Surviving rows: i3 (10:20), i4 (10:40), c4 (11:00) — **3 rows in state**. c4 produces no output: it matches i3 on `ad_id = A` and satisfies 11:00 ≥ 10:20, but 11:00 ≤ 10:50 is false, so it falls outside the 30-minute range; it does not match i4 (`ad_id` A ≠ C). The job emitted exactly the 4 rows from part 1 and nothing more.

**Step 5 — What happens if the streams then go idle.**

A watermark is $\max(\text{event time}) - \text{delay}$, so with no new events the maxima do not change and both watermarks freeze at $W_{imp}$ = 10:30 and $W_{clk}$ = 10:50. No further eviction occurs; the 3 rows stay in the state store indefinitely (they are part of the checkpoint and survive restarts, which is what gives the query fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5]). That is correct and harmless — the state is *bounded*, not necessarily empty. It only becomes a problem when a frozen watermark coexists with a stream that keeps producing, which is the failure mode analysed in the next problem.

Analysis — **Why the rule is asymmetric.** Students almost always guess that each side evicts by its own watermark, i.e. an impression at $t_i$ is dropped once $W_{imp} > t_i$. That rule is wrong and would silently lose matches: in this trace it would have dropped i1 at batch 4 ($W_{imp}$ = 10:10 > 10:00), yet c3 at 10:25 still had to match it in batch 6, and c4 at 11:00 still had to be tested against it in batch 8. The correct question is always 'which *other* side could still produce a partner for this row?', and the answer uses the other side's watermark plus the largest forward offset the predicate allows. The offset is one-sided (30 minutes forward, 0 backward) precisely because the predicate is one-sided.

**Edge cases the boundary exposes.** The comparison is strict. i3 at 10:20 is retained when $W_{clk}$ = 10:50 exactly, and would be evicted by the next click that pushes $W_{clk}$ to 10:51 or later. Boundary behaviour in a specific micro-batch can differ by Spark version because eviction runs alongside the batch that advanced the watermark; the exam-stable fact is the *rule* (opposite watermark plus the range bound), not the exact micro-batch index. A second edge case: eviction requires the opposite stream to keep producing. A stalled input freezes its watermark and therefore freezes the eviction of the *other* side's rows, even though that other side is perfectly healthy.

**Common mistakes.** (1) Trying to evict with a `.filter()` or a batch job: eviction is internal to the stateful operator and is what the watermark buys you; a stateless filter cannot know what has not yet arrived. (2) Believing that a join with a watermark gives *complete* results. It gives results that are complete only for events at or above the watermark: rows arriving below the watermark are treated as too late and their potential matches are lost. That is the price of bounded state and is exactly why the delay must be chosen from observed out-of-orderness, not guessed. (3) Assuming state emptiness means correctness. A permanently frozen 3-row state is fine; a permanently frozen watermark in front of a live stream is not.

**Generalisation and observability.** The same arithmetic drives state-retention decisions anywhere the platform keeps keys alive across micro-batches, and it is why the state store is checkpointed at all — storing processing state is what enables fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5]. Operationally, watch the **State Store Metrics** panel in the Spark UI of the streaming query (number of rows in state, memory used, number of state updates per batch). If the row count grows monotonically, either the range condition is missing, a watermark is missing, or one side's watermark is frozen by upstream lag. Because matched output is appended to Delta with transaction-log-backed exactly-once guarantees [source 1], you can safely stop, fix the query, and restart from the checkpoint to let eviction resume without duplicating already-written rows.
Problem 3

**Scene: a stream-stream join with watermarks, part 3 — the asymmetric-lag and no-watermark failures.**

Same job, same predicate, same 10-minute watermark on `event_time` on both sides. Each buffered row occupies about **1 KB** in the state store (payload plus object overhead plus index entries).

**Scenario A (asymmetric lag).** The impressions topic goes silent: the last impression ever produced is i3 at 10:20, so $W_{imp}$ freezes at 10:10 forever. Clicks keep arriving at **5,000 events per minute** with timely event times. (i) Which side of the state store grows, and why? (ii) How many rows and how many megabytes of state have accumulated after 30 minutes? After 6 hours? (iii) If the state store budget for the query is 2 GB before executors start spilling and failing, roughly when does the job break?

**Scenario B (no watermark).** A developer removes both `.withWatermark(...)` calls but keeps the same ON clause. (i) What is the maximum amount of state the join can hold, and what happens to the query? (ii) What is the cheapest correct fix? (iii) What does Spark do if you write the same join as a `LEFT OUTER` stream-stream join with no watermarks on either side, and why is that different from the inner-join case?
Hint: Ask which watermark controls the eviction of the click rows. If it never advances, nothing on the click side can ever be evicted — no matter how punctual the clicks are.

Worked solution
**Step 1 — Recall the eviction rules derived in the previous problem.**

Impression rows are evicted once $W_{clk} > t_i + 30$ min. Click rows are evicted once $W_{imp} > t_c$.

**Step 2 — Scenario A: identify the growing side.**

$W_{imp} = \max(\text{impression event time}) - 10\ \text{min}$. The impression stream has stopped, so its max stays at 10:20 and $W_{imp}$ is pinned at **10:10** forever. Click eviction depends entirely on $W_{imp}$, so every click with event time greater than 10:10 is **permanently un-evictable**. Clicks keep arriving at 5,000 per minute, all with event times well after 10:10 (they are timely), so they all accumulate. Meanwhile $W_{clk}$ keeps advancing, so the *impression* side stays healthy and small — its 3 rows are evicted on schedule. The growth is entirely one-sided, which is precisely why this is called the asymmetric-lag pitfall: two watermarks keep the state symmetric and bounded *only while both inputs make progress*.

**Step 3 — Scenario A: quantify the growth.**

Clicks retained at time $T$ after the stall $\approx 5{,}000\ \text{rows/min} \times T$.

- After 30 minutes: $5{,}000 \times 30 = 150{,}000$ rows; $150{,}000 \times 1\ \text{KB} = 150{,}000\ \text{KB} \approx 150\ \text{MB}$.

- After 6 hours (360 minutes): $5{,}000 \times 360 = 1{,}800{,}000$ rows; $1{,}800{,}000 \times 1\ \text{KB} \approx 1.8\ \text{GB}$.

- Break-even against a 2 GB budget: $2{,}000\ \text{MB} \div (5{,}000 \times 1\ \text{KB per min}) = 2{,}000\ \text{MB} \div 5\ \text{MB/min} = 400$ minutes, i.e. roughly **6 hours 40 minutes** of impression downtime. Note the growth is linear in *wall-clock downtime*, not in total data volume, and restarting the query does not help: the state is checkpointed and is restored on restart [source 5], so the job fails again.

**Step 4 — Scenario B: no watermark.**

With no watermark there is no notion of 'too late', so Spark can never prove that an unseen row will not match a buffered row. Therefore **every row from both sides is retained for the lifetime of the query**: state is unbounded, and its size is the total number of clicks plus the total number of impressions ever seen. At 5,000 clicks/min, the click side alone is $5{,}000 \times 60 \times 24 \times 1\ \text{KB} \approx 7.2\ \text{GB}$ per day, on top of the impression side. There is no threshold at which this stabilises; the query degrades as the state store spills to disk, micro-batch durations climb, GC pressure rises, and the executors eventually fail with out-of-memory errors that recur on every restart. **The cheapest correct fix is not to shrink anything, it is to add the two watermarks back**, on the event-time column, with a delay chosen from the observed maximum out-of-orderness of each topic (for example `withWatermark('event_time', '10 minutes')` on both sides) plus keeping the 30-minute range condition in the ON clause. That single change turns Scenario A's unbounded growth into a bounded, self-draining state.

**Step 5 — Scenario B, outer join variant.**

A `LEFT OUTER` / `RIGHT OUTER` / `FULL OUTER` stream-stream join is different because the query must *emit* something for rows that never matched. Deciding whether an unmatched impression is 'unmatched so far' or 'unmatched forever' is impossible without watermarks, so Spark rejects such a query at analysis time and requires a watermark on **both** sides before it will run. That makes the outer case the cleanest exam trap: an inner join without watermarks runs and dies slowly, while an outer join without watermarks fails immediately.

Analysis — **Why the asymmetry happens at all.** A watermark is a promise made by one input about its own future. $W_{imp}$ = 10:10 says 'no impression older than 10:10 will be processed any more'. That promise is about *impressions*, but it is consumed by the *click* side to decide when a click can stop waiting for a partner. When the impression topic dies, the promise is never renewed, so the click rows wait forever. The correct mental model is a two-sided handshake: each side's state is released only when the other side has publicly given up on it. This is why the platform's word for the mechanism is state management, not filtering — the state store exists to hold the buffered rows, and processing state is what enables fault tolerance and exactly-once semantics across restarts [source 5].

**Diagnosing the two failure modes.** The signature of missing watermarks is a state row count that grows linearly forever from the first micro-batch, with no periodic drops. The signature of asymmetric lag is a state row count that drops regularly on one side and grows linearly on the other; in the Spark UI you typically see the same per-batch input rate but a monotonic rise in state memory used. The fix for the first is to add `withWatermark` to the event-time column of both streams (per the rule already established: the watermark must be applied to the event-time column, not to processing time). The fix for the second is upstream: monitor per-topic lag, alert when one input stalls, or insert a guard that fails or pauses the query rather than letting state grow without bound. Adding a bigger watermark delay never fixes asymmetric lag — it makes it strictly worse.

**Edge cases and traps.** (1) A watermark delay that is too large is not 'safer'. It delays eviction on both sides, inflating the *bounded* state by exactly (arrival rate × extra delay) bytes; a delay of 10 minutes instead of 1 minute on a 5,000 clicks/min stream adds about $5{,}000 \times 9 \times 1\ \text{KB} \approx 45\ \text{MB}$ of steady-state buffer. (2) A watermark delay that is too small silently drops legitimate late pairs, producing a correct-looking but incomplete attribution — the hardest bug of the three, because there is no error and no metric drop, only a smaller output count. (3) A watermark going backwards is impossible by construction because it is a running maximum minus a constant; if you see 'state growing forever' with watermarks defined, suspect that one input's watermark is being derived from a column that is not actually the event time, or from a stream that is not producing. (4) Where a stalled input is expected and unavoidable, the pragmatic design is to make the *lagging* side deterministic — for example by joining the click stream to a small, fully-known dimension table loaded periodically rather than to a live impression stream — so that no unbounded keyed state is required on the fast side. Because chained streaming pipelines on top of Structured Streaming are the recommended pattern for high-volume, low-latency workloads and can ingest directly from an event bus such as Kafka [source 2], the impression topic's health is something the pipeline itself can be instrumented to watch. The final output is still written append-only into a Delta-backed streaming table, where the delta log's exactly-once guarantee [source 1] and the streaming-table definition — a Delta table with native support for streaming and incremental processing, designed for append-only ingestion and low latency [source 3] — mean that a restart after fixing the stall resumes cleanly without duplicating already-emitted attribution rows.

**Generalisation.** The same three-question checklist applies to any stateful streaming operator you are asked about: what indexes the state (the equi-join key or the window key), what bounds it (the range condition or the window boundary), and what releases it (the watermark of the relevant input). If any of the three is missing, state is not bounded; if all three are present but one input stalls, state is bounded only in theory.

actions.text: Now let's put watermarks to work on a real exam-style scenario: Problem 1 — a stream-stream join. This is the kind of question the certification loves, because it combines two of the trickiest ideas in Structured Streaming — event-time joins and bounded state.

Here's the scene. We're joining an ad-clicks stream to an ad-impressions stream on ad_id, and both streams carry a 10-minute watermark on event_time. Your job: decide which click-impression pairs actually join, and when each unmatched row gets evicted from state.

The hint tells you the key insight right away: two different numbers govern this join. The join predicate controls whether a pair matches at all, and the watermark controls how long a row is kept around waiting for a match. Keep those two rules separate in your head — mixing them up is the single most common mistake here.

In the worked solution, we write down both rules explicitly. Rule one: metadata only, and Spark buffers both sides in the state store until data arrives. Rule two: a buffered row is evicted once its side's watermark advances past that side's last-seen event time minus the ten-minute delay. Nothing in a stream-stream join is joined until data arrives — there's no eager matching.

Now the analysis: why does this method work? The ON clause matches ad_id, while the watermark bounds how much historical state we hold. Without the watermark, Spark would have to keep every row forever, because it can never be sure a late-arriving match isn't coming. The watermark gives Spark permission to forget — that's what makes the join both correct and bounded.
Problem 2 sharpens the eviction rule. Read the scene carefully and then try the hint before you look at the solution — the point here is to derive the rule yourself rather than recall it.

The hint states the eviction rule precisely: a row is evicted by the watermark of the opposite side — the side it is waiting to join with. Let that land. It's the asymmetry that trips people up, and it's exactly what the exam tests.

The analysis explains why the rule is asymmetric and, crucially, what happens when the two streams lag unevenly. Two watermarks keep the join state symmetric and bounded — but if one stream stalls, its watermark advances slowly, and that side of the state grows without bound. That's the asymmetric-lag pitfall, and it's a favorite exam trap.

scenes.title: Interactive: Coding a Windowed Aggregation and Stream Join

content.html:
⚡ Windowed Aggregation & Stream Join

Write event-time windowing code using PySpark. Use withWatermark and groupBy(window(...)) to aggregate events. Check the expected windowed counts below.
Loading Python…

Output

—

✅ Test Cases

▼

📘 Solution

from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()
# ...
events = spark.readStream.format("rate").load()
windowed = events.withWatermark('timestamp', '10 minutes').groupBy(F.window('timestamp', '10 minutes', '5 minutes')).count()
query = windowed.writeStream.outputMode('complete').format('console').start()

actions.text: We just saw conceptually how a watermark bounds state and how a window spec decides which events land where. Now let's write that logic ourselves. This coding widget has an editor where you'll compose a windowed aggregation and a stream-stream join in PySpark, then run it against test cases and compare the emitted rows to what you predict.

actions.content: This is the editor where you write your windowed aggregation and stream join code.

actions.text: Start with the windowed aggregation. The pattern to build is events dot withWatermark on event_time with a ten-minute delay, then groupBy a window of event_time, ten minutes duration and five minutes slide, and finally a count. Before you run anything, ask yourself: how many rows will a sliding window emit compared to a tumbling one? Make that prediction first.

actions.content: Run the code to see the emitted windowed counts.

actions.text: Now compare the actual counts to your prediction, and vary the window duration and slide. If you widen the slide so windows overlap more, the same events belong to more windows, so the emitted row count grows. Notice that withWatermark must be applied before the groupBy — place it after and the watermarked semantics are silently disabled, and that is exactly the exam trap this exercise is built to catch.

actions.content: Open the test cases to check your output against the expected results.

actions.text: Once the aggregation passes, extend the editor to a stream-stream join between two watermarked streams. Both sides need a watermark and a bounded event-time constraint, or the engine keeps every state forever. Inspect which rows the join actually produces and confirm the join output respects the watermark on each input.

scenes.title: Check: Stream Joins, Windows, and Watermarks

questions.question: A fraud-detection pipeline built on Databricks ingests card-authorization events that must feed a downstream risk model. The requirement is: results must be emitted with a target latency no greater than 30 seconds, and each authorization event must appear in exactly one output window so the model does not double-count suspicious activity. Which window type and parameters satisfy BOTH the latency and non-overlap requirements simultaneously?

options.label: Tumbling window of 30 seconds on the event-time column; every event belongs to exactly one window and output is emitted at each window boundary.
Sliding window of 30 seconds duration with a 10-second slide on the event-time column; events overlap across windows but results arrive faster.
Session window with a static 30-second gap on the event-time column; the gap guarantees non-overlap.
Tumbling window of 60 seconds on the processing-time column; the wall clock is always available so no event-time column is needed.

questions.analysis: Tumbling windows are fixed-length and non-overlapping, so each event falls into exactly one window — that satisfies the non-overlap requirement. Because the window duration is 30 seconds, results are emitted at each window boundary, which keeps latency within the 30-second target. Option B is wrong because sliding windows overlap: an event can belong to more than one window, which would cause double-counting in the fraud model (the teaching material explicitly warns that in sliding windows an event can appear in two windows). Option C is a distractor that conflates session windows with fixed windows: session windows are dynamic-length and end when no event arrives for the gap period, so the '30-second gap' does not bound latency at 30 seconds — a long-running session could hold results indefinitely. Option D is wrong on two counts: a 60-second tumbling window exceeds the 30-second latency target, and windowed aggregations in Structured Streaming must operate on an event-time timestamp column, not the wall clock (processing time) — the certification vocabulary distinguishes event time from processing time [source 3]. Streaming tables in Lakeflow are designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming, which is the underlying architecture that makes sub-30-second tumbling feasible [source 3].

questions.question: You are joining two streams in Databricks Structured Streaming: ad_clicks(event_time, ad_id, user_id) and ad_impressions(event_time, ad_id, campaign). Both streams call .withWatermark('event_time', '10 minutes') and are joined on ad_id with the standard time-range condition event_time BETWEEN impression_time - INTERVAL 10 MINUTES AND impression_time + INTERVAL 10 MINUTES. Which TWO statements about the join result are correct?

options.label: A click whose event_time is more than 10 minutes later than every impression's event_time will not match that impression, because the watermark has advanced past the join range and the buffered impression state is evicted.
The join buffers rows from both sides in the state store; the watermark bounds how long each side is retained, preventing unbounded state growth.
Even without calling withWatermark on either stream, the join will still evict old rows once the join window condition is satisfied.
Because both sides specify a 10-minute watermark, the join can safely buffer rows indefinitely as long as the ad_id keys match.

questions.analysis: Correct answers are A and B. In a stream-stream join, Spark must buffer both sides so that a late-arriving match can still be found — this is exactly the state store behavior described in the source material: 'Store processing state to enable fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics' [source 5]. The watermark acts as the eviction boundary: once the watermark (max event_time seen minus the 10-minute delay) advances past the join range, the buffered row is discarded and future matches are impossible, so a click arriving far too late cannot match (option A). Option B correctly states that the watermark bounds retention, which is precisely why an unbounded join will otherwise grow state forever. Option C is wrong because the exam rule is explicit: withWatermark must be applied to the event-time column BEFORE the aggregation or join to take effect; without it, state is never bounded. Option D is a common misconception — a watermark does not permit infinite buffering; it is the very mechanism that forbids it by evicting state once the watermark passes. Note that streaming pipelines in Databricks are built on Spark Structured Streaming, so these state-eviction semantics apply directly to Lakeflow pipelines as well [source 2].

questions.question: A Databricks engineer deploys a continuous aggregation from a Kafka event bus into a Delta Lake streaming table using Spark Structured Streaming. The pipeline groups events by a 5-minute tumbling window on event_time and writes to a Delta table with a 1-minute trigger. After three days of continuous operation the driver's state store memory climbs monotonically and the job begins throwing OutOfMemory errors, even though the input rate is steady. Which single change is MOST likely to fix the unbounded state growth?

options.label: Move the .withWatermark('event_time', '<delay>') call so it runs on the event-time column immediately BEFORE the .groupBy(window(...)), so Spark can evict completed windows from the state store.
Switch the window type from tumbling to sliding, because sliding windows share state across overlapping windows and therefore use less memory.
Change the output mode from append to update, because update mode is the only mode that supports state eviction.
Increase the number of shuffle partitions so the state store is distributed across more executors and per-partition memory drops.

questions.analysis: The single most likely fix is A. Without a watermark, Structured Streaming cannot know when a window is 'done,' so it must retain every open window's aggregation state forever — that is the textbook cause of monotonically growing state. The exam rule is precise: withWatermark must be applied to the event-time column BEFORE the aggregation (or join) to take effect; placing it after the aggregation is a no-op. Option B is wrong because sliding windows keep MORE state than tumbling windows (each event belongs to multiple windows), so switching would worsen the problem. Option C is wrong: output mode affects how rows are emitted to the sink (append vs update vs complete) but does not introduce state eviction — only a watermark does. Option D is wrong: increasing partitions distributes state but does not bound it; total state still grows without a watermark. The underlying reason eviction is even possible is exactly the mechanism described in the source material: 'Store processing state to enable fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics' [source 5] — the state store is bounded only by an explicit watermark, and Delta Lake sinks preserve exactly-once semantics across that state [source 5].

questions.question: A student claims: 'A session window with a 30-minute gap and a tumbling window with a 30-minute duration are functionally equivalent, because both close after 30 minutes of no new events.' Which statement BEST identifies the error in this reasoning?

options.label: Session windows are dynamic-length and close after the gap elapses since the LAST event, whereas tumbling windows are fixed-length and close on clock-aligned boundaries regardless of whether events arrived; a silent session and a busy session produce very different outputs.
Session windows are fixed-length and tumbling windows are dynamic-length, so the two are swapped in the student's claim.
Both window types require a slide interval, and the student simply forgot to specify it for the session window.
The two are in fact equivalent in Structured Streaming; the difference is purely cosmetic in the SQL syntax.

questions.analysis: The student's error is a classic conflation of session windows with a fixed, gap-less window. Session windows are dynamic-length: the window boundaries are driven by data — each session ends when no event has been observed for the configured gap, so the window length is a property of the data, not of a fixed clock. Tumbling windows are fixed-length and non-overlapping: the window boundaries are clock-aligned (for example, [00:00, 00:30), [00:30, 01:00)) and the window closes whether or not any events arrived. Consequently, a busy stream and a silent stream produce identical tumbling windows but different session windows. Option B is wrong — it inverts the definitions. Option C is wrong: session windows have no slide interval; the slide interval is a sliding-window parameter. Option D is wrong because the two windows produce different output rows, different latencies, and different state footprints, which is exactly why the exam tests the distinction. The windowing taxonomy (tumbling, sliding, session) is grounded in the same architecture that makes low-latency streaming tables possible in Lakeflow pipelines built on Spark Structured Streaming [source 2] and is consistent with 'Limit input rates to maintain consistent batch sizes and prevent processing delays' — a concern that applies differently to fixed windows and to dynamic sessions [source 5].

actions.text: That wraps up the harder territory — windows, watermarks, and stream-stream joins all working together. Time to see how it holds up under exam-style pressure: four integrated questions that pull those ideas into one place.

Take each one on your own and commit to an answer before you move on — these are designed to be reasoned through, not guessed. Once you submit, I'll walk you through anything that tripped you up, especially the traps we flagged along the way.

scenes.title: Checkpoints: The Recovery Anchor

elements.content: Checkpoints: The Recovery Anchor
A streaming query is production-ready only if it can stop and restart without losing or double-counting records.

Checkpoints persist progress and state so a query resumes exactly where it stopped — every micro-batch is recorded before it is committed.

Delta Lake's transaction log then guarantees exactly-once processing, even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the table. [source 1]

Triggers decide when work actually runs — not whether it runs.

Progress lives in the checkpoint, so the answer to "where does progress live?" is always: the checkpoint location, not the trigger. [source 5]

Worked example: a 60-second query processes micro-batch #47, writes to Delta, then crashes before commit. On restart, the checkpoint reports #46 as the last completed batch, so Spark re-runs #47 from the stored input offset — the target table sees those records exactly once. Missing the checkpoint means #47 replays as duplicates, or is lost entirely. [source 5]
Exam relevance: recovery, exactly-once, and trigger selection recur on the Data Engineer Associate exam. [source 1]

actions.text: Now we move into the part of streaming that decides whether your pipeline survives a restart. The topic is checkpoints — and I want you to think of them as the recovery anchor for a streaming query.

Here is the framing for the whole lesson: a streaming query is production-ready only if it can be stopped and restarted without losing records or double-counting them. That single property is what separates a demo notebook from something you would actually run in production.

Checkpoints are how that property is achieved. A checkpoint persists progress and state to reliable storage so a query can resume exactly where it stopped. Without it, Structured Streaming has no memory of what it already processed, and a restart means starting over or reprocessing.

Triggers answer the second half of the puzzle: when does work actually run? A trigger decides the cadence of micro-batches — not whether data has arrived, but how often the engine checks. That cadence is your main lever for balancing end-to-end latency against cluster cost.

To make this concrete, picture a sixty-second query processing micro-batches on a fixed trigger interval. We will walk through what happens to the checkpoint and the offsets when that query is killed mid-batch and restarted — and why the numbers still add up.

And keep the exam in mind here: recovery, exactly-once semantics, and trigger selection are recurring objective areas on the Data Engineer Associate exam. So treat this page and the next few as high-yield material rather than background theory.

scenes.title: Anatomy of a Checkpoint

elements.content: Anatomy of a Checkpoint

A checkpoint is the only place where Spark writes the durable evidence that lets a streaming query resume: the query plan, the source offsets consumed, the files committed, and the operator state. Delta Lake tables guarantee exactly-once processing as sources and sinks [source 5], and the transaction log preserves exactly-once even with concurrent readers or writers [source 1]. Every streaming write therefore carries .option("checkpointLocation", path), and that path must be stable, durable, and exclusive to one query [source 5].

commits/ — what finished

One file per completed micro-batch; the log of atomic, replayable units [source 1].

Missing → Spark cannot tell which batches already landed.

offsets/ — where to resume

Source offsets and the batch ID that consumed them.

A batch is only valid when its offsets are still reachable.

state/ — what survives

Aggregations, dedup sets, and both sides of stream–stream joins.

Without it, restart reprocesses from scratch [source 5].

metadata/ + sources/ — the contract

Pinned query plan and per-source fingerprints.

Change the source or plan and resume can be refused.
Worked example: a 2-minute trigger over 60 minutes produces 30 commit files; delete commits/18 and batch 18 re-runs, so downstream Delta rows are written twice unless its offsets were also discarded.

actions.text: Checkpoints are the recovery anchor for every streaming query, so let's open up the checkpoint directory and see exactly what's inside it. What you get under checkpointLocation is not one file — it's a small set of artifacts, each with a distinct job.

The headline idea first: a checkpoint is the only place where Spark writes durable progress. That's what makes the query restartable. Miss the checkpoint, and a restart either re-reads data you already processed or skips data you never processed — neither is what you want in production.

The commits directory answers one question: which micro-batches finished. Each completed batch drops in a single file, so on restart Spark just reads the highest commit and knows exactly where it left off. Declare the write, commit it — those are the only two states that matter here.

The offsets directory pairs with it: this records the source offsets each batch actually consumed — Kafka partitions and positions, file paths, sequence numbers. Together, commits plus offsets are what let Spark resume from the exact point of failure rather than from the beginning or from the middle.

Then there's the state store. Any stateful operator — aggregations, dedup sets, stream-stream joins — keeps its accumulated state here, so that state survives a restart without being rebuilt from scratch. This is the directory that quietly grows to a terabyte if your watermark is too loose.

Finally, metadata and sources together act as the contract. They pin the query plan and the source fingerprints — file formats, schema, source identity. Change a source path, a schema, or the operator set in a way Spark can't reconcile, and the checkpoint is invalidated. You'll get an error rather than silent corruption, but you still have to recreate the checkpoint from scratch.

Keep this worked example in mind: a two-minute trigger over sixty minutes is roughly thirty commits and thirty offset entries, plus whatever state the aggregations accumulated. In the exam, that's the shape of the question — trigger interval over a time window tells you how many commits and offsets you should expect. Let's do a quick check now.

actions.topic: What breaks if you delete or lose the state directory but keep commits and offsets?
actions.prompt: Think about a running stream-stream join. If state is gone but progress files remain, would Spark recompute state or refuse to restart — and why?

scenes.title: Check: Checkpoints and Recovery

questions.question: A data engineer runs a Structured Streaming query over an append-only ingestion Delta table and needs the query to resume exactly where it stopped after the cluster is restarted. Which option must be set on the streaming query to make it recoverable?

options.label: trigger(processingTime='10 seconds')
outputMode('append')
checkpointLocation('/mnt/checkpoints/ingest_query')
withWatermark('event_time', '10 minutes')

questions.analysis: The checkpointLocation option points the streaming query at a durable directory where Spark writes the query's progress, offsets, and state. On restart, the engine reads this checkpoint and continues from the last committed micro-batch instead of reprocessing everything from the source. It is the recovery anchor described in this unit's lesson objective: configure a checkpoint so a streaming query resumes exactly where it stopped. Option A only controls how often micro-batches are triggered; it provides no recovery metadata. Option B controls what rows are emitted (append vs. update vs. complete) and does not persist offsets. Option D controls late-data tolerance and state eviction but does not store the query's progress. The source material reinforces this need to store processing state to enable fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5].

questions.question: Which statements correctly describe what happens when a streaming query with a valid checkpointLocation is restarted after a cluster restart? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Spark reads the offsets stored in the checkpoint and skips micro-batches whose source offsets were already processed.
Spark replays every micro-batch from the very beginning of the streaming source, regardless of the checkpoint contents.
Stateful operators such as windowed aggregations reload their prior state, so state is not lost across the restart.
The checkpoint guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the Delta table sink.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: the durable offsets in the checkpoint record which source offsets were committed, and the engine resumes from there, skipping already-processed micro-batches. Option C is correct: stateful operators persist their state (e.g., open windows and buffered join rows) in the checkpoint and reload it on restart, so windowed accumulations are not lost. Option D is correct because the Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing, even when there are other streams or batch queries running concurrently against the table [source 1]; combined with the checkpoint's stored offsets, this gives end-to-end exactly-once semantics. Option B describes the classic misconception: without a checkpoint (or if it were ignored) Spark would have no record of progress, but with a valid checkpoint it does not replay from the source beginning. The source material also states that processing state is stored to enable fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5].

questions.question: A data engineer deletes the checkpointLocation directory of a running streaming query, then reruns the exact same query code against the same Delta table sink. Explain the likely consequence for the sink contents and for exactly-once guarantees, and give one specific change to the streaming source or query plan that would have made the existing checkpoint unusable anyway.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) State that deleting the checkpoint erases the stored source offsets and state, so the restarted query has no memory of what it already processed and will typically reprocess all data currently readable from the source (e.g., the full current Delta table snapshot or, for a Kafka topic, from the configured starting offset) — 40% (2) Explain that this breaks exactly-once against the existing sink: rows already written before the delete can be written again, producing duplicates in the sink, unless the sink write is idempotent or the query uses MERGE / an idempotent sink pattern — 30% (3) Give at least one plausible change that invalidates an existing checkpoint, such as changing the source table, altering the query's plan/schema (added or reordered columns, changed aggregation), or pointing the query at a different source — 20% (4) Clarity and correct use of Databricks/Structured Streaming terminology — 10%.
questions.analysis: Deleting checkpointLocation is the classic mistake in this unit: the checkpoint is the recovery anchor holding committed source offsets, query progress, and operator state. Without it, a restart looks like a brand-new query; it reprocesses whatever the source currently exposes and re-appends to the sink, so previously written rows appear again and exactly-once is lost against that sink. The Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even with concurrent streams or batch queries [source 1], but that guarantee depends on the checkpoint recording which source offsets were already committed; deleting it removes that record. Checkpoints are also tied to the query's plan: a changed source, a modified query (different columns or aggregation), or a different source table can make the checkpoint unusable, because the stored offsets and state no longer match the new plan. The source material notes that processing state is stored to enable fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5].

Once you've submitted, I'll join you to walk through anything that gave you trouble — so just focus on getting your own best answer down first.

scenes.title: Delivery Guarantees: At-Most-Once to Exactly-Once

elements.content: Delivery Guarantees: At-Most-Once to Exactly-Once
What the sink contains after a mid-batch failure — and how source + engine + sink combine to deliver exactly-once
The Observable Definition

A delivery guarantee is a post-failure property of the entire pipeline: given a crash after a micro-batch is partially written, at-most-once leaves the sink missing records, at-least-once leaves it with possible duplicates, and exactly-once leaves it as if the failure never happened. [source 5]

It is not a configuration flag — it emerges from source replayability, engine checkpointing, and sink idempotency acting together.
How Structured Streaming + Delta Lake Achieve Exactly-Once

1. Source replays. Kafka offsets or a Delta table can be re-read from the last committed position; a socket or non-replayable API cannot.

2. Engine checkpoints. Before committing a micro-batch, Structured Streaming writes a Write-Ahead Log (WAL), then commits the sink; on restart the WAL replays, giving at-least-once by default.

3. Sink is idempotent. Delta Lake's transaction log makes the replayed write a no-op, upgrading at-least-once to exactly-once. [source 1][source 5]
Worked Example: Crash Mid-Batch with WAL + Delta
Suppose a streaming query is on batch 17 when the driver crashes. Here is what each sink contains after the driver restarts and replays from the checkpoint.
⚠ Exam trap: exactly-once is a joint property of source + engine + sink. No trigger setting can grant it alone — a non-replayable socket source fails regardless of checkpointing.

actions.text: Building directly on the checkpoint you just ran: delivery guarantees are where all the pieces we've covered — checkpoints, sinks, sources — finally come together. Let's define them precisely.
Today's topic is delivery guarantees, from at-most-once all the way to exactly-once. The key word is 'after' — we are not describing normal operation, we are describing what survives a failure.

Here's the observable definition you should memorise. A delivery guarantee is a post-failure property of the pipeline. Concretely: what does the sink contain after a mid-batch failure? At-most-once means rows may be missing. At-least-once means rows may be duplicated. Exactly-once means neither.
Notice the framing here: define the guarantee by what the consumer observes in the sink, never by what the trigger or the engine claims. That's the exam-safe mental model.

So how do we actually get exactly-once? Three ingredients must line up. First, the source must be replayable — Kafka offsets and a Delta table both are, because they can re-serve the same ranges. A raw socket, or any non-replayable source, is not.

Second, the engine. Structured Streaming writes a write-ahead log before it commits a micro-batch. That gives you at-least-once by default on a restart — the batch will be replayed, but replay alone does not remove the risk of duplication.

And third, the sink. Walk through this worked example: the query crashes on batch 17, halfway through. Without an idempotent sink, replaying batch 17 writes the same rows twice. With Delta Lake, the transaction log records that batch 17 already committed, so the replay becomes a no-op — a duplicate-free re-execution.

Which brings us to the exam trap. Exactly-once is a joint property of source plus engine plus sink together. No trigger setting, no configuration flag, can grant exactly-once on its own. If an option asks you whether a trigger can make a pipeline exactly-once, the answer is no.

Quick recap of this page: at-most-once loses rows, at-least-once duplicates them, exactly-once does neither — and it only happens when a replayable source, the checkpointed engine, and an idempotent Delta sink all line up. Next, we'll go kill a live streaming query and watch this play out.

scenes.title: Check: Delivery Guarantees and Exactly-Once

questions.question: A data engineer builds a Structured Streaming pipeline that reads from a non-replayable source (a source that cannot re-read offsets after a failure), writes micro-batches directly to a sink that overwrites file partitions by path, and configures no checkpointing and no idempotent transaction log. After a mid-batch failure during restart, what delivery guarantee does the sink most accurately exhibit?

options.label: At-most-once
At-least-once
Exactly-once
At-least-once for the source, exactly-once for the sink

questions.analysis: At-most-once is the correct classification because the source cannot replay its offsets (records consumed before the failure are lost) and there is no idempotent sink or checkpoint to re-emit or deduplicate them. Structuring Streaming normally provides at-least-once by default because it writes a Write-Ahead Log before committing each micro-batch; however, that WAL depends on a durable checkpoint location. With no checkpoint and no replayable source, the engine cannot re-consume the failed micro-batch, so only records delivered before the crash survive. At-least-once (B) would require a replayable source or a recorded offset; exactly-once (C) would require an idempotent sink such as Delta Lake's transaction log [source 1]; and option D misattributes guarantees to the source, which is not the same as a sink guarantee.

questions.question: Which statements about the role of the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) during a Structured Streaming restart are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The WAL is written before a micro-batch is committed, enabling the engine to determine which batches completed and to avoid re-emitting already-committed data.
The WAL guarantees exactly-once by itself, regardless of whether the source is replayable or the sink is idempotent.
On restart, the engine consults the WAL and checkpoint metadata to decide whether to re-run or skip the failed micro-batch.
The WAL is a substitute for checkpointLocation and eliminates the need for a durable checkpoint directory.

questions.analysis: A and C are correct. Structuring Streaming writes a Write-Ahead Log before committing a micro-batch, which gives at-least-once by default on restart, and on restart the engine uses the WAL plus checkpoint artifacts (commits and offsets directories) to decide whether to replay or skip the failed batch. B is wrong because exactly-once requires an idempotent sink such as Delta Lake, whose transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even with concurrent streams or batch queries [source 1], and also depends on how the sink is configured to deliver data [source 5]. D is wrong because the WAL must reside inside the durable checkpoint directory; without .option('checkpointLocation', path), the WAL is lost on restart and recovery is impossible.

questions.question: A pipeline ingests events with Auto Loader (which can re-list and re-read files after a failure) and writes to a plain Parquet directory using a non-atomic file-per-micro-batch write. A second pipeline uses the same Auto Loader source but writes to a Delta Lake table. Both configure the same checkpoint. Which statement best explains the resulting delivery guarantee difference?

options.label: Both pipelines achieve exactly-once because Auto Loader can always replay the source; the sink choice does not affect the guarantee.

The Parquet pipeline is at-least-once because replay may re-write duplicate Parquet files, while the Delta pipeline is exactly-once because the Delta transaction log records which micro-batch committed, making re-writes idempotent [source 1].
The Parquet pipeline is at-most-once and the Delta pipeline is at-least-once, because Delta only adds file-level atomicity, not idempotence.
Both pipelines are at-most-once because Auto Loader loses files that were partially read before the failure.

questions.analysis: The Parquet sink is not idempotent: replaying the source re-writes files by path, producing duplicates, so the guarantee is at-least-once. The Delta Lake transaction log, by contrast, guarantees exactly-once processing even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the table [source 1], because the commit is recorded atomically and re-attempting the same micro-batch is idempotent. Option A ignores the sink's role; option C reverses Delta's guarantee, which explicitly includes exactly-once semantics, and option D misstates Auto Loader's replay behavior. This matches the broader design principle that structured streaming sources and sinks should be chosen together to obtain exactly-once delivery [source 5].
