actions.text: Now let's check what you've absorbed about delivery guarantees and exactly-once processing. Work through each question on your own — I'll walk through anything that tripped you up once you submit.

scenes.title: Triggers: Deciding When Micro-Batches Run

elements.content: Triggers: Deciding When Micro-Batches Run

A trigger controls when a micro-batch fires. Because the checkpoint records every committed batch [source 5], the trigger you pick determines end-to-end latency, cluster-hours consumed, and the recovery anchor the query resumes from.
processingTime
Fixed interval, e.g. '5 seconds'. Latency ≈ interval + batch time. Continuous cluster cost.
AvailableNow
Processes all backlog, then stops. Cost-efficient scheduled incremental loads.
Continuous
Experimental low latency (ms), weaker exactly-once handling.

Worked example — latency vs. cost math. An interval of 5 s with a 3 s average batch time yields 8 s observed latency. The same job at 1 s interval still pays 3 s per batch, so 500 ms average latency costs the engine 3 s of compute every second — 3× the cluster-hours.
Exam caveat: Trigger.AvailableNow supersedes the deprecated Trigger.Once on current Databricks runtimes; choose AvailableNow for idempotent Delta sinks [source 1].

actions.text: Now let's move on to triggers — the mechanism that decides when a micro-batch actually runs. In Structured Streaming, a trigger is a setting on the write stream that tells the engine how to pace execution of each micro-batch.

A trigger controls when a micro-batch fires. Because the engine processes data in discrete batches, the trigger defines the cadence of those batches, and that cadence directly shapes both latency and cost.

The first mode is processingTime. You pass a fixed interval, like five seconds. Each batch fires on that interval, so the observed end-to-end latency is roughly the trigger interval plus the batch processing time. If a batch takes longer than the interval, batches queue up behind each other, so keep the interval comfortably above your typical batch duration.

Second, availableNow. This processes all of the available backlog, then stops the query on its own. Nothing is left running idle, so it is the cost-efficient choice for scheduled incremental loads — you spin the cluster up, drain what has arrived, and shut down.

Third, Continuous. This gives experimental low-latency processing measured in milliseconds, but it comes with weaker exactly-once handling. Know that caveat for the exam — if a question offers you millisecond latency with full exactly-once guarantees, that is a trap.

One more exam point: Trigger.AvailableNow supersedes the deprecated Trigger.Once on current Databricks runtimes. The old Once trigger is legacy, so if you see it alongside AvailableNow, pick AvailableNow.

Keep the underlying trade-off in mind: shorter intervals reduce latency but add fixed per-batch overhead and increase cluster-hours. So choosing an interval is a cost decision just as much as it is a latency decision.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Sizing a Trigger Interval Against a Latency SLO

elements.content: Problem 1

A streaming ingestion job on a four-node Databricks cluster (one driver plus three workers, eight cores each) reads an events stream and writes it into a Delta table. The business requirement is a freshness SLO (service-level objective): every event must be queryable in the Delta table within 30 seconds of its arrival in the source. Benchmarking shows that one micro-batch costs about 12 seconds of wall-clock time, dominated by fixed per-batch overhead — query planning, task launch, file discovery, and the Delta commit — and roughly independent of how many events the batch carries. (a) Derive the latency budget available for the trigger interval. (b) Select a trigger interval from the configurable set {1 s, 5 s, 10 s, 15 s, 30 s, 60 s} that satisfies the SLO with comfortable margin, and state the resulting worst-case end-to-end latency. (c) Explain what happens if you configure the interval exactly at the budget value.
Hint: End-to-end latency is the time an event waits for the next batch plus the time that batch takes to run and commit: L = T + P.

Worked solution
Step 0 — Name the model. The worst-case end-to-end latency of a micro-batch pipeline is the sum of two terms: how long an event waits for the engine to pick it up, and how long the batch that contains it takes to be processed and committed. Write L_worst = T + P, where T is the trigger interval and P is the micro-batch wall-clock time. P already contains planning, reading, transforming and the Delta commit, so no extra term is needed for the write.

Step 1 — Compute the latency budget. SLO = 30 s, P = 12 s, so T ≤ 30 − 12 = 18 s. Any processingTime trigger at or below 18 seconds is compliant under this model.

Step 2 — Pick a configurable interval under the budget. Take T = 10 s: L_worst = 10 + 12 = 22 s, which leaves 30 − 22 = 8 s — about 27 percent — of headroom. Choosing T = 18 s would give L_worst = 30 s exactly, i.e. zero headroom for a slow shuffle, a Delta commit retry, or a worker that is still starting up; arithmetically compliant but bad engineering.

Step 3 — Configure it.

(spark.readStream

.format('cloudFiles').option('cloudFiles.format','json')

.load('/mnt/landing/events')

.writeStream

.format('delta')

.option('checkpointLocation','/checkpoints/bronze_events')

.trigger(processingTime='10 seconds')

.toTable('bronze.events'))

The checkpointLocation is not optional: it is what makes the query restartable, and it is also what allows the engine to skip micro-batches that were already committed.

Step 4 — Verify. Worst case 22 s ≤ 30 s, headroom 8 s.

Step 5 — Check the model's own preconditions. (i) The additive form assumes the batch finishes before the next trigger fires, i.e. T ≥ P. Here T = 10 s < P = 12 s, so the engine cannot actually honour a 10-second cadence: it starts the next batch as soon as the previous one finishes, giving an effective cadence of about 12 s and a real worst case of about 2P = 24 s. That is still inside the SLO, but the honest headroom is 6 s, not 8 s. (ii) The model assumes P is stable; P must be re-measured after every significant change in volume or cluster size.

Analysis — Why the method works: a micro-batch engine is a sampling loop, and the sampling period is the trigger interval. An event that lands just after the source offsets were read for batch k waits a full interval T for batch k+1 to start, then P seconds to be read, transformed and committed. The two delays are additive, so the SLO is a budget that the interval and the batch time must share. That is the whole reason the interval is bounded by the SLO rather than being a free tuning knob.

Common mistakes. (1) Forgetting P entirely and setting T = 30 s 'because the SLO is 30 seconds' — the real latency becomes 42 s and the pipeline silently misses by 40 percent. (2) Believing that processingTime is 'how long a batch is allowed to take'. It is not a timeout; it is the interval at which the engine checks whether a batch can start, and the engine will never start a new batch while the previous one is still running. (3) Reading the additive model as exact. It is an upper bound that holds while T ≥ P; once P exceeds T the pipeline saturates, the interval is not honoured, and the governing bound becomes 2P. (4) Using .trigger(availableNow=True) as if it were a faster streaming trigger, which is the subject of a separate problem. (5) Ignoring chaining: if this job feeds a second hop, the 30-second budget is shared across hops, so each hop needs its own, smaller budget. That matters because streaming pipelines are routinely chained, for example a Lakeflow streaming table — a Delta table with support for streaming and incremental processing, designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming [source 4] — feeding a downstream aggregation.

Edge cases. A burst of late-arriving files enlarges P without warning. A Delta commit on a contended table can take seconds longer than the benchmark. And the moment the volume grows enough that P approaches SLO/2, no trigger interval can save the SLO — see p4 for that derivation. The defensible practice is therefore not 'set T once' but 'measure P, compute the window, choose T, and re-measure after every volume change'.
Problem 2

Same pipeline: 30-second freshness SLO, P = 12 s per micro-batch, four-node cluster (one driver plus three workers). The ingest rate is constant at 24,000 events per second, about 86.4 million events per hour, so the volume of data per hour is fixed no matter how the trigger is configured. Finance asks for the cheapest trigger that still meets the 30-second SLO. (a) Compute the number of micro-batches per hour at T = 10 s and at T = 30 s. (b) Compute the fraction of wall-clock time the cluster spends executing micro-batches (the duty cycle) at each interval, and decide whether both intervals are even achievable. (c) Compute node-hours consumed per wall-clock hour and per day at T = 10 s and at T = 15 s. (d) State the recommended interval and the saving relative to T = 10 s.
Hint: The cost driver is the number of batches, not the data volume, because the per-batch cost is assumed to be fixed.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Batch counts. Batches per hour = 3600 / T. At T = 10 s: 3600 / 10 = 360 batches per hour. At T = 30 s: 3600 / 30 = 120 batches per hour. Ratio = 360 / 120 = 3×, which is the 'cluster-hours roughly triple' figure that the naive cost argument quotes.

Step 2 — Duty cycle. Batch execution seconds per hour = batches × P.

At T = 10 s: 360 × 12 = 4,320 s of work to fit into 3,600 s of wall clock → duty cycle = 4,320 / 3,600 = 1.20, i.e. 120 percent. That is impossible. The scheduler cannot start a batch while one is running, so the real cadence degrades to 12 s: 3600 / 12 = 300 batches per hour at a 100 percent duty cycle. The 10-second interval is therefore nominal, not real.

At T = 30 s: 120 × 12 = 1,440 s → duty cycle = 1,440 / 3,600 = 0.40, i.e. 40 percent. Physically fine, but L = 30 + 12 = 42 s, which violates the SLO.

At T = 15 s (the candidate we actually want): 240 batches × 12 s = 2,880 s → duty cycle = 2,880 / 3,600 = 0.80, i.e. 80 percent. Physically fine (each 12-second batch fits inside a 15-second slot), and L = 15 + 12 = 27 s ≤ 30 s.

Step 3 — Node-hours. Node-hours per wall-clock hour = duty cycle × 4 nodes; per day multiply by 24.

T = 10 s (saturated): 1.00 × 4 = 4.0 node-hours per hour → 4.0 × 24 = 96.0 node-hours per day.

T = 15 s: 0.80 × 4 = 3.2 node-hours per hour → 3.2 × 24 = 76.8 node-hours per day.

T = 30 s (for reference only, it fails the SLO): 0.40 × 4 = 1.6 node-hours per hour → 38.4 node-hours per day.

Step 4 — Verdict. Convert node-hours to money by multiplying by the per-node price; at any fixed price the ordering is unchanged. T = 15 s saves 96.0 − 76.8 = 19.2 node-hours per day, a 19.2 / 96.0 = 20 percent reduction, while still meeting the SLO with 3 seconds of slack. T = 30 s would be 2.5× cheaper than T = 10 s, but 42 s of latency is 12 seconds over the limit, so it is not on the table. Recommendation: T = 15 s — the largest interval in the set that satisfies T ≤ 18 s, and therefore the cheapest compliant configuration.

Analysis — Why the method works. When the per-batch cost is a fixed overhead (planning, task launch, file discovery, commit), the hourly compute is batches × P, and batches = 3600 / T. Hourly compute is therefore proportional to 1/T: halving the interval doubles the compute for exactly the same data. The saving from a longer interval is not 'less work per record'; it is 'the same work, paid for less often'.

Where the model breaks. The assumption P = constant regardless of volume is a small-volume approximation. In reality P = P_f + P_v with P_v growing with the batch's data volume, so a longer interval means bigger batches and a larger P_v. Once P_v is comparable to P_f, the cost curve flattens and the 'longer interval is always cheaper' conclusion no longer holds automatically. Two practical consequences: keep batch sizes consistent so the prediction stays valid — limiting the input rate is the standard mechanism for maintaining consistent batch sizes and preventing processing delays [source 5] — and re-measure P after any volume change rather than trusting the original benchmark.

Raise the batch rate? The increased number of commits at T = 10 s is not a correctness risk. Delta Lake's transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing even with other streams or batch queries running concurrently against the same table [source 1], so a replayed micro-batch becomes a no-op rather than a duplicate. It is a performance risk, however: 300–360 commits per hour produce many small files, which pushes read amplification onto every downstream consumer of the table.

Common mistakes. (1) Comparing cost by data volume instead of by batch count, which hides the fixed-cost multiplier. (2) Assuming a 10-second trigger really fires every 10 seconds when P = 12 s — the duty cycle is already over 100 percent, so the extra spend buys nothing. (3) Optimising cost at the expense of the SLO: T = 30 s is the cheapest row in the table and the only one that is disqualified.
Problem 3

An engineering team inherits the 30-second freshness pipeline. To cut cost they replace the streaming trigger with .trigger(availableNow=True) and schedule the notebook every 5 minutes from the Databricks job scheduler. They argue: 'availableNow processes all available data as fast as possible, so it is at least as fast as the 10-second trigger.' The cluster is configured with auto-stop, so a run that follows a shutdown also pays about 3 minutes of cluster start-up. Micro-batch time is still P = 12 s. (a) Compute the average and worst-case end-to-end latency of this design. (b) State whether the 30-second SLO is met. (c) State the general rule that decides when availableNow is the correct trigger.
Hint: The cadence that matters for freshness is the schedule, not the trigger name; availableNow runs once per job run and then terminates.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Establish what availableNow does. availableNow is a one-shot trigger: within a single job run the engine processes all data currently available at the source as one or more chained micro-batches, then terminates the query. The cadence at which new data is picked up is therefore the cadence of the scheduled job, not the micro-batch time.

Step 2 — Average latency. A record arrives at a uniformly random point in the 300-second schedule, so it waits on average 300 / 2 = 150 s. Add one batch of processing: L_avg = 150 + 12 = 162 s.

Step 3 — Worst-case latency. A record arriving just after a run starts waits nearly the full schedule: L_worst = 300 + 12 = 312 s, i.e. about 5.2 minutes. The 99th percentile is essentially the same number, 312 s, because the wait is dominated by a deterministic schedule rather than by jitter.

Step 4 — Include cold start. With auto-stop, a run that follows a shutdown adds roughly 180 s before the first byte is read: L_worst = 300 + 180 + 12 = 492 s, over 8 minutes.

Step 5 — Compare with the SLO. 312 s against a 30-second SLO is 10.4× over budget; even the average, 162 s, is 5.4× over. The design fails (b) decisively, and it fails on average, not only in the tail.

The intuition the team used is wrong in one specific way: 'as fast as possible' describes how quickly one backlog is drained inside a run, not how quickly new events are noticed. Freshness is governed by the run cadence; availableNow simply has no mechanism for noticing data that arrives between runs.

Analysis — The general rule. Freshness is bounded below by the arrival cadence of the consumer. For a long-running stream the cadence is the trigger interval T; for a scheduled availableNow job the cadence is the job schedule S (plus any cluster start-up). availableNow is the right trigger exactly when the required freshness is coarser than the schedule — the classic case is a nightly or hourly silver/gold materialisation where running a cluster continuously is wasteful. It is the wrong trigger whenever the SLO is finer than the schedule, as here.

Common mistakes. (1) Confusing 'drains the entire backlog in one trigger' with 'keeps up with the stream'; the phrase availableNow describes backlog semantics, not cadence. (2) Forgetting the cluster-start term, which is often larger than the processing term once auto-stop is enabled. (3) Believing availableNow is a form of continuous processing; it is a bounded batch execution. (4) Assuming that switching to availableNow breaks recovery. It does not: the checkpoint still records offsets and state, and the engine's state store is what enables fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics across restarts [source 5]. When the sink is Delta, the transaction log keeps the write idempotent under replay [source 1].

Where the cost argument should have gone instead. If the cluster is genuinely over-provisioned, the correct lever is cluster size or autoscaling policy with the streaming trigger retained, not the trigger type. The interval and the SLO fix each other (see p1); the number of workers controls how much slack you can afford. Also note that cost is not reduced for free: chained hops multiply the per-hop delay, so a design that satisfies 30 s end to end with two hops has roughly 15 s per hop, and any hop converted to a scheduled availableNow job blows the whole budget.
Problem 4

Continue with the 30-second SLO and the four-node cluster (one driver plus three workers). Model the micro-batch time as P = P_f + P_v, where P_f is fixed overhead that does not parallelise (planning, task launch, the Delta commit) and P_v is the data-dependent part that scales with volume and splits across workers. At the original volume on 3 workers, P = 12 s, made up of P_f = 8 s and P_v = 4 s. Ingest volume then grows 4×. (a) Predict P at 4× volume on 3 workers and compute the worst-case latency at T = 10 s. (b) The team doubles the worker count from 3 to 6, halving the parallel part. Compute the new P and the new worst-case latency at T = 10 s. (c) Derive the condition under which any trigger interval can satisfy a latency SLO of S, and apply it to part (b). (d) Recommend a concrete fix.
Hint: Two regimes: if T ≥ P the latency is T + P; if T < P the batches run back-to-back and the latency is governed by 2P.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Part (a). At 4× volume the variable term scales by 4: P_v = 4 × 4 = 16 s, so P = 8 + 16 = 24 s. Since T = 10 s < P = 24 s, the pipeline is saturated: the next batch starts when the previous one finishes, giving a cadence of about 24 s and a worst-case latency of roughly 2P = 48 s. The naive additive estimate, 10 + 24 = 34 s, is already 4 s over the SLO, so the conclusion is the same either way — but the real number is 18 s worse.

Step 2 — Part (b). Doubling the workers from 3 to 6 halves only the parallel part: P_v = 16 / 2 = 8 s, so P = 8 + 8 = 16 s. Still P = 16 s > T = 10 s, so the pipeline is still saturated: cadence ≈ 16 s, worst-case latency ≈ 2 × 16 = 32 s > 30 s. Doubling the workers improved the latency from 48 s to 32 s, a reduction of 16 / 48 = 33 percent, not the 50 percent one might expect, because the 8-second fixed term does not shrink with parallelism.

Step 3 — Part (c). Derive the feasibility condition. Let S be the SLO and consider the two regimes.

Regime 1, clean (T ≥ P): L_worst = T + P ≤ S, so T ≤ S − P.

Regime 2, saturated (T < P): the trigger interval is not honoured; batches run back-to-back and L_worst ≈ 2P ≤ S, so P ≤ S / 2.

The saturated bound contains no T at all: once P > S/2, no choice of interval helps. A trigger interval satisfying the SLO in the clean regime requires both T ≥ P and T ≤ S − P, so a feasible window exists if and only if P ≤ S/2, and the window is then T ∈ [P, S − P]. For S = 30 s the condition is P ≤ 15 s.

Applied to (b): P = 16 s > 15 s, so the window is empty — T ∈ [16, 14] is contradictory. No trigger interval can meet the 30-second SLO in this configuration. Verify at the edges: T = 16 s gives L = 16 + 16 = 32 s; T = 20 s gives L = 20 + 16 = 36 s, and increasing T only makes it worse. This is the key insight of the problem: once P approaches the SLO, the trigger interval ceases to be the design lever.

For reference, the original configuration (P = 12 s) has the feasible window T ∈ [12, 18] s, and T = 15 s sits in the middle of it, which is exactly why 15 s is more robust than either 10 s or 18 s.

Step 4 — Part (d). Two levers, in order of leverage.

Lever 1, attack P_f = 8 s, because it is the term that parallelism cannot buy back. Concretely: switch file discovery from directory listing to Auto Loader file-notification mode; compact small files upstream so a batch reads fewer, larger files; reduce the shuffle-partition count so task launch overhead falls; enable optimised writes to reduce the number of Delta commits. Any 2-second reduction of P_f translates directly into a 2-second reduction of the SLO budget consumed.

Lever 2, add parallelism only after P_f is addressed. With P = 8 + 16/(w/3) for w workers: w = 9 gives P = 8 + 5.33 = 13.3 s, opening the window T ∈ [13.3, 16.7] s, where T = 15 s gives L = 28.3 s; w = 12 gives P = 12 s and T = 15 s gives L = 27 s. Note the cost: 12 workers at an 80 percent duty cycle is 9.6 node-hours per wall-clock hour, far above the original 3.2 — an example of buying latency with money rather than with cleverness.

Lever 3, when the SLO genuinely cannot be met at full rate, cap the input rate so batch sizes stay consistent and processing delays do not compound [source 5]. Re-negotiating the SLO or moving the hot path to a lower-latency Delta-based streaming table [source 4] are the remaining options.

Analysis — Why the derivation matters. The condition P ≤ S/2 is the single most useful inequality in micro-batch sizing, because it separates two very different problems. If P ≤ S/2, tuning the interval is sufficient and cheap: pick T inside [P, S − P], ideally near the midpoint so that a ±10 percent drift in P does not push you out of the window. If P > S/2, interval tuning is provably futile, and effort must move to reducing P itself. Students who skip this check produce designs that look correct on a cost spreadsheet and cannot possibly meet the SLO.

Why the 33 percent instead of 50 percent. This is a direct application of Amdahl's law. The speedup of adding workers is capped by the non-parallel fraction. With P_f = 8 s and P_v = 8 s at 6 workers, half the time is serial overhead, so doubling workers again from 6 to 12 merely takes P from 16 s to 12 s — a further 25 percent for twice the hardware. Diminishing returns arrive quickly, and they arrive in exactly the term that decides feasibility.

Edge cases and common mistakes. (1) Applying the additive model T + P when T < P. In that regime the pipeline is saturated, the interval is nominal, and the true bound is 2P — a 10-to-20 second error in a 30-second SLO. (2) Assuming the fixed overhead shrinks with autoscaling. It does not; auto-scaling adds workers to the parallel term and also adds a start-up delay that can leak into P. (3) Assuming autoscaling reacts instantly. A scale-up triggered by a growing backlog takes tens of seconds to add executors, during which P is unchanged and latency is already drifting. (4) Treating P as a constant measured once during a quiet period. P is the variable that decides feasibility, so it should be monitored continuously — for example by tracking batch duration and trigger backlog in the streaming query's metrics. (5) Forgetting that the latency budget is shared across chained hops: a pipeline that feeds a downstream aggregation gives each hop only a fraction of the end-to-end SLO [source 2]. A restart or a failover is also not free — the checkpoint restores offsets and state, which is what preserves exactly-once semantics into the Delta sink [source 5][source 1], but the restore itself consumes part of the budget.

actions.text: All right, now let's put everything we just discussed about triggers and cost into practice with a fully worked problem. This one asks you to size a trigger interval against a latency SLO — freshness for streaming ingestion.

Here's the setup: a streaming ingestion job runs on a four-node Databricks cluster, and every event must land in a Delta table within 30 seconds of arriving. Each micro-batch costs roughly 12 seconds of wall-clock time, regardless of how much data it carries. Your task is to pick a trigger interval and justify it.

Keep the hint in mind: end-to-end latency is the time an event waits before it is durably written. That waiting time is dominated by the trigger interval plus the batch processing time. So we cannot spend the whole 30-second budget on waiting.

Now walk the worked solution. Step 0 — name the model. The worst-case latency equals the trigger interval plus the batch processing time. Step 1 — compute the latency budget: 30 seconds minus 12 seconds of processing leaves us a maximum interval of 18 seconds.

Finally, the analysis: why does the method work? A micro-batch engine only emits data when a batch fires, so the interval is bounded directly by the SLO. Stepping down to a 10-second interval gives a worst case of about 22 seconds — comfortably inside the budget — while batches per hour jump from 120 to 360, roughly tripling cluster-hours for the same data volume. That tension between latency and cost is exactly what the exam wants you to articulate.

scenes.title: Check: Triggers and Cost

questions.question: A data engineering team must ingest append-only clickstream events into a Delta table with a stated end-to-end latency SLO of under 30 seconds, running 24/7 on an always-on cluster. Which trigger choice best satisfies this latency SLO while remaining a supported, production-grade option?

options.label: Trigger.AvailableNow, because it drains the full backlog as fast as possible and then stops the query
Trigger.ProcessingTime("5 seconds"), because the observed latency is roughly the trigger interval plus batch processing time
Trigger.Continuous("1 second"), because it delivers the lowest possible latency
No trigger at all, because Structured Streaming runs each micro-batch only when a new file lands

questions.analysis: Trigger.ProcessingTime("5 seconds") runs a micro-batch on a fixed 5-second cadence, and the observed end-to-end latency is roughly the trigger interval plus the batch processing time, so a 5-second interval plus a few seconds of processing comfortably stays under a 30-second SLO. Option A (Trigger.AvailableNow) processes all available backlog and then stops the query, which is the cost-efficient choice for scheduled incremental loads but is not suitable for a continuously running low-latency pipeline. Option C (Trigger.Continuous) gives experimental low-latency processing with weaker delivery guarantees than the other modes, so it is not the production-grade answer. Option D is simply false: without a trigger, a query using the default micro-batch trigger still runs on its own cadence rather than waiting for a new file to appear. Delta-backed streaming sinks retain exactly-once guarantees regardless of the interval you choose [source 1].

questions.question: A Lakeflow pipeline ingests Kafka events into an append-only streaming table and must deliver results with a latency SLO of about 15 seconds. The pipeline writes to a Delta Lake sink. Which two statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Using Trigger.ProcessingTime("10 seconds") keeps observed latency near interval plus processing time, so it satisfies the SLO while avoiding the cost of a 1-second interval
Using Trigger.AvailableNow is appropriate here because the pipeline must run continuously around the clock
Switching the sink from a Delta table to a plain Parquet directory would preserve exactly-once processing after a restart
The Delta Lake transaction log makes a replayed micro-batch a no-op, so the sink guarantees exactly-once processing even with concurrent streams or batch queries

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: for a 15-second SLO, a 10-second ProcessingTime interval is a reasonable trade-off because observed latency is roughly interval plus batch processing time, and a shorter interval would multiply cluster cost. Option D is correct: Delta Lake's transaction log provides exactly-once processing, and this guarantee holds even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently against the table [source 5] [source 1]. Option B is wrong because AvailableNow drains the available backlog and then stops the query, which is the opposite of a continuously running pipeline; it is the cost-efficient choice for scheduled incremental loads. Option C is wrong because plain Parquet writes are not idempotent: a replayed micro-batch would append duplicate files, whereas the Delta transaction log turns the replay into a no-op. Note that switching the sink does not change trigger semantics; the guarantee comes from the sink, not the trigger.

questions.question: A pipeline reads Kafka events and must run as a scheduled incremental load every hour, with no requirement for continuous sub-minute latency. Explain which trigger you would choose and why, and then explain which trigger mode has weaker delivery guarantees than the others — and why that matters when the sink is a Delta table.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Correctly chooses Trigger.AvailableNow and explains that it processes all available backlog once and then stops the query — 35%. (2) Justifies the choice in cost terms (the query does not hold an always-on cluster between runs, so the cost profile matches a scheduled incremental load) and contrasts it with Trigger.ProcessingTime, noting that ProcessingTime runs on a fixed interval and yields latency roughly equal to interval plus batch processing time — 30%. (3) Identifies Trigger.Continuous as the mode with weaker delivery guarantees (experimental, at-least-once style behavior) and explains that exactly-once depends on an idempotent sink, specifically the Delta Lake transaction log making a replayed micro-batch a no-op — 25%. (4) Clarity and use of Databricks and exam vocabulary (checkpoint, watermark, micro-batch, streaming table) — 10%.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: Choose Trigger.AvailableNow for a scheduled incremental load. It processes all available backlog and then stops the query, so the cluster is not held running between runs; that is why it is described as the cost-efficient choice for scheduled incremental loads. Contrast this with Trigger.ProcessingTime, which runs a micro-batch on a fixed interval and whose observed latency is roughly interval plus batch processing time. For latency SLOs in the low seconds it is appropriate, but for an hourly batch it wastes cluster time. The trigger mode with weaker delivery guarantees is Trigger.Continuous: it gives experimental low-latency processing but does not carry the same delivery guarantees as the other modes. This matters because the sink's behavior determines what you observe after a failure. A Delta Lake sink is idempotent: the Delta Lake transaction log guarantees exactly-once processing, making a replayed micro-batch a no-op even when other streams or batch queries run concurrently [source 1] [source 5]. A non-idempotent sink such as a plain Parquet directory does not get that protection, so a replay appends duplicates. Streaming tables in Lakeflow are Delta tables with support for streaming and incremental processing, designed for append-only ingestion and low-latency streaming, which is why the Delta sink is the natural target for this pipeline [source 3] [source 4].

actions.text: Let's check how well that trade-off settled in. This one pulls together trigger selection, batch counts, and delivery guarantees — three ideas we just walked through. Take your time and work through each question on your own, and I'll meet you after you submit to unpack anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Trade-offs: Latency vs Cluster Cost for a Streaming Ingest

elements.content: Decision — A platform team runs a Kafka-to-Delta ingestion pipeline for clickstream events, and the business has published a 15-minute freshness SLO on the serving table. The cluster runs every hour of the day, but the incoming event volume of about 40 GB/day is unevenly distributed, with a heavy burst between 18:00 and 21:00 and long idle stretches overnight. The team must pick a trigger strategy that keeps the end-to-end latency under the SLO while staying inside a fixed monthly cluster budget and preserving exactly-once delivery into Delta; these goals pull in opposite directions, because tighter triggers buy lower latency at the cost of more micro-batches and more cluster-hours, while looser triggers save money but risk breaching the SLO. The decision is hard because the numbers must be checked against the budget, not against intuition about 'real-time always being better', and because the chosen trigger must still coexist with the checkpointing and idempotent-sink machinery already configured in this unit.

Constraints — End-to-end freshness SLO of 15 minutes from event arrival to visibility in the Delta table  •  Event volume of roughly 40 GB/day, with a large peak burst in the evening and long idle windows overnight  •  A fixed monthly cluster budget that must not be exceeded, so cluster-hours spent polling an idle source are effectively wasted money  •  Exactly-once delivery into Delta, which requires the checkpointed query and the Delta Lake transaction log to be preserved  •  The trigger must work with the existing checkpointLocation configuration so the query remains restartable

processingTime('5 seconds')
+ Near-real-time end-to-end latency, since each micro-batch fires only 5 seconds after the previous one completes; + Strongest fit for genuinely interactive or second-level freshness requirements; + Keeps the pipeline simple because the same continuously running query handles peak and off-peak identically
− Generates the highest batch count of the three options: a 24-hour day produces up to 17,280 trigger firings, each with fixed per-batch overhead; − Burns cluster-hours during idle overnight windows when no new events have arrived, wasting budget on empty batches; − Requires the most operational tuning because small batches amplify scheduling jitter and file-count growth in Delta
Best for: Workloads whose SLO is measured in seconds and whose budget can absorb continuous cluster hours regardless of source activity

processingTime('1 minute')
+ Sub-minute latency with roughly 1,440 batches per day, a 12x reduction in batch count versus the 5-second trigger; + A reasonable engineering default when the SLO is expressed in minutes rather than seconds, giving ample margin under a 15-minute SLO; + Still runs continuously, so there is no risk of a missed schedule window causing events to sit unprocessed
− Still pays for cluster-hours at night, so it does not decouple cost from source idleness; − Latency is bounded by the interval, and a slow batch can stack behind the next scheduled firing under peak load; − Does not exploit the fact that the stated SLO of 15 minutes leaves far more headroom than one minute of latency
Best for: Teams that want near-continuous freshness and are willing to trade budget for a simpler mental model than a scheduled job

availableNow scheduled every 15 minutes by a job
+ Lowest cluster cost of the three, because the query drains the available backlog and then stops instead of polling an idle source around the clock; + Produces perfectly bounded batches whose size tracks actual arrivals, which keeps file sizes and state-store growth predictable; + Latency is deterministically pinned to the schedule interval, so the 15-minute SLO is met by construction rather than by luck; + Preserves exactly-once through the checkpointed Delta sink, since each scheduled run resumes from the checkpoint and the Delta Lake transaction log makes replayed micro-batches no-ops
− Guaranteed worst-case latency of the full 15-minute interval, leaving no slack if a run overruns or a schedule tick is missed; − A tight operational coupling to the scheduler: if the job does not fire, no data is processed until the next tick; − Less suitable if the business later demands second-level responsiveness, since the floor is the schedule period
Best for: Append-only incremental ingestion with a minutes-level SLO and a hard budget constraint, where the scheduler can be trusted

Recommendation: availableNow scheduled every 15 minutes by a job — The binding constraints are the fixed monthly cluster budget and the 15-minute freshness SLO, and Option C is the only candidate that satisfies both simultaneously: availableNow processes all available backlog and then stops the query, so cost tracks actual arrivals instead of wall-clock hours, which matters because the 40 GB/day workload is idle for long overnight stretches. Because the SLO is 15 minutes rather than seconds, the pinned interval is not a defect but exactly the tolerance the business specified, and the schedule still leaves headroom to shorten the interval later if freshness expectations tighten. The 5-second and 1-minute triggers both spend budget on empty batches at night to buy latency the SLO does not require; they are only justified when the SLO is stated in seconds. Exactly-once is not sacrificed by the switch: each scheduled run resumes from the existing checkpoint, and the Delta Lake transaction log makes a replayed micro-batch a no-op rather than a duplicate [source 1]. A streaming table in Lakeflow pipelines is a Delta table designed for append-only ingestion and incremental processing [source 3], which is precisely the shape of this sink, and Spark Structured Streaming underneath provides the state store that enables fault tolerance and exactly-once delivery semantics [source 5]. The recommended design therefore keeps the checkpointed query with exactly-once into Delta [source 1], sizes batches to real arrivals, and spends money only when there is data to move.

actions.text: Now let's apply everything we just covered about triggers to a real decision. Here's the scenario: a platform team runs a Kafka-to-Delta ingest pipeline. Notice they have a concrete situation with explicit constraints — not a vague 'make it fast' request.

The constraints are what drive the decision. An end-to-end freshness SLO of 15 minutes, an event volume of 40 gigabytes a day, a fixed monthly cluster budget, and a hard requirement for exactly-once writes into Delta. Hold onto those four numbers — every option has to be judged against them.

Option A is processingTime of five seconds. This gives you near-real-time latency, but look at the trade-off: the highest batch count and cluster-hours, plus the most operational tuning. You're paying for freshness you weren't asked for.

Option B is processingTime of one minute. Sub-minute latency with far fewer batches — this is a very reasonable default when your SLO is measured in minutes, not seconds. But our SLO is fifteen minutes, so we're still overshooting.

Option C is availableNow, scheduled every fifteen minutes by a job. This is the lowest cost, gives you perfectly bounded batches, and pins latency exactly to the schedule interval. The cluster only runs when there's work to do.

So the recommendation: given the fifteen-minute SLO and the budget, Option C is justified. availableNow decouples cost from idleness, keeps exactly-once through the checkpointed Delta sink, and leaves headroom to shorten the interval later if the SLO tightens. That's the exam-ready reasoning — match the trigger to the constraint, not to the fastest possible setting.

scenes.title: Unit Glossary: Streaming Data Engineering

elements.content: Structured Streaming — A Databricks/Spark engine that treats a live data stream as an unbounded table and incrementally executes a standard DataFrame query over newly arrived rows, rather than requiring users to write imperative per-record stream processing code.

Unbounded table — The logical abstraction in which a streaming source is modeled as a table that grows indefinitely as new data arrives; queries written against it are logically evaluated over the whole table but physically executed incrementally over only the newly appended rows.

Micro-batch — The unit of execution in Structured Streaming in which the engine repeatedly reads the newly available source data, executes the query plan on that slice, and writes results to the sink; each micro-batch is committed as an atomic unit so it can be tracked and replayed.

Trigger — The configuration that determines when each micro-batch is launched; common variants are processingTime(interval) for a fixed wall-clock interval, availableNow for processing all current backlog and then stopping, and the experimental Trigger.Continuous for low-latency processing with weaker exactly-once handling.

Output mode (append, update, complete) — The setting that controls which result rows are written to the sink on each micro-batch: append emits only newly finalized rows and is required for operations that cannot retract output, update emits only rows whose aggregate values changed, and complete rewrites the entire result table each batch and is only valid for aggregations.

Event time — The timestamp embedded in the data record indicating when the event actually occurred at the source; it is the time basis windowed aggregations and watermarks use, and it is distinct from the wall-clock time at which the record is processed.

Processing time — The wall-clock time on the cluster at which a record is processed by the streaming engine; it is simpler to use because it needs no watermark, but it produces results that depend on when data arrived rather than when events occurred, so it is unsuitable when late data matters.

Watermark — A moving threshold defined as event time minus a specified lateness bound, declared with withWatermark(column, delay); the engine assumes no events older than the watermark will still arrive, allowing it to finalize windowed results and safely evict state, so a missing or misplaced watermark causes unbounded state growth.

Late-arriving data — Records whose event time falls behind the current watermark and therefore arrive after the engine has finalized the relevant window; they are dropped from windowed aggregations by default unless the watermark delay is widened to accommodate them.

Tumbling window — A fixed-size, non-overlapping event-time window, expressed as window(col, duration); every event belongs to exactly one window, so the total emitted row count for N windows equals N, making it the simplest window to reason about for periodic rollups.

Sliding window — A fixed-size event-time window that advances by a slide smaller than the window duration, expressed as window(col, duration, slide); because windows overlap, a single event can appear in multiple windows, and the number of windows covering a time span equals (span − duration) / slide + 1.

Session window — An event-time window that groups events separated by less than a gap of inactivity and closes when no event arrives for the configured gap duration; unlike tumbling and sliding windows it has no fixed size, so each session's boundaries are data-dependent.

Checkpoint — A durable directory of metadata and state that lets a streaming query resume after a restart without reprocessing committed work; it records completed micro-batches, consumed source offsets, and operator state, and it is configured with .option("checkpointLocation", path) on every streaming write.

checkpointLocation — The write option, set as .option("checkpointLocation", path), that specifies the durable path where a streaming query stores its checkpoint artifacts; because it must be unique per query, reusing the same path across two queries corrupts recovery and causes failures.

Offset log — The checkpoint subdirectory (offsets/) that records the exact source offsets each micro-batch consumed; on restart the engine reads it to resume from the last committed offset rather than rereading the entire source.

Commit log — The checkpoint subdirectory (commits/) that records which micro-batches completed successfully; on restart the engine consults it to skip micro-batches already committed and avoid re-emitting them.

State store — The checkpoint component that persists the accumulated state of stateful operators—such as aggregation accumulators and stream-stream join buffers—so those operators can be restored exactly after a restart instead of recomputing from the beginning of the stream.

Write-Ahead Log — A durability mechanism in which the offsets and intended batch metadata are written to stable storage before the micro-batch is committed to the sink; if the cluster fails mid-batch, the logged information makes the batch replayable, which is what gives Structured Streaming at-least-once behavior by default.

Replayable source — A source whose offsets can be deliberately re-read after a failure, so the engine can re-consume the same records during recovery; replayability is a precondition for exactly-once, since without it the engine cannot know what it missed.

Idempotent sink — A sink for which writing the same replayed data again produces the same final result rather than a duplicate; idempotence is the second precondition (alongside replayability) for exactly-once, and Delta Lake acquires it through its transaction log.

At-most-once — The weakest delivery guarantee, in which each record is processed zero or one time; it occurs when no checkpoint is configured, so after a mid-batch failure some records that were read are never written and are lost.

At-least-once — The default guarantee of Structured Streaming, in which a record is processed one or more times; the Write-Ahead Log ensures no record is lost on restart, but a replayed micro-batch can be re-emitted, so duplicates are possible unless the sink is idempotent.

Exactly-once — The guarantee that every record is reflected exactly once in the final sink result; it requires both a replayable source and an idempotent sink, and it is achieved in Databricks when the sink is a Delta table whose transaction log turns a replayed micro-batch into a no-op.

Delta Lake transaction log — The ordered record (_delta_log) of every commit applied to a Delta table; because a replayed micro-batch carries the same transaction identity, the log detects it as already applied and suppresses the duplicate write, which is what makes Delta Lake an idempotent sink.
Streaming table — A table declared as a streaming source in a pipeline, read with spark.readStream; it exposes only newly appended data on each micro-batch rather than the full table contents.

Stream-static join — A join between a streaming DataFrame and a static (batch) DataFrame; the static side is read once and broadcast against each micro-batch, so it needs no watermark and does not grow state.

Stream-stream join — A join between two streaming DataFrames; because matching rows can arrive out of order, both inputs must be watermarked so the engine knows how long to retain buffered rows, and an incorrect or missing watermark causes ever-growing state.

Delta table as source and as sink — A Delta table can serve in the same pipeline as the streaming input (spark.readStream.format("delta")) and as the streaming output (writeStream.format("delta")), which makes it both a replayable source and an idempotent sink and therefore the foundation of reliable exactly-once pipelines.

actions.text: Before we close out the streaming unit, let's consolidate the terminology you'll be tested on. This glossary page pulls together every key streaming term with exam-accurate definitions. We'll walk through it in five groups, and I'll spotlight the ones that show up most often on the exam.

First, the core execution terms. Structured Streaming is the Databricks and Spark engine that treats a live data stream as an unbounded table — a table with no end. Under the hood, that table is processed in micro-batches, which is simply the unit of execution: each trigger fires one micro-batch.

The trigger is the configuration that decides when each micro-batch runs, and the output mode — append, update, or complete — decides which rows get written to the sink on every batch. Remember, exactly these five terms form the spine of the execution model.

Next, the time terms. Event time is the timestamp embedded in the data itself — when the event actually happened. Processing time is the wall-clock time on the cluster — when we happen to process it. Confusing these two is the single most common streaming mistake, so keep them firmly separated.

A watermark is a moving threshold expressed in event time — it tells the engine how long to wait for late-arriving data, which are records whose event time falls behind that threshold. And you have three window types: tumbling is fixed-size and non-overlapping, sliding is fixed-size and overlapping, and session groups events by gaps of inactivity.

Now reliability. A checkpoint is a durable directory of metadata and state that lets a query restart exactly where it left off. Inside it, checkpointLocation is the write option you set, the offset log records which offsets were consumed, the commit log records which batches were committed, and the state store persists aggregation state across batches.

For recovery you also need a replayable source — one whose offsets can be re-read — and an idempotent sink, where writing the same record twice produces the same result. Together with the Write-Ahead Log, these are what make fault tolerance possible.

That brings us to the guarantee terms. At-most-once is the weakest — records may be lost. At-least-once is the default of Structured Streaming — records may be duplicated. Exactly-once guarantees every record is processed once and only once, and into Delta tables it's achieved through the combination of a replayable source, idempotent writes, and the Delta Lake transaction log.

Finally the pipeline terms. A streaming table is declared as a streaming dataset, stream-static joins combine a stream with a static table, and stream-stream joins combine two streams — which require watermarks on both sides. And a Delta table can serve as both source and sink in the same pipeline, which is exactly what makes exactly-once into Delta achievable.
That's the full glossary — execution, time, reliability, guarantees, and pipeline terms. These definitions are the exact vocabulary the exam uses, so review them until they're automatic.

scenes.title: Lesson Check: Checkpoints, Triggers, and Guarantees

questions.question: A Structured Streaming ingestion job writes to a Delta Lake table. After each cluster restart, the target table contains duplicate rows for the events that were in flight at the moment of shutdown. The query uses processingTime('5 seconds') with a valid, durable checkpointLocation, and the sink is a Delta table. Which change best explains AND fixes the duplication?

options.label: The checkpointLocation must be deleted on every restart so the query rereads from the latest offsets a clean slate.
The trigger must be switched to Trigger.Continuous, because only continuous mode reuses the commit log to skip completed micro-batches.
The checkpoint was placed on an ephemeral path that is wiped by the cluster lifecycle, so the commits directory is lost and replayed micro-batches are rewritten to the Delta table as new data.
Delta Lake cannot act as an idempotent sink, so duplicates are expected; the only fix is to add a post-write deduplication batch job keyed on event_id.

questions.analysis: Delta Lake's transaction log makes a replayed micro-batch a no-op rather than a duplicate, and the checkpoint's commits directory is what tells the engine which micro-batches already completed [source 1]. If the checkpoint path is ephemeral (for example, under a cluster-scoped mount that is destroyed with the cluster), the commits and offsets records vanish on restart, so the engine replays batches from the original source offsets and writes them again. Option A is the classic student misconception inverted: deleting the checkpoint is exactly what causes re-reads; a durable checkpoint is the recovery anchor. Option B is wrong because Trigger.Continuous gives experimental low-latency processing with weaker exactly-once handling, not stronger. Option D is wrong because Delta Lake IS the idempotent sink [source 5]. The correct diagnosis is that the checkpoint was not actually durable across the restart.

questions.question: A team must land a Kafka events stream into a Delta table with a 15-minute freshness SLO, a fixed monthly cluster budget, and a hard requirement for exactly-once delivery. They currently use processingTime('5 seconds') and the job is over budget. Which configuration choices satisfy BOTH the freshness constraint AND the exactly-once requirement? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Switch to availableNow triggered on a 10-minute schedule, processing the full backlog each run and then stopping.
Keep processingTime('5 seconds') but disable the checkpoint to reduce I/O cost.
Switch to processingTime('5 minutes') with a durable checkpointLocation and a Delta Lake sink.
Switch to Trigger.Continuous for sub-second latency, which reduces cluster-hours by batching less often.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: availableNow processes all available backlog and then stops the query, which is the cost-efficient choice for scheduled incremental loads while still meeting a 15-minute SLO when run every 10 minutes. Option C is correct: a 5-minute processingTime interval yields worst-case latency of roughly trigger interval plus batch processing time, comfortably inside the 15-minute budget, and a Delta Lake sink with a durable checkpoint provides exactly-once [source 1][source 5]. Option B is wrong on two counts: disabling the checkpoint destroys recovery (no commits/offsets artifacts) and does not preserve exactly-once. Option D is wrong because Trigger.Continuous does not batch less often, it processes continuously, and it has weaker exactly-once handling—an exam caveat to memorise.

questions.question: A pipeline uses availableNow with a durable checkpointLocation writing to a Delta Lake streaming table. Explain, in three or four sentences, why availableNow can be simultaneously CHEAPER and provide STRONGER exactly-once behaviour than a short processingTime trigger such as processingTime('5 seconds'). Your answer should reference the trigger lifecycle and the checkpoint's role in replay.
questions.commentPrompt:
Rubric (total 20 points):
(1) Trigger lifecycle (6 pts): Explains that availableNow processes all available backlog in one or more micro-batches and then STOPS the query, so the cluster is only running while work exists, unlike processingTime which keeps the cluster live between intervals even when idle.
(2) Cost argument (5 pts): Ties the stopping behaviour to fewer cluster-hours and lower operational tuning overhead versus a short fixed-interval trigger.
(3) Checkpoint / exactly-once link (6 pts): States that the durable checkpointLocation preserves the commits directory (which micro-batches completed) and offsets directory (which source offsets were consumed), so on the next availableNow run the engine resumes from where it stopped rather than reprocessing; combined with the Delta Lake transaction log the replayed micro-batch becomes a no-op, giving exactly-once.
(4) Clarity and terminology (3 pts): Uses Databricks/Structured Streaming vocabulary correctly (micro-batch, commits, offsets, checkpointLocation, Delta Lake transaction log, idempotent sink). Deduct for vague phrasing such as 'it just works'.
questions.analysis: A strong answer notes that availableNow runs the query only long enough to drain the current backlog and then stops, so the cluster is not paid for idle waiting between intervals the way a processingTime('5 seconds') job would be. That same stopping behaviour is what strengthens exactly-once: each run resumes from the durable checkpoint, whose commits directory records completed micro-batches and whose offsets directory records the consumed source offsets. Because the sink is a Delta Lake table, the transaction log makes any replayed micro-batch a no-op rather than a duplicate, so the combination of availableNow plus a durable checkpoint plus a Delta sink satisfies the exactly-once guarantee without the continuous overhead of a short fixed-interval trigger [source 1][source 5].

actions.text: With that glossary fresh, let's see how the checkpointing, trigger, and delivery-guarantee ideas actually hold up. There are three items here, and one of them asks you to put the reasoning into your own words, so take a moment on that one.
Work through each on your own and commit to your answer before submitting — I'll join you right after to unpack anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: What Orchestration Is and Where Lakeflow Jobs Fits

elements.content: What Orchestration Is and Where Lakeflow Jobs Fits
The production discipline of task dependency management and scheduling — and Databricks' native orchestration layer

• Orchestration is the production discipline of managing dependencies between workflow tasks and scheduling them so data solutions can reach production [source 6]. Preconditions: you have multiple tasks with an execution order; orchestration adds scheduling, sequencing, and monitoring. Edge case: a single self-contained notebook run needs no orchestration.

• Lakeflow Jobs is Databricks' native orchestration engine for scheduling and monitoring data pipelines and ML workflows, formerly Databricks Workflows (renamed in late 2024) [source 1]. It schedules and automates multi-step pipelines by defining tasks, dependencies, triggers, and failure handling [source 2].

• Orchestration includes compute resource allocation and workflow monitoring on top of code that would otherwise be run by hand [source 6].
Worked Example: Ingest → Transform → Serve → Train (4 tasks, shared compute)

Each step is its own task on shared compute; orchestration adds observability, retries, alerting, and repair [source 2]. Exam angle: what a job orchestrates and when a workflow needs a job vs. an ad hoc notebook run [source 1].

actions.text: Great work on that checkpoint, everyone. Let's turn to a brand-new capability area: orchestration. At its core, orchestration is the production discipline of managing dependencies between tasks and scheduling them so that your data solutions actually reach production reliably. This is one of the exam objectives, so let's define it carefully.

Read that definition with me: orchestration is the production discipline of managing task dependencies and scheduling them so that data solutions reach production. Dependency management answers 'what must run before what', and scheduling answers 'when does it run'. Without both, your pipeline is just a collection of notebooks you run by hand.

Now here's the native engine on Databricks: Lakeflow Jobs — formerly known as Databricks Workflows. It schedules and monitors your data pipelines and machine-learning workflows. So when the exam asks what orchestrates work on Databricks, the answer is Lakeflow Jobs.

And here's the typical orchestrated flow: ingest, then transform, then serve, then train a model. Each step is its own task, each can run on shared compute, and the orchestration layer wires the dependencies between them. Let me point out something important about what orchestration gives you on top of your code — observability into each run, automatic retries, alerting when things fail, and repair so you can rerun just the broken part.

So why does this matter for the exam? Questions test two things: what a job actually orchestrates, and when a workflow needs a job rather than an ad hoc notebook run. Keep that distinction in mind — a notebook you run by hand has no dependencies, no schedule, and no retry policy. The moment you need any of those, you need a job. Let's build on this with the orchestration object model next.

scenes.title: Jobs, Tasks, and Runs: The Orchestration Object Model

elements.content: Jobs, Tasks, and Runs: The Orchestration Object Model
Four objects every exam stem is built from: job, task, job run, task run.
Definition — the container objects

• Job — a definition: one or more tasks plus schedule, configuration, triggers and failure handling. Created once by an engineer; it holds no data and no execution state. [source 3]

• Task — a single unit of work inside a job, pointing at a notebook, SQL, pipeline, script or JAR.

• Job run — one execution of a whole job, from first task start to last task end.

• Task run — the execution of one task within one job run; a job run is the parent of every task run inside it.
Worked example — a daily sales load: job "daily_sales" (created once, schedule 06:00) contains 4 tasks. It fires 30 times in a month ⇒ 30 job runs and 4 × 30 = 120 task runs. [source 6]
Object comparison

Task types inside one job

Notebook · SQL (query / dashboard / file) · Lakeflow pipelines · Python script or wheel · dbt · JAR · Run Job

All types coexist in a single job and share its schedule. [source 5]

Exam trap: a task run is not a job. A job run reports as healthy even when one task run inside it fails, provided a downstream or unrelated branch still executes. Read the system status and the task-level status as two separate questions. [source 2]

actions.text: Building on what we just covered, this page gives us the exact vocabulary we'll use for the rest of the orchestration unit: jobs, tasks, and runs. Everything you'll read in an exam stem about Lakeflow Jobs is assembled from these four objects, so let's get them nailed down precisely.

Start with the definition of a job. A job is a container object: it holds one or more tasks, plus the schedule and configuration that govern them. It's a definition — you create it once, and it describes intent. A job run is one actual execution of that job. So the job is the blueprint, and the job run is one trip through the blueprint.

Here's a worked example to make it concrete. Imagine a daily sales load: a job named daily_sales_load, scheduled to run every morning. Inside it, a notebook task to ingest files, then a SQL task to build an aggregate. Each morning the scheduler fires the job, and that firing is a job run — one parent execution that owns every task run underneath it.

This comparison table is worth memorizing along two axes: scope and lifetime. A job is a definition, created once. A task is a unit of work inside a job, also defined once. A job run and a task run are the transient executions — created and destroyed each time. And the last column tells you they show up in different places in the UI, which is exactly how you identify them in a scenario question.

Now, what can a task actually be? A single job is not limited to one kind of work. A task can be a notebook, a SQL query, dashboard, or file, a Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipeline, a Python script or wheel, a dbt project, a JAR, or even another job via Run Job. That flexibility is the point — one job can chain heterogeneous work into a single dependency graph.

And here's the exam trap that catches people. A task run is not a job, and — critically — a failed task run does not always mean the job run fails outright. If a downstream or unrelated branch still executes, the job run can report as healthy while containing a failed task run. Read the stem carefully: ask yourself whether it's asking about the job run's status or the task run's status.

One last design point before we move on: tasks run on job compute or serverless compute, not on an interactive cluster you happened to leave open. That means a workflow never depends on a cluster staying alive, which is why scheduled production jobs are both cheaper and more reliable. Keep that in mind — we'll come back to it when we cover deployment.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Job and Task Vocabulary

questions.question: A data engineer defines a pipeline that ingests raw sales files, transforms them through a bronze-to-silver step, and then trains a forecasting model. The engineer creates a single item in Lakeflow Jobs that contains all of these steps, plus a schedule and a notification configuration. In the orchestration object model, what best describes this item?

options.label: A task, because it represents one unit of work that executes on compute
A job, because it is a container holding one or more tasks together with its schedule and configuration
A job run, because it defines one execution of the pipeline
A task run, because it tracks the state of each step as it executes

questions.analysis: A job is a container of one or more tasks plus its schedule and configuration. The item described is the definition itself — created once and reusable — and it holds multiple steps (ingest, transform, train) along with a schedule and notifications. That matches the job level of the object model. Option A confuses a task with a job: a task is the unit of work inside a job, not the container that holds the schedule. Option C mistakes the definition for an execution: a job run is one execution of the job, produced each time the schedule fires or the job is triggered manually. Option D mistakes a task run, which is one task's execution, for the whole definition. A useful rule from the object comparison is that the job is created once, whereas runs are produced every time the job or a task executes [source 6].

questions.question: During debugging, an engineer inspects the run history after a scheduled execution of a three-task pipeline. Which statements correctly describe the relationship between the job run, the task runs, and the job definition in that execution? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The job run is the parent of every task run produced in that execution
A single execution creates one job run and one task run for each task executed in that run
The job definition is consumed by the run and ceases to exist once the run completes
Each task run belongs to exactly one job run, but a job can accumulate many job runs over its lifetime

questions.analysis: The object model places the job run above the task runs: the job run is the parent of every task run in that execution, so one execution yields exactly one job run plus one task run per executed task. Because the job is a definition that is created once, it persists across executions and can accumulate many job runs over its lifetime, while each task run is tied to exactly one parent job run. Option C is a common misconception: the definition does not disappear after a run — it is the reusable blueprint that the run instantiates. This distinction matters in the Databricks UI, where a job is referenced as a definition while job runs and task runs are referenced as executions. Keeping the parent-child relationship straight is also what makes debugging features such as partial runs and repairs sensible: repairs re-execute failed tasks within the context of the existing job run rather than creating a new definition [source 4].

questions.question: A team needs a scheduled workflow that ingests files arriving in cloud storage into bronze tables, applies transformations, and then runs an ML training notebook — all ordered so that the training step runs after the transforms complete. Which statement best identifies the workload orchestration pattern and the correct object types involved?

options.label: This is an MLflow experiment: each pipeline step is an experiment run and the job is the model registry
This is an ingest-transform-serve pattern: each step is a task, the ordered dependency between them is defined in the job, and the training step would run as its own task on shared compute
This is a Delta Live Tables pipeline: the job object is replaced by a materialized view, so no task definitions are needed
This is a single task: because files arrive continuously, all three steps must execute in one task to keep them atomic

questions.analysis: The typical orchestrated flow is ingest, then transform, then serve or train a model, with each step represented as its own task running on shared compute, and the dependencies between the tasks defined inside the job. That is exactly the pattern the team described, and Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestration engine that schedules and automates such multi-step pipelines by defining tasks, dependencies, triggers, and failure handling [source 2]. Option A confuses orchestration with MLflow experiment tracking; the job is the orchestration container, not a model registry. Option C confuses orchestration objects with Delta Live Tables constructs — a materialized view is a data object, not a replacement for a job definition. Option D is a common trap: continuous file arrival is a trigger concern, and forcing all steps into one task would defeat the purpose of dependency management and per-task monitoring [source 6].

actions.text: Let's pause here and check your grip on the job and task vocabulary we just covered — jobs, tasks, and the runs they produce. Take a careful look at each question and answer them on your own; a few of these options are built to look right at a glance, so read the wording closely.
Once you've submitted, I'll walk you through anything that tripped you up and we'll sort out the traps together.

scenes.title: Declaring Orchestration Dependencies as a DAG

elements.content: Declaring Orchestration Dependencies as a DAG
In Lakeflow Jobs, you declare per-task dependencies using depends_on. The engine infers a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from these declarations — you never draw the graph by hand. [source 2]

Worked Example: 3-Task DAG

Task A: no depends_on → starts at t=0s

Task B: depends_on = [A] → starts after A

Task C: depends_on = [A] → runs parallel with B

Total wall-clock = 10s + max(5s, 5s) = 15s

Fan-in and Fan-out

Fan-in: Task D depends_on = [A, B, C] → waits for all three to succeed.

Fan-out: Task A has no dependencies, and B, C, D all list A in depends_on → all three start once A succeeds.

Key rules: A task with no depends_on starts immediately when the job run begins [source 6]. The graph must be acyclic — circular dependencies are rejected because they could never resolve to a runnable order [source 2].
Exam trap: Listing a dependency in a comment or a task name does nothing — only depends_on creates an edge. Default run-if condition: 'run if all upstream dependencies succeeded' [source 3].

actions.text: Now let's get to the heart of Lakeflow Jobs: declaring orchestration dependencies as a DAG — a directed acyclic graph. This is the core exam objective for orchestration, so let's make sure the mechanics are crystal clear.

In Lakeflow Jobs, you declare dependencies per task using the depends_on field. The graph is never drawn by hand — it is inferred entirely from those declarations. Every edge you want between two tasks must come from an explicit depends_on on the downstream task.

Here's a worked example with three tasks. Task A has no depends_on, so it starts immediately when the job run begins and can run in parallel with any other independent task. Task B and Task C declare their upstreams, and the DAG is assembled from those declarations alone.

Two shapes you must recognize. Fan-in: a downstream task depends on several upstream tasks, and it waits for every single one listed before it starts. Fan-out: one upstream task unblocks several downstream tasks, so all of them become eligible the moment that upstream finishes.

The key rules to memorize: a task with no depends_on starts immediately, independent tasks execute in parallel, and the graph must be acyclic. Circular dependencies are rejected outright because they could never resolve into a runnable order. By default, a task runs if all upstream dependencies succeeded — other run-if conditions come in the next lesson.

And here's the classic exam trap: listing a dependency in a comment or mentioning it in a task name does absolutely nothing. Only depends_on creates an edge. If it isn't in depends_on, the scheduler won't see it — and that edge simply won't exist in the DAG.

scenes.title: Interactive: Assemble a Multi-Task Dependency Graph

content.html:
🕸️Interactive: Assemble a Multi-Task Dependency Graph

Databricks Lakeflow Jobs · task_key · depends_on · topological order · cycle validation

Step 1 / 9

Step 1 of 9

🎯

Create a Job

Select a task on the canvas to inspect it.

Upstream — depends_on

  • none (root task)

Downstream

  • none (leaf task)
Tip: a task's DAG depth is the longest path from a root task to it. Tasks at the same depth form one wave and run in parallel.

nodes.label: Create a Job
nodes.details: In Databricks Lakeflow Jobs (formerly Databricks Workflows), a job is the unit of orchestration: one job contains one or more tasks that together form a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Jobs are the scheduling and dependency layer that sits above notebooks, SQL, and pipelines.

nodes.label: Add Tasks
nodes.details: Drop tasks onto the job canvas. A task type can be Notebook, SQL, Python script, Lakeflow pipeline, dbt, JAR, or Run Job. Every task needs a unique task_key (the task's unique name inside the job) — this key is exactly what dependencies reference later.

nodes.label: Label & Configure
nodes.details: Give each task a meaningful task_key so depends_on stays readable (for example ingest_bronze, transform_silver). Configure per-task compute, parameters, retries, timeouts, and notifications. A task with no task_key cannot be referenced by any other task.

nodes.label: Connect depends_on
nodes.details: Declare depends_on: ["upstream_task_key", ...] on the downstream task. Direction is implicit — control flow always runs upstream → downstream — so you never specify an edge direction manually. The canvas redraws an arrow for every depends_on entry.

nodes.label: DAG Redraws
nodes.details: Lakeflow Jobs topologically sorts the DAG (resolves a linear order that respects every dependency) to produce the execution order. The Jobs UI redraws the DAG view after each dependency edit, showing tasks as nodes and depends_on as arrows.

nodes.label: Parallel Branches
nodes.details: Tasks whose depends_on are all satisfied become runnable at the same time — that is parallelism. Independent branches execute concurrently, bounded by the job's max concurrent runs setting and by the workers available on the attached compute.

nodes.label: Cycle Detected
nodes.details: A cycle (A → B → A) has no valid topological order. The job definition is blocked by a validation error before any task can run, so you must delete the offending depends_on entry and re-resolve the graph.

nodes.label: Compare to Target
nodes.details: Compare the resolved order to the target order. Tasks sharing the same DAG depth (longest path from a root task) belong to the same wave and should run in parallel. If the resolved order or the wave grouping differs from the target, the edges are wrong.

nodes.label: Repair Edges
nodes.details: Repair edges until the resolved order matches the target, then validate and run the job. Use the Jobs UI run history, the DAG view, and per-task output to confirm that the topology — not just the code — behaves as designed.

actions.text: So far we've talked about depends_on as the only thing that creates an edge. Now let's actually build a dependency graph and watch Lakeflow Jobs resolve it. On this canvas you'll step through the full lifecycle — adding tasks, wiring depends_on edges, and seeing the execution order resolve in real time.

actions.content: Use the arrows to walk through the DAG assembly steps.
Start at the first node: creating the job itself.
Each node's detail panel explains the orchestration concept at that step.
Jump ahead to where the DAG redraws after depends_on edges are added.

actions.text: Notice the difference here. Steps two and three both wire into step four with depends_on, and Lakeflow Jobs topologically sorts the graph — it finds a linear order that respects every dependency. Tasks whose dependencies are all satisfied become runnable at the same time, and that's exactly what parallelism means in a DAG. Independent branches run concurrently, bounded by the job's max concurrent runs setting.

actions.content: Now look at the invalid path — a cycle that breaks the graph.

actions.text: Here's the exam-critical trap: a cycle — A depends on B, B depends on A — has no valid topological order. The job definition is blocked by a validation error before any task can run. You must delete the offending depends_on entry and re-resolve the graph. Then you compare the resolved order to the target, and repair edges until the waves match. Use the upstream and downstream lists in the panel to trace exactly which tasks feed which, and confirm the topology behaves as designed before you run the job.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Dependency Graphs and Execution Order

questions.question: A job run begins with four tasks: taskA has no depends_on, taskB has depends_on = [taskA], taskC has no depends_on, and taskD has depends_on = [taskB, taskC]. Assuming every task starts successfully and there are no Run-if conditions, which tasks become runnable at the very start of the job run?

options.label: taskA only, because taskC must wait until taskB finishes to keep the branches balanced
taskA and taskC, because both declare no depends_on and therefore start immediately when the job run begins
taskA, taskC, and taskB, because depends_on only orders taskD after the upstream tasks
taskD only, because fan-in tasks are always scheduled first to reduce overall run latency

questions.correctAnswer: taskA and taskC, because both declare no depends_on and therefore start immediately when the job run begins
questions.analysis: Lakeflow Jobs infers the DAG from per-task depends_on declarations rather than from a hand-drawn graph, and a task with no depends_on starts immediately when the job run begins, so independent tasks execute in parallel [source 3]. taskA and taskC are the only tasks with empty dependency lists, making them the two roots of the DAG that become runnable at run start. Option A is a common misconception that parallelism must be balanced or throttled across branches, but no such balancing rule exists in dependency declaration. Option C confuses declaration syntax with runtime behaviour: taskB declares depends_on = [taskA], so it cannot become runnable until taskA completes. Option D reverses execution order, since a fan-in task with depends_on = [taskB, taskC] is precisely the node that must wait the longest, not the first to start.

questions.question: You are reviewing four proposed depends_on declarations for a five-task job (taskA through taskE). Select every declaration set that forms a valid DAG with no cycle.

options.label: taskA: none; taskB: [taskA]; taskC: [taskA]; taskD: [taskB, taskC]; taskE: [taskD]
taskA: [taskE]; taskB: [taskA]; taskC: [taskB]; taskD: [taskC]; taskE: [taskD]
taskA: none; taskB: none; taskC: [taskA, taskB]; taskD: none; taskE: [taskC]
taskA: [taskC]; taskB: [taskA]; taskC: [taskB]; taskD: [taskA]; taskE: none

questions.correctAnswer: Options A and C
questions.analysis: A valid dependency graph must be a directed acyclic graph: follow the depends_on edges in one direction and you can never return to a task you already visited [source 2].
