Option A is a classic fan-out/fan-in diamond, taskA forks to taskB and taskC, which rejoin at taskD, then taskE — no path returns to an earlier task. Option C has two roots (taskA and taskB) running in parallel, fanned into taskC, plus an independent taskD, and taskE downstream of taskC — also acyclic. Option B creates a cycle: taskA depends on taskE while taskE depends on taskD, taskD on taskC, taskC on taskB, and taskB back on taskA, so the chain loops. Option D also contains a cycle: taskA depends on taskC, taskC depends on taskB, and taskB depends on taskA. A frequent student error is to judge validity by looking only at the first or last line of the declaration list; cycles must be detected by tracing the full transitive closure of edges.

questions.question: A job run has been in the Running state for several minutes. The dashboard shows that taskIngest has succeeded, taskTransform has succeeded, but taskServe has not started yet and displays no error. taskServe declares depends_on = [taskQuality, taskTransform]. Explain why taskServe has not started, and describe what must happen in the DAG before it can become runnable. Refer to the orchestration object model and to the way Lakeflow Jobs infers execution order.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Correctly identifies that taskServe's depends_on list contains taskQuality as well as taskTransform, and that the unmet upstream dependency is taskQuality — 40%. (2) States the general rule that a downstream task becomes runnable only after all upstream tasks listed in its depends_on have finished successfully, and that Lakeflow Jobs derives this ordering from the declarations rather than from a manually drawn graph — 30%. (3) Connects the observation to the object model, distinguishing job run (parent execution) from task run (one task's execution) and noting that "not started" is a scheduling state of the task run, not a failure — 20%. (4) Clear, exam-oriented phrasing — 10%.
questions.analysis: taskServe has not started because its depends_on list names two upstream tasks, taskTransform and taskQuality, and only taskTransform has succeeded. In Lakeflow Jobs the graph is inferred from per-task depends_on declarations, and a task runs only after every upstream task it declares has completed, so the missing prerequisite is taskQuality [source 3]. A strong answer also distinguishes job run from task run: a job run is the parent execution, and each task produces its own task run, so taskServe's task run simply has not been scheduled yet — "not started" is a waiting state, not an error [source 2]. Learners often misread a stalled task as a failure or as a problem with compute, but the Runtime column showing no error combined with a succeeded sibling task is the signature of an unmet fan-in dependency. In an exam scenario, the correct next step is to inspect the upstream task run for taskQuality — check whether it is still running, whether a Run-if condition caused it to be skipped, or whether it failed — because taskServe cannot begin until that dependency resolves.

actions.text: Now let's put those dependency graphs to the test. Work through each question on your own — three questions, so give each one the same careful reading you'd give an exam item, and don't second-guess yourself into changing a correct graph into a broken one.
Submit whenever you're ready, and I'll walk through the tricky parts with you after.

scenes.title: Notebook vs SQL vs Pipeline Tasks in One Workflow

elements.content: Dimension  |  Notebook task  |  SQL task  |  Pipeline task

What the task executes
Notebook task: A notebook task runs an existing notebook (commonly a PySpark notebook) that must already exist in the workspace, and the job references it rather than inlining the code. [source 1]
SQL task: A SQL task executes a query, a dashboard, or a SQL file against a warehouse, so its unit of work is a set-based SQL statement or visualization rather than arbitrary code. [source 4]
Pipeline task: A pipeline task triggers a Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines update, meaning it starts a declarative pipeline whose datasets and dependencies are defined by the pipeline itself rather than by imperative task code. [source 3]

Typical parameterisation and how inputs reach the task
Notebook task: A notebook task is parameterised through notebook widgets or task base parameters, and a job can pass SQL query outputs forward as parameters to downstream producers. [source 4]
SQL task: A SQL task is parameterised in the SQL text itself, for example with named parameters or query outputs that substitute into the statement, which keeps the task purely declarative at the warehouse layer. [source 4]
Pipeline task: A pipeline task is parameterised by the pipeline definition and its configuration rather than by ad-hoc widgets, because the update is triggered as a whole and the pipeline resolves its own dataset dependencies. [source 2]

Compute requirement and where the work runs
Notebook task: A notebook task needs a job cluster (or serverless/job compute) capable of running the notebook language, and the typical workload is PySpark over Delta Lake, so the compute must be sized for DataFrame-level processing. [source 3]
SQL task: A SQL task needs a SQL warehouse, because it runs against the warehouse layer, and the compute is provisioned and billed as warehouse capacity rather than as a general-purpose cluster. [source 4]
Pipeline task: A pipeline task needs the compute that the Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines update requires, since the declarative engine itself schedules and executes the underlying Spark work when the pipeline is triggered. [source 3]

Best-fit use case
Notebook task: A notebook task is the default choice for custom transformation logic, such as Python/PySpark code that does not map cleanly to SQL. [source 1]
SQL task: A SQL task is ideal for set-based transformation and for BI-serving layers, including dashboards and materialized views (a materialized view is a precomputed query result stored for fast reads) that feed reporting. [source 4]
Pipeline task: A pipeline task is ideal for declarative, dependency-managed ingestion and transformation with data-quality expectations, because the pipeline manages dataset dependencies and can enforce expectations on the data. [source 3]

Position in the DAG and dependency behaviour
Notebook task: A notebook task declares dependency through depends_on, and because a task with no depends_on starts immediately when the job run begins, an independent notebook task can run in parallel with other branches. [source 6]
SQL task: A SQL task behaves the same way at the orchestration layer: it is a node in the DAG whose start is gated by its declared depends_on edges, so a SQL task can run in parallel with any task that does not depend on it. [source 6]
Pipeline task: A pipeline task is a single orchestration node that internally fans out into a declarative update, so downstream tasks wait on the pipeline task as a whole even though the pipeline itself may stage many datasets. [source 2]

Worked example: a job that mixes all three
Notebook task: Consider a job with tasks ingest (pipeline task), transform (notebook task), and serve (SQL task). The ingest task has no depends_on, so it starts immediately; transform declares depends_on: [ingest]; serve declares depends_on: [transform]. If ingest takes 120 s, transform 300 s, and serve 60 s, the critical path is 120+300+60 = 480 s, and the notebook task contributes 300/480 = 62.5% of the run time. [source 6]
SQL task: The same job shows why task type is a property of the task, not the job: the serve SQL task cannot start before the transform notebook task completes, because the dependency edge gates it, regardless of the fact that SQL is set-based and could in principle run on a warehouse in parallel with an unrelated branch. [source 6]
Pipeline task: If serve were instead declared with no depends_on, it would start at t=0 and run in parallel with ingest and transform, so the critical path would fall to max(120+300, 60) = 420 s, a 12.5% reduction — demonstrating that the dependency declarations, not the task types, determine execution order. [source 6]

Typical exam trap
Notebook task: A common trap is choosing a notebook task to trigger a declarative pipeline update; the correct tool is a pipeline task, because a notebook task runs notebook code and does not itself start a Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines update. [source 3]
SQL task: Another trap is choosing a SQL task to run Python; a SQL task executes SQL against a warehouse, so Python logic must go in a notebook task rather than a SQL task. [source 4]
Pipeline task: A third trap is assuming the task type is fixed at the job level; in fact a single job can contain notebook, SQL, and pipeline tasks together, because the task type is a property of the task, not of the job. [source 2]
Takeaway — Choose a notebook task when the work is custom PySpark/Python transformation logic that already exists in a workspace notebook and does not map cleanly to SQL.
Takeaway — Choose a SQL task when the work is set-based transformation or BI-serving, including dashboards and materialized views, and can be expressed as SQL against a warehouse.

Takeaway — Choose a pipeline task when the work is declarative ingestion or transformation with dependency management and data-quality expectations, and you want the pipeline to resolve its own dataset graph.
Takeaway — Remember that a single job may mix all three task types, and execution order is controlled by depends_on declarations rather than by the task type itself.

actions.text: Now that you've wired up a dependency graph, let's talk about what actually lives inside each node. In Lakeflow Jobs, every task has a type, and the task type tells the platform what kind of work to run. Today we compare the three you'll be tested on: notebook, SQL, and pipeline tasks.

This table is your reference for the whole lesson. It lines the three task types up against four dimensions: what the task executes, how it's typically parameterised, what compute it expects, and the workload it fits best. Read it left to right, and you basically have the exam answer key.

Start with execution. A notebook task runs an existing notebook — often PySpark — and that notebook must already exist in the workspace, or the task fails outright. It's the default choice whenever you need custom transformation logic that SQL can't express cleanly.

On parameterisation, this is where the task types diverge. Notebook tasks accept widgets, job parameters, and task values passed from upstream tasks. A SQL task takes parameters directly in the statement, or references a query object. Keep this in mind, because the next page builds directly on how those inputs reach the task at runtime.

Then there's compute. A notebook task attaches to a cluster — all-purpose or job cluster. A SQL task runs against a SQL warehouse. A pipeline task triggers a Lakeflow Spark Declarative Pipelines update, and the compute is managed for you. So the task type effectively decides where the work runs and how you pay for it.

Best fit, in one line each: notebook for custom logic, SQL for set-based transformation and BI-serving layers, and pipeline tasks for declarative, dependency-managed ingestion with data-quality expectations. Point at the task type that matches the shape of the workload, not the language you happen to like.

Dependency behaviour is subtle. Notebook and SQL tasks are nodes in the job's DAG just like anything else — they obey upstream and downstream links and run-if conditions. A pipeline task is a node too, but it launches a declarative flow whose internal datasets have their own dependency graph. So you get a DAG inside a DAG, and that confuses a lot of candidates.

Here's the worked example, and it's the key insight of the whole page: a single job can mix all three. One task ingests with a notebook, the next triggers a pipeline update, then a SQL task serves the gold table. The task type is a property of the task — not of the job.

And here's the typical exam trap. Candidates reach for a SQL task to run Python, or a notebook task to trigger a declarative pipeline update. Neither works. If the work is Python, it's a notebook task. If it's a pipeline update, it's a pipeline task. Match the type to the workload and you'll avoid the trap every time.

So, takeaway one: choose a notebook task when the work is custom, code-driven logic. Takeaway two, a SQL task when the work is set-based and serves BI. Takeaway three, a pipeline task when the work is declarative and dependency-managed. And remember, they can all coexist in one job, wired together by the dependency graph you just built.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Designing a Five-Task Ingestion-to-Serving Job

elements.content: Problem 1

Northwind Retail runs a daily order-analytics pipeline on Databricks. The five workloads for the run dated 2025-06-01 are:

1. **ingest_orders** — a declarative pipeline that reads roughly 1,200,000 raw order records per day from cloud object storage into the bronze layer using Auto Loader with automatic schema evolution.

2. **clean_orders** — a PySpark notebook that already exists in the workspace; it deduplicates order IDs, casts timestamps to UTC, drops rows with a null customer key, and writes the silver layer.

3. **gold_orders_daily** — a single SQL statement that aggregates silver into a gold table holding revenue by day and country.

4. **refresh_dashboard** — a SQL task that refreshes the 'Daily Revenue' dashboard that executives open at 08:00 UTC.

5. **validate_orders** — a Python script task that runs third-party data-quality checks: a row-count reconciliation between bronze and gold with a 0.5% tolerance, and a null-rate ceiling of 0.1% on the customer key in the gold table. It must fail the job run if any check breaks.

Ordering constraints: cleaning must follow ingestion; the gold aggregate must follow cleaning; the dashboard refresh must follow the gold aggregate; and validation must run only after the gold aggregate **and** the dashboard refresh have both succeeded.

Produce (a) the task list with the correct task type for each workload, (b) the `depends_on` list for each of the five tasks, and (c) a one-line justification for every edge you add.
Hint: Work in three passes: assign a type per workload, translate each English constraint into exactly one edge, then check the graph for cycles and for tasks that would start at t=0.

Worked solution
**Step 1 — match each workload to a task type.**

| Task name | Task type | Why this type |

|---|---|---|

| `ingest_orders` | Pipeline task (declarative pipeline) | Declarative ingestion with Auto Loader and schema evolution is expressed as pipeline code, not imperative PySpark; Lakeflow Jobs runs a pipeline as a task. |

| `clean_orders` | Notebook task (PySpark) | Custom row-level transformation logic that already lives in a workspace notebook — the default choice for bespoke transformation code. |

| `gold_orders_daily` | SQL task | Set-based aggregation over Delta tables; the statement is warehouse-executable SQL, not Python. |

| `refresh_dashboard` | SQL task | Refreshing a dashboard is a SQL-serving workload against a warehouse. |

| `validate_orders` | Python script task | The checks use a third-party library and must return a non-zero exit code to fail the run; that is imperative control flow, not a query. |

**Step 2 — translate each constraint into edges.**

- "cleaning must follow ingestion" gives the edge `ingest_orders → clean_orders`.

- "gold must follow cleaning" gives `clean_orders → gold_orders_daily`.

- "the dashboard refresh must follow the gold aggregate" gives `gold_orders_daily → refresh_dashboard`.

- "validation must run only after the gold aggregate and the dashboard refresh" is a **fan-in**: two parents, one child, so `gold_orders_daily → validate_orders` and `refresh_dashboard → validate_orders`.

**Step 3 — write the task definitions.** Each task declares only its immediate parents; Lakeflow Jobs infers the full graph from those declarations rather than requiring you to draw it.

| Task name | `depends_on` |

|---|---|

| `ingest_orders` | `[]` |

| `clean_orders` | `['ingest_orders']` |

| `gold_orders_daily` | `['clean_orders']` |

| `refresh_dashboard` | `['gold_orders_daily']` |

| `validate_orders` | `['gold_orders_daily', 'refresh_dashboard']` |

As a JSON task array this is:

```

[

{"task_key": "ingest_orders", "depends_on": []},

{"task_key": "clean_orders", "depends_on": [{"task_key": "ingest_orders"}]},

{"task_key": "gold_orders_daily", "depends_on": [{"task_key": "clean_orders"}]},

{"task_key": "refresh_dashboard", "depends_on": [{"task_key": "gold_orders_daily"}]},

{"task_key": "validate_orders", "depends_on": [{"task_key": "gold_orders_daily"},

{"task_key": "refresh_dashboard"}]}

]

```

**Step 4 — verify the graph is a DAG.** The edges are 1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 3→5, 4→5. A topological order exists: `ingest_orders, clean_orders, gold_orders_daily, refresh_dashboard, validate_orders`. Every edge points forward in that ordering, so there is no cycle. Counting: 5 tasks, 5 edges, and the unique topological order means the graph is a single chain that closes with a fan-in at validation.

**Step 5 — identify parallelism.** Only one task has `depends_on: []`, so only one task is runnable at the instant the job run starts. Every other task has at least one unfinished parent at that moment. In this particular design there is **no** parallel branch: the dashboard refresh and the validation task are sequentially related because validation waits on the dashboard. If the team later added a separate branch — say a `features_orders` notebook with `depends_on: ['clean_orders']` and a downstream `train_forecast` — that branch would run concurrently with the `gold_orders_daily → refresh_dashboard` branch, because nothing connects the two.

**Step 6 — scheduling sanity check.** If ingestion takes 12 minutes, cleaning 17, gold 5, dashboard 5, and validation 2, the critical path is 12 + 17 + 5 + 5 + 2 = 41 minutes, so the run that starts at 02:00 UTC finishes at 02:41 UTC, comfortably before the 08:00 UTC dashboard audience. Crucially, the fan-in does not add time here: `validate_orders` waits for the slower of its two parents, and both parents are on the same chain.

Analysis — **Why this method works.** `depends_on` is a *declaration of ordering*, not a description of runtime state. The graph is data, not code: the same five `depends_on` lists produce the same execution order on every run, in every workspace, regardless of how long individual tasks take or in what sequence the tasks happen to appear in the authoring UI. That determinism is exactly what makes an orchestrated pipeline reproducible in production, where orchestration means managing dependencies between workflow tasks and scheduling them so a data solution can actually reach production [source 6]. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestration engine that schedules and automates these multi-step pipelines by defining tasks, dependencies, triggers and failure handling [source 2], and it is the layer used for scheduling and monitoring data pipelines and ML workflows [source 1].

**Why fan-in is the right attachment point for validation.** Validation is a *gate*, not a producer. Attaching it to both upstream producers means it cannot observe a half-finished world: it sees the gold table and the dashboard state only after both are complete. If you attached validation to the gold aggregate alone, it could pass while `refresh_dashboard` was still mid-flight and still reading the previous gold snapshot, and the executive dashboard would silently serve stale numbers. The rule of thumb is: a validation task's parents are exactly the set of artifacts it inspects.

**Step-by-step design recipe (generalises to any job).** (1) List workloads and tag each with a task type. (2) Convert each English phrase containing "before", "after", "once … has finished", or "only if" into one directed edge. (3) A phrase with two requirements becomes two edges (fan-in). (4) Tasks with no incoming edge get `depends_on: []`. (5) Run a topological sort; if you cannot finish it, you have a cycle, and the job definition is invalid.

**Common pitfalls.** *Reversing the gate.* Writing `refresh_dashboard depends_on ['validate_orders']` together with `validate_orders depends_on ['gold_orders_daily', 'refresh_dashboard']` creates a two-node cycle — the dashboard would have to wait for validation that itself waits for the dashboard. The designer's instinct ("validate first, then publish") is understandable but backwards: the validator inspects the published artifact, so it sits downstream of it. *Forgetting a `depends_on` key.* An omitted key is equivalent to an empty list, and an empty list means "start immediately when the job run begins" — the task does not politely wait for the task listed above it. *Assuming list order is execution order.* The order of tasks in the job definition file or canvas carries no scheduling meaning whatsoever; two engineers can write the same five tasks in opposite orders and get byte-identical execution behaviour. Only edges schedule. *Over-connecting.* Adding redundant edges "for safety" (for example, `validate_orders` also depending on `clean_orders`, which it does not read) never shortens a run and can only lengthen the critical path, as quantified in problem p3.
Problem 2

A colleague submits the following job definition for a 07:00 UTC daily run. Tasks are written in the order shown, and the job must load raw clickstream events (`ingest_events`), clean them (`clean_events`), aggregate them into a gold table (`gold_events`), refresh a dashboard (`refresh_events_dashboard`), and validate the result against a 0.5% row-count tolerance (`validate_events`).

```

1. validate_events depends_on: ['gold_events', 'refresh_events_dashboard']

2. refresh_events_dashboard depends_on: ['validate_events']

3. gold_events depends_on: ['clean_events']

4. clean_events (no depends_on key present)

5. ingest_events depends_on: []

```

(a) Identify every defect in this definition. (b) State precisely what Lakeflow Jobs will do with it and what the runtime consequences are. (c) Give the corrected `depends_on` list for each task. (d) Explain whether the order in which the tasks are written affects execution order. (e) The team fixes the defect and re-runs; the first attempt fails inside `validate_events` because a source table was momentarily empty. Explain the cheapest way to re-run without repeating ingestion and cleaning, and why that matters for cost.
Hint: Look for a pair of tasks that each wait for the other, and for a task that has no `depends_on` key at all.

Worked solution
**Step 1 — defect 1: a cycle between tasks 1 and 2.**

Task 2 says `refresh_events_dashboard` requires `validate_events`. Task 1 says `validate_events` requires `refresh_events_dashboard`. Substituting, the dashboard must wait for validation, and validation must wait for the dashboard:

$$refresh\_events\_dashboard \rightarrow validate\_events \rightarrow refresh\_events\_dashboard$$

There is no topological ordering of these five tasks, because no assignment of positions can place the dashboard before validation *and* validation before the dashboard. The graph is not a DAG. A job whose dependency graph is cyclic cannot be scheduled: every task on that cycle would be permanently runnable-but-blocked, waiting on a parent that waits on it. This is not a runtime race you can retry your way out of — it is a defect in the job definition, and the DAG must be corrected before the job will run at all.

**Step 2 — defect 2: `clean_events` has no `depends_on` key.**

An absent key is not the same as "runs after whatever is listed above". The effective dependency list is empty, so `clean_events` is a root task and becomes runnable at the instant the job run starts — simultaneously with `ingest_events`, not after it. The runtime consequence is a race: `clean_events` reads the bronze table while ingestion is still writing it. Depending on which finishes first, the cleaner sees an empty bronze table (silver becomes empty, gold becomes empty, and the 0.5% tolerance check fails against a zero-row gold table), or it sees a partially loaded bronze table and produces gold numbers that are wrong but *within* tolerance on a small sample — a silent data-loss failure that is far more expensive than a loud one.

**Step 3 — the corrected definition.**

| Task | `depends_on` |

|---|---|

| `ingest_events` | `[]` |

| `clean_events` | `['ingest_events']` |

| `gold_events` | `['clean_events']` |

| `refresh_events_dashboard` | `['gold_events']` |

| `validate_events` | `['gold_events', 'refresh_events_dashboard']` |

Topological order check: `ingest_events → clean_events → gold_events → refresh_events_dashboard → validate_events`, with the extra edge `gold_events → validate_events`. Every edge points forward, so the graph is acyclic. Note the symmetry with p1: the validator keeps both parents because it inspects both the gold table and the published dashboard; it is the *gate*, and gates sit downstream of the artifacts they inspect.

**Step 4 — does the written order of tasks matter?** No. The scheduler derives the execution order exclusively from the `depends_on` edges. If the colleague re-orders the five blocks as `ingest, clean, gold, dashboard, validate`, or as `validate, dashboard, gold, clean, ingest`, the run behaves identically, because in both cases exactly one task has an empty dependency list and every other task has the same parents. The neighbour below a task in a YAML or JSON file is not an implicit dependency.

**Step 5 — cheapest recovery.** Re-run only the failed task and its descendants using a repair run rather than a fresh full run. A repair re-executes `validate_events` on the same job run and, if the check passes, marks the run successful without re-reading the 1,200,000-ish raw records or recomputing the gold aggregate. This matters because partial runs and repairs are specifically designed to make debugging failed tasks easier, faster, and cheaper [source 4]. On a job whose ingestion alone consumes 12 minutes of cluster time per run, repairing one 2-minute validation task instead of re-running the whole 41-minute pipeline is the difference between a two-minute fix and a full re-ingest on every iteration.

Analysis — **Why the method works.** The whole failure mode here comes from one principle: the dependency graph, not the file layout, is the schedule. `depends_on` is a static, declarative ordering constraint evaluated once when the run starts; it does not inspect data, it does not react to whether a previous task "looked finished", and it does not care where a task appears in the definition. This is why a cyclic definition is a hard error rather than a hang: the scheduler can prove, before executing anything, that no valid ordering exists.

**Why fans-in must be checked explicitly.** The cycle in this exercise is not an exotic construction — it arises from a very natural mistake. A designer who wants "no bad data on the dashboard" reasons *forward* (validate, then publish) and writes the gate above the publish step. The correct reasoning runs *backward from the artifact*: what does this task read, and which tasks produce those things? A validator reads gold and the published dashboard, therefore both are its parents. Whenever you find yourself writing "X depends on validate", stop and ask whether the validator actually inspects X's output. If the answer is no, the edge is reversed.

**Edge cases worth knowing.** (i) A task with `depends_on: []` is never "orphaned" or suspicious — root tasks are normal and are exactly where parallelism begins; the bug in this exercise was that a *middle* task accidentally became a root. (ii) Validation tasks that must observe a snapshot should also consider the `Run-if` condition, so that a validation failure can fail the job loudly rather than leaving the pipeline in a green-but-wrong state; dependency edges control *order*, and conditions control *whether* a task runs after that order is satisfied. (iii) A failed repair on a task whose upstream has since been re-run can validate a mix of old and new data, so repairs should be applied to the same job run whose upstream outputs are still the ones you intend to validate.

**Common mistakes in the wild.** Blindly copying the previous day's `depends_on` lists after renaming tasks — the string keys no longer match, and an unmatched parent name is typically rejected at definition time or silently leaves a task root. Using a dashboard refresh as a parent of the gold aggregation because "the dashboard shows the aggregate" — again a reversed edge. And treating the order of the tasks in the submitted file as evidence about behaviour; reviewers who argue about file ordering are arguing about nothing.
Problem 3

The corrected seven-task job from p1 and p2 is now extended with a forecasting branch. The measured median durations on a warm cluster are:

| Task | Duration (min) | Parents |

|---|---|---|

| `ingest_orders` | 12 | (none) |

| `clean_orders` | 17 | `ingest_orders` |

| `gold_orders_daily` | 5 | `clean_orders` |

| `refresh_dashboard` | 5 | `gold_orders_daily` |

| `validate_orders` | 2 | `gold_orders_daily`, `refresh_dashboard` |

| `features_orders` | 9 | `clean_orders` |

| `train_forecast` | 20 | `features_orders` |

The job run is scheduled to start at 02:00 UTC.

(a) Compute the earliest start and finish time of every task. (b) State the makespan of the run. (c) Compute what the makespan would be if all seven tasks were forced into a single serial chain. (d) Compute the new makespan if the team adds the edge `features_orders depends_on ['validate_orders']` in addition to its existing parent, and explain the sign of the change. (e) State which tasks run concurrently and which task is the final gate.
Hint: Compute earliest finish as (earliest start of the latest-finishing parent) + duration. The makespan is the maximum earliest finish over all tasks.

Worked solution
**Step 1 — recursion for earliest times.** For a task with parents $P$, its earliest start is $ES = \max_{p \in P}(EF_p)$, and its earliest finish is $EF = ES + d$. Root tasks have $ES = 0$ relative to the run start of 02:00 UTC.

**Step 2 — compute level by level (times in minutes after 02:00).**

| Task | ES | Duration | EF | Clock finish (UTC) |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| `ingest_orders` | 0 | 12 | 12 | 02:12 |

| `clean_orders` | 12 | 17 | 29 | 02:29 |

| `gold_orders_daily` | 29 | 5 | 34 | 02:34 |

| `refresh_dashboard` | 34 | 5 | 39 | 02:39 |

| `features_orders` | 29 | 9 | 38 | 02:38 |

| `train_forecast` | 38 | 20 | 58 | 02:58 |

| `validate_orders` | $\max(EF_{gold}, EF_{dashboard}) = \max(34, 39) = 39$ | 2 | 41 | 02:41 |

**Step 3 — makespan.** The makespan is the maximum earliest finish over all tasks:

$$\text{makespan} = \max(12, 29, 34, 39, 38, 58, 41) = 58 \text{ minutes}$$

The run finishes at 02:58 UTC. Note that the fan-in at `validate_orders` does *not* extend the run: validation is off the critical path by 17 minutes. The critical path is `ingest_orders → clean_orders → features_orders → train_forecast`, of length $12 + 17 + 9 + 20 = 58$.

**Step 4 — serial-chain counterfactual.** If the seven tasks were chained end to end:

$$12 + 17 + 5 + 5 + 2 + 9 + 20 = 70 \text{ minutes}$$

so the available parallelism saves $70 - 58 = 12$ minutes, or about 17% of wall-clock time. Those 12 minutes are exactly the tail of the non-critical branch: the two branches diverge after `clean_orders` and rejoin only if you connect them, so the shorter branch (gold → dashboard → validate, 12 minutes) is absorbed into the slack of the longer one (features → train, 29 minutes).

**Step 5 — adding the edge `features_orders depends_on ['validate_orders']`.** Now $ES_{features} = \max(EF_{clean}, EF_{validate}) = \max(29, 41) = 41$, so:

- `features_orders`: 41 → 50

- `train_forecast`: 50 → 70

- `validate_orders`: unchanged at 39 → 41

$$\text{new makespan} = \max(41, 58 \text{ replaced by } 70, 41) = 70 \text{ minutes}$$

The makespan grows by 12 minutes. The sign is always the same: adding an edge can only delay tasks, never accelerate them, because it can only raise a $\max$ over parents. This is the formal reason the "add a dependency for safety" instinct is an anti-pattern.

**Step 6 — concurrency and the gate.** After `clean_orders` finishes at 02:29, two branches run concurrently: (i) `gold_orders_daily` then `refresh_dashboard` then `validate_orders`, and (ii) `features_orders` then `train_forecast`. Within each branch execution is strictly sequential. `validate_orders` is the final gate for the reporting branch: it is the only task whose result determines whether the reporting pipeline is declared trustworthy, and it joins two parents. `train_forecast` happens to finish last, but it is a leaf in a different branch, not a gate.

Analysis — **Why this method works.** Earliest-start/earliest-finish recursion is the standard longest-path (critical-path) computation on a DAG, and it is legitimate precisely because the graph is acyclic — a cycle would make the recursion non-terminating, which is the arithmetic restatement of the structural defect in p2. The formula $ES = \max(EF_{p})$ also explains the two facts practitioners rely on daily: (i) parallelism is free whenever branches do not share a descendant too early, and (ii) the makespan is set by the *longest* root-to-leaf chain, so optimising anything off that chain has zero effect on when the job finishes.

**Where the real wins are.** In this example the critical path runs through `clean_orders` (17 min) and `train_forecast` (20 min). Halving the dashboard refresh from 5 to 2.5 minutes changes nothing at all, because the dashboard branch has 17 minutes of slack. Halving `clean_orders` to 8.5 minutes, by contrast, cuts the makespan by 8.5 minutes. This is why profiling an orchestrated job means finding the critical path first and then optimising only along it — a point that is easy to state and easy to get wrong when a slow-but-slack task is the noisiest one in the UI.

**Edge cases.** Durations here are medians on a warm cluster; on a cold cluster the auto-start of compute can dominate the 2-minute validation task, and the critical path can shift between runs. Dependency edges are deterministic, but durations are not: `depends_on` gives a fixed *order*, not a fixed *runtime*. If a branch is known to be data-dependent (for example, a SQL task whose output feeds parameters into a downstream task), the scheduler still only enforces order — passing one query's output as a parameter is a separate mechanism from ordering [source 4]. Also note the difference between the fan-in here and a true join with data semantics: `validate_orders` joins on *timing* only, since it reads the gold table and the dashboard rather than combining two data streams.

**Common mistakes.** (1) Reading the job's total runtime off the sum of all task durations — that over-counts by exactly the slack in non-critical branches (12 minutes in part (c) versus part (b)). (2) Believing that a task listed immediately after another in the UI is somehow faster, or that re-ordering tasks changes the critical path; only edges and durations do. (3) Adding a validation edge "just to be safe" and then wondering why the nightly run drifted from 02:58 to 03:10, which is precisely the 12-minute penalty computed in part (e). (4) Forgetting that a task with `depends_on: []` becomes runnable the moment the run starts, which is the mechanism that creates parallelism in the first place and the mechanism that produced the race condition in p2.

actions.text: Let's put that wiring knowledge to work on a fully worked design problem. You are given five described workloads and their ordering constraints, and your job is to produce the task list, the task types, and the depends_on edges — then explain why the design holds up.

Here is the scenario. Northwind Retail runs a daily order-analytics pipeline. We ingest raw orders with a declarative pipeline, clean them in a PySpark notebook, build a gold aggregate in SQL, refresh a dashboard with a SQL task, and run a Python validation script that must run after everything else.

Before you peek at the solution, work in three passes: assign a task type per workload, derive the edges from the stated constraints, then sanity-check the graph. That three-pass habit is exactly what the exam rewards — structure first, then detail.

Step one: match each workload to a Databricks task type. Ingestion becomes a pipeline task, cleaning becomes a notebook task, the gold aggregate and the dashboard refresh both become SQL tasks, and validation becomes a Python script task — five tasks, five deliberate choices.

Step two: derive the edges. Cleaning depends on ingestion; gold depends on cleaning; the dashboard depends on gold; and validation depends on gold and the dashboard — that last one is a fan-in, and it is the safest place to attach a validator.

Step three: verify the graph is acyclic and note that the only real parallel opportunity is the dashboard refresh alongside any branch not listed as a dependency. The resulting depends_on lists are empty, ingest, clean, gold, and finally gold plus dashboard.

Why does this method work? Because depends_on encodes ordering, not runtime state — the same graph yields the same order on every run. Fan-in keeps validation from firing early. And watch the classic pitfalls: adding validation as a dependency of the dashboard instead of the reverse, forgetting that an omitted depends_on means start immediately, and assuming task order in the JSON implies execution order.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Choosing Task Types and Wiring Dependencies

questions.question: A data engineering team must create a task inside a Lakeflow Jobs workflow that executes an existing PySpark notebook to perform custom row-level transformation logic across a large Delta table. The notebook already exists in the workspace and requires a notebook path plus parameter values at runtime. According to the task-type comparison covered in this unit, which task type is the DEFAULT and best-fit choice for this workload?

options.label: A pipeline task, because ingestion-to-transformation logic should always be declared inside a Delta Live Tables-style declarative pipeline definition rather than in imperative code.
A SQL task, because SQL tasks run against a warehouse and therefore can express arbitrary row-level Python transformation logic more efficiently than a notebook.
A notebook task, because it runs an existing notebook (often PySpark) and is the default choice for custom transformation logic; the notebook must already exist in the workspace.
A Python script task, because a Python script is interchangeable with a notebook task and is required whenever parameters must be passed into PySpark code.

questions.analysis: A notebook task runs an existing notebook (often PySpark) and is the default choice for custom transformation logic; the notebook must exist in the workspace. That matches the workload exactly: existing notebook, PySpark, row-level custom logic, and runtime parameters. Option A confuses the pipeline task, which executes a declarative pipeline definition and is the better fit for ingestion/declarative dataflows, not imperative custom logic. Option B is wrong because a SQL task runs a query, dashboard, or SQL file against a warehouse and is ideal for set-based transformation and BI-serving layers, not arbitrary Python. Option D is wrong because a Python script task is a distinct task type with its own path requirement; it is not interchangeable with a notebook and is not required merely to pass parameters. Note that Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestration engine that schedules and automates multi-step pipelines by defining tasks, dependencies, triggers, and failure handling [source 2].

questions.question: A lakehouse job ingests raw orders, cleans them, builds a gold aggregate, refreshes a dashboard, and runs a final validation. In the job definition the engineer writes the following six depends_on declarations: (1) clean depends_on ingest; (2) gold depends_on clean; (3) dashboard depends_on ingest; (4) validate depends_on gold; (5) audit depends_on validate; (6) report depends_on dashboard. The stated ordering constraint is: 'the validation must run only after the gold aggregate has been produced, and the dashboard refresh must run before the validation is launched.' Which statements about the dependency graph are CORRECT? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A. Because a task with no depends_on starts immediately when the job run begins, ingest starts immediately, while clean, gold, dashboard, validate, audit, and report all wait for their declared upstreams.
B. The graph violates the stated constraint, because validate depends only on gold and therefore can begin as soon as gold finishes, even if the dashboard refresh has not completed.
C. dashboard and gold are both downstream of ingest and can run in parallel branches once their respectiv e upstreams finish; report is the fan-in point for the dashboard branch.
D. audit and report satisfy the requirement that validation runs before everything else, because dependency edges are evaluated in the alphabetical order of task names.

questions.analysis: A is correct: dependencies are declared per task with depends_on and the graph is inferred from those declarations, never drawn by hand; a task with no depends_on starts immediately when the job run begins, so ingest is runnable at t=0 and everything else must wait. B is correct and is the classic silent violation: the written constraint requires validation to run after the dashboard refresh, but validate depends only on gold. Since gold and the dashboard both sit downstream of ingest, validate can become runnable at the same moment the dashboard is still executing, violating the stated order. C is correct: gold depends on clean and dashboard depends on ingest, so once ingest and clean complete, the gold branch and dashboard branch can proceed in parallel; report, which depends on dashboard, is a fan-in point on that branch. D is wrong on two counts: there is no alphabetical evaluation order in a DAG, and edge evaluation is governed by dependencies, not task names. To repair the graph without breaking anything, add dashboard to validate's depends_on list (validate depends_on gold and dashboard), producing the correct fan-in described in the worked five-task example. Partial runs and repairs make it easier, faster, and cheaper to debug a failed task in such a graph without re-running the whole job [source 4].

questions.question: A team must build one Lakeflow Jobs workflow with these constraints: (i) raw events must be ingested declaratively as a streaming pipeline; (ii) a PySpark notebook must clean and conform the ingested data; (iii) a warehouse query must build the gold aggregate from the cleaned data; (iv) a dashboard refresh must run after the gold aggregate exists; (v) a Python validation script must run after BOTH the gold aggregate and the dashboard refresh complete; (vi) a nightly report must run after validation and after the dashboard refresh. For EACH of the six steps, name the task type you would choose and justify it in one sentence. Then write the complete set of depends_on edges, state which tasks can run in parallel, and identify any place where the constraints are ambiguous or would force a cycle. Cite at least one source marker.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Task-type mapping (40%): pipeline task for ingestion, notebook task for cleaning, SQL task for the gold aggregate, SQL task for the dashboard refresh, Python script task for validation, and a script/SQL task for the report, each with a defensible one-sentence justification. Deduct half credit for any mapping that swaps notebook and pipeline, or that claims a SQL task can execute PySpark row-level logic. (2) Edge derivation (30%): the answer must state clean depends_on ingest; gold depends_on clean; dashboard depends_on gold; validate depends_on gold AND dashboard; report depends_on validate AND dashboard. Deduct proportionally for missing fan-in edges, especially report missing dashboard. (3) Parallelism and cycle check (20%): identifies ingest as the only task runnable at t=0; notes that after gold completes, dashboard and validate's gold prerequisite are both satisfied, so dashboard proceeds while validate waits on dashboard; explicitly checks for a cycle and reports none when the written edges match the constraints. (4) Source citation and clarity (10%): cites at least one [source N] marker accurately and uses Databricks terminology correctly.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. Step 1 — ingest raw events declaratively: choose a pipeline task, because pipeline tasks execute a declarative pipeline definition and are the best fit for ingestion dataflows. Step 2 — clean and conform in PySpark: choose a notebook task, because it runs an existing notebook (often PySpark) and is the default for custom transformation logic; the notebook must exist in the workspace. Steps 3 and 4 — gold aggregate and dashboard refresh: choose SQL tasks, because a SQL task runs a query, dashboard, or SQL file against a warehouse and is ideal for set-based transformation and BI-serving layers. Step 5 — Python validation: choose a Python script task. Step 6 — nightly report: choose a SQL task or a Python script task, depending on whether the report is a warehouse query or generated programmatically. Edges: clean depends_on ingest; gold depends_on clean; dashboard depends_on gold; validate depends_on gold and dashboard; report depends_on validate and dashboard. Initially only ingest is runnable, since a task with no depends_on starts immediately when the job run begins. After gold finishes, the dashboard refresh becomes runnable, and validate remains blocked until dashboard also finishes; that is the fan-in that enforces 'validation after both gold and dashboard.' report then fans in on validate and on dashboard, the latter already complete, so it adds no extra wait. No cycle exists because every edge points strictly forward in the ingest → clean → gold → dashboard → validate → report chain. Ambiguity note: if the written requirement said 'the report must run after validation but before the dashboard refresh,' that would conflict with the edge report depends_on dashboard and force a cycle, which the platform will reject as an invalid DAG. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestrator for the lakehouse, covering jobs, tasks, dependencies, triggers, and cron schedules, so all of this is configured as job metadata rather than drawn by hand [source 3]; the native engine schedules and automates multi-step data pipelines by defining tasks, dependencies, triggers, and failure handling [source 2]. Orchestration also includes compute resource allocation and monitoring of workflows, which is why the whole chain is modeled as one job rather than six independent scripts [source 6].

actions.text: This checkpoint pulls together everything we've discussed about choosing task types and wiring dependencies. Take each question on your own and work through it carefully — think about the task-type comparison, the depends_on edges, and the ordering constraints exactly as we covered them.
Once you submit, I'll join you to walk through what tripped you up and reinforce the reasoning. Go ahead and give it your best attempt.

hints: A multi-task job keeps everything under tasks. Each task needs a unique task_key plus exactly one task-type field: notebook_task, sql_task, pipeline_task, and so on. A task with zero or with two task-type fields is rejected by the Jobs API.

scenes.title: Design Decision: One Job with Many Tasks, or Many Small Jobs?

elements.content: Decision — A four-engineer data platform team owns a nightly medallion pipeline (bronze ingest → silver clean → gold aggregate → dashboard refresh → validation) that must satisfy a 02:00 SLA, serves three downstream consumers of the gold table, and is frequently debugged by re-running only the validation step after a fix. The team must decide now — before the next sprint — whether to encode the pipeline as one Lakeflow job with five tasks, five chained jobs (each wired with Run Job tasks), or a single monolithic notebook, and the wrong choice will either fragment observability or lock them into a rigid scheduling topology. The difficulty is that all three structures run the same transformation code, so the decision is not about the code at all: it is about which orchestration object owns the run history, where partial repair is legal, and which unit the SLA can be measured against [source 3][source 6].

Constraints — Five dependent steps (ingest → clean → gold → dashboard → validate) that must execute in that order every night, with validation fanning in after gold and dashboard.  •  A single nightly 02:00 SLA must be observable end-to-end, so the start and finish of the whole pipeline must belong to one run record.  •  Three independent consumers read the gold table, so the gold task's boundaries must be visible and stable to downstream owners.  •  The team must be able to re-run only the validation step after a code fix without re-executing ingest, clean, gold, or dashboard (partial repair).  •  The engineering team is four people, so operational overhead (number of schedulers, number of run histories to read, number of places a cron lives) is a first-class cost.

One Lakeflow job containing five tasks with declared depends_on edges
+ Because a job is a container of tasks plus schedule and configuration, and a job run is the single parent of every task run, the 02:00 SLA maps directly onto one run record with one start time and one finish time — exactly the observability the SLA demands [source 3][source 6].; + Partial repair is native: Databricks documents that 'partial runs and repairs make it easier, faster, and cheaper to debug failed tasks,' so re-running just the validation task after a fix does not re-execute the four upstream tasks [source 4].; + The dependency graph is inferred from per-task depends_on declarations rather than drawn by hand, so the validation fan-in edge is declared once and the engine enforces it; there is exactly one dependency graph to reason about [source 1][source 3].
− All five steps share one job-level schedule, so if validation later needs its own independent cron, it cannot have one without being promoted to a separate job.; − Task-level ownership is weaker than job-level ownership: the run history is one record, so attributing a slow task to a specific team requires reading task runs inside the job rather than reading a job that belongs to that team.
Best for: Tightly coupled steps that share one SLA and whose failures are repaired at task granularity.

Five separate jobs chained with Run Job tasks
+ Each step gets its own job definition, its own schedule, and its own owning team, which is real value when a step genuinely has an independent cadence or a different on-call rotation [source 2].; + A failure in one job can be retried, inspected, and monitored as a first-class unit, and each job's run history is isolated from the others [source 6].
− The end-to-end 02:00 SLA now spans five separate job runs linked only by Run Job task edges, so computing total latency requires joining five run histories rather than reading one — this is exactly the harder-to-reason-about latency the decision brief warns about [source 6].; − Partial repair becomes ambiguous: repairing the validation job is easy, but repairing 'the pipeline' means repairing one job among five, and the dependency chain must be reconstructed mentally rather than read from a single graph [source 2][source 4].; − Operational overhead scales with team size: four engineers now maintain five job definitions, five schedules, and five notification configurations for one nightly pipeline [source 3].
Best for: Steps with genuinely independent schedules or distinct owning teams that must be scheduled and monitored separately.

One monolithic notebook that performs all five steps sequentially
+ Fastest to author: one file, one commit, no orchestration objects to declare, which is attractive under a short deadline [source 2].
− There is no dependency graph to inspect, so the ordering constraint is buried in cell execution order rather than declared as depends_on — the engine cannot show which task is runnable or why a downstream step has not started [source 3][source 6].; − There is no partial repair: fixing the validation step means re-running the whole notebook, re-executing ingest, clean, gold, and dashboard against the three consumers of the gold table [source 4].; − There is no per-task monitoring, so the 02:00 SLA cannot be decomposed into per-step latency and a failure in validation is indistinguishable from a failure in ingest in the notebook's single output log [source 3].
Best for: Throwaway exploration or a one-off ad-hoc analysis where no SLA, no downstream consumers, and no repair workflow exist.

Recommendation: One Lakeflow job containing five tasks with declared depends_on edges — The binding constraints are the single 02:00 SLA, the shared dependency chain, and task-granular repair. Option A satisfies all three simultaneously: one job run is the parent of all five task runs, so the SLA is measured against a single run record rather than five joined histories [source 3][source 6]; the validation fan-in is declared once as a depends_on edge and enforced by the engine, so the ordering constraint cannot be silently violated [source 1]; and Databricks explicitly supports partial runs and repairs inside a job, which is precisely the re-run-just-validation workflow the team needs [source 4]. Option B only wins if a step gains an independent schedule or a different owning team, and Option C fails the SLA, monitoring, and repair constraints outright. Revisit the decision and promote a step to its own job only when one of those triggers actually fires.

actions.text: Building on the job and task vocabulary we just covered, let's apply it to a real design decision. Here's the scenario: a four-engineer data platform team owns a pipeline, and they need to decide how to structure it in Lakeflow Jobs.

Start by pinning down the constraints, because the answer has to fall out of them. We have five dependent steps — ingest, clean, and so on — a nightly 02:00 SLA, three consumers of the gold table, and critically, a team that needs to re-run just the validation step after fixing a bug. That last one is the constraint most people overlook.

Option A: one Lakeflow job containing five tasks with declared dependencies. You get a single run history, one dependency graph, and — this is the key point — Databricks lets you repair individual tasks inside a job run. So that 're-run just validation' requirement is satisfied natively.

Option B: five separate jobs chained together with Run Job tasks. Each step gets finer-grained scheduling and ownership, but now your run history is fragmented across five jobs, and reasoning about end-to-end latency becomes genuinely harder. Notice the tradeoff — flexibility bought with observability.

Option C: one monolithic notebook doing all five steps. It's the fastest to write, but you lose dependency visibility, you can't partially repair, and there's no per-task monitoring. On the exam, this option is almost always the trap.

So the recommendation is Option A. The steps are tightly coupled, they share a single SLA, and task-level repair gives us exactly what the team asked for. But here's the revision trigger worth remembering: if a step ever gains an independent schedule or a different owning team, promote it to its own job and trigger it as a downstream task. That keeps this decision honest as the pipeline evolves.

scenes.title: Lesson Assessment: Jobs and Task Orchestration Basics

questions.question: A data engineer defines one job containing four tasks: ingest, clean, aggregate, and validate. The engineer runs the job once. Which statement correctly describes the resulting orchestration objects?

options.label: One job run is created, and each of the four tasks produces its own task run; the job run is the parent of all four task runs.
Four job runs are created, one per task, and one task run is created for the whole execution.
One job run and one task run are created; the task run represents the aggregated status of all four tasks.
No job run is created until all four task runs complete, at which point a single task run is promoted to a job run.

questions.correctAnswer: One job run is created, and each of the four tasks produces its own task run; the job run is the parent of all four task runs.
questions.analysis: A job is the definition (the container of tasks plus schedule and configuration), and a job run is exactly one execution of that definition. Every task inside the job produces its own task run during that execution, and the job run is the parent object of every task run. Distractor B inverts the nesting; distractor C confuses a job run with a task run; distractor D invents a promotion mechanism that does not exist. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestration engine on Databricks, formerly Databricks Workflows [source 1][source 2].
answer: One job run is created, and each of the four tasks produces its own task run; the job run is the parent of all four task runs.

questions.question: A job declares three tasks with the following depends_on declarations: task ingest has no depends_on; task clean declares depends_on: [ingest]; task enrich declares depends_on: [ingest]. Which statements about the execution of this job run are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: clean and enrich can begin executing at the same time, as soon as ingest has finished successfully.
ingest starts immediately when the job run begins because it has no depends_on declaration.
The DAG for this job is inferred from the depends_on declarations rather than drawn by hand.
enrich could start before ingest finishes because tasks are executed in the order they are listed in the tasks list.

correctAnswer: clean and enrich can begin executing at the same time, as soon as ingest has finished successfully.
ingest starts immediately when the job run begins because it has no depends_on declaration.
The DAG for this job is inferred from the depends_on declarations rather than drawn by hand.
questions.analysis: Dependencies are declared per task with depends_on, and the graph is inferred from those declarations, never drawn by hand. A task with no depends_on starts immediately when the job run begins, and independent downstream tasks whose upstream dependency has completed can run in parallel, so clean and enrich form a parallel fan-out after ingest. Option D encodes the classic misconception that list order in the task list implies execution order; orchestration is driven strictly by declared dependencies, not by ordering in the tasks array [source 2][source 6].
answer: clean and enrich can begin executing at the same time, as soon as ingest has finished successfully.
ingest starts immediately when the job run begins because it has no depends_on declaration.
The DAG for this job is inferred from the depends_on declarations rather than drawn by hand.

questions.question: A team must ingest raw orders as they land in cloud storage, then apply custom PySpark transformation logic, then publish a gold aggregate for BI consumption. Which task-type assignment best matches each workload to the correct Lakeflow Jobs task type?

options.label: Pipeline task for ingestion, notebook task for the PySpark transformation, SQL task for the gold aggregate serving layer.
Notebook task for ingestion, SQL task for the PySpark transformation, pipeline task for the gold aggregate serving layer.
SQL task for ingestion, pipeline task for the PySpark transformation, notebook task for the gold aggregate serving layer.
Pipeline task for ingestion, SQL task for the PySpark transformation, notebook task for the gold aggregate serving layer.

questions.correctAnswer: Pipeline task for ingestion, notebook task for the PySpark transformation, SQL task for the gold aggregate serving layer.
questions.analysis: A pipeline task is best for declarative ingestion (for example, landing raw orders from storage), a notebook task is the default choice for custom transformation logic such as PySpark code, and a SQL task against a warehouse is ideal for set-based transformation and BI-serving layers such as a gold aggregate. Option B and C scramble the mapping; option D substitutes a SQL task for custom PySpark logic, which is a common but incorrect shortcut because arbitrary PySpark transformations cannot be expressed as a SQL query. Lakeflow Jobs schedules and monitors these data pipelines as its orchestration layer on Databricks [source 1][source 5].
answer: Pipeline task for ingestion, notebook task for the PySpark transformation, SQL task for the gold aggregate serving layer.

questions.question: A five-task job must ingest raw orders, clean them with PySpark, build a gold aggregate, refresh a dashboard, and run a final validation script that must execute only after everything else has finished. Describe the task type you would assign to each of the five workloads, then write the depends_on edges that encode the required ordering, and explain why the validation task must fan in from multiple upstream tasks rather than from the gold aggregate alone.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Correct task-type mapping, 40% — pipeline task for ingestion, notebook task for PySpark cleaning, SQL task for the gold aggregate, SQL task for the dashboard refresh, Python script task for validation. (2) Correct depends_on edges, 35% — clean depends_on ingest; gold depends_on clean; dashboard depends_on gold; validation depends_on both gold and dashboard (fan-in). (3) Justification of fan-in, 25% — the validation must not start until every upstream task it verifies has completed, so its depends_on must list all upstream predecessors; depending on gold alone would silently allow validation to start while the dashboard refresh is still running, violating the stated ordering constraint.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: assign a pipeline task to ingestion, a notebook task to the PySpark cleaning step, a SQL task to the gold aggregate, a SQL task to the dashboard refresh, and a Python script task to validation. Edge derivation follows the written constraints: cleaning depends on ingestion; gold depends on cleaning; dashboard depends on gold; validation depends on both gold and dashboard, forming a fan-in. The DAG is inferred from these depends_on declarations and is never drawn by hand. The key reasoning point is that a downstream task runs only after all of its declared upstream tasks finish, so validation must enumerate every predecessor it depends on; omitting the dashboard edge would allow validation to begin before the dashboard refresh completes. Lakeflow Jobs serves as the orchestration layer for such multi-step workflows [source 3][source 5][source 6].

actions.text: You've made some careful choices about how to wire up orchestration — now it's time to see how well those decisions stuck. Work through each question on your own, and think through your reasoning as you go, since a couple of these ask you to justify your design choices.
Take your time on each one and submit when you're ready — I'll be right here afterward to walk through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: From Static DAG to Parameterized Workflow

elements.content: From Static DAG to Parameterized Workflow
Unit: Orchestration  •  Prerequisite recap: jobs, tasks, depends_on, and runs from the orchestration object model
Lesson Goal

Turn a fixed multi-task DAG into a reusable workflow driven by parameters and conditions.

A hard-coded DAG is brittle: every new date, region, or input table forces a code edit.

Exam focus — given a job definition plus inputs, predict which tasks run and with which resolved parameter values.
Two Objectives

1. Pass values between tasks: job parameters, task parameters, dynamic value references, and task values.

2. Add control flow: Run-if conditions for branching and For each tasks for iteration.

Both objectives map directly to Databricks exam items on Lakeflow Jobs definitions.
Worked Example — Why a Parameter Beats a Hard-Coded Path

Hard-coded DAG: path s3://raw/orders/2024-01-01/ fails on 2024-01-02 and needs a code edit. Parameterized: path s3://raw/orders/{{job.parameters.run_date}}/ with default 2024-01-01 — one definition runs every day, unchanged. References: [source 2] [source 3] [source 5]

actions.text: Alright, let's pick up where we left off. So far we've built jobs as fixed dependency graphs — a set of tasks, wired together in a specific order. That works, but it's static. On this page, we shift from a static DAG to a parameterized workflow: a job that accepts inputs and behaves differently depending on what it receives.

We're still inside the Orchestration unit. As a quick refresher, we just covered the orchestration object model — jobs, tasks, and runs. Keep those three terms in your head, because everything we're about to do builds directly on top of them.

Here's our lesson goal. The idea is simple: take a fixed multi-task DAG and turn it into a reusable workflow — one that's driven by parameters and conditions rather than by values baked into the definition.

We have two objectives. First, pass values between tasks — using job parameters, task parameters, dynamic value references, and task values. Second, add control flow: Run-if conditions give you branching, and For each tasks give you iteration. Those four ingredients are the whole toolkit for this lesson.

Let's motivate it with a worked example. Suppose a task hard-codes a path like s3 raw orders slash twenty twenty-four, zero one, zero one. It runs — once, for that exact date. But tomorrow that task is wrong, and you're editing code, redeploying, and hoping you don't typo a date. That's the brittleness we're going to remove.

And here's the exam framing, so you know what to listen for: given a job definition and a set of inputs, you should be able to predict which tasks run, and with which resolved parameter values. That single skill ties this whole lesson together. Let's dive in.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Job and Task Parameters

questions.question: In a Lakeflow Jobs (formerly Databricks Workflows) multi-task job, which statement correctly describes the scope of a job parameter versus a task parameter?

options.label: A job parameter is defined once at the job level and is available to every task in the job, whereas a task parameter is scoped to one specific task.
A job parameter is scoped to a single task, whereas a task parameter applies to every task in the job run.
Job parameters and task parameters are both visible only inside the task where they are declared, and they are never shared.
Job parameters can only be consumed by SQL tasks, while task parameters can only be consumed by notebook tasks.

questions.correctAnswer: A job parameter is defined once at the job level and is available to every task in the job, whereas a task parameter is scoped to one specific task.
questions.analysis: Lakeflow Jobs lets you parameterize a workflow at two levels. A job parameter is declared at the job level and is exposed to every task, which is why it is the preferred mechanism for values that many tasks need (for example, a processing date). A task parameter is declared inside a single task definition and only affects that task. Option B reverses the two scopes. Option C is wrong because job parameters, by definition, are shared across tasks. Option D invents a task-type restriction that does not exist; both SQL and notebook tasks can receive parameters [source 3][source 2]. This distinction mirrors the classic exam trap of confusing 'available to the whole job' with 'available to the whole task'.
answer: A job parameter is defined once at the job level and is available to every task in the job, whereas a task parameter is scoped to one specific task.

questions.question: A job defines a job parameter named country = 'US'. One of its notebook tasks also defines a task parameter named country = 'CA'. Which two statements are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Inside that task, the task-level value ('CA') takes precedence over the job-level value ('US') for the name country.
Inside that task, the job-level value ('US') always wins because job parameters are global and cannot be overridden.
A notebook task still has to retrieve the effective value with dbutils.widgets.get("country") before the value can be used in code.
Because two values exist for the same name, the job fails validation with a duplicate-parameter error.

correctAnswer: Inside that task, the task-level value ('CA') takes precedence over the job-level value ('US') for the name country.
A notebook task still has to retrieve the effective value with dbutils.widgets.get("country") before the value can be used in code.
questions.analysis: Precedence follows specificity: when a name is defined at both levels, the task-level value overrides the job-level value for that task, so the notebook sees 'CA'. Option B is the most common misconception — it assumes global beats local, which is backwards. Option D is false; shadowing a job parameter with a task parameter is legal and not a duplicate-name error. Crucially, and this is the trap this checkpoint targets, being visible is not the same as being read: a notebook task must still pull the value through dbutils.widgets.get("country") to bind it to a widget-backed variable [source 3][source 1]. Students who assume a notebook can silently read a job parameter without widgets.get() lose these marks.
answer: Inside that task, the task-level value ('CA') takes precedence over the job-level value ('US') for the name country.
A notebook task still has to retrieve the effective value with dbutils.widgets.get("country") before the value can be used in code.

questions.question: You are building a notebook task inside a Lakeflow Job (formerly Databricks Workflows) that must consume a job-level parameter called run_date. Explain (a) how a job parameter reaches a notebook task, (b) the exact reference syntax you would use in the task configuration and in the notebook code, and (c) what will happen if the notebook calls dbutils.widgets.get("run_date") but no widget or parameter of that name is bound to the task. Support your answer with reference to formal precedence rules.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Correctly states that a job parameter defined at the job level is visible to every task, including this notebook task, and that scope is not limited to one task — 30%. (2) Provides the correct JSON reference syntax, e.g. "{{job.parameters.run_date}}" in the task's base_parameters (or equivalent job-parameters reference such as "{{job.parameters.run_date}}" used in a task's parameters block) and the dbutils.widgets.get("run_date") call to read it in the notebook — 30%. (3) Explains precedence: task-level parameters override same-named job-level parameters for that task; when only the job-level parameter exists, that value is used — 20%. (4) Notes the failure mode: if no widget or parameter named run_date is bound, dbutils.widgets.get("run_date") raises an error (InputWidgetNotDefined / value not found), because a notebook cannot implicitly read job parameters without an explicit widget binding — 20%.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: (a) Job parameters are declared at the job level and are available to every task, so a notebook task inherits run_date unless a task parameter of the same name overrides it. (b) In the task definition, reference the job parameter with the JSON placeholder syntax, for example "{{job.parameters.run_date}}" placed inside the task's parameters/base_parameters; in the notebook code, read it with dbutils.widgets.get("run_date") (or an equivalent typed widget such as dbutils.widgets.getArgument in some contexts) and assign it to a Python variable. (c) If run_date is not bound as a widget or task parameter, dbutils.widgets.get("run_date") fails at runtime with an InputWidgetNotDefined-style error rather than silently returning a default — this is exactly the trap where learners assume a notebook can read a job parameter without any explicit widget access. Precedence: task-level values override job-level values for the same name; job-level values fill in when no task-level value exists [source 3][source 2][source 1]. Students should also note that partial runs and repairs allow re-running a single failed task without re-running the whole job, which is why being able to re-bind run_date per repair matters [source 4].
