scenes.title: Dynamic Value References and Task Values

elements.content: Dynamic Value References & Task Values

A static DAG becomes reusable when tasks pass data through runtime values: built-in dynamic references are resolved by the orchestrator at execution time, while task values are custom data a producer publishes for downstream tasks. The run-time engine Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestrator for the Lakehouse [source 3], and orchestration requires managing these dependencies and scheduling the tasks that consume them [source 6].

Publish: dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key, value) stores one custom value per key inside the producing task run.

Values must be JSON-serializable and are size-limited; pass IDs and counts, not large payloads.
Consume: dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(taskKey="...", key="...", default=...) — taskKey names the producing task, and default is returned when the key is missing.
Read rule: only tasks that declare depends_on on the producer may read its values. Parallel or upstream tasks cannot — visibility follows the DAG edge.
Worked example: clean_orders sets rows_written = 48213; the downstream gold_aggregate reads it with a default=0 and aborts if the count is 0.

actions.text: Now that we've covered job and task parameters, let's tackle the next piece of parameterized workflows: dynamic value references and task values. This is how a downstream task consumes a value that only exists at run time — something you can't know when you author the job.

Start with this reference cheat sheet. These are the built-in dynamic references Lakeflow Jobs gives you out of the box — {{job.id}}, {{job.run_id}}, {{job.parameters.<key>}}, {{tasks.<task>.result_state}} for the status of an upstream task, and {{tasks.<task>.values.<key>}} to pull a custom value a producer task published.

To publish a value, a task calls dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set with a key and a value. Two things to remember for the exam: the value must be JSON-serializable, and there's a size limit, so don't try to push an entire DataFrame through it.

On the consuming side, a downstream task reads it with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get, passing the taskKey, the key, and optionally a default for safety. Pair that with the {{tasks.<task>.values.<key>}} reference and you get a clean producer-consumer handoff.
Here's the rule people get wrong: only tasks that declare depends_on on the producing task can read its values. Parallel tasks and upstream tasks cannot — the dependency must be explicit in the DAG.

Let's walk the worked example. clean_orders sets rows_written to 4200, and a downstream task reads that count with a default of zero. Notice the trap alongside it: if you use dbutils.notebook.exit, you only get a string result — so when you need a structured, typed task value, taskValues.set and get is the correct tool. We'll practice this in the next worked problem, where Task A passes a row count to Task B.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Pass a Row Count from Task A to Task B

elements.content: Problem 1

A Lakeflow Jobs job named orders_daily contains two tasks. Task A (notebook task, task_key = "ingest_orders") reads raw files, overwrites the Delta table bronze.orders, and on the run of 2024-11-27 writes exactly 184,732 rows. Task B (notebook task, task_key = "aggregate_orders", depends_on = ["ingest_orders"]) must execute its aggregation only when Task A wrote at least one row, and must exit early (a guarded no-op) otherwise. (a) Write the code that publishes the row count from Task A. (b) Write the code that reads it in Task B. (c) State exactly what value Task B receives on this run and what it receives if Task A did not execute at all during a repair run.
Hint: Publish the value after the write, not before; consume it with an explicit default.

Worked solution
Step 1 — publish the value in Task A. After the Delta write completes, compute the count and store it under a stable key: count = spark.table("bronze.orders").count(); dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="row_count", value=count). On this run count = 184,732, so the value stored for task_key "ingest_orders" and key "row_count" is the integer 184,732. The call must happen inside a job run (during an interactive notebook session the task-values API is not available), and it must happen before any dbutils.notebook.exit() or raised exception, because once the notebook exits the value can no longer be written. Step 2 — consume the value in Task B, always with a default: row_count = dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(taskKey="ingest_orders", key="row_count", default=0). Step 3 — branch on the returned integer: if row_count > 0: run the aggregation else: dbutils.notebook.exit("skipped: no new rows"). Step 4 — evaluate the two scenarios. On the 2024-11-27 run the get() returns the integer 184,732, the comparison 184,732 > 0 is True, and the aggregation runs. In a repair run where only Task B (and its downstream tasks) is re-executed because Task A previously succeeded, the value may still be present from the original run; but in a repair or partial run where Task A was never executed in that run and the value is absent, get() returns the default 0 and Task B exits cleanly instead of failing. Step 5 — note the type. Because task values preserve JSON types, 184,732 comes back as an integer, not the string "184732"; the comparison row_count > 0 therefore behaves numerically. If a value is ever routed through a widget or a string-valued parameter, coerce it defensively with int(row_count).

Analysis — The method works because task values are typed, DAG-scoped key-value pairs: a task publishes under task_key + key, and only tasks in the same job run can read them, which is exactly the coordination primitive an orchestrator needs when tasks are separate processes that share no memory [source 6][source 2]. The critical design choice is the default argument. get() without a default raises an error when the key is missing, which converts a benign 'Task A did not run' situation into a failed run; supplying default=0 turns it into a defined branch. This is why partial runs and repairs are cheaper to debug when values are read defensively [source 4]. Common mistakes: (1) calling set() before the write, so the count reflects the previous version of the table; (2) calling set() only inside the if count > 0 branch — this happens to work for a row count because absence and zero are both falsy, but it is a latent bug for any non-zero-valued payload such as a watermark timestamp, where absence would be silently read as 'no new data'; (3) key or task_key typos, which survive code review because they only fail at run time; (4) assuming the value survives across job runs — it does not, it is scoped to the run (and to the repair lineage of that run). Generalization: the same set/get pair carries file paths, watermarks, run modes, or a 'should_process' boolean, which is the standard pattern for gating downstream work in a multi-task DAG [source 3].
Problem 2

The same orders_daily job runs every night. The aggregation in Task B takes 42 minutes on a 4-worker cluster whose all-purpose-plus-jobs compute consumes 16 DBU per hour, and the downstream gold SQL refresh in Task C takes 9 minutes on a serverless SQL warehouse billed at 4 DBU per hour. On 2024-11-28 the source system is closed for a holiday, so Task A overwrites bronze.orders with 0 rows. (a) Show how Task A must publish the count so that a zero is distinguishable from a missing value. (b) Show how Task B and Task C are prevented from doing useless work. (c) Compute the DBUs saved on that day, and the annual saving if 15 such zero-row nights occur per year.
Hint: Publish 0 explicitly; never rely on 'the key is absent' to mean 'no rows'.

Worked solution
Step 1 — publish unconditionally in Task A. count = spark.table("bronze.orders").count() returns 0; then dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="row_count", value=count) writes the integer 0. The set() call must sit outside any conditional. If you wrote if count > 0: dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(...), the key would simply not exist on a zero-row night, and every consumer would have to guess whether 'missing' means 'no rows' or 'Task A failed/never ran'. Step 2 — guard Task B in code. row_count = dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(taskKey="ingest_orders", key="row_count", default=0); if row_count == 0: dbutils.notebook.exit("holiday: nothing to aggregate") else: aggregate. On 2024-11-28 the notebook starts, reads 0, and exits in seconds instead of burning 42 minutes of cluster time. Step 3 — stop Task C declaratively as well. Task C is a SQL task whose parameters come from configuration JSON, where the value is referenced as "order_count": "{{tasks.ingest_orders.values.row_count}}". Attach the Run-if condition {{tasks.ingest_orders.values.row_count}} > 0 to Task C so the task is never started when the count is 0; the reference is resolved before the task begins, and the guard prevents the warehouse from starting at all. Step 4 — compute the saving. Task B avoided: 42 minutes = 42/60 = 0.7 hours, and 0.7 h x 16 DBU/h = 11.2 DBU. Task C avoided: 9 minutes = 9/60 = 0.15 hours, and 0.15 h x 4 DBU/h = 0.6 DBU. Total per zero-row night = 11.2 + 0.6 = 11.8 DBU. Across 15 such nights per year = 15 x 11.8 = 177 DBU of pure waste avoided, before any reduction in failed-run notifications or on-call noise.

Analysis — This exercise separates two ideas that beginners merge: the presence of a value and the truthiness of a value. Publishing an explicit 0 makes 'there were no rows' a fact the job recorded, whereas an absent key means only 'no one wrote it', which is an operational ambiguity. The default in get() exists so that consumers of an absent key degrade gracefully rather than failing, which is precisely the behavior you want on repairs and partial runs where upstream tasks did not execute [source 4]. The Run-if condition is the second layer: guarding inside the notebook still pays for cluster start-up and notebook launch overhead, while a Run-if condition stops the task before it starts, and Lakeflow Jobs treats dependencies, Run-if conditions, and triggers as first-class job features [source 3][source 2]. Edge cases to watch: (1) a Run-if condition that references a task value from a task that is itself skipped can resolve to a missing value and fail the task at start-up, so the upstream set() must be unconditional; (2) task_key matching is exact and case-sensitive, so tasks.ingest_orders.values.row_count is not the same reference as tasks.Ingest_orders...; (3) task values are meant for small scalars — never publish a DataFrame, a row list, or a large result set; if you need to move bulk data, write it to a Delta table and pass the table name as the value. Generalization: the publish-always / read-with-default / guard-early triad is the standard way to make an idempotent nightly pipeline cheap on empty days.
Problem 3

Task D of orders_daily is a SQL task that reconciles the bronze and silver layers. It must compare the bronze row count published by Task A with the number of rows that actually landed in silver.orders, and it must receive the bronze count through its configuration JSON rather than through code. On 2024-11-27, Task A published 184,732, and silver.orders contains 184,520 rows. (a) Write the parameter reference and the reconciling query. (b) Compute the dropped-row ratio and decide whether the job should alert, given a 0.05% alert threshold. (c) Explain what happens if the reference is written incorrectly or the upstream value is missing.
Hint: The reference is resolved before the query starts, so a broken reference fails the task, not the SQL statement.

Worked solution
Step 1 — declare the parameter in configuration JSON. The SQL task's parameters field contains {"bronze_count": "{{tasks.ingest_orders.values.row_count}}"}; the double braces mark a dynamic value reference, tasks.ingest_orders identifies the producing task by its exact task_key, values selects the task-values namespace, and row_count is the exact key used in set(). Step 2 — use the injected parameter in the query. SELECT ({{bronze_count}} - COUNT(*)) AS dropped_rows, ({{bronze_count}} - COUNT(*)) * 1.0 / {{bronze_count}} AS drop_ratio FROM silver.orders. Step 3 — evaluate with the run's numbers. bronze_count resolves to 184,732; COUNT(*) on silver.orders returns 184,520; dropped_rows = 184,732 - 184,520 = 212. Ratio = 212 / 184,732 = 0.0011476, i.e. 0.1148%, which rounds to about 0.11%. Step 4 — compare against the threshold. 0.11% > 0.05%, so the reconciliation breaches the alert threshold and the job should raise an alert or fail this task by design; 212 rows is roughly double the tolerance of 0.05% x 184,732 = 92.4 rows, so the breach is real and not a rounding artifact. Step 5 — wire the ordering. Task D must declare depends_on = ["ingest_orders"] so that the producer is guaranteed to have finished before the value is read; the reference is resolved at task start, and without the dependency the read can occur before the value exists [source 6]. Step 6 — handle failure modes. If the key were mistyped (for example {{tasks.ingest_orders.value.row_count}} or a wrong task_key), or if Task A had been skipped in a repair run, the value would be unresolvable and the task would fail at start-up with a resolution error rather than running the query. The mitigation is to keep set() unconditional in Task A and, where the consumer is code rather than JSON, to use the default argument described in the previous problems.

Analysis — Passing a number into configuration JSON rather than into code is what lets a SQL task, a dashboard refresh, or any non-Python task participate in the same data contract: Lakeflow Jobs resolves dynamic value references before the task starts, so the reference behaves as an injected constant [source 4][source 3]. This is also why the failure mode is severe and early: an unresolvable reference fails the task at start-up, producing a dependency-resolution error rather than a SQL error, which is a common source of confusion when reading run logs. The accounting is worth internalizing — a drop ratio of (bronze - silver) / bronze is a proportional measure, so the same 212 lost rows are 0.11% of a 184,732-row day but 2.1% of a 10,000-row day; always pair an absolute threshold with a ratio threshold so small days do not hide under a percentage and large days do not alert on trivia. Edge cases: an empty silver table makes COUNT(*) = 0 and the ratio exactly 1.0, which should be alerted on but may indicate an upstream write failure rather than data loss; a zero bronze count makes the ratio a division by zero, so either guard the task with a Run-if condition requiring row_count > 0 or use a CASE expression; and task_key/case sensitivity means the reference must match the job definition character for character. Generalization: the same mechanism carries any scalar contract between tasks — an environment name, a watermark, a partition date — and it is the recommended way to parameterize non-notebook tasks in a multi-task DAG [source 1][source 2].

actions.text: Let's start with Problem 1. The same orders_daily job runs every night, and Task A writes into bronze.orders while Task B must only run its aggregation when A actually wrote at least one row — otherwise Task B should exit early. This is exactly the scenario we set up on the previous page, so now let's build it out for real.

Before we look at the solution, here's the hint that matters most: publish the value after the write, not before. If you publish a count before the table has been written, you're reporting a number that doesn't reflect what Task B will actually see. The order of operations here is the whole point.

Step one: in Task A, after the write completes, we call dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set with key row_count, and we feed it the result of spark.table on bronze.orders, followed by count. So the value we publish is the true, post-write row count. Then in Task B, step two, we read it back with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get, passing taskKey A, key row_count, and default equal to zero. That returned integer is what we branch on — if it's zero, exit early; if it's greater than zero, run the aggregation.

Now the analysis, and this is the exam-worthy part. Notice that the value comes back as a typed integer, not a string — task values preserve type, so you can compare and branch on it directly. They're also DAG-scoped, meaning they only flow along the dependency edges you declared; Task B can only see values that A published because the DAG says B depends on A. And that default argument isn't cosmetic — it's what keeps partial runs and repair runs from crashing when Task A never executed.

So to close Problem 1: publish after the write, read with an explicit default, and branch on the typed result. That's the pattern you'll be asked to recognize and reproduce on the exam. But there's a subtle trap hiding in that default value, and Problem 2 is designed to spring it on you.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Run-if Conditions

questions.question: A Lakeflow Jobs workflow defines a validation task with the Run-if condition 'All succeeded'. In a given run, the upstream cleaning task fails. Which of the following best describes what happens to the validation task?

options.label: The validation task is skipped, because 'All succeeded' only admits a run when every upstream dependency completed successfully.
The validation task runs anyway, because 'All succeeded' is equivalent to 'All done'.
The validation task runs and is marked as succeeded, because a failed dependency is treated as succeeded by default.
The validation task is retried automatically until the upstream task succeeds.

questions.analysis: This tests Test Point 1 and the frequently confused difference between 'All succeeded' and 'All done'. In Lakeflow Jobs, the Run-if menu ('All succeeded', 'At least one succeeded', 'All done', 'At least one failed', 'All failed') determines whether a downstream task is admitted, and the default condition is 'All succeeded', not 'All done' as many learners assume [source 3]. 'All succeeded' requires every upstream dependency to reach a successful terminal state; a single failed dependency disqualifies the task, so it is skipped rather than run. Option B is wrong precisely because 'All done' is the broader condition that fires after every upstream task reaches any terminal state, including failure. Option C is a misconception about how terminal states are interpreted—there is no notion of a failed task being counted as succeeded. Option D confuses Run-if with retry logic, which is a separate part of failure handling [source 2], not a property of the condition itself. 'All succeeded' therefore represents the most restrictive of the admission conditions and is exactly why the default matters: it means a failed task blocks its dependents unless the condition is changed to something more permissive [source 3].

questions.question: A five-task job has a cleanup task with Run-if set to 'All done'. Its upstream dependency, an ingest task, fails after three retries. Which statements correctly describe the Run-if semantics in this scenario? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The cleanup task is admitted because 'All done' fires once every upstream task has reached any terminal state, including failed.
The cleanup task would have been skipped if the Run-if had been 'All succeeded' instead.
Because the ingest task failed, the cleanup task inherits that failure and cannot run.
'All done' and 'All succeeded' are interchangeable labels for the same behavior.

questions.analysis: This targets Test Points 1 and 2—matching each Run-if option to the outcome it admits and explaining why 'All done' fires after failures while 'All succeeded' does not. 'All done' is the permissive condition: it checks only that every upstream task finished, regardless of whether it succeeded or failed, so a failed ingest task still satisfies the condition and the cleanup task runs [source 3]. Option B is correct because 'All succeeded' would have required every upstream task to succeed, and a failed ingest task would disqualify the cleanup task and skip it [source 3]. Option C inverts the semantics: a downstream Run-if task does not 'inherit' upstream failure; failure propagation is controlled entirely by the chosen condition. Option D is the common misconception that the two labels are equivalent—they are not, and the default is 'All succeeded', so learners who confuse them may accidentally block cleanup tasks they expected to run [source 3]. The distinction matters for reliability engineering: 'All done' is useful for tasks that must always execute (for example, final notification or teardown), whereas 'All succeeded' is appropriate for tasks whose output is only valid if all inputs were valid.

questions.question: A data engineer wants a notification task to fire only when a transformation task failed, and a separate audit task to fire only when all upstream tasks have finished regardless of outcome. Which Run-if configurations correctly implement both requirements? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Notification task: 'All failed'
Notification task: 'At least one failed'
Audit task: 'All done'
Audit task: 'All succeeded'

questions.analysis: This exercises Test Point 1 across multiple realistic requirements. 'At least one failed' admits the notification task when one or more upstream tasks failed, which precisely matches the stated requirement that it fire when the transformation task failed [source 3]. Option A, 'All failed', is too restrictive: it would only fire if every upstream task failed, not just one. Option C is correct for the audit task because 'All done' fires once every upstream task reaches any terminal state, whether succeeded or failed, which matches 'regardless of outcome' [source 3]. Option D, 'All succeeded', is the trap from Test Point 4: it is the default and the most common choice, but it silently skips the audit task whenever any upstream task fails, defeating the purpose of an always-run audit [source 3]. The general design pattern is to reserve 'All succeeded' for validity-dependent work, 'All done' for unconditional finalization, and the failure-family conditions ('At least one failed', 'All failed') for error handling and notifications, which is consistent with the broader failure-handling role of Run-if within Lakeflow Jobs orchestration [source 2].

scenes.title: Conditional Branching with Run-if Conditions

elements.content: Conditional Branching with Run-if Conditions

A Run-if condition is evaluated by the orchestrator before a task executes; it gates the task on the result_state of its upstream tasks and is the mechanism Lakeflow Jobs uses to express if/else control flow at task level. A task cannot return a branch decision to the job — the job graph must already contain every possible branch. Precondition: the task must declare at least one depends_on edge, because Run-if only reads upstream states. Edge case: with no depends_on, Run-if is ignored and the task runs unconditionally. [source 1]
The Six Run-if Options
All six options evaluate only upstream result_state values. [source 3]
Custom Condition Syntax

elements.html: {{tasks.<task>.result_state}} == SUCCEEDED

elements.content: Custom conditions combine dynamic value references with comparison and logical operators. The reference resolves to the upstream task's terminal state at runtime, so expressions are stateless and rerunnable. Invalid keys cause the task to be skipped, not failed. [source 2]
Worked Example: If/Else Gate
tasks.decide.result_state == "SUCCEEDED" → branch A runs
tasks.decide.result_state == "FAILED" → branch B runs
Both branches coexist in the DAG; only one executes per run. [source 4]

actions.text: Now let's build on the Run-if conditions we just covered and take them one step further with conditional branching. This is where a single job starts to behave like real control flow — a genuine if/else at the task level.

The key thing to internalize here: a Run-if condition is evaluated by the orchestrator, not by the task itself. The job decides whether a task runs based purely on the state of its upstream dependencies before that task ever starts.

Here are the six Run-if options you need to recognize. All succeeded is the default. Then you have at least one succeeded, all done, at least one failed, all failed, and finally a custom condition. Notice the crucial detail — all six evaluate only upstream result states. There is no mechanism for a task to report a branch decision back to the job.

When the built-in options aren't granular enough, you drop into a custom condition. This references upstream task states using the tasks dot task name dot result_state syntax you see in the formula, combined with equality and inequality operators — plus logical operators when you want to combine several checks into one gate.

Let's walk the canonical two-branch pattern. You have a decision task, then two downstream tasks that both depend on it. One runs only when the decision succeeded, the other only when it failed — a clean if/else.
Branch A fires when tasks.decide.result_state equals SUCCEEDED.
And branch B fires when that same state equals FAILED. Both branches coexist in the DAG — remember, only one of them will actually execute.

One design note worth carrying into the exam: keep your branch conditions readable. Deeply nested gating turns a job graph into something that is genuinely painful to debug and repair, so favor clarity over cleverness when modeling branches as tasks.

actions.text: We just covered run-if conditions conceptually, so now let's make them concrete. This simulation asks you to set the outcome of each upstream task and then watch which downstream tasks fire and which get skipped.

actions.content: Toggle each upstream task between SUCCEEDED, FAILED, and SKIPPED.

actions.text: Let's start with the simplest case: everything succeeds and the condition is All succeeded. All three upstream tasks pass and the downstream branch should run cleanly.

actions.content: Baseline: all upstream tasks succeeded under ALL_SUCCESS.
Now switch the Run-if condition and compare the outcome against the same upstream states.

actions.text: Watch how All done and At least one failed change the result even though the upstream outcomes stay the same. All done means the run-if fires whenever every upstream task has reached a terminal state, no matter the result.

actions.content: One failure now trips the AT_LEAST_ONE_FAILED condition.

actions.text: Finally, try the custom expression. A condition like checking whether validate's result_state equals FAILED lets you branch on one specific upstream task, and note how a skipped task propagates — downstream tasks with unmet conditions are skipped, not failed.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Branching and Looping

questions.question: A data engineer is authoring a Lakeflow Jobs For each task whose body must iterate over a list of region codes. The list is produced at runtime by an upstream notebook task named 'discover_regions', which publishes the array with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="regions", value=[...]). Which statement correctly identifies a valid source for the For each task's input array?

options.label: The array must be a literal JSON list hard-coded into the job definition, because For each cannot read values produced at runtime.

The array can be sourced from a dynamic value reference to the upstream task value, for example {{tasks.discover_regions.values.regions}}, so the iteration set is resolved when the For each task starts.
The array must be passed as a job parameter at trigger time; task values cannot feed a For each input because they are only readable inside Python notebooks.
The array is automatically inferred from the depends_on graph, so no explicit input value is required on the For each task.

questions.analysis: Lakeflow Jobs builds on the parameter and task-value mechanism covered earlier in this unit: a task publishes data with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key, value) and a downstream task reads it with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(...) or via the dynamic reference {{tasks.<task>.values.<key>}}. A For each task is simply another downstream task, so its input array may be a dynamic value reference to an upstream task value (option B), or a task/job parameter produced upstream. Option A is wrong because hard-coding contradicts the whole point of parameterized workflows; option C inverts the rule — task values are exactly the kind of upstream-produced value a For each can consume, not a reason it cannot; option D confuses the dependency graph with data flow, since depends_on declares ordering only, never payload. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestration layer that ties dependencies, triggers and task configuration together [source 2][source 6].

questions.question: A For each task iterates over an input array of 12 elements and is configured with a concurrency limit of 3. Which statements about how each iteration references its current element, and about the effect of concurrency on wall-clock time, are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Inside each iteration, the current element is exposed to the task body (for example through the {{input}} reference or the iteration's input value), so the body can branch on the element's value.

With a concurrency limit of 3, up to 3 iterations execute in parallel, and the remaining iterations are dispatched as earlier ones complete — so wall-clock time is roughly one third of fully sequential execution if each iteration costs the same.
For each iterations are guaranteed to start and finish in strict array order, and the concurrency limit only controls how many tasks the cluster can accept simultaneously.
Because the body can contain Run-if branching, an iteration can decide per element whether its downstream work should proceed, which is how iteration and branching compose.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: each iteration receives its current element as the iteration's input, so the body can reference and branch on it. Option B is correct: concurrency limits the number of simultaneous iterations; with 12 elements and a limit of 3, up to 3 run at once and the rest are scheduled as slots free, so ideal wall-clock time is approximately 12/3 = 4 iteration-durations rather than 12. Option D is correct because the unit already established that Run-if conditions admit or block a task based on upstream result states; applying that per iteration lets branching and iteration compose. Option C is the classic trap: For each does not guarantee sequential, in-order completion — ordering of dispatch and completion is not guaranteed at high concurrency, which is precisely why the concurrency limit is the lever on total runtime. This ties back to orchestration's core job of managing dependencies and scheduling tasks [source 6].

questions.question: A For each task is configured to read an input array. In scenario X the array is empty ([]); in scenario Y the array contains one element that is null ([null]). Which prediction matches Lakeflow Jobs semantics?

options.label: In both scenarios the For each task fails validation because an input array must contain at least one non-null element.

In scenario X the For each task completes successfully without spawning any iterations; in scenario Y the task spawns one iteration whose input value is null, and the task body must handle the null or it will error.
In scenario X the For each task hangs indefinitely waiting for an element; in scenario Y the null element is silently skipped and no iteration runs.
In both scenarios the For each task spawns exactly one iteration: an empty array yields one iteration with no input, and a null element yields one iteration with null input.

questions.analysis: An empty array is a valid, fully resolved input: the For each task has nothing to iterate over, so it completes successfully with zero child iterations. A one-element array containing null is also a valid input of length 1, so exactly one iteration is created and its current element is null — the body is then responsible for handling that null (for example, a guard or a Run-if condition), otherwise the iteration will error. Option A is wrong because empty arrays are legal, not a validation failure; option C invents a hang that does not exist and wrongly claims null elements are skipped; option D confuses 'zero elements' with 'one empty element', which are different lengths and therefore different iteration counts. This distinction matters because Lakeflow Jobs treats task values and parameters as runtime-resolved configuration, so the array's contents — not its mere presence — determine behavior [source 2][source 3].

actions.text: Now it's time to check how well branching and looping have settled in. This next set of questions covers how a For each task gets its input array, how iterations reference their current element, how concurrency affects timing, and what happens with empty versus null inputs.
Take each question one at a time and work through it on your own — read every option carefully before choosing. Once you submit, I'll walk you through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: For Each Task to Refresh a List of Dates

elements.content: Problem 1

A nightly backfill job has an upstream notebook task named compute_dates that queries a control table to find missing order dates for silver.orders. The control table lists every date from 2024-05-01 through 2024-05-12 (12 dates). A query against silver.orders shows that only 2024-05-01, 2024-05-02, 2024-05-03, 2024-05-10, and 2024-05-12 already have data; those five dates are present. The job must refresh every missing date exactly once. In compute_dates, write the dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set call that publishes the missing dates using key "dates". Then configure a For each task named refresh_dates to consume that array; its nested notebook task takes a parameter named date and sets it to the current element. Set concurrent-iterations to 4. Finally, compute (a) the number of iterations, (b) the maximum number of iterations running at once, and (c) the minimum wall-clock time for the loop if each iteration takes 6 minutes of cluster time, ignoring scheduling overhead.
Hint: Missing dates = all dates minus present dates. Number of waves = $\lceil \text{iterations} / \text{concurrent-iterations} \rceil$.

Worked solution
Step 1: Enumerate the full date range. The control table lists 12 dates: 2024-05-01, 05-02, 05-03, 05-04, 05-05, 05-06, 05-07, 05-08, 05-09, 05-10, 05-11, 05-12. Present dates in silver.orders are 05-01, 05-02, 05-03, 05-10, and 05-12, so 5 dates are already present. Missing dates = $12 - 5 = 7$ dates: 2024-05-04, 2024-05-05, 2024-05-06, 2024-05-07, 2024-05-08, 2024-05-09, 2024-05-11.

Step 2: In the compute_dates notebook, publish the missing dates as a JSON-serializable array using a task value:

```python

missing_dates = [

"2024-05-04", "2024-05-05", "2024-05-06",

"2024-05-07", "2024-05-08", "2024-05-09",

"2024-05-11"

]

dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="dates", value=missing_dates)

```

Step 3: In the job definition, add a For each task named refresh_dates. The input is the dynamic value reference to the producer task's key; the nested task parameter date uses the special {{input}} variable, which the For each task replaces with the current element:

```json

{

"task_key": "refresh_dates",

"depends_on": [{"task_key": "compute_dates"}],

"for_each_task": {

"inputs": "{{tasks.compute_dates.values.dates}}",

"concurrent_iterations": 4,

"task": {

"task_key": "refresh_one_date",

"notebook_task": {

"notebook_path": "/Repos/team/backfill/refresh_date",

"base_parameters": {"date": "{{input}}"}

}

}

}

}

```

Step 4: Compute the quantitative results.

(a) Number of iterations = length of missing_dates = 7.

(b) Maximum concurrent iterations = 4, because concurrent_iterations is set to 4.

(c) The loop runs in waves. Wave 1 starts 4 iterations simultaneously; wave 2 starts the remaining 3 iterations. Number of waves = $\lceil 7/4 \rceil = 2$. Each wave takes 6 minutes, so minimum wall-clock time = $2 \times 6 = 12$ minutes. Without the concurrency limit (default 1), it would be $7 \times 6 = 42$ minutes, so the limit provides a 3.5x ideal speedup while bounding cluster load to 4 concurrent iterations.

Final answer: 7 iterations, at most 4 running at once, minimum 12 minutes for the loop.

Analysis — This problem uses the parameterized-workflow pattern: an upstream task computes a small JSON-serializable array, publishes it with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set, and a downstream For each task expands that array into independent iterations. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestration tool for data, analytics, and AI workloads on Databricks [source 6], and it lets engineers schedule and automate multi-step data pipelines by defining tasks, dependencies, triggers, and failure handling [source 2]. The For each task is a single node in the dependency graph even though it spawns many nested task runs; downstream tasks depend on the loop as a whole. Common mistakes include hard-coding the date list inside the For each task instead of reading task values, using the wrong key name in {{tasks.compute_dates.values.<key>}}, and forgetting that the default concurrency is 1. Edge cases: an empty array produces zero iterations and the For each task still succeeds; a list of millions of dates is not appropriate because task values are size-limited. If one iteration fails, partial runs and repairs make it easier, faster, and cheaper to debug failed tasks [source 4], so you can repair just that date rather than re-running the whole loop. Orchestration also includes compute resource allocation and monitoring of workflows [source 6], and concurrent-iterations is exactly that resource-allocation knob.
Problem 2

Using the same job from the previous problem, compute_dates runs and finds that silver.orders already contains all 12 dates, so it publishes an empty array: dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="dates", value=[]). refresh_dates depends_on compute_dates with Run-if "All succeeded"; aggregate_silver depends_on refresh_dates with Run-if "All succeeded". (a) How many nested task runs does refresh_dates create? (b) What is the result state of refresh_dates? (c) Does aggregate_silver run? (d) Now suppose compute_dates fails with an exception before setting task values. What is the state of refresh_dates and aggregate_silver? (e) If refresh_dates instead used Run-if "All done", would it run after compute_dates fails, and what problem could arise when it tries to read {{tasks.compute_dates.values.dates}}?
Hint: An empty For each input is a successful loop with zero iterations, not a failure. Run-if "All done" admits tasks whose dependencies are in any terminal state.

Worked solution
(a) refresh_dates creates 0 nested task runs. The input array is empty, so the For each loop has zero iterations.

(b) refresh_dates result state is SUCCEEDED. A loop over zero items completes successfully; it is not an error.

(c) Yes, aggregate_silver runs. Its Run-if condition is "All succeeded", and its only dependency refresh_dates has state SUCCEEDED, so the condition is satisfied. aggregate_silver then performs its aggregation over silver.orders as usual.

(d) If compute_dates fails before setting task values, refresh_dates uses Run-if "All succeeded". Since its dependency did not succeed, refresh_dates is skipped (it does not execute and creates no iterations). aggregate_silver then sees that refresh_dates did not succeed, so aggregate_silver is also skipped.

(e) If refresh_dates used Run-if "All done", it would run even though compute_dates failed, because "All done" admits a dependency that has reached any terminal state, including FAILED. However, the dynamic reference {{tasks.compute_dates.values.dates}} cannot be resolved: compute_dates never successfully published the key "dates". The For each task would then fail at expansion time (or produce an undefined input), because the For each input reference itself has no built-in default syntax. The safer design is to keep Run-if "All succeeded" on the loop and let control flow prevent a doomed expansion.

Analysis — This problem isolates the semantics of empty iteration and dependency failure. The key fact is that a For each task is a control-flow construct: it evaluates its input reference at runtime, expands the array into nested runs, and succeeds when all of those nested runs succeed. Zero elements means zero nested runs and a SUCCEEDED parent. Students often assume that an empty loop fails or that downstream tasks are skipped; both assumptions are wrong. The second half tests the interaction between Run-if and dynamic value references. Run-if "All succeeded" is the conservative default because it requires every dependency to succeed before the loop reads task values; Run-if "All done" is useful for cleanup or notification tasks but dangerous for data-consuming loops because a failed producer leaves the key unset. Lakeflow Jobs lets data engineers schedule and automate multi-step data pipelines by defining tasks, dependencies, triggers, and failure handling [source 2], and orchestration involves managing the dependencies between workflow tasks and scheduling these tasks to be executed [source 6]. A common mistake is to put the loop before the producer in the dependency graph or to use "All done" on the loop to try to tolerate upstream failures. Edge case: if the producer sets an empty array, the loop still runs and succeeds; if the producer fails, the loop is skipped under "All succeeded" and downstream tasks are skipped as well. Partial runs and repairs make it easier, faster, and cheaper to debug failed tasks [source 4], so after fixing compute_dates you can repair the failed task and the loop will re-evaluate.
Problem 3

A developer is building the same refresh job. They write the For each task input as {{tasks.compute_dates.values.date_list}}, but compute_dates actually published with key="dates". They set the nested task parameter to "{{tasks.compute_dates.values.dates}}" instead of "{{input}}". They leave concurrent-iterations unset, so it defaults to 1. There are 8 missing dates to refresh, and each iteration takes 5 minutes. (a) Identify the two configuration errors. (b) Explain what the nested task would receive if the second error were not fixed. (c) Compute the wall-clock time with the default concurrency and with concurrent-iterations=4. (d) Give the corrected For each task configuration.
Hint: The input reference must match the producer's key exactly. The special variable {{input}} represents the current array element inside the nested task.

Worked solution
(a) Error 1: The input reference uses key date_list, but the producer wrote key dates. Lakeflow Jobs will fail to resolve {{tasks.compute_dates.values.date_list}} because no such task value exists (or it will resolve to an empty/null value depending on how the reference is handled), so the For each task cannot build its iteration list. Error 2: The nested task parameter is set to {{tasks.compute_dates.values.dates}} instead of {{input}}. The reference {{tasks.compute_dates.values.dates}} always points to the entire array, not the current element, so every iteration would receive the whole list.

(b) If the key error were fixed but the second error were not, each of the 8 iterations would pass the full list of 8 dates into the date parameter. The refresh logic would then try to process the entire list 8 times (or fail immediately if it expects a scalar date string). For example, iteration 1 would receive ["2024-06-01", ..., "2024-06-08"] as its date parameter, which is not a single date.

(c) With the default concurrency of 1, iterations run one after another: $8 \times 5 = 40$ minutes. With concurrent-iterations=4, the loop runs in $\lceil 8/4 \rceil = 2$ waves, each wave taking 5 minutes, so $2 \times 5 = 10$ minutes. The ideal speedup is 4x.

(d) Corrected configuration:

```json

{

"task_key": "refresh_dates",

"depends_on": [{"task_key": "compute_dates"}],

"for_each_task": {

"inputs": "{{tasks.compute_dates.values.dates}}",

"concurrent_iterations": 4,

"task": {

"task_key": "refresh_one_date",

"notebook_task": {

"notebook_path": "/Repos/team/backfill/refresh_date",

"base_parameters": {"date": "{{input}}"}

}

}

}

}

```

Analysis — The For each task is a task-template expansion mechanism. Its inputs field must evaluate to an array; the nested task definition then becomes a template where {{input}} is bound to each element in turn. This is why the nested parameter must use {{input}}, not a dynamic value reference to the producer task: the producer reference is constant across iterations, while {{input}} varies. Common mistakes include mismatched key names, using the producer reference inside the nested task, and forgetting that concurrent-iterations defaults to 1. The concurrency setting is an upper bound, not a guarantee: if the cluster has fewer available slots, actual parallelism may be lower. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestration engine in Databricks, formerly known as Databricks Workflows, and it lets data engineers schedule and automate multi-step data pipelines by defining tasks, dependencies, triggers, and failure handling [source 2]. Lakeflow Jobs (formerly Databricks Workflows) is the native orchestrator for the Lakehouse [source 3], and orchestration includes compute resource allocation and monitoring of workflows [source 6], which is exactly what the concurrent-iterations limit controls. Edge cases: an empty inputs array yields zero iterations and success; a malformed reference causes the For each task to fail before any nested run starts; and if one of the 8 iterations fails, partial runs and repairs make it easier, faster, and cheaper to debug failed tasks [source 4], so you can repair just that iteration instead of re-running all 8.
Problem 4

Design the job dependency graph for three tasks: compute_dates (notebook), refresh_dates (For each), and aggregate_silver (notebook). The aggregate must run only if every date iteration succeeded. Write the depends_on and Run-if for each task. Then, if the 7-date loop has concurrent-iterations=4 and each iteration takes 6 minutes, compute_dates takes 2 minutes, and aggregate_silver takes 3 minutes, compute the end-to-end wall-clock time from job start to aggregate finish. Assume no scheduling overhead and that iterations are independent. Finally, state what happens to aggregate_silver if one iteration of refresh_dates fails.
Hint: Model the For each task as one node in the DAG. Downstream tasks depend on the loop as a whole, not on individual iterations.

Worked solution
Dependency graph and conditions:

- compute_dates: no depends_on; Run-if default "All succeeded".

- refresh_dates: depends_on compute_dates; Run-if "All succeeded".

- aggregate_silver: depends_on refresh_dates; Run-if "All succeeded".

The graph is a chain: compute_dates -> refresh_dates -> aggregate_silver. The For each task is a single node even though it spawns 7 nested task runs.

Wall-clock calculation:

- compute_dates starts at t = 0 and finishes at t = 2 minutes.

- refresh_dates starts at t = 2 minutes. It has 7 iterations with concurrency 4, so number of waves = $\lceil 7/4 \rceil = 2$. Each wave takes 6 minutes, so the loop takes $2 \times 6 = 12$ minutes. It finishes at $2 + 12 = 14$ minutes.

- aggregate_silver starts at t = 14 minutes and takes 3 minutes, so it finishes at $14 + 3 = 17$ minutes.

Total end-to-end wall-clock time = 2 + 12 + 3 = 17 minutes.

If one iteration of refresh_dates fails, the refresh_dates parent task does not reach SUCCEEDED; its result state becomes FAILED (or partially completed, depending on the platform's reporting). Because aggregate_silver has Run-if "All succeeded", it is skipped. The loop's other iterations may still complete, but the downstream aggregate is gated. You can then use repair to re-run only the failed iteration and then run aggregate_silver after the loop succeeds.

Analysis — This problem tests the mental model that a For each task is a single node in the dependency graph with internal fan-out. Students often try to make aggregate_silver depend on each iteration or wonder whether the aggregate waits for all iterations; in Lakeflow Jobs it does, because the For each task's SUCCEEDED state is reached only after all nested iterations succeed. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestration tool for data, analytics, and AI workloads on the Databricks Data + AI Platform [source 6], and its orchestration manages the dependencies between workflow tasks and schedules these tasks to be executed [source 6]. The previous names "Lakeflow Jobs" and "Databricks Jobs" were renamed to "Lakeflow Jobs" in late 2024 [source 1], which is worth knowing for certification vocabulary. Common mistakes include putting aggregate_silver on a Run-if "All done" condition, which would let it run even if iterations failed, and assuming that concurrent-iterations changes the number of iterations (it only bounds how many run at once). Edge cases: if compute_dates fails, refresh_dates and aggregate_silver are both skipped under "All succeeded"; if refresh_dates gets an empty array, it succeeds with zero iterations and aggregate_silver still runs; and if concurrent-iterations is set higher than the cluster can support, actual parallelism is lower than the limit. Partial runs and repairs make it easier, faster, and cheaper to debug failed tasks [source 4], which is the intended recovery path when one iteration fails in a long backfill.

actions.text: Now let's put all of that together in our fully worked problem. We have an upstream task that computes the last seven missing dates, and a For each task that must refresh each of those dates in parallel, with limited concurrency.

Read the statement carefully. A developer is building this same refresh job. The upstream task produces the list of dates that need backfilling, and the downstream loop iterates over that list, running one parameterized iteration per date.
Before you peek at the solution, here's the hint: the input reference must match the producer's task-value key exactly. That naming contract is where most people lose points on the exam.

Here's the worked solution. Step one: the upstream task calls dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set with the key dates and the computed array as its value. Step two: the For each task consumes that value through the taskValues reference, and it defines a nested task whose parameter references the current element as input. Step three: you set the concurrent-iterations limit, say four, to bound cluster load while still overlapping the work.

The analysis ties the mental model together. The array must come from a task that has already run, the iterations are independent and unordered, and an empty array simply skips the loop instead of failing it. Hold onto those three facts — they're the exact semantics the certification tests. And this is a great one to try yourself, so take a moment and work through the dependency setup before we move on.

scenes.title: Design Choice: Branch Inside the Notebook or Model Branches as Tasks

elements.content: Decision — A data engineering team has built a nightly Lakeflow Jobs pipeline that ingests raw data, validates it, and then applies two different transformations depending on whether the validation passes or fails. The lead engineer proposes writing all conditional logic as if/else statements inside a single Python notebook task, while a staff engineer argues for modeling each branch as a separate task with Run-if conditions. The team must choose an approach that satisfies two hard operational constraints: the job must be debuggable directly from the job UI, and when a branch fails, they must be able to rerun only that failed branch without recomputing the entire pipeline. The decision is difficult because the in-notebook approach is faster to implement and locally testable, but it hides branching from the job graph, whereas the task-level approach makes branching visible and repairable at the cost of more tasks to maintain and configure. [source 3] describes Lakeflow Jobs as the native orchestrator for the Lakehouse and explicitly covers dependencies, the Run-if condition, triggers, and failure handling. [source 6] adds that orchestration includes managing dependencies between workflow tasks, scheduling, compute allocation, and monitoring. [source 4] notes that partial runs and repairs make it easier, faster, and cheaper to debug failed tasks.

Constraints — The job must be debuggable from the job UI: operators need to see each logical step, its status, and its logs without reading notebook code.  •  A failed branch must be rerunnable in isolation without recomputing upstream or sibling branches that already succeeded.

In-notebook branching (if/else inside one task)
+ Simplest to implement: only one task to create, configure, and schedule, with no dependency wiring.; + Easy to unit-test locally because all branch logic lives in ordinary Python that can be executed outside Databricks.; + Fewer moving parts means fewer task parameters and Run-if configurations to get wrong.
− Branch logic is invisible in the job graph, so the UI shows one monolithic task and cannot display which branch ran or why.; − Retrying an individual branch requires rerunning the entire notebook task, recomputing everything before the branch, which violates the repair constraint.; − It mixes orchestration concerns (when to run what) with transformation logic, making the notebook harder to reason about and reuse. [source 6]
Best for: Very fine-grained, value-level if/else decisions inside a single logical step, such as choosing a date format or skipping a nullable column.

Task-level branching with Run-if conditions
+ The job graph visibly shows each branch as a separate task with its own status, logs, and run history, satisfying the UI debuggability constraint. [source 3]; + Each branch can be repaired independently: Databricks repair runs allow rerunning only the failed task and its downstream dependencies, which is faster and cheaper. [source 4]; + Per-branch compute and permissions can be configured, so a heavy branch can use a larger cluster or a branch touching sensitive tables can run under a restricted role. [source 6]
− More tasks to create, name, and configure, increasing maintenance overhead and the chance of misconfigured dependencies.; − Run-if conditions must be carefully written using {{tasks.<task>.result_state}} and logical operators; a wrong condition can cause a branch to be skipped or run unintentionally.; − The overall job definition becomes longer and may require additional parameters or task values to pass data between branches.
Best for: Coarse, operationally meaningful branches such as validation gates, retry paths, or alternative processing routes that must be visible and repairable from the job UI.

Hybrid: task-level Run-if for coarse branches, in-notebook if/else for fine-grained value logic
+ Coarse branches appear as separate tasks in the graph, satisfying both the debuggability and isolated-repair constraints for operationally significant decisions. [source 3]; + Fine-grained value-level if/else stays inside the notebook, avoiding an explosion of tiny tasks for every small data-dependent decision.; + The job graph remains readable because only operationally meaningful branches are promoted to tasks, while low-level logic stays encapsulated.
− Requires a deliberate design decision about what counts as coarse versus fine-grained, which demands experience and can be inconsistent across engineers.; − Engineers must understand both in-notebook branching and Run-if conditions, increasing the cognitive load and the risk of duplicating logic in the wrong layer.; − The boundary can drift over time: what starts as a fine-grained condition may grow into an operationally significant branch that should be promoted to a task.
Best for: Teams that need visible, repairable coarse branches without turning every small conditional into a separate task, and that can maintain clear design guidelines.

Recommendation: Hybrid: task-level Run-if for coarse branches, in-notebook if/else for fine-grained value logic — The binding constraints are UI debuggability and isolated branch repair, and only task-level Run-if conditions satisfy both: they make each coarse branch a first-class task with its own status and logs, and Databricks repair runs can rerun just the failed branch without recomputing the whole pipeline [source 3][source 4]. However, pushing every small value-level if/else into its own task would create an unmanageable number of tasks and violate the simplicity that makes notebooks locally testable. The hybrid approach resolves this trade-off by using Run-if conditions only for coarse, operationally meaningful branches—such as the validation gate and the pass/fail transformation paths—while keeping fine-grained value logic inside the notebook. This is also consistent with Lakeflow Jobs' design: orchestration manages dependencies, scheduling, and monitoring of workflow tasks [source 6], while transformation detail belongs in the task itself. To prevent drift, the team should document the decision in each task description, stating why a branch is modeled as a task or kept inside the notebook, so reviewers can see the rationale for the graph shape.

actions.text: Now let's tackle a design decision that comes up constantly in real Databricks jobs. A data engineering team has built a nightly pipeline, and they hit a fork in the road: should the conditional logic live as if/else code inside a single notebook, or should each branch be modeled as its own task with a Run-if condition? This is not a cosmetic choice — it changes how the job behaves operationally.

Before we pick a side, let's anchor on the constraints. Two things are non-negotiable here. First, the job must be debuggable from the job UI — someone on call at 2 a.m. needs to see where things went wrong without reading the code. Second, it must be possible to rerun only the failed branch without recomputing the entire pipeline. Keep those two requirements in your head, because they're what decides the answer.

Option A is in-notebook branching — plain if/else inside the Python notebook. The upside is real: it's simple, it's a single task, and it's easy to unit-test locally. The downside is equally real. The branch logic becomes invisible in the job graph, retrying just one branch is awkward, and you end up mixing orchestration concerns with transformation logic — which is exactly the kind of coupling that hurts you in production.

Option B is task-level branching with Run-if conditions. Here the branches are first-class citizens in the graph. You get a visible DAG, independent retries and repair of each branch, and the ability to give each branch its own compute and its own permissions. The cost is more tasks to maintain and configure — but notice how directly that maps back to our two constraints on the previous element.

So the pragmatic answer is a hybrid, and this is worth memorizing for the exam. Use task-level Run-if conditions for coarse, operationally meaningful branches — validation gates, retry paths, anything an operator would want to see or rerun on its own. Keep fine-grained, value-level if/else where it belongs: inside the notebook, close to the data it's transforming.

And one piece of hygiene that separates good pipelines from mysterious ones: whichever option you choose, make the decision explicit in the task description. Write down why the graph looks the way it does. A reviewer six months from now should be able to see the reasoning without reconstructing it from the code. That's the takeaway for this page — coarse branches as Run-if tasks, fine-grained logic inside the notebook, and document the choice.

scenes.title: Lesson Review: Parameters, Branching, and Control Flow

questions.question: A data engineer defines a job with job-level parameter env = "prod" and a task named transform that declares its own task-level parameter env = "staging". Inside the transform notebook, the engineer runs dbutils.widgets.get("env") and also references {{job.parameters.env}} in the same task's cluster configuration. Which pair of values is observed?

options.label: The notebook returns "staging" and the reference resolves to "prod"
The notebook returns "prod" and the reference resolves to "staging"
Both return "staging", because task parameters override all references
Both return "prod", because job parameters always take precedence

questions.analysis: Task parameters are scoped to a single task and override a job parameter of the same name for that task. Thus dbutils.widgets.get("env") inside the transform notebook yields "staging". However, the reference {{job.parameters.env}} explicitly targets the job-level namespace, not the task-level one, so it resolves to "prod". This distinction between task-scoped parameter resolution and explicit job-namespace references is exactly what Lakeflow Jobs (formerly Databricks Workflows) enforces, and it reflects the lesson's checkpoint on job versus task parameter precedence [source 2]. Option B inverts the two namespaces. Option C incorrectly assumes job.parameters is shadowed by task parameters. Option D incorrectly assumes job parameters always win, contradicting the documented precedence.

questions.question: Task A runs a notebook that executes dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="row_count", value=spark.table("bronze.orders").count()). Task B depends on Task A and starts with: cnt = dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(taskKey="A", key="row_count", default=0). Task A's run completes with result_state = FAILED after publishing a partial count of 42 before failing. Which best describes Task B's observed value for cnt when it runs?

options.label: cnt == 42, because the value was published before the failure
cnt == 0, because a failed upstream task does not publish task values
An exception is raised because Task A did not succeed
cnt is undefined and dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get returns None

questions.analysis: Task values are only committed when the publishing task's run reaches a terminal successful state. If Task A fails, its taskValues.set calls are discarded, so Task B's read falls back to the default of 0. Task values are the mechanism for passing values between tasks, but they must be JSON-serializable, size-limited, and associated with a succeeded run [source 6]. Option A misstates the commit semantics. Option C is wrong because get() with a default never raises for a missing key. Option D is wrong because get() with an explicit default returns that default rather than None.

questions.question: A pipeline has four consumers of a For each task named refresh that iterates over a list of dates. They are: (a) ingest, which always succeeds; (b) validate, which sometimes fails; (c) aggregate, which depends on ingest and validate and is marked with Run-if = All succeeded; (d) reconcile, which depends on ingest and validate and is marked with Run-if = All done. On a particular run, ingest SUCCEEDED, validate FAILED, and the For each refresh was configured to iterate over an array that was empty. Select all statements that are true. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: aggregate does not run because at least one upstream task did not succeed
reconcile runs because All done admits a mix of succeeded and failed upstream tasks
refresh runs zero iterations and the task itself can still be reported as SUCCEEDED
refresh fails because an empty array is treated as a null element

questions.analysis: Run-if = All succeeded (the default) fires only when every upstream task has SUCCEEDED; because validate FAILED, aggregate is skipped, so Option A is correct. Run-if = All done fires after all upstream tasks reach a terminal state regardless of success or failure, so reconcile runs, making Option B correct. A For each task with an empty input array performs zero iterations and its run can be reported as SUCCEEDED rather than failing, so Option C is correct. Option D is incorrect: an empty array is not equivalent to a null element, and handling of a null element is a distinct edge case from the empty-array case described in the lesson [source 3]. Together these behaviors illustrate the Run-if semantics and For each looping model described in the workflow orchestration course material [source 3].

questions.question: Describe a reusable pattern for a validation gate that halts the entire pipeline when data quality checks fail, while still allowing a notification or reconciliation branch to run. Your answer should cover: (1) where the validation logic lives relative to the write task; (2) how the gate signals success or failure to downstream tasks; (3) how you configure Run-if on the downstream tasks to express both the halt path and the notification path; and (4) how you make the gate reusable across environments. Give a concrete example using a row-count threshold and a null-rate threshold, and explain what happens when the gate raises an exception.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Validation as its own task downstream of the write task, with a clear statement that it evaluates data already written to a Delta table — 20%. (2) Signaling mechanism: raising an exception or otherwise causing the validate task's run to end in FAILED, and optionally publishing a check result via dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set for downstream consumption — 20%. (3) Run-if configuration: downstream load/aggregate tasks marked All succeeded so they do not run when validate FAILED; a sibling notification/reconcile task marked All done or a custom condition referencing {{tasks.validate.result_state}} == 'FAILED' so it still fires — 25%. (4) Reusability: parameterize thresholds and table names via job parameters and task parameters referenced with {{job.parameters.<key>}}, no hard-coded values — 15%. (5) Concrete example with numeric thresholds (e.g., row_count >= 1,000,000 and null_rate <= 0.01) and a statement that when the gate raises an exception, the validate task's run is FAILED, the All succeeded branch is skipped, and the All done / custom-condition branch runs — 20%.
questions.analysis: A strong answer places validation in a task downstream of the write task, since data quality checks must evaluate the materialized data. The gate signals by failing its own run (typically by raising an exception after the check fails) and can publish a structured result with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set. Downstream load/aggregate tasks use Run-if = All succeeded so a FAILED validate causes them to be skipped, halting the pipeline; a sibling task handling notification or reconciliation uses Run-if = All done or a custom condition such as {{tasks.validate.result_state}} == 'FAILED'. Reusability comes from parameterizing thresholds and table names via job and task parameters referenced as {{job.parameters.<key>}}, avoiding hard-coded strings. In the concrete example, a row-count threshold of at least one million rows and a null-rate threshold of at most 1% are checked; if either fails, the validate task's run is FAILED, the All succeeded branch does not fire, and the All done / custom-condition notification branch still runs. This design is consistent with Lakeflow Jobs' role as the native orchestration layer for scheduling, monitoring, and controlling multi-step pipelines [source 6].

actions.text: This page is a cumulative review, so it pulls together everything from this lesson — parameter resolution, task values between tasks, Run-if conditions, and For each looping. There are four questions, including one short-answer, so take your time and work through each one on your own.
Give every question your best independent attempt before submitting — I'll be right here afterward to walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Trigger Types in Lakeflow Jobs

elements.content: Trigger Types in Lakeflow Jobs

Objective: Classify any scheduling requirement — manual, cron, file arrival, table update, or continuous — before writing configuration. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestrator for the Lakehouse, handling dependencies and scheduling for data, analytics, and AI workloads [source 3][source 6].

Manual / Run now

No recurring schedule; effective default when none configured [source 3]

Scheduled (cron)

Trigger fires on a cadence, e.g., nightly batch [source 3]

File arrival / Table update / Continuous

Event-driven or always-on ingestion triggers [source 6]

Key distinction: A trigger defines what starts a run; a schedule defines the cadence at which that trigger fires. Cron is a type of schedule, whereas manual and Run now produce no recurring schedule and are the effective default when no trigger is configured [source 3].

Worked example: "Refresh sales data every night at 2 AM" → trigger type = scheduled (cron); cron expression 0 0 2 * * ? fires daily. "Process files as they land in S3" → file arrival. "Always-on streaming ingestion" → continuous.

actions.text: Now that you understand how jobs, tasks, and runs fit together as an object model, let's talk about what actually kicks a run off. This page establishes the vocabulary of trigger types in Lakeflow Jobs — and it matters because you'll be asked to classify scheduling requirements before you ever write a configuration.

Here's our objective for this segment: by the end, you should be able to take any scheduling requirement and pick the right trigger type with confidence. That means knowing not just the five names, but the distinction between a trigger — what starts a run — and a schedule — the cadence at which that trigger fires.

Let's start with the simplest case: manual, or Run now. There's no recurring schedule here — the job runs only when someone or something invokes it. This is worth remembering because manual and Run now are the effective default when no trigger has been configured at all.

Next, scheduled triggers. These fire on a cadence defined by a cron expression — for example, every night at midnight. This is your go-to for fixed batch windows, and it's the most common trigger you'll see in production.

Then we have the event-driven family: file arrival, table update, and continuous. File arrival fires when new files land in a location — perfect for irregular upstream drops. Table update triggers when a Delta table changes, and continuous keeps the job running to process events as they come, which suits always-on streaming ingestion.

Here's the key distinction to lock in: a trigger defines what starts a run, while a schedule defines the cadence at which the trigger fires. And there's a classic exam trap here — a job carries one trigger type at a time, and changing the trigger type replaces the previous schedule rather than running both simultaneously.

Let's tie it together with a worked example. Suppose the requirement is 'refresh sales data every night at 2 a.m.' — that's a fixed nightly batch, so cron is your answer. If instead the data arrives whenever a partner uploads a file, you'd reach for file arrival. And if you need always-on ingestion from a stream, you'd choose continuous. Use this mapping and you'll classify any requirement correctly.

scenes.title: Cron Schedules: Syntax, Timezone, and Pause Semantics

elements.content: Cron Schedules: Syntax, Timezone & Pause Semantics

Cron schedules are the trigger layer of Lakeflow Jobs (formerly Databricks Workflows), the native orchestrator that schedules and monitors multi-step data pipelines [source 2].

Reading a cron string correctly — and knowing which timezone it fires in — is a graded, exam-critical skill.
1. Read the expression field by field

The Databricks schedule editor parses six positional fields in fixed order: seconds, minutes, hours, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. Fields are space-separated and positional — swapping two fields never raises an error, it silently produces a different fire time.

Special characters: * (every value), - (range), / (step), ? (no specific value — used only in day-of-month and day-of-week when the other is set).
2. Worked example
3. Timezone setting

Timezone is a job-level setting — independent of the cluster, notebook, and UTC.

Changing it shifts every future fire time; past runs are unaffected. Most exam distractors assume UTC.

Derivation: 0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI

0s + 30m + 6h = 06:30 local

MON-FRI ⇒ 5 fires/week

≠ “every second”, not hourly, not daily.

Pause / Unpause

Pause disables the trigger but does not delete the schedule.

Missed fire times are not replayed on unpause.

⚠ Exam trap: Cron schedules fire forward only. They never retroactively backfill a skipped interval — retroactive data movement is a separate backfill or repair operation, not a scheduling concern.

If a run is missed because the job was paused or the trigger window passed, the next matching fire time is the only chance until you re-run manually.
Key takeaway: Orchestration requires reading schedules correctly, binding them to a timezone, and understanding that pausing prevents — not postpones — a fire [source 6].

actions.text: Now let's zoom in on one specific trigger type: the cron schedule. This is where a lot of exam points hide, because the syntax, the timezone setting, and the pause behavior each trip people up separately.
Remember the framing from earlier in this lesson: cron schedules are the trigger layer of a Lakeflow Job. The job definition describes what to run; the cron schedule simply decides when it fires.

So how do we read one? Step one is to read the expression field by field. That is exactly how the Databricks schedule editor parses it — it does not care about your intuition, it walks left to right through each position.

And here's the part that surprises people: the Databricks schedule editor parses six positions, not the classic five. It starts with seconds, then minute, hour, day-of-month, month, and finally day-of-week. That leading seconds field is the single most common source of a wrong answer.

Look at this labelled breakdown diagram. It shows how the expression zero, thirty, six, question mark, star, MON through FRI maps onto an actual fire time in the selected timezone. Trace each field across to what it contributes.

Let's make that concrete with a worked example. We have the special characters to keep straight: star means every value, dash means a range, slash means a step, and the question mark is the no-specific-value marker used in the day-of-month position.

Here's the derivation. Zero seconds, plus thirty minutes, plus six hours gives us 06:30. The question mark lets the scheduler ignore day-of-month, and MON through FRI restricts us to weekdays. So this schedule fires at 06:30 every weekday — read it field by field and the answer never has to be guessed.
Step three is the timezone setting — and this is where the exam distractors live.

The timezone is a job-level setting. It is independent of the cluster, independent of the notebook, and independent of UTC. It belongs to the job. And because it is job-level, changing it shifts every future fire time — not just the next one.

Next, Pause and Unpause. Pausing disables the trigger, but it does not delete the schedule — the definition is still there waiting. And critically, any fire times that were missed while paused are not replayed. When you unpause, you resume forward from now.

Which brings us to the exam trap itself: cron schedules fire forward only. They never retroactively backfill a skipped interval. If a run is missed — because you paused, or because a run was still executing — the cron trigger will not catch it up. Filling that gap is a separate backfill or repair operation, and that distinction is exactly what the exam is testing.

So here's our key takeaway for this page: orchestration requires reading schedules field by field, confirming the job-level timezone, and treating pausing as a forward-only operation. Read the expression, check the timezone, and never assume a missed fire time will come back on its own.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Cron Schedules and Trigger Selection

questions.question: A nightly pipeline ingests files that a partner delivers to cloud storage at unpredictable times between 00:00 and 06:00. The team's requirement is strict freshness: the refinement (silver) task must run as soon as new data lands, and the whole job graph (ingest, refine, publish) must remain visible and independently retryable in the Lakeflow Jobs UI. Which trigger choice best satisfies this freshness requirement while preserving the visible dependency graph?

options.label: A schedule trigger with a cron expression that fires the job every 15 minutes between 00:00 and 06:00, with the graph of ingest, refine, and publish tasks wired by dependencies
A file-arrival trigger that fires the job when new files land in the partner's storage location, with the same graph of ingest, refine, and publish tasks wired by dependencies
A manual trigger run once each morning by an analyst after they visually confirm the partner files are present
A continuous trigger that keeps the entire job graph running permanently so data is refined the instant it appears

questions.analysis: The stated requirement is strict freshness with an unpredictable arrival time, and it also requires the job graph to stay visible and retryable. A file-arrival (data-arrival) trigger fires the job exactly when the objects appear in the configured storage location, so the silver task runs immediately after arrival rather than waiting for the next polling interval. Because a trigger only decides WHEN the job starts, the internal ingest-refine-publish graph, its dependencies, and its per-task retries are still modeled inside the job, which matches the design constraint that branches and tasks remain visible and independently repairable in the UI. Option A is the classic freshness trap: a 15-minute polling cron is a fixed-interval guess, so on an unlucky morning the data can wait up to 15 minutes, and the job may also fire on intervals with no new data. Option C trades freshness for human latency and is not automatable. Option D is wrong because a continuous trigger is designed for perpetually streaming workloads, not for a bounded nightly medallion (bronze/silver/gold layering, where data is progressively refined) refresh, and running the whole graph non-stop would waste compute and produce overlapping runs. This reinforces the unit's distinction that triggers decide when a job starts while dependencies decide which tasks run — see Lakeflow Jobs as the orchestration layer for scheduling and monitoring pipelines [source 1] and its role in managing task dependencies and scheduling [source 6].

questions.question: A Lakeflow Jobs schedule is configured with the cron expression `0 30 2 * * ?` and the cluster timezone is set to UTC, while the schedule's timezone is set to America/Los_Angeles. It is currently 2024-06-10 09:00:00 in Los Angeles (Pacific Daylight Time, UTC-7). Which TWO statements about the next fire time are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: The `2` in the cron expression means the job fires at 02:30 in the SCHEDULE's timezone (America/Los_Angeles), not at 02:30 UTC
Because the cluster timezone is UTC and 02:30 PDT equals 09:30 UTC, the next fire occurs at 2024-06-11 09:30 UTC — i.e., the cron fields are interpreted against the cluster timezone
The next fire occurs at 2024-06-11 02:30 in Los Angeles, which is 2024-06-11 09:30 UTC
