The `0 30 2` fields map to minute=0, hour=30, day-of-month=2, so the expression is invalid and the schedule never fires

questions.analysis: A standard Quartz-style cron expression used by Databricks schedules has the field order second minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. So `0 30 2 * * ?` means second=0, minute=30, hour=2, every day. Those clock fields are evaluated in the SCHEDULE's own timezone (America/Los_Angeles), so 02:30 means 02:30 local Pacific time, not 02:30 UTC — statement A is correct. Statement C is also correct: since it is already 09:00 on 2024-06-10 in Los Angeles, today's 02:30 has passed, so the next occurrence is 2024-06-11 02:30 PDT, which converts to 2024-06-11 09:30 UTC (PDT is UTC-7). Statement B is the exact distractor described in the test blueprint: it confuses the cluster timezone with the schedule timezone. Changing the cluster timezone to UTC does not shift when the job fires; it only changes the runtime clock inside the notebook. Statement D mis-maps the field order and incorrectly declares the expression invalid — `?` is a legal placeholder in the day-of-week field. This distinction is central to configuring triggers and cron schedules in Lakeflow Jobs [source 3].

questions.question: An engineer pauses a daily Lakeflow Jobs schedule for two weeks during a migration, then re-enables it. On the morning it is re-enabled, she expects the job to automatically catch up on the 14 missed days. Which statement correctly describes the actual behavior?

options.label: Re-enabling a paused schedule automatically backfills all missed runs for the days the schedule was paused
Re-enabling the schedule only triggers the next scheduled run from that point forward; missed past runs are NOT replayed automatically and require an explicit backfill or manual run
The schedule resumes exactly where it stopped and executes the queued runs one after another, so the 14 missed days run consecutively
Because a paused schedule is modeled as SKIPPED states, the downstream tasks will fire on the missed days automatically under an All done Run-if condition

questions.analysis: A paused schedule is simply inactive: the orchestrator does not compute or queue the runs it would otherwise have created. When the schedule is re-enabled, the cron expression is evaluated from the current moment onward, so only future fire times are honored. Statement B correctly captures this: automatic backfill of missed runs does not happen, and catching up requires an explicit action such as a backfill job run or a manual run for the desired dates. Statement A is the exact misconception described in the test blueprint — the assumption that a paused or skipped schedule is automatically backfilled. Statement C invents an unbounded catch-up queue that does not exist. Statement D misuses the Run-if vocabulary taught earlier in this unit: `All done` fires a downstream task only after the upstream tasks in the CURRENT run have all completed (regardless of success or failure); it has nothing to do with replaying missed historical days. To run the missed dates, the standard pattern is an explicit backfill: compute the missing dates (as in the earlier For each example using `dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set` with an array of dates) and feed them into a For each task, or trigger a backfill run for the affected range. Note also that a skipped task in the graph is not the same as a skipped schedule; task-level skip semantics are governed by Run-if. This reflects the role of Lakeflow Jobs as the layer for scheduling and monitoring data pipelines [source 1] and for managing dependencies and scheduling of tasks [source 6].

actions.text: Time for a checkpoint on what we just covered. Take each question one at a time, work through it on your own, and don't rush the cron expressions — read them carefully and think about which timezone each field is interpreted against. Give every option a fair look before you commit.
Once you submit, I'll walk through anything that tripped you up. Go ahead and give it your best shot.

scenes.title: File-Arrival Triggers: Wiring Jobs to Data Dependencies

elements.content: File-Arrival Triggers: Wiring Jobs to Data Dependencies

A file-arrival trigger converts a job from 'run at time T and hope the data is there' to 'run when new data actually lands'. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestration engine on Databricks — it schedules and automates multi-step pipelines by defining tasks, dependencies, triggers, and failure handling [source 2][source 6].
Configure the Trigger

• Location: cloud storage path or Unity Catalog volume to watch

• Polling interval: how often the trigger checks the location

• First check runs at the interval, not instantly

• Example: s3://landing/orders/, every 60 s

• Polling is event-agnostic — it reads a file listing, not a delivery notification
What Fires — and What Doesn't

• Fires once per newly detected batch since the last run

• A burst of ten files arriving between two polls = one run

• Files already at the location when you create the trigger do NOT fire it

• Each run consumes the whole batch, so gate downstream tasks on batch size

• The trigger records a high-water mark per location
The Trade-off

• Cost: detection latency up to one polling interval; always-on monitoring

• Benefit: no guesswork, no early runs on empty data

• A cron guess is either late (idle clusters) or early (wasted compute)
Where the Pattern Fits

• Partner export arriving on an irregular schedule

• IoT landing zone with bursty device uploads

• Third-party data drop with no delivery guarantee
Exam trap: file arrival detects files, not completion — a partially written multi-file delivery can start a run before the upstream writer finishes.

actions.text: Now let's move from fixed schedules to data-driven ones. Up to this point, every trigger we've discussed fires on the clock — cron says a certain time, the job runs, whether or not the data is actually there. File-arrival triggers break that pattern.
File-arrival triggers wire a job to a data dependency instead of a wall-clock time. In other words, the job runs when the files show up, not when we guess they will.

Concretely, a file-arrival trigger converts a job from 'run at this time' into 'run when this data arrives.' That single change removes the fragile game of estimating when an upstream delivery will land.
So how do you configure one? You specify two things.
First, the location you're monitoring — either a cloud storage path or a Unity Catalog volume. Second, the polling interval, which is how often Databricks checks that location for new files.
Next, be precise about what fires the trigger and what doesn't — this is exactly the kind of detail the exam tests.
The trigger fires once per newly detected batch of files since the last run. And critically: files that were already present when you created the trigger do not fire it. Only new arrivals count.

Now the trade-off, which is the heart of this pattern. There's a cost: detection is done by polling, so you inherit up to one full polling interval of latency, plus a small always-on monitoring cost. But in exchange, you remove all the guesswork and the wasted early runs that a naive cron schedule produces.
Where does this pattern fit best? Think irregular, unpredictable deliveries.

A partner export that shows up on no fixed schedule, an IoT landing zone where devices drop files as they come online, or a third-party data drop — all of these are natural fits. You stop predicting and start reacting to the data itself.

Finally, the exam trap. File arrival detects files — not completion. If an upstream writer delivers a multi-file batch and a run kicks off mid-delivery, you can start processing a partially written dataset. Keep that distinction sharp: the trigger tells you a file appeared, never that the upstream writer has finished. That's it for this page — let's build on it next.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: From Scheduling Requirement to Cron Expression

elements.content: Problem 1

A Lakeflow Job named `ingest_partner_orders` runs on a cluster whose system timezone is UTC. The business requirement is: the job must run every Monday through Friday at exactly 06:30 US Eastern local time. (i) Write the exact cron expression for the job's scheduled trigger. (ii) State the additional setting that must be configured so the expression means 06:30 Eastern rather than 06:30 UTC, and prove it numerically for both a January run and a July run. (iii) A colleague submits the five-field POSIX expression `30 6 * * 1-5`. Using Databricks' seconds-first cron parser, compute exactly how many times that expression fires in a non-leap calendar year and compare it with the cadence the business asked for.
Hint: Count the fields before you count the digits: the first field of a Lakeflow cron expression is seconds.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Field order. Lakeflow Jobs cron triggers use the Quartz-style field contract, not POSIX: `seconds minutes hours day-of-month month day-of-week [year]` [source 3]. The seconds field is mandatory and comes first. So the expression needs six fields minimum, and the first one is `0` (fire exactly on the minute boundary, not one second late).

Step 2 — Build each field.

- seconds: `0`

- minutes: `30`

- hours: `6`

- day-of-month: `?` — this field carries no constraint, because the constraint lives in the day-of-week field. In the Quartz contract exactly one of the two day fields is constrained and the other is `?`.

- month: `*` (all twelve months)

- day-of-week: `MON-FRI` (Quartz accepts names such as MON, TUE, or numeric 1-7; names are clearer and less error-prone in review)

Resulting expression: `0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI`.

Step 3 — The timezone setting. The cron expression is wall-clock text; the timezone is a separate property of the scheduled trigger, and it defaults to the workspace/cluster timezone, which here is UTC. Set the schedule timezone to `America/New_York` (an IANA zone name, not the abbreviations `EST` or `EDT`, which are fixed offsets with no daylight-saving rule).

Numeric justification. Eastern Standard Time is UTC-5, so 06:30 local is 06:30 + 05:00 = 11:30 UTC on a January weekday. Eastern Daylight Time is UTC-4, so 06:30 local is 06:30 + 04:00 = 10:30 UTC on a July weekday. The UTC instant promised by the business therefore moves by one hour twice a year. A trigger pinned to UTC with `0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI` would instead fire at 01:30 local in winter and 02:30 local in summer — it would be wrong in both seasons, never right in either. Only the `America/New_York` timezone setting makes 06:30 mean 06:30 to the business.

Step 4 — What the five-field expression actually does. Read `30 6 * * 1-5` with the seconds-first parser:

- seconds = 30

- minutes = 6

- hours = `*` (every hour of the day)

- day-of-month = `*` (every day of the month)

- month = `1-5` (January through May)

- day-of-week = absent, so it defaults to every day

So it fires at HH:06:30 for every hour HH from 00 through 23, every day from 1 January through 31 May, and then stops for the entire second half of the year. The number of firings is $24 \times 151 = 3624$ runs in a non-leap year (151 = 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 + 31 days from January through May). The intended cadence is 5 weekdays per week, which is roughly $5 \times 52 = 260$ runs per year. The misparsed expression therefore runs about 3624 / 260 ≈ 13.9 times more often than intended, at the wrong minute of every hour, and is silent from June to December.

Analysis — Why the method works: a cron expression answers only the question 'which wall-clock instants', never 'in which timezone'. Splitting the two — cadence in the expression, wall-clock meaning in the trigger's timezone field — is what makes a single expression correct across the DST boundary that a hard-coded UTC job would cross twice a year.

Pitfall 1, the field shift. The most common failure is writing the POSIX five-field form `30 6 * * 1-5`. Every field shifts one position left, so the day-of-week constraint is silently reinterpreted as a month constraint. This is not a syntax error, it is a valid expression that fires thousands of times too often, which is why it survives code review as often as it does.

Pitfall 2, `?` versus `*`. In the Quartz contract that Databricks cron follows, the day-of-month and day-of-week fields are mutually exclusive: one carries the constraint and the other must be `?` [source 3]. Writing `0 30 6 * * MON-FRI` leaves `*` (every day) in the day-of-month field, which is at best redundant and is rejected outright by strict Quartz validators. Reviewers should treat `?` in exactly one day field as a required artifact, not a stylistic choice.

Pitfall 3, `MON-FRI` is not a business calendar. The expression fires on Christmas Day, New Year's Day, Thanksgiving, and both DST-transition weekdays if they fall on a weekday, because it knows nothing about holidays. Databricks provides no built-in holiday calendar on a scheduled trigger, so a holiday gate has to be built explicitly — with a custom Run-if condition on the first task or an in-notebook check against a dates table.

Pitfall 4, DST anomalies beyond the shift. On the spring-forward day, local times between 02:00 and 02:59 do not exist; a job scheduled in that window silently skips that day entirely. On the fall-back day, local times between 01:00 and 01:59 occur twice; a job scheduled there can fire twice, duplicating work. 06:30 Eastern is outside both windows in the US, so this particular job is safe, but the general rule belongs in any design review: the wall-clock times a cron can promise safely exclude the DST transition windows. Generalized: choose the timezone field from the *business* calendar, not from the compute platform, and remember that one job object can hold exactly one trigger configuration [source 1][source 3].
Problem 2

The partner contract states that order files land in `s3://partner-landing/orders/` between 05:00 and 07:00 US Eastern on weekdays, but sometimes not at all. The job `ingest_partner_orders` currently uses the scheduled trigger `0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI` with timezone `America/New_York`, and its first task reads everything present in the landing path. On roughly one weekday in five the folder is empty at 06:30, so the notebook either fails on an empty DataFrame or writes a zero-row batch; on days when the partner is late (say 06:50), the run misses the file until the next day. Replace the trigger, state the exact trigger configuration, and explain how the run learns which file triggered it.
Hint: The requirement on the table is 'run when data exists', not 'run at a time'. Which trigger type matches that sentence?

Worked solution
Step 1 — Diagnose the mismatch. The current design encodes a *time* requirement (06:30) for a workload whose real requirement is an *existence* requirement (process the file when it arrives). Arrival time is nondeterministic (05:00-07:00) and can be absent entirely, so no fixed cron can satisfy it: any time you pick is either too early (empty folder, wasted or failing run) or too late (SLA miss on late days). The correct trigger type is File arrival, which starts a run when new files land in a monitored location [source 3][source 6].

Step 2 — Trigger configuration on `ingest_partner_orders`.

- Trigger type: File arrival (remove the scheduled trigger from this job).

- Location: `s3://partner-landing/orders/`.

- Fire behavior: run when the first new file appears, with the batching/interval setting chosen so a burst of files dropped in the same poll window is handled by one run rather than one run per file.

- The trigger polls the path, so the wall-clock gap between a file landing and the run starting is bounded by the poll interval — it is near-real-time, not instantaneous.

Step 3 — How the run learns which file triggered it. The file arrival trigger supplies the triggering path to the run through its built-in trigger parameter, URL-encoded (for example spaces appear as `%20`), so a task that consumes the parameter must decode it before opening the path. A more robust alternative is to ignore the parameter for reading and process the directory with Auto Loader (`cloudFiles`) on the same path, which tracks which files have already been ingested and picks up anything that landed after the run started at the next incremental read. The trigger answers *when to run*; Auto Loader answers *which files to read*.

Step 4 — Budget consequence. The cron fired on 260 weekdays per year whether or not data existed. With a file arrival trigger and an 80% delivery rate, the job runs roughly $0.8 \times 260 = 208$ times per year, and each of those runs has data to process.

Analysis — Why the method works: triggers are selected from the *event that makes work available*, not from a habitual daily time. File arrival matches nondeterministic arrivals with possible no-shows exactly; a cron matches a clock.

Edge cases to state explicitly. (1) Fire latency: because the trigger polls, it cannot promise 'within 30 seconds of landing'. You must size the poll interval against the downstream SLA, and you must never describe a file arrival trigger as a hard latency guarantee. (2) Bursts: if six files land inside one poll interval, the batching configuration decides whether you get one run or six; a run that starts before all six have landed will only see the first ones unless the read side (Auto Loader) is incremental. (3) Timeouts: in a 'wait for file arrival' style configuration, a day with no delivery produces no run at all, which is silent — no failure notification and no red row in the run history. If anyone downstream assumes a daily run exists, add a separate watchdog job that deliberately checks for the absence of a run or the absence of fresh data. (4) Late files: a file landing at 07:30 after the 06:35 run finished is not lost by Auto Loader, but it is only picked up when the next run occurs, so pair the trigger with an incremental reader rather than a 'read the whole directory' task.

Common mistakes. Treating a file arrival trigger as a schedule and still writing a cron expression for it; assuming the trigger de-duplicates files it already saw (it does not — the read side must be idempotent, which is also what makes partial runs and repairs cheap when a downstream task fails) [source 4]; and forgetting the parallel trigger type, table update, which is the right choice when the partner writes into a Delta table rather than a file path, because table update triggers react to committed table changes rather than to objects in storage [source 3].
Problem 3

Finance needs a job `report_finance_daily` to produce a report at 08:00 US Eastern every weekday from `silver.orders_daily`, whether or not the partner delivered files that day; on days with no delivery the report must state 'no delivery today'. The ingest job `ingest_partner_orders` now runs on a file arrival trigger. A teammate proposes: 'just add the 08:00 cron to the ingest job — it already has a trigger, so put the schedule next to it.' Explain why that is impossible, give the complete trigger settings for both jobs, and describe how the report determines whether today's data exists.
Hint: Ask how many trigger configurations a single Lakeflow job can hold, and remember that task values and Run-if conditions are scoped to one job.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Trigger cardinality. A Lakeflow job has exactly one trigger configuration. The file arrival trigger already occupies it on `ingest_partner_orders`, so there is no second slot to put a cron in. The teammate's proposal is not a configuration mistake that can be fixed with syntax — it is not representable in the object model [source 3].

Step 2 — Two jobs, two concerns, two triggers.

- `ingest_partner_orders`: trigger type File arrival, location `s3://partner-landing/orders/` (unchanged from part b). Event-driven, runs 0 or more times per day depending on delivery.

- `report_finance_daily`: trigger type Scheduled, expression `0 0 8 ? * MON-FRI`, timezone `America/New_York`. Field check: seconds = 0, minutes = 0, hours = 8, day-of-month = `?`, month = `*`, day-of-week = MON-FRI.

Numeric justification of the timezone setting, as in part (a): 08:00 Eastern is 13:00 UTC in winter (EST, UTC-5: 08:00 + 05:00 = 13:00) and 12:00 UTC in summer (EDT, UTC-4: 08:00 + 04:00 = 12:00). The `America/New_York` timezone absorbs that one-hour difference so the local promise to Finance never changes.

Step 3 — How the report decides whether today's data exists. Run-if conditions and task values are scoped to a single job and do not cross job boundaries, so the reporting job cannot read the ingest job's state or its `dbutils.jobs.taskValues`. Instead it derives freshness from the data itself: the first task runs a SQL task such as `SELECT max(delivery_date) AS max_date FROM silver.orders_daily`, and its query output is passed downstream as a parameter [source 4]. The report task then compares that returned date with today's date in `America/New_York`: equal means report the day's numbers, not equal means emit the explicit 'no delivery today' status. This keeps the report correct even when the ingest job never ran that day.

Step 4 — Why two objects are better than one. Each job keeps its own run history and repair surface, so a failed report can be retried without rerunning ingestion; permissions can be granted narrowly (Finance gets `CAN VIEW`/`CAN MANAGE RUN` on the report job only, not on the ingest job); and each job can be placed on compute sized for its own workload. Partial runs and repairs exist precisely so that only the failed piece is recomputed [source 4]; the two-job split gives that property for free across the event-driven and clock-driven halves of the pipeline [source 1].

Analysis — Why the method works: the design rule is one concern per job object, and the trigger is part of the job's identity. Merging an event-driven concern and a clock-driven concern into one job is impossible because the object holds one trigger; merging them into one *run* would also be wrong, because the two runs must be able to succeed and fail independently.

Edge cases. (1) DST: 08:00 is a wall-clock promise to a human audience, so the correct behavior is for the UTC instant to move by an hour in spring and autumn while the local instant stays fixed; the IANA timezone name does exactly that. Using `EST` as the timezone string would pin the report to winter time all year and make it run at 09:00 local in summer. (2) A scheduled report will fire on days when the source data is absent, so 'no delivery' must be a first-class, explicitly written output path in the notebook or SQL, not a crash and not an empty report. (3) If the freshness check itself fails (table missing, permission error), that must surface as a job failure, not as a silent 'no delivery' — a false negative in a finance report is more expensive than a red run.

Common mistakes. Assuming a Run-if condition such as 'All done' can reach across jobs and gate the report on the ingest run — it cannot; dependencies and run-if evaluate only among tasks inside one job. Assuming a job can be both event-driven and clock-driven. Adding an intermediate 'orchestrator' job with a cron and a Run job task that calls the report job: this is valid, but it does not merge the triggers, it only relocates the cron one hop away and adds a second run history to debug, so it should be chosen deliberately rather than as a reflex. Finally, forgetting that a downstream fixed-window consumer changes the *number* of reports, not the pipeline: the ingest job still ingests only when files arrive, and the report job still reports every weekday, including the days when the honest answer is 'nothing arrived'. The generalizable rule is that pipeline freshness is a property of the data (`max(delivery_date)`), never a property of another job's run state [source 1][source 4].

actions.text: Building directly on the trigger distinction we just made, let's work through three exam-style problems that turn a written scheduling requirement into a concrete cron expression, a trigger choice, and the settings that make it correct. We'll take them one at a time.

Problem one. A Lakeflow Job named ingest_partner_orders must run Monday through Friday at 06:30 US Eastern. Here's the trap: the team's clusters are configured in UTC. Read the requirement carefully — the time and the timezone are two separate things, and a job scheduler resolves them separately.
Before you count the digits, count the fields. Lakeflow Jobs uses a seconds-first cron syntax — six fields, not the five you may be used to from POSIX.

So the expression becomes: zero seconds, thirty minutes, six hours, question mark for day-of-month, star for month, MON-FRI for day-of-week. That reads 0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI. Then — and this is the part candidates lose marks on — you set the job schedule timezone to America/New_York, so 06:30 means 06:30 Eastern regardless of what the cluster is configured in.

Why does the method work? Because a cron expression encodes a wall-clock time, and the timezone setting is what anchors that wall-clock time to a real instant. Change the cluster to UTC and the expression alone would still fire at 06:30 UTC — the timezone field is what makes it Eastern. Now let's look at what happens when a fixed schedule is the wrong tool entirely.

Problem two. The partner contract states that order files land between 05:00 and 07:00 Eastern on weekdays — but sometimes not at all. The requirement on the table is 'run when data arrives.' A window that sometimes stays empty is exactly the case where a fixed schedule wastes runs and misses late files.

The diagnosis is a mismatch between the trigger and the dependency. When arrival time is nondeterministic and some days produce no delivery, you replace the fixed schedule with a file-arrival trigger on the partner landing path. The trigger fires on the event that actually matters — a file showing up — instead of guessing a time.

And this is why the method works: triggers are selected by the nature of the dependency, not by convenience. If the upstream is data, trigger on data. If the upstream is a clock, trigger on the clock. Next, the hardest of the three — a case where you need both.

Problem three. Finance needs a job, report_finance_daily, to produce a fixed reporting window every morning — but the ingest that feeds it is file-arrival driven. So how many trigger configurations can a single job hold? Ask yourself that before you reach for the answer.

The trigger cardinality rule is the key: a single Lakeflow Job can hold only one trigger type. You cannot bolt a file-arrival trigger and a cron schedule onto the same job. Where a fixed reporting window is still required downstream, you create a second, separate cron-triggered job and let it depend on the ingest.

The design rule behind this: one job, one trigger mechanism. If two requirements genuinely need different trigger semantics, that's a signal to split into two jobs wired by a dependency — not to fight the platform. And watch these pitfalls across all three problems: a five-field POSIX expression gets misread by the seconds-first parser, question mark and star are not interchangeable in the day fields, and MON-FRI silently skips holidays and DST-shifted fire times. Keep those in mind as we move on.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: File-Arrival and Trigger Behaviour

questions.question: A data engineer configures a Lakeflow Jobs file-arrival trigger on a cloud storage path that already contains several files written hours before the trigger was saved. The job is then enabled. Which statement best describes what happens?

options.label: The trigger fires immediately, once per pre-existing file, because the trigger scans the path the moment it is saved.
The trigger fires once immediately to process all pre-existing files as a single batch, then switches to normal incremental detection.
The trigger does not fire for the pre-existing files; it begins detecting only files that arrive after the trigger is saved and the job is enabled.
The trigger fires only if at least one pre-existing file is newer than the previous run of the same job, otherwise it stays idle.

questions.analysis: A file-arrival trigger is an event-based trigger: it detects new files that land in the watched location after the trigger is configured and enabled, and it starts a run when the arrival condition is satisfied. Files that already existed at configuration time are not treated as arrivals, so the trigger should not back-fill them [source 3][source 2]. Option A is the classic pre-existing-file trap — new engineers assume the trigger behaves like a crawler that ingests everything it can see. Option B is a misconception that the trigger does a one-time catch-up batch; it does not. Option D invents a timestamp-comparison rule that is not part of the trigger semantics; trigger evaluation is about new arrivals, not about comparing file mtimes to a prior run.

questions.question: Which of the following are required or configurable elements of a file-arrival trigger on a Lakeflow Jobs job? Select all that apply.

options.label: A storage location to watch (for example, a cloud storage path such as an S3, ADLS, or GCS prefix).
An arrival condition that determines when a run should start once new files are detected in the watched location.
A cron expression that governs the cadence of the trigger.
A strict guarantee that the upstream writer has fully closed and committed every file before the job begins its run.

questions.analysis: A file-arrival trigger is defined by where to look (the watched storage location) and by the condition under which a detected arrival should cause a run to start — for example, an arrival count or a waiting period after first detection [source 3][source 2]. Option C is wrong because a cron expression belongs to a scheduled trigger, not to a file-arrival trigger; the two are different trigger types, and conflating them is a common error [source 1]. Option D is wrong because file detection is not the same as upstream write completion: the trigger observes that something has landed at the path, and a partially written file can be visible before the writer finishes, which is why the arrival condition (such as requiring additional files or waiting before firing) matters. Do not assume the trigger has transactional knowledge of the upstream job.

questions.question: A pipeline must react to new data landing in cloud storage with the lowest feasible detection latency and a cost profile that scales with data arrival rather than with wall-clock time. Which trigger choice best matches this requirement, and why?

options.label: A file-arrival trigger, because it reacts to the event of a new file landing rather than waiting for a fixed cron fire time, so it does not burn compute polling an unchanged path on a schedule.
A cron schedule at a very fine granularity, because the schedule editor supports a seconds field, which makes cron latency strictly lower than any file-arrival trigger.
A manual / Run now trigger, because the engineer can start the job the instant the data lands, eliminating polling entirely.
A table-update trigger, because tables are always updated before files are written, so a table-update trigger is the earliest possible signal.

questions.analysis: The trade-off between polling and event-driven detection is the core comparison here. A cron schedule fires at fixed times regardless of whether data has arrived; if the data lands just after a fire, the run waits until the next tick, and if nothing has changed, the run may still be spent doing nothing — latency and cost are both tied to the calendar [source 3][source 1]. A file-arrival trigger is event-driven: it starts a run when new files are detected, so detection latency is tied to arrival rather than to the next scheduled tick, and idle periods do not force scheduled runs [source 2]. Option B is wrong because, even with a seconds field, cron is still clock-driven, not data-driven, and it does not observe the path at all. Option C is wrong because manual runs are not a recurring trigger and require a human. Option D is wrong because it assumes a guaranteed ordering between table updates and file writes that a storage-layer trigger does not provide.

actions.text: Now it's time to check how well the trigger concepts have settled. Work through each question on your own — read carefully, since a couple of these hinge on precise trigger semantics rather than the general idea.
Take your time, answer all three, and once you submit I'll walk you through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Choosing a Trigger Strategy Under Real Constraints

elements.content: Decision — A data engineering team maintains a medallion architecture (a layered pattern of bronze/silver/gold tables, where silver holds cleaned and conformed data) for a daily batch feed that lands as files in cloud object storage. The silver layer has a 5-minute freshness target: once the upstream file for a given business day is delivered, silver must be refreshed within five minutes. The upstream delivers files anywhere between 05:00 and 07:00 Eastern, and there is roughly one gap day per week when no file arrives at all. The job that refreshes silver is a single Lakeflow Jobs task, and the team is also bound by a hard limit on always-on compute. The decision is difficult because the freshness target pulls one way (react immediately to whatever arrives) while the budget constraint and the unpredictable arrival window pull another way (do not pay for a cluster that is waiting at 04:59). A candidate trigger strategy is judged against these constraints, not against an abstract notion of 'best' orchestration.

Constraints — Silver layer freshness target: at most 5 minutes after a valid upstream file lands in the landing zone  •  Upstream arrival window is unpredictable: files land anywhere from 05:00 to 07:00 Eastern  •  No always-on compute: the team cannot keep a cluster provisioned and polling 24/7 to satisfy the freshness target  •  One job holds exactly one trigger type, so a single job definition cannot simultaneously be cron-triggered and file-arrival-triggered [source 3][source 6]  •  Gap days: on average one day per week delivers no file, and the pipeline must not report failure on those days  •  Fixed reporting window: a downstream report must still be produced every day regardless of whether a new file arrived

Scheduled cron trigger only
+ Deterministic run windows: a cron expression such as 0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI is fully predictable, and operators can reason about the next fire time before it happens; + Cheapest monitoring: because the trigger is a clock, there is no polling service, no file-list scan, and no always-on compute sitting idle between fires; + The schedule timezone is a job-level setting independent of the cluster, notebook, and UTC, so a shift in daylight-saving rules is a single field change rather than a code change
− Gap days run a job that has nothing to process, producing wasted cluster startup and a misleading green run that did no work; − On late-arrival days the file can land after the cron fire, so silver is stale until the next day's run — directly violating the 5-minute freshness target; − Tightening the cron to catch late arrivals (for example firing every 15 minutes from 05:00 to 07:00) multiplies the wasted-run problem on gap days and raises the run count without a guarantee of catching the file
Best for: Feeds whose delivery time is highly predictable and where a bounded, scheduled staleness (for example, 'silver is fresh as of 06:30 every day') is an acceptable contract

File arrival trigger on the landing zone only
+ Immediate reaction to delivery: the file arrival trigger fires when a file is detected in the landing zone, so silver can be refreshed within the 5-minute target without guessing when the file will land; + No wasted runs on gap days: if no file arrives, the trigger never fires, so no cluster is started, no compute is consumed, and no misleading green run is recorded; + Because the freshness target is measured from file arrival, not from a clock, the trigger semantics match the actual requirement; + Auto Loader-style file detection on the landing zone gives the trigger a concrete event to key off, rather than a blind schedule
− Polling latency: file arrival triggers rely on the platform noticing a new file, so the effective delay between 'file lands' and 'trigger fires' is a polling interval, not zero, and must be inside the 5-minute budget; − No completeness guarantee: a file arrival trigger can fire on a partial delivery — for example, one of three expected partitions — so the job must itself check completeness before refreshing silver; − A file arrival trigger will not produce the downstream daily report on a gap day, because no file means no trigger, which conflicts with the fixed reporting window
Best for: Landing-zone feeds where the arrival time is unpredictable but the arrival event is reliable, and where the pipeline can validate completeness before consuming

Continuous trigger (always-on)
+ Near-instant freshness: a continuous trigger keeps the job running and reacting, so latency approaches the platform's minimum reaction time rather than a cron interval or a polling delay; + No need to design around a polling interval or a cron fire time, because there is no discrete trigger to miss; + Would be appropriate if the feed were truly streaming and the business required sub-minute freshness
− Breaks the budget constraint directly: continuous triggering requires always-on compute, which is explicitly forbidden by the hard limit on always-on compute; − Unnecessary for a once-daily batch feed: paying 24/7 for a workload that produces at most one file per day is pure waste; − Turns a simple daily batch into an operational responsibility — a continuously running job is a continuously failing job when something breaks, which raises the monitoring and on-call burden
Best for: Genuinely streaming sources with a sub-minute freshness requirement and a budget that explicitly funds always-on compute

File arrival on the landing zone, plus a separate cron job for the fixed reporting window
+ Satisfies the freshness target for the data path: the file arrival trigger fires on delivery, so silver is refreshed within the 5-minute target regardless of whether the file lands at 05:00 or 07:00; + Satisfies the reporting requirement on gap days: because one job holds one trigger type, a second cron-triggered job runs the report at a fixed window every day, even when no file arrived [source 3][source 6]; + Does not require always-on compute: file arrival and cron are event- and clock-driven, so compute is started by the trigger and can be released between fires; + Preserves the run-if and branching logic learned earlier: the report job can use Run-if conditions to distinguish 'file arrived and silver refreshed' from 'gap day, silver unchanged' rather than treating both as success
− Two job definitions to maintain, monitor, and permission separately, which is more operational surface than a single job; − The two jobs need a shared state signal — for example, the report job must know whether the file arrival job actually refreshed silver today — so a task value, a status table, or a table-update dependency must be designed and kept correct; − The completeness check still has to live inside the file arrival job, because the trigger itself does not guarantee the delivery is whole
Best for: Daily batch feeds with an unpredictable arrival window plus a fixed downstream reporting obligation, where freshness and reporting are genuinely two different requirements

Recommendation: File arrival on the landing zone, plus a separate cron job for the fixed reporting window — This option is the only candidate that satisfies every hard constraint simultaneously. The 5-minute freshness target is measured from the moment the file lands, and files land anywhere from 05:00 to 07:00, so only an event-driven trigger — file arrival on the landing zone — can react in time; a cron-only job either fires before a late file lands (stale silver) or fires repeatedly to hedge (wasted runs on gap days). The always-on compute constraint rules out the continuous trigger outright, and the fixed reporting obligation rules out a file-arrival-only design, because a gap day has no file and therefore no trigger. Because one job holds exactly one trigger type, the reporting obligation cannot be bolted onto the file arrival job; it must be a second, cron-triggered job, which also keeps the daily report deterministic and cheap to monitor [source 3][source 6]. The residual risks — polling latency inside the 5-minute budget and a partial delivery passing the trigger — are addressed inside the file arrival job with a completeness check, not by changing the trigger. In short, the constraints select a two-job topology: event-driven for freshness, clock-driven for the report [source 1][source 2].

actions.text: Alright, let's put triggers to work on a real decision. Here's the scenario: a data engineering team maintains a medallion pipeline, and they need to pick a single trigger strategy for one job. Read the constraints carefully before you jump to an answer.

Three constraints frame everything. The silver layer has a five-minute freshness target. Upstream files land somewhere between 05:00 and 07:00 Eastern, roughly one gap day per week when nothing arrives at all. And there's a hard limit on always-on compute — no permanently running cluster. Freshness, unpredictability, and budget. Every option has to be judged against all three.

Option A is the scheduled cron trigger. Its strengths are real: deterministic run windows you can reason about, and the cheapest monitoring, because a run either fired or it didn't. But look at the failure side. On the gap day, you burn runs that find nothing. And on a late-arrival day, the file shows up after your window has already passed, so the data goes stale until tomorrow.

Option B reacts to a file arriving in the landing zone. No wasted runs on the gap day, and an immediate reaction the moment delivery happens. The cost: you pay a polling latency, and a file-arrival trigger tells you a file showed up — it does not guarantee the delivery is complete. A half-written file can trip the trigger just as easily as a finished one.

Option C is continuous, always-on. It gives near-instant freshness, but that is exactly the wrong trade here. It breaks the compute budget constraint outright, and for a once-daily batch feed, always-on compute is simply unnecessary spend.

So the answer is a hybrid. Use a file-arrival trigger on the landing zone for the main pipeline, plus a separate cron-triggered job for the fixed reporting window. Two jobs — because one job holds one trigger type. And when you justify it in an exam, tie the choice explicitly back to the freshness target and the compute budget, not just to convenience.

Notice the shape of the recommendation, because this is how trigger questions are graded: state the constraint, eliminate the option that violates it, then defend the survivor. Option C dies on budget, Option A dies on late-arrival staleness, and Option B survives once you cover its completeness gap with a second, cron-driven job.

The Cron fields drive everything. Notice the five fields — minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week. Let's start with a simple every-hour schedule so the prediction pattern is obvious.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Trigger Design Decisions

questions.question: A team needs a nightly reporting job that must run every day at 02:00 US Pacific time, but it must only produce a report after the previous day's extract file has actually landed in the landing volume. The extract file usually arrives between 23:00 and 01:30 Pacific. Lakeflow Jobs enforces a one-trigger-per-job constraint. What is the correct number of jobs required, and how should they be wired?

options.label: One job, with a single file-arrival trigger on the landing volume and a cron schedule of 0 0 2 * * ? used together on the same job.
One job, with a cron schedule of 0 0 2 * * ? only; the report task itself should poll the volume and wait for the file to appear.

Two jobs: an upstream ingestion job triggered by file arrival on the landing volume, and a downstream reporting job triggered by a cron schedule, connected so the report only runs after ingestion succeeds.
Two jobs: an upstream job with a cron schedule of 0 0 2 * * ? and a downstream job with a file-arrival trigger, so the report waits on the file after the schedule fires.

questions.analysis: Because a Lakeflow job accepts only one trigger, you cannot attach both a file-arrival trigger and a cron schedule to the same job. Option A is therefore invalid: the platform allows only one trigger per job, not two coexisting triggers. Option B leaves correctness to ad-hoc polling inside a task, which wastes early runs before 23:00 and still does not guarantee the file is complete when the report reads it. The correct pattern is to split responsibilities across two jobs: the upstream job is the file-arrival trigger that fires once per newly detected batch of files since the last run [source 6], and the downstream job keeps the fixed 02:00 cadence with a cron schedule [source 3]. Option D inverts the direction of the dependency chain and reverses the semantics of each trigger, so the report would fire before ingestion. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestrator for the Lakehouse and exists precisely to manage these cross-job dependencies [source 3].

questions.question: A data engineer in Berlin writes the cron expression 0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI for a reporting job and expects it to fire at 06:30 local Berlin time. Which statements about making that cron time mean a specific regional time rather than UTC are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The schedule timezone is a job-level setting that is independent of the cluster timezone, the notebook session timezone, and UTC.

If the schedule timezone is left at its default, the 06:30 in the cron expression is interpreted in that default zone, so the engineer must set the job schedule timezone to the target region (for example Europe/Berlin).
Setting the cluster's Spark timezone to Europe/Berlin retargets the cron expression, because the schedule inherits the timezone of the compute that runs the job.
Changing the schedule timezone shifts every future fire time of the job, so the next occurrence after the change must be re-derived.

questions.analysis: The schedule timezone is a job-level setting that is independent of the cluster, the notebook, and UTC, so option A is correct; a fixed cron expression can only mean a specific regional time if that job-level timezone is set to the region [source 3]. Option B is correct because a timezone-aware interpretation of 06:30 must come from the schedule setting, not from the expression text alone. Option C is the classic distractor: it confuses the cluster timezone with the schedule timezone, and changing Spark's timezone on the compute does not retarget the trigger. Option D is correct because changing the schedule timezone shifts every future fire time, so the next occurrence changes and must be recomputed. The expression 0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI is read field by field as seconds 0, minute 30, hour 6, day-of-month ?, month *, day-of-week MON-FRI.

questions.question: A job is configured with a file-arrival trigger on a landing volume. A partner delivery drops 12 parquet files for one logical dataset into that volume within the same minute, but they arrive across two polling intervals: 8 files in the first interval and 4 files in the second. What should the engineer expect, and what is the correct mitigation?

options.label: The trigger fires once per detected batch, so the job may start twice and the downstream task processes 8 files then 4 files; the engineer should make the processing idempotent and able to handle a partial delivery before declaring the dataset complete.
The trigger fires exactly once after all 12 files land, because file-arrival triggers accumulate a delivery window and wait for the partner to signal completion.
The trigger fires 12 times, once per file, so the engineer only needs to ensure the task is cheap per file.
The trigger fires zero times because files that appear after the trigger was created are not considered new and require a manual Run now.

questions.analysis: The file-arrival trigger fires once per newly detected batch of files since the last run [source 6], so a multi-file delivery split across polling intervals can legitimately produce more than one run. Option A reflects this: the engineer must design the downstream task to be idempotent and tolerate a partial delivery rather than assuming all 12 files are present in one invocation. Option B is wrong because the trigger is event-agnostic and does not know about partner completion semantics — there is no delivery-window accumulation logic. Option C is wrong because the trigger batches newly detected files rather than firing per file. Option D is a partial truth distorted into a falsehood: files already present when the trigger is created do not fire it, but files that arrive afterwards — as here — do fire it, so no manual Run now is required. The correct mental model ties the trigger to detection batches, not to logical deliveries.
