scenes.title: Notifications: Destinations, Scopes, and Events

elements.content: Notifications: Destinations, Scopes, and Events
Wire a job's outcome to the people who must act on it — in Lakeflow Jobs, the native orchestrator for the Lakehouse [source 3].

Destinations

Where a notification lands

• Email address

• Slack / MS Teams channel

• PagerDuty on-call

• Generic webhook (workspace)

Precondition: destination must exist / be connected for the workspace before it can be selected.

Events

What triggers a send

• Run start

• Run success

• Run failure

• Duration warning (threshold in minutes)

Edge case: duration warning fires only once the run exceeds the threshold; a fast run never sends it.

Scope

How wide the rule applies

• Job level: whole job + every task

• Task level: one task, its own recipient list

Precondition: task-level rules are separate from job-level, not merged. A task with its own list does not inherit the job list.

Source: config surface for jobs, tasks and notifications [source 3].

Worked example — a nightly ingest job

Job-level rule: send only on failure to the on-call list, plus a duration warning at 45 min (expected runtime 30 min).

Task-level rule on the load task: send on success to #data-eng (skip the on-call list entirely).

Compute cost of tolerance: 30 runs/month × 365 days ≈ 1 success email/day to #data-eng, but only the 45-min warning hits PagerDuty.

Why the default matters

Failure-only + long-task duration warning preserves signal [source 6].

Notify-on-success to a broad list = alert fatigue: a daily success email to 200 people trains them to ignore the one failure that matters.

Tie-back: notifications are job and task configuration only — they are not Databricks SQL alerts and never retry, repair or restart a failed task [source 4].

actions.text: Now let's turn to a configuration surface that quietly decides whether your team trusts your pipelines: notifications. The goal here is simple to state and easy to get wrong — you want a job's outcome to reach exactly the people who must act on it, no more and no fewer.

First, destinations. This is simply where a notification lands. You can target plain email addresses, or connected destinations already configured for the workspace — Slack, Microsoft Teams, PagerDuty, or a generic webhook. The key exam point is that these connected destinations are workspace-level configuration, so they exist independently of any single job.

Next, events — what actually triggers a send. You can subscribe to run start, run success, run failure, and a duration warning that fires when a run exceeds an expected time threshold. So the event list is short, and pairing the right event with the right destination is the whole design exercise.

Then we have scope — how wide the rule applies. At the job level, the notification applies to the whole job and every task in it. At the task level, it applies to one specific task and can even carry a different recipient list. That distinction is a favorite exam trap, so hold onto it.

This routing diagram makes the fan-out concrete: one job, and its success, failure, and duration-warning signals routed to different destinations. Notice that a single job outcome is not a single message — different events go to different audiences.

Here's a worked example: a nightly ingest job. At the job level, we notify the data engineering on-call channel on failure. At the task level, we set a duration warning on the long ingest task, pointing at the team that owns that source system. One job, two scopes, two audiences — and notice the recipient lists are genuinely different.

And this is why the production default matters. Failure-only, plus a duration warning on long tasks, preserves signal — every message means someone needs to act. Notify-on-success to a broad list does the opposite: it trains people to ignore the channel, and that's alert fatigue. One nuance to be precise about: notifications are job and task configuration only. They are not the same feature as Databricks SQL alerts, and they never retry, repair, or restart a failed task — they only tell you about it.

scenes.title: Designing an Alerting Strategy That Keeps Its Signal

elements.content: Designing an Alerting Strategy That Keeps Its Signal

From configuring one notification to sustaining an alerting posture a production team can trust. Alerts are part of the broader orchestration layer that schedules, monitors, and governs pipelines in Lakeflow Jobs [source 3].

Route by severity and audience. The same job event means different things to different people, so the destination must be chosen per event type, not per job [source 1].

• Routine success digests → a team channel for visibility and trend-spotting.

• Failures → the on-call paging destination, because someone must wake up.

• Duration warnings → the pipeline owner, who can act before failure occurs.

Bind durations to timeouts. A duration warning threshold and a run timeout are a matched pair: the warning fires first at, say, 45 minutes, and the timeout kills the run at 60 minutes. Without the timeout, a silently stalled job keeps holding compute and blocks downstream tasks indefinitely [source 6].

Worked example

Job runs 60 min tonight. Warning at 45 min pages the owner; the 60 min run timeout stops it. Owner sees the alert, inspects the graph, and reruns only the failed task.

Non-negotiable

Every destination needs a named owner. An alert routed to a list nobody monitors is indistinguishable from no alert at all — a common failure mode reviewed on the next slide.
Lakeflow Jobs: scheduling, dependencies, monitors, and failure handling in one orchestration layer [source 1][source 2]

actions.text: We just covered how to configure a notification. The harder skill, and the one the exam really tests, is designing an alerting strategy that keeps its signal — one your production team can actually live with night after night without tuning it out.

The first principle is to route by severity and audience. Routine success digests go to a team channel, failures go to the on-call destination, and duration warnings go to the pipeline owner. Notice how the same job event is deliberately sent to different places depending on what it means — not to a single catch-all channel.

Here's a worked example. A job normally runs sixty minutes. You set a warning at seventy-five minutes and a run timeout at ninety. If the job stalls silently at minute sixty-one and never fails on its own, the duration warning fires at seventy-five and the timeout kills it at ninety. That pairing is what catches a hung job instead of letting it run all night quietly.

Two things are non-negotiable. Every destination needs a named owner, and failure notifications belong on the tasks that sit on the critical path — with task-level notifications when a specific task needs a different owner. Also remember the classic failure modes: notifying on every success, alert fatigue, no named owner, and alerts routed to a list nobody monitors.

For the Lakeflow Jobs exam scenario — engineers who didn't learn the nightly load had failed until morning — don't blame the schedule first. Check the notification event selection, check the destination, and check whether anyone owned that destination. That three-part diagnosis is the answer pattern the certification is looking for.

scenes.title: Lesson Review: Scheduling, Triggers, and Alerting

questions.question: A data engineer reviews an exam scenario: an ingest job must start whenever a partner drops new files into a Unity Catalog volume, but the partner's delivery time varies between 05:00 and 07:00 Eastern and sometimes no delivery occurs at all on a given weekday. The team clusters are configured with the UTC timezone. The proposed job definition sets a scheduled (cron) trigger of `0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI` and leaves the job schedule timezone at its default. Which single element of this configuration is the MOST fundamentally wrong for the stated operational requirement, and why?

options.label: The cron expression itself is malformed: a valid Databricks expression must begin with the minute field, not the seconds field, so the trigger would never fire.

The trigger TYPE is wrong: because arrival time is nondeterministic and some weekdays produce no delivery at all, the requirement is satisfied by a file-arrival trigger on the monitored location, not by a fixed schedule.
The only real problem is the timezone: setting the job schedule timezone to America/New_York while leaving the trigger as scheduled cron would fully satisfy the requirement.
The configuration must instead use a Databricks SQL alert on the target table, because alerts are the mechanism that starts a job when dependent data changes.

questions.analysis: The stated requirement is event-shaped, not clock-shaped: arrival time is nondeterministic (05:00–07:00 Eastern) and roughly one gap day per week produces no delivery. A scheduled (cron) trigger fires on the clock whether or not files exist, so it wastes runs on gap days and produces stale data on late-arrival days. The correct trigger type is a file-arrival trigger, configured with a monitored location (a cloud storage path or a Unity Catalog volume) plus a polling interval; it fires once per newly detected batch of files since the last run [source 3][source 6]. Option A is wrong: Databricks expressions are read seconds-first, so `0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI` is a well-formed expression meaning 06:30:00 on weekdays. Option C is partly true but incomplete — fixing the timezone alone does not remove the wasted-run and gap-day problems, because a schedule cannot react to nondeterministic arrival. Option D substitutes a Databricks SQL alert for job trigger semantics; an alert can notify you that dependent data changed, but it is not the job's scheduling trigger, and conflating the two is a classic exam distractor [source 3].

questions.question: A production review turns up four separate job definitions. For each, decide which statements are CORRECT about the interaction of triggers, schedules, timezone, and notifications. Select all that apply.

options.label: Selecting 'Run now' (or manual execution) produces no recurring schedule, and when no trigger is configured the job effectively behaves as manual — the recurring schedule exists only if a scheduled (cron), file-arrival, table-update, or continuous trigger is configured.
The schedule timezone is a job-level setting independent of the cluster timezone, the notebook, and UTC, so changing it shifts every future fire time without altering the cron fields themselves.
Enabling failure notifications on a job causes Databricks to automatically repair and re-run a failed task before the notification is delivered, so the run usually succeeds despite an error.
For a file-arrival trigger, files that already exist in the monitored location when the trigger is created do not fire it; only files newly detected after the trigger is configured are counted.

questions.analysis: A is correct: manual and 'Run now' produce no recurring schedule and are the effective default when no trigger is configured, so a job with nothing but tasks will not self-start [source 3][source 6]. B is correct: the schedule timezone is a job-level setting — it is not the cluster's timezone, not the notebook's, and not UTC by definition — so moving it from UTC to, say, America/New_York shifts every future fire time while the cron text stays the same [source 6]. D is correct: a file-arrival trigger fires per newly detected batch since the last run, and pre-existing files are deliberately excluded from firing so that creating the trigger does not immediately launch a catch-up run. C is the distractor to reject: notifications are an alerting mechanism; they inform humans or systems that something happened (e.g., a failure), and they do not themselves repair or re-run failed work. Databricks' actual repair capability is partial runs and repairs, an explicit debugging feature, not a side effect of notification configuration [source 4].

questions.question: A data engineer writes a job that ingests partner files from a Unity Catalog volume. The upstream partner sometimes delivers nothing on a given weekday, but when it does deliver, the files land anywhere from 05:00 to 07:00 Eastern. The team sets the job schedule timezone to America/New_York and configures a cron trigger `0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI`. Which statement BEST describes the resulting behaviour on a weekday when the partner delivers no files at all?

options.label: The schedule will not fire, because Databricks suppresses cron fires on days when the monitored location has no new files — a scheduled trigger and a file-arrival trigger share the same detection logic.

The schedule fires anyway at 06:30 Eastern, because a scheduled (cron) trigger is clock-based and knows nothing about file arrivals; the run executes against whatever data is present, which on a gap day means stale or empty input.
The schedule fires but is automatically converted into a file-arrival trigger for that day, polling the volume until the partner delivers, and then runs once the files appear.

The schedule fires at 06:30 UTC regardless of the timezone setting, because Databricks cron expressions always evaluate in UTC and the job-level timezone only affects how the UI displays the run history.

questions.analysis: A scheduled (cron) trigger is clock-based: it fires when the wall clock in the schedule timezone reaches 06:30 on a weekday, regardless of whether any files arrived [source 3][source 6]. On a gap day it therefore executes against stale or empty input — exactly the wasted-run and stale-data cost the alternative file-arrival trigger was designed to avoid. Option A invents suppression logic that does not exist: cron triggers and file-arrival triggers are distinct trigger types with distinct firing rules, and a cron trigger has no file-detection step at all [source 6]. Option C invents automatic trigger conversion, which is not a Databricks behaviour. Option D inverts the timezone rule: the job schedule timezone directly controls when the cron fires, so setting it to America/New_York makes 06:30 Eastern — not UTC — the fire time [source 6].

questions.question: During an end-to-end production review, the team must satisfy a hard 5-minute freshness target on the silver layer while respecting three constraints: (1) upstream partner files arrive anywhere from 05:00 to 07:00 Eastern, (2) there is roughly one gap day per week with no delivery at all, and (3) always-on compute is capped. The team proposes a file-arrival trigger on the partner landing path. Which statements about this design are CORRECT? Select all that apply.

options.label: Because the trigger fires once per newly detected batch of files since the last run, it adapts to the partner's nondeterministic arrival window and avoids the wasted runs and stale data a fixed 06:30 cron would cause on gap days.

The polling interval, together with the monitored location, is a required configuration element and contributes detection latency, so effective freshness is bounded by (polling interval + downstream task duration) rather than by file arrival alone.
Because file detection confirms upstream write completion, a file-arrival trigger guarantees that each partner delivery is complete and atomic before the run starts.
An event-agnostic polling approach adds a small always-on monitoring cost, which must be weighed against the cheaper monitoring of a scheduled cron under the always-on compute cap.

questions.analysis: A is correct: the file-arrival trigger fires once per newly detected batch of files since the last run, so it tracks the 05:00–07:00 arrival window and stays quiet on gap days, whereas a fixed 06:30 cron wastes runs and consumes stale input [source 3][source 6]. B is correct: the trigger requires a monitored location (cloud storage path or Unity Catalog volume) plus a polling interval, and polling adds detection latency, so end-to-end freshness is at least the polling interval plus downstream task duration — this is why a 5-minute target can be missed even when the trigger 'reacts' quickly. D is correct: polling is event-agnostic and carries a small always-on monitoring cost, which is the core trade-off against cron's cheaper monitoring under the compute cap. C is the distractor to reject: file detection is not the same as upstream write completion. A file appearing in the monitored location may still be mid-write or part of a multi-file batch that is not yet fully delivered, so the trigger fires on detection, not on confirmed completion; treating the two as identical is a common exam trap [source 6].

actions.text: This is the review page for scheduling, triggers, and alerting — a mixed set of exam-style scenarios covering trigger selection, cron correctness, timezone behaviour, and notification configuration.
Work through each one on your own and pick your answers carefully; the questions reward the exact reasoning patterns we practiced. Once you submit, I'll walk you through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Lesson Opener: Making Production Jobs Resilient

elements.content: Lesson Opener: Making Production Jobs Resilient
Exam objectives in scope

Objective 1 — Resilience

Configure retries and timeouts on jobs and tasks

Objective 2 — Diagnosis & Repair

Read the job run history; repair failed pipelines
Three failure-recovery semantics — do not mix them up

Retry — automatic, inside the same run; only fires if retries are enabled and retry count > 0; re-executes the failed task, dependent tasks stay blocked [source 3]

Repair run — manual, partial re-execution; runs only the failed and downstream tasks, reusing succeeded upstream task results [source 4]

Full re-run — from scratch; every task re-executes, including those that already succeeded
Worked example — which recovery action?
A 4-task pipeline: t1 OK → t2 OK → t3 FAILED → t4 unattempted. Retries = 0. Repair run re-executes t3 and t4 only — t1 and t2 are skipped, saving ~2/4 of cluster time [source 4].

Prerequisites (already covered)

Jobs · tasks · runs; parameters & task values; cron and file-arrival triggers; alerts [source 6]
Exam tip — scenario questions ask for the smallest correct action after a single task fails. If succeeded tasks are reusable, repair beats re-run. [source 2]

actions.text: That wraps up scheduling, triggers, and alerting. Now we shift gear into a topic that shows up constantly on the exam and constantly in production: making jobs resilient. In other words, what happens when something fails — and what you should do about it.

This lesson is framed around two exam objectives. Objective one is resilience — configuring retries and timeouts so that a job survives transient failures on its own. Objective two is diagnosis and repair — reading the job run history, finding the root cause, and repairing the pipeline without redoing work that already succeeded.

Before we go further, lock in this distinction — it is the single most examinable idea on this page. There are three failure-recovery semantics, and you must not mix them up. A retry is automatic and happens inside the same run. A repair run is manual and re-executes only part of the pipeline. A full re-run starts the whole thing from scratch.

So, retry first. A retry is automatic, it happens inside the same run, and it only fires when you have configured it. If a task fails and retries are enabled, Lakeflow Jobs waits the retry interval and tries that task again — the tasks that already succeeded are left untouched.

Here's a worked example. Picture a four-task pipeline: t1 succeeds, t2 succeeds, t3 fails, t4 never starts because its dependency never completed. Ask yourself — which recovery action is correct? If the failure in t3 was a transient network blip, a retry is the smallest correct action. If it was a genuine logic error, a retry just burns time, and a repair run that re-executes only t3 and t4 is what you want.

Everything here builds on what we already covered: jobs, tasks, and runs; parameters and task values; and cron and file-arrival triggers with alerts. Retries and run-if conditions are just new levers on the same object model you already know.

One last thing before we dive in — the exam tip for this lesson. Expect scenario questions that ask for the smallest correct action after a single task fails. The answer is almost never a full re-run. Think retry for transient faults, repair for partial re-execution, and full re-run only when nothing upstream is salvageable. Keep that hierarchy in mind as we work through the mechanics.

scenes.title: Retries, Retry Intervals, and Task Timeouts

elements.content: Retries, Retry Intervals, and Task Timeouts

Lakeflow Jobs, the native orchestration engine, defines failure handling per task: how many times to retry, how long to wait between attempts, and how long a task may run before it is declared timed out [source 3][source 2].

Retry configuration (per task)

• Max retries: cap on re-attempts after the first failure

• Min / max retry interval: exponential backoff bounds the wait between attempts

• Retry on timeout: opt-in flag; off means a timeout is terminal

Each task carries its own policy, so a flaky ingest task can retry while a deterministic validation task fails fast [source 3].

Timeouts bound runtime

• A timeout caps how long a task may execute before it is failed

• A timed-out task fails fast instead of blocking the DAG indefinitely

• If retry-on-timeout is enabled, the task then obeys the retry policy; otherwise it is terminal

Timeout plus retry is the exam-relevant combination to reason about [source 2].

Retries only rescue transient failures — cloud I/O blips, throttling, spot-instance loss. Deterministic code, schema, or data-quality errors fail again after the final retry; retries are never a substitute for a fix [source 2].
A retry re-executes the whole task, so writes must be idempotent: MERGE/upsert or overwrite are safe; a blind append duplicates rows.
Worked example: 2 retries at 1-min base backoff = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 min max wait before the final failure.

actions.text: Now let's look at the first line of defense for a flaky task: retries, retry intervals, and task timeouts. These are configured per task inside a Lakeflow Job, and getting them right is the difference between a workflow that self-heals and one that either fails constantly or hides a real bug.

Retry configuration lives at the task level. You set a maximum number of retries, a minimum and maximum retry interval so the wait between attempts backs off exponentially, and a flag for whether the task should retry when it times out. The cap on retries is what stops a permanently broken task from retrying forever and burning cluster cost.

Timeouts bound the runtime of a task. A timeout caps how long a single attempt may run, so a hung task fails fast instead of blocking the DAG indefinitely. And critically, once it times out, it still obeys the retry policy — that is, if retry-on-timeout is enabled, the timeout simply counts as another failed attempt.

This diagram shows the timeline you should picture in your head. Attempt one fails, we wait the base backoff, attempt two fails, we wait a longer backoff because it is exponential, and attempt three succeeds. Each retry re-executes the whole task, so the total run duration is the work plus all of those waits.

Here is the crucial nuance for the exam. Retries only rescue transient failures — cloud I/O blips, throttling, a spot instance disappearing. A deterministic failure like a schema mismatch or a data-quality error will fail again on the final retry. Retries are not a substitute for a fix; they buy you resilience against noise, not against bugs.

And because a retry re-executes the whole task, your writes must be idempotent. A MERGE upsert or a full overwrite is safe to replay, but a blind append will duplicate rows every time the task retries. This is one of the most common exam traps on this topic.

Let's ground it with the worked example. Two retries with a one-minute base backoff means the waits grow exponentially — so you can compute exactly how much extra wall-clock time a task adds before it finally gives up. When you size retry settings against an SLA, that math is the whole game.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Retry and Timeout Configuration

questions.question: A data engineer is tuning a Lakeflow Jobs task and wants to control two distinct behaviours: (1) the maximum number of times the task will be attempted before the run is declared failed, and (2) the maximum cumulative time the task is allowed to spend waiting between those attempts. Which statement correctly maps the retry configuration to these two behaviours?

options.label: The 'max retries' field bounds the number of attempts, while the 'min retry interval' and 'max retry interval' fields bound the cumulative wait between attempts.
The 'max retry interval' field bounds the number of attempts, while the 'min retry interval' field bounds the cumulative wait between attempts.
The 'timeout' field bounds the number of attempts, while the 'max retries' field bounds the cumulative wait between attempts.
The 'min retry interval' field bounds the number of attempts, while the 'timeout' field bounds the cumulative wait between attempts.

questions.analysis: In Lakeflow Jobs (formerly Databricks Workflows), a task's retry policy has two logically separate concerns. The attempt-count component is governed by the maximum number of retries the task is permitted: once that count is exhausted, the task moves to a terminal failed state. The wait-time component is governed by the interval fields, which define the lower and upper bounds on how long the orchestrator waits before each subsequent attempt. The minimum interval sets the earliest a retry may fire (useful for giving an upstream dependency or throttled API time to recover), while the maximum interval caps the backoff so a long-running exponential schedule cannot push the next attempt past an acceptable freshness window. Options B, C, and D all conflate these two axes: option B swaps the roles of the two interval fields, option C treats the task timeout (which limits how long a single attempt may run) as an attempt counter, and option D treats the minimum interval as an attempt counter. The orchestration contract that these controls live inside is Lakeflow Jobs, the native orchestrator for the Lakehouse [source 3], and the same engine is described as managing dependencies, triggers, retries, and failure handling [source 2].

questions.question: Which two statements about retry-on-timeout semantics are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: If a task exceeds its configured timeout because an upstream source system is briefly unavailable, a retry is appropriate because the timeout is a transient failure that a later attempt may clear.

If a task exceeds its timeout because the job's result would be logically wrong no matter how many times it is attempted (for example, a deterministic business-rule violation), the run should fail immediately rather than be retried.
A timeout must never trigger a retry, because a task that timed out has by definition produced corrupt output that cannot be recovered.
A timeout should always trigger a retry, regardless of whether the task is idempotent, because retries are cheaper than reruns.

questions.analysis: The decision to retry on timeout hinges on classification of the failure. A transient or environmental timeout — an upstream database briefly rejecting connections, a network hiccup, a cluster briefly resource-starved — is exactly the kind of fault the retry policy exists to absorb, so option A is correct: the next attempt has a genuine chance of clearing the condition without manual intervention. Option B is also correct: if the timeout is a symptom of a deterministic problem (a malformed assumption about the source data, a business rule that the input can never satisfy), retrying just burns compute and delays the alert that a human needs to see. Option C is wrong because it overgeneralises: a timed-out task has not necessarily written any output at all, and even when it has partially written output, the idempotency of the task governs whether the retry is safe. Option D is wrong for the same reason from the opposite direction — it ignores idempotency entirely. The orchestrator that owns these decisions is Lakeflow Jobs, described as managing schedule, automation, dependencies, triggers, and failure handling [source 2], and the official description of the platform confirms that retries sit alongside triggers and compute configuration inside the native orchestrator [source 3]. Note that in a production pipeline the timeout value should also be chosen so the retry fits inside the freshness SLA: if the timeout is 30 minutes and the inter-attempt interval is 5 minutes, a single retry already consumes 35 minutes, which may exceed the window the downstream consumer can tolerate.

questions.question: An ingestion task uses a plain append write to a Delta table (no merge, no deduplication key) and is configured with 3 retries. During a run, the task writes a batch of rows, then the cluster is preempted before the write is committed to the table's transaction log. Which outcome best matches the correct idempotency reasoning?

options.label: The retry is safe because the aborted write never committed, so the retry produces exactly one copy of the batch.
The retry is unsafe because the append is not idempotent; if the original write had committed before the failure, the retry would append a second copy of the same rows, producing duplicate data.
The retry is unsafe, but the duplicates can be prevented automatically by setting max retries to 0.
The retry is always safe for Delta tables regardless of the write mode, because Delta Lake enforces uniqueness by default.

questions.analysis: The key insight is that idempotency is a property of the write operation, not of the retry policy. A plain append has no natural key and no merge condition, so applying the same logical batch twice produces two physical copies. In the scenario described, the cluster is preempted before the write commits, so this particular retry happens to be harmless — but only because you got lucky. The orchestrator cannot distinguish 'append that never committed' from 'append that committed and then the task failed for an unrelated reason', and in the second case the retry will duplicate data. That is why the safe design is to make the write logically idempotent: use MERGE on a natural key, use a deterministic overwrite of a known partition, or route through Auto Loader with file-level checkpointing. Option A is wrong because it assumes the aborted write is the only possible state, which the engine cannot guarantee. Option C is wrong because disabling retries avoids duplicates only by removing resilience to every other transient failure. Option D is wrong because Delta Lake does not enforce row-level uniqueness in an append — it guarantees transaction semantics and serialisable isolation, not de-duplication of repeated logical payloads. This matters because the orchestrator layer, Lakeflow Jobs, is explicitly described as providing failure handling for pipelines [source 2], and a correct retry policy must be paired with an idempotent write to be safe [source 3].

actions.text: That SLA math is exactly what this checkpoint puts to the test. You'll be mapping the retry fields to the behaviours they control, deciding when a timeout deserves another attempt and when it should fail immediately, and reasoning about what a retry does to a task that isn't idempotent — safe to say, idempotent just means the operation, run twice, leaves the data in the same state as running it once.

Take each question on your own and think through the reasoning rather than pattern-matching the wording — the distractors here are built to mirror the traps the real exam uses. Once you submit, I'll walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Run-if Conditions: Controlling Behaviour After a Failure

elements.content: Run-if Conditions: Controlling Behaviour After a Failure

In Lakeflow Jobs (formerly Databricks Workflows), a task's behaviour after an upstream failure is set by the task's Run-if condition, not by the task itself [source 3].

Worked example: a 3-task DAG (ingest → transform → load). If transform fails and load uses the default All succeeded, load is Skipped; the run reports Failed.

The five Run-if options

• All succeeded — default; runs only if every upstream task succeeded

• At least one failed — runs if any upstream failed

• All failed

• At least one succeeded

• All done — runs regardless of upstream state

Failure semantics

• Failing task → state Failed; job run → Failed

• Direct and transitive downstream tasks → Skipped (not Failed)

• A Skipped task never executes; it is reported, not retried, and blocks the default All succeeded gate of its own children

DAG propagation: with All succeeded on every edge, a single skipped dependency propagates skipping down the DAG — task1 fails → task2 skipped → task3 skipped even though task3 never saw a failure [source 2].

data.text: Fallback path when primary branch fails
Cleanup required only after total failure
Cleanup / logging that must always run

elements.content: Source references: [source 1] orchestration layer; [source 2] tasks, dependencies, failure handling; [source 3] Run-if condition, notifications.

actions.text: Now here's a topic the exam loves: run-if conditions. These parameters control whether a task actually executes once its dependencies have finished. The key mental shift is this — you don't change the task itself to express post-failure behaviour, you change the condition attached to the dependency edge.

There are five options. All succeeded is the default and behaves exactly as you'd expect. Then we have At least one failed, All failed, At least one succeeded, and All done. Remember the framing: you're choosing the condition, not the task, to decide how the workflow reacts after a problem.

Now the failure semantics, and this is the classic trap. When a task fails, it reaches the state Failed. But its downstream tasks — both direct and transitive — end up Skipped, not Failed. The overall job run is still marked Failed, but the individual downstream tasks show as Skipped. Don't confuse the task-level state with the run-level state on the exam.

That skipping propagates down the DAG. If every edge uses the default All succeeded, then a skipped dependency causes the next task to be skipped too, and so on. The skip cascades all the way through until — as we covered on the previous page — a Repair Run or backfill picks up the missing work.

This decision table maps each condition against the state of the upstream tasks, and tells you whether the task runs. Use it to reason about typical scenarios: sending a notification only when something fails, running cleanup regardless of outcome, or routing to a fallback path. Let me walk you through the rows.

In Lakeflow Jobs, these conditions live on the dependency edges in your job definition. The typical exam scenario is exactly what we just described: attach an alert task with At least one failed so it fires only on failure, or use All done for a cleanup task that must run no matter what happened upstream.

Keep the source references handy — the orchestration layer and the run-if documentation are what the exam draws from. The core takeaway for this page: choose the condition to express post-failure behaviour, and remember that a failed dependency produces Skipped, not Failed, downstream tasks.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Choosing Retry and Timeout Settings for an SLA

elements.content: Problem 1

A nightly production Lakeflow Job has three tasks in sequence: Task 1 (ingest) calls an external REST API, Task 2 (transform) runs a Delta Lake transformation, and Task 3 (publish) writes a materialized view (a precomputed, stored query result) for a BI dashboard. The job must finish every night within a 30-minute SLA. Task 1's API intermittently returns HTTP 503 responses, and about one night in ten the API call hangs without returning. The team must be alerted only when the run genuinely fails after all recovery attempts. (a) Classify each failure mode and choose the correct control. (b) Configure Task 1's retries, minimum retry interval, and retry-on-timeout. (c) Choose a task timeout and verify the worst-case recovery time fits the SLA. (d) Configure the notification task so alerts fire only on genuine terminal failure. (e) Explain why Task 1's write must use MERGE rather than INSERT INTO.
Hint: Transient errors belong in retries; hangs are liveness failures and need timeouts. Budget worst-case attempts × timeout + backoff.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Classify each failure mode. An HTTP 503 is a transient, retryable server-side error: the same request may succeed on a later attempt. A hang is a liveness failure: the call never returns, so a retry alone does not help because there is no error to catch. The hang must be converted into a retryable timeout failure by setting a task timeout. This matches the failure-handling controls exposed by Lakeflow Jobs tasks [source 3].

Step 2 — Configure Task 1 retries. Set Maximum retries = 3, Minimum retry interval = 30 seconds, and Retry on timeout = true. If the per-attempt hang probability is p = 0.1, then four attempts fail only if all four hang. Assuming independence, P(all four hang) = (0.1)^4 = 0.0001, so the nightly hang risk drops from 1/10 to about 1/10,000. The 30-second interval gives the API breathing room without wasting SLA budget.

Step 3 — Set the task timeout and verify the SLA budget. Set Timeout = 5 minutes. Worst-case Task 1 duration is $$T_{\text{worst}} = (r+1)\,T_{\text{timeout}} + r\,I_{\text{retry}} = (3+1)(5\text{ min}) + 3(0.5\text{ min}) = 21.5\text{ min}.$$ The remaining budget is 30 − 21.5 = 8.5 minutes for Task 2, Task 3, and the notification task. If Task 2 typically takes 2 minutes and Task 3 takes 1 minute, the worst-case job duration is 21.5 + 2 + 1 + 0.5 = 25.0 minutes, which fits inside 30 minutes.

Step 4 — Notification task. Add Task 4 with Run-if = At least one failed, and make it depend on Task 1, Task 2, and Task 3. This task runs only when at least one upstream task is in a terminal failed state after retries. If the retries absorb the 503 or timeout, no task is failed, so no alert fires. If Task 1 exhausts all 3 retries, Task 1 is failed and the notification fires to the on-call destination. This implements the alerting principle of routing failures to on-call while keeping success digests separate [source 6].

Step 5 — Idempotent write. Use MERGE instead of INSERT INTO for Task 1's target write. MERGE updates existing rows and inserts missing rows based on a business key, so re-executing the whole task after a retry produces the same final table state. An INSERT INTO append would add the same batch again.

Step 6 — Add a duration warning. Configure a job-level duration-warning notification at, for example, 25 minutes so a silently stalled run is caught before it violates the 30-minute SLA [source 6].

Analysis — The method works because it separates transient failures from liveness failures. Transient failures (HTTP 503) are handled by bounded retries; liveness failures (hangs) are converted into bounded failures by a timeout. The key design equation is $$(r+1)T_{\text{timeout}} + r I_{\text{retry}} + T_{\text{other}} \le T_{\text{SLA}}.$$ Common student mistakes include setting retry-on-timeout = true without bounding the maximum retries, which can turn one hang into an indefinite retry loop; choosing a timeout that is too large (for example, 15 minutes with 3 retries gives 4 × 15 = 60 minutes, already double the SLA); placing a notification task with Run-if = All succeeded, which suppresses the alert precisely when a task fails; and assuming that notifications repair a failed run. Notifications observe failure; they do not recover it. Lakeflow Jobs provides tasks, dependencies, Run-if conditions, retries, and notifications as first-class orchestration controls [source 2]. For pipelines with partial writes, partial runs and repairs make debugging easier, but repair still depends on idempotent task writes [source 4].
Problem 2

A data engineer proposes this Task 1 configuration for the same 30-minute SLA job: Timeout = 10 minutes, Maximum retries = 5, Retry on timeout = true, Minimum retry interval = 30 seconds. The engineer argues that more retries always make the job more reliable. Compute the worst-case Task 1 duration. Is the configuration safe for the SLA? If not, propose a minimal change that preserves retry-on-timeout but fits the SLA.
Hint: Worst case is (retries + 1) × timeout + retries × retry interval.

Worked solution
Worst-case Task 1 duration: $$T_{\text{worst}} = (r+1)T_{\text{timeout}} + r I_{\text{retry}} = (5+1)(10\text{ min}) + 5(0.5\text{ min}) = 60 + 2.5 = 62.5\text{ min}.$$ Since the SLA is 30 minutes, Task 1 alone can consume 62.5 minutes, so the job violates the SLA even if Task 2, Task 3, and notification take zero time. The configuration is unsafe. A minimal change that preserves retry-on-timeout is to set Maximum retries = 2 and Timeout = 5 minutes: $$T_{\text{worst}} = (2+1)(5) + 2(0.5) = 15 + 1 = 16\text{ min}.$$ This leaves 30 − 16 = 14 minutes for the remaining tasks, so the SLA holds. If more resilience is desired, keep retries = 3 and reduce the timeout to 4 minutes: (3+1)(4) + 3(0.5) = 16 + 1.5 = 17.5 minutes, still under 30.

Analysis — This problem tests the budget discipline behind retry and timeout settings. More retries are not automatically better: each retry multiplies the timeout by another attempt and adds backoff, so retries and timeout must be chosen together. Retry-on-timeout is powerful but dangerous because it makes a hang retryable; without a small maximum retries and a timeout that fits the SLA, one hang can occupy the entire window. A robust production pattern is to set the task timeout, compute $$(r+1)T_{\text{timeout}} + rI_{\text{retry}} + T_{\text{other}} \le T_{\text{SLA}},$$ and then add a duration-warning notification at a threshold below the SLA. This keeps the signal meaningful: a genuine failure after bounded retries alerts the on-call destination, while a slow-but-progressing run alerts the pipeline owner [source 6]. The same reasoning generalizes to any workflow orchestrator that exposes task-level retries and timeouts [source 3].
Problem 3

A Task 1 ingest uses INSERT INTO silver.orders SELECT ... FROM staging_orders. The task is configured with 3 retries. On a night when the API hangs, the first attempt times out after writing 1,200 rows; the second attempt succeeds and writes the same 1,200 rows. The target table now has 2,400 rows for the same order IDs. (a) Explain why retries caused duplicate rows. (b) Rewrite the write as a MERGE that is safe under retries. (c) State two conditions under which MERGE still is not enough.
Hint: Retries re-execute the whole task, not just the failed HTTP call.

Worked solution
(a) Retries re-execute the entire task, including the write. INSERT INTO is append-only and not idempotent: the first attempt wrote 1,200 rows before timing out, and the retry appended the same 1,200 rows again. The result is 2,400 rows for the same order IDs. The failed HTTP call is not retried in isolation; the task's full body re-runs.

(b) A retry-safe write uses MERGE on a unique business key:$$\text{MERGE INTO silver.orders AS t}\\\text{USING staging_orders AS s}\\\text{ON t.order_id = s.order_id}\\\text{WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *}\\\text{WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *}.$$If each retry sees the same staging rows, the first attempt may insert 1,200 rows, and the second attempt updates those same 1,200 rows instead of appending a second copy. The final table has 1,200 rows, so the task is idempotent with respect to retries.

(c) Two conditions where MERGE is not enough. First, if staging_orders contains duplicate order_id values within the same batch, MERGE may fail or nondeterministically update the target multiple times; deduplicate the source first, for example with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC). Second, if the MERGE condition does not cover all business keys or does not match the target's true uniqueness constraint, updates can miss rows or overwrite columns with NULLs. A third practical condition is that an append-only event table may intentionally preserve every delivery, in which case MERGE would erase the duplicate-event semantics the table needs; for such tables, deduplication must happen downstream instead.

Analysis — Idempotency means that repeating an operation produces the same final state. Retries at the task level require idempotent writes because the whole task body re-executes. MERGE is the standard idempotent write pattern in Delta Lake when a stable business key exists. The common mistake is enabling retries on a task that writes with INSERT INTO append; the first timeout leaves a partial write, and the next attempt duplicates it. A second mistake is assuming MERGE is automatically safe: it requires a unique source key, a deterministic source, and a MERGE condition that covers the same keys the retry writes. In production, combine MERGE with a staging table that is itself overwritten on each attempt, so the source is deterministic. Lakeflow Jobs supports task-level retries and failure handling, and partial runs and repairs make debugging failed tasks faster and cheaper, but neither feature replaces idempotent task design [source 2][source 4]. The rule generalizes: retries plus non-idempotent writes equals duplicates; retries plus idempotent writes equals exactly-once-like behavior at the task level [source 3].

actions.text: Now let's put retries and timeouts to work on a full worked problem. Remember how we covered run-if conditions — here we tie everything together: a stated production symptom plus a hard SLA becomes concrete retry, timeout, and run-if configuration.

Problem 1: a nightly production Lakeflow Job has three tasks and must finish within a 30-minute SLA. Task 1 calls an external REST API that intermittently returns HTTP 503 responses, and about one night in ten that call simply hangs. The team must be notified when the run genuinely fails — so the retry logic has to absorb the noise without hiding a real terminal failure.

The hint frames the whole method: transient errors belong in the retry path, and hangs are a liveness problem, so they belong in the timeout path. An HTTP 503 is transient, and a hang is what we call a liveness failure — the task never returns.

The worked solution classifies each failure mode and then sets the knobs. First, retries with a minimum retry interval so 503s get absorbed. Second, a task timeout of five minutes — well under the 30-minute SLA — so a hang fails fast instead of eating the window. Roughly four attempts, each up to five minutes plus backoff, still stays inside budget.

The analysis explains why this works: the method separates transient errors from liveness failures, then budgets both against the SLA. The key pitfall — your worst-case duration is max retries times the timeout. If that product exceeds your SLA, retries themselves become the outage.
Problem 2 turns that into arithmetic. The hint gives you the exact formula to memorize: worst case equals retries plus one, times the timeout, plus the retry intervals. Let's apply it.

Here the worst-case Task 1 duration is computed directly from that budget discipline. Notice how the formula makes the tradeoff explicit — every additional retry multiplies against your timeout, so you cannot tune the two independently.

The analysis here tests exactly that budget discipline. The exam loves this trap: people add retries for resilience and accidentally blow the SLA. Always run the worst-case multiplication before you commit a retry count to production.
Problem 3 covers idempotency — repeating an operation produces the same result. This is where careless retries become dangerous.
Here Task 1's ingest uses INSERT INTO to write into silver.orders, selecting from a source. Ask yourself: what happens if that INSERT runs a second time?
The hint gives it away: retries re-execute the whole task, not just the failed step. There is no partial replay — the entire statement runs again from the top.

The solution spells out the consequence: with INSERT INTO, a retry appends the rows a second time, silently duplicating your data. The fix is to make the write idempotent — use MERGE so a re-run upserts to the same final state instead of blindly appending.

And the closing analysis ties it together: idempotency means repeating an operation leaves the same result. Retries are only safe when the task's writes are idempotent. So the exam-ready rule is this — retries handle transients, timeouts handle hangs, run-if fires the alert on genuine failure, and MERGE keeps retries from duplicating rows. Make sure worst-case retries times timeout fits your SLA, and never retry a non-idempotent append.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Failure Semantics and Run-if Conditions

questions.question: A Lakeflow Jobs job has a linear dependency chain: task_A (ingest) -> task_B (silver transform) -> task_C (gold aggregate). The default Run-if condition is left unchanged on every task. task_A fails and exhausts all its retries. What is the state of task_B and task_C?

options.label: task_B and task_C are each marked Skipped because their upstream dependency did not succeed
task_B and task_C are each marked Failed because the run inherits the upstream failure state
task_B is Skipped but task_C runs, because task_C depends only on task_A's source table and not on the DAG
task_B and task_C both start and are marked Succeeded with empty output, because Run-if defaults to 'At least one succeeded'

questions.correctAnswer: task_B and task_C are each marked Skipped because their upstream dependency did not succeed
questions.analysis: Run-if conditions are evaluated per task against the outcomes of that task's dependencies, and the default is effectively 'All succeeded'. When task_A fails, the condition for task_B evaluates false, so task_B is Skipped rather than Failed; task_C then evaluates its own condition against a skipped task_B and is also Skipped. Skipped is a distinct terminal state from Failed, which matters in the next question about how the overall run is reported. Option B conflates skipped downstream tasks with the failed task itself, option C invents table-level dependency resolution that Lakeflow Jobs does not perform for task ordering, and option D misstates the default condition (the 'at least one succeeded' style behaviour requires an explicit run-if setting). Lakeflow Jobs defines tasks, dependencies, and failure handling as first-class orchestration concepts [source 2].
answer: task_B and task_C are each marked Skipped because their upstream dependency did not succeed

questions.question: A pipeline runs task_bronze -> task_silver -> task_gold -> task_audit. The team wants task_audit to always execute its validation check, even when task_gold was skipped or failed, so that it can record a 'no data produced' row. Which statements about achieving this are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Setting task_audit's Run-if condition to an 'always' style condition (run regardless of dependency outcome) will let it execute when task_gold is Skipped or Failed
If task_audit's Run-if condition is set to 'All succeeded', it will not run when task_gold fails, so the audit row would be missing
Making task_audit depend on no upstream task at all would guarantee it runs before task_gold and after task_bronze
A task whose Run-if evaluates false can still be forced to run by enabling retries on that task

correctAnswer: Setting task_audit's Run-if condition to an 'always' style condition (run regardless of dependency outcome) will let it execute when task_gold is Skipped or Failed
If task_audit's Run-if condition is set to 'All succeeded', it will not run when task_gold fails, so the audit row would be missing
questions.analysis: The Run-if condition is exactly the control that decides whether a task executes given its dependencies' outcomes; an 'always'-style condition makes the task run even when upstream tasks are Skipped or Failed, while the default 'All succeeded' semantics suppresses it. So the first two statements are correct. Option C is wrong because removing dependencies removes ordering guarantees entirely: with no upstream dependency the task is not sequenced after task_bronze at all, and it certainly cannot run 'after task_gold' that way. Option D is a common misconception: retries are a reliability mechanism for a task that actually attempted execution and failed transiently, and they never override a Run-if condition that evaluated false — a Skipped task never enters the retry path. Lakeflow Jobs treats dependencies and the Run-if condition as the mechanism for controlling execution order and failure handling [source 3][source 2].
answer: Setting task_audit's Run-if condition to an 'always' style condition (run regardless of dependency outcome) will let it execute when task_gold is Skipped or Failed
If task_audit's Run-if condition is set to 'All succeeded', it will not run when task_gold fails, so the audit row would be missing

questions.question: A job ends with task_final as its last task. task_final has the default Run-if condition, and its immediate upstream task failed, so task_final is Skipped. All other tasks either succeeded or were skipped downstream of the failure. How is the overall job run reported?

options.label: The run is reported as Failed, because a task failure occurred even though the last task was only Skipped
The run is reported as Succeeded, because a Skipped task is not a Failed task and the final task did not fail
The run is reported as Cancelled, because skipping the last task implicitly cancels the run
The run is reported as Succeeded only if a notification was configured; otherwise it is Failed

questions.correctAnswer: The run is reported as Failed, because a task failure occurred even though the last task was only Skipped
questions.analysis: A run's overall result reflects the most severe outcome anywhere in the DAG, not merely the state of the final task. task_final being Skipped does not erase the Failed state of its upstream task, so the run reports failure. Option B encodes the misconception that 'skipped' is harmless; skipping is a consequence of an earlier failure, not a success. Option C invents a cancellation state that is not produced by Run-if evaluation. Option D is wrong because notifications are an observability concern and never determine the recorded run outcome — they report it, they do not compute it. Determining whether the run reports failure therefore requires reading the whole run history rather than just the terminal task, which is central to diagnosing failed runs [source 4][source 1].
answer: The run is reported as Failed, because a task failure occurred even though the last task was only Skipped

actions.text: Now let's put that knowledge to the test. These questions ask you to predict task states and reason about run-if conditions when something upstream goes wrong — so think each one through carefully and choose your own answers.
Take your time and work through them independently. Once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning with you and clarify anything that felt tricky.

scenes.title: Diagnosing Failed Runs in the Run History

elements.content: Diagnosing Failed Runs in the Run History
Objective 2 — triage a failed run from its state, timeline, task error, and logs [source 4][source 6]
1. Run states to recognise

A task run is Failed when its own code or data raised an error (for example, a schema mismatch), but Skipped when its upstream dependency failed and the Run-if condition evaluated to false.

That distinction decides the fix: a skipped task never executed, so repairing the upstream task should also repair the skipped one; a failed task must be repaired itself.

Recognise also Queued, Pending, Running, Succeeded, Timed out (retryable only if retry-on-timeout is enabled), Canceled, and Internal error (platform-side, not your code).
2. Triage order

Open the job run, then read the run timeline (Gantt) and find the first long or red segment — the earliest failure, not the loudest.

Open that task run, read its error message, then drill into cluster logs, driver logs, and the Spark UI for the stack trace [source 4].

Partial runs and repairs make it faster and cheaper to debug the failed task than to rerun the whole job [source 4].
Worked example: 08:00 job, 09:17 failure → first red segment at 09:12
3. Classify the root cause
Task logic or data
Read parameters and task values at failure time — a stale value is the classic dev-succeeds / prod-fails cause.
4. The diagnosis decision

Re-run unchanged only for transient infrastructure error (already retried) — repair run after fixing task logic, data, or a stale parameter — targeted repair plus backfill for a specific date range when output for past partitions is also wrong.
Diagnose before re-running: every fix maps to a state and a root-cause class.

actions.text: Now that we've reviewed how retries and timeouts are configured, let's talk about what happens when those safeguards aren't enough — and a run actually fails in production. This page is all about diagnosing failed runs directly in the Run History.

Our objective here is simple to state: given a failed run, use its state, the timeline, and the logs to triage the failure and decide what to do next. That decision — repair, re-run unchanged, or backfill — is the real deliverable of diagnosis.

First, the run states you need to recognise. A task run is Failed when its own code or data raised an error that wasn't caught. A task is Skipped when it never ran because an upstream dependency failed — that's a critical distinction the exam loves to test.

So remember: Failed means the task itself broke. Skipped means the task was healthy but its dependency never delivered. Also keep an eye out for Timed out, which is different again — the task was still running when its time budget ran out.

Next, the triage order — and this is the part worth memorising. You don't just open the failed task blindly. You work from the top down: open the job run, then read the run timeline, also called the Gantt view.

In the timeline you're hunting for the first long or red segment — that gives you the earliest point where things went wrong. Once you've found it, open that specific task run, read the error message, and only then drill into the cluster logs, driver logs, or Spark UI for the full stack trace.

Here's a quick worked example. Suppose a job normally starts at 08:00 but shows a failure at 09:17. Your first move is not to read the error — it's to look at the first red or unusually long segment in the timeline, because that tells you which task actually blew the budget.

Third, you classify the root cause. There are four broad buckets: a task logic or data error — bad code, a schema mismatch, or a data quality failure; an infrastructure error, such as the cluster failing to start, an out-of-memory condition, or spot instance loss; a timeout; or a dependency or skip caused by an upstream failure.

While you're classifying, always read the run's parameters and the task values at the moment of failure. A stale or malformed parameter is one of the most common reasons a task succeeds in development and then fails in production — the code is fine, but the input it was handed isn't.

Finally, the diagnosis decision. Diagnosis should always produce one of three outcomes: re-run with no change when the failure was transient infrastructure, do a repair run after you've applied a fix, or run a targeted repair plus backfill if a specific date range of data was affected.

The rule of thumb: only re-run unchanged for genuinely transient infrastructure issues. If there was any code or data problem, a blind re-run just reproduces the same failure — and often at a worse time.

Which brings us to the guiding principle of this whole page: diagnose before you re-run. Every root cause you identify should map to a specific state, a specific log, and a specific repair action. If you can't name the cause, you're not ready to press re-run.

That's the triage procedure end to end — states, triage order, root cause classification, parameters at failure time, and the final decision. Next, you'll get some hands-on practice with transient failures in the interactive lab.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Reading Run History and Root-Causing a Failure

questions.question: A nightly Lakeflow Jobs run has three tasks arranged in a linear dependency: ingest → transform → publish. Each task has its own retry policy, and no task uses the run-if condition, so every task keeps the default 'All succeeded'. The run history shows the following final task states: ingest = Succeeded, transform = Failed, publish = Skipped, and the overall run = Failed. Based on this timeline and task-state evidence, which task is the first failing task, and which task was merely skipped rather than failed?

options.label: transform is the first failing task; publish was skipped, not failed, because the default run-if condition blocks all downstream tasks after any upstream failure.
publish is the first failing task because it never executed; transform succeeded and the failure appeared only at the final step.
Both transform and publish failed; the Skipped label on publish is only a display artifact and the task did in fact fail.
ingest is the first failing task because every downstream failure is caused by the ingestion layer, so root cause always starts at the source task.

questions.analysis: The run history is the authoritative evidence: the timeline lists ingest = Succeeded, then transform = Failed, then publish = Skipped, with the overall job run = Failed. The first task to reach the Failed state is transform, so that is where root-cause investigation begins. Under failure semantics, the failing task reaches state Failed while direct and transitive downstream tasks are Skipped, not Failed, though the overall job run is Failed. Option B inverts the evidence by treating the skipped task as the failure. Option C misreads the Skipped label, which is a real, distinct terminal state, not a display artifact. Option D assumes ingestion is always to blame, which contradicts the recorded Succeeded state for ingest and is a common misdiagnosis pattern. This is why partial runs and repairs make it easier, faster, and cheaper to debug only the failed tasks [source 4], and why the run history is the diagnostic surface for multi-step pipelines defined with tasks, dependencies, triggers, and failure handling [source 2].

questions.question: A data engineer reviews a failed run and confirms the first failing task was a single 'Silver to Gold' task that uses a deterministic schema-evolution error; all upstream ingest and transform tasks finished successfully, and no downstream tasks are needed to recompute data that already exists. The engineer wants the smallest correct action. Which of the following statements correctly describe the repair-versus-retry-versus-rerun decision? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A repair run is a manual, partial re-execution of the pipeline; it re-runs the failed task and its downstream tasks while reusing the already-committed upstream results, which is faster and cheaper than a full re-run.

Because the error is deterministic, simply retrying the same task without any code or configuration change will not succeed, because deterministic schema and data-quality errors fail again after the final retry.
A full re-run from scratch is always required after any task failure, because upstream results are always invalidated by a downstream failure.

The engineer should first fix the root cause, then trigger a repair run limited to the failed task and its downstream dependencies, rather than retrying the unchanged task or re-running the entire job.

questions.analysis: The correct combination is A, B, and D. A repair run is a manual, partial re-execution: it re-runs the failed task and its downstream tasks while reusing already-committed upstream results, which is the faster and cheaper path for debugging [source 4]. Retries only rescue transient failures such as cloud I/O blips, throttling, or spot-instance loss; a deterministic schema or data-quality error fails again after the final retry, so retrying without change is wasted effort. The correct sequence is to fix the root cause first, then repair only the failed task and its downstream dependencies. Option C is incorrect: a full re-run from scratch is not always required because a Skipped or failed downstream task does not invalidate the already-Succeeded upstream outputs; the engineer should choose the smallest correct action that restores correctness. This distinction between a retry (automatic, same run), a repair run (manual, partial re-execution), and a full re-run (from scratch) is exactly the terminology the certification assesses across Lakeflow Jobs' tasks, dependencies, and failure handling [source 2].

questions.question: Consider a three-task Lakeflow Jobs pipeline with dependencies ingest → transform → publish. The latest run history shows ingest = Succeeded, transform = Failed after exhausting its retries, and publish = Skipped, with the overall run = Failed. The transform task failed with a transient cloud-storage timeout on all of its retry attempts, and the engineer determines the transient outage is now resolved. In 4-6 sentences, describe the evidence you would cite to justify the root cause, state whether the repair scope is the failed task only or the failed task plus its downstream tasks, and explain which action you would choose among (a) fixing and repairing, (b) retrying the run without any change, and (c) a full re-run from scratch. Name the key Databricks product and use correct Databricks terminology.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Evidence and root-cause naming, 30%: must cite the run history showing ingest = Succeeded, transform = Failed, publish = Skipped, overall = Failed, and identify transform as the first failing task using the Skipped-vs-Failed distinction. (2) Repair scope, 25%: must state that repair scope is transform plus its downstream tasks, because publish is Skipped (not Failed) and must be re-executed after the failed task is repaired; upstream ingest is reused. (3) Action choice, 30%: must choose the repair option and justify it: the failure was transient, but the retries were already exhausted in this run, so a new attempt is needed; a repair run is preferred because it is partial, faster, and cheaper than a full re-run, and a plain retry-without-change is unavailable after the run itself has already completed and failed. (4) Terminology and clarity, 15%: must name Lakeflow Jobs and use correct terms (task, dependency, run history, repair run, first failing task, Skipped). Deduct for confusing a retry with a repair run or claiming a full re-run is mandatory.
questions.analysis: A strong answer states that the run history is the authoritative evidence and names transform as the first failing task, because ingest = Succeeded and publish = Skipped are downstream effects, not causes [source 4]. Under failure semantics, the failing task reaches Failed while direct and transitive downstream tasks are Skipped, not Failed, and the overall job run is Failed. Because publish is Skipped, it has not produced its output and must be re-executed, so the repair scope is transform plus its downstream tasks; upstream ingest results are reused because they already Succeeded. The failure was transient, but the retries were already exhausted in this run, so a new attempt is required and the engineer should fix the root cause if any, then trigger a repair run rather than a full re-run. A full re-run is unnecessary because only the failed task and its downstream dependents need recomputation, and partial runs and repairs make it easier, faster, and cheaper to debug failed tasks [source 4]. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestration layer for scheduling and monitoring data pipelines and ML workflows, and the run history is the diagnostic surface for these decisions [source 1][source 2].

actions.text: Let's put that into practice. This checkpoint covers reading a run history, root-causing the first failing task, and choosing the right recovery action.
Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer — I'll walk through the reasoning with you once you submit.

scenes.title: Repair Runs, Partial Runs, and Backfill

elements.content: Repair Runs, Partial Runs, and Backfill
Selective re-execution of failed tasks and downstream dependencies
Definition and Core Mechanism

• A repair run re-executes only the failed task and the tasks that were skipped downstream, reusing the original run's parameters, task values, and job configuration. It does not re-execute already-succeeded tasks [source 6].

• Partial runs and repairs make debugging failed tasks faster and cheaper by avoiding redundant recomputation of expensive upstream work [source 4].

• You can select specific tasks to repair (for example, repair from the failing task onward) and optionally override parameters for the repair; a repair always re-runs downstream tasks of the repaired task [source 2].
Repair vs. Alternatives: Choosing the Right Recovery

• Repair = same run, minimal recompute. Full re-run = fresh run, all tasks, safest for non-idempotent pipelines [source 3]. Backfill = run a new job run with an earlier date-range parameter [source 1].

actions.text: Now that we've looked at diagnosing failures in the run history, let's turn to the recovery side of the equation. This page covers repair runs, partial runs, and backfill — three ways to get a broken pipeline healthy again without paying for work you've already done.

Start with the definition and core mechanism. A repair run re-executes only the failed task and the tasks that were skipped downstream of it. Critically, it reuses the original run's parameters, task values, and job configuration — it does not touch tasks that already succeeded. So the expensive upstream work stays cached in place and you only recompute what actually broke.

Two operational details matter here. First, you can select specific tasks to repair — for example, repair from the failing task onward — and you can optionally override parameters for that repair. But remember the rule: a repair always re-runs the downstream tasks of the repaired task, because their inputs have changed. Second, there's a correctness precondition. Repairs assume idempotent, partitioned, or MERGE-based writes. If you repair a non-idempotent append pipeline, you can silently duplicate data. That's an exam favorite.

Let's put repair next to its alternatives, because choosing the right recovery path is the actual skill being tested. Repair means same run, minimal recompute. A full re-run means a fresh run, all tasks, and it is the safest choice for non-idempotent pipelines. And backfill means running a new job run with an earlier date-range parameter — that's for filling historical gaps, not for fixing a failure.

One quick visual to anchor it: in the diagram on your slide there's a five-task DAG where task three is red, tasks four and five are skipped, and the repair run re-executes only tasks three, four, and five. Upstream stays untouched. That picture is worth memorizing — if you can redraw it from memory, you understand repair semantics. Take a moment now and compare those three recovery options against a scenario in your own work before we continue.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Repairing a Failed Multi-Task Pipeline

elements.content: Problem 1

A nightly Lakeflow Jobs pipeline has 5 tasks in a linear DAG and is scheduled to start at 02:00. The most recent run took 35 minutes and failed. Run history shows: Task 1 (ingest from cloud storage, 8 min) Succeeded; Task 2 (silver MERGE into a Delta table, 14 min) Succeeded; Task 3 (gold aggregate) Failed with a schema error; Task 4 (publish to dashboard) Skipped; Task 5 (send SLA digest) Skipped; the overall run state is Failed. The Task 3 error message states that the source column was renamed from customer_id to customer_key. The fix is a two-line change to the gold aggregation notebook, and the on-call engineer can apply and re-validate the fix by 07:15. Business owners require the gold tables refreshed before 08:00. The job cluster consumes 8 DBU per hour. The engineer must decide between a repair run and a full re-run. Compute the repair scope, the time saving, the DBU saving, and whether each option meets the 08:00 deadline.
Hint: Read the run history states first: only Task 3 actually failed, and Tasks 4-5 were Skipped rather than Failed, so the DAG did not complete.

Worked solution
Step 1 - read the evidence. The run history shows Task 1 Succeeded, Task 2 Succeeded, Task 3 Failed, Task 4 Skipped, Task 5 Skipped, and the overall run Failed. In Lakeflow Jobs, a task that raises a schema error reaches the Failed state, and its direct and transitive downstream tasks are marked Skipped, not Failed; the overall run still reports Failed. Lakeflow Jobs is the native orchestration layer on Databricks for scheduling and monitoring data pipelines, and it gives run history with these per-task states so that a failure can be localized to the task that actually broke [source 1]. Because Tasks 1 and 2 succeeded, their outputs are already written and valid: Task 1 ingested the raw input, and Task 2 completed its silver MERGE. Opening the Task 3 error message reveals the renamed source column customer_id to customer_key, which is the deterministic cause of the failure. Lakeflow Jobs lets data engineers schedule and automate multi-step pipelines by defining tasks, dependencies, triggers, and failure handling, which is exactly the metadata the repair decision uses [source 2].

Step 2 - fix the cause, not the symptom. A renamed source column is a deterministic schema error: every retry executes the same SQL against the same schema and fails again in exactly the same way. Retries are only useful for transient failures such as throttling or cloud I/O blips; they do not repair deterministic code, schema, or data-quality errors. The correct action is to update the gold aggregation to reference customer_key instead of customer_id, then re-validate the notebook or SQL task before launching anything. The units covered earlier in this unit already established that jobs expose tasks, dependencies, the Run-if condition, retries, and notifications, so the fix belongs in the task definition rather than in the retry policy [source 3].

Step 3 - choose the scope. The engineer should use Repair run and select Tasks 3, 4, and 5. A repair run re-executes only the failed task and the tasks downstream of it, reusing the original run's parameters and the successful upstream outputs. Task 2's silver output is reused, so Task 1 and Task 2 are not recomputed. This matches the documented purpose of partial runs and repairs: they make it easier, faster, and cheaper to debug and recover failed tasks [source 4]. The repair must include Tasks 4 and 5 because they were Skipped, not Succeeded; if the engineer repairs only Task 3, then the dashboard refresh in Task 4 and the SLA digest in Task 5 still have no completed execution for this run, and the business owner still does not get refreshed gold data.

Step 4 - quantify the saving. The successful upstream work that repair avoids is Task 1 plus Task 2: 8 + 14 = 22 minutes. The repair re-executes the failed-and-skipped branch: 35 - 22 = 13 minutes of work. The time saving relative to a full re-run is 22 minutes, which is 22/35 = 0.629, or about 62.9%. In DBU terms, the job cluster consumes 8 DBU per hour. A full re-run costs $(35/60) * 8 = 4.667$ DBU. The repair run costs $(13/60) * 8 = 1.733$ DBU. The saving is $4.667 - 1.733 = 2.933$ DBU, which is about 62.9% of the full re-run compute. If the effective price is $0.55 per DBU, the repair saves $2.933 * 0.55 = 1.61$ dollars per incident.

Step 5 - check the deadline. The fix is ready at 07:15. The repair finishes at 07:15 + 13 minutes = 07:28, which is 32 minutes before the 08:00 SLA. A full re-run finishes at 07:15 + 35 minutes = 07:50, which meets the deadline with only a 10-minute margin. The repair is not merely cheaper; it creates schedule slack. If the fix slips to 07:30, the full re-run finishes at 08:05 and misses the SLA, while the repair finishes at 07:43 and still meets it. Therefore the correct decision is a repair run of Tasks 3, 4, and 5.

Analysis — The method works because the run history separates task-local failure from run-level failure. Only Task 3 broke; Tasks 1 and 2 produced valid outputs. A repair run is defined by the DAG boundary of the failure: it re-runs the failed task and everything downstream, while reusing upstream outputs from the original run. That is why the repair scope is Tasks 3-5, not Task 3 alone and not the whole DAG. The quantification follows from separating reused work from recomputed work: $35 - (8 + 14) = 13$ minutes, giving a 62.9% reduction in both time and DBU. Common student mistakes include: (1) increasing Task 3 retries, which cannot fix a deterministic schema rename and only delays the failure until the retry budget is exhausted; (2) repairing only Task 3 and forgetting that Tasks 4-5 were Skipped, so the dashboard and digest still do not run; (3) selecting all five tasks, which wastes 22 minutes and 2.933 DBU of already-correct ingest and silver work; (4) assuming that Skipped means Failed, when Skipped is specifically the downstream consequence of an upstream failure and does not by itself indicate a broken task. The decision generalizes to any deterministic failure in a multi-task DAG: locate the first Failed task, confirm downstream tasks are Skipped, fix the deterministic cause, then repair from that task onward, provided the successful upstream outputs are still valid and still fresh.
Problem 2

The same 5-task pipeline is repaired from Task 3 through Task 5. Task 2's silver write is a MERGE and is idempotent. Task 4 refreshes a dashboard materialized view and is safe to repeat. Task 5 appends one audit row per successful run into audit.pipeline_runs using INSERT INTO. After the repair, the audit table contains 2 rows for the business date 2025-03-11, but the pipeline's logical success count for that date should be 1. Quantify the duplication and decide whether the repair was safe. Then propose the minimal change that makes future repairs safe. Finally, analyze the alternative: if Task 2's silver write had been a non-idempotent append, such as INSERT INTO silver_events with no deduplication key, would a repair starting at Task 3 be correct? Use a concrete daily row-count example.
Hint: A repair run re-executes the failed task and all downstream tasks, so every downstream side effect must be safe to run more than once.

Worked solution
Step 1 - identify the side effect that is not idempotent. The repair re-executes Task 3, Task 4, and Task 5. Task 3 writes gold tables and Task 4 refreshes a materialized view; both are safe to repeat in this scenario. Task 5 uses INSERT INTO, which appends a new row on every successful execution.
