If historical customer changes must be tracked, keep an SCD Type 2 customer dimension in silver and publish the current or aggregated view in gold. A slowly changing dimension (SCD) is a technique for tracking historical changes to dimension records.

Justification: bronze landing stores raw files; silver applies cleaning, conformance, and normalization; gold serves curated metrics. Managed tables are appropriate when Unity Catalog should own the storage location and lifecycle. If a table must survive DROP TABLE, use an external table instead. Tables are typically indexed by a primary key and can have foreign keys that support joins and normalized schemas [source p.193]. Object stores are excellent for large batch reads and writes, which is why the raw landing zone and the Delta lake storage layers work well here [source p.233].

Analysis — The method works because each medallion layer has a different contract: bronze preserves source fidelity, silver enforces clean and conformed rows, and gold publishes business-level aggregates. The object type follows the data shape: files use a volume, rows use a table. Common mistakes: storing raw JSON only in a Delta table and losing the original files; placing cleaned data in bronze because bronze is assumed to mean all ingestion; placing curated marts in silver; using a volume for rows that must be queried with SQL; using external tables by default when managed lifecycle is desired. Least-privilege grants become layer-specific: BI users read gold, data scientists read silver, and only ingestion jobs write bronze. Lineage is easier to trace layer by layer, and cost attribution can be reported per schema because storage and compute can be grouped by layer. Normalization avoids duplicated state and inconsistency, while gold intentionally denormalizes for query performance [source p.193].
Problem 3

Adopt the naming convention: catalog = <domain>_<env>; schema = bronze|silver|gold; object = <entity>_<qualifier>; volume = landing; file path = <source>/<entity>/<yyyy>/<mm>/<dd>/<entity>_<yyyy><mm><dd>.<ext>. For the prod retail domain, write the fully qualified three-part SQL names for orders_cleaned in silver and sales_daily_region in gold. Write the landing path for an orders CSV for 2026-04-28. Then suppose the session has USE CATALOG retail_prod; USE SCHEMA silver;. Explain how SELECT * FROM orders_cleaned resolves. Finally, identify one bad name and correct it: RetailProd.Gold.Sales Daily Region.
Hint: Three-part SQL name is catalog.schema.object; a volume file path is /Volumes/catalog/schema/volume/... and is not the same namespace.

Worked solution
Catalog: retail_prod. Schemas: silver and gold. Objects: orders_cleaned and sales_daily_region.

Fully qualified SQL names:

retail_prod.silver.orders_cleaned

retail_prod.gold.sales_daily_region

Landing path for the orders CSV on 2026-04-28:

/Volumes/retail_prod/bronze/landing/orders/2026/04/28/orders_20260428.csv

Session resolution: with USE CATALOG retail_prod; USE SCHEMA silver;, the unqualified query SELECT * FROM orders_cleaned resolves to retail_prod.silver.orders_cleaned. The current catalog supplies retail_prod and the current schema supplies silver. If you then query sales_daily_region without a schema qualifier, it fails or resolves against silver, not gold, because the current schema is still silver. You must write retail_prod.gold.sales_daily_region or switch with USE SCHEMA gold.

Bad name correction: RetailProd.Gold.Sales Daily Region uses uppercase, mixed case, spaces, and no environment-in-catalog convention. Correct it to retail_prod.gold.sales_daily_region. If the object is a view, it still uses the same three-part name. If the item is a file, it is not a three-part table name; it belongs under /Volumes/retail_prod/bronze/landing/... instead.

Analysis — This works because the naming convention maps cleanly onto the Unity Catalog namespace: the catalog encodes domain and environment, the schema encodes the medallion layer, and the object name encodes entity and qualifier. The three-part SQL name catalog.schema.object is different from the volume path /Volumes/catalog/schema/volume/path. Common mistakes: putting the environment in the schema, such as retail_prod.bronze_prod, instead of the catalog; repeating the layer in the object name, such as silver.silver_orders; using hyphens or spaces in identifiers; and confusing a volume path with a SQL name. A consistent SQL naming layer also supports composing SQL with other operations in frameworks such as Spark and orchestration tools [source p.47]. Normalization is a strategy for ensuring that data is not duplicated in multiple places, which is easier to enforce when silver and gold objects are named predictably [source p.193]. Layer-per-schema organization then enables least-privilege grants by schema, lineage tracking from bronze to silver to gold, and cost attribution by layer.

actions.text: Now let's put that object model to work. This page gives you three worked problems that build a full project layout — a catalog, three medallion schemas, and a landing volume — and then justify every placement and naming decision. This is exactly the kind of design question the exam loves, because it tests whether you can reason about environment boundaries, not just recall syntax.

Problem 1 sets the scene: you're the founding data engineer for an e-commerce company, and you need to design and write the DDL for the catalog, the three medallion schemas, and the landing volume. Before you write a single line, read the requirement carefully. The scenario tells you there is one catalog per environment, so the catalog itself is your environment boundary — not a schema, not a prefix in a table name.

Here's the hint that makes it click: the catalog is the environment boundary, and the schema is the medallion layer. Once you accept that mapping, the layout almost writes itself. Production gets its own catalog, development gets its own, and inside each one you create a bronze schema for raw ingestion, a silver schema for validated and conformed data, and a gold schema for business-level tables. Non-tabular raw files go into a volume, which lives under a schema — so the landing volume belongs inside the bronze schema, since those files are the rawest form of the data.

The worked solution uses retail as the domain, so the catalog becomes retail_prod, and the three schemas are bronze, silver, and gold. Then a CREATE VOLUME statement declares landing inside bronze, giving you a path where raw files land before any table touches them. Notice the create order matters: catalog first, then schemas, then the volume, because each object must have its parent already in place.

Now the analysis, which is the part the exam actually rewards. Why does this work? Because Unity Catalog nests metastore to catalog to schema to object, and each level is a separate securable you can grant on independently. That means you can hand a data scientist read access to gold without ever exposing bronze, or let a pipeline writer land files in the volume without granting them table privileges. Layer-per-schema organization gives you least-privilege grants, clean lineage tracking, and cost attribution per layer — all three fall out of the structure for free.

Problem 2 reuses the retail_prod catalog from Problem 1 and asks you to classify assets: raw clickstream JSON files, cleaned tables, and curated tables. The hint tells you to ask one question first — is the asset files or rows? Files go into volumes; rows go into tables. Then the second question: which layer owns it? Raw files belong in the landing volume under bronze, cleaned tables in silver, curated tables in gold.

The worked solution walks through each: raw clickstream JSON files belong in the bronze landing volume because they're unprocessed files, the cleaned and deduplicated clickstream rows belong in silver because that layer validates and conforms, and the curated clickstream metrics belong in gold because that's what analysts consume. The reasoning for each placement rests on one principle — a layer is defined by the guarantees it provides, not by the tool that wrote it.

The analysis here stresses why the method works: each medallion layer has a distinct job, so each object has exactly one correct home. Bronze absorbs raw, unvalidated data. Silver enforces quality and resolves duplicates. Gold encodes business logic on top of clean inputs. When you can recite what each layer guarantees, placement questions become deduction, not guesswork.

Problem 3 introduces a naming convention and asks you to map it onto the three-part namespace. The convention is catalog equals domain and environment, schema equals medallion layer, and object equals the noun that names the entity. Applied literally: retail_prod for the catalog, bronze, silver, and gold for the schemas, and names like orders, customers, or clickstream for the objects underneath.

The hint reminds you that the three-part SQL name is catalog dot schema dot object. That's the payoff of the convention — every fully qualified reference reads like a sentence describing where the data lives and what it is. retail_prod.silver.orders tells you the environment, the layer, and the entity in one glance, with no ambiguous prefixes.

The worked solution spells it out: the catalog is retail_prod, the schemas are silver and its siblings, and a table like orders is referenced as retail_prod.silver.orders. Once you write references this way consistently, cross-environment promotion and cross-layer joins both become predictable because the name itself carries the governance boundaries.

Finally, the analysis: this works because the naming convention and the medallion layers reinforce each other. A team that can derive a name from the layer, and a layer from the name, avoids the most common exam trap — mixing environments inside a single catalog, or burying raw files in gold. So remember the takeaway across all three problems: catalog is your environment boundary, schema is your medallion layer, volumes hold files while tables hold rows, and every grant you'll ever write attaches to one of those levels.

scenes.title: Managed vs External: Choosing Where Data Lives

elements.content: Decision — A financial services firm is building a governed customer transaction dataset inside Unity Catalog to back both a new Databricks analytics surface and two legacy consumers: an on-premises BI extractor that reads Parquet files directly from cloud object storage, and a regulatory archive job that must still be able to re-hydrate historical data after records are retired. The decision situation is that the same logical dataset is wanted in one governed place, but the engineers must now commit to either letting Unity Catalog own the underlying storage path and lifecycle as a managed object or registering the dataset as an external object that points at a path the team controls. The decision is genuinely hard because neither choice is free: the managed path minimizes operational work today but trades away the ability to recover data after a DROP, while the external path preserves recovery and legacy access but shifts storage location management, lifecycle policy, and storage cost back onto the team. Because this dataset sits at the center of the pipeline and downstream consumers already depend on it once it exists, the choice also carries a total opportunity cost of ownership — whatever is chosen here forecloses the other option for as long as the dataset remains a core production dependency [source p.145].

Constraints — Retention/restore requirement: a retention policy and regulatory restore requirement mean that data must survive the deletion of the governed object, so a DROP of the object alone must not be the end of the data.  •  Cross-engine and legacy consumers: an on-premises BI extractor and a regulatory archive must read the files at a known, stable cloud storage path outside Databricks SQL, so the physical location must be known and controllable by the data team.  •  Storage ownership and cost: the organization owns the storage account and must explicitly own lifecycle policy and storage cost allocation, rather than delegating the lifecycle of this dataset to the platform.  •  Unity Catalog governance: the dataset must still be registered in Unity Catalog with a fully qualified name and governed by the existing metastore, catalog, and schema hierarchy; the decision is about who owns the storage path, not about abandoning governance.

Managed object: Unity Catalog owns the storage path and lifecycle
+ Operationally simplest: Unity Catalog manages the underlying storage location, so the team does not create, register, or maintain an external location or storage path for this dataset.; + Lifecycle is centralized: because Unity Catalog owns the storage location and the object lifecycle, there is one place to reason about the object's existence and one fewer path convention to document.; + No path-drift risk: consumers and producers cannot inadvertently diverge on a storage path because the platform, not the team, decides where the physical files live.
− DROP TABLE deletes the data as well, so a single DROP removes both the metadata and the files — which directly violates the retention and restore requirement for this dataset.; − Legacy readers that expect a stable, team-owned object storage path cannot be pointed at the platform-managed path without the platform's cooperation, so cross-engine consumers become harder, not easier.; − Storage cost and lifecycle policy are effectively delegated to the platform's ownership of the path, which conflicts with the requirement that the organization explicitly own storage lifecycle and cost.
Best for: Datasets that are consumed only through Databricks SQL and engines reading governed objects, where staleness and lifecycle are acceptable and DROP-deletes-data behavior is actually desirable for cleanup.

External object: a table defined over a path the team controls in a shared external location
+ Data durability across DROP: because the table points at a path the team controls, DROP TABLE removes only the metadata and the underlying files remain, which satisfies the retention and restore requirement.; + Stable, known path for legacy consumers: the on-premises BI extractor and the regulatory archive can read the Parquet files at the same team-owned object storage path without depending on Databricks SQL.; + Explicit storage ownership and lifecycle: the team controls the bucket, the storage class, and the lifecycle policy, so storage cost and retention policy are owned rather than delegated.
− The team now owns location management: it must create and maintain the external location, keep the path convention stable, and ensure that the registered path and the physical layout do not drift apart.; − Storage cost and lifecycle policy are now the team's responsibility, which means the team absorbs the cost of keeping data that managed lifecycle would have cleaned up.; − External objects are a worse fit for high-frequency small-update workloads; object stores remain an inferior fit for transactional update patterns with many small updates per second, so this option is only sound if the update profile is batch-oriented [source p.233].
Best for: Retention-constrained shared datasets that must survive a DROP, be readable by non-Databricks engines, and be governed under an organization-owned storage path with an explicit lifecycle policy.

Managed object with a scheduled export of the same data to an external location
+ Keeps the primary object operationally simple, because the dataset itself remains a managed object owned by Unity Catalog.; + Adds a second copy at a team-controlled external location, so the retention and restore requirement is partially satisfied by the export rather than by the primary object.
− The retention and restore requirement is now satisfied by a derived copy, not by the governed object, which means the restoration path depends on the export job succeeding and on the export schedule.; − Two copies must be reconciled: the managed object and the external export can diverge, and the team now owns both the external location management of the export and the managed lifecycle of the primary.; − This doubles the surface area for cost and governance errors and is the most brittle of the three options against DROP, because the DROP still deletes the primary data even if a stale export happens to exist.
Best for: Situations where the primary dataset must remain a managed object for operational reasons but a separate, additive copy is acceptable for a limited, low-stakes restore scenario.

Recommendation: External object: a table defined over a path the team controls in a shared external location — The binding constraints are data survival across deletion, cross-engine and legacy access at a known path, and explicit storage ownership by the organization; these constraints are exactly the ones that a managed object fails. A managed object is disqualified because DROP TABLE deletes the data as well, which violates the retention and restore requirement, and because platform-owned paths conflict with team-owned lifecycle and cost. The scheduled-export option only partially satisfies retention by depending on a derived copy, and it adds a reconciliation burden without removing the managed object's core failure mode. The external object is the only option whose default behavior — DROP TABLE removes only the metadata while the files remain at the team-controlled path — matches the retention requirement, gives legacy and cross-engine consumers a stable object storage path, and keeps storage lifecycle and cost explicitly owned by the team. This choice also acknowledges the opportunity cost: because the dataset becomes a core production dependency for the BI extractor and the archive, the team is committing to the external-object pattern for this dataset and should evaluate that commitment consciously rather than by default [source p.145].

actions.text: Building on the container hierarchy we just covered, here's a question that trips up a lot of exam candidates: when you create a table, who actually owns the underlying files on cloud storage? That's the managed versus external decision, and it's one you'll make constantly in real projects.

Our scenario: a financial services firm is building a shared dataset that other teams and engines will consume. We have to decide whether to store it as a managed object or an external object in Unity Catalog. Two options, one decision.

Option A, a managed object. Here Unity Catalog owns the storage path and the full lifecycle of the data. It's the simplest thing to operate — you write the table and Databricks handles everything underneath. The catch is that dropping the table deletes the data too, because the catalog owns both the metadata and the files.

Option B, an external object. This is a table defined over a path that you control — say, a shared bucket that other systems already use. The data survives a DROP, which is the key advantage. But you take on location management and the storage cost, because that path is yours to maintain.

So what actually decides it? Four constraints. First, the retention and restore requirement: if a restore or retention policy says data must survive a drop, that pushes you toward external. Second, cross-engine and legacy consumers — other tools that read from a path directly. Third, who owns the storage account. And fourth, whether you need to restore the data independently of the catalog.

There's also a common hybrid worth recognizing: a managed object with a scheduled export of the same data. You get the operational simplicity of managed storage, plus a durable copy written out on a schedule — useful when you want both easy operations and a retention safety net.

So our justified recommendation for this retention-constrained shared dataset is Option B: an external object. When the requirement is that data must survive a DROP, external is the correct answer. And here's the exam cue phrase to remember — if you see wording like "data must survive table deletion" or "retain files after DROP," that's your signal pointing straight to external.

Quick recap: managed means Unity Catalog owns the path and lifecycle and a drop deletes the data; external means you own the path, the data survives a drop, and you carry the storage management. Let retention and restore requirements drive the choice, and watch for that survive-the-drop cue on the exam.

scenes.title: Lesson Assessment: The Unity Catalog Object Model

questions.question: A data engineering team is designing the Unity Catalog namespace for a retail analytics platform. They require a single top-level governance container for one cloud region that is attached to all of their workspaces and holds every catalog, including a catalog named sales. Which statement correctly identifies the hierarchy level and scope of that top-level container?

options.label: The metastore is a schema-level container; it groups tables, views, volumes, and functions inside a single catalog such as sales.
The metastore is the top-level container for a region; it is attached to workspaces and holds catalogs, so sales is a catalog that lives inside it.
The catalog is the top-level container for a region; it is attached to workspaces and holds metastores, so sales is a metastore inside the catalog.
The schema is the top-level container for a region; it is attached to workspaces and holds catalogs, so sales is a catalog inside the schema.

questions.analysis: The metastore is the top-level container for a region; it is attached to workspaces and holds all catalogs, and each catalog groups schemas. Option B is correct because it places the sales catalog inside the metastore. Option A inverts the hierarchy by calling the metastore a schema-level container (a schema is the level that groups tables, views, volumes, functions, and models). Option C inverts metastore and catalog by claiming catalogs hold metastores. Option D inverts schema and catalog and misplaces the top-level scope. A recurring certification trap is confusing the metastore with a catalog, or a schema with a catalog; the metastore is not a catalog, and a schema is not a catalog. The source's discussion of schema metastores in lakehouse patterns reinforces that a metastore is a metadata container rather than a namespace level that groups schemas [source p.245].

questions.question: A team must persist a shared dataset in Unity Catalog such that the files continue to exist even if the governing table object is dropped, because the path is a shared cloud bucket controlled by the platform team. Which design decision satisfies this requirement, and what happens on DROP TABLE?

options.label: Create a managed table; DROP TABLE removes only the metadata and leaves the files in place so the team can re-register them.
Create an external table; DROP TABLE removes the metadata and the files remain because the external location is under the team's control.
Create a view over the shared path; DROP VIEW removes the underlying files and the view, satisfying both metadata and data lifecycle control.
Create a managed volume; DROP VOLUME deletes only the directory listing while preserving the files for later table registration.

questions.analysis: The requirement is that data must survive a DROP, which is the distinction between external and managed objects. An external table points at a path you control, so DROP TABLE removes only the metadata and the files remain. Option A is wrong because a managed table is owned by Unity Catalog: DROP TABLE deletes the data as well. Option C is wrong because a view is a stored query, not stored data, and dropping a view never deletes files at the referenced path. Option D is wrong because the object type required for tabular data addressed by a path is a table, not a volume, and a managed volume's lifecycle is tied to Unity Catalog. The source material on external tables and external data locations defined on buckets illustrates that the external pattern keeps the data outside the table and only processes it when queried, which is the same principle that keeps the files intact after a DROP [source p.351]. Because object storage is an immutable technology that will remain usable regardless of platform evolution, keeping the authoritative files there and pointing an external table at them is a durable design [source p.147].

questions.question: A team is landing raw, non-tabular CSV files that must be governed by Unity Catalog and later converted to cleaned Delta tables, and their solution must survive a DROP of the container object. Select all statements that are correct for this requirement.

options.label: Create an external volume that points at a path registered through an external location so the files survive if the volume object is dropped.
Create a managed table over the landing path so Unity Catalog owns the storage and lifecycle, and DROP TABLE will retain the raw files.
Use a volume rather than a table because a volume is the governed logical container for files and directories such as CSV, JSON, images, and ML artifacts.
Use a view over the raw CSV files because a view stores the files themselves, so dropping the view cannot delete the underlying data.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: an external volume points at a path registered through an external location, so the data survives a DROP of the volume object, matching the requirement that storage lifecycle stays under the team's control. Option C is correct: the decision rule is to use a volume when the data is files and a table when the data is rows queried with SQL; CSV, JSON, images, and ML artifacts are the canonical volume contents. Option B is wrong because a managed table is owned by Unity Catalog and DROP TABLE deletes the data along with the metadata, which violates the survival requirement. Option D is wrong because a view is a stored query, not a stored copy of files, so it cannot be the landing container for raw files. The external-table analogy from the source, where an external data location and a file format are defined and data is processed when queried rather than ingested, supports why an external volume keeps files outside the object's lifecycle [source p.351]. Storing the authoritative raw files in object storage aligns with the view that object storage is an immutable technology and a wise place for durable data [source p.147].

actions.text: Now it's time to put this together. This is a short end-of-lesson assessment on the Unity Catalog object model — the hierarchy, choosing between tables, views, and volumes, and what DROP does to managed versus external objects. Work through each one on your own and read the options carefully; the distractors here deliberately echo the traps you'll see on the exam.
Take your time, answer independently, and once you submit I'll walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Unity Catalog Access Control Fundamentals

elements.content: Unity Catalog Access Control: The Three Building Blocks

Every authorization decision in Unity Catalog is a triple: a principal is granted a privilege on a securable object. Access is additive — GRANT adds, REVOKE removes, and there is no DENY statement. The absence of a grant is the denial.

1. Principals

Users, groups,
service principals

2. Securables

Metastore > catalog > schema
> table / view / volume

3. Privileges

SELECT, MODIFY,
USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA

Additive model: GRANT adds a privilege; REVOKE removes it. Example — GRANT SELECT ON data_science_db TO Sarah, later REVOKE SELECT ON data_science_db FROM Sarah. Access-control requests are common; DCL vocabulary is exam-critical. [source p.300]

Two privilege families: object privileges (SELECT, MODIFY, CREATE TABLE) act on the object itself; path privileges (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA) are required just to reach it.

Exam trap: SELECT on a table is not enough — without USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on the parents, queries return TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND, not a permission error. Path privileges are preconditions, not extras. [source p.226] [source p.383]

actions.text: Now let's move into access control, which is one of the most heavily tested governance topics on the exam. Every authorization decision in Unity Catalog boils down to three building blocks, and if you can recall them cold, you can reason your way through almost any permission question.

Building block number one: principals. These are the identities that receive access — users, groups, and service principals. Groups matter a lot here because a group can be a principal itself, and it can also be a member of another group, which is how inheritance starts to happen.

Building block number two: securable objects. These are the things you protect, and they form a strict container hierarchy — the metastore contains catalogs, catalogs contain schemas, and schemas contain tables, views, volumes, and functions. Remember that the hierarchy is not decorative: you have to traverse it, and we'll come back to that point in a moment.

Building block number three: privileges. These are the actual permissions — things like SELECT, MODIFY, USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, CREATE TABLE, and EXECUTE. Privileges are always attached to a principal, and they always act on a securable object.

Now, the critical mental model: Unity Catalog is additive. GRANT adds a privilege; REVOKE removes it. There is no DENY statement anywhere in the model. That means the absence of a grant is the denial — access is never explicitly forbidden, it's simply never given.

And here is the classic exam trap that follows directly from the hierarchy. A principal holding SELECT on a table will still get TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND until it also holds USE CATALOG on the catalog and USE SCHEMA on the schema. The table privilege is necessary but not sufficient — you must be able to reach the object before you can read it. Keep those two families of privileges separate in your head: object privileges that let you do the work, and path privileges that merely let you get there.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: GRANT and REVOKE on Securable Objects

elements.content: Problem 1

You are the data platform engineer for the retailer Northwind. The Unity Catalog metastore attached to the EU workspace contains the catalog `sales`, which holds three schemas: `sales.bronze` (9 raw-ingest tables), `sales.silver` (7 cleaned tables), and `sales.gold` (3 curated tables, among them the managed Delta table `sales.gold.orders`, which has 48 columns and is owned by the group `data_platform`). A group `analysts_eu` with 6 members exists. The security review imposes five requirements: (1) every member of `analysts_eu` must be able to run `SELECT` queries against `sales.gold.orders`; (2) no member may insert, update, delete, or merge rows in that table; (3) no member may query any table outside `sales.gold` — in particular, nothing in `sales.bronze` or `sales.silver`; (4) a previous migration accidentally ran `GRANT MODIFY ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO analysts_eu`, and the stray write capability must be gone; (5) the deployment script must be safe to re-run in every environment without error. Write the complete SQL script, run it in the correct order, and state the exact final state you expect from `SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE sales.gold.orders`.
Hint: A query succeeds only when three separate privileges line up: traverse the catalog, traverse the schema, and read the object.

Worked solution
Step 0 — confirm the objects exist before granting on them. Grants are recorded against real securables, so a typo in a three-part name either fails or silently targets nothing useful: `SELECT CURRENT_METASTORE();`, `SHOW SCHEMAS IN sales;`, and `DESCRIBE EXTENDED sales.gold.orders;` should return the metastore, the three schemas (`bronze`, `silver`, `gold`), and the 48-column table. `DESCRIBE EXTENDED` also confirms the owner (`data_platform`) and that the table is managed.

Step 1 — grant the path privileges first, and only down the branch the analysts need:

```sql

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG sales TO `analysts_eu`;

GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA sales.gold TO `analysts_eu`;

```

`USE CATALOG` lets the group resolve names inside `sales`; `USE SCHEMA` lets it enter `sales.gold`. Deliberately no `USE SCHEMA` is issued on `sales.bronze` or `sales.silver`, so those branches stay closed even before any data privilege is considered.

Step 2 — grant the object privilege at the narrowest object that satisfies the requirement:

```sql

GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO `analysts_eu`;

```

The privilege chain is now complete: `USE CATALOG` on `sales` → `USE SCHEMA` on `sales.gold` → `SELECT` on the table. Drop any link and the query fails.

Step 3 — subtract the stray write capability:

```sql

REVOKE MODIFY ON TABLE sales.gold.orders FROM `analysts_eu`;

```

`MODIFY` authorises `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, and `MERGE` on a table, so this single statement satisfies requirement (2) and removes the mis-scoped grant.

Step 4 — verify with the catalogue of grants on the object:

```sql

SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE sales.gold.orders;

```

Expected result (columns `Principal | ActionType | ObjectType | ObjectKey`):

| Principal | ActionType | ObjectType | ObjectKey |

|---|---|---|---|

| `analysts_eu` | SELECT | TABLE | `sales.gold.orders` |

Exactly one row. The absence of a `MODIFY` row is the proof that step 3 landed. Use `SHOW GRANTS ON SCHEMA sales.gold;` and `SHOW GRANTS ON CATALOG sales;` to confirm the two path privileges are recorded at their own levels.

Step 5 — negative testing as an ordinary member, not as an admin. Impersonating a member of `analysts_eu`, run `SELECT * FROM sales.gold.orders LIMIT 10;` (succeeds, 10 rows), then `SELECT * FROM sales.bronze.clickstream LIMIT 10;` (fails with `TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND`, because the missing `USE SCHEMA` is reported as "object not found" rather than as a permission denial), then `DELETE FROM sales.gold.orders WHERE order_id = 1;` (fails with `PERMISSION_DENIED` on `MODIFY`).

Re-running the whole script is safe: Unity Catalog grants are additive and idempotent, and `REVOKE` of a privilege that is not currently granted is a no-op rather than an error.

Analysis — The method is built on a three-link privilege chain. `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` are *path* privileges: they do not read any data, they only make a container addressable, which is why they are granted first and on the narrowest branch. The third link is the *data* privilege, granted at the object. Writing this as three statements rather than one statement on the catalog is precisely the principle of least privilege in practice: "giving a user or system access to only the essential data and resources to perform an intended function" [source p.75]. A common failure mode is to skip `USE SCHEMA` because "I already granted SELECT on the table"; the query then fails in a confusing way, because Databricks reports the missing path privilege as `TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND` so that the existence of the object is not disclosed. Another frequent mistake is testing as a workspace admin or metastore admin: those roles bypass privilege evaluation, so a test that passes as an admin proves nothing about the 6 analysts. Third, students assume `REVOKE` can fail when the grant is absent — it does not; it is a no-op, which is what makes the script safely re-runnable. A fourth trap is treating `MODIFY` as a labelling issue: on a schema-on-write table every write must conform to the integrated schema [source p.245], so `MODIFY` is a data-integrity privilege as much as a confidentiality one — a stray write grant can silently corrupt the gold layer that downstream reporting trusts. Finally, note that the ordering *between* the grants does not change the final privilege set (grants are additive), but the ordering of the `REVOKE` does matter operationally: put the revocation early in the script so the accidental write window closes as soon as possible.
Problem 2

The requirement in Problem 1 covers exactly one table: `sales.gold.orders`. Three candidate grant statements are on the table for review. Option A: `GRANT SELECT ON CATALOG sales TO analysts_eu;`. Option B: `GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA sales.gold TO analysts_eu;`. Option C: `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO analysts_eu;`. Current inventory: `sales.bronze` has 9 tables, `sales.silver` has 7 tables, `sales.gold` has 3 tables (`orders`, `order_items`, `dim_customer`), and the schemas also contain 4 views in `silver` and 6 views in `gold`. The ingest team creates approximately 4 new tables per month, distributed as 2 in `bronze`, 1 in `silver`, and 1 in `gold`. (a) Compute how many tables each option authorises today and how many unintended tables that represents. (b) Compute the same figures 12 months from now. (c) Choose the option you would defend in an audit and justify it. (d) Explain why `USE CATALOG` and `USE SCHEMA` must still accompany whichever option you choose.
Hint: Count the objects the grant reaches, not the objects the analysts will actually query.

Worked solution
(a) Today. Option A reaches every table in the catalog: $9 + 7 + 3 = 19$ tables, of which $19 - 1 = 18$ are unintended. Option B reaches every table in `sales.gold`: $3$ tables, of which $3 - 1 = 2$ are unintended (`order_items` and `dim_customer`). Option C reaches $1$ table and $0$ unintended tables. Expressed as over-exposure relative to the requirement, A is $19/1 = 19\times$, B is $3\times$, C is $1\times$.

(b) After 12 months. Growth is $4 \times 12 = 48$ new tables: bronze $9 + 24 = 33$, silver $7 + 12 = 19$, gold $3 + 12 = 15$, for a catalog total of $33 + 19 + 15 = 67$. Option A now reaches 67 tables, $66$ of them unintended — a single `GRANT` written today silently authorises 66 extra tables a year from now, with no further action by any administrator. Option B reaches 15 tables, $14$ unintended. Option C still reaches exactly 1 table: the new gold tables are not automatically exposed, and if one of them is later required, a new reviewed `GRANT` is issued. The view surface behaves the same way: today Option A also reaches $4 + 6 = 10$ views, so it authorises $19 + 10 = 29$ relations to satisfy a one-relation requirement.

(c) Choose Option C. It is the narrowest object that satisfies the stated requirement, so it exposes no unintended table and no view, and its exposure does not grow when other teams add tables. Option B is defensible only if the requirement is literally "all of `sales.gold`"; used here it hands the analysts two extra tables that nobody reviewed. Option A fails the audit outright, because it grants SELECT across the entire catalog, including raw and cleaned layers that may contain unmasked personal data.

(d) `USE CATALOG` on `sales` and `USE SCHEMA` on `sales.gold` are still required. A data privilege on an object does not by itself make the path resolvable: the engine must first be allowed to traverse the catalog and the schema. Concretely, the audit-ready script is:

```sql

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG sales TO `analysts_eu`;

GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA sales.gold TO `analysts_eu`;

GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO `analysts_eu`;

REVOKE MODIFY ON TABLE sales.gold.orders FROM `analysts_eu`;

```

Analysis — The arithmetic is the argument. Option A grows without bound as a function of other teams' productivity, while Option C's exposure is constant at 1 relation regardless of how many tables are created; the security cost of a grant is therefore not just what it reaches today but the derivative of that reach over time. This is why the review asks for a defensible *scope* rather than a convenient one, and why "least privilege" is framed as giving access to "only the essential data and resources to perform an intended function" [source p.75] — a catalog-wide grant is by construction not essential to querying one table. Two subtleties deserve attention. First, views are an escalation path: a view in `silver` may read tables that the analyst cannot query directly, so granting on a parent object can leak data through a view that was never meant to be public — an effect that resembles the federated-query pattern in which an OLAP engine reaches data in external systems and returns combined results to the caller [source p.351], except that the caller here is an unaudited group. Second, the future-proofing argument is often inverted by students: they grant broadly "so the team is not blocked later". The correct inversion is that a broad grant is a permanent, unaudited authorisation that fires again every time someone else creates an object; a narrow grant costs one reviewed statement per new requirement. A materialized view (a stored query whose results are physically maintained and refreshed) declared over a governed table inherits the same concern: whoever can read the materialized view reads the underlying rows, so scope decisions must be made over the whole relation graph, not over one table name.
Problem 3

Two related release-review questions about subtraction of privileges in Unity Catalog.

Part A. The script in Problem 1 is executed a second time during a deployment. What happens to `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO analysts_eu` and to `REVOKE MODIFY ON TABLE sales.gold.orders FROM analysts_eu`? Does the script error?

Part B. Your group hierarchy is: `analysts_all` (40 members) has two child groups, `analysts_eu` (6 members) and `analysts_apac` (11 members). In March someone ran `GRANT MODIFY ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO analysts_all`. The review now requires that no member of `analysts_eu` can modify the table. You run `REVOKE MODIFY ON TABLE sales.gold.orders FROM analysts_eu;`, then test as one of the 6 members and find that the `DELETE` still succeeds. Explain exactly what happened, and give the correct remediation. Also check the ownership edge case: the table is owned by `data_platform`, and one of the 6 analysts was added to `data_platform` by mistake last quarter.
Hint: Unity Catalog has no DENY: privileges are only ever added, so subtraction must happen at the source of the grant.

Worked solution
Part A. Both statements are safe. Grants in Unity Catalog are additive and idempotent: re-issuing `GRANT SELECT` leaves a single `SELECT` row in the grant metadata, not two. `REVOKE MODIFY` on a privilege that the principal does not currently hold is a no-op — it succeeds and changes nothing. The script therefore completes without error and the resulting state is byte-for-byte the same as after the first run. This is a deliberate design property, not an accident, and it is what allows the same deployment script to be replayed in dev, staging, and production. Verify it either way: both runs return exactly one `SELECT` row for `analysts_eu` from `SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE sales.gold.orders;`.

Part B. The statement you ran was a no-op, and the test failure is expected. `analysts_eu` never held a *direct* `MODIFY` grant on the table; the only grant row on `sales.gold.orders` names `analysts_all`. Because `analysts_eu` is a member of `analysts_all`, each of its 6 members holds `MODIFY` *through inheritance*, and inherited privileges are not stored on the child group. `REVOKE ... FROM analysts_eu` therefore removes nothing, exactly as if the grant had never existed. The output of `SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE sales.gold.orders;` still shows the row `analysts_all | MODIFY | TABLE | sales.gold.orders`, which is the effective source of the capability. Diagnostically: a grant row names the *grantee*, and the grantee here is the parent group.

Correct remediation. Removing `MODIFY` from `analysts_all` fixes the requirement but is far too blunt: it also strips the privilege from the other 34 members (40 − 6 analysts in `analysts_eu`, and the remaining members of `analysts_apac`), including the 4 legitimate order writers. Restructure instead:

```sql

-- 1. create a purpose-built group and add only the 4 legitimate writers to it

-- (via the account console or the account SCIM API, since group membership

-- is managed at the account level, not by SQL)

-- 2. move the write capability onto that group

GRANT MODIFY ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO `order_writers`;

-- 3. remove the broad inherited grant from everyone else

REVOKE MODIFY ON TABLE sales.gold.orders FROM `analysts_all`;

-- 4. re-verify

SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE sales.gold.orders;

```

Expected verification result: two rows — `order_writers | MODIFY | TABLE | sales.gold.orders` and `analysts_eu | SELECT | TABLE | sales.gold.orders`. The 36 members who are not in `order_writers` lose write access; the 6 analysts in `analysts_eu` retain read-only access.

Ownership edge case. Ownership is not a grant and cannot be revoked. The owner of a table can always read, modify, and drop it, and can grant privileges on it. Any of the 6 analysts who is a member of `data_platform` therefore retains full control over `sales.gold.orders` no matter how many `REVOKE` statements you issue. Check the owner explicitly — `SHOW GRANTS` does not show it:

```sql

SELECT table_owner

FROM sales.information_schema.tables

WHERE table_schema = 'gold' AND table_name = 'orders';

```

If the owner group contains people who should only read, fix it by transferring ownership rather than by revoking:

```sql

ALTER TABLE sales.gold.orders SET OWNER TO `data_platform`;

```

(after first removing the accidental member from `data_platform`), and re-run the verification.

Analysis — The core mental model is that a privilege is a *directed grant row* (grantee, privilege, securable) and an effective permission is the transitive closure of those rows over the group membership graph. `REVOKE` deletes a row; it cannot delete a path. This is why the statement in Part B is a syntactically valid no-op that produces a false sense of security, and why interviews and audits both probe it. The system has no `DENY` construct: privileges are purely additive, so the only ways to subtract a capability are (i) revoke the row at its source, or (ii) change ownership, which is the one privilege that `REVOKE` can never remove. This is the same shape as the immutability model of object stores, where an object cannot be modified in place and a change is expressed as a new write of the whole object [source p.232]: the state of an authorisation set changes by issuing new operations, never by editing what is already recorded. Two further points generalize. First, group hierarchies are shared infrastructure — a grant on a parent group fans out to every descendant, and the blast radius scales with membership, so a writer group should be flat and purpose-named (`order_writers`) rather than borrowed from an analytics hierarchy. Second, service processes need their own principals: the common ingestion pattern is a reader process that extracts from a source database and writes objects into storage for a downstream system to consume [source p.278], and such a process should never be given a human analytics group's credentials, because it will be granted write privileges that no human role requires. Troubleshooting rule of thumb: when a revoke "does not work", enumerate the grant rows on the object with `SHOW GRANTS`, then walk the membership graph from the denied principal upward until you find the row that names an ancestor group.
Problem 4

You must ship a verification script that runs in CI after every deployment of the `sales` catalog and fails the build if the analysts' access has drifted. It must prove four things: (a) `analysts_eu` holds the two path privileges and exactly one data privilege inside the `sales` catalog; (b) the only principal with a direct `MODIFY` grant on `sales.gold.orders` is the legitimate writer group `order_writers`; (c) the table is owned by `data_platform`, not by any group that contains analysts; (d) if the team later needs to read raw files from the governed volume `sales.bronze.raw_landing`, the same pattern is extended to the volume, and the script reports it. Write the SQL, give the expected result of each query, and state the exact assertion the CI job should enforce on the combined result.
Hint: Use the per-catalog `information_schema` views: they expose grants at each level of the hierarchy, which `SHOW GRANTS` only does one object at a time.

Worked solution
Step 1 — data privileges inside the catalog. The per-catalog view `information_schema.table_privileges` lists one row per (grantee, table, privilege) triple in that catalog:

```sql

SELECT grantee, table_schema, table_name, privilege_type

FROM sales.information_schema.table_privileges

WHERE grantee = 'analysts_eu'

ORDER BY table_schema, table_name, privilege_type;

```

Expected: a single row — `analysts_eu | gold | orders | SELECT`.

Step 2 — path privileges, which live at their own levels and never appear in `table_privileges`:

```sql

SELECT grantee, privilege_type

FROM sales.information_schema.catalog_privileges

WHERE grantee = 'analysts_eu';

-- expected: 1 row -> analysts_eu | USE CATALOG

SELECT grantee, schema_name, privilege_type

FROM sales.information_schema.schema_privileges

WHERE grantee = 'analysts_eu';

-- expected: 1 row -> analysts_eu | gold | USE SCHEMA

```

The second query is the guard against the most common silent regression: someone re-runs an older script that contains `GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA sales.bronze TO analysts_eu`, which would open a second branch of the catalog without touching any table privilege.

Step 3 — write-privilege drift on the target table:

```sql

SELECT grantee, privilege_type

FROM sales.information_schema.table_privileges

WHERE table_schema = 'gold'

AND table_name = 'orders'

AND privilege_type = 'MODIFY';

```

Expected: exactly one row — `order_writers | MODIFY`.

Step 4 — ownership, which is invisible to the privilege views:

```sql

SELECT table_catalog, table_schema, table_name, table_owner

FROM sales.information_schema.tables

WHERE table_schema = 'gold' AND table_name = 'orders';

```

Expected: `sales | gold | orders | data_platform`.

Step 5 — extension to the governed volume. Non-tabular files are read through a volume, whose grants are reported by `volume_privileges`:

```sql

GRANT READ VOLUME ON VOLUME sales.bronze.raw_landing TO `analysts_eu`;

SELECT grantee, volume_schema, volume_name, privilege_type

FROM sales.information_schema.volume_privileges

WHERE grantee = 'analysts_eu';

-- expected: 1 row -> analysts_eu | bronze | raw_landing | READ VOLUME

```

`READ VOLUME` is the minimum privilege for reading files; `WRITE VOLUME` would be required (and reviewed) only for landing data.

Step 6 — the CI assertion. Collapse the four checks into one row of counters and assert the exact vector:

```sql

SELECT

(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales.information_schema.table_privileges

WHERE grantee = 'analysts_eu') AS table_grants,

(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales.information_schema.catalog_privileges

WHERE grantee = 'analysts_eu' AND privilege_type = 'USE CATALOG') AS use_catalog,

(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales.information_schema.schema_privileges

WHERE grantee = 'analysts_eu' AND privilege_type = 'USE SCHEMA') AS use_schema,

(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales.information_schema.table_privileges

WHERE table_schema = 'gold' AND table_name = 'orders'

AND privilege_type = 'MODIFY') AS modify_grants,

(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales.information_schema.tables

WHERE table_schema = 'gold' AND table_name = 'orders'

AND table_owner <> 'data_platform') AS owner_drift;

```

Expected result: `(1, 1, 1, 1, 0)`. The CI job must compare this vector to the expected tuple and exit non-zero on any mismatch — this catches an extra table grant, an extra `USE SCHEMA` branch, a resurrected `MODIFY` row, and an ownership change in a single assertion.

Analysis — The design decision here is to verify from the metadata catalog rather than by running queries as a user. Query-based testing proves that the happy path works today; metadata assertions prove that the authorisation surface is exactly what was reviewed, which is the property an audit actually cares about, and they cover negative cases (a schema branch that should not be open) that a positive smoke test cannot see. The per-catalog `information_schema` views mirror the object model taught earlier: catalog-level privileges, schema-level privileges, table privileges, and volume privileges are stored at different levels, which is why one query can never answer "what does this group have?" and why the hierarchy must be walked level by level. Granularity matters here for the same reason it matters elsewhere in the platform: file-based data inside a governed volume and row-based data inside a table are different securables with different privilege names (`READ VOLUME` versus `SELECT`), yet both are reached through the same `USE CATALOG` / `USE SCHEMA` path chain. Two edge cases are easy to miss. First, ownership is not a privilege and never appears in the privilege views, so an ownership check must be a separate query. Second, inherited privileges do not appear in these views for the child group: if `analysts_all` held `MODIFY`, the `analysts_eu` row count would still be 0 while the effective permission would be non-zero — which is why the assertion also counts `MODIFY` rows on the table by *any* grantee and compares against the expected writer group. A defensible verification suite therefore combines: (i) the expected privilege vector for the group under review, (ii) the full set of grantees holding powerful privileges on the object, and (iii) the owner of the object. The final generalization is that the expected vector is an artefact under version control, exactly like the DDL: a change in access entitlement should show up as a one-line diff in a pull request, not as a surprise during an incident review.

actions.text: Now that you've tackled the checkpoint, let's put privileges, GRANT, and REVOKE into practice with a fully worked problem. This is exactly the kind of scenario the exam loves because it tests least privilege and scope discipline at the same time.

Here's the setup. You're the data platform engineer for a retail company. The group analysts_eu must be able to query sales.gold.orders, must not be able to modify it, and must not be able to query any other schema in the sales catalog. Read that last constraint carefully — controlling what they can't reach is just as important as granting what they can.

The hint gives us the mental model: a query succeeds only when three separate privilege links are all in place. Path privileges first — USE CATALOG on the catalog and USE SCHEMA on the schema — then the object privilege itself. Miss any link and the query fails, no matter how generous the final grant is.

Let's walk the worked solution. Step zero is confirming the objects exist. Then we grant USE CATALOG on catalog sales, and USE SCHEMA on schema sales.gold to analysts_eu. Those two path privileges open the door but expose nothing yet — they only let the group navigate to the objects they're allowed to touch.

Then we grant the actual object privilege: SELECT on table sales.gold.orders to analysts_eu. That's the narrowest object that satisfies the requirement — read access to exactly one table, and nothing else in the sales catalog.

Now the cleanup. An accidental write grant is floating around, so we run REVOKE MODIFY on table sales.gold.orders from analysts_eu. Notice the analysis here: grants are additive and idempotent, and revoking a privilege that was never granted is a no-op, not an error. That's why you can safely re-run the statement. Always verify the final state with SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE sales.gold.orders.

One big pitfall to call out before we move on. Granting SELECT ON CATALOG sales would read every current and future table in that catalog — that directly breaks least privilege. Always grant at the narrowest object that satisfies the requirement, and let the path privileges carry the reachability.
