Work through each one on your own — take your time. Once you submit, I'll join you to walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Choosing a Fine-Grained Security Pattern

elements.content: Decision — A data platform team supports 40 analysts spread across three regions, all of whom query one shared Delta table named customers in Unity Catalog. Compliance now requires that the email column be masked for every principal outside a small PII group, and every row must be filtered so each analyst only sees the region assigned to them. The data must not be duplicated, because the platform team already pays for storage, pipeline runtime, and downstream consistency work on a single copy, and cloning per-region copies would multiply those costs and create drift. The decision is hard because three plausible mechanisms all appear to satisfy the visible requirement, yet they differ sharply in where enforcement lives, what happens when a new consumer or notebook appears six months from now, and how much they cost to maintain as the team scales.

Constraints — 40 analysts across three regions query one shared customers table; no duplication of the data is permitted  •  Compliance rule is per-principal: email must be masked for everyone outside the PII group, and this must hold for current and future query paths  •  Unity Catalog has no DENY statement, so security must be expressed as grants plus filter and mask logic, not as explicit exclusions  •  The solution must survive new downstream consumers without a manual re-granting step for every new group  •  All query paths must remain ACID-consistent and return predictable results under concurrent updates

Option A — dynamic views
+ A view is conceptually simple: analysts read from a purpose-built view that already contains the row filter and the email mask, so the rule is visible in one place.; + Views compose naturally with existing SQL and CTEs; a five-table join expressed in a view reads like ordinary SQL and keeps complex logic readable [source p.303].; + Views do not duplicate data, so storage and pipeline cost stay flat.
− Every existing consumer must be redirected from the base table to the view; any notebook, dashboard, or Lakeflow job still pointing at the base table silently bypasses the rule.; − The base table must be locked down separately by revoking SELECT from all non-PII principals, which is a second enforcement step that can be forgotten for a newly created group.; − A view is not materialized, so the join and mask logic runs on every query; on a large table this can be expensive compared with a precomputed path [source p.350].
Best for: Environments with a small, known set of consumers and a team that can reliably retire direct base-table access.

Option B — row filter functions plus column masks on the base table
+ Row filter functions and column masks attach to the table itself, so they apply to every current and future query path, including consumers not yet written.; + There is no data duplication: the single customers table stays authoritative, which preserves ACID guarantees and avoids drift between copies [source p.304].; + Once authored and owned correctly, the policy composes with Unity Catalog grants, and ABAC tag policies can be layered on top to manage scale instead of writing per-group grants by hand.
− Filter and mask functions are code: they must be maintained, unit tested, and owned by a responsible team, otherwise a small change can silently widen access.; − Tuning a row filter requires moving filtering into the table access path, so an unindexed or poorly written function can degrade every query against the table.; − Because Unity Catalog has no DENY statement, the mask must be written as a positive predicate over groups; getting the predicate wrong means the absence of a grant direction rather than an explicit block.
Best for: Multi-region, multi-principal access on a single governed table where the compliance rule must survive new consumers and scale without manual per-group grants.

Option C — physically separate tables or schemas per region
+ The data boundary equals the security boundary, so the rule is trivially explainable to an auditor: an analyst has grants on the EU table and nothing else.; + Each region can evolve its own schema independently, which is useful when regional schemas genuinely diverge, as in single-tenant storage designs [source p.253].; + Accidental cross-region reads are impossible because the objects themselves are distinct.
− It duplicates data, multiplying storage and pipeline cost by the number of regions, and every model or transformation now needs regional variants.; − It cannot mask a column for an authorized region: a PII analyst in one region needs the full column, so the same table cannot present both a masked and unmasked view without adding yet another object.; − If you later need a unified view across tenants for reporting, non-uniform schemas across regions become a major complication [source p.253].
Best for: Truly isolated tenants with divergent schemas and no cross-region reporting requirement.

Recommendation: Option B — row filter functions plus column masks on the base table — The binding constraints are that the compliance rule is per-principal and must hold for current and future query paths, and that the data may not be duplicated. Option B is the only option that enforces at the table itself, so a new notebook or downstream consumer created next quarter inherits the row filter and the email mask without anyone re-granting or redirecting. Because Unity Catalog has no DENY statement, security is expressed by granting SELECT plus attaching a filter and mask, and Option B keeps that expression on one governed object. Option A can be bypassed by any consumer that still points at the base table, and locking the base table down is a second step that is easy to miss for a new group; Option C duplicates data, multiplies storage and pipeline cost, and cannot mask email for an authorized region without adding another object, directly violating the no-duplication constraint. The trade-off accepted in Option B is operational: the filter and mask functions must be owned, tested, and tuned, which is why the recommendation pairs them with ABAC tag policies to manage scale instead of writing per-group grants by hand.

actions.text: Now that we've seen row filters and column masks in action, let's step back and answer a design question you'll face on the exam and on the job: which fine-grained security pattern should you actually choose? This page gives you a scenario and three options to reason through together.

Start with the constraints, because they drive everything. We have a data platform team supporting forty analysts across three regions. They all share a single customers table. Compliance requires that email be masked for anyone outside the PII group. And critically — there is no duplication of the data allowed. Those four facts are your decision criteria.

Option A is dynamic views. A view is conceptually simple and the logic is easy to reason about in one place. But it's coarse — every consumer has to be redirected to the view, and you still have to lock down the base table separately. That's an operational burden that grows with every new team.

Option B is row filter functions plus column masks applied directly on the base table. Because the policy lives on the table itself, it applies to every current and future query path automatically — nobody can bypass it by forgetting to use a view. The trade-off is that those functions must be maintained, tested, and owned correctly. Governance becomes a first-class engineering responsibility.

Option C is physically separate tables or schemas per region. It's the simplest to explain and the simplest to audit. But it duplicates data, multiplies your storage and pipeline cost, and — here's the subtle trap — it still can't mask a single column for an otherwise authorised region. Separation solves rows, not columns.

So the recommendation is Option B: row filters and masks on the single governed table. Why? Because the compliance rule is per-principal and must survive new downstream consumers — and only table-level policy guarantees that. To manage scale, layer ABAC tag policies on top instead of hand-writing per-group grants. Remember this reasoning chain: per-principal rule plus no duplication plus future consumers always points to Option B.

scenes.title: Tag-Based Policies, Least Privilege, and Verifying Access

elements.content: Tag-Based Policies, Least Privilege, and Verifying Access
Write the authorization rule once, attach it to a tag, and let the platform apply it to every object that carries that tag.

Attribute-based access control (ABAC): one policy, written against a metastore-governed tag, carries privileges, row filters, and column masks; every object tagged with that tag inherits the policy automatically. Precondition: the tag must exist in Unity Catalog first, and the tag must be attached to the object before the policy takes effect.

Trade-off: a per-object GRANT must be repeated for every new table and re-audited as the estate grows, so N tables means N statements; a tag policy is authored once and applies to all N tagged objects. Tagging scales past a few hundred objects; hand-written grants do not. [source p.398]

Least privilege: grant to groups, not individuals, and only the access a principal needs for the task at hand — never carte blanche admin. Grant at the narrowest scope that satisfies the requirement; grant on catalog or schema scope only when the requirement is genuinely estate-wide. [source p.75]

Worked example: analysts_eu needs to query orders. Per-object: 3 grants (USE CATALOG sales, USE SCHEMA sales.gold, SELECT ON TABLE orders). Tagged: 1 policy on tag pii=gold, and the same policy covers 40 future tables in sales.gold with zero new GRANT statements. [source p.387]

Verify effective access with the platform's own metadata: SHOW GRANTS ON <object>; current_user() and is_account_group_member('group') inside a diagnostic query; the information_schema privilege views; and the audit system table that records who ran which statement. [source p.402]

Exam trap: after tightening permissions, a query can fail with a not-found error rather than a permission error — always check path privileges (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA) before assuming the object was deleted. [source p.387]

actions.text: Now let's build on that reasoning and move from hand-written grants to scalable governance. This page covers three things: tag-based policies, least-privilege hygiene, and how to verify the access you actually have.

Start with attribute-based access control, or ABAC. The idea is simple: you write the authorization rule once and attach it to a governable tag. That policy carries privileges, row filters, and column masks, and it applies automatically to every object that carries the tag.

Notice the contrast. Under ABAC, one policy governs the whole set — tag an object and the rule follows it. That is far more maintainable than per-object GRANT statements, which must each be repeated and re-audited as the estate grows.

That's the core trade-off to remember for the exam. Tag-based policies scale to thousands of objects because the policy is written once; a per-object GRANT must be repeated for every new object and re-audited every time the estate changes.

Next, least privilege in practice. Three habits: grant to groups rather than individuals, grant at the narrowest scope that satisfies the requirement, and only grant at the catalog or schema level when the need is genuinely estate-wide.

Here's a worked example. The analysts_eu group needs to query orders. Rather than granting them a broad catalog privilege, we grant on the specific schema or table the requirement actually touches — narrowest scope that satisfies the need.

You also need to verify effective access using the platform's own metadata. Use SHOW GRANTS ON the object, current_user() and is_account_group_member() in a diagnostic query, the information_schema privilege views, and the audit system table that records who ran which statement.

Finally, the exam trap. After you tighten permissions, a query can fail with a not-found error rather than a permission error. Always check the path privileges before assuming the object was deleted — missing access often masquerades as a missing object.

So to recap this page: ABAC via tags scales, least privilege means groups and narrow scopes, verify with the metadata views, and treat not-found errors as a possible permissions clue. Next we'll pull this together in the lesson assessment.

scenes.title: Lesson Assessment: Access Control and Fine-Grained Security

questions.question: Group `analysts_eu` must be able to read exactly one table, `sales.gold.orders`, must never modify it, and must not be able to reach any other schema inside the `sales` catalog. Which single set of statements achieves ONLY this, with nothing extra?

options.label: GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG sales TO analysts_eu; GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA sales.gold TO analysts_eu; GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO analysts_eu;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO analysts_eu;
GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG sales TO analysts_eu; GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO analysts_eu;
GRANT SELECT ON CATALOG sales TO analysts_eu;

questions.analysis: Unity Catalog access is additive and path privileges are required just to reach an object: a principal must hold USE CATALOG on `sales` and USE SCHEMA on `sales.gold` before a fully qualified reference to `sales.gold.orders` resolves at all, then needs SELECT on the table itself. Option A grants exactly those three privileges and nothing more, so requirements are met with the least privilege. Option B fails because USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are missing, so the name may not resolve even though SELECT was granted. Option C omits USE SCHEMA, so navigation stops at the catalog. Option D grants at catalog scope, which is a classic exam trap: catalog-scope SELECT does not replace the schema-level path privilege and over-broadens the principal far beyond one table. Unity Catalog has no DENY statement, so the absence of extra grants (not a DENY) is what keeps everything else hidden [source p.75].

questions.question: A per-principal rule must apply to every present and future query path against `sales.gold.customers` (an ad hoc SELECT, a dashboard, and a scheduled job), and the rule must not be silently bypassed. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Attach the rule with ALTER TABLE sales.gold.customers SET ROW FILTER <function> ON (<columns>), where the function returns BOOLEAN and is evaluated for every query against the table.
Enforce the rule only in the BI dashboard's SQL, since that is the main consumption path and is easier to change.
Create a dedicated service account for the scheduled job and always connect with it, so the rule is effectively guaranteed across all paths.
Expression can use current_user(), is_account_group_member('group'), and current_metastore(), so identity is evaluated per principal at query time.
Attach a DENY rule and rely on it to override inherited grants.

questions.analysis: A row filter function is a user-defined SQL function returning BOOLEAN that is attached to the table with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER <function> ON (<columns>); once attached, the engine evaluates the predicate for every query against the table, so the rule applies to all present and future query paths, and inside the filter identity functions such as current_user(), is_account_group_member('group'), and current_metastore() resolve to the calling principal. Option B is wrong because enforcing in a single consumer leaves every other path unprotected, which is the classic bypass trap. Option C is wrong because identity is then a single service principal for all callers and the rule cannot vary per principal. Option E is wrong because Unity Catalog has no DENY statement — the absence of a grant is the denial, not a DENY object.

questions.question: A query run as the user `ana` fails with an object-not-resolved or permission error against `sales.gold.customers`. The only grants in place are: `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.customers TO ana;` and `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.customers TO analysts_eu;` (ana is a member of analysts_eu). Diagnose the failure, then write the minimal set of statements that fixes it. Then, for the larger need: the SAME masking rule must be applied to hundreds of tagged tables with minimal maintenance — state the scalable mechanism and why it is preferred.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Path privileges diagnosis — 35%: the answer must state that SELECT is present but USE CATALOG on `sales` and/or USE SCHEMA on `sales.gold` are missing, so the name does not resolve; and must state that revoking from `ana` does nothing because access is inherited from `analysts_eu`. (2) Correct minimal fix — 25%: the GRANT statements must be `GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG sales TO analysts_eu; GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA sales.gold TO analysts_eu;` or `TO ana` with a stated justification that the grant is on catalog and schema (the table SELECT is already present). Full credit requires the correct `ON CATALOG` / `ON SCHEMA` syntax. (3) Scalable mechanism — 25%: must name row filter functions attached with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER, applied to tables, or the dynamic view wrapping the base table, plus a mention of tagging for bulk application. (4) Clarity and correct terminology — 15%: uses Unity Catalog terms correctly and avoids DENY.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. First, diagnose: SELECT on the table is already granted, but a fully qualified reference to `sales.gold.customers` requires USE CATALOG on `sales` and USE SCHEMA on `sales.gold` just to reach the object. This is the missing piece, so the fix is `GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG sales TO analysts_eu;` and `GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA sales.gold TO analysts_eu;` (or granted to `ana` directly, but the group grant is better practice and matches the additive model). Second, do not revoke from a user who inherits access from a group — that is a known trap and here it is also irrelevant because it does not address the failure. Third, the scalable mechanism for the same rule on hundreds of tagged tables is a row filter function attached with `ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER`, applied by tag/object enumeration; the rule lives in one function and is evaluated for every query, so there is no code to duplicate. A dynamic view wrapping the base table is the alternative but needs a view per wrapped table. Access is additive and there is no DENY statement, so the absence of extra grants is the denial [source p.387]; give only the access needed to do the job today, nothing more [source p.75].

questions.question: Which statement tests the fine-grained mechanisms correctly, assuming `email` is a sensitive column and the requirement is to hide the column's values — not to hide rows?

options.label: A column mask (a function returning the column's string type, e.g. mask_email(email STRING) RETURNS STRING) attached with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK <function>, so values are transformed per principal at read time.
A row filter attached to the table, with the predicate on the `email` column, is the correct way to hide the column for principals without the PII group.
Revoking SELECT on the whole table from the principal, because there is no way to hide only the `email` column while allowing the rest of the table.
Running GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.customers (email) TO pii_readers; to grant column-level access without a mask function.

questions.analysis: Hiding a column's values calls for a column mask: a function that returns the column's string type (for example, mask_email(email STRING) RETURNS STRING) attached with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK <function>, evaluated per principal at read time. This is the mechanism taught in the row filters and column masks worked example. Option B is the key trap: a row filter conceals rows, not columns — the predicate tests values and removes rows from the result, leaving the column present for the rows that survive. Option C is over-broad and defeats the stated requirement (the rest of the table should be readable). Option D uses invalid syntax and does not create a mask; column access is not granted by naming a column inside GRANT. As always, there is no DENY statement, so the mask — not a DENY — is what hides the values, and access should be as fine-grained as the requirement warrants [source p.387]; the additive grant model and the absence of any bypass path are the design constraints [source p.75].

actions.text: Time for the lesson assessment. This one pulls together everything we just covered on privileges, inheritance, row filters, column masks, and choosing the right mechanism at the right scope.

Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer before moving on — some of these are built around the classic exam traps, so read carefully. Once you submit, I'll walk you through the reasoning on anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Lineage in Unity Catalog: What It Captures

elements.content: Lineage in Unity Catalog: What It Captures
How Unity Catalog records data flow automatically as workloads execute, which objects it links, and where the lineage graph becomes visible in Catalog Explorer.
How lineage is captured: automatically, at runtime

Unity Catalog records lineage by parsing statements and jobs as they execute against the metastore, so no manual instrumentation such as dbutils tagging or custom audit hooks is required for supported workloads [source p.383].

Each execution produces a lineage event that stores the input tables or views, the operation performed, the output object, and the identity of the principal that ran it, keyed to the current metastore [source p.350].

Capture covers notebooks and jobs as well as Delta tables and views, including a view that wraps five base tables the way a materialized view precomputes its joins [source p.350].

Because the event is written when the query actually runs, an object that is only declared but never referenced does not appear in the graph.
Worked example: one notebook run, five captured assets

A daily job reads sales.raw.orders (Delta) and sales.raw.customer_events (Auto Loader streaming table), joins them, writes sales.silver.orders_enriched, and a dashboard queries that silver table.

Lineage records 4 upstream-to-downstream edges plus the job run, so a drop in dashboard freshness can be traced to the raw table without reading any code.
Entities linked by lineage

The graph connects notebooks, jobs and their tasks, Delta tables, views, dashboards, and registered models whenever they read or write each other [source p.350].

A view is treated as a first-class node: the graph retains the path from the base tables through the view to consumers, matching the composable-view pattern where lineage flows down to subsequent tables asynchronously [source p.350].
What is not captured automatically

Reads executed entirely inside a client such as a local pandas dataframe in a Jupyter notebook never reach the metastore, so the notebook appears without tables or columns [source p.383].

Likewise, a federated query that pulls from object storage, MySQL, or PostgreSQL through a path outside the catalog is logged only for the catalog endpoint actually touched, so the external systems are absent [source p.351].
Where to find lineage

Open the table or view in Catalog Explorer and switch to the Lineage tab to see upstream sources, downstream consumers, and the jobs or notebooks that produced them.

The view is always scoped to the current metastore: an event written in one metastore is not visible from a table registered in another, even if the object names match.
Lineage coverage at a glance — which object types are captured automatically.

data.text: External client read (local pandas / ODBC outside catalog)

elements.content: Takeaway: lineage is a runtime by-product of catalog-mediated queries — no extra code, and it stops at the metastore boundary.

actions.text: Now that we've covered what you can do with access control and fine-grained security, let's turn to something complementary — visibility. Unity Catalog doesn't just let you lock down data; it also records how data moves through your platform. That's what lineage is.

So the title of this page raises the core question: lineage in Unity Catalog — what exactly does it capture? In a nutshell, it's an automatic record of the data flow between the objects you use in Databricks.

The key thing to remember for the exam is the word automatic. You don't write any special instrumentation or add metadata by hand — Unity Catalog records lineage at runtime as your queries execute. It works by parsing the statements your jobs and notebooks submit.
Because it reads the SQL and DataFrame operations as they run, lineage is essentially a by-product of the catalog tracking what you already did.

So which entities get linked together? The graph connects notebooks, jobs and their tasks, Delta tables, views, dashboards, and models. When a notebook reads one table and writes to another, that edge shows up automatically.

Let's make it concrete with the worked example on the slide. A daily job reads sales.raw.orders — a Delta table — and writes to a curated sales table. From that single notebook run, four or five separate lineage relationships are captured: the input table, the output table, the notebook, the job, and the task that ran it.

Now the important caveat — and this is where exam questions love to hide. Some lineage is not captured automatically. If a read happens entirely inside an external client, or through a non-Databricks engine, Unity Catalog simply can't see it. Lineage only knows about activity it observes.

This table gives you the coverage at a glance. Notebooks, jobs, Delta tables, views, and dashboards are all covered automatically; the exception is anything running outside the platform's supported workloads. Skim this once, then use it as your quick reference.

Finally, where do you actually go to see it? Open the table or view in Catalog Explorer and switch to the Lineage tab. Remember, the lineage you see is scoped to the current metastore, so cross-metastore flows won't appear on the same graph.

Bringing it together: lineage is a runtime by-product of catalog activity. It asks no extra effort from you, but it also only sees what runs through supported paths. That single sentence is the takeaway to carry into the rest of this lesson on tracing data flow.

scenes.title: Reading the Lineage Graph: Upstream and Downstream

elements.content: Reading the Lineage Graph: Upstream and Downstream

Lineage is a directed graph: every table is a node and every transformation is an edge pointing from an input to an output. Tracing upstream means walking edges backwards toward source systems; tracing downstream means walking them forward toward consumers.

This directionality is exactly why a data engineer must set service-level expectations with source-system owners before building on them [source p.209].
Upstream: “Where did this come from?”

Walking backwards answers provenance: which raw tables, ingestion jobs, and intermediate transforms produced this row? Because each source system may itself carry upstream dependencies, lineage terminates only at a true producer such as an IoT sensor, a web app, or an operational database [source p.63].
Downstream: “What breaks if I change this?”

Walking forwards answers impact: drop a column or change a type and every downstream destination — dashboards, feature tables, pipelines — that consumes it may fail silently. Schema and format drift from upstream is the classic cause, so engineers deliberately keep a flexible schema in the analytical layer [source p.334].
Worked Example: Column-Level Downstream Impact

A source table sales.bronze.orders has a column customer_id. At column level, three downstream columns depend on it directly or transitively.

1. sales.silver.customers_clean.customer_sk (a join key)

2. sales.gold.order_summary.customer_segment (an aggregation input)

3. ml.churn_features.customer_id (a model feature)

Renaming the source column touches 3 dependent columns across 2 catalogs and 3 schemas.

Table-level lineage would have shown only which tables read orders — three pipelines.

Column-level lineage names the exact connecting columns and separates direct from transitive edges.

That precision decides the blast radius: the engine must recompile the join, the aggregation, and the feature table, but an untouched unrelated region column forces no recomputation at all.
Choosing the Right Surface: Graph vs. System Tables
Catalog Explorer graph: best for visual exploration and design-time impact analysis, but it is a rendered view, not a queryable relation.
System tables: best for programmatic, repeatable checks — queryable from SQL, so results can be scheduled, diffed, and version-controlled.

Exam trap: lineage describes data flow, not authorization. The lineage graph shows that a dashboard reads a table — it does not tell you who was allowed to read that table.

Access is governed by GRANT/REVOKE and row filters or column masks, which you built earlier in this unit. Lineage and privilege are orthogonal: a table can be fully traced but not readable by you.

Orientation rule: edges point with the data. To go upstream, follow edges backwards to sources; to go downstream, follow them forwards to consumers. Unbounded upstream dependencies mean the contract with the source owner defines your reliability guarantee [source p.209].
Checkpoint: Lineage Direction and Lineage Pitfalls

Q1. A gold table named sales.gold.orders breaks. Which traversal identifies the root cause, and what do you reach?

A. Downstream — the dashboards that read it

B. Upstream — the source tables and transforms that feed it

C. Column-level lineage — the exact dependent columns

Answer: B. Upstream is the standard debugging direction; C is a refinement, not the initial root-cause traversal, and A answers impact, the opposite question.

Q2. You must run the same impact check nightly and alert on any new downstream consumer. Which tool fits, and why?

A. The Catalog Explorer graph, because it is visual

B. System tables, because they are queryable programmatically

C. Row filter functions, because they enforce access

Answer: B. Repeatable automation needs a queryable relation; A is for human exploration, and C governs authorization, not lineage.

actions.text: Now that we know what lineage captures, let's learn how to actually read the lineage graph. The skill here is traversal — moving through the graph in both directions.

Think of lineage as a directed graph: every table is a node, and every edge represents data flowing from one object to another. The critical thing to remember is that edges point with the data — the arrow follows the flow, always.

Upstream answers the question 'Where did this come from?' When you walk the graph backwards, against the direction of the edges, you're tracing provenance — following which raw tables, files, or notebooks fed into this object. This is how you root-cause a broken metric or audit where a number originated.

Downstream answers 'What breaks if I change this?' Walking the graph forwards, in the direction the data flows, you get the impact analysis. Before you drop a column or rename a table, this is the view that tells you which dashboards, reports, and downstream jobs are about to break.

Here's a worked example that shows why column-level lineage matters so much. We have a source table, sales.bronze.orders, containing a column called customer_id. The question is: if that column changes, what exactly is at risk?

Table-level lineage would only tell us which tables are connected — it would flag the whole downstream table as affected. But column-level lineage drills into the exact downstream columns that depend on customer_id, so you can see precisely which fields break. That precision is what makes column lineage worth switching to during impact analysis.
So which surface should you use? Let's compare the two options and then hit the exam trap that trips people up.

The Catalog Explorer graph — the visual lineage view you click through in the UI — is best for visual exploration and impact analysis at design time. When you're investigating interactively and want to see the shape of the flow, this is your tool.

System tables, on the other hand, are best for programmatic, repeatable checks. If you need to run the same impact analysis every night, or query lineage as part of an automated pipeline, you go to the system tables — you don't click through a graph by hand.

Now the exam trap — write this one down. Lineage describes data flow, not authorization. The lineage graph tells you where data came from and where it goes; it does NOT tell you who was allowed to read the table. Access control and lineage are separate governance concerns, and exam questions love to conflate them.

One orientation rule to lock in: edges point with the data. So to go upstream you travel against the arrows, and to go downstream you travel with the arrows. If you keep that straight, you'll never confuse provenance with impact.
Let's do a quick checkpoint with two questions to test your understanding of lineage direction and the pitfalls.

Question one: a gold table, sales.gold.orders, breaks. Which direction do you traverse, and what are you looking for? Think about whether you want provenance or impact here — a broken table means you're chasing the cause, so you're going upstream.

Question two: you must run the same impact check nightly, automatically. Which surface do you choose — the visual graph or the system tables? Recall what we just covered: repeatable, programmatic checks belong in the system tables, while the graph is for interactive exploration. Take a moment to reason through both before we move on.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Lineage Fundamentals

questions.question: A data steward asks you: 'When Unity Catalog records lineage for the query INSERT INTO sales.silver.orders SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount FROM sales.bronze.raw_orders, what does that lineage capture at the column level?' Which statement best describes the difference between table-level and column-level lineage in this scenario?

options.label: Table-level lineage records only that sales.silver.orders was written from sales.bronze.raw_orders, while column-level lineage additionally maps each output column (order_id, customer_id, amount) to the specific input columns it was derived from, including intermediate expressions.
Table-level lineage records the full SELECT expression text, while column-level lineage records only the output table name and its partition columns.
Table-level lineage captures who ran the query and when, while column-level lineage captures the GRANT and REVOKE statements applied to each column.
Table-level lineage applies only to Delta Lake tables, while column-level lineage applies only to external tables created over object storage such as S3 buckets.

questions.correctAnswer: Table-level lineage records only that sales.silver.orders was written from sales.bronze.raw_orders, while column-level lineage additionally maps each output column (order_id, customer_id, amount) to the specific input columns it was derived from, including intermediate expressions.
questions.analysis: Table-level lineage answers the coarse question 'which tables fed which tables' — in this example, that sales.bronze.raw_orders fed sales.silver.orders. Column-level lineage is the finer-grained graph: it records that the output column order_id derives from the input column order_id, customer_id derives from customer_id, and amount derives from amount, and it preserves the derivation expression so downstream consumers can trace a value back through transformations. This is essential when you must answer impact questions such as 'if the source column amount changes semantics, which downstream columns and dashboards are affected?' The second option is wrong because lineage does not store the raw SELECT text as its primary output, and partition columns are a table property, not the definition of column-level lineage. The third option confuses lineage with the audit log and with the privilege model taught earlier in this unit: GRANT and REVOKE affect who may reference an object, not what lineage records. The fourth option invents a storage-format restriction; lineage is a catalog-level capability and is independent of whether data lives in managed Delta tables or is read through external locations. Note the ecosystem context: federated queries can combine object storage, MySQL, and PostgreSQL sources, and lineage must still describe which objects contributed to a result [source p.351].
answer: Table-level lineage records only that sales.silver.orders was written from sales.bronze.raw_orders, while column-level lineage additionally maps each output column (order_id, customer_id, amount) to the specific input columns it was derived from, including intermediate expressions.

questions.question: A platform team is documenting the boundaries of Unity Catalog lineage for an audit-readiness review. Select ALL statements that are correct about how lineage is captured and what it does NOT tell you. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Lineage is captured automatically for supported query paths — for example, queries executed through Databricks SQL warehouses, notebooks, and jobs — without engineers writing explicit lineage instrumentation.
Lineage is a substitute for the audit log: because lineage records the query paths, you do not need to retain audit records of who ran which statement against which object.
Column-level lineage reflects the transformation expressions used to derive output columns, so it can be used for impact analysis when a source column changes.
Lineage is captured for every external reader of a table, including third-party tools that read the underlying storage files directly without going through the Unity Catalog query path.

correctAnswer: Lineage is captured automatically for supported query paths — for example, queries executed through Databricks SQL warehouses, notebooks, and jobs — without engineers writing explicit lineage instrumentation.
Column-level lineage reflects the transformation expressions used to derive output columns, so it can be used for impact analysis when a source column changes.
questions.analysis: The first option is correct: for supported query paths the engine records lineage automatically as a by-product of query execution, which is why a medallion architecture (a layered bronze/silver/gold refinement pattern) builds its traceability for free. The third option is correct: because column-level lineage stores the derivation between input and output columns, it supports impact analysis — 'if this source column changes, which downstream columns, views, and dashboards are affected?' The second option is a classic exam trap and is false: lineage and the audit log answer different questions. Lineage tells you the data-dependency graph; the audit log tells you the accountability record — which principal executed which statement, when, and from where. Institutions with compliance obligations need both, and lineage is explicitly not a replacement for the audit log. The fourth option is also false and mirrors the other real trap: lineage is captured when access flows through the supported query path. A third-party reader that bypasses the catalog query path and reads files directly does not generate lineage, which is one reason direct storage access should be locked down. This matters at scale: moving large volumes of data, such as 10 TB per hour from a source database, through governed paths is an architectural decision with both latency and governance consequences [source p.102], and lineage coverage is part of that same architectural decision.
answer: Lineage is captured automatically for supported query paths — for example, queries executed through Databricks SQL warehouses, notebooks, and jobs — without engineers writing explicit lineage instrumentation.
Column-level lineage reflects the transformation expressions used to derive output columns, so it can be used for impact analysis when a source column changes.

questions.question: You are onboarding a new analyst who asks two questions: (1) 'Does lineage tell me who is allowed to read sales.gold.customers?' and (2) 'If a colleague queries the table from a supported Databricks SQL warehouse, will the lineage appear without anyone doing extra work?' Write a concise answer that (a) distinguishes lineage from the permission model (GRANT/REVOKE, ownership, inherited grants) and from the audit log, (b) explains what column-level lineage adds beyond table-level lineage, and (c) names one situation in which lineage will NOT be recorded.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric — award credit proportionally: (a) Correctly states that lineage is a data-dependency record (which tables/columns fed which tables/columns) and NOT an authorization record. Must explicitly contrast with GRANT/REVOKE and with inherited/explicit privileges and ownership from earlier in this unit — an answer that says 'lineage shows who can access' earns no credit here. Must also state that the audit log, not lineage, answers WHO ran WHAT and WHEN. (40%) (b) Explains table-level lineage as the coarse 'table fed table' graph and column-level lineage as the fine-grained mapping of each output column to its input columns and derivation expressions, and correctly identifies impact analysis as the primary use case. (35%) (c) Names at least one valid non-capture case: direct/external read of the underlying files bypassing the catalog query path, a tool or path not supported for lineage capture, or a non-query activity such as manual file manipulation. (25%) Deduct for answers that treat lineage and permissions as interchangeable, or that claim lineage replaces the audit log.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: (1) No. Lineage records data dependencies — which source tables and columns were read and which output columns were written, along with the derivation between them. It says nothing about authorization. The permission model from earlier in this unit governs access: objects carry ownership, privileges inherited from a parent object or a group membership, and privileges granted explicitly on the object, and GRANT/REVOKE change those. The audit log is the accountability record for who executed which statement and when; lineage is not a substitute for it. (2) Yes — for supported query paths such as a Databricks SQL warehouse, notebook, or job, lineage is captured automatically as a by-product of execution, with no manual instrumentation. (b) Table-level lineage tells you that sales.bronze.raw_orders fed sales.silver.orders; column-level lineage additionally tells you that the output column amount derives from the input column amount (and records the expression), which is what makes impact analysis possible when a source column's meaning changes. (c) Lineage is not recorded when a reader bypasses the supported query path — for example, a third-party tool reading the underlying storage files directly — because no catalog-mediated query plan is produced to observe. Note the surrounding ecosystem context: query engines increasingly federate across object storage and external databases [source p.351], and they materialize results into optimized physical structures such as materialized views [source p.342], all of which belong to the lineage graph yet require the query to actually pass through a supported path for capture.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Trace a Metric from Source Table to Dashboard

elements.content: Problem 1

A monthly revenue dashboard object `dashboards.monthly_revenue` reads from `gold.revenue_monthly`. The Unity Catalog lineage graph in Catalog Explorer shows the following direct dependencies for the relevant objects: `gold.revenue_monthly` is downstream of `silver.orders_clean`; `silver.orders_clean` is downstream of `bronze.orders_raw`; `bronze.orders_raw` also has two other direct downstream consumers: `silver.orders_quarantine` and `ml.features_orders`. The pipeline ingests 1,200,000 order rows per month from an external point-of-sale system into `bronze.orders_raw`. (a) Reconstruct the full upstream chain from the dashboard back to the raw source, listing every hop. (b) List all downstream consumers of `bronze.orders_raw` that appear in the graph, separating direct consumers from transitive consumers. (c) If the ingestion job adds a new column `discount_code` to `bronze.orders_raw`, which downstream stakeholders must be notified, and why is lineage the right tool to answer this?

Hint: Walk the directed graph one hop at a time: an edge `source_table_full_name → target_table_full_name` means the target reads from the source. Upstream means against the arrow; downstream means along the arrow.

Worked solution
Step 1 — identify the dashboard's immediate upstream. The dashboard object `dashboards.monthly_revenue` is a downstream consumer of `gold.revenue_monthly`, so the first hop upstream is `dashboards.monthly_revenue ← gold.revenue_monthly`. Step 2 — continue walking upstream. `gold.revenue_monthly` is downstream of `silver.orders_clean`, so the next hop is `gold.revenue_monthly ← silver.orders_clean`. Step 3 — continue. `silver.orders_clean` is downstream of `bronze.orders_raw`, so the final hop is `silver.orders_clean ← bronze.orders_raw`. The full upstream chain from raw to dashboard is: `bronze.orders_raw → silver.orders_clean → gold.revenue_monthly → dashboards.monthly_revenue`. (b) Direct downstream consumers of `bronze.orders_raw` are `silver.orders_clean`, `silver.orders_quarantine`, and `ml.features_orders`. Transitive downstream consumers (reachable through one or more hops) also include `gold.revenue_monthly` and `dashboards.monthly_revenue` via `silver.orders_clean`, plus any consumers of `ops.quarantine_report` or `ml.features_orders` if those edges are present in the graph. For the graph as stated, the transitive additions from the three direct consumers are `gold.revenue_monthly` and `dashboards.monthly_revenue`. (c) The stakeholders who must be notified are the owners and consumers of every downstream object: `silver.orders_clean`, `silver.orders_quarantine`, `ml.features_orders`, `gold.revenue_monthly`, `dashboards.monthly_revenue`, and any downstream reports. This is exactly the set of nodes reachable from `bronze.orders_raw` in the lineage graph. Data engineering practice requires communicating schema changes to downstream stakeholders so they can adapt their ingestion, transformation, and reporting logic [source p.63]. Lineage is the right tool because it provides the complete, queryable dependency graph, including transitive consumers that a manual inventory would likely miss.

Analysis — The method works because lineage is a directed graph where each row represents exactly one hop from a source object to a target object. Walking upstream is a reverse traversal; walking downstream is a forward traversal. The upstream chain is a path; the downstream set is the reachable set. In the medallion architecture (a layered design pattern: bronze = raw data as ingested, silver = cleaned and conformed data, gold = business-level aggregates), this path is the canonical bronze→silver→gold→dashboard flow. Common student mistakes: (1) reversing the arrows and confusing upstream with downstream; (2) stopping at direct consumers and missing transitive ones; (3) assuming the lineage graph is complete when some sources are external. For example, if `bronze.orders_raw` is an external table reading from an S3 bucket, the lineage may stop at the table and not show the S3 location, because external tables read from object storage at query time [source p.351]. Another pitfall is that federated queries can combine object storage and multiple databases, and the lineage system may not capture every external source [source p.351]. Finally, schema changes must be communicated to downstream stakeholders, and lineage is the authoritative way to enumerate them [source p.63].
Problem 2

You need to reproduce the downstream walk from `bronze.orders_raw` using SQL over `system.access.table_lineage`. The table has columns `source_table_full_name`, `target_table_full_name`, and `event_time`. For the last 7 days, the raw table contains 1,240 rows for the relevant catalog, but each logical edge can appear multiple times because each write operation and each Delta Lake optimization emits a lineage event. The observed edges and their duplicate counts are: `bronze.orders_raw → silver.orders_clean` appears 3 times; `bronze.orders_raw → silver.orders_quarantine` appears 2 times; `bronze.orders_raw → ml.features_orders` appears 1 time; `silver.orders_clean → gold.revenue_monthly` appears 4 times; `silver.orders_clean → ml.features_orders` appears 0 times; `gold.revenue_monthly → dashboards.monthly_revenue` appears 2 times; `silver.orders_quarantine → ops.quarantine_report` appears 1 time. All other edges have 0 rows. (a) Write a recursive SQL query that returns the distinct set of all downstream tables reachable from `bronze.orders_raw` within at most 4 hops. (b) Compute the distinct downstream tables. (c) Compute the total number of raw lineage rows traversed by the recursion if duplicates are collapsed with UNION (not UNION ALL) at each step. (d) Explain what would happen to the row count if you used UNION ALL instead.
Hint: Use WITH RECURSIVE, start with source = 'bronze.orders_raw', join on target_table_full_name = next source_table_full_name, and use UNION to eliminate duplicate rows at each hop.

Worked solution
(a) SQL:

WITH RECURSIVE downstream AS (

SELECT target_table_full_name AS table_name, 1 AS hop

FROM system.access.table_lineage

WHERE source_table_full_name = 'bronze.orders_raw'

UNION

SELECT t.target_table_full_name, d.hop + 1

FROM system.access.table_lineage t

JOIN downstream d ON t.source_table_full_name = d.table_name

WHERE d.hop < 4

)

SELECT DISTINCT table_name FROM downstream;

(b) Hop 1: silver.orders_clean, silver.orders_quarantine, ml.features_orders. Hop 2: from silver.orders_clean → gold.revenue_monthly and ml.features_orders (already seen); from silver.orders_quarantine → ops.quarantine_report; from ml.features_orders → none. So new tables: gold.revenue_monthly, ops.quarantine_report. Hop 3: from gold.revenue_monthly → dashboards.monthly_revenue; from ops.quarantine_report → none. Hop 4: from dashboards.monthly_revenue → none. Distinct downstream tables = {silver.orders_clean, silver.orders_quarantine, ml.features_orders, gold.revenue_monthly, ops.quarantine_report, dashboards.monthly_revenue}, a total of 6 tables. (c) Raw rows traversed if UNION collapses duplicates at each step: hop 1 processes rows where source = bronze.orders_raw: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 rows. Hop 2 processes rows whose source is any table discovered in hop 1: silver.orders_clean has 4 rows (to gold.revenue_monthly), silver.orders_quarantine has 1 row (to ops.quarantine_report), ml.features_orders has 0 rows. Total hop 2 = 5 rows. Hop 3 processes rows whose source is gold.revenue_monthly (2 rows to dashboards.monthly_revenue) and ops.quarantine_report (0 rows). Total hop 3 = 2 rows. Hop 4 processes rows whose source is dashboards.monthly_revenue (0 rows). Total raw rows = 6 + 5 + 2 + 0 = 13 rows. (d) If you used UNION ALL, duplicate edges would not be collapsed. Hop 1 would produce 6 rows. Hop 2 would join each of the 6 rows from hop 1 to the outgoing edges of its target: silver.orders_clean has 4 rows, so the 3 duplicate rows to silver.orders_clean would each produce 4 rows = 12 rows; silver.orders_quarantine has 1 row, so its 2 duplicate rows produce 2 rows; ml.features_orders has 0 rows. Hop 2 would produce 12 + 2 = 14 rows. Hop 3 would join these 14 rows to outgoing edges: the 12 rows arriving at gold.revenue_monthly would each produce 2 rows = 24 rows; the 2 rows arriving at ops.quarantine_report produce 0. Hop 3 = 24 rows. Hop 4 = 0. Total = 6 + 14 + 24 = 44 rows, more than triple the 13 distinct-edge rows. With deeper pipelines and more duplicates, UNION ALL can explode combinatorially.

Analysis — The recursive CTE works because lineage rows are one hop each, so a chain of length $k$ is a recursive join of $k$ copies of the lineage table. Using UNION (not UNION ALL) is essential when the same edge appears multiple times: UNION deduplicates rows at each recursion level, keeping the traversal linear in the number of distinct edges. UNION ALL would multiply duplicate edges and can produce exponentially many intermediate rows. Common pitfalls: (1) forgetting to limit the recursion depth (`WHERE d.hop < 4`), which can cause infinite loops if the lineage graph has cycles (a table that is both upstream and downstream, often through a view or a materialized view); (2) comparing table names with case sensitivity issues—Unity Catalog stores full names as strings, and `'bronze.orders_raw'` differs from `'Bronze.Orders_Raw'`; (3) event lag: a write that just happened may not have a lineage row yet, so the query can miss the newest edge. The prejoining technique is relevant here: if `gold.revenue_monthly` is a prejoined or materialized version of repeated joins, its lineage may come from a materialized view definition rather than a direct query [source p.302]. Some OLAP systems can convert federated queries into materialized views, which can obscure the underlying lineage [source p.351]. Always verify the lineage freshness and deduplicate before auditing.
Problem 3

A data quality audit must guarantee that the column `customer_id` in `bronze.orders_raw` is preserved through the pipeline. You switch from table-level lineage to `system.access.column_lineage`, which has columns `source_table_full_name`, `source_column_name`, `target_table_full_name`, `target_column_name`, and `event_time`. You find these lineage rows (duplicates omitted): (1) `bronze.orders_raw.customer_id → silver.orders_clean.customer_id`; (2) `silver.orders_clean.customer_id → gold.revenue_monthly.customer_id`; (3) `silver.orders_clean.order_total → gold.revenue_monthly.revenue_amount`; (4) `gold.revenue_monthly.customer_id → dashboards.monthly_revenue.customer_key`; (5) `bronze.orders_raw.discount_code → silver.orders_clean.discount_code`; (6) `silver.orders_clean.discount_code → gold.revenue_monthly.discount_amount`. (a) Write a recursive SQL query to find all downstream (table, column) pairs reachable from `bronze.orders_raw.customer_id`. (b) How many distinct downstream column pairs are reachable? (c) If the team drops `customer_id` from `bronze.orders_raw`, which downstream artifacts break? (d) Why is table-level lineage insufficient to answer this audit question?
Hint: For column lineage, the recursive join must match both table and column: `source_table = previous target_table AND source_column = previous target_column`.

Worked solution
(a) SQL:

WITH RECURSIVE col_downstream AS (

SELECT target_table_full_name, target_column_name, 1 AS hop

FROM system.access.column_lineage

WHERE source_table_full_name = 'bronze.orders_raw'

AND source_column_name = 'customer_id'

UNION

SELECT c.target_table_full_name, c.target_column_name, d.hop + 1

FROM system.access.column_lineage c

JOIN col_downstream d

ON c.source_table_full_name = d.target_table_full_name

AND c.source_column_name = d.target_column_name

WHERE d.hop < 10

)

SELECT DISTINCT target_table_full_name, target_column_name FROM col_downstream;

(b) Hop 1: silver.orders_clean.customer_id. Hop 2: gold.revenue_monthly.customer_id. Hop 3: dashboards.monthly_revenue.customer_key. The discount_code path (rows 5 and 6) is not reachable from customer_id because the recursive join requires the column name to match; row 5 has source_column = discount_code, so it is excluded. Thus there are 3 distinct downstream (table, column) pairs: (silver.orders_clean, customer_id), (gold.revenue_monthly, customer_id), (dashboards.monthly_revenue, customer_key). Note that the column name changes to `customer_key` in the dashboard, but the lineage row connects them, so the dependency is captured. (c) If `customer_id` is dropped from `bronze.orders_raw`, the breakage includes: the cleaning job that populates `silver.orders_clean.customer_id` will fail or produce nulls; downstream `gold.revenue_monthly.customer_id` will be missing; and `dashboards.monthly_revenue.customer_key` will break or show blanks. Any join or aggregation that uses these columns will also fail. (d) Table-level lineage would only show that `silver.orders_clean`, `gold.revenue_monthly`, and `dashboards.monthly_revenue` depend on `bronze.orders_raw`. It would not tell you which column is the root cause, so the audit could not distinguish between dropping `customer_id` and dropping `discount_code`. Column-level lineage is required to pinpoint the exact column dependency.

Analysis — Column-level lineage works because each row records a dependency between a source column and a target column, including rename and transformation mappings. The recursive join on both table and column follows the dependency edges. Common pitfalls: (1) assuming column names are preserved exactly; they often change (e.g., `customer_id` → `customer_key`), so you must follow the lineage rows, not string matching; (2) forgetting that a target column can be derived from multiple source columns (e.g., a concatenation or a sum), which would require the lineage system to record multiple edges into the same target column—the recursive join as written follows one-to-one paths and may miss multi-source derivations unless you start from all relevant source columns; (3) using table-level lineage for a column-level audit, which is a classic mistake in data quality reviews. The prejoining strategy can also complicate column lineage: when tables are prejoined and denormalized, a single target column may come from several source tables, and the lineage graph can be harder to interpret [source p.302]. Federated queries and materialized views can further obscure column-level origins [source p.351]. Finally, schema changes such as dropping a column must be communicated to downstream stakeholders [source p.63].
Problem 4

A data engineer runs the downstream lineage query for `bronze.orders_raw` at 09:00 on a Tuesday. The pipeline wrote to `silver.orders_clean` at 08:58, but the lineage system has an expected event lag of up to 45 minutes. The same edge `bronze.orders_raw → silver.orders_clean` appears 3 times in `system.access.table_lineage` for the last 24 hours because each write operation and each Delta Lake optimization emits a separate lineage event. Another engineer has created a table whose full name is `Bronze.Orders_Raw` (different letter case). Last week the team dropped `silver.orders_quarantine`, and its historical lineage rows disappeared from the system table. The pipeline runs 3 times per hour, and each run produces 2 lineage events per edge. (a) Why might the query at 09:00 miss `silver.orders_clean`? (b) How do you deduplicate the lineage query so that each logical edge is counted once? (c) Which of these names are considered distinct by a string equality comparison in the lineage system: `bronze.orders_raw`, `Bronze.Orders_Raw`, `BRONZE.ORDERS_RAW`? (d) If an upstream object is dropped, what happens to its lineage and why is that a problem for audit? (e) For one edge with 3 runs per hour and 2 events per run, how many raw lineage rows accumulate in 8 hours, and what would happen to a 3-hop recursive query that uses UNION ALL instead of UNION?
Hint: Lineage is eventually consistent; deduplicate with DISTINCT or GROUP BY; remember that string comparisons are case-sensitive; and dropped objects remove their lineage history.

Worked solution
(a) The write to `silver.orders_clean` happened at 08:58, only 2 minutes before the query. Because lineage events can lag up to 45 minutes, the lineage row for that write may not yet exist in `system.access.table_lineage`, so the query misses `silver.orders_clean` even though the table was written. (b) Deduplicate by selecting distinct source and target pairs:

SELECT DISTINCT source_table_full_name, target_table_full_name

FROM system.access.table_lineage

WHERE source_table_full_name = 'bronze.orders_raw';

or group by both columns and count events. (c) Unity Catalog object identifiers are generally case-insensitive for resolution, but the system tables store the full name as a string, and string equality is case-sensitive. Therefore `bronze.orders_raw`, `Bronze.Orders_Raw`, and `BRONZE.ORDERS_RAW` are three distinct strings for a SQL equality check. To avoid missing lineage, use the exact case as created or normalize with `LOWER()` on both sides. (d) When an upstream object such as `silver.orders_quarantine` is dropped, its lineage rows are removed from the system table, so the historical dependency chain is lost. For audit, this is a problem because you can no longer reconstruct which downstream objects were affected by that table, and a compliance review may fail. Lineage history should be exported or retained separately. (e) 3 runs/hour × 2 events/run = 6 raw rows per hour for one edge. In 8 hours, 6 × 8 = 48 raw rows for that single logical edge. If a 3-hop recursive query uses UNION ALL, these duplicates multiply: hop 1 might produce 48 rows for that edge; hop 2 would multiply by the duplicates of the next edge, and hop 3 again, producing thousands of intermediate rows. For example, if each of three hops has 48 duplicate rows, UNION ALL could produce up to $48^3 = 110{,}592$ rows for a single path, whereas UNION would keep 3 rows (one per hop).

Analysis — The method works because lineage systems are append-only event logs with eventual consistency. Each event is a fact about a write, and the same logical edge can generate many facts. Deduplication with DISTINCT collapses the facts into edges. Event lag means that a query immediately after a pipeline run can be stale; best practice is to wait for the lag window or to query by `event_time` with a bounded delay. Case sensitivity is a frequent source of false negatives: two names that look the same to a human can be different strings to the database, so auditing queries should either use exact case or normalize. Dropped objects remove lineage history because the lineage table stores references to object names, and if the object no longer exists, the rows are cleaned up; this is a critical audit gap. This connects to data engineering practice: schema changes and upstream dependencies must be communicated to downstream stakeholders [source p.63], and ingestion pipelines that write objects into storage should have orchestration that records lineage reliably [source p.278]. Enrichment joins can also generate complex lineage that is easy to misread [source p.312]. Always check lineage freshness, deduplicate, normalize case, and preserve history before dropping objects.

actions.text: Now that you understand how the lineage graph is captured and how to read it, let's put that into practice with a fully-worked problem. We'll trace a single metric all the way from a source table up to a dashboard, and then reproduce that same answer in SQL over the lineage system tables.

Here's Problem 1. A monthly revenue dashboard reads from gold.revenue_monthly, which is built from silver.orders_clean, which is built from bronze.orders_raw. Your task is to reconstruct the full upstream chain and name the downstream consumers of bronze.orders_raw.

Before you jump to SQL, take the hint. Walk the directed graph one hop at a time. Each lineage edge connects exactly one source to one target, so a full chain is really just a sequence of single-hop steps stitched together.

The worked solution starts by identifying the dashboard's input object, then follows the upstream edges hop by hop until we reach the raw table. In Catalog Explorer you'd do this visually — open bronze.orders_raw and read the downstream graph to walk forward to the dashboard.

To reproduce the walk in SQL, we query system.access.table_lineage, selecting source_table_full_name and target_table_full_name, and join rows repeatedly until we land on the dashboard object. This is exactly the pattern you'll reuse in Problem 2.

Finally, the analysis. This method works because lineage rows are each one hop, so the whole chain is a recursive join. And watch for the common pitfalls: duplicate rows per event, event lag before lineage even appears, case-sensitive catalog and schema names, and lineage disappearing entirely if an upstream object gets dropped.

That sets up what's next. In Problem 2 we take this exact visualization and reproduce the downstream walk from bronze using a recursive CTE — so pay close attention to how the recursive step mirrors the hop-by-hop traversal we just described.

scenes.title: Audit Logs and System Tables

elements.content: Audit Logs and System Tables
system.access.audit, table_lineage, column_lineage — what they record, how long they are kept, and who can read them
1. system.access.audit — who did what, when, to which securable

Every workspace request that touches a securable is written to system.access.audit with a timestamped event row. The core columns are: event_time, user_identity.email, action_name, request_params, source_ip_address, and response.status_code. Because the table is queried with plain SQL, an auditor can reconstruct the full request context — principal, verb, target object, origin IP, and outcome — without any application-side logging. This is the runtime enforcement counterpart to the GRANT/REVOKE decisions you practised earlier: the grants decide whether a statement succeeds; system.access.audit records that it was attempted [source p.387].
2. Lineage tables — the graph in queryable, timestamped form

system.access.table_lineage and system.access.column_lineage expose exactly the same relationships as the lineage graph in the Unity Catalog UI — source and target tables, source and target columns, the query that produced the edge, and the timestamp of the write. No manual instrumentation is required for supported workloads; lineage is captured at query execution time. Because each edge is a row, you can ask questions the UI cannot answer directly, for example: which downstream tables would be affected if column email of customers changed shape? [source p.63]
3. Retention — a bounded window, not an archive

Audit rows in the system table have a bounded default retention. For long-term compliance, export the relevant partitions to your own governed storage on a schedule before they age out [source p.283].
4. Access — auditing is itself a governed activity

Reading account-level audit data is restricted to privileged users. The access controls on the audit table follow the same least-privilege discipline you applied to data tables: grant to the smallest group that needs it, at the narrowest scope, and revoke when the requirement ends [source p.387].

actions.text: Now that we've traced lineage in the graph, let's look at where those records actually live. Unity Catalog exposes both audit events and lineage as queryable system tables in the system.access schema.

The three you'll be tested on are system.access.audit, system.access.table_lineage, and system.access.column_lineage. They behave just like ordinary Delta tables — you can SELECT, filter, and join them.

Start with system.access.audit. It answers who did what, when, and to which securable. Watch for the key columns: event_time, user_identity.email, action_name, request_params, source_ip_address, and response.status_code.
Remember the scope: every workspace request that touches a securable is recorded here. That's your primary evidence trail for compliance questions.
Second, the lineage tables. table_lineage and column_lineage expose the exact same relationships you just saw in the visual graph — but in a queryable, timestamped form.
So system.access.table_lineage and system.access.column_lineage let you run SQL over what the graph draws — perfect for building your own downstream-impact reports.
Third, and this is a common exam trap: retention. Audit rows in the system table have a bounded default retention window. It is not an archive.
If your compliance requirement extends beyond that window, you must export the data yourself — Databricks will not keep it forever on your behalf.

Finally, access. Auditing is itself a governed activity. Reading account-level audit data is restricted to privileged users only — you cannot simply grant any analyst permission to DELETE the audit trail.

So keep these four properties straight: audit columns, queryable lineage tables, bounded retention, and restricted access. They map directly onto the governance questions in the exam. Coming up next, a checkpoint on exactly these points.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Audit Logs and System Tables

questions.question: A compliance auditor asks your team: 'For the table sales.gold.customers, which notebooks, jobs, or dashboards built this table, and what upstream tables fed into it?' Which audit/system table should you query first?

options.label: system.access.audit
system.access.table_lineage
system.access.column_lineage
system.information_schema.tables

questions.analysis: system.access.table_lineage records the table-level relationships Unity Catalog captures at runtime: which notebooks, jobs, or dashboards read or wrote a given table and which upstream tables fed into it. That directly answers 'what built this table?'. system.access.audit answers 'who read this table?' (who accessed the object and when), not what produced it. system.access.column_lineage answers column-to-column dependency questions, which is a narrower granularity than the question asks. system.information_schema.tables is metadata about table definitions (columns, types, owner), not runtime build provenance. Choosing table_lineage when the question is about access (or vice versa) is one of the classic exam traps: match the governance question to the right table first, then look up columns. Recall from earlier in this unit that Unity Catalog captures lineage automatically at runtime, without manual instrumentation, for supported workloads. [source p.343] illustrates how runtime state changes (deduplication, latest-version selection) are computed by queries against a table, which is exactly the kind of runtime activity that lineage records.

questions.question: You are reviewing the columns of system.access.audit to answer a security investigation. Which of the following columns are representative audit columns, and what does each one answer? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: user_identity / request_params — who performed the action and what exact request was made
event_time — when the audited event occurred
action_name / service_name — which operation was performed and by which Databricks service
retention_days — the guaranteed default retention period for audit history

questions.analysis: system.access.audit is designed to answer 'who did what, when, and how'. Typical representative columns include the identity of the actor (for example user_identity), the request payload or parameters, the event_time of the action, and the action_name / service_name that identify which operation and Databricks service were involved. Option D is a deliberate trap: assuming audit history is retained forever (or that retention is a fixed, guaranteed default) is a misconception — audit retention is configurable and bounded, not infinite by default. Keep in mind the broader engineering habit from the source material of auditing storage behavior directly, for example understanding that update/delete transactions can create new files and retain old files that may need to be vacuumed [source p.304] — the same principle applies to audit tables: you must know the retention and cleanup behavior rather than assume it. Also remember that file-system-like metadata such as permissions and pointers is stored explicitly [source p.226], which reinforces that you should verify where the governance metadata actually lives before relying on it.

questions.question: A data steward asks: 'Which columns in downstream table sales.gold.customer_summary are derived from the column sales.gold.customers.email?' Which system table should you query, and why?

options.label: system.access.audit, because column dependency questions are recorded as audit events
system.access.column_lineage, because it links source columns to downstream columns at column granularity
system.access.table_lineage, because any column question can be answered by looking at table names only
system.information_schema.columns, because it stores the derivation expressions for each column

questions.analysis: The question is about which column depends on which column, which is a column-granularity lineage question, so system.access.column_lineage is the correct choice: it links source columns to downstream columns. system.access.table_lineage is the right table for the coarser question 'what built this table?', but it does not, by itself, answer which specific columns are derived from which other columns. system.access.audit is for access events (who read/wrote what, when), not derivation. system.information_schema.columns stores column metadata (name, data type, nullability, comments) but not the derivation expression. A related engineering caution from the source material is that database transactions can create new files representing new state while retaining old files for failure checkpoint references [source p.304] — this is why you should rely on lineage metadata rather than trying to infer dependencies from physical files or from a single snapshot of how the table currently looks.

scenes.title: Tags, Comments, and Metadata Discovery

elements.content: Tags, Comments, and Metadata Discovery
Governed data becomes discoverable data once assets carry durable, centrally managed metadata — and that metadata is read by policy, not by the privilege system itself.
Governed Tags vs. Informal Workspace Metadata

A governed tag is an asset in the metastore itself: a key-value pair with a defined allowed-value list, an owner, and a scope (catalog, schema, table, or column). It can be searched, audited, and — critically — referenced by an attribute-based policy. Informal metadata (a free-text comment, a notebook markdown note, a dashboard title) is workspace-local, ungoverned, and invisible to policy.

A governed tag differs from an informal note in four preconditions: it lives in the metastore; it has a declared key and permitted values; it is applied by a principal with APPLY TAG; and it survives schema evolution and table replacement.
Comments: Documentation That Makes Analysts Self-Serve

A comment on a catalog, schema, table, or column records meaning and ownership so an analyst can decide whether an asset is the right one without pinging the producing engineer. Comment text is also full-text searchable, so phrases like "customer email, masked for non-PII" become search terms that surface the asset. Edge case: a comment on a column does not inherit down to a renamed column unless the rename preserves the column id.
Worked Example: Two Search Paths, One Answer

Path A (UI): filter tag pii=true, owner = risk_eng, comment contains "email" → returns sales.gold.customers.email. Path B (SQL): SELECT table_catalog, table_schema, table_name, column_name FROM system.information_schema.column_tags WHERE tag_name = 'pii'; — the same asset is returned by both paths, proving tag, owner, and comment are all first-class search dimensions rather than descriptive prose.
Rule of scaling: tagging is metadata, not a privilege

elements.html: tagged objects=500⟹1 policy, 0 duplicate GRANTs of 0−500 re-audits

elements.content: Classification: PII, Sensitivity, and the Durable Anchor

Tags such as pii=true, sensitivity=high, or retention=7y give compliance reviews a stable anchor that survives table renames, clones, and schema evolution. A policy can then say "for every column tagged pii, apply mask_email" without ever naming a column. Because the tag travels with the object and lives in one metastore, a hundred new pipelines that land PII columns are governed on day one.

Exam trap: applying a tag does NOT grant or revoke a privilege. The tag is metadata; access is still enforced by GRANTs and by tag-based policies that themselves attach privileges. Tagging a column pii=true does not by itself mask it — a policy must be bound to that tag.

Sources: governed tags vs. informal notes [source p.268]; meaning and ownership captured in schemas and comments [source p.291]; schema and comment text as the durable anchor for downstream readers [source p.383].

actions.text: So we've covered lineage and audit logs. Now let's talk about the metadata that actually makes data findable: tags, comments, and metadata discovery. This is how governed data becomes discoverable data for the people who need it.

The key distinction is governed tags versus informal workspace metadata. Governed tags are centrally managed in Unity Catalog, they carry policy relevance, and they can be applied at every level: catalogs, schemas, tables, and columns. Informal notes scribbled in a notebook don't have that authority or that reach.

Here's the important framing: a governed tag is itself an asset in the metastore. That means it's queryable, it's filterable, and it's subject to the same governance model as everything else you've seen in Unity Catalog.

Comments are the documentation layer. A comment on a catalog, schema, table, or column records what the data means and who owns it. That's what makes analysts self-serving, because they can understand an asset without pinging the engineer who built it.

Let's walk through a worked example with two search paths that converge on the same answer. Path A is the UI: you filter tag pii equals true, owner is risk_eng, and you get your result set. Path B is a programmatic query against information_schema with the same conditions, and it returns the same objects.

Notice the rule of scaling here: tagging is metadata, not a privilege. A tag is a label that describes the data, it does not control who can read it. This is the exam trap — applying a tag like pii equals true does NOT grant or revoke any privilege. Access is still governed by grants, exactly as we discussed on the access control pages.

That brings us to classification. Tags such as pii equals true, sensitivity equals high, or a retention identifier serve as the durable anchor for compliance reviews and policy decisions. When a regulator asks what sensitive data you hold, the answer is your tag vocabulary, not a spreadsheet somebody maintains on the side.

So to pull this together: governed tags and comments turn governed data into discoverable, classifiable data. You find assets by filtering on tags, owner, and comment text. You classify sensitive data with a consistent tag vocabulary. And you always remember that tags describe, grants authorize. That separation is exactly what the exam expects you to articulate.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Tags, Comments, and Discoverability
