questions.question: A data engineer tags the column `customers.email` with the tag `pii` and governs a tag-based policy on that tag that masks the column. A separate analyst group outside PII has only `SELECT` on the table. Which statement correctly describes WHY the analyst can no longer see the raw email value after the tag-based policy is attached?

options.label: Label

The tag itself has no effect on the query result; the masking happens because a tag-based policy attaches a column mask to every object carrying that tag, and the mask is evaluated at query time for every access path
value
A

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: Tagging is the classification attribute; the policy does the enforcement. ABAC-style tag-based policies attach privileges, row filter functions, and column mask functions to a governable tag, and the policy automatically applies to every object carrying that tag — so the query result is rewritten by the mask function regardless of which SELECT path the analyst uses [source p.343]. The trap in the other options is confusing metadata (the tag) with access control: the tag alone neither grants nor denies anything; the tag alone also does not 'hide' the field — the mask function attached to the policy does that. Option traps also include confusing classification with a GRANT, or with a view rewrite, which are alternative enforcement mechanisms, not the tag itself.

questions.question: Select all statements that correctly distinguish METADATA from ACCESS CONTROL when engineering compliance documentation for a shared `customers` table in Unity Catalog. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A tag is metadata: it records a classification (for example, 'pii' or 'sensitive'), and by itself grants no privilege to any principal.
A comment is documentation: it stores a human-readable description on a catalog, schema, table, or column, and it does not grant or deny SELECT.
A GRANT is access control: it is the mechanism that determines which principals can actually read rows and columns, and it must be re-audited as the estate grows.
Attaching a tag to a column is equivalent to a GRANT because the tag name ('pii') is the same string used in the policy predicate.

correctAnswer: A
B
C
questions.analysis: The exam repeatedly tests the boundary between classification and permission. A tag records a classification attribute; by itself it grants nothing. A comment records documentation; by itself it grants nothing. Only a privilege statement (GRANT) actually permits access, and because GRANTs are per-object they must be repeated and re-audited as the estate grows — the reason tag-based policies scale to thousands of objects while per-object GRANT statements do not [source p.402]. Option D is the classic trap: the fact that a tag NAME and a policy NAME share the token 'pii' does NOT make the tag a permission; the tag is only an attribute the policy selects on.

questions.question: Describe the practical division of labor between (a) tags, (b) comments, and (c) GRANTs / tag-based policies when a compliance officer asks you to 'make the data findable, document its meaning, and classify sensitive columns'. Then state one thing each mechanism CANNOT do on its own.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric with weightings: (1) FINDABILITY — identifies tags as the mechanism that makes objects discoverable, and explains that a well-chosen tag vocabulary (for example `pii`, `domain=finance`) is what enables search across the catalog, not per-object documentation — 20%. (2) DOCUMENTATION — identifies comments as the mechanism that records meaning (schema and column descriptions), and notes that comments do not change access — 20%. (3) CLASSIFICATION AND ENFORCEMENT — distinguishes tag classification (an attribute) from tag-based policy enforcement (attaching privileges, row filters, and column masks to the tag so they apply automatically to every object carrying it) — 25%. (4) LIMITATION STATEMENTS — supplies at least two accurate limitations, e.g. 'a tag does not restrict access by itself' and 'a comment is not a permission, and installing it does not make a column searchable only from the table page' — 20%. (5) CLARITY — uses Databricks/Unity Catalog terminology correctly and answers in complete sentences — 15%. Accept a concrete worked example (e.g. tagging `customers.email` as `pii` and attaching a masking function through a policy) as strengthening proof.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. Tags are the classification metadata layer: they record what an object IS (for example, 'pii', 'sensitive', 'domain=finance') and are what make assets findable and governable across thousands of objects at once. Comments are the documentation metadata layer: they carry descriptions at the catalog, schema, table, and column levels so that humans and downstream consumers understand meaning; comments are not permissions. GRANTs and tag-based policies are the enforcement layer: they determine which principals can read which rows and columns. The reason tag-based policies outscale per-object GRANTs is that the policy is written once against the tag and then applies automatically to every object carrying the tag, whereas a GRANT must be issued per object and re-audited as the estate grows [source p.402]. The key exam trap is assuming a tag restricts access or that a comment is searchable only from the table page: neither is true — a tag alone is metadata, and comments are catalog metadata that the catalog search surface can surface, not a page-local annotation. The reason this matters operationally is that stale or unutilized permissions accumulate silently over time and become a security hole; the fix is monitoring plus an incident response plan, and coupling the two into a dashboard the whole data team can watch [source p.402].

actions.text: Let's put that idea to work. This checkpoint covers how tags, comments, and grants each play a distinct role when you're making data findable, documenting its meaning, and classifying sensitive columns. Take each question on your own and give it your best reasoning — I'll walk through everything with you once you submit.

scenes.title: Comparison: Audit Log, Table Lineage, Column Lineage, Query History

elements.content: Dimension  |  Audit Log (system.access.audit)  |  Table Lineage (system.access.table_lineage)  |  Column Lineage (system.access.column_lineage)

Question it answers
Audit Log (system.access.audit): Audit answers 'who accessed what, when, and with what result' by recording each access event against a securable such as a table, view, or catalog. [source p.204]
Table Lineage (system.access.table_lineage): Table lineage answers 'what object depends on what object' by recording, for each query execution, the source_table_full_name that was read and the target_table_full_name that was written or read downstream. [source p.62]
Column Lineage (system.access.column_lineage): Column lineage answers 'which individual field depends on which individual field' by decomposing each recorded table-to-table edge into the specific source columns and target columns connected by that query. [source p.62]

Granularity (the level of the record)
Audit Log (system.access.audit): Audit is event-to-object granularity: one row per user action against one securable, so a single SELECT touching five tables produces five auditable access events.
Table Lineage (system.access.table_lineage): Table lineage is object-to-object granularity: one row per (source table, target table) pair per query, so it cannot tell you which field moved the data. [source p.62]
Column Lineage (system.access.column_lineage): Column lineage is field-to-field granularity: one row per (source column, target column) pair per query, which is the only level at which you can answer 'what breaks if I rename this one column?'.

Time semantics
Audit Log (system.access.audit): Audit is strictly event-time semantics: event_time records the instant the access occurred, so the table is an immutable chronology of discrete actions.
Table Lineage (system.access.table_lineage): Table lineage is execution-time semantics: an edge is emitted when a query runs, and the edge persists as a statement about the relationship 'this query read that and wrote this' rather than about the moment a user looked at data. [source p.204]
Column Lineage (system.access.column_lineage): Column lineage inherits the same execution-time semantics as table lineage because it is derived from the same recorded query, so it appears only for query paths that Unity Catalog actually observed.

What it does NOT capture
Audit Log (system.access.audit): Audit does not tell you the relationship between objects, so it cannot answer impact analysis questions such as 'what breaks if I drop this table?' even though it shows every read of that table.
Table Lineage (system.access.table_lineage): Table lineage does not record permissions, grants, or denial outcomes, so a successful edge in table_lineage is not evidence that a user was authorized to read the source. [source p.63]
Column Lineage (system.access.column_lineage): Column lineage does not capture reads performed by external clients or non-Databricks engines, so lineage is deliberately incomplete for out-of-platform consumers. [source p.63]

Who can read it (governance precondition)
Audit Log (system.access.audit): Audit is readable by principals granted SELECT on system.access.audit, and because it contains user_identity.email and source_ip_address, access should be restricted to a compliance or security group under least privilege.
Table Lineage (system.access.table_lineage): Table lineage is readable by principals granted SELECT on system.access.table_lineage, and in practice this is granted more broadly because the table contains object names rather than user identities. [source p.64]
Column Lineage (system.access.column_lineage): Column lineage is readable by principals granted SELECT on system.access.column_lineage, and the same schema/column names that make it useful for impact analysis also make it sensitive metadata that should be scoped to data stewards.

Typical compliance use
Audit Log (system.access.audit): Audit supports evidence requests such as 'prove that only the PII group read customers.email in Q3', which is answered by filtering on action_name and then on request_params for the specific table and column. [source p.204]
Table Lineage (system.access.table_lineage): Table lineage supports change-management evidence such as 'list every dashboard, job, and model that consumes orders_raw before we migrate it', which is answered by walking downstream edges from the source table.
Column Lineage (system.access.column_lineage): Column lineage supports privacy-scoping evidence such as 'prove that masked_email never flows into the marketing export', which is answered by filtering source columns and confirming no downstream column edge exists.

Worked example on a medallion pipeline
Audit Log (system.access.audit): Audit example: if analyst alice@corp.com runs a SELECT on gold.revenue_monthly at 14:02:11Z, audit records one row with event_time = 14:02:11Z, user_identity.email = alice@corp.com, action_name = 'commandSubmit' or the equivalent read action, and response.status_code = 200. [source p.204]
Table Lineage (system.access.table_lineage): Table lineage example: if the job that builds gold.revenue_monthly reads silver.orders_clean and writes gold.revenue_monthly, table_lineage gains the edge source_table_full_name = 'silver.orders_clean' -> target_table_full_name = 'gold.revenue_monthly'; reproducing the full chain bronze.orders_raw -> silver.orders_clean -> gold.revenue_monthly -> dashboard requires joining these edges transitively. [source p.62]
Column Lineage (system.access.column_lineage): Column lineage example: the same job that maps silver.orders_clean.order_total into gold.revenue_monthly.revenue adds the field edge order_total -> revenue, so renaming silver.orders_clean.order_total is provably breaking for exactly one downstream column and for every consumer of that column. [source p.62]

Decision rule for exam question stems
Audit Log (system.access.audit): If the stem contains 'who', 'which user', 'when', 'from which IP', or 'was the read denied', the source is the audit log. [source p.204]
Table Lineage (system.access.table_lineage): If the stem contains 'what depends on', 'what breaks if I drop/rename', 'upstream', or 'downstream' at the object level, the source is table lineage. [source p.62]
Column Lineage (system.access.column_lineage): If the stem names a single column and asks which other columns or which downstream fields are affected, the source is column lineage. [source p.62]

Takeaway — Prefer the audit log when the governing question is about principals and access events, because it is the only one of the three that records user_identity.email, action_name, and response.status_code. [source p.204]

Takeaway — Prefer table lineage when the governing question is object-to-object impact, because it is the only source that records source_table_full_name and target_table_full_name edges suitable for transitive walking. [source p.62]

Takeaway — Prefer column lineage when the governing question is field-to-field impact such as a rename or a PII flow trace, because only field-level edges can prove or disprove a single-column dependency. [source p.62]

Takeaway — Never substitute lineage for audit: a successful lineage edge is a statement about object relationships, not about authorization, and lineage is not captured for every external reader, so an absence of a lineage edge is not proof that no one accessed the data. [source p.63]

actions.text: Now we arrive at the table that students most often get wrong on the exam. We have four governance data sources here — the audit log, table lineage, column lineage, and query history — and they are not interchangeable. Let's read this dimension by dimension, starting with the question it answers.

This is the decisive row. The audit log, system.access.audit, answers 'who accessed what, and when'. Table and column lineage answer a completely different question — 'what depends on what'. Those are different questions, so they resolve to different tables. If the question stem is about access or a suspicious read, that is audit. If it is about impact or dependency, that is lineage.

Next, the granularity ladder. Table lineage is object-to-object — this table feeds that table. Column lineage is field-to-field — this column feeds that column. Audit is event-to-object — a discrete action, performed by a principal, against a securable object. Notice how the grain gets finer as we move down that list, and that the finest grain does not come from lineage at all.

Time semantics matter too. An audit event is a point in time — it happened at a timestamp and it never changes. Lineage, by contrast, is an evolving graph; it reflects the current state of dependencies, not a historical record of who did what. So never treat lineage as a substitute for an audit trail.

And the row that catches people out: what each source does *not* capture. Recall from the previous page that lineage does not record who read the data — a suspicious SELECT that exfiltrates rows will leave no lineage trace at all, only a system.access.audit entry. Keep that asymmetry in your head; it is a favourite exam trap.

There is also a governance precondition. All these system tables live in Unity Catalog, so reading them requires the right privilege on the system schema — usually granted to account admins or a dedicated audit role. Being able to see lineage in Catalog Explorer does not mean you can query the audit log; those are separately governed surfaces.

Let's ground this with the medallion pipeline example. Suppose a regulator asks which pipelines consumed the customers table. That is an impact question — table lineage, downstream direction. Now suppose they ask who exported the PII column last quarter. That is an access question — the audit log, filtered by object and time. Same table, two different sources, because they are two different questions.

So here is your decision rule for the exam. Step one: read the stem and name the question in one phrase. Step two: map that phrase — 'who accessed what' goes to the audit log; 'what depends on what' goes to lineage. Step three: only then choose the source. If you pick the table before you have named the question, you will be pulled toward the more familiar option.

Two takeaway cards to bank. Prefer the audit log when the governing requirement is accountability — who did it, when, from where, and did it succeed. That is the security and compliance framing, and it is event-based by nature.

And prefer column lineage when the requirement is precision — tracing a single sensitive field through a chain of transformations, or proving which downstream column is polluted by an upstream change. Column lineage is what lets you answer at field level instead of object level.

One bright line: never substitute lineage for audit. If someone read a table without writing it, there is no lineage edge to show it — full stop. Audit logs prove access; lineage proves dependency. Bring those two sentences to the exam and to work, and this whole table collapses into a single reflex.

scenes.title: Trade-offs: Designing a Compliance Auditing and Metadata Strategy

elements.content: Decision — A financial services firm runs its analytics estate on Databricks with Unity Catalog. External auditors have certified that the firm must retain twelve months of access history for every sensitive securable, and internal analysts must be able to discover sensitive tables quickly for data-masking and least-privilege reviews. The built-in Unity Catalog system tables for audit and lineage are the only source of access history today, but their default retention window is far shorter than twelve months. The platform budget is fixed, so any added capability must be cheap to operate and must not create an ungoverned data copy outside Unity Catalog. The hard part is that the requirement has two independent halves — retention and discoverability — and the tempting single-tool answers each satisfy only one half, so the team must decide whether to accept a requirement violation, pay for a duplicate pipeline, or compose a hybrid.

Constraints — Regulators require twelve consecutive months of access history, with no gaps longer than one day, and no requirement that the history be queryable in under a second.  •  The built-in audit system table retains only a bounded default window that is shorter than twelve months, and that window cannot be extended by configuration alone.  •  The platform budget for this workstream is limited, so any added storage and orchestration cost must be small relative to the value of the data being retained.  •  The exported history must remain governed inside Unity Catalog; an ungoverned copy of audit data in a plain storage bucket is not acceptable.  •  Analysts must be able to find sensitive tables quickly, which requires a queryable, human-curated metadata surface inside the catalog.

Rely only on the built-in audit system tables
+ Zero new infrastructure, zero new orchestration, and zero added storage cost, because the tables are already maintained by the platform.; + It is the primary query surface for recent access questions such as 'who read this table yesterday?' and requires no ingestion latency.; + It composes cleanly with lineage: system.access.table_lineage and system.access.column_lineage expose the same relationships as the visual graph in queryable, timestamped form [source p.306].
− It cannot satisfy the twelve-month requirement at all, because the built-in audit window is bounded and shorter than the retention period, and history simply ages out of the system table.; − There is no rebuild path once records expire; the data is gone, so an audit failure cannot be remediated retroactively.; − It adds no discoverability: a system table of raw events does not tell an analyst which columns are sensitive today without a separate curated surface.
Best for: Short-horizon operational debugging where the retention requirement is genuinely shorter than the system default and no external auditor is involved.

Scheduled governed export of audit and lineage system tables to cloud storage
+ It directly closes the retention gap: an incremental scheduled job reads new rows from system.access.audit and the lineage tables and writes them to governed storage, so the union of exported history and live system tables covers twelve continuous months.; + It preserves the primary query surface: recent questions are still answered from the live system table, and only historical questions fall through to the export, so day-to-day latency is unchanged.; + It can reduce long-run storage cost by parking older history in a colder storage class, since the access pattern for an export is rare reads and the classic trade-off is cheaper storage in exchange for higher retrieval cost [source p.236].
− It introduces a new governed asset, a new orchestration schedule, and a new failure mode: a missed or failed run creates a permanent retention gap that cannot be backfilled from the system table.; − It adds incremental storage and orchestration cost, which must be justified against the budget even if the volume of audit rows is small.; − It has an ingestion latency between the live system table and the export, so the export is authoritative for history but not for the last few minutes of activity.
Best for: Compliance retention where the requirement is retention length and completeness, not sub-second freshness.

Manually curated metadata catalog of tags and comments
+ It is the strongest option for discoverability: governed tags on sensitive columns are searchable in Catalog Explorer and are exactly what tag-based policies consume, so a single tag drives masking and row filters without repeating per-object GRANT statements.; + It is cheap in infrastructure terms, since it adds no new pipeline and no new storage.; + It produces human-readable classifications that analysts can act on immediately, which raw audit events cannot provide.
− It captures no access history whatsoever, so it fails the twelve-month requirement completely and by design.; − It is a curation task, not a measurement: tags are asserted by people, so they drift from reality as schemas evolve and can silently miss a newly sensitive column.; − It cannot reconstruct who read a table on a given date, which is precisely the question an auditor asks.
Best for: Discoverability and policy targeting, where access history is sourced from somewhere else.

Hybrid: keep system tables as the primary query surface, add a scheduled governed export for long-term retention, and layer governed tags on sensitive columns
+ It satisfies both halves of the requirement simultaneously: the export covers the twelve-month audit history, and the governed tags make sensitive tables findable and policy-targetable inside the catalog.; + It keeps cost bounded by reusing existing capability rather than replacing it: the live system tables remain the primary surface for recent queries, and only the historical tail is exported [source p.306].; + It reinforces the layered design already taught in this unit: ABAC policies read the tags, the audit export records who actually touched the tagged objects, and lineage system tables record what was built from them.
− It has the highest operational complexity of the four options, because it runs a scheduled export, maintains a tag taxonomy, and must keep both in sync with schema change.; − It requires disciplined governance of the export itself: the export location is a new securable that must be granted narrowly, or the audit history becomes over-exposed.; − Two mechanisms mean two failure modes, and a silent tag drift or a missed export run each violate a different half of the requirement.
Best for: A regulated environment where both retention and discoverability are hard requirements and neither single tool covers both.

Recommendation: Hybrid: keep system tables as the primary query surface, add a scheduled governed export for long-term retention, and layer governed tags on sensitive columns — The binding constraints are the twelve-month retention rule and the fixed budget, and the two failure modes of the single-tool options are what decide this. Relying only on the built-in system tables fails outright, because the audit window is bounded and shorter than twelve months and expired rows cannot be recovered. The curated catalog alone also fails, because tags are asserted by people and record no access events, so it cannot answer 'who read this table in March?' no matter how good the taxonomy is. Only the hybrid satisfies both halves: a scheduled export of system.access.audit and the lineage system tables extends history to twelve months, and governed tags on sensitive columns make those objects discoverable and directly usable by tag-based policies for masking and least-privilege enforcement. On cost, the export does not duplicate the whole system: the live tables stay the primary surface for recent questions and only the historical tail is written to colder governed storage, which is the standard pattern of trading cheaper storage for higher retrieval cost on rarely read data [source p.236]. The remaining risk is operational, so the design must treat the export as a pipeline with freshness and completeness checks — and those checks are themselves lineage and audit questions answerable with the same system tables, which is why the three-layer design is preferable to any single mechanism.

actions.text: We just covered the difference between audit logs and lineage — those two signals tell you who touched the data and what depends on it. Now let's put them to work in a realistic design decision: a compliance auditing and metadata strategy under constraints.

Here's the scenario. A financial services firm runs analytics on Unity Catalog, and it needs to satisfy two things at once: a one-year audit retention requirement and fast discoverability of sensitive tables. That dual requirement is what we're designing for.

Now the constraints. Regulators require twelve consecutive months of access history. But the built-in audit system table retains a much shorter default window — so relying on it alone cannot meet the retention bar. On top of that, the platform budget is limited, so any solution has to justify its cost. And analysts must be able to find sensitive tables quickly. Notice how these constraints pull in different directions.

Option A is to rely only on the built-in audit system tables with zero extra spend. It's the simplest and the cheapest — no new assets to govern. But it fails the twelve-month retention requirement outright, so it's a non-starter for compliance.

Option B is a scheduled, governed export of the audit and lineage system tables into cloud storage. This meets retention — the history lives as long as you keep exporting. The trade-off is real: you add storage and orchestration cost, and that export becomes a new data asset that itself must be governed.

Option C is a manually curated metadata catalog — tags and comments only. It's excellent for discoverability, but here's the trap: it captures no access history at all, so it does nothing for the audit requirement.

That leads to the hybrid. Keep the system tables as the primary query surface for recent, hot access data, add a scheduled governed export to satisfy long-term retention, and layer governed tags on sensitive columns so analysts can find them fast.

So the recommendation is exactly that hybrid — and the key exam skill is the justification. Each requirement maps to one piece: retention to the export, query performance to the system tables, discoverability to the tags. You defend the added cost by showing that no single option satisfies all the stated constraints. When you see a design trade-off question, name the constraints first, then show which option breaks which one.

scenes.title: Lesson Exam: Lineage, Auditing, and Metadata

questions.question: A compliance officer asks: 'On what date did a specific human analyst query the gold.revenue_monthly table, and from what IP address did that query originate?' You have both Unity Catalog lineage and the audit system table available. Which source should you query first, and why does the other source fail to answer the question?

options.label: Query system.access.table_lineage, because lineage records the identity of every principal who executed a query against a table.

Query system.access.audit, because it records event_time, user_identity.email, source_ip_address, and action_name — the who, when, and from-where of access — whereas lineage records data dependency relationships, not access events.
Query system.access.column_lineage, because column-level records include the requesting user's email as a mandatory field for each downstream column.
Query either table, since lineage and audit are two names for the same underlying event store and differ only in their display format in Catalog Explorer.

questions.analysis: The question is an access/accountability question — 'who, when, from where' — which is the domain of the audit log. system.access.audit carries event_time, user_identity.email, action_name, request_params, source_ip_address, and response.status_code, so it can answer precisely this class of question. Lineage, by contrast, describes the recording of an audit trail of data through its lifecycle, tracking the systems that process the data and the upstream data it depends on — it answers 'what built this table' and 'what depends on this column', not 'which principal executed a read at this timestamp' [source p.83]. Option A is the classic exam trap of treating lineage as an access record; lineage has no obligation to record the querying principal per read event. Option C invents a field that column_lineage does not guarantee. Option D collapses two distinct system tables into one, which is exactly the misconception the checkpoint on audit logs warns about. The correctness of B also rests on the fact that the system table is queryable, timestamped metadata, not a mere visualization.

questions.question: A data scientist wants to rename the column customer_zip in silver.orders_clean. Before approving the change, the platform team must identify every downstream object that would break. Which of the following statements about using lineage for this impact analysis are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Switching to column-level lineage in the Catalog Explorer graph shows exactly which downstream columns depend on customer_zip, which is more precise than table-level lineage for a single-column rename.
The same column dependency relationships can be reproduced programmatically by querying system.access.column_lineage, which is preferable when the check must be repeatable in CI.
Because Unity Catalog captures lineage automatically for supported query paths, the downstream graph will also list every analyst who opened the affected dashboard in the last 30 days.
Lineage captured for the rename will include reads performed by external clients and non-Databricks engines that query the table directly, so the impact list is guaranteed complete.

questions.analysis: Column-level lineage exists precisely to answer 'which downstream columns depend on this single source column', so A is correct; the Catalog Explorer graph is the design-time visual tool for this. B is correct because the column_lineage system table exposes the same relationships in queryable, timestamped form, which is the right choice for repeatable, programmatic checks — the lesson's rule of thumb is that the graph is best for visual exploration and system tables are best for programmatic, repeatable checks. C is wrong twice over: lineage is not an access record (it does not list who opened a dashboard), and it records data dependency, not user behavior. D states the opposite of the documented limitation: lineage is captured automatically at runtime for supported workloads, but reads by external clients or non-Databricks engines are not captured. This is why the textbook asks engineers to implement strategies to respond to schema changes automatically and to communicate changes to downstream stakeholders even when automation can accommodate them — automation does not eliminate the need to inform impacted consumers [source p.269].

questions.question: A junior engineer proposes to store a 'PII' marker on a column by writing it into the column comment, and separately to grant SELECT on the table to a new group. A reviewer objects that these are categorically different operations. Which statement best explains the distinction as Unity Catalog models it?

options.label: Comments and tags are both metadata — descriptive attributes about the data — while a GRANT is a privilege, which is an enforceable authorization that controls whether a principal can act on the securable; metadata describes, privileges permit.
Comments are privileges and tags are metadata, so tagging a column can be used as a substitute for a GRANT because tags are enforced at query time.
Tags are enforced access controls just like privileges, so applying a governed tag to a column is sufficient to hide that column from a group without issuing any GRANT or row/column policy.
Privileges and metadata are the same category in Unity Catalog; both live in the same catalog as attributes and both are enforced during query planning.

questions.analysis: Unity Catalog separates descriptive metadata from authorization. Governed tags are centrally managed, policy-relevant labels applied to catalogs, schemas, tables, and columns; comments document meaning for humans and tooling. Neither, by itself, denies or permits an action. Privileges are the enforceable authorization mechanism, and a GRANT is what actually determines whether a principal can read or write a securable. Option B is a category error that inverts the two. Option C is the most seductive trap: a tag may participate in a policy, but a bare tag is not an enforcement edge — enforcement comes from the privilege model and the policy that consumes the tag. Option D collapses distinct concepts and would imply that commenting a table changes who can query it, which is false. This distinction matters operationally: metadata answers 'what does this column mean and is it sensitive', while privileges answer 'who is allowed to touch it' — and those are the two questions the lesson requires you to keep separate.

questions.question: A monthly revenue dashboard reads gold.revenue_monthly, which is built from silver.orders_clean, which is built from bronze.orders_raw. An external BI tool (not a Databricks engine) also reads bronze.orders_raw directly. A regulator asks two questions: (1) 'What upstream sources feed this dashboard?' and (2) 'Who read bronze.orders_raw last quarter?' Explain which Unity Catalog mechanism answers each question, how you would walk the chain for question 1 both visually and in SQL, and why the external BI tool is a specific limitation you must disclose for question 1. Address retention explicitly for question 2.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Correctly assigns question 1 to lineage (table-level for the chain, column-level if a specific column's dependents are required) and question 2 to the audit system table — distinguishes 'what built this' from 'who read this' (30%). (2) Provides the visual walk: open bronze.orders_raw in Catalog Explorer and follow the downstream lineage graph forward to the dashboard object; and the SQL walk: iteratively query system.access.table_lineage joining source_table_full_name to target_table_full_name until the dashboard is reached (25%). (3) Explicitly names the limitation that lineage is captured automatically only for supported query paths, so reads by external clients or non-Databricks engines are not captured, meaning the impact chain for the external BI tool may be incomplete and must be disclosed (20%). (4) States that audit records in the system table have a bounded default retention window, so a 'last quarter' query depends on the window still covering that period and long-term compliance requires an export strategy (15%). (5) Clarity and use of correct Databricks terminology (10%).
questions.analysis: Question 1 is a provenance question and belongs to lineage: data lineage describes the recording of an audit trail of data through its lifecycle, tracking both the systems that process the data and the upstream data it depends on [source p.83]. Visually, open bronze.orders_raw in Catalog Explorer and read the downstream lineage graph, walking forward bronze.orders_raw to silver.orders_clean to gold.revenue_monthly to the dashboard; for a single column, switch to column-level lineage. Programmatically, do the same hop-by-hop walk with system.access.table_lineage, joining source_table_full_name to target_table_full_name until the dashboard object is reached. Question 2 is an access question and belongs to system.access.audit, which records who did what, when, and to which securable via event_time, user_identity.email, action_name, and source_ip_address. The critical limitation to disclose: Unity Catalog captures lineage automatically at runtime for supported workloads, but reads by external clients or non-Databricks engines are not captured, so the external BI tool's direct read of bronze.orders_raw may not appear in the graph — the impact list is therefore not guaranteed complete, and engineers must still communicate schema changes to downstream stakeholders rather than assuming automation covers everyone [source p.269]. Retention: audit records in the system table have a bounded default retention window and are not kept forever by default; answering a 'last quarter' question is only possible if that window still covers the period, and durable compliance requires exporting audit data to your own long-term store. Finally, schema changes at the source are a realistic hazard here: external sources may change their schema, so a rename or drop upstream of the dashboard can break it even while automation accommodates the change technically [source p.344].

actions.text: Time to pull this unit together. This one is an exam-style set over everything we just covered on lineage, auditing, and metadata — so expect scenario questions that ask you to pick the right mechanism for a stated business question, reason about column-level impact, and separate the ideas of metadata from enforceable privileges.

Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer before moving on — the distractors here are modelled on the traps that show up on the real certification exam, so a quick guess won't teach you much. Once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning with you, especially where those traps were hiding.

scenes.title: Storage Credentials: Delegating Cloud Storage Access

elements.content: Storage Credentials: Delegating Cloud Storage Access

Definition. A storage credential is a Unity Catalog securable that encapsulates exactly one cloud identity — an AWS IAM role, an Azure managed identity (delivered through an access connector), or a GCP service account. Unity Catalog assumes that identity to read and write cloud storage on a user's behalf.

Precondition: the identity must already exist in the cloud account and carry a trust relationship back to the Databricks account before the credential can be created.
How the Delegation Model Works

1. Unity Catalog assumes the cloud identity at query time using a trust relationship — an external ID established for AWS, an access connector for Azure, or service-account impersonation for GCP — rather than a stored secret.

2. Because access is delegated, no long-lived cloud keys live in notebooks, cluster Spark configs, or application code. A remote connection elsewhere in the stack may still require correct credentials and privileges [source p.383] — the storage credential removes that burden for governed paths.

3. Granting an administrator blanket cloud access is an antipattern; the principle of least privilege says grant only what the task needs, and revoke it when the task ends [source p.398]. A storage credential is that principle applied to data access.
Required Privilege: CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL
Held on the metastore, typically by metastore admins only.
What It Does NOT Do

Binds no path. Grants no end-user access.

Answers only: which cloud identity?
Worked example: silver.orders_clean reads s3://acme-lake/orders/ through a storage credential that wraps IAM role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/acme-uc-storage.

actions.text: Next, we move into a topic that sits right at the boundary between Unity Catalog and the cloud itself: storage credentials. We just finished working through lineage, auditing, and metadata, so the natural next question is — when Unity Catalog reads a file out of cloud storage on your behalf, what cloud identity is it actually using? That's exactly what a storage credential answers.

Here's the definition. A storage credential is a Unity Catalog securable that encapsulates a cloud identity — an AWS IAM role, an Azure managed identity delivered through an access connector, or a GCP service account. Unity Catalog uses that identity to read and write cloud storage on the user's behalf. Remember the word securable — it means the credential is itself an object under Unity Catalog governance, so it can be granted, revoked, and audited just like a catalog or a table.
So how does the delegation model actually work? Follow the numbered steps on the slide.

Step one: at query time, Unity Catalog assumes the cloud identity through a trust relationship — an external ID for AWS, an access connector for Azure. Step two: the critical payoff — no long-lived cloud keys are ever stored in notebooks, in cluster Spark configs, or in code. That's the whole point of the delegation model. Your users never hold the keys; Unity Catalog holds them and hands out access on a per-request basis. This is a very common exam theme, so notice the phrasing: the credential is assumed at query time, not baked into the cluster.

Now, who's allowed to create one of these? Creating a storage credential requires the privilege CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL on the metastore. It's held on the metastore and typically granted only to metastore admins. That makes sense — a storage credential is effectively a set of cloud keys, so you don't want it in everyone's hands. If you see an exam question about who can create a storage credential, look for metastore admin or the metastore-level privilege.

Equally important is what the storage credential does NOT do. It binds no path — it doesn't say anything about which folder or bucket on the cloud it applies to. It grants no end-user access — it doesn't give a single user permission to read anything. It answers only one narrow question: which cloud identity may be used. Path binding is a separate job that we'll cover on the next page when we introduce external locations, and end-user access comes from grants on those objects, not from the credential itself.

Finally, keep this worked example in mind: a query that reads silver.orders_clean from s3://acme-lake/... actually needs three distinct things stacked together — the storage credential that supplies the cloud identity, and then the external location and grants that bind a path and authorize the user. The credential is only the bottom layer of that stack. If you can trace that three-layer chain from S3 path all the way up to a running query, you've understood the core of the storage governance lesson, and you're set up well for external locations on the next page.

scenes.title: External Locations: Binding Cloud Paths to Credentials

elements.content: External Locations: Binding Cloud Paths to Credentials
What an External Location Is

• Definition: a Unity Catalog securable object that pairs one cloud storage path with exactly one storage credential.

• Precondition: the storage credential must already exist in the metastore; the location merely binds it to a path.

• Example path: s3://acme-lake/raw/events
Path-Based Governance
READ FILES · WRITE FILES · CREATE TABLE

• Privileges are granted on the location, creating the path-level boundary.

• External tables and volumes created under that path then operate under the location's authority.

[source p.351] External data locations are defined at table creation with the file format, but data is not yet ingested.

[source p.233] Object stores are the gold standard of storage for data lakes, serving large batch reads and writes.

[source p.249] Zero-copy semantics mean engineers must understand the limits of shallow copying across object storage.

actions.text: Let's build directly on storage credentials and talk about external locations, the object that actually binds a cloud path to a credential.

So what exactly is an external location? Think of a storage credential as the identity that says "I'm allowed to talk to this bucket." An external location takes that identity and pins it to a specific path.

Formally, an external location is a Unity Catalog securable object that pairs a cloud storage path — for example s3://acme-lake/raw/events — with exactly one storage credential. That pairing is the whole point: path plus identity becomes a single governable object.

Now here's why that matters — path-based governance. Privileges are granted on the location itself, not on the underlying bucket. So you grant privileges at the Unity Catalog layer while the cloud path stays the boundary.

The three privileges you'll see on an external location are READ FILES, WRITE FILES, and CREATE TABLE. Any external table or volume later created under that path then operates under the location's authority — the location is the gatekeeper.

Watch the binding rules closely, because these show up on the exam. One storage credential may back many external locations, but each location references exactly one credential. And a location path must not overlap the metastore's managed location, nor nest inside another external location.

Here's the binding chain from the source: an analyst receives a GRANT of READ FILES on the external location, which resolves to the storage credential, which assumes the cloud IAM role, which finally reaches the bucket prefix. Notice how the privilege never touches the cloud path directly — Unity Catalog mediates every step. Keep that chain in mind as we move into the checkpoint.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Credentials and External Locations

questions.question: In Unity Catalog, you are defining governed access to files sitting in an Amazon S3 bucket. Which object holds the cloud identity (the IAM role or equivalent principal) used to authenticate to that cloud storage, as opposed to the object that binds a specific cloud path to a governed name?

options.label: The storage credential holds the cloud identity (the IAM role / principal); the external location holds the path binding to the cloud storage URL.
The external location holds the cloud identity (the IAM role / principal); the storage credential holds the path binding to the cloud storage URL.
Both the storage credential and the external location each embed a copy of the cloud identity, so either can authenticate to the bucket independently.
Neither object holds the cloud identity; the cloud identity is always supplied at query time by the user's interactive notebook session.

questions.analysis: A storage credential is the Unity Catalog securable whose job is to hold the cloud identity — for example, an AWS IAM role that Databricks assumes, or the equivalent managed identity on Azure/GCP — so that Databricks can authenticate to the cloud account. An external location is the securable whose job is to bind a specific cloud storage path (for example s3://my-bucket/landing/) to a governed name that can be granted on. Keeping these concerns separate is what allows one credential to back many paths while each path stays an independently securable object. Option B inverts the two roles, which is the classic exam trap. Option C is wrong: the identity lives in the credential, and duplicating it in the location would defeat the separation of concerns. Option D is wrong because authentication is not delegated to the user's notebook session; the credential is a first-class governed object precisely so that end users never need raw cloud keys. This separation mirrors the general cloud pattern in which an object store is a key-value store for immutable objects and must be authenticated to before any path can be read [source p.232], and remote connections to such stores typically require the correct credentials and privileges before data access is possible [source p.383].

questions.question: A platform team is onboarding a new S3 bucket into Unity Catalog. Select ALL statements that are true about the privileges required for the two setup operations and about what the resulting objects do (or do not do).

options.label: Creating the storage credential requires the CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL privilege on the metastore.
Creating the external location requires the CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION privilege on the metastore, plus the privilege to use the referenced storage credential.
A storage credential by itself grants a user the ability to read the data files in the bucket, because possession of the cloud identity is equivalent to data access.
A single external location may reference several different storage credentials simultaneously so that different teams authenticate with their own cloud identity against the same path.

questions.analysis: Options A and B are correct. The two operations are separate privileges on the metastore: CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL authorizes the creation of the credential object that encapsulates the cloud identity, and CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION authorizes the creation of the path-bound location object; the location creation also requires the ability to reference the credential it will use. Option C is a real student misconception and is false: the credential is an authentication artifact, not an authorization grant. A user can hold a valid storage credential and still be denied data because they lack a grant on the external location, catalog, schema, or table. This is exactly why Databricks ships two objects instead of one — authentication (can we talk to the cloud account?) and authorization (may this principal read this path?) are distinct questions. Option D is also false: an external location binds one cloud path to one credential, so the relationship is one credential per location, not many. That is the mirror-image trap of the previous misconception, in which learners over-correct and assume credentials are interchangeable. The underlying cloud reality is that object stores such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, and Google Cloud Storage sit beneath cloud data lakes, and a remote connection to such storage typically requires the correct credentials and privileges to establish the connection [source p.383][source p.232].

questions.question: A junior engineer claims: 'Once I create the storage credential for our S3 bucket, analysts can immediately query the Parquet files in that bucket through Unity Catalog — the credential covers it.' Which response best diagnoses the error and states the correct minimum path to governed access?

options.label: The engineer is right that the credential covers access, but they also need to restart the cluster before the credential takes effect.

The credential only establishes authentication to the cloud account, not authorization to the path or table; the engineer must also create an external location bound to the bucket path and grant the analysts the appropriate privileges on that location (and on the catalog/schema/table).
The credential is irrelevant here; the engineer just needs to grant SELECT on the bucket URL directly, since Unity Catalog treats URLs as securable objects.
The engineer should instead move the files into the lakehouse managed storage, because external locations cannot be granted to non-admin users at all.

questions.analysis: This question tests the core mental model: authentication is not authorization. The storage credential answers 'can Databricks prove it is allowed to talk to this cloud account?', while the external location answers 'which cloud path is this, as a governed object?' and grants answer 'which principals may read it?'. Option B restates that chain correctly. Option A is a fabricated operational detail: there is no cluster restart step that converts a credential into data access. Option C is wrong because Unity Catalog models the path through an external location, not by granting on a raw URL string. Option D is wrong because external locations can absolutely be granted to ordinary users; in fact, that is their primary purpose. The wider context is that object storage is increasingly the storage layer for cloud data warehouses and data lakes, and retrieval from such stores is normally governed by credentials and access policies rather than by moving the bytes around [source p.126][source p.232]. A common remedy at scale is not migration but lifecycle policy: for instance, if data is accessed only once a month, move it to an infrequent-access tier rather than hoarding it, which keeps cost down without changing the governed access path [source p.251].

actions.text: Time for a checkpoint on credentials and external locations. Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer before you move on — that's what makes the review useful afterward.
I'll walk through the reasoning and clear up anything that tripped you once you've submitted.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Grant Read-Only Access to an External Bucket Prefix

elements.content: Problem 1

You are the metastore admin for the Databricks account 123456789012, which uses Unity Catalog. Curated Parquet data for the events pipeline lands at s3://acme-lake/raw/events (1.8 TB across 12,480 Parquet files). The bucket acme-lake as a whole holds 9.7 TB across 67,300 objects, and the metastore's managed location is the separate prefix s3://acme-lake/managed (2.4 TB). The IAM role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-role already exists; its trust policy already allows the Databricks control plane to assume it, and its permission policy allows s3:GetObject, s3:ListBucket and s3:GetBucketLocation on arn:aws:s3:::acme-lake and arn:aws:s3:::acme-lake/*. The account-level group analysts (17 users) must be able to read every file under that prefix through Unity Catalog, but must never be able to write, delete, or drop that data. Write the four DDL/DCL statements that implement this, name the privilege required to execute each statement, quantify how much of the bucket the grant exposes, and state the verification commands.
Hint: Model the request as three independent decisions — identity, path, then principal — and write one statement per decision.

Worked solution
Step 0 — quantify the blast radius before granting anything.

Bucket size B = 9.7 TB = 9.7×10^12 bytes. Prefix size P = 1.8 TB = 1.8×10^12 bytes. Files F = 12,480. Bucket objects O = 67,300.

Exposure by bytes: P/B = 1.8/9.7 = 0.18557, i.e. 18.6% of the bucket.

Exposure by object count: F/O = 12,480/67,300 = 0.18544, i.e. 18.5%.

The two measures agree to within 0.1 percentage point, which is the numeric evidence that raw/events is a coherent, well-bounded subset of the bucket rather than an arbitrary slice of it.

Step 1 — create the storage credential (the identity leg).

Executed by a metastore admin who holds CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL on the metastore:

CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL acme_cred

WITH AWS_IAM_ROLE 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-role'

COMMENT 'Read-only identity for the curated acme-lake bucket';

Unity Catalog does not copy any secret here: it records the role ARN and later asks the cloud provider to mint short-lived, session-scoped credentials by assuming that role. The IAM permission policy on the role is therefore still the outer bound of everything UC can ever do at this path.

Step 2 — create the external location (the path leg).

This statement requires CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on the metastore and CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on the storage credential acme_cred itself (a two-object privilege check, because creating a location both consumes a privilege on the parent object and delegates the credential):

CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events

URL 's3://acme-lake/raw/events'

WITH (STORAGE CREDENTIAL acme_cred)

COMMENT 'Curated Parquet for event analytics; read-only for analysts';

The external location is the object that binds a concrete path to a concrete cloud identity. Declaring the external data location up front and pointing tables at it is the standard pattern for querying object storage without ingesting the data into the warehouse [source p.351].

Step 3 — grant to the principal (the principal leg).

Executed by the external location owner (or anyone with MANAGE on it):

GRANT READ FILES ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events TO `analysts`;

Add the following only if analysts must also register tables that point at this path — the scene explicitly says they only need to read, so it is omitted by default:

-- GRANT CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events TO `analysts`;

Note that READ FILES is a privilege on the location, not on the bucket and not on the metastore. Nothing about WRITE FILES, DELETE, or ALL PRIVILEGES is issued.

Step 4 — verify.

DESCRIBE EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events; -- URL, credential name, owner, comment

SHOW GRANTS ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events; -- expect exactly one row: READ FILES -> analysts

Then prove it end-to-end as a member of analysts, ideally with a row count rather than a LIMIT:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_seen FROM acme.events_raw; -- expected: 48,112,904

Finally prove the negative case, which is the point of the exercise: as the same analyst, attempt an INSERT or DELETE against the same table and confirm it fails with INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS rather than silently succeeding.

Summary of the privilege chain: CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL on the metastore (admin) → CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on metastore + credential (admin) → READ FILES on the external location (analysts). Three objects, three privileges, no administrative access for any analyst.

Analysis — Why the method works. The request is deliberately decomposed into three separable decisions: identity (which cloud role), path (which prefix), and principal (which group). Doing it as one blob of cloud permissions is what produces the classic cloud antipattern of handing a user administrative access to everything when they need a handful of roles [source p.398]. Keeping the three decisions separate is precisely what makes per-path least privilege enforceable and auditable: SHOW GRANTS ON EXTERNAL LOCATION answers the principal question, DESCRIBE EXTERNAL LOCATION answers the path-and-identity question, and the IAM trust/permission policy answers the cloud-side question in between.

The two-layer enforcement point. A UC grant never overrides IAM. If you ran GRANT WRITE FILES here, writes would still fail because the role's policy only contains s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket. That is a safety net, not a design: it means the UC grant is a latent capability that becomes live the moment someone edits the IAM policy. Never rely on the second layer to compensate for an over-broad first layer.

Edge cases and common mistakes. (1) Trailing slash is not the issue; path-segment boundaries are. The location s3://acme-lake/raw/events covers s3://acme-lake/raw/events/2025/01/file.parquet but NOT the sibling s3://acme-lake/raw/events_v2/2025/, even though the sibling's string begins with the same characters up to the underscore. (2) The location URL must not overlap the metastore's managed location; here managed storage is s3://acme-lake/managed and the curated prefix is s3://acme-lake/raw/events, which is why the statement is legal. (3) A user needs the table-level SELECT grant in addition to READ FILES for table-based reads; READ FILES alone covers path-based reads. (4) Granting READ FILES to a group is preferred over 17 individual grants, because offboarding then happens by group membership rather than by hunting grants — and the principle says to give privileges for the timespan when they are needed and take them away afterwards [source p.398].

Generalization. Any data pipeline that writes Parquet or Delta files into an object-store prefix, as in a Spark job that ingests three JSON sources and writes a Parquet-formatted Delta table to S3 [source p.346], should expose that prefix to consumers through exactly this triple: one credential, one external location per curated prefix, and one narrow GRANT per consumer group.
Problem 2

A colleague executes your Problem 1 statements and returns three test results from a user account (dana@acme.com) that is a member of analysts and holds no other Unity Catalog privilege. Test A: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acme.events_raw returns 48,112,904. Test B: INSERT INTO acme.events_raw VALUES (...) fails with [INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS]. Test C: SELECT * FROM acme.events_v2 — a table registered with LOCATION 's3://acme-lake/raw/events_v2/2025/' — fails with [INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS] on path s3://acme-lake/raw/events_v2/2025/. For each test, decide whether the result is the expected behaviour or a defect; for any defect, name the root cause and give the fix. Then state the exact output you expect from SHOW GRANTS ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events and what an unexpected extra row would mean.
Hint: Separate the two layers: a Unity Catalog INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS error and a cloud IAM AccessDenied error come from different places and have different fixes.

Worked solution
Test A — expected, and it is the positive acceptance test. Dana inherits READ FILES on external location acme_events through group membership, so the path s3://acme-lake/raw/events/... is readable. The row count 48,112,904 is the concrete assertion: a count, not a LIMIT, because a LIMIT 10 can succeed by reading only one file and would not prove that all 12,480 files are readable.

Test B — expected, and it is the negative acceptance test, i.e. the evidence that least privilege is actually enforced. The insert fails because analysts were granted READ FILES and not WRITE FILES on the external location. Two layers both block it: Unity Catalog has no WRITE FILES grant, and the IAM role's policy contains only s3:GetObject, s3:ListBucket and s3:GetBucketLocation. If this test had instead succeeded, the grant in Problem 1 would have been wrong and had to be revoked.

Test C — a defect, but not a defect in the grant. Root cause: prefix boundary. The external location is s3://acme-lake/raw/events, which covers exactly the directory raw/events/ and everything below it. The table acme.events_v2 lives at s3://acme-lake/raw/events_v2/2025/, a sibling directory whose name shares a prefix but diverges at the underscore; Unity Catalog resolves the location as a path-segment-bounded directory, so events_v2 is outside the location's scope and the read is denied. Note that dana may still have a valid SELECT grant on the table itself — that does not help, because Unity Catalog checks the storage privilege first.

Fix, option 1 (preferred if the second prefix is genuinely curated): create a second external location and grant read on it.

CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events_v2

URL 's3://acme-lake/raw/events_v2'

WITH (STORAGE CREDENTIAL acme_cred)

COMMENT 'v2 events, read-only for analysts';

GRANT READ FILES ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events_v2 TO `analysts`;

One caveat: because acme_cred's IAM policy currently allows s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::acme-lake/*, no IAM change is needed here. If the sibling lived in a different bucket, the IAM policy would have to be extended too — the UC grant can never exceed what IAM allows.

Fix, option 2: rewrite the table's LOCATION to sit under raw/events/ (for example raw/events/v2/2025/) so that one location covers both generations. This is the cheaper fix, and it is the right one if events_v2 is really the same curated dataset.

Diagnostic rule to remember: a Unity Catalog error names the missing UC privilege and the UC object to fix (GRANT ... ON EXTERNAL LOCATION), whereas a cloud-side failure surfaces as an IAM AccessDenied, meaning the fix belongs in the role's permission policy, not in SQL. Because UC stores only a reference to the role ARN, an IAM policy edit immediately changes the effective power of every existing UC grant.

Expected verification output. SHOW GRANTS ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events should return exactly one row:

Principal = analysts, ActionType = READ FILES, ObjectType = EXTERNAL LOCATION, ObjectKey = acme_events.

If analysts also needed to register tables, a second row CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE -> analysts would be legitimate. Any other row is out of policy: WRITE FILES or ALL PRIVILEGES means the destructive capability was handed out; MANAGE means analysts can alter or drop the location itself; a row for the group ALL USERS or for an individual user rather than the analysts group means the grant is broader or narrower than intended. Complement this with DESCRIBE EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events, which must show URL s3://acme-lake/raw/events and STORAGE CREDENTIAL acme_cred — if the URL is the bucket root or the credential is a different object, the location was misconfigured and the grants on it mean something different from what you intended.

Analysis — Method choice. Verification is written as two positive assertions and one negative assertion: read succeeds, write fails, and a named sibling path fails. A grant is not verified by the absence of complaints; it is verified by an assertion that would fail loudly if the grant were wrong. This mirrors the general principle that a person or system should be given only the privileges and data needed for the task at hand [source p.398] — if you cannot demonstrate that the unnecessary capability is absent, you have not tested least privilege, you have only tested the happy path.

Why the prefix-boundary failure is the most common defect. Practitioners mentally model object storage as a filesystem with directories, but a prefix is a naming convention over opaque keys, and a different category of storage — a genuinely POSIX-like managed filesystem service such as Amazon EFS exposed over NFS — is what would give you real directories [source p.202]. Because prefix matching is string-based and bounded at separators, raw/events and raw/events_v2 are unrelated locations. Other classic variants of the same mistake: pointing the table at the bucket root while the location covers a subdirectory, and pointing at a path with a different case (S3 keys are case-sensitive).

Edge cases worth rehearsing for the exam. First, table-level SELECT and location-level READ FILES are both required for table reads; students often grant one and expect the other to be implied. Second, if the external table was created with an explicit file format such as Parquet, that format is fixed at creation time and the reader does not re-infer it [source p.351], so a prefix that mixes formats can produce confusing failures that look like permission errors. Third, path-based reads require only the location grant, so an analyst can read a prefix without any table existing on it — which is exactly why the location, not the table, is the correct object to lock down.

Common mistakes this problem trains you to avoid. Granting on the metastore instead of on the specific location; assuming that a SUCCESS on a LIMIT query proves full read access; reading an IAM AccessDenied as a Unity Catalog grant problem and burning time writing GRANT statements that cannot help; and forgetting that every grant on a location is really a grant on every object under that prefix forever, including files written next year.
Problem 3

The analysts group now has READ FILES on external location acme_events (1.8 TB, 12,480 files, 18.6% of the 9.7 TB acme-lake bucket; the metastore's managed location is s3://acme-lake/managed at 2.4 TB). Three amendments are proposed at the next review. Proposal 1: also GRANT WRITE FILES ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events TO analysts, argued as 'so they can fix a bad file instead of waiting for the platform team'. Proposal 2: GRANT CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION ON METASTORE TO analysts so they can self-serve other prefixes without filing tickets. Proposal 3: keep READ FILES for analysts (17 users) and additionally grant CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE to a 3-person subgroup analyst_leads. Quantify the exposure of each proposal, decide which to adopt, and give the final SQL.
Hint: Quantify each proposal as (number of principals that gain the capability) × (bytes that capability reaches), then compare against the requirement.

Worked solution
Set the baseline and the requirement first. Requirement: read every file under s3://acme-lake/raw/events; never write, delete, or drop that data. Baseline: 17 principals hold READ FILES on 1.8 TB — that is 18.6% of the bucket, with zero destructive capability.

Proposal 1 — add WRITE FILES to analysts.

Principals gaining the destructive capability: 17 (the whole group). Bytes in scope: 1.8 TB across 12,480 files.

Immediate effect today: zero, because acme_cred's IAM policy only allows s3:GetObject, s3:ListBucket and s3:GetBucketLocation. That is the trap: the dangerous grant is inert now and is one IAM policy line away from being live. If someone later adds s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject to the role, all 17 analysts simultaneously acquire delete rights over 1.8 TB without any further SQL review, because the UC grant is already in place.

Second-order risk: files under this prefix may also back a zero-copy clone or another external table. Deleting files in the original object can wipe out the clone as well, because cloning typically creates new pointers to the same raw data rather than physically copying it [source p.249]. A single analyst 'fixing a bad file' can therefore corrupt several downstream objects at once.

Verdict: reject. 'To be safe' is the exact antipattern the principle warns about; privileges should be granted for the timespan they are needed and then removed [source p.398].

Proposal 2 — grant CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on the metastore to analysts.

Principals affected: 17. Paths reachable: any path the credential can read, not just raw/events.

Maximum exposure: with the current IAM policy that is the whole acme-lake bucket, 9.7 TB. Compared with the curated prefix, 9.7 / 1.8 = 5.39, so the change multiplies the reachable data by about 5.4×. If the IAM policy were later broadened, the ceiling rises again to every bucket that role can touch.

Corollary defect: the grant also destroys the audit story. DESCRIBE EXTERNAL LOCATION is only a complete answer when the set of locations is small and controlled by the platform team; if any of 17 analysts can mint new locations at will, an auditor can no longer enumerate which paths map to which identity by inspecting the locations you approved.

Verdict: reject. Self-service is the right goal, but it is implemented by the platform team creating one external location per curated prefix and granting READ FILES on it, not by decentralising the ability to bind arbitrary paths to a privileged identity.

Proposal 3 — READ FILES for all analysts, CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE for analyst_leads.

Principals with read: 17 (100% of the group), over 1.8 TB. Principals with DDL: 3, which is 3/17 = 0.1765, i.e. 17.6% of the group. Principals with destructive capability: 0.

This satisfies the stated requirement exactly: the 14 readers get read; the 3 users who must register tables pointing at the prefix get the ability to do so; nobody can write or delete. It also keeps the accountability chain intact, because table creation on that prefix is attributable to three named-account holders rather than to an anonymous group.

Verdict: adopt, with the CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE row dropped if it turns out nobody actually registers tables — the scene's stated requirement needs only READ FILES.

Final SQL:

GRANT READ FILES ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events TO `analysts`;

GRANT CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events TO `analyst_leads`;

-- must return two rows, no more:

SHOW GRANTS ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events;

-- negative test: must fail for a member of analyst_leads too

-- DELETE FROM acme.events_raw WHERE event_date < '2024-01-01';

Finally, in the same review, confirm that the external location URL does not overlap the metastore's managed location s3://acme-lake/managed. A location declared at or above the managed root would overlap managed storage and is not a valid configuration; the reason this setup is legal is that curated data (raw/events, 1.8 TB) and managed data (managed, 2.4 TB) are disjoint prefixes totalling 1.8 + 2.4 = 4.2 TB of the 9.7 TB bucket, leaving 5.5 TB — 5.5/9.7 = 56.7% — outside both.

Analysis — Method choice. The three proposals are compared on a single axis that the exam rewards: capability × reach × principal count. Proposal 1 is small reach with wide principal count; Proposal 2 is wide reach with wide principal count; Proposal 3 is exact reach with the minimum principal count. Framing least privilege numerically turns a philosophical argument into an engineering decision, and it makes the asymmetry obvious: reach and principal count multiply the same way risk does, so a grant that is inert today is still a liability because it will silently become active if the layer beneath it changes.

Why the method works. Identity, path and principal are separate decisions, and each proposal loosens exactly one of them. Proposal 1 loosens the action set (adds WRITE FILES), Proposal 2 loosens the path set (adds the right to create locations), Proposal 3 touches only the principal set and only for the DDL action that the requirement actually names. Because the layers are independent, you can reason about each change without re-deriving the whole model — that separability is the entire value of the design.

Edge cases. (1) A WRITE FILES grant on a location is a delete grant: writing and deleting both land on the same prefix, and object storage deletion is immediate and not reference-counted, which is why the zero-copy clone hazard is real [source p.249]. (2) If a location's URL were moved to the bucket root, the same grant text would expose 9.7 TB instead of 1.8 TB — the SQL would be unchanged, so the path string is a security parameter, not a cosmetic detail. (3) An external table registered with an explicit location and file format continues to read from that path without ingesting data [source p.351], so revoking a location grant breaks every table on the prefix at once — plan revocations as coordinated changes. (4) The pipeline that writes raw/events — for example a Spark job producing a Parquet-formatted Delta table in S3 [source p.346] — needs a separate write path and a separate credential; do not reuse acme_cred for producers.

Common mistakes. Granting WRITE FILES 'to be safe'; granting on the metastore or catalog level when the question is about one prefix; assuming an IAM-level restriction makes an over-broad UC grant acceptable; granting MANAGE on the location so someone can 'clean it up'; and forgetting that privilege reviews must also remove access, since least privilege is about the timespan as much as the scope [source p.398].

Generalization. The pattern scales: one storage credential per cloud identity, one external location per curated prefix, and one narrow GRANT per consumer group, re-verified by DESCRIBE, SHOW GRANTS, and a read test after every change.

actions.text: Let's walk through the worked problem for this lesson. The setup is a request many of you will face on the job and on the exam: an IAM role and a curated bucket prefix already exist, and you have to grant a group read-only access to that prefix. Notice the constraint — read every file, but never write or drop anything.

Read the scenario carefully. The bucket s3://acme-lake/raw/events holds curated Parquet files, and the IAM role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-role already trusts your Databricks account. That single detail means the cloud-side identity work is done. Your job is purely the Unity Catalog side.

The hint is the key insight for this whole lesson: model the request as three independent decisions — identity, path, and principal. A storage credential answers who can reach the cloud storage. An external location answers which path is governed. A grant answers which users get access, and at what level.

Now the worked solution, step by step. Step one: as a metastore admin, create the storage credential binding the IAM role. Step two: create the external location pointing at the bucket prefix and attach that credential. Step three: grant READ FILES on that external location to the analysts group. Step four: verify — describe the external location, list its grants, then actually read the data as a member of analysts.

One thing to watch: you only add CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on that location if the analysts also need to register their own tables pointing at the path. For a pure read-only requirement, READ FILES is all you need — and granting more than asked is exactly the trap the exam loves.

Why does this method work? Because the three concerns are separated. Identity comes from the credential, path from the external location, and principal from the grant. That separation is what makes per-path least privilege actually enforceable. And notice the three classic pitfalls: granting WRITE FILES just to be safe, granting on the metastore instead of on the location, and choosing a path that overlaps the metastore's managed location.

Let's move to the second problem, and this one adds a wrinkle: a colleague executes your statements, and something does not behave the way you expect. Take a moment to read the prompt before we continue.

scenes.title: Managed Tables vs. External Tables vs. External Locations

elements.content: Dimension  |  Managed table  |  External table  |  External location

What the object fundamentally is
Managed table: A managed table is a Unity Catalog table whose data files live in a Unity Catalog–chosen storage path, so the table object and its files are treated as one governed asset [source p.226].
External table: An external table is a Unity Catalog table whose data files live at a user-specified cloud path, so the table object is a pointer to files that pre-exist and outlive it [source p.383].
External location: An external location is not a table at all; it is a securable that grants READ FILES, WRITE FILES, and CREATE TABLE on a cloud path, authorizing access to storage rather than describing a dataset [source p.383].

Who chooses the storage path
Managed table: Unity Catalog chooses the path automatically by placing files under the managed location configured for the schema or catalog, so the user never types a cloud URL [source p.226].
External table: The user explicitly picks the path when issuing CREATE TABLE ... LOCATION 's3://bucket/prefix', and that path must fall under an external location the user has been granted on [source p.383].
External location: The path is part of the external location's own definition; a user holding privileges on it may only reference paths inside that registered prefix, not arbitrary URLs [source p.226].
