What DROP TABLE does to the data
Managed table: DROP TABLE on a managed table deletes the underlying data files as well as the metadata, because Unity Catalog owns the lifecycle of both [source p.85].
External table: DROP TABLE on an external table removes only the metadata pointer; the files remain in object storage and can be re-registered by another table or read directly [source p.85].
External location: DROP has no meaning for an external location itself: you revoke the grant or drop the securable, which removes an authorization path but deletes no tabular data by itself [source p.383].

Privileges required to create or use it
Managed table: Creating a managed table requires CREATE TABLE on the schema plus USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG on the enclosing objects, and no cloud-storage privilege is needed because UC writes to its own managed location.
External table: Creating an external table requires CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on the external location that covers the path, in addition to the schema-level CREATE TABLE and USE privileges.
External location: An external location is itself the privilege vehicle: READ FILES, WRITE FILES, and CREATE TABLE are granted on it, and holding them is a necessary precondition for external-table creation [source p.383].

Whether it governs non-tabular files
Managed table: A managed table governs only tabular data it created; it offers no mechanism for admitting raw Parquet, CSV, or image files that are not registered as a table [source p.383].
External table: An external table still governs only the tabular projection it defines; the surrounding non-tabular files in the same path are not managed by the table object [source p.383].
External location: An external location governs non-tabular files directly, because READ FILES and WRITE FILES apply to objects in the path regardless of whether any table references them [source p.226].

Failure and edge-case behavior
Managed table: If a managed table's schema or catalog is dropped, the data goes with it, which is why managed locations are typically protected by retention and backup policies to prevent accidental irreversible loss [source p.85].
External table: An external table pointing at a path covered by no external location cannot be created at all, and even a valid external location does not by itself grant SELECT on the table built on it.
External location: An external location can be revoked without dropping the tables that reference it, leaving those tables readable by metadata but unwritable; the files themselves are untouched.
Takeaway — Ask 'who owns the files after the table disappears?' — if Unity Catalog should own the lifecycle and you want automatic deletion, choose a managed table [source p.85].
Takeaway — If the storage path must outlive the table, support non-tabular files, or be shared with other engines, choose an external table backed by an external location [source p.383].

Takeaway — Remember the exam trap: an external table cannot be created without an external location covering its path, and privileges on that location still do not grant SELECT on the resulting table [source p.226].

actions.text: Now that we've seen how storage credentials get delegated and how external locations bind cloud paths to those credentials, let's put the three most commonly confused concepts side by side: managed tables, external tables, and external locations.
Here's the comparison table itself. We'll walk through it row by row so the distinctions stick. Read it as five questions, and for each one ask yourself how the three objects answer differently.

First question: what is the object, fundamentally? A managed table is a Delta table whose data lifecycle Unity Catalog owns end to end. An external table is also a Delta table, but the files live at a path you control. An external location is not a table at all — it's a securable object that authorizes access to a cloud storage path.

Second: who chooses the storage path? For a managed table, Unity Catalog picks the path under the managed location — you never specify it. For an external table, you choose the path, and it must sit under an external location. That single requirement is where most exam questions hide.

Third, and this is the decision cue worth memorizing: what does DROP TABLE do to the data? Dropping a managed table deletes the underlying data. Dropping an external table removes only the metadata — the files survive at your path. So the real question is: who owns the files after the table disappears?

Fourth: what privileges does it take? Creating a managed table needs CREATE TABLE plus USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG. Creating an external table needs CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on the external location. And to simply read files at a governed path, you need READ FILES or WRITE FILES on the external location.

Fifth: does it govern non-tabular files? Only the external location does. Tables are about tables; if you need to govern a folder of raw Parquet, images, or model artifacts, the external location is the object that reaches them. That's exactly why the external location exists as its own securable.

And the failure case ties it all together. An external table pointed at a path that no external location covers simply cannot be created — the authorization chain has to be complete before the table exists. Also note: holding privileges on an external location does not by itself grant SELECT on a table. Those are two separate checks.
So the takeaways. First: ask who owns the files after the table disappears. If the answer is Unity Catalog, it's managed; if the path must outlive the table, it's external.

Second: when the storage path must survive independently — shared with another engine, retained for compliance, or reused across workspaces — an external table is the right pattern, and it requires an external location covering that path.

Third, remember the exam trap directly: an external table pointing at a path covered by no external location cannot be created, and privileges on that location still do not by themselves grant SELECT on a table. Keep those two facts separate and you'll pick the right answer under pressure.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Storage Governance Decisions

questions.question: A data engineer runs DROP TABLE on two Unity Catalog tables: sales_managed (a managed table) and sales_external (an external table whose data files live at s3://acme-lake/raw/sales/). All other things being equal, what happens to the underlying files in each case?

options.label: Both tables lose their metadata only; the data files remain in cloud object storage in both cases.
Dropping the managed table also deletes its underlying data files, while dropping the external table removes only the metadata and leaves the files at the external path intact.
Dropping the external table also deletes its underlying data files, while dropping the managed table leaves its files in the managed storage location.
Neither drop touches any files; both managed and external data are preserved indefinitely until a separate VACUUM job is scheduled.

questions.analysis: This item tests the core managed-versus-external lifecycle distinction. For a managed table, Unity Catalog owns both the metadata and the data, so DROP TABLE removes the table's metadata AND deletes the underlying data files in the managed storage location. For an external table, Unity Catalog governs only the metadata; the files are owned by you at the external path, so DROP TABLE removes the metadata but leaves the files untouched. Option A is the most common misconception: learners assume 'drop' is always metadata-only, but that is only true for external tables. Option C inverts the two behaviors. Option D wrongly implies that VACUUM governs the drop lifecycle — VACUUM removes stale files from a Delta table's history, not the files of a dropped external table. This reversible-versus-destructive property is why external tables behave like a 'two-way door' for data you cannot afford to lose [source p.109].

questions.question: In Unity Catalog, which privilege must a principal hold on a path or external location to perform each of the following operations? Select all that apply.

options.label: READ FILES on the path or external location to read data files directly from that path.
WRITE FILES on the path or external location to write data files to that path.
CREATE TABLE on the external location to register a new external table at a path under that location.
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on the storage credential to register a table whose data lives outside the managed storage location.

questions.analysis: The three path operations map to three distinct privileges. Reading files at a path requires READ FILES; writing files to a path requires WRITE FILES; and registering a table at a path requires CREATE TABLE on the external location that contains that path. Option D is a fabricated privilege and a classic distractor: there is no separate CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE privilege in Unity Catalog — the registration privilege is CREATE TABLE scoped to the external location, while access to the underlying cloud identity is delegated through the storage credential. This design enforces the principle of least privilege: a principal gets only the privilege needed for the operation at hand, and no more [source p.398].

questions.question: An instructor states 'the external location is the table' and 'each storage credential may back only one external location.' Which of the following best identifies the flaw in both claims?

options.label: External locations and storage credentials are the same object, so the statements are redundant rather than wrong.

An external location is a governed object (a path plus a credential) but it is not a table — tables are registered at paths under it — and a single storage credential can back many external locations.
An external location is a table, but a storage credential may indeed back only one external location because of the external ID trust relationship.
External locations are deprecated in Unity Catalog, so both statements are irrelevant to the managed-versus-external decision as it is tested today.

questions.analysis: The first claim confuses layers: an external location is a Unity Catalog securable that binds a cloud path to a storage credential, whereas a table is a separate metadata object registered at a path under that location. The second claim confuses cardinality: a storage credential can serve many external locations, because the credential encapsulates a cloud identity that governs a broad set of paths, not a single one. Option A is a category error; option C repeats both misconceptions and wrongly appeals to the trust relationship; option D is factually false. The storage credential is the delegation mechanism, and the external location is one of the positions where that delegation is applied [source p.246].

actions.text: Let's see how well the managed-versus-external distinction and those path privileges have settled in. Work through each one on your own — read the options carefully, since the distractors here are built to sound plausible.
Take your time and commit to an answer for each. Once you submit, I'll walk through anything that tripped you up.
