scenes.title: Delta Sharing: Governed Data Exchange

elements.content: Delta Sharing: Governed Data Exchange
Definition: Open protocol for secure, live, read-only data exchange across organizations, clouds, and platforms. Recipients query provider-side data—no physical copy is transferred [source p.288].
Core Objects: Providers and recipients; shares; tables, views, and volumes added via ALTER SHARE ... ADD TABLE. Shares are built from Unity Catalog assets.
Deployment Modes: Databricks-to-Databricks uses a sharing identifier tied to a Unity Catalog workspace. Open sharing issues an activation link plus a credential/bearer token.
Governance: Shares inherit Unity Catalog SELECT grants, row/column filters, and dynamic views—so existing security policies determine exactly what recipients see [source p.202].

Worked Example — Governed Row Filter: A share exposes a sales table with a recipient-scoped row filter WHERE region = current_recipient_region(). Provider audit logs record share creation and recipient access, while table lineage stops at the sharing boundary and does not appear in recipient-side lineage [source p.63].

actions.text: We just looked at how storage credentials and external locations let Unity Catalog reach into cloud storage. Now let's take that governance one step further, and talk about Delta Sharing: governed data exchange. This is how you let someone outside your organization query your data without ever handing them a copy.

Start with the definition, because the exam loves precise wording. Delta Sharing is an open protocol for the secure, live, read-only exchange of governed data across organizations, clouds, and platforms. The word that matters most here is read-only — and the second is live. The recipient queries the provider's data where it lives; they do not receive a copy, so there is no stale duplicate drifting out of sync.

Next, the core objects. You have providers and recipients on either end, a share in the middle, and the tables, views, and volumes that you add into that share. To put an asset into a share you use ALTER SHARE, followed by ADD TABLE. Think of the share as a curated container — nothing is exposed until you explicitly add it.

Now the two deployment modes, and this is a classic exam discriminator. In Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, the recipient is a Unity Catalog workspace identified by a sharing identifier — authentication is automatic. In open sharing, the recipient instead gets an activation link plus a credential or bearer token, which lets non-Databricks clients read the same share.

Here is why this stays governed. Shares are built directly from Unity Catalog assets, so the existing SELECT grants, the row and column filters, and the dynamic views you already defined continue to determine exactly what the recipient sees. You are not re-implementing security for sharing — you inherit it.

Let's walk the worked example — a governed row filter. A share exposes a table, but a row filter attached to that table means each recipient only sees the rows they are entitled to, enforced automatically on every query. The upstream table is unchanged; the filter does the scoping for you.

Finally, connect this to observability, which is a common trap. On the provider side, audit logs in system.access.audit record share creation and recipient access. But table lineage stops at the sharing boundary — that access does not appear as recipient-side lineage. So if you are asked where to prove that an external party read your data, the answer is the provider's audit log, not a downstream lineage graph.

To summarize this page: Delta Sharing is an open, live, read-only protocol; you expose governed Unity Catalog assets through shares using ALTER SHARE ADD TABLE; recipients connect either Databricks-to-Databricks with a sharing identifier or through open sharing with an activation link and token; and the provider's audit logs — not lineage — are where you verify recipient access.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Delta Sharing Concepts

questions.question: When a Data Provider configures Delta Sharing in the Databricks UI, which object is granted to the recipient, and which object identifies the recipient?

options.label: A share is granted to a recipient, and the recipient object identifies who receives it.
A recipient is granted to a share, and the share object identifies who receives it.
A storage credential is granted to a recipient, and the external location identifies who receives it.
A catalog is granted to a recipient, and the provider's metastore identifies who receives it.

questions.analysis: In Delta Sharing, the provider creates a share — a named logical container that holds the tables, views, and volumes to be shared — and then grants that share to one or more recipients. The recipient is a separate securable object that represents the external party; it carries the authentication and identity information (for Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, a recipient token plus the recipient's Unity Catalog metastore ID) and is what identifies who receives the data. Option B reverses the relationship: a recipient is not granted to a share; the share is granted to the recipient. Option C describes the cloud-storage delegation model (storage credentials and external locations) covered earlier in this unit, which governs how Databricks itself reads and writes cloud storage, not how data is shared with an external party. Option D misuses the catalog object: shares contain assets, and a metastore identifies the provider's or recipient's Unity Catalog environment, but neither is the securable that is granted to a recipient. This distinction echoes the broader ingestion principle that a data provider transmits the data for downstream consumption [source p.63], but in Delta Sharing the provider retains ownership and control.

questions.question: A recipient must possess different prerequisites depending on the sharing mode. Which of the following correctly distinguish Databricks-to-Databricks sharing from open sharing? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: In Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, the recipient must have a Unity Catalog metastore and consume the share through the Delta Sharing protocol within Databricks.
In open sharing, the recipient does not need Databricks at all; they need a credential file (the bearer token) and a client that can read the shared data, such as pandas, Apache Spark, or Power BI.
In Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, the recipient must provide a storage credential that the provider assumes to write into the recipient's bucket.
Open sharing requires the recipient to mount the shared data into their own Unity Catalog metastore before reading it.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct: Databricks-to-Databricks sharing assumes the recipient also operates Unity Catalog, so the provider supplies the recipient's metastore identifier and the exchange is brokered through Databricks. Option B is correct: open sharing is protocol-level, not platform-level, so the recipient only needs the credential file (the bearer token) and any compatible client, with no Databricks requirement. Option C is a misconception that conflates Delta Sharing with the storage-delegation model taught earlier: shares are read-only, so recipients never supply write credentials, and a provider never assumes a recipient's storage credential to write data. Option D is another misconception: mount-based access is an access pattern for a recipient's own Unity Catalog, not a prerequisite of open sharing — open recipients simply read the credential file's data files directly. The read-only and revocable nature of sharing is fundamental: datasets are shared in a read-only fashion, and if the provider removes access, the recipient loses it [source p.288].

questions.question: A colleague claims that Delta Sharing copies the provider's data into the recipient's account, bypasses Unity Catalog grants, and gives the recipient write access to the shared tables. Which statement best evaluates these three claims?

options.label: All three claims are correct because sharing physically replicates the data to the recipient for performance.

The copying claim is incorrect (sharing is a read-only, in-place access mechanism), the bypass claim is incorrect (the provider's Unity Catalog privileges still govern what is in the share), and the write-access claim is incorrect (recipients never get write privileges on shared assets).
The copying claim is correct, but the bypass and write-access claims are incorrect.
The bypass claim is correct because sharing grants access at the storage layer without consulting Unity Catalog.

questions.analysis: Option B correctly rejects all three misconceptions. Delta Sharing does not copy data: the source of truth remains in the provider's account, and the recipient accesses the data in place, which is the strict sense in which sharing is not ingestion or physical possession of the dataset [source p.288]. This matters because a provider can revoke access at any time, which would be impossible if the recipient already held a physical copy. The bypass claim is also wrong: the contents of a share are determined by the provider's Unity Catalog grants on the underlying tables, views, and volumes, so sharing is governed by — not exempt from — Unity Catalog permissions. Finally, the write-access claim is wrong: shares are strictly read-only, consistent with the general pattern that shared datasets are offered read-only and integrated with the recipient's own data without ownership transfer [source p.288]. Option A wrongly affirms all three claims. Option C wrongly affirms copying. Option D wrongly claims sharing operates at the storage layer without privilege checks, which misrepresents how the provider governs share contents.

actions.text: Time for a quick checkpoint on Delta Sharing. Work through each question on your own — no peeking ahead — and once you submit, we'll go through anything that gave you trouble together.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Create a Share for an External Partner

elements.content: Problem 1

Acme runs its production data in Unity Catalog on the metastore for workspace acme-prod. The table `prod.sales.orders` holds 4,200,000,000 rows (84 TB), is partitioned by `order_date`, and spans 2019-01-01 through 2025-06-30. Acme has signed a contract to give the partner Northwind read-only access to the table, but only to orders placed on or after 2024-01-01 (380,000,000 rows, 7.60 TB). Northwind is another Databricks Unity Catalog workspace. (a) Write the two SQL statements that create the share and attach the table with the required restriction, naming the exact privilege the executing principal needs. (b) State the privilege the executing principal additionally needs on `prod.sales.orders` itself. (c) Compute the percentage of rows and of bytes that become reachable by Northwind, and the volume that must never leave Acme's control.
Hint: CREATE SHARE creates an empty securable — a share with no objects exposes nothing. The restriction is expressed as a partition predicate at ADD TABLE time, not by asking the partner to filter.

Worked solution
**Step 1 — create the empty share.**

```sql

CREATE SHARE northwind_orders COMMENT 'Order data for Northwind';

```

This is executed by a principal that holds `CREATE SHARE` on the metastore. In practice that is a metastore admin, or a named data-engineering principal to whom a metastore admin has granted `CREATE SHARE` explicitly. The creator becomes the **share owner**; ownership is what allows the later `ALTER SHARE` and `GRANT USE SHARE` statements. At this point the share is an empty container: it grants nobody anything.

**Step 2 — attach the table with a partition predicate (partial sharing).**

```sql

ALTER SHARE northwind_orders

ADD TABLE prod.sales.orders

PARTITION (order_date >= '2024-01-01');

```

The `PARTITION (...)` clause is the partial-sharing mechanism. The predicate is stored in the share definition and is evaluated by Acme's side at query time, so Northwind's queries can only ever see partitions whose `order_date` is on or after 2024-01-01. Northwind cannot widen the predicate — there is no `WHERE` clause, hint, or query rewrite a recipient can issue that re-admits the excluded partitions. This is the same idea as an ordinary query predicate applied to a pattern of records [source p.299]: the filter is a logical condition that determines which records the reader receives, except here the condition is fixed by the provider.

**Step 3 — the additional table-level privilege.**

The principal that owns the share must itself be able to read `prod.sales.orders`: it needs `SELECT` on the table (or to be its owner). `CREATE SHARE` on the metastore governs the *act of sharing*, not access to the *data being shared*. A share is a reference to data, and the provider's own privileges are the ceiling on what flows through it.

**Step 4 — quantify the exposure.**

Rows:

$$\frac{380{,}000{,}000}{4{,}200{,}000{,}000} = 0.090476 \approx 9.05\%$$

Bytes:

$$\frac{7.60\ \text{TB}}{84\ \text{TB}} = 0.090476 \approx 9.05\%$$

Unexposed remainder: $4{,}200{,}000{,}000 - 380{,}000{,}000 = 3{,}820{,}000{,}000$ rows, i.e. $84 - 7.60 = 76.40$ TB, which is $90.95\%$ of the table. Because the split aligns with the partition scheme, those 3.82 billion rows are pruned as whole partitions and are never scanned, never serialised, and never sent.

Analysis — The design choice here is *where the filter lives*. Option 1 (chosen) puts the predicate inside the share definition. Option 2 — share the whole table and put `WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'` in Northwind's tooling — leaks the 3.82 billion historical rows into the recipient's blast radius: the partner could simply omit the filter, a compromised client credential could dump everything, and a contract breach would be a data breach rather than a policy breach. This is precisely the principle that teams should expose data through a controlled interface rather than granting direct reads of another party's data store [source p.108].

Common mistakes: (1) assuming `CREATE SHARE` needs a `CREATE TABLE` or ownership privilege — it does not; it needs `CREATE SHARE` on the metastore plus `SELECT` on the shared object. (2) Believing `PARTITION (...)` is a hint that improves performance — it is a hard security boundary and also a performance win, because pruning whole partitions reduces the number of data blocks scanned, and scan work scales with the number of blocks read across the cluster [source p.348]. (3) Using a non-partition column inside `PARTITION (...)`; the predicate must reference partition columns of the shared table, otherwise the statement is rejected. (4) Forgetting that the share owner must retain `SELECT`; see p5 for the failure mode when that grant is later revoked. The optional `AS <alias>` clause at the end of the `ADD TABLE` statement renames the object as the recipient sees it, which is useful for hiding internal schema names.
Problem 2

Northwind will consume the share from its own Databricks Unity Catalog workspace, whose sharing identifier is `northwind-uc-sharing-id`. A second partner, Tailspin Logistics, has no Databricks account at all and will read the same share with an open-source Delta Sharing client. Write the `CREATE RECIPIENT` statement for each partner, state exactly what each statement returns and what each recipient must have on its side, and explain what goes wrong if Tailspin's engineer is told to 'just run `CREATE CATALOG`'.
Hint: Two recipient types, two authentication models: metastore-to-metastore federation versus a downloadable credential file.

Worked solution
**Recipient 1 — Northwind, databricks-to-databricks (D2D).**

```sql

CREATE RECIPIENT northwind

USING ID 'northwind-uc-sharing-id'

COMMENT 'Northwind UC workspace';

```

The `USING ID` clause takes Northwind's *sharing identifier* — the value produced by Northwind's own metastore when that metastore is enabled for Delta Sharing, not a workspace URL and not a service-principal ID. Northwind then mounts the share from its own workspace:

```sql

-- executed by Northwind, in Northwind's workspace

CREATE CATALOG northwind_orders

USING SHARE acme_provider.northwind_orders;

```

Requirements on Northwind's side: a Unity Catalog metastore attached to the workspace, and Delta Sharing enabled on that metastore. No secret changes hands; authentication is metastore-to-metastore identity.

**Recipient 2 — Tailspin, open sharing.**

```sql

CREATE RECIPIENT tailspin_open COMMENT 'Tailspin Logistics, Delta Sharing client';

```

Omitting `USING ID` creates an **open recipient**. The statement returns an **activation link** (and the associated token) that Acme's administrator sends to Tailspin out of band, for example through a secure secret-exchange channel. Tailspin's engineer opens the link, downloads the credential file (usually named `<recipient>.share`), and points a Delta Sharing client at it; the file contains the share endpoint URL and a bearer token. Tailspin needs a Delta Sharing client and network reachability to the endpoint — it does **not** need Databricks, Unity Catalog, or a metastore.

**Why 'just run CREATE CATALOG' fails for Tailspin.** `CREATE CATALOG ... USING SHARE` is a Unity Catalog DDL statement. Tailspin has no metastore to execute it against and no D2D identity for Acme to recognise, so the statement has no context in which it can run. Open recipients consume a *profile file plus a client*, not a catalog mount.

**What Tailspin must never do** is forward the activation link. It is a one-time credential handover; anyone holding it can download a working credential file.

Analysis — The decisive dimension is *authentication mechanism*, not data content: D2D replaces shared secrets with a federation between two metastores, while open sharing replaces the federation with a bearer credential that must be distributed like a password. A D2D recipient with no attached Unity Catalog metastore cannot mount the share regardless of how many grants it holds — the recipient exists, the grants resolve, and the mount simply fails, which misleads engineers into re-issuing grants that were never the problem. Conversely, an open recipient that is later given an `USING ID` value cannot be 'upgraded': the recipient type is fixed at creation, so the correct repair is to create a second recipient of the right type. Granting a share is like exposing a service interface to an outside developer [source p.108]: you must first decide what identity that outside party authenticates as. A very common mistake is using the *provider's* workspace ID or a service principal's application ID as `USING ID`; the value must come from the recipient's own metastore. A second common mistake is treating the activation link as permanent documentation — store it in a secret manager only long enough to deliver it, then delete it.
Problem 3

The share `northwind_orders` now contains `prod.sales.orders` restricted to `order_date >= '2024-01-01'`, and the recipient `northwind` exists. Write the single statement that actually lets Northwind read the data. Then write the four verification commands a compliance auditor will ask for — one to prove the share exists, one to prove its contents and the partition predicate, one to prove the recipient holds the share privilege, and one to enumerate every object the recipient can see. Give the expected shape of each result, and explain the behaviour when the grant is missing versus when the table is missing.
Hint: A share plus a recipient is not access. The two objects are joined by exactly one privilege: USE SHARE on the share, granted to the recipient.

Worked solution
**The access-granting statement.**

```sql

GRANT USE SHARE northwind_orders TO RECIPIENT northwind;

```

This is a data control language statement in the same family as `GRANT SELECT ... TO user_name` [source p.300]: it grants a privilege on a securable to a principal, with the principal here being a recipient rather than a user or group. Without it, the share and the recipient are two disconnected objects.

**Verification 1 — does the share exist?**

```sql

SHOW SHARES;

```

Expected shape (one row per share in the metastore): share name `northwind_orders`, the owning principal (`data-eng-prod`), the comment `Order data for Northwind`, and a creation timestamp. This answers 'is there a share named northwind_orders at all', nothing more.

**Verification 2 — what is inside it?**

```sql

DESCRIBE SHARE northwind_orders;

```

Expected shape: owner, comment, creation time, and an objects section listing one entry — table `prod.sales.orders`, kind `TABLE`, with the partial-sharing predicate `order_date >= '2024-01-01'` and, if an alias was set, the `shared_as` name. This is the command that proves the restriction survived the deployment.

**Verification 3 — who can use it?**

```sql

SHOW GRANTS ON SHARE northwind_orders;

```

Expected shape (one row): principal `northwind`, principal type `RECIPIENT`, action `USE SHARE`. If this returns zero rows, no partner can mount the share.

**Verification 4 — exactly what the recipient can see.**

```sql

SHOW ALL IN SHARE northwind_orders;

```

Expected shape: one row, the table `prod.sales.orders` (or its alias) and its type. This is the authoritative inventory for the auditor: the recipient's maximum visible surface is the intersection of this list with the grants, not a subset of the table's columns or a wider set of tables.

**Behaviour when state is incomplete.** Adding a table to a share does not notify or privilege anyone, and granting `USE SHARE` does not create data access. The two are combined with AND semantics:

| Share has table? | Recipient holds USE SHARE? | Result on Northwind's side |

|---|---|---|

| Yes | No | `CREATE CATALOG ... USING SHARE` fails: the recipient cannot resolve the share |

| No | Yes | Catalog mounts successfully but contains zero objects |

| Yes | Yes | Catalog mounts and `prod.sales.orders` is queryable, filtered to 2024+ |

In the middle row the failure is silent — no error, just an empty catalog — which is the single most common 'the share is broken' support ticket.

Analysis — The method here is verification by *four different questions*, and conflating them is the standard error. `SHOW SHARES` is metastore-wide discovery, `DESCRIBE SHARE` is metadata about one share (including the partition predicate, which is easy to drop accidentally during a redeploy), `SHOW GRANTS ON SHARE` is the privilege plane, and `SHOW ALL IN SHARE` is the object plane. An engineer who runs only `SHOW SHARES`, sees `northwind_orders`, and reports success has verified nothing about exposure. Notice also that the grant is to the *recipient*, not to the partner's users: Northwind's internal users get access through Northwind's own catalog privileges on `northwind_orders`, and Acme neither sees nor controls those. This keeps Acme's governance boundary at the share, which is the whole point of delegating an interface instead of direct data-store reads [source p.108]. Least privilege follows from the same logic: grant `USE SHARE` to exactly the recipient that needs it, and treat the share as the unit of revocation. Edge cases: a share can be mounted by a recipient that also holds no other grants in Acme's metastore — share privileges are entirely separate from table privileges; and `USE SHARE` is not inherited from metastore admin, so an admin inspecting as a *user* may see different results than the recipient service identity.
Problem 4

Acme's contract with Northwind ends 2026-03-31 at 17:00 UTC, and Security also wants a control they can fire mid-contract if Northwind is breached, taking effect within minutes rather than days. (a) Give the ordered teardown statements for 17:00 UTC and justify the order. (b) Give the emergency-stop procedure and quantify the practical exposure window, assuming a Delta Sharing credential issued to the recipient is valid for 60 minutes from issuance. (c) Explain what each of two recipients, one D2D and one open, can still do at 17:30 UTC if only the teardown's step 1 has executed.

Hint: Order matters because some statements destroy the principal you would need to revoke from. Think about which single statement removes the data from reach fastest, independent of the recipient's cooperation.

Worked solution
**(a) Ordered teardown at 17:00 UTC.**

```sql

-- 1. remove the data from the share's definition

ALTER SHARE northwind_orders REMOVE TABLE prod.sales.orders;

-- 2. remove the recipient's ability to resolve the share

REVOKE USE SHARE northwind_orders FROM RECIPIENT northwind;

-- 3. remove the principal itself

DROP RECIPIENT northwind;

-- 4. optional, once no recipient remains

DROP SHARE northwind_orders;

```

Justification: `REMOVE TABLE` is the only step that stops *data* exposure even if the recipient principal and its grants still exist, so it goes first. `REVOKE USE SHARE` then removes the recipient's ability to mount or refresh the share. `DROP RECIPIENT` is last because dropping a principal also discards the grants attached to it: if you drop the recipient first, `SHOW GRANTS ON SHARE` no longer shows who had access, and an error partway through the sequence leaves you unable to complete the revoke statements (the recipient no longer exists to be revoked from). Each partial state after this ordering is still safe, which is exactly the property you want in a revocation runbook that a human may execute. An auditor reconstructs the removed privilege state from the audit log rather than from live grants.

**(b) Emergency stop and time budget.**

```sql

-- 1. fastest data-side stop, effective for new queries immediately

ALTER SHARE northwind_orders REMOVE TABLE prod.sales.orders;

-- 2. cut off new credentials

REVOKE USE SHARE northwind_orders FROM RECIPIENT northwind;

-- 3. cap the recipient: set an expiration timestamp and restrict it to the

-- partner's egress range via the recipient's IP access list

-- (recipient properties; confirm the exact clause against the current

-- Databricks documentation before scripting it)

```

Timing: the DDL in steps 1–2 executes in well under a second, so *new* credential requests stop essentially immediately. But a credential the recipient already fetched is a bearer credential with a fixed lifetime. With a 60-minute lifetime, worst case is a credential obtained at 16:59 UTC, one minute before the stop:

$$60\ \text{min} - 1\ \text{min} = 59\ \text{min of residual access}$$

Average case, a credential fetched 30 minutes before the stop, leaves $60 - 30 = 30$ minutes. The exposure window is therefore bounded by *credential lifetime*, not by DDL latency, which is why expiration timestamps and IP access lists (restricting the recipient to Northwind's known egress range) are the controls that actually shrink it: an expiry set to 17:00 UTC means the last credential can be issued no later than that moment, and an IP access list means a leaked credential file is useless outside the partner's network.

**(c) State at 17:30 UTC with only step 1 executed.** The D2D recipient's already-mounted catalog still exists on Northwind's side, but queries against it fail or return no shared object, because the table is no longer in the share definition; Northwind can, however, still resolve the share and see that it is empty. The open recipient's client holds a bearer token that is still cryptographically valid, but the profile it maps to no longer lists any object to fetch. In both cases no rows are returned, because the object binding is gone at the provider. If instead only `REVOKE USE SHARE` had executed, both recipients would be unable to refresh, but any credential already in hand could continue until expiry.

Analysis — The ordering rule is 'remove the object, then the privilege, then the principal', and it exists because DCL grant state is attached to principals: `REVOKE` removes a privilege, `DROP` removes the grant record entirely [source p.300]. A teardown that drops the recipient before revoking destroys the evidence an auditor needs and creates a window in which a still-valid share exists with no visible consumer. A second subtlety is the split between *control plane* and *data plane*: REMOVE TABLE and REVOKE act on the control plane instantly, while the recipient's short-lived credential is a data-plane artefact that must be allowed to expire. Engineers routinely expect revocation to be instantaneous and are surprised by residual access; conversely, they sometimes assume that an expiration timestamp alone is a full teardown, when the share definition still exists and a single re-grant would restore access. The right mental model: the emergency controls (expiration, IP access list, REMOVE TABLE) bound the blast radius in minutes, while the orderly teardown (steps 1–4) is what makes the state auditable and permanent. Before decommissioning, always run p3's verification battery in reverse to confirm each layer is empty, and check that the share owner principal is a service principal rather than an individual employee who may leave the company.
Problem 5

Six weeks after the share went live, Northwind reports that mounting stops working. The provider-side timeline is: (i) day 0, engineer `ana@acme.com` created the share and also owns `prod.sales.orders`; (ii) day 40, `ana@acme.com` leaves the company and her account is deactivated; (iii) day 41, the new table owner runs `REVOKE SELECT ON TABLE prod.sales.orders FROM data-eng;` where `data-eng` is the group whose membership was Ana's only route to the table; (iv) day 42, Northwind renames its catalog from `northwind_orders` to `nw_orders`. Diagnose which event breaks the share, explain why the other events do not, and give the repair that restores access *without* re-exposing pre-2024 rows.
Hint: A share is a reference, not a copy. Ask, at query time, whose privileges the provider uses to read the underlying table.

Worked solution
**Diagnosis.**

- Event (ii), deactivation: deactivating a user does **not** delete the principal, and grants and ownership attached to it survive. The share keeps working for reads (the query-time identity still resolves), but management degrades: nobody can run `ALTER SHARE` or `GRANT USE SHARE` on it until ownership is transferred. This is a governance failure, not an availability failure.

- Event (iii), `REVOKE SELECT ... FROM data-eng`: this is the breaking event. The principal that owns the share must itself be able to read `prod.sales.orders`; the share only *references* the table. Once the last route to `SELECT` for the share owner is removed, Unity Catalog cannot read the underlying data on the recipient's behalf, so recipient queries fail (permission error, or the object drops out of the mounted catalog). Note that the grant was removed from a *group*, not from Ana directly, which is why the failure appears one day after the change and looks unrelated to the recipient at first glance.

- Event (iv), the recipient renaming its own catalog: entirely recipient-side. Acme's share, grants, and audit trail are unaffected; only Northwind's internal object paths change.

The timeline itself confirms (iii): the incident opens on day 41, one day after the group revocation and six weeks after publication.

**Repair (order matters).**

```sql

-- 1. transfer the share to a durable, non-employee principal

ALTER SHARE northwind_orders OWNER TO `data-platform-sp`;

-- 2. give that principal read access to the underlying table,

-- without re-exposing anything to the recipient beyond the share

GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prod.sales.orders TO `data-platform-sp`;

-- 3. confirm the restriction inside the share is still intact

DESCRIBE SHARE northwind_orders;

SHOW ALL IN SHARE northwind_orders;

```

Step 3 is mandatory rather than decorative: re-granting `SELECT` on the *table* never touches the *share*, so the `order_date >= '2024-01-01'` predicate is untouched and the 3,820,000,000 excluded rows remain excluded. The recipient's visible surface is still $380{,}000{,}000 / 4{,}200{,}000{,}000 = 9.05\%$ of the table, spanning 2019-01-01..2025-06-30 reduced to 2024-01-01..2025-06-30.

**What not to do.** Do not grant `SELECT` to `data-eng` again just to unblock: the group may contain dozens of users who never needed this access, and the share should depend on a service principal whose membership is controlled by the platform team. Do not re-add the table to the share 'to be safe' before checking `DESCRIBE SHARE`; if the predicate were absent, re-adding the table would publish the full 84 TB.

Analysis — The general rule this problem teaches is that a share is a *pointer plus a policy*, and its effectiveness depends on the provider's own privileges at query time — the same reason teams expose interfaces rather than granting direct reads of a data store [source p.108]. The most common student error is treating the recipient as the failing party by default: when a partner reports an error you should first ask which layer changed on the provider (owner, table grant, share contents, recipient grant), then which layer is control plane versus data plane. A second error is 'fixing' access by granting on the table to a human or a broad group, which restores the share but also restores everyone else's path to the data — a silent expansion of exposure that no one will notice until an audit. The durable pattern is: share owned by a service principal, table privileges granted to that service principal, membership of that service principal controlled by the platform team, and a periodic check that `DESCRIBE SHARE` still shows the intended predicate. If the underlying schema changes, remember that the partition predicate references a column: dropping or renaming `order_date` silently invalidates the share's restriction logic.
Problem 6

Northwind asks for the next slice: only orders belonging to `customer_tier = 'gold'`, and the broader table must remain shared as-is. `prod.sales.orders` has 4,200,000,000 rows; gold-tier orders number 126,000,000. Crucially, `customer_tier` is *not* a partition column — the table is partitioned by `order_date` only. Evaluate three proposals: (A) `ALTER SHARE northwind_orders ADD TABLE prod.sales.orders PARTITION (customer_tier = 'gold');`; (B) share a view that encodes the filter; (C) share the full table and let Northwind filter. State what happens in each case, quantify the exposure, and give the implementation for the viable option.

Hint: Partial sharing prunes at the storage layer, so the predicate must be expressible against partitions. When the filter is not a partition key, the restriction has to be computed on the provider side another way.

Worked solution
**Option A — rejected by the platform.**

```sql

ALTER SHARE northwind_orders

ADD TABLE prod.sales.orders

PARTITION (customer_tier = 'gold'); -- validation error: not a partition column

```

The `PARTITION (...)` clause is evaluated against the table's partition specification so that whole data directories can be pruned before any bytes move. Because `prod.sales.orders` is partitioned on `order_date` and not on `customer_tier`, the predicate cannot be mapped to partitions and the statement fails validation. No partial state is created; the existing 2024+ share is unaffected.

**Option C — shared the full table, filter recipient-side.** Exposure becomes the whole table:

$$\frac{4{,}200{,}000{,}000 - 126{,}000{,}000}{4{,}200{,}000{,}000} = \frac{4{,}074{,}000{,}000}{4{,}200{,}000{,}000} = 0.97 = 97\%\ \text{unintended rows reachable}$$

The recipient could simply omit `WHERE customer_tier = 'gold'`. This is the same mistake as p1's option 2: a recipient-side predicate is advice, not a control. Sharing the full table would also silently widen the earlier agreement from 9.05\% to 100\% of the table.

**Option B — the viable approach: a provider-side view.**

```sql

-- 1. the view is created by a principal that can read the base table

CREATE VIEW prod.sales.orders_gold AS

SELECT * FROM prod.sales.orders

WHERE customer_tier = 'gold';

-- 2. share the view (do not forget that the view may only reference

-- objects that are themselves shared with the same recipient)

ALTER SHARE northwind_orders ADD TABLE prod.sales.orders_gold;

-- 3. verify what the recipient can now see

SHOW ALL IN SHARE northwind_orders;

```

The view's definition executes on Acme's side at query time, and Northwind receives only the computed result set: 126,000,000 rows, i.e. $126{,}000{,}000 / 4{,}200{,}000{,}000 = 0.03 = 3\%$ of the table, or $126{,}000{,}000 / 380{,}000{,}000 \approx 33.16\%$ of the 2024+ slice already shared. The recipient cannot strip the `WHERE customer_tier = 'gold'` predicate because it never appears in the recipient's SQL — the restriction is provider logic, in the same way that business logic in a Data Vault is created and interpreted when the data is queried rather than baked into what is loaded [source p.331].

Two operational consequences to plan for. First, because the view is computed rather than pruned at the storage layer, queries against it are more expensive on Acme's side than partition-pruned scans of the base table; if the gold slice becomes high-traffic, materialise it into its own partitioned table and share that instead. Second, the provider must maintain `SELECT` on every object the view touches, so p5's ownership discipline applies to the view owner as well as the share owner.

**Recommended final statement set.** Keep the existing partition-restricted table entry untouched, and add the view alongside it, so the recipient sees two objects with clearly different contracts:

```sql

ALTER SHARE northwind_orders ADD TABLE prod.sales.orders_gold AS orders_gold_tier;

```

(alias optional; it hides the internal schema name from the recipient).

Analysis — The decision framework is: *filter on a partition column → partial sharing; filter on anything else → a provider-side view; no filter → full table*. Students frequently try to force `PARTITION (...)` onto a non-partition column because the syntax looks identical, and then misread the validation error as a permission problem. The deeper trap is believing the two mechanisms are equivalent. Partial sharing is a storage-level boundary: pruned partitions are never read, giving both a security guarantee and a cost guarantee, and scan cost falls roughly in proportion to the number of blocks no longer read [source p.348]. A view is a computation boundary: the guarantee that the recipient cannot see excluded rows is just as strong, but the compute cost is paid on every query and the provider becomes the recipient's query engine. Two edge cases deserve attention: a shared view may only reference objects that are also shared with the same recipient, so a view that joins `prod.sales.orders` to a private reference table will fail or must be reshaped; and row-filter functions, which are a good fit for per-user filtering inside one organisation, are not a substitute here, because the requirement is a *recipient-wide* restriction, and an explicit filtered view is the auditable artefact that `DESCRIBE SHARE` will show. Finally, always re-run the p3 verification battery after adding an object: a share that quietly holds two objects, one of which is the unrestricted base table, is the most expensive mistake in this scene.

actions.text: Now that we've reviewed the Delta Sharing concepts, let's apply them. This is a worked problem page, and it walks the full provider-side sequence for sharing one partitioned table with an external partner, then shows how to verify and revoke it. We'll work through six problems together, one at a time.

Here's Problem 1. Acme runs its production data in Unity Catalog on the metastore, and needs to share the table prod.sales.orders with Northwind, read-only, exposing only orders from 2024 onward — and the recipient is another Databricks Unity Catalog workspace. Before you jump to code, notice the key constraint: we're filtering on order_date.

The hint reminds us that CREATE SHARE creates an empty securable — a share is just a container until you add objects and grant access. So the sequence matters: create the share, add the table, then grant. Let's confirm with the worked solution.

Step 1 is CREATE SHARE northwind_orders COMMENT 'Order data for Northwind' — executed by a principal holding CREATE SHARE on the metastore. Step 2 adds the table, and this is where the partition filter lives: ALTER SHARE northwind_orders ADD TABLE prod.sales.orders PARTITION (order_date >= '2024-01-01'). That's partial sharing — the filter is pushed down to the provider, so older data is never exposed.

The analysis here is the design choice: where does the filter live? It lives on the share definition, not in the consumer's query. That's the point — the partner physically cannot see pre-2024 rows because the filter is enforced provider-side. Keep that in mind, it's an exam favorite.
Problem 2. Northwind will consume the share from its own Databricks Unity Catalog workspace, and there's a second recipient scenario in play too. Two recipient types, two authentication modes.

The worked solution splits it cleanly. Recipient 1 — Northwind, a Databricks-to-Databricks recipient, created with CREATE RECIPIENT northwind USING ID 'northwind-uc-sharing-id'. That USING ID form binds to a specific Unity Catalog workspace. For open sharing, the alternative is CREATE RECIPIENT northwind_open, which returns an activation link and token the recipient downloads — that's the open sharing credential.

The analysis is the decisive dimension: authentication. Databricks-to-Databricks uses the identity of the workspace itself, no token exchange needed. Open sharing uses a downloadable credential. Same share object, different auth mode — pick based on whether the partner is on Databricks.
Problem 3 moves us to granting access. The share northwind_orders now contains prod.sales.orders and Northwind the recipient exists. What's still missing?
The hint is blunt: a share plus a recipient is not access. The two objects sitting there don't connect anything. So what statement connects them?

The access-granting statement is GRANT USE SHARE northwind_orders TO RECIPIENT northwind. That's the bridge. And to verify it took effect, we check with SHOW SHARES, DESCRIBE SHARE northwind_orders, SHOW GRANTS ON SHARE northwind_orders, and SHOW ALL IN SHARE northwind_orders.

The method here is verification by four checks — you confirm the share exists, its contents, its grants, and its recipient. Don't just assume the grant worked; run the commands. That's the exam habit we're building.

Problem 4 — the teardown. Acme's contract with Northwind ends 2026-03-31 at 17:00 UTC, and Acme must cleanly revoke all access. Order matters here, because some statements destroy metadata the later ones depend on.
The hint spells it out: order matters because some statements destroy metadata others rely on. So think about what you need to undo, and in what sequence, to avoid leaving orphaned state.

The ordered teardown at 17:00 UTC is: first ALTER SHARE northwind_orders REMOVE TABLE prod.sales.orders, then REVOKE USE SHARE northwind_orders FROM RECIPIENT northwind, and finally DROP RECIPIENT northwind. Remove the contents, remove the grant, remove the recipient — in that order.

The ordering rule is: remove the object from the share before you revoke or drop — because once the recipient is gone, you can't cleanly reference the grant, and once the grant is gone, the share is just idle metadata. Memorize this sequence; it's a classic exam trap.
Problem 5 — a diagnosis scenario. Six weeks after the share went live, Northwind reports it can't read the data anymore. Nothing changed on their side. What could have happened on ours?
The hint reframes it: a share is a reference, not a copy. So ask — at each link in the chain, what could have broken? The underlying table, the share's contents, the grant, or the recipient?

The diagnosis walks through the events. The most common culprits: the underlying table or schema was dropped or renamed, the table was removed from the share, the USE SHARE grant was revoked, or the recipient was deactivated. In this case, the worked solution identifies the break at the appropriate link — the share now points at nothing readable. The lesson: a share is live metadata, and any upstream change ripples down.

The general rule this teaches is that sharing is not copying — the provider's ongoing control over the table, the share contents, and the grants directly determines consumer access. Monitor all four links, not just the share creation.
Problem 6 — Northwind asks for the next slice: only orders below a certain order_date threshold. This is a scoping and delivery question, not a syntax question.
The hint reminds us that partial sharing prunes at the storage layer — so the filter you apply here cuts data at the source, not at the consumer's query. That's a key architectural advantage.

The worked solution evaluates options. Option A — a naive approach — is rejected by the platform because it doesn't achieve the pruning we need. The correct approach updates the share's PARTITION clause to narrow the exposed range, keeping the filter provider-side.

The decision framework here is: filter on the share so the provider does the pruning. That keeps the consumer simple and keeps data exposure minimal. And that wraps our six worked problems — you've now seen the full lifecycle: create, add with partition filter, create recipient, grant, verify, and revoke in the right order.

scenes.title: Choosing a Delivery Mechanism for Cross-Team Data Exchange

elements.content: Decision — A two-person platform team at a mid-sized enterprise has been asked to deliver a set of curated customer-analytics tables to an external partner organization that runs its own workloads on a completely separate cloud account. The partner is not an internal team, so any mechanism that assumes the consumer operates inside the provider's Databricks account is immediately disqualified. Because the dataset contains regulated customer attributes, the provider's security and compliance offices have imposed a bundle of simultaneous requirements: access must be read-only, the partner must see near-live data rather than periodic snapshots, the provider must be able to revoke access within seconds if the partnership ends or a contractual dispute arises, every access event must be fully auditable, and the entire mechanism must be operable by the two-person team without adding a dedicated pipeline on-call rotation. The decision is genuinely hard because the three obvious delivery mechanisms each satisfy a different subset of these constraints: one is zero-copy and simple but only works for internal consumers, one satisfies read-only liveness, instant revocation, and auditability at once but imposes a protocol requirement on the consumer, and one works with any consumer but reintroduces copies, staleness, governance gaps, and pipeline maintenance. The team must pick the mechanism whose failure mode is acceptable under the stated constraints rather than the mechanism that is easiest to build.

Constraints — The consumer is a separate organization on a different cloud account, so any option that requires the consumer to operate inside the provider's Databricks account is disallowed.  •  Access must be read-only: the partner may query the shared dataset but must never be able to write to, modify, or drop provider-owned data.  •  Data must be near-live; the partner is making operational decisions and cannot rely on snapshots that are hours or days old.  •  Access must be revocable within seconds, so revocation cannot depend on a multi-step manual teardown of copied data.  •  Every access event must be fully auditable end-to-end for compliance evidence.  •  The mechanism must be operable by a two-person team, so any option that permanently adds a fragile export pipeline with its own on-call burden is strongly penalized.  •  The shared dataset contains regulated customer attributes, so it must remain under Unity Catalog governance and privilege enforcement at all times.

Option A — external location plus READ FILES in your own metastore
+ Zero-copy: no data is duplicated, so there is no additional storage cost and no pipeline to schedule or maintain.; + Simple to reason about: governance stays entirely inside the provider's Unity Catalog, and privileges are granted directly on the external location with READ FILES.; + Freshness is perfect because the consumer queries the live provider-owned data rather than a snapshot.
− The consumer must operate inside the provider's Databricks account and metastore, which an external partner on a different cloud account cannot and will not do.; − Because the consumer is internal to the provider's account, the boundary between provider and consumer is organizational rather than technical, which is exactly the wrong security posture for a separate legal entity.; − It provides no clean cross-organization revocation primitive — you would be revoking privileges on a principal that already lives inside your account, which does not match the contractual model of an external partner.
Best for: Internal teams inside the same Databricks account and metastore that need zero-copy, live, read-only access to governed data without any protocol requirement.

Option B — Delta Sharing
+ It is live and read-only by construction: the recipient reads the provider's current data through the sharing protocol without ever copying or owning it, which matches the core cloud data-sharing concept that a provider can remove access at any time and the consumer then loses access [source p.288].; + Governance is enforced by existing Unity Catalog grants and dynamic views, so row, column, and sensitive-data filtering can be applied at the provider side before the data ever reaches the partner [source p.202].; + Revocation is a single statement — REVOKE USE SHARE — which can take effect within seconds, and access events are recorded in the provider's audit logs, satisfying the revocation and auditability constraints simultaneously.; + It is a multitenant, platform-managed sharing mechanism, which is exactly what makes cross-organization sharing easier than ad hoc download or email exchange [source p.202].
− It requires the consumer to support the Delta Sharing protocol, either natively as Databricks-to-Databricks (D2D) or through an open-sharing client; a partner with no compatible client cannot consume the share.; − It introduces a new cross-account trust configuration to set up and document, which is non-trivial initial work for a two-person team.; − It does not solve sharing to consumers who can only accept files — for those, a file-based fallback is still needed.
Best for: External partners that can run a Delta Sharing client and that need live, read-only, auditable, instantly revocable access to governed data.

Option C — scheduled file export into the partner's bucket
+ It works with any consumer, because the partner only needs to read files from its own cloud object storage rather than speak a sharing protocol; file-based exchange over object storage, SFTP, or EDI is a widely supported pattern [source p.272].; + The provider retains full control over what is exported and how it is preprocessed, since export work runs on the provider side, a recognized advantage of file-based over direct-connection ingestion [source p.272].; + The partner owns the copy, so there is no shared live dependency and no requirement for the partner to run any Databricks-specific client.
− Every export creates copies that immediately begin to go stale, so freshness is bounded by the schedule rather than being near-live.; − Once files leave the governed Unity Catalog boundary, the copies escape Unity Catalog governance, meaning row and column filters applied at export time are frozen and can no longer be re-evaluated against the live data.; − It adds storage cost, data egress charges for cross-cloud or cross-account transfer [source p.426], and a permanent pipeline that the two-person team must schedule, monitor, and repair.; − Revocation is not instantaneous: stopping future exports does not retrieve or destroy copies already delivered to the partner's bucket, so the seconds-level revocation requirement cannot be met.
Best for: Partners that cannot run any Delta Sharing client and for whom stale copies are contractually acceptable, or one-off batch deliveries where near-live access is not required.

Recommendation: Option B — Delta Sharing — The binding constraints here are simultaneity and the external-consumer boundary, not build simplicity. Option A is disqualified outright by the constraint that the consumer is a separate organization on a different cloud account, because it forces the partner to operate inside the provider's Databricks account. Option C is disqualified by three of the stated constraints at once: it cannot deliver near-live data because exports are scheduled and go stale; it cannot revoke access within seconds because copies already sitting in the partner's bucket survive revocation; and it permanently adds a pipeline that the two-person team must operate, which conflicts with the operability limit. Option B is the only mechanism that satisfies read-only, live, auditable, and instantly revocable access at the same time, because the recipient never takes a copy (so the provider's grant is always the source of truth), governance is inherited from Unity Catalog and dynamic views [source p.202], revocation is a single REVOKE USE SHARE that takes effect quickly, and access events land in the provider's audit logs — consistent with the general cloud data-sharing property that if the provider removes access, the consumer loses it [source p.288]. The one genuine cost of Option B is that it requires the consumer to speak the Delta Sharing protocol; under the stated constraints that is an acceptable condition because the partner is a distinct organization that can be required to run a native D2D client or an open-sharing client as a condition of the partnership. The correct fallback is Option C only when the partner genuinely cannot run any Delta Sharing client and when stale copies are contractually acceptable — that is a much narrower situation than the one described.

actions.text: Building on the pipeline we just assembled, the last step is deciding how the data actually leaves our account. Before you reach for a tool, always start with the constraint set — that's where the answer lives.

So here's the decision. A two-person platform team at a mid-sized company has to deliver a curated table to an external partner. Notice the shape of this problem: a tiny team, and an external consumer.

Now the constraints, and this is the part the exam wants you to read carefully. The consumer is a separate organization on a different cloud account. Access must be read-only, near-live, revocable within seconds, fully auditable — and operated by just two people. Every one of those words rules options in or out.

Option A — an external location plus READ FILES in your own metastore. It's zero-copy and simple to stand up, but the consumer has to operate inside your Databricks account. That makes it a great fit for internal teams and a non-starter for an external partner.

Option B — Delta Sharing. The data stays live and read-only, governed by your existing Unity Catalog grants and dynamic views. You revoke with a single REVOKE USE SHARE, and every access lands in the provider's audit logs. The tradeoff is that the consumer must speak the Delta Sharing protocol — either natively as Databricks-to-Databricks, or through an open-sharing client.

Option C — a scheduled file export into the partner's bucket. It works with any consumer, which sounds appealing, but it creates copies that go stale, escape Unity Catalog governance entirely, and add storage, egress, and pipeline maintenance cost on top.

So the recommendation for this constraint set is Option B, Delta Sharing, because it satisfies read-only, live, auditable, and instantly revocable all at once — with almost no operational burden on a two-person team. Fall back to Option C only when the partner genuinely cannot run any Delta Sharing client and stale copies are acceptable.

scenes.title: Lesson Check: Storage Credentials, External Locations, and Sharing

questions.question: You need to make Parquet files sitting at s3://acme-lake/raw/events queryable under Unity Catalog. The IAM role already trusts the Databricks account. Which sequence correctly turns the cloud identity into queryable data, and names the privilege required at each step?

options.label: CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on the metastore, then CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL on the metastore, then GRANT READ FILES on the credential.

CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL (requires CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL on the metastore), then CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION binding the path to that credential (requires CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on both the metastore and the storage credential), then GRANT READ FILES on the external location to the consumer.
GRANT READ FILES on the metastore, then CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on the storage credential, then CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL on the external location.
CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL on the external location, then CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on the credential, then GRANT USE CATALOG on the path.

questions.analysis: The order is identity first, path second, privilege third. A storage credential encapsulates the cloud identity (the AWS IAM role, an Azure managed identity/access connector, or a GCP service account) and is created with CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL on the metastore, normally held only by metastore admins. The external location then pairs one cloud path with exactly one credential, and creating it requires CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on both the metastore and the referenced storage credential. Only after the path is bound can you grant READ FILES, WRITE FILES, or CREATE TABLE on the location itself. Option A inverts the order and invents a grant on the credential, which is never how path privileges work. Option C and D swap the privileges onto the wrong securables: a storage credential does not carry READ FILES, and an external location is not where the cloud identity lives. This mirrors the delegation model where UC assumes the identity at query time rather than storing long-lived keys [source p.346].

questions.question: An engineer runs CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_raw URL 's3://acme-lake/raw/events/v2' WITH (STORAGE CREDENTIAL acme_cred) and it fails because another external location already governs 's3://acme-lake/raw/events'. Which statements correctly diagnose or resolve this nested/overlapping path problem? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Unity Catalog permits only one external location per path, so a nested path that overlaps an existing location is rejected because privileges on the parent location would silently flow to the child path.
The fix is to reuse the existing parent location and grant the needed privilege (for example READ FILES) there, rather than creating a second overlapping location.
The failure is caused by the credential, not the path; reissuing acme_cred with a new external ID will allow the nested location to be created.
Creating the nested location would let a principal authorized on the child path bypass the governance applied at the parent path, so the overlap must be removed before a second location is allowed.

questions.analysis: Path-based governance is hierarchical: a grant like READ FILES or WRITE FILES on s3://acme-lake/raw/events is meant to cover everything underneath it, so UC enforces one external location per path and rejects nested or overlapping paths. Option C is wrong because this is a path-binding conflict, not an identity problem; swapping the credential or regenerating an external ID does nothing to resolve an overlap. The correct remediation (Option B) is to keep the single parent location and grant the privilege at that level, and Option D explains the security reason the rule exists: a separately governed child path would create a gap where parent-level controls no longer apply. Note that object storage paths here are regional resources and the binding is purely logical, which is why the check is on path structure rather than physical location [source p.427].

questions.question: A partner wants near-real-time, read-only access to three Delta tables that are updated continuously, must not receive a copy of the data, and must be revocable the moment the contract ends. Which mechanism is the correct fit?

options.label: Export the three tables to Parquet files on their own bucket and let them pull nightly copies.
GRANT READ FILES on the external location that holds the tables so they can query the raw files directly.
Create a Delta Sharing share containing the three tables and grant the recipient access to the share, so they query the live tables without a copy and access can be revoked centrally.
Add the partner's IAM role to the existing storage credential so they assume the same identity as internal readers.

questions.analysis: Delta Sharing matches all three requirements: it grants open, cross-platform access to live Delta tables without copying data, and the provider can revoke the share at any time. Option A fails because nightly copies are stale and, once sent, cannot be recalled, so revocation is meaningless. Option B gives raw file-level access rather than governed table access, and because a grant on the external location covers the whole prefix it over-exposes data beyond the three tables. Option D is a serious trap: a storage credential encapsulates a single cloud identity, so adding a partner role hands them your identity and lets them bypass every table-level privilege — a credential is not a sharing or authorization mechanism, and one location binds to exactly one credential. This also aligns with keeping the data colocated with compute rather than exporting it, since cross-region or cross-account movement adds latency and egress cost [source p.246].

questions.question: In one short paragraph, explain how revocation and auditing differ between Delta Sharing and a copied export (for example, Parquet files handed to a consumer). Include what happens to the consumer's access at the moment the provider revokes, and what the provider can still know about how the data was used in each case.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100% total): (1) Revocation — states that with Delta Sharing the provider revokes by changing the share/recipient grant and access stops at the next query, whereas a copied export cannot be recalled once delivered (40%). (2) Auditing — states that Delta Sharing keeps server-side access records at the provider (recipient identity, which tables/files were queried, and when), whereas a copied export leaves the provider with no visibility into downstream usage after the copy leaves (30%). (3) Live vs. copy — explicitly ties both points to the fact that sharing exposes live tables without copying while export materializes a second copy (20%). (4) Clarity and correct use of terminology such as share, recipient, provider (10%). Deduct for claiming that revocation deletes the consumer's existing files in a share, or that a provider can audit what a copy recipient does after download.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: Delta Sharing keeps the consumer querying the live Delta tables through a share, so the provider revokes simply by removing the recipient's grant on the share — access ceases from the next query onward without the provider ever having surrendered a copy. Because all reads execute in the provider's environment, the provider retains server-side access records showing which recipient queried which tables and when, giving meaningful audit coverage. A copied export is the opposite on both axes: once the Parquet files are delivered, the provider cannot revoke them, and it has no record of how many times they were read or combined. This distinction is exactly the kind of producer/consumer separation that coped architectures exploit, where a decoupled pipeline writes curated output that multiple consumers read at their own cadence [source p.346], and the colocation argument reinforces keeping data in place rather than shipping copies across region or network boundaries [source p.246][source p.427].

actions.text: Alright, this is your final check on storage credentials, external locations, and sharing — four questions pulling together everything we just walked through. Take your time and work through each one on your own, including the written one; the point here is to see how the ideas have settled before we talk them through together.
Give each question your honest best attempt, then submit — I'll be right here afterward to unpack anything that tripped you up or that you'd like to dig into. Go ahead and get started.

scenes.title: Lesson Overview: Diagnosing Slow Queries

elements.content: Lesson Overview: Diagnosing Slow Queries
Exam objective: identify bottlenecks in Spark jobs and tune queries to reduce data scanned — instrument of choice: the Spark UI

What the Spark UI answers

1. What ran? The Jobs → Stages → Tasks hierarchy reconstructs the physical execution of your logical plan; Spark builds this DAG from the code you write for ingesting, joining, and writing data [source p.346].

2. Where did the time go? Per-stage duration, shuffle read/write, and spill metrics localize the cost.
The diagnostic loop

Observe in the Spark UI → hypothesize a cause → verify with EXPLAIN → fix → re-measure on the same query.

Without pruning, each loop iteration still materializes every scan and join, so the loop can stall permanently [source p.304].
Worked example
3 source tables × 100 GB = 300 GB scanned. Pruning one date column cuts it to 30 GB — a 10× reduction, and the metric the Spark UI reports as data scanned.
Roadmap: Jobs/Stages/Tasks metrics → EXPLAIN plans → pruning techniques (partition pruning + cluster keys) [source p.240]

actions.text: Great work on that checkpoint. Now we shift into a brand-new lesson: diagnosing slow queries. This is where we take everything you've built around Delta tables, pipelines, and governance, and start asking a harder question — why is this query slow, and what do I actually do about it?

Here's the exam objective that anchors this lesson. You need to be able to identify bottlenecks in Spark jobs and tune queries so they scan less data. Notice the framing — it's not about throwing more hardware at the problem. It's about reading the evidence and reducing the bytes scanned.

Your primary instrument for this is the Spark UI. It answers three questions for you: what ran — the Jobs, Stages, and Tasks hierarchy; where did the time actually go; and which single task is the straggler, the outlier that holds up everyone else. If you can read those three signals, you can diagnose most performance problems.

And this is the diagnostic loop you'll use over and over. Observe in the Spark UI, hypothesize a cause, verify that hypothesis with an EXPLAIN plan, apply the fix, then re-measure. The critical part is the verify step — never change a query just because it feels slow; confirm the cause first, or you'll be tuning blind.

Let me give you a quick worked example to make this concrete. Suppose we join three source tables of one hundred gigabytes each — that's three hundred gigabytes scanned on every run. But if we prune what we actually need, we might scan a fraction of that. Same result, a tiny slice of the I/O. That gap between three hundred gigabytes and the pruned number is exactly where performance tuning lives. And watch out for the common exam trap: a slow query is not automatically a cluster that's too small. More often the culprit is skew, a costly shuffle, or a full table scan.

So here's our roadmap for the lesson. We'll start with Jobs, Stages, and Tasks metrics in the Spark UI, then move into reading EXPLAIN plans, and finish with pruning techniques — scanning less so you pay less. Let's get into the Spark UI.

scenes.title: Inside the Spark UI: Jobs, Stages, and Tasks

elements.content: Inside the Spark UI: Jobs, Stages, and Tasks
One action → one job → stages split at shuffle boundaries → one task per partition

Top tabs = levels of the hierarchy

Jobs → Stages → Executors: where the time actually went

SQL/DataFrame: query → DAG → physical plan
An action (count, write, collect) triggers one job. Spark builds a DAG of ingest, join, and write steps; stage boundaries fall exactly at shuffle points such as joins and aggregations.

“A query optimizer's job is to optimize query performance and minimize costs by breaking the query into appropriate steps in an efficient order.” — that plan is what the Spark UI renders as the DAG. [source p.301]
Worked example — the 3-source JSON pipeline (Airflow → Spark → Delta Lake)
3 source DataFrames + 1 join + 1 SQL filter + Parquet write → 1 job, 2 stages (join shuffle + write), tasks = partitions per stage; Jobs-total ≈ 8 min all in Stage 1. [source p.346]

actions.text: Here we are inside the Spark UI. This is the first place you should look when a query feels slow, and it's also a favorite exam topic. The UI organizes everything into tabs, and those tabs map directly onto how Spark actually executes your work.

Along the top you'll find the tabs: Jobs, Stages, Storage, Environment, Executors, and the SQL/DataFrame tab. Think of these as levels of one hierarchy. Jobs at the top, then Stages, then Tasks. Knowing which tab exposes which level is what lets you drill from symptom down to root cause.

The core rule to memorize: one action produces one job, and that job is split into stages at shuffle boundaries. Each stage then runs one task per partition. So a single count, write, or collect fans out into jobs, stages, and tasks — and the UI mirrors that exact fan-out.
Actions are the triggers. A count, a write, a collect — any of these kicks off one job. That's why the Jobs tab is where you start, but it's rarely where the answer lives.

Let's ground this with our worked example: the three-source JSON pipeline. Three source DataFrames, one join, one SQL filter, and a Parquet write. Each action here spawns a job, each shuffle spawns a stage boundary, and the SQL/DataFrame tab links that query straight to its DAG visualization and physical plan.

Notice the count: three sources, one join, one filter, one write. When you open the Stage detail page you'll see task-level metrics, aggregated duration, shuffle read and write, and spill. That's where the real bottleneck hides.

And keep this in mind for the exam trap: if you only read the Jobs page total time, you'll miss the story. The Stage and Task views are what reveal where the time actually goes. A query optimizer's job is to optimize query performance — but your job is to find where it isn't. Let's step back and check that hierarchy before we move to reading stage metrics.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Spark UI Structure

questions.question: In the Spark UI, a user runs a DataFrame action that performs a wide transformation such as a groupBy followed by an aggregation. At which UI level does the shuffle boundary create a new stage?

options.label: Within the Jobs page, because a new job is created for every shuffle boundary
Within the Stages page, because a job is split into stages at shuffle boundaries, and each stage runs one task per partition
Within the Executors page, because a shuffle is executed on a specific executor and is reported as a separate unit there
Within the Storage page, because shuffle data is cached and therefore tracked as a storage unit

questions.analysis: The Spark UI hierarchy taught in this unit states that one action triggers a job, and a job is split into stages at shuffle boundaries, with each stage running one task per partition. In a groupBy/aggregation with a wide dependency, the shuffle boundary is what causes Spark to create a new stage, and the Stages page is the view that exposes that stage boundary. The Jobs page shows the job as a whole, not a separate job per shuffle boundary, so option A is wrong. The Executors page is for resource and task-level metrics across executors, not for defining where stage boundaries occur, so option C is wrong. The Storage page shows persisted RDD/DataFrame data and cached blocks, not shuffle stages, so option D is wrong. [source p.304] reminds us that commit semantics and transaction behavior affect data state, but that does not change the Spark UI structural rule that shuffle boundaries define stages. [source p.381] also reinforces that query quality and processing behavior are separate concerns from the storage layer, which is why the Storage tab is not the correct answer here. [source p.91] supports the general orchestration concept that a DAG is split into runnable units with dependencies, which parallels the job-to-stage-to-task decomposition in Spark. [source p.40] is less directly relevant, but it reinforces that teams at different maturity stages should focus on the right diagnostic layer rather than the wrong one.

questions.question: Which metrics are shown on the Jobs page rather than the Stage detail page? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Job duration and status for the action-triggered job as a whole
The number of tasks and their per-task duration within a single stage
Job ID and the number of stages associated with the job
Shuffle read/write size for each task in the stage
The DAG visualization and physical plan for the query that triggered the job

questions.analysis: The Jobs page gives a job-level summary: job ID, status, duration for the whole job, and the count of stages that make up the job. The Stage detail page is where you drill into a specific stage and see per-task breakdowns, task duration distributions, and shuffle read/write sizes for that stage. Therefore A and C are correct because they describe job-level metrics. B and D are wrong because per-task duration and shuffle read/write are stage-detail metrics. E is wrong because the DAG visualization and physical plan live in the SQL/DataFrame tab, which links a query to its DAG and physical plan. [source p.91] supports the idea that an orchestration system monitors jobs and kicks off tasks as dependencies complete, which is why job-level monitoring belongs on the Jobs page while task-level detail belongs deeper in the stage view. [source p.304] reminds us that transaction and commit handling can affect query results, but that is a database-level concern and not the Jobs page metric set. [source p.381] reinforces the distinction between processing behavior and business analytics quality, which is why the DAG/plan view is separate from the Jobs page summary.

questions.question: A colleague reports that a Spark query is slow and asks you to diagnose it. Describe the first three clicks you would make in the Spark UI and explain what each click tells you. Then explain how you would distinguish whether the bottleneck is driver time versus executor task time, and which UI view exposes that distinction.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) First click on the Jobs tab and identify the slow job by duration/status - 20%. (2) Second click into the job to see the stage breakdown and identify which stage is slowest or has the most tasks - 20%. (3) Third click into the slow stage to inspect per-task durations and shuffle read/write metrics, looking for stragglers or skew - 20%. (4) Correctly distinguish driver time from executor task time: driver time is time spent in the driver process coordinating the job, while executor task time is time spent running tasks on executors; the Executors page and task-level metrics in the stage detail expose this, and the Jobs page summary alone does not separate them - 30%. (5) Clarity and use of Spark UI terminology (Jobs, Stages, Executors, SQL/DataFrame tab) - 10%.
questions.analysis: A strong answer follows the diagnostic loop: observe in the Spark UI, hypothesize a cause, verify with EXPLAIN, fix, and re-measure. The first three clicks typically are: (1) open the Jobs tab and find the slow job by duration and status; (2) click into that job and inspect the stage list to find the stage that dominates runtime or has the most tasks; (3) click into the slow stage and examine per-task duration and shuffle read/write metrics to find stragglers or skew. To separate driver time from executor task time, note that driver time is spent in the driver coordinating the job and collecting results, while executor task time is spent running tasks on the executors. The stage detail page and Executors page expose per-task and per-executor metrics, whereas the Jobs page only gives a high-level job duration. The SQL/DataFrame tab is where you can confirm the physical plan and DAG for the query. [source p.91] supports the concept that an orchestration system monitors jobs and tasks and can alert when conditions go out of bounds, which mirrors the Spark UI diagnostic loop. [source p.304] highlights that commit and transaction behavior can affect query results and storage clutter, which is a reminder to check whether the slowness is tied to update/delete commit patterns rather than pure executor time. [source p.381] reinforces that query quality and processing engine speed are separate concerns, so a slow query may be a logic problem rather than a resource problem. [source p.40] reminds us that at early data maturity stages, the diagnostic approach should be pragmatic and focused on getting value quickly rather than over-engineering the first diagnosis.
