scenes.title: Reading Stage and Task Metrics Like a Diagnostician

elements.content: Stage- & Task-Level Metrics: Reading a Job Like a Diagnostician

A stage is split at shuffle boundaries and runs one task per partition; diagnosing means comparing tasks inside a stage, not just adding up stage time. A wide transformation forces memory to buffer records before the hash repartition, which is exactly where spill metrics appear. [source p.337] Spark's own pipeline example notes that ingestion runs in cluster memory but a large source can still spill to disk. [source p.346]

1. Task Duration Distribution

Read min / median / max, not the average.

2. Shuffle Read / Write Size

Ambient cost of a wide transformation.

Worked example — reading the distribution

Stage of 200 tasks: min = 4 s, p50 = 5 s, p99 = 240 s, max = 300 s. Skew ratio = max / median = 300 / 5 = 60×.

Wall time ≈ slowest partition ≈ 300 s, while all healthy partitions finished by 5 s → a partition read all the keys of one hot join key.

elements.html: skew ratio=task mediantask max​
Tstage​≈imax​Ti​≫avg(T)

actions.text: Nice work on that checkpoint. Now that you know how the Spark UI is organized, let's put it to practical use. This page is about reading stage- and task-level metrics the way a diagnostician reads symptoms — the numbers tell you which of four problems you're actually facing: skew, excessive shuffling, memory pressure, or garbage collection overhead.

First, remember the unit of analysis. A stage is split at shuffle boundaries, and each stage runs on a set of partitions, one task per partition. So when you open a stage and look at the task list, you're really looking at how evenly the work was distributed across partitions — that's what makes the metrics readable.

Start with task duration distribution. Don't look at the average — compare min, median, and max. If the median task finishes in two seconds and the max takes two minutes, the work is unevenly packed, and that's your tell for data skew. A large max-over-median ratio is the single most reliable skew signal in the whole Spark UI.

Next, Shuffle Read and Shuffle Write sizes. These represent the ambient cost of a wide transformation — every GROUP BY, every JOIN that isn't broadcast, every repartition. Big shuffle numbers tell you either the transformation is inherently expensive or your join strategy is wrong, because a small dimension table that should have been broadcast is being shuffled across the network instead.

Speaking of skew, here's the formula worth memorizing: skew ratio equals the max partition size divided by the median partition size. A ratio near one means even distribution. A ratio of ten means the largest partition holds ten times the typical one — and since a stage's wall-clock time is bounded by its slowest task, one skewed partition can dominate the entire stage.

That's exactly why stage duration is approximately the max over tasks of each task's duration. Notice this is a maximum, not a sum — a thousand fast tasks finish in a blink, but one straggler holds the whole stage hostage. Anytime a stage takes far longer than the sum of its average task times would suggest, you know to check the distribution.

Let's walk through a worked example of reading that distribution. Suppose you see a stage with a hundred tasks, median duration of three seconds, and a max of ninety seconds. The suite finished in ninety seconds, not in three. Nothing about the code is wrong — the data volume per key is. The remedy is a salting technique or an AQE skew join, not more clusters.

This table ties it all together: each symptom mapped to the metric that reveals it and the tuning lever that fixes it. Skew maps to duration ratio and salting. Shuffle maps to shuffle bytes and broadcast joins. Spill maps to execution memory and larger partitions. GC maps to GC time and reduced object churn. Learn the pattern — metric, symptom, remedy — because exam questions will hand you a scenario and expect that mapping back.

And one last trap worth flagging now: don't treat high total duration as the problem itself. Total duration is the symptom. The metric that actually matters is which task is the outlier. Almost every distractor on the exam that says 'the job is slow, add more executors' is wrong — the right answer points at the outlier and the lever that fixes it. Let's try that in the interactive lab coming up next.

widgetConfig.description: Diagnose Spark stage performance: adjust shuffle partitions and data skew, observe task duration distribution, shuffle size, and spill.

actions.text: So let's put that diagnosis instinct to work. This explorer simulates a real Spark stage view, and your job is to read the task duration distribution the way you'd read it in the Spark UI. Start by looking at the controls, then we'll walk through a few scenarios.

actions.content: Shuffle partitions, skew factor, and shuffle volume — the three levers behind stage performance.
Balanced baseline: 200 partitions, no skew.
Watch min, median, and max task duration — in a healthy stage these sit close together.

actions.text: Notice the tight band. When min, median, and max are close, every task is finishing around the same time. That's the signal of a well-shaped stage — no single task is holding up the shuffle read on the rest of the cluster.

actions.content: Now inject a hot key at 0.85 skew — the classic skew signature.
The max task duration blows out while the median stays put — that's your outlier.

actions.text: See the disaster now. The median says the stage is fine, but the max task duration is enormous, and spill is climbing because one partition is chewing through a mountain of data. This is exactly the skew pattern we discussed — a few tasks dominate the stage runtime while most executors sit idle waiting for them.

actions.content: Crank partitions to 600 with no skew — shrinking each partition, not fixing the shape.
Task count is high, but check the durations — many tiny tasks mean scheduler overhead.

actions.text: Adding partitions here didn't help the runtime — it just fragmented the work into many small tasks and added scheduling overhead. More partitions is not automatically better. The lever that matters is flattening the duration distribution, not multiplying the task count.

actions.content: The fix: a sensible partition count with the skew gone — watch the distribution flatten.

actions.text: That's the flattened distribution — min, median, and max cluster together again, spill drops, and the stage finishes faster. Flatter tasks mean less waiting, shorter cluster wall-clock time, and lower cost. Before we move on, try dragging the sliders yourself and see how quickly a hot key can undo a good partition count.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Diagnosing Stage Bottlenecks

questions.question: You inspect the Stage detail page for a shuffle-heavy Spark stage in a Databricks job. The stage has 200 tasks. Task durations are: minimum 1.2 s, median 1.5 s, and maximum 92 s. Shuffle Read is roughly balanced across tasks, and Spill (Disk) is near zero on all tasks. Based on this evidence, what is the most likely diagnosis for the bottleneck?

options.label: The stage is dominated by data skew, because the maximum task duration vastly exceeds the median and only a few tasks dominate the stage runtime
The stage is spilling to disk, because the max task duration is high and spill is a prerequisite for long-running tasks
The stage is bottlenecked by the number of shuffle partitions being too large, because 200 tasks implies excessive scheduler overhead
The stage is bottlenecked by slow network shuffle, because Shuffle Read is balanced and therefore must be the dominant cost

questions.correctAnswer: The stage is dominated by data skew, because the maximum task duration vastly exceeds the median and only a few tasks dominate the stage runtime
questions.analysis: The key signal is the duration distribution itself: min=1.2 s, median=1.5 s, max=92 s. That is a max/median ratio of roughly 61x, which is exactly the pattern you learned to treat as a skew signature in the earlier lesson on reading stage and task metrics like a diagnostician. When a stage is skewed, a small number of partitions hold a disproportionate share of the rows, so those few tasks run far longer than the rest and effectively set the stage wall-clock time; the other ~195 tasks finish quickly and idle. Note the distractors: 'Spill (Disk) near zero on all tasks' rules out the spill explanation, because spill is a memory-pressure symptom, not a consequence of long duration; 200 tasks with balanced shuffle read argues against a 'too many partitions' scheduler-overhead story; and balanced Shuffle Read means no single task read dramatically more data over the network as its dominant cost. Exam takeaway: translate the histogram shape (long tail) into the named bottleneck (skew) before selecting any remedy.
answer: The stage is dominated by data skew, because the maximum task duration vastly exceeds the median and only a few tasks dominate the stage runtime

questions.question: A wide transformation (groupBy + join) runs for 40 minutes. You see Shuffle Write = 380 GB, Spill (Disk) = 0 GB on every task, and GC time = 0.4 s per task. Task durations are tightly clustered around the median with a max/median ratio of 1.3. Which statements about the dominant cost and the correct first corrective action are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The dominant cost is shuffle I/O, and the first corrective action should be to reduce shuffle volume by repartitioning on a high-cardinality key and/or choosing a more appropriate join strategy such as a broadcast join where one side is small
The dominant cost is shuffle I/O, and the first corrective action should be to add more workers to the cluster
The tightly clustered task durations confirm that skew is the dominant problem, so the first corrective action is to salt the join key
Spill (Disk) = 0 GB excludes execution-memory pressure as the named bottleneck for this stage, because spill is the observable symptom of a partition exceeding its execution memory

questions.correctAnswer: The dominant cost is shuffle I/O, and the first corrective action should be to reduce shuffle volume by repartitioning on a high-cardinality key and/or choosing a more appropriate join strategy such as a broadcast join where one side is small; Spill (Disk) = 0 GB excludes execution-memory pressure as the named bottleneck for this stage, because spill is the observable symptom of a partition exceeding its execution memory
questions.analysis: This item forces you to separate 'spill versus shuffle' using the metrics rather than by intuition. Shuffle Write = 380 GB indicates a very expensive wide transformation, and the flat task-duration distribution (max/median 1.3) plus negligible GC rules out both skew and memory-pressure as the named bottleneck. Therefore the correct diagnosis is shuffle I/O, and the first action is to reduce the shuffled bytes — repartition on a well-distributed key and/or switch to a broadcast join if one side is small enough — rather than buying more compute. 'Add more workers' is the classic exam distractor: it increases aggregate capacity but does not reduce the amount of data each shuffle partition must move, so wall-clock time and cost may improve only marginally while the underlying bottleneck persists. Zero spill means no partition exceeded its execution memory, so execution-memory pressure cannot be the named bottleneck for this stage. Finally, tightly clustered durations are the opposite of skew, so salting the key would be an incorrect remedy here, even though salting is a valid skew fix in other contexts. For context on how distributed systems scale horizontally by adding worker nodes and how a leader distributes tasks to those workers, see [source p.115], which explains that adding machines satisfies load but does not by itself reshape the data distribution. And for why joins — the very operation producing this shuffle — become substantially more complex and costly as processing moves closer to continuous execution, see [source p.93].
answer: The dominant cost is shuffle I/O, and the first corrective action should be to reduce shuffle volume by repartitioning on a high-cardinality key and/or choosing a more appropriate join strategy such as a broadcast join where one side is small; Spill (Disk) = 0 GB excludes execution-memory pressure as the named bottleneck for this stage, because spill is the observable symptom of a partition exceeding its execution memory

questions.question: A Spark stage on a Databricks cluster shows these metrics: Spill (Disk) = 240 GB total, GC time = 3.5 s per task, Shuffle Write = 12 GB, task durations with max/median ratio = 1.4. Which pairing of metric to most likely remedy is correct?

options.label: High Spill (Disk) combined with high GC time points to execution-memory pressure, and the most likely remedy is to increase the executor memory or reduce partition size so each partition fits in memory
High Spill (Disk) points to excessive shuffle network traffic, and the most likely remedy is to add more workers to spread the shuffle
High GC time points to skew, and the most likely remedy is to salt the key even though durations are tightly clustered
High Shuffle Write points to spill, and the most likely remedy is to lower the number of shuffle partitions to combine output files

questions.correctAnswer: High Spill (Disk) combined with high GC time points to execution-memory pressure, and the most likely remedy is to increase the executor memory or reduce partition size so each partition fits in memory
questions.analysis: The pairing question asks you to map each metric to its most plausible remedy, which is precisely the skill the exam objective 'tune queries to reduce data scanned' and the diagnostic loop reward. Here Spill (Disk) = 240 GB and GC time = 3.5 s per task are the co-occurring symptoms of a partition that does not fit in its execution memory: the executor keeps allocating and collecting objects under pressure, so GC time climbs while the engine writes overflow to disk. The natural remedy is to give each partition more headroom — raise executor memory and/or repartition to smaller partitions — so spill and GC both fall. Contrast this with the other rows: high spill is not primarily a shuffle-network symptom (note Shuffle Write is only 12 GB, far smaller than the 240 GB spilled), so 'add more workers' misattributes the cause; high GC time is not a skew symptom, and the flat duration distribution (max/median 1.4) explicitly contradicts skew, so salting is wrong; and lowering the number of shuffle partitions would make each partition larger and likely worsen spill, not fix it. On the broader point of treating data as a bounded batch versus an unbounded stream, note that the source material observes streaming systems have long been treated as 'an expensive novelty or a dumb pipe' before their business utility matured [source p.412]; the same discipline of naming the real bottleneck rather than adding capacity applies whether the workload is batch or streaming. For the general distributed-systems mechanism of distributing tasks to workers and replicating data for resilience, see [source p.115], and for the complications that joins introduce when moving toward real-time processing, see [source p.93].
answer: High Spill (Disk) combined with high GC time points to execution-memory pressure, and the most likely remedy is to increase the executor memory or reduce partition size so each partition fits in memory

scenes.title: EXPLAIN Plans: Reading the Optimizer's Mind

elements.content: EXPLAIN Plans: Reading the Optimizer's Mind

Three flavors, three questions

• EXPLAIN — logical plan only; what will run, no rewrite detail

• EXPLAIN EXTENDED — adds Catalyst optimizer rewrites (filter pushdown, join reorder)

• EXPLAIN COST — adds statistics-based cardinality and sizeInBytes estimates

• Stage chain: parsed → analyzed → optimized logical → physical [source p.337]

Operators that drive cost

• Scan — reports files, row count, sizeInBytes

• Exchange — a shuffle boundary; one stage ends [source p.348]

• Sort — global ordering, full repartition

• BroadcastHashJoin vs SortMergeJoin — decides shuffle size

Worked example: predicate pushdown

1. events = 4,000,000,000 rows; avg 120 bytes/row → sizeInBytes ≈ 480 GB

2. Query filters event_date = '2024-01-15' (1 of 365 days ≈ 0.27%)

3. Without pushdown: scan reports 480 GB, all partitions read

4. With pushdown: scan reports ≈ 480 GB × 0.0027 ≈ 1.3 GB and a smaller row count

5. Ratio 480 / 1.3 ≈ 369× less data scanned in step 4

Exam trap

A plan can look right yet still scan the whole table: the filter sits above the scan instead of inside it.

Fix: compare plan before/after the filter; pushdown must appear in the scan node. [source p.337]

actions.text: Building on what we just covered about diagnosing slow queries, let's turn to one of the most powerful tools in that toolkit: the EXPLAIN plan. This is literally how you read the optimizer's mind.

An EXPLAIN plan shows you exactly how Databricks intends to execute your query before it actually runs — the sequence of operators, the join strategies, and crucially, how much data each step expects to touch.

There are three flavors you need to know for the exam. Plain EXPLAIN gives you the logical plan — what the query means. EXPLAIN EXTENDED shows the parsed and analyzed plans, useful for debugging. And EXPLAIN COST gives you the physical plan with the optimizer's cost estimates — that's the one you use to reason about performance.

Now, these plan stages flow through the Catalyst optimizer: parsed, analyzed, optimized logical, and finally the physical plan. Pay close attention to the operators that drive cost. Scan nodes report statistics like sizeInBytes and row count for the files to be read. And watch for Exchange nodes — those are shuffles — along with Sort and the chosen join strategy, like BroadcastHashJoin versus SortMergeJoin.

Here's a worked example. Say you have an events table with four million rows, and you add a filter on a partition column. Before the filter, the scan reports the full sizeInBytes. After the filter, predicate pushdown appears directly in the scan node — the numbers drop. That's the optimizer pushing work down to the reader and skipping data it never needed.

And here's the exam trap to burn into memory: a plan can look perfectly correct on the surface, yet still scan the entire table because the filter was never pushed down to the scan. Always compare the plan before and after adding a filter — if the scan statistics don't shrink, the predicate isn't being pushed. That single comparison is often the difference between a passing and failing answer on performance questions.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Diagnosing a Plan and Cutting Bytes Scanned

elements.content: Problem 1

A Databricks workspace contains a Delta Lake table `sales` stored as Parquet files. The table is 8 TB ($8.0 \times 10^{12}$ bytes) and is not partitioned. It was written with a single giant file of 7.94 TB and 63,999 small files of about 1 MB each. A data engineer runs:

```sql

SELECT * FROM sales WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01';

```

The query takes 42 minutes. `EXPLAIN` returns a physical plan whose scan node reads:

```

FileScan parquet sales[order_id#1, customer_id#2, order_date#3, product_id#4, quantity#5, unit_price#6, total_amount#7]

PushedFilters: []

PartitionFilters: []

sizeInBytes=8.0e+12

PartitionCount: 1

```

The Spark UI SQL tab shows one task with duration 41 min 12 s and 63,999 tasks with duration under 200 ms. Stage metrics report Shuffle Read = 0 B, Shuffle Write = 0 B, Spill (Disk) = 0 B. The query only needs columns `order_id`, `customer_id`, and `total_amount`. Assume 5% of rows have `order_date >= '2024-01-01'`. The target cluster has 16 executors × 8 cores = 128 cores. Diagnose the two independent bottlenecks, propose the minimal set of changes, predict the new physical plan, and estimate the new runtime and bytes read. Show all arithmetic.
Hint: Two bottlenecks: one giant partition (parallelism/skew) and no pruning (full scan). Fix both.

Worked solution
Step 1: Read the scan statistics in the plan. The scan node reports `sizeInBytes=8.0e+12`, so the engine will read all 8 TB. Both `PushedFilters` and `PartitionFilters` are empty, confirming that the predicate `order_date >= '2024-01-01'` is not pushed to the file or partition layer. Because the table is not partitioned, there is no partition directory to prune. Catalyst must read every row to evaluate the filter. This is a full-table scan.

Step 2: Check the Spark UI. The stage has 64,000 tasks: one giant task of 41 min 12 s and 63,999 tasks under 200 ms. The giant task is reading the 7.94 TB file; the near-instant tasks read the 1 MB files. This is a parallelism problem: stage runtime is bounded by the largest task, so roughly 41 of the 42 minutes are spent on one task. Shuffle Read/Write and Spill are zero, so the bottleneck is purely the scan of a single oversized file, not a shuffle or memory spill.

Step 3: Apply the minimal fixes.

(a) Column pruning: replace `SELECT *` with `SELECT order_id, customer_id, total_amount`. Columnar serialization allows a database to scan only the columns required for a query, sometimes dramatically reducing the amount of data read [source p.239]. The table has 7 columns; reading 3 instead of 7 cuts the columnar read to roughly $3/7$ of the row data.

(b) Partition pruning: rewrite the table partitioned by `order_date`, e.g. `CREATE TABLE sales_partitioned PARTITIONED BY (order_date) AS SELECT * FROM sales`. Partitioning by a time field is extremely common because analytics often scan over a time range [source p.240]. After this, `WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'` becomes a partition filter and reads only the 2024+ partitions, about 5% of the data.

(c) Repartition to avoid the giant task: when writing the new partitioned table, set `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` to a sensible value, e.g. 256, and ensure files are right-sized (roughly 128 MB–1 GB). On 128 cores, 256 partitions gives about 2 waves of tasks, which avoids both a single straggler and excessive scheduler overhead. Run `OPTIMIZE` on the Delta table to compact small files.

Step 4: Re-run `EXPLAIN` to confirm the new plan. Expected scan node:

```

FileScan parquet sales_partitioned[...]

PushedFilters: [IsNotNull(order_date), GreaterThanOrEqual(order_date,2024-01-01)]

PartitionFilters: [IsNotNull(order_date), GreaterThanOrEqual(order_date,2024-01-01)]

sizeInBytes=4.0e+11

```

The `PartitionFilters` field confirms partition pruning; `PushedFilters` confirms row-group or file-level filtering. The `sizeInBytes` drops from $8.0\times10^{12}$ to about $4.0\times10^{11}$ (400 GB) before column pruning. After column pruning, the actual bytes read can be lower: if the 3 needed columns are about $3/7$ of the row width, the read is $400 \times (3/7) \approx 171.4$ GB. In the Spark UI SQL tab, bytes read should drop from 8 TB to about 171 GB.

Arithmetic:

- Original bytes read = 8 TB = 8,000 GB.

- After partition pruning: 5% of 8 TB = 400 GB.

- After column pruning: $400 \times (3/7) \approx 171.4$ GB.

- Reduction factor = $8{,}000 / 171.4 \approx 46.7$.

- If the job were purely I/O-bound and scaled linearly, new runtime $\approx 42 \text{ min} / 46.7 \approx 0.9$ min $\approx 54$ s. With 128 cores and 256 partitions, the scan is highly parallel; a conservative estimate is 2–3 minutes. The giant task is eliminated because the data is spread across 256 partitions.

- Also set `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` for any shuffle in the job (this query has none). For a shuffle-heavy query, 256 partitions on 128 cores means about 2 tasks per core, avoiding tiny tasks and scheduler overhead.

Analysis — Why it works: pruning is applied at the file and partition layer before rows are materialized. Partition pruning uses the directory structure (`order_date=2024-01-01/...`) to skip entire partitions; file-level `PushedFilters` use Parquet row-group statistics (min/max) to skip row groups. Columnar serialization reads only the columns required, reducing I/O [source p.239]. Prefiltering data early reduces the amount processed in later stages [source p.337]. The parallelism fix addresses skew: one giant file creates one giant task, and the map portion of a scan is embarrassingly parallel across blocks [source p.348], but only if the data is split into many blocks—one giant file defeats this. Repartitioning spreads data so the stage runtime is no longer bounded by a single straggler.

Common mistakes: (1) Filtering on a non-partition column (e.g., filtering `order_date` when the table is partitioned by `region`) yields no partition pruning. (2) Wrapping the partition column in a function (e.g., `year(order_date) = 2024`) disables partition pruning because the optimizer cannot map the function output to partition values. (3) Using `SELECT *` when only a few columns are needed. (4) Setting `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` too low (e.g., 1 or 8) recreates the giant-task problem; setting it too high (e.g., 10,000) creates scheduler overhead. Edge case: if `order_date` is a string, partition values must compare lexicographically consistently; ISO dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`) work. If the filter is on a timestamp column and partitions are by date, you may need `date_trunc` or an explicit cast that the optimizer can push. Generalization: always verify pruning with `EXPLAIN` and confirm with the Spark UI SQL tab's bytes read metric; iterate until `PartitionFilters` and `PushedFilters` appear and bytes read drop.
Problem 2

A Delta table `events` is 4 TB and is partitioned by `event_date`, a string column in ISO format `YYYY-MM-DD`. The table stores three years of data: 2022, 2023, and 2024, each year roughly equal in size. Query A:

```sql

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE year(event_date) = 2024;

```

runs in 18 minutes. Query B:

```sql

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE event_date >= '2024-01-01' AND event_date < '2025-01-01';

```

runs in 45 seconds. Both queries return the same count. `EXPLAIN` for Query A shows `PartitionFilters: []` and `sizeInBytes=4.0e+12`. `EXPLAIN` for Query B shows `PartitionFilters: [IsNotNull(event_date), GreaterThanOrEqual(event_date, 2024-01-01), LessThan(event_date, 2025-01-01)]` and `sizeInBytes=1.33e+12`. Explain why the two queries differ by a factor of 24 in runtime, compute the bytes scanned in each case, and state the general rule that a student should apply. Assume the cluster has 32 cores and both queries are I/O-bound.
Hint: One predicate can be pushed to the partition layer; the other cannot. Check whether the filter is sargable.

Worked solution
Step 1: Interpret Query A. The predicate is `year(event_date) = 2024`. `event_date` is the partition column, but `year()` is a function applied to it. Catalyst cannot invert `year()` to a set of partition values without evaluating the function for every possible partition. Therefore `PartitionFilters` is empty, and the scan reads all partitions: all 4 TB. `sizeInBytes=4.0e+12` confirms this. The query then applies `year(event_date) = 2024` row by row after reading all data.

Step 2: Interpret Query B. The predicates are direct range comparisons on `event_date`: `>= '2024-01-01'` and `< '2025-01-01'`. These are sargable: the optimizer maps them directly to partition directory values. `PartitionFilters` lists them, so only partitions for 2024 are read. Since each year is about $1/3$ of the table, 2024 is about $4/3 \approx 1.33$ TB. `sizeInBytes=1.33e+12` confirms this.

Step 3: Compute bytes scanned and runtime. Query A scans 4 TB = 4,000 GB. Query B scans 1.33 TB = 1,333 GB. Ratio of bytes scanned = $4{,}000 / 1{,}333 = 3.0$, so Query B reads about one-third the data. The observed runtime ratio is 18 min / 45 s = 1,080 s / 45 s = 24. The extra factor comes from two effects: (a) Query A applies a function to every row, which is CPU work; (b) Query B's partition pruning also enables file-level and row-group-level skipping, and the 2024 partitions may be read with better parallelism. If both were purely I/O-bound, the expected runtime ratio would be about 3; the observed factor of 24 shows the CPU cost of evaluating `year()` on 4 TB of rows plus the overhead of scanning many more files. A simple model: Query A reads 4 TB at 3.7 GB/s aggregate, taking about 1,080 s. Query B reads 1.33 TB at the same rate, taking about 360 s, but it also benefits from fewer files and less CPU, yielding 45 s. The key point is that partition pruning eliminates two-thirds of the I/O and nearly all of the function-evaluation cost.

Step 4: General rule. For partition pruning to work, the filter must be expressed directly on the partition column using a comparison that the optimizer can map to partition values. Avoid wrapping the partition column in a function. If a function is necessary, rewrite it as a range predicate on the raw column. Also note that partitioning by a high-cardinality column like `event_date` (one partition per day) can create too many small files; Databricks recommends partitioning by a coarser column (e.g., month) or using clustering or Z-order instead. Edge case: if `event_date` were a timestamp and partitions were by date, filter `event_date >= '2024-01-01' AND event_date < '2025-01-01'` or use `date_trunc('day', event_date)` carefully.

Analysis — Why it works: partition pruning is static pruning—the optimizer reads partition metadata and eliminates entire directories before the scan starts [source p.240]. Columnar storage further reduces I/O by reading only needed columns [source p.239]. Prefiltering data early reduces the amount processed in later operations [source p.337]. In Query B, the range predicate is sargable, so Catalyst produces non-empty `PartitionFilters` and skips 2022 and 2023 entirely. In Query A, the function-wrapped predicate is not sargable, so `PartitionFilters` stays empty and the engine reads all 4 TB before filtering rows.

Common mistakes: (1) Using `year()`, `month()`, `date_format()`, or `substring()` on the partition column. (2) Casting the partition column (e.g., `CAST(event_date AS DATE) = '2024-01-01'`) can also disable pruning unless the optimizer can push the cast. (3) Filtering on a non-partition column and expecting partition pruning. (4) Partitioning by a column that is rarely used in filters. The exam may present a query with a wrapped partition column and ask why it is slow; the correct answer is to rewrite the predicate as a direct range filter. Also verify with `EXPLAIN`: look for `PartitionFilters` in the scan node. If it is empty, pruning is not happening.

actions.text: Now that you can read a plan and spot a bottleneck, let's put that skill to work on a fully worked exam-style problem. We'll go from an EXPLAIN plan and Spark UI metrics all the way to a concrete tuning change — and measure the improvement.

Here's Problem 1. A Databricks workspace contains a Delta Lake table, sales, that is eight terabytes. The query SELECT star FROM sales, filtered on order_date greater than or equal to January 1st 2024, takes forty-two minutes to run. Look at the physical plan: the FileScan parquet operator has no pushed filter, and the partition count is one.

Before you scroll down, pause here. Two bottlenecks are hiding in that description — a single giant partition that kills parallelism, and a full-table scan that reads all eight terabytes. Try to name both before you read the solution.
The two bottlenecks are exactly that: one giant partition causing a parallelism problem, and a scan with no filter pushdown reading the entire table. Let's walk the worked solution step by step.

Step 1: read the scan statistics in the plan. sizeInBytes confirms a full-table scan, because no partition filter and no pushed filter appear. Step 2: open the Spark UI and look at the task distribution — one giant task with a very long duration sitting next to thousands of near-instant tasks. That is the signature of a parallelism problem, not a slow scan by itself. Step 3: rewrite the query — replace SELECT star with only the columns you actually need, filter explicitly on the partition column order_date, and repartition to a sensible shuffle partition count. Step 4: re-run EXPLAIN and confirm that PushedFilters and PartitionFilters now appear, then check the SQL tab in the Spark UI to verify the bytes read actually dropped.

So why does this work? Pruning is applied at the file and partition layer before any rows are materialized. That means less I/O, less shuffle, and less compute cost — all three fall together. And here's the common pitfall to remember for the exam: if you filter on a column that is not a partition column, or wrap a partition column inside a function, pruning is disabled and you're back to a full scan. With that pattern in hand, let's look at a second variant.

Problem 2 gives us a Delta table called events — four terabytes, partitioned by date. We're comparing two queries whose predicates differ only in form, which lets us isolate exactly what partition pruning depends on.
One predicate can be pushed down to the partition layer and skip whole directories; the other cannot. Ask yourself which one, and why, before you continue.

Step 1: interpret Query A. Its predicate compares the partition column directly against a literal, so the optimizer can translate it into partition directories and read only those. Step 2: interpret Query B. Here the partition column is wrapped in a function or compared in a way the optimizer can't invert, so the filter stays at the row level and every partition is scanned. Same data, same table — radically different bytes read.

Why it works: partition pruning is a static, file-layer optimization. The optimizer never needs to materialize a row to decide a partition is irrelevant — it just skips the directory entirely. Keep the predicate sargable — that means written as a plain comparison the optimizer can read — and pruning fires every time. That's the mental model to carry into the checkpoint.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: EXPLAIN Plans and Operators

questions.question: A physical plan for a join shows an Exchange node immediately below the join, and the Spark UI Stage detail page reports large Shuffle Read and Shuffle Write sizes for that stage. Which operator is responsible for this shuffle, and what is the most exam-accurate interpretation?

options.label: Exchange — Spark is redistributing rows across the cluster to co-locate matching keys, which is a wide transformation boundary; large Shuffle Read/Write sizes indicate an expensive join strategy that may be avoidable.
BroadcastExchange — Spark is replicating the small table to every executor, and large shuffle sizes prove the broadcast was too aggressive.
SortMergeJoin — the join itself performs the shuffle, and Exchange is only a reporting label with no runtime cost.
FileScan parquet — the scan performs the shuffle as part of predicate pushdown, so Exchange is simply an alias for the pushdown step.

questions.analysis: In the Spark physical plan, an Exchange node is the operator that repartitions data across executors, and it is exactly the node that marks a shuffle boundary; in the UI, a stage is split at shuffle boundaries, so a stage that shows large Shuffle Read and Shuffle Write sizes is a stage dominated by an Exchange. The exam-accurate reading is that the join is being implemented as a shuffle-based join (for example sort-merge join), meaning Spark is moving rows across the network to co-locate matching keys, which is a wide transformation. Option B is wrong because BroadcastExchange avoids the large shuffle entirely by replicating the small side; if you saw a broadcast you would generally not see huge Shuffle Write on both sides. Option C is a real misconception: SortMergeJoin is the join algorithm, but Exchange is the physical operator that actually performs the repartitioning and it has real runtime cost. Option D confuses the scan layer with the shuffle layer; FileScan reads files and does not repartition data. This connects back to the diagnostic loop taught earlier: observe in the Spark UI, hypothesize a cause, verify with EXPLAIN, fix, re-measure, and only then change the join strategy. For broader context on how shuffle-heavy execution differs from scan-dominated analytics, see the discussion of large-scale analytics workloads [source p.305].

questions.question: You are tuning a join where one side of the join is a small dimension table (about 8 MB after filtering) and the other side is a large 4 TB fact table. The physical plan currently shows an Exchange and a SortMergeJoin. Which statements justify replacing this with a broadcast join? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The dimension table is small enough that replicating it to every executor is cheaper than repartitioning the multi-terabyte fact table across the network.
A broadcast join eliminates the shuffle of the large fact table, so the Exchange node above the large side should disappear and the join becomes a wide-transformation-free operation for that side.
A broadcast join is always the correct choice for every join, regardless of the size of the smaller side, because it removes all network cost.

The decision to broadcast depends on the size of the smaller side relative to the configured broadcast threshold; if the dimension table grew to hundreds of gigabytes, broadcasting it would cause executor memory pressure and the shuffle-based join would become the better plan.

questions.analysis: A broadcast join is appropriate when one side is small enough that shipping a copy to every executor costs less than moving the large side across the network. Option A is correct for exactly that reason: with a 4 TB fact table, repartitioning the fact side is enormously expensive, while replicating an 8 MB dimension table is cheap. Option B is correct because the mechanism of a broadcast join is to avoid the shuffle of the large side entirely, so the Exchange node driving the shuffle-based join disappears and that side no longer triggers a shuffle boundary in the plan. Option D is correct and is the essential edge case: Databricks and Spark apply a broadcast threshold, and if the 'small' side grows past that threshold, broadcasting it forces every executor to hold a large copy, which causes memory pressure or spills and makes the shuffle join cheaper again. Option C is the classic misconception: 'broadcast is always better' is false, because broadcast has a fixed cost per executor and becomes pathological when the broadcast side is large. For the general principle that less data processed means more performant code, see [source p.341].

questions.question: A student runs EXPLAIN on `SELECT * FROM sales WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'` against an 8 TB Delta table. The physical plan shows `FileScan parquet sales[order_date, amount, ...]` with `PushedFilters: []` and `partitionCount=1`, while the corresponding logical plan shows a `Filter (order_date >= ...)`. The student concludes 'the filter is in the plan, so the data is being pruned.' Which statement is the exam-correct interpretation, and why is it the trap described as confusing the logical plan with the physical plan?

options.label: The student is right: the presence of Filter in the logical plan guarantees the physical scan will prune rows, because Catalyst always pushes predicates into the scan.

The student is wrong: `PushedFilters: []` means no predicate pushdown occurred, so the physical plan is scanning the full table despite the logical Filter; the logical plan shows what you asked for, while the physical plan shows what will actually run.
The student is wrong, but the fix is to add more workers, because an empty PushedFilters list means the cluster is under-provisioned for the scan.
The student is right to focus on the logical plan, because `partitionCount=1` only affects scheduling and has no relationship to parallelism or bytes scanned.

questions.analysis: The correct answer is B. `PushedFilters: []` is the physical plan's report that no predicate was pushed down into the file scan, so the scan node is reading the full 8 TB rather than pruning rows at the file layer. This is the trap called out in the checkpoint: the logical plan (the Filter node the student is reading) shows what you asked for, while the physical plan shows what will actually run. Option A is the exact misconception: Catalyst can push predicates, but it does not always succeed, and the physical plan is the authoritative source here. Option C is the exam distractor 'add more workers' seen elsewhere in the unit — adding workers does not fix a missing pushdown, and in the worked problem the real fix was tied to partition/parallelism and filter ability. Option D is wrong because `partitionCount=1` is not neutral: it means the scan is not parallelized, which connects to the worked problem where one giant task ran alongside thousands of near-instant tasks — a parallelism problem, not a scheduling footnote. For related guidance on avoiding unnecessary data processing, see [source p.341], and for the broader context of scan behavior in analytics systems, see [source p.305].

actions.text: Time to put that together. This checkpoint covers reading EXPLAIN output and operators, choosing a tuning lever for a join, and spotting when the plan actually prunes data — all the things we just walked through. Take a shot at each question on your own, and I'll join you right after you submit to talk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Pruning: Scan Less, Pay Less

elements.content: Pruning: Scan Less, Pay Less
Every pruning technique is a way to buy back bytes: bytes scanned drive both wall-clock time and DBU consumption.

Columnar files let a query read only the columns it names, not the full rows — columnar storage packs similar values next to each other and compresses them well, which reduces what must be scanned [source p.419].

Four pruning layers stack on top of that: partition pruning, predicate pushdown, column pruning, and Delta data skipping.
Worked example

sales = 8 TB, one partition (p=1), no pushed filter. 8 TB / 1 task = one giant partition. Repartition by order_date into 365 days: only 1/365 of the data (≈22 GB) is read — a ~99.7% reduction in bytes scanned.
Four pruning layers and what each costs

Partition pruning. A filter on a partition column eliminates whole directories before any Parquet file is opened. SELECT … WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' on a date-partitioned sales table skips every folder older than 2024.

Predicate pushdown. Filters are evaluated inside the file scan so rows that fail the predicate are never materialized. A PushedFilters entry in the physical plan proves it happened; its absence means the filter ran after the scan.

Column pruning. Reading only named columns exploits columnar storage — an analytic query touching 4 of 40 columns reads roughly 10% of the bytes [source p.419]. SELECT * defeats this entirely, so never use it in production.

Delta data skipping. Each file carries min/max statistics; a predicate that falls outside a file's range skips that file outright. Z-ORDER clusters related values into the same files, sharpening those ranges.
Partitioned Delta table
A date filter hits one partition; the others are greyed out as skipped, each with its own min/max statistics badge.

File layout hygiene. Batch systems perform poorly under many small-batch writes because each insert creates suboptimal small files and repeated create-object operations [source p.273]. Compaction and OPTIMIZE merge small files, so the scan opens fewer objects for the same bytes.
Cost link. Bytes scanned is the billing lever: fewer bytes read means lower runtime and lower DBU consumption, so pruning is cost control, not just a speed trick.

Exam trap. Wrapping a filter in a function, or using a non-deterministic expression, silently disables pruning — WHERE to_date(order_date) >= '2024-01-01' cannot be pushed down to the file scan, and the query gains zero bytes credit.

actions.text: Now let's shift from diagnosing slow queries to actually fixing them. This page is about pruning, and the phrase I want you to remember is the title itself: scan less, pay less.

Every pruning technique we'll cover is essentially a way to buy back bytes. Fewer bytes read means less I/O, less time, and lower cost. So think of pruning as a lever you pull on purpose, not an accident of how you wrote the query.

There are four pruning layers, and each one acts at a different stage of the scan. Read them top to bottom: partition pruning, predicate pushdown, column pruning, and Delta data skipping. Each layer removes work the previous one couldn't.

Start with partition pruning. When your filter targets a partition column, Spark eliminates entire directories before a single file is even opened. Nothing gets read from the skipped folders at all — that's the cheapest possible win.

Predicate pushdown goes one level deeper. Instead of reading every row and filtering afterward, the filter is evaluated inside the file scan itself. Parquet and Delta both support this, so rows that fail the predicate are discarded before they ever reach your cluster's memory.

Column pruning exploits columnar storage. If you only name three columns, only those three column chunks get read off disk. This is exactly why SELECT star is an anti-pattern — it forces every column to be materialized even when you need a handful.

Delta data skipping is the fourth layer, and it's Delta-specific. Each file carries min and max statistics per column, so the engine can skip whole files whose ranges can't possibly match your filter. Z-ORDER helps here because it co-locates related values into the same files, which makes those min/max ranges tighter and skipping far more effective.

One more thing that quietly undermines all of this is file layout hygiene. Lots of tiny files raise per-file overhead and dilute the benefit of skipping. Compaction and OPTIMIZE consolidate them so the pruning layers can actually do their job.

Here's the cost link, and it's the reason this topic matters beyond speed. Bytes scanned is the billing lever. Pruning isn't just a performance technique — it's a cost-control technique, because DBU consumption scales with the work the cluster does.

Watch out for the classic exam trap: wrapping a filter column inside a function, or using a non-deterministic expression, silently disables pruning. The optimizer can't reason about the column's raw values anymore, so it falls back to scanning everything. Keep filters on bare columns to preserve every layer we just covered.

actions.text: Let's put that pruning theory into practice. In this SQL sandbox you have a slow Spark SQL query over a Delta table that we'll rewrite and then verify with EXPLAIN. Our goal is simple: scan fewer bytes by pushing filters down to the scan node and dropping columns we never use.

actions.content: This is the starter query. Read it before editing — note which columns it selects and where the filter lives.

actions.text: First, let's run the query exactly as written so we have a baseline. Watch the bytes scanned and the plan operators reported in the output.

actions.content: Run the original unmodified query to capture the baseline plan and byte count.
Look for the scan node: without a partition filter or a pushable predicate, expect a full scan and a large bytes-scanned figure.

actions.text: Now rewrite the query. Add a filter on the partition column using its bare form, and select only the columns you actually need instead of star. Then run EXPLAIN again.

actions.content: Re-run after each edit so you can compare the plan and byte count against the baseline.
Compare your rewrite with the reference solution once you've made your first attempt — the key is a bare partition-column predicate and a trimmed column list.

actions.text: Now test the trap. Wrap the filter column inside a function, like a date conversion or an uppercase call, and run EXPLAIN again. You should see the pushed filter disappear and the bytes scanned jump back up — the optimizer can no longer reason about the bare column value. That is exactly the anti-pattern the exam expects you to spot.

scenes.title: Lesson Quiz: Performance Tuning and the Spark UI

questions.question: You open the Databricks Spark UI Stages tab for a job processing a Delta Lake join. A stage shows 4,000 tasks. The task duration column reports a median of 1.2 seconds, a minimum of 0.9 seconds, and a maximum of 24 seconds. Shuffle Read for the longest task is roughly 8x the median task's Shuffle Read, and Spill (Disk) appears only on that one task. No new shuffle boundary or extra stage was introduced, and the cluster has been stable for hours. Which action should you take FIRST to fix this stage?

options.label: Add more workers to the cluster so the long task has more CPU to finish faster
Investigate the key distribution causing skew and apply a repartitioning or salting strategy on the join or group-by key
Increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 16,000 so each task gets a smaller slice of data
Disable disk spill by increasing the executor memory per node so no task spills

questions.correctAnswer: Investigate the key distribution causing skew and apply a repartitioning or salting strategy on the join or group-by key
questions.analysis: A maximum task duration that is roughly 20x the median (24s vs 1.2s), accompanied by one task holding ~8x the median Shuffle Read and being the only task to spill to disk, is the classic signature of skewed keys, not of a uniformly overloaded cluster. The correct first move is to identify the hot key (e.g., group by the join key and count rows, or examine the SQL/DataFrame tab's operator metrics) and then redistribute that key using salting, a broadcast hint if the other side is small, or repartitioning the skewed column. Option A is the exam's favorite distractor: adding workers does not help when the work is concentrated in a single partition, because one task cannot be split across workers. This mirrors the checkpoint guidance that a large max/median ratio signals skew and that 'add more workers' is the wrong fix when the real problem is the data layout. Option C (raising shuffle partitions in bulk) may spread the median tasks thinner and add scheduler overhead without moving the hot key, so it usually does not eliminate the straggler. Option D hides the symptom rather than fixing the layout; spill is a consequence of the skew, and the skew remains. [source p.346]
answer: Investigate the key distribution causing skew and apply a repartitioning or salting strategy on the join or group-by key

questions.question: You run EXPLAIN on a query over a partitioned Delta table named sales. The physical plan's scan node contains a PartitionFilters entry for [order_date >= 2024-01-01], but there is NO PushedFilters entry, and the scan still reports a sizeInBytes value equal to roughly the full table plus the full row count. You expected the row-level filter on customer_id = 'C-991' to also be applied. Which statement best describes what happened?

options.label: Predicate pushdown occurred for both filters because the plan mentions PartitionFilters

Partition pruning eliminated the irrelevant order_date directories before reading, but the row-level customer_id predicate was NOT pushed down into the file scan, so those rows are filtered after being read
Predicate pushdown did not occur at all, so the entire table including every order_date partition was read
Missing PushedFilters is normal for Delta Lake and can be safely ignored because Delta performs its own filtering automatically

questions.correctAnswer: Partition pruning eliminated the irrelevant order_date directories before reading, but the row-level customer_id predicate was NOT pushed down into the file scan, so those rows are filtered after being read
questions.analysis: The scan node distinguishes two distinct optimizations. PartitionFilters reflects partition pruning: the filter on the partition column order_date allows Spark and Delta to skip whole directories before any file is opened. PushedFilters reflects predicate pushdown: filters are evaluated inside the Parquet/Delta scan so rows can be dropped at read time. If PushedFilters is absent for customer_id, the engine reads those rows and filters afterwards, which is why sizeInBytes and row counts still look large. Option A is wrong because the presence of PartitionFilters does not imply pushdown of non-partition columns. Option C is wrong because the PartitionFilters entry proves pruning did occur for the order_date partitions. Option D is a misconception — a missing PushedFilters entry is meaningful and is exactly how the exam tests whether you can read a plan. The lesson's checkpoint says it directly: a missing PushedFilters entry means no predicate pushdown. [source p.304]
answer: Partition pruning eliminated the irrelevant order_date directories before reading, but the row-level customer_id predicate was NOT pushed down into the file scan, so those rows are filtered after being read

questions.question:
A table trades is stored as Delta Lake, partitioned by trade_date, with 400 columns and 12 TB of data. The query below runs for 38 minutes. Identify the rewrites that will reduce bytes scanned (select all that apply).

SELECT *
FROM trades
WHERE symbol = 'AAPL' AND trade_date >= '2024-01-01'

options.label: Replace SELECT * with an explicit list of the columns actually used downstream, so column pruning can skip unread columns from the columnar files
Keep the trade_date filter so partition pruning can skip directories outside the date range
Add a redundant trade_date filter that is equal to the existing one to help the optimizer recognize the partition column
Add a cluster key or Z-ORDER on the high-selectivity column symbol so the row-level filter reads fewer files, accepting that inappropriate clustering can degrade other queries

correctAnswer: Replace SELECT * with an explicit list of the columns actually used downstream, so column pruning can skip unread columns from the columnar files
Keep the trade_date filter so partition pruning can skip directories outside the date range
Add a cluster key or Z-ORDER on the high-selectivity column symbol so the row-level filter reads fewer files, accepting that inappropriate clustering can degrade other queries
questions.analysis: Three of the four options directly reduce bytes scanned on this Delta table. Column pruning works because Delta/Parquet is columnar, so unselected columns are never read; the SELECT * pattern defeats that optimization. Partition pruning works because trade_date is the partition column and the filter eliminates whole directories. Clustering or Z-ORDER on symbol reorders data within files so the row-level filter can skip larger portions of files, at the cost of sorting overhead and the risk noted in the source that inappropriate clustering can degrade performance. Option C is a fake optimization: duplicating a filter does not change the physical plan, because the optimizer already deduplicates and simplifies identical predicates, so it produces no bytes-scanned reduction and is a classic exam distractor. Note the asymmetry across storage models: in a row-oriented database pruning centers on indexes, while in a column-oriented database selecting only needed columns is the primary lever. [source p.304]
questions.commentPrompt: Full credit requires selecting exactly the three correct options (explicit column list, retained partition filter, cluster/Z-ORDER strategy). Deduct 5 points per incorrectly selected distractor (option C). Deduct up to 5 points if the learner does not explain WHY column pruning and partition pruning act at different layers (storage layout vs directory structure).
answer: Replace SELECT * with an explicit list of the columns actually used downstream, so column pruning can skip unread columns from the columnar files
Keep the trade_date filter so partition pruning can skip directories outside the date range
Add a cluster key or Z-ORDER on the high-selectivity column symbol so the row-level filter reads fewer files, accepting that inappropriate clustering can degrade other queries

questions.question: You are the on-call data engineer and a nightly Delta Lake job that normally finishes in 12 minutes is now taking over 90 minutes. Write the diagnostic sequence you would follow, starting at the Spark UI observation and ending with a verified fix. Your answer must name the UI tabs and metrics you inspect (Jobs, Stages, SQL/DataFrame, Executors), describe how you read EXPLAIN plans and pruning indicators (PartitionFilters, PushedFilters, sizeInBytes), and identify at least one database-level technique you might apply from the sources. Use Databricks and Delta Lake terminology exactly as it appears in the product.
questions.commentPrompt:
Rubric (100 points total):
(1) Observation phase at the UI level — 25 pts. Must mention navigating Jobs to find the slow job, opening the Stages tab to compare min/median/max task durations, and using the SQL/DataFrame tab to reach the DAG and physical plan. Award partial credit for identifying skew (large max/median ratio) or spill as candidate signatures.
(2) Hypothesize and verify phase with EXPLAIN — 25 pts. Must describe running EXPLAIN and checking the scan node for PartitionFilters, PushedFilters, and sizeInBytes/row counts. A strong answer notes that missing PushedFilters means no predicate pushdown and that PartitionFilters indicates pruning by directory.
(3) Fix phase grounded in the sources — 25 pts. Must propose at least two concrete fixes chosen from: column pruning (avoid SELECT *), partition pruning, predicate pushdown, clustering/Z-ORDER on a high-selectivity key, CTE rewrite for readability and performance, or addressing skew via repartitioning/salting. Cite the source guidance that inappropriate clustering can degrade performance if proposing Z-ORDER or cluster keys.
(4) Re-measure and verify — 15 pts. Must describe re-running the job and comparing the same metrics (stage duration, spill, bytes scanned) to confirm the fix without regression, and ideally validate against anticipated real-world data sizes rather than tiny test datasets.
(5) Exam-style anti-distractor reasoning — 10 pts. Must explicitly reject the reflex to 'add more workers' before fixing the data layout, explaining that adding capacity does not resolve a skewed partition. Deduct 5 points if the learner recommends scaling the cluster as a first step.
questions.analysis: A complete answer follows the diagnostic loop: observe, hypothesize, verify, fix, re-measure. Observation: Jobs tab to locate the slow job and its action, Stages tab to compare min/median/max task durations and to spot a large max/median ratio signaling skew alongside Shuffle Read/Write and Spill (Memory)/(Disk) metrics, and the SQL/DataFrame tab to tie the query to its DAG. Hypothesis and verification: run EXPLAIN and inspect the scan node for sizeInBytes, row counts, PartitionFilters, and PushedFilters; a missing PushedFilters entry means predicate pushdown did not occur, so rows are filtered after reading. Fix: apply column pruning by naming only the needed columns, retain partition-column filters for partition pruning, and where appropriate use a cluster key or Z-ORDER on a high-selectivity column — while remembering that inappropriate clustering and key distribution strategies degrade performance. Where the plan is complex, prefer CTEs over nested subqueries or temporary tables for readability and typically better performance. Finally, re-measure the same metrics and benchmark against anticipated real-world data and query sizes, not a tiny test set, so the validation is meaningful. Throughout, resist the exam's favorite distractor of scaling the cluster first: when a single task or a skewed key dominates, more workers do not fix the layout. [source p.346] [source p.303] [source p.304] [source p.174]

actions.text: This is our capstone quiz for this lesson on diagnosing slow queries — it pulls together everything we just covered on the Spark UI, EXPLAIN plans, and pruning. Take your time with each question, including the short-answer one, and work through them on your own.
Once you submit, I'll walk through anything that tripped you up and we'll dig into the reasoning together. Go ahead and give it your best shot.

scenes.title: Lesson Overview: Partitioning, Liquid Clustering, and File Layout

elements.content: Lesson Overview: Partitioning, Liquid Clustering, and File Layout

Physical layout is the largest single lever on query cost. How Delta rows are grouped into files and directories determines how many bytes a query must scan before any pruning logic runs [source p.246].

The classic remedy for scan cost is colocation (placing compute next to the data blocks it reads), which preserves bandwidth for the shuffle step and lets filters on the map side cut bytes early [source p.246].

In Databricks, layout choices — partitioning and liquid clustering — are how you encode that colocation in the Delta transaction log.

Delta relies on object storage for large batch reads and batch writes, but badly on thousands of tiny updates per second — small-file churn is exactly the workload object stores penalize [source p.233].

Compaction fights that penalty by merging small files into larger ones so scans stay sequential and metadata overhead stays low.
Worked example — the arithmetic of layout

A Delta table has 8 TB and 100,000 files averaging 80 MB. If 1 day = 1 partition and the filter is order_date = '2024-03-15' (a 1/365 slice), partition pruning leaves ≈ 22 GB to scan — a 365× reduction. Without partitioning, the same query scans all 8 TB.
This scene's two objectives

1. Choose partitioning or liquid clustering for a given predicate set.

2. Pick the compaction strategy (OPTIMIZE / auto-compaction) that resolves a small-file problem.
Maps to Data Engineer Associate objectives
Both objectives fall under the performance-and-cost domain: identify bottlenecks, tune queries to reduce bytes scanned, and lower storage/compute spend on Delta tables.

actions.text: Alright, that wraps up our look at query tuning and the Spark UI. Now we're shifting gears into a topic that sits underneath almost everything we just discussed: partitioning, liquid clustering, and file layout. This is where you stop tuning individual queries and start shaping the data itself so that queries get faster without you touching them.

Here's the core idea for this whole lesson. Physical layout is the single largest lever you have over query cost on Delta tables. Layout determines how many bytes a query must scan, and bytes scanned drives both latency and the compute bill. A badly laid-out table can force a query to read everything; a well-laid-out table lets it skip almost all of it.

Delta stores its tables on object storage — cloud blob storage like S3 or ADLS — as a set of Parquet files plus a transaction log. Object storage gives us cheap, durable, scalable batch reads, but it offers no indexes and no cheap random access. So the only way to read less is to organize the files so that the engine can prune them before it ever reads a byte.

The classic remedy for scan cost is colocation — physically placing related rows next to each other on disk. Partitioning is the long-standing form of that idea: you split the table directory by column values, and queries that filter on those columns skip entire directories. As we'll see later, liquid clustering is the modern successor for the cases where fixed partitioning hurts more than it helps.

To make this concrete, the lesson includes a worked example where we do the arithmetic of layout on a real-looking Delta table: 8 terabytes, 100,000 files averaging 80 megabytes each. We'll compute how many files a filtered query must touch under different layouts, and you'll see the numbers diverge fast — that's the moment the concept stops being abstract.

So this scene has two clear objectives. First, when you face a large Delta table, you should be able to choose partitioning or liquid clustering with a reason, not a guess. Second, when you see a small-file problem, you should be able to name the compaction strategy that fixes it and explain why it works.

Both of these map directly to the Data Engineer Associate objectives, and as the slide notes, they both fall under the performance-and-cost domain. That's worth remembering: on the exam, layout questions are rarely just about speed — they almost always come bundled with a cost or a scan-volume constraint.

Keep that framing in mind as we go. Whenever you're deciding on a partition key, a clustering key, or a compaction job, ask yourself two things: how many bytes will a typical query actually have to read, and what does that scan cost me in compute? That single habit will carry you through the rest of this lesson and through the exam questions that follow.

scenes.title: How Delta Tables Are Stored on Disk

elements.content: How Delta Tables Are Stored on Disk
Two halves of every Delta table: an immutable transaction log, plus the Parquet data files it points to.

1. Log + data files. A Delta table = a _delta_log transaction log plus a set of Parquet data files. The log is the source of truth; the Parquet files are the payload.

2. Immutability. Writes never edit a Parquet file in place — new state means new files, while old files are retained for failure recovery.

3. Commits add up. Many small commits clutter storage and eventually require VACUUM — the small-file problem in storage form [source p.304].

4. Partitions are directories. A partition is a physical directory; the partition key is the column whose values carve the directory tree (e.g. order_date=2024-01-03/).

5. Why files split at all. Column files get fragmented precisely so a single field update doesn't force rewriting a whole column [source p.419].
Annotated tree: _delta_log folder + date-named partition folders + blue Parquet file icons with size labels; right panel shows per-file min/max statistics.
Worked example: 200 files × 500 MB = 100 GB. Per-file min/max on order_date lets 1 filter (last 7 days) skip 196 files → ~2 GB read instead of ~100 GB. 50× less I/O.

actions.text: Now let's open up the file layout itself. Before we can tune partitioning or clustering, we need a precise mental model of what a Delta table actually looks like on disk — because everything in this lesson builds on that picture.

Every Delta table is really two halves. On one side there's an immutable transaction log — a record of every commit, which is the source of truth for what the table contains. On the other side there's the actual data: Parquet files sitting on object storage. The log tells you which Parquet files count right now; the files hold the rows.

Put concretely: a Delta table equals a _delta_log directory plus a set of Parquet data files. The log is append-only and ordered, and each new commit points at a new set of files. That separation is exactly what gives us ACID behavior on top of plain object storage.

Here's the annotated directory tree. At the top you see the _delta_log folder holding the numbered JSON commit files, alongside folders named by partition value — in this case dates — and inside each of those are the Parquet files for that partition. This tree is the canonical exam picture of a Delta table.

Notice the structural point: a partition is a physical directory. The partition key is simply the column whose values split that directory tree. When a query filters on the partition column, the engine can skip whole directories without ever opening their files — that's partition pruning.

Now the worked example that ties it to cost. Suppose you have two hundred files of five hundred megabytes each, for a total of one hundred gigabytes. Because Delta keeps per-file min and max statistics on every column, a well-filtered query only needs to touch the files whose ranges overlap the filter — that's data skipping. Fewer, larger files with good statistics mean far less I/O.

So keep three things in mind from this page: log plus data files, partitions as directories, and per-file statistics driving data skipping. In the next few pages we'll use this layout model to decide when partitioning helps and when it hurts.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Storage Layout Foundations

questions.question: A Delta table lives on cloud object storage. Which pair of components fully describes its on-disk structure?

options.label: A single monolithic Parquet file plus a schema metastore entry
A transaction log directory (_delta_log) plus a set of Parquet data files
A row-based CSV manifest plus a set of JSON index files
A partitioned Hive warehouse directory plus a Hudi metadata table

questions.correctAnswer: B
questions.analysis: A Delta table is physically a _delta_log transaction log plus a set of Parquet data files: the log records the committed actions that define the table version, and the Parquet files hold the actual rows. Option A is wrong because a Delta table is never one monolithic file — it is an open set of Parquet files whose contents and membership change over time. Option C is wrong because Delta data files are columnar Parquet, not row-based CSV, and the metadata is JSON commit files inside _delta_log rather than a separate JSON index. Option D confuses Delta Lake with Apache Hudi and describes a warehouse-style directory layout rather than the log-plus-data-file structure. Note the precondition and edge case: the two-component description holds for every Delta table, but the set of data files is not static — each commit in the log may add or remove files while the table remains a single logical table [source p.243].

questions.question: Which statements about how Delta tables are laid out on disk and how data skipping works are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Delta data files are stored in Parquet, a format that carries per-file column statistics usable for pruning.
A partition is a physical directory, and the partition key is the column whose values split that directory tree.
Data skipping prunes files by reading every file fully and discarding rows that do not match the filter.
Fewer, larger files with good min/max column statistics generally mean less I/O than many tiny files with poor statistics.
Partitioning and the Parquet file format are the same thing: choosing a partition key changes the on-disk encoding to Parquet.

correctAnswer: A
B
D
questions.analysis: Option A is correct: Delta stores its data as Parquet, and Parquet files carry per-file column statistics (min/max, null counts) that pruning can use [source p.245]. Option B is correct: a partition is a physical directory and the partition key is the column whose values split that directory tree. Option D is correct: data skipping prunes files using per-file min/max column statistics, so fewer, larger files with good statistics mean less I/O. Option C reverses the mechanism — data skipping prunes whole files using statistics rather than reading every file and filtering rows afterward. Option E is the classic distractor that confuses partitioning with file format: partition key choice changes the directory layout, not the Parquet encoding, and the two concepts are independent.
