Work through all of them before you submit, then I'll walk through anything that tripped you up, especially around what drives data skipping. Go ahead whenever you're ready.

scenes.title: Partitioning Keys: Selection and Over-Partitioning Traps

elements.content: Partitioning Keys: Selection and Over-Partitioning Traps
A partition key is a candidate answer only if it is frequently filtered, low-cardinality, and evenly distributed.
Four Selection Criteria

1. Appears in frequent WHERE filters.

2. Low cardinality: hundreds, not millions, of distinct values.

3. Even value distribution across all values.

4. Used with narrow, selective filters that the optimizer can push down.
Date and time columns satisfy all four criteria — the reason date-based partitioning is the classic analytics default [source p.240].
Three Over-Partitioning Traps
High cardinality: partitioning on user_id or order_id creates millions of tiny directories.
Too many partitions: staying under ~10,000 keeps the log and scheduler from bogging down.
Skew: an uneven value distribution concentrates almost all rows in one or two partitions.
Rigidity cost: changing the key rewrites every data file, invalidates existing file statistics, and can leave thousands of small suboptimal files [source p.273].
Worked Example: 8 TB Table, Three Keys

order_date — 3 years ≈ 1,095 partitions, ~7 GB each. Passes all checks.

order_id — 4 M distinct values → 4 M partitions, ~2 MB each. Fails cardinality and file-size.

region — 5 values → 5 partitions, 1.6 TB each, one partition holds 60% of rows. Fails skew.
Exam Trap: Which Key Is Best?
A. user_id (high cardinality) B. order_date (low cardinality, filtered often) C. a random UUID D. order_id (unique per row)
Correct: B — the others create millions of tiny directories.

actions.text: Now let's build on the file layout we just examined and turn to partition key selection. Partitioning is the most direct lever you have for scan reduction, but it's also where candidates lose easy points — both by picking the wrong column and by over-partitioning. Let's walk through the rules the exam expects you to apply.

Start with the baseline rule: a partition key is a candidate answer only if it actually appears in frequent WHERE filters. Partitioning on a column nobody filters by buys you nothing — the engine still has to scan every directory. So the first question to ask is always, what does the workload actually filter on?

From that baseline, here are the four selection criteria. One: it appears in frequent WHERE filters. Two: low cardinality — a manageable number of distinct values. Three: even distribution across those values. And four: stability, meaning the value doesn't change often. If a column misses several of these, it's a distractor, not the answer.

Date and time columns satisfy all four criteria, which is why dates are the classic partition key. We filter by date constantly, a few years of data is a few hundred to a few thousand distinct values, the rows spread fairly evenly across days, and a given date never changes. That's why order_date is almost always the safe pick when it's on the table.

Now the other half of this topic — the over-partitioning traps. The exam loves these because they punish anyone who reaches for the highest-cardinality column. Let's take the three failure modes one at a time.

Trap one: high cardinality. Suppose you partition on user_id or order_id. That produces millions of tiny directories, where each one holds just a handful of rows. The small-file problem explodes, metadata overhead balloons, and query planning slows down more than the pruning ever helps. Never partition on an identifier that is nearly unique per row.

Trap two: too many partitions. The practical guardrail is to keep partitions at or above roughly one gigabyte each and stay well under about ten thousand partitions. If you're counting thousands of partitions, you're almost certainly partitioning too finely — this is the number the exam wants you to remember.

Trap three: skew. If the values are unevenly distributed — say one tenant produces ninety percent of the rows — partitioning concentrates most of the data in a single directory. That hits the classic hot partition, and the workers doing the heavy lifting become your bottleneck even though you pruned correctly elsewhere.

And remember the rigidity cost. Once you've partitioned, changing the key means rewriting the entire table, and it can leave behind many small files if the rewrite isn't managed carefully. That's why partition key choice is a design decision to get right up front, not something to casually switch later.

Let's put numbers on it with the worked example. Take an eight terabyte table and three candidate keys. If we partition on order_date across three years, that's roughly one thousand ninety-five partitions, about seven gigabytes each — well inside our guardrails. Now imagine two point four million partitions from an order_id or a large per-user count: those are millions of tiles of tiny data, and the guardrails collapse immediately.

Finally, the exam trap in the exact form you'll meet it: which of these three keys is best? Option A is user_id — high cardinality. Option B is order_date — low cardinality, filtered constantly, well distributed. Option C is order_id — essentially unique per row. The correct answer is B, because A and C both create millions of tiny directories and crush the small-file guardrail. If you take only one thing from this page, take that.

scenes.title: Liquid Clustering: One Layout to Replace Them All

elements.content: Liquid Clustering: One Layout to Replace Them All

Clusters allow finer-grained organization of data within partitions: sorting by one or a few fields colocates similar values and improves filtering, sorting, and joining [source p.240].

Liquid clustering keeps that benefit but makes the layout self-managing.
CLUSTER BY
CREATE TABLE t (...) CLUSTER BY (col1, col2) [source p.419]
ALTER anytime
ALTER TABLE t CLUSTER BY (new_col) — no rewrite
1–4 keys
Order by filter selectivity; higher cardinality first
Example key set: CLUSTER BY (order_date, customer_id, product_id) — newest-to-oldest, most-selective-first ordering of the filter predicates.
Not supported together with partitioning on the same table — choose exactly one layout strategy. Partitioning and clustering split column files differently [source p.419].

actions.text: Now that we understand why partitioning keys can be a trap, let's meet the modern alternative: liquid clustering. The tagline is bold — one layout to replace them all — and it's genuinely the direction Databricks is pushing for table layout.

Here's the core idea. Clusters give you finer-grained organization of the data than partitions alone. Instead of slicing your table into a few coarse directories, clustering lets Delta Lake decide how to physically group rows so that the values you filter on most often end up close together on disk — which means fewer files touched per query.

The syntax is a single keyword: CLUSTER BY. This one clause replaces both Hive-style partitioning and Z-ORDER. So if you're used to writing PARTITIONED BY and then running an OPTIMIZE Z-ORDER after the fact, liquid clustering collapses both of those concerns into one declaration.

In a CREATE TABLE statement you simply append CLUSTER BY followed by your column list — for example, CLUSTER BY (col1, col2). That's it. The layout is declared up front, and Delta Lake maintains it for you as data arrives.
And here's the part that really changes the game: you can alter the clustering keys at any time. That means the layout decision is not permanent — it's adjustable.

You run ALTER TABLE and specify a new CLUSTER BY clause, and critically — no full rewrite of the table is required. The layout adapts incrementally as new data lands. That makes clustering reversible and genuinely low-risk, which is something you could never say about choosing the wrong partition scheme.

So how many keys should you choose? The guidance is one to four. Too few and you don't get enough data skipping; too many and the clustering becomes fragmented and ineffective — much like over-partitioning.

Order matters. Put the most selective filter columns first, and generally favor higher-cardinality columns. A column with millions of distinct values clusters better than one with three. Contrast that with partitioning, where high cardinality was exactly what you had to avoid.

A realistic key set looks like this: CLUSTER BY order_date and customer_id, ordered by filter selectivity. Queries commonly filter on a date range and then narrow to a customer, so that ordering pays off.

One hard constraint to memorize for the exam: liquid clustering is not supported together with partitioning on the same table. You pick one approach per table. If a question presents a table with both PARTITIONED BY and CLUSTER BY, that configuration is invalid. Pick one layout and commit to it.

So to recap this page: CLUSTER BY replaces partitioning and Z-ORDER in a single declaration, the keys can be changed at any time without a rewrite, and you choose one to four of them, ordered by filter selectivity. Next, we'll check our understanding of when to reach for clustering versus partitioning.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Partitioning vs. Liquid Clustering

questions.question: On a Databricks Delta table, which DDL statement correctly declares a liquid clustering layout on the columns region and order_date?

options.label: CREATE TABLE sales (order_id BIGINT, region STRING, order_date DATE) CLUSTER BY (region, order_date)
CREATE TABLE sales (order_id BIGINT, region STRING, order_date DATE) PARTITIONED BY (region, order_date)
CREATE TABLE sales (order_id BIGINT, region STRING, order_date DATE) ZORDER BY (region, order_date)
CREATE TABLE sales (order_id BIGINT, region STRING, order_date DATE) CLUSTERED INDEX (region, order_date)

questions.analysis: Liquid clustering is expressed with the CLUSTER BY clause in the table DDL: CREATE TABLE t (...) CLUSTER BY (col1, col2). It replaces the older layout tools, so you do not combine it with PARTITIONED BY on the same table. Option B is the legacy Hive-style physical partitioning syntax, which creates directories per distinct value combination rather than an adaptive clustering layout. Option C is a sorting operation applied to data, not a table DDL declaration, and option D is an index concept drawn from row-based RDBMS design — analytics-oriented columnar systems evolved away from index-first layouts [source p.239]. The classic motivation for any of these schemes is reducing the bytes scanned, since partitioning splits a table into multiple subtables by a field and date/time splitting is extremely common in analytics [source p.240].

questions.question: An 8 TB Delta table called events is filtered almost exclusively with high-cardinality predicates such as WHERE user_id = 'U-88213' and WHERE session_id = '...'. A teammate proposes PARTITIONED BY (user_id). Which statements correctly describe the trade-offs of partitioning versus liquid clustering for this workload? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Partitioning on user_id would create millions of tiny directories and files, far exceeding the roughly 10,000-partition ceiling and falling well below the ~1 GB-per-partition guideline, so it should be rejected.
Liquid clustering can be declared on a high-cardinality column because it does not create one physical directory per distinct value — it organizes data incrementally into a clustered layout instead.
Because user_id has high cardinality, partitioning is the safer choice: the more distinct values a partition key has, the better partition pruning performs.
The clustering key can be changed later with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (...) without rewriting the whole table, so a wrong first guess is reversible rather than permanent.

questions.analysis: Option A applies the anti-pattern rule directly: never partition on high-cardinality identifiers such as user_id or order_id, because each distinct value becomes a physical directory and you blow past the ~10,000-partition ceiling while each partition shrinks below the ~1 GB target. Option B is the core reason liquid clustering exists: it is a single CLUSTER BY column set that replaces both partitioning and Z-ORDER, and it adapts incrementally instead of materializing a directory per value. Option D captures the reversibility argument — clustering keys can be changed at any time with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (...) without rewriting the table, which is not true of physical partitioning. Option C is the misconception: higher cardinality makes partition pruning worse, not better, because each pruned partition still contains few rows, and the file/directory overhead dominates. Clustering was historically designed as finer-grained organization *within* partitions, sorting and co-locating similar values to improve filtering, sorting, and joins [source p.240], and the broader analytics trend has been to move away from index-centric, high-cardinality lookup structures toward scan-pruning layouts [source p.239].

questions.question: A student must review four proposed table-layout designs and flag the one that is architecturally wrong — specifically, the distractor that keeps partitioning and liquid clustering on the same table. Which design statement is that error? (Select the single incorrect design.)

options.label: CREATE TABLE t (...) PARTITIONED BY (event_date) — a date partition key used in frequent WHERE filters, with each partition comfortably above ~1 GB.
CREATE TABLE t (...) CLUSTER BY (event_date, region) — a clustered layout whose keys can later be altered without rewriting the table.
CREATE TABLE t (...) PARTITIONED BY (event_date) CLUSTER BY (region) — using both a physical partition key and a liquid clustering key on the same table.
ALTER TABLE t CLUSTER BY (event_date, region) — migrating an existing table to a clustered layout declared at the column-set level.

questions.analysis: Option C is the distractor. Liquid clustering is designed as *one layout to replace them all*: it supersedes partitioning and Z-ORDER, so you declare either PARTITIONED BY or CLUSTER BY, not both on the same table. Layering a physical partition tree on top of a clustering key reintroduces the over-partitioning and small-file problems that CLUSTER BY was meant to eliminate. Option A is a valid legacy design as long as the key is low-cardinality and each partition stays above the ~1 GB floor. Option B is valid because CLUSTER BY takes a column set and the keys can be changed with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (...) without rewriting. Option D is valid — the same CLUSTER BY syntax applies in ALTER TABLE. Recall that a partition is a physical directory and the more distinct values a partition key has, the more directories and files you create; clustering instead sorts and co-locates similar values to improve filtering, sorting, and joins [source p.240], the finer-grained counterpart to partition-level splitting [source p.239].

scenes.title: The Small-File Problem and Compaction Strategies

elements.content: The Small-File Problem and Compaction Strategies

A small file is any Parquet data file far below the table's target size (about 128 MB by default, tunable up to ~1 GB for large tables). Because Delta Lake indexes, opens, and schedules work per file, the file count — not the total data volume — drives I/O, task, and metadata overhead. Below: how small files arise, how to detect them, and how Databricks compacts them.
Why Small Files Appear

• Streaming / micro-batch ingestion: each trigger lands a new file, so a 1-second stream can write ~86,400 files per day [source p.67].

• Frequent small MERGE / INSERT: row-at-a-time writes in a columnar store force many create-object operations and degrade badly [source p.273].

• Over-partitioning: a high-cardinality key such as user_id splits data into thousands of sub-target directories.

• High-shuffle writes: a wide GROUP BY or join with many output partitions flushes one file per task.
Why It Is Expensive

• I/O and task overhead per file: every file becomes at least one Spark task plus one open/close round trip to object storage.

• Weaker data skipping: min/max stats live per file, so many tiny files mean more scan nodes in the _delta_log plan.

• Metadata bloat: the transaction log grows with file count, slowing every read that must reconstruct the snapshot.

• Symptoms to look for: slow queries, thousands of near-instant tasks beside one huge task in the Spark UI, and a file count vastly larger than the data volume.
Worked Example: The Cost of Splitting

Suppose a 200 GB stream lands 1 MB files continuously:

• files = 200 GB ÷ 1 MB = 204,800 tiny files

• target size ~128 MB → 200 GB ÷ 128 MB ≈ 1,600 compacted files

• reduction ratio ≈ 204,800 ÷ 1,600 = 128× fewer files

A scan touching the whole table must schedule 128× more tasks before compaction, each paying an open/close round trip — exactly the high-create-object pattern described in the source [source p.273].
Many small files → OPTIMIZE → few target-size files
Remedies on Databricks

actions.text: That clustering discussion leads us directly to the opposite failure mode: the small-file problem. Delta tables degrade not just from bad clustering keys but from too many tiny files, and that is what we tackle now.

A small file is any Parquet data file far below the target size — roughly 128 MB by default, and up to 1 GB for large tables. The exact number matters less than the principle: each file carries fixed overhead, so file count, not data volume, drives cost.

Why do small files appear? Streaming and micro-batch ingestion write one file per trigger; frequent small MERGE or INSERT statements each produce new files; over-partitioning multiplies directories; and high-shuffle writes scatter output across many partitions. Notice the pattern — these are all normal, even recommended, ingestion behaviors. Small files are the byproduct of good practices.

And why is it expensive? Every file becomes a unit of I/O and a task in Spark. Thousands of tiny files mean thousands of tasks scheduled, thousands of metadata entries to consult, and a query that spends more time on overhead than on actual data. In the Spark UI you will see it as slow queries with an excessive number of tasks — a table whose files vastly outnumber its data volume.

Let's make that concrete. Suppose a 200 GB stream lands 1 MB files continuously — that is roughly two hundred thousand files. The data has not gotten bigger, but the number of tasks, file opens, and metadata reads has exploded by orders of magnitude. This is exactly the scenario that OPTIMIZE exists to fix.

Here is a side-by-side view. On the left, a table with hundreds of tiny files. On the right, the exact same data compacted into a few target-size files. Same bytes, same rows — but radically different read performance, because the right side turns hundreds of tasks into a handful.

The transformation in one line: many small files, then OPTIMIZE, then few target-size files. That is the compaction operation. It rewrites the small files into larger ones and records the change in the Delta log, so readers immediately see only the consolidated files.

On Databricks, your remedies come in three tiers. First, run OPTIMIZE to compact on demand. Second, enable auto compaction and optimized writes so the platform handles it as writes land. Third — and this is the exam favorite — on Unity Catalog managed tables, predictive optimization does this automatically. So before you schedule a manual run, ask whether the table is already managed and covered. Remember the interplay: aggressive partitioning amplifies small files, so compaction strategy and partition design must be reasoned about together. On the next page we will check your understanding of exactly these trade-offs.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Small Files and Compaction

questions.question: A data engineer runs a Databricks job that performs a Delta MERGE statement once every minute, updating a few dozen rows each time. After two weeks, the table holds only about 4 GB of data but the Spark UI shows stages with thousands of tasks and query latency has tripled. An EXPLAIN and directory listing confirm the data is spread across tens of thousands of tiny Parquet files, each a few hundred kilobytes. Which explanation best attributes the small-file problem in this scenario?

options.label: The table was stored using CSV instead of Delta Lake, so the format itself fragmented the data into many small objects.
The frequent small MERGE operations each rewrote files and produced many additional small files, because batch-oriented storage engines perform poorly with many small-batch operations.
The table is partitioned by a high-cardinality column such as user_id, which is the single required cause of small files in Delta Lake.
Liquid clustering was enabled on the table, and clustering keys always rewrite data into sub-128 MB files by design.

questions.analysis: The described workload is the textbook small-batch write pattern: many small MERGE or INSERT operations rather than a smaller number of large operations. As the source material explains, in batch-oriented columnar systems 'while it is common to insert one row at a time in a transactional database, this is a bad pattern for many columnar databases, as it forces the creation of many small, suboptimal files' [source p.273], and 'running many small in-place update operations is an even bigger problem because it causes the database to scan each existing column file to run the update' [source p.273]. That matches the observed symptom of tens of thousands of sub-megabyte files against only 4 GB of data. Option A is the classic format-confusion distractor: small files are a layout/write-pattern problem, not a storage-format problem — converting the same files to another format would not merge them. Option C is wrong because over-partitioning is one possible contributing factor, but the question stem attributes the cause to the frequent MERGE cadence, and nothing states the table is partitioned on a high-cardinality column; more importantly, no single cause is 'required.' Option D inverts liquid clustering, which consolidates layout incrementally rather than fragmenting it.

questions.question: An engineer inherits a streaming Delta table written by a near-real-time ingestion job using frequent micro-batches. The table now has roughly 8 million files averaging 4 MB each, and downstream SELECT queries are slow because of metadata and task overhead. The team wants a remediation that reduces file count going forward as well as cleaning up the existing backlog. Which TWO responses best fit this scenario? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Run OPTIMIZE on the table (optionally restricted to recently written partitions) to compact the many small files into fewer, larger files near the target size of roughly 128 MB up to 1 GB for large tables.
Convert the data files from Parquet to CSV so that each file can hold more rows and the file count drops automatically.
Enable auto compaction so that small files produced by the ongoing streaming writes are compacted as part of the write path, addressing the problem continuously rather than only once.
Change the partition layout by adding a high-cardinality key such as a per-event UUID so each small file lands in its own clean directory.

questions.analysis: The scenario is a live streaming writer continuously producing small files, so the correct response combines a one-time cleanup with an ongoing remedy. OPTIMIZE is the compaction command that rewrites many small files into fewer, larger files near the target size (roughly 128 MB default, up to 1 GB for large tables), which clears the existing 8-million-file backlog; auto compaction handles the future writes by compacting small files as part of the write path. Together they map to the two halves of the requirement. Option B is the format-confusion distractor: small files are a physical layout problem, not a storage-format problem, and CSV is explicitly discouraged — 'Data engineers should avoid using CSV files in pipelines because they are highly error-prone and deliver poor performance' [source p.418]. Option D makes the situation worse by introducing an over-partitioning trap on a high-cardinality identifier, which multiplies directories and small files rather than reducing them.

questions.question: A 500 GB Delta table is written by a batch job that appends a few thousand rows every 30 minutes and is partitioned by a date column. The table has about 120,000 files averaging 4 MB each. Queries that filter on date and a customer column are slow, and the Spark UI shows stages with very high task counts. Explain (a) the most likely cause of the small-file problem, (b) whether you would use OPTIMIZE, an automatic compaction mechanism, or a layout change to fix it, and (c) why the choice of storage format is not the root cause. Cite the reasoning you would give in an exam answer.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric (100%): (1) Cause attribution — 35%. Full credit requires identifying frequent small-batch writes (appends every 30 minutes) as the primary driver of many small files, and may note over-partitioning by date as a contributing factor; the answer must tie the file count to the write cadence rather than to hardware or networking. (2) Remediation choice — 35%. Full credit requires selecting OPTIMIZE for the existing backlog and an automatic compaction mechanism/auto compaction for ongoing writes, and justifying why an immediate layout change (for example adding a high-cardinality cluster key) is not the first remedy; partial credit if only one of the two compaction steps is named. (3) Rejecting the format-as-cause distractor — 20%. Full credit requires stating explicitly that small files are a physical layout and write-pattern problem, not a Delta Lake or Parquet storage-format problem, so changing the format would not merge files. (4) Clarity and correct use of exam vocabulary — 10%. Deduct for vague phrasing such as 'the table is just messy' without naming the mechanism.
questions.analysis: A strong answer states that the cause is the small-batch write pattern: appending only a few thousand rows every 30 minutes creates a new set of small Parquet files on each run, which is the pattern the source material warns about — 'while it is common to insert one row at a time in a transactional database, this is a bad pattern for many columnar databases, as it forces the creation of many small, suboptimal files and forces the system to run a high number of create object operations' [source p.273]. Date partitioning can compound this if each 30-minute write lands in the same or a few date directories, multiplying files per partition. The remedy is to run OPTIMIZE to compact the existing 120,000 small files into fewer files at the target size (roughly 128 MB, up to 1 GB for large tables) and to enable an automatic compaction mechanism so new micro-batch writes are compacted continuously; a layout change such as liquid clustering or a repartitioning is a secondary optimization and should not be the primary fix because the underlying write cadence is what generates small files. Finally, the storage format is not the root cause: the same bytes in Parquet, Delta, or any other format would still be split across many files unless a compaction or layout step rewrites them, so converting formats is the wrong fix and CSV in particular is a poor choice because it is 'highly error-prone and delivers poor performance' [source p.418]. A layout-oriented exam answer would also connect the slow filtered queries to the fact that data skipping operates on per-file statistics, so many tiny files with redundant statistics increase the number of files scanned and the number of tasks scheduled — the exact symptom reported in the Spark UI.

actions.text: As I just mentioned, compaction strategy and partition design have to be reasoned about together. So let's put that to the test — this checkpoint walks through a few scenario-style items on small files and compaction, exactly the shape you'll see on the exam.
Work through each one on your own and commit to an answer before moving on. Once you submit, I'll join you to go over anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Diagnosing and Repairing a Degraded Table Layout

elements.content: Problem 1

The `prod.user_events` Delta table in Unity Catalog is 40 TB and holds 1,095 days (3 years) of clickstream events. It was created with `PARTITIONED BY (event_date, user_id)`. The ingestion job appends a micro-batch every five minutes; each batch writes one new Parquet file per partition it touches. Today the table occupies 21,900,000 partition directories and 9,850,000 data files whose average size is 4.1 MB. A dashboard runs:

```sql

SELECT count(*) FROM prod.user_events WHERE event_date = '2025-03-01';

```

It takes 47 seconds and scans 38 GB. A second query filters only on `user_id = 918273` and scans the entire 40 TB. Propose the three-step repair, compute the expected directory count, file count, and bytes scanned for the date query after the fix, and state which table properties you enable.
Hint: Compute the average partition size before and after dropping the user_id key, and compare the original directory count against the roughly 10,000-partition guidance.

Worked solution
Step 0 — Diagnose the over-partitioning. The composite key (event_date, user_id) multiplies cardinality: 1,095 dates × ~20,000 active users per day ≈ 21,900,000 directories. The table is 40 TB = 40,960 GB, so the average directory holds 40,960 / 21,900,000 ≈ 0.00187 GB ≈ 1.9 MB. That is far below the roughly 1 GB per-partition floor and far above the well-under-10,000-partition ceiling; the layout is over-partitioned by a factor of 21,900,000 / 10,000 ≈ 2,190. Each micro-batch writes one file per touched partition, so the five-minute ingestion cadence turns over-partitioning into millions of 4.1 MB files; this is exactly the pattern where many small batch operations force the creation of many small, suboptimal files [source p.273].

Step 1 — Remove the user_id partition. Recreate or alter the table so the physical partition key is event_date only: `PARTITIONED BY (event_date)`. Directory count falls from 21,900,000 to 1,095, and the average partition grows to 40,960 / 1,095 ≈ 37.4 GB, comfortably above the 1 GB floor. Partitioning on a high-cardinality identifier such as user_id is the trap; partitions split the directory tree, and a key with millions of distinct values generates a runaway directory count.

Step 2 — Add liquid clustering. Execute:

```sql

ALTER TABLE prod.user_events CLUSTER BY (event_date, user_id);

```

Clustering provides finer-grained organization of data within partitions and colocates similar values [source p.240]. Order matters: event_date first because date filters dominate the workload and support range pruning; user_id second because it is a high-cardinality equality filter that benefits from colocation but would be a poor leading key. Clustering keys can be changed later with the same `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY` syntax without rewriting the table.

Step 3 — Compact and prevent recurrence. Run `OPTIMIZE prod.user_events;` to compact the 9,850,000 files toward the target size. At the 128 MB target: 40,960 GB / 0.125 GB = 327,680 files, a 9,850,000 / 327,680 ≈ 30× reduction. At the 1 GB target used for large tables: 40,960 GB / 1 GB = 40,960 files, a 9,850,000 / 40,960 ≈ 240× reduction. Then enable auto compaction and predictive optimization:

```sql

ALTER TABLE prod.user_events SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact' = 'true');

```

and enable predictive optimization at the Unity Catalog catalog or schema level.

Quantified effect on the date query. Before: the `event_date = '2025-03-01'` directory contains 9,850,000 / 1,095 ≈ 8,995 files of 4.1 MB, so the query opens 8,995 files and reads 8,995 × 4.1 MB ≈ 36.9 GB ≈ 38 GB. After clustering with event_date as the first key and OPTIMIZE to 1 GB files, that single date's 37.4 GB is packed into ≈ 38 files whose per-file min/max event_date statistics fall inside the date, so data skipping opens ≈ 38 files instead of 8,995 — roughly 237× fewer file opens — and the byte volume is the same 37.4 GB of genuine data rather than overhead. Delta can answer a pure `count(*)` from transaction-log metadata, so the real elapsed time improves even more. The `user_id = 918273` query benefits from the second clustering key: with 40,960 one-GB files and min/max user_id statistics per file, a single user's rows are colocated into a handful of files, replacing a 40 TB full scan with a scan of a few GB; this is the data-skipping payoff that indexes provide in row stores by mapping values to locations [source p.239].

Analysis — Partitioning is coarse: one directory per distinct key value, so the partition key must have low cardinality. The exam rule of thumb is to keep partitions at or above roughly 1 GB and the total partition count well under ~10,000; the original layout violated both by orders of magnitude. Liquid clustering is the better fit here because user_id has ~20,000 values per day and ~50,000,000 values overall — cardinality far too high to partition — yet it is a common equality filter. Clustering stores min/max statistics per file on the clustering keys and sorts data hierarchically, so a predicate on event_date prunes files by their date range and a predicate on user_id prunes files by their user range. That is strictly more expressive than partitioning, which prunes only on the exact partition columns. A common student mistake is to keep both: a table should not be partitioned and clustered on overlapping columns; the correct migration is to drop partitioning and adopt CLUSTER BY. Another mistake is to put user_id first because 'it is the most selective'; selectivity is irrelevant if the leading key destroys the min/max usefulness of the columns that appear in date-range filters. The ordering rule is: put the column used in the most frequent and most pruning-friendly filters first (usually a date), then finer keys. A third mistake is to think OPTIMIZE is optional. Clustering without compaction leaves millions of small files; OPTIMIZE both compacts and, on a clustered table, reorganizes rows to honor the keys. Auto compaction only handles files produced by the current write; it cannot remediate a 9.85-million-file backlog. Finally, if the dashboard is latency-critical, a materialized view (a precomputed, stored query result) can serve the aggregate, but it does not replace fixing the base table's physical layout. In a medallion architecture (a layered bronze/silver/gold data organization), this table is the silver layer; the same repair pattern applies to any large fact table whose ingestion cadence is faster than its compaction cadence.
Problem 2

You must choose the clustering key order for the 40 TB `prod.user_events` table (1,095 dates, 200 countries, 50,000,000 distinct user_ids). The three dominant queries are:

Q1: `WHERE event_date BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-07' AND country = 'US'`

Q2: `WHERE user_id = 918273`

Q3: `WHERE event_date = '2025-03-01' GROUP BY country`

Candidate A: `CLUSTER BY (event_date, country, user_id)`.

Candidate B: `CLUSTER BY (user_id, event_date, country)`.

Using per-file min/max statistics, compute what fraction of the 40 TB each query must scan under Candidate B for Q1, and under Candidate A for Q1; recommend one candidate.
Hint: Clustering keys are hierarchical: the first key defines the primary file grouping, and later keys only sort within that grouping.

Worked solution
Clustering is hierarchical. The first key sets the primary file grouping; each later key sorts within the group created by the keys before it. Data skipping then uses per-file min/max statistics on the clustering columns.

Under Candidate B, `user_id` is first. Each file collects rows for a set of users, and because every user is active across the full three-year window, a file's min/max event_date spans roughly all 1,095 days. The Q1 date-range predicate `BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-07'` overlaps every file's event_date range, so no file can be skipped: the fraction scanned is 1, i.e. ≈ 40,960 GB (40 TB). Q2 is excellent (one user's rows are colocated), but Q1 and Q3 become full scans.

Under Candidate A, `event_date` is first. Files are grouped by date, so a file's min/max event_date covers a narrow date range. The 7-day filter matches 7 / 1,095 = 0.00639 of the data: 40,960 GB × 0.00639 ≈ 261.7 GB. Within those date groups, `country` is second, so the `country = 'US'` predicate prunes to 1 / 200 of that: 261.7 GB / 200 ≈ 1.31 GB for Q1. Q3 scans 1 / 1,095 × 40,960 GB ≈ 37.4 GB for the single date and then groups by country. Q2 still benefits: `user_id` is the third key, so within each date-country file users are sorted and min/max user_id ranges are narrow; a single-user lookup reads a small number of files, on the order of a few GB rather than 40 TB. Clustering sorts data by one or a few fields and colocates similar values, improving filtering, sorting, and joins [source p.240].

Recommendation: Candidate A. The date-range and date-equality dashboards dominate, so the leading key must preserve narrow event_date min/max ranges. Candidate B would optimize Q2 but destroy Q1 and Q3.

Analysis — The central idea is that a leading high-cardinality key makes the statistics of every later key useless for skipping. Under Candidate B, a file's event_date min/max is broad because one user spans all dates, so a date predicate cannot prune; the file count stays the same but selectivity drops to zero. Under Candidate A, a file's event_date min/max is narrow because a file belongs to a date range, so the date predicate prunes aggressively; country and user_id then prune within the already-reduced set. This is why the ordering rule is not 'most selective column first' but 'most frequently filtered, pruning-friendly column first.' A common mistake is to assume that adding more clustering keys always helps every query; in practice a poorly ordered key set helps the query that matches the leading key and leaves the others as bad as no clustering. Another mistake is to put a high-cardinality identifier like user_id first because equality filters on it are selective; that choice fails range predicates on dates, which dominate analytical workloads. Edge case: if Q2 were the only query and user_id filters were extremely rare but always point lookups, Candidate B could be justified. For a mixed workload, Candidate A is the safer, more general layout. The number 1/200 for country assumes approximately uniform country distribution; with skew, the pruned fraction is the fraction of files whose country min/max includes 'US', which data skipping computes exactly from file statistics.
Problem 3

After migrating `prod.user_events` to `CLUSTER BY (event_date, user_id)`, the table still has 9,850,000 files averaging 4.1 MB. Your team proposes four options:

A) `OPTIMIZE prod.user_events;`

B) Enable auto compaction and wait for it to fix the backlog.

C) `ALTER TABLE prod.user_events SET PARTITIONED BY (event_date);`

D) `OPTIMIZE prod.user_events ZORDER BY (user_id);`

Pick the correct primary action, state what must be enabled afterward, and compute the file-count reduction at the 1 GB and 128 MB targets. The ingestion job appends ~2 GB every five minutes.
Hint: Distinguish remediating an existing backlog from preventing future small files.

Worked solution
Correct primary action: A, `OPTIMIZE prod.user_events;`. OPTIMIZE rewrites small files into larger target-size files and, on a clustered table, also reorganizes rows to honor the clustering keys.

Option B is wrong as a repair: auto compaction only rewrites small files produced by the current write transaction; it does not schedule a rewrite of millions of historical files [source p.273]. Waiting leaves the 9,850,000-file backlog in place.

Option C is invalid as a metadata-only change: an existing Delta table's partitioning is fixed at creation and cannot be changed with `ALTER TABLE ... SET PARTITIONED BY`; you would have to recreate or rewrite the table. It also would not fix file size, and date partitioning alone is coarser than the clustering already in place.

Option D is wrong: Z-ORDER is a legacy layout technique, user_id is high-cardinality, and Z-ORDER does not address the number of files; it also should not be layered on top of liquid clustering on the same table.

File-count reduction from OPTIMIZE. The table is 40 TB = 40,960 GB.

At the 1 GB target: 40,960 GB / 1 GB = 40,960 files, so 9,850,000 / 40,960 ≈ 240.5× fewer files.

At the 128 MB target: 40,960 GB / 0.125 GB = 327,680 files, so 9,850,000 / 327,680 ≈ 30.1× fewer files.

After the one-time OPTIMIZE, enable auto compaction:

```sql

ALTER TABLE prod.user_events SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact' = 'true');

```

and enable predictive optimization at the catalog or schema level. Also set `delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite = 'true'` so writes pre-compact on the write path.

Recurrence arithmetic: each five-minute micro-batch is ~2 GB. Without write-side compaction it can produce 2 GB / 4.1 MB ≈ 500 files per batch; at 288 batches per day that is 288 × 500 = 144,000 files per day. With optimizeWrite and auto compaction, the same 2 GB becomes about 2 one-GB files per batch, or ~576 files per day, keeping the file count stable between scheduled OPTIMIZE runs. The data is ultimately written out as a Parquet-formatted Delta Lake table [source p.346].

Analysis — The method choice is a two-phase strategy: OPTIMIZE is the remediation for the accumulated backlog, and auto compaction plus predictive optimization are the prevention mechanism for new small files. Students often reverse the two and rely on auto compaction to clean up a legacy mess, but auto compaction is transactional and incremental: it targets small files created by the write that is currently committing, not files written months ago. OPTIMIZE is the tool that scans existing files and rewrites them to the target size, and on a liquid-clustered table it also clusters the data, so the compaction and the layout fix happen together. Option C fails on two counts: partitioning is not mutable in place for an existing Delta table, and even if it were, directory-level partitioning would not consolidate 9.85 million tiny files. Option D fails because Z-ORDER does not reduce file count and because mixing Z-ORDER with liquid clustering is not the supported layout path. The target-size choice is a trade-off: 128 MB is the default and gives faster incremental writes, while 1 GB is preferred for very large tables because it reduces file-open and task overhead further. Choosing 1 GB here gives ~240× fewer files; choosing 128 MB still gives ~30×, which is enough to remove the worst overhead. A common pitfall is to run OPTIMIZE once and declare victory; without auto compaction and predictive optimization, the five-minute ingestion cadence re-creates the problem within days, as the 144,000-files-per-day arithmetic shows. Another edge case is concurrency: OPTIMIZE rewrites files and can conflict with concurrent writers, so schedule it outside peak ingestion or rely on predictive optimization's managed scheduling.

actions.text: Now that you've had a chance to work through those checkpoints, let's put the layout concepts together in a full worked problem. This one walks a badly laid-out table from symptom all the way to repair across three parts, and it's exactly the style of scenario the exam likes to test.

Problem 1 sets the scene. We have a Delta table called prod.user_events in Unity Catalog, partitioned by event_date and user_id. It's grown to forty terabytes, it's riddled with millions of tiny files, and date-only filters are running slowly. Your job is to propose a fix.

The hint tells you the diagnostic move: compute the average partition size before you change anything. That single number exposes the over-partitioning threshold — once your partitions dip below roughly a gigabyte, the directory count explodes and the metadata overhead swamps the actual read.

The analysis confirms it — the partitioning is coarse in the wrong way, because user_id produces runaway cardinality and skew. One directory per user per day is a directory explosion. The fix is to drop the user_id partition and move to liquid clustering with ALTER TABLE CLUSTER BY on event_date and user_id, then run OPTIMIZE to compact those small files and enable auto compaction and predictive optimization.

Problem 2 shifts focus to the ordering of clustering keys for a four-column table. This is where people lose easy points. Your hint: clustering keys are hierarchical, so the first key does the heavy lifting of co-locating data, and each subsequent key only refines within its parent.

The analysis drives it home — a leading high-cardinality column fragments the layout and defeats the pruning you were hoping for. The idea is to lead with the column that gives you the cleanest, most selective slicing, and let the rest refine from there.

Problem 3 changes the question. After migrating prod.user_events to CLUSTER BY, you still have a backlog of tiny files from the old layout. The hint asks you to distinguish remediating an existing backlog from preventing future ones — two different jobs that often get conflated.

The worked solution picks OPTIMIZE as the correct primary action — you compact the backlog with OPTIMIZE and THEN turn on the ongoing maintenance like auto compaction so the problem doesn't rebuild itself. The analysis frames this as a two-phase strategy: remediate first, then sustain. That sequencing is the exam trap to watch, so make sure you can state it cold before we move on.

scenes.title: Decision: Partitioning, Liquid Clustering, or Z-ORDER?

elements.content: Decision — A data platform team of five engineers at a retail analytics company must redesign the physical layout of a new 50 TB Delta table that stores point-of-sale events. The table is loaded nightly by a batch pipeline and queried interactively by two dominant filter patterns: dashboard queries filter on `event_date` for a rolling 90-day window, while customer-service tools filter on `customer_id` plus a 7-day date range. The current prototype is an unmanaged external Delta table partitioned by `event_date` only, and the team must decide before the table enters production. The decision is hard because each candidate layout satisfies one filter pattern well at the expense of the other, the storage layer offers no single option that is strictly dominant, and the team must also respect Unity Catalog managed-table availability, engine support for `CLUSTER BY`, and the operational burden of keeping the layout effective as data grows.

Constraints — The table is a new 50 TB Delta table that will receive nightly batch appends, so the chosen layout must tolerate continuous incremental ingestion without a full rewrite.  •  Production queries must prune efficiently for both `event_date` ranges and `customer_id` equality predicates, because the service-level objective is under 10 seconds for interactive dashboards and customer-service lookups.  •  The table must live in Unity Catalog, and the chosen DDL must be supported by the engines that will query it; if `CLUSTER BY` is unavailable on the target engine or the table is an external legacy table, liquid clustering cannot be used.  •  The team cannot afford a migration project that rewrites the 50 TB table every time the access pattern shifts, so reversibility of the layout decision is a first-class requirement.

Partition by event_date
+ Date is the classic low-cardinality partition key and appears in the most frequent WHERE filters, so date-window queries prune to the relevant day directories and scan very little data.; + The layout is cheap to create and familiar: engineers already understand directory-based pruning, and no new engine capabilities are required.; + It aligns naturally with append-only nightly loads, because each night's batch lands in its own partition directory.
− The `customer_id` filter gets no pruning benefit, so customer-service lookups still scan the full 90-day window or the entire table unless other statistics happen to prune files.; − High-date-cardinality tables risk over-partitioning: a 50 TB table with several years of daily partitions and small nightly appends can produce files far below the roughly 128 MB target and a partition count that stresses the metadata layer [source p.273].; − Changing the partition key later requires rewriting the table, so the decision is effectively permanent once production data accumulates.
Best for: Workloads whose queries are overwhelmingly date-range filters on a table with low date cardinality and large per-partition volumes.

Liquid clustering on (customer_id, event_date)
+ A single layout serves both filter patterns: `customer_id` equality predicates and `event_date` range predicates both benefit from data skipping, because the clustering keys cover the two dominant access columns.; + Clustering keys can be changed at any time with `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (...)` without rewriting the table, which directly satisfies the reversibility constraint.; + Layout adapts incrementally as data arrives, so nightly batch appends improve the clustering over time rather than degrading it, and the approach avoids the over-partitioning trap because it does not create directory-per-value structures.; + It replaces both partitioning and Z-ORDER with one mechanism, which simplifies DDL and operational reasoning for the team.
− It requires engine support for `CLUSTER BY` and a Unity Catalog managed table; external legacy Delta tables and older engines cannot use it.; − Clustering is not a point index: an individual `customer_id` lookup on a very large table still reads a clustered subset of files rather than one record, so millisecond point lookups remain out of scope [source p.239].; − Teams used to partition-directory mental models must learn a new pruning model and verify it with EXPLAIN rather than assuming directory isolation.
Best for: New large Delta tables with multiple recurring filter patterns where the layout must remain changeable as access patterns evolve.

Z-ORDER on (customer_id, event_date) with OPTIMIZE
+ It improves data skipping on the specified columns and is well understood by engineers who already run `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (...)`.; + It can be applied to an existing partitioned table without changing the partition scheme, so it is a compatible add-on to the current prototype.; + It works on engines that lack `CLUSTER BY` support, which matters if the target engine has not yet adopted liquid clustering.
− Z-ORDER is not self-maintaining: its effectiveness decays as new files arrive, so the team must schedule recurring `OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY` jobs, and each run rewrites data and consumes cluster time.; − It does not replace partitioning, so the table still suffers the over-partitioning and small-file risks of `event_date` partitioning [source p.273].; − The benefit is bounded by how well the existing files are sized: if the table already has millions of tiny files, Z-ORDER runs are expensive and their value is limited until compaction catches up.
Best for: Existing partitioned tables on engines without `CLUSTER BY` support, where a scheduled optimization job is operationally acceptable.

Recommendation: Liquid clustering on (customer_id, event_date) — The binding constraints are the dual filter patterns, the 50 TB scale, and the requirement that the layout remain changeable without a rewrite. Partitioning by `event_date` satisfies only the date filter and, at 50 TB with nightly appends, invites over-partitioning and small files that the insert and batch-size literature warns against [source p.273]. Z-ORDER improves skipping but does not replace partitioning and must be re-run to stay effective, so it fails the reversibility constraint. Liquid clustering on `(customer_id, event_date)` covers both the `customer_id` equality and `event_date` range predicates, can be altered at any time with `ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (...)`, and adapts incrementally to nightly loads, which is why it is the recommended default for new large Delta tables. The one caveat is that this choice is only valid if the target engine supports `CLUSTER BY` and the table is a Unity Catalog managed table; if either is false, the team should fall back to Z-ORDER with OPTIMIZE and accept the maintenance burden.

actions.text: We just fixed a degraded table layout — now let's make the design decision that prevents degradation in the first place. This page poses the classic layout question: partitioning, liquid clustering, or Z-ORDER? And as always on the exam, the answer is not "whichever is newest" — it's the option that fits the workload.

Here's the scenario. A data platform team of five engineers owns a new 50 terabyte Delta table. It's filtered mainly by event_date and customer_id, and the analysts want fast reads on both filter patterns.

Note the constraints before you leap to an answer. It's a brand-new table with no legacy code pinned to a partitioned layout, it's Unity Catalog managed, and the engine supports CLUSTER BY. That matters — constraints are what shift a design decision from "textbook best practice" to "the right answer for this team."

Option A is partitioning on event_date. It's cheap, familiar, and great for low-cardinality date filters — but it's rigid: if analysts start filtering by customer_id, that partition scheme can't help. And it invites over-partitioning, which snowballs into the small-file problem we just covered.

Option B is liquid clustering on customer_id and event_date. It's adaptive, reversible — you can change the clustering keys later without rewriting the table — and it supports both filter patterns at once. That flexibility is exactly why it's the default recommendation for new large Delta tables.

Option C is Z-ORDER with OPTIMIZE. It works, but only inside the files OPTIMIZE touches — it doesn't replace partitioning, and it degrades unless you keep re-running OPTIMIZE. Treat it as a complement, not a foundation.

So the recommendation: for this 50 TB table filtered by both date and customer_id, use liquid clustering on customer_id and event_date — one layout that serves both access patterns with no rewrite. Ready to test that reasoning? Let's kick it around.

scenes.title: Final Checkpoint: Layout, Clustering, and File Sizing

questions.question: A 40 TB events table is currently partitioned by event_date and user_id. Analysts constantly filter by event_date alone, by user_id alone, and by both together. The table now contains millions of tiny files and date-only filters run slowly. Which single layout change best resolves both the runaway file-count problem and the slow single-column filters at the same time?

options.label: Keep partitioning by event_date and user_id but increase the number of partitions so each filter column has its own directory level
Drop partitioning entirely and rebuild the table with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (event_date, user_id) so either column can prune files adaptively
Keep the user_id partition and add Z-ORDER BY user_id on top of the existing event_date partition
Keep the user_id partition and run OPTIMIZE more frequently to merge the tiny files inside each partition

questions.analysis: The worked problem in this unit establishes the correct two-step repair: first remove the user_id partition, which created a runaway directory count and skew, then convert to liquid clustering with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (event_date, user_id) so filters on either column prune data. Liquid clustering replaces partitioning and Z-ORDER with a single CLUSTER BY column set, and keys can be changed at any time with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (...). Option A worsens the problem because adding more partitions increases the directory count and produces even smaller files — over-partitioning is a documented cause of small files. Option C mixes two layout mechanisms on one table, the exact distractor this unit warns against: clustering is designed to replace Z-ORDER, not stack on top of partitioning. Option D merely compacts within the broken directory structure; frequent OPTIMIZE cannot fix a layout where user_id alone cannot prune event_date partitions, and compaction is a remedy for file size, not for an unpruneable filter. Note that clustering is adaptive and reversible, which is why it is the default recommendation over rigid partitioning.

questions.question: A streaming pipeline lands micro-batches into a Delta table every few seconds, and the table's file count now vastly outnumbers its data volume, with queries spawning thousands of Spark tasks. Which of the following statements about this situation are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The root cause is likely frequent small writes from streaming ingestion rather than a defect in the Parquet file format itself
Running OPTIMIZE on the table is an appropriate compaction strategy because it merges small files toward the target file size
The only permanent fix is to convert the data files from Parquet to a row-based format so each write produces one large file
The high task count and slow queries are consistent with per-file I/O, task, and metadata overhead accumulating across many small files

questions.analysis: This unit lists streaming ingestion, frequent small MERGE or INSERT statements, over-partitioning, and high-shuffle writes as the common causes of the small-file problem, and describes the symptoms as slow queries, excessive tasks in the Spark UI, and a table whose files vastly outnumber its data volume. Option A correctly attributes the cause to the ingestion pattern, not the storage format. Option D correctly maps the symptoms to per-file I/O, task, and metadata overhead — small files are defined as data files far below the target size (roughly 128 MB default, up to 1 GB for large tables). Option B is correct because OPTIMIZE is the compaction command that merges small files toward the target size. Option C is the classic misconception this unit explicitly rejects: small files are a layout and write-pattern problem, not a storage-format problem. Switching to a row-based format would destroy the columnar benefits without changing how many files each micro-batch write produces. For context on why open columnar formats matter in a lakehouse — interoperable data exchange without reserializing proprietary formats — see [source p.243].

questions.question: A transactions table stores rows keyed by transaction_id, each with a merchant_id, a transaction_date, and an amount. The table is 8 TB, and 70 percent of queries filter on transaction_date ranges, while a smaller but important workload filters on merchant_id across all time. The table is currently unpartitioned and consists of a few hundred files averaging 1.2 GB each. Two proposals are on the table: (1) partition by transaction_date only, or (2) use liquid clustering with CLUSTER BY (transaction_date, merchant_id). Evaluate both proposals and recommend one, justifying your answer with reference to cardinality, filter patterns, file sizing, reversibility, and the risk of over-partitioning or small files. State explicitly which proposal you reject and the strongest technical reason for rejecting it.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (total 100%): (1) Correctly identifies transaction_date as a low-cardinality column that appears in the most frequent WHERE filters and merchant_id as potentially higher-cardinality — 25%. (2) Recommends liquid clustering with CLUSTER BY (transaction_date, merchant_id) and explains that it lets either filter column prune data, whereas partitioning on transaction_date alone cannot help merchant_id-only queries — 25%. (3) Explains reversibility and key flexibility: clustering keys can be changed with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (...) without rewriting the table, whereas partitioning is rigid and changing it requires rebuilding — 20%. (4) Addresses file sizing: current files average 1.2 GB, which is at or above the roughly 128 MB default target, so neither proposal should introduce a small-file problem immediately, but date partitioning could if granularity is too fine — 15%. (5) Explains why partitioning is rejected: partition-only on date is acceptable for the common filter but leaves the merchant_id workload unprunable, and if the date granularity were pushed finer it would risk over-partitioning and small files — 15%. Award no credit for answers that recommend stacking partitioning and Z-ORDER on the same table, or that claim partitioning and liquid clustering should coexist. Clarity and correct use of Databricks terminology (Delta table, CLUSTER BY, OPTIMIZE, data skipping) may adjust the score within the bands above.
questions.analysis: A strong answer selects option (2). It notes that transaction_date is a low-cardinality, frequently-filtered column and is the natural first clustering key, consistent with the guidance to pick a low-cardinality key that appears in frequent WHERE filters. merchant_id is included as a second key because it supports the secondary workload and liquid clustering lets either column prune data, which partitioning on date alone cannot do. Liquid clustering replaces partitioning and Z-ORDER with one CLUSTER BY column set, and keys can be altered later without rewriting the table, making the decision reversible and low-risk — the unit's stated default recommendation when a layout must adapt to more than one access pattern. Option (1) is rejected because it optimizes only the dominant date filter and leaves merchant_id-only queries scanning all date partitions unless the engine happens to prune on file statistics; if the engineer tried to rescue merchant_id by adding it as a second partition level, the directory count would explode and drive over-partitioning and small files. The answer should also confirm the current average file size (1.2 GB) is not itself pathological, so the repair is about pruneability, not compaction. This reasoning reflects broader lakehouse design principles around open, interoperable storage and hidden file management [source p.243], and the general caution that columnar systems do not enforce primary keys, so key-based access depends on layout choices the engineering team controls [source p.343].

actions.text: This is the final checkpoint for this lesson, so it pulls together everything we've covered on storage layout, key selection, clustering syntax, and compaction. Take your time with each question and work through them on your own — the short-answer one especially rewards a careful, structured justification.

Give every question an honest attempt before you submit, including the ones that feel tricky. Once you're done, I'll be right here to walk through the reasoning and clear up anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Lesson Overview: Joins, Shuffles, and Caching

elements.content: Lesson Overview: Joins, Shuffles, and Caching
Lesson objectives

• Choose broadcast hash join vs. shuffle hash join for a given table size and cluster profile.

• Predict which stage dominates wall-clock time in a slow join.

• Cut shuffle cost with caching where it actually pays off.

• Justify the choice with shuffle bytes and runtime, not intuition.
Where this lesson sits
Earlier lessons covered reading the Spark UI and laying out Delta files [source p.346]. This lesson changes the execution plan itself: join strategy, shuffle, and caching.
Where wall-clock time goes in a slow join
Shuffle write + read = 60% of runtime — the target of this lesson.
Exam objective: given a slow join plus a cluster profile, select the correct optimization and predict its effect on shuffle bytes and runtime. [source p.304]

actions.text: Good work on the layout and clustering material. Let's shift gears now and open a new lesson: joins, shuffles, and caching. This is where we stop rearranging files and start changing the execution plan itself.

Here are the objectives for this lesson. Two things you'll be able to do by the end: first, choose between a broadcast hash join and a shuffle hash join for a given pair of tables; second, cut shuffle cost with caching, but only where caching actually pays off. Notice the phrasing — choose and predict, not just recognize. That's the level the exam asks for.

So you need to pick the right join strategy, and you need to reason about caching as a cost decision rather than a default habit. Both of those are decisions you'll make constantly in production pipelines.

Let's place this lesson in the unit. Earlier pages taught you to read the Spark UI — jobs, stages, tasks — and to lay out Delta files with partitioning and liquid clustering. Those were diagnostics and storage layout. This lesson changes the execution plan itself. Same tables, same result, very different runtime.

Now look at this bar chart. It shows where wall-clock time actually goes in a slow join, broken into file scan, shuffle write and read, the join itself, and the final write. Pay attention to which bar is tallest.

Shuffle write plus shuffle read together account for roughly sixty percent of runtime. That is the target. So when you're handed a slow join, your instinct should be to ask how much of this time is shuffle, and what would remove it — a broadcast, a better distribution, or Adaptive Query Execution doing the work for you.

One last thing before we dive in — the exam objective, stated plainly. You'll be given a slow join plus a cluster profile, and asked to select the correct optimization and predict its effect on shuffle bytes and runtime. Predict the effect. That means the underlying mechanics matter, not just the name of the technique, and that's exactly what we'll build over the next several pages.

scenes.title: Why Joins Are Expensive: The Shuffle

elements.content: Why Joins Are Expensive: The Shuffle

A shuffle is the dominant cost of a join: rows are serialized, spilled to local disk, then pulled across the network at a stage boundary.

Because it touches every surviving row, it usually outweighs the table scan that produced those rows.
Narrow transformations

select

filter / where

withColumn

No data crosses the network — each row stays in its partition.
Wide transformations

join

groupBy

distinct / repartition

Forces a shuffle: serialize, spill to disk, pull across the network.
Default join: sort-merge

Both sides exchanged on the join key.

Then sorted, then merged.

Both inputs pay the network cost.
Worked example: 5 × 10 repeat rows in the join key produce 5 × 10 = 50 output rows per match group, so a shuffle can amplify data rather than shrink it. [source p.323]
If neither input fits on one node, Spark switches to a shuffle hash join that repartitions both sides by join key. [source p.337]

actions.text: Let's start with the single most important cost driver in this lesson: the shuffle. Before we talk about any join strategy or tuning trick, we need to understand why joins are expensive in the first place.

The title says it directly — the shuffle is the dominant cost of a join. Everything else we cover about broadcast joins, join strategies, and caching is essentially a way to avoid, reduce, or pay for that shuffle more efficiently.

So what actually happens during a shuffle? Rows are serialized, spilled to local disk, then pulled across the network at a stage boundary. Notice the three distinct costs there: serialization on the CPU, disk I/O, and network transfer. That's why it dominates runtime far more than the table scan — the scan reads compressed columnar files locally, while a shuffle moves every surviving row between machines.

It helps to split transformations into two families. First, narrow transformations — things like select, filter, and withColumn. Each row stays in the partition it started in, and no data crosses the network. These are cheap.

Here's the key rule to memorize for the exam: a narrow transformation never moves data between partitions. The parent partition maps to exactly one child partition, so Spark can pipeline these operations together with no stage boundary in between.
Now the opposite family — wide transformations. Join, groupBy, distinct, and repartition all fall here. These force a shuffle.

The reason is simple: these operations need rows that share a key to land on the same partition, regardless of where they currently live. So Spark exchanges the data, and that exchange creates a new stage. Whenever you see a stage boundary in the Spark UI, a shuffle happened there.
Now let's look at what Spark actually does by default when you write a join. Unless the optimizer decides otherwise, Spark SQL's default join path is the sort-merge join.

And the sort-merge join is literally described by its name: both sides are exchanged on the join key, so both inputs get shuffled, then each partition is sorted, and finally the sorted streams are merged together to find matches. Two shuffles, two sorts, one merge.

Here's a worked example that makes the cost concrete. Suppose you have five rows on one side and ten rows on the other, all with the same join key. That key can only live on one partition after the shuffle, so all fifteen rows are pulled onto a single node. Scale that up to millions of rows sharing a hot key and you can see how a shuffle turns into a bottleneck.

That last line is a preview of what's coming: if neither input fits on a single node, Spark switches to the shuffle-heavy path rather than a broadcast. So the practical question throughout this lesson is always the same — can we avoid the shuffle entirely, or do we have to pay for it?

To summarize this page: narrow transformations move no data across the network; wide transformations force a shuffle that serializes, spills to disk, and transfers rows; and Spark's default sort-merge join shuffles both sides of the join. Because a shuffle touches every surviving row, it usually dominates runtime far more than the table scan. With that baseline in place, we can now look at the fast path that avoids the shuffle altogether.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Shuffles and Wide Transformations

questions.question: A Databricks job runs this pipeline: read a Parquet file, filter rows with a WHERE clause on a single column, add a derived column with withColumn, then join to a small 5-row dimension table and write the result with a GROUP BY aggregation. Which operation is the first point in the physical plan where data must physically move across the network between executors?

options.label: The Parquet file scan, because reading columnar files requires repartitioning the data before any transformation can begin
The filter and withColumn transformations, because each one reduces the row count and forces a redistribution to keep partitions balanced
The exchange feeding the aggregation or the join, because wide transformations such as GROUP BY and the join require repartitioning by key
The write to the target table, because columnar systems re-sort all data on write to create optimized files and this re-sort is the shuffle

questions.analysis: Wide transformations such as GROUP BY aggregations and joins depend on data grouped by a key value. If a given key value lives on multiple executors, the data must be redistributed so that all rows for one key land in the same partition — this is the shuffle, and it appears in the physical plan as an Exchange node. Narrow transformations (select, filter, withColumn) are pipelined within each partition and move nothing across the network, so options B and the filter portion of the stem are wrong. A file scan reads data into partitions but does not repartition by key, so option A misattributes the cost. The write may also trigger a shuffle if a partitioning or clustering scheme requires it, but it is not the first wide operation; the GROUP BY and join are already wide and come earlier in the plan, so option D is wrong. This follows the lesson's framing that narrow transformations such as select, filter, and withColumn are pipelined per partition while wide transformations force a redistribu­tion [source p.273].

questions.question: A physical plan shows an Exchange node sandwiched between a Scan Parquet node and a HashAggregate node. Which statements about this plan are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The Exchange node is the shuffle boundary; the network transfer of rows across executors happens here.
Because an Exchange appears, the preceding Scan Parquet must have been inefficient and is the real cause of the shuffle cost.
The Exchange exists because the aggregation is a wide transformation that requires all rows for a given key to be co-located in one partition.
Removing or replacing the Exchange is only meaningful if the operator above it (the aggregation or join) can be satisfied without a key-based redistribution.

questions.analysis: The Exchange node marks exactly where Spark redistributes data across the network, so option A is correct. It appears because a wide operator such as HashAggregate needs key-based co-location of rows, which option C states correctly. Option D is the operative engineering point: an Exchange can only be eliminated or converted to a broadcast if the downstream operator can be satisfied without a full key-based repartition — for instance by broadcasting a small build side instead of performing a shuffle hash join. Option B is the classic misconception this lesson warns against: a scan reads existing files and produces partitions but does not itself cause a shuffle, so blaming the Scan Parquet node for a cost the Exchange incurred is a distractor. This mirrors the small-file lesson's warning not to mistake a storage-layout observation for the cost an exchange actually produced [source p.273].

questions.question: A team reports that a nightly job writing an events table is slow, and the Spark UI shows shuffle write bytes equal to nearly the full table size. The physical plan contains a single Exchange immediately above a Scan Delta node and below the final Write node, and the write path includes a GROUP BY on a high-cardinality event_id. A junior engineer proposes rebuilding the Delta table's file layout to remove the shuffle. Which diagnosis and action is most defensible?

options.label: The Scan Delta node is the cause, so compacting the table with OPTIMIZE will remove the shuffle and reduce shuffle bytes.
The final Write node is the cause, so switching to insert-only writes will eliminate the shuffle cost entirely.

The Exchange is the shuffle boundary feeding the GROUP BY on event_id; because keyed aggregation on a high-cardinality key cannot avoid redistribution, the fix is to change the query (for example, broadcast or re-aggregate differently), not to rebuild the file layout.
Because event_id is high-cardinality, liquid clustering on event_id will eliminate the Exchange node and remove all shuffle bytes.

questions.analysis: The Exchange node between the Scan Delta and the aggregation is the shuffle boundary, and it exists because the GROUP BY on event_id is a wide transformation that requires all rows for a given key in one partition. Since event_id is high-cardinality, no layout choice removes the need to co-locate rows by that key at aggregation time; the fix must change the query plan, for example by broadcasting a small side or restructuring the aggregation. Option A follows the distractor pattern the lesson flags: blaming the scan for a cost the exchange actually caused — OPTIMIZE addresses the small-file problem, not shuffle redistribution, and the lesson treats small files as an I/O and task-overhead issue rather than a shuffle cause [source p.273]. Option B confuses write semantics with shuffle: truncate-and-reload and insert-only are update patterns that change table state, not plan-level shuffles [source p.342]. Option D correctly identifies high cardinality but then draws the wrong conclusion: the earlier layout lesson is explicit that clustering keys should not be chosen for high-cardinality identifiers such as user_id or order_id, and in any case clustering prunes files at scan time rather than removing an exchange needed to satisfy a keyed aggregation.

actions.text: Let's test what we just covered on shuffles and wide transformations. Work through each question on your own, and once you submit I'll walk through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Broadcast Hash Join: The Small-Table Fast Path

elements.content: Broadcast Hash Join: The Small-Table Fast Path
Mechanism

• Collect the small side to the driver

• Ship it to every executor

• Hash-probe it in memory

• Large side is never shuffled
Prefiltering data to create broadcast joins can dramatically improve performance and reduce resource consumption. [source p.337]
Eligibility

• Decided by size, not row count

• spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold = 10 MB

• Higher = more broadcast attempts

• Zero disables the fast path
Rule of thumb: broadcast the down-filtered side only
Worked example
24 GB fact joined to 40 MB dimension; threshold default 10 MB. Down-filter the dimension to 9 MB (~92,000 rows, ~100 B/row) - it now broadcasts and skips the 24 GB shuffle.

[source p.337] Table A is often a down-filtered larger table that the query engine collects and broadcasts. [source p.304] Know how your database handles commits. [source p.346] The DAG spills a large source to disk.

actions.text: Now we reach one of the highest-yield tuning techniques on the exam: the broadcast hash join. We just saw why joins are expensive — the shuffle. The broadcast hash join is the single most common way to eliminate that shuffle entirely, and it's the small-table fast path.

Here's the mechanism. Spark collects the small side of the join to the driver, then ships that entire dataset to every executor. Each executor builds a hash table from it locally and probes it against its own partition of the large side. The key insight: the large side is never shuffled. Only the small table moves, and it moves once, to everyone.

Now, eligibility. This is decided by size, not by row count — that distinction matters. The configuration spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold defaults to ten megabytes. If the estimated size of one side falls under that threshold, Spark picks the broadcast automatically. Memorize that ten megabyte default; it appears on the exam directly.

One important nuance from the source material: Table A is often a down-filtered large table rather than a genuinely small table. Prefiltering data before the join means the resulting side can be small enough to broadcast — even if the underlying table is large.

Let's make that concrete with a worked example. A twenty-four gigabyte fact table joined to a forty megabyte dimension. The dimension sits well under the ten megabyte threshold, so Spark broadcasts it, and the twenty-four gigabyte fact table never shuffles. Compare that to a sort-merge join, where both sides would be shuffled across the network.

A rule of thumb worth carrying into the exam: broadcast the down-filtered side. If you can shrink one input with a filter before the join, you unlock the broadcast path even when the raw table is large.

Finally, the exam trap. Broadcasting a side that is actually large causes driver out-of-memory errors or severe executor memory pressure.
