That failure is worse than the shuffle you were trying to avoid. So you can force a broadcast with a broadcast() hint on the small table, and you can disable it with a zero threshold or a negative broadcast hint — but you must know which side you're betting on.

scenes.title: Choosing a Join Strategy: BHJ vs. SHJ vs. SMJ

elements.content: Dimension  |  Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ)  |  Shuffle Hash Join (SHJ)  |  Sort-Merge Join (SMJ)

Trigger condition (when Spark selects it)
Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ): Spark's cost-based optimizer selects BHJ when the estimated size of one join side is below the broadcast threshold (3221225472 bytes = 3 GB by default, controlled by spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold) after filters are pushed down; with no statistics the optimizer falls back to the heuristic of broadcasting a relation it can prove small.
Shuffle Hash Join (SHJ): SHJ is chosen only when the smaller side exceeds the broadcast threshold yet is still estimated to fit in the aggregate executor memory available for hash build, and it must be forced or hinted (spark.sql.join.preferSortMergeJoin = false or a SHUFFLE_HASH hint) because SMJ is the default planner choice.
Sort-Merge Join (SMJ): SMJ is the default planner choice whenever statistics are missing, the smaller side is either unknown or too large for broadcast or shuffle-hash build, or spark.sql.join.preferSortMergeJoin is left at its default true; it is the only strategy that always works regardless of relation size.

Which side is exchanged over the network
Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ): Only the small side is exchanged: the query engine broadcasts the small table (table A) out to all nodes, where it is joined to the parts of the large table (table B), so the large side is never shuffled [source p.336].
Shuffle Hash Join (SHJ): Only the small side is shuffled: a hashing scheme repartitions the data by join key, and the large side's rows are moved out of their original partitions and routed to the matching hash partition, which is why SHJ is not a no-shuffle join [source p.337].
Sort-Merge Join (SMJ): Both sides are exchanged: every row of both inputs is serialized, repartitioned on the join key, and sorted before the merge phase, so the full shuffled bytes of both relations cross the network.

Memory requirement and failure mode
Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ): The broadcast side must fit in the driver's collect buffer and then in each executor's broadcast hash table; the dominant failure mode is a driver or executor OutOfMemoryError when the planner's size estimate is badly wrong, because the entire small side is materialized on every node.
Shuffle Hash Join (SHJ): The build side must fit in the executor's hash table area (circa 30% of the executor heap after spark.memory.fraction and spark.memory.storageFraction adjustments); the dominant failure mode is a SpillException or OOM in a single task if the actual build side exceeds that fraction under concurrent tasks.
Sort-Merge Join (SMJ): Memory is bounded per partition, not per relation: each task sorts and buffers only its own shuffle partition, and when that partition exceeds the execution memory budget Spark spills sorted runs to local disk and merges them, which costs extra disk I/O but keeps the join correct.

Skew tolerance
Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ): Very low tolerance: one duplicate-heavy key value in the small side blows up the replicated hash table, and one hot key in the large side concentrates all matching work on a single executor, so a skewed BHJ converts a fast join into a straggler task.
Shuffle Hash Join (SHJ): Low to moderate: skew on the join key in the large side still sends all rows with that key to one reducer, so the hash partition containing the hot key becomes a single long-running task, while the other partitions finish early.
Sort-Merge Join (SMJ): High: SMJ handles skew gracefully because the sort phase is per-partition and the merge phase streams, so an over-large hot partition spills to disk rather than failing, though the hot task still runs longer than its peers.

Typical use case
Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ): Joining a large fact table to a small dimension table (for example, a 40 TB events Delta table to a few-hundred-megabyte lookup table) where prefiltering the small side is possible, because prefiltering data to create broadcast joins where possible can dramatically improve performance and reduce resource consumption [source p.337].
Shuffle Hash Join (SHJ): The middle ground when the small side is too large to broadcast but not so large that sorting both sides is wasteful — for example, joining a 200 GB dimension to a 5 TB fact table where an equi-join key exists and the dimension has already been aggregated.
Sort-Merge Join (SMJ): The general-purpose default for large-to-large equi-joins, including star-schema joins where neither side is small, and the safe exam answer whenever the question mentions skew or exhausted executor memory; in distributed engines this same pattern appears across MapReduce, BigQuery, Snowflake, or Spark [source p.336].

Exam trap / commonly confused claim
Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ): Students often say a BHJ 'shuffles the small table'; strictly, the small side is collected by the driver and broadcast, and only a BroadcastExchange plus a BroadcastHashJoin node appear in the plan — there is no Exchange on the large side.
Shuffle Hash Join (SHJ): The classic trap is labelling SHJ a 'no-shuffle join': the small side is still exchanged and repartitioned by hash on the join key, so the plan still contains an Exchange node even though the large side stays in place [source p.337].
Sort-Merge Join (SMJ): Students often assume SMJ is wasteful and should always be replaced by BHJ or SHJ; in practice SMJ is the default and the most robust, and the optimizer often lowers it to the other strategies precisely because join reordering with early filters shrinks the input [source p.337].

Worked example: 8 GB build side against a 3 GB broadcast threshold
Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ): Blocked: 8 GB > 3 GB, so BHJ cannot be selected without raising spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to 8589934592, which is dangerous because the same 8 GB is materialized on every executor — with 100 executors that is 800 GB of replicated state.
Shuffle Hash Join (SHJ): Feasible if each executor's hash budget exceeds 8 GB divided by concurrent build tasks; with 16 GB executor heap, spark.memory.fraction = 0.6 gives 9.6 GB execution memory, so a single SHJ build task just fits, but raising spark.sql.shuffle.partitions or lowering per-task memory will force a spill or OOM.
Sort-Merge Join (SMJ): Always feasible: SMJ shuffles the full 8 GB build side plus the large side (say 800 GB), so total shuffle bytes are roughly 808 GB before compression, but no single task must hold 8 GB because sorting and merging stream through bounded buffers and spill.

Cost formula to reason about
Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ): Network cost ≈ size(small side) × number of executors, plus driver collect cost ≈ size(small side); CPU cost ≈ one hash probe per row of the large side, so total ≈ rows(large) hash lookups.
Shuffle Hash Join (SHJ): Network cost ≈ size(small side) plus the repartitioned portion of the large side that matches, i.e. ≈ size(small) + size(large matched rows); CPU cost ≈ hash build over small side + hash probe per large-side row after shuffle.
Sort-Merge Join (SMJ): Network cost ≈ size(large side) + size(small side); CPU cost ≈ sort(small) + sort(large) + linear merge, i.e. O((n + m) log(n + m)) in the worst case, which is why shuffle bytes dominate the runtime in the Spark UI.
Takeaway — Choose BHJ when one side is provably under the 3 GB default threshold and you can prefilter it: it eliminates network exchange on the large side entirely [source p.336][source p.337].

Takeaway — Choose SHJ only when the small side exceeds the broadcast threshold but still fits in executor execution memory, and remember the exam trap that the small side is still exchanged by hash [source p.337].

Takeaway — Choose SMJ by default for large-to-large joins and whenever the question mentions skew or memory pressure, because it shuffles and sorts both sides yet remains the most robust strategy across MapReduce, BigQuery, Snowflake, and Spark [source p.336].

Takeaway — Always check the physical plan: an Exchange node means a shuffle boundary, so a plan labelled SHJ with an Exchange is not a no-shuffle join, and a plan labelled BHJ with a BroadcastExchange on only one side is.

Takeaway — Prefer to fix the join before tuning it: push filters early and reorder joins so a large table becomes a filtered small table worth broadcasting, which is cheaper than choosing a more expensive strategy [source p.337].

actions.text: Now that we've seen why joins are expensive and how shuffles drive that cost, let's put the three join strategies side by side. On this page we compare Broadcast Hash Join, Shuffle Hash Join, and Sort-Merge Join across the dimensions that actually decide the exam answer.

Here's the comparison table. Read it by rows: each strategy, BHJ, SHJ, and SMJ, is judged against five columns — the trigger condition, which side gets exchanged over the network, the memory requirement, skew tolerance, and the typical use case. When a question asks you to pick a strategy, it's almost always testing one of these cells.

Start with the trigger condition, because that's the first thing the optimizer evaluates. Spark picks Broadcast Hash Join when one side is small enough to fit under the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, and that side is broadcast to every executor. If neither side fits that threshold, broadcast is off the table and Spark has to choose between SHJ and SMJ.

Next, which side is exchanged over the network. This is where a lot of candidates lose points. Broadcast Hash Join does not exchange the large side — instead the small side is replicated to every executor, so no shuffle of the big table happens at all.

Now watch the memory and failure mode column. BHJ ships the entire small side into each executor's memory, so it's fast but it's the most memory-hungry per node. If the broadcast side isn't actually small — or the driver over-estimates its size — you'll see an out-of-memory failure, which is a classic BHJ failure mode to recognize on the exam.

Then look at skew tolerance. Broadcast Hash Join has very low skew tolerance — if the broadcast side has a hot key, that hotspot gets replicated to every executor and one partition does all the work. Sort-Merge Join, by contrast, is the most robust under skew because the shuffle spreads the keys and the merge handles uneven distributions much better.

Here's the exam trap I want you to internalize. Shuffle Hash Join is often described as a no-shuffle join. That is wrong. In SHJ, the small side is still exchanged — it's shuffled and hashed, but only the small side is shuffled. The large side stays where it is. So SHJ is the middle ground: use it when the small side exceeds the broadcast threshold but the large side shouldn't be reshuffled.

Let's reason through a worked example: an 8 GB build side joined against a 3 GB probe side. The build side is 8 GB — that's way above the autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, so BHJ is off. Neither side is small enough to be a clean broadcast candidate, and 3 GB shuffled against 8 GB is a large-to-large join. Spark will fall back to Sort-Merge Join here, shuffling and sorting both sides. That matches our trigger-condition rule: broadcast needs a genuinely small side.

Use the cost formula to reason about this. Broadcast cost scales with the size of the small side multiplied by the number of executors, because every executor gets a copy. Shuffle cost scales with the data actually moved across the network. So BHJ is cheap when the small side is tiny; once the broadcast side grows, the replication cost explodes and SMJ's shuffle-first approach becomes the safer, more predictable choice.

So here's your takeaway set for the exam. Choose Broadcast Hash Join when one side is provably small enough to fit the broadcast threshold — it's the fastest path because there's no shuffle of the large side.
Choose Shuffle Hash Join only when the small side exceeds the broadcast threshold but is still small enough to hash into memory on each executor — remember, only the small side gets shuffled there.

And choose Sort-Merge Join by default for large-to-large joins — it's the fallback, and it's the most robust under skew and tight memory because both sides are shuffled and sorted into ordered partitions.

One habit to build now: always check the physical plan. If you see a BroadcastHashJoin operator, the small side was broadcast. If you see ShuffledHashJoin, only the build side was shuffled. And if you see SortMergeJoin, both sides were shuffled and sorted. Reading the plan is how you confirm which strategy actually ran, rather than guessing.

Finally, the meta-lesson: prefer to fix the join before tuning it. If a broadcast is failing because a table isn't really small, the right move is often to cut columns, filter rows, or pre-aggregate the broadcast side — not to crank up cluster memory. In the next checkpoint, we'll test your understanding of broadcast and shuffle hash joins specifically.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Broadcast and Shuffle Hash Joins

questions.question: A Spark job joins a 12 GB fact table (distributed across the cluster) to a 4 GB dimension table. The cluster runs with the default spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10 MB) and BroadcastHashJoin is not disabled. The dimension table is NOT down-filtered before the join. Based on size-based eligibility rules alone, which join strategy will Spark SQL choose, and why?

options.label: Broadcast Hash Join, because the dimension table is smaller than the fact table and Spark always broadcasts the smaller side regardless of size
Shuffle Hash Join (or sort-merge join), because the dimension table exceeds the broadcast threshold, so neither side fits the single-node broadcast requirement
Broadcast Hash Join, because the broadcast hint path automatically compresses the 4 GB table to fit within the driver's memory budget
Shuffle Hash Join, because broadcast is only used when BOTH sides are smaller than the broadcast threshold

questions.correctAnswer: Shuffle Hash Join (or sort-merge join), because the dimension table exceeds the broadcast threshold, so neither side fits the single-node broadcast requirement
questions.analysis: Broadcast eligibility is decided by size, not by row count or by which table is 'smaller.' With the default threshold of 10 MB, a 4 GB side is far above the limit, so Spark cannot collect it onto a single node. The material explains the best case as one where 'the data on one side of the join is small enough to fit on a single node (broadcast join)' and otherwise 'a more resource-intensive shuffle hash join is required' [source p.336]. Option A reflects the misconception that 'smaller' always means 'broadcastable'; Spark's decision compares each side against the configured threshold, not against the other side. Option C invents an auto-compression behavior that does not exist — the hint cannot shrink a table past memory limits. Option D misstates the rule: the broadcast threshold applies per candidate side, not to both sides simultaneously.
answer: Shuffle Hash Join (or sort-merge join), because the dimension table exceeds the broadcast threshold, so neither side fits the single-node broadcast requirement

questions.question: Which statements about broadcast hash joins and shuffle hash joins are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: In a broadcast join, the small table is collected and shipped in full to every executor node, and the large side is not reshuffled on the join key.
In a shuffle hash join, both tables are repartitioned by a hashing scheme on the join key and the matching partitions are joined per node.
Broadcasting a table that is too large can exhaust driver and executor memory, causing OOM failures or severe garbage-collection pressure rather than a speedup.
Setting a broadcast hint guarantees the join will broadcast successfully; Spark will override memory limits whenever the hint is present.

correctAnswer: In a broadcast join, the small table is collected and shipped in full to every executor node, and the large side is not reshuffled on the join key.
In a shuffle hash join, both tables are repartitioned by a hashing scheme on the join key and the matching partitions are joined per node.
Broadcasting a table that is too large can exhaust driver and executor memory, causing OOM failures or severe garbage-collection pressure rather than a speedup.
questions.analysis: The first option matches the described broadcast pattern: the query engine 'broadcasts the small table (table A) out to all nodes, where it gets joined to the parts of the large table (table B)' [source p.336], which means the large side is not shuffled for that join. The second option matches the shuffle hash join description: 'A hashing scheme is used to repartition data by join key... The data is then reshuffled to the appropriate node, and the new partitions for tables A and B on each node are joined' [source p.337]. The third option captures the real failure mode: forcing the broadcast of an oversized relation moves megabytes-to-gigabytes of data into every task, and because 'Shuffle hash joins are generally more resource intensive than broadcast joins' [source p.337], optimizers only choose broadcast when the small side truly fits — violating that precondition causes memory pressure, not a win. The fourth option is the classic distractor: a hint is advice, and Spark still enforces memory and threshold limits, so it does not magically bypass the single-node size requirement.
answer: In a broadcast join, the small table is collected and shipped in full to every executor node, and the large side is not reshuffled on the join key.
In a shuffle hash join, both tables are repartitioned by a hashing scheme on the join key and the matching partitions are joined per node.
Broadcasting a table that is too large can exhaust driver and executor memory, causing OOM failures or severe garbage-collection pressure rather than a speedup.

questions.question: A team complains that their join is slow even after adding a /*+ BROADCAST(dim) */ hint, and the job now fails with executor out-of-memory errors. The dimension table is 30 GB and is not pre-filtered. What is the MOST accurate explanation of what happened?

options.label: The hint forced an over-large broadcast: the 30 GB side is above any reasonable single-node budget, so it was shipped to every executor and exhausted memory
The hint had no effect, and the OOM was caused by the shuffle hash join repartitioning the fact table
The hint removed all shuffling from the plan, so no exchange nodes appear in the Spark UI and memory spiked for an unrelated reason
The hint succeeded and the OOM was caused by the optimizer collecting a down-filtered version of the 30 GB table onto a single node

questions.correctAnswer: The hint forced an over-large broadcast: the 30 GB side is above any reasonable single-node budget, so it was shipped to every executor and exhausted memory
questions.analysis: This tests the failure mode of broadcasting a table that is too large. Broadcast requires that one side be 'small enough to fit on a single node' [source p.336]; a 30 GB side does not, so forcing it in creates the memory blowup. Option B is wrong because the hint does take effect and the symptom (OOM, not slow shuffle) is specific to broadcast. Option C is wrong because even with a broadcast join, the large side's partitioning still yields an Exchange node in the plan, and the claim that a hint 'removes all shuffling' is false — a broadcast join avoids reshuffling the large side on the join key but does not delete every exchange. Option D is wrong on two counts: the table was not down-filtered, and the optimizer cannot synthesize a filtered version of a large table just because a hint is present. A better fix would be to pre-filter the dimension table to a broadcastable size, which 'can dramatically improve performance and reduce resource consumption' [source p.337], rather than forcing a broadcast.
answer: The hint forced an over-large broadcast: the 30 GB side is above any reasonable single-node budget, so it was shipped to every executor and exhausted memory

scenes.title: Reducing Shuffle Cost: Distribution, Keys, and AQE

elements.content: Reducing Shuffle Cost: Distribution, Keys, and AQE
The techniques that shrink or eliminate the exchange — before you ever tune hardware

A shuffle is the network exchange of rows at a stage boundary; the Exchange node in a physical plan is its footprint, and it costs far more than the scan or the write that surrounds it.

This page covers the six levers that shrink or eliminate that exchange: pre-distribution, filtering, key choice, AQE, partition count, and skew handling.
1. Pre-Distribution: Skip the Exchange Entirely

Pre-sort or bucket tables on the join key so recurring joins are co-located — rows with the same key already live on the same executor.

Example: with a known 1 TB / 2 TB join, pre-bucketing the 1 TB side into 200 buckets at write time removes the Exchange the source table reports at scan time [source p.240].
2. Filter & Pre-Aggregate First
Push predicates down and reorder joins so small, filtered tables land on the left; the engine collects and broadcasts them [source p.337].
3. Keys, Cardinality, and Skew

Use equi-join keys with even distributions. Heavy skew in the key — many rows sharing one value — makes the exchange lopsided; skew, not total volume, is often the real cost driver (the salting rule).

Related breakage: row explosion (5-×-10 repetition in a key produces 50 rows per match) [source p.323].
4. Adaptive Query Execution
AQE coalesces small shuffle partitions at runtime and can convert sort-merge → broadcast when a side turns out small [source p.336].
5. Tune the Partition Count

Match spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to the cluster: the default 200 oversubscribes very small clusters and undersubscribes very large ones.

After the exchange, hash each row on the key; a uniform hash sends 200M rows from a 2 TB table to 200 partitions as roughly 1M rows each.
6. Exam Trap: Partition Count ≠ Skew

Raising shuffle partitions fixes the number of tasks, not the shape of the data.

Skew needs salting or AQE skew-join handling; sorting the partition list will not move the hot key.
Checkpoint: Match the Symptom to the Fix

A join leaks 3 TB across the network and one Exchange shows a few huge partitions while the rest finish early: the smell is skew, not raw volume. Coalescing partitions by 200 → 800 leaves the hot key untouched — the fix is salting or enabling AQE skew handling.

If the Exchange had shown many tiny partitions instead, that is the partition-count problem: lower shuffle.partitions or let AQE coalesce them.

actions.text: We just covered broadcast hash join and choosing a strategy. But what if neither side is small enough to broadcast, and you're stuck with a real shuffle? Then your job is to shrink or eliminate the exchange itself. That's exactly what these techniques do.

Quick refresher on what we're fighting. A shuffle is the network exchange of rows at a stage boundary, so every partition on one side gets repartitioned by the join key. That means serialization, disk spills, and network transfer — it's the single most expensive wide transformation in Spark. Everything on this page is about avoiding that traffic.

Technique one: pre-distribution — skip the exchange entirely. If the same tables are joined repeatedly on the same key, pre-sort or bucket them on that join key once. Because both sides land in matching buckets, the recurring join becomes a co-located join: no reshuffle at each run, the data is already aligned.

Technique two: filter and pre-aggregate first. Push predicates down and reorder joins so the smallest possible dataset reaches the shuffle. If you can cut rows to a tenth of their size before the exchange, you just paid a tenth of the network cost — the cheapest shuffle is the one that never carries the data.

Technique three: keys, cardinality, and skew. Prefer equi-join keys with even distributions, and avoid cross joins entirely. Remember, the real cost driver is usually skew, not total volume — one oversized key can dominate a stage while all other tasks finish in seconds.

Technique four: Adaptive Query Execution, or AQE. At runtime — after the shuffle statistics are known — AQE coalesces small shuffle partitions and can even convert a sort-merge join into a broadcast join when one side turns out small. That means a query can change its plan while it's running, based on the actual data.

Technique five: tune the partition count. Match spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to your cluster. That default of 200 is wrong for a tiny cluster and wrong for a huge one — too few and you starve executors, too many and you drown in small tasks and tiny files.

And here's the exam trap, technique six: partition count is not skew. Raising shuffle partitions fixes how many tasks you have — it does not fix one fat key. A single key lands in a single partition no matter how many you create. Skew needs salting or AQE's skew-join handling.

Now apply it. A join leaks three terabytes across the network and one exchange dominates the runtime. Ask yourself: is the volume genuinely huge, or is it one skewed key? Is it a recurring join I could bucket once? Before you touch hardware, match the symptom to the fix.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Shuffle Reduction and AQE

questions.question: A Databricks job joins a 12 GB filtered dimension table (table A) to a 4 TB fact table. The engineer first applies the query's date and status predicates to table A, shrinking it to 9 MB, and then joins. Which statement best explains why this pre-filtering changes the shuffle profile of the job?

options.label: Pre-filtering the dimension does not affect the shuffle; the fact table's Exchange node dominates cost regardless of dimension size.
Pre-filtering makes the dimension fit under autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, so Spark can collect and broadcast the small side and never exchanges the 4 TB fact table on the join key.
Pre-filtering makes Spark choose a shuffle hash join, which removes all network traffic by hashing both sides locally before merging.
Pre-filtering pushes the join below the scan, converting the wide transformation into a narrow one so no stage boundary is crossed.

questions.analysis: Prefiltering data to create broadcast joins where possible can dramatically improve performance and reduce resource consumption. [source p.337] The broadcast threshold is a size test (spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold defaults to 10 MB), so a 9 MB filtered dimension becomes eligible, and in a broadcast hash join the large side is never shuffled. Option A ignores the fact that the exchange on the fact side is precisely what broadcast eliminates. Option C is wrong because SHJ still repartitions data by join key; it removes nothing from the network. Option D misstates the rule: a join remains a wide transformation that crosses a stage boundary unless the other side is broadcast. [source p.337]

questions.question: A nightly job reports that 200 shuffle partitions each process wildly uneven amounts of data: three partitions read 40 GB each while 180 partitions read under 200 MB each. Total shuffle volume is normal, but a handful of tasks run 30x longer than the rest, and the job does not OOM. Which two actions address the actual problem? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Enable and tune Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) skew join handling so oversized partitions are automatically split into subtasks.
Raise spark.sql.shuffle.partitions from 200 to 2,000 so each of the hot keys is spread across more partitions.
Salting or otherwise pre-processing the skewed join key so a single key value no longer concentrates 40 GB on one task.
Add a broadcast() hint to the small side and cache the large side, because caching removes the skew.

questions.analysis: The symptom is a skew problem, not a partition-count problem: increased shuffle partitions (option B) hashes more keys per partition but a single hot key still lands in exactly one partition, because the mapper distributes rows by hashing the key, not by splitting key values across tasks. [source p.348] The correct levers are AQE skew join handling, which detects and splits disproportionately large partitions, and salting/key preprocessing to break up the hot value (option C). Option D confuses skew remedies with broadcast/caching: caching does not change the shuffle partitioning and is not a skew cure. [source p.337]

questions.question: A query analyst complains that a 40 TB user_events table 'must be cached because the full table scan is slow' and proposes persisting the whole table to fix runtime. Which diagnosis correctly distinguishes this from a shuffle/partition problem — and what is the appropriate fix?

options.label: The scan cost is a file-layout problem, so the fix is partition pruning, clustering, and filter pushdown; caching the full 40 TB table does not reduce the bytes scanned.
The scan cost is a shuffle problem, so the fix is increasing spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to spread the scan across more tasks.
The scan cost is a broadcast eligibility problem, so the fix is adding a broadcast() hint on the 40 TB table.
The scan cost is a join-strategy problem, so the fix is disabling the broadcast join threshold to force a shuffle hash join.

questions.analysis: A full table scan is a layout problem: partitioning splits a table into subtables so time-range filters scan only relevant data, and clustering sorts data within partitions to colocate similar values and improve filtering, sorting, and joining. [source p.240] Caching a 40 TB table does not make the scan selective, and shuffle partitions (B) govern redistribution after a wide operator, not the scan itself. Option C misapplies the broadcast mechanism: a broadcast hint is only safe for small sides under the threshold; broadcasting a 40 TB table would crash the driver. Option D confuses the fix with the opposite of the recommendation — disabling broadcast to force SHJ still shuffles both sides and does nothing for scan cost. [source p.337]

scenes.title: Caching: When It Pays Off

elements.content: Caching: When It Pays Off
Persisting intermediates only pays when reuse is high; Delta Cache is a different mechanism entirely
cache() and persist(): What They Do

• cache() stores an intermediate DataFrame in executor memory (optionally disk); every repeated action then skips re-walking the full lineage [source p.250]

• persist() is the same mechanism with an explicit StorageLevel — MEMORY_ONLY, MEMORY_AND_DISK, or disk-only

• Caching materialises at the first action, not at declaration — the cache is lazy
Why It Pays Off: The Cold-vs-Hot Trade

• Same intuition as query-result caches: a 40 s cold query can return in ~1 s warm [source p.307]

• Worth it when the same result is reused many times — iterative ML loops, interactive exploration, several downstream aggregations over one join

• Not worth it for a one-shot job or a table read once: the cache occupies memory other stages need [source p.250]
Worked Example — Break-even Reuse Count

Cold join recompute = 12 s, cache write = 9 s, warm read = 1.5 s, memory pressure cost ≈ 2 s per stage

Break-even: 9 + n(1.5 + 2) < 12n → 9 < 8.5n → n ≥ 2; caching wins from the second reuse onward

actions.text: Now let's shift to caching and persistence. In Spark, recomputation is the default: every time you trigger an action on a DataFrame, the engine replays the entire lineage from the source. Caching lets you break that cycle — but only when it actually pays off.

There are two methods worth knowing. cache() stores an intermediate DataFrame in executor memory using the default storage level. persist() does the same thing but lets you specify a storage level — memory only, memory and disk, serialized, replicated, and so on. Use cache() when the default is fine; use persist() when you need to control the trade-off between memory pressure and speed.

The intuition is identical to a query-result cache in a traditional database. A 40-second cold computation that you hit five times costs 200 seconds without caching. Cache it once at 40 seconds, and the remaining four hits are cheap. But you paid memory and a one-time write cost to get there.

Let's do the worked example. Cold join recompute is 12 seconds, the cache write costs 9 seconds, and each warm read is 1 second. The break-even reuse count is roughly (9 − 1) ÷ (12 − 1), which works out to one reuse. So a second use already pays for itself. But run this job only once and you have spent 9 seconds writing to memory for zero benefit — and that memory may evict data other stages need.

Two closing points for the exam. First, Delta Cache is a different mechanism — it caches remote Parquet files on local SSD so repeats avoid the network read, not the lineage recomputation. Second, always call unpersist() when you're done, and remember the exam trap: caching never fixes a bad join or a full table scan. It only avoids recomputation.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Diagnosing an Expensive Join and Deciding on Caching

elements.content: Problem 1

A nightly Spark job joins a 2 TB Parquet fact table fact_sales to a 40 MB dimension table dim_product on product_key. The cluster has 10 executors, each with 8 cores and 32 GB RAM. The Spark UI shows six stages. Stage 5 is an exchange stage with shuffle write 1.1 TB and shuffle read 1.1 TB. Its 200 tasks have a median runtime of 3.9 minutes and a maximum of 4.1 minutes. The file-scan stage for the fact table runs for 90 seconds. Which stage is the bottleneck, and what evidence rules out data skew? Compute the ratio of the exchange-stage runtime to the scan-stage runtime.
Hint: Compare task runtimes and identify which stage moves data across the network.

Worked solution
The bottleneck is Stage 5, the exchange stage. It writes 1.1 TB and reads 1.1 TB of shuffled data, while the file-scan stage completes in 90 seconds. The exchange stage is a wide-transformation boundary: Spark redistributes rows by key so that each key ends up on one and only one node, which is the shuffle step [source p.348]. The file scan is a narrow transformation and does not move data across the network [source p.346].

Evidence against skew: skew would appear as a small number of tasks running much longer than the median. Here the maximum runtime is 4.1 minutes and the median is 3.9 minutes, so max/median = 4.1/3.9 = 1.05. A ratio below about 1.2 typically indicates an even distribution of work. All 200 tasks take similar time, so the exchange cost is a volume problem, not a skew problem.

Runtime ratio: with 10 executors × 8 cores = 80 task slots, 200 tasks run in 200/80 = 2.5 waves. At ~3.9 minutes per task, the exchange stage takes roughly 2.5 × 3.9 ≈ 9.8 minutes. The scan stage takes 1.5 minutes. The ratio is 9.8/1.5 ≈ 6.5, so the exchange stage dominates the job.

Analysis — The method is to read the physical plan and the stage timeline: wide transformations such as join, groupBy, and distinct insert an Exchange node and a stage boundary, whereas narrow transformations keep rows in place. Students often blame the file scan or the final write because those stages show large byte counts, but the exchange is the only stage that both writes and reads 1.1 TB over the network. The edge case to check is skew: a join on a key with a few hot values can make 1 or 2 tasks run 10–50× longer than the median; here the flat task distribution proves skew is absent. This diagnosis generalizes to any Spark job: locate the stage with the largest shuffle read/write, then compare max and median task duration before changing any strategy.
Problem 2

The same job uses the default spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold = 10 MB. The dimension table dim_product is 40 MB on disk. Explain why Spark selected a sort-merge join (SMJ) instead of a broadcast hash join (BHJ). Then calculate the total bytes that cross the network if the fact side after projection and filtering is 1.1 TB and the dimension side is 40 MB, assuming SMJ shuffles both sides on the join key.
Hint: Compare the dimension size to the threshold, then count write and read bytes.

Worked solution
Spark chooses a broadcast hash join only when the small side is at or below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold. The default threshold is 10 MB. The dimension table is 40 MB, which is 4 × 10 MB, so Spark does not consider it broadcast-eligible. With no hint and no threshold change, Spark falls back to the default join path: a sort-merge join, which exchanges both sides on the join key, sorts them, and merges them [source p.336]. In a Kimball-style model the fact table is long and narrow while the dimension is wide and short, which is exactly the shape that makes a small dimension a natural broadcast candidate [source p.325], but the 10 MB default blocks that choice here.

Shuffle bytes for SMJ: the fact side writes 1.1 TB to local disk and the dimension side writes 40 MB = 0.04 GB. Total shuffle write ≈ 1.1 TB + 0.04 GB ≈ 1.1 TB (the dimension is negligible). Each byte written is later read across the network, so total network traffic ≈ 1.1 TB written + 1.1 TB read = 2.2 TB. The exchange stage reported in the Spark UI matches this order of magnitude.

If the join had used BHJ instead, the 40 MB dimension would be replicated to each executor: 40 MB × 10 executors = 400 MB of network traffic, and the 1.1 TB fact side would not be shuffled at all [source p.336].

Analysis — The key insight is that broadcast eligibility is decided by size, not by row count or by whether a table is conceptually a dimension. A 40 MB table with 100 rows is still above a 10 MB threshold. Students often assume the default threshold is large enough for any dimension table, or they confuse SMJ with a shuffle hash join (SHJ); SHJ also shuffles the large side unless the small side is broadcast. The calculation shows why the exchange is expensive: SMJ pays to write and read the entire large side, while BHJ pays only to replicate the small side. Edge case: partition pruning or column pruning can shrink the fact side below 1.1 TB, but as long as the dimension exceeds the threshold, Spark still chooses SMJ without a hint.
Problem 3

You fix the join by either raising spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to 100 MB or adding broadcast(dim_product) to the join. Predict the effect on (a) shuffle bytes on the fact side, (b) the exchange stage for the join, (c) the number of stages, and (d) runtime. Assume the scan stage takes 90 seconds, broadcast build and probe add 60 seconds per executor, and the original exchange stage took 9.8 minutes.
Hint: Think about which side is replicated and which side stays put.

Worked solution
Either fix makes the 40 MB dimension broadcast-eligible: raising the threshold to 100 MB puts 40 MB below the limit, and the broadcast() hint forces BHJ regardless of the threshold. The physical plan changes from a sort-merge join to a broadcast hash join.

(a) Shuffle bytes on the fact side: 0. The large side is never exchanged; each executor probes the replicated dimension with its local fact partitions [source p.336]. (b) The sort-merge exchange stage for the join disappears. A small broadcast exchange remains to replicate the 40 MB dimension, but it writes and reads only 40 MB × 10 executors = 400 MB total, versus 2.2 TB before. (c) Stage count drops: the join no longer creates a shuffle boundary for the fact side, so the stage that wrote 1.1 TB and the stage that read it collapse into one stage. A job with six stages typically drops to four or five. (d) Runtime: the 9.8-minute exchange is eliminated. The new critical path is roughly scan 90 s + broadcast build/probe 60 s ≈ 2.5 minutes, plus any downstream aggregation. The saving is approximately 9.8 − 2.5 ≈ 7.3 minutes per run, or about 75% of the original join time.

At a nightly cadence, 7.3 minutes saved per night is 7.3 × 365 ≈ 2,665 minutes ≈ 44.4 hours per year.

Analysis — The method is to change the join strategy so that the large side is never repartitioned. Broadcast hash join works because the small side fits in memory on each executor and can be hash-probed locally; the large side is read once from its existing partitions. Students often predict that the broadcast hint eliminates all network traffic, but the small side is still replicated to every executor—400 MB here, which is cheap but not zero. Common mistake: raising the threshold globally to an enormous value (for example, 10 GB) can make Spark broadcast tables that do not fit in executor memory, causing OOM. The fix generalizes to recurring joins between a large fact table and a small dimension: broadcast the dimension once, or better, pre-partition the fact table on the join key so recurring joins skip the exchange entirely.
Problem 4

The joined result is 1.2 TB and feeds three downstream aggregations. The cluster has 10 executors × 32 GB = 320 GB total executor memory, and spark.memory.fraction = 0.6. Should you cache the joined result with MEMORY_ONLY or MEMORY_AND_DISK? Justify with numbers. When should you unpersist the DataFrame?
Hint: Compute usable memory, compare it to the DataFrame size, and count how many times the data is reused.

Worked solution
Usable memory for caching is 320 GB × 0.6 = 192 GB. The joined result is 1.2 TB = 1,200 GB, which is 1,200 / 192 ≈ 6.25 times the available memory. MEMORY_ONLY cannot hold the whole DataFrame, so Spark would evict partitions and recompute them, causing thrashing. Use MEMORY_AND_DISK: partitions that do not fit in memory spill to local disk, so the data is still cached and reused without recomputation [source p.346].

The joined result is read three times by three aggregations. Without caching, the three aggregations read 1.2 TB each from Delta Lake, for 3 × 1.2 TB = 3.6 TB of input I/O. With caching, the first materialization reads 1.2 TB and writes it to memory and disk; the next two reads come from the cache, which is local memory or local disk rather than a remote scan. The I/O reduction can be substantial, especially if the three aggregations are separate Spark actions.

Unpersist after the third aggregation completes. Call df.unpersist() at the end of the job, before the Spark session ends, so that memory and disk blocks are released for the next job.

Analysis — The method is a reuse-versus-cost calculation: caching pays only when the result is consumed more than once and the recomputation cost exceeds the cache write cost. Students often choose MEMORY_ONLY by default because it sounds fastest, but with a 6.25× size mismatch it thrashes and can be slower than no cache. The edge case is a single-use result: caching a DataFrame that feeds one aggregation adds write cost and memory pressure for zero reuse benefit. Also note that MEMORY_AND_DISK still consumes executor memory for the partitions that fit, so it competes with shuffle and join buffers. This decision generalizes to any multi-consumer intermediate in a pipeline: cache only reused, expensive-to-recompute DataFrames, and always release them when the consumer count is exhausted.
Problem 5

A teammate suggests broadcasting a 5 GB dimension table to avoid all shuffles. The driver has 16 GB of RAM. Evaluate this proposal. What is the failure mode, and how does Spark behave if you add a broadcast() hint that exceeds available driver or executor memory?
Hint: Broadcasting collects the small side to the driver and then ships it to every executor.

Worked solution
Broadcasting a 5 GB table means Spark must collect that table to the driver, serialize it, and then ship a copy to every executor. On a 16 GB driver, the 5 GB table plus serialization buffers, task metadata, and the driver's own heap overhead can exceed available memory and cause an OutOfMemoryError (OOM). Even if the driver barely fits it, shipping 5 GB to each of 10 executors adds 5 GB × 10 = 50 GB of network replication, which can be larger than the shuffle it was meant to avoid. That is the failure mode: driver OOM or a broadcast that is more expensive than the sort-merge join it replaced.

The broadcast() hint does not override memory limits. Spark will attempt the broadcast if the hint is present, but if the table cannot be collected or does not fit, the job fails with an executor or driver OOM, or Spark may fall back to a sort-merge join in some configurations. The hint changes the planner's preference, not the physical memory of the cluster [source p.336].

A safer rule: broadcast only when the small side fits comfortably within driver and executor memory, typically tens to low hundreds of megabytes. For a 5 GB table, either increase the threshold cautiously after measuring, or pre-partition the large table on the join key so the exchange is skipped without replicating 5 GB.

Analysis — The method is to distinguish planner hints from physical resource limits. A hint is a request, not a guarantee; the broadcast hash join still needs to materialize the small side on the driver and on every executor. Students often believe that broadcast() always wins and that it eliminates all network cost, but the small side is replicated to every executor. Common mistake: raising spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to a huge value (for example, 10 GB) so that Spark broadcasts medium tables that should be shuffled. The edge case is a dimension table that grows over time: a 40 MB table today can become 5 GB next year, so the broadcast decision must be re-evaluated. This generalizes to any join optimization: choose the strategy that minimizes the total bytes moved, and verify with the Spark UI after the change.
Problem 6

The job ends but you forget to call unpersist() on the cached 1.2 TB DataFrame. Explain the cost. Then describe a scenario where caching the joined result is a net loss, and explain how the warning about small commits cluttering storage is analogous.
Hint: Cached blocks occupy memory and disk until they are evicted or the Spark session ends.

Worked solution
Forgetting unpersist() leaves the cached blocks in executor memory and on local disk. The DataFrame is 1.2 TB, and usable memory is 192 GB, so the memory-resident partitions continue to occupy up to 192 GB of executor memory that later jobs need for shuffle, join, and aggregation buffers. The disk-resident partitions also remain in the local disk directories until Spark evicts them or the Spark session ends. Later jobs then face memory pressure, eviction, and spill, or they may fail with OOM. The cache is no longer useful because the three aggregations have already completed; keeping it is pure overhead.

Caching is a net loss when the joined result is read only once. In that case you pay the cost of writing 1.2 TB to memory and disk, plus the memory pressure during the write, but you receive no reuse benefit. A single-consumer intermediate should be streamed to the next operation instead of cached.

The analogy to commit clutter is that both practices retain obsolete data that must be cleaned up. The source material warns that running a large number of small commits can create files that consume significant storage and may need to be vacuumed periodically [source p.304]. In the same way, stale cached blocks and their local disk files consume resources until someone removes them. The remedy is lifecycle discipline: cache only reused DataFrames, and call unpersist() immediately after the final consumer finishes.

Analysis — The method is to treat caching as a scoped resource, not a permanent optimization. Memory and local disk are finite: 192 GB of usable executor memory cannot hold 1.2 TB, so the cache is partly on disk, and those blocks persist beyond the job unless unpersisted. Students often assume that cached data is automatically cleaned up when the DataFrame variable goes out of scope, but Spark's cache is tied to the Spark session, not to Python variable lifetime. The edge case is a long-lived notebook or an interactive session where many cached DataFrames accumulate and evict each other, slowing every query. Common mistake: caching at the start of a pipeline because it feels safe, then forgetting to release it. This generalizes to Delta Lake file maintenance and commit hygiene: retain only what the current workload needs, and remove the rest deliberately.

actions.text: Now let's put all of that join and caching knowledge to work on a fully worked problem. We'll walk through a realistic nightly job that's slow, diagnose it step by step, and decide whether to cache.
Here's the setup. A nightly Spark job joins a 2 TB Parquet fact table to a 40 MB dimension table. The Spark UI shows runtime dominated by a single exchange stage.
The hint tells us the method: compare task runtimes and identify which stage dominates. Let's work it through.

Step one, diagnose. Read the physical plan. The bottleneck is an exchange stage with heavy shuffle read and write. Critically, all 200 tasks take roughly the same time — that uniform distribution rules out skew as the culprit.
The worked solution confirms it: the bottleneck is Stage 5, the exchange stage that shuffles both sides of the join. The file scan is not the problem — the shuffle is.
Step two, explain why. The same job uses the default spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold of 10 MB. Our dimension is 40 MB — four times the threshold.
Compare the dimension size to the threshold. 40 MB exceeds 10 MB, so the broadcast optimization is skipped.

Because broadcast eligibility fails, Spark falls back to a sort-merge join and shuffles both sides of the 2 TB fact table across the network. That's exactly what produces the dominating exchange stage.
The key insight: broadcast eligibility is what silently governs which join strategy Spark picks. Miss the threshold and you pay for a shuffle you never intended.
Step three, fix. You either raise spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold above 40 MB, or explicitly wrap the dimension with broadcast(dim).

The hint asks which side is replicated and which stays put. With a broadcast hash join, the 40 MB dimension is replicated to every executor, and the 2 TB fact table stays in place — no shuffle at all.
The predicted effect: shuffle bytes on the fact table fall to near zero, and the exchange stage disappears entirely.
Step four, the caching decision. The method is to change the join strategy, and then decide whether to cache.
The joined result is 1.2 TB and feeds three downstream aggregations. That reuse is what makes caching worthwhile here.

Compute usable memory and compare it to the Dataset. With roughly 320 GB of usable memory for caching across the cluster, a 1.2 TB result fits comfortably. So cache it with MEMORY_AND_DISK and unpersist when the job ends.
Usable memory for caching is 320 GB, the 1.2 TB result is larger than memory alone, so MEMORY_AND_DISK is the right storage level — the spill goes to disk rather than failing.
This is a reuse-versus-cost calculation. The result is reused three times, so recomputation is expensive — caching wins.
Now the pitfalls. A teammate suggests broadcasting a 5 GB dimension to speed things up.
Remember: broadcasting collects the small side to the driver first. A 5 GB table is not small. Pulling it onto the driver can OOM the driver and crash the whole job.
So broadcasting a 5 GB table means Spark tries to collect it onto the driver — that's a classic out-of-memory failure. Over-broadcasting is a trap, not a fix.
The method here is to distinguish planner hints from actual runtime behavior. A hint doesn't change physics — a big table is still big.
Finally, the forgetting problem. The job ends but you forget to call unpersist() on the cached DataFrame.
The hint: cached blocks occupy memory and disk until the cache is explicitly released or the cluster terminates.
Forgetting unpersist() leaves the cached blocks holding memory and disk, starving other jobs running on the same cluster.
Treat caching as a scope: cache it, use it, and release it. That keeps the cost bounded to exactly where the reuse happens. Let's check your understanding of joins, shuffles, and caching.

scenes.title: Lesson Check: Joins, Shuffles, and Caching

questions.question: A Databricks cluster runs Spark with the default configuration, meaning spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold = 10 MB. A query joins fact_events (1.8 TB, stored in Delta Lake) to a filtered dimension table dim_campaigns_2024 that the optimizer estimates at 340 MB after filter pushdown. There is no broadcast() hint anywhere in the query, and no bucketing or partitioning on the join key on either side. Which physical join strategy will Spark SQL most likely select, and what is the primary reason?

options.label: Broadcast Hash Join, because the dimension table has fewer than 10 million rows and row count is the eligibility rule.
Broadcast Hash Join, because the broadcast() hint is implied whenever one side is a dimension table.
Sort-Merge Join, because neither side fits under the 10 MB auto-broadcast threshold and Bucket joins are unavailable, so Spark must exchange both sides on the join key and merge them.
Shuffle Hash Join, because it exists precisely for the case where the smaller side exceeds the broadcast threshold but is still much smaller than the large side.

questions.analysis: Eligibility for a Broadcast Hash Join is decided by byte size against spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (default 10 MB), not by row count, and not by the semantic role of the table. At an estimated 340 MB, dim_campaigns_2024 is 34x over the default threshold, so automatic broadcasting will not trigger. Absent an explicit broadcast() hint or bucketing on the join key, Spark SQL falls back to its default wide-join path, the sort-merge join: both sides are exchanged (shuffled) on the join key, sorted, then merged. Option A is a classic exam trap — the row-count heuristic is intuitive but wrong; the threshold is expressed in bytes. Option B is also wrong: Spark does not silently broadcast 'dimension-like' tables; broadcasts must be justified by size or forced by hint. Option D is the most seductive distractor: SHJ does exist as a middle path when the smaller side is too big to broadcast, but Spark does not autonomously promote to SHJ purely from relative size comparisons — its planner is driven by threshold and cost, and SMJ is the default fallback. The relevant reported behaviour here — 'the shuffle bytes are dominated by the exchange' — is consistent with an SMJ of two unbroadcastable sides, and later we will see the fix is usually to pre-filter the dimension down below the threshold so that a Broadcast Hash Join becomes eligible [source p.337].

questions.question: A recurring nightly job joins streaming_enriched (a 4.2 TB Delta table) to region_lookup (a 6 MB CSV loaded as a Delta table) on region_id. A teammate adds a /*+ BROADCAST(region_lookup) */ hint and, on a separate branch, refactors the large table to be bucketed by region_id with 256 buckets, matching the join key. Which of the following statements about the effect on shuffle volume and runtime are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: With the BROADCAST hint, streaming_enriched is not exchanged over the network on region_id; only the 6 MB region_lookup is serialized to the driver and shipped to each executor. [source p.337]
With the BROADCAST hint, the overall shuffle bytes drop to roughly 0 because the small side is replicated in-memory rather than shuffled across the cluster. [source p.250]

If the bucketed side is 256-bucket-bucketed on region_id, and the other side is repartitioned (or bucketed) to exactly 256 partitions by the same hash function, Spark can eliminate the exchange for the bucketed side and turn the join into a narrow, per-bucket merge.
The BROADCAST hint overrides cluster memory limits, so even if region_lookup grew past the executor heap, the hint would still succeed and the plan would remain a Broadcast Hash Join.

questions.analysis: Option A is correct and matches the textbook description: in a broadcast join the small side (table A) is sent out to all nodes and joined locally against the parts of the large table (table B) [source p.337]. The large side is not exchanged on the join key, so its shuffle volume is effectively zero for that exchange. Option C is correct: bucketing on the join key means the data is already physically distributed by the join key's hash, so a matching-bucket join can skip the runtime exchange entirely and become a narrow per-bucket merge — this is the same idea as 'pre-partition or bucket tables on the join key so recurring joins skip the exchange'. Option B is a real exam trap: broadcast joins do not cost zero. The small side is replicated to every executor, so if you have 200 executors and the broadcast side is 6 MB, the driver ships about 1.2 GB of total network traffic. That is far less than shuffling 4.2 TB, but it is not zero — you cannot describe it as 'roughly 0'. Option D is false and repeats an earlier checkpoint distractor: a hint is a preference, not a force. If the broadcast side grows past what the driver/executor memory can hold, Spark will abandon the broadcast at runtime and fall back to a shuffled join rather than OOM the cluster. In other words, the hint cannot silence memory limits, and it cannot guarantee the plan.

questions.question: A data engineer reports that a Spark job's shuffle write stage is spilling 800 GB to local disk, and the Spark UI shows an Exchange node on the join key between fact_orders and dim_customer. The engineer's proposed fix is to increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions from 200 to 4,000, arguing that 'more partitions means less shuffle per partition, which means less total shuffle.' Which statement best evaluates this proposal?

options.label: The proposal is correct: shuffle bytes are inversely proportional to the number of shuffle partitions, so 4,000 partitions will reduce shuffle bytes by roughly 20x.

The proposal is misguided: the total shuffle volume is set by the Exchange on the join key, not by the partition count, and if the real problem is skew (a few hot keys holding most of the rows), more partitions just produces more small files and scheduler overhead without eliminating the hot partitions.
The proposal is correct: the Exchange node is caused by the file scan, so reducing partition size will let the scan push more predicates down and reduce total bytes.
The proposal is misguided: the fix is to cache fact_orders and dim_customer, since caching eliminates the shuffle entirely.

questions.analysis: The shuffle volume is determined by the Exchange on the join key, which serializes and repartitions the rows being joined — not by how many partitions those rows are later split into. Increasing shuffle partitions only changes how the same bytes are sliced; the total bytes remain the same. This is exactly the distractor pattern flagged in the earlier checkpoint: 'options that propose more shuffle partitions as a cure for skew' and 'options that blame the scan for shuffle cost.' Option A is arithmetically appealing but false. Option C misattributes the cost to the file scan; the Exchange, not the scan, is writing the 800 GB. Option D conflates caching with shuffle elimination — cache() and persist() avoid recomputation, not the first exchange. The right diagnosis is to first ask whether this is a partition-count problem or a skew problem. A healthy way to check is to inspect the per-task shuffle-read sizes in the Spark UI: if one or two tasks read hundreds of times more than the median, you have skew, and AQE's skew join handling or a targeted salting/bucketing strategy is the appropriate fix, not a global partition burst. If, instead, the task sizes are uniform but tiny, the fix is often to reduce and repartition before the join, pre-aggregate, and align with the join key.

questions.question: A pipeline computes an enriched_orders DataFrame by joining raw_orders to customer_profile and product_catalog, then filters to the last 90 days and calls .cache() before feeding four separate downstream dashboards. Each dashboard triggers a distinct aggregation. A colleague argues that the cache should be removed because 'caching is a general performance fix and we should just let the query engine re-read the source tables each time.' Write a short evaluation of whether the cache is justified in this specific case, and specify which storage level you would choose and why. Be explicit about what conditions would invalidate the caching decision.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Correctly identifies that caching pays off when the SAME intermediate DataFrame is reused by multiple downstream actions, and that four dashboards satisfy this condition — 30%. (2) Correctly notes that the cached intermediate is already filtered and joined, so it is a 'hot' reusable artifact; explains that without caching, each dashboard recomputes the joins and shuffles, so the cache saves repeated Exchange + merge work — 25%. (3) Chooses an appropriate storage level (e.g. MEMORY_AND_DISK or MEMORY_ONLY_SER) with justification tied to data size vs executor memory and the cost of recomputation vs the cost of spilling — 25%. (4) States edge cases that would flip the decision: cached result is larger than total executor memory and causes heavy eviction; the source tables change frequently so the cache goes stale; only one downstream consumer exists; or the four dashboards are actually scheduled hours apart so the cache expires before reuse — 20%. Deduct for answers that describe caching as a universal speedup without the reuse precondition. Accept 'do not cache' answers only if they argue a specific, quantified invalidation (e.g. cache larger than memory causes thrash), not merely a general distrust of caching.
questions.analysis: A reference answer covers four points. First, caching is not a general-purpose performance fix; cache() and persist() help when an intermediate result is reused across multiple actions, because they avoid recomputing the same plan. In this pipeline, enriched_orders feeds four dashboards, so the reuse condition is met: without caching, each dashboard re-executes the joins and the accompanying shuffles on the join keys. Second, the intermediate is already filtered (last 90 days) and pre-aggregated/joined, so caching stores a downstream, smaller artifact — the same 'prefilter before the expensive operator' principle that the join-reordering discussion recommends when it advises applying filters early and moving small tables to the left to reduce the data each join processes [source p.337]. Third, memory is not free: caching a table larger than executor memory causes eviction and spill, which can be worse than recomputation. A safe choice in many Databricks workloads is MEMORY_AND_DISK or MEMORY_ONLY_SER, because it tolerates pressure: hot partitions sit in memory, cold ones spill to disk rather than forcing recomputation. Fourth, the decision flips if the source tables are mutated between dashboard refreshes (the cache goes stale and must be invalidated), if the cached intermediate exceeds what the cluster can hold, if the dashboards are actually served from a query-results cache with a short TTL anyway (in which case materializing a Delta result may be more durable), or if only one downstream consumer exists. The exam-relevant framing is that query results cache and DataFrame cache both target 'hot' data with frequent access — the same tier reasoning that puts query results in a cache for fast repeated reads [source p.250] — but both must be justified by reuse and by fitting in memory.

actions.text: Let's check what we just covered on joins, shuffles, and caching. Work through each question on your own — take your time and reason it through from the sizes, thresholds, and settings given.
Once you submit, I'll walk through the answers with you and we'll dig into anything that gave you trouble. Go ahead and get started.

scenes.title: Lesson Overview: Photon, Cluster Sizing, and Cost Optimization

elements.content: Lesson Overview: Photon, Cluster Sizing, and Cost Optimization
Final lesson of the unit: compute engine choice, cluster shape, and cluster lifecycle jointly determine both wall-clock runtime and the monthly bill [source p.153].
Exam objective
Given a workload profile, pick compute type, cluster size, autoscaling min/max, and Photon.
Three levers
Engine (Photon on/off), shape (node type, workers, autoscale), lifecycle (job vs all-purpose).
Cost model
Total = (DBU rate × DBU-hours) + (VM price × runtime). Judge every optimization on both terms.
Worked example — estimating a bill before you run

A nightly job runs 8 workers × 2 hours = 16 worker-hours. At $0.40/DBU and 2 DBU/worker-hour: DBU cost = 16 × 2 × $0.40 = $12.80. Cloud VMs at $0.30/worker-hour: $4.80. Total ≈ $17.60. Halving runtime via Photon saves both terms; adding idle workers only inflates the VM term.
Roadmap: 4 checkpoints • 2 worked cost problems • hands-on cluster sizing simulator. High-throughput jobs should stay in one availability zone to keep bandwidth high and egress free [source p.426].

actions.text: That wraps up our deep dive into performance tuning. Now we open the final lesson of this unit — and it's the one where everything we've built comes together at the wallet level: Photon, cluster sizing, and cost optimization.

Here's the title and the frame for this whole lesson. Up to now we've optimized for speed — pruning, join strategies, caches. From this page forward, we optimize for speed and money at the same time. And on the exam, those two are almost never separate questions.

Start with the exam objective, stated exactly as the certification states it. Given a workload profile, pick the compute type, the cluster size, the autoscaling settings, and the Photon option that best fit it. Notice what that means: you aren't asked to recall a definition — you're handed a scenario, and you have to make four coordinated decisions and justify them.

Those four decisions collapse into three levers, and this is the mental model I want you carrying into every scenario question. Lever one: the engine — Photon on or off. Lever two: the cluster shape — node type, worker count, and the autoscaling minimum and maximum. Lever three: the lifecycle — a job cluster versus an all-purpose cluster, plus the auto-termination setting. Engine, shape, lifecycle. Those three levers jointly determine both the runtime and the bill.

Now the cost model in one line — and I want you to actually memorize this, because it prunes away most wrong answers. Total = the DBU rate times DBU-hours, plus the cloud VM price times runtime. Two terms, always. The DBU term is Databricks' own billing unit; the VM term is what the cloud provider charges for the machines. Every optimization you evaluate has to be judged against both terms. A change that halves runtime but doubles worker count can easily lose money — and that's precisely the trap these questions set.

Let's do a quick sanity check with the worked example on the slide. A nightly job runs eight workers for two hours — that's sixteen worker-hours on the VM side, and eight workers times two hours of DBU consumption on the Databricks side. Both meters are running simultaneously. So when you hear someone say 'let's just add more workers,' your first instinct should be: more workers cut the runtime, but do they cut total cost? It depends which term dominates for that workload. We'll work that arithmetic properly a few pages from here.

Finally, the roadmap so you know what's coming. Four checkpoints, two worked cost-estimation problems where we actually estimate a bill before running anything, and a hands-on cluster sizing simulator where you'll drag worker counts and watch latency and cost move in opposite directions. And the preview of cost-aware practices: right-sizing from Spark UI metrics, job clusters for scheduled work, spot instances for fault-tolerant batch, and instance pools to cut start-up time. Let's begin with the engine lever.

scenes.title: Photon: The Vectorized Query Engine

elements.content: Photon: The Vectorized Query Engine

Photon is a native C++ vectorized engine that replaces parts of the Spark execution engine at runtime; your Spark APIs, SQL, and DataFrame code are unchanged — it is a switch, not a rewrite.

Instead of interpreting one row at a time, Photon passes whole batches of column values through each CPU instruction, cutting per-row overhead.

Where Photon wins big (CPU-bound work):

• Large table scans

• Wide aggregations and joins

• String-heavy transformations

• Delta MERGE / DELETE / UPDATE writes [source p.343]

Cost nuance — always compare DBU-hours, never DBU rates. The Photon DBU rate is higher per unit, yet total spend frequently drops because wall-clock runtime shrinks. A job that cost 10 DBU-hours at $0.55 = $5.50 can become 3 DBU-hours at $0.80 = $2.40 — cheaper at the invoice even though the rate went up.

Worked example: baseline 10 DBU-h at standard rate vs. Photon 3 DBU-h at premium rate.
Exam trap: “Enable Photon to speed up every job” is false. Photon ≠ AQE, Delta caching, or autoscaling. Poorly written UDFs replaced by native functions win more than any engine swap [source p.359].
Photon barely helps: I/O-bound jobs, Python UDF-heavy pipelines, tiny datasets, and per-row inserts [source p.273].

actions.text: The first engine lever is Photon — Databricks' vectorized query engine. Let's be precise about what it is and what it is not, because the exam tests exactly that distinction.

Photon is a native C++ vectorized engine that replaces parts of the Spark execution engine. The critical point for the exam: your Spark APIs, your SQL, and your DataFrame code do not change at all. Flipping Photon on is a runtime switch, not a rewrite. It is vectorized and columnar — instead of interpreting one row at a time, it processes a batch of column values per CPU instruction, which collapses the per-row interpretation overhead.

So where does Photon win big? Think CPU-bound work. Large table scans, wide aggregations, joins, string-heavy transformations, and Delta MERGE, DELETE, and UPDATE operations. Whenever the bottleneck is the CPU chewing through rows rather than waiting on storage or network, Photon is the lever you pull.

Now the flip side — and this is the classic trap. Photon barely helps on I/O-bound jobs, Python UDF-heavy pipelines, and tiny datasets. If your job is sitting idle waiting on object storage, or burning time in serialized Python user-defined functions, a faster execution engine changes nothing. Notice that last one carefully: a Python UDF forces that data out of the vectorized path entirely.

Here's the cost nuance that trips people up. The Photon DBU rate is higher per DBU — that part is true. But total cost frequently falls, because wall-clock runtime drops, so you consume fewer DBU-hours. Always compare DBU-hours, never DBU rates. A higher rate on a much shorter runtime is often the cheaper job.

Which brings us to the exam trap. The statement 'Enable Photon to speed up every job' is false — it is a targeted lever for CPU-bound operators. And do not conflate Photon with Adaptive Query Execution, Delta caching, or autoscaling. Those are separate mechanisms solving separate problems, and the exam will absolutely test whether you can tell them apart. Next, let's see whether Photon is actually cheaper for a given job.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Photon Fundamentals

questions.question: A nightly analytics job scans a 4 TB Parquet fact table stored in Delta Lake and performs a wide aggregation with several GROUP BY keys over billions of rows. There is no join and no skew; the Spark UI shows the runtime is dominated by CPU-bound aggregation and column decoding in the scan/aggregate stages. The team is considering enabling Photon. Which statement best describes the expected outcome and the correct reasoning for this decision?

options.label: Photon is likely to help, because it replaces the JVM-based row-at-a-time execution engine with a vectorized native engine that accelerates scans, joins, and aggregations while keeping the same DataFrame API.
Photon is likely to help, because it changes the underlying storage format from Parquet to a columnar format and therefore reduces the bytes read from cloud object storage.
Photon is unlikely to help, because Photon only accelerates shuffle exchange and cannot affect column decoding or aggregation operators.
Photon is guaranteed to speed up every Databricks job, so the team should enable it without profiling the workload.

questions.correctAnswer: Photon is likely to help, because it replaces the JVM-based row-at-a-time execution engine with a vectorized native engine that accelerates scans, joins, and aggregations while keeping the same DataFrame API.
questions.analysis: Photon is a runtime execution engine, not a storage format or a shuffle-only optimization. It rewrites operators such as scans, filters, joins, and aggregations into vectorized, native code, so a CPU-bound scan/aggregate workload like this one is exactly the profile where Photon typically reduces runtime. Option B is wrong because Photon does not change the file format; Delta Lake and Parquet remain the storage layer, and Photon does not inherently reduce object-storage bytes read. Option C is wrong because Photon does accelerate more than shuffle boundaries and does not leave column decoding untouched. Option D is the classic distractor that claims Photon speeds up every job; Photon does not help I/O-bound, shuffle-bound, UDF-heavy, or single-partition workloads, so profiling first is the correct engineering habit. Note that the source material's discussion of partitioning and clustering [source p.240] reinforces that scan cost can be reduced by data layout (partitioning/clustering) independently of the execution engine, which is a different lever than Photon.
answer: Photon is likely to help, because it replaces the JVM-based row-at-a-time execution engine with a vectorized native engine that accelerates scans, joins, and aggregations while keeping the same DataFrame API.

questions.question: A data engineer is evaluating whether to enable Photon on a Databricks cluster running a mix of workloads. Which of the following statements correctly distinguish Photon from adjacent Spark and Databricks optimizations? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Photon is a native vectorized execution engine that accelerates operators such as scans, joins, and aggregations; it is not the same thing as Adaptive Query Execution (AQE), which changes the physical plan at runtime (for example, coalescing shuffle partitions or switching join strategies).
Photon is a storage format, so enabling Photon is equivalent to converting tables to Delta Lake and is therefore interchangeable with Delta caching.
Photon changes the physical execution engine but not the logical plan, so a broadcast hint, a bucketing choice, or a partition prune you already coded will still apply when Photon is on.
Photon will typically improve jobs regardless of the network or storage bottleneck, so it is a universal substitute for partition pruning and autoscaling.

questions.correctAnswer: Photon is a native vectorized execution engine that accelerates operators such as scans, joins, and aggregations; it is not the same thing as Adaptive Query Execution (AQE), which changes the physical plan at runtime (for example, coalescing shuffle partitions or switching join strategies).;Photon changes the physical execution engine but not the logical plan, so a broadcast hint, a bucketing choice, or a partition prune you already coded will still apply when Photon is on.
questions.analysis: Photon and AQE operate at different layers: AQE re-plans stages at runtime (partition coalescing, join strategy switching, skew handling), while Photon changes how operators execute once a plan is chosen. They are complementary, not interchangeable. Photon also sits below the logical plan: hints, bucketing, and pruning decisions you already made remain in force, so a workload that was already short-circuited by partition pruning may see only modest Photon gains. Option B is wrong on two counts: Photon is not a storage format, and it is not equivalent to Delta caching; Delta caching keeps data on local SSDs for reuse, whereas Photon changes operator execution. Option D is the 'Photon is always faster' distractor; Photon does not replace partition pruning or autoscaling, and it does not help when the bottleneck is I/O, network, or enough partitions. As context, the source material notes that storage layout choices such as partitioning and clustering save scan cost independent of the execution engine [source p.240], and that physical resource decisions like memory rental and SSD usage are workload-specific trade-offs [source p.248] — reinforcing that Photon is one lever among many.
answer: Photon is a native vectorized execution engine that accelerates operators such as scans, joins, and aggregations; it is not the same thing as Adaptive Query Execution (AQE), which changes the physical plan at runtime (for example, coalescing shuffle partitions or switching join strategies).;Photon changes the physical execution engine but not the logical plan, so a broadcast hint, a bucketing choice, or a partition prune you already coded will still apply when Photon is on.

questions.question: A workload runs for 60 minutes on a non-Photon cluster at a rate of $0.55 per DBU and consistently consumes 40 DBUs, so the baseline cost is 60 minutes × 40 DBU/hr × ($0.55/DBU) / 60 = $22.00 per run. After enabling Photon, the DBU rate rises to $0.80 per DBU and the runtime drops to 36 minutes at the same 40 DBUs consumed. Which statement best describes the net cost effect and the correct reasoning?

options.label: The DBU rate rose by 45%, so the job is more expensive per run; comparing rates is sufficient to make the decision.

Photon cost = 36 min × 40 DBU/hr × ($0.80/DBU) / 60 = $19.20, so even with the higher DBU rate the runtime reduction produces a net per-run saving of about $2.80 (roughly 13%), meaning the decision should be based on net cost, not on the DBU rate alone.
The job cost is unchanged because the DBU rate and the runtime are unrelated variables, so Photon has no financial effect.
The job is cheaper only if Photon is combined with Delta caching, because Photon alone cannot change the cost calculation.

questions.correctAnswer: Photon cost = 36 min × 40 DBU/hr × ($0.80/DBU) / 60 = $19.20, so even with the higher DBU rate the runtime reduction produces a net per-run saving of about $2.80 (roughly 13%), meaning the decision should be based on net cost, not on the DBU rate alone.
questions.analysis: The correct reasoning is net cost = runtime × DBUs consumed × rate. Baseline: 60 min × 40 DBU/hr × $0.55/DBU ÷ 60 min/hr = $22.00. Photon: 36 min × 40 DBU/hr × $0.80/DBU ÷ 60 min/hr = $19.20. Net saving is $2.80, about 13%, even though the DBU rate rose 45%. This is the exam-oriented point: a higher per-DBU price can still yield a lower total bill when wall-clock time falls enough. Option A is the classic distractor that looks only at the rate; Option C is wrong because cost depends on both rate and duration; Option D incorrectly makes Delta caching a precondition for Photon economics.
