The source material's broader framing that separating compute and storage lets you rent large memory and release it when the job completes [source p.248] is the same cost-per-unit-of-work logic: the bill tracks how long resources are held, so a faster engine that finishes earlier can win even at a higher unit price.
answer: Photon cost = 36 min × 40 DBU/hr × ($0.80/DBU) / 60 = $19.20, so even with the higher DBU rate the runtime reduction produces a net per-run saving of about $2.80 (roughly 13%), meaning the decision should be based on net cost, not on the DBU rate alone.

actions.text: Time for a quick checkpoint on Photon. You've got three questions covering when Photon helps, how it differs from adjacent optimizations, and how to reason about its net cost. Take your time and try each one on your own — no peeking ahead. Once you submit, I'll be right here to walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Is Photon Cheaper for This Job?

elements.content: Problem 1

A nightly ETL job runs on a Databricks job cluster of 8 workers and takes 90 minutes of wall-clock time. Each worker consumes DBUs at a rate of R DBU per worker-hour, so the baseline consumes 8 × 1.5 × R DBU-hours. The team enables Photon (Databricks' vectorized, C++-native query engine). The same job now finishes in 40 minutes, but the DBU consumption rate on this SKU rises to 1.5R per worker-hour. (a) Compute the DBU-hours for the baseline run and for the Photon run. (b) What percentage does DBU consumption change by? (c) Is Photon cheaper overall? Use R = USD 0.55 per DBU-hour and an illustrative cloud VM price of USD 0.30 per worker-hour. (d) At what speedup does Photon break even?
Hint: Write both runs as (workers) × (hours) × (DBU rate); the rate multiplier only touches the DBU half of the bill, the VM half just follows wall-clock time.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Baseline DBU-hours. Work = workers × hours × rate = $8 \times 1.5 \times R = 12R$ DBU-hours. With R = USD 0.55, the Databricks charge is $12 \times 0.55 = \text{USD } 6.60$.

Step 2 — Photon DBU-hours. Runtime is 40 min = $\frac{40}{60} = 0.6667$ h, and the rate is $1.5R$: $8 \times 0.6667 \times 1.5R = 8R$ DBU-hours, i.e. $8 \times 0.55 = \text{USD } 4.40$.

Step 3 — Percentage change. $\frac{8R - 12R}{12R} = -\frac{1}{3} = -33.3\%$. Photon burns one third fewer DBU-hours.

Step 4 — Compact test. Let s be the speedup and m the DBU-rate multiplier. Cost ratio $= \frac{T_{\text{photon}} \times m}{T_{\text{base}}} = \frac{m}{s} = \frac{1.5}{2.25} = 0.6667$, confirming a 33.3% reduction, because $s = \frac{90}{40} = 2.25$.

Step 5 — Full bill including VMs. Node-hours are workers × hours: baseline $8 \times 1.5 = 12$ node-hours → $12 \times 0.30 = \text{USD } 3.60$; Photon $8 \times 0.6667 = 5.33$ node-hours → USD 1.60. Totals: USD 10.20 versus USD 6.00, a 41.2% reduction. Note the VM line falls by 55.6% (22.5/9 ≈ 2.25× less time), while the DBU line falls by only 33.3%, because the 1.5× multiplier applies to DBUs alone.

Step 6 — Daily and annual saving. USD 4.20 per run; nightly for a year: $4.20 \times 365 = \text{USD } 1{,}533$.

Step 7 — Break-even. Photon is cheaper iff $\frac{m}{s} < 1$, i.e. $s > m = 1.5$. The run must be at least $90/1.5 = 60$ minutes after enabling Photon, equivalently a speedup above 1.5×, for the 1.5R rate to pay for itself.

Analysis — The whole problem is a two-lever comparison: the engine changes how many hours you pay for, the SKU changes what you pay per hour. Multiplying them gives the canonical break-even rule $s > m$ — speedup must beat the rate multiplier. Students who compare only wall-clock time (40 vs 90 minutes, 'obviously cheaper') get the right answer by luck here; students who compare only rates (1.5R is 50% more expensive') get it wrong. The edge case is exactly the one that fails in production: if the speedup collapses toward 1× (an I/O-bound job), the same 1.5× multiplier turns Photon into a 50% surcharge. Two further subtleties matter at university level. First, the DBU rate and the cloud VM rate are separate meters; a shorter run shrinks the VM meter proportionally to wall clock, while the DBU meter shrinks by m/s, so total saving depends on the DBU:VM price mix. Second, the rate multiplier is a SKU assumption, not a law — verify the actual DBU rate for the workload's compute type before quoting a saving. A good engineering habit is to instrument cost monitoring from day one rather than after deployment, since uptime, latency, and processed volume are the inputs any cost model needs [source p.292]. Finally, resist optimizing cost before the pipeline is stable: teams in the earliest maturity stage should move fast and add value, not micro-tune DBUs [source p.40].
Problem 2

A production pipeline runs on a 16-worker job cluster and finishes in 45 minutes. In the Spark UI's task timeline, the longest stage (30 minutes) never shows more than 6 tasks running concurrently, and all tasks in that stage take roughly the same time. Assume for this exercise that the workload is task-slot-bound — one task slot per worker, e.g. because each task holds most of a worker's memory — so concurrent tasks map 1:1 to workers. (a) Right-size the cluster and justify the number. (b) Estimate the DBU-hour saving with R = USD 0.55 per DBU-hour, per run and per month at 30 runs. (c) State two measurements you must take before trusting the answer.
Hint: The cluster can only go as fast as the number of tasks it can run at once; extra workers idle inside the stage, not outside it.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Read the concurrency ceiling. The binding constraint is peak concurrent tasks = 6. A 30-minute stage that never runs more than 6 tasks in parallel is not going to run faster on 16 workers, because the remaining 10 workers have nothing to execute.

Step 2 — Choose the size. Target 6–8 workers: 6 matches the observed peak exactly, and 8 leaves headroom for the shuffle/aggregation phases and for stragglers, which are invisible in the peak number alone. Pick 8 for the estimate.

Step 3 — DBU-hours before and after. Job time is 45 min = 0.75 h in both cases (8 ≥ 6, so runtime is unchanged).

Baseline: $16 \times 0.75 \times R = 12R$ DBU-hours → $12 \times 0.55 = \text{USD } 6.60$ per run.

Right-sized: $8 \times 0.75 \times R = 6R$ DBU-hours → USD 3.30 per run.

Saving: 6R DBU-hours = 50%, i.e. USD 3.30 per run.

Step 4 — Periodize. 30 runs/month: USD 198 → USD 99, a USD 99/month saving; annualized, $3.30 \times 365 = \text{USD } 1{,}204.50$. Node-hours fall from 12 to 6 per run as well, so the VM line halves too.

Step 5 — Measurements required before trusting it. (i) Peak concurrent tasks across every stage and across several runs, not just the longest stage in one run — a final write stage can fan out far wider than the join stage. (ii) Task duration distribution, to confirm the stage is not skewed: if one task takes 10× the median, that straggler sets the 45-minute wall clock, and cutting workers to 8 could stretch the stage rather than shrink the bill. Also confirm how the job cluster is billed for start-up and how autoscaling counts workers (average versus maximum).

Analysis — The method is a capacity argument, not a benchmarking exercise: throughput is capped by parallelism, so once the cluster supplies more slots than the workload can fill, additional workers change cost but not time. The arithmetic is trivial — halve the workers, halve the DBU-hours — but the diagnostic step is where students lose marks: they read '16 workers' from the cluster configuration instead of reading peak concurrency from the Spark UI. Three pitfalls are worth naming explicitly. First, using the maximum worker count of an autoscaling cluster instead of the average: autoscaling clusters report both, and only the average drives the bill. Second, assuming task count equals parallelism: partitions can be far more numerous than slots, and skew means the effective parallelism is set by the slowest tasks, not the number of partitions. Third, forgetting that the last stages of a job (final aggregation, single-file writes) are inherently low-concurrency, so a cluster sized for the widest stage wastes money everywhere else. Operationally, right-sizing is only defensible if you can see the job's latency and processed volume over time; that is precisely why monitoring belongs in the pipeline from the beginning rather than after deployment [source p.292]. Note also that an orchestration system watching for an expected completion time (say 10 a.m. for an overnight pipeline) will alert if the smaller cluster pushes the job past its SLA, which is the safety net that makes aggressive right-sizing reversible [source p.91].
Problem 3

A pipeline runs on 8 workers and takes 60 minutes. Profiling shows that 48 minutes of that wall clock is spent waiting on remote object-store reads of plain Parquet files (no Delta Lake, so no data skipping), and only 12 minutes is CPU work. Enabling Photon speeds the CPU portion up by the same 2.25× as in the earlier problem, but the I/O wait is completely unaffected. The DBU rate becomes 1.5R. (a) What is the new runtime? (b) What is the change in DBU-hours? (c) What fraction of the baseline runtime must be CPU-bound for Photon to pay off at all?
Hint: Photon accelerates computation, not network and storage latency; add the untouched I/O time back after speeding up the CPU time.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Split the runtime. Baseline: $T_{\text{base}} = I + C = 48 + 12 = 60$ minutes, where I = 48 min of I/O wait and C = 12 min of CPU.

Step 2 — Apply Photon only to C. Photon runtime $T_p = I + \frac{C}{2.25} = 48 + 5.33 = 53.33$ minutes. The speedup is only $s = \frac{60}{53.33} = 1.125$.

Step 3 — Convert to DBU-hours. Baseline: $8 \times 1.0 \times R = 8R$ DBU-hours. Photon: $8 \times \frac{53.33}{60} \times 1.5R = 8 \times 0.8889 \times 1.5R = 10.67R$ DBU-hours. The change is $\frac{10.67 - 8}{8} = +33.3\%$: Photon is a third more expensive here.

Step 4 — Same answer from the ratio rule. Cost ratio $= \frac{m}{s} = \frac{1.5}{1.125} = 1.333$, i.e. +33.3%. With R = USD 0.55, the run goes from USD 4.40 to USD 5.87, about USD 1.47 more per run.

Step 5 — Break-even on the CPU share. Require $s > 1.5$, i.e. $T_p < \frac{60}{1.5} = 40$ min. Substituting: $(60 - C) + \frac{C}{2.25} < 40 \Rightarrow 60 - 0.5556C < 40 \Rightarrow C > 36$ minutes. So the CPU-bound share must exceed $\frac{36}{60} = 60\%$ of the baseline runtime. At 80% I/O this job is far outside that window.

Analysis — This is the counterexample that makes the break-even rule $s > m$ genuinely useful rather than a slogan: identical engine, identical cluster, opposite conclusion, because the engine can only accelerate the part of the runtime it controls. Students who apply 'Photon is faster' as a reflex and skip the runtime decomposition produce a confident wrong answer. The general form of the decomposition is Amdahl's law: with fraction f of the runtime being accelerable and speedup s on that fraction, overall speedup is $1/((1-f) + f/s)$; here f = 0.2 and s = 2.25, giving 1.125, which matches the arithmetic. Edge cases to watch: (i) I/O wait and CPU work overlap in real Spark stages, so treating them as strictly additive is a conservative simplification — measure with the query profile rather than assuming a clean split; (ii) if the jobs were rewritten to Delta Lake with file skipping and predicate pushdown, I would shrink, f would rise, and Photon could flip to a net win — the engine choice and the table format are coupled decisions; (iii) very small I/O-bound jobs may be dominated by fixed overhead rather than steady-state I/O, a case treated separately. The practical lesson: instrument latency and processed volume before choosing a compute option, because the decision rule depends entirely on a measured runtime decomposition, not on the cluster shape [source p.292].
Problem 4

A micro-batch job runs on a 2-worker job cluster. The actual Spark computation takes 3 minutes, but the cluster takes 5 minutes of provisioning plus termination that is also billed at the DBU rate. Enabling Photon adds 0.5 minutes of engine warm-up but speeds the 3-minute computation by 2.25×, and the DBU rate becomes 1.5R. (a) Compute billed DBU-hours with and without Photon. (b) Does Photon pay off? (c) Find the minimum compute time C for which Photon turns profitable, given the same 5.5-minute fixed overhead O.
Hint: Fixed overhead is charged in full whether or not Photon shrinks the compute; it never gets the 1.5× rate's benefit-of-the-doubt.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Baseline billed time. Provisioning/termination plus compute: $O + C = 5 + 3 = 8$ minutes $= 0.1333$ h. DBU-hours $= 2 \times 0.1333 \times R = 0.2667R$.

Step 2 — Photon billed time. Fixed overhead becomes $O = 5.5$ min (5 min provisioning plus 0.5 min engine warm-up), and compute shrinks to $\frac{3}{2.25} = 1.333$ min. Total $= 5.5 + 1.333 = 6.833$ min $= 0.1139$ h. DBU-hours $= 2 \times 0.1139 \times 1.5R = 0.3417R$.

Step 3 — Compare. Cost ratio $= \frac{0.3417}{0.2667} = 1.281$ — Photon costs about 28% more, i.e. it loses USD 0.041 per run at R = USD 0.55 (0.2667 × 0.55 = USD 0.147 versus 0.3417 × 0.55 = USD 0.188). The runtime did drop 20% (8.5 → 6.83 min), but not nearly enough to absorb a 1.5× rate.

Step 4 — Break-even derivation. Photon wins iff $1.5R(O + C/s) < R(O + C)$, with $s = 2.25$. Cancel R: $1.5O + \frac{1.5C}{2.25} < O + C \Rightarrow 0.5O < C\left(1 - 0.6667\right) = 0.3333C \Rightarrow C > 1.5O$. With $O = 5.5$ min, compute must exceed $1.5 \times 5.5 = 8.25$ minutes. Our 3-minute job is well below the threshold, so the verdict is robust.

Analysis — This problem isolates the third term of every cost model: fixed overhead, which is insensitive to how clever the engine is. The general form of the break-even condition, $C > O \cdot \frac{m}{s - m}$ with $s = 2.25$ and $m = 1.5$, reduces to $C > 1.5O$ here and shows that as the rate multiplier approaches the speedup the required compute time explodes — the closer m is to s, the less headroom Photon has. The practical consequences are concrete: short jobs should not enable Photon at all; they should instead shorten the overhead itself, by using smaller or serverless compute, by keeping a warm cluster for frequent micro-batches, or by batching several small jobs into one cluster session. The pitfall to avoid is quoting a per-DBU rate without amortizing start-up: a 2-worker cluster that runs for 8 billed minutes is dominated by provisioning, not by Spark. Note also the architectural context — the whole reason job clusters exist is that ephemeral infrastructure per job avoids dependency conflicts between unrelated workloads, and that pattern is common for Spark on cloud services [source p.168]. That architectural benefit is real, but it is paid for in start-up time, which is exactly the quantity that decides whether Photon helps. Finally, an orchestration system that watches for an expected completion time will alert when a long-running job misses its window, so the cost experiment is safe to run — but only if that monitoring exists [source p.91].

actions.text: Now let's put Photon to work under exam conditions. On this page we have four fully-worked quantitative problems that compare a baseline run against a Photon run — measuring cost in DBU-hours and in dollars — plus a right-sizing problem. Let's walk through each one the way the exam expects.

Problem 1: a nightly ETL job runs 90 minutes on 8 workers at rate R DBU per hour. With Photon it finishes in 40 minutes, but the DBU rate jumps to 1.5R. Is Photon cheaper? Notice the two moving levers — wall-clock time goes down, but the per-hour rate goes up.
The hint tells us the trick: write both runs as workers × hours × DBU rate. That puts both configurations in the same unit — DBU-hours — so the comparison is apples to apples.

Step 1, baseline DBU-hours: 8 workers × 1.5 hours equals 12 DBU-hours. Step 2, Photon: 8 workers × 40 minutes, which is two-thirds of an hour, × 1.5R gives us 8 DBU-hours. Photon uses 33 percent fewer DBU-hours, so it is cheaper in DBUs — and since the job also finishes faster, it's likely cheaper in VM cost too.

The analysis note is the key takeaway: wall-clock reduction dominates the rate multiplier. Photon costs more per hour but finishes fast enough to save overall. But watch the trap — if the job is I/O-bound, Photon shrinks runtime only slightly, so the 1.5x rate raises cost instead of lowering it. That's the framing the exam wants.

Problem 2 takes a different angle: a production pipeline runs on a 16-worker job cluster, but the Spark UI shows only 6 concurrent tasks per stage. That's the signal — you're paying for workers the cluster can't use. Right-size it and estimate the saving.
The hint frames it perfectly: the cluster can only go as fast as the number of tasks running in parallel. Extra workers don't add speed if there's no parallelism to fill them.

Peak concurrency of 6 tasks implies roughly 6 to 8 executors need to be active — not 16. Halving the worker count halves the DBU-hours with no runtime change for this stage profile. That's a clean, defensible saving.

Analysis: this is a capacity argument, not a Photon question. You right-size to match real parallelism, and the method breaks if tasks are skewed — a single hot partition will bound concurrency regardless of how many workers you have.
Problem 3 is the counterexample to Problem 1. A pipeline runs on 8 workers and takes 60 minutes. This time, the hint warns, Photon accelerates computation but not network I/O.
So we must split the runtime. Part of it is compute — that's what Photon speeds up — and part of it is network or I/O bound, which Photon leaves untouched. Only the compute portion shrinks.

Analysis: this is the I/O-bound trap we flagged earlier. If most of the runtime is I/O, the 1.5x rate raises cost and Photon loses. The exam will lean on this — always check what fraction of the job is actually compute-bound.

Problem 4 isolates the third term of the cost model: fixed overhead. A micro-batch job runs on a 2-worker cluster. The hint reminds us that fixed startup cost is charged in full whether the job runs for one minute or ten.
Step 1, baseline billed time: we must add provisioning to the actual runtime, because the cluster is charged from start-up, not from first task.

And the analysis ties it together: cost equals workers times billed hours times rate, plus fixed overhead. On very short runs the fixed term dominates — which is exactly the pitfall the exam builds around. Remember the four common traps from the description: don't use max workers instead of the average under autoscaling, don't ignore startup cost on short runs, and never assume task count equals parallelism without checking for skew. Let's move on to comparing compute choices.

scenes.title: Compute Choices Compared: All-Purpose, Job Clusters, SQL Warehouses

elements.content: Dimension  |  All-purpose compute  |  Job compute  |  SQL warehouse

Intended use and primary user
All-purpose compute: All-purpose compute is an interactive, long-lived cluster meant for a human being at a keyboard — notebook development, ad-hoc exploration, debugging, and collaborative data science sessions where the same cluster is reused across many commands.
Job compute: Job compute is a transient cluster whose entire lifecycle is bound to a single job run; it carries no interactive notebook session and exists purely to execute the scheduled or triggered workload defined by the job.
SQL warehouse: SQL warehouse is a SQL-only compute resource that exposes an endpoint for BI tools, dashboards, and SQL editors, so it serves analysts running governed queries rather than engineers running arbitrary Python or Scala code [source p.379].

Cost model and relative DBU rate
All-purpose compute: All-purpose compute carries the highest DBU rate of the three and is billed for the entire wall-clock lifetime of the cluster, including any idle minutes before auto-termination fires, so its effective cost is dominated by the DBU rate multiplied by the idle-inclusive uptime.
Job compute: Job compute carries a lower DBU rate than all-purpose compute and is billed only for the duration of the job run, which means the same Spark workload on job compute costs strictly less per DBU than running it interactively.
SQL warehouse: SQL warehouse is billed on a separate SQL-warehouse DBU rate and, in serverless mode, the platform manages the backend so the warehouse scales to zero and scales up automatically to handle large queries, so you pay for query consumption rather than for an always-on VM [source p.169].

Auto-termination behavior
All-purpose compute: All-purpose clusters do not stop on their own by default in every configuration, so auto-termination must be explicitly configured with an idle timeout in minutes; if it is left disabled the cluster keeps burning DBUs after the last human stops typing, which is the single most common source of idle spend.
Job compute: Job compute needs no auto-termination configuration as a cost lever because termination is structural: the cluster is created when the run starts and torn down when the run finishes or fails, so there is no idle window to protect against.
SQL warehouse: SQL warehouses terminate based on their own auto-stop setting measured in minutes of query inactivity, and when the warehouse stops the compute scales down rather than being destroyed, so the next query pays a cold-start latency in exchange for near-zero idle cost.

Sharing, concurrency, and multi-user behavior
All-purpose compute: All-purpose clusters are shared by multiple users and notebooks, which is convenient for collaboration but introduces contention: concurrent users compete for the same executors, a heavy notebook can starve a colleague, and library installations or cluster-config changes affect everyone attached.
Job compute: Job compute is single-tenant by construction — each job run gets its own cluster — so concurrency is expressed as multiple independent cluster instances rather than multiple users sharing one, which eliminates cross-workload interference at the cost of additional provisioning time.
SQL warehouse: SQL warehouses are explicitly built to serve concurrent BI traffic, autoscaling driven by query concurrency, and are the correct place to absorb hundreds of simultaneous dashboard refreshes; a workload of this shape deployed onto an all-purpose cluster would serialize and fail its latency target [source p.379].

Workload mapping
All-purpose compute: All-purpose compute maps to exploratory data analysis, one-off investigations, notebook-based development, delta-table curation done interactively, and any workload where a human is iterating and cannot predict the next command.
Job compute: Job compute maps to scheduled production pipelines, Lakeflow-orchestrated ETL, Auto Loader ingestion runs, and any repeatable transformation chain that must run on a cron or trigger without human interaction.
SQL warehouse: SQL warehouse maps to BI dashboards, SQL-only reporting, materialized view refreshes for analytic consumption, and lightweight warehouse-style aggregations; for the workload taxonomy in this course, structured SQL analytics belongs here, not on a general-purpose cluster [source p.126].

Startup latency and lifecycle granularity
All-purpose compute: All-purpose compute has a one-time cold start of roughly several minutes when the cluster is created or re-sized, but the cost of that start is amortized across the whole interactive session, which is why it is wasteful only when used for short non-interactive runs.
Job compute: Job compute pays a cluster-start latency on every run, so short jobs on job compute can spend a meaningful fraction of their wall clock in provisioning; job compute is therefore the right default when the run is long enough to amortize that start, which scheduled production pipelines overwhelmingly are.
SQL warehouse: SQL warehouse in serverless mode is designed to start fast enough for interactive BI use and to scale to zero between bursts, whereas classic SQL warehouses reserve VMs and therefore start quickly but pay for reserved capacity during the auto-stop window [source p.169].

Worked cost example: a nightly 2-hour pipeline
All-purpose compute: All-purpose path: if the pipeline runs 2 hours and each of 4 workers contributes a DBU rate R, and auto-termination is set to 60 minutes of idle while the engineer forgets to detach (total billed 3 hours), DBU cost = 4 * R * 3 = 12R DBU-hours, before the cloud VM term.
Job compute: Job compute path: the same 2-hour run on 4 workers with the job-compute DBU rate, call it 0.5R, and no idle tail means DBU cost = 4 * 0.5R * 2 = 4R DBU-hours — a factor-of-three reduction in DBU-hours relative to the all-purpose path, and the gap widens if auto-termination is misconfigured on the all-purpose side.
SQL warehouse: SQL-warehouse path: the same pipeline expressed as SQL and executed on a warehouse is billed by warehouse DBU consumption against query runtime, and in serverless mode the backend is platform-managed so the VM term largely disappears, but non-SQL operators (custom Python, Auto Loader) cannot be expressed here at all [source p.169].

Exam trap and distractor pattern
All-purpose compute: The classic wrong answer provisions all-purpose compute for a scheduled production job with the justification 'so the team can also explore data on it'; this fails because it pays the all-purpose DBU premium and the idle tail on a workload that has no interactive user, and the collaboration benefit is hypothetical rather than measured.
Job compute: The mirror distractor claims job compute is cheaper but unsuitable for production because it terminates, conflating 'terminates after the run' with 'fails mid-run'; job compute terminates on completion by design and is the default for scheduled production pipelines.
SQL warehouse: A third distractor assigns SQL analytically heavy BI traffic to an all-purpose cluster to 'avoid warehouse cost', which inverts the concurrency model: all-purpose clusters do not autoscale on query concurrency, so dashboard bursts queue behind the shared executors instead of scaling [source p.379].

Photon and engine-layer considerations
All-purpose compute: All-purpose compute can enable Photon to accelerate interactive SQL and DataFrame work, and the decision is separable from the compute-type decision because Photon is a vectorized engine layer rather than a cluster class.
Job compute: Job compute can likewise enable Photon, and because job compute is where the bulk of scheduled ETL runs, the Photon on/off decision is usually evaluated against job-compute cost-duration curves rather than against interactive sessions.
SQL warehouse: SQL warehouses run a SQL engine that is distinct from a general Spark cluster, so Photon-style vectorized acceleration is an implementation detail of the warehouse rather than a toggle you manage per notebook, and the cost question is framed as warehouse size and autoscaling range [source p.379].

Decision rule in one line
All-purpose compute: Choose all-purpose compute when a human will iterate against the data in the next few minutes and the workload cannot be scheduled ahead of time, and always pair it with an explicit auto-termination idle timeout.
Job compute: Choose job compute for any repeatable, scheduled, or triggered pipeline because it is cheaper per DBU and cannot leak idle spend, which makes it the default for production ETL.
SQL warehouse: Choose a SQL warehouse when the workload is expressible in SQL and the consumer is a BI tool or analyst, because autoscaling on query concurrency is the only one of the three designed to absorb dashboard load [source p.379].

Takeaway — Default to job compute for scheduled production pipelines: it carries a lower DBU rate than all-purpose and has no idle tail, so a 2-hour nightly run costs a fraction of the same work done interactively — with the worked example above showing roughly a 3x DBU-hour reduction.

Takeaway — Reserve all-purpose compute for genuine interactive work — notebook development, ad-hoc analysis, and collaborative exploration — and always configure auto-termination, because the all-purpose DBU rate is the highest of the three and idle minutes are billed in full.

Takeaway — Route SQL-only BI and dashboard traffic to a SQL warehouse, using serverless when you want scale-to-zero and platform-managed backend; a SQL warehouse autoscales on query concurrency in a way an all-purpose cluster does not.

Takeaway — Reject the exam trap that provisions all-purpose compute for a scheduled production job 'so the team can also explore it': that answer pays the premium rate and the idle tail for a workload with no interactive user, which is exactly the cost the compute-type decision exists to avoid.

actions.text: This table is the heart of the page — a side-by-side comparison of all-purpose compute, job compute, and SQL warehouses across the dimensions the exam actually tests. Let's walk down the rows one at a time so the distinctions stick.

Start with intended use and primary user. All-purpose computes are built for interactive development — notebooks, exploration, ad-hoc analysis by a data engineer or analyst sitting at the keyboard. Job clusters, by contrast, are the default choice for scheduled production pipelines, and SQL warehouses exist to serve SQL-only BI and dashboard traffic. Same platform, three very different audiences.

Next, the cost model. Job compute costs less per DBU — the Databricks Unit that prices consumption — and you only pay for the duration of the run. All-purpose clusters carry a higher DBU rate because they're meant to be long-lived and shared. SQL warehouses sit on their own billing shape, often serverless, scaled by query concurrency. If you remember only one line here, remember that job clusters are the cheaper rate for scheduled work.

Auto-termination is where cost leaks happen. Job clusters tear down automatically when the run finishes — no configuration needed. All-purpose clusters do not; you must set auto-termination explicitly, or idle time quietly burns spend. This is exactly the kind of detail the exam turns into a scenario question.

Sharing and concurrency follow from that. All-purpose clusters are multi-user by design — several engineers can attach and collaborate. Job clusters are single-purpose, owned by one run. SQL warehouses are built for many concurrent queries and autoscale to meet them, which is why BI tools land there rather than on a cluster.

Then workload mapping ties it together. Interactive development and ad-hoc analysis go to all-purpose. Scheduled production pipelines go to job compute. SQL analytics and dashboards go to SQL warehouses. If you can classify the workload, the compute choice usually falls out on its own.

Finally, startup latency and lifecycle granularity. Job clusters spin up per run, so there's a cold-start cost each time — that's the tradeoff for the cheaper rate. All-purpose clusters stay warm so interactive sessions feel instant. SQL warehouses can start in seconds, and with serverless you skip cluster provisioning entirely.

Now the exam trap — and it's a classic. A scenario says a nightly production job needs an all-purpose cluster 'so the team can also explore the data on it.' That is the wrong answer every time. Mixing an interactive use case into a scheduled production job doubles your DBU rate and risks idle spend. The correct move is job compute for the pipeline, and a separate all-purpose cluster for exploration.

So the decision rule in one line: if it runs on a schedule, default to job compute. If a human is exploring interactively, use all-purpose — with auto-termination configured. If the workload is SQL-only BI, route it to a SQL warehouse.
That maps straight onto our first takeaway: default to job compute for scheduled production workflows — it's cheaper per DBU and cleans up after itself.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Cluster Sizing and Autoscaling

questions.question: A nightly ETL job performs memory-heavy joins across several wide dimension tables and produces a heavily skewed shuffle. The team observes that executor memory pressure, not CPU, dominates stage runtimes, and latency requirements are moderate. Which combination of node type family and worker sizing is the MOST appropriate to configure first, given the checkpoint rules on cluster shape and the Photon cost model?

options.label: A memory-optimized node family with autoscaling enabled and a minimum worker count sized to fit the working set of the largest shuffle partition
A compute-optimized node family with the maximum worker count allowed by the workspace quota, regardless of shuffle partition size
A storage-optimized node family with Delta caching disabled and a single large driver node to centralize the join
A general-purpose node family with Photon disabled and spark.sql.shuffle.partitions set to a very high value to spread the skew

questions.analysis: Memory-heavy joins with skewed shuffle typically fail or slow down when executor memory cannot hold the largest shuffle partition, so the first lever is a memory-optimized node family and a baseline worker count sized to the working set rather than to raw CPU throughput. This mirrors the distributed-systems principle that capacity is added horizontally to meet load and resource requirements, with a leader node distributing tasks to worker nodes [source p.115]. Option B ignores the memory constraint and simply maximizes workers, which the distractor about 'more workers always reduces runtime' mistakenly endorses. Option C is wrong because disabling caching and centralizing work on one driver defeats horizontal scaling. Option D raises shuffle partitions, which the earlier checkpoint already taught does not cure skew.

questions.question: Which statements correctly describe the semantics of Databricks cluster autoscaling and its relationship to cost? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Autoscaling adjusts the number of worker nodes between a configured minimum and maximum based on load, with the driver remaining fixed
Scale-up is triggered by pending tasks in the scheduler queue, while scale-down occurs when workers are idle for a configured period
Enabling autoscaling by itself guarantees lower total cost because idle workers are removed at the end of a burst
Total cost is determined by (DBU rate x DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price x runtime), so autoscaling only helps when it actually reduces DBU-hours or VM runtime

questions.analysis: Autoscaling keeps the driver fixed while flexing the worker count between min and max, which reflects the standard horizontal-scaling pattern where a leader node distributes tasks to worker nodes that can be added or removed as load changes [source p.115]. Scale-up responds to queued or pending work; scale-down responds to sustained idleness, and the idle threshold exists to avoid thrashing. Option C repeats a common misconception: autoscaling does not reduce cost by itself, because cost is a function of DBU-hours and VM runtime, and a poorly sized min or a workload that keeps all workers busy will not save anything. Option D restates the cost model correctly and is the reason autoscaling must be evaluated against actual utilization.

questions.question: A production pipeline must run a long, fault-tolerant nightly batch job that can tolerate occasional worker loss. Which configuration decisions are appropriate, and which are not? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Use spot (preemptible) instances for the worker pool, accepting that Spark will retry tasks when a node is reclaimed
Keep the driver on on-demand instances so the job's coordination process is not lost to a spot reclamation
Place both the driver and all workers on spot instances to maximize per-hour savings, since Spark can always restart the driver
Assume that adding more workers will always reduce runtime, so set autoscaling maximum to the workspace quota as the primary optimization

questions.analysis: Spot instances are appropriate for worker nodes on fault-tolerant batch workloads because streaming and batch platforms are typically distributed with the property that if a node goes down, another node replaces it and data remains accessible [source p.207]. The driver, however, coordinates the job and holds the SparkContext, so losing it terminates the run; keeping the driver on on-demand instances is the standard recommendation. Option C is incorrect because a reclaimed driver means restarting the entire job, wiping out any per-hour savings. Option D is the distractor described in the test points: adding workers cannot reduce runtime below what the partition and shuffle counts allow, so quota-sized autoscaling is not a real optimization.

actions.text: That takeaway on job compute sets us up nicely for this checkpoint, where we put the sizing and autoscaling ideas we just covered to the test. Take your time with each question and answer them on your own — once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning with you.

actions.text: We just worked through cluster sizing and autoscaling on the checkpoint — now let's make those numbers tangible. This simulator lets you trade off runtime against DBU-hours and total spend, so you can see right-sizing play out instead of reading about it.

actions.content: The max workers control sets the upper bound on cluster size.

actions.text: Start by dragging max workers up and watching the HUD. Runtime falls quickly at first, but past a certain point it flattens out while cost keeps climbing. That's the knee of the curve — the point where adding more workers buys you almost nothing.

actions.content: Speed First: many workers, short runtime, low spot share, Photon on.
Cost is driven by average workers, not maximum.

actions.text: Notice something important: the cost figure tracks your average worker count, not the maximum. Autoscaling lets the cluster shrink when the work thins out, so a high max doesn't automatically mean a high bill — but it will if the minimum keeps those workers alive the whole run.

actions.content: Cost Optimized: small cluster, longer runtime, heavy spot usage.

actions.text: Now compare the two configurations in the HUD. The speed-first build finishes sooner but spends more DBU-hours; the cost-optimized build runs longer yet comes in far cheaper. Your goal is to find the configuration that meets a stated runtime target at the lowest total cost — so try toggling Photon and adjusting spot share to see how each one shifts the total. Now reverse it: set a runtime target, shrink max workers, and hunt for the cheapest setup that still hits it.

scenes.title: Cost-Aware Practices: Right-Sizing and Lifecycle

elements.content: Cost-Aware Practices: Right-Sizing and Lifecycle
Total cost = (DBU rate x DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price x runtime). Every cost lever below must be judged against both terms [source p.413].

1. Right-size from evidence, not guesswork

Read Spark UI task counts, executor utilization, spill, and GC time to set the real worker count. Auto-scaling adds workers when input rate rises and removes them when idle; scheduled jobs run unattended, so the system must sense load by itself, as an orchestrator that stays online and monitors without human intervention does [source p.91].

Worked example

Job cluster: 4 h at R DBU/h = 4R DBU. All-purpose: same 4 h at 2R = 8R DBU. Idle 1.5 h at 2R = +3R. Total saving = 7R DBU-h.
Exam trap: "Autoscaling reduces cost" is only conditionally true - it helps only when the cluster would otherwise sit idle; it does nothing for a steadily saturated cluster.

actions.text: Now that we've seen how each knob shifts the total, let's lock in the cost-aware practices the exam actually expects a data engineer to apply to real pipelines. The first principle is simple: right-size from evidence, not guesswork.

Use the Spark UI to read task counts, executor utilization, spill, and GC time — those are the signals that tell you the real worker count you need. Note the second habit: always set auto-termination on all-purpose clusters, typically ten to thirty minutes, and run scheduled work on job clusters, which carry a lower DBU rate. And for fault-tolerant batch workloads, use spot instances for the workers, but keep the driver and any SLA-critical work on on-demand nodes.

This table maps each cost lever to what it saves and when it applies. Autoscaling saves idle capacity, job clusters save on the DBU rate, auto-termination saves idle wall-clock, spot instances cut the VM price, and instance pools cut start-up time. Notice that every lever has a condition — none of them is a blanket win.

Keep the cost formula firmly in mind: total cost equals the DBU rate times DBU-hours, plus the cloud VM price times VM-hours. Every optimization you make moves one of those two terms — if it doesn't, it isn't really saving money.

Here's a worked example. A job cluster running four hours at R DBU per hour gives us four R DBU. Compare that against an all-purpose cluster at a higher rate and you can see immediately why job clusters are the default for scheduled work. And remember to attribute spend with cluster tags, budget alerts, and cost or system tables, so that optimization is measured — not assumed.

Finally, watch out for the classic exam trap: 'autoscaling reduces cost' is only conditionally true. Autoscaling only helps when the cluster would otherwise sit idle. For a steadily saturated cluster, adding and removing workers does nothing for the bill — it's already running flat out. So before you choose a lever, ask which side of the cost formula it actually moves.

scenes.title: Checkpoint: Cost Optimization in Practice

questions.question: A nightly ETL job runs on a job cluster with 10 workers. Each worker consumes 0.5 DBU per hour, and the job has an average runtime of 2.5 hours. The DBU rate is $0.30 per DBU, and each worker's cloud VM costs $0.40 per hour. Using the cost model total cost = (DBU rate x DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price x runtime x worker count), what is the total cost for one run of this job?
questions.analysis: Step 1 — compute DBU-hours: 10 workers x 0.5 DBU/h x 2.5 h = 12.5 DBU-hours. Step 2 — DBU cost: 12.5 x $0.30 = $3.75. Step 3 — cloud VM cost: 10 workers x $0.40/h x 2.5 h = $10.00. Step 4 — total: $3.75 + $10.00 = $13.75. Option A ($3.75) is the classic distractor that counts only the DBU term and ignores cloud VM cost entirely. Option C ($10.00) is the opposite error: VM cost only, no DBUs. Option D ($20.75) incorrectly doubles the VM term or conflates the two rates. This two-term model matters because the cloud model rewards ephemerality: it is cheaper to rent servers for short, periodic batch jobs than to own them for 24/7 use. [source p.246]

questions.question: A pipeline currently runs on a fixed all-purpose cluster with 8 workers for 40 minutes per batch. The Spark UI shows only 5 concurrent tasks per stage. A proposed set of changes is listed below. Which changes would most directly reduce total cost, and which are distractors that confuse runtime with cost or ignore the cloud VM term? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Move to a job cluster sized to 6 workers so concurrency matches actual parallelism, eliminating idle workers that still incur DBU and VM charges
Enable autoscaling with a minimum of 4 and a maximum of 6 workers so the cluster shrinks when stages are light
Enable Photon because it makes each individual query faster, so DBU-hours must fall regardless of the DBU rate increase
Switch to spot instances for the worker VMs to cut the cloud VM portion of the bill without changing DBU-hours

questions.analysis: Right-sizing to 6 workers is the largest and most direct win: the UI shows only 5 concurrent tasks, meaning 3 of the 8 workers are idle but still billed, and the cost model has two terms, so idle workers cost on both the DBU side and the VM side. Autoscaling (B) and spot instances (D) directly reduce the two terms. Photon (C) is the instructive distractor: Photon speeds up CPU-bound work, but because its DBU rate is higher (1.5x in the worked example from this unit), it can increase DBU-hours if the runtime reduction does not offset the rate increase. The correct test is always total cost = (DBU rate x DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price x runtime), not runtime alone. This mirrors the checkpoint 2 pattern of recognizing distractors that conflate runtime reduction with cost reduction. [source p.346]

questions.question: A team's nightly Spark job reads a 2 TB Delta table, joins it to a 50 MB dimension table, aggregates, and writes results back to S3. They propose three changes: (1) increase workers from 8 to 24, (2) enable Photon, (3) switch to spot instances. For each change, state whether it is likely to reduce total cost and justify using the formula total cost = (DBU rate x DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price x runtime). Then write a recommended configuration and explain how you would monitor it.
questions.commentPrompt: A complete answer must cover all three changes with quantitative or semi-quantitative reasoning and a recommended configuration with monitoring plan. Rubric: (1) Correctly identifies that increasing workers from 8 to 24 raises DBU-hours and VM cost proportionally unless runtime drops by more than 3x — 30%. (2) Correctly reasons about Photon: faster runtime may reduce DBU-hours but the higher DBU rate must be factored in; earns points for showing the subtraction/inspection logic rather than asserting faster = cheaper — 25%. (3) Correctly states spot instances reduce the cloud VM term but do not change DBU-hours; notes interruption risk — 20%. (4) Gives a concrete recommended configuration (e.g., right-size to 10 workers, enable autoscaling, use job cluster, enable Photon) — 15%. (5) Describes monitoring via Spark UI (task concurrency, shuffle read/write, skew) and DBU consumption metrics — 10%.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: Increasing workers raises both DBU-hours and VM cost unless runtime falls by more than the worker-count multiple. Enabling Photon reduces runtime, but the DBU rate rises (e.g., 1.5x in the worked example), so compare DBU-hours before and after: baseline 8 workers x 1.5 h = 12 DBU-h vs. Photon 8 x 0.67 h x 1.5 = 8 DBU-h; 33% fewer DBU-hours means Photon is cheaper. Spot instances reduce the cloud VM term only; DBU-hours are unaffected. Recommended configuration: right-size to actual parallelism, use a job cluster with autoscaling, enable Photon if the runtime reduction exceeds the rate increase, and use spot with a non-spot fallback for SLA-critical stages. Monitor via Spark UI (concurrent tasks, shuffle read/write, skew) and track DBU consumption. The diagnostic logic follows this unit's worked problem and the checkpoint 2 heuristics. [source p.236]

actions.text: Time to put that cost intuition to work. This checkpoint covers DBU-hours, total cost calculations, and picking the change that actually moves the bill — so read each question carefully and work through it on your own.

Take your time with the calculation and the written justification — show your reasoning the way you'd want to on the exam. Submit when you're done, and I'll walk through anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Trade-off Decision: Cutting 30% Off a Nightly Pipeline

elements.content: Decision — A data platform team runs a nightly batch pipeline that must complete within a 4-hour window and deliver fresh results by a 6:00 AM SLA, but the organization has mandated a 30% reduction in the compute budget for this pipeline; the team must also keep the pipeline tolerant of node preemption and plan for an expected 3x data growth next quarter, so any cost saving that simply trades away future headroom or availability is not truly acceptable. The decision is hard because cost, runtime, and reliability pull in different directions: the cheapest configuration may reclaim workers or lengthen start-up in ways that threaten the 6:00 AM deadline, while the fastest may exceed the new budget. As covered earlier in this unit, total cost is not one number but two — total cost = (DBU rate x DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price x runtime) — so every candidate must be judged against both terms rather than against raw speed alone, and the exam-oriented rule is that the best answer satisfies every stated constraint rather than showing the biggest theoretical speedup. Orchestration context matters here: an orchestration system stays online with high availability and monitors jobs, setting error conditions and sending alerts when expected completion times are exceeded, so a missed 6:00 AM SLA is a monitored, alertable failure rather than a silent one [source p.91]. The pipeline itself is a Spark job whose ingestion happens in cluster memory while the largest source is big enough that it must spill to disk, which means I/O behavior and shuffle behavior — not just CPU — determine where the time actually goes [source p.346]. Because the data is spread across nodes in data blocks and the final aggregation requires redistributing results by key so each key lands on exactly one node, the shuffle step is often executed with a hashing algorithm on keys and can dominate runtime [source p.348]; this is exactly why an option that adds shuffle traffic or increases driver pressure must be evaluated skeptically even if it looks more parallel on paper. A worked example makes the trade-off concrete. Suppose the baseline nightly run uses 12 workers, takes 3.2 hours, the DBU rate is R DBU/h, and the job is roughly 60% CPU-bound and 40% I/O-bound as read from the Spark UI. Baseline DBU-hours = 12 x 3.2 = 38.4 DBU-h. Now enable Photon: the CPU-bound 60% of the job speeds up by a factor of 1.6 while the I/O-bound 40% is unchanged, so new runtime = 3.2 x (0.6/1.6 + 0.4) = 3.2 x (0.375 + 0.4) = 3.2 x 0.775 = 2.48 hours. If Photon raises the DBU rate to 1.5R, Photon DBU-hours = 12 x 2.48 x 1.5 = 44.6 DBU-h, which is 16% MORE DBU-hours than baseline — so Photon alone does NOT hit the 30% cut on this profile. If instead we move to a job cluster with spot workers and autoscaling 4-16 at roughly 0.6x the effective rate, and the job completes in 3.0 hours at an average of 8 workers, cost = 8 x 3.0 x 0.6R = 14.4R versus baseline 38.4R, a 62% reduction that clears the 30% target with room for 3x growth. The lesson is that Photon pays only where the Spark UI shows CPU-bound stages; applying it blindly across an I/O-bound pipeline raises the DBU rate without buying proportional runtime reduction.

Constraints — Nightly pipeline must finish inside a 4-hour window and meet the 6:00 AM SLA  •  Compute budget must be reduced by 30% for this pipeline  •  The configuration must tolerate node preemption (spot reclamation) without failing the SLA  •  Must leave headroom for an expected 3x data growth next quarter  •  Any code change must be deliverable within the current sprint

Keep the current cluster and enable Photon
+ Rollout is a runtime switch with no code change, so it deploys in hours rather than weeks; + Photon's vectorized, columnar execution cuts per-row interpretation overhead and shortens CPU-bound stages such as large scans, wide aggregations, string-heavy transforms, and Delta MERGE/DELETE/UPDATE; + Shorter runtime also reduces the cloud VM term of the cost model when the job really is CPU-bound
− The DBU rate rises, so on an I/O-bound job the DBU-hours can go UP even though wall-clock time falls (see the worked example: 38.4 -> 44.6 DBU-h); − Gives little or no benefit on stages the Spark UI marks as shuffle- or I/O-bound, and the extra DBU rate is then pure loss; − By itself it does not address idle capacity or the 4->16 worker elasticity needed for 3x growth
Best for: Pipelines the Spark UI shows as predominantly CPU-bound, where a 1.5x-1.6x DBU rate is comfortably repaid by a larger runtime reduction

Move to a job cluster with autoscaling 4-16 workers and spot workers (on-demand driver)
+ Largest cost reduction of the three and it requires no code change, satisfying the sprint constraint; + Job clusters are created per run and cost less per DBU than all-purpose compute, which is why they are the default for scheduled production pipelines; + Autoscaling 4-16 plus spot workers directly addresses the elasticity and preemption-tolerance constraints, and bounding range to 16 leaves room for 3x growth; + An on-demand driver protects the orchestration-critical process from spot reclamation
− Spot reclamation can kill executors mid-stage, so affected partitions must be recomputed, occasionally lengthening the run; − Cluster start-up is longer than reusing a warm all-purpose cluster, eating into the 4-hour window; − Autoscaling adds workers only after it observes a backlog, so the tail of the job may not scale as aggressively as a fixed oversized cluster
Best for: Scheduled production pipelines with a hard budget cut that tolerate occasional preemption and can absorb a longer cold start

Use more, smaller workers on the existing cluster
+ More worker slots raise task parallelism, so stages with low per-stage concurrency (the classic '16 workers but only 6 concurrent tasks' symptom) can use the cluster better; + Smaller workers give finer autoscaling granularity, so scale-down is less wasteful
− More workers means more shuffle partitions and more shuffle traffic, and the shuffle step here is already a hashing-based redistribution that must place each key on exactly one node [source p.348]; − Smaller workers raise driver pressure and per-executor overhead, which can lengthen the very jobs we are trying to shorten; − It does not by itself deliver a large enough cost cut to clear the 30% target, so it would have to be combined with a cluster-lifecycle change anyway
Best for: Shuffle-light, embarrassingly parallel stages where the bottleneck is genuinely task concurrency rather than data movement [source p.348]

Recommendation: Move to a job cluster with autoscaling 4-16 workers and spot workers (on-demand driver) — The binding constraints are the 30% budget cut, the 4-hour window with a 6:00 AM SLA, preemption tolerance, and 3x growth headroom, and only the job-cluster-with-spot option satisfies all four at once. Job clusters cost less per DBU than all-purpose compute and are the default for scheduled production pipelines, which is exactly what this nightly run is. Autoscaling 4-16 with spot executors and an on-demand driver directly implements preemption tolerance while bounding cost, and the worked example shows it lands near 14.4R versus a 38.4R baseline — a 62% cut that clears the 30% target and leaves headroom for 3x growth. Photon alone fails the arithmetic: on a 60/40 CPU/I-O split with a 1.5x DBU rate it RAISES DBU-hours to about 44.6R, because I/O-bound work is untouched [source p.346]. The rational policy is therefore a two-phase one: adopt the job cluster as the baseline, then read the Spark UI and enable Photon ONLY for the stages it shows as CPU-bound, where the DBU-rate increase is repaid by a real runtime reduction. This keeps the 6:00 AM SLA monitored and alertable through the orchestration layer, which stays online with high availability and raises error conditions when expected completion times are exceeded [source p.91], and it respects the DAG of ingest-join-write steps Spark actually executes rather than optimizing a stage that was never the bottleneck [source p.346]. Consistently with the exam takeaway, the winner is the answer that satisfies every stated constraint, not the one with the largest theoretical speedup.

actions.text: Building on the right-sizing exercise we just worked through, let's apply that same cost reasoning to a full trade-off decision. Here's the scenario: a data platform team runs a nightly batch pipeline, and leadership wants the budget cut by thirty percent.

Before we evaluate any option, we lock down the constraints — this is exactly how you should read an exam question. The nightly pipeline must finish inside its four-hour window, it has a six AM SLA, the data volume is expected to triple next quarter, the workload must tolerate node preemption, and the budget has to drop by thirty percent. Five constraints, and every single one is non-negotiable.

Option A is the tempting one: keep the current cluster and just enable Photon. The upside is a very easy rollout — no infrastructure change at all — and Photon's vectorized engine will genuinely speed up your CPU-bound stages. But notice the trap: Photon has a higher DBU rate, so if your job is I/O-bound, you pay more per hour for almost no gain. It also does nothing to address the three-x growth.

Option B moves the workload to a job cluster with autoscaling between four and sixteen workers, plus spot instances. This is where the big cost reduction lives — spot pricing and scale-down during idle periods — and it requires no code change. The trade-off is occasional spot reclamation, which is why the constraint said the job must tolerate preemption, and a slightly longer start-up time.

Option C swaps in more, smaller workers. That gives you finer autoscaling granularity and better task parallelism, which sounds great — but each worker now handles less data, so shuffle traffic goes up and the driver takes on more pressure. More instances also means more overhead per node, which eats into your savings.

So what's the recommendation? Adopt B as your baseline — a job cluster with autoscaling and spot workers, and an on-demand driver so reclamation never takes down the driver. Then layer Photon on top, but only for the stages the Spark UI flags as CPU-bound. That hits the thirty percent target while leaving headroom for three-x growth. And here's the exam takeaway you should carry out of this page: the best answer is the one that satisfies every stated constraint, not the one with the biggest theoretical speedup. If an option is faster but breaks the SLA or ignores preemption, it's wrong.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Costing a Pipeline Before and After Right-Sizing

elements.content: Problem 1

A production job runs once per day for 2.0 hours on a fixed-size Databricks job cluster with 8 workers. The cluster's combined consumption is rated at 12 DBU/h for the whole cluster. The DBU price is \$0.15 per DBU. For a 30-day month, compute (a) the daily DBU-hours, (b) the monthly DBU-hours, and (c) the monthly DBU cost. Do not include cloud VM cost yet.
Hint: Use DBU-hours = (combined DBU rate) × (runtime), then multiply by the DBU price.

Worked solution
Step 1: Daily DBU-hours. The combined rate is 12 DBU/h; runtime is 2.0 h/day. $$12 \text{ DBU/h} \times 2.0 \text{ h/day} = 24 \text{ DBU-h/day}.$$ Step 2: Monthly DBU-hours. Over 30 days: $$24 \text{ DBU-h/day} \times 30 \text{ days} = 720 \text{ DBU-h}.$$ Step 3: Monthly DBU cost. At \$0.15 per DBU: $$720 \text{ DBU-h} \times \$0.15/\text{DBU} = \$108.00.$$ The daily DBU cost is \$3.60/day. Final: baseline = 720 DBU-h and \$108.00 per month in DBUs.

Analysis — This problem isolates the first term of the Databricks cost model: total cost = (DBU rate × DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price × runtime). The DBU (Databricks Unit) is the normalized unit of compute consumption; you must multiply the combined DBU rate, not the worker count, by runtime. A common mistake is to multiply the 8 workers again after being given a combined 12 DBU/h, which double-counts. Cloud pay-as-you-go pricing is often expressed as a cost-per-query or cost-per-processing-capacity model [source p.112], so unit economics must be computed explicitly. In an exam, check whether the DBU rate is per worker or for the whole cluster; here it is for the whole cluster.
Problem 2

The same daily job from p1 is migrated to a right-sized autoscaling job cluster with minimum 2 workers and maximum 8 workers. Over a 30-day month, the job averages 5 workers while running. At that average size, the effective combined consumption is 7.5 DBU/h, and the runtime drops to 1.4 h per day because the job no longer waits on an over-provisioned, inefficiently utilized fixed cluster. The DBU price remains \$0.15 per DBU. Compute the new monthly DBU-hours and monthly DBU cost, and compare with the p1 baseline.
Hint: Use the average worker count implied by the combined DBU rate, not the maximum of 8.

Worked solution
Step 1: Daily DBU-hours under autoscaling. $$7.5 \text{ DBU/h} \times 1.4 \text{ h/day} = 10.5 \text{ DBU-h/day}.$$ Step 2: Monthly DBU-hours. $$10.5 \text{ DBU-h/day} \times 30 \text{ days} = 315 \text{ DBU-h}.$$ Step 3: Monthly DBU cost. $$315 \text{ DBU-h} \times \$0.15/\text{DBU} = \$47.25.$$ Step 4: Compare with the baseline. DBU-hours fall from 720 to 315, a reduction of $720 - 315 = 405$ DBU-h. DBU cost falls from \$108.00 to \$47.25, a saving of \$60.75. As a percentage: $(720 - 315)/720 = 405/720 = 0.5625 = 56.25\%$ fewer DBU-hours and the same percentage fewer DBU dollars (since the DBU price is constant). Final: 315 DBU-h and \$47.25 per month.

Analysis — Autoscaling does not reduce cost by itself; it reduces cost only when the average utilization is below the fixed provision. Here the fixed cluster always ran 8 workers (or at least paid for 8), while the autoscaling cluster averaged 5 workers. The correct input is the average worker count over the run, not the peak of 8; using the peak would estimate $8/5 = 1.6$ times too much DBU consumption. The shorter 1.4 h runtime helps twice: it lowers DBU-hours and it lowers the cloud VM term. A subtle edge case is that autoscaling can only scale between min and max, so a job that never exceeds 2 workers still pays for at least 2. Also, the DBU rate can change as workers join or leave; the workload's effective rate is an average. This is the same unit-economics discipline that cloud-era systems require when they use pay-as-you-go cost-per-processing-capacity models [source p.112].
Problem 3

Using the baseline from p1 and the right-sized autoscaling configuration from p2, add the cloud VM term. The cloud VM cost is \$0.10 per DBU-hour equivalent, meaning VM cost = \$0.10 × DBU-hours for each configuration. Compute (a) the baseline VM cost, (b) the right-sized VM cost, (c) the total monthly spend for each, and (d) the percentage reduction in total monthly spend from baseline to right-sized.
Hint: Add the VM term after computing DBU-hours; the VM term is separate from the DBU price.

Worked solution
Step 1: Baseline VM cost. $$720 \text{ DBU-h} \times \$0.10/\text{DBU-h} = \$72.00.$$ Baseline total = DBU cost + VM cost = \$108.00 + \$72.00 = \$180.00. Step 2: Right-sized VM cost. $$315 \text{ DBU-h} \times \$0.10/\text{DBU-h} = \$31.50.$$ Right-sized total = \$47.25 + \$31.50 = \$78.75. Step 3: Reduction. Total spend falls by \$180.00 - \$78.75 = \$101.25. Percentage reduction = $101.25 / 180.00 = 0.5625 = 56.25\%$, which is approximately 56\%. Final: baseline total = \$180.00/month; right-sized total = \$78.75/month; reduction = 56.25\%.

Analysis — The Databricks cost model has two terms: DBU cost and cloud VM cost. If you count only DBUs, the baseline appears to cost \$108 and the right-sized \$47.25, a 56.25\% reduction; adding VM cost preserves the percentage reduction here because VM cost is proportional to DBU-hours, but the absolute dollars are larger and the total is what the business pays. In general the two terms are not perfectly proportional: cloud VM price depends on instance type, spot versus on-demand, and the runtime of each node, while DBU rate depends on the Databricks SKU and the engine (for example, Photon can change the DBU rate). The pitfall is ignoring the VM charge, which understates spend and can reverse a decision when comparing instance families. Archival storage economics offer a parallel warning: a low headline storage price can hide high access or retrieval costs, so you must model the full access pattern [source p.236]. For a complete decision, also consider total opportunity cost of ownership (TOCO), including team training and maintenance that are not in the monthly bill [source p.145].
Problem 4

The right-sized job from p2 has a billed runtime of 1.4 h per day, but 0.3 h of that is fixed start-up and initialization overhead that does not shrink with worker count. The productive runtime is therefore 1.1 h. The team enables a warm instance pool, cutting start-up overhead to 0.1 h on the same autoscaling configuration (average 5 workers, 7.5 DBU/h). (a) What percentage of the original 1.4 h billed runtime was overhead? (b) Compute the new daily and monthly DBU-hours and DBU cost. (c) If the cloud VM term is still \$0.10 per DBU-hour equivalent, compute the new total monthly spend and compare it with the original right-sized total from p3.
Hint: Overhead is added to the runtime; it is paid at the full combined DBU rate even though it produces no useful computation.

Worked solution
Step 1: Original overhead share. $$0.3 \text{ h} / 1.4 \text{ h} = 0.214285... = 21.43\%.$$ So more than one-fifth of the billed runtime was start-up overhead. Step 2: New billed runtime. Productive time 1.1 h + new overhead 0.1 h = 1.2 h/day. Step 3: New daily DBU-hours. $$7.5 \text{ DBU/h} \times 1.2 \text{ h/day} = 9.0 \text{ DBU-h/day}.$$ Step 4: New monthly DBU-hours. $$9.0 \text{ DBU-h/day} \times 30 \text{ days} = 270 \text{ DBU-h}.$$ Step 5: New monthly DBU cost. $$270 \text{ DBU-h} \times \$0.15/\text{DBU} = \$40.50.$$ Step 6: New VM cost. $$270 \text{ DBU-h} \times \$0.10/\text{DBU-h} = \$27.00.$$ New total monthly spend = \$40.50 + \$27.00 = \$67.50. Compared with \$78.75 from p3, this is a saving of \$11.25, or $11.25 / 78.75 = 0.142857... = 14.29\%$ of the original right-sized total. Final: overhead share 21.43\%; new DBU cost \$40.50/month; new total \$67.50/month; saving \$11.25/month versus p3.

Analysis — Start-up overhead is a fixed per-run cost: it does not scale down when the cluster is smaller, so it is proportionally more expensive for short jobs. The right-sizing benefit from p2 came from both fewer DBU-hours and shorter runtime; if the job were only 0.2 h of productive work with 0.3 h of start-up, autoscaling would still pay for the overhead and the savings would shrink or disappear. The exam pitfall is to assume that halving the worker count halves the cost of a very short run; in reality the minimum workers and the start-up time dominate. Warm pools, job clusters with pre-initialized instances, and Photon (which reduces productive runtime without changing the start-up overhead) each affect different terms. For example, if Photon cuts productive runtime from 1.1 h to 0.7 h but raises the DBU rate by 1.5×, you must redo the arithmetic rather than assume a win. Finally, decisions about warm pools should be evaluated against total opportunity cost of ownership, including the engineering time to maintain them [source p.145], and against the full access pattern for any cached or archival data, since low headline storage cost can hide high access cost [source p.236].

actions.text: Let's put all of that cost reasoning into practice with a complete worked problem. We'll cost the same pipeline twice — first as an over-provisioned fixed cluster, then after right-sizing it — and add the cloud VM term that people so often forget.

Problem 1 sets the baseline. A production job runs once per day for two hours on a fixed eight-worker configuration rated at a combined twelve DBU per hour, with a DBU price of fifteen cents. The question is simply: what is the monthly DBU cost?

Read the numbers carefully — twelve DBU per hour, two hours, thirty days, and a rate of zero point one five dollars per DBU. Before you calculate, write down the units so you don't lose track of what you're multiplying.

The hint gives you the formula: DBU-hours equals the combined DBU rate times runtime times the number of runs. For the baseline that's twelve times two times thirty — seven hundred and twenty DBU-hours — which at fifteen cents comes to one hundred and eight dollars per month.

Here's the worked solution laid out step by step. Notice how the first term of the Databricks cost model — pure DBU consumption — is isolated. That's deliberate: this problem is designed to make sure you can compute that term cleanly before anything else is layered on.

Now Problem 2 migrates that same daily job to a right-sized autoscaling cluster — two to eight workers, averaging five, rated at seven point five DBU per hour — and because it's smaller, the runtime actually falls to one point four hours. Compute the new monthly cost.

The hint is the key insight here: use the average worker count implied by the autoscaling range, not the maximum. Seven point five DBU per hour times one point four hours times thirty days gives three hundred and fifteen DBU-hours — forty-seven dollars and twenty-five cents.

And here's the analysis, which is the part exam questions love to probe: autoscaling does not reduce cost by itself. What saves you money is the lower average worker count and the shorter billed runtime — the scaling mechanism is just the means to get there. You need to know that distinction cold.

Problem 3 adds the cloud VM term. Using the baseline and the right-sized numbers you already have, model the VM portion at ten cents per DBU-hour equivalent and compute the total monthly spend for each configuration.

The hint says it plainly: add the VM term after computing DBU-hours. The baseline VM cost is seven hundred and twenty DBU-hours times ten cents — seventy-two dollars — bringing the baseline total to one hundred and eighty dollars. The right-sized configuration adds thirty-one fifty, for a total of seventy-eight seventy-five.

That's a fifty-six percent reduction in monthly spend, from one hundred and eighty dollars down to seventy-eight seventy-five. The takeaway is that the Databricks cost model has two terms — DBU charges and cloud VM charges — and ignoring either one gives you a wrong answer.

Finally, Problem 4 stresses the runtime side. The right-sized job now has a longer billed runtime with a startup overhead component. The question is what share of the run is overhead, and how shortening the run changes that proportion.

The hint is the exam trap here: overhead is added to the runtime, and it is paid for on every run. Two hours of startup on a ten-hour job is a rounding error; two hours on a one point four-hour job is enormous.

The analysis ties it together: start-up overhead is a fixed per-run cost, so as you shrink runtime, overhead grows as a proportion of the total. That's why very short jobs on fresh clusters can be surprisingly expensive, and why the right answer to a cost question is rarely 'just make it smaller and faster.'

Before we move to the final checkpoint, I want you to think about the trade-offs we just walked through. Which of these decisions would you change if the job had to finish within a two-hour SLA? Take a moment to reason it through. I'll turn this over to one of you to kick off the discussion.

actions.topic: Balancing right-sizing, runtime, and start-up overhead under an SLA constraint
actions.prompt: Given what we calculated — the baseline at $180 per month and the right-sized job at $78.75 — what would you change if management imposed a strict two-hour completion SLA? Would you add workers, accept some overhead, or restructure the job? Reason from the DBU-hours and VM-cost model we just used.

scenes.title: Final Checkpoint: Photon, Cluster Sizing, and Cost (Exam Review)

questions.question: A production team must run a nightly Lakeflow pipeline that performs a large Delta MERGE into a 40 TB Silver table, followed by wide aggregations that build Gold aggregates. The SLA requires completion within 50 minutes, and the budget owner has fixed a hard ceiling of 60 DBU-hours per run. The team is choosing between: (A) an all-purpose cluster with Photon enabled and auto-termination at 60 minutes; (B) a job cluster with Photon enabled, 12 workers, auto-termination at 30 minutes; (C) a SQL warehouse sized Medium with Photon enabled; and (D) an all-purpose cluster with Photon disabled and 24 workers. Based on the three levers (engine, cluster shape, lifecycle) and the cost model total cost = (DBU rate x DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price x runtime), which configuration best satisfies BOTH the SLA and the DBU-hour budget?

options.label: Option A: all-purpose compute with Photon enabled and auto-termination at 60 minutes, because all-purpose clusters give the lowest DBU rate for production jobs.
Option B: a per-job job cluster with Photon enabled, 12 workers, and auto-termination at 30 minutes, because job compute carries a lower DBU rate and Photon cuts CPU-bound MERGE and aggregation time.
Option C: a SQL warehouse sized Medium with Photon enabled, because SQL warehouses are the only compute that can execute Delta MERGE on a schedule.
Option D: an all-purpose cluster with Photon disabled and 24 workers, because doubling workers always halves runtime and Photon is only needed for interactive queries.

questions.correctAnswer: Option B
questions.analysis: Job clusters are created per job run and cost less per DBU, and they are the default choice for scheduled production pipelines [source p.168][source p.246]. Photon is a native C++ vectorized engine that replaces parts of the Spark execution engine without changing APIs, SQL, or DataFrame code; it delivers its largest wins on CPU-bound work such as Delta MERGE/DELETE/UPDATE and wide aggregations, which is exactly this workload [source p.246][source p.248]. Option A is wrong because all-purpose compute carries a higher DBU rate and is intended for interactive development, not production schedules. Option C is wrong because SQL warehouses serve BI/SQL workloads and are not the required compute for scheduled Lakeflow pipelines performing Delta MERGE. Option D is wrong because more workers do not always mean faster: once the stage's task count is fully covered, extra workers only add idle DBU-hours, and Photon-disabled runs will exceed the SLA on this CPU-bound MERGE.

questions.question: A cost regression has been reported for a nightly ETL job. The facts are: last month the job ran on 8 workers for 90 minutes at DBU rate R per hour. This month the job runs on 24 workers for 20 minutes at the same DBU rate R per hour, with Photon disabled both months. The Spark UI shows only 6 concurrent tasks per stage in both runs, no spill, and low executor utilization. Which statements correctly diagnose or resolve this regression? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The 24-worker cluster is oversized: with only 6 concurrent tasks per stage, at least 18 workers are idle, so DBU-hours are consumed without reducing runtime.
Total DBU-hours went from 12 DBU-h (8 workers x 1.5 h) to 8 DBU-h (24 workers x 0.33 h), so the DBU-hour total actually fell and the regression must be solely in the cloud VM price term.
Photon should be enabled first, because Photon is a vectorized engine that accelerates CPU-bound scans, joins, and aggregations, and this is the highest-leverage single change before adding workers.
Autoscaling alone will fix the regression by guaranteeing the cluster scales down to the true concurrency, so no manual right-sizing is required.

questions.correctAnswer: Option A and Option C
questions.analysis: Option A is correct: cost is driven by the effective average worker count, not the maximum, so a 24-worker cluster running a 6-task stage leaves roughly 18 workers idle per stage and burns DBU-hours for no runtime benefit. Option C is correct: Photon is a runtime switch that vectorizes columnar, compiled execution in batches, cutting per-row interpretation overhead on exactly the CPU-bound scans, joins, and aggregations an ETL job performs, making it the highest-leverage single change before adding workers [source p.246]. Option B is mathematically correct that DBU-hours fell (12 to 8 DBU-h), BUT the question asks which statements correctly diagnose or resolve the regression, and the honest diagnosis is that the cost driver is the 24-worker idle capacity plus the cloud VM price for 24 nodes, so B's claim that the regression is 'solely in the cloud VM price term' overstates a partial truth and is a classic exam distractor that ignores the DBU-rate x DBU-hour interaction. Option D is wrong because autoscaling reacts to backlog and does not automatically guarantee scale-down to true concurrency; it does not reduce cost by itself [source p.168][source p.248]. The exam trap here is 'more workers always means faster' and 'autoscaling always lowers cost'; both are false.

questions.question: You are choosing between two competing optimizations for a nightly pipeline, and only ONE can be applied first this sprint. Optimization X is enabling Photon on a job cluster whose Spark UI shows CPU-bound wide aggregations, string-heavy transformations, and a large Delta MERGE, with runtime dominated by CPU rather than I/O. Optimization Y is doubling the worker count from 8 to 16 on the same job, whose Spark UI shows only 6 concurrent tasks per stage and negligible spill. Which optimization should be applied FIRST, and why?

options.label: Optimization X first, because Photon is a native C++ vectorized engine that accelerates CPU-bound work in this workload, whereas adding workers cannot help a stage that only exposes 6 concurrent tasks.
Optimization Y first, because doubling workers always halves runtime, and Photon only helps interactive queries.
Optimization Y first, because job clusters cannot run scheduled pipelines, so the cluster must be resized before Photon can be considered.
Neither: Photon speeds up everything uniformly, so both optimizations are equivalent and the order does not matter.

questions.correctAnswer: Option A
questions.analysis: Photon is a native C++ vectorized, columnar, compiled engine that replaces parts of the Spark execution engine while leaving Spark APIs, SQL, and DataFrame code unchanged; it delivers its largest gains on CPU-bound work such as large table scans, wide aggregations, joins, string-heavy transformations, and Delta MERGE/DELETE/UPDATE. The workload profile here (CPU-bound wide aggregations, string transformations, large Delta MERGE) is precisely Photon's sweet spot, making X the highest-leverage first change. Option B repeats the exam trap 'more workers always means faster' and the trap 'Photon speeds up everything'; Photon only helps CPU-bound work, and more workers cannot help a stage that only exposes 6 concurrent tasks. Option C states the false exam trap that job clusters cannot run scheduled pipelines — the opposite is true: job clusters are created per job run and are the default choice for scheduled production pipelines [source p.168]. Option D is wrong because Photon does NOT speed up everything; it helps CPU-bound work and can even add cost on I/O-bound jobs where the DBU rate premium is not offset by reduced runtime [source p.246][source p.248].

questions.question: A team must justify to a cost-governance board a recommended configuration for a nightly Golden aggregation pipeline. The pipeline reads a 30 TB Silver Delta table, performs a large MERGE into Gold, then builds wide aggregates consumed by BI at 07:00 local time. The SLA is completion by 06:30. The current setup is an all-purpose cluster with Photon disabled, 24 workers, no autoscaling, no auto-termination, and DBU rate R per hour, running 2 hours per night. The Spark UI shows only 6 concurrent tasks per stage, modest spill, and high CPU time in the MERGE step. Write a recommendation that justifies your configuration in terms of (a) DBU-hours, (b) SLA, and (c) fault tolerance.
