Include the cost formula total cost = (DBU rate x DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price x runtime), a concrete numeric DBU-hour comparison between the current and the recommended setup, and explicitly identify at least one exam trap you are avoiding. Use Databricks terminology precisely (job cluster, Photon, autoscaling, auto-termination, delta MERGE).
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric (100 points total): (1) Correct identification of job compute as the recommended lifecycle for a scheduled production pipeline, with a lower DBU rate than all-purpose, AND auto-termination set — 20 points. (2) Enabling Photon with justification tied to the CPU-bound Delta MERGE and wide aggregations, citing that Photon is a runtime switch with largest wins on CPU-bound work — 20 points. (3) Right-sizing from Spark UI evidence: the 6 concurrent tasks per stage prove the 24-worker cluster is oversized, so recommend roughly 6-8 workers and state WHY cost is driven by the effective average worker count, not the maximum — 20 points. (4) Concrete numeric DBU-hour comparison: current = 24 workers x 2 h = 48 DBU-h; recommended = 8 workers x ~1 h = 8 DBU-h, a ~83% reduction, and statement that total cost = (DBU rate x DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price x runtime) — 20 points. (5) Fault tolerance discussion: driver on on-demand while workers may use spot instances, auto-termination prevents idle spend, and the SLA buffer to 06:30 accounts for occasional spot reclamation — 10 points. (6) Explicitly names at least one exam trap being avoided ('Photon speeds up everything', 'autoscaling always lowers cost', 'more workers always means faster', or 'job clusters cannot run scheduled pipelines') — 10 points. Deduct up to 10 points for vague phrasing, failure to cite the cost formula, or missing numbers.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: recommend a per-job job cluster with Photon enabled, autoscaling min=4/max=8, auto-termination at 15 minutes, driver on on-demand and workers allowed on spot. Rationale: (a) DBU-hours — current is 24 workers x 2 h = 48 DBU-h; recommended is 8 workers x ~1 h = 8 DBU-h (Photon cuts CPU-bound MERGE time and halves the wall clock, and right-sizing per Spark UI cuts idle workers), roughly an 83% reduction. Because total cost = (DBU rate x DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price x runtime), both terms shrink: fewer DBU-hours and fewer VM-seconds. (b) SLA — Photon's vectorized, columnar, compiled execution targets exactly the CPU-bound MERGE and wide aggregations here, and right-sizing matches workers to the 6 concurrent tasks; together these comfortably meet the 06:30 deadline with buffer. (c) Fault tolerance — driver stays on on-demand so a spot reclamation cannot kill the run; auto-termination prevents idle spend; the modest spill noted in Spark UI should be re-checked after right-sizing and Photon, and if spill persists, shift to a memory-optimized node family. Exam traps avoided: 'more workers always means faster' (false — 6 concurrent tasks), 'Photon speeds up everything' (false — Photon helps CPU-bound work, not all workloads), 'autoscaling always lowers cost' (false — it reacts to backlog and does not reduce cost by itself) [source p.168][source p.246][source p.248].

actions.text: Now it's time for the final checkpoint on Photon, cluster sizing, and cost. This set is deliberately harder and mirrors the certification's format and distractor patterns, so read each scenario carefully and work through it on your own.
Give every question a genuine attempt — including the written recommendation at the end — and I'll join you right after you submit to walk through the reasoning and any traps you hit.

scenes.title: Why CI/CD for Databricks Pipelines

elements.content: Why CI/CD for Databricks Pipelines
From manual clicking to code: reduce drift and enable automated promotion

• Manual clicking creates drift: dev and prod jobs silently diverge, no diff or review possible.

• CI validates and tests every commit; CD promotes the same tested artifact through environments.

• Databricks Asset Bundles (DAB) describe jobs, pipelines, and permissions as YAML in Git.

• Exam objective: package jobs/pipelines as bundles; deploy across dev, staging, and production [source 1].
Data environment: a set of applications and physical infrastructure that enable storage, transfer, processing, and transformation, isolated for testing before production [source 6].

Continuous Integration (CI): validate and test every commit.

Continuous Delivery (CD): promote the same tested artifact through environments [source 5].

Worked example: A job configured manually in dev (3 tasks) is copied by hand to prod (2 tasks). Drift rate = 1/3 ≈ 33% divergence. With bundle promotion, the same artifact is deployed to both targets, drift = 0.
Exam objective: package jobs and pipelines as Databricks Asset Bundles; deploy bundles across development, staging, and production targets [source 1].

actions.text: Great work on that cost exercise. We're now entering a new lesson, and this one ties together everything you've built so far: why we do CI/CD for Databricks pipelines. Up to this point you've been creating jobs, notebooks, and pipelines by hand — now we shift to treating all of that as code.

Start with the problem. Manually clicking a job together produces drift: the dev job and the prod job silently diverge, and nobody can diff or review the change. If someone tweaks a schedule or a cluster setting in prod, that change lives only in the workspace — there is no version history, no pull request, and no way to answer the question 'what changed, and when?'

CI/CD gives us two disciplined halves. Continuous Integration means we validate and test every commit — the moment code lands, our automated checks run. Continuous Delivery means we promote the same tested artifact through environments, from dev to staging to production, without rebuilding or modifying it along the way.

One thing worth pausing on: a data environment is just a set of applications and physical infrastructure — in our case, a workspace plus the catalogs and compute that back it. CI/CD is the mechanism that moves our definitions cleanly between those environments.

Here's the worked example that makes it concrete. A job configured manually in dev sits in someone's workspace, wired to that workspace's paths and cluster. When it's time for prod, someone retypes it — different name, slightly different cluster, maybe a forgotten parameter — and now the two jobs have quietly drifted apart with no record of what diverged.

That brings us to the exam objective itself. You need to package jobs and pipelines as Databricks Asset Bundles, and deploy those bundles across development, staging, and production targets. Those two phrases — 'package jobs and pipelines' and 'deploy bundles across targets' — are the exact wording the certification uses, so get comfortable with them now.

Here's the mental model to carry forward: a Databricks Asset Bundle, or DAB, describes jobs, pipelines, and their permissions as code in YAML, versioned in Git. The bundle is the unit of promotion. Build once, deploy many — you never rebuild per environment. That single idea is the answer to a surprising number of exam questions, so hold onto it while we look at the bundle's anatomy next.

scenes.title: Anatomy of a Databricks Asset Bundle

elements.content: Anatomy of a Databricks Asset Bundle
Bundle root holds databricks.yml — the single declarative source of truth.
It declares the bundle name, the workspace host, include patterns, and the targets block (dev / staging / prod) [source 6].
resources: block declares jobs, pipelines, and model serving endpoints — each with its own permissions block.
sync: include/exclude controls which files upload; artifacts: builds wheels or JARs before deploy.
databricks bundle init scaffolds from a template: default-python, default-sql, or dbt-sql.
Requires the modern Databricks CLI (v0.205+); older CLI builds have no bundle commands.
Bundle root structure: databricks.yml, resources/, src/, tests/, .databricks/

Worked example: a 15-file project with 3 declared jobs + 1 pipeline = 4 resources; sync.exclude: ['tests/*', '.databricks/*'] uploads 9 source files instead of 15, and artifacts.whl builds once then deploys to dev → staging → prod [source 1].

actions.text: Now let's open up the bundle itself. A Databricks Asset Bundle is really just a folder of declarative configuration sitting next to your source code, and that folder is what CI/CD tools deploy from.
At the root of that folder lives a single file: databricks.yml. This is the one declaration of truth for the whole project — everything the CLI needs to know about the bundle starts here.

Inside it you'll find the bundle name, the workspace host it targets, any include patterns for extra config files, and critically the targets block. That targets block is where you define dev, staging, and prod — each with its own host, workspace path, and variables.

Next comes the resources block. This is where you declare the actual Databricks objects the bundle owns — jobs, pipelines, and model serving endpoints — along with their permissions, so access control travels with the definition instead of being clicked in by hand.

Then there are the sync and artifacts sections. Sync include and exclude rules control which files get uploaded into the workspace, so you can keep tests or data out of the deployment. Artifacts tell the bundle to build wheels or JARs before deployment, so custom libraries ship with their dependencies.

You don't have to author any of this from a blank page. The command databricks bundle init scaffolds a project from a template, and three are worth memorizing: default-python, default-sql, and dbt-sql.

One practical trap to remember: this all requires the modern Databricks CLI, version 0.205 or later. Older CLI builds simply have no bundle commands at all, so if a command isn't found, check the CLI version first.

And here is the directory structure in one picture. At the bundle root you'll see databricks.yml alongside a resources folder holding the job and pipeline definitions, a src folder for notebooks and code, a tests folder, and a .databricks folder that holds local state the CLI manages for you. That layout is what makes a repo boundary and a deployment boundary the same thing — which is exactly why bundles anchor a CI/CD workflow.

scenes.title: Check: Bundle Basics

questions.question: A data engineer is onboarding to a new team and is told, 'The bundle definition lives at the bundle root.' Which file must they open first to find the bundle name, the workspace host, the include patterns used during sync, and the targets block?

options.label: databricks.yml, located at the bundle root, which holds the bundle name, workspace host, include patterns, and the targets block
requirements.txt at the project root, which pins the Python dependencies and is read first by the Databricks CLI during validation
The notebook under src/ that contains the pipeline definition, because bundle metadata is annotated as comments inside the notebook itself
A generated job JSON file inside the .databricks/state directory, which is checked into Git and acts as the single source of truth for the bundle

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: The bundle root holds databricks.yml: this single YAML file declares the bundle name, the workspace host, the include patterns used to decide which files are synced, and the targets block that separates environments such as dev, staging, and prod. Option B is a real file in many Python projects but only pins libraries; the CLI never reads it as the bundle definition. Option C reflects the distractor trap for this objective: students conflate the notebook path with the resource definition. A notebook may be referenced by a resource, but it is not the bundle definition itself. Option D is a state artifact produced during deployment; it is derived from databricks.yml and must never be treated as the source of truth. This distinction is exactly why bundles exist: CI/CD = continuous integration (validate and test every commit) + continuous delivery (promote the same tested artifact through environments), and immutable, reviewable YAML in Git is what makes a change diffable at all. As noted in the course framing, isolated live and staging environments let engineers test ETL services and data pipelines before promoting them to production [source 6], which only works if the environment topology is declared in a versioned root file. Note the preconditions: databricks.yml is authoritative only when it sits at the directory the CLI treats as the bundle root; if you run the CLI from a subdirectory, you must point it at the root, otherwise validation fails or reads the wrong target.

questions.question: Reviewing a teammate's databricks.yml before a promotion, you see a top-level resources: block and a targets: block. Select ALL statements that correctly describe what these blocks declare and how they interact.

options.label: The resources: block declares jobs, pipelines, and model serving endpoints, and each resource can carry its own permissions block that governs who may view, run, or manage it
The targets: block declares the environments (for example dev, staging, and prod) and binds each one to a workspace host plus any target-specific overrides such as resource identifiers or permissions
A notebook path listed under sync: include patterns is itself a resource declaration, so any notebook that is uploaded to the workspace automatically becomes a deployable job or pipeline
The resources: block is optional if the target is defined, because target-level overrides are merged and can reference artifacts directly without an explicit resource declaration

questions.correctAnswer: A
questions.analysis: The resources: block is the declarative home for the things Databricks actually deploys: jobs, pipelines, and model serving endpoints, each of which can specify its own permissions block so that access control is defined as code rather than clicked into a workspace UI. The targets: block is the environment axis; it names environments such as dev, staging, and prod and binds each to a workspace host with target-specific overrides, which is what allows the same tested artifact to be promoted rather than rebuilt, the essence of build once / deploy many. Option C is the intended distractor trap. sync: include/exclude controls which files are uploaded to the workspace; uploading a notebook does not create a job or pipeline, because a notebook path is not a resource definition until a job or pipeline resource references it. Option D is wrong in both directions: resources do not become optional just because a target exists, and artifacts (wheels or JARs built before deployment) are inputs consumed by resources, not substitutes for them. The environment separation that makes this safe is described in the source material as splitting infrastructure resources into live and staging so engineers can test ETL services and data pipelines before promotion [source 6]. The broader framing that this course bridges traditional application lifecycle management with data engineering practice reinforces why each concern gets its own block [source 3]. Two edge cases matter in review: if the same resource key is defined in multiple targets, you must know Databricks' merge order or you will silently deploy the wrong identifiers; and if a permissions block is present but the referenced principal does not exist in the target workspace, deployment fails rather than degrading gracefully.

actions.text: Now let's check that the anatomy of a bundle actually stuck. Take a few minutes to work through each question on your own — read the options carefully and pick what you genuinely think is right.
Once you submit, I'll walk through everything with you, including anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Git Integration in Databricks

elements.content: Git Integration in Databricks

Git folders (formerly Repos) clone a remote repository directly into the workspace, so notebooks and bundle YAML are versioned in the same tree. Git provides the trigger surface for CI/CD — an external runner still executes the pipeline.

Git folder = repo clone in workspace. One Git folder per repository structure; supported providers include GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps, and AWS CodeCommit. Credentials are stored per user or via a service principal. [source 1]

Working model: branch → PR → main. CI validates the bundle on the pull request; deployment happens only on merge to main. Build once, deploy many — the same tested artifact is promoted dev → staging → prod. [source 5]
Worked Example: A Bundle Change Flows Through the Pipeline

A developer edits databricks.yml to add a job resource and opens a feature-branch PR. CI runs on the PR: it validates the bundle syntax and resolves the target. If validation passes and the PR merges to main, the external runner deploys the same artifact to the staging target and then to production. [source 6]

actions.text: Let's talk specifically about how version control connects to the Databricks workspace. Git folders are the bridge between your remote repository and everything you author inside Databricks.

A Git folder, which used to be called Repos, clones a remote repository directly into your workspace. The key idea: one workspace supports one Git folder per repository structure, and supported providers include GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps, and AWS CodeCommit. Credentials are stored per user or through a service principal.

Think of it this way: a Git folder is a repo clone living in the workspace, so you edit files in place and the changes map straight back to the remote repository. This is what lets code and infrastructure live together.

The working model is a feature branch, then a pull request, then a merge into main. CI validates the bundle on the PR, and deployment happens on merge. And here's the exam trap: Git folders give you version control and a trigger surface, but they are not a CI/CD system by themselves — an external runner still executes the pipeline.
Let's walk through a worked example of how a bundle change flows through this system. Watch how a single edit travels from branch to deployment.

A developer edits databricks.yml to add a job resource. Because the bundle config lives in the same repository as the source code, the code and the infrastructure are reviewed together — that's the whole point of keeping them in one repo.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Package an Existing Job as a Bundle

elements.content: Problem 1

Your team operates a hand-created job in the dev workspace. The inventory from `databricks jobs list` gives: job_id = 472199304817563, name = daily_sales_etl, a single notebook task pointing at /Workspace/Repos/team/sales/etl/bronze.py, a daily trigger with cron 0 0 6 * * ? in timezone UTC, max_concurrency = 1, timeout_seconds = 7200, and max_retries = 2. Leadership wants this exact definition to be deployable to dev, staging and prod without anybody re-clicking the job in the UI. (a) Write the exact command sequence that scaffolds a bundle project named daily-sales-etl using the default-python template and then captures the live job into it. (b) List the files and directories the scaffold creates, name the generated resource file, and explain how the bundle discovers it at validate/deploy time.
Hint: Scaffold first with `databricks bundle init`, then use `bundle generate job --existing-job-id` rather than retyping the JSON by hand.

Worked solution
Step A — scaffold. From an empty working directory inside a Git checkout:

```bash

databricks bundle init default-python --name daily-sales-etl

```

With `--name` supplied, the interactive prompts for project name are skipped; you still answer the template questions (include a Python package? no; use serverless? no). The template writes:

```

daily-sales-etl/

databricks.yml # bundle root: name, include, variables, targets

resources/ # resource declarations (jobs, pipelines)

daily_sales_etl.job.yml # created in Step B

src/ # notebook / library source that gets synced

bronze.py

tests/ # unit tests for the Python package

```

Commit this immediately (`git add -A && git commit -m "chore: scaffold bundle"`), because the next step only produces a reviewable diff if there is a clean baseline.

Step B — capture the running job. Confirm the identifier first, then generate:

```bash

databricks jobs list --output json | jq '.[] | select(.job_id == 472199304817563)'

databricks bundle generate job --existing-job-id 472199304817563 --key daily_sales_etl

```

The `--key` value becomes the resource key, so the job is addressable as `daily_sales_etl` for `bundle run`. The command serialises the live job definition (name, task list with notebook_path, schedule with cron 0 0 6 * * ?, max_concurrency 1, timeout_seconds 7200, max_retries 2, cluster spec, permissions) into `resources/daily_sales_etl.job.yml`, and — if the file is not already covered — ensures the root `databricks.yml` has an include glob:

```yaml

bundle:

name: daily-sales-etl

include:

- resources/*.yml

```

That include glob is what makes the bundle load the generated file: every `*.yml` under `resources/` is parsed and merged into the deployment plan, so a resource file that is not matched by any include pattern is silently ignored. Verify the capture with `git status` (the new file must appear) and `databricks bundle validate` before touching anything else.

Analysis — The method choice matters more than the typing. Hand-recreating the job in YAML is an act of transcription: you re-derive every field from a UI screenshot, and any field you forget (retry policy, timeout, task-level cluster) is a silent regression once the bundle overwrites the live job. `bundle generate job` reads the job object the service already stores, so feature parity is guaranteed by construction — whatever runs today is what the YAML says today. This mirrors the general CI/CD principle that you promote the artefact that was tested rather than a re-typed copy of it [source 3]. Typical student errors: (1) running `bundle generate` outside the bundle root, which fails because there is no `databricks.yml` to attach resources to; (2) creating the file under a directory the `include` globs do not match, then wondering why `validate` shows no job; (3) forgetting the `--key`, so the generated resource key is auto-derived from the job name and later `bundle run <key>` commands fail with 'resource not found'; (4) generating into a dirty working tree, so the generated file is mixed into unrelated changes and the review is useless. Edge case: `bundle generate` snapshots the job as a static declaration — it is not a live link. After generation, edits in the Databricks UI no longer flow back into the bundle, and the next `bundle deploy` will overwrite UI edits. That is the intended direction of truth (Git is the source of truth) but it must be stated explicitly to the team, otherwise someone 'fixes' production in the UI and the fix disappears at the next deployment.
Problem 2

The generated `resources/daily_sales_etl.job.yml` contains hardcoded Unity Catalog identifiers: the notebook task runs with `base_parameters: {catalog: "dev_sales", schema: "bronze"}` and the job's `run_as` / warehouse references assume the dev workspace. There are 6 hardcoded occurrences of the literal string `dev_sales` across the bundle (2 in the job YAML, 2 in src/bronze.py defaults, 1 in databricks.yml, 1 in tests/conftest.py). Rewrite the configuration so the same bundle deploys to dev (catalog dev_sales), staging (catalog staging_sales) and prod (catalog prod_sales), all using schema `silver` in staging and prod but `bronze` in dev. Show the root `bundle`/`variables`/`targets` blocks, the parameterised job snippet, the resolved value table for the three targets, and a command that proves no environment-specific literal is left behind.
Hint: Declare `variables:` once with a safe default, override per target, and reference them as `${var.name}` inside the resource file.

Worked solution
Root `databricks.yml`:

```yaml

bundle:

name: daily-sales-etl

include:

- resources/*.yml

variables:

catalog:

description: Unity Catalog catalog that receives this environment's data

default: dev_sales

schema:

description: Target schema for the bronze notebook

default: bronze

workspace:

host: https://dev-workspace.cloud.databricks.com

targets:

dev:

default: true

mode: development

workspace:

host: https://dev-workspace.cloud.databricks.com

staging:

mode: production

workspace:

host: https://staging-workspace.cloud.databricks.com

root_path: /Workspace/Users/svc-deploy@corp.com/.bundle/${bundle.name}/${bundle.target}

variables:

catalog: staging_sales

schema: silver

prod:

mode: production

workspace:

host: https://prod-workspace.cloud.databricks.com

root_path: /Workspace/Users/svc-deploy@corp.com/.bundle/${bundle.name}/${bundle.target}

variables:

catalog: prod_sales

schema: silver

```

Parameterised job resource:

```yaml

resources:

jobs:

daily_sales_etl:

name: daily_sales_etl

max_concurrency: 1

timeout_seconds: 7200

schedule:

quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 6 * * ?"

timezone_id: UTC

tasks:

- task_key: bronze

notebook_task:

notebook_path: ../src/bronze.py

base_parameters:

catalog: ${var.catalog}

schema: ${var.schema}

max_retries: 2

```

Resolution: the user's local machine runs the default target (`dev`), so `databricks bundle validate` with no `-t` flag resolves catalog = dev_sales, schema = bronze. Selecting a target overrides the declaration:

| Target | catalog | schema | mode |

|---|---|---|---|

| dev (default) | dev_sales | bronze | development |

| staging | staging_sales | silver | production |

| prod | prod_sales | silver | production |

The resolution rule is: target-level `variables` beat the top-level `default`; a variable with neither a default nor a target override is an unresolved value, and `databricks bundle validate` fails with 'variable catalog has no value' rather than deploying a broken job.

Proof that no literal is left behind — after parameterisation the only permitted occurrence of the dev catalog is the declared default, so the expected grep count is exactly 1:

```bash

grep -rn "dev_sales\|staging_sales\|prod_sales" databricks.yml resources/ src/ tests/ | wc -l

# expected: 1 (the default: dev_sales in databricks.yml)

```

Remaining hardcoded occurrences in `src/bronze.py` and `tests/conftest.py` must be replaced by reads of `dbutils.widgets.get("catalog")` and an environment fixture, otherwise the 6 → 1 reduction is only cosmetic.

Analysis — Why variables rather than three copies of the job file: one declaration plus per-target overrides makes environment differences explicit, enumerable and diffable, which is precisely what stops dev and prod from silently diverging. It also implements the build-once / deploy-many promotion model: the same Git commit carries the same YAML and the same notebook, and only the variable injection differs per environment [source 5]. The classic pitfall is the one this exercise is built around: leaving a literal catalog name in the resource YAML or in the notebook. The bundle then deploys successfully, `validate` passes, and every environment — including prod — writes into `dev_sales`. Nothing errors; you discover it when a production dashboard shows dev numbers or when staging and prod tables are missing. A second, subtler pitfall is the order of precedence: a target that overrides only `catalog` still inherits the top-level `schema` default, so a staging run can quietly land in `dev_sales.silver` rather than the intended `staging_sales.silver` — check the resolved table, not the file. Edge cases to teach explicitly: `mode: development` prefixes job and pipeline names with `[dev <user>]` and pauses their triggers, so a dev deployment will not fire at 06:00 UTC — that is intentional and is the reason the same cron is safe to commit; and any target that deploys into a production workspace should set an explicit `root_path` under a service principal to avoid writing artefacts into a personal user folder. Generalisation: the pattern `variable declaration + per-target override + CI grep gate` is the same mechanism used for cluster sizes, instance types, service principals and notification destinations, so students should treat catalog/schema as the first of many parameterised knobs.
Problem 3

The bundle is committed and parameterised. You now need to ship it to dev first: validate the same commit that will later go to staging and prod, deploy it, and run the job on demand to prove it works. Write the exact command sequence for the dev target, state what each command actually does to the workspace, explain what a non-zero exit code from each step means, and state how many deployments and how many validations are needed before all three environments carry the identical commit.
Hint: The order is validate → deploy → run, and `run` needs the resource key, not the job name.

Worked solution
The sequence for dev is a strict three-phase pipeline:

```bash

# 1. Validate: build the deployment plan against the dev target, no workspace mutation

databricks bundle validate -t dev

# 2. Deploy: sync files and create/update the job in the dev workspace

databricks bundle deploy -t dev

# 3. Run: execute the job resource named by its key

databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t dev

```

What each phase does:

1. `bundle validate -t dev` parses `databricks.yml`, resolves every include, resolves every `${var.*}` against the dev target, resolves every `${bundle.*}` and `${workspace.*}` reference, and type-checks the resource schema (cron expression, task keys, notebook paths). It exits 0 with a summary such as 'Validation OK! Found 1 job(s)' and exits non-zero on any unresolved variable, unknown field or duplicate resource key. Crucially it mutates nothing, which is why it is the gate that runs on every pull request.

2. `bundle deploy -t dev` performs two separate actions: it synchronises the local files matched by the bundle's `sync` rules into the workspace destination (the notebook lands at the target's `root_path`), then calls the Jobs API to create or update the job named by the resource key. A first deploy creates job id 472199304817563's replacement and writes the deployment state locally under `.databricks/bundle/dev/`. A second deploy of the same commit is a no-op and prints no changes — that idempotence is what makes the pipeline re-runnable. A non-zero exit means the sync or the API call failed: insufficient workspace permissions, a `run_as` identity that does not exist in that workspace, or a cluster policy that rejects the declared node type.

3. `bundle run daily_sales_etl -t dev` starts the job (bypassing the paused dev trigger) and streams the run lifecycle, returning the run URL and, on failure, the task error. To pass values at run time for a one-off smoke test:

```bash

databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t dev --params catalog=dev_sales,schema=bronze

```

Promotion arithmetic: because each environment is a distinct target with its own workspace host, one commit must be validated 3 times and deployed 3 times — 3 validates, 3 deploys, 3 runs for the full dev → staging → prod promotion of a single artefact. The number of builds, however, is 1: the notebook and YAML are uploaded from the same Git commit, so the count of distinct artefacts is 1 while the count of deployments is 3. That asymmetry is the whole point of the model — you build once and deploy many [source 5]. Staging and prod reuse the identical command sequence with `-t staging` and `-t prod` appended; nothing else changes, and the only permitted difference is the variable values resolved from the target block.

Analysis — Splitting validate from deploy is what makes the pipeline safe: validation is read-only and cheap, so it can run on every push and every pull request, while deployment is a mutation that must happen only after review. This is the continuous-integration half of CI/CD — validate and test each commit — feeding the continuous-delivery half, which promotes the same tested artefact through environments rather than rebuilding from a branch [source 3]. Students most often err in three ways. First, they run `bundle deploy` without validating locally, discover a typo only after the workspace job has already been updated. Second, they try `bundle run daily_sales_etl` without `-t`, which silently targets the default target and produces a 'job not found' error if the job was only ever deployed to prod. Third, they interpret 'validation OK' as 'the job is correct' — validation proves the configuration resolves and is schema-valid, not that the notebook produces the right rows; a post-deploy check of the target table (row count and the `catalog` column value) is still required. Edge cases worth flagging: in `mode: development`, the deployed job name carries a `[dev <user>]` prefix and its schedule is paused, so a successful deploy does not mean a run happened — use `bundle run` for an explicit smoke test; and if the bundle contains a pipeline as well as a job, `bundle run` needs the pipeline key, since a pipeline has no notebook task to invoke. Generalisation: the same three-phase contract — validate, deploy, run/verify — reappears in every promotion gate, including production, and the only thing that changes between environments is the target flag [source 6].
Problem 4

Diagnostic scenario. After the first prod deployment, the ops team reports that the nightly job did run in production (42 minutes, 8 workers, 1.2 million rows written), but the rows landed in `dev_sales.silver.orders`, and the production table `prod_sales.silver.orders` is still empty. Two candidate causes were raised: (A) the prod target was deployed with the wrong `-t` flag, and (B) a literal catalog name remained in the code. Reproduce the reasoning that identifies the true cause from the evidence, give the fix, and state the CI check that would have blocked this deployment.
Hint: A wrong target would still resolve `${var.catalog}`; ask what the running task actually received as a parameter.

Worked solution
Evidence analysis. The job ran in the production workspace with the production cluster shape (8 workers, 42 minutes) — that part of the target resolved correctly, so the deployment itself landed in the right place. What failed is the write destination: 1.2M rows appeared in `dev_sales.silver.orders`, which is the dev catalog resolved from the top-level `default: dev_sales`.

Distinguishing the two candidates:

- If cause (A) held — deploying with `-t dev` by mistake — the job would have been created in the dev workspace, the run would not appear in the production workspace at all, and the cluster shape would be the dev shape (2 workers, ~6 minutes), not 8 workers / 42 minutes. The observed run contradicts (A).

- Cause (B) holds because a hardcoded literal short-circuits variable resolution. If `src/bronze.py` still contained `spark.table("dev_sales.silver.orders")` or the notebook read a widget with a literal fallback (`dbutils.widgets.text("catalog", "dev_sales")` followed by a read of the widget default rather than the job parameter), then the target's `variables: catalog: prod_sales` is never consumed, and the prod run writes to dev. Variable resolution happens in the bundle, not in the notebook: the YAML can resolve perfectly while the code ignores the resolved value.

Fix, in order:

```bash

# 1. Locate every literal in the code and config

grep -rn "dev_sales\|staging_sales\|prod_sales" databricks.yml resources/ src/ tests/

# expected after fix: exactly 1 hit (the declared default in databricks.yml)

# 2. Read the parameter, never a literal fallback

# src/bronze.py must use: catalog = dbutils.widgets.get("catalog")

# 3. Re-validate all three targets, then redeploy prod

databricks bundle validate -t dev && databricks bundle validate -t staging && databricks bundle validate -t prod

databricks bundle deploy -t prod

databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod

```

Preventive CI gate (blocks the PR that introduced the literal):

```bash

# fail the build if an environment-specific literal escapes the default declaration

count=$(grep -rn "staging_sales\|prod_sales" resources/ src/ | wc -l)

if [ "$count" -ne 0 ]; then echo "hardcoded environment literal: $count hit(s)"; exit 1; fi

```

The same gate should also assert that the parameterised code path actually reads the widget: `grep -c 'dbutils.widgets.get("catalog")' src/bronze.py` must be at least 1. Data remediation is a separate, manual step: the 1.2M rows in `dev_sales.silver.orders` are valid dev data (the run was clean) but must not be confused with the production table, and the prod job must be re-run to populate `prod_sales.silver.orders` before the downstream consumers resume.

Analysis — This is the highest-value lesson in the scene because the failure is silent. Nothing in the deployment pipeline errors: `validate` resolves the variables correctly, `deploy` succeeds, the job runs green, and the only symptom is that the wrong table grew. The diagnostic method is to derive conclusions from independent evidence rather than from the most obvious hypothesis — the cluster shape and the workspace in which the run appears discriminate cleanly between 'wrong target' and 'hardcoded literal'. Students routinely jump to the wrong-target explanation because it is easier to imagine than a residual literal hidden in a notebook's widget default. The generalisable rule is that parameterisation is only complete when it reaches the code, not just the YAML; a variable that is declared, overridden and never read is decoration. Typical edge cases: a widget declared with a default value silently masks a missing parameter, because the notebook runs happily with the default; notebooks invoked without `base_parameters` inherit those defaults; and shared notebooks called by several jobs can hardcode a schema that is correct for one job and wrong for the others. This is why the grep gate belongs in continuous integration rather than in a documented convention — a rule that is not enforced by a failing build is a rule that will be violated [source 3][source 6]. One more governance point: after the fix, the production deployment must be executed by a service principal with a production `root_path`, so the audit trail shows an automated deployment of a reviewed commit rather than a human running ad-hoc commands against prod [source 5].
Problem 5

Write the CI/CD workflow that promotes `daily-sales-etl` from review to production. On every pull request touching the bundle, all three targets must be validated; on merge to `main`, dev is deployed and run automatically, staging is deployed after a manual approval, and prod is deployed after a second approval. Reuse the single artefact from the merge commit — no rebuild between environments. Also state the rollback procedure and how many approvals, validations, deployments and job runs the full promotion to prod consumes.
Hint: Validation is the PR gate; approvals gate the deployments; the artefact is the merge commit, not a fresh build per environment.

Worked solution
Workflow `./.github/workflows/bundle.yml` (structure is identical under GitLab or Azure DevOps; only the syntax changes):

```yaml

name: bundle-cicd

on:

pull_request:

paths: ["databricks.yml", "resources/**", "src/**"]

push:

branches: [main]

jobs:

validate:

if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'

runs-on: ubuntu-latest

strategy:

matrix:

target: [dev, staging, prod] # 3 parallel validate jobs

steps:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4

- uses: databricks/setup-cli@main

- run: databricks bundle validate -t ${{ matrix.target }}

env:

DATABRICKS_HOST: ${{ secrets[format('DATABRICKS_HOST_{0}', matrix.target)] }}

DATABRICKS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets[format('DATABRICKS_TOKEN_{0}', matrix.target)] }}

deploy-dev:

if: github.event_name == 'push'

runs-on: ubuntu-latest

environment: dev

steps:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4

- uses: databricks/setup-cli@main

- run: databricks bundle validate -t dev

- run: databricks bundle deploy -t dev

- run: databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t dev

deploy-staging:

if: github.event_name == 'push'

needs: deploy-dev

runs-on: ubuntu-latest

environment: staging # requires manual approval

steps:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4 # same commit SHA as deploy-dev

- uses: databricks/setup-cli@main

- run: databricks bundle validate -t staging

- run: databricks bundle deploy -t staging

deploy-prod:

if: github.event_name == 'push'

needs: deploy-staging

runs-on: ubuntu-latest

environment: production # requires manual approval

steps:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4

- uses: databricks/setup-cli@main

- run: databricks bundle validate -t prod

- run: databricks bundle deploy -t prod

```

Why this is 'build once, deploy many': every job checks out the same merge-commit SHA from `main`; the bundle uploads files from that SHA. There is no per-environment branch and no per-environment rebuild, so the bytes running in prod are byte-identical to the bytes validated on the pull request; only the resolved variables differ [source 5].

Budget arithmetic for one accepted, promoted feature:

- Validations: 3 on the pull request (one per matrix target) + 1 per deploy job = 6 `bundle validate` invocations.

- Deployments: 1 (dev) + 1 (staging) + 1 (prod) = 3, all from the same SHA.

- Automated job runs: 1 (the dev smoke test). Staging and prod run on their own schedules after deployment, because the schedule (0 0 6 * * ? UTC) is declared in the resource and targets in `mode: production` keep their triggers active.

- Manual approvals: 2 (staging, production).

- Distinct build artefacts: 1.

The inverse formula also matters: promoting one change to prod costs 6 validations and 3 deployments, so a validation that fails on a pull request has negative cost relative to one that fails after merge — that is the economic argument for validating all three targets before review, not just the default target [source 2].

Rollback: identify the last-known-good commit in `main`, revert it (`git revert <sha>`) and let the same workflow redeploy, or, for an incident, re-run the production deploy job on the last green SHA. Then confirm recovery with a post-deploy check rather than assuming it worked:

```bash

# expected: prod count grows by ~1.2e6 rows per nightly run, and no new rows in dev

databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod

```

Automated rollback triggers to configure: a job run failure rate above threshold, a post-deploy row-count check returning zero, or a freshness check showing the prod table has not advanced within its SLA window.

Analysis — The architecture separates three concerns that beginners conflate: integration (validating every commit against every target — cheap, read-only, mandatory on pull request), delivery (deploying the reviewed artefact to an environment behind an approval), and verification (proving after deployment that the target state was reached). Deployment pipelines exist precisely to give this visibility into production readiness without manual copying and reconfiguration, which is why approvals are attached to environments rather than bolted onto individual commands [source 1][source 2]. The deployment pipeline is the governed, automated path for promoting content across environments [source 1], and the promotion itself follows the build-once/deploy-many discipline with explicit environments dev → staging → prod [source 5]. Common mistakes: (1) rebuilding per environment, for example compiling a wheel separately in the prod job, which silently breaks the identical-artefact guarantee — if the bundle declares `artifacts:`, the build must happen once and the produced wheel must be the one uploaded to all three targets; (2) storing a single `DATABRICKS_TOKEN` for all environments, so a compromised CI runner holds prod credentials for a dev-only change — use per-environment secrets or, better, OIDC-federated service principals; (3) omitting `validate` before `deploy` inside the deploy jobs, leaving no guard against a mis-resolved variable in the environment being mutated; (4) treating the job's own success as post-deploy verification when the failure mode in p4 (writing to the wrong catalog) produces a green run. Edge cases: scheduled runs in production targets will fire on the declared cron as soon as deployment completes, so deploying at 05:55 UTC overlaps the 06:00 UTC run — either deploy outside the window or set `max_concurrency: 1` (already declared here) so the second run queues instead of double-writing; and a first-time promotion to a brand-new environment must create the catalog and schema before deploying, since the bundle manages jobs and pipelines, not Unity Catalog metastore objects. Generalisation: the same skeleton — matrix validation on PR, gated deploys on merge, explicit rollback trigger — carries over to any bundle content, whether jobs, Lakeflow pipelines or model serving endpoints, and the metrics that tell you whether it works (deployment frequency, lead time, change-failure rate, time to restore) are the DORA set that promotion pipelines are designed to move [source 5][source 6].

actions.text: Let's put all of that into practice with a full worked problem. We have a hand-created job living in the dev workspace, and we need to package it as a Databricks Asset Bundle so the same definition can deploy across dev, staging, and prod. Read the setup carefully — every detail matters.

Problem one gives us the starting point: a manually created job named daily_sales_etl that runs the notebook at /Workspace/Repos/team/sales/etl/bronze.py on a daily schedule. Our goal is to take that working job and express it as code, so we can promote the identical definition to every environment. Before you peek at the solution, try the hint on your own.

The hint points you toward the scaffold: run databricks bundle init with the default-python template. That single command gives you databricks.yml, a resources folder, a src folder, and a tests folder — the skeleton of every bundle you'll author.

Here's the worked solution. Step A is the scaffold. Step B is capturing the existing config — and this is the key move: databricks bundle generate job with the existing job id writes your current job definition straight into resources/daily_sales_etl.yml. You are not retyping the job; you are extracting the source of truth that already runs in production.

And look at the analysis, because this is the exam-worthy insight: the method choice matters more than the mechanics. Generating the YAML beats hand-writing it, because generate guarantees feature parity with the job that already runs. The classic pitfall is leaving literal catalog names in the YAML — do that, and every environment silently writes to dev data. That's exactly the trap the next problem tackles.

scenes.title: Check: Git and Bundle Authoring

questions.question: A data engineer has committed an updated databricks.yml and a new resources/daily_sales_etl.yml to a feature branch and opened a pull request. The engineer wants the same tested artifact to reach the dev, staging, and prod workspaces. According to the Git-plus-bundle workflow taught in this unit, which sequence of operations correctly moves from commit to deployed resource?

options.label: Merge the pull request to main, then run databricks bundle validate, then run databricks bundle deploy with the appropriate target.
Run databricks bundle validate on the pull request, merge the pull request to main, then run databricks bundle deploy with the appropriate target for each environment.
Run databricks bundle deploy to prod directly from the feature branch after a successful commit, then run databricks bundle validate as a post-deployment check.
Edit the generated YAML directly in the target workspace UI, save it, and let the Git folder sync the change back to the repository automatically.

questions.correctAnswer: Run databricks bundle validate on the pull request, merge the pull request to main, then run databricks bundle deploy with the appropriate target for each environment.
questions.analysis: The correct order is validate → review/merge → deploy, because continuous integration validates and tests every commit on the pull request, while continuous delivery promotes the same tested artifact through environments only after the change is reviewed and merged. [source 3] describes applying CI/CD pipelines to promote data pipeline artifacts between environments safely and reliably, and [source 5] describes artifact promotion as build once / deploy many across dev→staging→prod. Option A reverses validation and merge, so the merge happens without any gate. Option C is the classic distractor trap: deploying before validating means an unvalidated artifact can reach production, and validation after deployment cannot prevent the damage. Option D is a double error: it edits generated YAML directly in the workspace instead of in the bundle source, and it assumes the Git folder syncs workspace edits back — bundle deployment is push-based from the repository, not a round-trip sync. Note the concrete workflow numbers from the earlier worked example: the manual job daily_sales_etl ran /Workspace/Repos/team/sales/etl/bronze.py on a daily schedule, and once captured with databricks bundle generate job --existing-job-id <job-id> that definition becomes the single source of truth deployed to all three targets.
answer: Run databricks bundle validate on the pull request, merge the pull request to main, then run databricks bundle deploy with the appropriate target for each environment.

questions.question: A team is onboarding an existing, manually created job named daily_sales_etl into a Databricks Asset Bundle so that one definition can deploy to dev, staging, and prod. Which statements about the scaffolding commands are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: databricks bundle init scaffolds the bundle structure, creating databricks.yml, resources/, src/, and tests/ from a template such as default-python.
databricks bundle generate job --existing-job-id <job-id> captures the current job definition from the workspace and writes it into a file under resources/.
databricks bundle init rewrites the underlying notebook logic in src/ so that it matches the deployed job's schedule and cluster settings.
databricks bundle generate job reads the job definition from the bundle's resources/ directory and pushes it into the workspace as a brand-new job.

correctAnswer: databricks bundle init scaffolds the bundle structure, creating databricks.yml, resources/, src/, and tests/ from a template such as default-python.
databricks bundle generate job --existing-job-id <job-id> captures the current job definition from the workspace and writes it into a file under resources/.
questions.analysis: The first two statements are correct. databricks bundle init is the scaffolding step: it creates the bundle skeleton — databricks.yml, resources/, src/, and tests/ — from a template such as default-python. databricks bundle generate job --existing-job-id <job-id> is the capture step: it reads the live job definition out of the workspace and writes it into resources/daily_sales_etl.yml, which is exactly how the manually created daily_sales_etl job was packaged in the earlier worked problem. The third statement is wrong because init only creates structure and placeholder code; it never rewrites the business logic of an existing notebook to match schedules or cluster settings. The fourth statement inverts generate's direction: generate pulls configuration from the workspace into the bundle (workspace → files), it does not push files into the workspace (files → workspace) — that push happens later at deploy time. Distinguishing these directions matters because the whole point of the Git-plus-bundle workflow is that the repository, not the workspace, becomes the source of truth; [source 5] frames this as artifact promotion with a build once / deploy many discipline, and [source 6] frames it as isolating environments so ETL services and pipelines are tested before promotion to production.
answer: databricks bundle init scaffolds the bundle structure, creating databricks.yml, resources/, src/, and tests/ from a template such as default-python.
databricks bundle generate job --existing-job-id <job-id> captures the current job definition from the workspace and writes it into a file under resources/.

scenes.title: The Bundle Lifecycle Commands

elements.content: The Bundle Lifecycle Commands
Four daily commands: validate → deploy → run → destroy, plus inspection helpers. Each acts on a different layer of the workspace.

validate

Resolves variables + target, checks config. Workspace untouched.

deploy -t <target>

Uploads synced files, creates/updates resources, writes state under .databricks/bundle/.

run <resource>

Triggers the deployed job or pipeline; accepts --params overrides.

destroy -t <target>

Tears down resources. Use --auto-approve in CI so the pipeline does not hang.

A validator doesn't build anything — it only resolves and checks. deploy is the only command that mutates the workspace and writes the target's state directory, so it is the unit CI runs on merge.

Practitioners split resources into isolated environments (dev, staging, prod) before promoting pipelines, so a failed deploy never reaches the live target. [source 6]
Worked example: a CI job runs validate on the PR, then deploy -t prod on merge. Split the same failing config into dev/staging first. [source 5] [source 1]

actions.text: Now that you've authored your bundle, let's look at the commands that actually move it through its lifecycle. These are the four daily verbs every data engineer working with Databricks Asset Bundles needs at their fingertips.
Think of them as a loop: validate, deploy, run, and destroy. In practice you'll spend most of your time in the first three, and reach for destroy only when you're cleaning up a target.

First, validate. This resolves variables and the target, checks the whole configuration, and touches nothing in the workspace. As we just covered on the previous page, that last part matters: validate is purely a local sanity check before you risk any real change.

Second, deploy with the -t flag for your target. This uploads synced files, creates or updates the jobs and pipelines, and writes deployment state under the .databricks bundle slash target path. That state folder is how the CLI knows what already exists when you deploy again.

Third, run. You name the resource, pass the target, and the CLI triggers the deployed job or pipeline for you. This is also where you can hand in parameter overrides with the params option, which is exactly how you'll run the same job against different inputs without redeploying.

Fourth, destroy. This tears down the deployed resources for a target. Note the warning here: use auto-approve in CI, otherwise the command waits for an interactive confirmation and your pipeline just hangs. That is a very common, very annoying gotcha.

Here's the worked example to make it concrete: a CI job runs validate on every pull request, and on merge it deploys to staging, runs a quick smoke test, and then promotes to production. Notice that validate guards the door, and destroy only appears when a full environment needs to be torn down. You'll also want the inspection helpers in your toolkit, so let's discuss where you'd wire each of these commands into your own promotion pipeline.

actions.topic: Where would you place validate, deploy, run, and destroy in your team's CI/CD pipeline?
actions.prompt: Think about which commands belong on a pull request, which on a merge to main, and where auto-approve matters for destroy.

scenes.title: Interactive: The Promotion Pipeline

content.html:
🚀 The Promotion Pipeline

Commit → validate → dev → test → staging → production

1 / 7
🎯

Select a stage

Click any revealed node

Click a stage in the diagram to see the exact command it runs and the artifact it produces.

nodes.label: Commit & Push
nodes.artifact: Git commit SHA — one immutable version of the code.
nodes.details: A developer pushes to main. GitHub Actions starts the workflow defined in .github/workflows/bundle.yml on the push event. The runner checks out the repository and installs the Databricks CLI, which is the program that actually talks to the workspace.
nodes.detailsAlt: The push triggers a Databricks Workflow job whose task uses a Git source (branch main). Databricks pulls that revision itself and runs the task on Databricks compute — there is no external CI runner to maintain or patch.
nodes.tip: Both runners execute the same Databricks Asset Bundle. Only the machine that runs the CLI differs.

nodes.label: Bundle Validate
nodes.artifact: Resolved bundle configuration — nothing is written to the workspace.
nodes.details: Runs before anything is deployed. The CLI loads databricks.yml, resolves every ${var...} substitution for the chosen target, checks the YAML schema and verifies workspace authentication. Exit code 0 means the bundle is well-formed and the release may continue.
nodes.detailsAlt: In a Databricks Workflow the same guard is a validation task that runs databricks bundle validate on Databricks compute before the deploy task — same CLI, same exit code, same gate.
nodes.tip: Exam angle: bundle validate never creates or modifies resources. It is the safest possible check and always runs first.

nodes.label: Broken Variable
nodes.artifact: Non-zero exit code — the release is blocked before any environment is touched.
nodes.details: Rename ${var.catalog} to ${var.catalogg} in databricks.yml and leave the target's variable mapping untouched. Validation fails immediately with an unresolved-variable error and the workflow stops here — bundle deploy never runs, and no workspace is modified.
nodes.detailsAlt: In a Databricks Workflow the failure surfaces on the validate task itself: the task fails, every downstream deploy task is skipped, and nothing reaches the workspace.
nodes.tip: A typo costs seconds here. The same typo discovered after a production deploy costs a rollback.

nodes.label: Deploy to Dev
nodes.artifact: Bundle resources materialised in the dev workspace.
nodes.details: The GitHub Actions job runs the deploy command for the dev target. The bundle creates or updates workspace files, jobs, pipelines and schemas, and records deployment state so that the next deploy knows exactly what changed.
nodes.detailsAlt: As a Workflow task, deploy runs on Databricks compute under the job's own identity (a service principal). That identity must hold the permissions to create those resources — permissions are part of the promotion design, not an afterthought.
nodes.tip: bundle deploy is idempotent: re-running it after an unrelated change touches only what actually differs.

nodes.label: Integration Test
nodes.cmdNote: runs the job, asserts the result
nodes.artifact: Test results plus verified output tables in dev.
nodes.details: Run the pipeline end to end against a small fixture dataset in dev. Assert expected row counts, schema contracts and data-quality expectations. A failing test stops the promotion — no red build ever reaches staging.
nodes.detailsAlt: A Databricks Workflow encodes the same idea as a job with dependent tasks: run the pipeline task, then run the test task. If the test task fails, the job fails and the promotion gate stays shut.
nodes.tip: Test in dev, then promote what you tested — same commit, different target.

nodes.label: Deploy to Staging
nodes.artifact: Bundle resources in the staging workspace.
nodes.details: Identical code, different target. Only the variables change — catalog and schema names swap from dev to staging — so the same artifact lands in a production-shaped environment that is still safe to break.
nodes.detailsAlt: The Workflow selects the target the same way through task parameters, and the bundle resolves which variables apply at run time.
nodes.tip: Targets live in databricks.yml: one bundle, many environments, zero duplicated code.

nodes.label: Deploy to Production
nodes.artifact: Bundle resources in production — promotion complete.
nodes.details: Gated. In GitHub Actions the production job waits on an environment approval before it runs. Only then does the exact commit that passed staging reach production — nothing is rebuilt along the way.
nodes.detailsAlt: In a Databricks Workflow the gate is the permissions on the production target: whoever holds them, and whatever approval policy you configure, decides when production moves.
nodes.tip: Promote the artifact; never rebuild it per environment. The commit that passed staging is the commit that ships.

actions.text: Now let's put those lifecycle commands together and watch them run end to end. This diagram is a live promotion pipeline — each node is a stage from commit to production, and we can step through it one stage at a time.
