actions.text: Notice the deliberately broken variable branch here. When a variable name doesn't resolve, bundle validate returns a non-zero exit code and the release is blocked — bundle deploy never runs, and no workspace is touched. That's the whole point: a typo costs seconds at validation, not a rollback in production.

actions.content: The detail panel shows the command, its note, and the artifact for each stage.

actions.text: Keep stepping all the way to the final production deploy. Notice that the same commit flows through every environment — only the target variables change. And on the end-to-end picture: whether your runner is GitHub Actions or a Databricks Workflow, the same bundle and the same CLI commands execute. That equivalence is exactly the kind of comparison the exam loves to test.

scenes.title: Check: Lifecycle Commands

questions.question: A data engineer runs three commands against the same bundle and target in this order: 'databricks bundle validate', then 'databricks bundle deploy -t prod', then 'databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod'. Which statement correctly describes which of these commands mutate workspace state and which are read-only with respect to the workspace?

options.label: validate is read-only (it resolves variables and the target, checks the config, and touches nothing in the workspace), while deploy uploads synced files and creates or updates resources, and run triggers the already-deployed job or pipeline
validate is read-only, deploy is read-only because it only writes local state under .databricks/bundle/<target>, and run is the only command that changes anything in the workspace
all three commands mutate workspace state, because validate must upload the bundle to the workspace in order to resolve variables such as ${workspace.host} before it can check the configuration
validate and deploy both mutate workspace state, but run is read-only because triggering a job only reads the deployment state file rather than writing it

answer: validate is read-only (it resolves variables and the target, checks the config, and touches nothing in the workspace), while deploy uploads synced files and creates or updates resources, and run triggers the already-deployed job or pipeline
questions.analysis: The lifecycle commands were taught with a strict distinction: 'databricks bundle validate — resolves variables and the target, checks the config, and touches nothing in the workspace'; 'databricks bundle deploy -t <target> — uploads synced files, creates or updates resources, and writes deployment state under .databricks/bundle/<target>'; and 'databricks bundle run <resource> -t <target> — triggers the deployed job or pipeline, accepting --params overrides.' So validate is read-only with respect to the workspace, deploy is the mutating step that materializes files and resources, and run acts on what deploy already created. The trap distractor reverses the mutation model by claiming validate must upload to resolve variables; validation deliberately avoids any workspace write, which is exactly why it is safe to run on every pull request, consistent with the CI/CD practice of validating every commit before promotion [source 3]. Another distractor treats deploy as read-only merely because it writes local state; in fact the local state under .databricks/bundle/<target> is a record of the remote changes it just made, not a substitute for them. Note the edge case: run does not perform a hidden deploy — if the resource has never been deployed to that target, run fails because there is nothing deployed to trigger.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the bundle deployment state file and the 'databricks bundle run' command are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The deployment state is written under .databricks/bundle/<target>, so each target (dev, staging, prod) keeps its own record of what was synced and which resources were created or updated
'databricks bundle run' triggers the job or pipeline that is already deployed to the target and accepts --params overrides for that specific execution
'databricks bundle run' implicitly deploys the code first, so you never need to run 'databricks bundle deploy' before running a resource
The deployment state file is shared across all targets in a single global location, which is why deploying to prod can silently overwrite your dev environment

answer: The deployment state is written under .databricks/bundle/<target>, so each target (dev, staging, prod) keeps its own record of what was synced and which resources were created or updated
'databricks bundle run' triggers the job or pipeline that is already deployed to the target and accepts --params overrides for that specific execution
questions.analysis: Correct: deploy writes deployment state under .databricks/bundle/<target>, and the <target> path segment means the state is per-target — dev, staging, and prod each track what was uploaded and which resources were created or updated for that environment. Correct: run triggers the deployed job or pipeline and accepts --params overrides, which is how you re-run an existing artifact with different parameters without redeploying it. The distractor 'run deploys the code first' is the classic bundle misconception and is false: run operates on what deploy already produced, so the correct promotion order is validate → deploy → run, and running against an undeployed resource simply fails. The distractor about a single shared state file is also false: because state is namespaced by target, deploying to prod does not clobber the dev record, which is precisely what allows build once / deploy many across the dev→staging→prod promotion chain [source 5]. This per-target separation mirrors the CI/CD principle of isolated environments where pipelines are tested before promotion to production [source 6].

actions.text: So let's see how the lifecycle commands we just walked through have landed. Take a few minutes to work through each question on your own — no peeking ahead — and once you submit, I'll jump in so we can go over anything that gave you trouble.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Promote One Bundle to Production

elements.content: Problem 1

Your team owns the bundle `sales_pipeline`. It currently holds one job resource, `daily_sales_etl`, whose single task `bronze` runs the notebook `src/etl/bronze.py` and writes to `${var.catalog}.sales`. You must now promote this one bundle across three environments with these hard requirements:

1. dev reads `dev_catalog`, staging reads `staging_catalog`, prod reads `prod_catalog` (Unity Catalog is Databricks' governed metastore — the namespace that owns catalogs, schemas, tables and volumes).

2. Prod must run as the service principal `8f3d2c1b-0a49-4e77-9c2e-6b5a1d0e7f42` in the workspace `https://acme-prod.cloud.databricks.com`.

3. Only prod may hold the daily 06:00 UTC schedule.

4. Dev must run in development mode: job names prefixed with `[dev <user>]` and schedules paused automatically.

5. No YAML file may be duplicated per environment.

Write the bundle configuration and give the exact release command sequence, showing what each command produces.
Hint: Variables get a default, targets override variables and add target-only settings under `resources:`; dev mode is a target flag, not a separate file.

Worked solution
**Step 0 — repository layout (unchanged by environment).**

```

sales_pipeline/

databricks.yml # the ONLY environment-aware file

resources/daily_sales_etl.yml

src/etl/bronze.py

tests/test_bronze.py

```

**Step 1 — declare the variable once, with a dev default.**

```yaml

variables:

catalog:

description: Unity Catalog the pipeline writes to

default: dev_catalog

```

The default exists so `databricks bundle validate` with no `-t` flag still resolves. It is deliberately the *safe* environment.

**Step 2 — declare the targets and let each override the variable.**

```yaml

bundle:

name: sales_pipeline

include:

- resources/*.yml

workspace:

root_path: /Workspace/Users/${workspace.current_user.userName}/.bundle/${bundle.name}/${bundle.target}

resources:

jobs:

daily_sales_etl:

name: daily_sales_etl

max_concurrent_runs: 1

tasks:

- task_key: bronze

notebook_task:

notebook_path: src/etl/bronze.py

base_parameters:

catalog: ${var.catalog}

targets:

dev:

default: true

mode: development # names become [dev <user>] daily_sales_etl; schedules paused

workspace:

host: https://acme-dev.cloud.databricks.com

variables:

catalog: dev_catalog

staging:

mode: production

workspace:

host: https://acme-staging.cloud.databricks.com

root_path: /Workspace/Shared/.bundle/${bundle.name}/${bundle.target}

variables:

catalog: staging_catalog

```

**Step 3 — attach prod-only settings.** Only the prod target carries `run_as`, an explicit host, a permissions block, and the schedule:

```yaml

prod:

mode: production

workspace:

host: https://acme-prod.cloud.databricks.com

root_path: /Workspace/Shared/.bundle/${bundle.name}/${bundle.target}

run_as:

service_principal_name: 8f3d2c1b-0a49-4e77-9c2e-6b5a1d0e7f42

permissions:

- group_name: data-eng-oncall

level: CAN_MANAGE_RUN

- group_name: analytics-readers

level: CAN_VIEW

variables:

catalog: prod_catalog

resources:

jobs:

daily_sales_etl:

schedule:

quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 6 * * ?"

timezone_id: UTC

pause_status: UNPAUSED

```

The `resources:` block *inside a target* is a target-level override of the shared resource, so the schedule exists only when `-t prod` is used.

**Resolved configuration per target** (what `bundle validate` prints back):

| Target | `${var.catalog}` | Job name in workspace | Schedule | Identity |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| dev | `dev_catalog` | `[dev alice@acme.com] daily_sales_etl` | none / paused | deploying user |

| staging | `staging_catalog` | `daily_sales_etl` | none | deploying user |

| prod | `prod_catalog` | `daily_sales_etl` | `0 0 6 * * ?`, UNPAUSED | service principal |

**Step 4 — release.** Three commands, executed in order by CI:

```bash

databricks bundle validate -t prod # read-only: resolves variables + target, touches nothing

databricks bundle deploy -t prod # uploads synced files, creates/updates the job,

# writes state under .databricks/bundle/prod

databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod # triggers the already-deployed job

```

Expected results: `validate` succeeds with no workspace mutation; `deploy` prints the uploaded files and the created/updated job ID; `run` returns a run URL for *that* job ID and does **not** deploy code first. Because the dev target has `default: true`, a bare `databricks bundle deploy` hits dev, never prod.

Analysis — This is build-once-deploy-many: a single revision of the same files is validated once and resolved differently per target at deploy time [source 5]. The environments themselves are isolated sets of storage, compute and catalog resources, which is exactly the dev→staging→prod promotion path [source 6], and the goal is a structured, governed promotion instead of manual copying and reconfiguration [source 1]. The method works because Databricks Asset Bundle variable resolution happens *after* target selection: `${var.catalog}` is a placeholder, and the target supplies the value. That means the artifact under test in staging is the same artifact shipped to prod — only the resolved variable changes, which is what makes the promotion reliable [source 3].

Typical student errors: (a) copying `databricks.yml` into `databricks-dev.yml`, `databricks-staging.yml`, `databricks-prod.yml` — this reintroduces exactly the drift CI/CD exists to remove, because the three copies can now disagree; (b) hardcoding `prod_catalog` inside `resources/daily_sales_etl.yml`, which sends dev test data into the production catalog; (c) putting the `schedule:` block in the shared job resource so staging also fires a daily run — dev mode pauses dev's schedule, but staging runs with `mode: production` and will happily execute; (d) putting `run_as` or the prod `workspace.host` at the top level of `databricks.yml`, which breaks dev and staging; (e) assuming `bundle run` deploys — it does not, it only triggers what a previous `deploy` created. Generalization: any per-environment difference — catalog, schema, warehouse ID, cluster policy, notification email — should be a variable with a safe default plus a target override, never a forked file.
Problem 2

Given the bundle below, state the value of `${var.catalog}` that each invocation resolves, and say which one wins when two sources disagree.

```yaml

variables:

catalog:

default: dev_catalog

targets:

dev:

default: true

mode: development

variables:

catalog: dev_catalog

staging:

mode: production

variables:

catalog: staging_catalog

prod:

mode: production

variables:

catalog: prod_catalog

```

Invocations:

(a) `databricks bundle validate`

(b) `databricks bundle validate -t staging`

(c) `databricks bundle validate -t prod`

(d) `databricks bundle validate -t prod --var="catalog=prod_catalog_v2"`

(e) `BUNDLE_VAR_catalog=hotfix_catalog databricks bundle deploy -t staging`

Additionally: if an engineer runs (d) against the *prod* workspace and the run succeeds, how many catalogs exist in play, and which one do the scheduled 06:00 runs write to tomorrow?
Hint: Precedence is CLI `--var` > environment variable > target `variables:` > top-level `default:`.

Worked solution
**Rule.** Bundle variable resolution is a strict precedence chain, evaluated top-down until the first value is found:

1. Command-line override: `--var="catalog=..."`

2. Environment variable: `BUNDLE_VAR_catalog=...`

3. Target-level `variables: catalog:` for the selected target

4. Top-level `variables: catalog: default:`

If no `-t` is given, the target marked `default: true` (here, `dev`) is selected *first*, and then the chain runs.

**Answers.**

| # | Command | Selected target | Resolved `${var.catalog}` | Why |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| a | `validate` | dev (default) | `dev_catalog` | target override equals the default here, so both agree |

| b | `validate -t staging` | staging | `staging_catalog` | target override beats the default |

| c | `validate -t prod` | prod | `prod_catalog` | target override beats the default |

| d | `validate -t prod --var catalog=prod_catalog_v2` | prod | `prod_catalog_v2` | CLI flag is highest precedence and *overrides the target override* |

| e | `BUNDLE_VAR_catalog=hotfix_catalog bundle deploy -t staging` | staging | `hotfix_catalog` | env var outranks the target's `staging_catalog` |

**The prod-workspace question.** After (d) deploys, the *job definition* in the prod workspace is resolved with `prod_catalog_v2` baked into `base_parameters.catalog`. The prod target's own `variables:` entry still says `prod_catalog`, but it is no longer consulted — deployment state under `.databricks/bundle/prod` stores the resolved configuration that was applied. So two catalog names are conceptually in play (`prod_catalog` in source, `prod_catalog_v2` deployed), and the 06:00 schedule writes to **`prod_catalog_v2`**, because the schedule lives in the deployed job, not in Git. Re-running `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` *without* `--var` reverts the job to `prod_catalog` — the classic "who changed production?" incident.

Analysis — The method works because variables are *late-bound*: the YAML in Git is environment-agnostic, and the environment is chosen by `-t`, with CLI and environment overrides layered on top for one-off runs. Understanding the chain matters because a CI pipeline that passes `--var` for a hotfix can silently outrank a reviewed target definition, and the deployed job keeps the resolved value until someone deploys again. The high-precedence `--var` flag is a feature (it lets you re-point a single run at a repaired catalog) and a risk (it lets an unattended CI job write to an unintended catalog).

Where students go wrong: they assume the target's `variables:` entry always wins, so they expect (d) to yield `prod_catalog`; they assume `--var` only *adds* a variable rather than replacing it; and they confuse "what is in Git" with "what is deployed". The third mistake is the expensive one: `validate` is read-only, `deploy` is the only command that writes the resolved configuration into the workspace, and `run` merely triggers it. That is why the safe workflow is `validate -t prod` first — it resolves every variable and reports a mismatch before any state changes. Generalization: treat `--var` as break-glass. If a value must differ per environment permanently, it belongs in the target, under review, in Git.
Problem 3

A teammate submits this `databricks.yml` for review. It deploys "successfully" but causes four incidents. Identify each defect, state the concrete symptom it produces, and give the corrected fragment.

```yaml

bundle:

name: sales_pipeline

workspace:

host: https://acme-prod.cloud.databricks.com

resources:

jobs:

daily_sales_etl:

name: daily_sales_etl

run_as:

user_name: alice@acme.com

schedule:

quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 6 * * ?"

timezone_id: UTC

pause_status: UNPAUSED

tasks:

- task_key: bronze

notebook_task:

notebook_path: src/etl/bronze.py

base_parameters:

catalog: prod_catalog

targets:

dev:

default: true

mode: development

variables:

catalog: dev_catalog

staging:

mode: production

variables:

catalog: staging_catalog

prod:

mode: development

run_as:

user_name: alice@acme.com

```
Hint: Look at where the schedule, the catalog, `run_as`, and `mode:` live — and remember what `mode: development` does to names and schedules.

Worked solution
**Defect 1 — the schedule is in the shared resource.** Symptom: staging deploys the job *with* an UNPAUSED 06:00 trigger, so staging fires daily and overwrites staging tables that a reviewer was inspecting; dev escapes only because dev mode pauses schedules. Diagnosis: a shared resource is the wrong scope for something that must exist in one environment. Fix: move the block under `targets.prod.resources.jobs.daily_sales_etl.schedule`.

**Defect 2 — `catalog: prod_catalog` is hardcoded.** Symptom: a dev run of the notebook writes into the production catalog, mixing untested rows with production data — a data-corruption incident, not a config nuisance. Fix: `catalog: ${var.catalog}` with per-target overrides.

**Defect 3 — `run_as` names an individual (`alice@acme.com`).** Symptom: the job starts failing the day Alice changes teams or her token is revoked, and every run is attributed to a person rather than a workload identity in the audit log. Fix: `run_as: { service_principal_name: 8f3d2c1b-0a49-4e77-9c2e-6b5a1d0e7f42 }` under the prod target.

**Defect 4 — `mode: development` under prod.** Symptom: the production job is renamed `[dev alice@acme.com] daily_sales_etl`, its schedule is auto-paused so nobody notices, and a second job appears alongside the real one. Fix: `mode: production` for prod.

**Corrected skeleton:**

```yaml

resources:

jobs:

daily_sales_etl:

name: daily_sales_etl

tasks:

- task_key: bronze

notebook_task:

notebook_path: src/etl/bronze.py

base_parameters:

catalog: ${var.catalog}

targets:

prod:

mode: production

workspace:

host: https://acme-prod.cloud.databricks.com

root_path: /Workspace/Shared/.bundle/${bundle.name}/${bundle.target}

run_as:

service_principal_name: 8f3d2c1b-0a49-4e77-9c2e-6b5a1d0e7f42

permissions:

- group_name: data-eng-oncall

level: CAN_MANAGE_RUN

variables:

catalog: prod_catalog

resources:

jobs:

daily_sales_etl:

schedule:

quartz_cron_expression: "0 0 6 * * ?"

timezone_id: UTC

pause_status: UNPAUSED

```

**Diagnose before you deploy:** `databricks bundle validate -t prod` resolves and prints the configuration without touching the workspace; `databricks bundle summary -t prod` shows the resolved resource tree so you can confirm the schedule exists *only* there. Note also that the top-level `workspace.host` in the original pins every target to the prod workspace — dev and staging would have deployed to production URLs.

Analysis — Every defect here is a *scope* error rather than a syntax error, which is why the bundle validates and deploys happily: nothing is malformed, it is merely attached to the wrong level. The mental model is a three-layer merge — top level (shared, environment-agnostic), target level (environment-specific), and per-resource target override (one resource, one environment). The schedule, `run_as`, `permissions`, catalog and host must each be placed according to which environments legitimately differ.

Common student mistakes: thinking the schedule must live with the job it triggers (it does not — it is an environment attribute); using `user_name` in `run_as` because "it works in dev"; assuming `mode: development` only changes naming and forgetting it also pauses schedules, which turns a mis-set mode into a silent no-run rather than a loud failure; and leaving `workspace.host` at the top level after adding targets. In production you want failures to be loud, not silent. Generalization: whenever you add a setting to `databricks.yml`, ask "would this line be *wrong* in any other target?" If yes, it belongs inside a target.
Problem 4

A team currently maintains three hand-copied bundle files: `dev.yml`, `staging.yml`, `prod.yml`. Each shares 46 configuration lines, of which 11 must be identical in all three environments (bundle name, include patterns, task structure, notebook paths, cluster policy ID, and so on). The team ships a configuration change 24 times a year, and on any given change each file is edited correctly with probability 0.95. Compare this against the single-file bundle from Problem 1 in which the same change is made once with probability 0.95. Quantify (a) the number of edits per change, (b) the number of file pairs a reviewer must diff, (c) the probability that all environments end up consistent, (d) the expected number of drifting releases per year, and (e) why one file is safer even when its edit is wrong.
Hint: Consistency in a 3-copy world requires three independent correct edits: multiply the probabilities.

Worked solution
**(a) Edits per change.** Three copies means the same field is edited 3 times. One file means 1 edit. Reduction: 3 → 1, i.e. two-thirds of the edit work disappears, along with the chance of forgetting one.

**(b) Reviewer diffs.** With 3 files there are C(3,2) = 3 pairwise comparisons to prove agreement (`dev` vs `staging`, `dev` vs `prod`, `staging` vs `prod`). With one file there is 1 change under review. The three-file review cost can also be stated as 3 × 46 = 138 lines to eyeball versus 46.

**(c) Probability all environments agree.** Three independent edits, each correct with p = 0.95:

$$P(\text{all consistent}) = p^3 = 0.95^3 = 0.857375$$

So P(at least one divergent environment) = 1 − 0.857375 = **0.1426**, about 14.3% per change. With a single file, P(all environments consistent) = p = 0.95, so P(inconsistent) = 0.05 — but see (e).

**(d) Expected drifting releases per year.** Three-file world: 24 × 0.1426 ≈ **3.4 drifting releases per year**. Equivalently, expected number of wrongly edited files per release is 3 × 0.05 = 0.15, giving 24 × 0.15 = 3.6 wrong file edits per year — but only the ones that break the *pairwise* agreement show up as drift, hence the 3.4 figure. Single-file world: 24 × 0.05 = **1.2 incorrect configuration revisions per year** — and crucially none of them is a *disagreement* between environments.

**(e) Why one file is safer anyway.** In the three-file world a divergence is *silent*: staging and prod can both validate, deploy and run green while enforcing different catalogs or different cluster policies, so the first evidence is a business report that is wrong. In the single-file world, a wrong edit is wrong *everywhere*: `databricks bundle validate -t staging` fails first, and prod never receives the bad revision, because promotion is ordered dev → staging → prod [source 5]. The one-file failure mode is a loud, consistent halt; the three-file failure mode is invisible drift.

Analysis — The arithmetic is doing real engineering work here: it converts a vague sentiment ("duplicated config is bad") into a number (≈3.4 drifting releases per year). The key structural insight is that consistency across N copies requires N independent correct actions, so the whole-environment consistency probability is p^N, which decays geometrically with the number of environments — three environments already cost you 5% consistency, five would cost 22.6%. Build-once-deploy-many collapses N edits into one edit and turns the remaining risk from *divergence* (different behaviour per environment, undetectable by validation) into *uniform error* (identical behaviour everywhere, detectable in the first environment that deploys) [source 5].

Mistakes students make: assuming 0.95 per file means 0.95 overall; adding probabilities instead of multiplying them; and counting only "wrong edits" without asking whether a wrong edit is *detectable*. That last distinction is the whole point — the environments exist to make errors visible before production [source 6], and a governed, repeatable promotion path is what gives the team visibility into production readiness [source 2]. Generalization: any time a fact must hold in N places, either derive it from a single source of truth or accept a p^N consistency budget; the correct fix is almost always the single source of truth plus per-environment *values*, not per-environment *files*.

actions.text: Let's put everything from this section into one worked problem. We'll take a single bundle and promote it to production, where it needs a different catalog, a service principal identity, and a schedule that only exists in prod. The catch? We may not duplicate any YAML per environment.

So here's the setup. The team owns a bundle called sales_pipeline. Staging and production must read different catalogs, production has to run as a service principal, and only production may hold a daily schedule. Same files, no per-environment copies.
Here's our guiding hint: variables get a default, targets override variables, and any setting you place under a target only applies to that target. That single rule is the whole solution.

Now the worked solution, step by step. Step one declares the catalog variable with a dev default, then overrides it per target: dev_catalog for dev, staging_catalog for staging, prod_catalog for prod. Step two configures the targets — dev uses mode: development, which prefixes names with [dev <user>] and pauses schedules, while staging and prod use mode: production. Step three attaches the prod-only settings: run_as with the service principal, an explicit workspace.host, a permissions block, and the schedule entry living only under the prod target. And step four is the release: validate with -t prod, deploy with -t prod, then run the daily_sales_etl job against prod.

And here's the analysis that ties it together. This is build-once-deploy-many — the same files, the same tests, just different resolved variables. The common pitfall is copying databricks.yml for each environment, which reintroduces exactly the drift that CI/CD is meant to remove. Keep it in one file, and let target overrides do the work.

scenes.title: Choosing an Environment Promotion Strategy

elements.content: Decision — A four-person data team must promote Databricks Asset Bundles across development, staging, and production while a single platform team owns the workspace administration. The decision is hard because the team needs production-like test data to validate pipelines realistically, yet it has limited budget, no dedicated release engineer, and a mandate to keep the same Git-versioned bundle artifact deployable to every environment without duplicating YAML. Isolation strategy determines how much blast radius a bad deploy can cause, how much configuration surface the team must maintain, and whether production-critical workloads can run safely alongside experimental iteration. The design question is not whether to use CI/CD for Databricks Pipelines, which was established earlier in this unit as the cure for manual drift, but where the environment boundary should physically sit inside the Databricks account.

Constraints — 4-person data team plus one platform team; no dedicated release engineer is available to operate or review promotions full time.  •  Separate catalog per environment is required, so Unity Catalog namespace isolation must be enforced by configuration rather than convention.  •  Production-like test data is needed in staging, which means staging must be able to host realistic volumes, credentials, and compute behavior.  •  Limited budget: the number of workspaces, metastores, and service principals must stay as small as the isolation requirement allows.  •  One Git-versioned bundle definition must deploy to all targets without duplicating YAML per environment [source 3].  •  Production must be protected from a dev-time mistake such as a runaway job, a leaked personal token, or an accidental catalog write.

One workspace with bundle targets and variable overrides
+ Cheapest and fastest to stand up: only one workspace, one metastore attachment path, and one set of default permissions to configure.; + All iteration happens in a single place, so developers never context-switch between workspace URLs and the bundle's targets block carries the only per-environment difference.; + Variable overrides for catalog and service principal keep the YAML single-sourced, consistent with the promote-one-bundle pattern taught earlier in this unit.
− Isolation is logical, not physical: compute quotas, secrets, and permissions are shared, so a production job and an experimental job compete for the same cluster limits and the same secret scope.; − A misconfigured target can bind to the production catalog because the boundary is enforced only by variable values, not by an infrastructure edge.; − Interactive interactive iteration in the same workspace where production runs creates a realistic path for a developer's personal credentials to touch production data.
Best for: Teams whose most critical workload is still non-production, or prototypes where speed of iteration dominates the risk of shared blast radius.

A workspace per environment
+ Strongest isolation: each environment has independent credentials, independent compute quotas, and a separate metastore or catalog attachment, so a runaway job in dev cannot consume production capacity.; + Independent service principals mean a leaked dev token grants no production access, which satisfies least-privilege expectations for audited environments.; + Production-like test data can be loaded into staging without any chance of colliding with production job state or secrets.
− Three times the setup: three workspaces, three sets of workspace-level permissions, three service principal bindings, and three configuration surfaces to keep aligned.; − Three times the cost and ongoing maintenance surface, which is exactly the resource the four-person team does not have because there is no dedicated release engineer.; − Every workspace-level setting such as cluster policies, secret scopes, and Git folder credentials must be replicated and drift-checked manually, reintroducing the drift problem CI/CD was supposed to solve [source 3].
Best for: Organizations with a platform team large enough to operate multiple workspaces and regulatory requirements that demand physically separate production tenancy.

Hybrid: dev and staging share a workspace, production runs in its own workspace
+ Production gets a genuine blast-radius boundary because it lives in a separate workspace with its own metastore and its own service principal credentials, so dev-time mistakes cannot reach production compute or secrets.; + Day-to-day iteration stays cheap: dev and staging share one workspace, so the team maintains two workspaces instead of three and keeps one interactive environment for fast feedback.; + Staging can hold production-like test data at realistic volume because it shares the dev workspace's quota but can be wired to a staging catalog, satisfying the realistic-test-data requirement without a third workspace.; + The bundle remains single-sourced: targets in databricks.yml point dev and staging at the shared workspace and prod at the isolated workspace, so no YAML is duplicated per environment.
− dev and staging still share compute quotas, secrets, and some permissions, so a heavy staging load can starve a developer's interactive session.; − Two configuration surfaces must be maintained rather than one, so the operational cost sits between Option A and Option B and must be justified by the production boundary.; − A mistake in the shared dev/staging workspace can still corrupt staging data, meaning staging is not a fully independent rehearsal of production.
Best for: Small teams that need a real production boundary but cannot staff three independently operated workspaces; the recommended call until a second production-critical workload or a compliance requirement forces full separation.

Recommendation: Hybrid: dev and staging share a workspace, production runs in its own workspace — The binding constraints are the four-person team with no dedicated release engineer and the limited budget, which rule out Option B's three independently operated workspaces [source 3]. At the same time, the requirement that production be protected from dev-time mistakes and the requirement for a separate catalog per environment rule out Option A's fully shared workspace, because logical isolation through variable overrides alone cannot stop a leaked dev token or a runaway job from touching production compute and secrets [source 5]. Option C satisfies both edges: it keeps day-to-day iteration to two workspaces and one single-sourced bundle, while giving production its own workspace, metastore, and service principal so the blast radius of a mistake is physically contained. The promotion flow still follows the build-once-deploy-many model, with CI validating the bundle on the pull request and deployment on merge, so the same tested artifact reaches every target [source 5]. Option A remains acceptable only until the first production-critical workload arrives, at which point the shared-boundary risk becomes the dominant cost.

actions.text: Now let's put that single-file idea to the test with a concrete decision. A four-person data team must promote Databricks Asset Bundles across multiple environments. Before we pick a strategy, we need to be explicit about the constraints we're designing against.

Here's the constraint set. We have a four-person data team plus one platform team — that's it. Each environment has its own catalog, so isolation isn't optional. We need production-like test data in staging, which means the staging workspace has to behave like production. And critically: limited budget, with no dedicated release engineer. Remember those last two — they rule out anything that adds ongoing operational overhead.

Option A is one workspace with bundle targets and variable overrides. This is the cheapest and fastest path — a single workspace, a single bundle file, and target overrides swapping catalog names and variables per environment. But understand the tradeoff: compute quotas, secrets, and permissions are all shared, and the isolation is logical, not physical. A runaway job in dev competes for the same cluster resources as production.

Option B is a workspace per environment. This gives you the strongest isolation — independent credentials, independent quotas, genuinely separate blast radii. The cost? Three times the setup, three times the spend, and three times the configuration surface to keep in sync. For a four-person team with no release engineer, that maintenance burden is the real expense, not the license cost.

Option C is the hybrid. Dev and staging share a workspace, so day-to-day iteration stays cheap and fast. Production runs in its own workspace, with a separate metastore and its own service principal credentials. You get real isolation where it matters most — production — while keeping the developer loop lightweight.

So the recommendation is Option C. It gives production a genuine blast-radius boundary while keeping everyday iteration cheap. Option A is acceptable only until the first production-critical workload arrives — at that point, shared quotas and shared secrets become an incident waiting to happen. For the exam, memorize this mapping: constraints in, tradeoff out, recommendation with a stated expiry condition.

scenes.title: Exam Practice: Asset Bundles and CI/CD

questions.question: Your team keeps one Databricks Asset Bundle in Git that must deploy to dev, staging, and prod. Staging and prod currently read the same catalog because the catalog value is hard-coded in the job's notebook task. You have already declared a bundle variable named `catalog` with a default of `dev_catalog`, and staging already has `mode: production`. In which file and which block must you change the value so that only staging points at `staging_catalog`, without duplicating any YAML file per environment?

options.label: In `databricks.yml`, add or edit the `targets` block so that the `staging` target overrides the `catalog` variable with `staging_catalog`, leaving the `variables` block default at `dev_catalog`.
In `resources/<job>.yml`, add a second `resources` block scoped to staging that hard-codes `staging_catalog` in the task's notebook parameters.
Create a second copy of `databricks.yml` named `databricks.staging.yml` inside a `staging/` folder and commit it alongside the main bundle root.
In `databricks.yml`, add a `sync:` include pattern matching the staging environment so the uploaded files carry a staging-specific catalog value.

questions.analysis: The bundle root's `databricks.yml` holds the `bundle` metadata, `include` patterns, the `variables` block with the default value, and the `targets` block where each environment is declared and overridden. The earlier worked problem in this unit established exactly this pattern: declare `catalog` once with a `dev` default, then override per target (dev → `dev_catalog`, staging → `staging_catalog`, prod → `prod_catalog`), because 'No YAML may be duplicated per environment.' Option B is a distractor built on the misconception that resources are per-environment files; resources declare jobs, pipelines, and endpoints once, and per-environment variance belongs in targets. Option C mirrors the real-exam trap of copying YAML per environment, which breaks build-once/deploy-many artifact promotion and defeats the purpose of a single versioned artifact [source 5]. Option D confuses `sync` (which controls what gets uploaded to the workspace) with variable resolution (which happens at validate/deploy time against the target).

questions.question: A developer deploys the bundle with `databricks bundle deploy -t dev`, where the `dev` target is configured as `mode: development`. Select all statements that correctly describe what `mode: development` does or how it interacts with the rest of the lifecycle. (Choose three.)

options.label: It prefixes deployed resource names with the current user, e.g. `[dev alice@corp.com] daily_sales_etl`, so multiple developers can deploy the same bundle into one shared workspace without collisions.
It automatically pauses schedules defined on jobs and pipelines, so the dev deployment does not compete with production for cluster capacity or overwrite production output.
It runs `databricks bundle validate` implicitly and rewrites the resolved `databricks.yml` in the workspace, changing the target back to production on the next deploy.
It enables `--production` on the `databricks bundle run` command so the deployed job executes with production-grade retry semantics and interrupt protection.
It does not upload or mutate any workspace state at all; it only reports what the production deployment would look like.

questions.analysis: `mode: development` is the target-level switch that makes a bundle safe to deploy into a shared workspace: names are prefixed with the deploying user identity, and schedules are automatically paused, which is why the earlier worked problem specified dev uses `mode: development` while staging and prod use `mode: production`. Option C is wrong on two counts: `validate` is a separate command that touches nothing in the workspace, and no command silently retargets a bundle from dev to production. Option D invents a `--production` flag on `bundle run`; no such flag exists in the bundle CLI, and production behavior is controlled by the target's `mode` setting, not by a run-time flag. Option E describes `databricks bundle validate`, which resolves variables and the target but is read-only — it does not apply `mode: development` semantics at all. The engineering point behind build-once/deploy-many is that the same committed artifact is promoted through environments, and only the target changes between them [source 5].

questions.question:
You are the release engineer for a 4-person data team promoting a Databricks Asset Bundle from staging to production for the first time. Two candidates propose release procedures.

Candidate 1: 'Point the bundle at prod by editing `databricks.yml` directly in the Databricks workspace Git folder, then run `databricks bundle deploy -t prod --production` from the workspace notebook so the deployed resources are stamped production-grade. Keep a per-environment copy of `databricks.yml` in a `prod/` folder in Git for auditability.'

Candidate 2: 'Merge the reviewed pull request into `main`, let CI run `databricks bundle validate -t prod`, then have the release job run `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` followed by `databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod` when the schedule should start.'

(a) Identify every incorrect or unsupported claim in Candidate 1 and explain why it is wrong. (b) State why Candidate 2's command sequence is the correct order, including which commands mutate workspace state and which do not. (c) Explain which target setting — not a CLI flag — controls production behavior, and why the same committed bundle can safely serve dev, staging, and prod.
questions.commentPrompt:
Rubric (100 points total):
(1) Incorrect-claim identification (40 pts): explicitly names the non-existent `--production` flag on `bundle deploy` (or `bundle run`) and states that production behavior is set by `mode: production` on the target, not a CLI flag (15 pts); rejects editing `databricks.yml` directly in the workspace Git folder, explaining that authoring happens on a branch and enters the workspace through Git, not by hand-editing deployed state (10 pts); rejects the per-environment `prod/databricks.yml` copy, explaining that per-environment YAML copies break the single-artifact model, cause drift, and are what the target/variables override design exists to avoid (15 pts).
(2) Command sequence and mutation semantics (35 pts): states that `databricks bundle validate -t prod` is read-only — it resolves variables and the target, checks the config, and touches nothing in the workspace (15 pts); states that `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` is the step that uploads synced files, creates or updates resources, and writes deployment state under `.databricks/bundle/<target>` (10 pts); states that `databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod` triggers an already-deployed resource and does NOT deploy code first (10 pts).
(3) Same-bundle promotion rationale (25 pts): names `mode: production` as the target setting controlling production behavior (10 pts); explains that one committed bundle serves all environments because targets override variables (for example `catalog`) and mode, while resources are declared once, implementing build-once/deploy-many artifact promotion (15 pts).
Penalties: answers that merely restate 'CI is good' without naming concrete commands or blocks receive no points in sections (1) and (2). Answers that assert `bundle run` deploys code cap section (2) at 15 pts.
questions.analysis: Reference answer. (a) Candidate 1 contains three defects. First, there is no `--production` flag on `databricks bundle deploy` (or `bundle run`); the CLI does not accept it, and production semantics come from declaring `mode: production` on the target. Second, editing `databricks.yml` directly inside the workspace Git folder bypasses branch, pull request, and CI validation, which is precisely the drift problem CI/CD exists to eliminate — the working model is feature branch → pull request → main, with CI validating the bundle on the PR and deployment happening on merge. Third, maintaining a separate `prod/databricks.yml` copy contradicts the single-artifact promotion model: you would be deploying a different artifact to production than the one tested, which destroys comparability and reintroduces the manual, un-diffable drift this design removes [source 5]. (b) The correct order is validate → deploy → run. `databricks bundle validate -t prod` resolves variables and the target and checks the configuration while touching nothing in the workspace; `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` is the only step in this sequence that mutates workspace state, uploading synced files, creating or updating resources, and recording deployment state under `.databricks/bundle/prod`; `databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod` then triggers the deployed resource and may accept `--params` overrides — it never deploys code first. (c) What controls production behavior is the target's `mode: production` setting, not a CLI flag. The same committed bundle safely serves all three environments because resources — jobs, pipelines, and model serving endpoints, including their permissions block — are declared exactly once, while per-environment differences are expressed as variable overrides inside each target (dev → `dev_catalog`, staging → `staging_catalog`, prod → `prod_catalog`) plus the mode. This is the Databricks realization of the general build-once/deploy-many pattern, in which an artifact is promoted across dev → staging → prod rather than rebuilt per environment [source 5], and it keeps infrastructure resources isolated so pipelines can be tested before promotion [source 6]. Distinguishing junior from production-grade practice here is exactly the stated aim of the course material on applying CI/CD to promote data pipeline artifacts safely and reliably [source 3].

actions.text: Time for some exam practice. The questions ahead are scenario-based, just like the real thing — read each one carefully and pick the option or write the answer you believe is correct, all on your own.
Do your best on each question without second-guessing yourself too much. Once you submit, we'll go through everything together and unpack the reasoning behind each one.

scenes.title: Testing Pipelines Before Deployment

elements.content: Testing Pipelines Before Deployment

Tests are a mandatory gate: no bundle reaches Dev, Staging, or Prod until CI passes. Data teams split live and staging infrastructure to create isolated environments for testing pipelines before promotion [source 6].

Build once, deploy many — the same tested artifact is promoted, never rebuilt per environment [source 5].
Exam objective: given a pipeline defect, select the correct test type — unit, integration, or data-quality.
The Cost of Late Defects

• CI catch: minutes of rework on a pull request

• Prod catch: hours of remediation plus eroded trust

• Worked example: a null-key filter bug broken in one column

– 5M rows/day × 3 days = 15M bad rows to backfill

– ~6 engineer-hours of quarantine, delete, and re-run

– same bug caught by a unit test: ~2 minutes in CI
Testing Pyramid for Data

• Many fast unit tests — transformation logic on small frames, no Spark session required

• Fewer integration tests — read and write real Delta tables in an isolated schema

• Very few end-to-end job runs — full bundle run against a staging target

• Ratio in practice: ~50 unit : ~10 integration : ~1 E2E per pipeline
CI gates every pull request — deployment only on merge [source 5]

actions.text: Before any bundle gets promoted to an environment, it has to pass tests. That's what we're covering now: testing pipelines before deployment. This is the quality gate that sits between your code and every downstream consumer.

The rule here is simple and non-negotiable: tests are a mandatory gate. No bundle reaches dev, staging, or production without passing them. In the Databricks Asset Bundle lifecycle, validation and testing happen before the deploy command, not after.

And this is directly on the exam blueprint. The objective is: given a pipeline defect, select the appropriate test type — unit, integration, or data-quality. So you need to recognize not just what each layer tests, but which one catches which class of defect.
Let's talk about why this matters economically. The cost of late defects is the strongest argument for testing early.

A bug caught in CI costs minutes of rework on a pull request — you fix it, rerun, and move on. The exact same bug found in production costs hours of remediation, plus it erodes trust in the data. Every stakeholder who consumed a wrong number starts double-checking your tables, and that trust is hard to rebuild.
How should we structure those tests? Use the testing pyramid, adapted for data pipelines.

The base is wide and fast: many unit tests on transformation logic, running against small in-memory DataFrames. The middle narrows: fewer integration tests that actually read and write tables. And the tip is thin: very few end-to-end job runs. The pyramid shape matters because it keeps the suite fast enough to run on every commit — invert it and your CI becomes the bottleneck.

Finally, remember where this runs and how promotion works. CI gates every pull request, and deployment only happens on merge — the same tested artifact is then promoted from dev to staging to production. That's build once, deploy many: you never rebuild per environment, so what you tested is exactly what ships. Let's see this in practice with a unit test next.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Unit-Test a Transformation

elements.content: Problem 1

Your team owns the PySpark function `clean_customers(df)` in `src/myproject/transforms.py`. Its contract is: (1) trim leading and trailing whitespace from `email` and lowercase it; (2) drop every row whose `customer_id` is null; (3) keep only the most recent row per `customer_id`, where recency is determined by the `updated_at` timestamp column in descending order. The input DataFrame has schema `customer_id STRING, email STRING, updated_at TIMESTAMP`. Write a pytest unit test that fails if any one of those three rules breaks. Use the following six input rows:

| customer_id | email | updated_at |

|---|---|---|

| C1 | ` ALICE@Example.COM ` | 2024-01-01 10:00:00 |

| C1 | ` Alice@EXAMPLE.com ` | 2024-03-15 09:30:00 |

| C2 | ` Bob@EXAMPLE.com` | 2024-02-01 08:00:00 |

| C2 | `bob@example.com` | 2024-01-15 07:00:00 |

| C3 | `carol@example.com` | 2024-02-10 11:00:00 |

| NULL | `dave@example.com` | 2024-02-11 12:00:00 |

The test must run locally with no cluster and no table read or write, and must assert the row count, key uniqueness, and the surviving trimmed/lowercased email value separately.

Hint: Build the input with `spark.createDataFrame([...], schema)` and compare against an expected DataFrame built the same way; use `assertDataFrameEqual` after `orderBy('customer_id')`, then add separate assertions for count, null keys, uniqueness, and one email value.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Put the transformation under test in context. The contract has three independent rules, so the test must be able to fail for each one. A minimal correct implementation is:

```python

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

from pyspark.sql.window import Window

def clean_customers(df):

df = df.filter(F.col('customer_id').isNotNull())

df = df.withColumn('email', F.lower(F.trim(F.col('email'))))

w = Window.partitionBy('customer_id').orderBy(F.col('updated_at').desc())

return (df.withColumn('_rn', F.row_number().over(w))

.filter(F.col('_rn') == 1)

.drop('_rn'))

```

The order matters for reasoning about the test: dropping null `customer_id` first removes the row that has no key, then the email is normalised, then the window function selects the latest row per key.

Step 2 — Build the input with a literal local Spark DataFrame and call the function:

```python

import pytest

from datetime import datetime

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

from pyspark.testing import assertDataFrameEqual

from myproject.transforms import clean_customers

@pytest.fixture(scope='session')

def spark():

return (SparkSession.builder

.master('local[2]')

.appName('unit-tests')

.config('spark.sql.shuffle.partitions', '2')

.getOrCreate())

def test_clean_customers_trim_lower_drop_null_latest(spark):

schema = 'customer_id string, email string, updated_at timestamp'

input_data = [

('C1', ' ALICE@Example.COM ', datetime(2024, 1, 1, 10, 0, 0)),

('C1', ' Alice@EXAMPLE.com ', datetime(2024, 3, 15, 9, 30, 0)),

('C2', ' Bob@EXAMPLE.com', datetime(2024, 2, 1, 8, 0, 0)),

('C2', 'bob@example.com', datetime(2024, 1, 15, 7, 0, 0)),

('C3', 'carol@example.com', datetime(2024, 2, 10, 11, 0, 0)),

(None, 'dave@example.com', datetime(2024, 2, 11, 12, 0, 0)),

]

input_df = spark.createDataFrame(input_data, schema)

actual = clean_customers(input_df)

expected_data = [

('C1', 'alice@example.com', datetime(2024, 3, 15, 9, 30, 0)),

('C2', 'bob@example.com', datetime(2024, 2, 1, 8, 0, 0)),

('C3', 'carol@example.com', datetime(2024, 2, 10, 11, 0, 0)),

]

expected = spark.createDataFrame(expected_data, schema)

actual_sorted = actual.orderBy('customer_id')

expected_sorted = expected.orderBy('customer_id')

assertDataFrameEqual(actual_sorted, expected_sorted)

# Independent failure-reason assertions

assert actual.count() == 3

assert actual.filter('customer_id IS NULL').count() == 0

assert actual.select('customer_id').distinct().count() == actual.count()

c2_email = actual.filter(actual.customer_id == 'C2').collect()[0].email

assert c2_email == 'bob@example.com'

```

Step 3 — Derive the expected output row by row. C1 has two rows; the latest `updated_at` is 2024-03-15 09:30:00, so its email `' Alice@EXAMPLE.com '` is trimmed to `'Alice@EXAMPLE.com'` and lowercased to `'alice@example.com'`. C2 has two rows; the latest is 2024-02-01 08:00:00, so `' Bob@EXAMPLE.com'` becomes `'bob@example.com'`. C3 has one row, so `'carol@example.com'` survives unchanged. The row with `NULL` customer_id is dropped. Therefore expected row count = 3, distinct customer_id count = 3, and no NULL customer_id appears.

Step 4 — Run the test locally:

```bash

pytest -q tests/test_clean_customers.py

```

The local SparkSession starts in a few seconds, and there is no cluster, no Unity Catalog table, and no Delta write. A failure identifies the broken rule: the `count() == 3` assertion catches a failure to drop nulls or to deduplicate; the `IS NULL` filter catches a missing null-key drop; the distinct-count assertion catches duplicate customer_id values; the C2 email assertion catches a broken trim or lower operation.

Analysis — `assertDataFrameEqual` compares schema and values, so it is stronger than a row-count check; however, Spark does not guarantee row order, so the test sorts both sides by `customer_id` before comparison. If your PySpark version lacks `assertDataFrameEqual`, use `from chispa.dataframe_comparer import assert_df_equality` and call `assert_df_equality(actual_sorted, expected_sorted, ignore_row_order=True)` [source 3]. The edge case that breaks this test in production is a tie in `updated_at` for the same customer_id: `row_number()` picks an arbitrary winner, so two runs can return different emails. Add a deterministic tie-breaker, for example `orderBy(F.col('updated_at').desc(), F.col('email').asc())`, or switch to `rank()` and define an explicit conflict rule. A common mistake is asserting only `actual.count() == 3`: a function that returned the first three rows of the input would pass that assertion but fail the email-value assertion. Another common mistake is comparing `actual.collect()` to a Python list without sorting — the test becomes flaky. Unit tests like this are the fast gate that lets you promote the same transformation artifact through dev, staging, and prod without manual reconfiguration [source 6][source 3].
Problem 2

A teammate submits the following test and claims it proves `clean_customers` is correct:

```python

def test_clean_customers_on_prod():

df = spark.table('prod_customers')

clean_customers(df).write.mode('overwrite').saveAsTable('tmp_clean_customers')

assert spark.table('tmp_clean_customers').count() > 0

```

Classify this as a unit test or an integration test, and justify the classification using the scope and external dependencies of the test. Then rewrite it as a true unit test that uses literal input rows and a literal expected DataFrame, and that would fail if the email is not lowercased. Finally, state one thing the original integration test is still useful for that the unit test cannot cover.
Hint: The discriminator is external dependency and scope, not the fact that both tests use a SparkSession.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Classify. The test reads from `prod_customers`, a real Unity Catalog table; it writes to `tmp_clean_customers`, another real table; and it asserts only that the output row count is greater than zero. It therefore depends on external state (catalog, permissions, existing data, cluster or SQL warehouse) and mutates a table. By definition, that is an integration test, not a unit test. The claim that it proves `clean_customers` is correct is false: the assertion `count() > 0` passes if the function returns any non-empty garbage, including rows with untrimmed uppercase emails, duplicate customer_ids, or null customer_ids.

Step 2 — Rewrite as a true unit test. Construct the input inside the test and compare against an exact expected DataFrame:

```python

from datetime import datetime

from pyspark.testing import assertDataFrameEqual

from myproject.transforms import clean_customers

def test_clean_customers_email_is_lowercased(spark):

schema = 'customer_id string, email string, updated_at timestamp'

input_df = spark.createDataFrame([

('C1', ' MIXED@Example.COM ', datetime(2024, 1, 1, 10, 0, 0)),

], schema)

expected = spark.createDataFrame([

('C1', 'mixed@example.com', datetime(2024, 1, 1, 10, 0, 0)),

], schema)

assertDataFrameEqual(clean_customers(input_df), expected)

```

This test has no table reads, no table writes, no cluster, and no shared mutable state. If `F.lower` is removed, the actual email is `'MIXED@Example.COM'`, the expected is `'mixed@example.com'`, and the test fails.

Step 3 — What the integration test still covers. The integration test is useful for verifying Unity Catalog permissions, Delta Lake write semantics, schema evolution, and end-to-end freshness on real data — checks a unit test cannot make. Use it as a post-deploy verification or staging integration test, not as the gate for the pure transformation logic [source 5][source 6].

Analysis — Definition: a unit test exercises one function in isolation, with all inputs constructed inside the test and no external I/O, network, cluster, or shared mutable state. Preconditions: deterministic, fast (often under a second; a local Spark test is still acceptable at a few seconds), and runnable on every commit. An integration test exercises multiple components — storage, catalog, compute, permissions — and may mutate real state; it is slower, environment-dependent, and can fail for reasons unrelated to the transformation. Common misconception: 'it runs in pytest, so it is a unit test' — the file and runner do not determine the category; dependencies do. Another misconception: 'it uses Spark, so it is an integration test' — a local in-process SparkSession with literal DataFrames is still a unit test of the transformation logic. Edge case: a unit test that accidentally calls `spark.table(...)` or writes Delta output has crossed into integration and must be moved to a slower suite. The exam trap is exactly this distinction: unit tests cover pure transformation logic; reading from or writing to a real table is an integration test [source 6]. Keep unit tests as the fast CI gate and integration tests as the environment-specific verification step before production. Structured, governed promotion across environments should not rely on manual copying or reconfiguration [source 1][source 3][source 5].
Problem 3

Your CI workflow runs three shell steps in order on every pull request:

```bash

databricks bundle validate -t prod

pytest -q

databricks bundle deploy -t prod

```

The test suite contains 12 tests. A developer changes `F.lower(F.trim(F.col('email')))` to `F.trim(F.lower(F.col('email')))` and pushes. On the CI runner, 11 tests pass and 1 test fails in 4.2 s. The shell uses `set -e` semantics (or the CI platform's equivalent, where a non-zero exit stops the job unless the step is explicitly allowed to fail).

(a) State the exit code of `pytest -q` and explain exactly what happens to the deploy step. (b) Write the minimal GitHub Actions job that enforces this gate and ensures `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` runs only after a green test suite. (c) Name one failure mode where the gate itself would be misleading and explain how to handle it.
Hint: Trace exit codes: validate exits 0, pytest exits 1, so the deploy command never starts. `needs:` is cleaner than putting all three commands in one step.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Exit-code trace. `databricks bundle validate -t prod` resolves the target and variables, checks the bundle configuration, and touches nothing in the workspace; with a valid bundle it exits 0. `pytest -q` runs 12 tests: 11 pass and 1 fails, so pytest exits with code 1. Under `set -e`, the shell stops immediately; GitHub Actions also marks the step failed and skips later steps in the same job by default. Therefore `databricks bundle deploy -t prod` never executes, and the bundle is not promoted. The red test blocks the deploy, which is exactly the intended safety property [source 5].

Step 2 — Minimal GitHub Actions gate. Separate the read-only validation and tests from the mutating deploy, and use `needs` so the deploy job is skipped when the test job fails:

```yaml

name: bundle-ci

on: [pull_request]

jobs:

validate-and-test:

runs-on: ubuntu-latest

steps:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4

- run: pip install -r requirements.txt

- run: databricks bundle validate -t prod

env:

DATABRICKS_HOST: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_HOST }}

DATABRICKS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_TOKEN }}

- run: pytest -q

deploy:

needs: validate-and-test

if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'

runs-on: ubuntu-latest

steps:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4

- run: databricks bundle deploy -t prod

env:

DATABRICKS_HOST: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_HOST }}

DATABRICKS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DATABRICKS_TOKEN }}

```

With this structure, a pull request runs `validate-and-test`; the `deploy` job has `needs: validate-and-test`, so if pytest exits 1, GitHub Actions does not start the deploy job. On `main`, after a green run, the deploy job executes. This is the build-once, deploy-many pattern: the same bundle artifact is validated and tested once, then promoted across environments rather than rebuilt per environment [source 5][source 3].

Step 3 — One misleading failure mode: a flaky test. If the failure is caused by nondeterministic row order or a tie in `updated_at` rather than a real regression, the gate blocks a good change and trains the team to bypass it. Handle it by fixing determinism (add a tie-breaker in the window `orderBy`, sort DataFrames before comparison), or by quarantining the flaky test in a separate non-blocking job while keeping the deterministic unit tests as the gate. A second failure mode is `pytest -q` collecting zero tests (exit code 5); treat exit code 5 as a failure in CI, not as success, because a deleted or misnamed test file would otherwise silently remove the gate.

Analysis — The method works because `databricks bundle validate` is read-only while `bundle deploy` mutates workspace state; gating the mutation behind a fast, deterministic unit-test suite gives immediate feedback without touching production [source 5]. The common mistake is putting all three commands in one shell step and forgetting that some CI systems do not use `set -e` by default; then `pytest` fails but the shell continues and `deploy` runs, which is the exam trap. Another mistake is using `|| true` after `pytest`, which masks the failure. Edge case: `databricks bundle validate -t prod` may itself need workspace credentials in CI, but the unit tests should not — they run on a local SparkSession with no table I/O. The gate belongs in the integration phase of the pipeline: build, tests, scans, deploy, then post-deploy verification [source 5]. CI implementation phases include build, tests, scans, and deploy; the unit test is the test phase that produces a pass/fail signal before promotion [source 2]. If the organization has separate dev, staging, and prod environments, the same test gate should run before each promotion, and the artifact should be promoted rather than rebuilt [source 6][source 3].

actions.text: Building on that, let's put it into practice with a fully worked problem: unit-testing a PySpark transformation before the branch is ever merged. Here's Problem 1.

Your team owns a function called clean_customers that takes a DataFrame and does three things: it trims and lowercases the email column, it drops any rows where customer_id is null, and it keeps only the latest row per customer_id. Your job is to write a unit test that fails if any one of those rules breaks.

The hint keeps this simple. Build the input with spark.createDataFrame, pass it straight into clean_customers, and compare the result to an expected DataFrame. Notice the key exam point — there's no cluster dependency on a real table here, and each test runs in a few seconds.

Step one of the worked solution: put the transformation under test in its own importable module, so pytest can call the function directly instead of re-running a whole notebook. Then feed it a small hand-crafted input and assert on the output DataFrame.

Now the analysis. assertDataFrameEqual compares schema and data together, so it catches an unintended change in column types, not just row values. And remember the trap: a good test fails for the right reason — assert row count, key uniqueness, and the trimmed column value separately, rather than just trusting that the function returned without throwing.
Problem 2 reframes the question: a teammate submits a test and claims it's a valid unit test. Your task is to judge whether it actually is one.
The hint points you at the discriminator: external dependency. If the test touches a live table, a remote service, or real cloud storage, it's no longer a unit test.

In the worked solution we classify first — read the test and isolate what it actually depends on. Then we apply the definition: a unit test exercises one function in isolation, with all inputs constructed in-memory. Anything reading from or writing to a real table is an integration test, and that's exactly the exam trap to watch for.
Problem 3 moves to CI. Your CI workflow runs three shell steps in order, and you need to reason about what happens when one of them fails — specifically whether the bundle deploy still proceeds.

The hint tells you to trace exit codes. Validate exits 0, pytest exits non-zero on a red test, and because shell steps abort on a non-zero exit, the deploy step never runs. That's the whole mechanism — a red test blocks the deploy.
Step one is the exit-code trace: run databricks bundle validate — zero. Then pytest — a non-zero return. The shell stops there, so the databricks bundle deploy command is never reached.

And the analysis explains why the method works: databricks bundle validate and the test run are gates, and their exit codes short-circuit the sequence. Run the suite with pytest -q so a single red test genuinely blocks the bundle deploy in CI. That's the pattern to carry into your own pipelines.

scenes.title: Check: Testing Fundamentals

questions.question: A team runs a nightly Databricks job. The notebook reads a Delta table and loads it to another table. When the job fails, an engineer sees that the table `catalog.orders.silver_orders` had 0 rows when the job ran. The team determines that the upstream bronze table never received data because the upstream job was skipped. No code changes were made to the ETL notebook itself. Which category best describes this failure?

options.label: A unit test failure in the silver transformation code
An integration or data-quality problem across pipeline stages
A deployment failure in the Databricks Asset Bundle
A syntax error in the notebook source file

questions.analysis: The transformation code itself is fine; the failure arises because an upstream dependency (the bronze ingestion job) did not produce data before the silver stage ran. Data engineers deliberately split resources into live and staging environments so that ETL services and data pipelines can be tested end-to-end before being promoted to production, precisely because cross-stage defects like this only surface when the whole chain runs together [source 6]. A unit test only exercises a single function or notebook cell in isolation and would not reveal a missing upstream run. A bundle deployment failure would show up during `databricks bundle validate` or `databricks bundle deploy`, not as an empty source table. A syntax error would cause the notebook to fail immediately at parse time. The correct classification is therefore an integration or data-quality issue.

questions.question: A pytest file contains the following: a fixture decorated with `@pytest.fixture(scope="session")` that returns a `SparkSession` built by `SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()`, followed by several test functions that accept this fixture as a parameter but never call `SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()` themselves. What is the primary purpose of this fixture?

options.label: It replaces production data with synthetic data so tests never touch production
It provides a single shared SparkSession reused across all tests in the session, avoiding repeated startup cost
It automatically deploys the bundle to staging before each test runs
It writes test results back to the production Delta table for auditing

questions.analysis: A pytest fixture with `scope="session"` is instantiated exactly once for the entire test session and is injected into each test that declares it as a parameter. Reusing one `SparkSession` avoids the expensive repeated JVM/Spark context startup that would otherwise dominate test runtime. The fixture is a test-infrastructure convenience, not a deployment tool: deployment of a Databricks Asset Bundle happens through `databricks bundle deploy -t <target>`, which is the CI/CD stage that promotes artifacts between isolated environments (dev → staging → prod) rather than something pytest itself performs [source 6]. Option A describes test-data isolation, which is a separate concern handled by test-data management, not by the SparkSession fixture. Option C confuses the fixture with the deployment pipeline. Option D is a clear distractor because writing to production during tests would be dangerous. The Databricks exam expects you to know that fixtures provide shared resources, not lifecycle actions.

questions.question: You are designing the test strategy for a new ETL pipeline that ingests from a cloud object store, transforms with PySpark, and writes to a Delta table. A colleague proposes the following tactics. Which TWO tactics are appropriate for a pre-deployment test suite in a CI/CD pipeline? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Run unit tests against transformation functions using small, in-memory DataFrames
Run integration tests against a dedicated staging environment with staging-only credentials
Deploy straight to production, then run tests against real production data to verify correctness
Replace all automated tests with a manual review of the notebook source code

questions.analysis: The safe pattern is to test at two levels before promoting anything: unit tests that exercise transformation logic on small in-memory DataFrames (fast, isolated, no external dependencies), and integration tests run against a dedicated staging environment that uses staging-only credentials. This mirrors the standard CI/CD principle of promoting artifacts through isolated environments (dev → staging → prod) so that ETL services and data pipelines are proven before they touch production [source 6]. A CI/CD pipeline is explicitly the mechanism that promotes artifacts between environments safely and reliably [source 3]. Options C and D are the classic distractor traps: testing with production data risks corrupting live tables and violates data-isolation principles, and replacing automated tests with manual review removes the repeatability and regression detection that CI provides. Deployment pipelines exist precisely to avoid manual copying and reconfiguration between environments [source 1].

actions.text: Time to check how the testing fundamentals landed. You've got a few questions here covering test types and pytest fixtures — take your time and work through each one on your own.
Once you submit, I'll walk through the reasoning with you, so give it your best shot before you do.
