scenes.title: Worked Problem: Integration and Data-Quality Tests

elements.content: Problem 1

Your bundle `daily_sales_etl` is deployed to target `dev` and writes `dev_catalog.silver.orders` from `dev_catalog.bronze.orders`. For orchestration date `2025-06-15` the bronze snapshot holds 5,412,309 rows; 5,412,297 of them are distinct on the business key `(order_id, order_ts)`, so 12 rows are repeats of a key already seen, and 1,200 of the distinct rows carry `is_test_account = true`, which the silver job filters out. The documented `status` domain is {COMPLETE, PENDING, CANCELLED, RETURNED}. The unit suite `tests/unit/test_clean_orders.py` already passes in 1.4 s. Write the integration test module `tests/integration/test_silver_orders.py` that (a) triggers the deployed job against the dev target, (b) asserts no null `order_id`, (c) asserts no duplicate `(order_id, order_ts)`, (d) allows only the documented status values, and (e) keeps the row count within 0.5 % of the expected silver count. State every expected number, then say which assertions fail when a colleague merges a branch that emits `COALESCE(status, 'UNKNOWN_review')` on 37 rows and whose `LEFT JOIN` to a status-lookup table fans out 12 extra rows.
Hint: Compute the expected row count and the tolerance band *before* writing assertions — the band decides whether the test can pass at all.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Fix the boundary of the test. The unit suite already covers `clean_orders(df)` on small in-memory frames built with `spark.createDataFrame` in 1.4 s. The integration test must cover what the unit test cannot see: catalog resolution, the `run_date` job parameter, the Delta write mode, and the physical schema of the table that consumers read.

Step 2 — Trigger the deployed bundle once per test module. Never call the transformation function directly (that just repeats the unit test), and never re-run the job once per assertion (a run here takes roughly 4 minutes, so four per-test runs would add ~16 minutes and each assertion would read a different commit of bronze):

```

databricks bundle validate -t dev

databricks bundle deploy -t dev

databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t dev --params run_date=2025-06-15

```

Step 3 — Compute the expected numbers first.

$$\text{expected silver rows} = 5{,}412{,}297 - 1{,}200 = 5{,}411{,}097$$

$$\text{tolerance budget} = 0.005 \times 5{,}411{,}097 = 27{,}055 \text{ rows}$$

so the count assertion accepts the band $5{,}411{,}097 \pm 27{,}055$, i.e. roughly 5,384,042 to 5,438,152 rows.

Step 4 — The module. Use a module-scoped fixture so the job runs exactly once:

```python

# tests/integration/test_silver_orders.py

import pytest

from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient

JOB_ID = 4815162342

RUN_DATE = '2025-06-15'

TABLE = 'dev_catalog.silver.orders' # fully qualified: never rely on the session default

STATUS_DOMAIN = {'COMPLETE', 'PENDING', 'CANCELLED', 'RETURNED'}

EXPECTED_ROWS = 5_411_097

REL_TOL = 0.005

@pytest.fixture(scope='module')

def silver(spark):

WorkspaceClient().jobs.run_now(

job_id=JOB_ID, job_parameters={'run_date': RUN_DATE}).result() # ~4 min

return spark.table(TABLE)

def test_no_null_order_id(silver):

assert silver.filter('order_id IS NULL').count() == 0

def test_no_duplicate_business_key(silver):

dupes = (silver.groupBy('order_id', 'order_ts')

.count().filter('count > 1').count())

assert dupes == 0

def test_status_domain(silver):

seen = {r.status for r in silver.select('status').distinct().collect()}

assert seen <= STATUS_DOMAIN, f'undocumented statuses: {seen - STATUS_DOMAIN}'

def test_row_count_within_tolerance(silver):

actual = silver.count()

deviation = abs(actual - EXPECTED_ROWS) / EXPECTED_ROWS

assert deviation <= REL_TOL, f'{actual} rows, {deviation:.4%} off'

```

Note the operator in the duplicate check: `HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`, not `> 0`.

Step 5 — Healthy run. Null `order_id` count = 0 (pass); duplicate key groups = 0 (pass); distinct status = {COMPLETE, PENDING, CANCELLED, RETURNED} which is a subset of the domain (pass); actual = 5,410,890 rows, so deviation $= 207 / 5{,}411{,}097 = 0.0000383 = 0.0038\%$, far inside the 0.5 % budget (pass). All four checks are green.

Step 6 — The `COALESCE(status, 'UNKNOWN_review')` branch. `test_status_domain` fails and its message names the offending value: `undocumented statuses: {'UNKNOWN_review'}` (37 rows). Because the same branch also fans out 12 rows through a `LEFT JOIN`, `test_no_duplicate_business_key` fails with 12 duplicate groups. The row count becomes 5,410,902, so deviation $= 195 / 5{,}411{,}097 = 0.0036\%$ and the tolerance check still passes. Conclusion: the tolerance check is a smoke alarm, not a semantic guard; the domain and uniqueness checks are what catch the regression.

Analysis — Why this method works. An integration test earns its 4-6 minute cost only because it exercises the seam the unit test cannot reach: catalog resolution, the `run_date` parameter, the Delta write, and the table contract that downstream consumers depend on. Data engineers deliberately split resources into live and staging areas precisely so that this kind of pipeline test runs against an isolated environment rather than against data other teams are using [source 6]. That isolation is what makes the later promotion path (dev to staging to prod, each target overriding its own catalog variable) meaningful, because the build-once/deploy-many model assumes the artifact under test is the same one that eventually ships [source 5].

Where students go wrong. (i) Calling `clean_orders()` from the integration test re-tests the unit boundary and never triggers the job. (ii) Triggering the job inside every test function multiplies cost and lets different assertions read different commits of bronze, which produces intermittently failing tests that no one can reproduce. (iii) Writing `HAVING COUNT(*) > 0` marks every distinct key as a duplicate. (iv) Hard-coding a row count copied from last month's run instead of deriving it from the bronze snapshot for the same `run_date`. (v) Writing `spark.table('silver.orders')` without the catalog qualifier, so the test silently reads whichever environment the session defaults to. Edge cases worth naming: an empty bronze partition must fail the count assertion rather than pass vacuously, and a new value in `status` is a contract change that needs the same review as a function-signature change. This generalizes to any hop in a medallion architecture (a layered bronze-to-silver-to-gold data design): test the boundary where the contract lives.
Problem 2

Express rules (b)-(e) from the previous problem as a declarative data-quality check suite in the style of Deequ or Great Expectations rather than as hand-written `assert` statements. The suite runs against `dev_catalog.silver.orders` on the regression run: the table holds 5,412,297 rows, of which 12 rows are duplicates by the business key, 37 rows carry the undocumented status `UNKNOWN_review`, 0 rows have a null `order_id`, and the expected row count derived from the de-duplicated, test-account-filtered bronze snapshot for the same `run_date` is 5,411,097. The suite's row-count tolerance is 0.5 % relative. Compute each metric, state the assertion and threshold you would attach to it, decide pass or fail for each, and state the overall gate result. Also explain how you chose the 0.5 % figure, given that the daily partition receives at most 0.3 % of its rows as late arrivals within 48 hours.
Hint: A metric is a number; an assertion is a policy over that number. Compute the metrics before you argue about thresholds.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Compute the four metrics. Let $N = 5{,}412{,}297$.

Completeness of `order_id`: $(N - 0)/N = 1.000000$.

Uniqueness of `(order_id, order_ts)`: $(N - 12)/N = 5{,}412{,}285/5{,}412{,}297 = 0.99999778$, reported as 0.999998.

Domain compliance of `status`: $(N - 37)/N = 5{,}412{,}260/5{,}412{,}297 = 0.99999316$, reported as 0.999993.

Relative row-count deviation: $|5{,}412{,}297 - 5{,}411{,}097| / 5{,}411{,}097 = 1{,}200 / 5{,}411{,}097 = 0.0002218$, i.e. 0.02218 %.

Step 2 — Attach one assertion per metric, choosing the threshold family explicitly.

| Metric | Assertion | Threshold | Result |

|---|---|---|---|

| Completeness(order_id) | is complete | `= 1.0` | 1.000000 -> PASS |

| Uniqueness(order_id, order_ts) | is unique | `= 1.0` (equivalently `>= 1.0`) | 0.999998 -> FAIL |

| Compliance(status, domain) | is contained in set | `= 1.0` | 0.999993 -> FAIL |

| RowCount deviation vs baseline | is within relative tolerance | `<= 0.005` | 0.0002218 -> PASS |

Step 3 — The gate. Two assertions failed, so the quality gate returns FAIL and the pipeline stops before the artifact is promoted to staging. Only checks explicitly declared non-critical (a warning rather than a blocker) are allowed to fail without failing the gate; completeness and uniqueness of a business key are never warnings in a silver table, because every downstream join depends on them.

Step 4 — The declarative form. In Great Expectations style the four rules are rows of configuration, not code:

```python

suite = [

{'expectation': 'expect_column_values_to_not_be_null', 'column': 'order_id'},

{'expectation': 'expect_column_values_to_be_unique',

'column': 'order_id__order_ts'}, # a derived composite key column

{'expectation': 'expect_column_values_to_be_in_set', 'column': 'status',

'value_set': ['COMPLETE','PENDING','CANCELLED','RETURNED']},

{'expectation': 'expect_table_row_count_to_be_between',

'min_value': 5_411_097, 'mostly': None, 'rel_tol': 0.005},

]

```

In a Deequ-style analyzer you would emit the metrics as a metrics repository (column `completeness`, `uniqueness`, `compliance`, `size`) and attach the same thresholds as check constraints. Either way the *rules are data*: the suite can be versioned, diffed in a pull request, and applied to staging and prod unchanged.

Step 5 — Justify the 0.5 % figure rather than picking a round number. The partition legitimately receives up to 0.3 % of its rows as late arrivals within 48 hours, i.e. up to $0.003 \times 5{,}411{,}097 = 16{,}233$ rows. The tolerance must not fire on those, so 0.3 % is the floor. The tolerance must also be small enough to catch real defects: if one of the 24 hourly source files is never ingested, the loss is about 1/24 = 4.17 % of the partition, and 0.5 % < 4.17 % keeps that failure visible. So the shipped tolerance must satisfy 0.3 % < tolerance < 4.17 %, and 0.5 % is a reasonable point inside that window.

Analysis — Why declarative checks are preferred here. The rule set is expressed as configuration (metric, assertion, threshold, criticality) instead of imperative `assert` statements, which means the same suite can be pointed at `dev_catalog.silver.orders` and `prod_catalog.silver.orders` without editing code, and each run can persist its metric values to a results table so you can see whether completeness has been creeping down for three weeks. That directly supports the CI/CD objective of promoting artifacts between environments safely and reliably [source 3], and it is what makes a post-deploy verification step meaningful rather than ceremonial in a pipeline with dev, staging and prod stages [source 5].

The distinction students most often blur is metric versus assertion. A metric is a number (completeness = 0.999993). An assertion is a policy about that number (must equal 1.0). When the uniqueness check fails, the wrong fix is to relax the threshold until it passes; the right diagnosis is that 12 duplicate rows exist. The threshold is a statement about the data, and moving it hides a defect. A second common error is choosing a tolerance by feel and then discovering it is either so tight that late-arriving data makes the build red every Monday, or so loose that a dropped hour passes silently — the 0.3 % / 4.17 % window above is the reasoning that prevents both.

Edge cases to state explicitly: domain compliance assumes the `status` domain is a documented interface that changes only through review, so a legitimately new status is a suite change, not a data defect; uniqueness on the two-column key requires a derived composite column in frameworks that expect a single column; and a row-count check that passes at 0.022 % deviation tells you nothing about whether the 1,200 test-account rows were filtered, because that error is smaller than a tolerance sized for late arrivals. Volume checks and semantic checks answer different questions.
Problem 3

A nightly integration run on `2025-06-16` compares `dev_catalog.silver.orders` (5,379,001 rows for the `run_date` partition) against the de-duplicated, test-account-filtered bronze snapshot of 5,411,097 rows. The suite uses a relative tolerance of 0.5 %. Compute the absolute row budget, the observed deviation, and the pass/fail decision, and state how many rows are unreconciled beyond the budget. Then explain which tolerance style (absolute, relative, or both) you would ship for (i) a deterministic batch job reading one complete partition and (ii) an Auto Loader streaming silver table, and why asserting an exact row count is a design error once late-arriving data is in scope.
Hint: A tolerance is only meaningful relative to the smallest defect you need it to detect.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Convert the relative tolerance into an absolute budget.

$$\text{budget} = 0.005 \times 5{,}411{,}097 = 27{,}055.5 \text{ rows}$$

Step 2 — Compute the observed gap.

$$|5{,}411{,}097 - 5{,}379{,}001| = 32{,}296 \text{ rows}$$

Step 3 — Normalize.

$$32{,}296 / 5{,}411{,}097 = 0.0061519 = 0.6152\%$$

Step 4 — Decide. $0.6152\% > 0.5\%$, so the check FAILS. The number of rows beyond the budget is $32{,}296 - 27{,}055.5 = 6{,}240.5$, i.e. roughly 6,240 rows more than the tolerance allows. Those 6,240 rows are the ones an engineer must reconcile: the difference is on the order of a quarter of one hourly file, which should send you to the ingestion audit rather than to the tolerance setting.

Step 5 — Choose the tolerance style.

(i) Deterministic batch job, one complete partition: relative tolerance is the correct default because it scales with partition size, but pair it with a small absolute floor so that a tiny partition (say 40 rows in a backfill) cannot hide a 3-row loss inside 0.5 %. Ship `abs_dev <= 0.005 * expected or abs_dev <= 2`, whichever is stricter.

(ii) Auto Loader streaming silver table: neither form is stable on its own, because the table grows while you query it. Assert instead on a bounded window — compare silver rows for a closed `run_date` that the watermark has marked complete — or pin both sides to one instant and compare like with like, for example $\text{silver}(VERSION\ AS\ OF\ t) = \text{dedup}(\text{bronze}(VERSION\ AS\ OF\ t)) - 1{,}200$. Add a growth assertion alongside the count assertion: the count must be non-decreasing between two reads 30 seconds apart, and the read is retried up to a bounded number of times (say 6 attempts, 5 minutes total) before failing. Otherwise you have a race, not a test.

Step 6 — Why exact counts are a design error. A late-arriving file changes the true expected count after the assertion was written. An exact-count test therefore either goes red for a non-defect or gets rewritten with a hard-coded new number on every incident, which trains the team to ignore it. Compare against a *recomputed* baseline for the same commit, not a frozen constant.

Analysis — The key insight is that a tolerance is a discriminating instrument and must be smaller than the smallest defect it is supposed to catch. Two boundaries bracket the choice: the legitimate noise floor (late arrivals, at most 0.3 % here, which the check must tolerate) and the smallest real failure (one missing hourly file out of 24, about 4.17 %, which the check must catch). Any value outside that window is either permanently flaky or permanently blind. Students commonly pick 5 % because it 'stops the build going red'; that value sits exactly above the 4.17 % single-file failure, so the test would silently pass while an entire hour of orders disappeared. Going the other way and asserting an exact count guarantees failures on any delayed data.

Edge cases that decide whether the number means anything: a partition boundary that has not been closed yet by the watermark, a backfill that legitimately rewrites history and changes both sides, a timezone difference between the orchestration `run_date` and the event timestamp used in the comparison, and a `MERGE` that makes a re-run idempotent so the count is unchanged rather than doubled. Each of these changes the expected value without any code defect, which is exactly why the baseline must be recomputed at assertion time from the same source snapshot [source 3]. For streaming, snapshot consistency is the whole problem: reading a Delta table while Auto Loader commits new files makes a count assertion non-reproducible, so you either close the window or use time travel to pin both tables to one version.
Problem 4

A CI pipeline for `daily_sales_etl` has one free slot in the fast lane and four candidate tests. T1 asserts that `clean_orders()` lowercases email and drops rows with a null `customer_id` on a 3-row frame built with `spark.createDataFrame`. T2 triggers the deployed job on target `dev` and then asserts that `dev_catalog.silver.orders` contains no null `order_id`. T3 runs the same assertions against `prod_catalog.silver.orders`, on the argument that 'production data is the only realistic data'. T4 asserts that `dev_catalog.silver.orders` has freshness within 2 hours of ingestion time and that `status` only takes the four documented values. Classify each test as unit, integration, or data-quality, give the execution order for the pipeline, and justify rejecting T3. Then answer the exam-style question: your colleague says 'T2 and T4 both check that order_id is never null, so they are the same test class' — which is the code-correctness test and which is the data-quality test, and what is the rule that tells them apart?
Hint: Ask what is under test: the code that produced the data, or the data itself?

Worked solution
Step 1 — Classify by what is under test, not by what is asserted.

T1 is a unit test. It runs in-process on an in-memory DataFrame, performs no I/O, touches no cluster and no catalog, and finishes in seconds. It answers: does the transformation logic implement the contract?

T2 is an integration test. It crosses three boundaries the unit test cannot see — triggering a deployed job, resolving a catalog, and writing/reading a Delta table — and it is bound to the dev environment. It answers: is the code correctly wired into the platform?

T4 is a data-quality test. It encodes expectations about the data itself (freshness, domain compliance) independently of which code produced it. The same suite would be meaningful if the job were rewritten from PySpark into SQL.

T3 is misclassified rather than merely misplaced: pointing an integration test at `prod_catalog` breaks the isolated-environment rule, because the test data changes underneath the test, the test can pollute a table other teams read, and a genuine assertion failure would page an on-call engineer for a non-incident [source 6].

Step 2 — Execution order. Unit suite first (seconds, no environment), then the integration test (deploy to dev, trigger the job, ~5 minutes of environment-bound work), then the data-quality gate on the table the integration test just produced (cheap aggregate queries, tens of seconds). This ordering is the testing pyramid applied to data: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few full job runs, and the expensive ones only run after the cheap ones are green, so a logic bug never costs five minutes of cluster time to discover.

Step 3 — The exam-style distinction. T2 is a code-correctness test: its failure means the code violated a contract that is knowable in advance, and it would fail on any input that exercises the same path. T4 is a data-quality test: it can fail while the code is perfect, because an upstream system started sending `status = 'UNKNOWN_review'`. The rule is: a correctness test has an expected output derived from the transformation's contract; a quality test has an expectation about the state of the data and only ever fails when the data changes, not when the code changes. In the exam, when both 'integration test' and 'data-quality test' look plausible for the same description, name the system under test: deployed job and catalog wiring -> integration; table contents and their statistical properties -> data quality.

Analysis — The reason integration tests are placed after unit tests is economic before it is architectural: defects caught in CI cost minutes, and the same defects found in production cost hours of remediation plus trust in the pipeline. A fast suite that runs first gives the cheapest possible feedback, while the environment-bound suite runs once the cheap signals are green. Isolated staging areas exist precisely so that pipeline tests can run before promotion without touching live resources [source 6], and the dev-to-staging-to-prod promotion model only holds together if the tests that gate promotion are reproducible in each environment [source 5].

Common misconceptions this problem targets. First, treating a null check on a table written by a job as automatically 'an integration test' or automatically 'a data-quality test' — the classification follows the system under test, not the SQL keyword. Second, assuming more realistic data always means a better test: production data is realistic *and* uncontrollable, so a test that depends on it can pass or fail depending on what another team deployed at 03:00, which is the classic non-reproducible test. Third, using production as the integration environment and calling that 'end-to-end testing'; this also risks write access to shared tables, which is why the isolated dev target with its own catalog override exists in the first place. One useful generalization: if the same assertion text would be sensible in a data contract reviewed with the producing team, it belongs in the data-quality suite; if it would be sensible in a code review of the transformation, it belongs in the unit or integration suite [source 3].
Problem 5

The integration fixture writes its results to the shared table `dev_catalog.silver.orders`. Two CI runs of the same branch start at 10:00:00 and 10:00:20, both trigger the job for `run_date = 2025-06-16`, and the job appends its output (it does not replace the `run_date` partition). The second run's assertions read a table that now contains both runs' rows. A healthy single run produces 5,410,890 rows; the expected count from the de-duplicated, filtered bronze snapshot is 5,411,097 and the tolerance is 0.5 %. Compute what the row-count assertion and the uniqueness assertion report, explain why the failure is a test-design problem that also exposed a real pipeline defect, and rewrite the fixture so that the tests are hermetic — including teardown, given that a crashed runner never executes its own cleanup.
Hint: Isolation in tests is the same idea as an ephemeral environment in CI/CD: never let two runs share a mutable resource.

Worked solution
Step 1 — What the assertions now see. Two healthy runs append, so the table holds $2 \times 5{,}410{,}890 = 10{,}821{,}780$ rows.

$$\text{deviation} = |10{,}821{,}780 - 5{,}411{,}097| / 5{,}411{,}097 = 5{,}410{,}683 / 5{,}411{,}097 = 0.99992 = 99.99\%$$

That is 99.99 % against a 0.5 % budget, so `test_row_count_within_tolerance` fails hard. The uniqueness check also fails: every `(order_id, order_ts)` that ran twice now appears twice, so it reports 5,410,890 duplicate groups. The null check still passes (append does not create nulls) and the status-domain check still passes, which is a useful reminder that a green null check says nothing about duplication or volume.

Step 2 — Two defects, not one. The flaky test exposed a real pipeline defect: the silver job is not idempotent for a given `run_date`, so a retry of the same logical run doubles the data. The fix belongs in the job (a `MERGE` on `(order_id, order_ts)` or `replaceWhere` on `run_date`), and the test should keep failing until that fix lands. The second defect is test design: the fixture writes to a shared, mutable table, so two runs cannot execute concurrently.

Step 3 — Make the tests hermetic. Parameterize the target schema instead of hard-coding it, so each run owns its own namespace:

```

databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t dev \

--params run_date=2025-06-16,silver_schema=it_gh_12345_1

```

The job writes `dev_catalog.${silver_schema}.orders`, and the test reads the same fully qualified name. Two concurrent runs then write to `it_gh_12345_1` and `it_gh_12345_2` and cannot interfere.

Step 4 — Teardown that survives a crash. Put cleanup in a `yield` fixture so it runs even when an assertion fails, and keep the statement idempotent:

```python

@pytest.fixture(scope='module')

def silver(spark, schema_name):

run_job(run_date='2025-06-16', silver_schema=schema_name)

try:

yield spark.table(f'dev_catalog.{schema_name}.orders')

finally:

spark.sql(f'DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS dev_catalog.{schema_name} CASCADE')

```

Because a killed runner never executes `finally`, add a nightly garbage-collection job that drops every `dev_catalog.it_*` schema older than 24 hours, and give the job trigger a timeout (say 30 minutes) so a hung run cannot hold a schema indefinitely. Finally, register the module with `@pytest.mark.integration` and exclude it from the fast lane with `pytest -m 'not integration'`, so the expensive, environment-bound suite runs only after the unit suite is green.

Analysis — The arithmetic matters less than the principle it demonstrates: with a shared mutable target, a test outcome depends on whether another process happened to run at the same time, which makes the test non-reproducible and therefore useless as a release gate. Test isolation is the same discipline as ephemeral environments in a delivery pipeline — each run gets a disposable, addressable slice of the environment so that state cannot leak between runs [source 5]. When the suite is later promoted to staging and production, the same rule applies with higher stakes: tests may read isolated dev resources, never production data that other teams are mutating, because a test that depends on data changing underneath it fails for reasons unrelated to the code [source 6].

Common mistakes and edge cases. Leaving teardown out entirely, which accumulates orphan schemas until the dev catalog hits a name or storage limit. Putting cleanup in a fixture that is not scoped to the resource's lifetime, so a session-scoped schema is dropped while another module still reads it. Using `DROP TABLE` in a fixed order when `DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE` is both shorter and order-independent. Assuming `yield` teardown runs after a `SIGKILL`, which is why a GC sweep is required rather than optional. And the subtle one: making the test pass by loosening the tolerance instead of fixing the non-idempotent write — the 99.99 % deviation is not noise, it is a duplicated dataset, and the correct response is to fix the job and keep the test strict. This is also the point where bundle parameters earn their keep: the same declarative job definition runs in dev, staging, and prod with different variable overrides, so per-run isolation costs one parameter, not a duplicated YAML file [source 3].

actions.text: We've unit-tested transformations, but that's only half the story. Integration and data-quality tests verify that the whole job actually produces trustworthy data. Let's work through five problems that show up in this format.

Problem 1 sets the full scene: your bundle daily_sales_etl is deployed to a target, and you need tests that run the job against the dev catalog, assert no null order_id, assert no duplicate order_id and order_ts pairs, restrict status to documented values, and keep row count within a tolerance of the bronze source.
The hint tells you exactly where to start: compute the expected row count and the tolerance band first, so your assertion has a real number to compare against instead of a guess.
The worked solution walks step by step: fix the boundary of the test, trigger the job with the dev target, then query the resulting Delta table with declarative assertions.

The analysis explains why this method works. An integration test exercises the real job end to end, so it is slower and environment-bound — which is exactly why it runs after the unit suite passes and always against isolated dev resources, never production data.

Problem 2 shifts the focus: express those same rules as declarative data-quality checks in the style of Deequ or Great Expectations. The hint makes the key distinction clear — a metric is just a number, but an assertion is a policy that fails the job when that number breaches a threshold.

Here the solution computes four metrics, applies thresholds to each, and lets the framework enforce them. That is why declarative checks are preferred — they separate what you measure from how you react.

Problem 3 introduces tolerance on a nightly run. A tolerance is only meaningful relative to the source, so the solution converts the relative tolerance into an absolute row-count band before asserting anything.

Problem 4 puts the decision in a CI pipeline with limited time. The question is what is under test: the code that produces the data, or the data itself. That classification decides whether you place a unit test or an integration test in the funnel.

Finally, Problem 5 raises isolation. The fixture writes results to a shared location, and isolation in tests is the same idea as an ephemeral dev cluster — your assertions should only ever see rows your own run produced.

Across all five, the through-line is this: integration tests validate the pipeline end to end in an isolated environment, and data-quality assertions encode expectations as measurable policies. Try them yourself — use the hint if you get stuck, then reveal the solution to compare.

scenes.title: Check: Integration and Data-Quality Testing

questions.question: A team maintains a silver-layer Delta table named silver_orders, produced by a Lakeflow pipeline that reads a bronze table, casts order_date to DATE, deduplicates on order_id keeping the latest ingestion_timestamp, and enforces the contract that customer_id is never null. The team's release gate must catch a defect where a downstream engineer accidentally deletes the deduplication step. Which assertion set is the correct scoping of a data-quality test for the silver-layer table at the release gate?

options.label: Assert that the Lakeflow job finished with state SUCCEEDED and that the job run duration was under the historical median, since a passing job run is sufficient evidence the silver contract holds.

Assert the row count of silver_orders equals the row count of the bronze source, assert order_id has no duplicate values, assert customer_id contains no NULLs, and assert order_date is of type DATE with no values outside the expected business window.
Assert that a single Python function clean_orders(df) returns without raising an exception when given one hand-built three-row DataFrame, and treat that as the release gate for the silver table.
Assert that the workspace bundle validates and deploys successfully against the staging target, since deploy success proves the silver table satisfies its contract.

questions.analysis: The correct scoping for a silver-layer data-quality test is a set of assertions on the data itself in the target environment: uniqueness of the deduplication key (order_id), non-null enforcement of the declared contract column (customer_id), type conformance (order_date as DATE), and completeness or acceptance checks against known business bounds. These tests run after the pipeline writes to silver and read the written table, which is why they are classified as data-quality tests rather than unit tests — the pyramid places many fast unit tests on transformation logic and fewer integration tests that read and write tables [source 3]. Option A is the classic 'validate only that the job completed' trap: a SUCCEEDED job run proves the code executed, not that the deduplication or null-enforcement rules still hold, and it would pass on the very defect described. Option C confuses unit and integration boundaries: a three-row DataFrame fixture in a unit test exercises clean_orders(df) in isolation and is exactly the level at which cheap, fast tests belong, but it cannot certify the silver table in the environment where the defect would surface. Option D confuses deployment success with data correctness; validate and deploy confirm bundle configuration and resource creation, not row-level contracts [source 6].

questions.question: A four-person data team has separate Unity Catalog catalogs per environment (dev_catalog, staging_catalog, prod_catalog) and a limited budget with no dedicated release engineer. The lead proposes pointing the nightly pytest suite that runs assertion checks against silver_orders at prod_catalog so the tests exercise the most realistic data. Select all statements that correctly explain why running these data-quality tests against production data is the wrong choice and what to do instead.

options.label: Reading prod_catalog from an automated CI suite widens the blast radius: a test that legitimately fails can page on-call staff, write test artifacts or temporary tables into production, and consume production compute that other workloads depend on.

Production data frequently contains PII and other sensitive records, so automated suites that are not run under the production service principal and audit trail introduce a governance and access-control violation that would not occur in an isolated environment.

Running tests against production data is acceptable provided the assertions are read-only and the suite finishes in under five minutes, because the isolation requirement applies only to write operations.

The tests should target staging_catalog, whose data is production-like but whose compute quotas, secrets, and permissions are isolated from production, so a red test blocks promotion without touching live tables.

questions.analysis: Data engineers split infrastructure resources into live and staging to create isolated environments where ETL services and pipelines can be tested before promotion to production [source 6]. Option A is correct because the pre-release test stage exists precisely to keep failures from reaching live systems: a red test against prod_catalog would fail in the place where failure is most expensive and could leave side artifacts or contend for production compute. Option B is correct because production catalogs are governed by access controls and audit requirements; a CI suite reading PII without the production identity and approval path is a governance breach, not a testing shortcut. Option D is correct because staging provides production-like data behind an isolation boundary, which is the environment the release gate should block on. Option C is the distractor that mirrors a real misconception — the belief that read-only access makes production testing safe. Isolation covers compute quotas, secrets, and permissions as well as writes, and the only production access that belongs in a release pipeline is a deliberate, approved post-deploy verification step, not the everyday assertion suite [source 5].

questions.question: During a production release review, an engineer reports: 'Our release gate only runs databricks bundle validate, then deploys, then confirms the Lakeflow job transitioned to SUCCEEDED. Since the last release, the deduplication on silver_orders broke and duplicate order_id rows reached consumers.' Which diagnosis most accurately identifies the scoping defect in the release gate?

options.label: The gate is missing unit tests — adding pytest cases for the deduplication helper function would have caught the duplicate rows that reached consumers.

The gate is missing integration and data-quality tests that read the written silver table and assert row-level contracts such as order_id uniqueness, so it validates deployment configuration and job completion rather than the data the pipeline produced.
The gate should have run databricks bundle run with --params overrides against the production target, because the job run command is what deploys the corrected code before execution.
The gate should have used mode: development in the production target so that resource names are prefixed and schedules are paused, which prevents duplicate rows from being written.

questions.analysis: The defect is one of scoping across the testing pyramid: validate and deploy confirm bundle configuration and resource creation, and a SUCCEEDED job run confirms execution, but none of these read the silver table to check its contract. Integration tests that write to and read from tables, plus data-quality assertions on uniqueness, null rates, and acceptance bounds, are the layer that catches duplicate order_id rows before consumers do [source 3]. Option A reflects the misconception that more of the fastest tests at the bottom of the pyramid would substitute for the missing layer; unit tests run against hand-built DataFrames and never see the writer behavior that produced duplicates. Option C confuses the lifecycle commands: bundle run triggers the deployed job and accepts parameter overrides, but it does not deploy code, so it cannot be the fix. Option D misapplies mode: development, which prefixes resource names with the user identity and pauses schedules for developer-targeted deployments — it is not a production configuration and it has no effect on row-level duplication [source 5].

actions.text: Now let's put that into practice with a short check on integration and data-quality testing. Read each question carefully and work through all of them on your own — take your time, and commit to an answer for every one before you move on.
Once you submit, I'll walk through the results with you and we'll unpack anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Environments: Dev, Staging, and Production

elements.content: Environments: Dev, Staging, and Production

• Environment = a set of applications plus the physical infrastructure that enables storage, transfer, processing, and transformation [source 6]

• Objective: identify the four isolation levers in Databricks — workspaces, Unity Catalog catalogs and schemas, compute, and permissions
01 · Workspaces
One workspace per environment isolates compute quotas, secrets, and access — physical, not just logical, separation [source 5]
02 · Catalogs
Unity Catalog: dev_catalog, staging_catalog, prod_catalog — distinct schemas hold raw, clean, curated layers
03 · Compute + Identity
Jobs run as a least-privilege service principal; dev clusters stay small, prod clusters are sized for SLA
Definition. An environment is isolated iff (a) data paths are disjoint, (b) identities differ, and (c) a dev job's write attempt to a prod catalog fails at the permission layer, not in code review.
Worked example. prod_catalog.orders with 12M rows; empty dev_catalog.orders — a hard-coded path writes test rows to live billing and must fail CI [source 6]

Guardrails

Code identical; only config differs

Never write to production tables

No hard-coded prod paths

actions.text: Building on the checkpoint we just worked through, let's look at the concrete pattern the exam expects for separating environments. This is a core objective: identifying how Databricks isolates dev, staging, and production.

The title here names the three classic environments. An environment is simply a set of applications plus the physical infrastructure they run on — so dev, staging, and production each get their own isolated slice of the platform.

That definition matters because teams deliberately split their infrastructure into live and staging areas, precisely so ETL services and pipelines can be exercised before promotion. You test in isolation, then promote with confidence.

Isolation starts at the workspace layer. One workspace per environment keeps compute quotas, notebooks, and job definitions from bleeding across boundaries — your dev notebook can't accidentally reference a production cluster.

The second layer is the catalog. In Unity Catalog, the typical separation is dev_catalog, staging_catalog, and prod_catalog — a three-level namespace where the catalog itself becomes the environment boundary.

Third, compute plus identity. Jobs run as a least-privilege service principal, so the identity executing a dev job simply does not hold write privileges on production tables. That's isolation enforced by permissions, not just by convention.

Here's the formal definition worth committing to memory: an environment is isolated if and only if data, compute, and identity are all separated. Miss any one of those three and you have a leak, not an environment.

Concretely, look at the worked example — prod_catalog.orders with twelve million rows. That table lives in the production catalog, guarded by a production identity, reachable only from production compute. Every clause of the definition is doing real work here.

And the guardrails that keep this honest: the code stays identical across environments, only configuration differs — paths, catalog and schema names, cluster sizes, and identities. That's exactly what bundle targets express. Dev jobs must never write to production tables, and pipelines must never hard-code production paths.

scenes.title: Comparison: Environment Isolation Approaches

elements.content: Dimension  |  Separate workspaces per environment  |  Per-environment catalogs and schemas in one workspace  |  Branch-based development (Git branches as environments)

Isolation strength
Separate workspaces per environment: Separate workspaces provide the strongest isolation because compute clusters, secrets, Unity Catalog credentials, and workspace-level permissions are physically partitioned, so a mis-scoped grant in dev cannot reach production data [source 6].
Per-environment catalogs and schemas in one workspace: Per-environment catalogs in one workspace isolate data and permissions logically through Unity Catalog namespace boundaries (dev_catalog, staging_catalog, prod_catalog), but compute, secrets, and workspace-level identities remain shared across all environments [source 5].
Branch-based development (Git branches as environments): A Git branch isolates only code artifacts; it does not create any boundary around data, compute, or permissions, so two branches deployed to the same workspace read and write the same catalogs and share the same cluster identities.

Cost and overhead
Separate workspaces per environment: A workspace per environment triples the governance configuration surface and typically triples the fixed cost of workspace-level features, since each workspace needs its own metastore attachment, network configuration, and CI service principal [source 6].
Per-environment catalogs and schemas in one workspace: A single workspace with per-environment catalogs adds almost no incremental platform cost, because the existing workspace, compute policy, and metastore are reused; the added overhead is the catalog-and-schema bootstrap and the per-target variable overrides in databricks.yml [source 5].
Branch-based development (Git branches as environments): Branch-based development adds zero infrastructure cost by itself, but teams repeatedly pay hidden cost because branch deploys typically overwrite a shared dev workspace and force reconfiguration whenever two branches collide.

Operational complexity
Separate workspaces per environment: Separate workspaces require duplicated setup of users, groups, secret scopes, cluster policies, and bundle targets, so a four-person team without a dedicated release engineer must maintain three times the configuration surface [source 5].
Per-environment catalogs and schemas in one workspace: Per-environment catalogs keep one workspace, one set of cluster policies, and one bundle, so the only recurring operations are adding a catalog-schema bootstrap step and overriding the catalog variable per target [source 5][source 6].
Branch-based development (Git branches as environments): Branch-based development looks operationally simple because branches are a familiar Git primitive, but it pushes complexity onto humans who must remember which branch maps to which catalog and which compute, a mapping Git does not enforce.

Release safety
Separate workspaces per environment: Separate workspaces give the strongest release safety because a failed staging job physically cannot touch production compute or credentials, and production approvals are enforced at the workspace boundary [source 5].
Per-environment catalogs and schemas in one workspace: Per-environment catalogs give good release safety for data and permissions because production reads and writes prod_catalog only, but a misconfigured variable override can still point staging at prod_catalog since the workspace is shared [source 6].
Branch-based development (Git branches as environments): Branch-based development offers weak release safety because merging a branch is a code event, not a deployment gate; the same artifact can be run against production tables if the branch is deployed without a target override.

Fit for team size and constraints
Separate workspaces per environment: Separate workspaces fit larger or regulated organizations that have a platform team, independent credentials, and budget for per-environment quotas, as in the workspace-per-environment option where isolation and independent quotas justify three times the setup work [source 5].
Per-environment catalogs and schemas in one workspace: Per-environment catalogs fit the common lightweight case, such as a four-person data team with one platform team, limited budget, and no dedicated release engineer, because it delivers separate catalogs per environment with minimal cost [source 5][source 6].
Branch-based development (Git branches as environments): Branch-based development fits individual feature work and code review, not environment provisioning, so it should be paired with either of the other two approaches rather than used as the environment boundary itself.

Artifact and configuration model
Separate workspaces per environment: In separate workspaces the same bundle artifact is deployed to each workspace, and per-target variables override only configuration such as the catalog name, honoring the build-once-deploy-many principle across physical boundaries [source 5][source 6].
Per-environment catalogs and schemas in one workspace: In per-environment catalogs the identical bundle is promoted across targets inside one workspace, and only the catalog variable is overridden (dev to dev_catalog, staging to staging_catalog, prod to prod_catalog) while the artifact bytes stay constant [source 5].
Branch-based development (Git branches as environments): In branch-based development the artifact differs per branch rather than per target, which violates build-once-deploy-many because the code, not just the configuration, changes between environments [source 5].

Worked example under the 4-person constraint
Separate workspaces per environment: Option B, a workspace per environment, would require roughly 3 times the setup and cost for a 4-person team, so it is only justified if the shared-compute risk in one workspace is unacceptable [source 5].
Per-environment catalogs and schemas in one workspace: Option A, one workspace with bundle targets and variable overrides, costs one workspace and one bundle file, with three catalogs bootstrapped once, and satisfies separate catalog per environment plus production-like test data at the lowest cost [source 5][source 6].
Branch-based development (Git branches as environments): Branch-based development would not satisfy the constraint of a separate catalog per environment without additional catalog or target configuration, because branches do not create catalogs, so it fails the exam's isolation requirement.

Exam trap and definition edge cases
Separate workspaces per environment: Definition precondition: an environment is isolated only if compute, permissions, and data boundaries all exist; separate workspaces meet all three, but only after governance setup is duplicated in every workspace [source 6].
Per-environment catalogs and schemas in one workspace: Definition precondition: a catalog boundary must be enforced by Unity Catalog grants and a per-target override in databricks.yml; if the override is missing, staging silently reads prod_catalog and the environment is not isolated [source 5].
Branch-based development (Git branches as environments): Exam trap: treating a Git branch as an environment; branches isolate code only, not data, compute, or permissions, so a branch does not constitute an environment under the exam's definition [source 5][source 6].

Takeaway — Choose separate workspaces per environment when isolation strength, independent credentials, and independent compute quotas outweigh three times the setup cost and duplicated governance configuration [source 5].

Takeaway — Choose per-environment catalogs and schemas in one workspace for the common lightweight pattern: a small team, limited budget, no dedicated release engineer, but a hard requirement for a separate catalog per environment [source 5][source 6].

Takeaway — Never choose a Git branch as the environment boundary: branches isolate code only, not data, compute, or permissions, so pair branching with one of the other two approaches as the real isolation mechanism.
Takeaway — In all cases promote the same built artifact and override only configuration per target, such as the catalog variable, to satisfy build-once-deploy-many [source 5][source 6].

actions.text: Now that we know how to express environments as bundle targets, the real question is: how do you keep those environments isolated from one another? This page compares the main approaches, dimensioned by isolation strength, cost, operational complexity, and release safety. This is a classic exam objective.
Start with isolation strength. Separate workspaces per environment give you the strongest isolation — compute, permissions, and data are cleanly separated. But that strength comes at a price.

That price is cost and overhead. Every separate workspace means duplicated governance setup — the same Unity Catalog grants, the same cluster policies, the same cluster configs, all maintained per environment. Per-environment catalogs inside one workspace are the common lightweight pattern that avoids most of this duplication.

Operational complexity tracks closely with that. Separate workspaces are more moving parts to administer, but their blast radius is smaller — a misconfiguration in dev cannot touch prod. Fewer workspaces mean fewer things to manage, but weaker boundaries.

Here is the trap the exam loves. Never treat a Git branch as an environment. A branch isolates code only — not data, not compute, not permissions. If two people point at the same workspace and the same tables from different branches, they are writing to the same place. That is not isolation.

Whatever approach you choose, one rule holds in all cases: promote the same built artifact and override only configuration per target. The code that passes tests in staging is byte-for-byte the code that runs in production — only the catalog names, paths, and connection settings change.

So to pull it together — assess isolation strength first, then weigh cost, operational complexity, and release safety against your team-size constraint before you commit to an approach. Let's put that reasoning to the test. Given a four-person team with a modest budget, which isolation approach would you choose, and what would you be giving up? Take a moment and discuss it.

actions.topic: Choosing an environment isolation approach under a four-person team constraint
actions.prompt: You have a four-person team with a limited budget. Weigh isolation strength, cost, operational complexity, and release safety. Would you choose separate workspaces, per-environment catalogs in one workspace, or branch-based development? What trade-off are you accepting?

scenes.title: Check: Environment Isolation and Promotion

questions.question: A data platform team uses one Databricks workspace with a single asset bundle repository configured with the targets dev, staging, and prod. Each target overrides the catalog variable (dev_catalog, staging_catalog, prod_catalog) and uses mode: production for staging and prod. Which statement correctly describes what is shared and what is separate across these three environments?

options.label: The bundle source code is shared, but the compute, secrets, and workspace permissions are shared as well because isolation is logical, not physical.
The bundle source code is separate per target, but the Unity Catalog catalogs are shared because they are defined only once in the bundle.
The bundle source code is shared, the Unity Catalog catalogs are separate per target, and the compute, secrets, and workspace permissions are shared because isolation is logical, not physical.
Each target clones the repository into its own workspace, so compute, secrets, and catalogs are all physically separated.

questions.correctAnswer: The bundle source code is shared, the Unity Catalog catalogs are separate per target, and the compute, secrets, and workspace permissions are shared because isolation is logical, not physical.
questions.analysis: The exam expects you to separate logical isolation from physical isolation. In a one-workspace, multi-target setup, the same bundle source is deployed to every target, and variable overrides such as catalog are applied per target, so the catalogs are separate. However, compute quotas, secrets, and workspace permissions are shared because they all live in the same workspace; isolation is logical, not physical (source material). Distractor A is partially correct but wrongly claims the catalogs are also shared; distractors B and D misdescribe how bundle targets and workspaces interact. [source 6]
answer: The bundle source code is shared, the Unity Catalog catalogs are separate per target, and the compute, secrets, and workspace permissions are shared because isolation is logical, not physical.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguish code promotion from configuration override in a Databricks asset bundle promotion workflow? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Code promotion means the same artifact is built once and deployed many times, so the tested bytes are the ones that reach production.
Configuration override means the same bundle source is deployed to a different target with different variable values, such as a different catalog.
Rebuilding the artifact separately for production from a different branch is the recommended way to promote code, because it guarantees the production build is fresh.
Hand-editing production resources in the workspace UI is acceptable when the change is small, because the bundle will reconcile on the next deploy.

correctAnswer: Code promotion means the same artifact is built once and deployed many times, so the tested bytes are the ones that reach production.
Configuration override means the same bundle source is deployed to a different target with different variable values, such as a different catalog.
questions.analysis: Build once, deploy many is the defining property of artifact promotion: the exact artifact that passed tests is what lands in production, so you never test one build and ship another (source material). Configuration override is a separate mechanism: the bytes stay the same while variables like catalog are resolved per target. Option C is the classic trap: rebuilding per environment means production is not running the tested artifact, and promoting from a different branch breaks the branch-equals-environment assumption. Option D is also a trap, because edifying production by hand creates drift that the bundle does not automatically reconcile. [source 5]
answer: Code promotion means the same artifact is built once and deployed many times, so the tested bytes are the ones that reach production.
Configuration override means the same bundle source is deployed to a different target with different variable values, such as a different catalog.

questions.question: A 4-person data team has one platform team, needs a separate catalog per environment, needs production-like test data, and has a limited budget with no dedicated release engineer. They must choose between (A) one workspace with bundle targets and variable overrides, and (B) a workspace per environment. Compare the two options against the constraint set, state clearly which assets are shared and which are separate under each option, and recommend one option with a justification that a certification grader would accept.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Correctly identifies that Option A shares compute quotas, secrets, and permissions and achieves only logical isolation - 25%. (2) Correctly identifies that Option B provides the strongest isolation with independent credentials and quotas at roughly three times the setup and maintenance cost - 25%. (3) Maps both options against the stated constraints (4-person team, one platform team, separate catalog per environment, production-like test data, limited budget, no dedicated release engineer) - 25%. (4) Makes a defensible recommendation tied to the constraints, e.g. Option A for cost and speed or Option B for strict isolation, and explicitly rejects the traps of rebuilding per environment, hand-editing production, and treating branch as environment - 25%.
questions.analysis: A complete answer states that Option A deploys the same bundle source to multiple targets with per-target variable overrides, so code is shared and catalogs are separate, but compute, secrets, and workspace permissions are shared because isolation is logical, not physical. Option B gives physical separation, independent credentials and quotas, at the cost of roughly three times the setup, cost, and configuration surface. The recommendation must be tied to the constraints: with a 4-person team, one platform team, limited budget, and no release engineer, Option A is usually the pragmatic choice, provided you accept logical rather than physical isolation. The traps to explicitly reject are rebuilding the artifact per environment, editing production by hand, and assuming branch equals environment. [source 6][source 5]

scenes.title: Promoting Code and Configuration with Bundles

elements.content: Promoting Code and Configuration with Bundles
Exam objective: describe how a Databricks Asset Bundle moves through dev, staging, and production — one artifact, promoted unchanged, reconfigured per environment.
What a bundle declares

• Code: notebooks and Python files

• Resources: jobs, pipelines, clusters

• Variables: catalog, cluster size, run-as

• All three live in databricks.yml

• One target per environment: dev, staging, prod

• Secrets come from secret scopes, never Git [source 5]
Promotion flow

1. Open a pull request (PR = reviewed change set)

2. CI runs tests + databricks bundle validate

3. Deploy dev, then staging

4. Run integration tests on staging

5. Pass an approval gate

6. databricks bundle deploy -t prod [source 5][source 6]
Worked example: staging must read staging_catalog, prod reads prod_catalog. One YAML, two targets; only the variable changes — the notebook logic is byte-identical [source 1].
Golden rule: build once, deploy many — promote the same artifact, vary only environment configuration [source 5].

actions.text: Now that we've covered how to test pipelines before deployment, let's put it all together and see how code and configuration actually move through environments using Databricks Asset Bundles.

This page maps directly to an exam objective: describe how a Databricks Asset Bundle moves through dev, staging, and production. Expect questions that ask you to sequence the promotion steps or identify what changes at each stage.

First, recall what a bundle actually declares. It contains code — notebooks and Python files — along with resources such as jobs and pipelines, and variables. All of this is described in databricks.yml, and you define one target per environment, typically dev, staging, and prod.

Here's the promotion flow. You open a pull request, which is a reviewed change set. CI runs your tests and executes databricks bundle validate. You deploy to dev, then to staging, run integration tests there, pass an approval gate, and finally run databricks bundle deploy -t prod. Note the -t flag selects the target environment.

Consider this worked example. Staging must read from staging_catalog while production reads from prod_catalog. Only configuration changes between environments — variables, catalog names, cluster sizes, and the run-as service principal. Secrets are injected from secret scopes and are never committed to Git.

Remember the golden rule: build once, deploy many. Promote the same artifact and only swap configuration per environment. And always keep a rollback plan — retain the last known-good commit and re-deploy it rather than editing production resources by hand.

scenes.title: Decision: How to Promote Configuration

elements.content: Decision — Your team maintains a Databricks Lakeflow job called nightly_ingest that reads bronze events, cleans them through clean_customers, and writes silver.orders. It currently runs in one workspace against one production catalog, and the configuration that points it at the right catalog, schema, compute, and secret scope lives partly in a notebook, partly in a hand-edited job parameter, and partly in the heads of two engineers. The team has just won audit requirements that demand a defensible answer to the question 'what exact configuration produced the silver.orders table on the night of March 14?'. At the same time, a hard governance rule states that development jobs must never touch production data, and the platform team has forbidden the creation of a second production workspace for cost reasons. The decision is therefore not whether to promote configuration, but through which mechanism: you must choose an ALM (Application Lifecycle Management, the governed route by which artifacts move from development to production) mechanism that is reproducible, auditable, and rollback-safe, while fitting inside a single production workspace and a small team with no dedicated release engineer. What makes this genuinely hard is that the cheapest mechanism on the first run and the cheapest mechanism over a year are opposite answers, and the exam will ask you to justify the choice from the constraints rather than from a feeling that branching is 'more enterprise'.

Constraints — One team only, with no dedicated release engineer and no budget for a second production workspace, so the mechanism must be operable by the same engineers who write the pipelines.  •  A single production workspace exists; therefore isolation between environments is achieved logically through Unity Catalog catalogs and schemas, compute policies, and permissions rather than through physically separate workspaces [source 6].  •  Strong audit requirements: for any production table, it must be provable which artifact version and which configuration values produced it, and that proof must survive personnel changes.  •  Development jobs must never touch production data, so the mechanism must guarantee that a dev target resolves to dev catalogs and dev compute before any code executes.  •  The production deployment action must be attributable to a named identity that is not an interactive human session, so that the audit log distinguishes machine deployments from ad-hoc debugging.

Bundle variables with per-target overrides in one codebase
+ There is exactly one version of the pipeline code; environment differences are expressed as declared variables (catalog, schema, compute, secret scope) resolved at deploy time by the target, so the artifact is built once and deployed many times, which is precisely the build-once/deploy-many property CI/CD theory prescribes [source 5].; + Every configuration change is a Git commit, so the audit question 'what produced this table?' is answered by a commit hash plus a target name rather than by an engineer's memory.; + The same bundle validate and test suite can run in CI before any production deploy, and a service principal can execute the production deployment so the deploy is machine-attributable.; + Rollback is a revert commit followed by redeploy, which restores both code and configuration together; rolling back one without the other is the classic source of 'works in staging, fails in prod' incidents.
− The team must invest up front in externalizing configuration that is currently hard-coded or tribal knowledge, which is real work before the first benefit appears.; − Variable overrides add a layer of indirection: a developer can no longer read one file to see the whole picture, and a typo in a target override fails only at deploy time unless validation is wired into CI.; − Because there is one workspace, a misconfigured dev target that resolves to a production catalog is a governance incident rather than a technically blocked action; the guardrail is validation and review, not physics [source 6].
Best for: Teams that need reproducibility and auditability from a single code line, accept logical rather than physical isolation, and can afford a short up-front configuration investment.

Long-lived per-environment branches with hand-edited configuration
+ It feels immediately familiar to anyone with a Git background, and the first dev-to-prod promotion can be done by engineers who have never touched an ALM tool.; + Each branch can diverge freely, so an urgent production hotfix does not have to wait behind unreleased development work.
− Long-lived branches guarantee drift: the dev branch accumulates features the prod branch lacks, and the configuration files diverge until merging them is a manual conflict-resolution exercise.; − It directly violates build-once/deploy-many, because the artifact you tested is not the artifact you promote; you are testing a different commit with different configuration, which is exactly the failure mode artifact promotion exists to prevent [source 5].; − Merging configuration by hand across branches is unauditable in practice: Git history records that files changed, but not which resolved values were active at deploy time, so the March 14 question cannot be answered from the repository alone.; − The drift cost compounds; the longer the branches live, the more expensive the eventual reconciliation, and that cost lands on the same four engineers.
Best for: Short-lived hotfix branches off a single trunk, not as a permanent environment mechanism.

Manual edits in the production workspace UI
+ It is by far the fastest mechanism the first time: an engineer adjusts a parameter in the workspace, reruns the job, and the immediate problem is solved.; + It requires no tooling investment, no bundle structure, and no CI integration, so it imposes zero learning curve on the team.
− It is un-auditable in the sense the audit actually cares about: the platform may log that a job definition changed, but the repository does not record which configuration produced a given table, so you cannot reconstruct the March 14 state with confidence.; − It is unreproducible: repeating the deployment for a rebuilt environment, a disaster recovery exercise, or a new catalog requires a human to remember every click.; − It is impossible to roll back cleanly, because there is no previous version to restore to; you are reconstructing the prior state from memory while production is broken.; − It is the single most likely route by which a development job touches production data, because the only thing standing between a dev setting and production is an engineer's care [source 6].
Best for: Nothing that must survive an audit; it is only defensible for a throwaway debugging session in a non-production workspace.

Recommendation: Bundle variables with per-target overrides in one codebase — Two constraints decide this. First, auditability: with per-target variable overrides the deployed configuration is a commit plus a resolved target, so the artifact that produced any table is reconstructible from Git, whereas a branch-per-environment scheme tests one commit and promotes another and manual UI edits leave no repository record at all; this is the build-once/deploy-many property the CI/CD literature identifies as the core of artifact promotion [source 5]. Second, the dev-never-touches-production rule combined with a single workspace means isolation is logical, enforced by Unity Catalog catalog and schema resolution plus compute policy rather than by physical separation [source 6]. Option A makes that resolution explicit and reviewable, so a misconfigured target is caught by bundle validate and the test suite in CI before execution rather than discovered in production. The recommended rollout is: bundle validate and the unit and integration suites must pass as CI gates, the production deployment is executed by a service principal rather than by an interactive user session, and no job reaches production on a Friday without a green suite. A worked example makes the stakes concrete: suppose a production incident costs 4 engineer-hours to diagnose and remediate, and the team ships 20 configuration changes per quarter. If manual UI editing causes even one avoidable incident per quarter, that is 4 x 4 = 16 engineer-hours per quarter, or 64 engineer-hours per year, against an estimated 12 engineer-hours of one-time bundle setup and roughly 1 hour per quarter of override maintenance (12 + 4 = 16 engineer-hours per year). The bundle pays for itself within the first quarter even if it prevents a single incident, and it does so while also producing the audit trail that manual editing cannot produce at any price.

actions.text: So far we've kept environments isolated. Now the practical question: once your bundle works in dev, how do you actually move its configuration into production? Let's frame this as a decision under constraints.

First, the constraints we're working under. One team, no dedicated release engineer, a single production workspace, strong audit requirements, and one hard rule — development jobs must never touch production data. Those constraints eliminate a lot of options before we even start.

Option A: bundle variables with per-target overrides, all in one codebase. The same artifact is deployed everywhere, and each target — dev, staging, prod — supplies its own values. Every change is explicit, lives in Git, and is fully reviewable. This preserves the build-once principle.

Option B: long-lived per-environment branches with hand-edited config. It looks convenient, but it causes drift between branches, makes merges painful, and quietly breaks build-once — the exact thing we just spent the last pages protecting.

Option C: manual edits in the production workspace UI. Fastest the very first time, and that's the trap. It's un-auditable, unreproducible, and impossible to roll back cleanly — the opposite of what an audited production environment demands.

That leaves our recommendation: Option A. Bundle variables with per-target overrides, gated by bundle validate plus the test suite in CI, and a service principal executing the production deployment. Reviewable, reproducible, and consistent with the isolation and audit requirements we just covered.

scenes.title: Lesson Check: Testing and Environment Promotion

questions.question: A data engineer is investigating a defect in the clean_customers(df) transformation that trims and lowercases emails, drops rows with null customer_id, and keeps only the latest row per customer_id. The bug is in the deduplication logic and no tables are read or written. Which test layer is the correct and most cost-effective place to catch this defect?

options.label: A unit test that calls clean_customers on a small in-memory DataFrame and asserts the deduplication result
An integration test that runs the full silver.orders job against the production catalog
A data-quality check that runs on the gold-layer table after the nightly scheduled job completes
An end-to-end job run against a copy of production data taken immediately after the release

questions.analysis: The defect is purely in transformation logic with no table I/O, so it belongs to the unit layer of the testing pyramid — many fast tests on transformation logic using a local SparkSession and assertDataFrameEqual or chispa, taking seconds per test. Option B is wrong because integration tests that read and write tables are slower and environment-bound and are used to verify I/O and cross-table contracts, not pure deduplication logic. Option C misplaces the check at the data-quality layer, which validates declarative rules on produced tables rather than catching a logic bug at the source. Option D is the classic distractor trap of deploying first and testing in production, which the lesson explicitly rejects: defects caught in CI cost minutes, while the same defects found in production cost hours of remediation [source 6].

questions.question: A team is promoting a Lakeflow pipeline from the dev catalog to the staging catalog and then toward production. Select all statements that correctly describe safe promotion between environments. (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Configuration such as the target catalog should be parameterized per environment rather than hard-coded so the same artifact can be promoted unchanged
The promotion should pass through an approval gate before the production deployment step executes
Because the staging run succeeded, the production job can skip the approval gate to reduce lead time
Tests should run against isolated dev resources using a least-privilege service principal, never against production data

questions.analysis: Option A is correct because building the artifact once and deploying it many times requires environment-specific configuration (such as the Unity Catalog target) to be parameterized, not hard-coded per branch, so the same artifact is promoted unchanged [source 5]. Option B is correct because governed promotion includes an approval gate before production deployment [source 5]. Option D is correct because teams split infrastructure into live and staging areas to test ETL services before promotion, and tests must run against isolated dev resources rather than production data [source 6]. Option C is the distractor trap that skips the approval gate; staging success is evidence for promotion, not a substitute for the governance step [source 5].

questions.question: Describe the correct sequence of steps to promote a Databricks pipeline change from pull request to production deployment. Your answer must name the gates and checks at each stage, explain where an approval gate belongs, and explain why configuration such as the target catalog must be parameterized rather than hard-coded per branch.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Correct ordered sequence — pull request triggers CI, build/package the artifact, run the fast unit test suite, then run integration and data-quality tests against isolated dev resources, then an explicit approval gate, then deploy to staging, then production deployment with post-deploy verification and rollback trigger — 40%. (2) Names the gates and checks at each stage (unit suite passes before slower integration tests; tests never touch production data; least-privilege service principal used) — 25%. (3) Explains that the approval gate sits between verified staging and production so a human or policy authorizes the production deploy — 15%. (4) Explains parameterized configuration with the build-once/deploy-many rationale so the same artifact moves unchanged and only environment parameters (such as the target catalog) differ — 20%. Deduct for any answer that tests directly in production, skips the approval gate, or treats configuration as hard-coded per branch.
questions.analysis: A strong answer follows the pipeline order: a pull request triggers continuous integration, which builds and packages the artifact (build once), runs the fast unit suite on transformation logic locally, and then runs the slower integration and data-quality tests against isolated dev resources using a least-privilege service principal, never production data [source 6]. Once staging is verified, an approval gate authorizes the production deployment step, after which post-deploy verification and a rollback trigger apply [source 5]. Configuration such as the Unity Catalog target must be parameterized so that the same artifact is promoted unchanged rather than recompiled per branch, which is the build-once/deploy-many principle [source 5].
