Once you submit, I'll walk through the results with you and we can dig into anything that felt uncertain. Go ahead and give it your best shot.

scenes.title: Observability Signals for Databricks Pipelines

elements.content: Observability Signals for Databricks Pipelines
Monitoring asks "did it fail?" — observability asks "why, where, and how do I fix it?" Data engineers need both to run production pipelines.

data.text: Did the job start, finish, and how long did each task take?
Cluster driver & executor log streams; system.lakeflow.job_task_run_timeline
What exception or error message stopped this specific task?
Spark UI stages, tasks, shuffles, spill, memory
Where is time or memory being wasted — transforms, joins, or partitions?
system.billing.usage, system.access.audit, DESCRIBE HISTORY on Delta tables
What data or metadata changed, who changed it, and how much did it cost?
Expectations / declarative checks (Deequ or Great Expectations-style) [source p.184]
Is the output still correct — or just technically "green"?

elements.content: Mean time-to-detect (MTTD) per signal source — lower is better.

Worked example — the exam trap

Job 7 fails at 02:14. Run history shows Failed; logs show FileNotFoundException on s3://orders/dt=2025-06-01. Status is a symptom; the diagnosis lives in the logs. If a question offers "the job status" as the root cause, it is the distractor.

Data engineers split resources into isolated dev/staging/prod environments to test pipelines before promotion [source 6]; CI/CD promotion moves the same artifact across those environments [source 5][source 3].

actions.text: Now that we understand the mechanics of joins and shuffles, let's shift into the production mindset of this lesson: when a pipeline breaks or runs slow, how do you find out why? This is exactly where the distinction between monitoring and observability becomes critical.
Observability Signals for Databricks Pipelines. As a Data Engineer Associate, you need to know which signal to pull when something goes wrong — and the exam will test exactly that.

Monitoring answers a narrow question: did it fail? Observability answers a much harder one: why, where, and how do I fix it? Production engineers need both — a terminal status of Failed or Timed out is just a symptom, not a root cause. The diagnosis lives in the logs and metrics.

This table is your map. Each observability surface on Databricks — the Jobs run history, driver and executor logs, Spark UI metrics, system tables, and Delta table history — answers a different question. When you see a failure symptom on the exam, your first job is to match it to the correct surface to inspect first.

And here's the payoff — mean time-to-detect across four signal sources: run status, logs, metrics, and data-quality checks. Notice how the low-effort signals often lag far behind the deeper ones. Fast detection comes from wiring up the right signals before you need them.

Let's walk through the worked example: an exam trap. Job 7 fails at 02:14. The tempting answer is 'the job failed, restart it.' The correct answer is to open the run history, drill into the failing task, then read the executor logs to find the real cause. Status is where you start — logs are where you finish. Keep that discipline and you'll handle these questions cleanly.

scenes.title: Interactive: Query Job Run History

content.html:

scenes.title: Check: Monitoring Fundamentals

questions.question: A platform team operates a production Lakeflow pipeline that ingests bronze events with Auto Loader, transforms them into a silver table, and serves a gold aggregate. The team has dashboards showing job duration, cluster CPU, and failure counts, but when a downstream analyst reports that gold revenue figures look wrong for the last three days, no alert fires and the on-call engineer has to manually query intermediate tables to locate the origin of the discrepancy. Which statement best distinguishes the team's current capability from observability in this scenario?

options.label: The team has monitoring because they collect predefined metrics and alerts on known failure signals, but they lack observability because they cannot answer arbitrary new questions about internal state, such as why gold revenue drifted, without writing new queries and redeploying instrumentation.
The team has observability because they have dashboards for duration, CPU, and failures, and monitoring would additionally require distributed tracing across every notebook and cluster.

The team has neither monitoring nor observability, because monitoring only counts as such when it is implemented with Databricks SQL alerts and observability only exists when Unity Catalog lineage is enabled.
The team has observability because they can manually query intermediate tables after the incident, and monitoring is simply the automation of those manual queries into scheduled alerts.

questions.analysis: Monitoring is the practice of collecting predefined metrics against known signals and alerting when those signals cross thresholds; it answers questions you anticipated in advance. Observability is the property that lets you interrogate the system's internal state to answer unanticipated questions, typically by combining rich, high-cardinality telemetry (logs, lineage, metrics, events) with flexible query and drill-down. In this scenario the team monitors three known things (duration, CPU, failure count) but discovers a correctness symptom they never instrumented for, so they fall back to manual ad-hoc queries — the classic gap that observability closes. Option B reverses the definitions. Option C invents extra preconditions (specific Databricks features) that are not required for the concepts to apply. Option D conflates manual querying with observability as a system property, and mischaracterizes monitoring as merely scheduled queries. This distinction matters operationally because, as [source 6] notes, data engineers isolate environments so pipelines can be validated before promotion, and post-deploy verification (including verifying correctness, not just completion) is a standard CI/CD stage documented in [source 5]. Classic deployment-pipeline tooling such as Fabric's Deployment Pipelines advances artifacts across environments [source 1], but it does not give you the internal-state interrogation that observability provides once a pipeline is running in production. Reference: [source 6], [source 5], [source 1], [source 3].

questions.question: An on-call engineer receives four symptom reports from a production Databricks workspace (select all that apply): (1) a scheduled Lakeflow job cluster terminated with exit code 1 before the first task started; (2) an Auto Loader stream is running but the bronze table has received zero new files for six hours despite S3/ADLS arrival; (3) a downstream analyst says the gold aggregate columns are populated but metrics are wrong; (4) an engineer needs to see which upstream tables a silver table was built from and which downstream jobs consume it. Which of the following assignments correctly pair each symptom with the Databricks observability surface best suited to diagnose it?

options.label: Symptom (1) → the run history and cluster event log of the job: examination of the terminated run and cluster driver/stdout logs reveals provisioning or driver-startup failures before tasks executed.

Symptom (2) → the Lakeflow/streaming pipeline event log and Auto Loader checkpoint/state inspection: the stream can be running while a checkpoint or file-notification problem prevents new files from being picked up.

Symptom (3) → structural monitoring on Unity Catalog lineage and column-level profiling of the silver and gold tables: correctness drift requires inspecting data lineage and the actual values, not just run status.
Symptom (4) → the Databricks job run history and cluster CPU metric: lineage information can be derived from job run metrics and therefore does not require a separate catalog surface.

questions.analysis: Each symptom maps to a different Databricks observability surface because the failure modes live at different layers. (1) Driver/cluster startup failures never reach task execution, so the signal is in the run history entry and the cluster event/driver logs — option A. (2) A running stream with zero ingestion is a state problem, not a job failure; Auto Loader's checkpoint, schema inference state, and the pipeline event log are where you look — option B. (3) Wrong-but-populated values are data-quality issues, so you need lineage (which upstream wrote these rows) plus profiling of the actual columns, exactly the kind of declarative checks described in the integration and data-quality test material — option C. (4) Is wrong because lineage is not recoverable from run metrics and CPU readings; it is a catalog-level metadata surface, and using job run metrics to answer lineage questions is a real student misconception. Being able to distinguish these surfaces mirrors the CI/CD principle in [source 5] that post-deploy verification must check the right signal, and the environment-isolation principle in [source 6] that pipelines are tested in staging before promotion so production symptoms are diagnosable. Note also that deployment-pipeline tooling like Fabric's Deployment Pipelines [source 1] governs how content moves between environments but does not, by itself, provide the in-production observability surfaces above; end-to-end automation of these concerns is the explicit goal of the course described in [source 3]. Reference: [source 5], [source 6], [source 1], [source 3].

questions.question: A nightly batch job in a production workspace produced six rows in the run history for the last seven days. In chronological order they were: Succeeded, Succeeded, Failed, Canceled, Skipped, Timed out. The team adopted a conditional-task pattern where task B has a condition 'Run if all dependencies succeed, otherwise mark as skipped'. Which interpretation of the run-history states is correct, and what does each state tell you about where to investigate?

options.label: Failed means the task ran and returned a non-zero result and requires reading the task-level error and its logs; Canceled means a user or a policy (for example, a repair or overlapping schedule) stopped the run before it completed; Skipped means the task never executed because its dependency condition evaluated to false; Timed out means the task exceeded its configured maximum duration, which may or may not indicate a code defect.

Failed, Canceled, Skipped, and Timed out all mean essentially the same thing — the task did not finish successfully — so the engineer should treat them interchangeably and rerun the job rather than distinguishing them.

Failed means the cluster was unavailable; Canceled means the task succeeded on retry; Skipped means the task ran but produced zero rows; Timed out means the task was blocked by a dependency that never completed.
A run marked as Blocked is not a distinct state in Databricks; 'Blocked' is simply a legacy alias for 'Canceled', so both should be interpreted as user-initiated cancellations.

questions.analysis: Databricks run history uses distinct terminal states that encode different root-cause locations. Failed = execution began and returned a non-success result, so the actionable evidence is the task error message plus stdout/stderr and cluster logs. Canceled = execution was stopped externally (a user, a repair run, a superseding schedule, or a policy) — not a code defect — so the question is who or what canceled it, not what the code did. Skipped = the task's condition evaluated to false (for example, the conditional 'Run if' pattern you're using), which is expected behavior and not an error. Timed out = the task exceeded its configured maximum duration; this may reflect a genuine defect (pathological data skew, deadlock) or a sizing/misconfiguration problem, so you must distinguish. Blocked is a genuine and distinct state in the Databricks run-history model: it means a task was prevented from starting because an upstream dependency failed, which is different from Canceled (which stopped a running task). Options B and C collapse or distort the meanings; option D wrongly denies that Blocked is its own state. Being able to discriminate the run-history states is part of post-deploy verification described in [source 5] and is exactly the vocabulary the certification expects, because it depends on terminology like environment and target states that come from standard CI/CD vocabulary [source 3]. Reference: [source 3], [source 5].

scenes.title: Reading the Spark UI: Jobs, Stages, Tasks

elements.content: Reading the Spark UI: Jobs → Stages → Tasks

A slow query is rarely uniform: one stage, and often one task, dominates wall-clock time. Drill Jobs → Stages → Tasks to reach the culprit without guessing. This mirrors the discipline from the previous scene — isolate the offending unit before rewriting code, exactly as you trigger a job against an isolated dev target in the style of a CI/CD pipeline [source 6].
Navigating the Hierarchy

• Job = one triggered action or query

• Stage = a shuffle boundary; every exchange splits stages

• Task = one partition's slice of a stage

• Read the Tasks table: max, median, and p75 duration side by side
Core Metrics to Read

• Task duration: max vs. median — the ratio is the skew signal

• Shuffle read/write and spill (memory + disk)

• Input size, output rows, GC time

• Too few partitions show up as long per-task times

Signature example: 200 tasks report a median duration of 3 s, but one task runs 240 s — a max/median ratio of 80. Max ≈ 240 s + 199 × 3 s = 837 s of the job's total. Fixing one partition (salting the skewed key) drops the stage to roughly 5 s, cutting the job from ~14 min to about 5 s without touching any other stage.

Exam trap: a long total duration is usually one stage — locate the max-task outlier before changing code. Configure the same metric checks in dev/staging so a skew signature never reaches production [source 5].

actions.text: Let's extend what we just practiced on performance troubleshooting. When a query feels slow, the Spark UI is your diagnostic instrument. It organizes execution into a strict hierarchy: Jobs, then Stages, then Tasks.
Navigating that hierarchy matters. You start at the highest level — the Job — and drill downward until you reach the exact Stage and Task where the bottleneck lives. Never guess; let the UI lead you.

A Job maps to a single triggered action or query. A Stage is the set of tasks that can run together without a shuffle boundary. And each Task is one unit of work on a partition. That nesting is what makes drill-down possible.

Here are the metrics to actually read: task duration — maximum versus median; shuffle read and write; memory and disk spill; input size; and GC time. Together these tell you whether you're facing skew, spill, or serialization overhead.

Look at this signature example. Two hundred tasks report a median duration of two seconds, but one task takes four minutes. That spread — maximum far above median — is classic data skew. One partition got far more work than the rest.

And here's the exam trap. A long total duration is usually one stage, and inside that stage, one outlier task. Find the max-task outlier before you touch any code — otherwise you optimize the wrong thing and waste everyone's time.

Bottom line: a slow query is rarely uniform. Jobs, Stages, Tasks — descend the hierarchy, then read duration distribution, spill, and shuffle. That's the diagnostic loop, and it's exactly what the exam expects you to demonstrate.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Diagnose a Skewed Nightly Job

elements.content: Problem 1

A nightly Delta MERGE job on Databricks normally completes in 12 minutes. Last night it took 95 minutes. The Spark UI shows exactly one shuffle stage with 200 tasks. The median task duration is 3 s; the maximum task duration is 9 min 20 s. The stage reports shuffle read of 180 GB and 40 GB of disk spill. The cluster has 10 workers, each with 8 cores. The MERGE joins a 2 TB fact table to a 50 MB dimension table on the key customer_id. The key is not uniformly distributed: one value, C-0001, accounts for 22% of all fact rows. Diagnose the root cause and describe the fix. Then state how you would verify the fix before production.
Hint: Start with Jobs → Stages; sort tasks by duration. Compare max to median and check where the time is concentrated.

Worked solution
Step 1 — localize. In the Databricks Jobs UI, open the failing run and go to the Stages tab. Sort stages by duration; one shuffle stage dominates the 95 minutes. Click that stage and sort the Tasks table by Duration descending. The 200 tasks have median 3 s and max 9 min 20 s = 560 s. Compute the skew ratio: $$\text{ratio} = \frac{560\,\text{s}}{3\,\text{s}} \approx 187.$$ A ratio near 1 means uniform work; here one task is 187× the median. Check concentration: average shuffle read per task is $$180\,\text{GB} / 200 = 0.9\,\text{GB}.$$ If C-0001 is 22% of fact rows, the hot task can read roughly $$0.22 \times 180\,\text{GB} \approx 39.6\,\text{GB},$$ about 44× the average. The 40 GB spill is consistent with one reducer sorting a 39.6 GB partition with insufficient memory. The long tail is in one stage and one task, not spread evenly. Step 2 — diagnose. A max/median ratio above roughly 3× plus heavy shuffle read indicates key skew on the join or MERGE key, not a cluster-size problem. This stage is a wide dependency: the shuffle moves 180 GB because all rows for customer_id are hash-partitioned to one reducer. The single hot reducer becomes the critical path. If the cluster had 20 workers instead of 10, the hot task would still run on one core in one executor; the other 159 cores would idle. Therefore adding workers raises cost without shortening the critical path. Step 3 — fix. First enable Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) skew join handling. In Databricks Runtime, AQE is on by default (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true). Set: spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true; spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor=5; spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes=256MB. AQE detects partitions whose size exceeds factor × median partition size and the threshold, then splits the skewed partition into sub-partitions that run in parallel. If skew persists, salt the hot key: append a random suffix 0..N-1 to C-0001 on the large table and replicate the 50 MB dimension row for C-0001 N times with the same suffixes. Choose N so the hot partition shrinks below the threshold; N=64 gives $$39.6\,\text{GB}/64 \approx 0.62\,\text{GB}$$ per sub-partition. Alternatively, because the dimension is only 50 MB, broadcast the small side: broadcast avoids shuffle entirely if you raise spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (default 10 MB, can be raised up to 8 GB in Databricks). After the change, confirm spill drops from 40 GB to below 2 GB and runtime returns near 12 minutes. Verify the fix in an isolated staging environment before production: data engineers split infrastructure into live and staging areas precisely so they can test ETL services and pipelines before promoting them [source 6]. Use CI/CD to promote the same artifact through dev → staging → prod with an approval gate and post-deploy verification [source 5]. Artifact promotion follows build once / deploy many, not rebuilding per environment [source 5]. This also gives visibility into production readiness [source 2].

Analysis — Why the method works. Spark's shuffle uses hash partitioning: all rows with the same key hash to the same partition. For customer_id = C-0001 with 22% of 2 TB = 440 GB of fact rows, the hash maps every such row to one reducer. That reducer must sort and merge its partition while the other 199 reducers finish in 3 s and sit idle. The critical path is the single hot task, so the job's wall-clock time is bounded by that task plus overhead. AQE skew join works because it subdivides the hot partition at runtime, converting one serial task into many parallel tasks. Salting works because it changes the key so the hash function spreads the hot rows; broadcasting works because it removes the shuffle for the small side. Common mistakes: (1) looking at average task time instead of max/median, which hides the long tail; (2) assuming spill always means memory shortage and buying more RAM per worker, which does not split the hot partition; (3) adding workers, which is the most common wrong answer on the exam because it addresses cost and total throughput, not the critical path; (4) enabling AQE but leaving skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes too high, so the hot partition is not detected; (5) salting only the large table but not the dimension table, which causes missing joins. Edge cases: AQE skew join only applies to supported shuffle operations such as sort-merge joins and grouped aggregations; it cannot fix skew in a range join or a single large file read. If skew is on the MERGE key and the target table is partitioned, also check partition pruning. Generalization: always localize first (Jobs → Stages → tasks), quantify the skew with max/median and shuffle-read concentration, choose a fix that changes the partition or dependency structure, then verify in staging [source 6] and promote through CI/CD with post-deploy checks [source 5].
Problem 2

A teammate proposes doubling the cluster from 10 workers (8 cores each) to 20 workers to fix the 95-minute job. The job still shows one shuffle stage with 200 tasks: median 3 s, max 9 min 20 s, shuffle read 180 GB, disk spill 40 GB. Evaluate the proposal with numbers. Then write the promotion sequence for the actual fix, assuming the team uses Databricks Asset Bundles and isolated dev, staging, and prod catalogs. Name the CI/CD stages and the approval gate.
Hint: Compute how many cores can work on the hot task. Then recall the bundle promotion flow.

Worked solution
Critical path calculation. The job has 200 tasks, but the wall-clock time is not the sum of task times divided by cores. Spark runs one task per core; the hot task takes 560 s. With 10 workers × 8 cores = 80 cores, the hot task still occupies exactly 1 core. With 20 workers × 8 cores = 160 cores, the hot task still occupies exactly 1 core. During those 560 s, the other 159 cores are idle because they have no partition to process. The maximum theoretical speedup from doubling workers on the critical path is 1× for the hot task. Adding workers may reduce queueing or retries slightly, but it cannot split a single task. Cost per hour doubles: 10 workers → 20 workers. If runtime stays near 95 min, cost per run doubles with no SLA improvement. Therefore reject the proposal. The correct fix is to change the data distribution: enable AQE skew join handling and/or salt the hot key, or broadcast the 50 MB dimension. Promotion sequence with Databricks Asset Bundles: (1) developer opens a pull request with the fix; (2) CI runs unit tests, integration tests, and databricks bundle validate; (3) deploy to dev (databricks bundle deploy -t dev) and run integration tests against the dev catalog; (4) deploy to staging and run the same integration tests against staging data; (5) pass an approval gate; (6) deploy to prod with databricks bundle deploy -t prod [source 5]. A bundle declares code, resources (jobs, pipelines), and variables in databricks.yml with one target per environment [source 5]. The artifact is promoted build once / deploy many; only configuration is overridden per target [source 5]. Data engineers isolate staging precisely so pipelines are tested before production [source 6]. Promoting data pipeline artifacts between environments safely and reliably is the core CI/CD skill [source 3]. Deployment pipelines also give visibility into production readiness [source 2]. After production deployment, run post-deploy verification: check that spill drops below 2 GB and runtime returns near 12 min; define a rollback trigger if the stage max/median ratio or spill exceeds thresholds [source 5].

Analysis — This problem tests whether you can distinguish a cluster-size problem from a data-distribution problem. The exam frequently offers 'add more workers' or 'increase cluster size' as a distractor. The diagnostic signal is the task distribution: median 3 s is healthy, max 560 s is pathological, and the ratio is 187×. If all 200 tasks took ~28 s, the median would be high and adding workers could help by increasing parallelism, assuming the shuffle partitions can be split. If the average task time is high and the max/median ratio is near 1, the bottleneck is throughput or too few partitions, not skew. Another edge case: if the job has a single input file larger than the split size, Spark may create one task for that file; AQE skew join will not fix it—you need to repartition or compact files. Common mistakes: (1) computing 'average task time' and concluding the cluster is slow; (2) assuming more workers automatically parallelize a single task; (3) skipping staging and testing the fix directly in production; (4) rebuilding the artifact for each environment instead of promoting the same build. The correct exam answer names AQE skew join, salting, or broadcast, and it verifies in staging before production [source 6].
Problem 3

After enabling AQE skew join, the stage now shows 200 tasks, median 3 s, max 12 s, shuffle read 180 GB, spill 2 GB. The job runs in 13 minutes and the SLA is 15 minutes. A junior engineer wants to salt the hot key anyway. Should you? Justify with numbers. Then consider a variant: what if the max were still 9 min 20 s but spill had dropped to 1 GB? What would you check next?
Hint: Max/median is a screening heuristic, not an absolute rule. Look at absolute times and SLA.

Worked solution
First decision: do not salt. New max/median ratio = $$\frac{12\,\text{s}}{3\,\text{s}} = 4.0.$$ The heuristic says >3× may indicate skew, but the absolute max is only 12 s, and the job meets the 15-minute SLA at 13 minutes. Spill dropped from 40 GB to 2 GB, a 20× reduction, which proves AQE split the hot partition. Salting adds a random suffix to the hot key, replicates the dimension row, and introduces a join correctness risk; it also adds shuffle and CPU overhead. When the critical path is already small and the SLA is met, salting is not warranted. Second variant: if max were still 560 s but spill were 1 GB, then the hot task is still serialized but no longer memory-bound. Check whether AQE actually detected the partition: spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes may be too high (e.g., 256MB while the hot partition is 200MB). Lower it, or check whether the operation is a supported skew join (sort-merge join, grouped aggregation). If the operation is a non-equi join or a range join, AQE skew join does not apply; salt the hot key on both sides or broadcast the small side. Also verify in staging before production [source 6], and use the bundle promotion flow with an approval gate [source 5].

Analysis — This problem teaches that max/median > 3× is a screening heuristic, not a hard threshold. The absolute task time matters: a 4× ratio with a 12 s max is harmless; a 4× ratio with a 9 min max is not. Spill is a symptom of memory pressure on the hot partition, not the definition of skew. A hot partition can be skew without spill if it fits in memory. The exam may give a scenario where AQE is enabled but skew persists; the correct next step is to inspect the skew join threshold and the operation type, not to add workers. Another common mistake is salting without checking whether the hot key is used in a non-equi join; salting a key for a range join does not work because the range predicate spans multiple salted values. Generalization: always verify the fix with end-to-end metrics (runtime, spill, max task time) and promote through isolated environments [source 6] using CI/CD [source 5].

actions.text: Now that we know how to read the Spark UI, let's apply that diagnostic loop to a fully worked exam scenario. Problem one: a nightly Delta MERGE job on Databricks that normally completes in twelve minutes is now taking ninety-five minutes.

Look closely at the numbers the Spark UI gives us. One stage, two hundred tasks, a median task time of three seconds but a max task time of nine minutes and twenty seconds. Shuffle read of a hundred and eighty gigabytes, and forty gigabytes of disk spill. That max-to-median gap is the first clue.
Before you guess at a fix, start with Jobs, then Stages, and sort tasks by duration. Your goal at this step is to localize where the time actually goes — never jump straight to a solution.

Step one, localize: the long tail is concentrated in a single shuffle stage, not spread evenly across the job. Step two, diagnose: a max-to-median ratio above roughly three times, combined with heavy shuffle read, points to key skew on the join or MERGE key — not a cluster-size problem. Step three, fix: enable Adaptive Query Execution skew join handling, and where skew persists, salt the hot key or broadcast the small dimension table. Then confirm that spill actually drops.

Why does this method work? Skew concentrates many rows onto one partition, so a single executor grinds through the hot partition while the others sit idle. That is why adding workers raises cost without shortening the critical path — and it's the most common wrong answer on the exam.
Let's test that instinct with problem two. A teammate proposes doubling the cluster from ten workers to twenty. Should you approve that change?

Work it out before you answer. Compute how many cores can actually work on the hot task. Even with double the workers, the hot partition is still confined to one task, so the critical path barely moves.

The critical path calculation confirms it: the job is bound by that single long task, and horizontal scaling only adds parallel capacity for work that doesn't exist. This problem tests whether you can distinguish a skew bottleneck from a resource bottleneck — the exam returns to this distinction again and again.

scenes.title: Check: Spark UI Diagnostics

questions.question: A Spark UI stage for a Silver-layer aggregation shows 200 tasks. The median task duration is 2.1 seconds, but the maximum task duration is 47.8 seconds. Only three tasks exceed 45 seconds, and each of those three processes a partition roughly 20x larger than the typical partition. Which diagnosis and remediation is MOST appropriate?

options.label: Interpret the max-versus-median gap as data skew caused by an uneven key distribution; remediate by salting the hot keys, pre-aggregating the large partitions, or repartitioning on the skewed key before the aggregation.
Interpret the max-versus-median gap as a GC pause and increase spark.executor.memory for every executor in the cluster.
Interpret the max-versus-median gap as normal variance from cluster scheduling and take no action, because the median duration is healthy.
Interpret the max-versus-median gap as a disk-spill problem and enable automatic broadcast join on all joins in the job.

questions.correctAnswer: Interpret the max-versus-median gap as data skew caused by an uneven key distribution; remediate by salting the hot keys, pre-aggregating the large partitions, or repartitioning on the skewed key before the aggregation.
questions.analysis: Data skew is diagnosed precisely by comparing the maximum task duration to the median (or 75th-percentile) task duration within a single stage. When a small number of tasks dominate the wall-clock time and their input sizes are disproportionately large, the cause is uneven key distribution in a shuffle, not random scheduling noise. Salting, pre-aggregating hot keys, or repartitioning on the skewed key are the standard remediations. Option B misreads the symptom as memory pressure (GC pauses affect all executors, not three tasks). Option C ignores the fact that skewed stages make overall job latency unpredictable and can break SLAs. Option D confuses skew with a spill problem and recommends an unrelated join strategy. This reasoning builds on the observability lesson: Spark UI metrics answer 'why, where, and how do I fix it?', not just 'did it fail?', and choosing the correct surface to inspect first is the exam objective [source 5][source 6].
answer: Interpret the max-versus-median gap as data skew caused by an uneven key distribution; remediate by salting the hot keys, pre-aggregating the large partitions, or repartitioning on the skewed key before the aggregation.

questions.question: A Spark UI stage detail page shows the following executor metrics for a shuffle-heavy join: 'Shuffle Write: 4.2 GB', 'Disk Spill: 18.7 GB', and 'Memory Spill: 3.1 GB'. The job is running on a fixed-size cluster and the stage now exceeds its SLA. Which statements correctly describe how to read these metrics and what to do? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Both memory spill and disk spill indicate that a task could not fit its working set in executor memory; memory spill happens first when data evicts from the in-memory execution pool, and disk spill is the more severe fallback when even serialized in-memory structures no longer fit.

Disk spill is more expensive than memory spill because it involves serializing to disk and subsequent disk reads; reducing the shuffle-read partition size (repartitioning before the join) or increasing shuffle partition count can reduce it.

Because disk spill is present, the recommended fix is always to scale out the cluster by adding more workers before considering any change to the shuffle partitioning strategy, since spill can never be fixed by repartitioning.

Enabling Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) with spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true and coalescing small shuffle partitions can reduce spill by combining tiny partitions that would otherwise become overhead.
Memory spill and disk spill are the same metric reported by two different Spark versions, and neither can be acted upon without enabling Photon.

correctAnswer: Both memory spill and disk spill indicate that a task could not fit its working set in executor memory; memory spill happens first when data evicts from the in-memory execution pool, and disk spill is the more severe fallback when even serialized in-memory structures no longer fit.

Disk spill is more expensive than memory spill because it involves serializing to disk and subsequent disk reads; reducing the shuffle-read partition size (repartitioning before the join) or increasing shuffle partition count can reduce it.

Enabling Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) with spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true and coalescing small shuffle partitions can reduce spill by combining tiny partitions that would otherwise become overhead.
questions.analysis: Memory spill and disk spill describe two levels of the same failure mode: the executor's execution memory pool is exhausted, so Spark evicts data. Memory spill is the first fallback (data remains in the JVM heap in serialized/deserialized form), while disk spill is the more severe fallback that serializes to local disk and later reads it back. Because disk I/O is orders of magnitude slower than in-memory access, reducing the size of each shuffle-read task — through repartitioning before the join or increasing the number of shuffle partitions — directly reduces spill. Enabling AQE and coalescing small partitions reduces per-task overhead and can prevent tiny partitions from wasting memory, which reduces spill. Option C is wrong because it treats scaling as the only remedy; repartitioning is often cheaper and cannot be skipped. Option E is a distractor that invents a false equivalence and unnecessarily ties the fix to Photon. These signals come from Spark UI metrics, one of the core observability surfaces alongside Jobs run history, driver/executor logs, system tables, and Delta table history [source 5][source 6].
answer: Both memory spill and disk spill indicate that a task could not fit its working set in executor memory; memory spill happens first when data evicts from the in-memory execution pool, and disk spill is the more severe fallback when even serialized in-memory structures no longer fit.

Disk spill is more expensive than memory spill because it involves serializing to disk and subsequent disk reads; reducing the shuffle-read partition size (repartitioning before the join) or increasing shuffle partition count can reduce it.

Enabling Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) with spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true and coalescing small shuffle partitions can reduce spill by combining tiny partitions that would otherwise become overhead.

questions.question: A nightly Delta Lake MERGE job that upserts into a Silver table begins failing its SLA. Spark UI shows a shuffle read volume that is stable over time, no skew (max task duration is within 1.5x of the median), but consistent disk spill of ~12 GB per stage. The team cannot increase cluster size because of a budget freeze. Which remediation should be attempted FIRST?

options.label: Enable Adaptive Query Execution (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true) with coalesce and skew-join hints, so Spark can consolidate small shuffle partitions and adjust join strategy at runtime without changing cluster size.
Immediately scale the cluster horizontally by adding more workers, accepting the budget overrun because spill can only be fixed by adding memory.
Repartition the table on disk into far more files and use OPTIMIZE with ZORDER to eliminate the spill, accepting that this does not affect shuffle behavior.
Switch the job from MERGE to INSERT OVERWRITE to eliminate shuffle entirely, since MERGE always spills by design.

questions.correctAnswer: Enable Adaptive Query Execution (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true) with coalesce and skew-join hints, so Spark can consolidate small shuffle partitions and adjust join strategy at runtime without changing cluster size.
questions.analysis: When neither skew nor fluctuating input explains spill, and the constraint forbids adding compute, the correct first move is to reduce per-task working set with configuration rather than hardware. AQE dynamically coalesces small shuffle partitions and can switch a sort-merge join to a broadcast join at runtime, which directly shrinks the memory footprint of each task and can eliminate spill. Option B violates the stated budget constraint and treats scaling as the only remedy, which is false — repartitioning and AQE are non-hardware fixes. Option C conflates storage layout (OPTIMIZE, ZORDER) with shuffle behavior; it can help file-skipping and read performance but does not by itself eliminate shuffle spill. Option D is a distractor that overstates the cost of MERGE; MERGE does perform a shuffle for the join, but INSERT OVERWRITE also shuffles and would break the upsert semantics. This is an example of choosing among scaling, repartitioning, and AQE for a given symptom, using the observability surfaces introduced earlier [source 5].
answer: Enable Adaptive Query Execution (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true) with coalesce and skew-join hints, so Spark can consolidate small shuffle partitions and adjust join strategy at runtime without changing cluster size.

actions.text: This checkpoint picks up straight from that diagnosis work — reading the Spark UI and matching each symptom to the right remediation. Work through each question on your own and commit to an answer before you submit.
Once you're done, I'll walk through the reasoning with you — especially the distinction between skew and resource bottlenecks that we just practiced.

scenes.title: Troubleshooting Ingestion Failures

elements.content: Troubleshooting Ingestion Failures
Failure classes, Delta Lake enforcement, checkpoint locking, and triage order
Failure Classes and Their Signals

• Schema drift: unexpected columns arrive; Delta schema enforcement raises on unexpected columns.

• Malformed or corrupt records: Auto Loader writes them to the rescued data column.

• Permission and credential errors: principal lacks GRANT or secret is expired.

• Source connectivity or timeout, plus rate limiting from the upstream API.
Triage Order (avoids rework)

1. Source reachability — is the endpoint up and answering?

2. Credentials — does the job principal still hold the grant?

3. Schema — has the writer changed shape?

4. Data quality — are individual records malformed?

Checkpoint rule: a checkpoint locks the schema; non-evolutionary changes restart-fail the stream.
Worked example (checkpoint locking)

Stream started 3 days ago (t0 = 72 h) with a 6-column schema.

At t1 an upstream team adds a 7th column.

Restart at t1 fails in ~15 s because the checkpoint holds the original schema; no rows are produced after t0.

Sources: CI/CD pipeline stages, artifact promotion and environments [source 5]; isolated staging areas for testing ETL services before production [source 6]; CI/CD automation that separates junior from production-grade practitioners [source 3].

actions.text: Now that we know where to look for observability signals, let's apply that discipline to a specific and very common failure area: ingestion. Ingestion failures are the single most frequent category of production incidents you'll face, so let's break them down systematically.

Ingestion failures fall into four broad classes, and each one leaves a distinct signal. Schema drift means unexpected columns arrive and Delta Lake's schema enforcement rejects them. Malformed or corrupt records show up in Auto Loader's rescued data column. Permission and credential errors surface as authentication failures. And source connectivity, timeouts, and rate limiting present as unreachable endpoints or throttled requests. Learning to read these signals is what separates fast diagnosis from guesswork.

The triage order matters enormously, because working in the wrong sequence creates rework. Always start with source reachability — is the endpoint up and answering? Then verify credentials. Then check the schema. Only last should you dig into data quality. If you chase a schema error when the real problem is an expired credential, you'll waste an hour on a five-minute fix.

Let's walk through a worked example to make this concrete. A stream started three days ago — that's t0 at seventy-two hours — reading a six-column source. Now a seventh column appears upstream. The stream restart-fails immediately. Why? Because a checkpoint locks the schema at the moment the stream first started. Any non-evolutionary schema change is rejected on restart. The fix isn't to restart harder — it's to evolve the schema deliberately.

So the key takeaway for this page: know your four failure classes, respect the triage order, and remember that checkpoints lock your schema. With that foundation, you're ready to diagnose and fix a real failing stream in our next worked problem.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: Fix a Failing Streaming Ingestion

elements.content: Problem 1

Acme Retail runs a Databricks Auto Loader streaming ingestion job that reads newline-delimited JSON order events from s3://acme-raw/orders/ and appends them to the bronze Delta table main.bronze.orders_raw. The stream is configured with a checkpoint at s3://acme-checkpoints/bronze/orders_raw/ and a schema location at s3://acme-checkpoints/bronze/orders_raw/schema/. It has run continuously for 183 days, ingesting roughly 11 GB and 4.2 million events per day. On day 184 the upstream producer ships a new event contract that (a) adds a new nullable string column loyalty_tier and (b) renames the existing column cust_id to customer_id. No file is truncated, no JSON is malformed, and the producer certifies zero duplicate or dropped events. Within two minutes of the first new file landing, the stream fails with an Auto Loader schema-inference error stating that the schema inferred from the new file does not match the schema recorded for the stream. The downstream silver pipeline main.silver.orders is a Delta MERGE keyed on cust_id and is now stalled. Determine (1) what the error does and does not tell you, (2) the correct fix for each of the two contract changes, and (3) how to stop a single unparseable record from ever failing an entire micro-batch again.
Hint: Ask first whether the contract change adds information or redefines an existing column — those two cases have different fixes.

Worked solution
Step 1 — Read the error precisely. The message is a schema-INFERENCE mismatch against the schema recorded for the stream; it is not a data-corruption error and not a bad-record error. Three facts confirm the diagnosis. First, the message names two schemas and compares them; it never mentions a malformed payload, a corrupt record, or a rescued-data entry. Second, the failure begins at the exact arrival of the first file produced by the new contract, not intermittently after a random file. Third, the last successful run in Jobs run history (or system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline) processed every file produced before the contract deploy. Metadata mismatches fail deterministically and at once; malformed-data failures fail intermittently depending on which file arrives. Nothing already in bronze is damaged: 183 days × 11 GB = 2,013 GB (about 2.01 TB) and 183 × 4.2 million = 768.6 million rows were all ingested under the old contract, and a schema comparison never rewrites them. Auto Loader compares the schema it infers at read time with the schema it persisted earlier, so this error is a metadata reconciliation failure, not lost data.

Step 2a — Classify change (a): adding loyalty_tier is an ADDITIVE (evolutionary) change. Auto Loader can absorb it in place. Set .option('cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode', 'addNewColumns') (this is also the default when no explicit schema is supplied at stream start), restart the stream against the SAME checkpoint, and the schema recorded in the schema location is extended with loyalty_tier. Historical rows read back as NULL for that column, which is semantically correct: before day 184 the field did not exist. Restart cost here is minutes, not hours. Note that mergeSchema is the analogous option on batch Parquet/Delta readers; for a streaming Auto Loader source the option that governs this behaviour is cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode.

Step 2b — Classify change (b): renaming cust_id to customer_id is NOT evolutionary. A rename is invisible as a rename. Auto Loader observes only 'old column absent, new column present' — the same observation it would make for a drop plus an add. If you simply turn on addNewColumns and reuse the old checkpoint, the stream restarts GREEN and is silently wrong: customer_id is added to the schema, cust_id remains in the schema and is now NULL for every new row. The downstream MERGE keyed on cust_id stops matching, and you have produced silent data loss with a healthy-looking pipeline. This is the exam distractor — changing only the reader option while reusing the old checkpoint leaves the stream broken (or worse, quietly corrupted). The correct fix is a full refresh into a NEW checkpoint and a NEW table: create main.bronze.orders_raw_v2 with the new contract schema, point it at a fresh checkpoint such as s3://acme-checkpoints/bronze/orders_raw_v2/, and backfill all 183 days from the retained source files. Auto Loader is a file reader, so the raw JSON is still the source of truth and can be replayed. Once v2 is verified, repoint the silver layer at v2 through a view or table alias so no downstream consumer code changes, and keep v1 available for rollback for one contract cycle (blue/green style) [source 5].

Step 3 — Protect the downstream. Enable the rescued-data column so that one unparseable record can never fail a batch. For Auto Loader, cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode = 'rescue' (with the rescued data column, named _rescued_data by default, enabled via rescuedDataColumn in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines) means a record that does not match the declared schema is not dropped and does not raise: the fields that do match are extracted and the raw payload is preserved in _rescued_data. You then either filter rescued rows out of the append or route them to a dead-letter Delta table inside foreachBatch, for example: df.writeStream.foreachBatch(lambda batch, epoch: batch.filter('_rescued_data IS NOT NULL').write.mode('append').saveAsTable('main.quarantine.orders_bad_records')). The trade-off is real: rescue mode weakens strictness, so a rescued-row count becomes a first-class service-level indicator you must alert on, or you have simply moved the failure from a loud crash to a quiet leak.

Step 4 — Size the backfill with numbers. Incremental ingestion processes 11 GB in 9 minutes on a 4-worker cluster, that is 11/9 = 1.22 GB per minute. Backfill throughput scales roughly with workers: 16 workers gives 4.89 GB per minute, so 2,013 / 4.89 = 411.75 minutes, about 6.9 hours. 32 workers gives 9.78 GB per minute, so 2,013 / 9.78 = 205.9 minutes, about 3.4 hours. Compute cost is essentially flat: 16 × 6.9 = 110 node-hours and 32 × 3.4 = 110 node-hours. Doubling parallelism halves the outage window at roughly the same total node-hours, which is exactly why a backfill should run on a large, short-lived cluster rather than a small overnight one.

Step 5 — Verification and cutover. Run SELECT COUNT(*) FROM main.bronze.orders_raw_v2 WHERE _rescued_data IS NOT NULL; to bound the quarantine volume, and SELECT COUNT(*) FROM main.bronze.orders_raw_v2 WHERE customer_id IS NULL; which must return 0 for all rows ingested after day 184. Reconcile row counts for the backfill window against the producer's certified 768.6 million events, then cut silver over to v2. Ship all of this through the bundle pipeline — databricks bundle validate, deploy to dev, then staging, integration tests, approval gate, then deploy -t prod — rather than editing the production job by hand [source 5][source 6], so the new checkpoint path and reader options are reviewable in Git [source 3].

Analysis — Why the method works. Auto Loader persists its inferred schema outside the data path, in the schema location you supply, and compares every newly inferred file schema against that record. That persistence is what makes ingestion stable across restarts, and it is also what breaks when the upstream contract changes: the stream fails loudly rather than silently re-inferring a different schema each run. The decision rule that falls out of this architecture is: an additive change adds a column to a schema that is otherwise unchanged, so the recorded schema can be extended in place and the checkpoint reused; a rename, a drop, or a type change (for example int to decimal, or widening decimal(10,2) to decimal(12,2)) breaks the identity or the type of a column that existing files and existing downstream logic already depend on, so no schema extension can reconcile it — you need a new checkpoint, a new table, and a replay of the source.

Definitions and preconditions, with edge cases. A checkpoint is the durable streaming state directory containing offsets, commit metadata, source progress, and (for stateful operators) operator state; its central precondition is one-to-one ownership by exactly one streaming query at a time, and its key edge case is that reusing a checkpoint with a different query definition can fail or silently resume at the wrong position. A schema location is the directory where Auto Loader stores the inferred schema it compares against; its precondition is that it is stable across restarts, and its edge case is that it may be deleted on purpose but that deleting it alone does not constitute a safe full refresh. Full refresh is the controlled operation of dropping the target data, discarding the streaming state, and reprocessing all source data from the beginning; in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines this is a first-class operation that drops the target tables, clears the checkpoint, and reprocesses from source, whereas in a hand-written Auto Loader job you implement it by choosing a new checkpoint location and a new target table. The rescued data column is a payload-preserving column that captures records or fields that do not match the declared schema; its precondition is that downstream consumers either filter it or monitor it, and its edge case is that turning it on converts hard failures into silent incompleteness if nobody watches the count.

Where students typically go wrong. First, deleting the schema folder and restarting the existing stream, believing this is a full refresh — the offset log still claims those files are processed, so historical files are not reprocessed and the recorded schema and the source state end up inconsistent. Second, enabling addNewColumns for a rename and declaring victory when the stream turns green; the tell is that cust_id is NULL for every new row, and the downstream MERGE keyed on cust_id stops matching, producing silent loss. Third, assuming schema evolution retrofits history: schema evolution only changes how files are read, so you must decide case by case whether NULLs before the change date are semantically acceptable (a slowly changing dimension, that is, tracking how an attribute's value changes over time, often wants exactly this) or whether you need an explicit backfill or sentinel value. Fourth, treating the rescued data column as a substitute for schema management rather than as a safety net with a monitored metric. The generalization: whenever a stream fails, decide whether the change adds information (evolve in place, keep the checkpoint) or redefines existing information (full refresh into a new checkpoint and table), and always budget the replay cost before you start.
Problem 2

An on-call engineer triages four incidents on the same Auto Loader ingestion pattern over one week. Incident 1: the producer adds an optional column device_type; the stream fails at the first new file and would fail on every retry. Incident 2: the producer changes order_total from int to decimal(12,2) without renaming it; the stream fails at the first new file. Incident 3: the producer renames cust_id to customer_id; the stream fails at the first new file. Incident 4: one producer instance writes a truncated JSON line every few hours; the stream fails intermittently, on roughly one run in six. For each incident, classify the change as evolutionary (in place) or non-evolutionary (full refresh), name the correct remediation, and state the estimated downtime given that the historical data is 2,013 GB and that a 16-worker backfill processes 4.89 GB per minute. Then state the single diagnostic that separates Incident 4 from Incidents 1 to 3.
Hint: A contract change fails deterministically at the first new file; a bad record fails probabilistically.

Worked solution
Classification rule. Evolutionary means: the change adds information without redefining any existing column, so the recorded schema can be extended in place and the checkpoint can be reused. Non-evolutionary means: the change either redefines an existing column (rename, type change) or removes one, so no schema extension reconciles it and you must use a new checkpoint and a new table with a replay.

Incident 1 (new optional column device_type): evolutionary. Remediation: set .option('cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode', 'addNewColumns') and restart against the same checkpoint; the schema location gains device_type and historical rows read as NULL. Estimated downtime: one restart, on the order of minutes, plus no backfill because NULL is the correct historical value.

Incident 2 (order_total int to decimal(12,2)): non-evolutionary. The column name is unchanged, which is exactly what makes this a trap: Auto Loader still sees a type mismatch against the recorded schema, and a type change is not something addNewColumns resolves. Remediation: full refresh. Create main.bronze.orders_raw_v2, point it at a new checkpoint such as s3://acme-checkpoints/bronze/orders_raw_v2/, backfill from the retained source files, verify, then cut silver over.

Incident 3 (cust_id renamed to customer_id): non-evolutionary, same remediation as Incident 2. A rename is indistinguishable from a drop plus an add, so the recorded schema keeps cust_id (now permanently NULL for new data) if you merely enable addNewColumns and reuse the checkpoint.

Incident 4 (truncated JSON line every few hours): neither. This is a bad-record problem, not a schema-contract problem. Remediation: enable the rescued data column (cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode = 'rescue' with the rescued data column enabled, the same column Lakeflow pipelines expose) and route records where _rescued_data IS NOT NULL to a dead-letter Delta table or quarantine table; monitor the quarantined-row count as an SLI. Estimated downtime: none, if you can tolerate rescued rows being quarantined during the fix; the next restart applies the change.

Backfill arithmetic for Incidents 2 and 3. Historical volume is 2,013 GB. At 4.89 GB per minute on 16 workers: 2,013 / 4.89 = 411.75 minutes = 6.86 hours, call it about 6.9 hours of replay on the backfill cluster, plus verification and cutover time. If you instead run 32 workers at 9.78 GB per minute: 2,013 / 9.78 = 205.9 minutes = 3.43 hours. Both configs consume about 110 node-hours (16 × 6.86 = 109.8; 32 × 3.43 = 109.8), so parallelism buys outage-window reduction at flat compute cost.

The separating diagnostic. Determinism. Incidents 1 to 3 fail on the first file that carries the new contract and fail again on every retry, because the comparison is between schemas and the input is the same shape every time. Incident 4 fails only when a truncated file happens to arrive, so the failure rate tracks the producer's defect rate and a retry may succeed. Observable confirmation: in the deterministic cases, Jobs run history and the driver log show the same schema-mismatch message on every attempt and the last fully successful run precedes the contract deploy; in Incident 4 the error names a specific file or payload and the failure timestamps are scattered.

Analysis — Why this rule is the right generalization. Auto Loader's contract with you is that the first successful read fixes the schema; every later read is compared against that fixed reference. A change that only adds fields leaves the reference valid and extensible, so the cheap path (extend the schema, keep the checkpoint) is both correct and safe. A change that alters a field's identity or type invalidates the reference itself, so the only honest options are to build a new reference (new checkpoint and schema location) and a new target, then replay history. Trying to force the old checkpoint to accept a renamed or retyped column means you are asking a metadata store to guess intent it cannot observe.

Edge cases worth naming. Not every added column is safe to treat as purely additive: if the new column is later declared NOT NULL downstream, historical NULLs will propagate. Widening and narrowing type changes have a further asymmetry — widening leaves the old values representable, so you can sometimes choose to reinterpret rather than replay, but only if you can state and test that invariant explicitly; narrowing can genuinely lose information and always needs a replay plus a validation rule. Dropping a column is also non-evolutionary in practice, because downstream logic and existing Delta files still reference it. Finally, a schema change is not the only way to see a schema error: an upstream producer that starts emitting a nested object where a string used to be, or switches a timestamp format, looks additive at the top level but breaks parsing below it, which is why rescued data should be on for production ingestion regardless of the fix you choose.

Common student mistakes. Treating 'the stream is green' as evidence of correctness — after a rename with addNewColumns the job succeeds while writing NULL keys, and the failure surfaces days later in the silver MERGE. Confusing a type change with a new column because the name did not change. Assuming rescue mode is a fix rather than a safety net: rescue preserves the payload but does not restore the semantic meaning of a field, and it converts loud failures into quiet incompleteness unless the rescued-row metric is alerted on. And treating the four incidents as one problem class, when the first three are contract-management failures and the fourth is a producer-quality failure requiring a quarantine pattern rather than a schema decision. Operationally, this is why the fix must ship as a reviewed artifact with validate and integration steps on the path from dev to staging to prod, and with an approval gate before production [source 5][source 6], instead of as a manual option change applied to the live job [source 3].
Problem 3

A teammate proposes the following fix for the day-184 failure in which cust_id was renamed to customer_id: 'The schema is just a file under s3://acme-checkpoints/bronze/orders_raw/schema/. Delete that folder, restart the existing stream with addNewColumns enabled, and Auto Loader will re-infer the schema from the newest files. No backfill needed, no new table needed, no downtime.' Evaluate this proposal precisely: state what the checkpoint stores, what deleting only the schema folder actually causes, what a correct full refresh must include, and how it should be promoted to production. Give the backfill time for 2,013 GB at 4.89 GB per minute as part of your cost picture.
Hint: The schema is the smallest part of streaming state; ask what else the checkpoint remembers.

Worked solution
What the checkpoint stores. A Structured Streaming checkpoint directory is durable query state, not a cache. It contains the offsets log (which source files and partitions have been consumed), the commit log (which micro-batches were durably completed), query metadata (including the query and the source identity), a sources directory holding per-source planning state, and a state directory when the query has stateful operators. For Auto Loader, the inferred schema lives in the schema location you supply, which is commonly a sibling or child of the checkpoint. The precondition that matters here is one-to-one ownership: exactly one streaming query may own a given checkpoint at a time, and its recorded schema is compared against every newly inferred file schema. The edge case that breaks naive fixes is that the schema location and the offset/commit logs are separate pieces of state that must stay mutually consistent.

What the proposal actually does. Deleting only the schema folder removes the reference schema, so on restart Auto Loader re-infers from the files it reads next. But the offset and commit logs still assert that every file through day 184 has already been processed, so the stream does NOT reprocess the 183 days of history; it only re-infers from new files. Two things follow. First, the historical 768.6 million rows never receive any treatment of the renamed field — they keep the old physical column, and the re-inferred schema now describes only new files, so the table is read under a schema that does not match what actually sits in its older Parquet files. Second, and worse, the pipeline is now two incompatible schemas wearing one table name, with no record in the checkpoint of when the break happened. Any consumer that reads the table with a schema-on-read expectation, or that runs a MERGE keyed on a column whose meaning changed halfway, gets silently wrong results rather than an error. This is the checkpoint-lifecycle trap: changing a reader option while reusing a checkpoint does not refresh anything, and in the rename case it leaves the stream broken in the quiet sense — running, but semantically wrong.

What a correct full refresh must include. One: a new checkpoint location (for example s3://acme-checkpoints/bronze/orders_raw_v2/) that owns none of the old offsets or commits, so no stale progress state is inherited. Two: a new target table with the new contract schema (main.bronze.orders_raw_v2), leaving the old table intact as the rollback artifact. Three: a backfill that replays all retained source files under the new schema, sized explicitly — 2,013 GB at 4.89 GB per minute is 411.75 minutes, about 6.9 hours on 16 workers, or 205.9 minutes, about 3.4 hours, on 32 workers for roughly the same 110 node-hours. Four: a reconciliation and validation step, for example SELECT COUNT(*) FROM main.bronze.orders_raw_v2 WHERE _rescued_data IS NOT NULL; to bound quarantined records and a null-key check on the new key column to prove the rename was handled. Five: a cutover that leaves downstream code unchanged, typically by repointing a silver view or alias at v2, plus a rollback trigger and an explicit retention window on v1. Six: rescued data and quarantine routing enabled so the replay cannot be aborted by a single malformed record.

How to promote it. The change set — new reader options, new checkpoint path, new target table, and the silver view repoint — should live in the bundle and travel through the standard path: pull request, CI running tests and databricks bundle validate, deploy to dev, then staging, integration tests, approval gate, then databricks bundle deploy -t prod [source 5]. That gives reviewable, reproducible promotion of artifacts and configuration instead of manual copying between environments [source 1], and it keeps the build-once, deploy-many principle intact while the production backfill runs [source 5]. The broader CI/CD rationale is that data pipelines need the same discipline as application code precisely because environment separation is what makes a risky replay safe to test before it touches live data [source 6][source 3].

Analysis — Why the proposal is tempting and why it is wrong. It is cheap and it makes the error message disappear, which is exactly the signature of the most dangerous class of fix. The underlying misconception is that the schema file is the whole of streaming state, whereas the schema is only the smallest, most visible part; the offsets and commit logs are what give a stream its exactly-once semantics and its position. Editing one piece of state and leaving the others means the stream's behaviour is now defined by the mismatch, not by either piece alone. A related misconception is that a full refresh is a reader-option change; it is not — a full refresh is a lifecycle operation with a new state directory, a new target, a replay, and a cutover, and in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines it is exposed as an explicit operation that drops the target tables, clears the checkpoint, and reprocesses from source, which is a useful mental model even when you implement it by hand.

Edge cases and preconditions. If the source files have a retention policy, for example a 30-day lifecycle rule on s3://acme-raw/orders/, a 183-day replay is impossible and the correct answer becomes a forward-only migration with an explicit backfill limit and a documented gap; always check source retention before promising a full refresh. If the stream is stateful — say it does deduplication or sessionization — a new checkpoint resets that state, which can change results for events that straddle the cutover, and the plan must say whether late-arriving records from before the cutover are expected. If multiple downstream consumers read the bronze table directly rather than through a view, the cutover must be coordinated, which is an argument for routing consumers through a Unity Catalog view or alias from the start. And if the pipeline is already running inside a Lakeflow pipeline with expectations, the rescued data column and the quarantine table give you the place to attach data-quality metrics rather than ad hoc monitoring.

Common mistakes to watch for. Deleting the checkpoint entirely and restarting with the same table name, which either duplicates 768.6 million rows or, if you also truncate, destroys the rollback artifact. Backfilling into a new table but forgetting to size the cluster, turning a 7-hour window into a 27-hour one on too few workers. Forgetting the rescued data column during the replay, so the very first malformed historical file aborts the backfill and you have to start the window over. Promoting by hand-editing the production job rather than through the bundle targets, which leaves production configuration out of Git and makes the next incident unreproducible [source 5][source 3]. Finally, treating 'the stream is green' as the success criterion; the success criteria are reconciled row counts, zero unexpected null keys, and a bounded and monitored rescued-row count.

actions.text: Now let's apply everything we just practiced to a concrete ingestion failure. This worked problem walks through an Auto Loader stream that suddenly stops working after six months in production.

Here's the scenario. Acme Retail runs a Databricks Auto Loader streaming job reading JSON files from cloud storage. One day the upstream source adds a new column and renames an existing one. The stream, which had been running flawlessly for half a year, fails with a schema-evolution error. Take a moment to read the situation carefully before we jump to the fix.

Before you reach for any configuration option, the hint tells you to ask one question first: does this contract change add information, or does it change information? Adding a new column is an evolutionary change. Renaming a column or changing its type is a non-evolutionary change. That single distinction determines your entire remediation path — and it's exactly the kind of trap the exam loves.

Let's walk the solution step by step. Step one: read the error precisely. The message is a schema-inference mismatch against the checkpointed schema — not data corruption, not a missing file. Confusing these two failure classes is the first distractor. Step two: decide based on the change type. The new column is evolutionary, so you enable schema evolution with addNewColumns or mergeSchema. The renamed column is not evolutionary, so it forces a full refresh into a new checkpoint and a new table. Step three: protect downstream by routing unparseable records to a rescued data column or a dead-letter Delta table so a single bad record can't fail the whole batch.

Now the analysis, and this is the crucial insight. Auto Loader persists schema state inside the checkpoint. So when you change the reader option but reuse the same old checkpoint, the fix silently does nothing — the stream stays broken because it's still comparing against the stale checkpointed schema. You must account for the checkpoint lifecycle, not just the reader. That reuse-the-checkpoint mistake is the most frequent exam distractor on this topic. Notice how the method works because it treats the checkpoint, not the reader, as the source of truth for schema.

scenes.title: Check: Ingestion Troubleshooting

questions.question: A nightly Lakeflow pipeline ingests JSON files into a Bronze Delta table using Auto Loader with a fixed schema. One morning the run fails with the error text: 'Provided schema does not match the schema of the existing data. Found new column event_ts of type STRING; expected columns [...]'. No new workspace principals were added, and the storage credential was verified as valid in the same run. Which failure class does this error text describe, and what is the correct diagnostic conclusion?

options.label: A permission error, because the storage credential must have been revoked; the fix is to re-grant READ FILES on the external location.
A malformed-record error, because the JSON payload contains a stray field that must be quarantined into a rescued data column before the run can proceed.
A schema-drift error, because the upstream producer added a new column (event_ts) that is not present in the declared schema; the file structure was valid but its shape changed.
A checkpoint corruption error, because Auto Loader's checkpoint cannot track a second schema; the fix is to delete the checkpoint directory and restart.

questions.analysis: Schema drift is the addition, removal, or type change of a column in the upstream data. The error explicitly names a new column (event_ts) that does not match the declared schema, which is the textbook signature of drift — not ACL failure, not corrupt JSON. Option A is wrong because permission errors surface as authorization/credential failures in the logs, and credentials were confirmed valid. Option B is wrong because a malformed record would fail JSON parsing or produce a rescued-data entry, not a declared-schema mismatch on a clean new column. Option D is a distractor trap: deleting checkpoints is a last-resort remedy and is not justified by a simple additive drift [source 3][source 6].

questions.question: Your team uses Auto Loader to land raw events into a Bronze Delta table, and you observe a mix of failure signatures across recent runs. Which TWO signals, taken together, indicate that bad records should be routed to a rescued data column or a dead-letter table rather than triggering a full refresh with a new checkpoint? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A subset of rows fails type coercion (for example, an integer field arrives as the string 'N/A'), while the vast majority of rows parse cleanly.
Every file in the landing zone fails with an identical 'value does not match expected type' error, and no rows have ever been written successfully.
The upstream producer accidentally renamed a critical primary key for all future files, so the historical and future schemas are fundamentally incompatible at the source.
Individual records contain malformed nested JSON or missing required keys, but the overall file and table schemas remain stable over time.

questions.analysis: Options A and D describe per-record defects where the schema as a whole is intact — the classic case for a rescued data column (a side column Auto Loader populates with rows that could not be parsed) or an explicit dead-letter table, so good rows continue to land and bad rows are isolated and inspectable. Option B describes a system-wide failure, which usually points to a broken parser or a bad deployment, not to record-level quarantine. Option C describes a genuine breaking schema change at the source, which is the scenario that justifies schema evolution or, if history can no longer be reconciled, a deliberate full refresh with a new checkpoint [source 5][source 6]. Distinguishing isolated bad records from an incompatible schema is precisely the triage this objective tests [source 3].

questions.question: An ingestion pipeline has failed for three consecutive nights. The error log shows a new column named discount_pct appearing in every incoming file, and this column is not present in the existing Delta table schema. You are asked to recommend a remediation path AND to describe how you would isolate any individual records that still fail after the fix. In your answer, (a) name the failure class, (b) state whether schema evolution or a full refresh with a new checkpoint is appropriate and justify it in one or two sentences, and (c) describe the mechanism you would use to isolate remaining bad records.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Failure class correctly identified as schema drift (additive column) — 25%. (2) Recommends schema evolution (for example, adding the column or enabling automatic schema evolution) rather than a full refresh, with a justification that the change is additive and the existing history is still valid — 35%. (3) Explains that a rescued data column or dead-letter table isolates malformed records while permitting valid rows to land — 25%. (4) Clarity and use of Databricks/Delta Lake terminology (schema evolution, rescued data, checkpoint) — 15%. Award partial credit for correct identification of the class but an incomplete remediation, and deduct credit for recommending a full refresh without justification.
questions.analysis: Reference answer: (a) This is an additive schema-drift event — the producer added discount_pct to every file, so the declared Delta schema no longer matches the incoming data. (b) Schema evolution is the correct choice, because the change is additive and non-breaking: existing columns and historical rows remain valid, so nothing requires a rebuild. A full refresh with a new checkpoint would discard the incremental state Auto Loader relies on and force reprocessing of all source files, which is only justified when history can no longer be reconciled (for example, a key rename or type change that invalidates prior data). (c) Remaining individual malformed records would be captured by Auto Loader's rescued data column or written to an explicit dead-letter table, so that valid rows continue to land while the offending records are quarantined for inspection and replay. This separation of schema-level drift from record-level defects is the core decision this objective assesses [source 5][source 6][source 3].

actions.text: Building on that idea of the checkpoint as the source of truth, let's now put your ingestion troubleshooting instincts to the test. Take each question on your own first — read the error text carefully and let the phrasing guide your diagnosis.

Work through all three questions independently, then submit. Once you're done I'll walk through each one with you and unpack anything that tripped you up, so give it your best attempt before you check in.

scenes.title: Job and Cluster Failures, Retries, and Alerting

elements.content: Job & Cluster Failures, Retries, and Alerting

Failures outside the data itself — clusters, dependencies, and timeouts — require observability surfaces beyond Delta table history. The four failure families below are the ones exam scenarios test most often.
1. Cluster-level

• Init script / library install failure

• Spot-instance loss mid-shuffle

• Driver OOM (collect, too many partitions)

• Autoscaling lag vs. burst load
2. Dependencies

• Upstream failure blocks downstream (state = Blocked)

• Missed schedule window

• Dependency timeout waiting on parent

• Skipped tasks hide the real break
3. Recovery

• Task retries with exponential backoff

• Repair run: re-execute only failed tasks

• Idempotent MERGE makes reruns safe

• Never re-run the whole DAG blindly
4. Alerting

• Job notifications: start / success / failure

• Destinations: email, webhook (Slack, PagerDuty)

• SLA-driven alert on run duration

• Route to on-call only on P1 signals
Worked example — SLA regression
Daily p95 run duration over 30 days. The dashed SLA line marks the 45-minute budget. From day 18 the p95 crosses it and stays high — a regression, not noise.

Sources: [source 3] CI/CD for pipeline artifacts · [source 1] governed promotion across environments · [source 5] build-once / deploy-many promotion, approvals, rollback · [source 6] isolated environments for pipeline testing

actions.text: Now we shift from ingestion troubleshooting to a broader class of production problems: job and cluster failures, retries, and alerting. These are failures that happen outside the data itself — the data may be perfectly fine, but the platform, the dependencies, or the timing let you down.

Let's start with cluster-level causes. These are the environment problems: an init script or library install failure, a spot instance being reclaimed, the driver running out of memory, or autoscaling lag where the cluster simply can't add workers fast enough. None of these are about your data — they're about the compute your job landed on.

Next, dependency and schedule failures. When an upstream task fails, every downstream task that depends on it is blocked — you'll see that state shown as Blocked in the run graph.
