You can also hit a missed schedule window, or a dependency timeout where the upstream task just never finishes in time. The keyword here is that the failure cascades downstream.

So how do we recover? Three mechanisms. First, task retries with exponential backoff — the failed task waits progressively longer between attempts. Second, repair runs, which re-execute only the failed tasks instead of the whole pipeline. And third, idempotent MERGE writes — because a rerun only makes sense if running it twice produces the same result as running it once.

Finally, alerting. Job notifications can fire on start, success, or failure, and can be routed to email or webhook destinations. Beyond that, SLA-driven alerting watches run duration — it doesn't care whether the job technically succeeded, only whether it finished in time.

This chart makes SLA alerting concrete. It plots daily p95 run duration over thirty days, with the dashed threshold line marking the SLA. Notice how the duration drifts up over time and eventually crosses that line — the job still succeeds, but it's now violating the SLA. That's the signal an alert should catch, long before anything actually fails.

The takeaway for the exam: distinguish cluster failures from dependency failures from schedule failures, remember that repair runs target only failed tasks, and remember that SLA alerting is duration-based rather than success-based. Let's keep that framing as we move into the next scenario.

scenes.title: Decision: Remediating a Failing Production Pipeline

elements.content: Decision — Your team operates a production Lakeflow job that writes an idempotent MERGE into a Delta table; the job normally completes well within its service-level agreement, and the cluster is healthy with no resource pressure. Tonight the job failed, and the business requires the Delta table to be refreshed before the SLA expires in 45 minutes; a full rerun from scratch takes 90 minutes, so a naive restart cannot meet the deadline. A detailed look at the failure shows that 3% of incoming records are malformed — they cannot be parsed or violate a Delta Lake constraint — and those same records will keep failing every scheduled run until the root cause is removed. The decision is hard because the fast options risk either breaching the SLA or leaving the root cause in place, and the safe options consume more time than the SLA allows, so you must choose an option that satisfies the deadline and also removes the recurring failure. This scenario builds directly on the observability and ingestion-troubleshooting material you already covered: you must read the job run history and task-level error message before acting, and you must distinguish malformed-record failures from schema drift or permission errors [source 3].

Constraints — The SLA requires the Delta table to be refreshed within 45 minutes; any option judged acceptable must finish inside that window.  •  The job writes an idempotent MERGE, so any rerun or partial replay must preserve exactly-once semantics and not duplicate or corrupt already-landed rows.  •  The cluster is healthy, so the constraint is time and data quality, not compute capacity; adding cluster resources does not shorten a 90-minute full run enough to meet the SLA.  •  The 3% malformed-record rate is a recurring root cause; an acceptable option should remove or contain it rather than just restart the symptom.  •  The remediation must be auditable and reviewable, consistent with the promotion and configuration practices already covered [source 6].

Full rerun from scratch
+ Datasimply and safe: a complete replay of the MERGE reproduces the intended final table state with no partial-state ambiguity.; + Requires no new tables, code paths, or follow-up steps, so operational complexity is minimal.; + Because the MERGE is idempotent, rerunning the whole job cannot duplicate rows that already landed.
− The full job takes 90 minutes, which exceeds the 45-minute SLA by 45 minutes, so it cannot meet the deadline.; − It does nothing to identify or quarantine the 3% malformed records, so the next scheduled run will fail again.; − It wastes work by recomputing partitions that already succeeded, tying up the cluster for no business benefit.
Best for: Using when the SLA is not binding or when the failure is so widespread that no partial state can be trusted.

Repair run for failed tasks only
+ Fast and surgical: it retries only the tasks that failed, so it can land the good data well inside the 45-minute window.; + It preserves the idempotent MERGE semantics because the repair re-executes the same merge logic rather than writing an ad hoc load.; + It builds on the run-history and task-level diagnostics you already learned to read.
− It does nothing to stop the same malformed records from failing the next scheduled run, so the incident will recur.; − It leaves the 3% bad records unresolved in the source, meaning the repair may fail again on the same malformed input.; − It provides no durable evidence trail explaining why those records are bad, which weakens post-incident review.
Best for: Using when the failure is transient and the bad input has already been fixed or removed upstream.

Quarantine malformed records and let the good data land, then backfill
+ It protects the SLA because the good 97% of records land through the MERGE immediately, and only the malformed 3% are diverted.; + It removes the recurring root cause by capturing bad records into a quarantine table instead of letting them fail every run.; + It keeps the write idempotent and leaves an auditable trail that supports the review and configuration practices covered earlier.
− It adds a quarantine table and a follow-up backfill step, increasing pipeline complexity and operational overhead.; − It requires a later backfill or correction job to reconcile quarantined records, so the final table is temporarily incomplete.; − If the quarantine rule is too broad, valid edge-case records can be diverted and silently excluded from the main table.
Best for: Using when the SLA is binding and the bad records are a recurring, identifiable subset that can be captured and corrected later.

Scale the cluster and rerun the full job
+ It keeps the simple full-replay semantics of option A while attempting to shorten wall-clock time.; + It requires no changes to the pipeline logic or quarantine handling.
− The cluster is already healthy and the full job takes 90 minutes, so adding capacity alone will not reliably bring a 90-minute job under 45 minutes.; − It still ignores the 3% malformed records, so the recurring failure remains.; − It increases cost without addressing the actual bottleneck, which is data quality and pipeline design, not compute capacity.
Best for: Using when the failure is purely a resource-contention problem and the input data is known to be clean.

Recommendation: Quarantine malformed records and let the good data land, then backfill — Option C is the only option that satisfies all the binding constraints simultaneously. The 45-minute SLA rules out a full rerun, because the full job takes 90 minutes and the cluster is healthy, so scaling compute does not close that gap. A repair-only run meets the deadline but leaves the recurring malformed records in place, so the next scheduled run fails again and the root cause remains. Quarantining the malformed records lets the good 97% land through the idempotent MERGE within the SLA, preserves exactly-once semantics, and removes the recurring root cause by capturing bad records for correction later. The cost is a new quarantine table and a follow-up backfill step, which is acceptable because the alternative is a repeated SLA breach. This recommendation also aligns with the unit's emphasis on reading observability signals before acting and on treating malformed records as a distinct ingestion failure class [source 3], and it fits the governed, reviewable promotion practices you already studied [source 6].

actions.text: Let's put all of that troubleshooting knowledge to work on a realistic scenario. Your team operates a production Lakeflow pipeline, and it must deliver results before a service-level agreement — or SLA — deadline in 45 minutes. The job writes an idempotent MERGE into a Delta table, about 3% of the incoming records are malformed, and the cluster itself is perfectly healthy.

Those constraints matter. The SLA requires the Delta table to be updated on time, the write is idempotent so re-running is safe at the data level, and the cluster is not the bottleneck — the failure is coming from the data itself, not the infrastructure.

Option A is a full rerun from scratch. It is the simplest and safest choice for data correctness — a complete recompute from the source. But this is exactly the trap: the full job takes 90 minutes, and we only have 45, so it breaches the SLA every single time.

Option B is a repair run for failed tasks only. It is fast and surgical, and it gets us back under the SLA quickly. But notice the flaw: it does nothing to stop those same malformed records from failing the next scheduled run. We would be treating the symptom, not the cause.

Option C is to quarantine the malformed records and let the good data land, then backfill the quarantined rows later. This protects both the SLA and the pipeline itself. The cost is added complexity — a new quarantine table and a follow-up backfill step to manage.

And Option D would be to scale the cluster and rerun the full job. It keeps the data complete, but remember: the cluster is already healthy. Throwing more compute at a data-quality problem just bills you more while the malformed records keep failing.

So our recommendation is Option C combined with a repair run. It meets the SLA, keeps the write idempotent, and — most importantly — removes the recurring root cause instead of just restarting a symptom. That is the pattern the exam rewards: identify the constraint, isolate the real cause, and justify the trade-off. Take a moment to consider which constraint mattered most in your reasoning.

actions.topic: Choosing a remediation strategy under SLA pressure
actions.prompt: In this 45-minute SLA scenario, which constraint drove your decision most — time, data correctness, or root-cause prevention? Argue for the option you would defend to a skeptical stakeholder, and explain what you would monitor afterward to confirm the fix held.

scenes.title: Check: Exam-Style Troubleshooting Scenarios

questions.question: A nightly Delta Lake MERGE job that normally completes in 12 minutes now takes 95 minutes. The Spark UI shows a single shuffle stage with 200 tasks, a median task duration of 3 seconds, a maximum task duration of 9 minutes 20 seconds, shuffle read of 180 GB, and 40 GB of disk spill. A teammate proposes immediately resizing the cluster from 8 to 24 workers. Based on the diagnostic signature, what is the most likely root cause and the correct first remediation?

options.label: Key skew on the MERGE/join key, producing one oversized partition; remediate by salting or repartitioning the skewed key (or enabling Adaptive Query Execution) rather than scaling the cluster
Insufficient cluster capacity; remediate by scaling the cluster horizontally to more workers so the long task has more CPU
Excessive garbage collection across all executors; remediate by increasing executor memory and tuning the GC policy on every node
Too many partitions causing scheduler overhead; remediate by coalescing the stage down to far fewer partitions

questions.analysis: The signature is a long-tail duration distribution inside a single shuffle stage: a max/median ratio of roughly 186x (9m20s vs. 3s) vastly exceeds the ~3x heuristic taught in the skew worked problem, and it is combined with heavy shuffle read (180 GB) plus 40 GB disk spill. That combination localizes the problem to key skew on the join or MERGE key, not cluster size [source 1]. Because the work is concentrated in one or a few partitions, adding workers leaves the oversized partition unchanged — the classic exam trap of 'scale the cluster for skew.' The correct first move is to redistribute the skewed key (salt the key, pre-repartition, or enable AQE skew-join handling) so the long tail collapses. Option B reflects the scaling misconception the lesson explicitly warns against. Option C is wrong because GC time is not the discriminating metric here; spill and shuffle read rule. Option D is wrong because with 200 tasks and one pathological long tail, coalescing would make skew worse, not better.

questions.question: An Auto Loader streaming ingestion job that has run successfully for six months now fails. The error states that the stream's inferred schema does not match the checkpointed schema. The source has (1) added a brand-new column and (2) renamed an existing column. Which statements about the correct remediation are true? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: Adding a new column is an evolutionary schema change and can be handled by enabling schema evolution (e.g., addNewColumns/mergeSchema) so the stream continues from the existing checkpoint
Renaming a column is a non-evolutionary change; it requires a full refresh into a new checkpoint and typically a new target table
Editing the reader options without refreshing the checkpoint is sufficient to resolve both the added and renamed column
Because a checkpoint locks the schema, the stream will restart-fail until the checkpointed schema and the incoming schema are reconciled

questions.analysis: A streaming checkpoint persists the schema, so once it is written, any incompatibility between checkpointed and incoming schema causes a restart-fail loop — this is why option D is correct and must be fixed deliberately. Evolutionary changes (adding a new column) can be absorbed by enabling schema evolution such as addNewColumns or mergeSchema (option A), letting the stream continue against the existing checkpoint. Non-evolutionary changes (renaming a column, or changing its type) cannot be reconciled by evolution flags; the stream must be fully refreshed into a new checkpoint and a new target table (option B). Option C is the exam trap: editing reader options alone does not rewrite the checkpoint, so the mismatch persists — you must either evolve (for additions) or full-refresh (for renames/type changes). This mirrors the ingestion-troubleshooting lesson and the deployment principle of building once and deploying many, where configuration changes are governed rather than silently patched in place [source 2].

questions.question: A production pipeline reports 'Succeeded' in the pipeline UI, yet the downstream gold table is empty. Describe, step by step, how you would triage this discrepancy. Reference at least the observability surfaces you would use and the data-level checks that could explain a green pipeline run with an empty result set.
questions.commentPrompt: Grading rubric: (1) Distinguishes pipeline run status from data readiness — the run succeeded, so the failure is in the data path, not orchestration; must state this explicitly (~25%). (2) Names concrete observability surfaces and what each answers, e.g., Job run history (did the task complete?), task-level logs (what did the task actually read/write?), Spark UI (did the stage run and how many rows were processed?), Delta table history / Time Travel (what versions and what operations touched the gold table?), and system tables (~20%). (3) Probes data-level causes: upstream source returned zero rows or a filtered partition; a filter/join predicate dropped all rows; a schema or partition mismatch wrote to an unexpected location; a MERGE matched nothing because keys changed; a checkpoint advanced past unread data (~35%). (4) Articulates the remediation decision and how to verify the fix, plus clarity of expression (~20%).
questions.analysis: A 'Succeeded' run only asserts that the orchestration and tasks completed without an exception; it says nothing about whether rows were produced, so the first move is to separate monitoring ('did it fail?') from observability ('why, where, how do I fix it?') [source 1]. A strong answer traces the data path: inspect task-level logs for the counts actually read and written, use the Spark UI to confirm the stage executed and how many rows flowed, use Delta table history/Time Travel to see the latest operations on the gold table, and query the relevant system table for the run timeline. Then it probes data-level causes — an empty upstream partition, a filter or join that eliminated all rows, a partition/schema mismatch that wrote elsewhere, a MERGE whose keys no longer match, or a streaming checkpoint that advanced past unread data — and states how to verify the remediation. The key exam skill is refusing to accept the green status and instead following the artifact lineage to the point where data should have appeared but did not.

questions.question: A 3 a.m. batch job has failed three nights in a row with a different failure code each time, and the on-call runbook simply says 'restart the job.' Which sequence best reflects correct incident response for a pipeline that is failing repeatedly?

options.label: Restart the job immediately; if it fails again, scale the cluster up and retry until it succeeds
Use the run history and task-level logs to localize the failing task and read the precise error, determine the failure class, fix the underlying cause, and only then re-run
Disable the failing task and promote the remaining stages to production to preserve the SLA
Reset the checkpoint on every failing run so the job starts from a clean state each night

questions.analysis: Repeated failures with varying codes signal a persistent, unaddressed root cause, so the disciplined response is localization first: query the run timeline to find the failing task, read its error text, classify the failure (schema drift, malformed records, permission/credential error, source connectivity, or rate limiting), then remediate the cause before re-running [source 1]. Option A is the classic 'restart without fixing the data' trap and also blindly scales the cluster, which the lesson warns against. Option C would silently produce incomplete results and violates the governed promotion principle that data artifacts must move through explicit, tested gates rather than being disabled or skipped to hit an SLA [source 5]. Option D is dangerous because a checkpoint carries the schema and progress state; resetting it on every run discards that state and can re-read or skip data, and it does not address the actual defect. The correct answer reflects both the observability lesson (use the surface that answers 'why, where, and how do I fix it?') and the deployment lesson (fix safely, then promote) [source 2].

actions.text: Time to put all of that diagnostic instinct to the test. These scenarios pull together observability, Spark UI reading, ingestion, and job recovery into integrated exam-style items — so treat each one the way you would on the real thing: identify the constraint, localize the symptom, and reason toward the correct fix.

Work through all four on your own, including the written one — write out the steps rather than just picking an answer. Try each one independently before submitting, and once you're done I'll walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: The Certification Blueprint: Five Domains

elements.content: The Certification Blueprint: Five Domains

Exam Mechanics

Scenario-based multiple choice, no partial credit

≈45 questions in 90 minutes; passing score near 70%

Pacing and elimination matter as much as recall

Question Phrasing

“MOST efficient / LEAST expensive / LEAST code”

Expected answer: managed, declarative, Databricks-native

Eliminate manual or over-engineered options first
Domain Weights (approximate, verify current guide)
ELT plus Incremental Processing together = 51% of the exam.
Weights shift between exam versions — always check the official guide. Practice sets map to all domains [source 1].
Worked Example: Budgeting Study Hours by Score Impact

Suppose you have 50 study hours left and a practice test shows these per-domain scores: Lakehouse Platform 85%, ELT with Spark SQL & Python 60%, Incremental Data Processing 55%, Production Pipelines 70%, Data Governance 80%.

Expected exam contribution = domain weight × score: ELT 29% × 60 = 17.4 points; Incremental 22% × 55 = 12.1 points; Lakehouse 24% × 85 = 20.4 points; Production 16% × 70 = 11.2 points; Governance 9% × 80 = 7.2 points. Total ≈ 68.3% — below the ~70% threshold.

To gain the most points, raise the lowest-weighted-score products: Incremental (22 × 55) and ELT (29 × 60) have the most room to grow. Allocate 30 of 50 hours there, not to already-strong Lakehouse or Governance. This mirrors DORA-style pipeline health thinking: measure, target the bottleneck, then act [source 5].

Strategic consequence: A domain you never study is a hard ceiling on your total score. Remaining study hours belong to the weakest domain, not the most comfortable one.

Treat the five domains like isolated environments in a CI/CD pipeline: each must pass its own gate before promotion, and skipping a stage creates a production risk [source 6][source 2].

actions.text: Now that we've wrapped up the troubleshooting scenarios, let's pull the whole certification into focus. This is the blueprint page — the five domains you'll be tested on, their weights, and how the questions are actually phrased. Everything you've built in this course maps onto this page.

First, the mechanics. This exam is scored, the questions are scenario-based multiple choice, and there is no partial credit — an answer is either right or wrong. You get roughly forty-five questions in ninety minutes, with a passing threshold near seventy percent. That means pacing and answer elimination matter just as much as raw recall. If a question eats four minutes, you've spent someone else's time.

Here are the domain weights, approximate and always worth verifying against the current official exam guide, because they shift between versions. Lakehouse Platform sits around twenty-four percent. ELT with Spark SQL and Python is the largest at roughly twenty-nine percent. Incremental Data Processing is about twenty-two percent, Production Pipelines about sixteen, and Data Governance around nine.
Look at the bar chart — five domains on the X-axis, exam weight on the Y-axis. Notice the shape of it: two bars tower over the rest.

ELT plus Incremental Processing together make up fifty-one percent of the exam. Over half your score sits in two domains, and those are exactly the chapters we spent the most time on — Spark SQL and DataFrames, ingestion with COPY INTO and Auto Loader, and streaming with Delta.

Second, watch the phrasing. Questions follow exam-objective style: which approach is the MOST efficient, the LEAST expensive, requires the LEAST code. When you see superlatives like that, the expected answer is almost always the managed, declarative, Databricks-native option — not the hand-rolled one.
So let's turn that into a worked example for budgeting your study hours. The principle: allocate hours by score impact, not by comfort.

Suppose you have fifty study hours left and a practice score breakdown in front of you. You do not split those fifty hours evenly across five domains — that would be nine or ten hours each, which under-invests in the domains that carry the most points and over-invests in the ones you already know.

And here's the strategic consequence, which is the real lesson of this page: a domain you never study is a hard ceiling on your total score. So your remaining hours belong to your weakest domain, not your most comfortable one. On the next pages we'll map each of these five domains back to what you've already built.

scenes.title: Map Every Domain to What You Already Built

elements.content: Map Every Domain to What You Already Built

Four domains, four artifacts, one page. Read left to right: the domain name states the objective, the practice column names the features, and the artifact column is the memory you retrieve under exam pressure [source 1]. A crosswalk is a governed promotion of content across environments, so mapping each domain to a produced artifact is the same discipline as promoting pipeline assets from dev to staging to prod [source 6].

data.text: a Delta table queried from a notebook
SQL and PySpark jobs using joins, CTEs, UDFs
Auto Loader, COPY INTO, MERGE units
a bundle promoted across environments with tests and job-run monitoring [source 6]
grants, a row filter, and a column mask on a governed table

elements.content: Weights sum to roughly 100%. Read across each row: the weight tells you how many exam items reward it, so a 29% row earns nine more items than a 9% row.
Study inventory: every row where you cannot name your own artifact is the first place to re-practice — before touching any new material.
Exam framing: "given a scenario requiring X, which Databricks feature applies?" is answered from the artifact column, not from a memorized definition.
Worked example: the ELT artifact is an idempotent MERGE — rerun the same batch twice and row count stays 1,000, not 2,000, because the merge key matches on the first pass.

actions.text: Here's the crosswalk I promised. One page, four domains, four artifacts. The idea is simple: instead of memorizing abstract domain names, you map each domain to something you already built and already understand.

Read it left to right. On the left is the domain and its weight on the exam. In the middle, where you actually practiced it in this course. And on the right, the artifact you produced. If a domain name feels abstract, the artifact column is what makes it concrete.

Now walk down the rows. Lakehouse Platform, about twenty-four percent — you practiced that in the workspace, Delta table, and cluster-type units, and the artifact was a Delta table queried from a notebook. ELT with Spark SQL and Python, the heaviest at twenty-nine percent — that came from the transformation units, and your artifact was SQL and PySpark jobs using joins, CTEs, and UDFs.

Notice the weights sum to roughly one hundred percent, and notice how you read across each row. Incremental Data Processing at twenty-two percent — Auto Loader, COPY INTO, and MERGE units, where you built that idempotent upsert pipeline. Production Pipelines at sixteen percent — asset bundles, testing, and observability, where you promoted a bundle through environments with tests and job-run monitoring. And Data Governance at nine percent — Unity Catalog units, where you applied grants, a row filter, and a column mask on a governed table.

Here's how to actually use this. Treat the table as a study inventory. Any row where you cannot name your own artifact in the right-hand column is the first place to re-practice — before you touch any new material. That's your priority list, ranked for you.

And this is the exam framing that ties it together. When you see a question like 'given a scenario requiring X, which Databricks feature applies?', you answer it from the artifact column — from the thing you built and remember — not from a memorized definition. That's what we just covered with the worked example.

Take the ELT artifact, for instance: an idempotent pipeline. If a question describes a scenario demanding re-runnable loads without duplicates, that artifact is what surfaces the answer. Your memory of building it is stronger than any list of terms.

scenes.title: Check: Exam Structure and Domain Weights

questions.question: A candidate is building a study plan and wants to maximize return on study time. Based on the exam blueprint, which reasoning correctly connects domain weight to marginal return?

options.label: All domains are weighted equally, so study time should be split evenly across them
The domain carrying the most scored items deserves the largest share of study time because each additional correct answer there moves the total score the most
The hardest domain should always get the most time regardless of how many items it contributes
The domain a candidate already finds most familiar should get the most time because confidence compounds

questions.analysis: Marginal return on study time is driven by how many scored items a domain contributes to the total. If a domain carries the most items, each incremental improvement in that domain produces more correct answers, and therefore more points, than the same improvement in a smaller domain. Option A is a common misconception that assumes uniform weighting, which contradicts the idea of a weighted blueprint. Option C confuses difficulty with yield: a hard domain with few items offers a low ceiling on point gain. Option D is the 'study what feels comfortable' trap, which maximizes comfort rather than points. The blueprint concept is the same governed, structured promotion discipline described for deployment pipelines, where each stage has a defined role rather than equal weight [source 1].

questions.question: An exam item is phrased: 'A team must ingest streaming files into Delta Lake with the least code and the lowest operational cost while keeping schema changes managed automatically.' Which three signals in that objective indicate what the expected answer looks like? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: The phrase 'least code' signals a managed, declarative feature rather than a hand-written parser or custom loop
The phrase 'lowest operational cost' signals favoring a serverless or auto-scaling managed service over a permanently oversized always-on cluster
The phrase 'managed automatically' signals a built-in schema evolution mechanism such as Auto Loader with schema evolution enabled
The phrase 'streaming files' signals that the expected answer must avoid Delta Lake entirely and write raw Parquet

questions.analysis: Exam objectives are written as constraints that point at a specific product feature. 'Least code' pushes toward a declarative managed capability instead of custom code; 'lowest operational cost' pushes toward serverless or elastically scaled compute rather than a fixed oversized cluster; and 'managed automatically' points at built-in schema evolution, exactly the distinction between evolutionary changes (add a new column, enable schema evolution with addNewColumns or mergeSchema) and non-evolutionary changes (rename or type change, which require a full refresh to a new checkpoint). Option D is wrong because writing raw Parquet would discard Delta Lake's schema enforcement and transaction guarantees, which the objective implies must be retained. This is the same 'build once, behave predictably per environment' discipline that CI/CD promotion imposes on data pipeline artifacts [source 3].

questions.question: A candidate reviews a chapter, recognizes the diagrams, and thinks 'we covered it,' then skips the practice items. Which statement best describes why this is a trap for exam readiness?

options.label: Recognition is not the same as being able to build it unaided under time pressure with unfamiliar wording
Reviewing a chapter is always sufficient, and practice items only confirm what is already known
Practice items only matter for the domain a candidate has already mastered
Familiarity with a tool's logo is the strongest predictor of a correct answer on scenario items

questions.analysis: The trap substitutes 'we covered it' for 'I can build it unaided.' Passive recognition of diagrams and chapter headings does not prove the candidate can apply the concept to a novel scenario stem, which is how the exam is delivered. Option B is the misconception itself, stated plainly. Option C inverts the purpose of practice, which is to find gaps, not to celebrate existing strengths. Option D confuses branding familiarity with applied skill. The reliable test is whether the candidate can reproduce the behavior and reach the correct decision, the same standard by which CI/CD practices are promoted through isolated environments rather than assumed correct because they were reviewed [source 5].

actions.text: Now let's put that blueprint knowledge to the test. These three questions check whether you can connect domain weight to where study effort actually pays off, read what exam-objective phrasing is telling you, and spot the trap of mistaking recognition for readiness.
Take your time and work through each one on your own — I'll be right here after you submit to walk through anything that tripped you up.

scenes.title: Domains 1–2 Review: Platform and ELT

elements.content:
Domains 1–2 Review

Platform & ELT: high-yield exam facts
Domain 1 · Platform
Platform essentials (Domain 1)

• Delta Lake = ACID transactions + time travel over object storage; storage and compute scale independently [source 1]

• Managed (Unity Catalog) table: UC owns data files and lifecycle; DROP deletes the data

• External table: metadata in UC, files at a LOCATION you control; DROP keeps files

• All-purpose cluster = interactive dev; job cluster / serverless = scheduled, cost-sensitive runs [source 5]

• CREATE OR REPLACE rebuilds; CTAS derives a new table from a query; LOCATION redirects storage
ELT + trap cluster (Domain 2)

• Preference order for performance: Spark SQL > DataFrame API ≫ Python UDFs [source 3]

• Widgets/parameters make one notebook reusable across environments (dev→staging→prod) [source 6]

• "MOST efficient / LEAST code / MOST scalable" → choose the declarative, Databricks-native option [source 1]

• OPTIMIZE + ZORDER: file layout & data skipping; VACUUM: retention only

• Time travel cannot read versions VACUUM already deleted — retention sets the floor
Worked example — VACUUM sets the time-travel floor (7-day retention)

Day 0 write → v0 | Day 2 → v1 | Day 4 → v2 | Day 6 → v3

Run VACUUM on Day 8 with retention = 7 days (168 h).

Cutoff = Day 8 − 7 = Day 1.

Files younger than Day 1 are protected, so v1–v3 survive; v0 is deleted.

Exam takeaway

"Restore yesterday" succeeds (v1, v2, v3 remain).

"Restore to v0" errors — retention, not a bug.

If retention < cutoff window, older versions are gone permanently, so set retention before relying on time travel.
Quick check: A nightly job must cut cost and run unattended — which compute? (A) all-purpose (B) job cluster (C) driver-only (D) notebook cluster — Answer: B

actions.text: Alright, now that you've had a crack at those mixed-domain questions, let's consolidate the two heaviest domains into one high-yield review — Domain 1, the Platform, and Domain 2, ELT with Spark SQL and Python. These are the facts and decision rules the exam actually tests, so treat this page as your compression layer.

We start with Platform essentials. Delta Lake gives you ACID transactions and time travel directly over object storage, and compute is separated from storage so you can scale each independently. Know the compute rule cold: all-purpose clusters are for interactive development, while job clusters or serverless compute are the correct answer for any scheduled, cost-sensitive workload.

On table semantics, remember who owns the data. With managed tables, Unity Catalog owns both the data and its lifecycle. With external tables, the data stays at a path you control — you're only managing the metadata. And CREATE OR REPLACE, CTAS, and LOCATION each answer a different exam scenario, so read the question for which one it's really asking about.

Now the ELT decision rules and the trap cluster. When performance is the criterion, prefer Spark SQL or the DataFrame API over Python UDFs — native functions always win. Use widgets and parameters to make notebooks and jobs reusable. And prefer declarative SQL unless the scenario explicitly demands procedural logic. Watch for the trap wording: most efficient, least expensive, requires the least code, most scalable — under those constraints, the Databricks-native declarative option usually beats a hand-written loop or a self-managed cluster.

Let's walk the maintenance worked example, because this combines VACUUM and time travel. Follow the timeline: a Day 0 write creates version zero, Day 2 gives us v1, Day 4 gives v2, Day 6 gives v3. VACUUM removes the files that are no longer referenced, and crucially it sets the time-travel floor — you can never read a version whose files have already been vacuumed away.

Here's the exam takeaway. If someone restores yesterday, that succeeds because the recent versions — v1, v2, and v3 — are still on disk and haven't been vacuumed. The moment a version falls below the retention floor, it's gone. Keep the Delta maintenance vocabulary straight: OPTIMIZE and ZORDER handle file layout and data skipping, VACUUM handles retention.

Let's close with the quick check on this page. A nightly job must cut cost and run unattended — so which compute, which table type, and which statement style would you pick, and why? Take a moment, then we'll compare your reasoning against the Domain 1 and 2 traps.

scenes.title: Worked Problem: A Production-Grade ELT Task

elements.content: Problem 1

**Scenario (exam-style, Databricks/Delta Lake).** A retail CDC feed writes a daily micro-batch into the Delta table `bronze.orders_raw`. Yesterday's drop contained 4,218,764 rows covering 4,180,347 distinct `order_id` values, because the producer replays the last 30 minutes of change events on every run. The same `order_id` can therefore appear several times in one drop, with different `amount`, `status`, and `updated_at` values. The downstream table `silver.orders_current` must hold **exactly one row per `order_id`**, namely the version with the **latest** `updated_at`, and the job that builds it must be **safely re-runnable**: running it twice in a row must leave the target in the same state as running it once. `bronze.orders_raw` is 6.2 GB; the target starts empty. Write the deduplication + load logic and justify why it is idempotent.
Hint: Deduplicate with a window on `order_id` ordered by `updated_at` descending, keep `row_number() = 1`, and land the result with `MERGE INTO` — never `INSERT OVERWRITE` on a 6.2 GB table.

Worked solution
**Contract first (state the three clauses before typing code).** (1) `silver.orders_current` has exactly one row per `order_id`; (2) the surviving row is the one with maximum `updated_at`; (3) re-running the job is a no-op in terms of final table state.

**Step 0 — size the problem.** Rows in = 4,218,764. Distinct keys = 4,180,347. Extra (duplicate) rows = 4,218,764 - 4,180,347 = **38,417**, i.e. 38,417 / 4,218,764 = **0.911%** of the batch. So ~99.1% of the input is already clean; the job is a *collapse* problem on a small minority of keys, not a filter on the whole batch. That matters later when we choose MERGE over overwrite.

**Step 1 — deduplicate inside a window.** `DISTINCT` is wrong here: identical rows are rare, while *changed* versions of the same key are common, and `DISTINCT` has no notion of "newest". Use a window partitioned by the key and ordered by recency:

```python

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

from pyspark.sql.window import Window

raw = (spark.read.table('bronze.orders_raw')

.withColumn('updated_at', F.col('updated_at').cast('timestamp')) # never sort timestamps as strings

.withColumn('ingest_ts', F.col('ingest_ts').cast('timestamp')))

w = (Window.partitionBy('order_id')

.orderBy(F.col('updated_at').desc_nulls_last(),

F.col('ingest_ts').desc())) # deterministic tie-breaker

deduped = (raw.withColumn('rn', F.row_number().over(w))

.filter(F.col('rn') == 1)

.drop('rn'))

deduped.createOrReplaceTempView('deduped_orders')

```

The full batch has 38,417 duplicate keys but the *sample below* shows the mechanics. Six raw rows:

| order_id | amount | status | updated_at | rn |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 1001 | 120.00 | shipped | 2025-03-02 11:02:00 | 1 |

| 1001 | 120.00 | placed | 2025-03-01 09:14:00 | 2 |

| 1002 | 80.50 | placed | 2025-03-01 22:40:00 | 1 |

| 1003 | 240.00 | delivered | 2025-03-03 19:31:00 | 1 |

| 1003 | 240.00 | shipped | 2025-03-02 08:05:00 | 2 |

| 1004 | 15.99 | cancelled | 2025-03-02 07:12:00 | 1 |

Filtering `rn = 1` keeps 4 of 6 rows: order 1001 → 2025-03-02 11:02:00, order 1002 → placed, order 1003 → delivered, order 1004 → cancelled. Note that for order 1001 the newest row also changed `status` from `placed` to `shipped`, which is exactly why we cannot take the first row we see.

**Step 2 — land it with MERGE.** Because `deduped_orders` has at most one row per `order_id`, the merge condition matches at most one target row and Delta will not raise a multi-match error:

```sql

MERGE INTO silver.orders_current AS t

USING deduped_orders AS s

ON t.order_id = s.order_id

WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *

```

**Step 3 — audit the result.**

```sql

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_now, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS keys_now FROM silver.orders_current;

-- first run: 4,180,347 / 4,180,347

SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) c FROM silver.orders_current

GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; -- must return 0 rows

```

**Step 4 — prove idempotency.** Let $f(T)$ be the job applied to target state $T$: $f(T) = \mathrm{merge}(\mathrm{dedup}(S), T)$. Since $\mathrm{dedup}(S)$ contains exactly one row per key, each source row maps to exactly one key; the matched branch writes the *same* column values that are already stored when the source has not changed, and the not-matched branch inserts nothing new on the second run. Therefore $f(f(T)) = f(T)$: the second daily run is a no-op, with 0 rows inserted and 0 rows actually modified (Delta still reports the matched row count, but the values are identical).

Analysis — **Why the method works.** The window function is a *set-to-set* transformation that resolves multiplicity in the source before any write happens; MERGE is a *keyed upsert* that resolves the write in the target. Separating those two concerns is what makes both halves provable. The exam almost always hides the trap in ordering: if you merge first and deduplicate later, the same `order_id` from the source matches the same target row twice, and Delta raises `DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE`. Deduplicate first, always.

**Common mistakes.** (a) Sorting `updated_at` as a string: '2025-03-2' and '2025-03-02' order differently under lexical comparison, so cast to `timestamp` explicitly. (b) Ignoring ties: two rows with identical `updated_at` make `row_number()` non-deterministic across runs, which silently breaks the idempotency you claimed — add a deterministic tie-breaker such as `ingest_ts` or the source file path. (c) Leaving `updated_at` nullable: with `desc_nulls_last()` a null-timestamp row is only kept if it is the sole version of that key, so route null keys/timestamps to a quarantine table rather than letting them define "current".

**How it generalises.** This is the canonical silver-layer pattern in the medallion architecture (bronze = raw landed data, silver = conformed, deduplicated entities, gold = business-level aggregates) and the upstream half of a Type 1 slowly changing dimension (SCD Type 1: overwrite the attribute with the newest value, keep no history; SCD Type 2 would instead add valid-from/valid-to columns and keep every version). Operationally, package the job as a versioned artifact and promote the *same* built artifact through dev → staging → prod rather than editing per environment — the build-once/deploy-many principle behind artifact promotion [source 5], with isolated staging environments kept separate from live ones [source 6]. Parameterise the catalog/table names per environment; keep the dedup logic byte-identical.
Problem 2

**Scenario.** The Day-3 incremental drop into `bronze.orders_raw` contains 1,204,881 rows; all of them reference orders that already exist in `silver.orders_current`, which now holds 4,180,347 rows. Because the producer replays a 30-minute window, 2,317 of those rows carry an `updated_at` that is **older** than the value already stored in the target. For example, order 1003 is stored as `status = 'delivered', amount = 240.00, updated_at = 2025-03-03 19:31:00`, and the Day-3 file contains a replay of its earlier state: `status = 'shipped', amount = 240.00, updated_at = 2025-03-03 06:00:00`. Your Day-3 job uses the `p1` logic (`WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *`). (a) What goes wrong, and what is the numeric blast radius on a metric counting delivered orders for 2025-03-03 (currently 41,208)? (b) Rewrite the MERGE so late data cannot regress the target. (c) A teammate proposes adding `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE` to 'clean up' the target. Evaluate that proposal.
Hint: Add a predicate to the matched branch and ask what 'not matched by source' means when the source is an incremental batch, not a full snapshot.

Worked solution
**(a) What goes wrong.** `WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *` is unconditional: any source row that matches on `order_id` overwrites every target column, regardless of which record is newer. The Day-3 dedup output contains one row per order, so the *replayed* 2025-03-03 06:00:00 state is the survivor for order 1003 — the target regresses from `delivered` back to `shipped`. Numerically: the "delivered orders on 2025-03-03" metric falls from 41,208 to 41,207, a 1-row error from 1 row of the batch; scaled over the full drop, the 2,317 late rows can flip up to 2,317 / 4,218,764 = **0.055%** of the batch, which is small in percentage terms but is a *wrong* answer, and it is exactly the kind of silent corruption that is not caught by a row-count check.

**(b) Guard the matched branch with a recency predicate.**

```sql

MERGE INTO silver.orders_current AS t

USING deduped_orders AS s

ON t.order_id = s.order_id

WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET *

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *

```

With a strict `>`, order 1003's Day-3 replay (06:00:00 < 19:31:00) fails the predicate and is skipped: `status` stays `delivered` and the metric stays 41,208. Strictness matters — using `>=` retasks the engine to rewrite rows whose timestamp is *equal* to the stored one, produce no value change, and re-introduce non-determinism if two records share a timestamp but differ in payload. `>` makes "no new information" an explicit no-op.

**(c) The `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE` proposal is wrong and destructive here.** `NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE` means: a row exists in the target with no corresponding key in the source. That semantic is only sound when the source is a **full snapshot** of the entity. Day-3's source is an *incremental* batch of 1,204,881 rows, so every target key that simply did not change today would look "missing": 4,180,347 - 1,204,881 = **2,975,466 rows deleted**, i.e. 71.2% of the silver table. If deletes are genuinely required, either (i) treat the source as a full snapshot (or a CDC stream that emits explicit `op = 'D'` tombstones) and apply `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND t.order_date = current_date() THEN DELETE`, scoping the delete to today's partition, or (ii) model deletion as a soft-delete flag set by the CDC stream, and never use source-absence as evidence of deletion.

Analysis — **Why the method works.** The predicate moves the "which version wins" decision from the *pipeline schedule* (whatever arrived last) to the *data itself* (`updated_at`), which is the only thing that stays correct when batches arrive out of order, are replayed, or are backfilled months later. It also preserves idempotency: replaying the same batch again still fails the predicate and writes nothing.

**Common mistakes.** (1) Putting the recency filter in the source (`WHERE s.updated_at > ...`) instead of the merge condition — you cannot reference the target column `t.updated_at` in the source query, so the filter must live in the `WHEN MATCHED AND` clause or in a pre-merge join. (2) Using `UPDATE SET status = s.status` while other columns arrive with different timestamps (column-level staleness), which silently mixes vintages within one row; column-level conditions (`SET status = s.status` guarded per column) or a per-column `staged_at` are the fixes. (3) Assuming MERGE deletes: MERGE **never** deletes a target row merely because the source stopped sending it — deletes only happen in an explicit `WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE` branch, and that branch is dangerous the moment the source is incremental instead of a full snapshot.

**Operational generalisation.** A regression like this should be caught before promotion, not after: data-quality assertions on the target (delivered-order counts, duplicate-key counts) belong in the pipeline's test stage, which is the CI/CD pattern of promoting pipeline artifacts between environments safely and reliably [source 3], with post-deploy verification and a defined rollback trigger [source 5]. Version-control the corrected MERGE as a new artifact, promote it through staging first — the staging-versus-live separation exists precisely so this class of bug is found before it reaches production [source 6].
Problem 3

**Scenario (exam variation).** `silver.orders_current` is 6.2 GB stored across 4,860 files (average ~1.3 MB each) in Delta Lake. Each day the source produces 1.2M changed rows (about 1.8 GB). Four candidate designs are proposed to keep the table current:

- **A.** `INSERT OVERWRITE` the whole target from a fresh full read of `bronze.orders_raw` (deduplicated).

- **B.** Incremental ingestion (Auto Loader or `COPY INTO`) feeding the windowed dedup from `p1`, landed with the guarded `MERGE` from `p2`.

- **C.** Append every incoming batch without deduplication and let analysts query a `materialized view` that applies `row_number()` at read time.

- **D.** `TRUNCATE` the target, then re-insert the deduplicated full snapshot.

Which approach keeps the table current with the **least effort**, and what is the daily write amplification for the winner versus option A? Assume B rewrites only the files touched by the matched keys: roughly 9% of target files.
Hint: Compute bytes written per day for each option; "least effort" in the exam means least bytes written, least operator intervention, and automatic handling of new files.

Worked solution
**Step 1 — define 'current' and 'least effort' precisely.** `current` = exactly one row per `order_id`, reflecting the newest `updated_at`. `least effort` = fewest bytes rewritten per day, no manual file bookkeeping, and no orchestration change when new files land. Those three criteria are what the exam scores.

**Step 2 — compute daily write amplification.**

- **A (full overwrite):** reads the full source and writes the full target: 6.2 GB target + ~1.8 GB of changed data folded in ≈ **8.0 GB written per day**.

- **B (Auto Loader/COPY INTO + guarded MERGE):** Auto Loader tracks which files have already been processed, so ingestion reads only new files (1.8 GB). The MERGE rewrites only the files containing matched keys: 9% of 6.2 GB = **0.56 GB written per day**.

- **C (append + read-time view):** 1.8 GB/day appended *plus* the full 6.2 GB scanned on every query; the table grows without bound (30 × 1.8 GB = 54 GB after a month) and every analyst pays the dedup cost.

- **D (TRUNCATE + insert):** same 8.0 GB/day as A, but worse — the target is unreadable or empty inside the transaction window, so consumers see a gap.

Ratio of A to B: $W = 8.0 / 0.56 = 14.3$. Over a 30-day month, A writes 240 GB versus B's 16.8 GB — **14.3× less write amplification** for the same resulting table state.

**Step 3 — pick B, and state why in exam language.** Incremental ingestion discovers new files automatically (no listing code to maintain) and MERGE is a keyed upsert, so only affected files are rewritten. Month-over-month the table size is roughly constant (~6.2 GB) instead of growing by 1.8 GB per day, because duplicates and stale versions are resolved on write rather than on read.

**Step 4 — sanity-check the ledger (what each option does *not* do).**

| | one row per order_id | writes/day | table growth | new files auto-detected |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| A overwrite | yes | ~8.0 GB | none | n/a (full re-read) |

| B incremental + MERGE | yes | ~0.56 GB | none | yes |

| C append + view | only at query time | ~1.8 GB | +1.8 GB/day | depends on ingestion |

| D truncate + insert | yes, after a gap | ~8.0 GB | none | n/a |

Only B satisfies all three criteria simultaneously; C is disqualified by unbounded growth and repeated compute, A and D by write amplification and (for D) by an availability gap.

Analysis — **Why the answer is B.** The exam phrases the question as "which approach keeps the table current with the least effort" and rewards recognising that the expensive part of an ELT job is usually the bytes written, not the rows read. MERGE writes a deterministic function of the *keys that changed*; overwrite writes a function of the *whole table*. When the daily change set is ~1.8 GB against a 6.2 GB table, that difference is a factor of 14.3, and it widens as the table grows.

**Where students go wrong.** (1) Choosing A because "overwrite is simpler and therefore less effort" — it is *simpler to author* and far more expensive to run, and it also rewrites history: any downstream consumer reading during the overwrite sees a partially-rewritten state unless you swap tables. (2) Choosing C because a materialized view sounds free. A materialized view is a table whose contents are maintained by re-evaluating a defining query, so it shifts the dedup cost to every refresh and every query and does nothing about unbounded append growth. (3) Choosing D because TRUNCATE is fast — it is fast and it is unsafe, since it removes availability and destroys any rows the current incremental source did not resend.

**Edge cases to state explicitly.** If a MERGE must also remove records, remember it never deletes target rows that are absent from the source; add an explicit, partition-scoped delete branch or model deletion as soft-delete flags — and be certain the source is a full snapshot before doing so. If the target is partitioned and the merge predicate does not include the partition column, Delta must scan every file and the 9% rewrite advantage evaporates; partition on a predicate the merge actually uses. Table maintenance (compaction) should target the rewritten files, not the whole table.

**Deployment framing.** The winning design still has to be promoted safely: the incremental-ingestion-plus-MERGE job should be defined as infrastructure (parameters for catalog and paths per environment) and shipped through the same pipeline stages — build, test, scan, deploy — with dev → staging → prod promotion, so the promotion mechanism itself is testable rather than manual [source 5]. Isolated staging and live environments for data pipelines are the standard way to validate a change like this before it touches production tables [source 6], and deployment pipelines exist precisely to give visibility into production readiness instead of copying configuration by hand [source 2].
Problem 4

**Scenario.** Six months into production, the upstream JSON feed makes two changes in the same week: (1) it **adds** a new field `fulfillment_center` to every record; (2) it **renames** the field `amt` to `order_amount` without changing its meaning. An Auto Loader stream (`cloudFiles`) reads this feed and writes the deduplicated silver table. After the changes, the stream fails on restart with a schema-inference mismatch against its checkpoint, and separately 26,158 of the 4,218,764 records in the batch (0.62%) are missing required fields or contain malformed JSON. Redesign ingestion so that (a) additive changes flow through, (b) the rename is handled correctly, (c) malformed records do not stop the pipeline, and (d) the failure cannot recur silently.
Hint: Classify each change as evolutionary (additive) or non-evolutionary (rename/type change) — the two require opposite remedies, and the checkpoint locks the schema.

Worked solution
**Step 1 — classify the two changes before touching configuration.**

- *Add `fulfillment_center`* → **evolutionary**. New nullable column, no existing consumer breaks.

- *Rename `amt` → `order_amount`* → **non-evolutionary**. A rename is observed by the reader as *one dropped column plus one added column*; the inference layer cannot know these are the same field.

This classification is the whole exam point: additive changes are absorbed, structural changes are not.

**Step 2 — absorb the additive change.** Enable schema evolution on ingestion so the new column is added to the streamed schema and lands in the target:

```python

(spark.readStream.format('cloudFiles')

.option('cloudFiles.schemaLocation', '/checkpoints/orders/schema')

.option('cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode', 'addNewColumns') # additive only

.option('rescuedDataColumn', '_rescued_data')

.load('s3://landing/orders/')

.writeStream.option('checkpointLocation', '/checkpoints/orders/data')

.option('mergeSchema', 'true')

.trigger(availableNow=True)

.table('silver.orders_staged'))

```

`addNewColumns` adds columns that appear in the data without failing the stream; `mergeSchema = 'true'` lets the Delta write accept the widened schema.

**Step 3 — treat the rename as a data-migration event, not a config flag.** After the rename, `order_amount` arrives populated and `amt` arrives null (or absent). If you simply let schema evolution add `order_amount`, you get a table where `amt` is null for all new records and `order_amount` is null for all historical ones — a silently broken column with a 50/50 split. Correct procedure: (i) stop the stream; (ii) keep the old checkpoint for the old schema and start a **new checkpoint and new target table** for the new schema (`silver.orders_staged_v2`); (iii) backfill by unioning history projected onto the new schema (`amt AS order_amount` for old partitions, `order_amount` for new ones); (iv) publish a compatibility view `silver.orders_v` that exposes `order_amount` so downstream readers never see the split. The checkpoint's schema is frozen, so a non-evolutionary change is only recoverable by writing to a fresh checkpoint — restarting the old stream against the changed source is exactly what produced the failure.

**Step 4 — isolate malformed records instead of failing the batch.** With `rescuedDataColumn` set, records that cannot be parsed against the declared schema are not dropped: the offending fields (or the whole payload) are captured in `_rescued_data`, and the rest of the record is preserved. 26,158 / 4,218,764 = **0.62%** of the batch is affected. Route those rows to a dead-letter table for reprocessing:

```sql

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW bad_rows AS

SELECT *, current_timestamp() AS quarantined_at

FROM silver.orders_staged

WHERE _rescued_data IS NOT NULL; -- 0.62% of the batch

```

Because that fraction is small, quarantining does not threaten the pipeline's SLA; failing the whole batch over 0.62% of rows does.

**Step 5 — make the failure loud and non-recurring.** Record the inferred schema version alongside the batch; add an assertion that fails the job (not the stream) when the incoming field set differs from the recorded one by more than additive changes. That converts a 3 a.m. restart failure into a pre-promotion test failure.

Analysis — **Why it works.** Admission control is the organising idea: ingestion should accept and *record* novelty rather than reject it, but it must be able to tell "new column" from "changed column". `addNewColumns` plus `mergeSchema` handles the first; a new checkpoint plus a backfill handles the second; `rescuedDataColumn` handles corrupt records without taking the batch down. All three are separable, and the mistake students make is to reach for one switch (`mergeSchema`) for all three problems.

**Common mistakes.** (1) Believing `mergeSchema` can express a rename. It cannot — it will add `order_amount` as a new all-null column and leave `amt` all-null for new data, producing a column that looks healthy in the table listing but is wrong for half the rows. (2) Editing reader options in place and restarting the old stream: the checkpoint schema is locked, so the stream fails again with the same mismatch; the fix requires a new checkpoint location. (3) Dropping malformed rows silently with a permissive mode, which turns a 0.62% data-quality problem into an invisible one — the rescued column exists so the bad rows remain auditable. (4) Assuming a schema change alone justifies a full table rewrite: for the additive case, only ingestion config and the write's schema merge flag are needed.

**Generalisation and platform practice.** The same split applies to any streaming ELT: evolutionary change → widen schema in place; non-evolutionary change → new checkpoint, new table, backfill, compatibility view. This matters because the artifact you are changing (stream definition + job code) must be version-controlled and promoted between environments rather than patched live; deployment pipelines provide a structured, governed promotion of content across environments without manual copying or reconfiguration [source 1], and data-pipeline CI/CD exists to promote those artifacts between environments safely and reliably [source 3]. Isolating the repair in a staging environment first — separate from live resources — is what prevents a config edit from becoming a production outage [source 6].

actions.text: Now let's pull the Domain 1 and 2 material together with one production-grade ELT task — exactly the style of problem the exam uses to separate a working answer from the expected answer.

Here's the scenario, exam-style. A raw orders table keeps receiving duplicate and late-arriving records. Your job: produce a deduplicated silver table with exactly one current row per order_id, keeping the record with the latest updated_at, and make the job safely re-runnable on every daily run. Notice the two hidden requirements — deduplication and idempotency — they are what the question is really testing.

Before reading the solution, try yourself. The hint: deduplicate with a window on order_id ordered by updated_at in descending order, filter row_number equals one. Hold onto that — it's the shape of the answer.

Now the worked solution. Contract first: state the three conditions the result must satisfy. Then read the source, apply a window partitioned by order_id and ordered by updated_at descending, filter row_number equal to one, and MERGE INTO the target — ON order_id, WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET star, WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT star. Deduplicate before the merge, never inside it.

Why does the method work? MERGE is idempotent — re-running the job leaves the target in the same state. And deduplication must happen before the merge, or the engine can raise a multi-match error when two source rows touch the same target key. Two exam rewards you for knowing: MERGE never deletes rows missing from the source, and late-arriving rows whose updated_at precedes the stored value simply won't win the match.

Problem two is a direct extension — the Day-3 incremental drop into bronze. There's a predicate trap inside the WHEN MATCHED branch. Read the hint, then check your instinct against the worked solution.

The scenario: this incremental load shows the classic symptom of a MERGE matched branch that overwrote good rows with stale ones. The fix is to add a predicate to that branch — only update when the incoming updated_at is newer than the stored one. That's the second Domain 2 trap the exam loves to plant.

One beat on the pattern before we move on: any MERGE that touches an update column carrying a version or timestamp needs a guard predicate on the matched branch. Without it, you're silently accepting out-of-order writes.

Problem three flips the mode from "write the solution" to "select the approach." Same silver.orders_current story, but now the question is which strategy keeps the table current with the least effort. Scan the options before I reveal the reasoning.

The scenario is an exam variation — the phrasing shifts, but the underlying question is the same: incremental ingestion plus a MERGE, versus full overwrite on each run. On Delta, the expected answer is MERGE fed by Auto Loader or COPY INTO, because that's the pattern that stays current incrementally and stays within cost.

Step one in the worked solution: define what "current" and "late" mean for this table. Step two: measure the cost of each option in bytes written per day. Step three: pick the option whose cost curve stays flat as the table grows. That reasoning step is what the exam is scoring — not just the letter.

Why answer B? Because the exam phrasing — "keeps the table current with the least effort" — is a Delta-Lake idiom for incremental ingestion plus MERGE. Full overwrite is correct semantically but fails the "least effort" clause once volume grows. That's the discriminator between a working answer and the expected answer.

Problem four is the production twist — six months in, the upstream contract starts drifting. Schema evolution, admission control, and governance decisions all collide in one scenario. This is the Domain 3–5 crossover problem in miniature.

The scenario: the upstream source adds columns and tweaks types on a rolling basis. Your job is to decide — do you evolve, enforce, or quarantine each change? Read the hint: classify every change as evolutionary or breaking before you choose a knob.

Step one of the worked solution: split the two changes. An additive column is evolutionary — mergeSchema absorbs it, autoMerge within MERGE handles it, and overwriteSchema is never the right tool. A destructive type change is breaking — you must decide whether to enforce and let the write fail, or quarantine the invalid rows and page the on-call. Step two: wire the chosen policy into the pipeline, not into ad-hoc notebooks.

Why it works: admission control is the gate. Every row either meets the contract and lands in the silver table, or fails and is routed to quarantine with a reason. That's what lets you keep the table current without silently corrupting it — and it's the pattern that ties Domains 2, 3, and 5 together at certification time.

Take a moment with the four problems as a set. The exam hides the same three decisions inside every scenario: dedupe before you merge, guard the matched branch, and choose your schema-evolution knob deliberately. If you can name those three moves on any question stem, you're ready for the Domain 1 and 2 traps we're about to compare.

scenes.title: Check: Platform and ELT Traps

questions.question: A data engineering team is designing a new analytics workload on Databricks. The data lives in cloud object storage owned and governed by the central platform team, is read by external BI tools that query the storage path directly, and must survive cluster recreation and workspace deletion without data loss. The team wants to minimize Databricks-side storage cost, and the workload is a nightly batch job that runs for about 20 minutes. Which combination of table type and cluster type best satisfies the stated cost and lifecycle constraints?

options.label: Managed Delta table on an all-purpose cluster, because managed tables are easier to govern and all-purpose clusters support interactive notebooks
External Delta table on a job cluster, because the data lifecycle is owned by the storage path and the ephemeral job cluster minimizes compute cost
Managed Delta table on a job cluster, because managed tables give automatic lifecycle management and job clusters are the cheapest compute
External Delta table on an all-purpose cluster, because only all-purpose clusters can read external locations registered in the metastore

questions.analysis: The two traps here are the managed/external choice and the cluster choice, and each is decided by a stated constraint. Because the data must be readable directly from the object storage path by external tools and must survive workspace deletion, the table must be EXTERNAL (managed tables have their data lifecycle tied to the metastore object, so dropping the table can drop the files). Because the workload is a short nightly batch job with no interactivity requirement, a JOB cluster is the cost-optimal compute: Databricks bills job compute at a lower rate and it terminates automatically, which is the whole point of choosing it. Option A fails the lifecycle constraint (managed table) and the cost constraint (all-purpose compute for a batch job). Option C inverts the table choice; managed tables are 'easier' only until the storage-ownership requirement is violated. Option D fails both constraints, and its justification is false: all-purpose clusters have no exclusive privilege on external locations (Unity Catalog governs external locations independently of cluster type). Note that cost and lifecycle, not raw feature capability, are the deciding factors.

questions.question: You must transform 4 TB of Parquet data into a curated Delta table. The requirement is a per-row string cleanup plus a windowed sessionization computed with a bounded lookback. The team is optimizing for the FASTEST end-to-end transformation, and the code must be maintainable by a team of 12 engineers. Select all statements that correctly guide the choice among Spark SQL, the DataFrame API, and a Python UDF.

options.label: For the per-row string cleanup that is expressible with built-in functions, a Python UDF is the slowest option because it forces row-by-row serialization between the JVM and the Python worker, defeating Photon
Spark SQL and the DataFrame API compile to the same Catalyst logical plan and physical execution, so for the windowed sessionization either is a valid performance-equivalent choice
A Python UDF should be preferred over Spark SQL whenever the logic is complex, because Catalyst can optimize Python bytecode just as aggressively as built-in expressions
If the per-row logic genuinely cannot be expressed with built-ins, a pandas (vectorized) UDF is generally faster than a row-at-a-time Python UDF, but still slower than pure built-in expressions

questions.analysis: The exam's recurring trap is 'it works but it is non-declarative', so the performance question is really a question about whether the engine can see and optimize your logic. Option A is correct: a Python UDF is a black box to Catalyst and Photon; each row is pickled across the JVM/Python boundary, which is why a UDF that is functionally identical to a built-in can be an order of magnitude slower on 4 TB [source 3]. Option B is correct because Spark SQL and the DataFrame API are two front-ends over the same Catalyst optimizer and physical plan, so the windowed sessionization has equivalent performance in either, and the maintainability tie-breaker goes to the API your team already uses consistently [source 5]. Option D is correct and is the useful nuance: if the logic truly is not expressible with built-ins, vectorized pandas UDFs amortize the serialization cost over Arrow batches and beat row-at-a-time UDFs, though they still cannot match a native expression. Option C is the classic wrong answer: it claims the optimizer can optimize Python bytecode, which is exactly what it cannot do.

questions.question: A Delta table receives 500,000 small files per day from a streaming writer. Analysts report that point lookups on a high-cardinality 'customer_id' column are slow, and the table has accumulated six months of file history. You must distinguish what OPTIMIZE, ZORDER, and VACUUM each actually change on disk and in table history. Which sequence of operations correctly addresses the fragmentation and the lookup latency while preserving the ability to time-travel back 14 days?

options.label: Run VACUUM with a 0-hour retention to delete the small files, then run ZORDER on customer_id; this cuts storage and improves lookup latency
Run OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (customer_id) to compact small files and co-locate related values, then run VACUUM with a retention greater than 14 days so time-travel history survives
Run ZORDER alone, because ZORDER performs compaction as a side effect and no separate OPTIMIZE is required
Run OPTIMIZE with the default settings, then immediately run VACUUM RETAIN 0 HOURS; OPTIMIZE alone produces the file layout needed for fast point lookups on customer_id

questions.analysis: The three operations are distinguished by what they touch. OPTIMIZE performs file compaction: it rewrites many small files into fewer larger files, changing the on-disk layout. ZORDER is a data-clustering option of OPTIMIZE: it co-locates rows that share values in the ZORDER columns so that data skipping can prune files during point lookups on high-cardinality columns. VACUUM is orthogonal to both: it deletes files no longer referenced by the current table version, which is what actually reclaims storage, and its retention window is what controls how far back time-travel can go. Option B is correct because it names each operation by its real effect: OPTIMIZE + ZORDER for layout and pruning, VACUUM with retention greater than the required 14-day time-travel window so history is preserved. Option A is wrong because VACUUM with 0-hour retention destroys the 14-day time-travel requirement, and it does not improve read layout. Option C is wrong because ZORDER does not run compaction on its own; it is an option on OPTIMIZE and requires OPTIMIZE to actually rewrite files. Option D is wrong because plain OPTIMIZE without ZORDER does not produce the clustering that speeds point lookups on customer_id, and the 0-hour vacuum again breaks time-travel.

actions.text: This is the checkpoint we just set up for Domain 1 and 2 — the platform positioning and the ELT traps that mirror the most common wrong answers on the exam.

Take each question on your own and commit to an answer before you move on; the whole point here is to feel where the constraints bite. Work through all three, then hit submit and I'll walk through what tripped you up.

scenes.title: Domains 3–5 Review: Incremental, Production, Governance

elements.content: Domains 3–5 Review: Incremental, Production, Governance
Domain 3 — Incremental Data Processing (~22%): Choose the Right Ingest Pattern

• Auto Loader for continuously arriving cloud files: schema inference + evolution; rescued data column captures malformed records.

• COPY INTO for straightforward, idempotent batch file loads — tracks ingested files to prevent duplicates on re-run.

• Streaming tables & materialized views for declarative incremental pipelines: define the target, let the engine compute deltas.

• Decision rule: files arriving continuously + evolving schema → Auto Loader; small, known file sets → COPY INTO.
Domain 4 — Production Pipelines (~16%): Automate Promotion, Isolate Environments

• Databricks Asset Bundles package jobs, pipelines, and configuration as code; CI/CD promotes the same built artifact through dev → staging → prod instead of rebuilding per environment [source 5].

• Environment isolation (exam favorite): separate workspaces or catalogs per environment; credentials live in secret scopes, never in code; environment-specific values resolve as parameters at deploy time [source 6].

• Artifact promotion is build once, deploy many — the most common trap is rebuilding binaries per environment, which silently reintroduces the bug you just fixed.

actions.text: Now let's close out the blueprint with the final three domains: incremental data processing, production pipelines, and data governance. These are the last pieces of the puzzle, and they tie directly back to the deployment work we just completed.

Domain 3 covers incremental data processing at roughly twenty-two percent of the exam — the single heaviest domain in this group. You need to know when to reach for each ingestion tool: Auto Loader for continuously arriving cloud files with schema inference and evolution, COPY INTO for straightforward idempotent batch file loads, and streaming tables with materialized views for declarative incremental pipelines.

The decision rule here is the exam's favorite kind of question: it never asks whether a pipeline runs. It asks who can read the data, whether a re-run is idempotent, and whether a failed run can be safely retried. Keep that trap cluster in mind as you read every scenario.

Domain 4 covers production pipelines at about sixteen percent. The headline concept is Databricks Asset Bundles — they package jobs, pipelines, and configuration as code, and CI/CD promotes the same built artifact through dev, staging, and production rather than rebuilding for each environment.

Environment isolation is the favorite deployment topic. Separate workspaces or catalogs per environment, credentials held in secret scopes rather than in code, and environment-specific values resolved as parameters at deploy time — those three details are exactly what the exam expects you to name.

Domain 5 is governance. Unity Catalog supplies the three-level namespace — catalog dot schema dot table — centralized grants, row filters and column masks for fine-grained access, and automatic lineage for impact analysis. Notice that these map straight onto the CI/CD and environment work we just did: the target catalog is the deployment boundary, and the grants are what make promotion safe. Take a moment to connect the three domains in your own notes before we move to the study plan.
