outlines.title: Worked Problem: Diagnosing Slow Reads on an Ingested Table
outlines.description: Fully-worked diagnostic problem that moves from symptom to evidence to the correct maintenance command.
keyPoints: Statement: a streaming-ingested Delta table takes 90 seconds to run a simple filtered aggregate; DESCRIBE DETAIL reports numFiles = 12,000 and sizeBytes = 180 GB.
[Table] DESCRIBE DETAIL before and after maintenance: numFiles 12,000 to 240, sizeBytes 180 GB to 180 GB, unchanged row count after SELECT COUNT(*).

Worked solution: (1) confirm file count and average file size (180 GB / 12,000 ≈ 15 MB — far below target), (2) run OPTIMIZE with a date-range WHERE clause, (3) re-run DESCRIBE DETAIL and DESCRIBE HISTORY to confirm the new commit, (4) re-measure the query.

Analysis: bin-packing removes per-file overhead (listing, footer reads, task scheduling) which is why the full aggregate speeds up; a highly selective single-partition predicate may gain little because OPTIMIZE does not reorganize rows within files.
Common pitfalls: running OPTIMIZE on every micro-batch, forgetting that OPTIMIZE is not free (it rewrites bytes and incurs compute), and expecting OPTIMIZE to remove duplicates.
outlines.teachingObjective: Diagnose a small-file problem from table metadata and justify an OPTIMIZE strategy.

outlines.title: Z-ORDER BY: Multi-Dimensional Clustering for Data Skipping
outlines.description: Explain how Z-ORDER co-locates related rows so file-level statistics let Delta skip files entirely.
keyPoints: Given a selective filter on a high-cardinality column, choose Z-ORDER columns so Delta can skip files using min/max statistics.
Z-ORDER is multi-dimensional clustering: rows are ordered across several columns so values that co-occur in queries land in the same files.
Syntax: OPTIMIZE events ZORDER BY (event_date, user_id); it is always applied as part of an OPTIMIZE run, never standalone.
Effect: tighter per-file min/max ranges in the file statistics that Delta maintains for skipping — fewer files scanned, less I/O, shorter queries.
Selectivity rule: pick columns used frequently in WHERE filters with high cardinality (for example user_id, device_id, event_ts), not low-cardinality flags.
Limits and traps: keep to about four columns, returns diminish beyond that, and Z-ORDER does not replace partitioning — do not also partition on the same high-cardinality column.
outlines.teachingObjective: Select Z-ORDER columns and predict their effect on data skipping and read performance.

outlines.title: VACUUM and Retention: Cleaning Up Stale Files Safely
outlines.description: Teach how VACUUM removes unreferenced files, why retention exists, and how vacuuming too early breaks time travel.
keyPoints: Given a time-travel requirement, choose a VACUUM retention setting that does not delete files older versions still need.
VACUUM physically deletes data files that are no longer referenced by the current table version and are older than the retention threshold.
Default retention is 7 days (168 hours); VACUUM table RETAIN 168 HOURS is explicit, and VACUUM table DRY RUN lists what would be deleted without deleting.
Retention protects readers: time travel queries, streaming readers on an older snapshot, and concurrent long-running jobs may still read those files — deleting them causes FileNotFound errors.
Going below 7 days requires setting spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled=false, which is explicitly unsafe and breaks time travel.
Exam trap: VACUUM is irreversible and does not rewrite the transaction log — it frees storage by deleting files, while older history entries remain in the log but become unreadable.
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply VACUUM with a retention setting that satisfies the table's time-travel and concurrency requirements.

outlines.title: Trade-off Analysis: Maintenance Frequency versus Time Travel Needs
outlines.description: A constrained decision task: choose a maintenance policy for a table that must satisfy a latency SLA while auditors need 30 days of history.
keyPoints: Constraints: nightly ingestion of 500 GB into a Delta table, dashboards must return in under 5 seconds, auditors require 30 days of history, storage cost is a stated concern.
Option A — hourly OPTIMIZE plus Z-ORDER and VACUUM with the default 7-day retention: fastest reads, highest compute cost, breaks the 30-day audit requirement.
Option B — daily OPTIMIZE plus Z-ORDER after ingestion and VACUUM with the default 7-day retention, with audit history served from a separate append-only history table.
Option C — minimal maintenance with 30-day retention and no VACUUM: preserves time travel at the cost of degraded read latency and rising storage.
Pros and cons must be weighed against the SLA, the audit window, and the fact that VACUUM cannot be undone.

Recommended: Option B — maintain the hot table after each ingestion window and keep the extended history in a separate table, because VACUUM deletes files irreversibly and cannot coexist with a 30-day time-travel SLA on the same table.
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a maintenance and retention policy under conflicting performance, cost, and compliance constraints.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Sizing and Scheduling a Maintenance Runbook
outlines.description: Fully-worked quantitative problem that computes target file counts, chooses Z-ORDER columns, and writes the maintenance SQL for a stated SLA.
keyPoints: Statement: an events table is 1.2 TB with 24,000 files (average 50 MB), partitioned by event_date, queried with filters on user_id and event_date; the team needs 30 days of time travel and faster selective reads.
Step 1 — size the compaction: at a 256 MB target, 1.2 TB / 256 MB ≈ 4,900 files, so OPTIMIZE should cut file count by roughly 5x, reducing per-file overhead proportionally.

Step 2 — choose clustering: OPTIMIZE events WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS ZORDER BY (user_id), keeping high-cardinality user_id for data skipping and event_date for range pruning.
Step 3 — set retention safely: VACUUM events RETAIN 720 HOURS (30 days) to match the time-travel SLA; validate first with VACUUM events RETAIN 720 HOURS DRY RUN.
Step 4 — schedule: run compaction after each ingestion window on recent partitions, and run VACUUM on a separate, less frequent schedule.

Analysis and pitfalls: over-partitioning plus Z-ORDER on the same column duplicates effort; running OPTIMIZE too often wastes compute; using the default 7-day retention silently breaks the 30-day audit requirement.
outlines.teachingObjective: Compute and justify a concrete OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER, and VACUUM plan for an exam-style scenario.

outlines.title: Summary: Maintenance Roles, Order of Operations, and Exam Traps
outlines.description: Consolidate the lesson into a decision summary and pre-empt the most common certification distractor patterns.
keyPoints: Three roles to keep straight: OPTIMIZE compacts files, Z-ORDER BY lays data out for data skipping, VACUUM deletes stale files.
Order of operations after ingestion: OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (...) on recent partitions, then VACUUM on its own less frequent schedule with a safe retention window.
Exam trap 1: OPTIMIZE does not sort, merge, or deduplicate rows and does not change query results.
Exam trap 2: Z-ORDER is bounded (about four columns), has diminishing returns, and never replaces partitioning.
Exam trap 3: VACUUM is irreversible, defaults to 7 days, and deleting files still needed by time travel or concurrent readers causes FileNotFound failures.
Unit link: layout operations commit add/remove file actions to the transaction log, so versioning and time travel remain consistent until VACUUM removes the underlying files.
outlines.teachingObjective: Consolidate maintenance decision rules and avoid the certification exam's most common traps.

outlines.title: Spark SQL, DataFrames, and the Databricks Execution Model
outlines.description: Establish the mental model for the whole unit: what a DataFrame is, where the SparkSession comes from, and why SQL and PySpark are two syntaxes over one engine.

outlines.title: Reading Data into a DataFrame and Inspecting the Schema
outlines.description: Teach the read-then-inspect habit: how to load files and tables into a DataFrame and how to verify the schema before writing any transformation.
keyPoints: File reads: spark.read.format('csv'|'json'|'parquet').option('header', True).schema(...).load(path) — always chain the reader, never call it twice.
Table reads: spark.table('catalog.schema.table') returns a Delta table with its schema and statistics already known, so no inference is needed.
Inspect before you transform: printSchema(), dtypes, columns, count(), describe()/summary(), and display(df.limit(10)).

Exam trap: for CSV, Spark does not read the header or infer types unless you set option('header', True) and inferSchema=True; inferSchema also costs an extra pass over the data, so a declared schema is preferred.

outlines.title: Key Terms: Spark SQL and DataFrame Fundamentals
outlines.description: Reference glossary of the unit's core vocabulary, defined precisely enough to answer definition-style exam items.
keyPoints: SparkSession — the single entry point to Spark; in a Databricks notebook it is pre-created as the variable `spark` and manages configuration, catalog access, and DataFrame creation.
DataFrame — an immutable, lazily evaluated, distributed collection of rows with a named schema; every transformation returns a NEW DataFrame rather than mutating the original.
Transformation vs. action — transformations (select, filter, withColumn, groupBy, orderBy) are lazy and only describe a plan; actions (show, display, count, collect, write) trigger execution.
Lazy evaluation — Spark accumulates transformations into a logical plan and executes nothing until an action is called, which is precisely what allows Catalyst to optimize the whole plan at once.
Schema — the column names, data types, and nullability metadata of a DataFrame; printSchema() renders it as a tree and dtypes returns (name, type) pairs.

Delta table — a table whose data files plus a transaction log live in cloud object storage; read it with spark.table('catalog.schema.table') and the schema, statistics, and history come along with it.
Temporary view — a session-scoped SQL alias over a DataFrame created with df.createOrReplaceTempView('name'), letting the same data be queried with spark.sql('SELECT ... FROM name').

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Read, Inspect, Filter, and Select
outlines.description: A fully worked end-to-end problem that combines reading with an explicit schema, inspecting it, then filtering and selecting columns — in both PySpark and SQL.
keyPoints: Problem: from the raw file /databricks-datasets/retail/orders.csv (columns order_id, customer_id, order_ts, amount, status) return order_id, customer_id, and amount for only 'completed' orders placed in 2024 with amount >= 100, and state the resulting schema.

Step 1 — read with a declared schema: orders = (spark.read.option('header', True).schema('order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE, status STRING').csv(path)); then verify with orders.printSchema() and orders.count().

Step 2 — filter and select with the DataFrame API: orders.filter((col('status') == 'completed') & (year(col('order_ts')) == 2024) & (col('amount') >= 100)).select('order_id', 'customer_id', 'amount').

Step 3 — the SQL equivalent: SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' AND YEAR(order_ts) = 2024 AND amount >= 100; call explain() on both results to confirm they produce the same plan.

Analysis and pitfalls: an explicit schema avoids the extra scan that inferSchema performs and prevents silent type mismatches; filter is an alias of where; use & and | (not Python's `and`/`or`) and parenthesize each condition; and because DataFrames are immutable you must capture the returned DataFrame or nothing changes. A NULL in amount or status makes the whole predicate NULL, so those rows disappear — use isNull()/na.fill() deliberately.

complete relations (CSV) or documents (XML and JSON), and these are written into
files sequentially.

Examples and Types of Data Architecture
Because data architecture is an abstract discipline, it helps to reason by example. In
this section, we outline prominent examples and types of data architecture that are
popular today. Though this set of examples is by no means exhaustive, the intention is
to expose you to some of the most common data architecture patterns and to get you
thinking about the requisite flexibility and trade-off analysis needed when designing
a good architecture for your use case.

--- [source p.252] (page 252) ---
Single-Tenant Versus Multitenant Storage
In Chapter 3, we covered the trade-offs between single-tenant and multitenant
architecture. To recap, with single-tenant architecture, each group of tenants (e.g.,
individual users, groups of users, accounts, or customers) gets its own dedicated set
of resources such as networking, compute, and storage. A multitenant architecture
inverts this and shares these resources among groups of users. Both architectures are
widely used. This section looks at the implications of single-tenant and multitenant
storage.
Adopting single-tenant storage means that every tenant gets their dedicated storage.
In the example in Figure 6-10, each tenant gets a database. No data is shared among
these databases, and storage is totally isolated. An example of using single-tenant
storage is that each customer’s data must be stored in isolation and cannot be blended
with any other customer’s data. In this case, each customer gets their own database.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Derive a Revenue Report with when/otherwise and Casts
outlines.description: A fully worked problem that builds a small reporting dataset by deriving several columns at once, then proves the SQL and DataFrame versions are equivalent.
keyPoints: Problem: from the raw orders DataFrame produce order_id, order_date (DATE), amount as DECIMAL(10,2), amount_with_tax (amount * 1.08 as DECIMAL(10,2)), and revenue_band in {high, medium, low} using thresholds >= 1000 and >= 100, sorted by amount descending.

Solution (DataFrame API): orders.select(col('order_id'), to_date('order_ts').alias('order_date'), col('amount').cast('decimal(10,2)').alias('amount'), (col('amount') * 1.08).cast('decimal(10,2)').alias('amount_with_tax'), when(col('amount') >= 1000, 'high').when(col('amount') >= 100, 'medium').otherwise('low').alias('revenue_band')).orderBy(col('amount').desc()).

Solution (SQL): the identical SELECT with CAST(... AS DECIMAL(10,2)), CASE WHEN amount >= 1000 THEN 'high' WHEN amount >= 100 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'low' END, and ORDER BY amount DESC; compare df.explain() output for both to confirm one plan.

Analysis: withColumn is a projection — it appends or replaces a column by name and returns a new DataFrame; chaining many withColumn calls on a wide table inflates the logical plan, so deriving five columns in a single select/selectExpr is usually the cleaner and more optimizer-friendly choice.

Common pitfalls: CASE branches are evaluated top-down so a broad first condition swallows later ones; casting a non-numeric string yields NULL rather than raising an error, so validate before casting; and orderBy is still lazy — nothing is sorted until an action such as display() or write() runs.

What Is a Query?
We often run into people who know how to write SQL but are unfamiliar with how
a query works under the hood. Some of this introductory material on queries will be
familiar to experienced data engineers; feel free to skip ahead if this applies to you.
A query allows you to retrieve and act on data. Recall our conversation in Chapter 5
about CRUD. When a query retrieves data, it is issuing a request to read a pattern of
records. This is the R (read) in CRUD. You might issue a query that gets all records
from a table foo, such as SELECT * FROM foo. Or, you might apply a predicate
(logical condition) to filter your data by retrieving only records where the id is 1,
using the SQL query SELECT * FROM foo WHERE id=1.
Many databases allow you to create, update, and delete data. These are the CUD in
CRUD; your query will either create, mutate, or destroy existing records. Let’s review
some other common acronyms you’ll run into when working with query languages.

Practical Issues with Common File Formats
Engineers should also be aware of the file formats to export. CSV is still ubiquitous
and highly error prone at the time of this writing. Namely, CSV’s default delimiter is
also one of the most familiar characters in the English language—the comma! But it
gets worse.
CSV is by no means a uniform format. Engineers must stipulate the delimiter, quote
characters, and escaping to appropriately handle the export of string data. CSV also
doesn’t natively encode schema information or directly support nested structures.
CSV file encoding and schema information must be configured in the target system
to ensure appropriate ingestion. Autodetection is a convenience feature provided in
many cloud environments but is inappropriate for production ingestion. As a best
practice, engineers should record CSV encoding and schema details in file metadata.
More robust and expressive export formats include Parquet, Avro, Arrow, and ORC

The 2020s: Engineering for the data lifecycle
At the time of this writing, the data engineering role is evolving rapidly. We expect
this evolution to continue at a rapid clip for the foreseeable future. Whereas data
engineers historically tended to the low-level details of monolithic frameworks such
as Hadoop, Spark, or Informatica, the trend is moving toward decentralized, modu‐
larized, managed, and highly abstracted tools.
Indeed, data tools have proliferated at an astonishing rate (see Figure 1-3). Popular
trends in the early 2020s include the modern data stack, representing a collection
of off-the-shelf open source and third-party products assembled to make analysts’
lives easier. At the same time, data sources and data formats are growing both in
variety and size. Data engineering is increasingly a discipline of interoperation, and
connecting various technologies like LEGO bricks, to serve ultimate business goals.

capabilities, allowing customers to pull and push data. For example, many CRMs
offer APIs that their users can integrate into their systems and applications. We see
a common workflow to get data from a CRM, blend the CRM data through the
customer scoring model, and then use reverse ETL to send that data back into CRM
for salespeople to contact better-qualified leads.

Schema
What is the expected form of the data? What is the file format? Is it structured,
semistructured, or unstructured? What data types are expected? How does the data
fit into a larger hierarchy? Is it connected to other data through shared keys or other
relationships?
Note that schema need not be relational. Rather, data becomes more useful when we
have as much information about its structure and organization. For images stored in
a data lake, this schema information might explain the image format, resolution, and
the way the images fit into a larger hierarchy.
Schema can function as a sort of Rosetta stone, instructions that tell us how to read
the data. Two major schema patterns exist: schema on write and schema on read.
Schema on write is essentially the traditional data warehouse pattern: a table has an
integrated schema; any writes to the table must conform. To support schema on
write, a data lake must integrate a schema metastore.

--- [source p.342] (page 342) ---

ing a new table version.
Insert only. Insert only inserts new records without changing or deleting old records.

that columnar databases don’t typically enforce primary keys. The primary key would

A wide table can potentially have thousands of columns, whereas fewer than 100
are typical in relational databases. Wide tables are usually sparse; the vast majority
of entries in a given field may be null. This is extremely expensive in a traditional
relational database because the database allocates a fixed amount of space for each
field entry; nulls take up virtually no space in a columnar database. A wide schema
in a relational database dramatically slows reading because each row must allocate all
the space specified by the wide schema, and the database must read the contents of
each row in its entirety. On the other hand, a columnar database reads only columns
selected in a query, and reading nulls is essentially free.
Wide tables generally arise through schema evolution; engineers gradually add fields
over time. Schema evolution in a relational database is a slow and resource-heavy
process. In a columnar database, adding a field is initially just a change to metadata.

The Distributed Monolith Pattern
The distributed monolith pattern is a distributed architecture that still suffers from
many of the limitations of monolithic architecture. The basic idea is that one runs a
distributed system with different services to perform different tasks. Still, services and
nodes share a common set of dependencies or a common codebase.
One standard example is a traditional Hadoop cluster. A Hadoop cluster can simulta‐
neously host several frameworks, such as Hive, Pig, or Spark. The cluster also has
many internal dependencies. In addition, the cluster runs core Hadoop components:
Hadoop common libraries, HDFS, YARN, and Java. In practice, a cluster often has
one version of each component installed.

Schema
What is the expected form of the data? What is the file format? Is it structured,
semistructured, or unstructured? What data types are expected? How does the data
fit into a larger hierarchy? Is it connected to other data through shared keys or other
relationships?
Note that schema need not be relational. Rather, data becomes more useful when we
have as much information about its structure and organization. For images stored in
a data lake, this schema information might explain the image format, resolution, and
the way the images fit into a larger hierarchy.
Schema can function as a sort of Rosetta stone, instructions that tell us how to read
the data. Two major schema patterns exist: schema on write and schema on read.
Schema on write is essentially the traditional data warehouse pattern: a table has an
integrated schema; any writes to the table must conform. To support schema on
write, a data lake must integrate a schema metastore.

outlines.title: CSV vs Parquet vs Delta: Which Format, When
outlines.description: A side-by-side decision table across the dimensions that actually drive format choice on the exam and in practice.
keyPoints: [Table] Rows = CSV, Parquet, Delta; Columns = schema handling, storage layout, required read/write options, atomicity and ACID support, incremental and streaming support, typical role in the lakehouse
CSV: human-readable text, no embedded schema, needs header/sep/inferSchema, no ACID, best for interchange and small or arriving-from-outside files
Parquet: columnar and self-describing, schema travels with the data, efficient column pruning and predicate pushdown, but no transactions, no time travel, no concurrent-write safety

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Choosing and Applying a Write Mode for a Daily Refresh
outlines.description: A worked decision-and-code problem about refreshing a partitioned Delta table without duplicating or destroying data.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a partitioned Delta table /mnt/silver/events is partitioned by event_date; each night one day of late-arriving events must be replaced while all other days stay untouched, and the job must be re-runnable
Worked solution (option A): df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("replaceWhere", "event_date = '2024-06-01'").save("/mnt/silver/events") — atomically replaces only matching partitions
Worked solution (option B): set spark.conf.set("spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic") and write with mode("overwrite") so only the partitions present in the DataFrame are replaced

Analysis: plain mode("overwrite") with dynamic overwrite off would delete the entire table, and mode("append") would duplicate the day's rows on every re-run — neither satisfies the re-runnability requirement
Analysis of pitfalls: replaceWhere requires the predicate column to be a partition column for prune-based replacement, and the DataFrame must match the predicate or rows outside it can be lost

A wide table can potentially have thousands of columns, whereas fewer than 100
are typical in relational databases. Wide tables are usually sparse; the vast majority
of entries in a given field may be null. This is extremely expensive in a traditional

the space specified by the wide schema, and the database must read the contents of
each row in its entirety. On the other hand, a columnar database reads only columns
selected in a query, and reading nulls is essentially free.
Wide tables generally arise through schema evolution; engineers gradually add fields
over time. Schema evolution in a relational database is a slow and resource-heavy
process. In a columnar database, adding a field is initially just a change to metadata.

Queries, Modeling, and Transformation
Up to this point, the stages of the data engineering lifecycle have primarily been about
passing data from one place to another or storing it. In this chapter, you’ll learn
how to make data useful. By understanding queries, modeling, and transformations
(see Figure 8-1), you’ll have the tools to turn raw data ingredients into something
consumable by downstream stakeholders.
Figure 8-1. Transformations allow us to create value from data
We’ll first discuss queries and the significant patterns underlying them. Second, we
will look at the major data modeling patterns you can use to introduce business logic
into your data. Then, we’ll cover transformations, which take the logic of your data
models and the results of queries and make them useful for more straightforward

--- [source p.418] (page 418) ---
CSV: The nonstandard standard
We discussed CSV in Chapter 7. CSV is a serialization format that data engineers love
to hate. The term CSV is essentially a catchall for delimited text, but there is flexibility
in conventions of escaping, quote characters, delimiter, and more.
Data engineers should avoid using CSV files in pipelines because they are highly
error-prone and deliver poor performance. Engineers are often required to use CSV
format to exchange data with systems and business processes outside their control.
CSV is a common format for data archival. If you use CSV for archival, include a
complete technical description of the serialization configuration for your files so that
future consumers can ingest the data.

--- [source p.245] (page 245) ---
Schema
What is the expected form of the data? What is the file format? Is it structured,
semistructured, or unstructured? What data types are expected? How does the data
fit into a larger hierarchy? Is it connected to other data through shared keys or other
relationships?
Note that schema need not be relational. Rather, data becomes more useful when we
have as much information about its structure and organization. For images stored in
a data lake, this schema information might explain the image format, resolution, and
the way the images fit into a larger hierarchy.
Schema can function as a sort of Rosetta stone, instructions that tell us how to read
the data. Two major schema patterns exist: schema on write and schema on read.
Schema on write is essentially the traditional data warehouse pattern: a table has an
integrated schema; any writes to the table must conform. To support schema on
write, a data lake must integrate a schema metastore.

--- [source p.284] (page 284) ---
Practical Issues with Common File Formats
Engineers should also be aware of the file formats to export. CSV is still ubiquitous
and highly error prone at the time of this writing. Namely, CSV’s default delimiter is
also one of the most familiar characters in the English language—the comma! But it
gets worse.
CSV is by no means a uniform format. Engineers must stipulate the delimiter, quote
characters, and escaping to appropriately handle the export of string data. CSV also
doesn’t natively encode schema information or directly support nested structures.
CSV file encoding and schema information must be configured in the target system
to ensure appropriate ingestion. Autodetection is a convenience feature provided in
many cloud environments but is inappropriate for production ingestion. As a best
practice, engineers should record CSV encoding and schema details in file metadata.
More robust and expressive export formats include Parquet, Avro, Arrow, and ORC

The Background and Skills of a Data Engineer
Data engineering is a fast-growing field, and a lot of questions remain about how
to become a data engineer. Because data engineering is a relatively new discipline,
little formal training is available to enter the field. Universities don’t have a standard
data engineering path. Although a handful of data engineering boot camps and online
tutorials cover random topics, a common curriculum for the subject doesn’t yet exist.
People entering data engineering arrive with varying backgrounds in education,
career, and skill set. Everyone entering the field should expect to invest a significant
amount of time in self-study. Reading this book is a good starting point; one of the
primary goals of this book is to give you a foundation for the knowledge and skills we
think are necessary to succeed as a data engineer.

Are we saying that SQL is a be-all and end-all language? Not at all. SQL is a powerful
tool that can quickly solve complex analytics and data transformation problems.
Given that time is a primary constraint for data engineering team throughput, engi‐
neers should embrace tools that combine simplicity and high productivity. Data
engineers also do well to develop expertise in composing SQL with other operations,
either within frameworks such as Spark and Flink or by using orchestration to
combine multiple tools. Data engineers should also learn modern SQL semantics for
dealing with JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) parsing and nested data and consider

A proficient data engineer also recognizes when SQL is not the right tool for the job

The 2020s: Engineering for the data lifecycle
At the time of this writing, the data engineering role is evolving rapidly. We expect
this evolution to continue at a rapid clip for the foreseeable future. Whereas data
engineers historically tended to the low-level details of monolithic frameworks such
as Hadoop, Spark, or Informatica, the trend is moving toward decentralized, modu‐
larized, managed, and highly abstracted tools.
Indeed, data tools have proliferated at an astonishing rate (see Figure 1-3). Popular
trends in the early 2020s include the modern data stack, representing a collection
of off-the-shelf open source and third-party products assembled to make analysts’
lives easier. At the same time, data sources and data formats are growing both in
variety and size. Data engineering is increasingly a discipline of interoperation, and
connecting various technologies like LEGO bricks, to serve ultimate business goals.

Python, and JVM-based languages—platforms ranging from data warehouses to dis‐

As data storage and access patterns become more complex and outgrow the useful‐

Single-Tenant Versus Multitenant Storage
In Chapter 3, we covered the trade-offs between single-tenant and multitenant
architecture. To recap, with single-tenant architecture, each group of tenants (e.g.,
individual users, groups of users, accounts, or customers) gets its own dedicated set
of resources such as networking, compute, and storage. A multitenant architecture
inverts this and shares these resources among groups of users. Both architectures are
widely used. This section looks at the implications of single-tenant and multitenant
storage.

Columnar Serialization
The serialization formats we’ve discussed so far are row-oriented. Data is encoded as
complete relations (CSV) or documents (XML and JSON), and these are written into
files sequentially.
With columnar serialization, data organization is essentially pivoted by storing each
column into its own set of files. One obvious advantage to columnar storage is that it
allows us to read data from only a subset of fields rather than having to read full rows
at once. This is a common scenario in analytics applications and can dramatically
reduce the amount of data that must be scanned to execute a query.
Storing data as columns also puts similar values next to each other, allowing us
to encode columnar data efficiently. One common technique involves looking for
repeated values and tokenizing these, a simple but highly efficient compression
method for columns with large numbers of repeats.

amount of data scanned as much as possible. In addition to scanning only data in
columns relevant to a query, we can partition a table into multiple subtables by
splitting it on a field. It is quite common in analytics and data science use cases to
scan over a time range, so date- and time-based partitioning is extremely common.

scheme applied within a columnar database sorts data by one or a few fields, colocat‐

values.

Indexes, Partitioning, and Clustering
Indexes provide a map of the table for particular fields and allow extremely fast
lookup of individual records. Without indexes, a database would need to scan an
entire table to find the records satisfying a WHERE condition.
In most RDBMSs, indexes are used for primary table keys (allowing unique identifi‐
cation of rows) and foreign keys (allowing joins with other tables). Indexes can also
be applied to other columns to serve the needs of specific applications. Using indexes,
an RDBMS can look up and update thousands of rows per second.
We do not cover transactional database records in depth in this book; numerous tech‐
nical resources are available on this topic. Rather, we are interested in the evolution
away from indexes in analytics-oriented storage systems and some new developments
in indexes for analytics use cases.

--- [source p.301] (page 301) ---
Optimize your join strategy and schema
A single dataset (such as a table or file) is rarely useful on its own; we create value
by combining it with other datasets. Joins are one of the most common means of
combining datasets and creating new ones. We assume that you’re familiar with
the significant types of joins (e.g., inner, outer, left, cross) and the types of join
relationships (e.g., one to one, one to many, many to one, and many to many).

--- [source p.317] (page 317) ---
Third normal form (3NF)
The requirements of 2NF, plus each table contains only relevant fields related to
its primary key and has no transitive dependencies.
It’s worth spending a moment to unpack a couple of terms we just threw at you. A
unique primary key is a single field or set of multiple fields that uniquely determines
rows in the table. Each key value occurs at most once; otherwise, a value would map
to multiple rows in the table. Thus, every other value in a row is dependent on (can
be determined from) the key. A partial dependency occurs when a subset of fields in
a composite key can be used to determine a nonkey column of the table. A transitive
dependency occurs when a nonkey field depends on another nonkey field.
Let’s look at stages of normalization—from denormalized to 3NF—using an ecom‐
merce example of customer orders (Table 8-1). We’ll provide concrete explanations of
each of the concepts introduced in the previous paragraph.

From indexes to partitions and clustering
While columnar databases allow for fast scan speeds, it’s still helpful to reduce the
amount of data scanned as much as possible. In addition to scanning only data in
columns relevant to a query, we can partition a table into multiple subtables by

Session window. A session window groups events that occur close together, and filters
out periods of inactivity when no events occur. We might say that a user session
is any time interval with no inactivity gap of five minutes or more. Our batch
system collects data by a user ID key, orders events, determines the gaps and session
boundaries, and calculates statistics for each session. Data engineers often sessionize
data retrospectively by applying time conditions to user activity on web and desktop
apps.
In a streaming session, this process can happen dynamically. Note that session win‐
dows are per key; in the preceding example, each user gets their own set of windows.
The system accumulates data per user. If a five-minute gap with no activity occurs,
the system closes the window, sends its calculations, and flushes the data. If new
events arrive for the use, the system starts a new session window.

--- [source p.132] (page 132) ---
One of the central problems of managing batch and stream processing is unifying
multiple code paths. While the Kappa architecture relies on a unified queuing and
storage layer, one still has to confront using different tools for collecting real-time
statistics or running batch aggregation jobs. Today, engineers seek to solve this in
several ways. Google made its mark by developing the Dataflow model and the
Apache Beam framework that implements this model.
The core idea in the Dataflow model is to view all data as events, as the aggregation
is performed over various types of windows. Ongoing real-time event streams are
unbounded data. Data batches are simply bounded event streams, and the boundaries
provide a natural window. Engineers can choose from various windows for real-time
aggregation, such as sliding or tumbling. Real-time and batch processing happens in
the same system using nearly identical code.

high batch frequency. (In truth, DBAs and engineers have long used micro-batching

consumption.)

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Deduplicating a Change Feed
outlines.description: A fully worked window-function problem that keeps the latest record per key and removes deleted records, with analysis of determinism and performance.
keyPoints: Statement: from customers_cdc(customer_id, name, email, updated_at, op), keep the single latest record per customer_id and drop records whose op is 'delete'

Worked solution (Spark SQL): WITH ranked AS (SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, op ASC) AS rn FROM customers_cdc) SELECT customer_id, name, email, updated_at FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 AND op <> 'delete'

Worked solution (PySpark): w = Window.partitionBy('customer_id').orderBy(col('updated_at').desc()); df.withColumn('rn', row_number().over(w)).filter((col('rn') == 1) & (col('op') != 'delete')).drop('rn')
Analysis: row_number() is preferred over rank() because ties would otherwise return more than one row per key; adding a deterministic tiebreaker in ORDER BY guarantees stable results across reruns

Common pitfalls: MAX(updated_at) joined back to the source is slower and breaks on duplicate timestamps; partitioning by the wrong column leaves duplicates; filtering on rn before ordering the window gives arbitrary survivors
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to deduplicate a change feed with a window function and justify why row_number() is the safe choice.

Queries can have wildly different execution times, depending on how they’re exe‐
cuted. A query optimizer’s job is to optimize query performance and minimize costs
by breaking the query into appropriate steps in an efficient order. The optimizer will
assess joins, indexes, data scan size, and other factors. The query optimizer attempts
to execute the query in the least expensive manner.

each other. You won’t directly work with a query optimizer, but understanding some

Third normal form (3NF)
The requirements of 2NF, plus each table contains only relevant fields related to
its primary key and has no transitive dependencies.
It’s worth spending a moment to unpack a couple of terms we just threw at you. A
unique primary key is a single field or set of multiple fields that uniquely determines
rows in the table. Each key value occurs at most once; otherwise, a value would map
to multiple rows in the table. Thus, every other value in a row is dependent on (can
be determined from) the key. A partial dependency occurs when a subset of fields in
a composite key can be used to determine a nonkey column of the table. A transitive
dependency occurs when a nonkey field depends on another nonkey field.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Replacing a Python UDF with Built-in Functions
outlines.description: A fully worked rewrite that turns a slow row-by-row Python UDF into an equivalent chain of native PySpark functions, with an analysis of why the rewrite is correct and fast.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a `customers` DataFrame has `full_name` (inconsistent casing), `phones` (array of strings with punctuation) and `email`. The existing pipeline uses one Python UDF to trim and title-case the name, one to strip phone punctuation, and one to count valid phone numbers. Rewrite it with no UDFs.
Worked solution — name: `trim(initcap(col('full_name')))` replaces the title-case UDF
Worked solution — phones: `transform(col('phones'), p -> regexp_replace(p, '[^0-9+]', ''))` replaces the cleaning UDF
Worked solution — count: `size(filter(col('phones'), p -> length(regexp_replace(p, '[^0-9]', '')) >= 10))` replaces the counting UDF
Analysis: the native chain is visible to Catalyst, stays on the JVM, and uses no per-row Python handoff — typically an order-of-magnitude improvement on wide tables
Pitfalls: null arrays break transform unless guarded with `when(col('phones').isNull(), lit(None))`; regexp_replace before length is essential for correctness

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Deduplicate and Rank Without Self-Joins
outlines.description: A fully worked analytical problem that combines deduplication, top-N per group, and conditional aggregation in two window passes rather than a cascade of joins.
keyPoints: Problem statement: an `events` table has duplicate rows per `user_id`, plus a `category` column. Produce one row per user with the latest event and that user's top two categories by event count.
Worked solution — dedupe: `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC)` and filter `rn = 1`
Worked solution — top-N: aggregate counts per user and category, then `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY cnt DESC, category)` and filter `rn <= 2`
Worked solution — reassemble: collect the two surviving categories with `collect_list` into an array column, then join back to the deduplicated row
Analysis: two window scans replace a self-join plus a correlated subquery; the shuffle cost is bounded by the partition keys
Pitfalls: ties need a deterministic secondary sort key; null `event_ts` sorts first in ascending order and can silently win the ranking

Indexes provide a map of the table for particular fields and allow extremely fast
lookup of individual records. Without indexes, a database would need to scan an
entire table to find the records satisfying a WHERE condition.

be applied to other columns to serve the needs of specific applications. Using indexes,

away from indexes in analytics-oriented storage systems and some new developments
in indexes for analytics use cases.

Queries can have wildly different execution times, depending on how they’re exe‐

by breaking the query into appropriate steps in an efficient order. The optimizer will
assess joins, indexes, data scan size, and other factors. The query optimizer attempts
to execute the query in the least expensive manner.
Query optimizers are fundamental to how your query will perform. Every database
is different and executes queries in ways that are obviously and subtly different from
each other. You won’t directly work with a query optimizer, but understanding some
of its functionality will help you write more performant queries. You’ll need to know
how to analyze a query’s performance, using things like an explain plan or query
analysis, described in the following section.

Continuous CDC
Continuous CDC captures all table history and can support near real-time data inges‐
tion, either for real-time database replication or to feed real-time streaming analytics.
Rather than running periodic queries to get a batch of table changes, continuous
CDC treats each write to the database as an event.
We can capture an event stream for continuous CDC in a couple of ways. One
of the most common approaches with a transactional database such as PostgreSQL
is log-based CDC. The database binary log records every change to the database
sequentially (see “Database Logs” on page 161). A CDC tool can read this log and
send the events to a target, such as the Apache Kafka Debezium streaming platform.
Some databases support a simplified, managed CDC paradigm. For instance, many
cloud-hosted databases can be configured to directly trigger a serverless function

One of the central problems of managing batch and stream processing is unifying
multiple code paths. While the Kappa architecture relies on a unified queuing and
storage layer, one still has to confront using different tools for collecting real-time
statistics or running batch aggregation jobs. Today, engineers seek to solve this in
several ways. Google made its mark by developing the Dataflow model and the
Apache Beam framework that implements this model.
The core idea in the Dataflow model is to view all data as events, as the aggregation
is performed over various types of windows. Ongoing real-time event streams are
unbounded data. Data batches are simply bounded event streams, and the boundaries
provide a natural window. Engineers can choose from various windows for real-time
aggregation, such as sliding or tumbling. Real-time and batch processing happens in
the same system using nearly identical code.

The MDS limits itself to batch techniques that treat data as bounded. In contrast,

Recall continuous CDC, discussed in Chapter 7. CDC, in this form, essentially sets up

Cloud-based systems based around object storage support zero-copy cloning. This
typically means that a new virtual copy of an object is created (e.g., a new table)

Practical Issues with Common File Formats
Engineers should also be aware of the file formats to export. CSV is still ubiquitous
and highly error prone at the time of this writing. Namely, CSV’s default delimiter is
also one of the most familiar characters in the English language—the comma! But it
gets worse.
CSV is by no means a uniform format. Engineers must stipulate the delimiter, quote
characters, and escaping to appropriately handle the export of string data. CSV also
doesn’t natively encode schema information or directly support nested structures.
CSV file encoding and schema information must be configured in the target system
to ensure appropriate ingestion. Autodetection is a convenience feature provided in
many cloud environments but is inappropriate for production ingestion. As a best
practice, engineers should record CSV encoding and schema details in file metadata.

Schema
What is the expected form of the data? What is the file format? Is it structured,
semistructured, or unstructured? What data types are expected? How does the data
fit into a larger hierarchy? Is it connected to other data through shared keys or other
relationships?
Note that schema need not be relational. Rather, data becomes more useful when we
have as much information about its structure and organization. For images stored in
a data lake, this schema information might explain the image format, resolution, and
the way the images fit into a larger hierarchy.
Schema can function as a sort of Rosetta stone, instructions that tell us how to read
the data. Two major schema patterns exist: schema on write and schema on read.
Schema on write is essentially the traditional data warehouse pattern: a table has an
integrated schema; any writes to the table must conform. To support schema on
write, a data lake must integrate a schema metastore.

outlines.title: Idempotency: How COPY INTO Tracks Processed Files
outlines.description: Explains the file-level bookkeeping that makes COPY INTO safe to retry, and the boundary conditions where that safety breaks down.
keyPoints: For every loaded file, Databricks records the file path, its size, and its last-modified timestamp
A file is skipped only when path, size, and timestamp all match a previously processed file
Consequence 1: unchanged files are never reloaded, so retrying an orchestrated job is safe
Consequence 2: a file rewritten at the same path with a new timestamp or size is loaded again, while a deleted and re-created identical file is skipped
Consequence 3: file metadata is retained for 7 days by default - after that window a re-run can re-ingest the same files, and no row-level deduplication ever occurs
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain idempotent file loading and how COPY INTO tracks processed files

What is the expected form of the data? What is the file format? Is it structured,
semistructured, or unstructured? What data types are expected? How does the data
fit into a larger hierarchy? Is it connected to other data through shared keys or other
relationships?

have as much information about its structure and organization. For images stored in
a data lake, this schema information might explain the image format, resolution, and

outlines.title: Directory Listing vs File Notification
outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison of the two Auto Loader discovery modes across the dimensions that actually drive the selection decision.
keyPoints: [Table] Rows: initial setup effort, cloud infrastructure required, IAM permissions, per-trigger cost model, latency to detect a new file, practical file-volume ceiling
Directory listing: no extra cloud resources, cost grows with the number of objects re-listed on every trigger, fine for thousands of files or low-frequency scheduled runs
File notification: requires a cloud event queue plus an IAM role (SQS/SNS on AWS, Event Grid with a Storage Queue on Azure, Pub/Sub on Google Cloud) but avoids repeated listing of huge prefixes
Decision rule to memorise: high file count and low-latency targets push you to file notification; small volumes and restricted permissions push you to directory listing
Exam trap: notification mode still needs a periodic directory-listing backfill to catch files that arrived while the queue or notification service was unavailable
outlines.teachingObjective: Choose between directory listing and file notification using explicit decision criteria.

outlines.description: A quantitative worked problem comparing the per-trigger listing cost of directory listing at scale against event-based notification.
keyPoints: Statement: a prefix holds 12,000,000 objects; the stream triggers every 5 minutes; the cloud LIST operation returns 1,000 keys per call and costs $0.005 per 1,000 requests
Step 1 — calls per scan: 12,000,000 / 1,000 = 12,000 LIST calls
Step 2 — listing cost per scan: 12,000 x $0.005 / 1,000 = $0.06
Step 3 — scans per day at a 5-minute trigger: 288; daily listing cost = 288 x $0.06 = $17.28, roughly $520 per month before any compute

These days, if you’re considering writing a data ingestion connector to a database
or API, ask yourself: has this already been created? Furthermore, is there a service
that will manage the nitty-gritty details of this connection for me? “APIs” on page
254 mentions the popularity of managed data connector platforms and frameworks.
These tools aim to provide a standard set of connectors available out of the box
to spare data engineers building complicated plumbing to connect to a particular
source. Instead of creating and managing a data connector, you outsource this service
to a third party.

ways (e.g., CDC, replication, truncate and reload), set permissions and credentials,

CDC and database replication
CDC can be used to replicate between databases: events are buffered into a stream
and asynchronously written into a second database. However, many databases natively
support a tightly coupled version of replication (synchronous replication) that keeps
the replica fully in sync with the primary database. Synchronous replication typi‐
cally requires that the primary database and the replica are of the same type (e.g.,
PostgreSQL to PostgreSQL). The advantage of synchronous replication is that the
secondary database can offload work from the primary database by acting as a read
replica; read queries can be redirected to the replica. The query will return the same
results that would be returned from the primary database.
Read replicas are often used in batch data ingestion patterns to allow large scans
to run without overloading the primary production database. In addition, an applica‐

What Is a Query?
We often run into people who know how to write SQL but are unfamiliar with how
a query works under the hood. Some of this introductory material on queries will be
familiar to experienced data engineers; feel free to skip ahead if this applies to you.
A query allows you to retrieve and act on data. Recall our conversation in Chapter 5
about CRUD. When a query retrieves data, it is issuing a request to read a pattern of
records. This is the R (read) in CRUD. You might issue a query that gets all records
from a table foo, such as SELECT * FROM foo. Or, you might apply a predicate
(logical condition) to filter your data by retrieving only records where the id is 1,
using the SQL query SELECT * FROM foo WHERE id=1.

CRUD; your query will either create, mutate, or destroy existing records. Let’s review
some other common acronyms you’ll run into when working with query languages.

Credential Handling
Incorrectly handled credentials in notebooks and data science code are a major
security risk; we constantly see credentials mishandled in this domain. It is common
to embed credentials directly in code, where they often leak into version control
repos. Credentials are also frequently passed around through messages and email.
We encourage data engineers to audit data science security practices and work collab‐
oratively on improvements. Data scientists are highly receptive to these conversations
if they are given alternatives. Data engineers should set standards for handling cre‐
dentials. Credentials should never be embedded in code; ideally, data scientists use
credential managers or CLI tools to manage access.

whether a database, object store, or filesystem. In the pull model, data is retrieved

source table snapshot on a fixed schedule. You’ll learn more about ETL and extract,

From indexes to partitions and clustering
While columnar databases allow for fast scan speeds, it’s still helpful to reduce the
amount of data scanned as much as possible. In addition to scanning only data in
columns relevant to a query, we can partition a table into multiple subtables by
splitting it on a field. It is quite common in analytics and data science use cases to
scan over a time range, so date- and time-based partitioning is extremely common.
Columnar databases generally support a variety of other partition schemes as well.
Clusters allow finer-grained organization of data within partitions. A clustering
scheme applied within a columnar database sorts data by one or a few fields, colocat‐
ing similar values. This improves performance for filtering, sorting, and joining these
values.

Message Queues and Event-Streaming Platforms
Message queues and event-streaming platforms are widespread ways to ingest real-
time data from web and mobile applications, IoT sensors, and smart devices. As
real-time data becomes more ubiquitous, you’ll often find yourself either introducing
or retrofitting ways to handle real-time data in your ingestion workflows. As such,
it’s essential to know how to ingest real-time data. Popular real-time data ingestion
includes message queues or event-streaming platforms, which we covered in Chap‐
ter 5. Though these are both source systems, they also act as ways to ingest data. In
both cases, you consume events from the publisher you subscribe to.
Recall the differences between messages and streams. A message is handled at the
individual event level and is meant to be transient. Once a message is consumed, it
is acknowledged and removed from the queue. On the other hand, a stream ingests

Fault tolerance and resilience. Event-streaming platforms are typically distributed sys‐

replaces it, and the stream is still accessible. This means records aren’t lost; you may
choose to delete records, but that’s another story. This fault tolerance and resilience
make streaming platforms a good choice when you need a system that can reliably
produce, store, and ingest event data.

Reliability and Durability
Reliability and durability are vital in the ingestion stages of data pipelines. Reliability
entails high uptime and proper failover for ingestion systems. Durability entails
making sure that data isn’t lost or corrupted.
Some data sources (e.g., IoT devices and caches) may not retain data if it is not

ingestion systems leads directly to the durability of generated data. If data is ingested,
downstream processes can theoretically run late if they break temporarily.

Know how your database handles commits

i.e., a notion of committing several operations simultaneously in a way that maintains
a consistent state. Please note that the term transaction is somewhat overloaded; see
Chapter 5. The purpose of a transaction is to keep a consistent state of a database
both while it’s active and in the event of a failure. Transactions also handle isolation
when multiple concurrent events might be reading, writing, and deleting from the
same database objects. Without transactions, users would get potentially conflicting
information when querying a database.

databases create new files to represent the new state of the database and retain the old

realize by implementing streaming? If I get data in real time, what actions can I

In addition, consider establishing an SLA with upstream providers. An SLA provides
expectations of what you can expect from the source systems you rely upon. An
example of an SLA might be “data from source systems will be reliably available and
of high quality.” A service-level objective (SLO) measures performance against what
you’ve agreed to in the SLA. For example, given your example SLA, an SLO might

quality, and anything else of importance to you. Upstream owners of source systems
need to understand your requirements so they can provide you with the data you

outlines.title: Lesson Recap and Exam Takeaways
outlines.description: Consolidate the four ingestion paths and the decision rules students should carry into the certification exam.
keyPoints: JDBC batch for simple, low-frequency database reads; CDC when deletes and updates must be captured incrementally
Kafka for continuous event streams; managed connectors for SaaS and database sources with minimal code
Always account for credential handling, schema drift, ordering guarantees, and exactly-once semantics
Exam takeaways: map the scenario to source type plus freshness requirement, then choose the lowest-effort path that meets the latency
Next unit preview: transforming and modeling the data you have just ingested

nesting in certain columns. The Spark job combines the three sources into a single

outlines.title: Medallion Architecture: The Three Layers
outlines.description: Introduce the medallion (multi-hop) design pattern that organizes lakehouse data into bronze, silver, and gold layers of progressively higher quality.
keyPoints: Describe the medallion architecture as a data design pattern that organizes lakehouse data into bronze, silver, and gold layers to progressively improve data quality and structure [source 2]
Identify the quality progression: bronze = raw, silver = validated, gold = enriched and business-ready [source 6]
Explain why progressive refinement solves the problem of data arriving in inconsistent raw states before it reaches analysts and models [source 1]
Explain that each hop is a purpose-built table that decouples ingestion, cleansing, and consumption
[Chart] Horizontal layered diagram: source systems → bronze → silver → gold → BI dashboards and ML consumers
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe the purpose of bronze, silver, and gold tables

Bronze is drawn in bronze/copper tone with rough raw data blocks, Silver in grey with tidy structured blocks, Gold in gold tone with polished aggregated summary blocks. Arrows show data flowing left to right and being progressively refined. All text and labels in English. Flat vector style, minimal, no people.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Retail Orders from Raw Events to Gold
outlines.description: A fully worked design-and-code problem that moves a realistic streaming retail order source through bronze, silver, and gold.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a retailer streams order events (JSON with nested line items, late-arriving updates, duplicate retries) into cloud storage; design the medallion flow and write the key transformations
Worked step 1 — Bronze: use Auto Loader to append raw JSON files into a bronze table with ingestion metadata, no parsing, no deduplication
Worked step 2 — Silver: explode and type-cast line items, apply a MERGE on order_id to keep the latest version, drop duplicates, and enforce the expected schema
Worked step 3 — Gold: aggregate silver into a daily sales mart by store and product category, and expose a star-schema fact table with conformed date and product dimensions

Analysis: why MERGE on a business key works for late-arriving updates; pitfalls include merging before deduplication, losing the raw record needed for replay, and hiding a schema change by silently dropping columns

outlines.title: Decision: How Many Layers Does This Pipeline Really Need?
outlines.description: A constrained design decision about whether to materialize all three layers, with pros, cons, and one justified recommendation.
keyPoints: Constraint: a five-person team ingests streaming CDC from a production database and serves three BI dashboards; storage cost and refresh latency both matter
Option A — full three-layer materialization: highest data quality and replayability, but more jobs, more storage, and more orchestration to maintain
Option B — bronze + gold only, skipping silver: faster to build and cheaper, but business logic gets duplicated per dashboard and reprocessing becomes brittle
Option C — bronze + silver as Delta tables and gold as views over silver: lowest storage, but dashboard latency and cost move to query time

Recommendation: keep all three layers, but land silver incrementally with MERGE and expose gold as views until query cost justifies materializing them — justified because bronze guarantees replay, silver centralizes conformance, and gold views avoid premature storage cost

outlines.title: Fact Tables, Dimension Tables, and Grain
outlines.description: Introduces the two building blocks of a Kimball dimensional model and the grain declaration that makes a fact table unambiguous.

Grain: what a single fact row represents (for example, one order line item); declare the grain in words before writing any code
Keys: natural or business keys identify entities in the source system; surrogate keys are warehouse-generated integers that join facts to dimensions

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Declare the Grain for a Retail Sales Model
outlines.description: A fully worked example that turns a business question into a fact table grain plus its associated dimensions and measures.

outlines.title: Type 1 vs Type 2 vs Type 3: Comparing SCD Strategies
outlines.description: Introduces slowly changing dimensions and compares the three classic strategies side by side across the dimensions that decide an implementation.
keyPoints: [Table] Compare Type 1 / Type 2 / Type 3 across: history preserved, rows added per change, extra columns, key handling, reporting impact, and implementation effort
Type 1 overwrites the old value — no history, same row count, ideal for correcting data-entry errors
Type 2 adds a new row version with EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate (9999-01-01 for the open record) and an is_current flag — full history, row count grows
Type 3 keeps previous and current values in additional columns (Original ZipCode / Current ZipCode) — limited to a fixed number of changes, rarely used
Exam trap: Type 2 requires a surrogate key, because the business key is no longer unique once multiple versions exist

outlines.title: Worked Problem: A Type 2 SCD Row-Versioning Walkthrough
outlines.description: A fully worked example that shows exactly which rows a Type 2 dimension must contain before and after an attribute change.
keyPoints: Statement: customer_id 4471 moves from ZIP 10001 to 94105 on 2024-03-15; the customer dimension is Type 2 with a surrogate key — show the required change
Before: one active row — customer_sk = 981, customer_id = 4471, zip = 10001, EFF_StartDate = 2021-06-01, EFF_EndDate = 9999-01-01, is_current = true
Step 1 — expire the current row: set EFF_EndDate = 2024-03-15 and is_current = false; never overwrite the old ZIP value in a Type 2 dimension
Step 2 — insert the new version: customer_sk = 1492 (a brand-new surrogate key), customer_id = 4471, zip = 94105, EFF_StartDate = 2024-03-15, EFF_EndDate = 9999-01-01, is_current = true

Analysis: the surrogate key is what keeps historical facts pointing at ZIP 10001 after the change; the classic pitfalls are updating in place (that is Type 1) and reusing the same surrogate key for the new version

outlines.title: Implementing SCD Type 1 and Type 2 on Databricks
outlines.description: Maps SCD theory onto concrete Databricks mechanisms: Delta MERGE for Type 1, and MERGE or APPLY CHANGES INTO for Type 2.
keyPoints: Type 1 with Delta: MERGE INTO dim_customer USING staging ON dim_customer.customer_id = staging.customer_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET ...
Type 2 with a two-step MERGE pattern: first expire the matched current row (EFF_EndDate = change date, is_current = false), then insert the new version from the staged change
Delta Live Tables / Lakeflow: APPLY CHANGES INTO ... STORED AS SCD TYPE 2 generates the versioning, sequencing, and current flag for you
dbt snapshot models deliver the same Type 2 behaviour through dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to columns
Always derive the effective date from the source change timestamp, never from the pipeline run time, or backfills will corrupt the history

outlines.title: From Silver to Gold: What Gold Tables Are For

outlines.title: Anatomy of a Denormalized Gold Table
outlines.description: Shows how a fact table plus its dimensions collapse into one wide, read-optimized table, and states the guardrails that keep the grain intact.
keyPoints: Denormalization = deliberately re-introducing redundancy so BI queries do not have to join at read time
[Table] Star schema (sales + dim_customer + dim_product + dim_date) versus the single wide gold table it becomes: columns, joins needed, typical query

A wide gold table mixes fact measures (quantity, unit_price, discount_amount, net_revenue) with flattened dimension attributes (customer_name, customer_segment, product_category, store_region, order_date)
Trade-off: redundant storage and wider rows in exchange for removing join and shuffle cost from every query
Guardrail: keep the fact grain exact — join each dimension on its unique key (or the current SCD version), or row counts silently explode
[Image gen_img_1] Diagram of a wide denormalized gold table: fact measures beside flattened customer, product, and date attributes
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe the structure of a denormalized gold table and the trade-offs it encodes

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Denormalize a Star Schema into a Gold Table
outlines.description: A fully worked solution that joins a silver sales fact to its dimensions to produce one wide gold Delta table without changing the grain.
keyPoints: Problem: given silver.sales (grain = one row per order line item), dim_customer, dim_product, and dim_date, write gold_sales_wide as a single denormalized table

Solution: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold_sales_wide AS SELECT s.*, c.customer_name, c.customer_segment, p.product_category, d.year, d.quarter FROM silver.sales s LEFT JOIN dim_customer c ON s.customer_key = c.customer_key AND c.eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01' LEFT JOIN dim_product p ON s.product_key = p.product_key LEFT JOIN dim_date d ON s.date_key = d.date_key
Analysis: a LEFT JOIN against a dimension that is unique on its key (or filtered to the current SCD Type 2 version) preserves the fact grain — verify by comparing COUNT(*) before and after the join
Pitfall: joining a Type 2 dimension without the current-version filter fans out rows and duplicates revenue in every downstream dashboard
Pitfall: a dimension filter placed after the join (for example WHERE c.customer_segment = 'Retail') silently converts the LEFT JOIN to an inner join and drops rows
outlines.teachingObjective: Write a denormalizing transformation that preserves the declared fact grain

outlines.title: Centralizing Business Logic in the Gold Layer
outlines.description: Introduces business logic and derived data as shared definitions, and contrasts one governed definition with the scattered per-dashboard anti-pattern.
keyPoints: Business logic = the definition of a metric or rule: net revenue after returns, the window that makes a customer 'active', profit after marketing cost [source p.346]
Anti-pattern: the same metric re-implemented in every dashboard, notebook, and ad hoc query — the numbers drift and nobody can reconcile them
Fix: encode the logic once in the gold transformation (or a governed semantic/metrics layer) and let consumers select the finished result
DRY principle: derived data should be computed and stored in one place, not recomputed downstream with slightly different rules
Classic examples: ad-spend attribution, exclusion of auto-canceled orders, currency conversion, and refund handling

outlines.title: Where Should Business Logic Live?
outlines.description: A decision under real constraints: put logic in gold table columns, in views or materialized views, in a semantic/metrics layer, or in each BI tool.
keyPoints: Option A — materialized columns in the gold table: fastest reads and one physical definition, but every change requires a rewrite and backfill
Option B — gold views and materialized views: logic stays queryable and refreshable; materialized views in Databricks SQL add refresh cost and staleness
Option C — semantic / metrics layer: one governed definition serving many tools, at the price of adopting and maintaining the layer [source p.346]
Option D — logic inside each dashboard: rejected — it duplicates definitions, breaks lineage, and guarantees metric drift
Constraints and recommendation: materialize stable, high-traffic metrics as gold columns; keep volatile or team-specific definitions in a governed semantic layer; never encode them per dashboard
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a placement for business logic given governance, latency, and change-frequency constraints

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Encode Profit Logic Once
outlines.description: A worked computation of a net-profit metric including exclusion rules and a cost allocation that must stay identical for every consumer.
keyPoints: Problem: compute daily profit per product category = net revenue − COGS − allocated marketing cost; exclude auto-canceled orders; net out refunds
Solution: pre-aggregate refunds to the order-line grain, join marketing cost allocated by date and channel, then aggregate once to date × category and write the result to gold
Analysis: if refunds are joined at transaction grain without pre-aggregation, each refund is counted once per line item and the deduction is inflated
Analysis: incremental writes must be idempotent — re-running a day should MERGE on the date key rather than append a second copy of the day's profit
Pitfall: filtering canceled orders before versus after the allocation join changes the allocation denominator and quietly shifts every ratio downstream
outlines.teachingObjective: Implement a derived metric once, with correct exclusions and idempotent incremental writes

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Profit After Marketing Costs
outlines.description: A fully worked attribution problem showing how two defensible rules produce the same total but contradictory per-item profit — the mechanical root of duplicated metrics.
keyPoints: Problem statement: an ad platform reports 10 clicks and $80 of spend for an order containing item X (price $40, 6 clicks) and item Y (price $60, 4 clicks). Compute profit per item under (a) naive attribution and (b) price-weighted attribution.
Worked solution (naive, equal cost per click $8): X cost 6 × $8 = $48 → profit $40 − $48 = −$8; Y cost 4 × $8 = $32 → profit $60 − $32 = $28; total profit $20
Worked solution (price-weighted): X share = 40/(40+60) = 40% → cost $32 → profit $8; Y share = 60% → cost $48 → profit $12; total profit $20
Analysis: both allocations are exhaustive and additive, so total profit is invariant; the per-item profit for X flips from −$8 to +$8 purely from the rule choice

Analysis — pitfalls: mixing attribution methods across consumers, re-computing at a different grain (order vs item), double-counting spend when joins fan out, and recomputing a metric non-idempotently so totals drift on each run
outlines.teachingObjective: Compute a derived metric under two attribution rules and explain why rule choice, not data, causes disagreement.

outlines.title: Risks of Duplicated and Inconsistent Metrics
outlines.description: Connects duplicated logic to its business consequences: eroded trust, silent drift, wasted reconciliation effort, and hidden coupling.
keyPoints: Trust erosion: when two dashboards show different revenue or profit, stakeholders stop believing both and revert to spreadsheets
Silent drift: a rule corrected in one copy but not the others, so definitions diverge gradually with no error raised
Reconciliation cost: engineers and analysts burn hours tracing which number is correct instead of acting on it
Hidden coupling: dashboards silently depend on logic buried in another team's notebook, so a small refactor breaks reporting
Exam trap: 'recompute the metric in the BI tool for speed' is an antipattern, not a performance technique — it creates a second definition

outlines.title: Unit Glossary: Transformation and Modeling Terms
outlines.description: Complete definitions of the key terms from this unit, anchored in the medallion, dimensional-modeling, and derived-metric material.
keyPoints: Business logic — the rules that convert stored data into decision-ready values, such as profit = revenue − cost − marketing spend
Derived data — any value computed from other data rather than captured at the source; every gold metric, KPI, and ML feature is derived data
DRY (don't repeat yourself) — the principle that each piece of knowledge, including a metric formula, has exactly one authoritative representation
Single source of truth (SSOT) — the design rule that a metric is defined once and every consumer reads that definition instead of re-implementing it
Metrics layer / semantic layer — a governed catalog of metric definitions (formula, grain, dimensions) served to SQL, BI, notebooks, and ML consumers
Attribution model — the rule that assigns shared costs to items or channels; naive attribution splits costs equally, price-weighted attribution allocates proportionally to price
Grain — the level of detail a fact or metric is recorded at (order, item, day); comparing metrics at different grains produces silently wrong numbers
Conformed dimension — a dimension (for example, date or customer) shared by multiple fact tables so metrics can be combined consistently across the warehouse
outlines.teachingObjective: Recall and define the unit's core transformation and modeling terminology.

outlines.title: The Core Data Quality Dimensions
outlines.description: Introduces the six dimensions used throughout the Databricks Data Engineer Associate exam, each framed as the question it answers and a concrete check that implements it.
keyPoints: Completeness: are required values present? Check: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) / NULL rate per column.
[Table] Dimension comparison: dimension | question answered | example failure | example check expression.
Accuracy: do values reflect reality? Check: reconciliation against the source system of record or a trusted reference table.
Timeliness: is the data fresh enough for its use case? Check: MAX(ingestion_timestamp) within an expected freshness window.
Uniqueness: is each real-world entity represented once? Check: COUNT(*) equals COUNT(DISTINCT business_key).
Validity and consistency cover domain/format conformance and cross-field or cross-table agreement, e.g. shipped_date >= order_date.
outlines.teachingObjective: Define the six quality dimensions and pair each with an executable check pattern.

outlines.title: Completeness vs. Accuracy vs. Timeliness vs. Uniqueness
outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison of the four dimensions named in the lesson objective, organized by the decision-relevant dimensions learners must reason about in exam scenarios.
keyPoints: [Table] Columns: dimension | question answered | typical failure mode | primary metric | Databricks check pattern | what it does NOT prove.
Completeness proves presence, not correctness — a row full of placeholder values is complete but inaccurate.
Accuracy proves agreement with reality, which usually requires a reference dataset or source-system reconciliation.
Timeliness is measured against a business freshness requirement (for example, 30 minutes), never an arbitrary threshold.
Uniqueness requires a declared business key; uniqueness on a surrogate or partition column is meaningless.
outlines.teachingObjective: Discriminate between confusable dimensions using a decision-relevant comparison table.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: From Business Requirement to Testable Rule
outlines.description: Fully-worked translation of a vague stakeholder requirement into four executable quality rules, with the reasoning behind each rule made explicit.
keyPoints: Problem statement: the sales team says 'our orders table should be complete, current, and free of duplicates so the daily revenue dashboard is trustworthy'.

Step 1 — decompose the sentence into dimensions: completeness (customer_id, order_total present), uniqueness (one row per order_id), timeliness (loaded within 30 minutes of order creation), accuracy (order_total matches the payment gateway).
Step 2 — write each rule as an executable SQL assertion, for example SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL; expected result 0.
Step 3 — attach a threshold, severity, and owner to each rule so the test can fail loudly rather than silently.
Analysis: rules must be falsifiable and deterministic; a rule like 'data looks reasonable' is not testable, and a rule with no threshold produces alert fatigue.
outlines.teachingObjective: Demonstrate a repeatable procedure for turning business expectations into executable quality rules.
