Data control language
You most likely want to limit access to database objects and finely control who has
access to what. Data control language (DCL) allows you to control access to the
database objects or the data by using SQL commands such as GRANT, DENY, and
REVOKE.
Let’s walk through a brief example using DCL commands. A new data scientist
named Sarah joins your company, and she needs read-only access to a database called
data_science_db. You give Sarah access to this database by using the following DCL
command:
GRANT SELECT ON data_science_db TO user_name Sarah;
It’s a hot job market, and Sarah has worked at the company for only a few months
before getting poached by a big tech company. So long, Sarah! Being a security-
minded data engineer, you remove Sarah’s ability to read from the database:
REVOKE SELECT ON data_science_db TO user_name Sarah;

reused among different fact tables. A dimension that is reused across multiple star
schemas, thus sharing the same fields, is called a conformed dimension. A conformed
dimension allows you to combine multiple fact tables across multiple star schemas.
Remember, redundant data is OK with the Kimball method, but avoid replicating the
same dimension tables to avoid drifting business definitions and data integrity.
The Kimball data model and star schema have a lot of nuance. You should be aware
that this mode is appropriate only for batch data and not for streaming data. Because
the Kimball data model is popular, there’s a good chance you’ll run into it.

a pipeline that ingests data from three API sources in JSON format. This initial
ingestion step is handled in Airflow. Each data source gets its prefix (filepath) in an S3
bucket.
Airflow then triggers a Spark job by calling an API. This Spark job ingests each of
the three sources into a dataframe, converting the data into a relational format, with
nesting in certain columns. The Spark job combines the three sources into a single
table and then filters the results with a SQL statement. The results are finally written
out to a Parquet-formatted Delta Lake table stored in S3.

Materialized views
We mentioned materialized views in our earlier discussion of query caching. A
potential disadvantage of (nonmaterialized) views is that they don’t do any precom‐
putation. In the example of a view that joins five tables, this join must run every
time a marketing analyst runs a query on this view, and the join could be extremely
expensive.
A materialized view does some or all of the view computation in advance. In our
example, a materialized view might save the five table join results every time a change
occurs in the source tables. Then, when a user references the view, they’re querying
from the prejoined data. A materialized view is a de facto transformation step, but the
database manages execution for convenience.

Figure 1-5. The Data Science Hierarchy of Needs
Although many data scientists are eager to build and tune ML models, the reality is
an estimated 70% to 80% of their time is spent toiling in the bottom three parts of
the hierarchy—gathering data, cleaning data, processing data—and only a tiny slice
of their time on analysis and ML. Rogati argues that companies need to build a solid
data foundation (the bottom three levels of the hierarchy) before tackling areas such
as AI and ML.
Data scientists aren’t typically trained to engineer production-grade data systems, and
they end up doing this work haphazardly because they lack the support and resources
of a data engineer. In an ideal world, data scientists should spend more than 90% of
their time focused on the top layers of the pyramid: analytics, experimentation, and
ML. When data engineers focus on these bottom parts of the hierarchy, they build a
solid foundation for data scientists to succeed.

Schema
What is the expected form of the data? What is the file format? Is it structured,
semistructured, or unstructured? What data types are expected? How does the data
fit into a larger hierarchy? Is it connected to other data through shared keys or other
relationships?
Note that schema need not be relational. Rather, data becomes more useful when we
have as much information about its structure and organization. For images stored in
a data lake, this schema information might explain the image format, resolution, and
the way the images fit into a larger hierarchy.
Schema can function as a sort of Rosetta stone, instructions that tell us how to read
the data. Two major schema patterns exist: schema on write and schema on read.
Schema on write is essentially the traditional data warehouse pattern: a table has an
integrated schema; any writes to the table must conform. To support schema on
write, a data lake must integrate a schema metastore.

Data Architecture
Chapter 3 covers the basics of data architecture, as storage is the critical underbelly of
the data engineering lifecycle.
Consider the following data architecture tips. Design for required reliability and
durability. Understand the upstream source systems and how that data, once inges‐
ted, will be stored and accessed. Understand the types of data models and queries that
will occur downstream.
If data is expected to grow, can you negotiate storage with your cloud provider? Take
an active approach to FinOps, and treat it as a central part of architecture conversa‐
tions. Don’t prematurely optimize, but prepare for scale if business opportunities
exist in operating on large data volumes.

The strict modeling approaches we’ve described, especially Kimball and Inmon,
were developed when data warehouses were expensive, on premises, and heavily

Nonrelational databases: NoSQL
While relational databases are terrific for many use cases, they’re not a one-size-fits-
all solution. We often see that people start with a relational database under the
impression it’s a universal appliance and shoehorn in a ton of use cases and work‐
loads. As data and query requirements morph, the relational database collapses under
its weight. At that point, you’ll want to use a database that’s appropriate for the
specific workload under pressure. Enter nonrelational or NoSQL databases. NoSQL,
which stands for not only SQL, refers to a whole class of databases that abandon the
relational paradigm.
On the one hand, dropping relational constraints can improve performance, scala‐
bility, and schema flexibility. But as always in architecture, trade-offs exist. NoSQL
databases also typically abandon various RDBMS characteristics, such as strong con‐
sistency, joins, or a fixed schema.

Zero-copy cloning
Cloud-based systems based around object storage support zero-copy cloning. This
typically means that a new virtual copy of an object is created (e.g., a new table)
without necessarily physically copying the underlying data. Typically, new pointers
are created to the raw data files, and future changes to these tables will not be recor‐
ded in the old table. For those familiar with the inner workings of object-oriented
languages such as Python, this type of “shallow” copying is familiar from other
contexts.
Zero-copy cloning is a compelling feature, but engineers must understand its
strengths and limitations. For example, cloning an object in a data lake environment
and then deleting the files in the original object might also wipe out the new object.

Data definition language
At a high level, you first need to create the database objects before adding data. You’ll
use data definition language (DDL) commands to perform operations on database
objects, such as the database itself, schemas, tables, or users; DDL defines the state of
objects in your database.
Data engineers use common SQL DDL expressions: CREATE, DROP, and UPDATE. For
example, you can create a database by using the DDL expression CREATE DATABASE
bar. After that, you can also create new tables (CREATE table bar_table) or delete a
table (DROP table bar_table).

The Tight Feedback Between Applications and ML
Another area we’re excited about is the fusion of applications and ML. Today, appli‐
cations and ML are disjointed systems, like applications and analytics. Software
engineers do their thing over here, data scientists and ML engineers do their thing
over there.
ML is well-suited for scenarios where data is generated at such a high rate and
volume that humans cannot feasibly process it by hand. As data sizes and velocity
grow, this applies to every scenario. High volumes of fast-moving data, coupled with
sophisticated workflows and actions, are candidates for ML. As data feedback loops
become shorter, we expect most applications to integrate ML. As data moves more
quickly, the feedback loop between applications and ML will tighten. The applications
in the live data stack are intelligent and able to adapt in real time to changes in the
data. This creates a cycle of ever-smarter applications and increasing business value.

Local instance volumes
Cloud providers also offer block storage volumes that are physically attached to the
host server running a virtual machine. These storage volumes are generally very low
cost (included with the price of the VM in the case of Amazon’s EC2 instance store)
and provide low latency and high IOPS.
Instance store volumes (Figure 6-6) behave essentially like a disk physically attached
to a server in a data center. One key difference is that when a VM shuts down or is
deleted, the contents of the locally attached disk are lost, whether or not this event
was caused by intentional user action. This ensures that a new virtual machine cannot
read disk contents belonging to a different customer.
Figure 6-6. Instance store volumes offer high performance and low cost but do not
protect data in the event of disk failure or VM shutdown
Locally attached disks support none of the advanced virtualization features offered by

physical disk failure can lose or corrupt data even if the host VM continues running.
Furthermore, locally attached volumes do not support snapshots or other backup
features.

we use disks as a local cache and hence don’t need all the advanced virtualization

replication and redundancy and is serving as a cache rather than permanent storage.

the data must be in a usable form. The process for converting data into a usable

Big Data...for the 1990s
Products that claim to support “big data” at petabyte scale will often use benchmark
datasets small enough to easily fit in the storage on your smartphone. For systems
that rely on caching layers to deliver performance, test datasets fully reside in solid-
state drive (SSD) or memory, and benchmarks can show ultra-high performance by
repeatedly querying the same data. A small test dataset also minimizes RAM and SSD
costs when comparing pricing.
To benchmark for real-world use cases, you must simulate anticipated real-world data
and query size. Evaluate query performance and resource costs based on a detailed
evaluation of your needs.

Total Opportunity Cost of Ownership
Any choice inherently excludes other possibilities. Total opportunity cost of ownership
(TOCO) is the cost of lost opportunities that we incur in choosing a technology,
an architecture, or a process.1 Note that ownership in this setting doesn’t require
long-term purchases of hardware or licenses. Even in a cloud environment, we
effectively own a technology, a stack, or a pipeline once it becomes a core part of
our production data processes and is difficult to move away from. Data engineers
often fail to evaluate TOCO when undertaking a new project; in our opinion, this is a
massive blind spot.

options, effectively excluding data stacks B, C, and D. You’re committed to data stack

Storing data isn’t as simple as just saving it to object storage or disk and forgetting
about it. You need to think about the data storage lifecycle and data retention. When
you think about access frequency and use cases, ask, “How important is the data to
downstream users, and how often do they need to access it?” This is the data storage
lifecycle. Another question you should ask is, “How long should I keep this data?” Do
you need to retain data indefinitely, or are you fine discarding it past a certain time
frame? This is data retention. Let’s dive into each of these.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: GRANT and REVOKE on Securable Objects
outlines.description: A fully worked SQL problem that grants least-privilege read access to a group and revokes a mis-scoped write grant, with analysis of why the ordering and scope matter.
keyPoints: Problem statement: group `analysts_eu` must be able to query `sales.gold.orders`, must not be able to modify it, and must not be able to query any other schema in the `sales` catalog
Worked solution (path privileges first): GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG sales TO analysts_eu; GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA sales.gold TO analysts_eu;
Worked solution (object privilege): GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO analysts_eu;
Remove the accidental write grant: REVOKE MODIFY ON TABLE sales.gold.orders FROM analysts_eu;
Analysis: grants are additive and idempotent, and REVOKE of a privilege that was never granted is a no-op rather than an error — verify the final state with SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE sales.gold.orders
Common pitfall: granting SELECT ON CATALOG sales reads every current and future table in the catalog, which breaks least privilege; grant at the narrowest object that satisfies the requirement
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to write correct GRANT and REVOKE statements that produce a least-privilege access state.

Security
Security must be top of mind for data engineers, and those who ignore it do so
at their peril. That’s why security is the first undercurrent. Data engineers must
understand both data and access security, exercising the principle of least privilege.

outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison of the three ways a principal can hold authority over an object, across the dimensions that appear in exam scenarios.
keyPoints: Compare three sources of authority: object ownership, privileges inherited from a parent object or group membership, and privileges granted explicitly on the object

The table data is spread across nodes in data blocks; the MapReduce job generates
one map task per block. Each map task essentially runs the query on a single block

block might contain hundreds of megabytes, the full table could be petabytes in size.

parallelism; the data scan rate across the full cluster essentially scales linearly with the
number of nodes.

not gathering results to a single node; rather, we redistribute results by key so that

Single-Tenant Versus Multitenant Storage
In Chapter 3, we covered the trade-offs between single-tenant and multitenant
architecture. To recap, with single-tenant architecture, each group of tenants (e.g.,
individual users, groups of users, accounts, or customers) gets its own dedicated set
of resources such as networking, compute, and storage. A multitenant architecture
inverts this and shares these resources among groups of users. Both architectures are
widely used. This section looks at the implications of single-tenant and multitenant
storage.
Adopting single-tenant storage means that every tenant gets their dedicated storage.
In the example in Figure 6-10, each tenant gets a database. No data is shared among
these databases, and storage is totally isolated. An example of using single-tenant
storage is that each customer’s data must be stored in isolation and cannot be blended
with any other customer’s data. In this case, each customer gets their own database.

keyPoints: Problem statement: `sales.gold.customers` must show full email addresses only to the PII readers group, and EU analysts must see only customers in their own region

Compare the trade-off: tagging scales to thousands of objects because the policy is written once, while per-object GRANT statements must be repeated and re-audited as the estate grows

Apply least privilege in practice: grant to groups rather than individuals, grant at the narrowest scope that satisfies the requirement, and grant on catalogs or schemas only when the requirement is genuinely estate-wide

Verify effective access with the platform's own metadata: SHOW GRANTS ON <object>, current_user() and is_account_group_member() in a diagnostic query, the information_schema privilege views, and the audit system table that records who ran which statement
Exam trap: after tightening permissions, a query can fail with a not-found error rather than a permission error — always check the path privileges before assuming the object was deleted
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to apply tag-based policies and verify effective access for a principal.

The principle of least privilege means that a person or system should be given only the
privileges and data they need to complete the task at hand and nothing more. Often,

everything, when that person may need just a handful of IAM roles to do their work.

The evolution from rows to columns
An early data warehouse was typically built on the same type of RDBMS used for
transactional applications. The growing popularity of MPP systems meant a shift
toward parallel processing for significant improvements in scan performance across
large quantities of data for analytics purposes. However, these row-oriented MPPs
still used indexes to support joins and condition checking.
In “Raw Ingredients of Data Storage” on page 191, we discuss columnar serialization.
Columnar serialization allows a database to scan only the columns required for a
particular query, sometimes dramatically reducing the amount of data read from the
disk. In addition, arranging data by column packs similar values next to each other,
yielding high-compression ratios with minimal compression overhead. This allows
data to be scanned more quickly from disk and over a network.

The table data is spread across nodes in data blocks; the MapReduce job generates
one map task per block. Each map task essentially runs the query on a single block
—i.e., it generates a count for each user ID that appears in the block. While a
block might contain hundreds of megabytes, the full table could be petabytes in size.

We mentioned materialized views in our earlier discussion of query caching. A
potential disadvantage of (nonmaterialized) views is that they don’t do any precom‐
putation. In the example of a view that joins five tables, this join must run every

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Trace a Metric from Source Table to Dashboard
outlines.description: A fully-worked lineage tracing problem: identify the upstream chain for a dashboard metric, then reproduce the answer with SQL over the lineage system tables.
keyPoints: Statement: a monthly revenue dashboard reads gold.revenue_monthly, which is built from silver.orders_clean, which is built from bronze.orders_raw. Reconstruct the full upstream chain and name the downstream consumers of bronze.orders_raw.
Step 1: in Catalog Explorer, open bronze.orders_raw and read the downstream lineage graph to walk forward to the dashboard.
Step 2: reproduce the walk in SQL over system.access.table_lineage using source_table_full_name and target_table_full_name, joining rows until you reach the dashboard object.
Step 3: switch to system.access.column_lineage when the question asks which column, not which table, must be preserved.

Analysis: why the method works (lineage rows are one hop each, so a chain is a recursive join) and common pitfalls (duplicate rows per event, event lag before lineage appears, case-sensitive catalog/schema names, and lineage disappearing if an upstream object is dropped).

outlines.title: Trade-offs: Designing a Compliance Auditing and Metadata Strategy
outlines.description: A constrained design decision: choose how to satisfy a one-year audit retention and discoverability requirement using Unity Catalog capabilities.
keyPoints: Constraint set: regulators require 12 months of access history; the built-in audit system table retains a shorter default window; platform budget is limited; analysts must be able to find sensitive tables quickly.
Option A — rely only on built-in system tables: simplest, lowest cost, but cannot satisfy the 12-month retention requirement.
Option B — schedule a recurring export of audit and lineage system tables to governed cloud storage: meets retention, adds storage and orchestration cost and a new asset to govern.
Option C — maintain a manually curated metadata catalog of tags and comments only: excellent for discoverability, but captures no access history and does not satisfy the audit requirement.

Recommendation: a hybrid — keep system tables as the primary query surface, add a scheduled governed export for long-term retention, and layer governed tags on sensitive columns for discoverability. Justify it against cost and the stated retention constraint.

The principle of least privilege means that a person or system should be given only the
privileges and data they need to complete the task at hand and nothing more. Often,

everything, when that person may need just a handful of IAM roles to do their work.

outlines.description: Put the three most commonly confused storage-governance concepts side by side so students can pick the right one under exam conditions.
keyPoints: [Table] Columns: what it is, who chooses the storage path, what DROP does, privileges required, and whether it governs non-tabular files.

outlines.title: Delta Sharing: Governed Data Exchange
outlines.description: Introduce Delta Sharing as the open protocol that lets a provider expose Unity Catalog data to recipients without copying it, and connect it to the governance students already know.
keyPoints: Define Delta Sharing: an open protocol for secure, live, read-only exchange of governed data across organizations, clouds, and platforms, where recipients query the provider's data rather than receiving a copy.

The core concept of cloud data sharing is that a multitenant system supports security
policies for sharing data among tenants. Concretely, any public cloud object storage
system with a fine-grained permission system can be a platform for data sharing.
Popular cloud data-warehouse platforms also support data-sharing capabilities. Of
course, data can also be shared through download or exchange over email, but a
multitenant system makes the process much easier.
Many modern sharing platforms (especially cloud data warehouses) support row,
column, and sensitive data filtering. Data sharing also streamlines the notion of
the data marketplace, available on several popular clouds and data platforms. Data
marketplaces provide a centralized location for data commerce, where data providers
can advertise their offerings and sell them without worrying about the details of
managing network access to data systems.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Create a Share for an External Partner
outlines.description: Work through the full provider-side sequence for sharing one partitioned table with a partner over Delta Sharing, then review how to verify and revoke it.
keyPoints: Problem statement: share the table prod.sales.orders with the partner Northwind, read-only, exposing only orders from 2024 onward, where the recipient is another Databricks Unity Catalog workspace.
Step 1 — CREATE SHARE northwind_orders COMMENT 'Order data for Northwind'; executed by a principal holding CREATE SHARE on the metastore.
Step 2 — ALTER SHARE northwind_orders ADD TABLE prod.sales.orders PARTITION (order_date >= '2024-01-01'); partial sharing pushes the partition filter to the provider so older data is never exposed.

Step 3 — CREATE RECIPIENT northwind USING ID 'northwind-uc-sharing-id' COMMENT 'Northwind UC workspace'; for open sharing the alternative is CREATE RECIPIENT northwind_open, which returns an activation link and token the recipient downloads.

Step 4 — GRANT USE SHARE northwind_orders TO RECIPIENT northwind; verify with SHOW SHARES, DESCRIBE SHARE northwind_orders, SHOW GRANTS ON SHARE northwind_orders, and SHOW ALL IN SHARE northwind_orders.

outlines.title: Choosing a Delivery Mechanism for Cross-Team Data Exchange
outlines.description: Decide how to deliver curated data to an external partner under explicit governance, freshness, and revocation constraints, then justify one recommendation.
keyPoints: Constraint set: the consumer is a separate organization on a different cloud account; access must be read-only, near-live, revocable within seconds, fully auditable, and operated by a two-person team.
Option A — external location plus READ FILES in your own metastore: zero-copy and simple, but the consumer must operate inside your Databricks account, so it only fits internal teams.

Option B — Delta Sharing: live and read-only, governed by existing Unity Catalog grants and dynamic views, revoked with REVOKE USE SHARE, and recorded in the provider's audit logs; requires the consumer to support the Delta Sharing protocol, either natively (D2D) or through an open-sharing client.

Option C — scheduled file export into the partner's bucket: works with any consumer, but creates copies that go stale, escape Unity Catalog governance, and add storage, egress, and pipeline maintenance cost.

Recommendation: Option B for this constraint set, because it satisfies read-only, live, auditable, and instantly revocable at once; fall back to Option C only when the partner cannot run any Delta Sharing client and stale copies are acceptable.

From indexes to partitions and clustering
While columnar databases allow for fast scan speeds, it’s still helpful to reduce the
amount of data scanned as much as possible. In addition to scanning only data in
columns relevant to a query, we can partition a table into multiple subtables by
splitting it on a field. It is quite common in analytics and data science use cases to
scan over a time range, so date- and time-based partitioning is extremely common.
Columnar databases generally support a variety of other partition schemes as well.
Clusters allow finer-grained organization of data within partitions. A clustering
scheme applied within a columnar database sorts data by one or a few fields, colocat‐
ing similar values. This improves performance for filtering, sorting, and joining these
values.

tables for better query performance. For instance, if you have a very large table

queries to more efficiently access portions of very large datasets. BigQuery also allows
you to partition a table into smaller segments, allowing you to query only specific
partitions instead of the entire table. (Be aware that inappropriate clustering and key
distribution strategies can degrade performance.)

Queries can have wildly different execution times, depending on how they’re exe‐

Know how your database handles commits
A database commit is a change within a database, such as creating, updating, or delet‐
ing a record, table, or other database objects. Many databases support transactions—
i.e., a notion of committing several operations simultaneously in a way that maintains
a consistent state. Please note that the term transaction is somewhat overloaded; see
Chapter 5. The purpose of a transaction is to keep a consistent state of a database
both while it’s active and in the event of a failure. Transactions also handle isolation
when multiple concurrent events might be reading, writing, and deleting from the
same database objects. Without transactions, users would get potentially conflicting
information when querying a database.

the data processing and storage technologies—i.e., will you use Spark or a cloud

outlines.title: Reading Stage and Task Metrics Like a Diagnostician
outlines.description: Teach the specific stage- and task-level metrics that reveal skew, excessive shuffling, memory pressure, and garbage collection overhead.
keyPoints: Task duration distribution: compare min, median, and max — a large max/median ratio signals skew
Shuffle Read and Shuffle Write sizes: large values indicate an expensive wide transformation or a bad join strategy
Spill (Memory) and Spill (Disk): data did not fit the execution memory of the partition
GC Time and peak execution memory: high GC time points to oversized partitions or inefficient object churn
Scheduler Delay and task launch time indicate overhead when partition counts are too high
[Table] Metric vs. symptom vs. typical remedy: skew / shuffle / spill / GC, with the tuning lever for each
Exam trap: treating high total duration as the problem — the metric that matters is which task is the outlier
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to read stage and task metrics to name a specific bottleneck and propose a fix.

Object stores for data engineering applications
From the standpoint of data engineering, object stores provide excellent performance
for large batch reads and batch writes. This corresponds well to the use case for
massive OLAP systems. A bit of data engineering folklore says that object stores are
not good for updates, but this is only partially true. Object stores are an inferior fit for
transactional workloads with many small updates every second; these use cases are
much better served by transactional databases or block storage systems. Object stores
work well for a low rate of update operations, where each operation updates a large
volume of data.
Object stores are now the gold standard of storage for data lakes. In the early days
of data lakes, write once, read many (WORM) was the operational standard, but this

The Cloud-Scale Data OS and Improved Interoperability
Let’s briefly review some of the inner workings of (single-device) operating systems,
then tie this back to data and the cloud. Whether you’re utilizing a smartphone,
a laptop, an application server, or a smart thermostat, these devices rely on an
operating system to provide essential services and orchestrate tasks and processes.
For example, I can see roughly 300 processes running on the MacBook Pro that I’m
typing on. Among other things, I see services such as WindowServer (responsible for
providing windows in a graphical interface) and CoreAudio (tasked with providing
low-level audio capabilities).
When I run an application on this machine, it doesn’t directly access sound and
graphics hardware. Instead, it sends commands to operating system services to
draw windows and play sound. These commands are issued to standard APIs; a
specification tells software developers how to communicate with operating system

--- [source p.82] (page 82) ---
Timeliness
Are records available in a timely fashion?
Each of these characteristics is quite nuanced. For example, how do we think about
bots and web scrapers when dealing with web event data? If we intend to analyze
the customer journey, we must have a process that lets us separate humans from
machine-generated traffic. Any bot-generated events misclassified as human present
data accuracy issues, and vice versa.
A variety of interesting problems arise concerning completeness and timeliness. In
the Google paper introducing the Dataflow model, the authors give the example of an
offline video platform that displays ads.5 The platform downloads video and ads while
a connection is present, allows the user to watch these while offline, and then uploads
ad view data once a connection is present again. This data may arrive late, well after
the ads are watched. How does the platform handle billing for the ads?

--- [source p.273] (page 273) ---
Inserts, Updates, and Batch Size
Batch-oriented systems often perform poorly when users attempt to perform many
small-batch operations rather than a smaller number of large operations. For exam‐
ple, while it is common to insert one row at a time in a transactional database, this is
a bad pattern for many columnar databases, as it forces the creation of many small,
suboptimal files and forces the system to run a high number of create object opera‐
tions. Running many small in-place update operations is an even bigger problem
because it causes the database to scan each existing column file to run the update.
Understand the appropriate update patterns for the database or data store you’re
working with. Also, understand that certain technologies are purpose-built for high
insert rates. For example, Apache Druid and Apache Pinot can handle high insert
rates. SingleStore can manage hybrid workloads that combine OLAP and OLTP

Streaming Pipelines and Real-Time Analytical Databases
The MDS limits itself to batch techniques that treat data as bounded. In contrast,
real-time data applications treat data as an unbounded, continuous stream. Streaming
pipelines and real-time analytical databases are the two core technologies that will
facilitate the move from the MDS to the live data stack. While these technologies have
been around for some time, rapidly maturing managed cloud services will see them
be deployed much more widely.
Streaming technologies will continue to see extreme growth for the foreseeable
future. This will happen in conjunction with a clearer focus on the business utility
of streaming data. Up to the present, streaming systems have frequently been treated
like an expensive novelty or a dumb pipe for getting data from A to B. In the future,
streaming will radically transform organizational technology and business processes;

--- [source p.93] (page 93) ---
Streaming
Streaming data processing is inherently more complicated than batch, and the tools
and paradigms are arguably less mature. As streaming data becomes more pervasive
in every stage of the data engineering lifecycle, data engineers face interesting soft‐
ware engineering problems.
For instance, data processing tasks such as joins that we take for granted in the
batch processing world often become more complicated in real time, requiring more
complex software engineering. Engineers must also write code to apply a variety
of windowing methods. Windowing allows real-time systems to calculate valuable
metrics such as trailing statistics. Engineers have many frameworks to choose from,
including various function platforms (OpenFaaS, AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Func‐
tions) for handling individual events or dedicated stream processors (Spark, Beam,
Flink, or Pulsar) for analyzing streams to support reporting and real-time actions.

We utilize a distributed system to realize higher overall scaling capacity and increased
availability and reliability. Horizontal scaling allows you to add more machines to
satisfy load and resource requirements (Figure 3-4). Common horizontally scaled

progress, and completion of workloads. When a workload is started, the leader node
distributes tasks to the worker nodes within its system, completing the tasks and
returning the results to the leader node. Typical modern distributed architectures also
build in redundancy. Data is replicated so that if a machine dies, the other machines
can pick up where the missing server left off; the cluster may add more machines to
restore capacity.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Diagnosing a Plan and Cutting Bytes Scanned
outlines.description: A fully worked exam-style problem that walks from an EXPLAIN plan and Spark UI metrics to a concrete tuning change and a measured improvement.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a Delta table sales is 8 TB; the query SELECT * FROM sales WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' has run time 42 minutes; the physical plan shows FileScan parquet with no pushed filter and a partition count of 1
Worked solution step 1: read the scan statistics in the plan to confirm full-table scan behavior and huge sizeInBytes
Worked solution step 2: check the Spark UI and find one giant task with a long duration next to thousands of near-instant tasks — a parallelism problem
Worked solution step 3: replace SELECT * with the required columns, filter on the partition column order_date, and repartition to a sensible shuffle partition count
Worked solution step 4: re-run EXPLAIN to confirm PushedFilters and PartitionFilters appear, and verify reduced bytes read in the Spark UI SQL tab
Analysis: why it works — pruning is applied at the file and partition layer before rows are materialized, so less I/O, less shuffle, and less compute cost
Common pitfall: filtering on a column that is not a partition column or is wrapped in a function, which disables pruning

transactional applications. The growing popularity of MPP systems meant a shift

particular query, sometimes dramatically reducing the amount of data read from the
disk. In addition, arranging data by column packs similar values next to each other,
yielding high-compression ratios with minimal compression overhead. This allows
data to be scanned more quickly from disk and over a network.

Colocation of compute and storage has long been a standard method to improve

Single-Tenant Versus Multitenant Storage
In Chapter 3, we covered the trade-offs between single-tenant and multitenant
architecture. To recap, with single-tenant architecture, each group of tenants (e.g.,
individual users, groups of users, accounts, or customers) gets its own dedicated set
of resources such as networking, compute, and storage. A multitenant architecture
inverts this and shares these resources among groups of users. Both architectures are
widely used. This section looks at the implications of single-tenant and multitenant
storage.
Adopting single-tenant storage means that every tenant gets their dedicated storage.
In the example in Figure 6-10, each tenant gets a database. No data is shared among
these databases, and storage is totally isolated. An example of using single-tenant
storage is that each customer’s data must be stored in isolation and cannot be blended

Batch-oriented systems often perform poorly when users attempt to perform many
small-batch operations rather than a smaller number of large operations. For exam‐

suboptimal files and forces the system to run a high number of create object opera‐

From indexes to partitions and clustering
While columnar databases allow for fast scan speeds, it’s still helpful to reduce the
amount of data scanned as much as possible. In addition to scanning only data in
columns relevant to a query, we can partition a table into multiple subtables by
splitting it on a field. It is quite common in analytics and data science use cases to
scan over a time range, so date- and time-based partitioning is extremely common.
Columnar databases generally support a variety of other partition schemes as well.
Clusters allow finer-grained organization of data within partitions. A clustering
scheme applied within a columnar database sorts data by one or a few fields, colocat‐
ing similar values. This improves performance for filtering, sorting, and joining these
values.

Indexes, Partitioning, and Clustering
Indexes provide a map of the table for particular fields and allow extremely fast
lookup of individual records. Without indexes, a database would need to scan an
entire table to find the records satisfying a WHERE condition.
In most RDBMSs, indexes are used for primary table keys (allowing unique identifi‐
cation of rows) and foreign keys (allowing joins with other tables). Indexes can also
be applied to other columns to serve the needs of specific applications. Using indexes,
an RDBMS can look up and update thousands of rows per second.
We do not cover transactional database records in depth in this book; numerous tech‐
nical resources are available on this topic. Rather, we are interested in the evolution
away from indexes in analytics-oriented storage systems and some new developments
in indexes for analytics use cases.

An obscure but frustrating problem is row explosion. This occurs when we have a
large number of many-to-many matches, either because of repetition in join keys or
as a consequence of join logic. Suppose the join key in table A has the value this
repeated five times, and the join key in table B contains this same value repeated 10

suppose that many other repeats are in the join key. Row explosion often generates
enough rows to consume a massive quantity of database resources or even cause a

We often run into people who know how to write SQL but are unfamiliar with how
a query works under the hood. Some of this introductory material on queries will be
familiar to experienced data engineers; feel free to skip ahead if this applies to you.
A query allows you to retrieve and act on data. Recall our conversation in Chapter 5
about CRUD. When a query retrieves data, it is issuing a request to read a pattern of
records. This is the R (read) in CRUD. You might issue a query that gets all records
from a table foo, such as SELECT * FROM foo. Or, you might apply a predicate
(logical condition) to filter your data by retrieving only records where the id is 1,

An obscure but frustrating problem is row explosion. This occurs when we have a
large number of many-to-many matches, either because of repetition in join keys or
as a consequence of join logic. Suppose the join key in table A has the value this

enough rows to consume a massive quantity of database resources or even cause a

Encryption over the wire
Encryption over the wire is now the default for current protocols. For instance,
HTTPS is generally required for modern cloud APIs. Data engineers should always
be aware of how keys are handled; bad key handling is a significant source of data
leaks. In addition, HTTPS does nothing to protect data if bucket permissions are left
open to the public, another cause of several data scandals over the last decade.
Engineers should also be aware of the security limitations of older protocols. For
example, FTP is simply not secure on a public network. While this may not appear
to be a problem when data is already public, FTP is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle
attacks, whereby an attacker intercepts downloaded data and changes it before it
arrives at the client. It is best to simply avoid FTP.
Make sure everything is encrypted over the wire, even with legacy protocols. When in
doubt, use robust technology with encryption baked in.

outlines.title: Caching: When It Pays Off
outlines.description: Teach when persisting an intermediate result saves more than it costs, and how Delta Cache differs.
keyPoints: cache() and persist() keep an intermediate DataFrame in executor memory and optionally disk, so repeated actions skip recomputing the full lineage
It pays off when the same result is reused many times: iterative ML loops, interactive exploration, or several downstream aggregations over one join

Encryption over the wire is now the default for current protocols. For instance,
HTTPS is generally required for modern cloud APIs. Data engineers should always
be aware of how keys are handled; bad key handling is a significant source of data
leaks. In addition, HTTPS does nothing to protect data if bucket permissions are left

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Diagnosing an Expensive Join and Deciding on Caching
outlines.description: A fully worked diagnosis and fix for a slow nightly join, including the caching decision and its pitfalls.
keyPoints: Statement: a nightly job joins a 2 TB fact table to a 40 MB dimension table; the Spark UI shows runtime dominated by a single exchange stage
Step 1 — diagnose: an exchange stage with heavy shuffle read and write, not the file scan, is the bottleneck; 200 tasks all taking similar time rules out skew
Step 2 — explain: the 40 MB small side exceeds the 10 MB spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, so Spark fell back to sort-merge join and shuffled both sides
Step 3 — fix: raise the threshold or add broadcast(dim); predicted effect is that shuffle bytes on the fact table fall to near zero and the exchange stage disappears
Step 4 — caching decision: the joined result feeds three downstream aggregations, so cache it with MEMORY_AND_DISK and unpersist when the job ends
Analysis: why each step works, and the pitfalls — over-broadcasting can OOM the driver, caching a read-once result wastes memory, and forgetting to unpersist keeps the cost after the job finishes
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply join strategy selection and caching judgement end to end on a realistic slow-join scenario.

Hybrid Cloud
As more established businesses migrate into the cloud, the hybrid cloud model
is growing in importance. Virtually no business can migrate all of its workloads
overnight. The hybrid cloud model assumes that an organization will indefinitely
maintain some workloads outside the cloud.
There are many reasons to consider a hybrid cloud model. Organizations may
believe that they have achieved operational excellence in certain areas, such as their
application stack and associated hardware. Thus, they may migrate only to specific
workloads where they see immediate benefits in the cloud environment. For example,
an on-premises Spark stack is migrated to ephemeral cloud clusters, reducing the
operational burden of managing software and hardware for the data engineering
team and allowing rapid scaling for large data jobs.

Generally, clouds support their highest network bandwidth and lowest latency
between systems and services within a zone. High throughput data workloads should
run on clusters located in a single zone for performance and cost reasons. For exam‐
ple, an ephemeral Amazon EMR cluster should generally sit in a single availability
zone.
In addition, network traffic sent to VMs within a zone is free, but with a significant
caveat: traffic must be sent to private IP addresses. The major clouds utilize virtual
networks known as virtual private clouds (VPCs). Virtual machines have private
IP addresses within the VPC. They may also be assigned public IP addresses to
communicate with the outside world and receive traffic from the internet, but com‐
munications using external IP addresses can incur data egress charges.

formance scaling. While storage standards such as redundant arrays of independent
disks (RAID) parallelize on a single server, cloud object storage clusters operate at
a much larger scale, with disks distributed across a network and even multiple data
centers and availability zones.

Are records available in a timely fashion?
Each of these characteristics is quite nuanced. For example, how do we think about

the customer journey, we must have a process that lets us separate humans from
machine-generated traffic. Any bot-generated events misclassified as human present

outlines.title: Photon: The Vectorized Query Engine
outlines.description: Explains what Photon actually is, which operators it accelerates, and how to reason about its net cost when the DBU rate is higher.
keyPoints: Photon is a native C++ vectorized engine that replaces parts of the Spark execution engine; the Spark APIs, SQL, and DataFrame code are unchanged — it is a runtime switch
Vectorized, columnar, compiled execution processes batches of column values per CPU instruction, cutting per-row interpretation overhead
Largest wins on CPU-bound work: large table scans, wide aggregations, joins, string-heavy transformations, and Delta MERGE/DELETE/UPDATE
[Table] Photon helps vs. Photon barely helps: large scans/aggregations/joins/Delta writes (helps) vs. I/O-bound jobs, Python UDF-heavy pipelines, tiny datasets (little or no gain)
Cost nuance: the Photon DBU rate is higher per DBU, but total cost frequently falls because wall-clock runtime drops — always compare DBU-hours, not DBU rates
Exam trap: 'Enable Photon to speed up every job' is false; and Photon is not the same as AQE, Delta caching, or autoscaling

outlines.description: Fully-worked quantitative problems that show how to compare a baseline run against a Photon run in DBU-hours and in dollars, plus a right-sizing problem.
keyPoints: Problem 1 statement: a nightly ETL job runs 90 minutes on 8 workers at rate R DBU/h. With Photon it finishes in 40 minutes but the DBU rate becomes 1.5R. Is Photon cheaper?
Worked solution: baseline = 8 workers x 1.5 h = 12 DBU-h. Photon = 8 x (40/60) x 1.5 = 8 DBU-h. Photon uses 33% fewer DBU-hours, so it is cheaper in DBUs and likely in VM cost too (shorter runtime)
Problem 2 statement: a pipeline runs on a 16-worker cluster but the Spark UI shows only 6 concurrent tasks per stage. Right-size it and estimate the saving

outlines.title: Trade-off Decision: Cutting 30% Off a Nightly Pipeline
outlines.description: A constrained decision problem where three candidate cost-reduction strategies are weighed against an SLA and a budget cut.
keyPoints: Constraints: 4-hour nightly pipeline, 6:00 AM SLA, 3x data growth expected next quarter, must tolerate node preemption, and the budget must drop 30%
Option A — keep the current cluster and enable Photon: pros are easy rollout and shorter CPU-bound stages; cons are a higher DBU rate and little gain if the job is I/O-bound
Option B — move to a job cluster with autoscaling 4-16 workers and spot workers: pros are the biggest cost reduction with no code change; cons are occasional spot reclamation and longer start-up
Option C — use more, smaller workers: pros are better task parallelism and finer autoscaling granularity; cons are more shuffle traffic and higher driver pressure

Recommendation: adopt B as the baseline (job cluster + autoscaling + spot, on-demand driver), then add Photon only for the stages the Spark UI shows as CPU-bound — this hits the 30% target while leaving headroom for 3x growth
Exam takeaway: the best answer is the one satisfying every stated constraint, not the one with the biggest theoretical speedup

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Costing a Pipeline Before and After Right-Sizing
outlines.description: A full monthly cost calculation comparing an over-provisioned fixed cluster with a right-sized autoscaling job cluster, including VM cost.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a job runs 2 hours per day, every day, on a fixed 8-worker configuration rated at a combined 12 DBU/h; the DBU price is $0.15. Compute the monthly DBU cost
Worked solution (baseline): 12 DBU/h x 2 h x 30 days = 720 DBU-hours; 720 x $0.15 = $108.00 per month
Right-sized configuration: autoscaling 2-8 workers averaging 5 workers at 7.5 DBU/h, runtime falls to 1.4 h. Compute the new monthly cost: 7.5 x 1.4 x 30 = 315 DBU-hours; 315 x $0.15 = $47.25
Add the cloud VM term: if the VM portion is $0.10 per DBU-hour equivalent, the baseline adds 72.00 and the right-sized adds 31.50 — total monthly spend falls from $180.00 to $78.75, a 56% reduction
Analysis: cost is driven by the average worker count under autoscaling, not the maximum; the saving comes from both fewer DBU-hours and a shorter billed runtime
Common pitfalls: ignoring the VM charge and counting only DBUs; using peak worker count in the estimate; forgetting that start-up overhead makes very short runs proportionally more expensive

outlines.title: Git Integration in Databricks
outlines.description: Show how version control connects to the workspace and how branch-and-merge workflows trigger bundle validation and deployment.
keyPoints: Databricks Git folders (formerly Repos) clone a remote repository into the workspace; a workspace supports one Git folder per repository structure
Supported providers include GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps, and AWS CodeCommit; credentials are stored per user or via a service principal
Working model: feature branch → pull request → main; CI validates the bundle on the PR, deployment happens on merge
The bundle config lives in the same repository as the source code, so code and infrastructure are reviewed together
Exam trap: Git folders give version control and a trigger surface, but they are not a CI/CD system by themselves — an external runner still executes the pipeline

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Package an Existing Job as a Bundle
outlines.description: Convert a hand-created job into a Databricks Asset Bundle, validate it, and deploy it — with the reasoning behind each step.
keyPoints: Problem: a manually created job 'daily_sales_etl' in the dev workspace runs the notebook /Workspace/Repos/team/sales/etl/bronze.py on a daily schedule. Package it so the same definition can deploy to dev, staging, and prod.
Step 1 — scaffold: databricks bundle init with the default-python template creates databricks.yml, resources/, src/, and tests/
Step 2 — capture existing config: databricks bundle generate job --existing-job-id <job-id> writes the current job definition into resources/daily_sales_etl.yml
Step 3 — parameterise: replace hardcoded catalog/schema with ${var.catalog} / ${var.schema} and declare variables: with a default
Step 4 — verify then ship: databricks bundle validate -t dev, then databricks bundle deploy -t dev, then databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t dev

Analysis: generate beats hand-writing because it guarantees feature parity with the job that already runs; the classic pitfall is leaving literal catalog names in the YAML, which makes every environment write to dev data
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply the bundle-authoring workflow end to end on a realistic existing job.

outlines.title: The Bundle Lifecycle Commands
outlines.description: Present the four command families a data engineer uses daily, and what each one actually changes in the workspace.
keyPoints: databricks bundle validate — resolves variables and the target, checks the config, and touches nothing in the workspace
databricks bundle deploy -t <target> — uploads synced files, creates or updates resources, and writes deployment state under .databricks/bundle/<target>
databricks bundle run <resource> -t <target> — triggers the deployed job or pipeline, accepting --params overrides
databricks bundle destroy -t <target> — tears down the deployed resources; use --auto-approve in CI so the pipeline does not hang
Inspection helpers: databricks bundle summary, databricks bundle schema, and databricks bundle open
outlines.teachingObjective: Match each bundle CLI command to its effect and its place in a CI/CD pipeline.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Promote One Bundle to Production
outlines.description: Deploy the same bundle to a production target with a different catalog, a service principal, and a schedule that exists only in prod.
keyPoints: Problem: staging and production must read different catalogs, production must run as a service principal, and only production may hold a daily schedule. No YAML may be duplicated per environment.
Step 1 — declare variables: catalog with a dev default, then override per target (dev → dev_catalog, staging → staging_catalog, prod → prod_catalog)
Step 2 — configure targets: dev uses mode: development (names prefixed with [dev <user>], schedules paused) while staging and prod use mode: production
Step 3 — attach prod-only settings: run_as: <service-principal>, an explicit workspace.host, a permissions block, and the schedule entry present only under the prod target
Step 4 — release: databricks bundle validate -t prod, databricks bundle deploy -t prod, then databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod

Analysis: this is build-once-deploy-many — the same files, the same tests, different resolved variables. The common pitfall is copying databricks.yml per environment, which reintroduces exactly the drift CI/CD is meant to remove
outlines.teachingObjective: Deploy a single bundle artifact across dev, staging, and production targets using variable and target overrides.

outlines.title: Choosing an Environment Promotion Strategy
outlines.description: Weigh three realistic isolation strategies for promoting bundles, then commit to one recommendation under explicit constraints.
keyPoints: Constraint set: a 4-person data team, one platform team, separate catalog per environment, production-like test data needed, limited budget and no dedicated release engineer
Option A — one workspace, bundle targets with variable overrides: cheapest and fastest, but compute quotas, secrets, and permissions are shared and isolation is logical, not physical
Option B — a workspace per environment: strongest isolation and independent credentials and quotas, but three times the setup, cost, and configuration surface to maintain
Option C — hybrid: dev and staging share a workspace, production runs in its own workspace with a separate metastore and service principal credentials

Recommendation: Option C. It gives production a genuine blast-radius boundary while keeping day-to-day iteration cheap; Option A is acceptable only until the first production-critical workload arrives
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify an environment isolation choice for bundle promotion under realistic cost and governance constraints.

outlines.title: Testing Pipelines Before Deployment
outlines.description: Establishes why testing is a mandatory gate before any pipeline is promoted, and maps the layers of testing used for Databricks pipelines.
keyPoints: Exam objective: given a pipeline defect, select the appropriate test type — unit, integration, or data-quality.
Defects caught in CI cost minutes; the same defects found in production cost hours of remediation and erode trust in the data.
Testing pyramid for data: many fast unit tests on transformation logic, fewer integration tests that read and write tables, very few end-to-end job runs.
Tests execute automatically in CI on every pull request, before any bundle is deployed to any environment [source 5][source 6].
Build once, deploy many: the same tested artifact is promoted from dev to staging to production rather than rebuilt per environment [source 5].
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain why pipelines must be tested before deployment and distinguish unit, integration, and data-quality tests.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Unit-Test a Transformation
outlines.description: Fully worked example of writing a pytest unit test that proves a PySpark transformation is correct before the branch is merged.
keyPoints: Problem statement: the function clean_customers(df) trims and lowercases email, drops rows with null customer_id, and keeps only the latest row per customer_id — write a unit test that fails if any of these rules breaks.

Worked solution: build the input with spark.createDataFrame, call clean_customers, and compare against an expected DataFrame using assertDataFrameEqual or chispa — no cluster, no table, a few seconds per test.
Analysis: a good unit test fails for the right reason — assert row count, key uniqueness, and the trimmed column value separately, not just that the function returned without error.
Exam trap: unit tests cover pure transformation logic; reading from or writing to a real table is an integration test, not a unit test.
Run the suite in the CI stage with pytest -q; a red test blocks the bundle deploy [source 4][source 5].
outlines.teachingObjective: Write a passing unit test for a PySpark transformation using fixtures and DataFrame assertions.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Integration and Data-Quality Tests
outlines.description: Fully worked example of testing a bronze-to-silver job against an isolated dev catalog with data-quality assertions.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a job writes silver.orders; write tests that (a) run the job against the dev catalog, (b) assert no null order_id, (c) assert no duplicate (order_id, order_ts), (d) allow only the documented status values, and (e) keep row count within a tolerance of the bronze source.

Worked solution: trigger the job with the dev target, then query the resulting Delta table with assertions; express the rules as declarative data-quality checks in the style of Deequ or Great Expectations-style frameworks [source p.184].
Analysis: integration tests are slower and environment-bound, so they run after the unit suite passes and always against isolated dev resources, never production data [source 6].
Pitfalls: asserting exact row counts on late-arriving or streaming data, forgetting to clean up test tables, and letting tests depend on production datasets that change underneath them.
Exam phrasing: distinguish a test that validates code correctness from a test that validates data quality — the exam often offers both as plausible answers.
outlines.teachingObjective: Design and justify integration and data-quality tests for a Delta Lake pipeline.

outlines.title: Environments: Dev, Staging, and Production
outlines.description: Explains how Databricks isolates environments and why isolation is a prerequisite for safe promotion.
keyPoints: Exam objective: identify how Databricks isolates environments through workspaces, Unity Catalog catalogs and schemas, compute, and permissions.
Teams split infrastructure into live and staging areas precisely so ETL services and pipelines can be tested before promotion [source 6].
Typical separation: a workspace per environment and/or dev, staging, and prod catalogs in Unity Catalog, with jobs running as a least-privilege service principal.
Code stays identical across environments; only configuration differs — paths, catalog and schema names, cluster sizes, and identities — which is exactly what bundle targets express.
Guardrails: dev jobs must never write to production tables, and pipelines must avoid hard-coded production paths.
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe how Databricks environments are isolated and what must differ per environment.

outlines.title: Comparison: Environment Isolation Approaches
outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison of the main ways teams isolate Databricks environments, with the trade-offs of each.
keyPoints: Exam objective: compare isolation approaches and choose one given cost, isolation strength, and team-size constraints.

[Table] Environment isolation options: separate workspaces vs. per-environment catalogs and schemas in one workspace vs. branch-based development — dimensioned by isolation strength, cost and overhead, operational complexity, and release safety.

Separate workspaces give the strongest isolation of compute, permissions, and data, but duplicate governance setup and increase cost; per-environment catalogs inside one workspace are the common lightweight pattern.
Exam trap: treating a Git branch as an environment — branches isolate code only, not data, compute, or permissions.
Whatever the choice, promote the same artifact and override only configuration per target [source 5][source 6].
outlines.teachingObjective: Select an environment isolation strategy and defend it with trade-offs.

outlines.title: Promoting Code and Configuration with Bundles
outlines.description: Walks through the concrete promotion workflow for a Databricks Asset Bundle from development to production.
keyPoints: Exam objective: describe how a Databricks Asset Bundle moves through dev, staging, and production.
A bundle declares code (notebooks and files), resources (jobs, pipelines), and variables in databricks.yml, with one target per environment such as dev, staging, and prod.

Promotion flow: pull request, CI runs tests and databricks bundle validate, deploy to dev then staging, run integration tests, pass an approval gate, then databricks bundle deploy -t prod [source 5][source 6].
Only configuration changes per environment — variables, catalog names, cluster sizes, run-as service principal — while secrets are injected from secret scopes and never committed to Git.
Rollback plan: keep the previous good artifact and re-deploy the last known-good commit instead of editing production resources by hand.
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe and sequence the steps that promote a tested bundle into production.

outlines.title: Decision: How to Promote Configuration
outlines.description: A constrained decision on the mechanism used to move configuration between environments, ending in one justified recommendation.
keyPoints: Constraints: one team, a single production workspace, strong audit requirements, and a rule that development jobs must never touch production data.
Option A — bundle variables with per-target overrides: one codebase, explicit per-environment configuration, fully reviewable in Git; recommended.
Option B — long-lived per-environment branches with hand-edited configuration: causes drift, painful merges, and breaks the build-once principle.
Option C — manual edits in the production workspace UI: fastest the first time, but un-auditable, unreproducible, and impossible to roll back cleanly.
Recommendation: Option A, gated by bundle validate plus the test suite in CI, with a service principal executing production deployments.
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a configuration promotion strategy against explicit constraints.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Diagnose a Skewed Nightly Job
outlines.description: A fully worked Spark UI diagnosis: statement, step-by-step solution, and an analysis of why the fix works and what commonly goes wrong.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a nightly Delta MERGE job that normally runs in 12 minutes now takes 95 minutes; Spark UI shows one stage with 200 tasks, a median task time of 3 s, a max task time of 9 m 20 s, shuffle read of 180 GB, and 40 GB of disk spill
Step 1 — localize: open the Jobs → Stages view, sort tasks by duration, and confirm the long tail is concentrated in a single shuffle stage rather than spread evenly
Step 2 — diagnose: a max/median ratio above roughly 3x plus heavy shuffle read indicates key skew on the join or MERGE key, not a cluster-size problem
Step 3 — fix: enable Adaptive Query Execution skew join handling; where skew persists, salt the hot key or broadcast the small dimension table; confirm spill drops after the change

Analysis: skew concentrates many rows on one partition, so one executor processes the hot partition while the rest idle — adding workers raises cost without shortening the critical path, which is the most common wrong answer on the exam
outlines.teachingObjective: Diagnose and remediate a skewed shuffle stage using Spark UI evidence.

outlines.title: Troubleshooting Ingestion Failures
outlines.description: Catalogues the four failure classes in ingestion pipelines and the correct triage order.
keyPoints: Failure classes: schema drift, malformed or corrupt records, permission and credential errors, source connectivity/timeout, and rate limiting
Delta Lake enforcement: schema enforcement errors on unexpected columns, and the rescued data column Auto Loader populates for malformed records
Streaming checkpoints: a checkpoint locks the schema, so non-evolutionary schema changes restart-fail the stream
Triage order that avoids rework: source reachability → credentials → schema → data quality
[Chart] Bar chart of incident counts by ingestion failure class over the last quarter, highlighting schema drift as the most frequent cause
outlines.teachingObjective: Map an ingestion failure message to its failure class and begin triage in the correct order.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Fix a Failing Streaming Ingestion
outlines.description: A fully worked ingestion failure: an Auto Loader stream that stops after an upstream schema change.
keyPoints: Problem statement: an Auto Loader stream reading JSON from cloud storage fails with a schema-evolution error after the source adds a new column and renames another; the stream has been running for six months
Step 1 — read the error precisely: a schema-inference mismatch against the checkpointed schema, not a data-corruption error

Step 2 — decide: evolutionary change (add new column) → enable schema evolution with addNewColumns/mergeSchema; non-evolutionary change (rename or type change) → full refresh into a new checkpoint and table
Step 3 — protect downstream: route unparseable records to a rescued data column or a dead-letter Delta table so one bad record cannot fail the batch

Analysis: the checkpoint stores the schema, so the fix must account for the checkpoint lifecycle — changing only the reader option while reusing the old checkpoint leaves the stream broken, a frequent exam distractor
outlines.teachingObjective: Choose the correct schema-evolution and checkpoint remedy for a failing streaming ingestion job.

outlines.title: Decision: Remediating a Failing Production Pipeline
outlines.description: A constrained remediation decision where learners compare options and justify one recommendation.
keyPoints: Scenario and constraints: a production pipeline must deliver before an SLA in 45 minutes; the job writes an idempotent MERGE into a Delta table; 3% of records are malformed; the cluster is healthy
Option A — full rerun from scratch: simplest and safest data-wise, but the full job takes 90 minutes and will breach the SLA
Option B — repair run for failed tasks only: fast and surgical, but does nothing to stop the same malformed records failing the next scheduled run
Option C — quarantine malformed records and let the good data land, then backfill: protects the SLA and the pipeline, at the cost of adding a quarantine table and a follow-up step
Recommendation: Option C combined with a repair run — it meets the SLA, keeps the write idempotent, and removes the recurring root cause rather than just restarting the symptom
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a remediation strategy for a failing production pipeline under explicit SLA and data-quality constraints.

outlines.title: The Certification Blueprint: Five Domains
outlines.description: Open the final lesson by laying out the exam blueprint — the five domains, their approximate weights, and the question style — so students budget study time in proportion to scoring impact.
keyPoints: Exam mechanics: scored, scenario-based multiple choice with no partial credit; roughly 45 questions in 90 minutes with a passing threshold near 70% — pacing and answer elimination matter as much as recall

Domain weights (approximate — always verify against the current official exam guide, since weights shift between versions): Lakehouse Platform ~24%, ELT with Spark SQL and Python ~29%, Incremental Data Processing ~22%, Production Pipelines ~16%, Data Governance ~9%
[Chart] Bar chart: the five domains on the X-axis, exam weight percentage on the Y-axis, to show that ELT plus Incremental Processing together exceed half the exam

Question phrasing follows exam-objective style: 'which approach is the MOST efficient / LEAST expensive / requires the LEAST code' — the expected answer is usually the managed, declarative, Databricks-native option
Strategic consequence: a domain you never study is a hard ceiling on your total score, so remaining study hours belong to the weakest domain, not the most comfortable one

outlines.title: Domains 1–2 Review: Platform and ELT
outlines.description: Compress the two heaviest domains — the Lakehouse Platform and ELT with Spark SQL and Python — into the high-yield facts and decision rules the exam actually tests.
keyPoints: Platform essentials: Delta Lake provides ACID transactions and time travel over object storage; compute is separated from storage; all-purpose clusters are for interactive development while job clusters or serverless compute are the correct answer for scheduled, cost-sensitive workloads

Table semantics: with managed tables Unity Catalog owns the data and its lifecycle, while external tables keep the data at a path you control — CREATE OR REPLACE, CTAS, and LOCATION each answer a different exam scenario

ELT decision rules: prefer Spark SQL or the DataFrame API over Python UDFs whenever performance is the criterion; use widgets and parameters for reusable notebooks and jobs; prefer declarative SQL unless the scenario explicitly demands procedural logic

Trap cluster: 'MOST efficient / LEAST expensive / requires the LEAST code / MOST scalable' — under these constraints the Databricks-native declarative option usually beats a hand-written loop or a self-managed cluster

Delta maintenance vocabulary the exam expects you to distinguish: OPTIMIZE and ZORDER for file layout and data skipping, VACUUM for retention, and the fact that time travel cannot read versions VACUUM has already removed

outlines.title: Worked Problem: A Production-Grade ELT Task
outlines.description: Walk through one representative ELT exam problem end to end — statement, worked solution, and the reasoning that separates a working answer from the expected answer.
keyPoints: Statement: a raw orders table receives duplicate and late-arriving records; produce a deduplicated silver table with exactly one current row per order_id, keeping the record with the latest updated_at, and make the job safely re-runnable on every daily run

Worked solution (PySpark): read the source, apply a window partitioned by order_id and ordered by updated_at descending, filter row_number() = 1, then MERGE INTO the target ON order_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
Analysis — why it works: MERGE is idempotent, so re-running the job leaves the target in the same state; deduplication must happen before the merge or the engine can raise a multi-match error

Pitfalls the exam rewards you for knowing: schema evolution (enable mergeSchema where appropriate), late-arriving rows whose updated_at precedes the stored value, and the fact that MERGE never deletes rows missing from the source

Exam variations to expect: the same scenario phrased as 'which approach keeps the table current with the least effort' — the expected answer is MERGE fed by Auto Loader or COPY INTO ingestion rather than a full overwrite

outlines.title: Domains 3–5 Review: Incremental, Production, Governance
outlines.description: Cover the remaining three domains — incremental data processing, production pipelines, and data governance — at the decision-rule level, tying them to the deployment work done in this unit.

outlines.title: Comparison: Confusable Databricks Options
outlines.description: Put the most commonly confused pairs of Databricks features side by side, so the exam's scenario wording can be matched to the right option quickly.
keyPoints: [Table] Four confusable pairs compared across the dimensions the exam varies: cost, latency, code volume, and how much of the pipeline Databricks manages
Ingestion: Auto Loader (streaming file arrival, schema inference and evolution, incremental by default) versus COPY INTO (idempotent batch file loads, explicit schema, SQL-first)

Processing: hand-written MERGE logic (full control, more code, you own idempotency) versus Delta Live Tables and streaming tables with expectations (declarative, managed orchestration, built-in data-quality enforcement)
Deployment: all-purpose cluster for interactive development versus job cluster or serverless compute for scheduled production runs — and why the exam pairs 'cheapest' with the latter

Selection heuristic: read the constraint word first (least code, lowest cost, most scalable, must evolve schema), then choose the option that satisfies that constraint rather than the one you personally use most
