units.title: Databricks Platform Foundations
objectives: Students will be able to navigate the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform and locate the core services used by data engineers.
Students will be able to configure workspaces, compute, and repositories to run their own development work.

lessons.title: The Databricks Data Intelligence Platform
objectives: Students will be able to describe the lakehouse architecture and how the control plane and data plane relate.
Students will be able to identify the main Databricks components relevant to the Data Engineer Associate role.

outlines.title: Lesson Orientation: The Data Intelligence Platform
outlines.description: Frame the lesson's exam objectives and roadmap, and set expectations for the platform foundations unit.
keyPoints: Exam objective: describe the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform and the components a data engineer uses daily
Lesson roadmap: lakehouse architecture, control plane vs. data plane, and the core platform services
Unit context: this lesson is the first of four covering platform foundations, workspaces/notebooks/compute, SQL and Unity Catalog, and Git folders
How this lesson maps to the certification blueprint: platform architecture, ingestion, transformation, and productionizing workloads
outlines.teachingObjective: Understand the scope and exam relevance of the lesson.

outlines.title: What Is the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform?
outlines.description: Introduce Databricks as a managed, multi-cloud platform built on Apache Spark and unify its major service families.
keyPoints: Databricks is a managed cloud platform founded by the creators of Apache Spark; it runs on AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud
It unifies data engineering, analytics, and machine learning workloads on a single copy of data
Core service families a data engineer touches: Workspace and Notebooks, Compute (clusters and SQL warehouses), Workflows/Jobs, Delta Live Tables, Databricks SQL, and Unity Catalog
Exam phrasing to expect: 'Which Databricks component should be used to accomplish X?' — success depends on knowing each service's purpose
[Chart] Bar chart: relative exam blueprint weight by domain (platform, ingestion, transformation, productionizing) to show where platform knowledge pays off
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain what Databricks is and name the platform's main service families.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Platform Positioning
outlines.description: Quick checks that the learner can place Databricks correctly among cloud data platforms and recall the major service families.
keyPoints: Identify Databricks as a managed, multi-cloud platform built on Apache Spark
Match a stated task to the correct Databricks service family
Distractors mirror real exam traps, such as confusing an analytics service with an orchestration service
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify foundational platform knowledge before moving to architecture.

outlines.title: The Lakehouse: Unifying Lake and Warehouse
outlines.description: Explain how the lakehouse design combines the economics of a data lake with the reliability and governance of a data warehouse.
keyPoints: Data lake: low-cost object storage holding open-format files (Parquet, JSON, CSV) with no transactional guarantees
Data warehouse: strong ACID (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) transactions, fast SQL performance, and governance, but proprietary formats and higher cost
Lakehouse: keeps data in open formats in object storage and adds a transactional metadata layer on top
Delta Lake provides that layer, enabling ACID transactions, schema enforcement, upserts, and time travel over Parquet files
One copy of structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data serves BI, data engineering, and machine learning workloads
[Table] Side-by-side comparison of data lake vs. data warehouse vs. lakehouse across data types, ACID support, cost, and openness
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe the lakehouse architecture and the problem it solves.

outlines.title: Data Lake vs. Data Warehouse vs. Lakehouse
outlines.description: Compare the three architectures across the dimensions exam questions test, so the learner can justify a choice under stated constraints.
keyPoints: Storage format and openness: raw files in object storage vs. proprietary warehouse tables vs. open Delta tables in object storage
Transactional guarantees: none vs. full ACID vs. full ACID through the Delta transaction log
Workloads supported: machine learning and semi-structured data vs. SQL BI vs. both on one platform
Cost and scaling model: storage and compute scale independently in a lakehouse
Exam trap: the lakehouse is not 'a warehouse with extra storage' — the open format and unified governance are the distinguishing features
outlines.teachingObjective: Contrast lake, warehouse, and lakehouse architectures to support scenario-based decisions.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Lakehouse Architecture
outlines.description: Assess understanding of Delta Lake's role and the trade-offs between lake, warehouse, and lakehouse designs.
keyPoints: Explain what Delta Lake adds to files stored in object storage
Choose the appropriate architecture for a described workload and constraint
Distractors include plausible but incorrect claims, such as 'the lakehouse requires loading data into a proprietary store'
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm the learner can articulate lakehouse benefits and limits.

outlines.title: Inside the Lakehouse: Storage, Metadata, Compute, Governance
outlines.description: Walk through the four layers of the Databricks lakehouse so the learner can place each service on the architecture diagram.
keyPoints: Storage layer: cloud object storage (Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage, Google Cloud Storage) holds raw Parquet data files — cheap and effectively unlimited
Metadata layer: the Delta transaction log (_delta_log) records commits and enables ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel
Compute layer: Spark clusters, Photon-accelerated engines, and Databricks SQL warehouses read directly from object storage
Governance layer: Unity Catalog provides a unified catalog, permissions, lineage, and auditing across tables, files, and models
Architectural principle: compute and storage are separated, so each can be scaled and priced independently
outlines.teachingObjective: Map the lakehouse layers and identify which Databricks service owns each layer.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A clean layered architecture diagram of a lakehouse on a cloud platform, showing four stacked layers from bottom to top: cloud object storage with Parquet data files, a Delta Lake metadata/transaction log layer, a compute layer with Spark clusters and SQL warehouses, and a governance/catalog layer. Arrows show compute reading data from storage and the catalog governing access. Professional flat infographic style, blue and teal palette, all labels in English, no human figures

outlines.title: Explore the Lakehouse Architecture
outlines.description: An interactive architecture diagram where learners click each layer to see its responsibility and trace what happens when a query runs.
keyPoints: Click a layer (object storage, Delta log, compute, Unity Catalog) to reveal its role and the Databricks service that implements it
Trace a query end to end: request from the workspace, planning in the control plane, execution on compute in the data plane, read of data from storage
Toggle a workload type (BI SQL query vs. Spark ETL job) and watch which components become active
Probe common misconceptions: does data move into Databricks' control plane? Where do the files actually live?
outlines.teachingObjective: Reinforce the placement and interaction of lakehouse components through guided exploration.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Lakehouse Layers and Delta Lake
outlines.description: Test layer-by-layer knowledge, including Delta Lake capabilities and the significance of separating compute from storage.
keyPoints: Identify which layer or service is responsible for a described capability
Recognize Delta Lake features: ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and upserts on open files
Distractors include mixing up storage and metadata responsibilities, a frequent exam confusion
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify the learner can locate services within the lakehouse architecture.

outlines.title: Control Plane and Data Plane: What Runs Where
outlines.description: Explain the two-plane model, which is central to Databricks security, networking, and cost questions on the exam.
keyPoints: Control plane: the Databricks-managed backend — web application, notebook and query editors, job scheduler, cluster manager, and workspace metadata, hosted in the Databricks cloud account
Data plane: the compute and data in the customer's cloud account — cluster virtual machines plus the cloud object storage that holds the actual data
Classic compute launches in the customer's cloud subscription; serverless compute runs in a Databricks-managed account within the same region
Communication flows in both directions: the control plane sends orchestration and configuration commands to the data plane, while results, logs, and metadata flow back
Exam trap: the customer's data stays in the customer's cloud storage — it is not copied into the Databricks control plane
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe the control plane and data plane and the direction of traffic between them.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A two-box architecture diagram contrasting a Databricks-managed control plane with a customer cloud account data plane. The left box shows web UI, notebook editor, job scheduler and cluster manager icons; the right box shows compute clusters and object storage buckets. Bidirectional arrows are labeled to show orchestration commands flowing out and results and logs flowing back, with a note that customer data remains in the customer account. Flat professional infographic style, blue and orange palette, all labels in English, no human figures

outlines.title: Control Plane vs. Data Plane
outlines.description: Compare the two planes across the dimensions that drive exam scenarios: location, contents, data sensitivity, and failure impact.
keyPoints: Location: Databricks-managed account vs. customer cloud account or region
Contents: workspace UI, schedulers, cluster manager, metadata vs. virtual machines, serverless compute, and object storage holding the data
Data handling: control plane stores configuration and metadata, while sensitive data stays in the customer's storage and is governed by cloud permissions
Failure impact: control plane outages affect the interface and scheduling; data plane issues affect job execution, and results are typically resilient because data is stored separately
Use it to answer 'where does X live?' and 'who is responsible for securing Y?' style questions with confidence
outlines.teachingObjective: Distinguish the responsibilities and boundaries of the two planes.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Control Plane and Data Plane
outlines.description: Exam-style questions on plane responsibilities, data residency, and serverless versus classic compute.
keyPoints: Determine where a described resource resides: control plane, customer data plane, or serverless data plane
Reason about what happens to workloads when one plane is unavailable
Short-answer item asks the learner to explain why separating the planes helps with security and compliance
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm mastery of the two-plane model before summarizing the component landscape.

outlines.title: Core Components for the Data Engineer Associate
outlines.description: Consolidate the platform map of services a data engineer uses daily and preview the next lesson in the unit.
keyPoints: Workspace: the developer entry point holding notebooks, queries, dashboards, folders, and Git-backed Repos
Compute: all-purpose clusters for interactive development, job clusters for scheduled runs, and SQL warehouses for SQL analytics — all managed in the data plane
Pipeline and orchestration services: Workflows/Jobs for scheduling and orchestration, and Delta Live Tables for declarative, quality-enforced pipelines
Governance and analytics: Unity Catalog for catalogs, permissions, and lineage; Databricks SQL for BI-style querying on lakehouse data
Takeaways: the lakehouse unifies storage and workloads on open formats, the control plane orchestrates while the data plane executes, and every exam scenario can be traced back to this architecture
Next lesson: Workspaces, Notebooks, and Compute — configuring the environment you will use throughout the course
outlines.teachingObjective: Identify the main Databricks components relevant to the Data Engineer Associate role and connect them to the lakehouse architecture.

lessons.title: Workspaces, Notebooks, and Compute
objectives: Students will be able to create a notebook, attach it to a cluster, and run cells in multiple languages.
Students will be able to select an appropriate cluster configuration for a given workload.

outlines.title: Lesson Orientation: Workspaces, Notebooks, and Compute
outlines.description: Frame the lesson objectives and connect them to the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform foundation built in the previous lesson.
keyPoints: Objective 1: Given a workspace, the data engineer must create a notebook, attach it to compute, and run cells in more than one language.
Objective 2: Given a workload description, the data engineer must select an appropriate cluster configuration.
Builds directly on the previous lesson: the lakehouse architecture is now accessed through the workspace, notebooks, and clusters.
Exam relevance: workspace navigation and compute selection are foundational Data Engineer Associate task domains that later lessons (SQL, Unity Catalog, Git folders, pipelines) all assume.
Roadmap for this lesson: workspace navigation, notebook and language basics, attaching clusters, cluster configuration choices, and two applied decision scenes.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Workspace Navigation and Notebook Basics
outlines.description: Check retention of the workspace tour and notebook fundamentals before moving to multi-language cells.
keyPoints: Identify the sidebar areas that expose Workspace, Catalog, Compute, and Jobs.
Distinguish a notebook from a folder and from a file in the workspace browser.
Recognize where cluster state (Running, Pending, Terminated) is displayed.
Trap to expect: confusing the workspace browser with the Catalog Explorer.

outlines.title: Navigating the Databricks Workspace
outlines.description: Give students a reliable mental map of the workspace so they can find notebooks, compute, and data quickly during the exam and on the job.
keyPoints: Sidebar services used by data engineers: Workspace, Catalog, Compute, Jobs & Pipelines, SQL Warehouses, and Marketplace.
Workspace browser: your personal home folder versus shared folders; notebooks, folders, and files are the three object types you will create.
[Image] A schematic mockup of the Databricks sidebar and notebook editor with labeled regions: cell list, results pane, cluster selector, Run / Run all.
The Compute tab is where all-purpose clusters, job clusters, and cluster policies are listed and managed.
Exam framing: 'Where would the data engineer go to...' questions are answered by mapping the task to a specific sidebar service.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A clean, professional schematic mockup of a data analytics platform web interface, not a real product screenshot. Show a left-hand navigation sidebar with icon-plus-label rows and a main content area split into a notebook editor on the left and a results pane on the right. Include a dropdown in the top toolbar representing a compute selector. Use an abstract, flat, infographic style with no real logos or brand marks. All labels and text in the image must be in English.

outlines.title: Multi-Language Cells and Magic Commands
outlines.description: Students practise switching cell languages inside a single notebook and observe how state is shared between language contexts.
keyPoints: The notebook default language is chosen at creation, but any individual cell can override it with a magic command.
Magic commands to master: %python, %sql, %scala, %r for language switching; %md for markdown; %sh for shell; %pip for library installation.
The Spark session is shared across cells in a notebook, so a registered temporary view created in one language is queryable from another.
Observe how results render differently per language: SQL returns a table, Python returns output or a DataFrame preview, Scala returns a typed result.
Common trap: assuming a Python variable is directly visible inside a %sql cell — it is not, unless it is registered as a temporary view.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Notebooks, Cells, and Languages
outlines.description: Verify that students can choose the correct cell language and predict what is visible across cells.
keyPoints: Select the correct magic command for a described task.
Predict whether a value created in a Python cell is readable from a SQL cell.
Distinguish %md, %sh, and %pip from the four execution languages.
Trap to expect: a distractor that claims each cell runs in an isolated session.

outlines.title: Attaching Compute and Executing Cells
outlines.description: Explain the notebook-to-cluster relationship and what actually happens when a cell runs.
keyPoints: A notebook must be attached to a running cluster before any cell can execute; a detached notebook cannot run code.
The driver node coordinates the run and holds the Spark session; executor nodes perform the distributed work and return results to the driver.
[Image] A notebook shown attached to a cluster, with the driver and executor nodes drawn as abstract blocks and results flowing back to the results pane.
Cell lifecycle states to recognize: queued, running, finished, and error; Run all executes cells top to bottom while Run below executes from the cursor.
Exam trap: one cluster can serve many notebooks and one notebook can be re-attached to a different cluster — the attachment is not permanent.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A clean technical diagram in a flat infographic style showing a notebook document on the left connected by an arrow to a compute cluster on the right. Draw the cluster as one highlighted coordinator node labeled 'driver' and three smaller identical nodes labeled 'executor' arranged in a row beneath it, with abstract connection lines between them. Use muted professional colors and no brand logos. All labels and text in the image must be in English.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Create a Notebook, Attach a Cluster, and Run Multi-Language Cells
outlines.description: A fully worked, end-to-end task that mirrors the first lesson objective and the corresponding exam objective.
keyPoints: Problem statement: In a fresh workspace, create a notebook in your home folder that prints a greeting in Python, computes an aggregate in SQL over a table registered from Python, and reads that same table from a Scala cell — all while attached to a single all-purpose cluster.
Worked solution, step 1: Create the notebook and keep the default language as Python; name it so its purpose is obvious.
Worked solution, step 2: Create an all-purpose cluster with a current LTS runtime, 2 workers, and an auto-stop timeout; wait for state Running.
Worked solution, step 3: Attach the notebook, run the Python cell to build a DataFrame and register it with createOrReplaceTempView, then run a %sql cell and a %scala cell against that view.
Analysis: this works because one Spark session is bound to the notebook, so temp views are visible to every language context — a Python variable is not.
Common pitfalls: running a cell while the cluster is still Pending; expecting %sql to see a raw Python variable; forgetting that auto-stop terminates the cluster and clears notebook state.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Cluster Configuration Concepts
outlines.description: Assess understanding of the individual cluster configuration controls before students combine them into a workload decision.
keyPoints: Match a configuration control (runtime version, node type, worker count, autoscaling, Photon, auto-stop) to its effect.
Identify what happens to cost when autoscaling shrinks a cluster and when an idle cluster auto-stops.
Recognize when a single-node cluster is appropriate versus a multi-node cluster.
Trap to expect: a distractor that treats Photon as a storage format or Unity Catalog feature rather than a query engine acceleration.

outlines.title: All-Purpose Clusters vs Job Clusters
outlines.description: A side-by-side comparison of the two cluster categories students must be able to choose between on the exam.
keyPoints: [Table] All-Purpose vs Job Cluster across dimensions: who creates it, who can use it, lifecycle and termination, relative DBU cost, autoscaling support, and primary use case.
All-purpose clusters: created manually or by API, shared interactively by multiple users, used for notebooks and ad hoc exploration, higher cost, stopped manually or by auto-stop.
Job clusters: created by the job scheduler for a single run, isolated to that run, cheaper per DBU, terminated automatically when the run completes.
Decision rule: interactive development and exploration use an all-purpose cluster; scheduled, automated production pipelines use a job cluster.
Exam trap: all-purpose clusters can also run jobs, so 'job' in the question does not automatically mean job cluster — look for whether the work is interactive or scheduled.

outlines.title: Cluster Sizing and Cost Explorer
outlines.description: Students manipulate cluster configuration parameters and observe the resulting trade-offs in parallelism, runtime, and cost.
keyPoints: Increase or decrease the number of worker nodes and observe the effect on parallel task capacity and total cost.
Toggle autoscaling and set minimum and maximum workers to see how the cluster grows and shrinks with demand.
Switch worker node types and toggle Photon acceleration to compare throughput gains against cost per hour.
Set an auto-stop timeout and observe how much idle time is billed before the cluster terminates.
Goal: build intuition that 'best' cluster configuration always means best for a stated workload, not simply the largest cluster.

widgetOutline.concept: Cluster configuration trade-offs

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Choosing a Cluster Configuration for a Workload
outlines.description: Exam-style scenario questions requiring a cluster recommendation for a described workload.
keyPoints: Given a nightly batch transformation job, select the most cost-appropriate cluster category.
Given a small dataset and a single analyst, select a single-node versus multi-node configuration.
Given an unpredictable data volume, select autoscaling over a fixed worker count.
Trap to expect: options that ignore the workload's schedule, cost constraint, or data size and simply pick the largest configuration.

outlines.title: Decision Under Constraints: Right-Sizing a Nightly ETL Cluster
outlines.description: Students weigh concrete cluster options against explicit cost, runtime, and reliability constraints and defend one recommendation.
keyPoints: Constraints: a nightly 500 GB transformation must finish before 06:00; the monthly compute budget is fixed; the pipeline must tolerate spot instance interruption; the team also needs interactive notebooks during the day.
Option A — large fixed multi-node all-purpose cluster: fast and always available, but the highest DBU rate and idle cost when the pipeline finishes early.
Option B — autoscaling job cluster on a current LTS runtime with spot workers and Photon: lowest cost per DBU, scales with volume, isolated per run, but needs a retry policy for spot reclamation.
Option C — single-node cluster: cheapest and simplest for small data, but cannot parallelize a 500 GB transformation within the time window.

Recommendation: Option B, because the workload is scheduled and volume varies, so job-cluster pricing plus autoscaling meets the runtime window while respecting the budget; keep the all-purpose cluster for daytime interactive work.
Exam takeaway: justify a cluster choice with the stated constraint (schedule, size, latency target, budget), never with 'it is the biggest'.

outlines.title: Key Takeaways and Exam Checklist
outlines.description: Consolidate the lesson into a short recall checklist that bridges to the next lesson on Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog navigation.
keyPoints: Core daily workflow: find or create a notebook in the workspace, attach it to compute, and run cells — no attachment means no execution.
One Spark session per notebook means temporary views are shared across languages, and magic commands switch the language per cell.
Choose cluster category first (all-purpose for interactive, job for scheduled), then size it (node type, workers, autoscaling, Photon, auto-stop).
Exam checklist: map each 'where would the engineer go' question to a sidebar service, and justify every cluster choice with the workload's constraint.
Next lesson: Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog navigation, where these workspace and compute skills are applied to querying governed data.

lessons.title: Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog Navigation
objectives: Students will be able to use the SQL editor and SQL warehouses to query tables.
Students will be able to browse catalogs, schemas, and tables in Unity Catalog Explorer.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Entering the Databricks SQL Workspace
outlines.description: An entry checkpoint that verifies learners can locate the SQL surfaces in the Databricks workspace and distinguish them from the compute they used in earlier lessons.
keyPoints: Identify the workspace sidebar entry points for SQL Warehouses, the SQL Editor, and Catalog Explorer
Distinguish the Databricks SQL experience from notebook-based all-purpose compute
Recognize the exam trap that confuses a SQL warehouse with a cluster
Recall that queries are executed on compute, not in the browser editor itself
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm readiness to work with the SQL editor and Unity Catalog before new content is introduced.

outlines.title: The SQL Editor and the Query Lifecycle
outlines.description: Tours the browser-based SQL editor and traces exactly what happens between typing a query and seeing a result set.
keyPoints: The SQL editor is the browser-based surface for writing, running, saving, and scheduling queries against Unity Catalog objects
Every query runs on a SQL warehouse, which is the compute; the editor is only the client interface
Query lifecycle: SQL editor → SQL warehouse (compute) → Unity Catalog (names and permissions) → Delta tables in cloud storage
The editor bundles a schema browser, results grid, query history, visualizations, and query parameters
[Chart] Flowchart of the query lifecycle from editor to result set, showing where each step can fail
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to use the SQL editor and SQL warehouses to query tables.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A clean, modern UI mockup illustration of a cloud-based SQL query editor interface: a left sidebar showing a hierarchical catalog and schema tree with labels in English such as 'main', 'sales', 'orders'; a central code panel containing a short SELECT statement; and a bottom results grid with several rows of sample tabular data. Flat vector infographic style, blue and grey palette, no company logos, no faces, all text and labels in English.

outlines.title: SQL Warehouses: Types, Sizing, and Scaling
outlines.description: Explains warehouse classes, T-shirt sizing, autoscaling behavior, and how cost controls such as auto-stop work.
keyPoints: Warehouse types: serverless, pro, and classic, which differ in startup latency, resource isolation, and pricing model
T-shirt sizes run from 2X-Small to 4X-Large and set the number and size of clusters; size up for concurrency, not to make a single bad query fast
Autoscaling is configured with minimum and maximum clusters; auto-stop shuts the warehouse down after a set number of idle minutes
Photon is the vectorized execution engine that accelerates supported SQL workloads without query rewrites
[Table] Warehouse type comparison across dimensions: startup time, isolation, cost model, and best-fit workload
Exam trap: auto-stop suspends compute and does not delete or lose data stored in Delta tables
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to use SQL warehouses to query tables and choose an appropriate warehouse configuration.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: SQL Warehouses and Query Execution
outlines.description: Checks understanding of warehouse types, sizing, autoscaling, and where query execution actually happens.
keyPoints: Select the correct warehouse type given a stated startup-time or isolation constraint
Interpret a minimum/maximum cluster setting and predict scaling behavior under concurrent dashboards
Explain what auto-stop does and does not do to stored data
Match a workload description to an appropriate T-shirt size rationale
outlines.teachingObjective: Assess mastery of SQL warehouse configuration before moving to Unity Catalog navigation.

outlines.title: Interactive: Tracing and Breaking the Query Path
outlines.description: Learners click through the end-to-end query path, then deliberately break it at each node to see which error the platform returns and why.
keyPoints: Click each node in the flow to reveal its responsibility: client, compute, governance layer, and storage
Toggle between serverless, pro, and classic warehouses to observe the difference in startup step
Inject a fault at each node (wrong warehouse, missing privilege, missing table) and predict the resulting error
Compare where failures surface: the editor, the warehouse, or Unity Catalog
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to reason about which component is responsible for a query outcome.

outlines.title: Unity Catalog: The Three-Level Namespace
outlines.description: Introduces the metastore, catalog, schema, table hierarchy and the three-part naming convention used everywhere in Databricks SQL.
keyPoints: Object names use three levels: catalog.schema.table, for example main.sales.orders
Above the catalog sits the metastore, which is attached to workspaces and owns the identity and permission model
Object types governed by Unity Catalog include tables, views, volumes, functions, models, and connections
Default names are the main catalog and the default schema; names can be fully qualified or set with USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA
Managed versus external tables, and Delta as the default table format
[Chart] Hierarchy diagram from metastore to catalog to schema to table with a highlighted fully qualified path
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to name and locate any table with a fully qualified Unity Catalog name.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A three-level hierarchical infographic of a data catalog namespace: a single metastore node at the top branching downward into several catalog nodes, each catalog branching into schema nodes, each schema branching into table nodes. One highlighted path is labeled with the fully qualified name 'catalog.schema.table' in English. Flat vector infographic style, blue and grey palette, clean labels, all text in English, no logos, no people.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Unity Catalog Namespaces and Naming
outlines.description: Tests the ability to read, write, and reason about two-part versus three-part object names and namespace defaults.
keyPoints: Given a query, determine whether the table reference resolves correctly under the session's current catalog and schema
Distinguish one-part, two-part, and three-part names and when each is sufficient
Identify the correct object level for an operation on a catalog, a schema, and a table
Recognize the trap where a user assumes the default catalog applies to another workspace
outlines.teachingObjective: Assess accurate use of Unity Catalog namespace naming.

outlines.title: Hands-On: Querying Across Unity Catalog Namespaces
outlines.description: A simulated SQL sandbox where learners explore a fake Unity Catalog, set session context, and run correctly qualified queries.
keyPoints: Run SHOW CATALOGS, SHOW SCHEMAS IN, and SHOW TABLES IN to discover the available namespace
Use USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA, then re-run a previously failing unqualified query to see it succeed
Write SELECT statements against a three-part name and compare against a two-part reference
Observe the error returned when a namespace part does not exist and correct the reference
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to use the SQL editor to query tables by their Unity Catalog namespace.

outlines.title: Catalog Explorer: Browsing Metadata, Permissions, and Lineage
outlines.description: Walks through Catalog Explorer navigation so learners can inspect objects, grants, and data lineage without writing any SQL.
keyPoints: Navigate the tree from metastore to catalog to schema to table using search and filter, and read column names, data types, and comments
The table detail pages expose Overview for location and owner, Sample Data, Details for the schema, Permissions, Lineage, and Insights
The Permissions tab shows granted and inherited privileges and illustrates how grants cascade from catalog to schema to table
The Lineage tab shows upstream and downstream tables and the notebooks or jobs that read and write the object
Exam trap: catalog browsing is itself governed by privileges, so a user without SELECT may see the table name but no sample data
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to browse catalogs, schemas, and tables in Unity Catalog Explorer.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A UI mockup illustration of a data catalog explorer screen: on the left a collapsible tree of catalogs and schemas with English labels, on the right a details panel with tabs labeled Overview, Sample Data, Details, Permissions, Lineage, and Insights, and a small node-and-arrow lineage graph beneath. Flat vector infographic style, blue and grey palette, no company logos, no faces, all text in English.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Catalog Explorer and Governance Signals
outlines.description: Assesses the ability to interpret the metadata, permission inheritance, and lineage information surfaced by Catalog Explorer.
keyPoints: Predict what a user with only schema-level privileges sees when browsing a table in Catalog Explorer
Explain how a privilege granted on a catalog differs from one granted directly on a table
Read a lineage graph and identify which notebook wrote to a given table
Match each Catalog Explorer tab to the question it answers
outlines.teachingObjective: Assess interpretation of Unity Catalog metadata, permissions, and lineage in the UI.

outlines.title: Worked Problems: Locating, Qualifying, and Querying Objects
outlines.description: Three fully worked problems that practice translating a plain-English request into correct namespace exploration and query syntax, each with an analysis of why the approach works.
keyPoints: Problem 1: A colleague says the table lives in the sales schema of the main catalog. Write the query that returns the five most recent orders, with a worked solution using main.sales.orders and ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT 5

Problem 2: You inherit an unfamiliar workspace. Write the exact statement sequence to discover every catalog, then every schema in the target catalog, then every table in the target schema, with the worked SHOW CATALOGS / SHOW SCHEMAS IN / SHOW TABLES IN solution

Problem 3: A user must see a table in Catalog Explorer but must not be able to read its rows. Specify the privilege levels needed, with the worked answer distinguishing USE on catalog and schema from SELECT on the table
Analysis: Why grants cascade down the catalog, schema, table hierarchy, and why granting on every table individually is an anti-pattern that breaks as schemas grow
Common pitfall: assuming a two-part name resolves in another workspace, where the default catalog or schema differs
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to apply Unity Catalog naming, exploration, and privilege rules to concrete tasks.

outlines.title: SQL Warehouse vs. All-Purpose Compute
outlines.description: A side-by-side comparison of the two compute surfaces a data engineer chooses between, framed around the decision of which to use for SQL work.
keyPoints: [Table] Comparison dimensions: interface, supported languages, workload shape, concurrency, startup behavior, cost model, and fit with dashboards and alerts
SQL warehouse: SQL-only, optimized for BI and dashboards, supports serverless, pro, and classic types, integrates directly with the SQL editor and query scheduling
All-purpose compute: notebook-driven, multi-language, suited to Spark ETL, data exploration, and machine learning workloads
Key distinction: notebooks can contain SQL, but the SQL editor, alerts, and dashboards are delivered by a SQL warehouse
Exam trap: treating a SQL warehouse as a general-purpose cluster, or expecting an all-purpose cluster to back a dashboard
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to choose the correct compute surface for a given SQL or notebook task.

outlines.title: Lesson Checkpoint: Databricks SQL and Unity Catalog Navigation
outlines.description: A cumulative end-of-lesson assessment covering the SQL editor, SQL warehouse configuration, the Unity Catalog namespace model, and Catalog Explorer.
keyPoints: Trace a query from the editor through the warehouse and Unity Catalog to the Delta table
Select the appropriate warehouse type and sizing rationale for a stated scenario
Resolve and correct fully qualified object names under a given session context
Interpret Catalog Explorer permissions and lineage information to answer a governance question
Explain in writing why catalog, schema, and table are three distinct privilege levels
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify mastery of both lesson objectives before progressing to Git folders and the developer workflow.

lessons.title: Git Folders and the Developer Workflow
objectives: Students will be able to connect a remote Git repository and manage branches inside a Databricks workspace.
Students will be able to explain how version control fits into collaborative data engineering on Databricks.

outlines.title: Lesson Orientation: Git Folders and the Developer Workflow
outlines.description: Frame the lesson: why version control belongs inside the Databricks workspace and what the Databricks Certified Data Engineer Associate exam expects about a data engineer's developer workflow.
keyPoints: Lesson objectives: connect a remote Git repository and manage branches inside a Databricks workspace
Explain how version control fits into collaborative data engineering on Databricks
Roadmap: Git folder concepts → connecting a repository → branches → the pull-commit-push loop → team collaboration
Exam framing: the Data Engineer Associate exam tests Git folder operations and workspace-level Git configuration
Prerequisite recall: workspace navigation, notebooks, and compute from the earlier lessons in this unit
outlines.teachingObjective: Situate Git-based version control inside the Databricks developer workflow and state the lesson objectives

outlines.title: What Is a Databricks Git Folder?
outlines.description: Define a Git folder (formerly Databricks Repos) as a workspace object that syncs a remote Git repository, and contrast it with a plain workspace folder.
keyPoints: A Git folder syncs a remote Git repository (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps) with a folder in the Databricks workspace
Enablement prerequisites: a workspace admin enables Git integration, and each user links a Git personal access token (PAT) or OAuth credential
Terminology change: 'Repos' were renamed 'Git folders' on the platform — exam items may use either term
Supported content: notebooks (.py, .sql, .scala, .r) plus other repository files such as .md, .yaml, and .json
Exam trap: a Git folder is not the same object as a workspace folder — workspace folders are not version-controlled
outlines.teachingObjective: Identify what a Databricks Git folder is and what it is not

mediaGenerations.prompt: Clean technical diagram: on the left a cloud Git repository icon labelled 'Remote Git Repository (GitHub / GitLab / Azure DevOps)', on the right a Databricks workspace panel labelled 'Workspace', connected by a two-way arrow labelled 'clone / pull / commit & push'. Inside the workspace panel a folder icon labelled 'Git folder' contains small notebook file icons and a branch label 'main'. Flat infographic style, muted blue and grey palette, all labels in English, no people.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Git Folder Fundamentals
outlines.description: Check that students can distinguish Git folders from workspace folders and recall the prerequisites for connecting a repository.
keyPoints: Distinguish a Git folder from a workspace folder and from a notebook
Identify the two enablement prerequisites: workspace Git integration and a user Git credential
Recognize the Git providers Databricks supports (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps)
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify understanding of Git folder concepts and connection prerequisites

outlines.title: Connecting a Remote Git Repository
outlines.description: Walk through creating a Git folder step by step, from adding a Git credential to choosing a repository, branch, and sparse checkout path.
keyPoints: Step 1 — add a Git credential (PAT or OAuth) for your provider under your user settings
Step 2 — from the workspace, use Create → Git folder, paste the repository URL, and select the branch to check out
Optional — sparse checkout limits the checkout to selected directories, which keeps large monorepos manageable
Exam trap: most creation failures are credential or permission problems, not problems with the repository itself
Git folder permissions (CAN READ / CAN RUN / CAN EDIT / CAN MANAGE) are separate from workspace object permissions
outlines.teachingObjective: Connect a remote Git repository into a Databricks workspace using the correct sequence and settings

outlines.title: Interactive: The Sync Cycle Between Remote Repository and Git Folder
outlines.description: Students walk an interactive flowchart of the sync cycle and see what each Databricks action does to the remote repository and the local checkout.
keyPoints: Clone: the selected branch is pulled into the workspace Git folder
Pull: fetch and merge remote changes into the local checkout
Commit & Push: stage changes, write a commit message, and publish commits to the remote branch
See what happens when a teammate pushes while you still have uncommitted local edits
Click any stage to reveal both the Databricks UI action and the equivalent Git command
outlines.teachingObjective: Trace the clone/pull/edit/commit/push cycle and predict the state of the remote repository after each action

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Connecting Repositories and Syncing Changes
outlines.description: Test the sync cycle and the failure modes that appear when local and remote histories diverge.
keyPoints: Order the pull → edit → commit & push sequence correctly
Diagnose a rejected push caused by remote changes made since the last pull
State what a pull does to the working checkout versus what a commit does to the remote
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply the sync cycle and diagnose divergence between local and remote histories

outlines.title: Branches Inside a Databricks Git Folder
outlines.description: Explain how branches are created, switched, and reconciled from within the Databricks Git folder UI, and how branch state interacts with notebooks and jobs.
keyPoints: Create a branch from the Git folder's branch control and switch branches without leaving the workspace
Databricks requires a clean working tree before a branch switch — commit, discard, or resolve conflicting changes first
Merge a finished branch locally or open a pull request in the Git provider when branch policies require review
Revert a commit and discard changes are different operations; exam items test which one preserves shared history
Jobs can run against a Git reference (branch, tag, or commit), which is how versioned code reaches production
outlines.teachingObjective: Manage branches inside a Databricks workspace and relate branch state to notebooks and jobs

outlines.title: Interactive: Branch and Merge Sandbox
outlines.description: Students manipulate a branch-and-merge model to see how divergent commits arise, where the merge base sits, and when Databricks reports a conflict.
keyPoints: Simulate two teammates editing the same notebook on separate branches
Adjust commits on each branch and watch the merge base move
Force overlapping edits to trigger a conflict and see where it is detected
Compare a feature-branch strategy against committing directly to main and observe the conflict surface
outlines.teachingObjective: Predict conflicts and merge outcomes from branch state and commit history

widgetOutline.concept: Git branch, commit, and merge workflow inside a Databricks Git folder

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Branches and the Developer Workflow
outlines.description: Check branch operations: switching, merging, reverting, and discarding, and the conflict conditions around each.
keyPoints: Predict Databricks behaviour when you switch branches with uncommitted changes
Choose the correct operation to undo a bad commit versus to throw away local edits
Explain the conditions under which Databricks reports a merge conflict
outlines.teachingObjective: Select the correct branch operation for a given situation and anticipate conflicts

outlines.title: Git Folder vs. Workspace Folder vs. Local Git Client
outlines.description: Compare the three places a data engineer can keep code in a Databricks-centric workflow across the decision-relevant dimensions.
keyPoints: [Table] Git folder / workspace folder / local Git client × version control, native Databricks execution, permissions model, CI/CD suitability
Choose a Git folder for shared, versioned code that notebooks and jobs must run against a branch, tag, or commit
A plain workspace folder is sufficient for scratch exploration and non-versioned work, but provides no history or backup
A local Git client fits developers who edit outside Databricks and only sync code in when it needs to run on the platform
Exam trap: assuming workspace folders are versioned or recoverable — they are not
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify where code should live based on versioning, execution, and collaboration requirements

outlines.title: Exercise: Recover a Diverged Feature Branch
outlines.description: A fully worked problem: the learner pushes work on a feature branch, a teammate merges to main, the next pull conflicts, and the branch must be recovered with a clean history.
keyPoints: Statement: your feature branch and the remote main branch have both advanced; switching or pulling now surfaces a conflict on a shared notebook
Worked solution: pull → inspect the conflicting notebook in the diff view → resolve each conflicting cell → commit & push → open a pull request
Analysis: why Databricks requires a clean working tree before branch changes, and why the merge base determines which cells conflict
Common pitfall: discarding changes instead of resolving them, which silently destroys a teammate's edits
Variant: undo an accidental commit with revert versus rewriting history, and explain the consequence for everyone else on the branch
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply conflict-resolution and history-recovery procedures to a diverged branch

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Version Control in Collaborative Data Engineering
outlines.description: Assessment of the lesson's second objective: explain how version control fits into collaborative data engineering on Databricks, plus targeted Git folder operation questions.
keyPoints: Explain how Git folders let a data engineering team share reviewed, versioned code inside the workspace
Short answer: describe the path from feature branch to reviewed merge, including where review happens
Diagnose the most likely cause of a failure when creating a Git folder from a private repository
Distinguish commit, push, pull, merge, and revert in a Databricks Git folder
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain the role of version control in collaborative data engineering and apply Git folder operations

outlines.title: Lesson Wrap-Up: Version Control in the Databricks Workflow
outlines.description: Consolidate the lesson and connect it forward to the rest of the Databricks Data Engineer Associate course.
keyPoints: Key takeaways: connect a Git credential → create a Git folder → branch, commit, and push like any Git workflow, but inside the workspace
Version control is what makes notebooks shared, reviewable, and production-safe for a data engineering team
Exam-ready checklist: know the rename from Repos to Git folders, the prerequisites, and the clean-tree rule before branch switches

outlines.title: Delta Lake Architecture at a Glance
outlines.description: Frame Delta Lake as a storage-layer protocol that turns untrusted Parquet files in cloud object storage into a reliable, transactional table, and preview the lesson's focus on the transaction log.
keyPoints: Delta Lake is an open table format plus a transaction protocol layered on top of Parquet data files in cloud object storage [source 6]
Three components: Parquet data files, the _delta_log transaction log, and the metadata/protocol actions that bind them together
Storage and compute are decoupled — Spark, Databricks SQL, and other engines read the same table state from the same files
Exam focus: Delta Lake is the storage layer; Databricks is the platform that implements and manages it
[Chart] Stack diagram: cloud object storage (bottom) → Delta protocol and transaction log (middle) → compute engines (top)
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe how Delta Lake layers ACID guarantees over cloud object storage.

outlines.title: Delivering ACID on Top of Object Storage
outlines.description: Map each ACID property to the concrete Delta Lake mechanism that provides it, and explain what cloud object storage alone cannot guarantee.
keyPoints: Object stores provide cheap, durable, virtually unlimited storage but no multi-file transactions, no schema enforcement, and historically weak consistency on listings [source p.235]
Atomicity: each commit is one JSON file written all-or-nothing under a monotonically increasing version number
Isolation and consistency: readers see a consistent snapshot defined by the log, never a half-written table
Durability: both Parquet data files and log entries live in replicated, durable object storage

[Table] Map each ACID letter to its Delta mechanism: Atomicity → single JSON commit file; Consistency → log-defined snapshot and schema enforcement; Isolation → optimistic concurrency control; Durability → replicated object storage

outlines.title: Anatomy of the _delta_log Directory
outlines.description: Walk through the physical layout of the transaction log: numbered JSON commit files, atomic actions, and periodic Parquet checkpoints.
keyPoints: Commit files are named by zero-padded version: 00000000000000000000.json, 00000000000000000001.json, and so on
Each commit contains atomic actions — add, remove, metadata, protocol, and commitInfo — recorded as newline-delimited JSON [source 5]
Checkpoint files (for example 00000000000000000010.checkpoint.parquet) are written periodically so readers do not replay the entire log; _last_checkpoint points at the newest one
Practical inspection: list the _delta_log directory, read a commit file, and compare with DESCRIBE HISTORY and DESCRIBE DETAIL output
[Video] Animated write: a transaction appends a single JSON commit and atomically makes newly written Parquet files visible to readers

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Reconstructing Table State from the Log
outlines.description: A fully worked problem in which learners derive the active file set and row count of a Delta table at a given version by applying the commit actions in order.
keyPoints: Problem statement: given the actions in commits 0 through 4 of a table, determine the set of active Parquet files and the total row count at version 4

Given data: version 0 → add file A (1,000 rows) and file B (1,000 rows); version 1 → add file C (500 rows); version 2 → remove file A; version 3 → add file D (500 rows); version 4 → metadata update only

Worked solution: start from version 0, apply each commit in ascending order, drop any file listed in a remove action, then sum the row counts of the surviving files — active files are B, C and D, giving 2,000 rows
Analysis: remove actions only unregister a file from the log; the Parquet file physically remains until VACUUM, which is why log state and storage state differ
Common pitfalls: applying commits out of order, ignoring remove actions, or assuming a metadata-only commit changes the data

outlines.title: The Log as the Source of Truth: Concurrency and Isolation
outlines.description: Explain how readers obtain a snapshot from the log and how writers use optimistic concurrency control to commit safely without locking data files.
keyPoints: Readers never scan the directory for files — they read the log to obtain a snapshot, then open only the Parquet files that snapshot references
Writers use optimistic concurrency control: read the current version, attempt a commit at version N+1, and retry if another writer won the race [source 3]
Serializable isolation means concurrent transactions produce the same result as some serial ordering of those transactions
The monotonically increasing version number is what makes time travel, audit history and reproducible debugging possible
Exam trap: concurrency is coordinated through the log, not through locks on the data files; multiple readers and multiple writers are supported

outlines.title: Tradeoffs: Choosing a Table Format for a Workload
outlines.description: A constrained design decision in which learners weigh three storage options and justify a single recommendation using the transaction-log concepts from this lesson.
keyPoints: Constraint: a nightly batch job appends new events only (no updates or deletes), multiple writers occasionally overlap, and the team wants predictable cost with strong debugging ability
Option A — plain Parquet in object storage: lowest cost and no log overhead, but no ACID, no schema enforcement, no history, and unsafe concurrent writers
Option B — Delta Lake table: ACID commits, schema enforcement, version history, safe concurrent writes, at the cost of a small per-commit log overhead and periodic maintenance
Option C — managed warehouse table: strongest built-in governance and SQL tooling, but higher cost and less openness for non-SQL engines

Recommendation: choose Option B (Delta Lake) — the append-only pattern still needs concurrent-write safety, schema enforcement, and version history for debugging, so the small log overhead is easily justified

outlines.title: External (Unmanaged) Delta Tables
outlines.description: Explains external Delta tables — data at a path you control, metadata in the catalog — and the DROP TABLE behavior that is a recurring exam trap.
keyPoints: Objective: create an external Delta table with an explicit LOCATION and predict what DROP TABLE does

outlines.title: Worked Problems: Table DDL and Metadata Inspection
outlines.description: Two fully worked DDL and metadata problems that mirror the lesson objective of creating tables and inspecting their metadata.
keyPoints: Problem 1: create a managed table transactions(txn_id INT, acct_id INT, amount DECIMAL(10,2), txn_date DATE) partitioned by date, then confirm format, location, and file count

outlines.title: DML on Delta Tables: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
outlines.description: Covers the row-modifying statements and explains each as one atomic commit against the transaction log.
keyPoints: Objective: perform INSERT INTO, INSERT OVERWRITE, UPDATE ... WHERE, and DELETE ... WHERE on a Delta table
Every DML statement is a single atomic commit appended to the _delta_log, so readers always see either the old table or the new table, never a partial write
UPDATE and DELETE use copy-on-write by default: the affected files are rewritten, then the commit swaps the file list that readers resolve
DELETE FROM t with no predicate removes every row but keeps the table, its schema, and its history — a cheap reset compared to dropping the table
Exam trap: INSERT OVERWRITE replaces the entire table's contents while INSERT INTO appends; also, a DELETE predicate that matches nothing still creates a commit
outlines.teachingObjective: Execute INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE and explain the resulting commit

outlines.title: MERGE: Upserts in One Atomic Statement
outlines.description: Introduces MERGE INTO as the canonical upsert and synchronization pattern for Delta tables.
keyPoints: Objective: write a MERGE INTO statement that upserts and deletes rows based on a join key
Syntax: MERGE INTO target USING source ON target.key = source.key WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (...) VALUES (...)
Add WHEN MATCHED THEN DELETE for delete-on-match, and WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE to make the target an exact mirror of the source
MERGE is the standard slowly-changing-dimension and CDC-upsert pattern and commits atomically — one version, all clauses applied together

Exam trap: duplicate keys in the source raise an error because one target row would be updated multiple times — deduplicate the source first, typically with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC)

outlines.title: Worked Problem: A MERGE-Based Upsert Pipeline
outlines.description: A fully worked incremental-load problem that builds a deduplicated source and merges it into a dimension table, including the analysis of why each step is required.
keyPoints: Problem: an incoming daily extract staged in staging_customers must update changed customers in dim_customer, insert new customers, and remove customers absent from today's snapshot — all without duplicating rows
Solution step 1: deduplicate the source with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) and keep row_number = 1, because a non-unique join key makes MERGE fail

Solution step 2: MERGE INTO dim_customer AS t USING deduped_source AS s ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.name = s.name, t.updated_at = s.updated_at WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (customer_id, name, updated_at) VALUES (s.customer_id, s.name, s.updated_at) WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE

Analysis: the join key must be unique in the source; the ON clause must reference only source columns on the source side; the whole merge is a single commit, so a reader never sees a half-applied update, and the previous table state stays reachable through time travel

Pitfalls to compare against: INSERT OVERWRITE discards history and rewrites the whole table, and delete-then-insert takes two commits so it is not atomic; MERGE also does not by itself give you SCD Type 2 history — that requires explicit effective-date and current-flag columns

outlines.title: Inside the Transaction Log: Versions as Ordered Commits
outlines.description: Explain how version numbers are produced and how a reader reconstructs any historical state of the table.
keyPoints: Each successful write adds one commit file to _delta_log (for example 00000000000000000010.json) and increments the table version by exactly one
The state of a table at any point in time is recreated by starting from the original table and processing only the commits made prior to that point [source 5]
Delta periodically writes Parquet checkpoint files so readers do not have to replay thousands of JSON commits [source 3]
Version numbers are monotonic and never reused; the log is the table — deleting it destroys the table's history as well as its data
DESCRIBE HISTORY returns version, timestamp, operation, operationParameters, and userMetadata for every commit ever applied
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain how the transaction log encodes an ordered version history that makes time travel possible.

outlines.title: Querying History: Time Travel Syntax
outlines.description: Show the exact SQL and PySpark syntax for reading a historical version by number and by timestamp.
keyPoints: SQL by version: SELECT * FROM my_table VERSION AS OF 5; — SQL by timestamp: SELECT * FROM my_table TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-05-01T10:00:00'
PySpark: spark.read.option("versionAsOf", 5).table("my_table") or spark.read.option("timestampAsOf", "2024-05-01").table("my_table")
Use DESCRIBE HISTORY my_table first to discover the version or timestamp you actually need
Exam trap: TIMESTAMP AS OF resolves to the latest version committed at or before that timestamp, not the version nearest in time [source 2]
Time travel is strictly read-only — querying an old version never changes the current table
outlines.teachingObjective: Query a historical table version by version number and by timestamp.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Auditing a Table with Time Travel
outlines.description: A fully worked scenario in which a bad load must be isolated and the table rolled back, with the reasoning behind each step.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a nightly job appended 40,000 duplicate rows into delta.`/mnt/raw/events`; you must prove which version is clean, quantify the damage, and recover the table
Step 1 — inspect history: DESCRIBE HISTORY /mnt/raw/events; the suspect commit shows operation = 'WRITE', operationParameters.mode = 'Append', and the offending userMetadata
Step 2 — quantify: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events VERSION AS OF 12) AS good_rows, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events) AS bad_rows;
Step 3 — roll back: RESTORE TABLE events TO VERSION AS OF 12; then re-run the corrected pipeline

Analysis: this works because the log lets any version be reconstructed from immutable commits; common pitfalls are running RESTORE before DESCRIBE HISTORY (wrong target version), forgetting that VACUUM may have deleted the required data files, and assuming RESTORE erases the bad commit (it does not — it adds a new one)
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply time travel to audit and recover a table, explaining why each step works.

outlines.title: RESTORE TABLE: Rolling Back to a Prior Version
outlines.description: Explain restore mechanics, its interaction with the log, and the operational limits that make it fail.
keyPoints: Syntax: RESTORE TABLE my_table TO VERSION AS OF 5; or RESTORE TABLE my_table TO TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-05-01T10:00:00'
RESTORE does not delete history — it creates a new commit whose resulting state equals the old version, so version numbers keep increasing
Because a restore is itself a commit, the restore operation is time-travellable: you can query the state that existed just before the restore
Standard recovery pattern: bad write → find the last good version with DESCRIBE HISTORY → RESTORE → re-run the corrected pipeline
Limits: RESTORE fails if the required data files were removed by VACUUM (default retention is 7 days) and requires MODIFY permission on the table
outlines.teachingObjective: Restore a table to a prior version and describe the caveats that govern success.

outlines.title: ACID on Object Storage: What Delta Lake Guarantees
outlines.description: Map each ACID property onto the concrete Delta Lake mechanism that delivers it on top of cloud object storage.
keyPoints: Atomicity: a commit either fully applies or not at all, so readers never observe a partially written set of Parquet files
Consistency: readers always see a valid table state produced by an ordered sequence of commits, with schema and constraint enforcement applied
Isolation: concurrent writers are serialized through optimistic concurrency control on the log, and each reader sees a consistent snapshot of the table [source 3]
Durability: once the commit is written to the durable log store, the change survives failures of compute clusters

Delta achieves this on object storage by treating the log directory as the single source of truth and requiring mutual exclusion on log writes; readers use snapshot isolation while writes are serialized at a serializable level
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain how Delta Lake delivers ACID guarantees on top of object storage.

outlines.title: Concurrency Control: Optimistic vs Pessimistic in Delta Lake
outlines.description: A side-by-side comparison of the two concurrency-control strategies so learners can reason about conflict behavior under real workloads.
keyPoints: Compare optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency across mechanism, when conflicts surface, typical exception, and retry strategy
[Table] Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency in Delta Lake: mechanism, conflict detection timing, failure mode, isolation level, retry pattern
Optimistic concurrency control: no locks are held during the transaction; Delta reads the log at commit time and aborts the write if a conflicting commit appeared since the transaction began
Pessimistic concurrency: Delta takes mutual exclusion on the log store so that conflicting writers are serialized rather than detected after the fact

Exam framing: both approaches yield the same isolation guarantee (serializable writes, snapshot reads) — the decision-relevant difference is whether a conflict is avoided up front or detected and retried

outlines.title: Lesson Opener: Why Delta Tables Need Maintenance
outlines.description: Frame the problem that maintenance operations solve: repeated writes fragment a Delta table into many small or unhelpful files, which slows every subsequent read.
keyPoints: Given a Delta table with degraded read performance, identify the small-file problem and the stale-file problem as the likely causes.
Every write — INSERT, MERGE, UPDATE, streaming micro-batch — can add new Parquet files; file count grows much faster than data volume.
Many small files impose per-file overhead: directory listing, footer reads, task scheduling, and open/close cost dominate query time.
Stale files left behind by updates and deletes still cost listing, storage, and metadata even though the current table version does not reference them.
[Image] Diagram compares 'Before OPTIMIZE — 12,000 small files' with 'After OPTIMIZE — 240 files' for the same data volume.
Exam framing: maintenance operations change physical file layout and add commits to the transaction log — they do not change the logical table contents.
outlines.teachingObjective: Recognize the symptoms and causes of poor Delta table file layout before choosing a maintenance operation.

outlines.title: OPTIMIZE: Compacting Small Files
outlines.description: Teach the compaction command, its syntax and return metrics, and when it should be run in a pipeline.
keyPoints: Given a table with many small files, run OPTIMIZE to rewrite them into fewer, larger files and verify the result with DESCRIBE DETAIL.
Syntax: OPTIMIZE table_name [WHERE predicate] [ZORDER BY (col1, col2)]; it returns metrics such as numFilesAdded, numFilesRemoved, and bytes.
OPTIMIZE performs bin-packing — it packs files toward a target size (roughly 100 MB to 1 GB; Databricks targets about 256 MB) and does not sort rows.
It is scoped: with a WHERE predicate you compact only a partition or date range, which keeps cost down on large tables.
The operation commits a new version to the transaction log using add and remove file actions, so time travel to earlier versions still works.
Exam trap: OPTIMIZE does not merge or deduplicate rows, and OPTIMIZE on every streaming micro-batch is wasteful — rely on auto compaction or optimized writes instead.
outlines.teachingObjective: Run and interpret OPTIMIZE for file compaction and explain its effect on the transaction log.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Diagnosing Slow Reads on an Ingested Table
outlines.description: Fully-worked diagnostic problem that moves from symptom to evidence to the correct maintenance command.
keyPoints: Statement: a streaming-ingested Delta table takes 90 seconds to run a simple filtered aggregate; DESCRIBE DETAIL reports numFiles = 12,000 and sizeBytes = 180 GB.
[Table] DESCRIBE DETAIL before and after maintenance: numFiles 12,000 to 240, sizeBytes 180 GB to 180 GB, unchanged row count after SELECT COUNT(*).

Worked solution: (1) confirm file count and average file size (180 GB / 12,000 ≈ 15 MB — far below target), (2) run OPTIMIZE with a date-range WHERE clause, (3) re-run DESCRIBE DETAIL and DESCRIBE HISTORY to confirm the new commit, (4) re-measure the query.

Analysis: bin-packing removes per-file overhead (listing, footer reads, task scheduling) which is why the full aggregate speeds up; a highly selective single-partition predicate may gain little because OPTIMIZE does not reorganize rows within files.
Common pitfalls: running OPTIMIZE on every micro-batch, forgetting that OPTIMIZE is not free (it rewrites bytes and incurs compute), and expecting OPTIMIZE to remove duplicates.
outlines.teachingObjective: Diagnose a small-file problem from table metadata and justify an OPTIMIZE strategy.

outlines.title: Z-ORDER BY: Multi-Dimensional Clustering for Data Skipping
outlines.description: Explain how Z-ORDER co-locates related rows so file-level statistics let Delta skip files entirely.
keyPoints: Given a selective filter on a high-cardinality column, choose Z-ORDER columns so Delta can skip files using min/max statistics.
Z-ORDER is multi-dimensional clustering: rows are ordered across several columns so values that co-occur in queries land in the same files.
Syntax: OPTIMIZE events ZORDER BY (event_date, user_id); it is always applied as part of an OPTIMIZE run, never standalone.
Effect: tighter per-file min/max ranges in the file statistics that Delta maintains for skipping — fewer files scanned, less I/O, shorter queries.
Selectivity rule: pick columns used frequently in WHERE filters with high cardinality (for example user_id, device_id, event_ts), not low-cardinality flags.
Limits and traps: keep to about four columns, returns diminish beyond that, and Z-ORDER does not replace partitioning — do not also partition on the same high-cardinality column.
outlines.teachingObjective: Select Z-ORDER columns and predict their effect on data skipping and read performance.

outlines.title: VACUUM and Retention: Cleaning Up Stale Files Safely
outlines.description: Teach how VACUUM removes unreferenced files, why retention exists, and how vacuuming too early breaks time travel.
keyPoints: Given a time-travel requirement, choose a VACUUM retention setting that does not delete files older versions still need.
VACUUM physically deletes data files that are no longer referenced by the current table version and are older than the retention threshold.
Default retention is 7 days (168 hours); VACUUM table RETAIN 168 HOURS is explicit, and VACUUM table DRY RUN lists what would be deleted without deleting.
Retention protects readers: time travel queries, streaming readers on an older snapshot, and concurrent long-running jobs may still read those files — deleting them causes FileNotFound errors.
Going below 7 days requires setting spark.databricks.delta.retentionDurationCheck.enabled=false, which is explicitly unsafe and breaks time travel.
Exam trap: VACUUM is irreversible and does not rewrite the transaction log — it frees storage by deleting files, while older history entries remain in the log but become unreadable.
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply VACUUM with a retention setting that satisfies the table's time-travel and concurrency requirements.

outlines.title: Trade-off Analysis: Maintenance Frequency versus Time Travel Needs
outlines.description: A constrained decision task: choose a maintenance policy for a table that must satisfy a latency SLA while auditors need 30 days of history.
keyPoints: Constraints: nightly ingestion of 500 GB into a Delta table, dashboards must return in under 5 seconds, auditors require 30 days of history, storage cost is a stated concern.
Option A — hourly OPTIMIZE plus Z-ORDER and VACUUM with the default 7-day retention: fastest reads, highest compute cost, breaks the 30-day audit requirement.
Option B — daily OPTIMIZE plus Z-ORDER after ingestion and VACUUM with the default 7-day retention, with audit history served from a separate append-only history table.
Option C — minimal maintenance with 30-day retention and no VACUUM: preserves time travel at the cost of degraded read latency and rising storage.
Pros and cons must be weighed against the SLA, the audit window, and the fact that VACUUM cannot be undone.

Recommended: Option B — maintain the hot table after each ingestion window and keep the extended history in a separate table, because VACUUM deletes files irreversibly and cannot coexist with a 30-day time-travel SLA on the same table.
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a maintenance and retention policy under conflicting performance, cost, and compliance constraints.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Sizing and Scheduling a Maintenance Runbook
outlines.description: Fully-worked quantitative problem that computes target file counts, chooses Z-ORDER columns, and writes the maintenance SQL for a stated SLA.
keyPoints: Statement: an events table is 1.2 TB with 24,000 files (average 50 MB), partitioned by event_date, queried with filters on user_id and event_date; the team needs 30 days of time travel and faster selective reads.
Step 1 — size the compaction: at a 256 MB target, 1.2 TB / 256 MB ≈ 4,900 files, so OPTIMIZE should cut file count by roughly 5x, reducing per-file overhead proportionally.

Step 2 — choose clustering: OPTIMIZE events WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS ZORDER BY (user_id), keeping high-cardinality user_id for data skipping and event_date for range pruning.
Step 3 — set retention safely: VACUUM events RETAIN 720 HOURS (30 days) to match the time-travel SLA; validate first with VACUUM events RETAIN 720 HOURS DRY RUN.
Step 4 — schedule: run compaction after each ingestion window on recent partitions, and run VACUUM on a separate, less frequent schedule.

Analysis and pitfalls: over-partitioning plus Z-ORDER on the same column duplicates effort; running OPTIMIZE too often wastes compute; using the default 7-day retention silently breaks the 30-day audit requirement.
outlines.teachingObjective: Compute and justify a concrete OPTIMIZE, Z-ORDER, and VACUUM plan for an exam-style scenario.

outlines.title: Summary: Maintenance Roles, Order of Operations, and Exam Traps
outlines.description: Consolidate the lesson into a decision summary and pre-empt the most common certification distractor patterns.
keyPoints: Three roles to keep straight: OPTIMIZE compacts files, Z-ORDER BY lays data out for data skipping, VACUUM deletes stale files.
Order of operations after ingestion: OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (...) on recent partitions, then VACUUM on its own less frequent schedule with a safe retention window.
Exam trap 1: OPTIMIZE does not sort, merge, or deduplicate rows and does not change query results.
Exam trap 2: Z-ORDER is bounded (about four columns), has diminishing returns, and never replaces partitioning.
Exam trap 3: VACUUM is irreversible, defaults to 7 days, and deleting files still needed by time travel or concurrent readers causes FileNotFound failures.
Unit link: layout operations commit add/remove file actions to the transaction log, so versioning and time travel remain consistent until VACUUM removes the underlying files.
outlines.teachingObjective: Consolidate maintenance decision rules and avoid the certification exam's most common traps.
