units.title: Querying Data with Spark SQL and PySpark
objectives: Students will be able to query and transform data using both Spark SQL and the PySpark DataFrame API.
Students will be able to choose efficient query patterns for common analytical problems.

lessons.title: Spark SQL and DataFrame Fundamentals
objectives: Students will be able to read data into a DataFrame and inspect its schema.
Students will be able to filter, select, and derive columns using SQL and DataFrame operations.

outlines.title: Prior-Knowledge Check: SQL and DataFrame Vocabulary
outlines.description: Diagnostic quiz at the start of the lesson to surface gaps in prerequisite SQL and DataFrame vocabulary; every item is worded the way the certification exam words it.
keyPoints: Recall the semantics of SELECT, FROM, and WHERE and how each maps to a DataFrame operation.
Distinguish a transformation from an action in a distributed data processing context.
Identify what a DataFrame schema describes (column names, data types, nullability).
Quiz: 3 single-choice items at easy difficulty, used diagnostically rather than for a grade.
outlines.teachingObjective: Surface prerequisite gaps before introducing Spark SQL and DataFrame operations.

outlines.title: Spark SQL, DataFrames, and the Databricks Execution Model
outlines.description: Establish the mental model for the whole unit: what a DataFrame is, where the SparkSession comes from, and why SQL and PySpark are two syntaxes over one engine.
keyPoints: SparkSession is the single entry point to Spark; a Databricks notebook pre-creates it as the variable `spark`, and everything (spark.read, spark.sql, spark.table) hangs off it.
A DataFrame is an immutable, lazily evaluated, distributed table with a named schema — transformations describe work, actions trigger it.
Spark SQL and the PySpark DataFrame API both compile to the same Catalyst-optimized plan, so either path returns the same result.
The driver builds the logical plan, Catalyst rewrites it, and executors run tasks over partitions; display() renders results in the notebook while collect() drags every row back to the driver.
[Image gen_img_1] Execution-flow diagram: notebook → SparkSession → logical plan → Catalyst optimizer → physical plan → tasks on executor nodes.
outlines.teachingObjective: Understand what a DataFrame is and how Spark SQL and the DataFrame API relate to one execution engine.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A clean flat infographic showing the Apache Spark execution flow inside a Databricks notebook: a notebook page containing a SparkSession object, an arrow into a 'Logical Plan' box, then a 'Catalyst Optimizer' box, then a 'Physical Plan' box, then arrows fanning out to four executor worker nodes each holding partition blocks of a table. Minimal technical diagram style, dark blue and teal palette, thin lines, no people, all labels and annotations in English.

outlines.title: Reading Data into a DataFrame and Inspecting the Schema
outlines.description: Teach the read-then-inspect habit: how to load files and tables into a DataFrame and how to verify the schema before writing any transformation.
keyPoints: File reads: spark.read.format('csv'|'json'|'parquet').option('header', True).schema(...).load(path) — always chain the reader, never call it twice.
Table reads: spark.table('catalog.schema.table') returns a Delta table with its schema and statistics already known, so no inference is needed.
Inspect before you transform: printSchema(), dtypes, columns, count(), describe()/summary(), and display(df.limit(10)).

Exam trap: for CSV, Spark does not read the header or infer types unless you set option('header', True) and inferSchema=True; inferSchema also costs an extra pass over the data, so a declared schema is preferred.

[Table] Inspection method → what it returns → when to use it: printSchema (tree of names/types), dtypes (list of name-type pairs), describe (count/mean/min/max per numeric column), display (rendered rows), count (row count, triggers a job).
outlines.teachingObjective: Read data into a DataFrame and inspect its schema.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Reading Data and Schema Inspection
outlines.description: Mid-lesson checkpoint verifying that learners can choose the right read pattern and read a schema correctly before moving on to transformations.
keyPoints: Given a requirement, select the correct reader options for CSV, JSON, and Parquet sources.
Interpret the output of printSchema() and dtypes, including nested struct and array types.
Distinguish spark.table(...) from spark.read.table(...) and know when each is required.
Quiz: 3 items at medium difficulty mixing single- and multiple-choice, with distractors that mirror real exam traps such as inferSchema defaults and header handling.
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm schema-reading and data-loading fluency before introducing transformations.

outlines.title: Key Terms: Spark SQL and DataFrame Fundamentals
outlines.description: Reference glossary of the unit's core vocabulary, defined precisely enough to answer definition-style exam items.
keyPoints: SparkSession — the single entry point to Spark; in a Databricks notebook it is pre-created as the variable `spark` and manages configuration, catalog access, and DataFrame creation.
DataFrame — an immutable, lazily evaluated, distributed collection of rows with a named schema; every transformation returns a NEW DataFrame rather than mutating the original.
Transformation vs. action — transformations (select, filter, withColumn, groupBy, orderBy) are lazy and only describe a plan; actions (show, display, count, collect, write) trigger execution.
Lazy evaluation — Spark accumulates transformations into a logical plan and executes nothing until an action is called, which is precisely what allows Catalyst to optimize the whole plan at once.
Schema — the column names, data types, and nullability metadata of a DataFrame; printSchema() renders it as a tree and dtypes returns (name, type) pairs.

Delta table — a table whose data files plus a transaction log live in cloud object storage; read it with spark.table('catalog.schema.table') and the schema, statistics, and history come along with it.
Temporary view — a session-scoped SQL alias over a DataFrame created with df.createOrReplaceTempView('name'), letting the same data be queried with spark.sql('SELECT ... FROM name').
outlines.teachingObjective: Define the unit's core vocabulary precisely for exam recall.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Read, Inspect, Filter, and Select
outlines.description: A fully worked end-to-end problem that combines reading with an explicit schema, inspecting it, then filtering and selecting columns — in both PySpark and SQL.
keyPoints: Problem: from the raw file /databricks-datasets/retail/orders.csv (columns order_id, customer_id, order_ts, amount, status) return order_id, customer_id, and amount for only 'completed' orders placed in 2024 with amount >= 100, and state the resulting schema.

Step 1 — read with a declared schema: orders = (spark.read.option('header', True).schema('order_id STRING, customer_id STRING, order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DOUBLE, status STRING').csv(path)); then verify with orders.printSchema() and orders.count().

Step 2 — filter and select with the DataFrame API: orders.filter((col('status') == 'completed') & (year(col('order_ts')) == 2024) & (col('amount') >= 100)).select('order_id', 'customer_id', 'amount').

Step 3 — the SQL equivalent: SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' AND YEAR(order_ts) = 2024 AND amount >= 100; call explain() on both results to confirm they produce the same plan.

Analysis and pitfalls: an explicit schema avoids the extra scan that inferSchema performs and prevents silent type mismatches; filter is an alias of where; use & and | (not Python's `and`/`or`) and parenthesize each condition; and because DataFrames are immutable you must capture the returned DataFrame or nothing changes. A NULL in amount or status makes the whole predicate NULL, so those rows disappear — use isNull()/na.fill() deliberately.
outlines.teachingObjective: Read data into a DataFrame, inspect its schema, and filter and select columns with both APIs.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Selecting, Filtering, and Deriving Columns
outlines.description: Checkpoint quiz on the three core column/row operations just practised, phrased as exam objectives.
keyPoints: Select columns and rename them with alias, drop, and selectExpr.
Filter rows with compound predicates, including NULL-safe comparisons.
Derive a new column from existing columns and cast it to an explicit type.

Quiz: 3 items at medium difficulty, mixing single-choice, multiple-choice, and one short-answer item that asks the learner to write a one-line filter predicate, with distractors modelled on real exam traps such as `and` versus `&` and comparison against NULL.
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify that learners can select, filter, and derive columns in either API.

outlines.title: Playground: SQL and DataFrame Side by Side
outlines.description: A hands-on coding playground where learners run the same transformation twice — once in PySpark and once in Spark SQL — over a small shared DataFrame and watch the schema change after each run.
keyPoints: An editable PySpark cell is wired to a small in-memory orders DataFrame; running it renders the result as a table.
A mirrored SQL cell queries the same DataFrame registered as a temporary view, so learners can compare row counts and schemas immediately.
Guided missions: select two columns; filter to a single status; derive amount_with_tax = amount * 1.08; rename a column; drop a column; cast amount to decimal(10,2).
A live schema panel shows the output schema after every run, making it visible which operations preserve types and which introduce new ones.
A hint button reveals the SQL-to-DataFrame translation for the current mission, reinforcing that the two syntaxes are interchangeable.
outlines.teachingObjective: Build fluency by executing equivalent SQL and DataFrame transformations on the same data.

outlines.title: Selecting, Filtering, and Deriving Columns
outlines.description: Consolidate the core transformation vocabulary of the lesson into one reference slide with the DataFrame API on one side and the SQL mirror on the other.
keyPoints: Column selection and reshaping: df.select('a','b'), df.select(col('a'), col('b').alias('c')), df.drop('x'), and df.selectExpr('a', 'amount * 1.08 AS amount_with_tax').
Row filtering: df.filter(...) and df.where(...) are identical; combine predicates with & | ~ and wrap each condition in parentheses to control precedence.
Deriving columns: df.withColumn('amount_with_tax', col('amount') * lit(1.08)), explicit casts with col('amount').cast('decimal(10,2)'), and conditional values with when(...).otherwise(...).
Every one of these returns a NEW DataFrame — DataFrames are immutable, so reassign (df = df.withColumn(...)) or chain the calls.
[Image gen_img_2] Transformation-chain diagram: source DataFrame → filter → select → withColumn → new DataFrame, with the original DataFrame shown unchanged beneath the chain; caption in English.
outlines.teachingObjective: Filter, select, and derive columns using SQL and DataFrame operations.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A clean flat technical diagram of a PySpark transformation chain. On the left, a table labeled 'Source DataFrame' with columns order_id, amount, status. Arrows flow right through labeled boxes: 'filter(status = completed)', 'select(order_id, amount)', 'withColumn(amount_with_tax)'. On the right, a new table labeled 'New DataFrame' with the added column. Below the chain, the original Source DataFrame is drawn unchanged with the caption 'the original is never modified'. Minimal infographic style, blue and grey palette, no people, all labels and text in English.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Derived Columns, Casting, and Conditionals
outlines.description: Harder checkpoint quiz targeting the operations where exam candidates most often slip: withColumn versus select, casts, and CASE-style logic.
keyPoints: Choose the correct expression to add or replace a column with withColumn, selectExpr, or select.
Predict the result of casting between types, including what happens when a cast fails.
Apply conditional logic with when/otherwise and reason about the order of the branches.

Quiz: 3 hard items mixing single-choice, multiple-choice, and short-answer, with distractors that mirror real exam traps such as a failed cast silently returning NULL and an otherwise() branch that never executes.
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify precise understanding of derived columns, casts, and conditional expressions.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Derive a Revenue Report with when/otherwise and Casts
outlines.description: A fully worked problem that builds a small reporting dataset by deriving several columns at once, then proves the SQL and DataFrame versions are equivalent.
keyPoints: Problem: from the raw orders DataFrame produce order_id, order_date (DATE), amount as DECIMAL(10,2), amount_with_tax (amount * 1.08 as DECIMAL(10,2)), and revenue_band in {high, medium, low} using thresholds >= 1000 and >= 100, sorted by amount descending.

Solution (DataFrame API): orders.select(col('order_id'), to_date('order_ts').alias('order_date'), col('amount').cast('decimal(10,2)').alias('amount'), (col('amount') * 1.08).cast('decimal(10,2)').alias('amount_with_tax'), when(col('amount') >= 1000, 'high').when(col('amount') >= 100, 'medium').otherwise('low').alias('revenue_band')).orderBy(col('amount').desc()).

Solution (SQL): the identical SELECT with CAST(... AS DECIMAL(10,2)), CASE WHEN amount >= 1000 THEN 'high' WHEN amount >= 100 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'low' END, and ORDER BY amount DESC; compare df.explain() output for both to confirm one plan.

Analysis: withColumn is a projection — it appends or replaces a column by name and returns a new DataFrame; chaining many withColumn calls on a wide table inflates the logical plan, so deriving five columns in a single select/selectExpr is usually the cleaner and more optimizer-friendly choice.

Common pitfalls: CASE branches are evaluated top-down so a broad first condition swallows later ones; casting a non-numeric string yields NULL rather than raising an error, so validate before casting; and orderBy is still lazy — nothing is sorted until an action such as display() or write() runs.
outlines.teachingObjective: Derive multiple columns with casts and conditional logic and prove SQL/DataFrame equivalence.

outlines.title: Spark SQL vs. PySpark DataFrame API
outlines.description: A side-by-side comparison that gives learners a decision rule for choosing between the two interchangeable interfaces, framed the way the exam frames it.
keyPoints: [Table] Side-by-side comparison of Spark SQL and the PySpark DataFrame API across: readability for set-based logic, parameterization and dynamic columns, testability and reuse, where the code physically lives, and typical exam framing.
Both compile to the same Catalyst-optimized plan — correctness and performance are equivalent, so the choice is about team, tooling, and maintainability rather than speed.
Choose SQL when the transformation is self-contained and set-based: reporting queries, Databricks SQL dashboards, shared views, and quick ad-hoc exploration.
Choose the DataFrame API when you need parameters, loops over dynamic column names, unit tests, or orchestration inside a Python workflow.

Interoperability is the practical answer: df.createOrReplaceTempView('orders') exposes a DataFrame to SQL, and spark.sql(...) returns a DataFrame you can keep chaining — mix them freely in one pipeline.
outlines.teachingObjective: Choose efficiently between Spark SQL and the DataFrame API for a given transformation.

outlines.title: Lesson Assessment: Spark SQL and DataFrame Fundamentals
outlines.description: Closing assessment covering the full lesson — reading and schema inspection, filtering and selecting, deriving and casting columns, and interface choice.
keyPoints: Read data from files and tables into a DataFrame and describe its schema.
Filter, select, rename, cast, and derive columns using equivalent Spark SQL and DataFrame expressions.
Explain why transformations are lazy and how that enables Catalyst plan optimization.
Select the appropriate interface for a given transformation and justify the choice.

Quiz: 5 hard items spanning single-choice, multiple-choice, and short-answer, with distractors mirroring real exam traps such as inferSchema cost, immutability of DataFrames, NULL comparisons, and failed casts returning NULL.
outlines.teachingObjective: Assess mastery of reading, schema inspection, and filter/select/derive operations in both APIs.

lessons.title: Reading and Writing Data
objectives: Students will be able to read from and write to Delta, Parquet, and CSV sources with explicit options.
Students will be able to control write modes and explain their effect on target tables.

outlines.title: Reading and Writing Data: Lesson Roadmap
outlines.description: Frame the lesson against the exam objective and preview the four decision points: read options, write modes, schema evolution, and format choice.
keyPoints: Exam objective: read from and write to Delta, Parquet, and CSV sources with explicit options
Exam objective: control write modes and explain their effect on target tables
One API, two directions: spark.read (DataFrameReader) and df.write (DataFrameWriter), both driven by .format(), .option(), and .load()/.save()
Default behaviour is the single biggest source of exam distractors: default format is parquet, default write mode is error/errorifexists
Lesson roadmap: explicit read options → write modes → schema evolution → format selection and a worked end-to-end pipeline
outlines.teachingObjective: Understand how this lesson maps to the certification objectives for reading and writing data.

outlines.title: Reading Data with Explicit Options
outlines.description: Teach the explicit read pattern for CSV, Parquet, and Delta, and explain which formats need options and which do not.
keyPoints: General form: spark.read.format("csv"|"parquet"|"delta").option(key, value).load(path); table shortcut spark.read.table("catalog.schema.table")
CSV is the option-hungry format: header defaults to false, sep defaults to comma, and every column is typed as string unless inferSchema or an explicit schema is supplied
inferSchema requires an extra full pass over the data, so production code supplies an explicit DDL schema string to .schema() for speed and deterministic types
Delta and Parquet are self-describing: schema comes from the files (Parquet footer) or the Delta transaction log, so an explicit read schema is optional
Malformed CSV rows are handled by the read option mode PERMISSIVE/DROPMALFORMED/FAILFAST or by capturing rejects in badRecordsPath
outlines.teachingObjective: Read from Delta, Parquet, and CSV sources with explicit options and predictable schemas.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Reading Data and Read Options
outlines.description: Verify that students can pick the correct read pattern and option set for CSV, Parquet, and Delta sources.
keyPoints: Default format and default CSV options (header=false, string-typed columns)
inferSchema cost versus an explicit DDL schema
Correct method chaining for DataFrameReader (format → option → load)
CSV malformed-record handling via read mode and badRecordsPath
Distractor type: options that look like write settings but are being applied to a read
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm correct selection of read formats, options, and schema handling.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Reading a CSV and Landing It as a Delta Table
outlines.description: A fully worked end-to-end read-and-write problem with a concrete statement, solution code, and analysis of the option choices.
keyPoints: Problem statement: /mnt/raw/orders.csv is pipe-delimited with a header row and 40 million rows; land it as a Delta table at /mnt/bronze/orders and replace any previous content

Worked solution (read): schema = "order_id LONG, customer_id LONG, order_ts TIMESTAMP, amount DECIMAL(10,2)"; df = spark.read.format("csv").option("header", True).option("sep", "|").schema(schema).load("/mnt/raw/orders.csv")
Worked solution (write): df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/mnt/bronze/orders")
Analysis: an explicit schema avoids the second full scan that inferSchema causes and prevents amount from being inferred as string or timestamp from being inferred as string
Analysis of pitfalls: omitting option("sep", "|") yields a single column named after the whole line; omitting mode("overwrite") makes the second run fail with the default error/errorifexists mode
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply explicit read options and a chosen write mode to build a reproducible bronze ingestion step.

outlines.title: Write Modes and Their Effect on the Target
outlines.description: Explain each write mode's exact behaviour on an existing target and how Databricks tables differ from raw paths.
keyPoints: Four save modes via df.write.mode(...): error/errorifexists (default), overwrite, append, ignore
overwrite: replaces the data in the target — with Delta the existing data files are removed atomically and replaced, the table itself is not dropped and recreated
append: adds new files to the target without touching existing data; the natural mode for incremental loads and streaming micro-batches
ignore: if the target already exists the write is silently skipped — no error, no data change, which makes failures invisible in production
error/errorifexists: the default — the job throws if the target path or table already exists, which surprises candidates who assume append is the default
mode() also governs df.write.saveAsTable("catalog.schema.table") and DataFrameWriterV2 methods such as createOrReplace, append, and overwrite
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain the effect of each write mode on the target table or path.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Write Modes
outlines.description: Test precise recall of write-mode semantics, including the default mode and its failure behaviour.
keyPoints: What happens on the second run of a job that writes with the default mode to an existing target
Difference between overwrite and ignore when the target already exists
That append never removes or rewrites existing data files
Distractor pattern: modes named for insert semantics but applied to a whole-path write
Write modes applied through write() with mode strings versus DataFrameWriterV2 method calls
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm mastery of write-mode behaviour and defaults.

outlines.title: Lab: Read, Reformat, Write, and Inspect
outlines.description: A hands-on coding widget where students change read options and write modes and immediately see the resulting schema, file listing, and table history.
keyPoints: Choose a source format (CSV with configurable delimiter/header, Parquet, Delta) and observe how the inferred schema changes
Toggle inferSchema versus an explicit DDL schema and compare the schema and the simulated scan cost
Switch the write mode between error, overwrite, append, and ignore and watch the target file listing and row count update
Run a second identical write to reproduce the default-mode failure and then fix it
Inspect the resulting _delta_log entries and table history after each write
outlines.teachingObjective: Build hands-on fluency with read options and write-mode effects.

outlines.title: Schema Evolution: mergeSchema and overwriteSchema
outlines.description: Teach how Databricks handles incoming data whose schema differs from the target, and which option unlocks which behaviour.
keyPoints: Delta enforces schema on write by default: appending a DataFrame with a new column fails rather than silently altering the table
To add new columns on append, set the write option: df.write.option("mergeSchema", "true").mode("append").format("delta").save(path)
To replace the target schema entirely during a full refresh, set: df.write.option("overwriteSchema", "true").mode("overwrite").format("delta").save(path)
overwriteSchema only takes effect with mode overwrite — the classic exam trap pairs it with append, where it is ignored
mergeSchema is additive only (it cannot drop or retype columns), and a full schema overwrite invalidates existing readers and cached plans, so downstream consumers must be checked
outlines.teachingObjective: Control schema evolution during writes with the correct options.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Schema Evolution and Write Options
outlines.description: Assess whether students pair the right schema-evolution option with the right write mode.
keyPoints: mergeSchema with append versus overwriteSchema with overwrite
What happens when overwriteSchema is combined with mode append
Why mergeSchema cannot remove or retype an existing column
Schema enforcement on write by default and the error it produces
Distractor pattern: options that sound interchangeable but control different behaviours
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm correct pairing of schema-evolution options with write modes.

outlines.title: CSV vs Parquet vs Delta: Which Format, When
outlines.description: A side-by-side decision table across the dimensions that actually drive format choice on the exam and in practice.
keyPoints: [Table] Rows = CSV, Parquet, Delta; Columns = schema handling, storage layout, required read/write options, atomicity and ACID support, incremental and streaming support, typical role in the lakehouse
CSV: human-readable text, no embedded schema, needs header/sep/inferSchema, no ACID, best for interchange and small or arriving-from-outside files
Parquet: columnar and self-describing, schema travels with the data, efficient column pruning and predicate pushdown, but no transactions, no time travel, no concurrent-write safety
Delta: Parquet data files plus a _delta_log transaction log, giving ACID writes, schema enforcement and evolution, time travel, and streaming sources and sinks
Decision rule: land raw external files as CSV or JSON into bronze, then convert to Delta for anything that is refined, updated, appended incrementally, or queried concurrently
outlines.teachingObjective: Select the appropriate file format for a given ingestion and serving requirement.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Choosing and Applying a Write Mode for a Daily Refresh
outlines.description: A worked decision-and-code problem about refreshing a partitioned Delta table without duplicating or destroying data.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a partitioned Delta table /mnt/silver/events is partitioned by event_date; each night one day of late-arriving events must be replaced while all other days stay untouched, and the job must be re-runnable
Worked solution (option A): df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").option("replaceWhere", "event_date = '2024-06-01'").save("/mnt/silver/events") — atomically replaces only matching partitions
Worked solution (option B): set spark.conf.set("spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic") and write with mode("overwrite") so only the partitions present in the DataFrame are replaced

Analysis: plain mode("overwrite") with dynamic overwrite off would delete the entire table, and mode("append") would duplicate the day's rows on every re-run — neither satisfies the re-runnability requirement
Analysis of pitfalls: replaceWhere requires the predicate column to be a partition column for prune-based replacement, and the DataFrame must match the predicate or rows outside it can be lost
outlines.teachingObjective: Choose a write mode and options that achieve an idempotent, partition-scoped refresh.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Integrated Reading and Writing Scenarios
outlines.description: Exam-style scenario questions that combine read options, write modes, and schema evolution in one item each.
keyPoints: Scenario: read a pipe-delimited CSV with an explicit schema and append only new rows to an existing Delta table
Scenario: a nightly full refresh where the source added two columns, and the target must reflect them
Scenario: a second run of a job that used the default write mode — predict the failure and the fix
Distractor pattern: plausible option names (mergeSchema, overwriteSchema, ignoreCorruptFiles, header) placed in the wrong direction or the wrong mode
Distractor pattern: mixing read-side mode options (PERMISSIVE, FAILFAST) with write-side modes (append, overwrite)
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply read and write configuration correctly in combined exam-style scenarios.

outlines.title: Summary and Exam Traps
outlines.description: Consolidate the lesson into a short decision checklist and a list of the defaults and mispairings that cost points on the exam.
keyPoints: Read pattern: format → option(s) → load; CSV needs explicit header/sep/schema, Parquet and Delta read their schema from the data itself
Write pattern: df.write.format(...).mode(...).option(...).save(...), with error/errorifexists as the default mode you must override deliberately
Write modes in one line each: overwrite replaces, append adds, ignore no-ops silently, error fails fast
Schema evolution: mergeSchema for additive appends, overwriteSchema for full refreshes — and only with mode overwrite

Top exam traps: assuming append is the default, pairing overwriteSchema with append, confusing read-side mode options with write modes, and picking CSV where Delta is required for updates or concurrency
outlines.teachingObjective: Consolidate read/write patterns and the defaults most likely to be tested.

lessons.title: Aggregations, Joins, and Window Functions
objectives: Students will be able to aggregate and join datasets to answer analytical questions.
Students will be able to apply window functions for ranking, running totals, and deduplication.

outlines.title: Lesson Roadmap: Aggregations, Joins, and Window Functions
outlines.description: Frame the lesson and map the three query patterns — grouped aggregates, multi-table joins, and window functions — onto the exam objectives for querying data on Databricks.
keyPoints: Position in Unit 3 (Querying Data with Spark SQL and PySpark): aggregations → joins → window functions

Exam objective mapping: the Databricks Certified Data Engineer Associate exam assesses foundational data engineering tasks on the Databricks Data + AI Platform, including querying and transforming data
Three skill checkpoints: grouped aggregates, join semantics and join strategies, window functions for ranking, running totals, and deduplication
Teaching pattern for the whole lesson: every analytical question answered twice — once in Spark SQL, once in the PySpark DataFrame API
Prerequisite carried forward: reading data into a DataFrame and inspecting the schema
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to describe the three query patterns covered in this lesson and where they sit in the exam blueprint.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Aggregation Vocabulary and Prior Knowledge
outlines.description: Short diagnostic quiz confirming that students can distinguish aggregation semantics and move between Spark SQL and the DataFrame API before new material is introduced.
keyPoints: Distinguish the return shape of GROUP BY versus an ungrouped aggregate
Compare count(*), count(col), and countDistinct(col) and when each is correct
Recognise the equivalent Spark SQL and PySpark DataFrame API forms of the same query
Exam-style distractor: which query silently drops nulls from a count?
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to recall aggregation vocabulary and translate between Spark SQL and the PySpark DataFrame API.

outlines.title: Aggregating Data: groupBy, agg, and Spark SQL GROUP BY
outlines.description: Teach the aggregation building blocks — grouping keys, aggregate functions, and post-aggregation filtering — in both Spark SQL and the PySpark DataFrame API.
keyPoints: Two equivalent forms of the same query: df.groupBy("region").agg(sum("amount").alias("revenue")) versus SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM sales GROUP BY region
Core aggregate functions: count, sum, avg, min, max, countDistinct, stddev, percentile_approx — and what each one ignores

[Table] Aggregate function reference: function | what it ignores | typical use case (count(*) counts rows; count(col) skips nulls; avg(col) skips nulls; countDistinct handles exact distinct counts but costs a shuffle)
Grouping by multiple keys, filtering with HAVING (not WHERE) after the aggregation, and ordering results by the aggregated alias
Exam trap: an aggregate with no grouping key returns a single row rather than an error, which is often the intended answer
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to write grouped aggregations in both Spark SQL and the PySpark DataFrame API.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Monthly Revenue by Region
outlines.description: A fully worked aggregation problem that filters, groups, aggregates, and sorts a Delta table in both APIs, with analysis of the shuffle and the common mistakes.
keyPoints: Statement: from sales(region, order_date, amount, customer_id), return each region's monthly revenue, order count, and distinct customer count for Q1, ordered by revenue descending

Worked solution (PySpark): df.filter(col('order_date').between('2024-01-01','2024-03-31')).withColumn('month', date_trunc('month', col('order_date'))).groupBy('region','month').agg(sum('amount').alias('revenue'), count('*').alias('orders'), countDistinct('customer_id').alias('customers')).orderBy(desc('revenue'))

Worked solution (Spark SQL): SELECT region, date_trunc('month', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers FROM sales WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-03-31' GROUP BY region, month ORDER BY revenue DESC
Analysis: grouping on keys that are not the partition columns forces a shuffle — filtering before grouping shrinks the shuffled bytes and is the single highest-leverage optimisation here
Common pitfalls: filtering the aggregate with WHERE instead of HAVING, expecting avg() of an integer column to return a decimal, and using count(customer_id) when nulls must also be counted
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to aggregate and filter a Delta table to answer a revenue question in both Spark SQL and PySpark.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Aggregations Under Exam Conditions
outlines.description: Quiz on aggregation correctness and performance, with distractors written to mirror the traps that appear in real Databricks certification items.
keyPoints: Select the query that returns exactly one row per group
Distinguish HAVING from WHERE in an aggregated query
Diagnose an incorrect revenue figure caused by count(col) dropping nulls
Identify the pre-aggregation filter that reduces shuffled data
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to evaluate and correct grouped aggregation queries.

outlines.title: Joining Datasets: Types, Semantics, and Row Counts
outlines.description: Teach join types, join syntax in both APIs, and the join-strategy levers (broadcast versus shuffle) that determine performance on Databricks.
keyPoints: Join types and what they keep: inner, left / right outer, full outer, left semi, left anti, cross
Syntax in both APIs: df.join(other, on='customer_id', how='left') versus SELECT * FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
[Table] Join type vs output rows: inner (matched rows only), left (all left rows, nulls for unmatched right), left semi (left columns only, matched rows), left anti (left rows with no match)
Broadcast join: the small table is replicated to every executor, eliminating the shuffle — Databricks applies it automatically when a side is below spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold
Most common errors: ambiguous column names after the join, join-key type mismatches, duplicate column names, and null join keys that never match
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to choose a join type from the question wording and explain when a broadcast join applies.

outlines.title: Comparison: Which Join Type Returns Which Rows?
outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison of the join types students most often confuse, across row-count, null-handling, and output-column dimensions.
keyPoints: [Table] Inner vs Left vs Left Semi vs Left Anti: rows returned | null handling on the join key | columns in the output | typical use case
Semi and anti joins are filters, not column-adders — a frequent exam distractor that offers semi when the expected output includes right-side columns
Null join keys never match in Spark, so a left join on a nullable key produces unmatched rows rather than a match
Row explosion: joining on a non-unique key multiplies rows — always check key cardinality before joining
Read the question wording: 'customers who ordered' = semi, 'customers who never ordered' = anti, 'including customers with no orders' = left
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to select the join type that produces a specified result set.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Joins and Join Strategies
outlines.description: Quiz on join semantics and join strategy selection, using exam-style distractors around row counts and broadcast thresholds.
keyPoints: Predict the row count produced by a left join versus an inner join on the same inputs
Identify the condition under which a broadcast join is chosen
Spot the row-explosion trap caused by a non-unique join key
Choose between a left semi join and an inner join for a given question
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to reason about join output size and select an appropriate join strategy.

outlines.title: Window Functions: Partition, Order, Frame
outlines.description: Introduce the anatomy of a window function and the three exam-relevant patterns it unlocks: ranking, running totals, and deduplication.
keyPoints: Anatomy: function(...) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... ROWS BETWEEN ...) — a window aggregates without collapsing rows, unlike GROUP BY
Ranking family: row_number (no ties, always unique), rank (gaps after ties), dense_rank (no gaps after ties)
Running total: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
Deduplication pattern: row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY primary_key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1 keeps the latest version of each record
[Chart] Diagram: rows split into partitions, ordered within each partition, with the sliding frame highlighted to show which rows feed each output row
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to read and write a window specification and choose the correct ranking function.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A clean instructional diagram explaining the anatomy of a SQL window function. On the left, a table of rows is split into three horizontal partitions by colour. On the right, the same partitions are shown ordered by a date column, and a sliding window frame is highlighted over three consecutive rows with a bracket. Arrows connect a code label 'OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)' to the highlighted frame. Flat, professional, infographic style with a light background, minimal colour palette of blue, grey, and amber. All text and labels in English.

outlines.title: Interactive: Window Function Playground
outlines.description: A hands-on code playground where students change the window specification and immediately see how ranking, running totals, and deduplication results change.
keyPoints: Run the same SELECT with different PARTITION BY and ORDER BY clauses and compare the output row by row
Swap rank(), dense_rank(), and row_number() on data containing ties and observe the differences
Apply the deduplication pattern (filter row_number = 1) and verify that exactly one row per key survives
Compare a windowed SUM with the same SUM from groupBy to see identical totals but a different number of output rows
Change the frame clause (ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW versus the default) and observe how running totals shift
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to predict the effect of a window specification change on the result set.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Window Functions and Deduplication
outlines.description: Harder quiz testing window-specification reasoning and the deduplication idiom under exam-like conditions.
keyPoints: Predict the value of row_number() when ORDER BY ties occur and no tiebreaker is supplied
Distinguish rank from dense_rank on the same ordered partition
Choose the correct window specification for a per-customer running total
Separate a working deduplication query from variants that keep duplicates
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to evaluate window function queries for correctness and determinism.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Deduplicating a Change Feed
outlines.description: A fully worked window-function problem that keeps the latest record per key and removes deleted records, with analysis of determinism and performance.
keyPoints: Statement: from customers_cdc(customer_id, name, email, updated_at, op), keep the single latest record per customer_id and drop records whose op is 'delete'

Worked solution (Spark SQL): WITH ranked AS (SELECT *, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, op ASC) AS rn FROM customers_cdc) SELECT customer_id, name, email, updated_at FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 AND op <> 'delete'

Worked solution (PySpark): w = Window.partitionBy('customer_id').orderBy(col('updated_at').desc()); df.withColumn('rn', row_number().over(w)).filter((col('rn') == 1) & (col('op') != 'delete')).drop('rn')
Analysis: row_number() is preferred over rank() because ties would otherwise return more than one row per key; adding a deterministic tiebreaker in ORDER BY guarantees stable results across reruns

Common pitfalls: MAX(updated_at) joined back to the source is slower and breaks on duplicate timestamps; partitioning by the wrong column leaves duplicates; filtering on rn before ordering the window gives arbitrary survivors
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to deduplicate a change feed with a window function and justify why row_number() is the safe choice.

outlines.title: Lesson Summary: Query Patterns and Exam Traps
outlines.description: Consolidate the three patterns, the traps that cost marks, and the performance levers students must recall under time pressure.
keyPoints: Three patterns to recall instantly: grouped aggregate, correctly-typed join, windowed rank / running total / deduplication
Exam traps to memorise: count(col) silently skipping nulls, semi versus inner join confusion, default window frames versus an explicit frame, rank versus row_number on ties
Performance levers: filter before grouping, broadcast the small table, project only needed columns, and avoid SELECT * on wide tables
Self-check before moving on: can you write each of the three patterns from memory in both Spark SQL and the PySpark DataFrame API?
Next lesson preview: UDFs, higher-order functions, and efficient query patterns
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to recall the three query patterns and the exam traps associated with each.

lessons.title: UDFs, Higher-Order Functions, and Query Patterns
objectives: Students will be able to use built-in and higher-order functions in preference to Python UDFs.
Students will be able to explain why native Spark functions outperform row-by-row Python UDFs.

outlines.title: Prior-Knowledge Check: Native Functions and Query Vocabulary
outlines.description: Open the lesson with a diagnostic quiz that confirms students can recognise built-in Spark functions and the vocabulary used throughout the UDF and higher-order function material.
keyPoints: Identify which built-in function performs a given column transformation without a UDF
Distinguish DataFrame API expressions from Spark SQL expressions that produce the same result
Recall the vocabulary needed for this lesson: lambda expression, higher-order function, row-by-row evaluation, serialization overhead
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm prerequisite command of built-in function vocabulary before introducing UDFs and higher-order functions.

outlines.title: Lesson Roadmap: UDFs, Higher-Order Functions, and Query Patterns
outlines.description: Orient students to the three-part structure of the lesson and make explicit that the exam consistently rewards native functions over Python UDFs.
keyPoints: Part 1 — Why native Spark functions outperform row-by-row Python UDFs in the Catalyst and Tungsten execution model
Part 2 — Higher-order functions such as transform, filter, exists, and aggregate for arrays and maps
Part 3 — Reusable query patterns: deduplication, top-N per group, pivot, and anti-joins
Builds directly on the previous lesson's aggregation, join, and window function material
Exam signal: questions that describe a working but slow row-by-row solution usually expect a native rewrite
outlines.teachingObjective: Preview the lesson structure and the exam framing for the UDF-versus-native-functions decision.

outlines.title: Why Native Spark Functions Beat Python UDFs
outlines.description: Explain the execution-model reasons behind the performance gap so students can justify — not just remember — the preference for native functions.
keyPoints: Native functions are understood by the Catalyst optimizer and can be folded into whole-stage code generation on the JVM
A Python UDF is an opaque black box: Catalyst cannot inspect it, push predicates through it, or reorder it
Every Python UDF row crosses the JVM-to-Python boundary, paying serialization and process-transfer cost per record
Vectorized (pandas) UDFs reduce that overhead with Arrow batches but still block optimizer-level rewrites
Decision rule: reach for a UDF only when no built-in or higher-order function can express the logic
[Table] Native function vs Python UDF vs pandas UDF across execution location, per-row overhead, and optimizer visibility
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to explain why native Spark functions outperform row-by-row Python UDFs.

mediaGenerations.prompt: Clean technical infographic comparing two Spark execution paths side by side. Left path labelled 'Native Spark Function': a DataFrame flows into a Catalyst optimizer box, then into a single JVM task box with whole-stage code generation. Right path labelled 'Python UDF': a DataFrame flows into a Catalyst optimizer box drawn with a dashed outline suggesting opacity, then a per-row arrow crosses a boundary into a separate Python worker process and back, drawn as many small back-and-forth arrows representing serialization overhead. Flat minimal vector infographic style, muted blue and orange palette, no people, no real logos, all text labels in English.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: UDF Mechanics and Performance Vocabulary
outlines.description: Check that students can reason about where a UDF executes and why that placement costs performance, using the exam's typical distractor patterns.
keyPoints: Explain the role of the Catalyst optimizer and why it cannot optimise inside a Python UDF
Identify the per-row serialization cost incurred when data crosses between the JVM and a Python worker
Select the correct statement about when a UDF is genuinely unavoidable
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify understanding of the execution-model argument for avoiding row-by-row Python UDFs.

outlines.title: Higher-Order Functions: Working with Arrays and Maps
outlines.description: Introduce the higher-order function family that lets students process nested arrays and maps without exploding rows or writing UDFs.
keyPoints: Lambda shorthand: x -> expression, and referencing nested fields with element.field inside the lambda
transform(array, x -> ...) keeps the array shape; filter(array, x -> ...) removes elements
exists(array, x -> ...) returns a boolean, and aggregate(array, start, (acc, x) -> ...) folds the array to a single value
Array and map helpers that replace hand-written loops: array_distinct, array_union, array_contains, map_filter, map_zip_with
[Table] Higher-order function / what it returns / one-line PySpark example for each
Use explode_outer only when you truly need one row per element — higher-order functions keep the grain intact
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to use built-in and higher-order functions in preference to Python UDFs.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Replacing a Python UDF with Built-in Functions
outlines.description: A fully worked rewrite that turns a slow row-by-row Python UDF into an equivalent chain of native PySpark functions, with an analysis of why the rewrite is correct and fast.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a `customers` DataFrame has `full_name` (inconsistent casing), `phones` (array of strings with punctuation) and `email`. The existing pipeline uses one Python UDF to trim and title-case the name, one to strip phone punctuation, and one to count valid phone numbers. Rewrite it with no UDFs.
Worked solution — name: `trim(initcap(col('full_name')))` replaces the title-case UDF
Worked solution — phones: `transform(col('phones'), p -> regexp_replace(p, '[^0-9+]', ''))` replaces the cleaning UDF
Worked solution — count: `size(filter(col('phones'), p -> length(regexp_replace(p, '[^0-9]', '')) >= 10))` replaces the counting UDF
Analysis: the native chain is visible to Catalyst, stays on the JVM, and uses no per-row Python handoff — typically an order-of-magnitude improvement on wide tables
Pitfalls: null arrays break transform unless guarded with `when(col('phones').isNull(), lit(None))`; regexp_replace before length is essential for correctness
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to translate a row-by-row Python UDF pipeline into equivalent native PySpark expressions.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Higher-Order Function Selection
outlines.description: Test whether students can pick the right higher-order function for a described requirement and predict its return type.
keyPoints: Choose transform vs filter vs exists vs aggregate for a stated array-processing requirement
Predict whether an expression returns an array, a boolean, or a scalar
Recognise the exam trap of reaching for a UDF when a one-line higher-order function already answers the question
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify students can match higher-order functions to requirements and reason about their return types.

outlines.title: Interactive: Higher-Order Function Playground
outlines.description: A runnable playground where students experiment with higher-order functions on nested array data and compare them against an equivalent UDF implementation.
keyPoints: Edit and run lambda expressions against a small sample DataFrame containing array and struct columns
Toggle between a native higher-order implementation and a Python UDF implementation of the same logic
Observe the returned schema and the reported execution path for each version
Guided challenges: keep only valid phone numbers, sum nested order line prices, and flatten a struct array without exploding
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to write and reason about higher-order function expressions through direct experimentation.

outlines.title: Query Patterns: Deduplication, Top-N, Pivot, and Anti-Joins
outlines.description: Consolidate the recurring analytical shapes that appear on the exam and show the idiomatic Spark SQL or PySpark expression for each.
keyPoints: Deduplicate to the latest record per key with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC)` filtered to rank 1
Top-N per group by ranking inside each partition instead of self-joining aggregates back to the base table
Conditional aggregation in one pass: `sum(when(status = 'paid', amount).otherwise(0))` instead of multiple filtered joins
Set-style patterns: `left_anti` for rows that exist in one table but not the other, `left_semi` for the reverse question
Keep the grain intact with higher-order functions and explode only when one row per element is genuinely required
[Table] Pattern / Spark SQL form / PySpark form / typical exam cue phrase
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to choose efficient query patterns for common analytical problems.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Query Patterns Under Exam Conditions
outlines.description: A timed-feel checkpoint on the analytical patterns, with distractors modelled on the mistakes candidates actually make in the exam.
keyPoints: Select the pattern that returns the latest record per key without a self-join
Distinguish left_anti from left_semi from an inner join with a null filter
Recognise the distractor that explodes a nested array when a higher-order function would preserve the grain
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify students can apply deduplication, top-N, and set-style patterns under exam-style wording.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Deduplicate and Rank Without Self-Joins
outlines.description: A fully worked analytical problem that combines deduplication, top-N per group, and conditional aggregation in two window passes rather than a cascade of joins.
keyPoints: Problem statement: an `events` table has duplicate rows per `user_id`, plus a `category` column. Produce one row per user with the latest event and that user's top two categories by event count.
Worked solution — dedupe: `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC)` and filter `rn = 1`
Worked solution — top-N: aggregate counts per user and category, then `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY cnt DESC, category)` and filter `rn <= 2`
Worked solution — reassemble: collect the two surviving categories with `collect_list` into an array column, then join back to the deduplicated row
Analysis: two window scans replace a self-join plus a correlated subquery; the shuffle cost is bounded by the partition keys
Pitfalls: ties need a deterministic secondary sort key; null `event_ts` sorts first in ascending order and can silently win the ranking
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to implement deduplication and top-N per group efficiently with window functions.

outlines.title: Native Functions vs. Python UDFs vs. Pandas UDFs
outlines.description: A side-by-side decision table that consolidates when each option is the right call, so students can answer any UDF-selection question on the exam.
keyPoints: [Table] Three columns — Native / Higher-Order Functions, Python UDF, pandas (vectorized) UDF — compared across execution location, per-row overhead, optimizer visibility, language flexibility, and typical speedup
Native wins on every performance dimension and is the default answer; pandas UDFs are the fallback when logic needs Python but batch-level vectorization is acceptable
Plain Python UDFs are the last resort and the option the exam most often marks as incorrect in a performance-optimisation question
Decision rule worth memorising: built-in → higher-order function → pandas UDF → Python UDF
Note the exam distinction between a scalar UDF, a vectorized UDF, and an aggregate function applied with groupBy
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to justify why native Spark functions outperform row-by-row Python UDFs and select the right alternative.

outlines.title: Final Checkpoint: UDFs, Higher-Order Functions, and Query Patterns
outlines.description: Close the lesson with a mixed assessment that combines performance reasoning, higher-order function selection, and query-pattern choice.
keyPoints: Rewrite a described row-by-row Python UDF using native or higher-order functions
Explain in one or two sentences why the native rewrite is faster, referencing the optimizer and the JVM-to-Python boundary
Choose the correct query pattern for a deduplication or top-N-per-group requirement
Identify which of four candidate solutions the exam would consider the efficient one
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify the lesson's two objectives together: preferring native and higher-order functions, and explaining the performance rationale.

units.title: Data Ingestion Fundamentals
objectives: Students will be able to ingest batch and incremental data into the lakehouse from common sources.
Students will be able to select an ingestion approach based on source type and freshness requirements.

lessons.title: Ingestion Patterns and Design Choices
objectives: Students will be able to compare batch, streaming, and incremental ingestion patterns.
Students will be able to match ingestion patterns to latency, volume, and reliability requirements.

outlines.title: Ingestion Patterns and Design Choices
outlines.description: Open the lesson by locating ingestion at the front of the data engineering lifecycle and framing pattern selection as a deliberate design decision rather than a default.
keyPoints: Identify the ingestion stage of the data engineering lifecycle and explain its role in moving data from source systems into the lakehouse [source p.260]
Distinguish the three canonical ingestion patterns: batch, streaming, and incremental
Define bounded vs unbounded data and map each to a pattern [source p.260]
Explain why the pattern choice is a one-way door that constrains downstream storage, transformation, and cost [source p.66]
outlines.teachingObjective: Frame ingestion as a design choice driven by requirements.

outlines.title: Batch vs Streaming vs Incremental: Side by Side
outlines.description: Place the three ingestion patterns next to each other across the dimensions the exam tests: latency, volume, processing model, and tooling.
keyPoints: [Table] Compare batch / streaming / incremental across latency, data volume, processing model, and Databricks tooling
Batch: triggered by a predetermined time interval or size threshold; operates on bounded data; typically highest throughput per job [source p.66]
Streaming: continuous processing of unbounded data; requires checkpoints and state management for near real-time delivery
Incremental: ingests only changed rows via change data capture (CDC), minimizing reprocessing and cost
Recognize exam phrasing that pivots on 'lowest latency' versus 'lowest cost' versus 'least operational overhead'
outlines.teachingObjective: Compare batch, streaming, and incremental ingestion patterns on decision-relevant dimensions.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Ingestion Patterns
outlines.description: Check whether learners can distinguish batch, streaming, and incremental patterns and their defining characteristics.
keyPoints: Classify a described pipeline as batch, streaming, or incremental
Distinguish bounded from unbounded data
Identify which pattern is continuous by default
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify recognition of the three ingestion patterns.

outlines.title: Requirements That Drive the Choice: Latency, Volume, Reliability
outlines.description: Introduce the three requirement axes learners must extract from any ingestion scenario before selecting a pattern.
keyPoints: Evaluate latency requirements and place them on the spectrum from real-time to near real-time to scheduled batch [source p.66]
Evaluate volume and throughput: payload size, events per second, and horizontal scalability of the ingestion path [source p.236]
Evaluate reliability requirements: exactly-once vs at-least-once delivery, idempotency, retries, and dead-letter queues [source p.260]
Determine the data destination after ingestion, since destination format shapes the pattern as much as the source does [source p.260]
outlines.teachingObjective: Identify the latency, volume, and reliability requirements that drive ingestion design.

outlines.title: Reading Ingestion Metrics
outlines.description: Give learners a small plotted dataset of pipeline latency and cost so they can evaluate design claims against evidence rather than intuition.
keyPoints: [Chart] Line chart: end-to-end latency (seconds) for a batch pipeline, a micro-batch stream, and a continuous stream across a simulated 24-hour window
[Table] Throughput (events/sec), monthly compute cost, and operational complexity score for each pipeline
Evaluate the claim 'the continuous stream is always the most expensive option' and mark it supported, refuted, or insufficient
Evaluate the claim 'the hourly batch pipeline meets a 15-minute freshness SLA' and justify the verdict from the X-axis readings
outlines.teachingObjective: Evaluate ingestion design claims against latency and cost data.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Requirements Mapping
outlines.description: Test the ability to translate stated latency, volume, and reliability requirements into an ingestion pattern.
keyPoints: Select the pattern that satisfies a stated freshness SLA
Identify the requirement axis that eliminates a candidate pattern
Recognize when volume alone does not justify a streaming architecture
outlines.teachingObjective: Match ingestion patterns to stated latency, volume, and reliability requirements.

outlines.title: Choosing an Ingestion Approach Under Constraints
outlines.description: Work a constrained design decision: options with explicit pros and cons, ending in one justified recommendation.
keyPoints: Constraints: 2 TB of files arriving nightly via SFTP, a 6-hour freshness tolerance, a hard monthly compute budget, and a strict schema-evolution requirement
Option A: scheduled batch load — lowest operational complexity, highest freshness lag
Option B: continuous Auto Loader stream — lowest latency, highest standing compute cost
Option C: incremental CDC from the upstream database — minimal reprocessing, but dependent on source system access and log retention
Deliver one recommendation with an explicit justification tied back to each constraint, and name the condition that would change the answer
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify an ingestion design decision against explicit constraints.

outlines.title: Interactive: Ingestion Pattern Selector
outlines.description: Learners manipulate a decision flowchart, changing one requirement at a time, and observe how the recommended ingestion pattern changes.
keyPoints: Answer decision prompts covering source type, freshness requirement, data volume, and reliability guarantee
Follow the flowchart to a recommended pattern and read the trade-offs surfaced for that recommendation
Change a single input (for example, freshness from 6 hours to 30 seconds) and observe the recommendation flip
Reinforce that no single pattern is universally correct — the requirements decide
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply a decision procedure to select an ingestion pattern.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Design Decisions
outlines.description: Assess whether learners can apply the decision procedure to fresh scenarios rather than recall definitions.
keyPoints: Choose the best ingestion pattern for a described production scenario
Identify the requirement that makes a streaming approach unnecessary
Recognize distractors that confuse ingestion frequency with transformation frequency
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply pattern selection to realistic ingestion scenarios.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Matching Patterns to Six Source Scenarios
outlines.description: A fully worked classification problem: six source scenarios are assigned an ingestion pattern and a Databricks implementation, with the reasoning made explicit.
keyPoints: Statement: classify six sources — a Kafka clickstream, a nightly SFTP CSV drop, CDC from a PostgreSQL OLTP database, IoT sensor telemetry, a quarterly HR extract, and a SaaS REST API — and select a pattern for each

Worked solution: assign streaming to the Kafka clickstream and IoT telemetry, incremental CDC to the PostgreSQL source, batch to the CSV drop and HR extract, and a polled connector to the SaaS API, with a one-line justification each

Analysis: explain why latency dominates the decision for two sources and cost dominates for the remaining four, and why the choice of key/partition column matters for the streaming cases [source p.180]
Common pitfall: defaulting to streaming when an existing batch SLA already satisfies the business requirement, which inflates cost without adding value
outlines.teachingObjective: Classify real sources into ingestion patterns and justify each assignment.

outlines.title: Push vs Pull, Synchronous vs Asynchronous, and Delivery Guarantees
outlines.description: Cover the mechanics that sit underneath every ingestion pattern and that the exam uses as distractor material.
keyPoints: Compare push, pull, and poll ingestion models and identify the source characteristics that force each one [source p.260]
Distinguish synchronous from asynchronous ingestion and describe the failure mode of each
Differentiate at-least-once from exactly-once delivery and explain the role of idempotent writes in achieving the stronger guarantee [source p.178]
Explain how dead-letter queues and buffering absorb event-rate spikes and support reliability requirements [source p.238]
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain ingestion mechanics and delivery guarantees across patterns.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Mechanics and Guarantees
outlines.description: Test the supporting mechanics — push/pull, sync/async, and delivery guarantees — that appear as distractor options in exam questions.
keyPoints: Select the ingestion model a given source type requires
Distinguish at-least-once from exactly-once and identify what makes a write idempotent
Identify the purpose of a dead-letter queue
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify understanding of ingestion mechanics and delivery guarantees.

outlines.title: Key Takeaways and Exam Traps
outlines.description: Consolidate the pattern-to-requirement mapping and flag the traps that most often cost marks on ingestion design questions.
keyPoints: Summarize the mapping in one line each: batch for scheduled, high-volume, cost-sensitive loads; streaming for unbounded, low-latency feeds; incremental for minimizing reprocessing
Exam trap: selecting streaming for data with no stated latency requirement
Exam trap: confusing ingestion frequency with transformation frequency
Exam trap: ignoring destination constraints such as schema evolution and data type changes [source p.234]
