lessons.title: Loading Files with COPY INTO
objectives: Students will be able to load files from cloud storage into a Delta table with COPY INTO.
Students will be able to explain idempotent file loading and how COPY INTO tracks processed files.

outlines.title: COPY INTO: Loading Files into Delta
outlines.description: Opens the lesson by positioning COPY INTO as the SQL, idempotent, incremental way to load files from cloud object storage into an existing Delta table, and previews the exam objective it satisfies.
keyPoints: Exam objective: load files from cloud storage into a Delta table with COPY INTO
One declarative SQL statement that runs in notebooks, jobs, and Databricks SQL warehouses and always targets an existing Delta table
Retriable by design - re-running the same statement loads only files that have not been processed yet
What it replaces: spark.read + INSERT INTO (no file tracking) and hand-written MERGE upserts over landing-file drops
[Chart] Bar chart: rows inserted on run 1 versus three identical re-runs of the same COPY INTO statement - run 1 tall, re-runs at zero - to preview idempotency
outlines.teachingObjective: Frame the lesson around the exam objective for loading files into Delta with COPY INTO

mediaGenerations.prompt: Clean technical infographic diagram of a data ingestion flow: on the left a cloud object storage folder drawn as a stack of file icons labeled 'landing path'; in the middle a box labeled 'COPY INTO'; on the right a Delta table drawn as a layered cylinder labeled 'Delta table'. A dashed arrow skips past the middle box and is labeled 'already-processed files skipped'. Flat vector style, muted blue and grey palette, all labels and text in English, no human figures.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: COPY INTO Foundations
outlines.description: Checks the base facts students need before touching syntax: what COPY INTO targets, what happens on a re-run, and which file formats it accepts.
keyPoints: Target table must already exist - COPY INTO loads into a Delta table but does not create it
Supported file formats include CSV, JSON, PARQUET, AVRO, ORC, TEXT, and BINARYFILE
Distractor to reject: 're-running COPY INTO appends the same rows again' - already-processed files are skipped
Distractor to reject: 'COPY INTO removes duplicate rows from the table' - tracking is file-level, not row-level
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm foundational facts about COPY INTO before introducing full syntax

outlines.title: Anatomy of a COPY INTO Statement
outlines.description: Breaks the statement into required and optional clauses so students can read and write any variant the exam presents.
keyPoints: Required pieces: the target table, the FROM source path or external location, and FILEFORMAT
Example: COPY INTO my_catalog.my_schema.sales FROM '/Volumes/landing/sales/' FILEFORMAT = CSV
PATTERN filters files using glob syntax (*, ?, [abc]) and is not a regular expression; FILES lists exact file names instead
FORMAT_OPTIONS passes reader options such as header, delimiter, and inferSchema; COPY_OPTIONS controls load behaviour such as mergeSchema and force
[Table] Clause breakdown: clause, required?, example value, exam note - including VALIDATE, which reports on files without inserting rows
outlines.teachingObjective: Identify every clause of a COPY INTO statement and know which are required

outlines.title: Build It: COPY INTO Statement Builder
outlines.description: An interactive SQL workspace where students assemble a working COPY INTO statement clause by clause and receive immediate syntax and option-placement feedback.
keyPoints: Clause palette: target table, FROM path, FILEFORMAT, PATTERN, FORMAT_OPTIONS, COPY_OPTIONS
Error feedback for missing FILEFORMAT, unquoted string paths, and unknown option keys
Preview panel shows which files the PATTERN would match and whether the run would be a no-op
Re-run button executes the same statement twice to demonstrate the zero-new-rows re-run message
outlines.teachingObjective: Construct a syntactically valid COPY INTO statement and place options in the correct clause

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Syntax and Options
outlines.description: Tests clause selection and option placement, the two places exam questions most often hide a wrong answer.
keyPoints: Choose the right clause for the job: PATTERN for a glob over a directory, FILES for an explicit list, VALIDATE for a dry run
Distractor: 'PATTERN uses regular expressions' - it uses glob wildcards
Distractor: 'VALIDATE also inserts the data' - it only reports on the files
Option placement rule: reader options belong in FORMAT_OPTIONS, load behaviour belongs in COPY_OPTIONS
outlines.teachingObjective: Select the correct COPY INTO clauses and options for a stated scenario

outlines.title: Worked Problem: A Daily CSV Drop with Headers
outlines.description: A fully worked COPY INTO for a daily CSV landing path, including the verification queries and the reasoning behind every clause chosen.
keyPoints: Problem: load every CSV written under /Volumes/landing/orders/ whose name begins with part-, where the first row is a header, into the existing Delta table dwh.orders
Solution: COPY INTO dwh.orders FROM '/Volumes/landing/orders/' FILEFORMAT = CSV PATTERN = 'part-*.csv' FORMAT_OPTIONS ('header' = 'true', 'inferSchema' = 'true')
Verify: capture the row count and run a duplicate check on the natural key before and after a second identical run
Analysis: the header option stops the first line being loaded as data, and the narrow PATTERN keeps unrelated edge files out of the tracked-file set
Pitfall: omitting FILEFORMAT or assuming the file extension implies the format produces confusing parse errors
outlines.teachingObjective: Write and verify a complete COPY INTO statement for a header CSV landing path

outlines.title: Idempotency: How COPY INTO Tracks Processed Files
outlines.description: Explains the file-level bookkeeping that makes COPY INTO safe to retry, and the boundary conditions where that safety breaks down.
keyPoints: For every loaded file, Databricks records the file path, its size, and its last-modified timestamp
A file is skipped only when path, size, and timestamp all match a previously processed file
Consequence 1: unchanged files are never reloaded, so retrying an orchestrated job is safe
Consequence 2: a file rewritten at the same path with a new timestamp or size is loaded again, while a deleted and re-created identical file is skipped
Consequence 3: file metadata is retained for 7 days by default - after that window a re-run can re-ingest the same files, and no row-level deduplication ever occurs
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain idempotent file loading and how COPY INTO tracks processed files

mediaGenerations.prompt: Clean technical infographic showing file-level bookkeeping: on the left a set of file icons each with a small tag showing 'path / size / last modified' fingerprint symbols; a comparison arrow leads to a table on the right labeled 'tracked files in Delta' with two result rows labeled 'LOADED' and 'SKIPPED'. A small inset clock icon in the corner is labeled 'metadata retained 7 days'. Flat vector style, muted teal and grey palette, all labels and text in English, no human figures.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Idempotent Loading
outlines.description: Probes the mechanics and the limits of idempotency, the single most tested concept for this command.
keyPoints: What makes COPY INTO idempotent: comparison of file path, size, and last-modified timestamp
Which change forces a reload: a file overwritten in place with new content
Distractor: 'COPY INTO deduplicates rows sharing a primary key' - it does not, MERGE is the row-level tool
Retention limit: after roughly 7 days without tracking, previously loaded files may be processed again
outlines.teachingObjective: Predict whether a given re-run will load, skip, or duplicate data

outlines.title: Simulate: Re-Running COPY INTO Overnight
outlines.description: A hands-on simulation of a landing folder across several days where students add, overwrite, and delete files and watch which ones COPY INTO loads or skips.
keyPoints: Add new files, then run COPY INTO and see only the new files counted as loaded
Overwrite an existing file with a new timestamp and observe it being re-ingested
Advance the simulated clock past 7 days and watch the retained file metadata expire
Live counters for loaded files, skipped files, and cumulative rows inserted
outlines.teachingObjective: Observe idempotent behaviour and metadata expiry through direct experimentation

widgetOutline.concept: COPY INTO file tracking and idempotent incremental loads

outlines.title: Choosing the Statement: COPY INTO vs INSERT INTO vs MERGE
outlines.description: Side-by-side decision table for the three SQL commands that put data into a Delta table, with the situation that makes each one correct.
keyPoints: [Table] Dimensions compared: input shape, idempotent on re-run?, schema evolution, row-level deduplication, typical exam scenario
COPY INTO: file-based batches, file-level idempotency, append-only, the right choice for landing-file drops
INSERT INTO: rows or query results, no file tracking, not idempotent across re-runs - a retry duplicates data
MERGE: business-key upserts and row-level deduplication, the right tool when a re-run must not duplicate rows
Boundary note: continuous, high-volume, ever-arriving file ingestion is a different mechanism, covered in the next lesson
outlines.teachingObjective: Select the correct ingestion statement given a source shape and a re-run requirement

outlines.title: Exam Trap Drill: COPY INTO
outlines.description: A harder, scenario-shaped quiz built from the distractors that appear most often on the real associate exam.
keyPoints: Trap: 'COPY INTO creates the target table if it is missing' - it does not
Trap: 'Re-running COPY INTO loads all files again' - only new or changed files load
Trap: 'COPY INTO guarantees no duplicate rows' - duplicates can still arrive from rewritten files or after metadata retention expires
Trap: 'PATTERN is a regex' and 'FILEFORMAT is optional' - both are false
Expect scenario wording: pick the ingestion command given a landing path, an existing Delta table, and a re-run requirement
outlines.teachingObjective: Recognize and reject the standard exam distractors for COPY INTO

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Tripled Row Counts After a Re-Run
outlines.description: A debugging walkthrough in which an orchestrated COPY INTO job produced duplicate rows, taken from evidence gathering through diagnosis, repair, and hardening.
keyPoints: Problem: an orchestrated COPY INTO job loaded 120,000 rows on day 1, then loaded the same 120,000 rows again on days 9 and 10; the table now holds 360,000 rows
Diagnosis: the job was paused longer than the 7-day metadata retention window, so every file looked new, and upstream had also rewritten files in place with fresh timestamps
Repair: re-run monthly/merge cleanup - deduplicate the table with MERGE or DROP DUPLICATES against a natural key
Prevention: schedule the load inside the retention window, scope PATTERN to immutable partition prefixes, and land files in write-once folders such as /landing/orders/ingest_date=YYYY-MM-DD/
Analysis: idempotency is a property of file identity, not of table content - COPY INTO must never be relied on for row-level deduplication
outlines.teachingObjective: Diagnose and remediate duplicate rows caused by broken idempotency assumptions

outlines.title: Reading the Numbers: A Week of COPY INTO Runs
outlines.description: Students read a small run log from a production COPY INTO job and judge whether each stated claim is supported, refuted, or cannot be determined.
keyPoints: [Table] Run log by day: files in landing path, files skipped, files loaded, rows inserted, elapsed seconds
[Chart] Line chart across Mon-Sun showing files loaded versus files skipped, with loaded spikes only on the two days new drops arrived
Claim A - 're-running nightly reloads everything': refuted, because skipped counts are high on the five unchanged days
Claim B - 'loaded files track new arrivals': supported, because loaded count equals the number of new files on each landing day
Claim C - 'elapsed time is proportional to rows inserted': insufficient, because the longest run processed the fewest files but the largest single file
outlines.teachingObjective: Interpret COPY INTO run metrics and evaluate claims against the evidence

lessons.title: Auto Loader and Cloud File Ingestion
objectives: Students will be able to configure Auto Loader to incrementally ingest new files at scale.
Students will be able to choose between directory listing and file notification ingestion modes.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Ingestion Foundations
outlines.description: A short bridging quiz that verifies the Lesson 1-2 prerequisites — ingestion patterns and COPY INTO — before Auto Loader is introduced.
keyPoints: Distinguish batch, streaming, and incremental ingestion before touching Auto Loader configuration
Recall when COPY INTO is the better tool: SQL-first, bounded file sets, retry-safe at the directory level
Trap to expect: confusing COPY INTO's file-level bookkeeping with Auto Loader's per-file state tracking
Trap to expect: assuming 'streaming' always means lower latency and lower cost
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm prerequisite vocabulary from ingestion patterns and COPY INTO before introducing Auto Loader.

outlines.title: Auto Loader: Incremental Cloud File Ingestion at Scale
outlines.description: Introduce Auto Loader (the cloudFiles source) as Databricks' scalable incremental file ingestion mechanism and position it against COPY INTO.
keyPoints: Auto Loader is the cloudFiles structured streaming source: it detects and ingests only the files that are new since the last run
Exam objective: configure Auto Loader to incrementally ingest new files at scale — thousands to billions of objects — without re-scanning the whole prefix
Complements COPY INTO: pick Auto Loader for continuous or scheduled incremental ingestion, schema evolution, and very large file counts
Supported sources: AWS S3, Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, Google Cloud Storage, plus Unity Catalog external locations and volumes
[Chart] Illustrative bar chart comparing files scanned per run: COPY INTO full-prefix listing versus Auto Loader incremental discovery
[Diagram] End-to-end path: cloud storage bucket -> Auto Loader (cloudFiles) -> Delta Lake bronze table
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain what Auto Loader is and when it is preferred over COPY INTO.

mediaGenerations.prompt: Clean technical architecture diagram for a data engineering slide. On the left, a cloud object storage bucket containing many small file icons. An arrow leads into a central engine box labelled 'Auto Loader (cloudFiles)', which contains three small labelled sub-blocks: 'incremental file discovery', 'schema inference', and 'checkpoint / state store'. A second arrow leads from the engine into a Delta Lake table on the right labelled 'bronze table'. Flat vector infographic style, professional blue, teal and grey palette, generous white space, all text labels in English.

outlines.title: Under the Hood: State, Schema, and Discovery Modes
outlines.description: Explain the mechanisms that let Auto Loader scale — the state store, the schema store, schema evolution, and the two file-discovery modes.
keyPoints: Auto Loader maintains an internal RocksDB state store under checkpointLocation listing already-processed files — this is what makes ingestion incremental and effectively idempotent
Two discovery modes: directory listing (the default, which re-lists the prefix on every trigger) and file notification (which subscribes to cloud-native file events)
schemaLocation persists the inferred schema; when a new file introduces a new column, Auto Loader evolves the schema automatically
Records that do not match the schema land in the _rescued_data column instead of failing the stream, governed by cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode
Exam trap: schemaLocation and checkpointLocation are different directories and must not point at the same path
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe Auto Loader's state store, schema handling, and the two file-discovery modes.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Auto Loader Foundations
outlines.description: Checks understanding of what Auto Loader does, how it tracks state, and how it differs from a plain file-based streaming read.
keyPoints: Identify the role of checkpointLocation and schemaLocation in an Auto Loader read
Recognise that Auto Loader processes only new files and never silently reprocesses the full prefix
Trap to expect: claiming Auto Loader requires a running cluster 24/7 — it works with scheduled availableNow runs too
Trap to expect: assuming a mismatched record fails the stream, when it is captured in _rescued_data
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify understanding of Auto Loader's core mechanics before configuration details.

outlines.title: Configuring Auto Loader: Essential Options
outlines.description: Walk through the minimum viable Auto Loader read and the production options that the exam expects candidates to recognise.
keyPoints: Minimal read: spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles").option("cloudFiles.format", "json").load("abfss://path")
Required in production: cloudFiles.schemaLocation for the schema store and checkpointLocation for streaming state
cloudFiles.useNotifications = true switches the source from directory listing to file notification mode
Trigger choice: processingTime for continuous streaming versus availableNow to run incrementally as a scheduled batch job
Exam trap: .option("cloudFiles.format", ...) describes the file format (json, csv, parquet, avro) and is not interchangeable with .format("cloudFiles")
[Diagram] Schema inference and evolution: new files widen the schema while mismatched fields are diverted to _rescued_data
outlines.teachingObjective: Read and write a correct Auto Loader configuration with the essential options.

mediaGenerations.prompt: Technical infographic showing Auto Loader schema evolution. Three JSON file icons arrive left to right: the first file shows columns 'id, name'; the second shows 'id, name, email' with the new column highlighted; the third shows a mismatched field. Arrows from all three converge into a single merged Delta table schema below, where 'id, name, email' are shown as accepted columns. A separate small bin to the right is labelled '_rescued_data' and holds the mismatched field. Flat vector style, professional blue and amber palette, clean layout, all text labels in English.

outlines.title: Auto Loader Configuration Builder
outlines.description: A hands-on playground where the learner toggles Auto Loader options and immediately sees the generated PySpark read statement plus the runtime consequences of each choice.
keyPoints: Toggle cloudFiles.format (json, csv, parquet, avro) and watch the generated read statement update
Switch useNotifications on and off to see the cloud infrastructure and IAM permissions each mode requires
Add or omit schemaLocation and checkpointLocation and observe the validation warnings that appear
Compare trigger settings — availableNow versus a processingTime interval — and see how each changes the run pattern
Compare inferred schema versus a user-supplied explicit schema for the same sample file
outlines.teachingObjective: Build a working Auto Loader read statement through guided experimentation.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Auto Loader Configuration
outlines.description: Targeted quiz on option names, required paths, and the difference between file-format options and source format.
keyPoints: Match each option to its purpose: cloudFiles.format, cloudFiles.schemaLocation, checkpointLocation, cloudFiles.useNotifications
Identify which options are mandatory for a production streaming read
Trap to expect: swapping .format("cloudFiles") with .option("cloudFiles.format", "csv")
Trap to expect: pointing schemaLocation and checkpointLocation at the same directory
outlines.teachingObjective: Test accurate recall and application of Auto Loader configuration options.

outlines.title: Directory Listing vs File Notification
outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison of the two Auto Loader discovery modes across the dimensions that actually drive the selection decision.
keyPoints: [Table] Rows: initial setup effort, cloud infrastructure required, IAM permissions, per-trigger cost model, latency to detect a new file, practical file-volume ceiling
Directory listing: no extra cloud resources, cost grows with the number of objects re-listed on every trigger, fine for thousands of files or low-frequency scheduled runs
File notification: requires a cloud event queue plus an IAM role (SQS/SNS on AWS, Event Grid with a Storage Queue on Azure, Pub/Sub on Google Cloud) but avoids repeated listing of huge prefixes
Decision rule to memorise: high file count and low-latency targets push you to file notification; small volumes and restricted permissions push you to directory listing
Exam trap: notification mode still needs a periodic directory-listing backfill to catch files that arrived while the queue or notification service was unavailable
outlines.teachingObjective: Choose between directory listing and file notification using explicit decision criteria.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Migrating to File Notification Mode
outlines.description: A fully worked migration: a production pipeline ingesting four million small JSON files per day from S3 must move from directory listing to file notification without losing data.
keyPoints: Statement: 4,000,000 new JSON files per day land in s3://raw-events/; the business requires files to be visible within 5 minutes; today the run spends most of its time issuing LIST calls
Step 1 — enable notification discovery: cloudFiles.useNotifications = true, letting Auto Loader provision the SQS queue, SNS topic, and IAM role, or supply an existing queue on locked-down accounts
Step 2 — keep schemaLocation and checkpointLocation on durable storage and preserve both across the change so already-seen files are not reprocessed
Step 3 — set a trigger interval that satisfies the 5-minute freshness target and schedule a one-off backfill listing pass to catch files created during the migration window
Step 4 — verify with a reconciliation count: files in storage versus rows landed in the Delta table, per hour
Analysis: notification mode removes the O(total objects) listing cost, but the backfill pass is what guarantees correctness — a common exam distractor is assuming notifications alone are complete
outlines.teachingObjective: Migrate a large-scale Auto Loader pipeline from directory listing to file notification mode.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Choosing a Discovery Mode
outlines.description: Scenario-based quiz requiring a justified choice between directory listing and file notification.
keyPoints: Given a file volume, freshness target, and permission model, select the correct discovery mode
Recognise the infrastructure each mode requires and who must grant it
Trap to expect: recommending notification mode where the team cannot create queues or roles
Trap to expect: assuming notification mode eliminates the need for a periodic backfill scan
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply the discovery-mode decision criteria to realistic scenarios.

outlines.title: Choosing an Ingestion Mode Under Real Constraints
outlines.description: Three constrained scenarios are weighed against each other; each requires one justified recommendation rather than a generic 'streaming is better' answer.
keyPoints: Scenario A: 500 files per day, one-hour nightly SLA, no cloud-admin rights -> directory listing with a scheduled availableNow trigger
Scenario B: 20 million small files per day, two-minute freshness target, platform team can grant IAM -> file notification mode
Scenario C: a shared bucket where you cannot create queues and files arrive sporadically -> directory listing with a longer trigger interval, cluster autoscaling, and a file-count alert
[Table] Options x pros and cons x cost profile x operational risk, scored against file volume, latency target, and permission constraints
The recommendation for each scenario must name the constraint that decided it, and state the residual risk that remains after the choice
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify an ingestion-mode decision against explicit volume, latency, and permission constraints.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Counting the Cost of Directory Listing
outlines.description: A quantitative worked problem comparing the per-trigger listing cost of directory listing at scale against event-based notification.
keyPoints: Statement: a prefix holds 12,000,000 objects; the stream triggers every 5 minutes; the cloud LIST operation returns 1,000 keys per call and costs $0.005 per 1,000 requests
Step 1 — calls per scan: 12,000,000 / 1,000 = 12,000 LIST calls
Step 2 — listing cost per scan: 12,000 x $0.005 / 1,000 = $0.06
Step 3 — scans per day at a 5-minute trigger: 288; daily listing cost = 288 x $0.06 = $17.28, roughly $520 per month before any compute
Step 4 — under file notification mode the repeated listing disappears; cost shifts to per-event delivery, so the same workload becomes volume-proportional rather than object-count-proportional
Analysis: directory-listing cost scales with total objects x trigger frequency, so shortening the trigger interval multiplies cost — an exam-favourite trap when a question asks how to reduce latency
outlines.teachingObjective: Quantify and interpret the listing cost of directory-listing mode at high file counts.

outlines.title: Unit Check: Auto Loader and Cloud File Ingestion
outlines.description: A mixed, exam-weighted quiz closing the lesson: configuration, discovery-mode selection, schema evolution, and cost reasoning.
keyPoints: Write or repair an Auto Loader read statement containing the required options
Select a discovery mode from a scenario and justify it in one sentence
Explain how schema evolution and _rescued_data protect a long-running ingestion stream
Trap to expect: mixing up the option that names the file format with the format that names the Auto Loader source
Trap to expect: omitting checkpointLocation or schemaLocation from a production configuration
outlines.teachingObjective: Assess mastery of Auto Loader configuration and cloud file ingestion mode selection.

Students will be able to describe how Kafka and Lakeflow Connect feed streaming data into the lakehouse.

outlines.title: Databases, Kafka, and Managed Connectors: Lesson Roadmap
outlines.description: Frame the lesson as the two remaining ingestion paths beyond files: direct database connections and streaming platforms.
keyPoints: Beyond files: databases and streaming sources demand different ingestion mechanics than COPY INTO or Auto Loader
Lesson objectives: JDBC ingestion from relational databases, change data capture concepts, Kafka streaming, and managed connectors
Exam mapping: Databricks Data Engineer Associate ingestion tasks — JDBC, CDC, streaming, Lakeflow Connect
[Table] Roadmap: JDBC batch read | snapshot + CDC | Kafka streaming | managed connector, with the freshness each delivers
Guiding question: what is the source type, and how fresh must the data be?
outlines.teachingObjective: Frame the lesson scope and connect it to the certification exam ingestion domain.

outlines.title: Direct Database Connections with JDBC
outlines.description: Explain how Spark reads from and writes to relational databases over JDBC, including parallelism, pushdown, and credentials.
keyPoints: Read with spark.read.format("jdbc") using url, dbtable or query, user, and a password pulled from a Databricks secret scope
Control read parallelism with partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound, and numPartitions
Predicate pushdown sends filters to the source database and reduces the bytes transferred across the network
Exam trap: omitting partitionColumn forces a single-partition read, so a large table loads slowly with no parallelism
JDBC alone re-reads the whole table on every run; combine it with a watermark or CDC when you need incremental loads
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to configure a parallel JDBC read from a relational database on Databricks.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: JDBC Ingestion
outlines.description: Test configuration knowledge and common JDBC failure diagnosis.
keyPoints: Select the options required to make a JDBC read parallel
Diagnose why a JDBC read produced only one partition
Identify the correct credential handling approach (secret scope, never an inline password)
Distractors mirror exam traps: dbtable versus query, numPartitions versus fetchsize, lowerBound semantics
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify students can configure and troubleshoot JDBC ingestion.

outlines.title: Change Data Capture: Initial Snapshot Plus Increments
outlines.description: Introduce CDC as the mechanism that keeps a Delta table synchronized with a source database without full reloads.
keyPoints: CDC captures INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE by reading the source transaction log or database triggers
Batch-oriented CDC applies periodic deltas; continuous CDC applies change rows to the target near-real-time
Standard pattern: take an initial snapshot, then apply subsequent changes with MERGE INTO using primary key plus sequence
Exam trap: a nightly full reload is not CDC — CDC requires true change records, including deletes
[Chart] Line chart: cumulative rows processed per day over 30 days, full reload versus snapshot + CDC
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to explain how snapshots and change records keep a target table consistent.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A clean, professional technical infographic of change data capture. On the left, a relational database with a transaction log icon; an arrow labeled "change records (INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE)" flows to a Delta table on the right, and a separate labeled arrow shows the "initial snapshot". Numbered steps indicate order of operations. All labels and text in English. Flat vector style, blue and teal palette, no human figures.

outlines.title: Interactive: CDC Pipeline Explorer
outlines.description: Students drive a simulated source database, choose a CDC mode, and watch how snapshot plus increments land in the target Delta table.
keyPoints: Toggle operations on the source table: INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE
Switch between batch-oriented CDC and continuous CDC and compare refresh latency
Observe how MERGE INTO resolves repeated updates and removes deleted rows
Reset the simulation to inspect how the initial snapshot is captured
Read the change log panel to see exactly which records flowed into the target
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to reason about how change records are applied to a Delta target table.

widgetOutline.concept: Change data capture into a Delta table

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Change Data Capture
outlines.description: Test CDC concepts, MERGE semantics, and mode selection by latency requirement.
keyPoints: Distinguish CDC from a periodic full refresh
Identify the correct MERGE semantics for updates and deletes
Choose batch-oriented versus continuous CDC given a stated latency requirement
Distractors mirror exam traps: append-only writes for deletes, snapshot-only recovery, missing merge keys
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify students can select and reason about CDC approaches.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Snapshot Plus CDC from SQL Server to Delta
outlines.description: A fully worked JDBC-to-Delta ingestion problem: land a source snapshot, then apply hourly change records with MERGE.
keyPoints: Statement: ingest the sales.orders table from an on-premises SQL Server into a Bronze Delta table with a nightly snapshot and hourly change capture
Step 1: define the JDBC read with url, dbtable, partitionColumn=order_id, lowerBound, upperBound, and numPartitions=8
Step 2: land the snapshot into bronze_orders and record the high-watermark timestamp for the next run
Step 3: apply change records with MERGE INTO bronze_orders tgt USING changes src ON tgt.order_id = src.order_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
Analysis: a sequence or timestamp is required so out-of-order changes do not overwrite newer values; deletes need an explicit WHEN MATCHED AND op = 'DELETE' THEN DELETE branch
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to implement a snapshot plus incremental CDC pipeline end to end.

outlines.title: Kafka and Event-Streaming Platforms
outlines.description: Describe how Kafka topics, partitions, and consumer offsets feed continuous streaming data into the lakehouse.
keyPoints: Kafka is a distributed, append-only log: producers write records into topics that are split into partitions by key
Consumers track their position with offsets; ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, never across the whole topic
Delivery semantics range from at-most-once through at-least-once (the common default) to exactly-once with transactions and idempotent sinks
Exam trap: assuming Kafka deletes consumed messages, or that a consumer can re-read in global order after a restart
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to describe the Kafka model and its ordering and durability guarantees.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A professional technical infographic of an Apache Kafka cluster: one topic divided into three ordered partitions, each drawn as a sequence of record boxes with increasing offsets; producers on the left appending records, and a consumer group on the right reading with committed offsets. A final arrow leads to a Delta Lake table labeled "bronze". All labels and text in English. Flat vector style, blue and orange palette, no human figures.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Kafka and Streaming Ingestion
outlines.description: Test Kafka configuration options, ordering guarantees, and streaming reliability mechanics.
keyPoints: Select the options required by spark.readStream.format("kafka")
Reason about ordering guarantees per partition versus per topic
Identify the role of checkpoints in achieving exactly-once streaming ingestion
Distractors mirror exam traps: subscribe versus subscribePattern, startingOffsets versus endingOffsets, missing checkpointLocation
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify students can configure and reason about Kafka streaming ingestion.

outlines.title: Lakeflow Connect and Managed Connectors
outlines.description: Explain how managed connectors move data from SaaS applications and databases into the lakehouse with minimal code.
keyPoints: Managed connectors handle authentication, schema drift, and incremental extraction so you do not hand-roll each pipeline
Lakeflow Connect ingests from databases and SaaS sources such as Salesforce into Unity Catalog tables on a schedule
Ingestion gateways and private connectivity keep traffic inside your network for on-premises sources
Exam trap: managed connectors are not zero-configuration — they still require a destination schema, a schedule, and correct grants
Decision rule: reach for a managed connector first and drop to JDBC or CDC only when it cannot meet the source or latency need
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to describe how managed connectors such as Lakeflow Connect deliver ingestion.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A clean architecture infographic of managed ingestion. On the left, source icons for a SaaS application and an on-premises database; in the center, a managed connector service box labeled with authentication and schema-drift handling; on the right, Unity Catalog tables in a Databricks lakehouse; a shield icon represents a secure private-network gateway. All labels and text in English. Flat vector style, blue and green palette, no human figures.

outlines.title: Choosing an Ingestion Path: JDBC vs CDC vs Kafka vs Managed Connector
outlines.description: Compare the four database and streaming ingestion paths across the dimensions that drive a design decision.
keyPoints: [Table] Path comparison: JDBC batch | snapshot + CDC | Kafka streaming | managed connector — across latency, incremental support, source impact, operational effort, and code volume
Freshness: JDBC typically daily or hourly, CDC seconds to minutes, Kafka continuous, managed connector governed by its schedule
Effort and source impact: JDBC re-reads and loads the source; CDC reads a log with lower source impact; managed connectors are lowest effort overall
Decision rule: pick the lowest-effort path that satisfies the freshness and source constraints — do not reach for Kafka when a nightly JDBC read suffices
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to select an ingestion approach based on source type and freshness requirements.

outlines.title: Knowledge Check: Managed Connectors and Design Choices
outlines.description: Test scenario-based selection among managed connectors, CDC, JDBC batch, and Kafka.
keyPoints: Given a SaaS CRM source and a near-real-time freshness requirement, pick the appropriate connector
Compare a managed connector against a hand-rolled JDBC pipeline on effort, maintenance, and schema drift
Identify when CDC is required instead of a nightly batch reload
Distractors mirror exam traps: full reloads described as incremental, connector permissions in Unity Catalog, unsupported freshness expectations
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify students can map a scenario to the correct ingestion path.

outlines.title: Lesson Recap and Exam Takeaways
outlines.description: Consolidate the four ingestion paths and the decision rules students should carry into the certification exam.
keyPoints: JDBC batch for simple, low-frequency database reads; CDC when deletes and updates must be captured incrementally
Kafka for continuous event streams; managed connectors for SaaS and database sources with minimal code
Always account for credential handling, schema drift, ordering guarantees, and exactly-once semantics
Exam takeaways: map the scenario to source type plus freshness requirement, then choose the lowest-effort path that meets the latency
Next unit preview: transforming and modeling the data you have just ingested
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to summarize and apply the ingestion-path decision rules.

objectives: Students will be able to organize lakehouse data into bronze, silver, and gold layers.
Students will be able to produce well-modeled gold tables that analysts can trust.

lessons.title: The Medallion Architecture
objectives: Students will be able to describe the purpose and content of bronze, silver, and gold tables.
Students will be able to design a layered transformation flow for a realistic data source.

outlines.title: Medallion Architecture: The Three Layers
outlines.description: Introduce the medallion (multi-hop) design pattern that organizes lakehouse data into bronze, silver, and gold layers of progressively higher quality.
keyPoints: Describe the medallion architecture as a data design pattern that organizes lakehouse data into bronze, silver, and gold layers to progressively improve data quality and structure [source 2]
Identify the quality progression: bronze = raw, silver = validated, gold = enriched and business-ready [source 6]
Explain why progressive refinement solves the problem of data arriving in inconsistent raw states before it reaches analysts and models [source 1]
Explain that each hop is a purpose-built table that decouples ingestion, cleansing, and consumption
[Chart] Horizontal layered diagram: source systems → bronze → silver → gold → BI dashboards and ML consumers
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe the purpose of bronze, silver, and gold tables

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Retail Orders from Raw Events to Gold
outlines.description: A fully worked design-and-code problem that moves a realistic streaming retail order source through bronze, silver, and gold.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a retailer streams order events (JSON with nested line items, late-arriving updates, duplicate retries) into cloud storage; design the medallion flow and write the key transformations
Worked step 1 — Bronze: use Auto Loader to append raw JSON files into a bronze table with ingestion metadata, no parsing, no deduplication
Worked step 2 — Silver: explode and type-cast line items, apply a MERGE on order_id to keep the latest version, drop duplicates, and enforce the expected schema
Worked step 3 — Gold: aggregate silver into a daily sales mart by store and product category, and expose a star-schema fact table with conformed date and product dimensions

Analysis: why MERGE on a business key works for late-arriving updates; pitfalls include merging before deduplication, losing the raw record needed for replay, and hiding a schema change by silently dropping columns

outlines.title: Decision: How Many Layers Does This Pipeline Really Need?
outlines.description: A constrained design decision about whether to materialize all three layers, with pros, cons, and one justified recommendation.
keyPoints: Constraint: a five-person team ingests streaming CDC from a production database and serves three BI dashboards; storage cost and refresh latency both matter
Option A — full three-layer materialization: highest data quality and replayability, but more jobs, more storage, and more orchestration to maintain
Option B — bronze + gold only, skipping silver: faster to build and cheaper, but business logic gets duplicated per dashboard and reprocessing becomes brittle
Option C — bronze + silver as Delta tables and gold as views over silver: lowest storage, but dashboard latency and cost move to query time

Recommendation: keep all three layers, but land silver incrementally with MERGE and expose gold as views until query cost justifies materializing them — justified because bronze guarantees replay, silver centralizes conformance, and gold views avoid premature storage cost

outlines.title: Type 1 vs Type 2 vs Type 3: Comparing SCD Strategies
outlines.description: Introduces slowly changing dimensions and compares the three classic strategies side by side across the dimensions that decide an implementation.
keyPoints: [Table] Compare Type 1 / Type 2 / Type 3 across: history preserved, rows added per change, extra columns, key handling, reporting impact, and implementation effort

Type 2 adds a new row version with EFF_StartDate, EFF_EndDate (9999-01-01 for the open record) and an is_current flag — full history, row count grows
Type 3 keeps previous and current values in additional columns (Original ZipCode / Current ZipCode) — limited to a fixed number of changes, rarely used
Exam trap: Type 2 requires a surrogate key, because the business key is no longer unique once multiple versions exist

outlines.title: Worked Problem: A Type 2 SCD Row-Versioning Walkthrough
outlines.description: A fully worked example that shows exactly which rows a Type 2 dimension must contain before and after an attribute change.
keyPoints: Statement: customer_id 4471 moves from ZIP 10001 to 94105 on 2024-03-15; the customer dimension is Type 2 with a surrogate key — show the required change
Before: one active row — customer_sk = 981, customer_id = 4471, zip = 10001, EFF_StartDate = 2021-06-01, EFF_EndDate = 9999-01-01, is_current = true
Step 1 — expire the current row: set EFF_EndDate = 2024-03-15 and is_current = false; never overwrite the old ZIP value in a Type 2 dimension
Step 2 — insert the new version: customer_sk = 1492 (a brand-new surrogate key), customer_id = 4471, zip = 94105, EFF_StartDate = 2024-03-15, EFF_EndDate = 9999-01-01, is_current = true

Analysis: the surrogate key is what keeps historical facts pointing at ZIP 10001 after the change; the classic pitfalls are updating in place (that is Type 1) and reusing the same surrogate key for the new version

outlines.title: Implementing SCD Type 1 and Type 2 on Databricks

outlines.title: Anatomy of a Denormalized Gold Table
outlines.description: Shows how a fact table plus its dimensions collapse into one wide, read-optimized table, and states the guardrails that keep the grain intact.
keyPoints: Denormalization = deliberately re-introducing redundancy so BI queries do not have to join at read time
[Table] Star schema (sales + dim_customer + dim_product + dim_date) versus the single wide gold table it becomes: columns, joins needed, typical query

A wide gold table mixes fact measures (quantity, unit_price, discount_amount, net_revenue) with flattened dimension attributes (customer_name, customer_segment, product_category, store_region, order_date)
Trade-off: redundant storage and wider rows in exchange for removing join and shuffle cost from every query
Guardrail: keep the fact grain exact — join each dimension on its unique key (or the current SCD version), or row counts silently explode

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Denormalize a Star Schema into a Gold Table
outlines.description: A fully worked solution that joins a silver sales fact to its dimensions to produce one wide gold Delta table without changing the grain.
keyPoints: Problem: given silver.sales (grain = one row per order line item), dim_customer, dim_product, and dim_date, write gold_sales_wide as a single denormalized table

Solution: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold_sales_wide AS SELECT s.*, c.customer_name, c.customer_segment, p.product_category, d.year, d.quarter FROM silver.sales s LEFT JOIN dim_customer c ON s.customer_key = c.customer_key AND c.eff_end_date = DATE'9999-01-01' LEFT JOIN dim_product p ON s.product_key = p.product_key LEFT JOIN dim_date d ON s.date_key = d.date_key
Analysis: a LEFT JOIN against a dimension that is unique on its key (or filtered to the current SCD Type 2 version) preserves the fact grain — verify by comparing COUNT(*) before and after the join
Pitfall: joining a Type 2 dimension without the current-version filter fans out rows and duplicates revenue in every downstream dashboard
Pitfall: a dimension filter placed after the join (for example WHERE c.customer_segment = 'Retail') silently converts the LEFT JOIN to an inner join and drops rows
outlines.teachingObjective: Write a denormalizing transformation that preserves the declared fact grain

outlines.title: Centralizing Business Logic in the Gold Layer
outlines.description: Introduces business logic and derived data as shared definitions, and contrasts one governed definition with the scattered per-dashboard anti-pattern.
keyPoints: Business logic = the definition of a metric or rule: net revenue after returns, the window that makes a customer 'active', profit after marketing cost [source p.346]
Anti-pattern: the same metric re-implemented in every dashboard, notebook, and ad hoc query — the numbers drift and nobody can reconcile them
Fix: encode the logic once in the gold transformation (or a governed semantic/metrics layer) and let consumers select the finished result
DRY principle: derived data should be computed and stored in one place, not recomputed downstream with slightly different rules
Classic examples: ad-spend attribution, exclusion of auto-canceled orders, currency conversion, and refund handling

outlines.title: Where Should Business Logic Live?
outlines.description: A decision under real constraints: put logic in gold table columns, in views or materialized views, in a semantic/metrics layer, or in each BI tool.
keyPoints: Option A — materialized columns in the gold table: fastest reads and one physical definition, but every change requires a rewrite and backfill
Option B — gold views and materialized views: logic stays queryable and refreshable; materialized views in Databricks SQL add refresh cost and staleness
Option C — semantic / metrics layer: one governed definition serving many tools, at the price of adopting and maintaining the layer [source p.346]
Option D — logic inside each dashboard: rejected — it duplicates definitions, breaks lineage, and guarantees metric drift
Constraints and recommendation: materialize stable, high-traffic metrics as gold columns; keep volatile or team-specific definitions in a governed semantic layer; never encode them per dashboard
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a placement for business logic given governance, latency, and change-frequency constraints

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Encode Profit Logic Once
outlines.description: A worked computation of a net-profit metric including exclusion rules and a cost allocation that must stay identical for every consumer.
keyPoints: Problem: compute daily profit per product category = net revenue − COGS − allocated marketing cost; exclude auto-canceled orders; net out refunds
Solution: pre-aggregate refunds to the order-line grain, join marketing cost allocated by date and channel, then aggregate once to date × category and write the result to gold
Analysis: if refunds are joined at transaction grain without pre-aggregation, each refund is counted once per line item and the deduction is inflated
Analysis: incremental writes must be idempotent — re-running a day should MERGE on the date key rather than append a second copy of the day's profit
Pitfall: filtering canceled orders before versus after the allocation join changes the allocation denominator and quietly shifts every ratio downstream

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Profit After Marketing Costs
outlines.description: A fully worked attribution problem showing how two defensible rules produce the same total but contradictory per-item profit — the mechanical root of duplicated metrics.
keyPoints: Problem statement: an ad platform reports 10 clicks and $80 of spend for an order containing item X (price $40, 6 clicks) and item Y (price $60, 4 clicks). Compute profit per item under (a) naive attribution and (b) price-weighted attribution.
Worked solution (naive, equal cost per click $8): X cost 6 × $8 = $48 → profit $40 − $48 = −$8; Y cost 4 × $8 = $32 → profit $60 − $32 = $28; total profit $20
Worked solution (price-weighted): X share = 40/(40+60) = 40% → cost $32 → profit $8; Y share = 60% → cost $48 → profit $12; total profit $20
Analysis: both allocations are exhaustive and additive, so total profit is invariant; the per-item profit for X flips from −$8 to +$8 purely from the rule choice

Analysis — pitfalls: mixing attribution methods across consumers, re-computing at a different grain (order vs item), double-counting spend when joins fan out, and recomputing a metric non-idempotently so totals drift on each run
outlines.teachingObjective: Compute a derived metric under two attribution rules and explain why rule choice, not data, causes disagreement.

outlines.title: Risks of Duplicated and Inconsistent Metrics
outlines.description: Connects duplicated logic to its business consequences: eroded trust, silent drift, wasted reconciliation effort, and hidden coupling.
keyPoints: Trust erosion: when two dashboards show different revenue or profit, stakeholders stop believing both and revert to spreadsheets
Silent drift: a rule corrected in one copy but not the others, so definitions diverge gradually with no error raised
Reconciliation cost: engineers and analysts burn hours tracing which number is correct instead of acting on it
Hidden coupling: dashboards silently depend on logic buried in another team's notebook, so a small refactor breaks reporting
Exam trap: 'recompute the metric in the BI tool for speed' is an antipattern, not a performance technique — it creates a second definition

outlines.title: Unit Glossary: Transformation and Modeling Terms
outlines.description: Complete definitions of the key terms from this unit, anchored in the medallion, dimensional-modeling, and derived-metric material.
keyPoints: Business logic — the rules that convert stored data into decision-ready values, such as profit = revenue − cost − marketing spend
Derived data — any value computed from other data rather than captured at the source; every gold metric, KPI, and ML feature is derived data
DRY (don't repeat yourself) — the principle that each piece of knowledge, including a metric formula, has exactly one authoritative representation
Single source of truth (SSOT) — the design rule that a metric is defined once and every consumer reads that definition instead of re-implementing it
Metrics layer / semantic layer — a governed catalog of metric definitions (formula, grain, dimensions) served to SQL, BI, notebooks, and ML consumers
Attribution model — the rule that assigns shared costs to items or channels; naive attribution splits costs equally, price-weighted attribution allocates proportionally to price
Grain — the level of detail a fact or metric is recorded at (order, item, day); comparing metrics at different grains produces silently wrong numbers
Conformed dimension — a dimension (for example, date or customer) shared by multiple fact tables so metrics can be combined consistently across the warehouse
outlines.teachingObjective: Recall and define the unit's core transformation and modeling terminology.

outlines.title: The Core Data Quality Dimensions
outlines.description: Introduces the six dimensions used throughout the Databricks Data Engineer Associate exam, each framed as the question it answers and a concrete check that implements it.
keyPoints: Completeness: are required values present? Check: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) / NULL rate per column.
[Table] Dimension comparison: dimension | question answered | example failure | example check expression.
Accuracy: do values reflect reality? Check: reconciliation against the source system of record or a trusted reference table.
Timeliness: is the data fresh enough for its use case? Check: MAX(ingestion_timestamp) within an expected freshness window.
Uniqueness: is each real-world entity represented once? Check: COUNT(*) equals COUNT(DISTINCT business_key).
Validity and consistency cover domain/format conformance and cross-field or cross-table agreement, e.g. shipped_date >= order_date.
outlines.teachingObjective: Define the six quality dimensions and pair each with an executable check pattern.

outlines.title: Completeness vs. Accuracy vs. Timeliness vs. Uniqueness
outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison of the four dimensions named in the lesson objective, organized by the decision-relevant dimensions learners must reason about in exam scenarios.
keyPoints: [Table] Columns: dimension | question answered | typical failure mode | primary metric | Databricks check pattern | what it does NOT prove.
Completeness proves presence, not correctness — a row full of placeholder values is complete but inaccurate.
Accuracy proves agreement with reality, which usually requires a reference dataset or source-system reconciliation.
Timeliness is measured against a business freshness requirement (for example, 30 minutes), never an arbitrary threshold.
Uniqueness requires a declared business key; uniqueness on a surrogate or partition column is meaningless.
outlines.teachingObjective: Discriminate between confusable dimensions using a decision-relevant comparison table.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: From Business Requirement to Testable Rule
outlines.description: Fully-worked translation of a vague stakeholder requirement into four executable quality rules, with the reasoning behind each rule made explicit.
keyPoints: Problem statement: the sales team says 'our orders table should be complete, current, and free of duplicates so the daily revenue dashboard is trustworthy'.

Step 1 — decompose the sentence into dimensions: completeness (customer_id, order_total present), uniqueness (one row per order_id), timeliness (loaded within 30 minutes of order creation), accuracy (order_total matches the payment gateway).
Step 2 — write each rule as an executable SQL assertion, for example SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL; expected result 0.
Step 3 — attach a threshold, severity, and owner to each rule so the test can fail loudly rather than silently.
Analysis: rules must be falsifiable and deterministic; a rule like 'data looks reasonable' is not testable, and a rule with no threshold produces alert fatigue.
outlines.teachingObjective: Demonstrate a repeatable procedure for turning business expectations into executable quality rules.

outlines.title: Reading a Quality Metrics Report
outlines.description: Learners interpret a small week-long metrics table of null rates, duplicate rates, and ingestion lag, then judge whether given claims are supported, refuted, or unsupported by the data.
keyPoints: [Table] Daily metrics for seven days: total_rows | customer_id_null_pct | duplicate_order_pct | max_ingestion_lag_minutes | rule passes.
Claim 1: 'Completeness improved steadily all week' — evaluate against the null-rate trend, noting one mid-week regression.
Claim 2: 'Uniqueness is within tolerance' — evaluate against the duplicate-rate column and the stated 0.1% threshold.
Claim 3: 'Timeliness never breached its 30-minute SLO' — check whether max lag exceeded the SLO on any day.
Recognize that a metric can pass its own threshold while the dataset still violates a related dimension, so passes must be read per-dimension.
outlines.teachingObjective: Evaluate claims about dataset quality using quantitative quality metrics.

outlines.title: Where Should Quality Checks Live?
outlines.description: A constrained design decision: enforce quality checks at ingestion, during transformation, or at the serving layer, with pros, cons, and one justified recommendation.
keyPoints: Option A — at ingestion (bronze): earliest detection and cheapest remediation, but blocks or quarantines raw data and can mask upstream fixes.
Option B — during transformation (silver): checks run where business rules and joins already exist, but defects already persisted into bronze.
Option C — at serving (gold): protects consumers directly, but detection is late and remediation requires expensive backfills.
Constraints: 30-minute freshness SLO for the executive dashboard, a 1% null tolerance on customer_id, and a small platform team.

Recommendation: enforce critical, cheap, deterministic checks (completeness, uniqueness, schema) at ingestion, and business-rule accuracy checks in the silver transformation layer, with a final serving-layer assertion on the published contract.
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a placement strategy for quality checks under explicit business and platform constraints.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Computing and Thresholding Quality Metrics
outlines.description: Quantitative worked problem where learners compute completeness, uniqueness, and freshness metrics from raw counts and decide pass or fail against stated thresholds.
keyPoints: Given: 5,000,000 total orders, 175,000 rows with NULL customer_id, 4,992,500 distinct order_id values, latest ingest timestamp 47 minutes behind the latest order.
Step 1 — completeness: null rate = 175,000 / 5,000,000 = 3.5%, which exceeds the 1.0% tolerance, so the check FAILS.
Step 2 — uniqueness: duplicate rate = (5,000,000 - 4,992,500) / 5,000,000 = 0.15%, which exceeds the 0.10% tolerance, so the check FAILS.
Step 3 — timeliness: 47-minute lag exceeds the 30-minute freshness SLO, so the check FAILS; two of three dimensions breached in the same batch.

Analysis: thresholds must match the grain of the table and the business use case; also note that a 0.15% duplicate rate on a line-item table would be a false alarm because line-item grain legitimately repeats order_id.
outlines.teachingObjective: Compute dimension-specific quality metrics and apply thresholds correctly.

outlines.title: Why Duplicates and Late Data Break Pipelines
outlines.description: Frame the lesson by connecting duplication and lateness to the data quality dimensions covered in the previous lesson, and set the lesson roadmap.
keyPoints: Recall from Unit 6 Lesson 1: uniqueness and timeliness are two of the core data quality dimensions; this lesson makes them operational

outlines.title: Where Duplicates Come From
outlines.description: Catalogue the concrete sources of duplicated rows in Databricks pipelines so students can diagnose the root cause rather than blindly deduplicating.
keyPoints: At-least-once delivery: message queues and event-streaming platforms (Amazon SQS, Kafka, Kinesis) redeliver messages after failures — exactly-once is not guaranteed at the transport layer
Replayed ingestion: re-running a batch job, re-processing a checkpointed stream from an earlier offset, or backfilling a historical window appends the same events twice
Non-idempotent writes: an append-only (INSERT) pipeline produces a new copy of every record on every run, so pipeline re-runs multiply rows
CDC and source-system quirks: database replication and change-data-capture can emit an update as a new row, and multi-row updates emit one row per change
Exam trap: a MERGE whose SOURCE contains multiple rows for the same key is not a deduplication fix — it can fail with a duplicate-match error or multiply target rows
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to identify the specific mechanism that produced duplicate rows in a given pipeline.

outlines.title: Deduplication Strategy: Key Plus Ordering
outlines.description: Establish the general recipe for deduplication: choose the right key, choose a deterministic tie-break, then keep exactly one row per key.
keyPoints: Step 1 — Choose the key: the natural/business primary key, or a composite key (e.g., order_id + line_item_id) if the entity is a line item
Step 2 — Choose the tie-break: the record with MAX(updated_timestamp), MAX(version), or MAX(ingestion_time) wins; this must be deterministic
Step 3 — Keep one row per key: a window function (ROW_NUMBER) or an insert-only pattern read with MAX(created_timestamp) at query time
Exam trap: DataFrame.dropDuplicates() on all columns only removes rows that are identical across EVERY column — one differing field and the duplicate survives
Exam trap: an ORDER BY without a unique tie-breaker makes 'latest' non-deterministic when two records share the same timestamp
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to select an appropriate deduplication key and deterministic ordering rule for a given table.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Deduplicate Then Upsert into Delta
outlines.description: A fully worked, end-to-end deduplication and idempotent upsert problem from a bronze events table into a silver Delta table.
keyPoints: Problem statement: bronze.orders_events contains an average of 1.8 rows per order_id with different updated_at values, plus re-run duplicates from a backfill; build silver.orders with exactly one current row per order_id, and make the job safe to re-run any number of times

Step 1 — Dedupe the source: CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW deduped AS SELECT * FROM (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, ingestion_time DESC) AS rn FROM bronze.orders_events) WHERE rn = 1
Step 2 — Upsert idempotently: MERGE INTO silver.orders t USING deduped s ON t.order_id = s.order_id WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
Step 3 — Verify: SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM silver.orders GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 must return zero rows, and the row count must be unchanged after a second run

Analysis: the method works because the window function reduces the source to a single deterministic row per key, and the MERGE predicate makes the write a function of the data rather than of run count; the classic pitfalls are skipping Step 1 (duplicate-match errors or multiplied target rows), using >= instead of > on the timestamp (needless rewrites and version churn), and forgetting a tie-break so 'latest' flips between runs
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to build a re-runnable deduplication and upsert job from a bronze table into a clean silver Delta table.

outlines.title: Comparison: Four Deduplication Patterns
outlines.description: A decision table comparing the deduplication patterns students will meet on the exam, across the dimensions that actually decide the choice.
keyPoints: [Table] Rows: dropDuplicates(); ROW_NUMBER window + filter; Delta MERGE upsert; insert-only (append everything, query MAX(created_timestamp))
[Table] Columns: correctness when non-key columns differ; safe to re-run (idempotent); compute and storage cost; preserves history; typical use case
dropDuplicates is cheapest but only exact-row matches; ROW_NUMBER is the general-purpose batch workhorse; MERGE is required when you must update a target incrementally
Insert-only preserves full history and makes late arrivals first-class, at the cost of table growth, lookup overhead, and the need for a record sunset date
Exam guidance: match the pattern to the requirement — 'must be idempotent on re-run' points to MERGE, 'must keep one current row per key in a batch job' points to ROW_NUMBER
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to choose the appropriate deduplication pattern for a stated requirement.

outlines.title: Late-Arriving Data: Event Time vs Process Time
outlines.description: Introduce the three clocks in a data pipeline and explain why late-arriving records cause missed or double-counted results.
keyPoints: Three distinct clocks: event time (when the action happened at the source), ingestion time (when the record reached the platform), and process time (when the pipeline handled it)
Late data is normal: offline mobile devices, network outages, batch backfills, clock skew, and timezone bugs all deliver events out of order
Windowing aggregates computed on process time assign an event to the wrong window; re-running them appends a second answer and double counts
Watermarks bound how long a streaming query waits for late events, balancing result latency against state size and dropped records
Exam trap: aggregating with append-only writes plus process-time windows both misses late events and duplicates results when a window is recomputed

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Late Data Without Double Counting
outlines.description: A fully worked problem showing how to absorb late-arriving orders into a daily revenue aggregate idempotently, without inflating totals.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a streaming job writes daily revenue per region to gold.daily_revenue. Orders can arrive up to 48 hours after their event time, and the job is restarted nightly after maintenance. Neither the totals nor the row counts may drift across restarts
Step 1 — Define event-time windows: group the deduplicated stream by window(event_time, '1 day') and region, then attach a watermark of 2 days so the job waits long enough for realistic lateness

Step 2 — Make the write keyed and idempotent: use foreachBatch to MERGE INTO gold.daily_revenue t USING batch s ON t.day = s.day AND t.region = s.region WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET revenue = s.revenue WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *

Step 3 — Recompute, then overwrite by key: because each batch carries the complete (or more complete) window, a keyed upsert replaces the stale value instead of adding to it; append-only INSERT would add a second row per key per run and double count

Step 4 — Verify: after a restart that replays the same window, SELECT day, region, COUNT(*) FROM gold.daily_revenue GROUP BY day, region HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 must return zero rows and daily totals must be unchanged

Analysis: the method works because the merge key is the aggregate grain (day + region), so replay is a replace rather than an increment; the classic pitfalls are appending instead of upserting, keying on a surrogate column so each run creates new rows, choosing a watermark shorter than the real arrival lag (late events silently dropped), and leaving unbounded state because no watermark was set at all
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to implement a keyed, idempotent write that absorbs late-arriving records without double counting results.

outlines.title: Schema on Write: Enforcement vs. Evolution
outlines.description: Introduce the central tension of this lesson: protecting downstream consumers with schema enforcement while still absorbing legitimate upstream schema changes with schema evolution.
keyPoints: Delta Lake validates every write against the target table's schema by default — that default behaviour is schema enforcement (schema on write).
Schema evolution is the deliberate, opt-in relaxation of that validation so compatible upstream changes, most often a new column, can be absorbed.
Exam framing: given a scenario, state whether enforcement should block the write or evolution should accept it, and name the exact option that enables it.
Both mechanisms serve one goal — analysis-ready tables that downstream jobs, dashboards, and ML features can trust.
[Table] Two-column contrast: enforcement (mismatch rejected, no option required) vs. evolution (mismatch accepted only when explicitly enabled).
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain schema enforcement on write and decide when to allow schema evolution.

outlines.title: How Delta Lake Enforces Schema on Write
outlines.description: Detail exactly what Delta Lake validates on every write and what the resulting failure looks like in a notebook.
keyPoints: On write, Delta Lake compares the incoming DataFrame to the table schema: column names, data types, and nullability must be compatible.
Extra columns in the DataFrame, missing columns from the table, and incompatible type changes are all rejected by default.
A nullable source column cannot be written into a NOT NULL target column, and incompatible type families are not silently coerced.
The failure surfaces as an AnalysisException describing the schema mismatch — recognising this message is an explicit exam objective.
Enforcement is a safety net: it prevents a 'successful' pipeline run from quietly corrupting a downstream table.
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain schema enforcement on write and decide when to allow schema evolution.

outlines.title: Worked Exercise: Diagnosing a Schema Mismatch
outlines.description: Walk through a full diagnosis of a failing append job and two corrective patterns — conform the data, or evolve the table.
keyPoints: Problem: a nightly append of (order_id, customer_id, amount, region) targets a Delta table defined as (order_id, customer_id, amount).
Step 1 — read the AnalysisException carefully: identify the extra column and confirm no type or nullability mismatch is hiding underneath it.
Step 2, fix A (conform): select only the target columns in the DataFrame before the write, keeping the table schema fixed and stable.
Step 3, fix B (evolve): write with option("mergeSchema", "true") so the new column is added to the table and back-filled with NULL for existing rows.
Analysis: enforcement matches by column name, not by position, so column ordering alone never causes the error; mergeSchema is purely additive and never renames or drops columns.
outlines.teachingObjective: Use merge schema options to absorb upstream schema changes safely.

outlines.title: The Evolution Toolkit: Four Knobs You Must Know
outlines.description: Present the four schema-change controls, what each one covers, and the operation each applies to.
keyPoints: mergeSchema — a read option for Parquet discovery and a write option for DataFrameWriter; it unions differing schemas and adds new columns as NULL.
spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled — the session- or table-level switch that enables schema evolution for MERGE and streaming writes.
overwriteSchema = true — replaces the table's schema together with its data on an overwrite; destructive and rarely the right production answer.
ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMNS and ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE — explicit DDL when schema change should pass through change management rather than happen per write.
Renaming or dropping columns is not covered by any of these options; it requires column mapping to be enabled on the table.
outlines.teachingObjective: Use merge schema options to absorb upstream schema changes safely.

outlines.title: Worked Exercise: Evolving Schema Inside a MERGE
outlines.description: Full worked solution for upserting source records that carry a brand-new column into an existing target Delta table.
keyPoints: Problem: a MERGE upsert from staging, which now includes loyalty_tier, into a silver.customers target that does not yet have that column.
Key insight: mergeSchema is a DataFrameWriter option and does not apply to MERGE; schema evolution inside MERGE is controlled by spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled.
Worked solution: set the session configuration, then run the standard MERGE with matched and not-matched clauses — the new column must be handled on both branches.
Analysis: autoMerge only adds top-level columns or widens compatible types; conflicting types such as INT into STRING still fail the write.
Pitfall: leaving the session configuration enabled leaves evolution silently active for unrelated writes later in the same notebook.
outlines.teachingObjective: Use merge schema options to absorb upstream schema changes safely.

outlines.title: Tradeoffs: Enforce, Evolve, or Quarantine?
outlines.description: Choose a schema-change policy for a shared ingestion pipeline under explicit operational, cost, and compliance constraints.
keyPoints: Setting: one ingestion job feeds dozens of downstream tables, and the upstream team ships ad-hoc column additions without a published schema contract.
Option A — strict enforcement: fail fast on any mismatch, zero silent corruption, but every upstream change pages the on-call engineer.
Option B — blanket autoMerge everywhere: never breaks on additive changes, but typo-duplicated columns and unbounded schema drift accumulate silently.
Option C — enforce at the landing zone, quarantine mismatched batches, and evolve explicitly into curated silver tables.

Recommendation: enforce by default, publish an additive schema contract with upstream, and allow evolution only at the integration layer where changes are provably additive — backed by schema-change detection alerts.
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain schema enforcement on write and decide when to allow schema evolution.

outlines.title: Exam Focus: Schema Evolution Traps and Recap
outlines.description: Consolidate the lesson into the decision rules and trap patterns that appear most often on the certification exam.
keyPoints: Default is enforcement: any question stating that a write failed with a schema mismatch is testing that you do not reach for overwriteSchema first.

overwriteSchema is destructive and replaces both data and schema; reserve it for deliberate rebuilds.

outlines.title: Why Declarative Pipelines Exist
outlines.description: Frames the shift from hand-written orchestration code to declaring datasets, and previews the lesson's exam objectives.
keyPoints: Define a declarative pipeline: the developer declares datasets and their queries, and the framework derives the execution order

Recognise that a pipeline is a graph of datasets, not a list of scheduled tasks
Exam trap: 'declarative' does not mean 'no code' — you still write the transformation logic, just not the orchestration

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Bronze to Gold in SQL and Python
outlines.description: A fully worked end-to-end problem that declares three chained datasets twice — once in SQL, once in Python — and analyses why the code order does not matter.
keyPoints: Statement: raw JSON events arrive in raw_events; declare bronze (streaming ingest), silver (deduplicated and cleaned) and gold (daily aggregate) datasets with the correct dependencies
Worked solution (SQL): three CREATE OR REFRESH statements whose FROM clauses form the chain bronze -> silver -> gold, with no ordering hints anywhere in the script
Worked solution (Python): three @dp.table functions that read LIVE.bronze_events and LIVE.silver_events respectively, returning transformed DataFrames
Analysis: execution order is a consequence of dataset references, not of statement position, so the same pipeline graph is produced by both languages
Common pitfalls: using a batch read where a streaming read is required; referencing a physical path instead of the pipeline dataset name; assuming files execute top-to-bottom

outlines.title: Key Terms: Declarative Pipelines
outlines.description: Consolidated definitions of the unit's core vocabulary, written in the phrasing the certification exam uses.
keyPoints: Declarative pipeline — a pipeline expressed as a set of dataset definitions; the engine infers execution order, retries and refresh from the resulting graph
Dataset — a named output of a pipeline, produced by exactly one query, materialised as a streaming table, materialized view or temporary view
Pipeline graph — the directed acyclic graph of datasets connected by references; edges are inferred from the tables a query reads
Streaming table — a dataset processed incrementally as new data arrives, declared with CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE or @dp.table over a streaming read
Materialized view — a dataset the framework recomputes as its inputs change, declarable in both SQL and Python
LIVE schema — the pipeline-local namespace used to reference another dataset in the same pipeline instead of a physical table name
Expectation — a declarative data-quality rule attached to a dataset that can warn, drop or fail rows at refresh time
Pipeline mode and trigger — the settings that decide whether a pipeline runs continuously or on demand, covered later in this unit
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain how declarative pipelines differ from hand-written orchestration code.

outlines.title: The Core Decision: Which Dataset Type Do You Declare?
outlines.description: Opens the lesson by framing the three dataset types a Lakeflow declarative pipeline can produce, and why choosing the right one is both an exam decision and a production cost decision.
keyPoints: Objective: distinguish streaming tables from materialized views, and select the right dataset type for a given requirement.
A declarative pipeline can produce three dataset types — streaming tables, materialized views, and views — and the type is fixed by the declaration you write.
Streaming tables ingest new data incrementally; materialized views persist the result of a query and refresh it during a pipeline update.
Exam trap: 'every dataset in a declarative pipeline is a materialized view' is false — the declaration (CREATE STREAMING TABLE vs CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW) governs semantics.

outlines.title: Side-by-Side: Streaming Table vs Materialized View
outlines.description: A decision-grade comparison of the two dataset types across the dimensions the exam and real pipelines care about: processing model, semantics, sources, refresh, cost, and best-fit use case.
keyPoints: [Table] Streaming table vs materialized view across: processing model, data semantics, typical source, refresh behavior, compute cost, and best-fit use case.
Streaming table: incremental, append-only processing; consumes from streaming sources such as cloud files read with Auto Loader, message buses, or another streaming table.
Materialized view: the result of a query is persisted and refreshed on each pipeline update; it can be incrementally refreshed when the defining query is incrementally computable.
Both are registered in Unity Catalog as regular tables and can be read with an ordinary SELECT — reading them is not what distinguishes them.

Decision rule: append or change-data-capture semantics from a streaming source → streaming table; complex joins, aggregations, and serving-layer business logic over existing tables → materialized view.
outlines.teachingObjective: Compare streaming tables and materialized views across decision-relevant dimensions.
