outlines.title: Streaming Tables: Incremental, Append-Only Ingestion
outlines.description: Explains the processing semantics of streaming tables in detail — incremental reads, append-only behavior, CDC handling, and checkpointing.
keyPoints: Streaming tables process data incrementally: each pipeline update consumes only data that has not been processed before.
Their native semantics are append-only; to apply updates and deletes, use AUTO CDC (APPLY CHANGES) in Python or APPLY CHANGES INTO in SQL.
Streaming tables are backed by Delta Lake and use checkpoints to track the source offsets already consumed, which is what makes incremental reads and restart-from-failure possible.
Typical sources: cloud object storage via Auto Loader, event-streaming platforms, and upstream streaming tables — a batch table read with readStream-style semantics is not a streaming source.
Exam trap: adding a filter or a cast does not turn a streaming table into a materialized view; the declaration, not the transformation, decides the dataset type.
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain the incremental, append-only semantics of streaming tables and how CDC is layered on top.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Declaring the Right Dataset for an Ingestion-to-Serving Pipeline
outlines.description: A fully worked problem that takes a realistic requirement from classification through SQL declaration, with an analysis of why the split works and where learners typically go wrong.
keyPoints: Problem statement: JSON order files land continuously in cloud storage; a daily revenue aggregate must be served to BI; the pipeline must not reprocess the entire history on every update.
Step 1 — classify the ingestion hop: continuous file arrival means CREATE STREAMING TABLE raw_orders AS SELECT ... FROM STREAM read_files(...), i.e. Auto Loader.

Step 2 — classify the serving hop: a grouped aggregation over an existing table means CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS SELECT date_trunc('day', order_ts) AS day, sum(amount) FROM raw_orders GROUP BY 1.
Step 3 — verify incrementality: the aggregation is a deterministic grouped aggregate over an append-only input, so the engine can refresh it incrementally instead of recomputing the full history.

Analysis: why the split works (incremental at the edge, recomputable at the serving layer), and the pitfall of declaring the ingestion hop as a materialized view, which forces a rescan of the landing zone every update.
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply dataset-type selection end to end, from requirement to working SQL declaration.

outlines.title: Materialized Views: When the Result Is the Product
outlines.description: Explains what a materialized view persists, when it can be refreshed incrementally, and which queries force a full recompute.
keyPoints: A materialized view stores the result of a query and refreshes that result as part of a pipeline update — it is a persisted, queryable table in Unity Catalog.
The engine incrementally refreshes a materialized view only when the defining query is incrementally computable; otherwise it recomputes the full result on each update.
Non-deterministic expressions — current_timestamp(), rand(), and similar — make the query non-incrementally-computable and force a full recompute of the affected materialized view.
Materialized views are the natural fit for serving-layer aggregations, multi-table joins, and dimensional models that business consumers query repeatedly.
Exam trap: a plain VIEW is not a materialized view — a view recomputes at query time and caches nothing, so it cannot deliver materialized-view performance.
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain materialized view persistence, incremental refresh eligibility, and full-recompute triggers.

outlines.title: Controlling Refresh: Updates, Full Refresh, and Incremental Processing
outlines.description: Covers how a pipeline update decides what to process, when a full refresh is warranted, and how refresh policy interacts with each dataset type.
keyPoints: Objective: control refresh behavior and incremental processing for each dataset type.
A pipeline update processes every dataset that has new data available, whose definition changed, or that was explicitly requested with a full refresh — plus the datasets that depend on it.
A full refresh clears the data of the selected dataset and its dependents and reprocesses everything from the source; reserve it for backfills, logic corrections, and unrecoverable schema changes.
By default streaming tables process only new source data, while materialized views process only changed input data when their query is incrementally computable.
Exam trap: a full refresh on a streaming table can replay the entire available source history and reprocess all change data — it is not equivalent to a normal incremental update.
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain pipeline update semantics, full refresh scope, and incremental processing defaults per dataset type.

outlines.title: Choosing a Refresh Strategy Under Cost and Latency Constraints
outlines.description: A constrained decision exercise: three plausible pipeline designs for the same requirement, each with pros and cons, ending in one justified recommendation.
keyPoints: Scenario: a two-billion-row sales history, a dashboard with a 4-hour freshness SLA, and a strict monthly compute budget that rules out reprocessing everything every 15 minutes.

[Options] Option A: streaming table ingestion + incrementally refreshed materialized view for the aggregate; Option B: full-refresh materialized view every 15 minutes; Option C: a plain VIEW over the streaming table queried directly by BI.

Pros and cons: A has the lowest steady-state cost and the best latency; B is simplest to reason about but recomputes the full two-billion-row history on every update; C stores nothing but pushes all compute to query time with no caching.
Decision dimensions: data volume, update frequency, freshness SLA, cost per pipeline update, and the need to replay or backfill history.
Recommendation: Option A — incremental processing at the ingestion edge and an incrementally refreshed aggregation at the serving layer, reserving full refresh for backfills and schema changes.
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a refresh strategy by weighing cost, latency, volume, and correctness constraints.

outlines.title: Why Declarative Pipelines Need Expectations
outlines.description: Frames data quality as a first-class declaration inside the pipeline definition rather than a downstream afterthought, and previews the three expectation actions.
keyPoints: Objective: explain why expectations are declared on a dataset instead of validated after the load.
An expectation is a named constraint attached to a dataset that is evaluated on every pipeline update.
Three actions map to three outcomes: warn (keep the record), drop (discard the record), fail (stop the update).
[Chart] Bar chart: records in the raw stream, records passing validation, and records dropped or failed for one sample update.
Exam trap: expectations are not a replacement for pipeline modes or triggers — they only govern what happens to invalid records.
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain the role of expectations in a Lakeflow declarative pipeline.

outlines.title: Expectation Syntax: SQL and Python
outlines.description: Presents the concrete syntax for declaring named expectations and selecting the warning, drop, or fail action in both SQL and Python pipeline code.
keyPoints: Objective: write an expectation and select its violation action using correct Databricks syntax.
SQL: CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW — omitting the ON VIOLATION clause means warn only.
Python: @dp.expect("valid_email", "email RLIKE '^[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@'" ), @dp.expect_or_drop(...), and @dp.expect_or_fail(...) decorate the dataset function.
Expectations are attached at the dataset level, may be multiple per dataset, and are evaluated per update on streaming tables and materialized views alike.
Exam trap: expect_or_drop removes only the violating rows — it does not remove rows from upstream tables, and expect_or_fail aborts the entire update.
outlines.teachingObjective: Write SQL and Python expectations that warn, drop, or fail on invalid records.

outlines.title: Warn vs Drop vs Fail: Choosing the Action
outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison of the three expectation actions across the dimensions an engineer must weigh when writing production expectations.
keyPoints: Objective: choose the correct expectation action for a stated data-quality requirement.
[Table] Rows = warn / drop / fail; columns = SQL keyword, Python decorator, effect on the violating record, effect on the update, effect on downstream tables, typical use case, main risk.
Warn keeps all rows and records a metric only — useful for monitoring before enforcement.
Drop preserves pipeline continuity but silently reduces volume, which can distort downstream aggregates if not monitored.
Fail is a hard gate: it blocks the update and protects downstream consumers at the cost of pipeline availability.
Exam trap: confusing "the update fails" with "the record is quarantined" — only drop behaves like a quarantine.
outlines.teachingObjective: Differentiate warn, drop, and fail behaviors and match them to requirements.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Writing Expectations for an Orders Pipeline
outlines.description: A fully worked problem that writes expectations for an ingestion-to-silver orders pipeline, with a worked solution and an analysis of why each action was chosen.
keyPoints: Statement: given a raw orders streaming table with columns order_id, customer_email, amount, order_ts, write expectations that reject null order_ids, drop malformed emails, and fail on negative amounts, then explain the ordering.

Worked solution — SQL: CONSTRAINT valid_order_id EXPECT (order_id IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW; CONSTRAINT valid_email EXPECT (customer_email RLIKE '@') ON VIOLATION DROP ROW; CONSTRAINT non_negative_amount EXPECT (amount >= 0) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE.

Worked solution — Python: @dp.expect_or_drop("valid_order_id", "order_id IS NOT NULL"), @dp.expect_or_drop("valid_email", "customer_email LIKE '%@%'"), @dp.expect_or_fail("non_negative_amount", "amount >= 0").
Analysis: fail is reserved for violations that signal an upstream contract break (negative money), because dropping them would corrupt revenue reporting; drops are used for row-level noise.
Common pitfall: writing every expectation as expect_or_fail makes the pipeline fragile to a single bad record.
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply expectation syntax to a realistic pipeline and justify each action.

outlines.title: Where Expectation Results Land: The Pipeline Event Log
outlines.description: Shows how results of every expectation are recorded as structured events and what each metric in the event payload means.
keyPoints: Objective: locate expectation results in the pipeline event log and read their structure.
Each update emits data-quality events containing the dataset name and, per expectation, the expectation name, dataset, passed_records, and failed_records.
Warned and dropped rows are distinguished by the expectation's action, not by separate counters — a drop reduces the dataset's row count, a warn does not.
The pipeline UI surfaces the same data as a Data quality tab, but the event log JSON is the authoritative source for programmatic alerting.
Exam trap: assuming an expectation with failed_records = 0 means the expectation was not evaluated — it simply means no violations occurred in that update.

outlines.title: Tradeoffs: Choosing an Expectation Policy for Production
outlines.description: A constrained decision problem: select an expectation action policy for three constraints in a production pipeline and justify one recommendation.

Option B — fail everywhere: strongest guarantee, but a single bad batch breaks the freshness SLA.
Option C — drop identifiers, fail on contract-breaking violations, warn on non-critical fields: differentiated enforcement.

outlines.title: What Changes When You Ship a Pipeline

outlines.title: Triggered Mode in Depth
outlines.description: Explains exactly what happens on each run of a triggered pipeline and which trigger types are available.
keyPoints: Triggered pipelines start compute, evaluate the full pipeline graph in dependency order, refresh every dataset once, then stop — you pay only for the run, not for idle time

Trigger types: manual (Run now / API), scheduled (time-based cadence such as every 15 minutes or a cron expression), and file arrival (new files detected in a source location, typically via Auto Loader)
Each run is incremental for streaming tables: source checkpoints mean only new or changed data since the last successful run is processed
Materialized views are recomputed from their defining query on the triggered run, so their freshness equals the trigger cadence
Best fit: batch or micro-batch SLAs (nightly finance rollups, hourly BI refreshes), cost-sensitive workloads, and pipelines with no hard sub-minute latency requirement
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe the run lifecycle of a triggered pipeline and select the right trigger type for a stated freshness requirement.

outlines.title: Triggered vs Continuous: Choosing Under Real Constraints
outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison across the dimensions that actually drive the mode decision in production and on the exam.
keyPoints: [Table] Triggered vs Continuous across five dimensions: freshness / stale-data window, compute cost model, setup and operational overhead, behaviour on failure and retry, and typical use case
Freshness: triggered = freshness equals trigger cadence; continuous = streaming tables refresh as new data arrives with seconds-to-minutes latency
Cost: triggered bills per run and stops when idle; continuous bills for an always-on cluster, so it must be justified by a hard latency SLA
Only production deployment mode supports continuous pipelines with automatic retries — development mode is for iteration, not for always-on serving
Common hybrid pattern: a continuous pipeline for bronze/silver streaming tables feeding a scheduled triggered pipeline that rebuilds gold materialized views

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Selecting Modes and Triggers for Three Pipelines
outlines.description: A fully worked selection problem with three concrete pipelines, a worked solution, and an analysis of why the method works.
keyPoints: Problem statement: pipeline A rebuilds a nightly finance rollup read at 07:00; pipeline B emits fraud-risk signals that must be at most 1 minute stale; pipeline C must begin ingesting the moment a file lands in the landing zone

Worked solution: A = triggered, scheduled trigger aligned to the nightly window, production deployment mode; B = continuous mode, production deployment mode, always-on compute; C = triggered with a file-arrival trigger (Auto Loader detecting new files)
Worked solution continued: A and C keep compute cost near zero between runs, satisfying the cost constraint without violating either SLA
Analysis — why the method works: the mode is derived from the freshness SLA, not from data volume; the trigger type is derived from what signals new work (a clock vs an external event)
Pitfall to avoid: choosing continuous mode for a daily dashboard, which pays 24/7 compute for data nobody reads until the morning — a classic distractor in certification questions

outlines.title: Deploying with Unity Catalog: Target Catalog and Schema
outlines.description: Walks through how a pipeline is bound to a Unity Catalog target and what that means for governance and discovery.
keyPoints: A pipeline has exactly one target catalog and one target schema; every dataset the pipeline declares is published into that location and registered in Unity Catalog
Datasets appear as managed tables and views with full column-level lineage from source to consumption — no manual DDL or CREATE TABLE is required

Development mode uses an isolated cluster that starts on demand and does not automatically retry failures — use it for iteration; production mode uses the configured compute policy and retries failed runs
One pipeline owns its target schema: two pipelines writing to the same schema can conflict, so separate consumers get separate pipelines or separate schemas
Access is governed by Unity Catalog grants (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, SELECT, MODIFY) applied to the pipeline's owner or service principal — running a pipeline never bypasses Unity Catalog permissions
outlines.teachingObjective: Deploy a pipeline into a specified catalog and schema and explain the resulting governance and lineage behaviour.

outlines.title: One Pipeline or Two? Deploying Dev and Prod
outlines.description: A concrete deployment-design decision with three options, explicit constraints, and one justified recommendation.
keyPoints: Constraints: protect production datasets from developer mistakes, keep iteration fast and cheap, keep pipeline definitions reproducible and reviewable, and stay within a small team's operational budget
Option A — a single pipeline with a parameterised target schema switched by deployment mode: minimal setup, lowest cost, but a misconfigured run can write into the production schema

Option B — separate development and production pipelines built from the same source repository, each with its own target catalog: full isolation and a clean promotion path, with a small amount of extra configuration to maintain
Option C — one pipeline writing straight to production, with developers using manual runs: simple, but there is no safe place to iterate and no promotion process to audit

Recommendation: Option B — isolation and reproducible promotion outweigh the extra configuration; A remains acceptable only for throwaway exploration, and the development/production deployment mode is not a substitute for a separate non-production target
outlines.teachingObjective: Choose a deployment topology and defend it against explicit constraints.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Deploying an Orders Pipeline Step by Step
outlines.description: A fully worked deployment problem covering pipeline settings, triggers, permissions, and post-deployment verification.
keyPoints: Task: deploy the orders pipeline from the previous lesson so that its datasets land in `prod_catalog.sales`, refresh every 30 minutes, and automatically retry on failure

Step 2 — mode and trigger: keep pipeline mode = triggered, add a scheduled trigger every 30 minutes, and set deployment mode = production so compute comes from the configured policy and failed runs retry

Step 3 — permissions: grant USE CATALOG on `prod_catalog` and USE SCHEMA plus SELECT / MODIFY on `sales` to the pipeline's service principal; confirm the schema is owned by this one pipeline and no other pipeline writes to it

Step 4 — verify: run the pipeline, confirm each dataset appears in Catalog Explorer with lineage back to the landing zone, and confirm downstream consumers query `prod_catalog.sales` rather than the raw source; analysis note — a successful run proves nothing until the schema is checked and consumers are repointed

outlines.title: Batch vs Streaming: Bounded and Unbounded Data
outlines.description: Introduce the distinction between bounded (batch) and unbounded (streaming) data, and explain why streaming is chosen for low-latency use cases.
keyPoints: Define bounded vs unbounded data: batch processes a fixed, complete dataset; streaming processes a continuously arriving dataset with no predefined end
Choose streaming when data must be acted on with near-real-time or up-to-the-millisecond latency
Common streaming sources: message queues and event-streaming platforms (Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, Google Cloud Pub/Sub)

Exam trap: 'unbounded' does not mean 'schema-less' — streaming DataFrames are still structured and require a schema

outlines.title: Batch DataFrame vs Streaming DataFrame
outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison of the batch DataFrame and the streaming DataFrame (unbounded table) model so learners can spot the API differences the exam tests.
keyPoints: [Table] Compare Batch DataFrame vs Streaming DataFrame across: creation API, underlying data model, schema handling, execution model, and typical sink

outlines.title: Micro-Batch Execution and Triggers
outlines.description: Explain how Spark Structured Streaming executes as a series of micro-batches and how triggers control the cadence of each batch.
keyPoints: By default Structured Streaming uses the micro-batch engine: it repeatedly queries the source for new data and processes each chunk as a small batch
Each micro-batch is an ordinary Spark job executed against the logical streaming DataFrame
Triggers control cadence: processingTime (e.g., 'every 5 seconds'), availableNow, once, and the experimental continuous mode
Micro-batch achieves near-real-time latency while retaining the reliability and exactly-once semantics of batch processing
Exam trap: 'continuous' is a distinct, experimental low-latency mode — do not confuse it with the default micro-batch processingTime trigger

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Read and Write a Streaming DataFrame
outlines.description: A fully worked solution building a minimal streaming read, transform, and write pipeline in PySpark.

outlines.title: Tumbling vs Sliding vs Session Windows
outlines.description: Contrast the three window types across the dimensions the exam tests, so learners can pick the right one for a given requirement.
keyPoints: [Table] Compare tumbling, sliding, and session windows on: fixed vs dynamic length, overlap, extra parameter, and whether an event can appear in multiple windows
Tumbling: fixed duration, non-overlapping, every event belongs to exactly one window
Sliding: fixed duration PLUS a slide interval; overlapping, so an event can belong to several windows
Session: no fixed length — window boundaries are set by a gap of inactivity, and an event can join multiple sessions
Exam trap: a sliding window with duration 10 min and slide 5 min produces overlapping windows; a duration equal to the slide makes it behave like a tumbling window

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Assigning Events to Tumbling and Sliding Windows
outlines.description: A fully worked problem that makes window boundary arithmetic concrete, including the analysis the university-depth question demands.
keyPoints: Problem: events arrive with event times t = 0, 3, 7, 12 minutes. Assign each event to (a) tumbling windows of 5 minutes and (b) sliding windows of 10 minutes with a 5-minute slide
Worked solution (tumbling, 5 min): [0,5) → {0, 3}; [5,10) → {7}; [10,15) → {12} — every event in exactly one window
Worked solution (sliding, 10 min duration / 5 min slide): [0,10) → {0, 3, 7}; [5,15) → {7, 12} — event 7 appears in TWO windows

Analysis: the window start is floor(event_time / slide) * slide for sliding windows, so an event near a boundary is emitted once per window it belongs to; this is why sliding windows produce more output rows than tumbling
Common pitfall: grouping by the wall clock (current_timestamp) instead of the event-time column — results then depend on when the query ran, not when the event happened
outlines.teachingObjective: Compute window assignments for tumbling and sliding windows from raw event times.

outlines.title: Watermarks: Bounding State and Handling Late Data
outlines.description: Define the watermark, explain how it bounds streaming state, and describe how late events are treated under different output modes.
keyPoints: Define a watermark: a moving threshold equal to (max event time seen so far − delay); events earlier than it are considered too late to be processed
Explain that the watermark lets Spark evict completed windows from the state store — without it, state grows forever
State the exam rule: withWatermark must be applied to the event-time column BEFORE the aggregation or join to take effect
Describe how late events behave: in append mode aggregates are finalized when the watermark passes the window end, so records arriving later are dropped
Exam trap: a watermark does NOT change window boundaries or delay individual records — it only governs when results are finalized and state is cleaned up
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain watermark semantics and their role in bounding state.

outlines.title: Design Tradeoff: Choosing the Watermark Delay
outlines.description: A constrained design decision where learners weigh result latency, completeness, and state cost to pick and justify a watermark delay.
keyPoints: Decision: choose a watermark delay for a real-time aggregation pipeline that must balance freshness, accuracy, and cluster memory
Option A — short delay (e.g. 1 min): lowest result latency and smallest state, but more late events silently dropped
Option B — long delay (e.g. 30 min): higher completeness, but larger state store and delayed results
Option C — no watermark: no dropping, but unbounded state growth and no append-mode finalization (not viable for production)
Recommendation: set the delay to the observed p99 event lateness, emit the metric for dropped-late-events, and revisit if the SLA or event skew changes
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a watermark delay by balancing latency, completeness, and state cost.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: A Stream-Stream Join with Watermarks
outlines.description: A fully worked problem on joining two watermarked streams, showing how watermarks bound join state and which pairs actually match.
keyPoints: Problem: join an ad-clicks stream to an ad-impressions stream on ad_id, both with a 10-minute watermark on event_time, and determine which pairs join
Worked solution: Spark buffers both sides in the state store; a click joins an impression when their ad_id matches and the click arrives within the watermark window of the impression
Worked solution: an unmatched row is evicted from state once its watermark passes that side's last-seen event time minus the delay
Analysis: two watermarks keep the join state symmetric and bounded; if one stream lags badly, its watermark advances slowly and its side of the state grows — an asymmetric-lag pitfall
Common pitfall: performing a stream-stream join with NO watermark forces Spark to keep all state forever and the job will eventually fail
outlines.teachingObjective: Compute stream-stream join matches and reason about how watermarks bound join state.

outlines.title: Delivery Guarantees: At-Most-Once to Exactly-Once
outlines.description: Defines the three delivery guarantees in terms of what a consumer observes after a failure, then explains how Structured Streaming plus Delta Lake achieves exactly-once.
keyPoints: Distinguish at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once by what the sink contains after a mid-batch failure
Structured Streaming writes a Write-Ahead Log before committing a micro-batch, giving at-least-once by default on a restart
Exactly-once requires an idempotent sink: the Delta Lake transaction log makes a replayed micro-batch a no-op instead of a duplicate
The source must be replayable — Kafka offsets and Delta tables are; a socket or a non-replayable source is not
Exam trap: exactly-once is a property of source + engine + sink together, not something a trigger setting can grant on its own
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain how source replayability, the WAL, and an idempotent Delta sink together produce exactly-once processing.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Sizing a Trigger Interval Against a Latency SLO
outlines.description: A fully worked problem in which a streaming ingestion job must satisfy a 30-second freshness SLO on a four-node cluster, and the student must select a trigger interval and justify it.
keyPoints: Problem statement: an events stream must land in a Delta table within 30 seconds of arrival; each micro-batch costs about 12 seconds of wall-clock time regardless of volume
Step 1 — compute the latency budget: available trigger interval = SLO minus batch processing time (30 − 12 = 18 seconds)
Step 2 — pick a configurable interval under the budget, e.g. processingTime('10 seconds'), giving worst-case ≈ 22 seconds of latency
Step 3 — compute cost: batches per hour at a 10-second interval = 360 versus 120 at 30 seconds, so cluster-hours roughly triple for identical data volume

Analysis: why the method works (latency = interval + processing time, so the interval is bounded by the SLO) and the pitfalls (forgetting processing time, using availableNow for a continuous SLO, ignoring auto-scaling)
outlines.teachingObjective: Compute a trigger interval from a latency SLO and quantify the resulting cost trade-off.

outlines.title: Trade-offs: Latency vs Cluster Cost for a Streaming Ingest
outlines.description: A decision scenario under explicit constraints: three trigger strategies are compared and one is recommended with justification.
keyPoints: Constraint set: 15-minute freshness SLO, event volume of 40 GB/day, a fixed monthly cluster budget, and a requirement for exactly-once into Delta
Option A — processingTime('5 seconds'): near-real-time latency, highest batch count and cluster-hours, most operational tuning
Option B — processingTime('1 minute'): sub-minute latency with far fewer batches; a reasonable default when the SLO is minutes, not seconds
Option C — availableNow scheduled every 15 minutes by a job: lowest cost, perfectly bounded batches, latency pinned to the schedule interval

[Recommendation] Given the 15-minute SLO and the budget, Option C is justified: availableNow decouples cost from idleness, keeps exactly-once through the checkpointed Delta sink, and leaves headroom to shorten the interval later

outlines.title: Declaring Orchestration Dependencies as a DAG
outlines.description: Explains how depends_on turns a collection of tasks into a directed acyclic graph, how parallelism is inferred, and how the default run-if condition gates downstream tasks.
keyPoints: Exam objective: define orchestration dependencies so downstream tasks run only after the correct upstream tasks finish
Dependencies are declared per task with depends_on; the graph is inferred from those declarations and never drawn by hand
A task with no depends_on starts immediately when the job run begins, so independent tasks execute in parallel
Fan-in (several upstream tasks feeding one downstream task) means the downstream task waits for every listed dependency; fan-out means one upstream task unblocks several downstream tasks
The graph must be acyclic — circular dependencies are rejected because they could never resolve to a runnable order
Default behaviour is 'run if all upstream dependencies succeeded'; other run-if conditions are covered in the next lesson
Exam trap: listing a dependency in a comment or a task name does nothing — only depends_on creates an edge
outlines.teachingObjective: Build a multi-task job whose dependencies form a valid directed acyclic graph (DAG).

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Designing a Five-Task Ingestion-to-Serving Job
outlines.description: A fully worked design problem: given five described workloads and their ordering constraints, produce the task list, task types, and depends_on edges, then analyse why the design works.
keyPoints: Problem statement: ingest raw orders with a declarative pipeline, clean them in a PySpark notebook, build a gold aggregate in SQL, refresh a dashboard SQL task, and run a Python validation script that must run after everything else
Step 1 — choose task types: pipeline task for ingestion, notebook task for cleaning, SQL task for the gold aggregate and for the dashboard refresh, Python script task for validation
Step 2 — derive the edges from the constraints: cleaning depends on ingestion; gold depends on cleaning; dashboard depends on gold; validation depends on gold and dashboard (fan-in)
Step 3 — verify the graph is acyclic and that the only parallel opportunity is the dashboard refresh and any branch not listed as a dependency
Worked solution: depends_on lists of [], ['ingest'], ['clean'], ['gold'], ['gold','dashboard'] for the five tasks respectively
Analysis: why the method works — depends_on encodes ordering, not runtime state, so the same graph yields the same order every run; and why fan-in is the safest place to attach validation

Common pitfalls: adding a validation task as a dependency of the dashboard instead of the reverse, forgetting that an omitted depends_on means 'start immediately', and expecting task order in the JSON to imply execution order

outlines.title: Design Decision: One Job with Many Tasks, or Many Small Jobs?
outlines.description: A constrained design decision between structuring a pipeline as a single multi-task job, several chained jobs, or one monolithic notebook, ending in a single justified recommendation.
keyPoints: Constraint set: the pipeline has five dependent steps, a nightly 02:00 SLA, three consumers of the gold table, and a team that needs to re-run just the validation step after a fix
Option A — one job with five tasks: single run history, one dependency graph, repairable per task, simplest scheduling
Option B — five jobs chained with Run Job tasks: finer-grained scheduling and ownership per step, but fragmented run history and harder-to-reason-about end-to-end latency
Option C — one notebook doing everything: fastest to write, but no dependency visibility, no partial repair, and no per-task monitoring
Recommendation: Option A for this pipeline, because the steps are tightly coupled, share one SLA, and Databricks supports repairing individual tasks inside a job run
When to revisit: if a step gains an independent schedule or a different owning team, promote it to its own job and trigger it as a downstream task

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Pass a Row Count from Task A to Task B
outlines.description: A fully worked parameter-passing problem: Task A loads a bronze table and must tell Task B how many rows were written so that Task B can skip downstream processing when the count is zero.
keyPoints: Statement: Task A writes bronze.orders; Task B must run its aggregation only when A wrote at least one row, otherwise exit early
Solution step 1: in Task A, after the write, call dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="row_count", value=spark.table("bronze.orders").count())
Solution step 2: in Task B, read it with dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(taskKey="A", key="row_count", default=0) and branch on the returned integer
Solution step 3: when the value is needed inside configuration JSON instead of code, reference it as {{tasks.A.values.row_count}}
Analysis: task values are typed and DAG-scoped, and the default argument is what keeps partial or repair runs from failing when Task A did not execute

outlines.title: Conditional Branching with Run-if Conditions
outlines.description: Show how the Run-if menu and custom conditions express if/else control flow at the task level, and walk through the canonical two-branch pattern.
keyPoints: [Table] Run-if options: All succeeded (default), At least one succeeded, All done, At least one failed, All failed, and Custom condition
Custom conditions combine {{tasks.<task>.result_state}} with == / != and logical operators for fine-grained gating
Classic if/else: two tasks both depend on a decision task; one runs when the state is SUCCEEDED and the other when it is FAILED
Branching is decided by the orchestrator from upstream state — a task cannot return a branch decision to the job
Design note: keep branch conditions readable; deep nested gating makes job graphs hard to debug and repair

outlines.title: Worked Problem: For Each Task to Refresh a List of Dates
outlines.description: A fully worked looping problem: an upstream task computes the list of dates needing a backfill, and a For each task runs one parameterized iteration per date.
keyPoints: Statement: an upstream task computes the last seven missing dates; a downstream loop must refresh each date in parallel with limited concurrency
Solution step 1: the upstream task calls dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="dates", value=["2024-05-01", ...]) with the computed list
Solution step 2: a For each task consumes {{tasks.compute_dates.values.dates}} and defines a nested task whose parameter references the current element as {{input}}
Solution step 3: set the concurrent-iterations limit (for example 4) to bound cluster load while still overlapping the work
Analysis: the array must come from a task that already ran, iterations are independent and unordered, and an empty array simply skips the loop instead of failing it

outlines.title: Design Choice: Branch Inside the Notebook or Model Branches as Tasks
outlines.description: A design decision under explicit constraints: implement conditional logic as if/else code inside one notebook, or model each branch as a separate task with Run-if conditions.
keyPoints: Option A — in-notebook branching: if/else inside Python. Pros: simple, one task, easy to unit-test locally. Cons: branch logic is invisible in the job graph, harder to retry an individual branch, and mixes orchestration with transformation logic
Option B — task-level branching with Run-if: pros visible graph, independent retries and repair of each branch, per-branch compute and permissions. Cons: more tasks to maintain and configure
Constraint set: a nightly job that must (a) be debuggable from the job UI and (b) allow rerunning only the failed branch without recomputing the whole pipeline
Recommendation: use Run-if conditions at the task level for coarse, operationally meaningful branches (validation gates, retry paths) and keep fine-grained value-level if/else inside the notebook
Hygiene: whichever option is chosen, make the decision explicit in the task description so reviewers can see why the graph looks the way it does
outlines.teachingObjective: Implement conditional branching in a workflow.

outlines.title: Trigger Types in Lakeflow Jobs
outlines.description: Establish the vocabulary of job triggers so students can classify any scheduling requirement before writing configuration.
keyPoints: Identify the trigger types available on a Lakeflow job: manual / Run now, scheduled (cron), file arrival, table update, and continuous [source 3][source 6]
Distinguish a trigger (what starts a run) from a schedule (the cadence at which the trigger fires)
Recognize that manual and Run now produce no recurring schedule and are the effective default when no trigger is configured
Given a business requirement, select the trigger type: fixed nightly batch → cron; irregular upstream file drops → file arrival; always-on streaming ingestion → continuous
Exam trap: a job carries one trigger type at a time, and changing the trigger type replaces the previous schedule rather than running both
outlines.teachingObjective: Classify scheduling requirements into the correct Lakeflow Jobs trigger type.

outlines.title: Cron Schedules: Syntax, Timezone, and Pause Semantics
outlines.description: Teach students to read, write, and reason about cron schedules inside the Databricks schedule editor, including the timezone setting that most exam distractors exploit.
keyPoints: Read a cron expression field by field as the Databricks schedule editor parses it, starting with the seconds field before minute, hour, day-of-month, month, and day-of-week
Apply the special characters *, -, /, and ? and understand a weekday expression such as 0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI
State that the schedule timezone is a job-level setting independent of the cluster, the notebook, and UTC, and that changing it shifts every future fire time
Explain Pause / Unpause behaviour: pausing disables the trigger without deleting the schedule, and fire times missed while paused are not replayed
Exam trap: cron schedules fire forward only — they never retroactively backfill a skipped interval, which is a separate backfill or repair operation
[Image] A labelled cron-field breakdown diagram showing how 0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI maps to a fire time in the selected timezone
outlines.teachingObjective: Construct and interpret a job cron schedule, including its timezone and pause behaviour.

outlines.title: File-Arrival Triggers: Wiring Jobs to Data Dependencies
outlines.description: Show how file-arrival triggers replace fragile 'guess the arrival time' cron schedules with a data-driven dependency.
keyPoints: Configure a file-arrival trigger by specifying the monitored location — a cloud storage path or a Unity Catalog volume — together with the polling interval
Recognize that the trigger fires once per newly detected batch of files since the last run, and that files already present when the trigger was created do not fire it
Explain the trade-off: event-agnostic polling adds detection latency and a small always-on monitoring cost, but removes guesswork and wasted early runs
Apply the pattern to irregular upstream deliveries such as a partner export, an IoT landing zone, or a third-party data drop
Exam trap: file arrival detects files, not completion — a partially written multi-file delivery can start a run before the upstream writer has finished
outlines.teachingObjective: Configure a file-arrival trigger and justify it over a time-based schedule for irregular upstream data.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: From Scheduling Requirement to Cron Expression
outlines.description: A fully worked exam-style problem that converts a written scheduling requirement into a concrete cron expression, a trigger choice, and the settings that make it correct.
keyPoints: Problem statement: an ingest job must run Monday–Friday at 06:30 US Eastern; team clusters are configured in UTC; an upstream partner drops files 'between 05:00 and 07:00 Eastern on weekdays, but sometimes not at all'

Part (a) solution: write the expression as 0 30 6 ? * MON-FRI using the seconds-first field order, then set the job schedule timezone to America/New_York so 06:30 means 06:30 Eastern regardless of the cluster's UTC configuration
Part (b) solution: replace the fixed schedule with a file-arrival trigger on the partner landing path, because arrival time is nondeterministic and some days produce no delivery at all
Part (c) solution: where a fixed reporting window is still required downstream, create a second, separate cron-triggered job, because a single job can hold only one trigger type

Analysis: why the method works and the pitfalls — a five-field POSIX expression is misread by the seconds-first parser, ? and * are not interchangeable in the day fields, and MON-FRI silently skips holidays and DST-shifted fire times
outlines.teachingObjective: Translate a written scheduling requirement into a correct cron expression and trigger configuration.

outlines.title: Choosing a Trigger Strategy Under Real Constraints
outlines.description: A constrained decision exercise: pick a trigger strategy for one pipeline given a freshness target, an unpredictable upstream, and a fixed compute budget.
keyPoints: Constraints: 5-minute freshness target for the silver layer, upstream files arriving anywhere between 05:00 and 07:00 Eastern with roughly one gap day per week, and a hard limit on always-on compute
Option A — scheduled cron: deterministic run windows and the cheapest monitoring, but wasted runs on gap days and stale data on late-arrival days
Option B — file arrival: no wasted runs and immediate reaction to delivery, at the cost of polling latency and no guarantee the delivery is complete
Option C — continuous: near-instant freshness, but always-on compute that breaks the budget constraint and is unnecessary for a once-daily batch feed

Recommendation: file arrival on the landing zone, plus a separate cron-triggered job for the fixed reporting window — two jobs, because one job holds one trigger type; justify the choice against the freshness and cost constraints explicitly
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a trigger strategy against explicit freshness, reliability, and cost constraints.

outlines.title: Notifications: Destinations, Scopes, and Events
outlines.description: Introduce the notification configuration surface so students can wire a job's outcome to the people who need to act on it.
keyPoints: Identify the notification destinations a job can target: email addresses and connected destinations such as Slack, Microsoft Teams, PagerDuty, or a generic webhook configured for the workspace
Select the notification events to subscribe to: run start, run success, run failure, and a duration-warning threshold for runs that exceed an expected time
Distinguish job-level notifications, which apply to the whole job and every task, from task-level notifications, which apply to one task and can carry a different recipient list
Explain why a production default of failure-only (plus a duration warning on long tasks) preserves signal, while notify-on-success to a broad list creates alert fatigue
Exam trap: notifications are job and task configuration only — they are not the same feature as Databricks SQL alerts, and they never retry, repair, or restart a failed task

outlines.title: Retries, Retry Intervals, and Task Timeouts
outlines.description: Explain per-task retry and timeout configuration in Lakeflow Jobs and when retries actually help versus hide a deterministic bug.
keyPoints: Retry configuration is set per task: maximum number of retries, minimum/maximum retry interval (exponential backoff), and whether to retry when the task times out
Timeouts bound how long a task may run; a timed-out task fails fast instead of blocking the DAG indefinitely, and then obeys the retry policy if retry-on-timeout is enabled

Retries only rescue transient failures (cloud I/O blips, throttling, spot-instance loss); deterministic code, schema, or data-quality errors fail again after the final retry — retries are not a substitute for a fix
[Table] Configuration comparison: no retry vs retry with backoff only vs retry-on-timeout enabled — trade-off between run duration, cost, and blast radius
Exam trap: a retry re-executes the whole task, so writes must be idempotent (MERGE/upsert or overwrite are safe; blind append duplicates rows)
[Image] Retrieval-augmented diagram: stacked attempt timeline showing attempt 1 fail, backoff wait, attempt 2 fail, longer backoff, attempt 3 succeed — all labels in English
outlines.teachingObjective: Configure retries and timeouts to make jobs resilient.

outlines.title: Run-if Conditions: Controlling Behaviour After a Failure
outlines.description: Teach the run-if conditions that determine whether a downstream task executes, and how dependency failure produces skipped rather than failed tasks.
keyPoints: Run-if options for a task: All succeeded (default), At least one failed, All failed, At least one succeeded, All done — choose the condition, not the task, to express post-failure behaviour
Failure semantics: the failing task reaches state Failed; direct and transitive downstream tasks are Skipped, not Failed — the overall job run is Failed
Typical exam scenario: add an alert/notification or cleanup task that runs only when something fails (At least one failed) or always runs (All done)
A task can only run when its dependencies satisfy their run-if condition; with All succeeded, a skipped dependency propagates skipping down the DAG
[Table] Run-if decision table: condition × state of upstream tasks × whether the task runs — mapped to typical use cases (notification, cleanup, fallback path)
outlines.teachingObjective: Reason about dependency and run-if semantics when tasks fail.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Choosing Retry and Timeout Settings for an SLA
outlines.description: Fully-worked problem that turns a stated production symptom and an SLA into concrete retry, timeout, and run-if configuration, with an analysis of why the settings work.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a nightly 3-task job must finish within 30 minutes; Task 1 calls an external REST API that intermittently returns HTTP 503 responses; the API call hangs roughly one night in ten; the team must be notified when the run genuinely fails
Step 1 — classify the failure: an HTTP 503 is transient, so it belongs in the retry path; a hang is a liveness problem, so it needs a timeout
Step 2 — set Task 1 to 3 retries with a 30-second minimum retry interval and retry-on-timeout enabled, so 503s and hangs are both absorbed inside the SLA budget
Step 3 — set a task timeout of 5 minutes (well under the 30-minute SLA) so a hang fails fast rather than consuming the window; ~4 attempts × up to 5 minutes plus backoff stays inside budget

Step 4 — add a notification task with run-if = At least one failed so alerts fire only on a genuine terminal failure; also ensure the Task 1 write uses MERGE, because retries re-execute the whole task
Analysis and pitfalls: max retries × timeout must fit the SLA, a timeout can be retried indefinitely if retry-on-timeout is enabled carelessly, and retrying a non-idempotent append duplicates rows
outlines.teachingObjective: Translate an SLA and an observed failure mode into a concrete retry, timeout, and run-if configuration.

outlines.title: Diagnosing Failed Runs in the Run History
outlines.description: Teach a systematic triage procedure using the job run history, task-level details, logs, and the run timeline.
keyPoints: Run states to recognise: Queued, Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, Skipped, Timed out, Canceled, Internal error — and the difference between a failed task and a skipped task

Triage order: open the job run → check the run timeline/Gantt view for the first long or red segment → open that task run → read the error message → drill into cluster logs / driver logs / Spark UI for the stack trace

Classify the root cause: task logic or data error (code/schema/quality), infrastructure error (cluster start failure, out-of-memory, spot loss), timeout, or a dependency/skip caused by an upstream failure
Read the run's parameters and task values at failure time — a bad or stale parameter value is a common cause of a task that succeeds in development and fails in production
Output of diagnosis: a decision between re-run with no change, repair run after a fix, or targeted repair plus backfill for a specific date range
outlines.teachingObjective: Diagnose failed runs using the job run history.

outlines.title: Repair Runs, Partial Runs, and Backfill
outlines.description: Explain how repair runs re-execute only failed and skipped tasks, how partial runs and parameter overrides work, and when a repair is the wrong choice.
keyPoints: A repair run re-runs only the failed task and the tasks that were skipped downstream, reusing the original run's parameters, task values, and job configuration — it does not re-execute already-succeeded tasks
Partial runs and repairs make debugging failed tasks faster and cheaper by avoiding redundant recomputation of expensive upstream work [source 4]

You can select specific tasks to repair (for example, repair from the failing task onward) and optionally override parameters for the repair; a repair always re-runs downstream tasks of the repaired task
Correctness precondition: repairs assume idempotent, partitioned, or MERGE-based writes — repairing a non-idempotent append pipeline can duplicate data

Repair versus alternatives: repair = same run, minimal recompute; full re-run = fresh run, all tasks, safest for non-idempotent pipelines; backfill = run a new job run with an earlier date-range parameter
[Image] Conceptual diagram: a 5-task DAG where task 3 is red, tasks 4-5 are skipped, and a repair run re-executes only tasks 3, 4, and 5 — all labels in English

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Repairing a Failed Multi-Task Pipeline
outlines.description: Fully-worked problem where a learner must scope a repair run correctly and quantify the savings versus a full re-run, with a robustness analysis.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a nightly 5-task DAG ran for 35 minutes; Task 1 (ingest, 8 min) and Task 2 (silver MERGE, 14 min) succeeded; Task 3 (gold aggregate) failed with a schema error; Tasks 4-5 were skipped; the schema fix is a two-line change; business owners want gold tables refreshed before 08:00
Step 1 — read the evidence: run history shows Task 3 Failed, Tasks 4-5 Skipped, overall run Failed; opening the Task 3 error message reveals the renamed source column

Step 2 — fix the cause, not the symptom: update the gold aggregation to use the new column name and re-validate the notebook; do not simply increase retries, because a deterministic schema error will fail again
Step 3 — choose the scope: use Repair run so only Tasks 3, 4, 5 re-execute, reusing the original run's parameters and Task 2's silver output; Task 1 and Task 2 are not recomputed
Step 4 — quantify: repair recomputes only the failed and skipped branch (~35 − 22 = roughly 13 minutes of work) instead of all 35 minutes, cutting both compute cost and time to SLA

Analysis and pitfalls: a repair is only safe because Task 2's silver write is a MERGE and not a destructive overwrite; if a skipped upstream write were non-idempotent, a full re-run or a scoped backfill would be correct; repair also re-runs downstream tasks, so downstream side effects must be safe to repeat
outlines.teachingObjective: Scope and justify a repair run using run-history evidence.

units.title: Governance with Unity Catalog
objectives: Students will be able to manage data assets and access controls through Unity Catalog.
Students will be able to apply security, lineage, and auditing practices to lakehouse data.

lessons.title: The Unity Catalog Object Model
objectives: Students will be able to describe the catalog, schema, table, view, and volume hierarchy.
Students will be able to create and organize governed objects for a data engineering project.

outlines.title: Introducing the Unity Catalog Object Model
outlines.description: Orient students to Unity Catalog as the unified governance layer and introduce the nested namespace that every later scene builds on.
keyPoints: Unity Catalog is the unified governance layer for data and AI assets across workspaces, compute, and engines in the Databricks Data Intelligence Platform
All governed objects live inside one nested namespace: metastore → catalog → schema → tables, views, and volumes
Every object is addressed by a fully qualified name, for example sales.gold.orders
[Table] Governed (Unity Catalog) vs ungoverned (hive_metastore) objects: scope, access control, lineage, and discoverability
Exam framing: given a governance task, identify which level of the hierarchy it applies to
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain why Unity Catalog's unified object model is the foundation of governance in Databricks.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A clean, professional infographic of a nested governance hierarchy: a metastore box at the top containing catalog boxes, each catalog containing schema boxes, each schema containing three object boxes labelled Table, View and Volume. Layered rounded rectangles connected by thin lines, flat minimal corporate design, neutral blue and grey palette, no people, all labels in English.

outlines.title: Metastores, Catalogs, and Schemas
outlines.description: Establish the container half of the hierarchy: the metastore, catalogs, and schemas, including the DDL that creates them and how names resolve.
keyPoints: The metastore is the top-level container for a region; it is attached to workspaces and holds all catalogs
A catalog groups schemas; a schema (formerly 'database') groups tables, views, volumes, functions, and models
DDL: CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS sales; followed by CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS sales.gold;
Context switching with USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA determines the default catalog/schema used to resolve unqualified names
Exam trap: catalogs and schemas are containers only — they hold no data themselves
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe the metastore, catalog, and schema levels of the hierarchy and create them with DDL.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: The Container Hierarchy
outlines.description: Confirm students can place metastore, catalog, and schema correctly before object types are introduced.
keyPoints: Identify which level groups schemas (catalog) and which level groups tables and volumes (schema)
Decompose a fully qualified three-part name into catalog, schema, and object
Distractor watch: a metastore is not a catalog, and a schema is not a catalog
Distractor watch: tables are not the only object type that can live inside a schema
outlines.teachingObjective: Correctly locate each container level of the Unity Catalog hierarchy.

outlines.title: Tables and Views Under Governance
outlines.description: Cover the tabular object types and explicitly flag that non-tabular files are governed by a different object type, setting up the volume prerequisite.
keyPoints: Tables are the primary tabular objects; Unity Catalog manages Delta tables as either managed or external
Managed table: Unity Catalog owns the storage location and lifecycle, and DROP TABLE deletes the data as well
External table: the table points at a path you control; DROP TABLE removes only the metadata and the files remain
Views and materialized views are query-defined objects governed by the same permission, lineage, and auditing model
Non-tabular files cannot live in a table — Unity Catalog governs them with a different object type, the volume
outlines.teachingObjective: Distinguish managed and external tables and views, and recognize that files need a different governed object.

outlines.title: Volumes: Governing Non-Tabular Files
outlines.description: Teach the volume object fully before any quiz or exercise depends on it: what it is, its two modes, its path, and when to choose it.
keyPoints: A volume is a governed logical container for files and directories — CSV, JSON, images, ML artifacts — accessed at /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume>
Managed volume: Unity Catalog manages the underlying storage location; external volume: points at a path registered through an external location
Use a volume when the data is files; use a table when the data is rows queried with SQL
Volumes inherit the same privileges, auditing, and lineage model as tables and views, so file access stays governed
Exam trap: a volume has no schema and no ACID guarantees — reading a volume returns files, not rows
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe what a volume is, distinguish managed from external volumes, and decide when a volume is the right object.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Choosing the Right Object Type
outlines.description: Assess object-type selection now that table, view, and volume have all been taught, including the volume case directly.
keyPoints: Select the correct object type for storing non-tabular files under governance — the volume, not the table
Distinguish managed from external objects when the requirement is that data survives a DROP
Distinguish a table from a view when the requirement is a stored query rather than stored data
Distractor watch: a volume is not a schema, and a table cannot directly hold raw files
outlines.teachingObjective: Match a stated requirement to the correct Unity Catalog object type.

outlines.title: Worked Problems: Creating Governed Objects
outlines.description: Fully-worked DDL problems that create catalogs, schemas, tables, and a landing volume, with analysis of why each choice is correct.
keyPoints: Problem 1: Write idempotent DDL that creates a catalog and schema for a retail analytics team
Problem 2: Create one managed table and one external table, then explain how DROP TABLE differs for each
Problem 3: Create the volume sales.raw_landing and land raw CSV files into it — explain why a volume is used instead of a table
Analysis: object ownership determines data lifecycle; the classic pitfall is creating objects in hive_metastore where Unity Catalog governance does not apply
Full solution walkthrough with the expected DDL and the grading points that earn credit
outlines.teachingObjective: Create governed objects correctly and justify the object type chosen for each requirement.

outlines.title: Explore the Unity Catalog Hierarchy
outlines.description: An interactive hierarchy explorer in which students click through metastore, catalog, schema, and object levels and read the fully qualified names.
keyPoints: Click through the metastore → catalog → schema → object tree and read the fully qualified name of each node
Toggle between container levels to see which object types may live inside each one
Switch the current catalog and schema to see how unqualified names resolve
Immediate feedback on which level a governance action such as create, grant, or drop applies to
outlines.teachingObjective: Reinforce the hierarchy and naming model through hands-on exploration.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Namespaces and Naming
outlines.description: Verify that students can resolve names, write fully qualified references, and read volume paths correctly.
keyPoints: Resolve an unqualified object name using the current catalog and schema context
Write the fully qualified path of a file inside a governed volume
Distractor watch: /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/<volume> is a filesystem path, not a three-part SQL name
Distractor watch: renaming or moving an object changes its qualified name and the grants attached to it
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply correct naming and path conventions across all governed object types.

outlines.title: Worked Problems: Organizing a Data Engineering Project
outlines.description: Worked project-organization problems that design and create the catalog, schema, and volume layout for a medallion-style data engineering project.
keyPoints: Scenario: one catalog per environment, medallion schemas bronze, silver, and gold, plus a landing volume for raw files
Problem 1: Design and write the DDL for the catalog, the three schemas, and the landing volume
Problem 2: Decide where raw files, cleaned tables, and curated tables belong, and justify each placement
Problem 3: Apply a naming convention and map it onto the three-part namespace
Analysis: layer-per-schema organization enables least-privilege grants, lineage tracking, and cost attribution
outlines.teachingObjective: Create and organize a complete set of governed objects for a realistic data engineering project.

outlines.title: Managed vs External: Choosing Where Data Lives
outlines.description: A constrained decision scene weighing managed against external objects and committing to one justified recommendation for a shared dataset.
keyPoints: Decision: store a shared dataset as a managed object or as an external object in Unity Catalog
Option A — Managed: Unity Catalog owns the storage path and lifecycle, simplest to operate, but DROP deletes the data
Option B — External: you control the path, for example a shared bucket; data survives DROP, but you own location management and storage cost
Constraints that decide it: retention policy, cross-engine and legacy consumers, storage ownership, and restore requirements
One justified recommendation for a retention-constrained shared dataset, plus the exam cue phrase that signals it
outlines.teachingObjective: Choose between managed and external objects under explicit constraints and defend the choice.

outlines.title: Lesson Assessment: The Unity Catalog Object Model
outlines.description: End-of-lesson assessment covering the hierarchy, object selection, and lifecycle behavior with exam-style distractors.
keyPoints: Hierarchy and scope questions across the metastore, catalog, schema, and object levels
Object-selection questions requiring a choice between table, view, and volume for a stated requirement
Lifecycle questions on what DROP does to managed versus external objects
Exam-objective phrasing with distractors that mirror real certification traps
outlines.teachingObjective: Demonstrate mastery of the Unity Catalog object model and the creation and organization of governed objects.

lessons.title: Access Control and Fine-Grained Security
objectives: Students will be able to grant and revoke privileges on securable objects.
Students will be able to apply row and column-level security to protect sensitive data.

outlines.title: Unity Catalog Access Control Fundamentals
outlines.description: Establish the three building blocks of Unity Catalog authorization — principals, securable objects, and privileges — and how GRANT/REVOKE operate on them.
keyPoints: Identify the three building blocks of authorization: principals (users, groups, service principals), securable objects (metastore > catalog > schema > table/view/volume/function), and privileges
Explain that access is additive: privileges are added with GRANT and removed with REVOKE, and Unity Catalog has no DENY statement — the absence of a grant is the denial
Distinguish object privileges (SELECT, MODIFY, CREATE TABLE) from path privileges (USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA) that are required just to reach the object

[Table] Securable object to common privileges: catalog -> USE CATALOG, CREATE SCHEMA; schema -> USE SCHEMA, CREATE TABLE, CREATE VIEW; table -> SELECT, MODIFY; volume -> READ VOLUME, WRITE VOLUME; function -> EXECUTE
Exam trap: a principal with SELECT on a table still gets TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND until it also holds USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA on the parent objects
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to name the principals, securable objects, and privileges that form the Unity Catalog security model.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A clean professional infographic diagram of a four-level hierarchy for a data governance platform: a top-level metastore box, branching down to catalog boxes, then schema boxes, then table, view, volume and function icons at the bottom. Dashed arrows labelled USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA point down the hierarchy, and solid arrows labelled SELECT, MODIFY and EXECUTE point to the leaf objects. A separate small figure of a person icon and a group icon on the left is labelled principals, with arrows labelled GRANT pointing toward the objects. Flat vector style, blue and grey palette, all labels and text in English.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: GRANT and REVOKE on Securable Objects
outlines.description: A fully worked SQL problem that grants least-privilege read access to a group and revokes a mis-scoped write grant, with analysis of why the ordering and scope matter.
keyPoints: Problem statement: group `analysts_eu` must be able to query `sales.gold.orders`, must not be able to modify it, and must not be able to query any other schema in the `sales` catalog
Worked solution (path privileges first): GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG sales TO analysts_eu; GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA sales.gold TO analysts_eu;
Worked solution (object privilege): GRANT SELECT ON TABLE sales.gold.orders TO analysts_eu;
Remove the accidental write grant: REVOKE MODIFY ON TABLE sales.gold.orders FROM analysts_eu;
Analysis: grants are additive and idempotent, and REVOKE of a privilege that was never granted is a no-op rather than an error — verify the final state with SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE sales.gold.orders
Common pitfall: granting SELECT ON CATALOG sales reads every current and future table in the catalog, which breaks least privilege; grant at the narrowest object that satisfies the requirement
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to write correct GRANT and REVOKE statements that produce a least-privilege access state.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Privileges, GRANT, and REVOKE
outlines.description: Exam-style checkpoint on privilege types, GRANT/REVOKE syntax and scope, and the behavior of revoking access.
keyPoints: Determine which privilege must be granted for a principal to simply reference a catalog or schema in a fully qualified table name
Select the correct GRANT statement form for a table versus a catalog versus a schema
Predict the outcome of REVOKE on a privilege that the principal never held
Reason about the difference between granting SELECT at table scope and granting SELECT at catalog scope
Distractors mirror common exam traps: assuming a DENY statement exists, ignoring USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA path privileges, and confusing MODIFY with SELECT
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to apply privilege semantics and GRANT/REVOKE syntax to exam-style scenarios.

outlines.title: Inherited Grants, Explicit Grants, and Ownership
outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison of the three ways a principal can hold authority over an object, across the dimensions that appear in exam scenarios.
keyPoints: Compare three sources of authority: object ownership, privileges inherited from a parent object or group membership, and privileges granted explicitly on the object
[Table] Dimension rows: who can grant or revoke, whether the authority can be revoked without transferring the object, whether it survives a DROP and re-CREATE, and which SQL statement reveals it
Ownership: the owner holds all privileges on the object and the sole right to grant on it; ownership is changed with ALTER ... OWNER TO, not with GRANT
Inheritance: privileges granted on a catalog or schema flow down to contained objects, and privileges granted to a group flow to every member including future members
Exam trap: revoking a privilege from a user does not help if the user is still a member of a group that holds the same privilege — check group membership first
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to determine why a principal has access by distinguishing ownership, inheritance, and explicit grants.

outlines.title: Interactive: Simulated Privilege Evaluator
outlines.description: A sandbox where learners write GRANT and REVOKE statements against a simulated Unity Catalog hierarchy and then run queries as a selected principal to see which succeed or fail.
keyPoints: Write GRANT/REVOKE statements on a mock catalog, schema, table, and function
Switch the active principal among a user, a group member, and a service principal
Run a query as that principal and observe whether the engine resolves the object or returns a permission error
Watch the evaluator display the resolution chain: USE CATALOG, then USE SCHEMA, then the object privilege, marking each step as satisfied or missing
Test the inheritance rule by granting at schema scope and observing the effect on every table beneath it
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to predict the effective access of a principal from the grants in place.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Ownership, Inheritance, and Effective Access
outlines.description: Exam-style checkpoint on resolving why a principal can or cannot reach an object.
keyPoints: Determine the single change that restores least privilege when a user inherits excessive access from a legacy group
Identify which statement transfers full control of an object rather than granting a single privilege
Predict the effect of granting at catalog scope versus schema scope on future tables created later
Reason about a failed query that reports a missing table when the real cause is a missing path privilege
Distractors mirror real exam traps: assuming group grants can be revoked individually, assuming DROP and re-create resets ownership, and confusing ALTER ... OWNER TO with GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to diagnose access outcomes from ownership, inheritance, and explicit grants.

outlines.title: Row-Level Security with Row Filter Functions
outlines.description: Introduce row-level security in Unity Catalog: row filter functions attached to a table that silently restrict which rows each principal can see.
keyPoints: Describe the mechanism: a user-defined SQL function that returns BOOLEAN is attached to a table with ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER <function> ON (<columns>) and is evaluated for every query
Identify the identity functions used inside the filter: current_user(), is_account_group_member('group'), and current_metastore()
Contrast the two implementation styles: attaching a row filter to the table itself, versus shipping a dynamic view that wraps the base table with a filtering predicate
Explain the guarantee: the filter is applied by the engine before results are returned, so it cannot be bypassed by rewriting the SELECT statement or by querying through a derived view
Exam trap: a row filter restricts rows, not columns — and it is removed with ALTER TABLE ... DROP ROW FILTER, not with REVOKE
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to explain how row filter functions restrict visible rows per principal.

outlines.title: Worked Example: Row Filters and Column Masks
outlines.description: A fully worked DDL example that protects a customers table with a column mask on email and a row filter on region, plus a query that demonstrates the resulting behavior for two principals.
keyPoints: Problem statement: `sales.gold.customers` must show full email addresses only to the PII readers group, and EU analysts must see only customers in their own region
Column mask solution: CREATE FUNCTION sales.gold.mask_email(email STRING) RETURNS STRING RETURN CASE WHEN is_account_group_member('pii_readers') THEN email ELSE '***@***.com' END;
Attach the mask: ALTER TABLE sales.gold.customers ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK sales.gold.mask_email;
Row filter solution: CREATE FUNCTION sales.gold.region_filter(region STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN RETURN is_account_group_member('global_admins') OR region = 'EU';
Attach the filter: ALTER TABLE sales.gold.customers SET ROW FILTER sales.gold.region_filter ON (region);

Analysis: both functions run inside the engine at query time, so the masked value and the filtered rows appear in every SELECT; the masking function must be owned and EXECUTE-able by the querying principal

Common pitfall: masking the column but leaving SELECT on the raw column available through a different table or view that was populated before the mask was applied — apply masks at the source table, not only downstream
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to implement column masks and row filters and predict the output each principal receives.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Row and Column-Level Security
outlines.description: Exam-style checkpoint on fine-grained security implemented with row filter functions and column masks.
keyPoints: Select the correct DDL to attach a masking function to a column versus a filtering function to a table
Determine which predicate inside a filter function correctly compares the querying principal to a group
Predict the output of a SELECT issued by a member of the masked group
Reason about why a dynamic view and a row filter can produce the same visible result but differ in maintenance
Distractors mirror real exam traps: confusing SET MASK with SET ROW FILTER, using a user name where a group check is required, and assuming a row filter can hide a column
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to apply row filter and column mask syntax to protective scenarios.

outlines.title: Choosing a Fine-Grained Security Pattern
outlines.description: A decision under constraints: three ways to deliver row and column-level security, their costs, and one justified recommendation for a given scenario.
keyPoints: Constraints: 40 analysts across three regions, one shared `customers` table, a compliance requirement to mask email for everyone outside the PII group, and no duplication of the data
Option A — dynamic views: coarse and easy to reason about, but every consumer must be redirected to the view and the base table must be locked down separately
Option B — row filter functions plus column masks on the base table: applies to all current and future query paths, but functions must be maintained, tested, and owned correctly

Option C — physically separate tables or schemas per region: simplest to explain and audit, but duplicates data, multiplies storage and pipeline cost, and cannot mask a column for an authorised region

Recommendation: Option B on the single governed table, because the compliance rule is per-principal and must survive new downstream consumers; layer ABAC tag policies on top to manage scale instead of writing per-group grants by hand
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to justify a fine-grained security design against explicit constraints.

outlines.title: Tag-Based Policies, Least Privilege, and Verifying Access
outlines.description: Move from hand-written grants to scalable governance: attribute-based access control via tags, least-privilege hygiene, and the tools that reveal effective access.
keyPoints: Explain attribute-based access control (ABAC): policies attach privileges, row filters, and column masks to a governable tag, and the policy applies automatically to every object that carries that tag
Compare the trade-off: tagging scales to thousands of objects because the policy is written once, while per-object GRANT statements must be repeated and re-audited as the estate grows

Apply least privilege in practice: grant to groups rather than individuals, grant at the narrowest scope that satisfies the requirement, and grant on catalogs or schemas only when the requirement is genuinely estate-wide

Verify effective access with the platform's own metadata: SHOW GRANTS ON <object>, current_user() and is_account_group_member() in a diagnostic query, the information_schema privilege views, and the audit system table that records who ran which statement
Exam trap: after tightening permissions, a query can fail with a not-found error rather than a permission error — always check the path privileges before assuming the object was deleted
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to apply tag-based policies and verify effective access for a principal.

mediaGenerations.prompt: A flat vector infographic showing a database table on the left with several rows, where one column is highlighted. Two shields protect it: one shield labelled row filter covers a subset of rows and shows rows being hidden, and a second shield labelled column mask covers the highlighted column and shows stars replacing the values. On the right, a small panel shows two different user silhouettes each seeing a different view of the same table. Clean professional blue and grey palette, no human facial features, all labels and text in English.

outlines.title: Lesson Assessment: Access Control and Fine-Grained Security
outlines.description: Closing assessment that combines privilege grants, inheritance, row filters, column masks, and verification under exam conditions.
keyPoints: Determine the minimal set of statements that gives one group read access to a single table while hiding a sensitive column
Identify the correct place to enforce a per-principal rule so that it applies to all present and future query paths
Diagnose a failing query from its error message and the grants in place
Select the scalable mechanism when the same rule must apply to hundreds of tagged tables

Distractors mirror persistent exam traps: granting at catalog scope for a narrow need, expecting a DENY statement, revoking from a user who inherits access from a group, and assuming a row filter can conceal a column
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to resolve mixed access-control and fine-grained-security scenarios at certification difficulty.

lessons.title: Lineage, Auditing, and Metadata Discovery
objectives: Students will be able to use lineage to trace data flow from source tables to dashboards.
Students will be able to use audit logs and tags to support compliance and discoverability.

outlines.title: Lineage in Unity Catalog: What It Captures
outlines.description: Introduce automatic lineage capture in Unity Catalog and the entities it connects, setting up the rest of the lesson on tracing data flow.
