keyPoints: Describe how Unity Catalog captures lineage automatically at runtime as queries execute — no manual instrumentation required for supported workloads.
Identify the entities linked by lineage: notebooks, jobs, Delta tables, views, dashboards, and models.
Distinguish automatic runtime lineage from lineage that is not captured (for example reads by external clients or non-Databricks engines).
Locate lineage in Catalog Explorer on the table's Lineage tab, scoped to the current metastore.
[Table] Lineage coverage: object type (notebook / job / Delta table / view / dashboard) vs. lineage captured automatically (yes/no)
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain how Unity Catalog automatically captures lineage at table and column level.

outlines.title: Reading the Lineage Graph: Upstream and Downstream
outlines.description: Teach students to traverse the lineage graph in both directions and to choose between the visual graph and the queryable system tables.
keyPoints: Trace upstream (source) and downstream (consumer) chains from any table to answer 'where did this data come from?' and 'what breaks if I change it?'
Switch to column-level lineage to see exactly which downstream columns depend on a single source column.
Choose the right tool: the Catalog Explorer graph is best for visual exploration and impact analysis at design time; system tables are best for programmatic, repeatable checks.
Exam trap: lineage describes data flow, not authorization — the lineage graph does not tell you who was allowed to read the table.
outlines.teachingObjective: Use lineage to trace data flow from source tables to dashboards.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Lineage Fundamentals
outlines.description: Verify that students can identify what lineage captures, how to navigate it, and what it does not tell them.
keyPoints: Confirm the difference between table-level and column-level lineage.
Confirm that lineage is captured automatically for supported query paths and is not a substitute for the audit log.
Distractors mirror real exam traps: confusing lineage with permissions, and assuming lineage is captured for every external reader.
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain how Unity Catalog automatically captures lineage at table and column level.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Trace a Metric from Source Table to Dashboard
outlines.description: A fully-worked lineage tracing problem: identify the upstream chain for a dashboard metric, then reproduce the answer with SQL over the lineage system tables.
keyPoints: Statement: a monthly revenue dashboard reads gold.revenue_monthly, which is built from silver.orders_clean, which is built from bronze.orders_raw. Reconstruct the full upstream chain and name the downstream consumers of bronze.orders_raw.
Step 1: in Catalog Explorer, open bronze.orders_raw and read the downstream lineage graph to walk forward to the dashboard.
Step 2: reproduce the walk in SQL over system.access.table_lineage using source_table_full_name and target_table_full_name, joining rows until you reach the dashboard object.
Step 3: switch to system.access.column_lineage when the question asks which column, not which table, must be preserved.

Analysis: why the method works (lineage rows are one hop each, so a chain is a recursive join) and common pitfalls (duplicate rows per event, event lag before lineage appears, case-sensitive catalog/schema names, and lineage disappearing if an upstream object is dropped).
outlines.teachingObjective: Use lineage to trace data flow from source tables to dashboards.

outlines.title: Audit Logs and System Tables
outlines.description: Introduce the system tables that hold audit and lineage records, their key columns, and their retention and access characteristics.
keyPoints: system.access.audit records who did what, when, and to which securable, with columns such as event_time, user_identity.email, action_name, request_params, source_ip_address, and response.status_code.
system.access.table_lineage and system.access.column_lineage expose the same relationships as the visual graph, in queryable, timestamped form.
Retention matters: audit records in the system table have a bounded default retention window, so long-term compliance requires an export strategy.
Access is restricted — auditing a system is itself a governed activity, and only privileged users can read account-level audit data.
outlines.teachingObjective: Use audit logs and tags to support compliance and discoverability.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Audit Logs and System Tables
outlines.description: Check that students can name the right system table for a given governance question and recall its key columns and limits.
keyPoints: Match compliance questions to tables: 'who read this table?' versus 'what built this table?' versus 'which column depends on this column?'
Recall representative audit columns and what each one answers.
Distractors mirror real exam traps: choosing table_lineage when the question is about access, and assuming audit history is retained forever by default.
outlines.teachingObjective: Use audit logs and tags to support compliance and discoverability.

outlines.title: Interactive: Audit Log and Lineage Explorer
outlines.description: A hands-on SQL workspace where students filter audit records and traverse lineage system tables, seeing how one governance question maps to one table and one filter.
keyPoints: Filter system.access.audit by action_name, user, and time window to answer 'who accessed this table last week?'
Traverse system.access.table_lineage hop by hop to build an upstream chain, and compare the result with the column-level view.
Compare the audit result set with the lineage result set for the same table to see why they answer different questions.
Feedback panel flags common mistakes: missing time filter, forgetting deduplication, and querying lineage when the question is about permissions.
outlines.teachingObjective: Query system tables to reconstruct data flow and access history.

outlines.title: Tags, Comments, and Metadata Discovery
outlines.description: Show how governed tags and comments turn governed data into discoverable, classifiable data, and where that metadata interacts with policy.
keyPoints: Distinguish governed tags (centrally managed, policy-relevant, applied to catalogs, schemas, tables, and columns) from informal workspace metadata.
Use comments on catalogs, schemas, tables, and columns to document meaning and ownership so analysts can self-serve.
Discover assets by searching and filtering on tags, owner, and comment text in the catalog UI, or programmatically via information_schema.
Classify sensitive data with tags such as PII or sensitivity level so compliance reviews and policy decisions have a durable anchor.
Exam trap: applying a tag does not by itself grant or revoke a privilege — tagging is metadata, and access is still governed by grants.
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply tags, comments, and catalog search to make governed data discoverable and classifiable.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Tags, Comments, and Discoverability
outlines.description: Test the distinction between metadata and access, and the practical use of tags and comments for compliance and discovery.
keyPoints: Choose the correct mechanism for a stated goal: making data findable, documenting meaning, or classifying sensitive columns.
Recognize that metadata is not a permission and that permissions are not documentation.
Distractors mirror real exam traps: assuming a tag restricts access, and assuming a comment is searchable only from the table page.
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply tags, comments, and catalog search to make governed data discoverable and classifiable.

outlines.title: Comparison: Audit Log, Table Lineage, Column Lineage, Query History
outlines.description: A side-by-side comparison of the four governance data sources students most often confuse, framed around the question each one answers.
keyPoints: [Table] Rows: system.access.audit, system.access.table_lineage, system.access.column_lineage, query history — Columns: question it answers, granularity, time semantics, retention, who can read it, typical compliance use.
Highlight the decisive dimension: audit answers 'who accessed what', lineage answers 'what depends on what' — these are different questions with different tables.
Note the granularity ladder: table lineage is object-to-object, column lineage is field-to-field, and audit is event-to-object.
Use the table as a decision aid: read the question stem, name the question, then pick the source.
outlines.teachingObjective: Select the correct governance data source for a given compliance or impact-analysis question.

outlines.title: Trade-offs: Designing a Compliance Auditing and Metadata Strategy
outlines.description: A constrained design decision: choose how to satisfy a one-year audit retention and discoverability requirement using Unity Catalog capabilities.
keyPoints: Constraint set: regulators require 12 months of access history; the built-in audit system table retains a shorter default window; platform budget is limited; analysts must be able to find sensitive tables quickly.
Option A — rely only on built-in system tables: simplest, lowest cost, but cannot satisfy the 12-month retention requirement.
Option B — schedule a recurring export of audit and lineage system tables to governed cloud storage: meets retention, adds storage and orchestration cost and a new asset to govern.
Option C — maintain a manually curated metadata catalog of tags and comments only: excellent for discoverability, but captures no access history and does not satisfy the audit requirement.

Recommendation: a hybrid — keep system tables as the primary query surface, add a scheduled governed export for long-term retention, and layer governed tags on sensitive columns for discoverability. Justify it against cost and the stated retention constraint.
outlines.teachingObjective: Select an auditing and metadata strategy that satisfies retention, compliance, and cost constraints.

outlines.title: Lesson Exam: Lineage, Auditing, and Metadata
outlines.description: A harder exam-style set covering the whole lesson, with distractors modelled on the traps that appear on the real certification exam.
keyPoints: Scenario items that require choosing between lineage and audit data for a stated business question.
Items on column-level lineage for downstream impact analysis and safe schema change.
Items on governed tags, comments, and the difference between metadata and privileges.
Distractors mirror real exam traps: retention myths, treating lineage as an access record, and assuming lineage exists for every external reader.
outlines.teachingObjective: Answer exam-style questions on lineage, audit logs, and metadata without falling for common distractors.

lessons.title: Storage Credentials, External Locations, and Data Sharing
objectives: Students will be able to configure storage credentials and external locations for cloud data.
Students will be able to explain Delta Sharing as a governed way to exchange data across teams.

outlines.title: Storage Credentials: Delegating Cloud Storage Access
outlines.description: Introduce the storage credential as the Unity Catalog securable that delegates cloud storage access, and establish why it exists before external locations are introduced.
keyPoints: Define a storage credential: a Unity Catalog securable that encapsulates a cloud identity — an AWS IAM role, an Azure managed identity (access connector), or a GCP service account — which Unity Catalog uses to read and write cloud storage on the user's behalf.

Explain the delegation model: Databricks assumes that identity at query time using a trust relationship (an external ID for AWS, an access connector for Azure), so no long-lived cloud keys are stored in notebooks, cluster Spark configs, or code.
Identify the required privilege: creating a storage credential requires CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL on the metastore, typically held only by metastore admins.
Recall what a storage credential does NOT do: it binds no path and grants no end-user access — it answers only 'which cloud identity may be used'.
[Table] Storage credential vs. cloud IAM role vs. external location: who defines it, what it holds, and what each one can and cannot grant.
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe what a storage credential is and why Unity Catalog needs one to access cloud storage.

outlines.title: External Locations: Binding Cloud Paths to Credentials
outlines.description: Show how an external location pairs a cloud storage path with a storage credential, creating the path-level boundary on which Unity Catalog privileges are granted.
keyPoints: Define an external location: a securable object that pairs a cloud storage path (for example s3://acme-lake/raw/events) with exactly one storage credential.

Explain path-based governance: privileges are granted on the location — READ FILES, WRITE FILES, and CREATE TABLE — and external tables and volumes later created under that path operate under the location's authority.
State the privileges needed to run CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION: CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on the metastore plus CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on the referenced storage credential.

Apply the binding rules: one storage credential may back many external locations, but each location references exactly one credential, and a location path must not overlap the metastore's managed location or nest inside another external location.
[Diagram] Path-to-credential binding chain: analyst → GRANT READ FILES on external location → storage credential → cloud IAM role → bucket prefix.
outlines.teachingObjective: Configure an external location that binds a cloud storage path to a storage credential, and grant path-level privileges on it.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Credentials and External Locations
outlines.description: Check that students can distinguish the storage credential from the external location and know which privilege each operation requires.
keyPoints: Distinguish which object holds the cloud identity and which object holds the path binding.
Select the correct privileges for CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL and CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION.
Reject distractors that claim a storage credential by itself grants data access or that one external location may use several credentials.
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify understanding of the storage credential → external location chain and its privileges.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Grant Read-Only Access to an External Bucket Prefix
outlines.description: Fully work an end-to-end request: the cloud IAM role already exists, so grant the analysts group read-only access to a curated bucket prefix and verify the result.
keyPoints: Problem statement: s3://acme-lake/raw/events holds curated Parquet; the IAM role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-role already trusts the Databricks account; analysts must be able to read every file under that prefix but must never write or drop data.
Step 1 — CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL acme_cred WITH AWS_IAM_ROLE 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/uc-storage-role'; this is executed by a metastore admin holding CREATE STORAGE CREDENTIAL.

Step 2 — CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events URL 's3://acme-lake/raw/events' WITH (STORAGE CREDENTIAL acme_cred); this binds the path to the identity, and requires CREATE EXTERNAL LOCATION on both the metastore and the storage credential.
Step 3 — GRANT READ FILES ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events TO analysts; add CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on the same location only if analysts must also register tables pointing at that path.

Step 4 — verify with DESCRIBE EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events, SHOW GRANTS ON EXTERNAL LOCATION acme_events, then read the data (SELECT from a registered external table or a path-based read) as a member of analysts.

Analysis: the method works because identity (credential), path (external location), and principal (grant) are three separate decisions, which is what makes per-path least privilege enforceable; pitfalls — granting WRITE FILES 'to be safe', granting on the metastore instead of on the location, and choosing a path that overlaps the metastore's managed location.
outlines.teachingObjective: Configure storage credentials and external locations for cloud data and grant least-privilege path access.

outlines.title: Managed Tables vs. External Tables vs. External Locations
outlines.description: Put the three most commonly confused storage-governance concepts side by side so students can pick the right one under exam conditions.
keyPoints: [Table] Columns: what it is, who chooses the storage path, what DROP does, privileges required, and whether it governs non-tabular files.

[Table] Rows: Managed table — Unity Catalog chooses the path under the managed location, DROP deletes the data, needs CREATE TABLE plus USE SCHEMA/USE CATALOG; External table — the user picks a path that must sit under an external location, DROP keeps the data, needs CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE on that location; External location — not a table at all, it is the securable that authorizes path access through READ FILES / WRITE FILES / CREATE TABLE.
Decision cue: ask 'who owns the files after the table disappears?' — with managed tables Unity Catalog owns the lifecycle, with external tables the storage path outlives the table.
Exam trap: an external table pointing at a path covered by no external location cannot be created, and holding privileges on an external location still does not by itself grant SELECT on a table.
outlines.teachingObjective: Choose between managed tables, external tables, and external locations when designing governed storage.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Storage Governance Decisions
outlines.description: Test the managed-versus-external decision and the privilege each path access operation demands.
keyPoints: Predict what happens to the underlying files when a managed table and an external table are each dropped.
Select the correct privilege for reading files at a path, registering a table at a path, and writing to a path.
Reject distractors that treat an external location as a table, or that assume one credential may only serve one location.
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify understanding of storage governance decisions and path-level privileges.

outlines.title: Interactive: Storage Access Troubleshooting Simulator
outlines.description: Students assemble a storage credential and external location, then diagnose the failures returned by path access, table creation, and query operations.
keyPoints: Choose a cloud identity for the storage credential and observe that an incorrect trust configuration surfaces only at first data access, not at object creation time.
Bind a path in the external location, then attempt three operations — listing/reading files, creating a table at the path, and writing a row — and see which privilege each one requires.
[Diagram] Decision tree the simulator walks: is the path covered by an external location? is the credential valid and usable? does the principal hold the privilege this operation needs?

Read three injected failure messages and match each to its root cause: invalid credential, path outside any external location, or missing READ FILES / CREATE TABLE / WRITE FILES privilege on the location.
outlines.teachingObjective: Diagnose and fix configuration and privilege errors across the storage credential → external location → operation chain.

widgetOutline.concept: Unity Catalog storage access evaluation: storage credential → external location → privilege → attempted operation
keyVariables: storage credential binding and trust validity
granted privilege (READ FILES / WRITE FILES / CREATE TABLE / SELECT)

outlines.title: Delta Sharing: Governed Data Exchange
outlines.description: Introduce Delta Sharing as the open protocol that lets a provider expose Unity Catalog data to recipients without copying it, and connect it to the governance students already know.
keyPoints: Define Delta Sharing: an open protocol for secure, live, read-only exchange of governed data across organizations, clouds, and platforms, where recipients query the provider's data rather than receiving a copy.
Identify the core objects: providers and recipients, shares, and the tables, views, and volumes added to a share with ALTER SHARE ... ADD TABLE.

Distinguish deployment modes: Databricks-to-Databricks sharing, where the recipient is a Unity Catalog workspace identified by a sharing identifier, versus open sharing, where the recipient receives an activation link plus a credential/bearer token.

Explain why the exchange stays governed: shares are built from Unity Catalog assets, so existing SELECT grants, row and column filters, and dynamic views continue to determine exactly what a recipient sees.

Connect to observability: provider-side audit logs in system.access.audit record share creation and recipient access, while table lineage stops at the sharing boundary and does not appear as recipient-side lineage.
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain Delta Sharing as a governed way to exchange data across teams and organizations.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Delta Sharing Concepts
outlines.description: Check student grasp of shares, recipients, provider/recipient roles, and the difference between Databricks-to-Databricks and open sharing.
keyPoints: Identify which object is granted to a recipient and which object identifies the recipient.
Distinguish Databricks-to-Databricks sharing from open sharing by what the recipient must possess.
Reject distractors that claim Delta Sharing copies data, that it bypasses Unity Catalog grants, or that recipients obtain write access.
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify understanding of Delta Sharing concepts and object relationships.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Create a Share for an External Partner
outlines.description: Work through the full provider-side sequence for sharing one partitioned table with a partner over Delta Sharing, then review how to verify and revoke it.
keyPoints: Problem statement: share the table prod.sales.orders with the partner Northwind, read-only, exposing only orders from 2024 onward, where the recipient is another Databricks Unity Catalog workspace.
Step 1 — CREATE SHARE northwind_orders COMMENT 'Order data for Northwind'; executed by a principal holding CREATE SHARE on the metastore.
Step 2 — ALTER SHARE northwind_orders ADD TABLE prod.sales.orders PARTITION (order_date >= '2024-01-01'); partial sharing pushes the partition filter to the provider so older data is never exposed.

Step 3 — CREATE RECIPIENT northwind USING ID 'northwind-uc-sharing-id' COMMENT 'Northwind UC workspace'; for open sharing the alternative is CREATE RECIPIENT northwind_open, which returns an activation link and token the recipient downloads.

Step 4 — GRANT USE SHARE northwind_orders TO RECIPIENT northwind; verify with SHOW SHARES, DESCRIBE SHARE northwind_orders, SHOW GRANTS ON SHARE northwind_orders, and SHOW ALL IN SHARE northwind_orders.

Analysis and pitfalls: the provider must also retain SELECT (or appropriate access) on the underlying table; revocation follows a deliberate order — ALTER SHARE ... REMOVE TABLE, then REVOKE USE SHARE, then DROP RECIPIENT; adding an expiration or an IP access list to the recipient is the emergency stop; D2D recipients need an attached Unity Catalog metastore, while open recipients need a Delta Sharing client.
outlines.teachingObjective: Create a share, add governed data to it, define a recipient, and grant access through Delta Sharing.

outlines.title: Choosing a Delivery Mechanism for Cross-Team Data Exchange
outlines.description: Decide how to deliver curated data to an external partner under explicit governance, freshness, and revocation constraints, then justify one recommendation.
keyPoints: Constraint set: the consumer is a separate organization on a different cloud account; access must be read-only, near-live, revocable within seconds, fully auditable, and operated by a two-person team.
Option A — external location plus READ FILES in your own metastore: zero-copy and simple, but the consumer must operate inside your Databricks account, so it only fits internal teams.

Option B — Delta Sharing: live and read-only, governed by existing Unity Catalog grants and dynamic views, revoked with REVOKE USE SHARE, and recorded in the provider's audit logs; requires the consumer to support the Delta Sharing protocol, either natively (D2D) or through an open-sharing client.

Option C — scheduled file export into the partner's bucket: works with any consumer, but creates copies that go stale, escape Unity Catalog governance, and add storage, egress, and pipeline maintenance cost.

Recommendation: Option B for this constraint set, because it satisfies read-only, live, auditable, and instantly revocable at once; fall back to Option C only when the partner cannot run any Delta Sharing client and stale copies are acceptable.
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a governed data-exchange design under explicit freshness, revocation, and audit constraints.

outlines.title: Lesson Check: Storage Credentials, External Locations, and Sharing
outlines.description: Final lesson assessment covering credential configuration, external location binding, path privileges, and Delta Sharing, with distractors modelled on real exam traps.
keyPoints: Order the steps that turn a cloud IAM role into queryable data, and name the privilege required at each step.
Diagnose a failed external location creation caused by an overlapping or nested path.
Choose between a share, an external location grant, and a file export for a given consumer profile.
Explain in one short paragraph how revocation and auditing work differently for Delta Sharing than for a copied export.
outlines.teachingObjective: Demonstrate mastery of storage credentials, external locations, and Delta Sharing in exam-style questions.

units.title: Performance Optimization and Cost Control
objectives: Students will be able to diagnose and improve slow queries and pipelines.
Students will be able to tune compute and storage layouts to control cost.

lessons.title: Query Performance Tuning and the Spark UI
objectives: Students will be able to read the Spark UI to identify bottlenecks in stages and tasks.
Students will be able to use EXPLAIN plans and pruning to reduce data scanned.

outlines.title: Lesson Overview: Diagnosing Slow Queries
outlines.description: Frame the lesson around the exam objective of diagnosing and improving slow queries, and introduce the Spark UI as the primary diagnostic instrument in Databricks.
keyPoints: Exam objective: identify bottlenecks in Spark jobs and tune queries to reduce data scanned
The Spark UI answers three questions: what ran, where did the time go, and which task is the straggler
Map the diagnostic loop: observe in the Spark UI, hypothesize a cause, verify with EXPLAIN, fix, re-measure
Common exam trap: assuming a slow query means the cluster is too small — often the problem is skew, shuffle, or a full table scan
Lesson roadmap: Jobs/Stages/Tasks metrics, EXPLAIN plans, and pruning techniques
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to state the diagnostic workflow used throughout the lesson and connect it to the Data Engineer Associate performance-optimization domain.

outlines.title: Inside the Spark UI: Jobs, Stages, and Tasks
outlines.description: Explain the hierarchical structure of the Spark UI and how a query maps onto jobs, stages, and tasks so learners know where to look first.
keyPoints: Spark UI tabs: Jobs, Stages, Storage, Environment, Executors, and the SQL/DataFrame tab
Hierarchy: one action triggers a job; a job is split into stages at shuffle boundaries; a stage runs one task per partition
The SQL/DataFrame tab links a query directly to its DAG visualization and physical plan
Stage detail page shows task-level metrics, aggregated duration, shuffle read/write, and spill
Exam trap: reading only the Jobs page total time — the Stage and Task views reveal the real bottleneck
[Diagram] Hierarchical view: action → job → stages (shuffle boundary) → tasks per partition; annotate which UI tab exposes each level
Labels in the diagram should be in English
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to navigate the Spark UI and locate the job, stage, and task that correspond to a given query.

mediaGenerations.prompt: Clean technical diagram of the Apache Spark web UI navigation: a browser-window mockup with tabs for Jobs, Stages, Storage, Environment, Executors and SQL, plus an inset showing an action branching into a job, that job splitting into stages at a shuffle boundary, and each stage splitting into tasks per partition. Flat vector infographic style, blue and orange accents, white background, no faces, all text labels in English.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Spark UI Structure
outlines.description: Verify that students can map an action to its job, stages, and tasks and know which UI view exposes which metric.
keyPoints: Identify the UI level at which a shuffle boundary creates a new stage
Distinguish metrics shown on the Jobs page versus the Stage detail page
Recognize distractors that confuse driver time with executor task time
Short-answer: describe the first three clicks you would make to diagnose a slow query
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to locate the correct Spark UI view for a given diagnostic question.

outlines.title: Reading Stage and Task Metrics Like a Diagnostician
outlines.description: Teach the specific stage- and task-level metrics that reveal skew, excessive shuffling, memory pressure, and garbage collection overhead.
keyPoints: Task duration distribution: compare min, median, and max — a large max/median ratio signals skew
Shuffle Read and Shuffle Write sizes: large values indicate an expensive wide transformation or a bad join strategy
Spill (Memory) and Spill (Disk): data did not fit the execution memory of the partition
GC Time and peak execution memory: high GC time points to oversized partitions or inefficient object churn
Scheduler Delay and task launch time indicate overhead when partition counts are too high
[Table] Metric vs. symptom vs. typical remedy: skew / shuffle / spill / GC, with the tuning lever for each
Exam trap: treating high total duration as the problem — the metric that matters is which task is the outlier
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to read stage and task metrics to name a specific bottleneck and propose a fix.

outlines.title: Interactive: Spark Stage Metrics Explorer
outlines.description: Students manipulate partition counts and a data-skew factor and watch how task durations, shuffle size, and spill respond in a simulated Spark UI stage view.
keyPoints: Adjust the number of shuffle partitions and observe per-task duration distribution
Introduce skew into a key and watch a small number of tasks dominate the stage runtime
Observe when partitions become too small and scheduler overhead rises
Identify the configuration change that flattens the task duration distribution
Connect the flattened distribution back to reduced cluster time and lower cost
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to predict how partitioning and skew affect stage runtime and choose a tuning action accordingly.

widgetOutline.concept: Spark stage execution, task skew, shuffle, and spill diagnosis

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Diagnosing Stage Bottlenecks
outlines.description: Assess the ability to translate stage and task metrics into a named bottleneck and a first corrective action.
keyPoints: Given a task duration histogram, identify skew as the cause
Distinguish spill from shuffle as the dominant cost
Recognize the exam distractor 'add more workers' when the real fix is repartitioning
Match each metric (spill, GC time, shuffle write) to its most likely remedy
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to diagnose skew, spill, and shuffle problems from Spark UI metrics.

outlines.title: EXPLAIN Plans: Reading the Optimizer's Mind
outlines.description: Introduce logical and physical EXPLAIN output, the operators that matter for cost, and the statistics that predict data scanned.
keyPoints: EXPLAIN versus EXPLAIN EXTENDED versus EXPLAIN COST: what each returns and when to use them
Plan stages: parsed → analyzed → optimized logical → physical, produced by the Catalyst optimizer
Scan nodes report statistics such as sizeInBytes and row count for the files to be read
Watch for Exchange nodes (shuffles), Sort, and the join strategy: BroadcastHashJoin vs. SortMergeJoin
Exam trap: a plan that looks correct but still scans the whole table because the filter is not pushed to the scan
Compare the plan before and after adding a filter to see predicate pushdown appear in the scan node
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to read a physical EXPLAIN plan and identify the operators that dominate data scanned.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Diagnosing a Plan and Cutting Bytes Scanned
outlines.description: A fully worked exam-style problem that walks from an EXPLAIN plan and Spark UI metrics to a concrete tuning change and a measured improvement.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a Delta table sales is 8 TB; the query SELECT * FROM sales WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' has run time 42 minutes; the physical plan shows FileScan parquet with no pushed filter and a partition count of 1
Worked solution step 1: read the scan statistics in the plan to confirm full-table scan behavior and huge sizeInBytes
Worked solution step 2: check the Spark UI and find one giant task with a long duration next to thousands of near-instant tasks — a parallelism problem
Worked solution step 3: replace SELECT * with the required columns, filter on the partition column order_date, and repartition to a sensible shuffle partition count
Worked solution step 4: re-run EXPLAIN to confirm PushedFilters and PartitionFilters appear, and verify reduced bytes read in the Spark UI SQL tab
Analysis: why it works — pruning is applied at the file and partition layer before rows are materialized, so less I/O, less shuffle, and less compute cost
Common pitfall: filtering on a column that is not a partition column or is wrapped in a function, which disables pruning
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to convert EXPLAIN evidence and Spark UI metrics into a specific, justified query rewrite.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: EXPLAIN Plans and Operators
outlines.description: Assess whether students can interpret plan output and choose the correct tuning lever for the operator they see.
keyPoints: Identify the operator responsible for a shuffle in a physical plan
Decide when a broadcast join is appropriate and when it is not
Recognize that a missing PushedFilters entry means no predicate pushdown
Exam trap: confusing the logical plan (what you asked for) with the physical plan (what will run)
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to interpret physical plan operators and match them to tuning actions.

outlines.title: Pruning: Scan Less, Pay Less
outlines.description: Present the family of pruning techniques that reduce the data read by a Databricks query, and connect each to a cost outcome.
keyPoints: Partition pruning: filters on partition columns eliminate whole directories before any file is opened
Predicate pushdown: filters are evaluated inside the file scan (Parquet/Delta) rather than after reading all rows
Column pruning: selecting only needed columns exploits columnar storage — avoid SELECT *
Delta data skipping: per-file min/max statistics and file-level skipping; Z-ORDER co-locates related values to boost skipping
File layout hygiene: many small files raise overhead, so compaction and OPTIMIZE improve scan efficiency
[Diagram] A partitioned Delta table where a date filter eliminates all but one partition folder, with skipped files greyed out using their min/max statistics
Cost link: bytes scanned drives both runtime and DBU consumption, so pruning is a cost-control technique, not just a speed technique
Exam trap: filters wrapped in functions, or non-deterministic expressions, silently disable pruning
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to select the right pruning technique for a query and explain its effect on data scanned and cost.

mediaGenerations.prompt: Flat vector infographic of a Delta table laid out as folders by date partition. A query predicate arrow points at one highlighted partition; the other partitions are greyed out and labelled as skipped, with small min/max statistics badges on files. Clean technical style, blue and grey palette, white background, no people, all text labels in English.

outlines.title: Interactive: Rewrite the Query and Verify Pruning
outlines.description: A hands-on SQL sandbox where students edit a slow Spark SQL query, run EXPLAIN, and watch the reported bytes scanned and plan operators change.
keyPoints: Edit the starter query to add a partition-column filter and remove unnecessary columns
Run EXPLAIN and inspect whether PartitionFilters and PushedFilters appear on the scan node
Compare bytes scanned before and after the rewrite to see the pruning effect
Try a failed rewrite that wraps the filter column in a function and observe pruning disappear
Practice the skill in the language used on the exam: Spark SQL on Delta tables
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to rewrite a query to enable pruning and verify the improvement through its EXPLAIN plan.

outlines.title: Lesson Quiz: Performance Tuning and the Spark UI
outlines.description: A capstone assessment combining Spark UI diagnosis, EXPLAIN interpretation, and pruning decisions under exam conditions.
keyPoints: Diagnose a stage whose max task duration is 20x the median and select the best remedy
Interpret an EXPLAIN snippet and decide whether predicate pushdown occurred
Choose the query rewrite that minimizes bytes scanned for a given filter
Identify the exam distractor that recommends scaling the cluster before fixing the data layout
Short-answer: outline the diagnostic sequence from Spark UI observation to verified fix
outlines.teachingObjective: Students will be able to apply the full diagnostic workflow to unfamiliar exam-style scenarios.

lessons.title: Partitioning, Liquid Clustering, and File Layout
objectives: Students will be able to choose partitioning or liquid clustering keys for large tables.
Students will be able to resolve small-file problems through compaction strategies.

outlines.title: Lesson Overview: Partitioning, Liquid Clustering, and File Layout
outlines.description: Frames why physical table layout is the single biggest lever on both query latency and storage/compute cost, and previews the two objectives of this lesson.
keyPoints: Explain why physical data layout determines how many bytes a query must scan
Identify when to choose partitioning versus liquid clustering keys for large Delta tables
Determine the compaction strategy that resolves a small-file problem
Map each layout decision to a Databricks Data Engineer Associate performance-and-cost exam objective
outlines.teachingObjective: Set expectations for the lesson and connect table layout to query performance and cost.

outlines.title: How Delta Tables Are Stored on Disk
outlines.description: Builds the mental model of a Delta table as a transaction log plus Parquet data files, and introduces partitioning and data skipping as the mechanisms that let a query avoid reading data.
keyPoints: A Delta table is a _delta_log transaction log plus a set of Parquet data files
A partition is a physical directory; the partition key is the column whose values split that directory tree
Data skipping prunes files using per-file min/max column statistics — fewer, larger files with good stats mean less I/O
[Image] Annotated directory tree of a Delta table showing the _delta_log and date-based partition folders containing Parquet files
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe how Delta tables store data and how data skipping reduces scanned bytes.

mediaGenerations.prompt: Clean technical diagram of a Delta Lake table on disk: a top-level table folder containing a '_delta_log' folder and several date-named subfolders, each subfolder holding several Parquet data files drawn as blue file icons with size labels. A small annotation panel on the right shows 'min/max statistics' used for data skipping. All labels and annotations in English. Flat, professional infographic style, no people.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Storage Layout Foundations
outlines.description: Checks whether students can describe a Delta table's on-disk structure and the purpose of data skipping before moving into key selection.
keyPoints: Identify the two components of a Delta table on disk
Explain what data skipping uses to prune files
Recognize a distractor that confuses partitioning with file format
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify understanding of Delta storage structure and data skipping.

outlines.title: Partitioning Keys: Selection and Over-Partitioning Traps
outlines.description: Teaches the criteria for a good partition key and the failure modes (over-partitioning, high cardinality, skew) that the exam loves to test.
keyPoints: Choose a low-cardinality partition key that appears in frequent WHERE filters — date is the classic choice
Avoid over-partitioning: keep partitions at or above roughly 1 GB and well under ~10,000 partitions
Never partition on high-cardinality identifiers such as user_id or order_id
Partition on a column with even value distribution to prevent skew and hotspotting
Partitioning is rigid: changing the key rewrites the table and can create many small files
outlines.teachingObjective: Select appropriate partition keys and recognize over-partitioning anti-patterns.

outlines.title: Liquid Clustering: One Layout to Replace Them All
outlines.description: Introduces liquid clustering as the modern replacement for both Hive-style partitioning and Z-ORDER, including CLUSTER BY syntax and key-selection guidance.
keyPoints: Liquid clustering replaces partitioning and Z-ORDER with a single CLUSTER BY column set: CREATE TABLE t (...) CLUSTER BY (col1, col2)
Clustering keys can be changed at any time with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (...) without rewriting the table
Layout adapts incrementally as data arrives, so clustering is reversible and low-risk
Use 1 to 4 clustering keys ordered by filter selectivity, typically higher-cardinality columns
Liquid clustering is not supported with partitioning on the same table — pick one
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain liquid clustering and choose clustering keys for a large table.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Partitioning vs. Liquid Clustering
outlines.description: Assesses the decision between partitioning and liquid clustering, including syntax recall and the reversibility argument.
keyPoints: Match CLUSTER BY syntax to the correct DDL statement
Select the better layout strategy for a described cardinality and filter pattern
Spot the distractor that keeps partitioning and clustering on the same table
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm students can choose and express the correct clustering strategy.

outlines.title: Interactive: Liquid Clustering Key Explorer
outlines.description: Students experiment with clustering keys, data volumes, and query filters to see how many files a query must scan and how layout choice changes cost.
keyPoints: Pick 0 to 4 clustering keys from a sample table's columns
Apply a query filter and observe files scanned, bytes read, and estimated cost
Compare a good key order against a poor one and against no clustering
Observe why high-cardinality keys help when they match the filter predicate
outlines.teachingObjective: Develop intuition for clustering-key selection through hands-on simulation.

widgetOutline.concept: Liquid clustering key selection and data skipping

outlines.title: The Small-File Problem and Compaction Strategies
outlines.description: Explains what causes small files, why they are expensive, and the Databricks features that compact them, including the interplay with partitioning.
keyPoints: Small files are data files far below the target size (roughly 128 MB default, up to 1 GB for large tables); each file adds I/O, task, and metadata overhead
Common causes: streaming ingestion, frequent small MERGE or INSERT statements, over-partitioning, and high-shuffle writes
Symptoms: slow queries, excessive tasks in the Spark UI, and a table whose files vastly outnumber its data volume
Remedies: run OPTIMIZE to compact files, enable auto compaction and optimized writes, and rely on predictive optimization on Unity Catalog managed tables
[Image] Side-by-side comparison of a table with hundreds of tiny files versus the same data compacted into a few target-size files
outlines.teachingObjective: Diagnose small-file problems and select an appropriate compaction strategy.

mediaGenerations.prompt: Two-panel technical illustration for a data engineering slide. Left panel: a table folder overflowing with hundreds of tiny Parquet file icons labeled 'many small files, high overhead'. Right panel: the same table compacted into four or five large file icons labeled 'few target-size files, fast reads'. An arrow labeled 'OPTIMIZE' points from left to right. All text labels in English. Flat, professional infographic style, no people.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Small Files and Compaction
outlines.description: Tests recognition of small-file causes and the correct compaction response, mirroring the exam's scenario-style performance items.
keyPoints: Attribute a small-file problem to its most likely cause
Choose OPTIMIZE versus auto compaction versus a layout change for a described scenario
Reject the distractor that treats small files as a storage-format problem
outlines.teachingObjective: Verify diagnosis and remediation of small-file problems.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Diagnosing and Repairing a Degraded Table Layout
outlines.description: A fully worked exam-style problem that takes a badly laid-out table from symptom to repair, with an explicit analysis of why the fix works and the pitfalls to avoid.
keyPoints: Problem: an events table partitioned by event_date and user_id has grown to 40 TB with millions of tiny files, and date-only filters run slowly — propose a fix
Solution step 1: remove the user_id partition, which created a runaway directory count and skew
Solution step 2: convert to liquid clustering with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (event_date, user_id) so filters on either column prune data
Solution step 3: run OPTIMIZE to compact small files to the target size, then enable auto compaction and predictive optimization
Analysis: why clustering beats partitioning here, the over-partitioning threshold, and why the ordering of clustering keys matters
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply partitioning, clustering, and compaction decisions end to end.

outlines.title: Decision: Partitioning, Liquid Clustering, or Z-ORDER?
outlines.description: Presents the three layout options as a constrained design decision with pros, cons, and one justified recommendation for a given workload.
keyPoints: Option A — Partitioning: cheap and familiar for low-cardinality date filters, but rigid and prone to over-partitioning and small files
Option B — Liquid clustering: adaptive, reversible, and key-flexible, the default recommendation for new large Delta tables
Option C — Z-ORDER (with OPTIMIZE): works but must be re-run to stay effective and does not replace partitioning
Recommendation: for a new 50 TB table filtered mainly by date and customer_id, use liquid clustering on (customer_id, date) — it supports both filter patterns without a rewrite
Constraints that shift the answer: Unity Catalog managed table availability, engine support for CLUSTER BY, and existing partitioned legacy tables
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify a layout decision under explicit constraints.

outlines.title: Final Checkpoint: Layout, Clustering, and File Sizing
outlines.description: A mixed exam-style assessment covering the full lesson — storage structure, key selection, clustering syntax, and compaction.
keyPoints: Select clustering keys for a described query workload
Identify an over-partitioning or small-file anti-pattern from symptoms
Match compaction and clustering commands to their intended effect
Reject distractors that confuse partitioning, Z-ORDER, and liquid clustering
outlines.teachingObjective: Assess mastery of partitioning, liquid clustering, and file-layout optimization.

lessons.title: Joins, Shuffles, and Caching
objectives: Students will be able to apply broadcast and shuffle hash joins appropriately.
Students will be able to reduce shuffle cost and use caching where it pays off.

outlines.title: Lesson Overview: Joins, Shuffles, and Caching
outlines.description: Frame the lesson and connect it to the diagnostics and storage-layout work already covered in this unit.
keyPoints: Lesson objectives: choose between broadcast and shuffle hash joins, and cut shuffle cost with caching where it actually pays off
Where this sits: earlier lessons taught you to read the Spark UI and to lay out Delta files; this lesson changes the execution plan itself
Exam objective: given a slow join plus a cluster profile, select the correct optimization and predict its effect on shuffle bytes and runtime
[Chart] Bar chart of where wall-clock time goes in a slow join — file scan vs. shuffle write/read vs. join vs. write — showing shuffle dominating
outlines.teachingObjective: Understand the scope of the lesson within the Performance Optimization and Cost Control unit.

outlines.title: Why Joins Are Expensive: The Shuffle
outlines.description: Establish the shuffle as the dominant cost of joins before any tuning technique is introduced.
keyPoints: Narrow transformations (select, filter, withColumn) keep each row in its partition and move no data over the network
Wide transformations (join, groupBy, distinct, repartition) force a shuffle: rows are serialized, spilled to local disk, then pulled across the network at a stage boundary
Spark SQL's default join path is the sort-merge join — both sides are exchanged on the join key, sorted, then merged
Because a shuffle touches every surviving row, it usually dominates runtime far more than the table scan
[Table] Narrow vs. wide transformation comparison: example operators, data movement, typical cost profile
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain why joins incur a shuffle and why the shuffle, not the scan, is normally the bottleneck.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Shuffles and Wide Transformations
outlines.description: Verify that learners can identify when a shuffle occurs and where it appears in the execution plan.
keyPoints: Identify which operators trigger a shuffle and which do not
Recognise an Exchange node in a physical plan as the shuffle boundary
Distractor pattern: options that blame the file scan or the write for a cost that the exchange actually caused
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm understanding of shuffle causes and their appearance in the Spark UI and physical plan.

outlines.title: Broadcast Hash Join: The Small-Table Fast Path
outlines.description: Teach the broadcast hash join, its eligibility rule, and how to force or disable it.
keyPoints: A broadcast hash join collects the small side to the driver, ships it to every executor, and hash-probes it — the large side is never shuffled
Eligibility is decided by size, not by row count: spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold defaults to 10 MB
Force it with a broadcast() hint on the small table; disable it with a zero threshold or a negative broadcast hint
Exam trap: broadcasting a side that is actually large causes driver OOM or executor memory pressure — a worse failure than the shuffle you avoided
[Chart] Bar chart comparing bytes shuffled for the same query under sort-merge join vs. broadcast hash join
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply a broadcast hash join when one join side is small enough to fit under the broadcast threshold.

outlines.title: Choosing a Join Strategy: BHJ vs. SHJ vs. SMJ
outlines.description: Place the three join strategies side by side on the dimensions that decide the exam answer.
keyPoints: Compare the three strategies Spark can select: Broadcast Hash Join, Shuffle Hash Join, and Sort-Merge Join
[Table] Rows: BHJ / SHJ / SMJ; Columns: trigger condition, which side is exchanged, memory requirement, skew tolerance, and typical use case
BHJ does not exchange the large side over the network, but replicates the small side to every executor
SHJ shuffles only the small side and leaves the large side where it is — the middle ground when the small side exceeds the broadcast threshold
SMJ shuffles and sorts both sides; it is the default and the most robust under skew and tight memory
Exam trap: SHJ is often described as a no-shuffle join — the small side is still exchanged
outlines.teachingObjective: Select the correct join strategy from table sizes, memory limits, and skew characteristics.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Broadcast and Shuffle Hash Joins
outlines.description: Test strategy selection and the configuration that controls it.
keyPoints: Given two table sizes and a threshold value, predict which join strategy Spark will choose
Recognise the failure mode of broadcasting a table that is too large
Distractor pattern: options that claim the broadcast hint always overrides memory limits, or that SHJ removes all shuffling
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm the ability to choose between broadcast and shuffle hash joins appropriately.

outlines.title: Interactive: Join Strategy and Shuffle Cost Explorer
outlines.description: Learners manipulate table sizes, the broadcast threshold, and shuffle partition count to see the chosen strategy and its cost.
keyPoints: Drag the size of each join side and the broadcast threshold to watch Spark switch between sort-merge and broadcast hash join
Read the shuffle-bytes and stage-count readouts while varying spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
Toggle the broadcast hint on and off to see the physical plan change and the cost move with it
Trigger the failure case deliberately: broadcast a large side and observe the memory pressure warning
Debrief: choose the strategy from measured table sizes, not from habit
outlines.teachingObjective: Predict how configuration choices change join strategy and shuffle cost.

widgetOutline.concept: Spark join strategy selection and shuffle cost

outlines.title: Reducing Shuffle Cost: Distribution, Keys, and AQE
outlines.description: Present the techniques that shrink or eliminate the exchange before tuning hardware.
keyPoints: Pre-partition or bucket tables on the join key so recurring joins skip the exchange entirely
Filter and pre-aggregate before the join, and let join reordering and predicate pushdown shrink what reaches the shuffle
Use equi-join keys with even value distributions and avoid cross joins; skew, not total volume, is often the real cost driver
Adaptive Query Execution coalesces small shuffle partitions and can convert a sort-merge join into a broadcast join at runtime when a side turns out small
Tune spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to the cluster — the 200 default is wrong for both very small and very large clusters
Exam trap: raising shuffle partitions does not fix skew; skew needs salting or AQE skew-join handling
outlines.teachingObjective: Reduce shuffle cost through layout, filtering, join keys, and adaptive execution settings.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Shuffle Reduction and AQE
outlines.description: Assess knowledge of the levers that reduce shuffle volume and when each applies.
keyPoints: Match each technique — bucketing, pre-filtering, partition tuning, AQE — to the problem it actually solves
Diagnose whether a reported symptom is a partition-count problem or a skew problem
Distractor pattern: options that propose more shuffle partitions as a cure for skew, or caching as a cure for a full table scan
outlines.teachingObjective: Confirm the ability to reduce shuffle cost using the right lever for the observed symptom.

outlines.title: Caching: When It Pays Off
outlines.description: Teach when persisting an intermediate result saves more than it costs, and how Delta Cache differs.
keyPoints: cache() and persist() keep an intermediate DataFrame in executor memory and optionally disk, so repeated actions skip recomputing the full lineage
It pays off when the same result is reused many times: iterative ML loops, interactive exploration, or several downstream aggregations over one join
It does not pay off for a one-shot job or a table read once — cached data occupies memory that other stages need
Delta Cache is a different mechanism: it caches remote Parquet files on local SSD, so repeats avoid the network read rather than the lineage recomputation
Always unpersist() when finished; an abandoned cache quietly inflates memory cost and can cause eviction of working data
Exam trap: caching never fixes a bad join or a full table scan — it only avoids recomputation
outlines.teachingObjective: Decide whether caching an intermediate result is worthwhile for a given workload.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Diagnosing an Expensive Join and Deciding on Caching
outlines.description: A fully worked diagnosis and fix for a slow nightly join, including the caching decision and its pitfalls.
keyPoints: Statement: a nightly job joins a 2 TB fact table to a 40 MB dimension table; the Spark UI shows runtime dominated by a single exchange stage
Step 1 — diagnose: an exchange stage with heavy shuffle read and write, not the file scan, is the bottleneck; 200 tasks all taking similar time rules out skew
Step 2 — explain: the 40 MB small side exceeds the 10 MB spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, so Spark fell back to sort-merge join and shuffled both sides
Step 3 — fix: raise the threshold or add broadcast(dim); predicted effect is that shuffle bytes on the fact table fall to near zero and the exchange stage disappears
Step 4 — caching decision: the joined result feeds three downstream aggregations, so cache it with MEMORY_AND_DISK and unpersist when the job ends
Analysis: why each step works, and the pitfalls — over-broadcasting can OOM the driver, caching a read-once result wastes memory, and forgetting to unpersist keeps the cost after the job finishes
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply join strategy selection and caching judgement end to end on a realistic slow-join scenario.

outlines.title: Lesson Check: Joins, Shuffles, and Caching
outlines.description: End-of-lesson assessment covering join strategy selection, shuffle reduction, and caching decisions.
keyPoints: Select the appropriate join strategy for given table sizes, thresholds, and cluster memory
Predict the effect of a broadcast hint, a bucketed join key, or an AQE change on shuffle volume
Decide whether caching a specific intermediate result is justified, and justify the storage level
Distractor pattern: exam-style traps that confuse broadcast with shuffle hash join, blame the scan for shuffle cost, or present caching as a general performance fix
outlines.teachingObjective: Demonstrate mastery of join strategy selection, shuffle reduction, and caching for the certification exam.

lessons.title: Photon, Cluster Sizing, and Cost Optimization
objectives: Students will be able to select cluster sizes, autoscaling, and Photon based on workload characteristics.
Students will be able to apply cost-aware practices such as right-sizing and job clusters.

outlines.title: Lesson Overview: Photon, Cluster Sizing, and Cost Optimization
outlines.description: Frames the final lesson of the unit: how compute engine choice, cluster shape, and cluster lifecycle jointly determine both runtime and bill.
keyPoints: Exam objective: given a workload profile, select the compute type, cluster size, autoscaling settings, and Photon option that best fit it
Three levers: the engine (Photon on or off), the cluster shape (node type, worker count, autoscaling min/max), and the lifecycle (job vs all-purpose, auto-termination)
Cost model in one line: total cost = (DBU rate x DBU-hours) + (cloud VM price x runtime) — every optimization must be judged against both terms
Preview of cost-aware practices: right-sizing from Spark UI metrics, job clusters for scheduled work, spot instances for fault-tolerant batch, instance pools for start-up time
Roadmap: 4 checkpoints plus two worked cost-estimation problems and a hands-on cluster sizing simulator
outlines.teachingObjective: Select cluster sizes, autoscaling, and Photon based on workload characteristics.

outlines.title: Photon: The Vectorized Query Engine
outlines.description: Explains what Photon actually is, which operators it accelerates, and how to reason about its net cost when the DBU rate is higher.
keyPoints: Photon is a native C++ vectorized engine that replaces parts of the Spark execution engine; the Spark APIs, SQL, and DataFrame code are unchanged — it is a runtime switch
Vectorized, columnar, compiled execution processes batches of column values per CPU instruction, cutting per-row interpretation overhead
Largest wins on CPU-bound work: large table scans, wide aggregations, joins, string-heavy transformations, and Delta MERGE/DELETE/UPDATE
[Table] Photon helps vs. Photon barely helps: large scans/aggregations/joins/Delta writes (helps) vs. I/O-bound jobs, Python UDF-heavy pipelines, tiny datasets (little or no gain)
Cost nuance: the Photon DBU rate is higher per DBU, but total cost frequently falls because wall-clock runtime drops — always compare DBU-hours, not DBU rates
Exam trap: 'Enable Photon to speed up every job' is false; and Photon is not the same as AQE, Delta caching, or autoscaling
outlines.teachingObjective: Select cluster sizes, autoscaling, and Photon based on workload characteristics.

mediaGenerations.prompt: Clean technical infographic split into two panels comparing query execution models: left panel labelled 'Row-at-a-time' showing a CPU core pulling one row at a time from a table, with a narrow pipe; right panel labelled 'Vectorized (Photon)' showing a CPU core processing a whole column batch of values at once through a wide pipe, with SIMD-style parallel arrows. Minimal flat design, blue and orange accent colors, no people, all text labels in English.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Photon Fundamentals
outlines.description: Assesses whether the learner can identify when Photon improves a workload and can reason about its net cost rather than its DBU rate.
keyPoints: Given a workload description, decide whether enabling Photon is likely to improve runtime
Distinguish Photon from adjacent optimizations (adaptive query execution, Delta caching, autoscaling, partition pruning)
Reason about net cost when the DBU rate rises but runtime falls
Recognize distractor options that claim Photon speeds up every job or that confuse Photon with a storage format
outlines.teachingObjective: Select cluster sizes, autoscaling, and Photon based on workload characteristics.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Is Photon Cheaper for This Job?
outlines.description: Fully-worked quantitative problems that show how to compare a baseline run against a Photon run in DBU-hours and in dollars, plus a right-sizing problem.
keyPoints: Problem 1 statement: a nightly ETL job runs 90 minutes on 8 workers at rate R DBU/h. With Photon it finishes in 40 minutes but the DBU rate becomes 1.5R. Is Photon cheaper?
Worked solution: baseline = 8 workers x 1.5 h = 12 DBU-h. Photon = 8 x (40/60) x 1.5 = 8 DBU-h. Photon uses 33% fewer DBU-hours, so it is cheaper in DBUs and likely in VM cost too (shorter runtime)
Problem 2 statement: a pipeline runs on a 16-worker cluster but the Spark UI shows only 6 concurrent tasks per stage. Right-size it and estimate the saving
Worked solution: peak concurrency 6 tasks implies roughly 6-8 executors are needed, not 16; halving worker count halves DBU-hours with no runtime change for this stage profile
Analysis: why wall-clock reduction dominates the rate multiplier, and why the method fails if the job is I/O-bound (Photon shrinks runtime only slightly, so the 1.5x rate raises cost)
Common pitfalls: using the maximum worker count instead of the average under autoscaling; ignoring fixed start-up cost on very short runs; assuming task count equals parallelism without checking skew
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply cost-aware practices such as right-sizing and job clusters.

outlines.title: Compute Choices Compared: All-Purpose, Job Clusters, SQL Warehouses
outlines.description: Side-by-side comparison of the compute types a Databricks data engineer must choose between, across the dimensions the exam tests.
keyPoints: [Table] Compare All-purpose compute, Job compute, and SQL warehouse across: intended use, relative cost, auto-termination behavior, sharing/concurrency, and which workloads map to each
Job clusters are created per job run and cost less per DBU — the default choice for scheduled production pipelines
All-purpose clusters are for interactive development and ad-hoc analysis and must have auto-termination configured to avoid idle spend
SQL warehouses serve SQL-only BI and dashboard workloads, with serverless or classic options and autoscaling driven by query concurrency
Exam trap: provisioning an all-purpose cluster for a scheduled production job 'so the team can also explore data on it' — the classic wrong answer
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply cost-aware practices such as right-sizing and job clusters.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Cluster Sizing and Autoscaling
outlines.description: Tests configuration reasoning: worker counts, autoscaling min/max, node type families, driver sizing, and spot versus on-demand.
keyPoints: Given a workload profile (memory-heavy joins, skewed shuffle, bursty concurrency), choose the appropriate node type family and worker count
Reason about autoscaling semantics: min/max workers, what triggers scale-up and scale-down, and why autoscaling does not reduce cost by itself
Decide when spot instances are appropriate and which node (driver) should stay on-demand
Identify the distractor that claims adding workers always reduces runtime regardless of partition and shuffle counts
outlines.teachingObjective: Select cluster sizes, autoscaling, and Photon based on workload characteristics.

outlines.title: Interactive: Cluster Sizing and Cost Simulator
outlines.description: A hands-on simulator where learners trade off runtime against DBU-hours and total spend by changing cluster shape and lifecycle settings.
keyPoints: Adjust worker count, autoscaling min/max, node type, spot share, and runtime to see how DBU-hours and total cost respond
Observe the knee of the curve: past a certain worker count runtime stops falling but cost keeps climbing
See how autoscaling changes the effective average worker count, and why cost is driven by that average and not by the maximum
Enable or disable Photon to watch the runtime/rate trade-off play out in the total cost figure
Goal: find the configuration that meets a stated runtime target at the lowest total cost
outlines.teachingObjective: Select cluster sizes, autoscaling, and Photon based on workload characteristics.

widgetOutline.concept: Cluster sizing and cost trade-off

outlines.title: Cost-Aware Practices: Right-Sizing and Lifecycle
outlines.description: A practical checklist of the cost-control habits the exam expects a data engineer to apply to real pipelines.
keyPoints: Right-size from evidence, not guesswork: use Spark UI task counts, executor utilization, spill, and GC time to decide the real worker count

[Table] Cost lever vs. what it saves vs. when it applies: autoscaling (idle capacity), job clusters (lower DBU rate), auto-termination (idle wall-clock), spot instances (VM price), instance pools (start-up time)
Set auto-termination on all-purpose clusters (typically 10-30 minutes) and always run scheduled work on job clusters
Use spot instances for fault-tolerant batch workloads; keep the driver and SLA-critical work on on-demand nodes
Attribute spend with cluster tags, budget alerts, and cost/system tables so optimization is measured, not assumed
Exam trap: 'autoscaling reduces cost' is conditionally true — it only helps when the cluster would otherwise sit idle; it does nothing for a steadily saturated cluster
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply cost-aware practices such as right-sizing and job clusters.

outlines.title: Checkpoint: Cost Optimization in Practice
outlines.description: Assesses whether the learner can compute total cost and pick the configuration change that actually reduces it.
keyPoints: Compute DBU-hours and total cost for a given cluster configuration and schedule
Given a described pipeline, identify the single change with the largest cost impact (job cluster vs. Photon vs. more workers vs. spot instances)
Recognize distractors that conflate runtime reduction with cost reduction, or that ignore cloud VM cost entirely
Justify decisions in short written answers using DBU-hours and SLA constraints
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply cost-aware practices such as right-sizing and job clusters.

outlines.title: Trade-off Decision: Cutting 30% Off a Nightly Pipeline
outlines.description: A constrained decision problem where three candidate cost-reduction strategies are weighed against an SLA and a budget cut.
keyPoints: Constraints: 4-hour nightly pipeline, 6:00 AM SLA, 3x data growth expected next quarter, must tolerate node preemption, and the budget must drop 30%
Option A — keep the current cluster and enable Photon: pros are easy rollout and shorter CPU-bound stages; cons are a higher DBU rate and little gain if the job is I/O-bound
Option B — move to a job cluster with autoscaling 4-16 workers and spot workers: pros are the biggest cost reduction with no code change; cons are occasional spot reclamation and longer start-up
Option C — use more, smaller workers: pros are better task parallelism and finer autoscaling granularity; cons are more shuffle traffic and higher driver pressure

Recommendation: adopt B as the baseline (job cluster + autoscaling + spot, on-demand driver), then add Photon only for the stages the Spark UI shows as CPU-bound — this hits the 30% target while leaving headroom for 3x growth
Exam takeaway: the best answer is the one satisfying every stated constraint, not the one with the biggest theoretical speedup
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply cost-aware practices such as right-sizing and job clusters.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Costing a Pipeline Before and After Right-Sizing
outlines.description: A full monthly cost calculation comparing an over-provisioned fixed cluster with a right-sized autoscaling job cluster, including VM cost.
keyPoints: Problem statement: a job runs 2 hours per day, every day, on a fixed 8-worker configuration rated at a combined 12 DBU/h; the DBU price is $0.15. Compute the monthly DBU cost
Worked solution (baseline): 12 DBU/h x 2 h x 30 days = 720 DBU-hours; 720 x $0.15 = $108.00 per month
Right-sized configuration: autoscaling 2-8 workers averaging 5 workers at 7.5 DBU/h, runtime falls to 1.4 h. Compute the new monthly cost: 7.5 x 1.4 x 30 = 315 DBU-hours; 315 x $0.15 = $47.25
Add the cloud VM term: if the VM portion is $0.10 per DBU-hour equivalent, the baseline adds 72.00 and the right-sized adds 31.50 — total monthly spend falls from $180.00 to $78.75, a 56% reduction
Analysis: cost is driven by the average worker count under autoscaling, not the maximum; the saving comes from both fewer DBU-hours and a shorter billed runtime
Common pitfalls: ignoring the VM charge and counting only DBUs; using peak worker count in the estimate; forgetting that start-up overhead makes very short runs proportionally more expensive
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply cost-aware practices such as right-sizing and job clusters.

outlines.title: Final Checkpoint: Photon, Cluster Sizing, and Cost (Exam Review)
outlines.description: A mixed, harder set of scenario questions that closes the unit and mirrors the format and distractor patterns of the certification exam.
keyPoints: Given a workload and a budget constraint, select the compute type, cluster configuration, and Photon setting that best satisfy both
Diagnose a described cost regression using runtime, DBU rate, and worker count information
Choose between competing optimizations when only one can be applied first
Avoid the recurring exam traps: Photon speeds up everything, autoscaling always lowers cost, more workers always means faster, and job clusters cannot run scheduled pipelines
Short-answer item: justify a recommended configuration in terms of DBU-hours, SLA, and fault tolerance
outlines.teachingObjective: Select cluster sizes, autoscaling, and Photon based on workload characteristics.

outlines.title: Why CI/CD for Databricks Pipelines
outlines.description: Motivate code-based deployment of data pipelines and introduce Databricks Asset Bundles as the exam-relevant mechanism for packaging and promoting work.
keyPoints: Manually clicking jobs together produces drift: the dev job and the prod job silently diverge, and nobody can diff or review the change
CI/CD = continuous integration (validate and test every commit) + continuous delivery (promote the same tested artifact through environments)
Databricks Asset Bundles (DAB) describe jobs, pipelines, and their permissions as code in YAML, versioned in Git
Exam objective: 'package jobs and pipelines as Databricks Asset Bundles' and 'deploy bundles across development, staging, and production targets'
The bundle is the unit of promotion — build once, deploy many; you never rebuild per environment
outlines.teachingObjective: Explain why pipeline deployment must be codified and name the Databricks mechanism used to do it.

outlines.title: Git Integration in Databricks
outlines.description: Show how version control connects to the workspace and how branch-and-merge workflows trigger bundle validation and deployment.
keyPoints: Databricks Git folders (formerly Repos) clone a remote repository into the workspace; a workspace supports one Git folder per repository structure
Supported providers include GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure DevOps, and AWS CodeCommit; credentials are stored per user or via a service principal
Working model: feature branch → pull request → main; CI validates the bundle on the PR, deployment happens on merge
The bundle config lives in the same repository as the source code, so code and infrastructure are reviewed together
Exam trap: Git folders give version control and a trigger surface, but they are not a CI/CD system by themselves — an external runner still executes the pipeline
outlines.teachingObjective: Describe how Git folders and branching workflow combine with bundles to form a CI/CD loop.

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Package an Existing Job as a Bundle
outlines.description: Convert a hand-created job into a Databricks Asset Bundle, validate it, and deploy it — with the reasoning behind each step.
keyPoints: Problem: a manually created job 'daily_sales_etl' in the dev workspace runs the notebook /Workspace/Repos/team/sales/etl/bronze.py on a daily schedule. Package it so the same definition can deploy to dev, staging, and prod.
Step 1 — scaffold: databricks bundle init with the default-python template creates databricks.yml, resources/, src/, and tests/
Step 2 — capture existing config: databricks bundle generate job --existing-job-id <job-id> writes the current job definition into resources/daily_sales_etl.yml
Step 3 — parameterise: replace hardcoded catalog/schema with ${var.catalog} / ${var.schema} and declare variables: with a default
Step 4 — verify then ship: databricks bundle validate -t dev, then databricks bundle deploy -t dev, then databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t dev

Analysis: generate beats hand-writing because it guarantees feature parity with the job that already runs; the classic pitfall is leaving literal catalog names in the YAML, which makes every environment write to dev data
outlines.teachingObjective: Apply the bundle-authoring workflow end to end on a realistic existing job.

outlines.title: The Bundle Lifecycle Commands
outlines.description: Present the four command families a data engineer uses daily, and what each one actually changes in the workspace.
keyPoints: databricks bundle validate — resolves variables and the target, checks the config, and touches nothing in the workspace

databricks bundle destroy -t <target> — tears down the deployed resources; use --auto-approve in CI so the pipeline does not hang

outlines.title: Worked Problem: Promote One Bundle to Production
outlines.description: Deploy the same bundle to a production target with a different catalog, a service principal, and a schedule that exists only in prod.
keyPoints: Problem: staging and production must read different catalogs, production must run as a service principal, and only production may hold a daily schedule. No YAML may be duplicated per environment.
Step 1 — declare variables: catalog with a dev default, then override per target (dev → dev_catalog, staging → staging_catalog, prod → prod_catalog)
Step 2 — configure targets: dev uses mode: development (names prefixed with [dev <user>], schedules paused) while staging and prod use mode: production
Step 3 — attach prod-only settings: run_as: <service-principal>, an explicit workspace.host, a permissions block, and the schedule entry present only under the prod target
Step 4 — release: databricks bundle validate -t prod, databricks bundle deploy -t prod, then databricks bundle run daily_sales_etl -t prod

Analysis: this is build-once-deploy-many — the same files, the same tests, different resolved variables. The common pitfall is copying databricks.yml per environment, which reintroduces exactly the drift CI/CD is meant to remove

outlines.title: Choosing an Environment Promotion Strategy
outlines.description: Weigh three realistic isolation strategies for promoting bundles, then commit to one recommendation under explicit constraints.
keyPoints: Constraint set: a 4-person data team, one platform team, separate catalog per environment, production-like test data needed, limited budget and no dedicated release engineer
Option A — one workspace, bundle targets with variable overrides: cheapest and fastest, but compute quotas, secrets, and permissions are shared and isolation is logical, not physical
Option B — a workspace per environment: strongest isolation and independent credentials and quotas, but three times the setup, cost, and configuration surface to maintain
Option C — hybrid: dev and staging share a workspace, production runs in its own workspace with a separate metastore and service principal credentials

Recommendation: Option C. It gives production a genuine blast-radius boundary while keeping day-to-day iteration cheap; Option A is acceptable only until the first production-critical workload arrives
outlines.teachingObjective: Justify an environment isolation choice for bundle promotion under realistic cost and governance constraints.
